THEATRE REVIEW

KING LEAR

Young Centre for the Performing Arts

If King Lear is primarily a domestic play about a father and his daughters -- and at ground level it is -- the new Soulpepper production handles the matter exceptionally well. If its about other, larger things as well, the production falls seriously short.

William Websters Lear makes his first appearance walking down the dead centre of the stage, with the air of a man who has made a decision he secretly fears may be wrong and is therefore all the more determined to prove right. Arrogant and irrational he may be, but he is no hypocrite and he is not consciously manipulative. He really is in desperate need of his daughters' love and feels perfectly entitled to ask them for public demonstrations of it. The deal he offers them -- land for love -- does not appear to be pre- arranged. Nancy Palk's Goneril seems genuinely surprised to be put on the spot and, fulsome though her protestations are, she might even mean them. Brenda Robins Regan is more calculating, and this contrast between the two villainesses is kept up until the end; one burns hot, the other cold, until their mutual destruction over their passion for Edmund.

In this context, the refusal of Cordelia, the favourite child, to flatter her father, logically destroys his world. His banishment of her is paternal petulance raised to a higher power; the highest, since hes the king. The mood intensifies once he's resigned his rule. The jabs of regret over Cordelia, which set in early, alternate with his attempts to reconcile his pride and his new dependence on her siblings; their attempts are too, since much of her father's behaviour is intolerable, and Goneril at least seems to have a case. The most original stroke in Joseph Zieglers production is to have Lear embrace her just before cursing her with sterility; for a moment she thinks he intends a reconciliation. Webster seems to have thought through every word he utters, and everything in these scenes comes through fresh, unforced and surprising, right down to the desperation of "reason not the need, which opens up a wider perspective even while setting the seal on the play as a study of domestic in-fighting. This is how families actually behave: striking ludicrous bargains, clinging to shreds of dignity, indignantly claiming the moral high ground. The beatific obverse of these scenes is the reconciliation with Cordelia (Patricia Fagan, touching here though unduly priggish elsewhere) in which Webster is simple, direct and moving as he is again when he dies, convinced that his slaughtered girl is breathing. He seizes on all the wandering details that Shakespeare so generously provides.

This, however, leaves out the whole stupendous middle of the play. Webster deals just as powerfully and intelligently with Lears madness, and with the revolutionary insights to which it leads him, but they remain just things he says. Ziegler's production is sharp on text, fuzzy on context. An intermission stops the play in its tracks just when it's gathering steam. The ensuing storm doesnt exactly drown the actors, but it drowns the interplay between them. Diego Matamoros Fool, after beginning superbly as the merciless voice of Lear's conscience, almost literally fades out. David Storch does a resourceful job on Edgar's succession of crazy voices, but cannot link them to whats going on around him or to the scholar- hero, whom he plays rather well. The mock-trial scene in the hovel goes for astonishingly little. Some of the staging is ungainly, with Soulpeppers newly unveiled thrust stage turning out to have poor sightlines (Edmund's death, flat on the deck, is practically invisible) and even poorer acoustics (at least, I'm not used to hearing these actors mumble). Christina Poddubiuks set, two adjacent arches giving on to a brick wall, is usefully stark; her costumes are a very mixed bag, traversing periods in what is presumably in a quest for universality. Kents disguise, a mixture of Che Guevara and Desert Rat, is appealing, and Lear returning from hunting as a 19th-century English squire is excellent. But to put the Duke of Albany, a vital but underwritten moral force who needs all the dignity he can get, into a skirt (because Albany means Scotland) is a drag not only on the actor but on all the scenes in which he appears -- notably the last one, which only happens to be the greatest scene ever written.

The faults can't be put down to inexperience: Soulpepper hasn't done much Shakespeare, but its individual members certainly have. This is a company with talent pouring out of its ears: It has a magnetic Edmund in Jonathan Goad, even if nothing he does later quite matches up to the contemptuous silence of his first appearance; it has a deliciously smug Oswald from Kevin Bundy thats as good as any Ive seen; it can spare Oliver Dennis for a glorified walk-on; and it can even bring life to the minute uncredited role of the Captain who hangs Cordelia. Webster is one of our best actors though, unlike most who get to play Lear, he isn't famous. This has its disadvantages, since a star tends to account automatically for the reverence in which the other characters hold the king. But it does mean that we get to see Lear as a man rather than a role, and that takes us a long way. But all these constituent parts fail to add up. I don't ask that the production have a Concept; concepts are things beloved of critics that often look better in program-notes and interviews than on the stage. I would like it to have an identity.

- Until October 18. 416-866-8666.

2006-09-14-directs-regularly-at-shaw-act:
Joseph ziegler: Dual theatre player knows how a scene feels from the inside

"To tell you the truth," says Joseph Ziegler, I don't turn down very much work. Ziegler's work is acting and directing. The combination is a common phenomenon in Canadian theatre, almost a defining one: Robert Lepage, Martha Henry, Brian Bedford, Jim Mezon, Christopher Newton, Richard Monette, Albert Schultz, Diana Leblanc, David Ferry, the Daniels Brooks and MacIvor -- the list, traversing styles, backgrounds and generations, goes on and on. And thats not even counting the notable directors who were actors, and successful ones. Its a small world in which, as Ziegler says, "in order to make a living, you have to do everything." Generally, though, one side of the career equation takes precedence over the other. Ziegler, pictured below, uniquely, has kept the two in perfect balance.

His talents seem, if anything, to have been feeding on one another. Start with the acting, to which he brings the great complementary qualities of delicacy and gusto. In last year's A Whistle in the Dark, he gave a magnificent performance as a brawling Irish paterfamilias, a bully with a big mouth and a jellied spine. He followed it with a bristling account of the cynical Dr. Relling in The Wild Duck, for Soulpepper, of which company he is one of the 12 founding members. He'll be repeating the Whistle performance at the beginning of next year; before that, for the holidays, he recreates, for the third time, his delightful Scrooge in A Christmas Carol.

As a director, hes been a regular at the Shaw Festival for the past four seasons, distinguishing himself last year with a lucid and compelling Major Barbara (I love directing Shaw -- to try and get to what hes saying -- not soften it or make it polite) and this year with an intense production of The Heiress, with Tara Rosling in the title role ("we all say we strive for theatre that's 'dangerous; I think Tara really was dangerous"). He inaugurated Soulpeppers new home in the Distillery with Thornton Wilder's Our Town, which he first staged for the company in 1999; a fine production the first time around, it seemed just about perfect the second. And last week saw the opening of his Soulpepper production of King Lear, commonly supposed the biggest play of all, and the first show ever to use the Young Centre's Charles and Marilyn Baillie Theatre in its thrust-stage fomration.

I dont fool myself into thinking weve solved all the problems of a great play. Lear is huge. You can hardly make a dent in it. But we have a fantastic cast. It contains most of the actors who have appeared in different combinations at Soulpepper earlier this year, with the redoubtable William Webster in the title role. "Bill's been preparing for the part his entire life practically. It's impossible to do, but were doin it." (Ziegler shares with his leading actor a conversational habit of dropping g's when makin' a point.)

As youd expect, Ziegler has acted in the play in the past; he was Edgar to Douglas Campbells Lear, in John Hirsch's Stratford production of 1985. A lot has stuck with me from being in it and hearing it (and from seeing other productions over the years), but even late in rehearsals he's found himself making new discoveries and asking new questions. The realization, for example, that Lear regrets his irrational fury over his daughter Cordelias "most small fault" far earlier in the play than anyone remembers: Its his early insight, it obviously gets lost, but he's never afraid to look at himself.

This is Soulpepper's fourth Shakespeare production, and Ziegler has directed all but one of them. As an actor, he reckons that hes acted in some 25 or 30 Shakespeare productions. Hamlet, with Paul Gross at Stratford in 1999, was his first Shakespeare as a director, though he isnt certain that Stratford realized it at the time. He subsequently directed the play again, in a far more intimate production for Soulpepper, with the company's artistic director Albert Schultz in the lead. Both Gross and Schultz were, for our times, remarkably gentle Hamlets, a coincidence that I attributed to Ziegler's direction. He says now that "Albert was wonderfully vulnerable" in opening himself up to Hamlet, both in rehearsal and performance, but seemed surprised by my description of the performance as gentle. He does say "if I had any influence on Albert, it was in the get thee to a nunnery scene with Ophelia. He thought that's when Hamlet attacks Ophelia; I said 'Hes trying save her here. " And that's how it played.

It seems to have been pre-destined that Ziegler would spend his life working on classical and near-classical plays, and that he would do it in Canada, though he is in fact American. He grew up in Minneapolis, home of the Guthrie Theatre, founded by and named for the Stratford Festival's first director and run in Zieglers boyhood by its second: The plays and people I grew up watching were those that Michael Langham brought there. Logically, then, he came to Canada in 1976 to attend the National Theatre School, intending to return home immediately afterwards. However, by the end of his time there, "I knew I wanted to be here." Another Stratford veteran, the actor and teacher Douglas Rain, had instructed him, irrefutably, that if you can do Shakespeare, you can do anything. Ziegler himself went to Stratford, swiftly coming to notice there in juvenile roles, mainly with the festivals Young Company, which at that point, pleasingly enough, was run by the returning Langham. (Langham and Hirsch are the only Stratford chiefs never to have been actors. They were still, according to Ziegler, "real actors' directors. It's usually in TV that you work with directors who know nothing about acting.") His own break into directing came in 1991, when Robin Phillips, with whom he had worked at Stratford and elsewhere, took over the Citadel Theatre in Edmonton, and asked Ziegler and his wife, Nancy Palk, to come out for a season. Phillips instincts are unpredictable and, for the most part, impeccable. Most people whove been in the rehearsal hall with Robin will tell you that it's one revelation after another. He said, 'Should I think of you as a director? I said, I'd love to.'  His trial run, in the studio, was a two-hander about Jean-Paul Sartre and Simone de Beauvoir, with Bill Webster as Sartre and Phillips designing; the following year he did The Diary of Anne Frank "on the thrust" (an interesting challenge for a play that is, by definition, about confinement). He went on to direct for Theatre New Brunswick and did a couple of murder mysteries at the Shaw. And then came Soulpepper: "They were kind enough, or rash enough, to ask me to direct." And theyve continued to. Albert is very loyal to the founding members. Ill suggest something to him, like I'd like to do Noel Coward's Blithe Spirit, and hell say, why not Present Laughter instead. And Present Laugher is what they did. Ziegler presents himself, somewhat self-deprecatingly, as Soulpeppers voice of caution. "I thought we should only do one play in our first season; Albert insisted on two. He thought we should do five in our second;' I thought that was too many." Nobody, including Zigeler, doubts now that in both cases Schultz was proved right.

The two parts of Ziegler's career have of course affected and modified one another. I had a lot less patience as an actor than I do as a director. I am learning to think of theatre as a continuing process, rather than as just something on its way to a first night. When I act, I now think of the whole play a lot more; I used to be much more selfish as an actor -- in a way that actors ought to be. As a director -- I cant help but be affected by my work as an actor. Sometimes -- here he sounds a little bashful -- "I ask an actor if hell let me play it for a minute," the idea being not to have the actor imitate him but to give himself the sense of how a scene feels from the inside. Like many -- but by no means all -- actor-directors, he is, by his own admission, more a verbal, less a visual director though he points out that even for Phillips, an acknowledged pictorial master, directing was a matter of "text first, acting second, concept third." He himself spends "a lot of time fixing the physical form of a scene -- actors do much better, more effortless acting when they're in the right place." Major Barbara was visually very striking, and Our Town was beautifully choreographed. Those who work with Ziegler say that he's growing all the time. Those of us watching have been getting the same impression.

2006-09-21-a-haunting-production:
GHOSTS

Tom Patterson Theatre, Stratford

- - -

If the shade of Henrik Ibsen ever casts a spectral glance in the direction of Southern Ontario, it should be feeling uncharacteristically cheerful. Each of our three major classical companies has, in the last two years, mounted a first-rate production of an Ibsen play. Following Soulpepper's scintillating, heart-rending Wild Duck and the Shaw's spring-cleaned Rosmersholm, we have Stratford's account, obviously less adventurous but equally powerful, of the one about syphilis.

Sorry, that's a very reductive way of describing Ghosts, and one that Ibsen scholars have been shooting down for at least a century. The play's ineradicable final image is of a young man's brain softening before us, while his tortured mother debates whether to administer the killing medicine. But the disease itself isn't mentioned until the play is two-thirds over, and even then, as a Stratford program-note reminds us, never by name. It's only the ultimate manifestation, the ultimate symbol, of the subject at which the play has been banging away all evening: the ills we inherit from the society, and the family, into which we are born.

Oswald Alving, a Norwegian artist who went off to live a free life in Paris, is felled by an illness passed on by his much- respected but thoroughly dissolute father, the Captain, in whose memory his widow is about to open an orphanage. This is a self- consciously ironic act on Mrs. Alving's part, since she was on to her husband long before his death. The orphanage is the last chapter in a cover-up story that included her taking in the Captain's illegitimate daughter as her maid. When we first meet her, Mrs. Alving is a strong, intelligent woman who has shed many illusions. In the few hours covered by the action of the play, she will be compelled to shed many more. She may well be the unluckiest tragic protagonist since Oedipus, that other enforced seeker of truth, and like Oedipus she is still alive at the end of the play, still condemned to the agonies of choice.

Ibsen's reluctance to call Oswald's malady by its name didn't spare him the maledictions of Victorian critics. The play's London notices from 1891 -- "an open drain; a loathsome sore unbandaged." - - have passed into legend: These jaded days, one rather envies those reviewers their capacity for shock and the vigour with which they expressed it. It wasn't just the VD that repelled them; the play has an incest theme as well, which didn't charm them, and to top everything off, it puts the outraged moral majority on stage in the person of Pastor Manders, who recoils in horror when he discovers Mrs. Alving reading "advanced books." Ibsen is as skittish about saying exactly what might be in these books as he is about calling syphilis by its name or giving us details about the late Captain's dissipated habits or the temptations that Oswald encountered in Paris. Once upon a recent time, this evasiveness seemed very irritating, and actors of the Pastor had their work cut out to keep him from appearing a mere buffoon, an Aunt Sally set up for us to feel superior to. But not any longer: Time has caught up with the play and Manders, with his condemnation of things he hasn't read and his blanket appeals to scriptural authority, not to mention his advocacy of abstinence for young people who can't afford to marry, is back in the saddle. The parallels between the STDs of Ibsen's age and our own hardly need underlining -- they're in danger, indeed, of seeming glib -- and the play ends with what is, in effect, a mimed debate about euthanasia, fought out within the anguished soul of a mother.

Diana Leblanc's production, her best since her celebrated Stratford grand slam with Long Day's Journey into Night and The Cherry Orchard, beautifully mines the play's twin veins of irony and inexorability; it unfolds on a constructively cluttered domestic set (by Charlotte Dean) and is suffused with the sound of piano music and the sight of distant firs. Mrs.. Alving is a wonderful role for Martha Henry, who appears grey-haired and in a lush purple dress, sense and sensuality in a context rigidly confined. Perhaps the most revealing thing the character says is that those "advanced books" had told her little that she had not already learned from experience; like many women, in and out of plays, she is instinctively ahead of a society that insists on keeping her behind. She is also both watchful and witty. For all her articulate passion, some of the finest moments in Henry's performance are the silent ones: her tolerant smile as she watches Manders make a fool of himself, the tightening of her knee as she passes the moral point of no return. She has spent her life surrounded by clowns and cheats; the play shows her shedding them, leaving her with only her son to cling to, and then facing the cruellest disillusion of all: Enlightenment doesn't come cheap.

Peter Donaldson gives the Pastor his full measure of unthinking authority, blinkered sincerity and, rather delightfully, gullibility. He also adds a note of affronted, repressed sexuality; Mrs. Alving once threw herself at him (and he is, believably, a man she could have loved) and now her maid, for quite other reasons, seems likely to do the same. He's thrown into confusion by both of them. Every so often there's a sign that his mind might open, and this becomes a rich part of the pattern.

Brian Hamman, a find, is a touchingly open-faced, bewildered Oswald, and Adrienne Gould gives a striking account of the maid Regina, especially in her last ruthless scene. Gary Reineke completes the cast as her adoptive father, the carpenter Engstrand, an unscrupulous Dickensian creep, with a sanctimonious talent for pressing the Pastor's buttons; the performance unfolds slowly (that's quite independent of the man's walking with a limp) and with possibly excessive relish, but it makes its points.

But what it doesn't suggest is that Engstrand may, somewhere, have a legitimate case of his own. The other characters all do, and it's part of the greatness of the play, faithfully reflected in this production, that though the author's own stance is hardly in doubt, he doesn't make anything easy.

- In repertory until Sept. 23.

2006-09-22-role-playing-dames:
FANNY KEMBLE

Studio Theatre, Stratford

- - -

Fanny Kemble, born in England and married in America, was a 19th- century actress and abolitionist. She came by the acting genealogically; the Kembles were the great theatrical dynasty of their day, and Fanny's aunt was the paradigm of tragediennes, Sarah Siddons. The origins of her anti-slavery sentiments are uncertain, but they were brought into the sharpest relief when she was on tour in the United States. While playing in Philadelphia, she was wooed and won by a Southern gentleman who, in the immemorial way of stage- door Johnnies, had fallen in love with her performance of Juliet. Shortly afterwards, he inherited a plantation in Georgia with all appurtenances, human and animal, attached. You could not make such a story up.

It has attracted the attention of more than one actress, who has seen in it the seeds of a one-woman show. The one who has actually brought it to the stage is Domini Blythe, herself a British-born performer (and from a theatrical family) who has made most of her career in North America -- especially at Stratford where she stands out even among a golden generation of actresses. To put the story into shape, she turned to a real writer and director in Peter Hinton, and he has come up with a real play, in a super-real production.

That doesnt mean that, in his text at least, hes solved all the problems inherent in both the narrative and the genre. His framework is a come-back performance by Fanny, long after she has put both her career and her marriage behind her. She looks back on both of them, and especially on the issues of freedom and servitude as they have manifested themselves in her personal and professional lives; the latter, it seems, was mainly devoted to Shakespeare, and it's with a Shakespearean recital that she's making her present come-back. It is, in both the good and bad senses, an obvious device. One grows tired of hearing the stage manager knocking on Fannys door with the five-minute call (its always five minutes; time seems to be standing still) and with her own reiterated question: "Who shall I enter as tonight?" The idea may be that Fanny has lived her life as a series of roles, but the woman we meet seems to have been very consistent; her circumstances may have changed but she hasn't. It's entertaining, though, to hear her reminisce about her relatives (her aunt Siddons "spoke in blank verse when instructing a servant" and never cracked a smile onstage or off), and stimulating to hear her reflect on the instances of slavery and subjection in the plays to which she devoted her talents. Even Juliet, she reflects, only does two things on her own initiative: fall in love and kill herself. Everything else is some mans idea. I dont think this is quite fair -- it's Juliet, not Romeo, who first proposes marriage, and it takes some guts for her to swallow that sleeping-potion -- but it's a provocative point. Dont get her started on The Taming of the Shrew.

Even before she discovered that her husband was a slave-owner on a large scale, Fanny knew that in her own marriage she had been, in a sense, sold. Or so the play tells us. We cant be sure whether this was her own insight or Hinton's; Kemble was herself an able and voluminous author, and the script makes much use of her writings, but the result sounds seamless. When read, though, the script seems very much the work of the man who wrote The Swanne; it has the same anchoring use of verse structure, the same relish for and freedom with historical detail, the same strange wind blowing through it.

It changes gears from the first act to the second. Before the intermission, Fanny's experiences on the plantation are a ghostly presence at the back of the plays mind; after it, they take over. In particular, Fannys black maid Psyche, merely mentioned in the first half, becomes the figure through whom Fanny discovers the physical and emotional facts of slavery. She challenges Fanny's right to record in her journals the stories that Psyche has told her. This seems to be a pre-emptive strike at what would later be called cultural appropriation -- of which the play itself is of course both an example and an effective defence.

Much of Psyche's story concerns a friend of hers, a slave called Jenny Hill who ran away and whose escape Psyche herself was too timid to join. This seems to be all Hintons work, derived from the merest hint in Kemble, and it unbalances the play; we have come, after all, to investigate not Psyches psyche but Fanny's. But it's powerful stuff in itself, and it inspires superb work from Blythe who, in impersonating Psyche, finds a majestic defiance even in her confession of her fears. Acting after all is appropriation, by definition; and this actress, whose primary role is another actress, is here its living justification.

In the rest of the play she is witty, graceful and quicksilver versatile, with her emotional changes and exchanges superbly placed and graded under Hinton's direction. He always has his performer in the right physical and mental place, and -- thanks to Robert Thomson -- the right light.

He also has, from Tamara Marie Kucheran, a superbly evocative dressing-room set; trunks, open or closed, erect or supine, evoke both the heroine's theatrical world and her marital one, and a black dressing table belongs triumphantly to both.

- In repertory until Sept. 23.

Black & White Photo: Stratford Festival / Many actresses are drawn to the story of Fanny Kemble, but Domini Blythe has joined forces with dramatist Peter Hinton to make it happen.
2006-09-23-following-in-his-mentor-s-foo:
The first production at Torontos new opera house is the work of a first-time director. Its easy to lose sight of this in light of the more obvious excitements of the occasion: the Canadian Opera Company's attainment of its own welcoming and acoustically perfect home and its audacity at starting operations with the complete four- part cycle of the Ring of the Nibelungs. Also, Das Rheingold, chronologically the first opera of the tetralogy but in this case the last to reach the stage (the three subsequent instalments had made their bows, one by one, in the company's old quarters at the Hummingbird Centre), is directed by the same man who has designed all four, so the visual continuity is impeccable. There is, in fact, an air of inevitability about the whole process.

The man is Michael Levine, a national treasure whose work isnt seen in Canada nearly often enough, though he was born and grew up in Toronto and recently moved back here. Along with Richard Bradshaw, the COCs artistic director and the cycle's conductor, he must be considered one of the major architects of Canada's Ring. (Of course in the real world, or even the Wagnerian world, rings dont have architects. They have forgers. But that word has an unfortunate, well, ring.) In Levines words, asking him to direct was one of Richard's wild, unexpected ideas." But it had, from the start, its own logic.

Levine joined the more experienced, and very varied, team of Atom Egoyan, Francois Girard and Tim Albery. He helped create, and interconnect, their worlds. Finally, he got to round off the process himself or, Rheingold being the beginning of the story, to show how it started.

There's also a career logic to this. Levine, when I talked to him this week in his studio on the seventh floor of a converted garment- district building at King and Spadina, told me that he had trained in London at "one of the best courses around, the Central School of Art and Design. This was in 1979; the Thatcher government had just taken office in the United Kingdom but had yet to have much effect, and I felt like I was living in the Victorian period; I got a flat for (ps)7 a week. London still felt like a lot of little villages." He had "three excellent years at Central, where one of his occasional instructors was Philip Prowse, head of design at what was then, and may be still, Britains most adventurous repertory theatre, the Citizens in Glasgow.

I'd written letters to all the theatres -- Glasgow was one of two that replied. Philip came into the Central's studio one day, I showed him my work, and I got an assistant designers job at the Citz. I was so excited, I arrived two weeks early, without even a place to stay, went to the theatre and said I'll do anything, I'll sweep the floors. And I was sweeping the floor when Giles [Havergal, the Citizens artistic director] walked in and asked 'Who are you?' I said, Im the new designer.' "

As a London critic at the time, I used to find myself flying to Glasgow about once every two weeks, since the Citz had a style and a repertoire unlike any other. It would stage, with unblushing sang- froid, classic plays that one would otherwise know only from textbooks, bring them to outrageous life and then immediately move on to something else. Levine and I were both surprised to find that I had seen the first play he had ever designed on the stage -- at, he recalls, a budget of (ps)200. The play was Torquato Tasso by Goethe, and I remember it as first-rate Citz; one feared it would be boring, but was riveted. Levine also designed an obscure Jacobean comedy, The Custom of the Country, which the production set in Hollywood: not the place, the myth. Levine now expresses doubts about this idea, but I remember falling helplessly apart when one of the characters appeared as Mickey Mouse, complete with tail.

Levine was only there for a year but the experience was formative. "There was a fantastic team of people, working for nothing -- nothing being something when you're straight out of college. More specifically, Philip Prowses work was a huge influence on me; he had a way of working that was stylized, but off the cuff. He had an incredible rapport with the people he worked with, a wonderful way of getting results. The overlapping of direction and design made an impression on me; I never felt anything -- direction, design, acting -- should take the first role. Philip had a specific design rule: He felt that things should feel permanent on stage. He wasnt big on scene changes. I like scene changes. But I have a certain respect for Philip's ideology. He taught me that if you create something on stage, you have to have a good reason for destroying it."

The burning of Valhalla at the end of Gotterdammerung presumably counts as such a reason, especially as we have now seen in Rheingold how that palace was built. We see it as an architects' model with, just behind it, a great door representing a part of that model in its fully realized state -- though Levine admits that not everyone has got the connection, and I have to count myself among those who missed it.

Prowse took the overlapping of direction and design quite literally. He became a director in his own right, in demand for plays and operas way outside Glasgow. And so Levine has been following, if belatedly, in his mentors footsteps. He has found the experience "glorious -- I enjoyed every minute of it. Even as a designer, he has always made a point of attending as many rehearsals as possible, so he can be there to help solve problems as they come up. Not that directing hasnt also been daunting. Technical rehearsals, in his dual role, were like being in the eye of a tornado."

"And even in the rehearsal room it can be a terrible blind roller coaster ride; you don't know what you're doing. The singers come with the emotions of the piece already inside them, but not always the intentions of it. Most of the discussions we have had were about finding those intentions. You have people who may have sung the role in six or seven productions; you have to borrow some things and reject others. Its a difficult minuet; you have to earn their trust. All of my singers, though, have been really amenable.

One doesnt necessarily expect a designer to be an actors' or singers' director, but Levine seems to me to have drawn first-rate vocal and even physical characterizations from his Alberich (Richard Paul Fink), first wheedling, then snarling; from Loge (Richard Berkeley-Steele), the sardonic outsider among the gods; and from the majestic scold, Fricka (Judit Nemeth). His conception of the two giants is to have each represented by a team of actors, carrying the seated singer about.

Singers dont necessarily take to sitting down (though some do their finest work in the boardroom setting Levine and Albery have designed for the villains in Gotterdam-merung), still, Levine seems to have persuaded them. And perhaps the most moving in Rheingold comes when the gentler giant Fasolt (Robert Pomakov) calls for more gold to cover the eyes of the beautiful goddess Freya, whom he is about to lose.

On his home ground, so to speak, Levine, with much billowing drapery, has designed wonderful settings for the Rhine itself, whose maidens toss about fluffy white pillows; for the approach to Valhalla; and for Alberichs industrial-revolution smithy, where junior Nibelungs toil and where the master himself turns magically into a dragon. He goes from Toronto to New York where a Levine- designed production of Madama Butterfly opens the new season at the Met.

Looking in the opposite direction -- backward -- he won this year's Dora design award, in the opera/musical category, for a revived production of Wozzeck that he designed years ago. His acceptance speech was charming -- in an evening for the most part painfully short on charm or any good qualities -- but bemused. A noted British director once described Levine to me as a great designer and a very nice man." On the strength of one meeting and years of observation, I'd go with that.
2006-09-30-healey-s-generous-lives-up-to:
Authors latest play covers wide social, emotional ground

Michael Healeys latest play is called Generous, and it lives up to its title. It's generous in the social and emotional ground it covers, in the quality and quantity of barbed laughter it provokes, in both the sharpness and the compassion of its insights into relationships, and in the spirit that animates all these. It's generous, too, in the opportunities it offers its actors, a superb bunch who reply in kind. It returns its author, after the blur of Rune Arlidge and the fiasco of The Innocent Eye Test, to his rightful place at the top of the heap.

Its also a generous, or a least a complicated, play structurally, though I think Healey has been making it sound more complex than it is. He describes it as being four two-act plays, each with its own title, with their first acts grouped in succession on the near side of the single intermission, and their second acts.

In fact, its just one play in a number of scenes. It's true that these scenes take place across a wide expanse of time, and that each of the earlier ones seems to feature a discrete group of characters. But these people, or some of them, converge as the evening proceeds, and as its theme -- the costs and rewards of virtue -- comes into focus. Compared to the technical games played in many of Alan Ayckbourn's plays, or in Caryl Churchills Top Girls (which Soulpepper has blessedly announced for revival next year), the tricks of Generous are kids stuff. Still, it makes sense to approach the play scene by scene, applying to each of them the title, or sub-title, the author intended.

We begin, then, with PMO," set 15 years ago in Ottawa, with a minority government on the verge of collapse. Inspired by an apercu attributed to Brian Mulroney when discussing a member of his cabinet ("slit her throat), this shows us a loyal junior minister (Heritage) behaving like the knights who murdered Thomas a Becket; that is, taking a remark of her leader somewhat too literally and stabbing a rival MP in the neck, fatally wounding herself in the process.

She bleeds to death right in front of us and her colleagues but only one of them notices, let alone cares. The rest are far too concerned with fending off an imminent vote of non-confidence; the air, if you can believe this of our rulers, is thick with profanity.

The mode, which persists for this episode only, is frank cartoon, with most of the casting cross-gender. The scene was given a showing of its own last year at a political-theatre evening, and I remember it as being more substantial and, frankly, funnier than it is here. Daryl Cloran's direction, in stark contrast to his handling of the rest of the play, is frantic in the wrong way, and never manages to focus our attention on the character who, as it turns out, matters most. Still, Fiona Reid's grey-haired PM is a sight to see, looking terrific in trousers, dispensing high-octane ruthlessness as his world falls apart and finally asking how will this country survive without us?" He means it, too.

We move on to "The Death of the Alberta Report, set in Calgary at roughly the same time. A female oil executive, in between telephonically juggling husband and lover and agreeing to shop for her son at that great leveller, Canadian Tire (where retail goes to puke its guts out"), grants an interview to a phenomenally persistent journalist, and takes his breath away by refusing even to pretend to care about the environment. Were charmed by her frankness, even if he isnt.

Actually, he is charmed, as she proves by seducing him. She's a creature of iron impulse, fuelled by a fear of approaching death. Yanna McIntosh returns in this role to something like her best form, her wit and elegance blazing and her anger almost keeping pace with them. She looks great in trousers, too. Tom Barnett as her prey does a fine job of, essentially, keeping his own counsel. This scene establishes what the play proves best at: balancing power-play with sexual tension.

And now it's now, as "One Party Rule, set in the present, shows another erotic encounter, or the aftermath of one, where the worldly authority rests with the woman. Shes a widowed judge; hes a clerk in her office, her junior in every sense. They have just had what she is determined will remain a one-night stand. He wants to stay. And not just because he wants to help himself; he also wants to help her. Reid as the judge, a commanding woman in an unaccustomed state of fragility, and Jordan Pettle as the clerk, infuriatingly perky and endearingly sensitive, play this scene magnificently, with Cloran's direction exactly charting every physical and emotional move. The scene also has a wonderful delayed curtain-line.

It isn't the end, though, because next comes Lily," a wholly mimed scene in which a young couple take delivery of a tub of KFC and ferociously fight over it, because he wants to eat it -- all of it -- and she, who is Lily, doesnt think he should.

Meanwhile, the delivery-guy (McIntosh, in the single funniest performance of the evening) gawps in silent amazement and waits to be paid. The scene also affords us a momentary glimpse of Pettles clerk; it plays like a Monty Python gag but signals that the pieces, or some of them, may eventually fit together.

And so they do in the second half, whose arrival signifies that I should stop giving everything away. Anyway: the continuation of "Lily reveals that she, the judge and the clerk are variously linked and that at least two of them have the urge to do good for people; the clerk tags himself, not at all sheepishly, as the I- love-you guy." (He's talking about real relationships, not bumper stickers.) Lily herself persists into the renewed "Death of the Alberta Report, in a brief appearance that makes Michelle Monteith's edgy performance click into place.

McIntoshs exec is still alive, and wants to go into politics: to do good, if you believe her, and I think you should.

She is still ruthless, though, as hinted in the subtitle; she wants to take her ex-fling (who in Barnetts performance has subtly but inexorably matured) with her.

The last scene disposes simultaneously of PMO" and "One Party Rule. The conscientious objector from the first scene (Ari Cohen, a little too emphatically distraught) reappears in the judge's chambers, having long quit politics for the law. The clerk, who seems increasingly to speak for the author, suggests he should return. Asked why aren't politicians revered?" he answers, "Because we give them an impossible task. Govern us, we say, take our money and govern us, and we will hate you for it.... They become the nexus of our self-loathing."

The implication is that both parties (and, I suppose, all Parties) should get over it. He has a proposition for the judge, too, which she answers in a speech so perfectly balanced by both writer and actress that I found myself simultaneously hoping that it would be the end, since I couldnt see how anything could follow it, and that it wouldnt, because I didn't want the play to stop.

There is no grand finale, no final reunion of all the characters; nor should there be. Some ends are left rightly loose. (Some wrongly, too. There's a part of the judges back-story of which I cannot make sense.) We are shown people trying to do the right thing, personally or socially or both, and are left to judge whether it matters that they may be doing good in order to feel good.

It seems that in most cases, though maybe not all, it doesnt. That may not be profound, but it is acute, certainly when delivered with as much wit and surprise, both verbal and visual, as it is here.

Yannik Larivee's set is a bit cumbrous for all the changes required of it, but the pieces look good when they arrive.

Generous is a good play about politics and an even better play about love. It's also the first play of the new Toronto season. If it yields a better one, we will have been insanely lucky.

- Generous runs through Oct. 29 at the Tarragon Theatre, 416-531- 1827.

robert.cushman@nationalpost.com

Colour Photo: Michael Cooper / Michael Healey's Generous, featuring Fiona Reid and Ari Cohen, is a return to form for the playwright.
2006-10-03-his-words-may-lie-but-his-per:
Theatre Review

HERE LIES HENRY

Buddies in Bad Times Theatre

Daniel MacIvor's Here Lies Henry -- accent on the ambiguous verb - - is the initial offering in the farewell season of his company, da da kamera. It's also a revival of a production first seen in 1995. MacIvor shares with Daniel Brooks the credit for "creating" it, with Brooks taking responsibility for "direction and dramaturgy" and MacIvor for "text and performance." The last of those four components is the most important. I didn't see the show the first time around, and my early exposure to MacIvor's work came through a series of shows that I didn't much like. But after Cul-de-Sac and now this one, I realize that my initial antipathy to MacIvor's plays was largely due to the fact that MacIvor himself wasn't in them.

I doubt if there is an actor in Canada who is better than he at doing what he does. What he does is assemble a battery of physical and vocal mannerisms and, at lightning speed and with immaculate control, fuse them into a coherent persona. The character he plays is invariably on some kind of edge. Henry, whom he plays here, is gay, lonely and angry. Or that's what he says; but he could equally well be straight, gregarious, happy (though I think that's a long shot) and answering to the name of Cedric.

For Henry is by his own admission, or his own proclamation, an inveterate liar. Though of course this, as in the famous Cretan paradox, could be a lie.

Which raises the question, one that arises in nearly every MacIvor play that I've seen (the recent A Beautiful View may be an exception): Who cares? It seems futile to wonder whether or not a fictitious character is telling the truth. It's especially so when he's the only character in the play, meaning there can be no checks or balances built into the structure. I know this may well be the point -- the unreliable narrator and all that -- but it's never struck me as a very interesting one.

There are certain points where MacIvor makes it work. Henry appears to us as a man with a load of grievances, willing to take the sins of the world on his shoulders after committing them through sheer spite; he's the guy who gave away Anne Frank's hiding place, he's the man who taught Mohammed Atta how to fly a plane "because New York thought it was so fucking great." This, though you may not believe me, is a very funny moment, not least because it carries a heavy moral charge.

One realizes that at this juncture Henry is certainly fantasizing, but one also accepts that he's the kind of man who, in certain frames of mind, would have wanted to do such things, and for just such reasons. At other times -- or throughout, really -- he has a lot of charm. This is partly because he's a frankly confessed loser, self-deprecating even at his most aggressive, and partly because MacIvor's skill is spellbinding in itself.

He's especially fine at raising running gags to a higher power; the tics that make Henry tick include a cough every time he mentions his father (a heavy smoker who has passed on his habit) and a very exotic kind of hiccup when he mentions his mother. These and much else are seamlessly woven into a fabric that also includes updated topical asides and occasional unembarrassing button-holing of the audience.

The naivest question you can ask of an actor is how he remembers his lines, but on this occasion one really would like to know, because it seems impossible. Brooks' direction puts MacIvor into a tight spare box bounded by Andy Moro's cruelly precise lighting and, from Richard Feren, a sound-score that is as much as any play will ever need. Some of the best craftsmen in Canadian theatre support one of its supreme talents -- who is still, as far as I can tell, in search of something substantial to say.

- Here Lies Henry runs until Oct. 15. 416-975-8555

Colour Photo: Buddies in Bad Times / Daniel MacIvor the playwright benefits greatly from the casting of Daniel MacIvor the actor in Here Lies Henry.
2006-10-07-tiny-dynamite-s-anthony-sizzl:
robert.cushman@hotmail.com; Tiny Dynamite runs through Oct. 8 at Tarragon Extra Space, 416-531-1827.

Toronto theatre programs are usually flush with statements of intent, and with biographical information about the actors, directors, designers and technicians responsible for the play in hand. They can go strangely quiet, though, when telling us about the author unless he or she is actually on the premises.

"He or she" is right in relation to Tiny Dynamite, which is the inaugural production of an outfit called Theatre Smash. Having searched both program and press kit, cover to cover, I still have no idea about the life and career of the playwright. I don't even know whether the person, whose name is Abi Morgan, is male or female. It may be superficial to care about such things but I can't help wondering.

I have gathered that Morgan is Welsh, which with that name is no particular surprise, and the play does remind me of the kind of lyrical-psychological drama that was much in vogue in Britain's fringe theatres some 20 years ago and, very likely, still is. ("Theatre Smash develops and produces contemporary theatre work with a global twist," says the press release. I think that means they do plays from other countries.) It seems to have been discreetly Canadianized for this production, but that's largely a matter of accents. Like many plays of its type, it's stronger on mood than on substance.

It concerns two young men, lifelong friends, called Lucien and Anthony. Lucien is a risk analyst, by nature and by profession. Anthony is contrastingly rash; as a boy he was struck in the chest by lightning and he's been attracting electricity, literally and metaphorically, ever since. The experience doesn't seem to have impaired his brain, though Lucien sometimes treats him as if it has. It has robbed him of socialization skills or, perhaps more accurately, of the desire to have them. In the two men's shared past is the memory of a girl, now dead, who was important to both of them.

Taking their annual holiday together -- in the country, by the water -- they encounter Madeleine, a free-spirited part-time waitress whose presence brings everything back. (If this were Proust, she'd be a pastry.) Much compulsive retelling of their old story ensues -- the author is unlikely to have seen The Drawer Boy, but to a Toronto audience, the resemblance is striking -- leading to a kind of exorcism.

We have to take an awful lot on trust, principally the effect on the men of their new acquaintance. Just why does she stir up these memories? Would any girl have done? If that's the case, the situation isn't very interesting. If it isn't, we're hindered by the fact that Madeleine as written is just your standard theatrical waif; Perrie Olthuis, the first-time professional actress who plays the part, can't do much to give her definition. Also we have nothing to measure her against; however much they talk about her, the ghost in the boys' past remains just that, a ghost. The play presses for an emotional response it doesn't justify.

Then, too, Lucien, whose adventure the play turns out to be, is so reticent that the piece gets to seem pointless; other people have to tell us what he feels. Steven McCarthy plays him gaunt, gauche and -- we assume -- sensitive, but all the attention goes to Anthony who, as played by Dylan Trowbridge, is not merely magnetic but charismatic. This is a performance with a bubbling interior, a stew of exuberance and resentment, and also with a preternaturally sharp outline. The electricity the character courts and embraces seems literally to surround him, even when the lighting and sound effects aren't going full blast.

The play's technical and atmospheric demands are altogether extremely well-handled in Ashlie Corcoran's production. All three actors are required to take headers into the wings, where a lake is supposed to lurk, and their unnervingly persuasive dives are matched by equally blood-curdling splashes.

Now what else has Abi Morgan written?

Colour Photo: Michael Walton / From left to right, Dylan Trowbridge, Perrie Olthuis and Steven McCarthy star in Tiny Dynamite.
2006-10-13-monette-s-coming-out-hosanna-:
For many years now the lobby of Toronto's Tarragon Theatre has been dominated by a large photograph of a man dressed, handsomely, as Elizabeth Taylor dressed as Cleopatra. It's a picture of Richard Monette in the title role of Michel Tremblay's Hosanna, as produced at the Tarragon in 1972. Hosanna, the Montreal drag-queen locked into a love-hate relationship with a rough-trade partner, is a role that Monette looks back on as "a huge event in my professional life." And this is doubly a time for looking back, since Hosanna is being revived at the Young Centre for the Performing Arts in a production by John Van Burek, the play's English co-translator with the late Bill Glassco, who directed that original production. Meanwhile Monette is about to complete a record-breaking 14 years as artistic director of the Stratford Festival; the 2007 Stratford season, of which the details were announced last week, will be his farewell.

"In my professional life," Monette says, "Hosanna brought me from being a good actor -- in some people's minds -- to being a star actor. Bill Hutt said that it was one of the few star performances he'd seen by a Canadian." Monette still wonders whether those last three words make the compliment somewhat backhanded, though I don't think he needs to worry.

"I was playing Orestes opposite Monique Mercure's Electra at Centre Stage," Monette remembers, "and she suggested that I get the script. I read it, and I wrote to Bill Glassco saying, 'Please, please, please, could I have an audition?' And because I was a squeaky wheel, he agreed to see me. I said I'd like to read it in a French Canadian accent, and he said no." Doing it without the accent, though, Monette sounded like "a New York hairdresser from Greenwich Village," so finally Glassco allowed him to try it his way. "And when I did that, it exploded. Bill told me afterwards that in his mind he'd already cast somebody else. Then he changed his mind."

Ironically Mercure, the actress who had egged him on to try for the role, was critical when she saw, or rather heard, him do it. "Monique didn't like my accent; she thought I was making fun of the accent. But I am French-Canadian, and I based it on one of my aunts; I spoke just the way she spoke but in English. Michel writes in joual, which is what my family spoke." Richard Donat ("brilliantly cast"), who acted opposite Monette, spoke in an English accent, and the contrast seemed to work.

It fits too with the play's underlying theme. Hosanna, says Monette, was "slightly scandalous to people" when it opened; it dealt, through Hosanna's infatuation with Liz Taylor, with the theme of celebrity ("which was very big then"), and also of course with gender-bending. "It was regarded as being outspoken, with gayness, salty language and nudity. But it's also a political play, with Hosanna representing Quebec -- a transvestite in other people's clothes." It's a plea for Quebec to be itself and stop emulating America, represented in this case by Hollywood. Tremblay himself, though, told the actor: "I think what makes it work is its heart." Monette agrees. "It was shocking, but it was human. The difficulty with playing the role -- or the trap -- is it's easy to see Hosanna as getting her come-uppance because she's got a big mouth. She's a bitch, but funny. The problem is in making the character charming in the second act. But it's a fabulous role. It's got everything."

According to Monette, "Hosanna put Tremblay on the map in English- speaking Canada." It also put Monette on the map.

You can trace a straight line from his performance in Hosanna to his current eminence at Stratford. In the audience at that 1972 production was Robin Phillips, who was about to begin his own regime at the festival and, duly impressed, invited Monette to be part of it. He had acted at Stratford before, in minor roles; one of them was Eros in Antony and Cleopatra, with Christopher Plummer and Zoe Caldwell; and it was Caldwell's Cleopatra headdress that, in a nice gesture to tradition, he wore as Hosanna. (It's one thing that makes that Tarragon lobby photo so striking.) Under Phillips, Monette played leads, starting with Hamlet, and began directing. He continued doing this, with increasing success, under three succeeding regimes, before assuming the top job in 1994

Will he miss it? "While I'm doing it, I don't think I'll miss it, but I know that when it's over, I will. At the time, every day seems an age, but it's all gone by in the blink of an eye."

- Hosanna runs until Oct. 28 at the Young Centre for the Performing Arts. Call 416-866-8666 or visit youngcentre.ca for tickets.

Black & White Photo: Nir Bareket / Salvatore Antonio as Hosanna at the Young Centre for the Performing Arts, the role that was first played by Richard Monette in 1972. "It brought me from being a good actor to being a star actor," he says.
2006-10-14-william-webster-can-t-escape-:
Evenings when he isn't playing King Lear at the Young Centre, William Webster is playing King Lear at the Young Centre. That is, on his nights off from playing the title role in Shakespeare's tragedy for Soulpepper, Webster is appearing in the same space, and on the same thrust stage, as the one echt actor in a fantasia on Shakespearean themes presented by Moonhorse Dance Theatre and titled Ever Thus. In this he figures as the paterfamilias of a theatrical troupe who, arriving at the site of their next gig, elect, rather than checking into their digs like normal folks, to run through spoken and choreographed selections from their repertoire. Webster himself begins, with great and endearing authority, by casting a weary here-we-go-again eye and voice over the empty space. Another op'nin', another show (Porter, C.). 'Twas ever thus (Shakespeare, W.).

Later, he gets to do a few lines of Lear, including the start of the storm scene, spoken over eerie music rather than the usual thunderclaps. This is rather effective, and starts you wondering whether in an actual production it might not work better than the customary battle between actors and sound effects. He also appears, more or less in his own person, as part of a bafflingly interpolated Q&A sequence, talking about the Lears he has appeared in, at Stratford and elsewhere, before getting the chance to play the king himself. The gag here is that he and his fellows keep getting interrupted, and have to move to another part of the stage. I felt cheated; I wanted to hear Bill Webster's anecdotes.

Ever Thus is a refined but also weakened version of a longer piece tried out last year at the late lamented Theatre Centre and titled The Castle. That was set, as far as I could make out, in a hotel doubling as a haunted pile. It was obscure, but it had a certain brooding quality, and it included more substantial slabs of text: Webster got to throw a quizzical new light on Lear's awakening.

It seems unreasonable to expect dancers to handle blank verse, but in The Castle some of them got away with it. Standards have slipped in this regard. Of the four movers and shakers only Claudia Moore (the piece's director and choreographer) makes much of her lines, and even she is far less compelling a dramatic presence than previously. She plays, mainly, Lady Macbeth; or rather the spirit of the play the Lady inhabits. Significant lines are intoned, irrespective of character. Sometimes the performers swap significant words that recur from play to play; it's like flipping through a Shakespearean Concordance. The actual dancing tells us, among other things, that Hamlet was a neurotic youth who had issues with women, but that hardly counts as a revelation.

- - -

A more stimulating sidelight on Shakespeare in general and King Lear in particular can be had from Shakespeare and the Queen's Men, a joint theatrical-academic project on view at the Glen Morris Theatre, on the University of Toronto campus, and subsequently beyond. The Queen's Men were an Elizabethan theatre company who flourished briefly in the 1580s, in London and on tour, before disappearing from the record in mysterious, and conceivably sinister, circumstances. This was just before Shakespeare began his career, and the present enterprise is staging and discussing three plays that definitely or conceivably influenced him. Robert Greene's Friar Bacon and Friar Bungay, about rival magicians, may have inspired The Tempest, though personally I doubt it. The other two are uncontested sources: The Famous Victories of Henry V, which is like a whistle-stop tour through most of the English histories (not just the obvious one), and The True Chronicle History of King Leir and His Three Daughters.

This play is Shakespeare's Lear without the sub-plot and with a happy ending. In the latter respect it resembles the post- Shakespearean adaptations that found the death of Cordelia and the attendant darkness an intolerable affront to natural justice. No less a figure than Tolstoy agreed; an incorrigible moralist, he thought the old King Leir a perfectly decent play, crammed with religious feeling, that Shakespeare went and ruined. Indeed, the changes Shakespeare made, after an opening that he followed closely, are breathtaking; Lear's madness, the storm, the Fool, all the social and sexual insights are his invention. He must have been driven. Though I also like to think that, when Burbage or whoever brought the old play to his door and demanded an update, his first response was, "Well, that spelling has to go for a start."

The old play, though you can't help watching it without making comparisons, stands up nicely. Certainly it does in Peter Cockett's production, which adheres as closely as possible to the Queen's Men's own conventions, known or surmised: a platform stage, generic costumes, men in the female roles and, except in the crucial matters of music and fights, minimal rehearsal. The actors, like their forebears, learned their words from individual "parts," containing only their own lines and the immediate cues. So, as one of them told me, when they came together they really had to concentrate. It's tempting to wonder if a comparable freshness might be achieved by applying the same methods to actual Shakespeare productions, but that is probably to yearn for an innocence past recall.

The present show unfolds like a grown-up pantomime, with strong overtones of Cinderella and her Ugly Sisters: Gonorill and Ragan, as they're called here, are explicitly jealous of young Cordella's beauty, while her courtship by the King of France becomes a full- blown romance. At the end the two of them invade Britain, jointly and successfully; the couple that stays together, slays together. The siblings (Matthew Krist, Derek Genova, Julian DeZotti) are among the best I've seen in any version.

The play's main weakness is that its narrative outruns its characters, so that it seems long: Defeat the baddies already, one wants to call out; we know it's coming. Leir himself hardly undergoes much development. He's deceived, then quickly undeceived, then he suffers and becomes saintly on account of it. But he doesn't so much learn charity as put it on, like a new suit of clothes. Don Allison plays him with authority, and later with a twinkling benevolence that put me in mind of Stephen Fry.

The most accomplished performer, though also the one whose cleverness is aptest to overstep convention, is Alon Nashman, who doubles a randy French courtier (the play, again like pantomime, is never afraid to snatch at the nearest joke) with an eager English assassin, sent to dispatch the king and his even holier henchman Perillus, a figure whom Shakespeare seems to have sliced three ways: into Kent, Gloucester and the Fool.

CONCERT REVIEW

Barbra Streisand

Air Canada Centre, Toronto

I was a Barbra Streisand fan in 1963, the year of her first album. I stopped being one, while remaining something of an admirer, circa 1967, by which time she had half a dozen LPs behind her, all filled with original takes on terrific songs, and was in between playing Funny Girl onstage and onscreen. Your attitude to Streisand may well be defined by which of those performances you prefer. In the show she was an endearing singing actress in a musical; in the movie, where practically nobody else gets to sing a note, she is already on her way to being -- in a word she professes to hate, but which there is really no avoiding -- a diva. In the decades since, she has increasingly devoted herself to the production of technically perfect performances of mediocre material. So the wonder of her Tuesday night performance in Toronto -- part of what's being promoted as her farewell tour, though divas can always change their minds -- was how much of the old Barbra was back.

The repertoire, for a start, was almost unimpeachable; the worst it got was The Way We Were and her own Evergreen, which are at least passable. Otherwise, nearly everything was reclaimed from those early records, with a special emphasis on the songs of Harold Arlen: Not, alas, A Sleepin' Bee but Come Rain or Come Shine, which was buoyant; When the Sun Comes Out, which was all-purpose dramatic but excitingly so; My Shining Hour, which was new for her and the closest she came to touching as opposed to just impressing me; and a sizzling and sardonic Down with Love. This last was the nearest she came all night to singing a comedy song. The irreverent Brooklyn inflections that used to light up her performances are apparently gone beyond recall. She isn't a funny girl any longer, at least not in song, and that's a loss.

She still sings Funny Girl, lots of it. Her show starts, thrillingly, with the overture to the theatre version, and she's meticulous about telling us which songs were dropped and which interpolated. Thus she segues from The Music that Makes Me Dance, with its long and lovely lines, to My Man, the Fanny Brice staple that replaced it in the film. This must count as one of the great bad songs, and Streisand sang it with surprising restraint, which is the wisest course; unless you actually are Fanny Brice, giving yourself over to the song's melodrama can be embarrassing. And, of course, she sang People. This is one of those occasions on which a score's best-known song is one of its worst, but she took some of the banality out of it by setting it in its dramatic context and including the verse.

People may or may not need people, but they do seem to need platitudes. That song aroused some of the most frenzied cheers of the night, along with Somewhere, announced as a hymn to peace. She might even have got away with that one had the preening quasi- operatic quartet known as Il Divo not administered the coup de grace by joining in. Left to their own devices, they performed My Way as a joint tribute to Frank Sinatra, who should have had more tact than to sing it, and to the present star, who does have the tact but can tolerate having it sung at her. This amounted to more varieties of cheese than you could cut with a single knife.

Since we seem to be asked to pass judgment on the woman as well as the singer, I must say that, a few pious moments aside, I liked the Streisand who talked to us on Tuesday. In her black dresses and trademark long blonde hair, she was a superb sight, and vocally she was in immaculate, unfaltering control; a slight rasp only adds texture. She doesn't have the ability of a Sinatra, Garland or Astaire -- or of herself when young -- to cut to the heart of a song, or of the listener, with a single well-turned

phrase, but that doesn't stop her from delivering fine versions of Rodgers and Hart's Where or When or of I Stayed Too Long at the Fair.

She finished -- well, barring the encores -- with the other famous song from Funny Girl and by far the better one, the defiant take-no-prisoners number. It sounds especially defiant here because she sings the "stiff upper nose, kid" triumph-over-adversity reprise. This sounds a bit strange, coming from someone who's just been cheered to the echo and beyond, but there's no gainsaying it. Don't rain on her parade.

- Barbra Streisand plays her final Canadian show at the Air Canada Centre tomorrow.

Colour Photo: Brent Foster, National Post / No one short of Fanny Brice herself could have sung Funny Girl's selections quite like Barbra Streisand.
2006-10-21-ottawa-musical-montreal-play-:
Bring back The Wrong Son, and can someone explain Hosanna?

One of the best things to have happened recently in the Toronto theatre was also one of the least trumpeted. It was, in effect, a two-night stand, though I hope it will return in some more permanent form. The Wrong Son, a new musical by Allen Cole that premiered last month in Ottawa as the first production of the new regime at the National Arts Centre, was given two concert performances at the Harbourfront Arts Centre.

These featured the original Ottawa cast and musicians, and traces of the staging, in the form of projections of Peter Hinton's production. These suggested that the show must have looked stunning. All the same, Hintons most tangible contribution to the Harbourfront presentation (for which he was listed as "consulting director") was in the quality of the acting. We had the near-best of both worlds: the simplicity and immediacy of the concert format combined with the depth of performance obtainable from actors who have rehearsed their way into their roles.

And the piece itself is fascinating, the prolific Coles best that I have heard. Inspired by, rather than based on, a 1940s novel, it tells of Ryle, a Halifax piano player, returned with issues from the Second World War, whose new romantic and professional relationship with his female singer is threatened by the reappearance after many years of his vengeful wife. There is a shooting, and our musician finds himself on the run. He hitches a ride with another troubled young man, Cornell Tremble III, on his way to confront the father whom he hasn't seen since he was given up for adoption as a child and whom he has reason to believe is hoarding a considerable stash of cash. But it's Ryle who turns up at Cornell IIs remote house by the Bay of Fundy, and whom the old man embraces as his son.

There is a strong Maritime wind blowing through Coles treatment of the story, but the score has more to do with time than with place. It isn't, for the most part, folksy. It's more jazzy and cinematic. The first act, in fact, is film noir pastiche, and though its expertly done, its a seam that has been pretty thoroughly explored elsewhere. The second act, though, changes into something altogether more rich and strange, as old Cornell's love for his new- found son overrides any consideration that Ryle may not actually be that son, and as feelings that Ryle had thought long buried begin to re-emerge. The plot, too, revs up as characters reappear in unexpected combinations and circumstances, with a couple of cops in dogged chase. (They also form a chorus, one of whose functions is to act as the voice of Ryle's conscience, which is fairly dogged on its own account.)

The last section of the show is seriously tense, with a narrative and emotional power that invite comparison with Sweeney Todd. Like Sweeney, this is almost a through-composed piece, with occasional dialogue scenes whose brevity makes them stand out all the more starkly. Coles lyrics have a strong sawn-off quality; his music includes at least three independently beautiful melodies and much close-knit dramatic music that verges on chamber opera. It was tautly and lusciously played, in Toronto as in Ottawa, by the Arraymusic Ensemble, the shows co-producers, with Bob Stevenson conducting.

The cast boasted two stellar

actress-singers in Tamara Bernier, an ambiguous ingenue as Ryle's pet thrush, and Corinne Koslo, tough and vibrant as his ex. Frank Moore was both moving and disturbing

as the old man. (The projections

revealed that in the full staging he was dressed in yellow, with his house done up to match. Cool.) Ryle himself is largely a passive character, certainly an enigmatic one, but David Keeley, just sitting on a stool in a black sweater, established him as the piece's magnetic centre. Martin Julien gave the real Cornell a seedy swagger, and Randi Helmers and John Millard were an unimpeachable pair of avenging angels. The total effect was of yearning melancholy with the kick of a mule. Bring it back.

Maybe its because Im an Anglo -- and a British Anglo at that -- but I've never been able to get very interested in Michel Tremblay's Hosanna as an allegory of the divided soul of Quebec, or even to detect how that could be the case. I certainly dont believe that thats what has kept the play alive for 30 years. It survives on the wit, compassion and scabrous detail with which Tremblay depicts the relationship between Hosanna, the drag-queen hairdresser humiliated when impersonating Elizabeth Taylor impersonating Cleopatra (his favourite role, though probably not Taylor's), and Cuirette, the biker-lover who jealously helped engineer his/her downfall. Tremblay's ability to show this menage on its own terms -- no sensationalism, no special pleading -- seems daring even now.

That shines through, along with the plays evocation of Montreal at a certain time, even in the new production by John Van Burek (the original translator, with Bill Glassco), which is rather dull. Jean- Stephane Roys lumbering Cuirette is vocally and physically indistinct; and though Salvatore Antonio's Hosanna looks a peach, he misses out on the verbal glitter that keeps the first act afloat.

He and the play only begin to come together in the long agonized monologue that comprises much of the second half; and they finally close (with Roy, too, beginning to pull his bearish weight) when the play itself does. The two movingly reconcile, or something like it, and Hosanna, self-stripped of finery, admits that he is "a man." Forgive my innocence, but I'm not sure whether this means he intends to give up drag, and whether, if it does, Tremblay is not more of a puritan than we might have suspected. And though the very best people have tried to explain it to me, I don't see how this would equate with Quebec turning its back on strange gods and embracing its own identity. You can, of course, compare anything to anything but this is ridiculous.

- Hosanna runs through Oct. 28 at the Young Centre; 416-866- 8666.

Colour Photo: Nir Bareket / Jean-Stephane Roy, left, as Cuirette and Salvatore Antonio as Hosanna in Hosanna, playing at the Young Centre for the Performing Arts.

THEATRE REVIEW

DON JUAN

Stratford Festival

This year's Stratford Festival has been rife with classic French comedies. The Studio Theatre offered a production of Pierre Corneilles The Liar in which the actors changed roles at every performance and goosed the script and one another throughout the evening. It was fun, but the laughs had almost nothing to do with the text. They could have been doing any play.

As impressively formal as The Liar was engagingly informal, Stratfords production of Moliere's Don Juan began its run in English and closed it in French. The casting, with a couple of presumably mono-lingual exceptions, was the same in both versions. I caught the last English performance and the first French one, and I preferred the latter. I have no quarrel with David Edney's translation, but the playing seemed zingier in the original, and Molieres own text stood up better to the monumental style adopted by the director, Lorraine Pintal of Theatre du Nouveau Monde in Montreal.

Don Juan is a curious play and, even by Molieres standards, a loose-knit one. It is, despite its hero's international reputation, remarkably unsexy. It's one of the authors jokes that in the course of the play the legendary lover never actually scores with a woman. We meet him in the aftermath of his seduction of Dona Elvira, who twice appears to announce her retreat to a convent, first reproachfully, then forgivingly. In the course of abducting her Juan slew her father, whose statue famously appears at the end of the evening to drag him down to hell. Theres also some talk of his pursuing a couple of beauties by sea, but he's shipwrecked and instead has to work his charms on a pair of peasant girls, quite successfully until they start comparing notes. Much of the play is an extended debate between Juan and his servant Sganarelle, who speaks for conventional society and whose main beef against his master is not that he exploits women but that he refuses to be ashamed of it, any more than he is of killing his elders or bilking his creditors. What it all comes down to is that Juan doesn't believe in his societys morality, for which the shorthand is God. Theres a famous scene in which he offers gold to a starving hermit on condition that he blaspheme -- though, like other famous scenes, it never seems to have a theatrical impact to match its critical prestige. (It doesn't help that the production overplays its hand by making the poor anchorite seems more symbol than man). The closest Juan comes to repentance is to pretend a reformation when his father threatens to disinherit him. But he admits to Sganarelle that he's merely experimenting with another vice, though a peculiarly fashionable one; he may be a hypocrite, but he isnt hypocritical about it. Hes also physically brave, and his code stands up well against that of Dona Elvira's avenging brothers, whose values don't differ much from those of the Taliban. In the end, hes like the heroes of some Greek tragedies; he falls victim to a system that his author doesnt necessarily endorse but knows will always win. On a less exalted level, Moliere's play recalls the much-misunderstood last episode of Seinfeld, whose four principals ended up condemned by people far more selfish and sanctimonious than they were.

Moliere may have admired his Juan but he didn't much like him. That at least is the impression left by Colm Feores performance, which is fast and fluent (in both tongues), steely and unyielding but bloodless, even faceless. This last quality, though, may come with the productions territory. In Daniele Levesque's bleached settings, which are both gorgeous and austere, Juan lives in a house whose most prominent furnishings are a quintet of tailors' dummies, crowned in the last sacrificial act by candelabra. He changes identities as naturally and frequently as he changes his clothes; he cant really be a hypocrite because he has no centre to which he can be false. Benoit Brieres Sganarelle, by contrast, is foursquare and full-blooded: a combination of fear, greed and pious horror, who is endearing because he is recognizable. He never gets to change his clothes. He's also a master of clowning routines; indeed he starts the show with one, done almost entirely in Italian. Moliere, a Frenchman adapting a Spanish story, naturally set it in Sicily, though the geography throughout is very vague.

The costumes, by Francois St. Aubin, gracefully elide periods. Sevententh-century fig is reserved for Jean-Louis Roux as Juan's papa, who pays social calls in full Louis Quatorze regalia, incorporating a hint of armour; his performance, unhappily stiff in English, makes iconic sense in French. Similarly but differently, Gareth Potters Pierrot, slowed down in translation by a laborious Newfoundland accent, is charming in the original. The Statue of the Commander is transfixing in both versions; hes a hologram, with a crumbling visage and with the voice of Christopher Plummer. His impact is blunted, though, when Juan's death and damnation are represented by a dance with a female demon whom he, gallant and unrepentant to the last, is unable to resist; it makes intellectual sense but theatrically it's an anti-climax. Brieres final plaintive cry for his "wages," however, redeems it. In all its a grand, imaginative production: the kind of thing that may be commonplace in Quebec but can knock our chaussettes off in Ontario.

Colour Photo: Stratford Festival / Colm Feore as the bloodless, faceless and, despite its hero's international reputation, remarkably unsexy Don Juan.
