THEATRE REVIEW

OF MICE AND MEN

Bluma Appel Theatre, Toronto

John Steinbeck's Of Mice and Men, at least in its dramatized version, is one of those works that everybody knows but hardly anybody gets to see. Now, suddenly, two productions are upon us. CanStage have revived it as the opening production of their new season, and there is another revival scheduled next year at Stratford. The Toronto version, a co-production with Theatre Calgary, suggests that the best-laid plans can sometimes work out. Its excellent, and it looks magnificent.

Within the play itself, set among itinerant ranch-hands in the depths of Depression America, hopes are things that are born to be frustrated. They are also contagious. The dream shared by the duo at the heart of the story -- Lennie, the slow-witted giant who seems fated to crush everything he loves from his pet mouse on up, and George, his friend and protector -- communicates itself to almost everyone they meet. They talk, endlessly, about buying their own place; Lennie cant get enough of hearing George tell about the rabbits he'll be able to tend, and -- shades of Tom Sawyer and Huck Finn -- the circuses and ball-games they'll be able to slope off and attend. Candy, the fat crippled hand kept on to clean out the flophouse, overhears them and immediately wants in. Crooks, the black worker turned bitter and suspicious after years of being patronized and excluded by men in desperate need of someone even they can look down on, pours scorn on the idea but is still tempted by it. Curlys Wife, married to the bosss mean and jealous son and branded a tramp by all the men, has her parallel fantasy, one that likely shared by at least half the women in America; she dreams of being swept off to Hollywood and making it in the movies.

Steinbeck wrote Of Mice and Men as a novel and then turned it into a play. It was begging to be one -- the book's dialogue is insistently speakable -- and it took naturally to its new medium. There is no way that, without prior knowledge, you would suspect the stage version of being an adaptation. It is devilishly well- constructed, with all the seeds of ultimate destruction carefully sown and meticulously watered. The climactic encounter is between Curly's Wife and Lennie; they barely know one another, but by the time it happens we can practically prophesy how the meeting is going to go down. We can foresee its aftermath as well. But for all the authors control, and his rightful insistence that these men are what their era has made them, the characters remain people, not puppets; people who, in their isolation and their hopelessness, could easily be our contemporaries.

The play begins with George and Lennie on their way to their next job, and Dennis Garnhums production gives us the necessary time to get acquainted. George loves Lennie, feels responsible for him, and is frequently and inevitably exasperated by him; Shaun Smyth's edgy performance keeps all the shades in view, and moves naturally towards the acceptance of tragic necessity. Ashley Wright brings off a complementary balancing act as Lennie, reaching deeply and affectingly into the trusting recesses of a one-track mind. When they reach the ranch, they are confronted by a further roomful of good performances, most of them by actors new to Toronto: Sterling Jarvis brings a sardonic cackle to Crooks (the play isn't big on laughs but hes responsible for those it has), while Stan Lesks Candy amounts to a plaintive and appealing hill of flab. The scene in which he is pressured into allowing his sick old pet dog to be shot is the play's emotional signature, an emblem of what happens to the helpless, and the production wrings every drop of tension out of it. Candy's physical if not temperamental opposite would have to be the foreman Slim, the most sympathetic character -- in terms of both attracting and extending sympathy -- is played as such by John Kirkpatrick; in an atomized society he is the only person capable of charity. Even the devoted companionship of George and Lennie, which the others think phenomenal, doesnt extend beyond themselves. The only false notes are struck by Lisa Norton who seems to be playing the woman from the mens point of view rather than her own. She plays her character's anger at the expense of her hurt, and adopts a kewpie-doll voice presumably intended as her passport to Tinseltown.

The sets, by John Jenkins and Allan Stichbury, are spectacular: Vast expanses of golden corn (glowingly lit by Kevin Lamotte) majestically accommodate the play's hopeful first scene and its despairing last; in between we get an alternating series of timbered interiors. There's one scene that ends abruptly and confusingly; otherwise the constant changes offer bold statements rather than, as is usually when scenery gets shifted in full view, awkward apologies.

- On until Nov. 11. 416-368-3110

Black & White Photo: Trudie Lee / As George, Shaun Smyth, right, offers an edgy performance that moves naturally towards the acceptance of tragic necessity. Ashley Wright, left, reaches deeply into the trusting recesses of a one-track mind.
2006-11-02-musical-s-past-is-revealed-by:
PIPPIN

Royal Alexandra Theatre, Toronto

- - -

There have been two Golden Ages of, or at least for, Stephen Schwartz. There was a point in the 1970s at which three hit shows for which he was both composer and lyricist -- Godspell, Pippin and The Magic Show -- were running simultaneously on Broadway. He is now experiencing, in Toronto at least, a more modest renaissance. Wicked, his most recent piece, is back in town for an extended run, and a revival of Pippin has just checked in at the Royal Alexandra Theatre.

There is one thing that all the above musicals have in common: They are terrible. (I have to take the awfulness of The Magic Show on trust, but it has been universally attested.) That doesn't necessarily mean the scores are; Schwartz at his best writes decent lyrics and better music, though they always come in tied to mawkish and/or pretentious entertainments. Pippin's score is his best -- in what was once considered a pop-rock vein but now sounding more like mainstream Broadway -- but Roger O. Hirson's book, and the show's entire concept, qualify for both the above adjectives, though "pretentious" predominates. Moreover, the current version (which originated at the Goodspeed Opera House in Connecticut, home and forcing-house of musical revivals) suffers from a fatal disease: de- Fossefication.

Bob Fosse directed and choreographed the original Pippin. It was part of the cycle that he began with the film Cabaret and continued with Chicago, Dancin' and All That Jazz. These were all self-hating productions that set show business against itself. The master showman used all his devices -- he gave us the old razzle dazzle, as they say in Chicago -- while ending up railing at his audiences for accepting them and himself for using them. Personally I found all this self-flagellation tiresome. If he despised himself so much for playing tricks, he should have either stopped playing them or shut up about it. The latter would have been preferable, since he played them so well, and never better than in Pippin.

Some shows can work when de-Fossefied; the phenomenally successful revival of Chicago is not, whatever people tell you, as good as the original but it's more palatable -- and more enjoyable - - precisely because its creator's obsessions are toned down and kept at a distance. Besides, the underlying material is strong and the story interesting. Pippin doesn't have those luxuries. Its hero is the son of the Emperor Charlemagne (whose chivalrous reputation, though the show makes no pretentions to historical authenticity, is thoroughly debunked) and a hopeless idealist. In the first act he tries such youthful pursuits as war, sex, parricide (revoked -- this is a musical) and benevolent rule on his own account, and finds them all wanting. In the second, in which the action and background of the first are almost completely forgotten, he pursues his quest for "a higher purpose" and finds it, to the surprise of everyone except the audience, in the love of a young widow and her son. This is not at all what the people telling the story had in mind. They are a garish troupe of strolling players -- Pippin himself seems to be with them but not of them -- who try to seduce him with lights, costumes, music and, well, razzle dazzle. (Once Fosse got an idea, he stuck with it.) Without these things, they jeer, he is just ordinary, and who wants to be that?

It's very thin stuff, but the original production made it work with staging that pinned your attention from the opening hallucinatory number, Magic to Do, in which a white-gloved corps leaped out from a black box. In the new version (directed by Gabriel Barre, choreographed by Mark Dundy) the gloves are still on but the box has opened -- the set's predominant shade is murky blue. In the battlefield sequence, where Fosse and his colleagues earnestly set out to inform us that War is a Bad Thing, there's another fleeting homage to the master: the reappearance of his trademarked Steam Heat trio -- a girl and two guys in derbies doing an insolent strut -- but no sign of his overall architecture. (In the original Pippin, the threesome became known -- rather tastelessly -- as the Manson Trio.) It's significant, not to say mendacious, that Bob Fosse's name appears nowhere in the program though this is a show that nobody would be reviving now if he hadn't done it first. It's still his idea but without his ceaseless inventiveness, which is all that made the idea fly.

Some of the show's language seems to have become more permissive with the years, and there is an apparent attempt to link the fable's temptations of celebrity glitter to the age of American Idol. To quote the title of Fosse's last show (his only flop): big deal -- though, in fairness, the ending here does seem harder-hitting than I'd remembered it. As for the performers, as the Leading Player who is meant to be a Satanic charmer, Cabaret's backdated emcee, Andre Ward, grinning a lot, is long on Satanism but decidedly short on charm. Joshua Park's Pippin compensates in the latter department, and has real appeal as well; he is always direct and never merely winsome. Mickey Dolenz brings off Charlemagne with the same bluff imperturbablity that got him through the even grimmer circumstances of Aida -- though for some reason he looks, when not wearing his crown, as if he had wandered in from Fiddler on the Roof.

- Until Dec. 3. (416)-872-1212

Black & White Photo: Mirvish / No one wants a winsome Pippin: Joshua Park brings the charm.
2006-11-03-dynamite-diego:
THE CARETAKER

Young Centre for the Performing Arts, Toronto

- - -

With the sole exception of William Hutt, no Canadian actor makes as powerful or as sharply-defined an impression the moment he sets foot upon a stage than Diego Matamoros. In Soulpepper's revival of The Caretaker, the play that in 1960 instantly established Harold Pinter as a major dramatist and that remains his masterpiece, Matamoros plays Davies, the tramp who inveigles his way into a junk- laden West London flat owned or inhabited by two brothers and promptly becomes the cuckoo in their nest. In Albert Schultz's production he's a cuckoo in a crow's nest; the play is performed in the round, or more accurately in the square, with the audience on four sides and the only entrance a hole in the floor, below which stretches, or so we assume, an invisible flight of steps. This bedsit is an attic -- the worst of two worlds.

Davies is part wheedler and part bully, ruthless but also helpless. Matamoros keeps both his passive and his aggressive qualities going all the time. His British accent is impeccable; London rather than the Welsh that's been traditional for the role ever since its creation by the late Donald Pleasence, but then Davies, a.k.a. Jenkins, is very cagey about where he's from. "I've been around," is all he'll say when a challenger tries to pin him down on the subject. Much of the play's comedy, and what used to be thought of as its mystery, comes from his habit of going off in tangents, generally of his own creation, whenever faced with a question he can't or won't answer, "I was over there," he says eagerly when asked if he had served in the colonies. "I was one of the first over there." (Matamoros underplays the bravura of this; maybe it does need to be Celtic.) The room's impressive collection of objets trouves includes a store-bought Buddha. Asked his opinion of such things he says, vaguely, "they're all right, ain't they?" Telling his own stories, though, he can be richly specific, as witnessed in his account of the monastery to which he once trekked in quest of a pair of free shoes, only to be told by the monk on duty to "piss off out of it." (Davies threatened to report him to his Mother Superior.) Davies is his own worst enemy. If he is offered a pair of shoes, he invariably finds something wrong with it. Offer him a bed and he'll complain of the draft or of the chance of being asphyxiated by the (unplugged) gas stove alongside. Confide in him and he'll betray you. Offer him the chance to stay on as caretaker -- practically a sinecure -- with a red smoking jacket to wear on the job, and he'll use it to undermine you. Inevitably, he'll overreach himself, and he is after all a homeless old man living on what remains of his wits. An English director once described him as the last great character to be created by a British playwright, the last one can imagine future actors thirsting to play (hence, in a nutshell, the subsequent decline of modern drama); and this accurate assessment is fully embodied in Matamoros' performance.

Aston, the brother who brings him home, is a gentle, enigmatic man who has undergone a lobotomy in a mental hospital; he tells Davies about this, or at least he talks about it when Davies is present, in the longest and most celebrated speech in the play. Here the production runs into trouble. Traditionally, Aston tells his story quietly while sitting on the side of his bed. He can't do that here, because a quarter of the audience would be looking at his back; so Damien Atkins has to deliver it standing up and even moving around. This inevitably leads him into illustrative acting that is out of key, not only with the writing, but with the delicacy of the rest of his performance. Aston has built himself a cocoon, and it gives him strength. There are lines that cannot be crossed, and Davies crosses them. He taunts Aston with his incarceration (though when he desperately admits that he, too, once glimpsed the inside of such an institution, we start wondering just how much the two men may have in common), and then -- unforgivably -- sneers at his dream of building a shed. This illustrates Pinter's own contention that the play is not about the impossibility of communication but about its dangers. The Caretaker is one of those modern plays, including The Wild Duck and The Iceman Cometh, about men enslaved to their illusions.

Aston's brother Mick, the only character who seems to have solid links to the outside world (a business of his own and even, as he insists, a van), has his own dreams, mainly concerned with interior decoration; it's unclear to what extent his prose arias on the subject are merely ploys to bewitch, bother and bewilder, or how much he actually believes in them. But they're virtuoso turns, as are his celebrations of London bus routes, and Matthew Edison's delivery of them is beguiling if rather too subdued. (Pinter's style, like his world, is not far removed from that of Steptoe and Son. It needs the same comic energy.) Where Edison excels is in his prowling around the stage, putting the fear of God into Davies. He does it, we realize, to protect his brother. It's an irony that Mick, the wide boy, the one with the street smarts and the mental map of London, is also the most benevolent character in the play. The fact that he succeeds gives the play something of a happy ending. It comes with a cost; even Mick feels trapped and Davies is as pitiful as he was pitiless.

The ending, and the whole set-up, were reprised by Pinter in the more polished surroundings of No Man's Land but, dazzling exercise in high comedy though that is, The Caretaker is the greater play. It depends, of course, whether you prefer your Pinter smooth or scruffy. In this case, I'll take the scruff.

Schultz's production is not as unvaryingly superb as his No Man's Land but it's fine, with the play's succession of power-shifts made brilliantly clear. The ending is wonderfully balanced. The new stage formation doesn't solve this space's sight-line problems (as in the thrust-stage King Lear, if a character lies on the floor he's dead to us), but it creates a valuable sense of compression and enclosure. Lorenzo Savoini's set is absolutely right; the stage looks so specific to time and place that one ceases to wonder whether it's been thriftily recycled from American Buffalo.

The show is, frankly, a relief. After a triumphant beginning with Our Town, Soulpepper's first year in the Distillery has yielded a succession of near-misses varied by one outright fiasco. The Caretaker returns the company to its best, if not quite its very best, form.

- Until Nov. 25. 416-866-8666.

2006-11-04-play-descends-into-skid-row-s:
Most of Toronto's theatres have sailed into the new season with all guns blazing: Buddies in Bad Times has disinterred Here Lies Henry, the Tarragon has been Generous, CanStage has delivered itself Of Mice and Men and the Factory has fed us with Apple. Its fallen to Theatre Passe Muraille to lower the tone with a new play from Tom Walmsley, the aptly titled Descent.

I wouldnt want to be vicious about this; the play is seldom actually dull but it's vague and apparently aimless. The descent of the title is executed by Susan, a young woman whose sexual life has been, by her own account, comparatively sheltered and who is just about to get wed; indeed she gets the show off to a misleadingly spirited start by singing Nellie McKay's I Wanna Get Married. First, though, she wanna treat herself to what she describes as the female equivalent of a stag night, with two guys at once. Her chosen partners are a pair of heavy drinkers, both named Randy and chiefly distinguishable by the fact that only one of them has pretensions to being a poet.

But in treating Susan as the central character, I am drawing less on the play itself than on the publicity, which says she is, and on the shows logo, which is a striking portrait of Susan herself, or at least of the actress playing her. On stage, though, she seems no more important than any of the other four characters, all of them male, all of them at some point or to some degree lusting after her. Apart from the two Randies, in whose very basic pad the first act is set (the set is drastically minimal, presumably by design), we have two crumbs from the comparatively upper crust: Robinson, a publisher for whose patronage the poetic Randy half-heartedly hopes, and James, his assistant and acolyte whom everyone else despises for reasons that arent terribly clear. The action, or at least the talk, unfolds in a series of short, sharp bursts, punctuated by blackouts. There is humour but, at least on the second night when I saw it, hardly any laughs.

The most irritating thing about the play is that it takes for granted characters and relationships that it hasn't established. The second act, which is set in an abandoned church, seems at first to be picking up exactly where the first left off. (There's a car theft in both.) It then looks as if it might be happening in Hell; most of the characters have religious yearnings.

Eventually it transpires that we are still on Earth, after a lapse of eight years during which all these people have kept in touch, which, since they barely existed in the first place, is hard to credit. One of them seems to be dead, though he unfortunately wont lie down. There are some half-hearted farcical developments, on the Joe Orton model, concerning the robbing and moving and dumping of a corpse. Susans marriage has happened, but it hasn't worked out, though by the end of the evening she has managed to realize at least half of her eight-year-long fantasy. She gets to make some embittered speeches from the pulpit. All the characters engage in monologues and they are, by and large, the best things in the play.

Indeed, the whole play, despite its various voices, feels like a monologue. It's a journey into its authors personal Skid Row; theres no self-pity in it but it does rely heavily on the awareness, on both sides of the curtain, of Walmsley's own alcoholic past and late Catholic conversion; also on the guilty liberal conviction that the worse off a play's characters are, the better we will be for looking at them.

Kate Lynch, whose last Walmsley production (Three Squares a Day) was rather good, cant lend any focus to this one. The performances are casual to the point of shapelessness. Deborah Hays Susan is the best, especially in her later, jaded diatribes, which have real style. Brendan Murray gets some chipper conviction into the poetic Randy (who defines himself, accurately enough, by not writing like Blake). Christopher Morris as his buddy and namesake is likable enough but looks as if he would like somebody to throw him some motivation. As the rich and reviled Robinson, John Blackwood is thoroughly at sea. Paul Fauteux as James swims in his wake with more authority but no more persuasiveness, but then he is playing one of the more tenuous characters in modern drama.

Peter Cockett, who directed the three plays in the recent Shakespeare and the Queen's Men project, described himself during a post-performance Q&A session as less a director than a facilitator." By his own account, he set some ground rules and then let his actors get on with it, just as their Elizabethan forebears, whose rehearsals were rushed and rudimentary, would have had to do. The results -- the modern ones, I mean -- were always lively and often impressive. They are unlikely to have been exact replicas of the original interpretations; indeed, the whole idea of "interpretation may have been an intrusion, though an unavoidable one. What we bring to these plays of the 1580s is, inescapably, irony.

I am thinking especially of The Famous Victories of Henry V, the most enjoyable of the three shows and the only one I saw in the Queen's Men on Tour" section of the enterprise. (The touring date was the Tranzac Club, whose ale-drenched atmosphere was thoroughly appropriate. The audience thronged around the fit-up platform stage like Elizabethan groundlings, though a few of us softies managed to secure chairs.)

The Famous Victories has attracted academic interest as a source not only of Shakespeares Henry V but of the two parts of Henry IV that precede it. It covers breezily in about two hours the ground that we are accustomed to traversing in nine. Unsurprisingly, there isnt much subtlety. This Prince Hal is first a merrily unrepentant highway robber, then, after being rebuked by his royal father, turns instantly into a storybook hero who, on becoming king himself, leads all the lads off to victory in France. There are none of the heart- searchings and transitions you find in Shakespeare; and, though we still get the scene when the new king cuts loose his former cronies, there is hardly a hint of a Falstaff.

This Henry's attitude to all things and people French is unabashedly contemptuous and acquisitive. It must have warmed every patriotic Elizabethan heart. We now see things a little differently, and Paul Hopkins, playing the role here, could hardly avoid winking with us at his own outrageousness. His was altogether an irresistible performance, bold and fluent and charming. (At a couple of points he helped himself to the audience's beer.) He went, as his remote predecessors must have done, with the flow; only now it was a different flow.

The production revealed, too, that crudity can have its own complexity. There is a scene (echoed in Shakespeare, though he spread it out among various episodes) in which soldiers, pressed into service, take leave of home and loved ones, the latter represented by one alternately heartbroken and lascivious wife. Its part pathos, part broad farce; the actors played both modes, full out and simultaneously, and the results were both rich and instructive.

The new Queens Men also followed the old in relying heavily on typecasting; thus Don Allison played the king in all three plays -- in Famous Victories, he played two of them -- and always, I'll swear, wore the same crown. Similarly, Alon Nashman was always principal clown, and a virtuoso one, though he sometimes seemed to be playing in a different rhythm from the others, with more curlicues and pauses. But I daresay Richard Tarlton, the original star and the first great comedian in English stage history, did the same. I don't know how much this project taught scholars about how plays were done then. It certainly showed the rest of us a lot about how they might be done now.

- Descent runs through Nov. 19 at Theatre Passe Muraille, 416- 504-7529.robert.cushman@hotmail.com

2006-11-11-quaint-musical-demands-we-car:
There is a new book out whose sub-title is The Dream of a Canadian Musical Theatre. Its principal title is Broadway North, which strikes me as a very strange choice indeed. The author, Mel Atkey, has cast himself as both advocate for and chronicler of an independent and indigenous Canadian musical. So why has he chosen a label that, apart from being a runaway cliche in itself, explicitly looks to the United States for validation?

The Broadway (South) success of The Drowsy Chaperone allows the book an upbeat ending, though the vagaries of timing have meant that it has to be squeezed into a last-minute epilogue. But, of course, Chaperone has been given an American overhaul in staging and casting, and was a pastiche of American models in the first place.

Now at CanStage we have the world premiere of The Story of My Life, a musical that's practically a study in cross-pollination. Its authors are Canadians now based in New York. Its director is American. Of its two actors, one has spent most of his career in the United States, though he has also worked at Stratford; the other is a Canadian treasure who also enjoys star status on Broadway and whose name, not to keep you in too much suspense, is Brent Carver. The presentation offers very few grounds for complaint. The piece itself is close to unbearable.

It doesnt, as it happens, owe much to Broadway. It does, though, owe a lot to off-Broadway, and to a tradition of small or at least smaller musicals thats been flourishing in Greenwich Village and points north ever since New York discovered The Threepenny Opera in the mid-1950s. There's a useful history of the genre in the CanStage program, though one that's sometimes reckless in the scope of what it includes; it tries, for example, to rope in A Chorus Line. I saw A Chorus Line in its tryout at the Public Theatre and even then it was not, believe me, small.

Even off-Broadway musicals that are small dont have to be winsome (see Urinetown). But they very often are. And sometimes, as happens in The Story of My Life, that winsomeness is wedded to a throbbing emotionalism, a demand that we care about the people in front of us, however little reason we may be given to do so, because the authors care so much, dammit, and they have integrity, as is proved by the fact that theyre working on a modest scale. The word for this is sentimentality. Big musicals, of course, are hardly immune to it, but if I had to choose, I'd say that they do it less offensively if only because, with all that space at their disposal, they can spread the goo around a bit so that we can lap it up in a less concentrated form.

The Story of My Life is about two men, friends from boyhood, who grow up in a small town where it always seems to be winter. At any rate, Glenn Davidson has designed it as a snowscape dotted with piles of books. The prime reason is that much of the show takes place in and around the town bookstore. The town's name is Angel Falls and it might be either here or there, Canada or the United States; I dont remember ever being told which. I did get the feeling, though, when one of the characters moved to a successful literary life in an equally unspecified big city, that he was in New York rather than Toronto. The wider cultural references, too, seem to be American: Melville and Twain.

One of the cleverer things in the show is a recurring situation in which a character attends a funeral incognito, a la Tom Sawyer. Coming down a few pegs, there are constant references to Its a Wonderful Life. Alvin, who stays in Angel Falls to run his dad's bookstore (into the ground, eventually) is fixated on that picture, and especially on its angel Gabriel. So he sure picked the right place to live. Thomas, his buddy, is less fixated on both the town and the film; he refers to the latter as Frank Capra's feelgood Christmas movie." This is one of the more trenchant lines in Brian Hills book, which is both a lot shorter and a little more barbed than Neil Bartrams score, and Carver as Thomas fell on the tart words with every appearance of delight.

Alvin, like Jacob Marley, is dead to begin with, and Thomas has come back home after many years' absence to deliver his eulogy, in accordance with a long-ago promise (mutual). This, of course, leads to flashbacks, beginning with the friends' boyhood snowball fights. We see the school-age Thomas trying to protect Alvin from the consequences of his own neediness, not to mention his nerdiness, and we also see Thomas unexpectedly discovering a vocation as a writer and moving away to pursue it. We see various things, but theyre never more than incidents, and claustrophobically repetitive. Alvin eventually claims that Thomas has built his career on retelling stories that Alvin told him first and indeed had actually lived, but we have no way of judging the validity of this claim; even if its true, we don't know how much Thomas (who snarls "I never share credit") may have added in the way of style and imagination. Aren't all authors thieves? Throwing away his scripted funeral speech, Thomas decides to look in his heart and, in effect, improvise the show we have just seen that, he implies, will tell his hearers about Alvin. Only it wont; the show has told us little about Alvin and virtually nothing about Thomas. Which is why The Story of My Life is so deadly.

Well, because of that and its overall quaintness. In one respect, the show does progress a bit beyond its stylistic forebears from the 50s and after; it offers what I can only call explicit acknowledgement of implicit homosexuality. This, we infer, is what caused Thomas to call off his marriage and Alvin never even to come close. Thomas puts his fiancee on ice in one of the better songs, certainly one of the more slyly conversational. The score in general is competently crafted but pallid. It pleads for sympathy; even a bouncy song about an inspirational teacher has too much of the puppy- dog about it. Carver is in beautiful voice throughout, though I wish that on this occasion some of the harder edges of his acting had found their way into his singing. Jeffrey Kuhn is first-rate as Alvin, touchingly eager to please when young, powerfully embittered when older. The director is Michael Bush. This isn't the dream of a Canadian musical, and it's too mild even to be the nightmare of an American one.

- The Story of My Life runs at CanStage Berkeley Theatre through Dec. 9.; 416-368-3110.

2006-11-17-smashing-portrait-of-a-crumbl:
INSOMNIA

Buddies in Bad Times Theatre

- - -

The name of Daniel Brooks on a theatre bill promises, if it doesn't always guarantee, an adventurous production, one thats visually and sonically mesmerizing. This seems to be the case even when Brooks himself isnt the director. Chris Abraham has staged Insomnia -- which Brooks wrote 16 years ago with Guillermo Verdecchia and in which he also acts -- in a manner that might pass for Brooks' own work and was confessedly inspired by it. Banks of downstage lights flash in the audience's faces between scenes; other lights bathe strips of stage in red, making the affected parts look like lines of carpet, along which characters nightmarishly hurtle. Humming, screeching sound effects further shatter our nerves (lighting and sound are by Andrea Lundy and Richard Feren respectively, though at this stage in the game it seems almost superfluous to say so). None of this is gratuitous. The production reinforces the text with absolute precision.

That texts immediate subject is a breaking marriage, and it carries complete conviction. The larger subject seems to be contemporary society, all of it, and thats a lot chancier. The protagonist, John F., is a blocked writer, receiving little consolation from his wife Gwen, because she no longer has any to give. Maybe she never did; she knows it's over, even if he can't accept it and even though they have a child.

The pleadings and recriminations are starkly depicted in a series of very sharp, very short scenes. There arrives from California Johns brother William, an executive with Disney. At one point John, desperate, asks him for a job, only to be told that to work for the Mouse would require his becoming a completely different person, i.e. it isnt going to happen. John is indeed an insomniac (the condition drives him to take baths at 5 a.m.) though the title might also apply to Gwen, since his being awake keeps her awake. William's wife, Kate, though, is a narcoleptic, which would seem to be completely the opposite. William's own sleep patterns appear normal, which is suspicious in itself. John is attracted to Kate, and William appears to seduce Gwen, though around here the play slips beyond my literally minded ken. William announces that he has a plan to change his brothers life; his motives may be kindly or malevolent, but they involve him hypnotizing Gwen, and everyone but John going off to Japan. John, left behind, rediscovers his politically activist self and makes a long speech, one requiring a virtuosity in acting and performance that it doesnt actually get, in which he demolishes the entire spectrum from Noam Chomsky to Ann Coulter. (They are, he points out, essentially the same.)

He then smashes some windows -- I think -- and goes to jail. There is an ironically reassuring epilogue, whose point may be that you can paper over the cracks but the cracks will still be there. Which is all well and good, but somehow the device seems tired.

I'm not persuaded by the title image either, though it's undeniably effective in inducing critics -- including this one -- to affirm that this Insomnia will certainly keep you awake. The best parts of the script and all the parts of the production just about enforce it. Brooks himself, after a long break from performing, returns to the stage to play John; he may be only a journeyman actor, but his own belief in what hes doing ensures ours, especially in the early scenes where hes misery incarnate. Randy Hughson is not the most obvious choice for William, who is Mr. Success, but if he doesn't have the sleek profile he certainly has the mental measure, and its power; he also keeps us hoping against hope that, being Randy Hughson, he may really be a good guy and that, in its way, is helpful. Fiona Highet's Gwen, a bleak survivor awaking to agony, and Colombe Demers' Kate, a beautiful sphinx, are irreproachable.

- Insomnia runs until Nov. 26. Call 416-975-8855 for ticket information.

Black & White Photo: Guntar Kravis / Daniel Brooks and Fiona Highet as John and Gwen, whose marriage is on the rocks. Going to bed angry doesn't solve anything.
2006-11-18-that-s-a-lot-of-lawrence-to-c:
robert.cushman@hotmail.com; The Oxford Roof Climbers Rebellion runs through Dec. 17 at the Tarragon Theatre, 416-531-1827.

Alan Bennett's first play, Forty Years On, contains a detachable monologue about T.E. Lawrence. It describes him, in the anguished aftermath of the First World War, striding through London in his Arab headdress, flowing robes and scimitar, "in which uniform -- I quote from memory here -- he hoped to pass unnoticed in the Charing Cross Road." "Who am I? he would cry out in his despair. To which passersby would reply, You are Lawrence of Arabia. And I claim my (ps)5."

Some years before Bennett, another English playwright, Terence Rattigan, had given Lawrence a play of his own, a biographical piece titled Ross. The climax of that was the protagonist's capture and rape by the Turks, and his horrified realization that he had enjoyed it; horrified because it was not just his body that had been violated but his sense of his own -- to use the word fairly literally -- integrity. He had thought he was untouchable. The same incident is recounted, and given much the same interpretation, in a new Canadian play, The Oxford Roof Climbers Rebellion, by Stephen Massicotte.

The enigmatic, charismatic Lawrence is an obvious candidate for treatment on stage (and, of course, on film) but the narcissistic, masochistic Lawrence can also be a tough sell. Massicottes play shows us the postwar Lawrence as a fellow of All Souls College, where one of his fellow fellows is another young vet, poet Robert Graves, still in a state of intermittent shell shock from his experiences on the Western Front. The Oxford vice-chancellor, Lord Curzon, also happens to be the Foreign Secretary, so he is doubly in authority over them: certainly over Lawrence, who despite his protestations of disillusion and disengagement, is still involved with the British mandate in Arabia and Mesopotamia.

Graves is incensed by the mass sacrifice of his slaughtered comrades, Lawrence not so much by that as by his government's breaking of the promises he made to the Arabs whom he had roused to fight for them. In Lawrence's pre-war student days, he and his pals had climbed the highest, most dangerous towers in Oxford for the fun of it; now he and Graves (an experienced rock-climber) go climbing for a purpose. Lawrence goads and infuriates Curzon by hanging an Arab flag from the college spire. He and Graves also stage a pre- situationist protest involving a herd of deer, and issue manifestos appropriating lines from Gravess poems.

Or misappropriating them: That is the view of Gravess wife, Nancy, with whom he keeps a grocery store. Nancy is a more pragmatic progressive: socialist and feminist and suspicious of the possibly erotic bond between her husband and his friend.

The Graves's marriage is another line of plot; so are Curzon's attempts to get either man to deliver the address at what seems to be the first-ever Remembrance Day service. There is also Jack, Lawrences manservant, roused to murderous rage -- first at Curzon, then at Lawrence -- when his soldier son is killed in a Mesopotamian ambush. And looming behind everything, of course, is the birth of the current Middle East; in the later scenes words like "oil and jihad" and "insurgency and Iraq" are voiced, the last inducing a perceptible audience shiver.

That is a lot to cram into one short play. This one manages to get everything in on a narrative level, and seems in retrospect impressively shaped, but it doesnt carry much weight in actual performance. Scenes are rushed, issues crowded and characters rarely come to life. Here's Lawrence, striking attitudes, one of which is an acknowledgment that he strikes attitudes; there's Graves, having his meltdowns; the others just wander on and off as needed.

Nor does the plays style always match its ambitions. There are some barbed exchanges, as the setting and characters seem to demand, but some of the writing is sloppy. What does Curzon mean when he says that Lawrence "was veritably dismissed from the Paris peace talks? (Virtually," perhaps?)

Richard Roses direction doesn't supply much tension, and though Tom Rooney's Lawrence ("Ted" to friends) has the right blend of agony and mischief, his performance, which should drive the play, has a faltering rhythm. Jonathan Crombie does all that seems required of Graves, and Michelle Giroux, in a voice that's three- quarters Maggie Smith and the rest Emma Thompson, is superbly worried and imperious as Nancy. Victor Ertmanis and Paul Rainville fill in efficiently as Curzon and Jack. The title (singular, so Lawrence is the protagonist, even if he seems to share the limelight with Graves) suggests a sandbox revolt, an absurd gesture while the real action is going on elsewhere. Fair enough, but it makes the play itself seem out of proportion. The smaller action is too small, the bigger frustratingly out of reach.

Colour Photo: Cylla Von Tiedemann / Michelle Giroux and Jonathan Crombie in The Oxford Roof Climber's Rebellion, playing at the Tarragon Theatre.
2006-11-21-mum-s-not-the-word-with-theat:
Ross Petty continues to reinvent a classic genre

This Christmas, not for the first time, Ross Petty will produce Aladdin in Toronto. But this year, for the first time with this or any other of his shows, he fulfills a long-cherished dream of taking the show to other places as well: to Vancouver, Edmonton, Calgary, Regina, Saskatoon and -- after the Toronto run -- Ottawa. Petty's holiday entertainments are commonly known as "pantomimes, but he never gives them that label. The reason is that, after all this time -- and Petty has been involved with these shows, as producer and/or performer, for more than 20 years -- people hearing the word pantomime" still say, "Is it Marcel Marceau? In North America, pantomime" is just a longer synonym for "mime. But in Britain, which provided the inspiration for Pettys shows, pantomime is very verbal. It comes with words that are spoken, sung and -- in the mandatory sections involving audience participation -- improvised.

You take a familiar story: It could be European (Cinderella), Eastern (Aladdin), or even English (Robin Hood). You tell it, with as many diversions as possible in the shape of comedy routines and popular songs. You cast as many well-known, or at least well-loved, performers as possible. Your comic female lead will be played by a man (the pantomime dame) and your hero by a woman (the principal boy). That, pretty much, is the panto as it exists right now in Britain, though not all the conventions are cast in stone; the principal boy seems to be dying out, though the dame remains immutable.

Petty has been adapting and transforming for Canadian audiences for more than 20 years. His first encounter in 1982 consisted of seeing his future wife, Karen Kain, appearing in Aladdin at the Royal Alexandra Theatre in Toronto, in what must have been the twilight of theatrical colonialism. Kain was the token Canadian" in a show that otherwise made no concessions to where it was playing.

"Id never, says Petty, bemused but smitten, seen anything like it."

The following year Paul Elliott, the British producer, cast Kain and Petty, now married, in the most English of panto subjects, Dick Whittington. They played, literally, opposite one another: She was the Good Fairy, he was the villainous King Rat, the natural prey of Dick Whittington's famous Cat. Elliott, Petty says now, was "testing the waters -- if he had a show he would bring it over, but it was all hit-and-miss. Petty became his co-producer in 1986, partly because I wanted to have control of my life, instead of waiting for the phone to ring." And once he'd taken over the whole operation, he set about turning the shows into "a different hybrid than British audiences would be used to seeing.

In its way, though, the Petty panto has been a logical development of the British prototype. It, too, uses local talent and local topical references. It still has a singalong near the end of the second act, with kids brought up from the audience and given prizes. It has been, on the whole, more businesslike about the actual storytelling. It has persevered with the dame (sometimes in Pettys own person) but has dropped the principal boy -- the latter being a convention that has always had audiences outside Britain thoroughly perplexed.

We really came into our own," says Petty, "with the arrival of Ted Dysktra. He has an actors sensibility. He works well on his feet.

He also has what Petty appealingly calls the lunacy factor." Dykstra is the actor/writer/director probably still best known for being one half of Two Pianos, Four Hands and with a penchant for the rock 'n' roll bizarre; he starred in the Toronto production of Hedwig and the Angry Inch, and will direct The Rocky Horror Show for CanStage next year. (He also gave one of the best comedy performances Ive ever seen in Soulpeppers A Chorus of Disapproval.) Dykstra himself credits the beginning of the change to another actor/director, Jim Warren, who "began dragging Ross's shows across the pond and getting rid of the sexist and racist jokes. The texts they had were beyond repair, and Jim began insisting that they write new stuff. Ross was scared to change but Jim pushed him.

When Dysktra was asked to succeed Warren, he'd never seen an English panto, and he too was scared; he then decided that fear had always produced his best work and accepted. His own inspiration was closer to home.

I thought of The Simpsons as a template. They did all these things at first. They take contemporary culture and apply it to old stories, ideas and relationships. I was doing a cartoon series at the time called Bobo Roach. We hired a writer from there, Dave Finley."

Before Finleys advent, Pettys programs had been notoriously coy about the shows' authorship. Some of the scripts might have been folklore, and indeed played that way. Two years ago Dykstra and Finley did Aladdin, the show they're reviving now (with some new jokes; they seem especially proud of having one about Svend Robinson).

Last year it was Snow White and the Group of Seven, a title that gives the clearest pointer to the new Canadianizing of the form. Though the heroines non-dwarfish friends werent painters, but a boy band, made up of alumni of Canadian Idol. In Aladdin the singalong number is If I Had a Million Dollars.

"And you can't says Dykstra, get more Canadian than that." Except perhaps by casting wrestler Bret "Hitman Hart as the genie. This idea of Dykstra's turned out to be a real coup.

I have," says Dykstra. "walked down the street with a lot of famous people, but Ive never seen the reaction Bret Hart gets. Lawyers, homeless people, everyone.

One piece of casting thats remained constant is Petty himself -- still invariably the villain, and loving it.

As a performer, I'm a stage animal. This gives me a chance to get in front of a live audience again. And the response here is an experience you couldn't get anywhere else. Getting hissed as soon as I come on: you really need the energy of the audience." (In Snow White, of course, the baddie is the Queen, so playing the villain entailed playing the dame as well, even though Petty had never had "any great desire to play the dame. And indeed, the combination didnt really work; you cant be lovable and hissable at the same time.) The energy inspires Dykstra as well: You get the greatest feeling of accomplishment, to sit through this and make everyone feel that they've had a good time."
2006-11-24-stars-of-a-silver-screed:
DIRECTOR'S CUT

Factory Studio Theatre

- - -

Connoisseurs of unwitting irony will find an overflowing potful of the stuff at the Factory Studio. Director's Cut is a play about a writer-directors blighted attempt to make a movie, and it is itself the work of a writer-director. Jim Millan, founder and outgoing chief of Crows Theatre -- a company with a certain reputation but, to put it gently, an uneven track record -- wrote the play himself and has staged it in collaboration with Jillian Kelley, a Newfoundland director who two years ago won the highly prestigious Siminovitch Prize. Both these emperors may have impressive suits of clothes in their wardrobes at home, but they aren't wearing them here.

Stop me if you've heard this one before: A man with a vision sets out to make a film and finds that vision hopelessly compromised by mercenary producers, egocentric actors and -- let us be frank -- his own susceptibility to bullying, flattery and big budgets. The twist here, which I think they hope will kill you, is that the luckless visionary is Canadian while the philistine producer and airheaded stars are American. To be fair, the play never pretends that its all the Yanks fault. We can't tell whether our hero, Jeff, who seems in disarray throughout, has any talent or whether his initial idea had any merit. He wanted to make a lyrical flick about a picturesquely lost young woman and ended with something about a virus with the power to destroy the Internet. Worse, he tries to fuse the two. We know from the start that the movie is a disaster, because the whole thing is told in flashback. There is no suspense and no reason to take an interest, since the characters are not just cartoons but caricatures. (In theatre reviewers' jargon, a cartoon is an idea intentionally simplified to make a satiric point. A caricature is simple and nothing else -- a cartoon with the juice squeezed out.) The dramatic framework has Jeff and his trusty editor making off with the original footage to shoot a documentary about how it all went wrong. They make their way to Hollywood to confront their former producer, and the show ends with the three of them sitting down together for, in effect, a screening of the play weve just seen. Thats the second time in three weeks that this instant- retrospective device has surfaced on a Toronto stage -- the first was The Story of My Life -- and it doesn't look any lovelier the second time around.

The American actors Jeff is lured into hiring are an intense monolingual blond, bizarrely cast as a brooding Italian, and a wired dog-loving comedian who would be bizarrely cast as almost anything. Forest Whitaker is also supposed to be on board (we don't meet him) but he walks out, leaving the team scrambling desperately for someone close by to replace him. This is the cue for the play to start dropping the names of Canadian actors (Paul Gross? Colm Feore? Don McKellar? --No! shouts everybody in unison at the last suggestion) in a bid for laughs thats even more desperate. I can think of just one good play about the movies, Kaufman and Harts Once in a Lifetime; it's one of the funniest plays ever written and it doesn't mention a single real name. I confess I did laugh when the imported starlet expressed puzzlement at the fragrant names of Toronto theatre companies ("Tarragon? Pepper?") but, like everybody else, Ive been laughing at that one for years.

Given the obvious impossibilty of the project on hand, the money- man emerges as the most sympathetic character around; at least hes trying to salvage something and he isn't even particularly obnoxious. In fact he's notably controlled; this gives Ron White, who plays him, a distinct advantage over the rest of the cast, and very smoothly he takes it. Everyone else is left frantically mugging. Gord Rand is an actor who can seem different in every role he plays. He takes versatility to the point of unrecognizability, and as Jeff he is, at least in his first and most frantic scenes, unrecognizably bad. Hes a little more endearing later on when he quietens down. Chris Earle as his sidekick is cheerful in a neutral sort of way, except for a strange bout of monster-impersonation. I suspect that both these performances are fighting for their lives. Of those who act the actors, Amy Rutherford does the eye-fluttering bit efficiently if repetitively, while Ryan McVittie seems even more listless and scattershot than the guy hes playing. Michelle Latimer completes the stage cast as the token Canadian in the film cast; she has little to do and it works out for her. The stage has a false proscenium to make it look like a movie screen. VideoCabaret do all their shows in this kind of frame, but they usually find stylish things to put inside it. Also, their scene changes are virtuoso jobs; the ones we get here, though advertised as providing filmic fluidity, look no different from the hasty transitions we see in nine Toronto productions out of 10. "Be arch, be funny, be clever," the producer instructs his team. This show, a self-indulgent lampoon of self-indulgence, scores one out of three.

- Until Dec. 10. 416-504-9971

2006-12-08-god-bless-this-one:
THEATRE REVIEW

A Christmas Carol

Young Centre for the Performing Arts

Dickens makes it all right to cry. There is no shortage of books, films and even plays that know how to jerk the tears; we yield to most of them while despising ourselves for doing so. The difference with Dickens may have been best summed up in George Orwell's phrase about him; that he was generously angry, though I would add that he was also imaginatively angry. He doesnt present us with scenes of deprived or even dying children merely for emotional effect; he links them to the society around them without ever colluding into dehumanizing the victims or turning them into statistics. And hes also, of course, generously and almost continuously funny; his unique potency -- possibly even stronger when he's transferred from page to stage -- is his ability not so much to make us laugh till we cry as to keep laughter and tears in play simultaneously. And nowhere is this more evident than in that concentrated essence of things Dickensian, A Christmas Carol.

In Soulpepper's production, now on view for the third time, the joy is captured in its purest form when Joseph Zieglers magnificent Scrooge awakens from his dream to find that its still Christmas Day and that he has time to put his repentance into practice. He overflows with pleasure; as he addresses the "remarkable, intelligent boy" who has the good fortune to be standing underneath his window at the crucial moment, it's as if he's hugging himself and most of the human race and we, as its representatives, are returning the compliment. Zieglers ecstatic caperings in this scene are on a level with those of Alastair Sims sublime movie miser, and though he can't compete with the elongated and emaciated Sim in the matter of resembling a Victorian illustration come to life, he is a rather more believable businessman. This is a fleshy flinty Scrooge with years of life still before him, to be used for better or worse; so his reformation means something in human terms as well as mythical. His misanthropy is of course as extravagant as his later benevolence; Edgar Johnson, Dickens' biographer, pointed out that a man who suggests that any idiot with "Merry Christmas" on his lips should be laid to rest with a twig of holly through his heart, must have an active sense of humour thats bound to make him a soft touch for the spirits. Zieglers Scrooge puts up a good fight but caves early; from the moment he catches a glimpse of his own lonely schoolboy self, he's a goner. Looking on at the happiness he's missed out on, the wrong paths hes taken, this Ebenezer is very moved and very moving. Watch him, a spectral onlooker, joining in the dance at the Fezziwigs party, a moment of gratification that falls back into yearning. The character is inhibited, the actor is restrained; so the final release of both is overwhelming.

He's finely supported by other veterans of this show's previous outings: Oliver Dennis prince of Cratchits, John Jarvis as all four ghosts (Jacob Marley and the Christmas trio), Patrick Galligan as Scrooges nephew and a bevy of others. Jarvis sometimes thunders his warnings more than is necessary, and Galligan occasionally generalizes his messages of good cheer, but these are venial sins. Michael Shamata's adaptation remains ideal; it gets everything in, without strain. His production has changed somewhat; we have seen it before on a proscenium stage but now it's done in the round. This works well when Scrooge is being jostled, physically and emotionally, by the merrymakers on the streets of London -- we get a stereoscopic view of his isolation. Its less happy when those same citizens appear standing in a ring with a plan of the city pinned somewhere around their chests. Some scene changes, too, are cumbersome; the Fezziwig bash takes forever to get started, with surprisingly laboured performances from Kevin Bundy and Maggie Huculak as the founders of the feast. But the soul of the piece remains, more vibrant than ever. Dickens, as has often been pointed out, didnt exploit the Christmas spirit; he invented it. In every sense, he makes us feel good. And, as in previous years, a collection at the doors for the Daily Bread Food Bank allows us to put those feelings to some practical use. Which, in its way, is one of the best and most fitting ideas Soulpepper has ever had.

- Until Dec. 23. Call 416-866- 8666 for tickets.

2006-12-09-gotta-love-those-rockettes-ra:
The Rockettes, the pride of Radio City Music Hall in New York, have apparently been performing their Parade of the Wooden Soldiers routine for decades. It is indeed some kind of classic. The long line of massed high-kickers in their confectionery uniforms -- white pants slashed with red, black and yellow busbies topped by white feathers, scarlet tunics and with cheeks rouged to match -- give a good new name to military discipline as they wheel, form squares, subdivide and reunite, and at the number's climax face what seems to be their first experience of actual fire. They faint dead away, each one into the waiting arms of the next, toppling over like a brigade of dancing dominoes. It's entrancing.

Elsewhere in the Radio City Christmas Spectacular, now visiting Toronto for the first time in its 74-year existence, the Rockettes show off their tapping prowess in a treatment of the Twelve Days of Christmas that seems to change rhythm and tempo with each new chorus. Have you noticed that in most musicals, a simple kick-line invariably brings down the house? Nobody, though, cheers the Rockettes for doing it; we simply take their prowess for granted, which is one of the best things about them. They are also on hand for Carol of the Bells, a sleigh-ride sequence in which they are somewhat upstaged by the scenery, as glistening a piece of Hallmark art as you are likely to see blown up for the stage, and for Christmas in New York, a first-act finale to which their presence lends, barring the odd hint of skyscraper on the backcloth, the only element of authenticity. The program synopsis rightly insists that Christmas in Manhattan is different from Christmas anywhere else, but in this show it might as well be anywhere else. A big tree doesn't cut it. They have those all over.

This Spectacular, for those of us who have never caught it in its native habitat, is simultaneously like nothing, and like everything, you've ever seen. It is lavish, and if it doesn't seem imaginative now, you can tell that it must have been so once. It is, apart from the Rockettes, utterly generic. (All right, they're generic, too, but they define their genre.) Its spirit is that of every middle- of-the-road seasonal special you remember from your youth or have caught in reruns on PBS. It has, rather surprisingly, a sliver of continuity. This concerns Santa Claus, and how hard-worked he is at this time of year, and how much he loves it, and us, and being here.

Santa, it seems, loves Toronto like Barbra Streisand loved Toronto for the couple of days that she was among us. She, as you may have heard, sent her scouts out to learn thenames of local eateries so that she might charm us by dropping them. Santa's bonhomie is, as befits his vocational ubiquity, rather less specific. I still wonder why Santa, Barbra and most other entertainers feel they have to ingratiate themselves with us like that. Do they really think we're so starved for recognition? Why don't they just do what they do, and trust us to love them for that?

Anyway, John Paul Almon, the guy in this show's red suit, probably does the ho-hoing as well as anyone could, and it isn't his fault that I kept yearning for him to get stuck in some faraway chimney for the evening's duration. I felt even less indulgent toward Mrs. Claus (Bethe Austin), who always seems on the verge of really laying into her old man about his never being home for the holidays, but never quite gets around to it. (For a more acidulous approach to the same topic, see the Surabaya Santa number in Songs for a New World.) Still, when Santa serenades his Subordinate Claus with What Are You Doing New Year's Eve, the lyric does seem to have been made for them. I've always liked that song anyway. The show also makes a foredoomed attempt to be up-to-date -- up to what date I'm not quite sure -- with something called Santa's Gonna Rock and Roll, which I would describe, if this were not so charitable a season, as an abomination.

All gestures toward modernity are abandoned in the final scene, The Living Nativity, which has been on the bill since 1933 and which is, I imagine, much like the new movie on the subject, only shorter. It's also like every high-school Christmas pageant there ever was, except for its livestock. It features three real camels and as many sheep, the camels having considerably more personality. It's simple and presumably sincere, hewing to the received story with no revisionist doubts permitted. It has of course no place for the Rockettes (though the mind does start mulling the possibilities) or indeed for Santa, so all but the devout and the very traditionally minded are likely to find it an anticlimax. In tone it has nothing to do with the rest of the show; in attitude it has everything, proving that you can have your plum pudding and eat it, too.

There can be few shows further removed from Radio City than Head- Smashed- In Buffalo Jump, a collaboratively written piece by Un Spun Theatre. Four members are credited with co- creating and performing it; a fifth, Brendan Gall, with co- creating and directing. And there are two "additional" co- creators, a distinction that suggests all creators are created equal, but some are more equal than others.

In fact this show, too, is liable to break into the non- verbal. It starts with the four actors prowling the stage doubled up as if in the throes of severe stomach ache: the kind of prelude that has long given experimental theatre a bad name. It improves when it starts talking, but not enough. The opening must be meant to suggest alienation, and the action, which varies between the very simple and the maddeningly obscure, throws the feeling at us in handfuls. We are in Parkdale. There is Michelle ( Tricia Lahde), an agoraphobic young woman whom we meet hammering on the door of her superintendent, Dennis ( Chris Hanratty). He takes her into his apartment and as far as I could tell -- it isn't always clear whose room

we're in -- she takes possession of his bed, though without allowing him to share it with her. Dennis, lonely, is OK with this, though frustrated, and obtains a walkie-talkie set through which they can converse, or through which she can give him orders. She renames him Bear and herself Thea.

Thea conceives a plan for saving the world, or at least for doing something to it, and gets Bear to enlist the help of Andrea (Shira Leuchter), known to the media as "the Parkdale Angel" for having once stopped an old man from jumping out of his window. In fact, Andrea is not that angelic, is indeed one tough and maybe criminal cookie, and she certainly isn't as docile as poor old Bear. Nevertheless, she plays along.

The remaining character is Dusan (Christopher Stanton), proprietor of the pawn shop on the corner -- do you remember that old song? -- and who indeed does business with Andrea until she hasn't a thing left to hock. He is Czech and, as often seems to be the case with Central European men in Canadian plays, has a show- business past about which he utters reminiscent soliloquies. His accomplishments include playing the accordion ("is hard," he says reasonably, "to practise squeezebox in secret"), but his main talent, as so often in such cases, is for magic. He also talks about Canada, and about the images he had of our various cities before coming here. The last place on his list is the small Alberta town that had buffalo like other places are popularly supposed to have lemmings, and whose picturesque name gives the play its picturesque title. The implication, I guess, is that the characters also are so many doomed mammals. Or maybe not.

Anyway, having presented these people with varying levels of compellingness (Bear and Thea are the best conceived, though all the performances are OK), the show can't think of much to do with them. The story is attenuated, long-drawn-out and, especially at the end, confusing. It hardly makes a statement about Parkdale, let alone Toronto, let alone, in spite of Dusan's travelogue monologues, Canada.

The piece was a success on the fringe; blowing it up even to the size of the Young Centre's smallest space hasn't helped. "Co- creation" can produce good, even very good, work, but the odds are usually heavier than when you start with a script by a single playwright. When the actors write it themselves, they are likely to concentrate on what they feel good about performing, while letting context go by the board. And it's a sad fact, in theatre as in life, that group ideas are usually received ideas.

- Radio City Christmas Spectacular runs through Dec. 31 at the Hummingbird Centre, 416-872- 2262; Head-Smashed-In Buffalo Jump runs at the Young Centre through Dec. 16, 416-866-8666.

2006-12-16-can-t-get-away-from-christmas:
So I was eating a bowl of pasta in a downtown restaurant, pretty much blotting out the seasonal music that was oozing out of the speakers like aural spaghetti sauce, when a song that clearly wasn't Winter Wonderland or the one about chestnuts roasting on an open fire made its way through the miasma and pinned my attention. It was, I realized, a song I dimly recalled, titled The Man with the Bag-- Santa Claus, of course -- and sung, I was fairly sure, by Kay Starr. I hate not being sure of these things.

And then, half an hour later, I was sitting in the auditorium of the smallest space of the Harbourfront Centre, waiting for the start of The Stronger Variations presented by the movement-based group Theatre Rusticle, and expecting something stern and experimental. As the lights went down, the first thing we heard was another selection of pretty holiday music, starting with that very same Man with the Bag, and this time I was certain it was Kay Starr. Which was not only serendipitous but proved what turned out to be one of the production's central points; which is that, for better or worse, at this time of the year you cannot get away from commercialized Christmas spirit. You can't even escape it in an extended, and brilliantly executed, piece of movement-theatre based on a play by August Strindberg.

It's actually inherent in what Strindberg wrote, just begging to be used and embroidered. His one-act play The Stronger is a two- hander for a wife and a mistress. You can't call it a duologue because the wife does all the talking. It's Christmas Eve, she's been shopping and she drops into a cafe where she spies the woman whom she suspects, probably rightly, of sleeping with her husband. The song Guess Who I Saw Today? is not on this show's soundtrack, but you can imagine the wife returning home, greeting her spouse and giving that number's punchline a new twist by saying or singing "guess who I saw today? I saw her."

You might also say that the wife is following her shopping expedition with a fishing expedition. She talks about her home and family, commiserates with the other woman (or the Other Woman) on her singleness. And it's left to the audience to decide which of the two characters, the talker or the silent one, is actually "the stronger." It's notable, though, that star actresses have traditionally preferred to play the mistress, maybe not just because they didn't want to be bothered with learning lines.

Theatre Rusticle's adaptation, directed by Allyson McKinnon, started out on the Toronto fringe with three women -- Liza Balkan, Viv Moore, Lucy Rupert -- sharing and alternating the roles of wife and mistress. For this new and elongated version they are joined by three men -- Patrick Conner, Misha Albert, Matthew Romantini --playing husbands and lovers. The portions of text we hear (they're too substantial to be called fragments) seem to work equally well within and across gender lines.

The show begins with the sexy sextet, in a line as if on a moving platform, sidling and twisting on, in time with the happy music. They're dressed in time to it as well; in 1950s suburban happy gear, the men in casual black and white and the women sporting a lot of pink. They seem to have stepped out of the same scrubbed suburbia as the corps in the Radio City Christmas Spectacular, and the two shows in fact present rather similar world views with overlapping musical scores, except that the show at the Hummingbird offers it in all seriousness while this one up-ends it.

The same words, carefully lifted from the original, recur in duologue after duologue. Each gets started with a cheery reminiscence of an ill-omened wedding party at which bride and groom were plainly bored with one another before the marriage had even started. There are barbed condolences about loneliness

that cut both ways. Each shopper flourishes the gifts he or she has bought for the family; always it's a doll for the girl of the family ("It's for my daughter," says Wife No. 1, as if taking up position in a territorial dispute), a knife for the boy and a pair of slippers decorated with tulips for one's partner. Each of these props takes on a significance farcical or sinister or both. (One of the men screams that he's gone right off tulips.) The pattern doesn't stand quite as many variations as it gets, but it does stand up to most of them.

The performers move superbly, speak at least acceptably and even sing a bit, though most of the music, as noted, comes pre- performed. It isn't there, by the way, just to be mocked; it has its own presence, and even its own dignity. When the voice of Bing Crosby chimes

authoritatively in Count Your Blessings Instead of Sheep, it's impossible not to feel that he has a point, even if -- especially if -- it's one that the characters on stage would find it hard to appreciate. When the three guys glide to the Christmas Waltz, there is a kind of impossible grace to it, however mordant the context. And What Are You Doing New Year's Eve? -- which works cleverly in the Radio City show as a solicitous duet for Mr. and Mrs. Santa Claus -- works even better here as a bittersweet sword to be flourished over the head of someone who'll be spending it alone. (The record they've chosen, by Nancy Wilson, is especially good.) Altogether this is a rich show, it may be worth repeat visits. It could become an annual anti-Christmas staple.

Tony Nardi is an actor best known to Toronto theatre audiences for his work with Soulpepper, for whom he gave notable performances in A Flea in Her Ear, The Winter's Tale, Miss Julie (Strindberg again) and The Lesson. He is also in great demand on television, often for playing Italians, or anyway Italian- Canadians. His dissatisfaction with the ethnic stereotyping to which he has found himself subject, occasioned the first of his Two Letters, extended solo rants (that's a description, not a judgment) that he has been performing in various spots around town over the past month or two. I saw and heard the second Letter, which is focused more on theatre than on TV, and which arose from a long letter he sent some Toronto

theatre critics after a production -- in which he did not appear - - of a Goldoni play he felt both they and the director had misunderstood, largely because of their shared ignorance of the Italian commedia tradition from which it sprung.

It --Nardi's performance, not the Goldoni production -- was quite the firework display. There was plenty in it with which to quibble. It went, in its earlier stages, much too fast, as if the actor were nervous of holding the audience's attention with a script he'd written himself. It kept referring back to friends and advisors -- "ghosts" he called them -- who had obviously figured prominently in the first letter, but who remained a mystery to me. It kept going off on tangents; some of these were explosively enjoyable but at others I found myself putting my attention on hold, trusting it would turn itself back on when Tony returned to his main point. (It did.)

The point itself seemed to amount to a fairly standard actors' complaint to the effect that most directors are not to be trusted, and should not be allowed to come between the actors and the play. This is true, and some of Nardi's recreations of the despairing anecdotes with which actors regale one another are hilarious, but it remained unclear exactly what he intended to do about it. Nor am I sure that he did wisely to pin his whole argument on one production, or that he was correct to speak consistently of "Goldoni" and " commedia dell'arte" as if they were synonymous.

I raised this last point at a question- and-answer section after the show. He continued to disagree, and I confess that he convinced me he knew more about both subjects than I did. In fact, he'd already proved it, not by telling but by showing. The final section of his Letter was a kind of dream sequence in which a teacher of commedia went on trial. Nardi jumped between judge, defendant and other participants, bringing stock characters to dizzying life at a pace that now seemed the product of inspiration rather than panic. It was planned and written, but it had the manic flavour of improvisation. I think it was commedia; it was certainly virtuoso. If he wants to help our theatre and himself -- well, as that other commedia descendant Mr. Punch used to say -- that's the way to do it.

- The Stronger Variations ends tonight at the Studio Theatre, Harbourfront Centre, 416-973- 4000. Two Letters is being performed for the benefit of the Actors' Fund on Dec. 19 and 20 at the Factory Theatre Rehearsal Hall (3rd floor), 416-504-9971.
