2006-12-23-frank-sinatra-is-total-theatr:
Duke Ellington once described Frank Sinatra as "total theatre. The truth of that is apparent in the new box set Sinatra Vegas (Reprise, $94.99), four CDs and a DVD of live performances at an assortment of desert hot spots between 1961 and 1987. I don't know if it's true to say that Sinatra was better" in front of an audience than he was in a recording studio; theres a level of perfectionism on his best records that was obviously unattainable when he was winging it. Nor did he necessarily inhabit songs -- the thing he did better than anyone else -- more completely when he was playing to a crowd. The truth is perhaps the other way around. The inwardness that distinguishes his studio ballad performances is recreated -- immediately, at the drop of a downbeat -- in the middle of what would normally be a clattery, rowdy room. Studio Sinatra is already intense drama; add visuals and live response, and you do indeed have theatre, exhibited within each song in purest, concentrated form.

You have that theatrical essential, contrast: not only between numbers but within them. Sinatra, increasingly, it seems, as he got older, breaks down the traditional saloon singers distinction between "ballads and swingers." The first song on the DVD (a performance at Caesars Palace in 1978) starts, conventionally enough, with All of Me, an up-tempo song he had recorded back in 1954, and that he continued to sing in the same Nelson Riddle arrangement. (Part of the interest in these discs is in noting how many songs that Sinatra never revisited in the studio nonetheless continued to slip in and out of his club and concert repertoire. One wonders how, with so much to choose from, he went about selecting them.) Just hearing him break, apparently out of nowhere, into that curt percussive opening phrase -- "All of me -- is exhilarating enough. Then you notice that on the second line -- can't you see I'm no good without you" -- though the pace remains the same, the tone has changed; its now sensitive going on vulnerable, a transition thats consummated by the time he gets to "your goodbye left me with eyes that cry near the end of the song. A plain, even maudlin lyric is not so much transformed as redeemed; the feelings behind it are laid bare but never lingered over; the overall mood remains driving and slangy.

The contrasts within the song mirror in microcosm the conflicts within the performer, between the impeccable singer and the extremely peccable talker. If, as a singer, Sinatra is a great actor, as a comedian and raconteur he's somewhere between mediocre and crass. His monologues here mainly consist of heavy-handed name- dropping, and to a passing but obviously heartfelt tribute to the great songwriters: I wonder what we would have done without Rodgers and Hart?"

Not much, apparently. These discs are loaded with R&H songs, including the perennial Lady Is a Tramp, a number that seems to be one of everybody's Sinatra favourites except mine. This is one song on which I find him too self- aggrandizingly flip, too out of touch with the original. Again, though, the DVD has the best of it; this time, when he changes the lyric to "thats why this chick is a champ, he injects some affection into the swagger. And when he gets to the really tender songs, the effect, visual as well as aural, can be extraordinary. George Harrisons Something is a song about not being able to find words; hence its instrumental bridge. When Sinatra sings it here, elaborating on what was already a majestic performance on record, his hands perform a fierce ballet of frustration while his voice crests. There's something in the way she moves but he can't describe it, and though that only makes him love her more, hes taking a beating from the struggle to articulate it.

Theres more than a hint of anger, one that surfaces again in his remarkable piano-accompanied performance of Send in the Clowns, anger turned inward: Losing my timing this late in my career." Some chance. Physically he seems, at the age of 68, in very good shape. The voice, by this date, is grainy and craggy, a weathered effect that, for the most part, he knows exactly how to exploit. And yet it can sometimes shed decades, as in Someone to Watch over Me, with its magically ingenuous verse. Every time, as soon as the music starts, the crudity of the Sinatra image falls away, and though we certainly remain aware of the man and his legend, he himself seems concerned only with the song.

His commitment to the individual value of each number may explain why he sang so few medleys: only two that I'm aware of in the whole of his recorded works. One of them turns up here, and it's a splicing together of two long existing Riddle arrangements: songs from disparate sources that fit together with seamless narrative logic. The Gal that Got Away -- the Judy Garland classic, sounding, with its gender reversed and its dynamics reduced, even more lost and harrowing than when she sang it -- is interrupted halfway through by a persuasive backstory in the form of It Never Entered My Mind: Rodgers and Hart again, and their masterpiece. Sinatras sensitivity on this date even extends to the inevitable My Way. "I hate this song, he mutters as he goes into it, a statement that cheered me enormously. He then proceeds to prove us both wrong, at least temporarily, by phrasing the thing with amazing subtlety. He actually understates it; bombast is left until the final stanza, and even then most of it is left to the orchestra.

Ive dwelt on the DVD because there is -- officially, at least -- very little visual evidence available of Sinatra in performance. The four CDs, though, all have their share of revelations. The several tunes that recur from one disc to another show Sinatra's claim never to have sung a song the same way twice to be true. Disc 1 (The Sands, 1961) gives us the singer in his absolute Kennedy-era prime, about a year into running his own record company. There are joyous versions of two numbers from his band- singing days with Tommy Dorsey: The One I Love Belongs to Somebody Else and Without a Song, the latter another example of his doing the lyricists a favour by uncovering the emotion, a kind of awed happiness, in whose direction they were rather vaguely pointing. It also includes Just One of Those Things, reclaimed for heartbreak; Billy May's uproarious arrangement of On the Road to Mandalay; Moonlight in Vermont, with some phrasing thats daring in concept and prodigious in execution; and You Make Me Feel so Young, which, when he sings it, is my favourite song.

Disc 2 (The Sands, 1966) is a kind of trial run for the canonical Sinatra at the Sands album. Hes with the same great band, Count Basie's, doing almost exactly the same program; One for My Baby has gone missing, and indeed is absent from the entire box, even though it's generally and justly regarded as the quintessential Sinatra saloon song, and therefore the quintessential Sinatra live performance. That apart, snobs of the alternate take, of which the disc is one long example, will seize on it and pronounce it superior to the authorized version: rightly, I think. A bonus track has Sinatra talking about working with Basie: It was like a juggernaut. When the orchestra started and it came at you, you knew you had to be part of that or you got lost. I tried to stay in the realm of what the orchestra was playing I hung back just a little bit, I guess thats the way to say it." Sinatra talking about his own music is always illuminating; a shame he did it so seldom.

Disc 3 (Caesars Palace, 1982) brings a band without strings, and rethought versions of some Sinatra standbys: I Cant Get Started, in which he manages to sound quizzical, world-weary and heartsore all in one line, and Night and Day sung to quintet arrangement with, one imagines, furrowed brow and certainly with furrowed voice. Yearning is what he does best; more and more in these performances, the ageing Sinatra seems to be singing about the unattainable. His voice goes astray on some long notes at the end of These Foolish Things, and it doesn't matter.

Disc 4 (The Golden Nugget, 1987) begins with I've Got the World on a String, the trumpet intro to Riddles 1953 arrangement still unmistakable, and takes in yet more R&H; a deep, fragile Spring Is Here, and My Heart Stood Still with a big climax that he takes full-throatedly, though admittedly its the orchestra that does the heaviest lifting. There's also Hoagy Carmichael's I Get Along without You Very Well, whose haunted first line should give you goosebumps and which he typically introduces as "a song about a big liar."

Much in the Vegas ethos and Sinatra's embracing of it, such as his stated distrust of people who didn't drink, sticks in the craw now. (It did then.) But when he sings, he transforms it and himself. There have been many fine popular singers but no other who has operated at, or maybe even aspired to, this level as an artist.

Cinderella in Muddy York

Tarragon Extra Space

The brother-and-sister team of Ann and David Powell, known as Puppet mongers, has been presenting Cinderella in Muddy York, for audiences aged five and up, since 1990. They and their mostly stringless dolls retell the old story by setting it in 1834, the year the town of York changed its name to Toronto. The heroine is now the daughter of an absentee father whose second wife has come over from England -- with her own two daughters, of course -- and who proceeds to take her disenchantment with Upper Canada out on poor Ella, whose cinder-grey dress inspires her familiar sobriquet.

This is more motivation than the trio of intruding harpies customarily gets, and indeed the domestic relations in this 50- minute production are sketched both more subtly and more fully than is customary in your average family spectacular. This Stepmother doesn't know shes being cruel; she merely suffers from a severe case of entitlement. She calls Cinderella "dear in sweetly reasonable tones even while ordering her to prepare cups of herbal tea that will be sympathetic to her allergies. As for Cinders step- siblings, the show is far too modern to call them the Ugly Sisters but it's still hard to think of them any other way. They are named Zelda and Imelda; one of them looks like Miss Piggy and the other has a figure like a tent-pole and a face like a hatchet. They are allowed a measure of farcical poignance when they go galumphing at the ball. When they get to try on the Slipper of Destiny, one of them has a foot that's too big to fit, the other has a foot thats too small.

The ball is thrown to celebrate the citys re-branding, and the guest list includes an array of starchy couples destined to donate their names to major thoroughfares. (Mr. and Mrs. Henry Eglinton Mr. and Mrs. Donald Valley"). The celebration is also a chance for the Lieutenant Governor of Ontario to marry off his son, a shy and studious young fellow named Mr. Charming Prince. As in the original story, the ball is a three-night affair, and it's only at the last midnight that the heroine almost forgets to leave. As in no other version that I know, she says -- while leaving the room and shedding her shoe -- what her name is. This is very practical of her, but it leaves young Charming looking distinctly twittish. Armed with this vital information, why doesn't he just send a flunkey from door to muddy door asking for a young lady by the name of Ella? They could always fall back on the footwear routine in the event of contesting claims.

This particular Ella shows traces of post-Beauty and the Beast Disney feminism; she wonders why she cant be a doctor or lawyer and she has premonitory doubts about the idea of getting married. When Mr. Prince pops the question, however, she accepts immediately. The show, directed by Sue Miner, is sweet but skimpy. The Canadian historical setting is about the limit of the scripts inventiveness. As for staging, the Powells bring off one pocket-sized coup in the transformation of pumpkin into coach. They manipulate their puppets in full view of the audience, and also share the stage with them in narrating and even in acting roles. They are unlikely to give Ronnie Burkett any sleepless nights, whether in point of technical wizardry, richness of detail or intensity of performance. Ann's stage-presence is modest, in both the good and bad senses; David's is plain overbearing. They take bows at the end of the show. The puppets don't.

- Cinderella at Muddy York runs until Jan. 1 at the Tarragon Theatre. 416-531-1827

I may never have properly grasped the meaning of the word "thorough" until I read George Gershwin: His Life and Work by Howard Pollack (University of California Press). This 900-page volume takes its subtitle both very literally and very logically. Most life-and-work books take the two components in tandem. This one segregates them. The life gets the books first part, which is long, and the work gets the second, which is longer.

Each part is, of course, further subdivided. The biographical section proceeds by topic, starting with Gershwin and his Family. But of course George, though childless, had a family -- the most artistically significant being his elder brother and prime lyricist, Ira -- throughout his too-brief life, so he dies at the end of the first chapter. He dies again at the climax of other chapters concerned with his friends, his personality, his relation to the music of his time (popular, concert, theatre and jazz) and his own compositional studies. These last, Pollack, fighting the myth of his subject as an "untutored genius" who preferred to remain untutored, reveals to have been far more wide ranging and persistent than has usually been suspected.

Gershwin was writing for Broadway (including one full score) before he was out of his teens. He hit his stride as a successful commercial songwriter in 1919 when, at the age of 21, he wrote Swanee, which in hit single terms -- sheet music then, of course, rather than record sales -- remained the biggest smash he ever had. Five years after that, he made his debut as a concert-hall composer with Rhapsody in Blue, another Greatest Hit. He had already composed his first opera, a one-act piece titled Blue Monday, which had been inserted in (and speedily removed from) a Broadway revue. When the Rhapsody was unveiled in 1924, Gershwin's best musical-comedy work still lay ahead, though only by a few months: Lady Be Good, starring Fred and Adele Astaire and bringing a new Jazz Age pulse and wit to the American stage, premiered at the end of that same year. He went on alternating concert with light- theatre work, though statistically the latter predominated by a wide margin.

So he confused people, though not, it appears, himself; he never seems to have regarded one kind of musical form as intrinsically superior to another, or to have thought of any assignment as being a diversion from his natural path. He knew his own talent, but he wasn't boastful, merely confident. He seems to have charmed most who knew him and everyone who worked with him. Pollack argues that musical and critical opinion about Gershwin has always split along popular and "classical" lines, but not in the way you might expect. Classicists, suspicious of Gershwins philharmonic ambitions and skeptical about his structural skills, have always claimed to prefer the show tunes. Populists have been tickled pink that one of their own should have made the crossover, and may even have felt shamefaced about holding him back. Exhibit A here is the 1945 biopic, significantly titled Rhapsody in Blue, which strongly suggests that George broke the heart of his old music teacher -- an imaginary character -- by his continual backsliding into writing pop songs.

Pollack debunks some small but persistent Gershwinian myths. Countless books and articles, attempting to convict Porgy and Bess of racism, have quoted Duke Ellingtons objections to Gershwin's lamp-black Negroisms. This has always seemed to me to sit oddly with Ellington's personal and professional admiration for Gershwin (the feelings were mutual), and, it now turns out, the Duke never said it. The phrase was written by a theatrical journalist with an ideological axe to grind who appended it, along with a few other comments of his own, to an interview with Ellington. Ellington was upset, and tried to get the record changed, but the words stuck.

John OHara, on the other hand, did say, "George died on July 11, 1937, but I dont have to believe it if I don't want to." It doesn't mean, though, that he had lost a friend; OHara, we learn, was one of the few who disliked Gershwin the man. That, though, may make his words all the more moving. For nearly all who heard it, Gershwins music epitomized his time and his place, so when he died, at the age of 38, both friends and strangers felt that America had lost its voice. The early death contributed, of course, to the legend; it cemented the golden-boy status, making Gershwin seem like the Gatsby of composers. And it still hurts: I remember as a child, decades after the event, listening to a radio show about him and my incredulity at discovering that the man who had composed all those wonderful songs had died so young O'Hara's words, quoted at the very end of the program, seemed to me exactly right.

Having dealt with the life by category, Pollack, a professor at the University of Houston and an all round music man, like his subject, proceeds through the work in strict chronology. A fiend for detail, he gives you all the facts about all the music; who produced, conducted or performed it, who replaced whom on tour, what luminaries were in the first-night audience, what the reviewers said. He makes a good analytic case for all the concert music. He makes me want to listen again to An American in Paris, which I have always thought of as movie music before the fact. When it comes to the musicals, he provides detailed synopses of the plots, and where the songs fit into them He admits in a preface that these

Its easy to see why. Most of these shows were farces, and its hard to keep the plot of a farce in your head when you're not actually watching it. And they all seem to have the same plot, involving mistaken identities and the temporary separation of Boy and Girl by rich and snobbish parents. All the same, it's worth persevering. Its received wisdom that the songs are only loosely anchored to their texts, and can easily be moved from one spot to another, or even from one show to another. Pollack proves this wrong. Some of the songs, the ones we dont know, are quite specific plot songs, and even the famous ones have reasons for being where they are. In Lady Be Good, the title song -- which isn't a love song, more a conspiracy song -- serves a vital narrative function, and a witty one, while Fascinating Rhythm is an anthem to syncopation that has no place in the story but comes along just when the show needs to explode.

It's become the fashion to reassemble these shows and their scores into new products, as in the Broadway successes My One and Only and Crazy for You. (The former is being staged this year at the Shaw Festival.) In narrative terms, though, neither of these shows makes any more sense than did the originals; in fact, they make less. To judge from the book of Girl Crazy, the Gershwin show with the greatest concentration of standard songs, the main fault with these old libretti is not inconsequentiality but longwindedness; they run their jokes into the ground. They need streamlining rather than radical alteration.

And on a related note: Hearing these scores with their original orchestrations, or informed reconstructions when the originals have been lost, is like hearing them for the first time. Check out the Roxbury series of recordings (on the Nonesuch and New World labels) and be scintillated. Some Golden Age composers, Richard Rodgers or Harold Arlen, may have written finer autonomous melodies, but none has had Gershwins focused theatrical energy. Pollack even makes a persuasive case for a couple of semi- operettas, Rosalie and Song of the Flame, to which no one else has paid attention in decades.

Better known are the political comic operas: Strike Up the Band, Of Thee I Sing, Let Em Eat Cake. These are exercises in the whimsical- satirical, and are recurringly topical, though it's possible that they seem harder-hitting when described than when actually staged.

Of Thee I Sing seems to demand revival every time there's a presidential election (it starts with a parade of voters brandishing such placards as Vote for Prosperity and See What You Get), but the one Id most like to see now is Strike Up the Band, which demands it on a more permanent basis: i.e., every time theres a war. This show exists in two versions. In the first, which closed out of town in 1927, the United States, at a tycoon's behest, goes to war -- with Switzerland -- to make the world safe for cheese; in the second, a hit in 1930, it embarks on a similar conflict over chocolate. I guess that means they sweetened it. Pollack challenges the received opinion that they also softened and weakened it. He may be right; the revised version certainly has the stronger score, augmented as it is by I've Got a Crush on You and Soon and a rip-roaring showstopper titled Mademoiselle from New Rochelle. There must be a way of amalgamating the best of this shows textual and musical worlds.

Even a writer as conscientious and comprehensive as Pollack has to skimp on something. In his case its the individual songs. Some he examines in detail, throwing in exhaustive lists of artists who have recorded them. Many others, including my own personal favourite, They Can't Take That Away from Me, he merely acknowledges as existing. Nor is he always the most enlivening writer. (He has a habit of saying "for his part" or for her, their, or its part whenever he wishes to switch attention from one person, group or thing to another. For my part, I wish he wouldn't.)

He catches fire, though, when he comes to deal with Porgy and Bess, the summit of Gershwins achievement, the work to which everything else leads, though not necessarily directly: "The opera essentially sounds like nothing else, not even, as sometimes claimed, Gershwins own musical comedies."

For all that, it's an opera made, quite legitimately, out of show music, which I think accounts for Pollack's conviction that its sheer verve makes many other operas sound tepid in comparison. We take for granted that Pollack loves Gershwin-- why else would he have bothered? -- but this is the only place where his enthusiasm shines through his prose: "Gershwin's superb abilities as a musical dramatist, including terrific handling of elaborate ensembles shows its author to be deeply humane in his sensitive understanding of the weakness and resilience, the haplessness and dignity, of an oppressed but tight-knit group. Better than anything else he ever wrote, the work reveals Gershwin as not only a brilliant artist, but a great and complex one."

He did write more. He spent the two years left to him in Hollywood, where he wrote three movie scores (two of them for Astaire) that show him at his highest power as a songsmith. Literally all the songs are winners, and most of them are classics. Then he died of a brain tumour. Ira, who lived another half century, never got over it; that was his tragedy. American music never got over it, either. And that has been part -- a large part -- of its glory.

2007-01-09-from-italy-with-a-valentine:
ORPHEUS DESCENDING

Royal Alexandra Theatre, Toronto

- - -

Seana McKenna, playing Lady Torrance in Tennessee Williams Orpheus Descending, begins as a hard-bitten retailer who is not about to take any guff from anyone. Lady is the daughter of an Italian immigrant -- at various times she refers to him and herself as "wops and dagoes" -- who settled in a small town in the deepest South and ran a winery there; that is, until he and it were set on fire by longer standing residents who objected to the proprietor's selling drinks to black people. Lady subsequently married, or as she tells it was bought by, Jabe Torrance, a much older merchant whom she hates and who has now fallen gravely ill, leaving her to mind the store. Also in Lady's past are a rich younger lover and a miscarried child. She is, when we first meet her, one angry, bitter and sarcastic Lady.

Into town, into the store and into her life comes Val Xavier, a glamorous young vagrant of 30, who might be the Williams dream male personified. Hes a reformed stud; he wears a snakeskin jacket thats his most treasured possession save only for his guitar, which carries autographs of idols from Leadbelly to Satchmo; and he claims, among other picturesque things, that his temperature is always a couple of degrees above normal, "same as a dog's. He also claims an impressive track record in warming up women. Lady, who could use some warming, eyes him at first with sardonic distrust, an emotion that McKenna communicates superbly.

In fact, she does everything superbly. Hers is as complete a performance as ever I have seen in Toronto, distinguished by the way it blends wit with passion. She lives each moment with full-blooded intensity, and links each to the next with flawless logic. She melts to Val of course, as he to her, but her knife-edge never dulls. The play's climax takes her on a rattletrap progress from vengeance to triumph to tragedy, and her end, after she has been so fully alive, could hardly hurt more. Its impossible while watching her to imagine the part played by anybody else. The contact between her and Jonathan Goads Val, especially in their first long scene of approach and avoidance, is exemplary in its tautness and variety.

Miles Potter's production, announced in the program as based on the 2005 Stratford Festival production," is that same terrific staging with a re-angled set and a handful of cast changes. Peter Hartwell has straightened out the bar counter that dominated his set on the platform stage of the Tom Patterson, from horseshoe to horizontal. We lose some surprise entrances but, surprisingly in a larger theatre, we gain concentration; and the counter now makes an even more effective platform for Val's humiliation at the hands of the local yokels. Goads performance, always good, is now even better. Val is probably a harder role than Lady -- shes a person with a documented history, he's an ideal whose past is kept determinedly cloudy -- but Goad earths him with unassuming self- confidence. (Critics love to be oxymoronic, but this time it fits.)

As at Stratford, I kept changing my mind about the play itself, thinking it at one moment Williams' masterpiece, and at the next a supreme act of unwitting self-parody. Potter admits in his program note, "its not clean, its not neat, it doesn't tie up, but says that's its glory. In fact, though, his triumph has been to take a piece that doesnt make logical sense and to treat it as if, at least moment by moment, it does. Hence it also makes emotional sense; more than a slapdash, self consciously bold" production could hope to do. This is an ensemble show with all the connecting lines in place. Disconnected parts of the Orpheus myth -- his musicianship, his descent into a Hell here identified with darkest Dixie, his final immolation -- are scrambled together and fastened onto Val, who is less a characterization than a collage. It may also have too many characters, or at least too many given intriguing traits that arent developed. The most persistent and alluring is Carol, the county tramp who sees Val as a kindred lost, or freed, soul; she's given an electrically bedraggled performance by Dana Green. But all the actors seize their chances. Michelle Fisk and Brigit Wilson are delightfully censorious as the town biddies who complain in their turn of other citizens indulging in "hypocriticism -- another thread that's left undeveloped. Catherine Fitch is haunting as the sheriff s wife, who paints visionary pictures while going progressively blind, and Thom Marriott powerfully impassive as her husband who claims, ambiguously, to hate violence. Walter Borden irrupts periodically as the painted-faced Uncle Pleasant with his Choctaw call" that serves as both Vals fanfare and his epitaph, and David Francis, with monstrously protruding eyebrows, conveys all the hatred festering in the dying Jabe, though not all the murderous power -- though this is the one point at which the production itself falters. Costumes, music, lighting and sound are all ideal. This is as close to a definitive performance as we will see, anywhere. Grab it.

- Until Feb. 11. For tickets call 416-872- 1212.

2007-01-10-every-jack-needs-his-chloe-se:
To prepare for the new season of 24 beginning this Sunday, we're spending the week reviewing Jack Bauer's exploits to date. Today, how Mr. Bauer measures up to other secret agents.

- - -

Mary Lynn Rajskub doesn't think Chloe O'Brian should ever die. She says so in a 24 fan magazine. She's biased, of course, since she plays Chloe, but most followers of the show would agree with her. She's the first funny character the show has had since George Mason, in the second season, forestalled a death from plutonium poisoning by crashing an airplane into the desert for the public good. George was a wisecracker, and the closer he got to his end the wittier he became. Chloe's humour is the opposite, and maybe more durable; earnest and tactless and incredibly good at her job, she doesn't know she's funny. There are, I know, some Chloe-haters out there who don't get the joke either, but the rest of us have found her increasingly delightful and surprisingly sexy. I can forgive the show for killing off George, Tony, Michelle and even Edgar (though it's hard); like its hero, Jack Bauer, it has to keep up a reputation for ruthlessness. But I would never forgive it if anything happened to Chloe.

Compared to its Fox stablemate Prison Break, 24 has been short on memorable characters, but Chloe has entered into the culture: if not witty in herself then the cause of wit in others, even in other fictional stories. There's a character in Little Miss Sunshine, identified in the credits as Pageant Assistant Pam, who has to marshal the beauty contestants in the movie's last frantic section. We don't get a clear look at her to begin with, but then someone gives her an order on her walkie-talkie and she snaps back "copy!" And just as we're thinking how much that word and that voice remind us of Chloe, she comes into full view and it is Chloe. Or at least it's Rajskub, an accomplished comedienne even when not playing Chloe or --as in this case--knowingly ripping off Chloe.

Anyway, Chloe cant die because she's Jack's love interest. I realize that this on past evidence is not something a lady would advertise when buying life insurance, but maybe I phrased it the wrong way around. Jack is her love interest, even if she doesn't fully realize it; at all events she hero-worships him ("don't worry," she remarked insouciantly last season while watching him take out the opposition, "he's good at this") and will do anything for him. This is just as well because he's always asking her to do things for him, some of them dangerous and most of them borderline illegal. They're a team, even if they're rarely together, what with her being mostly in the CTU office and him out in the field. She makes him possible; it's her prowess at the computer (she carries geekiness to the point of genius) that allows him to make full use of his toys. As good as he is with old stuff like guns, Jack's real weapon is the multitasking cellphone.

And either he has a better model than anybody else or he's more resourceful at using it.

Here he joins hands with a long line of action heroes. They've all combined their native strengths with the fanciest hardware. Beowulf went out to fight the monster Grendel equipped with the latest thing in axes. Achilles started with the unfair advantage of being invulnerable (save his heel) but his thoughtful mother still had him fitted out with a new suit of armour before he went to smite the Trojans. The 20th century cheapened the tradition by equipping its superheroes with superpowers -- which, cheating still more, they had to change identities to wield. But the old ways made something of a comeback with James Bond, who started his later cinematic adventures by picking up gadgets from John Cleese. (A dubious source, I'd say.)

The Bond of the new Casino Royale seems to have been influenced by Bauer. He's less suave than in his previous incarnations; he even declares, admittedly at a moment of exceptional weariness, that he doesn't care whether his Martini is shaken or stirred. Bauer of course is notorious for never tasting a drop or taking a bite during any of his day-long vigils. More crucially, the new James breaks the rules, infuriating his long-suffering superiors in the way that Jack has been doing since hour one of Day One.

Bond still hasn't taken on Bauer's weltschmerz; he actually had premonitory traces of it in Casino Royale the book, but his author dropped the idea thereafter. Jack does have doubts, mainly stemming from the death of his wife at the end of Season 1. However well Kiefer Sutherland plays him, though, it's never been possible to take them seriously; they're just gestures. I see from that same 24 fanzine (honest, boss, my kids brought it into the house, I just happened to peek at it) that we'll be meeting Jack's father, regrettably not played by Donald Sutherland, even though Jack himself has always seemed like one of nature's orphans. Here 24 seems in its turn to be taking a leaf from Prison Break, whose brother-protagonists suddenly acquired a dad, and as suddenly lost him.

I see too that the late President Palmer's brother will now, in a sort of alternate-universe tribute to Bobby Kennedy, have succeeded him in the White House. Wayne Palmer was always a more corruptible figure than his saintly sibling, so he may also be more fun. David Palmer was always a boring character, and in the first season, he seemed to come not only from a different plot but from a different script. And when the two did finally meet up at CTU it was unfortunate, if I may quote a young lady of my acquaintance, that the president brought his dialogue over with him. I don't suppose there's much chance we'll see any more of the disgraced President Logan or, sadly, of his feisty disillusioned wife, a role in which Jean Smart set the bar for acting higher than it's ever been raised in this show before. I wonder if she ever shacked up with Aaron, the White House security man, whom she plainly adored and to whom she came a lot closer than Chloe ever has to Jack. I hope at least that he comes back, if only for sentimental reasons. Did you know that -- apart from Jack, Palmer (deceased) and Tony (ditto) -- he's the only character to have figured in every season to date? Solid and hulking, his immovable earpiece standing out in stark relief from his hairless dome, he has progressed over five years from virtual walk-on to untrumpeted hero. I don't recall ever seeing an interview with Glenn Morshower, who plays him, but I'll bet he doesn't think Aaron, who's had some near-misses, should ever die. Even if he does, I don't.

- Tomorrow, watching in real time.

Hows this for a sample of realistic telephone conversation? It's drawn from Wendy Lill's new play, Chimera.

FIRST MAN: Youre not serious. This is a joke, right? Where did you hear this?

SECOND MAN: I heard it from my son-in-laws best friend. He grew up in White Cloud.

FIRST MAN: Your son-in-law's best friend? Grew up in White Cloud? Unbelievable.

Unbelievable is right. We don't, in the play itself, actually hear Second Mans contribution to the exchange, and phone chats in which only one of the participants is audible are notoriously hard to dramatize. One character always ends up repeating, for the audiences benefit, what the other has just told him. All the same, this specimen is quite exceptionally clunky. The clunkiness is unfortunately typical of the way in which the people in Chimera talk to each another, even when they're both in the same room with only a desk or table between them. Which is the unexciting formation in which these characters, in various combinations, find themselves for far toomuch of the evening.

The play is one of those in which the author takes an Issue, and dumps a collection of representative types on stage to deal with it. In this case the topic is stem-cell research, or a particularly contentious subset of it: the possible emergence, sometime in the future, of a crossbreed of human and animal, named after the mongrel monster of Greek mythology known as the Chimera. What may be setting off this possibility is the implanting, for medical research purposes, of embryonic human cells into the brains of rhesus monkeys. The author's method of humanizing her characters is to endow each of them with a few hand-me-down hang-ups to be dragged out at convenient moments. This has the unlooked-for effect of short circuiting the debate and preventing the ethical questions from being properly aired. Discussion may not be the highest form of drama (Shaw, with whom its generally identified, was less a dialectician than a crazy comedian in whiskers) but it is preferable to soap opera.

Lill is helpfully frank about her own method. She has one of her creations, a lobbyist who at first seems irrelevant but is later revealed as the plays evil genius, outline his strategy: "First, one assembles a cast of characters. The inexperienced cabinet minister, the fundamentalist MP and we mustn't forget the muckraking reporter trying to get back in the game." (That we mustn't forget is sinister cardboard-villain talk at its most outrageous.)Well, then. The inexperienced minister is saddled with the Justice portfolio, and, though all in favour of progress, shes faced by a confusion in the law over whether it might be permissible for monkey cells to be imported into humans as well as vice versa. The fundamentalist member (for White Cloud -- "Alberta" as he has to keep explaining), who sits opposite her, spearheads the Unfair to Apes and Unclean for Humans campaign and amasses a lot of popular support until he gets up in the House and a) is outed as a former geography teacher who taught his pupils creationism; and b) starts quoting from that fine old anthem Who Put the Bop (In the Bop-She- Bop-She-Bop), which on his lips sounds ridiculous. The muckraking scribe attracts the hostility of everyone in the play, which suggests hes doing his job right, and seems intended as the play's protagonist without having been properly groomed for the position.

He forms something of a bond with the scientist conducting the actual research, a septuagenarian lady from the North of England, who believes that she may be on the way to finding a cure for autism. This seems to me an unanswerable argument, but nobody else in the play ever engages with it. This, I suppose, is true to life, or at least to life as presented on talk shows where people keep pushing their own line without taking any notice of anyone else's. One feels like shouting, as off-stage voices in this plays parliamentary scenes constantly do, Answer the question. Of course nobody ever does, in the real world or on stage, but on stage, especially in what purports to be a play of ideas, is one place where one would like them to try.

The playwright, herself a former NDP MP, has decent impulses. She extends sympathy to most of her characters, including the rightwing Christian with whom she can have little politically -- though maybe something philosophically -- in common. She also builds up a reasonable head of narrative steam by the end of her first act. But it goes off the boil, done in by flaccid dialogue and by-the- numbers construction. This is another of those plays, assembled in short fidgety scenes, that leave you feeling that their subjects would be better treated on television. The writing probably wouldnt be any better, but the production values might lend an air of documentary urgency. And maybe it would be better in the theatre to approach such a subject as documentary rather than to invent a Chimerical case and try to pump feeling into it

Presumably by way of reflecting the genetic theme, all the characters have personal issues about the issue. The scientist is estranged from her son, an actor. The childless minister, putting her career first, once had an abortion and wonders if she did the right thing. Her aide squabbles with his wife about daycare and ear infections. Even the lobbyist flashes pictures of his grandchildren. And the journalist, himself a childhood friend of the minister's, had a twin brother afflicted with Down's syndrome and carries a load of guilt about how he behaved to him. This gives him a repentant curtain line thats meant to touch the heart but comes across like perfect kitsch.

Mary Vingoes staging switches from one conversation to another, and from one side of the stage to the other, in a manner that seems trudging and even grudging. Nor does her direction do much to help the performers who are left trying to put a brave face on material in which they seem to find it hard to believe. That at least was the impression left on Tuesday when actors one knows to be good were continually fumbling (not forgetting) their lines, which is generally a sign of underlying discomfort. In fact, the one who did best was the only one new to me, Joan Gregson, whose tart accent helps her authenticity no end. David Fox as the Bible-thumper imposes himself, as he usually does, through force of personality (by the way, I've yet to read a review of Snow Cake that does justice to -- or even mentions -- his massively moving performance in that picture) and David Jansen puts some cynical flesh on the hungry bones of the reporter. Geoffrey Pounsett and John Dolan are somewhat defeated and Philippa Domville almost entirely so. The biologist lady, presumably speaking for her author, cites Darwin, not as preaching the survival of the fittest but as saying, more or less, "only connect." It's a noble idea, but connective tissue is precisely what this show lacks.

As many readers have pointed out, the "unidentified woman" seen with George Gershwin in the picture that accompanied last week's column was in fact the young Ginger Rogers. I have also to apologize for a mistake in the article itself: The neo-Gershwinian confection My One and Only is being staged this year at the Stratford Festival, not the Shaw.

- Chimera runs through Feb. 11 at the Tarragon Mainspace, 416- 531-1827.

2007-01-18-saving-the-last-dance-for-mom:
The departed banned in China THEATRE REVIEW

Singkil

Factory Studio Theatre

Catherine Hernandez's play Singkil is set in present-day Scarborough, but takes its title from a centuries-old Philippines dance. It remains a living tradition and depicts, so we are informed, the travails and eventual triumph of a princess lost in a forest. She eventually finds her way out with the help of a prince, though the play also tells us that the prince was a later addition and that in the pristine version she worked out her own salvation. This may be very empowering but it makes what already sounds like a vague all-purpose scenario even mistier. In this play it's a metaphor that won't do what its author wants it to do, and so turns into an unwanted superstructure.

The princess here is Mimi, who is in her twenties, the daughter of Filipino immigrants. Her mother Maria recently died, though she gets plenty of stage time in dreams and flashbacks. Maria was a former Singkil performer, who gave it up to get married, against the advice of her friend and dancing-partner Norma. Norma used to dance the handmaiden to Maria's princess and seems now to be carrying this role over into her real life. She arrives in Toronto in the wake, so to speak, of Maria's funeral with the declared intention of looking after Nestor, the husband, and the undeclared one of healing the breach between Mimi and her late mother. Mimi had hated Maria for reasons that, when revealed, seem less than Earth-shattering, at least in theatrical terms. (Most of us feel more tolerant about the behaviour of people in plays than we might about the behaviour of people in real life.) She also hates Singkil, for reasons that go beyond a young person's routine resentment of alien customs that set her apart from her peers; with Mimi it's personal. The play traces how she comes to love and forgive her mother; or, to put it another way, how she learns to dance.

The parts are all there, decently written but loosely assembled. The show is the second major offering, following Banana Boys, from the Asian-Canadian theatre group fu-Gen; and dance, as you would expect given the story, plays a prominent part in Nina Lee Aquino's production. Indeed, it begins with a dance, an erotic pas de deux that's very striking, though it turns out to be not an illustrative introduction to Singkil itself but theatrical shorthand for some actual love-making between Mimi and her boyfriend Chase. Or maybe -- I doubt

it but we aren't given enough information to decide -- what we are watching is one of those later Singkil accretions, with Chase cast as the unwanted prince. He does a lot of sticking around, though Mimi keeps changing her mind about whether she wants him or not. She can certainly act like a princess, in the uncomplimentary sense, and so, we gather, could her mother before her, whom marriage and motherhood in a new country left feeling bored and marooned. We are left, when all is finally explained and atoned for, with the feeling that the love of mother and daughter is a fraught but beautiful thing. But we knew that already and the play does little to make it new.

The later, more emblematic dancing never seems more than decoration, though it's tastily done (choreographer, Clare Preuss). Real Singkil is apparently performed on a symbolic forest of bamboo poles, and Camellia Koo's set pays tasteful homage to that concept, at the expense of suggesting any convincing Canadian domesticity that might set it off. Nadine Villasin's Mimi is very immediate, if occasionally rough at the edges, while Karen Ancheta's Maria smoother but more distant (even given that she's dead). Rose Cortez finds it hard to get beneath Norma's aggressively chatty exterior, and Leon Aureus, required to play the unassuming Nestor at two widely-spaced periods of his life, seems stranded midway between them. Chase, the boyfriend, is given a lively performance by David Yee, an Asian actor who looks European, which in this play is confusing. Chase tries, a little too eagerly, to reunite Mimi with what he presumes to be her own culture, and it makes a difference whether he is doing this from inside or out.

The play bears a fortuitous resemblance to Pedro Almodovar's Volver; both have estranged generations of women finding reconciliation, skeletons in family cupboards (more numerous and extreme in the movie) and a mother with a musical past, though the Spanish one's talent is for singing rather than dancing. It's unfair to compare a beginning playwright with a brilliant director at the height of his powers: The liquid movie is obviously in a different class from the lumpy play. In one respect, though, Hernandez' vision is more inclusive than Almodovar's; it finds a place for men, and -- Singkil revisionism notwithstanding --a generous one. Both are fundamentally warm-hearted works, but the play has structural cracks that make it feel chilly. - Until Jan. 28. 416-504-9971

Robert.cushman@nationalpost.com

2007-01-20-welcome-back-to-t-o-three-out:
This is the colour to wear this week as part of the annual Windfall Clothing fundraiser Serendipity is sweet. A fortuitous festival of Canadian theatre is going on in Toronto at the moment, with the metropolitan transfer of Stratford's Orpheus Descending joined by the return to the city of three outstanding shows from past seasons.

Leading the pack is Half Life, which now displaces The Drawer Boy as the best combination of Canadian writing, acting and direction that I have seen. It was first seen in 2005; its toured in the interim, here and abroad, with a couple of cast changes but the original actors are now all back in place. Watching John Mightons play a second time, I found myself wondering how many drafts it must have gone through before reaching its canonical form. Its themes and actions dovetail in a seemingly casual, effortless pattern that must actually have taken much hard labour to work out.

Patrick and Clara are two old people in a nursing home. Patrick is spry, aware and sardonic; Clara is sweet, confused and wheelchairbound. They fall in love, convinced that they are resuming an inconclusive romance that flared for a brief period during the Second World War. The first time I saw the play, I believed that this had indeed been the case; this time I doubted it. Donald, Clara's son, is sure that it couldn't have happened; he speaks with theoretical authority, as a psychologist specializing in the limitations of the human memory. He believes these limits to be a good thing, speculating on how unbearable existence would be if we lacked the capacity to forget, and pointing out that even the most capacious computers have built-in limits. He also, in what he believes to be in his mothers best interests, thwarts her and Patricks stated desire to get married. It's an age-reversed Romeo- and-Juliet situation, with an additional bittersweet twist; we are programmed initially to expect the divorced Donald to get together with Patrick's daughter Anna. Antagonism over their elders puts paid to that, though they seem initially to complement one another: shes an artist, hes a scientist, and they're both professionally frustrated.

In the play's first scene, Donald propounds a theory about limited attention spans, drawn from his experience of trying to tell a story at a party, and the theme echoes through the play. The action is full of conversations that are broken or simply lost, and the play is accordingly made up of short scenes which, however, are never sketchy. Relationships are touched lightly but fully, notably that between Donald and Clara; he visits her daily but can think of little to say; she still thinks of him as her brilliant boy. Some of the best writing in the play concerns the ability of children to feel an intensity of happiness -- and, by unspoken corollary, of unhappiness -- unattainable to adults, which is one thing that makes cruelty to children so uniquely abhorrent.

The play packs a lot in. It gives us, as well as the criss- crossing connections at its core, a sense of the life of the home; its hard, come the final curtain, to believe that we have only met two members of staff and one semi-official visitor. Its discretion makes the occasional shock all the more powerful, as when Patrick is discovered at the start of a scene, tied to a chair. It also enjoys itself with recurring motifs: telephone numbers and the ability to recall them are significant, as are entry codes; Patrick was a code-breaker in the war and he still has the knack. One of the key scenes is set on Remembrance Day. Its extraordinary, too, how a play dealing in tiny encounters turns out to have cosmic range. Half life can be a measure of geological time as well as of the shrunken existences experienced by some of the plays' characters -- by all of them and all of us, if we are to believe Donald. He thinks it a blessing that time swallows us all up; the local vicar finds it an unbearable idea for which belief in God is the only salve.

Randy Hughson's performance of the latter role is the most improved since the first opening. Before, he seemed to function chiefly as comic relief; he is still funny, funnier if anything, but he can make us sense the dormant despair that his compulsive cheeriness keeps at bay. (He does like, when chatting with the old folks, to dwell on all the terrible things they have come through; the play lets us hear some hilariously harrowing snatches from one of his sermons.) Barbara Gordon shifts brilliantly between ages as a dyspeptic resident (who says when hearing of a deceased inmate "at least she wont have to do any more crafts") and a brisk late- arriving nurse; and Maggie Huculak is equally fine as the underpaid caregiver she replaces, one in whom an uncommon sympathy and efficiency co-exist with a tendency to pilfer from the patients. Diego Matamoross Donald has lost some of the deprecatory wit that used to light up his first scene, but his intellect and his weary good nature are still splendidly in place. Laura de Carteret sometimes goes for easy options as Anna, but I suspect hers is the least developed role. The two central seniors are beyond praise, with Carolyn Hetherington's supremely gentle Clara radiating a grace that outlives lucidity and Eric Peterson's Patrick showing cantankerousness giving birth to courtesy. Daniel Brookss production is scenically, sonically, emotionally and intellectually immaculate.

In the early years of the 20th century, there was an American playwright named Clyde Fitch who was so successful and prolific that he once had two plays open against each other on the same night. Daniel Brooks notched up a similar record last Wednesday, which saw the openings, or re-openings, both of Half Life and of Monster, which Brooks and Daniel MacIvor created together in 1999, which Brooks directs and which MacIvor, all on his own, performs. If Monster (which, for obvious reasons, I saw at a preview) had been my first encounter with MacIvor solo -- I missed it the first time around -- I would undoubtedly have been knocked out. As it was, I was still mightily impressed, but could not shake a sense of being served the mixture-as-before. Like the later Cul-de-sac, it evokes a community with something nasty happening behind every window; like the earlier Here Lies Henry, it has a narrator-protagonist -- though this one does more narrating than protagonizing -- who projects his own violent discontents on to the rest of the world. At one moment hes ingenuous, at the next diabolical, and the transitions, as usual with MacIvor, are both instant and awesome. The blood- freezing tale he unfolds begins with a young couple next door, whose altercations Mac- Ivor voices in a quick-change register and rhythm that suggest Ronnie Burkett without his puppets. She wants a child, he doesn't; and he could be right because we shift to a young boy's axe-murder of his father, which in turn is fondly, or at least obsessively, remembered by another kid who lives next door. The crime inspired a movie; we meet its director, a recovering alcoholic, and the more prosperous producer who claims the film was his in the first place. There is wit as well as horror in the writing and, of course, in the acting: MacIvors ability to people a stage while standing virtually immobile is phenomenal, and Brooks gives him the cool, cruel atmospheric backup to which he and we are accustomed. The upshot -- that there is a monster in all of us, perpetrators or scavengers -- is not that profound, or even that involving, but in performance and presentation, this is theatre at a very high technical level.

Monster is part of the farewell season of MacIvors production company, da da kamera. Brooks now runs the Necessary Angel company, which gave birth to Half Life. His predecessor, Richard Rose, now runs the Tarragon where, if you're still with me, Half Life was first staged, though not as a Tarragon production. That theatre's own best play of 2006, Rosa Labordes Leo, about two young men and one young woman of variously revolutionary dispositions growing up hopefully in Allendes Chile and drastically in Pinochet's, is now back where it started, and standing up to a second viewing less well than I had hoped. It once looked deceptively modest, with ramifications; it now seems to have more to be modest about, though stylishly written and interestingly fluid in construction. Some of the edge has gone off Rose's direction with its central conceit of a triangular stage for a triangular relationship. The plays jump- cuts from the personal to the political and back are now less jumpy and less cutting than I remembered them, and without this shifting focus both levels of concern seem pro forma. Its still worth seeing, and the performances are excellent. Leo himself, accidental hero and central consciousness, in love with both his companions, mopes and twitches beautifully. Cara Pifko is sharp and glittering as the shared girlfriend and muse, with a sideline (mysterious or maybe just underwritten) in kleptomania. Sergio Di Zio is best of all as the most committed of all, taking an engagingly single- minded character and making him flesh and blood.

- Half Life runs through Feb. 3 at the Bluma Appel (416-368- 3110). Monster runs through Feb. 4 at Buddies in Bad Times (416- 975- 8555). Leo runs through Feb. 4 at the Tarragon Extra Space.

New World Stage: Combined festival brings a heady mix of global theatre Torontos Harbourfront Centre used to house, at different times, two theatrical festivals. There was the biennial World Stage season and there was the International Dance season. This year the two combine in the New World Stage International Performance season, which is planned to be an annual event accommodating drama, dance and the increasingly fluid and disputed area between them. As well as being a more diverse occasion than previously, the New World Stage is also a longer one. The old World Stage seasons were typically crammed into a few weeks. This one is spread over a more leisurely six months, beginning tomorrow and stretching into June.

At least, it should seem more leisurely to audiences and critics. The organizers, probably, will never let up. For Tina Rasmussen, the season's artistic director, this should seem like par for the course. The festival is the culmination of two years' heavy globetrotting that may have peaked at the Edinburgh Festival, where she saw 66 plays in nine days. (You can do this in Edinburgh, easily.) Its a peculiarly intense kind of tourism, with an equally intense kind of souvenir-shopping attached. "You want, says Rasmussen, to bring your travelling experiences back with you."

She didnt have to travel very far to collect her opening production, Dollhouse. This is Ibsen's A Doll's House, as rendered by the New York company Mabou Mines, a troupe so long-established and well-regarded that it must count as the Establishment of experimental theatre.

Lee Breuer, the director, offers a new spin on what the company calls Ibsens feminist "anthem. (Their quotation marks.) It certainly offers a bizarre take on the plays title by having all the male roles played by little people" (or, to put it another way, very short men) while the women are all around six feet tall. This might make the patriarchal system seem more outrageous than ever, or it may make the women's eventual victory somewhat predictable. We shall see. The idea as described certainly sounds good for at least 10 minutes of stunning theatre, though it leaves you wondering what they will do for an encore.

Mabou Mines has built-in Canadian content. It takes its name from a community in Nova Scotia, where the company's founding members planned their inaugural event back in 1970. So it seems fitting, or at least a nice coincidence, that one of the home-grown contributions to the season (World Stages world does include Canada) should come from Halifax. This is Revisited, presented by the 2b theatre company (as opposed, presumably, to the Not 2b theatre company), a show that started life as a "revisitation of Thornton Wilders Our Town but ran into problems over rights. So the canvas was extended to take in other (comparatively) early American writers including Willa Cather and Walt Whitman, making it in effect Revisted Revisited. The format is simple; a storyteller and his audience sit at a table, and the man calls up characters from his small-town memories, characters who proceed to people the stage. It's one of the shows about which Rasmussen herself sounds most enthusiastic. It has, she says, a terrifically honest, non- strident ending; it makes you recall why you fell in love with the theatre."

There are people who fell in love with the theatre in the early 1970s, or at least had their eyes more fully opened to its human and imaginative potential, when they saw Sizwe Bansi is Dead. This is the play created in South Africa by the white playwright Athol Fugard and two black actors, John Kani and Winston Ntshona, as an enactment of how it felt to live under apartheid. (It wasn't an explicit protest play; the protest was built in.) The play, which had to be virtually smuggled out of its native country and had a shattering impact across the world, has outlasted the system that provoked it into being. Toronto will be seeing a new production directed by Peter Brook, who merits the title "legendary theatre director if anyone does.

This isnt the same as the production of the other Kani- Ntshona- Fugard collaboration The Island, which played in Toronto with Brook directing the two original performers. This is a new, from-the- ground-up production with different actors and performed in French. It was first staged at the Theatre des Bouffes-du-Nord in Paris, which has been now Brooks base for more than a quarter of a century.

Technically small but has massive reverberations": That could be a description of Sizwe Bansi, but in fact it's Rasmussen's summary of Belgian show Aalst -- a True Story, which reduces staging to two people in a single chair -- a method she describes, undoubtedly accurately, as "something you wouldnt see anywhere else. Aalst is faction" theatre, based on newspaper and TV reports, about a crime -- the murder of two children by their parents -- and its effect on the town in which it happened. Im also looking forward to another more elaborate collective piece, Particularly in the Heartland, whose logo is a heart decorated with the stars and stripes. Presented by another New York company, The TEAM (Theatre of the Emerging American Moment), it's described as "a new play about losing sight of America, and trying to fall back in love with it. If the company can catch that emerging moment, it should be exciting. They are, according to Rasmussen, a very young, exuberant, athletic company," with an average age of 27.

And for relaxation after all this intensity, we can anticipate The Spiegel Show, starting June 1, which is happening in the Spiegeltent'n tavern. This is a space that doesnt yet exist but will be erected on the model of a "travelling, wooden circular dance hall, popular in the 1920s in Belgium. The entertainment within it, however, will not be Belgian; it will be Torontonian, drawn from local comic and musical talent. Rasmussen directs it herself, and she -- a passionate, quiet-spoken lady -- promises a salubrious salon and an evening thats sexy and salacious." Sounds just like what we'll need as summer sets in.

2007-01-26-it-s-the-levels-man:
Mabou Mines Dollhouse

Premiere Dance Theatre,

Harbourfront Centre

- - -

No need to unroll a red carpet to welcome Mabou Mines to town; they've brought their own. The stage floor is covered in red when we take our seats, though everything around and behind it is dour and bleak. Then billowing red curtains start descending, enfolding the backs and sides of the stage and even parts of the auditorium. (Hey everyone, we're in a theatre.) A lady enters and takes her place at a piano, and her face is red too, at least the area around her eyes; it turns out much later that this is to make her look Chinese, which I don't think she is. An even plusher curtain falls at the front of the stage, making it look as if the show is over before it's even begun. But it rises again, revealing a large packing case, which when opened discloses a fully operational doll's house, which is quickly put together to serve as the environment for what follows.

Which, under the title Mabou Mines Dollhouse, is a re-imagining by New York's senior experimental company of the Ibsen play generally known in these parts as A Doll's House and regarded as the modern theatre's first and finest feminist manifesto. The beginning is rather impressive. The show's ending is very impressive. The miniature setting falls away for Nora Helmer, pampered and patronized wife of the banker Torvald Helmer, not just to declare her new-found independence, but to declaim and even sing it. The scene has been transported to an old-style opera house, the heroine waxing passionate on a balcony, surrounded by puppet couples in private boxes; the consciousnesses of the lady puppets, or some of them, are visibly elevated while the gentleman puppets look, as far as I could tell, perturbed or simply uncomprehending. Nora, announcing her departure, strips off everything she wears, including her flaxen Nordic wig. From below Torvald, who is in bed, looks up aghast.

Nora is somewhat under six feet tall, Torvald somewhat under four. The other female and male characters are cast to the same scale. (The tallest of all, presumably on the principle that the last should be first, is the maid, who is also pregnant.) This, along with the nursery setting, which incorporates tiny furniture and a rocking horse, is the production's central and most obtrusive device, and it makes most of the actual play -- everything in fact until the finale -- very heavy going. The set is a relentless actualization of what the play offers as a metaphor. The casting takes that concept and duly dolls it up. It has, of course, its own built-in ironies. Here are these women, submitting to these men who are actually much smaller than they are. Here are these men, condemning their women to live on a scale to which they themselves are or should be accustomed. Once you're past the initial surprise, the evening settles down to become an interminable statement of the obvious.

For all his revolutionary credentials Lee Breuer, the director, isn't out to undermine Ibsen; he's out to underline him. This goes not only for the play's message, which is unaltered, but for its method. The plot involves blackmail, guilty secrets and convenient confidences; most productions try to play down the melodrama, but this one, in a joyless sort of way, revels in it. The actors strike exaggerated attitudes at every twist of plot or change of mood. The music played is by Grieg, since the work's national origin is another thing the production is at pains to emphasize. The language is English, but the pronunciation is, or so I assume, authentic Norwegian. Nora's name comes out as something like "Nula," and she is always Fru Helmer, never Missus. And since her husband calls her a doll and a little bird, she twitters and flutters throughout. Indeed, the entire cast is in a constant state of pirouette.

The text, already substantial, is lengthened by some nightmare sequences in which a corps of bogeys act out the heroine's worst fears of having corrupted her children by her earlier feckless behaviour. The production also offers the revelation that 19th- century people, even people in classic 19th-century plays, had sex. The minor characters of Krogstad and Mrs. Linde go down on one another -- sequentially, not simultaneously -- right in the middle of their friends' dollhouse. More importantly we're left in no doubt that riotous times in bed are what kept Nora and Torvald together, especially Torvald. But even this isn't new. A fine production in one of the Atlantic Theatre Festival's first seasons, directed by Michael Langham, set the whole last duet in the bedroom, achieving devastating results without getting childish about it. That's one of the most irksome things about productions like Breuer's; they behave like they're first with the latest when they're actually old hat.

Bad acting, whether done accidentally or on purpose, is never invigorating to watch. It's especially enervating when the actors themselves are discernibly good, as most of them are here. Maude Mitchell as Nora does everything that's asked of her and then some, and Mark Povinelli strikes some very impressive sparks off Torvald, especially when strutting all over his domestic domain or when recalling his fury at having the obsequious Krogstad working in his office. I've never heard the latter bit better done. It's one of the few occasions when the production is genuinely funny, as opposed to just trying to be. Another is the same actor's cry of "No more melodrama!" immediately before launching into another bout of it. Not funny is having the Chinese pianist exit in a huff when someone makes a derogatory remark about her native land. She has to be pacified with cries of "It's in the script!" Ron Rosenbaum's fascinating new book The Shakespeare Wars has a wonderfully apposite sentence about "antiquated academic avant-gardistes who can't get over the stunning revelation that a play isn't real ('It's, like, artificial, man')."

The actors all talk through throat mics, in accordance with the director's longstanding belief that unamplified sound is unacceptable to modern audiences who want to hear every subtle modulation; not that many of those are in evidence here. Audiences who know the play will feel patronized; those who don't will probably feel baffled. But then there's that last scene, to which there's even more than I have outlined. There's a suggestion that Torvald is dreaming it. Then he wakes up and finds that it's real. He runs offstage and out through the auditorium, calling out his wife's name. It's her triumph, his tragedy. And it beats any amount of traditional door-slamming.

- Until Feb. 4. Call 416-973-4000 for tickets.

2007-01-27-waiting-for-the-major-three-m:
Morris Panych has written a historical play, though he has claimed not to be much interested in getting the facts right. On the strength of What Lies Before Us, I believe him; but I also believe that on this occasion his indifference has done him in.

He gives us three men marooned in the Rockies in the 1880s while doing surveying work on the Canadian Pacific Railroad. One of them appears to be English, another Scottish and the third is definitely Chinese. We are some way into the play before we get any precise information about why they're there, and it isn't that precise even then. I don't think the word "Canada" is spoken from one end of the evening to the other. The Englishman, an empire builder by temperament if not by ability, sometimes speaks rhapsodically, not to say deliriously, about what their project will do for the country when it's completed, but what actually lies before him and his companions is less glorious and less susceptible to factual verification. For the most part, we have a play about these three guys stuck in a tent.

It's a gloriously realistic tent, with its camp beds and its tin bath. Panych has not directed this play himself, but he has sent along his regular designer Ken MacDonald who, in collaboration with Robin Fisher, has done his usual great job. But what goes on inside it is unanchored behaviourism. The two Brits can't stand one another, what with Ambrose the Scot being an unhappy cynic and Keating the English chappie an optimistic idiot. They cannot, however, get away from one another. It is impossible while contemplating them not to be reminded, as in so many other plays, of the indissolubly united tramps in Waiting for Godot. They, too, are waiting for someone; in their case it's an army Major who is going to rescue them. The certain knowledge, gained from looking at the program, that the Major is not going to arrive is dispiriting in a way that the non-appearance of Godot never was. This play could really use another character. The ones we have are stick- figures, who bicker away at each other on the apparent principle that if they keep at it long enough, one of them will say something amusing. Occasionally one does -- this is Panych, after all -- but not enough to keep the entire first act from being painfully tedious.

The second is unexpectedly better. Ambrose -- Vladimir to Keating's Estragon -- has defied expectation by not only talking about getting away but actually making a serious attempt to do it. I don't think it's giving much away to say that he fails. After the intermission we find him afflicted with gangrene and Keating with, believe it or not, rabies. One faces amputation, the other insanity. We've spent the first act watching them dancing aimlessly on the edge of despair. We now see them sunk in the pit itself, and it's far more satisfying. Ambrose, always miserably self-aware, keeps a journal which he hopes others will find after his death: "I want the world to know the terrible things this country can do a man's writing style." So the play does have things to say about Canada, after all.

And while it may not have a Pozzo figure, it does have a Lucky: Wing, the Chinese cook who infuriates Keating by not being able to speak or understand a word of English. He is especially riled by Wing's inability to run him a bath, which he treats as a new phenomenon, though we're also given to understand that they've been there for ages, and the situation must surely have presented itself before. Beckett's Lucky, you'll remember, has a stunningly effective speech constructed entirely of gibberish. Panych's Wing has an equivalent aria, the last thing in the play, spoken in his native language, which, of course, for most of the audience, might as well be gibberish. It, too, is effective, even moving, quite possibly more than it would be if we did understand it. Wing has spent the entire play being insulted and abused, but the last words are his. This, I guess, is What Lies Before Us: Canada united and multicultural, with former hierarchies reversed. Wing is played by Wayne Sujo, who is working on this particular railroad for the second time; he was in the opera Iron Road, which played in Toronto a few years ago and really was an exciting piece of theatre.

What Lies Before Us really isn't. It's tempting to say that the play would seem better if its author had directed it but I'm not so sure. The current staging is Jim Millan's farewell production as artistic director of Crow's Theatre, a company that crested with the premiere more than a decade ago of Brad Fraser's Unidentified Human Remains and the True Nature of Love. I've often felt that Millan and Crow's have been living on Unidentified Human Remains ever since but I cannot see what they could have done here that they haven't. David Storch and Matthew MacFadzean certainly do their damnedest as the Anglophone duo; MacFadzean, in particular, as the manically insular Keating comes close to making a human being of a caricature. Keating is satirized as a walking compendium of received ideas, but he's one himself--a startlingly simplistic portrait from a writer of Panych's sophistication.

Cabaret-U-Mano is a puppet show, hailing from Montreal, in which the dolls dance to records, and their handlers move right along with them. It's at its best when the people and the puppets seem to merge; when, in effect, you cannot tell the dancers from the danced. Most of the accompanying music consists of camped-up pop classics, which are then camped ever further up by the show itself. The flavour is insistently faux erotic; a bony marionette doing a striptease isn't my idea of a turn-on but chacun a son gout. The puppeteers, some of whom are very clever, seem to be making fun of the puppets, which is a change after several centuries of the reverse.

- What Lies Before Us runs through Feb. 24 at the Berkeley Street Theatre, 416-368-3110; Cabaret-UMano runs through Feb. 18 at the Diesel Playhouse, 416- 971-5656.
