2007-02-03-soulpepper-gets-to-the-core-o:
Soulpepper's production of The Threepenny Opera gets to the core of the piece. I would say that it gets to the heart, except that this Bertolt Brecht-Kurt Weill classic doesn't have one. It might, I guess, be accused of having compassion. There are songs in it, especially towards the end, that depict the misery of the poor with an angry bitterness that feels authentic. But they aren't really about social justice.

Brecht wrote the piece in 1928; and in later years, after he'd got religion (i.e. Marxism), he tried in rewrites and prefaces and notes to make it politically correct. But he wasn't a socialist here. He wasn't even an anarchist. He was a nihilist, seeking a righteous pretext for his own violence. It can get monotonous (how many times in one evening do you want to be informed that the world is a heap of excrement?) but it's certainly compelling. There's a consistent vision.

It's Brecht's vision even though Weill, a brilliant chameleon of a composer, carries it along with a score that's alternately abrasive and seductive. It's Brecht's, despite the fact that he doesn't seem to have written much of it. He got the story and characters from John Gay's The Beggar's Opera, the first British musical, whose 18th-century whores and highwaymen he transformed into whores and bank-robbers of no identifiable period. He delegated most of the actual work to his longsuffering mistress and amanuensis, Elisabeth Hauptmann, while taking, in his usual endearing fashion, all the credit himself. The Soulpepper program makes some amends, crediting Hauptmann with "German translation" and Brecht with "adaptation and lyrics." The present English translation of the German translation is by the late Robert David Macdonald, a mischievous Scottish fellow; he, or somebody, has accentuated the apolitical by squeezing into one of the songs a skeptical reference to Karl Marx that I don't remember from any other version.

Something else about the program: It announces a play "in three acts" while also telling us, with perfect truth, that there will only be one intermission. Tim Albery, the director and something of a tease himself, stops the action right in the middle of a scene. It's the one in which Captain Macheath, a.k.a. Mack the Knife, visits his favourite brothel and is betrayed to the police by his favourite doxy whose name, like that of most Brechtian sexworkers, is Jenny and who has been bribed by Mack's unwelcoming new in-laws the Peachums. The break works, as does the re-positioning of two important songs to places where they make greater narrative and atmospheric sense.

The Beggar's Opera was cavalier about plot; the Threepenny update is downright insulting. It takes place in a fantasy London that's Edwardian as much as it's anything but keeps referring to the coronation of Queen Victoria, some 70 years earlier. It thinks the Old Bailey is a prison rather than a courthouse, and has a man condemned to death at an hour's notice and without a trial. Albery tidies up, somewhat, the ramshackle structure while keeping faith with the play's savage inner chaos.

Nothing is more savage than the ending; Mack is saved from the gallows by a royal pardon. In Gay, this is a joke on the audience ("give 'em a happy ending"); in Brecht, it's a joke on the world ("man eats man, and money talks"). In both, the implausibility is freely admitted from the stage. So Gay anticipated Brecht's alienation effect by 200 years. The show puts paid to the idea that Brecht used alienation as a means of keeping his own passionate feelings in check; he took to it naturally, as the perfect vehicle for imposing his own icy coldness on his audience.

The first thing we see in the Soulpepper production is a side of beef, hanging; d'bi.young.anitafrika as the narrating Ballad Singer seems to be playing a butcher's assistant. She rasps rather than sings Mack the Knife, underlining a brutality in the song (this isn't the pop version) that could probably be trusted to do its own work. But she's a glittering presence, and she moves furniture on and off stage with a splendid air of contempt. Crime in this world is a business like any other; Mack, who is thinking of diversifying into banking, is the thug and seducer as tycoon. He's played by Albert Schultz, sleek, slicked-down and heartless. (That's a compliment.) He's only roused to emotion, and some especially powerful singing, by the prospect of his own death. Patricia O'Callaghan is his bride Polly, dainty of voice and walk and steely of grip, while the senior Peachums are gleefully and vindictively played by William Webster and Nancy Palk; Webster punches home his anti-moralizing songs in great style. Stuart Hughes is delightfully Caledonian as Mack's buddy, the Chief of Police (by a careful irony, the only character with feelings) and Jennifer Villaverde as his daughter rises impressively to a vengeful spot of mock-coloratura, she being another of the hero's cast-offs. Mack's gang is excellent.

Lorenzo Savoini's set consists of two platforms. In front, in keeping with the pervasive imagery of gluttony and hunger, is a giant dinner-table; behind is an abattoir or anything else you fancy. The only staging flaw is that too much singing happens beyond the great divide, tough on vocalists who are untrained (mostly) and unamplified (blessedly). Sarah Wilson's performance of Pirate Jenny (the second most famous song) is a blur when it starts upstage, a triumph when it finishes down. This apart, Paul Sportelli's musical direction, with a couple of actors doubling in the band, is superb. The vengeful, menacing ensembles, tightly and fiercely choreographed by Patti Powell, are tremendous; they hate, but the hatred is earned. This is a devil of a show to get right, and this production is almost the best I've seen. On the first night it got cheers, which were deserved; it didn't, despite being both a musical and an opera, get a standing ovation. That's because it chills.

- The Threepenny Opera runs through March 10 at the Young Centre for the Performing Arts; 416- 866-8666.

2007-02-08-forecast-is-for-funny:
COMEDY REVIEW

Tip of the Melting Iceberg

Second City, Toronto

Many years ago, children-- so many that I can remember neither the date nor the title of the show -- there was a Toronto Second City revue that struck me at the time and strikes me still as one of the funniest things I have ever seen. One of the items that have stayed with me is set in a TV newsroom, where a report about the world coming to an end in five millennia was misread on air as "in five minutes," leading to much consternation and dropping of defences. The weatherman was especially affected. You guys, he said tearfully to the two anchors, "are the only friends I've ever had." Actually, Jack, one of them replied, "I never liked you much."

I was reminded of this last item by a scene in the new and excellent Second City show Tip of the Melting Iceberg. It picks up the same comic principle of people revealing themselves in extremis and goes deeper with it. Three guys, old friends, have come to their favourite meeting spot. One of them is about to get married, and has asked one of the others to be his best man, leaving the third feeling rejected and resentful. The chosen one reveals some truly shocking news about his own prospects, thus putting a crimp in everybodys plans. After the initial, and surprisingly slight, intake of breath, the audience watches in delight as the trio go into competitive paroxysms of self pity, self-absorption and plain old selfishness.

It could be that selfishness is at the root of all comedy. Its certainly at the root of farce, and revue-sketch humour is farcical almost by definition; it doesn't have the time to be anything else. This Second City show, smartly directed by Steven Morel, is especially well-equipped in this respect since, as its title suggests, it is from time to time about the environment. (We've learned by now that its only from time to time that Second City revues bear any relation to their titles. Weve also learned to live with it.) So it can satirize the things we do and the ways in which we ignore or excuse them. The opening number depicts a man juggling cellphone calls while driving through a built-up area and eventually hitting something in his path. The closing number, a song, sounds for a distressing moment as if the company is about to go earnest and preachy on us, but it soon regains its poise and reverts to being cynical, which is far more effective, even as propaganda. Somewhere in between there's an apoclayptic weather report from the near future; it doesn't cover Quebec, which has independent weather, and is disquietingly evasive about just what has happened to Halifax.

The five writer-performers are great. Anand Rajaram keeps shyly and uncharacteristically in the background for the first 20 minutes or so; this turns out to be a strategy since he first makes his mark as a worker in an office so nervous about racial profiling that it wont even allow him to recommend a good Indian restaurant. Rajaramis himself a one-man -- sorry one-person-- commentary on colourblind casting since he appears to equal effect in numbers where his ethnicity couldnt matter less and in numbers where it couldn't matter more.

Jim Annan is perhaps the most inner-directed of the team, untouchable within each of his personae, whether as a Canadian border guard applying for a gun like the Americans have (he'd prefer an AK-47) or a male panda in a zoo whod rather chew bamboo than help perpetuate his species though, push come to shove, hes prepared to settle for doing both at once. Annan, who is squat, has a Mutt-and- Jeff thing going with Scott Montgomery, who is lanky, and who shines especially as a corporate bozo trapped at a reception in the AGO, reeling off descriptions and interpretations of the exhibits at virtuoso speed while proudly maintaining an attitude of philistine contempt.

There are two ladies present. Lauren Ash specializes in outsize voices, reserving the deepest, slowest and lonesomest for a girl with multiple physical afflictions and an imaginary boyfriend whose invitation to take her to the prom she has, for obvious logical reasons, to refuse. (He's devastated; he thought he was real.) Leslie Seiler is a smooth blond, presenting Air Canada's new itemized-billing scheme; as she sweetly explains to a client, if you're going to order all those tasty in-flight drinks, then you'd better reserve bathroom privileges as well.

This, then, is a fast-moving, good-looking (designs by the feted Camellia Koo), quickthinking and, on occasion, rather courageous show. The theatrical funniness in Tip of the Melting Iceberg builds, so that you laugh till you cry.

- Indefinite run. Call 416-343- 0011 for ticket information.

2007-02-10-a-boy-who-would-be-king-of-so:
There was Half Life, and there is still Orpheus Descending, but the most moving play in Toronto, as well as one of the most delightful, is Danny, King of the Basement at the Lorraine Kimsa Theatre for Young People.

It's another welcome revival of a recent success. David S. Craigs play, mounted by his Roseneath Theatre company, turns up on the former YPTs main stage four years after making its debut in the same theatre's studio. In the interim, it has been on numerous Canadian tours and has been seen in other productions abroad. It's new to me, however, and though I had gathered that it was a play about homelessness and child poverty" that never became journalistic or didactic (there isnt a social worker or activist in sight), nothing had prepared me for the dazzling economy of the writing.

Within five minutes of curtain rise, and without being force-fed a thing, we have ingested nearly all the salient facts about young Danny Carter and his single mother, Louise. In one short, fast scene we have seen them executing an early-morning flit from their latest home and Louises latest boyfriend. (We don't meet him, just hear him snoring, but Louise's "he didnt turn out to be Prince Charming, did he? tells us all we need to know about that relationship, all three sides of it.) We have seen them take the St. Clair streetcar -- charmingly represented, like all transportation in this show, by a cut-out on wheels -- to their new home. This is not, as Danny -- who has now moved eight times in two years --expects it to be, a shelter. Its a flat: 92B Clinton St., B for basement. We have discovered that Danny, having had to grow up fast, has a close and playful relationship with his mom. His encyclopedic memory for subway stops and the order they come in helps her find her way about town, which is sort of cool; she calls him Mr. Banker" and actually lets him take charge of their cash, which sort of isn't.

Louise is the only adult we actually see, though we hear plenty about others. The two other visible characters are kids. We get three social levels placed side by side, with problems that reflect off one another. Penelope is the daughter of the woman who lives in the rest of No. 92 and, in the aftermath of a divorce, rents out its basement; as Danny learns, "rich people can think they're broke. Penelope goes to ballet classes and acting classes and is very clothes- and- status conscious. She resents having been taken out of private school, and she especially resents her neighbour and public-school classmate Angelo. Angelo does have two on-site parents, but his father is out of work and his resentment over this has turned into him a monster who yells at his son for being unable to score at hockey. Dannys assessment is that he sounds like a dinosaur," and thats the shape in which we glimpse him through his window, shadow-play style. It's no great surprise that the three kids, initially hostile, quickly become friends, or that the catalyst for their doing so is Danny's unstoppable imagination. In his fantasy life, which proves very infectious, hes a "game agent who reports, gathers information, hangs out." In his game, Louise is an agent posing as his mother. (Angelo objects, "Shes your real mother. Danny, worried that his friend might crack under interrogation, replies, it's probably safer for you to think that.") Danny has had a lot of practice in imagining things; he has had to imagine a winter coat and winter boots. He also believes, or wants to believe, that his father is in the Rocky Mountains, fighting fires. Eventually, some of his dreams, plus what he regards as a shameful secret, crash in on him, and he becomes for a time truly homeless.

Craig isn't one of your sadistic playwrights, and there is, of course, a happy ending, at least for these characters. Still I doubt if any adult is going to sit through this play without crying. (Children, officially the target audience, will likely be more resilient.) Richard Greenblatts production is lovely in its speed, fun and ability to distinguish between compassion and sentimentality. It also looks great, against a colourful set by Andjelija Djuric that amounts to a witty reduction of downtown Toronto, with the OCAD building putting in a whimsical appearance on the skyline. The ace up the shows sleeve, though, is its casting of grown-up actors as the kids. This device could be, and often has been, embarrassing, but here it proves liberating. Actors, by definition, play; that part of the child stays alive in them longer than it does for most people, and this piece, whose motive force is imagination, lets them tap right into that. They make an emotional connection that's direct, unforced, and totally unpatronizing.

In fact, Jacklyn Francis, as grownup Louise, seems to be playing at a disadvantage; she places so much emphasis on the mother's conscientious cheerfulness that we lose sight of the desperation beneath it. The juvenile roles, though, bring out the best in three of the best. Yanna McIntosh has a gift of directness that she has compromised in some recent roles by trying too hard or doing too much, but shes in top form as a perfect Penelope, focused and complete whether being impossible or being concerned. And also when being hurt; Penelope has two cellphones, one for each of her parents to call her up and abuse the other. Caught between them ("Im just a kid, says Ms. Hardboiled. Talk to each other."), she throws both phones into the trash; it's hard to conceive of a more wrenching image of the child as battleground. Cliff Saunders, last seen as Bilbo in Lord of the Rings, provides a private kick when Angelo has to read in class from The Hobbit; throughout he has a hotline to pre-teen bewilderment and pre-teen strength. Freshness and alertness are Jordan Pettle's stock-in- trade, and they find a wonderful conduit in Dannys progression from King of Moving (his own phrase) to King of the Basement, a better thing to be.

Dannys last traumas seem rushed in the writing, and hence in the playing; this is the only part of the play that made me wonder what it would be like with real kids. Otherwise, no complaints. Stanislavsky said that acting for children should be the same as acting for adults, only better; he might have said the same about writing and here is proof of both. I forget who said that if your play has a message you'd better not let your characters know what it is but, whoever he was, he gets vindicated, too.

Talking of kings and basements: In the COC's production of Gounods Faust, I really liked the climactic descent to Hell, via instant trapdoor, of Faust and Mephistopheles, while the wronged Marguerite did the hangmans job for him and achieved instant apotheosis, going literally through the roof. I know the music critics have been rough on this production, and I agree that having Faust and Mephisto exchange identities is too clever by half. Again literally: man into fiend makes sense but the reverse doesn't. Still, it seems to me that by bringing salvation and damnation back into play, this Faust restores some of the gravitas that belongs to the legend and that the opera sacrifices by reducing the whole thing to a lachrymose love-story. If all Faust wants to do with his magic powers is seduce one village maiden, then his pact with the devil seems like a waste for him personally and an irrelevance for the audience. Or, to put it another way, the end of the show forgets the beginning. Admittedly, you could say the same of Goethe's Faust, or a least of the Part 1 that was Gounods inspiration, but Goethe came back with a Part 2 that gives the hero bigger fish to fry. He also gets to escape, though Ive never been quite clear from what; Goethe was too much the philosopher to have believed in damnation, and that's enough to make any treatment of the Faust story problematic. Gounod's music does believe, but only at the unquestioning level of a 1950s movie epic. (I confess: coming to opera from musical theatre I cant help hearing Marguerites Jewel Song as a parody of Leonard Bernstein's Glitter and Be Gay, rather than the other way around.) Anyway, I found this production, directed and designed by Nicholas Muni, visually thrilling with its evocation of, and constant return to, Faust's cabalistic study. The new opera house continues to be one of the best places to go for exciting stagecraft.

- Danny, King of the Basement runs through Feb. 25 at the Lorraine Kimsa Theatre for Young People, 416-862-2222; Faust is in repertory through Feb. 25 at the Four Seasons Centre for the Performing Arts, 416- 263-8231.

2007-02-17-the-end-came-mercifully:
There's a new offering from the company known as Mammalian Diving Reflex, a name that may have some meaning for the people behind it but has always seemed to me like three vaguely imposing words pulled at random from the dictionary. I have similar trouble parsing the title of this production, which is Diplomatic Immunities: The End. I'll have a wild guess. It means that the world is a dangerous place in which no one, regardless of nationality, is secure. So tear up your passports. This is certainly the burden of the show itself, a mix of videotaped interviews and live improvisation with just a smidgen of script that no one, least of all its creators, would call a play. There are eight credited "research artists," four of each sex, whom it would be equally inaccurate to call a cast; nevertheless, they are the people who are on stage throughout.

Near the end of The End, there's a video section in which a classroom ful of kids are asked what song they would most like to hear at, or just prior to, the end of the world. The majority vote goes to We Are the Champions, and one of the (ahem) cast proceeds to sing it live, on stage and off-key. With its built-in complacency, and its dismissive reference to "losers," that song strikes me as a cheesy choice for a global epiphany. Maybe the bad singing is meant to be a comment on that, or maybe it's meant to be touching in its honesty. You never know.

That same inquiry, about ideal requests to be forwarded to some universal DJ, has been echoing through the evening. The Mammalian research artists have been out on the streets of Toronto asking people questions, including that one, and they line up a few members of the theatre audience and ask them as well. We know that when the victims of 9/11 were facing their own version of the end of the world, music was not what was on their minds; they wanted, insofar as they had a choice, to get in touch with their families. That's probably how most of us would react. But none of this show's respondents, live or taped, mentioned such a thing, and only one said that, on the whole, he would prefer silence. (Myself, if forced to select music at the close, I wouldn't go for a song at all. I'd choose Bach, if only as some kind of atonement for not having listened to him enough when I was alive.)

Still, if the answers to this and other queries were mostly mushy and banal, the questioned were only taking their cues from the questioners. When one of the live subjects on the first night demurred at assessing his feelings about the end of the world, he was asked how he would feel if only part of it were about to end. Partial apocalypse sounds like a contradiction in terms; it certainly lowers the tone. Nor is it ever very clear what the show has in mind when it talks about the world ending. It could be ecological catastrophe, or nuclear war, or some kind of Biblical Armageddon.

We are given some preliminary information about the taped subjects, but it goes by too fast, and there are too many of them, for us to keep track. Only two make a vivid impression, both, as it happens, in different branches of the same business. One is the proprietor of a Queen Street sex store, who blames everything on greed and capitalism; he's not the only person in the show to make this case, but he's the most lucid. The other is a middle-aged, crack-addicted prostitute who presents the authentic face and voice of hopelessness. Asked how she would like to die -- another of the show's favourite questions -- she says "nobody dies in their sleep anymore." That's a line more haunting than most playwrights could devise.

It may also mean that we're concerned here not with some curse peculiar to our own age but with our old friend the Human Condition, that is, we all die. The show isn't sure and it doesn't pretend to be. Darren O'Donnell, who conceived and directed it, has said more than once that most conventional theatre, with scripts and actors, is boring. I wouldn't argue with that. But it doesn't follow that unconventional theatre is necessarily any less boring. Sheer performing skill, though not an end in itself, can be useful in holding boredom at bay. Of the current Mammalian Diving octet, only O'Donnell himself has any significant credentials in this respect, and his energy level here is unusually low. When he and his colleagues are left to talk among themselves, the results are painful, stilted trying to pass as casual. One of the four men (I'm not sure which; their names went by very fast) is a possible exception; he presides over the live interviews and does so with authority and nice comic timing. Two of those grilled on the first night -- by fellow audience members as well as from the stage -- responded with good-natured dignity; nobody, as the show says, is forced to participate, but it doesn't seem to have occurred to the team that having one person interrogated by a group automatically smacks of bullying. A third victim was an outright volunteer, with cheek to spare; quizzed on his claim that he gave 20% of his income to charity, he said that he included under that heading money spent on taking out women who didn't end up sleeping with him. Well, it's a point of view.

The things we do right are as much on the show's mind as the things we do wrong. At the end we're all asked to stand and recite a credo of good intentions, beginning with the declaration that each one of us is the best person in the room. As I didn't feel I could make that claim for myself, I stopped lip-synching fairly early on I'm all for happy endings but this is ridiculous.

- Diplomatic Immunities: The End runs through Feb. 25 at Buddies in Bad Times Theatre, 416-975-8555.

Color Photo : Tyler Anderson, National Post / Playwright Darren O' Donnell conceived and directed Diplomatic Immunities: The End.;
2007-02-21-a-unique-kind-of-eulogy:
THEATRE REVIEW

ELEGIES: A SONG CYCLE

BERKELEY STREET THEATRE, TORONTO

- - -

In what may be a financial first, the listed sponsors for Elegies include the Mount Pleasant Cemetery. There is an obvious congruence here between the backer and the thing backed; as its title suggests, William Finn's song cycle really is about dead people, real ones, personally known to the author. Im also reminded, in a backhanded way, of an advertising slogan that I used to see as I drove past Torontos most celebrated resting place. "Yes," it said, we have plots available. I often thought of putting them in touch with some playwrights of my acquaintance.

Elegies doesn't have a plot, but it does have a shape. It begins with papers raining down on the floor, as if from the twin towers on 9/11, and it ends by returning to that date. This, unfortunately, is the show's weakest point. But well start with the strengths, some of them surprising. This is a piece that continually risks sentimentality and self-pity, but nearly always avoids them.

Finn is the composer-lyricist of March of the Falsettos and its sequel, Falsetto land, two musicals that always struck me as more admirable for their ambitions than for their achievements; they tried to musicalize complex relationships but often failed to find the words that would make them concrete and dramatic. Elegies goes after simpler game; for the most part if offers soliloquies rather than conversations. In a series of songs -- initially conceived, I believe, for private commemoration rather than public performance -- Finn pays tribute to a lost generation of New Yorkers. Grief is the theme, but comedy is often the vessel; there are more laugh-out- loud lines here than in some musicals that go begging for them; the rhymes, unusually for this writer, are as neatly wrapped as the observations. And the music, wayward but piercing, offers just the right kind of support.

Those mourned include one genuine theatrical celebrity, the volcanic producer Joseph Papp ("Joe Papp / never took crap / except from writers "). Others are off-Broadway cult-figures, like the actress Peggy Hewitt (who was loved / and she knew it) and Jack Eric Williams, known to me as the original mountainous Beadle of Sweeney Todd, but also a composer. This last tribute is cleverly framed as a letter to another composer, Ricky Ian Gordon, with instructions to pass on regards to the other triple-barrelled songsmiths (hello, Jason Robert Brown; hello, Michael John La- Chiusa) of the generation below Finns own. There's some refreshing barb here.

You may not have known these people when the songs start, but you do by the time they end. It makes you all the readier to respond to those that strike closer to home. Mark's All-Male Thanksgiving memorializes what seems to have been an annual gay ritual; later in the show comes a song commemorating Mark himself. This arouses dangerous memories of a kind of song that used to be inescapable in New York cabaret -- the "my lovers just died of AIDS and its your fault" song -- but rises above them. It leads into a potentially even more dangerous kind of lament. Mark had a friend, Monica, who also died too young, and Finn offers his version of a song she might have sung to her daughter. Note the tact of that; it isn't palmed off as what she actually would have sung and, because of that remove, it's moving. Theres also a lovely tune called Venice, about a curmudgeonly member of the Thanksgiving group who wanted to take his friends there. And these in turn prepare us for Finn getting really autobiographical with a stoically cheerful number sung by his dying mother, being taken for her last drive, and a eulogy by the younger son who was at the wheel. It sounds as if it should be dreadful but it isnt. Finn writes from his heart but keeps himself, for the most part, out of the picture.

The production, by Acting Up Stage who last year gave us the excellent John and Jen, is very good, with witty and sensitive staging by Lezlie Wade and impeccable musical direction by Wayne Gwillim. The performances are mostly good and, in the case of Thom Allison who pretty much plays Finn, superb. He shows off an amazing technique without showing off; he holds long pealing notes in the middle of lines that don't disrupt the flow and flashes a satanic grin that modulates into a compassionate smile. He also does a very good Quentin Crisp impersonation. Barbara Barsky does well by the mother's song, and even better by an early acerbic number for a teacher with high standards and low expectations. Steven Gallagher starts the show arrestingly, though hes oddly starved of solos later on. Eliza-Jane Scott rises to Monicas song though she too often loses the thread of her other material. Michael Strathmore has an agreeable bounciness, which is just as well as he has to sing a thing called My Dogs, the punchline of which hardly justifies its length. I also resisted a tribute to someone called Fred who read Jean- Paul Sartre and hated Frank Sinatra, mainly, I suspect, for the sake of the rhyme.

And then there's the 9/11 finale, which is meant to put a significant seal on the show with a full-length number but only adds a portentousness that very nearly does it in. It's two songs in one- -for one of the victims phoning home, and for his widow, remembering the call. It doesnt begin to do justice to the desperate anguish of the situation. It merely dishes out show-song platitudes (of a New Age variety) at an interminable length, suggesting that the characters have all the time in the world. That is exactly what they didnt have.

- Until March 3. For ticket information call 416-368-3110.

2007-02-23-back-with-the-ussr:
THEATRE REVIEW

THE RUSSIAN PLAYS

HARBOURFRONT STUDIO THEATRE

Hannah Moscovitch's The Russian Play, the jewel of last year's Summerworks festival, is back in town, pluralized. The original three-actor piece has now been joined by a monologue entitled USSR that is almost as good. The resultant double bill runs until Sunday as part of the Hatch season of "emerging performance projects" at Harbourfront. It deserves, measuring shortness of run against quality of product, to be the hottest ticket in Toronto.

The original Russian Play starts off as a knowing satire on the traditional Western view of Slavic gloom. Mention is made of the tragic stories associated with Tolstoy and Chekhov, and we are then told a tale in which some of that spirit is transmuted into the later era of Stalin and the KGB. It concerns Sonya, who works in a small-town flower shop, conveniently placed near the local graveyard. At the age of 16, she has an affair with Petya, the gravedigger, who impregnates her and then goes back to Moscow, where he has a wife. "OK," says the narrator tartly (she says nearly everything tartly), "so heart of Sonya is broken, but heart is very strong organ." Besides, says Sonya herself, "what can gravedigger do for you -- dig your grave when you are dead." In fact, in the course of the play, Petya does precisely this for two of his nearest and dearest. Sonya moves to Smolensk, where she is kept by Kostya, a rich young kulak who treats her well until she starts pining for her sexy sexton. Kostya has secret police connections and calls on them to get her out of his way. The play's last section is an extraordinary combination of bleakly funny and heartbreakingly sad.

Moscovitch never puts a word wrong, and her mastery of tone is perfectly reflected in Natasha Mytnowych's direction. The production has now acquired a set (designed, like most sets at the moment, by Camellia Koo) consisting of a couple of screens craftily lit by Kimberly Purtell from behind, where characters glide on stage to miraculous effect. There is, as before, moody guitar accompaniment from Tom Howell, plus some other music composed by Claire Jenkins. The show also employs a choreographer, Monica Dottor, who has devised some haunting erotic pas de deux. Michelle Monteith is both the flinty narrator and the tender-hearted Sonya, two sides of the same kopeck, both ringing absolutely true. Everything she does is devastatingly strong, nothing is excessive and nothing unwanted spills over from one part of the play or the performance to another. There is no better acting currently happening in this town. As the two men by whom Sonya is loved and betrayed, Aaron Willis and Shawn Campbell are perfect on a smaller scale, one defiant in his perfidy, the other shamefaced.

USSR gives us an even later Russia, or perhaps a Russian diaspora. The protagonist-narrator is Elena, a Moscow doctor (unemployed, or at least unpaid) in the post-Soviet era who met a Canadian businessman, married him, came back with him to Toronto and bore an adored child. Loneliness and the language barrier undo her, and the ending is as stark as that of the companion play. The text is witty and so, in a satanically compassionate way, is the narrative development.

In both these plays, the law of unintended consequences is working flat-out and remorselessly. (As it also does, come to think of it, in Moscovitch's earlier play Essay, which proved that she could also handle a contemporary non-ethnic theme, without a hint of pastiche.) The publicity sells the play as being about "mail order brides," but that undersells it. It also implicitly claims that the play is about relations between Russia and Canada, and this maybe oversells it. It doesn't matter. This time the same director and lighting person also share the design credit; the production unfolds on a stage floor covered with table lamps, all but one of which have gone out by the time the action turns decisively dark. As Elena, Maev Beaty flawlessly conveys the sardonic vulnerability that, to this date at least, is the author's hallmark; I said there was no better acting in Toronto than Monteith's in the first play but I didn't say there was none as good.

- Runs until Feb. 25. For more information call 416-973-4000.

2007-02-24-actors-lurch-across-the-stage:
We are someway into The Sheep and the Whale before we hear of either a sheep or a whale. The sheep turn out to be sacrificial offerings in a Muslim ceremony. The play is largely about ethnic traditions and ethnic differences. It takes place on a ship that's nominally Russian but is actually controlled by a conglomerate, and whose crew and passengers are from all over. It's roaming around the Straits of Gibraltar, surrounded by separate civilizations. I don't know quite where the whale fits in. He's a blue one, who at some point in the past -- the play is full of flashbacks -- was sighted by a ship's doctor, the most sympathetic and enlightened person on board, who swum out fascinated to get closer to him. Maybe he (the whale, not the doctor) symbolizes the natural world that makes racial conflicts seem not only obscene but absurd.

The Sheep and the Whale is the first play of Moroccan-Canadian writer Ahmed Ghazali; he wrote it in French and it was translated by Bobby Theodore. It arrives in Toronto bearing golden opinions and a prize. It also arrives as a verbose mess, with a cast made up of poses rather than people. It starts with a storm at sea, which as in other plays from The Tempest on down, is confusing but exciting. Once the storm is over, the excitement lets up but the confusion doesn't.

The Russian freighter has hit a smaller boat, killing all but one of its human cargo of Moroccan refugees. Having thus acquired the bodies, the captain is obliged to find a home for them. None of the surrounding countries, however, will take them; a reflection, presumably, of what would have happened had the victims been alive. The big ship has, or had, its own stowaway: a black African whom the doctor befriended and who has now vanished; he's the object of a vicious manhunt by the sailors. There is also a tourist couple on board, the man Moroccan and the woman French. They are in a state of attraction-repulsion about one another and one another's cultures, demonstrated by some rough sounding sex they have just offstage. Once she wanted to learn Arabic, but he was against it. Now she only wants to go home and so, incompatibly, does he. It's thanks to him that we learn about the sheep sacrifice; as a boy he was very squeamish about cutting a ram's throat while facing Mecca. We also get a glimpse of the vessel's owners, represented by an American huckster-tycoon who delivers the company spiel in a cartoon scene that, in writing and performance, takes failed satire to an unnerving level of ham-handedness. All these elements are thrown in together but so inconclusively that when the end comes, it feels like an intermission. Relief, as the house lights come up, dukes it out with incredulity.

Some of the shapelessness can probably be blamed on Soheil Parsa's direction. (The show is a co-production between Cahoots Theatre Projects and Parsa's own Modern Times company with input from the host house, Theatre Passe Muraille.) The actors lurch clumsily across the stage, even in good weather, and they handle the dialogue in much the same way. Faced with lines too formal and too weighed down with ideas to pass as normal speech, they do what actors usually do when denied stylistic guidance: try hard to make everything sound realistic. That means forcing passion onto words that won't take the weight. It also means the most atrocious anthology of forced laughter, both individual and choral, that I have ever heard come off of a stage. (Some of the laughs in the auditorium sounded pretty forced as well.) It may be unfair to blame the performers themselves, since at least some of them are known to be good: Julian Richings, for example, who, as the idealistic doctor with a thing about whales, here puts himself through great gyrating corkscrews in an attempt to convey conviction. Or Soo Garay, whose solution to playing a walking symbol is to never stop shouting. Jim Warren as the skipper survives best, buttressed as he is by a handy ship's telephone and a ripe Russian accent. He proves his ethnicity by asking the French lady down to his cabin to view a rare edition of Anna Karenina. That's one funny line we can be reasonably sure was meant that way.

Blind Submission is confusing in a less grandiose fashion. It's the work of three actor-playwrights who wrote three separate plays, each about a person either suicidal or a rescuer of suicides. These have been sutured together, so we watch them in alternating chunks. Each performer, as well as playing his or her own protagonist, appears in other roles in the other plays, making the whole thing extremely hard to follow. Nor do the plays uncover much new ground: How much more is there to say about the travails of growing up both gay and Jewish? There are sparks of good writing, and the creative three --Dmitry Chepotevsky, Heidi Waters and especially Jenn Griffin -- wear their actors' hats with grace.

- The Sheep and the Whale runs through March 11 at Theatre Passe Muraille, 416- 504-7529; Blind Submission closes tomorrow at Theatre Centre, 416-539-0988.

2007-02-27-no-thanks-for-all-the-memorie:
THE POLISHED HOE

Enwave Theatre, Harbourfront

- - -

In theory, Colin Taylor and Alison Sealy-Smith have done a neat, economical job of adapting Austin Clarke's novel The Polished Hoe for the stage. The book is, for the most part, a long, purposefully rambling monologue in which Miss Mary Mathilda, doyenne of the Caribbean island of Bimshire, confesses to having murdered the white owner of the local plantation and gives the reasons why. The stage version retains the novel's confessional format, but makes some alterations, logical and sensible ones, to the order in which the information is handed out.

That is not enough to make a play, let alone an enlivening evening in the theatre. Reading the novel is like taking a long walk through very rich mud. The exertion is caused not so much by the intricate patois of Mary Mathilda's speech as by her habit of going off on long digressions. There is a reason for these: They amount to a miniature history of black-white relations in the West Indies. The dead man, symbolically named Mr. Bellfields, had exercised a droit du seigneur on any plantation woman who took his fancy, but Mary had been his long-time favourite (he was her master, she was his mistress) and had fathered her son -- now grown- up and an English-educated doctor. Everybody on the island had reason to hate Mr. Bellfeels (as they call him in the book), and Mary tells us what those reasons were. The way in which she does it is fine on the page, at least for a reader equipped with stamina and patience. Digression in the theatre , though, is death.

And so, even more, is what Kenneth Tynan, reviewing another novel adaptation, described as "exposition in its least dramatic form -- retrospective narration in the first person." That, unrelieved, is what the dramatized Polished Hoe gives us. The only variation comes in there being two police officers to take down the protagonist's statement. First there is the young Constable; he is then relieved by his superior, the Sargeant, a contemporary of Mary's and one who has long admired her from afar. He has his own memories, and the best scene in the play comes when the two go out from the living room of the Bellfields' Great House into the fields themselves; here we at least have the tension of two sets of recollections working against each other.

Otherwise there is no present tense action, no present-tense conflict. This won't do. There are many plays in which much of the action has occurred before the curtain rises, but -- apart from brilliant sketches like Hannah Moscovitch's USSR -- there are no good ones in which everything has. The Polished Hoe often bears a remarkable resemblance to Ibsen's Ghosts, what with its exhumation of an abusive relationship, its hints of an unfulfilled attraction between the two principal characters and its incorporation of a saucy maid throwing herself at an older gentleman (though the Sargeant is far more responsive to Gertrude, Mary Mathilda's young domestic, than Ibsen's Pastor Manders would ever have allowed himself to be). We also, as in Ibsen, get spectral presences located just off the main acting area, but here they aren't the younger generation preparing to repeat the mistakes of their elders and so kick-start the plot into new life; here they really are ghosts, or at least thin flashback figures acting out fragments of Mary's story in a desperate attempt to add some variety to the evening. Things happen in Ghosts. Even in the supposedly action-less Chekhov we get such exciting events as the selling of a cherry orchard -- and The Polished Hoe (a weapon, incidentally, not a woman, though funnily enough that might work) recalls that play, too, with its magnetic chatelaine and her inarticulate admirer. And don't give me Waiting for Godot; stuff happens there too, if only in the ebb and flow of feeling between the two tramps. But nothing happens in The Polished Hoe.

The adaptors don't do much for their own script in their other guises of director and leading player. Taylor's staging and pacing are ponderous. Sealy-Smith, young for her matriarchal role, gives an efficient account of Mary Mathilda, but considering the weight of personal and racial tragedy the character is required to bear and the reverence in which she is said to be held by everybody else on the island, efficiency is not enough to cut it. Nor does it take in the sly humour that permeates the novel and could surely find a place in the play. Lacking these elements, the performance becomes monotonous. Tony Thompson's Sargeant is monotonous too, but his is a rather splendid kind of monotony. This Barbados actor (the show is a co-production by our Obsidian Theatre Company and their Frank Collymore Hall) has a vast, slow, respectful presence, impassive but not unfeeling. Indeed his recollection of a long-lost love (three rejection letters and out) is the one touching moment in the evening. Jamaal Grant also does his bit for the honour of the force as the Constable, just graduating from being wet behind the ears.

- Runs until March 4. Call 416- 973-4000 for more information.

2007-03-02-a-good-sign-of-the-apocalypse:
THEATRE REVIEW

THE FOUR HORSEMEN PROJECT

FACTORY THEATRE

- - -

You might describe The Four Horsemen Project as an archival extravaganza, though that, like most other possible descriptions, would sell it short. Some years ago Kate Alton, a choreographer, and Ross Manson, director of the Volcano theatre company, heard a recording by The Four Horsemen, a quartet of 1970s Toronto experimental poets who were wedded to sounds more than to words, and whose works were intended to be heard rather than read. They meant their poems as visceral experiences. Alton and Manson, with a quartet of dancers who are more than dancers, have set out to expand that experience, using the Horsemen's poems as base. They have triumphantly succeeded.

The original Horsemen were Rafael Barreto-Rivera, Paul Dutton, Steve Mc- Caffery and BP Nichol who is now dead. He seems also to have been the most influential of the four, and one of his creations -- a pome is your body -- serves both as the show's finale and as its overall theme.

The mix also includes some cheeky animation, designed by Bruce Alcock. Nichol and company described what they did as "intermedia," or so a television show of the time assures us. We're more likely to call this idea "mixed media," though even that is beginning to sound a little faded.

Anyway, part of this production's strategy is to pit its own more advanced tools at the service of the old idea. We start with a clip from that sober old TV documentary projected on the stage's back wall. Then it's dragged down to the floor and the first performer to appear, the joyous Naoko Murakoshi, begins not so much tapping as rhythmically stomping on it. She manages to make what could be a gesture of dismissal into a tribute. She also talks, introducing us to the word-jazz and foot-percussion that will be the foundation of the show. She plays with the words "a drum and a wheel," becoming both as she whirls round in circles that may not be ever-decreasing but are certainly ever-accelerating. And the words themselves keep pace, scrolling in different formations all over the acting area. I don't think they're all that wonderful as literature, but that isn't the point. The writers seem to have been laying a perfect foundation for a show of which they are unlikely to have conceived.

The three other performers are Jennifer Dahl, Andrea Nann and Graham McKelvie; they, too, can use their voices as well as their limbs, and they all have stellar personalities. Nann and Dahl are the sophisticates -- "worldlings," the Elizabethans would have called them, though maybe here it should be "wordlings" -- to Murakoshi's gamine. McKelvie, who appears older than his female colleagues, often regards them with beguiling bemusement; he works through it, as he also gets to share an erotic duet with Dahl.

The most enchanting things about the show are its cheek and its colour. Alton's choreography comes from all over; there is even a Hawaiian number with ukuleles. Manson's direction, much helped by Itai Erdal's lighting, knits everything together, makes everything flow.

Some sequences outstay their welcome but the show as a whole doesn't. Toronto has recently been inundated with tributes to the Beat poets who were the Horsemen's precursors. Here the beat really goes on.

- Runs until March 4. Call 416-504-9971 for more information.
2007-03-03-devastation-all-around-there-:
At the start of Scorched, Wajdi Mouawad's play about memory, kinship and genocide, 10 of Toronto's finest troop on stage and fix the audience with their best impassive stares. There is one among them who, though looking initially no less baleful than the others, stands out as the only cast member wearing a suit and tie. This is Alon Nashman who plays, delightfully, a Quebec lawyer with a talent for mangling the language that goes beyond mere malapropism. Life," he tells his clients, "is not a bowl of berries, especially it seems when youre caught between the devil and the Blue Danube."

Linda Gaboriau, who translated the play from French, has been most creative with these addled aphorisms. Of course, they eventually begin, like all running gags, to limp a little, and there is the question of what theyre doing here at all. The play is anything but a comedy, and "comic relief" in a sombre context can become a mechanical and even demeaning device. One can, though, make a case for the relevance of this one. The play is partly about language, about its power to recall and record events and maybe to redeem them. Some of it concerns the attempts of a Taliban-like regime to eliminate reading and writing, especially among women.

There are things in Scorched I respect, but I didn't much like it. It's another Quebec play (Mouawad is Lebanese-Canadian) in which abstraction trumps action. Thats not to say that it doesnt have lots of story. Like Mouawad's Tideline, it's a quest play concerned with honouring the dead. A male and female twin come to the lawyers office to hear the will of his old friend, their mother. She came to Canada a devastated woman from a devastated Middle Eastern country; unnamed of course, according to the annoying belief that one can get at the particular from the general rather than the other way about. She has left her children letters to deliver to their father, whom they never knew, and their brother, of whom theyve never heard. So the daughter, and later the son, set off for the old country, where they discover one horrific piece of history after another: reprisals and counter- reprisals for an original offence nobody can now remember. And wherever they go, the siblings keep running into David Fox whose recurring appearances as a series of reminiscent elders, each more doddering than the last, become another running gag.

In counterpoint, we watch the story of the mother, Nawal, herself. She is played at three stages of her life by three different actresses, though a single player (Valerie Buhagiar, who wavers between nagging and genuinely fierce) plays a friend who's with her two-thirds of the way. Janick Hebert is appealing and later troubling as the teenaged Nawal whose newborn boy is torn from her by order of a malevolent mother. Kelli Fox is the fortyish Nawal who's become literate and is politicized when she finds herself in the middle of an atrocity. She has a set-piece speech describing it, and its a sign of whats wrong with the play that even Fox, who can do grief and anger better than anyone, can't stop it from sounding like a set piece, though it's supposed to be a spontaneous reaction. Conversely, Nicola Lipman gives a shattering account of Nawal in her sixties, testifying at the trial of a torturer, with a speech that actually is a prepared statement.

The things the play tells us (or, more accurately, reminds us of) are genuinely terrible. The dramatic test is whether they are any more terrible for being told us by these people in this story, and apart from Lipmans speech, I dont think they are. The play stakes an awful lot on metaphor. The initially battling siblings, for example, reflect the country from which they came. (And even, come to think of it, the one they're in now. She's a mathematician. Hes a boxer. Whats that supposed to add?) Internecine warfare occasions a particularly brutal case of incest, and the whole play can be taken as a scrambled riff on the Oedipus theme, down to the abandoned child rescued on a mountainside. It's also about mother- daughter hatred, and that's one theme too many, with a posthumous reconciliation that smacks of fairy dust.

The twins are excellently played by Sophie Goulet and Sergio Di Zio who, doubling as the young Nawals lover, more than confirms the promise he showed in Leo. Theres one more actor, Alex Poch- Goldin, who's held in reserve till near the end and turns out to be a devastating secret weapon. Nearly everyone in Richard Rose's production indulges at some point in unfocused rhetorical acting but they're a fine crew in a mostly swift and adroit staging. There's a scene in which characters from one time frame run round the perimeter of the stage while characters from another conduct a conversation in the middle. Like much else, it starts out impressive and ends up obscure.

- Scorched runs through March 31 at the Tarragon Theatre. Call 416-531- 1827 for ticket information.

2007-03-07-an-exotic-domesticity:
THEATRE REVIEW

JOHN AND BEATRICE

TARRAGON THEATRE

- - -

Beatrice sits munching an apple in a sparsely furnished room at the top of a 33-storey building with a broken elevator. She is awaiting a suitor. She had advertised for one, placing posters all over town that promise a substantial reward to any man "who can interest, move and seduce her. In that order." Up the stairs puffs John, who, as a self described bounty hunter, feels that this is an offer right in his line. When he enquires about that reward, Beatrice informs him that her dad, a plastic garbage-can king, was decapitated in a freak auto accident, that she is the heir to his fortune and that the building and most of the block on which it stands belong to her. John takes up the triple challenge and does very well at it, mainly by telling stories, both piquant and poignant, about his own early life. In fact, it looks as if he's won.

The situation in Carole Frechette's John and Beatrice may not seem the most plausible you have ever encountered, but it plainly wasn't meant to be. Beatrice is a fairy-tale heroine: a latter-day Rapunzel with a tower block for a tower, a Sleeping Beauty whose slumbers are broken up into abrupt little naps. At least, that's how she sees herself. The play is a fantasy about a fantasist. John's a yarn-spinner as well, but his stories seem more grounded, even if his way of life--helping old ladies find lost pets, hunting down chainsaw killers, living off the rewards and only accepting payment in $20 bills -- sounds a trifle exotic. He might be the modern version of the woodcutter who wins the princess. But times have moved on, and we might guess from the characters' names that they are mismatched. Their ideal partners would probably be called Dante and Janet.

There's a preciousness about the play, especially in its second half, that can get on the nerves, but I never felt like giving up on it. There is a human current running through it -- far more so than in some of the more elaborate plays that have been fetching up in Toronto recently and more too than in Frechette's other (and in my mind over praised) plays like Elisa's Skin and Helen's Necklace. There is also wit. I actually believed in John's story about how he got started on his strange career: rescuing a young woman from drowning and finding, after he had moved in with her, that she had become something other and less romantic. "Her voice was too shrillher dress was too fancy." (The translation is by John Murrell, who habitually gives Frechette a head start over other Francophone Canadian playwrights arriving on Anglophone stages.) John has learned something about love, if only not to look for easy definitions of it. Beatrice, despite having had, she says, 14 men in her life, is still clinging to received ideas from some age of innocence. "Someone told me," she says inter alia, "that if you love a man you cook him a rack of lamb." Ah, that fine old French culture.

After John has theoretically won Beatrice and she has theoretically succumbed, the two perform a sped-up version of what married life might be, looking forward in much the same way that the nonagenarian couple of Ionesco's The Chairs look back. It isn't encouraging. Their emotional vocabularies don't match. ("Don't push me," says John, metaphorically. She does, literally.) The ending is trite, but the play survives. It's a paradox: You never believe in these people, but you still want to know what happens to them.

It's very well done. Leah Cherniak's direction keeps the juices flowing and makes the most of the few sequences of violent action. Yannik Larivee's set, with a checkered floor and walls tapering in exaggerated crooked perspective, is an eye-catcher. Under Lesley Wilkinson's lighting the colour of those walls changes from faded ochre to orange-red, while constantly changing vistas tease us through the solitary window. Otherwise, the most notable visual features are the bottles of drinking water, brand undetectable, that litter the floor, and on which Beatrice seems to subsist. (What good is sitting alone in your room? Not much, apparently.) But it's the acting that makes the evening. Rick Roberts' John is a fine compound of burliness and sensitivity. Caroline Cave's Beatrice is a woman passionately determined to be disappointed by life. There are even moments at which, moving from grinning incredulity to squeaky- voiced disparagement, she seems to be channelling Jon Stewart responding to something more than usually outrageous in the news. This is a visually compelling, vocally rich performance that draws on both the princess and the clown: a psychological striptease -- a physical one too, in one rather specialized regard -- that still leaves a secret at the core.

- Runs until March 24 at the Tarragon Theatre. For tickets call 416-531-1827.

THEATRE REVIEW

HOUSE

BUDDIES IN BAD TIMES THEATRE

- - -

Daniel MacIvor's House begins with just a chair on stage. Well, it is billed as a stand up, sit down, one man comedy nightmare. When the author-performer, the one man in question, walks on the stage, the first thing he does is pick up the chair and throw it offstage. He then walks off himself and returns with another chair, a straight-backed thing indistinguishable from its predecessor. This doesnt meet his standards either; he flings it away, walks off again and returns with a third, again identical. And this time - - obeying the comedians sacred Rule of Three--he does sit down on it and starts talking. He is standing up again pretty soon; there is, it turns out, more standup than sit-down in this routine. The sedentary position would hardly do justice to the character's rage.

So what else is new? This revived play, marking positively the last appearance of MacIvor's production company da da kamera, is another of MacIvors studies in anger and loneliness. Its the most concentrated of them, the least complicated apart from a few sequences where the hero's misery train gets derailed for some spookily-lit monologues within the monologue, and probably the most entertaining. MacIvor plays Victor, who works for a septic-tank company. This isn't what he wanted to do with his life. He wanted to be an engineer. But like the man in the Peter Cook sketch who wanted to be a judge but "didnt

have the Latin" and so went down the mines instead, Victor has been mis-routed by circumstance. In this case the circumstance is a hysterically controlling mother, determined that her son shall go into septic tanks like his father before him. His father isnt still in septic tanks; he got out to go work for a circus -- actually it sounds more like a fairground--as the Saddest Man in the World. One way and another, Victor seems to have inherited a lot from him.

Vic also tells us about his sister who has a houseful of dogs, with

MacIvor controls the play with one of which she's in love. He also speaks of his wife, who is also his third cousin and who despises him for his job and, probably, for other reasons. She also seems to have a secret career, secret from Victor anyway, as a dominatrix. And Vic, with good reason, belongs to a therapy group presided over by a cheerful soul to whom he refers to as Joseph- call-me- Joe-and-I-won't. (This recurring phrase is both funny in itself and a sign of the heros obsessiveness.) Vics best friend in the group is a kleptomaniac. And he isn't happy at work because, not only is it not what he wants to do, but everybody there ignores him, especially his boss.

MacIvor controls the play, under Daniel Brooks's direction, with crack timing and a gimlet eye. The play is one of his earliest and he seems to have updated it a little. When welcoming the audience -- hes very upfront about the fact that were all in a theatre -- he congratulates us on not having stayed home to watch "a TV show about an angry doctor." That reference to the other House must be newly added, but it ties in very well with one of the main script's chief devices: a violent spasm, coupled with a shout, that overcomes the speaker every time the word "house" crops up in his text. Finally, we get to his issues with his own house; these turn out to be crucial and to bring together elements from both his marriage and his job.

This cumulative section, though, is the weakest part of the play. There's too much that strains credulity, even given Vics lavish capacity for self-deception. The play is stronger on anecdote than on narrative. The details are sometimes scary and sometimes the best kind of funny, the kind that takes you totally by surprise, while also being totally logical. There is also an epiphany, whose intended seriousness I wouldnt want to guess at and to which your response will depend on your taste in epiphanies. Anyway the production, crowning da da kamera's final retrospective, is a testimony to MacIvor's high talent, and a stimulus to wondering where he will take it from here.

- Until April 1. Call 416-975-8555 for more information.

2007-03-10-cartoon-history-of-canada-out:
The white politicians and entrepreneurs are back doing what they do best: swindling, land-grabbing and oppressing the native population. The native population are doing what they do best, resisting fiercely while squabbling among themselves so as to make victory even less likely. And Michael Hollingsworth, an artistic director of Video Cabaret and author and stager of most of their works, is doing what he does best, which is making vicious fun of the lot of them. At least I have to assume it's what he does best, since in 10 years or more of watching his work Ive never seen him do anything else.

The History of the Village of the Small Huts, Video Cabarets cartoon history of Canada, has now reached its seventh instalment, The Saskatchewan Rebellion. It's 1884, and that new-fangled railroad contraption is continuing with its mission, adumbrated in the preceding Canadian Pacific Scandal, of crossing the continent, spike by spike, encroaching and disinheriting everything that stands in its way. Doing a show about it may count as performing CPR. This time the victims are the Metis of Saskatchewan, whose struggle is led by Gabriel Dumont and the returned, and possibly deranged, hero Louis Riel, and the Cree, under Chief Big Bear. The grasping Donald Smith heads the Company; John A. Macdonald, as complacently power drunk, or just drunk, as before happily -- well, more or less happily -- supplies, at public expense, the massive infusions of cash so grandiose a project requires.

History, in short, repeats itself; and so does Hollingsworth. Much of what he does as a director certainly bears repeating. After all this time, one takes his black-box staging methods for granted, but there's nobody else who does what he does, at least nobody who does it with live actors rather than puppets. (His actors, or at least the people they play, may resemble puppets, but thats another thing.) On a tiny stage in the back room of a pub -- Hollingsworth, in a welcoming speech, called it a "cosmic dollhouse" -- seven actors playing an average of four roles apiece perform prodigies of quick change in gorgeously exaggerated costumes (designed by Astrid Janson and Sarah Armstrong) and a positive forest of wigs. Andy Moro supplies lighting of pinpoint precision and awesome lack of spillage, and the performers achievement in invariably hitting their marks deserves a round of applause of its own. The scenes are innumerable and, of course, short. This, as I've noted before, prevents both players and spectators from getting closely involved with any of the characters. Despite the proximity of stage and auditorium, and the clownishness of the performance style, which you'd think would be ingratiating, Video- Cabaret thrives on keeping everything at a distance. Its live theatre pretending to be canned.

Theres good and bad to this, and The Saskatchewan Rebellion offers both. The political intrigues are hard to follow, not I think, because they're especially confusing as narrative, but because the characters executing them are so bloodless. We know they're despicable, even before theyve opened their mouths, so we stop being interested. This goes, by the way, for the Metis leader Gabriel Dumont, who is decidedly bloodthirsty, as well as for the white men; the show spreads its satire around, though it reserves its contempt for the Caucasians. Video- Cabaret shows have, Ill swear, a special sound: a sneering acoustic. Words come out slow and curdled, surrounded by dead air. This show, though, has slightly more emotional content than most. When the military and the Mounties set about starving the Cree off their lands and into reservations, it's moving as well as horrific. Some of this is due to the performance of Michaela Washburn as the Cree chief, a tiny figure -- not so much Big Bear as Baby Bear -- of piteous dignity, especially when trying to be crafty in the face of firepower. (Washburn is the only woman in the cast, and only one of the roles she plays is female.) The other outstanding turn comes from Mac Fyfe as Riel. If the show uses video techniques, then he is the only character permitted a close-up. We see him right downstage, his face to us and his back to the judge, as he is tried, convicted and condemned to hang. He is also on his knees, though this fact is concealed from us until he gets up; the lighting is that good. Earlier, as a charismatic leader, he has teetered brilliantly on the edge of insanity, a religious zealot who seems to be his own God. Fyfe, uniquely, plays just the one role, and he's the Riel thing. The script goes in for some low-rent anachronisms: the victors declare that theyre going to party like it was 1885. Far more agonizing is when John A., at a temporary low point and reaching for the bottle, sings "my kind of town, Oblivionville is"; it doesnt even scan, and he does it over and over again In related news, it's the rich what gets the pleasure and the poor what gets the blame, throughout.

- The Saskatchewan Rebellion runs through April 8 at the Cameron House. Call 416-703-1725 for tickets.

2007-03-13-beam-me-up-boatswain:
THE TEMPEST

University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, Mich.

- - -

Patrick Stewart's Prospero lives in an Arctic hut. Thats the set-up for a sensational new production of The Tempest by the Royal Shakespeare Company that opened last year in Stratford-on-Avon, England, then formed part of a three play RSC residency at the University of Michigan in Ann Arbor (which is where I saw it), and is now playing at the Novello Theatre (formerly the Strand) in London. Somehow -- perhaps, as he himself suggests, by heavenly providence -- the rotten boat into which the magicians enemies consigned him when they threw him out of his Milanese dukedom fetched up amid the tundra. Years later, when he raises the tempest in The Tempest, his magical powers prove strong enough to blow those same enemies all the way from North Africa to the North Pole, or somewhere close.

In leading this classical contingent, Stewart returns to his roots. He was an RSC stalwart -- the kind of actor people call "reliable" -- for about two decades before his abrupt ascent to international fame as Captain Luc Picard, a role for which his aquiline authority made him a perfect, if unexpected, fit. He has come out the other end, not just an ex- Star Trekker but a full star presence, his Shakespearean skills not just intact but enhanced. His Prospero is a craggy, hairless seer (Stewart has been bald for as long as anyone can remember; even when young he was nobody's juvenile lead) who is angry and powerful but not, by current standards, especially bleak or bitter.

He may hound and despise his foes but his ruling passion is his love for his daughter, Miranda, an affection wrinkled with humour. Many actors have raised laughs from Prospero's obsessive injunctions to Ferdinand, Mirandas betrothed, to honour her chastity until marriage. Stewart conveys that, though he means every word of it, he is also laughing at himself, at his own inability to leave it alone. He trusts them just far enough to assign them separate bunk beds in what the text calls his cell. He has done it up well, and one notes that he has been able to provide climate-appropriate clothing; Maria Gales enchantingly impetuous Miranda wears a woolly bonnet, a heavy coat made out of multi-coloured scraps and a clumping pair of jackboots. Maybe her dad had Ariel and his other spirits run them up cheap.

Rupert Goold, a young director mounting his first RSC Shakespeare, has done the most important thing possible for any play; he has created a world, a breathtaking one. The set, designed by Giles Cadle, has as its signature device a traverse curtain that continually wipes away one icy vista and replace it with another; the barren island has never seemed bleaker or more specific. The sense of place is an enormous stimulus to the actors, and especially to the shipwrecked courtiers whose scenes, so often tedious, are here gripping and even witty.

On their way home to Italy from celebrating a royal marriage in Tunis, they look as if they had been travelling first-class on the Titanic and were tempest-tossed while half-way through dinner. So they come ashore wearing Eddie Bauer life jackets over their evening clothes. This makes them look incongruous but also dangerous. The barbed banter of the corrupt Sebastian and Antonio is not only comprehensible but viciously funny. Meanwhile, their victim, the virtuous and garrulous Gonzalo (James Hayes), has his stature enhanced; his Utopian vision of the island transformed manages to seem both absurd and impressive, and the same goes for his speech of blessing in the last scene. Meanwhile, the irredeemable Antonio (Ken Bones) grows ever more impassive; physically he resembles his brother Prospero (he's bald too), and it's a blistering irony that when Miranda discovers the "brave new world" of men, its her uncle, so like but unlike her father, whom she first salutes.

The court party has earlier been exposed to one of the most stunning effects I have ever seen. The phantom banquet that tantalizes the weary and famished travellers here takes the form of a giant seal, drawn in on a sled. They slice it open, and start tearing out pieces of bloody blubber.

As they begin to eat, out of the belly of the beast there springs up a harpy Ariel (Julian Beach) who, even in his earlier unwinged state, is as far removed as possible from the traditional balletic sprite: He is tall, gaunt and flour-faced; he moves with the deliberation of Frankensteins monster, and his voice is a minatory croak. He is authentically other-worldly, but though technically inhuman, he can reach out towards feelings. It's as important here that Ariel should beg mercy for Prospero's victims as that Prospero should grant it. Their parting when Ariel claims his freedom is uncommonly moving. The goddesses wedding masque becomes an Inuit fertility rite; the clown scenes arent very inventive, but they do maintain the play's power dynamics, as between a rather lightweight Caliban and the two sots he's unwise enough to worship. The productions end is a powerful fusion of harmony and discord; as Stewarts Prospero prepares to return to civilian life, his cell splits apart and, instead of merely breaking his magic staff, he hurls it into the ruins where it catches fire and explodes.

The Tempest is extraordinary, but the RSC's other two productions, Antony and Cleopatra and Julius Caesar, also won very favourable response from the Ann Arbor audience. These were the kind of alert, responsive houses that actors rise to. The RSC, which everyone in England was recently giving up for dead, has spectacularly bounced back.

- The Tempest runs at the Novello Theatre, London, to March 24. Visit www.rsc.org.uk or call 011-44-870-950-0940 for more information.

2007-03-17-civilization:
There is a recurring kind of bad acting that I seem to keep banging on about, and that I can best define as "passion in excess of the object." It usually manifests itself as nagging and pleading. Two characters, let us say, are having an argument. The actors turn the thoughts and emotions into grievances, to be stuffed desperately down one another's throats. There is a lot of this about, maybe because we have lost our feeling for the weight of words, and so try to colour them, garishly.

Bad acting is not the exclusive province of bad actors. Lucy, a new production at Can Stage, is the work of genuinely talented people. Damien Atkins' play stars Seana McKenna, who is more than talented; she is, quite simply, the best. She plays Vivian, an anthropologist who is also the mother of an autistic daughter, the Lucy of the title. Lucy, now aged 13, has been brought up by Vivian's divorced husband who wants some time off with his new girlfriend. So Vivian has to take care of the child for a year, though she has always shrunk from human contact and never wanted to be a mother, either before or after becoming one. But she eventually bonds with Lucy, deciding after a consultation with a knowledgeable but unsympathetic therapist that she and her daughter have a lot in common. In fact Vivian comes to believe that she is autistic too -- hence her lack of the conventional social skills and instincts -- and that autism represents the shape of things to come. Or rather, a return to the shape of things that were: Civilization was a huge mistake, and modern society is destroying itself by its overbearing insistence on notions like Feeling and Sharing and Community.

I don't know how much scientific basis there may be to this, or even how much Atkins himself believes it, but it's an undeniably provocative idea, even an appealing one, that runs refreshingly counter to today's mushy orthodoxies. The first act can't shake off the disease-of-the-week disease, but it still gives us an economically constructed, sympathetically observed view of Lucy's condition and Vivian's attempts to cope with it. We can see for ourselves the similarities between them, and we begin to think that the play is hitting us over the head with the irony of it all. It turns out that Atkins has far more in mind. When Vivian gets to state her case, her auditor and shocked antagonist is her former research assistant. In earlier scenes this lady has been a mere device, a foil whose function has been to ask the right questions at the right moment, and Philippa Domville, who plays her, has not been able to bring her to life. Now, faced with an idea that repels her, she becomes a raging fury, generating far more heat than light. She devalues her own case even as she tries to make it; which cannot have been the intention. The scene becomes a screamfest and even McKenna, usually the most fastidious of actresses, gets caught up in it. She gets off some wonderful sharp zingers ("You can decide for yourself, am I the future or am I a bitch?" encapsulates both the character and the argument very nicely, with wit working in the service of meaning) but too often the sense of what she is saying is swamped by the sheer belligerence of it. It all goes by too fast and too furious.

The earlier scenes offer McKenna good jagged writing to depict a good jagged personality, and she inhabits every twist, turn and hesitation of it. She plays her final desperation to the hilt, and does the same for some disconcertingly plain speaking: "You do this every day?" Vivian asks her husband incredulously, when first confronted with the specifics of looking after Lucy. Lucy herself is seen in double focus; she's a clinical study in the symptoms of autism (Meg Roe handles the remoteness and the ferocity splendidly) and she's a lyrical narrator, letting us know what she really thinks, especially about her mother. The two strands converge at the end of the first act, when Lucy creeps into Vivian's bed and Vivian finds that she can, first frighteningly and then joyfully, hear with her daughter's ears, see with her eyes. It's a tricky scene, to put it mildly, and it's done here with a lot of flashing lights and clangorous sounds that remain just tricky. Eda Holmes is a fine but uneven director, and this production has got away fromher.

Teresa Przyblski contributes a chilly unit set that does duty for everywhere without quite convincing as anywhere. Brendan Murray as the medic and Tony Munch as Vivian's ex are competent though Munch's compulsive arm-gestures are reminiscent of the seals in A Fine Romance who flap their fins to express emotion The last scene finds the two guys and the uptight assistant (whose business it doesn't quite seem to be) uniting against Vivian who wants to take Lucy to Africa, presumably to connect with something fine and primal. There's a paradox for you, a play and character that seemed to be coming out against fashionable touchy-feeliness ending up as touchy- feely as they come.

- Lucy runs through April 14 at Berkeley Street Theatre, 416- 368-3110.
