2007-03-24-action-reclaims-bad-acting:
Last week I tried to describe a recurrent form of bad acting that I called "passion in excess of the object." I also referred to "nagging and pleading." This week my vocabulary in this matter received a welcome boost.

I attended a rehearsal of Action, a Sam Shepard play from the 1970s, that opens next Thursday at the Equity Showcase Theatre. It's a play whose four characters exist in largely unexplained states of obsessive despair. Toward its end we find a man called Jeep (played in this production by Brendan Gall) concentrating

all his energy on gutting a fish while meditating on the frightening fact that he always seems to be eating. Meanwhile, another man, Shooter (Greg Palmer), is crouched under a chair that he's pulled down on top of himself and from which he declares that he will never move, ever. It would be hard to claim that these two guys and the women (Maev Beaty and Aviva Armour-Ostroff ) who share their space communicate with one another, but they do in some sort converse.

Brendan Healy, the director, working on a scene between Jeep and Shooter, gave Palmer a note that struck me as very perceptive. "Can you," he said, "not play deny? Just set the record straight." The concept of "playing deny" is not one that I had encountered before, but it seemed to sum up much that had been bothering me for years. An actor states a feeling or an opinion but inside of just stating it ("setting the record straight"), which can be very powerful, he speaks as if he expected to be contradicted. He is denying something that hasn't actually happened, refuting an objection that hasn't been made. A querulous note sets in. It happens all the time.

Bad acting, as I noted last week, can happen to good actors. The interesting thing about Healy's production in this context is that it sets out to reclaim Bad Acting, to give bad acting a good name. Of course, it all depends what you mean by bad acting. The kind that I've been going on about is something for which Healey and his actors have, I discovered, as little time as I do. Bad acting can only be defined in opposition to what we think of as good acting, and it's these players' contention that we've come to equate good acting with "naturalistic acting." And that this, especially in the constricted form in which we encounter it in films and television, may represent surface reality but does not represent "truth."

I've heard that song before, and I have problems with it. For a start, it seems to me that surface reality -- how people actually talk and behave -- may not be the whole of human life but is an important part of it; if you ignore it you are halfway to treating people as symbols, which is often bad theatre, or to regarding "reality" as some kind of bourgeois mystification, which is always bad politics. I think, too, that if you asked most people what they thought of as good acting, they would say that it was "natural acting." Here I have to quote, yet again, from Kenneth Tynan who once wrote: "the rise of the natural style is an event of ubiquitous date that has taken place roughly twice in every century from the sixteenth onward [Garrick] staggered the public by the naturalness of his manner [Edmund Kean's] command of natural speech revolutionized a theatre inured to Garrick's rantings Breaking decisively with the past, the Moscow Art

Theatre under Stanislavsky inaugurated an acting method founded

on the cataclysmic idea that actors should act natural."

Acting changes because behaviour changes. It's very largely a matter of rhythm. We can respect history but when it comes to judging something new, we respond to what makes us laugh, what makes us cry, what makes us believe.

What we believe depends on the kind of play we're watching. We can accept people expressing their emotions in song or in blank verse, but we want those forms to be personalized. Audiences are very good at identifying conventions and adjusting to them (though much ink has been wasted by theorists who don't believe that they are or should be). The kind of Bad Acting Healey & Co. are trying to reclaim is not bad at all. It's extravagant acting for extravagant circumstances. Palmer made a very good point when he said that what passes for naturalism on TV is actually unnatural. It's circumscribed. When an actor on screen receives bad news, he tries to react to it as quietly and subtly as possible. In real life, we don't actually do this. We cry, we scream, we explode.

The characters in Action are at the end of their respective tethers, and Healey is encouraging his cast to express their desolation as graphically as possible. Gall is breathing differently from the way actors usually do -- "pushing out all your air before talking" -- which, as he says, "puts you in a dangerous place." Let me confess that I'm not convinced that Shepard's play needs the extreme treatment to which this production seems bent on subjecting it; I hear it lighter, more conversational, in line with the old principle that the way to play an absurd situation is to treat it as absolutely normal. That makes it funny, which I suspect is what will happen anyway once it gets in front of an audience. But what I saw was powerful in its own terms, and the more I saw, the more it grew on me.

- Action runs March 29 to April 1 at Equity Showcase Theatre. Call 416- 533- 6100 for ticket information.

2007-03-28-a-child-s-play:
THEATRE REVIEW

THE RED HORSE IS LEAVING

Theatre Centre, Toronto

- - -

In The Red Horse Is Leaving, Erika Batdorf plays her own mother. That is Thaya Whitten, a Nova Scotian woman of multiple talents; primarily she was a painter, but she was also a jazz musician and some kind of performance artist. She was also mentally ill, with a doubleedged attitude to the drugs prescribed for her condition. She depended on them, but she also feared addiction and worried how they might affect her creativity.

Batdorf, herself an accomplished performer, begins this solo show with a long and sometimes very funny silent sequence showing the artist in her studio. Distractedly (the piece might almost be said to be a continuing pun on the different meanings of the word "distraction"), she juggles a cigarette and a cup of coffee, neither of them probably the most advisable of substances. At one point she seems to be attempting to paint with the cigarette. She makes a shaky but determined approach to the canvas on her easel, then realizes that the brush she has chosen is not the one she wanted and shakes her head in gentle frustration. When she sits down, her knee visibly trembles.

When she starts talking she talks directly to us, breaking the fourth wall in a manner that seemed to me too self-conscious for its own good. To draw attention to the fact that you're shattering a convention is a strange kind of double-bluff. It fits perhaps with Whitten's own nervous self-awareness as a performer. Drawing on her subject's journals, Batdorf presents her as simultaneously in a gallery and in a theatre. She is conducting a participatory lecture on painting. What, she asks, is the purpose of art or, more specifically, what is the artist's motive? Profit, communication, self-expression? She opts, I think, for the last, telling aspiring artists that "the only thing you have to offer the world is you." She alludes to her own reputation as "a controversialist" and to the way she shocked the folks back home: "Women in the Lutheran Church didn't do such things."

Her subject for the day, both as painter and lecturer, is fear. She suggests that the colour of fear might be red, and offloads a splodge of it onto her canvas. She then calls for further suggestions from the house, and various spectators step forward to add their own chosen shades to the composition. There is nothing embarrassing about this audience participation; Batdorf is an underplayer, and the attitude she presents -- firm in her ideas, diffident in their presentation -- makes everyone feel at ease. On the first night assorted volunteers contributed black, green and yellow to the picture; Andy McKim, Theatre Passe Muraille's newly appointed artistic director here making his debut as a directed artist, opted for aubergine, which Whitten- Batdorf translated as "black-purple."

I can understand being afraid of aubergines. In the end, though, I find it hard to conceive of fear as a colour, which may explain why I found this whole section of the show oddly whimsical. At the end of it, though, a phone rings, and it was in Batdorf 's reaction to that I truly saw fear, stabbing and unadorned.

One section of this show, sympathetically directed by Todd Hammond, bleeds imperceptibly into the next, and it seems that suddenly we are back in the studio, watching and hearing a verbalized elaboration of the opening silent sequence. We see Whitten battling with her psychological and chemical demons, trying to keep the world of patrons, dealers and caregivers both at hand and at bay. One sly reference to her daughter Erika summons up a whole familiar pattern of the grown child caring for the ailing parent, all the more piercing and constant when the disorder is mental rather than physical. It's also, of course, in the circumstances of the show itself, a fine inside joke. Batdorf, however, whether as writer-compiler or as actress, never presumes on the special relationship. This is a loving portrait, and both she and the audience are nourished that fact, but it's an objective and unsentimental one. It's also tantalizingly incomplete, but that probably comes with the territory.

- The Red Horse is Leaving runs until April 8 at Theatre Centre, 1087 Queen St. W. Call 1-888-222-6608 for tickets and information.

2007-03-30-a-post-apocalypse-hee-haw-sin:
THEATRE REVIEW

PARTICULARLY IN THE HEARTLAND

Enwave Theatre

- - -

The TEAM (acronym for Theatre of the Emerging American Moment) begin their contribution to WorldStage by hanging around the stage in casual, mainly rural gear giving out with off-key renditions of The Star Spangled Banner, Take Me Out to the Ball Game, American Pie and other anthems. They are indeed from the U.S., though they have done most of the work on this show in the U.K. They then invite us, as a reciprocal gesture, to sing O Canada. On the first night we sang, on the whole, better than they did.

It seemed, for the longest time, as if we might also be able to act better than they do. This proves in the end not to be the case; there's talent on that stage. But we have to travel an obscure and whimsical road to find this out. The particular stretch of heartland depicted in Particularly in the Heartland is Kansas, known to all of us as a region of strange and terrible storms. The latest twister, or whatever it is, has left the three Springer children -- Sarah, Todd and Anna -- alone in their homestead, their parents having vanished on a trip to Wal-Mart. They receive three visitors who become part of the household. One is a heavily pregnant young woman named Tracy Jo who, at her first appearance, turns to the audience and confides, "I'm an alien-- ssh." The second is an older woman called Dorothy who has reversed the trajectory usually associated with her name by being blown to Kansas from Oz, or at least from New York. (She seems to have been in a plane crash.) The third is the ghost of Bobby Kennedy.

Some kind of allegory is obviously intended. There has, perhaps, been a nuclear devastation that has cut these characters off from the outside world. The values of Middle America are being tested. The set-up, though, is confusing, as well as being almost interminable. It involves a lot of not especially expert whirling about; the company boast of their "exuberant physicality," but the results suggest that we have been taking the physical skills of some of our own groups entirely too much for granted. Kristin Sieh, playing Sarah, does get to do some fairly spectacular skipping.

It isn't clear what the intruders are meant to add. Tracy Jo, the earliest arrival, does get to tell Dorothy, "I was poor, tired and huddled once too -- but I was here first, just remember that," which is sort of neat, but what is gained by making her an alien? Is Bobby meant to represent the lost hopes of liberalism? He doesn't make much of a case, though when RFK says of JFK, regarding the Cuban missile crisis, that he believed in "America's right to moral leadership of the planet," and hence resisted a pre-emptive strike, something stirs.

Something stirs, too -- indeed it's a turning-point -- when one of the young Springers says, "I'm a Christian," and Dorothy, a sophisticate from the financial sector, murmurs, "That's awesome." Strict belief has always been a fertile ground for both drama and comedy, and it proves so here, with Todd placing his hands over his ears when he hears swearing and Sarah protesting at the use of the word "evolution." But it's hard to see why a family of evangelical Christians should be standing in for the whole of Kansas or indeed Kansas for the whole of red-state America. These characters aren't being mocked, but they aren't being much tested either. The show includes a question-and-answer session, where on the first night someone -- not a plant, I'm sure -- asked the Springer kids what they thought happened to their parents. They replied that they must have been taken up to heaven in what they call the Rapture leaving the children to carry on living on Earth. They admitted to being puzzled as to why they themselves should have been thought unworthy of apotheosis, but put it down to childish misdemeanours. They referred us to a series called Left Behind, depicting children left in just such a situation. Anyway, I was glad that question got asked. Without it, we would have been hopelessly lost.

The sequence also showed the actors' capacity to stay completely in character while improvising. Libby King and Frank Boyd touchingly complete the sibling trio, Lucy Kendrick Smith's more sympathetic moments as Dorothy are very good, and though I don't remember the original well enough to be sure, I suspect that Jake Margolin may well be doing a first-rate impersonation of Bobby; he's authoritative, anyway. In the show's final sequence, Bobby's ghost gets to play Marley's ghost in a group reading of A Christmas Carol, or parts of it, whose mixture of admonition and benevolence seems to be the show's own message to us. It's an impressive end, and the people up there seem genuinely nice.

- Until April 1. Call 416-973-4000 for more information.

2007-03-31-let-s-go-conquer-mexico:
If you go to see a play knowing only that it has something to do with the European conquest of the Americas, and if the first word of text you hear is "1492, then I think you might be pardoned for imagining that you are in for something concerning Christopher Columbus. This is the first point but far from the last at which One Reed Theatre Ensemble, creators and presenters of Nor the Cavaliers Who Come with Us, will turn out to have wrongfooted you.

It seems that 1492 was also the year in which the Holy Roman Emperor Charles V, formerly Charles I of Spain, discovered he was broke, having shelled out all he owned to buy his imperial title from the Pope who had it to sell. So, to replenish his coffers, Charles looked west. And the conquistador with whom the play is concerned is not Columbus but Cortez, conqueror of Mexico.

One Reed is a company composed of four actors -- Frank Cox O'Connell, Megan Flynn, Marc Tellez and Evan Webber -- who trained together at the National Theatre School, and discovered a shared interest in Mexican history and its ramifications for the present. They approached it from different angles: Tellez comes from a Mexican-American family; O'Connell was, in his own description, more the guilt-ridden white guy, trying to find the roots of my power." On graduation, they shared their research materials with a director, Daniel Mroz, and this show, developed over the past two years, is the result. It had a successful Toronto run at last years Summerworks, and is now being re-staged, in a slightly extended version, at the Glen Morris Studio on the University of Toronto campus. I saw a final run-through, which happened also to be the first run-through in this space. There were, though, no signs of uncertainty. It was a very accomplished performance.

Nor the Cavaliers is anything but a straightforward historical drama. More than half of it is concerned with a present-day figure billed simply as the Tourist (Webber) who journeys to Mexico to test what he describes as his own secular socialist principles, which he has found falling out of favour even in his native Canada. It seems odd in one way, fitting in another, that he should choose to visit a country whose traditions are the opposite of secular. Weve learned that it owes much of its present and historical form to the demands of a grasping church. We already know, and the play further informs us, that the soldiers who conquered it were also missionaries; they plundered and killed under the banner of Christ. But they came up against the natives' loyalties to their own gods, loyalties even more passionate and, for the invaders, profoundly disorienting.

The show switches backwards and forwards between past and present, but the present predominates. This, as far as I was concerned, was if not a mistake then a source of regret. I wanted to know more of the history and was frustrated, not just by its being constantly interrupted, but by its being relayed to us in gobbets that are written and acted in a style that I can best describe as intense but secretive. A central figure is a native woman who makes common cause with Cortez, spurring him on to greater excesses. She operates by incantation. " 'I will murder all the men and rape the women -- say it, she commands him, and he does. He says it, that is, but presumably he goes on to do it. We are dealing with her ancestral inter-tribal hostilities; she is a Mayan avenging herself on the Aztecs. Thats interesting, but I confess I got the information not from the performance but from talking to the cast and director afterwards.

Back in today, the Tourist finds refuge with a horse doctor in whom many of the old habits of thought live on. He talks about the lie of equality" and gives as his model of society the relation between horse and rider; together they are stronger than either could be alone but one, the rider, has to be in unquestioned control. These sentiments don't stop him happily cohabiting with a liberal-minded lady whose pet cause is the release of "women in chains, but he regards her activities with patronizing benignity. The Tourist is shocked by his host's attitudes but doesnt have much of an answer to them.

Atmosphere is provided, and changes in time and space effected, by a liberal and inventive use of homemade actorly effects. The evening all but commences with some piercing flamenco-style chanting by Flynn, accompanied by a complex rhythm of hand-claps from the men. Actors seem literally to somersault from one role and scene to another. Sand is strewn liberally across the stage; at one point Flynn, as the horse-medics domestic, stirs into an ever- increasing circle, a magical image. The performers are very good at all the devices they employ, but the air of a post-graduate drama- school exercise is still very much present; technique predominates over substance. In the first quarter of the show, Flynn told me, we share the tools that we have, we ask the questions so that you can come up with an answer." I couldn't find one.

- Nor the Cavaliers Who Come with Us runs through April 6 at the Glen Morris Studio, 1-888-222-6608.

2007-04-02-the-show-that-watches-us-even:
Last week's penultimate episode in the current season of Prison Break featured an unpretentious, but still spectacular, procession down the streets of Panama City. Strutting out in front, jaunty and dapper in white duds and, naturally, a Panama hat, was T-Bag, the serial killer and bisexual sex offender, now being used as a decoy to catch others who escaped with him from Fox River Prison at the end of the first season.

Behind him, keeping tabs and ready to pounce, were two minor characters, toughs in the pay of the mysterious Company that seems to control America if not the world. A safe distance after them came Bellick, the disgraced prison warder turned bounty hunter, itching to deprive T-Bag of US$5-million in formerly buried treasure or at least to collect on the reward for his apprehension.

Keeping their eyes firmly fixed on him were Sucre-- the nicest of the original escapees, pressured into an unholy alliance with Bellick -- and Michael, the show's hero and mastermind, lured here by an e-mail from Sucre that Sucre never actually sent. He's the real object of the Company's trap, but being super smart he's already figured that out; he wants, though, to turn in T-Bag, since he has on his conscience the people T-Bag has killed before and since Michael reluctantly engineered his release. (Michael had actually been an engineer before getting himself locked up.)

Michael is being trailed by Mahone, the haunted federal agent whom the Company has blackmailed into killing all of the Fox River Eight; at the last count, he'd offed three of them.

And Mahone was being tracked by Linc, Michael's brother, whom the Company framed for murder and whose escape from the chair was Michael's motive for organizing the prison break in the first place.

The show obviously relished its own wit in parading these characters, so ingeniously united and re-united. Wit, verbal and structural, is one of Prison Break's most attractive features. Among TV drama series, it occupies a space between The Sopranos, which is completely character-driven, offering not so much a narrative arc as a narrative mosaic, and 24, which is completely plot-driven, so much so that when the plot falters, as it has this season, we have nothing left to cling to. Playing for time, 24 goes down narrative blind alleys that seem hopelessly arbitrary because the people, Jack Bauer included, are puppets. And they aren't funny --not even Chloe this season.

Prison Break also has its tangents and dead ends, but we enjoy them because we like following the characters. That goes even for the despicable ones. There are, it's true, many fans who heartily wish T-Bag dead as soon as possible, but his debased insouciance, and Robert Knepper's brilliant Southern- fried performance, have the rest of us hooked. And a flashback to his own abused white- trash childhood humanized him without too much sentimentalizing him.

Strangely, Kellerman, the company hit man now hung out to dry, has never aroused the same public hatred, though he must have killed as many people (and nursed incidentally a similar hopeless passion for one unattainable woman); he too, as played by Paul Adelstein, has style and a believable streak of humanity. There is a surprising degree of complexity here. The driven Mahone (William Fichtner), Nemesis on barbiturates, keeps winning our sympathy. Even the brutish Bellick (Wade Williams) has his sad-funny moments; he's a middle-aged man still living with his mother with whom, be it noted, he enjoys the only affectionate parent-child relationship on the show. He has also now been arrested, twice, for murders actually committed by T-Bag.

Prison Break's prison break came at the end of the first season. I asked at the time if a sequel would have to be called Prison Broken, and doubted that it could possibly work. I was wrong. The second season has surpassed the first. It's been fascinating to see the characters dispersed, their storylines separating out and then crisscrossing with what seems a fair imitation of inevitability. The central motifs -- the conspiracy, the framing of Linc, the treasure, the price on the fugitives' heads --act like magnets.

The show also boasts one of the most compelling romances in TV drama history: Michael (Wentworth Miller, who's turned wry watchfulness into a style) and Sara (Sarah Wayne Callies), the disgraced prison physician, belong together precisely because they're both so withdrawn, so guarded (pun partially intended), so painfully intelligent. The plot keeps pulling them apart, and they've barely got to kiss, so one roots for them all the more.

Last Monday's episode -- maybe the best there's ever been -- ended with Sara, about to get 12 years for aiding and abetting, finding an unlikely saviour in the repentant Kellerman, entering the courtroom flashing a smile that's a patented blend of sheepishness and arrogance, promising to reveal all about the Company. Bets are being taken on whether he, unlike all the others who have tried, survives to tell his tale. It's hard to believe that the show would have the heart to kill him off, or that the villains would have the opportunity. But if he comes through then bang must go the conspiracy, so what will the promised third season have to beat its head against?

Something, plainly, will have to go painfully wrong for somebody in tonight's season finale. We'll be left, once again, hanging from a cliff for several months, cursing and blessing Prison Break for leaving us there.

2007-04-07-it-drags-a-bit-but-you-d-expe:
Commercially, the best thing that ever happened to The Rocky Horror Show was The Rocky Horror Picture Show. Artistically, if the word means anything in this context, it was probably the worst.

Many people, I know, don't believe that there was a stage Rocky Horror Show before the movie. But there was; I saw it. It debuted in the upstairs space at Londons Royal Court Theatre in 1973 and then moved up the street into a converted cinema in the Kings Road, Chelsea -- just the right locale for a fashion-conscious cross- dressing rock musical that was also a spoof on low-budget Frankenstein-monster pictures. It ran there for years, a neat and stylish little entertainment that never took itself too seriously. Recently, it was voted the most memorable production ever at the Royal Court, a theatre that has generally taken itself very seriously indeed. You may regard this either as an intolerable insult to the high-minded house of John Osborne, Edward Bond, Caryl Churchill and Sarah Kane, or as serving them right.

Anyroad, hit though it was in London, Rocky Horror flopped ignominiously in New York, which normally would have skewered its chances in the rest of the world. But then there came the movie, cheap and grungy (so I'm told, I've never seen it). This, too, tanked until audiences discovered the bliss of shouting responses back at the screen. The movie became a cult, and subsequent stage productions, of which there have been many, have had to imitate it.

The new CanStage production, directed by Ted Dykstra, seems to proceed on the principle of joining what it cant beat. It gives us a warmup prologue in which Eddie Glen, in cockney cheeky-chappie mode, welcomes us and invites our participation. He tells us pretty much what to shout (slut," mainly) and when we can shout it. The first-night audience certainly took him at his word, and then some. But there is a difference between shouting at actors on a screen and actors on a stage. The latter is boorish. Even at a movie screening, though, I would guess that the sound of people in the auditorium tirelessly trying to show how much smarter they are than the entertainment theyre watching would be "smugly. (That's an adjective I've just coined meaning smug and ugly. But it fooled spell-check, which thinks its an adverb.) And now that the whole thing has become a ritual, with preprogrammed responses, its pointless. There's no spontaneity here. We have amateur performers competing with professionals. They fail, of course. But they do succeed, much assisted by a zealously insensitive amplification system, at drowning out the original's words.

Ill admit that this hardly counts as desecrating a masterpiece. Richard OBrien, who wrote the book, music and lyrics, is a minor talent (his one subsequent musical, T. Zee, was a disaster that hasn't even had a schlock movie to rescue it) who, once in his life, got lucky by getting clever. His lyrics are insolent rather than witty (damn it, Janet" is about as funny as they get, though "there's a light shining over at the Frankenstein place is my favourite line), but his tunes heat the place up. However, like most rock, pastiche or otherwise, they are static rather than dramatic.

Stasis turns out to be the shows main problem or, perhaps more appositely, its main drag. Dykstras direction has more zing and energy than anything -- certainly anything musical -- seen on the Bluma stage in some years but, staking so much on keeping things moving, it's defeated by a second act that jumps up and down instead of progressing. You probably know the deal. Brad and Janet, all- American teenagers in love, seek refuge from a storm in the castle of Dr. Frank 'n Furter, a mad scientist who also happens to be omnisexual. He seduces both Brad and Janet, using identical lines on both (this, staged on an upright bed, is the productions best scene) and, it's safe to say, changes their lives forever. He test- tube incubates a hunk called Rocky, not apparently to take over the world but to have a new boy toy to play with. And, boy, is Frank mad when Rocky starts playing with others. This doesn't get us very far, so the show starts remembering its sci-firoots and drags in a Dr. Strangelove clone to thwart Franks rather vague plans. The upshot is that two of Franks minions take off in a rocket for the transsexual planet of Transylvania (and you thought it was a country), while Frank, for some reason, immolates himself.

The cast perform at fever pitch; they stay on it, too, which is impressive. Adam Brazier's Frank doesn't have the glitter or the surprising pathos of the roles creator, Tim Curry, but he has a commanding grin and an even more commanding voice. There is comparably strong acting and singing from Ron Pederson and Mairi Babb as the kids. Eddie Glenn reappears in a couple of cameos, in one of which he gets to lead the most invigorating number, Hot Patootie." Jody Ripplingers choreography is rote but reasonable; Erika Connor's costumes are, in all senses, sensational. The show's narration is delivered by the revered John Neville, on grainy inserts of black-and-white film. He does it with great style (and has a lovely dismissive parting line, probably of his own invention), but the device does deprive us of the originals most delightful moment, in which an onstage narrator, a staid BBC type, suddenly got caught up in the big Time Warp number. Perhaps because he was on film, Neville got shouted down by the audience more than anyone. This made it even harder to follow the story. It also, since he himself was in the first night audience, seemed very rude.

- The Rocky Horror Show runs through April 21 at the Bluma Appel Theatre. Call 416-368-3110 for details.

2007-04-09-this-pork-chop-from-new-jerse:
Its so good to have it back. The exhilaration kicks in all over again with the title sequence, which was always the most enticing in TV history and grows richer at each viewing. (And listening, I'd swear they've turned up the volume on the soundtrack song.) Tony Sopranos drive home through the landscape of his life is now as rich with memories for us as for him. And maybe were better off than he is; the drive sometimes seems like the most fun Tony ever has.

The Sopranos, however energized by violence and humour, has always been an elegiac show. It began, after all, with a panic attack and Tony's admission to his shrink that the great days of being a mob boss were in the past. Last night's episode, the first in the concluding batch of nine, worked in a fist fight and a murder, but was still low-key. It showed us Tony at his most vulnerable and at his most vindictive.

It might have been subtitled The Blooding of Bobby Baccala. Bobby (Steven R. Schirripa) has always seemed the most likeable, even innocent, of the Jersey hoods. Tonys sister Janice once told her own shrink that Bobby wasnt like the others, and then went ahead and married the poor widowed guy. We learned last night that Bobby had yet to "pop his cherry" in the sense that he'd never killed anyone; even when hunting, he only used a bow and arrow, to give the deer a fair chance. A great proponent of fair play and going by the book, Bobby; he even objected to Tony, Carmela and Janice inventing their own rules for Monopoly on the grounds that Parker Brothers put a lot of thought into it.

They were playing the game at Bobby and Janice's lakeside place up near the Canadian border. This gives Tony plenty of opportunity for his favourite pastime of gazing desperately or contemplatively into stretches of water. Its his 47th birthday, shadowed by his having been brought up on a gun-possession charge that threatens to morph into something more substantial.

We notice that though Bobbys frame was definitely not made for shorts and singlet, and Janice (Aida Turturro) is ampler than ever, Tony seems to have lost weight and Carmela is trim as she always was; James Gandolfini and Edie Falco have weathered the seasons and the acting honours in excellent condition. Janice, irritating as ever, brings up more discordant childhood memories than Tony cares to hear ("makes us sound like a dysfunctional family"). He lobs insults at her, literally across the board; Bobby, in a mood of chivalrous disgust, leaps to her defence (the Sopranos -- you go too far); there's a fight from which Tony emerges bloodied. He takes a peculiarly nasty revenge, one that combines business with pleasure.

He and Bobby meet up with a couple of drug dealers from Montreal: prescription-drug dealers, that is, offering to unload expired osteoporosis pills at a huge discount. (Canadian content note: This may be the first time The Sopranos has acknowledged Canada's existence. We learn that Bobbys own granddaddy had entered the U.S. from here--illegally, since he had a past as a political agitator. Plus ca change. Bobby, of course, would now like to erect a wall to keep latter-day undesirables out. And his in-laws say Amen.)

The deal can be sweetened if Tony will knock off the worrisome brother-in-law of one of his new partners. He deputes Bobby to do the deed; and not, he says, with a bow and arrow. Bobby complies, shooting the guy, who looks as much surprised as appalled, while hes doing his laundry. Bobby then returns, as these men always do, to the loving bosom of his family (he and Janice have a darling two- year-old daughter). Whether something has died inside him, we can't tell, and may never be able to. But the conflict that underpins the show, between Tony's better and worse natures, has found another mirror in another of his subordinates -- who will probably get the promotion that Tony, disillusioned with nephew Christopher, has promised him. Hes proved himself.

The episode was crammed with comic detail: the resigned swagger in Tonys eye when the cops come to arrest him; Meadow's shrill legal protests over her father's humiliation, and the silence (embarrassment? Schadenfreude?) of the respectable doctor neighbours; Tonys unexpected prowess at old movie-star impersonations, especially of W.C. Fields; Janice and Carmela doing karaoke, with Carmela having to look over her shoulder at the words on the screen. Plus a couple of prize false trails: We see Tony lying in bed, his face twisted in what we take to be a nightmare about a drowned child and find that hes actually been receiving a birthday blow job from Carmela; a "welcome home" sign at a party turns out not to be for Tony out on bail but for the peculiarly loathsome New York boss Phil Leotardo, back from a heart attack. We find, incidentally, that the New Yorkers refer to Tony as "pork chop from New Jersey." Yes, it was a quiet episode, but fires have been lit.

- Robert Cushman will critique each of the remaining eight episodes in this space.

2007-04-12-just-gotta-get-right-outta-he:
REVIEW

WE WILL ROCK YOU

Canon Theatre, Toronto

- - -

Theres a line in We Will Rock You that asks, in effect, what you get when you combine pre-packaged soulless entertainment with a brain-washed audience. The answer, though the show itself seems unaware of it, is that you get We Will Rock You.

It's a jukebox musical built around the songs of Queen. A story has been devised, into which the numbers have to be more or less arbitrarily stuffed. It's the same formula used for Mamma Mia!, with better music and lyrics, an even worse book, incomparably less slickness in presentation and the same general level of dumbness. The plotline thats been dreamed up by Ben Elton, the British comedian, is science-fictional and somewhat evangelical. Elton has also directed the show, presumably in imitation of the wildly successful London original; this, though, is a strictly Canadian production, with on-the-whole good local talent. As payback for that, we have a slew of pandering local references, making the show the latest big musical to play like a Ross Petty pantomime, only not as good.

We are in the year 2307, with the whole world controlled by an Internet corporation called Globalsoft. As tyrannies go, it does indeed seem fairly soft; its most repressive act is to ban live rock music. Consumers are confined to whatever downloaded enervating entertainment the company thinks is good for them. I dont know if other kinds of live music have been forbidden since, apart from one sneering reference to modern jazz, the show never acknowledges that such things could have existed. It believes the words "rock and music" are synonymous. Its worldview is as totalitarian as the one it purports to oppose; it's also more frightening since it bears a closer resemblance to things as they are.

Queen wrote a song called Killer Queen, so that's the name -- and the number -- that the show bestows on its villainess, Globalsofts boss. Its unclear how she maintains her hold on power since all she seems to care about is her bikini wax, but megalomaniacs are notoriously narcissistic. And that's how Alanna Bridgewater acts and sings this one, with more effort than effect. She has a sneering sadistic henchman called Khashoggi; he's Evan Buliung, a fine actor trying valiantly to lower his standards. Opposing them are two youths whose brains have somehow remained unwashed: Galileo Figaro, whose dreams are inexplicably filled with shards of old lyrics, and Scaramouche, whose social and sartorial independence earn her the scorn of her peers at Ga Ga (virtual)High. This latter-century Winston and Julia are embodied, very well, by Yvan Pedneault and Erica Peck. Figaro and Scaramouche join a rebel cadre known as the Bohemians, and they themselves are of course named after references in Queens biggest and most puzzling song, Bohemian Rhapsody, which never gets fully performed in the show proper. I guess integrating and making sense of it would have been too much of a dramaturgical challenge.

Our young couple take the musical into the 21st century by having sex (non-virtual) on their first date and refusing to shut up about it afterwards. The show itself takes a dim view of the new millennium, pegging its dawn as the moment at which music started to go profit-driven and homogenized. (It blames this on "boy bands.") This is rubbish. Rock has been a million-dollar electric machine since the 1950s, and it staggers the mind how a culture that has everybody buying the same records can pass itself off as nonconformist. The attitude is a product of the hype it affects to despise. A music so enslaved to technology was begging to be commodified, asking in fact for the download-future as depicted in We Will Rock You. And, I know its foolish to ask logical questions of a show like this, but I will anyway: If the music of Queen is supposed to stand for artistic and personal freedom, how come the baddies get to sing it as well?

In fact the music fares rather badly here, despite the best endeavours of the cast and of Rick Fox's onstage band, which is revealed late but was there all the time. (But if it was there, doesn't that make the conflict sort of redundant? And if the Killer Queen is so powerful and evil, why does she fold so easily? Sorry, Ill shut up.) The only songs that really work are Crazy Little Thing Called Love and the title number, both of them done as straight-on performances. The rest are hobbled by being told to illustrate plot and character situations for which they were never designed. A lot of Queens songs actually have the teasing tendril- trailing quality of seeming to have been extracted from some unwritten musical. But they weren't written for this musical (even though the band's surviving members are on its wagon). The show irons out their ironies and reduces them to noise.

What else? Spectators are issued with little green light-sticks that they obediently wave in the air. Audiences (and not just for this show): Refuse participation. You have nothing to gain but your self-respect. Arlene Phillips choreography might be excused on the grounds that those who execute it are supposed to be robots, but couldnt the robots have been more imaginatively programmed? Elton's script does run to a few good jokes, all of them crammed into one scene in the second act and entrusted to a pickled hippie, played with pleasing relish by Jack Langeduk. But even he is only there to fulfill the show's main purpose, which is to make a narcissistic generation feel nostalgically good about itself. - We Will Rock You plays until May 27. Call 416-872- 1212 for ticket information.

2007-04-13-dolls-without-the-house:
THEATRE REVIEW

JOHN GABRIEL BORKMAN

Young Centre for the Performing Arts, Toronto

- - -

After Soulpepper's recent production of Ibsen's The Wild Duck, it's a shock to find the company going into reverse gear with its new production of John Gabriel Borkman, a ghastly piece of museum- theatre that thinks it's being experimental.

The show is actually a co-production with the fringe group Theatre Columbus; it combines their aesthetic with some of Soulpepper's resources. Ibsen's last great play, his last but one of any kind, takes to what should be thrilling extremes his technique of advancing the present through exposing the past. J. G. Borkman himself is a financier whose empire crashed when he was caught embezzling on a huge scale. He did five years in jail, and has served another eight of more or less voluntary imprisonment on the top floor of his own house. He only sees one visitor, his old clerk Foldal; the two men humour one another's illusions, which, in Foldal's simple opinion, is what friendship is about. Down below sits Gunhild, Borkman's massively embittered wife, who is visited by Ella, her twin sister and Borkman's former love, sacrificed long ago to his ambition. Both women also want vindication, and both cling to it in the form of Borkman's son Erhart. He, however, wants no part of either of their plans, having attached his own to the notoriously worldly lady who lives down the street.

The play as written has a cast of eight, of whom five are simultaneously on stage for the big confrontation scene. In Leah Cherniak's production it's performed by only three actors; they carry dolls, each representing a single character, so that we'll know which they're meant to be at any given moment. Sometimes an actor will hold two dolls and have a conversation with herself, looking like a Punch and Judy man. In the last scene the dolls are dropped altogether; this may mean that Borkman and the sisters, out in the snow after years of being cooped up, are finally revealing their real selves. Or it could mean that, with only the three principal characters present, we no longer need mechanical aids. The convention never comes clear.

The dolls and doubling concept (read: gimmick) prevents the actors from engaging with the text, the characters, and one another. It saves them, in fact, the trouble of acting. The results are predictably depressing.

This, of course, is something that Ibsen is always suspected of being but doesn't have to be. If his plays are to transcend their superficial gloom, they have to be presented with passion and wit, two qualities for which this production substitutes melodramatic posing and an occasional laugh at the play rather than with it. Borkman is probably deluded and unquestionably selfish; his predicament may be cruelly comic, but he sees himself as tragic, and he needs to be played on that scale. Casting Michael Simpson, an actor good at playing endearing elders, is downright weird; the character becomes merely pettish and the play pointless, though Simpson does play young Erhart as effectively as a middle-aged character man is ever likely to do. The one role for which he would be perfectly suited is that of old Foldal, but this has gone, in the evening's only instance of crossgender casting, to Nancy Palk. She plays it well, though less well than she plays the Borkmans' perpetually surly maid. Her major role though is Gunhild. This, uniquely in this show, is a role in which she might very well be cast in more conventional circumstances, but she muffs it here; the woman's ice-cold anger comes off as mere spitefulness. Martha Ross (who, with Cherniak, is Theatre Columbus' guiding spirit) is a soft- centred Ella: competent but bland. The director doesn't seem to have much interest in actually guiding actors through a scene. In their long establishing duet, the two actresses recite their lines, shouting when they sense that some violent emotion might be called for. It has all the shape and force of a first read-through.

The visual interest here is confined to the opening moment when we glimpse the actors, and the dolls, through a scrim. The poster looks far better than the play; it depicts not dolls but marionettes, with broken strings. If there's a joke there, it hasn't landed on stage. Borkman is a play we hardly ever see, and one that Soulpepper might have cast superbly from its own ranks; there are at least two potential, though widely different, Borkmen among the company's regulars. To do it like this is an opportunity criminally wasted. - Until April 21. Call 416-866-8666.

Robert.cushman@nationalpost.com

2007-04-14-our-town-revisited-a-nurse-di:
Two shows in from the East Coast, both of a quality high enough to discourage Toronto from feeling smug about itself. On the other hand, Toronto may be entitled to ask why it always gets to see these things last. One of these two productions has already toured to Australia.

Revisited, which to date is going only as far as Germany, comes to us from the 2b theatre company of Halifax, as an indigenous contribution to the WorldStage season. Its audience (28 max) sits around a large table in a small room; the table is the stage though the actors, all two of them, mostly stand at its sides (and ours) and lean into it. The title is double-edged. The piece started out as a revisiting, or reduction, of Thornton Wilder's Our Town, itself a play about revisiting the past, but was prevented by Wilders estate from hewing too closely to the original material. So the troupe reworked their text (make that triple-edged) and supplemented it with references from other chroniclers and celebrants of small- town America: Sherwood Anderson, Willa Cather, Edgar Lee Masters (he of Spoon River Anthology) and, somewhat outclassing the others, Walt Whitman.

Its still very much Our Town. We still have a narrator guiding us through a day in the lives though this one, unlike Wilder's Stage Manager, gets to impersonate the people he describes. The focus is narrower. We concentrate on the young couple, here renamed Tom and Lucy, whom we follow from courtship to marriage to the bride's early death. We also have her wish to, yes, revisit just one day from her past, and her heartbreaking realization that we never value the stuff of our existence while its happening. There is some reference to the vast pitiless framework of time and space, and to the Great War after which the town and the country and the world will never be the same. There is a sterner concentration (because, in an hour- long show, so much else has to be left out) on the disturbing character of the towns lonely, alcoholic and ultimately suicidal music teacher. One element that isn't in Wilder is the revelation that Tom's mother writes stories; she gets short-listed for a prize from the Atlantic Quarterly but fears that her stay-at-home husband will never let her make the trip to the ceremony. We never are told how that turns out. I felt cheated.

Its all beautifully done, but I couldnt see the point. Revisited is hardly a re-interpretation; it doesn't tell us anything that isn't already there in Our Town. Still, the delicacy and inventiveness of Christian Barrys production may be their own justification. The director shares co-creation credit with the actors. Steven McCarthy, the narrator, carries a small sack of dirt that he scatters artistically across the tabletop to show how Main Street intersects with the railroad station. The contents of the same sack do duty for the burial mounds of the last section. McCarthys soft-voiced performance is searching, confiding and evocative. He brings a gentle and whimsical touch to the respectable ladies of the town and sends an uninhabited suit and shirt whistling down a clothesline the length of the table to represent one of the men. He plays, in fact, all the roles except one. That one is Lucy, to whom Michelle Monteith brings a combination of toughness and fragility to which the word "sensitive" hardly does justice. Her face is alight with each successive emotion. An actual spotlight, pitiless and sympathetic, epitomizes the staging; for the actors it's a gift and an opportunity, and they rise to both.

The Factory Theatre's main season is over but its staying up past its normal bedtime to host a bunch of guest-shows, under the umbrella title of Performance Spring. The first of these visitors is Tempting Providence which comes from Newfoundland and, unlike Revisited, is about where it comes from. It tells the real-life story of Myra Grimsley Bennett, who died a decade and a half ago at the age of 100, having arrived from Britain in 1921 with the official job description of nurse. In practice she was also doctor, surgeon, midwife and vet, the sole medical presence to a rugged stretch of country unlinked by roads. (Arriving in the summer, she hadnt quite realized what she was getting herself into.)Her initial contract expired after two years but, though racked with homesickness, she stayed on anyway, because she was needed.

It's to the credit of Robert Chafe, the author, that though the play tells a story that could clearly not have been invented, it doesn't feel like a documentary. Its first act, though, feels repetitive. In a rapid but protracted series of vignettes we see Nurse Bennett, the very sound and picture of a no- nonsense angel of mercy, working most hours, conquering local prejudice, local superstition and local hearts. A local heart of which she makes a particular conquest belongs to Angus, who manages to interrupt her professional ministrations just long enough to propose and be accepted. Probably it didnt happen quite like that, but its charming to pretend it did. Act 2 slows down and is shorter; it concentrates on an injury to Angus's brother and an epic sleigh ride to get him to proper treatment and avoid amputation. It's this exploit that seems to have sealed the Bennett legend. Honours followed, and even a real road. Jillian Keiley, a legendary Canadian director whose work has hardly been seen here, delivers an unobtrusively virtuoso production. Chairs and a table are arranged and re-arranged to suggest the various locations, but the focus is still firmly on the acting. Deidre Gillard-Rowlings finds exactly the right brisk rhythm for Myra and sticks to it; she also sticks to the same brisk pace and here we might have used some variation. Darryl Hopkins makes Angus the same sympathetic helpmate on stage as he must have been in life; and Robert Wyatt Thorne and Melanie Caines fill all the other roles to near-perfection. - Revisited runs through April 19 at the Brigantine Room, York Quay Centre, 416-973- 4000; Tempting Providence runs through April 22 at the Factory Theatre, 416-504-9971.

2007-04-16-the-final-days-are-all-about-:
Actors from The Sopranos

routinely pay tribute to the astonishing quality of the scripts they receive. I don't recall reading as many testimonials from the writers to the performers, but I imagine that the feeling is mutual. We, the viewers, are as likely to think in terms of casting as of acting; every character seems exactly right, and who can tell how much is skill and how much is judgment. In a long-running series, the mechanism becomes self-perpetuating. The more we get to know these characters, the more we can believe in them. And the likelier even the most repulsive are to arouse our sympathy.

Last night's episode, written by Terence Winter and one of the best there's ever been, gave us this full-strength. It had two main plot threads. One concerns the making and initial screening of Christopher's long-promised movie; the made man has finally made it, coming up with a gangster-slasher flick called Cleaver. (As in axe, though we're told there have been rumblings from Eldridge Cleaver's estate.) The other treats of Johnny Sack (Vincent Curatola), the imprisoned New York boss who is now not only orange-suited but distressingly wired-up. He's been diagnosed with terminal cancer, and over the next hour, he and his wife and daughters will move us close to tears. In his coolness and intelligence, Johnny has always been an attractive character, but he has never been what you'd call admirable. But dignity, mortality and family devotion go a long way, and not just with Johnny. Little Carmine (Ray Abruzzo), the ineffectual malapropping New York heir-apparent who describes Chris' movie as blending "the sacred and the propane," sounded very sensible (and still funny) when heeding his wife's desire not to end up "the wealthiest widow on Long Island." Phil Leotardo (Frank Vincent), his putative successor whom I had pegged last week as "exceptionally loathsome," turned our feelings around when gently telling his grandchildren about their family's humiliating arrival at Ellis Island when an immigration officer unfamiliar with their real name Leonardo "named us after a ballet costume." One of the kids pipes up that "leotards are for modern, not ballet," but as Phil insists, the principle's the same: "Leotardo: That's my f- -- in' legacy."

Legacy, and the cares of office, held this episode together, more tightly than most. Johnny asks how he'll be remembered and pronounces with ashen authority that being numero uno is "a thankless job." Over in the other storyline Tony congratulates his nephew Chris on having made a movie that will survive long after they've all been forgotten; later, he's on the verge of crying when, having recognized himself in the film's brutish protagonist, he laments, "All these memories and for what?" and concludes, "I think [Christopher] despises me. He wants to see me dead."

A word about casting. The Sopranos often uses actors, Curatola and Vincent among them, who came to acting through other things: most famously Steven Van Zandt, now so identified with his role as Silvio that he looks incongruous when reverting to his previous identity as a Springsteen guitarist. The casting directors seem especially fond of casting directors. There's Peter Bogdanovich in his recurring role of shrink's shrink (one line last night, and it was a killer), while this episode was virtually stolen by Sydney Pollack as a former oncologist turned prison-hospital orderly (he killed his wife and her aunt and the mailman). He was wonderfully wise and philosophical. The oneoffs on this show can be as rich as the regulars or the in-betweens. It has such texture, the result of familiarity reinforced by continuing invention. James Gandolfini's Tony gives a knowing nod to the FBI guys who surprise him as, in a moment we've come to know and love, he collects his newspaper in the driveway, then complains to Carmela "that's the last time I'm going down for the paper. It's too dangerous, has been for years." We laugh; he doesn't. At other times, he's very aware; indeed the thing that sets Tony apart from his colleagues, making him both more human and more dangerous, is that he has empathy. He can see someone else's point of view; and he can use it. One of the things that Gandolfini does best is to shake his head and smile, when he knows what's going down and no one knows he knows. This episode's final shot shows Tony and Chris, at the latter's daughter's christening, looking over one another's shoulders in an embrace that's half- loving, half-fearful. It's as powerful and prophetic as the door that shuts out Diane Keaton from the men's counsels at the end of The Godfather. Even now, entering its home stretch, The Sopranos surprises.

- The last episodes of The Sopranos air Sunday nights on The Movie Network at 9 p.m.

2007-04-17-a-double-dose-of-bleak-futuri:
THEATRE REVIEW

Noble Parasites

Theatre Passe Muraille, Toronto

Mike McPhaden, author of the greatly overpraised Poochwater, has come up trumps in spades, giving us a pair of futuristic fables that amount to a double dose of dystopia. Or, coming right on top of We Will Rock You, a triple dose. The new deal, though, comes minus the happy ending.

The overall title Noble Parasites applies most obviously to the double bill's first half, subtitled The Bookworm. (It applies to the second piece by strained metaphor or not at all.) We are, says the program, "deep underground, centuries from today." Society, though presumably it still reproduces itself, has gone monastic; its members dress up in the starkest form of ecclesiastical couture and devote themselves to mortification of the flesh. They do not, though, have to do the mortifying themselves; their bodies have been invaded by multitudes of bugs whom they both welcome and worship. Top of the heap is the mighty tapeworm, who practically has hymns sung to him.

Somewhere offstage is someone or something very powerful called the Witch, though I couldnt make out if the characters were in thrall to her or at war with her -- or both. Food is scarce, and the citizens regulation greeting is happy in my hunger. Literacy in the world of The Bookworm has become very circumscribed (they've probably banned rock music as well). Education consists of learning sets of rhymed verses praising the goodness and rightness of this limited world. Young people parrot them in oral exams designed to gauge their fitness for adulthood. What happens to them if they fail is not spelled out, but it obviously isn't nice.

We meet Lindy, whos about to take the test, and her cousin and instructor Fran, whos both stimulated and spooked by Lindy, having acquired forbidden knowledge of how things used to be. McPhaden tells a good suspenseful story, laced with insouciant black humour. He dallies somewhat in the section establishing the young heroines, not much helped in Rebeca Brown's production by Kate Hewlett's Lindy drifting in and out of conviction and Amy Rutherfords Fran never getting there in the first place. Things perk up with Julian Richings arrival as the examining Minister, looking like a cadaver in a cassock. He smells a rat (which, in this play's climate, must be very easy to do) and puts Fran in the exquisitely ironic position of not knowing whether she wants her protege to succeed or fail. And the examiner shows enough intellectual ambivalence for the screws to turn even tighter.

The second play, Sea Change -- "a city park, decades from today" - - is a kind of long-range prequel to the first. The two pieces are in fact linked by a single object, a copy of Reader's Digest. (Im not telling how.) Things are materially better than they will later become, but the rot has already set in; technology is omnipresent, individuality is eroding and life is cheap. Ironically, the person who feels least at home in a world where people have computers literally in the palm of their hands is a former video-game designer. Hes been overtaken. He has billion-dollar election- rigging secrets in his briefcase, but he's no match for two young women: a peddler of uplifting pamphlets who can change identities in an instant and a gun-toting adventuress. There are any number of twists and turns. This spy-spoof is less imaginative satire than its companion piece but brisker entertainment. Richings manages to be taut and bemused at the same time, and the two women are all kinds of tough. I blame both plays, or the worlds of both plays, on global warming, as I am surely meant to do. Warm is the new cool. - Until April 29. Call 416-504- 7529 for ticket information.

2007-04-20-finding-salvation-from-segreg:
THEATRE REVIEW

SIZWE BANSI IS DEAD

Enwave Theatre, Harbourfront Centre

- - -

At 82 years old, 60 of which he has spent as the foremost director in the English theatre, Peter Brook has earned the right to coast. And anyone who knows of the spectacular productions that dotted his earlier career might think initially that is what he is doing in his production of Sizwe Bansi Is Dead. It's a simple show with only two actors, but it doesn't even have what you might call the spectacle of starkness. The performers have the support of props, door frames and recorded jazz. It's all very relaxed. It's also tremendously taut: the mature work of a master.

It comes to Toronto's WorldStage from Brook's own world stage, the Bouffes du Nord in Paris, where, since the 1970s, he has maintained an international acting troupe. This has always had a strong African component, and Sizwe Bansi is a legendary South African play. It was created, also in the '70s, by the white playwright Athol Fugard and two black actors, John Kani and Winston Ntshona. Since one of the characters is a photographer, it seems apt to call it a snapshot of life under apartheid. Brook's production (in a French translation, with English surtitles) is, as far as I know, the first major staging with actors other than those who originated it.

The original, staged in London in 1973, derived much of its extraordinary power from its sense of release; Kani and Ntshona (who had to travel as Fugard's servants to be allowed to leave home) were not only testifying to their own lives, but to their own talents. This was storytelling theatre that used humour to illuminate a dire situation. Styles, the cameraman, begins it by recalling his former life on a Ford assembly line where, for just one day, the workers were treated as human beings because the current Henry Ford was paying a visit. After that, it was business as before, but Styles, one of the few workers who could read, had relished the factory boss's brief dependence on his skills. The experience inspired him to quit the line and open a studio. Into it, just as he's finished telling his tale, walks Sizwe Bansi, a worker from another township, needing a portrait. He also needs another identity, as we learn from a series of conversations between Sizwe and an ingenious friend and from Sizwe's letter home: dictated, since he can't write. Sizwe Bansi is dead but he will, at a daily cost, survive.

The play's record, the image of black life in that time and place, is not so much of atrocity as of continual indignity. It is possible, as Brook would apparently like us to do, to extrapolate from the situation on stage and apply it to horrors in our own times, but the piece has lost some of its power. We no longer have the knowledge that these actors came from that situation and would be going back to it. My strongest memory of the original is of Winston Ntshona's baffled Sizwe railing, Lear-like, at the pass laws for blacks: at the "dompas" (it came out sounding like "dumb pass") whose possession governed his life and whose loss would make him a criminal. Pitcho Womba Konga, in Brook's production, is quieter, more stoical, almost wry.

This is altogether a lighter production than the original. (Lighter in the most basic sense--it is, if I can trust my memory, far more brightly lit.) This has something to do with time, something probably with the logical French language and the ironic French temperament. But, if the delivery is light, it carries a heavy freight. Konga, dreaming awkwardly of his future, has wonderful moments of delicate comedy, pipe in his mouth, assuming a manager's pose. The photography theme is constant and vital to the plot. It's a service that Styles, reflecting on early ghastly experiences with family groups ("37 New Brighton smiles on the same photo--never again") has, without knowing it, been setting himself up as a saviour. Habib Dembele gives him a joyous, elfin quality and balances it with good-humoured man-of-the-world exasperation as Sizwe's friend and other rescuer, the man who exhorts him to grab at salvation, even when he finds it literally lying in the gutter. Between them, these actors create a world for us. The play is little like Fugard's unaided works, which are drier and also duller; it's full of pungent detail, shrugged or mocked at, understated to shock. Dembele plays several roles, Konga only one, but they both give the impression of enormous versatility and enormous mutual trust. The level of contact here--actor to actor, actors to audience -- is remarkable. Brook, in the simplest way, has done it again. - Until April 22. Call 416-973-4000 for ticket information.

Robert.cushman@nationalpost.com

2007-04-24-if-shakespeare-was-a-wise-guy:
Compared with The Godfather, to which it so often pays sly homage, The Sopranos has never been that much of a bloodbath. In the first three episodes of the final series, we had been down to a whack a week, always someone minor. We have now, on two consecutive Sundays, seen the elimination of a contender for boss of New York, a story that acts as sideshow and counterpoint to the principal saga of Tony Soprano and his mostly ageing Jersey boys.

For the most part this week, we were either on the road with Tony and Paulie, taking a hurried trip to Florida prompted by an FBI investigation into a corpse they disposed of 25 years ago (Tonys first hit, we were told), or we were with senile Uncle Junior, incarcerated in a facility for criminal mental cases. The two storylines took no note of one another's existence, though we did see Tony and Paulie passing a road sign that read "hitchhikers may be escaping inmates," while Junior, who shot Tony nearly fatally at the start of the previous season, could be heard asking if his nephew had yet apologized to him.

But there were, as always, links. This show now has such a backlog of finely woven material that everything that happens in it reflects on something else. Tony remarked at one point that  'remember when is the lowest form of conversation. Hes probably had quite enough of it talking to his shrink. But this episode had him trapped for long periods with the unstoppably reminiscent Paulie, who it seems, is not only Tony's lieutenant, but was, in earlier years, a surrogate father. I don't think the latter aspect of their relationship has been well set up in previous seasons, but having brought it on the show made the most of it. Its a connection that Paulie seems to relish and that Tony finds at the least embarrassing and at the most highly dangerous. Paulie may talk too much and to the wrong people. The tensest sequence in this instalment found them alone on a rented fishing boat (The name? Sea Vous Play), reminiscent -- as we were too insistently reminded of in dreams and flashbacks -- of the one on which the two guys and Silvio shot the informing Big Pussy. Tony, inspired perhaps by his nephew Christophers chopper movie, plainly thought of doing Paulie in with an axe, and Paulie knew it.

Paulie is an unwilling solitary, one of this family show's few major figures to be childless and unmarried. The other is Corrado Junior, who has also thought of Tony as a substitute son (when he hasn't been trying to dispose of him) and who also talks a lot. But he cant reminisce much, because most of his memory has gone. What remains is the ability to tell some (very funny) jokes and the opportunity to organize illicit poker games, played for candies, with real (definitely not diet) Coke for refreshment: some comedown for a former don. He takes one inmate under his wing, an angry young Asian whom at one confused point Corrado Junior addresses as "Anthony." And here again -- a Shakespearean image of disorder -- the rude son comes near to killing the father dead.

Theres another common factor in the two narratives: incontinence. Junior, when off his medication, can't control his bladder. Down in Florida lives --apparently rather well--Beansie, confined to a wheelchair after being viciously run over by Richie Aprile seasons ago. He excuses himself from the dinner table to empty my bag, prompting Paulie -- a survivor of prostate cancer -- to murmur, "Kill me first." Junior seems to agree; he goes back on his meds, at the cost of being sedated into a living death. This inmate won't be escaping any time soon.

This was a low-key episode, after the previous weeks fireworks display. (The show seems to be alternating them.) But the themes continue to develop, as Tony loses faith in one subordinate after another and as his business loses any glamour it may have had: Tony, who once trafficked in jewellry and Rolex watches at least, is now reduced to beach furniture, expired Fosomax and Black and Decker power drills. The show is great at brand names, and I doubt if its product placement. Paulie's peace offering to the Sopranos is a deluxe espresso machine. Who's at the door? asks Tony, when its delivered. "Williams- Sonoma," answers Carmela.

Fancy gifts or not, the mob and most of its members are decaying, and they know it. And this really is the answer to those who complain, as a reader did on the National Posts letters page last week, that the show glorifies crime. It certainly appeals, as fiction always has, to a human fascination with outlaws and violence. Like other such "despicable" works as Macbeth and Crime and Punishment, it takes a killer for its protagonist and tells the story largely from his point of view. Like them, too, it has a religious context. These people are all believers: Paulie has worked out exactly how much time he'll have to spend in purgatory, and he reckons he can do the time. Tony's conscience is more sophisticated. He draws lines. But he can't stop himself from crossing them. The show doesn't have to judge him for us. He judges himself.

2007-04-28-all-dressed-up-nowhere-to-go-:
Once on The Simpsons, when Homer expressed reluctance to visit Japan, Marge tried to cane his mind by saying "you liked Rashomon." "That's not how I remember it," said Homer.

Ha ha. Still, our abiding sense of Japanese art as being about shifting perceptions, epitomized in the very title of that movie, is doubly reinforced in 36 Views. It deals with the contrasting and overlapping reactions to Japanese culture of Asians and Westerners and it is itself the work of a Japanese-American dramatist, Naomi Iizuka.

The title derives from a series of prints by Hokusai, a 19th- century Japanese artist, and the play unfolds in 36 scenes, each numbered off at the side of the stage and accorded delicate pictorial accompaniment. (Hokusai actually bequeathed 46 views, but the author obviously felt enough was enough.)The action concerns the discovery of a "pillow book," the work of an 11th-century Japanese noblewoman. Only it isn't; it was run up, initially for laughs, by a young 20thor 21st-century forger, American, and an artist- associate, Asian. Their work dazzles both scholars and buyers. So all kinds of questions emerge. If the work is beautiful anyway, what does it matter whether it's "authentic"? Can you put a cash price on imagination? In Shakespeare's Troilus and Cressida, Troilus asks rhetorically, "What's aught but as 'tis valued?" To which his big brother Hector says "value lies not in particular will." So, are there absolutes?

The matter is complicated in the play, as it always is, by personal emotions. If the play has a central figure, it's an American named Wheeler. Wheeler's a dealer. (No, honestly.) But with his keen appreciation of the market value of Japanese artifacts, there seems to co-exist a genuine infatuation with Japanese art and with at least one Japanese person, a beautiful scholar. She doesn't reciprocate. So the play in its 36 episodes, some of which are mere fragments, tantalizes us with facts and fancies, seen from different angles, though they hardly amount to three dozen completely different ones. And to show how much these angles are the products of conflicting or intersecting cultures, it offers a mixture of theatrical styles. At dialogue-level, this is a Western work, but its staging partakes of Japanese kabuki techniques, with visible stagehands.

At least, that's the idea. What actually comes across is a commonplace story of love and fraud, told in a confusing order, with a couple of extra actors lurking under tables and occasionally helping the other performers out with costume changes that they could perfectly well execute themselves.

Yasmina Reza's play Art was a far more scintillating examination of the ways in which different people may react to the same picture, while Pacific Overtures, the Stephen Sondheim-John Weidman- Harold Prince musical, fuses American and Japanese stagecraft to far more dazzling effect, reflecting the clash of cultures and the variables of human perception, while throwing in a solid history lesson at the same time.

36 Views, according to the Toronto program, has received a truly terrifying number of workshop productions in the United States, reinforcing my own perception that "workshopping" has become an end in itself.

David Ferry's production, for the Actors Repertory Company, is lovely in its sets, costumes, lighting and especially in Jamie Nesbitt's projections. But in other respects, it's heavy-handed, with performances that border on lifeless. The actors are as likely to intone their lines as to speak them. This is especially noticeable in a choric sequence that has them all putting on their best prose-poem voices in what is presumably meant to suggest the wisdom of the ages. But it affects the chattier sections as well. John Fitzgerald Jay makes Wheeler's fumbling attempts at erotic advances seem like the best scene in the play, or at least the most humanly credible, but the character's other drives are stuck in neutral. As the object of his affections, Ginger Ruriko Busch has a bewitching presence, all the mystery of old Japan in a svelte new dress, but not the authority to back it up, so she becomes less mysterious than anonymous. As the principal faker, Gordon Bolan renders gifted naivete as simple blandness, while Marjorie Chan turns the colleague who supposedly spurs him on with her charm and energy into a grinding bossyboots. Gary Reineke has some amiable moments as a senior expert ("We used to call ourselves Orientalists - - that's how old I am") but is at sea when his character is required to expound on weightier matters. As a prying journalist, Kyra Harper acts as if she were in a thriller, which is pretty much what her scenes require but puts her out of sync with everybody else. The play seems to call for a synthesis of styles; the actors have trouble deciding which they're in at any given moment.

If the show had a bigger budget, one would be tempted to use one of the script's better lines against it: "All it is is money, jazzed up to look like art." As it is, it does look like art. But it doesn't feel like it.

- 36 Views runs through May 5 at the Berkeley Street Theatre Downstairs, 416-368-3110.
