2007-05-04-the-award-fits-him-like-a-bus:
Robert Lepage, Canada's favourite

theatrical son, received the Europe Theatre Prize here last Sunday. You don't actually have to be European to get the prize, which is given "in recognition of a life devoted to art theatre." You do have to have made an impact on Europe and to play according to European rules, which basically mean "director as auteur." Lepage obviously qualifies on both grounds, big time.

In his acceptance speech -- which was charming, marked by the surface diffidence and deep rooted confidence that characterize his stage work, and like his stage work was equally fluent in French and English -- Lepage said "it may seem strange that the European Prize should go to a North American, but Europe is not just a continent, it's maybe a modern idea of the world, of rapprochement." He added: "Maybe the jury noticed this in my work. In which case, I'm profoundly grateful."

At a symposium two days earlier Don Rubin of York University's theatre department had noted that, within Canada, Lepage was regarded as a Quebecois artist, while to the rest of the world he was simply Canadian. (Other countries really don't care about the differences between our provinces.)

But this distinction seemed to break down in Thessaloniki, where the word "Canadian" wasn't heard very much. If Lepage himself seemed to prefer "North American," the emphasis elsewhere was very much on his identity as a Quebecer. On a later panel I was asked how Lepage's work was received in English Canada,

to which I replied "not often enough." We seem to see most of his shows only after they've toured the rest of the world. I was able to add, though, that when they were received in Toronto, it was generally with immense enthusiasm. There have been missteps such as Geometry of Miracles (the one about Gurdjieff and Frank Lloyd Wright) and Elsinore (the virtuoso but pointless oneman show that gave new meaning to the phrase " Hamlet without the prince"), but there have also been triumphs that have been received as such. These have ranged from one- man plays that really were plays ( Needles and Opium, The Far Side of the Moon) to the ensemble masterpiece The Seven Streams of the River Ota. I might have added that his opera doublebill of Duke Bluebeard's Castle and Erwartung showed that he can work magnificently within the disciplines of someone else's prescribed texts. And I did say that his own works, however collaboratively they may have been created, have ended up as texts, the best of which have proved sturdy enough to withstand production by other people.

For their public presentation Lepage and his Ex Machina company offered an hour's worth of "Works in Progress." From The Andersen Project, commissioned by the Danish government to mark the bicentennial of Denmark's most celebrated fabulist, came The Shadow, a scary piece about a dark fairy tale (a sort of Silhouette of Dorian Gray) that overwhelms everyday life. Lepage himself claims to identify with Hans Andersen, but this scene on its own could do little more than tantalize. Two scenes from a piece called Lipsynch gave little indication of what the whole might be like, or even why it has that title. The first, a monologue about child prostitution, was disturbing in a surprisingly conventional way; the other, a more complex episode about a brain surgeon whose work follows him remorselessly home, allowed one of his male actors to give an unnervingly convincing performance of an old lady. Finally from The Far Side of the Moon, a work now surely very far in progress, we had Lepage himself reprising his rolling-on-the-floor dance of a man imitating his own filmed image: still haunting, though suggestive out of context of the Marx Brothers' mirror routine in Duck Soup without the laughs.

A Latvian director, Alvis Hermanis, received a subsidiary Europe Prize for "New Theatrical Realities." His acceptance speech was worthy of note.

"Artists," he said, "now wear suits like businessmen [and] drink mineral water rather than whisky." But they still present themselves as rebels, prizing anger over compassion: "Our brains are too large, our hearts are sometimes too small. But we have to try anyway."

Lepage, I think, has always done this. The dazzling high-tech of his shows never effaces -- indeed it highlights -- their humanity. He shows us man adrift in space but not dwarfed by it. European or North American, Quebecois or Canadian, he deserves to be honoured.

THEATRE REVIEW

SAINT JOAN

Festival Theatre,

Niagara-on-the-Lake

- - -

A veteran theatre critic once divided the many performances he had seen of George Bernard Shaw's Saint Joan in to tough and tender Joans. By that yardstick, Tara Rosling, in the opening production of this years Shaw Festival, must be ranked among the tender. When she makes her first appearance at the castle of Robert de Baudricourt, whom she cajoles into sending her to the French court, she has the invulnerability of total innocence. Shes sublimely confident, hardly needing to raise her voice to make a point, and in perpetual possession of what can literally be described as a winning smile. It wins her the awed respect of craven kings and seasoned soldiers, virtual command of the French army, and a series of bruising victories over the occupying English. Rosling makes all this credible, and any lingering doubts as to whether her initial brightness can darken, when Joan discovers that not everybody loves a winner after she's won, are conclusively dispelled. Her resolve when Joan finds herself deserted by her allies is both effective and affecting; so is her desolation when, on trial by the Inquisition, she briefly believes herself deserted by God as well.

It's a shining performance, but some things are missing, as they tend to in tender Joans. Cutely cropped though she is, it is hard to believe in this Joan as a soldier among soldiers or even as a military pragmatist. Also, that smile does not translate into actual gaiety, the common-sense humour with which Joan deflates so many of her adversaries. Roslings voice pipes rather than chuckles; when a judge at her trial rebukes her for giving pert answers, it rings oddly as what we have been hearing from her are mystified sobs. There are times when this Joan seems reduced to a supporting player in her own drama. And though the final cry of the rejected saint, How long, O lord, how long? might well pierce heaven, it is less successful at piercing the theatre.

This is partly because it lacks context. As Shaw wrote it, Joans cri du coeur concludes an epilogue -- the Dauphin's dream -- that brings us up to date on the burned heretic's rehabilitation and canonization and shows her former friends and enemies first worshipping her and then, once again, deserting her. Its a scene that directors and commentators have traditionally found troublesome, though in fact it does its job well. Jackie Maxwells solution at the Shaw is to turn the epilogue into a prologue. Before the official text gets started, we have a ghostly parade of characters mouthing a condensed and re-ordered version of what would normally come at the end. It is clever (though I should think anyone who does not know the play must be wondering who all these people are) and it does cast an interesting ironic pall over what follows; we know from the start that Joan does not stand a chance, before or after death. But it means that when we get to where the epilogue should be, there is virtually nothing left of it. The finale does not have a build.

The prologue is performed, against a hideously starry sky, in costumes suggesting the First World War, and the period keeps switching thereafter between the early 20th century and Joan's own early 15th. It makes a sort of sense; Shaw's play premiered only five years after the so-called Great War, which has in any case become accepted theatrical shorthand for any kind of armed conflict. But if it does not do any harm, it does not do any good either. The message seems to be that all wars are essentially the same and equally damnable. Shaw, the pacifist, might well have agreed but it does not happen to be what this particular play is about; if it was, Joan would have to be one of its villains, and the production certainly does not present her that way. There is a jokey line about Hell being preferable to the French wars; its delivered here with an ominous solemnity, which as always with Shaw makes it not more effective but less.

The productions great virtue is the overall strength of its acting, and even more of its interacting. Ben Carlson, unexpectedly cast old, brings all his pace and lucidity to Bishop Cauchon, and as his hostile ally the Earl of Warwick, Blair Williams is suave perfection. Their debate on Joan's spiritual and political heresies is the Shaw Festival doing what it does, or should do, best. Though placing this scene, the only one in which Joan herself does not appear, just before the interval does not do the heroine's status any favours. The scenes actually a three-hander; Peter Krantz, as the fanatically patriotic English chaplain, splendidly humanizes a one-joke role, while his later breakdown when confronted by the reality of her execution brought me closer to tears than the Maid herself ever did. Reaction to tragedy is often more moving, because its more accessible than tragedy itself; a fact also demonstrated on a smaller scale by Andrew Bunker as the more constructively traumatized Brother Martin. Harry Judge is a fey, funny Dauphin, Patrick Mc- Manus a terrifically likeable Dunois and Thom Marriott makes so much of the bullying La Tremouille (who "pretends to command the army") that his early exit, however a fair judgment on the character, is downright cruel to the audience. - In repertoire through October 27. Call 1-800-511-SHAW for more information.

Some plays begin by assailing the audiences eyes. A few make their first appeal through the ear. David Frenchs Leaving Home is among the select few to make their initial impact by way of the nose. The pleasant aroma of cooking fish assaults our nostrils as we take our places for Soulpepper's revival, the first Toronto production, surprisingly, that this Canadian textbook classic has received since its premiere in 1972. The cooking is done in a fully equipped kitchen, stage right; the rest is living- cum-dining room. The phrase kitchen sink drama is always taken to be synonymous with squalor, economic and possibly moral, but in fact when sinks, stoves and fridges do appear on a stage, it's a sign that were dealing, at the very least, with the respectable working class, and very likely with the aspiring lower middle. The people in Leaving Home have elements of both.

It was the first of Frenchs cycle of plays concerning the Mercer family who came from Newfoundland to live in Toronto but never really felt comfortable there. Jacob, the father, resents nearly everyone, and especially his two sons, Ben and Billy, the former of whom has driven the wedge in further by going to university. Mary, Jacob's wife, is a peacemaker but by no means a doormat. Young Billy has got his girlfriend pregnant (they've played Vatican roulette and lost), and the pair are set to marry on the day of the play. Joining them for a pre-nuptial lunch is the brides mother, another transported Newfoundlander and an old flame of Jacobs; she brings along her latest boyfriend, an undertaker whom she nicknames Lazarus because "at night he rises from the dead." (She talks that way a lot.) The elders in this play are masters and mistresses of the fine parental art of making their children want to sink through the floor.

When it was first produced, Leaving Home was hailed as a beacon of the new Canadian drama. Anywhere but in Canada it would have seemed fearfully old-fashioned: a box-set family drama working its way to a neat resolution. Compare what Thomas Murphy, another first- timer, was doing in Ireland with family tensions in A Whistle in the Dark a decade before. To its credit, French's play doesn't pretend that its most serious problems are soluble, but it still manages a final epiphany that seems unconnected to whats preceded it. But it also has the old-fashioned virtues of involvement and suspense. Once past the necessary lumps of exposition, it sinks its hooks in and never lets go.

I was tempted to say it has the virtues of a well-made play, but in fact its rather oddly made. The title refers to Ben's decision to move out of his parents' house, a plan that he divulges to his mother early on and that she accurately predicts will drive his father wild. Never mind that Dad himself has often suggested that its time for his son to act like a man and be independent; as far as hes concerned, anything that Ben says or does must be wrong, and he's perfectly capable of yelling that any of his previous remarks on the subject shouldn't be dredged up and held against him. This kind of compulsive wrong-footing within families is painfully familiar (and hardly confined to fathers and sons), but Im not convinced that the peculiarly nasty example of it that French presents here is really, as he seems to want us to think, a mask for deep, inexpressible affection. Whatever: This relationship is the heart of the play, and the rest of it begins to seem like an elaborate irrelevance. In theory, one can see that the plight of Billy and his bride, who have grave misgivings about their shotgun marriage, is a variation on the theme; they, too, have urgent reasons for leaving home. But their relationship is only sketched in and is abandoned just when it seems that it might get interesting.

Ted Dykstras production, on a dream of a realistic set by Patrick Clark, is cunningly staged and finely orchestrated. There is a surprising amount of humour, and some inspirational casting. Kenneth Welsh's paterfamilias is magnificent, or it is if you overlook the trifling fact of some three-quarters of his lines being, at least to my immigrant ears, incomprehensible. But from underneath all the gabbling and the slurring (which, among other things, obscures what seems to be a major theme about the hostility between Protestants and Catholics), there emerges a man in whom anger and bewilderment have overridden anything else. Welsh finds a rhythm of resentment into which everything fits: spasms of bonhomie; brief excursions on the dance floor; ghastly, distorted chop-logic; bouts of physical violence. It's impossible to approve of him, almost impossible to like him, but we get a very clear sense of the barriers hes beating against; Welsh practically erects them onstage. His chief antagonists labour under the disadvantage of being as consistently right as he is wrong: Diane DAquila occasionally hits a discordantly plaintive note but her Mary is otherwise suitably rocklike, while Jeff Lillico does a very good job of stating the case for flight while wishing that he didn't have to.

As the mother-in-law-to-be, Jane Spidell is a revelation; she has always been a fastidious actress, and she still is, but her inner poise here enables her to present a late-blooming hedonist whose demonstrativeness embarrasses everyone around her while delighting us. Her mortician beloved, Harold (a.k.a. the formaldehyde kid), is the indispensable Oliver Dennis; he never gets to speak a word but in his black-clad lanky silence, a drink never out of his hand, he suggests that a great comic creation has waited 35 years to find proper expression. "I think," says Jacob at a moment of uproar, "that we should all take an example from Harold," and it's to Denniss credit that its the most explosively funny line in the play. Anthony Johnston and Martha MacIsaac do their best for the underwritten not-so-happy couple; it isn't MacIsaac's fault (though it may, on consideration, be the productions) that the scene in which she proves herself her mothers daughter by running her hand up the imperturbable Harold's leg seems to belong to some other character in some other play. Sex, in this play, is pretty much beneath the surface, and it should probably stay there.

- Leaving Home runs through June 23 at the Young Centre, 416-866- 8666.

The latest-but-one episode of The Sopranos chased me around Europe for a week, never quite catching up in time for me to write about it. So, here is a combined view of both that instalment and its successor: Episodes 4 and 5 of the current and final series. This at least reduces my danger of revealing sensitive information and having to enter the Critics' Protection Program.

As it happens, these two episodes fit very snugly together. They both explore the basic Sopranos theme of fathers and children, and especially of fathers and sons. I've often felt that the most important relationship in the show is the one between Tony and Anthony Junior. He's always wanted to keep A.J. out of the mob, for which, in any case, the kid has little talent. But Tony's hopes that A.J. might avoid it by emulating the academic success of his sister Meadow have been consistently and conclusively dashed. So, Tony makes fleeting, self-conscious contact whenever he can; memories still linger from the first season of father showing son how to change a tire ("We do it ourselves in this house") or the two of them sharing a furtive dish of ice cream.

One thing that A.J. inherited from his dad was a proneness to panic attacks. It was this that forced his parents a couple of years ago to abandon their plans to pack him off to a military academy. (He was far from willing, anyway: "I look like a dork," he said, surveying himself in his uniform.) There was a ghastly echo of this incident last week in the story of young Vito, son of the gay gangster who got bumped off in the previous season. That story seemed drawn out at the time, but it's justified itself in the sequel. Young Vito (did his parents call him V.J.?), unnervingly Goth, is acting up violently, and his mother appeals for help to the two ganglords on whom she has a claim: Phil Leotardo, her cousin, and Tony, her husband's old boss. Tony is the more sympathetic of the two when attempting a man-to-man talk - Phil being Phil, it's hardly a contest - but he doesn't actually get anywhere with his old friend's son. Half the time, young Vito points out, Tony has called him young Carlo. As usual, the strands here are drawn very tight: Carlo is the guy who replaced Vito on the mob's construction scam, and Tony often laments that he isn't nearly as good an earner. "Maybe," he tells Carlo, with a characteristic blend of tolerance and brutality, "you should try [fellatio]". And it's with a similar mix of cynicism and conscientiousness that Tony disposes of the young Vito problem; he won't pony up the $100,000 needed for the family to move to Maine ("you can't," he says, "have a geographical solution to a psychological problem"), but he will contribute $18,000 to have the boy removed to a camp in Idaho, where corporal punishment is not only allowed but, it seems, encouraged. It's a far nastier place than Tony once had in mind for his own son. And there's no reprieve as there was for A.J.; Vito Junior is virtually kidnapped, screaming, in the middle of the night.

This may be the worst thing Tony's ever done. Even here, though, it's possible to construct a kind of defence for him. He intended to pay for the Maine move out of his gambling winnings, only there weren't any. Tony's gaming compulsion has been abruptly introduced this season but it fits who and what he is. It's now cost him another in his diminishing line of old friends: Hesh, the Jewish financier, to whom he paid off a $300,000 loan at the end of Episode 4, accompanied by sheepish expressions of sympathy over the death of Hesh's girlfriend, the apparent victim of a heart attack. Tony used to be proud of having a Jew in his inner circle, but that kind of thing can turn on a dime. In debt and resenting it, Tony says things like "don't be shy, Shylock" while Hesh, who didn't dare not make the loan, has his own unflattering remarks about unpredictable Italians. And, on the subject of race, the Sopranos didn't seem too thrilled about A.J. having gotten himself a Hispanic fiancée.

The story of this engagement was spread over the two episodes. In 4, the barely adult A.J. proposed, was accepted, and then rejected. It was his best chance at escape, and 5 showed a depressed, regressing A.J., sprawled across his parents' couch, watching Tom and Jerry. Robert Iler's performance has been trashed over the years, but I've always found him convincingly insecure, not least in the tentative beard he's grown as a stab at maturity. Meadow, showing unusual concern, thought him suicidal. (And we remembered that the one time A.J. showed any interest in school is when he discovered doubt and existentialism). Irony of ironies: When Tony pushes him out of the house to hang with people his own age, they turn out to be junior gangsters from college, the student sons of Tony's lieutenants. The fathers are immensely proud of their offspring's scholastic achievements, even while the offspring are developing their own line in violence and extortion. (One of them is young Carlo who, when we meet him, doesn't seem in the least like young Vito.) A.J. seems to dig it; he's on track to become part of the world his father wanted to keep him out of.

James Gandolfini has seldom been more moving than in Tony's latest consultation with Dr. Melfi, recalling how, when your children are ill, you long to change places with them and take their pain; as always he makes you aware both of the reality of the feelings and of the sinister limitations of the space in which they operate. Keeping A.J. happy and uninvolved would, I think, be Tony's idea of salvation, and it looks like he isn't going to get it.

Conversely he wants to keep Christopher, his nephew and effectively his other son, very much involved, and that too is backfiring. Tony has come, after an initial burst of pride, to resent Chris's movie-making and he can't resist mocking Chris - who's in Alcoholics Anonymous - both for his attempts to stay on the wagon and for his periodic falls off it. The others laugh at a man who doesn't drink but it's Tony, the intelligent, who really knows how to twist the knife.

Episode 5 continued Chris's feud with Paulie Walnuts, his rival as loosest cannon in the arsenal who, in one scene, drives his car all over Chris's expensive garden: definitely bringing the fight home to your enemy. Later, Paulie tramples on even more sacred ground by prophesying a future for Chris's daughter as a stripper in the Bada Bing. Goaded beyond endurance, Chris shoots - but he shoots somebody else, a comparative innocent. The motives for this, the week's statutory whack, are mixed, but the victim may have sealed his own fate by uttering the word "Mafia," the first time it's been spoken, to my recollection, since the famous “Meadowlands” episode in which Tony's daughter asked him if he was a member. Tony's blustering reply was that there was no such thing as the Mafia; It was merely "an ugly stereotype."

That wheel, too, came full circle in Episode 5 when Tony denounced Chris' movie as "a very unflattering picture of Italian-Americans." The same allegation has of course been made of The Sopranos itself. The show's complexity is its best defence; second-best, perhaps, is this reminder (it's actually a running gag) that Tony agrees with his detractors, and that the show itself is way ahead of them.

2007-05-15-requiem-for-the-newly-departe:
Christopher Moltisanti is dead. As if that wasn't shocking enough, he died a mere ten minutes into Sunday's episode of The Sopranos, ignominiously, in a car-crash. People have been speculating on Chris' demise for some time, especially with the show entering its own deaththroes, but the core characters, those who have been around since the very beginning, have seemed to possess a kind of immunity. Yes, Tony's mother Livia left us early on, but that was principally because of the death of the actress playing her. Chris' girlfriend Adriana was shockingly murdered two seasons ago, and her death continues to reverberate, but it had taken time for her to become a major player. And her death, when it came, was the climax of an episode. Big Pussy, the first major casualty, had most of an hour devoted to his demise; his was a most ceremonious offing.

Of late, the show has been getting more cavalier with its send- offs. Hesh and Uncle Junior have been effectively sidelined, but they are still technically alive. Even more remarkably, the episode about Chris' death turned out not to be about Chris' death but about everyone's reaction to it, especially Tony's. Because Tony killed him. This was not altogether unexpected, since Chris, once the favoured surrogate son, had come to to represent all kinds of threat. But for it happen like this? While chauffeuring Tony, Chris swerves and hits another car. Chris, the relapsed junkie, protests that he has too much dope in his system for him to risk being caught in the driver's seat. ("I'll lose my licence"). He's so badly hurt that he might die anyway. So Tony, whose superficial bruises give him a lumpy look for the rest of the episode, helps him along. You might call it a mercy-killing, but you'd have to be feeling very generous. Incidentally David Chase, the series' creator, co-wrote this episode; it was as if he too had to do this job himself. His hands-on presence may also account for the episode's insistent -- maybe too insistent -- symbolism.

Carmela's reaction is concern for Tony -- she doesn't know, of course--and quasi-maternalgrief for Chris; remember how, when he was close to death once before, she prayed that he would recover and get out of the Life? (Not that she's got out of it herself.) Paulie Walnuts, Chris' old foe and colleague, expresses unexpected sympathy, probabaly sincere, or as sincere as anyone in this milieu ever gets. ("You were his dad, I was his Dutch uncle" he says to Tony, who was Chris' uncle.) But the old indignant Paulie bounces back, when his mother --actually his aunt, but we don't have to go there -- dies too. The two wakes are held on the same day, and the one for Mrs. Walnuts, or whatever her name was, loses out; hardly anyone shows up. (Tony and Carmela do pay a flying visit.) "What kind of testament is that," Paulie asks, "to her spirit and generosity?" And maybe we should count in the two young ladies in the car that got away; the one driving won't go back to help because "I'm on my learning permit after dark." Much the same position as Chris, really.

But it all centres on Tony, his vestigial guilt and his overriding relief. He tries unload some of the latter response on Carmela, with little success. He actually confesses it to Dr. Melfi, twice. The first time he even confesses the murder. Then he wakes up. The Sopranos' dream-sequences fool you every time, especially in this episode, which has a dream-like feel throughout. The second, real, psychiatric session cunningly reprises much of the first,imaginary, one, with the most incriminating details left out. The combination of brutality and evasiveness in these scenes are James Gandolfini at his best.

Then, in a sequence strikingly reminsicent of his near-death experience when Junior shot him, Tony goes to Vegas: Not, primarily, to play the numbers (though he does, and for a change wins) but to meet and bed an old girlfriend of his nephew's. Presumably the sexual rivalry he always felt with Chris has been sated. She turns him on to peyote, and he ends the episode having a Carlos Casteneda moment in the desert. "I get it," he shouts, though what he gets is unclear. Whatever it is, I doubt that it will last. We've met new Tonys before, and have stopped wanting to believe in them. One of the last things Chris got to say to Tony was "whatever happened to 'stop and smell the roses?'" Nothing much. It couldn't, as long as Tony remains Tony and his life the life.

Maybe his real son has a chance. AJ remains part of the gang of student Sopranos, and this week participated in the beating and humiliation of a black boy who had the misfortune to be on his bike when it was hit by a rashly opened car door. (This has been an episode of road rage.) But he seemed less happy about it than he did about the torturing of another kid, and he seems to be worried by all kinds of things he's never thought about before, from the Middle East conflict to Wordsworth's words on the world being too much with us. He talks to his shrink about the hopelessness of it all. But then again, it could just be words. The show often shows us feelings, fine or foul, flaring up and being smothered by the process of life. Tony's and Carmela's marriage should have foundered a dozen times but it goes on. Tony's desert revelation was counterpointed by the side-effect of one of his business deals: a load of asbestos dumped into a river. Earlier he had hurled a Cleaver coffee-mug, a souvenir of Chris' movie, into the wilderness beyond his own home. And on both occasions, his beloved ducks feebly quacked.

THEATRE REVIEW

A MONTH IN THE COUNTRY

COURT HOUSE THEATRE,

NIAGARA-ON-THE-LAKE

- - -

Ivan Turgenev wrote a play called A Month in the Country, and so, 150 years later, did Brian Friel. Friels play is billed -- not just chronologically -- as "after Turgenev," and large sections of it do indeed follow very closely after. There are others in which it keeps a more radical distance.

One thing that Friel, Irelands most venerated living playwright, has surprisingly not done is to alter the original's time and place. Classic Russian plays have in the past been quite successfully transplanted to later periods in Ireland, but here we are still in the vast wasteland of provincial Russia in the 1840s. And though the dialogue can be racily contemporary, there is nothing about it -- not, at least, on the lips of the Shaw Festival's Canadian cast -- that sounds especially Irish.

What Friel has done, for the most part to great effect, is to sharpen both the absurdity and the heartbreak of the main plot bequeathed him by his predecessor. Here again we have Natalya Petrovna, young wife of a rich landowner, flirting inconclusively with the admirer, Rakitin, whom shes been keeping on a string for years (and whose self-lacerating, unconsummated passion is based on Turgenevs own feelings for a married opera singer). Here we have Belyayev, the household's new, young tutor suddenly arousing the interest both of Natalya and of her teenage ward Vera, of whom she becomes maliciously jealous. What in Turgenev is incipiently farcical becomes explicit in Friel, without in any way devaluing the emotional confrontations which, decorous in the original, come at us here with their white gloves off.

This is the only version I've seen of A Month in the Country to hold my attention throughout; usually Ive flagged somewhere in the middle as the characters seemed to be going endlessly around in the same circles. Tadeusz Bradeckis excellent production is ruthless but not heartless. It enables Fiona Byrne, in what must be her finest performance to date, to expose all the self-indulgence of Natalya, who believes the world owes her a romance, without skimping either on the pain she suffers or that which she causes. David Jansen's Rakitin, more puppy-dog than lapdog, is adequate while hardly probing the depths of the man's agony or of his ironic selfzcontempt, but Martin Happer is suitably guileless as Belyayev and Marla McLean a revelation as Vera, a character whom I have never known to register as more than a necessary ingenue but is here capable

of real feeling and real anger; her scenes with Natalya, who is trying simultaneously to befriend and exploit her, are among the strongest in the show.

There is an extraordinary tragifarcical performance by Blair Williams as Natalyas uncomprehending spouse, whose main interest is his threshing machine: Suddenly provoked into paroxysms of jealousy over the wrong man, he as quickly subsides into terrified acquiescence. He is the character most altered: Turgenev wrote him as stolid, but Friel, picking up on hints, makes him a volatile mothers boy, with Patricia Hamilton giving a grandly judicious account of the mother. She, too, has acquired a new dimension (in fact, a whole new backstory), and Friel has in general dealt more freely with the minor characters than with the major ones, with varying results. With the local doctor, who provides rich material in the first place, he's been completely successful. Ric Reid, emphasizing the man's peasant background and emotional dyspepsia, plays the doctor as a resentful hanger-on who despises himself and everyone else, especially those who laugh at his terrible jokes. Its a superb performance, as remote as possible from Reids fine gentle Inquisitor in Saint Joan (which is about bad things happening to good people because good people do them), and most delicately partnered by Sharry Flett as the spinster companion whose face speaks finely shaded volumes and with whom he eventually pairs off. He has a further fine foil in Michael Ball as an unprepossessing neighbour who admires Vera and pays the doctor to act as go- between: a nice enough fellow whose dramatic fate it is to bring out the worst -- the most selfish or the most desperate-- in everyone.

The role of Herr Schaaf, an older and Germanic tutor, has been much extended, given a more extended line in randiness and a wholly new one in malapropisms. David Schurmann plays him well, but he far outstays his welcome. Confession: I once played Schaaf, and was heard to complain that the brevity of the role proved that Turgenev was a novelist, not a playwright. Chekhov, I grumbled, would have known how to keep his small-part actors active throughout. I should have been careful for what I wished. Two servants who pursue an inconclusive courtship in the original have also had their relationship upgraded so that it becomes part subplot, part commentary on the self-inflicted torments of their employers. No complaints about the performances of Moya O'Connell and Thom Marriott but they become intrusive.

The show has too active a periphery. But its centre holds. - A Month in the Country is in repertoire through October 6. Call 1-800- 511- SHAW for tickets.

2007-05-19-bloody-miserable-bunch-these-:
Sarah Kane hanged herself at the age of 28, having written six plays and suffered a short lifetime of depression. Those facts hang heavy in the mind of anyone entering a theatre to witness one of her famously bleak plays, which provoked both shock and awe in England in the 1990s and are gradually making their way over here. Their dark vision, the implicit argument goes, is drawn from the author's own experience, so it has to be authentic.

It's a kind of blackmail, but I'll give in to it. I'll also agree that the actual language of her plays is remarkable, particularly in the case of Crave, a kind of quartet for voices that's staged here by Nightwood Theatre. But these qualities in themselves don't necessarily make a masterpiece. Crave is hard work. It repays the effort, more in stabbing moments than as a whole, but the difficulty isn't a recommendation in itself.

The four people in Crave are identified simply as A, B, C and M. In Jennifer Tarver's production they stand in a series of adjacent alcoves, created by the bends of the folding screen that constitutes Teresa Przybylski's set, lit with cruel virtuosity by Kimberly Purtell. They deliver alternating monologues, many of them composed of a single line. There are hints of plot lines, in which the monologues sound like splinters of dialogue; one speaker seems to be answering what another has said, though frequently the call and the response will be separated by a remark from somebody else altogether.

The speakers are, to an extent, characters. A briskly introduces himself by saying "I'm not a rapist I'm a pedophile." He also, disconcertingly, has the play's tenderest lines about love and longing, many of them assembled into the play's one extended and extremely eloquent speech, composed as a single run-on sentence and delivered as such, or at least as far as human breath permits, by Hardee Lineham. His performance is altogether a memorable blend of seediness and torment, a sharp physical and mental outline, sadly set off by a bulging belly. He talks at one point of "this woman with the desolate eyes for whom I would die." This could be C, who seems as a child to have been abused by her father or grandfather or both, and will carry the scars to what will undoubtedly be an early death. It's impossible not to see her as figuring Kane herself, but it's also a tribute to the writing that she's no self-indulgent mouthpiece. As played by Michelle Monteith, who can do amazing things with the word "bereaved," she swings between soulful and spiteful.

B -- the sketchiest figure, though Carlos Gonzalez-Vio plays him well enough--is a self-consciously tough young man, locked in an approach-and-avoidance scenario with M, a self-possessed sophisticated lady whose biological clock is beginning to sound alarms. (B: "I need to be seduced by an older woman." M: "I'm not an older woman." B: "Older than me, not older per se.") M is played with unfaultable style by Maria Ricossa. Her alphabetical distance from the other characters suggests that she may exist on a different plane. Perhaps the play is an elaborate therapy session and she's the shrink. Or perhaps the author was just being a tease. But when C cries out, over and over (and over and over) "what have they done to me?" it's M who sharply tells her to "grow up and stop blaming mother." C sees M as her neglectful mother anyway (maybe that's what's the initial's about) but M vigorously denies it. It's some ingenious cat's cradle that we have here.

The text is studded with black aphorisms. "The outside world," says A, "is vastly overrated." "If I die here," proclaims C, a little less resonantly, "I was murdered by daytime television." The latter, though, may be a comment less on the world at large than on the kind of institution in which Kane herself ended her life. It's surely the author herself whom we hear through the confession "I am an emotional plagiarist, stealing other people's pain." That's almost a writer's job description, disturbed or otherwise.

As for what the characters are craving: It has to be that old thing love, sought as always in impossible places. The climax must be when the four entreat "LEAVE. COME BACK. STAY" in unison and in capital letters.

"Don't forget," C admonishes us, "poetry is language used for its own sake." I don't know if that's a recommendation or a warning, but it's tempting to refer her back to her author, with the observation that dramatic poetry is language used for drama's sake. It doesn't even have to be verbal, and in fact Tarver, a director who excels at making the abstract concrete, does the visual thing superbly here.

I am three-quarters convinced. If the production is revived, I shall go again.

- Crave closes tonight at the Young Centre for the Performing Arts, 416- 866-8666.

2007-05-23-family-ties-hold-strong-a-j-s:
There was a surprisingly lame bit of writing in Sunday's episode of The Sopranos. A.J., still depressed over the breakup of his engagement and just about everything else, is surprised in his room by big sister, Meadow. He tells her how screwed-up the world is ("do you realize we're gonna bomb Iran") and criticizes her for watching Borat ("it's not fair to the people involved"). She tries to buck him up, telling him that no matter what privileges she's enjoyed, this is an Italian family, and he, the son, will always be the favourite.

That's probably true enough. But it was uncomfortably explanatory for this show, and Jamie-Lynn Sigler as Meadow certainly couldn't bring it to life. A.J.'s sociopolitical conscience also sounded rather pat -- as if the show itself were assuring us that it was keeping up with world events -- though it's psychologically plausible. A boy who's always led a sheltered, uninquistive life is suddenly shocked into awareness, and swallows everything at once. He's 20 and experiencing all the customary years of adolescent disillusion rolled into one.

A.J.'s also being affected by the college classes he's been auditing. Last week, it was Wordsworth on materialism; this week, it's Yeats on the apocalypse and The Second Coming: "Things fall apart, the centre cannot hold " A.J. can identify with that on every level. Carmela, who's always had a conflicted relationship with high culture, went into indignant worried-mother mode with one of the episode's two funniest lines: "What kind of poem is that to teach college students?"

She had a lot to be worried about. This was the episode in which A.J. tried to commit suicide in his parents' pool. Tony, seeing it just in time, threw down the sandwich he was eating, jumped in and rescued him. His first reaction after fishing the boy out was to shake him and say angrily, "What's wrong with you?" His next was to ask, "Are you all right?" and his third was to break down in tears, hold him and say, over and over, "Oh, my baby." The scene, as written by Terence Winter and acted by James Gandolfini and Robert Iler, was wrenchingly moving.

In a way, it brought father and son back from the brink. Tony, who the previous week murdered his surrogate son, this week saved his real one. I doubt if anybody was surprised. Blood really is thicker than water. By this stage, I think, most of us have stopped judging Tony. We just watch, fascinated, as he blunders from one action or response to another. Our stand-in, of course, is his shrink, Dr. Melfi, whom we saw this week in one of her periodic sessions with her own therapist. (And who, one wonders, treats him? Does this pattern of infinite regress at some point turn back on itself?)

I once heard of a psychiatrist who said that Tony's therapy accomplished absolutely nothing, and praised the show for its realism in this regard. The selfsatisfied Dr. Kupferberg, who has a vicarious fascination with Melfi's gangster patient, points to research indicating "talk therapy serves to validate sociopaths." Which may be the show ruefully kidding itself: It's talk therapy and we're the shrinks.

Is Tony a sociopath? He recognizes loyalties outside himself,and he doesn't kill for the satisfaction of it, so he isn't a psychopath. One of the few mob characters who might qualify for that description is the late Christopher Moltisanti, who sacrificed his girlfriend and capriciously murdered a (legitimate) colleague. The others have ties. Even Paulie loved the mother who was really his aunt. Even the awful Phil Leotardo is partly motivated by the desire to avenge his brother. But their community feelings stop short within their own organizations, often under their own roofs.

The metaphors have been getting graphic. Phil and Tony, the New York and New Jersey bosses, are now jointly responsible for unloading asbestos onto the landscape. No wonder Tony's annoyed that A.J.'s new concerns include the environment. Paulie rather hilariously brings the themes together when condoling with Tony over A.J.'s death wish: "All these toxins we're exposed to --it's a wonder there aren't more kids [attempting suicide]."

The Soprano family continues to play the self-righteousness game, as, come to think of it, does almost everyone on the show. "I am intimately acquainted with the Soprano family curse", says Carmela, acidly accusing Tony of always "playing the depression card." A.J., in family therapy, blames everyone, including his grandmother Livia for informing him on her deathbed that life was garbage. (I'd forgotten that. Everything on this show comes back to bite you.) Tony clings to the idea that he has redeeming features: "I'm a good guy, basically. I love my family." Indeed he does; this week he all but killed a guy to prove it, one who'd insulted his daughter. (There were no actual deaths this week, which may presage a bloodbath to come.) He even likes to think of himself as a good citizen. In the very first episode he drew a line, while talking to Melfi, between his own actions and those of terrorists blowing up children (the kind of thing that now appalls A.J.). And even now, the only way in which he'll try to ingratiate himself to the FBI is to offer them (probably) useless information on a couple of Arabs who used to frequent the Bing.

That storyline may or may not be going anywhere; it keeps recurring, but tenuously. We are presumably in for a showdown between Jersey and New York. This week ended with Tony visiting Phil, who refused to see him, merely taunting him from what looked weirdly like a medieval turret (or at least like something from Monty Python and the Holy Grail). Little Carmine, who'd brokered the abortive meeting, here went beyond mere malapropism to favour Tony with a sublimely mixed metaphor that was the show's other funniest line: "You're at the precipice of an enormous crossroads." With only two episodes to go, we all are.

- The Sopranos airs Sunday nights on The Movie Network at 9 p.m.

Daniel MacIvor's Marion Bridge isn't a monologue, contains no physical or emotional violence and is tolerably realistic. It is MacIvor's attempt -- written a decade ago; partly, we are told, to please his mother -- to come up with a play that resembles other people's. In this endeavour it is fairly successful and fairly entertaining. But I wouldn't say it was exciting.

The title refers to a spot in Cape Breton to which two of three sisters once paid a fondly remembered childhood visit; the third, the youngest, got somehow left behind, as seems to have been her fate throughout life. She is the one still living with their mother, who is now at the point of death. So the others, in early middle age, come home to help out, or at least to be present. Agnes, the eldest, arrives from Toronto; she's an unsuccessful actress with a drink problem. Theresa, the middle one, is a nun, from a good-works order in New Brunswick. Agnes, who fancies herself as a cynical wisecracker, has a lot of fun making jokes about Theresa's calling. Louise, the stay-at-home and the only one not named after a saint, is in the process of memorizing a compensatory catalogue of the canonized. She's gruff and abrupt and organizes her life around "her show," a TV soap to which she's addicted but which she later abandons when it gets too silly. Theresa, though, begins to get hooked on it.

Their quirks are amusingly portrayed. I especially enjoyed the way Theresa picked up on Agnes's fashionable use of the word "whatever," going on to claim that the trouble with today's world is that it's become a "whatever" society. (There's a neat reversal of this exchange at the end of the play.) Theresa, defending her vocation to the world and herself, is an interesting character. But Louise is little more than odd, and Agnes, with her block about entering her mother's sickroom, adds nothing new to the familiar notion of the bruised sophisticate who returns and learns. The inevitable rapprochement between the sisters involves an offstage visit to their estranged father and his younger girlfriend which, as we hear about it, is sad-grotesquefunny but no kind of revelation, and a climactic return trip--by all three, this time -- to the fabled Marion Bridge, which isn't as resonant as it's presumably meant to be. In fact, it casts doubt on the validity of the title, and hence of the play. Each sister is afforded a lyrical soliloquy, and these accomplish even less.

The author's own production, for the Company Theatre, is expectedly well staged, and decently acted though, on the night I was there, Caroline Gillis as Agnes seemed both unsure and over- emphatic. Emmy Alcorn, whose Mulgrave Road company in Nova Scotia premiered the play in 1998, gives an arrestingly throaty account of Louise, banging around her own little world on emotional auto- pilot, but it's Sarah Dodd (the one hold-over from Company Theatre's previous show, A Whistle in the Dark) who gives the show its centre, making a perfect unpatronizing case for Theresa in both her doubts and her certainties.

The Young Centre, down in the Distillery, is currently awash in small-town drama. Marion Bridge occupies one space, while Soulpepper's Leaving Home, which I think of as a displaced small- towner, shares another with the same company's revival of the Thornton Wilder play that explicitly maps out and sums up the whole genre. Joseph Ziegler's production of Our Town, coming round now for the third time, is as lovely as ever, if not lovelier. Albert Schultz's Stage Manager, beautifully pitched, embodies the play's stance of detached compassion, while presiding (I assume with artistic director's pride) over a stageful of sparkling, perfectly integrated performances. John Jarvis's newspaper editor, reaching out in brow-mopping embarrassment to his about-to-be son-in-law, has actually improved since last year, more of a person, less of a turn. Richer, too, is Jeff Lillico, as the equally reluctant object of the man-to-man chat; in the great drugstore proposal scene, he practically bursts out of his skin to prove himself worthy of the girl he suddenly realizes he adores. Then there are the serene and chippy mothers of Nancy Palk and Jane Spidell; Oliver Dennis's doctor, contented even to complacency; Martha MacIsaac's bride, whose porcelain fragility conceals an even more touching strength; Diego Matamoros's professor with topography on tap; and William Webster's sodden choirmaster, fixing his fellow citizens with a silent despairing glare. As an exemplar of Soulpepper at its expansive best --casting in breadth, playing in depth -- this ranks second only to Platonov, which had the advantage of a richer text. Our Town is a string of cameos rather than a dynamic painting. It has you beguiled with its evocation of an America long gone, then irritated at yourself for succumbing to sentimentality, then reassured that Wilder sees the narrowness of Grover's Corners, N.H., as acutely as you do yourself. For all the freedom of its stagecraft, it's a play about limitations --humanity's in the world, the world's in the cosmos --and it's both a celebration of those limits and a lament. The Stage Manager's philosophizing have the accent of cracker-barrel, but he knows it and so does the play, of which he is the voice but not entirely the soul. This is the best imaginable production. - Marion Bridge closes tonight. Our Town is in repertoire through Aug 19, both at the Young Centre. For information, call 416-866-8666.

2007-05-28-the-fence-sitters-of-love-nee:
THE PHILANDERER

Royal George Theatre, Niagara-on-the-Lake at the Shaw Festival

- - -

George Bernard Shaw's The Philanderer, his second play, would have us believe that, in London in the 1890s, there was an establishment known as the Ibsen Club, named for the great Norwegian playwright and providing a comfortable environment for all the well- heeled advanced thinkers of their day.

Like Shaw himself, his fictitious clubmen and clubwomen seem to have had a limited idea of what their idol actually stood for. Ibsen was never a great one for causes; he even denied, despite A Dolls House, that he was a feminist. The "Ibsenism" that the characters in The Philanderer go on about seems to be a vague label for anything progressive but boils down in practice to relations between the sexes.

Any enlightened young thing applying for membership has to be certified, to the horror of the older generation, as either an unmanly man or an unwomanly woman. This has nothing to do with homosexuality. It doesnt even ban relationships between members, which in fact, seem to be encouraged. But partisans of what the title character calls the advanced view -- our view are supposed to move easily from one partner to the next, to take rejection in their stride, and to abstain from jealousy, possessiveness and all the other appurtenances of romantic love.

Somewhat thin and protracted as a story, the play, like most of Shaw, is an astonishingly confident outpouring of language. The characters are mainly stock figures brought to new and vivacious life by sheer force of dialogue. The chat, as usual with Shaw and especially with Shaw on sex, is witty but chilly; but it's one of his most fascinating plays, because it's one of Shaws most personal. The philanderer himself, Leonard Charteris -- confident, articulate, superficially solicitous and invincibly self-centred-- is an engaging but merciless self-portrait. He may not be the sexual late bloomer that his author was, but for all his presumed conquests, theres still something virginal about him -- as there is, admittedly, about most of Shaw's characters; they may be constrained by the theatrical conventions of their time but one suspects that, even when safely offstage, they would be more talk than action.

We see Leonard getting on with a new love before being off with the old, or at least before the old is off with him. Both ladies are fellow club members. Grace Tranfield, to whom he's currently paying court, is a widow, the most sensible and truly liberated person in the play. Julia Craven, his unwilling ex, stalks, threatens, cajoles and throws tantrums, both in and out of the club, which she has obviously joined under thoroughly false pretenses; she is, at least if you happen to be in her line of fire, the womanly woman from hell. If Charteris has too little heart, Julia has too much.

He finally palms her off on a more pliable admirer, a Dr. Paramore, who happens to be treating her father for a fatal but, as it turns out, non-existent disease. You might say -- and Shaw would surely want you to -- that the father has Paramores disease, while the daughter has paramours disease.

Alisa Palmer's production, yet another bloom in the Shaw Festival's opening bouquet, is both handsomely and humorously designed by Judith Bowden. It has Ben Carlson in scintillating form as Charteris, Deborah Hay as a Grace more than worthy of the name and Nicole Underhay as a Julia whos almost totally wrong. Julia is one of natures dark ladies, but this one is light of hair and, greatly compounding the damage, of temperament. She's a rare case in Shaw where wit is inappropriate.

Also too lightweight, though for other reasons, is Peter Krantz's Dr. Paramore, whose great discovery is disproved by foreign researchers who have been granted more animals to torture. He seems less a medical star in danger of falling than a student worried about his grades.

The heroines fathers, the twin voices of outraged convention, are splendidly played. They are both members of notoriously reactionary professions -- Julias is a soldier, Grace's is a theatre critic-- and they are given buffo performances by Norman Browning and Peter Hutt, the one rumbling, the other apoplectic.

Shaw wrote a "lost" last act that is to be given at some performances later in the season. It should be worth catching, since it has more weight and more poise than anything in the rest of the play. The official final curtain is here an anti-climax. When Julia tells Charteris at the end of the play that she could kill him, we ought to believe her; the stage direction tells us that the other characters sober up, realizing that they are in the presence of real grief.

Grace, having herself effectively dumped Charteris, takes Julia's side, telling her "never make a hero of a philanderer." He laughs, but the laughs on him. Its a difficult gear change to pull off, but it's what the play's about. The man who laughed at love and the woman who staked everything on it -- the Shavian and the anti- Shavian -- have both had their ideals shattered. Ibsen himself, the perennial questioner and non-joiner, would have approved. He would never have joined a club that would have him as a mentor. - George Bernard Shaws The Philanderer is in repertoire through October 7 at the Shaw Festival in Niagara-on-the-Lake. For tickets call 1-800- 511-SHAW or visit www.shawfest.com

2007-05-29-musicals-don-t-have-to-be-as-:
MACK AND MABEL

Festival Theatre, Niagara-on-the-Lake, Ont.

- - -

Im in the camp with those, including the composer-lyricist himself, whose favourite Jerry Herman score is Mack and Mabel.

Mack is Mack Sennett, the pioneering maestro of early silent film comedy, and Mabel is Mabel Normand, his favourite leading lady and the love, the show insists, of his life. (And he of hers, but stuff happens.)

The show flopped when it was done on Broadway in 1974, but its tunes have kept it alive, and just listening to them all flow past in the overture to the Shaw Festivals production makes you understand why.

We get invigorating foretastes of the commanding and pulsating Movies Were Movies, the pugnacious Big Time, the poignant I Won't Send Roses, the enchanting Look What Happened to Mabel and much else. There are so many goodies in this medley that it can afford to hold the show's closing number, called I Promised You a Happy Ending. It isnt a particularly good song, but its crucial to understanding a) what the musical is trying to do and b) why, with all its attractive qualities, it doesn't work.

The show is a first-person narrative with flashbacks. Mack, adrift in a horrible new world where actors talk, starts the proceedings by singing at us that "movies were movies when during the titles you knew / You'd get a happy ending.

By the end of the evening, Mack is fantasizing of just such a fadeout for himself and Mabel, even while acknowledging that there was no reunion and that Mabel really wound up an unemployable drug addict caught up in a murder scandal. At least, thats how things played out in the shows original book, written by the late Michael Stewart, and many people blamed the production's failure on the implied downer of its finale.

The script has since been reworked (by Francine Pascal, Stewart's sister) so that there really is a happy ending. Mack and Mabel get to make one more picture together and, for all we are told, live happily ever after. This feels false, because it is false, although not so much false to history as false to the shows own purpose.

Mack and Mabel tells two stories: the story of silent comedy and the story of a love affair. For a time, the two tales get along together. Its lovely when Mabel, a deli waitress, comes to Mack's New York lot to collect payment on a sandwich and gets caught up in the action, revealing herself to be a great natural comedienne. It's neat, and musically and lyrically delightful, when she first sees herself on the screen, and understands just what has happened to the former queen of corned beef and salami." Its a thrill when the whole Sennett operation hits the big time and sets off for California, full of beans and schadenfreude: "This time, exults an unusually frank lyric in Big Time, we wont say 'those lucky bastards' / this time those lucky bastards are us."

The romance gets off to a bittersweet start when Mack, a workaholic, admits that he isnt the flower-sending type and Mabel ruefully accepts him. When Mabel muses later that there are things time doesnt heal, it's an admission worth the price of admission.

But, even in the original unsweetened book, there are fatal flaws. The love songs may engage the characters' emotions and ours, but the love story doesnt. Its a formulaic affair, with predictable complications arising from Mack frustrating Mabel's ambitions of becoming a dramatic artiste. The story of the Sennett studio also becomes formulaic, and here it's the fault of the score, or of what the score is asked to do. Mack outlines his philosophy (I Want To Make the World Laugh). He invents the Sennett Bathing Beauties (Hundreds of Girls). He invents the Keystone Kops (Hit Em on the Head). The numbers are cheery and repetitive, both individually and as a group, and they dont get us anywhere.

Molly Smith's production, the last item in the Shaw's impressive opening hand, is slick and spectacular, on sets by William Schmuck that are skeletal, mobile and appropriately filmic. But it cant conceal the fact that the show itself is largely static, however energetic the scenery and the performers might be.

A show that failed with Robert Preston and Bernadette Peters is unlikely to succeed with anyone else, but Niagaras two leads sing their numbers and play their characters very well.

Benedict Campbell, rhythmically barking his songs, is as driven and driving as Mack should be and more sympathetic than might be expected. Glynis Ranney is likable, too, and sings beautifully, but makes no visible or audible connection between Mabel as Brooklyn gamine and Mabel as Hollywood goddess.

Gabrielle Jones belts admirably as a showgirl-of-all-trades, the only other character to get anything approaching a solo, though her Tap Your Troubles Away number is ruined by generic choreography that realizes too late that it's meant to be caustic commentary.

This production makes the half-heartedness work for it, giving the performers shy solo lines and letting the whole thing build. At its best Mack and Mabel is exhilarating. But its best doesn't happen often enough. - Mack and Mabel is in repertory through Oct. 28. For tickets, call 1-800-511-SHAW or visit www.shawfest.com

THEATRE REVIEW

KING LEAR

Festival Theatre, Stratford, Ont.

- - -

There was a medieval theory known as the King's Two Bodies, that distinguished between the monarch as a mortal man and as the repository of an ongoing and imperishable tradition. Playing King Lear in this years opening production at Stratford, Brian Bedford seems to be offering us the Kings Two Voices.

He comes before us in a husk in rich robes, leaning for support on his favourite daughter's arm, and his first line is delivered so feebly that the audience has to strain to hear it. One wonders if the actor, who hasn't played heavyweight tragedy in a long time, may have bitten off more than he can chew. So it goes until his authority is challenged, first by Cordelia, then by Kent, at which point it reasserts itself. The voice crackles, swells, and even roars, while the tottering old man turns into a tyrant fully capable of lifting a sword and, if not prevented, doing serious damage with it.

At one level, Bedford is playing games with us. But then, so is Lear. He adopts a senescent pose to justify taking what I can best describe as a spiritually early retirement, and its impossible to tell whether hes doing it to fool his courtiers or to fool himself. He oscillates throughout that opening scene between wheedling weakness and imperious strength.

Ironically, when he has given away his temporal power, he seems more vigorous than ever, a bluff squire devoting himself to hunting, riding, eating and drinking hard. His mind -- this may be his real undoing--is fully alert too; he may not be wise, but he's smart. Bedford is not, I think, an actor to whom madness comes easily, but he is superb at presenting baffled logic.

He's also great at making connections; the curse of sterility that he places on Goneril arises directly out of his conviction that

she has broken the bond between the generations. His sudden pity for the poor arises from his consciousness of his own vulnerability. I have known Lears who were more searching and more terrible in the storm (which the production places after the interval), but I have never seen one who got on such intimate quizzing terms with the mock- madman Poor Tom. Bedford makes the keyword nothing echo through the play.

The quiescent Lear only reappears, for real this time, after he has been through the purgation on the heath and the searing insights at Dover. The reconciliation with Cordelia, after hes been nursed back to some kind of health, is disappointing. Where he is great is in the scene where they are dragged to prison. His gentle insistence on the happiness theyre about to share, and his amused contempt for the fools around them, come from a deep place, and are profoundly moving.

So too is his death, in which the two voices seem to be sounding as one, and which is illuminated by at least one stunning innovation: When this Lear thinks he sees Cordelia's breath stirring, he isn't looking at her body but straight ahead, at some phantom in his own imagination. I never

imagined before that Bedford could bring me to tears. But then Ive never seen him before in a part that required him to.

With this production of Lear, Bedford pulls off, in fact, a double surprise. He succeeds in the foolhardy task of directing the play while starring in it. His is a conventional production, done in Elizabethan costumes (which, designed by Ann Curtis, supply a helpful courtly atmosphere) and on a stage bare except for a huge golden throne at the beginning. There is at least one major cut: We lose the mock-trial of Goneril and Regan. True, its only in the Quarto text, not the later Folio. But if, as some scholars think, this shows Shakespeare having second thoughts, then Shakespeare got it wrong.

It's a vital stage on Lear's journey, and without it Bedfords performance seems incomplete. So does the role of the Fool, whom we never see again. It hurts more, as both roles are extremely well played. Bernard Hopkins Fool is an ageing comic, anxious for his master, not for himself.

Kent cannot be much of a stretch for Peter Donaldson, but he's a tower of strength, especially at the end where his sorrow helps cue our own. The revelatory supporting performance, though, is Scott Wentworth's Gloucester, a bustling man of the world whose enforced awakening is at least as powerful as Lears own.

The production makes no fashionable bones about its Ugly Sisters: Goneril (Wenna Shaw) and Regan (Wendy Robie) are forceful twin studies in self-justifying malevolence, differing only in stature and hairstyle. If they are allowed to be refreshingly bad, then Cordelia (Sara Topham) is permitted to be good though, running against the temper of the times, she works too hard at it. The editing means that shes down to just one suitor, the King of France (Tim MacDonald) who, scooping lines from his absent rival, emerges far more strongly than usual. Dion Johnstone's Edmund makes little impression beyond his first flash soliloquy; Gareth Potter has the usual trouble establishing the virtuous Edgar but as Poor Tom he's excellent. The ducal husbands are Wayne Best, a Cornwall whose asperity crosses easily into brutality, and Graham Harley who, in moving Albany from milquetoast to avenger, shows Lear's own ability to turn on a dime.

One last subtlety:When Lear at the end says "and my poor fool is hanged," audiences have always taken for granted that he means the Fool, while the unsentimental insist that he means Cordelia. Bedford has it both ways. His Lear is confused; he thinks that he means the Fool, then you can see him jerked back to reality as he remembers that the actual victim, there dead beside him, is someone ever more precious. "Break heart, I prithee break" says Kent; and it does. So, I think, will yours. - King Lear is in repertory at the Stratford Festival until Oct. 28. THEATRE REVIEW

OKLAHOMA!

Festival Theatre, Stratford, Ont.

- - -

I've never noticed it before, but I realized at the new Stratford production that were three-quarters of the way through Oklahoma! before anybody mentions Oklahoma. And even at that, it only happens in the subplot. Ali Hakim, the itinerant peddler supposedly from Persia, having recently escaped a shotgun wedding to the flirtatious Ado Annie, bids her what he calls a Persian goodbye. This seems to involve up-ending the recipient and implanting a smothering kiss on her lips that leaves her begging for more. At which point Will Parker, her actual affianced, gets mighty jealous and treats her to "an Oklahoma hello," which is the same sort of gesture, only with more gusto.

So, it starts as a joke. But in the next scene, which always plays like a finale ahead of its time, the entire company delivers another kind of Oklahoma hello by singing the title song, one of the great goosebump moments in the American musical. But this time, as the wind comes sweeping down the plain and Richard Rodgers music sweeps right along with it, they're saying hello to Oklahoma itself, the brand new state that has yet to come into existence. Curly the cowboy and Laurey the rancher, the newlywed hero and heroine, are its symbols, their union prefigured in The Farmer and the Cowman, the challenge square dance that opens the show's second act and looks forward to "when this territory is a state / And joins the

Union just like all the others." Up until then, we havent heard a word about it. Which just shows how cunning the apparently artless Oscar Hammerstein was.

Oklahoma!s opening is a legendary paradigm of simplicity: A woman sits outside a farmhouse silently churning butter while a male voice approaches from offstage singing about a beautiful morning. It's one of those songs that's so much a part of our lives its hard to believe anyone actually sat down and wrote it. The tableau develops into a love scene thats mostly tall tales and quarrelling. Then we get news of the outside world, i.e. loose-living, high- rising (seven storey) Kansas City. Both the serious and the comic love plots involve the tensions between the two ways of life that have to become one. The burning question that notoriously underpins the long first act -- will it be Curly or Jud Fry, the brooding and reclusive hired hand, who gets to take Laurey to the box social? -- is less trivial than it looks. It's literary shorthand for which of them will marry her. That has traditionally been enough to fuel a romantic comedy, and is here a further shorthand of its own. By the time the explosive square dance begins, an epic has snuck up on us.

Some of the surprise is necessarily lost on the Festival Theatre's stage, where everything looks epic to begin with. But the show can handle it -- after all, it was one of the first musicals to become a widescreen movie -- and Patrick Clarks sets combine the broodingly spacious with the comfortably particular. Donna Feores direction and choreography are immensely spirited, although the acrobatic production numbers seem to exist for their own enjoyable sake rather than to further or deepen the story.

There isn't the subtlety or the pathos of the Trevor Nunn-Susan Stroman production that recently played in London and New York, though this staging does follow that one in dispensing with the traditional doubles for Laurey's dream ballet and letting the principals dance out their own conflicts. The result is a huge gain in power and coherence both for the sequence itself and for the show as a whole.

Blythe Wilson is still primarily a singing rather than a dancing Laurey, which is fine since she has the two loveliest songs: the not- quite-defiant Many a New Day and Out of My Dreams which, wistful and sweeping at the same time, may be the best of all Rodgers waltzes, which is saying something.

She is also an acting Laurey, strong but troubled. Dan Chameroys Curly is more problematic; as fine an actor as he's become, he looks and sounds strangely sneaky here. (And what one would give to hear Oh What a Beautiful Mornin' as the first audience did, unamplified and coming from somewhere rather than everywhere.) In fact, he seems rather less wholesome than David W. Keeleys Jud, a surprisingly open-faced outsider whose frustrations are not only powerful but sympathetic, both in his Lonely Room solo and in the mocking Pore Jud, a brilliantly sarcastic sequence that also finds Chameroy at his best.

But then Hammersteins lyrics in this show are the funniest he ever wrote. His dialogue can sparkle, too, especially when shrugged through by Jonathan Ellul, whose Persian is unmistakably and unashamedly Jewish. Kyle Blair is a winning Will with, as the song says, plenty of room to spin a rope, and plenty of skill to take advantage of it. Lindsay Thomas, though, spoils Ado Annie by over a- doing her. The character, of course, has no subtlety: all the more reason for the actress to have some. Nora McLellan as Aunt Eller wraps the show up as surely as one of the ribboned boxes at the social.

Berthold Carriere's conducting makes the score a joy, which admittedly is no trick. Or, as the Broadway historian Ethan Mordden unanswerably asked, when debunking the myth of the show's failure at its Boston tryout, How could an audience not like Oklahoma!? - Oklahoma! is in repertory through Nov. 4. No Canadian actress does language, especially curlicued, high- comic language, like Fiona Reid. She has the first hour of Tony Kushner's Homebody/Kabul entirely and entrancingly to herself. She plays a London woman, the homebody of the title. She tells us that she is married, though the most intimate contact she and her husband now have consists of sampling one another's antidepressants. She also has a daughter, and there isn't much communication there either. Her chief delight is reading: "I have," she confesses, "read too many books. I haven't read many books, but I've read too many."

The books she favours are slightly out-of-date travel guides and histories; she's currently engrossed in one about Afghanistan. Its style has infected her own; she speaks in long and ornate sentences rendered even longer by her constant fear that she may have misspoken herself and must therefore go back and start again. Reid doesn't drop a stitch of this dense verbal knitting; she renders confusion with devastating, hilarious lucidity. More than that, she creates a character out of syntax, a print-dress sort of lady who's modest and worried but has a questing soul. She tells us about visiting a store and finding to her amazement that she can understand the proprietor, even though he's speaking Pashtun. Soon, so the rest of the play informs us, she will journey to Kabul herself and never come back. The year is 1998. The Taliban rule; the Americans have not yet bombed.

Kushner is a wonderful writer of lines, speeches and sometimes even scenes, but his plays, including the trophied Angels in America, are a mess. This one, as per its title, is two plays, or a monologue with a play attached. The monologue is superb, the play is confused and at times banal. Husband Milton and daughter Priscilla journey to Kabul to bring the homebody's body home. They're told she has been killed, hideously. Milton wearily believes it, Priscilla angrily doubts it. Weariness and anger are their character notes. They squabble for much of the play over their feelings about the vanished woman, a subject in which it's impossible to take much interest since the homebody herself told us very little about their relationship and we've never seen it for ourselves.

Priscilla, donning a burqua, hits the Kabul streets in search of her mother, or at least her mother's body, and runs almost immediately into potentially deadly trouble. She's rescued by a Tajik poet, who offers to act as her guide and interpreter, though not without his own agenda. Sanjay Talwar plays this role with an appealing blend of politeness and passion. He also codirects with Jon Michaelson; their production, once Reid is offstage, takes a long time to gather fresh momentum. Lesley Faulkner, whom I remember being iridescent as the surrogate Marilyn Monroe in After the Fall, is allowed to play Priscilla on a single grating note, even when going rapturous over the Afghan landscape. Her dad experiences a similarly shop-soiled transcultural epiphany by doing drugs. He's your stereotypical uptight Englishman, though Michael Spencer-Davis gets to transcend the type. The family's surname is Ceiling, and the play tries to show all its members breaking through theirs, but there are no clear connections between their successive actions.

Speaking of connections, Milton's supplier is a British consular type named Quango Twistleton, who has gone native for the narcotics; Kris Holden-Ried, new to the stage, gives him a quiet (i.e., semi- audible) charm. Deena Aziz brings the show back close to its opening level as a former librarian seeking Western asylum and desperately conflicted about it. A speech in which she rails against oppression, both homegrown and imported, constantly switching between languages as between targets, is a tour de force.

Words themselves are a recurring motif. The Tajik poet writes his verses in Esperanto, which he prizes for its "hyper-rational ungainliness." Milton works in computer language, another rational and ungainly tongue, which, when he speaks it, becomes its own poetry. Language, as this play's best writing and acting show, is a powerful tool. But it doesn't make a play.

- Homebody/Kabul runs through June 9 at the Berkeley Street Theatre (downstairs). Call 416-368-3110 for more information.
