TO KILL A MOCKINGBIRD

Avon Theatre, Stratford, Ont.

- - -

You can blame it on my age or on the educational system that raised me, but I have never read Harper Lee's To Kill a Mockingbird. I've never seen the movie, either. Nor, until Wednesday, had I seen the stage version. But I knew that the story involved an upstanding white lawyer in the Deep South defending a black man railroaded on a rape charge. I entered the Stratford theatre expecting something corny, but gripping.

What do you know, I was right. At least, I was on the mark when it came to the trial scene. For my fellow ignoramuses: It's 1935 in Macon, Ala. Atticus Finch has been nominated to represent Tom Robinson, accused of violently assaulting 19-year-old Mayella Ewell. It's obvious that her real abuser is her father Bob, a vicious guy who represents white trash at its trashiest, and Atticus easily establishes that Mayella led Tom on and that he, justifiably terrified, got out of the place as soon as possible.

But it's the Deep South, and Tom has already narrowly escaped a lynching. We have all the suspense of courtroom drama, plus the adrenalin of feeling that we are on the side of the angels.

Or, with Peter Donaldson playing Atticus, of the archangels.

Donaldson does a magnificent job of humanizing a man who, except for one brief moment of excess judicial fervour at the end, is always in the right. He fights passionately in a case he knows he's likely to lose. His final appeal to the jury's sense of decency is superbly sculpted, oratorical acting at its finest, alternating moral fervour with lashing irony. He can see the point of view of the people he's fighting.

A widower, he's a model father to his two young kids, leaving them in no doubt of where righteousness lies while admonishing them to be tolerant even of the crazy, bigoted old lady next door. And, despite being out of practice, he can bring down a mad dog (canine variety) with a single rifle shot. I can't believe that Gregory Peck (Atticus in the film) could have been as effective. Peck was Mr. Decency. With Donaldson, there's always a dark side lurking, throwing the light into relief.

The court proceedings also benefit from David Francis the scrupulously upright judge, and from Steve Ross, a freebooting prosecutor with no apparent scruples whatever. Dion Johnstone's Tom is pitiable with no loss of dignity, and Dayna Tekatch's Maryella pitiable with no dignity whatsoever, only a stubborn brattiness that's the residue of having been continually beaten down. How much she believes her own lies is unknowable, at least in this adaptation, but she desperately needs someone she can look down on. If she avoids caricature, Wayne Best as her pappy falls right into it; there's no sense -- in writing, acting or direction -- of what might make him tick.

Unfortunately, To Kill a Mockingbird (hate that cute title) isn't just a racial-prejudice drama. It's an out-of-the-mouths-of-babes drama. Much of it is seen through the eyes of Jem and Scout, Atticus's son and daughter, and of their friend Dill, who comes and goes for reasons that may make sense in the novel but are a timewasting drag on the stage. The story is told by Scout's older self, who presumably stands in for the novelist.

Christopher Sergel's adapatation is a lazy, unimaginative piece of work, dumping things on stage just because they're in the book; and this narration is the worst of it; it reduces the actress, Michelle Giroux, to bestowing long looks on the scene of her childhood and intoning languid prose about it.

Whatever the script and production pretends, this isn't Scout's story; she's just in it. The kids have their mischievous side, but they have all the right instincts; Dill, at the trial, comments on all the "contempt" there is in the world. They are appealingly played by Abigail Winter- Culliford (Scout), Spencer Walker (Dill) and especially by Thomas Murray as Jem, but they slow the play down. Child actors tend to be weak on timing unless dynamically directed which, in Susan Schulman's production, they are not.

The climax, ineffectually staged in the half-light, depends on the intervention of a hermit-like figure we've heard about but have not previously seen: Call him a recluse ex machina. This may work on the page or on the screen, both of them are better suited to atmospheric foreshadowing; on the stage, it's just flat.

The show is decked out with authentic-sounding backwoods music and a gospel choir. You couldn't have a play about the South without them. Everyone knows that. - To Kill a Mockingbird is in repertory at the Stratford Festival until Oct. 27. Call 1-800-567-1600 or visit www.stratfordfestival.ca for tickets.

With its penultimate episode, The Sopranos has turned into a gangster drama. Or rather, its become like other gangster dramas. Just as The Godfather closed with Michael Corleone disposing, in montage, of all his enemies, so in this one the body count has gone way up, as the bosses of New York and New Jersey have finally turned on one another.

One of the accusations that Tony Sopranos mother and uncle flung at him (behind his back) in the very first episode was that he was "thumbing his nose at New York." It's been a long road, but that struggle has finally come to a head. Only, this being The Sopranos, things are not going so smoothly, at least not on the Jersey side. They start out all right, with Silvio paying a social call on Burt Gervasi, the snitch who'd been trying to persuade him to cross over to Phil Leotardos bunch in New York, and efficiently garrotting him. (Burt commenced the episode by picking up the newspaper in his driveway. Always a dangerous thing to do. Ask Tony.) So, no qualms about Silvios loyalty.

Phil knows it, because he promptly places Sil on his hit list, along with Tony himself and, to his subordinates' surprise, Bobby Bacala, the apparently harmless former driver. Tony gets wind of this, via FBI Agent Harris, and lays counter-plans, calling guys from Italy to execute his New York rivals. But maybe he laid on too many intermediaries, or maybe you can't trust outside help, because the guys who go gunning for Phil end up shooting an innocent lookalike and the mans daughter.

Cunning Phil has gone to ground. He despises the Sopranos for not being a real Family at all, just "a jumped-up crew" and his delegates certainly seem more efficient than Tonys. Sunday's episode ended with Bobby dead and Silvio in a coma. Bobby, in a prolonged but effective sequence, gets shot while shopping for one of his favourite model trains. Silvio is bushwhacked in his car, just outside the Bada Bing. There's a memorable shot of half-naked girls and their customers fleeing as he bites the dust.

Lest we feel too sorry for Sil, the sight of him crawling on the ground couldnt help but raise memories of Adriana in a similar position as he disposed of her a few seasons ago: by common consent, the most shocking whacking ever on The Sopranos.

Remember how good Steve Van Zandt was in that scene, making clumsily nice with Adriana up to the moment of drawing his gun? Have we seen the beginning and end of Van Zandt the actor? He was quoted in Vanity Fair as saying that hed never acted before The Sopranos and might well never do so again. At the very least, he might work in commercials. Or, he could just go back to music.

Last seen running for his life was Silvio's car-mate Patsy Parisi. We can probably assume that he was a loyalist, not a rat. But when he gets his breath back, Patsy -- as the Soprano empire crumbles around him--may feel a modicum of satisfaction for the death of his twin brother. Previously, he had to slake any thirst for vengeance by urinating in Tony's pool.

This week saw Tony covering that pool. Perhaps its a seasonal thing, perhaps its to discourage A.J. from a second suicide attempt. By episode's end, Tony was out of the house, having sent wife and kids off separately and ensconcing himself in a safe house with a few anonymities and Paulie.

Paulie wasn't on Phils list; maybe his loyalty is compromised; maybe (and more likely) Phil, rightly, didnt think him important enough. Paulie has had his stab at changing sides, and it worked out bitterly for him. And though Tony, a few weeks ago, thought seriously of killing him, it seemed to be more for his loose mouth than for any suspicions.

Anyway, Tony has had this week to face a far more wounding rejection. Dr. Jennifer Melfi has abandoned him. At a dinner party full of psychiatrists, Dr. Elliot Kupferberg, the shrink's shrink, repeated his admonitions about therapy for sociopaths serving only to enable them, and even let fall the identity of her patient. This seems appallingly unprofessional, and I had a hard time believing it. But it cues what is presumably Tony's last consultation. The Duchess of Melfi, as I like to think of her, tells him that, after seven years, she can do nothing more for him. Tony reacts with furious self-pity. Every word he says --about his troubled son, his career-challenged daughter --fits in with what Melfihas read about sociopaths hypocrisy and sentimentality.

Tonys love for his family may count for little against his other activities, but it seems real. And isn't Melfijust angry with herself for having, as she now sees it, been taken in for so long, and for having made no difference? (In the latter case, she's wrong. The differences were for the better. The worse would have happened anyway.) She tries to be clinical and impersonal in dismissing him, but what comes out is the opposite. The scene plays like a marital breakup, as bitter and petty as the one Tony and Carmela had. Only, they got together again -- Tony and Melfiare unlikely to do so.

But there is, come to think of it, no guarantee that Tony and Carmela will set eyes on one another again, at least not alive. Would The Sopranos dare do that to us? I doubt it.

But I wouldn't take bets on it.

It was a kick to see and hear the Toronto Symphony Orchestra at Roy Thomson Hall play the opening theme music from Monty Python's Flying Circus. It was announced in the program as the Liberty Bell March by John Philip Sousa, but few in the audience were fooled. We knew what was really on their minds. And if it wasn't on theirs, it was on ours.

They played it well. Well, they would, wouldn't they? It was part of an orchestral mini-concert (highlight: the Nimrod section from Elgar's Enigma Variations) preceding the real business of the evening, Not the Messiah (He's a Very Naughty Boy), an oratorio based on Monty Python's Life of Brian, with Eric Idle himself as co- author, narrator and even singer. He is also the cousin of the conductor, Peter Oundjian, whose position as music director of the TSO, plus the participation of the new Luminato festival, helped this "Ontario oratorio" become as such.

As well as being a filleted adaptation of the movie, the new piece functions as an homage to, or more frankly, an exploitation of, all things Python. For example: As is well known, Brian was born in a stable to the Non-Virgin Mary while a more momentous birth was taking place just next door. ("Is it A.D. yet?" "It's about a quarter to.") And There Were Shepherds -- that's the title of one of the numbers, if an oratorio has numbers. In it, the shepherds sing about how happy they are in their jobs because, simply, "we like sheep." They don't, they make it clear, have much time for any other variety of livestock. They are as enhusiastica bout sheep as others have been known to be about Spam. There's also a strong hint that they enjoy shepherding as much as others might enjoy, say, lumberjacking. This theme becomes more explicit at the other end of the legend when Brian is about to be crucified. One of his fellow prisoners sings A Fair Day's Work, which is really the imperishable Python anthem about cross-dressing timber cutters as it might have been structured by Gilbert and Sullivan.

I don't remember exactly how Brian, in The Life of, came to the cross, but I'm sure there was a reason. In Not the Messiah, which is less a narrative than a series of jump-cuts, it just sort of happens. It can't be traced to his involvement with the People's Front of Judea; though that, which provided the best scene in the film, also provides the best song here. Entitled What Have the Romans (as in "what have the Romans ever done for us?"), it covers exactly the same satiric ground but does so within the satisfying disciplines of rhyme and meter. Honour the lyricist who can make creative use of the word "aqueduct." John Du Prez, Idle's composing collaborator, has written an amusing and eclectic score, and in something called The Final Song reaffirms the talent he showed in Spamalot for writing Andrew Lloyd Webber pastiches that are better than Andrew Lloyd Webber. Of course, it isn't the final song. It has to give way to a full-scale rendition of Always Look on the Bright Side of Life.

By "full-scale" I mean that it involved the orchestra, 32 members of the Toronto Mendelssohn Choir, all five of the evening's featured vocalists, and four bagpipers who wandered on and off the platform from time to time, piping. It also, most definitely, involved the audience, who were vocally enthusiastic throughout. A young relative of mine surmised that they were composed about equally of Python fanatics and symphony regulars who had never heard a joke before. Myself, I suspect a considerable overlap.

But much of the evening's appeal undoubtedly depends on its sense of lesemajeste. I don't mean by that irreverence towards the Bible. The show begins with a rather heavy-handed anti-hymn, O God You Are So Big ("and we are garbage in your sight") and it retains the exhortations of Brian, the reluctant messiah, that his flock should learn to think for themselves. But this element is muted, and the music actually dilutes it.

The fun really was in seeing formally garbed musicians and singers get with pop rhythms. It was a kick to behold the Toronto Mendelssohnians solemnly doowopping or simply behaving like massed survivors from the era of the Ray Conniff

Singers. It was just about irresistible when a fit of swaying took hold of choristers, soloists and those members of the string section who didn't happen to be playing anything at the time. (They cradled their instruments and swung themselves.) Shannon Mercer (soprano) and Christopher Sieber (tenor) shared an orgasmic Mozartian duet that was a riot; Jean Stilwell (mezzo) came as close as anyone could to reproducing musically the sound of Terry Jones in drag; and Theodore Baerg (bass) stood at the side and enjoyed himself. Their operatic diction, however, often got in the way of the words. Idle (baritone-ish, said the program) presided with his customary humour and charm, qualities that were shown by his conducting cousin to run in the family.

2007-06-09-the-world-shows-us-our-toront:
Maybe it takes foreign visitors to make us really look at our city. The confluence of the Luminato and New World Stage festivals has brought us two companies from abroad who have mounted site- specific productions in parts of Toronto to which your average theatre-goer, or indeed your average theatre, rarely travels. One of them even brought along a Toronto play.

This was Risk Everything, originally seen as the last component of George F. Walker's Suburban Motel cycle, and now presented by a Polish troupe, TR Warszawa, at Mc-Bride's Bicycle Shop, way out west on Dundas. The play centres on Carol, whose philosophy is that of the title, and who has exercised it by stealing $68,000 from a thug called Steamboat. She is now holed up, terrified but unrepentant, with her comparatively practical daughter, Denise, and Denise's timid husband, R.J. They receive one visitor, on whom Carol avidly and lubriciously fastens; he's Miki, a porn-film director known in this production, though not in Walker's original, as Miki Fucky. Walker's work is not exactly short on sex and violence, but here both are way upfront.

The play is performed against big store windows giving on to the street, so part of the fun for the official audience comes from watching the reactions of the unofficial audience outside. The people on Dundas West greeted with commendable sang-froid the sight of Carol sitting on the toilet or of Miki attacking her, equipped with a huge strap-on. The street life, in turn, contributed to the play; when a police car drove by, sirens sounding, the whole cast hit the floor as if by prior arrangement. Sometimes the two worlds met; when characters, especially Carol, went out into the street and accosted passersby, or when, twice, a white SUV roared to a halt disgorging from its trunk the bloodied figures first of R.J., then of Miki, both of them having rashly tried to intercede with Steamboat. His response is to deliver them both back home with dynamite stuck to their chests. This is one effect that worked better in the original when it was done deadpan.

The Polish production is announced as a mixed-media show. In practice, this means that there's a functioning TV on the set. But the script calls for that, anyway; R.J. is addicted to the tube, and the play is partly about his efforts to wean himself from it. There are surtitles, though the cast frequently attempt the English text, or approximations of it, and this is rather charming. Essentially, we are getting Walker's none-too-subtle original with the volume turned up and the result, though prolonged, is both impressive and invigorating. Carol's risk-everything code, a mixture of greed and disrespect for the lives of others, has always struck me as a playwright's confection, but it benefits from the full-out performance of Aleksandra Konieczna, who is shamelessness personified. Agnieszka Podsiadlik's Denise is a good sober counterweight, and Jan Drawnel's R.J. a delight, always on the verge of protest without ever quite getting there.

From Australia, Urban Theatre Projects takes us a little closer to home (home, in Toronto theatre circles, being approximately Queen and Bathurst) with a piece that in fact is called Back Home and is presented in "an undisclosed Toronto backyard," which turns out to adjoin the Centre for Addiction and Mental Health on Queen West. The dramatic setting, though, remains Australian. Four youngish men, bearing the names of their actors (Aaron Fa'Aoso, Buddy Dannoun, Leo Tanoi, Shannon Williams), gather for a reunion barbecue. One of them is Middle Eastern, one Caribbean, one Black Australian, one Native Australian. All, by mainstream accounting, are minority; all feel themselves to be marginalized; they alternate between sharing their grievances and taking them out on one another. Buddy, the host, is an aspiring DJ, and here too amplified music punctuates the action. Here, though, it's pivotal rather than decorative, in a production (by Alicia Talbot) that stakes as much on naturalism as the Poles do on style, though the results are oddly similar: overlong but powerful. This is also a magical-mystery-tour production; you board a bus at York Quay to get to the action, and en route you get a lecture on Toronto's native heritage

- Risk Everything closes tonight at McBride's Bicycle Shop. Back Home also closes tonight; board the bus at Harbourfront Centre, 7:15 p.m.

THE BLONDE, THE BRUNETTE AND THE VENGEFUL REDHEAD

Studio Theatre, Stratford, Ont.

---

If there were to be an award for the year's best male performance at the Stratford Festival, it might well go, despite what is already serious competition, to Lucy Peacock.

In The Blonde, the Brunette and the Vengeful Redhead (revived from last season) Peacock plays seven characters, but the most memorable may be the one man among them. He's certainly the most unsparingly drawn, both by the actress and her Australian author Robert Hewett. He's Graham, the husband of Rhonda, the redhead of the title, whose vengeance was directed at the blond of the title, with whom she suspected Graham of having an affair, on the advice of their neighbour, the brunette, also of the title. The redhead ended up in jail and Graham promptly started a new affair with the brunette.

So he has, really, a lot to feel sorry about.

Most of his sympathy, though, is directed at himself. We first see him (from the back) relieving himself, and he continues to relieve himself, verbally. He has, we gather, been very hard done by, and everything is somebody else's fault, mostly some woman's. He does admit to a few twinges of guilt around his old mate, the brunette's husband. (No more neighbourly barbecues for them.) If it took another man to understand this guy so embarrassingly well, it may well have taken a woman to give him so clear and witty an outline. That's not to say that Peacock ever mocks or patronizes Graham. She plays him with the same sympathy and conviction that she extends to the five women and one child who make up the rest of her portrait gallery. But the circumstances of a one-person show almost dictate a certain amount of detachment, for both actor and audience. Peacock is as fully inside each of her characters as any actor can ever be. She also has an individual voice and stance for each of them. But each comes on stage bearing an implicit weight of comparison with the others.

Hewett takes a single traumatic incident, at a shopping mall, and examines a selection of those it affects: a catalogue, we come to realize, that could be extended almost indefinitely.

Rhonda is the only one we meet twice; she's quiet and confused at the start, quiet and steely at the end. There's a capable English doctor, aware that her colleagues refer to her as "that Pommy bitch" (a strange usage, given that the scene has been transplanted from Australia to Canada). There's a bereaved boy, played more precisely and also more movingly than last year. There's the blowsy brunette, whose story differs significantly from Rhonda's even when they're supposedly describing the same events. There's an elderly woman with reserves of compassion that are genuine but limited.

And there's the blond mistress, who's Russian and a surprise. Peacock has lapsed into excessive underlining in the first couple of scenes, but otherwise she remains perfect. The writing takes a sentimental dip at the end, but it's full of believable observations and incorporates one moment of classically packed irony that radiates in memory across the entire play. Geordie John-son's direction is spot-on, both during the scenes and between them. As Peacock changes costumes in silhouette and, more significantly, wigs, we listen to Stephen Woodjetts' musical score, which is like water dropping, and look at projections that suggest that malls, in any country, are accidents that cannot wait to happen. - The Blonde, the Brunette and the Vengeful Redhead is in repertoire until Sept. 2. Call 1-800-567-1600 or visit www.stratfordfestival.ca for tickets.

2007-06-11-they-re-wonderful-and-s-marve:
In 1927, there was a Broadway musical called Funny Face that was in terrible trouble on the road but, after drastic surgery, came in as a hit. In 1983, there was a Broadway musical called My One and Only that was in terrible trouble on the road but, after drastic surgery, came in as a hit. Both these shows had scores by George and Ira Gershwin. In fact, My One and Only started out as something between a revival and an adaptation of Funny Face.

Something else: Each of these shows starred the top Broadway dancer of its day. Funny Face had Fred Astaire, playing not so much opposite as alongside his sister Adele. My One and Only had the towering Tommy Tune, piquantly matched with the diminutive Twiggy. Tune, a superb razzle-dazzler of a choreographer, also took over the direction, and his staging, plus his ruthless overhaul of the show's book, are what made it work. All the same, what arrived in New York was a rewrite of a rewrite of a rewrite of something that, even in 1927, had been regarded as awful. Its new success was a triumph of personality. It could hardly be duplicated. When Stratford announced a revival, I thought Stratford was mad.

As Ira Gershwin himself might have put it, I couldn't have been wronger. From its opening sequence -- three debonair male performers, hoofing and scatting through I Can't Be Bothered Now -- the show is a knockout, a Stratford musical that delights as a musical rather than as a classical company having fun. Indeed the joy starts even earlier, with Berthold Carriere's big festival band sounding jazzier, or at least brighter and more syncopated, than it ever has before, as it bounds through the Gershwin selection that constitutes the overture. Gershwin and dancing, the overwhelming bulk of it tap, make this show go.

How much Michael Lichtefeld's direction and choreography owe to Tune's, I couldn't say, but they're exhilarating just the same. It isn't just the steps, which are wonderfully executed by everyone. It's the way the steppers look in the extravagant hues of David Boechler's extravagant costumes. And it's the way both clothes and people move against the clean geometric lines of Douglas Paraschuk's Art Deco sets which, taking their inspiration from Mondrian, pay an abstractionist's homage to pre-Depression New York. For, despite everything, the show retains the original's time and place, or at least the idea of them.

It also has a story; not much of one, but enough. Billy Buck Chandler from Texas falls in love with Edythe Herbert from England. She's famous for having swum the Channel; he wants to be famous for flying the Atlantic but is thwarted by the kind of mechanical complications known in the trade as Second Act Problems.

The lovers get to wander as far afield as Morocco and a desert island that turns out to be Staten. That's all there is to the plot, really, barring a bit of blackmail that isn't too interesting. The score retains five songs from the original Funny Face but is otherwise Gershwin from all over. It's chary, though, of becoming a parade of greatest hits --making it superior to the later, similar and better-known Crazy for You, which had an equally inconsequential book, but far more of it. There may not be much substance in My One and Only, but there is drama. It's in the dancing and the music that summon up excitement, urbanity and loopy romance, and songs and choreography that are always right for the moment and the people.

The leads don't have the vertical tension of Twiggy and Tune, but they're excellent. They also, like the whole show, demonstrate the versatility of tap. Cynthia Dale, honouring her predecessor with traces of Cockney, vocalizes a bittersweet ballad, while seemingly unaware that her feet are continuing to do their own unpreventable thing. It's nice work if you can get it; which happens to be the song she's singing.

Laird Mackintosh is all impeccable impetuosity. His finest hour, maybe the show's, is the title number. It comes as a challenge-duet with Mark Cassius as a certain Mr. Magic who's teaching him to be a smooth yet ardent wooer and has finally to get out of his chair (something he very rarely does) to demonstrate. What follows is bliss, with a narrative charge. David W. Keeley, harmlessly sinister, and Dayna Tekatch, perkily persistent, are a secondary couple who's dialogue doesn't help them much, but who finally get to do a number (the original Funny Face) that's worth waiting for. The only number that disappoints, here as on Broadway, is the finale Kickin' the Clouds Away, simply because the tune itself falls short. If they'd asked me for a Gershwin mock-spiritual, I'd have suggested Clap Yo' Hands. But they didn't, and it's 24 years too late now.

There's a difference between the dancing here and that in Oklahoma! that tells as much about the shows themselves and the times that gave birth to them as about these productions. The rambunctious production numbers in Oklahoma! look like hard work, and win our applause for it. The performers (largely the same ones) in My One and Only bewitch us by making it look easy. They look, too, as if they could keep it up forever. I can't recall having as much fun at a Stratford musical. - My One and Only is in repertoire until Oct. 28. Call 1-800-567-1600 or visit www.stratfordfestival.ca for tickets.

Black & White Photo: David Hou, Stratford Festival / Cynthia Dale, centre, plays Edythe Herbert in the Stratford Festival's production of My One and Only, a musical that carefully avoids becoming a parade of greatest hits while showcasing some of the best tunes by George and Ira Gershwin. ;
2007-06-12-bada-whimper-the-success-of-t:
Mother of God, what was the end of Tony? There he was, as so often before, in a restaurant with his immediate family, or three- quarters of it: Meadow was late. The room was filled with menacing strangers, or just ordinary customers who seemed menacing because The Sopranos was on its final countdown and something had to happen. Tony had chosen a song from the jukebox: Dont Stop Believing. And, at the words don't stop, everything did. The sound cut out and the screen went to black, as viewers all over North America cursed their TV sets for breaking down at this of all moments. A couple of seconds of this. Roll credits.

A lot of people felt cheated. Some think the ending means that Tony got whacked. They point to Bobby Baccilieri at the beginning of this final season saying that you don't see or hear your own whacking; everything just goes black and stops. Not that thats how it seemed to go down for Bobby when he got his in the model-train store during the penultimate episode. At the end of that show, Tony had a flashback to their conversation, which might have been premonitory. Its likelier, though, that it was David Chase messing with our minds. I don't think Tony died. In fact, if that's what were meant to believe, then I do feel cheated. If it was going to happen, I wanted to see it.

What I felt was shock, followed by frustration that was almost immediately overtaken by a sense of fitness. On a narrative level we got the "life goes on" ending that many of us had come to expect. I would guess that if Chase had ended the show a couple seasons ago, as he once threatened, he would have settled for Tony being either killed or sent down for a good long time.

But as the show progressed, it came to seem less like a story and more like a series of probing variations on an elegiac mood. The last scene parallels the finale of the first season. That gave us the four Sopranos (one sometimes forgets that the show is named for all of them, not just for Tony) dining in their glory at their favourite Italian restaurant. At a nearby table, raising congratulatory glasses, sat Tonys four principal lieutenants: Big Pussy, Silvio, Paulie and Christopher. There was an almost Shakespearean sense of the king surrounded by his counsellors, and a comparable richness of texture: We already knew all of these people very well.

Compare that to now: Pussy and Christopher dead by Tony's own hands (literally in Chris's case), Silvio on life-support, Paulie cajoled or coerced into taking a crew-captains job he feels to be jinxed, Tonys relations with his wife and kids in a permanent state of runaround. Hesh, Artie, Uncle Junior and, most woundingly, Dr. Melfiare all, in their different ways, out of his life. The restaurant is now a run-of-the-mill diner (a possible significance of the episode title, Made in America), and nobody seems to demur at the choice. Expectations have been scaled-down all round. And the FBI are closing in with charges that Tony's lawyer warns him he's unlikely to beat.

On the plus side, hes made his peace with New York. Phil Leotardo, disowned by his subordinates, has been gruesomely disposed of, gunned down in his car like so many others. His twin grandchildren were in child-seats in the back, leaving his wife -- sorry, widow -- uncertain what to be more distraught about. It seemed unlikely that anything could make us feel sorry for Phil, but this scene managed it; his one redeeming feature was that he was gentle with his kids. Tony was tipped off to Phils whereabouts by Agent Harris, his surprise new friend and kindred spirit. In one of the episode's more delicious moments, we saw Harris with his very own goomar, a lady agent whose post-coital confidence, judging from her expression, he had just betrayed. Right to the finish, this show could give us a whole character in a single silent moment. There's nobody left with an obvious motive to do Tony in. But one doubts that Phils death gave him much satisfaction. One doubts that anything does.

If that were all, the show could have ended on a bitter sweet fade-out. The cut to black was more like a slap in the face. It was also a shared joke, less about

the show as narrative than about our expectations of it. Over the years, The Sopranos has created a unique bond with its audience. We have bought into it on a deep level, one that partakes of soap opera (as most drama does) but also transcends it. We have wanted to know what, finally, happens to these people. Its a tribute to the writing, and perhaps even more, to the acting, which, from the highest ranks to the lowest, has rarely been less than superb.

If the actors were perfectly cast in the first place, they were then given the chances to dig and to expand, and they took them. What other show, to take a single example, could have created and then dropped a figure as compelling as Svetlana, the sexy, one- legged Russian caregiver? We were left longing for closure and dreading it, partly because we simply didn't want the show to end, partly because we sensed that any definitive ending would be unsatisfying -- there were just too many possibilities to choose from. Hence the extraordinary tension of the last episode, far exceeding that of its more obviously action-packed predecessor.

We were certainly teased with possibilities and allusions. A man disappeared into the washroom and we half expected him to come out with guns blazing, like Al Pacino in The Godfather. Meadow was late because she was terrible at parallel parking, but this, both funny and suspenseful, turned out to signify nothing beyond itself. The show did, in fact, offer more closure than you might think -- most of the story-lines and character-arcs were tidied up in downbeat ways -- but as for what really happened, or would happen, to Tony himself, we don't know. In most TV shows, it wouldnt matter. But The Sopranos pretty much created its own form. No other TV drama has gone on so long, so well, with so persistent a narrative thread so brilliantly diversified, and in doing so it created expectations that couldnt possibly be met. And it ended by acknowledging that.

Immediately before tuning in for the last episode, I re-watched the first, and it was fascinating to see how the surfaces had changed while the essentials remained the same. Everything was very clearly laid out, with far less subtext than we've become accustomed to and a lot of voice-over. James Gandolfini's Tony was as brutal and as charming as ever, but far more open-faced, less creased. Robert Ilers A.J. was just a pudgy little boy, and presumably cast for that reason. The way in which his character has developed (it never, of course, matured) now seems extraordinary. The fractious relationship between Tony and Carmela was already in place; so, to an amazing degree, was that between Tony and Chris. Tonys awareness that he had "come in at the end" was proclaimed at the very start and has only got sadder.

There was, too, our unwillingness -- reflected, almost to the end, in Dr. Melfi -- to give up on Tony, and his discomforting inability to let us. The received wisdom is that in the last season, Tony irredeemably coarsened. I don't agree. Even in his final, shell- like state, he was insisting that Bobby's children be provided for, and if some of that was self-interest (if others paid, he wouldnt have to) not all of it was. You cant speak of Tony's "flashes" of humanity; he's been human all the way through. That doesnt make him a tragic hero -- one more reason for denying him a tragic ending. But he may be an example of tragic waste. Or, bearing in mind what hes always passed off as his primary line of work, Tragic Waste Disposal.

2007-06-13-much-sharper-than-a-serpents-:
I have seen some anti-Semitic Venetians in my time, but those in Stratford's new Merchant of Venice really take the cannoli.

In Richard Rose's fascinating if uneven production, done in modern costumes with Renaissance trimmings, they start the evening with what seems to be a parody of the Last Supper, and proceed to cavort around in carnival pig masks ideal for fantasy Jew-baiting.

The normally negligible character of Solanio (Bruce Dow) achieves unexpected prominence when he does his vicious impersonation of Shylock's laments over the loss of his daughter and his ducats. He leaves no doubt that it's the latter commodity that touches the Jew most dearly. Not that this same Solanio is all that charitable to his fellow Christians. He thinks himself snubbed by Antonio in the opening scene and seems to relish the merchant's ruin as keenly as Shylock does himself. The Jew is not the only one who can bear a grudge.

Antonio, finely played by Scott Wentworth, is a complex figure within whom gentlemanliness and generosity co-exist with sexual possessiveness over his friend Bassanio and an ingrained prejudice that seems religious and professional rather than racial. He calls Shylock not "gentle" but "Gentile Jew," rationalizing it with a quick and patronizing, "This Hebrew will turn Christian; he grows kind." Maybe it's the same religious emphasis that leads this production's Portia to object to the Prince of Morocco's "persuasion" rather than his "complexion," or maybe someone is just being chicken. But few people in this show are very nice.

Ron Kennell, an outstandingly funny Launcelot Gobbo, has his old blind father (Bernard Hopkins) in genuine distress with his false account of his own death. Gratiano (Gareth Potter) is a loudmouthed bigot, though not without charm when among friends. As for Lorenzo (Jean-Michel LeGal), his eyes light up when he elopes with Jessica, not at her but at the casket of cash she's stolen from Shylock: for him, too, it's the ducats, not the daughter.

There's also some straightforward xenophobia. Portia's mocking catalogue of her foreign wooers is much enlivened by having them all present on plinths, striking exaggerated national poses and talking in exaggerated national accents. The Princes of Morocco (Jamie Robinson) and Arragon (Tim MacDonald), when choosing among the caskets, parade their ethnic foibles at full cartooned length, though at the expense of their moments of sober self-realization. The stage is alight with tensions and animosities in a production that probes as sharply into the text as this season's King Lear -- and with more imagination.

Unfortunately, the character on whom much of this should converge is a smudge. Graham Greene's Shylock is an outwardly assimilated businessman (his friend Tubal looks far more Orthodox) with a cantankerous sense of his own worth. His response when Antonio's bond becomes forfeit is to have himself measured for a new suit. (Is there a legal pun here?) His body language is excellent: Watch his mock cringe before Antonio and his real cringe, with a fatalistic shrug attached, before the Duke. But he cannot handle the verse, which he crumbles into disconnected, unintelligible little packages. He's stronger in the prose of "hath not a Jew eyes," which emerges here not as a timeless plea for tolerance but as a perverse statement of equality. "If you wrong us, shall we not revenge?": I've never heard that emphasis before, and it's very powerful.

The show's star curtain call goes, however, not to Shylock but to Portia and Bassanio, and it's their play: a darkly witty piece about love and its handmaiden, jealousy. Severn Thompson's Portia, in a most unbecoming dress that's short in front and bunched behind, starts out giggly and golden-girlish. She gathers strength as she watches Sean Arbuckle's Armani-clad Bassanio, a disarmingly sincere opportunist, choose the right casket. (She's given him some unsubtle musical hints beforehand.) Her offer to help rescue Antonio is a competitive bid to prove her love stronger than his. And Antonio responds in kind. After Portia, in male disguise, has saved his non- kosher bacon, he insists that Bassanio surrender his ring in payment, precisely because it was a gift from his wife. You can see this sad, gay man perk up at the idea, egged on by all the boys in Venice.

So the last scene of newlywed squabbles, graced also by a promising Nerissa from Raquel Duffy, packs an unusual and many- layered punch. A final attempt to draw all the threads together, though, overreaches itself. Sara Topham's excellent Jessica ends the play fearful and alone, with a Hebrew hymn reproaching her over the sound system. Directors are always trying to read these regrets into the Jew's renegade daughter, and one can understand why, but there's no textual evidence for them. I hate to say it, but Shakespeare's Jessica seems perfectly happy among all those rich and lucky Christians. - In repertoire through Oct. 27. Call 1-800-567-1600 for details.

2007-06-15-this-is-the-moor-who-offers-m:
The Stratford season continues its investigation into racism in Renaissance Venice with a new production of Othello, the festival's first in 13 years. It is, of course, casting problems that have kept the play, theoretically one of the most popular of Shakespeare's, off the boards for so long. It no longer seems permissible to cast a white actor in the title role, not many black actors have amassed the classical experience to bring it off, and there are few actors of any colour with the tempestuous power, both vocal and temperamental, to play it at all. And even Iago, which seems a foolproof role, in fact isn't. It's easy to make a great villain entertaining. It's hard to make him believable.

David Latham's production boasts a good Othello, a superb Iago, and a mounting tension that gets started around the middle of the play and goes through the roof at the end. It's also staged straightforwardly and traditionally costumed. Philip Akin, the first Stratford Moor to be both black and Canadian, is a visibly battle- scarred warrior with an unassuming authority and considerable charm.

Where Akin and the play swing into life is in the central temptation scene, which is beautifully built by all concerned. Othello first seems secure enough in his wife's love to brush aside Iago's insinuations. But the worm has already entered his soul, and in what follows, we practically see it taking possession. By the end of the scene, literally and figuratively on his knees, he is Iago's creature, his partner in jealousy. Akin charts the rest of the decline with terrifying accuracy. He hits a speed bump in the approach to the murder of Desdemona: Lacking Othello's extravagance of soul, he makes "it is the cause" sound more spiteful than sacramental. But he recovers to find an impressive emotional logic in the despairing acceptance of guilt that culminates in suicide.

Jonathan Goad's Iago is a self-prized realist envenomed at the thought of the self-prized hero. Iago hates everyone and has affection for no one. He is, apart from Richard III, Shakespeare's only sociopath; and even Richard has a late fit of conscience. Goad, young as Iago should be (he admits to 28), captures all the chilled inhumanity and the self-deprecating humour that conceals it. The most fluent verse-speaker in the company, he still conveys the prosaic doggedness of Iago's mind. Articulate though he is in both modes, he is still the first Iago to make me believe in his final vow of silence. He has sealed off every other avenue of human contact; now speech goes as well. We are left with his final glance at the corpses on the bed and the knowledge that, for him, they make everything worthwhile.

Lucy Peacock's Emilia begins with quiescent resignation; you shudder at her marriage to Iago, but you understand it. She proceeds, like all good Emilias, to take over the play; first as Desdemona's worldly confidante, then as her avenger. The racing excitement of the last scene is largely down to her as she uncovers the plot; so is its emotional power. She's the audience's representative on stage; as with Peter Donaldson's Kent at the end of King Lear and Peter Krantz's de Stogumber in the Niagara Saint Joan, we are moved in large part because of this. She's a more heartening figure, because she is a more active one, than either of them. Othello heats us. Iago chills us. But the lumps in our throats are Emilias's fault. - In repertoire until Sept. 22. For more information, visit Stratfordfestival.ca.

2007-06-16-no-gentrification-in-walkervi:
The Luminato festival focused heavily on the plays of George F. Walker, and two segments of that Walker Project are still around, playing in tandem. The Factory Theatre has revived its last year's production of Escape from Happiness and has added to it a new staging of the play to which that play is a sequel, the ironically titled Better Living.

Or is it ironic? My feelings about Walker's plays continue to bounce around. They have a style and a vision that are unlike anybody else's, they have a casual, eccentric wit that keeps me engaged and listening and, whether set in run-down Parkdale houses or suburban motels, they create a section of Toronto --call it Walkerville--full of people on the edge, living just inside or just outside the law. The problem is I don't believe in them. I don't mean that I don't believe such people exist, but that the ones Walker puts on stage rarely seem more than their author's puppets. Which makes the plays, for all the things that happen in them, seem weightless and ultimately unsatisfying.

Better Living, which is now 21 years old, is directed by Ken Gass with exemplary zip and precision, and it boasts an unbeatable cast. Nora, who, with eccentric determination, is renovating the basement of her East End house and would like to renovate her family along with it, is played by Clare Coulter, a past mistress at presenting a kind of batty integrity that almost amounts to secular sainthood. She's in her own world, though so far inside it that the messages she sends the outside world can sometimes, not for the first time with this actress, be indecipherable. She has three daughters. Elizabeth (Irene Poole, playing emphatically on the nose) escaped the house to become a lawyer; returning to it often makes her feel angry and frustrated. Mary Ann (Sarah Manninen, who's very funny) is the mother of a child whose whereabouts, as well as whose father's name, she keeps forgetting. Gail (Lisa Norton, leaving Shaw Festival gentility way behind her) has what seems to be mutually satisfactory sex with her boyfriend Junior (Brandon McGibbon, agreeably goofy), though when she moves out temporarily, he stays put.

The catalyst for the comings and goings is the return after several years of Nora's husband, Tom, an abusive ex-cop who left home in the wake of his family's self-defending attempts to kill him. You have to love a man who can take a hint. Now, however, he wants to bring order into their lives, so that they'll be able to defend themselves against the plundering hordes of people less fortunate than they are. Such do exist, and they have a nasty habit of being foreign. Fascist Tom may be, but, as played by Ron White, he attracted much of my sympathy simply by virtue of being the only person on stage who was neither shouting nor twittering. Well, almost the only one; his blessed calm is shared by Oliver Becker as Nora's singularly unshockable priestly brother. The two men have little else in common; in fact, brother, or should that be Father, Jack was a prime mover in Tom's planned demise.

Anyway, White's sleek performance develops a healthy decibel level of its own, as the residents and visitors line up with or against him. Some of them alternate, especially Elizabeth; the ferocity of Poole's performance may partly derive from the frequency, and the unaccountability, with which she is required to change sides. Nora, too, begins to warm to her ex, but only by refusing to acknowledge that he is her ex. This cognitive- dissonance device is repeated in Escape from Happiness, and it's no more persuasive here than it is there. All the same, Nora's stubborn refusal to see evil, even when she used to be married to it, has its own strength and it stands at least a chance of prevailing.

It's tempting to describe Walker's plays, with their casual violence, as black comedies, but it might be more accurate to call them sunny tragedies. They have an underlying benevolence: better living indeed. He deserves his place as the foremost Canadian playwright of his generation, but I wish there were more competition.

Tough!, a slightly later Walker play given a complementary production in the Factory Studio, does have believable characters: believable to a fault. It's a play about teens, for whom Walker turns out to have an excellent ear. Bobby has got Tina pregnant and has to decide whether to do the decent thing or carry on being happily promiscuous. Tina is going to keep the baby but has no intention of forcing Bobby into anything. Jill, Tina's friend, has never liked Bobby and is aggressively on his case and in his face.

A straightforward three-actor production would, I suspect, seem grindingly obvious: the sort of thing that gets toured to schools for sociological uplift. Gass has had the inspired idea of dividing each role four ways among a multi-cultural cast. So each character becomes an archetype compounded of individuals. Technically, too, the show gets terrific mileage out of overlapping dialogue, choral speech, and surprise movement. Nina Lee Aquino is associate director and her choreographic skills are well in evidence.

The 12 young performers (down to 11 on my night) worked exhilaratingly together, with Bethany Jillard, blonde and proud, outstanding among the Tinas. The assorted Bobbies ran a delightful gamut of feckless resentment while the various Jills gave an uncompromising joint account of one of the least sympathetic characters in contemporary drama. The show has closed, but you can bet it will be back.

- Better Living runs through July 1 at the Factory Theatre. Call 416-504-9971 for details.

2007-06-18-shakespeare-would-not-be-amus:
Richard Monette's last Shakespeare production at Stratford falls into a category that I don't remember ever encountering: the Self- Administered Insult.

For years now, people have been glibly accusing Monette of mounting gag-laden, over-the-top productions of practically everything. The allegations have continued despite a string of good- to-excellent shows that answered to that description in no way whatsoever: King Lear, The Tempest, The School for Scandal, The Importance of Being Earnest, Troilus and Cressida, Cat on a Hot Tin Roof, Henry VIII, Henry IV Part One, Edward II I could go on. So, he might have decided that if the label of irresponsible farceur were to be hung around his neck regardless, then he may as well earn it. He may have reasoned that The Comedy of Errors, an actual farce that he had already directed with some success several years back, would be the ideal vehicle. If those were really his thoughts, I sympathize. But he was very, very wrong.

The moment that best sums up the show comes when Aegeon, the Syracusan merchant condemned to death for arriving ransomless in the hostile city of Ephesus, is paraded through the streets, accompanied only by the Duke (a surprisingly minimal escort for a man on death row) and carrying a placard that reads "My End Is Near." He turns it around, to reveal a picture of the departing Monette himself. Ha, ha.

In a similar vein, we get a property camel borrowed from My One and Only and labelled accordingly, and a reference to the scarcity of tickets for Oklahoma! There's also an actor who crosses the stage in a penguin suit emblazoned with the words "for the critics." Sorry; I can't speak for the other guys, but I only like penguins onstage when they're real. These self-referential japes might pass muster on the last night of the run. They might even, conceivably, have raised some indulgent laughter on the first night (though they didn't). What audiences in between will make of them I cannot imagine.

Maybe the gags wouldn't matter if they were isolated moments in a production that otherwise offered a focused and inventive account of the play (though such a production wouldn't have included them in the first place), but Monette doesn't seem to trust his author an inch. Everything is sent up, though the first rule of farce -- which I have never seen successfully broken -- is that everything has to be taken seriously. Otherwise, it isn't funny. Aegeon's death- sentence shouldn't be funny; it's the real deal that frames all the craziness.

The Comedy of Errors is the play about two sets of identical twins -- two masters named Antipholus, two slaves named Dromio -- separated at birth, turning up as young adults in the same city and constantly being mistaken for one another, until every person in town suspects every other person of having gone mad. Nobody wants a reverential production; the best production I ever saw was done as a musical, and it wasn't The Boys from Syracuse. But the actors have to believe in the situations, or we won't. They should not be wasting their time and ours by signalling what rubbish they think it all is.

The show is a compendium of unfunny gags, with no roots in character or situation. The Duke of Ephesus can't pronounce his city's name without getting his sibilants soaked, and the conjuror Dr. Pinch emerges, after an elaborate buildup from both script and staging, as a robed nonentity whose comic presence is zero. The acting in general is at as low an ebb as I remember at Stratford.

One of Monette's unacknowledged strengths has always been the basic one of making sense of the text. He seems to have given up on it this time. Allegra Fulton renders about 50% of the jealous Adriana's lines incomprehensible, while Sophia Walker as her ingenue sister raises that score to somewhere around 90%.

There are a few survivors. Tom McCamus, who arrives late, brings a welcome burst of energy and efficiency as the resident Antipholus. Bruce Dow makes the visiting Dromio's anatomizing of the spherical kitchen-wench, a geography lesson in herself, into a pleasantly salty vaudeville routine. He and his twin (Steve Ross) share an affecting reunion scene that's moving even at the very end of a production like this. Back at the very beginning, Brian Tree delivers Aegeon's long tale of woe with a dry doggedness in misery that I liked. I also confess to a weakness for the Greek tragic chorus that oohs and aahs its way through his trial before rousing itself to deliver the most famous of Greek tragic tags, the one about calling no man happy until he is dead. It doesn't connect to anything that follows, but it was fun. That, though, was before I realized that the whole evening was going to be like that.

Did I mention the mechanical Komedy Kat that chases a real dog in between scenes to which neither of them has any connection? I guess it's an apt motif for a show that's just one non sequitur not following another. - In repertoire until Oct. 26. For tickets, call 1-800-567-1600 or visit www.stratfordfestival.ca.

2007-06-19-a-little-bit-of-canada-in-a-n:
Tonight, for the first official time, Michael Therriault will reveal himself to West End audiences by slithering 50 vertical feet down the front cloth of the Theatre Royal, Drury Lane.

Therriault is repeating in London the award-winning performance he gave last year in Toronto as Gollum in the musical of The Lord of the Rings. That performance was contortionist enough, but it didn't incorporate this particular acrobatic feat. True, he has the support of an invisible wire, and he has had six weeks of previews to get used to it. Still, when I had tea with him at a London hotel just before those previews were due to start, he confessed to being "terrified. But," he added, "I'm proud that I'm actually doing it."

And that's just the start. Gollum, this time around, goes out as hair-raisingly as he goes in. One criticism made of the Toronto show was that its climax, Gollum plunging to his death in the fiery craters of Mount Doom, was insufficiently clear. Its restaging involves Therriault falling backward from a height of three metres "onto a giant bean-bag." And in between these extremes, he acts and sings -- very well, if his Toronto performance is any guide.

When I talked to Therriault, he had been in rehearsal for almost two-and-a-half months, while accepting that "most of my rehearsing will come in previews." In the midst of all the show's spectacle, Gollum's is an intimate role, most of whose scenes are either on his own or with the two principal hobbits, Frodo and Sam.

A couple of days before our meeting, I had dropped in on a technical rehearsal and found it to be very technical indeed, with acting about the last thing on anybody's mind. The stalls were a solid bank of computers. The director, Matthew Warchus, looked commendably unfazed by the task of helming one of the most complex and expensive shows in theatrical history.

Warchus is co-adaptor of The Lord of the Rings as well as director, so one of his jobs has been to cut it. According to producer Kevin Wallace, the show will be brought down to three hours by combining the kingdoms of Gondor and Rohan. Personally, I would have liked to see the same amalgamation imposed on the show's two races of Elves, but they remain separate. However, the song Lothlorien, which even I found a bore in Toronto, has been turned from a static solo by Galadriel into a full-scale Elvish anthem. The show, Wallace says, is now "more of a musical" with a clearer storyline.

Its Canadian content is now minimal. Three of the four major hobbits remain from Toronto, but they were British to begin with. The new Aragorn is a French performer, Jerome Pradon, but Toronto audiences may remember him as the title character in the ill-fated musical Napoleon.

And then, of course, there is Therriault, the self-described "small-town kind of guy" from Acadia who still seems slightly bemused at finding himself near the centre of a West End megamusical. This despite a Broadway stint in Fiddler on the Roof and a TV triumph as Tommy Douglas. He's endearingly self- deprecating about his position among Canadian actors. He won his spurs at the Stratford Festival, where he was one of the great young discoveries of the Richard Monette regime and one of the first graduates of the conservatory.

When it came time to leave Stratford to play the star role of Leo Bloom in the Toronto company of The Producers, he was not merely scared, but "depressed." His gloom should soon have lifted. His performance as the timorous accountant was a triumph and established him as a genuine acting-singing-dancing triple threat.

And it might well have paved the way for Gollum. Both characters share a certain manic obsequiousness. Both spend time crawling on the ground. And Leo's attachment to his blanket has a definite kinship with Gollum's passion for his Precious.

2007-06-23-the-dora-plethora:
If we are to judge by this years Dora nominations -- and for once we can -- the 2006-'07 season was the one in which the kids beat the grown-ups at their own game. Or rather games. Three productions from the Lorraine Kimsa Theatre for Young People have between them been nominated in so many categories in the main, or General Theatre, division that the company has hardly any shows left over for the Theatre for Young Audiences section, which is where they usually go.

Of those three shows, two -- I Think I Can and Danny, King of the Basement -- really were among the best things of the year. The third, Seussical, really wasn't, though some of its individual participants were. I Think I Can, the Florence Gibson-Shawn Byfield piece about empowerment through tap-dancing, is up for outstanding new musical (the Doras shrink from the word "best), and I dont see how it can lose, unless someone feels churlish about the fact that it doesnt have any songs. But then, its two competitors, Bird Flu over the Cuckoo's Nest, the best Second City revue in years, wasn't notable for its songs either, and neither was CanStages The Story of My Life, which had a lot of them. I think I Think I Can can, and will. It should also get outstanding production of a musical, given that the competition is Story of My Life, We Will Rock You (which may win but shouldnt), Seussical and what we apparently have to refer to as Richard O'Brien's The Rocky Horror Show. (Who does Mr. OBrien think he is -- Monty Python?) No mention here, or anywhere else, for Songs for a New World, though it was a better show than most of them, and very stylishly staged. That brings us (oh these subtle distinctions) to outstanding direction of a musical, a category that this year has found room for Seussical, as well as the atrociously directed (ah, but by Ben Elton, whos famous) We Will Rock You. Here, too, I Think I Can's Conrad Alexandowicz should waltz, or hop, off with it; though he might have serious competition from Christopher Bond and Hilton Battle over at Evil Dead: the Musical where staging and performance prevail over (mostly) terrible material. Battle could also be a winner for best choreography.

Seussical comes into its own in the musical performance categories. George Masswohl's Horton the Elephant should win by a trunk over Yvan Pedneault (We Will Rock You) and Rick Ward (Evil Dead). Id cheer, too, if Corinne Koslos Gertrude McFuzz flew off victorious; I might do the same for Sarah Cornell (Evil Dead), Melody Johnson (I Think I Can) or Erica Peck (We Will Rock You) but the bird has it, if only by a tail feather.

On to more solemn stuff. The big surprise in the new-play category is the omission, apparently on a technicality, of Wajdi Mouawad's ambitious Scorched. I wasn't one of its big boosters, but it obviously deserved to be there, especially as most of the pieces that are feel like barrel-scraping, including Michael Hollingsworths The Saskatchewan Rebellion, which isnt even new. So the field should be clear for Michael Healey's generous Generous. Though last time Healey won, I'd prophesied hed lose: Apologies in advance, Michael. Scorched does make it into outstanding production of a play (Im confused, too) and will very likely win. What should win is Orpheus Descending but it wasn't even nominated; as a joint product of the Mirvishes (too commercial) and Stratford (too Stratford) it didn't stand a chance, given the Doras notorious reverse snobbery. Its even more scandalous that Miles Potter's direction didn't get a nod, though Ill admit that the actual best direction nominees are all worthy and hard to choose between; put a gun to my head and Ill squawk for Chris Abraham (Insomnia). Seana McKenna's transcendent Orpheus performance has been recognized, and should be a sure thing, which doesn't mean it is. Fiona Reid (Homebody/Kabul and Generous) should be the runner-up but isnt there; sometimes one despairs. Outstanding male performer will probably be Kenneth Welsh in Leaving Home; this Canadian classic" must be Soulpeppers most-nominated production ever, which, given the Doras' past neglect of the company's magnificent Ibsens and Chekhovs, suggests that there might just be a little parochialism at work here. And its certainly astonishing that The Threepenny Opera was completely ignored in all the musical categories.

Most ludicrous category: featured role (either gender) in a play or musical. There is, of course, enough talent here in any season to furnish four awards. With them all squeezed together, Id plump for Jane Spidell in Leaving Home. The Ensemble (i.e., everyone) in Danny, King of the Basement also got nominated; this is a cop-out, though they were all great, especially Jordan Pettle (who should have been named for Generous, anyway). The set, costume, lighting, sound and musical direction categories are embarrassments of (mostly) riches, though I'm perplexed that The Rocky Horror Show didn't get a costume nomination for sheer wit while Seussical did.

Down in the Independent Theatre division, I note that Hannah Moscovitchs The Russian Play didnt get an outstanding new play nomination, though it's far superior to anything that did. Michelle Monteith (female performance) mercifully did, and deserves to win, despite stiff competition from Sarah Dodd (Marion Bridge, glad they singled her out) and Deena Aziz (Homebody/Kabul). Male performance should go, please, to Thom Allison, who in Elegies: A Song Cycle was star-quality personified; though Ryan Kelly was superb in Will the Real J.T. LeRoy Please Stand Up, which should also have been among the best new plays. Poaching on to the Opera division: I pause on the verge of asserting that Lady Macbeth of Mtsensk should win everything to recall that Das Rheingold was wonderful, too, both in itself and as the capstone of the COC's Ring Cycle. Also, though Nicola Beller Carbones Lady MofMwas amazing, so, too, were the duelling divas of Elektra, Susan Bullock and Ewa Podles. Operatic candidates also infiltrate the General division, notably in musical direction, though how you measure Richard Bradshaws big band against, say, Rick Fox's (We Will Rock You) is beyond me.

As for Monday's awards show itself: It will be better than last year's. It has to be.

2007-06-28-man-as-masterpiece-between-st:
Obituary of William Hutt.

William Hutt was Canada's greatest actor. Everybody knows that. But he was even more than that. The bulk of his career was spent at the Stratford Festival playing Shakespeare. By the time he played his last role there -- Prospero, fittingly enough, in The Tempest, the great valedictory play -- he had become the finest Shakespearean actor in the world.

This was a matter of taste and talent, of course, but even more of strength and endurance. Actors who go on acting into their eighties usually settle for gnarled or delicate cameos. Hutt didn't have to settle. In his last decade of life he still had the resources to play Prospero and King Lear, each for the fourth time. And with experience there naturally came unrivalled authority. He knew his way around these texts as nobody else could, but he never stopped exploring them. Playing his last Lear in 1996 (he was 76, which is theatrically old but chronologically young for the monarch who admits to being "fourscore and upwards" ) he husbanded his resources but spared nothing in voltage when his rages actually came around. Power was allied to finesse. In Lear's last scene, as the king's mind wandered around the brute fact of his daughter's dead body, his technique was quicksilver. Writing about his penultimate Prospero (1999) I cited "the taut, flexible viola voice, the sustained and witty phrasing, the architectural prowess that built each speech into an ongoing wave of sense and sound, the fusing of these to create a character." At the time this was rumoured to be his farewell performance; it turned out to be anything but. When he did play his last Prospero it was different again, less bravura (probably of necessity) but more intense. "Our revels now are ended" wasn't peaceful; it was angry.

That Hutt should have had such a career is itself a tribute to the Canadian theatre. It has thrived on continuity, a tradition that he himself helped to establish. He was in the very first Stratford season in 1953, playing small parts but already attracting notice. This steadily grew, "steadily" at this point being the operative word. In 1957 he had his first major success, as Polonius in Hamlet. In 1967, playing the title role in Richard II, he became, in Stratford and Canadian terms, a star. He sometimes

went off to London or New York or even to other Canadian theatres, but there were still very few Stratford seasons he missed. At some point in the 1970s he became recognized as the festival's doyen, an authoritative figure offstage as well as on. From what I have read, and what I saw myself as a visitor, he was not yet a great actor, though he was obviously a remarkably accomplished one, one who could time a throwaway line in comedy as perfectly as he could unroll a bolt of rhetoric in tragedy. The performance, for me at least, that lifted him into a new dimension was his Feste the jester in Twelfth Night (1980); astoundingly relaxed in speech or song, he cast a spell every time he opened his mouth.

The two sovereign English classical actors of the twentieth century were the chiselled, elegant John Gielgud and the volcanic Laurence Olivier. Hutt, more than any British actor, was the natural heir of both of them, combining their qualities; and he grew to be as good as either. (He also, by all reports of his towering Lady Bracknell in The Importance of Being Earnest, had moments of challenging Dame Edith Evans.) He surpassed Olivier as James Tyrone in Eugene O'Neill's Long Day's Journey into Night; his sudden plea to his morphine-addicted wife -- "can't you stop now?" -- was an immensely moving cry from the heart, that took you by surprise even on a second viewing. He couldn't surpass Gielgud as the bar-room poet of Harold Pinter's No Man's Land but he equalled him; the tiptoed way that he manoeuvred around his rich host's elegant carpet to get himself a drink was a masterpiece in itself, even before he got to the long speeches. It was extraordinary in itself that he should be attempting so new and taxing a role in his eighties, and for a company (Soulpepper) with which he had never worked before; it was thrilling that he brought it off so consummately.

He said after his last stage performance that he wanted to go on acting on the screen, and he had a marvellous epiphany in the TV series Slings and Arrows as an old actor finally getting his chance at playing Lear. (It might be counted as Hutt's Lear No. 4 .) He was, to a certain extent, playing himself; if you knew him it was hard not to see the kind, witty, sharp-tongued, theatrically wise Bill Hutt who knew Shakespeare in general, and that play in particular, inside out. In one sad respect the role was unwittingly prophetic; the actor he played was dying of cancer, and it's leukemia that has now taken Hutt himself. The speed of his passing is a shock, but maybe a good one. It capped a life and a career supremely well spent.

2007-06-29-the-arch-old-knight-of-york:
It has passed into both civic and theatrical legend that Camelot and what was then the O'Keefe Centre opened at the same time. The Alan Jay Lerner-Frederick Loewe musical began its pre-Broadway tour in 1960 as the opening attraction of Front Street's cavernous emporium. Deals were done to make it so, but the inevitable result was two sets of teething traumas happening at once. The show opened unhappily, and key members of the creative team were whisked in and out of hospital with heart attacks as they attempted to fix it. Still, whatever the problems on that first night long ago -- which included a four-hour running-time -- what appeared on the stage must have been a miracle of excitement compared with what's going on there now. We have another touring Camelot, though this one is probably not headed for Broadway.

It's one of those catchpenny revivals with a sort of star in the lead. Michael York is playing King Arthur, and he's the main reason why the show's a disaster. It seems cruel to say so, since musical theatre has never been his thing (nor indeed has any other kind of theatre), and he does seem to have been cast for niceness. But that's the problem. His Arthur goes through the entire show with a self-deprecatory smile and vocal inflections to match. It's meant, I suppose, to be disarmingly charming, but it becomes physically painful to watch and to listen to. He seems to be apologizing for his emotions rather than feeling them. If we cannot believe, passionately, in Arthur's agony and in his idealism, the show makes no kind of sense.

In this very free version of Arthurian legend, the king's idealism consists in his introducing to Britain the concepts of law and justice, to be administered by the knights of the structurally egalitarian Round Table. The agony comes when his queen, Guenevere, betrays him with his best friend and perfect knight, Lancelot. Guenevere is put on trial and condemned to the stake, leaving Arthur to face what his devilish bastard son Mordred calls the "magnificent dilemma" of sparing her, thus destroying his ideals, or killing her, thus destroying his love.

There's tragic force there, and even this production can't quite destroy the soaring poignancy of the show's ending, in which Arthur, via a reprise of the previously jingly title-song, sends off a young hopeful called Tom of Warwick (i.e. Thomas Malory, future author of the Morte d'Arthur) with instructions to keep the Camelot story alive. It doesn't, though, come anywhere near disguising the weaknesses inherent in what has gone before. If ever there was a flawed musical with elements of greatness, Camelot is it. Lerner's book, admittedly with a fearsome amount of ground to cover, varies between solemn and flippant, generally settling on arch. Archness also pervades many of his lyrics. Loewe's music similarly veers between stately and stodgy, occasionally alighting on lovely; though, it's somehow typical that the loveliest song of all, Follow Me, should be sung, mostly offstage, by a character we barely meet to one whom, a mere half-hour in, we are about to lose. Michael A.M. Lerner (A.J.'s son) has adapted the script, and somewhat streamlined it, though he's added a baffling silent prologue and has cut a couple of the merrier songs from a score that couldn't really afford to lose them.

The staging (Glenn Casale) and sets (John Iacovelli) are very makeshift. Rachel York has charm and spunk as Guenevere, while showing again that it's impossible to play this role without sounding exactly like Julie Andrews, not only in the range and colour of her singing, but in the roguishness of her speech. That said, her singing of Before I Gaze at You Again, not previously a song to which I've ever paid much attention, is the evening's high point. An actor with the unlikely name of Time Winters gets all the available fun out of King Pellinore, a transplanted English clubman who arrives at court in search of the Questing Beast, like (he says) all the Pellinores before him, and then forgets about it for the rest of the show. He's fortunate, for purely technological reasons, in not having to sing. We have suffered much recently from overbearing sound systems; now here's one that's underbearing. It makes everyone, from the vibrant Ms. York to the modest Mr. York, sound as if their vocal cords have been wrapped in cotton wool. - Camelot runs until June 30. For more information call 416-872-2262.
