2007-06-30-the-people-have-spoken:
The People's Choice Award, a sort of extramural Dora, is voted for, online, by people who, it is assumed, are neither theatre professionals, such as comprise the juries for the Doras themselves, nor critics. In fact, they are ordinary punters making their preferences known in the teeth of the self-proclaimed experts. This is healthy. Last Monday, the prize went, hearteningly, to Evil Dead the Musical, a show that had been nominated in four of the official categories but lost in all of them. With that off my conscience, let me tell you what I think of Evil Dead.

I think it's terrible, at least as far as its actual writing is concerned; the staging and some of the performances are excellent. By now, we have learned to dread any show that has "the Musical" in its title. The suffix can mean one of two things, except in cases like this one where it means both of them. One is that the show's source material has already been so thoroughly worked over that the latest version needs to come equipped with some kind of distinguishing mark. The other is that musical theatre itself is regarded as a debased sub-genre, only viable as a source of campy fun. The result has been a long series of shows, spoofing things that nobody took seriously in the first place. Low-grade horror movies are favourite targets. The cycle probably started with The Rocky Horror Show, to which Evil Dead pays explicit homage. It has a dance-number called Do the Necronomicon, whose lyric describes it as being like The Time Warp only better. The judgment is arguable; but when a derivative show has to make a defensive joke of its reliance on another derivative show (to pre-empt the audience's noticing for themselves) we have reached a very advanced stage of enfeeblement indeed.

Evil Dead started as a Toronto fringe show, and probably worked very nicely there. It has since been to off-Broadway and back. It derives from a couple of cult movies, neither of which I've seen. This may conceivably disqualify me from judging the show, but a piece of entertainment is supposed to be able to stand on its own feet. I did get the impression that the enthusiastic audience with whom I saw the show already knew the material backwards, and were getting their kicks from being reminded of it. Maybe the award was less Popular and more cult-fanatical than I'd first thought.

Anyway, those who know the story in advance have an advantage over the rest of us, because the show itself doesn't tell it very well. It starts out with five young people -- a department-store salesman (houseware), his girlfriend, his kid sister, his best buddy and a tall pneumatic sex-mad blonde whom the buddy has been lucky enough to pick up--off to spend a weekend in a deserted cottage in the woods. This information is dispensed in an opening number that's almost entirely inaudible, so you have to pick up most of the information for yourselves later on. Anyway, the cottage is spooked, and by evening's end, four-fifths of the quintet have been turned into Candarian Demons, whatever they are, each transformation being announced by the victim's cackling "look who's evil now." The only one left standing is the salesman himself, and he's had his moments. Converging on their story is that of the daughter of the house's owner, a frantic academic, and her ineffectual boyfriend whom she never lets finish a sentence. The daughter gets to sing a long country-flavoured (i.e., whiny) song whose title is All the Men in My Life Keep Getting Killed by Candarian Demons. Apart from being a candidate, musically and lyrically, for Worst Song Ever Written for a Musical, even a cult-spoof one, it leaves us no wiser as to what, if anything, distinguishes a Candarian from any other kind of demon. The show skimps on its basic mythology even more shamelessly than it does on establishing its characters. What it really cares about is gore, as humans and demons set about slaughtering one another. Our indomitable houseware hero loses a hand quite early on; this is ingeniously handled as indeed are all the effects, all credit to the directors, Hinton Battle (who's also the adroit choreographer) and Christopher Bond, and to the very droll sets by David Gallo. The blood spatters very inventively; though the point does seem to be quantity rather than quality.

When asked who were the authors of Oklahoma!, Cole Porter, who himself always wrote both music and lyrics, replied "Rodgers and Hammerstein -- if you can imagine it taking two men to write one score." The gods alone know what he would have made of Evil Dead whose music is credited to four composers --Frank Cipolla, Melissa Morris, George Reinblatt and the aforementioned Christopher Bond -- who have failed between them to come up with a single distinctive tune. Reinblatt also wrote the lyrics, to which the idea of building a comedy song, as opposed to throwing in a couple of random jokes, seems completely foreign. His book, though, has its moments. I liked the failure of the nerdy boyfriend even to announce that he, too, was evil now without being interrupted; and I loved the response of his lady to the news that the hero's girlfriend was the only demon with a habit of making bad puns: "And she's the one you let live?" she says, in tones of censorious wonder. The towering Sarah Cornell, who can be smart and wide-eyed at the same time, does this delectably, as she does the entire role; she's less successful as the blonde bimbo, but as this character isn't around very long, it doesn't matter. Ryan Ward does unblinking yeoman service as the protagonist from retail, and the rest (there were some understudies on when I saw it) are enthusiastic if not exactly subtle. The show itself doesn't matter; the trend behind it does. It consists of people who have contempt for musicals expressing that contempt by writing them.

- Evil Dead the Musical runs through Aug. 4 at the Diesel Playhouse. Call 416-971-5656 for details.

THE CASSILIS ENGAGEMENT

Court House Theatre, Niagara-on-the-Lake, Ont.

---

In 1909, at the age of 39, St. John Hankin, playwright, drowned himself. It may be the worst loss ever inflicted on English drama by an early death. The Shaw Festival tipped us off to this a few years ago with its production of Hankin's The Return of the Prodigal and it now reinforces the point with The Cassilis Engagement.

Hankin wrote Edwardian society comedies that owe something to Shaw and more to Wilde, but are trimmer and more mordant than either. They show greed, jealousy and snobbery bubbling beneath a placid surface and finally boiling over. The Cassilis Engagement is subtitled "a play for mothers," and it turns on the efforts of Mrs. Cassilis, a widowed member of England's county gentry, to prevent her son Geoffrey from contracting an unsuitable marriage. Geoffrey's fiancee is a lower-class London girl called Ethel Borridge, which in name alone is enough to condemn her. Mrs. Cassilis determines to kill the match with kindness. She invites Ethel down to her place in Leicestershire for a prolonged visit, asking her to bring her own mother, and trusting that the sheer incongruity of their presence in such surroundings will both alarm Ethel and awaken Geoffrey. It turns out to be a fruitful scheme, in ways that even its progenitress might not have foreseen.

Hankin was anything but a sentimentalist, and Ethel is anything but a victim. Her mother has scrimped to give her an education, hoping that she can use it to marry money; there's a senescent earl waiting in the wings, but Geoffrey will more than do. Meanwhile, Mrs. Cassilis' friends and neighbours look on aghast, horrified that she should give such creatures houseroom, let alone be friendly to them.

Christopher Newton's production contains three marvellously complex performances. Mrs. Cassilis is a mixture of long-suffering and long-sighted: a nice woman who hatches a nasty plan that requires her to act nice. Goldie Semple lays out these layers superbly. The feral maternal protectiveness, the flickers of conscience, the natural graciousness purposefully perverted, are all there; so is a sense of loss in the midst of success. Mrs. Borridge is a hearty vulgarian whose transparent opportunism and dropped "aitches" (she's only too 'appy to make herself at 'ome) embarrass her daughter as thoroughly as they amuse or appall her hosts -- which, since she herself has trained Ethel to be upwardly mobile, is choice indeed. Mary Haney plays her vigorously and successfully for laughs until her ambitions begin to fall apart, at which point she becomes enraged, desperate, and -- in her terror -- terrifying. Social climbing may be a joke; poverty isn't.

Watching mother and daughter exhibiting their tricks and manners to the scandalized toffs is rather like watching Eliza Doolittle's "not bloody likely" scene from Pygmalion extended over most of an evening. (Hankin's play came first.) The greatest of the play's many ironies, though, may be that Ethel is so full-blooded a character as to make much of Mrs. Cassilis' best-laid plan superfluous; she was bound to revolt against this environment even without her mother on hand. Trish Lindstrom makes her hard, vivacious and fundamentally honest, able to buck the expectations all around her rather than deny her own nature. A scene in which she entertains the company with a music-hall song (lyrics by Newton himself ) is a real set- piece, delightful in itself and laying bare all the conflicts.

The men's roles are decidedly subordinate, but David Leyshon almost saves the baffled Geoffrey from complete and utter drippiness, and as an ageing rake playing devil's advocate, Patrick Galligan has a diverting swagger, though he seems excessively aware, not so much of his place in the world as of his place in the play. There is a third mother in the cast, a countess who communicates mainly via epigram and represents the minor aristocracy at its intolerant worst. There's a similar character in The Return of the Prodigal, and the problem with both of them is to stop them turning into cut-rate Lady Bracknells, revelling in their own outrageousness; Donna Belleville, like her predecessor, fails to solve it. Her daughter is the girl everybody thinks Geoffrey ought to marry, a mouse in jodhpurs; Charlotte Gowdy plays her dowdy, but in an appealing sort of way that includes one modest moment of genuine suffering. As Mrs. C's confidante who gets drawn gradually into the plot, Laurie Paton conveys subtle and supple gradations of shock and fascination with both those on both sides of the tracks. In a good Shaw season, this show is the best yet. - In repertoire until Oct. 5. Call 1-800-511-SHAW or visit www.shawfest.com for tickets.

I love Ken MacDonald's set for the hotel in Hotel Peccadillo. It's the rich relation of his crazy design for the one-man play Earshot, with its violently exaggerated perspective. Here we get a corridor flanked by two lines of doors that get outlandishly smaller the farther away from us they are. At their apex is a tiny chair. At one moment, a full-sized actor brings it right downstage, where proportions are normal, and sits on it. It's hilarious.

The Hotel Peccadillo, then, is quite the kinky establishment. It, and the play that contains it, have previously been best known in England as Hotel Paradiso. The original is by Georges Feydeau, the master of 19th-century French farce (and his sometime silent partner Maurice Desvallieres, who lives on in parentheses). The new version is a free update by Morris Panych, who is also the director. He has stayed fairly close to the classic structure. In Act 1, various couples plan independently to commit adultery in a shady inn. Act 2: They all arrive simultaneously and are all elaborately thwarted. Act 3: They have to explain themselves to jealous spouses and, for the most part, get away with it. Feydeau wrote many

plays of this kind, and the proof of his genius is that his third acts, where the knots are tangled tighter before being cut, are invariably the funniest.

Panych has also found equivalents for all the original characters though he has changed their external features and, in some cases, their essences. His protagonist, Pinglet, is now a psychiatrist with a dragon lady for a wife. Pinglet has written books in praise of monogamous marriage, so it's somewhat embarrassing that he should find himself with an urge to seduce the wife of one of his patients. She's willing, indeed eager, since her husband neglects her; this is because he's a professional critic (of everything, apparently, from paintings to, yes, hotels) for whom nothing -- in art, life or probably plumbing -- can ever live up to his ideals. A new character is Feydeau himself, who takes over the role of the hotel manager and combines it with that of a commentator, lamenting how much more uptight everybody is now than in his day. He has some very funny lines. So, at one time or another, do most of the other characters. There is also some very funny staging.

But it's all to no purpose. Or rather, it's to too much purpose. Panych has come up with something that nobody needs: a moralizing farce. The fact that his morality -- for which he makes a very good case--is other people's immorality doesn't slow the play down. His target is today's new puritanism, as exemplified by Pinglet, whose couch is a site for preaching fidelity. It seems to me that Panych overrates the new repressiveness and underrates the old, of which, as it happens, Feydeau himself was an exemplar. (In his work, I mean. In life, if that's the right term, he died of syphilis.) Panych has got Feydeau wrong. Those belle epoque farces, however many frilly knickers they have on display, are the opposite of aphrodisiac. They show respectable bourgeois people making fools of themselves and very relieved to return to normality with their virtue, and more importantly their reputations, still unscathed. "This would happen when my wife's not here to help," says Feydeau's protagonist (though not Panych's) when overcome by tummy troubles in the act of coveting his neighbour's wife. At least, he says it in the version I'm familiar with. Maybe it's a translator's caprice. But it fits.

The point is, they all have reason to fear being found out. In Panych's version, nobody does, except Pinglet, and even he's a borderline case. The mainspring of farce has been removed, and what remains is mere rushing around, well-choreographed, but essentially aimless. The mechanism has been tampered with, too. Feydeau's cast includes an upright barrister with four young daughters and a stammer that comes and goes, a device that proves crucial to the denouement. Panych substitutes a dashing airline pilot with a retinue of nubile flight attendants. This looks like a wholesale lift from a later and lesser French farce, the 1960s hit Boeing- Boeing, currently enjoying a brilliant surprise revival in London, in accordance with the rule that yesterday's escapism is today's classic (and vice, quite often, vice versa). The pilot also has a speech impediment, but it means nothing, since in this set-up he has nothing important to conceal or reveal.

The most centred and economical of the Niagara performances is given by Benedict Campbell as the critic. The slyest and juiciest comes from Lorne Kennedy, whose Feydeau has the delivery of a scripture-citing devil and the coiled posture of a jackknife. The most rewardingly energetic, vocally and physically, is Patrick Galligan's Pinglet, who in addition to driving the plot along gets to deliver some verbal tirades that fizz with the authentic farcical mixture of doubt and desire. The object of his attentions is Charlotte Gowdy, whose character's subtleties have gone out the window along with her inhibitions, but who is a delightfully sullen sex object even so. And there is that set, exploiting the full depth and width of the Festival stage but still unable to dispel the impression of a lot of talented people rattling around in a void. - In repertoire until Oct. 7. Call 1-800-511-SHAW for more information or visit Shawfest.com.

2007-07-07-crammed-with-first-rate-actor:
Caryl Churchills Top Girls is a play requiring seven superb female performers. Its come to the right place. The upper echelon of theatre around here -- what might be called the Toronto- Stratford-Niagara axis -- is crammed, almost to embarrassment, with first-rate heroic actresses. The top girls assembled for Soulpepper's production could hardly be bettered. It's a sobering thought, or maybe an intoxicating one, that they could be equalled, maybe two or three times over.

The play itself, which might be called the flagship British feminist drama if it didnt fly its flag at such an oblique angle, was first staged in London in 1982 and was a dazzler. It still dazzles, especially in its first scene, though some of its later passages have frayed a bit. That opener, though, is a feast -- of wit, imagination and other things.

Let us now praise famous women, a selection of whom from history or legend are assembled for dinner at a smart London restaurant. There is Lady Nijo, an imperial Japanese concubine who became a nun, played by Robyn Stevan with a delectable air of stoicism triumphing over deep sadness. There is Chaucers Patient Griselda, given a tender-tough performance by Cara Pifko; she has in common with Lady Nijo the experience of being forced to surrender her children to demonstrate her fealty to her husband and the society he represents. Bringing us slightly more up to date is Isabella Bird, Scots Victorian traveller; her incredulity at some of the tales told by her medieval companions allows Kelli Fox to deliver the most explosively funny moment of the evening. Ann-Marie MacDonald is hilariously unruffled as Pope Joan who rose (probably apocryphally) to Peter's chair by disguising herself as a man and was only rumbled when she gave birth in the street during a procession, whereupon she was dragged off and, as MacDonald blandly recounts it, stoned to death. She doesn't seem, all things considered, to bear much of a grudge. Looking very grudging indeed at the end of the table, and hardly saying a word, is Liisa Repo-Martell as Dull Gret who, in a Breughel painting, led a punitive expedition into Hell. She looks slightly happier to be there, though, than the waitress; Diana Donnelly says not a word but conveys, while bringing the food and pouring the drinks, a lofty resentment of everybody and everything.

The party has been convened by Marlene, a present-day lady celebrating her promotion to boss of the Top Girls Employment Agency. Her guests are women who have inspired her but whom she has, in her own mind, surpassed. They reflect her own issues with career, children and siblings. The rest of the play shuttles, more or less naturalistically, between Marlenes office and her sisters home in Suffolk, the world she left to become successful. Megan Follows plays Marlene brilliantly, with a hard edge that never becomes a mannerism. She is the only actress to play one role throughout; the others recur in two or three guises apiece.

Alisa Palmer's orchestration of the restaurant conclave is visually excellent and aurally pretty good. (Some bits are hard to hear, even given the author's fondness for overlapping dialogue.) Her touch slackens, though, in the office scenes. Churchill is a superb dramatic writer --every scene, speech, line, makes a point and connects with the others -- but her language, unlike Pinters, isnt the kind that brings its own style with it; the peculiar London brittleness, barbed and chatty, here proves elusive. The director has also changed a delicate structure into a fragmentary one by redividing it from two acts into three. Marlene and her colleagues may see themselves as beating the patriarchy but they're actually joining it, a point that's made in cartoon style when a young woman presents herself for an interview so intent on coming off like a brash young man that she practically is one. Here, more than anywhere, I missed the pace and poise of the original production.

This version surpasses the original, though, when it gets to the last scene, a squaring-off between Marlene and her sister Joyce. Some of their domestic differences seem to have been fetched up from old theatrical stock, and the way in which their political opposition is framed--one is rabidly pro-Thatcher, the other virulently anti -- now sounds dated. (It actually seemed simplistic at the time: not the issues, but the reduction to personalities. To be fair, I think the plays aware of that.) But the actresses, Follows and Fox, ride right over the limitations; playing consummately with and against one another, they give us the authentic feel of fury. Foxs triptych of roles -- taking in braw comedy, worried concern and outright blazing anger -- is one of the evening's triumphs, a magnificent performer handing out everything she's got. Repo-Martell is also especially fine when her Dull Gret gets reincarnated as Angie, the sullen and bewildered teenager who becomes a self-elected battleground for the sisters. Joyce brought her up but shes infatuated with Marlene and her world. Unfortunately, theres no place for her in that world, as Marlene herself brutally points out, plenty of children are getting left behind. The point, a good one if less than cataclysmic, is lightly made within the play's kaleidoscopic pattern, then driven home in a later scene that's chronologically earlier. The plays technical insouciance once made it seem like a masterpiece. It doesnt any more, but it still counts for a lot.

- Top Girls runs through Aug. 4 at the Young Centre for the Performing Arts. Call 416-866-8666 for details.

STRATFORD, Ont. - Friends, family and members of Canadas theatre royalty gathered in Stratford for the funeral of legendary actor William Hutt Monday, cramming into the pews to pay their respects.

The word on everybody's lips was "generosity". It cropped up equally in the speeches and tributes that formed part of the service itself, and in the informal reminiscences of the relatives, colleagues, admirers, friends and fellow Stratford citizens gathered outside the church waiting for the doors to open.

Stratford's St. James Anglican Church, which holds about 500, had 15 rows of pews designated for friends of Hutt.

Hutt, who died last Wednesday at 87, was universally recognised as Canadas greatest actor, certainly the greatest to have devoted his life to the theatre of his native country. He was in the Stratford Festivals first season in 1953, and spent most of the rest of his career there.

Albert Schultz of Toronto's Soulpepper Theatre - who gained formative experience acting alongside Hutt at Stratford and went on to direct him in some of his finest performances - spoke of Hutt's grace and courage in his last days when greeting those who had come to his house to pay their last respects.

Reminiscing about Hutts love of good food and drink, he said, "He taught me how to mix a Martini, he tried to teach me how to drink it."

Schultz also paid tribute to Hutt the actor: He moved me to such deep delight and such deep tears. His legacy will never be matched.

Richard Monette, Stratfords outgoing artistic director, read from a sermon on the subject of death by George Herbert, the 17th-century poet and clergyman. It was one that Hutt himself had often read - a text almost forbidding mourning: "Speak to me in an easy way. Laugh as we always laughed at the little jokes we enjoyed together. Let my name be ever the household word." And - in words that might have been coined for Hutt's contribution to Canadian theatre - there is absolute continuity. All is well.

Peter Hutt, Hutt's nephew and an actor in his own right, paid emotional tribute to a 40-year friendship whose "beginning was the advent of my thinking life." Acting with the legend was nothing less than sublime, he said. Voicing everybodys thoughts, he added that he had believed "Billy would outlive us all."

Martha Henry, who made her Stratford debut in 1962 as Hutts daughter in The Tempest, quoted a speech from Eugene O'Neill's Long Days Journey into Night in which, years later, she had played his wife. Referring to her first meeting with Hutt, she said, that was 45 years ago and weve loved each other ever since.

As expected, Hutt's funeral was attended by Canadian, and especially Stratford, theatre royalty. Along with Monette and Henry, dozens paid their respects including Fiona Reid, Seana McKenna and Peter Donaldson.

---- The festival's general director, Antoni Cimolino attended. There were also representatives of Ontarios other major classical companies, including Jackie Maxwell, director of the Shaw Festival, and her predecessor, Christopher Newton.

Former Stratford artistic director Robin Phillips delivered the eulogy, speaking of how Hutts miraculous voice had provided a conduit for Shakespeare's imagination.

He also insisted that Hutt devoted himself more than any other man to his country's cultural development.

The phrase "the theatrical community" can be glibly overused, but on Monday's hot afternoon it genuinely existed, in memory of a man and and an actor whose legacy, as Schultz accurately said, "will never be matched."
2007-07-12-fate-s-hand-is-gentle-in-stei:
The Stratford production of John Stein-beck's Of Mice and Men begins beautifully as a bucolic fable, with vagrant workers George and Lennie caught as in a snapshot, washing themselves by a riverbank in practically the last peaceful moment either of them is to know. The end of the play will find them back in the same spot, with Lennie, the simple, mouse-crushing giant, about to be shot by the friend and protector who feels compelled to kill him rather than stand by and see him lynched.

George and Lennie have reached the end of a long, ineluctable line. Martha Henry's production captures the sense of fate that traps a stageful of men, and one woman, victims alike of their own natures and of the Great Depression. It does so, though, in excessively gentle fashion, and certainly with less power than was unleashed in last year's CanStage production at the Bluma Appel Theatre, though it may well be the case that Of Mice and Men is simply not a play that one should see twice in quick succession; its insights, psychological and sociological, aren't that transfixing. And though its narrative is beautifully, inexorably structured, you may need time to forget it before succumbing to it again.

The rolling, golden cornfield sets of the CanStage production are missed, though they would hardly be practicable on the Tom Patterson stage. John Pennoyer, much aided by Bonnie Beecher's dappled lights, does a more modest but still evocative job on the great outdoors and a solid one on the bunkhouse and barn that house most of the action. It's more than unfortunate, though, that the play's most crucial scene--an accidental catastrophe that begets more catastrophe -- should be given a staging that's triply remote: on top of a platform, at one end of the stage and behind a rail.

The performances are rather remote, as well: accurate, but faint. Graham Greene's hulking Lennie, the man who kills the things he hugs, is powerful and somewhat affecting, but he seems to be existing on an island of his own. There is little sense of the binding comradeship he has with George, or of their touching dependence on one another. In George's case, the dependence is liberally laced with exasperation, but the impatience shouldn't blot out everything else. In Nicolas Van Burek's performance, surly and explanatory, it does. The bunkhouse crew have flavour, but it's damped down. Jerry Franken is endearingly gnarled as Candy, the crippled oldster who buys into George and Lennie's dream of buying their own farm somewhere, but the scene in which his buddies bully him into letting them kill his mangy old dog is surprisingly lacking in tension.

The presence of Franken, one of the original actors in The Drawer Boy, does, though, make one wonder how much Michael Healey's play owes to Of Mice and Men. Both plays have as their central device a clever man repeatedly telling a life-preserving story to a simple man who has heard it a hundred times before and wants to hear it a hundred times more.

Stephen Russell, though rather mature for the role, is a sympathetic authority figure as Slim, the foreman, and Brian Hamman a magnetically unsympathetic one as Curly, who's the boss's son and doesn't care who knows it. The role of Curly's wife is the one point at which the Stratford production decisively beats last year's Toronto one. The CanStage actress played her as if through the eyes of the men in the play, as a piece of arrant jailbait. Jennifer Mawhinney, though no less sexual, grants her a trapped, vulnerable identity of her own. - In repertory through Sept. 22. Call 1-800- 567-1600 for tickets.
2007-07-14-dreams-come-true-against-all-:
William Saroyan's The Time of Your Life is a play that's impossible not to love, one that sends you out of the theatre with the heady sensation of wishing you had written it yourself. Soulpeppers production is one of the best things the company has done, certainly its finest new achievement since setting up shop in the Distillery. Written in the perilous year of 1939, and set in a San Francisco honky-tonk, the play presents a crowded stageful of American dreamers and, while fully acknowledging the odds against it happening, shows most of their dreams coming true. One of its minor but defining characters is Harry, an aspiring hoofer and comedian, played here by Jeff Lillico, a young actor whose stature increases by -- literally in this case -- leaps and bounds. After unrolling a stream-of-consciousness routine thats plainly ahead of its time, Harry declares I'm funny -- but they don't laugh." This line, in its blend of pride and frustration, just about sums up the plays view of the human condition. It also, to make the bitter even more sweetly ironic, garners the biggest laugh of the evening, a moment that doesnt so much rock the house as bond it.

Saroyan, the program tells us, died saying "I thought they would make an exception for me and the play's optimism seems, on the surface, just as unreal. It presents a world in which whores and innocents can find true love, preferably with one another (but then in Saroyan's world the whores are innocents) and in which strikers and strike-breakers lie down together like lions and lambs. The one unsympathetic character is an officious sadist from the vice squad, and when he gets struck down everybodys happy. At roughly the same time, a pinball freak whos been playing the machine the whole length of the play finally succeeds in making the Stars and Stripes pop up on it. This, the play implies, is how things should be; America should be standing up against Hitler, who in this perspective is a vice cop writ large. Saroyan knew something about genocidal tyrannies; his family was Armenian.

Large-cast plays set in bars traditionally inspire great ensemble work, and so it is here. They can also become merry whirls, an option that Albert Schultz's production, though rich in comedy, steadfastly refuses to take. It moves at a measured pace and a subdued volume that are initially disconcerting but gather increasing force, providing breathing-space for everybody and everything. Actors perform duologue scenes while those not involved but still on stage go into suspended animation, giving the whole thing, on Lorenzo Savoini's spare and mellow set, the look and feel of a genre-painting.

The play seems to be taking its tone and tempo from its central figure, a philosophical philanthropist named Joe. Joe spends his days and nights drinking champagne (a unique tipple among the habitues of this particular saloon) at a corner table, buying newspapers by the batch but not reading them, sending out for whatever takes his fancy and performing acts of random kindness. Joseph Zieglers Joe is another in his line of terrifyingly good performances, sad and witty and gentle, delightedly inquisitive about his fellowmen while personally unreachable, authoritative, even when sitting hunched over and moving with appropriate stiffness on the rare occasions he gets up. Joes attitude to the American Way is, like the play's, ambiguous; he takes great delight in such profitable national icons as toys, guns and chewing gum, while feeling guilty over the pile he himself has made from robbing the poor -- not, one suspects, illegally. There seems also to be a broken heart in his past, as he shares with a sympathetic stranger (Jennifer Villaverde) his memories of the woman he never married and his dreams of the children they never had -- the third one was my favourite." This is the most magical scene currently on the Toronto stage. The second most magical has Ziegler challenging Kevin Bundy's wholly delightful Tom, his protege and gofer, as to which of them can chew the most sticks of gum at one time. The contest, which coincides with major plot developments, is refereed by Stuart Hughes giving the performance of his life as a moccasined yarn-spinner, quick on the draw and slow on the drawl, whose most outrageous yarn is true.

The bar boasts a second guardian angel in the unlikely shape of its proprietor Nick, whom Derek Boyes makes likeable but too obviously soft-shelled. There are lesser roles, too, where the texture turns soggy: Oliver Dennis, too emphatically sententious as a cop with a conscience, and Martha MacIsaac, too emphatically tearful as an incipient war widow. Patricia Fagan, though, cuts sentimentality triumphantly off at the pass, being moving and even believable as the tart with a heart.

The text calls for a great deal of music, on mouth-organ or jukebox, and the production, as beautifully orchestrated aurally as visibly, picks him up on this and raises the stakes on piano. Jazz singer Denzel Sinclaire, making a good acting debut as a vagrant with an unexpected gift, does the playing; he also gets to sing Little Girl Blue, something that Saroyan didnt think of but should have done Everybody wants a job at Nicks; a newsboy (Benjamin Head) breaks out into When Irish Eyes Are Smiling, and gets a hand if not an engagement. More seasoned actors adorn some of the tiniest roles: John Jarvis and Jane Spidell as a pair of society slummers, and William Webster and Les Carlson as a pair of drunks. Webster has the play's first line: "This is a free country -- isn't it? The plays answer is an emphatic yes, with reverberating reservations. There can hardly be a Joe to look after every saloon in the land, and he makes a mysterious exit from this one, leaving behind him an air of hopeful melancholy. In his lyrics to Zip, from Pal Joey, Lorenz Hart asked, "Will Saroyan ever write a great play?" That was in 1940. On this showing, it's clear he already had.

2007-07-21-a-hip-hop-catfight-in-highpar:
Note: A Midsummer Night's Dream runs through Sept. 2 at the Dream in High Park. Call 416-367-1652 for information.

The Dream in High Park, presented annually by CanStage, is the dean of our alfresco Shakespeare theatres. It's a responsibility that weighs unusually heavy this summer, owing to the disappearance of the local competition. Shakespeare in the Rough has suspended operations, ShakespeareWorks seems to have died of shame, and Oakville's Festival of Classics has had its plug pulled. Barrie's Theatre by the Bay and Newmarket's Resurgence Company are both mounting programs devoid of Shakespeare, unless you count Resurgence's inclusion of a one-man Hamlet already seen elsewhere. The painful part of all this is that most of these organizations have in recent years maintained higher standards than high-profile High Park, where a populist policy too often translates into a slapdash product.

That's what we get this year with A Midsummer Night's Dream, directed by ahdri zhina mandela. It's been puffed as a Caribana or hip-hop Dream, but that's just noisy topdressing; what's underneath is formless and anonymous, dependent on the individual actors' highly variable skills. For all its popularity -- this is the sixth Dream in High Park since the whole thing started in 1983 -- is an appallingly difficult play whose three worlds of lovers, fairies and clowns have a habit of wandering aimlessly off in their own directions. This is especially likely in an open-air show where the absence of lighting, at least for the first half of an evening, tends to flatten everything out. The Dream is usually thought of as the ultimate pastorale, but if those scholars are right who think that it was first written as a kind of nuptial cabaret, it could be one of the few Shakespeare plays that was meant to be played indoors.

I sometimes pray to get to the end of just one year without having to see a production of A Midsummer Night's Dream. This, of course, means I'm jaded. The better part of me believes that A Midsummer Night's Dream is as great a play as ever was written, and every so often that better part gets fortified by productions that serve it up whole, fresh and alive. Kate Lynch's all-female interpretation at Theatre Passe Muraille was one, Miles Potter's conventional but consistently intelligent version in Oakville another, and David Ferry's uproarious staging last year in Newmarket a third.

The best of the current High Park performances is in fact inherited from that third show. This is Maev Beaty's Helena, an earnest beanpole (she carries a yoga-mat around and executes a sun-salute in her first soliloquy), careering like a weather-vane from self-abasing to self-righteous and throwing her heart and soul into both extremes. Holly Lewis's Hermia, a miniature termagant, is an effective foil for her, and the two of them put up a good cat fight. Their male counterparts go, as usual, for less: Richard Harte is a vigorous Demetrius but Antonio Cayonne, a first-time actor, brings from his other life as an oral poet a trick of trying Lysander's lines out in different word-orders before hitting on the right one. ("The course of true love never did run smooth" is subjected to especially prolonged torture.) This elaborate speech-impediment may be the dumbest comic idea a Shakespeare production has ever come up with. The one thing you don't want to do in these plays is stop the language in its tracks.

This production, in its different departments and in various modes, does it all the time. The fairies are just pushy, right down to the singing girl-group of Peaseblossom, Cobweb and Mustardseed, intoning their lines in chorus while destroying their sense. Kevin Hanchard's Oberon does make sense, but it's a crabbed, ungiving kind of sense, aiming possibly at sinister but getting off at morose. Karen Robinson, an excellent dramatic actress but not exactly light of touch, is a monstrously coy and overbearing Titania. She does better as her mortal doppelganger, Hippolyta, progressively asserting herself over Hanchard's Theseus to the extent of pinching some of his best lines. Maybe it's a blow for feminism.

And so, perhaps, is the transformation of two of the hard-handed men who put on the play of Pyramus and Thisbe into hard-handed women. It totally disregards, of course, the fact that male camaraderie has a different tonality from male-female and that the scenes are written the first way. It also makes nonsense of Francis Flute the bellows-mender (still male) being cast as Thisbe; why would he be, when there are real women available? The mechanicals' rehearsal scenes are as juiceless as I have ever known them. Their actual performance begins with a rap treatment of the prologue, which is at least ear-catching, but it runs out of ideas afterwards. Steven Gallagher's Peter Quince, played as a young and earnest amateur director, is moderately delightful, but Matthew Kabwe's Bottom is short on personality and shorter still on humour, resulting in a sizeable portion of the play getting lost in the woods. There is a tail attached to Bottom's bottom in his transformation scene--a first, I think--but he hasn't been granted much of an ass's head, maybe because no mortal headpiece could compete with some of the things that seem to be growing out of the fairies' skulls, especially Oberon's.

Sarah Dodd's Moonshine has a nice moment when she loses it and seems about to attack the spectators with her lantern; she doubles as Egeus, whom she tries very hard to make funny, maybe to make up for a lack of laughs elsewhere. Whatever, turning Hermia's father into Hermia's mother makes hay of the play's sexual politics; the point, well brought out in the Lynch production, is that she's oppressed by men.

Cut to the end: Colin Heath, a formidably acrobatic Puck who's also been acting agreeably, has to deliver his valediction -- an actor-audience moment if ever there was one -- surrounded by the rest of the cast screeching and cavorting. It's the show's crowning moment of tone-deafness.

2007-07-23-genesis-of-blanche-dubois-sum:
SUMMER AND SMOKE

Royal George Theatre, Niagara-on-the-Lake, Ont.

---

Tennessee Williams' Summer and Smoke contains as much pointed or lyrical or funny writing as any of his plays, but it lacks a driving force. It's the neglected elder sister to A Streetcar Named Desire; they were written more or less simultaneously, around 1945, but Streetcar got to Broadway sooner and became first the hit and then the classic. It's the stronger play, but there is a chronological irony in its having been the first to arrive at the ball. Streetcar is, in some sense, the sequel to Summer and Smoke: not a literal or immediate sequel -- Streetcar takes place just after the Second World War and Summer just before the first one--but a spiritual and psychological one.

More specifically, Alma Winemiller, the heroine of Summer and Smoke, suggests what Blanche DuBois might have been like before she went off the rails (or the trolley tracks). The play concludes with Alma taking the first step toward becoming Blanche by picking up a newly arrived travelling salesman, in emulation of the town tramp -- the town in this case being Glorious Hill, Miss.

Up until then, Alma has been the picture of cultured propriety. The daughter of a minister, she runs the town literary society and is a singing teacher by profession. (Blanche was a teacher, too.) Her name, as she makes sure everybody knows, is the Spanish word for "soul," and love for her means finding a soul mate.

Ever since childhood, though, she has been fascinated by John, the boy next door, a doctor and the son of a doctor, whose philosophy is strictly materialist and whose notions of affection are notoriously physical. Halfway through the play he makes a pass at her, which she rejects. The rest of the evening shows both of them changing, passing one another -- I hate to say like ships in the night, but it's unavoidable -- and ending up, or so we are meant to believe, in one another's former places.

Alma is in some ways a more interesting character than Blanche. She's more obviously intelligent, sharper-tongued and less of a poseuse, and she presents us with a process rather than a result. At the Shaw Festival, she's magnetically played by Nicole Underhay, who manages to be convincingly vibrant and convincingly repressed, not just by turns but at the same time. Which is the essence of Alma: She has something to repress, something fierce. The things she doesn't have, that Blanche does, are a compelling narrative and a worthy antagonist.

It isn't that Summer and Smoke lacks structure. It's loaded with it, indeed loaded down with it. There are two matching acts: a summery one in which passions begin to flare and a wintry one in which they are cruelly doused. And, of course, there are two matching principals with opposing principles. John, though, both in the writing and here in the performance, is a shadow, though a very loquacious one. Unlike Stanley Kowalski, he comes out of no recognizable social or family background; he's just the idea of a debauchee, with the details of his debauches left conveniently vague. He claims by the end of the play to have come around to Alma's side, but the evidence -- he's getting married and taking his doctoring seriously -- remains strictly theoretical. Jeff Meadows, looking goofy and acting stolidly, can do nothing to bring him to life, and for all that Underhay can bring -- she's especially fine at conveying agonized disappointment, nobly borne but with a sardonic edge -- their scenes together, which take up much of the play, begin to drag horribly.

The director, Neil Munro, hasn't helped by cutting the play's prologue, which shows us the hero and heroine as children and sets up their relationship for the rest of the play. (Or are we using different texts?) This means that in the later scenes, ghostly childish voices that we don't recognize keep referring us back to things that we haven't been told about.

The production overall has a moody, broody quality that holds promise for the first 10 minutes but then declines into sluggishness. It also looks gloomier than Williams -- who knew about atmosphere if he knew about anything -- seems to have intended, with Peter Hartwell's harsh-looking set mostly suffused, courtesy of Alan Brodie's lighting, in dark leaf patterns. It's all right for the town square, but most of the action takes place in John's and Alma's adjacent houses, which here have a perplexing habit of encroaching on one another's territory. They are also full of lace curtains that the actors unaccountably keep hiding behind. This staging plays hell with a crucial plot development that's confusing enough in the first place: the shooting of a character we know little about by another of whom we know less.

There are some excellent supporting performances. Sharry Flett is outstanding as Alma's mother, who has driven her further into herself by declining into a premature senility in which mischievous irresponsibility is hard to distinguish from outright malevolence. Peter Hutt is fine as her clerical spouse, ostentatiously long- suffering. Guy Bannerman is good as his medical neighbour and counterpart, and Brigitte Robinson and Melanie Janzen are delightful as contrasting pillars of Alma's poetry circle; that old-time gentility, censorious or timed, is very economically summoned. Jonathan Gould brings up the play's rear with surprising sweetness as the visiting fireman who may be setting Alma on the road to ruin. Unless it's the other way around. - In repertoire through Oct. 27. For info, call 1-800-511-SHAW.

2007-07-27-playgirl-of-the-western-world:
Lady Augusta Gregory was a natural-born playwright. That's the revelation of this year's Shaw Festival lunchtime show, a double bill of her plays (she wrote short) under the umbrella title of The Kiltartan Comedies. Kiltartan, Scottish though it sounds, is in Galway, Ireland, and was the country seat of the lady's husband, a member of parliament and former governor of Ceylon. She figures in text-books as the co-founder, with W.B. Yeats, of Dublin's Abbey Theatre, the house that, beginning in 1904, made modern Irish drama possible. The books also say that she contributed importantly to that drama herself, but we've seldom had the chance to judge for ourselves on stage. Our loss; but now, our gain.

Of course, she wrote rich dialogue; she was Irish, wasn't she? (Anglo-Irish actually. And Protestant. And conflicted.) Unlike some of her compatriots, though, she didn't let her pen or her characters' tongues run away with her. She had a firm narrative sense and also a spatial one, too. She wrote pictures as well as words. The abiding image from The Rising of the Moon, the first and stronger of the Niagara duo, is of two men sitting back to back on top of a barrel, to which a reward notice has been posted. One of them is a police sergeant, nervously watching the coastline for a Home Rule agitator -- we are in the early, and comparatively benign, days of the Troubles -- thought to be very dangerous. The other is a ragged ballad-vendor whose presence makes the sergeant even more uneasy, but whose absence might be worse. It's obvious to the audience that the balladeer is in fact the wanted man, and it is eventually made clear to the sergeant as well. The question becomes, will the policeman let the man go or turn him in and claim the 100 bounty --equal, the program tells us, to $18,000 of today's money? On the one hand there is the cash, plus his professional duty. On the other, since, of course, he

himself is Irish, there is the memory, craftily played upon by his musical antagonist, of the yearning patriotic songs the sergeant heard and sung in his youth, and of all they stand for. He makes his choice, but the play's last line finds him still exquisitely uncertain of whether it was the right one.

Douglas E. Hughes delivers this character beautifully, crowning a delightful performance of a man beset by doubts and fears, trying to be inflexible. Patrick Mc-Manus confirms the promise held out by his Dunois in Saint Joan of being a first-rate romantic actor, whimsical and dangerous. He also sings like a bird. Harry Judge and Andrew Bunker complete the cast as a couple of raw, embarrassingly conscientious constables. The comedy in the play helps build the suspense, allowing Micheline Chevrier's production to be both tense and relaxed

Spreading the News, the second play, is a more conventional rural comedy, about the multiplying power of rumour. A minor altercation at a fair grows, by the time the story has been told at second-and third-and fourth-hand, into a full-blown case of murder with an agricultural implement. Not even the reappearance of the supposedly dead man can quite halt the villagers' suspicions; they believe in ghosts. The play covers some of the same ground as one of the Abbey's most famous products, The Playboy of the Western World, and it's hard not to feel that it does it far more economically. You may get a little tired of a stage full of simpletons, no matter how gloriously they talk or how wildly they fantasize, but this play, too, has a political sting. Its authority figure is an English magistrate (Douglas Hughes again, in contrastingly complacent mode) confident that he can untie the local Gordian knot with the same unflinching methods he used in other colonies. We end with the prospect of the imaginary opponents about to be consigned to the same real holding cell, there to beat the real daylights out of one another. And, of course, rhapsodizing about it. A ripe and ready team of locals include Mary Haney as an apple seller whose deafness is part of the problem and nothing of the solution, Guy Bannerman looking forward with some reason to another unlucky day, and Tara Rosling as his formidable wife. (She looks more like his daughter and acts more like his mother, which may be the point; these men are babies, whatever the chronology.) Maybe the Shaw could offer us another double bill, combining one of Lady Gregory's plays with one by her professional partner, Yeats, whose dramatic works are, because of the poet's non-dramatic prestige, better regarded and more often revived. I'll bet the lady would come out on top. - In repertory until Oct. 6. For more informaton, call 1-800-511-SHAW.

2007-07-28-you-were-poked-by-second-city:
The new Second City revue, Facebook of Revelations, begins in time-honoured fashion with a musical number. Second City programs never list the titles of anything, be it sketch or song, but I think we can take it that this opener is called Safe Bet: The Musical. It's a spoof of all the We Will Rock You-Mamma Mia shows that hang "songs you already know" on the thinnest or most pretentious of storylines. (Sometimes on both.) Every cliche of the genre is in place, paraded at whistle-stop speed. It's a joke that needed to be made, and the six Second City writer-performers make it very well.

They then start taking swipes at environmentalism, both outside (a sketch about a road trip) and in (a scene about a dinner party). God knows, environmental self-righteousness, like any other kind of self-righteousness, is a ripe subject for satire. And the Second Citizens, who are probably satirizing themselves, seem prepared to take it to the limit; the second item has a very tough finish. The scenes, though, are cleverer than they are funny, and this turns out to be a problem with the entire first half of the show, culminating in an extended routine, largely mimed, about a baseball rookie whose beaming incompetence brings colleagues, fans, and even the team mascot on to the field in protest. I'd probably find it more hilarious if I knew or cared more about baseball, but I can see that it's very well done. Still, after the sustained and no less acute hilarity of the last two Second City shows, this one is a letdown.

Things improve considerably after the intermission; it can't just have been that by that point I'd had more to drink. Marital breakups and Afghanistan are beautifully skewered-- both, remarkably, in the same number. Dad, trying desperately to explain to the children over breakfast, why Mom is no longer around without actually saying a word against her (he does drop his guard to the extent of saying, ruefully "oh, yes, Mommy yells"), tells them she has gone Over There and embarks on a wonderful non-stop rodomontade about our conflicted reasons for being There in the first place and the probable outcome of same. It's like Tony Kushner's play Homebody/ Kabul only much, much shorter; and, I'm inclined to think, better. As a bonus, we get the sight of two full-grown actors (very full, in one case) getting to play the kids whose moods swing between terror and oblivion, tearful and cheerful.

And then, there is a number about two screw-sorting robots who fall in love with one another on the job. (According to the male robot, you can tell how a female is going to age by looking at her motherboard.) The idea isn't the newest in the world but it's done here with great invention and finesse, and is even a little moving; the lady robot asks her minder please not to erase her memory for the day, and is greeted with a bland, patronizing "Whatever would you want that for?" So, what we have just seen must happen every day. Talk about bittersweet. It seems appropriate that this sketch should be followed immediately by one about human office workers who behave like robots. They are planning to murder their boss. He doesn't seem to have done anything to deserve it. But you know how people are once they get an idea in their heads.

The star performer here (and a veteran of those two great predecessor revues, Bird Flu Over the Cuckoo's Nest and Tip of the Melting Iceberg, is Lauren Ash. Only she isn't so much a star as a terrific featured player who has honed her talents to the finest edge. Dark-haired and comfortable-looking, she does everything with razor-sharp economy, whether playing a love-sick computer, a homicidal drone or a pharmacist censoriously refusing to dispense a morning-after pill. Ash does grievance very well indeed. Jim Annan, another Second City familiar -- short, fair and maniacal -- doesn't have enough to do, but is always welcome when doing it. He has his best moments here when lurking on the fringes. Scott Montgomery is a tall guy with a gift of the non-stop gab, some of his tirades being scripted (the Afghan one), others seeming at least partly improvised. Marty Adams is the most prominent newcomer, if only because of his pronounced chubbiness. He is both the coy male robot and the rambunctious child performing prodigies of slow-motion naughtiness, but his finest hour comes as an oleaginous call-in host who never gets any calls. Except tonight, when members of the audience are drafted to play the callers, thereby imposing on the cast the necessity of being somewhat spontaneous. (Even if they already know where they're going, they have to work out how to get there.) This is one of the best-conceived items in the evening. Darryl Hinds and Karen Parker both have their moments, but have some way to go The show's title declares itself in a gospellish closing number whose theme is "Jesus wants you in his facebook." It returns us to the realm of bright ideas that don't really go anywhere, but it's enthusiastically put over by the ensemble and it sends us away reasonably happy.

- Facebook of Revelations runs indefinitely at the Second City. Cal 416-343-0011 for details.

2007-08-03-a-tale-of-old-billy-the-bard:
Few things set my teeth more sharply on edge than the sound of people talking about "Bill Shakespeare." There's a full dose of it in Shakespeare's Will, a one-woman play in which the person doing the talking is Anne Hathaway, the poet's wife or, when we meet her, his widow. Generally, when Shakespeare is "Billified," the intention is to take him down a peg. That doesn't seem to be what Anne has in mind, but the diminutive is so jarringly anachronistic that it comes out that way anyway. Why can't she call him Will, as anyone else of her generation would have done? Especially as there's an unexploded pun on that name in the play's title and in its basic situation: Anne reminiscing while waiting to read her late mate's final testament. He didn't leave any debts. If he had, the play might have been called Shakespeare's Bill.

Nobody would want or expect Vern Thiessen, Anne's ghostwriter, to write a whole play in 17th-century pastiche. What one hopes for, as with any historical piece that isn't aggressively agenda driven, is language that keeps faith both with its imagined period and with ours. And that, apart from that one oft-repeated lapse, is what Thiessen offers us. This is a perfectly intelligent, decently written play. It still strikes me as pointless: an example of drama once-removed. Miles Potter, who directs it, says in his program note that "you could change the character's name and you'd still have a good play." But that's disingenuous. The only reason that anyone's interested in Anne Hathaway is because of whom she married. Unfortunately, the one thing we know about that marriage is that we don't know very much. She was eight years older than he was; she was pregnant when they wed. They had three children in all, one of whom died young. He left their native Stratford-on-Avon for London, where he had a successful career as actor, playwright and theatrical shareholder. He returned home in his last years, and he bequeathed his wife -- notoriously -- their second-best bed (with, to be fair, all the trimmings). That's all. The play is scrupulous

about not adding to it.

Such inventions as it comes up with are concerned with Anne alone. But we can't buy the play as the dreams of an everyday Elizabethan housewife, because our awareness of who her husband was hangs immovably around the evening's neck.

What did she think of him? Thiessen hazards a few guesses: that she was more experienced than he was and more amused by him as a lover than impressed; that his family background (including its presumed Catholicism) appalled her father; that she suspected, and somewhat resented, his bisexuality; that they had an open marriage, of which she took full advantage during his long absence; that she wasn't best pleased by the noisy, boozy friends (including, surprisingly, Francis Bacon) he brought back from the capital; that she heartily disliked her spinster sister-in-law, Joan. What -- the really compelling question -- did she think of his plays? We can't be told, because probably she never saw any of them. To do so, she would have had to travel to London, and there is no reason to believe that she ever did. (The play suggests that Shakespeare actively discouraged her.) Conceivably she wasn't interested, which would be interesting in itself, but which isn't explored. What did he think of his work? What, especially while away, did he think of her? She doesn't know, so neither can we. It's a hell of a hole.

The play tries to fill it by having Anne tell us things about herself that could be equally true of any woman: that she liked the sea (this is by way of being a leitmotif

), that she liked men, and that she was devastated by the death of her son Hamnet, a death for which the author has a wholly new explanation. We are told that Will himself was cut up by it, too, to the extent of not being able to visit the boy's grave. Much is made of his having been named after an old Stratford friend of Shakespeare, Hamnet Sadler. Nothing is made of the haunting question: How could his father, not so many years later, have brought himself to write a play whose hero had an almost identical name? Wouldn't the mere act of writing out that name so many times have burned up his quill? Did it function as an act of exorcism, or was it a case of the artist's proverbial heartlessness? And wouldn't Anne have heard about it somehow?

Germaine Greer has a book coming out about Anne Hathaway that, she says, proclaims the marriage to have been happy and Anne to have been practically Shakespeare's muse. I don't see where the evidence can come from, but then I can't see much evidence to the contrary, either. The trajectory Thiessen presents -- a canny but trusting woman fighting off disillusion, but finally thrust into it --makes sense on its own terms, but the development is sketchy. But there's enough to enable Seana McKenna to shine. The production has her going up and down a flight of steps more often than seems necessary, but she is completely in command of her own highs and lows. She encompasses roguishness, sensuality, wit --both defensive and aggressive -- and scalding pain, neither underplaying nor overdoing. The performance may justify the choice of play: You will know, coming out, that McKenna is a superlative actress. But you probably knew that going in as well. - In repertory through to Sept. 20. For more information, call 1-800-567-1600 or visit Stratford-festival. ca.

2007-08-04-a-stitch-in-time-makes-nine-s:
Soulpepper, Albert Schultz reminded me, will be 10 years old next July. Its a decade since the classical theatre collective of which he is the artistic director (there's a contradiction in there somewhere but I don't think it matters) astounded us all with its production of Schillers Don Carlos, a 200-year-old play that nobody in Canada had ever seen. Since then, the company has become a vital part of the landscape. Its hard, depending on your angle of vision, to believe that it has been around such a short time or that it has survived so long.

And, of course, after eight inaugural seasons at Harbourfront, Soulpepper is now in its second year on its own premises in the Distillery District. When I met with Schultz this week in the pub down the cobbled street from the Young Centre, what was on my mind was not the upcoming anniversary but the current achievement. Soulpepper now has three productions running on its two major stages -- Top Girls in the smaller space, Our Town and The Time of Your Life rotating in the larger one -- and all are first-rate. I don't know of any other Toronto company that has ever achieved such a thing, or of one that could. What gives Soulpepper its edge and popularity is name-and-face recognition; broadly speaking, the people on stage are the organization. The core actors -- the dozen listed in the program as founder members, plus one or two others -- have, for the most part, stuck around. This kind of actor-based persistence in a main-stream company is very rare.

One factor in this is that Schultz himself, apart from blossoming as a director, also continues to act, more often these days than ever. He's currently in rehearsal in Chekhovs Three Sisters, directed by Laszlo Marton, the Hungarian who has already given Soulpepper some of its greatest productions including two other Chekhovs, Uncle Vanya and Platonov, and Ibsens The Wild Duck. The cast includes founding veterans like Diego Matamoros and others who have grown up within the company. Everybody knows one another, says Schultz. "That's the secret of this company, the driving force behind it. It's really exciting to be in a rehearsal room watching someone like Patricia Fagan, whom you spotted in theatre school and have seen grow every year, to see what shes doing, just a couple of weeks into rehearsal." A third layer of the cast contains the inaugural members of Soulpeppers Academy.

I've been with these people every day for 12 months. I've taught them, acted with them, directed them, made music with them -- theres not a single one of those 15 people I dont have a relationship with.

It helps to have your own building. "Joe Ziegler [actor, director and founding member] says that, when he walks into the front door of the Young Centre, he feels at home." Audiences, I think, feel the same, and I buy Schultz's statement that the company is richer and deeper because of its proximity to itself; all the operations are under one roof. That said, it's taken until now for Soulpepper to find its feet in its new surroundings. The companys two worst productions ever ( The Importance of Being Earnest and John Gabriel Borkman) have been here, and last years repertoire seemed lightweight, full of worthy but small-scale (and newish) plays. It can't be coincidence that this season, bigger and bolder, has also been better.

One thing Soulpepper has always had going for it is that in Toronto almost any classic is a rare classic; even Hamlet was the play's first major Toronto outing in decades. There are still areas that remain largely untouched: most of English-language drama before 1900 for example. Schultz wants "to explore the repertoire a bit more broadly"; he admits that the company has been nervous of Restoration comedy because none of us have any experience of it. Next year, though, they are mounting The Way of the World, directed by the National Arts Centres Peter Hinton, probably the most stylish director in Canada.

What else does Schultz dream about? "A bigger, 500-seat theatre across the street where we could put our successes." (That doesnt seem too likely.) I'd like to be able to tour internationally while still maintaining a 12-month repertoire at home. (Also difficult, but necessary. Soulpepper sometimes produces world-class work, and the world should see it.) "More money. We get the lowest urban subsidy of any company in the country. What I'm trying to avoid is either stuffing the repertoire with one-or-two-person shows or cutting down on rehearsal time. We do seven weeks average Thats what makes us what we are."

You cant, says Schultz, "put a bunch of actors together and expect them to be an ensemble." That's an exaggeration; ensemble has happened in ad hoc productions in Toronto, and in less concentrated circumstances at the Shaw and Stratford Festivals. And there have been Soulpepper productions full of good actors giving good performances but never amounting to more than the sum of those parts. But the higher mathematics of ensemble has occurred gratifyingly often: in Marton's Ibsen and Chekhovs, in Schultzs own productions of Ayckbourn and Pinter and Saroyan, in Zieglers Our Town, right back to that initial Don Carlos directed by Robin Phillips. Play, actors and audience unite in understanding -- the manifestation in performance of the unifying Schultz identifies in the best rehearsals: "an incredible amount of shorthand."

2007-08-10-junkyard-homer-lays-waste-to-:
Studio Theatre, Stratford, Ont.

In Woody Allen's Stardust Memories, an admirer of the artist- director contemplates his swish automobile and says, "I think it symbolizes the authors car." In Peter Hintons wondrous production of The Odyssey, a vandalized and dilapidated car occupies the centre of the stage, and it symbolizes practically everything. At the start it's both the sacked city of Troy and the famous horse that brought about its downfall. When Odysseus sets off on his 10-year voyage home to Ithaca, it becomes his ship, with a mast pointing up from somewhere behind its trunk. Later, its sail unfurls to represent the shroud that his wife, Penelope, weaves to keep her suitors at bay.

The car even plays a car; at least, when Menelaus dispatches Odysseus' son Telemachus with a friendly "take my chariot," he tosses him the keys. With actors crouching and lurching behind its rain-soaked windshield, it provides a spectacular image for storms at sea. (Odysseus and his men spend a lot of time being tossed on the waves; that is, when they -- the men anyway -- arent being eaten like sheep by one-eyed monsters or turned into pigs by bright- eyed witches.) And there are times when the car functions simply as an intriguingly versatile acting space. When Nigel Shawn Williams Odysseus finally makes it home, dressed as a beggar, he encounters the faithful swineherd Eumaeus (Walter Borden). The two of them take shelter beneath the hood, sharing crusts and embittered observations and generally sounding one another out. It's a quietly amazing scene, magnificently played by both.

Obviously, this version of Homer's epic, first staged in England 15 years ago, crosses periods as well as countries. Its the work of Derek Walcott, the West Indian poet, and its principal inflection is Caribbean. Its Homeric substitute (powerfully rendered by Jeremiah Sparks) is a singer, Blind Billy Blue.

The text remains remarkably true to the structure of the original -- sometimes, with its flashbacks within flashbacks and its glancing allusions to the obscurer corners of myth, to the point of confusion. But the details are punched-up. Its man-eating Cyclops (Roy Lewis) is a dictator and Philistine and proud of it, from the period of the Colonels. This allusion, grimly funny as the episode is as a whole, is one of the few mistakes. Timelessness is one thing. Faded topicality is the opposite.

Conversely, when Odysseus descends into Hades, its delightful to find it modelled on the London Underground, with the hero's late mother (Joyce Campion) impatiently awaiting her train, handbag in hand.

Walcott ties the story together with constant references to, and even appearances by, Odysseus' former companions. Agamemnon, struggling in the fatal net, is, in this production, an unforgettable image. Odysseus young pilot Epenor is the haunting double of Telemachus (both played excellently by In-Surp Choi.) As for the theodicy

in The Odyssey: the goddess Athene makes periodic appearances, usually in disguise, and toward the end theres a brief but startling attempt to turn the ragged, mocked Odysseus into a Christ figure.

The first half of the show, depicting the wanderings, is endlessly inventive, but it's the second, the homecoming, that's the more powerful. A centred story will always be more dramatic than a picaresque one, and this one builds superbly to the drawing of Odysseus bow and the slaughter of the suitors, their hundred names called out as the same few actors fall obligingly dead, time after time, in an endless variety of poses. It doesnt get dull. The subsequent hanging of the maidservants, the most controversial passage in the poem, is mooted but never executed. It's left, so to speak, hanging; we await the modernized sequel, The Penelopiad, due in Ottawa next month.

Williams' Odysseus is a seven-league step forward for him as an actor: witty, lucid, anguished, commanding every moment of the play. The most heart-stopping of them all he shares with Barbara Barnes- Hopkins as the old nurse Eurycleia when she is the first to recognize him.

Allegra Fulton survives an initial brittleness to become a riven, independent Penelope. She also plays Circe and a delicious Helen who, post-Troy, has become a high-suburban hostess in a yellow pant- suit and stilettos. Steve Ross makes a strikingly insolent principal suitor, Sophia Walker does an alluring teenage princess, and Ian Deakin is bluffly likable in a string of roles.

The production is not so much multicultural as cross-cultural. Black and white actors throw themselves with equal enthusiasm and equal success into the shows alternating idioms. The wonders in Hintons staging hardly stop: great balls that drift down from above and turn into what look like balloons (though solid enough not to burst when people sit on them); the revelation, in Carolyn M. Smith's set design, that Ithaca, furnished with transparent Philippe Starck chairs and tables, was aeons ahead of its time; Robert Thomson's solid walls of light dividing the stage. Walcotts script is poised between celebration and requiem, as, come to think of it, is Homers, and the production honours both of them. It's a great ride. - In repertoire until Sept. 28.

2007-08-11-cuckoos-marriage-and-conrad-b:
Summerworks is a juried festival, which makes it surprising that something as awful as Fabuloso (Tarragon Mainspace) should turn up there. Not that juries aren't fallible, but at alternative theatrefests their mistakes are likelier to lie in the direction of earnestness and pretension.

Fabuloso, by the American John Kolvenbach, is blatantly commercial in every respect except its awkward 75-minute length. The show has received an unprecedented amount of hype due to the presence in the cast, after a long time away from the stage, of Nicholas Campbell. He has a few quiet moments here that are rather affecting, but most of the time he is shouting or gabbling or both. He plays one half of a frantically fractious engaged couple seen invading the home of another couple, married, whose relationship has reached an advanced state of stagnation. Or so we are told; we're asked to take an extraordinary amount on trust.

The husband and the male intruder are boyhood friends who haven't seen each other in years. The hosts, as the play all but comes out and says, accept their unruly guests as substitutes for the children whom, for reasons unexplored, they have never had. But there is no reality to either pair, and the play simply lurches from one scene to the next. Surest sign of a failed piece of theatre: The audience starts clapping just before the final scene, in the kind hope that it's all over.

Summerworks has another cuckoo-in-the-nest play, In Full Light, by young playwright Daniel Karasik.

A teenage girl is knocked down, injured but not killed, by a motorist who, oozing contrition, goes to the victim's mild-mannered father, proffers $6,000 in recompense, and will not be denied. Later he claims to have lost his job and his home and moves in with the family, eventually making off with the wife's jewels and (ambiguously) her affections.

Meanwhile, the daughter throws herself, violently, at the nervous bird-watching young man in the house opposite. It's even hinted that she too is a trickster, having invited the accident to attract his attention. This part of the play is as contrived and overwrought as its heroine. The other half, though, is excellent.

The intruder might be either a con man or an acute study in psychological need; the script keeps both options open and so, insidiously, does David Ferry's performance.

The best Summerworks play I saw was Paul Dunn's Offensive Shadows (Tarragon Extra Space), advertised as a sequel to A Midsummer Night's Dream.

It's also a prequel; we learn, in their own past-tense voices, what happened to Shakespeare's four lovers before he introduced us to them: Demetrius, a nerd, was engaged to Hermia before she met Lysander, a jock; Helena was always the wallflower. We then get a speedy run-down of their adventures in the woods, as they would have remembered them; then their adventures on a reunion picnic, five years after the whirlwind weddings with whose results they are now predictably but not hopelessly disillusioned.

Many productions of the Dream have discovered how close these characters are to modern teenagers; Dunn's very funny, and sometimes probing, script keeps that idiom going while cunningly recalling lines and themes from the original. Performances (Jessica Greenberg, Mark McGrinder, Jason Mitchell, Kimwun Perehinec) and direction (Michael Shamata) are pitch-perfect.

There's more past-tense narration (stuff is catching) in Hannah Moscovitch's Mexico City (Tarragon Extra Space), in which a married couple from 1960 tell us of their adventures in the titular town, finally breaking down and talking to each other when the local customs get to them. Brendan Gall (the birdman from In Full Light) and Molly Atkinson, who could be louder, are the actors.

It's a squib but expert and entertaining, especially by comparison with Yogyakarta, with which it shares a double-bill and which concerns revolution, hostage-taking and idealistic Canadian ignorance in Indonesia. Written by Alan Dilworth (in better form as director of Mexico City), it never gets beyond stating familiar positions. Its best feature is a slanting frame of a set, designed by Camellia Koo.

Another, slightly better, hostage-play, Martin Julien's Home Free (Factory Mainspace), also has a few ideas and no place to take them. "Inspired by, but not based on" last year's abduction of Christian pacifists in Iraq, it shows one captive's gay partner asking the authorities back in Canada to let him, and their relationship, play a more visible role in the rescue effort. The actors, especially Hume Baugh, do their best to personalize the characters, but they remain debating points --obscure ones.

I suppose these plays could be described as "political." But if political drama is to amount to anything, beyond making its perpetrators feel important, it has to offer more than the repackaging of stuff we can read in the papers.

It also has to mean more than making jokes about Conrad Black, though that's mostly what we got at Summerworks edition of The Wrecking Ball (Theatre Passe Muraille), whose formula is plays written on topical topics at a week's notice. The closing item, by Linda Griffiths, was titled Simply Black. But it turned out to be good: an imagining of its protagonist's reapplication for Canadian citizenship that worked as literary parody, as performance (David Ferry again, with Griffiths herself dark-glassed and silent as his lady) and as drama of some depth and ambiguity If it was a hatchet job, the hatchet was double-edged. Which is what political theatre, like any other kind of theatre, is supposed to be.
