2007-08-14-singing-and-dancing-at-death-:
Thomas Mann's short story Tristan has a delicate, fragile plot and a steely, ironic tone: a velvet fist in an iron glove. It tells of Gabrielle Kloterjahn, a rich merchant's wife who, in the early years of the 20th century, seeks treatment at an expensive Alpine spa for what turns out to be a case of TB. She attracts the attention of a fellow inmate, an author (of one book) named Detlev Spinell. Discovering that before her marriage she had played the piano, Spinell consructs a romantic fantasy of Gabrielle as an artistic princess snatched from her true vocation to become the wife of an unappreciative philistine and -- worse yet -- the mother of a rudely healthy child. Spinell is right about one thing: Gabrielle is a gifted pianist, as she proves when he inveigles her into playing selections from Tristan and Isolde. But the excitement brings on a fatal worsening of her condition.

Wagner's love music wreaks a subtler brand of aphrodisiac havoc in the story than it does in the opera. Physically, Mann's couple never come close. Their affair never happens, and is thus very hard to dramatize. It might perhaps work as a play of Chekhovian nuance, or as a chamber opera. The Shaw Festival's attempt has something of both, being a high-strung musical with a lot of dialogue. It's an honourable try, in which nobody's intelligence gets insulted; but the combination proves self-defeating. It's nearly an hour before there seems any reason for the show to be a musical at all.

Paul Sportelli and Jay Turvey take joint credit for the book, music and lyrics, though I imagine that Sportelli, the Shaw's musical director, is chiefly responsible for the sounds and Turvey, a long-serving Festival actor, for the words. The lyrics are sensitive and sensible, with a neat habit of cross-referencing one another -- though sometimes too audibly pleased with their own rhymes -- and the music has been excellently scored for a string quartet, just the right arrangement (or arrangements) for the tale's physical and emotional climate. It reaches an impressive height at the end of the first act when Jeff Madden's Spinell sings, thrillingly, of the One Face that has enthralled him. The title comes from a line in the original, but Mann's mordant dryness has been left a long way behind -- which might not matter if only the show were consistent about it.

Madden plays Spinell very well as a man who's dreamed of being in a romantic musical and thinks he's blundered into one. The show seems inclined to humour him, though it's hindered in this regard by Glynis Ranney's hausfrau Gabrielle, who obstinately refuses to radiate and who has been given songs that lower the musical tone from silvery post-Sondheim to leaden Lloyd Webber. Another obstacle is the lurking, unromantic spirit of Thomas Mann himself. When Spinell agonizes over a letter to Herr Kloterjahn, Mann observes, in words that must go straight to the heart of every scribbler, "a writer is a man who has a more difficult time writing than anyone else." That line, alas, has not found its way into the musical, but much of the subsequent confrontation between the two men is there, some of it spoken, some sung. It makes Spinell seem both naive and patronizing -- in short, insufferable. So he seems in the book, but the show then tries to rescue him. In the story, his principal antagonist is not Gabrielle's husband but their baby. This is obviously difficult to stage; the Shaw has already balked this season at casting 12-year-olds in Summer and Smoke, and a baby would certainly be pushing it. Spared this humiliating encounter, Spinell is able to emerge with some of his illusions intact, even -- something Mann never countenanced -- as the Tristan of his own imaginings.

You wouldn't think to go looking for musical-comedy energy in a supporting cast of sick people interspersed with the occasional hypochondriac, but the show does its best. A couple of characters have been invented; others have been enlarged from mere hints in the text. In theory, that's legitimate; in practice, it means that the central narrative gets crowded out. Mann has a single throwaway sentence about the sanatorium's housekeeper and her unrequited yearning for the doctor-in-charge. Here, their relationship is expanded so that it almost becomes a sub-plot but never quite makes it. A woman "with an ear disease" (Donna Belleville in a melodious reprise of her agreeably twittering performance from The Heiress) is elevated to a full-blown case of comic deafness. A retired general (a kindly performance by Neil Barclay) is also given jokes that don't work, along with regrets that do: A song called Happy, about the statistical improbability of ever being it, is one of the authors' best inventions.

But both the writing and Eda Holmes's direction are full of loose ends and unresolved opportunities. We're someway into the action before either of the leading characters gets a song (Gabrielle has actually been forbidden to sing, and the repressed Spinell hardly seems the type), so it ought to be a big deal when they do; in fact, it passes unnoticed. One patient (the dancing Jane Johanson) has been so traumatized that she can only utter the three words "isn't it strange." So what's she doing joining in a celebratory number about a sleigh ride -- a trip, incidentally, on which she isn't going? "Hey, it's a musical" really doesn't cut it. It is neat, though, that Isn't It Strange should be the title of Gabrielle's big song, and that Johanson should make a spectral appearance in it, just as she has made a celebratory one during the fateful piano recital. This involves a transparent, two-dimensional piano that lights up and wheels around the stage. That's nice, but it has nothing to do with the rest of Judith Bowden's design, which is lumpenly realistic, or with the production as a whole. - Tristan is in repertoire through Oct. 6. Call 1-800-511-SHAW for ticket information.

2007-08-18-more-of-the-same-but-that-s-o:
The new Cirque du Soleil production is called Kooza, which apparently is a Sanskrit word meaning both "box" and "treasure." According to the program, the show "tells the story of the Innocent, a naive but charming clown striving to find his own place in the world." We're also told that it's an attempt to take the Cirque back to its roots and to pay tribute to the spirit of the clown who "cajoles us into tenderness and paints our smiles into sweetness."

In fact, it's nothing like as bad as that sounds. Indeed it is, like most Cirque shows, rather wonderful. But I can't see that it's much different from its predecessors. Cirque shows, to the extent that I've ever been able to follow them on a narrative or -- so help me -- an intellectual level, have always seemed to be about naive clown-figures going on journeys and finding themselves in kingdoms populated chiefly by acrobats, jugglers and, yes, other clowns. The protagonist wanders among and around them until it's time to go, at which point he does. I'll concede that this quest has an especially magical beginning. Our young pilgrim opens what I have to call the Semi-Eponymous Box and out of there springs -- as if on a spring -- a Jack. He functions forthwith as the hero's partner, guide, philosopher (I guess) and friend.

Another concession: The show does send in more clowns than usual. One of them is a clown in a crown: an august master-of-ceremonies figure who can still be as giggly and irresponsible as any of his confreres. A departure in the lineup is a large shaggy dog, or rather -- in keeping with the no-animals-allowed policy by which this circus has set itself apart from all others -- a human being in an outsize doggy costume. There are also cops, from the Keystone precinct. There are more chases in this show than in any Cirque I recall.

As always, though, the performers who make us catch our breath are the daredevils. The Cirque always hires the best, and at least two of this year's troupes within the troupe are phenomenal. About half-way through the evening, there's a high-wire act. Of course, there's always one of these, and part of the suspense that they generate lies in our curiosity as to how they can possibly top the memories of previous years. This crew ups the ante by pretending to lower it. There are two wires, one above the other. The one beneath, though terrifying enough to you and me, is for beginners, who can be satisfied with little more than walking from one end of the line to the other and back without falling hundreds of feet to the floor. Wimps, really.

It's on the high high wire, literally in parallel, that the advanced stuff happens. Up here is where a couple of guys insouciantly pedal bicycles along the wire, singly at first, and then in a kind of tandem, courtesy of a plank that hooks on to both riders' shoulders. And then, from somewhere even higher in the Big Top, a chair descends and settles snugly on the plank. It goes without saying that a third man will then sit on the chair and perform a few casual stunts of his own. Somewhere around this point, we notice that some kind souls at ground level are holding out a security blanket. This may be the greatest shock, since Cirque du Soleil has always disdained anything remotely resembling a safety net. It turns out, though, that the contraption isn't there to cushion any falling human bodies (not, of course, that there are any) but to receive the chair when its occupant tosses it down with what we would once have referred to as gay abandon. Well, chairs cost.

But you ain't seen nothin' yet: not until a turn that the program calls the Wheel of Death but that I think of as the Human Hamsters. Two men spin through the air on a pair of gigantic rings, rotating high, low and wide on a single axis. They perform comparatively modest gymnastic feats while cradled within their respective discs; tiring of this, they climb on to the outer surfaces and perform acrobatics that are absolutely incredible.

The geometric beauty of such feats eclipses even their daring. The performers, poised perpetually on the edge of self-destruction, seem to be defying time as well as space; there's a kind of serenity in watching them, a hypnotic sense of mortality being held at bay. Elegance rules, too, in the exploits of a fellow who does his stuff on top of a self-assembled tower of chairs. Chairs seem to be very important in this show.

It isn't all lovely. There's a more literal kind of magic act, a conjuror who belongs more to music-hall than to circus and who, unlike the athletes and acrobats, is hardly the best of his kind. He also breaks with Cirque convention by talking to us, at length, in English. He does have some respectful fun with audience participation, though in this respect the clowns have beaten him to the punch. On the night of my visit, they commandeered a charming young lady from the house, made her disappear in the first act and didn't bring her back until the second, after we'd forgotten about her, I'm sure they treated her well wherever they'd taken her, but it did mean she'd had to miss the high-wire.

There's also a garish tinge to the show, probably bearing witness to the Cirque's long residence in Las Vegas. There are dancers dressed up as human skeletons, and a nightclub chanteuse who sings behind some of the acts without adding much to them. What any of this has to do with Kooza's proclaimed Age of Innocence, I cannot figure. But it must be hard to stay pure and ethereal in the midst of all that earthly merchandise.

- Kooza plays through Oct. 7 at the Grand Chapiteau. Call 1-800- 361-4595 for details.

2007-08-20-on-the-edge-of-the-carpet:
A DELICATE BALANCE

Tom Patterson Theatre, Stratford, Ont.

---

The ambience could hardly be more different, but A Delicate Balance, directed by Diana Leblanc, is the Mary Poppins of productions: practically perfect in every way.

Edward Albee's 1966 play is the counterweight to his earlier and more celebrated Who's Afraid of Virginia Woolf. The older play raises its curtain on a perpetually and bitterly battling married couple and shows by the end that, though nobody would describe theirs as a good marriage, they will survive together. A Delicate Balance begins with a couple who seem to have everything, and leads them, wittily and remorselessly, into despair. Of the two plays, I think it wears better. It's certainly the more economical.

Here are Tobias and Agnes, a prosperous pair of old-middle-aged WASPs. Tobias has inherited wealth (and some unseen servants), though he does seem troubled by taxes. Agnes runs his life for him. Agnes' younger sister Claire lives with them, and is an alcoholic by most people's definition, a mere drunk by her own. (Alcoholics, she says, "couldn't help it; I could, and wouldn't." Actually, nearly everyone in this play has a marked talent for putting it away; it seems to be a mark of caste.)

Julia, the couple's daughter, is on her fourth marriage and she now returns home in flight from it, just as she has done from the previous three. On this occasion, though, she is preceded, indeed pre-empted, by Harry and Edna, her parents' best friends, who have come down with a severe case of existential angst. Driven from their house by a nameless terror, they seek--practically demand -- refuge with Tobias and Agnes. They are not welcome, though it seems they cannot be dislodged.

Agnes especially dreads their presence. She begins the play with an elegant meditation on the possibility, which she seems to regard as a near certainty, that she will someday lose her mind. Her guests may be bringing that day closer. Their terror (Agnes calls it a plague) could be catching. And the two marriages, it seems, are very much alike; both have been marked by a progressive loss of intimacy. We gather that there was once a summer in which both husbands were unfaithful with Claire.

Skeletons get rattled, including that of Tobias's and Agnes's son who died in childhood; this is Albee's perpetual lost-boy motif (an adoptee himself, he even has the gall to name the kid Teddy) but it's more skillfully integrated than in Virginia Woolf, where it's a last-act device to keep the party going. If Agnes is abrasive, Tobias is seemingly placid, doing his best to be everybody's friend. Agnes goads him to take a stand, to stop withdrawing, which is what, in the literal sexual sense among others, he has been doing for years.

The six Stratford performers, individually and in battle formation, are about as good as anything gets. Leblanc orchestrates them on a drawing-room set by Astrid Janson that's complete and comfortable, save in one signficant detail: a carpet that juts off both sides of the platform sides, right into space. It's symmetrical, which is reassuring, but it's also disconcerting. We're not used to having the scenery exceed its prescribed boundaries in this way. It perfectly figures the precariously delicate balance that Agnes in particular is desperate to maintain.

The sensation of keeping chaos at bay is brilliantly evoked by Martha Henry, who weaves her way through the complex Henry Jamesian periods in which Agnes expresses herself with a patrician confidence terrified of letting its guard down. Close-cropped and as elegant as her surroundings, this Agnes never relaxes. Even when she descends to one-liners, her wit freezes. Fiona Reid's Claire, by contrast, crackles; she is the self-licensed jester, fastening on everybody's weaknesses and especially her own. Alone in this menage, she shows few signs of suffering, but she's a buccaneer of the wisecrack. Michelle Giroux' superbrat Julia is very much one of the family. She arrives to find that the intruders have taken over her room, so her fears and resentments get channelled into territorial warfare. The most strategic site in the room is, naturally, the handsomely pannelled bar. When the visitors offer to pour the drinks, both sides know it to be an act of conquest and when Julia, arms outstretched, rushes to prevent it, we have a scene of high tragic farce.

The central figure, though, the one on whom the pressures converge, is Tobias, whom David Fox keeps as amiable as possible for as long as possible. His mask slips quite early, in a self- lacerating speech about a pet cat whom he felt as a boy no longer loved him, and for whose death he now blames himself. Plainly, he feels the same loss, and the same guilt, in his marriage. But even this he delivers with a shambling grace, letting himself off the hook even as he baits it. Only at the end does Fox release the danger, shouting at the unwelcome Harry that he wants him to stay. Maybe he's doing this, as he protests (too much), from friendship; maybe it's to defy Agnes, who wants the opposite; maybe it's all furious sarcasm, geniality raised to the power of a threat. Or maybe Tobias, whose Biblical namesake gave shelter to an angel with gratifying results, wants to catch the plague -- he practically says "bring it on." It could be a blessing. Harry and Edna might be like the uninvited guests in a T. S. Eliot play, furies or guardians of mercy, depending on how you treat them.

James Blendick's Harry, describing the terror in slow, honey- sweet tones, leaves no doubt of its reality; Patricia Collins' Edna breaks down in pitiable tears. At times, just as believably, he's Tobias' good country club buddy, and she's a strict-but-fair godmother, slapping Julia for her own good. And at others, they treat the place as if they own it and have a right to. It's very funny, in every sense. They come and go and return and leave. It's as if they've held a mirror up to Agnes and Tobias, and the image has been rejected. Tobias returns to apologizing, Agnes to meditating on madness, and they and their realtives to their matching solitudes. If it's possible for a play and a production to be both lucid and mysterious, that is the achievement here. - A Delicate Balance is in repertoire until September 28. For tickets, call 1-800-567-1600 or visit Stratfordfestival.ca.

2007-08-23-tis-true-we-have-seen-better-:
Kenneth Branagh's film of As You Like It tells the story very well. The problem is, in this play there isn't much story to tell. Once past the first act, it's mainly mood and wit and bitter-sweet philosophizing about love, and here--partly through casting, partly through a wide sentimental streak -- the show falls short.

Branagh takes the privilege of film to fill in the parts that Shakespeare left out; whenever possible, he substitutes action for exposition which, given the medium, is a good thing. Indeed, he starts before the play does, showing us Rosalind and her father the duke, pre-banishment, surrounded by friends, family and entourage, happily watching a Kabuki show. The reason they're doing this is that they're members of the English colony in Japan, living in a comfortable enclave of their own, following the host country's "opening up" to foreign commerce at the end of the 19th century. All this has to be explained in the opening titles, which is suspicious in itself; a relocation idea that worked wouldn't need so much nervous justification. Anyway, the performance is interrupted and the domestic peace shattered when hostile warriors, having gained entrance underwater, swarm in and dispossess the good duke in favour of his not-good brother. Rosalind has to watch her father brutally struck to the ground, before he gets up and makes his escape to the Forest of Arden. Apart from that, my lady, how did you enjoy the play?

Well, conceivably the Kabuki cross-dressing convention gave her the inspiration for her own male disguise when she, too, is kicked out of court. But nothing is made of the connection; nor is the tension between Asian and European used to point up the play's own contrast of court and forest. When we get to the woods, we find them peopled, apparently indiscriminately, with representatives of both hemispheres. Corin and Audrey are of the West, Phebe, Silvius and William of the East; they're all well acted, Phebe in particular, but there doesn't seem to be any pattern at work. If Branagh wanted to do a multicultural production, he should surely have just gone ahead and done it, rather than setting up a rarefied historical setting that was bound to get us asking specific questions. By the end of the play, the Japanese element has been pretty much forgotten, while all it has yielded en route are a few pretty pictures, and the casting of Charles the wrestler as a sumo champ. He's a silent mountain of a man, whose lines have all been reassigned to someone else. This makes the report on his condition after his defeat by Orlando ("he cannot speak, my lord" -- but he never has) funny in ways that may not have been intended.

After all that build-up, the actual wrestling match proves disappointingly perfunctory. On the other hand, we do get (very briefly) to see Orlando fight the lioness that's about to devour his brother Oliver, and that's a lot more fun than hearing the repentant Oliver tell us about it afterwards. As a textual editor, Branagh earns full marks, cutting and rearranging the text to maximum effect and obviously understanding the bits that are left. He gives his actors chances and some of them respond in kind. Brian Blessed, playing both dukes, takes the two-sides-of-the-same-personality shtick to the limit, serene and genial in one frame, a neurotic tyrant in the next, while Alfred Molina makes a splendidly snobbish Touchstone, a bottom-pincher in town and a determined seducer in the country. He is also able, something I've never seen before, to reduce the friendly shepherd Corin to a state of terror, turning their discussion on manners into an interrogation.

The de Boys boys are black, and excellent: David Oyelowo gets more vigour and humour out of Orlando than most actors manage, and Adrian Lester (on familiar green turf, since he was once a highly- praised Rosalind in an all-male As You) does as well by the even sorrier role of Oliver. Their squabbling is powerful, and so is their making-up. There the compliments have to stop. Kevin Kline obviously has some

idea of the melancholy Jaques, but his chances of communicating it are ruined by his own habit of breaking up each of his lines three ways, and by his director's bright idea of keeping the camera roaming around him during his big speech; all the world may be a stage, but we don't have to circumnavigate it. He's also the one character who's harmed by the cuts; there seems in the end no reason for him to have been in the play. A Rosalind would have to be truly appalling to make you reach the same conclusion, but Bryce Dallas Howard barely scratches the surface either of the heroine's passionate abandon or of iced-water good sense. I also wondered why, since she's American, she's speaking nasal estuary English (that's cockney minus the flavour), but maybe she's trying to fit in with Romola Garai's Celia. It's a flat sound anyway, and it drains the mock-wooing scenes -- which are the heart of the play -- of much of their richness. The music department tries to compensate with slurpy underscoring, but that just cheapens the play. The final reconciliations raise the customary goose-bumps, so the play still works, but the glow is far fainter than it should be. - As You Like It airs tonight at 9 p.m. on The Movie Network

2007-08-24-hostages-of-excitement:
Passions can flare over many things. Toward the end of the first act of Pentecost, the stage erupts in a dispute over a religious painting. It's a fresco, on the wall of a church in an unnamed Central European country, that might be either an imitation Giotto or something that Giotto imitated. If the latter is true, then perspective, the Renaissance and the modern era of painting all got started long before, and far away from, their official time and place of origin. Three art historians, all with a personal as well as professional stake in the outcome, are arguing furiously. Just when it seems the tension can't go any higher, it does. The church door is flung open and a Jeep rolls on stage, peopled by displaced representatives of every country and culture east of what used to be the Iron Curtain. They have guns. They take the experts hostage and, with them, and perhaps more valuably, the painting.

Pentecost is many things, and one of them is that rare commodity - - a viscerally exciting play in which you can't wait to discover what happens next. Its author, David Edgar, is one of Britain's most accomplished public playwrights, writing large plays on large themes; since the 1970s he has been anatomizing his own country, present and past. (He wrote the legendary adaptation of Nicholas Nickleby whose revival we will shortly be seeing in Toronto.) More recently he has gone global. Pentecost, which was first produced in 1994, seems if anything to have gained in topicality. It may originally have been a response to events in Yugoslavia. It could just as easily have been sparked by Iraq and Afghanistan.

Of the three original disputants, only one, Gabriella, is a local; she's a museum curator for whom the early dating of the painting is a matter of both professional and national pride. Oliver, a visiting English critic, is easily won over to her side, and he gets the backing to have the picture removed and cleaned. The third party is Leo, a U.S. academic, specifically hired to prove them wrong. That's before his life and theirs get torn apart. His paymasters are the local Catholic and Orthodox hierarchies, opponents in most things, including which of them is the rightful inheritor of the building, but united in their determination to keep the fresco where it is. This church, like the country it stands in, has had many identities: It was a mosque under the Ottomans, a prison under the Nazis and a shrine of atheism under the Communists. Today, the country, as Gabriella says, is making a mess of the free market.

The insurgents have got in, from a camp on the border, with the intention of getting out. Survivors of atrocities from across the continent, they demand asylum in the west. Threats are made, offers are offered, suspense ratchets, and

--as expected--captives and captors bond. They all speak different languages (including a made-up one for what the play calls "our country") but, mercifully for the audience, most of them have English as a default tongue. Edgar is very scrupulous as to when and how this gets used.

Language here is subject as well as medium: from the inscription on the Statue of Liberty, both a standing promise and a standing rebuke, to the local peculiarities of a tongue that has the same word for "to" and "from." ("This would explain the taxis" says Oliver.) Pentecost is the festival of speaking in tongues. And with Stoppardian neatness, if not quite Stoppardian wit, at least two of the play's climaxes turn on linguistic misunderstandings and resolutions. It connects with an ongoing debate about art: as value in itself, as religious or national symbol, as bargaining chip. Themes and story are thrillingly advanced when the refugees erupt in a multi-cultural songfest that's both convivial and competitive and that has a bitter explosive finish. There's even a love plot. It feels perfunctory (Edgar is at his weakest when conversation is divorced from ideas), but it also feels necessary. And it is beautifully set up: "This is Illyria, lady" says Oliver to Gabriella, at once Balkanizing the story and universalizing it.

And, of course, Stratfordizing it. Indeed, the play began its life, like that other current studio triumph The Odyssey, in the equivalent space at the English Stratford; they premiered there within two years of one another. (Here, it's been within two days.) The refugees' Jeep dominates this production, just as a wrecked car does The Odyssey. There must be more garage space backstage at the Stratford Studio than anyone suspected. A Bulgarian director, Mladen Kiselov, has been appropriately recruited, and he gets unflinching commitment from his cast. Lucy Peacock caps a terrific season with a Gabriella who's both flinty and flirtatious, wringing amazingly various shades from such English-as-a-second-language expressions as "okeydoke" and "tallyho." John Koensgen is a wry and gentle, if excessively diffident, Oliver; Jonathan Goad may be too fresh- favoured for the abrasive Leo, but both his tirades and his one- liners are magnetic. Adrienne Gould gives a firebrand account of the refugees' leader, a Palestinian who's a multiple exile on her own account.

The staging goes against the published script in denying us a proper look at the painting, which is a loss since its subject -- Mary mourning the dead Jesus -- is as important as its provenance. Someone in the play describes Marxism as a good idea that hasn't been tried; the same of course has been said of Christianity. The play wants, I think, to harvest the most humane elements of both while lamenting the improbability. It calls to mind George Orwell's description of Dickens: "generously angry." It's a genuinely inspiring evening. - Pentecost is in repertoire until Sept. 21. Call 1-800-567-1600 for ticket information.

2007-08-25-it-will-take-two-to-replace-h:
There have been some grievous losses in and around the theatre this year: William Hutt, Ed Mirvish, Bluma Appel. But the death of Richard Bradshaw hits especially hard. He was in his prime and had just begun what should have been a brilliant new chapter of his career. He gave Toronto its long-awaited, and long-despaired-of, new opera house, and presided over its triumphant opening season.

He didn't, of course, get the Four Seasons Centre built all on his own. But it's certain that without his charm, enthusiasm and dogged pertinacity it wouldn't have happened. (He told me that a CEO once offered a handsome personal donation, on top of what his company had provided. "Sorry," said Richard. "Opera is a very expensive business. I need much more than that." "All right," said his benefactor, taken aback but fascinated. "How much do you need?" And gave it.) The Canadian Opera Company now has a home that's a pleasure to visit in itself, and that serves, with superbly unfussy concentration, the art that it houses. It's no surprise that Bradshaw and Jack Diamond, the architect, became such good friends. They brought out the best in one another. And in doing so he made our city a better place to live.

But Bradshaw was already doing that, in the COC's less glamorous lodgings at the Hummingbird Centre. The complete Ring cycle was planned to give the new house a magnificent baptism, and it did, but three-quarters of it had already come into being at the old address, including the Gotterdammerung that was dramatically the high-point of the series. The huge conference-table in that production -- another gift from the business world, you might say, though this time in an imaginative sense -- was as powerful an image as the Toronto stage has yielded in years.

The COC's best shows have been as important theatrically as musically: the Ring, Elektra, the superbly integrated Lady Macbeth of Mtsensk that lit up this past season. That, of course, is how opera is supposed to work, and it is certainly what Bradshaw wanted; I have known few people as acute and enthusiastic about the arts in general and those of the stage in particular. His decision to let Michael Levine design all four Ring operas and direct one of them was a brave hunch, superbly vindicated. As a musician, of course, he led from the front, or at least from the pit, and many of the company's most exciting evenings were under his baton.

It will obviously take two people to replace him; at least I'm not aware that the world is swarming with candidates who could be both artistic director and principal conductor. It's probable that standards will be maintained; the coming season, after all, is already in place and, operatic planning being the long-term thing that it is, so is much that will come after. His shrewdness and geniality, though, are irreplaceable. He was, in addition to everything else, fun.

"Richard Bradshaw," said the minister at his funeral, "abhorred eulogies." He still deserves them.

From tragic business to Funny Business, the new musical promoted from the Fringe to the cabaret space at the Diesel Playhouse.

One man may seem incompetent, another not make sense

While some may seem like quite a waste of company expense.

They need a brother's leadership, so please don't do them in;

Remember mediocrity is not a mortal sin.

Those lines aren't from Funny Business. They're from a much older satire on office politics, Frank Loesser's How to Succeed in Business Without Really Trying, and I quote them, partly because it gives me pleasure just to type them out, partly because they show what the musical theatre has lost --lethal satire masquerading as bland acceptance. These days we get the reverse, as in Funny Business whose script keeps pulling the rug out from beneath itself and pulling its punches in doing so. How to Succeed impaled its characters; Funny Business lets them off all possible hooks.

A Toronto communications company is under pressure to improve its performance or reduce personnel. The kindly boss decides to mount a talent-show to restore morale. Head office (in Winnipeg) decrees that one of the four performers -- heads of marketing and sales, the receptionist, an intern -- shall be fired by the end of the performance. The intended entertainment is abandoned in favour of an elimination contest There's a further reversal at the end that I won't reveal except to say that it represents the ultimate cop-out. There's some bad-mouthing and some back-biting, but everything is directed at sending the audience home if not happy, then fuzzy. The office details are very vague.

Daniel Abrahamson's score includes one clever item in which the senior personnel jealously compare their finances, the numbers deflatingly displayed on computer screens. Otherwise we get cheery tunes with no profile and words to match That's another lost Loesser lesson: You can't have sharp lyrics without sharp music (which hardly anyone writes any more). Some ideas here are funny, but there's no way they can land. The cast work hard: Trevor Campbell makes the office junior a charming loser and Alison Wool-ridge is, aptly, a department head you wouldn't want to get caught under. Lana Carillo and J. Sean Elliott are respectively perky and smirky, both qualities written into their roles but overdone, and Chris Trussell charmless beyond the call of duty. Authors and producers are very young and have bold plans for rescuing the commercial theatre. And Frank Loesser was right about mediocrity.

- Funny Business runs throughOct. 7 at the Diesel Playhouse. Call 416-971-5656 for details.

2007-08-31-an-earnest-effort-of-lesser-i:
Oscar Wilde's lesser comedies -- meaning all those that aren't The Importance of Being Earnest -- are tricky animals: curious combinations of epigrammatic satire and high-flown society melodrama. Even in An Ideal Husband, the best of the second-best, the two elements rarely coalesce; they come at us in alternating swatches. Wilde resolved the discord in The Importance, his last play, by making his text -- with its ceaseless cascade of genteel insults -- into verbal farce, and his action into situation-farce. The guilty secrets that haunt the protagonists of the earlier plays are still there, rattling around in their closets: babies, left abandoned in handbags, grow up to lead double lives that necessitate their being called Ernest in town and Jack in the country. Plot and dialogue are saying the same ominous thing: Transgress the rules of society and you will never be forgiven.

The plots and jokes of the earlier plays say it too; however, being melodramas, they provide their heroes and heroines with escape clauses, generally taking the form of the love of a good woman. This, as Wilde himself must have feared and was anyway soon to discover, makes them far less realistic than the apparently fantastical Importance. If An Ideal Husband is the most interesting of the experimental hybrids, that's partly because the scandal it exhumes is a good, solid political one. In his youth, Sir Robert Chiltern, a high-flying upcoming statesman, profited from a spot of insider trading. If this is revealed, it will spell the end both of his career and of the piece of high-minded legislation he is currently sponsoring. Enter Mrs. Cheveley, who is a woman with her own past -- sexual naturally -- and a blackmailing adventuress. (It's a rule in society drama of this period that any Mrs. will be at least one of these things. To be a lady, you have to be a Lady.) She threatens to dish the dirt on Sir Robert, and though she's eventually thwarted -- I don't think that's giving much away -- she manages en route to shake the marital confidence of the trusting and virtuous Lady Chiltern almost to its foundations: to bring her, indeed, to the brink of destroying her own reputation.

Richard Monette's production is the final attraction both of this Stratford season and of his undervalued fourteen-year reign as artistic director. So I wish that it were better. It fails to harmonize the play's two voices (I'm not sure it even tries) and it's sometimes plain to the point of being dull; Michael Gianfranesco's sets are nondescript, Francois St-Aubin's frocks and frock-coats mostly unbecoming. Monette does succeed, though, in making us take the serious bits seriously. When Tom McCamus and Brigit Wilson, as the embattled and embittered Chilterns, start going for one another at full decibel level, the hammers resound, the tongs blaze and the actors cut through the stilted words to the perfectly valid emotions beneath. Elsewhere, he locates the beating heart behind the stuffed shirt, and even finds some self- deprecating humour; she doesn't have that luxury and is stuck with being indignantly virtuous.

The good Lady Chiltern and the bad Mrs. Cheveley were at school together, and the latter has never stopped being jealous of the former. Dixie Seatle is excellent in the few moments at which she plays this grudge for real, but most of the time she settles for being a cut-rate Mata Hari, with an arrantly artificial laugh. Self- congratulatory laughter is rather a feature of this show. The play contains a bevy of society dames, delivering withering witticisms that sound like Lady Bracknell's leftovers, even though they obviously aren't. These attendant harpies are presumably meant to suggest the social pressures that could bring Sir Robert crashing down, but Wilde doesn't give them much of a context, and neither does the production. A succession of toothy or just mouthy ladies lines up to deliver unsupported specialty turns. Sometimes they get exit applause, an almost infallible sign that bad acting has just occurred. I said almost infallible: Brian Tree, as the elder statesman Earl of Caversham, gets a hand too, and he deserves it.

Not, I admit, that his happily harrumphing performance does much to establish the play's political ambience. Where Tree scores is as the heavy father to the dashing Lord Goring, who is the play's nearest approach to a unifying force. Goring figures as compassionate commentator, self-satisfied man about town, cheerful comic wooer and resourceful saviour of his friends the Chilterns. That's a lot to combine; David Snelgrove dishes out the elements one by one without reconciling them. He's best when playing with his romantic partner, whom Sara Topham, after an uncertain start, makes both sensible and delectable. Their union is part of a surprisingly satisfying last act, one in which, by a rich accumulation of plot twists and petardhoistings, realists and idealists alike are revealed to have feet of clay and to be all the better for it. Here Wilde's wit works, not as a collection of one-liners but structurally. The production rises to it, and fends off anti- climax.

In a broader sense it doesn't. An Ideal Husband is the final entry in a Stratford week that was otherwise an unbroken -- and, in my experience, unprecedented -- series of triumphs: The Odyssey, A Delicate Balance, Pentecost. In that context it's a letdown. But the successes count for more than the disappointment, in quantity, quality, and in sheer variety. This regime is going out in glory. - In repertoire until Oct. 27. Call 1-800-567-1600 for tickets and information.

2007-09-01-things-dreamtof-in-his-philos:
Two of the best Hamlets I have seen were from actors named Albert: Finney in London, Schultz in Toronto. They had other things in common besides the name. Both were, in literal terms, too old for the character they were meant to be playing, who is said in the play to be 30 and who for most of the time seems younger. Both were physically stocky, active actors, far removed from the frail, sensitive Hamlet stereotype. Finney, in particular, was slagged for this; the conventional wisdom was that he didn't look or sound like an intellectual and so couldnt conceivably be one. In fact, both Alberts seemed to me to cut straight to the centre of Hamlet, which is that he never stops -- cannot stop-- thinking.

In which respect, he is like his author. That is the theme of a recently published book that is in fact called Shakespeare the Thinker (Yale University Press, $35.95) and is the work -- posthumous, alas -- of a British scholar and critic, A. D. Nuttall.

Nuttall belongs in the tradition of what I would call enjoyment- based critics who have survived the batterings of at least three generations of literary theorists. The most celebrated of these is Harold Bloom, who says on the dust-jacket that "Tony Nuttall is my hero! So he should be, since Nuttall does what Bloom did in his Shakespeare: The Invention of the Human, and does it better. Like Bloom, he surveys all the plays (or nearly all -- he leaves a couple out), and he is as trenchant and suggestive as Bloom--in that book, anyway --is bullying and windy.

You can read page after page of Bloom rhapsodizing about Falstaff, his favourite, without being any the wiser as to why Bloom loves him so much. You may also reach the conclusion that he thinks the two parts of Henry IV to be very bad plays, since he seems contemptuous of everything in them that isnt Falstaff, i.e, half of each play. Nuttall has comparatively little to say about Falstaff, but what he says (an astonishing compound of gargantuan appetite and sharp intelligence. His love for Hal is deep, his selfishness complete") touches all the bases. He crams the Henry IV plays and Henry V into a single section, so he, too, leaves a lot out, but in his case, the losses are focused and, I think, implicitly acknowledged. He concentrates on Prince Hal, who "knows from the first that he has an enormous responsibility and a very difficult job to do and grows up to be a king who is still acting, naturalistically, brilliantly."

This, of course, is character criticism, something that was officially declared dead in the 1930s by a generation who thought that "character

had no meaning in drama (or in the novel) and that everything was image and symbol. This mandarin movement has in its turn been decried by the successive waves of structuralists and historicists (each of whom have one valid thing to say, and just keep saying it), but psychological humanism -- I can't think of a better phrase for it -- still gets a bad academic rap. It's considered ludicrous to speculate on what happened to characters before they entered the play (or, in the old scholarly catchphrase, to ask how many children had Lady Macbeth?"), but, as Nuttall points out, thats what audiences -- and, he might have added, actors -- do all the time, and good playwrights work from that premise.

Nuttall isnt writing "performance-based criticism, and he only mentions two specific productions, both of them occasions that confounded their audiences' preconceptions by making them cry. (One was Vanessa Redgrave, playing Imogen in Cymbeline.) But he has a range of reference that goes from classics to comics, or from philosophy to Star Trek; he relates Captain Kirk saying: Are you feeling emotion, Mr. Spock?" to Prospero's surprise at finding that Ariel, the "mysterious electrical being has feelings. I hope he got to see the stunning Royal Shakespeare Company production of The Tempest in which Patrick Stewart, Captain Kirks successor, played Prospero in an Arctic setting that, in a totally unexpected way, fulfilled his own stipulation that the staging must be neutral."

Nuttall doesnt often play critic-as-director; what he does, far more valuably, is to offer literary readings that are theatrically aware. Nor, despite his title, does he make claims for Shakespeare as a systematic philosopher. What he does is to trace ideas that a supremely intelligent writer kept discovering in the stories he set out to tell and anticipate most of what has been thought since.

Some he traces from play to play. In the early Henry VI, he finds squabbling noblemen propelled into civil war by the very act of taking sides; they pick flowers and, before they know it, it's the Wars of the Roses. Much later, we find history shaped in Julius Caesar by the kinds of thoughts the protagonists can think, the kinds of speeches they're equipped to make. Another early play, The Two Gentlemen of Verona ("How bad is a bad Shakespeare play? Not very.), sets the scene for later comedies by showing male friendship in conflict with heterosexual love," with the latter invariably winning out. It works in tragedy too: Romeo essentially leaves Mercutio for Juliet; Iago takes a terrible revenge on Othello whos abandoned him for Desdemona.

Sometimes, Nuttall gets too ingenious. His description of Angelo, the wrecked Puritan of Measure for Measure, as a sort of inverted Christ-figure, taking the sins of the world on his shoulders for the sake of a higher legalistic good, is a fascinating if strenuous read, but I cant see any way it could be made to work in the theatre. On the other hand, he makes more imaginative sense of Antony and Cleopatra and the contrast between "cold, dry Rome and wet, formless, erotic" Egypt than anyone I've ever read; I want to see it staged by a director who's read him. I think Nuttall may have a considerable influence on future productions. At the very least, I expect to see him quoted endlessly in program notes.

2007-09-08-three-sisters-who-break-your-:
Chekhov's Three Sisters yearn to go to Moscow. It's the one thing about them and their play that everybody knows. The first huge virtue of Laszlo Marton's Soulpepper production is that it rescues this premise from being a theatrical joke and makes it both fresh and forceful.

Listening to the play's opening speeches, we register the facts and the feelings as never before. We take in just how long Olga, Masha and Irina have been living in their provincial fastness, and how their lives are still dominated by the memory of their father the general who brought them here. Marton has staged this prelude formally, the cast lined up in chairs against the back wall. We seem to be suspended in time; there are even distant echoes, musical and visual, of the general's funeral. The sisterhood's initial hopefulness rings out clear; so do the mundane rumblings of the people around them that will eventually swallow them up. Five minutes into the play, your heart is already breaking.

Suddenly, it's raining, and we're firmly in present time, the sisters virtually dancing in anticipation of Irina's name-day party. Another of the production's signal achievements is that it makes us believe in them as siblings; they have all the closeness and all the shared jokes. It's typical, both of them and of the production, that in the traumas of the third act, with the town on fire, they break out into a pillow fight. Olga, the reluctant headmistress and more reluctant spinster, is often played as a wraith-like figure from a different generation altogether; d'bi.young.anitafrika gives her the family passion and the family warmth; confronted with Masha's infidelity to her husband (another teacher) she's torn, visibly and agonizingly, between sympathy and disapproval. Megan Follows' Masha, all nerves and irony, disintegrates before our eyes as she first yields to, then loses, the married officer Vershinin. Patricia Fagan's Irina is a radiant study in hopefulness continually lowering its sights, forced to compromise in love and in life, and losing even what she's settled for. The complexities of feeling that percolate within and around this family are brilliantly captured. Nicolas Billon's English version is exceptionally lucid.

There is, as usual in Marton's Chekhov productions, a physicality that is both exciting in itself and a huge release for the actors, whether they're playing joy or -- more frequently -- desperation; sometimes it's joy to stave off desperation. When Michael Simpson's drunken doctor, in his great aria of self-disgust, his belly protruding over his long-johns, washes himself off, he practically drowns himself in the basin. (He also -- a signature Marton motif -- has an intense relationship with a chair.) A role that is often sentimentalized here takes on a new leering identity, a stubborn refusal to take anything seriously that melts for a brief moment when he shouts at Andrei, the sisters' even more hapless brother, to get out of town fast. Kevin Mac-Donald gets electric in Andrei's most intense sequence of self-flagellation. It's typical of Chekhov that this should immediately be followed by a shrewish outburst from his wife, Natasha, typical of Marton that she should deliver it from a window immediately above him.

The stage is small, but Lorenzo Savoini's brick-backed set, with the onstage candles atmospherically realized in Kevin Lamotte's lighting, makes the room seem large. Characters huddle in corners or against walls in a frantic search for intimacy: Irina fending off the hopeful attentions of Mike Ross's kindly bearded Baron or Andrei making his spectacularly ill-fated (because successful) proposal to Natasha.

Sarah Wilson plays Natasha's initial shyness and later cruelty to the max, with one hysterical uncomprehending outburst that combines them. Stephen Guy-McGrath's Soliony, the play's other destructive outsider, has a mad spasm that's even more frightening. In general, the company's newer younger actors are good at the emotional extremes, less so at imposing themselves in between. The most relaxed performances come from Soulpepper's two middle-aged statesmen: Diego Matamoros embodies all the embarrassment and irritation of Masha's cuckolded husband, continually arriving just too late to find his wife in some kind of flagrante. Equally well- meaning and equally ineffectual -- indeed the two supposed rivals spend a surprising amount of convivial time together --is Albert Schultz's Vershinin, drifting in and out of his affair without quite knowing what's hit him or, especially, her. His famous philosophizing is perfectly genuine -- he's Russian, after all; it's also a mask for guilt. The lovers' farewell is triumphantly tragicomic: she jumping into his arms; he trying to disengage himself while she clings frantically to his coat, as if that might hold him.

Even the smallest parts are well played; the two aged retainers (Dawn Greenhalgh and Les Carlson) better than well. The junior officers (James Dallas Smith, Michael Blake) are amiable spectators; even the silent maid (Jennifer Villaverde) has a validating moment of terror. Irony cuts through the play like a knife, but this isn't one of those Chekhov productions that falls over itself to be funny; I laughed only once. Rather, it banishes gloom by giving pain its full weight and putting it in personal and historical perspective. It's comic in the largest sense, and brimming with life. There have been some very fine productions in and around Toronto this year, but this one tops them all.

- Three Sisters runs through Sept. 29 at the Young Centre. Call 16-866-8666 for more information.

2007-09-15-greatest-what-if-play-ever-wr:
Friedrich Schiller, Germanys national playwright, died just over 200 years ago. For most of that time, hes been a reproachful emblem of how the English-speaking theatre neglects the European classics. Things, however, are looking up, Schiller-wise. Nine years ago, his Don Carlos was Soulpepper's inaugural production, and a triumph. The same company's Mary Stuart, in a tense and thrilling production by Joseph Ziegler, is a worthy companion-piece.

Mary Stuart is the greatest what-if play ever written. Its central scene is a confrontation between Mary Queen of Scots and her cousin, captor and nemesis, Elizabeth I. This never happened, indoors or -- as the play has it -- out. The historical dethroned Mary did indeed cross the border into England seeking asylum, and the historical Elizabeth did lock her up in Fotheringay Castle and finally have her beheaded there on charges of treason. But the real Elizabeth refused Marys entreaties for a face-to-face encounter, since she knew that if she agreed, she would be obliged -- for reasons personal, ethical and political -- to pardon her.

Schillers Elizabeth knows it, too, and so do her canniest counsellors. But in the play, she disregards their advice and yields to flatterers who persuade her that an encounter will be a perfect chance to humiliate her rival. For a time it looks as if both ladies will get their druthers. Mary, who's been through three husbands and a lover at the least, gets to act the tactful penitent; her virginal relative gets to gloat. And then they both lose it. Elizabeth twists the knife once too often; Mary snaps and says unforgivable things. And history, having received a powerful new kick in the farthingale, returns to its appointed path.

The threat Mary represents to Elizabeth, and to England, is part genealogical, part spiritual and part erotic. If Elizabeth is literally a bastard, then Mary has a claim. The Catholic church thinks so; it also needs Mary as a devout champion of the true faith against the Protestant usurper. But she's not only a religious symbol, shes a sex symbol. These attractions combine, to intoxicating effect, on a young gentleman named Mortimer who has been converted simultaneously to the worship of Rome and of Mary, and has vowed to deliver her. (The collateral damage would include her keeper, his own uncle.)Mortimer is Schillers own invention, but he had plenty of doomed historical equivalents.

Peter Oswald's translation (recently staged in London, and I prefer the Canadian production) is sharply angled for modernity. The politicians who, equally devoid of remorse and of personal malice, manoeuvre for Mary's death, ring any number of contemporary bells. So, even louder, do the inflamed zealots like Mortimer who set off on assassination missions after taking the sacrament and being granted absolution in advance; they could be suicide bombers.

Zieglers direction only falters at what should be the climax of the climax. The queens quarrel-duet has built up a good head of steam, but it fizzles at the end; instead of a last locking of eyes and minds, we have Mary delivering her last defiance to Elizabeth's departing back. Otherwise, the production (which I saw at a preview) has tremendous energy, pace and point. The play is, among other things, a good romantic yarn; it starts with a bang and ends with a shock.

Schiller may have blackened Elizabeth, and he undoubtedly sentimentalized Mary, but he packed both roles with subtleties, showing how each finds reflected in the other what she most fears, and most desires, in herself. Yanna McIntosh's Mary is beautifully in the moment, bursting with suppressed pride, packed with grace. Nancy Palks Elizabeth is a regal flirt, toying with everyones emotions, including her own and -- in a familiar image that is here made fresh -- left alone with her power at the end.

There is a very strong supporting cast. David Storch may be somewhat mature for Mortimer, but he digs deep -- deeper, possibly, than his author could have anticipated--into the psyche of a twisted idealist, a philosophic firebrand. Stuart Hughes balances him with a flamboyant account of the Earl of Leicester, a self-hating survivor who flatters both queens (unhistorically in one case) and deceives both. William Webster's Lord Burghley offers a third way: an understated statesman, the most civil of civil servants, the most conscientious and the most lethal. There is good work as well from C. David Johnson (unrecognizable as a terrified secretary), Jim Warren and, as the one retainer Mary's allowed to retain, Hazel Desbarats.

ChristinaPoddubiukhas designed a handsome and sombre set, though one that denies the one exterior scene its proper sense of release. Her costumes, too, are rich, though their scheme is a bit hard to follow. The ladies wear period frocks; the men have suits but also ruffs -- except for Leicester who goes ruffless (maybe he has the wrong kind of neck) and the French ambassadors, who are thoroughly modern millefeuilles. But then, when it comes to style, Paris has always been ahead of everybody else's time.

- Mary Stuart runs through Oct. 13 at the Young Centre, 416-866- 8666.

2007-09-18-the-one-that-they-want:
I was fortunate when attending High School Musical to be briefed on the production's antecedents by a member of its target demographic, a well-spoken, well-dressed young lady of about six. "First," she explained, "it was a TV show. Then a movie. Then a book. Then shoes." She and her contemporaries were as polite and enthusiastic as they were knowledgeable. They hold out great hope for the future of theatre audiences. It's unfortunate that the object of their affections doesn't do the same for the future of theatre.

Its fans are obviously in no position to know this, but High School Musical is a show that sets new levels of unoriginality. And I'm not referring to the way in which this latest Disney product cannibalizes its own previous incarnations. I mean the way in which it recycles everything else. The characters may be highschoolers, but the show starts out like every old college musical there ever was, with students merrymaking and cheerleaders pom-pom-pomming on what we presume to be the steps of the library. Not that there's much evidence that anyone in this academy ever cracks a book. But then they never did in Good News or Best Foot Forward, either.

Sorry to get so archeological. What we more immediately have here is a mix of Grease and Hairspray, a product that could be the most alarming tonsorial development since Sweeney Todd. As the students at East High in Albuquerque, N.M., begin to sort themselves out, we learn that the population divides into Jocks and Brainiacs. Troy, a Jock (basketball) and Gabriella, a Brainiac (math) and new around here, met up over the summer and they reminisce about it, in what sounds like a weak, not to say virginal, imitation of that old Grease-y favourite, Summer Nights. The Hairspray analogies start oozing when we meet Sharpay, East Side's Queen Brat, who for years has ruled the school's third clique, the Thespians, with a whim of iron. The Thesps are mounting a home-grown musical entitled Juliet and Romeo, with a happy ending in which the lovers survive and move to Toronto. (Or wherever else High School Musical happens to be playing.) Sharpay takes it as read that she will play Juliet, and she gets all snarky and Machiavellian when Gabriella proposes to audition, since Gabriella can maybe sing and is certainly nicer. For some reason, the teenaged manipulators who oil the plots of these shows are never fun; they're just obnoxious. Somewhere along the line, High School also pays homage, to put it tactfully, to The Telephone Hour from Bye Bye Birdie, A Chorus Line passim, and even - - in the character of Troy's dad, who's also the school coach and who first jeers, then cheers, his son's inclination to try out for the musical himself -- Billy Elliott. And Ms. Darbus, the crabby drama teacher, who is kind of fun, is a close cousin of Miss Hannigan from Annie.

We have no reason, beyond the fact that she's the heroine, to think that Gabriella would make a better Juliet than Sharpay, though it's probable that Ryan, Sharpay's twin brother and performance partner, would be a less credible Romeo than Troy, who at least is interested in girls. But it's best not to go too deeply into plot and motivation. As if Sharpay's machinations weren't enough, the Jocks and Brainiacs, fearful of losing their respective star attractions, hatch impenetrable plots to stop them auditioning and then immediately repent and concoct even murkier schemes to repair the damage. Everything hinges on a last-minute alteration to the audition schedule, but how this comes about and why it couldn't immediately be put right is very unclear. The book is credited, if that's the word, to somebody with the magical name of David Simpatico. The songs for which the story periodically stops (they certainly don't move it forward) are the work of 13 composers, working in various combinations, and none of them sounds like the new Gershwin, or even the new Marc Shaiman. The score's nadir may be something called Stick It to the Status Quo, which is meant to be that ghastly thing called "empowering," but is actually just jerky.

The show may be stale but the production and performances are surprisingly fresh. Jeff Calhoun's direction is smooth, Lisa Stevens' choreography is energetic and Kenneth Foy's sets are excellent -- with their rows and rows of overhead lights, they are impressively spacious and make institutional architecture look like a good idea. John Jeffrey Martin and Arielle Jacobs are an appealing Troy and Gabriella, the only two people in nthe show who resemble real human beings. The rest of the cast don't get that chance, but they caricature with vigour. Chandra Lee Schwartz and Bobby List are as amusing a pair of terrible twins as anyone has a right to expect, given their material, and Ellen Harvey as Ms. Darbus does a very good Carol Burnett; even her passion for the drama is weirdly, indeed alarmingly, believable. Nice too is Olivia Ogama as the timid composer of the show-within-the-show which, for all we are allowed to see or hear of it, may be a masterpiece. (Though, on the basis of the one song we do hear, probably not.) Like everyone else, she gets to pair off at the end; in her case, it's with the school's resident newsreader, who spends the entire show making hysterically cheery announcements and mysteriously gets to the end of the evening without somebody strangling him. I notice that though the casting is proudly multicultural, the actual couplings are strictly intra- racial. And though Ryan, too, is allowed to find a partner, that encounter is kept very coy and upstage. School fiction, in any genre, is always aimed at an audience younger than the characters it depicts -- nobody finds their own contemporaries glamorous --but in this show, the gap yawns wider than ever before. - High School Musical runs until Sept. 23 at the Princess of Wales Theatre. For tickets, call 416-872-1212 or visit mirvish.com.

2007-09-22-literature-on-trial-the-pillo:
Once upon a time, there was a natural-born playwright whose name was Martin McDonagh. He was Anglo-Irish, and he had an older brother who went off to America to be a screenwriter. Maybe Martin was jealous or something; but anyway, he holed himself up at home for nine months and wrote the drafts of seven plays. The first of them was called The Beauty Queen of Leenane, and when it was staged it knocked its audiences sideways because here, for the first time in generations, was a piece that had them on the edge of their seats, panting to know what would happen next. The author seemed to have dramatic construction in his bones, along with a gift for characters who lived, dialogue that was both taut and flavoursome, humour that was mostly black and action that was largely violent. His other plays turned out to have the same qualities. And the reason this story is told in the past tense is that, at the age of 37, McDonagh has announced that he has quit the theatre for novels and movies, which is frustrating but also sort of fitting. The tale is told.

The Pillowman, which gets the Toronto season off to a blazing start, stands apart from the rest of McDonaghs work in that it isnt set specifically in Ireland and might well be a meditation on his own talent. It's about storytelling and its consequences. Its central character is a writer, largely unpublished, named Katurian Katurian; his parents, he says, had a warped sense of humour. (This turns out to be an understatement.) Katurian claims to despise autobiographical fiction, but he admits that one of his own stories might be taken that way; it's called The Storyteller and the Storytellers Brother. This storytellers own brother is named Michal and is mentally challenged. He loves to hear Katurian's stories; one of his favourites is called The Pillowman, and it's about a fluffy puffed-up figure whose mission is to talk children into committing suicide so as to save them the trouble of doing it later in life when theyre really unhappy. Katurians work is full of abused and murdered children. He now has reason to believe that a series of horrific child-killings have been committed by his brother, acting out the stories Katurian told him.

The brothers have been hauled in for questioning by two policemen, officials of what they themselves cheerfully describe as a totalitarian state." They are certainly freer with the beatings and the electrodes and the threats of summary execution than cops in democratic countries are supposed to be, but any political comment is merely a veneer, a method of pushing the play's themes to extremes. You don't have to be a fascist to deplore child abuse, or even to want to punish it, but Katurians plight is intensified by his living in a society that can routinely censor books and destroy manuscripts. This for him could be a fate worse than death. And he has a point: People die, art has at least a chance of living on. The question -- one that neither liberals nor conservatives have ever conclusively settled -- is whether it should, if it has a demonstrable chance of inspiring harm. That the person committing the harm may, like Michal, not be responsible for his own actions doesnt let literature off the hook: rather the reverse.

These questions are brilliantly dramatized, as opposed to merely discussed, in a scene between the brothers that David Ferry has directed magnificently. Shaun Smyth, who was excellent last year as the tale-teller in Of Mice and Men, is downright superb as this one. He not only brings out Katurian's fear, vanity, protectiveness and flashes of obstinate heroism, but shows how each bleeds into the others. Paul Fauteux's Michal, in whom self-centredness reaches the pitch of virtuous indignation, is his distorted mirror-image.

The two interrogators -- a self-proclaimed good-cop/bad-cop duo - - have their own issues with the issues, both personal and literary They, unlike the brothers, are played American. Oliver Becker, the foot soldier, sounds like Tony Soprano, and, like Tony, the more layers he reveals, the better he gets. Richard Mc-Millan, the guy- in-charge, is more like something out of Guys and Dolls. He does good things, especially in the matter of comic timing, but he undersells the characters intelligence, sophistication and -- above all -- weariness, so a vital thread in the plays texture goes missing. But a huge amount remains, in wit, tension and sheer presence.

The title turns out to have all kinds of resonance, especially for Katurian himself. There's also self-questioning. In The Beauty Queen the audience practically cheered the brutality on; here it appals, wherever it comes from. Which doesn't mean that it doesnt compel. Reconcile that, says the play. Or, thats show business. And they all, or some of them, lived unhappily, ever after.

- The Pillowman runs through Oct. 27 at the Berkeley Street Theatre. Call 416-368-3110 for information.

2007-09-25-a-most-winning-loser:
THE DROWSY CHAPERONE

Elgin Theatre, Toronto

Dancap, whose self-proclaimed mission is to bring Broadway to Toronto, made a happy start on Sunday with a show that's already taken Toronto to Broadway.

It's hard to imagine The Drowsy Chaperone without Bob Martin's glorious performance as the Man in Chair, and frankly I wouldn't want to, but the thing has been known to happen. It's happening right now in New York, where Martin has been released from the Broadway production on account of his chronic inability to be in two places at the same time. He's now reprising his iconic role on the first leg of the road-company tour, though future further-flung destinations will have to do without him. And of course, as has often been told, the show actually started its life without him, at least on stage. Back in 1998, the musical, in miniature form, was his wedding-present from a group of friends. When he himself joined the group, as writer and performer, the show began its transforming journey from spoof musical to portrait of the kind of guy who loves, and indeed lives, spoof musicals.

Of the four Chaperones I've encountered, my previous favourite, the happiest compromise between wits and glitz, was the version that Daniel Brooks directed in 2001 at the Winter Garden. But now that The Drowsy Chaperone has wafted downstairs (in her sleep, presumably) to the Elgin, all earlier bets are off. This is Casey Nicholaw's superbly snappy Broadway staging, but with its heart more firmly in the right place, which is to say wherever Man in Chair happens to be sitting or, quite often, flitting.

It's quite a melancholy heart. The show's now-famous conceit is that Martin's narrator-figure plays us his prized original-cast album of an archetypally frothy 1920s musical, which promptly comes to life before our eyes, while our host scampers around its edges like a small boy begging desperately to be let in. Though he adores the piece, he's frank about admitting the places where its enchanting silliness gives way to mere foolishness. As he says, musicals are what life should be like but never is. In life, as we see and hear for ourselves, records skip, phones ring and lives get wrecked -- the last point being illustrated in the enchanting capsule biographies that he provides of the show's original performers and in what he lets slip concerning his own lonely existence and failed marriage. (Are we surprised that a solitary musical buff should have been married? Well, as he says himself, "Don't make assumptions.") These speeches were always there, but they've never struck home as wittily or as poignantly before. Martin's character is also justifiably disenchanted with the modern theatre, which he sums up as "Elton John, must we continue this charade?", a line that comes at us literally out of the dark -- The Drowsy Chaperone being, as far as I know, the only musical ever to start with a black-out. So this apparent tribute to the derrieregarde is actually a trail-blazer. Martin doesn't merely lead it; he conducts it, with a perfect command of pitch and tempo. Has there ever been so winning a loser?

He and Don McKellar wrote the book, Lisa Lambert and Greg Morrison the score. There's little danger, I think, of anyone's equating these pastiche songs with Golden Age originals, and Larry Blank's wildfire big-band arrangements sound as if they were written for a 1960s revival rather than for the real thing. But then, as I never tire of pedantically pointing out, the whole premise is flawed because there were never original-cast recordings of 1920s shows, not in America (there were in England), and certainly none that included full dialogue, then, now or in-between. But the music is still energizing and the lyrics witty, though I refuse to believe that Ira Gershwin or P.G. Wodehouse, who seem to be the models here, would ever have been so stuck for a rhyme with "stumble" that they had cravenly to invent one. (Plum and Ira weren't no stumble-bums.) But there's one authentically wide-eyed line -- "love has no intention to offend" -- that's enchanting, especially as softly delivered by Georgia Engel, who plays the show' shy chatelaine. Oh, didn't I mention the plot-within-a-plot? It's set in a country house and it involves a wedding, or several. Bride-in-chief is an actress who's about to give up art for life (in both senses) and who has a standout number about it called (I Don't Want To) Show Off, in which she does, extravagantly. Andrea Chamberlan carries this off stunningly, that being the only conceivable way to carry it. It's the piece de resistance of Nicholaw's choreography, meaning that you can't resist it, but most of the numbers are tonics. So are David Gallo's sets, which convert a one-room apartment to a wonderland, and Gregg Barnes' costumes. Question: Is Martin the show's token Canadian or are all the others the token Americans? Anyway, bouquets to most of them, especially the women, including Nancy Opel's contralto profunda in the title role. The intrusion of a number from a quite different musical with an Oriental setting remains a special joy, though the authors may not realize that they've fast-forwarded into the age of Rodgers and Hammerstein and Lerner and Loewe, with what looks like Eliza Doolittle post-transformation intruding on the court of Siam. This would be the second-half opener, except that the Man in Chair detests intermissions. Which is fair enough; his show couldn't sustain one. It's definitely in the little-jewel category, and it hardly stops flashing. - The Drowsy Chaperone is at the Elgin Theatre until Oct. 14. For tickets visit www.dancaptickets.com.
