2007-09-27-more-mr-nice-guy-our-theatre-:
When we left The Office -- taking care, I hope, to switch off all the lights, because the Dunder Mifflin paper company doesnt look capable of withstanding any significant amount of extravagance -- Ryan was about to ascend from the depths of Scranton to the heights of Corporate. Four years ago, at the beginning of the shows first season, Ryan was a mere intern, so this is Irony. Michael, his boss, who had been confidently salivating for the Corporate gig, chose instead to return to his old perch and to the arms of his former girlfriend, the currently unemployed Jan. Or, more accurately, to her new and spectacular cleavage. More accurately still, he didn't have a choice; New York didn't want him.

Nor did they want Jim or Karen, Michaels subordinates, who were likewise condemned to return to base. Jim, like Michael, was all set to burn himself on an old flame, in his case the receptionist Pam. Meanwhile Dwight, Michaels second-in-command, is still entangled with Angela, Ms. Uptight from the Christian Right, a nervous relationship because they're two very nervous people. When Michael, with a degree of neurotic complacency excessive even for him, bequeathed his old position to Dwight before himself being interviewed for his new one, Dwight set about establishing his own reign of petty terror. It included lectures on the origins of paper and the appointment of a secret deputy. It must have left his staff nostalgic for Michael's rule of benign neglect. Which is just as well, as theyve now got it back.

So, at the political level, The Office returns tonight without much in the way of suspense, unless of course Ryan screws up in the Big Apple and is ignominiously returned to base. But that doesnt seem to be his style. On the personal level, though, much is uncertain, since the various romances have always been rocky and will doubtless continue to be. Trouble is that, funny though The Office undoubtedly is -- very funny at times -- I don't much care. And this perplexes me, because in the past I have become invested in the love affairs of TV characters who were far less skillfully depicted than the ones here. You might say, I suppose, that I'm not meant to care: that these are self-centred people, satirically conceived, whom we are expected to observe with ironic detachment. But that isnt the way the show has worked out. Indeed, the main thing that bothers me about it is how it has progressively broken faith with its sardonic origins.

There was a revealing moment in the last season finale. Jim, undergoing his own New York interview, was asked what he thought of Michael. He replied, hes a very nice guy. There was a "but" attached, and Jim may have been hypocritically saying what he thought management wanted to hear. But in fact he was right. Michael, as Steve Carell now plays him, is a nice guy. He wasn't three years ago, and Jim wouldn't have said he was. Back then the show was closely modelled on the BBC series that inspired it. Ricky Gervais David, the British Michael, was a monster, oozing smarmy incompetence. Carells Michael is also incompetent but, at least as we have him now, he's well-meaning. When he spouts political correctness he seems to believe it, for reasons that are at least partly humane. The British Office was also more believable as an office, and more geographically rooted. Instead of NBC's generic Scranton it was set in Slough, the appropriately despondent outer London township that inspired the normally kindly John Betjeman to write a poem beginning Come, friendly bombs, and fall on Slough.

American TV has a habit of softening up British comedy, most notoriously in the Fawlty Towers travesty that tried to persuade us that Basil and Sybil really loved one another. Even All in the Family was, to my mind, a pale reflection of Till Death Us Do Part. Here in Canada, too, we can do good misanthropy; at its best, Ken Finklemans The Newsroom had the insouciant savagery (and the workplace credibility) that The Office misses, or that I miss in The Office. The U.S. networks let it through just once -- in, ironically, the biggest comic success theyve ever had, Seinfeld. But then I don't think they ever noticed: at least, not until that show's much underrated final instalment rubbed their noses in it. Curb Your Enthusiasm, which makes it manifest, is strictly a cable creation.

North American fans of The Office tend to believe that the series has improved over the years, citing its greater depth of human interest. I dont dispute that -- the longer a series goes on, the more varied characters it is likely to generate -- but I dont think that's quite the point. Much probably has to do with the talents of Carell himself: He can do self-absorbed and self-pitying, but he wasn't born to be unlikeable. This may have been why the show has imported a later adornment of The Daily Show, Ed Helms, to portray the uncrackable insensitivity that Carrell lacks. (Helms Daily Show shtick was to cheerfully insult people, and it carries over.) Thats not to deny either Carell or the show itself their bouts of lunatic inspiration. Nobody is going to forget the bus ride to last season's beach party, with Michael encountering opposition from his black colleague Stanley and telling him to "go to the back of the bus" and then, realizing what he'd said, amending it to the front of the bus. Or the middle of the bus. Or drive the bus. Id class with that the Benihana Christmas episode in which Michael found himself unable to remember which of two Japanese waitresses he was attempting to score with. Stevie Wonder, he pointed out, is married; did anyone think that he loved his wife less, just because he couldnt tell what she looked like?

Tonight's season opener is called "Fun Run," and has Michael organizing a charity run in order to ward off a supposed curse on the office. Think of it as Exercise to Exorcise. - Season Four of The Office premieres tonight at 9 p.m. on Global and NBC.

2007-09-29-when-the-wages-of-virtue-are-:
The last Tarragon Theatre season began with a play called Generous. The new one starts with a play called Benevolence. It seems unlikely, but the Tarragon may be setting itself up as the home of the good guys.

Or maybe not. In Michael Healey's Generous, there were good deeds that went unpunished but not very many. In Morris Panych's Benevolence, the wages of virtue are even more dubious. The particular act of benevolence that sets things off is performed by Oswald Eichersen, an uptight orthotics salesman. One impulsive day he gives a $100 handout to Terence Lomy, a homeless man who's been sleeping outside his apartment for weeks. The gift arouses Terence's ingratitude or his vindictiveness --it's never quite certain which. Maybe it's just direction-less opportunism. Anyway, Terence takes it upon himself to rescue Oswald from his humdrum, hemmed-in existence and bring out the free spirit that declared itself in that first uncharacteristic gift. Not that Oswald isn't usually nice; it's just that he isn't usually that decisive.

Terence uses their new acquaintance to enrich himself at Oswald's expense, in more ways than financial, and to enmesh Oswald in a life of crime. He isn't your everyday tramp, though he may be your everyday literary tramp; he has a vocabulary and a range of literary references that are at least the equal of his victim's, and he has criminal connections.

Terence manages to estrange Oswald from his girlfriend, who's frigid and domineering (and a real estate agent, if you need further proof ), and introduces him to a friendly hooker who is cut out for a higher calling. The various transactions and encounters occur in a porno movie theatre that used to be an art house.

Panych directs the play himself and, as usual, he gets a superb set from Ken MacDonald. When we first glimpse it, through a scrim before the play commences, we think we're looking at a mirror image of the auditorium in which we are seated. When the curtain rises and the lights kick in, we find ourselves in what looks to me like an exact reconstruction of one of the two surviving movie theatres in my own neighbourhood though these, I'd have you know, are art houses. (Well, some of the time.)

There's a beguiling tone to the play, and to the production, but the overall feeling is thin. In the first half the writing seems to be aiming toward an airy funniness that it reaches only intermittently, while in the second, the action, most of it offstage and reported, gets increasingly random. Indeed, the world outside hardly seems to exist. The play seems to be preaching a liberationist message not unlike that of Panych's Feydeau adaptation, Hotel Peccadillo, but it twists and turns confusingly. The upshot, I guess, is that Oswald is victimized by his opponent (whom his girlfriend, Audrey, in a rare moment of insight, pegs as his alter ego) but is still the better for the experience. But, though the dialogue keeps harking back to the initial act of charity, it never establishes a causal connection of any weight.

It was once said of Peter Ustinov that he wrote not so much plays of ideas as ideas for plays, and that is what Panych, who somewhat resembles Ustinov in wit and whimsy, has come up with here. The abstraction emblazoned in the play's title hovers above the evening without ever being seriously examined.

Tom Rooney gives a lovely performance as Oswald, delicate even in humiliation. This actor really is one of the good guys, able to hold decency up to a comic light without ever becoming either harsh or sentimental. (The orthotics business seems right for him; his life pinches him like, well, a tight shoe.)

Stephen Ouimette brings the necessary bravura to the loamy Lomy but cannot make him real. It's hardly his fault that his early departure makes the play seem even more inconclusive, or that while he is there his role depends excessively on the incongruity of hearing a derelict talking about Kurosawa. He also pontificates on Oswald's own failed attempt at screenwriting: one of the play's loosest ends.

Jennifer Wigmore's role as Audrey amounts to one compelling scene of self-discovery, sandwiched between two bouts of caricature. Gina Wilkinson seems to have decided, probably rightly, that on the role of the tart subtlety would be wasted.

The cast is completed by Colin Heath, playing a succession of furtive patrons embarrassed, inconvenienced or just plain scared by the events going on around them. Or maybe he's playing the same patron on successive visits; I wasn't sure. Anyway his performance, almost entirely silent, is very effective, as befits a former cast member of Panych's The Overcoat.

The director's choreographic sense, at least, is as strong as ever. Visually and dramatically, everyone here is put in the right place at the right time.

- Benevolence runs through Oct. 27 at the Tarragon Theatre, 416- 531-1827.

2007-10-02-the-king-and-i-and-many-more-:
You might expect a miniseries called The Tudors to be the most ambitious treatment of a dynasty since Dynasty. You would be wrong. This Irish-Canadian co-production on an English historical theme confines itself to just one member of the family, the fat one with the wives. Only that's not how he appears in this show, which takes a narrow view even of its one starring monarch. It's the young and agile Henry VIII whom we meet here, and only the first two of his half-dozen spouses figure in the credits.

"It's good to be king," announces the cover on the published version of the show's scripts, a tagline that nicely captures the tone -- nudgingly and unoriginally jovial -- of the texts themslves. Michael Hirst, who conceived and wrote the show, certainly doesn't think he's being unoriginal. "The story of young Henry VIII", he writes. "presented a rich and so-far untapped vein. He engineered the change in England from Catholicism to Protestantism, which was so profound that nobody had ever tackled it dramatically before." Nobody? Shakespeare didn't allude to it in his Henry VIII? Robert Bolt didn't go on and on about it in A Man for All Seasons? And as for Henry himself being an untapped vein -- it's only four years ago that there was a series actually called Henry VIII with Ray Winstone playing the king in ripe Cockney: a startling idea that worked because the actor invested it with such juice and vigour.

The Tudors, at least in its first episode, is the standard fancy- dress brew of sex and duplicity and duplicitous sex. It's easy on the violence, though: Somebody gets assassinated in the very first scene, but it doesn't even rate a viewers' warning. (I expect this to change when the king gets down to the business of snuffing out conspiracies and interrogating the past lovers of future wives.) The Henry we meet is already tired of his first wife, Katherine of Aragon, and especially of her failure to bear him a son. He consoles himself short-term with various ladies-in-waiting and long-term with investigating the possibilities of divorce. He also wants war with France; and he trusts his minister, Cardinal Wolsey, to provide him with "just cause." Wolsey seems to be playing Dick Cheney to Henry's George Bush, though what he is secretly intriguing for is peace. He's also angling to be Pope, and he's capable of throwing a foreign Bishop violently against a wall to make his ambitions clear. Sam Neill plays a very smooth and powerful Wolsey, waking velvet echoes of James Mason at his most sinister.

Jonathan Rhys Meyers's Henry, meanwhile, is nobody's fool, not even the Cardinal's. The late Margaret Webster, a distinguished Anglo-American theatre director who began her career working on local pageants, said that the experience had taught her that anyone - - man, woman or child -- could, with the aid of the famous Holbein makeup and stance, be made to look the living image of Henry VIII. Most Henries have made at least a gesture in that direction. Rhys Meyers, though, has none of it. A pre-credits sequence informs us that, before his elder brother's death, Henry was intended for the church, and he looks it here: Not only is he not fat to the point of emaciation, he looks both sallow and callow. Underneath, he's a calculator: rather like the revisionist view of Henry V -- Shakespeare's, not history's -- to whom he explicitly compares himself. (He's talking about the warrior Henry, but it's the long- sighted politician whom he really resembles.) "What," worries one of his advisors, "if he doesn't know what's in his best interests?" But he proves that he does, taking himself off from council chamber to bed chamber for a vigorous tumble with the nubile (and married) Lady Elizabeth Blount. Yes, it's good to be king. You might not think it possible for a nude scene to look anachronistic, but this one does. Henry also plays a fierce game of tennis: the "real" (i.e. royal) indoor variety, that's more like squash.

The show can't wait to break the news that the Tudors and their entourage were, if not just like us, then just like the people we read about in the tabloids. At some level they obviously were, but it might be more satisfying to make that discovery for ourselves than to be continually prodded into it. There's an art to anachromism, especially verbal; it has to have a style of its own, and Hirst's attempts aren't exactly Shakespeare, or even Shakespeare in Love. They aren't all jokey, either. "As a humanist," says Sir Thomas More, who seems to have been reading too many of his own biographies, "I have an abhorrence of war." He also speaks of "the principle of collective security and universal peace," and says that the treaty with France "encourages the creation of pan-European institutions." A man for all seasons, indeed, including one 400 years in the future. Nobody has yet promised to bring back "peace with honour" but Henry will do that when he gets back from the Field of Cloth of Gold, which is obviously about to be given sumptuous treatment.

- The Tudors debuts tonight at 9 p.m. on CBC.

2007-10-04-twelve-maids-but-it-still-nee:
Crisp and trenchant and witty, Margaret Atwood's The Penelopiad is a book that cries out to be read aloud. In Atwood's own stage version, the cries are half answered, but only half; the author's voice comes through from time to time but mostly the play steers an uneasy course between recitation and dramatization. Or perhaps, since Atwood's text is a response to The Odyssey, I should say that it reverses Homer by showing that if you try to sail between Scylla and Charybdis, you can still end up being dashed by one and drowned by the other.

The show is a first-ever collaboration between Canada's National Arts Centre and Britain's Royal Shakespeare Company. This is more notable historically than artistically, as the result displays neither organization -- and indeed, neither nation's theatre, -- at anything like its best. Nor does it hold out much hope for Atwood's proving as notable a playwright as she is a novelist. Both on page and stage, The Penelopiad tells the story of The Odyssey from the viewpoint of the hero's wife, that by-word for patience and fidelity. The fidelity remains in this version--at least Penelope, as narrator, says it does -- but the patience is wearing thin, certainly within her own head. She addresses us as a dead woman: current and permanent residence, Hades.

When Homer's Odysseus returned from 10 ten years of war and 10 years of wandering, he celebrated by killing the hundred suitors who had been besieging his wife and feasting on his foodstuffs. As an encore, he hanged a dozen female slaves who had been sleeping with the intruders. The latter act has struck many readers down the ages as, to put it mildly, gratuitous, and Atwood agrees with them. She structures her own book around the deed and the various characters' responsibility for it. Guilt is sloughed off by Odysseus, who ordered the executions, and his son Telemachus, who carried them out, but bitterly acknowledged by Penelope who, we learn, encouraged her twelve favourite maids to make nice with her tormentors in order to find out what they were thinking, but failed to warn anyone about it.

Atwood finds the Homeric story shocking, and with reason. But she can't do much with her shock except state it, and then re-state it. This works all right in a novella but not in a play. If we are to care about the maids' deaths, we must have felt that they were once alive, and these women have no dramatic life: not as individuals, not as a chorus. Atwood actually calls them a chorus in the book, and she gives them a series of odes describing how miserable the life of a slave girl, even a favoured slave girl, inevitably was. Some of these interludes are plaintive, more are sardonic. They are a lot more fun to read than they are to hear, at least in this production.

The same goes for Penelope's monologues, which are the backbone of both incarnations. Gone almost entirely, and much missed, are her commentary on everyday afterlife in the underworld, and on what she occasionally hears or glimpses of the continuing world upstairs. (She knows about the Internet, but who was Hitler?) There's an acid laugh on nearly every page of the book, starting with Penelope's observation that Odyesseus "got away with everything" and that getting away was one of his "specialties." The words are still there in the play, but they aren't funny. Penny Downie, the fine Australian actress (now living in Britain) who plays the queen, is the main reason for seeing the show; in fact, I would settle for re- naming The Penelopiad The Pennydowniad. (It's certainly easier to pronounce.) She can be very powerful, and she can tell a joke; like Seana McKenna, whom she most resembles among Canadians, she was once a virtuoso Chorus in Henry V. This evening's at its best when Downie just stands and delivers, but even she settles too easily and too early for doom and gloom.

The rest of the cast, and the production team, are divided about equally between both countries. Canada supplies some actresses with good track records (Corinne Koslo, Jenny Young, Kate Hennig, Philippa Domville) but both they and their British sisters could be anybody, whether gyrating in the chorus or stepping out of it to play individual supporting roles, of both genders; the British Sarah Malin is a very matey Odysseus. Music is by a U.K. composer, Warren Wills; his main contribution is to drown out the words of the songs. In one number, a sea shanty, this may be a blessing: Best not to have speculate on whether the awful lengths to which Atwood is prepared to go in seach of a rhyme are meant to sound horrible. It's performed in sailor suits twice; Penelope remarks that in Hades, "a certain amount of vapid dancing goes on," and Veronica Tennant, the choreographer (ours), takes her at her word. The direction, by Josette Bushelle-Mingo (theirs), is just dull: a visual and emotional void.

Chances are that it worked better in both respects at its first stop, the intimate Swan at Stratford-on-Avon (which is many people's favourite space) than it does at the yawning NAC, which is unlikely to be anybody's. But there's an irony here; it's impossible not to compare The Penelopiad to the dramatization of The Odyssey itself that the NAC's own director, Peter Hinton, mounted this year at the Canadian Stratford. That was an infinitely more imaginative production of a superior play, one that re-invented its original instead of plonking it down while losing the best bits. When it comes to specific elements the two stories have in common -- the killing of the suitors and the portrayal of Helen as a brittle minx - - the contrast is painful.

2007-10-05-working-hard-to-work-hard-to-:
'This is quite nostalgic for me" says Marvin Hamlisch.

Thirty-odd years ago, he wrote the music for A Chorus Line, a musical about the Broadway audition process that captured the thrills and despairs of a career in musical theatre. His place on the production team also made him part of the show's own mechanism of selection, life imitating art in the casting of a musical about casting a musical.

Now, he's one of the five "marquee judges" on CBC's Triple Sensation. This is a six-part series in which aspiring performers aged 16-26, from across Canada, compete for a $150,000 scholarship to any training institution in the world that will accept them. The title means that all the contestants have to prove themselves as actors, singers and dancers It could almost be the Chorus Line Reality Show.

The shows follow the winnowing process. This Sunday and next, we watch kids assembling in Toronto, Vancouver and Montreal for open call auditions. Forty from each region are chosen for assessment by the Marquee Panel. Apart from Hamlisch, they are Cynthia Dale, musical star at the Stratford Festival; Adrian Noble, former director of the Royal Shakespeare Company; Broadway choreographer Sergio Trujillo (Jersey Boys); and the show's executive producer and guiding spirit, Garth Drabinsky.

Drabinsky's great gift is to believe absolutely in the importance of whatever project he is involved in and to communicate that passion to other people. (I worked for him in the past, and enjoyed the experience.) I believe him when he speaks of this show as a producer's tribute to performing talent, and as a clarion-call to the importance of funding training in the performing arts.

He has also hit on something that goes beyond the immediate context.

The initial task of the Marquee Panel is to select a dozen finalists who are then treated, or subjected, to a series of rigorous Master Classes in each of the relevant disciplines. The 12 record their experiences in video diaries. What's captured is the strange mixture of collusion and conflict that takes over every class, every group audition, every rehearsal, and probably every business meeting.

The short list will go down to ten, then to a final six who will make it to the elimination round in front of the same five judges who, by this time, are themselves emotionally invested.

There is an element here of the American Idol blood-sports attraction. What's different is that the whole process has been completed before the show even goes to air. Another is that nobody gets publicly humiliated Another is the sheer range of abilities that are tested. And another is the judges themselves, who are rigorously but sympathetically involved, and do not line up in any good-cop, bad-cop formation.

"If this was just a talent contest," says Hamlisch, when I spoke to the group at the penultimate selection stage, "none of us would have showed up. I always hoped that there'd be a more civilized way to do this, but auditions are the only way."

An incorrigible performer and compulsive joker, Hamlisch at one point accompanies one of the auditionees when he leans that she's doing one of his favourite songs, Broadway Baby.

Trujillo points out the economic necessity of nurturing a breed, if not of triple sensations then of triple talents. The days of separate singing and dancing ensembles are long gone.

That leaves the acting. There's a strong emphasis here on delivering monologues, mainly from Canadian plays, and even more on Shakespeare, on the sound principle that if you can play Shakespeare you can play anything and that his rhythms are after all musical.

You don't have to be good at everything to be great at something; there have not, after all, been many Triple Sensations in the real world. The series will probably throw up some talents who have fallen at particular fences but could still be heard from.

What is impressive is a talent-show that doesn't present itself as the fast track to stardom, but as one in which the final goal is further training. The comment of one young man stays with me: "I don't necessarily want to be a star. But I want to make a living." - Triple Sensation airs Sunday at 8 p.m. on CBC.

2007-10-06-it-s-curtains-for-actors-dire:
The Stratford Festival said semiofficial farewells to Richard Monette in a gala performance on Sept. 17. I call them semi- official because, obviously, Monettes 14-year term of office as Stratford's artistic director doesn't come to an end until the current season does, at the beginning of November. But there are new shows to open, so the Monette regime has had its say.

No one attending that gala could have been left in any doubt that it was, whatever its ups and downs, an engaging and successful say. Its conclusion has been further marked by the publication of Monettes memoir, This Rough Magic (Stratford Festival, $39.95), as told to David Prosser, Stratfords director of literary services. (Prosser has done an excellent job; the book reads fluently, and sounds like Monette talking.) The book officially stops short when Monette gets the top job -- it's supposed to be the story of how he got there, not what he did there--but in fact the preceding chapters are littered with flashes-forward, as when an incident from the past, or a play previously directed or acted in, reminds him of one that cropped up again during his own reign. Each chapter has as its title a phrase from Shakespeare: "Poor naked wretches" headlines Monette's fascinating account of his stint in the London cast of Oh! Calcutta!.

He describes, with retrospective sour amusement, the sudden crippling stage fright that overtook him while appearing in Toronto in 1998 and that effectively put paid to what was then one of the best acting careers in Canada. It has since subsided enough to allow him to make one acting appearance (successfully, in Filumena) during his Stratford reign, but only one. For all that, he has been very much an actors director -- or an actor-as-director -- and the gala was, in the way of things, primarily an actors testimonial. It glowed with laughter and affection.

The main complaint might be that there wasn't much Shakespeare on view for an evening commemorating an era at a Shakespearean theatre and mounted on the Festival Theatre platform stage, which was built for Shakespearean purposes (and which Monette himself has accurately described as the Festival's most vital asset). There were no performances of the big speeches. I suspect this might have been different if Bill Hutt had lived, but, as it was, all we got was a montage of lines from the plays that Monette himself has directed. This kind of thing can be embarrassingly precious, but David Latham arranged these extracts cunningly so that one fed logically into the next, and then seized gleefully on those that might have direct relevance to the dedicatee himself, who was handily seated in a front row, stage left. Scott Wentworth relishingly reeled off Falstaffs unblushing defence of his own moral character. Walter Borden, looking straight at the artistic director whos about to be succeeded by a triumvirate, delivered himself of Lear's intention to divide in three his kingdom.

In fact, the show, directed by Andrey Tarasiuk, was remarkably free of bloat, bombast or unearned sentiment. Christopher Plummer and Martha Henry delivered tributes. Peter Donaldson, shrouded in a parka, announced in stentorian tones you arrive in the snow, and you leave in the snow, before presiding over a disrespectful conspectus of Monette's rehearsal techniques. Dan Chameroy revealed an unexpected side of his talents with a Monette impersonation that, for a moment, had us all fooled. Lucy Peacock, who has spent her entire career at Stratford and seems in the last couple of years to have entered on a brilliant new chapter of it, sang Before the Parade Passes By, from Hello, Dolly!, and delivered authentic musical-comedy goosebumps. These were only topped by Brian Bedford and Seana McKenna reprising the balcony scene from Private Lives and providing a virtual master class, not just in the acting of Coward but of emotion-flecked high comedy in general.

Also, a penguin, currently starring in Monettes production of The Comedy of Errors, crossed the stage bearing a sign saying "the critics hated it; the audiences loved it." All good fun on this particular night, but I cling to the belief that the audience might have loved it even more if the laughs had had anything to do with the play that the author wrote. Theres a far better defence of Monette's brand of populism in the book, where he remarks that with few exceptions (I'm glad he said that) "the critics turned up their noses at my decision, in Henry IV, to explore the comedy inherent in the scenes with Hotspur." As he says, discontinuity of character, of style, of tone, is one of the hallmarks of Shakespeares genius. Hes far more sensitive to text than most reviewers have given him credit for.

There have been missteps in the Monette regime (some choices in middlebrow modern plays and "family experiences" have been shockers), but the full record has been overwhelmingly positive. Reverting to Henry IV, he says at the book's end (admittedly in parenthesis), "Future artistic directors, take note: I may have a Falstaff in me yet." That's a piece of casting thats occurred to many people in the past few years, contemplating the mans rumbustious voice and personality. (The last, by his own admission, self-created; he grew up shy and troubled.) It's good to know that he agrees. Good, too, that he contemplates more acting. At the end of the evening--just before an appropriate rendition of the title song from Camelot led by Tom McCamus -- Antoni Cimilino, Monette's second-in-command and his successor as supremo, stressed that this was not necessarily goodbye; he also remarked on the love that had welled up through the entire night. That is what you would expect on such an occasion, but it was no less moving for that.

2007-10-10-no-such-thing-as-a-free-monda:
Monday, Monday. So good to me. Or it used to be. When I was just a theatre critic, my Mondays were free. No plays open on a Monday night and few even play then. Television, of course, is relentless. So, by way of getting my feet a little wetter, I settled down on Monday for a night of regular viewing.

8 p.m. Global. Prison Break. Sara is definitively dead, her head delivered in a box to Lincoln, who -- for reasons both selfish and un -- can't bring himself to break the news to her loving, incarcerated Michael. Informed sources (in the real world) suggest that this development is the result of a complex series of negotiations and ultimata between the producers, the network and the actress concerned who is off -- in Canada -- having a baby. I think it's regrettable since: a) both the actress and the character were attractive; b) there was real chemistry between her and Michael, actually helped by the psychological and often physical distance between them; and, frankly, it hurts; c) Michael is left devoutly planning his latest escape in ignorance of what's gone down, which makes him look rather foolish and thereby reduces the stakes. Doubtless there will be a fearsome scene when he finds out; Wentworth Miller, pent-up in his penitentiary, can certainly do intensity and he can do anger. But he's no more a tragic hero than Jack Bauer on 24 (well, maybe slightly more) and the writers of both shows are getting above themselves if they think otherwise. These thriller soaps aren't Shakespeare. They aren't The Sopranos. They aren't even Deadwood.

And though I can't give up on Prison Break, it is marking time. The titular premise was maybe good for only one, so to speak, outing. It got a miraculous second-season second wind with the ex- cons and their pursuers interacting on the outside. Now that they're back inside again, in a Panama jail where the prisoners have been left to their own devices, it's repetitive and the fact that the inmates have taken over the asylum makes it, oddly, less urgent. There are no compelling new characters this season, and the old ones are in a rut. Bellick, grandly played by Wade Williams, has surely suffered enough, even for a sadistic weasel of a corrupt corrections officer. At least T-Bag got to murder somebody this episode; I mean it's been weeks.

9 p.m. CBC. Intelligence. I've been with Prison Break since the beginning. Intelligence was new to me (stop nodding your head) and I wondered what it would be like to come in on the middle of a densely- plotted thriller. It is, of course, hopelessly confusing, though some things seemed strangely familiar. "Previously on Intelligence" (this usage seems to have become standard, thanks to 24), somebody's brother got framed for something; indeed, once the episode got started, "tell us where your brother is right now" seemed to be the key line, uttered by bullying and -- as far as I could tell -- crooked cops, most of them with shaven scalps. They were going bald- headed at the job of nailing the wrong man. A nightclub got raided by a SWAT team whose leader, not getting the attention he felt he deserved, was reduced to yelling "turn the f---ing music off." By the end of the hour things were a little less murky, and I could tell that Intelligence was intelligent. This Canadian series has been bought by the U.S.; they shouldn't need to change it much.

10 p.m. Stayed with CBC for The National. Top story of the day seemed to be that "Peter is away tonight." We were told that a visiting dignitary to our troops in Afghanistan "would be treated like any other Canadian" and the point was driven home by having posed for an interview outside a Tim Hortons. A piece about refugee Somali students at Canadian universities (title: The Lucky Ones) was very well done, genuinely heart-warming. All CBC programs were regularly interrupted by last-minute Ontario election ads, all of them desperate. Put all their messages together and you come up with there being thousands more cops on Ontario's streets, none of whom can find a family doctor.

11 p.m. Comedy Network. Jon Stewart, in fine quizzical form, mused on President Musharraf 's triumph at the Pakistani polls ("I find him charming, but 98%?") and getting positively metaphysical when interviewing John Oliver on President Bush's mixed messages on the word "torture." "I'd expect" said Oliver, wonderfully indignant, "you at least to support our words: our brave fighting words, many of them making the ultimate sacrifice: losing their definition." Orwell would have approved. Stewart's interview of Vicente Fox was, as his interviews often are, an anticlimax, prompting only the thought that the former Mexican president looks rather like John Cleese, had he elected to play Manuel rather than Basil. Stephen Colbert, on the other hand, did a super interview; he's usually better talking to people he pretends to agree with (right) rather than those he pretends to oppose (left) but this time he had a fellow liberal -- George Saunders, author of The Braindead Megaphone, attacking talk-show hosts -- whose ironic sense matched his own. Colbert is also in two minds about Columbus Day, though not for the fashionable reasons: "You don't think an American could have discovered America? We live here. How hard could it be?"
2007-10-11-fashion-victim-ugly-betty-is-:
Watching the first two episodes of Ugly Bettys second season, I started wondering about categories. These are important in television, because without them no one would know where to send the awards. But they matter to viewers as well. Great art may confound expectations, but that's hardly the issue here. Most of TV is entertainment designed to fit into a box: literally and metaphorically. We like to know what kind of rise it is trying to get out of us.

I think Ugly Betty is a holy horror, but it has won plenty of prizes. And most of them have been for comedy. This is strange, because it doesn't have any laughs. Its title character, a perky but determinedly unglamorous young Mexican who lands a job as editorial assistant at a New York fashion magazine, is accident-prone; America Ferrara, who plays her, can take an endearing pratfall, and regularly does. But the humorous potential in that is limited, and besides, its offset by the characters all-around pluckiness in the face of a world dead set against her. She has to watch her boss's back while a perfidious and amoral rival plots to unseat him from the editorial chair, though not from the wheelchair to which he's currently been consigned. Shes lost her boyfriend to some promiscuous schemer (not the same one) though at close of play last week she seemed about to get him back. She was also, however, being blackmailed; her dad is stranded in the old country without a U.S. visa, and she can get him fast-tracked back if she stoops to a bit of personal betrayal. Agony. This last wrinkle might be a lost shard from some cop or spy or terrorist drama. Looked at another way, its like a daytime soap with production values. Or The Devil Wears Prada going on forever.

If it's comedy, it can only be so in the default sense: That is, that it's drama so weightless that we refuse to believe that anybody meant it seriously. The other elements include a transsexual amnesiac, an office flunky who has issues over her long-lost father and her all-too-present mangy dog and a very elegant convicted murderess on the run. Some of this is played for pathos, some for absurdity and some -- most -- for whatevers nearest to hand. Its overheated without ever coming to the boil.

Somewhere on Ugly Betty's trophy-shelf sits a Teen Choice Award for Best Villain, given to Vanessa Williams. There's specialization for you. And the lady has had to work hard for it. She plays Wilhemina, the ambitious bitch-goddess (her middle name might be Success) who schemes to marry the hapless editors proprietor- father and is making out with a hunky bodyguard. Thats as well as putting Betty through the wringer, though she's not above pretending to make common cause with her. ("I am black, you're Mexican.") When things threaten to go wrong for Wilhemina, we glimpse the flames of hell burning in the fireplace behind her; she then proceeds to the office roof where she takes out her rage by smashing a row of mannequins. For all that, she isnt really scary. The show wouldnt let her be.

Its survival is obviously due to something. It has a basic knack of narrative pacing, and it has Ferrara, who is the closest thing on it to three-dimensional. But the ugly duckling defying the spoiled beauties always strikes a chord and Ferrara too has won a Teen Choice Award -- for Breakout. This may be true in an ethnic as well as a personal sense; she's a rare Hispanic heroine, though this is hardly likely to count in Canada as it does in the States. And going from ethnics to ethics, she's had a scene in which she indignantly decries the idea of a beauty-shoot built around victims. This did have a comic build to it as well as a moral one. It was nicely off- hand. But it stood pretty much alone.

The wily Wilhemina has an assistant called Marc: a gay stereotype- -placed within the fashion world, hes a double stereotype without the saving grace of wit. The nearest hes come, after being attacked by a fake nun, is I don't think I'll ever be able to watch The Sound of Music again. Hes unscrupulous and sycophantic but, when he accidentally does something nice, hes capable of saying "I'm a good person -- no, I'm a great person", crowing like Peter Pan and meaning it. This is the kind of having-it-both-ways that has degraded the once noble concept of irony. I think Marc may have written Ugly Betty.

- Ugly Betty airs tonight at 8 p.m. ET on Citytv and ABC.

2007-10-13-what-s-the-thing-again-oh-rig:
The Shakespearean adaptation calling itself The Prince Hamlet comes in at just under two hours, which means, of course, that nearly half of the original has been cut. This is a Hamlet with no political background. If this production's Denmark is a prison, it's guarded from the inside. There are no Polish wars or Norwegian incursions, no mention of Fortinbras, let alone a personal appearance to claim the throne and clear up the bodies. This version ends with Horatio's recap about carnal, bloody and unnatural acts, all of them strictly domestic.

It also begins with that speech, so that the main action becomes a major flashback, within which, in this treatment, there are other minor flashbacks. The official opening scene doesn't happen, at least not in its usual form. It's transported, or bits of it are, into the second scene, as an audio-visual illustration of Horatio and Marcellus's account to Hamlet of their initial sighting of his father's ghost. Soon after this we see for ourselves the dishevelled prince intruding on the terrified Ophelia, instead of just hearing from her dad about it. And much later -- a matter of extrapolation rather than interpolation -- we see her watery end even as the queen describes it.

The show is the initial offering of a new company, Toronto-based and internationally staffed, called Why Not Theatre. They aim, by their own account, "to see and hear [ Hamlet] as if for the first time" and "to simply tell the story, simply." They have succeeded. The production, directed by Ravi Jain and Katrina Bugaj, is lively, exciting and very intelligent. This does not, despite some of the implicit claims that seem to be floating somewhere above the program notes, make it unique. I have seen full-length productions, with the lines spoken in their accustomed order, that were just as illuminating. They have generally been done, though, by actors more experienced than these, and one reason for welcoming this production's reduced running-time is some -- not all -- of its nine actors would be hard-pressed to hold our attention for longer.

And it is true that the cuts, and the transpositions, and the occasional transfer of a speech from one character to another, keep those of us who have heard this text rather too often on our toes. But the treatment would also, I think, make sense to someone who'd never seen the play before; that's more than you can say for most Shakespearean collages that only work, despite their pretensions to freshness, as japes for the jaded. Some things have been filled out, and others filleted, but the spine of the original remains unaltered.

Some of the staging really is illuminating. When Claudius, in what is now the first scene, announces his marriage to his brother's widow, he appears to be presiding at that brother's funeral, and it's chilling; no wonder Hamlet is traumatized. (Relentless strobe- lighting may have something to do with it as well, though it's probably meant as effect rather than cause.) The king is standing on a rostrum at the time and he spends a significant amount of time there. The only other furnishing is a movable arras-curtain, used for its accustomed purpose of concealing eavesdroppers. This production, though, places us on the eavesdroppers' side. When Hamlet, out of sight though not of hearing, tells Ophelia to get her to a nunnery, we watch the reactions of Polonius and, more importantly, of Claudius, increasingly alarmed at the realization ("those that are married already, all but one, shall live") that he has been rumbled. When the closet scene comes around, we're again on Polonius's side of the arras as he waits to be stabbed, though this time it's less exciting; maybe it's a trick that only works once in an evening. The fight is very sharply staged. Jain, Why Not's guiding spirit, studied at the Lecoq mime school in Paris, as what Canadian experimentalist did not, and his staging is appropriately, and aptly, physical.

Hamlet's four soliloquies are here down to two-and-a-half; he shares the "rogue and peasant slave" diatribe with a taunting chorus. We still, as the production must mean us to do, get inside his head, a thoughtful and sensitive head, progressively corroded by experience. Philip Graeme, an Anglo-Canadian actor well worth keeping an eye and ear on, gets the essential point about Hamlet; that his is a mind that will take on anything. He even brings "to be or not to be" to fresh life, springing it out of left field and with a remarkable knack for landing with perfect logic on words that other actors have left unstressed.

Matthew Bulgo is a bluff and loyal Horatio, Rory Sheridan a funny Polonius, and Kathryn Merry a poignant spirited Ophelia who goes arrestingly to her death singing the Bus Stop song, a.k.a. A Paper of Pins. She also benefits from having her two mad scenes collapsed into one. Sean Donovan's Claudius must be the least fleshly usurper on record, and he's too lightweight in other ways as well, but the production at least allows him to be credibly conscience-ridden.

Gertrude, one of the most opaque characters in Shakespeare, remains that way in Liz Pounsett's performance; I think she drinks the poisoned cup on purpose, but it's impossible to be sure. Laertes (Aron De Casemaker) has nothing to distinguish him beyond his mohawk haircut. This Danish play contains a real Dane, Troels Hagen Findsen, who does most of the Gravedigger's part in what I assume is his native tongue. He also plays Rosencrantz in a cloth-cap, opposite a Guildenstern (Will O'Hare) in a bowler. And Why Not?

- The Prince Hamlet runs through Oct. 21 at the Winchester Street Theatre. Call 416-262-3198 for details.

2007-10-17-even-drug-dealers-can-use-a-l:
I was complaining last week about TV shows that refuse to stay in their allotted categories, or even decide what kind of thing they want to be in the first place. If any show has managed to confound preconceptions and get away with it, its Weeds.

It started, I suppose, as a sitcom: a sour-cute idea about a youngish widowed mother, a respected member of her California community and sexy as hell, supporting herself and her two sons by selling dope. Just about everybody in the town of Agrestic, it seemed, was her willing client. As a premise that's intriguing, but limited. What -- the bane of all sitcoms --could you do but restate it?

Weeds' solution has been to darken everything while remaining flippant about it. From the start it incorporated a broad vein of satire about shockable hypocrisy (the Christian right has always been good for a laugh) and municipal corruption, sometimes disguised as municipal incompetence. This has become steadily less good- natured.

Also, Nancy, the protagonist, has been plagued by roosting chickens. Back in the pilot episode, she was affronted at the idea of kids dealing or even using; the third and current season has found her own elder boy as a runner. The nice black family who were her suppliers have been supplemented by others -- black, Mexican and even Armenian-- who are not nice. The cliffhanger ending of the last season found Nancy in her kitchen with about a dozen guns trained on her. Its true that most of her assailants were too preoccupied with cracking wise at one anothers expense to pose a serious threat; collectively, they were the gangs that couldn't shoot straight. But there was always the possibility that, individually, one or two of them could. And people on the show have been killed, occasionally, though never the sympathetic ones. As the star, Nancy has tenure and she acts as though she knows it; she may get desperate but she's never despairing. She has, though, found herself in deeper -- or harder. Its no longer just pot that shes dealing with. Our heroine is involved with heroin.

Weeds is compulsively watchable (nobody writing about it has been able to avoid the word addictive) and it remains ambushingly funny. From recent episodes I treasure the memory of a filling- station attendant remarking of a cryptic customer, "I know it's a cliche, but I think he was being ironic," and the revelation that drug dealers like driving Priuses. (Because they're quiet.) Mary- Louise Parker brings a knife-edge comic presence to Nancy; also, the California climate permits, or maybe compels her, to go around all the time in skimpy black dresses. She has, too, a wonderful foil in her for-want-of-a-better word-friend Celia, who started as your average censorious neighbour and has matured into downright malevolent, though not without having a certain amount of right on her side. And since shes only a featured player, she really suffers.

All the same, you can still hear the grinding of gears, or perhaps the sound of bases being covered. One problem that has always dogged Weeds is that there was no premise behind the premise. We jumped in, as the ancients would say, in medias res. We never saw Nancy in her former life or learned how -- as opposed to why -- she got into her current one. In the first scene of the pilot, she was in a PTA meeting, virtuously opposing the presence of sugary drinks in school; in the second scene, she was on her merry way in her car, selling to what was already an established customer base. I know its a cliche, but I think the show was being ironic. And in its breezy way it worked. The trouble is, though, that Nancy is a premise before she's a person. The sitcom is just that: situation comedy. It resists development. Compare (and Weeds is good enough, and ambitious enough, to justify the comparison) The Sopranos, which wasn't primarily comic, and in which the menace was real, but which was funny --indeed funnier, because the comedy grew from the characters. Sitcoms used to be stationary, or at any rate repetitive. That tradition may have peaked in Seinfeld, where the characters aimlessness virtually forbade any possibility of a story. When a sitcom develops a continuing narrative, as the current trend is, it becomes a bastard form: not an impossible one, but the strain shows.

With its harried mom, loutish big brother and puzzled small one, Weeds is somewhat like Malcolm in the Middle, without a Malcolm in the middle. Though if young Shane isnt a genius on the Malcolm level, he's still plenty bright; he was able to supply the full text of the proverb "tempus fugit," which I, despite the classical education flaunted above, never could. Weeds falls between the comparative realism of Malcolm (a bolder show, despite its more conventional trappings) and the sheer camp of Desperate Housewives. I never thought I'd mourn the demise of the laugh track, but I do miss what the laugh track signified: a whole-hearted commitment to laughter. Weeds has left it a little late to become drama; its stuck at bizarre. Its also taught us that Little Boxes sung by Elvis Costello sounds exactly the same as Little Boxes sung by Randy Newman, and that it's a tiresome, patronizing song whoever does it.

2007-10-19-tinkering-with-tv-gums-up-the:
When Trey Anthony's 'da Kink in My Hair was a stage play, it was a breakout event: first on the Toronto fringe, then at the small uncommercial Theatre Passe Muraille, then in the big and commercial Princess of Wales, where its run kept getting extended, then in London, and tomorrow -- the world. It was by far the most successful show ever to have been written, staged and performed by and about black Toronto women, or indeed black Canadian women. It broke out in other ways, too. By the time it arrived at the Princess of Wales, it was a combination of play and musical. It was also a show whose characters addressed the audience in person, breaking right through the fourth wall.

So it's disappointing, indeed dispiriting, that the new TV version of 'da Kink should have stepped right back again. The characters remain within the frame, which itself seems to have shrunk. The TV series, like the play, is set in a Toronto hairdressing salon operated by two sisters, originally from Jamaica. The proprietor, Novelette, a.k.a. Nettie (Ordena Stevens-Thompson), is ambitious and efficient; her sister Joy (played by Anthony herself ) is a freer or at least more feckless spirit, who has come to Canada to help out. Next to them in prominence is Starr, a trainee, played by Anthony's co-writer, the striking Ngozi Paul. There's also a male stylist, Nigel, who fancies himself big-time and can't understand why Starr, at least at this writing, doesn't feel the same.

Joy put in time in Jamaica raising Nettie's son Dre, now an teenager facing the usual problems of fitting in at a new school -- added to the ongoing struggle over whether he is, spiritually speaking, his mother's son or his auntie Joy's boy. The fact that two of the show's five principals are male suggests a capitulation to received ideas of what a TV series, especially a comedy series, is supposed to be about. So also, to use an appropriately conservative phrase, does the new focus on the family. In the stage show, the spotlight was very much on the customers; their lives and experiences were explored through the things they said while sitting in the stylist's chair, or just by how they liked to have their hair done. ("The hair," says Nettie in the TV show, "tells you everything.") A picture of a community was built up. That hasn't happened yet in the new medium. All that domesticity is getting in the way.

To be fair, the new Kink is one workplace show in which convincing work gets done. We learn about the hours, the scheduling, even the actual techniques. We also believe that everyone involved is either good at the job or will be very soon. Well, it makes a change from The Office. Unfortunately, although the authors seem to have been at pains to make the concept less theatrical, they've actually made it more stagy. It feels like a filmed play, even though it isn't one. Make that a videotaped play; film is slicker. 'Da Kink is billed as a comedy, but it plays like a soap -- and nothing as sophisticated as shampoo. A daytime soap at that, with the same leaden pacing, both of writing and performance.

"Everyone relax, Nigel has arrived," says Nigel, arriving. Starr's status is announced by her being told "gentle now, trainee." A posh lady in the first episode was hardly through the door before telling the room "my daughter is -- miracle of miracles -- getting married." "Oh yes," said Nettie, anxious that nothing should be missed, "the society wedding of the year." Talk about exposition.

Well, all right, it's tough setting things up. It might be easier -- on the viewers at least -- if the actors could make less of a meal of it. Anthony herself, continually whirling about to show off Joy's vitality, is the worst offender. She was fun onstage, but she hasn't adapted. I've seen three episodes of 'da Kink (the second airs on Sunday), and though I've sometimes sensed the texture of humour, I haven't laughed once. Episode 3 involves Joy taking the day off to sell jerk chicken at Caribana, and running into trouble for not having a permit. It does seem sort of basic. Also, Nettie meets a man who is personable and divorced and can fix the air conditioning. I wonder where that will lead.

The show does offer Torontonians the pleasure of name-checking; Nettie is addressed as "Empress of Eglinton Avenue." And even viewers further afield may appreciate the bits involving Dre's troubles at school, scorned by a girl he likes for wearing Nikes whose logo includes a tell-tale extra 'e'. As Starr says, remembering her own shy schooldays, "making friends is torture" -- for both sexes. Glad to have that equality recognized.

Dre has also been caught by his outraged mother with a girl in his room, though as tolerant Joy says, "It wasn't a full panty- dropping episode." Well, it makes a change from Weeds -- though both shows have involved jokes about: "coloured people's time" i.e. being late.

There has so far been nothing in the TV show to match the searing monologue about child abuse delivered on stage by d'bi.young. Maybe there won't be; 'da Kink seems to be after tamer game. But, either as comedy or drama or something in between, it needs to get hot to be hot. As hot, in fact, as it once was. - 'da Kink in My Hair airs Sundays on Global

Black & White Photo: / The magic is missing from the popular stage production turned television series -- somewhat ironically, because the direction is still a bit too stagy. Global ;
2007-10-20-the-disease-of-the-century-pl:
The Canadian Stage Company -- no longer, it seems, to be known as CanStage -- often does revivals but seldom does classics, which puts it in awkward territory. If the company were in the music business, you'd say it does high-class pop covers; how long before a new production of Equus? If the plays are British, they tend to fall into the category that William Goldman identified in his Broadway chronicle The Season as the Snob Hit. The Elephant Man, a play whose author is American but that got its start in London and is set there, definitely qualifies. It has a period setting and is based on real events. It also counts as a Disease of the Week Play, or, bearing in mind the extremity of its central character's affliction, a Disease of the Century Play.

Bernard Pomerance's piece takes the story of John Merrick, the hideously deformed young man whose face and body were covered by masses of bony protuberances, and makes of it both a poignant personal history and a lecture-demonstration on the hypocrisies of Victorian, and by possible extension modern, philanthropy. It works better in the first aspect than in the second, especially in this production with Brent Carver playing Merrick.

The play's convention -- self-evidently a wise one -- is to use no make-up or prosthetics to portray the character's plight; everything is conveyed by the actor's stance and the amount of inner pain he can convey. I used to think that any competent actor obeying these rules could play Merrick with the identical results: a conclusion I drew from having seen both the original London actor and the original London understudy and finding them effectively indistinguishable, as well as indistinguishably effective. Carver proves me wrong. There is an ironic tilt to his head, as well as a resigned slump in his frame, as he is stood up in front of a hospital faculty to have his condition described. (It's known now as Proteus syndrome.) Paring everything down, he achieves a grace of body, and of soul. In Pomerance's account, Merrick relishes beauty, longs for love and worries about those whom he believes, extraordinarily, to be even worse off than he is. He whimsically ascribes his own evil fortune to his mother, a beautiful woman, having been frightened by an elephant when she was pregnant. Carver abandons the beauty-of-suffering quaverings that have marred some of his recent performances and asks hard questions in a soft voice. He brings a fastidious comic sensibility up to the edge of tragedy.

All the same, we don't learn much about Merrick, biography apart, except that he was sensitive. Against him, the play sets Frederick Treves, an ambitious young surgeon who rescues him from a brutalized existence as a fairground freak and, with the aid of public subscription, sets him up in relative comfort at the London Hospital. This benevolent act also turns out to be a shrewd career move for Treves and in the second act, the author, in an oblique way, sets about flaying him --and us --for it.

Treves is played by Geraint Wyn Davies, last seen in a Canadian theatre as that other sculptor of human material, Professor Henry Higgins. He is excellent in the first half as businesslike baby- faced saviour and forgivably at sea later on when beset by financial and moral crises that are neither explored nor explained.

Under Treves's protection, Merrick, who at first repelled all who looked upon him, becomes a pet of society: a frillier freak in a fancier fairground. In a sequence that plays like a high-school idea of irony, lords and ladies are paraded before us, each exclaiming that they see reflected in Merrick the best aspects of themselves. We too, are implicitly arraigned for congratulating ourselves on our compassion for his compassion. That is not, in fact, a bad index of how this kind of play works, but I don't know where it leaves the author, who is profiting from the situation on his own account.

In the play as written, and originally produced, there is a kind of rigour to his approach, with each scene prefaced by Brechtian subtitles. Robin Phillips's production tastefully dispenses with these, but is left with short scenes that refuse to meld. His staging is elegant, to no particular purpose; the wrought-iron set, which he seems to have designed himself, is impressive when you enter the theatre but unhelpfully vague once the action starts. Phillips has steered the two central roles well but can't do much with the lesser ones. There's a baffling bit of sub-plot in which Jack Wetherall gets to describe Barry MacGregor as "a moral swamp"; Michael Spencer-Davis makes sadly little of the bullying showman who exploits Merrick and later comes cringing back but compensates as a sleek and pompous prelate. The key-role of a star actress who, more reasonably than most, finds in Merrick a kindred spirit is played by Kate Trotter who makes her as grandiloquent off stage as she may have been on: a pity since the vocal posturings seem to be swathing a decently sympathetic performance

- The Elephant Man plays through Nov. 3 at the Bluma Appel Theatre, 416-368-3110.

2007-10-25-the-several-sides-of-sarah-si:
As a stand-up comic, Sarah Silverman plays wide-eyed and brash. As the protagonist of her own TV show she plays wide-eyed and naive; brash, too, but with a brashness that seems to take its owner by surprise. The sitcom Sarah has been known to apologize, something the stand-up Sarah would never do. (The talk show Sarah has done it, sort of, but that's a third persona, combining elements of the other two.)

The most celebrated line from Silverman's club act --and probably the best --is "I was raped by my doctor; that's kind of bitter- sweet for a Jewish girl." It ranks with, and may well have been influenced by, Lenny Bruce's acceptance of Jewish guilt for killing Jesus: "Yes, we killed him. My family killed him. We killed him because he didn't want to be a doctor."

Silverman has echoed that more directly, too: "I'd kill him again, if he came down here in his Birkenstocks." There is a difference, though. I wouldn't want to push the idea of Bruce-as- moralist too heavily -- he obviously got a personal charge out of shocking people -- but it's plain that he was making savage fun of anti-Semitism. He ridiculed the Christ-killer libel by yoking it to a more benign stereotype, the upwardly-mobile doctor-lover, fostered by Jews themselves. (It's not a joke that would occur to Gentiles to make.) But that was 40 years ago. Silverman operates in an entertainment world in which it's OK to be Jewish. She's early- Barbra Streisand for the 21st-century.

Her demeanour -- demure and mentally if not physically gawky, sets off the forthrightness of her sex and bodily-function jokes. (She's disinclined to separate the two.)

She gets closer to actual outrageousness when she takes on other races: "The best time to have a baby is when you're a black teenager." "[My black boyfriend] has to start loving himself before I can stop hating his people."

A talk-show reference to "Chinks" famously got her into trouble; she said sorry, but also said that it made her wonder about her own people: "Are we losing our control of the media?" But she is also, in effect, making common cause with black comedians in their observation of how the culture, their own included, depicts African- Americans.

Each episode of her TV show concludes with her telling her dog (played by her dog) what she has learned from this week's adventures. In one, "I learned that older black women are wise beyond their years and younger black women are prostitutes." In her solo act, she has the perfect response to her critics: "I don't base my material on stereotypes -- I base it on fact" -- a dazzling piece of double-bluff that first rebuffs the imputation of bias, and then reinstates it, twice as hard.

It's the real Sarah commenting on the imaginary Sarah. (Not that I'm sure which is which. Or that she is.) This sets her apart from the boring majority of stand-ups, of any race or either gender. They rant; she characterizes. She's in the same self-ironizing game as Stephen Colbert.

She has a regrettable weakness for atrocious puns. The first episode of her current TV series was called "Bored of the Rings", and it wasn't even a Tolkien parody. It started with her invading a church whose bells had been keeping her awake, and demanding "to speak to the manager." (She must be super-sensitive. When I was an undergraduate I lived next door to King's College Chapel, Cambridge, which has the most clangorous chimes west of Notre Dame. It took me just two Sundays to learn to sleep through them.) "He's called Jesus of Nazareth," she said, "not Jesus of Noisareth."

I felt like switching off right there, but she promptly redeemed herself by looking around the building, which was absolutely packed, and muttering "no wonder no one goes to church anymore -- Jesus." The absurdity of the Sarah character --a self-proclaimed "mixture of ignorance and arrogance" -- comes into sharper relief when there are others present, and is more endearing too. The action progressed to find her recruited by two nice WASP ladies who were against killing babies, an uncontroversial cause if ever there was one; it took her an improbably long but very funny time to discover that they were militant anti-abortionists. Shock-horror from Sarah, who had had three abortions, looked forward to more and seemed to regard the whole procedure as rather cuddly.

Actually, tweaked and recut a bit, this show might make good pro- life propaganda; the ladies, despite their stern appearance ("were you,' asked Sarah, "styled by angry lesbians?"), were acted with perfect seriousness. In the way it distributed its sympathies, the show perfectly reflected most people's mixed feelings on the issue. It took place, like all the other episodes, in Valley Village, Calif., a community that seems able, like The Simpsons' Springfield, to expand and contract at will.

It feels like a village but supports not only a crowded church but a thriving full-time abortion clinic, saved from destruction at the last minute by Sarah's two best friends, a pair of overweight gays, roused from all-night session of Dungeons and Dragons (they haven't progressed to video games) to ride to the rescue in full medieval fig.

One of them took an arrow in his posterior which Sarah removed using the clinic's suction-pump. This is what you call elegant construction. The sitcom shows a capacity for affection that the stand-up Sarah would never have countenanced. That's what happens when you let other people into your world, and have to make up stories for them: tolerance.

- The Sarah Silverman Program airs tonight at 10:30 p.m. on the Comedy Network.
