2007-10-27-sins-of-the-father-hannah-mos:
Hannah Moscovitch is 29, so it's a bit early to go hunting for grand patterns in her work. Nevertheless, the four plays of hers I've seen, all of which I like a lot, do seem to have a common theme. That theme, an inherently dramatic one, is entrapment. Her new play, East of Berlin, presents this in classic form. Its hero might be under a Greek curse. He might also be under a Biblical curse. There's a note in the program that's labelled "The Sins of the Father," but even without that it would be impossible to sit through this piece's packed 90 minutes without that text coming to mind.

The father's sin in this play is a damnable one; he was a doctor at Auschwitz. Like so many Nazis, he fled to Paraguay after the war, with his wife and his young son, Rudi. The play is Rudi's monologue, interspersed with encounters with two other people. Rudi has grown up in ignorance of his father's past (he's now a real estate salesman) until a friend, a more precocious and inquisitive boy called Hermann with equivalent skeletons in his own family closet, clues him in. Rudi, now in his late teens, is naturally appalled. He confronts his father, who doesn't exactly deny the charges but doesn't admit much guilt either: He had no choice, he would have been punished had he refused, and so on. (According to Jonah Goldhagen's Hitler's Willing Executioners -- admittedly a tendentious book -- this isn't true.) His wife reveals that she urged him to stay, which seems all too plausible.

These parental encounters are narrated, not shown, but we do witness the crucial conversations with Hermann, which end in a seduction. Hermann is gay, Rudi isn't, but it's Rudi who makes the advances, primarily as a way of getting back at his old man. This isn't enough rebellion, though, so Rudi takes himself off to study in Berlin. He's financed by a grant from a Nazi foundation; I usually despise exclamation points, but !

Dropping out of medical school (the apple doesn't fall, etc.), he spends his time in the archives, researching his father's guilt. There he meets Sarah, a German-Jew-ish-American girl investigating her own family's history, i.e., the same subject from the opposite side. The two fall, axiomatically, in love. Moscovitch, who has reported on love in previous plays, here proves herself capable of presenting it: economically, delightfully, movingly.

Both are turned on by the differences between them; and for Rudi especially -- if he shocked his father with a gay fling, then how about a Jewish marriage? Naturally, he puts off telling Sarah the whole truth. When it comes out, he's faced with an impossible choice: of loyalties, of betrayals. And it isn't his fault, any more than it was Hamlet's or Oedipus's. Less, really. But that never let anybody off the hook. We're always told that plays should ask us questions. Usually the questions are rigged. But when Rudi at the end asks our approval for whatever it is he's about to do (what he actually says, chillingly, is "This is the only solution, isn't it?") we are thoroughly implicated. Also, we wouldn't know what to tell him. Psychologically, this is truthful; morally, it's just; dramatically, it's terrific.

The play's first half is disconcerting: not in subject, but in tone. Moscovitch's sense of humour, dark but not cynical, is at full alert here, but as we don't yet know whom Rudi is talking to, or why, he comes off more glib than troubled. It's only in retrospect that we understand; and even at that a line like "I thought you were resettled -- I mean dead" sticks in the gullet. The evening doesn't fall into what I'd call theatrical present tense until Sarah appears, from then on it moves like fate on wheels, prompting lumps in the throat and knots in the stomach.

Alisa Palmer's direction is both sensitive and tense. Camellia Koo's set is magnificent: a long, ashen book-lined wall that does duty for any number of drawing-rooms and libraries, culminating in the Auschwitz archive and, by extension, the camp itself. Michael Walton supplies superbly ominous lighting, and John Gzowski a haunting sound score, full of half-heard melodies.

As for the acting: Brendan Gall's Rudi, like the play itself, takes time to come into focus, but it develops into a wrenching study of gangling guilt and of hope perpetually deferred. Paul Dunn's Hermann, edgy and chipper, brings a surge of energy whenever he appears. Diana Donnelly, who has moved with increasing assurance since her initial misstep with Major Barbara, hits full stride here; her Sarah has exactly the right measure of wariness and abandon. Moscovitch has usually been lucky in her interpreters, and they in her; the match here is just about perfect

- East of Berlin runs through Nov. 25 at the Tarragon Extra Space. Call 416-531-1827 for more information.

Color Photo: Cylla Von Tiedemann / Two friends discover a family secret. Paul Dunn, left, and Brendan Gall star in East of Berlin. ;
2007-10-31-more-sickness-than-health:
You know about metatheatre: a play or show that comments on its own nature or its own circumstances. The original production of Le Malade Imaginaire, Moliere's last play, is a strong contender for greatest metatheatrical event, ever. (Don't rush; it opened and closed in 1673.)

In this satirical comedy about a hypochondriac, the title role was played by the author himself who was himself very ill and who pulled off an unrepeatable coup at the fourth performance by dying, right there on stage.

That's the legend, anyway. When the audiences at the three previous performances heard about it, they must have felt cheated. But even they had been treated to a jolt of what we preposterously call post-modernism, though it's obviously as old as Aristophanes. They got to hear Moliere, who had already made fun of doctors in his other plays, railing in his protagonist's persona about the theatrical libels perpetrated on the medical profession by that intolerable scoundrel Moliere. Laugh? They thought he'd die.

This scene still comes off well in the Pleiades Theatre revival entitled Dying to be Sick. Unfortunately, it's about the only scene that does.

The translation, by Adrienne Clarkson and Pleiades' founder John Van Burek, may well be very good (it leaves in tasty gobbets of the original French, just as Van Burek's Goldoni translations regaled us with the occasional mouthful of Italian) but most of the actors mash it up so much that it's hard to be sure.

This isn't altogether their fault; the director, Brendan Healy, has put them into grotesquely exaggerated wigs and frocks, and ordered up strangled accents and coy balletic poses to match. Almost the only person on stage allowed to act like a human being is Hardee Lineham as Argan himself, the perpetual patient; he delivers a funny and credible account of a tetchy tyrant, high on his own imagined sufferings, living only for his next prescription enema.

The production must think that his humanity will be thrown into sharper relief if he's surrounded by shrieking cartoons who might be his bad dreams come to life.

It doesn't work that way, though. The play's satire on human credulity, especially in matters of health and mortality, may be forever pertinent, and its jabs at the price of drugs certainly strike home right here and now, but it's still a one-joke assembly- line piece that needs all the reality it can get.

Argan, like many earlier Moliere figures, is an obsessive who takes his delusions out on his immediate family. Like his predecessors he has a daughter whom he wants to marry off to a man who'll humour his fantasies (she, of course, is in love with someone else) and a wise maidservant who does her best to save him from himself.

In this production, the maid (Michelle Polak) is a cackling ninny, the daughter (Stephanie Broschart) a simpering gold-digger -- a shallowly cynical idea quite unsupported by the text -- and her true love (Karl Ang) a nondescript accomplice.

It may have been my fancy but I sensed that all these actors were having qualms about taking their director's medicine and would have preferred to play their characters undoctored. The actress playing Madame Argan, who really is a gold digger, seemed on the other hand to be enjoying herself going over the top, and I found it hard to forgive her for it. It is of course possible for actors to achieve truth through caricature, but they probably need to be more accomplished or experienced than most of those here.

The only one who doesn't let his trappings play him is Alex Poch- Goldin as the youngest of the play's parade of venal quacks. You can understand what he's saying and why.

There are no trappings on Victor Ertmanis as the hero's brother- in-law -- the one who offers to take him to a comedy by Moliere -- and his entry brings a breath of fresh air. But he dissipates it when he starts belabouring his points; as the play's voice of reason, he shouldn't sound so desperate about his own arguments.

The play ends with a harlequinade sequence -- it's officially called a ballet --in which the hypochondriac, cured of thinking himself incurable, is mockingly transformed into a physician.

William Hutt, in an otherwise forgettable Stratford production, once did this enchantingly, tossing off phrases in Latin as if in a dream. This production, true to its own logic -- and it does know what it's doing, even if what it is doing is wrong -- makes it more of a nightmare.

It doesn't have either the skills or the resources for the job, and it seems to go on forever, but my impression was that Argan died at the end of it. That would make it the author's own joke, trumped; at least one other revival has had the same idea.

But as Moliere himself was uniquely equipped to remind us: Dying is easy, comedy's hard. - Dying to be Sick runs until Nov. 4 at the Theatre Centre. Call 416-872-1212 for more information.
2007-11-01-comedy-that-goes-down-like-a-:
There's a promo going around for the new season of It's Always Sunny in Philadelphia that's a parody of Friends. It starts, as Friends used to, with its principal characters crowding one another on a sofa in front of a fountain. Then they fall in. And just to make the point clear, the screen flashes a title proclaiming that this show is UNFRIENDLY.

I'm all in favour of Friends being taken down a peg, but I have to admit that it managed to maintain its impetus for most of its lifespan. The Philly show seems to have exhausted its energies at the start of its third season.

Like Friends, it rotates around an urban watering-hole; only instead of a yuppie coffee shop where a couple of the characters work, we get a run-down Irish pub where all of them do. (So it's also, in socio-economic-televisual terms, a poor man's Cheers.) The five leads, Mac, Charlie, Dennis, Dee and Frank, are all very similar to one another. Frank is Dee and Dennis' adoptive father -- they're twins --and probably Charlie's biological one, though this has yet to be fully acknowledged. Frank is played by Danny De-Vito, who only joined the team in the second season and who looks as if he's slumming.

The characteristics they all share are greed, sloth, lust (usually frustrated) and ignorance. This makes them pretty representative of the human condition, but it's just about all there is to them; the quintet have congealed into a mass, so that who does what in any given story-line looks arbitrary. Selfishness and stupidity may not on their own be enough to power a comedy, at least not over the long haul.

Sunday's kick-off episode starts out with Frank decrying the idea of what he calls "global heating." That turns out to be the best line in the show; the writers, Rob McElhenny (who

plays Mac) and Glenn Howerton (who plays Dennis) are too laid- back to go in much for verbal wit. What they rely on is people doing outrageous things with straight faces, and after a while this becomes self-defeating.

The gang find a baby abandoned in a dumpster. Dee and Mac decide to take care of it; at least Mac decides that Dee will take care of it while he basks in the glory of instant fatherhood. It gets worse. Told that the kid would look great in commercials, they set about blacking him up, since the market is already flooded with white mites. I hear the sound of writers' desperation.

Meanwhile, in related stories, Frank and Charlie go trawling through the trash for other valuable objects, which goes absolutely nowhere, while Dennis gets embroiled with a hippie tree-hugger (literally) who's cast aspersions on his own born-again environmentalism. That's the best part of the show.

Next week's show is better. Mac and the twins try out for the NFL's Philadelphia Eagles. The guys pour scorn on Dee's efforts because she's a girl with scoliosis, but mainly because she's a girl. Meanwhile, Frank has an acid trip which is deeply unamusing. More entertainingly, the regulars confront a rival clan, the McPoyles, who boast their own sports champion, Doyle McPoyle. Some of their interchanges almost count as character comedy.

It's Always Sunny started with modest ambitions and an even more modest budget and, but it may have been spoiled by success. At the moment, though, it's (almost) never funny in Philadelphia.

2007-11-03-season-starts-with-decades-be:
Theatre Passe Muraille begins its new season by reviving its greatest of the decade. This new production of Michael Healey's The Drawer Boy is, in fact, a multiply commemorative occasion. It marks the 40th anniversary of TPM itself. It's the first offering under the theatre's new artistic director, Andy McKim, and, by the same token, a valedictory tribute to his predecessor, Layne Coleman, under whose aegis the play was first staged. It's also a tribute to TPM's own origins, since The Drawer Boy is partly inspired by The Farm Show, the collective production of 1972 that first put this theatre on the map. And, if I may, it's a personal milestone for me. The Drawer Boy was the first substantial new play I reviewed for the National Post, and I still remember the delight I felt at discovering it. Its initial impact and subsequent reverberations, across the country and outside it, remain unsurpassed, and very nearly unrivalled; among later plays only Kristen Thomson's I Claudia and John Mighton's Half Life come close.

Healey himself has written subsequent plays, Plan B and Generous, that are more adventurous technically and wider-ranging intellectually. None, though, has characters with the autonomous life of those in The Drawer Boy or a story that unfolds with the same folkloric ease. It feels, still, like the one play its author had to write; one that welled up within him and may have taken even him by surprise.

It's a simple enough tale. In the '70s, a young actor working on a project not unlike The Farm Show billets himself for research purposes on an Ontario farm run by two middle-aged men, lifelong friends, named Morgan and Angus. The actor's name is Miles, after Miles Potter, who was both a member of the actual Farm Show troupe and, nearly 30 years later, the first director of The Drawer Boy.

Angus suffered a brain injury in the Second World War that robbed him of all but the shortest-term memory; he is, however, a genius at figures. He loves to hear Morgan tell him the story of his accident and of the two Englishwomen -- "the tall girl" and "the taller girl" -- whom the two friends loved and lost. Angus, who was once a gifted draughts-man, figures in this narrative as "the drawer boy." Miles overhears the story, and puts it in the show. (He hasn't been getting very far in rehearsals with his impressions of the inner life of cows destined for slaughter, maybe because Morgan, who has a cruel streak, has been putting him on.) He invites his hosts to a rehearsal; Morgan is incensed at hearing his words onstage, but Angus is enchanted. He begins to remember things. And Morgan has to reveal some hidden truths.

The play is a fable, maybe a simplistic one, about the power of performance, both for spectators and participants. Like Hamlet, though less calculatingly, Miles uses a play to catch his auditors' conscience; and The Drawer Boy in fact includes a hilarious riff on the Danish play, though without any direct reference to the play scene. What it isn't, whatever Healey's intentions may have been, is much of a tribute to The Farm Show. Admittedly, that production was long before my time in Canada and it probably wouldn't have been my kind of theatre anyway, but it does seem that what moves Miles about his hosts' history, and what moves us, has very little to do with farming or indeed with Ontario. It could have happened to anybody.

It's impossible to avoid comparing this new production with the original, and I'm not going to try. Ruth Madoc-Jones's direction doesn't have the richness and detail

of Potter's, but it's very lucid and in clarifying the last scenes, which seem rather hurried in the writing, it may even have the edge.

It does have a younger pair of farmers, so the chains that bind them, both of affection and resentment, weigh less heavy. Randy Hughson's Angus doesn't have the unique massive presence of David Fox but that ends up working to his advantage. Fox was so much himself that one couldn't imagine his ever being any different; with Hughson, glimpses of the sensitive and intelligent man he once was keep peeping through, and the effect is immensely moving. When he cried, I did, too, as I never have at this play before. And earlier on, with Hughson using his quick-fire timing to convey Angus's instant memory lapses, I laughed, too. It's a joy to see this actor in a substantial role again.

John Jarvis's Morgan lacks the agrarian authenticity brought to the role by Jerry Franken, but in all other respects he's fine. The dialogue in this play remains wonderfully sure and resonant, and Jarvis gets the two best lines. One is Morgan's sardonic response to Miles's query about the farmer's alternating round of tending and killing: "Miles, it's an emotional roller coaster." (I've been Healey's willing slave ever since first hearing it.) The other is his memory of the words spoken to him by the woman who was leaving him: "This is the worst thing I could possibly do to you. Don't you dare help me."

Miles is the least flashy role and Tom Barnett, who created it, got less attention than his colleagues. In retrospect, this was unfair; his eager solidity is much missed in Frank Cox-O'Connell's performance, which starts out as a flapping cartoon, though it acquires some stature when Miles himself becomes part of the story instead of just listening to it. It's a little easier, too, to understand why he agrees to perform all the ludicrous chores that Morgan sets him. As a docile actor, he's just taking direction.

- The Drawer Boy runs through Nov. 18 at Theatre Passe Muraille. Call 416-504-7529 for details.

2007-11-07-dirtys-delicious-darlings-eye:
'Iwant," said one of the spoiled-rotten young things on Dirty Sexy Money ,"to be a human being." This was in the first episode, which aired six weeks ago, and it struck me at the time that she'd come to the wrong show. Now I'm not so sure. Nobody is going to give DSM, as it shall henceforth be known, marks for ruthless realism. But it is succeeding on all levels, and to do that it has to create its own kind of truth.

It's enjoyable social-calendar, eye-candy trash. It has a mystery plot as its baseline, not nail-bitingly tense, but compelling in a relaxed way that's rather refreshing. It has the apparently effortless wit that TV shows so often find it easier to attain when they are not structured or marketed as comedies. It's very well acted.

Besides, how would most of us know whether it was real? DSM centres on the Darling family, who are darling in the way that's only possible when the head of the house is a millionaire, probably multi. (Not a billionaire. There is one of those on the show, and Papa Darling describes him as such, as if aware of the gulf between them. Not that he sounds very awestruck about it. He seems to loathe the guy. Where the right lies, if it lies anywhere, is yet to be revealed.) The younger Darlings carry on as if they too were millionaires, or at least have splendiferous allowances; Trickle- down economics can work if your circumstances are rarefied enough.

Set against all this corruption (we assume) and decadence (we know) is our hero Nick, a New York lawyer primarily engaged in representing charities pro bono; That is, he works like a dog and gets thrown a bone. Nick's late father, known as Dutch, devoted his life to being the Darlings' consigliere, and Nick has been offered the chance to go the same route.

Despite initial skepticism, that borders on repulsion, Nick accepts: for a variety of reasons that include discovering who, if anyone, killed his dad. Peter Krause plays Nick and he brings to the role, and to the antics that surround him, an expanded version of the amused bemusement that distinguished his performance in Six Feet Under (which I heretically think was a less good show).

Krause has marvellous chemistry with Donald Sutherland, who plays Tripp, the Darling-in-chief; The two are partners in a Faustian bargain of which both are well aware and that neither cares to bring to the surface. What goes on between them is not just a battle of wits, but a battle of wit, and both performances quietly gleam.

An enemy of Tripp's warns Nick that "He's not what you think he is." But Nick doesn't know what he thinks Tripp is, and neither do we. The show's richest men are very nice to Nick -- suspiciously so - - and Nick is very nice to everyone, in a tolerantly judgmental sort of way. He behaves like everybody's uncle -- perhaps, in view of his ancestry, their Dutch uncle.

Tripp Darling is cultured. He gives his chauffeur (who doubles as personal airplane-pilot, and trebles as fall-guy every time a family member commits a traffic offence) a copy of Xenophon and tells him to keep at it; The rewards will justify the effort.

Sutherland does this kind of thing beautifully, with a great paternalistic purr. He has more trouble keeping his immediate family in line. He's recently discovered -- or did he always know? -- that his wife Letitia (a majestic Jill Clayburgh) was carrying on for forty years with his late friend and lawyer. As a result, one of Tripp's children isn't his -- so Letitia has been getting in Dutch, as well as vice versa -- but we have been left guessing which. They're a fine collection, all raised to believe that money can buy anything and anybody.

There's Patrick, a senate hopeful, who's played, very well, by Willliam Baldwin. He's being groomed as a future president of the U.S. and he does seem to have a few ideals. However his chances of even making it to senator are jeopardized by an affair with a transsexual hooker. (That's what the exasperated Nick calls her. Patrick denies she's a hooker.)

There's Karen, on the brink of her fourth marriage, but still with her hooks into Nick,

her childhood sweetheart: "He deflowered me," she informs her current fiance, who seems commendably unfazed. It may be an index of how deeply the show has its hooks into me that I've come to detest Karen for her transparent campaign to snatch Nick from his nice normal wife Lisa. It would be cool if she turned out to be the bastard, making her Nick's half-sister, but I doubt the show would go there.

On the other hand, it has given us the Darling twins, Jeremy and Juliet, in whom the sense of entitlement (and resentment over it) reaches delirious depths, and who revel in their "twintuition" which they carry to the verge of being twincestuous.

The remaining sibling is Brian, a priest with an illegitimate son whom he's trying to pass off as a Swedish orphan. At first I thought Brian was a Catholic priest, but it turns out he's married; I'm not sure whether that makes his situation more or less shocking. He started out as the most obnoxious character, and he's still the sharpest-tongued, but as life has closed in on him he's become rather endearing.

The show also features guest celebrities. Some are kept waiting, unheard and unseen, on the ends of phones ("Hey, Condi!"), some appear as themselves (Dan Rather covers a Darling party), some even act (Peter Bogdanovich, perhaps the world's best cameo performer, put in a delightful appearance in the first week, though I have no idea who he was meant to be).

For all its mix of schadenfreude and voyeurism, DSM avoids the airless camp of Dynasty or Dallas, still the definitive plutocratic soaps. (Which reminds me: Juliet, told by Jeremy that Pluto's not a planet, replied ineffably, "It will always be a planet to me.") It's kept grounded by being viewed through the quizzical eyes of Nick, whose status as narrator must mean that he'll be alive at the end, unless of course they're going to pull a Sunset Boulevard on us.

I hope, anyway, that everything will be wrapped up in a single series. That would be so much classier. Though with all that Dirty Sexy Money at stake, I wouldn't want to bet on it.

- Dirty Sexy Money airs tonight at 10 p.m. on A-Channel.

2007-11-07-it-s-time-to-lose-that-1950s-:
Each week in our All About series, we introduce our subject on Tuesday, feature a first-person essay on Wednesday and open up the pages to our readers on Thursday. This week we look at TV snobs. Are you ashamed of what you watch? Send your thoughts to allabout@nationalpost.com

Dr. Rob Buckman, oncologist, author, medical educator and comedian, recently reconnected his television. Before that, he and his family had passed through a two-month period of disconnection (from the TV, not from one another). The fault, he says, was not in the programs, but in him. "I've got a seriously addictive personality. If the TV is on, I can only memorize what's on the TV."

His children were similarly hooked, as children tend to be. Most of the family "found it easier to watch cartoons" than to concentrate on schoolwork, housework or just work. The exception in the Buckman household is his wife, also a doctor, who, he says, "can read, talk on the telephone, make notes and watch television all at the same time. Whereas I can't even do one of those things at a time."

He did rent DVDs , during the period of abstinence, but this proved a worse situation. The Buckmans found, like so many before them, that they had a pile of discs that they could never find the time to watch, all stacked up and reproachful. So, three or four weeks ago, they rejoined the world; Principally, Buckman insists, so that his wife could watch CNN. ("I do, too" he claims.) But they try, he says, "not to watch repeats of cartoons and sitcoms. We have a rule: My wife has the remote."

Surprisingly, perhaps, they have only signed on for the basic service. They don't, for example, get HBO. Buckman acknowledges that this means missing out on some good shows, at least until they come out on DVD or reappear on the networks. He especially likes Dexter, which he feels has "conflicts beyond most characters on TV, even The Sopranos." (We differ here. Seriously).

He doesn't find any conflict between abjuring most television, and himself pursuing a TV career which, he says, "is going on quite nicely" with regular guest-expert appearances on TVO, Citytv, CTV "and so on."

Only he doesn't regard it as a career. He calls it "an explaining sideline: part of my general shtick of trying to explain complex stuff simply."

So Buckman's first abandoning, then rationing, his TV watching is "a reflection on the household, not on the medium. We needed to go into rehab, and then get back."

He is not a TV snob, or rather he isn't an anti-TV snob. In fact, he doubts if many people are any more. "That attitude of 'I wouldn't have one in the house' is very '50s. Like saying now that you wouldn't have a computer. It would be a bit of an embarrassment to people."

Buckman was a kid in London in the 1950s, as was I, and back there and back then, that attitude was certainly widespread, if only because a television was still a comparative rarity.

My father was in the retail trade so we were among the privileged ones and it seems to me, looking back, that nobody had the right to be snobbish about TV, if only because in England it didn't banish radio. (It still hasn't.)

Television was a large part of my education; seeing a BBC children's version of A Midsummer Night's Dream, when I was seven or eight, was probably the formative cultural event of my life. There was a lot of drama on TV in those days -- first adaptations from the stage and then, increasingly, original scripts -- and it was taken for granted that they'd exist and be good; unlike today when the single play, on both sides of the Atlantic, is a rare and much- trumpeted event, surrounded by a general presumption that it's going to fail.

I have a friend in New York, a major theatre and movie buff, who confines his TV watching to three events a year: the Oscars, the Tonys and -- perhaps by way of expanding his horizons -- the Miss World contest. Otherwise he despises TV as a hopelessly inartistic medium; The screen is too small.

It is, though, the long-form drama series that seems to have rekindled interest in TV among the cultural classes. One noted Canadian actress, who describes her watching as "selective but very loyal," says that her impression of TV was certainly affected by The Sopranos, which she agrees was "the nonpareil," though she personally preferred Six Feet Under ("about the best thing television had ever produced") and The West Wing.

She was turned on to the latter by her teenager, which must be a very common phenomenon; My own viewing over the last two decades has been guided by my children, from Sesame Street to Jon Stewart. And she does know people who won't have a TV, or will only watch the public stations: "I can't even get them to watch the Shopping Channel." So she's eclectic. But professional standards come into play here; She rates the Shopping Channel's presenters very highly indeed.

The only person I know in Canada who doesn't own a television is the actor and Soulpepper stalwart William Webster. At least I thought he didn't own one. It turns out he does -- he inherited it when a relationship ended -- but never turns it on. "I didn't want to waste time, as I had before, switching channels, trying to find a political debate that wasn't degrading, rude and uncivil." (Good luck.)

"I was becoming interested in poetry; Having spent 40 years reciting it, I wanted to understand it. So I'd rather spend my time reading good books, the occasional newspaper, trying to make sense of what's in The New York Times or The New Yorker."

He's very thorough about this, maybe confirming Buckman's diagnosis: "I live in the 19th century. I don't have a computer. And when I did see something on TV, I used to hate the bad acting, like bad vaudeville. I thought I'd rather go to a play. I'm very snobby. I'm sure I'm missing a lot. I've never seen The Sopranos. I did see an episode of The Office-- the U.K. version -- and I thought, 'I like this' -- the sense of eavesdropping on all the banalities and horrors of group existence, the intrigue and gossip that we all love as human beings."

But it's nature programs, which he used to enjoy, that prompt his most sweeping denunciation of the medium. "I thought 'if I have to see one more alligator chomping down on a bloated hippo somewhere...' It's all about the excesses of American capitalism. It's all about the food chain."

For more All About, visit nationalpost.com/allabout
2007-11-08-home-violent-home:
THEATRE REVIEW

LULLABY

Simone Interiors,

1690 Queen St. West

---

At the back of an interior design story in gentrified Parkdale, a new company called Dark Horse Theatre has staged a play about the gentrification of Parkdale. That, at least, is the hook. Looch, an aspiring young businessman, and his girlfriend Leandra buy a house, renovate it, and let out the basement. Their prospective tenant is a middle-aged guy named Kenny who claims to be an old inhabitant of the neighbourhood. He looks and sounds down and out but is able to offer $1,500, cash, in advance. You'd think he'd won the lottery.

As a matter of fact, he has won the lottery; at least so he says, and Thelon Oening's Lullaby never explicitly contradicts him. It does tell us that Kenny has done time, probably more than once. These two factors put together are enough to make him an atypical case on which to build a play about the old, local order being forced to give way to the new. (Well, maybe it isn't about that, but that's what it's been touted as being about.) In much the same way, our yuppie couple seem exception-ally feckless as home-owners; enough goes wrong with the place, quite apart from what Kenny gets up or down to, for us to wonder if they ever bothered to have it inspected. But then they do seem to be trusting a lot in Looch's rich dad to see them through; they need him, as both Looch and Leandra are having job problems. These, however, are kept shadowy.

The construction of Lullaby is about as rickety as that of the house it depicts. This matters, though, surprisingly little. Oening, a new writer, has a gift for pungent and free-flowing dialogue, and Kenny is a creation. He isn't a totally original creation; he's one of those cuckoo-in-the-nest home-breakers (as opposed to housebreakers) who abounds in modern drama and whose archetype is the tramp in Pinter's The Caretaker. David Ferry is a master at this kind of role; he played another wheedling, threatening, cash- flashing intruder in Daniel Karasik's In Full Light, at Summerworks. There are differences, though: Kenny is a yarn-spinning melancholic with anger simmering; Ferry is very powerful when it boils over. He plays deafening music, he keeps intruding on his landlords' living- quarters, drinks and does drugs. He also takes what seems to be a genuine -- if intrusive -- interest in

the lives of his hosts, especially Leandra.

She is going through professional and emotional withdrawal; and the play is very persuasive at charting her attraction-repulsion towards Kenny: She's afraid of him; she comes to depend on him (and his store of champagne and dope and painkillers); and she feels protective towards him. "You must stop trying to buy people," she tells him, and it's certain that his money isn't making him happy. Amy Rutherford's Leandra is her best performance to date. She sounds, for the first time, as good as she looks, and she achieves a remarkable vocal and emotional fullness in a confined space. Dusan Dukic's Looch, by contrast, is excessively low-keyed, but he does have the sketchiest, most schematic role; he grows as hostile towards Kenny as Leandra is indulgent, and ends up seeing him as a rival, though, of course, he can't bring himself to acknowledge it. This is the second play in two days to feature a fight between its two male characters, and this one is vicious.

Jennifer H. Capraru, the director, clearly lays out the play's emotional geography but runs into problems, probably not of her own making, with the physical. A site-specific production raises high expectations of scenic realism; otherwise, why not set the play on a conventional stage? Here we have a living-room that changes without warning into a bedroom, and a basement that seems to be on the same level as the rest of the house. When you stop believing in a play's spatial dynamic, you start having problems with its character dynamics as well. This aside, the design is excellent; as might be expected, since it's by Tamara Marie Kucheran, who's also responsible for the Passe Muraille revival of The Drawer Boy and, last year at Stratford, for the gorgeous Fanny Kemble. The play's title is a poser; it doesn't acquire any relevance until the play is almost over, and it seems arbitrary and sentimental when it does. But it isn't quite the end; and when Ferry's Kenny shuffles off into the night, leaving chaos behind him, he moves you not as a figure on a sociologist's graph, but as a complex, inexplicable human being. - Performances run through Nov. 18. For tickets, call 416-460-9306.

2007-11-08-the-dragon-awakens-in-more-wa:
For the second time this week, I find myself writing about dirty, sexy money. Sexy money, anyway. According to the Galafilm documentary China's Sexual Revolution (airing tonight on CBC) there are more sex shops in China's biggest cities than in most cities in the West. And 75% of the worlds sex toys are made in China. But then, isnt 75% of everything?

They had a lot of catching up to do, and fast. It's happening" says the commentary "at warp speed. There was the cultural revolution, and then there was the economic revolution--pretty much its opposite -- and the sexual revolution is their child: a troublesome one as you might expect, coming from such incompatible parents.

The film, written and directed by Josh Freed and Miro Cernetig, takes us on a guided tour of China's new strip clubs, massage parlours and talk radio shows and liberated blogs that are not so much confessional as exultant. A young lady called Muzemei recorded the sounds of her own love-making and posted it on the Internet; it was so popular the server crashed for days. (Shes a revolutionary," says one observer. "Ten years ago she would have gone to jail.)

It all looks like a hyped-up version of our own world: the gospel according to Sex and the City, except that Sex and the City never took itself as gospel. The liberated sex presented here acts as if had something to prove. In that respect, its the cultural counterrevolution, as earnest as its opposite.

Some of the most compelling parts of the film--if only because they are, to us, the strangest -- concern that earlier time, when Red Guards patrolled towns and villages, and when immoral behaviour - -holding hands, for example-- would lead, at the very least, to a terrifying bout of enforced self-criticism.

The rejection of all this is quite explicit. I don't care what Chairman Mao thinks of my life" says one contemporary young woman. Well, he is dead. And, as the film delights in pointing out, when alive he was a hypocrite, a man of imperial tastes who thought a steady diet of virgins would keep him young.

But the old legacy still persists, and in a malign and unexpected way. China's "one-child policy produced a conflict between the imposed economy and the traditional peasant desire for a male heir. Science came to the rescue; female children were aborted. The result is that young men now outnumber young women by the millions.

No wonder the smart young females in the cities look so pleased; they have freedom and choice. The men, especially the poorer ones, end up frustrated. Theres a huge demand for prostitutes. And, though the statistical disproportion in the countryside is presumably the same as in the towns, the poor young women who have emigrated from the villages, end up supplying it.

China has the fastest-growing sex trade in the world. The film presents Chinas sexual revolution as primarily a woman's thing (maybe because of the Western tradition that women talking about sex make better copy); it also seems to be a rich person's thing.

As expected, there are many of the older people who deplore it. It may be all right for Europe, says one. There even homosexuality is normal." (This is the only time that subject is mentioned. Maybe it just doesnt happen in China. Like in Iran.) "But China doesnt want it.

So who," asks the commentary, in one of those bright summaries guaranteed to set the teeth on edge, "will win? The older generation, or generation sex? How far have they come from Mao to now?

There are clues apparently: It may be impossible to chain the new sexual dragon," (shot of a statue of a dragon, with a chain around its neck) "but parents are coming around. And indeed one mother does say, tolerantly or maybe just resignedly, that she looks at the world and it's just like television, a sigh that might echo round the world.

Where, the film inquires as if not expecting an answer, will it all lead: To a brave new world of sexuality or a Great Leap Backward?" Well, probably neither, but on the evidence provided the former's likelier than the latter, and certainly more likeable.

"This, says one contributing female expert, is one of the funniest periods in China for a long time." A male professor, who has some misgivings about the way things may be going, is still very clear about the alternative, one that he himself lived through: "If the cultural revolution comes again, he says, I will kill myself."

- China's Sexual Revolution airs tonight at 9 p.m. on CBC.

THEATRE REVIEW

NO GOOD REASON

Young Centre for the Performing Arts

---

There are two characters in Stephen Baetz's No Good Reason, both of them shell-shocked soldiers from the First World War. We meet them on the terrace of a military hospital in Kent that is dedicated to the recuperation of only the Canadian troops. One of them, Will, is an officer who is compulsively re-living the horrors of active service. In the first couple of brief scenes, we watch him hurl himself, wordlessly and alarmingly, around the stage, while his companion Sam, who is wheelchair-bound but seems better adjusted, watches with concern.

The play proceeds on the premise that a play about the horrors of one war will automatically get us thinking about those of all wars. To an extent that's true, but those thoughts aren't going to be either deep or disturbing unless the play itself is. We need to care about the characters in their own right before we can make any useful comparisons.

These two boys never come to life. The script keeps hopping from one aspect of their situation to another, never alighting long enough to illuminate anything. They act as mutual
therapists:Will gets Sam out of his chair, Sam jollies Will out of some of his terrors. There are bits about their girls back
home: Will has a fiancee whom, in his shattered state, he's afraid to contact; Sam speaks of a love who is plainly a fantasy. There are flashbacks to the traumas of the trenches. There are references to a tyrannical doctor who's trying to make Will forget when Sam knows that his only hope is to remember. It all gets to seem like filler. Even the characters' doubts about what it was all for -- the aspect that's meant to remind us of Iraq and Afghanistan-- are perfunctory.

The familiar "you be your girlfriend and I'll be you" routine (nothing physical; it's about help in writing a letter home) yields a couple of lines that are funny in a better sense. It turns out that one of the pair may not even be Canadian. This crops up late in the play, but for some reason the outcome is given away in the publicity.

There's a well-staged fight, but for the most part Leslie O'Dell's production can make the play nothing but dull. Christopher Stanton, once past his early contortions, gives a decent account of Will, but Mark McGrinder's Sam is done in by a continuous vocal smirk, which is intended to convey ambiguous cheerfulness; his attempts at bolstering his companion's morale sound positively nannyish. Perhaps, if a playwright wants to get us thinking about modern warfare, he should choose a different conflict. It's true that 1914-18 was the entrance to the chamber of horrors in which we still live, but dramatically and otherwise it's been done -- to use a rather too appropriate phrase -- to death. There have been innumerable literary and dramatic treatments of this war, and it's hard to add anything new. At any rate, it hasn't happened here. It's cruel, but true, that the best comment on this play is its title. - Performances run through Nov. 10. For tickets, call 416-866-8666.

Almost the last thing that happens in Stephen Sondheim's Sweeney Todd is that the boy Tobias goes mad. This comes just after Sweeney, the vengeance-crazed demon barber of Fleet Street, has dispatched his two arch-enemies, Judge Turpin and his beadle, and after a more innocent bystander has also bitten the combined dust of Todd's tonsorial parlour and Mrs. Lovett's pie-shop. (The two are partners. In every sense.) It also follows Sweeney's turning on Mrs. Lovett and killing her, too; in most productions he does this by shoving her into her own baking-oven, but in John Doyle's staging, which comes to Toronto after successful seasons in London and New York, he has one last recourse to his trusty razor. Tobias then kills him, after informing him that he really oughtn't to go killing people, which is the only moral statement the show makes and the only one it needs. It's hardly surprising that the kid ends up off his rocker.

Which is how and where we find him as Doyle's production begins, held in a straitjacket, from which he is presently released to enact the story whose finale I have just given away. (I haven't spoiled anything. Sweeney is not about mystery but about Fate.) This version has two major conceits. One is narrative: The show is set in an asylum whose inmates are assisting in Tobias's theatrical psychotherapy. The other is technical: In this musical, which is virtually through-composed, the actors are also the orchestra. And so cunning are Sarah Travis's minimalist orchestrations, and so pointed the disposition of the actor-musicians about the stage, that the musical device also becomes a dramatic one.

A major consequence of the concept is that the show becomes about Tobias, who here gets to start it off with the uniquely haunting Ballad of Sweeney Todd. (Apparently the song's been cut from the upcoming movie. I can't imagine. Though I have seen the trailer, which seems reluctant to admit both that the film is a musical and that there is anyone in it besides Johnny Depp.) Edmund Bagnell, this production's Tobias, is vocally compelling, with just a couple of cracks, and visually compulsive; we watch the story through his eyes, noting in particular his trembling devotion to Mrs. Lovett, the protectress whom he in turn wishes to protect; their duet Not While I'm Around has never made more sense, has never indeed seemed more of a duet.

The weight of the show still falls on Sweeney and his co-worker. The current Todd is David Garry, newly promoted from standby. He gets through very creditably, looking every inch the fanatic Victorian tradesman, but he doesn't have the madness that propels both the character and the work, so some of the crucial sequences become monotonous. I've only seen one great Sweeney and that was the original, Len Cariou. I've rarely seen a Mrs. Lovett who was less than superb, but Judy Kaye may be the best of them all. She does make heavy cockney weather of the dialogue, but there isn't much of that; she gets every ounce out of the songs, not just melodically (she has one of the best voices in musicals) but dramatically and comedically. She knows exactly when to point a line with parlando, without ever breaking the flow. Not even Angela Lansbury was funnier with The Worst Pies in London, and no one has done nearly as well with By the Sea, which here becomes not a specialty turn but a delightful window into the woman's genial but fatally limited soul. She also stomps around the stage playing the tuba, with what looks like gusto, and, to remarkable effect, tinkles on the triangle.

Doyle's players-in-a-madhouse idea seems to owe something to Marat/Sade; certainly one recurring image -- the pouring of blood into a bucket to denote a death -- directly recalls the legendary Peter Brook production. No gore actually spills from throats here; the stage is bathed in red light instead, while the victims don spattered white coats. It's effective, as is Doyle's set, a bare room with one towering set of shelves, filled with knick-knacks. The whole production is gripping, but it's also limiting; it's fashionable to decry Harold Prince's original gigantic staging, but its physical size suited the show's emotional size. It released the tragedy in the melodrama. Perhaps a vibrant Sweeney, which this production has never had, would make the difference.

The performance level in general is down from New York, with a callow expressionless judge and a beadle whose physical slightness allows him to spend time standing in an upright coffin but who is vocally and dramatically thin as well. Doyle's New York production had the best beadle I've ever seen in Alexander Gemignani who's about to join this touring version to take over Sweeney. It also had the best Johanna in Lauren Molina; she's still playing it but her dizzy, spunky heroine has inexplicably dwindled into a thing of shreds and patches. The best of the supports is Katrina Yaukey, wittily playing the rival barber Pirelli in "push", which someone once suggested as the opposite of drag. I've never quite believed that the piece itself, tour-de-force of musical-theatrical writing though it is, is Sondheim's masterpiece; it lacks the intellectual and emotional range of Pacific Overtures and Into the Woods and the fun of Forum. It still dwarfs most other musicals of the last ... it still dwarfs most other musicals.

-Runs through Dec. 9 at the Princess of Wales Theatre. Call 416- 872-1212 for more information.

It's taken a long time, but the third season of Prison Break has begun to get exciting in the way one took for granted with its predecessors.

Last week's episode was a double, which in itself is usually enough to ratchet up the tension. And as it went into its second hour, we actually got an escape attempt. This week's "fall finale" - - how did we get suckered in to using these absurd names? -- was even better. And it ended with our hero, Michael Scofield, actually being escorted out of Panama's Sona prison by the authorities, presumably to somewhere worse, though it's hard to imagine what that might be.

We, the viewers, are probably not free of Sona yet, as most of the supporting cast remains locked up inside there. Sad for them, and also for us, because as hellholes go, Sona is boring.

It's also been looking progressively less hellish, and on a sunny day it resembles a holiday camp with generous visiting hours. It's boring because it isn't believable. This makes it a marked contrast to the comparatively credible penitentiary of Fox River, Chicago, where the first season happened.

That setting had a strange double effect; we were perfectly happy to stay there for the duration and observe the daily round, but also invested enough in the escape team to wish desperately for their plans to succeed.

Season Two gave us the escapers on the outside and was even better. It was fun to see the team continually splitting and re- forming; and since they were on the run and in constant danger of re- capture, the escape theme was still playing full blast -- even though it depended improvisation rather than Michael's genius for long-range planning.

He seemed, by the end, to have defeated his enemies, saved his brother who had been framed for murder and sentenced to the chair, and united with the woman he loved. But then there was a cruel twist, with Michael south of the border and back behind bars.

Back there with him were three of his worst enemies: one fellow fugitive and two highly compromised fellow-pursuers. This seemed like it might be fun, but it hasn't worked out that way.

The show seems at its wits' end about what to do with most of its personnel, and it has to contend with our resentment about the people it's got rid of.

And then there's the hoosegow itself, one in which the prisoners were so unruly that the authorities left them to run their own lives, only swooping down from time to time to make an example of some unfortunate inmate. I don't know if this variation of the lunatics taking over the asylum has ever happened in real life, even in Central America, but it sure doesn't ring true here.

So Michael has nothing real to fight against. Lechero, the kingpin felon whom the guards left to impose his own reign of terror is actually, in comic-book terms, quite an engaging figure, though very hard to understand.

Basic comprehension has always been a problem with this show; the downside of Wentworth Miller's glamorous intensity as Michael has been that most of what he said came out as a mutter. Now, with half the cast sporting exotic accents, it's worse.

So what awaits, after the fall (finale)? Or does anything? Prison Break, like every other network series, is about to be grounded by the TV writers' strike, which means that Michael and his scapegrace brother Linc (ironically on the outside while Michael's been in), and those remaining few they hold near and dear, may be in limbo forever.

The upside of this is that we can invent our own developments. I vote, first of all, for Dr. Sara to be brought back to life. I know the producers and the actress have both denied this will happen, and that Linc actually saw Sara's head in a box. But we didn't see it, and Linc can sometimes be dumb as an ox.

Michael is a lesser figure without his constantly-deferred love interest. Ex-prison officer Bellick, who's shown signs of moral rehabilitation, should be encouraged to pursue them; he's been through enough south of the border to warrant redemption, and his humiliation long since ceased to be funny.

T-Bag should be given something to do, or at least something amusing to say. And the all-powerful Company, whose shadowy machinations were a great counterpoint in the first two seasons, should become less shadowy.

We clutch at straws, those of us who struggle to retain our loyalty to shows that used to be great. There is a good reason. The long-form thriller serial -- the pulp relative of the TV novel created by HBO -- is a form still young and worth praying over.

BLITHE SPIRIT

Young Centre for the Performing Arts, Toronto

In the vast corpus of Noel Coward's work, Blithe Spirit ranks as a medium play: Below Hay Fever, Private Lives and Present Laughter, but ahead of most of the others. It's also a medium play because there's a medium in it:Charles Condomine, a successful English novelist, calls -- for research purposes only -- on the services of Madame Arcati, the Ouija-board lady from the local village, and she inadvertently conjures up the ghost of Charles' late wife Elvira, much to the displeasure of his current wife, Ruth. Charles isn't too pleased either, suddenly finding himself caught between two brides, of whom only one is technically alive though both are kicking.

Morris Panych's Soulpepper production is an unevenly blended cocktail of truth and exaggeration. He's on his best behaviour with the scenes between Charles and Ruth, which he takes with the same playful seriousness that distinguished his Shaw Festival production of Coward's Design for Living. Joseph Ziegler and Fiona Reid depict, with maximum sharpness, a match in which supposedly comfortable badinage covers an emotional void. It helps, of course, that both actors are superb comic technicians. Reid, in a knockout series of evening frocks, manages, as usual, to locate the most flammable word in any sentence and then ignite it. Ziegler, forced to cater to a mischievous former beloved invisible to everyone but him, is very droll in his double takes; he also strikes to the spoiled childish heart of a man who's been both bullied and protected by all the women who have ever entered his life. Neither performance, though, can quite sustain the length of the evening. It's largely the fault of the writing: Ruth more or less fades out, while Charles sticks around to do the plot's heavy lifting without being granted much of a personality. (Coward himself knew this; he refused to play the role himself, except when trapped into it on tour.) By the end, Ziegler has been reduced to playing prim crossed with cute. The Christmas season chez Soulpepper has come to mean Joe Ziegler seeing ghosts, and I did get to feeling nostalgic for his matchless Scrooge. (It will be back next year.)

Brenda Robins, red of hair and suit, and unearthly-white of face, is an unusually abrasive Elvira but without the melting flirtatiousness that one assumes Coward intended would balance the equation. (He did have a weakness for throaty charmers.) As for Madame Arcati, the happy medium, there are historically two ways of playing her: The full-flower eccentricity of Margaret Rutherford, whose original performance is providentially preserved on film, or the cheerfully practical businesswoman epitomized by Jenifer Phipps in a Shaw production that made me think more highly of the play than I have before or since. Nancy Palk offers a bit of both: She makes a bracing first impression, but the production pushes her way over the top. Madame boasts of being able to bicycle up hill and down dale, but calisthenics in the drawing room are much too much. So too, and more, is the maid Edith. The script decrees that she performs all her duties at the double, but that doesn't mean she has to go everywhere with knees bent, crouched in the starting position. Melody A. Johnson, who plays her, seems to have been directed to be insanely funny, something of which she is more than capable but not when the production stands over her and makes her do it.

The one unquestionably triumphant thing about this show is its look. Ken MacDonald's set and Charlotte Dean's costumes transport us to a vanished world where doctors made house calls in evening dress, or indeed to a vanished world where doctors made house calls. Everything that isn't explicitly ghostly is done in shades of grey; the cups in the china cabinet match the upholstery on the sofa. In scale and proportion, this is a paragon among country-house settings, majestic without being overpowering. At the end, when the ghosts turn to poltergeists, the set even gets to do a turn of its own, with furnishings flying all over the place. It could even afford to go on longer and more violently; this is a rare example of Panych erring on the side of restraint. Overall, there's a whiff of superior summer theatre about this winter show, starting with the choice of play. It's Soulpepper punching below its weight. - Blithe Spirit runs until Dec. 15. For tickets and show information, call 416-866-8666.

Black & White Photo: Sandy Nicholson / Brenda Robins as Elvira and Joseph Ziegler as Charles may have complicated relations with the spirit world, but at least their doctor makes housecalls. ;

The commercial hook for PU-239 is the presence of George Clooney and Steven Soderbergh as executive producers. Nowadays it seems that everybody and his brother can be an executive producer -- this production lists seven -- but it's quite possible that without Clooney's and Soderbergh's endorsement, the film would never have been made. Which would have been a pity.

PU-239 is weapons-grade plutonium. The film, written and directed by Scott Z. Burns (writer of The Bourne Ultimatum, producer of An Inconvenient Truth) from a short story by Ken Kalfus, is about two Russian men stranded and shafted after the collapse of the Soviet Union: Timofey, a nuclear plant worker, and Shiv, an aspiring Moscow gangster.

There's a malfunction at Timofey's plant and, after trying to prevent it, he is fired without compensation, since to give him anything would constitute an admission of criminal negligence on the part of management. (Truths don't get more inconvenient than that.) He does depart with a dose of radiation sufficient to kill him in just a few days, and a pouchful of plutonium, fissionable material that he hopes to sell so as to secure a future for his wife and young son. Which is how he gets mixed up with Shiv.

Shiv is an enthusiastic young hustler, trying to make his way in a world that has collapsed into one big black market. He's in the protection racket, but finds he's encroached on the territory of mobsters far more powerful than himself. He has a couple of sidekicks dumber than he is but also more dangerous. (Or more dangerous because they're dumber. They are, it turns out, especially dangerous to themselves.)

Shiv takes some convincing that Timofey is actually in possession of an untouchable powder that he's prepared to sell at the bargain rate of US$30,000. But as he is in desperate need of funds himself, to pay off the big guys he unwittingly crossed, he agrees to go into partnership.

Healsogets personally involved. Shiv has a son himself -- by a hooker girlfriend who professes not to be sure if the boy is even his -- and what starts out as a strained thematic parallel turns into a dramatic bond.

The film divides into two parts of which the second is the more engrossing. In the first half, we keep cutting between Timofey's story and Shiv's, and it's an uneven contest. For all the horror of what happens to Timofey, and despite good performances from Paddy Considine and Radha Mitchell (tough and tender as the wife), the treatment is lachrymose.

Oscar Isaac's Shiv, on the other hand, is funny, quick-witted, and desperate in the best gangster movie tradition. He's a small- timer who scams money from street traders supposedly to fight Chechen terrorists, and for whom every walk down the street is an opportunity to lift some windshield wipers.

Shiv is also, naturally, a fan of American pop culture, though he's hazy about some of the details: Sharing with his son, he comes up with a delirious concoction in which the CIA pursue that well- known Chicago hood Jesse James, who in turn gets mixed in with Jesse Jackson, of the Jackson Five ("the most powerful family in America").

When Timofey and Shiv combine, each feeding off the other's desperation, the movie kicks into its highest gear. The two initial stories keep folding back on one another, to dramatic and blackly comic effect. One of the achievements -- an ambiguous one, I suppose, but an achievement nonetheless -- is that we lose our moral bearings. If our heroes' deal goes through, lethal material will be made available to the highest bidder.

Nevertheless, as we watch them shuttle between two pitiless gangland kingpins -- one old, one young -- we find ourselves desperately hoping that they will succeed and that they won't be killed or screwed. The personal hits harder than the political; which may not have been the Clooney-Soderbergh intention. This is an American production, mostly peopled by American actors, plus Steven Berkoff, once the arch "bovver" boy of theBritish theatre, grown unrecognizably fleshy but as terrifying as ever. (His "legitimate" counterpart, though-- the nuclear CEO -- sounds disconcertingly Scottish.) It's full of American gangster tropes which, as most recently demonstrated in David Cronenberg's Eastern Promises, have long since gone international.

Here, though, the genre is really raw; the underworld is the world--gangster-capitalism at its purest with no social safety net. The ending is, all things considered, less bleak than it might be. But not by much. - PU-239 airs tonight at 9 p.m. on Movie Central

2007-11-17-this-is-your-family-on-drugs-:
Daniel MacIvor's retreat into conventional narrative play- writing continues apace. Though "apace" may not be the right word for his new play, How It Works, a slight piece in a slow production.

It's a mildly interesting, mildly entertaining play about relationships ruptured and possibly repaired. It starts well, with Al, a cop, and Christine, a pharmacy cashier, having a beer together at a Halifax pub called the Thirsty Duck. (I think. They just refer to it as The Duck. Im all in favour of plays set in Halifax, but most of the time this one could be going on anywhere. Call it universal. Or just vague.) This is their first flesh-and-blood encounter after striking up an acquaintance online, and author and actors capture the promise and discomfort of a first date that isnt quite a first date. Al, the first to arrive, sits there, happily lip- synching to a record of Trouble in Mind, until Christine arrives to find him covered in the mild embarrassment that's almost obligatory in a white man caught singing the blues. They get on. We learn that both are ex-marrieds, though it subsequently transpires that Christine is referring to a youthful two years spent in a convent. So she's a bride of Christ; though if she never took her vows, wouldnt that make her more a fiancee of Christ? And is her name significant? Anyway, the idea later yields a couple of fairly funny lines but doesnt contribute as much to her strength of character as seems to be hoped.

Tom Barnett gives a well-grounded performance of Al; he's the only member of the cast who never forces a note. Caroline Gillis's Christine is strong and likeable, though shes never as solid again as she is in that first scene. But then neither is the play. Tom has insisted that he cant be involved with anyone who does drugs, and we find when we follow him home that this isn't just professional. His 19-year-old daughter, Brooke, is hooked on crystal meth (though the program gets more specific about this than the play does) and is lying and stealing to support her habit. From here on, the play declines into a routine family-problem drama, decked out with a few tricks and aphorisms. We see Brooke with her mother who, when we first meet her, is getting dressed for a date of her own. This turns out to be the reddest of herrings, and Fiona Highet cannot make the woman anything but brittle. Her relationship with Al is never credible, least of all when it gets shown to us in flashbacks; these include a satire on old-fashioned experimental theatre that is briefly amusing but seems to belong in some other show.

Christine manages to convince both of Brooke's parents that shes the person who can, if not cure Brooke, make her face up to her situation. And, yes, its a credit to both MacIvor and Gillis that this is believable, in terms of who Christine is, if not of what she actually does. This connects with the play's prologue, a short credo that Gillis delivers very well, and with its title, How It Works, in that we all have stories inside us that we need to let out. Brooke's is of a youthful trauma that triggered her addiction. What the incident was is signalled many scenes before its actually revealed. I appreciate that the play probably isnt aiming at suspense, but it creeps in anyway, the issue being not what happened to Brooke but when she will put us all out of our misery by telling. Bethany Jillard has Brooke's teenage rhythms down perfectly; so has the writing, but neither is able to develop them. The final note is one of carefully qualified optimism: an honourable posture but, with the characters faint and the action fragmentary, no more than a posture.

MacIvor's direction proceeds laboriously from one episode to another and -- on a set dourly designed and lit by Kimberly Purtell - - from one anonymous rostrum to another. Recorded songs between scenes, mostly with a country sound, depress the mood and the pace still further. Most of the world, the theatre world anyway, is a Daniel MacIvor fan, and I was able to join the club myself when I finally caught up with his one-man shows. But after the flash of those solo plays (and, to be fair, of his twohander A Beautiful View, in which he didn't act but which he directed superbly), the drabness of this one is a shock, and an unwelcome one Instead of attitude, platitude.

- How It Works runs through Dec. 16 at the Tarragon Theatre. Call 416-531-1827 for details.

THEATRE REVIEW

DIRTY DANCING

Royal Alexandra Theatre

---

There's a cute variation at Dirty Dancing on the customary pre- show mixed message of welcome and admonition.

We're advised that the show takes place in 1963, "long before cellphones." As I remember, it was long before drum machines as well, but that doesn't stop the proceedings from commencing with a pounding beat that sounds decidedly anachronistic. No intrusive beeps from the auditorium could hope to compete.

Dirty Dancing is subtitled "The Classic Story on Stage." I confess, here and now, that I never saw the classic story on screen, but my impression is that Eleanor Bergstein, who wrote both, is trying to recreate the movie experience as closely as possible with live actors.

If I did know the movie, I would probably consider this a pointless exercise; I don't usually have much interest in reliving cherished memories second-hand, and un-cherished memories may be even worse.

Coming -- so to speak -- fresh, I was impressed by the dogged and inventive determination of director James Powell to make the show as fluid as possible. The stage rises and falls with military precision and metronomic regularity, projections (designed by Jon Driscoll) are brilliant in their clarity and family-album evocative.

In a world full of We Will Rock You and High School Musical: The Musical, or whatever they called it, Dirty Dancing looks positively artistic.

It doesn't always sound that way, but then I don't suppose many people are going to see it in order to savour the wit and wisdom of Bergstein. The level of acting -- let's not get pretentious here, the level of linereading-- is atrocious, but then so are many of the lines.

MonicaWest, thefemale lead, does have a freshness, or at least a naivete about her that suits the character she's playing, who goes in for being painfully sincere. She is, as everybody in the theatre but me already knew, Frances Houseman, a doctor's daughter who comes with her father, mother and jealous-but-loving older sister (who looks and behaves younger) for a last holiday in the Catskills.

It was, she tells us as the family car makes a circular progress around the stage, the last summer before the Beatles (man, you North Americans were late developers), the last time anyone ever called her by her nickname of Baby. For some reason, it never occurs to anyone to call her Frankie, which would suit her perfectly.

Baby is an idealist whose ambition is to join the Peace Corps. In the meantime, she has more immediate moral and social problems to confront and, it must be said, she comes through them all with flying colours: She never meets a spasm of doubt that can't be dispelled in three seconds. She falls for Johnny, a boy from the other side of the tracks; he teaches Latin dancing to guests bored with the foxtrot.

This -- the Latin dancing, I mean -- is the dirty dancing of the title, though it looks pretty antiseptic here. Still, it's enough to prejudice Baby's decent-but-blinkered dad against Johnny, especially when he's called in to salvage a botched abortion suffered by Johnny's regular mambo-partner, a situation for which he holds Johnny morally (i.e. biologically) responsible.

There's no reason why he should hold Johnny responsible, except that without this misunderstanding, the central relationship would have no complications whatsoever. In terms of what actually happens between them, the boy never comes close to losing the girl for a moment. Doctor Dad, I regret to say, is played in an especially appalling performance by actor Al Sapienza (Mikey Palmice of The Sopranos) who sounds as if he wouldn't want to be held accountable for a word that falls from his lips.

Meanwhile the show treats us to snapshots of resort life and entertainment (including a full half-minute of authentic-sounding borscht-belt comedy), and generally behaves like Wish You Were Here updated by a decade.

Given the speed of the proceedings, this works. So, against all the odds (which include a strenuous, but blank, leading man in Jake Simons) does the main story. We can even stand for the insistent morality which includes inflicting a last-minute comeuppance on the camp's resident loose woman.

The show only gets unforgivably cheesy when it gets on the subject of civil rights; A very '70s sounding rendition of We Shall Overcome is followed by a momentary projection of Martin Luther King, Jr. It demeans a great man to reduce him to the theatrical equivalent of a T-shirt logo, and it's insufferable of the show to congratulate itself on how far ahead it is of the times it depicts.

It's all supposed to tie in with the mental struggles, dropped in at widely-spaced intervals, of a trainee hotelier over whether to journey south to join the Freedom Riders. First he will, then he won't, then -- but I wouldn't want to spoil anything.

Big musicals in Toronto always include at least one recruit from the classical theatre, served up as a sacrificial offering; here it's Dylan Trowbridge, late of Shaw: having seen him at his best, I can testify that he isn't at it here.

The dancing, given the show's premise and title, is routine; the climax of choreography, story and show is supposed to come when Baby, as Johnny's replacement partner, finally manages the Lift; but it never really registers that she hasn't been Lifted already.

As a musical, though, the show does have its own integrity in that it isn't really a musical. There are many songs, either authentically of the period or written for the movie, like the famous and deeply undistinguished The Time of My Life, but they're all used as backgound, whether prerecorded or rendered live. There is some late slippage when a couple of minor figures take on the function of a commentating chorus, but none of the leads ever sing in character, or sing at all.

This story-with-dance idea has been done before, in an artier way, in Contact, but this is somehow more likeable. A convention is established and adhered to. I admire that. - Dirty Dancing is at the Royal Alexandra Theatre for an indefinite run. Call 416-872-1212 for more information.
