2007-11-23-my-ventilator-is-playing-god-:
Craig Ewert is, or was, a professor of computer sciences in Chicago who took early retirement and, to get out of Bushs America" moved to Harrogate, a spa town in the north of England.

There he was stricken with ALS, or Lou Gehrigs disease. Facing a life of deteriorating paralysis -- in his terms, with no life at all- -he decided to kill himself, with as little pain and as much dignity as possible. He went to Switzerland, one of two countries in the world (plus the state of Oregon) that permits medically-assisted suicide and the only that allows it for non-citizens.

He met in Zurich with Ludwig Minelli, popularly known as "Doctor Death but actually a human-rights lawyer, who runs Dignitas, an organization devoted to providing precisely this service.

The documentary The Suicide Tourist (CTV, tomorrow) tells the story of Ewert and his extremely supportive wife Mary.

It also follows, in counterpoint, the story of another pair of Dignitas clients: George Coumbias, a Greek-born immigrant to Vancouver who rose from janitor to president of L'Oreal in Japan. Now in his seventies, he has suffered four serious heart attacks and expects a fifth: I can't play tennis or golf, I cant have sex. What are they going to tell me next, no more good food and wine?"

He has serious fears: "Im a very private person; I want to be able to feed and clean myself. So far, George's story and Craig's parallel one another. But there is a difference. Georges wife Betty (theyve been inseparable since 1958") is in perfect health but doesn't want to survive him. They have an assisted-suicide pact.

Craig's case seems -- to me, anyway -- perfectly cut-and-dried; as he says, confronting his choices, "Ive got death, or Ive got suffering and death, and he's perfectly entitled to choose the former.

George's, or rather Bettys, is murkier, and its understandable that the doctor to whom Minelli refers both couples should have no hesitation in writing a prescription for Ewert but balks at giving one to Mr. and Mrs. Coumbias.

Simply, it goes against his training. But the question remains: Doesn't a sane woman have a right to end a life that she believes she will find insupportable? And who's to say that, when her husband dies, she wont kill herself anyway?

John Zaritskys film won the audience vote as best Canadian picture at this year's Hot Docs International Documentary Festival. It isn't a debate. Dissenting voices are only heard through the comments of their opponents; Craig Ewert trenchantly observes that without modern technology he would be dead anyway, and the Christians who complain about doctors who practise euthanasia playing God" ignore the fact that doctors play God all the time by preserving lives that in earlier ages would have been lost. "My ventilator is playing God, he says. (You could of course extend this argument to every medical advance since Hippocrates, but I dont think that invalidates it.)

These touches apart, the film is an elegy and -- at two hours -- an unduly prolonged one; a judgement that may sound heartless but is in the circumstances appropriate. Ewert, whose gets the bulk of the screen and voice-over time, is an intelligent and sympathetic man, but in the end he has only one thing to say: that his life has become intolerable and, having weighed the options, he has the right to end it. I wouldnt give him an argument but, in the interests of variety if not of balance, I would have liked to hear someone else give him one.

Minelli makes the surprising but rather persuasive point that Dignitas can actually prevent suicides; by offering desperate people a civilized option, it can prevent them from rushing into things and give them the opportunity to change their minds.

Still, if there's one really disturbing thing in the film, it's Minellis admission that, to maintain objectivity," he never actually attends a death: "I do not mix the potion.

We, however, do attend Craig Ewerts death. We hear the designated attendant hand him the draught and say, Mr. Ewert, if you drink this, you're going to die," and we witness him swallowing it and asking for apple juice to drown the taste.

It's solemn enough, and revealing enough, for me to swallow my own customary doubts about the effect of film cameras on supposedly spontaneous moments, and the thought-processes of the people who allow or even welcome them.

Theres a momentary cheat when were treated to a montage of what are presumed to be the dying man's last memories; it isn't exactly sentimental, but it breaks the code of realism that otherwise justifies the film. But it regains its dignity when Mary Ewert holds her late husbands hand, then gets up, takes off her glasses off and kisses him. She doesnt cry, or not on camera. And you think, "yes, it would have been worse if she'd had to watch him die painfully." And we all die.

- The Suicide Tourist airs tomorrow at 7 p.m. on CTV.
2007-11-24-once-more-on-the-yellow-brick:
E.Y. alias "Yip" Harburg, who wrote the lyrics for the 1939 movie of The Wizard of Oz and had a substantial if largely uncredited part in fashioning the screenplay, always used to claim that it was a political film. A lifelong leftist and a devout Roosevelt man, he said that when the Scarecrow, the Tin Woodman and the Cowardly Lion made their respective bids for a brain, a heart and "da noive," they were paying tribute to the man in the White House who had given America the qualities it needed to combat the Depression: intelligence, compassion and courage. It's uncertain whether he meant us to identify FDR with the Wizard himself who, you may remember, turns out to be something of a fraud.

Not altogether, though. It's he who, when pushed, teaches the three supplicants that they're at least as good as the poseurs who claim to have the virtues they themselves seek, and that all they really need is self-confidence. It's the same lesson that the Good Witch imparts to Dorothy about how to find her way home -- but only after she's learned it for herself. This message of self-reliance prompted the movie historian Ethan Mordden to call The Wizard of Oz the best right-wing musical ever made (and just in time for war, he noted). It's a judgment that would have flabbergasted Harburg, who gloried in having one of the fattest FBI files of anyone in show business; an investigator once asked him, quite seriously, if his Happiness Is a Thing Called Joe was a song about Stalin. But there is a cockeyed truth to it (and Yip always delighted in paradoxes, provided he was the one coining them). It proves, if nothing else, that extremes can meet.

It also suggests that The Wizard of Oz is a fable rich enough to be put to use in diverse ways. The film took liberties with the 40- year-old book it was based on; the Kansas dust bowl that Dorothy famously decides she isn't in any more was a different place in 1939 than it had been in 1900. L. Frank Baum's story had become the basis of a hugely successful, and thoroughly escapist, stage musical long before MGM acquired the movie rights; and, as we've seen, the movie isn't escapist, though it is about (temporary) escape.

Despite The Wiz and, please God, despite Wicked (which really is a fairy tale and not in a good way), the film still defines how everyone sees the story. The stage version now on view in Toronto hews very closely to the movie, including some material retrieved from the cutting-room floor. It's the work of an English actor, John Kane, and was first staged by the Royal Shakespeare Company, who gave it a mind-blowingly bounteous production. Our Young People's Theatre can hardly summon the same resources, but, on its own more modest terms, it's almost as effective. And it does put its own stamp on the story, while unobtrusively updating it.

The focus of Allen MacInnis's production is more psychological than sociological. In a program note, he lays great stress on Dorothy's trip to Oz being a dream; this, of course, is built into any version of the story, but the correspondences between the girl's real friends, foes and family, and her fantasy ones are sharper here than usual. I wish that Michael Gianfrancesco (sets) and Steve Lucas (lights) had found a way of reproducing the movie's alternation of sepia and full colour, but they have given the show a charming miniaturist look with an overarching theme. Once we get to Oz, we can see clear to the back wall of the stage, pulleys and lighting- grid in full view, and the theatre itself becomes a metaphor. The Munchkins are puppets, seen from the neck up; they look like relatives of Fozzie Bear, treated to a makeover in blue.

Most importantly, while the show treats the script, the lyrics and Harold Arlen's music with the utmost respect, nobody on stage acts as if they'd seen the movie. All the characters are freshly thought. When Saccha Dennis's Dorothy sings Over the Rainbow, it's an expression of hemmed-in teenage anger frustration rather than Judy Garland wistfulness, and a song you may never have wanted to hear again comes back to life. So does the girl herself. She's surrounded and supported by some of the best musical-theatre performers in Toronto, not to mention a dog who trots on and offstage with indomitable pertinacity. George Masswohl, an unassuming tower of strength as Uncle Henry, mutates into a very funny Emerald City Guard; Molly Atkinson, a salt-of-the-earth Auntie Em, has a nice sense of self-satire as the Good Witch. The three companions are Paul McQuillan, an enchantingly floppy Scarecrow; Thom Allison, a Tin Man in a Campbell's soup can who delivers some ringing vocal variations on If I Only Had a Heart; and Shawn Wright, an appealingly bashful Lion, though without -- inevitably -- the underweening majesty of Bert Lahr's King of the Forest. (This is the one role where comparisons can't help bearing down; it was written for Lahr, mainly by Harburg, as Dorothy was never written for Garland.) Sam Moses's Professor Marvel takes his sweet time, but he's a bumbling whiz of a Wizard; a shame that the available technology doesn't permit his exit by balloon. Sharron Matthews is more believably threatening as Miss Gulch than she is as the Wicked Witch, but, in the latter role, she does get to kick off The Jitterbug, a restored swing tune (Arlen at his rhythmic best), that becomes the most invigorating number in any current Toronto musical. Movie musicals slavishly transferred to stage are a plague, but this is something different: the latest chapter in the progress of a classic.

- The Wizard of Oz runs through Dec. 30 at the Lorraine Kimsa Theatre for Young People. Call 416-862-2222 for more information.

2007-11-27-laughing-at-civilization-s-de:
(From The National Post, November 28, 2007) Kenny Hotz and Spencer Rice were assigned each other's names in a photo caption yesterday in Arts & Life. 

According to the sheriff in No Country for Old Men, the world started going to hell when people stopped addressing one another as "sir" and "ma'am." He may just have meant Texas, but I think he was including the world. He may well have had a point, one that stretches as far north as Canada. Here, the decline of civilization is being hastened by the weekly gross-out contest known as Kenny vs. Spenny.

I said the decline of civilization, not the decline of television. The show can be pretty funny. (Well, maybe scratch the pretty part.) By presenting these supposed friends in state of perpetual competition, it implicitly invites us to pick sides. I had better admit that I, true to critical type, identify with Spenny, witheringly dismissed on the show's Web site as a "neurotic adult- type," rather than with Kenny, pegged by the same source as "a witty wise-cracker and brilliant schemer." I think Kenny must have written that, always supposing of course that Kenny can write. Spenny is the subtler performer, for what -- in this context -- that's worth.

Last week's episode had the duo vying to create the best viral video. As an exercise, this may have been a trifle superfluous as all their shows are viral videos in the first place; they look cheap, and the two participants are bidding against one another for audience approval even when no vote is taken. Last week, one was taken and Kenny won, despite Spenny's inventive Cute Extravaganza, for which he mustered a whole floor full of rabbits, puppies and uncooperative babies, the mother of one of whom was heard to declare "this is the stupidest thing I've ever signed him up for." Even Spenny's desperate attempt to lower himself to Kenny's level by, in the dainty words of the synopsis, "consuming excrement," availed him nothing. Kenny gained his viral victory by having himself filmed "on top of Paris Hilton": i.e. posing on a roof against a cut-out of the Eiffel Tower. Spenny thought this was cheating, but the landscape of these two isn't a country for old or young men. The most hilarious thing about this show may be the ritual warnings about its being "suitable for adult viewing only."

Tonight we find out who can eat the most meat. Kenny starts out by concentrating on tongue and Spenny on turkey, both true to character. Which reminds me: Is turkey, meat, strictly speaking? There are some who would consider poultry a separate category. Sorry I brought it up. Which also reminds me ... no, I won't go there. But you can, if you watch the show. I won't, of course, give away who wins, but it's probably no secret that both guys get to craving a change of carnivorous diet. Kenny, after crooning to some strips of bacon, fries them up before our very eyes. ("My rabbi's gonna be pissed.") There's also a scene in which he has to make out with an old lady. You can't help feeling that she's the one who's lowering her standards. This is no country for her, either.

As has been reported here and elsewhere, Kenny vs. Spenny is our latest export, with the U.S.'s Comedy Central using our boys to fill the space vacated by striking writers. It's certainly one of those shows programmed to connect with every American's inner frat-boy. But if it keeps getting more strenuously outrageous that may just be because of the desperation that overcomes the majority of sitcoms as each begins to exhaust its initial premise. And Kenny vs Spenny is a sitcom, and as crafted and artificial as they come, despite its pretense of being reality TV (which of course is also a pretense). Despite, too, its primitive production values, which make The Sarah Silverman Program look like vintage Carol Burnett.

Not all sitcoms degenerate. Little Mosque on the Prairie has come along very nicely, outgrowing the giggling folksiness signified by its title in favour of a raised-eyebrow jollity that occasionally erupts into a genuine hoot. Tomorrow night's episode has Baber stricken with fear of what may be the Evil Eye, and is called "Best Intentions." That could almost be a generic TV comedy title (though it wouldn't do for Kenny and Spenny). I haven't seen this episode, but I would like to pay tribute to last week's episode, which had Samantha Bee as a guest star, proving that she can be just as funny when she's restrained as when being extravagantly wide-eyed and incredulous on The Daily Show. No, funnier. She fitted into the situation; she reacted to other people's lines and delivered her own as if she believed in them. In short, she acted. The show's three statutory plot lines were nicely rhymed, with a satisfying pay-off. An especially pleasant strand involved the efforts of Carlo Rota and Sheila Mc-Carthy's mixed-married couple (would this make McCarthy the Muslim equivalent of a shiksa?) to work from the same home, with predictably nonproductive results. Rota's unclassifiable ethnicity (English accent, Italian name, Canadian passport) has take him in the last few TV seasons between being unnervingly all-knowing at a reception-desk in At The Hotel, tortured and then self-torturing as Chloe's errant ex on 24, and funny and unruffled here. Through it all, he's stayed urbane. And he always seems to get the smart, funny girls. - Kenny vs. Spenny airs at 10 p.m. tonight on Showcase; Little Mosque on the Prairie airs Wednesdays at 8 p.m. (8:30 NT) on CBC.

2007-11-28-satiated-seymour:
LITTLE SHOP OF HORRORS

Bluma Appel Theatre, Toronto

---

It's business time again at the (bop-she-bop) Little Shop of Horrors. The place has never looked or sounded better.

Little Shop of Horrors is something unique: a rock musical that's unpretentious, unsentimental, witty, lean as well as mean. It derives, as is well known, from a 1960 movie -- not so much Grade B as Grade Z-- that Roger Corman shot in two days on a leftover set: It became an off-Broadway musical in 1982, with Howard Ashman, who also directed, writing the book and lyrics and Alan Menken the music. Their score is rooted in 1960s Brill Building pop, so you might say the show represents the perfect melding of two schlock genres, each containing at least some seeds of sophistication. These seeds, to adopt the show's own warped horticultural imagery, were lovingly watered and tended by the authors until they blossomed into musical comedy numbers in the sharpest American tradition. The story's setting and ethos are established in an opening number called Skid Row (Downtown), and if you remember Uptown ("where people don't pay much rent") -- well, this song is pretty much its mirror image, but accentuating the negative. (It also sounds a bit like Up on the Roof might have done, had it been reworked as Down in the Gutter. The Gutter, in this show, is an S &Mnightclub.) Soon after this, Seymour, the unawares botanical genius who is our protagonist, sings of his existence as an overworked flower-shop assistant and underloved orphan, his voice pounding in time with his heart: "I keep asking God, what am I for / He says, gee, I'm not sure." Ashman's early loss -- first to Disney, then to death -- was a grievous one; Menken's music has never been the same without him-- he subsequently took to writing with Tim Rice.

Perversely but triumphantly, the show makes us care about its characters and situations by exaggerating them; the music blows them up, the words bring them down to something resembling Earth. Seymour is the nerd of all nerds transformed into a cross between Faust and Frankenstein. Audrey, his blond beloved and co-worker, is the waif of all waifs, oppressed by a dentist boyfriend who enjoys his work. (As she sings, "I know Seymour's the greatest / But I'm dating a semi-sadist." In her accent, the rhyme works.) And the plant that Seymour discovers during an eclipse of the sun and on which he bestows the loving name of Audrey II, turns out to be the monster of all monsters. At first, for all his expert care, it refuses to grow: "What," he sings at it rhetorically but unwisely, "do you want from me, blood?" Well, yes. It wants to eat everyone. And does. But first, it makes the flower shop's fortune and also the guilt-ridden Seymour's, its strangeness and its awesomely increasing dimensions bringing in customers where none were before. Michael Gianfrancesco's flock-wallpapered set for the Canadian Stage Company's revival suggests that this may have had something to do with its looking less like a retail outlet than like someone's dilapidated living room.

Ted Dykstra's direction is immensely gleeful and polished. He and his choreographer, Jody Ripplinger, have staged each number with maximum punch and point. Every song lands, musically and lyrically; I've seldom heard more laughs at a musical. Note, for example, the mental and physical struggle between Orin the dentist, asphyxiating on his own laughing-gas, and Seymour whose "ethical dilemma" leads him briefly into rapid-fire Gilbert and Sullivan. Little Shop may not be as distinguished a musical as Sweeney Todd, but the two have some surprising similarities of theme and structure And, a scene in Sweeney reminds us, barbers once doubled as dentists.

There are some flaws. The all-purpose girl group who act as chorus -- their iconic names are Crystal, Chiffon and Ronette -- are too pushy for their own good -- and the show's. Sheldon Davis, as the little shop's little owner, is likewise effortful, especially at being Jewish. Rejean Cournoyer is a fine Elvis-clone of an Orin (whose mother, observing his proclivities, told him, "Son, be a de- en-tist") but he's ineffectual as a succession of later characters, all of them emissaries of the establishment, tempting the hero with riches. So the conscientious torments of Ron Pederson's Seymour, which should drive the second half, go for less than they should; he's also the victim of a harsh sound system which makes it hard for him to come off as shy.

Otherwise, he's the singing and dancing Seymour of your dreams, incisive even when dithering. Patricia Zentilli's Audrey I, a gentle vision whom nature intended to be pre-Raphaelite but whom fate has painted post-Pollock, may even surpass your dreams, especially when she sings Somewhere That's Green, a yearning hymn to plastic- covered suburbia. Best of all is Audrey II, voiced by Jeff Jones as a soul singer who starts all wheedle and ends all gravelly gloat, andmanipulatedby actor-puppeteer Eric Woolfe to take over the stage, and potentially the world, with grasping tendrils and yawning mouth.

This plant deserves an award: a Flora Dora. - Little Shop of Horrors runs until Dec. 15. For tickets, call 416-368-3110.

2007-11-30-the-yellow-pages-of-the-blues:
We were old, says Solomon Burke, summing up the glories of the concert we've just watched, we were all together. And," -- pause for a laugh -- "we weren't getting paid.

Burke is one of the headiest of the blues headliners featured in Lightning in a Bottle, which memorializes a 2003 show at Radio City Music Hall in New York City, which itself memorialized an entire American musical tradition.

Martin Scorsese, whose The Last Waltz is one of the most celebrated of all concert movies, is the executive producer of Lightning, and he appears on stage to make a brief introduction. The film, however, is directed by Antoine Fuqua, and very well.

The film cuts between performances on the night of, and rehearsals for, the show; with some stills and newsreel clips to fill in the sociological background, plus footage of artists like Muddy Waters and John Lee Hooker who, for the best of mortal reasons, couldnt make the gig.

Otherwise, everyones there. As one participant says, they must have looked in the Yellow Pages under blues."

"We try, says Scorsese to tell the story of this music from the beginning," and we start with Angelique Kidjo rapturously chant- singing Zelie, identified in a caption as adapted from a West African source. Fast forward to Mavis Staples and a 1928 injunction from Blind Lemon Jefferson, See That My Grave Is Kept Clean, her husky voice grazing the title phrase and turning it into gospel- blues.

David "Honeyboy Edwards, introducing his own Gamblin' Man, tells us that he hustled all over Mississippi" and that he started performing when he was 13; that too was in 1928. ("Every time I got tired they gave me a drink of whisky. I guess he got hooked.)

Odetta, whom I think of as a folksinger and who still looks amazingly young when she talks, but like a tragic seer when she sings, does Leadbelly's Jim Crow Blues, whose title speaks for itself.

We also get to hear Odetta sweeping in on a rehearsal with the great, and now late, Ruth Brown, and exclaiming I dont know why this brilliant woman has to compete with the band."

The musicians -- among whom Dr. John is repeatedly prominent -- look suitably chastened, and cool it. Brown herself, who was recovering from a stroke, muses that "most of the great singers of blues are men, because that allows them to vent their feelings.

For herself, she harks back to her 1950s R & B hit Mama, He Treats Your Daughter Mean, a time when, I didnt understand the blues. Now I have a reason to sing them." Singing, we learn, saves her from screaming; she reprises that teenage hit in a mature rasp.

Brown also joins forces with Staples and Natalie Cole to deliver the ultimate female put-down, Men Are Like Streetcars (with Bill Cosby onstage as the bemused object of their attentions). Cole, looking torch-singer glamorous in a beaded dress but sounding wildly good, is also the performer entrusted with W. C. Handy's St. Louis Blues, the centrepiece, as it happens, of one of her father's best albums.

Handy, we are told, did not so much write songs as transcribe them; and in rather the same way the film downgrades the "classic blues of the 20s and the women who sang them -- even Bessie Smith, whose likeness is briefly glimpsed but whose name is never mentioned. Shes lost somewhere between the early rural blues and the later varieties that cross-pollinated with country, jive and rock.

Or, to put it another way, in the gulf between acoustic and electric. The concert, and the film, pretty much divide into those two halves. For home viewers, the first half is the better, with the musicians' faces as compellingly gnarled as their voices. There's even a health warning, from Vernon Reid: A lot of these guys weren't sympathetic figures. Leadbelly shot a man dead. We project a lot of sentimentality on them -- because they made a great sound."

The second half, a cumulative jam session, is more a case of "you had to be there. There are still many moments to make you feel you were. Steve Tyler and Joe Perry look and sound like the Rolling Stones must have wished they did.

Burke, looking like a house with a white fedora for a chimney, sits in a straight-backed chair and delivers Turn On Your Love Light, a hand-clapper and audience-swayer that possesses even him, so that he stands up and takes his hat off. He also has a bizarre, scary anecdote about having to sing for the Ku Klux Klan.

King also has a story, about singing in the more liberal precincts of the University of Maryland and being booed because he was blues and the students wanted soul and R & B. (It was like being black twice.") "They thought, he says, taking the final spot, they would save the oldest till last."

Not quite accurate, or at least not in terms of his age: It may be more of that sentimentality, because he has so much reputation and presence, but when he sings and plays Sweet Sixteen, the same number with which he eventually won over the Maryland campus, you would swear that he extracts the sweetest and strongest sounds ever to come out of a guitar.

After all that, it's something of a come-down to learn from the final credits that the whole thing has been a glorified commercial for Volkswagen. (Something about the blues moved from the Mississippi Delta to Chicago and New York, and they can take you the same route.) But at least, as Solomon Burke testifies, the proceeds went to charity.

2007-12-01-get-thee-behind-a-typewriter-:
Linda Griffiths's Age of Arousal is a historical fantasia about the British suffragette movement. Its action unfolds over the single year of 1885, but the author has avowedly crammed into that time events and currents of thought from 1869 to 1914. The title is a pun; it refers to both intellectual and sexual arousal. Indeed it could be a multiple pun, since the actions and reactions of the five women in the cast are at least partially determined by how old they are.

At the senior end, there's Mary Barfoot, who's served time for militant activities and begins the play with a powerful account of how it felt to be force-fed, that is tortured. Now retired from front-line protest, she does her bit by running a secretarial school, giving women the tools to achieve the economic independence that has to precede all the other kinds. She owns a set of Remington typewriters that take on a practically totemic significance for all who behold them. Her admiring though increasingly mutinous assistant, with whom she has a physical as well as a professional relationship, is Rhoda Nunn, who is in her thirties. Rhoda re- encounters a trio of former acquaintances, the Madden sisters, who since the death of their father have been leading wretched lives of genteel poverty; they are, in order, Alice, Virginia and Monica. Monica, at 21, is the youngest person in the play and works as a shopgirl; Alice and Virginia, both middle-aged and more inhibited by their upbringing, sit at home and starve. Mary takes the sisters in and introduces them to the brave new world of secretarial training.

The one male in the play is Everard, Mary's cousin and a youngish ex-doctor. He falls in lust with Monica and in love with Rhoda, who fascinates him both as a woman and as a Woman; he is beginning to "get" feminism in the way one might get religion. Rhoda responds, warily but hungrily; she is the one character who might be said to cross a sexual bar line, Alice settling happily for celibacy and Virginia for dressing as a man with no emotional consequences, or at least none that are made very clear.

The play has a pattern rather than a story, and the dominant thread is how women relate to men when they feel theoretically obliged to break free of them. (Monica is the only one who doesn't feel that. She's a pre-post-feminist.) To a lesser extent, it's about how men relate to women in the same historical circumstances. However, this love-plot, for want of a better term, descends into melodrama. Fierier, if transient, sparks are struck by observations like Alice's when confronted by the Remingtons: "But men are secretaries." So they were, and it was technology that made the difference; there was a time when it was as revolutionary for women to get behind a boss's typewriter as it later became for them to escape from it. There's also a more elaborate, intellectually suggestive sequence in which the characters attend an avant-garde art exhibition and give us their impressions of Impressionism, experienced as both visual revelation and social threat. Such chronological cross-lighting effects, though, are surprisingly rare. We're shown little of what historically happened. It's theory divorced from practice.

This is all the more frustrating when you confront the published text. For this, Griffiths supplies a personal and historical essay that's far more compelling than anything that appears onstage. Among much else, it contains a nuts-and-bolts outline of the fight for women's suffrage and of how, as in all revolutionary movements, the moderates parted company from the militants. It may be too big a canvas for Griffiths, or anyone else, to encompass in a play but it could make a wonderful film--one that no one, as far as I know, has ever attempted.

The dialogue in Age of Arousal is elegant, sometimes witty, but it always seems to be floating above the ground, even when the people are supposed to be suffering. This extends to substantial passages in which the characters utter their thoughts, unheard by their companions; the author calls this "thought-speak" and says that it's different from the Shakespearean soliloquy or aside. She's right; those Elizabethan speeches are dynamic, the actors talk to us. Hers are static and unhelpfully flowery. But nothing is ever new, and her idea was given a thorough and more vigorous workout by Eugene O'Neill in his 1920s marathon Strange Interlude, itself memorably burlesqued by Groucho in the Marx Brothers' Animal Crackers.

Anyway, in Maja Ardal's production, the convention is difficult to discern; the texture is soggy, and the colours run. The set (by Julia Tribe) evokes nowhere in particular, and among the actors it's every man for herself. An English accent goes very well with Clare Coulter's customary air of abstracted hoity-toitiness; whether her magisterial eccentricity is what the role of Mary actually requires is another matter. Ellen-Ray Hennessy and Maggie Huculak do the elder sisters as comic turns, especially Hennessy whose Virginia is burdened by the plot with alcoholism and a trip to Berlin from which she brings back only red herrings. Gemma James-Smith has a more rewarding role as Monica and brings some freshness and energy to it. Sarah Dodd does the most powerful work as Rhoda, though, like most actors trapped in limbo, she sometimes pushes too hard to get out of it. Dylan Smith's main qualification for Everard seems to be that he's actually British; he seems too young and underpowered for the role. Maybe I'm being genderist (hey, I think I've invented a word) but the man's inner struggles strike me as the most interesting in the play. That, at least, is to the play's credit. It has the honesty to be conflicted.

- Age of Arousal runs through Dec. 16 at the Factory Theatre. Call 416-504-9971 for information.

2007-12-05-bentonville-s-befuddled-beast:
It would be stretching the truth to say that Wal-Town is a film about Wal-Mart. Rather, it's a film about a journalist who writes a story about a half-dozen Quebec activists who cross the country, twice, distributing leaflets about and mounting pieces of street theatre outside its stores. That's more degrees of separation than anyone needs.

It also suffers from a sense of deja vu. As an attack on Wal- Marts hiring, firing, pricing and outsourcing practices, it makes no points that werent made in Wal-Mart Nation a couple of years back, and it's not nearly as effective. Wal- Mart Nation was a CBC News-world production, so it makes little sense to blame the new show for being too Canadian. It's tempting, though, because Wal- Town, a co-production of Productions Grand-Nord Quebec Inc. and the National Film Board of Canada, is selfdefeatingly nice, whimsical and polite. It takes its name from the protesters themselves, who have adopted it as a parody of their target.

We should start with Jason, a freelance writer who in 2004 boarded the protesters van to chronicle their cross-continental magical mystery tour. He is very earnest and has the general air of a nineteenth-century Mormon. He had a commission from Corporate Knights, the corporate social responsibility magazine, and his professed aim was to be objective. Or, as he puts it, I think Im going to have a multi-angled, multi-dimensional viewpoint." Too multi-dimensional, it turns out, for the publication, which prides itself on being provocative. Too multi-dimensional as well for Jason himself, who has a personal epiphany. While sitting in his bath he tells us that on his second trip with the group he was determined to take an active part in their protests. And indeed we see him taking part in a play-demo, urging customers to "step up and see the Beast of Bentonville, a fellow-performer with a golden-painted Happy Face. He's cornered and contained" (their word) as bemused passersby are instructed "this is only a short-term solution. They can say that again.

It's rather sweet to be thrown back into the 1960s ambience of the Wal-Town six, who are like Merry Pranksters without the acid, either in their veins or in their thoughts. The film devotes a lot of time to showing the activists sitting around the campfire questioning their own motives and the efficacy of their methods. Of course, everything has to start small, as Wal-Mart itself did, but by 2004, anti-globalization was not exactly a newborn babe. When youre opposing an organization that constitutes the 22nd biggest economy in the world (bigger, to repeat the obvious, than most countries) youre unlikely to achieve much by dressing up in clown suits and handing out pamphlets to customers who drive away without reading them, usually making rude remarks as they go.

Wal-Mart's customers are, as the Wal-Towners themselves admit, the hardest moral nut they have to crack. It's hard to argue with people who want, and need, to buy stuff at rock-bottom prices. That does not, however, explain why Wal-Mart cant devote some of their billions of profits to paying their employees a decent wage, or why they come down so hard on any attempts to secure one. In 2004, we pass through Jonquiere, Que., site of the only Wal-Mart with a unionized workforce; in 2005, its been closed down. Management's claim that it was unprofitable seems a little too convenient. A former mayor of Guelph complains that Wal-Mart, after knocking on the town's door for ten years, has finally bought its way in. A company spokesman asks rhetorically to be shown a town where businesses have been decimated since Wal-Marts arrival; we cut to a row of boarded-up storefronts in Sault Ste.-Marie. In Stratford, Ont., which has held out, a shop owner, in business since 1938," says that "theyve doughnut-ed every town they've gone into. There certainly seem to be no holes on Stratford's main street, though the town, which I know rather well, may have gone too far the other way; there isnt even a supermarket within walking distance of the town centre. There are merry tales of a Quebec Wal-Mart where the staff had to pay for the Christmas party, and even then, the manager of the store won the prize." Monty Burns lives. And thats without getting into the business of child labour abroad, as Wal-Mart has, with the lawsuits to prove it.

It's all stirring stuff, even if we've heard it before, but in this program we only get it in little bits. It makes the cardinal error of believing that protesters are more interesting than what they're protesting against, and that those who chronicle the protests are more interesting still.

"Is that what it comes down to? asks one of our crusaders. Everybody making a lot of money?"

"It came down to that years ago," says a jaundiced but satisfied shareholder. And there the conversation ends, just when it was getting somewhere. This is a red-hot subject, but the treatment is milky white.

-Wal-Town premieres tonight at 10 p.m. on TVO.

2007-12-05-well-at-least-it-has-that-cat:
Irving Berlin's White Christmas

Sony Centre for the

Performing Arts, Toronto

The best critical summary that I know of the film White Christmas was made by one of its stars, the late, great and delightfully honest Rosemary Clooney.

Introducing its title song at one of her concerts, she said that it was a picture that could be enjoyed at the appropriate time of year but had best be avoided at all others. It's certainly no masterpiece of narrative logic. I was once able to share with Clooney my bewilderment over a plot development in which her character, up till then half of a struggling singing-sister act, suddenly gets a booking as the headlining chanteuse in a swank New York showroom. Rosemary, who knew all about the realities of show business, said that she'd never understood it either.

The new stage version of the film, which started out in San Francisco in 2004 and has been trundling around the continent every winter since, is billed as Irving Berlin's White Christmas, which is fair enough, as Berlin's music and lyrics are the most it has going for it. The show's book is credited to David Ives and Paul Blake, who have brought off the remarkable feat of fashioning a narrative even less coherent than its source.

For the benefit of those who keep their TV sets switched off each December: Two Second World War buddies, Captain Bob Wallace and Private Phil Davis, team up as a song, dance and comedy act. Ten years into peacetime they have the entertainment world at their shuffling feet.

They meet the aforementioned sisters, Betty and Judy Haynes, and romance ensues, with no rivalries but some misunderstandings, at least between Bob and Betty. They incidentally are named after the real-life siblings of the performers who first played them, Bing Crosby and Clooney. The other members of the original quartet were Danny Kaye and Vera-Ellen, and the movie traded heavily on the star status of its cast. It also tapped into the wartime nostalgia of a uniquely peaceful decade.

The two guys find their former much-loved general reduced to running an unsuccessful ski lodge in Vermont. They rescue him from bankruptcy by putting on a show (the lodge has a barn), calling on their performing colleagues to make up the cast and on their old military colleagues to make up the audience. The general cannot choke back his tears. Neither, helpless slobs that we are, can we.

The sentiment of the stage White Christmas is actually the least objectionable thing about it. What brings it down is the grinding anonymity of its performance. The script doesn't exactly help.

In the movie, Phil saved Bob's life and has been calling him on it ever since; this gives their relationship a hint of edge. That's completely vanished here, along with the subtler details of Phil's scheming that brings Bob to Vermont in the first place. (He thought he was going to Florida.) The structure is that of a putting-on-a- show show: We get to see some of the numbers on the way through, but virtually nothing at the finale. It's a let down.

Wallace and Davis are supposed to be top-of-the-line performers, able to make the all-powerful Ed Sullivan do their bidding. With Crosby and Kaye, this is credible. Without them, it isn't; the characters have no character, and the actors here don't supply any.

In a role designed to feed into both Bing's affability and his reserve Graham Rowat (Canadian born but American based, so splitting the difference in a bi-national cast), is somnolent. His partner, Tony Yazbeck, is a deft if slightly heavy hoofer with no particular comic flair. Their ladyloves, Kate Baldwin and Shannon O'Bryan, are livelier but hardly earth-shattering.

The only charismatic on board is Kate Hennig as an ex-trouper with an Ethel Merman voice and manner who's wound up behind a reception desk and can't wait to get back out in front of it. A late replacement, she's jubilantly and justifiably confident, despite having some appalling shtick thrown at her before, after and even during her big number.

But the authors are shameless; they throw in a (literally) screaming queen of a stage manager and a couple of squawking brain- dead chorines, the problem being not that these stereotypes are insulting, but that they're boring. And that's not to mention the ultimate horror: a supposedly adorable little girl who goes into a routine, even as the audience prays that she won't. Meanwhile, some of the best grown-up talent in town is consigned to cameos (Paula Wolfson) or to the chorus (Jennifer Stewart).

The director is Walter Bobbie, known for class work like the never-ending revival of Chicago. That makes his presence here mystifying, but his production is at least slick; the sets are both lavish and useful, and though Randy Skinner's choreography isn't going to get any marks for innovation it's certainly crisp, especially in tapping.

And there are the songs. Berlin's film score was made up of good new songs and better old ones, and the stage version widens the net, trawling up irresistible classics like Let Yourself Go and I've Got My Love To Keep Me Warm, plus a couple of treasurable rarities, Love and the Weather and Falling Out of Love Can Be Fun.

These last are done as plot numbers and they don't fit. Still, it's good to hear them. Otherwise: Well, it's that time of year -- you could rent the movie.

- Irving Berlin's White Christmas runs until Jan. 5. at the Sony Centre in Toronto. Call 416-872-2262 for information.

2007-12-06-what-would-jesus-watch-the-pa:
Tonight is the 300th episode of ER. And the fictional characters seem to be in on this extra-textual fact, because they're celebrating by having a betting-pool on admissions: "142 -- if we keep them cranking, we could hit 300," says one of the team in the expository tones so typical of medical staff at the beginning of a show.

Those betting it will happen get a windfall in the shape of a whole convention of food-poisoning victims. Even this doesn't quite bring the numbers up to the required level. Will there be a last- minute casualty that will push them over the top?

Well, I wouldn't want to spoil it for you.

The official reason for all this gambling in the ranks --not to mention the gastric disorders -- is that it is, in the premature way they do these things in TV land, Christmas. So the episode is doubly celebratory. All departments are doing their seasonal bit and "surgery drew the nativity scene." This means that, due to a complicated chain of events, we get to see somebody trying to take a swab from a camel.

The festivities also account for the guest appearance of Reiko Aylesworth, a pleasure to see since she's unlikely to be coming back to her old role on 24 any time soon. (She was Michelle, who is fairly definitively dead.) She plays the hospital chaplain, and her presence gives rise in the script to such unaccustomed words as "proselytizer" and "acolyte," as well as more colloquial phrases like "are you banging the chaplain?" Both levels of discourse are understandable; who wouldn't want to be Ayleseworth's acolyte?

She's also there to serve a higher purpose by offering counsel to troubled regulars, and presiding over a final scene in which she exhorts the personnel to remember the patients who have touched their lives (cue a succession of split-second flashbacks) and to feel justifiably proud of themselves.

The other visiting star is Peter Fonda. He plays a father reunited with his Down's syndrome son on the very day that his terminally-ill wife is to have her plug pulled. Fonda gives this all he's got (this includes a vocal delivery full of calculated hesitations, but how else do you act this kind of thing?) and the situation is as undeniably affecting as it's manipulative. It also reminded me of why, though I can always get sucked into shows like ER while actually watching, I can never get hooked. Medical soaps don't have any of the elements that might keep me tuning in: They aren't funny, they don't have suspense from one episode to the next and their characters are uniformly superficial. And they are numbingly formulaic: Every week there's a life to be saved, of someone we hardly know. (The same formula of Six Feet Under, only in reverse.)

The most believable medical series ever was The Sopranos, which had a lot of scenes set in hospitals. But they were seen, always, from the point of view of the patients, which made them a lot easier (and also more painful) for most of us to identify with. Maybe medical professionals feel the same bond with ER and Grey's Anatomy but I wouldn't bet on it. Not even at Christmas.

Also involving a nativity play --in fact starting with one -- is The Pagan Christ on CBC. A voice-over tells us that one third of the world's population subscribes to basic Christian beliefs, including - - in fact dominated by -- that Jesus was a real person. The film charts the growing disbelief in this of the Canadian religious journalist Tom Harpur, who nonetheless still considers himself a Christian, an allegorical one. For him "the Jesus figure stands for [everybody's] higher self." The film is based on his recent book of the same name.

What sparked his historical doubts were strikingly detailed resemblances between the Christian legend and the myths surrounding numerous Egyptian gods: the birth, the miracles, the resurrection. (He also identifies the Egyptian goddess Isis as "the black Madonna.")

Whether this makes Christianity a plagiarism or just another example of the confluence of myth is left unexplored, but Harpur has plenty of other ammunition. He suggests that Christianity in its official form was imposed by Constantine, the first Christian Emperor of Rome who, to hold the Empire together, insisted that the new state religion be accepted, lock, stock and fairy tales. As in Communist Russia, to disbelieve meant banishment and death.

This is very plausible, and the film strengthens its hand -- in what may be an unfairly emotive way -- by juxtaposing scenes from "The Holy Land Experience," a Christian theme-park in Orlando, Fla. (yes, next door to Disneyworld), guaranteed to turn off any rational person. It also gives pundit time to genial Christian traditionalists of a less fundamentalist aspect; but it's hard not to concur with a pair of English scholarly sceptics. According to them, the orthodox argument amounts to "those other stories are just stories, ours really happened," which is not intellectually respectable.

The Harpur faction are also emphatic that there are no historical references toJesus till 140 years after his death; the Gospels are self-justifying oracles (as well as contradicting one another) and other texts are fragmentary and ambiguous. It all comes as a cold shower, even to non-Christians like myself who have always taken for granted that Jesus was a real and admirable -- and revolutionary -- man. It also raises questions: If he didn't exist, then what did the early Christians believe, and why? They were persecuted, before they started in persecuting others. It's a fascinating pro-gram nonetheless. - The Pagan Christ airs tonight, 9 p.m. on CBC; ER airs at 10 p.m. on CTV.

2007-12-08-turtles-turtles-rah-rah-rah-t:
It was Theodore Roosevelt who said "I don't go so far as to say that the only good Indians are dead Indians, but I believe nine out of 10 are": a statement that's not only hateful but violently ungrammatical. (Nine out of 10 are good? Nine out of 10 are dead? He's unlikely to have meant either of those things.) Roosevelt's statement has been adopted, and adapted, by the Turtle Gals Performance Ensemble for the title of their new show, The Only Good Indian..., subtitled There's No Indians Like Show Indians...

Teddy himself is a character in the show; when he isn't outright vilifying native Americans, he and his wife are taking them to the White House to provide exotic entertainment. He also has an ongoing and not especially friendly relationship with Buffalo Bill Cody who keeps asking him for money. Cody, of course, was one of the founding fathers of the business there's no business like, and his Wild West shows were trailblazers in the matter of exhibiting and exploiting Indian performers. The experiences of four actual Indian writers, musicians and actresses from the 19th and early 20th centuries are here juxtaposed with those of a contemporary quartet being screen- tested for roles in movies. The man they're auditioning for is invariably the spitting image of Buffalo Bill.

The message seems to be that nothing changes. That, though, is a hard point to get across without falling into monotony yourself, and this piece keeps saying the same things. The four Turtle Gals onstage are Falen Johnson, Cheri Maracle, Jani Lauzon and Michelle St. John; they also wrote the show, along with Monique Mojica. The director is Yvette Nolan. The script, we are told, is largely drawn from the writings and utterances of the historical women themselves. There are also songs, not all of them of native origin; I'm still trying to work out what Music! Music! Music! is doing there. On the other hand, the inclusion of two songs from Annie Get Your Gun (one of them parodied) is a clear case of ironic justice.

The foursome do some lovely a cappella harmonizing. As actresses, they play women far better than they play men; their Bill and Teddy are not just caricatures but clumsy ones. They also do far better as the women of the present than of the past, who don't come with enough context to be compelling.

The movie-test scenes are far more immediate; the players are drawing, presumably, on their own experiences that seem, in their seesawing mix of companionship and competitiveness, to be the same as those of most other performers, only more so. Their main complaint is that they're being used, still, as sex objects; I can't say that I've noticed that in recent films to be more the case with native women than with non-native ones (except that the natives get less work anyway) but I defer to their first-hand knowledge. The world, showbiz and other, does seem to be defined here in terms of Indian women versus white men, which does leave a lot out: Indian men, for example. The show is better-humoured than I've probably made it sound, with the performers' own talents making the strongest part of their case.

From Turtle Gals to Theaturtle, the sole visible proprietor is Alon Nashman. This gifted actor is director, designer and narrator of The Snow Queen, a dramatical-musicalchoreographical presentation of the story by Hans Christian Andersen. This, when I was child, always struck me as grimmer than Grimm; its habitat, physical and spiritual, is Arctic. Shards of glass from a black-magic mirror provoke moral blindness in any eye they may fall into; one such victim being the boy Kay who falls under the spell of the evil Queen of the title. Kay's devoted sister, Gerda, travels the snowscape in search of him. The story must have given C. S. Lewis several hints for The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe, but his story is livelier; Andersen's, despite a kind of happy ending, is bleak. Nashman tells it well, though he's best when it gives him specific roles to play, notably that of a helpful crow. The Tokai String Quartet play a nerve-sharpening musical score composed by Patrick Cardy. The dance element is supplied by Kate Alton, whose scattered appearances as the Snow Queen don't add very much.

Turtle Gals, Theaturtle, Sweeney Turtle. Well, perhaps not; but Sweeney Todd, now with a new and improved leading man, has points of contact with The Snow Queen. The musicians in the latter show occasionally lean in to become part of the action; in John Doyle's production of Sweeney the actors, as is well known, are the musicians, and there is often a consonance between who they are and what and how they play. Moreover, the new Sweeney, Alexander Gemignani (he was Beadle Bamford when this production was in New York), is a musician by birthright, son of Stephen Sondheim's regular conductor. He's confined here, Sweeney not being much of a communicator, to a few blasts on the trumpet; vocally, he lacks the bravura to bring off the character's fall into madness, but he is excellent in the earlier scenes, the very picture of dour, impassive vindictiveness. I'd never registered before just how sparely and skilfully Hugh Wheeler's book (from a play by Christopher Bond) dovetails with Sondheim's score. Lauren Molina's dotty and faithful Johanna and Benjamin Magnuson's ingenuous Anthony are as good now as they were in New York. The show as a whole, with Gemignani's Sweeney and Judy Kaye's superlative Mrs. Lovett, is better than it was in New York.

- The Only Good Indian... runs through Dec. 16 at the Tarragon Extra Space (416-531-1402); The Snow Queen runs through Dec. 15 at the Young Centre (416-866-8666) Sweeney Todd closes tomorrow at the Princess of Wales Theatre (416-872-1212).

2007-12-12-lives-of-lonely-loose-lipped-:
A British TV drama series can usually be counted on to start with a bang. The first episode of The Whistleblowers is no exception; it begins with a virtually naked man running in terror down a London street. A young man and woman-- we subsequently learn that they're lawyers, colleagues and lovers -- are driving down the same street and narrowly miss running him over. They witness his recapture by a pair of strong-arm guys who advise them to go home and forget about it. Our couple, whose names are Ben and Alisha, obey the first half of the instructions but not the second. Fairly soon, they discover that the fugitive is a suspected terrorist and that his captors are holding him, a long way under the radar, for "enhanced interrogation."

It looks like the beginning of a series-long intrigue, a sort of anti-24, or a domestic successor to the BBC's brilliant Washington- set The State Within. In fact, though, the situation is wrapped up within the episode. Ben and Alisha drag this semi-judicial thuggery into the light, and get it stopped -- this example of it anyway. Flushed with success but unemployed -- their bosses, bowing to official pressure, have dispensed with their services -- they decide to open their own agency. This agency will provide counsel and support for lonely citizens eager to follow their example by blowing the whistle on all kinds of institutional malfeasance. Next week, we see them confronting a cover-up by a pharmaceutical firm that has carelessly released a deadly virus; the week after, they investigate the suicide of a boy pushed out of a rich school and into a poor one. The rest of the six-part series has them taking on "the immigration service, the drinks industry and an environment agency." (I quote from the press release.) There's corruption everywhere.

I don't doubt it, but in going after so much of it, the show has boxed itself in almost before it's started. It's the latest variation on the old private eye format: You bring us your problems, we'll put them right. It has, of course, grown up a bit; our heroes can expose symptoms, but there's no suggestion that they can heal the underlying rot; they're more Philip Marlowe than Perry Mason. The creator and prime author is Tony Marchant, who 20 years ago was one of Britain's most promising left-wing playwrights. What he's come up with here is reasonably compelling, but without much individuality. The storytelling is sometimes confused (some establishing flashbacks in the first show take forever for the viewer to process) and the characters are paper-thin. Richard Coyle and Indira Varma do what they can for Ben and Alisha without getting much beyond her being the plucky practical one and him being rash and whimsical. Their assistant, a semi-hard-boiled investigator named Kenny (Daniel Ryan) is implausible comic relief. Guest actors are the best: Douglas Hodge, Allan Corduner (Sullivan in Topsy- Turvy), David Threlfall and Josette Simon make up a welcome parade of British old-stagers.

Nearly everyone, though, gets done in at some point by the script's methods of exposition. "What's waterboarding?" asks Ben, all innocence; either he doesn't read the papers or he's trying out for U.S. Attorney General. Before too long he gets to see for himself. So do we; and though it's hard to watch, it's still one of the best sequences in the show. The victim himself is only there because he was implicated, also under torture, by an outsourced innocent who happens to be a citizen of Canada. So at least the writers read the papers, and have heard of Maher Arar. Considering how close to the bone all of this is, the story should be more gripping than it is.

The next two episodes do offer some variations on the format. We get a reluctant whistleblower and a fake whistleblower. The reluctant one is a microbiologist blackmailed by Big Pharma into covering up what they falsely tell him are his own mistakes. So far the villains in the series have been easily identifiable; they wear silk shirts, eat in expensive restaurants and speak in what used to be known as BBC accents. They also regard all other people as expendable. The fake whistleblower is a teacher, employed by one school but a mole for another. "Well, you try living on my salary," he tells the virtuous legal eagles; the author of this third episode, Steve Thompson, is an ex-teacher himself, and that line must have come from the heart. A boy gets sacrificed because his emotional problems might compromise the school's position in the academic league tables. But the show can't just leave it there. The school also has to be a bastion of the religious right, teaching creationism in science classes. Presumably this reflects the beliefs of the rich man whose millions are funding the place, but neither he nor the situation are ever explored. This is the best, most complex instalment of the three, but it's still hampered by characters who converse in sound bites. "If they can do this," says the bereaved mother, "if they can refuse to help my son ..." Ben completes the thought for her: "Then think about how many other kids may be in need." Worthy thoughts, wooden words. - The Whistleblowers airs at 9 p.m. ET on Wednesdays beginning tonight on TVO.

2007-12-14-the-voice-of-jane-sex-money-a:
Every 10 years or so, the novels of Jane Austen hit our large and small screens with a collective thud. As there are only six books in the Austen canon, the movie studios this time around have felt obliged to supplement them with such cinematic fancies as Becoming Jane (the early life of a classic author) and The Jane Austen Book Club (the posthumous life of a classic author).

Meanwhile British television has been working its way, yet again, through the approved texts. Three of these adaptations are playing on TVO over the next three Sundays.

Leading off is Northanger Abbey, Austen's first novel, though not published until after her death.

It starts with a mild shock. Theres an introductory voice-over, delivered in creamily ironic tones by Geraldine James, billed here as "the Voice of Jane Austen."

She introduces us to our heroine, Catherine Moreland, one of 10 children in a genteel English country family and known when growing up as a tomboy whose favourite pastimes were cricket and baseball. Baseball? Surely Andrew Davies, the adaptor, notorious for smuggling jokey anachronisms into ancient texts, is tossing a bone to the North American market. But no, its authentic voice-of-Jane. America's national pastime was an English ex-sport.

Catherine, we learn, progressed from ball games to reading. She immersed herself in Gothic novels like Ann Radcliffe's The Mysteries of Udolpho, the original bodice-rippers.

Northanger Abbey is at once a spoof of the genre, an example of it and a reproach to it. Catherine, at least in this TV version, cant take a simple trip in a stagecoach without visions of highwaymen and ravishments dancing in her head.

Her destination is the spa town of Bath, the mecca of Regency England high society. Everythings more free and easy in Bath, says one of the visiting bucks.

From there she progresses to Northanger Abbey itself, a Gothic pile after her own heart. Extending the invitation to stay is the owner, one General Tilney, who looks like the place's grinning ogre. There should be lightning playing around his head.

For Catherine the place has two major attractions. One is the General's son Henry, a highly eligible young clergyman. The other is the abbeys potential as a repository of ghostly secrets.

Davies is the most prolific of TVs literary adaptors and one of the most skillful. There are only two reasons for objecting to this.

One is that Davies is, or used to be, an excellent TV dramatist in his own right; in the 1980s he wrote A Very Peculiar Practice, a cunning combination of two popular genres -- campus and medical -- and one of the best miniseries ever, a comedy that got deeper and darker as it went on.

The other is that his adaptations get further and further away from the words the novelists actually wrote. He keeps the plots and characters but he loses the style. Without Jane Austen's running commentaries, all you're left with a series of courtship anecdotes in pretty frocks.

Davies tries to get around this by modernizing not only dialogue but action. In practical terms, that means he makes explicit what Austen kept veiled and decorous.

This Northanger Abbey may be the first Jane Austen ever to include a nude scene: a back view only, and part of a dream, but still. "Nothing to be afraid of," says the Rev. Harry. One of Catherines friends gets seduced by an unscrupulous officer, and we get an actual bedroom scene.

Yes, Austens novels really are about sex and money, but there's still a feeling of being nudged. As in: You thought Jane Austen was repressed and spinsterish? This'll learn ya.

Its no substitute for an accurate, witty account of the protagonists progress. Felicity Jones' Catherine is a pretty miss from 21st-century suburbia. She doesn't, as all Austen heroines should, learn from her mistakes; its hard to wince with her or to rejoice.

JJ Feilds agreeable Henry has the right stuff; so, in a quieter vein, does Catherine Walker as Eleanor, his guardian angel of a sister. She gets married at the end of the story, to a suitor we haven't met before, and with the blessing of her hitherto implacable father.

The Voice of Jane chimes in again, cheerfully acknowledging the improbability and pondering whether her tale may be said "to recommend parental tyranny or reward filial disobedience."

The artificiality is delicious, but the TV script balks at going all the way with it. It gives us an earlier meeting between Eleanor and her betrothed.

Northanger Abbey is its author's slightest work, and so the more difficult to translate to another medium.

Mansfield Park and Persuasion, two of the major novels, lie ahead. We'll see.

- Northanger Abbey airs on Sunday at 9 p.m. on TVO.

2007-12-15-it-s-a-wonderful-life-plus-mu:
The conventions governing the interactive murder mysteries at the Mysteriously Yours dinner theatre are as rigid as those for Japanese Kabuki or Greek Old Comedy. You start with a source, some popular movie that's taken on iconic significance. Thus the current show, It's a Wonderful Death!, is inspired, as hardly needs saying, by the 1946 Frank Capra-James Stewart picture of almost the same name that television and American sentimentality have turned into a Christmas classic. You assemble its characters, or variations on them, in a confined space. You isolate one of them -- usually some old geezer with more money and less charity than is good for him -- and establish that each of the others has reason to wish him dead. Then you kill him. He will be played by Jean Daigle, director, co-writer and star; his early disposal in one role makes it possible for him to return in another -- generally a bulky cop with a Newfie accent - - and investigate his own demise. He will interrogate the other actors, and also members of the audience who have been summarily issued with temporary identities and even the occasional spoken line. He will have us all vote on the murderers identity, and at the end he will say which of us got it right. I never do.

Sometimes it works, sometimes it doesnt. It has a lot to do with the fecundity of the material that the authors have chosen to lampoon. ("Parody" is too flattering a word, plunder too harsh.) If your target is The Godfather, you can expand it to draw on the whole tradition of gangster movies, and the audience's awareness of it. But It's a Wonderful Life isnt a genre picture in that sense. Its a one-off, a moralizing fantasy: Instead of mobsters, it features angels; in place of a godfather, God. George Bailey, a.k.a. Jimmy Stewart, is in despair at his failure to protect his savings-and-loan clients from the depredations of the local Mr. Big, but a heavenly emissary saves him by showing him--in a reverse-Scrooge effect -- how much worse his world would have been had he never existed. It's an alternate-universe movie.

One result of this is that the characters, whichever plane of reality they may currently be inhabiting, are shadowy. The nefarious Mr. Potter, George's wife, Mary, his fighter-pilot brother Harry, their feckless Uncle Billy, Violet the local tramp -- none of them are substantial enough to make fun of. A good joke has to have its basis in some kind of reality. Anyway thats the best excuse I can offer for the flatness of the script here. The authors -- Brian Caws, Brian Smith and Daigle -- even fail, for the first time in my experience, to offer solid reasons to suspect every one of the characters. Its one thing not to know who did it; it's another not to care.

I never thought I'd say such a thing about a Mysteriously Yours production, but this show may be the victim of its own sophistication. It keeps the motif of God sending down an angel to take care of good ol George. This deity doesnt run to a burning bush, but he does speak -- in much the best effect of the evening -- from within a suddenly illuminated chandelier. (And his voice, not too surprisingly, is the voice of Daigle.) This seraph, recruited from somewhere far in the East (that is, beyond Ottawa),manifests himself as the investigating cop -- not, I would say, an easy fit and one that the show has no idea what to do with. Still, it makes the attempt and even goes metaphysical on us in the process. We must, we are told, find a motivation that will fit our suspect in both worlds. This fairly made my head spin, and I gave up on any serious attempt to spot the culprit. When the time came to hand in our ballots, I didn't exactly spoil mine, but I did vote for Mr. Potter as the author of his own demise; he seemed to have by far the best reason. I was wrong, of course, and my conclusion (in which, incidentally, I was not alone) was roundly scorned by Daigle at the last judgment. I have to say, though, that when the truth was revealed, it struck me as cheating, even by the elastic standards previously established around here. Maybe the real truth is that It's a Wonderful Life was never meant to be a murder story, or even the farfetched excuse for one; its too, well, bloodless. Maybe they were confusing it with Its a Wonderful World, a Stewart vehicle of the previous decade, that really was a comedy-thriller. Though, since it isn't a famous title, probably not.

What compensations can I list? The menu, though I wish I'd ordered the steak. A couple of musical numbers for Brigitte Solem as Violet; shes flat -- her voice anyway -- but I think thats the point. She welcomes George's brother back from the war with I'm Just Wild about Harry, fitted out with wonderfully excruciating, new lyrics. "Those Axis powers/They fought for hours." Daigle, who as that "scurvy little spider" looks and sounds like James Gandolfini playing Winston Churchill, and who, in his subsequent police persona, manages as ever to make bullying the audience seem positively endearing. We know its for our own good. I wonder, as Ive done before, whether this superb comedian might be lured away from his present, obviously profitable activity and persuaded to act in, say, Moliere. I wonder similarly whether the whole Mysteriously caboodle might be persuaded to expand its horizons and try some other format. Or at least if it might acknowledge that its performance space actually includes a stage and that it might utilize it from time to time instead of leaving the cast to weave ceaselessly between the customers' tables.

- It's a Wonderful Death! runs indefinitely at Mysteriously Yours. Call 416-486-7469 for details.

2007-12-19-placing-euro-disney-in-artist:
Walt Disney spent four years of his boyhood on a Missouri farm. The experience doubtless contributed to his sense of the natural world as a backdrop, to his anthropomorphic approach to animals and to his general good ol' folksiness. Just as important, according to Walt Disney: Once Upon a Time (in CBC Newsworld's Wild Docs slot), was his mother's habit of telling him fairy tales at dinnertime. The traditional, and fairly horrific, European stories ate deep into his imagination. Add this to his innate technical, pictorial and entrepreneurial talents and you have what this film's commentary calls "a worldwide empire," built, in a memorably jaw-breaking phrase, on "turning the phantasmagorical into the cinematographical."

"It all started," as you may have heard before, "with a mouse." We hear again the story of how the struggling Disney operation, after having a couple of its best ideas stolen right out from under it, came up with the fabulously squeaky and rubbery Mickey (voiced by Walt himself ), whose debut picture Steamboat Willie, the first animated feature with synchronized sound, conquered the world. What is new in this telling is the way that it juxtaposes Disney's creations with those of earlier authors and illustrators, starting with the British ones: Richard Dadd, Arthur Rackham and most notably Beatrix Potter. He then moved beyond and behind them. The director of Once Upon a Time, Samuel Doux, places Mickey and his friends within a literary and pictorial tradition. Emulating his subject's bent for intrusive cuteness, he even has a couple of cartoon rodents of his own sitting at the side of the frame and saying, in marvelling tones, "we are distant cousins of Mickey Mouse."

The device is only used once and momentarily, making you wonder why it's there at all. For the most part, the film is a conventional mixture of clips, montage and talking heads. Doux is French, and his main point -- a fascinating one -- is to show Disney as a very American artist paying consistent homage to European art. Partly this is a matter of source material; we are told that of the 17 feature-length films in which Disney himself had a hand, 14 derive from European sources. He was self-taught, with "a suspicion of culture in general," but, in a familiar paradox, "he had a fascination with more learned culture." He was shy

of it, but he also wanted to co-opt, and perhaps to be coopted by it. (In that sense he might be said to represent the essence of studio-era Hollywood, though, among those using flesh-and-blood performers, MGM came close.)

He came back from his own first trip to Europe loaded down with art books. He also, again like the other studios but more so, assembled a creative team drawn from the European diaspora. The result was a fruitful clash of traditions. The stern engravings of Gustave Dore inspired the fearsome forests of Sleeping Beauty and Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs, where the trees come to terrifying life. Meanwhile, the Dwarfs are sheer cuddly Americana (nobody before Disney had thought to give them distinct personalities, let alone names), bluebirds start warbling at any hint of romance and the musical score is liable to turn to syrup, though less so than in later Disney pictures. Snow White herself, we learn -- "the first time the studio had to animate a human character" -- was consciously designed as a combination of Shirley Temple and Janet Gaynor, with a singing voice even more irritating than Temple's, which at least came naturally. But she also has a touch of Fay Wray menaced by King Kong. Most intriguing nugget: The mature and still beautiful actress singing the mirror-gazing Queen removed her false teeth to provide the voice for a Witch, whose visual inspiration was Honore Daumier.

Pinocchio gives us an Italian story set in a village that's pure Bavaria. Salvador Dali said that there were three great surrealists in Hollywood: the Marx Brothers (that's three already, but never mind), Cecil B. DeMille and Disney. He especially loved Disney's Pink Elephants Parade. Walt proposed a collaboration, something called Destino that was meant as a supplement to Fantasia. We are shown the 18 seconds of animated test for a picture that remained unmade: a "great American-European cultural partnership" left unrealized.

Disney's favourite book apparently was Alice in Wonderland, and he consciously planned Disneyland as a trip through the looking- glass. The Alice movie took him 15 years to make, and it's tempting to ask why, if he loved the book so much, he had to desecrate it. But the clips shown here suggests that he didn't, or not as much as one remembers. His Alice is a very fair descendant of the original as drawn by John Tenniel, and it's irresistible to watch Jerry Colonna, complete with shriek and moustache, laying down his vocal for the March Hare. Anyway the film -- which, it's surprising to learn, lost money -- is integrity itself compared to what the Disney corporation later did to the Winnie The Pooh stories, text, visuals and all. The latest picture we're shown here is The Jungle Book. The Bare Necessities number is shown in a French-dubbed print, which is charming but does rather destroy the pun in the title. Disney was never at his happiest with English Lit. What turned him on were the old French, Italian and especially Germanic titles, wild woods and bare mountains, given his personal once-over. Nature sweet of tooth and red of claw.

- Walt Disney: Once Upon a Time airs tonight at 10 p.m. on CBC Newsworld.
