2007-12-22-letters-from-a-blithe-spirit:
THE LETTERS OF NOEL COWARD

Edited by Barry Day

Knopf

800 pp., $47

---

How, on a given day, did Noel Coward decide which of his talents to use? The acting, singing, directing and producing would obviously be scheduled in advance, but how about the writing choices? What prompted him to compose a song, a play, a story, a novel, a poem, a diary entry or -- something he seems to have done at some point on most days --a letter?

Probably it wasn't a problem. Coward was a single-minded multi- talent, an enviable combination. One of his charms seems to have been that, while always ferociously busy, he had time for people; for friends, colleagues and family. Though in his case "family," at least in the blood-relative sense, boiled down to one person. The same man who created Mrs. Worthington, that song in which the stage- struck mother and her awful progeny are forever immolated, owed his own career to Mrs. Violet Coward's maternal determination to put him on the stage, at the age of 11. He never forgot it, and neither did she. The theatre was his passport out of genteel suburban poverty, and it was hers as well: literally -- her son was able to take very good care of her, and incidentally of his father and brother, for whom he had little personal warmth -- but also vicariously. She bathed in his glow, and he loved the fact that she did. Even before she changed his life by securing him a role in a London Christmas show, she was his confidante. When sent away to stay with relatives, he wrote her longing letters beginning "Dear Darling old Mummy- snooks," or "mother duckie."

Homesickness, Barry Day observes, was "a condition that was to apply for many years to come when he was separated from his mother." Day, who has previously edited a handsome and formidably complete collection of Coward's lyrics, has not so much annotated the letters (he explicitly rejects footnotes) as contextualized them. He has in fact given us a Coward biography, with the letters -- including some written to the subject rather than by him -- as the chief exhibit. What becomes clear is that you could tell most of the Coward story, at least up until 1954, when Violet died, by his letters to her, so concerned was he that she be made to feel part of it. The filial tone changes somewhat as he grows older, or perhaps just as he grows more successful. The salutation is shortened to "Darling," and the signature is "Snoop." Hers, to him, is "Snig." These exchanges were probably more fun for them to write than they are for us to read. (Though they are restraint itself compared to the way Coward habitually greeted Alexander Woollcott, the self-anointed wit of the Algonquin Round Table; he was "Dearest Acky-wacky-weesa." It may have suited him. He certainly doesn't seem to have been very grown- up.)

Regular and affectionate though the letters to Violet may be, they are informative rather than revealing. He has, after all, a duty to put a good face on everything. Troubles with temperamental actors are treated as jokes, and any personal unhappiness goes unmentioned. His love life is strictly out of bounds, and not only when writing to Mum. Probably the love of Coward's life was his American manager and producer, Jack Wilson, but as their relationship cools it's Wilson's professional rather than his personal conduct that comes in for censure. Livid though Coward obviously was at Wilson's grievous mismanagement of his finances, he cannot bring himself to be rude to him. He tries to make allowances. And this is consistent with all of his friendships. Coward, by many people's testimony, was a very kind man. He certainly seems to have found it hard to be explicitly unkind. You feel that he swallowed a lot of bile.

It seems to be the flip side of his refusal to admit emotional vulnerability. "To hell with God-damned L'Amour," he writes to Marlene Dietrich, who's been sending sorrowful epistles about her (mostly) unrequited passion for Yul Brynner; "it always causes far more trouble than it's worth." He liked to pretend that he himself was above it, though we know from other sources that he wasn't. If he disparaged romance, he exalted friendship, particularly in that of theatrical peers such as the Lunts and of the small circle of helpers and associates whom he came to think of as his "family." One of them was theatrical designer Gladys Calthrop, whom he addressed as "Cock" and to whom he wrote nearly as often as he did to his mother, and far less guardedly. From Jerusalem: "I flew here yesterday and it's a fair f--ker except for the Arabs and Jews fighting each other and me having to faire the gentil promenade."

This was 1938, and the prelude to his career, still too little known or appreciated, as a wartime agent. He shared with Winston Churchill (here "my dear Winston," though they admired rather than liked one another) the distinction of being among the few Englishmen to have been consistently right about Hitler. He was sent to Paris to help set up a Bureau of Propaganda, an assignment that found him at first enthusiastic and then disillusioned, before setting off as a roving observer-entertainer through the United States, Australia and most of the Asian Front. Thence home to write, direct and star in In Which We Serve (and he didn't even like movies).

He did his greatest work before the war, became a figurehead during it and fell from favour after it. Notoriously, he attacked the new young playwrights of the 1950s, just as he himself had been attacked in the '20s for writing such radical plays as The Vortex. That was in print; in person the story was, again, something else. One of the most cheering entries in his Diaries is the realization that, against all his instinctive prejudices, he is "on [Harold] Pinter's wavelength." He expands on this here in letters to the playwright: "You cheerfully break every rule of the theatre that I was brought up to believe in, except the cardinal one of never boring for a split-second. I love your choice of words, your resolute refusal to explain anything ..." It's one of the best concentrated pieces of Pinter criticism I've read.

He also maintained mutually admiring correspondences with John Osborne, Edward Albee and, despite grave philosophical differences, Arnold Wesker. This section, a record of talent saluting talent, is the most valuable and revealing in the book.

Almost the last letter printed is from his 70th year, three years before his death. His doctors, to his fury, had told him to exercise and give up smoking. He writes, "I suppose I could make very old bones indeed -- look at Mum -- but I'm not at all sure I want that. I've never wanted to be the last to leave any party." The letter was written to Gladys Calthrop. It was signed Yours, LAZARUS.

---

FROM 'NOELIE' WITH LOVE - To his secretary, Lorn Loraine, about actress Tallulah Bankhead, who had given him an Augustus John painting only to demand it back, Coward wrote, "Tallulah, apart from being a conceited slut, is a black liar. She gave me the bloody picture.Why in hell should I wish to be lent an Augustus John portrait of a pear drop? Send it back!" A year or two later, American theatre director Jack Wilson was considering casting the actress. Coward wrote again to Lorn, "The play he has for Tallulah is based on a Henry James novel. It is very gentle and subtle and if Miss Bankhead can discipline herself to refrain from farting to get a laugh or bouncing ping-pong balls off her tits, it might be a success." - When he was 64, Coward wrote to Laurence Olivier ("Larryboy"), "It is being slowly and painfully beaten into my skull that I am no longer a precocious boy of 19, although when I look in the mirror at this lovely little heart-shaped face with all those pretty little jowls hanging from it, I find it hard to believe." - The next year he wrote to his friends the acting team Alfred Lunt and Lynn Fontanne, "I have had several chins taken away in London by a brilliant plastic surgeon ... I now look an old 12."

2007-12-31-plots-that-dare-not-show-real:
Letitia Prism, the Victorian governess immortalized in Oscar Wilde's The Importance of Being Earnest, once wrote a three-volume novel. Few ever got to read it because she absent-mindedly confused the manuscript with the baby she was minding at the time, depositing the former in a perambulator and the latter, famously, in a handbag. This mischance condemned her to the ranks of the great unread, but it didn't stop her from firmly enunciating an aesthetic credo. Asked how her novel ended she replied, "The good ended happily, the bad unhappily. That is what fiction means."

And that is what it did mean, for centuries. There were some variations allowed, depending on what kind of piece you were writing. In Shakespeare's comedies -- the pop hits of their day -- justice was dispensed strictly on the Prism principle. His tragedies were more, shall we say, realistic. The bad still ended unhappily, but so very noticeably did the good, or at least the more prominent among them. A few virtuous people were permitted to survive, to clear up the bodies and to suggest the persistence of a moral order in the universe.

This, though, was not enough for the puritan critics of that or subsequent ages. One in the next generation, contemplating the cruel ends of some of Shakespeare's loveliest ladies, asked "in that case, what profiteth it us to be virtuous?" It's a good question, to which no one has ever come up with a good answer. If literature and drama say anything about virtue, it is that it had better be its own reward.

Our own pop culture has a long tradition of denying this. The Hollywood Code laid it down that virtue should always be triumphant, or at the least that crime should never be seen to pay. Television paid implicit allegiance to the same Code. In recent years, though, the cage has been rattled and this year it has shattered. The TV event of 2007 was the finale of The Sopranos. The best-regarded movie was No Country for Old Men. And in both, the arch-criminal walks away.

It would be a stretch perhaps to say that Tony Soprano ends happily. His world has contracted, there are criminal charges in his future that he'll find difficult to beat, his friends and colleagues are either alienated or dead. Nevertheless, last thing we see, he's still alive and eating with his family, even though the series' tone, and all our expectations of the gangster genre, have led us to expect a violent ending in which he may very well perish. The deal was: "You die, and we'll forgive you your sins, and we'll forgive ourselves for liking you." Well, it worked for James Cagney; his was a black-and-white world in which the black was more exciting but was also condemned. The Sopranos is a crime story told almost entirely from the criminals' point of view, a theme on which the best subsequent HBO series have been playing variations. The Wire alternates cops with robbers, suggesting there's little to choose between them; Deadwood mixed them up almost indistinguishably. Showtime's Dexter is a sympathetic serial-killer serial. And this has filtered through to other networks -- the most likeable characters in Prison Break are the ones behind bars, not all of them unjustly. It's a grey, grey world.

No Country for Old Men presents a black one. Once Hollywood would have soft-pedalled Cormac McCarthy's novel or ignored it entirely. The Coen brothers take it literally, with bleak relish. The character we identify with is morally ambiguous; he's also brutally - - but casually -- killed off. Much the same thing happened in Hitchcock's Psycho, but this time it happens near the end of the picture, leaving us no time to readjust, and there are no good people to avenge him. There are decent folks, but they're ineffectual. The villain meanwhile is as close as the movies have come to presenting cold, unredeemable evil. And he gets away, wounded but alive. Maybe justice will catch up with him somewhere down the road, but there's a strong suggestion that he's invincible. And there's naught for our comfort; he isn't even charming.

Wilde's Lady Bracknell, who did get to read Miss Prism's novel, pronounced it a work "of more than usually revolting sentimentality." If nothing else, our new works are an escape from decades, maybe centuries, of having to view the world through Prism's prism. Lady B might well have found the ambiguities of The Sopranos disturbing, but she would have been right at home with the bleakness of No Country. It could have been her country. She was, after all, "a monster without being a myth. Which is rather unfair." Like life.

2008-01-03-the-wire-the-beginning-of-the:
If you look on US television as a Goliath, then it makes a sort of sense that the writers who have most successfully challenged the conventions of the drama series should all be called David. David Chase gave us The Sopranos, David Milch Deadwood, and David Simon The Wire. Of these three HBO treasures, the first has run its course, the second was cut unconscionably off in its prime, the third is about to begin its fifth and last season.

All three Davids produce their shows, and by all accounts exercise tight control. Chase and Milch also direct, but Simon is the only one of these auteurs who is strictly an author. He writes or co-writes an impressive proportion of The Wire’s scripts, and has a story credit on every episode. Before coming into television he was a journalist, a crime reporter on the Baltimore Sun. His experiences on that beat were the inspiration for The Wire, the story of a beleaguered police detail trying to bring down the drug-lords controlling the housing projects of West Baltimore. The show’s first series concentrated on that theme while casting side-glances at a few others: municipal corruption for example. Subsequent series, while keeping the same core of characters, have widened the focus to look at Baltimore’s politics, its waterfront, its school system. The general picture has been one of greed, graft and hopelessness: a world from which drugs – doing them, or dealing them, or both – offer the only hopes of escape.

This new series introduces us to another level of Baltimore society, the press - specifically Simon’s old employer the Sun with which he has a well-documented love-hate relationship. Strangely, this world of which he was actually part rings less true on the screen than do the cops and gangsters whom he merely observed. Both the setting and the characters look right (one of the newsroom veterans happens to be a dead ringer for a senior writer at the Toronto Star) and there is a nice weary swagger to some of the dialogue: “at the Sun, God still resides in the details” says an editor, instructing a reporter in the difference between evacuating a building and evacuating a person. But there is, at least in the first two episodes, something self-consciously expository about both the writing and the acting of these guys; though it’s interesting that the city editor, who seems to be the focal figure, is played by Clark Johnson, the director who piloted The Wire’s pilot.

It’s taking time for these scenes to connect with the rest of the show on a narrative level, though there are promises from the publicity department that we’ll be seeing hard-hitting stories muzzled by the paper’s corporate owners. That’s what’s always been happening to the cops on The Wire, in constant danger of having their investigations thwarted or muzzled by jealous or incompetent superiors, fearful of having their own secrets uncovered. And already there’s a thematic connection. The paper is threatened by downsizing; so are the cops. They can’t even get overtime. The boys (and girls) on The Wire have seen their detail dissolved, reformed, dissolved again, ever since it first got together in Episode One. It’s all of course a question of priorities. “One thieving politician trumps 22 dead bodies” says the perpetually angry Detective Jimmy McNulty. “That’s good to know.” One of the recurring ironies in The Wire is that even those who might be on the side of the angels make careful, self-interested choices as to which angels they’ll serve.

There are people who think The Wire even better than The Sopranos, and certainly it tells us more about the texture of Baltimore than The Sopranos ever did about New Jersey. It has a wider focus. But it also has a shallower one. It’s more about plot than about character. It’s impossible to imagine The Wire depicting a relationship as deep and tangled as that between Tony and Carmela, or coming up with a figure as juicy as, say, Paulie Walnuts. There are certainly engaging figures; my own favourite is Bubbles, the junkie informant (Andre Royo) surprisingly still with us and even on his feet after five years. It’s also been nice to chart the rise of Lester, the supercool cop with a genius for processing information, doing what he does best after years relegated to the pawn-shop control. (He’s played, with superb unflappability, by Clarke Peters, whom I remember as a fixture in London musicals in the 70s and 80s. Style’s always good.) On the whole though we react to, and sympathise with, the cops as a team rather than as individuals. We do sympathise with them, even though Simon has emphatically disclaimed any possibility of glorifying or ennobling them. They are guys, doing a job, for their own reasons, mainly self-interested. But it seems to be a job worth doing, even though the show acknowledges its hopelessness. Strike down one gang and another appears. (The Wire is the best possible argument for drug legalisation.) This is almost the first show (not quite – there was the ill-fated Line of Fire) to give equal time to cops and criminals. The most haunting figure among the outlaws has been the young D’Angelo Barksdale who, in the first series, went down to serious time so that his gang-lord uncle might get off. It was his mother who persuaded him to do this, and it was horrifying, but her arguments made a certain sense. What other support-system was he going to find? In the new series one of the newsmen suggests a story on “Dickensian lives of city children.” He’s being sentimental and opportunistic as hell, but he’s also right. These conditions are out of Dickens. And these TV shows are the new form of novel that chronicles them for us.

2008-01-05-forget-the-doras-here-s-the-c:
Alook back at some of the best performances of 2007 and the shows they came in:

Seana McKenna ( Orpheus Descending) The best came first, since this scalding performance was unsurpassed by anyone this year including McKenna herself; though Shakespeare's Will, her Stratford solo, confirmed that she can do anything--except, apparently, sing madrigals. The Orpheus ensemble in Toronto was slightly less starry than it had been at Stratford but hardly less good.

Eric Peterson, Carolyn Hetherington, Diego Matamoros and all ( Half Life) Another ensemble return, heart-rending and impeccable. Like the play.

Daniel MacIvor ( Monster, House) This retrospective season cemented MacIvor's fearsome legend as a theatrical soloist. His plays elsewhere, involving other actors, were less exciting.

Maude Mitchell, very tall, and Mark Povinelli, very short, mixing their own metaphor in Mabou Mines Dollhouse, a visiting show from New York whose Ibsen deconstruction was alternately exasperating and invigorating. In a contrastingly sober WorldStage import, Aalst (from Belgium), Felix van Groeningen and Lise Pauwels, as child- murderers, took naturalistic behaviourism as disturbingly far as it can go. Habib Dembele and Pitcho Womba Konga ( Sizwe Bansi Is Dead) History lived.

Anand Rajaram ( Tip of the Melting Iceberg), the best Second City revue in ages. Thom Allison (Elegies, The Wizard of Oz) Star quality. Yvan Pedneault, Erica Peck, Jack Langeduk ( We Will Rock You) Fresh Canadian talent in a stale British show.

Albert Schultz and Company ( The Threepenny Opera) Soulpeppers fresh and mature combining on a largely excellent production of the hardest tuner in the repertoire.

Jordan Pettle, Yanna McIntosh and Cliff Saunders ( Danny, King of the Basement) playing children, for children, as seriously and skilfully as if they were playing grown-ups for grown-ups, in a play that's a genre classic.

Michelle Monteith and Maev Beaty ( The Russian Plays) A revived Hannah Moscovitch play paired with a new one, both inspiring virtuoso acting. Monteith, an acrid waif, was the young actress of the Toronto year, sharing honours with Steven McCarthy in the beautiful Revisited (from Halifax) and with a fine team in the exacting Crave.

Nicola Lipman ( Scorched) Stonily impressive, in a play and production not so much scorched as overheated.

Joseph Ziegler, Family and Associates ( A Whistle in the Dark) Yet another perfect remount, with Ziegler's Falstaffian patriarch matched against Allan Hawco's terrifying tearaway.

Susan Bennett and Ryan Kelly

( Will the Real JT Leroy Please Stand Up), transcending camp in a Sky Gilbert play that does the same, even if its author doesn't want it to.

Jane Spidell and Oliver Dennis

( Leaving Home), turning marginal characters in one of those "Canadian classics" into newly polished comic jewels; in the central role, Kenneth Welsh was equal parts incomprehensible and enchanting.

Tara Rosling ( Saint Joan) Moving if not exactly soldierly, and surrounded by a sterling Shaw Festival crew. Opening week also found this company at its best in The Circle (everybody), A Month in the Country (nearly everybody), The Philanderer ( Ben Carlson and Deborah Hay). Later on and better still, Goldie Semple, Mary Haney and Trish Lindstrom were a transcendent trio in The Cassilis Engagement, a real discovery. As were The Kiltartan Comedies and their young leading man, Patrick McManus.

Fiona Reid ( Homebody/Kabul) She had a very good year but this was matchless virtuosity. Sarah Dodd ( Marion Bridge) The best in this, she also shone in Whistle and Age of Arousal, which also featured Clare Coulter in a world of her own.

Brian Bedford ( King Lear) Moving as he's never been (and more so than Ian McKellen's quizzical king in the U.K. and U.S.). Also Scott Wentworth's superb Gloucester. Elsewhere in Stratford's opening batch: Cynthia Dale and Laird Mackintosh in My One and Only, exhilarating, like the show. Lots of people in a provocative Merchant of Venice. Jonathan Goad, magnetic, and Lucy Peacock, overwhelming, in Othello, both also shone elsewhere and she was the actress of the year.

Two George Walker ensembles,

veteran ( Better Living) and juvenile ( Tough).

Soulpepper Unlimited. Four great shows. If Top Girls, the newest script, also seemed the thinnest, it called for and got seven superb performances. The Time of Your Life (Joe Ziegler again presiding), Mary Stuart (Nancy Palk v. a grown-up Yanna McIntosh) and Three Sisters had whole stagefuls of them.

Everyone ( A Delicate Balance, The Odyssey, Pentecost) Richard Monette's Stratford regime all-but-concluded with three superbly exciting shows on successive nights. Nigel Shawn Williams's Odysseus was a giant step.

Shaun Smyth and Paul Fauteux

( The Pillowman) Brothers in the best new foreign play. Brendan Gall, Paul Dunn and Diana Donnelly ( East of Berlin). Friends, enemies and lovers in the best new Canadian play. Though both pieces transcend boundaries.

Bob Martin ( The Drowsy Chaperone) Call him irreplaceable. Philip Graeme ( The Prince Hamlet) A partial text, a complete performance. Brent Carver ( The Elephan Man) Fresh light on a faded play. Randy Hughson ( The Drawer Boy) A new way to play a role thought to be definitively taken. David Ferry Ubiquitous.

Judy Kaye ( Sweeney Todd) The best Mrs. Lovett -- and there have been lots.

Ron Pedersen, Deborah Zentilli and a man-eating plant ( Little Shop of Horrors) Pedersen also good, along with Adam Brazier, in the earlier Rocky Horror Show, but second time was the charm.

Kurt Browning ( Peter Pan) Skating and flying. Kate Hennig ( White Christmas) A show-stopping surprise. And, in this show, a relief.

It was also the year we lost Bill, Ed, Bluma and Richard: One great artist, two great enablers, and one who was both.

2008-01-08-not-quite-a-step-up-y2k-for-t:
You might guess that a jPod would be the next thing up from an iPod.

Guess again.

In Douglas Coupland's new TV series, based on his novel, jPod is the name given to a haphazard team of video-game designers all herded together during the Y2K computer panic (remember that?) because all their surnames began with the letter J. So we have a show whose premise is a pun, if that. It may have seemed delightfully inconsequential on the page. On the screen it's just silly.

I mean, by my simple arithmetic the show's co-workers, employees of a huge Vancouver company called Neotronic Arts, have been herded now for seven years, time enough for even the most intransigent organization to have acknowledged that its computer had bungled and to have done something to put it right.

The show, at least on the strength of tonight's first episode, makes nothing of its characters' shared initial, maybe because there's nothing that could be made. It just seems a too-cute way of getting together a variegated bunch of employees for another workplace comedy. At the centre of it is Evan Jarlewski (David Kopp), the team's "gore specialist," which involves finding new ways of putting "carnage and violence into video games while conforming to industry quality codes."

You might think that this job description would make him quite cutting edge but it seems that video violence in and of itself is, well, so 20th century. This at least is what I gleaned yesterday morning from hearing Coupland himself, who talks very engagingly about his own creations (as about most other things), discuss the matter in a radio interview with Shelagh Rogers. According to Coupland, Evan is the repository of traditional moral values in a world hell-bent on shedding and shredding them. And he does seem innocent, or at least charming, compared to his immediate colleagues: Casper Jesperson, self-renamed Cowboy, a Yalie obsessed with sex and death (especially from lung cancer) and obnoxiously proud of his physique; John Doe, who commits the serious crime of "bringing extra-buttery popcorn into the work environment"; Brianna Maria Jyang, known as Bree, who's a control freak; and Kaitlin Joyce, who seems to be a new arrival (once the computer's glitched, it stays glitched) and who wants out ASAP.

So there they are, rubbing along well enough as far as we can tell, when -- like every team in every TV office including The Office, not to mention 30 Rock -- they get saddled with a new supervisor who doesn't understand.

This one is more a Steve Carrell loser than an Alec Baldwin winner. He is Steve Lefkowitz, "VPinCharge of Vision," and without, as far as I can tell, a J to either of his names, which must prove that there's one rule for the bosses. At an initial departmental meeting (the episode's highlight), Steve proposes gentling up the department's latest product by incorporating an animal into it.

He suggests a turtle and the entire crew go on a turtle hunt. Steve also thinks the new game will benefit from having an X at the end of its name that will automatically "make it way cooler." Let's hear it for the author of Generation X, making sporting fun of the book that made him famous.

Let's also add this up: Evan, the gore specialist, is standing up for old-fashioned gentleness against a man who loves turtles. Well, who doesn't love a paradox?

Evan faces similar contradictions in his private life. His father is an ex-engineer turned actor whose new dream is to speak at least one line in a TV show. (He's played by Alan Thicke, who in his time has spoken many.) He's also conducting a halfhearted affair with a school contemporary of his son's whose repeated insistence that she was popular are the show's low point.

Mother, meanwhile, prides herself on being a middle-class lady who grows very good pot; and where on current TV have we heard something like that before. More excitingly, she kills a guy who looks like he's intruding on her operation; and she and an unwilling Evan spend much of the show trying to dispose of what the specialist in imaginary bloodletting calls " a real live dead body." He also says "if it was too easy to get rid of bodies, we'd run out of people; as a species, we're a disaster." I'm not denying that there are good lines.

But it's late in the day to make comic capital out of people acting cavalier over little things like murder. Black comedy has been around too long to be shocking, especially when the whole context is weightless. We are promised future instalments in which the characters are faced with "Chinese gangs ... sexual swingin' ... British royalty," but on the evidence so far this is another show acting cool over people who think they're acting cool.

Add it to the bulging list that we call Irony, a once noble concept that has come to mean what we have in place of humour. This particular specimen is amiable, but so far that's all. - jPod airs tonight at 9 p.m. on CBC.
2008-01-10-you-can-t-make-this-stuff-up-:
Jon Stewart had an otherwise empty box on his screen occupied by the words "Space Reserved for Clever Pun." Stephen Colbert called as of old for The Word to appear and no word was there. As of Monday, the late-night twin-pins of faux news and comment have been back, bucking the writers' strike. Or maybe being bucked by it.

In practical terms, Stewart and Colbert without writers -- living, we have to assume, on their own wits -- has meant shows reduced to monologues and interviews. So far, this has worked out better for Colbert, who is essentially a one-man band, than for Stewart, who has always relied on a cohort of comic correspondents to whom he can act as incredulous straight man. (The best of them, before he struck out on his own, was Colbert.) At their best, Stewart's monologues have been great, but when they have fallen flat there has generally been something funny -- and transparently scripted--from the supporting corps to pick up the slack. The interviews have always been chancy. They have worked when political; depending on the guest pundit's affiliation, Stewart has been able to share his liberal outrage with the pundits with whom he agreed, or raise incredulous eyebrows at those with whom he didn't. When some showbiz figure has wandered by to promote a new movie, he has seemed at a loss; on these occasions The Daily Show with Jon Stewart has stopped being a parody of a chat-show and turned into an uninspired example of the real thing.

There were no visiting movie stars this Monday or Tuesday, though I suspect the show may have to fall back on them fairly quickly. Monday found our boy just a little too convincingly nervous as he acknowledged his new solitude, made passing reference to the Iowa and New Hampshire primaries that were the day's main news story, and then proceeded to the industrial action unfolding -- at least in theory -- just underneath his own window.

There's a nice irony about his position -- a boss who must have crossed a picket line of which he was an ideological component -- but he didn't make much of it. Stewart's most treasurable talent has always been stripping the surface absurdity from a situation to reveal the absurdity underneath. This time, though, he managed it only once, when suggesting that the $1.99 exacted for downloading his own show from iTunes had nothing to do with making a profit and was just "a shipping and handling charge."

He seemed relieved to get to the interview, which was with Ron Seeber, a very tough-looking professor of labour relations at Cornell.

Having established that they were both, guardedly, on the writers' side, Stewart was able to get to the funny stuff, to the jargon of it all ("They've walked away from the table; is it a nice table?") and, by some mysterious logical process, to anti-Semitism ("the whole reason I got into this business was I thought we controlled it"). He signed off with, by my watch, a good five minutes to spare, time that he effectively bequeathed to his friend, colleague and employee Colbert.

Tuesday found Stewart in much better shape, acknowledging the limitations of the unscripted life ("any movie reference I make is going to be from the '80s") and getting down to the impending presidentials.

This involved an aghast look when calling all the candidates, especially Mitt Romney, on the changes in their invocations of "change," and re-running footage to expose the gap between the stuff that happens and the stuff that gets said.

This has always been his greatest public service, and he was at his best showing us Hillary Clinton's supposed meltdown and then asking, "Was that all?" (Even the BBC had been taking the pool-of- tears stuff seriously.) He even managed to get one of his own team back: John Oliver, the snippy Englishman, insisting that every thing he was saying was strictly off the cuff, while standing before a projection of himself, in his writing persona, walking in a protest- circle, and also insisting that as a foreigner, he wasn't affected by Guild regulations anyway.

"My brain's not on strike, brother," said Stewart, interviewing David Frum on his disillusion with the Bush administration of which he was once a booster. Here Stewart, playing the standard interview game, was at a disadvantage compared with Colbert when speaking to the similarly disenchanted Andrew Sullivan, worried about America's standing in the eyes of the world.

"You care what the world thinks?" Colbert asked, sounding generally incredulous. Colbert's trick, in his persona of self- intoxicated right-wing blowhard, is to play devil's advocate so well that the devil feels embarrassed to have shown up.

Without unions, Stephen correctly pointed out, we could go right back to the good old days of child labour. Colbert is now so thoroughly within his role, and can think against himself so well on his feet, that he maybe can do without literary help. Noting petulantly that there was nothing on his auto-prompter, he turned it into a comment not only on the studio situation but on himself: "I always thought the machine read my thoughts and played them back." (I paraphrase, but that was the thought.)

The Colbert Report pronounced its title in English fashion on Monday, but on Tuesday it had regained its confidence and gone back to Gallic. One almost trembles for the day when the White House shifts leftward, as it may make Colbert's pose as voice of America untenable. Still, I don't suppose Limbaugh and O'Reilly are going to fade away when that day comes, so we may still need Colbert to expose them by saying the same things with more panache. And if we don't -- well, he's a talent; he'll survive. And he could always go back to supporting Jon Stewart. Maybe they could be a double act.
2008-01-12-we-shoulder-one-more-play-on-:
Canada, we are frequently told, found its national identity in the First World War. Whether or not that is true, it often seems to have found its theatrical identity there: not at the time, but in retrospect. Play after play takes us back to the years in which Canadians, with horrifying cheerfulness, shouldered the military burden of being citizens of the British Empire. Maureen Hunters Wild Mouth is the latest to arrive bearing the revelation that war is hell and that that war was especially so.

In some ways, the play takes the historical issue back to its roots. Its set on a Saskatchewan farm, on which both the farmer and his wife are English immigrants. They have had one son killed in the Somme; another is over there now; and the youngest is raring to go. They are visited by the farmer's sister, who has also lost a son to the war and is furiously embittered about it. Her stated aim is to understand what drives young men to destroy themselves and others. She seeks enlightenment in particular from a Lithuanian farm labourer, himself a decorated soldier who's been invalided out. After considerable goading, he obliges with a practical demonstration of what carnage is like by plunging his hand into a bucket of intestines and showering her with the blood. This is the showiest scene in the play but its too forced to be genuinely dramatic. Its the author, rather than Bohdan, the ex-soldier, who is straining for effect.

She finds a lot of them down on the farm. There is apparently a buffalo jump nearby, and the air is full of thundering hooves, along with the more immediate complaints of slaughtered livestock and refractory tractors. (Though, as often happens at the Tarragon, the atmospherics are upstaged by the sound of a train on the tracks outside the theatre, a real live noise blessedly innocent of being a metaphor for anything.) Some of the rural touches seem to be there for their own sake, a rival focus of interest fighting the play's ostensible theme. Is this a play about the prairies or a play about the trenches? Most of the characters may belong to the same family but there seems to be no urgent reason for them to be occupying the same stage.

Possible connections are left lying about unused. Take the farmer, Logan (Ian D. Clark, appropriately stalwart), and his wife, Roberta (Brenda Robins, branching fiercely out with a North Country accent and a grey wig, but too undisguisably agreeable for the suspicious termagant the play seems to have in mind). They're from the old country and have lost one child, and hazarded another, in its service, despite living thousands of miles away. Are their allegiances in any way split? Do they have unpatriotic doubts? They dont give sister Anna much of an argument or much of an agreement either. Their daughter Claire (Sarah Allen) has no links to the war theme, beyond fancying Bohdan and getting jealous when he starts taking an interest in her aunt. Her bellicose young brother, Jamie (a spirited debut performance by Simon Rainville), starts out by branding Annas pacifism as treason; later on, either he or his author grows tired of this and he settles for other forms of attention-getting: loudly reciting advertising slogans, for example. (These do have a certain period charm.) I suppose you could claim that both he and Anna are trying to make a dent in their relatives' unshakeable stoicism, which they read as complacency, but you'd have to be quite desperate to do it.

As Anna, Sarah Orenstein occasionally falls back on stonewalling histrionics but most of the time she blazes; Oliver Beckers Bohdan is rather conventionally broody. Theres one other character, an older farmhand called Aloysius, a veteran of earlier wars; he doesn't say much, and most of what he does say he mutters, but since he's acted by David Fox his mutterings are quite compelling, while his physical presence is completely so. He also plays the violin, an accomplishment that gets him the final curtain, its good for a dying fall. But the play as a whole is so low-key, despite everything thats presumed to happen in it, that a melancholic ending merely seems like more of the same.

Theplay does lookgood, or nearly: Yannik Larivee has encased it in a slatted box -- floor, walls and ceiling -- receding in deep focus and marred only by a small screen at the back, carrying miniature views of the outside world. It's a nice thought, but it makes the place resemble a primitive movie theatre in a converted barn. R.H. Thomson's production starts off well with most of the cast at dinner --an image that recurs several times --but it doesn't manage to inject much energy. Also, though we accept that actors in small theatres have to move their own furniture, they should maybe not try too hard to do it in character.

SALT-WATER MOON

Young Centre for the Performing Arts, Toronto

---

Soulpepper sems to be working its way through David French's Mercer cycle, a set of plays that chugs through mid-20th-century Canadian history by following the fortunes of a Newfoundland family who, like the author's own, moved to Toronto. The company had a big success last year with Leaving Home, the first-written play of the series; it now jumps ahead to the third, Salt-Water Moon. But it also jumps back, since Salt-Water Moon shows the small-town courtship of the young couple whom we met in Leaving Home as fractious parents, marooned in the metropolis.

Jacob Mercer has been away from home for a spell -- in Toronto, in fact -- and he comes back to win Mary Snow, with whom he had once spent the night and whom he believes still loves him. So, indeed, she does -- otherwise there'd be no other plays in the cycle -- but there is the small matter that in Jacob's absence Mary has got engaged to someone else, a solid young citizen with prospects. Mary is "in service;" Jacob arrives at her employers' door, on a balmy night in 1925 when everyone else in town is off at a funeral, staking everything on his own charm.

Here he has a lot in common with the play, the clue to which is its beguiling title. Whatever painful baggage the two characters and their unseen community may be presumed to be carrying, this is a lightweight mood-piece. The mood is beautifully realized in Ted Dykstra's production, which has the enhancements of Victoria Wallace's set (practically archetypal in its porch, garden and picket fence), Leigh Ann Vardy's melancholy seductive lighting and a haunting sound-scape with the concluding bonus of a recorded song from Melanie Doane. Most of all it has the Jacob of Jeff Lillico, a sharp-edged and sharp-witted scapegrace with heartsick vulnerability at his core, ready to tell any number of lies in the service of what he genuinely feels. Shakespeare in All's Well That Ends Well has a character describe our lives as "a mingled yarn, good and bad together," yarn meaning wool. Jacob's life is a series of mingled yarns, the kind you tell, true and false together. Lillico spins them with enchanting speed and control, his exhilarating expertise even extending to some momentary spasms of song and dance. He's had the practice. This actor has specialized in musicals at the Shaw, modern classics at Soulpepper and is about to embark on a full round of Shakespeare at Stratford. This is playing the system in a very good way. And if he doesn't gather a Dora for his present performance, I am fully prepared to be hornswoggled.

The play's dynamic is that Jacob's newly citified confidence meets Mary's home-brewed suspicions, partly rooted in her status as an orphan, with a younger sister whom she is determined to rescue from a brutal-sounding institution: hence her marriage plans. Krystin Pellerin makes these revelations very affecting. She plays Mary's stony anger, though, at the expense of conveying any dormant affection for Jacob; so the pre-ordained happy ending, though it still gladdens the heart, seems arbitrary. It isn't easy to imagine either of these youngsters growing into the middle-aged figures who we saw portrayed, only last year, by Kenneth Welsh and Diane D'Aquila. Pellerin does bring an authentic Newfie sound to the play; with Lillico's accent you have to believe very strongly in the transformative powers of a year spent in Ontario.

Salt-Water Moon is a slighter play than Leaving Home, but it's also more likeable and has fewer loose ends. Its principal weakness is that though we hear, evocatively, about the decline of the local fisheries and, less evocatively, about the shadowing trauma of the recent war, neither theme seems to have entered into the blood and being of the couple we actually see. It's background, part of the "this is our country, look at it" aesthetic that underlies most of French's plays, not to mention others of the time, such as David Fennario's Balconville. It was probably a necessary phase for Canadian drama to pass through, but it's difficult to imagine the plays being taken as seriously anywhere else. But here is here, and the plays have cut a distinctive new panel in Soulpepper's tapestry. A company whose repertory roams the world needs to come home now and then. - Salt-Water Moon runs until Jan. 31. Call 416-866-8666 for more information.

2008-01-17-we-don-t-need-another-hero:
It seems likely that the Oscars, like the revolution, will not be televised. They will happen but, because of the writers' strike, just as a stage event, as happened in prehistoric times. I think this is defeatist. Why shouldnt the show go on?

My sympathies in the dispute are with the writers. The Oscars, though, are one occasion on which Id happily see the networks roll right over them. Every year I watch the final credits roll and think: All these people got paid -- a lot, presumably -- for writing this mindless, sycophantic rubbish?

This year why not let the actors (it's nearly always actors; outside of actual nominees no-one else is presumed to exist in Hollywood on Oscar night) make up their own presentation speeches? They could hardly do worse. Of course, we'd have to do without all the special tributes, and probably the production numbers that traditionally clutter up the evening, but think of how much earlier wed all get to bed. And how much more happily.

As for a host -- well, I suppose thered still have to be one, but if it's Jon Stewart, he's a stand-up guy and he can make it up as he goes along, or at least memorize his lines without first writing them down, just as we currently have to tell ourselves hes doing on The Daily Show. Im not sure whether the rules would mean sacrificing the interminable red-carpet interviews and sound-bite replies that ritually precede the main event, but let's ditch them anyway, just to be on the safe side. We could end up with a movie celebration that's actually about the movies. Theres a radical notion.

Meanwhile, the imminent disappearance of American drama series, cut off before they could get their stories straight, is supposed to herald a grand opportunity for shows made in Canada. The CBC, in particular, has been jubilant about its new slate of productions.

On the evidence so far, theyre being over-optimistic; their viewing figures may go up, but that in itself won't stop the audience from fondly missing the shows that it's missing. Bottom of the heap at the moment is MVP, which has been shamelessly plugged as Desperate Hockeywives. This is loose labelling, because so far the show has only come up with one wife who could be called desperate, and thats because in the storys opening moments she became a widow. More precisely, it's because she discovered that her husband, the supposed star of his team, had left no insurance and that his team, or at least its snaky manager, was not prepared to shell out to keep her in the style to which she had become accustomed.

By the end of the second episode, she's been reduced to working as a cashier at a gas station where the manager finds himself, one trusts to his embarrassment, facing her across the till. This scene might have seemed more convincing if the camera hadnt made such a big deal of showing us that this was a full-service station, meaning that the manager would have had no reason to enter the office at all.

Otherwise, the focus has been on desperate girlfriends: actual, potential or disposable. There are three principal ice-aces vying for, or trying to avoid, these ladies attentions: one new guy, one bad guy and one guy with no discernible characteristics except that he's the captain and seems intended to be the hero.

The main thing wrong with the show, apart from its plodding pace and slurpy background music, is that it has virtually nothing to do with its ostensible subject. Far be it from me to wish there were more hockey on television, but the characters here could be any spoiled, rich people.

There have been virtually no scenes in the locker room and none at all on the ice. John Ferguson, general manager of the Toronto Maple Leafs, was quoted in yesterday's National Post as saying nothing that goes on outside the game, outside these walls, distracts me or us from our purpose." Well, I suppose he would say that, but the implications sound more dramatic than anything on MVP, whose characters spend all their time partying. We dont have a sense of what the pressures are, where they stand in the league, or who their most dangerous opponents might be.

Its like the Oscars, come to think of it, where all that really matters is who's wearing the best frocks. Or, in this case, who isn't wearing them.

Its also very predictable. We know, from the moment they set eyes on one another, that there are going to be sparks flying between the widows bratty wannabe-a-ballerina daughter and the rookie who's taken over the departed's status, paycheque and house. We can guess that therell be trouble when the young mans small- town girlfriend finally manages to put her grandmother in a home and arrives to claim her share of the high life.

Meanwhile, the skipper pursues a virginal daycare worker while the script trips over itself trying to find reasons to keep them apart. (She's also being wooed by her old English Lit teacher, a far more eligible suitor, even if he does insist on quoting Chaucer in modern translation. And him a scholar, too.)

I was never a fan of the real Desperate Housewives but at least it knew it was ridiculous. MVP, completely devoid of wit, doesn't even have camp appeal. Maybe it isnt trying to be serious, but its certainly solemn. - MVP airs Friday at 9 p.m. on CBC. Also, catch Robert Cush-man talkin' tough about Tony -- Soprano, that is -- in Halifax on Jan. 21 at 7 p.m. at the University of King's College. For more information call 422-1271 ext. 136.

Fancy frocks? Duelling dudes? Is it the Oscars?

2008-01-18-of-scum-and-stubbornness-expl:
William Sampson can still laugh. That may be the most surprising - - though certainly not the most shocking -- revelation in Confessions of an Innocent Man, David Papermy's film about Sampson's three-year ordeal in a Saudi Arabian prison, tortured and condemned for a crime he plainly did not commit.

It's angry laughter, obviously, but it's also self-mocking and, at the same time, self-approving. He says that when he was finally released and arrived at Heathrow (after a flight spent half-fearing that the plane would land somewhere else and he'd be taken back) he looked in the mirror and saw "Charles Manson on a bad day." He qualifies that: "I didn't look as bad as I thought." He had reason to look bad: He had spent the last two and a half years of his imprisonment in solitary confinement, practising every form of non co-operation short of a hunger strike. He prowled his cell naked with his body covered in his own excrement. He is, by his own proclamation, a stubborn son of a bitch, and that's what got him through. He's justifiably proud. And honest. There's more than one kind of confession going on here.

The film is based on Sampson's book of the same title, and though it comes with a commentary spoken (in craggy, oracular tones) by Martin Sheen, it's Sampson himself in interviews who does most of the storytelling. The narrative is plainly laid out. We learn about Sampson's life as a business consultant in Riyadh, part of an expatriate British colony (he himself has dual U.K. and Canadian citizenship) boozing it up in an officially -- and rigorously --dry country.

Then, we learn about the day in 2000 when his life changed forever; a car-bomb killed a British engineer and the Saudi authorities, anxious to allay any suspicions of homegrown terrorism, pinned the crime on a Dutch friend of Sampson's who happened to be in the car behind. Under interrogation, he implicated Sampson and another expat (a Scot, as it happens, like Sampson himself ). Then followed confessions extracted under torture, a kangaroo trial, and death sentences that were never carried out, though Sampson was subjected to a mock execution. He was also further tortured, and named a fourth man. The tortures (including the notorious falanga, beating on the soles of the feet) are meticulously described and discreetly shown, in brief and shadowy but still disturbing dramatized scenes; so, almost as disturbingly, is Sampson's "dirty protest." He also tells about being raped.

About the only flaw in the film is how little it tells us about Sampson's three fellow victims. Two of them are interviewed, but we don't learn much about what they endured or how they reacted. (Raf Schyvens, the Dutchman, does speak of his remorse for having involved his colleagues, but nobody blames him for it. Nor should they.) We get the impression that Sampson was singled out for special treatment, but whether his bloody-mindedness was the cause of this or its result is never made clear.

Sampson says that his parents "had a very bad marriage ... They should never have been allowed to get married." But they did and he, as he says with typical mordancy, was the result. Nevertheless his father James, who lives in Vancouver and twice visited his son in his Saudi jail, emerges as the prime mover in his

son's eventual release (and possibly therefore in that of Sampson's companions). He got, as is well known, little help from his government, who were more concerned with diplomatic niceties.

Sampson senior speaks of "the scum that work for the Canadian Foreign Affairs Department -- the lowest scum on Earth. At least," he adds, fearful of encountering even worse, "I hope they are." His feelings are understandable, though the film itself suggests that Sampson's trial lawyer, for whom "oily" seems the appropriate word and who genially admits that Samspson may have suffered "some mental torture," might be a strong contender.

It's difficult, certainly, to stomach the evasiveness of Prime Minister Chretien (caught saying "it's not clear" Sampson was tortured) or the self-justifications of those lower down, claiming that firm protests would only have made matters worse. They are firmly debunked by Francine Dube, whose articles in the National Post did much to make the Sampson case a cause celebre, while in Britain, which hardly seems to have done a better job of defending its nationals, a reporter for the Guardian (some issues can make strange journalistic bedfellows) draws the moral that, if your government finds out about your misadventures abroad, then you are, as he caustically puts it, expendable.

A spokesman for Human Rights Watch makes the fairest summary: There may be a case for tactful diplomacy (meaning, not antagonizing countries with a lot of oil) but in this case it was inappropriate and probably self-defeating. By a crowning irony that Sampson himself might appreciate, he and his friends were finally released in exchange for prisoners from Guantanamo Bay. The film refrains from drawing the obvious moral that torture is indefensible, even when our side is doing it, but it's implicit. There are few surprises in this film, except in matters of detail including, as I began by saying, details of character. You switch on expecting to be angered and sickened, and you are. - Confessions of an Innocent Man airs tomorrow at 7 p.m. on CTV.

2008-01-19-one-room-twelve-men-lots-of-a:
Reginald Rose's Twelve Angry Men is justly famous as a prize exhibit from one of those recurring Golden Ages of American Television: in this case, the 1950s era of the live, original drama. The TV play became, with minimal alteration, a movie, and Rose subsequently wrote a theatre version that has been in heavy rotation ever since. The stage play does make changes to the original, mainly for the worse; they pad and sentimentalize. But they don't interfere with the impact of the piece, which remains the non-stop attention- grabber it has always been.

You probably know the set-up. A jury settles down to consider its verdict in a New York murder case. A teenager is on trial for murdering his father. (Both are probably black, though the word isn't mentioned; we only hear, with unctuous delicacy, about "these people." I don't know if the author was trying for universality, or trying to spare '50s sensibilities, but I suspect the latter. Anyway, the crime plainly occurred in one of the inner city's virtual ghettos.) There appears to be a mountain of evidence against the accused, starting with the fact that he was overheard threatening to kill his father. Eleven of the jurors are disposed to cut the discussion short and send the boy to the chair -- which, this being a first-degree murder, is undoubtedly where he would go. But the 12th, an architect, if it matters, has doubts. He never claims to know definitively that the prisoner is innocent, but he cannot convince himself that he is guilty either. Gradually, in the face of ridicule, indifference and belligerent hostility, he wins the others over to his side. It's a thrilling and heartening process. Also, in a world in which the presumption of innocence is increasingly being called into question, a newly pertinent one. It's a feel-good evening, in that it vindicates all our best liberal sentiments, but democracy deserves its demonstrations, too.

The play is one-of-a-kind, providing all the excitement of a courtroom drama while dispensing with the judge, the lawyers and the prisoner at the bar. There turn out to be some very leaky components in the prosecution's case, and the jurymen, once aroused, take delight in pulling them apart. This should, of course, have been the defence's job, but we are told that the accused was represented by a court-appointed advocate who really couldn't be bothered. This element of the play is a little hard to swallow -- not the defence's negligence, but the acumen and enthusiasm of the jury, who practically re-stage the proceedings as they should rightfully have proceeded.

They turn out to be first-rate sleuths, so we get the thrills of a trial-play and a detective-play at the same time. There is much pacing-out of floors, and examining of weapons, and discussion of how much of a crime would be clearly visible from across the tracks of an elevated railway. (There's nostalgia for you. New York's Third Avenue El was mostly closed down in 1955, one year after the date of this play.) And the excitement mounts when the remaining reactionaries among the Clean Dozen are provoked into attempting their own counter-demonstration. One of them actually yells at an opponent "I'm going to kill you." Aha.

Along with exciting action goes compelling characterization. Most of the 12 angries only become so when they start getting enraged with one another, but you might call them the Cross Section, an account of the varied sociological strata they represent. (Given, that is, that they're all white and all male.) They start out, inevitably, as types, but their personalities become more sharply defined according to how they agree or disagree.

The present production, directed by Scott Ellis, comes from New York's Roundabout Theatre (it opened there in 2004 and has been touring for a couple of years) and it's a display of steadily gathering force; the ensemble grows tighter as the individuals become more distinct. I wasn't crazy about Richard Thomas's performance as Mr. Valiant-for-Truth, which is in a style I've seen described as Hollywood-sincere, all italics and exclamation-points. But no one could say he isn't sympathetic.

Mike Boland is an unobtrusively authoritative foreman and Alan Mandell a dignified octogenarian reproach to some of his younger, brasher colleagues (the characters, that is, not the actors). But the two stand-outs are the two hold-outs, the last to be converted: Kevin Dobson as a blithe bundle of prejudice who wants to bring the debate to a speedy end so he can get to the ball-game, and Julian Gamble, a massive presence as a more complicated kind of loudmouth, one whose personal issues poison his view of the case and who eventually dissolves in what looks like a heap of blubber. His collapse is one place where the stage adaptation weakens the original script --his motivation is made too explicit -- but it still works. And there's a nice developing irony: The man who couldn't see what there was to discuss becomes a fanatic for driving things to a conclusion; he may not mind being on a hanging jury but he doesn't want a hung one. It's a little sentimental when he and his opponent reach a kind of silent rapprochement, but not much. This is one of those rare occasions on which the phrase "never a dull moment" is the literal truth.

- Twelve Angry Men runs through Feb. 10 at the Princess of Wales Theatre. Call 416-872-1212 for details.

THEATRE REVIEW

PALACE OF THE END

Berkeley Street Theatre

---

Arrange the following three atrocities in order of their atrociousness: (1) An American female soldier at Abu Ghraib is photographed pointing at a pile of naked Iraqi prisoners arranged in a pyramid, and she and her male colleagues subject them to other forms of sexual humiliation; doubtless you've heard about it; (2) A gentle Baghdad bookseller, his wife and two daughters are murdered by American soldiers claiming to be looking for insurgents; the elder daughter, aged 13, is also raped; (3) A pregnant Iraqi woman, a communist (like everybody, she says) is interrogated by Saddam Hussein's torturers, who want to know the whereabouts of her husband; she is beaten and raped in front of her 15-year old son; when she refuses to talk, her other son, aged eight, is tied to a ceiling-fan and spun round and round at increasing speed; when this too proves ineffective, he is placed naked on the snowy roof of the building where his mother can hear him coughing until he dies.

It's a tough call between (2) and (3), but I'd vote for (3). That also seems to be the opinion of Judith Thompson, who has written a monologue around each event and has arranged them in the order cited. The overall title, Palace of the End, derives from the Baghdad torture-fortress that is the setting for the last story. That narrative is as harrowing as anything I have ever heard in a theatre, though if the evening as a whole is intended to be anti- war (or anti the U.S. war in Iraq; everyone's anti-war) then it backfires. The emotional effect is to make you feel that anything-- even the cruel mess the Americans have made-- would be preferable to leaving the country in Saddam's power.

The effectiveness of the three individual plays is not in direct proportion to their horror-quotient. In fact, it's the reverse. This is accentuated in David Storch's production, which boasts, in order of appearance, one superb performance, one that is fine, and one that is passable.

The first benefits enormously from being the only one told by a perpetrator rather than a victim. This immediately adds complexity. The woman identified in the program as "An American Soldier" is of course Private Lynndie England, who took the fall, along with her boyfriend, for the Abu Ghraib abuses, and can actually be seen as a kind of victim herself. In fact, that's how she sees herself, though not for the OK political reasons. She's incensed at the messages about herself that she finds posted on the internet, especially the ones that describe her as ugly white trash. ("I think if I was an actor, I would have to call that a bad review.") Hell, she'll have us know, she was never ugly, and even back home in the South there were girls worse-looking than her. She's very defensive, though. It's plain that being posted as a prison guard made her feel more desirable than she'd ever felt in West Virginia. She felt she had to prove herself to her male buddies, and she could only see the prisoners as means to that end. At home she'd needed someone (specifically, an unfortunate crippled girl) to feel superior to, and to join in humiliating. Thompson is brilliantly successful in getting inside her character's mind, understanding her without excusing her. So is her actress, Maev Beaty, playing here triumphantly against type: She's fleshy, querulous, allowing us to connect the dots that the woman herself is hardly aware exist.

The second play features "A British Microbiologist and Weapons Inspector." He's Dr. David Kelly (unlike Lynddie, he gives us his name) who committed suicide after outing himself as having "sexed up" the Weapons of Mass Destruction report for the benefit of Tony Blair. The bookstore victims were his friends, and -- at least in Thompson's telling--it was learning of their fate that turned his mind around; he passed from thinking the invasion justified, and therefore worth a little falsehood, to killing himself for having helped make it possible. We meet him just before the moment of death in the peaceful English countryside. Julian Richings plays him very quietly and very sympathetically, but the play is out of focus; unlike its predecessor, it can't make the narrator as compelling as the horrors he narrates.

This brings us to "An Iraqi Mother," who also has a real-life analogue, though one likely to be unknown to
most: Nehrjas Al Saffarh, who survived her torture under Saddam only to be inadvertently killed by the U.S. (Her home was bombed in the first Gulf War.) Arsinee Khanjian is bland and monotonous when setting her character up for us, but develops considerable intensity when describing her actual ordeal. She has the misfortune of being handed the play's most pretentious
element: a mystical dream of future peace and reconciliation that hardly measures up to the hideous realities that have gone before. The ending also suffers from a forced attempt by author and director to draw all three characters together; the first two are mute audience to the third though their reactions remain inscrutable. Having them all talk about their respective journeys "through the looking-glass" doesn't do much for artistic unity either. These are three shards, wrenching ones, from the tragedy of Iraq. There is no way that they, or any other three, can add up a to a full picture. - Palace of the End runs until Feb. 23. For tickets, call 416-368-3110 or visit canstage.com.

Black & White Photo: Chris Gallow, Canstage / Julian Richings, Maev Beaty and Arsinee Khanjian each present a heart-rending monologue on the war in Iraq, but bringing their stories together was a bit more of a challenge. ;

THEATRE REVIEW

SMALL METAL OBJECTS

Eaton Centre, Toronto

---

So there we were, sitting on benches (hell on the back, but the show's only an hour long), in a makeshift open booth just south of Sears, gazing out at three heavily populated levels of shopping mall, and at the catwalks and escalators that connect them. We had headphones clamped to our ears, or earphones clamped to our heads. We must have looked odd.

We were there to witness small metal objects, brought to us by the Back to Back Theatre of Australia, and the first offering in this year's World-Stage season. (The production moves next week from Toronto Vancouver.)

In this piece four actors are placed within a large and crowded public space; the premiere was at a railway station in Melbourne. They act out a drama that we may be able to see, if we can find the right direction in which to look, and that we can hear, courtesy of those headsets.

It concerns two modest-sounding men, Gary and Steve, who have a mutual-support system going. Gary has a wife and children -- he will also shortly be a grandfather -- and boasts, quietly, of all the things, including his life, that he would be willing to sacrifice for their sakes.

Steve has never even had a girlfriend and is emotionally dependent on Gary; he's terrified when Gary reveals that he is about to have a knee operation, even though Gary reassures him that this is a procedure that has seldom, if ever, proved fatal.

The two turn out, rather surprisingly, to be drug dealers; and they are contacted, first by cellphone, then in person, by a far smoother operator named Alan who needs their product for a function he's hosting that evening. The problem: Gary has to reclaim his stash from a nearby locker, Steve refuses to move from the spot to which he is presently rooted and Gary will not abandon him.

Alan has to call in heavy reinforcements, in the shape of a very upscale motivational psychiatrist. If she can't succeed in uprooting Steve, Jim will have to find an alternative source of supply: in Scarborough. (Just why these four Aussies are transacting their purely domestic business right here in Toronto is a question, obviously, not to be asked.)

According to Bruce Glad-win, director of both the company and the production, the show operates on two levels. One of them is situational: the depositing of actors and audience among a crowd of people who aren't in on the act. It doesn't work too well.

Maybe the Eaton Centre is too big and self-absorbed a space; anyway, the actors are hard to pick out (of course, if they'd done the show inside Sears, they would have been visible for miles), and the hoped-for spontaneous interaction between them and perplexed members of the general public mostly failed to materialize.

If there were any spirited verbal dust-ups going on, they failed to communicate themselves through my cans. Nor did we weirdos in the bleachers attract more than passing curiosity. There is a mildly hypnotic fascination about watching the metropolitan shoppers, heedlessly thronging; all human life was probably there, but we never got to find out about it. And really, why is this stuff about mingling with the public and making the spectators part of the spectacle regarded as such a big philosophical deal? We know already.

The other aspect of small metal objects is the play itself, and that is far more satisfying. (I don't understand the title, and I've yet to read an article or review that attempts to explain it.) The Back to Back company is partly composed of actors who, in the group's own words, "are perceived to have an intellectual disability." These include Sonia Teuben, whose idea the show was and who plays Gary, and Simon Laherty who plays Steve.

Teuben's voice and delivery are pinched, concerned and urgent; Laherty's is blockish and deliberate. Their rhythm, a mental connection riddled with pauses but essentially unbroken, may remind you of early Pinter. The counterpoint of question and reassurance may also remind those with long memories of the television duologues of Peter Cook and Dudley Moore.

Their would-be clients, by contrast, are played by for-want-of-a- better-word normal actors (Jim Russell and Caroline Lee); and the kick comes in seeing the worldly, successful couple failing to impose their will on the two in the margins. They can't break Steve's stubbornness or Gary's loyalty: not with money, not even with sex.

When the lady, who's like a walking, talking copy of Cosmopolitan, offers as a last resort to go down on Steve and is refused, her fury at the man she's conditioned to despise knows no bounds. For once, the humble and meek get exalted; and if the mighty aren't exactly put down from their seats, they are at least obliged to shuffle a little. The actors may be physically hard to discern, but aurally they're very present. This theatre production is terrific radio. - In Toronto until Saturday. Call 416-973-4000; at the PuSh Festival in Vancouver from Jan 30-Feb 3.

2008-01-26-it-all-comes-out-in-the-wash-:
The title of Lynn Nottages play Intimate Apparel refers to a series of elegant undergarments run up by Esther, a 35-year-old black seamstress in 1905 New York. Esther is gifted but unlettered and, she has come to believe, unloved and unlovable. However, she strikes up a correspondence with George, a Caribbean man working on the Panama Canal. Since she can neither read nor write her letters have to be ghosted, and George's read to her, by two of her best customers, one a white society woman and the other a black prostitute. George comes to New York, and the two pen-pals embark on what is, to all intents and purposes, an arranged marriage.

Well, at least they've arranged it themselves. Mr. Marks, an orthodox Jewish cloth merchant, is waiting for a bride, about whom he knows nothing, to arrive from Romania; meanwhile his beliefs forbid him to let another woman so much as touch him, which Esther, for all her apparent prudishness, would obviously like to. Meanwhile Esthers white client, Mrs. Van Buren, is trapped in a loveless marriage, while Mayme, her black client, has sex and nothing else. That leaves Mrs. Dickson, in whose house Esther and her sewing machine reside; she married late to a much older man who has left her a widow. This loquacious lady comes on like the leading lady in the black Broadway production of Hello Dolly!. Everyone in this play is childless; everyone acts as Esthers friend and confidant, with the notable exception-- at least, once they've actually met and the knot has been tied--of her mail-order spouse.

Nottage is a rising and much-decorated American playwright, and this has been her most successful play. It trades in patterns and parallels, rather like the plays and novels of the time and place that it depicts. Both Esther and George are the children of slaves; the other characters are in other acquired or inherited chains. The title too has ramifications; Esther's personal as well as professional relationships are based on the clothes she makes; these include an eye-catching smoking-jacket, made from silk bought from Mr. Marks, thats her wedding present to George. It plays a pivotal role in the subsequent action. Theres also a sense of style in the dialogue, along with some lines and situations that pierce the heart. There is also a weakness for coincidence in plotting, that stops bashfully short of full-blooded melodrama. The challenge, as the action roams, along with Esther herself, from one room to another on a compartmentalized set, is to avoid becoming diffuse and episodic. The play doesn't quite manage it, and the Obsidian Theatre Company's production cannot pull up the slack; in fact, it lets it drop even further

Philip Akins direction has its heart in the right place. The wed- ding-night scene of George and Esther is handled with notable delicacy, as a mixture of promise and shadow. But the productions pacing is off; most of the time it trundles, meaning not only that it's generally slow but that when it should pause, it doesn't. The scenes between Esther and Mayme include a couple of what should be heart-stopping revelations; here, both actresses just carry on without blinking an eye. The result is that all the performances, with the exception of Alex Poch-Goldins Mr. Marks, sometimes fall out of focus; Marium Carvells hearty Mrs. Dickson hardly ever falls into it. Individually, the actors are fine. As Mayme, whose boudoir includes a piano and who should by rights have been a musician, Lisa Berry is warm with flamboyant flashes of anger. As Mrs. Van Buren, dreading another visit to the opera and reaching out to Esther as her only link to life, Carly Street is glamorously cool with a rage that's subdued but that burns even hotter when released. It's good to see Street, condemned in Lord of the Rings to be lacklustre in a lacklustre role, back on form, "form being the operative word since Esthers custom-made corsets look especially good on her. The problems posed by mounting this play in this elongated space may be insuperable, and Tamara Marie Kucherans set-design fails to solve them, but her costumes are, as the script requires them to be, superb.

Kevin Hanchard's George is difficult to judge in the first half of the play, when he's still in Panama; hes in shadow, barely glimpsed, and an actor you cant see rapidly becomes an actor you don't hear. When he finally emerges, he paints a sharp portrait of goodwill giving way rapidly to frustration (New York is cold, especially when you're unemployed) and then to outright selfishness and irresponsibility: Just Like a Man, in fact. The decline, though, both of his character and of the marriage, is presented in predictable terms; and this rebounds on Raven Daudas Esther, who certainly manages to centre the play but whose transitions from Point A to Point B often leave us guessing, even though both points are fully present in their own right. Daudas Esther is full of incipient passion: a woman who is far from frigid but who has held herself in for so long that she doesn't know the code for letting go. The story is told almost entirely from her point of view (she's hardly off stage) so any blame that may attach to her is hard to register.

As for music: I wish the production had found something less obvious than Scott Joplins most famous tune to evoke the ragtime era; and though its delightful when Mayme tempts Esther into joining her in one of those bawdy blues about a handy man", their vocal style is surely anachronistic. It's a decent evening, one that holds out the frustrating promise of being more.

- Intimate Apparel runs through Feb. 3 at the Berkeley Street Theatre Upstairs, 416-368-3110.
