2008-01-30-the-marvelous-ms-moscovitch:
THEATRE REVIEW

THE RUSSIAN PLAY/ESSAY

The Factory Theatre, Toronto

---

Hannah Moscovitch's Essay and The Russian Play were first seen, in that order, at two successive Summerworks festivals. They obviously deserved further exposure, and having suggested in these pages that they should be revived as a double bill, I feel like basking in the results. It's a fact, though nobody seems to be making a fuss about it, that all the new plays to have opened on major Toronto stages in the past few weeks are by women. These two are the best of them. Both combine a biting wit with an unsentimental humanity. Both show a priceless quality to shift an argument, or an emotional state, on a dime.

Both plays have casts of one woman and two men. Comparing them, Ken Gass, the Factory's artistic director, asks us to query how much the "position of women in society ... has changed from Stalinist Russia to the halls of contemporary academe." Given that Pixie, the young lady in Essay, bursts into tears in her teacher's office and is offered Kleenex, while Sonya in The Russian Play is starved and tortured by the Soviet secret police for having displeased her influential lover, I'd say we've come a long way, baby. Essay is a campus play, set in a history department. Jeffrey, a teaching assistant, is querying Pixie, an undergraduate, on her choice of essay topic; asked to write on a military leader from 18th or 19th century Europe, Pixie wants to write on the obscure figure (well, I'd never heard of her) of Elisabeth Farnese, wife of Philip V of Spain, rather than on Napoleon like everybody else. Jeffrey suggests that she is letting her feminism-- of which he, as an enlightened young man, approves -- get in the way of her historical perspective. She rather dashes his preconceptions by saying that she isn't a feminist, though she later says, maybe for the sake of a quiet life, that, all right, she is. Otherwise, she sticks to her guns, and at the suggestion of the departmental head, a Professor Galbraith, ends up writing on Elisabeth and Napoleon.

The essay turns out badly. So Jeffrey thinks, and the professor seems to agree with him. He still advises -- again for the sake of a quiet life -- giving her a passing grade; after all, she's just one student, probably passing through on her way to what he, with cankered joviality, calls "women's studiesology"; and anyway, what can you expect of a girl named Pixie? He also suggests, with reference to the (I agree, appalling) concept of "herstory," that it might be possible to write about the historical significance of Napoleon's horse, and call the result "horsestory." Jeffrey is both incredulous and incensed by all this, and he calls on Pixie to rebut it and stand up for her principles. When she stays silent, he accuses her of behaving "like a lobotomy in a skirt," which is when she cries. At this moment, as at the climax of David Mamet's Oleanna, to which this play owes an acknowledged debt, we witness a teaching career imploding before our eyes: less violently than in Mamet, and less irretrievably, but still making the audience catch its breath and then review its reactions.

The play is really about Jeffrey whose political correctness happens to coincide with high academic and intellectual standards and a fatal lack of professional smarts. Jordan Pettle hits him off perfectly, as a study in impetuosity constantly reining itself in too late. (Like all Moscovitch's protagonists, he falls into traps that he really had no hope of avoiding.) He, like his two colleagues, is repeating his performance from Michael Rubenfeld's admirable original production. Richard Greenblatt is the professor who can never forgive Jeffrey for missing a conference at which he himself was a keynote speaker, but who seems genuinely pained by his juniors' missteps; he can behave decently for dubious reasons. He's also the vehicle for some hilariously barbed satire on campus politics: Why, he asks, should the cultural studies brigade act as if they want to take over his department ("they already have their own") and why is the sociology building so much nicer than his? With the boys fighting it out like this, Pixie wisely takes refuge in silence; or maybe she really doesn't have anything to say. Claire Jenkins' performance leaves the question appropriately open; what she does convey beyond question is a refusal to fit into anybody's ideological preconceptions. Like the play itself.

The Russian Play is a scintillating exercise in style (owing more to Chekhov's short stories than his plays, whatever the script says) which also manages to be a moving meditation on poverty, oppression and love. I have now seen Michelle Monteith's performance as Sonya three times, and I can't say that it has improved; it was perfect the first time and it still is, impossibly mature, both technically and emotionally, in its instant switches from sardonic narrator to trusting heroine and back again. That the two women are in fact one is only revealed at the end, though I can't see any point in keeping that secret. As before, Monteith gets strong support from Shawn Campbell and Aaron Willis as the two (married) men in her life, which is more than you can say of Sonya herself; one, a poor gravedigger, breaks her heart, the other, a rich factory-owner, breaks her body. Also as before, and also invaluable in their contributions to matters of atmosphere and tension, are Tom Howell's violin-playing and Kimberly Purtell's cruelly acute lighting. The play's scale, and its key, may be minor but the overall achievement, under Natasha Mytnowych's direction, is major. - The Russian Play/ Essay runs until Feb. 17. Call 416-504-9971 for more information.

2008-01-31-ah-stay-on-the-island-best-to:
This is a non-spoiler alert. There have been no advance screeners of tonights season premiere of Lost, so I am unable to drop any subtle hints of what might be going to happen. Or even, which would probably be more likely, any clumsy hints.

So let's go back to last season's finale. Actually, lets stop flattering the networks by echoing their self-aggrandizing audience- baiting talk of "premieres (which are usually extended recaps) and finales" (which, rarely finalize anything, because of there is another season to consider) and just refer to first, last and, when necessary, in-between episodes. Last seasons last episode of Lost found Jack, the show's nearest approach to a hero, at the point of leading his fellow plane-crash survivors, and other acquired flotsam, off The Island. He seems nearer to doing it than ever before, due to the descent from the skies (by parachute), of an English chick -- "bird, we used to call her --named Naomi, who has access to a boat and the complicated methods of getting in touch with it. At least, she had these things; she doesn't have them any longer because shes been shot.

Anyway, she may not have been all she seemed. On this show, as on so many others, it would be surprising if she was. Which of course means that she may be. Arguing against her authenticity is a television message, received in another part of the island and another part of the plot, from a woman with a much posher English accent, whose name is Penelope and who doesnt seem to have heard of Naomi or her boat. And then there's Ben. He's the shrivelled- looking guy in charge of the Others who were on the island first and have been making the castaways lives -- and sometimes their deaths - - miserable ever since they first got there. It took Ben a long time- - the better part of two seasons, really -- to reveal his full evilness, so maybe the writers didnt know about it then, either. It's getting quite hard to remember the first season of Lost, when the central conflict had yet to be declared and the whole thing seemed to be a cross between Survivor and a maturely-cast Lord of the Flies, complete with mysterious Beast. Ben, who is currently a captive of the good guys, has been warning them that if they trust Naomi, even posthumously, they'll all be killed. Well, of course he would say that. But one of the many irritating things about Ben is that he sometimes tells the truth when he ought to be lying. (Another irritating thing is that there seems to be no good reason for his underlings to render him unquestioning obedience. Its not as if he could beat them up. But thats often the case with criminal masterminds in fiction.)

I don't like Lost. I'm tempted to call it the triumph of style over substance, except that mystification and hand-me-down glamour arent stylish. Decadent" would be more like it, though, without the depraved fun that might suggest, I cant in all honesty dismiss it out of hand, as I usually end up at the end of an episode wanting to know what will happen next. What I don't want to know, and what the show insists on telling me, is what happened last. Something like half the series' footage consists of flashbacks to the characters lives before they made their fatal, or at least fateful, flight plans. The latest episode gave us a twist on this with an elaborate flash-forward: Jack, back home in Los Angeles, unsuccessfully attempting suicide, and then roaming around as a junkie unable to get his prescription filled. Which is really humiliating because hes a doctor. It's uncertain whether this is meant to be a literal prophecy, or just a projection of Jack's fears while still on the island of what will befall him if ever he gets off.

Its meant, obviously, to add depth to his character. But it doesnt work, just as the flashbacks don't work for him or any of the others. In their marooned state, the characters are as miserable a bunch as have ever threatened to go into indefinite syndication, but at least they have some action to sustain them. In their previous lives, they sit around feeling sorry for themselves. And they do it in the same glossy, airless television-land inhabited by the characters of all television soaps with aspirations to seriousness. It fits that Jack was a doctor in his former life, as was Juliet, one of his two bait-and-switch love-interests on the island; medical series have always been the shows with the most pretension to reality and the least connection with it. We are meant to think that the show's random collection of stereotypes have significance beyond themselves because they all have skeletons in their closets and because the landscape they currently inhabit is full of unexplained secrets and -- in the bad peoples lair -- complicated technological gizmos. Well, not always that complicated: Its rather charming, in the age of most series' multi-tasking cellphones, to find that Ben's gang still rely on the humble walkie- talkie. I mean, when did you last even hear that phrase?

Well, all right, there are some people I like. I cheered when Hugo a.k.a. Hurley, the fat fellow whose help is spurned by the tough guys, came to their rescue by driving his van right through the ranks of the opposition. Then theres Desmond, the ex-monk who was also a designer for the Royal Shakespeare Company. You have to love the details; I suspect that one was dreamed up by some studio- bound American scribe with fantasies about the British classical theatre. (Ive met some RSC designers, and none of them struck me as possible action-heroes. Still, you never know till you're tested.) Desmond has also read all of Dickens except Our Mutual Friend: Shame he missed that one, it's almost the best, but at least he has something to look forward to. Unlike his friend and compatriot Charlie the rockstar, whom he has failed to save from drowning. When, I wonder, did British characters become indispensable accessories for American TV shows? Does it go back to Daphne on Frasier? Or further still?

The isle is full of noises. The background music does most of the acting. So of course it always has, until the best HBO shows taught us to do without it. Now its pretty much a rule:Music that substitutes for drama means a show that cant be taken seriously. That doesn't always matter; many shows don't need or want to be taken seriously. Some even have a sense of humour: Lost probably thinks it has, but it has yet to yield a single intentional laugh. Its ultimate source, I think, may be the 60s cult series of all cult series, The Prisoner, an interlocking series of mazes. Lost aspires that way, but gets -- well, lost. It wouldnt be surprising if the whole thing turned out to be a dream. That would be the ultimate decadent touch.

-The season premiere of Lost airs tonight at 9 p.m. ET on CTV.

2008-02-02-spelling-bee-musical-comes-to:
There were times in The 25th Annual Putnam County Spelling Bee, which comes to us as a hit Broadway musical with an off-Broadway size and sensibility, when I felt like standing up and shouting at the people on stage "Shut up and spell. This is not really a reflection on William Finns music and lyrics; they are hit-and- miss, like all of his work, but the hits are palpable. It is a compliment to Rachel Sheinkin's book, though maybe a backhanded one. After all, the script and score of a musical are meant to work in perfect synergy, neither one making you miss the presence of the other. The best spoken jokes in this show are so good that it would take a Porter, a Loesser or a Sondheim to compete with them in song.

Competition happens to be what this show is about. Putnam County is a generic American small town, six of whose high-school students (all played by adult actors) have reached the local finals of the arcane national ritual so painstakingly identified in the title. Presiding over the proceedings is a former winner who has grown up to be a successful realtor, a career choice that Roberta Duchak, who plays her in this touring production, makes seem very credible. Helping her out is a school vice-principal who once had an unspecified cloud hanging over his head but claims to have got out from under it now. His job is to read out dictionary definitions of the operative words when the contestants request it, as they invariably do, and also to use those words in sentences, which he apparently makes up out of his own head. His inventions can take plodding literalism to hilariously inspired levels (Billy, put down that phylactery, we're Episcopalian"); they may not be very illuminating to prospective spellers but they certainly shine a light on the mind that came up with them. Douglas Kalbs pinched pedagogue shares the evenings comic dividends with the young finalists themselves, who are prodigies to their parents and both freaks and geeks to their peers. That's a double burden even before you factor in the pressures of the game itself. It's fun to see them wrestle with the words, especially in the initial stages when nobody gets anything wrong, even when, say, a girl with a lisp is obliged to cope with the word "cystitis. The process is varied by having four members of the audience play additional contestants, who are first flattered with easy words (would you believe, cow?) and then flattened with impossible ones. One splendid lady at the Toronto premiere temporarily derailed the show by getting her hard word right, which is certainly more than I could have done, forcing them to find another one with which to dismiss her. It was the highlight of the evening, but there is, of course, no guarantee that it will be repeated.

Back in the plot, its initially funny when the kids, too, begin to mess up and get eliminated. Chip Tolentino (Justin Keyes) successively succumbs to embarrassment, incredulity and rage when the sight of a rivals sister in the audience gives him an erection. (It doesn't help that the word he's being asked to spell is titup.") Gradually, we realize, glumly, that these young people have issues, which are illustrated in little inset scenes:Meet Logainne Schwartzandgrubenierre (Dana Steingold) whose name, a spelling bee in itself, derives from her having two live-together daddies who make irreconcilable demands on her; Olive Ostrovsky (Va- nessa Ray) with, or rather without, her self-absorbed absentee mother; and the multilingual Marcy Park (Katie Boren), trying to face down impossible parental expectations. All three performers are excellent, with Ray especially charming and Boren hitting sudden rebellion out of the ballpark, but the only character who makes adolescent angst entertaining is a touchy, though definitely not touchy-feely, fellow called William Barfee. He is overweight and spells out words with what he calls his Magic Foot: cue the choreography. Eric Roediger, who plays him with a marvellous air of injured self-absorption, is making, amazingly, his professional debut; though since in the program he thanks his wife, it must be a belated one.

As for the score, it starts with a winsomely jolly title tune, in a familiar vein, and reaches its creative and thematic peak with Olives My Friend the Dictionary. ("I love the indented border/ Every words in alphabetical order.") It has turbulent sequences that manage to be simultaneously apt and distracting, and strenuously off-kilter dramatic numbers that try hard to flesh out what the book has barely sketched in. It recalls the confessional mode of A Chorus Line, with the difference that those characters had a vocational reason for expressing themselves in song and dance, and had real desperation driving them. American musicals used to glorify winners; now they're likelier (cf. Wicked) to glorify losers, which might be a step forward if only they were prepared to dig deeper into the people with whom they profess to sympathize James Lapine, who usually does more complex pieces, directed this show that comes on oddball but ends up deep in the mainstream The laughs predominate; go for them and you'll be all right.

- The 25th Annual Putnam County Spelling Bee runs through Feb. 10 at the Elgin Theatre. Call 416-872-5555 for more information.

Five weeks ago, Pearson International Airport joined the big leagues. It became the site of an exciting chase, culminating in the take-down of a terrorist and the arrest of a possible accomplice. It was fictitious, of course, but it got the new drama series The Border off to a pounding start.

The Border, apart from contributing to CBC's new drama push, is part of a movement to shine a glamorous light on government departments with less than glamorous titles. In The Border it's Immigration and Customs Security; in Global's The Guard, it's the Canadian Coastguard's Search and Rescue Team. The latter sounds as if it should be more thrilling, but so far it's The Border that's hit the ground running.

Not that it hasn't done some stumbling. The remainder of the premiere dealt with the disputed fate of the putative accomplice, a Canadian citizen whose crimes seemed to be: a) being of Syrian origin; b) occupying the next seat on the incoming flight; c) letting the terrorist slip him the name of a good orthodontist -- an excuse regarded by the hardliners at CSIS as so much dental floss. The CSIS boss wanted to send the man back to Syria, with all that that would entail. The decent chaps at ICS would have none of this. And so the battle of the acronyms was joined, and won by the good guys with disappointingly little effort. I had imagined that we were just at the start of an intricate intrigue, in the manner of 24 in its great days, but The Border, like The Guard, has turned out to be not a serial but a series --i.e. a show in which the same characters face similar problems every week. (Both try to kid you that they have continuity by starting each week with one of those "previously on ..." announcements that only sound good when delivered by Kiefer Sutherland.)

Well, at least The Border seems committed to exploring every region in which the country belonging to us abuts the country belonging to them. "Them" is of course the United States, and they have been behaving very themmishly, indeed. The hawkish CSIS man (as portrayed by Nigel Bennett) just about counts as a crypto-American, but he has turned out to be the merest curtain-raiser. In the second episode, the Yanks sent in the cavalry, in the shape of a young lady from Homeland Security, an immigrant herself, with an an attitude like Ann Coulter with security clearance. Robert Fulford has already complained in these pages about the show's unwavering anti- Americanism; in the given context, I can't see that that's so bad -- it's not as if the Maher Arar case didn't happen -- but I do agree that the execution is formulaic. (My esteemed colleague is also right about the show's comic-relief computer geek being an unsuccessful attempt to emulate 24' s Chloe; his winsomeness has nothing to do with his skills whereas Chloe's unsociability was the essence of hers.) Agent Bianca seems to have taken one look at Canada and decided that on behalf of her employers this land is their land, and she can never quite understand why ICS head Major Mike Kessler should see things differently. He's played, very well, by James McGowan.

Every episode of The Border contains innumerable scenes of Mike and Bianca going eye-ball-to-eyeball, Bianca saying "You Canadians! Unbelievable!" when the major complains about a little thing like having his country's air space violated. Last week's episode, however, ended with the two of them sloping off to buy one another a drink, so this could be the beginning of a beautiful friendship. But this was an episode that never established the suspense it was striving for.

The previous week was much sharper: a four-cornered struggle between our guys, Bianca's guys, escaped Islamist terrorists and the Quebec police that involved two former Stratford Festival luminaries, Graham Abbey and Nazneen Contractor, trekking through the province's wider regions and nearly succumbing to both friendly and unfriendly fire in the process. Abbey isn't quite Jack Bauer, but he is shaping up nicely in the cat-with-nine-lives category. When The Border's narrative is firing properly, it doesn't matter too much that its characters are from stock.

It matters more in The Guard, which announces itself as being "character-driven." This turns out to mean that its principals have issues. This means they spend a lot of time moping at home instead of getting out and interacting on the job. Miro, the Duty Captain, has an online relationship with a sex worker who has misappropriated his credit card. Of Miro's team of Rescue Specialists, Laura is pouting about being passed over for Miro's job. And Andrew, having failed to rescue a child in the first sequence of the first episode, keeps having flashbacks about it, which are damaging his relationship with his own family. People say anonymously angsty things such as "we can't live like this." It's like daytime TV with an adventure gimmick. And maybe there's been a basic miscalculation about how exciting the setup is. Every week, the team goes out, and either it saves lives or it doesn't. Lost or saved, we don't know the people whose lives are at stake, so we can't much care; and there are no ramifications in the wider world.

- The Border airs Mondays at 9p.m. onCBCandTheGuardairs Tuesdays at 10 p.m. onGlobal.

2008-02-05-painfully-funny-with-extras-r:
Our hero, trying to impress a deeply religious girl and her priest, goes on about what a good place Heaven must be. "It's gonna be brilliant up there", he enthuses; then, trying to be more specific, he adds "it'll be like Ibiza."

This is the humour of self-embarrassment, carried to such extremes and with such conviction, that it can be genuinely painful. Ricky Gervais is back.

He shares his thoughts on the hereafter in the first episode of his new -- well, officially new to Canada-- series Extras. This also featured a running gag about cerebral palsy. He--or, to be pedantic, Andy Millman, the character he plays -- meets a woman who suffers from it. "Don't worry," she says, as if to ease his obvious discomfort. "Oh, good," he replied, this in the circumstances being the best he can come up with in the line of polite chit-chat.

Extras arrives on the Comedy Network a few years after being seen in the U.K. and the U.S., not to mention worldwide availability on DVD. It's still a treat for anyone who likes the comedy of the excruciating. Gervais' character, a mixture of the fawning and the incompetent, is close kin to the one he created as David Brent in the original version of The Office, with the crucial difference that this time he isn't anybody's boss and so is in no position to hurt anyone except himself -- at which he is a virtuoso. In The Office, Gervais' character was at the top of a small heap; Extras finds his new character at the bottom of a big one. Andy is a fortyish actor, a late beginner in the profession but keen. Having yet to be given a single line to speak in any medium, he is working as what the world in general calls an extra and what he himself calls a background artist. ("Just for the pocket money," as he says, convincing nobody, including himself.) He has a friend, Maggie, who's also in the background business, and with roughly the same number of social skills. He is also cursed with an agent whose attributes include "having trouble with his cellphone -- and technology generally." Stephen Merchant, Gervais' co-writer, plays him with an air of listless self-deprecation that could be either charming or alarming, depending on whether or not you're his client.

So what Andy actually does is hang around movie sets in uncomfortable and unbecoming costumes, waiting to be called and hoping to make contacts. And he does meet some real-life stars. In the first episode, it was Kate Winslet, uttering friendly obscenities that sounded amusing because a) she was Kate Winslet, and b) she was dressed as a nun, for a film that seemed to be The Sound of Music with realistic Nazis. (As she said herself, the best way to get an Oscar is to do a Holocaust picture.) Last week, Andy met Ben Stiller, taking a flight at directing ("I'm one of the world's most successful comedy actors, but what does that mean?"). He, too, was making an ostentatiously humanitarian picture, which didn't stop him throwing a very nasty, and very convincing, tantrum when crossed -- by Andy, as it happened. This was tough, since Andy had spent the entire show trying to ingratiate himself, feigning enthusiasm over classics like The Seven Samurai: "I love all the number pictures."

Gervais can almost make you believe that Andy believes that he means it. That's because, though his character is pushy, his delivery isn't. He's quite the understater --even working from a script, he sounds improvised.

It's the verite aspect that makes the show work, enhanced of course by the celebs sending themselves sportingly up. (One assumes they know what they're doing. Though sometimes -- especially with Stiller -- one hopes that they don't.) The Stiller episode was notably well-constructed, with Andy the architect of his own misfortune; the Winslet episode not so much. But the persona Gervais has constructed is fascinating. He's a misanthropic sycophant, a self-defeating combination that's common enough in real life but under-exploited in fiction.

There's an obvious danger of repetition. However, there have been two seasons of Extras, and the Comedy Network has cannily jammed them together. In the first season, Andy tells us that he's written a TV series. (Shades of George Costanza, of whom Andy may be the unsanitized version-- if you can imagine that.) We assume this is another of his hopeless projects, but in the second season it gets written, and even made. And then the suits -- this may be the BBC, but they're still suits --move in and start to change it. This is a more fertile situation. Plus, these shows have A-list guests of the acting calibre of Ian McKellen (who does the self-satirizing classical actor bit better than anyone) and Patrick Stewart. It also has Gervais reacting to the accusing headline "TV bully kicks dwarf in face" with the observation that "there's no such thing as bad publicity."

It's tempting to call Gervais' comedy of masochistic cruelty typically English, but its most notable TV antecedents are American: The Larry Sanders Show and, later, Curb Your Enthusiasm. Both of those, though, are set in a world of real celebrity (as well as, like Extras, featuring real celebrities). Extras, however, is seedier. It's unlikely ever to be sweetened into a vehicle for Steve Carell.

2008-02-07-the-search-for-zandile-is-sti:
THEATRE REVIEW

Have You Seen Zandile?

Burton Auditorium and

Equity Showcase Theatre

The African Theatre Ensemble, who produced Have You Seen Zandile?, say that Gcina Mhlophes play is an attempt to escape the South African tradition of apartheid drama with its persistent rhetoric of victimhood. Thats a praiseworthy aim.

All the same, it's hard to believe while watching the play, which is based on the author's own childhood, that any black South Africans could have lived through the apartheid years as untouched by the system as these characters appear to be. As a contribution to Black History month, it seems surprisingly unhistorical.

Its a flimsy piece in other ways, too. Its ostensible theme is the power of storytelling. Zandile is a Zulu girl -- eight at the start of the play, 18 at the end -- whose parents have separated and who lives with her much-loved and much-loving grandmother. Granny, or Gogo, is an inspiring storyteller whose imaginative powers rub off on Zandile.

Their happy life together is interrupted when Zandiles mother appears (in a white car, a point that's stressed but not elucidated) to reclaim or, more precisely, to kidnap her. Zandile spends her teenage years in a maternal environment more repressive and protective than she has been accustomed to; she misses her grandmother desperately, but still makes friends and does well at school.

Finally, through an amazing coincidence involving her best friend's boyfriend being related to her own family, she is able to find out where her Gogo lives. What happens in the last scene should probably not be revealed, but it doesnt come as much of a surprise.

We are in effect watching pages from a scrapbook, assembled on the thinnest biographical premise. Zandile invents an imaginary friend; thats one scene. She talks to flowers, and drills them as if they were a glee club; that's another.

Her Gogo, having lost her, wanders through the auditorium desperately asking the spectators "have you seen Zandile?"; but if that, as per the title, is meant to be the emotional heart of the play, it stops beating very quickly. And so to adolescent confidences between Zandile and her more earthbound friend Lindiwe, which seem to be there mostly to fill in the time before the final curtain.

I saw the play at the Workman Theatre on Queen Street, where it wasn't much helped by flat direction (from Bunmi Oyinsan) and even flatter lighting. It is helped, somewhat, by accompanying drums and, a lot, by its actors. dbi. young portrays the growth from childhood to young womanhood with unfettered grace and unabashed immediacy. Though, there are times, especially when she and Lindiwe discuss menstruation and "sleeping with boys," when one feels that she has played this role before, in her own play blood.klaat, and with better material.

Joke Silva, a star actress from Nigeria (via the U.K.), doubles - - unrecognizably -- as both grandmother and mother; shes especially fine as the latter, when granted a humanizing monologue about her own musical aspirations and how they were blighted by marriage. (Which, to be fair, is one up to the power of storytelling.) Olivia Duodu rounds out the cast, cheerfully if without her colleagues' distinction, as the girlfriend with the fortunate connections.

- Have You Seen Zandile? is at the Burton Auditorium at York University until Feb. 8 at 9:30 a.m. and at Equity Showcase Theatre Feb. 7-8 at 2:30 p.m. and 8 p.m., and Feb. 9 at 8 p.m.
2008-02-09-a-hard-life-in-steeltown-cana:
The playwriting debut of J. Karol Korczynski occurred three years ago with a piece called Canada House. He and the Canada House Artistic Co-op have now come up with a successor piece, Canada Steel, with a third, Canada Square, on the way. Canada House focused on drug-dependency, crystal meth mostly, presented as a means for the bosses to keep the workers docile. In Canada Steel, the only drugs at issue are legitimate medicinal ones, with the main subject the wreckage, institutional and human, of what used to be a great industry, the steel mills of Hamilton.

Gus, a former steelworker prematurely retired for mental-health reasons, has already lost his house; he now finds that his union will no longer pay for his medication. He tends to go off his meds anyway; and his resultant towering rage is much exacerbated by his attempts to phone the union to discover what has happened to his health plan. His calls get routed to India, where they are fielded by a young lady named Bhopal; initially unhelpful, she gradually becomes more and more invested in Guss problems, partly because she has similar ones of her own; her outsourced job is about to be sourced even further out, to Burma. In his lighter moments, Gus pursues a Homer Simpson-ish vendetta against an unseen next-door neighbour, and dons a Leafs jersey to watch the team play on TV, going berserk when they actually win the Cup. (The play, like Canada House, is set in the future.)

Meanwhile Guss wife, Rose, discovers, in a dumpster, an outsize piece of progressive art depicting the steelworks; idealistically, she thinks it should be exhibited, and pragmatically, she suspects it's worth money. Still further meanwhile, Gus and Rose, who aren't that progressive, worry that their daughter Roxie may be taking up with a lesbian. This occupies a lot of space in the first act and is totally forgotten in the second.

Les, the yuppie smoothie, in whom Rose is trying to pique an interest in the painting and with whom she goes to bed a couple of times, is by a strange coincidence the very same official who holds her husbands fate in his hands. The union is now virtually indistinguishable from the company. Act 2 finds most of the cast -- with the virtual inclusion of Bhopal, on the line from Mumbai but visible in person -- converging on Less pad, a situation for which the technical word is "farcical. And some of it is played for farce, though without either the preparation or the development to make it work in more than isolated flashes. Les instructs his aggrieved visitors on the ways of the new globalized world, telling them that they don't get it." In fact, they do, and so do we, but that doesn't stop Les from going on telling us. Mayhem ensues, with a coda that seems split between the authors instincts for apocalypse and his ideological obligations toward hope.

The play straggles and bellows, and Graham Cozzubbos production just sits there and lets it happen. Some of the acting is disgracefully bad, with a succession of fluffed lines on the second night suggesting a general lack of confidence. Gus's unstoppable anger may partly explain the hammering monotony of Daniel Kash's performance, but there is no equivalent excuse for Alison Woolridge's Rose, played on a single note of aggrieved aggression. Brian Marler's Les is a reprise of the role he played in Canada House, and as uneasy now as he was then, but Caroline Gowdy has reasonable moxie as Roxie. It would not normally be a compliment to say that an actress phones her performance in, but Pragna Desai, who has to do just that, progresses delightfully from anonymously unhelpful to earnestly concerned to blazingly defiant. But then, as befits a telephone operative, she has all the best lines.

- Canada Steel runs through Feb. 17 at the Tarragon Theatre Extra Space. Call 416-531-1827 for details.
2008-02-13-sophie-s-sophistry-cringewort:
The American TV networks, made nervous by the writers' strike, are said to be looking greedily at new Canadian shows; and the CBC, which has a raft of new shows to offer, has been patting itself on the back at the prospect. One of the shows in which the Americans are said to be most interested is the comedy series Sophie They must really be desperate. I can't imagine Sophie being anyone else's choice.

Remember the play, and later film, A Taste of Honey? It concerns a white teenage girl, pregnant by a departed black lover, counselled and comforted by a gay male friend, and periodically invaded by a dissolute mother who has man-problems of her own.

Sophie, probably by accident rather than design, reassembles many of these elements. There are, of course, some differences. A Taste of Honey was firmly set in 1950s working-class England; Sophie emphatically positions itself in the middle-class here and now. (Though the "here" part, at least, is very vague. Canadian the show may be, but it has no sense of place. Its spiritual home seems to be a fantasy version of the fantasy New York of Friends. This rootlessness may, of course, be what recommends it to the Americans.)

Sophie herself is no teenager but the glossy owner of a glossy talent agency. Her pregnancy was the result of a one-night stand with someone unknown; she assumed, up until delivery, that the father was her regular boyfriend Rick. Rick is now her ex, having taken up with Sophie's best friend Melissa; he is also, and viciously, her professional rival.

Matt, the gay confidant, is a doctor. There are two mother figures, and it would be hard to say which is the more destructive. The better-intentioned one is Estelle, longtime client of Sophie's and longtime lover of Sophie's late father; Estelle has an adopted Chinese daughter whom she, being an actress who once played Stratford, has named Ophelia and who has grown up judgmental and impatient with Estelle's fantasies. ( Shades, but sadly faint ones, of Absolutely Fabulous, a much-imitated show that is, of course, inimitable.)

Sophie's embittered birth-mother is called Judith; she's as focused on her own grievances as Estelle is on her stalled career, but she can sometimes be a force for good. As played by Mimi Kuzyk, she's the best thing on the show. But most of the actors are good; or at least blameless. It's the writing. And the producing.

The character of Melissa brings back our old friend the dumb blond, all pout and wiggle and benevolent intentions. Otherwise -- black, gay and Asian elements notwithstanding -- the characters aren't stereotypes. They aren't anything. They seem to have been assembled by a computer, collectively and -- in the case of Sophie herself -- individually. She has something for everyone; she is, to quote the press-release, " hot-tempered, loving, generous, practical and filled with a sense of wonder."

That is, she's a blur. What's supposed to be funny about her? Her personality? Her situation? If it's the latter, does the humour arise from her being a single mother, or from her being an embattled professional? The show has as much trouble juggling her two roles as she does; it tends to focus on each one, on alternate weeks.

Tonight's episode is marginally better than its predecessors, despite being another round between Sophie and Rick and having no role for Judith. Both agents are after "Miriam Cambridge, the hottest young star in town." ("I discovered her, I nurtured her," says Sophie late in the half-hour, which doesn't make sense. We've been led to believe that Miriam's already a star, and that neither has previous history with her.) But along the way we do get to hear of actors being malevolently sent off to the wrong auditions.

Middle-aged Estelle shows up for a hip-hop musical, and tries fearlessly, or just shamelessly, to ingratiate herself; she pronounces herself "rad" and says "I'm down with that." But even this goes sour.

Sophie tries to titillate us with a glimpse of a supposedly glossy world and to reassure us by showing us its inhabitants coming croppers. It then reassures us further by telling us that some of its people are really nice and the rest are harmless. Comedy without danger: It's a familiar formula. It's also a dead zone.

The show doesn't have a laugh track, which I guess is an advance for civilization, but it also doesn't have laughs. I mean that literally. What it has is the presumption of comedy. Featureless people make weightless remarks, while plucked strings on the soundtrack try to make us believe that, if this isn't funny, then at least it's cute.

There's a lot of it around. But if CBC is going to imitate American television then surely it should be setting its sights on the best of the cable shows rather than the worst of the networks. It's been known to aim high in the past. Just think: They cancelled This is Wonderland and they gave us this.

-Sophie airs tonight at 8:30 p.m. on CBC.

2008-02-16-condos-are-a-sham-and-other-f:
(From the National Post, February 23, 2008) In last Saturday's review of Second City's Tazed and Confused, Ashley Botting was mistakenly credited with a role in a playground sketch that was written and performed by Karen Parker. The Post regrets the error. 

The new Second City revue, Tazed and Confused, contains only one number that's actually about Tasers, and even that has nothing to do with airports and little with the RCMP. Rather, it's a song for the three women in the six-strong cast, about stun guns being the new approved feminist weapon for self-defence. It isn't one of the stronger items in the show. The second part of the title, though, may be an additional pun; people are con-fused because they live in con-dominiums, and the show has a lot to say about that. At its beginning, its close and immediately following the intermission, the show offers con-dolences (that one's mine) to all those cramped and alienated souls who have bought into high-priced highrises. This recurring theme-- they call it the Condo Con--might be more inventively handled, but it has its moments. One of them involves a male performer saying that he likes the condo life because he's a voyeur, and then yelling at a female performer as to what the hell she's looking at.

I will spare you the rest of my customary rant about the disconnect between Second City's revues and their titles, only pausing to remark that this new edition--a good show, not a great one -- has even less political content than most. As always, the writers are also the performers. They are more consistently excellent in the latter capacity than in the former, which is par for most courses. The veteran in the lineup is fair-haired Jim Annan, who is especially winning as a divorced dad, who's granted custody of his daughter on her birthday weekend and monitoring the video game she and her friends insist on playing. It's called Dungeon Master, and it worries him; though, as he admits on one of his forays into the kiddies' quarters, clad in underpants and mask, daddy and his girlfriend "are playing a similar game upstairs." The Second Citizens are often at their best in sketches that require them, or some of them, to play children, and this is one of their best.

The Dungeon Master himself is Marty Adams, confined to an alcove whence he cackles gleefully, in monkish cowl and with jerking jowl. Adams is, to mince words, an exceptionally plump performer, and his girth is put to use in many scenes, including one in which he seems to be playing a baby and another in which he's an orangutan. Still, the most distinctive of the men is Darryl Hinds, who claims the best moments in the two best numbers. In one, he's Tonto, the Lone Ranger's sidekick, querying both his companion's status ("how can you be the Lone Ranger? We're always together") and his own (though his hurt claim to belong to the First Nations -- "because we were here first" -- is met by the Masked One with mocking incomprehension). He's even more sensational as a victorious football player giving very basic answers to very dumb questions ("What was your strategy?" "I ran very fast and tried to catch the ball") and then flabbergasting everyone with his response to a smart one.

A newcomer among the ladies is Ashley Botting, a brunette who ranges from thoughtful to hysterical and sings unusually well. She teams up with Leslie Seiler, an acerbic blond, to represent the travails of youngish mothers at a playground, comparing their offspring ("I always wanted a little girl, but you take what you get") while keeping a suspiciously distant watch over their well- being. Seiler also does a surprise strip. She and Anna recombine as an elderly couple, who make the brisk decision to forego decay in favour of mutually assisted suicide; this sketch, Waiting for Godot meets The Savages, is not completely successful, but it moves the customary goal posts. The cast is completed by Karen Parker, a mischievous presence who's at her best as a yowling pre-teen, happily traumatized by her Dungeon Master. There is expectedly smart direction by Doug Morency, and unexpectedly (at this address) stylish design by Camellia Koo. We take Second City for granted, but it's a true civic adornment, an asset to Toronto's comic present and -- judging from the way its alumni get around-- the rest of the world's comic future.

- Tazed and Confused runs indefinitely at The Second City. Call 416-343-0011 for details.
2008-02-19-ready-to-be-flambed-chef-scho:
Irecently found myself helping with the cooking at Rundles. Rundles is the most highly rated restaurant in Stratford, Ont., which is saying something.

Usually, when I go to Stratford, my main purpose is to see plays. But in between shows, one has to eat; and for years now, Stratford has been one of the best places in Canada in which to do that.

During the winter, when the theatre festival shuts down, most of the top eating places do likewise. Their chefs and proprietors occupy themselves at the Stratford Chefs School, which each year takes on a dozen prospective cooks and has its own culinary stars, plus "celebrity chefs" from here and abroad, to teach them.

The school is now the subject of a reality TV show, Chef School, which is why I was one of a select party of journalists assembled in the kitchen. We were getting a taste, so to speak, of what the students went through. Mercifully, nobody filmed us while we were getting it.

I was lying when I said I helped. All I did was wave a blowtorch in the direction of a square of sweetened pasty whose intended destiny was to form the outer casing of a delectable morsel billed on the menu as "caramelized Russian pastry." My blowtorch technique, though, was lacking, and my contribution ended up charred, blackened and discarded.

We were working according to the instructions of Matteo Baronetto, an impossibly young-looking maestro from Milan (he was 30, but I was reliably informed that he had to produce ID when attempting to buy cigarettes); we subsequently ate an amazing lunch for which we had some theoretical responsibility but that really came down to Matteo and his assistant. The previous evening we had eaten an almost equally spectacular dinner cooked by the students under Matteo's direction. Take it from me, the Stratford Chefs School is doing good work.

That said, it deserves a better TV show. Chef School falls into a familiar trap. In following the fortunes of its dozen aspirants, it stakes nearly everything on "human interest."

The young people we meet (their median age is early 20s), furiously interacting with one another, might be training for anything. Jim Morris, who runs Rundles and is co-director of the school, observes at one point that there's "a crazy element to people who cook for a living."

The opening episodes have been higher on craziness than on cooking, which, for a show airing on a specialty food network, is rather curious. As a group, these kids -- rowdy and uncertain and swearing a lot -- are much like any others. The only thing that makes them interesting is what they're studying.

There are long stretches when the show might better be called All About Alex. Alex is a bushy-eyebrowed 21-year old who seems to have antagonized all his fellow students. He enraged them on the very first day by arriving early and grabbing the best room in the residence. (I can't see what was so terrible about that. Somebody had to do it.)

He needs, according to his schoolmates, to always be the focus of attention, and the show certainly gives it to him. "I don't know what's wrong with Alex -- the way he works," somebody says, to which he responds -- at least the editing makes it look as if he's responding -- "I'm not a train wreck ... I like to cause accidents."

The school, like the restaurants behind it, has an eclectic approach to cuisine -- unlike, as Morris points out, a typical French cooking school --and it has an extra-culinary curriculum that is similarly wide-ranging.

The philosophy of Morris and his co-director Eleanor Kane (proprietress of the Old Prune, another of the town's finest) is that "students must learn to be articulate about culture and cuisine." So there is, among other things, a yoga class, which seems to work for Alex.

Stress levels rise, obviously, for the first class evaluation, which is the subject of the show's fourth episode. There was still a bias towards the banal: We had a montage of people saying "it's exam day" and telling the camera they were nervous about it. We got the point. But this instalment was still the best to date because it was what they, and we, were there for.

Assigning the dishes and judging the results was Neil Baxter, Rundles' chef and therefore quite likely the best in the country. He seemed to be a very calming presence, but also seemed quite perturbed by much of what he witnessed. He's the kind of teacher who's so gentle he's cruel, because you want so much to please him and his judgments are delivered in such pained, measured tones.

Everybody emerged with a passing grade, even Alex who announced, "I'm on the road to perfection," and then proceeded to drop stuff. "I've got a lot on my plate now," he said afterwards. (I'm not picking on him; the show does. And who knows, he could get his own series out of this.)

Another student, Joyce, was praised for the quality of her sweetbreads but chided for serving them on a brown paper towel. Then there was David who unhappily charred his arctic char. "I wouldn't consider it burnt, exactly," he said, but it sure looked burnt to Chef Baxter, and even to me; since David was the student with the most professional experience, it was comforting to see that it could happen to him too, though he understandably didn't see it that way.

The Stratford Chefs School runs a two-year course, and there's always attrition in the second year. So there's pressure. Chef School the show tries hard to make us feel that pressure but doesn't seem to trust its subject. That's the trouble with reality shows. They aren't very real.

- Chef School airs tonight at 10 p.m. ET on Food Network Canada.

2008-02-19-southern-belle-in-a-cold-clim:
THE CLEAN HOUSE

Bluma Appel Theatre, Toronto

Sarah Ruhl's The Clean House is a North American play that has gone warmly South. Its Toronto production seems misguidedly intent on cooling it down again. The author, who is thirtyish and much- lauded, has said that her initial idea came from an overheard remark at a party; a doctor was complaining that her maid, a Brazilian, refused to clean her house. "I did not," she said "go to medical school in order to clean my own house."

That line has gone straight into the play where it's spoken by Lane, a physician who does indeed have a Brazilian maid called Mathilde. Mathilde used to be depressed and her pills have left her with an antipathy towards cleaning anybody's house. What she really wants to be is a comedienne; she comes from a funny family, and both of her parents pretty much died laughing.

The play's unstressed point is that this is the best way to go; and who would argue? Well, Lane and her sister Virginia ("like the state", though the name may have another significance) both would, at least to begin with. They are crazy about having spotless surroundings, though while Lane wants someone else to do the work, Virginia likes to do it herself. And since she's through with cleaning her own place at approximately 3:12 every day (well, she says "approximately," though to anyone else it sounds unnervingly precise), she has more than enough time to take care of Lane's, which is a great blessing for Mathilde.

Both sisters are married; we never meet Virginia's partner -- she doesn't seem to see much of him herself -- but Lane's husband Charles is a player. He's a surgeon who falls in love with, and leaves his wife for, a breast-cancer patient named Ana.

Ana laughs a lot; she also knows how to cry despite coming from a country, Argentina, where crying is said to be officially discouraged.

"They fall in love," says a subtitle, as surgeon and patient do just that. Only here there are no titles. I only know that they existed in previous stagings from reading American reviews supplied to me by Canadian Stage: A generous gesture, since those reviews point to a purposeful craziness -- the ethnic quotient makes the term "magical realism" impossible to avoid -- that Alisa Palmer's production either damps down or misses entirely.

Charles and Ana declare their passion, mid-mastectomy, in operatic duet. Ana's half of this is ringingly performed by Mary Ann McDonald, an accomplished singer who also gives a joyous, and eventually moving, spoken performance.

Joseph Ziegler plays Charles, and though he acts charmingly, his singing is muted. The song is accompanied by a dance, and this too lacks something in abandon. When Mathilde "imagines" her parents, we see them in mimed flashbacks; these are preserved, but in a nervous hole-and-corner fashion. Judith Bowden's chilly set is more attuned to the play's title than to its spirit, though Kevin Lamotte's lighting is, by its own lights, superb.

Mathilde is on a quest for the perfect joke, and eventually she finds it and tells it, though tactfully not out loud. In its first half, the play's devices may seem cute or cloying, but they justify themselves in the second, which is a generous testament to all kinds of love, including euthanasia.

It is also quirkily funny; Charles' announcement that he is shacking up with Ana according to Jewish law, despite the fact he isn't Jewish, occasions as well-built a comic scene as I have recently encountered. Later, with Charles off in Alaska chopping down yew trees with prophylactic properties, the four women draw unexpectedly together by sharing a bowl of chocolate ice cream: a lovely image.

Seana McKenna and Fiona Reid play the sisters, but it's a partnership that provides less than promised; they're both mistresses of timing, so their performances dovetail nicely, but they don't strike any fresh sparks off one another. Both are in familiar modes: Reid fluffy and neurotic, McKenna steely on top and jellied underneath, with a glance that could shame any basilisk and a touching forgiveness at the end.

The play's heart, though -- and the evening's salvation -- isn't really with them, it's with the two women from South America: Ana, and Mathilde, the latter of whom has two households understandably vying for her non-domestic services and whom Nicola Correia-Damude plays boldly and delightfully.

She starts the play by telling a joke in Portuguese. I suspect that non-Portuguese-speakers may not be missing much, but her body- language suggests that it's hilarious. - The Clean House is at the Bluma Appel Theatre until March 8. For more information call 416- 368-3110.
2008-02-20-so-tell-me-about-your-tedious:
When I first heard about In Treatment, I assumed it was going to be a reality series. My mistake, and a foolish one: It would be ethically impossible for a real psychiatric session to be filmed for public consumption. (Now go ahead and tell me that someone, somewhere has done it.) But if it is going to have any credibility, a fictional show about psychoanalysis or psychotherapy should adhere to stringent naturalistic standards. It should probably be improvised. Certainly it should not sound written.

In Treatment does sound written, in a glib if high-minded way, like a 1950s Hollywood melodrama directed by Ingmar Bergman. Based on, but not slavishly tied to, a successful Israeli series, it airs five nights a week.

Monday to Thursday, Paul, a rumpled, middle-aged therapist of Irish extraction (to put it another way, he's played by Gabriel Byrne), acts as inquisitor and sounding board for three individual patients and one couple.

On the fifth day, the shrink himself gets shrunk, consulting with a senior therapist called Gina on how his week has been. Generally, it has been terrible.

A minor reason for this may be that some of his patients are tedious, to us and probably to him. They include Alex, a young veteran of the Iraq war who tries for favoured-patient status by buying Paul an espresso machine, and a couple wondering whether or not to abort their second child.

Another patient is dull for viewers but disturbingly fascinating to him: shes Laura, a narcissistic anesthesiologist who may be the least convincing medical professional in TV history, and certainly the one you would least trust to put you under. She delivers unbearably pat monologues about her state of mind, tells Paul that shes in love with him and berates him for not responding.

She also tells him about the sex she's having with Alex, whom -- in the soapiest of soap opera developments -- she encountered outside Paul's office one day when he got his appointment time wrong. (If it were really true to its own pretensions, this show wouldnt step beyond the consulting room.)

Like many in his profession, Paul works from home. (A nice place, somewhere in the New York hinterlands.) This becomes a problem for him, since his physical proximity to work emphasizes his psychological distance from his family; at least thats how his wife resentfully sees it.

She has an affair, which she tells him about, and he winds up sleeping on his own couch. That couch sees a lot of drama, much of it way beyond the normal call of psychiatric duty. It gets bloodied when Paul's pregnant patient has a miscarriage right on the premises (one problem solved, you might think, but the couple come back for more).

It's the site of gymnastics, including backflips, performed by Pauls youngest and most interesting patient, a 16-year old athlete with parental and relationship problems. She broke both her arms in an accident but is obviously recovering, at least physically. Shes seeing Paul for "evaluation" rather than therapy, so maybe it's permissible for him to put his arm around her when she's in distress. But it looks like crossing a line.

Thats undoubtedly how Gina, his own therapist, would see it. Shes a martinet on doctor-patient etiquette.

The show has some things going for it. One is Mia Wasikowska's performance as Sophie, a model of teenage bewilderment and teenage disdain. I'm not sure that her scenes are better-written than the others, but her freshness and spontaneity certainly make them seem so.

Byrne himself is fine, a patient and unwearying listener when on the job; very weary indeed and far from patient when hes the patient. So his scenes with Dianne Wiests excellent Gina, whom he likes but distrusts (or maybe trusts but dislikes), have a special charge.

Paul's confessions to Gina (and his rows with his wife, who's given a good, brittle performance by Michelle Forbes) have something of that. Pauls bathroom seems to see even more action than his couch -- so far its hosted one suicide attempt and any amount of vomiting -- and it's interesting to see how much of the turmoil in his life he reveals, how much he conceals or how much he exaggerates.

But this makes In Treatment a more conventional show than it promised to be, or was promoted as being. Its focus is not the therapy, but the therapist. As his patients keep complaining, it's all about him.

Talking of melodrama and false promises: Damages started its run on Monday. It's the latest high-gloss, big-dollars serial, masquerading as a thriller about legal and corporate skullduggery: Dirty Sexy Money without the humour or -- so far -- the sex. It stars Glenn Close (as a crueller Cruella), Ted Danson and a newcomer, Rose Byrne, as an ingenue who proclaims "phoney is not my strong suit." It is the show's.

- In Treatment airs weeknights at 8:30 p.m ET on The Movie Network and 9:30 p.m PT on Movie Central.

2008-02-21-imagine-laughing-and-actually:
THEATRE REVIEW

THE ODD COUPLE

Young Centre for the Performing Arts, Toronto

---

There are many compliments to be paid to the Soulpepper company's revival of The Odd Couple, but the chief among them -- the one that contains all the others -- is that it refuses to be a gag machine. Neil Simon's comedies can hardly help being funny (at least the best of them can't, and The Odd Couple, though an early work, may be the best of all), but they can also leave you feeling pummelled with wisecracks and starved of humanity. In the words of a Broadway sage: You laugh, but you don't enjoy it. The screen adaptations of Simon's plays have just this soulless quality. If they are to breathe, the plays need a live audience to breathe along with them, and Tuesday's first-night house was in harmony with the actors from our first sight of the supporting quartet of poker players in Oscar Madison's smoky, dusty apartment.

The story, by now, is folklore. Oscar takes in his friend and fellow-divorce Felix Ungar, who is as compulsively neat as Oscar himself is fecklessly untidy, and the two set up house together. In effect, they re-enact their marriages, with the same disastrous results.

There isn't much plot; there isn't even much character development once the basic psychological facts have been established. But there is a mastery of incident, and of verbal and physical knockabout, hardly any of which feels externally imposed. (Simon gets an amazing amount of mileage from having somebody unexpected at the other end of the phone or ringing the doorbell. Unexpected by the characters, that is: The audience can nearly always guess. It's remarkably satisfying.) Above all, there is the friction between two men who really like, but cannot stand, one another.

Stuart Hughes' direction gets the most from every word and every situation, without forcing a thing. He has a set, by Lorenzo Savoini, that conjures up not only the room in the apartment that we do see but the half-dozen that we don't, plus the flat across the hall. He has costumes, by Erika Connor, perfectly attuned to the personalities of those who wear them and to the period -- just before the 1960s became "The Sixties" -- that they inhabit. Above all, he has a central couple whose oddities come out enchantingly even.

Albert Schultz is a gentler, goofier, paunchier Oscar than we are accustomed to. He isn't, in other words, Walter Matthau looking like a human razor blade and making with the one-liners as if they, too, were weapons, of the automatic variety. Even a rank showbiz line like "what is that, the Curse of the Cat People?" -- Oscar's response to one of the verbal guilt-trips that Felix lays on everyone around him -- comes from Schultz like a genuine, baffled inquiry: angry, yes, but also concerned. Diego Matamoros's Felix is pettishly perfect, from his trim receding hairline and uptight specs on down, not to mention out. He hugs his neuroses while giving them plenty of geographical space. This actor is, among much else, a champion clown, whether terrifying his pals with gestures in the general direction of suicide or executing a dainty ballet when proudly setting the table for a dinner of London broil. An overweeningly proud cook, he looks his happiest in an apron. Still, what really unites the two men, and the two performances, is an underlying sadness. Though in Felix's case it isn't all that underlying; he parades it, and it's hilarious.

One of Felix's domestic achievements is to kill his buddies' poker-game with acts of culinary kindness. The visiting gamesters are Michael Hanrahan, Oliver Dennis, Derek Boyes and Kevin Bundy, in roughly that order of effectiveness as individuals and with impregnable credibility as a collective. These are good New Yorkers' parts -- the production's big surprise is the impact made by Amy Rutherford and Krystin Pellerin as the coo-coo Pigeon sisters, two English birds nesting in the apartment upstairs whom Oscar thinks ripe for the plucking but who start unexpectedly coo-cooing over Felix. They are perfect, in voice, manner and -- in dolly dresses that look quantifiably Quant -- appearance.

It's Felix's virginal thwarting of Oscar's dreams of scoring that drives the great rift between them. Once that has been established and the recriminations have mutually and furiously flown, the play has little more to say and starts to run out of gas though not, thanks to what has gone before, of goodwill. There's no flagging in the performance; the stage remains charged with energy, and so does the auditorium.

I wouldn't want Soulpepper to embark on a Simon cycle; the appeal of this show has much to do with seeing this company's two signature actors in joyous partnership. But everything else backs them up, down to the inspired choices of music between scenes and even at the curtain call. You laugh, and you enjoy it. - The Odd Couple plays in repertory at Toronto's Young Centre for the Performing Arts until April 19. Call 416-866-8666 for information.
