2008-02-23-i-was-the-critic-who-stood-an:
Late in 1979, Britain's Royal Shakes peare Company, at a high artistic tide and a low financial ebb, issued a press release. It announced that in 1980 it would only be able to afford one new production at its London home, the Aldwych Theatre, to sit alongside the customary Shakespearean transfers from Stratford-upon-Avon. That one, however, would be a whopper: an adaptation, in two full-length parts, of Charles Dickens novel The Life and Adventures of Nicholas Nickleby.

This may sound like hindsight, but my first reaction was, "What a good idea." Dramatizations of novels often flounder, but I had come to believe that this was due not to any fundamental incompatibility between page and stage, but simply because stage versions never gave themselves enough time. Dickens was a writer with an obviously theatrical genius, who -- had he written when plays rather than novels were the dominant form -- might have been the greatest English playwright since Shakespeare. Stage versions of his books often dwindled into a collection of famous catchphrases and basic plot lines; the richness, the variety and the passion got lost. But this didnt have to happen. A fringe company called Shared Experience had recently mounted a version of Bleak House, which, with no sets or costumes and only six actors, managed to cover the whole book, no subplot or minor character left behind. It was breathtaking.

The RSC's Nickleby was obviously going to be a bigger deal physically; they had a company of 40. It was a very strong company, forged over several years by the recognizably great artistic director Trevor Nunn, who was to co-direct Nickleby with young protege John Caird. What distinguished Nunn's work was its humanity - - he seemed to love actors -- and its full-bodied intensity; his comedies were rib-breaking and his tragedies terrifying, and Dickens would give him huge scope for birth. He had recently directed Ian McKellen in the greatest Macbeth I or most other people had seen. McKellen was no longer with the RSC, but I encountered him in Aldwych at Nicklebys first official all-day performance.

Im looking forward to this, he said, "more than to anything I've ever seen." A couple of months later I asked if the event had lived up to his great expectations. Oh, much more, he said. He added that what he loved most was the feeling that the show had been created by the actors --his ex-colleagues -- to share with the audience.

The show did indeed unfold like a sumptuous gift, from them to us. Watching the impetuous, impoverished young Nicholas and his family progressing through the cruelties and the kindnesses of early Victorian England we laughed, we cried and were made to feel -- as George Orwell wrote of Dickens -- "generously angry." Part One lasted four hours, Part Two four-and-a-half; and since so much of the show was comic, one ended up feeling light-headed. I think it was at the third intermission of the second show that an acquaintance voiced my own thoughts by saying, I don't want this to end. We were completely caught up in the shows world. At the end, I happily defied critical tradition by standing up and joining in what appeared to be unanimous tear-stained cheers.

So it was a shock to find that the reviews were mostly not that good, with "not really a play" the burden of complaint. My own review in The Observer was a rave, beginning with the words theres a lot to be said for length. But what turned the tide was a column by the late Bernard Levin in The Times. There were lines round the block the next morning. The production was brought back twice within the year, then went to New York, on to television and into legend.

There have not been many revivals. But in 2006, Jonathan Church, the new artistic director of the Chichester Festival Theatre, finding himself in straits similar to the RSC's 28 years ago, mounted a new production with similar success. Co-directed by Church and actor-director Philip Franks, it was revived last year, toured in Britain, and now plays its only North American date at the Princess of Wales Theatre, starting today, all day. This has given David Edgar a chance to have a second look at his play. Some people are surprised to learn that Nickleby has a playwright, and Edgar, whom I reached by phone at his home in Birmingham, admits to mild irritation at the persisting legend that, back in 1980, "45 actors and two directors" did it all themselves -- though it was created on the basis of a five-week workshop before I delivered.

Edgar, then as now one of Britain's best large-scale public playwrights, was an inspired choice of adaptor. He reminded me that the original production happened "quite early in Thatcherism" when there was debate as to whether the vaunted Victorian values were truly "about self-help or about philanthropy. The social and economic divisions in society are now, if anything, stronger." And so it is in Dickens. One of Nicklebys villains, the aristocratic cad Sir Mulberry Hawk is able to bet Pounds 50, while Nicholas is offered a munificent pound a week by Crummles -- and Pounds 5 a year at Dotheboys Hall. Mr. Crummles, no meany, is the archetypal strolling actor-manager with whom Nicholas and his oppressed companion Smike find employment, and whose repertoire in Edgars version includes a riotous rewrite of Romeo and Juliet.

Edgar has reduced the plays' running times to three and three- and-half-hours ("more of a pang to me than it was to the public") and thinks some of his changes may be improvements. We've lost a whole subplot from Part One; Part Two was more difficult, more a matter of filleting. Part Two is now a better play than it was, cleaner and clearer. And darker.

Though, it always had its dark passages, and they were very powerful. Edgar once described Dickens theory of human and social behaviour as "wouldnt it be nice if every day were Christmas." The novels and the play recognize that most days aren't, but insist that they should be. Meanwhile, the show is the richest kind of present, any day of the year. - To April 20 at the Princess of Wales Theatre. For tickets, call 416-872-1212 or visit mirvish.com
2008-02-25-jon-stewart-s-amiable-double-:
Jon Stewart, columnist. Solemn music played as Oscar's statue revolved, untouched and unclaimable. Then we cut to the stage, on which stood three silver columns. One of them rose, and out from under it stood our host. He seemed slightly nervous, slightly cool, which is what we expected of him.

It was a very short monologue. He stood at the front of the stage, apparently unfazed by the absence of a desk (which you cant always say for him on The Daily Show) and possibly moving less than any host in Oscar history. Its not just that he isn't Billy Crystal; he isn't even David Letterman, whom I remember as roaming around the stage in apparent agonies of embarrassment. Im not knocking him. I liked Letterman as an Oscar host. I respected his out-of-placeness. Its the only time I've ever found him funny.

Stewart takes to it more naturally, while seemingly aware that he still has a reputation as an iconoclast to take care of. The stars in the theatre audience probably share his ambivalence. They'd like to make fun of the spectacle and what it represents, but theyre part of it. Jack Nicholson sat in the front row, as usual. At one point, he seemed to be threatening Stewart not so much through his teeth as with them.

The monologue fell into two parts. The first was about the writers strike and how grateful everybody was that it was over. It was surprisingly tame, hardly worth calling the writers back for. Then, by way of reflections on the self-congratulation about to run rampant ("We're going to spend the next four to five hours giving each other golden statues") we proceeded to consideration of the films themselves, or at least of the five nominees for best picture, all but one of them about psychopaths. (Thank God for teen pregnancy.)

Stewart's amiable double bind became apparent as he started listing and commenting on the nominees. Every title was greeted with fervent applause, by its clique of employees and supporters in the house, or -- who knows? -- by people who genuinely liked it. They seemed genuinely to think that Stewart agreed with them, though his purpose at this juncture was to make fun of them. "Thank God for Atonement," he said, and then after the cheering had died down, at last a film that does justice to the passion and raw sexuality of Yom Kippur. Some members of my family saw the punchline coming, others didnt, but we all found it funny. Personally, Ive been waiting for someone to make that joke ever since the novel came out. I also relished his words to Diablo Cody on her progression from exotic dancer to screenwriter for Juno ("I hope you're enjoying the pay cut"), and most of all to his Bushian admonition to keep movies about the Iraq war running in theatres for 100 years, despite their dismal commercial record: "Withdrawing the Iraqi movies will only embolden the audience -- YOU CAN'T LET THE AUDIENCE WIN."

Let him come back next year. Unless Stephen Colbert wants to do it. In character.
2008-02-26-at-age-80-oscar-s-heart-rate-:
If there can be a low-key Oscars show, this year's was it. For a start, or rather for a finish, it wrapped up before midnight. That's short --probably the shortest it's been in decades. Maybe this had something to do with the writers' strike; four writers were listed on the credits, plus another 10 including Jon Stewart for "special material," but they may well have been rounded up too late for anything elaborate. Mind you, this was hardly the first Oscar year that has left one wondering why it took so many people to come up with so little.

Anyway: no bloated and embarrassing musical numbers, other than the performances of the five nominated songs. And those adjectives could really only apply to three of the nominees, the three from Enchanted, each more vacuous than its predecessor. To think that these were composed by the Alan Menken who once gave us Little Shop of Horrors. To this has he come. To this have we all come. Can anyone imagine, in the golden age of Hollywood song, any picture having more than one song nominated, though many were the scores that deserved it. Anyway, the prize, to everyone's relief, went to a nice modest Irish lad for something folksy. "That guy is so arrogant," said Stewart, deftly puncturing the pretensions of everyone else. (Few Oscar recipients actually boast, unless they're James Cameron waxing Titanic, but most of the Americans have an overweening way of playing humble.) Shortly afterwards, Stewart topped this by acknowledging an error and bringing back the song's female co-author, who had been crowded out of the acceptance speech. Great to have a host who can think on his feet. He got better and better as the evening went on: our own representative in the land of cleavage and tuxedoes. He wore a tux too, of course, but we persuaded ourselves that it was camouflage.

It was not a night of surprises. The greatest suspense came from wondering who would make a first entrance by being discovered inside the set's central column (Stewart), who would manoeuvre their way round the back of it (Nicole Kidman) and who would make a regal entrance down the middle of the stage with the architecture cleared away (Helen Mirren). Queen Helen proceeded to present the best actor award to Daniel Day-Lewis without, as far as I could see, even bothering to look at the contents of the envelope. There had been the same acceptance of the inevitable in the earlier bestowal of the supporting actor prize on Javier Bardem. Everyone refrained from making the obvious jokes about what Bardem might have done to them with his cattle gun if he'd lost or what Day-Lewis might have done with anything available. The latter's award was to me the occasion of what might be called negative suspense. I'd hoped, very much against hope, that somebody else would get it, as there is effectively no one else in There Will Be Blood except Day-Lewis, and by the time the picture clocked up its second hour I felt I had had quite enough of him. Incidentally, was I imagining it, or does no woman get to utter a word in the whole long course of that movie? Even a bride about to say "I do" has to say it in sign-language.

Bardem thanked his mother in their native tongue, leaving one to ponder whether from now on all acceptance speeches shouldn't be made in Spanish; it seems a much faster language. Penelope Cruz, announcing the foreign film competitors, astonishingly said (in English) "congratulations to all our nominated countries." Not the films or their creators, but the countries. Sounds paternalistic to me. The off-screen announcer later reinforced the head-patting effect by informing us "this is the first Academy Award and the second nomination for Austria." Gallant little Austria. Still, the non-American part of the world got its sweet revenge later when the French Marion Cotillard surprised everyone -- including, very obviously and delightfully, herself -- by nabbing the best actress prize with her Edith Piaf. I was glad for her though, not having caught her at it, I was expecting a win for either Julie Christie or Ellen Page while forlornly rooting for Laura Linney.

You see the insidious things the Oscars do to you? They get you feeling sorry for your favourite losers; though, since everybody who gets nominated in a major category is either a millionaire already or will be very shortly, they can probably do without our pity. I discovered, what everybody else may already have known, that Joel Coen is the talkative brother; they were called to the podium three times, but you could hardly accuse No Country for Old Men of sweeping any boards: another cause of the low-keyness. Was Cormac McCarthy actually there? I was shocked; Hollywood is surely no country for him. Diablo Cody, by contrast, seems to have picked up Hollywoodspeak fast; "I worship you guys," she assured her unvictorious co-nominees in the original screenplay stakes. Jack Nicholson now personifies Old Hollywood; and we could wonder why he wore dark glasses when in the audience but no glasses when on stage presenting. Tilda Swinton, best supporting actress, maintained the good British (and Canadian, had we won anything) tradition of being pleased but incredulous: not just at her victory but at the whole parade.

Funniest line of the evening was Bob Hope's on the Oscar-judging process: "A secretary types out the final list, and is then taken out and shot." He said it, of course, a long time ago and in black and white. Most fatuous was wished on Renee Zellweger, who informed us that "some of the most exciting moments of your life have won Oscars." I told you they should have let the strike go on. I always enjoy the obituary section (and, not I promise you, in any ghoulish sense); Kitty Carlisle's name got respectful applause, but Betty Hutton's didn't. The fickleness of fame. But then, who is famous? Any dead person who wasn't an actor is routinely identified by profession. Well all right, "Bud Ekins, stunt artist" is information previously unknown to most of us, but do we really need to be reminded that Michelangelo Antonioni was a director? And who was Ingmar Bergman?

Them out there got to party on (though, be still my schadenfreude, it was raining in sunny Cal) while us out here got, by Oscar standards, an early night. I approve of Oscar losing weight, but I confess that his leaner look left me feeling shortchanged. Perhaps they are making the event less of a blockbuster because the movies that get to be contenders aren't busting many blocks either. Whoever thought the Academy Awards would live up to their name and become an art-house event?

2008-02-27-do-as-she-does-and-as-she-say:
The first lady of Canadian theatre is hitting the road. This month, plus the beginning of next, finds Martha Henry travelling to Vancouver, Edmonton, Regina, Winnipeg, Montreal, Toronto and St. John's.

Oh yes, and Chicago. But she isn't acting. She's auditioning other actors: a new intake for Stratford's Birmingham Conservatory for Classical Training. If the name sounds geographically confusing, bear in mind that Birmingham in this context is not a place but a benefactor.

The conservatory is a training program in classical performance that lasts 20 weeks, most of them occupying the spaces between one Stratford Festival and the next. When Henry was approached, in the fall of 2006, to be its new principal, it was, she told me over drinks at a Toronto hotel, "a complete surprise. In fact I said no. I didn't want to stop acting. But they told me that wasn't the idea."

"They," in this case, were Antoni Cimolino, Stratford's new general director and Marti Maraden, one of its even newer triumvirate of artistic directors; the other two are Des McAnuff and Don Shipley, and the team launches its first season this spring.

Henry is part of that season as an actress, with major roles in The Trojan Women and All's Well That Ends Well. The idea, plainly, is that she should lead by example as well as by precept and experience.

"They insisted that I should continue to act: Not necessarily just at Stratford, they're not guaranteeing me years of work there." (Though why would they ever want to let her go?)

Henry has not, by her own account, had "a lot of pedagogical experience," though she has taught before: at the National Theatre School in Montreal (at which, back in 1960, she had herself been one of the first students), at the Tarragon Theatre in Toronto and at Carnegie Mellon University in Pittsburgh, Pa. She was also the artistic director of the Grand Theatre in London, Ont., for several successful years, with a de facto role in the nurturing of actors if not their formal training.

When she began to think about the Stratford offer she "tried to look back and see how much of it had gone into my head and my bones. At the end of two weeks I thought, I could do that. And so far that's proved to be true."

"So far" means the greater part of one theatrical/academic year. Henry's steering of her first group, the class of 07/08 has been, according to Cimolino, a roaring success: "She's opened all kinds of doors, built all kinds of bridges." She says herself that "my greatest value is that I've done everything you can do as an actor; I've done stupid things, I've made all the mistakes." (She's also done a lot of things right, which I suspect her students may find equally inspiring.)

The conservatory runs a 20-week, six-day-a-week, course -- she hopes, next year, to expand it to 21 weeks -- divided into three terms. They come in September, and emerge in mid-February, having spent five months in the Tanya Moiseiwitsch Rehearsal Hall, named for Stratford's first great designer and situated in the theatre basement.

It sounds gruelling, not least for its principal who by her own admission is not a naturally early riser: "They go from 10 to six, alternating voice and movement every morning. I sit in on classes, and I meet with them every Sunday." The current group spent their first term working with a variety of teachers, including people from the company; they were also exposed to such visiting luminaries as Olympia Dukakis .

In their second term, David Latham -- Henry's predecessor as principal and now in charge of the expanding area of training within the main company -- worked with the students on Macbeth and taught them mask-work.

"David," says Henry, "teaches with enormous concentration on the depth in Shakespeare: what goes on underneath the text. I try to give them the skills to do that." (This includes "giving them yellow Post-it notes on diction.") In their third term, Henry has been working with them on Twelfth Night -- and finding new things in a text she thought she knew off by heart.

The Conservatory started during former artistic director Richard Monette's regime; it was one of his most cherished projects, along with the Festival theatre studio. Some of our best young actors emerged from the Conservatory's earlier years: Michael Therriault, Jonathan Goad, Michelle Giroux and others.

Goad and Therriault were already in the Festival company when they enrolled in the conservatory, and some other experienced actors have gone there; a notable example is Dan Chameroy, already a well- known performer in musicals who has painstakingly and rewardingly made himself over into a dramatic and character actor.

For the most part, though, the conservatory in Monette's time enlisted, as Henry says, "people fresh out of school." The new emphasis is slightly different: "The present directorate want actors capable of playing medium or big parts in the fairly new future. For that to happen, you need fewer people with more experience. Last year, from hundreds of applications, we took eight, not 12 (the previous customary intake). They mostly have two years in the professional theatre -- no more than that, before they develop bad habits."

Conservatory actors generally progress into the main company; the current batch have small roles in several of the coming season's shows and will have one of them, the perennially young play Love's Labour's Lost, more or less to themselves. "If you bring in twelve people every year willy-nilly, you end up after five years with a lot of the company being inexperienced young people. The company begins to look semiprofessional."

"I've enjoyed," Henry says, "watching these kids evolve, trying to make sure that what we're doing for them is the most constructive use of them in the long run. I don't care if they're in pain in week four, but I do care about their well-being at the end of week 20."

By their well-being, she means "their potential as actors. If they can absorb the Shakespearean text, they can do just about any text." Nor, obviously, can they all be expected to spend their entire careers at Stratford.

Henry herself hasn't, though she's been a powerful presence there ever since playing Miranda in The Tempest in 1962, fresh from her own training. "It's very important to me that the students come out of this being productive members of the society and the community; that they're proactive-- terrible word--in rehearsals or in the running of a theatre. I want artistic directors, in any theatre in the world, to be glad to have them. No theatre school can teach what the Conservatory can -- being exposed to designers, cutters, lighting designers, what it's like to make a wig, how to treat dressers and stage managers -- that's with the assumption that they already have a natural graciousness. I had to learn all this by hook or by crook. Nobody said to me 'this is the way you say hello to a wig.' "

After checking my notes on this, I phoned her to ask if I had made a mistake. Didn't she mean, how to say hello to a wigmaker? "No," she said firmly. "I want them to know how to talk to a wig."

2008-02-28-rocking-the-republic:
THEATRE REVIEW

ROCK 'N' ROLL

Bernard B. Jacobs Theatre, New York City

---

Everyone knows that it's unwise to assume that the characters in plays necessarily speak for their authors. Nonetheless, I'd always assumed that Tom Stoppard was waxing autobiographical in The Real Thing when he had his playwright hero say that he didn't like "the pop music which it's all right to like."

The example he gave of that category was Pink Floyd (as opposed, say, to Wayne Fontana and the Mindbenders). But it now turns out that Stoppard does like Pink Floyd. They're among the off-stage heroes of his newest play Rock 'n' Roll, along with former Czech president Vaclav Havel and a Czech rock-group called The Plastic People of the Universe. Havel of course was not a musician but he was, the play tells us, a fan.

Rock 'n' Roll, which is playing in New York after a triumphant run in London, is concerned with music and politics: to a large extent, with music as politics. Its action switches between England and Czechoslovakia in the years from 1968 to 1990.

The English scenes take place in a house and garden in Cambridge, the town in which Pink Floyd's lost hero Syd Barrett was born and to which he retreated after his early meltdown. He's glimpsed at curtain-rise leaning over the garden wall, playing on a pipe and singing, all summer-of-love like or, as the play would have it, Pan- like.

Currently in the house is Jan, a young Czech academic who's going home to greet the Prague spring, carrying with him a boxful of the rock albums he's come to love. When the Russian tanks remove Dubcek and restore repression, Jan remains seemingly uncommitted. His musical and personal idols are the Plastics, whom the regime detests not for what they say but for what they are: nonconformity personified. ("They're not heretics," Jan explains, "they're pagans.")

Jan, like other Stoppard protagonists, is sceptical of explicit commitment, which he interprets as an outlet for personal neurosis; he won't sign Havel's Charter 77. He still gets into trouble, and though the police don't bother to break him, they do break his record collection. Again, like other Stoppard protagonists (and probably Stoppard himself ) he changes his mind; takes a kind of stand. And, in a neat pincer movement, a more vociferous friend comes to admit that there is merit in Jan's idea of pure Plastic rebellion.

Rufus Sewell, from the London cast, plays Jan's mercurial qualities to the point, in the earlier scenes, of irritating whimsicality. But he's always attuned to what the character thinks and feels, and as both his manner and his hairstyle become increasingly and enforcedly sober, he grows, as he should, almost out of recognition. (His London successor was Dominic West, from The Wire; that I would like to have seen.)

The Czech scenes in fact are almost completely successful, especially in making us believe just how important the music was to these people, on every level. That theme is less convincing in the English scenes which can never make rock seem more than -- what in fact it probably was -- a pseudo-political indulgence.

Not that the music itself, which we hear in clips between the scenes, doesn't sound good; it's just that it doesn't connect with the characters. Head of the Cambridge household is Max, a fiftyish (when the play starts) professor who's a sorrowfully unreconstructed Stalinist. ("I speak," he says, "as one who's kicked in the guts by nine-tenths of anything you can tell me about Soviet Russia.") For him, the Czech Revolution is a frivolous sideshow, and Jan -- once his favourite student --a terrible letdown.

I can't imagine that Stoppard has much intellectual sympathy with Max, but he's given him some powerful speeches, especially about the way in which Russia becomes everyone's conscience-salving Aunt Sally. Max's wife, Eleanor, is a classics-teacher dying of cancer, and insistent on making her husband realize that his love for her is something that transcends materialism, dialectical or otherwise.

Two more fine British imports, Brian Cox and Sinead Cusack, play these roles very affectingly (Cusack doubles as Max's grown-up daughter who's also Jan's ultimate love-interest), but they can't make their part of the play coalesce with the other as anything more than theory. The point must be that emotions and beliefs have to inform one another, and that we are all capable of infinite self- deception about this, but the various romantic involvements don't really involve. Most Stoppard plays are about love and politics. In The Real Thing, the love elbowed the politics off the stage. Here it's the reverse.

There are also fewer laughs than in almost any other Stoppard play, though the text suggests that quite a few jokes have gone missing in the nads, or on the lips, of an American supporting cast obliged to speak with English accents even when they're playing Czechs.

Trevor Nunn's production can be surprisingly halting, with the actors -- including the leads -- prone to suggesting passionate conviction by addressing their companions as if they were slightly deaf. There are echoes here of many other Stoppard plays: Nothing wrong with that, but neither does it make the play -- what some British critics have proclaimed it -- his summarizing masterpiece.

Rather, it's an uneven play that no one else could have written and that at its best is very fine. I look forward to a Canadian production with, say, Joseph Ziegler, Lucy Peacock and Michael Therriault.

The piece ends with the characters, or some of them, joyfully attending a 1990 concert by the Rolling Stones, who've previously been hardly mentioned: Too bad it couldn't have been the Floyd or the Plastics, but history decreed otherwise. It's a good curtain, but it isn't a synthesis. It leaves too much out. - Rock 'n' Roll is at the Bernard B. Jacobs Theatre, New York City. For tickets call 212-239-6200 or 1-800-432-7250 outside New York.

2008-03-01-for-nanking-and-country-marjo:
In 1937, some 300,000 civilians in what was then the capital of China were killed, and some 80,000 women violated, by the invading Japanese army. This atrocity, or collection of atrocities, is less notorious than it should be, but to the extent that it is known, its known as the Rape of Nanking. This circumstance alone suggests that the fate of the women has not been ignored in comparison with the whole, but the central character of Marjorie Chan's play a nanking winter is convinced that it has.

More precisely, she is the central character of the play's first half. a nanking winter ("title is all lowercase says the publicity -- why?) is divided into two ill-fitting sections. The first concerns Irene, a present-day Chinese-American woman whose book on the massacre is about to be published. She is based on Iris Chang whose The Rape of Nanking is the best-known volume on the subject and who subsequently committed suicide. Irene is herself subject to fits of depression, during one of which she was hospitalized; while she was away, her publishers, with the consent of her husband, took it upon themselves to change her title from The Nanking Holocaust to the supposedly more reader-friendly The Nanking Incident. This would make it the only known example of a sales-hungry publisher opting to make a title less sensational.

Irene is understandably angry about this, and she takes her anger out on everyone around her. She has an especially unlovable habit of putting words into other peoples mouths and then blaming them for it. She plays this trick most notably on her husband, who, for the sake of rhetorical effect, is himself a Japanese-American man whose grandfather may possibly have been among the perpetrators. She also gets mad at her younger sister, who, admittedly, is annoyingly perky, and, of course, with her editor and the firms lawyer.

All present are at least agreed that that a suggested compromise title, Nanking: The Other Holocaust, would have represented the worst of all worlds, implicitly downgrading Armenia, Rwanda and others too heart-breakingly numerous to mention. But the idea that the term holocaust" is, so to speak, already taken, sparks another tirade from Irene. "All right she yells, let's talk about the Jews." However, when she starts doing just that, she comes up with something both interesting and unexpected. It turns out that the man who tried hardest to protect the Nanking victims was German; not only that, he was China's ranking Nazi. He reported back to Hitler on the open slaughter, convinced that the Fuhrer would be shocked and would protest. The result, apparently, was merely to convince the regime that its own genocide had better be carried out, as far as possible, in secret.

Chans first act tries to fuse domestic drama with polemic, succeeding with neither. We then move, via a transition that struck me as both cheap and inept, backwards in time and outwards in scope. We are in Nanking, in a convent thats serving as a refuge for a remnant of the Chinese and that's seeking official Japanese recognition as a secure zone. It's run by an American sister, whose ally is the good Nazi, Niklas Hermann. (The historical names have been changed.) The action takes in the rendition, through trickery, of 200 female refugees to serve as "comfort women.

The five actors from the first part play more or less corresponding roles in the second, but it would take far more imaginative writing and direction than we get here for so small a number to evoke horrors so huge. The script reduces the events to prison-camp melodrama, and Ruth Madoc-Jones production (for Nightwood Theatre) falls back, both at home and abroad, on unmotivated emoting. Grace Lynn King and Ella Chan, who play Irene and her sister, reappear as two young Chinese women both named Mei, randomly selected by their author to stand in for thousands. King gets to play a suicide for one half of the evening and a survivor for the other, and her fate seems equally arbitrary both times. Brooke Johnson flails as both the publisher and the nun; Leon Aureus reduces the various Japanese characters to a row of apologetic zeroes. Stephen Russell comes off best, as Niklas, but then hes playing the most compelling character, the play's equivalent of Oskar Schindler or Paul Rusesabegina. Being neither villain nor victim, he has some freedom of choice. Besides, the good German" always attracts sympathy: not, I think, because we're all secret Fascists, but because we like to believe in the possibility of redemption. Not that this one seems to have had much to be redeemed from; he was thousands of miles from home when his countrymens excesses began and, we are told, was speedily singled out by the Gestapo when he returned. But after Irenes revelations about him in Act 1, we view his actions in Act 2 through a doubly tragic lens. We can practically hear his masters picking up unwitting tips from his reports, and can see him being plunged from one catastrophe into another. This may be my own ethnicity speaking, but the play is more successful at suggesting the nightmare yet to come than it is at evoking the one that is supposed to be its subject.

- a nanking winter runs through March 16 at the Factory Theatre. Call 416-504-9971 for details.

2008-03-04-not-so-big-a-winner-oprah-s-n:
Oprah Winfrey is on the phone, asking if she may speak to Kim, please. Happily, Kim is at home, able to take the call. She is overcome ("I can't believe this!") to hear that Oprah her very self is on the line. She is practically delirious when she learns that she has been chosen as one of the contestants on the new charity game show, Oprah's Big Give. Isn't it lucky that the TV cameras just happened to be there in Kim's living room?

There is a lot to hate about Oprah's Big Give but the hysterically faked spontaneity of that early exchange is as good a way as any of conveying the tone. Kim is among 10 people selected to compete in the matter of giving away some of Oprah's money. (Well, let's assume it's Oprah's money.)

We were never told on Sunday's opening show whether the 10 had undergone a rigorous screening process or whether their names had been picked out of a hat. But it seems likely that they were chosen on a mix of throb-appeal and sob-appeal; they included Cameron, 22, "dot-com millionaire;" Brandi, 23, pageant queen but still equipped to empathize with the less fortunate ("I've had girls sabotage my efforts to win"); Rachael, 32, singer-actress, and a reality show natural ("I experienced physical and sexual abuse"); and Carlana, 38, TV producer and paraplegic.

They were sent out into Los Angeles, in teams of two, to raise money for deserving cases. Their efforts were monitored, and at the end of the show they were assessed by three -- I think we're supposed to call them "celebrity judges": a footballer, Chris Rock's wife and Jamie Oliver.

Their job, as on any "reality" elimination show, is to thin the ranks, week by week. Also on hand, again as in any such contest, is a breathless host, Nate Berkus, to tell us at the show's half-hour mark that the big givers were now "halfway through the challenge of changing someone's life."

His commentary tended to blend into the announcements ("coming up -- the pressure is on!") designed to hold us through the commercial breaks. And, sparing in her personal appearances but spiritually present, is the fairy godmother herself, who has done some good in her time but has turned into a caricature of gush: "This is a show designed after my own heart -- the biggest giver becomes the biggest winner." Because -- something of which the competitors were apparently not apprised until the very end -- the judges' ultimate favourite gets a US$1-million prize, which may or may not be more than he or she has raised in the course of the series. So much for virtue being its own reward.

With all these levels of personality involved, it was hard to concentrate on the actual charitable objects. We and the cameras raced back and forth between the widow of a murdered man, now facing the loss of her house; the mother of a Down syndrome child who herself is running a disability centre; a destitute Iraq war vet; and an idealistic young doctor carrying US$200,000 of student debt.

They all merged into one, especially as the focus was less on their problems than on those of their instant teams of caregivers. They too were confusing, not to say confused: one pair got lost on the road, earning them much eventual scorn from the judges.

They all succeeded in raising something: from friends, neighbours and the occasional well-primed corporation or approachable movie-star. (Make Target your target! Jamie, generous like a Foxx!) And the recipients were tearfully the better for it.

That much, I guess, is a good thing. And, intentionally or not, the show does reflect some painful truths. Charity is a competitive sport; in real life, the various organizations have to compete for our compassion, and they have the advertising and the fundraisers to prove it.

It also prompts questions. What happens to all the deserving American cases who don't happen to have attracted the attention of Oprah's researchers? What kind of society makes compassion dependent on the whims of millionaire entertainers? Why is there no safety net? Why, to take the most obvious example from Big Give's big opening, have the country and its army abdicated responsibility for the soldiers of whom they profess to be so proud? Jamie Oliver asked the couple on that case why they hadn't thought of calling in the marines. He may have had more of a point than he knew.

Of course, the show itself never grapples with these questions. It's too concerned with being an American Idol for charity-volunteers, with Oliver shaping up as a nice man's Simon Cowell.

In fact, it's worse; the more unfortunate contestants on Idol are embarrassing nobody but themselves, but Big Give makes a feel-good spectacle out of other people's poverty and bereavement. The judges' favourite moment, they told us, was of children sending balloons up to heaven with a message for their dad. The inspirational music barely stopped, though it was amusing that one of the background songs told us to "be careful what you wish for." Someone may be fired for that piece of irony.

As an extra touch of mild sadism, the contestants were judged not as pairs but as individuals, so everyone would know who'd let down the team. Just one person was let go this week, her identity of course kept secret until all the others had opened their envelopes and found plane tickets inside. So, the loser was expected to walk home?

Being America, there has to be a loser; otherwise, we'd never know about the winners. They're a generous people all right; in so merciless a society, they'd better be.

- Oprah's Big Give airs Sundays at 9 p.m. ET on CTV.

2008-03-06-by-any-other-name-she-s-still:
CYRANO DE BERGERAC

Festival Theatre, Stratford, Ont.

---

Edmond Rostand's Cyrano de Bergerac, the most celebrated romantic drama in the world repertoire, is also its most elaborate hard-luck story. Maybe that's the same thing.

Think about it. We have a swashbuckling hero, possessed of all the talents both martial and intellectual, but robbed of any confidence with women by his self-consciousness about his preternaturally long nose. He falls in love, dares for a moment to hope, finds that the lady has already fallen for a pretty young dunderhead and contrives to lend his rival his own eloquence in a kind of vicarious courtship. It works, until the rival realizes that the lady, brainy on her own account, is more smitten with his borrowed wit than with his native good looks. He resolves to do the decent thing and tell all, but is struck down in battle before he has the chance, leaving our hero, no less honourable, feeling morally prohibited from disillusioning his beloved. She does eventually work it out, but only after Cyrano has undergone a further 15 years of selfless devotion. And then it's too late because he's dying, struck down by a cowardly assassin. (Nobody ever fought him face-to-face and survived.) Rostand twists every possible knife; his Cyrano even finds time to remember, at death's door, that his mother had been too revolted by his ugliness to show him any kindness. It taps directly into everybody's store of erotic self-pity, and achieves a kind of greatness in doing so.

That isn't all it does. It's as funny as it is sad, with Cyrano's verbal gymnastics, brilliantly rendered in Anthony Burgess' translation, keeping pace with his virtuoso swordsmanship. This is a man who insults an enemy to death, composing a perfectly-rhymed ballad about him while they fight a duel; "when the poem ends, I hit," he promises, and delivers. He's also a free spirit, as feared a satirist as a soldier. He's an actual French figure from the 17th-century, raised to fantasy level by a writer from the 19th. Colm Feore, returning to a role he played at Stratford a decade and a half ago, is in command of every mood; his sword flashes, his wit stings and his energy seems inexhaustible. He reaches a kind of apotheosis in the play's seriocomic balcony scene; Cyrano, in a weird mixture of masochism and authorial pride, pushes aside ( "this is getting difficult") his handsome mouthpiece and pours out his own words, with no hope of reaping the benefit. Pathos mixed like this suits him better than pathos unadorned; his death scene brought a passing lump to my throat, but it didn't have me weeping the expected buckets.

For once, though, Cyrano has to share the emotional load. I called Christian, his unsuspecting competitor, a dunderhead, but I didn't mean it. Mike Shara, in a revelatory performance, gives him not only the customary good looks and good intentions, but sensitivity and even a brain; he may lack the gift of Gascon gab (Cyrano and his fellow cadets are countrymen of Alexandre Dumas' D'Artagnan, who puts in a token appearance) but he has a blunter kind of wit, and a poignant awareness of when he's been beaten. The play's a self-sacrifice contest, and Christian's less elaborate renunciation proves at least as moving as Cyrano's.

The production, by the star's wife, Donna Feore, gets off to a mystifying start with a small modern boy (played by their son) trying on a cadet's costume. As a framing device, it's unnecessary, and anyway never appears again. Once that's over, Mrs. Feore surrounds Mr. Feore with an excellent staging that gets the Festival platform swirling with action, as you might expect from an expert choreographer, but also fills it with intelligence. She shows you where to look and gives you things worth looking at and listening to. She only misreads one moment, when she has Wayne Best, otherwise admirable as the protagonist's friend Le Bret, shout his sympathy over Cyrano's rejection by the adored Roxane rather than confide it. Amanda Lisman, as the lady in question, simpers more than a bluestocking should, and their common enemy de Guiche is a more complex figure than the pantomime villain supplied by John Vickery. But there are some very nice small performances: Douglas E. Hughes as a drunken versifier; Robert Persichini doubling as a ham actor whom Cyrano drives from the stage and as the Gascons' commanding officer; Martha Farrell as a refreshment vendor whose adoration would strike Cyrano in a heap if only he could see beyond his nose. John Stead has arranged a fine duel and a great battle. Occasional passages are spoken in the original French, which may not be strictly logical, but is no less so than Shakespeare's anglophone Julius Caesar expiring with Latin on his lips. Besides, Burgess himself admitted that there could be no English translation for Cyrano's own dying word which is, and remains, panache. Which is also a fair summary of the whole show. - Cyrano de Bergerac is in repertory through Nov. 1. Call 1-800-567-1600 or visit stratfordfestival.cafor tickets and information.

2008-03-06-the-next-generation-of-angry-:
Three years ago, the young British director Rupert Goold and the somewhat older British actor Patrick Stewart collaborated on a magnificent production of The Tempest, set in the Antarctic. They have now reunited for a Macbeth set in what appears to be a refectory doubling as an abattoir. This is less magnificent but is still exciting.

The production started in England at the Chichester Festival, then played London's West End, is now at New York's Brooklyn Academy of Music and will shortly transfer to Broadway. It has more loose ends than The Tempest, whose frozen-island landscape found a logical place for every character, new castaways and long-term residents alike.

The ideas and the people in this Macbeth don't all sit together as well. The Scotland of this production is a fascist state, as witnessed by much video footage of goose-stepping troops. It's also a hereditary monarchy, though that seems to be a controversial innovation.

When King Duncan formally announces that his son Malcolm will be his heir, he sets off a murderous reaction in Macbeth who, fresh from the witches' prophecies, thinks the crown will be his. Goold, whose direction can be as masterful with small details as with big images, marks the moment superbly, and so does Stewart. His Macbeth is a Junker among the aristocrats, a professional soldier never quite sure where he stands with all the smooth civilians.

He's a divided man in another sense, the seemingly bluff warrior whose imagination keeps taking him by terrible surprise. Initially, the production signals this by changing the lights whenever its protagonist starts soliloquizing.

Later, when his scruples have been overcome but his terrors haven't, the gulf between himself and everybody else is still more boldly signalled. The banquet scene is staged twice, once on either side of the intermission. The first time we, like Macbeth, see Banquo's ghost; the second we, like the guests, see only a madman shouting at an empty chair.

So far, so riveting. And there are many other fine things. Lady Macbeth (Kate Fleetwood) is young and beautiful, a trophy wife with strong but limited ambition; we see what draws them together and what pushes them apart. Admittedly we get this in most productions, but this one does it with exemplary lucidity.

The scenes leading up to the murder of Duncan are brilliant; like many party hosts, this couple likes to confer and re-group in the kitchen. Later Macbeth practically takes up residence there; he briefs Banquo's murderers while preparing and then munching a sandwich -- anything to keep busy, and to remind himself why it's good to be a king.

The set is dominated by a fridge, a basin (useful for the play's hand-washing motif ) and at the back, a practical elevator with clattering gates, put to ominous use in almost every scene. The last battle is brilliantly evoked. It's made very clear that the invaders have entered Macbeth's own castle, and he has nowhere to run.

However, with so much realistic detail, we become very conscious of the parts that don't add up. Why is Banquo murdered on a train, after it's been made clear that he's gone out horseback riding? For the sake of a reverberant modern image, I guess, but the political colouring is overdone. It isn't really what the play's about (Shakespeare takes kingship for granted) and some of it is crudely laid on.

Then there are the witches. They first appear as nurses at a field hospital, attending to the Bloody Sergeant (whose speech has to be coughed and gabbled through, to justify the setting) before casually pulling the plug on him and revealing their true identities. Quite a coup, even though it means reversing the order of the first two scenes.

They then practically take up residence in Macbeth's home, as evidently in his mind. They don't just tempt him, they practically choreograph his downfall. This makes them too powerful and the hero too weak. Their cauldron scene is scampered through (wrong kind of cooking for this show) and though the trio of apparitions is cleverly done, as so many speaking corpses in a morgue, the filmed procession of Banquo's regal heirs is a mess.

Back to what is good. Macduff 's wife and children are allowed an early and charming appearance, to set up their subsequent slaughter. Macbeth himself, in another powerful departure from tradition, supervises the massacre in person. ("This deed I'll do," he says, and does it.)

The bereaved Macduff is finely played by Michael Feast, who holds the longest of pauses before responding to the intolerable news; the director was brave to put this in, and the actor, who makes it seem like the only possible reaction, justifies the courage.

Ross (Tim Treloar), who brings the bad tidings, is played as a well-meaning civil servant, terrorized by Macbeth's interrogators and guilty about it. And dominating everything is Stewart, whose jovial public face becomes that of an increasingly coarse and sadistic joker -- he hates the men he has to humour -- while his insides crumble.

He's Stalin with an inner life. He doesn't take you as deep inside the cankered mind as did Ian McKellen, the only great Macbeth I've ever seen. (Though older audiences compared him unfavourably to Olivier. These things depend on where you came in.) But it's an eloquent, unflinching performance in which every moment is freshly thought and every thought communicated.

It may be short on grandeur but it's long on truth. - Macbeth is at the Brooklyn Academy of Music until March 22. The show re-opens at the Lyceum Theatre in New York on April 8.

2008-03-07-at-least-the-fourth-wall-does:
THEATRE REVIEW

Democracy

Tarragon Theatre, Toronto

West Germany, under the 1970s chancellorship of Willy Brandt, is considering rapprochement with East Germany. A member of Brandt's cabinet wonders aloud whether "these new friends" can be trusted. A minor functionary in the government office, one Gunter Guillaume, is asked his opinion. "Half of me," he replies, "wants to say one thing. Half of me wants to say another." Brandt himself observes that that is "the position of the electorate as a whole on almost everything."

Democracy, the title of Michael Frayn's play about Brandt's rise and fall, is also its governing metaphor. It's about balancing contradictions: within states, within governments, within individuals. Half of me wants to say that it's a subtle examination of the political process and the people within it; the other half has to acknowledge that the production actually on view at the Tarragon is amazingly dull.

It's amazing because Frayn is a humane, witty and unpretentiously intelligent writer, skeptical without being cynical. He's also a self-aware craftsman constantly setting himself technical challenges and usually solving them, whether he's writing a farce about a farce ( Noises Off) or making discussions about nuclear fission dramatic ( Copenhagen). Democracy works on three levels: as a psychological study, a political intrigue drama and a spy story.

Gunter Guillaume has good reason for his confessed ambivalence; he's been sent from the East to worm his way into the chancellor's confidence. He succeeds, though without ever making Brandt like him -- the reverse, if anything. He himself, though, comes to practically worship the worldly, witty, charismatic Brandt, a condition he shares with a large proportion of the population. Guillaume is altogether an unusually benign kind of spy; if Brandt's intentions towards East Germany are truly positive, then East Germany is interested. Guillaume's job is not so much to undermine his quarry as to shore him up. Ironically, it's the detection of Guillaume's identity -- by a remarkably clumsy Secret Service -- that contributes to Brandt's eventual unseating. The wall, as we know, will come down anyway, the glory going not to Willy but to his less lovable successor Helmut Schmidt.

Much of the play is seen through Guillaume's eyes: When he isn't reporting back to his control, he's giving us one-sentence updates on his state of mind (the two conventions are sometimes hard to tell apart). Here, I think, Frayn falls into the same trap that ensnared him in an earlier play, Benefactors, in which the characters were always compelled to tell us what they felt. This compulsion to tell rather

than show destroyed Benefactors, and it damages Democracy. You keep wondering when the real play is going to start. Frayn was a novelist before he was a playwright, and both these plays read better than they act. At least, Democracy reads better than it acts in Toronto.

I was struck at first by the pace of Richard Rose's production; then I realized that what we were offered was not pace but mere speed. Complicated speeches are rattled off at an impressive lick by actors who seem to know what they're talking about, but after a while it all blurs together. This is a play that keeps cutting not just from one scene to another, but from one mode to another and there is no weight to any of them and no distinction between them. Visually, it's dispiriting: Guillaume describes his new workplace at the Palais Schaumburg as "a 19th-century ironmaster's dream of the aristocratic life," but it looks here as if he might have well have stayed home. Charlotte Dean's set is an arrangement of drab office furniture, which consigns some vital scenes to cramped quarters at the back of the stage. What really does the show in, though, is the casting. The Willy Brandt one remembers from newsreels was a fleshy, smiling charmer. R.H. Thomson's Brandt is as gaunt and dour as his surroundings. This isn't just a matter of reproducing history; the play itself keeps insisting on Brandt's humour, his knack for playing the crowd and his surface warmth. It also shows that there was darkness beneath: Brandt's rootless refugee past, his feeling of being unfathered, his doubts on just about everything. But there's no interest in penetrating beneath the mask when there's no mask.

It's Brandt's loneliness that helps draw Guillaume to him -- the two men turn out to have discontents in common (they're both in dried-up marriages for one thing, though Willy naturally had more access to consolation than Gunther). Guillaume seems to have been the kind of sad spy patented by John Le Carre -- he certainly comes in from the cold, without ever feeling at home in the warm. Alon Nashman gets Guillaume's plaintive externals right but can't ring many changes on the inner man. He doesn't grow on the job. With so little tension between the two central figures, the play becomes an affair of undifferentiated minor guys scurrying around in suits, hatching plots.

Graham Harley is the best of them, as a dedicated hack who's painlessly converted from Communism to Catholicism. With his English accent and air of spiritual dandruff, he might be on loan from Old Labour. Alex Poch-Goldin has the featureless and therefore thankless role of the German Democratic Republic spy-master who spends the play sitting at a cafe table downstage left receiving confidences. This points to the play's biggest technical problem: It wants to be fluidly impressionistic and massively specific. Half of me blames the production for not solving it. The other half thinks it's insoluble.

- Democracy runs through April 6 at the Tarragon Theatre, call 416-531-1827 for more information.

2008-03-08-the-passion-of-powell-david-h:
David Hare's Stuff Happens is a historical play about the Iraq War in which none of the characters is Iraqi. Well, almost none: There are a few words from Saddam Hussein mouthpieces early on, and there's an epilogue, a powerful one, in which an exile laments the crucifying of his country both under Saddam and under the Americans. Our only fault, he says, was not taking control of our own destiny. How that would have been achieved, he doesn't say. After all, he himself had to leave.

This is the last of a series of chorus-like speeches that dot the play. An early one, delivered by someone identified as Angry Journalist, says that a dictator was removed, and that arguing about the characters or motives of those who removed him is moralizing self-indulgence. Palestinian Academic chimes in halfway through to claim that the invasion was a sideshow, designed to deflect attention from the Middle East. These declarations stand starkly in the play, though the main action hardly engages with them. In a way, it embodies the worst suspicions of Iraqi Exile, Angry Journalist and Palestinian Academic. It's a racy account of the build-up to war, and of the manoeuvrings within and between the American and British governments. The last thing anybody has on their minds, or at least on their tongues, is the fates and wishes of the people on the ground.

This queasy vacuum is both the play's strength and its weakness. It may be Hare's liveliest play, one in which the characters don't just discuss politics but do them, and in which the story and characters come ready-made. The words, for the most part, don't; there are some direct quotes from documented speeches, but most of the dialogue is what the author himself has described as guesswork. It's very persuasive guesswork, as we eavesdrop on what may have gone on behind closed doors with the Bush and Blair cabinets and at the United Nations. Some of it undoubtedly improves on the original. (Colin Powell knows Iraq once had weapons because "we still have the receipts.") And even the recognized sound bites gain from being heard in a context. We get the whole of the Donald Rumsfeld response to looting from which the play takes its title. That doesn't make his words any more endearing, but it does make them less cavalier.

The play's thrust is that Bush and his closest advisors ducked and wove and stonewalled all qualms and disagreements, in order to pursue a course on which they had been set since 9/11--earlier, in Dick Cheney's case. This is unlikely to be news to anyone, but it's vigorously presented with a genuine sense of cut-and-thrust. There's a climactic White House meeting in which the gloves come off, and Cheney roams the room, expressing his contempt for conscientious objectors in general and Tony Blair in particular. It's capped by a shorter, more rueful scene in London where Blair's advisors tell him that power doesn't need to do deals; it just is.

The gathering sense of power, unanswerable and unanswering, is palpable in Joel Greenberg's production for his Studio 180 company. It goes at a driving but lucid pace, is shrewdly cast and well--in many cases, superbly -- acted. Fifteen actors, initially confronting us from three rows of mobile office chairs, play upwards of 70 roles. Half a dozen get a part apiece. If there's a centre, it's Nigel Shawn Williams' warm, troubled Secretary of State. Indeed, the play is largely The Passion of Powell. He's presented, with some simplification, as the unceasing voice of conscience and prudence, increasingly isolated by his colleagues (in one of the best scenes, he sits miserable and silent while they all join in Amazing Grace) and then outfoxed by his hoped-for allies at the UN. The play notably sidesteps the question of just why he finally fell into line. Nor, surprisingly, does it give much weight to his or anyone else's purely tactical misgivings concerning the invasion and its aftermath. (Which, if heeded, might conceivably have granted Iraqi Exile both sets of wishes.)

He's up against a trio of bullies and a couple of sphinxes. David Fox gives a wonderful account of Rumsfeld as a pedantic serpent, lost in contemplation of his own rhetoric; Hardee T. Lineham's Cheney is all withering vitriol, with the voice and stance of an assault-weapon; and Neil Foster weighs in as Wolfowitz. Yanna McIntosh's Condoleezza Rice, to whom I had greatly looked forward, is the nearest thing to a disappointment; this Condi plays her cards so close to the chest as to leave the actress almost nothing to do. Barry Flatman jumps into the front rank of Dubya doubles while chilling most of the obvious laughs. He's genial and he's impassive; he leaves open the question of how cunning he might be underneath it all.

Andrew Gillies cannot escape the patches of wetness that cling to most Blair impersonators (except Michael Sheen in The Queen) he still emerges with unexpected dignity, especially in a play from the British left. Indeed, it goes easy on him; the WMD dossier is eagerly mentioned, and then completely forgotten. (David Kelly is a no-show.) Among the multi-taskers, there's ear-catching work from Sarah Orenstein, Paul Essiembre, Sam Kalileh and Guy Bannerman.

The play essentially ends with the president's drop-in victory speech: the only scene actually set in Iraq. Ahead and unmentioned lie Abu Ghraib, the insurgency and the prospect of civil war. It's after we've all gone home that the worst stuff happens.

- Stuff Happens runs at the Berkeley Street Theatre Downstairs until March 29. Call 416-368-3110 for more information.

For a show that prides itself on being tough, The Wire has had an extraordinary knack for making its viewers cry. That quality wasn't too much in evidence in Sunday night's concluding episode: a bumper-length tying-up of loose ends --or to put it with appropriate grandeur -- arranging of destinies. But it was going full blast the previous week, one in which the emotional focus was on the Baltimore corner-kids who have been tugging at our consciences and our tear ducts for the last two of the show's five years. That episode ended with Michael on the run and Dukie disappearing into the crackhouse that from now on he would have to call home.

Before breaking our hearts, that same episode had made them race faster by showing us the mass arrest of the Marlo Stanfield crew, finally secured by the indefatigable sleuths of the Major Crimes Unit. It was the march of the good guys: a rare occurrence on The Wire and one that any other show would have saved for the finale. On this one we knew it couldn't last. And sure enough, the following week, corruption and face-saving at every level meant that the case crumbled.

I wonder if The Wire may come to be known as the Show of Great Penultimates. It has consistently reached its peak in the last-but-one week of each season: I think, for example, of the second season, the one that centred on the docks, with Frank Sobotka, the flawed but decent union leader, literally marching to his doom at the hands of the drug lords.

It's either fitting or ironic, take your choice, that the one season that defied that rule was itself the one before last. The magnificent fourth season-- the one that focused on the inner-city schools -- did have a wonderful penultimate episode, but it had an even better ultimate one, a rain of emotional hammer-blows that may be the most powerful hour of television drama ever. (When it was over, one just sat there, drained and shattered.)

What hit the hardest was the fate of Randy, the most easily likeable of the four central kids, driven by desperation to reveal his knowledge of a murder and branded a snitch forever after. We left him after he'd fallen through the system, consigned to a group home from which he stood a very good chance of emerging dead. The Wire has been very good at keeping track of past characters, if only in the briefest of cameos, but unless I missed something it has never been able to bring itself to tell us what became of Randy.

David Simon, The Wire's creator, is fond of likening his show to Greek tragedy in the sense that all its characters are trapped by fate, which in their case is Baltimore's decayed municipal system, itself an especially stark microcosm of modern America. He compares it to The Sopranos (The Wire's only peer) which he calls Shakespearean, in the sense that its people have free will.

There's something in that, though the contrast between the two theatrical forms isn't watertight and there's quite a lot of overlap between the two TV shows. Tony Soprano is a figure of Falstaffian amplitude (in more senses than one) but he's still trapped in his own inheritance. And there are at least one and a half characters in The Wire who aren't controlled by their environment.

The one is Omar, the freelance who makes his living by robbing the organized dealers; he is what he is, with his own code (completely ruthless with other criminals, he's "never hurt a taxpayer"), and he makes no excuses. He's also the greatest of the show's many wits; its comic highlight was the trial scene in which he informed a crooked lawyer that they were both in the same business.

The half is Jimmy McNulty, the rebellious cop, whose demons are his own, even though they're let loose by his frustration with the department in which he works. You can't, to make the most obvious Sopranos comparison, imagine any character in The Wire going to a shrink, but if they did, Jimmy, the most tormentedly self-aware, would be the best candidate. A mock-tragic hero, he received the fitting finale tribute of a fake wake.

I called Jimmy a cop. Nobody on the show does. For them, whether they're inside or outside the law, the word is always "police." The way they pronounce it with the accent often on the first syllable, it takes on mythological resonance. The highest compliment the force can bestow on one of its own is to say that he --or she-- was "good police."

This isn't always the same as what Bubbles, the recovered (hooray) addict, would call "good people," but there's a rough correlation. They exist at all ranks, but they become rarer the higher up you go; idealists like Cedric Daniels (upstanding even when sitting down), or even practical reformers like the twice-bitten Bunny Colvin, don't survive. Compromise pays, and outright malignity often takes the jackpot.

The pattern has been repeated at every interconnected level the show has explored: the docks, City Hall, the schools, the press. The last of these, by common consent, has been the show's weakest link; the characters, so morally complex at every other point, are here reduced to good guys, bad guys and nonentities. Even worse, the stated theme -- that society gets worse because the media had given up on in-depth reportage --is only stated, never felt.

We never believed that anything would be different if the Baltimore Sun (Simon's old employer and at least magnanimous enough to let its name be used) had higher standards. It was never, as everything else on the show has been, a life-and-death issue. It has made this last season the least good of the five.

It was also threatened by what seemed to be a classic case of shark-jumping: McNulty's invention of a serial killer in order to get back the slashed funds for Major Crimes. However, this justified itself in the end when the scheme unravelled and we saw everybody running for cover, the charge headed by the mayor who had won office on a program of "change" in which he at least seemed to believe. (A white politician in a black city, he sometimes seemed like a photo-negative Barack Obama.)

The only change we actually saw was life getting more brutal; on the streets, the Barksdales, who had family loyalty and some recognition of honour ("he a man," said Avon Barksdale when Cutty, the former "soldier," walked out of the life) gave place to Marlo, young sociopath, and he in turn to some brawling subalterns. Rawls, the consummate police politician, went on to state-capital glory; Major Valchek, prick of pricks, became commissioner. There were also a few redemptions: Bubbles, Cutty, Prez, who went from hopeless cop to hope-inspiring teacher, Carver who stayed in the force and was increasingly impressive. Bodie, his opposite number on the street, went down but at least went down fighting. And some people, like Bunk and Kima, just went decently on, which is a kind of redemption.

Mayor Carcetti and Dukie had never heard of one another, but every decision the former took, or failed to take, helped doom the latter. It's one thing to have that inclusive vision (a truly Dickensian one, incidentally); it's another to flesh it out as triumphantly and consistently as The Wire has. It hasn't had a lame episode, and The Sopranos, though still my hairsbreadth favourite, had a few.

Anyway, they're the twin peaks (ha) of American television. One final comparison: The Sopranos ended as abruptly as it did because it was about individual characters, and it had told us all it knew. The Wire ended with montage because it was about a world, which goes on and replicates itself. I haven't mentioned the acting. That would take another article, and it would be rhapsodic.

2008-03-12-very-much-actually:
Soulpepper's first Shakespeare production, eight years ago, was Twelfth Night, directed by Albert Schultz, in which experienced actors played the below-stairs characters and young and untried ones handled the love interest. It didn't work out too well; the older players stole the show, not just because of their greater experience but because the text itself handed them the opportunity. The same tactic is tried in the company's new As You Like It, again directed by Schultz, with far happier results. Some weathered stalwarts have supporting roles, and they are great, but the burden in this play has to fall on the young ones -- in this case the first generation of Soulpepper's academy -- and they shoulder it with considerable sensitivity and contagiously high spirits.

The opening orchard scene finds the actors gathering apples. There are more apples when the play moves to the Forest of Arden; the banished lords, pastoral exiles, get to munch them. An As You Like It with apples is a conventional As You Like It, and so this production proves. Costumed in non-specific modern dress, and with the various songs set as bluegrass, it takes the play pretty much as it comes. But then so, I suspect, did its author, who knew from themes -- in this case the realities and illusions of romantic love--but not from concepts. The pastoral convention, contrasting the suspect sophistication of the court with the supposed simplicities of the country, is a convention, not a subject. The play uses it, but is not about it. A production could make more of it than this one does, but it doesn't have to. The important thing is that the words and the action should be intelligible and they should be entertaining, and this show scores highly on both counts.

The junior players tend to turn the verse into sing-song; this is a shame, but it isn't a calamity, considering how much of the play -- and how much of the best of it -- is in prose. This includes the great mock-wooing scene in which Rosalind, in man's disguise, instructs her unknowing lover Orlando in the real facts of life ("men have died from time to time and worms have eaten them, but not for love"), all the while falling deeper and deeper herself. Sarah Wilson, a tall and tart Rosalind, gets the balance very well, though she's stronger on the disillusion than the illusion. She grows steadily through the play -- she's especially good at telling off the spoiled shepherdess Phoebe -- and by the end is the enchantress she should be; she earns the right to speak the epilogue. (Wilson is the only actor I know of to have passed through both the Stratford Conservatory and the Soulpepper Academy; she should be exceptionally well-schooled.)

Michael Blake's Orlando has presence and a welcome degree of humour. His big, bad brother Oliver, traditionally an unrewarding role, is exceptionally well played by Mike Ross, who makes a forceful jealous villain with a streak of self-doubt that lets him mature into a suitable suitor when it's time for him, too, to be paired off. As if this weren't enough, he's also the production's excellent musical director and plays the singing lord Amiens, a double role that involves him in some bemusingly quick changes. Jennifer Villaverde's Celia overdoes the pertness, likewise Amy Rutherford's Phoebe, though she at least is able to turn it to self-satire; Krystin Pellerin's Audrey is, blessedly, a bucolic country wench who's funny without a hint of caricature. Kevin MacDonald is affectingly vulnerable as the love-struck Silvius; Stephen Guy-McGrath is excellent as his older buddy Corin, bringing off another unrecognizable double as Charles, a wrestler who's here done up in full professional gear. His bout with Orlando is

very entertainingly done, both of them playing shamelessly to the on-stage audience. Equally well done, in a different vein, is the late quartet for unaccompanied voices on the meaning of love: "Like the howling of Irish wolves against the moon," says Rosalind, typically but not quite accurately, especially as she's part of it herself. Another young Academician, Lorenzo Savoini, has designed the set, which has elegant pillars (town) turning to spindly trees (country). Nice, though I wondered about the two red rocks lurking at the back of the forest. Sandstone?

As for the seniors, Diego Matamoros offers (can you bear to hear this?) another superb performance of the melancholy Jacques, a professed outsider who yet demands to be the the centre of attention:He graphically acts out the Seven Ages of Man, and also display an uncommon ambition -- in this role, anyway -- to be a rock star. Oliver Dennis's Touchstone, the more professional clown, is a dry and sparkling put-down artist; he also, reminding us of his Lucky in Waiting for Godot, has to carry a lot of baggage, literally. Michael Hanrahan is an urbane usurper apt to turn dangerously nasty. William Webster, though the halest stage octogenarian I've ever seen (he looks as if he should be carrying Orlando on his back rather than vice versa) is a splendid old Adam, and reappears for the ceremonial ending as Hymen the god of marriage, a role in which he beams radiant good will-- though it's unfortunate that he has to do it from the side of the stage rather than where this character belongs, dead centre.

The production is slapdash in some of its other choices. Duke Frederick subjects Oliver to a waterboarding, that being the most topical of tortures; too much dialogue is underscored by the splashing of water or the bleating of lambs, and by both at once at one crucial point. I don't see why "the second son of old Sir Rowland" shouldn't be allowed to announce himself as such when he makes his last-minute appearance; coincidence and Shakespearean comedy are hardly strangers. But the ancestral, eye-pricking magic that lies within this play is fully released in the multiple pairings at the end. Soulpepper has yet to offer us a great Shakespeare production, but this is their best try yet. - As You Like It runs in repertory until April 19 at the Young Centre for Performing Arts, Toronto. Call 416-866-8666 for tickets and information.
