2008-03-13-teenage-deutschland:
The musical Spring Awakening would be a first-rate production of the play Spring Awakening if only the songs didn't keep getting in the way. This isn't an example, like My Fair Lady, of an adaptation subtly tweaking its original, and coming up with something different but related. It's a case of two styles and periods at war with one another. The fact that this was plainly the intention doesn't make the result any more satisfying.

The play was written in 1891 by Frank Wedekind, at the beginning of a literary career as one of Germany's most reverberant iconoclasts; this, his first play, feels, still, like the one he owed it to himself to write. The musical is the work of Steven Sater (book and lyrics) and Duncan Sheik (music), and it has a similar urgency; it opened on Broadway in 2006 after the customary extended gestation period, was an instant sensation, and is being brought to Toronto next season by Mirvish Productions. Both concern a group of tormented adolescents in a German provincial town; their tortures are caused equally by their school curriculum, which is as narrow in scope as it is cruel in its demands, and by their sexuality, which they are not so much encouraged as forced to deny -- vainly, of course.

One girl, Wendla Bergmann, whose mother cannot bring herself to impart the biological facts, is made pregnant by Melchior Gabor, who knows more but obviously not enough. Academically, Melchior is his generation's prize student. His best friend, Moritz Stiefel, is also his polar opposite; he's the boy most oppressed by both varieties of ignorance, and he winds up committing suicide. Wendla also dies, at the hands of a backstreet abortionist procured by her mama--an event that the musical depicts with lip-smacking relish where the play is far more laconic and far more powerful.

Wedekind has been tagged, like most of his time and place, as an Expressionist, but in this play at least was more of

a hyper-realist. It's constructed in a series of short, sharp scenes, some of which retain some shock effect even now. Two scenes involve masturbation, one solitary, one group; there's a lyrical homosexual seduction as well as a fumbling hetero one. The musical's structure hews fairly closely to the play's, and is powerfully, furiously staged by Michael Mayer on a set appropriately resembling a school gymnasium.

Though the spoken script is kept strictly in period, the score is way out of it. The lyrics include references to stereos and phone calls, and -- a far deeper anachronism -- the tunes are rock. That is, a music that screams sexual know-how is applied to characters whose tragedy is that they don't have any. There's no pretence that the songs are forwarding the plot; they'reabout thekids expressing their inner drives. These don't change much over the course of the show. In fact, they boil down to two, desire and frustration. Listen to the CD, and you can't tell which character is supposed to be singing. You can tell that they're using a vocabulary, and a frame of reference, that wouldn't have been available to them. The message seems to be "this is how these adolescents would have expressed themselves if only they'd had our advantages." This is the present not so much illuminating the past as patronizing it.

There's a sense in which Wedekind asked for it; his last scene includes a Man from the Future, who persuades Melchior to follow him into the world rather than following his friend and his girlfriend into the grave. But that's just one scene, and besides, it's written with the same dark wit as the rest of the play. The musical's closing anthem, The Song of Purple Summer, makes for a flatulently sentimental subsitute.

In its own right, some of Sheik's music is lovely (the opening Mama Who Bore Me and the twice-used love song The Word of Your Body) or poundingly effective (The Bitch of Living). Sater's lyrics are the customary self-important approximations. The songs in the older rock musicals were dramatically ineffective because you couldn't hear the words; those in the newer ones are dramatically ineffective because you can. No lyricist in or out of the theatre is obliged to use rhyme, but if he is going to, then why not do it right? Why pair "idol" with "Bible" and think you're clever? The smartest Sater gets is pairing "f--ked" with "self-destruct"; that has some force to it.

One area in which the show gets fruitfully away from Broadway tradition is Bill T. Jones' choreography, which isn't graceful and fluent but awkward and restricted, as befits the environment; for once the term "knee-jerk" can be used as a compliment. The older people are sternly marginalized: first by being divided among just two actors (Kate Burton and Glenn Fleshler, both new to the cast, both good), second by not being allowed to sing except in ensembles. Most of the original kids remain, with Jonathan Groff vibrant as Melchior and Lea Michele touching as Wendla. The new misfit Moritz (Blake Bashoff ) actually fits in very nicely. As the supposed saviour of the American musical, Spring Awakening is the new Rent, which itself was hailed as the new Hair.

Each was seen as an improvement on its predecessor for dramatic sophistication, and that claim is true. Each has also been called a breakthrough in musical style, and don't you believe it. Songs that don't tell the story or develop the characters have been with us nearly as long as Wedekind's play. And did you know --I wonder if the authors of the show do -- that he was a singer-songwriter himself? - Spring Awakening runs indefinitely at the Eugene O'Neill Theater, New York City. For information call 800-432-7250.

2008-03-15-you-like-genres-we-ve-got-gen:
Marion J. Caffey is a director, choreographer and occasional author who has achieved success with a series of achingly superficial shows about popular music. He reaches some kind of nadir with 3 Mo' Divas, an evening of gold-plated copper-bottomed garbage.

It's a companion piece to his earlier 3 Mo' Tenors, which I haven't seen but which was apparently a response to the phenomenon of the original operatic Three Tenors. Caffey found those classical gentle-men's forays into the pop repertoire painfully forced, as well he might. So he rustled up three male singers with a pop grounding and an operatic range, and set them loose on all kinds of songs. 3 Mo' Divas is the female follow-up.

The rangy vocal demands necessitate two alternating casts, billed in strict no-losers-here fashion as Cast 1 and Cast A. (This brand of egalitarianism was anticipated years ago by Stephen Sondheim and Arthur Laurents, who in their musical Anyone Can Whistle divvied up a whole town into a Group A and a Group 1. They meant it, though, as satire.) I saw Cast A. I doubt if it matters much which you see, since the format is designed to stamp all the individuality out of both of them and their material, with every

song choreographed to within an inch of its death. Anyway, I saw the A team, which consists of Ramona Dunlap, Andrea Jones-Sojola and DeVonna Lawrence, all of whom have powerful and, when they're occasionally allowed to relax, pleasing voices.

They lift them first in a series of operatic arias (Puccini, Handel, Rossini, Gounod). They present these with a mildly competitive edge, flashing suspicious glances at one another out of the corners of their eyes; these displays of one-upwomanship are designed, I imagine, to reinforce the popular idea of the jealous classical diva, and to stop the audience from getting restive from all that culture. From this section, labelled Classical, they proceed to others billed as Broadway/Movies, Jazz/Blues, Soul and R & B, Soul Medley (hey, that's a lotta soul) and Spiritual/ Gospel. These ladies certainly

have chops; every opportunity to yell is enthusiastically taken and, I have to admit, enthusiastically received: White audiences seem to feel that if they scream back at black female singers who are screaming at them, they'll have soul, too.

The lowest point, provoking the loudest cheers, must be Dunlap's singing of God Bless the Child. This starts out as straight Billie Holiday impersonation, which seems pointless but is at least unobjectionable. It then lurches into wild-eyed melodrama that has nothing to do with the Holiday style or, more importantly, with the understated bitterness of the song itself. It crops up, surprisingly, not in the jazz section but under Broadway, on the grounds that it was once included in a compilation show called Bubbling Brown Sugar. Let the Good Times Roll, pure R & B, has made the same crossover, due to its originator Louis Jordan having once been the subject of the revue Five Guys Named Moe. You'd think that there were enough great Broadway and Hollywood songs in existence for this show not to have to go raiding other larders. The authentic ones they have chosen are hardly first rank: Little Shop of Horrors, the anthem from Rent about "seasons of lo-o-o-ove" and something from The Wiz. Conversely, an actual Broadway song, My Funny Valentine (let no one say that this show shies away from obvious choices) is filed under Jazz/Blues, a sequence incidentally that contains no authentic blues at all. But if jazz means originality, then Lawrence here brings off something unprecedented -- in my experience anyway -- by taking a breath between "valen" and "tine."

But then it doesn't matter what style they think they're singing: All the songs come out the same -- loud, superficial and vapid. A tribute to "Ella Fitzgerald, the first lady of scat," turns out to be a rote reproduction of Fitzgerald's famous How High the Moon routine, but stopping before it gets to the hard parts: i.e. the ones that would require actual improvisation. The whole is delivered with a glassy smugness that could hardly be further from the real Ella's selfless desire to please.

Yes, they prove that operatic voices can sing pop, or vice versa. They don't prove that there's any point in doing it when everything is homogenized: when opera gets miked and pop loses all connection with words and with meaning. Anyway, wouldn't it make better dramatic sense to start with the pop stuff and work up to the classical as a surprise? Not that this show is much concerned with drama, except insofar as it confuses it with hysteria; it's a concert whose connection with theatre is confined to real estate. The spirituals do make a reasonable finale; they can legitimately draw on both traditions, European and American, and they at least start out quiet. Earlier on, the threesome's harmonizing on Moody's Mood for Love is quite stylish. The avowed aim of 3 Mo' Divas is to provide a musical something for everyone -- which, as usual, results in nothing much for anyone. Director and entrepreneur Caffey seems to have never met a cliche he couldn't embrace. No mo'. Please.

2008-03-19-of-love-bus-drivers-and-homop:
A fondly-remembered exchange from an old radio show: the scene, a fashionable London soiree in the 1890s. "And who are you?"

"Oh, I'm merely the wittiest, most fascinating man in West End society."

"Are you sure?" "No, of course I'm not Shaw; he's that awful fellow in a red beard and knickerbockers. I'm Oscar Fingal O'Flaherty Wills."

"Oh, you're Wilde!" "So would you be if you were called Oscar Fingal O'Flaherty Wills."

(Ah, the days when comedy was literate.) Anyway, Oscar Fingal what-have-you figures prominently in A Man of No Importance, a winning-if-uneven 2002 off-Broadway musical now receiving its Canadian premiere, and he still isn't happy about his full name.

As a man who lives for fame, he frets that it's too long to fit on billboards. Wilde, I should make clear, isn't really a character in this show; he's a ghostly presence in the mind of the hero Alfie Byrne, a closeted gay bus driver in 1964 Dublin for whom fame is the least of his problems.

Alfie is prone to recite Wilde poetry to his passengers (they seem to like it), and he also runs a church drama group that specializes in Wilde plays; they've already done The Importance of Being Earnest, though not, as far as we're told, A Woman of No Importance. This year Alfie has set his sights on the lush tragedy Salome, which he thinks is a masterpiece. The church establishment -- the "sodality" they call it -- disagrees; it thinks the play pornographic, and it bans both the production and the group. Which is where we come in.

Alfie is packing up his props and thinking about his amateur-theatrical friends and the show they'll never give. He imagines them acting out the story of his recent life, playing all the people in it --including themselves. This elaborate device never really takes hold; it merely looks as if a small cast is doing a confusing amount of doubling.

This isn't just, or even principally, aputting-on-a-show-show --much of it is concerned with Alfie's emotional life, or lack of it. He's a middle-aged man who lives with his sister. Two attractive young people unwittingly force him to confront his own desires. One is Robbie, his driver, whom he secretly and unrequitedly loves. The other is Adele, an out-of-towner who steps onto Alfie's bus one day and whom he instantly casts as Salome, the virginal seductress.

Both show him that love, of any variety, is a messier business than he would like to think. His idolized Oscar makes spectral appearances, urging him to step out and come out. (Wilde plays a very similar role in Tom Stoppard's The Invention of Love, tempting and taunting the historically repressed A. E. Housman.) This, in a homophobic town,

doesn't work out too well either. Robbie has to work out his own salvation which, with a little unexpected help from his friends, he finally seems capable of doing.

Based on a little-known movie, the show is the work of Terrence McNally (book), Stephen Flaherty (music) and Lynn Ahrens (lyrics), the team that wrote Ragtime. This is a smaller work, in every way, that -- at least in this production -- never takes off as a musical. The songs vary in quality, but even when good they don't lift the story.

Lezlie Wade's direction doesn't turn the economy of scale to advantage; much of the staging consists of moving chairs around, and one important scene comes bewilderingly out of nowhere (and returns there). A vigorous pub band plays reduced orchestrations. An ambitious scene-setting title-song founders under the weight of its title phrase.

There are a couple of comic numbers, one titled Books and the other Art, that aren't bad (Ahrens can be a witty and perceptive lyricist) but seem to have come out of some other show, or at least to be sung by characters who need more development; one of them is the show's villain, a butcher who deals in ham offstage as well as on, and whose destructive bigotry is hardly established, let alone explored.

Flaherty's showbizzier tunes come off as derivative. Far more creative in its pastiche is Streets of Dublin, a rousingly atmospheric piece of Poguery, resoundingly sung by Kyle Blair as Robbie; he's the best singer in the cast, and one of the best actors. But his role too is underwritten, and even that song is some distance from the show's emotional centre.

That resides with Alfie himself whose Love Who You Love (it sings better than it reads) is a song both halting and lilting, and who is beautifully played by Douglas E. Hughes, a Shaw Festival regular who, on this evidence, has been underused at his home base. He is quiet, kind and contagiously fervent (and very Irish) in his worship of Art, lost and fumbling in everything else. His anguish could probably break the surface more powerfully than it does, but this is still a moving performance that knows what Alfie, and the show, are all about.

There is good support from Patty Jamieson as the sister (a loving shrew more vigorously desperate), Bethany Jillard -- who isn't the securest singer but makes a touchingly bruised Adele -- and Gary Krawford as a theatre-group veteran who tells Alfie that he's a terrible director and makes it sound the most affectionate of tributes.

There is a generous amount of wishful thinking, mixed in with shameless theatrical sentiment, in the way the show ends, but the generosity conquers. Oscar Fingal would probably drop all poses and agree. - A Man of No Importance is at the Berkeley Street Theatre until March 22. For more information call 416-368-3110.
2008-03-20-all-purpose-experimental-thea:
THEATRE REVIEW

THE MANSFIELD PROJECT

Factory Studio Theatre

---

After eight years spent excavating the short stories of Anton Chekhov, the remarkably talkative mimes of Theatre Smith-Gilmour have turned their attention to a slightly more recent tale-teller. The Mansfield Project is a dramatization of four pieces by Katherine Mansfield; there is no narrative overlap between the sections but they have been arranged so that each melts into the next.

The show begins with two men digging a grave, an image that when clothed in anything approaching modern dress, plants us firmly in the land of All-Purpose Experimental Theatre, European Division, Chekhov to Beckett. Two black-clad females stand at the back of the stage in mourning; First Gravedigger remarks to Second Gravedigger that now these women's lives will really start. He doesn't make that sound like a happy thing.

He's not wrong. The ladies are The Daughters of the Late Colonel. That's the title of the first Mansfield story before us, though you'll search in vain to find that information in the program, or anything at all about the author beyond vague generalizations concerning her "delicate words" and the "challenge" she presents.

Here's a radical suggestion: Suppose our theatre programs start devoting less space to beautiful mission-statements and declarations of how happy the actors are to be working with one another (or just working) and more to basic facts about the authors and the works they're plundering. Anything less seems rather rude.

I'm no Mansfield scholar myself, but I think I can see that this New Zealand-born writer who spent much of her short life (1888 to 1923) in England was trying to make universal art out of the British class system. The specifics count. The colonel's daughters find themselves part-liberated, part-terrified. Their father bullied them, and there are plenty of flashbacks here to show us just how he did it. They even worry about whether they have the right to bury him. (As opposed to what, you may ask. Well, this is not a wholly naturalistic story, and Theatre Smith-Gilmour wouldn't have it any other way.) They have a brother who's out in Ceylon, doing the work of the Empire; a mention of there being no proper postal system out there brings out the sound effects of pattering hooves. And they have a nephew, to whom they are devoted and whom they ply with cake that he, with some embarrassment, declines to eat. Above all, they have a maid, on whose cuisine they are dependent and of whom they would now like to get rid: understandably, since she appears here as a cooking monster out of Strindberg or Lewis Carroll.

As usual, directors Dean Gilmour and Michele Smith have come up with a staging that is swift, suggestive and economical. Having paid that ritual obeisance to their ingenuity, I have to note that in between the quick changes their shows are largely dependent on words, and that when it comes to delivering them they, as actors, are invariably less effective than the colleagues with whom they share the stage. In this instance Adam Paolozza, whose maid here is a really scarifying skivvy, and the consistently incisive Claire Calnan.

Gilmour is a stolid actor and, however hard his Colonel may bark, he doesn't have much bite. Calnan and Smith play the sisters, without establishing much family resemblance. Cal-nan is bracingly Anglo-Saxon; Smith, as always, relays her lines in a thick Gallic accent that makes everything she says come out twee and twittery. This has its charms, especially when her character gets to agonizing over whether, by not leaving crumbs out in the kitchen, they may be starving the mice. But it helps propel the whole thing into Theatre Smith-Gilmour's favourite mode of Gothic farce; and since Mansfield's stories, unlike Chekhov's, don't have a born playwright inside them struggling to get out, it's farce that fails to pay off. In terms of length The Daughters of the Late Colonel is the most substantial part of the evening, but it simply fades out in favour of the next bit.

That would be Carnation, a fairly pointless piece of sexual fantasy, which in turn gives place to Prelude, about a group of bloodthirsty children. This comes off like something out of Second City, a troupe who are always good as horrific kids (cf. the Dungeon Master sketch in their current revue); it's less amusing than the Second Citizens would be, but it probably has higher aspirations. Equilibrium is somewhat restored in Six Years After, which has Smith being touching as a bereaved mother on a cruise, with Gilmour as her oblivious, though apparently well-meaning, husband. It could be a nice dying fall, if it had something more solid to fall from. - The Mansfield Project is at the Factory Studio Theatre until April 13. Call 416-504-9971 for more information.
2008-03-22-what-s-graceland-got-to-do-wi:
There are some puzzles attached to Last Days of Graceland at Theatre Passe Muraille. One is, what is the play supposed to be about? Another is, what is it doing on a main Toronto stage? A third is, why is it being done so poorly?

The first query is perhaps disingenuous. Franca Miraglia, the author, makes it clear at the end of the evening, and at various points on the way, that the subjects on her mind are love and forgiveness, and that these are things of which she is in favour. So, probably the question should shift to that of why she has chosen to deliver this unobjectionable message in the way that she has, and especially to why she has set it where she does. The Graceland of the title is the one you thought it was, Elviss mansion; he isn't mentioned by name but his music is occasionally heard and his image appears once on the sleeve of an old LP that someone is brandishing. The place has been bought by a very rich unseen man, referred to (by an equally unseen, though obviously not unheard, public service announcer) as our imperial host, Kwan Wah Heen. Mr. Heen sounds like a piece of work: "surrounded by expensive wealth" according to the announcer (which, if I heard it right, must be the play's one intentional laugh-line). Before he closes the place for good and all, he has invited the public to come take a last look at it; 10 lucky visitors, chosen by lottery, will also get to cart off some memorabilia.

We focus on two of these pilgrims. One is Sandra, a young woman who has until recently been plying the specialized trade of "professional eulogist" -- that is, she writes and delivers nice speeches at the funerals of people she has never met. The other is Robert, a somewhat older science teacher (and, he rather ruefully tells us, after-school drama coach) whose still older male lover is dying.

It turns out that the meeting of Robert and Sandra is more than coincidence. Even before the mechanical details are revealed, we have gathered, with the assistance of copious flashbacks, that they both have problems with their nearest but not necessarily dearest. Sandra has long been estranged from her father, and the accumulated fallout has soured her on the eulogizing business. An admired author she was hired to glorify turned out to have more clay in his shoes than she could comfortably handle; confusingly, the play begins with her tribute to him, making us wonder whether we have wandered into the wrong stately home. Robert has issues around a girl in his past life and a boy in his present and maybe future one, plus the memory of a terminally ill younger brother on whom he turned his back; four separate people in his memories ask him to come to bed -- its his personal leitmotiv -- though the motivation behind the requests tends to vary. These back stories are uniformly banal, especially in the snippet form in which we receive them here. Patricia Vanstones production seems, to begin with, reasonably spry in its pacing, but it soon resolves into an awkward affair of bringing phantom characters on from the wings, spotlighting them behind screens, or -- the ultimate clunkiness --pushing those screens laboriously around to make room for the next unrevealing revelation.

So: Sandra is cured of her spikiness, Robert stops beating up on himself, and it seems they have one another to thank. The mechanics of bringing this about could hardly be more contrived; and what's Graceland got to do with it? The play has nothing to say about Elvis and hardly anything about his fans. I suppose there are meant to be symbolic overtones in the name itself, plus some intimations about hanging on to the past or letting go of it --it's unclear which course the play is advocating. Maybe it wants us to have a bit of both.

Apart from its physical liabilities, the direction is almost completely unsuccessful in getting credible work from its cast. Supporting actors, including a couple with good track records, either overplay remorselessly or retire defeated. Of the two leads, Catherine Bruhiers Sandra is just awful: wooden and strident. Jim Joness Robert is this Graceland's nearest approach to a saving grace; he can play anxiety without seizing up, and seems alone among the cast in not finding his lines literally unspeakable. I'll spare you the details of the uplifting final image; I'll merely say that the evening is a rocky road leading to a vat of syrup. This has not been a good season for new Canadian drama.

- Last Days of Graceland runs through April 6 at Theatre Passe Muraille. Call 416-504-7529 for details.

2008-03-25-doing-the-things-a-particle-c:
INVISIBLE ATOM

Theatre Passe Muraille Backspace

---

The Halifax theatre company known as 2b came to Toronto last year with Revisited, a beautiful reduction of Our Town performed by two actors on a tabletop. They are now revisiting us themselves with a piece called Invisible Atom that, despite its title, is as visually striking as its predecessor and even more minimalist, the size of the cast being slashed by 50%.

That sole actor is also the author. His name is Anthony Black, and Atom is his character's name. That, he stressfully stresses, is Atom "as in bomb," not Adam "as in apple," and indeed he carries on as if he were the last man on Earth rather than the first. Atom is a bastard -- literally -- who rose from unpromising beginnings to become, in his twenties, a high-flying financial trader. He now has the house, the car and other trappings that befit his earnings, though he does admit that the accompanying debt makes him feel as broke now that he's rich as he felt when he was poor. A former physics student, engaged to another, they have a son, Abraham("Abe the babe") whom Atom greets with delight as being the first person he's ever met who looks like him.

When we meet Atom, he's poised between life and death: most arrestingly so in Ann-Marie Kerr's moody and ingenious production that has him picked out by Leigh Ann Vardy's pinpoint lighting on a pitch-black stage, Video Cabaret style. He has hurled himself off a bridge and we catch him in free fall. "I have no time," he says, adding in a phrase that hauntingly collapses his background in science with his career in money, "who can own time?"

So what has brought him to this pass? Well, it all goes back to his birth, but in more recent times he has suffered: first, a loss of faith in both the morality and the efficacy of his business; second, a terrorist attack on his place of work on a day he happened not to be in it. He has, in the wake of these, embarked on a search for his biological parents that has taken him across the ocean and back and which resulted in severe disillusionment. Persisting in his genealogical research, he finds himself to be the latest in a very long line of bastards, a progression whose details the performer-playwright reels off in a continuous sentence virtuosic in its speed as in its wit. It seems, as far back as he cares to take us, that Atom is the multiply illegitimate descendant of Adam Smith, who was himself the unacknowledged issue of Isaac Newton. This is historically improbable on several counts, but its symbolic fitness is undeniable; the founders of modern physics and modern economics bequeath us this all too splittable Atom.

Pushing him finally over the edge, our hero has been offered the chance of renewed riches at high moral cost: a dilemma that I can only describe as the Last Temptation of Atom. (I rather hoped he'd succumb, but that's me.) His overall trajectory, a hectic downward spiral, is depicted and enacted with great narrative flair. Along the way, of course, he encounters many minor characters, who are impersonated with energy if no great depth: I certainly had my doubts about the sweet-natured taxi driver, a refugee from some devastated former Soviet state, who talks about the importance of "family" with the accent on the second syllable. In a class of his own is the insanely rich English businessman who turns out to be the kind of brutal Cockney wisecracker patented by the early Harold Pinter and most recently incarnated by Ralph Fiennes in Martin McDonagh's In Bruges. As in that film, so in Black's play and performance, I enjoyed him but I didn't believe in him.

Black does, however, keep us with his hero; in an appropriately cool manner, we sympathize with him, and we share in his suspense. I myself felt, as he unravelled, an increasing dread that he would mislay the cherished child he was supposed to be guarding; and I think the author meant me to. He gives us a haunted mind, desperately seeking exorcism; the detail is in the devils. - Invisible Atom runs until March 30. Call 416-504-7529 for information.
2008-03-27-this-hour-has-one-host-and-th:
Recently, This Hour took on The Hour, and you can still see the results on YouTube. This Hour Has 22 Minutes aired a sketch entitled "Strombeshi," in which an actor impersonating George Stroumboulopoulos gets together with an actor impersonating Jian Ghomeshi for a half-imaginary TV show in which "we talk about ourselves." It's a love-in between two guys congratulating themselves on being what it's probably no longer cool to call cool: on being young and successful and having daily or nightly shows of their own. ("You're great." "No, you're great".) It's pretty funny, especially when faux-Jian congratulates faux-George on the number of bands he wears on his wrist to signify his devotion to various charitable causes, one of them being "rubber depletion due to excessive wristbands." George also spends a lot of time expecting a text-message from Bono, which impresses Jian even when no message arrives.

Do you detect an imbalance here? George is the primary target, maybe because a television host is easier to satirize on television than a radio host. The best they could do with Jian was ask him why his radio arts show Q -- devoted to "Politics, Performance, People" -- wasn't called P. George comes with visuals. "Strombeshi" was set on what looked like George's set, complete with hideous (and, to judge from the way in which the host always seems to be straining forward while sitting on it, hideously uncomfortable) red plastic furniture. Even more fearlessly, it reproduced the tiny tuft of hair that sprouts beneath George's lower lip, whose function seems to be to supply a lonely note of gravitas to balance the boyishness.

There is also the fact that Jian's radio program is harder to make fun of because it's usually good, with an interviewer-host who sounds informed and entertaining; it certainly makes a refreshing change from the traditional CBC arts shows. (This estimate has, of course, nothing to do with the fact that Ghomeshi writes a column in this very section of this very paper.) The Hour with George Stroumboulopoulos is far more problematic, the problems beginning with the fact that this hour goes the full 60, minus commercials. That's a lot to fill every night of the week, especially when you're going up against Jon Stewart and Stephen Colbert and covering some of the same topics. Why, last week, would anyone but the severely cable-deprived want to hear George on President Bush's five-years-on Iraq speech when they could be hearing Jon? (To be fair, Stewart on this subject turned out to be surprisingly uninspired, like he'd done it all already. But it's the principle of the thing.) George's stock-in-trade on these occasions is very much like Jon's; he runs clips and interrupts them with incredulous expressions, visual or vocal. But he doesn't have Jon's delivery or Jon's personality or, from the sound of it, Jon's writers.

But then, is he supposed to be a comedian? Officially maybe not, but if the news is your pasture and irreverence your image, then it's a role you're more or less forced into.

You can't just pass yourself off as the alternative Peter Mansbridge (though that may well be what the Corporation originally had in mind). And if you have a studio audience ....

At the beginning of George's show, he invariably gets the same blast of sycophantic applause as Stewart or Colbert. The difference with George is that after the opening. The volume -- in terms of both

loudness and amount -- steeply declines. On Tuesday night, he interviewed a couple of Canadian residents who also happen to be American Democratic super-delegates. I lost count of the number of times he said he expected them to turn up wearing capes, but it wasn't funny even once. When they did arrive (in suits) they turned out not to have much to say, and he wasn't very successful at drawing them out.

There are some good things about the show. The brief sections, labelled The Set Up or The Bio, which set up the next subject or the next guest, are more helpful than the scrambled eulogies delivered by most talk-show hosts -- though we maybe don't need, at this date, to be informed that Senators Clinton and Obama are running for the Democratic nomination. And, as jumpy and off-putting as he is when talking to camera, George can be a decent interviewer when he meets somebody with whose flow he can go.

Sometimes he goes too easy. Last week he was chatting with Jenny McCarthy, the former Playboy model whose life changed when her son was diagnosed with autism and she herself became an activist for proper treatment. You'd think this would make her impregnably sympathetic; but she came on as if she were plugging her latest movie, and George was content to schmooze right along with her.

Things were much better on Tuesday when he met Chantal Kreviazuk; she's the most sensible and appealing of pop singers with a conscience (she slipped once into talking about her "artistry" when she meant her career, but we can overlook that); George let her make the running, which was the decent and clever thing to do. But he shouldn't have said that after the break, we'd be taking "our nightly nosedive into glitz and glamour." What does he think he's doing the rest of the time?

Thompson, National Post / George Stroumboulopoulos leans out of his presumably uncomfortable chair at a taping of The Hour in October. ; Black & White Photo: Halifax Films / This Hour Has 22 Minutes' Mark Critch, left, and Shaun Majunder bring the beast known as Strombeshi to life. ;; Caption:
2008-03-29-scandal-a-politician-and-a-ca:
You want timeliness? Greg Nelson's The Fall involves a politician who's renowned for his probity, caught up in a call-girl scandal. You want coincidence? The play is three years old; it was first produced at SummerWorks in 2005. But really, if you want this kind of thing to be topical, all you have to do is wait awhile. It'll come 'round.

Anyway, The Fall has more to offer. It is, in its expanded version at Tarragon, a tense, intelligent and economical play, very well presented, whose only weakness may be an excess of ingenuity. It's a twohander with four characters. We're in an Ottawa conference room: one long table, a chair and the audience on two sides. Despite the furniture, the people on stage rarely sit down; they have too much on their minds. First off, we meet Kate, a legal scholar, and David, a lawyer who has come direct from delivering a tear-inducing oration at the funeral of his father, Harry, who was a judge. A quarter-century ago, Harry was one of the prime backroom boys in the drafting of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms. Kate and David were college contemporaries. They even once dated. (Apparently, it was a disaster.) A more pressing memory for Kate is that of her very first job as a clerk in Harry's office. She emerged from it in possession of memories, ethical dilemmas and an incriminating file.

And suddenly, with just a change of lighting and the removal of David's glasses, we're back in time, in the same office, to find Harry confronted by Jane, a journalist, who has some goods on him -- or, more precisely, on one of his bosses, the minister responsible for pushing through the legislation in which Harry so passionately believes. Drugs are involved and, as aforesaid, an escort. It may all come out. To stop this from happening, Harry may have to violate the spirit of the very Charter he longs to establish.

It's a pretty problem, echoing across two generations. Added to the mix is that, whatever eulogies David may have recently delivered, in life he and his father did not get on. They were estranged for years. And, maybe because of this, David is a drunk.

The play keeps us on moral and theatrical tenterhooks. Both, though, are somewhat blunted by the number of levels involved. To put it another way, the storytelling is immediate but the issues are removed. Harry might move us more if he were covering for his own misdeeds, rather than somebody else's. And his agonies might be more agonizing if we saw them happening present-tense rather than in flashbacks. It works both ways; the fencing matches of the younger generation seem less urgent once we realize that they're only a series of feints for the real drama.

Which isn't to say that the fencing isn't effective in its own right. Nelson gives very good cat-and-mouse -- all the characters carry secrets that they only give up under pressure -- and he's very well served in this production. Jennifer Tarver, a director known for fine work on more abstract plays, proves equally adroit at adjusting the nuts and bolts of this one. She makes it weighty but not ponderous. Two of Toronto's best younger actors make up her cast. Sarah Dodd, in a pin-striped pantsuit with hair centre-parted and in a bun, makes little attempt to differentiate between the two women she plays, but the play neither asks nor permits her to; both are capable people in terrible binds, and Dodd, terse and wounded, does fine by both of them. Ashley Wright is squishier as the judged son than as the judging (and self-judging) father, but he is really offering us complementary halves of one riven man. The play tells us that, when you're in a tight corner, blackmail comes easy -- emotional blackmail if no other kind is available. Having griped last week about the recent standard of new plays in town, I have to say that The Fall is a definite rise.

- The Fall runs through April 27 at the Tarragon Extra Space. Call 416-531-1827 for details.

2008-03-31-the-elocutions-of-a-revolutio:
There was once--and still is, of course, in reruns -- a delightful musical number on The Simp-sons in which the kids at Springfield Elementary pay tribute to the Mediocre Presidents of the U.S.A. (William Henry Harrison! I died in 30 days!") John Adams didn't make that cut, nor should he. All the same, when you think about what the same song calls "caretaker presidents, its hard not to think of Adams, Americas second president (one term only) and first vice-president. Also, one might have thought that he was the Famous Founding Father least likely to get his own miniseries. But he has one now, and it's good.

This is Adams' second brush with showbiz stardom. He was one of the delegates to the Continental Congress whose deliberations were the subject of the musical 1776; and if not quite the leading man -- the show didnt have one -- he could be counted first among the casts equals. He was the prickly commentator at the Congress, impatient with his fellows' reluctance to get on with it and declare independence already. When it came time to prepare the document, he stepped down, knowing his own unpopularity, and -- with the encouragement of the canny and persistent Benjamin Franklin -- handed the job to the more personable Tom Jefferson.

The TV series takes much the same view of all these characters, and its second episode covers almost exactly the same events as the musical. But, with seven hours to fill instead of two, the series can afford to be more leisurely; it starts earlier in Adams' life and goes on much later. This allows Paul Giamatti to play an Adams whose resentments run far deeper than those of his singing counterpart but who also has more of a sense of humour -- about himself if about nobody else.

Hes surrounded by other illustrious Oscar losers: the luminous Laura Linney as his wife, Abigail, Tom Wilkinson stealing all available scenes as a peg-legged Franklin who seems to be auditioning for Long John Silver, and Sarah Polley, who emerges at the end of Episode Four as the grown-up version of the Adams only daughter, Nabby. We also get Stephen Dillane as Jefferson, presented here as a romantic malcontent with what seems to be an unrequited eye for Abigail, the ubiquitous Zeljko Ivanek as the recalcitrant delegate Dickinson; and David Morse, a George Washington who, with the aid of a prosthetic nose, is physically right on the money: He looks, in fact, as if he's stepped right off it.

I cannot tell a lie: In this version, Washington's elevation to the presidency comes as rather a surprise, because we have seen so little of him. Hes been at war while Adams battles have been fought in council, first at home, then -- on diplomatic missions to France, Holland and England -- abroad. Many of the textbook highlights of the American revolution -- the Boston Tea Party, the British capture of Philadelphia, Valley Forge, the British surrender -- have taken place offscreen. The show partakes of its hero's integrity by keeping him, and us, well away from them. Can you imagine old Hollywood being so scrupulous?

We began with Adams, lawyer and farmer, trudging through the merciless Boston snow. (A later episode will find him reassuring his 14-year-old son John Quincy, who's been posted to St. Petersburg, that the Russian winter has nothing to teach a Massachusetts man.) Almost the first thing he does on arriving home is to take off his wig, to reveal a perfect egg head; the key to Giamattis excellent performance is that, though gentlemanly fashion obliges him to wear those hairpieces (and he gets through a lot of them), he really cant bear them.

The main event of the first episode is his defence -- against all his political preferences but in line with his professional and personal ethics -- of British soldiers falsely accused of mowing down local townsmen. The trial was presented at possibly excessive length, but it's vital in setting Adams' character note; hes always prepared to do the unpopular thing. Theres a side of him that revels in it. Abigail has to advise him to shorten some of his learned courtroom rhetoric and, as usual, she's right. Theirs was a famously long and devoted marriage; Linney's role for the first two weeks seems confined to saying yes, John" and -- at moments of exceptionally high drama -- "no, John, which seems a waste. But she has more chances later.

While John is away at the congress, she runs the home and the farm, apparently (though it seems historically unlikely) without any hired help. By way of compensation, U.S. history develops an appealing habit of parading past her door, on its way to and from the war. When Nabby asks, Why do boys have all the fun?" Abigail pauses in her hoeing to reply grimly, "Because we let them.

She does get to join John in Paris and London, though even here her fun is limited. John proves no diplomat, and smarts when his efforts to get the French onside are slighted in favour of the smoother, more flirtatious Franklin. Ah, to be 70 again," says Ben, ogling the Versailles beauties. (Thats prior to being discovered playing chess in the bath with his Parisian mistress, who may seem 70 again, but not 60.)

John is secure with Abigail, however jealous and uneasy with everyone else. He knows his own worth, and the show persuades us that hes mostly right; there's an interesting contrast between Giamatti's way of worrying at his lines and the legato delivery favoured by his British co-stars. Theres too much heart-pumping music, a cheapening I thought HBO had outgrown; even the opening theme seems to think its The Magnificent Seven. Sets and costumes are sumptuous, as is the camerawork; the Dutch scenes look like Vermeers. As historical dramas go, this is less fun than Rome but more trustworthy. In both respects, it leaves The Tudors in the dust.

2008-04-03-there-s-no-u-s-history-withou:
Anew CNN series titled Black in America begins tonight with Eyewitness to Murder, a documentary about the assassination of Martin Luther King Jr. It's an excellent program. The presenter, Soledad O'Brien, seems to have talked to just about everybody still living who was present at, or around, the Memphis killing in 1968, and to many who were caught up in what happened later. Her interviews are lucidly interwoven with grainy footage from the day and with some helpful graphics. The sequence depicting the murder itself is about as tense and as scrupulous as any reconstruction could be.

Someone says that King's death marked the end of the Civil Rights era. It could equally be claimed that it marked the beginning, or at any rate the cusp of the progression from struggle to achievement. The point is never explicitly made, but the feeling is conveyed that the killing of King effectively discredited his opponents. That's poetically just, considering the lengths to which they had gone to discredit him. The film provides chilling -- and, at this distance, bleakly comic -- details of the FBI's poison-pen conspiracy against him, exacerbated by his being as fierce an opponent of the Vietnam War as he was of segregation. "I think J. Edgar Hoover had a personal dislike for Martin Luther King" says John Lewis, one of the King's young associates and obviously a master of understatement.

Lewis is now a Democratic congressman for Georgia. Andrew Young, an older and closer King aid and the most eloquent of the interviewees, became American ambassador to the UN. Their progress is some evidence at least for the truth of King's famous sermon about standing Moses-like on a mountain, viewing a territory that he might never reach but that his successors would. The irony of his having said that just a couple of days before his death is duly marked, but we're also told that it was a speech he'd given before -- whenever, in fact, he felt that danger was imminent. Which was a lot of the time; he's quoted as saying, "Every morning when I brush my teeth, I know this day may be my last." What really set the fear in motion was the killing of President John F. Kennedy, which brought assassination back into the American arena. There's a bloody bookend here: Two months after King's death, John Lewis was in a Los Angeles hotel room, awaiting a meeting with Bobby Kennedy. The meeting never happened. When he heard about the new assassination, Lewis tells us, "I broke down and cried." And he does again, on camera.

Two days later, King's presumed killer, James Earl Ray, was captured at Heathrow Airport in London. And the film is more about him than it is about King, which may seem to belie the series title, but is in accord with all studies of an assassination, documentary or dramatic. The climactic event happens, at latest, halfway through: The victim becomes a symbol and the perpetrator a protagonist. Ray was a poor white southerner with an extensive criminal record; his brother, interviewed by O'Brien, says that, however unprepossessing in appearance, "as a criminal he was fearless ... smart and intelligent ... smart enough not to get caught." His major crime, prior to the murder, seems to have been a bank robbery from which he walked away with US$30,000 in $20 bills -- thereby creating a literal paper trail that helped undo him. Ray was undoubtedly a racist (he wrote in a statement "I wouldn't say I hated King ... I think most preachers are a little phony") and he was undoubtedly in Memphis on the fatal day -- staying in a flophouse directly opposite the hotel balcony on which King was gunned down. That same day, Ray left Memphis, arriving two days later in Toronto. (There's a momentary shock here for locals; we see the street signs for Ossington and Argyle and wonder, till the narration clears it up, whether there's some American town with the same intersection.) His eventual aim was to get to some white-dominated country in Africa; he had the money for the trip, and the forged papers, but not quite well forged enough. Hence his arrest. The FBI were as zealously on his case as they had been on King's -- which, for the conspiracy-minded, may be suspicious in itself.

Ray confessed, then retracted the confession, but was convicted anyway. He claimed to have been duped by a mysterious man named "Raoul" who was never found. Certainly there are troubling gaps in the evidence. Ray's brother believes in his innocence; so, more startlingly, does the King family. We see footage of King's son Dexter visiting Ray in prison in 1997 and pledging solidarity. Ray died in jail in the next year, but we hear from lawyers who took up his cause and from those who opposed it. Your opinions when watching are likely to bounce about: convinced first that he was guilty, then that he was framed, then that he was involved but was part of a conspiracy (involving, it's alleged, the FBI, the Memphis police and the U.S. military). We're also told by a lawyer that "the fact that Ray lived all those years proves there wasn't a conspiracy." That sounds like the last word, but of course the conspirators could have been being super-subtle. If this were TV fiction, we'd know there was a conspiracy, a bottomless one. As it's fact, meticulously presented, we're left in fascinated uncertainty. - Eyewitness to Murder airs on CNN tonight at 9 p.m.

2008-04-04-ah-the-north-toronto-desert-t:
Our subject is Gross hypocrisy. I mean that in the nicest way. In Slings and Arrows, Paul Gross played a decent and talented artist haunted by the suspicion that he was a fraud. In The Trojan Horse, the new two-part thriller on CBC, he's a politician whose idealism masks unscrupulous ambition: the same persona turned inside out.

The Trojan Horse is the successor to H20, which saw Gross as Tom Mc-Laughlin, Canadian prime minister whose good deeds included donating his country's water supply to keep the folks in the United States from dying of thirst and whose bad included getting rid of his own father. Part one of this sequel showed Canada opting, by a 2% referendum majority, to become part of the U.S., and Gross vowing to take vengeance on an unspecified "them" for allowing this to happen. His plan is to become American president, and he has the backing of a limitlessly wealthy media tycoon (Kenneth Welsh) and of the all-powerful heads of the three major European secret services. He also sets about re-wooing his ex-wife, and he gets himself shot, non-fatally, so that he can stage a resurrection, thereby endearing himself to everyone who enjoys a good story.

That is where we left Tom last week. In part two, which airs on Sunday, the plot thickens. One thing that makes The Trojan Horse more fun than a series such as The Border is that it keeps several storylines going at once. There are the spy chiefs who have got hold of a computer progam guaranteed to fix any election and are prepared to put it at Tom's service. The MI5 man on this team of ruthless smoothies is played by the late William Hutt, visibly frail but still capable of knocking you to attention with an authoritative snap. The schemers have to eliminate everybody else who knows about it, incurring a lawyer whose long-lost journalist mother (Greta Scacchi) finds out about it, and starts investigating. She is our heroine, and the one uncompromised character in a show whose principal message is a plague on all their houses, especially the White one

This is currently occupied by Tom Skerritt, who's very good as a pious, spineless Republican who doesn't look or behave in the least like George Bush. He does have a secretary of state (Saul Rubinek) who's Kissinger without the accent and a security advisor (Rachael Crawford) who might be confused with Condi Rice. This week the Pres has to deal with an exceptionally ugly Saudi hostage situation, arranged for his benefit by his own staff. Unfortunately it also gives a leg-up to his Canadian rival.

Gross himself and John Krizanc are the writers, Charles Biname the director, and the thing moves like the wind. After his deathbed recovery, Tom and his bride "retreat to the dessert." So says the press release, but I regret to inform you that it's a typo. I challenge anyone, by the way, to make sense of the following sentence from the same document: "Biname shot to the desert of Saudi Arabia north of Toronto and the Badlands of Alberta substituted for the Sierra Dablo Mountains, the White House at the White House set in the Kleinberg Studios north of Toronto and was able to shoot for location for a day in London, England." It might have been nice, too, to make some mention of Hutt's death and to have added The Wire to the bio of Clark Johnson, who appears here as a killer with a conscience.

There are flaws. The story repeats itself; Scacchi gets attacked in hotel rooms on two continents. And it doesn't make good on all its pretentions. Though it professes to have a satiric side, it isn't very witty; there is a neat scene in which Rubinek and Ziegler, swapping scandals, trade a gay affair against an abortion, and Guy Nadon gets to say, "for two weeks I was the prime minister of Canada, so you know I'm harmless," but that's about all. The business of Canada surrendering itself isn't explored. Similarly, the contradictions in Gross' character are mentioned, but we'd have to see him actually in power for them to mean anything. When he finally has a showdown with Scacchi, she accuses him of some of the few things he hasn't done, and I'm not sure the show notices. And though the show mostly gets more exciting as its story gets more outrageous, the final twist lost me. I stopped believing, not in the action, but in the motivation. This isn't drama on the level of The Englishman's Boy, but it beats most of CBC as entertainment.

- The Trojan Horse continues Sunday at 10 p.m. on CBC.

2008-04-05-he-s-got-chicken-in-the-barn-:
The first-act curtain of Fire really lights one. Two, actually. On one side of the stage, there's Ted Dykstra, as a first-generation rock 'n' roller not unlike Jerry Lee Lewis, shaking the theatre as he pounds out Good Golly Miss Molly on voice and piano. On the other, there's Rick Roberts as a Bible-belt minister with resemblances to Jimmy Swaggart, finding his feet and his voice on his first venture into a radio studio. The real Lewis and Swaggart were cousins, but this piece makes them brothers, and renames them Cale and Hershel Blackwell. (Acknowledgments, I guess, to Otis Blackwell who cowrote Lewis's Great Balls of Fire and many of Elvis's hits.)Whatever, they turn out to be kin in talent as well as in blood. Both are natural, consuming -- and self-confusing --performers.

The point is made again at the start of Act 2; Roberts's Hershel, now thoroughly in his preaching groove, is as wild, as physically and vocally hyper-kinetic, as purposefully thrashingly hysterical, as Dykstra's Cale: perhaps more so, as Cale is already beginning to lose it. There's a musical as well as a psychological validity to this: rock -- Cale's brand of it anyway -- came out of the South, out of the church, and when Cale, in an attempt at reconciliation with his long-estranged brother, sings and plays some gospel, very affectingly, it's like he's coming home. The boys' father is a preacher and a musician, though he disapproves of the ways in which each has used his inherited gifts. The brothers also share a wife (sequentially, I should add: Cale first, though Hershel was the first to confide that he loved her, or lusted after her); she's named for that Miss Molly who sure loved to ball. She spends the evening trying to resolve her feelings for the two of them and to define her faith as a Christian, somewhere between Cale's diabolism and Hershel's bigotry.

Fire, with a script by Paul Ledoux and David Young and a score that's half pre-existing and half Ledoux originals, is a better show than it is a play. But to deal with the good part first. Dykstra played Cale 20 years ago and won a Dora for it; he's since said that he was too young for the part back then. He's strictly too old for its first part now, for all his tousled boyishness, but he has the heart of the role firmly nailed down. Versatility is one thing and this cast is loaded with it, but Dykstra, a goodness-gracious medium-sized ball of fire, is in a league of his own. Apart from the quality of his musicianship (he's also the MD), there's its energy, and the conviction of that energy, and the tact and delicacy with which it's dispensed. In the first act, he's both a natural star and a boy out of his depth. In the second, he's grown and grizzled and sunk. He's starved of opportunities post-intermission, as if a rock star's decline was pro forma and didn't have to be gone into, but he sinks his teeth into what he's got, whether drying out in jail or prostrating himself before his inflexible sibling who by this point has moved, profitably and disreputably, into politics.

Roberts's Hershel, pre-ordination, is stiff and unrevealing, but once the spirit's got to him, he's possessed and thrilling. Nicole Underhay gives herself over as fully to Molly who, what with having the first and last speeches, emerges as both chorus and protagonist. The actress can carry it; the character can't. Simply, it isn't about her.

Anyway we have three electric performances. Make that four, since Richard McMillan is absolutely fine as the minister-father, a fundamentalist who's allowed to be decent. When a character gets to do a number, spoken or sung, the authors give him good material. I have purist misgivings about a show that mixes old and new songs, especially when the subject is semi-biographical, but Ledoux comes through beautifully with Cale's gospel song. But though the script devotes too much time and effort to the brothers' earlier relationship and too little to the later -- there's a lot of Tom Sawyerish stuff (in which Molly also partakes) about swearing oaths of eternal devotion with blood cut from fingers -- but it never means much.

If Cale's decline is taken for granted, Hershel's becomes repetitive; politically, he ties himself to the coat-tails of an aspiring senator who happens to be both Molly's pa and Cale's ex-manager, and who is given a hesitant performance that weakens this plot-line considerably. James Macdonald's production is played out on a constricting set that seems mainly inspired by the railroad tracks where the Blackwell boys go for their youthful confession sessions but doesn't really evoke much of anything.

The actors and the music make the evening; when they're in command we have a tale of sound and fury, signifyin' somethin'.

- Fire runs through April 19 at the Bluma Appel Theatre. Call 416-368-3110 for details.

Color Photo: Cylla Von Tiedemann / Nicole Underhay and Rick Roberts in Canstage's Fire. ;; Caption:
2008-04-09-an-airborne-procedural-discov:
The Disaster -- sorry, Discovery -- Channel has a new season of Mayday, devoted to notable airplane crashes. It starts tonight with what is, from a Canadian perspective, the most notable of all: the 1986 destruction of Air India Flight 182 with 329 people, mainly Canadian citizens, on board.

This isn't exactly an under-told story, and there is something catchpenny about using it to launch a season, as there is about the overall title of the series itself. But the program itself is serious and informative, though it's a strange combination of dramatized reconstruction and investigative documentary.

The dramatized parts are inevitably the least successful. Since this was a catastrophe with no survivors, we can only have brief generic impressions (and the show, to its credit, does keep them brief) of what went on among the passengers. Conversation in the cockpit is reproduced, presumably in a literal reconstruction of the last recorded moments from the planes black box, retrieved from 6,000 feet below the surface of the ocean.

More questionable is the reenactment of the airport check-in scene in which a belligerent customer, known to history only as M. Singh, browbeats a harried clerk into sending his baggage through, despite his not possessing the appropriate ticket. The bag of course contains the bomb, and he isnt going with it. Maybe the scene had to be shown, but is it necessary for the angry non-passenger to be quite such an obvious caricature of a terrorist? And did the unfortunate agent have to be not only portrayed but named? We are told that she's had to live ever since with "her eternal sadness and heartbreak." Isn't that enough?

The Toronto-Bombay flight was approaching Ireland when it went down. We get scenes with the Shannon Airport aircraft controllers as the plane disappears from their radar, and a present-day interview with one of them. With all allowances made for the passage of time, the real and the acted personae hardly match up. But this ushers us into the interesting part of the film, which is an unusually intense, complex and meticulous police procedural. Canadian, British and Indian officials are all involved. Air Indias chief investigator, a Mr. H.S. Khola, spells out with a true sleuths delight the reasons why the black box was crucial to determining whether the crash was due to sabotage or mechanical malfunction: If there's any mechanical problem, the crew will be talking about the problem, they will not be silent about the problem. We hear this for ourselves in a twice-played scene. One moment the captain and his co-pilot are exchanging humdrum information about insurance seals, the next -- well, there isn't a next moment. Thats when theres silence. The computers went out, along with everything else on board.

It had to be "a devastating decompression or a bomb." The film rather gives the impression that the possibility of sabotage was only entertained after days, maybe weeks, of weighing the alternatives. In fact, it was already being alleged on the day of the disaster, with two organizations -- one of them, the Sikh extremist group that was eventually found guilty -- claiming responsibility. But it still had to be proved, with evidence from wreckage reclaimed from the bottom of the sea. A British salvage veteran, used to dealing with smaller craft, talks about the challenging of retrieving the shattered, scattered fragments of a jumbo jet.

Luckily -- if that's a permissible word in this context -- he found the right ones. Against comparably daunting odds, the RCMP tracked down -- via an electronics store in the small town of Duncan, B.C. -- the inoffensive stereo tuner that held the bomb. (It could hold just four sticks of dynamite, enough, in the right circumstances, to bring down an airliner: You don't need much.)

After the device that held the bomb came the suitcase that held the device. The pro-gam actually starts with the information, chilling at the best of times, that "every day, millions of pieces of luggage arrive at airports across the world," going on to advise us that "one bag led to an investigation unique in the history of aviation" -- rather a reductive view of a story that, on the films own showing, was a lot more complicated. Anyway, the resultant 20-year criminal investigation isnt really the concern here. It's about mechanics, including the information that the bombing led to the invention of new system for firewalling cargo holds that proved too costly to implement. The human cost can, in this context, be taken for granted and, for most of the film's length, it sensibly is.

The narration does pause to tell us, in dramatic tones, that the destruction of the passenger jet was a crime. But I think we knew that. - Mayday:Air India: Explosive Evidence airs tonight at 10 p.m. on the Discovery Channel.

Black & White Photo: Discovery Channel / Dont worry, thats not really a plane being ripped apart in mid-air, just a dramatic recreation from Discovery's Mayday. ;; Caption:
2008-04-10-air-farce-deserves-an-honoura:
For the last 10 years I have missed The Royal Canadian Air Farce -- missed it, in fact, as often as I could. But now that I will really have to miss it, with the announcement that the show's next season will be its last, I find myself becoming nostalgic. Watching the next-to-last season's finale, which went out last Friday, reminded me that the Air Farce regulars are real comic talents, however familiar their format and bland their material.

Luba Goy, for example, may not give very good Hillary Clinton (though she can put up a passable resemblance), but she gives excellent Luba Goy. Last week allowed her a turn as herself, stiff-upper-lipping over the show's imminent demise while drowning the sorrows she affected not to feel. ("I've been unemployed before -- and this isn't a very expensive wine.") The lines may not have been all that great ("rent-a-Luba, play-my-tuba" as she contemplated hiring herself out for future gigs at lower rates), but she was. Goy, unlike many people on TV comedy shows, is an actor, which is not the same thing as an impersonator. It means that she can give herself over to the situations she's involved in.

Friday found her as a Tim Hortons customer, incensed to discover that her rim had already been rolled. It wasn't the brightest of comic ideas, but it was rooted in and played for a certain kind of reality --a rarity in sketch-comedy shows that have increasingly become a matter of dropping names into limbo. And when Goy took another moment or few to lash out at the creepiest TV ads, she had her audience enthusiastically with her, especially when she took aim at the Pepto Bismol diarrhea spokesman ("if anyone should get whacked, it's him") and at that Alexander Keith talking statue that confronts me whenever I turn on my set ("still, unmovable, isolated and incapable of performing any meaningful action"). At times like these, Air Farce is performing a public service: comedy as safety valve.

Talking of taking aim, Don Ferguson's Colonel Stacy is still firing off that Chicken Cannon, with a relish that seems only slightly diluted by time (and with impeccably poker-faced support from his female assistant). There is a certain atavistic attraction to the routine after all these years, and I guess it's too late to wonder whether such a bizarrely cozy form of satire is very Canadian or just very Air Farce. My favourite of last week's targets: "Jim Flaherty, for telling Dalton McGuinty his province's finances have been screwed up ever since Flaherty himself was Ontario's finance minister."

There's an obvious logic to having the colonel do what he does. I'm still not clear about Sister Bessie giving out her Bessia Awards at the start of the show. Is a nun automatically funny or --gasp--daring? Blessings on the sister, though, for her gloss on Stephen Harper's citing of Rick Mercer as a credible commentator: "If you want credibility, watch Rick Mercer; if you want comedy, watch Question Period."

That's about as bitchy as Air Farce gets; and though it's possible that the laugh was meant to be on Parliament rather than on Mercer, I know which I prefer to believe. The Comedy Network, which specializes in trailers calculated to scare you off the actual product, has been running -- for what seems like an eternity -- a clip of Mercer saying "Today is flag day. Settle down, Stephen Harper, I said flag day." Well, you can't accuse them of false advertising. In its combination of lame joke and unctuous delivery, that line is perfect Mercer.

Settling down on Tuesday for an evening of CBC comedy (I earn my pay), I was a little dashed to find that the night's Rick Mercer Report was a repeat from February. But if they can rerun it, I can revile it.

Mercer's idea of humour seems to be to attend an event and have himself filmed there, grinning. On this show, he paid a call on Defence Research and Development Canada, got strapped into some whirling device, and mystifyingly remarked, " It's like my brother's wedding all over again." Later he went to the Canadian Auto Show, where he conducted interviews on the probing level of Entertainment Tonight.

For topicality, we had The Front Page, with snarky comments at which the audience laughed before the punch-lines, which sounded suspicious to me, and The Rant, in which Rick talks and walks very fast while the camera shoots him at 45-degree angles. He gave us " A Message from Elections Canada: Lower Your Expectations." Well, that might be worth a smile; the audience squealed.

This show turns up the laugh track, and the music, very loud. Like it has something to conceal. To be fair, Mercer can do better than this. He was an impressively crisp host on Canada's Next Great Prime Minister a few weeks ago, though Paul Martin on the judging panel had slyer comic timing.

After Mercer's frenzy, the more laid-back This Hour Has 22 Minutes came as a relief. It wasn't much funnier though. I think the best bit featured a thin girl on an exercise bike ("Ellen O'Hanlon, fitness enthusiast"), lamenting the privileges afforded to fat people ("They get 12 square meals a day"). But I'm stretching even to find that. This Hour fancies itself as more cutting-edge than Air Farce, but it seems like the same show done by younger people. (For years, I thought it was the same show.) Air Farce has recently said that it never set out to be satire, just

to be funny, but in practice it adheres to the same lame philosophy as the other shows: the belief that satire consists of mentioning a politician by name. And if you do it on CBC? Wow, you're brave. Actually, the funniest moments on Tuesday night came during the commercial breaks. Peter Mansbridge, trailing The National, buttonholed us through the screen Mercer-style and promised to tell us "why broadcasters want more money -- meaning you might pay more." But he is a broadcaster (isn't he?). An ad for the corp's new Bold channel promised us Intelligent Drama. Audacious Comedy. So that's where they're putting it.

Black & White Photo: Cbc / Rick Mercer plies his antics with musician Anne Murray. On his frenzied show, Rick Mercer Report, the Newfoundlander has an unctuous mien. ; Black & White Photo: / Jessica Holmes parodies Britney Spears on CBC's Air Farce Live, the best of the corp's Big Three comedy shows. ;; Caption:

Air Farce has recently said that it never set out to be satire, just to be funny, but in practice it adheres to the same lame philosophy as the other shows: the belief that satire consists of mentioning a politician by name. And if you do it on CBC? Wow, you're brave.

Actually, the funniest moments on Tuesday night came during the commercial breaks. Peter Mansbridge, trailing The National, buttonholed us through the screen Mercer-style and promised to tell us "why broadcasters want more money --meaning you might pay more." But he is a broadcaster (isnt he?). An ad for the corps new Bold channel promised us Intelligent

Drama. Audacious Comedy.

So that's where they're putting it.

2008-04-12-incomprehensible-but-on-purpo:
One of the characters in George F. Walker's Beyond Mozambique is Rocco, an Italian doctor with a Nazi past. These days, he lives in a well-appointed shack in some African country that presumably isn't Mozambique, and experiments on recently deceased human bodies in the hopes, he says, of finding a universal cure for cancer. His customary attire is jungle casual, but some mornings he puts on a tuxedo. This is to oblige his wife, Olga, who believes that she is her Chekhovian namesake from Three Sisters. She insists, though few would have guessed it to be an old Russian custom, on people dressing for breakfast.

The play is early Walker -- from 1974, when the actual Mozambique was still a year from independence while the Toronto theatre was revelling in having acquired it -- and its other characters have gone similarly Beyond. There is Tomas, a brain-damaged young Greek who supplies Rocco with fresh cadavers, not all of them by mere blameless grave-robbing. There is the Corporal, a trigger-happy ex-Mountie (the shows only gesture to Canadian content) who comprises the entire local police force and likes to have sex with 11-year-old girls. There is Father LiDuc -- half-Chinese, not that it shows -- the latest in a line of problematic priests sent out hebre by the Church in the reasonable hope that they wont come back; his particular hang-up is drugs, for which his tastes seem appropriately catholic. And there is Rita, a former porn star, whiling away the time until her boyfriend gets out of jail (for beating her up) and can produce her in an artistic sex film; she wants to be Susan Hayward in The Snows of Kilimanjaro or Rita Hay-worth in anything.

Well, doesn't that all sound like fun. Bits of it are. The young Walker arrived on the Toronto indie scene full of verbal flair and with a script stacked with monomaniacs. His gambit, like that of the British Joe Orton in the previous decade, is to treat the outrageous as normal, or at most as slightly vexatious. (You've murdered Old Joseph, Rocco admonishes Tomas one minute from the start. "I taught that old man to play dominos.") Orton loved to expose respectable hypocrisy while still showing it triumphant; Walker, here at least, is showing white society crumbling from within while besieged from without. Offstage, the natives are restless. At least, theyre going in for distant drumming which, over the course of the evening, becomes steadily less distant.

The difference between Orton and early Walker is that the former supplied firm farcical structures, leading to a climax. In Beyond Mozambique, the characters just flail around for the duration, exhibiting what an earlier era would have called their humours. Sometimes they get in one anothers way, but there's no real conflict or contact, and no build. There is indeed a climax. The alien sextet -- one of whom is by now technically dead, but that doesn't bother anyone -- are cornered by the indigenous insurgents, who send them a bloodstained message that reads "entertain us." The reviews from 30 years ago suggest that this was regarded as all very meta-theatrical; the rebellion was a mere symbol for the assumed displeasure of a bourgeois audience that had had too much. (Or maybe a radical audience that hadnt had enough. You never know.) Even now, its possible to feel more than a twinge of sympathy with the rebels' demand. It's what the relationship of audience to players should be: Weve shown up, you deliver. Nowadays, though, were less bothered about the nature of theatre, and we're likelier to take the ending straight. The Africans are saying "all right, let's see this culture of yours" and the Europeans respond with gobbets of Chekhov (Olgas obsession comes in handy here), backed by Tchaikovsky. Of course, Chekhov has always been Torontos (and many other places') favourite modern classic, so maybe Walker was being locally satiric after all. Or maybe he just wanted a flashy ending.

If he was arraigning Western decadence, I can't help thinking that lumping together porno-flicks with concentration camp experiments is being hyper-moralistic. Probably its all show; I cant believe that Walker was really intending to anticipate the ethical stance of Iranian President Ahmadinejad. Anyway this and much else is rendered moot in Ken Gass' revival, which unfolds in jerks and is vocally muddy to the point of incoherence. The performances arrange themselves on a steeply sliding scale. At the top of accomplishment is Sarah Orenstein, who sets up Olga as the type of the haughty, somewhat sexualized high comedienne, and clings to the convention like grim death. Joe Cobden comes in a good second as the doped-up padre, whom he plays with a kind of unshockable innocence that, come to think of it, typifies the play. (He may have the best single line when he describes the incurable insanity of both his parents as "a bizarre game of one-upmanship.") Somewhere in the middle are Dmitry Chepotevky's Tomas, who is meant to be incomprehensible, at least some of the time, and Richard Zeppieri, who makes the Corporals role seem unactable but has the excuse that it probably is. At the bottom are Tara Nicodemos Rita, with a delivery that strangles her words at birth, and--in the crucial role of Rocco -- Oliver Becker. This is an actor excellent at playing uncouth. But Rocco has to be thoroughly couth, at least on the surface. If he isn't, the play has nothing to mourn and nothing to demolish. That's on top of the fact that he too swallows his words so that vital information never gets dispensed. The play comes through as a curiosity. We also, the author included, have moved beyond.

- Beyond Mozambique runs through May 4 at the Factory Theatre; 416-504-9971.
