2008-04-15-tragedy-on-the-periphery:
Colleen Murphy's The December Man is a play prompted by the 1989 Mont-real Massacre. It invents a story peripheral to the main event and tells it backwards. That may sound doubly, if not triply, perverse. In fact the choices turn out to be inspired and the execution, by both the author and her interpreters, virtually flawless. Micheline Chevrier's production, a collaboration between Canadian Stage and Edmonton's Citadel Theatre, was received on its Toronto first night with pin-drop concentration, a signal achievement for a play with no intermission and a minimal number of laughs.

It's grim but it isn't heavy. Much of it is familiar domestic drama raised to an unfamiliar level. We start with a middle-aged, working-class couple, Benoit and Kathleen, who seem to be preparing their home for a special occasion. John Ferguson's set is perfect, with just the right degree of respectable chintz, and with a quiet ceremonial air to it that turns out to be absolutely appropriate. We think for a moment that these are parents preparing a celebration of their son's graduation. It turns out that they are executing a suicide pact, and they want the place to look nice when they're found. It's one of the play's accomplishments that their concern, Kathleen's especially, for propriety comes to seem honourable rather than ridiculous. We learn that they did have a son, Jean, and that he has killed himself ahead of them.

Jean was one of the male engineering students present in the room at the Ecole Polytechnique that was invaded by Marc Lepine, and, like all the other men, he was ushered out of the room before the slaughter of the women began. His guilt never left him. It took various forms. He learned karate, so as to be more prepared were there ever a next time. He stopped going to classes by day and stayed out all night, haunting movie theatres. (He saw Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles II, twice.) The model building that was his course project, and whose specifics he had explained to his semi-comprehending but proud and fascinated father, didn't work out; he couldn't get it to balance properly. Finally, he hanged himself. I'm not giving any of this unfairly away here. The play's construction means that it is its own spoiler alert

We're taken back, step by step, through the months that followed Jean's death and then through the months that preceded it. Just about everything rings true. Benoit and Kathleen squabble with one another and with their son like any family, especially one in which the parents have invested all their pride and all their hope in an only child who's almost bound to seem unresponsive. Most people get through stuff like this; these people are thrown into a situation in which they can't. Benoit works on an assembly line whose management has waited decades to install air conditioning; Kathleen was a cleaner, though she gave that up after losing Jean, thereby -- at least in her husband's estimation -- making her state of mind even worse. He, meanwhile, drinks and smokes. Kathleen, a devout Catholic, is sure she'll be reunited with Jean in heaven. Benoit is far less sure; there's a weird sense, coinciding with his undoubted weariness, that he is going

through with their plan partly to oblige his wife. They bicker over many things, but they would never let one another down. Brian Dooley and Nicola Lipman superbly embody both the strengths and the stresses of the marital bond. He's a big, caring and impatient man with a load of justified resentments and the usual fears and inhibitions about communicating with his son. Where the father blusters, the mother nags; she's a worrier whose world collapses when she has no one to worry for. Mourning does not become her. Not every couple would end the story as they do, but we believe that this one would, ordinary though the partners seem. The play makes ineluctable tragedy out of the mundane, like prime Arthur Miller: Death of a Salesman and His Wife, perhaps. In its end is its beginning, and it works both ways.

This means that the dramatic climax has to be the story's start. The author lays out for herself the task of dramatizing the terrible day as it would have appeared to these people -- the casual turning on of the TV, the frantic telephoning that would be comic in another context, the overwhelming but temporary relief--and she brings it off with total conviction. A rather similar challenge confronts the actor who plays Jean, who only comes onstage halfway through, after what I can only describe as one hell of a retrospective buildup. This, too, is brilliantly met, with Jeff Irving conveying the essence of a walking nightmare, shifting between blankness and hysteria. There is a hint that one of the murdered women was his girlfriend, or at least that he would have liked her to be. (The hint is dropped twice: the only instance of the play's overplaying its hand.) The actual details of the massacre are sparingly mentioned, but they're omnipresent; we catch glimpses of them in Kathleen's bitter acknowledgment of how many lives were wrecked, even her irrational jealousy of how some other victims were buried. Christmas is a recurring image in the play. There could be many other ways of dramatizing that one horrific December day, but it's hard to believe that there could be one more effective. - In Toronto until May 17. For more information, call 416-368-3110.

2008-04-17-elite-never-sounded-so-sweet-:
Jon Stewart said something on Monday night that I had given up hope of hearing on television. He said "I always thought elite meant good." He had been running the usual barrage of mind-numbing clips denouncing Barack Obama's "elitism." He then added, unanswerably, "If you don't think you're better than us, what the [bleep] do you think you're doing running for president?"

And when I hear a Canadian comedian come up with a line as smart and as heartfelt as that, I shall retract my criticisms of CBC's attempts at topical satire.

CBC itself has come under fire recently both for being elitist and for not being elitist enough. Last Thursday's Globe and Mail featured directly opposed columns on this matter by John Doyle, TV critic, and Russell Smith, pundit. Smith's article was the summation -- to date, anyway -- of his attacks on CBC radio for cutting down on its quota of classical music. Doyle has been responding by saying a) that any threat on that front is dwarfed by the censorship proposals implicit in Bill C-10, and b) that there's quite enough classical music available anyway. He's right about a), especially in light of the bill's ugly little phrase about art that's "contrary to public policy"; the response to b) must be that it depends where you live.

Anyway, Doyle went on to counter what he identified as "the widespread belief ... that CBC has come under fire both for being elitist and not elitist enough television isn't culture, it's lowbrow rubbish" by saying that, if you look beneath the surface, a popular show like The Office "illuminates the human condition" (indeed, and you don't have to look very far beneath) and that even ER instructs us that doctors have "very human foibles when it comes to human relationships." Well, yes, it does; so has every medical drama since Dr. Kildare and probably beyond, and it's hard to believe that most people didn't know it anyway. Complex drama means more than acknowledging that people can have jobs and sex lives. Doyle has a point, but when it comes to men in scrubs on soaps, he's pushing it. Smith's article pounces on the question of complexity. Complex art, he writes, has been regarded, traditionally and rightly, as more serious, longer-lasting, than simple art. Therefore, classical music has more right to subsidized airtime than the popular music with which the CBC proposes to replace some of it.

A problem here is that the phrase "classical music" muddies the waters. When we talk about a classic novel, or a classic play, or a classic painting, we're not talking about a particular kind of piece; we merely mean one that has been around long enough to have proved its survival value. More bluntly, we mean something old. "Classical music" can be new. It's a genre, hard to define but possible to recognize, if only by the negative qualities of not being pop or jazz and of being performed in concert halls and opera houses.

I have long nurtured the suspicion that when we say we want art that's "demanding" or "challenging" or even "offensive," we really mean we want it to be those things for other people. We ourselves have already met the demands, faced the challenges, swallowed the offence. I also think that what music you're comfortable with is very much determined by where, chronologically, your ears came in. I do agree that classical music, old or new, should have the greatest presence on CBC Radio 2, but I don't see why pop or jazz should be excluded as long as they're of the kind you can't readily hear elsewhere. As long, too, as they're presented in an illuminating way; they should be given the kind of context for which most commercial stations wouldn't have the time. And the management shouldn't be spooked by the idea that they might be catering to a minority audience. Minorities can be quite large. Even sport is a minority interest, hard though some people may find it to believe. In fact, with the possible exception of the weather reports, there's no type of program that interests everybody.

In this week's National Post, Marni Soupcoff made the case for abolishing all government funding for the arts. But her argument is historically flawed. There's always been subsidy. The great Florentine painters were subsidized by the Medicis, who were the government. The Athenian theatre festivals, on which the whole tradition of Western drama depends, were vast civic events. I want the CBC to get more money, not less. I want CBC radio to remain commercial-free and -- wild flight of fancy-- CBC television to return to being so. (The BBC has managed it, and for all its compromises it remains a beacon. British culture would be a wilderness without it.) I'd like to see a mindset in TV drama that glories in real achievements, rather than one that turns down Slings and Arrows, frets over the ratings for The Englishman's Boy and professes disenchantment with the narrative serial -- the one thing television can do better than any other performing medium. I would be happy to see the banishment of "reality TV." Just as -- to return to Stewart on Obama, and to Obama himself--I welcome broadcasters and even politicians who can express reasonably complicated thoughts, even if this lets their opponents thrash them in sound bites. Stewart actually offers the perfect wordplay for the CBC. It doesn't need to be "elitist." It does need to be elite.

Color Photo: Darren Stone, CanWest News Service / Protesters at the CBC Radio 2 studio in Victoria showed that classical fans aren't going to take the proposed changes to the station lying down. ;; Caption:
2008-04-18-between-kafka-and-arar-extrao:
A ccording to TVO, Extraordinary Rendition is very loosely inspired by the case of Canadian Maher Arar. The basing, if thats a word, seems to have been very loose indeed. In fact there's no internal evidence that the makers of this British film had the Arar case anywhere on their minds.

The story told here resembles the Canadian one in that its central character is kidnapped by secret service agents, flown to a Middle Eastern country to be interrogated on suspicion of having links to terrorist organizations, tortured into making a confession, and eventually released.

But Zaafir, the protagonist, is a British citizen seized not in an airport but on a London street, and his government seems totally unaware of his plight. There isn't even the token intervention offered by Canadian officials during Arars imprisonment, and there seems no question when Zaafir returns home of his being awarded any compensation. Canadian viewers lured in by the publicity may be either bemused or relieved to find that, in this telling, Canada is completely off the hook. It looks for a time as if the United States will be, too. Zaafir seems to have been abducted by homegrown operatives with a semi-official mandate, sounding as nasty as only British thugs in British TV films can. Were well into the story before we find that they're in cahoots with the CIA.

Zaafir (Omar Berdouni) is a college teacher, Muslim by religion and of Pakistani origin, with a newly pregnant, and Catholic, wife (Ania Sowinski). We see him before, during, and after his ordeal, though part of the point is that in experiences like this there really isn't any "after." The physical scars may heal, but the psychological ones remain indefinitely.

To drive this home, the three time frames are scrambled together. When Zaafir is in his cell or in the torture chamber, he hallucinates about his wife; when hes reunited with her, he hallucinates about when they were apart. Which is very credible, but no great revelation.

In fact Jim Threapletons film doesn't reveal much at all; his script is too little and his direction too much. The music, pounding or scraping, is constant, the dialogue muted, the editing jumpy and the chronology, as noted, scrambled. The intention must be to make us feel Zaafir's ordeal for ourselves, but what were mostly aware of us is the films technique. The precise locale of the rendition is left indeterminate. So is the background, and certainly the accent, of the chief inquisitor, though the fact that he's played by Andy Serkis may send extra chills down a viewer's spine. If you were going to be interrogated, you wouldnt want it to be done by Gollum in hot pursuit of his precious.

Or, in this film, in cool pursuit. Serkis plays good cop, lamenting that the people around him are animals. This statement, of course, means that he himself is the silkiest animal in the pack, continually complaining about how all this giving orders for beatings and waterboardings is preventing him from spending quality time with his family.

A subtler part of his method is to tell Zaafir as little as possible not only about where hes being held but why. Unfortunately, this leaves the audience as much in the dark as the victim. This isn't Kafka; we're dealing with a specific kind of abuse thats happening now. We dont need arty atmospherics to persuade us that torture and rendition are unspeakable practices. We could do with some insight into how it's allowed to happen and what it's supposed to achieve. In Zaafirs case this remains thoroughly obscure. Once hes confessed, he's released. The film starts with him being repatriated, i.e. unloaded at dead of night in a deserted British airport, bruised and confused, to the horror of the security staff. Everything else is flashback, or flashback within flashback.

Much the most interesting part comes, chronologically, after the release. To Zaafir, every conversation now seems like an interrogation. Even his wife loses patience. She sympathizes but she cannot comprehend. Neither can the official helpers. A wearily pedantic functionary (well played by Hugh Ross, though I couldn't tell whether he was meant to be a lawyer, psychiatrist, or civil servant) asks, "Were you maltreated?" Zaafir, understandably, storms out of the office.

The film starts with a caption: "Men without conscience are capable of any cruelty the human mind can imagine." It ends with another, more dryly informing us that there are currently 39 abduction complaints against the CIA. Those two statements provide more food for thought, and even for nightmares, than anything that comes between. - Extraordinary Rendition airs Sunday at 9 p.m. on TVO.
2008-04-19-on-this-front-it-s-not-so-pop:
For the second time in a row, the main stage at Theatre Passe Muraille is given over to a show that doesn't deserve to be there. The two cases aren't identical. Last month's Last Days of Graceland placed an implausible story in an impossible locale. The credibility of People Power, the new occupant, cannot be challenged either on the grounds of narrative or of setting. This is a history play, set in the Philippines during the Marcos years. It covers the 14-year period between the assassination of opposition senator Ninoy Aquino, and the flight, by popular demand and with American assistance, of the president with his family, and his replacement by the murdered man's widow, Cory. That's a lot to take on, more than this production has the resources for or, as far as I can determine, the ability to bring off.

Last Days of Graceland was scarred by bad acting. So is People Power, more consistently -- omnipresently, in fact -- but also more forgivably. For one thing, the players, members of a Filipino-Canadian troupe called Carlos Bulosan Theatre, are dealing with a subject close to their own hearts; a lot of emotion bounces off the stage and a certain amount of sympathy ripples back. For another, the actors are hobbled by their script, though since it's literally their script -- they wrote it themselves -- this really is a matter of withholding blame with one hand while bestowing it with the other. Which hand is which is hard to decide; maybe the woodenness of the acting is due to the banality of the script or maybe it's the other way around. Either way, it rarely sounds like real people talking. Best just to list the five creators (Leon Aureus, Rose Cortez, Nicco Garcia, Christine Mangosing, Nadine Villasin) and their director-dramaturge (Nina Lee Aquino, presumably no relation and certainly none that the program mentions) and move on.

People Power is a tribute to a popular movement that resulted in a non-violent revolution. But it portrays it in a sentimental-grotesque fashion that's not so much simplified as simplistic. The Marcoses themselves make token appearances, but they aren't even cartoons, just cardboard cut-outs. Also, though the show makes a point of impugning their attempts at populist ingratiation-- trying to win over the populace with fake smiles and sanctimonious slogans -- it uses exactly the same tactics itself. I've rarely seen so many excruciating excursions into the audience.

The majority of the characters are representative fictions. The constant doubling and the low-definition performances make the permutations difficult to follow, but mostly they seem to divide into heroic rebels, government stooges and in-betweens. There are a couple of society ladies who sip expensive drinks, complain about the help and share enthusiastically in the first lady's celebrated footwear fetish. One of them is a newspaper editor's daughter who's severely critical of her photographer-husband's penchant for taking pictures that might be embarrassing to the regime. Later she changes sides, though whether that's due to an access of conscience or to a sense of where her bread might henceforth be buttered is left unclear.

One corner of the stage houses recurrent scenes in a brothel where GIs stationed in Manila humiliate the girls, who alternately dream of revenge and escape. ("Yankees go home -- and take me with you;" it's the best line of the evening, though reminiscent of Miss Saigon without the songs, just as much of the rest suggests Evita.)

On an upper level, and in a scene that might take some kind of prize for confused staging, Filipino emigres in a far country that might be California are intimidated by agents of the CIA. We meet a prosperous family -- self-made father, self-righteous mother, one idealistic daughter and one complacent one -- apparently designed to symbolize the entire conflict. "What tortured people?" asks mama, newly informed of human-rights abuses and gazing around the stage as if she expected them to be visible from her dining table. "I don't see them." It's an all too typical moment. Intentionally or not, the show caricatures the people it disapproves of and sentimentalizes those it likes. Its feelings may be sincere, but its methods are second-hand.

Camellia Koo's set, well-furnished with oil-drums and festooned with stickers marked either "Marcos" or "Aquino," gives us the trappings of conflict, but if the people don't carry conviction either as symbols or as individuals, we've no reason to care.

And there's an additional handicap, one that's unusual in political drama: The story has a happy ending. What the play wants to happen, happened. Generally, shows designed to involve us in struggle leave us with the feeling that the struggle is still going on and that we'd all better sign up for it. I'm usually a sucker in the theatre for Popular Front rhetoric, but this time my blood refused to race. It just didn't feel the need. I have to report that there was a standing ovation on the opening night, but I suspect that it was partisan. It was cheering the Cause, not the effects.

- People Power runs through May 11 at Theatre Passe Muraille. Call 416-504-7529 for ticket information.

2008-04-22-don-t-blink-or-you-ll-miss-th:
Sky Gilbert's self-described "very gay little musical" starts with a song en-titled We're Much Too Drunk To Write a Musical, which is very disarming of it. As it turns out, Happy is a show that needs all the disarmament it can muster. It's not without its charms, but it deconstructs itself at such a rate that not only does it leave nothing standing, it hardly gets around to building anything in the first place.

Even the one-word title is a snare. It's presumably a joke on the more traditional meaning of "gay:" It also seems to be ironic, in that the story concerns a married male couple who think they've found a contented life together even if their author is positive that they haven't. (Sky Gilbert, meet Michael Coren. Different premises, same conclusion.) And that's before we get to the subtitle, which both mocks and reaffirms the belief that the musical is an inherently gay medium. (Doesn't work for Guys and Dolls, to name but one.) And this musical is certainly "little;" it has a duration of an hour and a quarter, a cast of four, pre-recorded piano accompaniment that frequently drowns out the unamplified singers and a score containing just three numbers. The rest of the evening is dialogue, though that's just as well since dialogue remains what Gilbert does best.

Now concentrate. That opening song is performed by Bob, a playwright and lyricist, and Sue, dramaturge and (again self-described) fag hag. Later they're joined by Dave, the composer who is Bob's personal and professional partner, and then by a young man who gains entry by claiming to be selling subscriptions for something called the Evening Star. Once in, he announces (in song) that he's AIDS. Not that he suffers from it: that he is it. Then there's a blackout, during which posters for the Xtra, the gay Toronto weekly, and Follies, the apogee of cult musicals, disappear from the walls of Bob's apartment. Camp, in other words, has been struck. We realize that Bob and Sue and Dave are writing a musical about Bob and Sue and Dave writing a musical, and that the musical they've been writing is the one that, up to this point but no longer, we have been seeing. What we're now seeing is a musical about the musical (about a musical) that they've been writing.

And the musical they were writing is about gay marriage, and it glorifies the union of Bob and Dave as being devoted but chaste. Only the real Bob is a hypocrite because he's been carrying on with the Evening Star boy who now reappears in his own person rather than as a symbol for AIDS. Now you might think that if Bob and Dave have found an arrangement that works for them, even with loopholes, that's a good thing and nobody's business but their own. Their author, however -- and this time I mean Gilbert -- seems more inclined to upbraid them for forsaking the promiscuity that he seems to think synonymous with homosexuality. Admittedly, this is less evident from the piece itself that from the surrounding literature and from some first-night guffaws from clued-in members of the audience.

Micah Barnes' music is traditional show-tune, jolly but undistinguished. Gilbert's lyrics are hard to judge since they mostly can't be heard. None of the men can sing them, and even Sharron Matthews, usually a musical-theatre dynamo, sinks beneath sound level, at least until she gets to belt out a solo, a sadder-but-wiser number in the line of The Ladies Who Lunch. Where Matthews really surprises is in her acting; she handles her speeches and her reactions with unsuspected ease, force and even subtlety. David Tomlinson captures the two sides of Bob, the prig and the slob; Jamieson Eakin makes something touching of a lost-boy stereotype, and though Jason Cadieux has little to do as Dave, he seems quite nice.

Part of Gilbert's purpose seems to be to blame gay authors of musicals, especially successful ones, for not dealing with gay subjects. He also has a go at fellow playwrights, taking potshots at Brad Fraser for depicting just such a lifestyle as he himself seems to be advocating. No, wait, that's in the play-within-the-play -- the hypocritical one -- so maybe it doesn't count. Either way, a piece as flimsy as this is hardly a solid foundation from which to attack other writers. In this show -- it isn't true of all his plays -- Gilbert doesn't seem to like anyone very much, including his own characters. As Bertolt Brecht so very nearly said, Happy is the show that needs no heroes. - Happy: A Very Gay Little Musical runs at the Buddies in Bad Times Theatre, 12 Alexander St., until April 27, 2008. Call 416-975-8555 for more information.

Black & White Photo: Courtesy Buddies In Bad Times / David Tomlinson, left, and Jason Cadeaux star in Happy. ;; Caption:
2008-04-23-pre-confederate-drudgery-work:
Each episode of Working Over Time begins with Jeff Douglas telling us about Donald Alexander Smith. He was the railroad financier and Hudson's Bay Company director who got to drive in the last celebratory spike on the Canadian Pacific Railroad. We get a momentary shot of Douglas impersonating Smith, looking every inch the Victorian worthy. Then we get a shot of him, looking not too impressed by the ceremony, as one of "the guys who drove all the other spikes." The series is about that guy, and about all those who came before and after him, doing all the impossible backbreaking jobs that created this country. It is in fact an alternative history of Canada.

It's a lot more gleeful than that sounds, largely due to the personality and the methods of Douglas himself. He takes us across the continent and down the centuries, finding out the things people had to do, doing them himself and conscientiously dressing for each part. He's delighfully informative and self-deprecating. Being taught by experts -- either those who are still obliged to live in the old ways or who are doing it as some kind of project -- he has repeated shots at doing as they do. Most of the time, he's not very good at it. But he isn't disgracefully bad either, and there's nothing demeaning about the process, either for him or for us. When he laughs at himself, as he frequently does -- either at the time or in retrospective commentary -- the laughter is warming, sometimes even healing.

Tonight's first episode, "Staying Alive," begins briskly with the injunction that "13,000 years ago, man's first job was to survive." Douglas is in moccassins -- maybe we've moved on a couple of millennia -- as he says that the ability to make fire in the most primitive circumstances was "the difference between life and death," and adds, "I guess I would have died." The next job was "to make a weapon out of a rock --hunting large animals before the arrow was invented." Cue shots of animals on cave walls, and Douglas being handed an Aztec weapon which might, he muses, have been used to hunt a mammoth. And then there was the business of skinning it.

That's just in comparatively temperate zones. We move to the Arctic, where "it's not too easy to find something to eat" and "I may get the chance to kill a baby seal--not sure how I feel about that." He learns to build a shelter, and then, shifting ground again to Queen Charlotte's Island on the West Coast, to take a giant tree and turn it into an ocean-going canoe. "They used these canoes to travel far distances; even" -- here's a jaw-dropper -- "as far as Japan." But trade and exploration cut both ways and, over on the other side of the country, Canada got its first European visitors. A thousand years ago the Vikings arrived, and "there goes the neighbourhood." Even the Vikings get some sympathy, though, as they'd come here in search of "low-grade bog ore," which you'd find just where you'd expect. Skipping a few more centuries, we also get to identify with the Jesuits who branched out from Quebec as missionaries to the First Nations but found that the tribes had a lot to teach them--about snowshoes, for example. We learn that, sleeping in log-houses, fifty people to a dorm, there was so much smoke you might go blind or die of a respiratory disease. There were other intruders with worldlier aims -- the Hudson's Bay company, for example. "It looks like the white guys are planning on staying, and that can't be good."

Tomorrow's episode shows that those white guys had at least to earn their keep. We backtrack to 1497, with John Cabot arriving, along with "18 to 20 guys from Bristol who did the actual work" but who found it preferable to staying in jail. Flash forward to 1837, and I mean "flash" because that is when somebody had the literally bright idea of building a lighthouse to cut down on the ships that were being wrecked on the coast of "New-found-land" (Douglas does deliver the province's name like that). We've always known that lighthouse-keeping was a lonely life, but did you realize that the light had to be re-charged every two hours, so someone in the family had to stay up all night? There were more companionable jobs. You could be a pioneer, learn how to plough and to flail ("Flail the grain," says Douglas' kindly instructor, "don't flail yourself"). It seems the only job tougher than the pioneer's was that of the pioneer's wife, keeping house and slaving over a hot log fire. A helpful lady (from a present-day pioneer village?) fills in a few more details. "Most of the time you're pregnant. It's a very difficult job." And kids at a later stage of development are naturally rambunctious. "Don't pull on Mommy's skirt," says Douglas, who at this point is wearing one, along with apron and mob cap, "mommy's trying to work here."

Not surprisingly, Douglas decides that what he always wanted to be was a lumberjack. He hadn't realized that this involved getting from the lower part of the tree to the higher, literally on a springboard. It's scary. It's also, like the whole show, a little exhilarating to watch, and a little shaming. And there's better or worse to come. This is Douglas's promise for the rest of the week: "We're gonna build towns [and] cities and come up with some of the messiest, smelliest, dirtiest jobs ever devised by the mind of man. I'm looking forward to it." - Working Over Time airs on History Television at 2 p.mand 9 p.m. until Friday.

2008-04-24-finding-drama-in-clinton-vs-o:
First they vamp till ready, then they pontificate. At 8:40 p.m., with the first actual vote results trickling in, the Fox Network decided to chance its arm. "Fox News projects Hillary the winner" it said in determined you-heard-it-here-first tones. This was as exciting as Tuesday evening got. The folks at CNN were a little more cautious; it took them another twenty minutes to project Hillary the winner. A projection sounds more scientific than a prediction, and CNN in particular had batteries of charts and statistics with which to back up its forecasts. They had to have something to while away the hours.

I had forgotten just how tedious election coverage, and primary coverage in particular, can be. It really isn't anyone's fault. We have an essentially static situation that, by tacit consent, has to be covered on a minute-by-minute basis. It started with all the commentators fixating on the exit polls while simultaneously assuring us that these didn't really count for anything. Nevertheless they persisted, rattling off the candidates' constituencies: young, black and Protestant for Obama, old, female and Catholic for Clinton. All were agreed that this was Hillary's race to lose. When it was clear that she wouldn't lose it, they spent the rest of the night telling us that they'd told us so. Their unanimity, as a playwright once said about the rare occasions when people on stage agree about anything, was wonderful. They also reiterated that this still left Obama ahead in the competition for the actual nomination, especially with his campaign having more money in the bank. Everyone took for granted that more money entitles you to an electoral advantage: A dismal phenomenon -- and I'm an Obama fan-- that might have merited some discussion but didn't get any.

A peculiarity of the coverage was that the format and the personnel on each network remained constant whatever program was ostensibly playing: Larry King Live was Larry King absent, and if Bill O'Reilly was present on his own show, he was uncharacteristically bashful about it. CNN had, as mentioned, the classier graphics. Wolf Blitzer stood by, with every appearance of comprehension, while a man with a pointer explained with the aid of three adjacent pie-charts how big a slice Hillary could hope to consume in any number of demographic contingencies. My head spun. Later they ran a map of the state, divided into regions, into light and

dark blue (I guess it's too late to change this confusing convention) according to probable electoral preference. Barack, we were informed, absolutely needed to win the bottom right-hand corner. We had barely absorbed this before being shown the same map as it might have appeared in previous contests. The things they can do with a flick of the switch, or whatever they use nowadays.

Periodically, CNN would leave Wolf at the door and travel to another part of the studio where Campbell Brown, looking peremptorily in charge, would interrogate her panel of experts, all chained to their lap-tops. There was one designated Clintonite, one for Obama, one real live superdelegate (with pronounced Obama leanings) and David Gergen, who did very well as resident wise man. Over on Fox, which one might have expected to be frothing with Republican disdain, the equivalent team was surprisingly restrained. If they were delighted at the spectacle of the opposition tearing itself in half so their own man could pick up the pieces, they weren't showing it. There was some rare tension in the studio when they seemed unable to locate Karl Rove (current job description: Fox News political analyst) but when he did materialize, with no horns visible, he too sounded reasonable and respectful. Maybe it's a plot. Fox commentators got very insistent about the prospect of Howard Dean's knocking his candidates' heads together and forcing them into a dream team--one that might easily become a nightmare and not just for the Republicans.

Otherwise, the most drama came in watching the leap of Hillary's advantage from 8% ("doesn't matter") to 10% ("this means business"). The greatest suspense came from wondering just how long the captions at the bottom of the screen could keep telling us we were "Moments Away from Clinton Victory Speech." At last Hillary mounted the podium (husband to the side of it, looking as if it wasn't his proper place) and ... how to put this ... conceded victory. She was courteous about Obama, and when his turn came, he was the same about her -- in the teeth, I must say, of some of his rowdier supporters. Barack can tell a very good joke, but otherwise rarely smiles; Hillary never says anything funny but smiles all the time. His oration was stirring stuff, and though he couldn't have been making those rolling periods up as he went along, he sounded as though he might be. I know that great speech-making isn't all it takes to make a president, but it isn't as if the electoral process -- in America or anywhere else -- gives a candidate a chance to demonstrate anything else. Or that the media, obsessed with "image" and how things will "play," would want it to. There was one hopeful sign: Later on, a Fox anchor badgered a couple of correspondents about whether "bitter" (that word has become journalistic shorthand, which is depressing in itself ) had done Obama any harm. Neither thought it had. If Obama can do nothing but raise the standard of political discourse, that will be something. It might even filter down to television.

2008-04-26-of-haggis-and-hummus-in-david:
The World Stage season brings to Harbourfront a Scottish play set in the Middle East: a double slice of exotica.

Damascus comes from the justly fabled Traverse Theatre in Edinburgh, which has maintained a reputation for literary experiments for over 45 years. Its the work of David Greig, a scarily prolific playwright who's also the dramaturge for the National Theatre of Scotland. Some of it has a rewarding thickness of text and texture beyond our usual expectations. Some more of it -- it's a long play by current standards -- feels like filler: intelligently selected but oddly placed.

Our protagonist is Paul, like his author -- who has taught play-writing workshops there -- a Scottish writer on a cultural mission to the Syrian capital. Paul is trying to sell English-as-a-second-language storybooks. We find him in the lobby of a somewhat grand hotel, jet-lagged from the flight in and impatient for the flight out; its Valentines Day and he'd like to be home with his wife. (It seems, all things considered, a badly planned trip.) His departure plans are frustrated by an airport bomb in Beirut. Meanwhile, he negotiates, professionally and personally, with Muna, a junior academic charged with vetting his volume.

Their longest encounter is a richly rewarding duologue that mingles the political, the linguistic and the erotic. Material that Paul had thought innocuous turns out to be highly charged; between the fundamentalists and the modernizers (the majority, according to Muna) he's crossing a minefield. Some of his preconceptions about the Arab world are challenged; though when she accuses the West of using Syria as an offshore torture-chamber, you may feel like shouting back that it couldnt happen without some enthusiastic Syrian cooperation. There is much talk of tenses: of the difficulty of transmitting into Arabic the stiff but subtle English conventions of present, future and past, perfect and imperfect. And this in turn becomes a vehicle of flirtation: Muna, who is younger than Paul, takes on the air of a perpetually postponed Future Indefinite. I cant place it, but I'm sure that somewhere in the Past Perfect I've met this device before, but no matter; Greig and his actors make it their own, Present Dynamic.

Ewen Bremner, playing Paul, is so deeply inside the character that the actual performance sometimes fails to get out; this is especially the case at the beginning when his muted rendition of a phone call home, mostly with his back to us, results in important information going missing. He still catches the essence of the pedantic, conscientious man cut loose from his moorings: the born Mr. Unlucky. Long before the end of the play, you begin to doubt whether hell get out of Damascus alive. (And Im not saying he doesn't, and I'm not saying he does.) Nathalie Armin complements him, almost perfectly, as Muna, feeling the pull, weighing her options. When the two come close to connecting, its like watching a British play that we saw last year at Stratford, David Edgars Pentecost, with its priorities reversed: In this dramatized clash of cultures, the personal trumps the public, in effectiveness if not in intention.

In fact, what goes on around this relationship is something of a blur. This is partly a matter of performance: Philip Howard's production feels like a decent piece of work that's been shipped into a space not so much too large for it as too awkwardly proportioned. But its also in the writing. Syria as a place in itself -- as opposed to part of some generic Middle East -- comes sharply into focus when Muna confronts Paul. But for much of the time, this could be just another story of a European losing and/or finding himself in a mysterious city.

For reasons of dramatic economy, theatrical economics or both, the hotel is strikingly short of both guests and staff. It seems to be run single-handedly by a young receptionist-barman named Zacharias, whose twin ambitions, for both of which he enlists Pauls assistance, are to bed an English-speaking girl and to sell the movie script of his life to Hollywood. He's winningly played by Khalid Laith, but in the end (he gets, surprisingly, the final curtain) he comes off less as a person than as a device. Wasim, Muna's superior (and ex-teacher, and ex-lover), a radical gone tame, might tell us more about the country but he remains, in Alex Elliotts performance, doggedly uninteresting; he and Muna converse in Arabic, which we hear as English, so we know when theyre being rude about Paul but he doesn't. It's similar to a device used in Translations, but it wears thin much quicker.

This may be the only play that recalls both Brian Friels opus and Casablanca (plus a good dozen other movies); its presided over -- from atop a spiral staircase -- by a lady pianist (played with excessive doominess by Dolya Gavanski) who seems, like Zacharias, to work a 24-hour day, supplying music appropriate to every mood and in every style. I'd hoped she might stretch to "we're off on the road to Damascus" -- Hope and Crosby meet St. Paul -- but no joy. As a conception she is, pardon my oxymoron, pure kitsch. Her background is, she tells us repeatedly, as eclectic as her repertoire: ex-Marxist, ex-Christian and transsexual. Presumably, she personifies Damascus, with the implication being that Damascus has something for everyone--but what city haven't you heard that about? Damascus the play has something for some people, but it requires patience.

- Damascus closes today at the Premiere Dance Theatre. Call 416-973-4000 for more information.

2008-04-29-if-only-john-adams-could-be-r:
One of the rousing lines in Hillary Clinton's Philadelphia victory speech was her promise of a return to the family home: "It's a long road to 1600 Pennsylvania Avenue and it runs right through the heart of Pennsylvania." She then asked her listeners to log onto her website and donate the fare to get her there. It's been a long time away, but she did get two terms out of her previous stay. Compare that to the tenure of the first inhabitants, John and Abigail Adams, who hardly had a chance to enjoy the place at all.

That at least is the impression given in John Adams, the HBO series that wrapped up last Sunday having got finer with each successive week. When the Adams moved into the White House it was still under construction, and they had to keep getting out of the way of the decorators. But then there weren't many places they did enjoy.

We had already seen them ill at ease in Paris, out of sorts in London, and -- in John's case -- foaming with frustration in Philly, trying to persuade his fellow delegates to the Continental Congress to act like men and make their defiance of Britain official. (John's view of the hearts of Pennsylvanians seemed notably less rosy than Hillary's.)

It was only on their farm in Massachusetts that they felt at home; and happiness to them meant being in one another's company. If you want a First Couple who could function both as political allies and devoted spouses, here they were. Their marriage lasted 54 years, and one of the signal achievements of the series and of its stars, Paul Giamatti and Laura Linney, was to make their bond believable and, especially at the end, moving.

By many people's accounts -- most definitely including his own -- John Adams was the forgotten man of the American Revolution. So making him the hero of a TV miniseries -- with George Washington, Thomas Jefferson, Benjamin Franklin and Alexander Hamilton reduced to supporting roles -- was a gesture worthy of the man himself.

Adams, who spent the last and crabbiest years of a long and crabby life justifying himself in memoirs and in criticisms of others' memoirs, would have been pleased. Or maybe he wouldn't. Probably he would have dwelt on mistakes and inaccuracies (it's a safe bet that there were many), refusing to hear any defence on the grounds of artistic licence.

The scattershot nature of history is one thing that the miniseries got right. I wrote of the earlier episodes that all the battles happened off-screen; and this remained true of the series as a whole. The only things that happened were deaths. First there was John and Abigail's oldest daughter, also called Abigail, succumbing to breast cancer, but not before undergoing a mastectomy -- without anesthetic, of course. We all but saw the knife go in, and most viewers must have looked away from the scene, praying for the camera to do likewise. (Sarah Polley played the younger Abigail, a role that in previous episodes had hardly tested her; one suspects she signed up mainly for the death scene.)

Then Mrs. Adams went, graciously and sensibly as she had lived, leaving John as piteously bereft as an actor on television has ever seemed. He himself went at age 90, on the very same day -- the Fourth of July, of all amazing dates -- as his old friend and enemy Thomas Jefferson. This phenomenal double coincidence was given a long build-up but, typically, no great pay-off.

The two men were afforded no in-person reconciliation. We heard their letters to one another in voice-over, with all the affecting reticence that period prose, quietly delivered, could afford. It wasn't completely satisfying; the production never seemed quite sure how central it wanted Jefferson to be; he wasn't in the title, he didn't get star billing, but sometimes his relationship to Adams seemed the point. Other times, it disappeared. History's fault, I guess.

The approach had the defects of its virtues, like Adams himself, who emerged as a man whose dignity was all on the inside. As Giamatti played him, he knew he was right but could never clinch the deal in public. We tend to praise great performances for their variety but their secret may actually be a kind of monotony; the actor finds a rhythm and holds to it.

Giamatti's keynote here was arrogance expressed as diffidence, and so bound to offend his hearers on both accounts. He perfected a delivery I'd describe as vocally hunched, as if some truths were too self-evident to need explaining. This made some of the politics hard going; one wanted him to explain himself more.

All the show's faults, though, were on the right side. We've become used to HBO taking the high road with contemporary drama; they've shown here that it's possible in costume as well. Excerpts from contemporary political journalism shows that, in terms of character assassination, our own age has hardly begun.

As for the actual dialogue, I don't know how much of it was reproduced from the record and how much was pastiche, but it sounded wonderful: "He did me and my reputation great insult," said Adams of Jefferson. Imagine the White House crowd talking with such simple force on The West Wing. Imagine them doing it in real life.

2008-05-03-it-was-a-pleasure-waiting-mr-:
And now the guy youve all been waiting for. In Brendan Gall's play Alias Godot, Alon Nashman plays the mystery man himself, the emblematic figure of non-appearance now made manifest. As befits a refugee from the universe of Samuel Beckett, he wears a bowler hat, though one in a better state of repair than you would expect to find on a Beckett tramp; the same applies to the white shirt and dark suit that complete his ensemble. He is, after all, Mr. Godot, a figure, or so we have always been led to believe, of some authority. He also wears handcuffs, since he's being detained in a dilapidated New York cop shop. This is far from any territory you might expect him to inhabit, a fact of which he is uncomfortably aware. There are people far away who expect his presence and, as he tells the two officers whove pulled him in, If I dont arrive quickly, they're likely to endow my absence with undue significance."

He has a mysterious package to deliver, which these days sounds sinister. So think the detectives, uncommonly jittery guys whose names, Vincent and Edward, are at least within shouting distance of Beckett's Vladimir and Estragon. They are joined, or rather invaded (twice, once in each act) by their own Pozzo and Lucky --here called Rocko and Linus -- whose powers outrank those of the police since theyre members of a Terrorism Unit, though as Godot, who has an extremely meticulous mind, points out, that should really be an Anti-Terrorism Unit. They seem grateful for the information.

Gall is divided into two parts, or at least his play is. The part that works is not so much a pastiche of the Beckettian model as a series of riffs on it, and it is hilarious. The other half is an examination of American, and by extension global, paranoia post-9/11, a subject on which it lacks anything new to say. In practice, the dislocation isnt that severe; the two modes overlap and the goodwill generated by the first carries over at least partway into the second. Also, Richard Rose has delivered a superb production; the director and performers paper over all the cracks except for the intentional ones in Teresa Przbylski's brilliantly bleak set, a severe frame on which everything looks good, including the actors' shadows.

Nashman plays the incarcerated Godot with a modest insistence that adds up to a peculiar kind of authority: prissiness so sure of itself, if not of its immediate circumstances, that it approaches the numinous. No wonder he makes his captors feel nervous. The very first thing he says, wonderfully linking the world hes come from to the world hes in, is "I was told I have the right to remain silent." He may have been read his rights, but that doesn't mean he's going to get them. Hes at the mercy of Bad Cop and Dumb Cop. As Victor, the bad one, David Ferry, his hair standing up on his head in a permanent state of greasy alert, gives what may be the performance of his life: The aggression that has seemed forced in some of his recent George Walker performances, here flows freely, set off as it is by the nervousness of a man whos his own ticking bomb scenario. He's permanently at the end of a very frayed tether.

Paul Braunstein's Edward is a good-natured soul adrift who, like his distant cousin Estragon, keeps getting beaten up by unseen gangs: in his case, youthful marauders feasting on what appears to be the corpse of a formerly great metropolis. Among the many other jazzed-up echoes from the source are a coat rack that sprouts leaves and Mr. Godots self-furnished job description as a farmer specializing in sheep and goats. Also, when Rocko and Linus appear, they keep falling over.

If the aggressiveness of Tony Nappos Rocco sometimes seems overdone, consider that the same criticism has been levelled at many Pozzos before him. Geoffrey Pounsett's Linus inherits from his role-model a virtuoso first-act diatribe crammed with verbal garbage -- in this case, it's a montage of police-state protocols, and the one point at which the old and new plays do achieve a kind of symbiosis -- and a second act spent in total silence: also in drag, which is a step beyond Europes Uncle Sam, if not Americas. The interaction between the five characters -- partly carried over, partly new -- has great theatrical impact, certainly in a production as charged with the right kind of energy as this one is.

Actually, the play has yet a third level, as police-procedural, real or parodied, but here it speedily runs out of gas. There's an offstage figure referred to as Jimmy Nicknames, a sort of Godot's Godot; but if Godot was obscure, Jimmy is simply confusing. The play moves towards an apocalyptic finish that it simply hasnt earned. Like Becketts first postwar, Cold War audiences, we bring our own existential dread into the theatre with us; but where his play distilled it into something new and personal, this one just plays with what we already know. People said the same thing 40 years ago about Tom Stoppard's Rosencrantz and Guildenstern Are Dead, another self-confessed Beckett knock-off, but one that also had the thickly populated landscape of Hamlet to draw from. It kept strictly and fruitfully to the rules of the Shakespearean plot. Gall has to invent his own, which proves paradoxically constricting. Also, he isn't as funny as Stoppard. But hes plenty funny, and the play, his first at full-length, is the most scintillating debut weve had this season. - Alias Godot runs through June 1 at the Tarragon. Call 416-531-1827 for ticket information.

2008-05-05-let-this-bea-warning-grand-th:
Edward Roy's latest cautionary tale for teenagers centres on a violent death. It begins with a vivid enactment of a video game whose name is the same as that of the play, Dead Ahead. Three whirling male contestants vie for gangland supremacy in Mega City. Game over, the trio of 17-year olds who've been battling it out are left to cope with their own lives, which are more humdrum but still potentially explosive. All three are the problem kids of problem families.

Andrew, the smartest, has controlling parents who've placed him in a private school away from his friends. Tiga, who's very needy, has a father who's dating a woman -- Tiga calls her "the skank" -- much younger than his mom. Cory, who has bullying tendencies and in whose basement the game is played, has lost his mother; ever since her death, his dad has turned drunk and -- especially towards Cory -- violent. He's also threatening to relocate his son and himself to Vancouver. By the end of the play, all three boys have witnessed or participated in a real-life killing. Will they cover it up or will they go to the police? Their friendship fractures under the strains of guilt and mutual suspicion. These are intensified by the presence of Megan, Andrew's girlfriend and part-time conscience. The other two resent her, especially Tiga, whom she riles up at their first meeting by pretending to believe he's gay.

The author is his own director, and his work in both capacities is tense, sensible and convincing. It avoids the platitudes of both the old and newer schools of youth theatre; there is little moralizing and less self-conscious toughness. There are some instructive peeks into the younger generation's store of general knowledge; they've heard of Hitler (he's mythology) but not of Stalin (he's only history). As to whether the four young people -- the only characters we see -- should or shouldn't snitch, the question is left open, though there's little doubt of the direction in which the play itself is tilting. (It may not match up with the audience's instinctive sympathies.)

The problem, when you consider it, is not unlike the one famously raised by E.M. Forster as to the comparative merits of betraying one's country or one's friend, though the question here is rather more immediate; it involves self-preservation as against self-sacrifice. And if you're looking for further hallowed comparisons, the sickening difference between mayhem on a video screen and in real life was anticipated nearly a century ago in the Irish classic The Playboy of the Western World, whose heroine came to recognize the "great gap between a gallous story and a dirty deed." Megan comes to the same conclusion, and much faster, though she may not express it as colourfully.

That said, the video game metaphor is the play's weak point, whether you take it as just a metaphor or as a possible case of cause and effect. There's no evidence that these kids, however they may horse around, really see themselves as candidates for gangland supremacy or that they're either the victims or the exponents of some culture of violence. They stumble into violence in real life, they're appalled by it when it happens and even, judging by their conversation, before it happens. The rest is teenage braggadocio and peer-pressure, of a kind that long predates the computer, in a pervasive broken-home environment that is distinctively contemporary but is also a different problem, or set of problems, altogether. All Dead Ahead the game does for Dead Ahead the play is get it off to an eye-catching start.

The acting is excellent, if occasionally forced, the actors being young but not that young. If there's a standout, it's Ben Lewis, who as Andrew has the most nuanced role, but Eli Ham (Cory) and Ashton Doudelet (Tiga) are equally involved and involving, while Sabryn Rock's Megan has the rhythms and attitudes of 21stcentury youth down to perfection. I saw the play with a house of seventh and eighth graders, and they never talked, coughed or snickered. - Dead Ahead runs until May 16. Call 416-862-2222 for more information.
2008-05-07-seeking-answers-across-the-di:
Halfway through his five-part series My Israel, Ralph Benmergui says that "everyone who comes here feels they're a victim of something or other." He speaks as a Sephardic Jew visiting an Ashkenazi-run country. His family emigrated to Canada from North Africa, and he attended an Ashkenazic Hebrew school in Vancouver where, as he ruefully admits to a Sephardic journalist friend in Israel, "they treated me like dirt ... we [Jews] were invisible."

"We're still invisible," chimes in his mother, from her Canadian kitchen. We meet her at the beginning and end of the show, and keep flashing back to her in between. Like any good Jewish mother, she worries about her very grown-up son going off to such a dangerous place. She's also proud of him for doing it --With good reason as it turns out, since My Israel is an outstandingly good-natured and inquisitive piece of work.

It's poised, as just about any examination of Israel must be, between despair and hope. Talking to an old Canadian friend who emigrated to Jerusalem decades ago and is fiercely patriotic without being bigoted, he says, "I feel everyone's grievance is real, but no one feels heard," and she doesn't disagree. An especially determined female settler says, "We're all victims -- the Israelis and the Palestinians -- it's the governments' fault." As to what those governments should be doing, that they're not, she doesn't elaborate and Benmergui doesn't press her, at least not in the footage we see.

That's the program's biggest failing; it keeps cutting away just when you want it to ask another question. Two and a half hours is a lot of TV time, but it isn't much in the real world. But then even if the conversations went on forever, they likely wouldn't resolve anything. We're dealing here with irreconcilables -- and not just between Jew and Arab -- that have, somehow and sometime, to be reconciled. Benmergui must have known that before he left, but the knowledge gives his show the tension of a quest. He's resolutely cheerful in his approach, so we get an apparently lightweight show with heavyweight implications.

Monday's episode centred on the Wailing Wall, which he approached with a suspicion that seemed equally rooted in modern scepticism and old-time religion ("isn't this a form of idol-worship? God doesn't dwell in bricks and mortar"), with a side trip to the Holocaust memorial of Yad Vashem ("the place where the reason for Israel becomes clear").

He got to spend Christmas in Bethlehem: "I went from the Wailing Wall to the al-Aqsa mosque to Manger Square in

one day" -- and if you think a North American Christmas looks secular, you should see Manger Square. The timing of his trip means that he also got to celebrate the Christian New Year in Israel. It's a festivity that some younger Israelis (defiantly disengaged, they don't like to believe there's a war on), have adopted with enthusiasm but, to Benmergui's Canadian eyes, with little success; at a quarter to midnight, he still can't find a party.

Yesterday's program was about "the new wall," security barrier or land grab, depending on your point of view. In effect, it works as both. "I know it's evil and not good," says Benmergui's Israeli driver, "but my family comes first." The harassment at the check points is shown, and is shaming, though the sad point it makes is less about Israel than about humanity: power, backed by self-righteousness, will always be abused. "The other" can always be demonized, as Jews know better than most. The series' last episode introduces us to intransigents on both sides (though none of them seem to be what you'd call good haters) and then to an Israeli and a Palestinian family, both bereaved in the conflict, who have come together in a reconciliation program. It's genuinely moving.

The struggle is so wearily familiar that it's almost a relief to be shown, in tonight's "Race and Class" episode, the tensions within Israel itself, a country where the city skylines look increasingly American while, outside them, "many live in poverty because security trumps everything, including social programs." One in three Israelis, we're told, lives below the poverty line. Israel is a place where "you have to make a choice, religious or secular, left or right, Ashkenazi or Sephardi," though the last, of course, may have been made for you. Benmergui's journalist friend has been able, it seems , to make a decent life for himself.

On the other hand, we're shown a Sephardi village where "going into town means crossing the railroad track" with a train threatening to mow you down every 15 minutes. The inhabitants must often feel a kinship with the refugees living in camps "that were not supposed to be permanent but have been here for 60 years."

Indeed the most kindred spirit Benmergui encounters is Mohammed Alatar, an Arab filmmaker -- American-Palestinian -- who shares his own sad, smiling mix of fatalism and hope. In fact, Alatar may be the more hopeful of the two, perhaps because he has to live it. He tells us, at different times, that "the disease is the occupation," but also that "Palestinian hatred is unsustainable" and that he's sure "Israel will still be here, 50, 100 years from now." Everyone agrees. All the same, the last shot is of Benmergui, this nice and charming man, beating his head against the Wailing Wall. - Ralph Benmergui: My Israel airs tonight at 9 p. m. ET on Vision TV.

2008-05-10-under-their-suits-fantasy-is-:
The first impression given by Sexual Practices of the Japanese is that they do it with dummies. The stage is lined with mannequins: not womannequins, since what we see is a line of empty grey suits, waiting to be inhabited, as in due course some of them will be. It's a striking opening to a Vancouver-born show that inaugurates the Factory Theatre's performing spring season, and that proves to be visually impressive throughout. Atmospheric, too, and intelligent and well performed for the most part, though some of its constituent parts outstay their welcome.

There are three in the cast: one man, Raugi Yu, and two women, Manami Hara and Maiko Bae Yamomoto. Hara and Yamomoto also co-wrote the show with Hiro Kanagawa and James Long, and Long and Yamomoto co-directed it. The first verbal section gives us the two women actors dressed as that old Japanese fantasy, two little maids from school. They quiz (male) members of the audience on their notions of Japanese women. As induced audience participation goes, it's quite disarming. Then they entice another guy on stage -- a very game specimen, on the first night -- and ask him searching questions about baseball, e. g., "in what city do the Seattle Mariners play during a home game?" (Seattle was one of the show's previous touring dates.) The relevance of this turns out to be the sex-symbol status of a Japanese Mariner, Ichiro Suzuki. Later on, in the show proper, one of the female characters will use him as prime fantasy material.

This is one of three narrative streams that run through the show, and if that terminology calls to mind Robert Lepage's masterpiece, The Seven Streams of the River Ota, the comparison is not inapt; apart from the Japanese setting, this production has some of Lepage's fluidity and pictorial panache. And his play, too, interwove its stories, though they were both more numerous and more complex. The authors of this show seem to have conceived of it as three separate plays, juggled together rather than placed end to end, but the audience is likely to experience them as one, and they do converge. One concerns the experiences of a young woman travelling to work on the Tokyo subway. (I don't think anybody actually says it's Tokyo, but that was my notion.) Jammed up against her fellow passengers she gets remorselessly and, of course, anonymously, groped. She doesn't find it erotic. Strung out as it is across the evening, this has considerable visceral impact (the lighting and sound are superb) but less as story. The emotional outcome is inevitable, yes, but also predictable. The text makes great ominous play with the reiterated subway announcement "Be Aware" but it may be raising our consciousness less than it thinks.

In another part of the urban jungle -- or, put another way, at the commuter's destination -- the CEO of a sex-toy company, one of those walking suits, plots new ways of heightening female pleasure and corporate profits. His female employees respectfully point out that he may be ignoring the human element, a statement he finds interesting. His is a hierarchical world; his wife respectfully packs him a lunch every day, even though he never eats it (and, he admits, he'd probably miss it if she didn't). Meanwhile, one of his subordinates instructs the other on how to cater -- psychologically -- to the men in authority above them. This is the only section in which characters interact, or perhaps one should just say co-exist. When the boss invites one of his assistants to a "love hotel," he finds himself unable, despite her charms, to take his mind off his work. And, meanwhile, the baseball fantasies rise to a climax; point made, I would have thought, quite early on, but perhaps you really have to care about baseball. However, this does inspire the funniest of the show's collision points: a duel in which the offensive and defensive weapons are ball player's bat and businessman's briefcase.

We have, then, a fantasia on Western views of Asian sexuality, whose upshot seems to be that the Japanese are having less fun than we've been led to believe but they're working on it. And since this fantasia is itself the product of a divided view -- the creators are Japanese-Canadians -- it has an extra level of wryness. They are complicit in what they're satirizing, and they feel the pain while keeping a certain distance from it. It's a tantalizing show, promising more than it delivers. Which I guess is another stereotype.

On the subject of good-looking shows: the Canadian Opera Company's production of Debussy's Pelleas et Melisande (director Nicholas Muni, designer Dany Lyne) ranks with the Ring and Lady Macbeth of Mtsensk among the best things to happen in the new house. A dual-levelled set, with a third layer occasionally dropped in for people to die on, conjures up both a feudal court in which the rulers prefer to keep the starving ruled down below and out of sight, and the shifts between dream and reality in a beautiful, mysterious work. Maybe the mystery turned off the first-night audience, whose response was phenomenally tepid by operatic standards. But even if diva-worship (and divoworship) is your main thing, you should be amply rewarded by Russell Braun's Pelleas, Isabel Bayrakdarian's Melisande, and above all -- certainly in acting terms -- by the great Pavlo Hunka as the jealous Golaud, working wonders with an anguished pianissimo. - Sexual Practices of the Japanese runs through May 18 at the Factory Theatre. Call 416-504-9971 for ticket information.

2008-05-12-narcissism-cubed-the-hills-is:
Yes. The Hills are alive, though I myself am flagging. MTV's reality-soap -- call it that for the moment --is airing what amounts to a day-long retrospective of the season so far leading up to a brand-new finale. I had planned on experiencing this marathon ahead of time, via a simulated model consisting of some 12 hours worth of DVDs. But time and fortitude ran out, and I had to do some skipping. I doubt that, in essential terms, I missed much. The Hills, like much long-running TV, is a show in which stuff happens but nothing much changes. Sort of like life.

The Hills revolves around four teen-and-twenties California career girls, and like most youth shows it's designed for a mostly female audience, younger than its characters, who wish they all could be California girls. So I am not, on several counts, its target demographic. Also, I have a strong bias toward acted and written drama, which The Hills prides, or at least advertises, itself as not being. Nor is it comedy, another genre I like. I smiled once during my Hills experience: Lauren Conrad, who plays -- sorry, who is -- the central character Lauren Conrad, was sitting at an outdoor cafe with a girlfriend and announced that she had planned a trip to the gym. "Don't bother to work out," said the friend; "eat your Pinkberry and enjoy life." That line had a shape to it, a certain elliptical swing. But it stands alone.

Lauren lives in Hollywood where she combines college with an intern job at Teen Vogue. (The show is an orgy of product-and-location placement.) The publicity tells us that she really does work there, though it's a mystery how she manages, given the demands on her schedule of recording her personal and professional life for the camera. The personal of course takes precedence. Season 3, the current one, began with Lauren locked in a bitter feud with her former roommate and best friend Heidi. The reasons, though often explained, remained obscure to me but they seemed to include Lauren's disapproval of Spencer, the boy of Heidi's dreams, who over the season has realized some of Lauren's worst fears. This is symbolized by his going from clean-cut to stubbled.

I wonder how they work these things out. The crew can't be on duty 24/7. Does a protagonist call up the producers and say "I'm going to break up with my boyfriend today -- be there"? And how do they ensure the boyfriend's compliance? And did Heidi, an event planner, get a promotion and a trip to Las Vegas because her bosses thought her worthy or because the show did? Fairly obviously, it's all set up. This show may have started with the actual circumstances of its participants' lives, but it must now be proceeding according to a pre-arranged plan. Though one would like to know who does the arranging.

Like all "reality shows" The Hills is heavily edited: more, probably, than most dramas. It's even more artificial than the Survivor model, which at least sets a bunch of people a common challenge and lets them get on with it. But some of its borrowings from the genre are useful. Characters are meticulously identified, by name and function, every time they appear, an especially valuable aid on a show where nearly all the girls are blondes. The titles used to tell us, for example, that "Justin" was "Audrina's ex-boyfriend", though they acted so close that he seemed more like an ex-ex. And indeed he's now billed as "boyfriend." There have been times when I would have welcomed such assistance with The Wire and The Sopranos. By the way, though sleeping-together is taken for granted, The Hills is sexless. Friends and Dawson's Creek were Bacchanalian by comparison.

The show may be contrived, but it doesn't sound written. I doubt that any writer could come with dialogue so lame. Note I said "lame," not "bad." There is an accuracy about the uninspired and unfocused way these people speak. Most of us, most of the time, think and talk as narrowly and narcissistically as they do (though the Hollywood setting accentuates the narcissism) and we all think our own concerns all-important. Most of us, though, don't get to share those concerns with the viewing public. The folks who live on on The Hills do narcissism cubed.

Crazily, it works; as with all soaps of any competence, taken in sufficient quantities it becomes addictive, or at least easier to watch than to turn off. Some make higher claims for it. The real-life Spencer, who is making a real-life bundle from personal appearances, has been quoted as saying "like, how much work is reading from a script? We're improv TV personalities. That's way harder." Now one knows -- or hopes -- that there's more to acting than "reading from a script" (Spencer really should get out more). But it's true that most of us instinctively judge acting by how "real" it seems, and in that sense improvised performance or reality-show performance or the unskilled hybrid performances on The Hills are off to a standing start. But they also get boring quicker. A perfect match of style, form and content, The Hills is also the perfect definition of what people grow out of.

2008-05-14-audacious-yet-vexatious:
Trevor Nunn had two inspired ideas for his production of My Fair Lady. One concerns the placing of the intermission. Traditionally the first act curtain has fallen, anticlimactically, in the midst of the Embassy Ball to which Professor Henry Higgins escorts Eliza Doolittle to test whether her transformation from Cockney flower-girl to posh-speaking lady is complete enough to convince the swellest of the swells. Nunn pauses instead on the preceding scene, Eliza about to set off for her ordeal, radiant but terrified: Cinderella on her way to the ball, which as pantomime writers have always known is by far the more uplifting and suspenseful way of doing things.

The other, smaller innovation also concerns the first act. Every time the action wanders outdoors we see newsboys hawking papers announcing that the king -- Edward VII, presumably -- is sick, dying or, finally, dead. So when we reach the Ascot Gavotte, the fashionable world has gone into mourning, and a number that everyone remembers as being clothed, audaciously, all in white, is now in black: Call it the audacity of surprise.

These two effects were stunning when the production opened at Britain's National Theatre in 2001, and they have a residual impact in the American touring production, "redirected by Shaun Kerrison," that re-opens the Toronto (formerly the North York) Centre for the Performing Arts after 10 wasted waste-land years. But they mean far less, because they no longer have a dramatic context. The acting strength that has always been the hallmark of Nunn's best work, in plays or in musicals, has diminished almost to vanishing point. Meanwhile, the tricksiness and over-elaboration that were mild blemishes on the show in London have become debilitating eyesores.

There is one life-saving performance, the Eliza of Lisa O'Haire who has a singing voice that lights up both the wistfulness of Wouldn't It Be Loverly and the rapture of I Could Have Danced All Night and who, British herself, finds the right spoken sound for both halves of her character's progress. (Some of the supporting accents in this show about accents are atrocious.) Her acting too is well up to conveying Eliza's native confidence,

hurt affections, and resilience. Her last two numbers are spoiled by the production's compulsion to illustrate and underline everything, but she splendidly holds up her end in the final, nearly wordless scene in which she comes back to the professor, here beautifully staged half as jest, half as challenge.

She doesn't, though, get much of a response from 'er 'Enry. Christopher Cazenove does reasonably when asked to play Higgins' passion for the English language and his casual lack of passion for anything or anyone else; he's all right, in other words, in the dialogue scenes that are taken verbatim from Pygmalion, either stage play or screenplay. But if he can cope with Shaw, he's at sea with Lerner and Loewe, and with the romantic patina -- romantic even in denial -- that their songs cast over the original. Higgins is a role famously written for a non-singer. But there are non-singers and non-singers, and Cazenove's Sprechstimme is numbingly defective in pitch, colour and even rhythm. (William D. Brohn's exacting new orchestration for Why Can't a Woman Be More Like a Man completely did him in.) Out with all those things go wit, charm and any reason for Eliza to fancy him. I've Grown Accustomed to Her Face, that paragon of anti-love songs, goes for nearly nothing.

It isn't completely his fault. I remember my relief when Alex Jennings, the fine Higgins I saw in London, was after all the busy-ness granted an empty stage on which to sing

that song; and my dismay as it started filling up with phantom flower girls to remind us of what he was missing, as if the song itself weren't already telling us. Eliza's Show Me is similarly disrupted by a parade of suffragettes with placards reading "deeds, not words": a sop, presumably, to someone's social conscience, like the presentation of Eliza's dustman dad (Tim Jerome, not so much horny-handed as heavy-handed) as short on benignity and long on neglect. Both his songs are staged as extended knees-up routines, though only one needs to be; British directors seem to regard American musicals as so many boxes of chocolates, and cannot bear to leave a single flavour untasted. Matthew Bourne's choreography is dreadful, alternately -- sometimes simultaneously -- cute and overblown. The initial visual impact of the Ascot scene is destroyed when the assembled toffs start high-stepping as if they themselves were horses, when the whole point is meant to be their unmoved stateliness. With a Little Bit of Luck involves a prolonged prance on dustbin-lids, recalling a routine in that great neglected movie musical It's Always Fair Weather. In fact, the staging keeps prompting memories of Gene Kelly and MGM: a lamppost or a sofa (Singin' in the Rain), a strap-hanging subway ride (On the Town).

O'Haire apart, the best things about the show are the ironic presence of Marni Nixon, the celebrated vocal ghost who dubbed Audrey Hepburn in the Fair Lady film, in the non-singing role of Mrs. Higgins, and the un-ironic excellence with which she plays it. Walter Charles has his moments as Colonel Pickering, though he's too little the gentleman, too much the buffoon. Distressingly further down the same road is Justin Bohon's Freddy, so exaggerated a twit that, though he has the voice to sing On the Street Where You Live, he completely forfeits the right. Anthony Ward's sets make an evocative job of Covent Garden (where the production has its most charming moments) and an imposing one of Higgins' monumentally book-lined study. His establishment is, as usual, impossibly large for a mere professor of phonetics: I counted four maids, two footmen and a housekeeper. Broadway has always been more starry-eyed about the British class system than Britain itself was. Which, though I'm not complaining, is the difference in a nutshell between the incurably romantic My Fair Lady and its impenitently satirical source. - My Fair Lady plays until May 31. For ticket information, call 416-872-1111.
