2008-05-17-never-meet-your-no-1-fan-the-:
It may be every writer's worst nightmare to be corralled for an indefinite period by his self-described No. 1 fan. Then again it may not. Let's admit, though, that if the writer has been knocked out in a car accident and wakes up to find himself incapacitated and at the fan's mercy, then that raises the stakes considerably. They go even higher when the fan is an ex-nurse with access to pain-killing drugs that give her traumatized patient a choice between agony and addiction.

Those who have read Stephen King's novel Misery and/or seen the film that was based on it will recognize the situation. Those who, like me, have done neither may still find it striking a chord since you can't help hearing things, especially about the movie. My ignorant impression is that Simon Moore's stage adaptation is a faithful one. And not knowing what happens once the basic set-up has been set up probably helped me to enjoy the Canadian Stage production, which I found thoroughly gripping, even though it moves slowly (this actually has its advantages) and lays on its effects with a trowel (this doesn't).

For my fellow innocents: Paul Sheldon is a best-selling novelist who has hit it particularly big with a sequence of decorously sexy period romances (what the trade used to call bodice-rippers) about a heroine whimsically named Misery. We first see him accepting an award, prior to taking off to his mountain hideaway to work on his latest. We next see him, book written and car crashed, pinned to a bed in the home of his ardent admirer Annie Wilkes. She has read his new manuscript, which he thinks his best, and she does not approve. She finds it pretentious ("stream of consciousness" he explains, breaking no ice whatsoever), and full of rude words. Worst of all, it has no Misery. But this is nothing compared to her wrath on going into town, buying a paperback of Paul's last Misery book (she can't afford hard covers), and finding that it really is his last Misery book. He's killed her. Annie isn't having this, any of it, and she forces Paul to: a) tear up his just-completed masterpiece and b) write a new story, Misery Returns, in which she does. It's hard to tell which of these two humiliations he finds more agonizing; though if Conan Doyle could yield to readers' entreaties and bring Sherlock Holmes back to life after pushing him over the Reichenbach Falls, Paul has at least the consolation of being in good company. (The company, perhaps, that Misery loves.) There are rumours, too, that the upcoming seasons of 24 and Prison Break will revive characters thought deceased; one wonders whose beds their authors have been strapped to.

So, Annie gets Paul off his back and into a wheelchair, and buys him a second-hand typewriter. (I'm not sure when the play is set, but it certainly wouldn't work if Paul had a computer. Though, of course, going for a hard drive is what got him into trouble in the first place.) Once partially mobile, Paul naturally sets about trying to escape, thereby getting Annie very upset. Reaching back into her experience on surgical wards, she ... I'll spare you the gory details, though David Storch's production doesn't. It gets very literal, inducing incredulous gasps from the audience that turn rather too speedily to giggles. There really are things you shouldn't do in a theatre, at least not without an anaesthetic. Anyway, if you had begun to wish that the play would stir its stumps a little, the action around here may make you regret your choice of metaphor.

In fact, the show's leisurely nature is what makes it work. We see everything from Paul's point of view, hear him screaming when his medication is withheld, share his musings on his helplessness and on his hopes of outwitting his captor. He's immersed, in fact, in his own stream of consciousness and we're in there with him, splashing for our lives. Tom McCamus makes the identification seductively easy; he's completely convincing, right from his calculated blend of modesty and arrogance when accepting his prize. His charm and suavity never quite leave him, even at his most desperate as he counts off the moments that separate him from final disaster. Annie is the showier role and Nicola Cavendish seizes it, right from the sugar-sweet smile with which she greets her awakening idol, a moment at least as scary as any of the more overtly menacing things she does later. She digs deep into Annie's memories of a twisted childhood, but she's less powerful when she switches into villainess mode, which she's either allowed or encouraged to do too early and too loudly; I wanted her to cut the cackle, literally.

Where the play and the actors excel is in giving life to the usually invisible bond between the oblivious entertainer and the audience who, in a mixture of grudge and gratitude, feels that she owns him and that he owes her. She, who for years has paid the piper, can finally make him dance to her tune. Each of them is comically oblivious of the other's values and modes of operation; they do know that they're in a life-and-death struggle. Rather less subtle are the setting that Britta Gerecke has dreamed up for Annie's stronghold, full of poles but short on walls, and James Fisher's supposedly spooky sound-score, which seems to think that the play is still a movie. The two forms have different ways of creating suspense, and what's effective in one can be ludicrous in the other. Which reminds me: The CanStage program note says Misery is the only work of King's to have made the journey from page to screen to stage. The writer must have forgotten the Broadway musical Carrie, a superflop so legendary a book was named after it. - Misery runs through May 31 at the Bluma Appel Theatre. Call 416-368-3110 for ticket details.

2008-05-21-age-gives-cohen-s-voice-a-maj:
"This," said the 74-year old maestro, "is the first time I've been on a stage in 14 years. Of course, back then I was just a crazy kid with a dream." Big laugh. Leonard Cohen is on a comeback tour, and he's kicked it off in the Maritimes: first stop Fredericton, second Halifax. In fact --however he may have looked, felt or sounded when he was a mere incipient sexagenarian -- his present age becomes him. Where once he had the hawk-like look of a youngish Al Pacino, he now has the foxy demeanor of an oldish Dustin Hoffman: dapper with a slight edge of disreputable. He looks sidelong at everything including, if such a thing is possible, himself. He seems especially surprised, though certainly not displeased, by his trio of female backup singers; "How," he appears to be wondering as, hat-in-hand, he watches them undulate, "could I have gotten this lucky, this late?"

He spends a lot of time clutching that fedora; nearly every moment, in fact, that he isn't actually singing. It gives him an air of humility ringed with confidence; it also summons the image of the wearily romantic chansonnier he must always have yearned to be: Charles Aznavour with a dust-and-ashes touch of Jacques Brel. Dust and ashes characterize his voice, which would be a growl if it had more body. It's a more attractive as well as a more compelling sound than the terror drone with which he started his recording career 40 years ago. It also sorts better with his material, which is downbeat even when the subject appears to be redemption.

Even his defining hit Suzanne sounds better coming from an old man than a young one; its fuzziness can at least be defended as the haze of memory. That song has always seemed to me to sum up the worst of the singer-songwriter school -- the kind of "poetic vision" that sees no further than the end of the next line. What does "she has touched your perfect body with her mind" mean? The man is just spraying adjectives around -- it's the kind of vagueness that a whole generation mistook for poetry, when it isn't even decent songwriting. The sole exception of the iconic singer-songwriter bunch is Randy Newman, who is always specific, even at his most oblique. But "specific" is what it should be about. Is there -- quite apart from the whiny tune, which even Cohen's mature voice can't disguise--any reason or relevance for the piled-up similes of Bird on a Wire?

Still, if there isn't reason, there is usually rhyme: one thing that Cohen's far better at than most of his peers. The comparatively recent That Don't Make It Junk has a very satisfying clunk. Hallelujah is a tour-deforce of rhyming, though it's a shame that Cohen now sings "do you" and "to you" rather than "do ya" and "to ya;" maybe he's trying for subtlety, but it's self-defeating. It weakens the song's alternation of sacred and profane. This mix is something that Cohen has gone in for ever since the gratuitous -- read: meretricious -- intrusion of Jesus in the middle of Suzanne. The imagery is usually Catholic -- odd, from a Jewish Buddhist --and it works far more powerfully in his political songs. At least, I assume they're political. First We Take Manhattan (Then We Take Berlin) seems to be an outpouring of all-purpose resentment; it could be the marching song of a crusading Fascist. Presumably it's meant more as a warning than an inspiration, though its power comes from putting you emotionally on the side of the devils. Even Democracy sounds as much threat as promise, even with its disarming reference -- maybe his best single line -- to the Sermon on the Mount "which I don't pretend to understand at all." Everybody Knows, one of my two favourite songs of his, is definitely warning, with an intoxicating touch of gloat. It's in this mode that Cohen's authority as writer and performer comes most satisfyingly together: here, and in my other favourite, Tower of Song, which brings all his recurring personae -- the lover, the outcast and the troubadour -- into a reasonably coherent whole, and sports a marvellously self-deprecating stanza about Hank Williams. Take along with these his best mordant-romantic songs, I'm Your Man and Ain't No Cure for Love.

He played a nearly three-hour show, with a half dozen built-in encores. The band moved beautifully between folk, pop, klezmer and-- with special credit to guitarist Bob Metzger --jazz. The backup ladies moved less beautifully -- they swayed their hips in a bored sort of way, as a part of the contract that they hadn't properly read -- but their harmonies and occasional solos were lovely; one of the trio is Sharon Robinson, Cohen's songwriting collaborator on Everybody Knows, among other things; one wonders how much of that song's tightness and straightforwardness are due to her. Cohen himself is in complete command, an impish, minor prophet vociferously honoured in his own country.
2008-05-24-desperation-and-despair-there:
Dawn Greenhalgh and Megan Follows play very well together as mother and daughter, which, at the risk of being simplistic, may have something to do with the fact that they are mother and daughter. That is certainly the hook for the Soulpepper production of Marsha Norman"s 'Night Mother, a New York hit in 1983 and a repertory staple ever since.

Closely related the actresses may be, but their styles are very different. That isnt a criticism; generations styles are different. Greenhalgh, in this play at least, is flossy and chatty; Follows, stark and withdrawn and unnervingly logical. The women they play share a house in a small Southern town. The action begins with Jessie, the daughter, informing Thelma, the mother, that she is about to kill herself with her late father's gun. The rest of the play consists of Thelma trying frantically to talk her out of it, and Jessie declining to be talked. It's a contrast between desperation, which spills out of Greenhalghs Thelma, and despair, which Follows hugs tight to herself as an accomplished fact. Both modes have their disadvantages when it comes to communicating with the audience -- Greenhalgh tends to gabble and Follows to mumble -- but both are powerful

Its an artificial piece with the trappings of realism. I should just have written you a note, says Jessie to Thelma, giving up, almost with a shrug, on making her mother see her point of view. And in real life, if that's the appropriate expression, writing a note is just what she would have done; at least, I've yet to hear of a suicide confronting a putative survivor immediately before doing the deed. Typically, they depart, with or without written communication, leaving the survivors to worry forever after about what went wrong and how they might have prevented it. Jessie wants to spare Thelma that, but she only succeeds in giving it to her in concentrated form. And the playwright works in a similar way. The purpose of the drama is less to probe the unknowable--a suicides motivation -- than to show us the essentials of what went on between and around the two women. In this its successful, though on a less than triumphant scale.

Thelma had a loveless marriage, and resents the bond between her husband and her daughter. Jessie's own marriage failed more dramatically; she and her estranged (though apparently still caring) husband have a thieving, drug-taking son. She also has a married brother, whom both she and Thelma seem to regard with, at fondest, amused tolerance. Jessie is also an epileptic, though she insists that her fits have nothing to do with her desire to kill herself. And she has always been reclusive; it seems her mother engineered her marriage in order to get her out of the house.

"You're my child," cries Thelma, at her wits end for arguments. Im what your child has turned into, replies Jessie, with devastating calm. It's a searing exchange, but we really have no means of gauging what changes may have occurred in Jessie over the years. Even by her own account, the seeds of self-destruction were always there. There's a sense, too, in which both women are plain wrong. They have reached the stage where the child becomes the parent, exacerbated by the fact of their living together. Part of the reason for their conversation is for Jessie to instruct her mother in the details of day-to-day survival: a course that Thelma, who isnt exactly senile, resents as impertinent but whose necessity she tacitly acknowledges. The mother, in fact, is about to be orphaned, and dreads it.

The domestic details are splendidly summoned in Ken MacDonalds neatly-furnished kitchen-living-room set, and the play makes us powerfully aware of the restricted lives they both live; they're in a very narrow community. But again, though that may be part of the reason for Jessie's decision, were never really told so. Jessie makes sardonic references to "Red China" but thats about as far as the play gets in acknowledging the outside world. It's true to life, I guess, but it's constricting for the audience as well. Night Mother is one of those plays thats frustrating and compelling at the same time; one of those high-toned American dramas (they generally win Pulitzers as this one did) obsessively, not to say monotonously, focused on the domestic. And it doesn't tell us as much about the psychology of mothers and daughters as it thinks it does: less, actually, than an apparently more extreme and melodramatic play like The Beauty Queen of Leenane.

Greenhalgh's performance, respectably blowsy, seems genuinely rooted in the plays landscape. Followss doesn't: She comes on, not just as more intelligent than her mother but as belonging to another social and intellectual world altogether, and the play suffers from it. The tension, in Alisa Palmer's production, comes and goes; or maybe its just that the audiences absorption in it does; much of it seems, despite the intimacy of the theatre, to be going on a long way away. The moments when the actresses come downstage to get in one another's faces and in ours -- jovially as well as tearfully -- send the dramatic temperature mercifully but too infrequently up. That doesn't count the ending; weve been told its coming for an hour and a half but despite or perhaps because of that, it's a genuine shocker. Nothing surprises like the inevitable.

- 'Night Mother runs until June 21 at the Young Centre for the Performing Arts. Call 416-866-8666 for details.

2008-05-26-it-s-bigger-it-s-bolder-it-s-:
Carey Perloff thinks the world of Canadian actors. She isn't Canadian herself, though shes a frequent visitor, especially to Stratford, Ont. She is in fact the artistic director of the American Conservatory Theatre of San Francisco, one of the most enterprising and distinctive resident theatres in the United States. I visited it last fall, and found Geordie Johnson, who a few years ago was Stratfords Richard II, rehearsing the all-American role of Starbuck in The Rainmaker. He was initially surprised at the casting but seemed to be taking it in stride.

Recently, Perloff has been working on a new version, by the British writer Timberlake Wertenbaker, of Jean Racine's Phedre, the most celebrated of French classical tragedies and a notoriously hard nut for the English-speaking theatre to crack.

Last year she found she had hit a wall. I thought," she told me, "that it would help Timberlake find her way to the next stage of the translation if we could try it out with people who have the acting chops to handle the language, and who can also play the sexuality -- it's death if you have cerebral actors.

Most American actors, apparently, cant do this, maybe because they dont have the practice; British classical acting, according to Perloff, has been spoiled by the all-pervasive Essex accent," a whining kind of debased Cockney. I agree, but I was relieved to get confirmation from an independent source.

Canadians speak the classics in a manner that's essentially, and blessedly, classless. So Perloff phoned Antoni Cimolino -- then executive director of the Stratford Festival, now in overall charge as general director. -- and a Stratford workshop was set up. Perloff came as director, bringing with her Olympia Dukakis to play the nurse. The Festival supplied the other actors, with Seana McKenna playing the desire-ravaged Phedre, Scott Wentworth as her husband Theseus, and Jonathan Goad as Hippolytus, her stepson and love-object: practically dream-casting for these roles.

The resulting rehearsed reading was, by all accounts, sensational; there has been talk ever since-- though as yet no official confirmation -- of a full-scale production at the festival in 2009. It would, on the face of it, be criminal for it not to happen.

McKenna, reflecting, in a conversation earlier this year, on the "very intense five days of the workshop, noted that you have to go with the Greeks; you can't dip your toes into the Aegean Sea -- you have to jump in." She should know; she was a fine Medea at Stratford a few years ago (in a production thats being revived in Toronto next season), and she appears at this years festival in The Trojan Women, opposite Martha Henry: the first time, amazingly, that these two female powerhouses have acted together.

As the cast also includes such terrific actresses as Yanna McIntosh (absent from Stratford for years) and Kelli Fox (completely new to the place) the amount of talent encamped on the plains of Troy looks quite extraordinary.

Which could be said of this year's Stratford company as a whole: A combination of festival regulars and newcomers that looks, on paper, like the strongest team ever to be assembled in Canadian theatre. One has to say "on paper because a barrage of gifted individuals doesn't always translate into an ensemble, and even when it does it can be hard to keep such a group together for a period of years -- which presumably is the intention. Also, an undeniable cloud hangs over the festival with the resignations of Marti Maraden and Don Shipley, two of the artistic directors responsible, with the surviving Des McAnuff, for assembling the actors in the first place.

Maraden will still be directing two plays, The Trojan Women and Alls Well That Ends Well, and I believe the protestations of all concerned that theyre too immersed in getting the actual shows on stage (what else could they do, after all) to let themselves get affected. Still, it's a downer.

But there's promise as well. Peter Hinton, who directs The Taming of the Shrew, told me that his cast contains half-a-dozen possible Petruchios (including one, Evan Buliung, who actually plays him). Adrian Noble, the former director of Britains Royal Shakespeare Company responsible for this years Hamlet (and also on the judging panel of TV's Triple Sensation on CBC), shares Carey Perloff's opinion of the local talent; though hes understandably less inclined than she is to disparage the standards in his homeland.

What he does say is that the festival actors are pound for pound, as good as youll see at the English Stratford at this moment" and that Canadian acting combines "the best of the North American method tradition with that of the British classical verse tradition. The quality of verse-speaking here is very high. There's a healthy respect for tradition -- which isn't always the case in the U.K.

His Hamlet, set at the beginning of the 20th century (you cant go any later than the First World War -- you need a hierarchical society") stars Ben Carlson, a Stratford debutant but with a formidable record in striking sparks from classic texts; his long speeches in the Shaw Festivals Man and Superman stopped the show the way actors do in musicals.

This is Carlson's second Hamlet -- he played the role last year in Chicago, coincidentally for another former RSC director, Terry Hands -- and one of three roles he's playing at Stratford. Together they amount to an actors democratic ideal: one whopping lead, one meaty supporting role (Tranio in The Shrew) and one lesser but still important part (First Lord in Alls Well).

He's been rehearsing all three at once, and admits that if he were doing Hamlet again, he might like a slightly less hectic schedule. But the mix, he says, is terrific; "It's why you get up in the morning; I think all actors should do [repertory] -- it flexes your muscles, gets your energy up.

The problem of course is that there arent enough Hamlets to go round, and this years Stratford company is crammed -- for better or worse, and we don't yet know which -- with star-quality actors playing only supporting roles: they include Fiona Reid, Tom Rooney (Horatio to Carlson's Hamlet, a nice touch since for three years in Ottawa the roles were reversed) and Randy Hughson who has a substantial part in Shrew but is otherwise confined to First Soldiers and Second Gravediggers.

It turns out, though, that this is at his own request: I was apprehensive about my own skill in terms of the verse; I wanted to check out the vibe." Hes found he likes the vibe on several levels ("youve got to jump in at Stratford, or you'll be trampled ... it's wonderful to sit in a rehearsal room and theres Martha Henry ... when you step on the festival stage for the first time, youre aware of all the history, you're struck by the power of that stage") but is beginning to feel impatient for bigger challenges.

The possibilities for this newly assembled company are exciting. It will be fascinating to see how it all shakes down. And I want to see that Phedre. - For tickets call 1-800-567-1600 or visit stratfordfestival.ca.

2008-05-27-a-cinderella-story-think-agai:
THE STEPMOTHER

Court House Theatre, Niagara-on-the-Lake

---

The Shaw Festival's production of The Stepmother is a companion piece to its production of Getting Married. Eustace Gaydon is a widower, a gentleman-speculator sorely in need of a cash infusion. His hopes are pinned on the will of his late sister, and he is furious when she turns out to have left all her money to her companion, Lois. So Eustace does the obvious thing. He invites Lois into his house, first as governess to his two young daughters, then as his wife. It's an even better investment than he'd hoped. Lois turns out to have great talent as a dressmaker, and Eustace sets her up in her own business -- using her own money of course.

Ten years pass and Lois, without quite realizing it, is supporting both of them. She also attracts the attention, ardent but mostly honourable, of Peter, the conveniently wealthy barrister next door. The rest of her overstretched time is spent tending to the growing Gaydon girls, the elder of whom is now in love with a boy whose father, knowing rather too much of Eustace's character and prospects, is dead set against it being a match. If you believe the title, the relationship between Lois and the Gaydon girls is the central topic of the play.

Don't believe the title. The contrast between the traditional bad stepmother and this very good one may be the stuff of theories and program notes, but the play itself hardly admits it's an issue. We are told absolutely nothing about Eustace's first wife, nor do we get any glimpse of Lois in her governess period. By the time the main action starts the girls are unshakably devoted to her -- they unself-consciously refer to her as "mother" --and she to them.

What remains riveting about the play -- and about the production -- is the ambience of love and money. The law decrees that Lois's property is her husband's, practically that she herself is; precisely the situation that the reluctant brides of Getting Married were bridling at. But in Shaw that's all in the head; Lois has physically to live it, just as she has to deal with actual sexual temptation that the audience believes in. (Nobody believes for a moment in the supposed erotic triangles of Getting Married.)

All the Gaydons are living hand-to-mouth, a reality brought home to us early on by the character of Eustace's maiden aunt Charlotte who keeps house for him and has to beg him for cheques to live on; Jennifer Phipps plays her to perfection, in sickness and in health though not in that order.

The drama comes as Lois realizes how horribly she is trapped, and as she fights to escape-- from her own conditioning, as much as anything else. The strain tells; Claire Jullien admirably presents a woman who has to keep carving out new roles while remaining true to herself. We see, and feel, several sets of scales dropping from her eyes.

Blair Williams' Eustace overdoes the debonair blackguard; he's best when most desperate, trying to keep up at least the pretence of self-respect. There's an ambiguity, too, about Patrick Galligan's Peter; he loves Lois all right, and his armour genuinely shines. But he too manipulates her, even if it's for her own good. Eustace, come to think of it, would probably make the same claim for himself; and half-believe it.

Marla McLean, an ingenue plus, unforcedly projects spirit and precocious wisdom; she's her stepmother's stepdaughter. Jesse Martyn makes her a charmingly impulsive swain, and there are valuable glimpses of the everyday from Guy Bannerman, a solicitor as implacable as the law itself, and Jenny L. Wright, solicitous in a more amusing way as Lois's disapproving assistant. This, you feel, is how the world went round and -- in the more painful scenes between husband and wife-- still does. - The Stepmother runs until Oct 4. For tickets and information call 1-800-511-SHAW or visit shawfest.com.

2008-05-27-a-game-of-clue-without-the-bu:
AN INSPECTOR CALLS

Festival Theatre, Niagara-on-the-Lake

---

J. B. Priestley's An Inspector Calls can be played quite effectively in a realistic mode, as a detective drama with sociological overtones and a delayed metaphysical twist.

The Shaw production, the first of its season, brings the play literally, down to earth. Peter Hartwell's set, one of his best, is a colonnade with an alarming elevator door at its back and a couple of adjoining planes -- tectonic plates, perhaps --jutting out in front.

On these sits the posh family dining room in which the play happens. Those lift doors clank like prison gates, and there seem to be chains hanging down from the ceiling. (This last detail struck me as a bit much.) The production was to have been directed by Neil Munro, and there is an identifiably Munrovian air of High Concept about it.

Jim Mezon took over when Munro fell ill, and he has done a first-rate job. The play has been beautifully choreographed to reflect the guilt-trips and power struggles that make up its action, and the excitement is all but continuous.

Benedict Campbell plays Inspector Goole, and he doesn't shout; he's a quiet but implacable interrogator (and apparently self-appointed judge) pressing insistently on the nerve of his subjects' collective conscience -- a commodity in which some of them have a greater share than others. He's calling on the Birlings, a prosperous family living in the north of England just before the start of the First World War. (The play was written just before the end of the Second.)

A young woman has killed herself by the excruciating method of swallowing disinfectant, and all present turn out to have had, unknown to one another, a hand in her downfall. Mr. Birling, one of the town's most prominent industrialists, started it off by firing her from his factory, when she helped lead a strike for higher wages.

Daughter Sheila had her dismissed from her next job in a dress shop, for seeming to laugh at her when she tried on something unflattering. Sheila's fiance Gerald Croft (an upwardly mobile match for the Birlings) kept the girl as his mistress, treated her well, but then cut her loose. Mrs. Birling and son Eric contributed as well, but since their guilts are only revealed after the intermission, it would be breaching the critical code to describe them here.

Whatever his stature as a moralist, Priestley at his best was a superb dramatic craftsman. Judicial process proverbially make for terrific theatre, and this play is one long trial-scene, with the witnesses varied enough and the story grim enough, to stop any threat of monotony in its tracks.

If there's a heroine it's Sheila, who fiercely admits her responsibility and is both agonized and repulsed by her relatives' ability to slip out of theirs; Moya O'Connell plays her with the same force and delicacy that lit up her debut last year in The Circle. Does the Shaw need another actress who can play blazing moral fervour and make us laugh? (Sheila has the play's few witty lines, mainly of the corrosive variety.) Well, never mind: It's got one now.

The shiftier young males, weak and drunken Eric and smug and sober Gerald, are well done by Andrew Bunker and Graeme Somerville; both men are capable of remorse, as long as there's no other option.

As for their elders: Mary Haney overdoes the ramrod aspect of Mrs. Birling, one of those committee ladies who give charity a bad name, but Peter Hutt is a persuasively oily and evasive Mr. B., a self-proclaimed, self-satisfied, self-made man.

This is the second suicide play to arrive on out stages in as many nights -- the first was Soulpepper's 'Night, Mother -- and it strikes me as a more persuasive, and certainly a livelier, account both of what might lead to such an event and of its effect on the survivors.

Like 'Night, Mother it has an ending -- in Priestley's case shamelessly borrowed from Gogol's similarly-titled Government Inspector -- that you can see coming from a mile off and that still pins you to your seat when it does. - An Inspector Calls runs until Nov. 2. For tickets and information call 1-800-511-SHAW or visit shawfest.com.
2008-05-27-marriage-isn-t-for-everyone:
GETTING MARRIED

Royal George Theatre, Niagara-on-the-Lake

---

Stephen Sondheim said it faster in a patter song from Company (A wedding, what's a wedding / It's a prehistoric ritual / Where everybody promises fidelity for ever / ...Thank you all. But I'm not getting married today), but Shaw said it first, in 1908 to be precise. And in both cases, the betrothed couple go ahead and do it anyway.

That apart, Getting Married is the most relentless of the author's talkfests. The last time it played at Shaw, the production imposed some kind of mood and shape on it by ignoring Shaw's instructions and setting it in a gazebo, a sort of pre-nuptial tent.

This new production, by Joseph Ziegler, puts the play back where Shaw said it belonged, in the Bishop of Chelsea's kitchen. It's handsomely designed by Sue LePage, but it doesn't have the same kind incipient air of carnal carnival. And it only comes to life at the start of the second half when a new character, who has been given a considerable build-up, justifies it by lighting up the show, which is the impact Shaw intended her to have but doesn't always happen.

We're in the Bishop's kitchen because his daughter is about to get hitched. She and her intended though, are less in evidence than the rest of the episcopal brood. Marriage, or the lack of it, is on all their minds.

We find that the young lovers want to call it off; they've also taken a look at the marriage contract and are shocked at the responsibilities he is expected to take on and the independence she is expected to give up. So, says the Bishop cheerily (he says everything cheerily), why don't all present sit down and try to work out a new rational contract of their own?

So they try. And of course they can't agree on anything. While their elders are arguing, the young people sneak off and tie the knot anyway, before a registrar. The world must be peopled.

This supposedly pivotal pair hardly exist as people: A fault in the play is made worse in this production, which gives us the groom (Gray Powell) as a ninny in knickerbockers and the bride (Krista Colosimo) as a pretty nothing. Of course it's tough to make an impression in a Shaw play when you aren't given much to say, but even the talkers here give us stray sparks rather than a cumulative verbal bonfire.

The ladies do best, by and large. Fiona Byrne's Lesbia is all businesslike sparkle, Nicola Correia-Damude has a throaty if anachronistic attractiveness as the free-talking, ultra-conventional Leo, and Sharry Flett is winningly selfless as Alice.

Peter Krantz has the General's boyish hurt but not his mannish bluster, while Peter Millard, initially a bracingly brisk Reginald, eventually runs out of changes. David Schurmann as the Bishop played the first night with viral laryngitis, which actually worked to his advantage; the scratches gave his customary golden voice some welcome new contours.

Michael Ball is familiarly cast as a genial greengrocer; Norman Browning is most unfamiliarly but delightfully cast as the Bishop's chaplain whose puritanical punchlines -- he's an adherent of the primitive church, and fiercely celibate -- are here delivered with unfailing pungency through the actor's disapproving nose.

The play breaks down, not before time, into a death-against-life contest between him and the production's late great arrival Mrs. George, mayoress of the town and the greengrocer's sister-in-law, given a transforming performance by Laurie Paton. She is the first person to mention sex though, typically, she does it in a cloud of metaphor while in a clairvoyant trance.

As she describes it, it seems to be a one-way process -- the woman giving everything to the man--but the actress casts a spell with it. When awake she's no less enchanting, a down-to-earth siren, bewitching every man in town except the Bishop, to whom she herself is in thrall -- platonically, of course. Her special prey is the dashing Hotchkiss, one of Shaw's philosopher kings who proves to be a philosopher fool. Here it's not even that fair a fight, since Martin Happer's performance, all right on looks, is frustratingly short on intellectual muscle.

So, having blazed, the play begins again to fizzle and, Shaw fan though I usually am, I ended feeling that, like the play's less regenerate characters, I still draw the line at Getting Married. - Getting Married runs until Nov. 1. For tickets and information call 1-800-511-SHAW or visit shawfest.com.
2008-05-28-what-bedding-through-yonder-t:
In the latest Stratford production of Romeo and Juliet, the prologue is assigned, unusually, to Friar Laurence. Peter Donaldson plays the role, and his delivery gives the new season and the new regime their best possible start. His Friar proves not only the most thoughtful but, in many ways, the most passionate person on stage.

He rages at the two feuding families of Verona, at the recalcitrant Romeo in his more self-pitying moments, but he's notably kinder to the more sensible Juliet, and his anger is generally constructive. Like everyone else in the play he's defeated by events, which themselves are an index to human fallibility, his own included. He appropriates the last speech as well as the first, and it's partly due to him that the play seems the tragedy of a society as well as of a couple of kids.

The society is in fact more powerfully present than the kids. Des McAnuff's staging is excellent, brawls, balls and all. The platform stage has been rounded off, warmly lit (by Robert Thomson) and elaborately but not overpoweringly built up. Heidi Ettinger's set is dominated by an arched Italianate bridge that can serve as a balcony, summon a place and even, in a fanciful way, link periods. The production starts contemporary with Vespas, prams and guns; it gets into fancy-dress for the Capulets' party and stays there, allowing, among other things, for the sword-fights to make sense.

We only return to the present for the final post-mortems: a satisfying and foreseeable rounding-off, even if you doubt the need for modern dress in the first place. (You can't "make" a play relevant. Either it is or it isn't. Though you can, admittedly, obscure its relevance.) The centrality of Donaldson's Friar may have something to do with his being the one character who doesn't need to change his clothes.

A trapdoor allows for popup appearances by Juliet's bed or the Friar's pharmacopeia, the latter probably once too often. Ettinger's summoning of the Capulet tomb is awesome, a line of permanent sepulchres stretching out behind Juliet's supposedly temporary one. In the final sequence, which involves rain, Lucy Peacock's Nurse makes an unscripted but very moving appearance to take pride of place among the mourners. Her early gossipy scenes are nothing special, but once things start to go wrong and the Nurse is roused successively to indignation and accommodation and grief, she is superb. She has an unforgettable moment, smoothing Juliet's sheets to camouflage her unease at having betrayed her. The production is good at small physical things as well as big ones.

It isn't as good at orchestrating all the performances. Some reputable actors do disappointing work: Steven Sutcliffe's Paris is ineffectual, and Evan Buliung so laboriously underlines Mercutio's sexy banter that one wonders what his friends see in him. He only becomes likeable when about to die, and it's hard to see what good an unlikeable Mercutio does the play. Some others are plain bad. Paul Dunn's clown Peter, though, is brilliant, while Lady Montague (Irene Poole) makes an unusually vivid impression, signalling her abrupt death via a couple of lines and a fair bit of directorial invention. Heading the other dignified household, John Vickery is an excellent Capulet, genial until crossed at which point he becomes volcanic.

As for the star-crossed twosome themselves: well, they're on the right lines, she wise beyond her years, he callow beneath his. When Gareth Potter's Romeo is finally shocked into maturity --at "then, I defy you, stars" -- he's impressive; earlier, he's never afraid to play the boy's emotional self-indulgence. What's lost between these extremes is any saving sense of a vital connection to Juliet. Nikki M. James gets much of Juliet through her eyes --especially in her first scene where she amusedly sizes up her elders' plans for her early marriage -- but hardly any through her voice. Her long speeches disappear into space, and even her shorter ones trail off. Missing, plainly, are experience and technique; this is one performance that may well improve greatly over the long Stratford haul. The balcony scene, at least, is charmingly impulsive from both parties, though her audibility is hardly helped by the intrusion of mood-music at the end of the lovers' meeting. The best TV has given up on this kind of pandering, and even movies show signs, so it's an odd time for the theatre to start.

Revving up the violence is another thing, but it's also the easy part. Romeo and Juliet was, as far as we can tell, the first full-blooded play about romantic love; Shakespeare in Love got that right. It remains, by centuries of consent, the iconic one. There's an audience out there, new with each generation, that wants to believe in it. - Romeo and Juliet runs until Nov. 8. For tickets and information call 1-800-567-1600 or visit stratfordfestival.ca

2008-05-29-something-is-fresh-in-the-sta:
HAMLET

Festival Theatre, Stratford

---

In his years at the Shaw Festival Ben Carlson mastered the art of delivering long prose sentences, lucidly and thrillingly and wittily, on a single breath. As Hamlet at the Stratford Festival he translates this same skill into blank verse, with results that are just as exciting and--Shaw being Shaw and Shakespeare being Shakespeare--considerably more moving.

In a production by the British director Adrian Noble that's without a single dead moment, he gives a performance without a single dead word or dead thought. It's world-class Shakespeare.

Carlson can be a difficult actor to sum up because he is so transparent. He offers no mannerisms that a critic can seize upon and call "interpretation." This makes him ideal for Hamlet who is less a character than a ceaselessly probing intelligence, a glistening, abnormally sensitive surface that reflects and refracts every idea that fate throws in its path.

He does, of course, have emotions and a situation, and Carlson gives full measure to Hamlet's initial grief, to the complementary qualities of gentleness and mordancy that allow him to see the best in some and the worst in others (Adrienne Gould's superb Ophelia gets it from both barrels), and the determination that alternately spurs and deserts him.

The Ghost's revelations excite him, to the point that he literally throws a fit, from which he emerges well on the manic side of depressive. When he's in company, he has purpose; he can't stop himself talking. When he's alone, he can't stop himself thinking.

The production, full of action in group scenes, leaves him pointedly alone on vast expanses of platform, for the soliloquies; and it's exhilarating to see Carlson, in his first appearance on the Festival stage, commanding both the space and the text. He has a remarkable gift for sounding spontaneous, conversational, freshly thoughtful without ever losing the shape of a speech.

"O that this too, too solid flesh would melt" is pure, baffled sadness; "O what a rogue and peasant slave" is vigorous self-directed anger, laughing at his own excesses ("O vengeance") and then resolute to put them to use ("about, my brains").

A couple of minutes later in "to be or not to be" he's thrown back to naked mind; the idea of suicide has occurred to him, he can't shake it and it leads him to a quieter and yet more helpless bafflement at his own failure to revenge. The most hackneyed of speeches is made fresh.

The last soliloquy, spoken against the sight and sound of the Norwegian army trudging off to their graves "like beds," is the ground zero of hopeless resolution. When he returns from England it's with a new philosophical resolve, a new gentleness and a steely new realism. And he's the first Hamlet I can remember who speaks to the skull of Yorick as if he actually did know him.

Every scene has a rationale, fresh but unforced. We see the Players rehearsing Hamlet's new speech for The Murder of Gonzago just before he instructs them in it. Claudius tempts Laertes over a game of pool. He also sets spies on his own spies. A few familiar ideas come up fresh: the use of silhouettes, for example, for the play within the play, and then in the play itself. The Ghost (James Blendick) enters in a conventional swirl of dry ice, but when he speaks it's with a truly eerie mix of the supernatural and the familiar.

His reappearance in Gertrude's closet is clearly the product of Hamlet's own imagination, a brake on an encounter that's becoming uncomfortably Oedipal. Maria Ricossa's elegant Gertrude is shallow in the wrong way (she makes nothing of Ophelia's drowning) but I at least believed that she and Hamlet were mother and son; in some productions they might never have met.

Scott Wentworth as Claudius doesn't play his love for her as deeply or tormentedly as he might (and he is sometimes surprisingly hard to hear) but he presents a smooth usurper-tyrant whose fits of rage extend, in the prayer scene, to himself. The mutual loathing of him and Hamlet is palpable.

The richest family grouping, though, is Polonius-Ophelia-Laertes, who share an affecting group hug when Laertes (Bruce Godfree, a bit suburban) leaves for France. Geraint Wyn Davies, the least doddery of dads, conveys real concern when he lectures his kids, and he gets their respect in return. Gould's Ophelia, loving and shockable, strikes any of number of new notes, including some on the piano (the production's use of music is exemplary); her elders show their affection by joining her in duets, a habit that has a horrific pay-off in a harrowingly unsentimental mad-scene. Earlier, she's silently shown her reaction to Hamlet's plans to go back to school; she's not in favour.

There's a bed on stage for the nunnery scene, making its eroticism first tender and then nasty. Tom Rooney is a lovely, supportive Horatio, Victor Ertmanis and Randy Hughson a funny pair of Gravediggers, and I could go on. This is a fantastic evening. - Hamlet runs until Oct. 26. 2008-05-30-any-more-post-civil-war-tensi:
THE LITTLE FOXES

Royal George Theatre, Niagara-on-the-Lake

---

This year's Shaw Festival plays are arranging themselves in pairs. Alongside An Inspector Calls, with J. B. Priestley calling down vengeance on his whirling Birlings, we have The Little Foxes, in which Lillian Hellman wields the hatchet on her horrendous Hubbards.

The Hubbards are a post-Civil War Southern family, rich but definitely not old money, a fact that gnaws at them even as they express their contempt for the soft slave-owning gentry whose immediate descendants they've dispossessed. They don't plant 'taters, they don't plant cotton; and them what plants 'em are best forgotten.

What the Hubbards are good at is trading in the stuff, the cotton anyway, and they have a deal brewing with a Chicago tycoon who would like some southern comfort in his brand. There are two Hubbard brothers, the domineering Benjamin and the smarmy Oscar, and a sister, Regina. Regina is married to Horace Giddens, a banker whose consent is needed to seal the deal. Horace is not, however, about to give it. He is a sick man, and says that he has done quite enough bad things in his life without adding to them now. Besides, he hates the Hubbards, especially the one he married. Regina reciprocates, her most pressing concern right now being to keep his ailing heart from beating for good and all.

Rounding out the clan are Oscar's wife Birdie, a good weak woman whom he terrorizes; their son Leo, a rotter and sneak who's his dad's spy in Horace's bank; and Alexandra, daughter of Horace and Regina, who stands an awful good chance of being married off to Leo. Or, considering what Leo's like, an appallingly bad chance.

Like Priestley, Hellman never stops telling you how terrible her terrible people are, and she's even less subtle about it. Where Priestley is insistently righteous, she's insistently self-righteous. Eda Holmes, director of this revival, quotes her as saying "I am representing for you the sort of person who ruins the world for us," and that us-and-them tone is significant. An Inspector Calls suggests that we're all implicated; Hellman seems to have dreamed up her characters in order to feel superior to them.

It can be a pleasure shared, since she's also supplied an efficient melodramatic plot for them to rattle about in: one that sets Regina against her brothers as well as the three of them against all decent -- or, in Horace's case, half-decent -- folks. But both plot and play can be hard to activate. There was a star-studded Stratford production--Martha Henry and William Hutt and Brian Bedford -- that I missed but that must have been roaring fun; the two versions I have seen --one with Elizabeth Taylor, one without -- were crashing bores. Holmes, however, keeps the play alive and suspenseful by the unexpected method of treating the characters as human beings. This goes especially for Regina, a woman who in middle age exhibits all the most endearing maternal and matrimonial features of Joan Crawford and Lady Macbeth, but who suffered a maimed childhood on her own account; Laurie Paton, whose season this is (so far), plays her with a creamy malice beneath which the scars still fester. Ric Reid is ideally rough and gruff as Ben and Peter Krantz sufficiently creepy as Oscar. Gray Powell and Krista Colosimo, the two juveniles from Getting Married, make far better impressions here with, to be fair, far juicier material; he as the mewling low-life Leo, she as Alexandra, whose declaration of independence cows even Regina, leaving us to wonder whether it heralds a new era of selflessness, or just more of the same.

David Jansen's Horace is a weak link, too lightweight and, beneath his grey hairs, too young for the company he's required to keep and the fight he's supposed to put up. Lisa Codrington also seems a little young but is otherwise splendid as Addie, the black servant who runs the Giddens house with all the authority of an ancestral retainer. The Hubbards have made their pile, we are told, by "cheatin' the coloureds;" Regina's coloureds take their revenge by being very selective with their loyalties: none for her, some for Horace and all the world for Alexandra who, Addie says, will marry Leo "over my dead body." So that's where the power lies. Sharry Flett, in a part that might have been written for her, finds a fluttery dignity nestling beneath the clipped wings. Like Blanche, Scarlett or any other self-respecting Southern heroine she can't help thinking of her old Kentucky home, or whatever part of the Dixie The Little Foxes is supposed to be happening in. Hellman wrote a sequel called Another Part of the Forest. Someone should revive that, in tandem or just for a change. - The Little Foxes runs until Nov. 1. 2008-05-31-we-must-sing-its-praises-ther:
Its always a kick to find that an admired actor can sing as well. Jonathan Goad, starring in and as The Music Man at the Stratford Festival, certainly can -- like a bird on certain notes. He also has nimble feet, roguish comic timing and oceans of shy charm.

But there's trouble, right here in River City, which you can take to mean either the Iowa town where the show is set or Stratford itself; and it makes this great musical -- a maverick posing as a conformist, like its hero -- slightly less than the total tonic it could be. The clue is in that word shy. Professor Harold Hill, the fake vendor of 76 trombones (and assorted other instruments), is a charmer all right, but his charm is of the shameless, barnstorming variety. He imposes himself on the River Citizens by sheer fast-moving, crisp-talking energy. Ya Got Trouble, which epitomizes the process, here becomes the chorus's number rather than his. Or maybe its just that I cant get Robert Preston's powerhouse inflections out of my head.

Now let's, as Harold himself might say if it suited him, shoot straight pool: Goad is not just streets but whole highways ahead of the last man to play this part at Stratford. His playing of Hills more sensitive side -- his immediate empathy with the disadvantaged, for example -- couldnt be bettered, and it extends to his love-scenes with Marian Paroo, the book-loving music teacher (or music-loving librarian). Harold is meant to be an experienced sexual as well as commercial con-man, whereas the heart that Goad wears on his sleeve is very evidently real; he doesn't really need the salvation she brings him. Still, there's genuine magic between them. Leah Osters acting is occasionally stiff, but she has the square root of Marian in her, and her singing is radiant, especially in her near-aria My White Knight. The highlight of the evening is Marian the Librarian, the odd-metered number in which Harolds incorrigible wooing leads to a mass outbreak of soft shoe all over the reading room. In Michael Lichtefeld's choreography, this includes a marvellous in-house parody of Romeo and Juliet. But his work, and the company's execution of it, is top-notch throughout, from the invigorating gymnasium-floor hop of Shipoopi (this show and West Side Story opened the same season, a great one for dances at the gym) to the displays of interpretive dancing presided over by Fiona Reid as the mayors wife. Its worth the trip to hear her say, "Ladies, let us attend to our Grecian urns" (or words to that effect).

Actually, the list of pleasures in Susan Schulman's production is endless. There's the show itself, for a start: a first-time-out one-of-a-kind masterpiece, whose librettist-lyricist-composer Meredith Willson, though a richly experienced musician, had never written a musical before and never wrote a good one again. It cant have hurt that for this one he had Frank Loesser as a mentor; rumour credits Loesser with having ghosted My White Knight and rumour is probably right. He encouraged Willson to mine his turn-of-the-century childhood, in just such a proud and sheltered Iowa township as the shows, and encouraged him to match a story that's funny and makes sense to a most out-of-the-ordinary score: one that takes in marches, ballads, barbershop, irresistible patter-songs and the extraordinary word-jazz opening in which kibitzing salesmen provide both the exposition and the sound of the train they're travelling on.

The Avon stage cant match the vistas of the shows previous airing at the Festival Theatre. Philosophically I approve of the decision to restrict musicals to the proscenium house, but I have to confess that The Music Man was one of two shows -- Fiddler on the Roof, also about a town, was the other -- that justified the epic look. Still, Patrick Clark's sets bring striped-suit ice-cream-parlour America to delectable life, and the population is by and large terrific. It includes such surprise musical casting as Sara Topham, doing some earnestly bedraggled hoofing, and Michelle Fisk, wonderfully warm, sharp and tuneful as the heroine's mother. Those more accustomed to this kind of thing include Eddie Glen, an expert sidekick; a formidable colla voce quartet (Laird Mackintosh, Shawn Wright, Jonathan Monro, Marcus Nance); and a malapropping Mayor (Lee MacDougall) who, like the hero he opposes, is delightful but a little short on threat. There are also some more-than-bearable children, headed by Christopher Van Hagen as the lisping boy who learns to sing Gary, Indiana. He is key to the redemptive ending, which comes a bit sudden in this production but casts a glow anyway. The Music Man beat West Side Story at the 1958 Tonys. Historians usually reckon this to be an injustice, but I'm not so sure. - The Music Man is in repertory through Nov. 1 at the Avon Theatre, Stratford. Call 1-800-567-1600 for more information.

2008-06-03-liza-would-be-proud:
THEATRE REVIEW

Cabaret

Avon Theatre, Stratford

The curse of Cabaret is that its a musical designed to shock that now has to make its way in a theatrical world inured to shock. Directors have responded by upping the ante, most notoriously in Sam Mendes London and Broadway revival, with its trick ending in a concentration camp, just in case we hadn't got the message that Nazi Germany was horrific. It was undeniably exciting, but talk about overkill. In Amanda Dehnert's Stratford production, the curse is lifted. Its the most powerful version I have seen since Harold Princes 1960s original.

Prince's production worked by seduction. It lulled you into Christopher Isherwood's world of cheap Berlin lodging-houses and seedily glamorous Weimar nightclubs. Then it stunned you with an apparently innocuous folk song that turned into a Nazi anthem, a single stone through a Jewish greengrocers window and the Kit Kat Klubs celebrated Gorilla Song, an insidiously sweet-sounding number whose punchline, she wouldn't look Jewish at all, really was a punch: a sucker punch that woke you up and made you realize how far and how easily you had travelled. (It certainly upset audiences of the time, or at least those unable to tell the difference between anti-Semitism and the dramatic depiction of the same.)

That surprise effect is now gone beyond recall; Dehnert and her choreographer Kelly Devine downplay the number -- it seems for the longest time that there won't be a gorilla in the room at all, and when one does appear you might wish they hadnt bothered. But it doesnt matter. Tomorrow Belongs to Me has had its chilling double effect (far more so than in the Mendes version), and the production has come up with a blow-in-the-face first-act ending worthy of Hal Prince himself in Sweeney Todd mode.

The production has one unprecedented ace up its sleeve in the form of Sean Arbuckle's revelatory Clifford, the American equivalent of the Herr Issyvoo of Isherwood's stories and the play I Am a Camera. (If there is a musical with a more complex and still-developing genealogy than Cabaret, I dont know it.) Instead of the usual onlooking patsy, hes a passionate, ironic and troubled figure who centres the whole show. He is a camera observing, but he also participates. When he inaugurates the final valedictory chorus in which Wilkommen turns into Auf Wiedersehen, it really seems to be his song. He also gets one of his own: A previously unheard, musically adventurous ballad that John Kander and Fred Ebb added to their score for the Mendes production, but that was cut.

Trish Lindstrom's is an unusual Sally Bowles, compelling but not quite convincing, not so much charmingly feckless as bitterly uncaring. She's an androgynous figure who might well attract the bisexual Cliff ("If we could see her through his eyes ...") but is less likely to be saleable to a German club audience as "the toast of Mayfair." But nobody could claim that her cabaret numbers lack edge, much of it turned against herself.

Equally chilling, but less controversially so, are Cory OBriens Nazi organizer and Diana Coatsworth's Nazi sympathizer, both with a surface charm that corrodes. For warmth you go in this production to Frank Moore's frantically self-deluding Herr Schultz, the middle-aged wooer who presses his suit with fruit, and to Nora McLellans Fraulein Schneider, whose two Weillish songs -- the buoyant So What and the desperate What Would You Do -- wear the best of any in the score.

Their doomed romance, like that of Sally and Cliff, is watched from the side by Bruce Dows cabaret host, who plainly never expected else. It was, I think, a bad day for the show when the emcee became accepted as the star part. He's a commentator -- a show-stealing role to be sure -- but an actor can hardly steal a show that he already owns. By current orthodoxy, he controls the whole thing -- there's just too much of him.

Dehnerts production at least avoids trying to make him, and the club he inhabits, symbols of Fascism and victims of it at the same time. In fact, she quite subtly makes the point that gays were destined to be as much victims of the new era as Jews. The cabaret of Cabaret bears little relation to the club depicted in the stories, in which Sally sings American standards, badly. Our idea of Weimar cabaret has become a fantasy about a fantasy to be simultaneously indulged and deplored: a dream of an age in which anything went, especially sexually, and in production of this show its moved, not to the show's benefit, from metaphor to all-devouring reality.

Bruce Dow, mohawk-pated, seems to be having a good time going through the sleazy motions -- we've long gone past mere seediness -- but hes at his best in a straightforward despairing number like I Dont Care Much, which he sings as if he actually does, very much. To be honest, some of the emcee's numbers, especially Two Ladies, are feeble even as written, and the production doesn't do much for them. It's the real-life characters, about to be engulfed in terror, and they make it tremendous. - Cabaret runs until Oct. 24. 2008-06-03-wit-romance-and-the-dance-hun:
Wonderful Town

Festival Theatre, Niagara-on-the-Lake

The Shaw Festival's production of Wonderful Town is a lot of fun with one major flaw. The spirit lifts when Paul Sportelli's pit band strikes up the overture, which kicks off with Swing!, the most invigorating of the encyclopedic collection of 1930s pop pastiches that make up Leonard Bernstein's terrific score. It then sinks a bit at the realization that this chamber outfit, very light on the brass, is too genteel to swing. Worse, it's muffled and slow. A similar lack of punch and speed dogs the evening, in the book scenes as well as the musical ones.

Wonderful Town needs pace because it doesn't have much substance. What it has lots of are flavour and pedigree. It's based on a play that was based on a book that was based on real life. Ruth and Eileen, the show's two heroines, are sisters who come to Greenwich Village seeking their fortunes as writer and actress respectively. (Ruth wrote the book -- the original one, I mean.) Ruth, by her own acerbic account, has trouble attracting men; bubbly Eileen has trouble holding them off. The wit and fizz of Bernstein's music are matched by those of the lyrics, the best and funniest ever to be penned by the team of Betty Comden and Adolph Green. It's a pity that these quintessentially urbane Manhattan madcaps, who wrote the deathless screenplay for Singin' in the Rain, didn't get to do the musical's book as well. They might have given it the smart 1930s zaniness for which its characters and its time-frame cry out.

The actual script (by Jerome Chodorov and Joseph Fields) is rather aimless. Since the show was written in 1953, it has the appearance of a well-made musical in which the plot sparks off the songs and the songs illuminate the characters, but in fact it's a series of sketches. The bond between the sisters is the evening's emotional core.

There's a love story too: Ruth, trying to sell her work to magazines, meets an editor at The (thinly-disguised) New Yorker: They fall for, and after the usual complications, get one another. Meanwhile, Eileen attracts the attentions of a gauche drugstore clerk (specialty: banana splits), a sleazy newspaper editor and the entire New York police force, every man-Seamus of whom is Irish. Arrested for taking her sister's place at the head of a conga-line otherwise composed of Brazilian naval cadets (it's perfectly logical) she becomes the toast of the station-house, its officers flatly refusing to believe that she isn't from the Auld Country herself.

In this scene the book, the score and Roger Hodgman's production reach simultaneous peaks. The coppers have been serenading their heroine with an ardent ballad, My Darlin' Eileen, which by a mere change of tempo reveals itself as a jig. New York's finest, headed by the diminutive and invaluable William Vickers, proceed to throw themselves around the stage at impossible angles. Jane Johanson's choreography here is a joy, as it is for most of the evening. Lisa Horner's Ruth climbing the rigging in the naval yard to escape the attentions of the dance-hungry Brazilians is an especially fragrant memory.

Ruth, who contemplates writing a book entitled One Hundred Easy Ways To Lose a Man and who is given a song of the same name, is the show's presiding spirit, one that Horner captures with near-perfect style, timing and delivery. All she lacks is the final spark of personality that would make her not only the show's main attraction, but its reason for being. Chilina Kennedy is as delectable and tuneful an Eileen as one could dare imagine. If the girls are great, the guys vary. Jay Turvey sings very nicely but is implausible as a hard-bitten journalist and unbelievable as a romantic lead. Thom Marriott has a rollicking time as a star football player out to grass for the football season, who gets one very funny song and a mother-in-law problem, which occasions a particularly inconsequential subplot.

Among the other Village archetypes, Speedy Valenti, jazz clarinetist and nightclub proprietor, seems in Lorne Kennedy's performance to have arrived on the scene 10 years too early; he's more hipster than hepcat. We get the lowdown on the lingo and the rhythm in the above-mentioned Swing!, a real musical and lyrical treasure of a number. William Schmuck's sets and Judith Bowden's costumes do the stage and the characters proud.

I've stated my reservations. but they shouldn't stop you from making yours. Praise be to the Shaw Festival for reviving a musical that isn't one of the usual suspects but is definitely in the great tradition. - Wonderful Town runs until Oct. 5. For tickets and information call 1-800-511-SHAW or visit shawfest.com.
2008-06-05-the-way-we-weren-t-with-swing:
Welcome to the 1970s, when people swung, though not mu s i c a l l y. They did other things too, of course, but on the evidence of tonights first episode, Swingtown isn't interested. It's a curiously limited portrait of a decade or even -- since it makes a big deal of being set in the U. S. bicentennial year of 1976, with July 4 fireworks exploding all over the screen -- a single year in that decade.

Dont you think, our heroine Susan Miller asks her friend Janet, that "theres an energy shift we're missing out on?" Just the kind of question that must have rolled effortlessly off people's tongues every day of the decade. Well, nobody could accuse Swingtown of not laying its themes on the table, right from the off. Susan and her husband Bruce are about to move, in a sociologically upward fashion, from one Chicago neighbourhood-- where Janets the neighbour -- to another. Observing them as they move in are their new neighbours, Tom and Trina Decker, who are licking their lips. Tom and Trina have an open marriage, and they cant wait to invite Bruce and Susan into it. In fact, it's the first thing that crosses their minds -- which, like that of the show, are of the one-track variety.

The episode actually starts with Tom and Trina, not as a subtle way of easing us towards meeting the Millers themselves but in order to generate as much steam as possible as quickly as possible. Tom is an airline pilot, and there he is in his cockpit, advising his passengers of their imminent touchdown in Chicago (where, says the weatherman, it's hot and wet) and with a stain on his shirt. No, its not what you think: A rookie flight attendant has spilled some coffee on him, and shes abjectly apologetic: what will his wife say? "My wife," purrs Tom, will love you, and so it proves. And we haven't even had the credits yet.

Susan and Bruce have the usual TV complement of troubled and troublesome kids, whom Susan (Molly Parker, in a charming variant of the awakening role she played in Deadwood) advances as an excuse for having missed out on "all that Woodstock stuff".

She says this while accepting Trina's offer of a Quaalude: her first, though, blushes over, she takes it with as little fuss as if it were a chocolate drop -- probably less. She and Bruce are attending the Deckers Independence Day party, at which their hosts have every intention of loosening them up. It works, too: The two couples end up in a happy four-way haze.

Not everybody has their potential . Janet, who is something of an emotional limpet and quite happy with her constricted life, thank you very much (I quote her pretty much directly), has tagged along to the party, and gets a nasty shock when she blunders into the basement. Janet is the kind who trails her old friends to their new home bearing her own prize-winning apple pie, while Tom and Trina favour ambling across the lawn with a house-warming bottle of Dom Perignon. (Make that house cooling, if Tom is half the man were meant to take him for.) Returning home after her glimpse of orgy, Janet takes to furiously scrubbing her stove -- at dead of night, mark you -- because, she tells her husband with the symbolism dripping off her like beads of sweat, we live in a pigsty. Janet is being set up, with extraordinary cheapness, as a straw-woman, a caricatured figure of repression; presumably she will either stay that way for the season or suffer some kind of erotic comeuppance. That apart, I can't see that the show has anywhere to go. Either Susan and Bruce will settle happily into their new liberated lifestyle, which will be nice for them but not very dramatic, or they will get messed up with love and jealousy and logistical problems, which would be soapy and predictable. It looks like we're in for Sex and the Suburbs or Not- So-Desperate Housewives. As for making us nostalgic for the 70s: First theyd have to convince us that the era they're depicting was a) attractive and b) real.

Which is what Mad Men, premiering Sunday on CTV, does for the 1950s, a period that it makes seem very far away and very close. We smile and wince at the casual-but-calculated sexism (in which both genders collude) while recognizing the underlying attitudes; they have not, after all, gone that far under. Mad Men is far more erotic than Swingtown shows any signs of being, because the bodies are attached to minds that have other things on them. It's a unique show: It has the trappings of a workplace sitcom (not that different from The Office, at first glance), but it spurns the situations and its comedy, though

abundant, is acrid. Thats especially the case in the first episode, "Smoke Gets in Your Eyes," which brings the advertising firm of Sterling Cooper and its creative director Don Draper (the excellent Jon Hamm), the firms (and the show's) star performer, up against the problem of pitching Lucky Strikes to a society that's beginning to know about lung cancer. No question that the admen and the Lucky Strikers put their mouths where their money is; they all smoke like chimneys, though that seems an ugly simile for a show that makes office smoking look elegant and office boozing enviable. Especially funny is the companys desperate attempt to find just one Jew on their payroll, so that a department-store magnate and possible client will feel at home. (They finally locate him in the mailroom.) Blacks, of course, are in strictly service positions, and even an Italian feels incurably self-conscious.

The patina is exactly right, like one of the edgier movies of the period, Sweet Smell of Success or The Apartment. It certainly looks better than the 70s, and of course sounds better. Mad Men is set in 1960, but its (and its characters') musical tastes hark back five years earlier: to Band of Gold or On the Street Where You Live (the Vic Damone version). We're on the cusp; these men in suits and women in skirts seem untouched by rock n roll and would be flabbergasted -- the men, anyway -- at any rumour of a counter-culture. They're in for shocks. Peggy (Elisabeth Moss, with the look and flair of a young Brenda Blethyn), gets ahead of the curve by going on the pill, to her doctor's lascivious disapproval; shes demure and shocked by advances, but still succumbs to the ambitious office jerk, days before his marriage; she could be naive or smart or both. Meanwhile -- or more accurately, next week -- Don arranges for his nervous wife to see a psychiatrist; and then phones him to find out the details -- and the shrink has no qualms about telling him. Its a boys' club all right, even apart from the scenes at the Playboy, but one in which all the members are headed for ulcers. It's about gloss and self-destruction, as opposed to Swingtown, which is just about gloss. I was this show's captive from the opening title-card, which told us that Mad Men was a phrase coined to describe Madison Avenue advertising executives and then added "they coined it."

- Swingtown premieres tonight at 10 p. m. on Global and CBS. Mad Men makes its network debut on Sunday at 10 p. m. on CTV.

THEATRE REVIEW

LOVE'S LABOUR'S LOST

Tom Patterson Theatre, Stratford, Ont.

---

Sometimes you can go home again. Michael Langham, director of the Stratford Festival for most of the 1960s, has returned to mount a new production of Love's Labour's Lost, the comedy with which he scored his most decisive early success at the festival and to which he has returned countless times since. He and the play are still fresh. This production, in which young actors from the Stratford Conservatory are bolstered by a few old reliables, is as magical as any version of the play I have seen -- or of any play, because, when Love's Labour's Lost is done well, it can seem like the best play ever written.

It's an early Shakespearean comedy that distills the essence of the form. One of the great Shakespearean themes is transience. Love's Labour's embodies it. It lulls its audience, as its characters are lulled, into believing that there is all the time in the world; and then shows, delicately but brutally, that there isn't. The situation -- there's hardly any plot -- is that the young King of Navarre and three of his attendant lords have taken a three-year pledge of monastic study, a vow they are immediately forced to break when the Princess of France -- with, naturally, three attendant ladies --arrives in the royal park on a diplomatic mission. Of course the four men fall in love with the four women. The latter are similarly interested but mock their wooers for making and then breaking their ascetic promises and, most of all, for the elaborate, fantastic ways in which they express themselves. Basically, they want the men to grow up.

The play satirizes the artificial wordplay that was all the rage in the literature of the time, but it also indulges in it, gloriously. All this is knocked on the head when news of a royal death arrives from France. It's a thunderclap moment, one that prompts a re-evaluation of priorities and -- usually unthinkable in comedy -- a postponement of any possible marriage. "Our wooing," complains Berowne, the most articulate and self-aware of the lords, "doth not end like an old play" -- though even more startling, if we're talking self-awareness, is the earlier line in which, when the boom falls, he shoos the supporting comics from the stage: "Worthies away, the scene begins to cloud." He practically cues the lighting.

The production looks gorgeous. Anyone downcast at the rumoured loss of the familiar Festival Theatre can stroll along the riverside to the Tom Patterson, where Tanya Moiseiwitsch's once-permanent facade has been reconstructed in all its stepped and balconied glory. Its spare elegance is offset by Charlotte Dean's ravishing Cavalier costumes. The women in particular look wonderful. Together set and clothes provide the perfect ambience: burnished and bitter sweet.

This done, the greatest challenge and the most vital is to make thelanguageentertaining and accessible. Some individual moments here might be better realized -- the great scene in which the young men progressively discover their shared perfidy falls short of its full, escalating impact -- but overall, Langham and his young cast do brilliantly. Every word tells. Ian Lake's Berowne is a verbal quick-change artist who can

alter moods, as the play itself does, on a dime. He makes a great put-down specialist and his cunning, heart-stopping speech about the educational glories of love really is glorious. Shane Carty's King is a good shy foil, Jon de Leon's Dumaine breaks beautifully into song, and Alanna Hawley is a naturally commanding Princess.

The courtiers' verbal excesses are echoed and expanded by their supposed inferiors ("they have been at a great feast of language and stolen the scraps"), with whom the older actors, and one a lot younger, have a field day. Peter Donaldson's Don Armado, the "fantastical Spaniard" -- proud, melancholy, noble and ridiculous -- is unlikely to have been bettered anywhere, certainly not in the magnanimity with which he acknowledges that the biblical Samson was on the whole better than he at carrying gates. And I flat refuse to believe that anyone has ever played his page Moth as charmingly, cheekily and skillfully as the phenomenal 11-year-old Abigail Winter-Culliford does it here. Their scenes, the most convoluted in the play, are fearlessly and flawlessly done, with Brian Tree, knowing and weathered as Costard the clown, expanding the duets into a triumphant trio.

More conventional but sufficient are John Vickery's booming schoolmaster and Gareth Potter's timid curate, who's almost hidden in his costume and makeup but does get to illustrate Costard's description of him as "a marvellous good bowler." Back on the courtly fringes, Steven Sutcliffe's Boyet is a delightful go-between, and Gordon S. Miller creates a whole character out of a star-struck forester's three-line attempt at flattering the Princess, a sign of the care the production takes and the rewards it reaps. This, with Hamlet, makes two great Shakespeare productions in one opening week. - Love's Labour's Lost runs until Oct. 4. For tickets and info, call 1-800-567-1600 or visit www.stratfordfestival.ca
