When My Name is Rachel Corrie was announced for production in New York, there were protests and the play was cancelled. It got on later, at another address. The same thing happened in Toronto; Canadian Stage announced a production and then abandoned it, and though the company denied that it was caving in to any kind of pressure, it's hard to believe the protestations. Anyway, the play is now on; and if objections ever were levelled on political grounds, they were misguided. Well, assuming you believe in freedom of speech.

Which is not to say that the play is impartial; it isn't. Rachel Corrie was the 23-year-old American peace activist who died in 2003 while trying to stop an Israeli bulldozer from demolishing a Palestinian home in Gaza. She may well have been naive-- standing in front of a bulldozer is naive -- and the play, assembled by Alan Rickman and Katharine Viner from Rachel's letters and journals, provides no evidence that she even attempted to talk to an Israeli. Her focus is entirely on the Palestinians whose lives she shared and whose hospitality she enjoyed, while remaining guiltily aware that she, unlike they, could leave at any time.

Her mother in Oregon, whose consciousness she raises, writes to her that this is the first time she's been aware that Palestinians have a case; where she lives, the words "suicide bombers" are enough to put a stop to any conversation. Rachel herself seems to have been in the opposite situation; suicide bombings, and all that they imply, never get into the conversation in the first place. Rachel isn't much concerned with context. When she talks of the Palestinians she knows practising "non-violent resistance," she sounds starry-eyed, not because they're really all potential terrorists but because she's using fancy words to describe the day-today process of getting by in an abhorrent situation. It is abhorrent, and no amount of "context" makes it less so: more, if anything. You end up rooting for Rachel.

You also, of course, mourn her death. But that doesn't necessarily mean that you want to know as much about her life as the play wants to tell you. It's a monologue, much of which is devoted to the protagonist's student years, trying to find a focus for her own idealism. Hers is a marathon role, brilliantly played by Bethany Jillard under the acute direction of Kate Lushington. In about a year's worth of work, Jillard has become our reigning interpreter of the contemporary North American teenager and early twentysomething; whether she's playing tough or vulnerable, whole or abused, shy or in-your-face, she has the accents, the attitudes and the rhythms down perfectly. She comes by them naturally, of course, but it's still a feat to shape them into a performance. The salient quality of her Rachel Corrie is its restlessness, emotional, intellectual and physical. (She turns somersaults or does handstands at moments of perplexity.) She can also, without any affectation, play passion. Rachel was something of a writer, as well as a cause looking for an outlet. She agonized about right and wrong, justice and injustice, before settling on the Middle East as her battleground. She seems to have been selfless, or a least no more concerned with playing out her own dramas than everyone is.

But her adolescent agonies are hardly unusual, and though that gives them a kind of representative interest, her words aren't inspired enough to sustain it. The thinking seems to have been that a bleeding political situation, a martyrdom, and an autobiographical paper trail should add up to a play. Some of the best parts are the letters she reads from her proud but worried parents; it's good to hear other points of view and theirs -- trying cheerfully to be supportive, but leaking any number of doubts -- are very recognizable. The piece goes from engaging to monotonous to baffling to gripping-- the baffling part being a pre-climactic retrospective detour -- the only point at which the play makes its heroine seem self-indulgent. It recovers itself to plunge into something like tragedy, with a ground-down Rachel's despairing conclusion that there may be more evil in the world than good; Jillard rises thrillingly to the challenge. She recovers her optimism, which I suppose means that the play does. But I'm not so sure; her end -- which, of course, we've been anticipating all evening -- still comes shockingly fast. Just one death, of course, in a world that's full of them, and no more to be lamented than anyone else's, but the theatre doesn't work that way. We suffer with those whom we've seen suffer, and here, whatever news she herself may bring of others, there's only one of them. - My Name is Rachel Corrie plays through June 29 at the Tarragon Extra Space. 2008-06-11-hard-headed-women:
Four of our finest actresses appear in The Trojan Women, giving performances that are predictably memorable. (I know that phrase confounds past with future, but we are dealing with myth here.) What goes on around them is not so great.

This is despite the perennial topicality of the play. It may even be because of it. Greek tragedy is full of refugee dramas, but Euripides' play is the one with which it is easiest for us to identify, and that fact may lull us, artistically speaking, into a sense of false security. The setting is the end of the Trojan war. Troy has been sacked, the men have been killed and their widows and daughters, the former queen Hecuba at their head, huddle on the plains in what might be a primitive tent city, awaiting deportation and slavery.

Euripides has the reputation of being a more naturalistic writer than his predecessors Aeschylus and Sophocles, and to some extent this is true. But he still wrote within the same conventions, for performance in huge amphitheatres, for actors in masks, for a singing chorus and with a maximum limit of three speaking actors in any one scene. This solved some problems for him, but creates many for us. Marti Maraden's production treats them as though they don't exist.

For example: The play contains the first, and maybe still the greatest, atrocity scene in world drama, great because it's presented as a breach in nature, something previously unimaginable. It represents the birth of realpolitik. Hector, the Trojan warrior, left a young son; the Greek council has decided that the child must be killed, lest he too grow up to be a hero. Soldiers appear on stage to tear him from the arms of his mother, Andromache; he is to be thrown from a cliff, his head dashed on rocks. This is all explained in the silent boy's presence. How is he supposed to react? How are his elders supposed to react to him? Euripides didn't have to bother about this, but we do, unless we're going in for extreme stylization. I've no idea what the answer is, but it hasn't been found at Stratford,

where they just say the lines and hope for the best.

Actually the best, in this scene, does happen in the form of Seana McKenna's Andromache, whose personal grief moves by astonishing gradation into universal agony. For Andromache, as for most Greek sufferers, it's all about her but that's all right because she's Everywoman. Martha Henry's hard-bitten Hecuba watches her intently, watching other people -- ironically, compassionately, angrily -- being something that Henry may do better than any other actor on Earth. And on Earth, curled up on it, is where her performance begins. She rouses herself to face one calamity after another.

Hecuba, who's already lost a home, a husband and innumerable sons, is further deprived of a grandson and two daughters. One of the latter is the prophetess Cassandra, who's been given as concubine to Greek general Agamemnon. This is the cue for Kelli Fox to enter in a Woodstock wedding dress that does her no favours. (John Pennoyer's costumes, mixing periods in the cause of timelessness, are generally unfortunate.) The quartet is completed by Yanna Mc-Intosh, creaselessly beguiling as Helen, the putative cause of all the trouble, begging and charming her way out of death by stoning, just as the vengeful Hecuba knew and dreaded she would.

These four performances have a rigour that the rest of the show lacks. Nicholas Rudall's translation strikes a reasonable balance between stark and casual, but it has some awful lapses. Sean Arbuckle, as the humane herald lumbered with bringing all the bad news, should not have to bear the additional burden of beginning a bulletin with "I'm not good at this." For one thing, he is good at it. And then there is the eternal problem of the chorus, composed of captives. The venerable Joyce Campion is the standout; her very presence testifying to a catastrophe that crosses generations. But here too the production gestures towards formality then backs away from it. The chorines are best when singing (music by Marc Desormeaux), second best when speaking in unison and weakest when trying to make individual lines sound both ominous and sensible.

That leaves the gods, who speak a prologue that's bland to them, but bitterly ironic for everyone else. Greek tragedy draws on a vast mythological corpus: The writers could light up parts of the canvas as they chose, confident that their audience could fill gaps and draw conclusions. It's not so much subtext as ubertext. Here we have Poseidon and Athena, miffed that the Greeks haven't been making them the proper sacrifices, capriciously plotting their downfall, which will happen after the play ends. Poseidon, god of the ocean, is in naval uniform, and the two of them appear to be hanging out on the gangway of some beached battleship. I find the Greek view of divinity, Euripides' anyway, very plausible. It's the only theology that answers that old question about bad things happening to good people. The gods have the power but, with all that immortality to play with, they long ago got bored with us. In another view, they are us magnified, mainly for the worse. The Trojan Women is maybe the prime example of a play that's great without being, in any conventional sense, good. It has no plot, only episodes. It ends with Troy in flames: the only possible climax but halfheartedly depicted here. If you want to know what burning Troy was really like then, in a Stratford season full of cross-references, stroll along the Avon and catch the First Player's speech in Hamlet. - The Trojan Women runs until Oct. 5. For tickets and information, call 1-800-567-1600 or visit www.stratfordfestival.ca.

2008-06-11-it-was-the-best-and-now-it-s-:
Soulpepper's Uncle Vanya was a great production when we first saw it in 2001. It keeps getting better. Back for the third time, it now has a quartet of central performances that, fine individually, have reached a phenomenal level of contact. They also inhabit an external world that in Laszlo Marton's production is more clearly and starkly depicted than ever.

There's very little glamour in this account of Chekhov's world. Uncle Vanya himself, for all his pretentions to (and actual possession of ) wit and culture, is drudging his life away as an absentee landlord's estate manager. In Diego Matamoros' performance he begins both the first and the last acts curled invisibly in an armchair, like a figure out of Lewis Carroll: a victim of depression in the first case and despair in the second, having failed to shoot either himself or the exploiting Professor on whom he blames his own failure. In between, he has fallen hopelessly in love with the Professor's beautiful young wife and had to endure the humiliation of seeing the local doctor get closer to first base with her than he could ever manage. Matamoros rolls all these disparate defeats into one ball of pain and frustration, without ever losing sight of the fact that the play is, in some sense, a comedy. As Sonya tells him, he will survive. That's the trouble.

Liisa Repo-Martell's Sonya is even more moving, and fiercely so. Any traces of waif-like fragility have long since departed this performance. She's a practical country girl, tormented by feeling unattractive. When she asks the doctor, whom she adores, if he could ever be interested in a "friend or sister" of hers, she curses her choice of words as soon as they're out of her mouth; though the cruellest irony is that he can't see through them, transparent as they are. Enlisting the match-making assistance of the beauteous Elena, she knows her doom before her friend can tell her of it, and she accepts it silently, but with tragic weight.

Kristen Thomson shows more clearly than ever before how Elena clings to her own comesticized image as a way of keeping emotional attachments at bay. Marton makes much of these characters' habits of rushing out -- from the room, the house, the district -- whenever a situation becomes painful or embarrassing. This applies even to the one supposed realist among them, Astrov, the doctor whom Albert Schultz plays as bone-weary. He has to come a long way -- on horseback, through the mud -- to make house calls, and Schultz, whose performance has become harder with the years (perhaps excessively so), is on a short fuse. He is violently impatient with the suicidal Vanya, but hardly less so with himself, for his professional foul-ups and for falling in love with Elena. Even his hymns of praise to forest preservation -- his one great passion -- are subdued and hurried, as if he hardly expected anyone to be interested and has grown a shell to pre-empt other people's laughter.

Apart from the occasional explosion (mainly from Matamoros) these people speak very quietly, because they know one another so well and can take their relationships for granted. So of course can the actors, who have played these roles since the production started. Even at the risk of some inaudibility (Michael Levine's set is less acoustically hospitable here than it was at Harbourfront), this deep sense of ensemble is as precious as it's rare. No one else in the cast has been able to put down such deep roots, with the possible exception of William Webster, who in the minute role of a bent-double servant functions, as I wrote before, as part of the scenery; he is the image of life going on, regardless. Michael Simpson, the production's other survivor, brings little more to old Waffles than a voice and a wig. Among the newcomers, Joseph Ziegler's Professor gets the Professor's tetchiness and pomposity, plus a new and credible smoothness, but doesn't as yet get very far beneath them. Hazel Desbarats as Vanya's pedantically besotted Maman is a more blatant eccentric than was the late and wonderful Charmion King; Patricia Hamilton, though not the world's most obvious peasant-woman, doles out the right measures of Russian tea and sympathy as the family nurse.

The play is an exposition of the law of unintended consequences. At one level it's farce. The Professor's plan to sell the estate may well be self-interested but it could be sensible; however, it gets nowhere because Vanya and Sonya, the people most affected, have more tormenting things on their mind. Then Vanya tries his hand as a tragic hero with ludicrous, agonizing results. This climactic scene has lost something in clarity. But other wonderful moments remain: Vanya's making love to a chair in place of Elena, Elena leaping into Astrov's arms when it's too late to matter. The production's physical dynamics still match its emotional, with the rain pelting down before, after and halfway through the action. This is a hard world, lit by a single electric bulb that's carefully rationed; there is, what with Astrov's forestry schemes, a topical emphasis on conservation. This is Chekhov unsentimental but loving. It's as good as theatre gets. - Uncle Vanya runs until June 21. Visit www.soulpepper.ca for more information.

2008-06-13-heavy-on-tragedy-light-on-the:
CBCs adaptation of Othello, The Tragedy of the Moor, is handsome, intelligent and -- inevitably -- limited. Some of the limitations are literal; a lot of the Shakespearean text is gone, including nearly all the long speeches.

Carlo Rota's Othello doesn't get to describe his wooing of Desdemona, or to rebut the charge of having bewitched her; indeed, no such charge is made. When his jealousy kicks in, his farewell to his military identity is reduced to a single line: "Othellos occupations gone" has gone.

He doesn't compare his own implacability to that of the Pontic sea, though implacability turns out to be something that Rota is good at. There's no willow scene; which is tough on the storys two leading ladies. Even Othellos sacrificial approach to the killing of Desdemona (it is the cause) is abbreviated. What gets lost in all this is the sacramental aspect of the play and the character: The key reason for his actions seeming not credible but also blasphemously misguided.

Which is strange in a way, because this production implies a religious conflict that isn't there in the original. Though many of the play's words have been cut, only one has been changed: The derogatory "thicklips" becomes Muslim. This Moor of Venice is ethnically correct as he isnt in Shakespeare, to whom "moor" just seems to have meant black.

After decades of being told that only black actors can play Othello (the truth is that few actors of any race can play him) its piquant as well as impressive to see him played by the racially inscrutable Rota: British-born and accented, Canadian-based and currently best known for Little Mosque on the Prairie.

Rota usually projects a humorous self-awareness that should be all wrong for Othello, but turns out to be all right. He establishes authority without effort ("put up your bright swords") and seems very sure both of himself and of his love.

Iago has to work very hard to crack that shell; some clever adaptation (by Matthew Edison and director Zaib Shaikh) makes it seem a longer, more varied and gradual process than it is in the theatre. The temptation takes place over a buffet-lunch; when the dam is burst, Othello finds an outlet in hacking away at a joint of meat.

A terrible logic, unfounded but unstoppable, takes over the two scenes in which he abuses his wife as a whore. His last speech is left intact; in fact we hear it twice, at beginning and end. (The play is a flashback.) And with it we reach greatness. Rota lays out the facts of the case calmly, sanely, tormentedly; it seems he'll go quietly. And when he whips out his knife and kills himself, it's total shock. Its a long time since Ive seen an Othello, on stage or screen, as good as this.

He couldn't be called the richest vocally: Lie thee down and roar, says Emilia when the Moor discovers the truth, but roaring isn't in Rotas register. But then neither is it in televisions, which effectively forbids shouting. The alternative method of conveying intensity is by whispering, and there's a lot of that here.

The cast includes a posse of Stratford Festival veterans -- Graham Abbey, Peter Donaldson, Jonathan Goad-- who can colour and personalize the verse at any volume; Abbey is the best Cassio I have ever seen.

The character most diminished is, unexpectedly, Matthew Deslippe's Iago, who ought to thrive on secrecy but here just seems furtive; he could be pegged for a villain a mile off. Losing the bulk of his soliloquies, he also loses any chance at a deeper demon-ism; he comes closest when laying his plans over a military map, moving the other characters around as if they were pawns -- which to him of course they are.

The show has been given a rich but indeterminate period look; theres nothing especially Venetian about its Venice (not a canal in sight) but its Cyprus is, if not Cypriot, then certainly North African. Othello should feel at home there.

Initially, indeed, he does, but he has brought his Venetian status as an outsider with him, and it makes him vulnerable. Since the casting entails omitting the insistent way in which everybody -- himself included -- refers to Othello as "black," we have to take his alienation to a large extent on trust. The concept, as so often when productions go all out for relevance, doesnt quite fit.

For once, we have an adaptation that says less about racism than the original. To be fair, the billing merely says "based on the play by William Shakespeare." It doesn't claim to be the play. But the closer it comes, the better it is. - Othello, The Tragedy of the Moor airs Sunday at 9 p. m. on CBC.

2008-06-14-spotlight-on-shakespeare-the-:
There's a line in A Midsummer Night's Dream about "the spiced Indian air," and the production that Luminato has brought to Toronto is legitimately drenched in it. The play also tells us that Oberon, king of the fairies, has come from the farthest step of India; whether he lives there, or was just holidaying, isnt revealed, but the Elizabethans associated the supernatural with the East. Either way, this production, directed by the British Tim Supple and cast with actors from all over India and Sri Lanka, has more than exoticism going for it. It has authenticity.

It was first staged in New Delhi in 2006, was then adopted by the Royal Shakespeare Company, and seems to have been touring ever since. The actors perform in English and, we are told, in some half-a-dozen Indian dialects; sometimes the language changes within the course of a speech. So to get much out of it, you either have to be fluent in several different tongues, or to know the original pretty well. The latter is advisable anyway since this show, like Black Watch, has been booked by Luminato into a big space with terrible acoustics; there are times when you cant tell which language is being spoken. Visually, too, the show probably loses from the lack of intimacy. Still, plenty of spectacle remains; and so does a great deal more.

Some scenes in this version make more sense than ever before, and not just the supernatural ones. The plight of Hermia, threatened with death or a nunnery if she refuses to wed the man of her father's choice, is a lot more immediate when set in a world that knows of arranged marriage, and even of enforced wifely sacrifice. When daddy (J. Jayakamur) relents, that carries weight, too. The now-customary doubling of Oberon with Theseus (P. R. Jijoy) and Titania with Hippolyta (Archana Ramaswamy) comes over as something more than routine; the mortal pair really learn from the travails of their dream-doubles. Titania, as it happens, is as sexy as hell; also mad as hell when Oberon demands custody of her changeling boy (who is rewardingly present) and horrified to her roots when she discovers the trick he's played on her. Horrified but not deeply shaken: So shes had sex with a man transformed to a donkey -- if youre immortal you get over it.

The production has been compared to Peter Brook's famous 1970 version, and they have things in common. A gym-like set; pervasive use of seemingly home-made music, joyous or eerie; actors who double as acrobats, though as much here out of sheer high spirits as to simulate magic; a bed that hangs suspended in air, though it doesn't in this case represent Titanias bower. When she retires to sleep, or when the mortal lovers do, theyre cocooned, marvellously, in giant pods; when they're subsequently discovered-- the mortals anyway -- they're entwined in pairs. Sumant Jayakrishnans set seems composed, initially, of silver foil: a flimsy back wall through which the actors erupt when we move from town to forest.

Helena (Shanaya Rafaat) and Hermia (Yuki Elias) seem to have been to an English boarding-school. They handle the original verse more expressively than anyone else and build a persuasive relationship of shared confidences and mutual jealousies, though it fades as the play goes on. The presiding spirit is Puck (Ajay Kumar) whose "what fools these mortals be" is stupendous in its other-worldy detachment. In the most astonishing visual sequence of the show, he ties intricate silken ropes around the quarrelling lovers so that they end up, most appropriately, in a boxing-ring.

This show is more insistently erotic than Brooks, and more entertainingly. When Bottom (Joy Fernandes) turns ass, his outsize ears are less noticeable than his outsize phallus: a joke that you might expect to, well, subside early on but that remains potent, in all sorts of ways. Its memory lingers on into his awakening, when he arrives at "me-thought I had..." and does not dare to elaborate. This whole speech in fact is miraculous, the crown of an entrancingly self-important performance, whose satisfied solemnity with the English language may recall Borat to some and Peter Sellers to others. (If that sounds racist, too bad; the sizeable Asian proportion of the audience were laughing too.) Quince (Vivek Mishra) is a bearded village elder, and the amateur actors' scenes of consultation and rehearsal are delightful. So much so that when the play of Pyramus and Thisbe actually arrives, it is -- apart from Quince's prologue, which is super --an anti-climax.

There are other imperfections. Some of the play feels skated over, whatever the language. There is a long dance sequence that communicates hardly anything except the desire to have a long dance sequence. But at the end, all, as Puck says, is mended. As he delivers his valediction, the other actors stomp and sway behind him, joyously and hypnotically. It really feels like magic. More and rarer than that, it really feels like a dream.

Blink, another Luminato show, is also like a dream but not such a good one. Its written and performed by the Soulpepper Academy; young professionals who have done excellent work with the parent company but here seem mostly stilted, as do the lines that theyve written for themselves. A danger of collective creation is that the participants can emerge convinced that they have newer news to impart than is actually the case. Here the messages are that war is awful, and that those who photograph it for a living may emerge scarred, and not just physically. I don't doubt either proposition, but this piece doesn't make them fresh, though Weyni Mengeshas staging, with its evocation of desert combat, initially suggests that it will. Mike Ross is persuasively taut and zoned-out as the cameraman back from Iraq, Sarah Wilson has a few urgent moments as his pregnant wife, but the others are playing ciphers or caricatures.

- A Midsummer Nights Dream closes tomorrow at the Canon Theatre. Call 416-870-8000 for more information; Blink closes tomorrow at the Young Centre. Call 416-866-8666 for details.

2008-06-17-a-carnival-of-sexes:
THEATRE REVIEW

THE TAMING OF THE SHREW

Festival Theatre, Stratford

---

Peter Hinton has enough imagination, invention, intelligence and cheek for four directors. This is a good thing. But his Stratford production of The Taming of the Shrew might actually be the work of four directors. It's never dull and bits of it are inspired, but it is confusing.

Its jumping-off point seems to be a historical paradox. The Shrew, a play that has been taken to advocate the subjugation of women, was written at a time in England when a woman was in charge. This production brings Elizabeth I onstage, both as a backdrop, courtesy of a hugely blown-up miniature, and in her own person. First, in what directors insist on referring to as "the rarely staged Induction," though I can hardly recall a production that didn't include it, she takes the place of the text's anonymous Lord; that is, she finds the tinker Christopher Sly passed out in front of an inn, and persuades him that he is a nobleman, for whom the play-within-the-play -- The Taming of the Shrew itself -- is performed. And when that play gets underway, the Queen, or someone looking exactly like her, starts appearing in it; she takes the role of the Widow who pairs up with the spurned wooer Hortensio in the last scene and seems about to give him a tough marital time. This is very hard to follow. It's also, in a production whose costumes and general ambience are aggressively Elizabethan, unconvincing. No acting troupe of the time, strolling or otherwise, would have put the Virgin Queen recognizably onstage (as a twice-married woman, yet) unless it fancied being hung, drawn and quartered. And though England is famously littered with pubs claiming that Queen Elizabeth Slept There, she would not have been caught on any premises patronized by the likes of Sly. Ins Choi makes less of the tinker's ordinarily juicy role that any actor I have seen, possibly because there's so much going on around him. The Queen herself (Barbara Fulton) is woefully uncommunicative as an actress, but seems to have been cast for her singing. Oh yes, she sings as well. So does most of the cast, especially the tavern wenches, who give out with ballads of the time (plus one that's been smuggled in from The Beggar's Opera) about the woes of wedlock: 15th-century hurtin' songs.

So, is Petruchio's "taming" of Katherina a hurtin' thing or a healin' thing? It depends here on which scene you're looking at.

Kate has a limp; that's a very literal reading of a line of Petruchio's that's probably meant as a joke, but it gives her a source of resentment to add to the usual ones of an unsympathetic father and spoiled younger sister. Irene Poole's is a very intense performance whose anger, as hasn't always been the case in her modern work, is kept within the bounds of the character. She also has a dormant wit that's sparked, to her visible surprise, by Evan Buliung's eloquent and unusually sensitive Petruchio. They fall in love at first meeting. This always happens in productions of the Shrew, for the very good reason that it's what happens in the play, but it's unusual for her to kiss him on demand as willingly as she does at the end of the wooing scene here. It does make the rest of the play seem sort of unnecessary, and more than usually cruel. But there are complications here too, as Buliung makes clear, with the help of the odd pronoun-change, that in depriving her of food and sleep, he's doing it to himself as well. She gives in, but, unlike most Kates, she doesn't happily play along. It's hard to know what to make of her submission speech, but she isn't playing it for irony. It provokes an alarmed squeak of protest from Adrienne Gould's Bianca, though since this kid sibling has hitherto been the usual tease and more than the usual flirt, it's a bit late in the night for her to start playing the sisterhood card. Anyway Petruchio seems genuinely touched, and the pair are all set for what critics from Harold Bloom to Germaine Greer have hailed as one of the few happy marriages in Shakespeare.

What Hinton seems to be at is providing a carnival of the period's shifting attitudes to relations between the sexes. But you have to pant to keep up. I've always believed that Katherina's turning point comes when she intercedes on behalf of a servant whom Petruchio is berating; it's the first time she's considered anybody's feelings besides her own. Add Hinton's to the long line of productions that have failed to mark this moment: surprisingly, since elsewhere masters and servants are much on his mind. The two themes collide when he turns the lackey Grumio into a woman, one whom Petruchio can beat as he would never dream of beating his wife. (Kate hits him, not the reverse.) The only thing that can be said for this muddying of the play's sexual politics is that it provides a good if unexpected role for Lucy Peacock. Intriguingly, she passes the oppression down to her subordinate Curtis (Paul Dunn), a stay-at-home drudge who begs for news of the outside world as if literally starved for it.

Over in the Bianca subplot, the help are having an even rougher time: A passing threat to slit the nose of the uppity valet Tranio is taken, like Kate's limp, literally, so that Ben Carlson turns up in the last scene nasally mutilated but still serving. I have no idea what Patrick McManus is doing with the page Biondello, for whom he looks both too old and too upscale. Still, what with Randy Hughson, Jeff Lillico and Juan Chioran as rival suitors (Tom, Dick and Harry in the Cole Porter translation) the stage is alive with good actors clinging fiercely to their author, their director and their own instincts. Best of the lot is Stephen Ouimette as father Baptista, giving a squirm of incredulous delight at getting his problem daughter off his hands. Santo Loquasto's set is a handsome complement to the spare modern lines of his Hamlet. As for what Elizabeth is doing in the middle of it all: I believe that Hinton thinks that the Queen has deposed the tinker and the play is her dream -- of what her life might have been, for better and for worse, as an ordinary woman. It's ingenious, but as usual in such cases, the play, knowing nothing of such things, buckles under the strain. - The Taming of the Shrew runs until Oct. 25. 2008-06-20-toward-russia-with-lovers:
The late Wendy Wasserstein described The Sisters Rosensweig, a 1992 New York success now being given a belated Toronto premiere by the Harold Green Jewish Theatre Company, as "neither a serious nor a comedic play." She then contradicted herself by saying "it is hopefully both."

It can't be both and neither. Let's not get into "hopefully," but just when did the pretentious "comedic" replace the perfectly serviceable "comic"? Maybe "comic" is considered too full-blooded a word. Chekhov's plays are both serious and comic. Wasserstein's, though moderately enjoyable in the Broadway middlebrow manner, is neither.

It's fair to invoke Chekhov because the play itself does. Not only is it about three sisters, but it starts with the birthday of one of them. We glimpse the celebration dinner table at the back of Phillip Silver's sumptuous set, just as we do in the first act of Three Sisters. Like their Russian counterparts, the Rosensweig ladies receive a succession of gentleman callers, some welcome and expected, others -- at least initially -- not.

The play takes place in London, though the sisters are American, originally from the Bronx. Sara, whose house we are in, has a high-profile job in the British office of an Asian bank. Pfeni uses Sara's place as a base. She's a journalist who used to cover international disaster zones but has now settled for glossy travel pieces; she's just got back from Bombay. That leaves Gorgeous, the only one to have stayed in the United States and the only one currently married. Back home in Massachusetts she's lucked into a career as a radio host, dispensing advice. She's managed to combine a gig as a tour guide with attendance at Sara's birthday.

Gorgeous is also the only sister to have stayed true to her Jewish roots. She's quite vociferous about it, as she is about most things that arise. Pfeni is indifferent, and Sara icily hostile. She's also a multiple divorcee, a situation that -- as she says in the play's most memorable line -- has given her a rich choice of surnames; the WASPish one she has settled on is Goode. She is desultorily dating a British businessman, whom her teenage daughter Tess describes as a Nazi. She also attracts the attentions of a furrier from New York, who seems to represent everything in her background from which she has been trying to escape. Pfeni, meanwhile, enjoys, when enjoyment is possible, an on-and-off liaison with a gay English theatre director.

This assortment of relationships gives the play a fractured, compartmentalized feeling. The same split focus occurs in Chekhov, but his plays are unified by some large event bearing down on all the characters: the sale of a cherry orchard, the army leaving town, a threatened or actual suicide.

The Sisters Rosensweig is set against something much bigger -- the disintegration of the Soviet empire -- but it's too big, and too far off, to impinge fully. It gives rise to twinges of social conscience in Pfeni and even in Sara. Young Tess is even planning a trip to Lithuania along with her activist boyfriend. But it doesn't amount to more than an intermittent plot device, and even the Jewish heritage theme doesn't count for as much as the author apparently wants it to. She seems to be blackmailing her characters with it, much as Gorgeous does. And it all seems mixed in, anyway, with an imposed guilt at having left America.

Why shouldn't Sara live in London if she wants to?

So the interest in the play comes down to the sisters' relationships with one another and -- more importantly, despite the title -- with their various men, and these don't carry enough of a charge. The not-quite-serious, not-quite-comic mode means in practice that both laughter and pain are muted. Wasserstein won't sell out with a happy ending but can't bring herself to write an unhappy one either.

Jim Warren's production is very assured, so well placed and well paced that you all but take it for granted. It doesn't manage, though, to place the sisterhood where it presumably belongs, at the centre of the play. There's a scene of reconciliation and reminiscence that works quite well as a set-piece, without ever persuading us these women could be related. (Their colourings, for a start, are wildly disparate, however many allowances you make for hair-dye.)

Individually, they're accomplished. Rosemary Dunsmore is icy, brittle and troubled as a Sara who's gone native with a vengeance (barely a trace of an American accent); Sarah Dodd is pained and confused, but with a winningly tolerant smile, as Pfeni; and Linda Kash shifts in to yenta overdrive as Gorgeous, though certainly garnering laughs on the trip.

Of the men, Richard Greenblatt's fur merchant makes wryness into a fountain of dramatic energy as well as humour, and as Pfeni's love interest, who turns out more loving than interested, Steve Cumyn has an effervescent time testing the waters of bisexuality. (Pfeni's character is apparently autobiographical, but that doesn't stop this relationship from seeming thoroughly manufactured.) Cumyn's performance is geographically impeccable, as is Michael Hanrahan's right-wing suitor with rumoured unsavoury tastes. Regrettably, he's confined to a single scene, but he does suggest unexplored depths, and he registers the evening's greatest moment of silent wit when he casts his eyes on a young man's ratty sweater and decides that it's taught him all he needs to know.

There's also a repeated device -- not quite a running gag -- whereby a character bursts into song, either sacred or profane, and is interrupted by someone's coming through the door. Music is important to these people, and the dramatist lets us know it. But she doesn't make us feel it. - The Sisters Rosensweig runs until Sunday. For information and tickets, call 416-366-7723 or visit stlc.com.

2008-06-21-al-gore-fights-king-cole-with:
So what do you do with all those suddenly outdated Toronto recycling bins and boxes? You recycle them: as stage furniture. They make up, in various configurations, the set for An Inconvenient Musical. Good luck doing anything as constructive with the new wheeled monsters that have taken their place.

An Inconvenient Musical is a riotously entertaining show that achieves the remarkable feat of mercilessly lampooning Al Gore's famous documentary while reinforcing its message. Gore himself appears as the narrator-figure, impersonated by Doug Morency with a perfectly judged air of self-satisfied self-deprecation. Having tried, he tells us, to get his point across by every other available means, he has finally settled on "the most powerful weapon on Earth:musical theatre."

The musical he presents is, like so many these days, largely a spoof of other musicals, but it avoids being irritatingly parasitic, perhaps because it actually has something on its mind. Here, as well as in some plot points, it resembles Urinetown -- less musically sophisticated, perhaps, but funnier. It isn't the kind of show that you would expect to have an intermission (it started out last year on the Toronto fringe where small is necessary), but it justifies the indulgence with a first-act closer that's terrific and a second-half opener that's sublime. The former is a bombastically prophetic number in Les Mis style celebrating The Day After Tomorrow ("the day after the day after today"). The latter is a very close parody of the Seasons of Love song that kicks off the second half of Rent, renamed Seasons We Love and performed by the cast -- all eight of them -- in mufflers and mittens: odd garb in which to complain about global warming but this is Toronto, a climate in which, as they complain with some bitterness, it can be hard to keep the faith.

The Rummoli Brothers wrote the script and collaborated with Waylen Miki on the score. The story's hero, played by Cyrus Lane with an impressive combination of square jaw and vibrant voice, is Gordon Green, a Middle American lad, whose dad has a job with an energy company and dies when working on a top-secret device called the Samoflange. (Gord loses his mom too. And his dog. And his guitar.) Following his nose and connecting the dots, Gordon arrives at the HQ of his father's former employer, mega-tycoon Cole Powers who wants to re-convert the world to, guess what, coal power, and has developed the Samoflange to bring this about, never mind that it kills everyone who comes within a few feet of it. (So some environmentalists complain about overpopulation. This'll show 'em.) Mr. Powers has also bought the state of Wyoming for his testing ground (on Craigslist for $640, no pets).

He has a slavering supporting trio of lesser-mega tycoons with military uniforms and fluctuating Dr. Strangelove accents. General Motors, General Electric and General Store, which I think runs Wal-Mart. Others of the same rank are mentioned but do not appear, including General Public "who never goes to the theatre unless he knows someone in the cast." In his fight against this dastardly conglomerate, Gordon falls in with a vegan cafe owner and cabaret artiste and her friends, most of whom have been drastically affected by pollutants. One of them claims to have mutated into C3P0 from Star Wars, though he's at least as reminiscent of the Tin Man from The Wizard of Oz. Whatever, he's played by Matt Baram with divine gentleness and tick-tock timing. The gang spearhead an anti-Cole resistance movement whose acronym is so crowded with consonants as to be unpronounceable by all but the exceptionally gifted, most of whom seem to be in the show. Gordon tries to write a protest song, but finds that neither folk, heavy metal, nor that freedom-fighters' favourite, doowop ("that's all the existing musical genres"), will serve his turn. Finally, though, he does come up with a lucky number. And that is where the plot really thickens.

One of the Rummolis, under what I take to be his real name of Kurt Firla, designed the production's numerous slide-shows and videos, which make great use of pie-charts and are highly accomplished, both as satire and in their own right. One of their figures looks like Ned Flanders, and the show as a whole recalls The Simpsons in the unflagging and unpredictable way in which it keeps its jokes coming -- and in its combination of comic licence and civic responsibility.

There are a couple of minor acting disappointments: Lee Smart's King Cole has a highly twirlable villain's moustache, but not much vocal clarity behind it. Since his role consists largely of malapropisms, that's a handicap; it's hard to understand what he isn't saying. Ayumi Iizuki vacillates uncertainly between heroine and villainess, though admittedly so does her role. She does get to sing a song about being Vice President, of Powers' Enward company, which Morency's Gore indignantly interrupts and then takes over, on the grounds that VP is his job, or at least his identity. David Suzuki also sings, a rousing anthem about non-passive resistance, in which he's unexpectedly and irresistibly joined by two bushes-full of small furry animals. He's played by Chris Gibbs. Aurora Browne and Sandy Jobin-Bevans complete the cast and are both very good. Nearly all the performers are Second City alumni and, much as I like revue, this musical shows them off better than almost any show I can remember at their home base. This show will burn up a lot of fossil-fuel before it's done. It's going a long way.

- An Inconvenient Musical runs through June 29 at the Factory Studio Theatre; 416-504-9971.

2008-06-23-as-long-as-no-one-knows-do-re:
How do you solve a problem like Maria? Maybe by not creating it in the first place.

It's obviously too late to wish that The Sound of Music had never been written. You could climb every mountain and still not find that dream, though the show is by far the least interesting of the Rodgers and Hammerstein musicals, including their three bona fide flops. The musical with the nuns and the Nazis is immovably in the cultural bloodstream, the object alike of swooning adoration and camp mockery. (Some people, I'm sure, combine both reactions.) It's also the only musical whose casting could become the subject of a TV reality show. Cabaret is a popular musical, too, a cult one as well, but it's impossible to imagine a show called The Search for Sally Bowles. The object of such a quest needs to have a certain innocence about her. We have to watch a parade of ingenues competing for the most ingenuous role of all.

And now we have the chance. Andrew Lloyd Webber produced a successful stage revival of The Sound of Music in London, having discovered his leading lady through a televised nationwide search, complete with voting viewers. Mirvish Productions are bringing the stage production to Toronto, and CBC is bringing How Do You Solve a Problem Like Maria? along with it, or rather, before it. Last Sunday and Monday, the vast field of contestants was narrowed down to 50, then 20, then 10. Starting next week, the hunt is really on: a further round of tests and auditions with Canadian viewers polled for their opinions on who will be Toronto's Maria.

It is, of course, a publicity stunt and, in essence, an old one. Think of the search for an unknown to play Scarlett in Gone with the Wind. But in those days, the public was supposed to be a hungry witness of the spectacle, not a participant. Now the electronic election has become the model, and nobody seems to find it in the least surprising.

It's frightening. For one thing, it abjectly denies the old showbiz wisdom that you don't give the public what they think they want, you give them what they never knew they wanted. This is a real live production we're talking about, not the nebulous chance of being acclaimed as a Canadian or American Idol. And the casting of its leading role is to be determined by a head-count among people with no professional expertise, in circumstances even more artificial than those of the usual audition. Lloyd Webber himself said it best, while mulling over the aspirants' videos before watching the Top 20 strut their stuff for him at the London Palladium: "On TV, everyone is reduced to the same screen size." It can't tell you very much about stage presence.

David Mirvish, interviewed in the Palladium lobby, said that it was all very fraught, they were all very talented, and he was glad he didn't have to make the decision. But he should be making it, or helping to make it -- it's his job. As for the show's director, whom one would expect to have something to say about the identity of his leading lady, he's so far been conspicuous by his absence. Do all these people feel happy about abdicating their responsibilities? The only professional whose opinion seems to count is the man everyone compulsively refers to as "Lord Lloyd Webber." In the words of the commentary the postulant Marias are offering up their talents before "the Lord himself." He, to his credit, is coming over shrewd and good-humoured -- the man who began his career with the air of an engagingly earnest schoolboy now seems like a tolerant, seen-it-all headmaster. Not bad for a mogul.

And, to be fair, the TV show is a cut above most of its talent-contest competitors. It has a sense of humour about itself, as demonstrated in a title sequence involving rival Marias biffing one another on the familiar mountain-top from the opening of the movie. The movie also inspires what the commentary describes as "a Maria essential-- singing while spinning," though the image of a twirling Maria derives entirely from Julie Andrews and her director's camera. You can bet that spinning wasn't essential when Mary Martin created Maria on Broadway. But that's another problem with Maria; her show has become a staged movie. Our host, Gavin Crawford, shows little sign of his comic past and the show has a disconcerting habit of photographing him curled up on windowsills like Peter Pan, but he probably copes as well as anyone could with the built-in sycophancy of the genre and with such portentous pronouncements on performance anxiety as "they may have excelled in Maria school, but this is the real world." "Maria school" is the jovial name given to the theatrical boot camp at which those on the long shortlist were put through the paces by a trio of professionals:a musical director, a vocal coach and a leading actor. Here, the program gets down to business, allowing us to see scenes being worked on and songs being worked through. Sequences like this were the best parts of last season's Triple Sensation, and Maria has so far been offering them in more concentrated form. It's a wall and we're the flies.

But it's still very artificial. The lucky Marias who got flown to London had to put on a show -- a carefully rehearsed production -- to get in a show. It's also, like all these things, protractedly cruel -- and it will inevitably get crueller. The Palladium culling process involved the young actresses parading before the Lord himself in unpredictable groups of one, two and three, left completely off guard as to which among them had passed and which had failed. The suspense, of course, was entirely for our benefit, and it was abetted by cutting between these individual triumphs and agonies and the spectacle of the entire group carolling about the hills being alive. Theatre has always been a blood sport, but traditionally it's only been the final stage of the game that gets acted out in public. I also wonder just how conclusive the popular vote will be. In the West End production, the role of Maria ended up going to a performer who was already fairly well known and well established. I suspect that the authorities have allowed themselves some wiggle-room. If not, well, that's their problem. - How Do You Solve a Problem Like Maria? airs Sundays and Mondays at 8 p. m. on CBC

2008-06-24-this-doc-doesn-t-belong-bille:
Arinze Eze is the writer, director, narrator and also the subject of Where I Belong, which was made under the auspices of the National Film Board, and is screened tonight on CBC Newsworld's The Lens. Eze's parents are Nigerian, and he grew up in Nigeria where he trained to be an engineer. However, he was born in Canada, and having a Canadian passport -- "my escape card" he calls it -- he was able to come here to pursue his career. It didn't prove that easy, and anyway his life took a turn. He ditched engineering to fulfill lifelong dreams of being an artist. He's a versatile one; his film shows him making music, making theatre and --particularly and most impressively -- painting. But the principal job description that he offers is filmmaker.

Where I Belong begins with the stark statement "I don't believe in Canada any more," voiced over shots of Eze trekking through the snow. He didn't just come to Canada; he came to Winnipeg in, he says "one of the worst winters." No wonder there was temperature shock. It doesn't seem to have lasted, though; later scenes show him braving the climate in an open-necked shirt. His deeper disillusion also seems to have been temporary. It makes an ear-catching opening, but that's about all.

The film, in fact, is very bitty. Much of it concerns Eze's relationship with his girlfriend Tina, who is not only white but Jewish, and their worries about how their respective families will react. Eze's parents are all set to visit him, though they're delayed for a long time by visa problems. "I was born in Canada," says Eze at this point, "but my parents can't come and visit me -- because they're Nigerian." This is a subject that deserves more investigation than it gets. Anyway, the restrictions were apparently lifted because the parents arrive, separately, mother first. Subtitles -- "3 days before Mom's arrival" -- provide what must be meant as a suspenseful countdown. But it's all build-up, no payoff.

That goes, as it so often does, for the publicity as well. "An African-Canadian man's interracial relationship with a white woman suffers parental disapproval when his Nigerian parents come to visit." So says the press release, which must have been watching some other film. When Mom does arrive, she couldn't be nicer, smarter or more understanding; and Pop isn't far behind (in either sense), insisting that love is the most important thing. Both parents, it's true, have warnings about the problems that may face the children of interracial couples, but nothing they say could be construed as in any way intolerant or obstructive. They actively support the relationship.

The irony is that it's already broken down: a casualty not of anything Eze's parents say but of what he and Tina fear they might say. It's left very vague; the couple remain close and are obviously still fond of one another. (As they say, "we have five years of history -- that doesn't go away.") The "pressures" that have driven them apart are, again, left unexplored. Tina, whom we always seem to see gazing into a mirror applying lipstick, admits that Eze is clearly not "a nice Jewish man" such as her own family would have wished for her, but how they dealt with the situation is never revealed. Tina is worried about Eze's mother being a born-again

Christian: "I hope," she says, "the religious conversation won't come up". (It doesn't: not that we hear, anyway.) Tina also says that she "doesn't want to come in the middle of [Eze's] family" -- but what about hers? Maybe her folks just didn't want to appear in the film, maybe they weren't asked, but their absence makes the picture very one-sided. I must confess to an antediluvian suspicion of people who like to enact crucial scenes from their private lives while the cameras are rolling. But if it's going to be done, I think it ought to be done thoroughly.

We all place an exaggerated value on our own experiences. Where I Belong, which won in the NFB's Reel Diversity Competition, "a national initiative in partnership with CBC Newsworld," looks like a film made because its director wanted to make a film, and found his autobiography the handiest subject. According to that press release, "a recent Statistics Canada study reports a 30% increase in mixed-race marriages since 2001, but family acceptance can be slow." That's worth making a film about. But Eze, the NFB and the CBC haven't made it. - Where I Belong airs today on CBC Newsworld at 10 p. m.

Black & White Photo: Allen Fraser, National Film Board Of Canada / Arinze Eze's Where I Belong looks at interracial relationships and the anxieties and reactions surrounding them. ;; Caption:
2008-06-26-lemon-zesty-jazz-is-in-the-fa:
CONCERT REVIEW

Sandy Stewart and Bill Charlap

The Old Mill, Toronto

There are some standard songs that are, paradoxically, so well-known that nobody sings them. It takes an extraordinary singer to make something fresh of Tea for Two or Smoke Gets in Your Eyes. Sandy Stewart, who is an extraordinary singer, did them back to back on Tuesday night, thought them through with no trickery, and took a rapt audience along with her.

She reclaimed the Tea song with what I would call a gentle garden swing, or perhaps a soft hammock rock: a languorous, hypnotic reading

that found space for a gently comic disgust for the line in the verse about being discontented with homes that are rented. It conveyed real pleasure, just as the Smoke song, an even tougher assignment, communicated real pain. She did the whole song out of tempo, first philosophically, then shocking us by sounding out the lyric's cruellest words -- I am without my love, "now laughing friends deride" -- like a tolling bell.

In the early 60s, Stewart was the girl singer on thea Perry Como TV show. Shes now a woman singer, physically compact, musically and dramatically mature, with a velvet voice, an understated wit and a subtle sense of dynamics secured by superb intonation. (She can bring off the occasional Judy Garland big finish, though I rather wish she wouldn't.) She also, with admirable forethought, gave birth to a son, Bill Charlap, who is the crown prince of the younger jazz pianists. Accompanying her, he's in more of a conservatory mode than when he himself is leader (though hes always been a musician who plays songs rather than chords); his instrumental choruses amplify and expand the moods his moms created: notably on After You, an alarmingly grown-up Cole Porter number about anticipated heartbreak -- one of those this is too good to last songs. Its flip side -- "too hot not to cool down" -- is Porter's Just One of Those Things, another of those warhorses that Stewart resuscitates by playing down the flipness. It's another of her rubato ballads, every word and image freshly thought, with a hint of Sinatra world-weariness at the edges.

A song that Porter should have written but didnt -- Jerome Kern and Oscar Hammerstein did -- is All in Fun, a gentle romantic spoof of Manhattan sophistication that Stewart phrases beautifully -- "our feet have left the ground -- a bit." She once recorded a wonderful Kern album, and from it she also included Remind Me, a blend of sentiment and commonsense: not so much bitter-sweet as tart-sweet. She and Charlap seem justifiably proud of one another, without overdoing it. Their encore could not have been lovelier or more fitting: Two for the Road, a collaboration of Henry Mancini and Leslie Bricusse, and the best song either man ever wrote.

Stewart and Charlaps performance was part of the Toronto Jazz Festival's Cabaret at the Old Mill series, which mostly features Canadian musical-theatre performers: tonight it's Patricia Zentilli, a Dora nominee for Little Shop of Horrors, and tomorrow Louise Pitre. It's an initiative Toronto greatly needs. But we need visitors too. Stewart is a beacon, quite possibly the best singer of this repertoire alive.

2008-06-27-tracking-the-truth-of-two-ter:
Heres a typical moment from tonight's instalment of The Naked Archaeologist. Our narrator and star, Simcha Jacobovici, fully clothed, says that there is evidence all over the Middle East of the truth of the story of Sodom and Gomorrah. Cut to a scene from an old movie: a newspaper editor saying, presumably to some reporter, "I thought I told you to kill that story." Funny.

Well, no, not really.

Actually, it's bloody irritating. The use of these commentative clips is Jacobovicis trademark: He, or his researchers, must spend as much time digging in the film archives as they do digging in the desert. As comic relief, its pathetic. As a means of reassuring the viewers that they don't have to feel intimidated by all that scholarship, it's close to insulting.

Its even more so because the tale Jacobovici has to tell is interesting. Its the story behind the story of Lot in the Book of Genesis. Two stories really. Part 1 is the familiar one of Abraham's nephew taking God's advice to evacuate the Twin Cities of the Plain (nomad that he was, he must have lived in one and made side-trips to the other) and of his wife, perhaps anxious about whether or not shed packed everything, looking back and being turned into a pillar of salt. Part 2, the bit they were more reticent about teaching you in school (at least in my day -- things might well have moved on since then), tells how Lots two daughters, under the impression that the two vanished towns accounted for the whole of humanity, seduced their father so that the world might be re-populated. Backward -- or at least sheltered -- in some ways, they were definitely forward in others. It may be the earliest known argument for providing women with a balanced education.

I had never realized before that the biblical story is the only written testimony we have to the existence of either Sodom or Gomorrah. This being the case, it's hardly surprising that scholars have regarded the whole tale as a fable. The favoured interpretation, apparently, is that the incest story was the Israelites' method of dissociating themselves from the rival tribes of Ammonites and Moabites, Lots progeny (as opposed to Abrahams). And since there was no archeological evidence, either, for the cities of the plain--five in all, of which one was supposedly spared -- there the matter rested.

Until recently. Treading, one assumes, in the footsteps of other explorers, Jacobovici takes us to an old Jordanian church (cue old-time chase footage as he drives through Iraq) on whose floor is an old mosaic -- as opposed to Mosaic -- map suggesting there really were such towns, and they really had been consumed by fire, divinely ordained or otherwise. And from there to another church where an inscription has been discovered honouring Saint Lot (this must be a translation unless the early Christians had prophetic and linguistic powers), suggesting that somewhere underneath is where Lot and his relations had relations. Jacobovici even finds some pillars of salt, though, as he says, these are unlikely to include the saline remains of Mrs. Lot unless she was a midget.

Indiana Jones taught us that archeologists can be swashbucklers. Jacobovici shows that they can also be cut-ups. It pays off: When he accosts people in the street, they say, "Hey, you're the naked archeologist" -- this despite the bright orange T-shirt he wears everywhere. Even his more sober colleagues and consultants like a bit of back-chat: We're not going to look too good ourselves, 3,000 years from now, says a respected emissary from the British Museum while meditating on a mummy.

Underneath it all, Jacobovici can get quite awestruck. "To be in a Bronze Age gate, at the Dead Sea, in a candidate for Sodom and Gomorrah is amazing, just amazing," he gleams. It is. But it doesn't compensate for the relentless jokiness of a show torn between smartening up and dumbing down. - The Naked Archaeologist airs Fridays at 10 p. m. on VisionTV.

Black & White Photo: Visiontv / "Here's where they gave gold ingots to beggars and then refused to sell them food" --just one of many reputed sins of the biblical cities of Sodom and Gomorrah, which documentary-maker Simcha Jacobovici pursues like a yukking Indiana Jones. ;; Caption:
2008-06-28-who-s-making-the-award-decisi:
One of this years Dora Award nominees is Tazed and Confused, a Second City revue. This isn't up, as you might think, for Best New Musical. It's in the running for Best New Play, authorship credited to the Ensemble.

Theres a part of me thats pleased by that. It introduces a pleasing note of irreverence into a procedure prone, by its nature, to sycophancy, solemnity and self-congratulation. Besides, the best Second City revues are better written than most plays. All the same, there's something about its selection that smacks of desperation.

Well-merited desperation, I have to say. All seasons are bad seasons for new plays, but 2007-08 was worse than most. There is a redemptive front-runner in Hannah Moscovitch's East of Berlin, which has to win, even though its victory will deprive us, come Monday, of watching the Ensemble troop onstage to claim the prize. (Almost as good as the Tonys, where every show has 17 producers.) Moscovitch might conceivably be hampered by the fact that shes running against herself, with her early play Essay also nominated because, though it has been seen in Toronto before, that was only on the Fringe, which doesnt count. Moscovitch's other revived (and better) early piece, The Russian Play, doesn't qualify because it got a rather brief run the previous season. OK, but why didnt Michelle Monteiths virtuoso performance in that piece get a Best Actress nod? I've always understood that though revived plays aren't eligible, revived performances are. (In fact, theres one nominated this year.) Keeping up with these rules is enough to make your head spin.

The rules may explain why Colleen Murphys The December Man, well represented in other categories, doesn't have a shot at Best Play; it may have been new to Toronto but it had already been done in Edmonton. Or did the jurors seriously think it inferior to Judith Thompson's Palace at the End, which was three monologues and maybe one-third of a good play? (And again with the acting: Maev Beaty, the best of the three monologists, is the only one not recognized.) The remaining contender is Brendan Galls Alias Godot: I dont think it should win, but I'm pleased to see it up there; it was a very funny play (and production, incidentally) that was generally underrated.

There's a category called Outstanding Production of a Play. It isnt the same as Outstanding Direction, though its hard to see how you could have one without the other. It means, if anything, Best All-Round Event. One that should certainly have been nominated, should very likely have won, is Studio 180's Stuff Happens, the Iraq show (and a far livelier one than Palace at the End). It hasn't received a single nomination in any category; even David Foxs sublime impersonation of Donald Rumsfeld has been passed over. Well, as Rummy himself said, stuff happens. Or, as just about everybody in Toronto theatre has been saying, its a scandal.

Especially in light of what has been nominated. Take the Obsidian Theatre Company's slow and unfocused staging of Intimate Apparel. (Though it deserves, as befits its title, its Best Costume recognition. Bravo, Tamara Marie Kucheran.) There seems to be a rule that Obsidian will be nominated whatever it does; surely black theatre in Toronto has got beyond needing that special treatment. Jewish theatre shouldn't get it either; what is the Harold Green Companys Rose doing there? A fine performance, certainly, by Lally Cadeau, but a mediocre play. And on the subject of logs being rolled, it can only be Top Girlss status as a feminist classic that has gained it more reclame (not just from the Doras) than Mary Stuart, The Time of Your Life or Three Sisters, which were superior Soulpepper productions of more challenging plays. Yes, Top Girls was an actresses' showcase; it still fell apart in its middle scenes.

On the topic of Soulpepper: I'm rooting for Joseph Ziegler ( The Time of Your Life) as Best Actor since a) he was marvellous; b) he was robbed a couple of years ago for A Whistle in the Dark; c) Id like that show to get a break. Id like it to extend to Stuart Hughes's Supporting Performance a category that also includes, pleasingly, Mr. and Mrs. Diego Matamoros, she being Robyn Stevan in private life. Both were delightful, but Mr. M was Dora-worthier in The Odd Couple, just as he was a couple of years ago in The Government Inspector. What is it about great comic acting that the Doras don't get? And why do they persist, insanely, in lumping supporting performances Male and Female, Play and Musical, in the same crowded category?

Oh yes, Musicals, Outstanding Production of. These include Can-Stages Little Shop of Horrors, directed by Ted Dykstra, and Fire, starring Ted Dykstra (wild as Jerry Lee Lewis). The former deserves to win. Dykstra (in the revived performance mentioned above) is up for Best Musical Actor and he deserves that, too, though Rick Roberts in the same show is competition. Id hate to choose between Nicole Underhay (also same show) and Patricia Zentilli ( Little Shop) for Best Musical Female. How could Fire have such great performances but still be such a drab evening? The script, that's why. (And the production, though the director's nominated nonetheless.) Most Ludicrous Category: Musical Direction. How do you compare The Time of Your Life with Eugene Onegin? No-Contest Categories: Opera Production. ( Pelleas and Melisande) and Touring ( Nicholas Nickleby). They Have To Be Joking Category: Anything including Dirty Dancing. Question of Questions: Given the flak that comes their way every year, from here and elsewhere, when will the Dora jurors get around to explaining their methods, their criteria and their identities?

2008-07-03-if-a-line-is-delivered-inaudi:
Sometimes, all's well that begins well. Fifty-five years ago the Stratford Festival got off to a terrific start by mounting what was then the most neglected of Shakespeare's so-called "dark comedies" and, in effect, reclaiming it for the repertoire. Tyrone Guthrie gave his production of All's Well That Ends Well an Edwardian-cum-Chekhovian setting, a choice repeated some 30 years later in a Trevor Nunn staging that went from Britain to Broadway. Now the play is back on the Festival stage, directed by Marti Maraden, whose program note opts unequivocally for a costume date of 1889 and whose production is redolent, like Nunn's, of autumn and railway stations.

It doesn't have the sophistication of Nunn's version, despite Christina Poddubiuk's sets and frocks. It's a decent production but it's soft at its centre. All's Well is about tough love. Helena, orphaned daughter of a doctor, falls in love with Bertram, the Count of Rossillion, in whose widowed mother's house she has grown up. She promises to cure the King of France of a fistula if he'll reward her with a husband of her choice. She does and he does. She picks Bertram, who isn't pleased at being summarily married off. He runs off to the Florentine wars and sets about seducing a virtuous young maiden of the parish. Helena takes the girl's place in bed, gets pregnant and, after exposing him at court, gets her man. We have to be persuaded that this is all for the best.

For this to happen, we need a Helena not afraid to show that, though her ends may be admirable, her means are ruthless, and a desperately callow Bertram in urgent need of salvation from himself. Daniela Vlaskalic's Helena is a girl scout, all light, no shade; Jeff Lillico's Bertram faithfully says and does all the things that are set down for him, but without any sign of passion or purgation. To be fair, the only good Bertram I've seen was the late Ian Richardson; he was able to draw a high-comedy line around the character, highlighting his insecurities and earning forgiveness for them. Leah Oster, so good in The Music Man, plays the almost-abandoned Diana, who is supposed to drive the revelations of the last scene, a task for which she lacks both the vivacity and the classical chops.

It's strange that the production should miss out on the sadness that dogs the play's centre, since it's so insistent on the melancholy that haunts its edges. Its presiding presence is Tom Rooney, as the Countess's clown Lavache. He gets all the laughs his author allows and a few over. Martha Henry plays his employer, beautifully, as strong of mind but frail of body; she visibly ages in the absence of her son and adopted daughter.

The king is Brian Dennehy, quiet but with authority to burn, and as the lord Lafew Stephen Ouimette is a jewel, able to bring down the house with a flicked-off line like "who's his tailor?" The object of the inquiry is Juan Chioran's towering Parolles, braggart soldier and Bertram's hanger-on, who looks to be on permanent furlough from the French Foreign Legion. The extended sequence of his unmasking by his fellow officers, who fool him into thinking he's been captured by the enemy, is a joy. It's also an awesome demonstration of company strength, what with Ben Carlson and Patrick McManus as the commentating brothers Dumaine (Carlson especially good as sardonic philosopher) and Randy Hughson a gleeful interrogator and double-talk specialist.

It's all a bit detached, though, with Parolles not really feeding into the play's general examination of human frailty or establishing his status as Bertram's evil angel; though of course, with Chioran being approximately twice Lillico's height, it must be hard for them to make eye (or any other kind of) contact. But this is the production's besetting fault; it's crowded with talent (it has Fiona Reid in the small role of the Widow and Michelle Fisk in the tiny one of Mariana) but it feels underpopulated. It can't be a coincidence that this season's version of the open stage, stripped of familiar balcony and columns, has played host to inaudibility in every single show. - All's Well That Ends Well runs until Aug. 23. For tickets and info, call 1-800-567-1600 or visit www.stratfordfestival.ca.
2008-07-03-power-to-the-steeple:
FUENTE OVEJUNA

Tom Patterson Theatre

---

The Golden Age of Spanish drama was roughly contemporary with the equivalent era in England, and Lope de Vega's Fuente Ovejuna is its most celebrated product. It's a body of work with a rarefied reputation outside its homeland, though, in my limited experience, when the plays are given in English, they always work. They come across as Shakespearean, only more so. Lope, in this play anyway, offers even more sheer story than Shakespeare, more blatant theatricality, including a lot of music and fighting, a huge relish for each passing moment, and a shifting social viewpoint that goes beyond Shakespearean ambiguity into a kind of populist absolutism. Fuente Ovejuna (literally, "the sheep well") is a play about a village whose inhabitants rise up against a local oppressor. It gives power to the people, and then has them surrender it to their feudal overlords.

The Stratford production, translated and directed by Laurence Boswell, who in Britain has been a pioneering Lope de Vegan for a quarter of a century, is uneven but exhilarating. It's 1476 -- about 130 years before the play itself was written --and a divided Spain is up for grabs; Commander Guzman of Calatrava persuades Rodrigo, the young Grand Master of the province, to throw in his lot with the Portuguese-backed forces of Castile rather than with those of the soon-to-be-celebrated and "most Catholic" monarchs Ferdinand and Isabella. Guzman lets slip that his soldiers are quartered in the tiny town of Fuente Ovejuna, and the second scene transports us there, to meet the really important people.

What we took for the main picture was only a frame, which will gradually dissolve to become part of the canvas. The villagers welcome the victorious Guzman back home with fulsome tributes; he, though, has his eyes on more tangible rewards. A notorious despoiler of peasant womanhood, he now has his sights set on the young and spirited Laurencia; he is only prevented from raping her in a field by the arrival of her admirer Frondoso, who has to flee for his life after rescuing her. He returns when the Commander is called back to battle, and marries Laurencia; but their wedding is interrupted when Guzman too returns, this time in snarling defeat and even more inclined than usual to exercise the Spanish equivalent of droit du seigneur. Frondoso is arrested, Laurencia abducted. She escapes with her honour apparently intact, but her clothes torn and her face bloodied. The villagers take collective action; armed with pitchforks, they storm Guzman's castle, and kill and dismember him. Their Catholic majesties send in a torture squad to investigate; the people outwit them by maintaining, even on the rack, that there is no guilty party: "Fuente Ovejuna did it." Or: It takes a village.

The play is an extraordinary, sometimes disconcerting, mix of comedy and drama. It applauds the villagers' steadfastness, but never seems to question the throne's right to have them tortured in the first place. They themselves may be heroic self-liberators or a vigilante mob. Boswell's staging of their summary justice as a slow-motion battle doesn't really work, but it does fit the play's try-anything spirit. On the other hand, he gets the full force, both frightening and inspiring, of the textbook-famous scene in which Frondoso and Laurencia (who, for reasons of dramatic convenience, have escaped the round-up) overhear their friends and neighbours, including a 10-year-old child, being interrogated. Jonathan Goad and Sara Topham play these militant lovebirds with a blend of playfulness and determination; this may be Topham's best performance, once past an over-emphatic discussion with her best friend, in which role Severn Thompson undergoes a similarly beguiling development.

The star villager, though, may be Mengo, a fat and self-serious lad whose attempts to protect his cousin from the Commander's depredations earn him a pitiless beating, and who goes through the rest of the play offering to bare his buttocks to show the results. "You're the best actor," somebody tells him; that may not be strictly true, but Robert Persichini certainly does superbly in a role that might have been written for him. The other locals range from James Blendick's sonorous patriarch, through Nigel Shawn Williams' easy-going poet manque, to Laird Mackintosh, one of several excellent recruits from Stratford's musicals division, as a bespectacled student who comes home to bemoan the invention of the printing press, or as this translation has it, "information overload." It leads, apparently, to books being published under the names of famous authors who didn't write them; here we may conceivably hear Lope himself disclaiming responsibility for some of the 2,000 plays with which he is credited. The greatest joy of this production may be the way in which it summons a community made up of distinct individuals; their council meetings, on a spare Peter Hartwell set of benches and floor grilles, are very compelling.

As their oppressor-in-chief, Scott Wentworth indulges in too much tooth-baring villainy but has subtler stuff in reserve. Stephen Kent shows nervous promise as a vacillating Grand Master. Stratford royalty Geraint Wyn Davies and Seana McKenna play the Spanish royalty, though neither performance is likely to add substantially to its owner's resume. (McKenna -- something I never thought I would say of her -- comes close to phoning it in.) The pair are depicted as benevolent autocrats, suggesting that Lope was sucking up to the dynasty that sheltered him. This production accepts that, putting a conservative spin on a play that can easily be interpreted as a blazing call to revolution. It isn't the very best show at Stratford this year but it may be the most encouraging. - Fuente Ovejuna runs until Oct. 4. For tickets and info, call 1-800-567-1600 or visit www.stratfordfestival.ca.
