2008-07-05-american-star-wows-stratford-:
At the Stratford Studio we get Brian Dennehy -- a star in the American theatre but a previously unknown quantity in ours -- in a double-bill of one-act classics. In the first, he plays a compulsive talker; in the second, a compulsive listener whose particular fix is the sound of his own recorded voice from the days when he too was a compulsive talker.

Eugene O'Neills Hughie, the first play, is a miniature hung round the neck of the authors marathon masterpiece The Iceman Cometh. That play is about a collection of lushes in a New York barroom, barricading themselves against the horrors of reality with booze and what O'Neill refers to -- with compulsive repetition -- as "pipe dreams." Hughie zeroes in on a guy who might be one of them: Erie Smith, small-time gambler and big-time drunk, returning after an extended bender to the cheap Manhattan hotel he calls home. What sent him off was the death of a Mr. Hughes, a. k. a. Hughie, the hotel night clerk and the regular recipient of Erie's nocturnal boasts and confessions. Without this sounding board, Erie feels desolate. But hope beckons. The desk is now manned by a new clerk, a wizened fellow whose name is also Hughes. Could he be the new Hughie? Erie tries his best to make him so, going on about his own past triumphs at the tables and with the ladies, and about how Hughie, trapped in wedlock and terminally timid, lived vicariously by hearing about them. In fact, Erie is reminiscing about his own reminiscences.

Dennehy, swaying expansively, captures Eries tarnished swagger, his frantic attempts to keep the daylight out and his possibly new acknowledgment that it may just be time to let it in. But his thunder is somewhat stolen by Joe Grifasis clerk, which perhaps is as it should be since his, when you come to think of it, is the title role, if only by right of inheritance. Grifasi, whose face is a medley of lines and pouches and whose manner makes unobtrusive seem like a bumptious overstatement, might at first sight be part of Patrick Clark's faultlessly persuasive set, but he has an identity of his own, and it's an ambiguous one. He could be humouring Erie, seeing right through him; he could be impressed. He might even -- to me it was the dominant impression -- be identifying with his predecessor; ruefully, silently acknowledging that his own predicament and personality, not to mention his marriage, are very similar to those of the late Hughie -- even while Erie addresses him as a man of the world whos above all that.

The clerk, because of his secrecy, is really a more interesting character than Erie, whose blowhard tactics are transparent from, as he himself might say, the get-go. What saves them is the salt and humour with which he expresses them; as Robert Falls, the plays director, says in a program note, O'Neill isn't usually credited with being funny but here, regurgitating the Broadway slang of his seriously misspent youth, he is. Certainly Dennehy, spouting the lingo, and Grifasi, absorbing it, make him seem so.

"Do you know Arnold Rothstein?" asks the new Hughie, impressed by this possibility at least, of an irritated Erie who would much rather not go there. Rothstein, plainly, is out of Eries league. He was the gangster whom Damon Runyon portrayed as The Brain ("however much money there is around, The Brain sooner or later gets hold of all of it") and though ONeill obviously lacked Runyon's comic genius, there's a sense in which he got there first and more authentically. Hughie, like The Iceman, lets us sniff the real stench that Runyon turned into perfume.

Hughie -- the real, the ex-Hughie, I mean -- must rank among the great non-appearing title characters, along with Mary Chases Harvey, that other legendary drunkards companion, and of course Samuel Beckett's Godot. Which gets us to the evening's other and probably even better half, Becketts Krapps Last Tape, in which Dennehy, having played a duet with another actor, plays a duet with himself. This is the play in which an old failed writer, who's been logging his own life on a tape recorder, listens to an entry from decades earlier, a time at which he still had love and hope but turned his back on them: on the former anyway with predictably dire effects on the latter.

Sam Beckett was a gentleman and a showman; he laid out his plays meticulously, with an infallible sense of timing. Jennifer Tarver, an expert Beckett director whom Stratford was smart to scoop up from the Toronto fringes, obeys his instructions implicitly and still emerges with a production that has an identity of its own. Beckett knew that when he had Krapp begin the play by eating a banana and a half and leaving the peel on the floor, we would wait for him to slip on it; so he does, but at a moment when we don't expect it. He doesnt fall; he merely flails, which Dennehy does brilliantly, before going on to fall foul of lifes more metaphysical banana skins.

His physical transformation is remarkable, from the expansive Erie to the reclusive Krapp whose closest contact with the outside world is in his jutting eyebrows. Phenomenal too is the contrast between the gnarled voice that issues from his lips, and that of the hopeful young litterateur that we hear on tape, so shockingly authentic that one almost suspects Dennehy of having laid down his vocal tracks some 30 years in advance. Both are authentically Dublin, but at vastly different stages of development. Every time one sees this play, its progress seems more ineluctable, towards a bitter dismissal that one prays in vain won't happen. Krapp, a more universal play than Hughie, is also a better one technically (Both, incidentally, were first staged in 1958, O'Neills posthumously.) Hughie pretty much

23

dances on one spot; Krapp, for all its seeming stasis and obsession with the past, has forward motion.

- Hughie and Krapps Last Tape run until Aug. 31 at the Studio Theatre, Stratford. Call 1-800-567-1600 for more information.

2008-07-08-tears-from-the-clowns:
THEATRE REVIEW

A LITTLE NIGHT MUSIC

Shaw Festival, Niagara-on-the-Lake

---

There's a wonderful tear-inducing moment at the end of A Little Night Music when the show's assortment of ill-sorted couples has been happily resorted, and the orchestra signals a reprise of the accidental hit song Send in the Clowns. Among the many pleasures in the Shaw Festival's pocket-sized revival is the discovery that the tune's re-entry can bring on as much sweet sorrow when sounded by a clarinet as by a full complement of strings. Musical director Paul Sportelli seems far more attuned to this work than to the brassiness of Wonderful Town. It's been orchestrated (by Jason Jestadt) for a chamber quintet, and though one misses the swell of a full orchestra propelling the first-act finale A Weekend in the Country, the taut tart beauty of Stephen Sondheim's score, the headiest written for a musical in the last 40 years, is undiminished.

The five instrumentalists balance the five liebeslieder singers who are built into the show as written. They function as commentators; the signal achievement of Morris Panych's production is to bring them closer than ever before to the characters and events on whom they're commenting, not only physically (hardly avoidable on this stage) but spiritually and emotionally as well. The chorus also take on personalities of their own, with Glynis Ranney at their head as a secular solicitous Mother Superior of the human condition. Conversely, the protagonists sometimes become observers, and very effectively. When Donna Belleville, wheelchair-bound as the ex-courtesan mother of the heroine, sings the autobiographical Liaisons, it's the most natural complement in the world to her actress-daughter's one-night stand with an old flame. When Juile Martell, as the kind of maid everybody ought to have, sings The Miller's Son, it's a realistic statement of her own sexual possibilities and a tolerant comment on everyone else's. The show is the most attentive and restrained production of anyone's work save his own that Panych has mounted since his CanStage version of Sondheim's Sweeney Todd. I guess that tells us who he respects.

There are drawbacks. The intimacy of the space and the sparseness of the backing permit unmiked singing, which is a blessing; but with the audience on three sides we lose words when the actors turn away, which is a pity (with lyrics of this quality, that's putting it mildly). And the constant peering of the performers through the birches that make up most of Ken MacDonald's set can get too cute.

More importantly, while the singing is mostly firm from the start, the acting takes time to cohere. The major exception here is Goldie Semple who, in this musicalization of Ingmar Bergman's Smiles of a Summer Night, plays Desiree Armfeldt, dramatic star of the Swedish stage, whose scheme to detach her former lover from his still-virginal child-bride -- a good idea from everybody's point of view -- steers the action. Semple seems taxed even by the narrow vocal demands of Desiree's songs; if her Send in the Clowns brought cheers on the first night, it could only be because she's the star and it's a standard. But her acting around the song, and in all her other scenes, is warm and sensitive enough to make amends; she's a mature, sensual woman, keenly alive to her own and everyone else's absurdity.

As Fredrik, the object of her affectionate designs, George Masswohl is as solid and reliable as a traditional family solicitor. Which, by profession, is what he is, but he's also supposed to be a passionate man in a mid-life crisis. Masswohl, when talking, conveys hardly any of this. When the music starts, though, he's another man, alert to every nuance. By the show's climax, which finds him fatalistically consenting to a game of Russian roulette, the two sides of the performance have come together.

Thom Allison, by contrast, remains bisected. He plays the Count, Fredrik's even-more-married rival, a role for which he has too much intelligence and too little machismo; his head-notes, though, are thrilling. As his acid-tongued and acid-minded spouse, Patty Jamieson is good in all departments, if you can accept that socially, if not intellectually, this Countess has married up.

The junior characters are delights. Panych puts Desiree's daughter, playing with dolls while eyeing her elders, at the centre of the action, and Michaela Bekenn justifies the position, especially with her ecstatic leaps as the county weekend looms into view. Justin Stadnyk as Frederik's frustrated seminarian of a son and Robin Evan Willis as the young stepmother he despairingly adores give the completest musicaldramatical-comical performances of all, though Willis could let up on the silliness later on. She does, though, confirm my long-held belief that her solo, Soon, is the most breathtaking song in the piece, rivalled only by the ensemble's miraculous Night Waltz; these are the two great true waltzes in a score composed in multiples of three-quarter time.

The worst of playwright Hugh Wheeler's book is its clunky attempts at epigram (mostly given to Belleville, who tactfully underplays them); the best is the way it organizes the story around the music. There are sections of the second half in which the plot rather elbows out the songs, but the two come together at the close. Shadowed by mortality, it's a perfect compromise of a happy ending. - A Little Night Music runs until Oct. 4. Call 1-800-511-SHAW or visitshawfest.com for information.

2008-07-10-a-life-of-rhyme-simon-callow-:
Shakespeares sonnets tell the story of one of the most graphic and self-destructive loves in the language. So says Simon Callow, the English actor -- and many other things -- who is performing a selection of them, under the title There Reigns Love, at this year's Stratford Festival: previewing now, opening Sunday.

Callow has been doing the sonnets, in one form or another, for nearly 30 years, off and on. He's done them once before in Canada, in 1999 as a one-night benefit for Soulpepper Theatre in Toronto: an occasion on which, he told me on the phone this week, hed noticed "a chap in the front row, looking very intent" who turned out to be Mike Myers. Of all people, he didnt quite add, though some of us might. It may be that Austin's powers of concentration were greater than mine. I remember that recital as an inspiring but somewhat taxing occasion; these are tough, dense poems, and I can't have been the only member of the audience whose concentration sometimes flagged.

This time, though, Callow will only be reciting 80 out of the published 154. I told him I was grateful for this concession, but he cheerfully dashed my confidence by revealing that when Id seen him at it in Toronto, hed only done 60.

This, though, he says, will be different; it will be more of a show, perhaps more of a play. It has a new title; one of hundreds of striking phrases that offer themselves up from the text (though, as he says, out of context those ardent quotations tend to sound like the names of Ivor Novello musicals). And he's learnt them. He won't be standing at a lectern, which is what he did at the National Theatre in London, back in 1979, when he read the entire 154 in a three-hour stretch, this time with John Gielgud sitting a little more expectedly than Mike Myers but perhaps more dauntingly, in the fifth row.

Callow was on the crest of a wave, having recently opened on the same stage as Mozart in Peter Shaffers Amadeus, which may to this day may be his celebrated stage role. (Hes in the movie, too, but as another character.) The performance was spurred by the theories of a scholar, John Padel, who had taken what Callow rightly describes as "the approach of almost anyone who reads the sonnets -- they start speculating about them as autobiography."

Padel was convinced that the original publishers of the poems had scrambled their order in order to obscure what might have been some embarrassingly famous identities, including those of the dark lady and "noble youth" with whom the poet seems linked in an obsessive triangle of love and jealousy.

Callow himself isn't so sure that the sonnets are literally autobiographical; he does think they provide a window onto intense and tortured feelings that Shakespeare himself must have experienced: a rare opportunity to hear the most reclusive of authors speaking in the first person.

There Reigns Love is not, Callow insists, a scholar's night out -- its entirely speculative. It has the trajectory and the journey of a play. It also, for the first time, has a director: the veteran Michael Langham, Stratfords artistic director through most of the '60s, who knows the Festival's various stages like nobody else and has, Callow says, "an incredible freshness --he makes no concessions at all to age."

Most of the actual rehearsing has been done, fast, in Stratford. The two men had met and discussed the work in London, where they both live, but Callows schedule at the time was typically full.

He was engaged in two projects, both of which might be considered late outcroppings of Amadeus: playing the psychiatrist in a touring production of Shaffers Equus and directing a Mozart opera, The Magic Flute.

This has been the pattern of his life for the last 20-odd years. In 1984, he published a book called Being an Actor, a combination of memoir and credo, and it started him on a second career. Or perhaps re-started him on a first; though acting had consumed him for years, his original ambition had been to write. That first book, which was both forceful and funny, led to others, including a superb biography of Charles Laughton and another, a three-parter still in progress, of Orson Welles.

His byline can also be found regularly on the arts pages of The Guardian. Along with writing has come directing films, plays, operas and musicals. He has also acted in plenty of movies, while his most noted stage-work has been less in plays alongside other actors than in one-man shows about writers: not just Shakespeare but Wilde and, most prolifically, Dickens.

He has become not so much an actor as "a person about the theatre" -- my description, not his, and one, I think, that he temporarily accepts with some misgivings -- and a uniquely valuable one: I would rather read him on the theatre than almost any critic; he not only has more practical knowledge and sympathy than most of us, he also writes better. But he does want, he says, to get back to stage acting.

Pushing 60, Callow reckons he has 10 more years to play the great classical roles that, so far, have surprisingly failed to come his way. His Shakespearean resume, for example, consisted for years of just the grizzled warrior Titus Andronicus and the young lover Orlando in As You Like It. (He may be the only actor to have played them in that order.) He's since played both Falstaffs, but in peculiar circumstances: in a stage version of Chimes at Midnight, Welles' film adaptation of Henry IV and in a musical of The Merry Wives of Windsor.

He insists that he won't play soldiers, which rules out Macbeth and Othello, but he does want to have another crack at Falstaff; who, one might quibble, was a soldier if a reluctant one. He certainly should play more Shakespearean leads. Meanwhile, he gets to come closer than most actors to playing the man himself. - There Reigns Love runs until Aug. 3. For tickets and information visit stratfordfestival.ca.

2008-07-11-men-in-blue-have-never-felt-s:
Good cop, bad cop, new spin. The central characters of Flashpoint, CTVs new drama series, are Greg, whose job is to talk people out of situations mortally dangerous to themselves and others, and Ed, who, when Greg cant make them see the errors of their ways, shoots them. Ed, a champion sniper, heads a team at Toronto's SRU, one of those dashing television acronyms, here standing for Strategic Reserve Unit. Greg seems theoretically to be his second-in-command, but in practice -- judging from the first two episodes, anyway -- it is he who makes the running, and he who deserves to.

There are other regular team members -- eight actors get over-the-title billing -- but we have yet to discover much about them. There's time for that, though; they all have back stories, or so says the media release, which comes in the form of a dossier and is written in the kind of prose that could make even Mad Men or The Wire sound bad.

Flashpoint isnt in their league. For one thing it follows the crisis-a-week formula, rather than telling a developing story. Like CBCs The Border (and so much else), it's a series rather than a serial (like the public broadcaster's Intelligence and so little else). But, on the evidence available, its better than The Border. The conflicts within the organization seem less contrived, those within the individual characters a little deeper.

Flashpoint brings the action show to the place the "adult Western" reached before that genre crawled into the desert and died. That is, the cops do drastic things to people, physically or psychologically, and then feel bad about it. Its the kind of situation that 24 is always promising but never gets around to delivering, and that even The Wire tended to shy away from. Ed's marriage seems to be in jeopardy, due to his involvement in his work (and maybe his inability to discuss it at home); Greg's has already broken up, depriving him of any contact with his son. At the end of each operational day, they take their guilts home and deposit them in what the promotional material, recklessly mixing its metaphors, describes as their over-stuffed closets.

The first two episodes give them plenty of food for self-examination. The first, inspired, like the whole series, by an actual Toronto happening, is a fairly basic hostage drama. An immigrant man shoots a (presumably) immigrant woman who refuses to let him back in her life; he then grabs a bystander and holds a gun to her head. Greg, on the ground, asks him to put down his weapon; Ed, on the roof, gets ready to ensure that he will. The group also includes a pixieish sniperess, but she takes a wrong turn on the way up, so Ed has the action to himself. We learn that the code-word for shoot! is "Scorpio"; we wait to learn whether Scorpio will rise or will be averted. The options keep changing, and the arrival of the gunmans son raises the stakes, especially the psychological ones for Ed. Casting notes: Stephanie Morgenstern, one of the shows two cocreators, plays the (understandably) silent hostage and Dragana Varagic, one of Toronto's finest but most under-used actresses, is the initial victim, who is very voluble while she lives, but speaks only in Croatian. So does her killer. This makes it hard, both for the SRU and for viewers, to get inside his head.

This doesn't hold for Episode 2, which is told very much from the viewpoint of what the SRU would call the subject. He, well played by Henry Czerny, is Jack, a widower whose young and beloved daughter has been called into hospital for a long-awaited heart transplant. But theres been a computer glitch, and an older man is first in line to receive the new organ. Father and daughter are told to go home. Whereupon Jack seizes a gun and the contested heart and insists that it be inserted according to his specifications. Our boys (and girls) speed to the scene. Ed stands ready, along with a tiresome young stud of a new recruit who would plainly prefer to shoot first and, if necessary, afterwards. But this is really Gregs scene. As a kind of bereaved father himself, he has a direct line into how Jack feels and he uses it, both compassionately and ruthlessly.

I said that Flashpoint is formulaic. Its formula is to plunge viewers into the crisis at the start and then flash up a "two hours earlier" title, so that we can learn how both sides got there. It works better in Episode

2, the situation being more detailed and more special.

The first episode is decently exciting; the second is, I'm tempted to say, indecently tense. Anything involving a sick child, especially with a distraught parent thrown in, has built-in emotional force. Not only did I want to know what happened, I wanted to know how the writers would get out of the corner into which they had painted themselves. I don't think they do. (The ending is very American, network rather than cable. Once we would have called it "Hollywood." I hope thats cryptic enough not to spoil anyones fun.) But I bought the feelings, if not all of the actual narrative, and Enrico Colantoni is excellent as decent, troubled Greg. So, with less to go on, is Hugh Dillon as less decent, more troubled Ed. So, I'm sure, will be all the decent, troubled others, once they get the chance.

- Flashpoint premieres tonight at 10 on CTV.

2008-07-12-money-sex-make-the-best-comed:
A few weeks ago at Stratford, Peter Hinton gave us a production of The Taming of the Shrew that rode wildly off in all directions. Now, in superb contrast, we have his take on The Way of the World, which turns out be ruthlessly concentrated and consistent. This makes it very funny and at times rather moving. Here in Canada, where we have very little tradition of playing Restoration comedy, it may be easy to underestimate just how magnificent an achievement this production is.

Written in 1700, The Way of the World is generally regarded as the pinnacle of the form. It still flopped with its first audience, and revivals in England have to this day been greeted with more respect than enthusiasm. The main stumbling-block is the plot which, though fairly simple in itself, is almost impossibly convoluted in the telling.

The author withholds vital information for ages, and then spills it out too fast to be followed. Hinton makes it clearer than in any other production I have seen. I understood everything until the last lap, in which two sets of characters -- one supposedly good, the other indubitably bad -- are engaged in competitive blackmail on remarkably flimsy premises. At least, I cant tell what they have on one another that's so terrible. But it doesn't matter much because here, and in all that leads up to it, the battle lines are so elegantly and forcefully drawn.

The production, a joint venture by Soulpepper (which supplies most of the actors) and the National Arts Centre (which supplies Hinton) unfolds on a compact stage, with the audience on three sides; we have them surrounded. We may be hazy on the factual details but never on the emotional stakes. We know precisely who loves, who hates, and who fluctuates.

Like all the plays of its school, indeed like most comedies from any school, The Way of the World is about money and sex. The pivotal character is Lady Wishfort, a widow, who has a lot of the former but hasnt been getting much of the latter. So shes a doubly easy mark, jealous of everyone (including her own twice-married daughter) and susceptible to most. Hinton and his fine designer, Carolyn Smith, pay a kind of visual lip service to the play's historical period with a mural serving as backdrop, depicting the beaux and belles of the time. But what goes on in front of it is dressed from the cusp of the 1950s and 1960s -- the London equivalent of Mad Men time. (A coffee-house wench has been transformed into a Playboy bunny.) It's a period, like Congreves own and most others, of rampant lust and desperate hypocrisy. It fits perfectly.

We start, emblematically, with two men playing cards, both hating to lose but hating even more to admit it. They are Fainall, the villain, and Mirabell, the hero. Both have designs on Lady Wishforts money; the moral difference between them is that Mirabell is capable of love. He seems actually to have made love, real or pretended, to every woman onstage, servants possibly excepted, but his genuine passion is for the lovely Millamant who keeps him, as she keeps most of London, on a string. She's playing an aggressive-defensive game as, in this world, she needs to. Mirabell and Millamant are supposed to be the summit Restoration couple, though it's sometimes seemed to me that theyve been refined almost out of existence, speaking jewelled prose but without much character. This time, though, I believed.

Millamant usually goes to a legend-in-her-own-lifetime actress: an Edith Evans, Maggie Smith or Judi Dench. Here shes Caroline Cave, young and breathtakingly lovely (beautifully gowned, too) with a sure sense of her own worth and grave doubts about others'. Some of the epigrammatic wit may be damped down (the line about dwindling into a wife, for example) but she finds a deeper comedy in the tension between vulnerability and surrender. The great "proviso" scene in which she and Mike Shara's Mirabell lay down conditions for a civilized marriage lives up to its reputation and beyond. Shara, in what is traditionally the duller role, really runs the play: a recognizable quite-spoken modern young man, watchful and testing and ambiguously decent -- even, at the end, compassionate.

The productions clarity is as much verbal as visual. Both aspects pay off brilliantly in Damien Atkins Witwoud, a kiss-curled fop whose every line is a killer, even when he himself is the victim. He and William Webster as his older chum Petulant push the time frame a few years forward; dressed in camp cast-offs from an English public school, they definitely suggest Carnaby Street. More broadly hilarious is Tanja Jacobs' Lady Wishfort, first seen doing game battle with a weight-reducer (and its vibrating belt), and later achieving pathos, though some of her words come out strangulated. (Or fail to.)

C. David Johnson is a powerfully malignant Fainall, a study in passionless jealousy while Nancy Palk, as his cohort Mrs. Marwood, plays jealousy saddled with passion (though she often seems marooned in a corner of the stage). John Jarvis is a bluff country squire, and the nicest man around; Randi Helmers plays a deliciously varied medley of maids; Michael Simpson is Mirabell's manservant, nefariously disguised as the Ladys servant, though hes at his best in his dainty delivery of the prologue.

The production gets in nearly every syllable of text, and has thought about every one of them. As a Soulpepper show, it's on par with Laszlo Marton's Chekhovs --and more like them than you might imagine. - The Way of the World runs through Aug. 2 at the Young Centre; 416-866-8666.

2008-07-15-marriages-mergers:
THEATRE REVIEW

THE PRESIDENT

Royal George Theatre, Niagara-on-the-Lake

---

Farce is always a race against time. Seldom, though, is that so literally the case as it is in The President, the insanely enjoyable one-act piece that is this year's lunchtime show at the Shaw Festival.

The title character, a Mr. Norrison, is president not of a country (he'd consider that small potatoes) but of a company. He runs a tight, happy and incredibly profitable ship but, at the very moment of taking a supremely well-deserved vacation, he finds both his plans and his livelihood threatened. A lovely young woman, entrusted to his care for a season by her father who just happens to be our tycoon's most vital potential investor, has got herself wooed, wed and impregnated by a poor and bearded taxi-driver who is also, wouldn't you know, a card-carrying Communist. (And she was supposed to be in school, getting finished.) Her parents are about to hit town. Hurricane Norrison has just one hour to transform the ill-chosen love of her life into a suitable son-in-law. He's up for the challenge. Just to keep himself and the audience on our respective toes, he has his secretary run in and announce the time every few minutes.

His secretary: The play is full of them. That dates it, though to exactly which date is hard to say. It was written in 1929, by Ferenc Molnar, head Hungarian honcho of the Continental boulevards, whose works have been the foundation of diverse English-language triumphs from Carousel to, well, to The President. The latter's original title was One, Two, Three, under which name it was filmed by Billy Wilder; the play, at least in this version, is much, much funnier. Molnar was as at home in Manhattan as he was in Europe, and Manhattan is where the play, in Morwyn Brebner's sumptuously snappy adaptation, is unquestionably set; if we didn't know it from the words, we'd know it from the Chrysler Building whose summit is located directly outside the presidential office window. The office and its staff seem rooted in the 1950s but the cabbie, volubly loyal to his Marxist principles even in the process of discarding them, is an emblematic figure of the '30s, as is the emigre Central European count, currently employed as a janitor but still empowered to sell ambassadorial positions to the highest bidder. It all merges into myth: the American dream with the velocity, and something of the undercurrent, of nightmare, one that hits us where we currently live. What after all could be more contemporary than a play about a makeover?

Working from a tongue-twisting text (try saying that fast), Blair Williams, a proven fine actor making as auspicious a directorial debut as I can remember, sets about making life as fiendishly difficult for his cast as possible. If the diminutive William Vickers comes onstage he will be plonked firmly down on a very high chair. When the actors aren't spinning around the stage, we must assume that they're spinning behind it. Those who double are required, having changed from one character to another, to come back as the person you first thought of. One of them, Mike Nadajewski, brings off a triple, his most eye-catching impersonation being of a secretary specially hired for her inability to provoke jealousy in even the most suspicious of spouses. Male, female or indeterminate, this company proves as impossible to intimidate as -- well, as so many Norrisons.

Norrison himself is Lorne Kennedy, dynamically dapper, going at a furious crackling pace without sweating a drop. He has other people to do that for him, lubricating their loyalty by a liberal application of what he calls "oil." He knows all his employees' private problems, and has a soothing word, sometimes even a soothing action, for all of them. He does not, of course, care an actual jot for any of them. For his transformation act, he needs a full force of helpful tradesmen, obsequious board members and tireless messengers. Manipulating them all, he can shift in a single breath from fixing a typist's broken engagement to ordering a barber to "shave the first man who walks through that door." His imperious rhythm even accommodates personal heartbreak over a faithless mistress, each spasm accorded precisely one second's indulgence in what becomes a sublime running gag, befitting Kennedy's sublime performance.

The production might be said to take place in the Kennedy era, since the unrelated Chilina Kennedy brings to the role of the impulsive young brideas muchingenuous edibility as she bestows on the darlin' Eileen of Wonderful Town, and even more bloody-minded determination. No wonder gentlemen prefer blondes; and if the Shaw feels like trying that piece again, there could hardly be a likelier Lorelei Lee. Jeff Meadows is suitably rubbery as her beloved, taught in record time to drive autos like the autocrats and drink pluto like the plutocrats, as Lorenz Hart put it in a song, entitled Disgustingly Rich, that might be this play's theme tune. Support is impeccable, with especially flavourful cameos from Thom Marriott and Michael Ball. Surveying what he has wrought, the president favours an especially admiring subordinate with a reflection on the malleability of "people -- as you call them." It gives a pleasantly acrid parting tang to what has otherwise been an hour of effervescence. Standing ovations at first nights, or first afternoons, have become debased currency. For this curtain-call, though, we were on our feet even before the actors were: a reception so rapid and unanimous as to put cheers and bravos back on the gold standard. - The President runs until Oct. 4. For tickets and information visit shawfest.com.

2008-07-18-a-war-with-the-army-you-have-:
In the first sequence of Generation Kill, a U. S. Marine, stationed in Kuwait just prior to the invasion of Iraq, laments to one of his buddies that the local population "still haven't cleaned up their trash from the last war." (Ive cleaned up his language a bit there myself. You cant write about Generation Kill in a family newspaper without doing that to almost every line.)

After this, the conversation gets more philosophical. A soldier reflects on the achievements of the ancient civilization around them and on all the killing that has gone on in and around it. It's destiny, he drawls. "White man's gotta rule the world." He himself is black.

Racial tensions flair within the battalion whose members are the subjects of this HBO series, the creation of David Simon and Ed Burns who gave us The Wire. I was going to say this is that shows long-awaited successor, though Generation Kill seems to have arrived in very short order. So do sexual tensions; at least, being gay is a favourite accusation that these guys fling at one another, though nobody seems to take it very seriously. This kind of hazing is just a standard way of passing the time.

As far as their reaction to the job at hand is concerned, the men seem gung-ho for combat, though this may be an act. Theres a memorable scene in the first episode in which the guys read the fan mail that the kids back home are sending them: not their own kids, but boys and girls who must have been told to write to them as a school assignment.

Some are straightforward bloody-minded hero worship; others sympathize with them over the terrible responsibility of killing people who after all are equally children of God. That prompts one guy to improvise a reply about how he's actually a killing machine who just can't wait to get himself as many Iraqi scalps as possible.

How much of this is bravado, how much is real? Now youre asking.

Anyway, kids letters aren't want they want from home. They want copies of Hustler. And then there comes among them, for embedding purposes, a journalist who used to write for that very publication (Boy, says one of his new compadres, "we are in the presence of greatness") but who is currently employed by Rolling Stone, which America's warriors naturally despise as a bastion of liberal wussiness.

He is a surrogate for the real life Rolling Stone correspondent Evan Wright whose book is the basis of the series. I welcomed his arrival, as a possible point of reference among a mass of soldiers whom I was having difficulty sorting out.

He hasnt served that purpose, though its been fun watching him alternately shocked and intrigued by the occupants of the vehicle to which he's assigned when the wagons finally start rolling. The call to action has been heralded by the unwonted arrival at the gates of Fort Matilda, Kuwait, of a long line of trucks from Pizza Hut. Prior to this the men have been largely cut off from the outside world, only roused to interest by a rumour, spreading like wildfire, of the death of J. Lo.

Among their other troubles is a sergeant-major, continually on at them to conform to the military code by shaving off the facial hair that's resulted from a battalion-wide moustache-growing contest. My sympathies, here, are rather with the sergeant-major. The facial decoration makes the characters even harder to tell apart than is usually the case in war films.

It isnt only masturbation fodder and palatable chow that the troops are lacking. Armaments and electronics are in chronically short supply. (A sign, we know, of what is to come. Or not to come.) Some of this seems familiar, from previous wars, or from books and films about them.

Were in a Catch-22 world of disgruntled grunts and incompetent or eccentric commanding officers. Or, keeping it in TV terms, this might be a new MASH, but one in which the characters we like stand a chance of getting killed. (There aren't any I'm attached to yet, but I assume that will change.)

The battalion commander, known as Godfather, has to rely for most of his information on the BBC. Finally he gets to send his men into Iraq proper with the following encouraging words: The general has asked this battalion to be Americas shock troops, and Godfather cant tell the general, 'We don't do windows.

Godfather speaks in a hoarse rasp, and his resemblance to Marlon Brando presumably earned him his nickname. Rolling Stone guy finally plucks up courage to ask him how come. "Throat cancer" is the answer. You a smoker? inquires the scribe. "No", says Godfather. Just lucky, I guess.

Generation Kills dialogue, as I trust has been made clear, is up to Simon-Burns standard. So is the underlying mordancy, with an extra touch of the absurd.

The first Iraqi we see, as the troops start rolling, is a solitary child gazing at the caravan from the roadside. When a squad of Iraqis surrender, they have to be "unsurrendered" because HQ can't think of anything practical to do with them that falls within the provisions of the Geneva convention: a decision that causes disbelief in the ranks.

This doesn't seem to be as fertile ground for its authors as The Wire was; they may well feel constraints about making any of the characters too engaging. The situation, of course makes the Baltimore streets --geographically closer but less historically immediate -- seem escapist by comparison. But even The Wire, though I can hardly believe it now, took its time to draw me in. We'll see.

- Generation Kill airs Sundays at 9 p. m. on The Movie Network.

2008-07-18-the-sun-will-come-out-tomorro:
A weekend in Niagara country that began with the waltzes and mazurkas of A Little Night Music continued with the breakneck farcical galop of The President. And after all that dancing came After the Dance.

The dancing here is occasionally literal but mainly metaphorical. The society depicted in Terence Rattigan's play seems to be suffering a collective hangover from one of Noel Coward's marvellous parties. Rattigan, Coward's successor as the boy-wonder playwright of the British theatre and forever linked with him in the critical imagination, wrote it soon after his establishing hit, the farcical French Without Tears. This one is English, with tears.

Set and written in 1939, under the imminent threat of the Second World War, it shows a generation still grappling with its guilt over having survived the First. David Scott-Fowler, a little too young to have perished at the Front, is doing a good job of drinking himself to death by way of atonement. Or maybe it's just that he's rich and weak-willed.

Anyway, he has the money to keep an open apartment for a group of like-minded friends, though unlike most of them he also has intellectual interests; in his soberer moments he works on a long-gestated and apparently unreadable book about an unmemorable European monarch.

David has a wife, Joan, who loves him more than either of them is disposed to admit. Into their lives comes Helen, a member of the next and more responsible generation, the one that knows -- though it's seldom explicitly mentioned -- that a war is about to begin.

Helen is the girlfriend of David's young relative Peter, whom David supports by employing him as an on-site proofreader for his literary endeavours, but it's really David on whom she has set her sights. She wants to reform him. She is prepared to sacrifice both his marriage and her own romance in the process.

The play failed with its first audience, who may have found its implicit warning of impending cataclysm too plausible to be necessary, and who may also have found the posturings of the previous decade's Bright Young Things somewhat beside the point. Or they might still have identified with that lost generation and resented seeing them used for moralizing purposes.

Interestingly, Coward-- supposedly the Brightest of them all -- was also one of those most earnestly inclined to wag a finger at their irresponsibility. He could have identified with both sides. Rattigan, one of the newer set, was to be lumped by posterity with the older, frivolous crowd; even his more successful plays fell out of favour in the '50s, so After the Dance stood hardly a chance.

But it's been rediscovered by an age that likes to unearth the bitterness in writers and worlds traditionally thought privileged and carefree. By that criterion, After the Dance ranks high among the 20th century's twilight-of-a-civilization plays.

Its effect depends on our finding the mad whirl of its characters' lives poisonous but seductive, and on the Scott-Fowlers and their circle being interesting both as symptoms and as individuals. A production eight years ago by the short-lived Montreal Young Company, for whom it was a surprising but rewarding choice, brought this off poignantly well.

Christopher Newton's production at Shaw, which should be thoroughly at home with the piece, does excellently with the collective aspect, more patchily with the personal. It boasts a fine clipped performance from Deborah Hay as Joan, loving and high-strung, pretending to be tough and carefree, clinging valiantly to an outworn code; and a fine flowing one from Neil Barclay as John, an amply-proportioned friend of the central couple, who seems permanently ensconced in their home and all but permanently on the sofa. He's as perceptive as he is parasitic, describing himself as able to change his life but unwilling to do so and David as just the reverse. He's right on both counts.

But that's a problem. John and, by extension, the play tell us more about the protagonist than they're dramatically able to show us. We have to take David's potential, for good and bad, on trust. What we actually see appears merely affable; and Patrick Galligan, a very sunny actor, cannot supply the missing elements of diabolism and waste. Helen, beavering away at him for his own supposed good, is similarly compelled to play on one note; Marla McLean starts her off with appropriate youthful urgency but turns into a nag. Ken James Stewart is good and fresh as her discarded intended, and among a pungent bevy of hangers-on there's a superbly pointed turn from Claire Jullien (understudying the official performer) as a soused survivor clinging to yesterday like there could never be a tomorrow. - After the Dance runs until Oct. 5. For more information call 1-800-511-SHAW or visit shawfest.com.

2008-07-19-the-first-voice-is-the-only-v:
To begin at the (real) beginning: When Under Milk Wood, Dylan Thomas play for voices," was first broadcast by the BBC, the First Voice -- that's how he was billed -- was Richard Burton. He shared the play's narration with a Second Voice, but he had the bulk of it, and he delivered the long opening speech -- the summoning of the South Wales village of Llaregubb at night, "starless and bible-black -- as if it were an incantation. In the 50 years since, most actors, in whatever medium, have followed his example. Kenneth Welsh breaks the mould.

In Ted Dykstras production, which originated at last years Luminato festival and has now been adopted by Soulpepper, Welsh is not only the first, but the only voice. He handles all the narration and impersonates all the 50-odd characters, vocally and to a great extent physically. His approach to the first, long, lush, adjective-driven overture is to treat the town and the night not as familiar entities, lying there just waiting to be evoked, but as buried treasure, whose constituent parts have to be revealed and enumerated with an archaeologist's sense of wonder and delight. Welsh has to climb down a ladder in the back wall of the stage in order to reach the place; once there, he sets about removing dust-sheets, metaphorical and literal. And that's the way he explores the whole day-in-the-life piece, less as a magician than as a scientist.

He is something of a magician as an actor, with a dainty roguishness of which archaeology probably knows little. He stretches out unself-consciously on the ground to depict female sexuality, blossoming or fulfilled. Thomas view of womanhood might be considered by the forward-thinking to be limited; the women of Llaregubb mostly divide into obliging wantons (Polly Garter, the late Rosie Probert), wannabe wantons (Gossamer Beynon, Mae Rose Cottage, BessieBighead, Myfanwy Price), harridans (Mrs. Pugh, whose sadistic shrewishness drives her husband to poisoning her, in cherished fantasies; Mrs. Ogmore-Pritchard, whose fanatical cleanliness drove both her husbands to poisoning themselves, for real) and malicious gossips. The only happily married men are a drunkard and a bigamist. The others are weaklings, interspersed with the occasional visionary: the blind Captain Cat, the Rev. Eli Jenkins who is the towns poet and historian. Welsh brings them all to life, with a different voice and stance for each. He is assisted by an onstage musician, Mike Ross, and -- most spectacularly -- by two onstage sound-effects artists, Jenna Dalla Riva and Brooke Graeff. They remind us that this was, originally, a radio play, though the BBC at its peak could never have competed with the actual smell of cooking onions that arises at a relevant moment. (And persists through others less relevant.)

In terms of performance, the only fault is that Welsh isn't actually very Welsh, and the lack of lilt makes some of the language less delicately witty than it could be. (This is especially the case with the censorious biddies in the grocery store, who sound less narrow than malignant.) The gentle, langourous voice that Welsh has conjured up for Polly Garter is delightful; it's also identical to the one that Rod Beattie uses to portray Mrs. Walt Wingfield, who as far as I know is pure Canadian.

I admired Welshs virtuosity, and I enjoyed being reminded of a text that I used to love but havent heard or thought about in years. But it is a text, rather than a play, and the solo treatment only underlines that. (And --nothing to do with this production -- I've come to distrust some of its easy rhetoric.) The problem with it is that it has no internal movement. Here it contrasts markedly with its most obvious analogue, Thornton Wilder's Our Town, which accepts that people dont change much but shows how time and events can bring them to agony and to ecstasy. Thomas was a greater writer than Wilder (or at least a greater wordsmith) but this, his only work in dramatic form, is as time-locked as its land-locked.

Its representative characters are Mog Edwards and Myfanwy Price, tradespeople who live at opposite ends of the village and write letters of undying love to one another but will never meet, on this day or any other. Other characters do meet, or at least collide, and the collisions keep Thomas' show on the road. The most celebrated moment comes when Polly Garter sings a contented song about all the men she has lain with, and the Rev. Eli Jenkins, sublimely unshocked or even uncomprehending, cries out thank the Lord, we are a musical nation." It's a lovely incongruous moment, a great first-act closer in productions with intermisssions. (This one is continuous.) But its impact is reduced when one actor, however skilled, is ventriloquising both roles. We lose the contrast and we lose the timing. There are similar difficulties when Mrs. Organ Morgan ("a martyr to music) talks about Polly Gs twin boys and her husband (its organ, organ all the time with him") thinks she's comparing Bach and Palestrina. It takes two to make a failure of communication.

If Under Milk Wood is any kind of play it's a comedy of humours: a parade of farcical obsessives, though without a farcical plot to sustain them. Its also sentimental, a quality driven home by Welshs and Dykstra's decision to ditch Thomas' ending in favour of the Rev. Eli's poem, "we are not wholly bad or good/Who live our lives under Milk Wood": a thunderingly obvious statement that can sound very nice in passing but hardly qualifies as terminally profound. This performance has its pleasures, even its splendours, but it adds a layer of cuteness to material that is quite cute enough to begin with.

- Under Milk Wood runs through Aug. 2 at the Young Centre. Call 416-866-8666 for details.

2008-07-23-will-the-real-shakespeare-ple:
THEATRE REVIEW

THERE REIGNS LOVE

Tom Patterson Theatre, Stratford, Ont.

---

"The expense of spirit in a waste of shame / Is lust in action ... " So begins the most powerful anti-love poem or, more clinically, anti-sex poem in the English language. So also begins There Reigns Love, a one-man show in which Simon Callow charts a path through Shakespeare's Sonnets, attaching them to a speculative account of the author's social and emotional biography.

Callow starts by enunciating that opening proposition clearly, almost primly. Then he warms up, pursuing the poem's argument against passion with considerable passion -- intellectual passion --of his own.

Suddenly, there's a complete break in mood, and he starts chatting to us, very charmingly and informally, in his own words. He talks about the autobiographical connotations that have habitually been read into the Sonnets, and advances a particular theory about them, one adumbrated by English scholar and psychoanalyst, John Padel.

The idea, briefly, is that the Sonnets were initially commissioned by the Countess of Pembroke, one of the most culturally inclined of Elizabethan noblewomen, to persuade her recalcitrant 17-year-old son, William Herbert (the mysterious "Mr. W. H." of the Sonnets' dedication) to marry and beget an heir. The first 17 poems in the published sequence were written in this vein, on the occasion of the earl's 17th birthday.

The subsequent Sonnets were published in jumbled order, to throw identity-hunters off the scent; Padel has reordered them so that they tell the story he wants them to tell. Meeting the young man, like a portrait painter taking the measure of the subject he's been hired to immortalize, Shakespeare became infatuated, and the tone of the poems more urgent and anguished.

Eventually a three-way relationship -- not necessarily consummated on all sides -- developed between W. H., W. S. and the poet's mistress, the eternally mysterious "Dark Lady" who, confronted by one admirer as literary go-between for another, might have uttered the 17th-century equivalent of "speak for yourself, dear John." Or, in this case, dear Will. Whichever Will it was.

Callow advances this thesis with great persuasiveness, occasionally interrupting himself to admit, disarmingly, that there may not be a word of truth in it. It certainly seems suspiciously neat, and also simplistic in its attempts to detect a one-on-one correspondence between poet and poems. But it does give an actor something to act.

Act it, under the direction of Michael Langham, Callow does. He doesn't impersonate and he doesn't dress up, but he's playing the man, or an idea of him.

Still, biographical theories apart, the material is recalcitrant. These are packed, thick poems; Callow doesn't do all 154 of them, but even two or three in succession can be a strain on an audience's concentration.

Although written by a great dramatist, their impulse is not dramatic, at least not cumulatively. Even the knottiest of Shakespeare's theatrical verse (some of the jealousy speeches in The Winter's Tale, for instance) is easier for an actor and audience to navigate; it's part of a clear story and there's usually another character at the receiving end. It's meant to be caught on the wing.

The Sonnets, like most non-dramatic poetry, are meant to be pondered at leisure. In Callow's performance, the pattern set in that opening aria is repeated: a forceful introduction followed by a conscientious attempt to negotiate the images and make the thought lucid. There isn't too much energy left over to convey emotion.

At least there wasn't on opening night, which was plainly under-rehearsed. Lighting cues went wrong, including one apparently meant to signify a pause before the end, but which the audience took to be the end. Callow, having acknowledged an ovation, had to add "there's a bit more" and then do an encore, which he did with considerable grace.

If he was nervous, it didn't show at that moment. But nerves were probably the reason why some of the Sonnets arrived several lines short of their official fourteen; the most celebrated of all, "shall I compare thee to a summer's day," arrived at its sublimely boastful conclusion (the poet is praising his own art, rather than his subject's beauty) by express train, bypassing some of the more picturesque stops along the way.

Romantic ardour is hard to convey when you're trying simultaneously to hack a path through thickets of metaphor and metaphysic. Callow is best when required to be bitter and baffled.

The beginning of the second half finds his imagined Shakespeare going on a long bus ride across England: A rather literal reading of some repeated images of travel and tiredness (and rather too literally staged), but one that Callow manages to tie to his hero's feelings of being used, and hating it, while unable to stop loving the users.

"Not marble nor the gilded monuments / Of princes shall outlive this pow'rful rhyme:" but in this account the power, and the transcendence of time, reside jealousy and frustration rather than love: Not that those feelings are ever easy to disentangle for anyone.

Here I did feel that I was hearing a man, a clever and suffering one. Was that man Shakespeare? Somehow it's hard to credit -- as I think it would be of any performance or any choice of writings.

The most self-referential image in the Sonnets is supposedly the one about the speaker's going here and there and making himself a motley to the view: Shakespeare apologizing for his career as an actor (and a touring actor at that). Looking at those words now in cold print, I find it hard to see them that way. They look more like another blind alley: the opaque mocking us by looking transparent.

I don't remember how Callow spoke them or even, to be honest, if he spoke them at all, but if he left them out I think his instincts were sound. The most apparently autobiographical lines could easily be the most misleading.

The Sonnets are largely a record of torment, and they continue to torment us. We approach these poems, written in the first person and without speech-headings, hoping that here at last will be Shakespeare speaking for himself. And what we find is just another character. - There Reigns Love runs until Aug. 3. For more information, visit stratfordfestival.ca or call 1-800-567-1600.

THEATRE REVIEW

BELLE MORAL: A NATURAL HISTORY

Court House Theatre, Niagara-on-the-Lake, Ont.

---

Ann-Marie MacDonald has a very good ear. I'm not referring to the aural appendage that sits in a jar of formaldehyde on the desk of Pearl Mac-Isaac, the amateur-scientist heroine of MacDonald's play Belle Moral. I mean the rhythmic sensitivity that enabled her to write expert Shakespearean pastiche for the otherwise feeble Goodnight Desdemona (Good Morning Juliet) and excellent conversational lyrics for the musical Anything That Moves. She is also a good actress and, in a logical world, her writing and histrionic talents would combine to produce good plays. But it hasn't happened yet.

Belle Moral, produced at the Shaw Festival in 2005 and now revived, remains a series of orations linked by whimsy: amusing for its first half-hour and progressively agonizing thereafter. (Shaw Festival programs always sport a quotation from GBS himself. An apposite choice for this one might be Saint Joan's "how long, O Lord, how long?") It's set on the very brink of the 20th century. Belle Moral is a stately house near Edinburgh whose owner recently died, willing the place to Pearl, his daughter, on condition she remain childless. Apparently he feared the perpetuating in the family of a strain of insanity, which may possibly be manifesting itself in Pearl's brother Victor, a madcap aesthete with suicidal tendencies.

Both siblings have a thing about dogs. The ear in the jar is a canine one, a present to Pearl from the local doctor who has his own designs on her and is encouraging her in her Darwinian pursuits; she hopes to use it to prove a genetic link between dogs and men, and thus perhaps a unity in all creation. By the end of the play the doctor has emerged as a villain and Pearl, a belle moralist on her own account, seems to have moved from science to mysticism. I say "seems" because all she does is make speeches; no process is dramatized. There are other elements: a mysterious painting executed by Pearl's mother, who died giving birth to her, and an even more mysterious woman who haunts the premises and whose identity is eventually revealed. But there is no dramatic traction. The plot's main practical effect is to break the play down into short scenes, necessitating trundling scene-changes that make the proceedings seem slight and ponderous at the same time.

In between the changes, Alisa Palmer's production is firmer than it was, and Fiona Byrne's performance of Pearl, always admirable, is now superb. Jeff Meadows' capricious Victor is less irritating and more contained than before, though the character isn't. Peter Hutt, the one major cast change, finds a diabolism in the doctor that his predecessor lacked, but falls foul of both the Scots accent and the play's web of ideas. When it comes to expounding philosophic positions -- something that Byrne does with exemplary fluency -- he has to take a breath after every couple words. Maybe he is trying to compensate for his character's being so relentlessly demonized; he remains a raging rationalist while all the others, in varying modes of fancy dress, line up for a photograph presumably intended to signify the supremacy of the imagination and the harmony of all creation.

Of the others in the lineup, Graeme Somerville, in a regrettably brief role as an honourable lawyer, comes closest to matching the leading lady for presence and sparkle. Donna Belleville, theShaw's first choice for maiden-aunt confidantes, does another one here, and in her case, the accent (what I'd call an Edin-burr) helps. Bernard Behrens plays, enchantingly, an ancient retainer who is referred to as Young Farleigh and has a strapping tall grandson greeted, even more hilariously, as Wee Farleigh. An earlier and very good laugh-line tells us that "you can't be pagan and Protestant -- or if you are you're a Catholic." But it leads nowhere. The play has virtually nothing to say about Christian sects, and very little about religion at all, except in the mushiest generalities. All very New Age-y, if 70 or so years before its time. I can only repeat what I wrote three years ago: There is no living connection between what these characters do and what they say. - Belle Moral: A Natural History is in repertory until Oct. 5. Call 1-800-511-SHAW for details and tickets.

2008-07-26-a-hotel-worth-checking-out-th:
I don't want to confuse anyone. The Gladstone Variations is a collection of four short plays that are given on-site productions at the Gladstone Hotel on Queen West. We will call them for the moment Plays A, B, C and D. A and B make up a double bill, C and D another. Both bills are performed simultaneously during each night of the run. That's not all; both are performed twice. You may see Play A and then move on to Play B, or you may do it the other way around. You may return the next evening and face the same options with Plays C and D. Or you may see C and D first. Myself, I saw them in strict alphabetical order, as arranged by the management who knew what was best for me.

When you see the plays, you get to do some walking. They take place in rooms, in lobbies and on landings all over the hotel and also on the sidewalk outside. The kicker is that of the 13 characters on board (or is it 14? -- one of the actors may be doubling), six (or is it seven?) appear in more than one play. And even apart from that, the action in one play sometimes impinges on that in another, with some of the evenings' impact depending on that fact. The amount of effort and ingenuity required to get all this synchronized is awe-inspiring.

As an event, The Gladstone Variations unquestionably succeeds. As for the individual plays: they vary. They all play off the implicit contrast between the posh watering-hole the Gladstone now is, and the dodgy hostel it used to be. The protagonists tend to be ghosts from the past who return to haunt the present. The obvious danger here is preciousness. Brendan Gall's The Card Trick (Play C), directed by Alan Dilworth, avoids it best. It has the advantage of a stunningly immediate performance by Richard McMillan as a bloodied down-and-out, desperately searching -- for reasons that are made somewhat but not entirely clear --for a lost little girl. (We get to see her, or at least some little girl, staring unavailingly through plate-glass windows. She's in one of the other plays, too.) McMillan starts the play lying outstretched in front of the hotel, a position from which he is evicted by a highly hostile bellboy. But he makes his way inside, and we follow him, up and down and even into a bathroom; of all the four plays, this is the one that makes the most extensive and ingenious use of the hotel's facilities. McMillan's character is no patsy: intellectually, if in no other way, he's smart. But he's also outnumbered and overpowered by staff and circumstances and what seems to be his own crushing sense of guilt. You can stand a few feet away from McMillan and see the real unblinking face of agony. And he can stand a few feet away from you and never lose it.

Richard Greenblatt, who ranks next to McMillan as the most prestigious actor on this particular block, also starts out supine on the sidewalk. He appears in Rick Roberts' The Tearful Bride (Play A), directed by Aaron Willis, as a concierge. When he gets up, he leads us into a bedroom where he tells us the story of a bride whose groom failed to show on their wedding night, and of an attendant bellhop who turned out to fit perfectly into his attendant tuxedo. These two roles of course acted out before our eyes (Marc Bendavid being nicely nervous as the help), though it's Greenblatt who does most of the talking. It's pretty clear that this is his memory of an early scene from his own career, a tale of broken dreams covered over with a professional gloss that has now become habitual. Partly because of this distancing narrative device, partly because it is for the most part geographically static, the play doesn't fit too well with its companions. It's like a New Yorker story thrust among pieces from The Walrus. But Greenblatt's performance makes a fascinating contrast with McMillan's: a study in how to keep your audience at emotional arm's length even while standing on top of them. It is in its indirect way almost as affecting.

Mike McPhaden's Requiem for a Hotel (Play B), directed by Ruth Madoc-Jones, gives us Janet Amos as a ginger-haired bag lady in a Tweetie-Pie T-shirt whom I momentarily took, when she approached us as we lined up for admission outside the hotel wall, for the real thing. The reality-quotient increased as we trailed her inside and watched her battle with the ATM in the lobby. (Others watched too, and watched us watching her. That's part of the fun: the rubbing-up of official spectators and unofficial, each group seeming to the other like parts of a show. This isn't about blurring distinctions. It's about accentuating them.) She's here for karaoke night, at which she always sings an Elvis song. Guess which one she chooses. I thought this item excessively fey, and I thought the same, only more so, about Julie Tepperman's I Grow Old (Play D), directed by Rebecca Benson, in which a man who, like the title, delights in quoting "Prufrock," comes to the hotel to lay some ghosts and to add to their number. One up for reality, though: At one point a social worker called to his aid finds that her car has been towed from the supermarket lot next door; I'd left mine there too, and felt panicked.

The staff includes Sanjay Talwar as a second, ambiguously courteous concierge, and Dov Mickelson as a second bellhop with skills to learn, being as he's discourteously sardonic in one play and sadistic in another. The sum is more than the parts: The hotel takes on a theatrical identity of its own. The show is a hit from the Fringe, produced by Tepperman and Willis for Convergence Theatre, which for these circumstances could hardly be more aptly named. - The Gladstone Variations runs at the Gladstone Hotel through Aug 3. Call 416-504-7529 for details.

THEATRE REVIEW

MRS. WARREN'S PROFESSION

Festival Theatre, Niagara-on-the-Lake

---

Bernard Shaw's first three plays, the ones he called Plays Unpleasant, are among his best. This shouldn't be the case; they deal with specific social abuses of the 1890s that are supposed to have passed into history. As it happens they haven't; and Mrs. Warren's Profession, the last of the trio, has the most pertinent subject of all: prostitution, prompted by poverty, on an international scale. Even if it were dated, though, it would still retain theatrical force; Shaw the pamphleteer can be a more engaging writer, even a more human one, than Shaw the self-satisfied sage.

Mrs. Warren's Profession is what used to be called a "strong" play, one in which social issues are expressed through family conflicts hot enough for melodrama. The central relationship here is what may be the strongest and most volatile of all: mother and daughter. When Mrs. Kitty Warren was a girl, she saw one of her half-sisters dying of lead-poisoning from working in a factory and the other respectably married off to a man who took to drink. She herself, possessed of looks and charm, worked as a barmaid for starvation wages until the penny dropped -- many pennies in fact -- and she followed her full sister Liz into a life of profitable shame. They progressed to opening their own chain of brothels, in Belgium, Austria and Hungary. Mrs. Warren has been able to raise her daughter Vivie handsomely on the proceeds, and to send her to Cambridge, where she became a mathematical prodigy. Mother and daughter have had very little contact over the years, but now -- at a holiday cottage in the English Home Counties -- they confront one another and Vivie, for the first time, learns the truth.

She learns it in two separate stages, which are the occasion of two great duets. These are the heart and soul of the play and of Jackie Maxwell's engrossing production, her best at the Shaw Festival so far. Vivie is an advanced young woman who is preparing for a career in accounting and prides herself on being realistic and unsentimental. It's Mrs. Warren's resentment of this attitude that brings on the revelations. Vivie's initial shock gives way to sympathy and approval as she agrees that, given her economic circumstances, her mother had no option. The first act curtain comes down on the two women in an affectionate embrace

It turns out, however, that even if Mrs. Warren is no longer on the game, she is still in it, and that it's still yielding munificent returns -- on which, of course, Vivie has been living. This shock doesn't wear off, Vivie flees to the London chambers of her friend and business partner Honoria Fraser (a vital offstage female character to balance the equally absent Aunt Liz, now living in cathedral-town respectability). Her mama follows her there, for a second confrontation which leaves them as irreconcilable as they were formerly reconciled.

"I am my mother's daughter," admits Vivie, and the two women overlap to a fascinating extent. Both are practical, active women with a horror of idleness and of hypocrisy, though they may differ on what constitutes the latter. Mary Haney's Mrs. Warren shifts accent, from suburban to outright cockney, at moments of anger or indignation, and the change reflects her willingness to fall back on emotional blackmail, packaged as maternal sentiment. "I wish you wouldn't rant, mother," is Vivie's reaction, but her own rationality is its own form of excess. The play ends with her implicitly forswearing not only daughterly affection, but emotional engagement of any kind. Shaw directs that she does this "with joyous content" but Moya O'Connell's Vivie suggests that something valuable is being given up. Haney has moments of playing the argument rather than the woman and O'Connell sometimes comes closer to tears than either Vivie or Shaw might think decent, but these are two very fine performances, electrifying in the way they advance, bond and then retreat. O'Connell has the passion of great candour, and Haney a residual warmth and jollity that show how Kitty Warren got where she is.

There are also four decidedly subsidiary men. The most fully drawn is Frank, a clergy-man's son and reprobate-in-training who courts Vivie and is part of what she gives up; Andrew Bunker gets both his charm and his honesty (about himself, at any rate) very well. His despised father, one of Mrs. Warren's many old flames, is Ric Reid who takes expert, if probably exaggerated, advantage of the opportunity to play a hangover. The man who drove him to it is Sir George Crofts, man-about-town and Warren enterprises' prime investor, whom Benedict Campbell plays with surprising but textually justified daintiness, with some of the airs of the traditional wicked squire. The quartet is rounded off by David Jansen's gentle Praed, an art-fancier whose function in Mrs. Warren's past (or even his knowledge of it) is left oddly ambiguous. His function in the present is to get everything wrong, by being idealistic about it. Here he stands in for the audience, led to expect a traditional country-house drama with family values (I owe this to David Edgar's brilliant introduction to the Penguin edition) and then seeing them overturned. Sue LePage's sets support this; they start with applause-begging vistas of the Surrey hills, reinforce, and then powerfully contract into a counting-house, which is what this finely unpleasant play is about. - Mrs. Warren's Profession runs until Nov. 1. Call 1-800-511-SHAW or visit shawfest.com for details.

2008-08-01-sparing-the-glamour-serving-t:
(From the National Post, August 2, 2008) Season one of Mad Men airs on Bravo!, on Wednesdays at 9 p. m. Season two of the TV series airs on A-Channel, on Sundays at 10 p. m. Incorrect information appeared in yesterday's Arts & Life section. 

Jon Hamm and Elisabeth Moss are giving great secretive performances in the two central roles of Mad Men. Their characters -- Don Draper, head of creative at the Sterling Cooper ad agency and Peggy Olson, his former secretary and now a junior copywriter -- have no relationship beyond the professional, that emotional distance being a crucial element of a show that thrives on defeating viewers' expectations. But they do in a sense belong together: They are two of a kind.

They admire one another. It's an admiration given willingly on Peggy's part, since she entered the show as an office novice while Don was the office genius. (And, at the start of the second season, still is, though cracks may be showing.) He, meanwhile, seemed hardly to notice her existence, except as a necessary cog in the machine, but proved willing to acknowledge and reward her talents, once they manifested themselves. He might even be proud of her, though he's never said so. Alone of the men in the office, he never patronizes, insults or exploits her; there was one scene towards the end the first season when both were at a low ebb and there even seemed to be an unspoken sympathetic bond between them.

Both actors excel at suggesting hidden depths, bottled feelings and mysteries even they themselves are unable to probe. One never knows just how naive -- or how calculating -- Moss's Peggy might be. Last season she managed to carry a baby almost to term without noticing; though in this case I'm not sure whether it was she or the show's writers who were in denial. Meanwhile she took control of an audition session for a radio spot as if by right. She's not only a born writer, apparently; she's a born director. (She gave Stanislavskian notes.) She'll probably end up running the place. And she's only 22. She pointed this out last Sunday, when the firm reluctantly decided to recruit or at least interview some youth, only to be told "you don't count." She's still a woman, and it's still only 1962. She also made Don's new secretary cry, just as she herself had once done. It may be neanderthal to say so, but she isn't as likeable as she used to be.

Don can be likeable because he's so hard to like. He's cold at work, cold at home -- though he'd clearly prefer to know how to be otherwise -- with his two children and his trophy housewife. Much of the first season was devoted to showing the elaborate lie he had been living, escaping the remnants of a miserable childhood by stealing the identity of an officer in the Korean war. We learned of this through flashbacks that felt hokey at the time but eventually justified themselves by the typical Mad Men method of failing to pay off. "You know what?" asked Robert Morse's fluffy senior partner when Don's would-be blackmailer confronted him with the evidence. "Who cares?" Our

sentiments exactly. (And how one misses Morse in the episodes in which he doesn't appear.)

Don is rather like Tony Soprano in that one grabs eagerly at any stray signs of decency in him. It's part of television lore how Mathew Weiner, the creator and principal author of Mad Men, earned a berth as a writer on The Sopranos by sending David Chase the unmade scripts of his own show. The two series have a surprising amount in common; they both show greedy male-dominated societies operating by what are supposed to be outdated rules. Both feature plenty of eating, drinking and (on the male side at least) extramarital sex. Both have featured roles for doctors and psychiatrists. Tony, though, has more self-knowledge than Don, or at least wants more. He famously told his shrink that he knew he'd come in at the tail end of something, that he was in fact an anachronism. Don is caught in an earlier phase of the same extended time warp; the big joke of the show -- or, more grandly, its central conceit -- is that it's set in a world that doesn't know it's about to change. Don, who's only in his thirties, scoffs at the cult of youth, and in his own terms he's right to do so. Youth culture, in his world, meant the Beat generation, a minority group that the establishment might regard with distaste, fascination or simply boredom, but that it felt no compulsion to join.

Don, the commuting suburbanite, lost a mistress from the Village to one of her contemporaries for precisely this reason. It was only later in the decade that youth became power. None of the Mad Men -- and maybe not even Peggy, the token Mad Woman -- has yet shown signs of seeing it coming.

Mad Men beats The Sopranos on visual style, but loses in other respects. Maybe the WASP corporate life is just less dramatic than a life of ethnically centred crime (or of crime-fighting; see The Wire). Mad Men is notably lacking in rich supporting characters; after a whole season I still can't fit name to face to personality traits among most of the junior guys in the office. The only one who stands about among the tail-chasing males is the art director, simply because he's a closeted gay (and Italian). There is Pete, the young and well-connected account executive, but he's such a snivelling heel that it's hard to take an interest (though not at all hard to believe). Out in lovely Ossining, N. Y, there's Don's wife Betty, played by January Jones -- a name unmatched since Tuesday Weld, with whom she shares a talent for portraying off-kilter fragility.

The tensions among the suburban wives often promise to be more fascinating than those among their Manhattan mates -- with a lone divorcee who lights up the screen whenever she appears -- but the show hasn't given them much rein. It's also been getting steadily less funny. Maybe there are a limited number of laughs to be garnered from showing racial and sexual prejudice. Or from advertising itself; we started on a highly satiric note with a campaign to make the health hazards of smoking glamorous. That was hard to top and the show, with a new product every week, has itself the equivalent of the "another death, another dollar" formula that encased Six Feet Under.

Maybe that's the point: It's just another job. What keeps us watching Mad Men isn't the glamour of the '60s or even the satire of it; that's worn off. It's the uncertainty of subtext, which is another term for grown-up drama.

-Season one of Mad Men airs Sundays at 10 p. m. on A Channel; Season Two airs Sundays at 10 p. m. on AMC.
