2008-08-02-puppets-are-better-actors-ave:
Note: Avenue Q runs through Aug. 31 at the Elgin Theatre. For tickets and information call 416-644-3665.

There are ways in which Avenue Q is like Chicago. Dont get too excited. Chicago was -- well, still is -- a musical that shamelessly revels in what it calls razzle-dazzle while affecting to decry and expose it. Avenue Q presents itself as a grown-up Sesame Street; it uses tropes and characters from the children's TV show to present a harsher view of the world than preschoolers should ever be exposed to. When the crunch comes, however, the stage musical turns far more preachy and sentimental than the thing it parodies. Indeed, even to say that is to be unfair to Sesame Street which, unless it has greatly changed since my kids were kids, has never been either of those things.

It's also, I confess, not wholly fair to Avenue Q, a musical with a good score, an OK book and -- in this touring version of the 2003 New York original -- some excellent performances. Its storyline concerns Princeton, a young man who comes to the fictitious street of the title because he cant afford lodging on any thoroughfare higher up the alphabet. He is, in fact, broke. "What," he sings, do you do with a BA in English? a question some of us are still asking, and a first line thats so good that the authors hardly bother to write the rest of the song. They do, though, hang in long enough to let Princeton declare that he still has a feeling that he "might make a difference to the human race." (You can see where this is leading. It's leading to a song called Purpose.) He knows he's among friends when the locals join in a competitive chorus entitled It Sucks To Be Me.

Among those whom it sucks to be are Brian, an unbooked stand-up comic; his -- careful now -- Asian-American fiancee, Christmas Eve (I a therapist but I have no clients); and a pair of male roommates called Rod and Nicky. The landlord is Gary Coleman, real-life former TV child star, whose fame is now so far in the past that the joke passed me by completely, though the writers think its a good one, judging by the number of times they repeat it. (Just to make it more confusing, Gary is played by a woman. His voice hasnt broken yet?) Perhaps most importantly, there is Kate Monster, a teacher's assistant, with whom Princeton embarks on a tentative relationship, because they're both rather tentative people--especially him.

Brian, Gary and Christmas Eve are played by real, full-grown actors. All the others are played by puppets, voiced and manipulated by other full-grown, and fully visible, actors -- just like on Sesame Street where the population is divided between Muppets and others. Here, though, the only reason for the divide seems to be to remind us of the source. Some of the parallels are rib-nudgingly close. Kate has a semi-namesake (but not a relative) called Trekkie Monster, who is all furry and growly. And as for Rod and Nicky: If you ever wondered whether Bert and Ernie were gay, well it turns out they were. Or at least Bert was. Or rather, Rod is. And closeted, and votes Republican. And though outing him may count as a fearless expose, it seems a thin exchange for the rich cross-talk act that Jim Henson and Frank Oz used to provide (and must still do, in reruns). This is despite the fact that Rods furious-denial song about My Girlfriend Who Lives in Canada ("Her name is Alberta / She lives in Vancouver") is rather funny.

The highly promising Robert Lopez and Jeff Marx wrote the shows music and lyrics, whose mock-educational content owes something to the actual Sesame Street but whose style recalls the off-Broadway musicals of the '60s: gentle and tuneful with the merest hint of a rock beat. (The lyrics also work in some subliminal Sondheim homages, while one song -- he made me a mix tape sounds like an update of the Ice Cream number from She Loves Me.) Kate's Theres a Fine, Fine Line is a fine -- if not quite fine, fine -- ballad thats searching as well as touching. Most other numbers are comic list-songs that depend on how inventively they can fill out their premise. Everyone's a Little Bit Lacist (that's how Christmas Eve sings it) does this very well; so does Schadenfreude, whose examples include "football players getting tackled / CEOs getting shackled." But The Internet is for Porn, Trekkie Monsters credo, just repeats itself, which, I suppose, fits the subject.

Princeton is winsomely played by Robert McClure, who doubles as Rod, and Kate is delightfully played by Anika Larsen, who doubles as Lucy the Slut; both bring off a different kind of doubling by acting alongside their puppets as well as through them, and always making the feelings match. I also liked the two Bad Advice Bears who get Princeton and Kate into bed. (So thats bad advice?) Brian is played by an actor called Cole Porter; he must be used to remarks on his name, so here's another one: How neat to have the only Jew in the show played by the only goy among the great songwriters. Jason Moore did the neat direction, and Jeff Whitty wrote the book, which has some good laughs but succumbs to uplift. Princeton goes through the show looking for his Purpose, and the show finally gives him one, in the shape of altruism. It then tries to make a joke of it and then goes sappy again. Like Chicago, it wants to have it both ways. And like Wicked (though Avenue Q's a better show) it hitches a ride off a far superior, and actually more adult, original. This isn't adaptation, or even thoroughgoing parody. It's freeloading.

2008-08-07-we-ll-always-have-freebooting:
How do you resist a show whose first spoken line is "have you seen a blowfish driving a sports car?" The question is addressed by the occupants of a speeding taxi to an old lady at a pedestrian crosswalk, and her reply is in the affirmative. Indeed, we ourselves have just seen her seeing it. She doesn't appear in the least fazed either by the question or by the vision that occasioned it. All she says, in a tone of familiar resignation, is "bloody Torchwood." It seems this kind of thing happens all the time in Cardiff, Wales.

Torchwood is a sci-fiseries from BBC Wales, named for an elite five-person force ("separate from the government, outside the police, and" -- the ultimate cachet -- "beyond the United Nations") dedicated to preventing aliens from taking over the Earth, a threat that presents itself regularly once a week. The crew, which resembles an elite franchise of Ghostbusters, is headquartered in Cardiff because that town, or a sliver of it, sits astride "a rift in time and space." (And I used to put it all down to those ethereal Welsh accents.) It's also where the aliens, showing remarkable consideration, always seem to launch their attacks.

The show is announced as a spinoff of the venerated kids'-series-turned-cult-classic Doctor Who. How and how far it has spun, I couldn't say, not having watched the parent show in years. Even with Torchwood itself I'm a bit out of touch, since what's about to hit our screens is the second season, and I've never seen the first. However, it's fairly easy to latch on to, and the show is obliging about supplying background information.

Torchwood is the brainchild of Russell T. Davies, who was also the creator of Queer as Folk. (It shows.) Its protagonist is Captain Jack Harkness, who's a cross between Jack Bauer and Batman, but with a sense of humour. He's glamorously played by John Barrowman, best known for his work in musicals and most recently seen in these parts as the acting coach on How Do You Solve a Problem Like Maria? Jack is kind of an alien himself but has seen the light. He still has unearthly powers: "I can't die, ever," he says, which rather spoils the suspense if you ask me. Of course, your average superhero never dies, but it's always a comfort to feel that he just conceivably might. Jack is also hungrily bisexual, but if you're going to live forever it obviously makes sense to try everything. Episode 1 ("Kiss Kiss, Bang Bang") brings him up against an extraterrestrial ex-companion, and ex-lover, Captain John Hart (James Marsters, once of Buffy the Vampire Slayer and hence in congenial territory). Apart from seeking power and riches for himself, Captain John wants to woo Captain Jack back to their old existence, freebooting around the galaxies. "How can you stay tied to one place?" he asks, casting a contemptuous eye on the lights of downtown Cardiff. But Jack, it seems, is not to be tempted from his principles. "I worked my way up through the ranks," he boasts, to which his former buddy replies, "I'm sure the ranks were very grateful."

This episode is stronger on style than on story. The techies (not trekkies) on Jack's team are chock full of unlikely data, but their efforts to explain themselves tend to be drowned out by the constant whooshing noises on the soundtrack. Also they mumble, very fast. I got the drift but not the details. Still, nobody on screen seemed to be taking it very seriously. The most prominent among Jack's subordinates, meaning the one most regularly exposed to threats of a violent end, is Gwen (Eve Myles), a sensitive ex-copper. My favourite, though, is the wonderfully named Burn Gorman; I very much liked his performance as the earnest Mr. Guppy in Bleak House and was therefore delighted to find him repeating it here, in the guise of a keen-as-mustard medic. I'm not sure why he and his chums travel by taxi, but maybe it's meant to sound an ironically comforting everyday note, like Dr. Who's phone booth. The blowfish, by the way, turns out to be a red herring.

I preferred Episode Two ("Sleeper") which introduces us to an alien with human interest. She, given a lovely performance by Nikki Amuka-Bird, is an apparently normal and loving young wife, torn between her acquired and inherent natures: think Third Rock from the Sun, played straight. The invaders in this one really mean business, rolling up their sleeves to get to work, they reveal horrendous canal-like abrasions, wherein reside all their malevolence. (They're probably also good for flashing at reunions.) This being a BBC show, I was taken back to what may have been the Beeb's first attempt at science fiction, a real macabre masterpiece, done live at that, called The Quatermass Experiment with which I was unwisely left alone when I was a smallish child. There was a traumatizing moment in that one when a character removed the coat wrapped over his hand to reveal that the hand had turned into a cactus. Yes, he was an alien plant. I've never screamed so loud in my life. Looking back, though, the continuity between then and now seems almost reassuring. Here we are in the 21st century, a point of which Torchwood makes a very big deal, and the extraterrestrials still want to take us over. It's nice to know that we're still desirable.

-The second season of Torchwood premieres tomorrow at 10 p. m. on Space.

2008-08-09-the-cushie-for-best-sketch-go:
Getting nominated for a Dora this year may have gone to Second City's heads. I don't mean that in a bad way, or not entirely. The best number in their new revue -- it comes at the end of the first half and begins the redemption of what has hitherto been a pretty dismal evening -- is a sketch about awards shows that nails absolutely everything. The prizes in this number are presented for documentary film, and they're called the Dockies.

It's all here. The hyperactive presenters trying to conceal their boredom and disgust with the entire proceedings. The caucus-race categories ("Best Photography. Best Final Credits. Best Photography of Final Credits.") The recidivist winners, clambering manically on stage to nab every trophy for their movie about lupus; there's a giggling couple who insist on taking the longest route to the platform every time, and then can never find their way off of it. The meaningless acceptance speeches, whether triumphalist or gee-shucks. The recidivist loser, crying foul; in this case she's a vindictive hausfrau (well, she looks like a hausfrau) whose nominated picture was Indo- Malaise: Chronic Fatigue Syndrome in the South Pacific. (Other nominated titles include C-C-Canada: A Stuttering Immigrant's Dream and One Hump or Two: Diversity in Camels). The presenters' assistant seems uncertain whether he's an usher or a bouncer, or if he's necessary at all. It's heaven.

The title of the show, which is less inspired, is Barack to the Future, though if this revue runs until November, some re-branding may be called for. To be fair, this is one Second City topical pun that actually justifies itself onstage, in the form of a number. It's the opener, in fact, showing President Obama pre-empting the Dockie winners by making his own acceptance speech, paying due tribute to his own "charismatic but humble Obama eyes." Once past this point however, and even with the help of an assassination attempt ("that's not funny, Hillary"), the sketch has no place to go. And at that it's ahead of most of the other sketches in the first half, which don't even have a place to start.

I will except a fairly funny item about a couple of pool guards unable to save a single client from drowning, except for one bratty little girl who rescues them. Otherwise, until the Dockies come along, it looks as if the Second Citizens, who didn't actually win that Dora, may be resting on their almost-laurels. Part 2, however, starts on another high, a number -- a mini-ballet really -- about two raccoons attacking one of the city's giant new garbage cans. (Whatever these things may or may not be doing for recycling, they're certainly proving a boon to urban comedy; first, An Inconvenient Musical, now this.) They come equipped with flashlight and picklock, as many of us have long suspected, and their grace and precision in overturning and exploring the receptacle is immaculate. Karen Parker and Leslie Seiler, in black fur and black masks, execute what a close acquaintance of mine has described as a paws de deux. It could be Toronto's answer to Cats.

Seiler, described in another number as "the femme fatale of funny," lives up to it throughout the evening. She is especially stunning as a Bay Street high roller with a busy schedule, doing speed-dating speedier than might be thought humanly, or humanely, possible. Parker, the only other lady present, is good to have around, especially when awful old ladies or awful little girls are required, but has fewer opportunities; the best thing that can be said about her turn as a Coronation Street woman avidly recalling her penurious youth is that she has an impressive command of the accent. (This ee-by-gum, when-I-were-a-lad satire has been thoroughly mined by everyone from Alan Bennett to Monty Python. Leave it to the natives.)

The excellent Darryl Hinds comes into his own (and has the best punchline of the evening, and indeed of many revues past) demonstrating what he claims to be a traditional Jamaican method of picking up girls. (Jamaicans in the audience showed hearty approval.) But he too is starved of material; he deserves better than to be the go-to guy for impersonating celebrities of colour, from Obama to -- an especially low point -- Omar Khadr. Marty Adams repeats his fat-man's specialty of miming, with relishing grossness, very small people; last time around it was a baby, this time it's an adult: a foot-and-a-half high, on a job interview. (Seiler is his interviewer, and it's another score for her.) In general, Adams makes a winning loser. There are two new faces, belonging to Kerry Griffin and Reid Janisse. Musical numbers are down to one, but it's good: a hymn to Canada ("you can-can do it," they sing, doing can-can kicks) that sounds genuinely cutting and genuinely patriotic. Bruce Pirrie directs, and on this occasion he's a better stager than editor. There's good wood here, but there's also too much that's dead.

- Barack to the Future runs indefinitely at Second City. For more information, call 416-343-0011.

2008-08-11-the-little-boy-that-changed-i:
Its common knowledge that the American plane that dropped the atom bomb on Hiroshima was called the Enola Gay. It's not so well known--at least it was news to me -- that the name was that of the pilot's mother. Sweet. More ominous is the news that one of the two accompanying planes -- the one charged with taking pictures of the operation -- was called Necessary Evil. The questions remain, how necessary and how evil.

Hiroshima, a first-rate documentary from the BBC, leaves no doubt about the evil, but is tight-lipped about the necessity. It restates the familiar conundrum about the bomb ending the war, saving thousands of lives at the cost of thousands of innocent others. It tips its hand only towards the end when it points out that the moral turning point for many people was not the immediate toll in lives but the radiation sickness that overtook the initial survivors -- some of whom had drunk acid rain to quench a raging thirst -- to an extent far greater than anyone had foreseen.

The film, written, produced and directed by Paul Wilmshurst, mixes archival footage, first-person reminiscence and freshly acted scenes. The mix, as always, is jarring; we get imagined dialogue among U. S. politicians, U. S. troops, and the Japanese high command who converse via subtitles. The most effective reenactments are silent scenes of the survivors stumbling and crawling to some kind of safety, with their older (real) selves narrating in voiceover.

The linking narration is spellbindingly lucid, and delivered (by John Hurt) with exemplary sobriety. Hiroshima was selected for sacrifice because it was a major military base, but also -- we learn in one of the more pungent lines of dialogue -- because "Kyotos out -- Stinson likes the temples too much." There are built-in ironies, horrible or hopeful. We get the expected shots of inhabitants obliviously pulling rickshaws or taking the subway to work on the morning of Aug. 5, 1945. The sighting of a reconnaissance plane leads to a bomb warning; people take shelter. Then theres an all-clear, and they go back to being sitting ducks. A doctor tells how his life was saved because, the night before, he'd been called to the bedside of a boy in a village some miles from the city. Cycling back the next day he encountered something like a body stumbling towards him. Trying to take its pulse he found there was nothing to hold on to-- "no skin."

One of the crew confesses that he didn't believe until the very last moment that the damn thing would actually go off. We hear few regrets from that quarter, though one of the men from Necessary Evil says that, looking back, the Japanese had been so demonized that nobody really cared. We are left with the last ironies: that Hiroshima is a thriving city again and that the most warlike nation has become the most pacific, as a direct effect of the bomb. But there isn't much moral accounting or much about afterthoughts. Early on, when dealing with the tests at Los Alamos, we get a freeze-frame on a figure identified as J. Robert Oppenheimer, accompanied by the familiar quotation about becoming Death, the destroyer of worlds. But he's never mentioned again. Maybe there should be a sequel.
2008-08-12-powerful-protestations:
THEATRE REVIEW

THE PASTOR PHELPS PROJECT

Cameron House, Toronto

---

This year's Summerworks festival was supposed to start with a protest. The Pastor Phelps Project, subtitled "a fundamentalist cabaret," was due to be picketed by members of the Reverend Fred Phelps' Westboro Baptist Church from Topeka, Kan. This congregation, notorious for their vociferous insistence that "God hates fags," had already signalled their attitude to the show pretty clearly by denouncing it as illiterate garbage: a piquant criticism for fundamentalists to make, even on the unlikely supposition that they'd actually read the script, since a substantial proportion of it consists of verbatim quotes from the Bible. Even the name of the group presenting it, Ecce Homo, is as much biblical as it is homosexual.

Anyway, the Phelpsians were prevented from entering Canada, let alone Toronto, so instead of protests, all we were left with on opening night were protests against the protests: local groups bearing signs reading "keep your hate out of Canada" (they've had to) and, more wittily, "you're not in Kansas any more" (though presumably they are).

The demo may have turned out to be a damp squib but the show itself, written and directed by Alistair Newton, surprisingly didn't. I say "surprisingly" since the Rev. Phelps' mission is so transparently hateful (in both senses) that satirizing it is like mounting an attack on a barn door; we're talking, after all, about people who were barred from this country because of their plans to picket the funeral of Tim McLean, the Greyhound bus victim, on the grounds that his beheading was a divine punishment for Canada's tolerance of sexual deviance. (Though, since they level this charge at virtually every state in the Western world including their own, it's hard to see why they singled out this one. For the publicity, I guess.) However, The Pastor Phelps Project is rousingly performed, with a lot of well-drilled hymn-singing that doesn't always come across as mockery. The show acknowledges complexity, even if it doesn't pursue it.

Fred Phelps himself appears as a frothing gesticulating figure in a fairground peepshow: Put a penny in the slot and activate him. We learn some surprising things about him, including the fact that he established his legal practice by defending African-Americans in civil-rights cases. Later, in a reversal of the old saw about strange bedfellows, we find him coming in for harsh criticism from the likes of Bill O'Reilly and Jerry Falwell. Admittedly they -- O'Reilly, anyway -- are attacking less for his sexual views than for his disrespect for U. S. soldiers killed in Iraq and Afghanistan. They, too, are signs of God's anger with sodomite America; it seems that, in the Phelpsian gospel, nearly everything is. At moments like these, the show seems to find it hard to decide which side it detests most, which is a kind of balance. It also brings in Ann Coulter, reeling off some of her craziest and most-recycled quotes, none of which have anything to do with Phelps. (Well, she does call Al Gore a fag.) She seems to be there purely so the show can parade another hate-figure (again in both senses). If they want to take her on, better they should give her her own show. Or, better yet, that they shouldn't.

Phelps, as portrayed by Carey William Wass, does have a kind of demented dignity; he sticks to his guns, to put it mildly. It's possible to see him as an originally good man gone bad, or at least mad. We also meet other members of his philoprogenitive family, notably his daughter and principal mouthpiece Shirley Phelps-Roper (excellent played by Evalyn Parry) whom we see interviewed by Tyra Banks for that well-known liberal bastion Fox News. Tyra is shocked by Shirley, and by the sheltered upbringing Shirley's wished on her own daughters, and so I guess we should be, but she too comes out of it rather well; at least nobody could call her a hypocrite.

The show skates over some of the Phelpses' other phobias: of the Jews for instance, who they claim are perpetrating the real Holocaust (and who apparently ran Nazi Germany. Not even pre-Nazi, but Nazi). And of Ireland. And Sweden. Much of what we do hear is cut-and-paste: a well staged version of the relevant pages from Wikipedia. But at the end the production transcends itself. A young boy, presumably with gay inclinations, has been watching and listening to Phelps and has been scared by him. Now, though, he prevents himself from being outright traumatized by conjuring up his own imaginings of the story of David and Jonathan; it's just as Biblical as that one homophobic verse in Leviticus, and it carries a lot more weight. - The Pastor Phelps Project runs until Aug. 17. For more information or to buy tickets visit summerworks.ca.

2008-08-13-surfing-channels-for-the-gold:
Hearken to the words of American essayist Chuck Klosterman, from four years past: In order to enjoy the Olympics, you can't think critically about anything; you just have to root for America (or whatever country youre from) and assume that your feelings are inherently correct. It strikes me that every wrongheaded sentiment in this country derives from the culture of inherent, unconditional rightness. I agree.

Im not sure that the feelings Chuck describes are shared by every spectator of the Olympics -- if they were, viewers from many countries would surely have switched off by now --but they certainly seem to permeate the TV networks. CBC and NBC have both been as patriotic in their Beijing coverage as events have allowed them to be.

In Canada, this hasn't been much. Here I must quote Chuck again, admitting his own susceptibility to the general malaise: "I'm sure Ill unconsciously find myself not-so-secretly hoping that America wins every

event -- except for speed walking-- for some reason, I always hope Canada dominates speed walking." He also referred to the speed walking juggernaut that is Canada. That was then. No speed-walkers, Canadian or otherwise, have travelled across my screen so far this year. Weve had to be content with the whitewater kayaking. "We want to know where Canada stands," insisted Ron MacLean. Where we stood, it turned out, was with David Ford in 18th place. This didn't sound all that impressive, but they put the best face on it, even if he wasn't going to get any medals. Ill say he did well. I think anybody who trusts himself to one of those things in those currents and comes out alive is a hero.

The Slovenian contestant did very well, and we learned -- these games are proving very educational-- that his country is full of white water, just like Canada. Maybe that counts as transferred patriotism.

In some ways, our most consistent export to the Olympics has been MacLean himself. The U. S. anchors have been bumptious by comparison, very gung-ho for their own boys and girls. (Except in the commercials, which on NBC have been remarkably free of Olympic content. On CBC, every advertiser wants to get into the act. Rona gives the impression of having sponsored the entire games themselves.)

Both countries have to face the problem of what to do on-screen when there are no actual events going on. Canada has opted for comedy, which after all is one of the things at which we are supposed to have reached Olympic standards. "Every Western town has its Chinatown," said one funny fellow. Does Beijing have its Western town?

It turns out that Beijing does. At least, we were treated to an excruciating saloon routine, in which a Chinese cowboy instructed a Canadian tenderfoot in the finer details of Wild West-ern lingo and etiquette. "Thank you, CBC comedian," said Ron, obviously wishing that the selectors had been a little more rigorous.

NBCs equivalent is The Olympic Zone (or The O-Zone, though nobody could call it layered) which is a sporting version of Entertainment Tonight. This, too, attempts to embrace the local culture; we've had a crash course on chopsticks. For something more immediately relevant, we had A Day in the Life of Michael Phelps, described as "uncomplicated but utterly remarkable;" by his own account it goes eat, sleep, swim, though the footage made it look like "eat, sleep, swim, pat dog." The eating is gargantuan. But maybe he was having us on.

That said, what has usually greeted me when I've turned to the Olympic channels has been beauty. For some reason, Ive always seemed to coincide with the synchronized diving, where the contestants vary between those who are merely fantastic and those who are superhuman. Of course, some people have higher standards than I do. Ive watched perfectly matched pairs perform impossible feats, only to hear an expert female commentator (who "dove herself") telling me what they did wrong, and sometimes commiserating with the judges on not having her advantages (i. e., having to award points without seeing the athletes in slow-motion). When you do watch them in slo-mo, they're unearthly. Maybe the Chinese could devise a way of having them perform that way in the first place. They'd probably have the best shot at it, because the things theyve been doing in diving, swimming (where their female champions are said to be 16, and look younger) and in gymnastics -- the most exciting Olympic event to happen on dry land -- have defied belief. Maybe it has something to do with playing at home; it certainly has a lot to do with being trained, from an early age. And, as one impressed but skeptical lady implied when discussing the opening spectacle on BBC News, perhaps its the product of a regimented society.

From what I've seen of the Olympics, they hug their winners, especially the young ones, every bit as affectionately as we do; they do seem to shun those who lose. I wonder what the Chinese TV coverage is like. Apart from being -- I assume -- technically perfect.

2008-08-16-three-plays-one-night-summerw:
Three shows from Summer-Works, two of them outstanding in their own right and also, as it happens, internally linked.

Erin Shields If We Were Birds (Theatre Passe Muraille Mainspace) reinvigorates a dramatic tradition that goes back to the Elizabethans. Shakespeare and Company often drew on the classical myths narrated by Ovid, sauciest of the Latin poets, in his Metamorphoses; indeed the Chairman of the Board drew on the same legend as Shields when writing the blood-bolstered Titus Andronicus. The story here is that of the rape of Philomela, a princess ravished by her brother-in-law, Tereus, who cut her tongue out to stop her from telling. Procne, Tereus' wife and Philomel's sister, nevertheless found out about it, and took a revenge ghastly even by mythological standards. (Shakespeares Titus, whose daughter had been subjected to similar treatment, swore to outdo Procne in vengeance, but even he couldnt quite bring that off. As an avenger, Procne is Titus plus Medea. Let's call it a tie.)

Erin Shields' re-telling of Ovids re-telling brings in an appropriately tragic chorus: five women from our own times who -- from Nanking 1937 to Bosnia 1995 -- have been subjected to other, thoroughly documented violations. This could seem like a crude bit of nose-rubbing relevance but, in fact, it works magnificently, due to the authors mastery of tone and the ease with which she can slide from one to another, a quality beautifully reinforced in Alan Dilworth's production. We have the girl-talk, pubescent and post, of the sisters sharing a bath, a scene written and staged with delicious tact. We have the urbane realpolitik of their sisters' sly father King Pandion, bumbling but ruthless (and played by David Fox in a manner not too far removed from his Donald Rumsfeld in Stuff Happens), bestowing the hand of his acquiescent elder daughter as payment to a military ally. We have domestic comedy from the domestics. And we have the stark narratives of those same servants as they tell how, and how brutally, they came to be enslaved, in a powerful mix of solo and unison speech. This is what the chorus in Stratfords Trojan Women should have been like -- though its true that Euripides offers less immediately grabbing material. Shields also supplies a binding metaphor: Like the classical Philomela, who was turned into a nightingale, these modern rape-victims become birds.

The sisters are perfectly cast, with Tara Rosling an inquisitive, trusting and finally heartbreaking Philomela, and Philippa Domville (in her best performance since the Chet Baker play Time after Time) a sensual, sophisticated and finally implacable Procne. Geoffrey Pounsett makes a reasonable stab at Tereus, but seems to be holding the horrors -- both those he inflicts and those he suffers --at arms' length. The production is a terrific event, and Shields is clearly a major talent.

She also acts: not in her own play but in Fewer Emergencies (Factory Studio); this is presented "in association with" Groundwater Productions, who mounted If We Were Birds, though in this case the principal producer is someone or something called Mitch. The vaunted British dramatist Martin Crimp wrote the play. Or maybe the plays: Fewer Emergencies is a three-piece suite, whose components form a pattern, one that's thematic and, up to a point, narrative. But the stories are told scrambled; theyre recalled in fact by a central female figure, prompted and/or interrupted by two -- or, in the middle section, three -- male interlocutors. They pull her up on nearly everything she says. (Did she mean this? Are these the right words? Is she serious?) Crimp may be the most piercingly precise stylist in the British theatre since Pinter -- Martin McDonagh, being Irish, doesnt count -- and he has put his own talent on trial here. In Brendan Healy's production, the actors sit on stools and speak through microphones; as in some nightmare talk-show. All the exchanges are precisely calibrated, everything brittle but impeccably conversational, nothing forced. Shields, who bears the brunt, proves as much a virtuoso at speaking another 's words as at writing her own. She plays a woman anatomizing a marriage -- we assume her own, though everythings third-person -- that she declined to leave, even though it was too perfect to be happy. The middle section involves a school massacre, meticulously described, and here the play does seem to me to stray into sensationalism, the author showing off how tough he is, in a way that If We Were Birds never does. Or maybe its just that such an event is literally closer to home than carnage in Africa or Central Europe, however contemporary. The men are Andrew Pifko, Ken MacKenzie (who's also the designer, a very rare double), and, briefly, Vahid Rahbani. Among the accomplishments required of the cast, and duly delivered, is the ability to harmonize in scat like the Swingle Singers. These two shows might make a fine, if searing, double bill.

Another multi-tasker, Claire Calnan, functions in Raising Luke (Passe Muraille Mainspace) as author, director and -- on the night I went --last-minute actress. The play, set in a convent, may need a Catholic audience, lapsed or current. The crises of conscience and vocation it presents seem specialized, and in a huddled and muffled production, remote. Nor does the staging make much sense of a convoluted time-scheme. Martha (well played by Maja Ardal) switches between being an ill-adjusted novice and being the mother of a troubled son (the titular Luke) with a highly guessable secret. Calnan herself played a more outspokenly sceptical nun who yet manages to survive within the order; even with a script in her hand, she was excellent.

-SummerWorks closes tomorrow. For schedule information, call 1-888-222-6608.

2008-08-19-my-pharaoh-lady:
George Bernard Shaw's idea of Julius Caesar was Shaw himself in a toga: an enlightened thinker and non-stop talker who was also a man of action. Shaw himself, of course, didn't command armies on the battlefield, but he got into a lot of political fights, and not just on paper. He was also a ladies' man who liked to present himself as above all that, or -- seen from another angle -- a prude who cultivated a reputation as a philanderer.

This is the image that, in stark variance with the historical record, he wishes on the middle-aged Roman general who in Caesar and Cleopatra encounters the teenaged Egyptian queen. In real life, they were lovers and had a child. In Shawspeak, they're teacher and pupil, he a little miffed that she doesn't fancy him, but only as a passing matter of pride, not passion. Their relationship is a dry run for that of Higgins and Eliza in Pygmalion, though a Pygmalion that nobody would have a hope of turning into My Fair Lady. (It was tried once, disastrously.)

Where Pygmalion has a plot, Caesar and Cleopatra just has history, most of it happening offstage. What happens onstage is debate, with Caesar winning every round. That sounds hopelessly undramatic, and yet the play -- certainly in Des McAnuff's Stratford production -- is knockdown entertaining. The trick is that Caesar -- the most enlightened of dictators and the most pacific of generals, one who likes to set prisoners free because it's so much more agreeable and less troublesome than locking them up, a man who doesn't flinch from killing but both abjures and abhors revenge and realpolitik --doesn't have an earthly clue. He's fighting a losing battle, not only against his own time but against all others. The moment he closes his mouth, human nature kicks in. It's about to kick him especially hard. Shaw teasingly claimed -- well, one hopes he was teasing-- that his Roman play was "better than Shakespeare," but in fact much of its effect depends on our awareness of Shakespeare. We are nudged about what awaits Caesar when he returns to Rome. We know Cleopatra will meet another, more congenial Roman and -- more cloudily -- that their story, unlike this one, will be a tragedy.

Ruthless, benevolent and with a hair-loss problem, this Caesar is the most engaging of Shavian supermen. Playwright and character were of a comparable age, even though Caesar was near the end of his career, and Shaw still practically at the start of his. At 78, Christopher Plummer is older than either of them, but he remains a heroic actor with a mischievous streak, and one who shows no signs of fading gently into the sunset. Not that he can't underplay: Caesar, like all the best Shavian heroes, expresses himself largely through deflationary wit; Plummer is a complete master of the throwaway that lands. (An increasingly rare talent, by the way.) He can also, and effortlessly, assume the grand manner; he's a self-puncturing figure, but the self that gets punctured, both visionary and practical, is real.

His mission with Cleopatra is to transform her from spoiled, frightened girl to poised, thoughtful queen. (Still spoiled, however, and murderous.) He gracefully introduces her to herself, and there is a definite sense that Plummer is performing the same service for Nikki M. James, who when she played Juliet at the beginning of the season was acting around the text, and now as Cleopatra is driving right through it. She has all the directness of the schoolgirl, all the imperiousness of the princess; in fact she only falters at the very end, when she gives us all of Cleopatra's sorrow at Caesar's departure but none of her relief. Here the production can't resist going for sentiment.

The best supporting performances are Steven Sutcliffe's prim British secretary, Gordon S. Miller's debonair art dealer, and -- best of all -- Paul Dunn's boy king Ptolemy, sulking and quaking on his throne. Peter Donaldson, as Caesar's chief officer, offers plenty of gruff loud loyalty, but surprisingly few grace notes; while Diane D'Aquila, failing to find the key to Cleopatra's bloodthirsty nurse, settles instead for battering the door down. And in a play that deals largely in types, some roles seem haphazardly cast; if the burning of Alexandria's library is to have either comic or dramatic effect, then the distraught tutor who brings the news has to be a really passionate pedant. Here Caesar, the author-as-philistine (again like Shaw himself ) has nothing to react to. The show, however, looks wonderful, in an appropriately witty way. The two leads meet between the paws of what Cleo calls "a baby sphinx," which here has a faint smile on its projected face. Elsewhere, Robert Brill's gracefully versatile sets are overseen -- and sometimes manoeuvred -- by an assortment of Egyptian gods in black and gold. Paul Tazewell's costumes adorn everyone except the minor Egyptian males, whom they tend to smother; the women are beautifully dressed (and, in a bathhouse scene that might have surprised the author, undressed).

The books say that Shaw was poking fun at the costume melodramas of his own day; I suspect that he also adored them, and this staging allows us the best of both worlds, spectacle worn at a rakish angle. The production is fast and easy. It's a lightweight evening. Which is both right and good. - In repertory at the Stratford Festival until Nov. 8. 2008-08-20-a-play-to-be-bused-out-of:
Joanna McClelland Glass is for all practical purposes an American playwright, but her birth certificate is Canadian. Her play Palmer Park is set in middle-class Detroit, which is an important part of the Stratford Festival's catchment area. It has an interesting subject and it has been cast with good actors, a few of whom even give good performances. Those are the excuses, the only ones I can think of. The play is awful.

The title refers to a downtown area where Glass herself lived for the six years immediately following the 1967 Detroit riots. House prices went into steep decline, allowing the upwardly mobile, black and white, to buy homes previously beyond their means. This much is explained to us in the first scene by Fletcher Hazelton, a black pediatrician, and his wife Linda; and by their newly-arrived next-door neighbours Martin Townsend, a white physics professor, and his wife Kate. And they go right on explaining to us for the rest of the evening, joined after a short while by three other local couples, one black, two white.

The ratio is important. Palmer Park prides itself on its diversity, but not on its statistical equality. The area -- and, very importantly, its school -- maintains a proportion of 65% white, 35% black; and, in the play's most arresting point, it's the blacks who are the most determined to keep it that way. If the balance shifted in their favour, the place would be perceived as black, and there would go the neighbourhood. Somebody uses the phrase "tipping point" -- anachronistically, I'd say. And go, or tip, it eventually does.

Before that happens, all the Palmer Parkers get on (I was about to say like a house on fire, but that obviously wouldn't be appropriate). They have social evenings. They go out in bi-racial pairs and knock on doors to raise money for the school, meeting responses crabby, generous or both. (All minor roles are done as cameos by the 10 principals.) But reality comes calling, in the form of the Board of Education, which proposes to bus in black kids from the underfunded, overcrowded school in the next district. Our home team protests, and makes helpful suggestions about improving the other school's facilities, but there is no way. Eden has to be abandoned. To see the aftermath, take a drive today through present-day downtown Detroit and its endless strip-mall suburbs.

It's rare to see a play so unabashedly committed to the cause of NIMBY. Of course, we're all middle-class hypocrites who in real life would have been firmly in Palmer Park's corner; but the theatre is a place where hearts may freely bleed, and the plight of Detroit's blue-collar ghetto-dwellers is likely to hit us harder than that of its doctors, teachers and realtors. The only way around this is to make the characters mean something to us as people. But this is where the play falls down. The writing is appallingly lazy. The Townsends and Hazeltons have a couple of establishing scenes, showing their initial mutual embarrassment and underlying goodwill.

(We're also told that both families have dogs, whose mention will always be good for a heart-tugging moment later on.) But nothing goes below the surface, and these supposedly central characters soon fade into a fuzz of people feeding us facts and trying to make them sound like conversation; whether they're talking to us or to one another, it all comes out the same. At the end, we hear that one couple's marriage has cracked, but we hardly registered its existence in the first place. The play falls foul of the danger inherent in autobiographical drama: the author's belief that her experiences will be as fascinating to everyone else as they are to her. Maybe this one should have been called Glass Houses.

There are some hopeful and rather embarrassing attempts at flash: an interminable and vaudeville sequence in which the men bond over their love of baseball, and a party-turn performance of -- of all unexplored things -- The Darktown Strutters' Ball. (Good song, but still). We see nothing of the children whose futures are supposed to be all-important, unless you count a two-minute interlude in which Kelli Fox and Yanna McIntosh switch from playing Kate and Linda to impersonating their young daughters; this enables McIntosh to renew delightful memories of her performance in Danny, King of the Basement, and she does elsewhere get to show off the sense of humour that she's neglected in recent years. She's too dynamic, though, to be a credibly contented stay-at-home mom. As Fletch, Nigel Shawn Williams gives one of his sympathetic accounts of beleaguered decency. I felt sorriest and/or angriest for Jane Spidell, a fine wasted actress, who has to cope with lines like "let me, Mrs. Motormouth, cut to the chase." Ron O. J. Parson's production seems to be trying to make all this seem natural, but there's no way.

The only good moments come when the play settles for public address as public address, instead of trying to pass it off as dialogue: when Dan Chameroy's nervous prof makes his doomed presentation to the Board of Education, or when, in the most powerful performance of the evening, Kevin Hanchard's assembly-line worker makes his rejoinder. The setting consists of fairly basic projections (pop groups and other memorabilia), and the costumes change to reflect the passage of time; as often happens in such cases, much of the acting is done by the hairstyles. This seems fitting for a play whose idea of establishing period is to have someone say, "We've got a new album. It's that Broadway musical Hair." - Palmer Park plays in repertory at the Stratford Shakespeare Festival until Sept. 21. 2008-08-23-call-me-supremely-unstageable:
Its surprising to find a dramatization of Moby Dick that doesn't begin with the summoning words Call me Ishmael. It is, of course, uncommon to find any stage version at all of the Herman Melville novel, given its bulk and metaphysical scope and its having as a title character what Kenneth Tynan, discussing Orson Welles's attempt half a century ago, "the supremely unstageable whale."

Morris Panychs new adaptation in the Stratford Studio not only does without the opening words, but without any dialogue at all. There is some voice-over narration, delivered indeed by Ishmael, the only survivor of Captain Ahabs doomed voyage, but it comes to us distorted by echoes and overlays, as if Panych, who also, of course directs, were determined to allow us as little verbal comfort as possible. There does seem to be progressively more of it as the evening goes on, in possible acknowledgment that the further the story goes, the more help we need.

Even those who haven't read the book can be counted on to know its bedrock premise: Ahab is in monomaniacal quest for the white leviathan that bit off his right leg. As crocodiles to Captain Hook, so whales to him. Hook, of course, was trying to avoid his fate, while Ahab positively courted his, but no matter: Each ends up in the belly of his respective beast. Melville clinches the matter, before the expedition gets under way, by having Father Mapple in the whalers' chapel preach a sermon on Jonah. (Did he, one wonders, deliver this same oration every Sunday? He could hardly have found another text as well-fitted to his congregation.)

Panychs production is, like his triumphant version of Gogols The Overcoat, a ballet for actors. As before, he has the expert collaboration of Wendy Gorling and Shaun Amyot, credited respectively with movement and choreography, though it's hard to see where one ends and the other begins. He also has rich spare settings (Ken Mac-Donald), wonderful weathered costumes (Dana Osborne), and superb lighting (Alan Brodie). Some things are brilliant; no one who sees it will forget the departure of the Pequod from Nantucket, the cast ranked on the rungs of a ladder, their shirt-tails billowing so they are at once the sailors and the sails. At the other end of the trip, each boat in the last whale-hunt is evoked by an actor running between two outstretched planks held by other actors. The final catastrophe, though, is a let-down; and though I didn't exactly tire of the continuous music by Debussy (to whose mysteries the show is nearly as much a homage as it is to Melvilles), I did begin to crave some variation. And I certainly didnt expect the Panych intermission; it breaks the spell.

But the main problem is that, where The Overcoat had a plot that could be recreated without words, Moby-Dick (he's a hyphenated whale in the original, though not in any adaptation) has a theme that's almost wholly dependent on them and a hero who only lives through them. You have to buy into the Biblical rhetoric of Melvilles Ahab, and to his habit of expressing himself in impromptu iambics, whether hubristically defiant (Id strike the sun if it insulted me) or incantatory ("what ho, Tashtego, let me hear thy hammer"); if you do, the effect is magical on page and could well be on stage. Without them, Ahab is just a seafaring man with one leg and a glint in his eye; David Ferry plays him effectively on that level, and there is an undeniable kick in seeing so verbal an actor robbed of his tongue. I could not, though, escape the suspicion that if he did open his mouth, what would come out would be the voice of Robert Newton as Long John Silver.

There isn't much conflict in Ahab; he defines the word "obsessive." But there are forces pulling at him; and these -- his good and bad angels --are convincingly externalized in the persons of Starbuck, the first mate (as opposed to the coffee shop), who's decently played by W. Joseph Matheson-- though he, too, could probably use some words -- and Fedallah, Ahabs personal harpooner to whom he virtually sells his soul, and who is wickedly well played by Shawn Wright, as a maritime Fu Manchu. (He doubles, ironically enough, as Father Mapple, preaching a commanding silent sermon.) But what emerges as the central relationship, and is virtually a love story, is that between Ishmael (Shaun Smyth, very sympathetic) and Queequeg, the heathen harpooner (Marcus Nance, both fearsome and endearing), who cradles the tiny idol of his tribal god, and bequeaths it as a sacred heartbreaking relic.

Great names these characters have, though most of them of course go unspoken; you have to a) know the book, b) know the actor and c) consult the program to work out that the droll figure doing imitations of Ahab behind his back is the third mate, Flask, played by Eddie Glen. There are three women in the cast, billed as Sirens, hence representing the lure of the sea and, finally, Moby Dick himself: a task for which they are far too dainty. So the supremely unstageable whale remains unstaged. Im not sure he has to be; the Welles production was before my theatre-going time, but I did once see a version at the Royal Exchange Theatre in which the stage was spread at the last moment with a huge tarpaulin which seemed to capture both monster and ocean. There's nothing like that here. But Panych's show has its own climax: an unexpected but perfectly logical epilogue that's a quiet knockout. Call me astounded

- Moby Dock is in repertory through Oct. 18 at the Studio Theatre, Stratford. Call 1-800-567-1600 for details.

2008-08-26-hang-on-to-nostalgia:
(From The National Post, August 27, 2008) The telephone number for ticket sales for Jersey Boys is 416-872-1111. Also, Rick Elice's surname was incorrectly spelled in Robert Cushman's review of the Dancap production of Jersey Boys. 

THEATRE REVIEW

JERSEY BOYS

Toronto Centre for the Arts

---

The truth about Jersey Boys is that it's a well-staged pop concert with a couple of good dramatic scenes. Make that one good dramatic scene and an epiphany. The latter occurs when the original Four Seasons, whose biography the show is, are reunited, years after having split up, at their induction into the Rock 'n' Roll Hall of Fame. They do a number, and in the middle of it each steps forward to tell us, with economy and dignity and even wit, what's been happening to them in the meantime.

The scene is the one that shows how it had all fallen apart. Tommy DeVito, the New Jersey kid with the talents of a musician and the instincts of a fixer, is now deep in debt to the mob and angry that his teammates don't give him enough credit for bringing -- and keeping -- the group together. (He exaggerates, but he has a point.) He's banished to Las Vegas. Nick Massi, the self-effacing bass player and vocal arranger, also takes his departure, on the grounds that he's tired of being one of four guys, with him as Ringo. (It might have been worse; he could have been George.) That leaves Bob Gaudio, the resident songwriter, and Frankie Valli, the lead singer whose stratospheric falsetto was the Seasons' signature.

It isn't just the group that falls apart at this point; it's the show, at least if you're judging it as any kind of drama. The four-way tensions that have sustained the piece melt away, and we start marking time in biography-land where stuff happens because stuff happened. There's a long sequence in which we hear about Gaudio trying to sell an "art song" that, from the buildup it's given, might be All the Things You Are and The Man I Love and the soliloquy from Carousel rolled into one, but that only turns out to be Can't Take My Eyes Off You. Jersey Boys is the most ambitious of jukebox musicals, and it may well be the best -- Ain't Misbehavin' was something different; a jukebox revue -- but it's still a jukebox musical. It isn't stupid like Mamma Mia!, but the numbers and the story bear no relation to one another, beyond the fact that the former was created by the people in the latter. There are a few half-hearted attempts to make the songs reflect character, but the lyrics are too generic for that to work. These are great pop songs, the early ones especially, but there's no way they're theatrical.

Well, they are in one sense: They foster a sense of occasion. The audience screams here when a song begins, because they recognize it and because they admire the actors for making it sound like the original. Once that nostalgic connection has been made, the songs fade into one another. Sergio Trujillo, the choreographer, has given them some stylish moves, probably better than the Seasons' own, but how many ways are there to stage four guys singing? And if I can indulge my own nostalgia: I was a teenager when those records came out, and what me and my mates loved about Sherry and Big Girls Don't Cry and (my own fave) Walk Like a Man, is that they were funny. Those bass voices solemnly confirming Valli's high-pitched exhortations sounded wonderfully absurd, we assumed on purpose. But maybe Americans hear it differently. It certainly doesn't happen here, where the contrasts are less extreme.

Which is not to take away from the four leads who are amazing, and who can also act. (They have a great sound system. You can tell who is singing what.) Each gets to tell a quarter of the story -- the show is divided into spring, summer, and you get the idea-- so there are hints of complexity, which the performers exploit. Andrew Rannells is open-faced and smart as Bob, Steve Gouveia pleasantly astringent as Nick. Jeremy Kushnier has Tommy's wise-guy desperation down perfectly; he gets, appropriately, to start the story off and he can never let go of the feeling that he owns it. Frankie himself, oddly enough, is the least distinctive as a character; the book (by Marshall Brickman and Rick Ellice) is at its best when setting up the boys and the Jersey background, but most of its jokes fall with a thud, its music-business scenes are Hollywood cliche, and it makes emotional demands regarding Frankie's wife, daughter and girlfriend that it never begins to justify. These domestic scenes are as bad as writing gets, and Joseph Leo Bwarie as Frankie has to bear the brunt of them. But he copes, and his vocals duly tingle the spine. The most thrilling musical moment in the show isn't a Seasons song at all; it's the young Frankie at a club segueing from I'm in the Mood for Love into its vocalese paraphrase ("there I go, there I go, there I go ...") You hear a star being born.

Nobody else makes an impression, except perhaps Jonathan Hadley as Bob Crewe, the swishy record exec. And thereby hangs a tale, or should. Crewe gets program credit for writing the lyrics, though according to the show itself Gaudio wrote both words and music for all the Seasons' songs. So was this another case of an industry guy cutting himself in? And wouldn't there at some point have been trouble about this? Either the show doesn't want to go there, or it hasn't been allowed to.

Des McAnuff's staging is fast, tight and tidy; it starts with a bang, before you can even catch your breath, and it keeps the coups coming, most notably the entry of a full brass section, strolling across a catwalk, instruments gleaming, in the middle of a number: the perfect visual correlative for what happens on the record. (Gaudio uses the phrase "objective correlative" in one scene; it reminds you that Brickman co-wrote Woody Allen movies.) Klara Zieglerova's set is unlovely -- this is Jersey -- but serviceable; though the Pop Art projections employed to lighten it up don't have much to do with anything. I persist in my eccentric belief that there's something unsatisfying in spending a whole evening watching talented performers expending most of their energies on trying to sound like other talented performers. I had fun, but now I'd like to see a musical. - Jersey Boys runs until Nov. 9. Call 416-872-01111 or visit dancaptickets.com for information.

2008-08-28-as-sincere-as-the-oscars-demo:
Some of the more revealing moments in the TV coverage of the U. S. Democratic National Convention have come on Larry King's show on CNN. He's had Republican pundits commenting on the day's proceedings. (He promises to have Democrats return the compliment at the Republican shindig next week.) I wouldn't say that most of the talk-show hosts and blond congresswomen he has assembled are notable either for subtlety or perspicacity; indeed, as time went on over the first two nights, Larry appeared increasingly bewildered that he'd invited them into his room. But on Monday night, Ben Stein, he of the money and on this occasion the brains, said something that struck home. He said that Michelle Obama's keynote about her husband's great personal qualities was a mass of cliches.

It hurts to say so, but he was right. On the other hand, what else did he expect? I can't think of any political system that puts such sentimental emphasis on a candidate's relationship with his or her spouse. What other democracy assumes that the voters are, in effect, electing a couple? It's as if the U. S. never got over the pain of separation from the British monarchy and still yearns for a pair of figureheads at the top. Maybe it still expects them to produce an heir. (Given the dynastic strain in American politics, that may not be so far-fetched an idea.) So there was Michelle, forced into telling the convention, and the world how much she loves her husband. As Ben said, that's nice, but really we could take it for granted. And as he should also have said, who cares? Not that his own pronouncements were so shiningly original. He expressed his disappointment (pundit-speak for delight that your opponents have done something you hope will damage them) that none of the Democratic speakers had expressed support for America's brave troops. That's a cliche in itself, and who could doubt that if the Democrats follow his advice during the remainder of the week, more cliches will result.

It's also a cliche to say that American politics, especially when televised, are a branch of show business. But nothing else makes sense. The videos that preceded Michelle's speech and Ted Kennedy's were exactly like the buildups given to lifetime achievement honorees at the Oscars: schmaltzy and, in this context, irrelevant. (Ted's was all about what a good uncle and yachtsman he is.) It says much for both speakers that they were able to rise above it when they reached the podium. Kennedy was irresistibly leonine; even Larry King's panel cheered him, metaphorically at least. (Well, Ben Stein did refer to the "disgusting" things Ted had done, presumably meaning Chappaquiddick, but we know by now that pols and commentators only indulge in these fits of morality to score points against their enemies, while keeping very quiet about the turpitudes of their allies.) Michelle, bromides aside, managed to make a prepared speech sound spontaneous, a talent that I, as an old broadcaster, greatly admire. And I believe that she meant every word of it. All the same, it was sad to see her, in effect, dumbing herself -- and her husband -- down. It's the opposite of what we've liked them for. And when her two daughters gave a cute hello to their daddy, brought to them live by video-link from Kansas City, with Stevie Wonder's Isn't She Lovely as their exit music, I wept; but not in the way I was obviously meant to.

Not that that would stop me voting for him, were I American, or will stop me rooting for him, as I'm not. But what is all this stuff about introducing us to the real Barack, and telling us that the Obamas are people just like us? By the time any politician gets to make a serious run for the White House, let alone actually secures his party's nomination, he's already way out of touch with the lifestyles of the poor and humble, or even -- to invoke both sides' favourite totem -- with those of the "middle class." (Nobody in America mentions the working class anymore. I wonder what happened to them.) Elitist? Michelle in her Tiffany blue gown looked pretty special to me. Besides, to repeat Jon Stewart's memorable comment, if you're running for the most powerful office in the world you'd better be better than the rest of us. If it comes to that, isn't that what John McCain's supporters keep claiming for him? Their default position is that he withstood four years' torture in the "Hanoi Hilton," a feat surely beyond most of us. I forget whether the talk-show jock who brought this up on the King show (and seemed to blame Obama for not having been through it) was or was not the same guy who objected to health care reform on the basis that an America that looked after its citizens from cradle to grave wasn't the American he grew up believing in. It didn't seem to be the possible cost of the plan that he objected to. It's the principle of the thing.

It's been wives' week. Hillary Clinton, resplendent in orange pantsuit, made the speech of her life, one that did sound prepared, but in a good way, hitting every point passionate and hard, with the cameras periodically cutting away to a beaming Bill, beaming especially bright at her (literal) shout-out to him. She commanded her troops to support Obama, and though she may, as the scoffers said, have been playing "the good soldier," I believed she meant it. It doesn't seem to have been enough, though, for some of her supporters. Larry, ramping up the incredulity that increasingly becomes him, interviewed a Democrat lady who refused to cast a vote for Obama because "he hadn't wooed [her] enough." (She presumably meant her vote at the convention, not in the actual election, though Larry disappointingly didn't press her on it.) So it wasn't about the country, it wasn't about the party, it wasn't even about Hillary, it was about her. Meanwhile the Republicans continue to use past quotes from Hillary in ads against Obama that disconcertingly punctuate the Denver love-in; if they think she's that wonderful, what were they doing in the other party? Meanwhile they counter the Democrat claims that McCain equals Bush by dissociating him from their incumbent leader. One wonders why the Americans bother to have political parties. Neither of them seems to stand for anything. Unless they're on the meat-market floor of a convention, in which case it seems they'll stand for everything.

2008-08-30-laughing-last-and-best-soulpe:
Farce depends on the combination of neatness and fluke. In a splendid example of life imitating art, two leading British playwrights, in the 1960s, came up with examples of the genre that's short enough to be presented in a double-bill, each having not only the same number of characters (eight) but the same division of genders (5m, 3f ). I don't know who at Soulpepper, 40 years later, first noticed this coincidence, but the cries of Eureka! must have been deafening.

The two plays in order of appearance (and reverse order of composition) are Tom Stoppard's The Real Inspector Hound and Peter Shaffer's Black Comedy. Stoppard's play is not, strictly speaking, a farce at all; farce has to play by earthbound rules, and Hound is a fantasia. Stoppard himself has said that it's about wish-fulfillment; and the characters doing the wishing are a couple of theatre critics whom the author depicts with, I have to say, extraordinary charity. (But then Stoppard himself was a reviewer before becoming a practitioner). One, Birdboot, is a jovial type, probably writing for a popular daily; the other, Moon, has intellectual pretensions, not all of them caused by his being a perpetual second string whose appearances in public are invariably greeted by cries of "Where's Higgs?" (We're told that the paper, these being far-off days, even runs to a third string, named Puckeridge. "What's he like as a critic?" Birdboot asks. "Nobody knows," is Moon's dark reply.)

Birdboot and Moon are attending the first night of an impossibly bad country-house whodunit, one in which the cleaning-lady answers the phone and unspools the entire exposition ("Hello, the drawing-room of Muldoon Manor") to persons unknown, and in which obligingly complete police announcements pour out of the radio every time it's switched on. This isn't parody; it's burlesque. (Though I have to admit that the radio device was used in all seriousness by a highly praised new Canadian play just a couple of years ago.) The cast includes a pretty young actress to whom Birdboot has been paying offstage court and a glamorous older one to whom he transfers his affections at first sight. Let this be a lesson to all who would mix pleasure with business: First Birdboot, then Moon, are drawn into the action of the play they're watching, with dire results. This, I have to say, is something that seldom or never happens in real life; but both men are drawn on by their dreams, Birdboot's of romance, Moon's of revenge. There is equally a sense (though it's not too well worked out) that the play, or maybe the theatre in general, is taking its own revenge on them.

This being Stoppard, the main fun is verbal, and Jim Warren's production too often flubs the tone. It does so especially with the critics. Michael Simpson's lip-licking Birdboot is almost completely off. Oliver Dennis's shiny-pated Moon is better, especially in his opening silence and his closing shock, but the production makes the cardinal error of having the two recite their reviews-in-progress to one another rather than as complementary monologues. The play-within-the-play is easier meat, though not that easy; peopled as it is with conscious stereotypes, it calls for both boldness and finesse, a trick best turned by Corinne Koslo's domestic drudge (named Drudge) and Mike Shara's ostentatiously mysterious stranger. Sarah Wilson, tennis-racquet in the ascendant, is a properly ingenuous ingenue; Caroline Cave's chatelaine is a stunner, but maybe too young for Birdboot's fickleness to have its full effect. In the title role (which certainly isn't the principal one),William Webster makes a spectacular entrance in waders but seems to be coming from the wrong end of the force-- super-sleuth rather than flatfoot. Small things such as this weigh down a play that's a fragile to begin with.

Black Comedy, by contrast, is cast-iron. If Hound is minor Stoppard, this is major Shaffer, indeed his best play, worth all the pseudo-profundities of Equus, Amadeus and The Royal Hunt of the Sun put together. Brindsley, a feckless young sculptor, waits in his flat for the arrival of the two men whom he needs to impress: a millionaire art-collector and the military father of his hyper-debutante fiancee. Then a fuse blows, and everything goes dark; except that, in a device Shaffer borrowed from the Classical Theatre of China, from the audience's point-of-view it's bright. This simple reversal, with gradations between, is fanatically maintained throughout, with results for which "hilarious" seems a pitiful understatement. Brin has borrowed furniture from the house-proud antique-dealer next door, and when this friend returns he has stealthily to re-turn it: in pitch darkness, with people present. (At one sublime point he takes out the wrong thing and has to bring it back.) Warren's direction this time is magnificent, and the actors slip into the highest of gear. Shara is the kind of youngish leading man Soulpepper has needed since... well, since he left the company in 1999; as a farce's essential, the-person-to whom-this-could-not-have-happened-at-a-worse-time, he not only manages the physical pirouettes sublimely, but he also manages to create a character who needs saving from himself. Cave, as his intended, is a perfect scream; as, in a different key, is Dennis as the floppy-haired-andwristed neighbour. (Quite a contrast in coiffures, his evening--of accents, too.) Koslo could hardly be better than in Hound, but as a teetotaller embracing tipsiness in the dark, she's every bit as good. Wilson is delectable as Brindsley's former lover and future salvation, though her brief impersonation of (in effect) Koslo's character in Hound is the half-evening's only spot of heavy-handedness. C. David Johnson gives much the same performance in both plays, but it's a good one. Like most Shaffers, Black Comedy has moments of being too big for its boots, or too long for its johns, but they pass, leaving tears of joy behind. - The Real Inspector Hound and Black Comedy run through Sept. 20 at the Young Centre for the Performing Arts. 2008-09-05-suckers-gone-civil-alan-ball-:
After creating a successful TV series about people who bury the dead, what rests but to create another series about the dead who refuse to stay buried? Alan Ball ( Six Feet Under) returns with True Blood, which is about vampires. Balls subjects, though, are not your ordinary blood-sucking revenants. Or rather, they are ordinary. Theyre domesticated. True Blood postulates a world in which vampires have come out of the coffin (I quote) and are demanding acceptance. Next thing you know, they'll be running for office.

Ball's victims have been liberated by the invention of a synthetic blood product (I think I heard someone say it was Japanese) that relieves them of the need to slake their thirst on humans. Needless to say, this is not enough to make all humans trust them. It certainly isnt enough in the small town of Bon Temps, La., which is where True Blood is set. Though the vampires have progressed enough to have their own pressure-group, the American Vampire Legion (we see their designated spokesperson, in a prologue sequence full of witty reversals, being interviewed by Bill Maher), they arouse extreme responses. There are the "vampire-drainers," who viciously prey on the former predators, and the fang-bangers, who want to have sex with them. It can be quite hard, psychologically speaking, to tell these two groups apart.

The Christian right, naturally, detests the vampires; its TV representative denounces them even while refusing to recognize their existence by actually talking to them. (Its for non-encounters like these that split screens were invented.) On the outskirts of Bon Temps someone has hung a sign reading "God Hates Fangs." So you can see where we're at. Vampires in this show are stand-ins for the victims of real-life intolerance, especially as encountered in pockets of rural America.

The obvious trouble with this approach is that gays, blacks and immigrants actually exist, and vampires don't. So the metaphor seems, shall we say, frivolous: certainly slight to build a whole TV series on. Here I

have to declare a lack of interest. Vampires as a subject bore me, whether theyre being used to induce thrills or giggles. (Yeah, I know about Buffy. So slay me.) Obsession with the occult seems to me the least attractive legacy of the 1960s. Still, if any show could convert me, this one would. At the end of the first episode I thought, well that was good, well written and well acted, but I dont know that I need to stay with it. At the end of the second, I was hooked. For now, at least.

True Blood, as you may have gathered, does not belong to the solemn end of the vampire spectrum. It's vamp-camp. But there is more to it. At the least, it represents the meeting of two kinds of Gothic: Transylvanian and Southern. Its central character (the heroine of a line of popular novels that I of course haven't read) is Sookie Stackhouse, whos a waitress at Merlottes bar (and undoubtedly grill) and is, by the look of things, over-qualified. She too has supernatural attributes, and they're far more interesting. She can read minds. It's caused her trouble since early childhood (she was diagnosed with ADD, which of course is the precise opposite of her actual condition) but shes learned to tune it out, at least some of the time. Its still played havoc with her love life; she can never get through a date because her knowledge of what her companion is thinking causes her either to laugh or to throw up. She's also a self-reliant person, who can swing a very nifty chain when confronted by villains.

She's played with abundant wit and gumption by Anna Paquin, once the little girl of The Piano, now proving how impressively nine-year-old child stars can grow up.

Scarcely less beguiling is Sookies best friend Tara (Rutina Wesley), first seen working at a hardware store where she confronts a troublesome customer with an aggressive lack of interest that would do credit to Canadian Tire. Tara would rather read a book, which she continues to do in her next job, behind the bar at Merlottes. Tara speaks well; she tells a male friend at a party your standards are so low, you always get lucky (not with her, he wouldn't be interested) and she affectionately sums up Sookie as "trouble waiting to happen." Tara has an obvious unspoken crush on Sookie's brother Jason, whose standards may also be low, or at least risky; he spends an impressive proportion of the show in and out of a succession of beds. ( True Blood has some of the raunchiest sex and most brutal violence yet seen on HBO. That is not a condemnation.)

Ball has talked in an interview of the shows "moral complexity." Ive yet to see it. But the characters are quirky, and the setting attractively earthy and, to viewers outside the locale, exotic. (Ball's a Southerner himself, so I suppose we have to take his word for a milieu in which half the cast sound like T-Bag from Prison Break, and a quarter seem about to behave like him.) And there is some variation among the vampires themselves; they all seem traditionally scary and repulsive, except for Bill (Stephen Moyer), Sookie's love-interest, a clean-cut respectful son of the old South who expired during the Civil War: a circumstance that fascinates Sookies grandmother (the great Lois Smith) who wants him to address her library group, the Descendants of the Glorious Dead. This elicits from Bill, who presumably should know, the response that theres nothing glorious about death, certainly not in war. Ball wrote and directed the opening episodes, and so far they're better than Six Feet Under. They're also less insufferably lofty than his screenplay for American Beauty, though I suppose if I lived in Louisiana I might think differently. The best thing about the show is that for longish stretches you can forget that it's about vampires at all. You may, however, find yourself thinking about the Republican Convention.

-The premiere episode of True Blood airs Sunday night at 9 p. m. on The Movie Network.
