2008-09-06-cinderella-at-the-distillery-:
ean Anouilhs Ring Round the Moon is a play built on extravagance and magic. You might deduce as much from its title, which admittedly was not Anouilh's own. He called his play, a wry twist on the Cinderella story, L'Invitation au Chateau, which would sound a lot more prosaic rendered literally into English than it does in French. The English title was the inspiration of the translator, Christopher Fry. In the immediate aftermath of the Second World War, Fry and Anouilh were regarded as complementary figures, young masters of verbal and theatrical legerdemain, restoring wit and fun and glamour to cultures starved by austerity and, in Frances case, scarred by occupation.

Immensely popular in the 40s and '50s, both men had fallen violently out of fashion by the committed '60s; when I was an undergraduate, my earnest friends could hardly pronounce either of their names without spitting. Of the two, Anouilh has since fared better; Frys own jingling verse plays have fallen almost completely (and probably unfairly) off the radar, but Ring Round the Moon, in prose, has survived. For reasons artistic or contractual or both, this is a rare example of a foreign play persisting in the repertoire for nearly 60 years without being re-translated. For all that, Im not sure that Fry's version does it full justice. Anouilh's characteristic tone is one of bitter-sweet farce, and though in this play the sweet predominates, there is an underlying toughness with which Fry, despite some lyrical moments and some very funny ones, seems uneasy.

It could still work, and it has done. But something is wrong with Joseph Zieglers Soulpepper production; maybe, its that as a director Ziegler is more logician than magician. (He's a magical actor, and if Soulpepper or any other Canadian company were to revive Anouilh's best play The Waltz of the Toreadors, hed be my first choice for the lead.) Individual scenes here make sense, but they dont fold into, or explode out of, one another. There isn't a rhythm.

The Cinderella is Isabelle, a penniless ballet-dancer who's invited to the chateau of Madame Desmortes who, naturally, is giving a ball. The invitation has actually been extended, though, by her nephew Hugo. Hugo has an identical twin brother, Frederic; theyre played, of course, by the same actor. Hugo is nasty, Frederic, nice, though this seems to boil down in practice to Hugo being worldly (he claims that the 10 minutes by which hes the elder have taught him all there is to know about women) and Frederic, shy. But Hugo is certainly manipulative, he wants Isabelle to attract Frederic, and thus arouse the jealousy of Frederic's unkind fiancee Diana Messerschmann, whose father is a former tailor from Kracow, now one of the richest men in the world and not enjoying it much. Hugo turns out not to be as dispassionate or uncaring as he'd like to think. Isabelles own feelings get involved, and hurt. Sub-plots and side-actions add to the overall mix of whimsy and satire.

Christina Poddubiuks delicate anteroom of a set promises enchantment that it never quite delivers. (Richer lighting might help; the first act in particular seems to unfold in shades of grey.) The ball itself is going on next door; it's well evoked by Mike Ross's musical score, less well by the dancing couples who periodically spill over onto the stage and whose efforts seem effortful. The plays most famous scene, tangential to the plot but vital to the mood, may be a tango-with-dialogue performed by Lady India, the millionaires self-consciously smouldering mistress, and his secretary Patrice, her reluctant other lover. It misfires here, with the words ill-matched to the moves and with Kristen Thomson radically miscast as a feather-witted femme fatale. (Her partner, Kevin Bundy, gets his petrified character perfectly.) Also off-key is Diana Donnelly's Diana, less spoiled than graceless.

Most of the performances are fine. Brenda Robins has never been better than she is as Isabelle's mother, a refugee from dowdiness intoxicated by glamour, and Brenda Bazinet, who plays her old friend and Madames tyrannized companion, never as good. Madame herself is Nancy Palk, giving the best of her grande-dame performances as a wheelchair-bound chatelaine who never does an unkind thing and never says a kind one; she unrolls her sentences with superb bite. (She looks as if shes about to break into Liaisons from A Little Night Music; not such a stretch as Sondheim and Prince considered this play and Jean Renoir's Rules of the Game as source-material before settling on Smiles of a Summer Night.) Somehow, though, she's never as much at the centre of the play as she should be. Nor, despite his charm and his constant presence as one brother or the other, is Jordan Pettle; Frederic gives him no trouble, and he has a very fair shot at Hugo, witty but without capturing the diabolism that presumably should drive the action. To be fair: For a self-proclaimed bastard, Hugo has a disconcerting habit of acting in everybodys best interests. Thankfully, the production has an

emotional core in Patricia Fagans Isabelle, rather drably gowned for the belle of the ball, but alight with moral and emotional fervour, and especially good at conveying varying shades of shame. She shares the best scene with Diego Matamoros, wearily ruthless as the melancholy Messerschmann; when the two of them tear up a selection of his bank-notes, her bitter cry of "let's not forget the poor" echoes in the mind. (These days Matamoros's authority on a stage almost constitutes unfair competition, but shes up to it.) The cast is completed by Richard Clarkin as Isabelles protector, who wants to add her to his butterfly collection, and John Jarvis, who seems a little spry and Jeevesian for the text's "crumbling butler" but is admirable nonetheless. This, though, is a play that should beguile you, then disturb you, then charm you all over again, all seamlessly. Here it's a bumpy ride that leaves you clutching at moments.

-Until Sept. 20 at Young Centre for the Performing Arts. Call 416-866-8666 for ticket information.

2008-09-09-why-less-can-be-more-the-debu:
The first episode of the new sci-fi-cum-terrorist show Fringe ends with the following remarkable exchange:

"How long has he been dead?"

"Five hours."

"Question him."

Well, it can't be vampires, because we already have a show about them. In fact, I know after watching the 90-minute pilot pretty much what's led us to this point, but to tell you too much would be spoiling. But I think that I can safely quote another couple of lines of dialogue that occur a few frames earlier. A supporting-role cop, male, remarks to a starring-role cop, female, "corporations have higher security clearance than we do." He then adds: "The truth is, we're obsolete." You mean, no more tense conversations betweenlaw-enforcement twosomes sitting in cars? That can't be. His other observation, though, is probably correct. So far -- and the plot could easily thicken--most of the skulduggery in this show is traceable to a multi-billion dollar concern with gleaming white offices called Massive Dynamic, who are into chemicals. Whether they're also in league with aliens remains to be seen.

Let's go back to the top. Fringe comes from creators who have worked on Lost and Star Trek, and it has the marks. But it begins more like 24, starting as that show did all those years ago with a mysterious incident on an aeroplane leading to the grisly demise of all on-board. This time, though, the captain has the presence of mind to put the plane on autopilot before succumbing himself, and it makes a safe landing at Logan Airport in Boston. (Dead, if you'll pardon the pun, on schedule: "Unlike" says a cop -- the same one, I think -- "any flight I've ever taken.") The 24 vibe returns later in the episode when a rogue civilian, who nevertheless is on the side of the good guys, goes Jack Bauer on a suspect from whom he requires vital information in a very short time. I hate to tell you that it works.

Our central character, though not so far a very involving one, is Olivia Dunham (Anna Torv), FBI Special Agent. What a pleasure to be able to type those last two words again; they bring back a cozier past. We first meet Olivia at a motel where she's having a romantic tryst with a colleague. I'm not clear why they couldn't go to his place or hers, but this rapidly ceases to be of any moment, as the guy inhales a dose of whatever it was that laid the passengers and crew so low and spends the rest of the episode hovering between life and death. Up to this point, Olivia has been professionally interested in finding who or what killed a whole planeload of people. Now, it's personal.

She's working, not too comfortably, with a high-up from Homeland Security (the new glamour-outfit in television land) who addresses her as "li-ai-son"; he's played by Lance Reddick, who seems to have been hired to repeat his upstanding policeman performance as Lieutenant Daniels on The Wire, but with less nuanced material; Daniels could be tough on his men, but this guy just seems rude. When Anna discovers a promising lead, he more or less tells her to stuff it and get back to her desk. She perseveres and the trail leads her to what the titles helpfully identify as "Baghdad, Iraq." (Oh, that Baghdad.) I doubt that the show itself went there; indeed I hope it didn't, not just for the sake of one brief scene in an anonymous hotel lobby in whose background men in headdresses may occasionally be glimpsed. Also hanging out there, and the object of the trip, is Pacey from Dawson's Creek. Well, I'm sorry but, given the basic level of competence that most TV shows can be trusted to deliver, one tends to respond to the actors less for what they're doing now than for what they've done before. Joshua Jackson, who was the best thing in Dawson's Creek, has aged (not too noticeably) into the best thing so far on this one. He's Peter, the near-genius son of a total-genius father whom Olivia needs to track down, and whose cooperation is secured by means of some simple blackmail. He and Olivia display the on-sight animosity that is an almost infallible fictional sign of deep romantic attraction. I'm not saying they're in one another's arms yet; I mean, she does have an out-of-action boyfriend.

Peter's dad is, literally, a mad scientist; he's been locked up for 17 years for nefarious chemical experiments. But he seems to want to atone, and one of his helpful actions is to devise a cocktail of drugs, including but not limited to LSD, that will en-able Olivia to make mental contact with her comatose partner. This is one of the many points in the show that requires Jackson to signal "you can't be serious." (He does it very well.)His father, who looks like Solzhenitsyn until he shaves his beard off, is John Noble, an Australian actor playing an Englishman. (Torv is an Australian playing an American; Jackson is a Canadian playing an American. Nobody's accent gives trouble.) The doctor is allowed to practise in his old underground lab, which since his enforced departure has been used as a storage room. The contrast of these surroundings with the glistening quarters of The Company (sorry again, wrong show; same idea) is its own moral comment. Representatives of both sides remark, ominously, on there being "a Pattern." Unravelling it is the mission to which Olivia, Peter and Dr. Frankenstein (his son's pet name for him) are summoned at episode's end by the former Lt. Daniels, who seems delighted to have his very own special detail again.

Is it good? It certainly moves fast. I'd quite like to know what happens next, which is not quite the same as dying to know. It's the difference between suspense and mere curiosity, which is also the difference between shows with human content and shows without. As a die-hard fan of 24 and Prison Break, I can hardly complain about lack of credibility, but those shows survive by making you invest in the people rather than the technology. That's as true for science fiction as for any other kind. It's amazing what they can do these days. Sometimes the art is to refrain from doing it. - Fringe debuts tonight at 8 p. m. on CTV and A.

2008-09-11-eye-for-actors-and-a-nose-for:
Note: Obituary of Richard Monette.

I wish Id seen Richard Monette's Hamlet or his Prince Hal, or the performance in Hosanna that made him a star. A giant picture of him as that sad, funny drag queen hangs in the lobby of Toronto's Tarragon Theatre, and it makes a wonderful mental contrast to the image of the orotund actor-manager who directed the Stratford Festival for a record-setting 14 years. The latter was a mask that grew pretty close to his face but one that he wore, I suspect, with a mischievous self-awareness. Nobody, despite the sculpted tones, would ever have called him pompous.

I knew Monette mostly as a director: of the Festival and of many of its plays. (I also knew him as a genial, generous and encouraging friend.) In both these directorial guises, he became to an extent the victim of his own publicity and his own success. Because his first successful production was of The Taming of the Shrew, he became typed as a director not just of comedy but of farce, and accused of loading every play with irrelevant business. There was some occasional truth to that; in his final Shakespeare production, The Comedy of Errors, he seemed, perversely, to be going out of his way to prove the accusations true. Most of the time, though, his detractors were seeing in his work what they had programmed themselves to see.

He wasnt a director for concepts. He was one with a keen and sympathetic eye for actors, as you might expect, and with a keen nose for the text, as perhaps you wouldnt. In recent years, he did a fine exploratory job on Troilus and Cressida, and an especially accurate and entertaining one on Henry IV, Part 1; the latter was attacked for not keeping the serious scenes serious and the "comic" scenes comic, as if it were not the genius of that play not just to alternate those genres but to fuse them.

Some of his best productions weren't comedies at all; he may even have been better off when he didn't have those skills to fall back on. I remember his atmospheric Cat on a Hot Tin Roof, his rowdy Inherit the Wind, and the more-than-stage-filling extravagance of The Three Musketeers. (All right, that was a kind of comedy, certainly an entertainment.) His King Lear was most memorable for William Hutts great performance, but it was a fine account of the play in its own right. The first of the two Tempests he did with Hutt (Richard himself preferred the second, but he was wrong) was one of the best-balanced productions of that minefield of a play that I have seen. And it wasnt just, or even principally, the clown scenes.

The administrative achievement of Monette's that nobody denied was that he balanced the theatre's books. The corresponding accusation was that he did it at too high a price, watering down the repertoire with populist choices. I could have done myself without some of the middle-brow family experience plays; I also wish, much as I love musicals, that the festival hadnt become enslaved to them -- though that didnt start with the Monette regime and hasn't ended with it. What seems to have been forgotten is the canniness with which he balanced the predictable with the truly adventurous. Considering the praise Stratford has received for staging a Greek play, it's worth remembering that Monette mounted a whole season of them. Or that a few years ago he programmed five Shakespeares in a season, including some of the most obscure. Or that in the Studio, which he founded, he presided three seasons in a row over the premieres of Peter Hintons insanely ambitious trilogy The Swanne.

Im glad that he got to play a part in the current season as "interim director" of Michael Langham's beautifulproduction of Love's Labours Lost, working on the text with young actors from the Conservatory that was another of his cherished innovations. Im grieved that he never got to play the Falstaff that he and many others knew he had in him. (That would have been quite a comeback.) The farewell gala that the company mounted for him last year on the Festival stage left no doubt how much he was loved. He is certainly going to be mourned. And he was still young.

robert.cushman@hotmail.com---------

'WE CARE ABOUT ART, NOT ABOUT MONEY':

Robert Cushman discussed Richard Monettes ascension to Stratfords top artistic position in his 2002 book Fifty Seasons at Stratford (McClelland & Stewart/Madison Press):

The Canadian theatre -- more than the American, and far more than the British -- has smiled on the actor-director. Most of Stratford's artistic directors have been established professional actors. ... None of them, though, had quite the thespian credentials of Richard Monette.

Monette is the only Stratford chief to have worked his way steadily up within the organization. Between 1965 and 1987 he had acted in 15 different seasons, progressing from walk-ons to leads. He had won additional fame, or notoriety, at the tempestuous general meeting that followed the dismissal of the Gang of Four in 1979; as the chairman of the [Stratford Festival] board of governors wound up the proceedings, leaving many questions still unanswered, Monette had screamed at him: "You pig!We have spent our life in this theatre. We have given our time, and we care about art, not about money all the time. You have no morals. I don't know how you can sleep."

For all the nerve that he had demonstrated, on-and offstage, Monette gradually developed a crippling stage fright that turned him from acting to directing; and after his first Stratford success with the 1988 Taming of the Shrew, he became the Festival's most frequent and reliable guest director. Obviously, he was being groomed for the top position. As was by now the custom, Monette spent the 1993 season shadowing and working with the outgoing director, David William, but in truth he had been serving a 30-year apprenticeship.

2008-09-12-oslo-descent-into-a-suicidal-:
If the title Norway. Today sounds ominously like an email address, there's a reason. The play comes from deep within the world of dot-commery. Its first scene is a conversation held online. Somewhere in Norway (today) a 20-year-old woman has entered a chat room, looking for someone to join her in a suicide pact. Her call is answered by a man of similar age in another country. What that country might be is never revealed, and probably doesn't matter, but one can't help wondering. The author, Igor Bauersima, comes from Switzerland, so maybe his hero does, too. I know the internet has broken down all kinds of barriers, but it still seems a handy coincidence that boy and girl are able to speak, or text, the same language. How's their German in Norway?

The boy's name is August, the girl is July, a. k. a. Julie, but don't let that put you off. Their contact switches, along with the play's action, from virtual to real; August flies to Norway -- with Julie, as we subsequently learn, paying the fare. She looks able to afford it; he certainly doesn't. We join them high on a mountainside overlooking a fjord, into which they propose to fling themselves. Only not just yet. Julie's brought a camera on which to record her last thoughts, August has brought a portable music player to assist whatever mood may arise, and they also have a tent, in which they propose to spend their last night. Guess what happens.

So it's Love and Death, or Love or Death, and it's cuteness and pain. (And the whole damn thing, to invoke an ancient movie title.) The pain comes through most clearly in Julie's stark opening statement in the chat room, the point at which this self-styled "existential comedy" comes closest to justifying the description. She wants to kill herself because life seems pointless. He wants to kill himself because his seems pointless, which is a bit different. He doesn't have a girlfriend. She isn't surprised.

Ieva Lucs' Julie is, at the beginning, impressively stark. Later on, I suspect, she suffers in translation. Speaking in English with a North American accent she sounds, inevitably, like a spoiled rich American girl, not so much implacable as bossy. She's better later, when she gets to soften up and even laugh at herself. August, by contrast, laughs at himself almost continually, as a defence mechanism. He's a great roller with the punches as, with his insecurities, he needs to be. This makes his the more rewarding role; and Steven McCarthy, a definite up-and-comer with electricity in his veins (he was great last year in Revisited), gives a bold performance of shyness: a neat feat.

We never believe he'll go through with it; we think she just might. Only she's set on doing it in her own time, and doesn't take kindly to having it accidentally anticipated. As they both perch precariously on the literal edge of doom, there are a fair number of laughs of the "I might have got killed!" variety. There are touching moments, too, including a sex scene that starts as fantasy because that's the most comfortable way in which these awkwardly-matched partners can get revved up. Besides, it's virtually (ha!) the way they met. Their love-making is seen live in silhouette, and also in projections, tasteful both ways; Sarah Baumann's production (for Theatre Smash) takes, and runs with, the play's idea of life as something that exists in order to be recorded on video. Or at least its characters' idea; audiences above a certain age may feel like voyeurs, not so much of activities as of a mindset. Like those characters, the play keeps approaching the brink -- of sentimentality or facile philosophizing -- and pulling back just in time. If love conquers all (and I'm not saying it does, go and find out for yourselves) that could be because all doesn't put up enough of a fight. The play's an odd blend of romantic comedy and fashionable angst that just about holds.

To give the most basic recommendation: It's a 100-minute play with only two characters and no intermission that isn't boring. - Norway. Today runs until Sept. 21 at Tarragon Extra Space. Call 416-531-1827 for information.

2008-09-13-rekindled-but-still-remiss-ho:
Wadji Mouawads Scorched, as translated by Linda Gaboriau, contains one line that, in the 18 months since the play was first seen at the Tarragon, has become justifiably famous. A French-Canadian lawyer, who has trouble with English idioms, talks about being caught "between the devil and the Blue Danube. He says a lot of things like that. In a modest spirit of emulation, I'd like to say that the revival of this extravagantly praised play leaves me feeling, more than ever, like a skeleton on the beach.

It is, I readily admit, a play of greater size and assurance than we're accustomed to. It erects an elaborate structure, with building blocks ranging from Greek myth to todays headlines, in order to tell a story about genocidal warfare and its effects on countries and families. It moves nimbly around time and space: from contemporary Canada to both the past and present of an unnamed ravaged country in the Middle East. The strongest resemblance is to Mouawads own birth country of Lebanon; one of the pivotal offstage events is a massacre in a refugee camp. But there are also ingredients that suggest Afghanistan, and places even farther afield such as Sudan or Somalia. An atrocity is an atrocity wherever it happens, true. But a generalized Everycountry does not necessarily bring it more forcefully home than an identifiable place from which we might extrapolate for ourselves. It also leads to generalized characters. The problem with Scorched is that its impressive machinery is operated by puppets.

There is one exception, one case in which a real insight is embodied in a real person. This is a torturer (Alex Poch-Goldin) who once had dreams of fame as a musician -- in a preparatory career as a sniper, he amused himself by playing air-rifle -- and regards his current vocation as another branch of show business; his victims are there to entertain him, i. e., to stop him from being bored. But even this revelation is weakened by having its subject be all too aware of it; he makes his avowal, flourishing, a red nose that's also a plot-point, before the tribunal that's trying him. The other characters are lay-figures jumping through predetermined hoops.

It starts hopefully enough. The Montreal lawyer summons a brother and sister, both young adults, to the reading of their late mothers will. Mother was an immigrant from the plays other country," and she and her children hadn't spoken in years. The air is thick with resentment, full of sullen silences; there are flashier scenes in Richard Rose's production, but this is the best. The siblings are dispatched by posthumous maternal fiat to find the father they thought dead, and a brother they never knew they had. The couple are very well played by Sophie Goulet and Sergio Di Zio; she is a mathematician, for symbolic reasons, and he is a boxer, for no discernible reason at all. Other questions arise. Why does the lawyer (delightfully played by Alon Nashman) get his English proverbs wrong but nothing else? It isnt very plausible or, after the first few times, very funny. It seems like a cut-price way of supplying "human interest," something the play otherwise lacks.

Denying it to us may be a reason for having Nawal the mother, whose flashback story unfolds in counterpoint with her childrens present-tense one, played by three different actresses: Janick Hebert, Sarah Orenstein and Nicola Lipman, in ascending order of age. This is despite the fact that she has a friend and contemporary who's played by one actress throughout; and the probability that, though all three performers are good, Orenstein as the middle one could play the entire woman herself. She's impressively flinty in what she does, but if she were allowed some variation, she might even persuade us that Nawal is one real woman instead of a series of poses. As it is, her only consistency is as a vessel of misfortune: robbed of a child when young, raped and tortured when older. Her positive attributes, like teaching herself to read in a savagely sexist culture, are painted on. Her decisive action, which comes out of nowhere, is to kill, offstage, a guerrilla leader of whom we have only just heard.

Orenstein, replacing Kelli Fox, is one of two changes from the original cast. The territory has indeed been purged of Foxes, since David Fox has been succeeded by Jerry Franken, his old sparring-partner from The Drawer Boy and elsewhere. A less idiosyncratic actor than his predecessor, Franken makes his constant reappearances as various elders seem less like a running gag, but he throws away one of the plays best speeches in which a long train of reprisals and counter-reprisals is traced back to end precisely nowhere.

That is the plays pithiest point. A woollier one is that civil war is a kind of incest. Cue the Oedipus legend, scrambled and repackaged. But Oedipus wasn't just a victim; he was an actor, who dedicated himself to discovering the truth. Nawal, from beyond the grave, sends her children to discover it, and it proves hideous. She could just as well have told them while she was alive, but maybe she thought sleuthing would be better for their souls. Or maybe it's just so there could be a play. Either way, the generations arrive at a posthumous reconciliation thats purest mush The first-night audience started applauding before this final scene: at best, a sign that the timing is off and at worst, that the audience not only thinks but hopes its over. Still, there was a standing ovation at the real close. I stayed in my seat. I'd hoped that a second viewing would make me like the play more. But it made me like it less.

-Until Sept. 28. Call 416-531-1827 for ticket information.

2008-09-16-he-s-a-bad-man-with-a-good-ac:
Fresh from hunching over the copy of the season premiere of House sent to my home by a cooperative network or two (yes, they make House calls), I have to report that nothing much has changed in the hospitals of New Jersey. Not, at least, in the one that we're concerned with. Dr. Gregory House, he without whom no medical procedure can proceed, is told by his colleague Wilson, who wants to bail on him, you spread misery because you cant feel anything else." Havent people been telling him that ever since this show started?

Someone close to me recently remarked that the principal achievement of House has been to make a whole generation believe that Hugh Laurie is American. For those of us who remember Laurie as Bertie Wooster and other characters almost as ineffably English, that's quite an achievement. It would, after all, have been easy to make House a British genius imported by the North American medical system (I know one or two of those), but they chose the hard way, and it's paid off. Lauries House is believably American. What he isnt is believably human.

This isn't the actor's fault; he deals expertly with what hes given. I was at a social gathering last week at which there were quite a few doctors present. I took the opportunity to ask them what they thought of House, and of medical soaps generally. They seemed to find ER the most realistic in its depiction of hospital routine. None of them were very keen on House. The most important objection I heard was that, in an age of increasing medical specialization, Houses all-round expertise just isn't credible.

House's neuroticism and misanthropy are, of course, supposed to make this show more "serious and adult" than other hospital dramas. In fact, they just make it more pretentious, and therefore more offensive. Weve had shows about gangsters, cops, admen and vampires that have transcended their genres, to become authentically dramatic or authentically comic, sometimes both. But doctors and surgeons, who you would have thought worthy of at least equivalent treatment, are still stuck in the old routine.

Maybe its because their jobs, or public perception of their jobs, make it look too easy. Here are people facing life-and-death situations on a regular basis, so that becomes the formula: a new crisis every week, with the professionals trying to balance these responsibilities with their personal problems, sometimes their personal demons. With House, this has become especially formulaic, because he's all demons. Every show has him being foul to people for half the running time while the rest is taken up by a patient, horribly sick from this week's plot-device gimmick. Tonight, its feminism.

We start with a high-powered lady activist threatening to sue the pants off an all-male boardroom for their dismal record of harassment. Suddenly, her assistant collapses, clutching herself and her clothing while screaming, "I cant get 'em off me. Her boss inquires of the assembled hopeless males, You gonna call an ambulance, or you just gonna sit there and stare?" Somebody, apparently, does dial the right number because next thing we know the patient's in hospital, where shes discovered to be pregnant, and not hysterically. But that isnt half the story, hers or House's.

House, the misogynist's misogynist, takes the opportunity to let off a few zingers about yesterdays sluts being todays empowered women. But he can't give the patient too much face time, because he's trying to stop Wilson from leaving him; its that personal. Wilson is grieving the death of his beloved, for which he may or may not hold House partly responsible. House even refuses to tend to the patient, though of course everyone knows he has the magic bullet, until Wilson changes his mind, which his colleagues call unprofessional and I call unbelievable. I dont care how much the show has invested in his being a bastard. Nobody could say this show spares doctors their own share of suffering, what with Wilson's bereavement and House's terrible limp and their female colleague having been diagnosed with Huntingtons chorea. She confides as much to the patient, who confides right back that her boss is one of those ideologues who treats

her own staff as badly as she accuses her opponents of treating theirs, but that shes a force of nature nonetheless. And we're meant to make the connection that this is how House's staff regard him. Have all the principles you want, but bow down to genius. Its very neat.

Now, its true that House's colleagues talk right back to him, but they're still his stooges, just as the patients are. Hes the one who gets all the good lines, from a snappy, "Im not busy, it's just a euphemism for 'get the hell out of here, " to an extended comparison between grief and Newark as two places you need to drive right past. All right, that last one may not be good, but they clearly took a lot of trouble with it; its the show's idea of style. Maybe it's the scrubbed-clean setting that makes hospital dramas so undramatic; everythings antiseptic, right down to the music that they pipe in to persuade us that emotions are happening. (All network shows do it, but these ones are the worst.) Its insulting to the audience, and to the actors -- as if they weren't trusted to act. Instead they rattle off diagnostic jargon as if they understood it, which by now they very well may. But they can't seem like real physicians, because they can't seem like real people. Is there a doctor in the House?

- House airs tonight at 8 p. m. on Global TV.

2008-09-17-soft-shoe-softies-on-so-you-t:
I dont know where the title of So You Think You Can Dance Canada? gets off being so mocking and derisive. This show proves Canada can dance, or at least the representatives of it who get to appear onscreen. Turning this show on is like tuning into the Olympics; the TV is full of people doing, very well, what most of us could hardly hope to do at all.

Mary Murphy was certainly impressed. One of the trio of judges on last week's opening round, she could hardly control her enthusiasm. Imported from the United States, she sounded as if Canada were a country she had only just discovered and could hardly wait to tell her friends about. "Some of the best dancers on the planet are here!" she squealed. Murphy's appearances on American TV have earned her the title Queen of Scream, a badge, to judge from the way its quoted in her biography, she wears with pride. But it really is more of a squeal than a scream, and its one of the most grating sounds to have emerged from my TV in recent months, rivalled only by Murphy's laugh, which, once started, goes on forever. The crazy thing is that when the former dancer quiets down and says something specific about the talent in front of her, it's on the mark. This despite the fact that neither she nor her two quieter colleagues -- who could hardly help being lower key but seemed equally judicious --had a bad word to say to, or about, anybody. A few of the initial parade of hopefuls had their hopes deliriously realized and were sent directly to the Heaven of the shows finals. A larger number were consigned to Purgatory, otherwise known as Choreography, where they are forced to execute steps other than the ones theyve dreamed up on their own. A very small number -- of those we were allowed to see, anyway -- were damned, meaning sent home and told not to come back. And even they were allowed to depart with encouraging words in their ears.

Compared to American Idol and its derivatives (not that AI isn't derivative itself ), this is a very kind show, low on embarrassment (unless you count Murphy's eruptions) and humiliation. Either the initial screening process had been ruthless at weeding out incompetence, or the producers were charitable about showing it to us. Or maybe having two left feet is a condition more easily acknowledged by the sufferer than being tone deaf. Anyway, everybody we got to see could actually do it. Nearly all the dancing on show was hip hop or something akin. From the casual viewers perspective, the more acrobatic or eccentric the gyrations were the better, since we only saw them in short spurts anyway and could hardly judge things like line or flow. (A lot of the dancing seemed, to this untrained eye, to bear little rhythmic relation to the music it was being done to. That may be one thing that Choreography is supposed to straighten out.) The show is both a celebration of, and made possible by, the return of dancing to the streets. At best, its the everyday made marvellous. One of my own favourite contestants (and, at 28, one of the oldest) was Karl, a scissor-legged performer, who said that dancing had saved him from a life with the gangs, and also that, I got my hip-hop influence from living in the street. I never knew what it was -- I was living it. Then there was Amanda, who appeared in tears because "my dad passed away -- I'm willing to bare my soul to express myself." She duly broke down at her audition, and was voluminously comforted by the judges.

I just wanna come up and give you a hug, Mary said. This is the kind of thing reality TV can't resist, and that one wishes it would. Anyway, Amanda was sent to Choreography -- "not just because your father died" -- but no further, which seemed fair. Honour and sympathy were both satisfied.

So this show belongs, with Triple Sensation and (I hate to admit) How Do You Solve a Problem Like Maria?, at the top end of the talent-show spectrum. It starts with a certain assumption of professionalism. Beyond that, it falls into all the cliches. We get the breathlessly inane narration (because theres nothing to say), the long line of aspirants shown being nervous before the audition and jubilant afterwards. We also get the inescapable fact that, since we see the auditionees for seconds at a time and in endless succession while the judges remain constant, its the latter whom the show ends up being about. But that may change as the concentration narrows. I wonder if, as the season progresses, anyone will get the chance or show the ability to dance slow. Even if the street style could produce an updated equivalent of the tap-dancing Astaire, could it also yield the Fred who danced with Ginger? Maybe that's a demand that will be made in later episodes, when the kids are left to someone else's devices. (Though I have heard it said, and it must be true, that there are far more good dancers than good choreographers.) Maybe the title will become more relevant, and more biting, as the weeks dance on. - The second episode of So You Think You Can Dance Canada airs tonight at 8 p. m. on CTV.

2008-09-20-mournful-mythic-and-middling-:
The Obsidian Theatre Company's new double bill is a conscious attempt to break out of what might be called the ghetto conception of black theatre. One play is a domestic drama in which black actors play contemporary urbanites who might be of any race. The other is an updating of a Greek myth that has been given a specifically black context but one whose geographical location is very far from here. This is a praiseworthy initiative, or pair of initiatives, but neither play is much fun to sit through.

Late, by Marcia Johnson, is about a recently bereaved woman and the new inhabitant of her basement, who's there on a sublet. This rather tenuous relationship needs considerable setting-up, involving flashbacks and a third, intermediary, character who is otherwise superfluous. Donna has been happily married to a jazz pianist whose abrupt departure from her life leads her into a frenzy of reminiscence, mainly concerned with her early-morning routine. Carol, the new arrival, recently abandoned by her own boyfriend, makes it her mission to rescue Donna from her grief, though she seems rather more in need of rescue herself. Anyway, the two of them turn out to be good for one another, though scenes that show it are both cloudy and sketchy.

Meanwhile there's Locksley, Donna's original tenant, who is also a musician and who goes on the road, thereby making room for Carol, until circumstances and an anxious mother conspire to persuade him that " '70s rock can get on without me." He gets some other good lines, plus a hopeless lust for Donna, but he doesn't get or contribute much else, and it's a shock to realize that we're meant to care about him as well as about the two underwritten women. All three characters have to, in some sense, move on, to come to terms with the conflicts between their dreams and their realities, but that's not much to take home.

Johnson is an experienced radio playwright, and her play unfolds in what is now the expected succession of short scenes. This means that we spend much time watching the actors moving furniture in the half-light, to effect changes that don't look all that startling when we get there. The 19th century had heavy scenic realism; the Elizabethans had non-scenic fluidity. We seem to have stuck ourselves with the worst of both worlds and -- more to the point -- the best of neither. We get plays without shape leading, inexorably, to performances with the same deficiency. Marjorie Chan's direction is pretty lax in terms of what it lets its actors get away with. Sabryn Rock has an attractively world-weary presence as Donna, but there is little sense that she and Edwige Jean-Pierre, a querulous Carol, are conducting a conversation, let alone a relationship. Each strikes an attitude and then waits for the other to strike hers. The general effect, in all departments, is of something well-meaning but shallow.

The mythic Medea was a woman who killed her children to spite her husband. Euripides, the first playwright to tell this story, was able to mask its lack of endearingness by not allowing us too close a look at the kids. Wesley Enoch's Black Medea boldly begins by letting us not only see, but hear the child (only one in this version), a recognizably modern boy who, in a clever touch, is playing with a model of a boat, an ancient Greek trireme. We brace ourselves to feel the horrors of the tale as we have never felt them before. But by the time, the actual infanticide rolls around, we don't care, having long lost touch with recognizable reality.

Or at least with any that we could recognize without more help than we're given. Black Medea is an Australian play, rooted in Australian Aboriginal culture. This Medea is a woman from a remote settlement who defies local tradition to marry a Jason who lives and thrives in the outside world. Eventually he proves unfaithful: not in the specific, shabby-but-motivated fashion of his classical prototype but by dallying with unspecified "sluts." The social gradations, the different worlds from which Medea and Jason have sprung and in which they both have to live, are never filled in. In fact, after a tight couple of scenes in which past and present do seem to be illuminating one another, the play, as directed by Philip Akin, just about abandons drama and falls back on incantation. A two-woman chorus comes on, to lure Medea back to the magical world from which she has descended and she -- well, she either regresses or she finds her true spiritual self, depending on how you want to look at it. The upshot seems to be that it's all right to murder your son, providing you paint your face before doing it.

The chorus rather lost me, but I think that at one point I heard them talking about a man "raping his mother," which sounds like the wrong myth. Any countervailing argument is muffled by a text that presents Jason as an opportunist wife-beater, and a performance (by Lindsay Owen Pierre) that carries no conviction even on that level. Medea, denied the clever plotting of the original, isn't even allowed the dignity of her own murderousness; she's more victim than avenger, and Audrey Dwyer's initially powerful performance eventually --or not so eventually --becomes monotonous. Black Medea is a more impressive piece than its companion (though I'm tempted to put "impressive" in quotes) but it's also more boring You may know the feeling.

- Late and Black Medea run through Oct. 5 at the Berkeley Street Theatre Upstairs. Call 416-368-3110 for tickets and information.

2008-09-22-escaped-crusaders-the-heroes-:
Since Heroes concerns a new breed of superheroes -- inexplicably gifted creatures who agonize about their powers -- a bit of navel-gazing on the genre as a whole may be in order. I'd say that it has gone, within living memory, through three different stages.

In the 1930s, when people could certainly use some reassurance, there was the classic era of comic books and motion-picture serials. This persisted well into the '50s, when the comics were still being published and the serials were turning up on TV and at what my generation called Saturday morning pictures." We got involved in the stories, just as folks in the Depression used to do, in the sense that we were excited over what would happen next, but we never seriously expected Superman or Captain Marvel to materialize and solve our problems for us.

Scroll on, and we get to a more devoutly unserious time, the era of Camp, in which the old icons are resurrected on TV and in movies to be simultaneously mocked and celebrated -- or maybe mocked before theyre celebrated. How, these productions implicitly inquired, could people ever have believed such junk? (The answer of course is that they didnt.)

And now, in a new Dark Age that I suppose we have to trace back to 9/11, but that also has something to do with the internet's enormous utility as a facilitator of cults, we have a brave new race of superheroes with identity crises. If Clark Kent had ever grown tired of donning his cape, we would have known what to tell him: Make all your phone calls from the office. But the heroes of Heroes, spread out across the world and largely unknown to one another, have problems less easily solved, problems both psychological and physiological. And we're being asked to take them seriously, and even to care about them. The long-form TV serial, a gift to world culture but easily abused, practically demands that we do.

Heroes kicks off its third season tonight with a two-hour special. Ive only been trusted with the first hour, so theres a limit to the amount of spoiling I can do. But I can reveal that we start with what looks at first blush like a routine political assassination (routine in TV terms, that is) but turns out to be a benevolent warning shot fired across the bows of New York Congressman Nathan Petrelli who may be about to abuse his powers on a scale of which most politicians could only dream. In the course of the hour, Nathan finds God and gives a TV interview in church. This attracts the attention of a really corrupt politician, of the worst kind: I mean the kind who's never seen without a bimbo girlfriend. This palooka plainly thinks he can use Nathan. I don't think he knows what hes getting into.

Meanwhile, in another part of the city and of the plot, theres Suresh who, in the bet-hedging words of Wikipedia, "does not have any known super-powers and has to make do with plain old scientific genius. This could take him far; he manages to isolate the gene that distinguishes super-humanity. This is something really new: a biological explanation for superheroes. You see what the show is trying to do? It's trying to domesticate these guys (and gals). It's giving them backstories, and real adversaries. No more saving mythical cities called Gotham from mythical villains called the Joker. The bad people here are a Company, probably identical to the one that Michael Scofield, with his comparatively limited abilities, is simultaneously trying to bring down on the same network. Holy conspiracies, Batman.

With all this solemnity going on, its no wonder that Heroes cant afford a sense of humour. Well, it almost can't. Over in Japan, there's the very engaging Hiro, a millionaires son and heir, proving that lines like I dont need a fleet of corporate jets -- I can teleport" are much funnier when they come at you as sub-titles. I wonder if the same treatment would benefit such hardboiled epigrams from the other hemisphere as "It's all behind me now, like a long night after a bad taco." You have to wonder how the actors on shows as badly written as this keep their faces straight. The closest thing to a central character, cheerleader Claire Bennett, has the gift of immortality (that's a plot point, not an aesthetic judgment), which is a real suspense killer. And yet Heroes tries to operate as a thriller. Of course it's billed as fantasy, but it taps into a desperate need to believe in something that will save us from ourselves. That's something new in the genre, and a bit creepy. The 1930s were even harder times. But its consumers seem to have had harder heads. - The season premiere of Heroes airs tonight at 9 p. m. on Global.

2008-09-26-fighting-the-good-clean-fight:
With a mildly rude song giving its ironic all on the soundtrack, a comfortable-looking middle-aged lady rides a bike with a basket along a provincial English street, looking like a benign version of Miss Gulch from The Wizard of Oz. She is actually Mrs. Mary Whitehouse, a morality crusader who flourished in Britain from the early 1960s right through until her death in 2001. And her opponents did indeed regard her as the reincarnation of the Wicked Witch of the West. Or, more accurately, of the Midlands.

The chief object of the Whitehouse wrath, at least in her earlier years, was the BBC. The Beeb, in what looks initially like a classic example of turning the other cheek but turns out not to be, has made her the subject of a dramatized film, cheerily entitled Filth. "This story took place," say the titles, "only with more swearing and less nudity." That's a teaser in more senses than one; the actual show has no nudity but it does have swearing. It begins pretty much as a cartoon: Mary exchanging friendly words with the local vicar, Mary cycling home, Mary pouring tea for her family when an early-evening discussion of pre-marital sex comes on the TV, taking her so completely by surprise that she drops the pot. At this point the show seems to be both trivializing and patronizing Whitehouse, treating her as a dear out-of-touch old thing, thereby underrating both her and the forces she opposed and provoked.

But it soon begins to dig deeper. We see Mary as a teacher (quite a good one, it seems) genuinely concerned for her students, upset that they're upset. Mary and her husband, a postman named Ernest, are played by Julie Walters and Alun Armstrong, two of the most endearing actors on God's Earth. Armstrong, especially, is a treasure, as a loving, supportive, quietly humorous partner both spurring his wife on and reining her in. (He points out that Clean Up National Television, her original name for her campaign, could give rise to an acrimonious acronym.) The Whitehouses are the only characters whom we actually see having sex: a joke that resonates on any number of levels. They certainly have a better marriage than their archenemy Sir Hugh Carleton Greene (Hugh Bonneville). Sir Hugh, brother of Graham (the novelist, not the actor), director general of the BBC at its most permissive period, treats his family with foul-mouthed casualness and ends up divorced. He's no more endearing at the office, ogling two successive secretaries and greeting their departures to get married as tiresome interruptions of his routine and without even token words of congratulation.

He refers to Mrs. Whitehouse as "that woman" and refuses to meet with her: a tactical error at the very least, since it quickly becomes obvious

that she has a sizeable constituency. He also refuses to allow her air time, though it's pointed out to him that if you're against censorship, you really shouldn't be censoring your opponents. His social life revolves around clubs and cricket matches. He is the cultural elitist of Stephen Harper's dreams.

But not so fast. The cunning of Amanda Coe's script is that, though it gives us plenty of reason to like Mrs. Whitehouse and plenty of reason to dislike Sir Hugh, it ends up leaving us in no doubt that she was wrong and he was right. The turning point for her is a public meeting at Birmingham Town Hall that she approaches in terror and exits in triumph. Present at the meeting is a young playwright whose radio play she's attacked. He asks for right of reply. She says that he's already had his time (fair point) by writing his filthy play (unfair abuse, shutting down debate). He responds by savagely lampooning her in a TV series called Swizzlewick. "Good show" says Sir Hugh, adding sotto voce, "pity it wasn't funny."

And so, for Mary, it hubristically goes: What starts as a reasonable desire to protect children from subject matter for which they may not be ready progresses into a desire to eradicate the mention, if not the actual existence, of any word or idea she finds personally disagreeable. (She asks Ernest, incredulously, if he can imagine such a thing as oral sex. His wistful silence suggests that he can.) She keeps tabs on the number of times the word "bloody" occurs in Till Death Us Do Part (progenitor of All in the Family). And it isn't just sex and language. It is, as always, religion and politics. She can't abide to see Christianity mocked or even criticized; she's shocked that the satirical show That Was the Week that Was ( The Daily Show without the underlying moral fervour but incredibly liberating in its day) should be lampooning the (Conservative) prime minister. She also gets around to attacking sci-fi violence in Dr. Who and -- in a semi-apocryphal incident that anticipates James Dobson's attack on Teletubbies -- deploring the lack of respect shown by the puppets on a kids' show towards their human co-stars. Generations of ventriloquists oppressed by their dummies must have risen up and cheered.

When Filth was aired in the U. K., a poster on the Times website summed Mary up perfectly: "too proper to enjoy vulgarity and too vulgar to enjoy anything else." And the film doesn't have to defend Greene personally: Merely by mentioning some of the shows that she attacked and he championed (there were many others) it reminds us that he presided over a golden age of television. Other responses to the show have said that Whitehouse would have been appalled by today's television, the game shows and the degradation. So she would; and so would Greene. But it's far more her legacy than his. It's the free market in action. The film concludes with Mary standing triumphantly outside the hallowed portals of Broadcasting House, the BBC's Central London HQ, about to receive an audience with a new director general who recognizes her existence. It's the beginning of an end.

- Filth: The Mary Whitehouse Story airs Sunday at 9 p. m. on TVO

2008-09-27-where-sultry-songs-don-t-fear:
I feel some trepidation in writing this, since I'm personally involved, but I'm greatly looking forward to next week's Canwest Cabaret Festival at the Young Centre. I've spent some of the happiest evenings of my life watching and listening to singers and songs in intimate surroundings, preferably with drinks available. It's an experience that's been hard to come by in Toronto in recent years; it exists, but you have to go digging for it. So it's heartening that there should be four days of the stuff, featuring some of Canada's performers, in a prime downtown location.

For 19 years now there's been an annual event in New York called the Cabaret Convention, a series of concerts mainly devoted to what's become known as the Great American Songbook: golden-age Broadway songs, Cole Porter, Gershwin, that brand of thing. (It's named after Mabel Mercer, the New York singer who epitomized that kind of repertoire in that sort of cafe setting.) During the first Convention, I sat on a panel on which we tried to determine what cabaret actually was. It became clear that for a lot of people, it meant mainly the title of a film; this was before the show on which the movie was based came back in revival glory. And beyond that, it meant, and continues to mean, the whole legend of louche, satirical Berlin nightclubs that the musical, somewhat freely, evokes. Well, that's if your fancy is German; if it's French the word "cabaret" is likelier to evoke Edith Piaf, Charles Aznavour and Jacques Brel. In the United States, and I think in most of the English-speaking world it's come to mean that Broadway catalogue and its extensions. In England, obviously, Noel Coward. In Canada, some of the later troubadours writing in the enigmatic confessional mode. Joni Mitchell, perhaps. Or Leonard Cohen.

Cohen (Oct. 2-3) is one of three composers featured in the Cabaret Festival's Songbook evenings: a trio of tributes, playing two performances each, alongside the less formal solo shows that make up the bulk of the programming, and covering between them quite a few waterfronts. Cohen, with his man-in-black mordancy, connects with the poet-as-singer traditions of Berlin and Paris, but also with the North American pop maestros of the '60s and after. In pop, but not quite of it, although -- like so many of the older American songwriters -- Jewish. With a twist: I don't know how many American songs there are called Hallelujah -- hundreds probably -- but there can't be any others this sardonic. Patricia O'Callaghan will be singing it, along with (among other things) one of those oddly yearning Cohen songs, Take this Waltz. Steven Page (one singer-songwriter saluting another), does the famous Famous Blue Raincoat and -- what may be the ultimate uncompromising title -- A Singer Must Die. Major Cohen love songs on parade include Dance Me to the End of Love from Maryem Tollar, and I'm Your Man from Sarah Slean. (I was surprised too.) Andrew Whiteman (Apostle of Hustle) rounds out the bill with some of the more biblical titles: Waiting for the Miracle and Waters of Babylon.

If there's a place where jazz intersects with cabaret, and even with show tunes, it's in the songs of Duke Ellington (Oct. 5). Ellington's Harlem was its own cabaret: metaphorically and, in the first years of his bandleading career at the Cotton Club, literally as well. Ellington, whose wide-ranging musical showmanship deserves the appellation of "total theatre" that he himself bestowed on Frank Sinatra, ran in effect his own repertory company, bringing out the compositional best in many of his instrumentalists as well as in himself. The Duke's arranger and alter ego Billy Strayhorn was responsible for at least two of the most achingly lovely tunes in the Ellington book, Something to Live For and Chelsea Bridge, both to be sung (though I don't think the latter has an official lyric) by Ada Lee. Strayhorn also wrote the startlingly precocious saloon song Lush Life, to be sung by Mary Margaret O'Hara, and the Ducal theme-tune Take the "A" Train, to be done by singer-pianist John Alcorn, along with the Ellington-Strayhorn Satin Doll.

There are plenty of songs, though, with music by Ellington alone: the matched pair of Don't Get Around Much Anymore and Do Nothin' Till You Hear from Me, both instrumentals are fitted out with flavourful lyrics. They're to be sung by Don Francks, a Canadian cabaret institution, along with I Got It Bad, conceivably the most famous Ellington song and one of the few that actually originated in a show -- as, surprisingly, did the zany Bli-Blip, to be sung by the evening's emcee, Andrew Craig. One of my own favourites, Take Love Easy, also originated in a show, albeit a different one. The song is being done by the great Jackie Richardson and it's from Beggar's Holiday, a Broadway update of The Beggar's Opera.

Which brings us to Kurt Weill (Oct. 4), whose Threepenny Opera was the greatest of such rewrites and who may sum up the world, or worlds, of cabaret more completely than any other composer. In his collaborations with Bertolt Brecht, he was Weimar Berlin. In the 1940s, he was Broadway, at its most adventurous, collaborating with writers from Langston Hughes to Ira Gershwin via Ogden Nash. In both those modes (and in a Parisian period between), he bequeathed whole sheaves of songs to a breed of intense recitalists whom Brecht's daughter once described to me as "all those ladies in black." Did the German and American Weills have anything in common? Well, to be superficial about it, they both wrote showcase songs about ladies called Jenny: the baleful Pirate Jenny, with Brecht, giving way to the cheerfully admonitory Saga of Jenny ("don't make up your mind") with Gershwin. Patricia O'Callaghan will sing both, as well as the Brechtian Bilbao-Song and Alabama Song, the latter in duet with Mary Margaret O'Hara who'll also perform the haunting Lonely House from Weill's Broadway opera Street Scene. Mike Ross salutes the Broadway Weill with two songs from his Nash collaboration One Touch of Venus, the famous Speak Low and the less famous but terrific I'm a Stranger Here Myself. The French Weill gets more of a look-in than is usual on these occasions from Sara Slean who also sings Lost in the Stars, a song that's practically become an anthem. Once again the emcee sings, in this case John Millard, presenting Weill at his most savage (Army Song) and most mellow (September Song). And there is every possibility that Albert Schultz, the festival's overall director, will reprise some of his Macheath numbers from Threepenny.

One more thing: Cabaret is a notoriously ephemeral art, literally flying by night. So if any of these promised songs fails to materialize, sue me. But it won't hold up in court. - Robert Cushman will be hosting the Songbook evenings at the Canwest Cabaret Festival.

2008-09-29-lifestyles-of-the-smug-and-ve:
The new season of Californication begins with David Duchovny, as our hero Hank, getting in his last round of rubberized sex before departing to the hospital for the vasectomy he promised his girlfriend. Scratch that: the vasectomy he promised his girlfriend he would have. The procedure turns out to have more complications than he'd anticipated, and he spends the rest of the episode in pain and telling everyone about it. The comic climax, if thats the word I want, occurs when he goes down on a woman in a darkened room at a party, and finds that he is servicing the wrong body. Its owner, naked, pursues him through the house, claiming that he violated her. Hank protests that he isnt "a rapey guy. And indeed, why would he be, given the way women throw themselves at him and his unbuttoned shirt, whether he's in a supermarket or at a social gathering? And I know this is Hollywood, geographically as well as generically, but this man is supposed to be a writer. In your dreams, script guys.

Duchovny plays Hank very believably, but that's part of the problem. I dont want to believe in him. Californication is the un-cool version of Curb Your Enthusiasm. Not that it doesnt try very hard to be cool, but that's also part of the problem. Larry David's show brings off the considerable feat of making you share a rich mans contempt for his surroundings, mainly by equating him with the people hes satirizing. The last thing Larry does is let himself off the hook; he's right there, wriggling. You aren't supposed to like him, merely to believe in him. Hank you are meant to love despite everything, much as his long-suffering partner Karen does. Californication is set among Los Angeles somewhat less rich and famous (they certainly arent at Larry's success level), and it makes a show of laughing at their smugness and venality. But it's drenched in envy of the sunshine life.

Season One ended with Hank and Karen eloping from her wedding to someone else. (Where have I encountered that romantic scenario before? Several places, but the Niles-Daphne plotline from Frasier comes most immediately to mind.) Season

Two picks up from there. Not only are Hank and Karen plainly made for one another, they have a 13-year old daughter to prove it: wise, or at least cynical, beyond her years and with a zombie voice. Which, given that she has to say I love L. A." with a straight face, is probably helpful. Karen (Natascha McElhone) is the only likeable person on the show, and much too good for her man; which admittedly is the normal state of affairs in romantic comedy (which is what Californication seems to think it is). Hank is supposed to be more honest than most of the people he mixes with, and he is probably smarter, but he remains the stereotype of a mixed-up artist, unable to resist temptation sexual, alcoholic or narcotic.

Californication -- did the show come into being because somebody thought of that pun, and had to find a peg for it? -- has been assailed by morality groups (especially in Australia and New Zealand, for some reason) but that doesnt mean its good. In fact, the protesters have an aesthetic point, whether or not they know it. Once we have grasped that the characters have sex and do drugs a lot, pausing only to compare notes, the show has nowhere to go. It takes more than sex to make a good sex farce; it takes ingenuity. Wit helps, too. As, frankly, does a feeling of guilt, which permissiveness tends to rule out -- though not completely, because jealousy can manifest itself in the most liberated of circumstances. Californication does touch on that, but mainly it's content to get high on its own audacity. To give us a little more to chew on, Hank is equipped with writers' block as well as a writers conscience; both are challenged this season when hes handed the opportunity to ghostwrite the memoirs of a music mogul. This may at least enable him to help his agent, it's generally believed, of course, that it's the agents job to help the client. but this one needs all the help he can get, being a personal and professional mess. I wouldnt dream of spoiling, but I will reveal that Hank's shenanigans in Episode One lead in Episode Two to his being obliged to call his agent's cell from a cell, the penal kind. Also that it contains one of the saddest, if not the most original, of lines: "I love you too, but what if thats not enough? Karen says that. She also says that the infuriating magic of Hank is that you can never stay mad at him for long." Its a cop out for the show to be telling us that, even if it's true. Especially if it's true. I was railing at House last week, but I'll give it this: You can stay mad at House, and nobody ever pretends different. - The season premiere of Californication airs tonight at 9 p. m. on TMN.

2008-09-30-all-the-stage-is-an-alleyway:
THEATRE REVIEW

The Crackwalker

Theatre Passe Muraille Backspace

Twenty-eight years on, Judith Thompson's first notable play stands up very well. The Crackwalker is a tragedy of the urban and marginalized, one that unlike later entries in the genre -- including some of Thompsons own -- never condescends to its characters or treats them as prepackaged ingredients in some political or metaphorical stew. The play is a social indictment, but it grants its people free will and watches compassionately as they abuse it.

There are four active characters and a fifth on the sidelines. This is the Crackwalker himself, an ambiguously named (crack cocaine? falling between the cracks?) homeless man who haunts the dreams of the others and sometimes intersects with their realities. He is what any of them might become. He falls just short, or breaks just free, of being a symbol. Michael Murphys production for the Staged and Confused company, which specializes in Canadian revivals, does a fine job of keeping the Crackwalker constantly on the fringes of the action and of everybody's consciousness, whether he's roaming a catwalk to the side of the main acting area or stumbling onto the stage itself. He gives the play an outer shape.

The inner shape is largely determined by the brief blossoming and steep decline of Theresa and Alan. Theresa, somewhat mentally challenged, is blessed or cursed with emotional amnesia. Her chief means of support is prostitution; she takes up unwelcomed residence on her best friends sofa. Marie Jones plays her with a powerful mixture of innocence and defiance, unshakably fixated on the next good and invariably passing thing.

One of those things is Alan, more intelligent but equally unable to cope: indeed, with fewer defences. He alternates between gentleness and rage, the latter fuelled by the memory of what the system, doctors especially, did to his father. He and Theresa marry, on what seems like a whim, and even more ill-advisedly, have a child. (Alan angrily rejects social services advice that Theresa should have her tubes tied.)

What happens to them and their baby is painful to watch, the more so if you've seen the play before and know what's coming. But it isnt sensational; theres a deep vein of pity caused by the fact that both parents are acting as lovingly as they know how. Rick Jon Egan doesn't quite capture the deep-seated paternal tenderness

that makes Alan both affecting and disturbing, but in all other respects he's admirable, a lanky vulnerable figure straight off the streets.

Its a peculiarity -- actually a weakness -- of the play that it sets up four principal characters and then largely neglects two of them. Alans friend and unwilling host (Hannah Miller) is contrastingly capable, except for being unable to break away from an abusive partner who is also Alan's partner in petty crime. (Craig Pike comes on in this role like a nice young actor uncertain of his surroundings and trying too hard.)

There is something pat and predictable about this second relationship; its participants are reduced to playing chorus to the central drama, rather than being co-equal with it. Nor, in this production at least, do the quartet's rare moments of peaceful co-existence function as the points of rest for which they were presumably intended. There are holes in the pattern. But the main threads are very strong. Very little has changed in our cities since the play was written, and the production doesn't have to strain very hard to remind us of that. But even if it had, the story of Alan and Theresa, and even the Crackwalker himself, would still strike home. - The Crackwalker runs until Oct. 11. For tickets and information, call 416-504-7529.

2008-10-01-assimilation:
Season Two of Little Mosque of the Prairie had what its producers are pleased to describe as a cliffhanger ending: Would Rayann accept or reject a marriage proposal from JJ? Carlo Rota, who plays Rayann's dad Yasir, is also, of course, a familiar face on 24, a coincidence that throws into sharp relief Little Mosque's rather undemanding standards when it comes to hanging from cliffs.

Still, suspense is holy, and I've been requested not to defile any of it by giving stuff away. This makes discussion of tonight's Season Three premiere a little delicate, but I'll do my best. The episode has two comic mainsprings. One is the jealous impulse of Amaar, the young Imam, to make his friend and roommate JJ look bad. The other is the inability of Yasir, who will obviously never make a TV previewer, to keep his mouth shut about information that his wife Sarah would like to dispense for herself.

I hope I've been discreet enough.

In any event, both plot-threads could be charitably described as gentle and accurately described as tame. These qualities have their place, and though Little Mosque has never been much on laughs (there are none tonight), it is capable of summoning smiles. But they're built on a weak foundation. There's the name for a start. It's no coincidence that the funniest fictions on television -- Seinfeld, The Simpsons, Frasier, all the way back to The Burns and Allen Show -- have generally had the simplest declarative titles. Little Mosque's title rivals Californication in the cuteness stakes; it settles for nudging allusion rather than wholesale theft. Put your premise in your title, and you're signalling that you have an idea so outrageous that it will do the rest of the work for you. This is rash. Premises are merely promises. If they're to be kept, they have to be worked on. And the premise of Little Mosque has proved, partly for honourable reasons, more self-cancelling than most.

There is the idea, built into that title, that there is something inherently incongruous in the idea of a flourishing Muslim community in a small Canadian prairie town. Balancing that, there is the desire to show that Muslims are just like anyone else, and thus deserving of a sitcom that's just like any other. The latter impulse is the one that's won out. The comedy of culture-clash -- and, more subtly, of clashes within a culture -- hasn't quite vanished but it has faded, leaving generic storylines in which the women just happen to have their heads covered.

On that basic TV comedy level, it's low energy. If it has the Canadian virtue of restraint, it has the Canadian vice of pokeyness. There are two peaks in tonight's episode. One involves Sarah finding an unexpected new recruit for her book club: a nice moment for Sheila McCarthy, who does downbeat really well, unlike some of her colleagues who tend to beat you over the head with how subtle they're being. The other has Yasir intruding on the studio of a redneck radio host; it has a punchline -- actually a punch-visual -- that's predictable but still sort of satisfying. Also it's potentially fruitful to see a Muslim character interacting with someone who does not, in principle, like him. This is rare on a show in which, for example, church and mosque get on like a couple of holy houses on fire. That, to be sure, is an admirable sign of the times. But it isn't very dramatic, and therefore not very comic. Comedy has traditionally ended with reconciliation, but it's supposed to be a hard-won fight. Assimilation, when you think about it, is almost the opposite of funny. - Season Three of Little Mosque on the Prarie begins tonight at 8 p. m. on CBC.
