2008-10-03-a-comeback-with-kick:
THEATRE REVIEW

FOLLIES: IN CONCERT

Festival Theatre, Niagara-on-the-Lake

---

I am lucky enough to have seen the original production of Follies in 1971 and unlucky enough to have seen it only once. It marked the zenith of any number of talents: composer-lyricist Stephen Sondheim, librettist James Goldman, director and producer Harold Prince, co-director and choreographer Michael Bennett, designer Boris Aronson and many others, including maybe the finest collection of actors, singers and dancers ever assembled on Broadway. The performers weren't all equally good in all departments, but each was superb where it counted, with the acting in particular the best I had seen in any musical up to that time.

There were 51 in that original cast, which is one reason why the show can never be properly revived, which in turn is why we fortunate ones alternately gloat and grieve over our memories. Follies' afterlife has been in cut down, sometimes extensively re-written editions, including one devised for concert performance: actors at music-stands and some token staging. This is the version that the Shaw Festival is mounting for four performances this season. Its limitations are obvious and inescapable. All the same, this is the most satisfying Follies, the most enjoyable and the most moving, I have seen since that first one.

Follies is actually about two kinds of follies: Ziegfeld and human. A theatre that served as home for one of those inter-war series of spectacular revues is about to be torn down, and the former producer is throwing the closing-night party to end them all. Former stars and former showgirls turn up in force:Among them two chorines from the 1940s, Phyllis and Sally, and their respective husbands (and former stage-door johnnies), Ben and Buddy. Ben is "the famous Benjamin Stone," writer and politician; Buddy is Buddy, travelling salesman for an oil company. Before their marriages, Ben had a fling with Sally, and 30 years later she is still fixated on him. The strands and implications of this cat's cradle are revealed in a retrospective song, Waiting for the Girls Upstairs, that even for Sondheim is a tour-de-force of accumulated evocative detail set to an accelerated soft-shoe rhythm; the tour becomes even more forceful when, halfway through the number, the characters' younger selves appear to act out their memories. Most of the characters, major or minor, have these youthful doubles, as past and present, nostalgia and disillusion, rub up against one another. Valerie Moore's Shaw production brings out these interactions very well -- I'd forgotten how powerful the moments are when a protagonist's old self turns on his or her young one, each blaming the other for past mistakes and present betrayals.

Another wonderful memento is the orchestral sound: Paul Sportelli has a full complement of musicians on stage (the pit would be too small) to render this score as it was meant to be heard; indeed, of all the show's original participants, the one best-served here may be orchestrator Jonathan Tunick, whose work is ear-tingling. He had of course an extraordinary score to work with, one in which contemporary expressions of angular angst are juxtaposed with word-and-note-perfect tributes to the old Broadway masters, each given a dramatic or psychological tweak. (The difference between the period pastiches of Chicago and of Follies is that those in the former never advance beyond the initial joke while those in the latter explore.)

Moore is a choreographer, but there's no way in these circumstances that she can begin to equal the point or the excitement of the original dances. Who's That Woman, the "mirror number" that just about sums up the show, is virtually meaningless. Even in the solo songs, there's a limit to how much someone can move around at a lectern. But some of the limitations are made to work: Static staging-- the participants in a scene a whole stage apart, points up the emotional distances that the piece is about.

There's one performance that's a musical and dramatic triumph: Glynis Ranney's Sally, affectionate, vulnerable, disturbed and offering the best rendition of In Buddy's Eyes I have ever heard. It's a shame that this version (like all the revisions, though less than some) softens the book material, especially at the end, which should find Sally catatonic. George Masswohl's Ben is authoritative and intelligent, Jay Turvey's Buddy proficient but lightweight. As Phyllis, Melanie Janzen is over-parted, lacking the woman's New York smarts and depleting Could I Leave You, the most devastatingly sardonic show-tune ever written, of its wit, its shape and its anger. Anger, however, makes an unexpected and very effective appearance in Goldie Semple's delivery of the show-stopping survivor's anthem I'm Still Here.

Her role as a perennial ex-star now consists entirely of that song; this text cuts all her dialogue and, here as elsewhere, every cut hurts. The show as conceived may be a third kind of folly, of the grand architectural kind. It needs its size to drive home its over-arching metaphor in which the death of old show business signifies the death of the American dream. You may not quite believe it (did audiences in the '30s really take the everlasting-love-at-first-sight stuff as words to live by?) but you have to believe the show believes it. What we have at the Shaw isn't enough, but it's a lot. Whatever your memories or lack of them, enjoy. And suffer. - Follies: In Concert closes tonight. Call 1-800-511-SHAW for information.

Color Photo: Mark Callan / If this makes you nostalgic for 1971, hightail it to the Shaw Festival! ;; Caption:
2008-10-09-a-fabulous-idea-kath-and-kim-:
The world could use a good and silly new sitcom, and Kath and Kim will more than do. Its drawn preliminary comparisons to Absolutely Fabulous; it isn't on that level, but then few things are.

Like AbFab, Kath and Kim is about a fractious relationship between a mother and daughter. The British show gave us a ditzy mom and her straitlaced offspring. This American one (based on a hit Australian series, hence doubly derivative) gives us two generations both alike in fecklessness. They are in fact in competition, a conflict less rich in possibilities but holding up well over the first two episodes. How well it can sustain is another thing.

Kath (Molly Shannon) is the mother, in her forties, divorced and dating. Kim (Selma Blair) is the daughter, twentyish, just married and already wanting out. Kim, in the opening moments of the pilot, arrives on Kath's doorstep, claiming that her husband has told her to "do things." Sexual things? asks Kath, interested. No, says Kim, he told me to cook dinner. (It later transpires that hed requested her to pop something in the microwave.) This isnt Kim's idea of being a trophy wife, which is apparently what she thought she was. She's miffed too that Kath, who is intent on staying in shape, has changed what was Kims bedroom into a miniature gym, throwing out all Kims possessions, including her collection of Care Bears. Soon afterwards, Kim's husband, a meek young man named Craig, arrives to reclaim her. "I'm putting my foot down", he says, but spoils it by adding, Please? He then tries blackmail: "If I go through that door, you wont see me again." Kim points out that this is unlikely, as the door is glass.

Craig works at the mall, in an electrical appliance outlet. Phil, who is Kaths boyfriend-going-on-fiance and truly adores her, also works in the mall. He's the proprietor of Phil's Sandwich Outlet, and theres a plot complication when he spots Kath eating a wrap at a rival establishment. The last Australian thing I saw, the stage play The Blonde, the Brunette and the Vengeful Redhead, also concerned jealousy, indeed outright mayhem, in a mall. Message: If youre Down Under, stay out of food courts.

Anyway, it's all very fitting, as Kath and Kim seem to spend most of their lives in malls. (Neither seems to have a job.) They're aggressively superficial. They live to shop, and also to eat. And to be admired. Kim is well up, too, on celebrity lore, remarking that if Britney Spears and Melanie Griffith could leave abusive relationships, then so can she. (Question: When did celebrities and performers become synonymous? Even today, its still possible to be famous for other things.) Kath seems a trifle more, shall we say, ironic about the celeb thing, saying at one point that she doesnt intend to be Catherine Zeta-Jonesed, which is quite hard to say.

And it can get quite witty: When Kim looks up from her magazine to announce that the stars are holding a rally against global warming, Kath murmurs, "How brave." And this time she isn't being ironic.

The shared narcissistic values of Kath and Kim reinforce my own grizzled conviction that nothing has changed in popular culture since the '80s, bar the odd dance step. This, in any but the most obvious sense, reduces the comic potential. I probably shouldnt push the AbFab comparison too hard, but the point of that show was that the Jennifer Saunders character was continuing to peddle a myth of the 60s that was long past its sell-by date. There was almost a moral element to the conflict between her and her daughter. Here Kim seems to be combining the roles of both daughter and spaced-out best friend, Joanna Lumley and Julia Sawalha. And Ab-Fab even had a third generation, the grandmother, making it even richer. If Kath has a mother, we've yet to hear about her. Also, the men in Absolutely Fabulous were marginal. In Kath and Kim they're front and centre, with the men, unusually in comedy, rather too good for the women (though presumably dumb for caring about them). I have a feeling that there's a lot of romance in this show, and that we're going to see both Kath and Kim bouncing back and forth between partners: a series of returns that could rapidly prove diminishing. So far, however, so pretty good. - Kath and Kim debuts tonight at 8:30 on E! and NBC.

2008-10-11-after-the-happily-ever-after:
The Tarragon's Extra Space has been twice blessed this year. At the beginning, it housed Hannah Moscovitch's East of Berlin; now, in a guest production by Joel Greenberg's Studio 180, we have Paul Dunn's Offensive Shadows, two thirds of which amount to the best new writing, and some of the best acting and direction, to have turned up since then.

The remaining third looks like an attempt to transform a piece that at 55 minutes was the deserved hit of last year's Summerworks into some-thing more befitting a full night out. It's ill-advised. Dunn's play is a riff on A Midsummer Night's Dream, and it takes its title from Puck's last speech to the audience: "If we shadows have offended/Think but this and all is mended." Puck himself, though, had no part in Dunn's original which focused on Shakespeare's four lovers -- Hermia and Lysander, Helena and Demetrius -- suggesting what they might have been like before their mixed-up night in the wood and speculating on what might have happened to them after it.

That's all still there, but first we get a little bit of Puck. His last lines in Shakespeare -- "Give me your hands if we be friends/And Robin shall restore amends" --are his first lines here, and he follows them up with a more recent but still classic paraphrase: "Clap hands if you believe in fairies." That's an equivalence I'd never noticed before, and it's also fun. He then embarks on a long monologue whose burden is that, in fact, people no longer believe in fairies, and that's bad, and it's all the fairies' fault. Specifically, it's Oberon's fault; Puck doesn't like his boss much, making it clear that he's a tyrannical and unappreciative employer as well as, to Titania, a louse of a spouse. Much of what this "rock-star fairy" tells us amounts to a jaundiced synopsis of the original story; to this Puck adds an account of what humanity has come to in the subsequent millennia, during which time its taken its cue from that tiresome old rationalist Theseus -- he who equated lunatics, lovers and poets. The consequences seem to have included global warming: cf. Titania's "forgeries of jealousy" aria, in which fairy quarrels were held responsible for the terrible weather people were having. That too was a topical speech in its time.

Andrew Kushnir plays Puck with some flair, greater energy, and a progressively diminishing store of rhythmic resource. But then he's stuck with a monotonous text that's increasingly reliant on undermining any lyrical expectations with a string of disgruntled four-letter words. Well, Puck it. It feels like padding.

It also doesn't fit, intellectually or chronologically, with the excellent stuff that follows. Dunn's original picks up from where Shakespeare's left off, not from unnumbered centuries later. It's true that his young quartet look, talk and behave like modern teenagers, but this is the case -- well, maybe not the talking part -- in many modern productions. His achievement is to show how exactly the parts fit. He gives us the back-story in a series of reminiscing monologues. We learn that, crudely put, Helena was the school slut and Hermia the school virgin, Demetrius a nerd and Lysander a jock. That's more differentiation than Shakespeare gave them, the men especially, but it's perfectly consistent with what he did tell us. It seems that Hermia was going with Demetrius, in a bored sort of way and with parental approval, until she set eyes on Lysander; Demetrius, on the rebound, had a one-time fling with Helena who proceeded to stalk him. They recall these things in a bemused sort of way, on the eve of their double wedding.

Flash-forward to five years later: the couples have reunited for an overnight picnic in the same old woods. They have somewhat lost touch. Lysander, still irritatingly successful, has moved with a discontented and frustrated Hermia to the Athenian equivalent of Silicon Valley. Demetrius and Helena, who stayed home, aren't too happily-ever-after either. Hermia, ever the princess, hates camping out; Helena is more than cool with it.

Lysander can still beat Demetrius at everything and eventually achieves the tryst with Helena for which he'd briefly panted five years earlier: a development that, as it turns out, satisfies nobody. The 21st-century text continues to play creatively with the 16th-century one: "is that a bush or a bear?" Hermia asks Demetrius as they glimpse the outline of the other couple coupling. Dunn plays absolutely fair with Shakespeare's creations and with his own; he's closer, in other words, to Rosencrantz and Guildenstern Are Dead than to Good Night, Desdemona (Good Morning Juliet). He never goes in for pastiche but he turns teenspeak into its own kind of poetry.

He gets a crackerjack production from Michael Shamata, one that goes at warp speed without ever losing clarity and in which every line shifts the balance. Jessica Greenberg, Kimwun Perehinec, Mark McGrinder and Jason Mitchell make a formidable foursome with Greenberg's Helena, which is the most flamboyant role, and Mitchell's Demetrius, which is the least, maybe coming out a fraction ahead. Having just seen the Shaw Festival's Follies, I found surprising similarities between that show and this one. Both depict the aftermath of a theatrical dream; both reassemble two couples with tangled erotic pasts; both show bright things coming inexorably to confusion; both end in reconciliation that's more like resignation. As an actor (three standout performances at Stratford this year) and playwright (with plays for Stratford and Theatre Direct before this one), Dunn is a striking double talent. Be patient with the evening's first part and you'll be richly rewarded by the rest.

At the beginning, it housed Hannah Moscovitch's East of Berlin; now, in a guest production by Joel Greenberg's Studio 160, we have Paul Dunns Offensive Shadows, two thirds of which amount to the best new writing, and some of the best acting and direction, to have turned up since then.

The remaining third looks like an attempt to transform a piece that at 55 minutes was the deserved hit of last years Summerworks into some-thing more befitting a full night out. It's ill-advised. Dunn's play is a riff on A Midsummer Nights Dream, and it takes its title from Pucks last speech to the audience: "If we shadows have offended/Think but this and all is mended." Puck himself, though, had no part in Dunn's original which focused on Shakespeare's four lovers -- Hermia and Lysander, Helena and Demetrius -- suggesting what they might have been like before their mixed-up night in the wood and speculating on what might have happened to them after it.

Thats all still there, but first we get a little bit of Puck. His last lines in Shakespeare -- Give me your hands if we be friends/And Robin shall restore amends --are his first lines here, and he follows them up with a more recent but still classic paraphrase: "Clap hands if you believe in fairies." Thats an equivalence I'd never noticed before, and it's also fun. He then embarks on a long monologue whose burden is that, in fact, people no longer believe in fairies, and thats bad, and its all the fairies' fault. Specifically, it's Oberons fault; Puck doesnt like his boss much, making it clear that he's a tyrannical and unappreciative employer as well as, to Titania, a louse of a spouse. Much of what this rock-star fairy tells us amounts to a jaundiced synopsis of the original story; to this Puck adds an account of what humanity has come to in the subsequent millennia, during which time its taken its cue from that tiresome old rationalist Theseus -- he who equated lunatics, lovers and poets. The consequences seem to have included global warming: cf. Titania's "forgeries of jealousy" aria, in which fairy quarrels were held responsible for the terrible weather people were having. That too was a topical speech in its time.

Andrew Kushnir plays Puck with some flair, greater energy, and a progressively diminishing store of rhythmic resource. But then hes stuck with a monotonous text thats increasingly reliant on undermining any lyrical expectations with a string of disgruntled four-letter words. Well, Puck it. It feels like padding.

It also doesn't fit, intellectually or chronologically, with the excellent stuff that follows. Dunn's original picks up from where Shakespeares left off, not from unnumbered centuries later. Its true that his young quartet look, talk and behave like modern teenagers, but this is the case -- well, maybe not the talking part -- in many modern productions. His achievement is to show how exactly the parts fit. He gives us the back-story in a series of reminiscing monologues. We learn that, crudely put, Helena was the school slut and Hermia the school virgin, Demetrius a nerd and Lysander a jock. That's more differentiation than Shakespeare gave them, the men especially, but it's perfectly consistent with what he did tell us. It seems that Hermia was going with Demetrius, in a bored sort of way and with parental approval, until she set eyes on Lysander; Demetrius, on the rebound, had a one-time fling with Helena who proceeded to stalk him. They recall these things in a bemused sort of way, on the eve of their double wedding.

Flash-forward to five years later: the couples have reunited for an overnight picnic in the same old woods. They have somewhat lost touch. Lysander, still irritatingly successful, has moved with a discontented and frustrated Hermia to the Athenian equivalent of Silicon Valley. Demetrius and Helena, who stayed home, arent too happily-ever-after either. Hermia, ever the princess, hates camping out; Helena is more than cool with it. Lysander can still beat Demetrius at everything and eventually achieves the tryst with Helena for which hed briefly panted five years earlier: a development that, as it turns out, satisfies nobody. The 21st-century text continues to play creatively with the 16th-century one: "is that a bush or a bear?" Hermia asks Demetrius as they glimpse the outline of the other couple coupling. Dunn plays absolutely fair with Shakespeare's creations and with his own; he's closer, in other words, to Rosencrantz and Guildenstern Are Dead than to Good Night, Desdemona (Good Morning Juliet). He never goes in for pastiche but he turns teenspeak into its own kind of poetry.

He gets a crackerjack production from Michael Shamata, one that goes at warp speed without ever losing clarity and in which every line shifts the balance. Jessica Greenberg, Kimwun Perehinec, Mark McGrinder and Jason Mitchell make a formidable foursome with Greenbergs Helena, which is the most flamboyant role, and Mitchells Demetrius, which is the least, maybe coming out a fraction ahead. Having just seen the Shaw Festival's Follies, I found surprising similarities between that show and this one. Both depict the aftermath of a theatrical dream; both reassemble two couples with tangled erotic pasts; both show bright things coming inexorably to confusion; both end in reconciliation that's more like resignation. As an actor (three standout performances at Stratford this year) and playwright (with plays for Stratford and Theatre Direct before this one), Dunn is a striking double talent. Be patient with the evening's first part and you'll be richly rewarded by the rest.

- Offensive Shadows plays through Oct. 19 at Tarragon Theatre Extra Space. Call 416-531-1827 for details.

THEATRE REVIEW

THE SOUND OF MUSIC

The Princess of Wales Theatre

---

The new production of The Sound of Music, by David Mirvish via Andrew Lloyd Webber, begins with singing nuns filling not only the stage but the auditorium. They come at us down the aisles, carrying candles. It's truly frightening, and makes you wonder what the show can possibly have in store when it gets to the Nazis.

This Austrian convent has been staffed with some of the best singing actresses in Canada, and they make a beautiful introductory noise. Then we suddenly burst through a cloudscape in the middle of the Princess of Wales' wide and wonderful stage, and there is Elicia MacKenzie's Maria, carolling and cavorting through an undulating Alpine seting that, as designed by Robert Jones, would take most people's breath away but seems to leave her with plenty. The hills are alive, and it's very impressive.

So is she. I still believe that turning theatrical casting into a branch of the reality TV industry is an abomination; democracy is a wonderful thing, but producers and directors should make their own artistic decisions. Still, judging pragmatically, this solution of the problem called Maria (to misquote a song that's one of my own least favourite things) is a very happy one. Apart from a voice that's gorgeous, clear and natural, she has a quality that may be unprecedented in this role: youth. Mary Martin, the first Maria, was middle-aged when she played it; Julie Andrews, the legendary one, may have been fresh and scrubbed, but she was born mature; the stage Marias I've personally witnessed, Petula Clark and Cynthia Dale, weren't spring chickens either. Maria, if you pay any attention to lyrics, is supposed to be eighteen going on nineteen. Nor is she a natural-born governess; she learns on the job. MacKenzie, tomboyish and impetuous, outwardly insecure but inwardly tough as old lederhosen, brings the show remarkably close to making sense.

She has the benefit of a production by Jeremy Sams that, especially in its early stages, is as intelligent as The Sound of Music is ever going to get. It's sometimes weighed down by memories of the movie; Mac-Kenzie, in her opening song, does the Andrews twirl as if it's in her contract and she can't wait to get it over. But note how the direction sets up My Favourite Things to make it credible that Maria and the Abbess (Noella Hurt, who acts stiffly but sings resoundingly) should be sharing such thoughts. The show also goes on looking sumptuous but it falters in the second half, where it falls foul of those two operetta perennials: love and war.

As a romantic musical, The Sound of Music, despite its chocolate-box reputation, really isn't up to much. It's largely a rerun of Rodgers and Hammerstein's earlier, and much superior, The King and I, with that show's love that could not speak or sing its name replaced by one that would like to but doesn't have the material. Maria and Captain von Trapp, the melting martinet, have never on stage or screen been granted a decent duet, while the script simply takes their mutual attraction for granted. (This is the one R&H score for which Hammerstein didn't also write the book, and it shows. Everything feels as if it's written in capital letters, though that may be partly due to the amplification, which makes singing sound great and acting sound awful.) There is no chemistry between MacKenzie and Burke Moses's untender Captain von Trapp, a block in a double-breasted suit. He does, to be sure, have the show's one truly heartwarming moment when he embraces his previously neglected children; that's because they are children, hence irresistible, especially when hurt or healed.

These seven junior Trapps are especially well-acted, despite the extremes of cuteness to which they have driven. The eldest (Megan Nuttall) forms part of one of the show's other couples, one that starts out with a good-old fashioned charm song that never gets followed up; their relationship's doomed by history (he's in the Party), a development that could be interesting but is hung out to dry. That's not the production's fault, nor is the fact that Maria's older highborn rival (Blythe Wilson) retires from the scene without a fight. But it could make more than it does of her cynical duets with the time-serving Max, whom Keith Dinicol plays with a twinkle that obliterates all his ambiguities.

What he's collaborating with is the Anschluss, which the production does its level best to make terrifying without much help from the text. (What's there is real enough; it's just that so much is left out.) The theatre itself becomes the Salzburg concert-hall in which the Trapp Family Singers' effect their trompe l'oeil transformation into the Trapp Family Refugees, and there are indeed storm troopers in the aisles, though they're still not as scary as the nuns. But no staging has the technical resources to compete with the film here, or in what follows. The production does add a new dark touch: Max, left behind, gets arrested. But we're given no time to ponder what might happen to him (or to thousands of others); we're whisked on to an uplifting finale. The Sisters reprise that meaningless mountain-climbing song, which is You'll Never Walk Alone minus the soul, in the bottom half of the stage, while in the top half the Trapps on their Alp are seen obeying the injunction, while fixing the audience with a collective grin that's pure postcard kitsch. It's certainly in keeping with the spirit of the show, if not with the general handsomeness of the production. It's just that after Cabaret and, in its way, The Producers, a (literally) escapist musical about Nazism seems -- I was going to say dim-witted but I'll settle for myopic. - The Sound of Music runs until Jan. 11. Call 416-872-1212 or visit mirvish.com for information.

2008-10-18-kept-on-a-tight-leash-the-cas:
There is a powerful, chilling scene at the beginning of Wild Dogs. Six of the shows seven characters stand at the edge of a wood, each calling out the name of a favourite hound who's disappeared into it. Their individual tones vary from wistful to hopeful to hopeless to desperate. The gradations, in Kelly Thornton's production, are haunting and, in at least one case, frightening. The effect is truly theatrical, something you couldnt get from a book. But its the only sequence in the evening of which that is true.

Wild Dogs is in fact based on a book--a novel by Helen Humphreys -- that I haven't read, but have read about -- enough, anyway -- to have learned that it's a story narrated in turn by each of the people in it. In other words, its a sequence of monologues. In this stage version from Nightwood Theatre, the monologues are retained, but are chopped up and intercut; Anne Hardcastle is credited not with having adapted the original, but with having "arranged it.

Plays based on novels dont have to be lifeless, though there's a better-than-average chance that they will be. Neither do plays composed of monologues; one of the most compelling plays I ever saw, Kennedy's Children (a 70s view of the 60s) was made up entirely of half a dozen people in a barroom talking to themselves. Once you realized that was all you were going to get, you adjusted and let yourself be lured in by language that was immediately witty and eventually moving, and that had innate stage presence. None of these things are true of the speeches in Wild Dogs, which has adopted a convention that seems increasingly arbitrary. The people in Kennedy's Children never broke out of their respective cocoons; that was the point. Those in Wild Dogs are figures in a shared story. On occasions, presumably when there's no help for it, they even interact. Only they havent been given the theatrical tools to do it.

They are all members of a depressed community; depressed economically and, for the most part, psychologically as well. The dogs have escaped, or been let go, largely because their owners can no longer feed them. The central character, or at least the narrator-in-chief, is Alice, who recently broke up with her boyfriend and who strikes up a new relationship with Rachel, a conservationist academic on a field-trip. This affair, like much of the rest of the play, falls into the category of things that are presumed to have happened but, in dramatic terms, never do. Tamara Podemski, playing Alice, soliloquizes well enough but seems still to be doing it when supposedly talking to the person she loves; Raven Dauda as Rachel responds in kind and, when left to herself, is something of a grouch.

Taylor Trowbridge gives a wrenching if inevitably unvaried account of a brain-damaged young woman who actively identifies with the wild things. The mens roles are more recognizably grounded, with Les Carlson affecting as a neglected ancient, Steve Cumyn touchingly creepy as a frustrated artist with an advanced degree in voyeurism and Stephen Joffe arresting, alternately pitiful and aggressive, as a boy peer-pressured into petty crime. His are the shouts that ring out most agonizingly in that initial sequence, and his later encounters with Alice, who sees in him an all-too-familiar reflection of her own youth, bring the proceedings briefly to life. But the attempt to render all the characters through their relations to their lost dogs simply misfires. It merely leaves the impression that all the exciting stuff is happening offstage, among a collection of mutts we naturally never meet. It's no accident that the most complete performance comes from Tony Nappo as the one figure outside the charmed circle, a hunter who is nobody's dog lover. He is given feelings to portray (from anger to guilt, but thats enough) and actions through which to convey them. And when he talks to us, he does seem to be telling a personal story rather than reciting a prose poem.

The production keeps all the performances to a rigorous line; there is no emotional or oratorical overflow, though the temptations that way must have been considerable. But this is another play enslaved to its own metaphor: literary theatre" in a sense beyond merely being taken from a book. Its the kind of thing that often gets rave reviews and even awards, so don't let me put you off when I say that I think it's deadly. - Wild Dogs continues until Nov. 8 at the Berkeley Street Theatre. Call 416-368-3110 for show information and tickets.

2008-10-20-life-like-lice-can-be-messy-a:
SCRATCH

Factory Theatre

Charlotte Corbeil-Coleman is the daughter of Layne Coleman, actor, director and former head of Theatre Passe Muraille, and Carole Corbeil, novelist, critic and plawright. Her play Scratch, begun eight years ago and reaching the Factory Theatre stage after many expansions and reworkings, started out as her reaction to two things: her mothers death from cancer and her own stubborn case of head lice. The names, and probably many of the circumstances, have been changed, but what occurs on the stage feels unshakably autobiographical, especially as the author herself appears in the central role. The other characters, each with their own take on the protagonist's double predicament, are her parents, her best friend, her mother's sister and a young man, known as the Poet, who is enlisted to care for the mother in the closing stages of her illness.

The first thing to be said about Corbeil-Coleman as a playwright is that her words swing. By that I mean that her dialogue, unlike that in 90% of purportedly realistic plays, never has you protesting that people dont actually talk like that. It isnt glib, fancy or stilted. But neither is it slavishly naturalistic. It has rhythm, wit and flavour. It also has a quick pulse. This is, obviously, a selfconscious play, and with a selfconscious shape. "If this were my story ..." says each of the characters, some of them repeatedly, as they watch Anna, the heroine, grappling with her twin afflictions. The one who comes closest to making it her own story is Madelyn, the friend, who watches, sympathetically aghast, as Anna seems to be withdrawing from her dying mother and refusing to visit her hospital bed, just when you would imagine the two of them might need each other most. At age 15, Anna's declared reaction to her imminent loss is that it makes her horny; she throws herself at the bemused Poet. (Nice man, comments her father, "terrible poet.") Madelyn, an aspiring painter, meanwhile wants nothing more than to be with Anna's mother, herself an artist who has always encouraged her. It isnt exactly Rashomon; nobody disagrees about the facts of the situation. Where they differ is over which facts, and especially which feelings, they want to stress.

The most questionable aspect of the production is the onstage presence of the author. Not that her performance is bad: Its actually very good, uncompromising in its head-tossing (and of course head-scratching) depiction of stubbornness as a form of evasion, or of innocence trying desperately hard to be experienced. It isn't that the author-actor tries to present herself in a good light; she's actually doubly hard on herself. It would be good to hear her voice mediated through someone elses. That could make it more sympathetic but not, I think, sentimental.

Apart from this, and from a habit of sending the actors walking around in circles (a device thats been patented by Scorched), ahdri zhina mandiela's direction is excellent. Monica Dottor gives a glowing, beautifully detailed account of Madelyn, while Mary Ann Mc-Donald's Mother pretty much defines the word gentle, even when being infuriating. Shes an unreconstructed spirit from the 60s or, to put it geographically rather than historically, she's the Annex made melting flesh. She denies her daughter the shampoo that might heal her hair because of the chemicals it contains. (We never do learn whether Anna used it at a later date. Or if not, why not.) She and her musician-husband (Kevin Bundy, very likeable especially when putting on brave faces) share, before tragedy strikes, a delectable variation on the traditional marital row over finances: "You are not" says Mother, striking an ambiguous blow for feminism, the only one not bringing enough money into the house. Ryan Hollyman does as much as is probably possible with the over-writing and underwritten Poet. Catherine Fitch plays his sharp-edged girlfriend, who is a bit of a caricature, plus several semi-official ladies who are rather more so; her most prominent role, though, is the Aunt, whom she eventually makes believable, even though her personality is primarily defined by her unwillingness to spend money on anything except taxis (for safety) and Kleenex (for just about everything). These are believable human quirks that somehow seem stagey when put on a stage. More importantly, one of the play's major climaxes falls into the same category of things that may very well have happened but still seem too good, or at least too neat, to be true.

There is something schematic about the play. Im not sure that it justifies its structure or even the metaphor thats emblazoned in its title: life equated with lice, messy with itchy. I don't know that it ends up making any particular statement about grief, loss or survival. But it does show them all happening -- believably, sometimes touchingly, and nearly always entertainingly. It's an impressive calling card. - Scratch runs through Nov. 2 at the Factory Theatre. Call 416-504-9971 for more information.

2008-10-22-they-try-to-get-out-as-they-d:
Well, talk about serendipity. This year's Toronto Arts Council Foundation Awards were announced and bestowed the day after the Young Centre opening of A Raisin in the Sun. Weyni Mengesha, who directed Raisin, won the Royal Bank of Canada Emerging Artist Award. Obviously this new production arrived too late to have been a factor in her winning the prize. But on the strength of this show, she's no longer "emerging"; she's emerged.

Lorraine Hansberry's play, first seen in 1959, is famous as the first work by a black woman ever to be presented on Broadway. In most respects, it's a traditional American domestic drama, with characters alternately oppressed by their social and familial circumstances and rising above them. The difference between it and its predecessors is that this family, the Youngers, is, in their own favoured word, "coloured." They liveinacramped, roach-infested apartment on the south side of Chicago, which they have a chance to leave when the matriarchal Lena comes into $10,000 of insurance money from the death of her husband. She proposes to spend it on a house, an initiative approved by everyone except her son Walter Lee, a frustrated 35-year old chauffeur who wants to get rich quick by investing in a liquor store. An even grimmer complication arises when a delegate from the all-white neighbourhood into which the Youngers propose to move informs them, in the nicest possible way, that they will not be welcome and tries to bribe them to go elsewhere.

There are side issues. Beneatha, Walter Lee's younger sister, is studying to be a doctor, to the skepticism of her relatives who wonder why she can't just settle for being a nurse. She has two suitors: a complacent rich boy, whom she treats with barely-concealed disdain, and a young Nigerian who wants her to go back to his homeland with him. (African trappings attract her and so, increasingly, does the African reality.) Walter's wife Ruth is pregnant with their second child; she works as a cleaning lady all the hours, apparently, that God sends, plus a lot more hours that she spends chained to her own family's ironing board. The play is about alternative methods of pulling free of an intolerable situation: out to the suburbs, up into business, back to roots.

It has some familiar American flaws. Characters are inclined to stop in mid-scene and indulge in uplifting monologues drawn from their pasts, which no one ever seems to feel the urge to interrupt. The play pulls more domestic punches, and is sunnier in outlook, than its exemplars O'Neill and Miller at their best (though it's a lot better than either of them at their worst) and its embattled optimism sometimes amounts to sentimentality. But if it's dated, it's only in a good way. It's both sobering and inspiring to sit through these people's travails with the words "Barack Obama" ringing through your mind. It's also good to be reminded of a time when playwrights knew how to tell stories, and knew how to activate family tensions and family joys (and when producers could supply a sizeable cast to help them do it). This play brings its circumstances alive from the first moment, when we hear, casually, of a young boy obliged to sleep on the sofa because there's nowhere else. Despite its abundance of plot, what really keeps the play in motion is its eye and ear for the seesawing of family feelings. It's also the strength of Mengesha's production, a joint presentation by Soulpepper and Theatre Calgary, whose keynote is emotional generosity.

It even survives what could be a crippling weakness: an uneven performance by Charles Officer in the pivotal role of Walter. He has some very good scenes, including one in which he promises a bright future to his son (Kofi Payton, who's delightful) and another in which he assails his mother for destroying his dreams. But he blurs his crucial transformations, which are also the play's; the climax becomes something you want to believe in rather than something you can. Abena Malika's Ruth also has her tentative moments, but she can be forgiven anything for the ecstatic aria with which she greets the news that at long last she'll have a house to clean that's actually her own. Alison Sealy-Smith brings to Lena an expansiveness -- vocal, physical and spiritual -- beyond anything I've seen from her before. She's sometimes been a bossy actress; here she's commanding, which is something else entirely. She summons, and surmounts, a family history of slavery and sharecropping; and she doesn't scant the woman's less lovable aspects, which include slapping her free-thinking daughter's face to make her profess a belief in God. (How unlovable Hansberry meant this to be is an open question. She also treats Ruth's threats to whop her young son as a source of comedy.) The younger Younger herself is Cara Ricketts, equally luminous whether being funny, flirtatious, dedicated or enraged. Michael Blake, casual and brash, and Awaovieyi Agie, humorous and intense, are the two young men in her life -- the two, you might say, who want to marry Beneatha. The white intruder, in a gloriously uncomfortable suit, is Diego Matamoros, his voice emerging from beneath his specs in a kind of benevolent sneer. Another bearer of bad news, even more traumatic, is played with vivid terror by Matthew Kabwe: a tiny role, but an example of how the production fills the play out to its edges. This is literally the case in Scott Reid's admirable set, which shows not only the apartment itself but glimpses of the two on other side, providing ample illustration of why the family yearns, so desperately, to get out. - A Raisin in the Sun runs until Nov. 15. For tickets and information call 416-866-8666.

2008-10-23-front-row-at-the-sideshow:
Politics is show business. That's the conclusion, indisputable if hardly a revelation, reached by Frost/Nixon at its own conclusion, and dropped neatly in our laps. The play makes a decent case for it, not least by being an example of it.

Decent, but thin. Peter Morgan's play centres on the 1977 television interviews in which David Frost elicited from Richard Nixon a first-time-ever admission that he had indeed been at fault over Watergate, both the burglary itself and the cover-up. It draws a parallel between the two participants. On the one hand, the disgraced president, saved from impeachment only by the pardon so opportunely bestowed by his successor, and obsessed with restoring his prestige, or at least with doing it no further harm; on the other, the gadfly entrepreneur, in search of a coup that might redeem a career in danger of fizzling on three continents. So the two men need one another, but for incompatible reasons.

Historically, Frost won. Theatrically, Nixon does. This is partly for technical reasons. To put it crudely, Nixon was a historical figure, Frost was a media one; which means (even more crudely) that the former asks to be acted and the latter to be impersonated. Actor Len Cariou's resume includes such self-destructive heroes as Coriolanus and Sweeney Todd, and some of that stature gets into his Nixon, whom he presents as wily but never weaselly. Nixon agrees to four interviews, of which only the last is to concern Watergate, and he gets off handily in the first three. So it's awesome to see his face crumble, as Cariou's graphically does, when he tumbles into giving an unguarded reply to an unexpected question; and it's impressive when (against advice) he walks back into the ring and confesses that he let himself and America down. Maybe he was just cutting his losses, but the play offers the tragic option and the actor takes it. A coda shows him wryly envying his adversary's ability to work a room and enjoy it. This, considering how high Nixon actually climbed, is guff, but you swallow it at the time.

One reason, other than a million-dollar fee, that Nixon agrees to the interviews is that he's persuaded that his opponent is an apolitical lightweight who's never even bothered to vote. This certainly squares with my own impression of Frost as a man of no particular convictions, or even performing talents, who happened to be the right age, and the right personality, for the British "satire boom" of the early '60s. It's why he's a less substantial figure than Jon Stewart, whose Daily Show is the contemporary equivalent of Frost's That Was the Week That Was, but who means what he says and is also (or therefore) funnier. The play's Frost takes a terrific professional and financial gamble that only pays off, or so we're told, because his assistant Jim Reston, who functions as the play's part-time skeptical narrator, unearths a crucial and hitherto neglected piece of evidence. All Frost has to do is spring it; there isn't even any suggestion that he's been purposely lulling his quarry into a sense of false security. (Well, he suggests it, but his staff aren't buying it and neither do we.) David Storch's quiz-kid Frost spends most of the evening running around like a self-absorbed squeaky-voiced chicken, in increasing fear of having its head chopped off. On this level it's a perfectly good performance -- actually quite an interesting one -- but it bears, even when he's supposed to be on camera, little relation to the twang-toned, unshakably confident (some would say complacent) inquisitor we know from the box -- a medium of which he was one of the first real masters.

The actor isn't helped by the play's efforts to give him a life outside the box. Morgan, the screenwriter of The Queen (a more substantial work on a more substantial subject) seems to be a documentarian rather than a dramatist; the script's most compelling scenes are transcripts. The made-up or guessed-at bits are plodding, and the Frost camp has most of them. There's even an attempt at love interest with the peripatetic Frost meeting his future fiancee sitting across the aisle in first class, a scene that neither the writing nor the performance make credible and that nothing could make relevant. There are also scenes involving Nixon superagent (in the 10% sense) Swifty Lazar, whose underlining of the politics-performance equation doesn't excuse their lameness.

Two actor-playwrights, Damien Atkins and Michael Healey, step persuasively outside their usual comfort zones as Frost aides, while Tom Mc-Beath seems ruggedly inside his as point man to Nixon. Ari Cohen's Reston is too much the shoulder-shrugger to carry any weight. Ted Dykstra's direction gives the play flash, which it needs, but it can't fill in the holes.

The story holds you. It just doesn't seem as significant as everyone thinks it is. Nixon's capitulation may have been cathartic for him but it can't have told Americans anything they didn't already know. It made no difference, except to David Frost's career which is only important if you're David Frost. And the stakes seem grotesquely disproportionate: a man jeopardizing his job against one who cashiered his country. The real drama was in Watergate itself. The interviews weren't even an epilogue: just a belated sideshow. - Frost/Nixon runs until Nov. 8. For tickets and information call 416-368-3110.

2008-10-25-headless-male-seeks-mate-chil:
First seen in 1999, Darren ODonnell's [boxhead], with text by Darren O'Donnell and direction by Chris Abraham, is a kind of Creation myth. (The current revival is by Crows Theatre, which is now Abrahams company, "in association with" Mammalian Diving Reflex, which has always been O'Donnell's.) It starts with a character identified as Dr. Thoughtless Actions, a young geneticist who awakens one morning to find that his head is enclosed in a box. Happily for him, he doesnt seem to suffer from claustrophobia but after a while he does get lonely. So this Adam gets himself a mate, a male one, by cloning himself. He and his new double, Dr. Wishful Thinking, are happy together but decide that they would be even happier if they had a child. After some experimenting they realize that this is impossible as, with the same DNA, they are really the same person. The fact that theyre the same gender can't help either, but it may be unfairly literal-minded to point this out.

Still, as long as I'm being literal, Id like to ask a question. The fact that Dr. Thoughtless wakes up unexpectedly boxed means that there was a time, culminating in the night before, when he wasnt. Does this mean that humanity has encased itself in limitations of perception that aren't natural but enforced? If so, whose fault is it? The play seems to be blaming God, or perhaps gods. The show unfolds behind a false proscenium and within an encompassing blackness. Apart from the two doctors, cavorting at ground-level, the only being we see is represented by a pair of roving eyes shining high up in the dark. They belong to a narrator, of the omniscient variety: a divinity, in fact, of Old Testament proclivities. He doesn't want them to take their boxes off. But his creations, if thats what they are, do have free will; the issue becomes whether or not they will exercise it.

In due course the narrator, too, splits up, and starts having arguments with himself: more enlivening, actually, than those the two mortals have. This may be because theres something intrinsically entertaining in the idea of gods having internal disagreements (the Greeks knew that); it's also because they have the more interesting voices: deep and fretful, as opposed to those of the scientists which are squeaky and querulous. I also found it appealing that the sonorous sounds and twinkling orbs, in a sea of nothingness, combined to remind me of Sesame Street's Cookie Monster with the colour-scheme reversed.

Down below, Thoughtless and Wishful pursue such ambitious projects as creating a voiceless echo; I have no idea whether these are meant to signify noble aspiration or crass foolishness, modern man and especially modern science getting above themselves. The names, though, rather suggest the latter. This doesnt stop them from being endearing, but it also severely reduces their level of interest, as of course does the fact that theyre interchangeable, and not just because they're clones. I realize that the show isn't exactly aiming at psychological realism, but like nearly all drama on which can be hung the term absurdist, it inevitably harks back to Waiting for Godot, but a Godot from which the contrasts between Vladimir and Estragon have been ironed out, leaving us only with image. One that makes its point early but then hangs around for the duration.

Still, its superbly realized in the mise-en-scene: in Steve Lucas lighting, in the percussion music of Romano Di Nillo, in the set (credited to O'Donnell, Abraham and Naomi Campbell, the producer) and in the performances of Andrew Shaver and Adam Lazarus, who seem not only to be playing the headless helpless duo on earth but to be supplying voices for the bodiless deities as well: a staggering feat on any number of levels.

Last Monday, the Stratford Festival paid tribute, in its principal theatre, to its late artistic director Richard Monette. This wasn't an occasion designed to be reviewed, but I can at least say that there was some lovely singing, solo and choral, and that Dan Chameroy was both hilarious and touching in his demonstration that he ceased to be afraid of the director when he found he could "do his voice." He recreated it flawlessly, largely in its moods of calculated exasperation: you hire singers, you get singers; you hire dancers, you get dancers; you hire actors -- pot luck -- the last delivered on an upward inflection, as a guttural snarl. Brian Bedford read simply and affectingly from Monettes autobiography, on how he fell in love with the theatre and what it continued to mean to him; Martha Henry spoke passionately, even fiercely, about his undervalued legacy. She also cued a tape of his famous outburst at the embattled AGM of 1980 when, still just an actor, he denounced the Festival board as "pigs." Id read about this many times, even written about it, but I'd never heard it before. It was amazing. So, too, was the montage of interview excerpts that closed the evening, allowing us to see a Monette still achingly young, before his tenure and even during its first years. As many of the speakers suggested, he could rage or tease for effect, but when he spoke of what he believed, he was transparently real. At the end, we gave a standing ovation, even though the stage was empty. As someone said afterwards, Richard would have loved it.

- [boxhead] runs through Nov. 2 at Buddies in Bad Times theatre. Call 416-975-8555 for ticket information.

It hurts to come late to a cult. The natural impulse is to take out one's frustration on the object thats being venerated. But with Flight of the Conchords, theres no chance. This show is wonderful.

For those who don't know, which I'm fondly hoping means most people over 30, Flight of the Conchords come from New Zealand and theyre a band, and I cant help it if that sentence looks ungrammatical. Seems like all the good plural band names were taken. Anyway, Flight aren't that plural, as there are only two of them. One, the taller and broader and clumsier of the two, is called Jemaine, and he's played by Jemaine Clement. The more compact of the two, marginally more competent especially at dealing with girlfriends, is Bret, played by Bret McKenzie. (The way he pronounces it, it sounds like Brit, and thats not just me, because some non-New Zealanders on the show hear it that way, and get confused.) So, yes, the actors have the same names as their characters. They explain this at some length in the shows trailer, which is in heavy rotation on the Comedy Network, and is unique among that station's ads in that it actually makes you want to watch the show it's plugging. (Most make you run screaming from the very idea.) Jemaine and Bret hawk their wares with exactly the kind of casual, downbeat solemnity that they project in the show itself. Jemaine grins. Bret smirks. Theyre self-deprecating even while self-promoting.

Clement and McKenzie actually are a band in, you know, real life; they write song parodies, of which they have built up a rich bank. The TV show is structured around these numbers. It shows us Jemaine and Bret trying to make it in New York and failing, at least to date, abjectly. In one episode (next weeks, actually) Bret and Jemaine are starving, reduced -- Jemaine is anyway -- to eating a sandwich that Bret has found on the street. We cut from this squalid domestic scene to a rap number titled Inner City Pressure that finds Jemaine, generally the more volubly aggrieved of the two, in his local convenience store, rhyming about "Counting coins on the counter of the 7-Eleven / From a quarter past six to a quarter to seven." Oh, and the manager's name is Bevan. Lovely sense of specifics these guys have. The number, like all the numbers on the show, is shot like a low budget video, with the two participants doing the work of a chorus by being caught lurking in improbable corners. That's also how they live their lives. When Bret acquires a girlfriend named Coco (Sutton Foster no less, Broadway star of Thoroughly Modern Millie and The Drowsy Chaperone), Jemaine insists on tagging along on all their dates.

Thats in Episode Four, which I strongly recommend, and which is called Yoko, Jemaine having seized on the rhyming significance of Cocos name to accuse her of breaking up the band. More constructively, he dissuades his friend from writing a two-hour ballad about climbing the highest mountain and persuades him to substitute more prosaic proofs of devotion.

In Episode Three, we meet Murray (Rhys Darby), the Conchords' manager and compatriot who operates semi-clandestinely out of an office in the New Zealand consulate and seems mildly surprised that his clients expect him to get them gigs. He also likes making lists and calling "band meetings," often in his car or in the park; he seems suspiciously happy that Jemaine isn't going to get a girlfriend any time soon. To make up for this, the boys have a rabid and unwanted groupie named Mel (Kristen Schaal, last seen by me as a gloriously unqualified would-be host on The Daily Show) who throws herself at them whenever they meet on the street while her husband looks philosophically on.

I dont know if Bret and Jemaine are students of classic British comedy; they have obvious hints of Ricky Gervais, but they also remind me of Peter Cook and Dudley Moore in their down-and-out mode: the would-be smooth exchanging philosophical gems with the incurably chirpy. As theyre the only New Zealand comedians I've ever seen, I can't say whether theyre typical, but they do give the impression of being a portent: a sign that their country has funnier things to offer the world than The Piano and Lord of the Rings. If their efforts to take a bite out of the Big Apple leave them choking, thats part of the joke. (And look how well the hick shtick has turned out for Canadians.) There's a new flavour about this show: dry slapstick. It shows in particular in the way that Jemaine in particular changes accents. He can sound unaccountably English, even when rapping: "Yes, my lyrics are sexist / but you ladies should know I'm trying to correct it." I hope the bad rhyme is intentional. Anyway, its hilarious. If this is a sitcom, and I cant think of any other way to classify it, it's the best in a very long time. I laughed very loud and very often.

- Flight of the Conchords premieres tonight at 10:30 p. m. on The Comedy Network.

THEATRE REVIEW

PYAASA

Theatre Passe Muraille Backspace

---

The principal characters of Pyaasa live in a tent under a bridge in Calcutta. There is Meera, who cleans the toilets in the house of a wealthy woman; her husband, whom we hear of but never actually meet and who performs the same function in a police station; and their daughter, Chaya. Chaya reads a lot and is eager for an education, tendencies that her mother deems socially inadvisable. The family are Untouchables, the lowest of the low. The caste system was officially banned in India in 1950 but seems too hard-wired into Hindu tradition to have disappeared. Besides, too many people have a stake in it. Anyone concerned with the evils bred of religion can add this to their list.

The play, which lasts 45 minutes, was written by Anusree Roy, who plays all the roles. Anyone wary of one-person shows can leave their fears at the door. Apart from a brief tendency to ramble, somewhere in the first third, this is a taut, inexorable piece of work, superbly performed. It starts with Roy squatting on the ground, in what looks like an attitude of hopelessness. She rouses herself and partakes in a scene, funny in a barbed way, between Meera and a superior servant in the same household, whom she differentiates through instant changes in voice and stance. One inclines haughtily downwards, the other demurely cowers while also, you feel, keeping her own ironic counsel. When Meera makes the mistake of actually looking at her antagonist, the latter complains that now she'll have to take a shower to wash away the uncleanness of it. Interestingly, the mistress of the house, when we finally meet her, doesn't seem especially concerned with this. She seems to regard Meera simply as a source of dirt-cheap labour, to be dismissed if ever she steps out of line. It's the middle orders who cling to the system, compensating for their own economic dependence by despising those even worse off than themselves. It's a familiar pattern, but Roy, by stating it firmly but lightly, brings it freshly home.

Meera herself has a certain psychic investment in her own status; in her own mind, she can avenge herself by "letting her shadow fall" on someone who's offended her. That same acceptance becomes rather less amusing when she tries to pass the oppression on to her own daughter, telling her that her only hope in life is to marry the right man, which seems to mean any who'll have her. As usual, the road to disaster is paved with the very best intentions. Meera secures Chaya a job at a tea stall run by her employer's son. Chaya is dazzled; she's never even tasted tea before. "Pyaasa" is a Hindi word meaning thirst, and Chaya has been, in several senses, parched. She falls into a trap, centuries old but newly baited by those she has most reason to trust. The play develops as a miniature tragedy, with a conclusion that draws on tradition even as it condemns it.

Roy's physical control is extraordinary; so is her empathy. She's able to switch instantly, and with total conviction, from gnarled mother to joyous child. She might be playing Juliet and the Nurse simultaneously. With a bare set, and David DeGrow's precision lighting, Thomas Morgan Jones' production gives the actress-author everything she needs. She gives everything in return. This is a rare kind of protest drama. It goes beyond anger. - Pyaasa run until Nov. 15 at Theatre Passe Muraille's Backspace. Call 416-504-7529 for information.

2008-11-01-they-don-t-think-they-can-dan:
Ihave never believed that A Chorus Line was, in the advertising phrase recycled for the current revival: "The Best Musical. Ever." But it is an essential musical, one that both explores and embodies the drives, on both sides of the curtain, that make the form come alive. It's about energy, transmitted and received. Theoretically, it's about performers, but it's also about audiences. It could, and has often been known to, drive an audience crazy.

You know the drill. Zach, a director-choreographer, is holding auditions for a new Broadway show. He has chorus roles for eight performers and a shortlist of twice that number. On the thin pretext that his choristers will have characters to play as well as songs and dances to perform, he interrogates them about their past lives and especially about what made them want to dance. Some of the resultant confessions are merely spoken, others are musicalized. And they're done with such skill and conviction that by the end, we're rooting for every one of them -- even while knowing that half of them are going to be rejected. Catharsis is practically guaranteed.

A Chorus Line premiered in 1975, and ran longer than any Broadway production up to that time. Of all its major creators, only one -- Marvin Hamlisch, who wrote the mostly excellent music--is still alive. A new production, closely based on the original, opened in New York last year, and its touring version is now playing in Toronto. It's directed by Bob Avian, who 33 years ago was co-choreographer to Michael Bennett, the show's director and presiding genius. The job of recreating Bennett's choreography, though, has gone to Baayork Lee, who was in the original cast.

Some things are as exciting as I'd remembered from when the show was new. The opening sequence, in which Zach puts all the aspirants through an exhausting series of dance combinations, has always been my favourite part, and this time around some things seemed to come up with extra sharpness: the individualization of the characters before they've even been formally introduced, their fumbles and silent curses, their taskmaster's patience and his ruthlessness.

This number has the thrill of a documentary; even when -- something that's unlikely to happen at an actual audition -- the performers start singing, in unison, I Hope I Get It, you still buy it, the sentiment seems so urgent, so heartfelt and so right. (That simple line is probably the best single moment in Edward Kleban's lyrics). After it's over, the convention changes; the subject matter remains different from that of the average musical but the form becomes the same: People sing about their life experiences and how they feel about them. There's a long ensemble number, with mini-numbers inside it, whose title is Hello Twelve, Hello Thirteen, Hello Love, but it's the smaller, more individualized songs that are more effective.

Or they could be. It depends on the performers. Maybe standards have slipped since the '70s, or maybe Bennett's successors lack his flair for talent spotting and talent driving. The present corps are uniformly excellent as dancers, variable as singers and even more variable as actors. The best performance comes from Bryan Knowlton as Paul, the Hispanic boy whose traumatic moment came when his parents discovered him working in a drag show; he handles this monologue (he doesn't have a song) beautifully, even with a few too many sobs at the end. After hearing it you watch his dancing with a keener eye; he justifies the attention. Emily Fletcher does all right, but less well than is possible, by the infallible role of Sheila, the wisecracking den-mother (or considering her comparative youth, den-sister). Elsewhere, the cosmetic-surgery song Dance Ten Looks Three, a. k. a. Tits and Ass, is ruined by over-aggressiveness, while Nothing, the tale of the Puerto Rican student terrorized by a posturing acting-teacher, is spoiled by being squawked. Michael Gruber's Zach is forceful but wooden. By contrast, the proclamation by his ex-flame Cassie (Nikkie Snelson) that she'd be proud to be in this chorus comes from the heart of the show, and is genuinely uplifting.

Robin Wagner's bare mirrored set remains the same; so do Theoni V. Aldredge's costumes, including of course the gold suits and top hats in which the entire company executes the exhilarating, regimented, high-stepping finale. People used to argue about this number: Was it a celebration or a bitter comment on the relegation of individuals to cogs in a dancing machine? Now, it hardly matters. The number, and the show, come to us as reminders of a better time. This musical, unlike the TV "reality shows" of which it's the unwitting ancestor, celebrates not the cult of stardom but the quest for meaningful work.

- A Chorus Line plays to Nov. 30 at the Canon Theatre. 416-872-1212 for details.

2008-11-06-rock-in-a-hard-place-the-thir:
Decades ago and an ocean away, John Cleese made himself over from a writer and performer on Monty Python's Flying Circus, the best sketch-comedy show ever, to writer, performer and principal creator of Fawlty Towers, the best situation comedy ever. Other people have attempted the same transition -- it's an obvious one, after all -- but its Cleese of whom I, perhaps incongruously, find myself thinking when I consider Tina Fey and her progress from Saturday Night Live to 30 Rock.

30 Rock is a show that can be very funny in bursts, but is also strangely unsatisfying. The reason, I suspect, is that Fey, unlike Cleese, has brought her previous comedy ethic with her. Like Fawlty Towers, and like many other shows, 30 Rock is a workplace comedy. Unlike Fawlty Towers (and unlike, say, The Office, especially in its British incarnation) it doesnt create a workplace that's credible, and hardly bothers to try. Actually it's almost insulting to call Fawlty Towers a sitcom; its best episodes were classic farce, Feydeau on a miniature scale. This means they had to be logically structured, not just physically but psychologically; Basil Fawltys seaside hotel may have been chaotic, but its chaos sprang from the thoroughly believable personality-deficiencies of its inhabitants.

Back when it started, 30 Rock held some of the same promise. It was intriguing to see Feys Liz Lemon lured by Alec Baldwin's megalomaniac studio head into working as head writer for crazy movie star Tracy Jordan. But as the series has progressed, it's drifted increasingly far from that premise. The show-within-the-show still exists, but not in any tangible way. Its amazing how little work is seen to get done. The mugging Tracy Morgan plays his semi-namesake; theres presumably more to Morgan in real life than there is to Jordan here, but he never lets us know it, and he isn't half as cute as the show thinks he is. Neither is Kenneth, the Southern pageboy (Jack McBrayer) whom everybody loves and fraternizes with but who, at the start of the Season Three, is still just a page. It's a wonderfully egalitarian set-up. It just isnt very plausible. Or very funny: I wouldnt say that comedy depends on hierarchy, but it can be a very useful tool.

The main reason to watch the show is Baldwin. There's always a kick, of course, in seeing a respected actor in such frivolous surroundings; the kick is doubled when he turns out to be so perfectly suited to them. In a way, Baldwin's performance is an enlargement of the devastatingly sadistic motivational speech he delivered in the film version of Glengarry Glen Ross, but cut loose from its moral bearings. He performs here with a monstrous insouciance that perfectly conveys the character while simultaneously suggesting that, personally, hes having the time of his life. It was great fun watching him in last weeks season premiere, forced to start again from the bottom of the company -- which, as always, is the mailroom -- and emerging from it in record time. Like the hero of How to Succeed in Business Without Really Trying, he obviously had a real talent for mail-roomery.

It was also fun to see Fey herself trying desperately to prove her maternal credentials to the lady from the adoption agency (a fearsome Megan Mullally). It was a plot-line that actually built, and was pleasantly reminiscent of her attempts last year to impress the committee of the co-op she wanted to buy into. She's likeable, but either she lacks the comic energy to maintain herself at the centre of things (she consistently loses out to Baldwin) or her character does. Her devastating Sarah Palin on Saturday Night Live (there must have been many people who wondered, when John McCain appeared on that show last week, just which lady he was standing next to) suggests that she is a finer mimic than she is an actress. Even on 30 Rock, she's notably funnier when she puts her glasses on. It seems that as a performer as well as a writer shes still operating by the scattershot (and often scatterbrain) methods of the show that launched her. 30 Rock aspires to be free-wheeling, and sometimes it succeeds. When it suddenly throws in a musical number, featuring an otherwise-wasted Jane Krakowski, the sheer incongruity can be delightful. Its also fond of little flash-forward vignettes like the ones on Family Guy. But if you're trying to be a cartoon, live actors can be an encumbrance; watching Baldwin's misadventures in Washington at the end of last season, I found myself thinking how much more savagely and economically bureaucracy used to be skewered on The Simpsons. Though I confess that with that show, the operative phrase is "used to be."

Jennifer Aniston is in next weeks episode, and she -- or to be charitable, her character -- is no less irritating than she was on Friends. 30 Rock is unhealthily fond of guest-stars; it seems like an admission that the regulars dont carry enough weight. (And it can be frustrating. It's always nice, of course, to see Edie Falco, but shouldn't she have better things to do with her time?) Its interesting that Seinfeld, which remains the nonpareil of network American sitcoms, hardly ever used them. It didnt need to, because it had four thoroughly grounded, idiosyncratic central characters. As a personality Fey often comes off as a cut-price Julia Louis-Dreyfus, but her function should probably be more that of Jerry Seinfeld: a comic by profession but, in practice, everybody else's incredulous straight guy. But that would necessitate there being an everybody else worth responding to, and a framework to support them. Yes, I did say the Seinfeld characters were grounded; their jobs, or the absence of them, carried conviction. It was also determinedly and refreshingly misanthropic, something 30 Rock, a true child of its age, never dares to be. It may have roots in TV "satire" shows and even, judging by its pace and setting, in classic screwball comedy, but there's never any threat. Everybody -- even Baldwin --is too busy making nice.

- 30 Rock airs tonight at 9:30 p. m. on Citytv.

2008-11-07-these-bullets-won-t-make-it-t:
How's this for a pedigree? The Black Rider, subtitled The Casting of the Magic Bullets and billed as a rock opera, is credited to Tom Waits, Robert Wilson andWilliamS. Burroughs. Their individual responsibilities are not disclosed, but the natural assumption is that Waits wrote the songs, Burroughs wrote the dialogue and Wilson, America's all-purpose theatrical visionary, came up with the concept and the original staging. The first English-language production was mounted in Edmonton in 1998 by a group called November Theatre, who have been touring and refining it ever since. It's their version, in what is announced as its final form, that has now been brought to Toronto.

I thought it 10% extraordinary and 90% tedious going on unbearable. To deal with the worst first: The piece derives (yet more pedigree) from a German folk tale that previously inspired, among other things, the non-rock opera Der Freischutz. It tells the story of a servant whose prowess as a marksman (he aimed at a stag to which was tied a wounded man, successfully shooting the stag while sparing the man) won him the title of Royal Huntsman. This post was passed through his descendants, until a daughter threatened to disgrace the family name by marrying a clerk; to prove himself a worthy shot, her beloved made, in effect, a deal with the devil, purchasing magic bullets with a fatal clause in the agreement.

This potentially haunting tale is obscured in the telling, partly by being narrated out of chronological order, and partly by being festooned with song, dance and movement that is sometimes effective and is sometimes just full of itself. The whole show is bent on proving how sinister it is. It comes with a frame, and not a terribly original one: The story is presented to us by a travelling fairground troupe so menacingly grotesque in themselves that their subject matter has a hard time measuring up. It's a freak show before it even gets started. Once under way, it takes a strenuously pseudo-Gothic view of people and events that is sometimes funny and more often merely mean.

Wilson is a venerated prophet of non-verbal theatre, so it's ironic that his ideas and his creations generally sound more interesting when he or someone else is describing them -- in words, of course -- than when they're actually experienced. Nothing gets more monotonous more quickly than the theatre of image, especially when the images are slow to change. The Black Rider, inescapably linear even if the lines are tangled, is far from being an extreme example of the genre; it has a lot of words, but they aren't all clear. Many of them, of course, occur in the songs. Waits has provided a jangling, commentative score that seems to take in everything except rock: There's operetta, folk and even some jaunty early jazz. The lyrics are foggy, doing little to further the action and not much to explain it. In short, they aren't very dramatic; which is disappointing since Waits, when he isn't writing for the theatre, is one of the few contemporary songwriters who might be able to. The show is all affekt (the German term seems appropriate), a matter of striking attitudes at the expense of narrative. Kevin Corey does have a nerd-ish appeal as the clerk, but in general you don't care enough about the characters even to wish them ill.

Now for the good stuff. Some of the attitudes, under Ron Jenkins' direction, are very impressive. Marie Nychka, the choreographer, has staged a wild ball. Much of the singing is muggy, but Michael Scholar Jr., as the diabolic tempter named Peg Leg, cuts through the haze with a ringing solo that warms up the theatre while chilling the blood. Rachael Johnston is marvellous as the heroine, especially when sharing a duet with her intended, he hiding under her skirts, she -- we have to assume -- standing on his shoulders. (This makes hers a literally towering performance.) Finally, within sight of the end, there's a slow-motion death-fall, hilarious and horrific at once, that comes as close as anything I've seen to making manifest the inexorable. It should invade the dreams of everyone who sees it. - The Black Rider runs until Nov. 16. Call 416-531-1827 for ticket and information.
