2008-11-08-sisters-are-doing-it-for-them:
The best parts of Soulpepper's production of Top Girls are better than ever. This includes the opening dinner-party scene, a festive gathering unlike any other in modern drama. (Or ancient drama, probably.) Marlene, who's just been promoted to managing director of a London employment agency, plays host to a collection of iconic women, real and fictitious, from earlier historical periods, whose travails and triumphs have, as she sees it, paved the way for her own success.

That's as may be. Marlene's trajectory and her personality seem brittle and superficial compared to those of her guests. Or maybe that's just the 1980s for you, that being the decade from which Caryl Churchill's play speaks to us, loudly if not always clearly. Anyway, what one responds to initially is the playwright's nerve in imagining such a scene, her wit in bringing it to life and the amazing ensemble strength of the performers. Their interplay in Alisa Palmer's production is pitch-perfect and fingertip-precise, especially when it comes to maintaining their lines of thought through the overlapping dialogue that increasingly dominates the festive board. What materializes is a delicate balance of acceptance and revolt. The most delicate of all is Robyn Stevan's Japanese court concubine, glorying in the small revenges she was able to take on her lord and master while accepting the system that he (literally) embodied. Broader fun comes from Ann-Marie MacDonald's Pope Joan, cheerily recalling how she was dragged from her horse and stoned to death when her gender was detected, and from Liisa Repo-Martell as Breughel's Dull Gret, virtually silent and stuffing unaccustomed delicacies, such as bread, into her bag as insurance against the bad times. And for total silence, there is Diana Donnelly's waitress, the only figure from Marlene's own time and a vivid reminder that, even in her world, not all girls are top girls. Or especially in her world.

The rest of the play rams this point home. It consists of short scenes from Marlene's own life and times, some domestic, some professional. The latter are largely devoted to interviews conducted by Marlene and two of her colleagues with prospective clients. These were always the weakest parts of the production (not counting its fragmenting decision to have two intermissions), and they haven't improved. They're written pretty much like revue sketches, so they demand absolute precision. The English accents are spot-on; this show's unsung heroine may be Diane Pitblado, the dialect coach. But the tone and pacing are off, and with them go the specifics of the question the play poses: whether these women, competing and sometimes succeeding in a male-dominated world, are taking on its worst characteristics (and thereby betraying the foremothers they boast about). It's a question that, in the Britain of 1982, had taken corporeal form in the person of Margaret Thatcher, whose famous words about there being no such thing as "society," adorn this production's set. There's no comparable figure now; we tried on the first night to close our eyes and think of Sarah Palin or even of Stephen Harper (ideologically a closer fit) but neither quite fills the bill. The play's politics are still pertinent, just as its form is still audacious, but neither comes as a surprise now.

Thatcher is explicitly invoked in the last of the play's domestic scenes; she's extolled by Marlene, excoriated by Marlene's sister Joyce (the perfect name, for some reason) whom Marlene, proudly metropolitan, is visiting in the rural village where they grew up. Joyce is raising Marlene's unacknowledged daughter Angie, who embodies the play's conflicts. She worships her glamorous, successful "aunt," but when she runs away to London, it's plain that London -- Marlene's London, anyway -- has no place for her. The Top Girls Agency could never find her a job; and Marlene (behind Angie's back, mercifully) is the first and coldest to say so. The scenes back at Joyce's place are brilliantly, suggestively written and brilliantly, suggestively played. First we see Angie hiding out in the backyard with a suspiciously younger friend: a hauntingly believable duet, this, between Cara Pifko and Repo-Martell, whose defiant, unhappy Angie is the counterpart of her Dull Gret, deserving more than the world will give her. Then, earlier in time but in the play's last scene, there's the duel, bitter but shot through with the remnants of sisterly understanding, between Marlene and Joyce, whose idea of political protest is to scratch the bodywork of posh cars. Top Girls is hardly a detailed naturalistic play, but these scenes, with their echoes of past conflicts, serve notice that Churchill could write an excellent one if she felt like it. As Marlene, Megan Follows, the one actress to play a single role, has lost some sharpness of definition but still fires fiercely on all cylinders. Kelli Fox's Joyce, her voice and stance aggressively akimbo, is the final panel in a triumphant triptych; in the first scene, she's been Isabella Bird, a Scots Victorian traveller paradoxically devoted to her homebody sister, and in the middle, she's the begging wife of the male colleague Marlene has displaced, a figure who in one brief scene sums up any number of contradictions. All three characterizations are perfectly judged and perfectly pitched: vocally, physically, stylistically. If there can be a first in this cast of equals, then she's the top.

- Top Girls continues at the Young Centre for the Performing Arts until Nov. 22. Call 416-866-8666 for ticket information.

THEATRE REVIEW

Emilia Galotti

Avon Theatre, Stratford, Ont.

This year's Stratford Festival -- uneven as they all are, but with an unusually high proportion of peaks -- concluded with something from abroad. This was a bold and welcome initiative. Its also, things being as they economically are, one thats unlikely to be repeated in a hurry. Pity.

The Deutsches Theater of Berlin brought us their much-travelled, much-heralded and much-reduced production of Emilia Galotti, a five-act drama by Gotthold Ephraim Lessing, here clocking in at a brisk 90 minutes, many of them devoid of dialogue. Lessing's play dates from 1772; it's a bourgeois tragedy about a prince who falls helplessly in lust with a daughter of the middle classes, the titular Emila, on the day shes about to marry someone else. An over-zealous chamberlain arranges to have the maiden abducted, her fiance winding up as collateral damage. Once he has her in his lair, the prince seems uncertain how to proceed; these arent the Middle Ages after all. Surprisingly, Emilia is allowed visits from her parents, who never had much time for aristocrats anyway. Their resentments are greatly encouraged by the prince's scorned fury of an ex-mistress, who gives Emilia's father a dagger for a present, and more or less tells him to get on with it. The play, at least in this version, ends up quite literally dancing on a knife-edge.

Michael Thalheimers production begins, also literally, with fireworks, presumably symbolizing the explosions taking place in the characters heads. It concludes with the heroine picking her way through a stage-full of elegantly swirling couples, none of whom we have seen before, and none of whom is permitted to take a final bow alongside the seven principals. (European actors sure love their curtain calls.) One wondered whether the dancing help had been flown over, or whether they were locally recruited, perhaps from imminently unemployed members of the Festival's company.

Between these bookend coups, the action unfolds in a long bare room with a single door at the back. It's anything but palatial, and theres nothing extravagant or historical about the costumes, either. The received wisdom on this production is that its banished the play's social conflicts in favour of the animal passions beneath. I only buy half of that. Emotion here is certainly front and centre, climbing up the walls and rolling all over the floor, but that doesn't banish the matter of class. Its built-in. Sven Lehmanns prince, poleaxed by his thwarted desire for a girl he's just seen in church, throws himself on the ground and thrashes about in agonies of frustration only available to someone who's been accustomed from birth to having anything he wants. Similarly, the chamberlain Marinelli (Ingo Hulsmann) ties himself into vocal and physical knots in which obsequiousness is bound up with imperturbability. He acts the perfect servant as if his life depended on it, which it very likely does, but the mask cant help slipping. Marinelli is one of those supporting characters who thinks the play should really be about him, and resentment is the natural result.

Its all excitingly theatrically, though it means that Lehmann has to go on graphically demonstrating that the prince is smitten long after we've gotten the message. A program note congratulating Thalheimer on his tried and trusted radicalism (isn't there a contradiction in there somewhere?) claims that, in his hands, the play is about "the failure of communication." Well, show me the play that isnt. Its true that what remains of the text in this production is raced through, with the actors jumping on lines that denote contradiction or misunderstanding, and that much is made of the royal lackey's misconstruing of his master's orders --or at least of his master, in time-honoured handwashing fashion, pretending that he has. But its also true that these actors arent concealing their feelings. They're letting them all hang out, in a manner rarely witnessed in polite company.

At least the men are. The women are more sphinx-like, and they're a fascinating pair. We never quite know what Regine Zimmermanns rail-thin Emilia is thinking or how much of a victim she is; she could be passive or calculating or just enduring. Probably shes all three. We can see what's driving Nina Hoss's cast-off countess (the rank is important). Shes a wonderfully poised and elegant figure, ravaged with jealousy, but exactly how much destruction she intends to wreak is left in doubt. The production is underscored with a single, almost continuous waltz; when it stops, the relief is brief and the silence even more oppressive.

It would be interesting to see this ruthless concentration applied to an English Jacobean play: The Changeling, say, or Tis Pity She's a Whore, to both of which this play bears some narrative resemblance. This is not the balanced, humane Lessing, Enlightenment personified, to whom Soulpepper introduced us with their production of his Nathan the Wise. (He must have been a good guy; he was the father of modern criticism.)One would like to encounter this play in its entirety some time, just to be sure. But if Thalheimer and his troupe have selected, I don't think they've distorted. This time around, Lessing is more.

THEATRE REVIEW

Kindertransport

Al Green Theatre, Miles Nadal JCC, Toronto

If there's anything more infallibly wrenching than a play that touches on the Holocaust, it's a play that touches on the Holocaust and involves children. Kindertransport falls into that second category, and there are scenes in it that duly make the heart pound and the eyes ache. For all that, it's a simplistic and half-baked piece.

This production, by the Harold Green Jewish Theatre Company, is the Canadian premiere of a British play by Diane Samuels that was first seen in London in 1993. The kindertransport was a scheme that evacuated Jewish children from Germany in the brief window between Kristallnacht and the outbreak of war, placing them with households in Britain and America. Eva, later Evelyn, is sent from Hamburg to live with a family in Manchester. We see Eva's birth mother sending her away; we see her meeting her adoptive mother and the development of their deep if sometimes fractious relationship; and we see the adult and anglicized Evelyn in later life, coping -- or failing to -- with her own college-aged daughter, who has Just Found Out. Scenes from the three time frames are played out contrapuntally.

Eva brings with her from Germany a storybook about the Rat-Catcher of Hamelin, who seems to be related to the Pied Piper, but is even more sinister; certainly he's a figure designed to scare children, and Eva/ Evelyn grows up mentally linking him to the Nazis. She herself might be suitable prey for a pack rat catcher. She can never throw anything away, and it's in her attic in London (where she's moved from up north) that her daughter Faith eventually comes upon the book. We hear it being read aloud, simultaneously, in the late 1930s and in the early 1980s, when the pfennig drops. This trite device is the kind of thing you might expect to find in an earnest instructional play for children. In fact something similar was used, only more imaginatively and effectively, in the stage version of Hana's Suitcase a couple of years ago at the Young People's Theatre in Toronto.

The author, according to her program note, based her script on three actual sets of memories, and it does have a composite feel about it, as if it were trying to take disparate stories, of survivors and their children, and make them fit together. The play gives us three overlapping sets of mothers and daughters, and it's at its best when tracing the interaction of Eva and her substitute parent Lil. This is a relation coloured by historical circumstances but not determined by them, meaning that the relevant scenes have a life of their own that doesn't necessarily cohere with the rest of the play. They are bridged to some extent by the performance of Jennifer Dzialoszynski who plays Eva, with complete physical and emotional authenticity, right up to the brink of adulthood. She shows us a girl by turns frightened, joyful, bewildered and stubborn, always loving or at least seeking love, and rather scary when circumstances lead her to rebuff it when it comes in unpalatable form. You can see why Lil, played by Patricia Hamilton with an admirable blend of sternness and forbearance, should be more drawn to Eva than she seems to be to her own flesh-and-blood daughters (whom we never meet): This one needs her more, and needs her more demandingly. And when history does intrude, notably when the two of them blunder into watching a newsreel

on the liberation of the camps, it does so economically and believably.

Other relationships in Christopher Newton's production are less convincing. Corinne Koslo as the grown-up Evelyn is fine (no Canadian actress can muster a more authentic North of England accent) until we realize who she's meant to be, at which point we -- or anyway I -- stop believing. The younger Eva may have been touchy at times; her older self is nothing but prickles, which may be acceptable in theory but not in practice. Some blame attaches to the thinness of the writing, which reduces the characters to attitudes, and more to the third-generation performance of Jenny Young, which is pitched on a single belligerent note; you might say, given her character's name, that she's going through a permanent crisis of Faith. Nancy Beatty has difficulty conveying the torment of a German-Jewish mother sending her child away, likely forever, and is thoroughly defeated by a later scene in which the two of them flatly refuse to listen to one another. Again, there's a valid idea there but it's worked out so crudely that credibility crumbles.

Fathers and husbands are kept strictly off stage; the one male actor, Anthony Bekenn, is billed as the symbolic Rat-Catcher but actually appears as a series of officials -- German and English, terrifying or benevolent or in-between -- whom he renders as a series of neat music-hall sketches. These include a wartime postman, mentally lumping Jews with Germans as undesirable aliens and refusing to hear the difference. (This does make a point.) Cameron Porteous, perhaps in reference to the triple time-scheme, has designed a three-arched set that works well for the several scenes that are set in railway stations (with announcements recorded, I suspect, by the director himself ), less well for the more numerous scenes that are supposed to go on in confined spaces like the all-important attic. There are also projections, which are helpful in letting us know where we are but are not especially atmospheric; at the preview I attended, they vanished temporarily due to a computer breakdown, and I don't think that the play suffered much from their absence. I suspect that this play would work best in an intimate theatre with a minimum of design. - Kindertransport is at the Harold Green Theatre until Nov. 23. For tickets and information call 416-366-7723 or visit hgjewishtheatre.com.

2008-11-14-an-austen-by-any-other-name-i:
That indefatigable screenwriter Jane Austen is at it again, this time in semi-modern dress. Lost in Austen is based on Pride and Prejudice, but it isn't a straight adaptation in BBC classic-serial style. Nor is it a wholesale updating in the manner of the movie Clueless, which re-worked Austen's Emma as a story of Beverly Hills. It's something in-between and quirkier.

Its heroine, who has the very Austen-ish name of Amanda Price, is a contemporary West Londoner in her twenties who's hooked on Austen in general and Pride and Prejudice in particular. She pines for the gentler manners depicted in her idol's novels, and especially for their courtlier courtships: Understandably, as when her own live-in swain gets around to proposing marriage, his fond words are swallowed up in a beer-sodden burp. She gets small comfort from her mother who urges her to settle for the available male in a manner that may put you in mind -- and certainly puts Amanda in mind -- of the matchmaking Mrs. Bennet. So when the bewitching Elizabeth Bennet, everybody's favourite heroine, materializes in Amanda's bathroom, Amanda is primed, if incredulous. After a certain amount of backchat about the differences between fact and fiction, Amanda ventures through Elizabeth's magic portal. Elizabeth does not come with her. Amanda finds herself an uninvited guest in the Bennet household, regarded by its inhabitants with a mixture of fascination, suspicion and outright resentment. It shouldn't happen to a dog.

As a matter of fact, it has happened to a dog. There used to be--maybe still is --a highly literate hound on children's TV called Wishbone, who week after week insinuated himself into classic stories without any of the human actors noticing the difference. In one episode he played Mr. Darcy, the aloof charmer who eventually wins Elizabeth, or whom Elizabeth eventually wins. Lost in Austen is more ambitiously, self-consciously intertextual.

Amanda suspects at first that she has wandered into some elaborate TV set-up. Encountering a Darcy rather less charming

than the one she has envisioned, she muses: "He's not Colin Firth. But even Colin Firth wasn't Colin Firth. They had to change the shape of his head with makeup." Amanda has certainly read the book -- she has the well-thumbed Penguin Classic to prove it --but she's equally affected by seeing it on film and TV. Confronted by some of the realities of 18th-century English life, she is taken somewhat aback. She also discovers that, in those days, Alaska was known as "Russian America." I don't know if this was actually the case, or if it's just a serendipitously topical invention of the author's.

The larger joke depends, of course, on our knowledge of the original; and it's one that might not work with any other classic novel. Only Oliver Twist still has the same degree of popular currency -- it has the advantage of having been a hit musical, but its nightmare landscape can hardly compare with Austen's as a receptacle for romantic wish-fulfilment. Guy Andrews' script does an excellent job of simultaneously inflating and puncturing the dream. He has an excellent ear for both Austen's idiom and Amanda's, though he might perhaps have credited his heroine with more of his own sensitivity; for one so steeped in the books, she takes few pains to avoid shocking and confusing her companions.

The humour of incongruity holds up delightfully in the first episode. In the second, the show starts to dig deeper, with results whose satisfactoriness has yet to be determined. Amanda has come in at the start of the story and she knows how it is supposed to end. However, with her presence and Elizabeth's absence, things start to go differently. She falls ever so slightly for Mr. Bingley, the destined mate of Elizabeth's sister, Jane, and he for her. But one detour leads to another with at least one startling and distressing result. How are they going to work their way out of that one? Maybe they won't.

Jemima Rooper is a perfect Amanda, pert and puzzled. Hugh Bonneville makes Mr. Bennet, sardonically resigned to not being master in his own house, into the most amusing and engaging character around, and Alex Kingston expands on the traditional gushing portrayal of Elizabeth, giving her claws. Guy Henry is a greasy beanpole as the fawning parson Mr. Collins, even more unsavoury in the flesh, as Amanda observes, than on the page.

Amanda has impressed the impoverished gentry with her income of Pounds 27,000 a year, and by the fact that she "rents in Hammersmith." That area has changed since my day, but not as much obviously as it has since the Bennets', who, misconstruing Amanda's slang, refer to its "otter-strewn thoroughfares." Elizabeth, presumably, is still exploring them. It had better not turn out to be a dream. - Lost in Austen airs Sunday at 8 p. m. on VIVA.
2008-11-15-the-trouble-with-being-teache:
The title character of Bashir Lazhar is a substitute teacher. He's standing in for at least two people, both of them women. One is his immediate predecessor in a Montreal classroom, who met a violent end by which her Grade 6 students are still, as both he and we assume, traumatized. The other is the wife whom he, a refugee, left behind with their own children in Algeria. She was a teacher, while he worked in a cafe. Her influence on him, his inheritance from her, are among several things that this 75-minute one-man play leaves unexplored or undeveloped. But what we do have is written with such sympathy and charm, and performed with such grace and power, that even our frustration rebounds to the plays credit. Were involved.

Evelyne de la Cheneliere's play begins with Bashir practising his first words to his class, trying out introductions stern, jovial, friendly or outright ingratiating. Just telling them his name is a challenge. Finally, he just chalks it up on the board and also, you feel, chalks it up to experience.

Under beautifully modulated direction from Jennifer Tarver, Raoul Bhaneja conveys the paradox of a man who feels himself in some sense a fraud but also realizes that he is in the one situation he was born for. The air of confidence he wears in class ceases to be a mask; talking to these children he knows who he is, even if his expectations of them seem unrealistically high. ("I'm going to read you a paragraph from Balzacs The Wild Asss Skin-- I'm sure you all know it.) But he wins them over, one of them at least, a girl who delivers an outstanding assignment on the meaning of violence, a subject that resonates on both sides of the desk. One of the outstanding achievements of the performance and the production is their ability to conjure up the presence of unseen characters; watching Bhaneja, you really feel as if you are in that classroom.

You are almost equally convinced by his dealings with the refugee board, to whom he presents a case beyond tears and soaked in angry irony, and with an increasingly unsympathetic (and, one imagines, stony-faced) school principal. The more he arouses his pupils' feelings, and his own, the more suspicion he arouses in staff and parents. He reaches out, clumsily, to a female colleague who he momentarily thought was reaching out to him. He chides his classs aspirations to study Spanish, suggesting that before learning a second language they should master their first. But he himself is teaching in, and therefore, of necessity, learning, a second language, and this gives a formality, and an extra layer of meaning, to everything he says.

The plays time-scheme isn't altogether clear. Some of it clearly flashes back to before the start of Bashir's teaching career, but its hard to work out how much. Are his worst stresses past or present? We have a character whos totally engaging from moment to moment, but in a cloudy context. Even the vaunted theme of violence and the response to it hangs somewhat in the air, undefined. But Bhaneja's body language -- the way he can suddenly spin around; the way he moves a chair in the principal's office, pretending to an assurance he cannot feel -- is as meaningful as his words. These can sometimes be very funny, intentionally or otherwise. Jokes," he sternly tells his class, "arent an excuse to stop working; and in Morwyn Brebners first-rate translation -- her second this year, following her sublime version of The President at the Shaw Festival -- they do a lot of work. The play is also a moving essay in what may be the most moving of themes: the potential, so often wasted or abused, for joy in childhood. This play centres on, and is performed by, a man, but its author, translator and director are all women. I don't know how much to read into that, but in addition to carrying an unbearable personal burden, Bashir can never shake the feeling of being a substitute's substitute. Hearing at the end of the play of another, female, teacher, he remarks with a kind of crushed approval that shell be maternal." Theres a lot going on in this play, not all of it realized, but the theme of what children and their various guardians need and deserve comes through beautifully.

- Bashir Lazhar runs through Dec. 7 at the Tarragon Extra Space. Call 416-531-1827 for more information.

2008-11-20-a-midsummer-s-night-sex-theat:
A program note for this new Canadian adaptation of Miss Julie reminds us that in 1888, when August Strindberg's original play was first published, it was described as "filthy," "debauched" and "repulsive." (And this in what we think of as permissive Sweden. But maybe things were different back then.) The same note goes on to remark, quite accurately, that in performance the play never turns out to be as much fun as those adjectives suggest. This production sets out to restore some of the excitement. Despite all kinds of deficiencies, it succeeds.

Miss Julie: Sheh'mah takes its new suffix from a First Nations word meaning "white person." The Canadian Miss Julie, like her Nordic namesake, is a rich man's daughter surrounded by servants. In this case the servants (in her word and theirs) are Indians. We meet two of them: the absent master's valet, here named Jonny, and his fiancee, Christie Ann the cook, in whose kitchen the action takes place. Just outside there's a party going on, and it's got Miss Julie very hot. During the course of the night -- in Strindberg's it's Midsummer's Eve -- she and Jonny, each of them with a barrelful of issues, have sex while ChristieAnn slumbers next door. It's her first time; it certainly isn't his, as he takes brutal pleasure in informing her. They make frantic plans to run away together, maybe open a hotel. The plans are dashed when the lady reveals that she has no money of her own. He slinks back into service; she, having passed through disillusion and degradation (in her own mind, at least) takes the traditional heroic way out.

The play has been re-set in the 1920s, so we are not, despite the attendant rhetoric, getting a full update. Kick Theatre, the new company responsible, announces itself in another note as "devoted to producing catalytic, dynamic theatre that reintroduces audiences to the cathartic power of the stage." That's a lot to take on. It also presumes a catharsis-starved audience, desperate to get its kicks from Kick. That sounds patronizing, as does the assumption that the audience would be unable to appreciate the tensions underlying Miss Julie unless those tensions are dug up and deposited in their own backyard. We've all read books, seen plays and watched movies depicting masters and servants. We have historical imaginations. We know about class. We can relate.

It may be splitting hairs, but I suspect that what happens in transplants like this one is that the actors relate to something immediate to them, and the audience picks up on that. Kick is right about one thing: Most translations of Strindberg are awful. Tara Beagan, credited as "play-re-wright" (a new word on me, and one that I'm not crazy to meet again) and herself part-Native, has come up with a text that has awkwardnesses of its own, but is mostly direct and dynamic. Part of this is certainly due to the added bite of making the social distinctions racial as well: something that illuminates Miss Julie's masochistic fascination as well as Jonny and Christie Ann's well-voiced resentments. But more of it comes from making the sex more explicit, verbally and visually, than Strindberg would have dared, though probably not more than he would have liked. Artistic choices merge with budgetary necessities. The play unfolds in real time; in the original merrymaking extras burst onto the stage while the lovers are presumed to be going at it in the wings. Here the party animals remain out of sight, while Jonny and Julie couple in plain view, violently and convincingly. It makes sense of a lot of things.

Melee Hutton's production has trouble with matters like getting people persuasively in and out of doors, but it keeps a firm grip on emotional temperature. This is despite some alarming unevenness in the acting. Christine Horne obviously knows what the pale and driven Miss Julie, in all her quivering self-destructive delicacy, is about, but in a play full of long speeches, she is embarrassingly unable to give shape or variety to any lasting more than a couple of lines. (She also does some strange physical things, like nearly strangling herself with a shawl that seems to be doubling as a blanket, and sliding off a bed with a pronounced bump.) Darrell Dennis has more technical command, as well as a sullen bravado that's right for Jonny; one thing that neither the original nor this adaptation does is to glorify the oppressed. But he swallows many of his words and, on the first night, stumbled over more. (The whole show, in fact, seemed under-rehearsed.) Gail Maurice infuses Christie Ann, who knows very well what the other two are up to, with an appealing air of tolerant disdain in her first scene, but she too fails to sustain. Teresa Przybylski's wood-lined set has a touch of setting to it, as if paying homage to the original Scandinavian location as well as the new British Columbian one.

And I have to confess: I have seen Miss Julie done by the top classical companies in Britain and Canada, in productions that were technically superior to this one; none of them held my attention as this one did. - Miss Julie: Sheh'mah is at The Theatre Centre until Nov. 29. For tickets and information call 416-538-0988.

2008-11-22-agent-of-change-jack-bauer-wi:
Redemption is all the rage in television's high-end action serials. Much of last week's episode of Prison Break was a requiem for Brad Bellick, the sweaty and scummy prison corrections officer who made life hell for his charges in Season 1, went completely rogue in Season 2, underwent innumerable humiliations when he himself was imprisoned in Season 3 and, having been thus purged, met a hero's end in the current Season 4. I shall miss Brad, if only for the pleasure of wondering whether he would revert to his previous rat status or make the ultimate sacrifice for the team. It had to be one or the other. He had been one of the show's more colourful characters, but it was painfully obvious that the authors had run out of things for him to do. But nobody could say they didn't give him a send-off.

On a grander scale, the writers of 24 seem to have been having the same problem with Jack Bauer. He ended Season 5 a broken man: lost his girlfriend, his confidence and apparently his vocation. He's coming back for a sixth season, but before that -- tomorrow night, in fact -- we get a two-hour special, bridging the gap between his last adventures and his next: a prequel to the sequel. It's set mainly in Africa, and it's actually called 24: Redemption.

So what does Jack need to be redeemed from? On one level it seems clear. Early in this show, a U. S. official arrives to serve Jack with a subpoena, one that has apparently been chasing him half-way around the world. The substance is that he broke the rules in his days as a counter-terrorist agent. More plainly, he tortured people. Kiefer Sutherland's Jack, looking as defiantly haggard as he has ever been when not actually being tortured himself and still doing most of his acting in a whisper, says that he will answer to his own conscience, which does indeed seem to be getting plenty of exercise. He gets ready to skip town (or, in this case, a small settlement) but is derailed, not for the first time, by the demands of a crisis greater than his own.

The country in which we and the U. S. legal system discover Jack bears the fictitious name of Sengala. In the past, 24 has left countries, mainly Middle Eastern ones, discreetly unnamed but this is the first time it has invented one, and it pokes a small hole in the show's admittedly fragile credibility. Sengala sounds like an anagram but is more of an amalgam: It combines some of the more brutal aspects, recent past and present, of Congo, Uganda, Rwanda, and Zimbabwe. There's a civil war on. A powerful prologue shows young boys being rounded up to serve in a rebel army, trained to regard their opponents as "cockroaches" (i. e. stooges for white oppressors) and to execute them. Jack is helping out an old buddy (Robert Carlyle) who's running a school. First, the two men have to protect their charges from being rounded up and turned into cannon-fodder. Then, with minimal help from the U. S. government and none at all from the United Nations, they have to somehow shepherd them to the capital, before that old 24 real-time window closes shut and the embassy is evacuated. To make it happen, Jack may have to surrender himself.

In the course of this self-imposed duty, Jack kills people (this is hardly a spoiler), but he doesn't beat anybody up. So he may already be on the road to reform and eventual atonement. His previous activities have,

of course, become notorious in the world outside TV fiction; his name has been bizarrely invoked to justify the current U. S. administration's own coercion practices. As has often been pointed out, there's a disconnect here; the "ticking-bomb" interrogation scenario favoured in 24 never seems to occur in the real world. What's less often mentioned is that it works both ways. Jack's fictitious activities can't really be condemned by the standards of real political life. With him, it's usually personal; the first time he brutalized anyone onscreen, it was to discover the whereabouts of his kidnapped wife and daughter, and I doubt if anybody blamed him. And in later examples, the situation has usually -- not quite always -- been engineered to show that he had no other choice. The show has found it convenient to portray him from time to time as weighed down by guilt, but it's never been very specific about the causes. What Jack probably feels worst about is his wife's death, which wasn't his fault. Earlier this year, I talked with Jon Cassar, one of the show's senior writer-producers, who admitted this vagueness, but promised it would be addressed in the coming season with Jack, the Dirty Harry of counterterrorism, emerging in his vaunted guise of tragic hero.

What awaits him on the home front is anyone's guess. The special is divided between the African action, exciting and self-contained, and the American, which seems to be a cryptic set-up for familiar things to come. Washington is as much of a cesspool as ever, though the show that pre-empted history by giving us a black president may be doing it again by giving us a female one. The episode shows us Cherry Jones, one of New York's premier stage actresses, getting sworn in, with our own Colm Feore hovering as First Dude. The lady shows signs of being as idealistic a C-in-C as was the late David Palmer, but her immediate predecessor (Powers Boothe, still massively alarming) has warned her that things change once you're in office. I don't know whether we'll be seeing more of him, but his right hand man (Peter MacNicol, the honourable weasel) will presumably still be around. We don't as yet get to meet anyone else we know, but it seems certain that, though CTU itself is no more, the fabulous Chloe will return, one hopes with better material than last season, as will the beloved Tony Almeda. So what if we saw him decisively killed onscreen; if Prison Break can resurrect a beheaded heroine, anything is possible. The two shows have in fact become very similar; Prison Break has made increasing use of torture as a plot-device, and even as a cathartic one, and both pit a loner, or a small band of loners, against a conspiracy aiming at world domination and infiltrating the higher reaches of government; 24 has recruited Jon Voight as its new mastermind. Both seem to be written and constructed on a succession of whims, and believability flew out of both their casements a long time ago. Both have characters who at least started out interesting, and on whom one can never quite give up. Both, despite everything, are the pulp TV to which I remain most hopelessly addicted. Perhaps I, too, am awaiting redemption. - 24: Redemption airs tomorrow at 8 p. m. ET/PT on Global, E! and Fox. Prison Break airs Monday at 8 p. m. ET/PT on Global and Fox.

It's been three years since Company Theatre made their astonishing debut with A Whistle in the Dark, a great Irish play for which they imported Irish director Jason Byrne. They have now brought him back to stage an Anglo-Scandinavian play, an occasion that only falls short of the previous one because the play itself does. It's still an extraordinary production with moments, sometimes whole sequences, of unsettling brilliance.

Festen is a stage version, by British playwright David Eldridge, of the 1997 Danish film of the same name, its script credited to Thomas Vinterberg (who directed the movie), Mogens Rukov and Bo hr. Hansen. It was released here as The Celebration, and if you smell irony there, you are right. Like A Whistle in the Dark (and indeed, on a smaller scale, Company Theatre's intermediate production Marion Bridge), Festen is a family drama, though hardly family entertainment. Helge is a rich man much into lodges; he is a Freemason and he also owns a hunting lodge. Helge's family -- less extended in the play than in the movie, for obvious reasons -- has assembled there for his 60th birthday. His two sons have followed him into the hospitality business, Christian, the elder, far more successfully than his brother Michael, who is embittered about it and about nearly everything else. He's a drunk and a wife-abuser. Christian isn't happy, either. They have a sister, Helene, a defensively free spirit who isn't ageing well, and they had another sister, Christian's twin, who recently committed suicide in her bath. All told, this must be the most dysfunctional Danish family to appear on a stage since the royal gang at Elsinore.

The text makes explicit allusion to Hamlet and to Hitchcock, both relevant sources. The latter yields a teasing mixture of propriety and suspense, the former a watery death, rumblings of incest and a hero given to guilting his relatives. Christian, rising at dinner to propose a toast to his father, opens a can of worms and flings it in the old man's face. The guests do their practiced best to pretend nothing is happening, but as the night proceeds and as morning takes over, the effort grows increasingly hard. No one can leave because the chef, Christian's best buddy, has thoughtfully removed their car keys. Community singing is the principal recourse; a raucous local equivalent of Happy Birthday is repeatedly struck up, and when Helene produces a black boyfriend, everyone joins in a merry racist chant.

The screen Festen is the best-known product of Denmark's Dogme group, whose puritan gospel enjoins handheld cameras, no extraneous music and strict location shooting. Byrne's production goes for a theatrical equivalent -- minimal furnishings, stage open to the bare brick walls, all stage lighting from visible lamps, house lights full on throughout -- that is actually the direct opposite. Lack of artifice is an artifice in itself, in either medium, but in the theatre you really see it. A single bed stands in for three bedrooms, simultaneously. Guests sit on chairs more spartan than you'd find at any posh party or any posh hotel. (The film prided itself on giving you the real thing.) I'm not complaining. This unlivable set (designer, John Thompson; lighting, Andrea Lundy) is thoroughly lived-in. Byrne is noted for not giving his actors set blocking; moves may vary from night to night. This works enormously well for a play whose characters are constantly required to react, or not, to the unbearable or the incredible. Each has to find his or her own way; and at the preview I saw, they all did. A small girl (Isabelle Lobo) eats her way with serene dedication through her elders' turmoil. Grandpa (Gary Reineke) favours the assembly with a fixed senile smile. The whole table gets up and plays a grimly funny game of nonmusical chairs. This isn't anarchy. The performances and the relationships are rooted.

They're less firmly rooted than in Whistle, because the text gives them less help. As in the film, you're left wondering what it's all for. Are we only here to see, yet again, the bourgeoisie exposed, the elders rotten, the youngers maimed? Probably yes. These characters don't just have skeletons in their closets; they're skeletons themselves. But they certainly rattle with style. Eric Peterson's Helge is more tetchy than tyrannical, if he carried more weight, the play might. Rosemary Dunsmore, though, is superb as his wife, alternately soothing and goading her offspring in a set speech dripping with poisoned politesse. (It's the high point of the play as it was of the film.) Allan Hawco and Philip Riccio, the company's founders, again play brothers, Hawco weak and vicious (last time he was strong and vicious), Riccio an ambiguous avenger. Caroline Cave is rather wasted as Michael's wife, who gives near as good as she gets but has to give most of it early. Tara Rosling transforms herself as Helene; as her nerves go, she seems more and more like a Nordic Janice Soprano. And so it goes, down a fine line that includes Earl Pastko's implacable maitre d' and Nicholas Campbell's understandably depressed tycoon. The entire cast is on red alert. This is about as close as we'll get to pure theatre, with all the limitations that implies and all the excitement. - Festen runs until Dec. 13 at the Berkeley Street Theatre. For ticket information, call 416-368-3110.

2008-11-29-the-relationships-worth-remem:
Theatre Passe Muraille's fall season of theatrical miniatures is now on its second leg. In one evening you can catch two shows, one in each of this theatres spaces.

On the main stage, theres Trudeau Stories, Brooke Johnson's unexpectedly engaging memoir of her relationship with the former prime minister, whom she met soon after he became former. It happened 20 years ago at the National Theatre School in Montreal; she was a final-year acting student, and he was a distinguished visitor at the school's fundraising ball. She, like most of her fellows, couldnt afford a ticket, but she got in as a student rep. Shed once asked Trudeau for an autograph, and he remembered. He asked her for a dance. It went well, though with some slight embarrassment on her part (she had toilet-paper stuffed inside her borrowed shoes) and they became friends. He was remarkably assiduous about returning her phone calls. They went to bars and restaurants together, discussed poetry, went on hikes. They did not become lovers, though there may have been a subterranean spark. She acknowledges, in the first of her many letters to him (so she kept copies?), that he has a reputation and she draws boundaries.

His attitude to her, meanwhile, emerges as not quite paternal, but paternally flavoured. He shows concern for her welfare and her career. He's intrigued by the theatre, even asks to attend a rehearsal, as if it were an area he would like to have cultivated, but for which he never had enough time. If they talked much about politics, we never get to hear of it. He just seems to have liked her. So do we.

For one thing, she's a credit to her old school. Her past professional work has made this abundantly clear, but its in especially sharp focus here. She talks to us, with a naturalness thats 90% complete, while also enacting a series of visual images of how she was -- and, sometimes, how he was -- at the time. It's like turning the pages of a live snapshot album; at the end of Allyson McMackon's production, as she recalls her reaction to the news of her old friends death, she replays them for us, at top speed, one after the other. What comes through, with a maximum of craft but a minimum of artifice, is a portrait of an especially attractive kind of young Canadian woman, forthright but reserved, humorously aware, as relayed by her older self. What comes through is not Trudeaus personality or even his fame, but their impact on someone who never expected to find herself exposed to them but kept her head and came to take them for granted. As history, it's just a footnote to a footnote. As autobiographical performance, it's delightful and, at just over an hour, doesnt outstay its welcome.

"This is a theatre. Youre only allowed to use the F-word if you're pretending to be poor." That observation, the sharpest piece of theatrical commentary I've heard all year, is proffered by Penny Lamb, teenager, to her younger brother, Ezra, who needs it. They are the two characters of Legoland, written by Jacob Richmond, co-directed by the author and Britt Small who is also ultra-democratically the stage manager, and originated by Atomic Vaudeville, from Victoria. The young Lambs grew up in a throwback hippie colony; Legoland is the name given by its inhabitants to everything outside their own walls, or whatever they have in place of walls. Penny and Ezra used to sneak out to visit it, and their escapades led to the fuzz (one anachronism deserves another) following them home and arresting everybody for growing stuff. Penny and Ezra were thrown into a Catholic boarding school, where Ezra, hyper-intelligent or at least hyper-articulate, developed AHDD while Penny was reviled, by the other girls and the staff, as a lesbian, which they use as a handy synonym for loser. She becomes a rabid fan of an especially sickly boy band; after theyve crashed and burned, shes revolted when their lead singer re-emerges as a particularly violent and misogynist white rapper. Funded by the cash they've made from peddling Ezra's prescription drugs, the pair set off for California so that Penny can give her former idol a piece of her mind. At the very least.

As they travel by Greyhound through the United States, they discover each state subject to an increasingly higher level of terror alert, each gradation named after a character from Sesame Street. (Elmo is the scariest.) Switching channels, Id say that Ezra and Penny are like a twisted version of Bart and Lisa, and that the smarty-pants Ezra also resembles the annoyingly omniscient baby from Family Guy, not least in his snooty quasi-British accent.

The Lambs tale is told to us by Penny herself, still in her school uniform, as part of her community service, in the hope (brainwashed, presumably) that having heard it we will depart to lead "fuller and lawfuller lives." Camille Steubel plays Penny; she has brilliant timing, and is very funny and occasionally touching. Amitai Marmorstein's Ezra looks like Little Lord Fauntleroy in specs and on anti-depressants, and he, too, is funny: not touching, but then I doubt if he's trying to be. He also operates puppets who impersonate additional characters including the menacing pop/rap star. Somewhere in the accompanying literature is a claim that Automatic Vaudeville want to offend. I dont think so: If you satirize everything, as they do, you offend no one, especially when your main focus is pop culture. Branding the everyday world as Legoland loses its sting, when youve already established that the people doing the branding are ridiculous. Both these shows were first seen in Toronto at Summerworks, though not by me. I'm glad to have caught up with them.

- Trudeau Stories plays at Theatre Passe Muraille, and Legoland at Theatre Passe Muraille Backspace, through Dec. 6. Call 416-504-7529 for more information.

THEATRE REVIEW

Road Show

Public Theater, New York City

Wilson and Addison Mizner were brothers, born just over a year apart in California in the 1870s. During the later decades of that century and the earlier decades of the next, they led colourful lives and acquired colourful reputations: Addison as an architect, Wilson as a playwright, theatrical manager and all-round entrepreneur, and both of them as flim-flam men. They are the subjects of Road Show, a musical by Stephen Sondheim and John Weidman that has reached New York after more than 10 years of planning: much more in Sondheim's case, since he's on record as having been fascinated by the Mizners since the beginning of his own career in the 1950s.

Road Show is the fourth title the current project has had; it was known in gestation as Wise Guys (still my own favourite title, but apparently abandoned because people thought it was about the Mafia), in workshop as Gold and in a production by Harold Prince that played Chicago and Washington a few years ago as Bounce. The current name refers not only to the brothers' constant travels but to an image much favoured by Wilson in particular: the more flamboyant and erratic of the two, he uses "the road," in surprisingly Tolkienian terms, as an everlasting symbol of adventure, opportunity and get-rich-quickness. Near the end of the show, he has a booze-and-cocaine fuelled vision of a dazzling multi-lane highway that finally convinces Addison that his brother has lost it. They both die penniless; the closing number finds them reunited in some kind of afterlife (Heaven? They doubt it), Wilson still urging further exploration. "Willie," sings an exasperated Addison, "we're dead" --one of those laconic Sondheim lines that in dramatic context are funnier than any epigram. (Others, in other shows, are "June" and "pay attention." Email your entries.)Wilson, though, is undeterred. He sees the road to eternity as "the biggest opportunity there is."

It's a lovely ending, half sardonic and half exultant, to a show with a mostly excellent score and, on paper, a fascinating story. But it still doesn't compute, and I suspect that the unfixable fault is history's. We are offered, to put it broadly, Addison as the conscientious plodder who gets results and Wilson as the conscienceless scamp who blows in and screws everything and everybody. In their youth, they journey to the Yukon where they actually strike gold: Wilson then gambles their claim away. Much later, they're involved in another gold-rush, the 1920s Florida land boom. Addison, with the support of a rich male lover who's always dreamed about backing artists, finds his fortune by designing crazily eclectic mansions for the wealthy and pretentious. Then Wilson arrives, takes over and ruins it all. (A market crash--pre-1929 --helps him do it.)

So there's a pattern, played out at the beginning and end of the show. There might, I suppose, be a risk of repetition if it operated in the middle as well, but in fact what happens is that the brothers go their separate ways, which means that the show's central dynamic gets suspended. There are, it's true, some emotional underpinnings, deriving from their parents. Papa Mizner was a go-getter, whose deathbed bequests to his sons are ambition and the road metaphor. Mama is a loving emotional leech who on her deathbed sings a song called Isn't He Something that's ostensibly about how much she loves them both, but it is really about Wilson, who (typically) isn't there, rather than Addison, who (typically) is, thus breeding more resentment. Mama is beautifully played by Alma Cuervo (who, both times the Sam Mendes production of Cabaret came through Toronto, was a superb Fraulein Schneider); she makes the song the emotional high point of the evening, both touching and troubling.

Of course, once it's over, she's dead; though she does, like the rest of the company, stick around as part of a ominous ensemble, perched on and around a brownish construction of platforms and alcoves, artfully composed of trunks and suitcases. This setting has been designed by the show's director, John Doyle, celebrated for his stripped-down actors-as-musicians revivals of Sondheim's Sweeney Todd and Company. This time he has a full-time band to play Jonathan Tunick's customarily fine orchestrations, but the production is still determinedly downbeat; there's no choreographer, and the staging seems designed to head off any possibility of applause after a song.

Each brother gets to head up a company number depicting his solo progress. Addison's Trip shows its subject wandering the globe, investing in doomed ventures, and accumulating the bric-a-brac that will eventually form the foundation of his architectural style. It's a slyly appropriate composition that glides beguilingly

The road is a symbol of adventure, opportunity and get-rich-quickness

and hopefully along, and then turns up the tension. Alexander Gemignani, who is both a fine character actor and one of the best singers in musical theatre, makes a charmingly ungainly Addison, though sometimes underplaying the moments when lightbulbs go off in his head. Michael Cerveris is good when Wilson goes to pieces, less adept at conveying raffish confidence. His major turn, That Was a Year, shows him in New York, marrying and living off a rich widow, writing plays, promoting jockeys and prize-fighters, and going bust. It's here that the production's austerity seems most at odds with the slam-bang careers it's chronicling. It shouldn't have to work so hard to convince us of its seriousness.

Weidman's script doesn't overstress the story's resonance as a representative American fable, but it's inescapably there, especially now. Sondheim's score, as intelligent and exploratory as expected, combines jagged with jaunty; it also includes a bewitching long-lined ballad (The Best Thing That Ever Has Happened) unlike anything in his previous work. But he hasn't got as deeply inside his characters as usual. It's far more Addison's show than it's Wilson's -- the opening number is about him -- but in the end, we don't know whether he's his brother's victim or the architect (sorry) of his own misfortune. If it is both, the proportions aren't clear. I doubt, though, that this is the end of the road for Road Show. There's too much gold there, too much bounce, for some theatre not to try it again. - Road Show is at the Public Theater in New York City until Dec. 28. Call 212-967-7555 for tickets and information.
2008-12-04-the-gift-that-keeps-giving-st:
Some time ago, Stephen Colbert had Tony Bennett as a guest on The Colbert Report and came close to blowing his cover. (His own cover, not Tonys.) Bennett is an obvious liberal, and Colbert duly pretended to bait him with his faux Bill O'Reilly shtick, something on the lines of "why do you have to do all these charity tours to poor countries?" But his heart obviously wasn't in it, and it was a relief when he gave it up and let the singer sing. And then, all pretence of opposition was thrown aside when, halfway through Bennetts rendition of They All Laughed, Colbert, obviously thrilled and having the time of his life, joined in. Lo and behold, he could sing. Rather well. Very nearly very well.

It was obvious, from his days as a reporter on The Daily Show, that Colbert was a first-rate actor-comedian with an intellectual top-dressing. On The Report hes had to confine himself to a single persona, but the quick-thinking virtuosity with which he's sustained it, through interviews as well as monologues, has been amazing. (There has been the odd slippage. In the run-up to the U. S. elections he seemed to be getting really angry underneath it all. So did Jon Stewart on his, but Stewart's format allows for it.) So perhaps it shouldnt have been a surprise when he came out as what used to be called an all-round entertainer.

Thats how he appears on A Colbert Christmas: The Greatest Gift of All. He sings, he dances -- or at least throws himself around in a rhythmic kind of way. (He doesn't lip-synch so well, though.) But this time he does it while staying in character. The Colbert of the Report has gone beyond being a mere parody of a bullying right-wing TV host. Come to think of it, he never has bullied; what he does is wheedle, belligerently. The Colbert-figure transcends politics. What he presents, with unflagging panache and almost unflagging precision, is a delirium of self absorption, narcissism on speed. He is, something that might once have seemed impossibly oxymoronic, a manic Jack Benny.

Like Benny, Colbert is vain, greedy and a coward, and so shameless about it, he's lovable. The format of his Christmas show -- which, in a typically Colbertian pre-emptive strike, has hit the airwaves and hence the DVD stores a full three weeks early -- is not the greatest, but it will serve. Colbert wants to get to the studio to record his TV special, but he cant leave his seasonal cabin in the woods

because theres a bear outside, and it might eat him. (The bear does eat a celebrity in the course of the show, but has to disgorge him. The celebrity is grateful. Not being digested by a bear was his Christmas wish.) Thankfully Elvis Costello, who has always looked and sounded somewhat Dickensian, is holding the fort and he sends progress reports on what seems like a cut-rate production. (Goats standing in for reindeer. And, more bemusingly, for mice.) But if Colbert can't get there to see the stars, they can come to see him.

Or maybe he dreams that they do. "I'm so high," says Willie Nelson, youre hallucinating me. ("Youre really high," Colbert agrees, harmonizing along there, very nicely.) Nelson, the favourite country singer of people who don't like country music -- I'm speaking personally here -- appears in miniaturized form as Fourth Wise Man in a nativity scene, offering a herb that smells more sweetly than either frankincense or myrrh. Colbert also greets "legendary country singer Toby Keith," who offers musical support to his War on the War on Christmas. (Separate church and state, some liberal said / I think its time we separated him from his head. I hope he knows hes being satirical.) And there is "legendary R & B singer John Legend," according to whom R & B stands for roots and berries and who has a suggestive joke about nutmeg; indie folk deity Feist, as an angel holding your prayers in strict sequence; and -- in a final glittering display of verbal front-loading-- "ageless icon of generosity and joy Santa Claus." The nicest turn of all, though, is done by Jon Stewart, dropping in from the cabin half an hour before yours -- the one where you used to live, and engaging his ex-employee in a duet about Hanukkah, a subject of which Colbert knows proudly nothing. Stewart has a shy falsetto of a singing-voice, much unlike the full-throated Colbert. But they go well together.

Colbert begins the proceedings with a rousing Christmas-song-to-end-them-all, including a line celebrating "a freshly hobbled Tiny Tim." But, for all the barbs, this is not so much an anti-Christmas special as a Christmas anti-special. It ends with Colbert and Costello duetting what must be the best seasonal song in years, which I can best sum up as tolerantly skeptical. ("There are worse things to believe in" is its refrain, and it lists some of them.)The lyric-writing throughout the show is first-rate. I'm not advocating Colbert doing regular musical interludes on The Report --it would spoil his image. But I'd like to see him some time in a revival of The Music Man. Who better to play a soft-centred egomaniac? - A Colbert Christmas: The Greatest Gift of All airs tonight on The Comedy Network at 10 p. m. Repeats Dec. 13 and Dec. 15 at 10 p. m., Dec. 24 at 6 p. m. and 11 p. m. and Dec. 25 at 8 a. m.

THEATRE REVIEWS

IT'S A WONDERFUL LIFE

Bluma Appel Theatre

A Christmas Carol

Young Centre for the Performing Arts

---

George Bailey, meet Ebenezer Scrooge. I'm sure you two will have a lot to talk about. After all, you're both known for having received life-changing supernatural visitations that hit you right in the festive season.

But first --and in deference to the fact that George's story, It's a Wonderful Life, is currently being told in Toronto as a staged radio play (yes, I saw your eyebrows ascend) -- a few words from our critic.

It's a Wonderful Life is brought to you by the Canadian Stage Company who got it from an American playwright, Philip Grecian, who of course got it from the 1946 Frank Capra movie that has come to epitomize the concept known as Capracorn. George is the bashful but determined do-gooder who functions in his archetypal American small town as a kind of one-man Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac, and whose benevolent stewardship of the family savings and loan company earns him the undying enmity of the bigwig plutocrat Mr. Potter, who resembles -- how can I put this? -- Montgomery Burns without the nuance. Due partly to the villainy of Mr. Potter, partly to the carelessness of his drunken uncle (George has always been good to his family) and partly to the value of his insurance policy, our boy is tempted to suicide and despair, not in that order. But he is saved by Clarence, an apprentice angel with an Irish accent, sent down from heaven to show George what he has accomplished in his life by bringing hope and happiness to his fellow citizens. By way of subplot, Clarence's successful execution of this mission wins him a promotion. Every time a bell rings, we are told, an angel gets his wings. Clap your hands if you believe in this.

George seems terribly slow on the uptake; Clarence makes it perfectly clear that he is giving him a counterfactual demonstration of what the town would have been like had he never been born, but he still keeps wondering why nobody recognizes him. Compare this with A Christmas Carol, which Soulpepper has brought back, in Michael Shamata's exemplary adaptation and production, for a fourth season: Scrooge catches on very early to what the three Christmas ghosts have in store for him, so we can concentrate on his reactions to their revelations. (All right, he does seem reluctant to realize that he himself is the unmourned corpse at Christmas Yet to Come, but who wouldn't be?)Compare, more importantly, that George is the innocent victim of one rich scoundrel, while Scrooge is used to indict a whole system in which he himself is a major participant. One is a good guy throughout; the other, far more dramatically, a bad one who changes. Of course Dickens' tale isn't realistic either; but it doesn't pretend to be. (Capra's does.) But, with the wit and imagination of a great writer behind it, it's real. (Capra's isn't.)

Whichmay explain why Soulpepper tells their story as if they believed in it, while CanStage tells theirs as if they were apologizing for it. It's a very elaborate apology, with a lot of talent behind it. As stated, the Grecian adaptation's conceit is that the show is being broadcast live from a 1940s radio studio. This is lovingly recreated in Donna Feore's production, which is an impressive feat of visual orchestration. We watch the stage actors playing radio actors, flirting and joshing and doing their knitting when they're not actually on mic and making a great show of reading from scripts when they are. A lady pianist supplies mood music, as if this were a silent movie. (If American radio drama was really like this, then American radio drama deserved to die.) In a party scene, the cast break into a brief Charleston; real radio actors wouldn't exert themselves like that, but it's fun to watch. So is John Gzowski, billed anachronistically as "Foley artist," doing the sound effects before our eyes. There are commercial breaks, mostly sung and gorgeously in period. But it all distracts from what's meant to be the play.

That it takes hold at all is principally due to Mike Shara, who gets better and better. Without any kind of Jimmy Stewart impersonation, he has George's aw-shucksiness shiningly to rights; this is a performance of unblinking excellence. Marla McLean is his de-serving marital partner, Patrick McKenna charms as Clarence and others more earthbound, and Juan Chioran gets to play two kinds of cad, the evil Potter and the bottom-pinching thesp who impersonates him. A strong supporting cast includes Douglas E. Hughes (playing God) and Leslie Arden (playing the piano), with Blair Williams as announcer and man-of-many-voices, three of them sequentially at one point. But it still all feels like cashing in on a famous title. The program reveals that the same adaptor has done another, straightforwardly theatrical, version of the same material, seen last year in Vancouver. As the old joke has it, what's a Grecian earn? At Christmas, I should imagine, quite a bit.

A Christmas Carol is worth the price just to see Joseph Ziegler's Ebenezer kicking off his slippers in an ecstasy of joyous reformation; his final rapprochement with Oliver Dennis's crown prince of Cratchits is a heart-warmimg bonus. Who knew being good could be so much fun? Ziegler's Scrooge is beautifully of a piece; the seeds of humour, if not of good humour, are sown in his early extravagant misanthropy, while his encroaching pain at the sight of opportunities past is very moving. Other welcome returning veterans are John Jarvis's quartet of spirits and Patrick Galligan's incorrigibly cheerful nephew, with Maggie Huculak as an assortment of wenches and crones. In terms of overall ensemble, CanStage cannot on this occasion be faulted. But Soulpepper has the soul. - It's a Wonderful Life runs until Dec. 20. Call 416-368-3110 for tickets and information. A Christmas Carol runs until Dec. 24. Call 416-866-8666.

2008-12-06-the-moliere-up-there-a-mexica:
Arriving with the recondite recommendation of being one of the best Mexican plays of all time," Sabina Bermans Moliere, translated by Shelley Tepperman, is actually set in France, and 17th-century France at that. It's about the rivalry between its title figure, the greatest French comic playwright, and his tragedian counterpart and sometime protege, Jean Racine. Racine narrates the play as an obituary tribute to the deceased Moliere, who famously died onstage while performing in, of all things, The Imaginary Invalid. Racine, obviously one of nature's revisionists, disputes this story, and otherwise seems torn between tearing his competitor down and crying him up. Its like Amadeus fought between equals.

Arriving in Paris as a gauche and prim unknown, Racine has every reason to be jealous of Moliere, whos already disgustingly successful as a dramatist, actor and impresario. Racine despises comedy as a frivolous and probably immoral genre, which puts him fully in agreement with the oddly named, and even more oddly titled, Monseigneur Prefixe, Archbishop of France. (You can be archbishop of a city, not a country.) Historically, Moliere was persecuted by the Church, who took his portrayal of a hypocrite in Tartuffe as an attack on religion and who got the play banned. That's bad enough, but this play's Archbishop makes it personal. It turns out the seduction scene in Tartuffe is actually a re-enactment of the Monseigneurs own attempt to debauch Racines wife, an actress in Moliere's troupe. Besides, the Archbishop disapproves of comedy as taking the mind of the impressionable King Louis XIV off its proper business of making war; I've heard some philistine arguments in my time but this one takes the gateau. He reckons that the royal sinews will be more effectively stiffened by a good dose of Racinian tragic verse and, incredibly enough, hes right. Early on, the Archbishop makes a wager that he can wipe the infuriating smile off of Molieres face by destroying his happiness, which is certainly fragile, given that he's being cuckolded by his young also-actress wife. (He makes a play out of it, of course.) Later, His Grace raises the stakes and goes after Moliere's life, enlisting Racines help to do it. The Churchs view seems to be that if tragedy is the lesser of two evils, it's still an evil, and Racine gets neutered by being given a civil-service job-- though not till after he's succeeded in writing Phedre.

The play switches at impressive speed between past and present, onstage and offstage, pratfalls and heartache, springing constant surprises as it does. It gets a superb production from Richard Rose -- conceivably his best ever. Charlotte Dean designed the revolving and resourceful sets and witty costumes, Rebecca Picherak did the lighting, and there isnt a moment at which the stage isnt both visually and aurally alive. I can't remember a time when the Toronto theatre was so full of good big casts, and this 13-strong company is one of the best, as alive when reacting in groups as when squaring off one-on-one. So it seems churlish to observe that, despite all the fireworks, what's supposed to be the central conflict doesnt catch fire.

Moliere is the title character but Racine is the central one. (Just as Amadeus, named after Mozart, is really about Salieri.) Rick Robertss Racine is the one involved in the play's crises of conscience, in its three-way battles of Church, state and art. Richard McMillan's Moliere is their victim but stands outside them. He has the best lines and the best attitude ("I know, he tells Racine, its more prestigious to make the audience suffer"), but his bedraggled life and triumphant career seem like a self-contained play going on inside the other one. Both actors give superlative performances, but their contest, the plays announced theme, is more spoken than felt.

The intrigues don't quite work either, since the most problematic role, the Archbishop, gets the most problematic performance. As often as Julian Richings extends his robed arms, like a malignant black bat, he remains petty bureaucrat rather than grand conspirator. The rest are a catalogue of excellence: Kyle Horton's inscrutable king, Nancy Palk doubling as his rambling mother and Molieres mother-in-law whos also his virtual first wife, Cara Pifko as the present and provocative Mme Moliere, Richard Binsley as the fabulist La Fontaine, Mike Ross, the production's musical director, periwigged at the harpsichord as the great Lully, Moliere's own MD, and flashing a time-serving grin when required. Just as performance, the evening is a cupful of coups. And, whatever my reservations about the script, the production couldnt be there without it.

I will, though, voice a couple of extra qualms. The translation has its off-moments; why keep calling Moliere a "comic rather than the more authentic and resonant comedian?" And why end with a song celebrating the cutting off of the kings head? Historically, this wasn't to happen until the Louis after next; also historically, this Louis did far more to promote and protect Moliere than the play allows. In theory, writers are free to take what liberties they please with the facts; in practice, truth has an uncomfortable habit of being not only stranger than fiction but more dramatic.

- Moliere runs through Dec. 28 at the Tarragon Theatre. Call 416-531-1827 for more information.
