Plays about rival poets are clustering on the Toronto scene. We have Moliere, which gives us an undeclared conflict between the eponymous comic genius and Racine, the tragedian who wants him dead. And we have Sylvia Plath Must Not Die, where the contenders are the suicidal Sylvia and Anne Sexton, her friend and fellow scribbler, who wants her alive. Or at least who wishes that Sylvia would refrain from suicide until she herself has committed it. She doesn't want her thunder stolen.

In this production, brought to us by the esteemed One Yellow Rabbit troupe from Calgary, Plath and Sexton share the stage with their respective husbands, Ted Hughes -- also of course a poet -- and Kayo Sexton -- emphatically not. "Is this going to be depressing?" Kayo asks Ted at the start of proceedings, disarmingly voicing the fears of everyone in the audience.

It turns out not to be depressing, at least not much, but it isn't very enlightening, either. Basically, it's a poetry recital, with the two heroines -- seated in their off-duty moments on twin Muskoka chairs -- taking turns at performing their own verses, interspersed with someprosejoustings with the twomen. Verses apart, the sources seem to be Plath's journals interspersed, I would guess, with brief linking sequences of the company's own inventions. Within these limitations, the production is up to One Yellow Rabbit's established standards of visual panache. Much of the credit for this must go to Denise Clarke, doubling as choreographer (her actual credit is "staged by," but same difference, I think) and Sextonimpersonator. The series of pas de deux she has contrived, done mainly to a Miles Davis record, gives graceful expression to the tensions and occasional rapprochements. The most seductive image she contributes, though, is her own as an elongated and inebriated Anne, sashaying and swivelling across the stage in an elegantly revealing black-and-white number, poetry in erratic but irresistible motion.

She also makes a good fist of making the spoken poetry flesh, though not quite good enough. She has a lot of style, but doesn't convey much substance. Making non-dramatic verse into viable theatrical language is always the Devil's own job, certainly over the course of a whole evening. There Reigns Love, Simon Callow's biographical arrangement of Shakespeare's sonnets seen this year at Stratford, was a case of the actor biting off more than the audience could chew. The poems of Sexton and Plath are more accessible, if only because they're more recent, but their cumulative effect is deadening. Either the poems are too dense or I am.

Clarke's attractions apart, the Sexton poems may work better because they seem directed at someone, and from a frank and engaging point of view, that of a free-wheeling promiscuous alcoholic. Plath's are far more tightly wound and inward-driven--more self-pitying, to put it unkindly -- and Onalea Gilbertson, fetchingly if primly adorned with an orange Alice headband, doesn't begin to bring them to life. She's muted until she gets to the showpiece poem Daddy, a dodgy enough piece to begin with, what with its comparison of the poet's father-and-husband problems to the Holocaust, but one that has been known to work theatrically as a kind of incantation. Here it's shouted, coming across as stridently sulky.

Sympathy, to the extent it's aroused at all, swings over to Hughes, a much-maligned figure in any case and played here by Michael Green with persuasive North of England pawkiness --meaning he comes across as earthy and puzzled. Andy Curtis' Kayo is not just puzzled but bewildered, a salesman by trade and agreeably all-American. Their scenes together presumably fall into the what-if category: conjectural but believable. The foursome seems to have been an ill-assorted couple of couples, Kayo and Sylvia monogamous, Ted and Anne anything but. It's doubtful, though, that they would have been any happier had they changed partners. - Sylvia Plath Must Not Die is at the Young Centre for the Performing Arts until Dec. 13. Call 416-866-8666 for tickets and information.
2008-12-10-all-hat-no-cattle-a-show-with:
The emblematic moment in Rich Kids: Cattle Drive comes early, when Kourtney tries for the first time to get on a horse. (I think it's Kourtney. The cast also includes a Courtenay. It's very confusing.) All the other nine spoiled darlings who have signed up for a stint on a Colorado ranch have managed it, but she's having problems. Joshua, the trail boss, is unsympathetic. He blames it on her jeans. "You've got to wear ranch jeans -- not Gucci jeans."

Kourtney is incensed -- as much as anything by the insult to her fashion sense: "First of all, who wears Gucci jeans?" Then she gets defiant; these are her jeans, and she's not going to change them: "If you don't like it, give me a stepping stool." Later on she muses on the indignity of it all: "I thought that comment about Gucci jeans was really mean and uncalled-for." And she reaches for the ultimate grievance: "It's like stereotyping. It's a racist comment in a way."

No question: Kourtney, or Courtenay, and company have been set up to be stereotyped. "There's more to me," says one, "than just being a spoiled brat." And though you know to laugh, you're not quite sure how. (She does say she has outside interests, like going to lunch.) Rich Kids: Cattle Drive has taken an understandably long time to reach our screens; it aired in the U. S. in 2005 under the title Filthy Rich:Cattle Drive, which sort of gives it away. After all, if you're going to do a show about a bunch of greenhorns learning to be cowboys and cowgirls, there's no intrinsic reason for them to be wealthy. The idea is to play into our desire to see the privileged ones make fools of themselves and suck it up. And they certainly play along: how consciously, is hard to tell.

At least two of them should know what they're getting into, being as they're actors and the children of actors. One of them is the son of Anthony Quinn, no less; the other's father is Robert Blake, known not just for his film and TV work, but for what his son Noah coyly refers to as "that little murder trial." Of all the philosophical gems with which these kids, in hallowed reality show fashion, introduce themselves, I think Noah's is my favourite. "I definitely allow the pendulum of life to take me on its journey," he says.

This particular swing of the pendulum has its participants given two days of training at Saddleback Ranch before being divided into two gangs and sent off to herd 100 head of cattle per group (one gets the red steers, the other the black) with, of course, a running competition going on between them, and trail boss Joshua pronouncing judgment at dinner as to who's done the best. The winning team gets massages, the losing team gets to do the dishes. If this

all seems too gritty a prospect, there are words of comfort: "Don't think they'll be leaving the world of gossip behind." Nor do they: "There's just the gossip on Britney," says one of the preliminary teasers, and you might think at that moment they mean Spears. But no, they mean one of their own, who spells it Brittny (her dad's a footballer) and who, even as they all fly from Los Angeles to Colorado in a luxury jet, is getting close with Alex, the junior Quinn. He, however, is "definitely keeping my options open," meaning that he's playing her off against Kourtney or Courtenay. Much of the first episode is devoted to everybody talking about this. The word is that in later instalments, Fabian ("son," so help me Wikipedia, "of an Ecuadorian businessman") emerges as the really obnoxious one. So far, though, the easiest one to distinguish is Alexander (not Alex) Clifford, because he's English, "eldest son of the Lord Clifford of Chudleigh." It's unclear why he chose to come, since he's never wanted to go to America, whose culture has in his mind consisted of McDonald's and -- I think I heard this right --Salem. But his presence, and a few pained remarks he makes about the others' lack of equestrian prowess, does put us in touch with a vanished age when the wealthy were expected to be able to ride.

This show, obviously, is the reality show eating its own tail, the foul mismating of at least two sub-genres. It comes with all the trimmings: sex (theirs), schadenfreude (ours), envy (ours and theirs), built-in opportunities for slapstick and a gloating narrator saying things like, "If they think they had it rough before, they're in for a rude awakening." It may also make you wonder what became of the dear old Western, including the comic variety in which Bob Hope or even Kenneth More (anyone else remember The Sheriff of Fractured Jaw?) would go incongruously riding on the range, but eventually come up trumps, which would include getting the girl, who was usually pneumatic and either Jane (Russell) or Jayne (Mansfield.) It also suggests that Dirty Sexy Money (I miss that show) was more of a documentary than we might have guessed. We can't, though, dismiss these young things quite out of hand, even if they do seem to regard allowances of US$20,000 a month as mere pittances. ("Do you realize," says one of the more aware, "that $2,000 a month is a lot for some people?") It isn't as if any of us would do better as impromptu cowhands, though it's also not as if anyone would ask us. They're doing it, in case you wondered, for charity -- and, however crummy, the show is a few steps up from Oprah's Big Give. They are being asked to do something real, and even interesting. They may also be getting, from the long-suffering Joshua, lessons in eloquence. Waking them up at 5 a. m. --a time few of them may have known existed, at least not as part of the morning -- he says "we're burning daylight here." That's Shakespearean. Like, literally. - Rich Kids: Cattle Drive airs tonight at 10 p. m. ET on Slice.

2008-12-11-with-all-eyes-on-these-guys-t:
SOMEONE WHOLL WATCH OVER ME

Berkeley Street Theatre Upstairs, Toronto

Frank McGuinnesss Someone Who'll Watch Over Me is partly a play about performance, so it's appropriate that its current revival should be, taken all around, the best-acted play in Toronto. Which at this moment is saying something.

Somewhere among Tom Stoppards juvenilia theres an apprentice play that he later summed up as Waiting for Godot in the condemned cell ... I'm sure you get the idea. The piece went professionally unperformed, but Stoppard's description of it would do very well for McGuinnesss play which, ever since its premiere in 1992, has been performed indeed. Becketts play, the greatest technical as well as philosophical influence on all drama since the Second World War, reduces the form to something like its basic necessities. He gave us two men, in a roadside limbo and without benefit of personal biographies, filling in the days with conversation and the occasional physical exercise to give themselves, in their own imperishable phrase, "the impression we exist." McGuinness, another Irishman, gives us three men whose identities are comparatively lavishly documented: an American doctor, an Irish journalist and an English teacher. And we do know where they are, though it's part of their torment that they don't know whether anybody else does. They are hostages, chained to the wall in a cellar-like room in Beirut. It may not quite be a condemned cell, but they have no way of being sure. Any one of them might be taken out and shot at any moment. Or any one of them might be released.

The play has a geometric structure; it gives us a pyramid and then inverts it. First there is one captive, then two, then three, then two again, then back to one. The games the men play are, obviously, meant to serve the practical purpose of keeping them sane; you could not perhaps say quite the same of the routines enacted by Becketts tramps, but then again maybe you could. (And Becketts play is more realistic than you might think; it was partly inspired by his experiences in the French Resistance.) McGuinness's prisoners write imaginary letters home, invent movie scenarios a la Kiss of the Spider Woman, recreate horse races and Wimbledon tennis finals. What start as competitive rituals develop into mutually supportive ones.

Initial conflict is guaranteed by the presence of the Irishman and the Englishman, dragging out ancestral hatreds that, in any real sense, they probably hardly feel. Edward, the Irishman, is a vulnerable loudmouth who sought a dangerous posting partly out of bravado, partly to escape an uncomfortable marriage; he's also a voluble atheist who refuses to read the Bible or the Koran, the only two books available, but whom we eventually find --perhaps for anything better to do -- deep in one of them. David Ferry brings a high level of both energy and intelligence to the role; its as close to being a rampageous performance as is possible in his confined position, but its precision-controlled. Vocally he never lets up, whether he's being wistful or aggressive, but he never loses sight, or lets us lose sight, of the fear that grows within him every minute. You can track a lot of this play's progress through the actors eyes: Ferrys blaze, those of R. H. Thomson as Michael, the Englishman, are pale and blinking. Michael, a widower, came to Lebanon as a language teacher after being laid off at home. He's prim and apparently vulnerable: a self-acknowledging sad sack, kidnapped when on his way to market to buy pears for a flan (his most prized recipe). He also seems to have gone through life fending off suspicions that he might be gay, suspicions raised again, at least momentarily, by his fellow prisoners. His lonely life (no children, wife died young) and unfashionable scholarship (he's a medievalist) may in fact have made him the best qualified to survive. Thomsons performance is often very funny, especially when he proudly summons up Virginia Wades victory at Wimbledon, complete with sound effects: a proud virtuoso turn by a man who's learned not to cower. There's a touch of Monty Python in Thomsons assumed Englishness, and it doesnt hurt a bit. Defensiveness gradually gives place to strength, which combines with the humour and adds up to grace. This is as fine a performance as I've seen him give.

As Adam, the American who serves as part-time mediator, Ryan Hollyman is less well defined than the other two, but so is his character. He's a blank slate to whom his companions assign qualities that may or may not be there. His terrors, though, are as vivid as theirs. The director (and producer) is Tegan Shoet, a newcomer who apparently supports her theatre habit by working as a lawyer; she gets as much variety into the staging as the constricted circumstances permit, and the mental contact between the actors is superb. Steve Lucass jutting three-cornered set is excellent, as is his merciless lighting.

The hostage-takers are kept offstage, like a collective Godot though one whose appearance is dreaded rather than desired. We dont even hear much about them. Here the play cheats; it may be the captors' strategy to keep the captives physically in the light (it's never switched off) and mentally in the dark (they dont even know what day it is) but they must have said something. They must be making demands of some kind, or why take hostages at all? But the characters say nothing about it, apparently keeping quiet for our benefit. We dont even know if they've been physically ill-treated; there are bruises on Ferry's legs but theyre never explained or even referred to. The tensions and resolutions between the cellmates are finely dramatized, their ongoing fight with their jailers not so much: a limitation thats frustrating but that may also, paradoxically, be a strength. There is a fourth voice written into the play, that of Ella Fitzgerald, whose recording of the almost title song (the Gershwins called it Someone to Watch Over Me) is both Edward's choice of imaginary Desert Island Disc and a key to the theme of both play and production: interdependence. - Someone Who'll Watch Over Me is at the Berkeley Street Theatre Upstairs in Toronto until Dec. 13. Call 416-368-3110 for tickets and information.

2008-12-12-a-good-anne-is-hard-to-find-t:
Arriving in good time to spoil everyone's holidays, Anne of Green Gables: A New Beginning is Kevin Sullivan's latest addition to the saga of the orphan girl with red hair and a funny way of talking. The subtitle derives from a presumption that the Old Beginning -- Lucy Maud Montgomery's -- wasn't good enough. The company responsible calls itself Anne Prequel Productions Inc., proving that second-guessing is now an industry.

You don't have to be a Montgomery fanatic to observe that, while her version was tart and taut, this one is aimless and endless. That sub-title is also a pun. We are here to witness "a new beginning" for the grown-up Anne Shirley of 1945, a successful novelist stricken with writers' block while trying to deliver a play, and consumed with worry for her only son who has yet to return from the war. So she retreats to the old place on P. E. I., where a rummage in the attic reveals things previously unknown about her childhood. It seems that, before coming into the care of the Cuthberts of Green Gables, Anne had done time in both a workhouse and a Great House, experiences that left an inexplicable lack of scars on the girl we met in the books. It seems that her father vanished, after causing her mother's death with his careless driving (of a horse and cart). Anne's path and her dad's occasionally re-crossed in her pre-Gables days, but it's been years since she heard of him and she now becomes obsessed with tracking him down. This gives her the stimulus to finish her play, though it's not clear how. Meantime she goes into prolonged flashback. We alternate between the present Anne and the past one.

The first thing we notice is that, carrot tops apart, they have absolutely nothing in common. Older Anne (Barbara Hershey) is a capable if dull woman who thinks and speaks just like everybody else. The younger one notoriously expresses herself in high-flown phrases drawn from early exposure to 19th-century romantic poetry ("My life," she observes early on, "does not have to be a graveyard of buried hopes") and it's impossible to believe that so compulsive a verbal tic would just disappear, whatever the passage of years. It gets little semi-orphan Annie into endless trouble, and viewers, too, may want to wring her neck: No reflection on the child actress, Hannah Endiott-Douglas, who's doing what's required, but she seems, for so supposedly smart a kid, pathologically incapable of knowing when to shut up.

What I called a workhouse is officially named the Bolingbroke County Poorhouse, and it seems to have been synthesized from the author-director's reading of Oliver Twist, Jane Eyre and The Count of Monte Cristo. Here Anne suffers much persecution, due to her criminal parentage and exotic vocabulary: "God punishes the disobedient," says the matron, adding, as an apparent afterthought, "with eternal damnation." (And Anne thought she was going to get off with standing in a corner.) Delivered, due to the sudden benevolence of authorities who must have had every reason to close the place years ago, Anne finds eventual refuge in the house of the rich and imperious Mrs. Thomas, unexpectedly played by Shirley MacLaine, who after all these years is still one of nature's gamines and ill-suited to imperiousness, or indeed to period drama. Not that it isn't nice to see her again, and she visibly brightens when allowed to deliver one of the script's two funny lines. At first she dispatches Anne to clean the stables, but eventually she takes to her, as one eccentric redhead to another. Mrs. Thomas owns the local lumber mill, and is having serious troubles with banks and unions. Anne gets embroiled in these, and it's all very confusing. Nor, in the eye of eternity or even of basic character development, does it get us anywhere.

There's some constancy in what I suppose we have to call the main plot, in the shape of Anne's summer-stock director (Ron Lea) who's always hanging around as if on the verge of proposing but never quite does. Anyway, no causal connection is ever established between the two timelines. This is a production without style, originality or imagination. It's aimed, obviously, at those who feel there can never be too much Anne, but even they may find that there can. - Anne of Green Gables: A New Beginning airs Sunday at 7 p. m. on CTV.

2008-12-13-cinderella-and-her-fabulous-f:
As Busby Berkeley probably used to say, and as his songwriters certainly wrote:

"What do you go for. Go see a show for.

Tell the truth, you go to see those beautiful Dames."

If the show is a pantomime, or as Ross Petty prefers to call it, a sillylicious family musical, you certainly do. Petty's Cinderella, upping the traditional panto average, offers no less than three Dames, all of them beautiful in their own eyes if nobody elses. Theres Petty himself, in full barrel-voiced-and-chested command, as Bertha Von Botox, Cinderella's scheming and tyrannical mother-in-law. In this show, which is unusually well-motivated for the genre, we actually see her trap Baron Hardup into marriage. (Usually it's a done deal before the curtain rises.) She does it partly through flower power -- she has an aphrodisiac purple petunia -- and partly through appealing to the Barons thespian instincts. Hes an ex-actor who puts on a funny accent when his passions are aroused. She herself boasts, or boasts of, a theatrical resume. She was in The Sound of Music (as an Alp) and was going to be at Stratford "until Des McAnuff found out I was Canadian," which is unfair but funny. Petty has mastered the art, which has eluded him in some previous years, of being convincingly female and convincingly villainous at the same time, at least as conviction goes in these parts. He takes no prisoners and despises those who do.

Then there are his daughters, the traditional Ugly Sisters: Dan Chameroy's Plumbum, who's mad about men, and Adam Braziers Carnivia, whos mad about food but wouldn't mind a nibble at a Prince. Individually, each is a hoot; together, they're a pair -- make that a quartet -- of hooters, even if the script has them ringing a few too many changes on the same basic jokes.

Still, the fact that it individualizes them at all is an accomplishment for the annals. This is the best script a Petty show has ever had: the work of a real writer, Chris Earle, who may be doing his best work. It has construction and development and all those other things that building firms ring you up with quotes for -- also some things they dont offer, such as jokes. (Did you know Michaelle Jean was Ukrainian? She brought perogies to Parliament. Dont worry, there's more where that came from.) There is some revisionism. Paula Brancati must be the least downtrodden Cinders on record; one of those post-feminist (or at least post-Beauty and the Beast, Disney version) heroines, she does few chores and is a champ at arm-wrestling, a talent that, typical of this show's foresight, comes in handy at the denouement. She and her dad face their personal recession by running a cafe whose menu seems to consist entirely of pumpkins, and you should be able to see where thats headed. To help it along theres Patty Sullivan's delightfully child-friendly Fairy Forgetful, who gets her instructions from a Fairy Godfather attached to some supernatural Cosa Nostra.

Meanwhile, there's the prince (Jake Epstein), whod rather be a pop star, the Artist Formerly Known as The Prince, though he still seems in line to be King as, once love-struck, he converses entirely in quotes from Elvis songs. Once upon a time he would have been played by a woman, but the convention of Principal Boy seems to have given way to Principal Boys Bodyguard. Playing the character formerly known as Dandini, but billed here as Tony and Tina, Karen LeBlanc sheds male attire and dark glasses to reveal great legs and a river-deep mountain-high singing voice. She also provides a new love interest for Buttons (the indispensable Eddie Glen), reprieved from his usual fate of standing around all gallant and heartbroken while the girl of his dreams makes off with the boy of hers. The roster of named characters is completed by Laurie Murdoch, doubling as baron and king and especially fine as the latter who has an inspired line in malapropisms.

The script's economy is matched by that of Ted Dykstra's direction. To be sure, there are true and false economies: I dont take kindly to a transformation scene that consists of a blackout followed by the heroines re-entry in a change of clothes. Still, when the carriage appears, it is drawn by real horses. More important, everything moves fast and sure. We're spared the traditional singalong sequence; instead, the statutory inveigling of kids from the audience is made part of the plot. They are judges (extraordinarily confident ones at my visit; either they'd been well-briefed or theyve learned from TV) at the So You Think You Can Prance contest thats a vital part of the ball. The prancing, whether real or wannabe, is of a high standard; for once, a panto has choreography (by Tracey Flye) that deserves the name. There are also great witty costumes by Erika Connor. And a moral: Never take directions from a barber-shop quartet. (I don't have time to explain.)

2008-12-18-about-those-bums-in-the-seats:
There is, obviously, no such thing as a homogeneous theatre audience. Even in and around Toronto, you don't see the same people at Dirty Dancing as you do at Festen, even though both are stage versions of movies. (These days, when people tell you they like "live theatre," they are likely to mean either stagings of films or animated jukeboxes.) There isn't, come to that, much overlap between the public for Stratford and Soulpepper and the public for the Canadian Opera Company. But for contrasts in audiences, the real place is New York City.

At a Sunday matinee of Road Show, the Stephen Sondheim-John Weidman musical at the Public Theatre, which I reviewed a couple of weeks ago, the house seemed made up of regular Public subscribers and upscale Sondheim fans. (Here there is a considerable overlap between groups.) These are older couples, probably from the East Side, in clothes from Barneys or Bergdorf's; the wives, one felt, were the prime movers in getting the tickets bought. They seemed to be trying hard to love the show, but only partially succeeding; discussions on the way out (the show has no intermission) were intense but inconclusive. They were still glad to be there rather than on Broadway. Not that they couldn't afford Broadway -- they all seemed comfortably heeled -- but that they knew it wouldn't have much to offer them, certainly not in terms of musicals.

Saturday night on Broadway itself reveals a much younger crowd. This is atypical, but the play, a revival of David Mamet's Speed the Plow, may still count as cutting edge, and two of the cast of three are stars of TV niche-hits: Jeremy Piven (Entourage) and Elisabeth Moss (Mad Men). The play is small-potatoes Mamet, a sliver off his cutthroat masterpiece Glengarry Glen Ross, with the locale changed from the real-estate shark pools of Chicago to the back offices of Hollywood, and with a woman permitted on the premises. Here, a young producer (Piven), who has sold his soul to commerce, is tempted to reclaim it by an apparently idealistic intern (Moss) who turns out to have her own agenda. It's well performed at dialogue level, though without the murderous elan it really needs. Piven's performance never suggests that he may have any depths to be stirred, not that the play gives him much help in this respect. Moss, in a role whose trajectory is remarkably similar to her shy-but-ruthless Peggy on TV, does her familiar thing but makes it fresh, which may be a definition of star quality; she seems to be carefully thinking every moment, and she never stops being ambiguous. If hers is the most interesting presence, the most immediately electric, at least when he gets handed a tirade, is that of Raul Esparza.

Esparza is the only actor whose resume is predominantly theatrical (he was Bobby in the recent revival of Company) as an aspiring hotshot who sees his one chance of a green light receding Fitzgerald-like into the distance and fights viciously, with both speech and fists, to get it back. The house, which was full of updated versions of the young execs who give Moss a tough time on Mad Men, audibly warmed to him. There was still a lingering sense of dissatisfaction, as of people being shortchanged by a short play that never really makes up in texture what it lacks in time. But even minor Mamet is better than anything else that's likely to be found on Broadway.

It is, for example, infinitely better than the approved dramatic hit August:Osage County, the most overrated American play since the last overrated American play. (There's one most seasons.) In this marathon drama, the most acclaimed piece to be set in Oklahoma since Oklahoma!, generations of a family converge on a homestead much less than 24 hours from Tulsa, to commiserate over an unexpected loss and to compete enthusiastically in the old American sport of heaving skeletons out of closets. That Wikipedia calls it "darkly comedic" should be warning enough; the self-consciously brooding title (the significance of the month is never made clear) supplies the rest. After running for 18 months, the play has long exhausted the hard-core New York audience. It now -- I saw a matinee -- gets bused-in groups from the suburbs, eagerly lapping up what they've been told is good for them. They exploded , pleasantly shocked, at every cheerfully salacious line the author, Tracy Letts, had provided for their delectation; they gasped approvingly at each Gothic revelation. Major plot twist: A mild case of incest turns out to be a severe case of incest. Most of the performances are caricatures: You can see rather better direction, and infinitely better acting, any night of any week in Toronto. It makes you wonder, all over again, why we're supposed to be so much in awe of New York: Why, for example, Dancap Productions tout the word "Broadway" in their publicity as if they were offering us a slice of the Holy Grail. To be fair, the original cast (from the highly-esteemed Steppenwolf company of Chicago) have taken themselves off to London; their replacements, with a few exceptions, are well below snuff. One of the exceptions is Estelle Parsons, who at a scarcely credible 81, plays a crop-haired and corrosive matriarch with a prescription-drug habit and selective memory loss. This is a role bound, in one of the flood of Canadian productions set to engulf us when the rights become available, to be played by Martha Henry, while the New York actress playing the most abrasive of the play's statutory three daughters is a dead ringer for Seana McKenna with about a tenth of the talent.

Downtown at the New York Theatre Workshop, the co-producers' handle is "Theatre for a New Audience." They looked pretty familiar to me: students and middle-aged theatre buffs, possibly academics and with a sizeable European contingent,

paying reverential homage to a Peter Brook production, from his Theatre des Bouffes du Nord in Paris, but performed in English. The one speaking actor in a cast of two is Bruce Myers, a long-time British member of Brook's international troupe whom I once described (to his delight, I believe) as "a Royal Shakespeare Company dropout." He's now narrator and title character in The Grand Inquisitor, a faithful rendition of the famous encounter, fromDostoyevsky's The Brothers Karamazov, between the persecuting ecclesiastic and a silent Christ returned to Earth and due for a second crucifixion. Myers has grown into a commanding, possibly a great actor, navigating long paragraphs with passion and logic and even wit, but beyond his presence there seems little point in putting onstage something that can as easily be read. And even on the page the Inquisitor seems to make a single point -- that mankind prefers the chains of authority to the responsibilities of freedom-- over and over again. Onstage and in the auditorium, the atmosphere was penitentially intense. Once again, the Theatre had found its Public.

2008-12-19-please-sir-i-don-t-want-any-m:
Did you know that Oliver Twist ends with the young hero standing before a holly-decked fireside and wishing everyone a Merry Christmas, straight to camera? Probably not, because it isn't in the book. But the producers of the latest BBC/PBS dramatization (currently airing in two parts on TVO) obviously had an eye to the time of year at which their production was likely to land in the schedules.

That isnt all thats wrong with it, but as a piece of clumsy opportunism, it's symptomatic. We all know that Charles Dickens invented the modern idea of Christmas as a time when people get festive and behave decently to one another; he wrote a joyous chapter to that effect in his first novel Pickwick Papers long before he institutionalized the idea by inventing Scrooge. That doesn't mean it has to be shoehorned into every adaptation of every story. It seems especially superfluous now, arriving on the heels of the updated Christmas Carol which we saw a week ago and which is bound to become a staple for at least the next few winters.

That version moves Dickens story to the present, with Scrooge as a London debt-collector repossessing pensioners TV sets when they need them most and stuck on a pretty nurse who rejects him for having the wrong values. Eventually, of course, and with some new and subtle variations, he acquires the right ones. The modernization does highlight some awkward questions: If Scrooge is abandoning his career grinding the faces of the poor, how is he going to subsidize his newfound philanthropy? But the new version plays an enjoyable game with our awareness of the old one. It can take whatever liberties it pleases: It still makes us laugh and cry as Dickens should. It's a genuine reinvention.

The new Oliver Twist, by contrast, stays in period and comes to us as a conventional adaptation. It makes all kinds of changes but hardly any of them work. It isn't a kaleidoscopic but essentially faithful rearrangement of the original, like the brilliant Andrew Davies Bleak House of a few seasons back. It does juggle and rework the plot, working hard from the first to provide a backstory for Olivers birth in the workhouse; Dickens himself, like a TV writer today, seems only to have given any thought to this about halfway through. Here Sally Phelps adaptation resembles Alan Bleasdale's fine version (which, at six years old, was hardly ready to be retired) but without any of the panache. It gives the skulking villain Monks, Oliver's half-brother, an overtly murderous role and amorous designs on the super-virtuous heroine Rose. This doesnt make either Monks or Rose less tedious than they are in the book. What does happen is that the sentimentality that in the novel is hived off within a few skippable chapters now engulfs the whole piece, which is what often happens when you fancy yourself tougher than a great writer: You make him soft.

One reason for this is that the adaptation is almost completely without humour. And one reason for that is that it retains, as far as I could tell, just one line of Dickens dialogue: I'm sure you can guess which one. Dickens' Oliver is a plucky little number; his TV equivalent (whose accent seems to fluctuate between coarse and posh according to the company hes keeping) improves on that by being an outspoken preteen advocate for social justice. After hes asked for more and has been dragged before the workhouse board, who are unsubtly seated around their own groaning board, he tells them just what he thinks of them and their dietary regulations. Which is admirable of him, but less cutting, less moving and less economic than the scene Dickens actually wrote.

Similarly, when Oliver gets to London and is brought to trial on a false pickpocketing charge, the ferociously ignorant magistrate of the original becomes a pantomime villain whose clerk informs him that he's sentenced a mere 22 people to death this week, "and it's only Tuesday." Incredibly, the same Mr. Fang later presides at Fagins trial for murder. And hereby hangs (operative word) a particularly appalling tale. Id feared that political correctness might rob Fagin of his Jewishness, but no: Timothy Spall, who seems perplexed as to whether he's playing villain or victim, affects a singsong Central European delivery, as if that would help with lines like never trust a goyim; we hate them as we hate bitter herbs. The judge, who has suddenly acquired a jury, instructs them in the case of "Fagin the Jew" who is accused of murdering a Christian child. Early Victorian England may have been both barbarous and bigoted, but it wasn't the Middle Ages. Nor was it The Merchant of Venice, but this Fagin is offered the chance of mercy if he will go down on his knees and "take Christ as your saviour." I wont spoil the ending for you.

I will reveal, though, that Bill Sikes (Tom Hardy) is not the usual hulking ruffian but a smooth operator out of a Guy Ritchie movie who never really meant to kill Nancy, just to rough her up a bit. The horror of that murder, and of Sikes subsequent flight, goes for nothing, which must be a first. He meets his fate, in a literal upending of the original, not on a rooftop but in a sewer. The Artful Dodger works very hard, shouldering the duties of three characters, which I suppose is clever. Further rewrites give Sophie Okonedo's Nancy more face time with Oliver than is customary; her contemporary cockney twang makes the character more immediate and more appealing than usual. Other mitigating female performances are Sarah Lancashire's surprisingly sexy Mrs. Corney (her partner Mr. Bumble has the pouchy look of Bert Lahr's Cowardly Lion) and Anna Massey, the best undamed actress of her British generation, making a sharp and benevolent mountain out of a textual molehill as the housekeeper Mrs. Bedwin. Oh yes, and the Artful Dodger and Bill Sikes' dog lived happily ever after. - Oliver Twist concludes this Sunday on TVO at 9 p. m.

THEATRE REVIEW

DANCING WITH STARS CAN BE MURDER

Mysteriously Yours, Toronto

---

A few years ago in these pages, I suggested that Jean Daigle -- star, director and co-author of the Mysteriously Yours interactive dinner-with-murder operation -- should add Tony Soprano to his gallery of parody impersonations. Well, now he's obliged, but not, unfortunately, in the context of a full-fledged New Jersey gangster spoof. Dancing With Stars Can Be Murder, threateningly subtitled The Finals!, takes for its target exactly what you'd expect: a reality TV show with celebrity input. Daigle's Tony appears, for no particular reason, to investigate the poisoning (for once it isn't a shooting) of a contestant who, in his own mind at least, was the favourite to waltz off with the prize.

To be exact, Daigle doesn't play Tony: he plays James Gandolfony, an actor famous for playing Tony. He's turned up to be one of the celebrity judges, but he arrives late, as Daigle's character always does. This is so he can double as the victim, who this time around sports a startling black wig, voluminous enough for three Liberace hairdos piled one on top of another. The performance that supports this creation is suitably flamboyant; and when it comes to the main business of the evening, interrogating his fellow actors and selected members of the audience about their connection with the deceased, he's as good at the amiable bullying as ever he was. And it certainly fits the Tony Soprano persona, first seen here in undershorts, dressing-gown and smoking a cigar. There's probably an explanation of why this getup, so ideal for going down to the end of the driveway to pick up the morning paper, should be Tony's choice of attire for a social-professional engagement, but I forget what it is. Anyway he himself seems faintly embarrassed by it, and glad of the chance to slip off at the intermission and get into something less loose. Daigle's ability to be simultaneously inside the proceedings and detached from them is what makes these shows go.

All the same, this isn't one of the good ones. It's an arbitrary mix of two pop-culture flavours -- three if you count the Agatha Christie whodunnit convention that underpins all the creations here -- that gets little out of any of them. Tony out of context seems like a waste. Parody of TV dance competitions hardly gets beyond telling us that judges and competitors alike are, to a man or woman, murderously jealous narcissists. (Well, if they weren't murderous, or potentially so, they wouldn't be here.)What ingenuity there is has gone into naming them: we meet choreographer Bruno Tarantella, recording starlet Mary Kate Lohanspears and prima ballerina Tatiana Imasonova -- accent, for full effect, on the third syllable -- who does show off a routine involving hammers with a dancing handyman from the audience who, on the night I attended, was damned impressive. I was also mildly tickled by Mary Kate's revelations about some anti-social behaviour earlier in the day that had resolved in her spending a full 90 minutes in police custody, and by her fear that if found guilty of homicide she might be subjected to a sentence even longer.

The choreographic quotient is disappointingly low, especially coming from a company who a year or so back was able to convert their formula into a neat mini-musical. And even the detection part is perfunctory. There was a time at Mysteriously Yours when you could expect a denouement after the denouement; when, once the crime had been solved, there was some kind of twist in the criminal's reaction. Now, the guilty party is identified, those of us who got it right are congratulated and the rest castigated (Daigle still does this very well), and we all go home.

Still, it's Christmas, and one wants to be nice, and there are worse ways of spending a holiday night out. The cast still rise splendidly to the odd improvisational challenge when a punter comes out with an unexpected response, and even when one doesn't. And, something that sets this dinner theatre apart from most others, the dinner part of the equation is very strong. Order with confidence, from a staff who remain charming and considerate and who, in some cases, have been there for years. Such ensemble consistency is rare, in restaurants as in theatres. The management must be doing something right. - Dancing With Stars Can Be Murder is playing at Mysteriously Yours ...Mystery Dinner Theatre's New Year's Eve Mystery Gala. Call 416-486-7469 or 1-800-668-3323 for tickets and information.

2008-12-30-not-much-under-the-hood:
THEATRE REVIEW

Chitty Chitty Bang Bang

Canon Theatre, Toronto

Boxing Night at Chitty Chitty Bang Bang was distinguished by the show's starting half an hour late. This is an especially cruel occurrence when the audience is full of children, though I have to say that this house took its enforced exile to the concession stands in the lobby with exceptionally good grace. Unspecified "mechanical difficulties" were cited for the delay, but we all had our suspicions. Finally, Steve Wilson, cast in the leading role of Caractacus Potts, appeared to confirm, admittedly with considerable charm, our darkest fears. The flying car, the production's title character and raison d'etre, wouldn't fly. It could still do all kinds of other things (e. g. "move laterally") and, honestly, we'd hardly notice, but we could have our money back if we liked.

But this patience was rewarded, because at the very end of the show, the car did in fact levitate, just as it was supposed to. (Well, I assume as it was supposed to: Maybe on a good night it belches fire and tap-dances as well.) I don't know how this happened. In the storyline proper, CCBB will only do complicated things, like letting her headlights light, if the person in the driver's seat says please. So I can only imagine that, during the intermission last Friday, someone talked to her very, very nicely.

The attraction at the Canon is the touring version of the London and Broadway stage musical of the Hollywood film musical of the Ian Fleming book. I missed all those previous incarnations, so I'm going purely on present evidence when I declare Chitty Chitty Bang Bang to be, in the face of enormous competition, the worst-constructed musical I have ever seen. It doesn't have enough of a story to fill its space, though it seems to think it does, and it stops and starts and sputters worse than CCBB herself could have done before Caractacus gave her a facelift.

For the benefit of my few fellow-ignorami, I had better explain. The show is set in England, depicted as so often in American musicals as an Edwardian never-never land. Caractacus is a young widower whose two children develop an attachment to a broken-down old crock that they prevail upon their dad to buy for them. Father is an inventor, with a special interest in sweets, and he tries to sell one of his creations to a confectionery magnate: a bit of action whose only uphsot is that Caractacus gets together with the tycoon's daughter to have a love affair. Retreating behind his garage doors, Caractacus performs on his new plaything (the car, not the lady) what seems to be a full wash and service. He does not however appear in any way responsible for her newly revealed supermechanical powers: a serious break in fairy-tale logic, especially given that these powers are said to be crucial to the rounding-up of the baddies at the end. Note I said "said to be." It happens offstage, which is where our newly shiny heroine spends most of the second act. The Magic of the Theatre has its limits.

Oh yes, the baddies. They're Vulgarians, from Vulgaria. Thick accents and muddy sound made me think at first that they were Bulgarians, but it turns out Fleming wasn't being xenophobic, just snobbish. Figures. Vulgaria is ruled, from the side of the stage, by a Baron and Baroness who mysteriously covet the car even before it's revealed to be a) road-worthy, b) amphibious, and c) gravity-defying; and who will stop at nothing to get it. The Baron giggles and likes toys; the Baroness cackles and hates children. (Presumably the Baroness is barren, and resents it, but like the rest of the show she isn't much on motivation.) She employs a Childcatcher to lure kiddies with sweets, catch them in nets, and then do God knows what to them; given a bit more stage time she could be seriously disturbing.

Just after his humiliation at the sweet factory, Caractacus leads an extended knees-up called Me Ol' Bamboo whose only rationale seems to be to reprise the Step in Time number that was so popular in Mary Poppins. Wilson does this, and everything else that's asked of him, with appealing shy chirpiness, though for someone in his line of work he's short on eccentricity. His offspring (Jeremy Lipton and Camille Mancuso on my night) are perfectly fine, while George Dvorsky and Elizabeth Ward Land are an enjoyably campy villain and villainess. Some of their backchat went, one hopes, over the heads of the youngest, but it's nothing compared to the badinage foisted on their comic spies (tall Dirk Lumbard and short Scott Cote), which may have you pining for the suave sophistication of Ross Petty's Cinderella. One might have expected more wit from a Fleming spy-spoof; but on second thoughts, perhaps not. There's also a whole pack of dogs, whose leader is a real professional.

Next up at the Canon is Medea, another play that ends --at least in the original Greek -- with its protagonist making a getaway in a heavenly car. Sweet are the uses of diversity: Bang Bang Chitty Chitty Bang Bang, we may still need you. - Chitty Chitty Bang Bang runs until Jan. 4. For tickets, call 416-872-1212 or visit mirvish.com.
2009-01-03-this-was-a-quartet-i-won-t-so:
The four shows of the year, the four that left you rubbing your eyes, wondering whether what you saw could really be happening: Company Theatre's Festen, Soulpeppers The Way of the World, Stratfords Hamlet and the Shaw Festival's The President. All were imaginative, fully-fleshed realizations of deeply challenging texts. All were ensemble achievements, with both the Stratford and Shaw shows throwing in a virtuoso performance at the top of the team.

Adrian Noble's production of Hamlet was something we hadnt seen at Stratford in years: a full-blooded main-stage realization of a Shakespeare play that created a world (pre-1914) in almost perfect harmony with the text. Take the one detail of Ophelias piano-playing, something that illuminated her relationship with her family and exploded in her mad-scene. The play was visually beautiful and thrillingly spoken, most of all, by Ben Carlson, whose blend of lucidity, intelligence, passion, wit and speed found their ideal outlet: a performance whose baffled anger haunts the

memory. (He made to be or not to be" sound fresh. And he's young enough to play it again.) Stratford's other great Shakespeare this year was Michael Langhams Loves Labour's Lost. Since Langham is in his 80s and has done the play often before, and since he was doing it now with largely unknown actors, this was routinely dismissed as old-fashioned and undercast. If to make complete intellectual and emotional sense of an elusive play, to look lovely, and to be both heart-tugging and riotously funny is to be old-fashioned, we're in serious trouble.

There were other good things at Stratford: a showmanly Caesar and Cleopatra, fine individual performances in The Trojan Women, the chance to see Fuente Ovejuna and an insanely strong overall company. But it was also a strange-feeling year, with two of its three new artistic directors having resigned before the opening, and one inexplicable choice among the new plays. So, next year, we start again, again.

And, disappointingly, without Peter Hinton, whose two Stratford productions werent among his best, but who more than compensated at Soulpepper with his Way of the World, a scenic update (to the 1950s) that unlocked the play. Traditionally its been about wigs, stars, epigrams and an incomprehensible plot; now it was about driving, sexy, funny and surprisingly young people in a context. Since we seldom see Restoration comedy in Canada, the achievement was taken for granted, but it was extraordinary. One hung on every word. Soulpepper's other big achievement was Weyni Mengesha's production of A Raisin in the Sun, with Alison Sealy-Smith giving the performance of her life. Unlike my big four, this show worked familiar conventions, but it worked them superbly, surmounting any fears that Broadways pioneering black play might now seem worthy but dull. Altogether, this was Soulpeppers Broadway year. The choice of The Odd Couple raised some eyebrows, and one wouldn't want them to make a habit of it, but it was Schultz and Matamoros Inc. in high comic gear, in other words, a treat.

Nothing, though, was as hilarious as the Shaw Festival's The President, Blair Williamss stunning debut production of this wonderfully hardboiled farce (Hungarian-American and combining the best of both). With Lorne Kennedy playing the lead in a perpetual state of fast-forward, it was a lunchtime show, but also the high point of a Shaw season otherwise good without being distinctive.

Festen was Company Theatres follow-up to A Whistle in the Dark. Jason Byrne, who directed both, seems to have an aesthetic that's unique: casual approach, rigorous results, with companies of strongly marked individual actors working in fruitful tension. Second place in Toronto's ensemble stakes goes to Studio 180s Stuff Happens: It didnt have the same ground-breaking feel but it did have super performances and -- courtesy of the Iraq war and the Bush administration -- a mordantly gripping story. Ensemble broke out again at the end of the year, with whole stagefuls of fine actors being better than their material: in the Tarragon's Moliere, CanStage's Its a Wonderful Life, and -- if were going to be stringent about it --in the threehander Someone Who'll Watch over Me at the Berkeley Street Theatre.

Best new Canadian play: Hannah Moscovitch's East of Berlin, whose cast serendipitously included Paul Dunn, author of Offensive Shadows which was the second best, and Brendan Gall, author of Alias Godot which was the third. All three plays witty and blessedly non-parochial, though Moscovitchs carried much the heaviest freight. Dunns might have done better if stripped of its new prologue and paired with his earlier Shakespearean knock-off High Gravel Blind, which some years ago was the inaugural play at Stratford's studio. There was the usual--actually, it seemed worse than usual -- complement of sloppily constructed new plays, dripping with self-importance, at Tarragon, Factory, Passe Muraille and elsewhere. Most disappointing British play: Democracy. (Could a Michael Frayn play really be this dull?) Best imported American play: Sarah Ruhl's The Clean House, though you might not have known it from the CanStage production. On the other hand that much-criticized organization did give us Judith Thompsons Palace at the End (overrated but respectable) and Little Shop of Horrors.

Best musical was, obviously, Jersey Boys. Though hang on, it wasnt: best musical was An Inconvenient Musical, hugely funny, with an original score, and all ours. Finally: I'm too often remiss about crediting costume designers; indeed, one of our leading playwright-directors has been putting it about that I'm fashion-challenged. So, after bows in the direction of Charlotte Dean ( Loves Labours Lost) and Tamara Marie Kucheran ( Intimate Apparel, fittingly) let me conclusively salute Erika Connor, who came up with creations (for The Odd Couple, Little Shop of Horrors, Cinderella) whose magnificence even I had to recognize. And finally finally: it's off my official beat but Tim Albery's COC production of War and Peace was another of the year's triumphs, if also, to my mind, another example of the staging excelling the thing staged.

2009-01-05-pinter-helped-lead-the-troops:
Maybe, if you're thinking of the 1960s as the British decade, your first stop should not be the Beatles. but Harold Pinter. He was in at the start. It was in April, 1960, that The Caretaker opened in London, and immediately became the Play To See. I doubt that any play since, British or other, has achieved the same instant and unquestioned cultural cachet. And it wasnt just a fashionable thing: The play has endured.

But in fact the thing -- the Pinter phenomenon -- had already happened; and not in the theatre but on television. Just a month earlier there had been a triumphant TV production of his previous full-length play The Birthday Party, a play that had famously crashed and burned on the London stage just two years earlier. There had, though, been a groundswell of critical and professional support that had ensured the author a reputation; and hed re-surfaced with a couple of one-act plays and some revue sketches. These had established his talent as a writer of dialogue that was pungently funny and also hung disturbingly in the air. He could conjure tension from words.

What they hadn't been able to show was that he could assemble these tensions into a good story. But this was what The Birthday Party, released into the living rooms of a nation, explosively proved. Admittedly it was a story from which bits seemed to have been left out; we never found out exactly why the jovially sinister Goldberg and Mc-Cann were terrorizing the reclusive mother's boy Stanley or where they were dragging him at the end. But that didnt matter; in fact in the context of this play, designed to tap into everybodys insecurities and everybody's evasiveness, it helped. That isn't always true -- sometimes, including in some of Pinters later plays, obscurity can just obscure -- but it is true here. It certainly held my family spellbound: "You didnt know what was going on," said my father, but you couldn't take your eyes off it. Or your ears: I remember my dad's astonished laughter when Goldberg rounded off the toasts and congratulations for Stanleys birthday with the traditional Yom Kippur greeting: "And well over the fast." The timing -- always Pinters greatest strength -- was uncanny; it came out of nowhere and was completely right. You could say the same of the play itself. After this firework display, the triumph of The Caretaker, a more contained piece with no rough narrative edges, was a walk.

Pinter claimed that his crosstalk mix of veiled threat and inconsequential defence derived from his East End youth, walking and talking his way out of trouble with anti-Semitic gangs. (Goldberg, the Jew as gangster and Pinter's only overtly Jewish character, may be his revenge. He's certainly drawn from life. Pinters father was a tailor. Goldberg, Ive always felt, had a previous career in gentlemen's outfitting.) The tramp and the two brothers in The Caretaker are avowedly based on people he met at a later period, as a struggling actor and writer. Davies, the possibly Welsh tramp who claims service in the colonies (I was over there--I was one of the first over there) is a tragi-comic creation worthy of Dickens. The English director Mike Alfreds claims that he's the last great character in British drama, and that the theatres subsequent decadence can be traced to its failure to come up with anything comparable. I think hes right, and not just about Britain. The Birthday Party has great lines; The Caretaker has great speeches. And always the words serve the action. Mostly they are action.

The Caretaker got Pinter tagged as "a kitchen sink dramatist," a label that stuck -- oddly, since, as he moved up socially, his plays did too. The Homecoming was the transition play: An East End family are visited by their son, now a successful academic, and his wife, who takes over; she has all the men on their knees. It's a brilliant, chilly piece, though not always credible: I imagine that Soulpepper, who are working their way through the Pinter canon, have it in their sights. I wish they, or someone,

would do The Collection, his most neglected play, first written for television and one of the very few TV plays to have transferred successfully to the stage. It's one of his most trenchant studies of sexual jealousy, the form of territorial warfare that most concerned him in his middle period. It was also the first of his plays to be directed by Peter Hall, whose icily elegant approach crystallized whats known as the Pinter style. Its a style from which subsequent productions have had to free themselves. Interestingly it's a style with which he himself as an actor had little to do. Playing a tyrant-boss in a revival of his early play The Hothouse he gave a brutally enjoyable performance, noticeably devoid of pregnant "Pinter pauses." But then, even as a playwright, I don't think he used pauses more than anyone else; he just notated them more.

Pinter did cultivate an image of inaccessibility, refusing to explain his plays to journalists or even actors. Theres a famous story of him directing one of his own plays and telling the cast, Of course, we cant be sure what the author meant here. Though to balance that, there's another story of him helping out an actor in a play of his that he wasn't directing by giving him the blessedly helpful note, "Well, he just wants to f---her, doesnt he?" I met him myself about a dozen times, unable on the first occasion to believe that it was happening: not because he was intimidating -- he couldnt have been friendlier -- but because he was such an established cultural fact. It was like being approached by T. S. Eliot.

To call Pinter a major talent is almost insulting. He was the greatest master of dramatic weaponry to appear in the last half-century. He had an innate feel for verbal and psychological violence: All plays are battles, but his are more nakedly so than most. That doesn't mean he always produced major work. The late short political plays are diminished, though they're recognizably the work of the same man; their torturers and interrogators are descendants of Goldberg and Mc-Cann and horribly believable. Maybe he could have written their scenes in his sleep but the fact remains he did write them, and nobody else could have. He was accurate -- and prescient -- in his attacks on American exceptional-ism, which he summed up as "Were American, so whatever we do is right," though his own counter position, amounting to "Its American, so it must be wrong," was just as simplistic.

Even the middle, and middle-class, plays strike me as inferior to the great early ones, with their cockney roots. The characters' idiom is impoverished and so, theatrically speaking, are they. For one very important thing, they aren't as funny. But thats a matter of degree: The heart is still there. Listening to John Gielgud reeling off the prose arias of the trickster-poet in No Mans Land, or hearing William Hutt deliver them 20 years later -- both actors plumbing the depths of the man's humiliation while letting us relish the way he tries to skate over them-- was to know, again, what drama is about.

Well, hello Ruby Tuesday. This is the night of the week that E! has reserved for the story of Ruby Gettinger, a seriously overweight woman from Savannah, Ga., whose family, friends and physicians all advise her that if she doesn't reduce her weight she will die, sooner rather than later. We are witnesses to her struggle.

The show is less exploitative than that probably makes it sound. It is, though, very repetitive, a characteristic it shares with all reality shows. Thats the category in which its being promoted, and it does raise the question of what the dividing line is between "reality (the quotes are mine, and I'd add italics to them if I could) and documentary. Or maybe the former is just the fancy name that TV channels now give to the latter. I think, though, that there is there is a dividing line, and that it's crossed about halfway through this shows appropriately super-sized opening episode.

For the first half were in the house that Ruby, who's in her thirties, shares with Jeff, her friend since childhood, and Jim, her teenage nephew who's taken refuge with her after leaving his unsympathetic parents. Frequent visitors are Georgia, another old friend, and her son Ben. Its just us and them and the camera crew. Georgia, whos almost too appropriately named, cooks a lot of meals for Ruby: I love to cook Southern," she says -- which seems to be a large part of the problem. Ruby weighs 500 pounds, and even that is a reduction of what she once was; she shows us a picture of when she weighed 700. How she lost that 200 is not revealed, though in view of what we're told later, it's a reasonable question. She has tried various diets over the years ("the grapefruit diet -- weve tried everything), but never for longer than five days. She has a very pretty face and a sunny personality, I love my life," she says, "but the physical parts awful. And we can see for ourselves the difficulty she has simply in finding a chair she can fit into and get out of, and the embarrassments that can cause. I've lived in this shell," she says, "since I was eight.

So there's Ruby, and theres her ready made support system that, up till now, has not always been supportive in the best ways. (Weve been enablers," they admit.) A trip to her family doctor -- which must have been restaged for our benefit, unless you really believe in coincidence-- convinces her that she is "a metabolic time bomb waiting to go off and that she must lose it or, well, lose it. And it's here that the show changes course, and becomes reality," in the TV sense that defines reality as a contest.

Now if this were a hard core cruel show, Ruby would be just one of a group of overweight people (we're well into the second half before anyone uses the word "obese) and there would be judges keeping track of how well they stick to their new regimes and expelling, with censorious comments, those who fail to measure up. Viewers might even be asked to vote on who was likeliest to fall off the wagon. Ruby, needless to say, doesnt go that route. Rubys contest is with herself, which is certainly a subtler and more humane way to go, but does leave all the participants with a very limited number of things to say, and the show with the obligation to have them keep saying it. Ruby's West Coast best friend" Brittany (a name that seems to crop up in every reality show, though with variant spellings) comes for the weekend; this is

a case of opposites attracting, since Brittany is a health nut. (She apparently travels with an exercise bike.) She introduces Ruby to health food stores, signs her up at a gym and buys Georgia a new cookbook.

Ruby gets a personal trainer and enlists in water aerobics. There being "no bathing suits in my size, she wears instead a dress with safety pins." Everyone wishes her well, and intends to do their best by her; it's genuinely refreshing to encounter a non-fiction show full of genuinely nice people. But we do have to spend a lot of time listening to Ruby telling us, either to camera or in voice-over, how she knows that this time she really has to make a change; and to her helpers telling us the same. This is morally better than the customary reality-show narrator telling us over and over again how tense everybody is (this shows only commentary comes from Ruby herself, which is a good thing), but its no less monotonous.

Obviously Ruby's problems go beyond what she eats. So, as well as her own doctor and an "obesity doctor, she goes, with all the normal trepidation, to a psychiatrist: If you'll forgive me putting it his way, she goes to a shrink to help her get shrunk. And he gets her to admit that there are passages in her childhood whose memory she has just blotted out. I would have thought filming such a consultation was a breach of psychiatric etiquette, but what would I know? Future episodes will take us further along this route. If we have been wondering about Rubys romantic life -- and we have -- she tells us that she had a boyfriend who said he would marry her if she lost weight and who left when she didnt. That was six years ago. We're promised that next week he'll return. Another coincidence, or just the magic of television and its industrious researchers? A happy ending is, I think, practically guaranteed. After all, even in the most savage of competitive shows, the humiliations of the losers are drowned out by the triumphs of the winners. And when there's only one person who can either win or lose, you can guess which way it's going to go. And morally it has to, for the sake of all the other Rubys who may be buoyed up by her example. This is one reality show" that could do some real good.

- Ruby premieres tonight at 10 p. m. ET on E!

Iassume that cops and allied trades really do say "copy that," meaning "OK" or "I've got your message and will carry it out" as frequently as TV would have us believe. As far as I'm concerned, the phrase, however authentic it may be, belongs to Mary Lynn Rajskub, who has used it to such effect as Chloe on 24 that the makers of Little Miss Sunshine, in which she had a cameo role, employed it as a gag to herald her appearance. Any other character who uses it is copying her. Copy that.

Few shows use it as promiscuously as Flashpoint, which has a lot of characters to spread it around. Flashpoint has some other fleeting resemblances to 24, in that it depicts a team of expert law enforcers dealing with crises on a weekly basis. It also has some structural similarities to another American show that's just starting up again, Damages. Both begin with flash-forwards to lure us into the main action, though where Damages takes us beyond the end of the main story, Flashpoint merely lures us in with tense moments from the episode we're about to see. These episodes are basically self-contained. This is how television drama series have traditionally unfolded, but after all the recent shows that have demonstrated the power of the ongoing narrative, the old formulas are getting to look, well, formulaic.

There is some internal development of course. The crew of Flashpoint's Strategic Reserve Unit have their personal problems, which are carried over from week to week. I didn't keep up with all of the first season, but my impression on returning for the second is that things haven't progressed much. Team captain Ed (Enrico Colantoni) is still uneasily balancing work and home; Greg (Hugh Dillon) is still the troubled loner. Both are still very well acted. Two of their younger henchmen and henchwomen are nurturing an off-again, on-again love interest. But their stories are inevitably subordinated to the short-term problem of the week.

This season's opener gives us Colm Feore, whom we discover in the teaser yelling at his SRU protectors "Where the hell's my wife?" (This could be his signature line of the year, given that he's also playing the president's husband in 24 and, at Stratford, Macbeth.)He's a billionaire tycoon turned philanthropist (another overlap with Damages -- the pool of possible plots is limited) hosting a gathering at the Royal York Hotel; one of the pleasures of this show is seeing Toronto cast as Toronto. He turns his back for a moment and his wife is abducted. She's held hostage as payment for misdeeds he committed while building his fortune in South America. ("You don't," he admits, "become what I am by being nice to everybody.") It's an unusual situation because, though SRU has no trouble finding the victim, they can't touch her; she's been fitted with a necklace bomb. Feore and Wendy Crewson, she especially, give noble performances as husband and wife.

Ed functions here as their personal bodyguard, and they take to him so much that he gets offered a paid-for suite (corporate rate) to share with his wife, who we imagine gets very few treats. ("When you're rich," says Feore, "you get things cheap." A truth for the ages.) But the events of

the day sort of take the shine off that. Personal feelings come more vividly into play in the next episode where, instead of swarming over a hotel, the team members get to intone "copy that" while laying siege to a house. Inside it a woman (Kristin Booth, very intense), driven hysterical by infertility, holds a knife to the throat of another woman whom she suspects of being her husband's mistress. Do they try to talk her down, or do they break in? There are good arguments on both sides, all professional, all coloured by personal experience.

If Flashpoint is the kinder, gentler, more contemplative, more Canadian cop show, Howie Do It proves, from its title on, that we can be as crass as anyone else and maybe crasser. This is Howie Mandel ("The best part of my job is you cheer just because I show up and work") resuscitating what he calls "the hidden camera prank show" -- as in Candid Camera, for those with long memories, and People Are Funny, for those with elephantine memories. He may even be parodying those shows, though such a thing may not be possible; indeed, they were probably more ingenious and sophisticated. The trick is that Mandel puts on a black wig and pretends to be a producer auditioning his victims for some other TV show; then, after they've humiliated themselves enough, he reveals himself in all his baldness, and they fall down and worship -- or at least in one case -- still look hurt. But presumably they all signed releases. Howie sprays water or blows gale force winds at guys auditioning to be weather reporters. He sends a gullible young man to pick up girls with ill-advised pick-up lines. ("You have nice legs. What time do they open?") He has a fellow dress up in a bunny suit and sing greeting telegrams at a funeral. He has one man watch while someone else makes love to his wife. He ends each segment with by screeching "This is Howie Do It!" Each of the embarrassments is single-track; it's impressed on us that all the participants in a scene except the one unctuously identified as "the mark" are professional actors, or otherwise in on the joke. This reminds me of an old comedian's maxim: A civilian audience will laugh at a comic dressed up as an old lady hurtling towards a brick wall, but for an audience of comics, it has to be a real old lady. Howie Do It is definitely comedy for civilians. There's a whole studio of them, convulsing themselves, even though all they're looking at is film clips. I watched my review copy right through to the end. I'm a saint. Don't copy that.

-The season premiere of Flashpoint airs tonight at 9 p. m. on CTV. The series premiere of Howie Do It airs tonight at 8 p. m. on Global.

2009-01-10-it-s-been-six-days-and-jack-h:
The events I am about to describe, or at least hint at, take place on your television screens over a period of two hours on Sunday night and another two on Monday. After that, we'll be back to an hour a week until we reach the titular total of 24. This is Season 7. As we join it, Jack Bauer is up before a Senate Committee, which is investigating his extensive record of torturing terror-suspects: not, you may feel, before time. (Jack would agree with you.) Tony Almeida, whom we saw graphically dead in Season 5, is (gasp) alive and (double-gasp) working with terrorists himself.

Jack appears before the committee wearing a suit, a state of affairs that we know from previous experience cannot continue long. And indeed, the proceedings have hardly got started before he's subpoenaed by the FBI who need his help in tracking down Tony. Well adjourn till this time tomorrow says the committee chairman, unaware that in the 24 universe "this time tomorrow" doesnt exist. Before the adjournment, the chairman seems to be standing in for all the prissy liberals whom Joel Surnow, the show's right-wing creator, famously holds in contempt. (Has there ever been a lawyer on 24 who wasn't a traitorous scum-bag?) Jack, meanwhile, pleads guilty to having perpetrated what the law defines as torture but asks if the government would rather have civilians killed than let him pummel the truth out of suspects. But, as has often been pointed out, the ticking bomb scenarios presented on 24 never seem to crop up in real-life investigations. Not to mention that none of the alleged torturers at Abu Ghraib and Guantanamo seem to have had Jack Bauers alternative track-record as daredevil heroes. Most people can tell the difference between fact and fiction, but the show itself seems to have them confused at this point. It makes a feint at examining the issues and then abruptly calls time.

Not that the Jack we meet in this new season is any less world-weary than the one we already know, but it remains a given rather than something explored. The "redemption" that was the subtitle of last years prequel doesn't seem to have taken. Or maybe it's just a slow process, not that this show has room for those. Some other things have changed. CTU as we knew it is no more, which seems less a case of throwing the baby out with the bathwater than of demolishing the bathroom altogether. In compensation, Jack does encounter the same personality-types at the FBI as at his old stomping grounds. Theres the suspicious, by-the-book senior agent (Jeffrey Nordling) who really needs to get real or get slapped. Theres the superefficient female agent (Annie Wersching) whose attraction-repulsion relationship to our hero suggests that she's being groomed as today's love-interest. (Someone should warn her of how badly these things always turn out.) Theres an operative who acts like a mole, and so probably isnt. There is, somewhere, a real mole. And there's an earnest, unintentionally funny computer genius, adept at hacking and tracking, who's played by comedienne Janeane Garofalo and who has to be the bizarro Chloe. One longs to see her going head to head, or screen to screen, with the real Chloe. Well, it might just happen.

In fact (why try to keep a secret that everybody knows?), Chloe does reappear this season, her skills and her hero-worship of Jack still intact. Did you know -- Jon Cassar, the producer told me -- that at CTUs nearest real-life equivalent, they call all their computer whizzes Chloe, regardless of gender? Meanwhile, there are the usual problems, and the usual infighting, over at the White House. Principled president Allison Taylor is poised to invade Sengala, the imaginary but all-too-believable African country where Jack was supposed to get Redeemed and where theres a genocide in progress. Not on her watch. In real life, her intervention might pose a pretty moral-political problem for liberals and conservatives alike; here, it's all mixed in with the domestic terrorist plot, which involves the theft of a firewall-destroying device capable of killing thousands and crippling the entire U. S. infrastructure. As Madam Prez, a troubled-but-determined Cherry Jones is starting to justify her high theatrical reputation, though

Colm Feore as her husband seems stuck with a stick of a role. He keeps ducking out to investigate the supposed suicide of his son. As of the close of Episode 4, it's all beginning to tie in. President Taylor is facing a one-hour ultimatum; she will undoubtedly get out of it, only to be faced by 19 hours of additional frustration. The season so far is decently tense, and more coherent than its immediate predecessors. But its also full of barefaced variations on tropes and characters weve met before: the ice-cold disaffected Brit, the psychopath threatening mass destruction to avenge a death in the family. How long before Jack and the president meet and discover a deep mutual respect? How are they going to bring back Aaron? Will Kiefer Sutherland's Jack maintain his record as the longest-serving TV character never to crack a smile, let alone a joke?

I confess these questions nag at me more insistently than any provoked by Damages, which is back with its own patented time-device: the prologue set six months hence in which Ellen (Rose Byrne) spills her guts to someone unseen before the main action sweeps us back into the present to explore the spillage. There is a pervasive and persuasive glitter about Glenn Close's unscrupulous lawyer, ferociously doing bad for good causes; she can even seem natural when acting natural on the Regis Philbin show. (He acts natural, too). But I cant get interested in her or in her personal Manichean divide: Its all too self-importantly slick. Ted Danson's corrupt billionaire is confined to a hospital bed in the first episode, but convalescence becomes him, even makes him sympathetic: True, he's supposed to have defrauded his stockholders and ruined his employees, but these days that just seems par for the course. Reality has caught up with this show, and mugged it. - 24's Season 7 premiere begins tomorrow at 8 p. m. ET/PT on Global and concludes Monday at the same time. Damages airs Sunday at 10 p. m. ET/PT on Showcase.
