2009-01-15-brooding-american:
THEATRE REVIEW

BURIED CHILD

National Arts Centre, Ottawa

---

Sam Shepard's Buried Child, strikingly revived by the English theatre company of the National Arts Centre under Peter Hinton's direction, is a play full of half-articulated relationships. It seems fitting that its first scene, maybe its best, should show a man in his seventies, lying on a couch in front of a silent television while sipping from a whisky-bottle, being harangued by his wife whom we can't see as she is offstage and presumed to be upstairs. Their conversation -- censorious and controlling on her part, sullenly defiant on his -- sets up a dynamic between them and reveals selected details of their family life, past and present, while leaving others in shadow.

The septuagenarian paterfamilias is called Dodge; his wife is Halie. They live in an Illinois farmhouse circa 1978. (That at least is when the play was first produced.) Halie, a vociferously religious woman, is about to pay a call on her priest, with whom she may be having an affair. She and Dodge had three sons; one, who might have been a football champ, is dead, in what are hinted to be sinister circumstances. The other two are still very much around. They are Tilden, who appears brain-damaged and who keeps coming in from the backyard

bearing corn and carrots that nobody can remember planting, and Bradley, who lost a leg in a chainsaw accident (well, how else?) and is fearsomely angry. Dodge lives in fear of Bradley, who has a habit of creeping up on his sleeping dad and cutting his hair off, which seems sort of Biblical. Hanging over, or perhaps under, them all, is the memory of the buried child of the title, whom we finally learn to have been the fruit of incest. This preoccupation may explain why when a real, now grown-up child appears -- Vince, the son of Tilden -- almost nobody recognizes him. With him he has brought his girlfriend Shelly, who at first recoils in horror from the scene-- she expected Norman Rockwell -- but soon rolls up her sleeves and does her best to sort it out. Among other admirable things, she defangs Bradley by depriving him of his artificial leg, leaving him twice emasculated.

It's tempting to describe this neo-Gothic set up as Cold Comfort Farm without the laughs. In fact, though, there is plenty of humour, all of it intentional. Shepard's writing glistens, in both inflationary and deflationary modes, and most of his characters stand tall -- even, or especially, Dodge, who takes nearly everything lying down. The relationships, taken one at a time, give actors and audience plenty to bite on. I can't see, though, that it all adds up to much beyond itself. There are too many holes in the storytelling (as opposed to the actual story) for that. And calling it post-modern doesn't help; it rarely helps anything.

There seems to be a presumption, extended to Shepard's plays since they started appearing in the '60s, that if you put a dysfunctional group of American people on a stage, you automatically have a statement about the whole country. There's an online study guide to Buried Child in which the phrase "the American dream" crops up in practically every sentence. But untilled soil, a deceased sports hero and the play's debut in the post-Vietnam era aren't enough to raise it above its station as fairly powerful personal fantasy. And maybe not all that personal: Its home-invasion plotline wakes echoes of Pinter's The Homecoming, while the abandoned child motif recalls the collected works of Edward Albee. The big revelation, when it comes, doesn't reverberate.

The NAC's program synopsis suggests that the ending, in which Vince takes over both the house and his granddad's signature red cap, may also be a hopeful new beginning. It looked to me more like the cycle about to repeat itself. (His girl has left.) American drama, though, is almost incapable of resisting a redemptive finale, so the program may be right. It's one thing that makes the rare plays that do face the darkness, Death of a Salesman or Glengarry Glen Ross, so impressive. And they are statements about America.

All that said, Hinton's production is hypnotic, monumental in scale and gesture, delicate and detailed in feeling. Eo Sharp's set, which I can best describe as all-over slatted, fills the vast and largely unfurnished stage so that the characters, under Robert Thomson's jagged or mellow lighting, seem marooned but not dwarfed. Troy Slocum's sound design is sharp and scary; when a glass breaks here, the next town must be quaking in its shoes. Company teamwork is impeccable, though individual performances vary. David Fox's Dodge, alternately craven and commanding, is superb; Randy Hughson shambles, perhaps a touch too endearingly, as Tilden; and Adrienne Gould, red-haired and determined as I've never seen her, climbs by degrees as Shelly should, though with some audible effort when she reaches the top. Clare Coulter's Halie is so piercingly right when merely heard that her actual appearance is an anti-climax, maybe because Halie is a self-righteous pillar of the community while Coulter always seems a born-again eccentric; the bright yellow dress that she wears when returning from cavorting with the clergy doesn't look right on her, though it blends perfectly with the yellow roses that Shelly is carrying at the time: an instance of the care with which this production calibrates its visuals. Alex Ivanovici's Bradley works hard for menace; Christie Watson's Vince is personable but without a perceptible arc, though he's the character who needs one. The play is widely regarded as its author's masterpiece; I find it imposing, but frustrating. My favourite Shepard play remains the compact and poetic Fool for Love; until I saw it I thought Shepard's followers so many sheep. - Buried Child runs until Jan. 24 at the National Arts Centre in Ottawa; Feb. 1 to 22 at the Leonor and Alvin Segal Theatre in Montreal.

2009-01-15-introducing-the-songless-sket:
THEATRE REVIEW

THEM AND US

Theatre Passe Muraille

---

Tracy Dawson, who is both author of them and us and one-quarter of its cast, is a former writer-performer with Second City and her play shows it. It's a collection of sketches. Most of them are well-written and some of them are funny, though seldom to a laugh-out-loud degree. Some of the other attractions of revue are missing as well, such as music, drinks, an intermission and a variety of authorial styles and viewpoints. We have no choice but to regard the proceedings as a play, and seen that way it gets frustrating and a little wearisome. Beyond the actors' skills, which are considerable, we have nothing to hold on to.

There is a unity of theme, but even that turns out to be counter-productive. All the episodes are about relationships, a subject that offers the advantage of being of potential interest to nearly everybody and the disadvantage of being the most obvious topic under the sun. You can always say something about it but, unless you do some serious digging, it's unlikely to be anything novel or arresting. These couples -- the vast majority of the scenes are dialogues -- all arrive at the conclusion that interacting with another person is difficult and sometimes painful, but better than the alternative. Anyone disagree?

I lied a bit when I said there was no music. More accurately, there's no original music, and nothing performed live. Quite a bit gets piped in, and to good effect. The show starts with the Sinatra-Basie record of Fly Me to the Moon, the four actors on stage self-consciously grooving to it. It's one of the wittiest things in the evening, especially with Michael Healey shuffling somewhere on the edges of hip, and Sarah Dodd looking pained but determined. A later scene finds a Nina Simone record used as an emotional touchstone for four people at a dinner party. Dawson herself and Gray Powell, the two younger members of the team, are the hosts; Dodd and Healey are, respectively, a woman reeling from a break-up and a guy who's somehow managed to become a single father without ever having dated. They know they've been set up to be set up, and it's sweet -- if something of a credibility-stretch -- to watch them wrestle with their pre-ordained roles. One wishes them well.

There's another festive gathering later on, a sour balance to the first. Dawson is the host, Powell is her ex and Dodd is a woman whose romantic prospects for the evening are ruined by a mix of jealousy, intoxicating substances, and -- this, I think, is the real crusher --a fatal mismatching of tastes in movies. It's tempting to say that all the best scenes here

are the group ones, but that doesn't hold for a protracted item in which the guys on one side of the stage and the gals on the other demonstrate the different ways in which signals may be interpreted and stories told by the two genders. The Summer Days, Summer Nights song in Grease did it more economically and entertainingly. Indeed, if you want a set of vignettes about feelings solitary or shared, then song, with its power to concentrate a moment, may be the best way to go.

The spoken duets here include two in which an older man (Healey) fences with a younger woman (Dawson): much younger in one case since he says, flustered-like, that she's his partner's daughter. (Would that be life-partner or business-partner? It does make a difference.) Their first encounter, a sort of prenup contract, has him saying that he doesn't believe in romantic love, which probably means that he does: Coming early in the evening, it's plainly meant to state a theme, but it isn't one that gets developed, just repeated. The most "serious" encounter, and the most dispensable, finds a doctor giving a patient a diagnosis of cancer, followed by an embrace; this scene is unprofessional, on a number of levels. The most obviously revue-ish items are an exchange of false comfort between two women in a coffee shop, and a monologue by Dawson about having flatulence on a date; nothing very wrong with either of them, but they don't seem to belong with the author's higher ambitions.

I have few complaints, though, about the performance. Ruth Madoc-Jones' direction is supple and fluid, the myriad transitions excellently handled with much credit to Kimberly Purtell's bare set and bold, sensitive lighting. Of the players, Dawson herself is better at timing her lines than exploring what's beneath them; it's unfortunate, too, that she has to make much of the running in the first quarter of the evening. (I doubt if it was meant to be The Tracy Dawson Show, but it does come on that way.) Powell does unobtrusively and resourcefully well, especially with the night's first monologue. Healey explores, endearingly, many shades of rumpled; at one point he had me convinced that he'd changed the colour of his hair, though all he'd really done was muss it up a little. Dodd shows off the greatest range, from rage to loss to (occasional) glee, and hits each unfussily on the nose; I've never thought of her as a revue performer, and I doubt if she has either, but she has the economy and versatility for it. Some of the scenes -- I almost said numbers -- do echo or complete others, but this doesn't add up to structure. It's as if a Second City running gag were being asked, single-handedly, to repeal the law of diminishing returns - Them And Us Runs until Jan. 31. Call 416-504-7529 for more information.
2009-01-15-the-new-corps-at-the-mother-c:
Previously on Being Erica ... Actually, that's a tough one, and I'd hate to be one of the people who has to prepare this show's instant updates. The thing is, when you look back at previous episodes, you find the action divided between the factually-previously and the fantasy-previously. Or between real reality and alternate reality. Or between the seriously-just-past and the might-have-been-more-distant-past. (Of course, even the factual parts are fiction, but enough is enough.)

It's not that confusing when you actually watch. Here is Erica Strange, 32, in Toronto and at an assortment of dead ends. She's a university graduate with literary ambitions, but neither her degree nor her talent have borne any fruit. In one day she loses both her next-best-thing-to-a-boyfriend and her job -- not that she liked either of them much anyway. Her family are constantly on at her about her career and marital prospects, or lack thereof. (Need I say she's Jewish?) To top it all, she suffers an allergic reaction from a free sample of flavoured latte and winds up in hospital. There she encounters Dr. Tom, a whimsical shrink whose professional credentials don't include a surname. He says he can help her. He asks her to write down a list of the events and decisions she most regrets. We don't get a very close look at this document, but it seems to contain enough material for 10 weeks of television. And so, almost before Erica knows where she is, she's somewhere else: back in high school in Episode one, and at university in Episode two, fortified in both cases by knowing now what she wishes she'd known then.

The show to date is half refreshing, half crackerbarrel. Much of the refreshment comes from Erin Karpluk, who plays Erica and who makes self-deprecation sexy. Michael Riley as Dr. Tom offers a pixie-ish variation on his accident-prone lawyer from This is Wonderland, the difference being that this guy doesn't make mistakes and is really pretty smug about it. (And speaking of Wonderland, Erica has a good claim to be today's Alice. That would make the doctor a cross between Humpty Dumpty and the Mock Turtle.) The today scenes are by and large delightful, well observed and entertainingly played. The problem is with the quasi-flashbacks. Erica, retuning to her old haunts and those with whom she haunted, does indeed make some different choices.

Some of them work out better than others, but at the end of them all she's still the same person. This moral, hinted at in the first week, is explicitly stated in the second, leaving you wondering where the show has left to go. We care enough about Erica to wonder what's going to happen to her now; what happened to her back then is beginning to get in the way.

Maybe one of Erica's mistakes is that she, a Torontonian, went to the University of Toronto; perhaps she needed to get away. Her alma mater appears, when revisited, to have been a terrifying place, ruled by elitist secret societies with appalling hazing rituals. But the locations are nice, and there's a sense of the city about the whole show that's pleasing, if occasionally puzzling; Erica applies for work with a publishing company that seems to live in the Opera House. Her writing ambitions came to the fore in Episode Two, which she narrates in voice-over as if reading stage directions; she even read the credits, getting one of them (I assume intentionally) wrong. There was none of this device in Episode One; and though I think I see its point, I hope it remains a one-off. If it persists, it could get seriously annoying.

---

Previously on Wild Roses ... Summarizing this, CBC's other new big one, is so efficiently done at the start of Episode Two that the viewer need feel no guilt about missing Episode One. Wild Roses is a simple tale of greed and grudge whose title remains mysterious. They might have called it Calgary, as it clearly yearns to be Canada's belated answer to Dallas, or perhaps Sex, Oil and Rock 'n' Roll. The sex to date is minimal. We do get to see some bull-on-cow action, though Mr. Big, as his owners fondly call him, fails to come through, and is finally sidelined by an overdose of bovine Viagra. This is one of the semi-comic interludes that dilute what ought to be flaring melodrama. The rock 'n' roll comes from Lucy, who gives up a European tour with her band so she can stay home and help her widowed mother and two sisters fight off the oil tycoon who's threatening to foreclose on their cherished ranch. He's doing this because a) the mother's spurned his advances; b) he's running low on black gold, and he's detected a fresh lode on the property; c) he's a bastard. This mixture of motives does not make him a complex character. Still less so is Lucy's daughter, pretty near the ultimate in spoiled bitches, who's cheating on her brand-new fiance, and shows her sluttish nature by always doing it standing up. This makes her easier to photograph, both for the show itself and for a blackmail plot. She also shows how stuck-up she is by listening to opera: not a convincing trait. But then the show's attitude to high culture is none too informed; its promos describe it as "Shakespearean," a claim largely unsupported by the dialogue. This in any case has to fight for its life against the onmipresent music, some of it fittingly country, most of it just bloated. The show's timing is historically unfortunate; we aren't really in the mood for the villainous David's gloating declaration that "the price of crude is going up." It's old-fashioned in more damaging ways: It's airless. To watch these dessicated lads and lasses riding the range is to weep for the network that gave us, only last year, The Englishman's Boy, and seems little inclined to follow it up. - Being Erica airs Mondays at 9 p. m. on CBC. Wild Roses airs Tuesdays at 9 p. m. on CBC.

2009-01-17-on-maddening-myth-mirvish-s-m:
I have two abiding memories of the 2000 production of Medea at the Stratford Festival. One is of the believability of Seana McKennas Medea and Scott Wentworths Jason as a couple in or after the last stages of marital breakdown, competing in blame and resentment. The other is of the way in which the play, otherwise done as naturalistically as Athenian tragedy will allow, began and ended with fragments of the original Greek and with the actors in the traditional tragic masks. We were taken on a journey from then to now and back again.

Restaged in Toronto with the same two leading actors, Miles Potter's production retains this double focus. We get both immediacy and immensity, both hit and myth. Within this giant pendulum swing, there are the personal oscillations, emotional and technical, of McKenna's Medea, by turns wronged refugee wife, silky sorceress, sardonic commentator and unappeasable fury. Medea, a kings daughter, avenges herself on the husband whos dumped her in favour of a younger princess, by having her supplanter and her father burned alive, and then by killing her own and Jason's two sons. She exults in the first deed; feels compunction but no guilt over the second. And certainly in Robinson Jeffers' domesticated but still resonant adaptation of Euripides original, she enjoys telling us, via the chorus, just how angry, clever and desperate she is and how appalling and contemptible are all men. It sometimes feels that its the actress as much as the character who's doing the enjoying, but she's so adept at changing gears, at stopping on the comic brink and plunging instantly back into the inferno, that it doesnt matter. Wentworths Jason, his voice a ringing sneer, hardly whitewashes Jason, but he makes his case as forcefully as she makes hers. (And Medea must have been hell to live with.) At the end, with his mask clapped on, he's the one who's trapped in tragedy. She gets away.

Michael Spencer-Davis and Nigel Bennett give affable support as, respectively, a confessedly weak king and one whos not quite strong enough. As the nurse who graduates from home help to atrocity reporter, a black-clad Patricia Connolly bites into every word, whether watchful or appalled, that she answers. If the production is slightly less powerful in a big house than it was at the Tom Patterson eight years ago, thats partly due to the upping of the chorus from three ladies to five. Then, they could be distinct people who sometimes merged; now, despite distinguished personal resumes (from Shaw, Stratford and elsewhere) they're the usual uncertain bunch, not quite individuals, not quite a collective. Until, that is, near the end, which is when the production shows its hand and clutches them within it. They beat on the doors of Peter Hartwell's imposing new set, behind which Medea is committing double filicide. They feel inexorable tragedy sweeping down, and they make us feel it. Flames spring up from altars to bar Jasons way, and to tell him and us that magic is at work and, beyond that, fate. Michael Beckers music and Peter McBoyle's sound design, both thrilling, deliver the aural coup de grace. The verbal comes from McKenna, ineluctable and unreachable. You already know the end.

It's worth, though, going beyond the end. Medea escaped to Athens, courtesy of King Aegeus to whom she'd promised release from sterility. She came through and he had a son, Theseus, whose second wife Phaedra became a tragic heroine on her own account, falling in love with her stepson and causing both his death and her own. And Phaedra is a role that Connolly played at Stratford two decades ago and that McKenna is to play there this year. Myth is continuous. And inescapable. - Medea runs through Feb. 9 at the Canon Theatre. For more information, call 416-872-1212.

2009-01-19-living-life-in-an-alter-ego-u:
Perhaps the best thing about United States of Tara is that the title isn't the best thing about it. Good, teasing pun though it is, the show itself more than lives up to it.

Tara, in this new joint offering from Dreamworks and Showtime, is a suburban lady in her late thirties. In Kansas, I think; the geography isnt stressed, though the character certainly is. Besides having a career, a husband and two teenage children, she also plays host to three alternate personalities. She has been able to keep them at bay through medication but now, distressed by side-effects, she has gone off her meds, and her alters, as everybody here calls them, are invading her life and her familys. The show, I should perhaps make clear at this point, is a comedy.

Which raises a ticklish question. Dissociative Identity Disorder (DID), from which Tara suffers, is a real and distressing condition, often stemming from childhood abuse. The show, from an idea by Steven Spielberg no less, is actually written by Diablo Cody, screenwriter of Juno, who is famous or notorious for not doing research. She does not examine the real-life implications of her premise in anything approaching clinical detail. She uses it as a device. But I don't think that constitutes exploitation. The show doesn't laugh at Taras condition. It uses it as a way of laughing at other things.

Ive seen three episodes. The first two both begin with Toni Collette's Tara talking to camera; the third doesn't, but I hope these prologues will return -- because they are, in a nervously informal way, smashing. She tells us, hand on chin ("while Im still lucid"), that shes an interior designer, currently fashioning a 17th-century rococo nursery for a rich client. ("I create opulent environments for women who hemorrhage money.") She has an extremely understanding husband, Max; a 14-year old prodigy of a son, Marshall; and a daughter, Kate, who is commencing being sexually active, maybe not as much as she'd like people to think but enough to provoke very mixed feelings in her mother. And it's primarily to deal with these feelings that Tara calls upon the services of her other selves. Or sacrifices herself on her alters.

The three are: T, a gum-chewing aggressive flirt of her daughters own age; Buck, a foul-mouthed jock with a different brand of aggression, which he puts down to service in Vietnam; and Alice, a picture-perfect housewife from televisions idea of the 1950s. Each comes complete with wardrobe and coiffure. Whether they could really manifest themselves so neatly is open to doubt. But I'm prepared to go with it, especially with Collette being splendid in quadruplicate. She's fine as T and also as Buck, but its Alice -- whom we dont meet until Episode Two-- who's the killer.

She represents old-style sitcom intruding on new-style, and leaving it largely speechless. (That makes her the comic photo-negative of January Jones' wife in Mad Men, a 50s figure engulfed by the onrushing 60s.) In one of the best scenes from any TV show in recent memory, Alice imposes her old-world wisdom, and impregnable sweetness, on an insecure teacher who's been giving her too-bright son a hard time in literature class. She also, literally, washes Kate's mouth out with soap. This doesnt go as well; its Kate, as you might expect, who has the hardest time with her mothers. Why, she asks, "can't mom just be manic-depressive like all the other moms?" Actually, special problems apart, this family doesn't seem any more dysfunctional than what TV has trained us to regard as the norm. Both Max and Marshall think that Tara is, or are, pretty neat.

Codys writing is razor-sharp in both speech and silence , the smart-ass quality less irritating than it sometimes was in Juno, or at least more evenly spread around. Brie Larsons Kate is something of a blur, especially vocally, but John Corbett is delightfully placid as Max, trying to sort out the various sexual demands and opportunities afforded by three women in the same body. (Buck doesn't turn him on.) There is an added attraction -- for viewers, I mean -- in Tara's sister Charmaine, played by Rosemary DeWitt who was Rachel in Rachel Getting Married, so may be making a career out of being the crazy ladys sensible sibling. (They dont even want me around when I'm me, complains Tara of the people she lives with. "Please," says Charmaine, it's all you.)

But the prize performance, Collette apart, comes from Keir Gilchrist (British-born, Canadian-based, if you care) as Marshall, with his Pabst movies and Thelonious Monk records, and his developing crush on a slightly older boy who involves him, to his dismay, in a church basement morality play ("We need an AIDS patient being flogged in Hell") that he advertises as cutting-edge.

And so it may be, compared to the school production of Grease, whose auditions provoke an especially memorable comment from Marshalls earnest would-be girlfriend: Even something mainstream like Miller or, God forbid, Wilder would be preferable to this --its not even good on an ironic level.

United States of Tara is good on an ironic level, and on other levels as well, levels more truly entertaining. "I'm not schizophrenic," says Tara, "I don't hear voices." She knows best. But, if I were being sloppy about it, I could say that this show does for schizophrenia what Weeds does for drug-dealing. And, in the patented cable TV game of subverting suburbia, it's the best thing since. - United States of Tara premieres tonight at 9 p. m. on The Movie Network.

2009-01-21-the-truth-of-the-matter-is-it:
I'm not gonna lie to you. Lie to Me isnt good. It isnt all that bad either: just standard-issue. The pilot, which is all I have to go on, is quintessentially pilot in the matters of getting its regular characters together, displaying their quirks, hinting at possible future interactions and giving them a couple of specimen plotlines in which to show their paces. Plots in which we can't get invested because we know we'll never see them again.

Its a new wrinkle on the detective-show formula. Wrinkle" really is the appropriate word here, since the central character, the apparently British Dr. Cal Lightman (Tim Roth) believes, in direct contradiction of Shakespeares King Duncan, that there is an art to finding the mind's construction in the face, and that he's got it. Hes a human polygraph, able to spot a liar by reading the minutest details of their face and body language. He seems infallible at this but, just in case, he has a support team of three: Dr. Gillian Lightman (Kelli Williams), a psychologist loaded with the human warmth that the brilliant Cal conspicuously lacks; Eli Loker (Brendan Hines), a young man whose name practically screams "TV series and who, we are told, never lies himself; and Ria Torres (Monica Raymund), whom we actually see being recruited. Shes an airport security officer whose prowess at spotting suspicious passengers so impresses Cal and Gillian that they hire her on the spot. She even spots them, though frankly they are acting so exaggeratedly suspicious that even I might have tagged them. Have you ever," she's asked, "had any specialized deception training? To which she smartly replies, I've dated a lot of men." There, Ive spoiled the one good line for you. But its worth catching her delivery of it.

We start with Cal himself interrogating a domestic terrorist who refuses to talk. "That's all right, says the doc, nonchalantly letting us in on his personal credo and the show's. I dont have much faith in words. The average person tells three lies in every 10 minutes worth of conversation." Its riveting stuff, but it turns out not to be the beginning of a storyline, but part of a lecture he's giving to the law-enforcement troops. Having no access to the body language at the show's story conference, I cant say whether this is a blatant imitation of the opening sequence of The Lives of Others or just a coincidence. Though I doubt that Cal believes much in coincidence.

He and his colleagues and their expertise are for hire to any law enforcement agency that needs them, though as always in these shows the need is expressed with suspicion verging on contempt. (One FBI guy dismisses them as a carnival show.) The genius team do have an inconvenient habit of suspecting the innocence of those whom the authorities have already determined to be guilty. Their lesser case tonight concerns a U. S. senator suspected of consorting with prostitutes, or at least a prostitute, and surprisingly reluctant to try and worm his way out of it. Most time, though, goes to a male high schooler apprehended at a murder scene, the victim being a lady teacher. The boy comes from a family of Jehovahs Witnesses, and it falls to the two doctors to interview his parents. One looks forward to seeing them questioned in their own home instead of doing it themselves on the doorstep of somebody else's, but no subtle revelations are in store. "Get out of my house, yells the father, when the question is raised of his responsibility for his son's thwarted sexuality. With his nostrils flaring and his fists clenched, he seems rather a waste of Dr. Cals subtle skills. Meanwhile the music swells, to relieve the actors of most of the burden of acting.

Not that they dont do their best, under what must be considerable pressure. They have to live, after all, with the knowledge that the camera is scrutinizing their minutest changes of expression on our behalf. Among the comparatively innocent, I was delighted to see Robert Wisdom, the great Bunny Colvin of The Wire and good, if miscast, as the jail boss in Prison Break's unfortunate Panamanian detour. He's back on the side of the law this time, with one scene as a helpful desk sergeant. Hell presumably reappear, but even that possibility isnt enough to counteract the deadening feeling that we're in for the same bunch of people going through the same predictable moves every week, even while seeming to start from scratch. They may be thwarted on the odd case -- this is 2009, after all -- but even that won't change the predictability of it all. None of them have yet displayed any compelling personal characteristics. Cal, who is divorced with a teenage daughter, is being built up as a misanthrope: I recommend happiness to you," says Gillian, his girl Friday. But that only makes the show seem like the police procedurals answer to House, with Roth the new Hugh Laurie. And at least Laurie gets to show off an American accent.

- Lie to Me airs tonight at 9 p. m. on Global.

2009-01-23-the-view-from-here-the-holoca:
Every father who is a soldier should think about his children ... They never will live a normal life. Those words are spoken at the beginning of the documentary film Inheritance, shown on PBS at the end of last year, by Monika Hertwig, daughter of Amon Goth, the Nazi death-camp commandant now best known for having been played by Ralph Fiennes in Schindler's List. The same words might also serve as an epigraph for Hannah Moscovitch's play East of Berlin, whose original production from last year is currently being revived at the Tarragon Extra Space in Toronto. Both the play and the documentary present a meeting between a Holocaust survivor and/or her child, and the child of one of the perpetrators.

And so does the movie The Reader. This does feature a perpetrator, and it also has two survivors, mother and daughter; in one scene, the two sides are present in the same courtroom, but they dont actually meet. Their interaction is conveyed to us through a mediating figure, the boy whose future is coloured by having an affair with an older woman who was once a camp guard. And the boys older self is played by the same Ralph Fiennes, whose portrayal of Amon Goth propelled Goth's daughter into contacting Helen Jonas, the Plaszow camp inmate who had initially escaped the gas chambers by being taken by Goth to work in his house and who was rescued from there by Oskar Schindler. Monika wanted -- well, what? To make amends? To seek forgiveness for crimes committed when she was a baby, but still in some sense hers? To seek some kind of common cause with a woman hurt, though far more grievously, by the same man who had blighted her own life? We can never know, and neither can she.

Inheritance brings Monika and Helen together at the site of the camp itself. James Moll's film is a fine and moving one, even if you may harbour some doubts about the TV companys role in setting the whole meeting up. Both women break down, but it seems that its Helen who has to do more of the comforting, even though Monika is a strong and striking figure in her own right.

Years after the war, Monika's mother committed suicide. So did Helen's husband, another survivor, with whom she had made a life in America. This is one of the correspondences between Inheritances true story and the fictitious one that unfolds in Moscovitchs impressive East of Berlin. Brendan Gall plays Rudi, a young German who grew up in Paraguay and discovered his father had been an Auschwitz doctor, responsible for selections at the ramp. Fleeing the knowledge, he goes to Berlin, where he meets and falls in love with Sarah, a young Jewish-American woman, the daughter of survivors; her mother, too, had eventually killed herself. Both feel an appealing streak

of perversity about their relationship, though Sarah is far from knowing the full truth of Rudi's background. When she does discover it, Rudi, who's narrator as well as protagonist, returns to South America. We leave him with a gun in his hand, about to shoot either his father or himself. It would be unfair to reveal which he does, though foreknowledge actually makes the play seem richer.

When Moscovitch saw Inheritance, she was, she told me, amazed and relieved to discover how much she had got right. She already knew, though, that what might seem the most improbable aspect of her play had happened in real life. The viewer of Inheritance develops a longing for Monika and Helen to become friends. It doesnt happen; Helen can muster respect and even sympathy for Monika, but not affection. Moscovitch had read books about second-generation reconciliations between Jews and Germans that did indeed lead to friendships and even love affairs. Writing a play about the Holocaust was, she says, "a terrifying thing to do because Im Jewish." The ethical problems are obvious; and it merges with a technical one. Writing about it directly means dividing your cast between victims and perpetrators. But victims aren't dramatically interesting, because they've been deprived of choice, and concentrating on the perpetrators might seem obscene. The best way to approach it, now, seems to be to focus on the inheritors, whose situation is a little easier to apprehend.

The Reader, Oscar nominations notwithstanding, fails at this, though theres a suicide in this one, too. It works initially as a sexual fantasy (initiation by an older woman) but when the identity of Kate Winslets ex-guard is revealed, it makes everything else in the picture seem trifling, even offensive. Why, in such a context, should we care about the petty torments and equivocations of Fiennes' emotionally blighted lawyer? Was Winslet's cruelty due in any way to her illiteracy, and is her learning to read supposed to be some kind of silver lining? If not, what is the movies conceit? What I feel, what I think, Winslet says, "doesnt matter; the dead are still dead." Well yes, but we knew that. If Winslet's thoughts and feelings are really so unreachable, which is indeed likely, maybe she shouldn't be the subject. When Fiennes goes to visit Lena Olins remarkably poised survivor in her remarkably swank apartment, she tells him that there is nothing to be learned from the camps. True or false, that statement blows up the whole of the preceding film.

East of Berlin leaves its Nazi offstage, but it makes him believable, through the words of his son whose shamefaced monologue is addressed, Moscovitch told me, to an imaginary audience of survivors. I hadnt realized that, but I can see how that premise makes the writing possible and makes it powerful. Approaching the Holocaust at two removes, it passes the Helen Jonas reality test. The Reader doesn't. "There's no catharsis to be found in the camps," Olins character tells us. Nor is there for Moscovitchs characters or for Helen Jonas or Monika Hertwig. But there may, in watching them, be some for us. - East of Berlin runs until Feb. 7. Visit tarragontheatre.comfor information.

2009-01-24-pop-goes-the-bard:
SHAKESPEARE AND MODERN CULTURE

BY MARJORIE GARBER

Pantheon

368 pp.; $34

---

Marjorie Garber writes that Prospero's "our revels now are ended" speech in The Tempest is "one of the passages in Shakespeare that I find real difficulty in reading aloud without a noticeable catch in my throat."

She isn't the only one, but it's heartening to find an academic critic (Garber is a professor of literature and chair of environmental studies at Harvard, as well as being the author of a dozen books) expressing such enthusiasm and exposing such vulnerability. The very idea of a professor reading Shakespeare aloud is an encouraging one, made all the more heart-warming by the fact that Garber's own prose -- fast, witty and aware -- both invites and survives the reading-aloud test. There isn't a page of Shakespeare and Modern Culture that I didn't enjoy.

Which makes it frustrating that the book as a whole is so disappointing. It starts from the uncontroversial proposition that Shakespeare's plays have insinuated themselves into just about every aspect of modern life, including some apparently incongruous ones, and that this has in turn affected the way we respond to the work itself.

She attempts to trace the relationship between 10 of the plays and their later analogues, "modern" in her sense stretching back into the 19th century and forward into the 21st. It's a field she's equipped to explore; it's rare to find an author, especially a scholarly one, who can treat both traditional and pop culture without condescending to either. But it's also a vast area, one that invites catalogues rather than conclusions. Too often, you come to the end of a chapter wondering what the author was trying to prove.

To each of her chosen plays she affixes a keyword, denoting a concept that later ages are said, not always persuasively, to have found especially attractive. To The Tempest, first in her book as it was in the First Folio, she assigns the word "Man," which can mean just about anything. She starts with an account of a Kentucky prison whose Shakespeare performance group has never, despite all colonialist theories, cast a black prisoner as Caliban; that's fascinating but she never goes back to it.

Her chosen theme for The Merchant of Venice is "Intention" -- the never-ending search to determine whether Shakespeare agreed with us about Shylock. Critics, especially modern ones, have decried the idea of "intention," but consider this: Almost every rehearsal of a play, whatever the theorizing behind it, inevitably becomes an attempt to discover what the author meant. The Merchant is a case whose problems might be summarized by two facts: It was a favourite play of the Nazis, and Jewish actors have always clamoured to play it. There are whole books about its history, and Garber adds little to them except a lively style.

Her best chapter is on Romeo and Juliet ("Youth"). Here she's able to zero in on two co-existing yet contradictory phenomena. One is that Romeo's name has entered the language with an identity precisely opposite to its namesake's in the play; instead of a lover faithful unto death, he's a boy too dishy to confine himself to one girl. (Remember Petula Clark's hit song Romeo, which begins "I studied Shakespeare when I was at school" and ends, "are you mine, or just only my Romeo?") The other is the way in which each young generation adopts (and adapts) the play as its own image of romantic revolt against social and familial intolerance. Garber has a lot to say about West Side Story, a show that's influenced all subsequent productions of Romeo and Juliet; something, too, about Tom Stoppard's screenplay for Shakespeare in Love, a movie that, wittily and movingly, affirms R&J as "the normative love story of our time," and knows in advance that we will agree.

Stoppard also figures largely in the chapter on Hamlet ("Character"), which provides a brilliant commentary on Rosencrantz and Guildenstern are Dead, though not quite as brilliant as the commentary that the play itself provides on Hamlet.

It also has some of the best of the (mainly) New Yorker cartoons with which Garber sprinkles her pages, as a neat way of reinforcing Shakespeare's omnipresence (subway commuter: "If it be not now, yet it will come; the readiness is all").

Also fun: Her referencing business-instruction manuals that cite Henry V ("exemplarity") as a leadership model, Henry's willingness to execute his friends being cited by one such book as "the ultimate pink slip," which, Garber gently points out, rather misses the play's complexities.

You might say the same for the constant invocations of Lady Macbeth ("Interpretation") by journalists writing about Hillary Clinton or Margaret Thatcher, which they could surely only do by disregarding marital context. (Bill as Macbeth might be possible casting, but Denis?) Garber has a soft spot for Mac-Bird, a forgotten satire on LBJ, whose idea of parody was to name Adlai Stevenson as the Egg of Head; this may or may not be fair to Stevenson, but it certainly isn't fair to Shakespeare, whose jokes were much cleverer.

As are Garber's: This book is probably just a pendant to her magnum opus, Shakespeare After All, which I passed up reading a year ago (I opted for A. D. Nuttall's brilliant Shakespeare the Thinker) but up with which I now intend to catch. It may, I fancy, say more in passing about Shakespeare's modernity and modernity's Shakespeare than this one does by concentrating on them. - Robert Cushman is the National Post's theatre critic.

2009-01-26-a-mushier-m-a-s-h-zone-of-sep:
For the third time in recent months, a character in a TV action drama finds himself, or in this case herself, standing, petrified, atop an unexploded bomb. This scenario should be more gripping in ZOS: Zone of Separation, which is set against a real and recent conflict, than it was amid the fantasy heroics of Prison Break or 24. But in fact it's less, precisely because the stakes and therefore the expectations are higher and they have not been met.

The person on the mine is Captain Sean Kovacs (Michelle Nolden), commander of an unarmed team of United Nations military observers in a Balkan town called Jadac, fictitious but resembling Sarajevo. Her job and her team's is to keep the town's Muslim and Christian populations from one another's throats; it isn't easy since just about everyone we meet from either side is either a fanatic or a racketeer or both. Kovacs is Canadian and a self-hating Albertan. (A rare breed as far as I know; anyway she doesn't like other Albertans.)The ante in the minefield incident is upped, theoretically, by the presence of two other potential victims, both children, and of a pair of distraught parents. On top of that, the entrapped Kovacs keeps having flashbacks, in hallucinatory black-and-white, to an earlier incident that left her somewhat traumatized and a male colleague almost completely so. And on top of that, high-pitched music on the soundtrack keeps alerting us to how tense and potentially pitiful it all is, though the tension is somewhat eased by our knowledge that the tough and tender Nolden has the show's top billing, and so is hardly likely to perish in the first episode. I know I must sound like a broken record about this, but the use of music to manipulate our emotions -- to do, in fact, what the writing and performance should be doing -- has become the sign that separates the serious TV shows from the soaps. ZOS, which has aspirations on the level of The Sopranos, Deadwood and The Wire, winds up instead in the semi-serious world of Flashpoint and The Border. (This may reflect its mixed parentage; ZOS is a show with CBC involvement that has ended up premiering in the tougher cable environment of The Movie Network.)

As it happens, Malcolm MacRury, the show's principal writer and one of its executive producers (Paul Gross is another), has a Deadwood past, and he's quoted as seeing the new show as a homage to that one. Both depict a frontier civilization, or lack of it, with a fragile rule of law. Notably, both feature a transplanted Englishman, an outwardly genial brute ruling the local roost as saloon-keeper, brothel-owner and gangster. Ian McShane's Al Swearengen, though, is a hard act to follow, and ZOS's George Titac, a Muslim from Manchester, doesn't have the flavour, the charm or, judging from the first two episodes, the complexity. He's played, forcefully, by the aptly named and cauliflower-faced Colm Meaney, who is in fact Irish. You've heard of colour-blind casting; this show specializes in what I'd be tempted to call accent-deaf casting, were it not that all the actors do the voices so well. Thus Allan Hawco, certainly Canadian, does a flawless cockney chancer as the new second-in-command of Kovacs' multicultural corps, with what seem to be nefarious sidelines that will doubtless be clarified later. Enrico Colantoni, such a nice if troubled guy on Flashpoint, is startlingly transformed into a bare-chested Christian paramilitary chief with rock-star ambitions and accoutrements. (This does take some swallowing.) His partner in -- almost exclusively -- crime is Lolita Davidovich, the cast's nearest approach to Hollywood celebrity, playing the glamorous widow of a Christian warlord.

Cast not against ethnicity, but rewardingly against type, is Rick Roberts as Major Hart, who is Canadian like Kovacs and who is also her UN opposite number, professionally and psychologically; he commands a newly-arrived force of definitely armed peacekeepers. In contrast to his predecessor, an accommodating officer from Azerbaijan (smoothly played by Hrant Alianak, whom I hope it's not unkind to describe as Canadian drama's all-purpose Eastern European), and despite bearing an occasional disconcerting resemblance to the chicken-shooting captain from Air Farce, he ain't about to take no guff from nobody. Indeed, part of his aim, and maybe the show's, seems to be to dispel all the polite cliches about Canada. Promotional material for the show suggests that some of his acerbity will turn out to be due to family problems back home. But that's rather how the show operates. It hands out neat backstories to its characters and gets them to act up. None of it feels organic or original. And the political background-- the element that's supposed to distinguish the show from other shows -- remains just that, a background. Only the most sensational aspects are allowed in.

Much of the first episode is devoted to a potentially provocative march by the Christian side of town, who wish to rebury their dead. It's a tinderbox waiting to happen, but when it does, it's dramatically ineffective. Maybe there's just too much else to be set up. Openers tend to be confusing; the show does get clearer and more purposeful in its second week. The principal conflict seems to be not between sects but between people: the battle of Kovacs and Hart who, put like that, sound rather like a comedy team. That may not turn out to be inapposite. The show's ambitions seem to include absurdist military satire on the order of MASH. But it hasn't happened yet. - ZOS: Zone of Separation airs Mondays at 10 p. m. on The Movie Network.

2009-01-31-caesar-comes-to-the-cinema-ou:
Last years Stratford Festival production of Caesar and Cleopatra (author Bernard Shaw, on a season pass from Niagara-on-the-Lake) began with a neat little coup-de- theatre. The audience arrived in the Festival Theatre to find itself confronted by the immobile figure of a beaked Egyptian deity, presumably with an actor inside. We waited, those of us who already knew the play, to hear him deliver the long prologue with which Shaw brings us up to speed on the Roman-Egyptian political situation c. 50 BC. But he fooled us: He just stood there until the lights went down, and then slid gracefully out of our sight via a trap door. Way to make your audience feel winked at.

In the filmed version of this production (see it in a Cineplex theatre at 1 p. m. today, or wait for it to hit TV) only the last beat of this faux-overture is retained, since sitting in front of a screen, watching nothing happening, would be a lousy way of initiating a dramatic experience. Thus truncated, it doesn't make much sense, but we do still get the transformation that follows: straight into the first desert encounter between the aged Julius Caesar and the teenaged queen, he haranguing the Sphinx as his spiritual equal, she hiding terrified between its paws. The sets for this show were always spectacular and I enjoyed being reminded of them. As to whether they'd make the same impression on a viewer who hadnt seen them onstage, I have my doubts.

The production was filmed onstage, before an audience, from an array of strategically-based cameras; so we only see the sets in undefined sections. Economics apart, this is probably the best way to do it, short of a complete studio rethink; which, for a show as detailed in its theatricality as this one, would probably be counter-productive anyway. We get this one complete with spectators who are enthusiastically audible and intermittently visible.

All the same, the best of this version is in close-ups and two-shots. The film emphasizes both the strengths and the weaknesses of Des McAnuffs original production. The strengths are in the two lead performances and in the way they bounce off one another. Shaw idealized Caesar by humanizing him, making him a mouthpiece for all the right political and ethical ideas (the Shavian ones, that is) while granting him a modicum of vanity and a superabundance of schoolboy impetuosity. He needs an actor equally adept at striking poses and deflating them. Christopher Plummer is superb at both. In his seventies, he may well be at the peak of his powers, vocally, intellectually, and maybe even physically. (Though we do notice, more than onstage, that a double has been slyly edged into place for his plunge into the harbour of Alexandria.) Whether in rhetoric or cross-talk, he never lets either the meaning or the rhythm of a line slip by him. Fifty years his junior, Nikki James can hardly have the same technical command, but she, too, captures every mood. Cleopatra, unlike Caesar, develops, and you can follow her here from frightened, credulous girl to a queen whose capricious authority Caesar can applaud if not approve. By reducing their relationship to a chaste interplay of teacher and student, Shaw sanitized history outrageously; but he had his agenda, and Plummer and James carry it out, almost to the letter. Theirs is, among other things, a contest in roguishness.

And along with it goes an embodiment of the play's central debate, between a virtuous, superhuman politics and a vindictive, expedient one: the former winning all the debating points and the latter, as always, carrying off the game. What should be surrounding and strengthening it, though, goes too often by default. Shaw wrote two alternative prologues; this production, wanting to get to the stars as soon as possible, spurns them both. This turns out to be symptomatic. When Rome and Egypt confront one another in the play's second act, the conflict is played out in the broadest terms; theres no cut-and-thrust, everyone -- especially the Egyptians, nearly all cast against type, which in Shaw is generally fatal -- shouts as though they were at a public meeting. Later, when Caesar and Cleopatras philosophies come into direct conflict, and they appeal to their friends and supporters for judgment, some small but significant cuts weaken the issues and reduce everyone's stature; it matters not just that Britannus, Caesar's ultra-respectable slave, casts his vote against his master but why he does.

These cuts were in the stage production, too. But cuts can sometimes make a play seem longer and, with the spectacle inevitably reduced, this play-on-film feels long in a way it didn't in the theatre. But the lead performances make it worthwhile. And there is a prologue of sorts. Plummer, in his own person, sits on the edge of the stage and welcomes us, and he could hardly do it more charmingly. We don't quite get the best of both worlds, but we do get a pleasing taste of both. - For more information on participating theatres, visit cineplex.com.Weekend Post

2009-01-31-cultures-come-together-but-th:
Theatrefront is a Toronto-based company that travels abroad, does workshops and brings the goods back home. Its previous production, Return, was subtitled The Sarajevo Project. Now comes Ubuntu (The Cape Town Project). Seven people are listed as creating the show, of whom one is the director and five -- two Africans, three Canadians -- make up the cast. (The seventh person, Deborah Hay, is also an actor but doesn't appear.) The impression it leaves is that the resident team thought it would be cool to collaborate with South African actors but, as so often happens with group creations, left the matter of what story they might want to tell to a prolonged afterthought.

There is an idea mooted, and it's a valid and provocative one. It's partly about the clash of cultures but more about their unity. One of the characters, a scientific academic, points out to his class -- and, more importantly, to us -- the implications of humanity having originated in Africa and of some of it having migrated, all over the globe, changing pigmentation through the millennia. So, despite passing tensions, the unprecedented array of faces on contemporary streets really represents a return to basics.

In more immediate theatrical terms, Theatrefront's hunch that black African actors would expose them to a vigorously physical style of playing that might rub beneficially, works a treat. Mbulelo Grootboom and Andile Nebulane start the play with some startlingly acrobatic vignettes of life under, and escaping from, apartheid. They have transmitted at least some of these skills to their white collaborators, who sometimes look a bit self-conscious in the mime sequences but nonetheless do very well. Early in the play, a plane from Cape Town makes a bumpy landing at Pearson. The bumpiness has more to do with spectacle than plot, but the doing is very good. After touchdown, plot and dialogue take over, and we're in dramaturgical trouble.

This is despite Grootboom and Nebulane being fine naturalistic actors, as well. They play father and son, named Philani and Jabba. The play unfolds in two time frames. Philani came to Toronto 20 years ago as a student, found work as a lab assistant and began sending money home to Jabba, then one year old. He also found love with a shy Canadian student with a consuming interest in the mating-calls of auks. The grown-up Jabba comes to Canada to find his father, his only clue a photograph showing Philani with Michael, the aforementioned academic. Michael used to wear glasses and now has apparently switched to contacts; we know where we are time-wise from how David Jansen, who plays him, puts on and takes off his specs.

The scenes of the past work better, especially a sweet love-in-the-library scene between Grootboom and, as the bird-fancier, the remarkable Michelle Monteith, who can infuse shades of meaning into the simplest lines without overloading them with "significance." Philani has a limp, explained by his having received surgical treatment back home from a revered doctor-counsellor, the Sangoma. Michael can't believe his ears when he hears this, nor can he credit Philani's insistence on the importance of tradition. As quite often happens in dramatic debating-scenes, at least one obvious argument goes unstated: That Western medicine has its traditions, too, many of which it has discarded in the light of subsequent knowledge. Anyway, this part of the story includes an inexplicable, or at least unexplained, death.

Jabba arrives to almost literally pick up the pieces; a fair amount of his story turns on intercontinental differences in burial practices. Of course, it's meant to signify more than that, but it doesn't have the backup. If you believe the publicity, the show is really about the impact on a second generation of interactions with the first. In other words, it's about the young (who also, for symmetrical reasons, meet in a library). The plan just about holds for Jabba, whom we meet early and whom Nebulane invests with an involving edge; though he, too, seems reluctant to ask obvious, if dramatically inconvenient, questions. (Odd how many conversations in plays end for that reason.) It doesn't work for his opposite number (Holly Lewis), who arrives late and is asked to shoulder a lot of unrealized angst. The plot is slender, implausible and time-consuming, climaxing in a revelation that may break new ground for half-hearted melodrama.

Which is a shame, because Daryl Cloran's production is technically excellent (it's a far more polished piece of work than Return, though with less to bite on). Lorenzo Savoini has designed a bold set, a revolving wall made out of suitcases, and even bolder lighting, and Christian Barry provides a cross-cultural sound score that starts with drums and builds from there. The show's ending, a funeral ceremony back in Africa, seems similarly planned to draw on the best of both worlds. But it requires a certain suspension of disbelief, not so much in the action as in the actors, the Canadian ones anyway.

- Ubuntu runs through March 1 at the Tarragon Theatre. Call 416-531-1827 for ticket information.

2009-02-03-go-ahead-and-like-what-you-se:
Maja Ardal is a veteran of three cold countries. Before she lived in Canada she lived in Scotland, and before that she lived in Iceland. You Fancy Yourself, her self-performed one-woman play, tells the story of a girl who came to Edinburgh from the even more frozen North in the early 1950s at the age of four, so I think we can take it that it's autobiographical. Our theatres, Passe Muraille especially, are currently so awash in reminiscent monologues that I approached this one suspiciously. My suspicions turned out to be unfounded. The show's a delight.

Ardal takes us on the journey of her surrogate figure, whom she calls Elsa, through her early years at home and at school. Elsa's father has arrived determined "to scale the citadels of Scottish learning," which I think means he's a teacher. (We never do find out how well he does at it.) Elsa is a resilient child, and it would be a stretch to say that she's persecuted, but she does bear the burden of being an immigrant in an age group that's especially xenophobic or-- since this is Scotland -- clannish. Socially, she's between classes. Her best friend Adelle lives in poverty with a sick chain-smoking mother, an aggressive brother and no one else. Elsa, who's a kind of Nordic Anne Shirley with a mind full of legends and fairy tales, fantasizes for Adelle's benefit about her father having met a glamorous end in the war. School life is dominated by a rich girl and her sycophants, who spend their breaks riding imaginary horses. Elsa can't help wanting to be accepted by the equestrian class who, knowing their power, alternate between excluding and admitting her. In dealing with them, Elsa comes close to betraying her friend. "You fancy yourself " is the taunt -- the dread accusation of getting above her position in the pecking order -- that the snobs throw at Elsa. The climax is her own triumphant realization that, yes, she does, in a way of which they can't conceive.

That's a bit too neat. Nor is the conflict of loyalties drawn as tight as it might be; we lose sight of Adelle, and especially of her family situation, for much of the play. (Having an interval is a mistake for this kind of show in this kind of space.) Adelle's folklore fantasies, and her newer dreams inspired by Hollywood, aren't that compelling either; if the show's meant to be about culture-clash, it doesn't make it. What count are the individual characters and vignettes. Under Mary Francis Moore's direction, Ardal begins the evening peeking shyly over the top of a trunk -- with Ubuntu at the Tarragon, Toronto has two shows playing whose main visual motif is luggage. A chunky presence in her own right, Ardal gets herself into the mind and body language of a small girl and shows us the world and its inhabitants as they appear to us all at that age: a mixture of documentary and horror-comic. She finds a distinct voice and stance for every character; most unusually in this kind of ventriloquial performance -- she doesn't rush the transitions.

The classroom provides the most drama, the most comedy, and -- whatever your background or gender -- the sharpest recognition. These primary-school kids seem to have the same teacher in every grade, a Miss Campbell, a sentimental battleaxe with a revisionist view of the Massacre of Glencoe, the 1692 atrocity in which, with encouragement from the English, the Campbell clan slaughtered the MacDonald clan in their beds. Literally, as the MacDonalds were their guests at the time. Miss Campbell, true to her family pride, believes that her ancestors have been much misjudged, and that the MacDonalds, always a shifty race, had it coming. My own observation is that the mutual suspicion may well persist to this day, between those who love soup and those who love burgers. As luck would have it, there is a David MacDonald in the class who, with his runny nose and attention deficit, reminds Elsa, who is nonetheless his only protector, of a troll. The show's finest scene is a singing contest at which the rich bitchette acquits herself atrociously, the despised David huskily but truly, Elsa herself outlandishly with windmill gestures and Adelle, tastefully disregarding all the direction Elsa has tried to give her, quite beautifully. Miss Campbell renders true judgment, thereby overcoming all her prejudices, except the unshakable one in favour of the poetry of Robert Burns. (Elsa's feelings about her friend's success are, not surprisingly, mixed, and drive her temporarily into the arms of the snobs.) Singing badly when you can sing well is really hard but Ardal -- without accompaniment, mind you -- makes all four vocal performances completely convincing and melts us with the last as surely as Adelle melts Miss Campbell. It's the crown of a virtuoso performance. She has every right to fancy herself. - You Fancy Yourself is at Theatre Passe Muraille Backspace until Feb. 14. Call 416-504-7529 for tickets and information.

2009-02-04-oh-that-old-joke-again-jon-do:
When the funniest line in a comedy show is, "Why did the chicken cross the road?" there has to be desperation in the air. To be perfectly fair to tonight's episode of The Jon Dore Television Show ("Dore Gets Old"), we do actually get to see the road-crossing chicken, and that's pretty neat. (I've never thought about this before, but getting a chicken to cross on cue can't be easy.) Also, just to show how self-aware everyone is, we immediately get a flashback to the writers' room, where the star's team tries, not too successfully, to explain to him the chicken's relevance -- the show is about getting old, and it's an old joke.

More exactly, the show is about the chubby, bearded comic's fear of getting old. There he is, at the top of the show, scraping tunelessly away at a violin and proclaiming, "The guilt is killing me -- I shot JFK"; then, if one non-sequitur can lead to another, we find he's in a skate park, about to execute a daredevil leap ("rad to the bone") whose failure leaves him writhing on the ground in, let us hope, pain. That, though, isn't the worst of it. A group of kids see him lying there, and make fun of him for trying stuff he's too old for. Worse yet, a passing group of young women express their revulsion at the idea of such a palsied granddad hitting on them. Dore, who thinks of himself as young, is appalled. Not to say terrified.

He visits his psychotherapist (a fixture on the show), to whom he confesses his revulsion. "I can," he either boasts or confesses (it works both ways), "live with terminal cancer. What I can't take is kids telling me I'm a dinosaur." He's onto something there. However, since he's chronically unable to stay on track, he ends up giggling with his shrink over the word "stegosaurus." He also calls on an anti-ageing specialist, who himself has reached the age of 54. ("More than half a century," calculates Dore, who really has problems with this.) So, realizing that even the professionals can't beat old age, he decides to join it. He takes himself to a seniors centre to find how its inhabitants can support lives so obviously not worth living. The trio he interviews turn out to have a lot more vitality than he does, especially one wrinkled lady who sounds as if she grew up in the north of England. They even seem to have better sex lives than he does; and of course this, even more than skateboarding, is what's really on his mind. The show ends with our hero in bed with an old lady (the delightful veteran actress Araby Lockhart, if I read the credits right) about to make ravenous demands on his body.

So Dore moves from demonizing old age to worshipping it. Both extremes are of course equally crass, a fact about which the show makes no bones. There is an old and honourable history of making comedy out of crassness. The trouble with Dore's show, despite its alternation between interviews and acted scenes, is that there's nothing outside the crassness. The interviews recall those that used to be regular features on The Daily Show with Jon Stewart; Ed Helms or Rob Corddry would go out to meet people with extreme views and sit there slack-jawed, egging their subjects on to even greater outrageousness. The Stewart show seems largely to have dropped this idea, whether due to a shortage of intrepid interviewers or of gullible interviewees. The point, as in a somewhat different way with Borat or Ali G, is that something or someone gets satirized. On this show, the only person who gets exposed is Dore himself, and he's a dummy to begin with. (There is, presumably, a gulf between Dore the character and Dore the performer, but we can only respond to what we see.) The acted parts are a little like Curb Your Enthusiasm, but only a little. Larry David's character always has a plot to move around in -- this gives us a line on his obnoxiousness, and makes it richer. It doesn't soften it, or stop us from guiltily identifying with it, but it does suggest that there may be a world, and even other people, elsewhere. Dore's show is all Dore, and he isn't fascinating.

Dore's declared idol is David Letterman, whom I hold more responsible than any other performer for degrading the once-noble concept of irony into a synonym for "being bad on purpose, and smug about it." The real running gag of the Dore show -- it's emblazoned in the title --is "look at me, I'm on television," as if the idea of being a TV comic were so delicious in itself as to preclude any necessity of actually being funny. Dore encounters a genie (of the lamp persuasion) who admonishes him, when he can't decide on his three wishes, to "think of the theme of the episode." Comedic self-awareness also has a history, stretching back to Aristophanes, but it shouldn't be all there is. "Dore," say his writers, "this is hip humour; maybe you are getting old." In his nightmares. In their dreams. - The Jon Dore Television Show airs tonight at 10 p. m. on the Comedy network.

Black & White Photo: Comedy Network / Jon Dore goes from loathing everything old to embracing frisky seniors, all in the span of 30 minutes. ;; Caption:
2009-02-07-nostalgia-squared-but-it-does:
The defining moment of Happy Days, A New Musical comes just after the beginning of Act Two when somebody says "Fonzie has never been the same since he jumped that shark." It tells you everything you need to know about the show, and I'm not talking exposition. It's a pathetic attempt at self-satire that tries to be knowingly ingratiating, but plays as desperate. Maybe, the giveaway line is intended to disarm all the critics, this one included, who have been polishing their own shark-jumping references ever since the show was announced. Again, too late: Right from its opening number this production presents an unmissable slowly moving target.

Basics: This "new musical" is an attempt to recapture the supposed magic of a 1970s attempt to recapture the supposed magic of the 1950s. That's nostalgia squared, which is more than anyone needs. (And even in its time the TV Happy Days, with its happy nuclear family, must have left some people wondering why they didn't just re-run Leave It to Beaver and have done with it. ) Second Basics: The TV original was one of those occasions on which a secondary character steals the show. But if he's going to work that larcenous magic again, he has at least to start out secondary. This show gives star billing, and what there is of story and conflict, to Arthur Fonzarelli, a. k. a. The Fonz, the leather-jacketed garage mechanic whose official billing is hero's best friend. However, it retains just enough of its prototype's rope to hang itself. Richie Cunningham, the ostensible protagonist, still gets to introduce the story and to narrate it. He also has a sort of trajectory of his own. But it's a measure of his and the show's ineffectuality that when he rounded off the evening by proposing to his girlfriend at the senior prom, we'd all forgotten that she even existed. Memo to whoever may currently be at work on Seinfeld The Musical: Don't build it around George.

Meanwhile the resources of the Fonz, whose most celebrated if contradictory characteristics are imperturbability and a short fuse, are tested by the return to town of his own former squeeze, the eponymously dressed Pinky Tuscadero, now some kind of star with her own entourage (total number: two, female, also in pink. I must say, for a homecoming celebrity, she makes a remarkably low-key entrance). Pinky's advent coincides with a developer's threat to Arnold's malt-shop, everyone's favourite hangout. The entire community, meaning Richie's friends and family, bands together to defeat this, their principal money-raising scheme being a televised wrestling-match between the Fonz and a pair of preening jailbirds, recently ex, called the Malachi brothers. The Fonz, however, has a bad knee, and rather than have this shameful fact revealed, he leaves town. Town, by the way, is Milwaukee, which is hardly a village, but apparently everybody in it notices his absence and is stricken by it. Anyway, somewhere on the road to Damascus or wherever he's headed, he has a visitation from his twin gods James Dean and Elvis (though in a world full of Elvis impersonators, this production has managed to unearth one who can't do it) and heads back. Meanwhile ... actually, there isn't a meanwhile. A very thin story has to be stretched over two hours. As Richie says, in the show's one genuinely bright moment of self-reference, usually he can get his problems sorted out in 30 minutes.

While I'm paying the odd compliment, I should acknowledge that Paul Williams' score isn't bad, especially the words, which were always this veteran popsmith's stronger suit. A number for the recidivist Malachis has them recalling their practice days when "we terrorized the playground on our stolen trikes." Williams' lighter lyrics are full of bright touches like that, though, typically of his generation, his ballads are gummy and vague. What does his songs in, though, is the extreme predictability with which they're placed. Everybody gets an Establishing Number; you just know that, after Richie's dad has taken himself off to his day's work at the hardware store, his stay-at-home wife will start singing about her dreams as an everyday housewife. But it's the book, Garry Marshall's attempt to cash in on his TV original, that's irredeemable. It parades the characters in a sustained bid for the applause of recognition, padding things out with increasingly hopeless anachronisms: jokes about the price of gas, about some crazy new business called "computers," even a skateboard. The energy-level is so low both on stage and in the auditorium (I've seldom heard so tepid a response at a musical) that when the second-act curtain went up on Arnold's "going out of business" sign, I thought for a moment that it meant the show.

The actors don't exactly suggest they're in a hit, but they throw themselves in and mostly come up floating. Felicia Farley's Pinky is a squawker; but Joey Sorge has the Fonz's moves down pretty much perfectly, Steven Booth bobs engagingly up and then down again as Richie, and as his mom Cynthia Ferrer, who has a twinkle that's nearly a sparkle, surprises everyone with a tap-routine -- everyone, at least, who's never seen a straitlaced lady in a musical before. Even by musical standards, this number is hideously unmotivated, but we take what we can get, and the cast do the same. - Happy Days continues at the Elgin Theatre through Feb. 15.
