2009-02-11-of-men-and-trees:
As of now, Shakuntala is the oldest play running in Toronto -- no great wonder, since it was written somewhere around the year AD 400. Up until last Sunday, though, it had to yield first place in the antiquity stakes to the Canon production of Medea, its senior by a handsome eight centuries. And yet the older play, a Greek tragedy, is far more accessible to us than the younger, a classic from India that I can best describe as comic-epic-mystic-romantic.

Some of Shakuntala's strangeness is formal, deriving from its frequent dependence on song and stylized dance. But the hardest thing for us to accept is the characters' lack of culpability. As much as people talk about Fate, the characters in a Greek play are comparatively free agents, with some responsibility for what the gods do to them and more for how they respond. But in Shakuntala, written by a court poet named Kalidasa and based on a story from The Mahabharata, everything is down to magic. The title character is a forest girl who lives a secluded life among hermits, though not so secluded that she doesn't have a couple of (in this production, anyway) giggly confidantes. King Dushyanta encounters her while disguised and on a hunting trip, woos her, weds her and gets her pregnant. He then returns home, promising to send for her. But Shakuntala's local hermit gets angry with her and pronounces a curse: She will vanish from the memory of the one who loves her best. And so it proves. When his pregnant bride presents herself at the palace, a puzzled king denies all knowledge. (Thereby, of course, proving that, despite having an abundance -- or, it seems, an embarrassment -- of other wives, he does love her. As tests go, it's arcane but effective.) Torn between anger and heartbreak, she is providentially snatched up in a cloud, to heaven but not to death. Eventually, with a few magical aids, the king finds her and the child there, and there is a happy ending.

If the play resembles anything in our tradition, it's the final romances ofShakespeare, especially Pericles, another story of long-suffering innocence finally rewarded. There are times in Charles Roy's production (for Pleiades Theatre, whose mission is exploration) when we can feel a similar kind of greatness. It takes a long time to arrive: until the beginning of the second half, in fact. The early courtship sequence is long, drawn out and coy, especially the scenes involving Shakuntala's friends, who treat us to a continuous display of twirling and squealing. The crucial scene of the hermit's curse is rushed and non-specific.

Roy's adaptation veers between neat versifying and prosaic bathos. As a director, he confronts a fearsome task with limited resources: The choreography (by Hari Krishnan) is more dutiful than beguiling, though Itai Erdal's lighting can be magical, especially when summoning a slow dawn. The cast is mixed, in both background and accomplishment. In the two leading roles, Anita Majumdar and Sanjay Talwar are, ethnicity notwithstanding, miscast. Talwar, a fine actor of gawks and geeks, makes the king's puzzled conscientiousness endearing sympathetic; but he is not a natural authority figure in a dramatic world that calls out for it. Majumdar, by contrast, is too worldly and controlled for Sakuntala's initial innocence. They both give us the outlines of their predicaments, but not the texture. The other players do a lot of doubling, some of it confusing. Indian audiences may know the story by heart; the rest of us need to have it told as well as decorated. It feels like a masterpiece, but we have to take a lot on trust. - Shakuntala runs until Feb. 15. Call 416-973-4000 for more information.
2009-02-12-off-with-their-hedsors-a-fini:
It's tough being a bad girl, and especially being a bad girl on a television "reality show." (I can no longer bear to type those last two words without quotes.) Last year, in Rich Kids: Cattle Drive, we saw a posse of them dispatched to earn their keep -- and a substantial catch prize -- in the Wild West. In The Girls of Hedsor Hall, another bunch of spoiled American females is sent off to an equally mythic, and possibly even tougher, environment: an English finishing school for young ladies.

In fact, the kids in this new show aren't all rich though, such are our expectations of the genre, it takes some time for that realization to sink in. There are a dozen of them, and introductions in the first episode tend to be rushed. (Confusion is compounded by the fact that the ranks include a Jennifer, a Jenna and a Jen. Couldn't the selection process have been rigged a little more constructively?) We may think we have them pegged as a bunch of Paris Hilton wannabes, but it turns out that many of them are don't-wannabes; they have abuse problems, substance or sexual, of which they want to rid themselves. This makes them more sympathetic, and the show more offensive.

Add to its many faults that the whole thing is set up on, literally, false premises. Research suggests that "Hedsor Hall," the English country home to which The Girls are consigned, is actually called Hedsor House and that, despite claims made in the script about a hundred-year pedigree, it's generally used as a convention centre. In fact, the whole idea of "the English finishing school" is probably a myth; when young English ladies have been "finished," they've been sent abroad, usually to Switzerland. The Girls of Hedsor Hall turns out to be a U. S. spinoff of a British show, Ladette to Lady. (There's a male equivalent, From G's to Gents, which is being given a simultaneous spin on MTV. Some bad ideas seem inexhaustible.) The two principal teachers at Hedsor Hall have been carried over from the parent production; they are Gill Harbord, headmistress, and Rosemary Shrager, "disciplinarian," an educational title unknown outside highly specialized establishments. Both ladies may be playing themselves, but they come across as very bad actresses. Ms. Harbord (I think I heard her title right) is toothy and mostly addresses her charges in tones of pained disapproval; Mrs. Shrager (ditto) is beefy and barks at them. Both are very easily offended. There is a third instructor in the shape of Tara Conner, a former Miss USA and a protegee of Donald

Trump, who is the show's executive producer and can add it to the list of things for which he stands accountable. Conner greets her trainees by telling them that she was once every bit as bad they are--bad meaning disrespectful or foulmouthed or drunken or slutty or some combination thereof -- but that Hedsor Hall has changed her. Her actual duties are a little vague.

The girls, having been treated to a ride through the countryside in a fleet of black cabs (renting a bus would probably have been cheaper but less picturesque), are decked out in school uniforms and provided with a pearl necklace apiece.

This makes some of them begin to feel like real ladies and makes others burst out laughing. They will have to surrender them if they're expelled, and it is of course built into the show that every week at least one of them will be. That will apply whether or not any of them has deserved it. That's both cruel and stupid. It makes American Idol, which at least professes to involve the deployment of actual skills, seem positively classy.

As a treat, and a test, the girls are let loose on their first evening at a cocktail party with some young men announced as -- I couldn't make such language up, but the show can and does -- "dignified members of British royal society." (They're so dignified that their dialogue comes with subtitles.) Some riotous behaviour ensues; one of the boys tells one of the girls that she looks like a horse, and for some reason we're meant to hold it against her that this makes her angry. Actually anyone who believes that the youths of the English upper class have anything to teach anyone about manners and morals is living in a snobbish -- and peculiarly American -- dreamworld. Maybe it's because I'm a Londoner, but I would like to state that any show that begins, as this one does, with establishing shots of Big Ben has no idea what, or where, it's talking about.

Next comes the first round of judgements, first in one-on-one interviews in the principal's office ( just them and us and the cameras), then in more public humiliation sessions before the whole school. Margie, a black girl with a big ass (her own description) and a rage problem (not her own description, though she wouldn't disown it) is told that all the other girls are in mortal fear of her. She breaks down in tears, saying that she desperately needs the chance; I wouldn't be surprised if she were the eventual winner. So I've revealed that she isn't kicked out tonight. Sorry. Jenna (I think it's Jenna), when asked what she does for a living, says that she strips and has an adult web-site. Miss Harbord ("how simply awful") is shocked beyond measure that she should be showing off her body and unmoved by the excuse that if she didn't she'd be homeless. She's even more appalled when the girl slams the door on her way out. Reality shows cannot bear too much reality.

"By tomorrow morning," the students are chillingly told, "we want you to conform" -- in other words, to change from televised objects to fantasy stereotypes. One of them, Amanda, is asked, "What are you doing about your cursing?" Since the offending words have been bleeped out, it's possible that she's merely being requested to swear more imaginatively in future, but probably not. Anyway, Amanda's unrepentant. Asked what she'd like to say to Mrs. Schrager now, she says, "I'd tell her to go f---herself." It's hard not to cheer her on. - The Girls of Hedsor Hall airs tonight at 10 p. m. on MTV Canada.
2009-02-14-you-could-call-it-the-threepe:
Look at it one way, and the musical of The Color Purple has four salient scenes. The first, immediately after curtain-rise, shows two small black girls, sisters, playing a clapping game; the date is 1904, the place is Georgia. The second occurs a few years later; Celie, one of the girls, has been virtually sold into marriage with a brutal farmer known as Mister. He really wanted Nettie, the other one, but their father judged her too pretty and clever to be sacrificed so he offered Celie, considered ugly but a hard worker, and threw in a cow as sweetener. Celie, by the way, was raped and twice pregnant by the time she was 14; her pa removed both of the babies at birth and disposed of them no-one-knows where. Now, Nettie arrives at the farm, but Mister attempts to force himself on her and Nettie runs off, promising to write.

She does too, every day for years, but Mister hides the letters from Celie. Eventually -- third vital scene -- another character finds them and tells Celie, thoughtfully withholding the information until the first-act curtain. This has the effect of making everything else that's happened so far seem irrelevant. Nettie has gone to Africa as a missionary, and a rather hurried sequence at the start of Act 2 shows her there. That's all we see of her until the last scene when, naturally, she comes home, bringing with her Celie's two children now, time having advanced to 1949, very fully grown. The music swells, and the show asks us to take as its emotional climax Celie's reunion with one character we barely know and two others we don't know at all. Judging by the musical's success on Broadway and elsewhere, this works for many people. I think it's a cheat, though--compared to some others in the genre--not a disgraceful one.

There is another way of regarding the show, and a more interesting one. This makes it the story of Celie's growth into self-reliance, both practical and emotional. No white characters appear, and few are mentioned. The show says, in tough terms, that oppression, especially of black women, didn't end when slavery did. Celie, for much of her life, might as well be Mister's slave. But after years of letting him exploit her domestic talents, she breaks free and goes into business for herself as a pants-designer. She has two mentors and role models. One is Sofia, the forceful woman who loves and marries Harpo, Mister's son by a former marriage, but leaves him; with the encouragement of his father and even of the as-yet-unliberated Celie, Harpo tries to beat her. (In all honesty Harpo, a mild if chirpy soul, didn't stand a chance.) The other is Shug Avery, a blues singer and old flame of Mister's, who comes back into his life and then leaves it again, taking Celie with her. Along with this goes Celie's spiritual progression. She starts as a conventional churchgoer; the first big number is a prolonged, jumping gospel sequence during which Celie looks, considering her social and physical condition, remarkably cheerful. The tragedies in her life threaten to destroy her faith, but she eventually arrives, prompted by Shug Avery, at a kind of pantheistic acceptance; at least, I think that's what the title song is about. The trouble with all this, though, is that it doesn't need the relationship of the sisters and makes it seem like a sentimental extra layer.

It could all be reconciled in the more spacious form of a novel, and the show is, of course, based on one, by Alice Walker. Steven Spielberg, by all accounts, made it work as a movie. And it makes a better musical than it would a play, music being a great lubricant. But it can't do everything, and Marsha Norman's book and Gary Griffin's direction have their work cut out imposing any kind of through-line. Themes and threads, notably Celie's lesbian relationship with Shug Avery, are forever being picked up and then put down again. More dialogue scenes might help, though the score (by Brenda Russell, Allee Willis and Stephen Bray, all theatrical first-timers) does an impressive job of dispensing information with flavour. ("If you think hard work been doggin' you before," sings the chorus when Mister takes Celie, "get ready for the Big Dog.") As usual, the music and lyrics are best when earthiest and most vernacular. When affirmation strikes, they go "contemporary," which is to say vacuous. You might call these numbers Threepenny Oprah, and indeed she's the principal producer. A second-act jive number alerts us that the 1940s have arrived; otherwise, two world wars and a depression pass by without anyone seeming to notice. And, as often happens in shows covering a lengthy time span, nobody seems to change physically until half an hour before the close at which point everybody ages very fast.

Otherwise, there are no quarrels with the show's look or with its performance. John Lee Beatty's sets are impressively framed by hanging Georgia moss. Donald Byrd's choreography is spirit-lifting and much enhanced by Paul Tazewell's costumes. Kenita Miller is a sweet, strong Celie; she even validates the convention that holding a single note very loud and very long is a sign of deep feeling. Angela Robinson similarly transcends type as a shimmering Shug, who's as warming when confiding in Celie as when stunning in a gold dress in a juke-joint. Stu James's Harpo switches charmingly between diffident and debonair, and Felicia P. Fields is a powerhouse Sofia. (A large lady, she gets the evening's biggest laughs when, pregnant, she arches her body backwards as an assault-weapon. Subtle it isn't.) Rufus Bonds Jr. is Mister, who reforms halfway through; he's good in both phases but two one-dimensional moods don't make one complex character. There's a trio of commenting church biddies who get rather irritating, and who turn up in the Africa number as part of a desperate attempt to yoke all the storylines together. Here, more than anywhere, the show buckles under its self-imposed strain. But it's an honest attempt. And given that "purple" usually denotes over-writing, over-acting or both, maybe the most impressive thing is how seldom it lives up to its title.

- The Color Purple runs through March 14 at the Canon Theatre. Call 416-872-1212 for more information.

2009-02-18-what-s-so-funny-about-peace-l:
Asweet-faced, mild-mannered comedian is a rarity, especially these days, soDemetriMartin stands out. After the customary apprenticeship in stand-up comedy and a writer-performer gig on The Daily Show with Jon Stewart, hes now driving his own vehicle, Important Things with Demetri Martin. Every week he will turn his gaze, filtered through monologues and sketches, on some imposing abstract topic. He starts tonight with timing.

Well, timing is widely known to be the vital ingredient of successful comedy, so I suppose you could say that anything Martin does would be relevant. And on that strictly technical level he succeeds: He gives all his jokes their best shot. In soliloquy, he's an oddball observationist on the order of Steven Wright or the late Mitch Hedberg, but without their wild air of grievance and discovery. Like them, he jumps from one topic to another, but he doesn't push each to its limits as they would. Martin can be agreeably whimsical, as when he wonders whether there were any Goths in Gothic times and how well they would fit in if there were. But thats hardly in the same league as Hedbergs meditations on king-and queen-size beds. (How come all you kings are the same size? Hey, I got one for your lady as well.")Martin also talks about how hard it is to make conversation with a baby. This is very true, but it's not an idea that he pursues to any great effect.

Nor does it have much to do with timing, except in the sense that everything does, especially since "timing as investigated here seems to be interchangeable with the grander and even more inclusive subject of time." One of his sketches --it's really more a succession of micro-vignettes -- has him taking off in a time machine (thinly disguised as a pop-dispenser) and capitalizing on his historical knowledge: Encouraged by an initial encounter with Mary Magdalene, he makes bets with a 1929 flapper on the likelihood of a crash and appears, laden with potatoes, to an Irish peasant girl at the height of the famine. In another, even more desultory item, hes a rookie cop shooting up the wrong apartment. Both these subjects would probably be funnier if he just riffed on them to the camera.

In his most sustained attempt at working with other performers, hes an actor playing a break-up scene with his girlfriend, unable to get angry with her but getting very angry with the director, who keeps telling him to get angry. ("Use it!" says the director, but all Martin can do is lose it.) I suppose that's about timing. Anyway it's reasonably ingenious. And it makes good use of Martins incurable good-natured-ness. Hes almost a throwback to the Zen comics of the '60s; irrespective of what he's actually saying, he seems to be signalling peace and love, brother.

You cant help liking Martin, if only for being one of the few comedians who doesnt keep complaining about his terrible luck with women. But likeable isn't the same as funny. He features a running gag that I liked, a recurring commercial about buying rings of escalating value for every occasion up to and including bankruptcy. And, in a final display of multidimensional timing, he plays a variety of musical instruments while turning the pages of a chart with jokes written on it. (Flip charts were his principal shtick on the Stewart show.)

Not every Daily Show alumnus proves a major comic when out on his own, or even while still there (think of Lewis Black and despair), and I wouldn't at the moment give Martin more than a passing grade. He seems bright enough. Maybe he should trust it more. Selfdeprecation is all very well, but if you're not careful, you may find your audience agreeing with you.

- Very Important Things With Demetri Martin airs tonight at 10:30 p. m. on The Comedy Network.

THEATRE REVIEW

Toronto the Good

Factory Theatre

Despite some appearances, the title of Andrew Moodie's Toronto the Good may not be altogether sarcastic . Its true that the plays cityscape includes random shooting, racial profiling, irresponsible journalism, overworked teachers of under-parented children, marital tension and a husband nerving himself to be unfaithful, but nearly everybody in it has good intentions and is drawn with sympathy and wit. Whether their personal and professional lives all fit neatly onto the one stage is another matter.

The play begins with a youngish man named Thomas Matthews being pulled over by a cop for no apparent reason other than he's black. It turns out that he's a Crown lawyer who--justice in this play being not so much poetic as ironic -- is engaged in defending a white policewoman accused of just such an act of discrimination. Politically, Thomas might be called centrist. For the prosecution is Simon Phillip, white and vociferously left. Multiplying the contrasts and correspondences, Thomas and his French-Canadian schoolteacher spouse are expecting their first child while Simon, in his wifes brief absence, is playing single father to his own two kids. Additional stresses in their respective lives include the Matthews fights over who renews the licence on the car and who gets to drive it (she's the one who ends up taking the TTC where, despite her condition, no one offers her a seat), and Simon's attempts to exploit his temporary freedom with a succession of strippers and hookers.

Its a lively, fractious, funny play that might be Torontos answer to The Wire, with the same cross-currents of black and white, conscience and compromise, public and private, office and street; and the same refusal of the characters to stay in their own docketed boxes. It even features the same professional groupings as The Wire: police, the law, the press, the schools. (No dockers, though; and only the merest whiff of drugs.)What it inevitably lacks is the length and breadth of The Wire. There's no time to let the characters' on-and off-duty lives breathe and develop and enrich one another. We end up with alternating slabs of, for want of better terms, social significance and human interest.

Both elements have their attractions. The legal procedurals are initially the more thrilling, milking all the paradoxes of black and white lining up against preconceptions. The scenes with the accused Officer McGill (Sandra Forsell), who initially talks a very convincing game, are especially gripping. Her victim/accuser (Marcel Stewart, who strengthens the Wire connection by looking like DAngelo Barksdale) fares less well. He disappears from the action before we even hear him state his case, which accordingly ceases to be of more than theoretical interest. Even the reversals begin to seem schematic. The rival attorneys wheel and deal, threaten and compromise, and end up in a shouting match, each brandishing the names of un-favourite politicians. (Ill raise you one Jack Layton for a Mike Harris.)

It's odd how false this scene sounds, given that another kind of specificity is one of the play's greatest strengths Its an acute joy to sit in a Toronto theatre and listen to characters literally mapping their daily lives, with actual street names and landmarks and intersections. This may be the first play to which audiences should bring a GPS. Both Thomas and Simon engage us with monologues, and Simons, addressing the getting of breakfast and the daycare run and the race to the courts, is a particular treat. (Though if, from what I could work out, he lives in East York and works downtown -- what's he doing later on the Gardiner?) His attempted dalliances -- all with black sex workers, unless I'm confused by colour-blind casting -- are meant, I suppose, to complicate his idealism, just as the snapping of patience in Thomass occasionalimpatience with his white wife is supposed to show that assimilation can have sharp edges. He gets interviewed by a Toronto Star reporter who gets very aggressive about what she sees as his privileged refusal to rock any boats. "My name," he says angrily, "is Thomas, not Tom;" but she misquotes and crucifies him anyway. The whole incident is incredible (and crudely played): the plays lowest point. Better, but still only sketched in, are the attempts of Thomas's wife to get through to a student with just too many strikes against her, and a hip-hop chorus that's a complete break in style and barely comprehensible.

Xuan Fraser gives a beautifully controlled performance as Thomas, urbane witheruptions, and Brian Marler a winning one as Simon, appealing with complications. Philip Akins production is handicapped by a playground set that serves little practical or metaphorical purpose, but it brings out all the scripts excitements. It starts like the urban play we've all been waiting for. It can't sustain that, but it ends on an oddly hopeful note thats both touching and persuasive. The character whos been keenest to leave town is resigned, maybe even reconciled, to staying. The city may not be Toronto the good, but it isn't all bad either. - Toronto the Good runs until March 1. Call 416-504-9971 for information.

2009-02-20-in-the-heat-of-the-night:
THEATRE REVIEW

Miss Julie: Freedom Summer

Bluma Appel Theatre

Katharine Hepburn famously ascribed the chemistry of Fred Astaire and Ginger Rogers to him giving her class and her giving him sex. August Strindberg's Miss Julie, the world's most famous intermissionless play, gives us that formulation with the genders reversed and the partners irredeemably out of step. Strindberg's Julie, virgin daughter of a 19th-century Swedish count, has class in spades and is not about to forget it, though she sometimes acts as if she'd like to. Jean is her father's valet and thus socially far beneath her; but he does have sex, or at least sexual experience, and in the course of the play, which unfolds on a hot midsummer night, he literally gives it to her. Their coupling is combustible and its aftermath dire.

For the second time this Toronto season we have a version of Miss Julie that updates and transplants the original. Last year, Miss Julie: She'mah situated the production in 1920s Canada, with a white Julie and a First Nations Jean. Now comes Stephen Sachs' Miss Julie: Freedom Summer, an American piece that comes to us as a coproductionby CanStage and the Vancouver Playhouse, and that turns up the heat by placing us in a Mississippi mansion in 1964, the turning-point year of the civil rights movement. Julie is a white judge's daughter; Jean, now John, and his fiancee Christine are of course black, she being the family's cook and he the chauffeur. I can't believe that nobody has yet dubbed this adaptation Driving Miss Julie, but if they haven't, then let me be the first. Anyway, it's the best production of Miss Julie, either straight up or with a twist, that I have seen.

I'm suspicious of revivals that implicitly suggest they're doing their originals some kind of favour by making them "contemporary." But this doesn't pretend to be the original play; it's a new text that follows the old one closely, but not exactly, while grabbing at what's most vital about it. Strindberg meant to shock with frankness, and the core of his play still seems brutal. But the conflict of aristocrat and servant no longer packs the same automatic punch; we understand it but we don't really feel it. Add race to sex and class, and you have a new dimension that reinforces the old. And by choosing the precise date that he has, Sachs gives us the sense that not just the central couple but the whole country is in heat.

Caroline Cave's Julie is white-hot from the moment she comes on stage, as the other characters observe and as the play requires. (Slow builds, I sometimes think, are wasted on Strindberg.) Slim and proud and desperate, acting with a treasurable combination of intelligence and sensuality, and with whiplash velocity, she encompasses both the self-assertion and the self-abasement of a woman who tempts and taunts and surrenders, sometimes in the space of a single sentence. Even actresses native to the territory can sound exaggerated when playing the Southern belle -- as can actual Southerners who aren't acting at all -- and Cave has her moments, but she always rescues herself. Inevitably we think of Tennessee Williams, and there is an astonishing correspondence between the baleful gentility of his heroines and that of Cave's -- and Strindberg's -- Julie. It's awfully plausible that, dressed up to elope, she should sorrowfully command John to execute her pet bird who's not wanted on the voyage, and then hysterically berate him for his inhumanity. She immediately sees herself as a slaughtered bird, and nothing could be more Tennessee than that. The equation only fails to balance at the end. Julie, in her own quaint way, chooses death rather than dishonour; a Williams heroine might talk like that but would never actually do it. (Blanche DuBois herself, according to her creator, would speedily have seduced some kindly stranger into releasing her from the New Orleans asylum.) Sachs is his own director, and I mostly relished the speed of his production, but its conclusion seems arbitrary when it should be ineluctable. Cave is more riveting with her hair metaphorically and literally down, rather than demurely up as she wears it at the end. But this is a still a whirlwind of a performance.

Kevin Hanchard matches her as a John with complementary hang-ups: sure of himself as a man, but still jumping shamefully to attention at the ring of the master's phone (a particularly effective update). He's cruel without being naturally callous; he has just as much compassion as he can afford. He's nettled and shamed not only by Julie but -- Strindberg's notorious misogyny being on hold in this play --by Raven Dauda's spirited and sensible Christine who, all dressed up in her Sunday-go-to-meeting, gives the play's religious imperatives an unaccustomed authority. She also, in an uncommonly handsome kitchen, attacks her chopping-block with an implacability that foreshadows the dispatching of Miss Julie's pet. Some of the scene setting is heavy-handed; John reads about Lyndon Johnson's signing of the Civil Rights Act and the murder of the freedom riders Goodman, Schwerner and Chaney in the same edition of the daily paper, dated the Fourth of July. And The Real Inspector Hound should have killed off the device by which, whenever someone turns on the radio, it's right at the start of either a song or a news bulletin. But most of the details fit beautifully into place. The brief shared dream of opening a jazz-club in Chicago--John as manager, Julie as hostess, Christine as cook-- rings true for all three of them; they must all have seen the same movies. The play Miss Julie is supposed to have the tension of an erotic nightmare. For once it does. - Miss Julie: Freedom Summer is at the Bluma Appel Theatre until March 7. For tickets and information call 416-368-3110

2009-02-21-the-second-time-as-farce-trav:
The key line in Travesties is spoken by Nadya Krupskaya, more helpfully known as Mrs. Vladimir Lenin, when relating an incident from one of her husband's periods of imprisonment. She positioned herself outside the jail where he should have been able to see her. But," she says, "something went wrong. I forget what. Tom Stoppards play, a classic since its London debut in 1974, is about things going wrong for people with the loftiest ideas, and being misremembered afterwards to boot. Its about history's clowns.

The Lenins spent some of the First World War years in Zurich. So did James Joyce. So also did Tristan Tzara, one of the daddies of Dada. They weren't there at exactly the same time, but Henry Carr, writing his memoirs some 60 years later, would like to think they were. These unreliable reminiscences, irresistibly confided to the audience, are the spine of the piece. Its a play-within-a-monologue.

Carr, too, really existed. He was a minor official in the British consulate whose one claim to fame is that he played Algernon in a production of The Importance of Being Earnest for which Joyce was the business manager and which resulted in the two of them suing one another over the cost of a pair of trousers. Carr remembers himself as being the consul; and the actual consul, Bennett, as being his manservant. He also recalls being the friend and confidant of all three revolutionary transients, joining in their heated debates about the nature, purpose and proper relation of art and politics. Also those of their female acolytes: Carrs sister, Gwendolen, is a disciple of Joyce's gospel of art for art's sake, while his sweetheart, Cecily, a librarian, supplies books and worship to Lenin. The two ladies names may clue you in to the fact that Carrs dreamworld draws heavily on his role in The Importance; he pictures himself as an Oscar Wildean dandy, obsessed with his tailoring (those disputed pants). Large sections of the play are written as close and pointed pastiche of the parent comedy. (Joyce to the exhibitionist anti-artist Tzara: I advise you to acquire some genius and, if possible, some subtlety before the season is quite over.")Add to this, among much else, a musical crosstalk routine, a bump-and-grind on a library desk, and a scene written entirely in limericks. It's a brilliantly witty, and brilliantly intelligent, carnival.

It also has its drawbacks, chief being that it has no emotional arc. It certainly has heartfelt moments, notably Joyce's impassioned advocacy of art as magic, at the climax of which he literally produces a rabbit from a hat. Stoppard has said that he agrees with Joyce, but he gives equally persuasive arguments to Lenin and Tzara, of whom he disapproves, and to Carr, the plain man as philistine. But nobody in the play actually goes through anything; there are no doubts, fears, or disillusions, and the only plot is Oscars. This makes it less satisfying than Jumpers, its Stoppardian predecessor and companion-piece. Jumpers is a moving as well as a sparkling work, but in Travesties everything depends on sparkle: a daunting assignment that Joseph Zieglers Soulpepper production gets an impressive four-fifths right. It gets full marks for logic and lucidity, less -- after a delightfully deadpan opening sequence -- on bravura. Christina Poddubiuk has designed an elegant and versatile set for the craziness to bounce off, including a clock that can move smartly backwards to underline the glitches in the hero's head. But the limericks, for example, go slow and unmusical, and the show in general could use more showbiz.

It is, though, splendidly acted: far better than the last London revival, in which Antony Sher's old-man act as Carr killed off most of the laughs. Soulpeppers Carr is Diego Matamoros, whose gift is to establish a rhythm and identity for every role he plays and explore from there. Here he does it twice over and, barring a few lapses in comic phrasing, superbly. As the old Henry, hes the image of a dry, tetchy English pundit, brooking no contradictions except his own. As the young one, he's a self-satisfying man about town, more priggish than debonair and more Wodehouse than Wilde: especially with Kevin Bundy ineffably wonderful as his man, a Jeeves with socialist leanings who's also a dab hand, and foot, at a hat-and-cane number.

Jordan Pettle brings a welcome flamboyance and precision to Tzara (Jack to Henrys Algy) and David Storchs Joyce, though sometimes too muted, is fine in his prophetic utterances, as well as sporting a great cartoon outline. Oliver Dennis and Maggie Huculak are pitch perfect as the Lenins who, despite Stoppard's extensive rewrites, remain largely sealed off in their own part of the play, as in the sealed railway carriage that carried them back to Russia. Sarah Wilson and Krystin Pellerin are treats as the two young ladies, who end up butting heads and minds in a vaudeville duet ("oh, Gwendolen...oh, Cecilee) that might be even more pointed with more talking, less singing. Pellerin, as a librarian successively stern and melting, is especially fine, surpassed for endearingness only by this production's bunny, definitive in its role. - Travesties runs through March 21 at the Young Centre. Call 416-866-8666 or visit soulpepper.cafor tickets.

This year's Oscars, some shill said before they started, would be like no other." That wasn't true -- theres no way of changing the essential nature of this self-congratulatory schmoozefest, except perhaps by doing it without an audience -- but these were supposed to be different because of the recession. On the strength of the first hour, I cant say I'd have noticed. The stage did seem smaller than usual -- the performing area was narrowed to a blue-tinted circle, with a few ugly pillars behind it --but that seems to have been a design choice, probably no cheaper, at least in money terms, than any other.

Is it possibly more economic to hire a song-and-dance man as host, rather than a comedian? It seems unlikely, and any way it turned out to be a non-issue since Hugh Jackman turned out to be more valuable to the occasion as a chat-dispenser than as a musical performer. After being given the briefest of introductions -- maybe economy was at work here, or at least an attempt at good taste -- he launched into a spiel about actors stretching themselves -- i. e. performing as characters from countries other than their own. It doesn't sound much to get excited about -- doing accents is a useful acting skill, but hardly what its all about -- but he was at least able to prove by enumeration that theres been a lot of it about this past year, most of it award-nominated. He then remarked that he, an Australian, had appeared this year as an Australian in a film called Australia, and all it had got him was the hosting gig. Next year, he said ins the spirit of downsizing, he was doing a film called New Zealand. All right, it's not that hilarious, but there was a certain point to it. And he was very assured doing it, and otherwise buttering up the audience, or at least the stars in the front row.

Maybe, if musicals give out on him, he can go into stand-up comedy, or its more fashionable stepchild, chat-show hosting.

His musical turn on the Oscars -- the reason, he imagines, for hiring him -- certainly let him down. Nothing wrong with the way he did it, but the material was awful. It was the old Billy Crystal routine of listing the nominated movies' names and doing bits round them, but without an ounce of inspiration.

A few points of interest. There were shout-outs to pictures like The Wrestler and The Dark Knight that werent nominated but everyone thought should have been. There was a bit about not having seen The Reader, presumably because a song-and-dance routine referecning the Holocaust might strike even Hollywood as an uncomfortable stretch. And Anne Hathaway got to duet with Jackman in the Frost/Nixon bit, and proved she can sing, too. Someone should take advantage of that sometime.

Anyway, Jackman is one of those actors who can talk to the audience in his own person and still sound natural. Others who in the first stretch could do it turned out to be Whoopi Goldberg (because shes a comic), Goldie Hawn (ditto, and also because she's still an enchantress) and Tilda Swinton (I don't know; maybe because shes British and experimental).

Steve Martin and Tina Fey did it brilliantly, introducing the screenwriters awards. They even managed to undermine,, if not the whole idea of the awards, then at least their intolerable self-seriousness. Bring them back next year. Cohosts. I wouldnt even mind if Jackman made three. They have whole year to write him a good song.

2009-02-24-separating-the-medleys-from-t:
Danny Boyle leaped in the air a couple of times when receiving his best director Oscar for Slumdog Millionaire. He then explained, nice Anglo-Irish boy that he is, that he'd once promised his children that, if he ever got an Oscar, he'd respond like Tigger. I thought that was endearing, especially when he added that his kids were now too old to remember that he'd said it.

Less endearing was his comment that he didn't know how the show looked to the folks at home, but from where he sat in the Kodak Theater, it was wonderful. Oh Danny Boyle, the pipes, the pipes are calling; and what they're saying, in their mournful Celtic way, is that for all us underprivileged gawpers, the show looked terrible.

Some of its awfulness was common to all awards shows. Some seemed to have been dreamed up specially, especially the weird, supposedly arty camera angles from which they shot the on-set TV monitors on which the customary montages were screened. These were mostly shot from high up and lopsided, so that it was impossible to see just what was being celebrated.

Even the annual roll-call of the recently deceased wasn't spared. I always look forward to the morgue montage -- it's genuinely informative -- but this year they really managed to cheapen it.

What kind of a crazy idea was it to intersperse the montage of scenes from the five best picture nominees with scenes from movies past to which they bore some faint resemblance? These all flashed by so fast, that only when something turned up in black-and-white could we get any purchase on which era it belonged to. Not to mention that most of the supposed connections were laughable. "Mad as hell and not gonna take it any more" doesn't bear much resemblance to the struggles of Harvey Milk. Hollywood's compulsive referencing of its own past may indicate a proper piety; it's more likely to be born of desperation.

If it isn't montages, it's medleys. We had one of the nominated songs (with dances) and another of the nominated incidental music (orchestra on stage); and it was impossible to tell the individual items apart. Though maybe it would have been impossible anyway.

Hugh Jackman, hosting, told us that musicals are back, and proceeded, with assistance from Beyonce and numerous others more anonymous, to celebrate them in a shapeless parade of intertwined snippets that began with Top Hat, White Tie and Tails, and then tried to reflect its glory onto a trip through the Dark Ages. If musicals being back means Mamma Mia!, better they should stay away.

Why not just let Jackman do a number? It's presumably what he was there for. I spent the latter part of the evening eating the kind words I wrote about him yesterday on the strength of the first hour. He isn't a comic, and he isn't an emcee. He looked like a fall guy.

One nice innovation: the acting awards were each announced by a team of five former winners saluting the current nominees, one apiece and face virtually to face. Some of them sounded as if they might actually have written their own speeches: Whoopi Goldberg, for example, commiserated with Amy Adams ( Doubt) on the difficulties of playing a nun (those constricting habits, plus "your love interest is always off-screen"), or Shirley MacLaine making Anne Hathaway cry by congratulating her for everything, including the singing voice that she'd earlier shown off by duetting with Jackman in the opening medley's Frost/Nixon bit.

All right, it's ridiculous to be touched by the sight of very rich people paying tribute to other very rich people; but Hathaway had a right to smile through tears, since she deserved to win for Rachel Getting Married and she must have known she hadn't a prayer. And, oh God, there was Sophia Loren, just beginning to look her age but only just.

Among the gents, Cuba Gooding gave a shout-out to Robert Downey, perhaps on behalf of all actors called Junior. Robert DeNiro solemnly inquired, "How did he do it? How for so many years id [Sean Penn] get all those jobs playing straight men?" Penn's victory was a palpable upset. Everyone expected best actor to go to Mickey Rourke, to whom I bear no malice; but the voters made the right decision, relieving us all of the necessity of crying over spilt Milk. (Other surprise: best supporting actress to Penelope Cruz. I think everyone expected it to go to Viola Davis. I certainly did. How could you miss with a single scene in which you get to upstage Meryl Streep?)

Slumdog Millionaire cleaned up and nobody, I imagine, was surprised or even displeased. It's a feel-good picture that knows, indeed revels in, its own unreality. (Of course it's contrived. That's the point.) And a lot of Mumbai kids got a trip to California. Heath Ledger's family collected his award with dignity; they didn't cry, but everybody else did. (Talk about a foregone conclusion; his living competitors must have wondered why they bothered to show up.)

Steve Martin, who must definitely have written his own stuff or at least had it tailored for him, hit the evening's high point early on by quoting something about writers living forever and then commenting "the man who wrote that is now dead." Best timing of the evening. Bring him back.

2009-02-27-what-happens-when-you-let-the:
Some years ago, William Finn, composer-lyricist of March of the Falsettos and other shows, underwent emergency brain-surgery. He then wrote a musical about it. When people start talking about unlikely subjects for musicals, they always say how crazy and brave it was for Andrew Lloyd Webber to write a show about cats. Personally, I always thought it was, especially in a culture as anthropomorphically-inclined as Britain, a bloody obvious idea, practically a no-brainer. Song-and-dance about a frontal lobe operation, though, is something else. You might call it a new brainer. Which is very nearly what Finn did call it.

A New Brain has its snags, but it's largely delightful, sometimes moving and has Finn's best score. James Lapine wrote the book, which, in terms of actual dialogue, is very sparing; we're someway into a fairly brief evening before we realize that the show is not, in fact, composed. The autobiography is not exact but is fairly blatant. The hero Gordon is, like Finn, a songwriter, though operating in less prestigious territory. He writes for a kids' show that's hosted by a human-sized talking and singing frog, and he despises the show, its star and his own contributions to it. He is lunching with his agent to discuss this situation when he comes over all funny and has to be rushed to hospital. The only other specific things we learn about Gordon is that, again like Finn, he is both gay (we meet his boyfriend) and Jewish (we meet his mother).

Acting Up Stage, who specialize in bringing offbeat American musicals to Toronto, have done this one very well, with the director, Daryl Cloran, delivering a faultless production that moves smoothly, sensitively and inventively from one mood to the next. The same can be said of Steven Gallagher's Gordon, a supple and touching performance that establishes a direct rapport with the audience, even though the writing gives him more predicament than personality. The show's trajectory is that a young man with issues finds that they matter less than the fact of being alive, especially when you've just had a narrow escape from being dead. The show's last rejoicing number is called I Feel so Much Spring. The cast, led by Gallagher, sing it beautifully, and we can appreciate the weight of feeling behind it, but it may leave you reflecting that off-Broadway uplift is not so very different from Broadway uplift. Frankly, any character could sing it, in almost any show

Finn has always had a gift for the plangent, at its best here in a song called I'd Rather Be Sailing that both aches and soars, especially as sung by Thom Allison. He plays Gordon's lover, whose passion for boats sometimes seems to eclipse his passion for Gordon (or that's how Gordon, a grumpy landlubber, tends to see it) but who still keeps faithful, anxious vigil at his bedside. What Finn is less good at is being clever: Barbara Barsky as Gordon's mother is handed a number called Throw It Out in which she visits her son's apartment and gets rid of his books, which she seems to be blaming for something. She enumerates books and titles, but they seem to be there for the rhymes, rather than for any specific light they shed on either character.

There's also a choric bag lady (Paula Wolfson), the painful reality of whose situation is eclipsed by her function as a metaphorical messenger, first of warning, then of goodwill. Better are the scenes inside the hospital, in which the terrors engulfing Gordon and his support-group are played off against the businesslike concerns of the medical staff: from a cheerily insensitive surgeon (Jonathan Tan) to a male nurse who swings between sympathy and resentment and who sums himself up in song as Poor, Unsuccessful and Fat. He's splendidly embodied by Steve Ross. The two elements come together in a hallucinatory sequence, most inventively choreographed by Marc Kimmelman, in which Gordon's memories of his father's racetrack gambling habit are played out by a ghostly, mocking array of doctors, nurses and friends.

Musical director Wayne Gwillim musters his forces impeccably; this is as well-sung a show as you'll find in Toronto. Remaining performers include Parris Greaves as a minister, Patricia Zentilli as a surprisingly soft-boiled agent and Allie Hughes, delightful as a waitress still smitten with childish adoration of Mr. Bungee, the frog-star employer who haunts Gordon's nightmares. He's played by Juan Chioran, who must be the tallest amphibian in captivity, and who seems happiest when he's allowed to take his head off and give Gordon a pep talk. His function seems to be to help our hero back to health by persuading him that writing cheerful songs for children can be a noble pursuit, as indeed it is. The really affecting journey in the show is a musician's one. Gordon's initial attempt to write a number called Frogs Have So Much Spring, in which neither he nor anyone else can believe, finally evolves into I Feel so Much Spring and, just before that, to the show's real climax Time and Music. Lindsay Anne Black designed the ingenious set; musical arrangements, carried over from the New York original, are by another fine composer (and finer lyricist), Jason Robert Brown. - A New Brain is at the Berkeley Street Theatre until Sunday. Call 416-368-3110 for tickets and information.

2009-02-28-we-all-could-use-some-medical:
Kristen Thomson's The Patient Hour turns out not to be what it seems. I have mixed feelings about this since, pardon my grammar, I like what it seems. I admire the audacity with which the play moves into unexpected territory, and in retrospect, I appreciate the cleverness of the hints dropped earlier on, both in the writing and in Chris Abrahams production. The first two-thirds of the play are funny, touching and engaging. The last section varies between the provocative and the pretentious.

We are in a hospital room: almost literally, since the patient, unseen, is presumed to be somewhere in the middle of the auditorium. She is an elderly woman, in critical condition after a stroke. The other characters -- her son, her daughter, the night-nurse and a mysterious female patient claiming to be from a room down the hall -- speak to her unresponsive form, therefore in effect to us, as well as to one another. This is the place to say that any doubts that lingered about Thomsons writing after her triumphant and self-performed I Claudia are here dispelled. She can write for performers other than herself, and she can write dialogue as well as monologue. It's true that her people often don't seem to be paying attention to one another, and that they often talk past one another. Thats clearly intentional, and after all, it worked for Chekhov.

Also obviously intentional is the pun in the plays title. Hospital vigils are doubly disconcerting, in that they're predominantly uneventful while the events that do happen are frequently alarming. They're typified by forced smiles and frayed nerves, and the play gives us full and believable measure of both. They can also exacerbate family tensions, and that seems to be the pattern here. Charles and Laura, brother and sister, havent communicated in years. Much of this is ascribed to Lauras having been in prison, or somewhere, for shoplifting: a farcical-sounding episode that Waneta Storms, who plays her, relates with great biting humour and aggressively rolling eyes. This is a tough, grimly amused performance from an actress who was everywhere in this city's theatres 10 years ago and has been much missed since. Charles, it seems, never visited her; neither did their mother, Dawn. Charles is an auto mechanic, a compulsive jokester driven by insecurity. Pushing 40 and never married, he contemplates making a pass at June, the nurse, who has been married and wishes she hadn't. The territory occupied by these two, each both hoping and dreading that the other will make a move, isnt exactly uncharted, but its sweetly explored. He makes clumsy attempts at flirting; she, flashing a semi-discouraging smile, makes awkward gestures at being flirted with.

Charles is played by Todd Thomson, who is the author's brother and bears a strong resemblance to her, both physically and in the warmth and wit of his acting. He's likely to hop up and squat on a chair to attract attention or to make a surprise entrance as an accident victim. Liisa Repo-Martells June, who had a career in pottery before switching to health care, offers a quieter, more businesslike study in shyness. The scenes between the two of them give what may be the most thorough workout ever given to the Canadian upward inflection, that vocal tic whereby every statement becomes both a question and a plea for approval. It works. As the most fully realized characters in the play, everything we hear from or about them rings true.

Patricia Fagan plays the unplaceable, and troubled, Young Patient who keeps wandering in to confide in the quiescent Dawn. She has a harrowing speech about having given birth to a dead child, a trauma from which she has not recovered. She doesnt seem to fit with what one knows about hospital routine, and the disconnect is reflected in the production. Julie Fox's set is impeccably, if economically, realistic, but there are strange discontinuities in the action, especially in the matter of exits and entrances. The director, though, absolutely knows what he is doing, and nearly --not quite--everything adds up by the end. Some things from the past are revealed at just the right telling moment, notably the fact that Dawn once worked in a prison. Her name, too, is probably significant; the play is full of cosmic metaphor (even the puzzle game that Charles brings to entertain his mom is called Planet Earth) that, I confess, struck me as less astronomical than astrological. In other words, it lost me. The parts of the play that I found most persuasive, either as pain or pleasure, are those grounded in experience rather than philosophy. There's a fair amount of what I would call wishful spinning. But compassion -- for the living, the dying and the dead -- comes through clearly and for the most part unsentimentally. The acting is unwaveringly superb. And frankly, everyone in or around Toronto theatre is in love with Kristen Thomson; this play will keep all those flames burning.

- The Patient Hour runs through March 29 at the Tarragon Extra Space. Call 416-531-1827 for details.
2009-03-04-truckers-in-a-dangerous-clime:
Those of us living in temperate zones like Toronto can stop complaining about what a terrible winter we're having. Ice Road Truckers, the new TV documentary show set in the Northwest Territories, proves to us that we just don't know from cold. You freeze all over just looking at it. And somebody like me, who flinches at the idea of a nighttime drive on the 401 even in the summer, can reflect on the truck drivers who are the central characters on this show. Their job is to drive supplies from Yellowknife to diamond-mining operations 300 miles farther north. And the roads they drive on, which have to be newly built every year, are made of ice. (The diamonds are described as "another kind of ice.") Some of us are terrified of driving on ice. These guys are scared -- well, apprehensive, they don't scare easy -- of driving off it. Or, more accurately, of falling beneath it. The establishing shots for each episode of Ice Road Truckers include 18-wheelers sinking, drivers presumably included, into the deep waters of instant hypothermia.

It's strictly a seasonal job. The ice road, built over permafrost, is good for only 60 days, which is just twice the time it takes to construct it, at an annual cost of $10-million. The rewards for the truckers are comparably big. One of them says that he can make a year's wages in eight nights; another, aged 25, looks forward to being a millionaire by 30. "The dash for the cash" is how they describe it at the start of each episode. It's nature's own reality show -- or nature's and commerce's -- and the narration is delivered in reality TV's exclamatory, heavily italicized tones.

We focus on a half-dozen truckers, and each episode concludes with a chart showing how much each of them has earned so far. "Some of them," we are lipsmackingly told, "will hit the jackpot, others will jack-knife." However, the jackpot contains legitimate earnings. There's no suggestion in the first two episodes that the TV company is offering any kind of top-up. (Well, on the History Channel, you'd hardly expect it.) This isn't some contest that's been artificially dreamed up by a network. It's what these guys would be doing anyway. That gives it its kick. The line between "reality" and documentary has been getting increasingly blurred, but this show --however it wants to bill itself and however unctuously it sometimes comes on--is on the respectable side of it.

The road will crack if they all start off at once, so they draw lots for departure times. The winner is Alex, the most experienced of the bunch, grizzled and jovial and something of a good-luck charm for the others. He sets off with a 220-pound load of diamond-processing material. ("Everyone's in a good mood," he says at the start, "unless you don't like my jokes.") Alex tells us, persuasively, that he loves being on the ice, but this time out he hits one of the many occupational hazards: an air leak. It's 40 below (Fahrenheit or Celsius, remarks a local radio announcer, at these temperatures it hardly matters) and has to keep moving, otherwise he'll freeze. But he also has to keep stopping; he's in for 13 hours on frozen roads.

At the other extreme is T. J., 21 and an ice-road virgin, who tells us that he "despises the cold," which initially suggests that he may be in the wrong line of work, or at least have chosen the wrong place in which to practise it. And wouldn't you know, first time out, he encounters the most dreaded of weather conditions, a whiteout. Here, as at several points, you get to wonder how the camera crew, unacknowledged in the cab with him, must have felt. Well, at least they had the satisfaction of providing T. J. with company. And the other guys, too: Long-distance driving encourages soliloquy -- these heroes have an audience for theirs

Existential drama? You bet. It's like a factual climate-reversed version of The Wages of Fear, the classic French film about truck drivers bearing loads of nitroglycerin, sometimes going up in flames when they hit a patch of rough ground. I don't know if comparable mayhem is in store for any of the designated protagonists on this show. We do meet the rescue teams who descend beneath the ice to salvage whatever, and presumably whomever, they can; fatality figures are quoted, but it's not clear whether they refer to divers, drivers or both. The truckers emerge with the expected blend of bravado and practicality, surface camaraderie and basic competitive solitude. The narration does its best to cheapen things with the reality show's patented rhetorical questions ("Is this rookie really cut out to go the distance on these roads?") and compulsive scoreboarding ("After 14 days of the dash for the cash, Alex is in the lead with $120,000"). But this hysteria is shamed by the guys themselves. "There's a whole lot of stupid rolling on the roads this year," says one of them. That's poetry.

-The premiere of Ice Road Truckers airs tonight on History Television at 9 p. m.

2009-03-06-two-women-of-many-words:
Last year at Passe Muraille, Anusree Roy gave us a one-woman play, Pyaasa, that showed her to be a good writer and an exceptional performer. The same qualities are on view in her new piece, Letters to My Grandma, but the result isn't as satisfying. There's nothing actually wrong with the piece itself, and there's much about its presentation that's perfect, but you're still left wondering at the end of its 50-minute length what it was all for.

Roy appears here in two roles. She's Malobee, who in her childhood emigrated with her parents from India to live in Toronto, and whom we meet in her early twenties when she's about to get married. And she's Malobee's beloved grandmother, whom the family left behind in India and with whom Malobee has constantly corresponded but

has never visited. Somehow, it never seemed to be the right time for the trip. Despite its title, the play contains as many letters from grandma as to her. Malobee sorts through a cache of correspondence on the day before her wedding, and it's this that sets off the reminiscences that make up the play.

It isn't all letters. There's an early funny scene in which we see Malobee's arrival in Toronto, dealing with airport administration on behalf of her family and going through the numerical intricacies of calling her grandmother via phone card. The old lady is now in a nursing home, and Malobee is much concerned -- it's a constant theme of the play -- that she's taking her medication properly. We hear grandmother herself dealing imperiously with her nurse. And, in the most obviously dramatic sequence, we flash back to her experiences as a semi-refugee in the chaos that overtook India at the end of the Second World War. We hear about the strains on her marriage, to a man who took off to work in Burma for years at a time. We gather that she is a survivor, and surmise that that's one of the things about her that her granddaughter loves.

Of the generation between them, we hear virtually nothing. And no real parallel emerges between the two people we do meet. The older woman's struggles in her birth-country dwarf those of the younger in her adopted one, though presumably we're meant to make some kind of connection between them. If Malobee (who I imagine is somewhat autobiographical) has undergone any great pressures in Canada, we don't hear about them. Her fiance is apparently British, but any tensions arriving from this are confined to the reactions of her grandmother, who carries bitter memories of the English but eventually admits that they may be all right in peacetime.

Pyaasa had more characters, more atmosphere and a bitterly ironic story. Letters to My Grandma is much slighter, more a two-headed lyric than a play. It does have an ear for detail, and Roy's acting, here as before, gets the best of two worlds: the formality of Eastern theatre and the naturalism of Western. She is very particular in delineating her roles, the grandmother's especially, while giving each a stark, stylized physical outline. She moves, and occasionally chants, with a grace that transcends prettiness. She executes thunderclap transformations from one role to the other, abetted by Thomas Morgan Jones' direction and, especially, David DeGrow's lighting. I don't know whether she's taken vows of theatrical solitude; personally, I'd like to see her follow Kristen Thomson's current example, and both act with and write for other performers. There's nothing aesthetically immoral about one-person shows, but a glut of them such as we are currently experiencing --mainly for economic reasons -- can leave an audience feeling starved. - Letters to my Grandma runs until March 8. Call 416-504-7529 for information.

2009-03-07-building-blocks-forbidden-pho:
Two shows for young audiences, both set in, from a Canadian perspective, exotic climes, both imaginatively staged, both with a message rather loosely attached. The Forbidden Phoenix, which comes to the Lorraine Kimsa Theatre for Young People, via the Citadel Theatre in Edmonton, is the more exotic of the two, perhaps surprisingly since much of its action depicts events that happened right here.

The inspiration of Marty Chan's play is the building of the Canadian Pacific railroad, with its heavy reliance on exploited immigrant labour from China. Chan filters this historical material through the traditions of China's classical theatre, in particular, the story of the Monkey King who, Chan tells us, "promised to find food for his tribe, and travelled west until he found a waterfall." Beyond this waterfall lies, surprisingly, Canada, and the railroad magnate Horne, performed here as a tyrant-figure from Chinese legend. It looks as though Sun Wokong, the Monkey King, has hardly left home at all.

This puts a dent in the playwright's declared purpose of writing a cautionary tale about racism and how to defeat it. There is no sense of differing cultures or even of differing ethnicities. It's true that Horne does occasionally speak in sneering tones of "cool-ees" (that's how he pronounces it) whom he delegates to do such suicidally dirty work as blasting open recalcitrant mountains with sticks of dynamite, but Sun Wokong is the only cool-ee we meet, and when he's not available Horne seems perfectly willing to sacrifice the lives of employees of his own race. Meanwhile, the civilization that the Monkey King has fled seems even more repressive than the one he's reached, ruled over as it is by a Dowager Empress, who grabs all produce and profits for herself and treats any opposition as blasphemy. Sun Wokong only goes west because she has banished him there, for hoarding rice to feed his son: a boy whom the Empress later kidnaps and whom she brainwashes into rejecting his father. This is foul but I can't see how it counts as racist.

The titular phoenix sits atop the hill that blocks the railway line, defying Horne's efforts to dislodge her and providing Sun Wokong with moral and sometimes physical support in his battle for justice. Her precise significance, though, baffled me, whatever it may have done for the young audiences for whom the show's intended. But they reacted enthusiastically to the look and sound of the show, though seemed lukewarm, as well they might, about its songs. Purportedly this is a musical, but the numbers (music by Robert Walsh, who also collaborated with Chan on the lyrics) do nothing to advance the story. The form entails freedom and fluidity, and Ron Jenkins's production, gorgeously designed by Leslie Frankish, brilliantly attaches this to the techniques of the Chinese opera. The conventions may muddy the show's politics, but they do great things in the imaginative sphere. Also in the personal: The relationship between Sun Wokong (Richard Lee) and his Monkey Son(Shannon Kook-Chun) is expounded in roughly equal proportions of dialogue, dance and acrobatics, with an emphasis on martial arts, and it's as moving as it's delightful. Michael Dufays and Lori Nancy Kalamanski are imposing villains, and the support-work is excellent.

Binti's Journey, revived by Theatre Direct as the opening production at its sparkling new premises in Wychwood Barns, is more single-mindedly set in Malawi. Adapted by Marcia Johnson from Deborah Ellis's novel The Heaven Shop, it presents a society living and, from what we see, coping with the omnipresent threat of AIDS. "Your father has AIDS" is almost the first line we hear, a common schoolyard taunt here directed at Binty, whom we meet as a child radio star and whom we follow, through her own narration, as her world and her family falls apart and is then, in a sort, reassembled. The heaven shop is the family business, and it makes coffins. Jajube Mandiela's Binti doesn't change much through these supposedly maturing experiences, but she's an appealing focal point. Among her colleagues, who double indomitably, Patrick Amporah is especially good as males ranging from Binti's brother to the uncle who takes her in when her parents die. He's an unsympathetic guardian, and Binti's life in his care becomes an updated Cinderella story. She later finds refuge with her grandmother, whose power and wisdom are signified by having her played by three actors speaking more or less in unison, a device that's impressive when it arrives and wearisome when it persists. The production, by ahdri zhina mandiela, works very well as a tale. It's a kind of love story. The play can be quite blunt about the brutal ways in which AIDS can be contracted, but at times it's in danger of treating it almost as a beneficent force. The perpetual dilemma for children's theatre is to be uplifting without being preachy or sentimental. Neither of these shows avoids the trap. Technically, though, they're on a high level.

- The Forbidden Phoenix runs through March 11 at the Lorraine Kimsa Theatre for Young People. For schedule information, call 416-862-2222.

2009-03-12-contemplating-love-amid-the-m:
THEATRE REVIEW

THEATRE PASSE MURAILLE BACKSPACE

---

Layne Coleman's Tijuana Cure is a first-person solo piece that prompts both empathy and embarrassment, with the former winning out. Coleman, best known as an actor and director (and also as former artistic director of Passe Muraille, whose Backspace is hosting this Smash Theatre production) is writing about his journey with his late wife, the novelist and critic Carole Corbeil, to a "last hope" clinic in Mexico. Their purpose was to try a diet cure for what proved to be Corbeil's fatal cancer. Coleman doesn't perform the piece himself, and the actor who stands in for him is in fact a woman, Ieva Lucs.

The Colemans' ordeal has already been the subject of a full-scale play, Scratch, by their daughter Charlotte Corbeil-Coleman (who is a momentary character in this one). That, though, changed the names and many of the details and emerged as an imaginative work in its own right. Tijuana Cure sticks, we must assume, to the facts, physical and mental. It's already been published in The Walrus; I didn't know this while I was watching it, but I did find myself thinking that the recurring queasiness I felt would not have been present if I had been reading the same material as a printed memoir. Live performance, and especially a live audience, change the equation. We're being asked to applaud someone, right then and there, on the quality of his grief.

The saving grace here is that we're also being asked to consider the quality of his happiness, and it's easier to rejoice in that. We are presented with what was plainly a lovely, loving marriage -- something that the theatre, for obvious reasons concerned with dramatic conflict, doesn't often ask us to contemplate. The title seems at first blush ironic, as we know that Carole wasn't cured and didn't survive. The play doesn't take us up to her death; it confines itself to the trip, in the course of which Layne's love for his wife wasn't exactly rediscovered -- it hardly seems to have gone away -- as reaffirmed. To that extent their pilgrimage produced, if not a cure, then a Tijuana tonic.

This of course is very moving, not least because the accompanying spectres of pain and loss must connect to the worst nightmares, imagined or lived, of everybody watching. These factors aren't obsessively dwelt on but they are always present, not least in the constant references to Carole's need for painkillers. We also partake as Layne girds himself--his phrase -- for an expanded role as his wife's mental and physical support. (The diet is an onerous one.) Somewhat more light-heartedly, we watch him doing battle with the rigours and uncertainties of travelling from Toronto to Tijuana via San Diego, and with his relishing of the local colour. Encouraged by Carole, who urges him to enjoy himself as much as possible, he inspects the local red-light district. This in turn connects with amorous memories of his youth: his falling in love with his wife, and some less satisfactory encounters earlier on, at least one of which is excruciatingly entertaining. These reminiscences and others, such as his excitement at seeing The Beatles on Ed Sullivan and the disgust they aroused in his puritanical father, are justified as having run through his head while he was in Mexico. But it seems a dubious peg. It's as if the author is trying to cram into the piece material that, however engaging in itself, doesn't belong there. Again, it would work fine in print. In the less forgiving medium of drama, it's padding.

The casting must be intended to provide a distancing effect, to avoid theobvious danger of self-exploitation. Up to a point it succeeds. Lucs, under Ashlie Corcoran's direction, makes no attempt to imitate Coleman, or indeed to do any kind of male impersonation at all. She's an actress with a strong physical and vocal presence that quite often goes into overdrive: I've never known so much juice to be squeezed from simple place-names. This wide-eyed over-emphasis, pervasive in the earlier parts of the evening, is the direct opposite of the discretion the play needs. It's the wrong kind of alienation. Later on, the performance settles down. A woman's body takes the curse off, while adding a comedic edge to, the narrator's rueful preoccupation with his own physicality. Lucs also of course gets to play all the women in the story, including Carole herself, whose spoken contributions are significantly minimal. That's a tactful decision on the author's part, and it communicates itself to the actress who becomes both simpler and more affecting as the play's emotions take hold. Naked autobiography in the theatre always seems to me like special pleading, sometimes amounting to emotional blackmail. This production, which I saw at a preview, can't avoid the first charge but keeps honourably clear of the second. - Tijuana Cure is at the Passe Muraille Backspace until March 28. Call 416-504-7529 for more information.

2009-03-14-they-were-only-waiting-for-th:
At the start of Blackbird, a man and a woman confront one another in charged silence across a very messy room. It turns out that their lives, and especially their prior relationship, are even messier. The man, Ray, looks to be in his late fifties, early sixties; we learn that the woman, Una, is 28, though in the current production she seems about five years younger.

They're in a staff room at Rays workplace; the reason it looks like a pigsty (I quote) is that the employees leave the detritus of a days snacking lying all over it. Ray's own position in the company (dental floss and allied products) is uncertain, but he claims it's something senior, though at one point he gets so intent on clearing up the garbage from the floor and tabletop that Una twits him with being the janitor. This he vehemently denies, and I think we can take it that he is telling the truth. Its typical of David Harrowers engrossing play that we can be more certain of what Ray isn't than of what he is.

The salient fact about the two characters is, however, undisputed. There's a certain amount of fencing and stonewalling before were told what it is, but the revelation comes early enough for it to be re-revealed here; besides, it would be impossible to discuss the play intelligibly otherwise. Ray and Una had a sexual relationship when Una was 12. Ray was sent to prison; since his release he has, he says, rebuilt his life. Una hasnt seen him since his arrest but now, having spotted his picture in a trade magazine, she's tracked him down. For revenge, retribution, reconciliation or just some unspecific notion of "closure"? We don't know and neither, probably, does she. As for Ray, he could be terrified to see her or pleased or intrigued or some combination. All the possibilities are there.

Blackbird was first staged at the Edinburgh Festival in 2005; it was subsequently staged in London and New York, winning all kinds of awards in both places. For the first 20 minutes of its Toronto production, its reputation seems overblown. Its tense, certainly, and intriguing, but it unfolds with the kind of freighted, sawn-off, semi-enigmatic dialogue thats become contemporary drama's default style. We think we know where we are with it: Basically, this being a British play, in oblique Pinterland, with a dash of Mamet menace. Our mistake. Those influences, or at least those resemblances, are certainly there, but to the play's own ends. It may seem secretive, but it isnt obscure. Harrower has, on this evidence, an impeccable sense of what can and cannot be said without cheating. He applies it to character, narrative and even to morality. His remarkable achievement is to move us beyond disgust.

There is no doubt that both Una and Ray are deeply damaged, and our instinctive reaction is to blame Ray. I wouldnt say the play discourages that reaction, but it does complicate it. We're made to contemplate the unsettling possibility that what happened all those years ago was love, which would have made the betrayal all the more intense. Then, in the play's last brilliant quarter of an hour, theres another reversal, one that changes all our perceptions. Were forced to recognize something that we have been tempted to forget -- what a 12-year-old child is actually like. Here, Harrower is, indeed, harrowing. I've said that he knows just how much to reveal. He also knows how and when to spring the revelations; he times his surprises for maximum impact. And still he leaves us wanting to know more. The play ends with the most unnerving set of unanswerable questions since Ibsen dropped the curtain on Ghosts without telling us whether or not Mrs. Alving was about to mercy-kill her son.

I would guess that both roles in Blackbird are fearsomely difficult, but Ray's is probably the more easily approachable. Hes in the more obviously dramatic situation, a cornered man governed by fear, the predator become the prey. That, at least, is the impression given in this Studio 180 production in which Hardee Lineham plays him, superbly, as a man built out of jelly. You believe in the facade he has constructed, as a pink-faced middle manager, and shudder at how easily it can be dismantled. Una suffers more from the productions decision to sever the play's connections to its national origins; there's no reason, of course, why it couldnt happen in Canada, but her manner of speech is hard-wired to the British tradition of opaque threat. She does sound like someone out of Pinter, and Jessica Greenberg seems to be playing a style rather than a person. She starts blankly aggressive, before switching to plaintive, a tone that dominates a long retrospective monologue, which, perhaps unwisely, is staged and lit as a set-piece. Its only in the last stretches, where Una's at her most open and vulnerable, that the performance finds some flexibility. This imbalance apart, Joel Greenberg delivers a taut production on a wonderfully anonymous set by Michael Gianfrancesco, an environment disdainful of humanity whose human inhabitants have clearly reacted in kind. The last of the play's open questions, or maybe the first, is its title; the author has referred offhandedly in interviews to Bye Bye Blackbird ("no one here can love or understand me") and to the Lennon-McCartney song, but I think he was kidding.

- Blackbird runs through April 4 at the Berkeley Street Theatre Downstairs. Call 416-368-3110 for details.
