2009-03-16-a-wire-gone-slack-the-line-pe:
Deja vu. Max and Jayne are having extra-marital sex in a Scarborough motel. Max is a cop, Jayne a lawyer, both of them disillusioned with their work and with one another. Outside in a car sits Max's partner Donny, who has gone past disillusion on the road to derangement and is now, as often, drunk. It might be a scene from a George F. Walker play.

As a matter of fact, it is. The publicity for The Line has been coy about this, but the first two episodes of this 15-part serial reproduce the action and dialogue from Adult Entertainment, one of the plays in Walker's Suburban Motel cycle of stage plays, an opus in which Max and Donny are recurring characters. Unlike the play, the TV show travels outside the motel room. We meet characters and witness events that in the theatre we only hear about. So when, at the start of Episode 2, Max staggers into the room with a knife stuck in him, we don't have to be told how it got there. We've seen.

That doesn't necessarily mean we believe. Even Walker's most enjoyable plays are finally unsatisfying, their characters insubstantial figures in a lightweight phantasmagoria. It's a personal tone all right, but it feels willed rather than imagined. His previous TV series, This is Wonderland (co-written, like this one, with Dani Romain), made this work; it was a series of pungent, darkly hilarious vignettes, with the minimum of connecting story. It also got up its characters for the occasion. Max and Donny, creatures of the stage, shrivel when exposed to the light of day, especially as the action they're involved in is, inescapably, a police procedural. And, even given that most of us derive our knowledge of cops and criminals from other TV shows, this one isn't very convincing. Max is a rogue cop; Donny, who has bought a part-interest in the motel and spends much of his time attending to it, is just a rogue. They don't seem to have anyone to report to.

The case they're concerned with, reprised and expanded from the play, centres on Carlos, a subordinate drug dealer just released from prison and trying, for economic reasons, to serve two masters: Andre, an established local kingpin, and Eddie, who works out of a Vietnamese restaurant even though, in Andre's sour estimation, he's really Hawaiian. Carlos's divided loyalties inevitably get him in trouble, and his complicated family life inevitably comes under threat. The cops have similar domestic problems: Donny is tempestuously estranged from his wife, and Max looks to be becoming so from his, an intelligent woman who suspects him of having married her for her exotic appeal. (She's black.)Max and Jayne keep bouncing in and out of one another's lives, or at least of the motel bed, and she enlists him to keep tabs on the unsavoury boyfriend of one of her clients. This doesn't turn out well, either. This show has more dysfunctional relationships -- husband-wife, parent-child, lover-mistress, gangster-hooker -- than anyone can keep track of. And that's before you get to the actual crimes.

The show does break new ground in the treatment of money laundering by showing us bills, of uncertain denomination, actually going round and round in a washing machine. By and large the crooks here are more vivid than the cops; though, as a close relative of mine remarked, "they wouldn't last a day in Baltimore." I've been trying to avoid the comparison to The Wire, but the similarities are inescapable, especially in a scene where Andre instructs his apprentice pushers on what to charge and to whom, like Stringer Bell lecturing his henchmen on the finer points of market share, only tamer. Both The Line and The Wire present concerned pictures of urban, or suburban, wastelands. But where The Wire quietly rages, The Line shrugs. It has the feel of a comedy show, though The Wire is in fact funnier as well as more serious. (Or because it's more serious.)

The acting here is good, though without the grounded electricity of Wonderland. Ron White, who's played Max onstage, plays him again, elaborating on his original troubled calm; Daniel Kash plays Donny, whose feet are so far off the ground it's irritating. Cle Bennett is fairly sympathetic as Carlos, while Wes Williams fairly menacing as Andre. Sharon Lawrence, of NYPD Blue, has been imported to play Jayne, as has Ed Asner, the iconic Lou Grant, to play her dad: a performance on which I can't comment as, in the four episodes I've seen, he hasn't appeared. Of course, he has plenty of time left; 15 hours is a long time in TV terms, or most other terms, and I do wonder how they're going to fill it. I can't claim, though, that my wondering has much to do with suspense. I may well keep watching. I'm interested; Walker, after all, is a real writer. But nothing so far has made me care. - The Line airs tonight at 10 p. m. on The Movie Network.

2009-03-16-we-need-the-ceeb:
Second in a week-long series

Ihad the luck to grow up on the BBC. One of the best things about Britain is that it has managed, despite constant political sniping, to maintain a publicly funded nationwide broadcasting service that doesn't have to be supported by advertising and that has made an enormous contribution to the cultural life of its country. I owe a lot of my education to it. We have a comparable thing in Canada. It's called CBC Radio. We don't at the moment have it on television: at least, not to the extent that we could.

Some of the reasons for this are political. Public broadcasting always gets hammered by governments, who believe that if the thing is going to exist at all it had damn well better function as their propaganda arm. This, by the way, has nothing to do with the supposed "liberal bias" of the CBC. One thing that comically unites left and right is the entrenched belief of both that there is some monolithic force called "the media" that is out to get them. The fallback position of both is that, in its news coverage at least, "the media" should be impartial and objective. Actually, for as long as broadcasting is conducted by human beings, complete objectivity cannot exist and would be boring if it did. The most we can hope for is conscientiousness, and CBC news does pretty well on that score.

As for what is known as "creative" programming: The CBC's job here is to encourage talent, and if artistic talent declares itself as left of centre -- well, maybe that's something to think about. It certainly isn't a merely fashionable or transient phenomenon. The Victorian novelists we now revere were savagely critical of "Victorian values." Whatever kind of show we're talking about, fact or fiction: A public broadcasting organization that didn't offend or annoy people wouldn't be doing its job. It's one of the definitions of democracy.

A friend in the business has advised me not to give in to nostalgia. Still, I want to indulge my own long enough to recall that at one time the world was quite envious of Canadian television, and especially of Canadian television drama. The BBC in the 1950s ran whole seasons of it. In the early '60s when one of the British commercial companies embarked on a series of edgy new plays -- they called it Armchair Theatre, which I guess dates it in two ways -- they hired a Canadian, Sydney Newman, to run it. (One of his beneficiaries was an emerging playwright called Harold Pinter.) This

was a case of a commercial station consciously competing with the standards set by the subsidized. A public broadcaster's job, like that of any public cultural organization, is to get stuff on that wouldn't get on otherwise. And to be pleased when it gets picked up or imitated by someone else.

I don't think that this ideal relationship has been changed by the advent of the multi-channel universe, though it has been refined by it. There will always be overlap, and there should be, but the profusion of niche stations should have relieved CBC TV of any lingering obligation to be all things to all people. But it's hamstrung by commercialism, and of course by commercials. Leave aside their irritant factor, or the extent to which advertisers may influence programming. It affects tone. Listen in Toronto to CBC Radio 1, through Metro Morning, The Current, Q, As It Happens (you have to bypass The Point, which is pointless), and through all the varieties of voice you get a consistency of quality -- urbane, caustic, inquiring -- that you seldom encounter on television.

The mindset of the ads also seeps into management psychology. It means the frenetic, and foredoomed, attempt to appeal to a phantasmal "popular" audience -- and not just for the sake of ratings; I think there's an existential fear of being thought uncool. (It's also, in a clear case of cross-media contagion, draining the soul from commercial-free Radio 2, the corporation music station.) It underlies the proud purchasing of senescent American game-shows. It accounts, especially when you add in the concomitant grovelling to a generalized "youth," for George Stroumboulopoulos getting his Hour every night rather

than a more reasonable half-an-hour a week. And it may explain why, when the CBC decided for the first time in years to do Shakespeare on television, it opted for a cut-to-the-bone Othello starring an actor from Little Mosque on the Prairie with no theatrical experience, classical or otherwise. It had its merits, but in a country boasting at least three major classical companies, each filled to bursting with first-rate players who've spent their lives doing Shakespeare, it hardly seems the best way of showing off our riches to the world. Or, more importantly, to one another. Why not an ongoing scheme to preserve and adapt Canada's best theatre productions (as with the Stratford Festival's Caesar and Cleopatra, that it was left to CTV to screen), alongside the fostering of new TV plays by current writers?

I say this in hope as well as frustration, since I can't bring myself to give up on CBC's once-proud drama tradition, and because there have in fact been encouraging, if limited, signs. There was the artistic triumph of The Englishman's Boy -- though we have yet to see or hear of a comparable successor. That show was something of a throwback in being a single play (in two parts, but still). The Single Play, whose demise used to be much lamented, has effectively been replaced by something more exciting and unique to television: the long-form narrative serial as pioneered in Britain ( Pennies from Heaven, The Singing Detective) and brought to fruition on American cable. CBC had a go at this with George Walker's funny and unsettling This Is Wonderland -- even if it was axed after two seasons. Since then there's been The Border, whose American sale everybody is very jazzed about but which in fact represents a retreat to the formulaic model of a self-contained episode -- meaning essentially the same episode -- every week. There's a better form out there, one that explores and doesn't manipulate, and CBC ought to be pursuing it.

You can't will such things into being. But you can provide the soil for them, and a public broadcasting system is ideally equipped to do so. Or it should be. But it can't, if it operates as a faux-commercial network. A subscriber-supported system isn't the answer either, if PBS is any guide; it's principally a buyer of foreign goods, and it seems to equate "culture" with anything in crinolines. (And pledge-breaks are even more annoying than ads.) Cable has proved a more creative alternative, but it's fragile; HBO's golden era may already be over. Like most of our cultural institutions, CBC is undersubsidized. Like them, it shouldn't be: not just because they create jobs or attract the attention of foreigners, though they do, but because they're good things in themselves. Like them it needs to be funded to a high standard, and then held to it.

2009-03-19-tale-of-a-getaway-gal-missing:
THEATRE REVIEW

FACTORY THEATRE

---

Florence Gibson's new play Missing is based on an earlier radio play of hers that in turn took off from an actual incident: the 1988 disappearance, still unsolved, of a woman named Lois Hanna from her home in Ontario. Gibson has changed many things. The historical Lois was in her twenties and single but her theatrical equivalent, Evelyn MacMillan, is in her thirties, wife of a London-area farmer and mother of three. The time has been moved back to 1974, presumably chosen as a date when contemporary feminism was still in its birth-throes and relations between the sexes that much starker. Evelyn may have been abducted, perhaps killed; she may have chosen to leave a family setup she found insupportable. The play's emotional thrust is towards the latter conclusion; but we are never definitively told.

Alongside the aftermath on the farm and the attendant police investigation, the play explores related relationships in local locations. Carol Seaforth, the detective assigned to the case, is herself married to a schoolteacher, their still-young relationship being in a precarious place. Their most immediate disagreements concern which of them has sacrificed most and whether or not they'll have children, but these are aggravated by his jealousy over the time she's spending with the bereaved Trevor MacMillan-- who, as it happens, is at least as hostile as he is unhappy.

We also spend time in a roadside diner, presided over by Janine, a salty dispenser of eggs, fries and ancestral wisdom, whose sole prop and assistant is Freddy, an elderly man whom she habitually addresses as though he were mentally backward (which he probably is) and devoid of feelings (which he isn't). They are, though, fond of one another. Onto the premises wanders a young woman calling herself Elaine, whom Janine promptly engages as a cook. Elaine speaks vaguely of a possibly abusive boyfriend, but gives very little else away. She also keeps changing hair styles and colourings, and eventually has plastic surgery: all of which encourages the suspicion, never fully verified, that she may be the errant Evelyn.

Gibson writes exceptionally colourful dialogue, and has some piercing insights into her chosen theme of domestic entrapment (of both genders), how or whether to escape it, and at what cost But she may have set herself an insoluble problem. Asking why Evelyn left turns out to be as fruitless as asking why Godot never arrived, and without comparable compensations. If Evelyn isn't Elaine, we know nothing about her: Her nearest-if-not-

dearest give away more than they realize, but it's still second-hand. If she is Elaine, we also know nothing about her, since Elaine very much isn't telling. And detective Carol's increasing tendency to project herself onto one or both of them gets us very little further.

The actors occasionally line up as a chorus, chanting or murmuring local gossip. It's an awkward device that feels as if it were left over from the radio version (though I probably wouldn't have liked it much on radio, either). It hints, though, at a greater formality than either the play or David Ferry's strangely muffled production manages to encompass. What seems to be an abstract pattern of feelings and ideas is superimposed on a naturalistic piece of storytelling drawn, after all, from life; and the two modes defeat one another. There are gestures towards stylization in the direction. Doors open and close without anyone passing through them. (Could this be a homage to the offstage slamming door of A Doll's House, most famous of all plays about domestic departure?) Props are minimal, and one character gets handed two bottles of invisible liquid purporting to be Coca-Cola. Gillian Gallow's set is dominated by a spiral tree, the second Factory design (following on Toronto the Good) to feature an image of no practical use to the play. A fight is staged with punches visibly pulled. Probably less purposeful in its artifice is the lack of contact, erotic or otherwise, in the scenes between the cop and the farmer, who hardly seem in the same space. Carol cannot have been intended to be as cold and shallow as Fiona Highet makes her seem. As Trevor, Alan Van Sprang shouts a role that's improbably articulate to begin with, and loaded with confusing subplot, though he does come through for the play's best scene, a broadcast appeal for his wife to return "so everything will be the same" -- which of course would be the problem.

There's a pervasive belligerence about the performances: especially Emma Hillier's as the farmer's eldest daughter, another of those sullen, sulky teenagers who are becoming a stage cliche, and Shauna Black's Elaine, opaque however you take her. Kyra Harper has the warmest and wittiest writing as Janine, though she gabbles some of it, and is probably too striking and eccentric a presence to be the point of balance the play seems to require. Guy Bannerman, though, makes a pleasing Freddy -- who, in the spirit of equality, makes a brief getaway of his own--and Andrew Gillies is excellently bewildered, resentful and furious, in that order, as the teacher without a pet. - Missing runs until April 5. Call 416-504-9971 or visit factorytheatre.ca for tickets and information.

2009-03-20-the-grown-ups-won-t-even-let-:
The play Spring Awakening includes a scene at the funeral of Moritz Stiefel, a 19th-century German schoolboy driven to suicide by the demands of a merciless academic curriculum. His disappointed dad proclaims to the world that the boy "was no son of mine," though he's cheered up by a sympathetic teacher who tells him that Moritz's marks probably wouldn't have been good enough to get him into the next grade anyway.

The musical Spring Awakening finds all this heartlessness a bit much to take, and substitutes a father who sobs silently while Melchior Gabor, best friend of the deceased and the show's true hero, sings one of the evening's frequent laments.

Frank Wedekind, the lifelong enfant terrible who wrote the original play in 1891, may have gone a bit far in this scene; even Teutonic parents disappointed by their children's exam results probably weren't that Hunnish. The adult characters in this, his first play, are mainly caricatures. But they're clean-lined efficient caricatures of a powerful social structure that it took some courage to attack.

The musical, more than a hundred years on, is aiming at safe targets, which it's as likely to exaggerate as to soften. The teachers here are not just blinkered and dogmatic, but actively vindictive. A girl in the play tells her friends that her father beats her; in the musical he also subjects her to full-scale sexual abuse, with a song attached. Maybe the authors think that Wedekind meant this but didn't dare say it, though given his explicitness on the subjects of masturbation, teenage homosexuality, pregnancy and abortion, that seems unlikely. Anyway the show appears torn between sensationalism and sentimentality. It's a very confused piece.

Some of the confusion lies in the rock score, which is as anachronistic in its words as its music. Some of the time, the kids in the story seem to be singing about their own desires and frustrations (as in West Side Story, only young people are allowed to sing; unlike in West Side Story, no other topics are allowed); other times, it feels as if the performers are grabbing their mics to offer their own gloss on how they would have reacted in comparable circumstances. The prevailing tone is, "dudes, you wouldn't believe this repression," and no, we don't, not when the lyrics are going on about cellphones and stereos. The show is taking a ride on past pain, and making a factitious parallel between youthful agonies then and now. Yes, adolescence is always a time for feeling misunderstood, but contemporary middle-class kids aren't being victimized like those in the play.

Young Melchior, a freethinking prodigy who's the idol of all the girls and probably great at games as well, blunders into sex with innocent Wendla Bergmann and gets her pregnant. Wendla's mother, whose blushes are here played for cheap laughs, has been too shy to tell her daughter the biological facts. But, on the show's own showing, if she hadn't got them from her mother, she'd have got them from her girlfriends, two of whom had already learned the hardest way. The show, mindful of what becomes a musical, can't resist going all lyrical over the union of Melchior and Wendla, though it's a fumbling, violent thing in the original (and here, until the music starts). The tag line in the ads is "you never forget your first time." Given that the first time in this case leads to death from a botched abortion, the sentiment seems dubious. It's the kind of slogan Max Bialystock might have dreamed up if he'd opted for Spring Awakening instead of Springtime for Hitler.

The cast is loyalty personified. Matt Doyle renders Melchior as a strong full-throated all-American boy, which seems to be what's required; Blake Bashoff is sad-funny as Moritz, who finds his sexual urges even harder to cope with than Latin and math, and also labours under a hair-style apparently modelled on Shockheaded Peter; Christy Altomare is a sweet Wendla, though one who looks better able to take care of herself than her story requires. As for the score:Duncan Sheik's music peaks very early with the poignant opener Mama Who Bore Me, though as a song for the girls when the show is more about the boys, it sends false signals. There are a couple more nice ballads and a lot of musical rough-housing, some of it effective.

Steven Sater's lyrics (he also wrote the book, which is best when closest to the play) at one point find a neat rhyme for "self-destruct" -- sorry about this being a family newspaper -- but are otherwise sloppy on craft and low on content, either narrative or psychological. The songs are interchangeable between characters: Listen to the CD if you don't believe me, and try and work out who's singing.

To paraphrase what I wrote of the New York production: The trouble with the old rock musicals was that you couldn't hear the words; the trouble with the new ones is that you can. - Spring Awakening runs until April 19 at the Canon Theatre. Call 416-872-1212 or visit mirvish.com for details.

2009-03-21-economy-of-humour-the-recessi:
In dishonour of the economic situation, the new revue at Second City has christened itself 0% Down, 100% Screwed, a title that for once takes topicality above the level of the vaguely relevant pun (cf. Barack to the Future, Tazed and Confused and almost any others you may or may not care to remember). Not only that, but the show keeps its announced theme going right through the first number and even into the second. After that, it pretty much drops the idea, but then we wouldn't want things to get monotonous, would we?

About that opening number. It presents five of the cast of the six, lined up across the front of the stage as a pick-swinging chain gang of, to generalize a little, ex-yuppies. Lamenting their various falls from financial grace, they each conclude by intoning the same universal sentiment: "Blame it on the Crisis." Above and on guard stands the remaining performer, who tells us with great deflationary flair that being as he has a cushy job in government, he isnt really affected. Now, this might be satire of the crisis, or it might be satire of satire of the crisis, but either way its an appealing beginning, not least for the way it shows off a very strong team.

The strongest of all is Darryl Hinds, who is impish and unquenchable and seems, this time around, rather underused, possibly because he's so good that he's always going to seem underused. The second number is really his, as a Toronto taxi-jockey whose current passenger would be a prime candidate for that chain gang. As he moans about the problems in his life, our driver counters with his own, which are extreme as hes an immigrant from Gaza, but which he is chivalrously inclined to play down, which of course makes them sound all the more insupportable and his passenger all the more insufferable, because plainly nobody knows the troubles this cabbies seen because nobody wants to know, and I don't think I can type another comma. The sketch goes on too long, like that sentence, but it makes its point, and Hinds couldn't be more whimsically devastating. And thats about it for the economic situation. The show has other fish to grill.

Visually, it may be the most stylish of all Second City shows. The director is Melody Johnson, a performing alumna of the troupe and one of its most distinctive comic actresses. She has infused the production with her own quirky physicality, both between numbers (the transitions are exceptionally smart) and within them. Camellia Koo, similarly distinguished, designs. The evenings highlight is a sketch depicting a children's puppet show at a public library. Now this might be accused of topical relevance, as we're told that budget-cuts may make this troupes version of Little Red Riding Hood into The Last Puppet Show, but the real drama lies in the relationship-spat between puppeteers, and the effect their jealousies and recriminations have on the life-size creatures at the end of their strings who are left to dangle, languish and collide. The marionettes are played by actual actors, and the detail, precision and wit with which its all been worked out are extraordinary.

In a slightly related vein I also liked, though not quite as much, the chubby Marty Adams' turn as a Marco Polo incensed at having been turned into a kids' game. Reid Janisse is aptly manic as a diabolical emissary from American TV faced with the apparently hopeless task of getting Canadian politicians to be rude to one another on camera. (I dont think it is all that impossible but never mind.) Leslie Seiler features as a floating psychic -- she does seem to float -- whose easy deductions about members of the audience inspire her two male acolytes to delirious flights of professional sycophancy. Numbers like this, which have to be at least partially improvised, seem to get the best out of Second Citizens these days; while the proper improvs that follow the main show (and are free if you come in late) were, on the night I went, extremely good. They seemed, bizarrely, to have better punchlines than the written stuff. Caitlin Howden functions as gamine second woman and Kerry Griffin as more or less permanent straight man. Hinds later assumptions include a dainty Barack Obama, paying a state visit to Ottawa, with Seiler in tow as a very fierce Hillary; keeping a few intellectual feet above the ground, this president projects an appropriate air of glazed bemusement, as if uncertain whether it's he or the Harpers who have dropped in from outer space.

I had few belly laughs from this evening, but much pleasure. It isn't among Second City's very best shows, but they are few and far between. It is, however, among their second very best.

- 0% Down, 100% Screwed runs indefinitely at Second City. Call 416-343-0011 for details.
2009-03-24-bound-to-earth-but-still-flap:
You've heard of milestone productions. And Up They Flew is a two-milestone production. It's the 25th anniversary show for Theatre Columbus, the Toronto company that combines a physical aesthetic with a literary bent. And it's the last play to be presented under the joint artistic leadership of the company's founders, Leah Cherniak and Martha Ross, who function on this show as director and author respectively.

They're going out on a high note of style and a low one of substance. To take the best first: And Up They Flew has a cast of seven actors who by the end of the evening stand revealed as a comic ensemble of intoxicating skill and cohesion. They also fall revealed, since the play, which is in part a bedroom farce that never gets to the bedroom, requires them to bump repeatedly into swinging doors, recalcitrant furnishings and -- especially -- one another. There are possibly more collisions here per minute than I have ever seen on a stage. To begin with, it just seems untidy but as it goes on it becomes its own medium (which reminds me, the plot includes a seance) and, indeed, message. The cast become so intoxicated by it that at one point they take off into a dance number, as if the characters' desperation has become the actors' joie de vivre. It's infectious.

Impressive though it is, it isn't all that funny. But then clown shows seldom are, certainly not when they go on for two-and-a-half-hours, and Theatre Columbus has its roots in clowning. Slapstick for its own sake rather quickly outstays its welcome; if we're to keep laughing we have to know just why the characters are behaving like accident-prone automata and, even more important, to care. And this is where And Up They Flew falls to Earth. It's billed as "Gosford Park Meets the Marx Brothers," which is both presumptuous and inaccurate. The show does include a human-mirror sequence like the one in Duck Soup but, good as they are, no one onstage amounts to one-third of a comic genius (i. e. a Marx brother). And any resemblance to Gosford Park is confined to setting the play in

a 1930s English drawing room and throwing in references to the class-system, at least insofar as one character is a servant while the others are all masters and mistresses.

It's also subtitled "a comedy about the 20th century," and it is, quite self-consciously, one of those plays set between the world wars in which people keep harking back to the carnage behind them and, if the author is feeling prophetic or is the beneficiary of hindsight, forward to what worse may come. There are many such plays in existence, some of them with the added attraction of having been written at the time; the Shaw Festival keeps reviving them. This new one has nothing to add beyond the stubbornly unhelpful conceit embodied in its title. Jane Ashbury wants to be the first woman to fly the Atlantic in the opposite direction to Amelia Earhart; in the meantime she and her husband are hosting a house-party. Jane enlists the help of her childhood friend Nora Duckworth whom she hires as a maid, keeping their old acquaintance secret so that her husband will not know of her own lowly origins. (He's big in toilet goods, and self-conscious about it). Another married couple is present, plus a bachelor with a Casanova complex and somebody's elderly aunt. There is a lot of lusting after others' partners, but though they go through the motions of not wanting to be found out, none of them seems really to mind very much. They also go through the motions of being worried over Jane's aviatrix ambitions, but again without much conviction. Her desire to fly away and rise above it all seems equally thin and whimsical. These people barely exist, so the farce doesn't function. Neither do the ideas. That British drawing-room society of the '30s was shallow and headed for a rude awakening has been said before, usually by the British. Why say it again, now, in Canada?

In fact, there is some Canadian content here. John Jarvis plays, deliriously well, a fellow who goes humorously mad and starts speaking with a Canadian accent. I'm not suggesting these conditions are coequal; his character is a traumatised war vet who starts channelling a slain Newfie comrade. He even talks of moving to Canada, though neither he nor the play gets far in this direction. He also has apocalyptic visions in which he foresees the atomic bomb, the oil race and Monty Python. Others delightful are Paul Braunstein as a dogged but not quite dashing seducer, and as the oracular aunt, the still-youngish Michelle Fisk taking subtle advantage of age's privilege to stay comparatively still and quiet. Julie Stewart puts on a bold comic face as a semi-willing adulteress (the spirit is willing, etc.) and John Cleland blusters effectively as the bathroom magnate. Of the two putative heroines, Lisa Norton has an intriguingly baleful air as Martha the reluctant, not to say incompetent, maid; Kerry Ann Doherty smiles prettily as Jane, but the character's a hole in the play. As a text, And Up They Flew is earthbound, but the production flaps wings. - And Up They Flew runs until April 4 at the Berkeley Street Theatre Upstairs. For tickets, call 416-368-3110 or visit theatrecolumbus.ca.

2009-03-27-it-s-always-sunny-in-rural-bo:
The first image on the opening credits of The No. 1 Ladies Detective Agency is of a brown finger pointing to a spot on a map of Africa. Up pops a title to tell us that it's Botswana, which is where our scene is set. This is informative, and also cute.

The same might be said of the pilot episode for this new series, based on a popular set of novels by Alexander McCall Smith. Darker themes occasionally peep through, but as detection series go, this one is as sunny as the climate. It's a co-production of HBO, the BBC and the Weinsteins of Miramax: I'm not sure what the last part of that partnership might be expected to bring to the table, but for the rest this is far more sly and cozy mainstream-British than tough and gritty cable-American. This first instalment has the special cachet of being cowritten and directed by the late Anthony Minghella and produced by the late Sydney Pollack, both of whom died before the rest of the season went into production; and it shows them both in uncommonly relaxed mood.

It revolves around Precious Ramotswe, a charming and ample lady from the bush, played winningly and amusingly if without great emotional variation by Jill Scott, best known as a singer-songwriter. Precious's beloved father died, leaving her his van and 180 cows; these turn out to be cash-cows, since she sells them and drives off to town (Gabarone) in the van to start a new life and a new business. The van breaks down en route, but is salvaged by a widowed auto mechanic (Lucian Msamati, who is brilliant) who becomes Precious's precious friend and, at last sighting, the nearest thing to a love-interest -- best to call it, for the moment, a like-interest. Precious also has a married past; she is divorced from a man who beat her, so savagely that her only child miscarried. This man, and his

shady lawyer, now want some part of her fortune; encountering them at her father's funeral, she remarks that it's the first funeral at which she's seen him since her baby's. This is one of those acrid moments that the show doesn't develop, at least not this week, but that lingers in the mind.

Precious sets up shop, on the irresistibly named Zebra Drive, as Botswana's Best (and, as she freely admits, only) Lady Detective. ("The bad men," says her car-fixing guy, already smitten, "had better watch out.") At first, business is slow to develop, as is mercilessly noted by Precious's sole employee Grace, a secretary just out of college with near-perfect scores and a very brisk and bespectacled manner. She's played by Anika Noni Rose (Dreamgirls), whose fast, clipped voice, superlative comic timing and general air of loyal disenchantment are irresistible; she raises the show's level from pleasant diversion to essential entertainment. She's a joy, whether comparing her own employability to that of less qualified but more pliable ladies ("nine times out of 10, short skirt gets the job") or opening a file in which the agency can record, as she punctiliously puts it, "every 'unch and every 'int." (Office equipment consists of two typewriters, each with missing keys; neither boasts a functioning "h.")

Grace also tangles with the male proprietor of next door's Last Chance Hairdressing Salon, who tells her "your hair and my scissors should spend some quality time together." "That man," says Grace severely, "is very much like a woman." Try getting away with that line in a European setting. Minghella's coauthor is Richard Curtis, of Blackadder and other things, and I suspect him of some of Grace's material. She may well, if 24 doesn't buck its ideas up a bit, displace Chloe O'Brian in my affections.

Business improves, and by the end of this double-length episode the firm has taken on, and solved, five whole cases. Precious's success-rate is attributed to her traditional "woman's intuition" which translates as an ability to make connections: to take a chance remark from one context and apply it constructively to another. She is as often asked to investigate misdemeanours as crimes. In time-honoured private-eye fashion, she's engaged by a woman digging for dirt on her husband, a scene that occasions a delectable triple-play between Scott, Rose, and Nikki Amukia Bird as the bristling wife, wanting to know "is my husband a philanderer of the first water?" ("Adulterer," snaps Grace unforgivingly from the outer office. It's the rule on this show that all men are guilty until proved innocent.) Cracking this one leads Precious into an ill-advised attempt to play Miss Marple and Mata Hari simultaneously, a process that leads to a highly foreseeable but still enjoyable reversal. At the other extreme of seriousness we have a child-abduction ring, involving an updated witch-doctor operation. Presiding over it is Idris Elba, Stringer Bell from The Wire, playing a totally different but equally chilling super-thug, and managing the African voice as persuasively as he did the American. (His native tongue is cockney, or what's now called estuary English.) This could be disturbing stuff but it's kept at a distance, just as the abuse in Precious' life is kept in the past. So far, this is a law-and-order series in which the good is always victorious; which makes it, certainly by HBO standards, rather tame. It also reverts to the old-fashioned formula of a different story, or stories, every week. Botswana has a happier history than most African countries, but life there can't really be that neat. It isn't that neat anywhere. - The No. 1 Ladies Detective Agency premiers this Sunday at 9 p. m. on HBO Canada.

2009-03-28-at-times-even-aquafit-can-cre:
Most of Another Home Invasion consists of Nicola Lipman sitting in a chair and addressing the audience. That's a lot more compelling than you might think.

The play was written by Joan Macleod, who seems to do her best work in monologues. She wrote The Shape of a Girl, a fine portrait of a teenager that was partly a response to the murder of Reena Virk. This play, which may be even better, takes us to the opposite demographic extreme. Lipman plays Jean, a woman of about 80 who is now the caregiver for her husband, Alec, who recently suffered a stroke. They live in the same house in their beloved North Vancouver that they've occupied for upwards of 50 years, but they are now awaiting relocation to another kind of home. The place they have set their hearts on is the nearby Kiwanis facility, which has one floor that takes couples. What fuels the play, giving it both passion and suspense, is Jean's and the audience's growing fear that this will not be allowed to happen.

Author and actress may do even better at summoning up unseen characters than Kristen Thomson in I Claudia. Actually, this play has a Claudia of its own, a lady from social services who monitors the couple's state of co-existence and (unequal) co-dependence. Claudia is fussy and bossy, but she has her uses; she persuades Jean to enrol in Aquafit classes, something that Jean at first resists and then embraces as the highlight of her existence. She won't hear of missing one, sometimes to the chagrin of her daughter, Bethie, who has to come over and hold the fort at home in her absence, and who operates according to a whole different body clock. (Jean's idea of a civilized dinnertime is something like 5:30 p. m.; Bethie likes to treat dinner as more of a midnight snack). Alec is vividly depicted as a man who once had the fortitude to conquer alcoholism, but is now in a condition that he cannot overcome. Jean has sons living in Toronto and Calgary, but her accessible family is completed by Bethie's teenage daughter, Amber, who comes over to do the vacuuming; for this Amber gets minimum wage and does, as Jean tartly remarks, minimum work. She apparently concentrates on upstairs, an area which, as Jean also tells us, nobody uses anymore.

One day, a man arrives on the doorstep, makes aimless conversation and, at one point, grabs Jean's arm when she seems in danger of falling. He seems, to Jean anyway, to be harmless if mysterious, but he's a crystal-meth addict and his visit has repercussions. He seems to be somewhat shoehorned into the play, but has the effect of speeding up what already seems an inexorable slide toward disaster. Alec's deteriorating condition is already putting the couple's planned future in jeopardy; now, an unexpected rally of strength hastens the process. Jean's home, and her hopes, are being invaded from all sides: by the system, by an intruder, by mortality. She rages, but she doesn't whine.

The play's great quality is its mixture of strength and gentleness. Jean describes her daily rounds, and her larger issues, economically, unsparingly and with an overridingly tart humour. These qualities are brilliantly reflected in Lipman's performance: mainly sedentary, like the life it's depicting, and so taking on extraordinary force on the occasions when she forces herself out of her chair. She can have a mean mouth: almost literally, given the firm, sardonic set of this actress's jaw. She only relaxes it at the end of the play, and the effect is like a burst of sunlight. On the most immediate level, the play's ending is a grim act of acceptance. But there is something about this character and this performance that dismisses defeat. Her horizons are limited, her battles are all personal, but she can still reflect on the deafening noise that might be made if all the women in her situation were to raise their voices in unison. This is as close as the play gets to the explicit raising of issues, and it justifies itself on every level. Richard Rose's direction coaxes the writing and the performance sympathetically along. For staging, he gives us the solitary figure surrounded by presumably symbolic autumn leaves.

The song Autumn Leaves actually plays on the soundtrack that precedes and follows the performance, along with such other relevant tunes as I'll See You in My Dreams and, most poignantly jaunty at the end, We Just Couldn't Say Goodbye. Maybe these were just chosen at random as old music to suit old people. But that would be quite a coincidence. - Another Home Invasion runs through April 19 at the Tarragon Theatre. For more information, call 416-531-1827.

2009-04-01-in-defence-of-livent:
For 18 months -- the last 18 months, really, of the company's active existence -- I was an employee of Livent Inc. (I came direct from there to the National Post, which may make me the only person to have worked consecutively for Garth Drabinsky and Conrad Black.) My official title at the Toronto-based theater production company was Director of Corporate Communications, which could have meant anything but eventually resolved itself into a cross between a speechwriter and a dramaturg. My time there lasted beyond the suspension of Drabinsky and Myron Gottlieb, but it was Garth who recruited me and it was largely him to whom I reported. And whatever others experiences may have been, I have to say that mine was positive.

I felt valued and appreciated; I worked alongside a phenomenal number of able --and likeable--people; and I believed, and still believe, that the company I worked for was producing good shows.

Its true, I realized early on, that you couldn't have a conversation with Garth that wasn't in some way a conversation about Garth. But once that was accepted, ideas were always welcome. I dont even recall being shouted at. The director of one Livent show, an American, told me that hed come to Toronto with some trepidation, having heard all the stories, but in fact found that he was being treated with nothing but courtesy and encouragement. He was still, he said, waiting for the other shoe to drop. I doubt that it ever did. People considered to be artists and/or intellectuals got considerate treatment.

In the wake of last week's trial verdicts, some pundits have taken to disparaging Livent-- not just in regard to the company's business practices, but its production of large-scale Broadway-style musicals. Starting with its mounting of The Phantom of the Opera from a [London/New York] template, said Rick Salutin in The Globe & Mail last week, Livent promoted theatre that wasnt "live in any meaningful way."

There is a fragment of a point here, but only a fragment.

Id date the international franchising of musicals to 1947, which is when Richard Rodgers and Oscar Hammerstein's Oklahoma! opened in London -- at the Theatre Royal, Drury Lane -- in a replica of its Broadway staging. As one historian has noted, R&H didn't just mail it over; they supervised it in person and insisted that it be done right. The show was enormously successful, and was followed over the next two decades by authentic remounts of other shows from the American musicals unfolding golden age. The best of them were, by general consent, among the most exciting theatre to be seen in London.

It would have been terrible if that had been all there was to the British theatre. But it wasnt. The same period saw the establishment of two major subsidized companies, the National Theatre and the Royal Shakespeare, and the

advent of unstoppable generations of new playwrights. And the same goes for the -- admittedly less distinguished --musicals that have been imported to Toronto, and everywhere else in the world, over the last 25 years: They haven't stopped anything else from happening, either new plays or new companies.

I know people talk as if the success of the megashows drained off attendance from smaller-scale homegrown Canadian productions, but I don't believe it. There isnt much overlap between the audiences in the first place, but those who are interested in both would find their way to both. In Toronto, Phantom ran at the Pantages for 10 years, so one visit would leave plenty of time over for catching other shows.

Personally,Id hate to see Phantom in anything but the original Hal Prince production. But I did want to see it, and all the other international hits before and since, if only to find out what all the fuss was about: a natural human impulse, I think, and not to be despised.

However, Phantom was only the starting point for Livent. Most of its subsequent energies went into the productions of brand-new shows, plus one major revival. These productions -- Kiss of the Spider Woman, Show Boat, Ragtime, Parade -- constitute a track record unmatched by any commercial producer, anywhere, in decades. (Fosse, the remaining show, wasn't in the same league.) Kiss, Ragtime and Parade reached a level of musical expressiveness and dramatic intelligence that leaves later lauded shows such as Wicked or Spring Awakening looking half-starved.

What of the criticism that these were all shows written and staged by Americans, on American subjects and with largely American casts, and all ultimately aimed at New York? Undeniably, Livent in general, and Drabinsky in particular, were dazzled by Broadway and wanted to be part of it. But that doesn't mean Canadian audiences couldnt identify with the shows and their characters. I might also point out that both Brent Carver in Kiss of the Spider Woman and Steven Sutcliffe in Ragtime are Canadian actors, and pillars of the community at that, but it would be disingenous. I too would like to have seen more Canadian actors, and some shows written by Canadians; some of the latter were in development when the company imploded, but I cant say how far they would have been developed.

But where, I wonder, would cultural nationalists draw the line? Would they disapprove of the foreign companies brought over by festivals like WorldStage and Luminato? How about the Stratford and Shaw festivals, where the actors are overwhelmingly Canadian but the basic repertoire is old European?

"Vertical integration" -- owning or building a chain of theatres and filling them with your own product, which was Livent's plan -- depends on generating a guaranteed stream of hits. This may have been possible for the Hollywood studios whose heyday was Livent's professed inspiration, but no theatre company can do it. This doesnt mean, however, that Livents actual shows were soulless or mechanized or developed according to the whims of focus groups. Yes, opinions were solicited (mine among them, if you must know), but then, to quote my favourite line from Gypsy, this is show business; everybody listens to everybody. The Livent process was not essentially different from the workshop method routinely practised by non-commercial theatres. It doesn't produce fail-safe results for them either.

Behind the criticism of Livent, I sense the familiar phrase "telling ourselves our own stories." The implication is that in Canada those stories should always be Canadian. But a story belongs to whoever wants to tell it and whoever cares to listen. Livent's stories, none of them safe or obvious choices for musicals, carried that conviction. The name meant something: Toronto theatre was livelier with Livent than without it.

THEATRE REVIEW

SHIRLEY VALENTINE

Bluma Appel Theatre, Toronto

---

Nicola Cavendish, playing the one and only role in Shirley Valentine, brings down the house with her description of marriage: "It's like the Middle East, isn't it? There's no solution." It's a neatly turned wisecrack, delivered with a winning mix of diffidence and confidence, as if the speaker were dubious about posing the question, but quite sure of the answer. I laughed as loudly as anyone else. But it was also the moment at which I stopped believing.

Like Hedda Gabler, with whom she doesn't have too much else in common, Shirley comes before us under her maiden name as a sign that she's locked in a stultifying marriage that has stifled the real her. She's 46 years old and living in Liverpool; she and her husband, after a long marriage with a grown-up son and daughter to show for it, have long since stopped communicating with one another. So Shirley talks to the wall (literally), letting off observations like the one quoted above. And though I've great respect for the wit and wisdom of Liverpudlian housewives, I doubt if they talk quite so much like late-night talk-show hosts. It's being done, far too obviously, for our benefit.

Willy Russell, another Liverpudlian, wrote the play just over 20 years ago. It first arrived in Canada in 1989, in a Vancouver productionfeaturingCavendish, who has been doing it on and off ever since, always under the direction of Roy Surette. Its current appearance at the Bluma marks her farewell to the role. (It's also a farewell for Martin Bragg, CanStage's outgoing artistic producer.)We see Shirley in two locations and at two stages of reawakening. In Act One, she's in her kitchen, preparing a dinner of "chips and egg" for her old man, who will undoubtedly be displeased since this is the day of the week when he eats mince meat. (Shirley's timing is impressive here, too. The eggs are done at precisely the moment her husband's shadow appears outside the door.)

Her friend Jane wants Shirley to accompany her on a two-week trip to Greece. She wants to go, but is sure she can't. But a final burst of spousal insensitivity tips the scales, and Act Two finds her on the beach at Corfu, counting an impressive array of blessings. She's briefly found love, or at least a man who knows his way around her body. More lastingly, she's found herself. Shirley Valentine has been reborn and she doesn't intend -- spiritually or geographically -- to go back.

Act One has her reflecting on her past and present lives. It is not without whimsy: Shirley's repeated "hey, wall" drove me up it. It's also an evasion; the play would have more credibility if she talked, honestly and consistently, to herself or to us. (She starts Act Two by addressing her confidences to a rock, but she doesn't keep it up.) Some of what she says is very funny indeed. What slew me the most were her reminiscences of her son's appearance as Joseph in the school nativity plays, greeting the news of no room at the inn with an indignant "but we booked!" (No mystery where that talent came from.) Some is authentically, enragingly sad, as when Shirley recalls a school principal who stigmatized her as stupid and ignorant, and refused to be convinced otherwise. And much seems like padding. Shirley tells us of a recent re-encounter with a once-posh former schoolmate who's now an expensive hooker. As she's Shirley's contemporary, she must really have husbanded her resources. (Or resourced her husbands. Or other people's.) It feels implausibly coincidental. And though I suppose you can connect it to the theme of realizing your destiny, it also feels irrelevant.

Because, however much she tells us about herself, we never know Shirley as a real person. The play's method is to tickle us, and then say "but seriously, folks." Cavendish, gorgeous though she is (and wonderful at an array of accents), is complicit in this. She just about rubs our noses in Shirley's sensuality and in her naivete. She gets so cozy with the audience and gets so many easy laughs -- they may be technically hard, but they're intellectually and emotionally easy -- that she loses any overall sense of loneliness and vulnerability. So in the second half of the play, she has to practically start over, and with material that's less grounded; she does her damnedest to move us, but she succeeds as an actress rather than a character. By accident or cunning, Russell has kept Shirley vague; he gives us a vessel into whom we can all pour our fears of having wasted our lives and our knowledge that the worst thing of all is regret, and then he throws us a redemption. And there are no ambiguities, no sense that freedom may come at a price. Shirley pays lip service to the idea that her husband may be as much a victim as she is, but we'd have to meet him to have an opinion about that. Compare that with the uncomfortable realities of the woman currently played by Nicola Lipman in Another Home Invasion. (That makes two one-woman plays in Toronto, performed by virtuoso actresses with the same first name. And they say Canadian theatre doesn't have trends.)

Of the two, Shirley Valentine is certainly more of a fun trip. Cavendish is irresistible. So is the whole package. But that isn't always a good thing. - Shirley Valentine is at the Bluma Appel Theatre until April 18. Call 416-368-3110 or visit canstage.com for tickets and information.

2009-04-03-singer-on-songwriters-elvis-c:
For a wonder, Spectacle is a show that lives up to its hype. Its full title is Spectacle: Elvis Costello With ..., which sounds both cumbersome and inconclusive, but is at least accurate. The idea is that Costello, the singer-songwriter who gives eclecticism a good name, plays host to a favoured musician or group of musicians. They talk about music, they perform it separately or together. And that's all. The season kicks off with a one-on-one: Costello sits down with Elton John. Next week finds him chatting up the three members of The Police, at the end of their reunion tour (the one that might have been called "the hello again and goodbye forever show). The week after that theres a guitar pull" -- which, as I understand it, differs from a jam session in being sequential rather than collective -- whose participants include Kris Kristofferson, Roseanne Cash and Norah Jones. Future guests range from Lou Reed to classical diva and sometime crosser-over Renee Fleming, via Tony Bennett. Oh yes, and Bill Clinton.

Rufus Wainwright and Mrs. Costello (Diana Krall) will represent Canada, and theres an admiring reference to Ron Sexsmith. We do seem numerically underrepresented (wouldn't Joni Mitchell be a natural? or k. d. lang?), especially as this is a British-Canadian co-production. It's already been shown in the United States, go figure, and it was actually shot in the U. S., at the Apollo Theater in Harlem, than which you could hardly get more legendary, though frankly from all we can see it could be any place with a stage and an audience. Still, its hard to imagine the U. S. coming up with such a project: The nearest equivalent I can think of is Inside the Actors Studio, but there the interviewer is the outsider-as-sycophant. The corresponding danger, when you have peer talking to peers, is that mutual admiration will descend into mutual back-scratching. But, on the evidence of the first two shows, the people concerned are too smart and too funny for that to happen. Costello and John have too much else to talk about, largely their enthusiasm for other performers, while the three Police-men have sharp-tongued reputations to protect.

Each show begins with Costello singing a number associated with his guest or guests. He then slips into host mode, a role to which he brings an unassuming eager-beaverness. As an

interviewer hes unashamedly raw; many TV inquisitors carry clipboards, but it's rare to see one consult his notes as frequently and openly as Costello does. His trademark unshavenness, too, makes him an unlikely prospect to succeed David Letterman or Jay Leno or even Jon Stewart. But he's a natural comic and, most importantly, hes informed and hes enthusiastic. He takes it for granted that his audience will also have those qualities, if not to his degree, and he builds on that.

The first Spectacle might easily have been re-titled in the plural: two pairs of spectacles, in fact, since his glasses and John's -- plain horn-rims against gaudy --make an engaging visual statement in themselves. Another is the way in which the blue-draped set matches the colour of John's shirt.

They talk about perceptions of success and failure. John shares his shock at having, in the first flush of his own success, driven to collect Martha and the Vandellas at a London airport and discovered that these Motown idols "had had to borrow money to get their clothes from the cleaners in order to make the tour at all. They share admiration for the hugely influential Laura Nyro, who may have been ahead of her time by seeming to be behind it; and for David Ackles who ended up as a teacher and who wrote splendid songs, one of which (Down River) they duet as a storming finale. Having decided long ago that Im not an Elton John fan (and his recent theatre scores did nothing to change my mind) I was ignorantly unprepared for the earthiness of his vocals here, or indeed for the information that Leon Russell is Johns biggest idol -- he told me of a great throat remedy."

The Police procedural sensibly brings the trio on separately, for indivdual interviews, before throwing them together for the conversational equivalent of a jam. (This also of course mimics their collective trajectory: dispersal and reunion.) Andy Summers talks about learning new harmonic possibilities on guitar from listening to Jimi Hendrix, and having to un-learn them when playing with punk groups ("you didn't have to be able to play at all). Stewart Copeland defines the split personality of his later career: I'm the composer guy, whos very sophisticated, and the drummer who aint." Sting, announced as "all-round good egg tells us that the bass is a great place to control the band from" and crosstalks with Costello on their songwriter-rivalry. (Costello, placatingly: "You thrive on a degree of competition. Sting, unhesitatingly: Yes, but I'm right.")

Spectacle isn't as pure and unflashy as all that. Its obviously heavily edited, and it breaks things up with irritating cuts to a visual checkerboard motif, backed up by computerised music, apparently designed to favour no known school of composition. It also keeps alluding to exciting performance-clips that then fail to appear. (Both these distractions are especially evident in the John show.)

The great thing, though, is that Costello never stops a conversation because it seems to be getting too serious. Its notable that all the participants in these first two shows are British, immersed in what is after all an American musical culture but still outside of it, and with an amused, articulate perspective. Also that they were part of the second invasion -- the post Beatles-and-Stones wave -- that could accommodate the pre-rock tradition rather than oppose it. From this perspective, Costello's marriage to Krall looks like the symbolic convergence of two musical cultures, with the added reconciling twist that it's the younger singer who does the older music. He duets with Summers on a tune by Charles Mingus (who, he says, "speaks more than other jazz writers to people from rock and roll). He celebrates the 1968-71 heyday of the singer-songwriter (incredibly rich") while lamenting the demise of the songwriter per se: a profession in which he himself could certainly have prospered even if hed never sung a note. He also says that "the quality of the music in the 60s and '70s is much better than what it is today;" he's probably right but, as the son of a British dance-band singer, hes better placed than most to realize that thats every generation's complaint. I look forward to seeing what he'll get out of Tony Bennett, whos been saying the same things in interviews for years, maybe because hes always asked the same questions. Will Costello kick that show off by singing I Left My Heart in San Francisco? And what will be President Clinton's theme song? - Spectacle premieres tonight at 9 p. m. on CTV.

Black & White Photo: Ctv / Spectacle host Elvis Costello and Elton John, two musicians from Britain's second invasion, meet on cable television. ;; Caption:
2009-04-04-it-s-the-end-of-the-world-as-:
Idon't know why One Wooden Shoe, a theatre company new to me, is called One Wooden Shoe, but its members seem to me a nice bunch of people with, collectively, an inquiring mind and a talent to amuse. That, anyway, is the impression left by their show Dedicated to the Revolutions, whose title is likewise something of a curveball. The revolutions it's dedicated to, six of them, arent of the barricaded variety. They are, in one way or another, scientific. The performers list them for us, vocally and by writing them on a chart: the Gutenberg, the Copernican, the Newtonian, the Industrial, the Darwinian, the Nuclear and the Information.

The Newtonian gets star billing. When we enter the theatre, five of the cast are playing a game involving the piling of toy bricks one on top of another until the tabletop tower theyve erected topples over, enabling its constituent parts to demonstrate their obedience to the law of gravity. The players stand around the table taking or awaiting their turn and behaving with the kind of studied casualness that people, especially when they're professional performers, always exhibit when trying to act as if they don't know people are looking at them. Now seems as good a time as any to introduce them. They are Frank Cox OConnell, Chad Dembski, Aimee Dawn Robinson, Erin Shields and Jacob Zimmer, who nicely rounds off the alphabetical list by being the prime mover of both the company and the show. He looks and behaves like an amiable don. OConnell, who has the most active stage presence, is more your livewire high school teacher. Robinson, who has a different but equal kind of authority, emerges as a compelling lecturer and natural mistress of ceremonies. Shields, also known as an accomplished playwright (her If We Were Birds was the hit of last year's Summerworks and is scheduled for next year at Tarragon) comes on here like an untidy but gifted student. Dembski is an imp.

Evan Webber, the young actor left over, is at the side of the stage performing his own experiment. He's testing the efficacy of Mr. Gutenbergs invention by writing out the Bible by hand while a printer (in the cause of a level playing field theyve chosen a model created in the same year that Webber himself was) does its own thing with the same material. They both plunge synchronously into Genesis, the mechanical scribe getting as far as the story of Lot (spicy stuff for a machine) while the human one has barely progressed beyond "in the beginning." In fairness, he has taken time off to include a drawing, though it doesn't seem to compare with the figures in a monk's illuminated manu-script. Game, set and match to Gutenberg, Id say. And Newton hasnt done too badly either.

Dedicated to the Revolutions is the kind of show after which people put the fear of God into me by saying, I can't wait to see what you're going to say about this one, to which I generally reply, "Neither can I." That doesnt mean its a bad show, rather that it isn't amenable to the orthodox rules. It certainly isn't a play, or even a revue; its more of a lecture-investigation with theatrical and musical illustrations. The performers dont have to act (which doesn't mean they can't) but they do have to command our attention. This they accomplish; theyre actually rather heavy on the charm. (They admit, freely and repeatedly, that theyre no more scientists than we are, though they've probably done more research more recently.) In terms of theatrical invention the production reaches its peak early in a sequence on distribution networks, which involves the depiction of different methods of interpersonal communication -- one to one, one to two, one to many -- through an assortment of tin cans and cables. They're at their foggiest when they get to Darwin, and try to distinguish between evolution and natural selection. The end of the world is also prophesied, though its comfortingly consigned to billions of generations in the future: How many billions is illustrated by having Shields engaged, like T. S. Eliots Macavity, in "complicated long-division sums."

At two points in the evening, the audience is allowed to participate -- though we to choose from a list of pre-selected questions to which the cast presumably have pre-rehearsed answers. (This doesn't stop them from going into huddles before replying.) Everyone's favourite, perhaps because it looks so funny just on paper, is: Be-fore Newton, how did things fall? The answer of course is, exactly the same way as they have since, but elucidating this point involves the actor concerned in a suspicious number of "you know"s -- about three a sentence, I calculated, though unlike Shields I didnt have a blackboard to help me.

Ive hinted that, despite its title, the show isn't political in any obvious sense. But protest, or at least mordant doubt, does slip in. There's a reference to the transformative effects of the Industrial Revolution on the owners and the children who worked for them. Mutually Assured Destruction (theres a nostalgic phrase) gets compared, under the Information heading, to "the belief that someone will rip you off" -- which, were told, most people actually don't. (Don't believe it, I mean, not dont rip you off, but I guess it works both ways.) At the end the group both expresses its doubts about, and pays tribute to Progress with an unexpectedly haunting tune whose refrain is "nothing ever wants to change but it does." Its both a celebration and a challenge. The show is casual to a fault, sometimes beyond but, as Galileo more or less said, I guess it works.

- Dedicated to the Revolutions runs through April 12 at Buddies in Bad Times Theatre. Call 416-975-8555 for schedule and ticket information.

2009-04-08-yes-junior-minister-in-its-de:
From the office that brought you The Office comes Parks and Recreation. Since NBC in the U. S. and Citytv here have been promoting the new show as a companion piece to the old one, and since it has two of the same executive producers (Greg Daniels and Michael Schur, if you care about executive producers) there seems little point in going over the similarities. They exist, that's all.

The Office, of course, is set in a wildly dysfunctional private organization; Parks & Rec, as its obviously destined to be known, is set in a mildly dysfunctional public one. Both shows are carried along by soliloquies to the camera, and both feature a star comedian as an ambitious manager. A key difference is the ambitions the central characters. Steve Carrell in The Office is all ego and insecurity, Amy Poehler in Parks & Rec is ego plus overflowing self-confidence plus what seems to be a genuine desire to do good for her fellow creatures. The U. S. incarnation of The Office is of course kinder and gentler than the U. K. original, but Parks & Rec is nicer still. As satire on government its no Yes Minister; its setting -- the folksy municipality of Pawnee, Ind. -- is rather far removed from the seat of any actual power. All the same, I suspect that if this show were British, and aired on PBS, people would be raving about it. It has the casual air of, say, To the Manor Born: off the wall but not so far off that it collapses in a manic heap on the floor. I've seen the pilot, and I like it.

It had me from the pre-credits sequence which has Poehler as P&R superintendent Leslie Knope (the K is silent, so much so that you have to go to the show's website to find it exists) intently interrogating a six-year-old on the quality of her sandbox experience: Was it great fun, some

fun, or not much fun? From here she progresses to extricating a drunk from the childrens slide where, as an adult, he has of course no right to be. Leslie, blond, bright-eyed and 34, is a hands-on lady. We follow her back to departmental HQ, where nobody is remotely as enthusiastic as she is, and then to a public meeting which, she tells us, is where the rubber of government meets the road of real human beings. The real human beings who attend are few in number but full of complaints -- about graffiti, loud music and profanity generally -- and they voice them, well, vociferously. Leslie finds this gratifying: "What I hear when Im being yelled at is people caring loudly." From the throng arises one especially powerful voice; it belongs to Ann, a nurse who says that she doesn't like politics (general applause) but wants to draw attention to a large pit -- really more of a chasm-- that some feckless developers have left outside her house and into which her musician boyfriend has recently, and injuriously, fallen. Rashida Jones plays Ann, and she emerges as second lead when Leslie announces that she intends not just to fill the hole in but to turn it into, naturally, a park. I think this is called empire-building. Leslie thinks of it as her own personal Hoover Dam project.

It seems that this scheme, with the two ladies as allies, is going to be the season's ongoing plotline. Having griped so often about shows that dont have plots but simply dish up repetitive situations every week, I feel mean when I doubt the development potential of this one. This, though, puts me in the same camp as Leslies colleagues, none of whom thinks she has a prayer but all of whom, so far at least, are going along for the sake of a quiet life. Or a quieter one than they'd have otherwise. They're a rich bunch, and its on their potential as well as Leslies that I pin my hopes. These are especially high for Rob (Nick Offerman), the boss of the outfit, a government official who's opposed government on philosophical grounds, and would like to turn it all over to Chuck E. Cheese (his dream employer). Then there's Tom (Aziz Ansari), who hits unsubtly on every woman in sight and identifies himself as a redneck from South Carolina, even though Leslie seems to think hes Libyan. More laid-back is Mark (Paul Schneider), a disillusioned urban planner who can just about remember having slept with Leslie. Junior member is April (Aubrey Plaza, the first female Aubrey Ive ever encountered), a taciturn intern with an interesting glower. So far she's the only character not to talk to the camera, or to anybody else much, probably because she's too bored. The others unburden themselves at every opportunity.

Writing, performance and direction share a beguiling, and occasionally cutting, offhandedness. This isnt an original style, as already acknowledged, but its still unusual enough to be refreshing. Like most good comedy, this show takes the self-centredness of all its characters for granted. Leslie's aim, we are told, is to be first female president of the U. S. A. and, with commendable impartiality, she lists her role models as Hillary, Nancy and Sarah. Which reminds me: If we're going to compare comedies featuring SNL alumnae, then on the evidence so far I'll take this over the frenzy of 30 Rock any day. It makes a nice rec. - Parks and Recreation premieres tomorrow on Citytv and NBC at 8:30 p. m.

2009-04-11-keeping-cool-in-king-louis-co:
Acompany called the Red Light District has taken up residence, perhaps appropriately, in the basement of the Drake Hotel, self-proclaimed Hot Bed for Culture. The play is Moliere's The Misanthrope, a French classic, but the atmosphere certainly isnt classic and, though it might be described as enthusiastically louche, it isnt French. It's Weimar refracted through Queen West. The actors, greeting us in slithery poses and insinuating tones, do everything but sing Wilkommen. It's the kind of divine decadence thats fascinated audiences ever since The Threepenny Opera, which is fitting since the production is directed by Johanna Schall, who is the granddaughter of Bertolt Brecht. And though the show doesnt have much to do with the chillier dogmas of alienation, it does realize the Brechtian ideal of making us view an old play through new eyes. And what we find is what was always there, made fresh.

As quite often happens with aggressive takes on classics, I started out somewhere between suspicious and hostile and was progressively converted. Or perhaps the word is seduced. Alceste, the title character of The Misanthrope, is an idealist who demands impossibly high standards of the world around him and -- mostly but not always -- of himself. He refuses to fib or flatter and is shocked, though not really surprised, by those who do those things. There are two chinks in his armour. One is a lawsuit over some disputed property, in which his amour-propre seems as much at stake as his legal rights. (He calls his unseen opponent every name under the sun without deigning to get into specifics.) The other is his love for the beautiful flirt Celimene, who's simultaneously besieged by an army of admiring sycophants, none of whom she seems exactly to discourage. If he were truly true to his principles, Alceste would just walk away. But he doesn't.

An exceptionally informative program note clues us in to the aimless, airless lives of the thousands of enforced hangers-on at the court of Louis XIV: the people of whom Moliere actually wrote. The production tries to enforce an equivalence between them and the young fashionistas of our own time: the people, in fact, whom you might see hanging out at the Drake. You cant truly equate an existence imposed by royal fiat (Louis way of de-fanging the fractious French nobility) with one freely chosen by a section of, as this production's update of Tony Harrison's already updated translation puts it, "mankind circa 2009." I mean, theres king pressure and theres peer pressure. This production has to do some forcing. But that granted, it makes good tense sense of a play that can easily come off as an inert conversation piece.

It's very much in your face. The space is confined, the music and the visuals are from clubland, and the actors, costumed flamboyantly a la mode, move around and among us, getting up close and sometimes personal. So they do with one another; sex keeps breaking out where in the original it's kept under decorous wraps. In many productions this kind of thing just seems like showing off, but here it works. Insofar as you can separate the two, this show is more concerned with love than with politics. Alcestes erotic torments trap him like a vise; the play, performed without an intermission, allows him no escape.

The Harrison translation, a classic in its own right, was first performed by the British National Theatre in 1973, in a production that substituted de Gaulles Elysee for Louis' Versailles. Its effects range from the self-flagellating fury of Alceste's Just how degrading can a passion get? to Celimenes sublime refusal of a rural retreat with her lover: "Im only 20; I'd be terrified / Just you and me all that countryside." There are times at the Drake when I wished the actors, most of them recent ex-students, would stop crawling and scampering about and give the couplets a chance, but they confront the combined challenges of text and staging with winning commitment. Ted Witzel's Alceste is sketchy on personality but dead-on in projecting his predicament; Eve Wyldens Celimene loses some vocal points in the wash, but is still the credible queen of a shallow society with tantalizing inklings of something better. Marcel Dragonieri is toweringly good as Oronte, the amateur poet who begs Alceste for an honest opinion and is arrogantly unforgiving when he gets it. (Jesus wept, explodes the misanthrope-critic, "its bloody rubbish.") Philinte, the friend who keeps urging the hero to temporize, can be interpreted, according to your preconceptions, either as the honest voice of reason or as a contemptible time-server; Reid Linforth, in the show's most original performance, makes him both, mercilessly teasing Alceste with the name of Celimene but coming eloquently through in his defence. In a world in which bisexuality is a given, two characters have their genders reversed. This doesn't really square with Celimenes attempt to excuse an incriminating letter by saying its from a woman, but it does prompt fresh performances from Simon Rainville as the gentle Eliante and from Kat Letwin as a marquise whose reading, from an iPhone, of an even pricklier communique, distinguishing every pronoun at top speed, is a riot. Spencer Evoy rounds off the beau monde as a still-male marquis, and Mairin Smit makes the prudish Arsinoe something more dangerous than the usual frump. Moliere's original subtitle was The Atrabilious Lover; this version settles for Why Contempt is Sexy. It makes its point. I wonder how Schall approaches her granddad's plays. - The Misanthrope plays through April 26 at the Drake Hotel. Visit thedrakehotel.cafor details.
