2009-04-14-on-swashbucklers-single-malts:
David Mamet is characteristically sparing with the information he provides in Glengarry Glen Ross, but he takes care to give us the essentials. This selective economy is what makes the play so funny, so scary and so convincing. Look at the title. Once you've got past the natural assumption that it refers to a duel to the death between two rival brands of malt whisky, you realize that Glen Ross (which I think is only mentioned once) is the name of a stretch of dubious Florida properties that the play's Chicago real estate salesmen used to peddle in their glory days, while Glengarry (which gets three or four name-checks) denotes the even more dubious lands in the same state that they're reduced to offloading now. "Now," strictly speaking, would mean 1983, which is when the play was first staged; "then" could mean 1965, a year that one character invokes with a mixture of nostalgia and desperation. But it's easy to adjust the dates in our heads to the present, especially given that the play revolves around the stark certainty of layoffs. This has always been a cutthroat business, if only because its hucksters never had anything substantial to huck. But what was once a matter of competitive honour has now become one of survival.

There are four men, working for the same firm, engaged in a sales contest whose outcome will leave one of them with a Cadillac, one with a set of steak knives and the other two on the street. They've mostly been in the game for years. Effectively holding their fates in his hands is a young, and much resented, office manager, who in turn answers to two unseen proprietors. It's remarkable how complete a picture we get, mainly through dropped hints, of the hierarchy, how it was built up and how it operates, and of the pattern of the salesmen's lives: days drumming up trade on the phone, morose lunches, evenings spent charming and fooling gullible customers, nights in lonely hotels. There's a camaraderie bred of custom and shared apprehension, but since these fears are competitive by definition, any of these guys can turn on a dime. There is a kind of professional pride at work, and sometimes it gets spread around, but nobody ever misses a chance to take advantage. This could be the best workplace play ever written.

It has a fittingly deceptive structure. The first act, set in a Chinese restaurant where you can practically smell the MSG, is composed of duologues: salesman and boss, salesman and salesman, salesman and potential client. We only reach full ensemble when we get to the office, in turmoil because someone has broken in and stolen the "leads" -- the prized list of lucrative contacts. So there are two dramas going on, the robbery and the sales, the first providing a steady throbbing ground-bass to the ebb and flow of the second, until both explode in rapid succvession.

Mamet's celebrated profanity-driven dialogue, full of hesitations and false starts, can be taken two ways: to denote people at the top of their game or at the end of their tether. David Storch's Soulpepper production mostly opts for the latter; it isn't the funniest Glengarry I've seen but it could be the saddest. Its defining portrait is Eric Peterson's Shelley "the Machine" Levene: the one-time sales champ now reduced to begging -- and bribing -- for scraps. It's easy to feel sorry for him, but Peterson doesn't play for sympathy as Jack Lemmon did in the film; there's always a mean crack waiting to burst out of him, and even his moments of triumphant swagger have their underside. As Richard Roma, the up-and-comer who stands where Levene once did, Albert Schultz, hair spectacularly slicked, plays like a quiet cobra, hypnotising his prey with a philosophical aria about self-gratification that works its magic by sound as much as sense. Less satisfyingly, he sounds the same subdued note among his colleagues, and some of the flavour goes, both from his aggression and his moments of apparent sympathy. Kevin Bundy plays his civilian victim well, without getting the delicious tension between his awe of Roma and his fear of his own wife. (The guy practically apologizes for not letting himself get swindled.) Schultz's anger though, when his prize fruit goes pear-shaped, is electrifying.

Twin performances that make the Mamet pauses sing come from Peter Donaldson as the most abrasive member of the sales force, nursing grudges from way back, and William Webster, jowly and pouchy, as the most pathetic, facing the same defeat as Levene but without the same fight in him. Jordan Pettle gets the manager absolutely right, savouring his power and, beneath his collegiate veneer, as ruthless and venal a barracuda as the boys out in the field. Ken MacDonald's sets do well by the restaurant, less well by the office; the two are symbolically linked when the wall menu of one turns into the contest-scoreboard of the other. I'm not convinced that a play at once so full and so spare needs this kind of illustration, but I guess it serves for a play in which dog voraciously eats dog after first sharing a table with him. - Glengarry Glen Ross runs until May 9. Call 416-866-8666 for tickets.

2009-04-16-the-doctor-is-back-in-and-he-:
Iwas very sniffy about the first season of In Treatment. I said that this show about a psychologist and his patients was just another medical soap, more highfalutin than most, but still focusing on the practitioner rather than on those practised upon. I have to eat crow. The second season strikes me as being a quantum leap on its predecessor, but this isn't because it's abandoned the things that, first time around, I felt were flaws. It's kept them, pushed them even further into the centre and proved them to be assets.

I started my first course of In Treatment assuming that Paul, the therapist so beautifully and tactfully played by Gabriel Byrne, would function as sounding board rather than protagonist. I was disconcerted when one of his female patients fell in love with him (cliche No. 1), when she bumped into a male patient just outside Paul's consulting room (cliche No. 2) and when the two patients started a relationship (need I go on?).

Paul himself was then dragged into the centre of the action, which was further complicated when his wife left him. Now it's true that even from the start Paul was a more interesting presence than most of the people he treated. But it still seemed like cheating: a betrayal of the quasi-realistic, quasi-clinical format the show had apparently laid down for itself.

In this new season, now in its second week, Paul's problems seem even more acute, and everything else reflects back on them. No longer does everything happen in a consulting room, either Paul's or that of his supervisor Gina (Dianne Wiest), the shrink's shrink. Notice was served of that in the first episode, which took place in a lawyer's office.

Paul, now divorced, has moved from Maryland to Brooklyn, pursued by a multi-million dollar lawsuit. One of his former patients is dead, maybe a suicide; Paul is being sued for negligence. Intellectually he knows this to be ridiculous; emotionally he can't be sure, for reasons not confined to the deceased having been the male half of Season 1's affair.

A member of the legal firm that Paul consults turns out to be Mia (Hope Davis), another former patient: one whom, years ago, he encouraged to have an abortion, a decision that, with her biological clock ticking, she now regrets. That first episode gave us a chain of reversals: the therapist in the hot seat, the tables re-turned as it turns out that the New York mal-practice specialist, with her big salary and high-achieving view over Manhattan, still needs her help.

And she'll be getting it, once a week. As before, we spend four evenings a week watching Paul in session with patients, and the fifth bringing his own problems, which include his patients', to Gina whom -- in an echo of the situation with Mia -- he first consults as a friend and then as a patient. Davis, hyper-active, and Wiest, hyper-calm, are both terrific, but so are all the other principals. Maybe New York just breeds classier neurotics, but Paul's current patients are a far more compelling -- and disturbing -- collection than his previous bunch.

There's April, an aggressively bright student who's been diagnosed with cancer and is refusing treatment because to acknowledge the need for it would be to give up control. Alison Pill is ferociously good in the role. ("I bet," she says with all the sarcastic confidence of a 23-year-old, "you're one of those people who still has a land line." Paul pleads guilty.) Also terrified of acknowledging weakness is Walter, a CEO whose company is under threat, whose daughter is doing dangerous volunteer-work in Rwanda and who is suffering attacks -- which he's had, he says, since childhood as if that made them less serious. John Mahoney does a fine job of showing the man's inner struggle between arrogance and need; he acts not just with his eyes but with the bags under them. I wonder: Is the world divided between those people who, in therapy and out, compulsively underplay their problems, and those who do the reverse?

Finally and most wrenchingly, there is Oliver, the 11-year-old son of a breaking marriage; his parents, who bring him to the sessions and compete for his love, are graphic illustrations of what has gone wrong. Aaron Shaw is amazing as this boy who, when Paul asks him about his school's history lessons, replies, "We don't have history, we have humanities. And right now we're reading this lame book called Lord of the Flies." Why is it lame, Paul asks. Because, says Oliver, "you've no need to crash on an island for kids to be mean." Oliver knows; he's overweight and his schoolmates, taking their cue from the lame book, have taken to calling him Piggy.

All these cases hit Paul where he lives -- or where he no longer lives. They all, in some way, involve children. His own daughter tells him, "there'll be no more hugs --not until you come home," which is plainly impossible.

In a lovely touch we see, behind them on a shelf, a turtle left behind after his last consultation with Oliver, who's supposed to be looking after him as a school project. ("If he dies, I fail.") In a sense, the connections between the stories are artificial, but it's the kind of artifice that makes for dramatic truth. The show is based, episode for episode, on an Israeli series, but the American writers, who include such successful playwrights as Warren Leight and Marsha Norman, have acclimatized it. Writing and direction are sober, and sometimes very moving. Byrne -- prickly when his own problems are in question, infinitely patient with his patients --is superb. However racking his doubts, you know that Paul is in the right profession. This is the best drama series since Mad Men, the best from HBO since The Wire. - In Treatment airs on Sundays and Mondays at 9 p. m. ET on HBO Canada.

The beginning and the end of The Last Days of Judas Iscariot are that Judas had a mother. At the start, she talks about the love that suffused him when he was born and about his burial in a potters field. At the close, she sings about them. The song isn't in Stephen Adly Guirgis' original script, but with Louise Pitre playing the role in David Ferrys Toronto production, musical additions are more than justified. An ambitious, provocative and furiously funny text translates into a magnificent night at the theatre.

Pitre proves as powerful a talking actress as she is a singing one. Another fine musical transplant is Adam Brazier, who plays Butch Honeywell, foreman of the jury at Judas trial. Judas is in Hell, but some people feel that after a couple of millennia he could use some clemency. So a trial is convened, in Purgatory, which here seems to be a suburb of Middle America. Butch has the play's last major speech, delivered to a catatonic Judas in his infernal cage, and it is as beautifully paced in the acting as it is in the writing. It's a mournful account of the sins in his own life, whose upshot is that we all betray. In doing so, Butch lost the person he loved most. So he has a fellow-feeling for Judas.

The trial is presided over to his extreme reluctance by Ted Dykstra, stupendously alarming in dark glasses and a Southern drawl. For Judas defence, there is an all-purpose feminist progressive (Janet Porter whos forceful, if sometimes too much so); for the prosecution, a toadying Egyptian riotously played by Morris Panych, who communicates infectious joy at being on a stage for the first time in years and untarnished skill at occupying the space.

Guirgis is transparently Catholic. He gives all his characters a case, and the space and energy to state it. I doubt if he approves politically of Mother Teresa, but she still emerges, in Aviva Armour Ostroff's performance, with dignity fiercely intact. Judas' story is examined from every conceivable angle. Caiaphas (Dykstra in a heavy beard, and very troubling) resonantly refuses to hear the Jews blamed yet again for the death of Christ; though Pontius Pilate (Philip Akin, massive as a four-star general), playing the antiterrorism card, is disposed to do just that. Various disciples declare Judas "a dick," but not a traitor. Great thing about a court of the dead: You can call anyone. Both sides call Satan who makes both the most powerful and the most disturbing case for the existence of God; the devil is Diego Matamoros at his smoothest and most terrifying.

Judas, condemned for carrying out a divine plan, got a raw deal. Hauntingly played by Shaun Smyth, he shuffles periodically onstage, the last time for a writhing encounter with a Jesus (Jamie Robinson) whose love he still cant accept but who also seems disinclined to accept his, at least on his terms. The court gives a verdict; the play doesnt. My own is that this is the most exhilarating play to come out of America, or maybe anywhere, in years. Here's the only bad news: The show is off already. Economics, and maybe casting logistics, made a run of more than 10 performances (in the Distillery's Fermenting Cellar) difficult. But the production is a revival of a show seen even more briefly four years ago. So, perhaps it can rise again, phoenix-like. Especially since the producing company is Birdland Theatre.
2009-04-22-playing-characters-who-played:
In HBO's Grey Gardens, Jessica Lange and Drew Barrymore play, respectively, Edith Beale and her daughter, also Edith Beale. Grey Gardens itself is their house in the Hamptons, which progresses from grandeur to acute decay to a kind of reclamation. One of the best scenes shows Lange as the elder and now aged Edie, sitting up in bed, singing along with an arrangement of Tea for Two that had been specially written for her in her younger days. Arriving at the last stanza, she forgets a line and comes in too early on the next one, the one about the sugar cake. So she has to ad lib her way through, so as to finish at the same time as the accompaniment, which she does with true upper-crust aplomb.

What I didn't know, when watching last Saturday night, was that Lange was reproducing, and reproducing exactly, the performance of the same song in the same circumstances given by the real Edie in the documentary film, also called Grey Gardens, made in 1975 by Albert and David Maysles: same cracked but accurate voice, same gaffe, same carelessly indomitable recovery. I didnt know but I soon found out, as HBO showed the Maysles film immediately after showing its own. This was a lot of semi-patrician eccentricity to take in one evening, but it was worth it. The Beale ladies were fascinating sociological and psychological phenomena, something between facts and artefacts. The same description might hold for the performances of Lange and Barrymore, both of whom immersed themselves in all the available biographical material, including of course the documentary, and both of whom emerged giving, with invaluable assistance from cameramen and makeup artists, skin-tight impersonations of the originals. But not just impersonations. These are performances that start from externals, which are certainly striking enough in this case, and then find rigorous justification for them. Acting often works like that.

The Beale women -- Big Edie and Little Edie-- were Jazz Age party girls who could never bring themselves to admit that the party was over, even though their later years were one monstrous hangover. That's the situation captured in the Maysles' documentary, which shows them reminiscing, recriminating and reconciling with extraordinary abandon -- though what remains unclear is whether they forgot the camera was there or enjoyed themselves playing up to it. (Some of both, probably.) The dramatized movies not-so-secret weapon is that it can show us the events and people that the documentary could only talk about. We are of course substituting one kind of unreliable narration for another, but we do get some kind of external purchase on the relationship. There are two eternal dynamics at work here: mother-daughter and ambitions-regrets. Either can yield powerful drama; together, theyre explosive.

Past and present alternate. Present here is the Maysles brothers coming to call and staying to shoot. Past takes us back to the 1930s; Big Edie is married to a rich businessman (Ken Howard) who commutes from New York and is increasingly appalled by her behaviour; nursing dreams of being a singer, she entertains lavishly (and apparently continuously) and has her own live-in young male pianist. Little Edie also has theatrical ambitions, and when daddy moves definitively out, she goes with him. It even seems she might make a go of it; at least she flirts and wheedles her way into an audition with a prominent producer. But an affair with a married man (Daniel Baldwin, whom one hopes is reconciled to roles that seem designed for his brother Alec) blows up in her face, and she hightails it back to mother. And there she remains. It's a perfect setup for two lifetimes of mutual blame, tempered by unbreakable, exasperated love. Why did Little Edie come home? To look after her mother, she says. Because she was scared to do anything else, her mother says. Both are obviously right.

Debt and dilapidation take over the premises, as also do an army of pet cats and scarcely less domesticated raccoons. (So that's why they filmed in Toronto. Though along with the raccoons, they got the services of top Canadian actors like Kenneth Welsh and Ben Carlson.) Luckily the Beales have a rich cousin, the former Jacqueline Bouvier (Jeanne Tripplehorn), who vacationed with them as a child and now, midway between being a Kennedy and an Onassis, is able to wave a magic wand and have the house restored to a semblance of its former status. And in her wake come the Maysles duo, who cant promise much in the way of monetary reward (as they put it, "the words documentary' and 'profit seldom occur in the same sentence") but who do end up bringing the two Edies something of the fame theyve always craved. There's a moment of apotheosis that's both funny and touching.

One of the minor felicities of Michael Sucsys script and direction is the balance held between the Maysles exploitation of their subjects and their affection for them. Balance indeed is the word throughout. The film keeps a high-comic tone, and its evolving period feel is immaculate (the music's great, with Lange doing a lot of singing and Barrymore a bit) but it never loses its grip on two women, each of them devastatingly clear-eyed about the other while being -- mostly -- a fantasist about herself. The human condition, in other words, carried to extremes; and these two can laugh at themselves as well as one another. Lange plays with a debutante drawl that grows into a grand, craggy snarl: the voice, as we know, of her original. Barrymore's tone, equally authentic, is Katharine Hepburn on ice, whether viperish, imperious or just riffing on her own frivolity; she's still a flirt. She addresses her mother, always, as "Mother darling," but there are no Joan Crawford overtones; it sounds natural and overbearing, but sincere. These are two superb performances, in an exceptional production. - Grey Gardens airs again today at 1 p. m. and 8 p. m., as well as on Sunday at 8:50 a. m. on HBO Canada.

2009-04-25-bitterness-is-a-nasty-theme-f:
Icould almost feel grateful to Hardsell. Theatre criticism can grind you down into a state of numbed acceptance in which you begin to wonder whether you could truly love or hate a show ever again. In the past two weeks I have been twice rescued. The Last Days of Judas Iscariot gave me something to love. And now theres Hardsell, a show to hate.

That isn't because it lacks competence. It comes, after all, from the highly rated Necessary Angel Company, here spreading fresh wings. Daniel Brooks, the company's new artistic director, created the show, in collaboration with its sole performer, Rick Miller. Brookss direction is probably perfect, certainly slick; Miller emerges as a faultless mimic (which we already knew), a decent ventriloquist (which we didnt) and an accomplished clown. A clown is what he's playing here, name of Arnie and bearing a strong resemblance to Krusty from The Simpsons. Not a vocal resemblance -- this isn't a reprise of Millers MacHomer--nor much of a physical one, though he does appear in war paint. But hes like Krusty in his avarice, cynicism and venality. He's not as commercially successful, but he's certainly commercial. Which makes for bitterness. Which is what the shows about.

Arnie is, he tells us, Rick Millers brother. And Rick Miller is an idealist, but a compromised one. He contributes to causes, does charity gigs, has a wife and (Arnie repeatedly tells us, with a kind of barbed relish) two lovely daughters. But he also hosts Just for Laughs, a deeply commercial operation; drinks Coca-Cola, and we all know about them; and is generally in the merchandising business. Why, the very show we're watching is sponsored by CIBC. Everyone is selling, everyone's for sale.

Well, yes. I agree. Whatcha gonna do? Not much, seems to be the answer. This is another blast of showbiz self-hatred; the kind of thing that, on a larger scale, kept the late Bob Fosse going, all the way from the movie of Cabaret to Big Deal. You play tricks, tell the audience how much you despise yourself for playing them, then play some more. In a more sober and searching manner, Wallace Shawn has also explored liberal guilt in duologue (My Dinner with Andre) and monologue (The Fever). Shawn took his own rap. Miller, though, is triple-bluffing. Instead of offering a straightforward mea culpa, he shifts his angst on to an imaginary evil sibling. And if we retort that Arnie, after all, is only Miller in disguise, then he can still score points for honesty, but without personally facing any music. Its infinite regress. And its not as if the theme is all that interesting, certainly not when its supposed avatar keeps excusing himself. The show has little to say, nowhere to go; all Miller-as-Arnie can do is vent till ready. He's technically adept at many things (his instant James Brown impersonation, twice repeated, is nice), but he's unrelentingly unfunny. That could very well be the idea, but it isnt a rewarding one. Visually, the show is fairly striking. Arnies face is white, his hair a shock of red, and he inhabits a whitish universe (designed by Ben Chaisson and Beth Kates) that's heavy on the video. The press release says that Hardsell is theatrical irony at its nastiest." They got that right.

The Madness of the Square is not a show you can hate. It's too inept for that. Marjorie Chans play (Cahoots Theatre Projects, in cahoots with Factory Theatre) tries to tell the story of Tiananmen through the experiences of four involved students with, at least to start, varying degrees of commitment. It proceeds on the dubious assumption that Chinese students in 1989 would have thought, talked and behaved exactly like Canadian students now, or at least like Canadian students with the concerns and the vocabulary of a campus soap. Theres Fan-Ying, initially aimless both scholastically and politically, whose ability to speak English leads to her becoming a talking head for foreign media, which in turn brings her dangerous notoriety. There's Shen, who's there because he fancies Fan-Ying. Theres Ding-Ding, the frivolous rich boy who foots the bill at the noodle-shop and thinks hes a wow with the ladies. And there's Sun-Yi, who's the dedicated one and who declares late on that the freedom she believes in is sexual freedom; though she seems to have a narrow view of this since she, a lesbian, strongly objects to two of her heterosexual friends getting married. There are also a more seasoned activist, who can be quite compelling, and a BBC reporter whos an embarrassment. Of course, even revolutionaries have private lives, but the play doesnt seem able to get beyond them. Its principal method of trying is periodically to assemble its actors in chorus formation and have them shout Brechtian chapter headings ("What happened to Sun-Yi ...") as if this would somehow lend epic weight to a forlornly sentimental script. (To be fair, Brecht often played this game, especially when he, too, set plays in China.) These interludes apart, Ruth Madoc-Jones stages the play well, but she cannot disguise the banality of the text or of most of the performances; Karl Ang and JohnNg are the only actors who don't come off helpless. There's plenty of video here, too, most effectively at the end when images of the square after the tanks went in have us retrospectively putting faces to the carnage. For that much, I guess, you have to give the play credit. But it remains a hopelessly naive attempt at a tragic subject, like children's theatre on a bad day. - Hardsell plays through May 9 at the Berkeley Street Theatre. Call 416-368-3110 for ticket information; The Madness of the Square plays through May 3 at the Factory Theatre. Call 416-504-9971 for details.
2009-04-25-how-bach-can-change-your-life:
THE CELLO SUITES

By Eric Siblin, Anansi, 304 pp., $29.95

- - -

At the beginning of the 21st century, Eric Siblin had an epiphany. He was staying at a hotel in Toronto, close by the Royal Conservatory of Music and, having just quit a job in Montreal as pop critic for The Gazette, was searching for some other music that might, he says, "occupy a central place in my life."

He saw a listing for a performance at the RCM of Bach's Cello Suites, went along, and had his life changed. Eventually he wrote a book: one that's partly about the composer, partly about Pablo Casals, who rediscovered the six Suites and made the talismanic recordings of them, and partly -- a large part -- about Siblin himself.

Bach does that to people. Of all classical composers, he seems the one most likely to reach out to those immersed in what academics used to call "secondary music." Siblin himself points to Disney's Fantasia (Stokowksi shaking hands with Mickey Mouse) and to the realization, in the 1930s and since, that Bach swings, which inspired, among others, Benny Goodman (Bach Goes to Town) and Django Reinhardt and, of course, the Swingle Singers, who made Glenn Gould feel "like lying on the floor and kicking my heels."

Contemplating "Bach's street cred," Siblin notes that "his peers in the classical pantheon, Mozart and Beethoven, aren't tampered with nearly as much. . . . Perhaps it has something to do with the steady beat of baroque music . . . or the possibility that Bach's reportedly great skill at improvisation is somehow embedded in the music itself."

Bach was a great rearranger, of his own compositions and others'. The Cello Suites, a lengthy series of unsupported solos for what was then a new-fangled instrument unaccustomed to such exposure, may seem an ascetic, rather forbidding introduction; more people probably get hooked on Bach via the Brandenburgs or the St. Matthew Passion. But each suite is in fact a set of dance pieces, rooted in popular rhythms.

Siblin constructs his book as something between a homage and a seance. His opus, too, is divided into six sections, each sub-divided, like each suite, into six sections: Prelude, Allemande, Courante, Sarabande, Gigue and one variable movement that might be Minuet, Boure or Gavotte. It's difficult, though, to see any particular correspondence between the sub-headings and their content. Except, that is, for the way in which Siblin begins each of his Preludes with an impressionistic account of what Bach was up to in each of his. These are evocative and helpful; he's especially good on the ominous fifth prelude and the explosive sixth. (Meaning, I think I can hear what he hears.) Otherwise there is, for better or worse -- I think for worse -- very little musical description and no musical analysis.

The three narrative threads unfold alternately, in what's presumably meant to be counterpoint, and they get in one another's way, as in a destructive kind of Siblin rivalry. The sections on the composer himself are the least satisfying. Siblin chafes at the stuffy image of Bach inspired by his best-known portrait (Shakespeare, his literary equivalent, has had the same image problem), pointing out that Bach fought a duel -- with a bassoonist -- and was sent to prison for defying a patron. But these were early, passing excitements.

Most of the time he seems to have led an industrious life, chiefly remarkable for the quantity as well as quality of the music he produced and the number of children he fathered, 20 of them. ("He was very prolific, Bach," said Bernard Miles, the British character actor and comedian, in a mock lecture; "used to practice on an old spinster up in the attic.")

Casals is easier, fierier meat: the prodigy from Catalonia who in 1890, at the age of 13, came across the sheet music for the Suites in a second-hand store in Barcelona at a time when hardly anyone knew they existed, and would devote a sizeable portion of his life to studying, practising and performing them. He and the Suites conquered the world in tandem. There was, besides, an exciting sub-plot to his life: a Catalan patriotism that found hope and then disillusion in the Spanish Civil War. "He was," writes Siblin, "a leftist in conservative eyes, but extreme leftists saw him as a well-connected monarchist."

Casals made his first recordings of the Suites in London and Paris, while desperately scanning the news from Spain. After Barcelona fell, and Catalan autonomy with it, he took up residence in the French Pyrenean village of Prades, as close to home as he could safely get. He remained an implacable enemy of Franco's regime for the rest of his life, refusing to play in any country that recognized it. When in 1958 he was begged to play in New York, for the United Nations, he was able to persuade himself that U.N. headquarters were extra-territorial; but he still refused to play the Suites, what Siblin calls "his spiritual signature."

Casals' decades-long stand against fascism is worth remembering any time you hear scorn poured on performing artists for getting involved in politics.

In the personal sections, we follow Siblin as he travels in America and Europe, seeking traces of both Bach and Casals; declines to explain to a Montreal waitress that he's going to a Bach recital when everyone else in town is off to hear U2; interviews world-class cellists; and meets Walter Joachim, a shuffling 80-year-old veteran of the Montreal Symphony who encourages him to learn the cello: "Not that I would ever be any good . . . I was too old for that ever to happen. But it would give me some insight."

And so, apparently, it does. He also, it seems, embarks on a quixotic quest to discover Bach's lost original manuscript, which fizzles out. He reintegrates his own split personality with a familiar but vivid case for classical music as the pop music of its day, pointing out that Bach premiered his own works in coffeehouses as well as churches, and that we could do with some of the same informality: "Why shouldn't the audience be able to unleash its bravos or reward a smoking instrumental solo in real time?"

And conversely, while acknowledging the fine and varied performances that have succeeded and in some ways improved on him, he writes that Casals "played the suites the only correct way -- by breathing life into them."

This is an untidy, sometimes frustrating book, but it's smart and passionate and it, too, breathes life.

(National Post)

Sky Gilbert has never been short on cheek, so it's no particular surprise that he should have written a play baldly entitled I Have AIDS. (It is not, he insists, autobiographical.) Still, there is a mild shock when his protagonist, in the first scene, says to his live-in lover, in between commenting on the latest developments on Beverly Hills 90210 and asking what's for dinner, "I almost forgot; I have AIDS." His partner's response is equally urbane, unruffled and unlikely.

The partner's name is Vidor; he's an interior designer, who emerges from the kitchen wearing an apron bearing the slogan "not your average housewife," and it's down to him that the play's setting has the kind of elegance that we've come to associate with Gilbert as with no other Canadian playwright. Prodon, the one who's ill, is a stand-up comic -- as is Gavin Crawford, who plays him -- and he proceeds to take advantage of his profession by picking up a mic and talking to us directly. He tells us, if I'm following correctly, that what we've just seen is a parody of the way gay men who are HIV-positive are supposed to behave in plays, now that the diagnosis is no longer a death-sentence. The rest of the evening is a demonstration of how they do behave, or at least of how this one would.

Prodon takes an abbreviated five-step journey from denial to acceptance. Denial consists of aggressive promiscuity, which is what he was doing anyway. This is a style he throws in the face of a visiting female health-worker, who asks for a list of his contacts and is told that this is impossible since there've been more than 10,000 of them, mostly anonymous. The lady is shocked and, up to a point, mocked. But only up to a point; Prodon's author, if not Prodon himself, is prepared to grant her some dignity, thereby reinforcing my conviction that, beneath all the bravado, Gilbert is a decently, and rather conventionally, talented playwright.

The health lady is played by Ryan Kelly; it's the first of three performances he gives in this show and probably the best, though the least showy. The second is of Lady Booty, a drag-queen who accompanies Prodon to a club where some of the activities are graphically demonstrated and others are even more graphically described. In the aftermath of this, Prodon changes his ways, takes his meds and plays host to a third guest, Ron, a lonely man who claims that only through contracting AIDS has he found a place in the world. He gives a long speech that touches both Prodon and the audience (Kelly got exit applause on the first night), but that leaves Vidor unmoved. His function throughout is to act as the voice of reason, or at least to disagree with Prodon while continuing to love him; he identifies Ron as "a man who defines himself by having AIDS" and he doesn't want Prodon to go the same route.

Nobody in Canadian theatre writes more fluent, speakable dialogue than Gilbert, and once again, as his own director, he gets excellent performances. David Yee as Vidor makes an admirable anchor, while Crawford goes from acid desperation to acrid acceptance. At the end he reverts to stand-up mode, telling us that the purpose of his story is to remind us that AIDS hasn't gone away from the lives of Canadian gay men, even though people like Stephen Lewis would have us believe that nowadays it's all about Africa. I doubt the continued existence of the noble-suffering AIDS plays against which Gilbert claims he's setting himself; at least, I don't get to see them. More to the point, as I watched the author's talents struggling to find a story to contain them, I renewed my long-held disbelief in the viability of illness -- any illness -- as a dramatic subject. Either you write a medical soap about the Search for a Cure or you end up with a hard-luck story, in which characters suffer from something they can't control and for which they aren't responsible. It's sad, indeed it's horrible, but it precludes free will and denies drama.

For a dramatist who writes marvellous dialogue and tells good stories and deals with choice, I commend you to the American Stephen Adly Guirgis, author of The Last Days of Judas Iscariot. Den of Thieves, a slighter but still terrifically enjoyable play of his, is being premiered here by Surface-Underground theatre, an Equity co-op: very well too, with Jamie Robinson giving his most assured performance yet as an almost-reformed kleptomaniac with Robin Hood tendencies and Lisa Norton riotously forsaking her Shaw Festival roots as an all-purpose moll. They are half of a gang of four -- two confirmed crooks, two trying to go straight through yet another addicts' program -- who get involved in what promises to be an easy heist and find that they've invaded the home of a Cosa Nostra family who spend the play's second half wondering how, or whether, to kill them. The Mafia characters are from stock, though with twists; some of the plot-turns are predictable, but in a satisfying way. What takes us by surprise is the contest in self-sacrifice that the captives engage in when there's no other option; this is moving, both in writing and performance, and not remotely sentimental. Guirgis is on about redemption again, though not here in an explicitly Christian context. He's also wonderfully funny. He's the real deal -- America's best since Mamet -- and it's criminal that none of our established theatres have acknowledged him. Not that they'd likely improve on these fine independent productions, but they could at least provide greater exposure.

- I Have AIDS runs through May 3 at Buddies in Bad Times Theatre. Call 416-975-8555 for details; Den of Thieves runs at the Walmer Centre Theatre through May 9. Call 416-924-1122 for more information.

An oddity of Producing Parker is that the title character isn't the star, though she is the protagonist. This new animated series is named after Parker Novak, a hard-working and capable TV producer in her late twenties, working on a daily TV program called The Dee Show. The Dee in question is an ego-driven talk-show host who soaks up all the attention, onscreen and off, while relying on underlings like Parker to do all the work. Kim Cattrall is the voice of Dee, and she's the only performer with a credit in the opening titles, even though its Kristin Booth, playing Parker, who does most of the heavy lifting on the show itself. No reflection on Cattrall but this really does seem a case of life imitating art. If you call it life; if you call it art.

Producing Parker begins niftily enough, with a good old-fashioned theme song. A 1950ish vocal group informs the heroine "you have to work your butt off / but you dont regret it / now you're in your element / with a full screen credit" not to mention you've got your staff / and the last laugh. Its catchy, though it does recall the title song of a certain Broadway musical, one that also concerned producers. Once it gets to story, however, the show is in the uncomfortable position of satirizing a genre that satirizes itself.

A lot of it has been done before, sometimes by shows with live actors. Parker, the plucky professional at the mercy of exploitative no-talent employers, is the cartoon version of Tina Fey in 30 Rock. She has an office full of wacky associates but no real friends and no love life. She does, however, have a talking dog, a device even more irritating here than it is on Family Guy. Its also borrowed from that show a habit of going off on split-second tangents. Whimsy can be used for satire, but it isn't the same thing. The commentary on The Simpsons -- back in its good days --depended on our believing, at some level, in the characters and in a sense that the show meant what it said. South Park, Family Guy and, now, Producing Parker don't bother to mean anything; theyre too concerned with being the cool beyond cool. They arent as smart as they think they are, and they aren't as fast. They're sitcoms that take advantage of animations limitless capacity for special effects, but not of its potentially dizzying depth of wit. They mistake frenzy for invention.

The format of Producing Parker is that Dee, while doing her show, will discover that someone has something she doesnt and that her whole team, mainly meaning Parker, will have to devote the next segment of their lives to getting it for her. The first show finds Dee hosting on a discussion on "what matters most to women" -- i. e. jeans -- and discovering from a British designer called Indigo Jones that she herself is posterior challenged --i. e. she doesn't have a fashionably big bum. (If that is the fashion, but plainly Dee will believe anything if it makes her feel insecure enough.) "Indigo Jones," says Dee indignantly, can kiss my ass. "If she can find it," a subordinate murmurs. That's quite funny, but the show goes on making the same joke for the next half-hour, with commercials for something called Booty Barn, scenes at a bar named Heinies and the loyal Parker trying out a posterior pump which gives her so much ballast that she goes flying through the air like Mary Poppins and gets mistaken for a terrorist. Talk about forced.

Episode Two is better (strange how often I find myself saying that) since Dees obsession is a little more rooted in reality -- hence more fruitfully comic -- and she herself puts in more than token appearances. This time, after hosting a show on model moms, she decides that what she wants is a baby. Too busy to do it the orthodox way ("You told them I'm a celebrity?" she asks indignantly when Parker relays the information about the nine-month waiting period), she settles instead for adoption. Chicago, Parker's pneumatic blond intern (amusingly voiced by Sarah Cornell, who played a similar role, in person and with a Swedish accent, in the Toronto production of the actual Producers), rings round the agencies and finds one that guarantees delivery in 24 hours or no charge. Once the blankets are off, the baby turns out to be Siamese twins, prompting Chicago to say its got two heads -- its gonna be so smart. So indeed it is -- I mean, they are: genius level, in fact. Of course it's Parker who has actually to look after them, and who proves a born mother, and of course they go missing just as Dee's about to present them to her TV audience, leaving the bereaved star to scream the reasonably immortal line, "This is the worst thing thats ever happened to me -- were talking about dead air, people." Dee, by the way, literally breathes fire when she's upset, like when someone mentions her age.

Others laying about the place include Simon (Aaron Abrams), a would-be writer who's relaxed to the point of total disengagement and is Parkers nearest thing to a two-legged buddy, and the studio head, a Martini-sipping dandy named Blake. Hes yet another Brit (though played by Peter Keleghan, who as far as I know is Canadian) and would rather be doing reality shows, featuring either sharks (he keeps one in his office) or zombies. Parker has a crush on him; strangely, as she's supposed to be so sensible.

Making Parker, rather than Dee, the pivotal figure is a bit of a cop-out and also self-defeating. If you have a monster as your central character, then you should make her central, rather than trusting that your audience will root for the underdog. (Parker is everyone's underdog, including the dog's.) Egomaniacal TV hosts can offer infinite comic potential. Remember The Larry Sanders Show. Think of what Stephen Colbert does four nights a week. And those shows were/are tough. Producing Parker only pretends to be, like so much TV comedy. Well, like so much comedy.

- Producing Parker airs tonight at 8:30 p. m. on TVtropolis.

I, CLAUDIA

Young Centre for the Performing Arts

---

Re-encountering Kristen Thomson in I, Claudia is like welcoming back an old friend. Or a gaggle of old friends, as behind her masks Thomson impersonates four separate characters.

Claudia herself, the 12-and-a-half-year-old child of a recent divorce, is of course the centrepiece, and must by now be the best-loved character in Canadian drama; a perceptible sigh of affectionate recognition goes round the auditorium at the first glimpse of those preternaturally wide eyes that seem simultaneously to accuse and beseech. But we also get to meet Drachman, the Central European showman turned Canadian school janitor who acts as master of ceremonies; Doug, the father of Claudia's father; and Leslie, the woman who has supplanted Claudia's mother.

Drachman, from the imaginary country of Bulgonia, remains the least satisfactory character; it seems that Bulgonians speak with an impenetrable accent, and anyway I'm not persuaded that the play needs Drachman's toy theatre with its red traverse curtain in order to establish its performing convention -- though, given that it does exist, Chris Abraham's production makes the discreet most of it. The school basement is Claudia's refuge, her shelter from a bullying world; the implication that its custodian is the only person who really understands her, as one outsider responding to another, is touching but vague.

Doug, Thomson's other male impersonation, is more successful and seems to have grown richer down the years. (We first saw the play in 2001.) I certainly don't remember being as struck before by his battle with a recalcitrant piece of candy, a struggle that has him complaining "I never saw a wrapper so in love with its lozenge" -- one of the many lines in the piece that sends laughter crashing through the theatre in waves before subsiding into sadness. Doug seems to disapprove of his son's new choice, and he's fond of Claudia, but he can't do much to help her. His new daughter-in-law has more in common with him here than he might acknowledge. Leslie has two scenes, and the first of them, this time around, is a bit of a blur. She comes into her own in her second, being fitted impatiently for her wedding dress, fearful that her great day will be spoiled, anxious about what kind of impression she will make, what kind of wife, and what kind of stepmother. She is currently, as she fears and as Claudia herself makes clear, the person Claudia hates most in the world.

She once suggested that she and Claudia should be girlfriends, to which Claudia's unspoken response -- relayed to us with all the scorn of immediate pre-adolescence -- was "Leslie, just look at yourself." Her dad had first introduced Leslie as "a special friend," on which Claudia's comment is: "I hate to be precocious, but I know a euphemism when I see one." The most legendary of the play's many devastating lines, this both demonstrates and describes Thomson's ear for believable exaggeration, applied to an age group at which exaggeration is the norm.

A lot of things go wrong for Claudia, quite apart from her situation at home. She's picked on by the smart girls at school; her pet goldfish, objects of both her love and her scientific curiosity, die on her. Her parents are, with wonderful tact, kept offstage, but we get to know them, at least through her eyes. We share in her possessive pride over her prescribed outings with her dad, treats that make her feel both grown-up and sad; we're torn up when she speaks fiercely and tearfully of her mother as the nicest person in the whole world, and of the token that she placed under her mother's pillow in the hopes it would bring about a reconciliation. When she tells about her dream of how the new wedding day should have turned out, we're totally, as I think she'd say, swept away in it: more exhilaratingly than we were when the play was first done. Claudia emerges as a brave and even noble figure, as well as a sad and funny one. (And really there's no need to feel too terrible about her long-range prospects; we know that Thomson's own parents divorced, and she hasn't turned out too badly.)

Thomson has since proved with The Patient Hour that she can write for other actors as well as for herself, and that she isn't limited to monologues. We also know that she's a fine actress in more conventional circumstances. Her Claudia, though, is unlike anything else she has done; maybe unlike anything anyone has done. It's both carefully distanced and shatteringly immediate. To watch this play and this performance is to adopt Claudia as your own child; you feel protective and you feel proud. - I, Claudia runs until May 23. Call 416-866-8666 or visit youngcentre.ca for details.

The ending of Prison Break is surprisingly satisfying. I can't go into details of course, but the justice meted out in tonights double length season finale is, for the most part, remarkably poetic. Any tears shed will, I think, be happy ones.

Apart from being happy that the show is ending well, devotees will, I think, be happy that its ending. And that's not because our nerves can't stand the strain of the characters constant hopes, setbacks and re-alignments. Or at least not in the way that the creators might have hoped. We look fondly back to the first season in which the angelically ingenious efforts of Michael Scofield to save his framed brother Lincoln Burrows from the chair were set against the more or less convincing, and certainly absorbing, texture of life in a Chicago prison. I thought the second season was even better; it was fascinating to watch the brothers and their fellow escapees -- some welcome allies, some not -- fanned out across the landscape, and then fanned in again, in their struggles to avoid re-capture by the law, or elimination by a corrupt administration, itself in thrall to the ruthless all-powerful Company.

Opinions differ as to when it all started to go to hell. Probably the crucial moment was the end of Season 2, when a logical happy ending was arbitrarily denied, probably by a network intent on prolonging a successful show. (And were they ever wrong. Ratings have plummeted.) Season 3 was a complete waste of time, with Michael and company thrust into another jail, in Panama, whose own chaos overtook the story itself. Season 4 endearingly tried to act as if Season 3 had never happened, but it too got engulfed. Other fatal moments: The apparent decapitation of the lovely Dr. Sara and her unsurprising return when the actress contract got sorted out. (We were glad to see her -- at least I was --but still.) The first mention of Scylla, the miracle device that can precipitate either total war or total peace, and its relentless promotion as the show's MacGuffin. (I've never really understood its connection to Lincolns incarceration, which Id thought was what the show was about.) All other mentions of Scylla. The advent of Gretchen, the Mata Hari who couldn't act, and her removal just as it was beginning to seem that she could. The final act of writers' desperation: the appearance of the brothers mother, who wed been told was dead, and her unmasking as the most evil and least convincing of the show's evil geniuses. (She really can't act; not this role anyway.) My husband," she tells Lincoln tonight, "used to call me Lady Macbeth, to which Linc replies, no wonder I never liked Shakespeare." At least, I think he does; shes shot him, so hes mumbling a bit. She then tells him that he's just too dumb. Some mom.

But just as the threat of execution is said to concentrate the mind wonderfully -- which, come to think of it, was this show's original premise -- so the imminence of its own extinction seems to have brought on a final spurt of energy. Tonights double-length finale couldnt exactly be called plausible, but it's edge-of-your-seat exciting. Almost to the end our heroes are having to dodge both acknowledged baddies and putative goodies. It might be amusing, someday, to tally up just who on this show has suffered the greatest number of unjust arrests. Linc? Sucre? Mahone?

It's also, as might have been anticipated, something of an old friends night. We all knew that Sucre would come back (and its hardly a spoiler, since it happens before the credits) but he's followed by some more surprising returns. There's one who functions as a deus ex machina, and just behind him another deus from an even shinier machine. Though since this guy --Im itching to tell you who it is -- seems to have had everyones fate in his hands for ages, you may get to wondering where he's been all this time. Strange are the ways of fate, and of actors' availability. We can count ourselves lucky that William Fichtners Mahone has hung in there (So who cares how many people hes killed? He's suffered and we like him) and that Robert Knepper's T-Bag-- serial killer, rapist and son-of-the-South -- has grabbed every stylish opportunity hes been given. His best recent moment, after some stooge said, "I never worked for the Company, was when he practically crooned the comment, six words that never come true." T-Bag keeps promising to escape the box in which his authors have confined him, and his attempts at rehabilitation have been haunting. I guess, though, that the redemption prize on this show has already been taken, by Brad Bellick, the formerly brutal warder who ended up taking one for the company, though definitely not for the Company. They might have thrown him a last posthumous bone.

24 also ends its season, though not its life, on Monday. So presumably --I havent been fed an advance copy of this one -- Jack Bauer will be rescued from death-by-bioweapon through a transplant from daughter Kim, currently being held hostage again. One hopes this is intentional self-parody, as in order to save her Jack once again has to take villainous instructions through an ear-piece, just as in Season 1, eons ago. And he may have to pretend-kill the lovely Renee for the second time this season. (Well, I trust it'll be pretend. Jack's relationships never go well, but there are limits.) 24, by starting each season pretty much from scratch, has an advantage on Prison Break, which had obligations towards continuity, and this season, following on a couple of bummers, has been unexpectedly tense. The ethics of torture have been discussed, in a dutiful but not unintelligent way. Jon Voigt has come, chewed scenery and been blown up. The lady presidents annoying daughter has been handed, at the 22nd hour, a decent plot-line. And Tony Almeida, resuscitated even more laughably than Dr. Sara, has been swinging metronomically from bad to good to bad again. There has to be another twist --Im betting on good-but-doomed -- or there won't have been any point at all. As at this point in previous seasons, America has been saved. Now we get to the important stuff. - The series finale of Prison Break airs tonight at 8 p. m. on Global. The season finale of 24 airs Monday at 8 p. m. on Global.

No, but I saw the movie. That is: Up until the new production at CanStage, my only acquaintance with John Patrick Shanley's Broadway success Doubt was via the screen version with Meryl Streep as Sister Aloysius, the iron-clad principal of a convent school in the Bronx, and Philip Seymour Hoffman as Father Flynn, the priest whom she suspects of improper conduct with an altar boy. I liked the film; apart from the merit of the central performances, I thought it one of the most successful examples I've seen of opening up an enclosed original. The glimpses we were shown of the school's daily life, of the students, of the contrasts between the comfortable, convivial dining table of the priests and the constricted refectory of the nuns, seemed to me nothing but enriching. The play, with four adult characters in narrow focus, is small beer by comparison. Quite possibly, though, if I'd seen them the other way around, I'd prefer the play. The point is, this is not material that stands up well to a second look.

The play's timeframe is the JFK early '60s. Its subtitle is A Parable, and it starts with Father Flynn delivering one, on the merits of doubt as an honest, flexible way of getting through life. Father Flynn is a modernizing priest who grows his fingernails long, writes with a ballpoint pen and wants to open up the annual carol concert to more contemporary material like Frosty the Snowman. All these things, especially Frosty, are anathema to Sister Aloysius, who rules with a rod of iron and believes that it's more beneficial for her students to fear her than to love her. Naturally, our sympathies are all with the open-hearted father (whose attributes include being a first-class football coach) and against the censorious sister. Cunningly, the play then begins to make us doubt, as strong evidence arrives that the priest has plied a 12-year-old boy with communion wine and may have gone further. The boy is especially vulnerable, as the first black pupil the school has ever had. Counter-complications arise when, in the best scene, the victim's mother pleads to let sleeping dog collars lie, while displaying a startling tolerance, for this time and place, of her son's possible gayness. Sister Aloysius won't be dissuaded and persists in what she regards as a crusade for truth and justice (and against an all-too-believable male clerical establishment), which Father Flynn regards as a witch hunt. Their cat-and-mouse game is absorbing at a first viewing, humdrum on repeat. Because beneath it, all is pretence and pretension.

In the play's last line, Sister Aloysius confesses that she, too, has doubts. Well, all very nice, but doubts about what, exactly? About the priest's guilt? Hardly; she seems totally convinced of it. About his capacity to wreak havoc in another parish? The matter is mentioned, but not pursued. About the underhanded tactics she's employed in entrapping him? (She admits to having sinned, and this may be what she means.)About the boy's fate, when his abusive dad finds out? About Frosty and fountain pens? About her own possible loss of vocation? All or any of these are conceivable; none is explored. It's a cop-out. The play ends where it ought to be beginning.

What we're left with, in Marti Maraden's production, is efficient but bloodless. As the big sister, Seana Mc-Kenna is excellent, as we knew she would be, but not beyond what we knew she would be. She doesn't take the same risks as Streep, who pushed the character to the brink of caricature and then pulled back, making her seem more human in the process. Nor does David Storch have the massive fleshly confidence that Hoffman brought to Father Flynn, and especially to his sermons; in other respects, though, he's fine, especially in the locker-room pep talk that shows us the man in his element, absolutely confident and unimpeachably Irish-American. As a young nun whose reactions mirror the audience's, Daniela Vlaskalic is over-the-top naive in her early scenes, but more persuasive when chastened. As the mother, Raven Dauda rides the obvious surface of every speech without connecting one mood to the next; emotionally, she's constantly ahead of herself.

It's been a week of shadow boxing. Hal Linden, the star of Tuesdays with Morrie, has said in some remarkably frank interviews that he finds Mitch Albom's original book "maudlin and sentimental," but that Jeffrey Hatcher's stage adaptation has cured all that. In fact, the play seems as cracker barrel as the book presumably is. Linden plays Morrie, sociologist and sage, now dying of Lou Gehrig's disease. Rick Roberts is Mitch, a former student who visits him weekly and finds his own life unspecifically transformed in the process. Mitch is an in-demand sports reporter, of whose success Morrie seems suspicious. Mitch has abandoned earlier ambitions to be a jazz pianist, though he has married a singer --an interesting wrinkle that the play doesn't seem to notice. Still, Emilie-Claire Barlow's (offstage) wifely singing of The Very Thought of You is the show's highlight. Both actors, in Ted Dykstra's production for the Harold Green Jewish Theatre, are good, though Roberts is initially too strident and Linden is your all-purpose secular rabbi. He gets his laughs, and the evening is painless, but all it leaves is a feeling of generalized goodwill.

Jonathan Garfinkel's House of Many Tongues tries to dramatize the Middle East conflict by showing us a house uncomfortably shared by the Palestinian who used to live in it and the Jewish general who owns it now. The house speaks, as does a camel (the house's would-be love interest). In Richard Rose's production, the actors, given impossible roles, vary only in their degrees of unnaturalness. The title refers not just to language barriers but to the proposal of the General's 15-year-old son to bring peace by having everyone practice cunnilingus. An alternative pun, given that the boy is said to have been found floating on the river in his cradle, might be Go Down, Moses.

- Doubt runs through May 30 at the Bluma Appel Theatre; call 416-368-3110 for details. Tuesdays with Morrie runs through May 31 at the Winter Garden Theatre; call 416-872-5555 for tickets. House of Many Tongues runs through June 3 at the Tarragon Theatre; call 416-531-1827 for more information.

THEATRE REVIEW

SEVEN JEWISH CHILDREN: A PLAY FOR GAZA

Theatre Passe Muraille Backspace

---

To dispose of some things that would be essential in most theatre reviews but are probably inessentials in this one: The performance of Caryl Churchill's 10-minute play Seven Jewish Children: A Play for Gaza, at Passe Muraille this past weekend, was admirably directed by Rose Plotek as a kind of spoken concert. Its 10 actors took turns reading the text at music stands, and most of them did it very well. Rosemary Dunsmore and R. H. Thomson were especially good

But that probably isn't what you want to know. You want to know if Churchill's already notorious play is anti-Semitic. It isn't. And it isn't just about Gaza. It's about facing the intolerable, either as a victim or as a possible aggressor, and especially about how you help your children to face it. The piece, more of a stage-poem than a conventional drama, is composed entirely of speeches. Each shows a parent debating about what to tell the child. How do you balance caution with reassurance? It's the most basic of parental challenges, taken to hideous extremes. The play presents situations in which it's rarely possible to know the right thing to do and never possible to know the right thing to say. It covers, in its short span, a remarkable amount of ground, historically and psychologically. As well as being about what people say to protect their children, it's about what they say to protect themselves.

We start with hiding out during the Holocaust: "Tell her it's important to be quiet ... Don't tell her they'll kill her." Then to the post-war revelations about the camps: "Tell her her uncles died ... Don't tell her they were killed ... Don't frighten her." Then, immigration to Israel: "Tell her it's sunny there ... Tell her we're going home." Then about the fact there are Arabs there: "Don't tell her I wouldn't have come if I'd known ... Tell her maybe we can share ... Don't tell her that." Then about the Six Day War: "Tell her how big their armies are ... tell her we turned them back." That, the briefest section, is the only one without negatives. But it's immediately balanced by a section on the first intifada: "Don't tell her they throw stones ... Tell her they're not much good against tanks ... Don't tell her they set off bombs in cafes ... Tell her, tell her, they set off bombs in cafes." That last line, by the way, disposes of the allegation that the play is fixated on Israeli atrocities and doesn't mention the Palestinian. (If the Israeli army hasn't committed any atrocities, then it's unique among all armies in world history. And though I'm Jewish, and generally pro-Israeli, I find that hard to believe.)

But then, it's amazing how much of this play's commentators have managed to ignore, including the "tell her ... don't tell her" alternation that is both the play's foundation and its bell-like refrain. (A review of the published script in Saturday's Globe and Mail managed to leave half the play out of its account, quite a feat with a work this short.) Most of the criticism has focused on the last section, the one that deals with the war in Gaza. It ends with a vengeful speech whose paragraph length, in contrast to all the previous measured one-liners, suggests hysteria. It ends: "tell her I look at one of their children covered in blood, and what do I feel? Tell her all I feel is happy it's not her." You can read that as generalized bloodlust or as a resurrection of the blood-guilt libel, but you'd have to ignore the last three words to do so. What we're being told is the plain truth: that the first instinct of any decent person in a war zone hearing of the death of a child would be relief that the child wasn't his or her own. And the second instinct would be to be ashamed of the first instinct, which is the progression for the speaker here. She draws back and says, again, "Don't tell her that." And then, "Tell her we love her." And then, "Don't frighten her." What else could she say?

Probably the experience of being in an enclosed space with this play is different from that of reading it. It makes you more inclined to empathize with the characters, less inclined to judge them. That's true even in this production's rehearsed-reading format, which precluded any heavy "acting" or remotely realistic staging: both, I'd say, to the good. It does begin, after all, with the Holocaust -- a subject on which, unlike the present-day Middle East, there's no room for moral or political debate -- and that beginning hangs heavy over the rest of the play; we aren't exactly given time to forget it. The later line "tell them they can't talk suffering to us" is as resonant as any in the play. (It was spoken here by Diana Donnelly, last seen as the descendant of Holocaust victims in East of Berlin.) Yes, I realize it's double-edged. I realize, too, that I've been going in for a certain amount of devil's advocacy. Churchill's own stated opinions outside the play are uncompromisingly pro-Palestinian, and I doubt if the play has got her into any fights with her chums at the Royal Court. But a playwright's ex cathedra attitudes aren't the same thing as her play; she probably wouldn't be much of a playwright if they were. Churchill at her best is a very good playwright and she's at her best here, with each apparently simple line carrying very complex freight. It dramatizes doubt -- unlike the eponymous Broadway confection that merely drops the name. Of course, a play so brief leaves a lot out. (The last major event at Passe Muraille was the marathon City of Wine. This theatre seems to like its plays very long or very short.) One could certainly conceive of a play that would examine the conflicted emotions of an Arab mother as she straps a suicide bomb onto her son. I doubt if those who hate this play would like that one very much either.
2009-05-23-relationships-start-off-on-th:
The lion of this year's Shaw Festival, at least in terms of share, is not the Irish maestro but an English one. The festival is reviving, in its entirety, the cycle of 10 one-act plays that Noel Coward wrote as vehicles for himself and Gertrude Lawrence, and that were first staged in 1936 under the umbrella title Tonight at 8:30. Niagara's opening triple bill is called Brief Encounters, after the legendary movie version of the playlet originally known -- and still known here--as Still Life.

This is the piece, a classic in both media, that taught the world about English railway stations and unconsummated English adultery. (At least it's unconsummated in the film; in the play it's an open question as to how thoroughly interruptus the coitus -- offstage, of course -- actually was.) Alec, a married doctor, meets Laura, also married, while they're both changing trains, and wins her heart by removing a piece of grit from her eye. Their affair, dogged by guilt and respectability, proceeds along a passionate but unhappy track, until finally derailed. (Well, if ever a metaphor was going begging ...) All their meetings that we see take place in the station cafe, where the staff conduct comparatively carefree flirtations, in ironic contrast to the customers who frequent the place in which they serve.

Jackie Maxwell, the director, has lined this play up with two others and found links between them, beyond the obvious one that they're all concerned with social codes. In We Were Dancing, a tongue-in-cheek fantasy set on Coward's favourite imaginary island of Samolo, the actors who played Alec and Laura reappear as a couple who fall into adulterous love with similar abruptness (in their case, because they were dancing) but refuse to keep it to themselves. Friends, spouses and relatives, once over being scandalized, give the lovers their blessing, at which point they rather rapidly get over it: a brief encounter indeed, and a nice insight into what might have befallen Alec and Laura had they persisted. Finally, we have Hands Across the Sea, which isn't about infidelity but which maintains continuity by transporting us from an outpost of the empire to a place obsessed with such. Lady Maureen Gilpin (a. k. a. Piggie) and her naval husband play host in their Mayfair flat to a couple they thought they knew from Malaya. This is a farce, of mistaken identities and ceaseless pixilated phone chat, that has been known to be very funny indeed, though it isn't here.

The plays -- the first two, anyway -- look great. William Schmuck has designed a travellers' rest that manages to make institutional austerity spectacular, thanks in large part to its remorselessly revolving doors, and a dazzling tropic isle that suddenly reveals the most wittily shimmering seas you ever saw. The changes between one play and the next are pretty spectacular, too. It's what goes on between them that's the problem, especially in Still Life, where Deborah Hay and Patrick Galligan make it hard to follow what's going on between the lovers, emotionally or even factually. The play is supposed to break your heart over the lost chances and brave choices of people who, because they're British, are too decent not to be repressed. (This is a myth, but everybody believes it and it's too late now.)But there has to be some passion to be repressed, and it's barely evident in this production; Hay is too young for the bind she's supposed to be in and Galligan too uniformly nice. They both have and provide a much better time as absurd reflections of their former selves in We Were Dancing, at one point breaking spontaneously into the title, and only, song. At least that's what the text says they do. Here, as if in defeated acknowledgement that they're not Noel and Gertie, they're joined by the whole company, in what looks like a Dorothy Lamour number infected by Bollywood. It's deafeningly lip-synched--I know that sounds like a contradiction in terms, but believe me -- and it's sort of fun, but it undermines the insouciant magic of the original. To the production's credit, it does manage to restore the right mood, with the curtain rising again on everybody's having apparently forgotten what they've just been doing. That's right; there are one-and-a-half plays on either side of the intermission. Cute.

The evening's secondary couple are Corinne Koslo and Thom Marriott, she at her best as the cafe manageress in the first play, he as a bemused intruder in the last. Michael Ball makes a lovely appearance in the middle one, looking like a wounded walrus. Goldie Semple is jarringly over the top in the first instalment, blessedly so in the other two. Her sozzled indignation is almost a lifesaver for Hands Across the Sea, a piece that otherwise looks and sounds marooned on what is suddenly a big and empty stage. It even swallows up the basic story. Meanwhile, up in the skyscape we get a procession of increasingly larger airships, as if that could somehow compensate for the lack of entertainment down below.

Back in Toronto, I recommend Fear of Flight, though more for its presentation than its substance. Originating (quite some time ago) with the Artistic Fraud company of Newfoundland, this depicts a storm-tossed cross-country plane trip, with vignettes of the passengers' past lives supplied by playwrights from all points along the flight path. Only one of these (written by Daniel MacIvor, performed by Mia Mansfield as an innocent lady travelling at the behest of Jesus, who in this incarnation sounds like a con man) is especially enlivening, but it's the group effort that counts. While hanging firmly on to their individual identities, the 14 actors combine brilliantly in a kind of acted ballet to which they also provide non-stop a cappella accompaniment. Jillian Keiley's production justifies the mountainous regard in which she's held across Canada. Actually, she'd already done that, for me, with her magnificent staging of Creon, the penultimate play in Ned Dickens's City of Wine cycle. The ultimate one, too--Seven, directed by Sarah Garton Stanley -- was a fine piece of vocal and visual orchestration, with the highest overall standard of acting (by mature York students) of the entire enterprise. Both plays brought the chorus to the forefront of the action: brilliantly so in Creon, which brought the Antigone story to new life, with too much repetition but to ultimately stirring effect in Seven. Collecting these last two episodes confirmed some of my earlier preconceptions, overturned others. Somebody remount the whole thing so I can write about it again. - Brief Encounters is in repertory through Oct. 24 at the Festival Theatre, Niagara-on-the-Lake. Call 1-800-511-SHAW for tickets. Fear of Flight runs through May 24 at the Factory Theatre. Call 416-504-9971 for details.
2009-05-25-the-king-et-al-a-production-t:
IN GOOD KING CHARLES'S GOLDEN DAYS

Royal George Theatre, Niagara-on-the-Lake

---

Bernard Shaw's In Good King Charles's Golden Days was the last of his plays to appear before the Second World War and the last to have remained in something approaching general currency. Like most of his late works, it's an unabashed discussion piece, with what might be called a relaxed attitude to character and even to theme. Relaxed but still active: The characters go where their author's interests take them, but they do so with a surprising degree of warmth. This is possibly Shaw's mellowest play, tormented though some of its characters are, and its current production is in the Shaw Festival's best tradition of articulate ensemble. There are no weak performances and a few outstanding ones.

The golden days are those of Charles II of England, the fabled "merry monarch" restored to the throne after the execution of his father and the brief republican rule of Oliver Cromwell. Charles may be most celebrated for the number of his mistresses, and he is here escorted, or pursued, by a trio of them:Nell Gwyn and a couple of duchesses. It was a time of scientific revolutions as well; Charles established the Royal Society and much of the play is set in the Cambridge home of that fellowship's leading light, Isaac Newton. An amiable but driven and tormented man, Newton is not pleased to have his house invaded and his work interrupted by a gaggle of celebrities; his highly respectable housekeeper Mrs. Basham is downright scandalized. She still buckles down and provides dinner for nine (with borrowed furniture), the list of uninvited guests being completed by George Fox, the first Quaker; the king's younger brother James, a fanatically unreconstructed Papist; and Godfrey Kneller, a portrait painter. They all parade their personal obsessions, a circus of ideas with the king as ringmaster.

This makes it, to juggle historical order in a way that both playwrights might approve, Shaw's most Stoppardian play, but it differs from Travesties (say) in having no central conflict, not even one as capacious as art vs. politics. And then there's the sex. The director, Eda Holmes, tries to unify the play by beginning with Newton's maid having an erotic daydream about the king; and later, when Charles goes home for an epilogue, having his sleeping couch surrounded by the phantasmal figures of his three lady friends before he wakes up to converse with the true chaste love of his life, his wife. But the real strength of the production, apart from graceful sets by Camellia Koo, lies in the wit, lucidity and occasional passion of the acting, and the way in which these qualities all flow together.

If there is an overall theme, it's in the struggle of Charles himself to maintain a precarious point of rest in a chronically violent world. It's splendidly captured by Benedict Campbell, who makes a deceptive start as a mere bluff and genial master of ceremonies, but who can unleash fury and scorn in an instant. The one thing this above-average sensual man cannot tolerate is intolerance, which means that he prizes good manners and that his one real enemy is his brother (a pugnacious Andrew Bunker).

Shaw's Newton is half genius, half virginal eccentric; Graeme Somerville, crowning a series of fine festival performances, imbues him with the priceless gift of making ideas sexy. In a time-travelling acknowledgment of Shaw's own acquaintance with Albert Einstein, Newton is provoked by Kneller (Ken James Stewart, prickly and promising) into a vision of a curvilinear universe, something that brings him both to exaltation and despair, since it would mean tearing up much of his own work (including a world chronology that Shaw himself pronounced mad). Also very fine is Ric Reid's proudly uncouth Fox, a variant on a familiar Shavian theme: the puritan seduced, if only intellectually, by art and female company. This comes principally in the form of Nicola Correia-Damude's Nell, who can declaim a tragic speech with no reference to its context and who charmingly drops a spoon when Newton expounds on gravity. The two haughtier wenches are done by a commanding Claire Jullien and, almost comprehensible through her French accent, Lisa Codrington. Mary Haney is briskly and expectedly superb as the housekeeper who will stand no nonsense (and is therefore much provoked); Laurie Paton is gravely enchanting as, in effect, the housekeeper's royal equivalent, the queen who came from Portugal and knows that, when these golden days are over, she'll have to return there. The royal domesticity, beautifully captured by both actors, was probably Shaw's idealized view of his own marriage. He seems to have lit on a historical period, taken what appealed (or appalled), and bound it together with sympathy rather than strict logic. So with this production: the Shaw's best Shaw in a number of years. - In Good King Charles's Golden Days continues to Oct. 9. For tickets and information call 1-800-511-SHAW or visit shawfest.com.
