2009-05-26-portrait-of-an-artist:
SUNDAY IN THE PARK WITH GEORGE

Royal George Theatre, Toronto

---

Of the two musicals that Stephen Sondheim and James Lapine wrote together in the 1980s, the first, Sunday in the Park with George, has generally been held in higher critical esteem than its successor, Into the Woods. The latter, based on fairy tales, has been disparaged as a kids' show, while the former is self-consciously about important things like Art. In fact, Into the Woods houses a seamless masterpiece, the modern theatre's nearest equivalent to A Midsummer Night's Dream, while Summer in the Park greatness, though it certainly exists, flashes disconcertingly on and off. Alisa Palmer's Shaw Festival production is uneven, but it's still the most satisfying I've seen, the only one in which the emotional resolutions of the evening's second half top the more cerebral pleasures of the first.

Like Into the Woods, Sunday in the Park has a first act that seems complete in itself until you experience the second; and that would in fact be cute but unsatisfying if you didn't experience the second. The first act climax is a tableau vivant representation of Georges Seurat's giant group painting A Sunday Afternoon on the Island of La Grande Jatte, a modern pastoral for a new industrial age. We've spent the evening thus far watching Seurat -- George to us -- on location, sketching the various weekending figures who make up both the picture's and the musical's supporting cast, and then refining the sketches in his studio. Now, we watch the final assembly. George moves the other actors around the stage until he has them where he wants them; meantime, they sing a soaring chorale at whose final tolling notes the painting has taken shape before our eyes.

Standing at the front of the group, placed there at the last moment as a form of amends, is Dot, George's former model and mistress, whoin real life is about to leave Paris for a new life with a new man in America. She's pregnant with George's child, but has been turned off by his absorption in his work. History tells us little about Seurat, and it naturally tells us nothing about the people -- soldiers, domestics, assorted bourgeois --in his painting; Lapine's libretto has had to invent biographies for them, none of which amount to more than grudging vignettes. A minor exception is an old lady who turns out, with endearing abruptness, to be the absentminded George's mother; a major one is Dot, who takes her name from Seurat's own pointillist

technique. (If Andrew Lloyd Webber had written this show, it would have been called Dots.) And that revolutionary style is reflected in Sondheim's score, its melodies marked out in stabbing, iridescent shafts of sound. And these motifs build and echo from one song to another so that a late number (Move On) becomes, not a reprise of an earlier one (We Do Not Belong Together) but an expansion and glorification of it.

The ache, the yearning and the discipline that distinguish Sondheim's music also find wonderful expression in Finishing the Hat, which might be called George's vocational number. It's hard, the song and the show tell us, being an artist. (Indeed. But then, it's hard being anything.) But it works more as a window into George's craft than into his character. He's aloof and dedicated, Dot is vivacious and instinctive, and the others are lay figures: by definition, of course. This thinness of personality is obviously intentional (it's telling that only George and Dot have numbers of their own) but it's also, in a Sondheim show, frustrating. Act Two moves us from 1884 to 1984 and from Paris to New York: Seurat's (fictitious) great-grandson, also called George, is a laser sculptor who calls his creations Chromolumes, his latest being a homage to his namesake's masterpiece. He's accompanied by his wheelchair-bound grandmother Marie, the daughter Dot was carrying. Unlike George the Brushwielder, who never sold a painting, George the Chromluminary is professionally feted and artistically frustrated;

he has to spend most of his energies raising money (his art, he sings sardonically, "needs a Foundation"). The satire on the art world is fairly facile -- these people, too, are dummies -- but when young George makes a pilgrimage to the Parisian park, where the spectral presence of Dot gives him the understanding and encouragement she could never offer his predecessor, the show takes on a new life. At least it does here, as I've never known it do before. This is largely due to Steven Sutcliffe, who may not have the vocal plangency of Mandy Patinkin, creator of the double role, but is a far more sympathetic actor. A trifle stiff as George One, he makes George Two a restless, vulnerable and wholly believable figure. When he sings the soul-searching Lesson #8 (title courtesy of Dot's old grammar book) the show's themes come together as his personal quest: past and present, tradition and innovation, Children and Art. That last coupling is the title of Dot's last great song: an example of unifying a show by main force. (Though what of childless non-artists? Are their lives nothing?)

Julie Martell as Dot/Marie may have a tougher job than her co-star, since she has to compete with memories of Bernadette Peters, who was incomparable. Surprisingly, for a young performer who's mainly done musicals, she's stronger as old Marie than as young Dot, and comes across better in speech than in song. The latter isn't just her problem; the Shaw tradition of unmiked voices is a noble one but Paul Sportelli's orchestra, giving an otherwise exemplary account of what sound like the original orchestrations, often drowns out the words. Two supporting actors stand out: Kyle Blair in what turns out to be the key role of American George's technical assistant (who opts to work for some less demanding employer, like NASA) and especially Sharry Flett, a revelation as French George's mama whose longings for life, and especially trees, as they used to be, have enormous resonance. The Act One finale is not, because of fussy staging, to be as stirring as it should be. The Act Two finale, immediately due to Sutcliffe but with Flett having helped prepare the ground, is moving even to tears. - Sunday in the Park with George is in repertory until Nov. 1. For show times and ticket information, call 1-800-511-SHAW or visit shawfest.com.

2009-05-28-a-drink-to-their-stealth:
Jim Mezon, in the Shaw Festival's production of A Moon for the Misbegotten, gives the most riotously funny performance I have ever seen in a Eugene O'Neill play. That, admittedly, is not much of a contest; in fact, I can't think of a single competitor. But if it's a departure in my experience of O'Neill, it's also a departure in my experience of Mezon. I associate him with chillingly powerful level-toned characters, men who don't need to raise their voices in order to command respect. I've sometimes wished that he would shout a bit, that he would, literally and metaphorically, get his hands dirty.

Well, here he does, plenty. He plays Phil Hogan, an Irish-American tenant-farmer, tilling unforgiving soil in 1923 Connecticut. Phil is a roaring, swaying drunk most hours of the day and night, except for maybe a few hours, say late morning, when he's just gearing up. Phil has three sons, who have understandably left home; and a daughter, Josie, a strapping lass with a self-nourished reputation as the town tramp. Josie isn't about to leave, for complicated reasons that furnish some of the play's comedy and more of its tragedy. She nags at Phil, he storms at her, but they're locked together and they know it. Jenny Young isn't built to Josie's physical scale, and you sometimes have to close your eyes and imagine somebody else. But what she lacks in heft, she makes up in tenacity. This is a generous performance, in rage as much as in love. Josie has a lot of both, though dispensing the former comes easier. She also has a lot of pain, some secrets and much pride, and the elements combust.

Father and daughter might easily have been transported from an actual Irish play; they have the brogue and the blarney though not, mercifully, the whimsy. Writing Irish seems to have released a richness and sharpness in O'Neill that you don't find elsewhere in his work, and the actors here seem to rejoice in it: "You're worse than dacent," goes one choice insult,

"you're vartuous." If the play were just about Phil and Josie, then it might be a masterpiece and Joseph Ziegler's production an unqualified delight.

But it isn't just about them. It's also about their landlord, Jim Tyrone Jr., a character based on O'Neill's alcoholic actor of an elder brother. Fearing that Jim may be about to sell the place from under them, Phil comes up with a plan to surprise him in bed with Josie so that he will marry her or, at the very least, refrain from evicting her. Jim has always admired Josie, especially -- as he confirms more than once -- her big breasts. A man with extensive experience of whores, Jim seriously doubts Josie's claim to be of their number. It's reckoned by all parties that romance and whisky will do their work, once the two young -- well, younger -- people are alone together under the moon from which the play derives its title.

Moon is one of O'Neill's very late, very long plays: three hours and up. There are acres of repetitive exposition and two minor characters who aren't really necessary. It's true too that by the time the moonlight rendezvous rolls around, we've been made exhaustively aware of the characters' tangle of conflicting expectations, and the scene is potentially richer for it. It turns out, though, that for O'Neill, still obsessed with his own family, the Hogans' predicament is secondary to the self-torment of Tyrone. There are several drawbacks to this: a) he isn't our brother; b) though he too has Irish blood, he speaks in the Yankee gin-mill slang that O'Neill never managed to make sing, interspersed with wiseacre aphorisms like "our land of the free and the get-rich-quick;" and c)-- the fatal one-- he's played by the spiritually clean-cut David Jansen, who at one point manages a passable physical approximation of the delirium tremens but gets nowhere near their despairing essence. The production still manages to squeeze some tenderness out of this strangest of love scenes, but it's a shadow of what it should be, which in turn makes the play's ending less bittersweet than frustrating. I should say that it beats any other production I've seen. It's still O'Neill, great through all his faults, and Mezon's performance is at once toxic and intoxicating: a cocktail of brute cunning and shamefaced compassion, with the ingredients contending for passage through every grimy pore. Not that Phil would ever lower himself to anything as adulterated as a cocktail. - A Moon for the Misbegotten continues until Oct. 9. 2009-05-29-billie-trying-to-be-a-hero:
BORN YESTERDAY

Festival Theatre, Niagara-on-the Lake

---

It's 1945. Harry Brock, a tough operator who made a fortune in scrap during the war, has arrived in Washington to corner the junk market for good and all. He has an ex-idealist lawyer to counsel him and a tame senator to sponsor the necessary bill. Harry doesn't break laws so much as bypass them, though he could certainly break legs if pushed. Ensconced with him in his very luxurious hotel suite is his girlfriend Billie Dawn, former Broadway chorine, who in addition to her obvious uses comes in very handy for putting her signature to documents she hasn't read. But then she doesn't read much of anything. That would mean putting on glasses, which she's convinced would ruin her looks.

Billie is the girl played by Judy Holliday in the movie Born Yesterday; they immortalized one another. The Shaw Festival has revived the Garson Kanin play on which the film was based, a play that might, especially at the Shaw, be subtitled Eliza Doolittle Goes to Washington. Harry gets to worrying that Billie might embarrass him in front of the high-toned people he needs to impress, so he hires someone to educate her. The someone is Paul Verrall, a journalist whose idealism is emphatically not ex-(man, he writes for The New Republic) and who wears glasses all the time. It comes as no surprise that Paul's pedagogy so transforms Billie that she gets to questioning her protector's business practices, especially the ways in which they run counter to what she has now learned about the U. S. Constitution. Along the way, I need hardly add, Paul and Billie fall in love.

The play is part screwball comedy, part melodrama and part -- a large part -- Democracy 101. It's also, of course, topical. The senator promises "no interference with free enterprise -- foreign or domestic." A hotel maid, taking in Sue LePage's supremely enviable set, observes, "While I'm getting $18 a week, I don't see why anyone should spend $235 a day," to which Paul dryly replies, "I know some people who'd call you a communist," to which she replies, "Tell them I'm thinking about it. Seriously." I'm not sure that the play ever improves on that for trenchancy: not when Harry's corrupted mouthpiece, who's drinking to forget, starts remembering; not when Paul starts quoting improving books, and dropping names like Tom

Paine; and certainly not when Billie starts quoting and name-dropping right back. The play is unquestionably on the side of the angels, but it gets mighty self-congratulatory about it.

Gina Wilkinson, directing, cannot unify the play's different styles, but she manages each very well on its own terms; hers is a very assured festival debut. An interpolated bellhops' ballet near the beginning points us down a blind and campy alley; and a prolonged game of gin rummy that's a classic on the screen just seems mystifying in long shot. But a symbolic book-burning is a fruitful invention, as is the decision to have Billie not merely boast of the five lines she once had in Anything Goes, but recite them. Funny in itself, it also feeds very nicely into Billie's adoption of that show's title song as her personal theme, which in turn guarantees that the audience's toes will be tapping for the curtain call.

The staging is smart and teamwork impeccable. As for individual performances, my only major beef is with Deborah Hay's Billie, a curious reservation to have since she's very talented and seems to be doing everything right: the teetering walk, the hard-boiled innocence, the corncrake voice. I blame the play. It banks heavily on the charm of hearing liberal verities delivered in a traditional dumb-blond squawk, thereby patronizing both the character and the audience. Eliza in Pygmalion didn't merely lose an accent, she gained a soul or rather discovered one that was there all along, but Billie only has a set of circumstances. Holliday humanized her, but she was unique.

The men in her life actually offer more scope. Gray Powell, latest in the Shaw's uncommon line of intelligent juvenile leads, is a perfect Paul, the picture of humorous integrity, while Thom Marriott makes Harry into a surprisingly complex brute, and unable at bottom to believe that he could be doing anything wrong. It isn't only his pride that is hurt when Billie deserts him, it's his ambitions. The dread that he too might be thought stupid really gets to him. And he does have his own smarts; when he's told that he can't have his cake and eat it, he says that it don't make sense, which it's about time somebody said.

There's reliable support work from Patrick Galligan and Lorne Kennedy, and Ali Momen makes a neat impression as Harry's cousin, a reluctant thug. The first night audience raised the roof, and the show does offer a good time. But Shaw, O'Neill and Sondheim offer better ones. - Born Yesterday is in repertory until Nov. 1. Call 1-800-511-SHAW or visit shawfest.com for tickets and information.

2009-05-30-back-to-the-future-stratford-:
Earlier this year. I chaired a panel, all of whose members have ended up pursuing careers different from, but related to, those they had originally envisaged. One of its members was Antoni Cimolino, general director of the Stratford Festival Theatre. Most of his working-life has been spent at Stratford, and in the early '90s he was an actor there, scoring some notable roles: Romeo to Megan Follows's Juliet and Laertes to Stephen Ouimette's Hamlet. But then he found that while onstage, his concentration was wandering. This is not a desirable quality in an actor; given the propensity of both Romeo and Laertes to engage in duels, it could even have been a physically dangerous one.

So Cimolino turned to directing, which both permits and demands a wider view of the whole process, and from there increasingly into administration. He was the right-hand man of Stratford's late artistic director, Richard Monette, and when Monette retired, he was promoted to the newly created position he holds now. The initial plan was that he would work in concert with a trio of artistic directors; after last year's well-publicized (though still largely mysterious) disagreements, the three were reduced to one, Des McAnuff.

"Des," said Cimolino, when I spoke to him recently over dinner and, later, by phone, "chooses the plays, the actors, the directors." But it isn't as if Cimolino has renounced all artistic interests. He says he doesn't miss acting but does miss directing; and this season, after abstaining for a year, he's returning to that role with Batholomew Fair, by Shakespeare's critic, eulogist, rival and drinking buddy, Ben Jonson.

It's a bold choice. This will apparently be the 400-year-old play's professional premiere; when the British director William Gaskill, an old mentor of Cimolino's, was told about it, his reaction was "good luck." It's a detailed, sprawling down-and-dirty realistic comedy of a kind far removed from Shakespeare. For one thing, as Cimolino notes, it tells you far more about Puritans -- the progressives, however uncomfortable, of their time. Speaking of "the brilliance in Jonson," he says what a thrill and a challenge it's been for the actors to "immerse themselves in the language, and in a very different view of London." It's almost a Jacobean documentary, so it's encouraging that Cimolino, unlike some recent British directors, is doing it in period.

The plays of Shakespeare's contemporaries are an obvious way for Stratford to extend its repertoire, and since I've been saying so for years, I'mobviously pleased to find Cimolino, with McAnuff's encouragement, going that route. The plays don't even have to be English; one of the treats of last season was the Spanish classic Fuente Ovejuna, which some customers, when placing their orders, referred to as "that play with all the vowels" but which they enjoyed when they got there.

"People were extremely moved by that play," says Cimolino. "In terms of Western thought, it's an important defence of average people. There's a direct line to Beaumarchais" -- the French playwright whose Marriage of Figaro prefigured the Revolution. Cimolino has an impressively wide range of cultural reference; Monette once divided Stratford's directors into the showmen and the intellectuals, and Cimolino, despite his image as an organization man, is one of the intellectuals. He envisages "more work from Shakespeare's contemporaries, from the Greeks, a broader range of European classics, work from non-Western culture," naming, as an example, the Indian writer Rabindranath Tagore. "We're the national theatre of a diverse population."

That kind of exploration involves risk, of course, and therefore money: Stratford this year is visibly drawing in its horns. There are only three Shakespeares this season, one of them at the Avon. Cimolino points out that this isn't unprecedented: "In 2000, we only did two." (He has the dates at his fingertips.) But the fact remains: Last year, when Stratford put "Shakespeare" back in its title, it made a great fuss over having five of his plays on the Festival stage and banishing musicals to the Avon. This year, West Side Story is in the main house. That may be good, bad or indifferent, but it's a change.

Of course, it's about funding. Stratford, battered by its own economy, and the world's, announced at one point that it was cancelling eight performances. These have now been restored, thanks to a $3-million grant from the federal government, and another $500,000 from Ontario. "Our forecast," says Cimolino, sounding cautious, "is pointing towards break-even." All this welcome money, though, comes out of tourism budgets; it's meant for marketing productions, not for creating them.

Support for that comes from the Ontario Arts Council and the Canada Council. Their combined contribution is $2.5-million, amounting to 4% of total revenue, which, Cimilino says, is "with the greatest respect, highly inadequate." This isn't just compared to the subsidized companies in the U. K. "Canadian Stage receives more support than we do, with a much smaller operation. We're the largest theatre in North America, and -- in percentage terms -- the least funded." He sees the arts councils' attitude as "how little funding can we give them, and still have them survive?" He's probably right.

He's also right that, whatever the vagaries of particular seasons, the festival is "a precious asset -- we should be making the most of it. We attract hundreds of thousands of audiences from all over the world." It's a myth, apparently, that American audiences ("half of them from Michigan") only support the musicals: "They can see those at home. They come for the classics."

They even, he says, enjoy Canadian plays. With more financial security, Stratford could do more new plays, more unfamiliar classics, extend rehearsal periods, tour productions (even to Toronto), and expand its educational programs, which include "teaching Shakespeare to teachers."

Above all, it can preserve and nurture its acting company, "the single greatest resource for acting of Shakespeare in the world," with the kind of continuity that has long since ceased to exist in the U. K. Seeing an actor like the late William Hutt "changes a young actor's idea of what the possibilities are. If there isn't a place for a Bill Hutt to work, then we're all the poorer for that."

And on a final inspirational note: "I don't think actors are as good as they can be, unless they tackle Shakespeare. He beggars our best talents but exalts them as well."

2009-05-30-ghosts-of-authors-haunt-etern:
The Crows Theatre production of Eternal Hydra is a visually impressive and finely acted staging of an interesting play. I have an unworthy suspicion, though, that the text and the presentation (but not the acting) may be working against one another.

Anton Piatigorskys play, which made a one-act debut in the Stratford studio a few years ago, now reappears as that almost extinct species, a two-acter, complete with intermission. It also belongs to the definitely thriving species, the literary fantasia. It begins by quoting the recently fashionable idea of the death of the author, and then proceeds to suggest that even writers and critics who might subscribe to it as a theory, tend to balk at it when it's their own rights that are being withheld. The author at the centre of this play, one Gordias Carbuncle (all names are fictitious, though no others are this unlikely) actually is dead, in the clinical sense, but won't lie down. He haunts an

English literary scholar named Vivian Ezra, whos adopted him as her pet cause and special subject, and has come into possession of the long-lost almost-complete manuscript of his magnum opus: 99 out of a projected 100 chapters of a novel entitled, with double appropriateness, Eternal Hydra. So: Who cut off its last head, and do we care? Or, as a possible publisher says of the book, "I know its great but is it any good?" Carbuncle had a James Joycean background, as well as Joycean ambitions: He is, or was an Irish Jew. That, somebody remarks to him in a flashback, is an unusual combination. Why do you think I left? he snaps back smartly. I have to confess, David Ferry's delivery of this line was my favourite moment of the evening.

Like all authors, dead or otherwise, Carbuncle wants recognition, and he gets very agitated when Vivien seems to be blowing his chances of posthumous publication. She demurs because the New York publisher wants simultaneously to issue a novel by a current black writer Pauline Newberry, in which Gordias is a character, meaning that thunder would be stolen and reputations possibly defamed. It turns out, though, that Gordias was quite the appropriator himself, when he got the chance. We see him in Paris, between the wars, exploiting, intellectually and sexually, the writer/researcher who's done much of his work for him. He makes a less successful pass at a stranded American writer from whom he nevertheless buys the story of her ex-slave grandmother in New Orleans, subsequently putting it in his book. And he fends off the advances of a gay admirer from whom he still succeeds in extracting a cheque.

My main memory of the Stratford production is that it left me wondering if that was all. Despite the extensions and expansions Piatigorsky has put in, I felt much the same now. The play has got more complicated but not necessarily more complex. It now ends with a complete departure: the acting out of the grandmothers story, depicting a suffrage meeting that turned into a race riot. Black people are killed, but a white politician is able to prosper by making their cause his platform. More appropriation, though presumably done with good intentions. And there the play ends, cutting us adrift from the characters we previously knew. Its frustrating, and not just on a narrative level. We're left wondering -- at least I was -- whether we've watched a literal enactment of the purloined story or whether Carbuncle might have touched it up a bit, maybe even transformed it. Does he really have any talent? He certainly has all the trappings, especially the drinking and the sponging. Really, of course, there is no "really." Piatigorsky himself invented everything, and he isnt dead, in any sense. He has a program credit to prove it. The play takes off from a critical theory that nobody has ever found interesting. And as for appropriation: All fiction writers appropriate. Otherwise, theyd have nothing to write about. Race doesn't make any difference. The only issues are copyright ones.

It's tempting to compare this play to those of Tom Stoppard or his lesser-known compatriot Terry Johnson. But they take off from actual figures and/or actual texts; theyre dizzying, but theres solid ground beneath them. They're less cerebral (meaning, among other things, that they're funnier, in texture and structure as well as in individual lines) and easier to follow, partly because you really want to follow them. In Chris Abrahams production of this one, the issues are murky, partly because the stage is. It has striking groupings and transitions, jolting lighting (John Thompson), scary sound (Richard Feren). But the atmospherics drown the text, blinding us with science. The acting, though, is terrific. Everybody doubles, in and out of time frames. Ferry adds the Louisiana pol to his Carbuncle, whos a double in himself: endearingly vain and insecure when dead, disturbingly so when alive, with a vein of self-hatred that may take this actor deeper, and stiller, than he's ever been before. Liisa Repo-Martell is authentic to the bone as a particularly British kind of scholarly sleuth, nervous but implacable, and Karen Robinson, forceful in her present-day persona, is both touchingly shy and heartbreakingly proud when transported to the past. Sam Malkin plays two generations of possible patrons, one of whom says of Gordias' masterwork "I know its great. But is it any good?"

I didnt know the Far East was obsessed with the Wild West, but I'll take Anand Rajaram's word for it. This shining ornament of Second City has devised a wordless entertainment, irresistibly titled Cowboys and Indians, in which Rajaram acts out a very rich fantasy life. A little mime goes a marathon for me, but it's wonderful to watch him dealing resentfully with an unwelcome alarm call, mounting a refractory and contemptuous horse (whom he also momentarily plays), cowering in jail, or climbing all over the audience, in angry search of whoever's done him wrong. He has an accompanist, Bob Wiseman, who conjures ruby-rich harmonies out of a honky-tonk; Rajaram turns on him, too, with a terrifying fury, suggesting meekness too long provoked Some people are appallingly talented.

- Eternal Hydra runs through May 31 at Buddies in Bad Times. Call 416-975-8555 for ticket information; Cowboys and Indians runs though June 7 at the Factory Studio. Call 416-504-9971 for tickets and schedule information.
2009-06-03-a-tempting-tyrant-colm-feore-:
MACBETH

Festival Theatre, Stratford, Ont.

---

Colm Feore playing Macbeth takes time to get into his stride, but it's an impressive one when he hits it. His earlier scenes have the strange effect of turning lucidity into a kind of obscurity. When he lays out the reasons why he shouldn't be killing Duncan, it seems an open-and-shut case; there's no agony, no doubt, no sense that he's actually feeling the very thing he seems to be arguing against. Yanna McIntosh's Lady Macbeth has her work cut out making any kind of dent in him. Macbeth may not be a clever man, but he's certainly an imaginative one; Feore gives us hardly a glimpse of the demons within.

This changes after the murder, in his baffled, agonized recounting of his inability to say "amen." From that moment, he's a lost soul and he knows it. The rest of the performance shows him coming to terms with this. It involves some revelatory approaches to familiar passages. Macbeth's rant, after the murder is discovered, about this being the end of the world ("nothing serious in mortality"), is generally played as an exaggerated attempt to cover up his own guilt; from Feore, it's an accurate account of his own spiritual state. Once enthroned, he slips into the role of self-preserving tyrant with cynical ease. His scene with Banquo's murderers is a reenactment of his own progress; once the tempted, he's now the tempter, and relishing it. It helps that Sean Arbuckle and Peter Hutt play the two killers not as the usual hardened thugs but as men with actual grudges and grievances, itches that need to be scratched.

It takes a ghostly visitation to shake this Macbeth; confronted by Banquo at the banquet, he climbs on the table and tries shooting a man already dead. It isn't guilt that possesses him, but weary frustration. At "blood will have blood" he's halfway down the road to the nihilism of "tomorrow and tomorrow and tomorrow," a mood that Feore, unusually and persuasively, prolongs into the final battle. He falters only at the revelation that Macduff is "not of woman born," as in too many productions, both actors rush over this ghastly sick pun-- the climax of the play -- as if they'd heard it already. This isn't a moving performance; Feore, at least in my experience, is not a moving actor, and Macbeth is not a moving character. He should, though, involve you in his nightmare, and Feore does this only occasionally. But he's fascinating and, in damned spots, harrowing.

His real ace is his command, both technical and intellectual, of the text. He continually comes up with surprising new readings that turn out to be absolutely valid. He acts the language, a rare but essential skill born partly of experience, and fully displayed here by only two other actors: Geraint Wyn-Davies, the suavest Duncan I've ever seen, and Tom Rooney, who for five glorious minutes turns the Scottish play into a play about a porter. McIntosh, who's done up to exploit a catchpenny resemblance to Michelle Obama, certainly has the ability, but she only comes into her own after she and her partner have spiritually split up: when they commiserate over their shared need for a good night's sleep, or in her own sleepwalking, which is terrifying. The couple's best moment isn't in the text; just before her death, she silently crosses the stage while her husband asks the doctor about "ministering to a mind diseased." He doesn't sympathize, but he identifies.

Des McAnuff's production is set in what his program-note calls "mythic mid-20th-century Africa." I doubt I'd have known if he hadn't told me. True, one actor appears in a golden robe, and the cast is about equally divided between black and white, plus a couple of Asians. But there's no discernible pattern to the division; and the witches, whom you'd think might benefit, are feeble. The idea seems to be that a regime is being changed through outside -- i. e. English -- intervention. "Stands Scotland where it did?" Apparently not, and God knows where England is supposed to be. This business is what I think of, perhaps unfairly, as American Shakespeare: the imposition of a concept that's at best peripheral and at worst irrelevant. Proof is that Macbeth himself, whom the play is about, never says a word about colonialism: For him, enemies are just enemies. The play's main interest isn't geopolitical, and casting Machiavellian aspersions on its shadowy "good" characters doesn't make them any more interesting. McAnuff's staging ranges from flashy to genuinely imaginative. The banquet is a tour-de-force, and tensions in individual scenes are intelligently exposed. But the production did leave me pondering, as never before, over one of the play's unanswered questions. Given his murderous fury over the prospect of Banquo's heirs succeeding him, does the childless Macbeth intend to try again some time with another Lady? And if so, what does he intend to do with the present one? It's enough to keep her up at night.

- Macbeth is in repertory through Oct. 31. For tickets and information call 1-800-567-1600 or visit stratfordfestival. ca.

2009-06-04-the-discerning-upper-crust-wo:
THE IMPORTANCE OF BEING EARNEST

Avon Theatre, Stratford, On.

---

The recent stage history of The Importance of Being Earnest has not, among high-grade Canadian companies, been a happy one. The new Stratford production doesn't just break that jinx; it treads it, rejoicing, beneath its several pairs of dainty but implacable feet. It gets everything right.

It makes the dialogue work and it makes the plot work. Perhaps the greatest satisfaction of Brian Bedford's production is the joy it dispenses at seeing the absurd symmetry of the action play itself out. In most stagings, the story of Earnest is ignored, perhaps because it's assumed that everyone knows it, while the lines get the wrong kind of attention: the laboured kind. Everybody falls in love at first hearing with this play's endless procession of jokes, but once you've heard them, you've heard them. If they are to keep on delighting us, they not only have to be impeccably delivered, they also have to be impeccably motivated. That's what happens here. Every line is keyed to what its speaker hopes to get out of it, or what he or she hopes to conceal with it. This goes even for the obvious, apparently detachable epigrams; they're counters in a non-stop game of one-upmanship.

As everyone knows, Oscar Wilde's play, like all English comedies and most English dramas, is about class, the ongoing joke being that the conflicts are kept invisible while being fearfully present in everyone's minds. Its first quotable line is the one about the lower classes owing it to their superiors to set a good example (otherwise, "What on earth is the use of them?"), and even before that we've been treated to a subterranean duel between master and man over the merits of the former's piano playing. Indeed, before a line has been spoken, Robert Persichini's manservant, wincing at each misplaced offstage note, has clued us in that this is to be an exceptional evening.

The program notes, including Bedford's own, make great play with the word "subversive;" and it's true that Wilde, on the eve of his own downfall, took great barbed pleasure in having aristocratic society condemn itself out of its own mouth. That doesn't exactly make it The Communist Manifesto; it's unlikely that even in 1895, when the barbs were fresh, they led to any acts of what Lady Bracknell calls "revolutionary outrage." As it happens Bedford, who himself plays Lady B without a trace of pantomime dame, creased me up more violently with that line than with any other of the evening. It's not merely that it was immaculately phrased in itself, though Bedford's entire third-act performance is a sublime comic concerto; it's the way in which it embodies, in its appalled dismissive-ness, the lady's entire mindset. She summons a spectre and then crushes it with the vocal equivalent of a glance. No wonder Jack Worthing compares her to a Gorgon.

Lady Bracknell may be the play's legendary role, but it's the two young men, Jack and Algy, who have to do the heavy lifting; they run the first act together and the second by turns. Their casting here is unimprovable. For a start, the actors' natural pulse rates --Ben Carlson's brisk, Mike Shara's languid -- complement one another as perfectly as they suit the characters. Both of them are leading double lives, but it's the respectable Jack who has the most to lose; his propriety begets anxiety, and Carlson, furtively hearty, plays both to the hilt. He's the production's motor. I've read of actors provoking hysterics when Jack, in mourning for an imaginary brother, produces a black-bordered handkerchief, but I've never experienced it before. Jack is the one character who knows his conduct is ridiculous but could never admit that he himself is. He really is earnest. Shara, in a waistcoat that Wilde himself

might have envied, is enchantingly shameless, a duck's back to his friend's moralizing water. And though this may be the least sentimental play ever written, the revelation that they are in fact brothers comes within a few yards of being touching.

The two girls match them, with Sara Topham's impregnable hauteur as Gwendolen balanced by Andrea Runge's demurer steeliness as Cecily. As Reverend Chasuble, Stephen Ouimette, a visual symphony of limbs and gaiters, wafts phantasmally through the manor-house garden; Sarah Dodd's Miss Prism melts delightfully though always respectably in his presence. I thought at first she overdid her suburban asperity towards Cecily, on whom she is after all dependent, but on reflection she makes an excellent point. Prism, though personally as blinkered as Lady Bracknell, is the play's social conscience, prevented as a governess from aping the aristocracy as the butlers and valets do. And she has her unwitting revenge. One wouldn't want to throw the baby out with the bath-water, but leaving it in a handbag is an outrage as revolutionary as Aunt Augusta knew in her threatened bones that it would be. - The Importance of Being Earnest is in repertory through Oct. 30. 1-800-567-1600.

2009-06-06-sisters-doing-it-for-and-to-t:
Some people believe that the fourth and final act of Chekhov's Three Sisters is the high-water mark of modern drama. And it might be if it weren't for the existence of the act that comes before it. Act 4 is a succession of personal Calvaries, shot through with laughter that's sometimes bitterly ironic and occasionally just plain funny. You could hardly ask for more. But in Act 3 you get it; you witness the ascent up the mountain, a process that involves hope and despair, depending on whom you're looking at; one person's triumph involves another's defeat and both, you know at the time, are going to be transitory.

That at least is how it goes in Martha Henry's amazing new production at Stratford, a triumph of what I can best call personal interlocking. It's the scene of the town fire. The house of the three Prozorov sisters has become an impromptu centre for disaster relief. Everybody they know in their provincial town drifts in and then out, among them the drunken old army doctor Chebutykin, confessing as so often before that he's forgotten all the medicine he ever knew. This time, though, it isn't a joke; he's killed a patient. James Blendick is an actor who can seem trapped in his own orotund delivery, and there are moments in this show when he's too much the one-man chorus. But he rises superbly to this, his great moment of truth-telling, and especially to the twice-repeated allegation that Natasha, the shrewish wife of the sisters' feckless brother is -- in Susan Coyne's live-wire adaptation -- "having it off with Protopopov," the unseen town councillor who seems to control everyone's destiny, including that of the man he's cuckolding.

The doctor's audience includes the schoolteacher Kuligin, who, in Peter Hutt's performance, is visibly but ambiguously shocked: Perhaps it's because he is easily shockable, perhaps it's because he's come to suspect that his own wife, the middle sister, Masha, is having it off with someone, or soon will be. And present, too, is the very someone, the philandering and philosophizing Colonel Vershinin. When Masha enters, there ensues the most extraordinary seduction scene. Tom McCamus has played Vershinin as a man whose word-spinning, though it may originally have been born of conviction, also comes in very handy as an erotic weapon. He now uses it quite consciously as such, drawing off his boots as he talks about mankind's terrible present and glorious feature; Lucy Peacock's Masha, taking a conscious decision to be hypnotized, removes her own shoes and then her shawl. That's as far as it goes, but it's enough to detonate Masha's admission to her sisters -- who don't want to hear it -- that she loves Vershinin and her headlong departure, we assume, to his bed.

As in any first-rate Chekhov production, everything has roots, everything has consequences. The aftermath for Masha and Vershinin is an enforced farewell that McCamus plays as the superficial mugged by the tragic, and Peacock, who these last few years has become a great actress, plays with a feral despair so abandoned -- in both senses -- that you can hardly believe you're watching it. She played Masha at Stratford 20 years ago, so she's strictly too old for it, but she makes that work for her; Masha, with her rage and her boredom and her lightning changes of mood, is a drama queen who knows it: Hedda Gabler with a human face. (She always wears black, and everyone knows what that means in Chekhov.)

Irene Poole's Olga is her own kind of ageless, with an unusual edge to her long-sufferingness; when Hutt's Kuligin, indomitably well-meaning, says that he should have married her, she responds with a wince that could mean "I wish" or "horrors" but probably the latter. Dalal Badr has fewer technical resources than her fellows, but her Irina is a very honest account of an anti-ingenue. She isn't "radiant" as Olga says, and she too knows it. She's a study in settling for progressively less; her longing for Moscow less heartache than toothache. Outside the sisterhood, too, everyone has a developing biography. Kelli Fox's Natasha progresses by easy stages from outsider to virago, never suspecting her own conduct; Juan Chioran's Solyony, desperate for acceptance, wins some sympathy for his sinister solitude before it turns murderous. Two male studies in failure wring the heart: Gordon S. Miller's waster Andrei, delivering his visions of the future to a baby that probably isn't his, and Sean Arbuckle's Baron, adjusting the cushions on his chair before embarking on an oration, and desperately seeking a word of love from a fiancee who can't give it to him. I've never wished more devoutly for a supernatural rewrite that might avert his fate. Then there are the small-part seniors: Joyce Campion's octogenarian nurse (the only character who gets a happy ending -- maybe Chekhov is just telling us to wait) and Robert King's uncomprehending Ferapont who at one point, through a delicious invention it would be unfair to reveal, gets the stage to himself.

Performances apart, Henry's direction is superb, alternating huddled scenes with lonely spacious ones and making a tour de force of the abortive second-act revelry; the intimate Tom Patterson stage, of course, increased the impact sixfold. There have been other productions of Three Sisters that I've hugely admired, but none that has involved me as deeply with the characters as this one. It's one of the great evenings in the Canadian theatre. And I expect it will get richer.

- Three Sisters is in repertory at the Stratford Festival through Oct. 3 at the Tom Patterson Theatre, Stratford. Call 1-800-567-1600 or visit stratfordfestival. ca for ticket information.

2009-06-08-with-the-bard-out-to-pasture-:
THEATRE REVIEW

Tom Patterson Theatre, Stratford, Ont.

Ben Jonson's Bartholomew Fair is a play that seemingly sprawls and sprawls before revealing itself to be quite cunningly organized. It's a poetic documentary, though written entirely in prose except for a few songs and a sustained burst of doggerel. Its setting is a shyster's carnival, and its cast divides into two groups: those, a mixture of cheats and fools, who visit the fair; and those, cheats all, who operate within it. Together, these make up as bulging a list of important characters as in any play ever written. They are assembled in groups, mixed up and finally brought together as the audience of a play within the play, this being a show literally in miniature as it's performed by puppets. The reunion is also, as so often in comedy, a mock-trial. Only the final judgment here is that there's no judgment: We're all human, all frail "flesh and blood." It is, depending on how you look at it, either a deeply cynical world-view or a joyously tolerant one.

Antoni Cimolino's Stratford production (the play's North American premiere, 395 years after its British one) takes the tolerant view which, especially in the theatre, has to be the right one. Jonson, notoriously censorious in his earlier plays, became surprisingly mellow and accepting in his late ones, of which Bartholomew Fair is the first and greatest. Maybe the retirement of his friend and rival William Shakespeare had something to do with it; the market in festive comedy was no longer cornered. Not that the two of them ever spoke the same dramatic language; Jonson's, here more than ever, is topical, satirical, aggressive and obscene. He could be lyrical, too, but never for long and never here. His style may be tough, but it swings, and the great attraction of this production is that all of the performers in it seem to relish what they're saying and whom they're playing. There's a real sense of discovery here, on both sides of the house. The limitation is that hardly anyone seems quite rightly cast.

That sounds dogmatic, but Jonson was a dogmatic writer. He's notorious for practising "humours" comedy, meaning roughly that his characters are obsessives, and he's still at it here. The obsessions have to be hit hard, fast and clear, which is partly a matter of temperament and partly of technique. Like last year's Love's Labour's Lost, this production is largely cast from Stratford's conservatory, with a top-dressing of older actors including some of the best there are. Neither side does as well now as it did then, partly because no director gets to acquire the inside-track knowledge of a Jonson play that Michael Langham had of Love's Labour's, partly because the juniors then were dealing with a play and characters essentially as young as themselves. The stand-out here is Ian Lake, who gives the neatest performance of the evening as Trouble-all, an amiable madman with a thing about judicial warrants. His appearance halfway through is the show's turning-point -- which, to be fair, it always is because it's through his crazy agency that the play's succession of vignettes begins to shake down into a plot.

There is a sort of title character, Bartholomew Cokes, a rich young booby who visits Bartholomew Fair upon Bartholomew's Day and undergoes his own massacre, being happily robbed of everything he owns, including his fiancee; Trent Pardy gives him some sweetness but not the ecstasy of innocence that should possess this most gullible of gulls. The prime role among the elders is Adam Overdo, the local judge, working undercover to expose "enormities" and getting everything wrong; he is beaten, insulted and put in the stocks but persists through all humiliations and three separate disguises. Tom McCamus gives him great sidelong charm but is never credible as the occupant of even the humblest bench; he has no height to fall from. Juan Chioran thunders wondrously as Zeal-of-the-Land Busy, baker turned Puritan, who goes to the fair to eat roast pig and denounce idolatry including that of the puppets by whom his hypocrisy is decisively exposed; what he lacks is a sense of place and position, say a cockney accent. Brian Tree gets the surliness and pugnacity

of Wasp, a servant with the shortest fuse on record, but not the volume. Lucy Peacock, spectacularly padded at all conceivable points, is chuckle-some casting as Ursla the pig-woman, who's practically the fair personified, but once she's established the character's girth and vulgarity she has no place to go.

There's satisfying work from Jonathan Goad as a gambling gallant who loses one heiress and gets another, older but richer (note that, in a comedy without a love story, he's the closest thing to a hero); from Randy Hughson and Victor Ertmanis as a pair of pimps who put a couple of respectable women on the game, right under their husbands' noses; from Jesse Aaron Dwyer as a conscientious cutpurse; Michael Spencer-Davis in the minute role of an officer; and Cliff Saunders who runs a great puppet-show. The show itself is a production highlight, and though some of the fairground jollity is run-of-the-mill, there is also some good surprise staging and an unusually intelligent placing of actors in the auditorium. Jonsonian comedy, combining a thick text with the action of a farce, is a tough act; this is an encouraging start at cracking it. - Bartholomew Fair is in repertory through Oct. 2. 2009-06-09-not-so-witty-but-gritty-and-f:
The stature of most musicals, as of most plays, is commonly determined by their ability to withstand stagings different from the ones they were born with. With West Side Story, no one has ever had the chance to put that to the test, since the show is driven by dance; Jerome Robbins' original choreography is literally built into the contract. Subsequent directors and choreographers have chafed over this, but I doubt if many audiences have minded. Those ensemble numbers remain thrilling and, with Sergio Trujillo in charge of their recreation, they work superbly at Stratford. Cool is a knockout, and the Dance at the Gym not far behind. In a lighter and less confrontational mode, I Feel Pretty is a delight. The dancing, then, is great. Otherwise, the production, with one very important exception, isn't a patch on the one that the festival delivered, also with Trujillo as choreographer, 10 years ago.

The exception is Chilina Kennedy's Maria, who takes a lightning journey from teasing and bewitching ingenue to devastated and devastating tragedienne; in the rage, despair and determination with which she greets her

brother's death at her lover's hands, she beats all other Marias I've seen, and most Juliets. In a show built for triple threats, she's the only member of the cast who acts, sings and dances with equal authority. Tony, like Romeo, usually comes in second (though he didn't here, last time around) and Paul Nolan's is, as one of his own songs puts it, no better than all right: engagingly, indeed aggressively, ardent in speech and movement but missing out vocally on the urgency and excitement of Something's Coming, which only happens to be the best song in the score. He gets his biggest applause for swinging himself up bodily to Maria's balcony: an impressive feat certainly but one that also lifts the audience, right out of the story. At that, though, it's of a piece with the self-admiring high note that all Tonys are all required to sustain at the end of Maria (the song, not the girl.). And that, of course, is Leonard Bernstein's fault.

How good is this score anyway? It's actually the least interesting of Bernstein's big Broadway quartet, less adventurous than On the Town or Candide, less fun than Wonderful Town. When it's violent, jagged and pulsating, it's very exciting, including the tough counter-themes that cut across the ballads. When those ballads are left to their own, strenuously soaring devices, you can only recall how much better Richard Rodgers was at writing passion, and how much better Stephen Sondheim, this show's lyricist, would be when he wrote his own music. But all right, as a totality the score works, In that respect it's like Arthur Laurents' book; Laurents thought that by giving his Jets and Sharks invented slang rather than the real 1950s thing, he'd avoid becoming dated, but the reverse has proved true. Still, however forced in its details, Laurents' script, which is certainly far more economical than Shakespeare's, grips and rushes you along; even the misbegotten movie has you gasping for breath, praying that stuff won't happen. Gary Griffin's Stratford production gets the adrenalin going, though I wondered more than usual why, when Maria demands Chino's gun, he meekly hands it over. With the grouping here, it just isn't a big enough moment. Tony and Maria's troth-plighting in the bridal store is, however, beautifully and playfully handled; such a shame that mock-hymn has to start solemnly up and spoil it.

But at least Kennedy and Nolan can sing it. Otherwise, the cast's vocal skills come in way behind their physical ones. The supports in this show don't require golden voices but they do need precision and a sense of how to phrase a line, especially a funny one. Gee Officer Krupke, which is full of them, is here just awful. The Tonight ensemble, usually a knockout, is ragged too. It isn't just the songs that suffer, it's the scenes and the characters. Anita (Jennifer Rias) is underpowered in everything except looks. Riff and Bernardo are colourless. Even the non-singing adults (with the possible exception of Mike Nadajewski's Gladhand) misfire. Take the cops: Lieutenant Schrank has been hardened by years on the beat but he isn't, as Dan Chameroy plays him, a B-movie sadist. And as for his subordinate (Bruce Dow): Gee, Officer Krupke, I never knew you were such a softie.

The production stakes a claim to originality by adding an extra character, a bemusing one. He's a boy (Kolton Stewart, a touching Macduff Junior in Macbeth) who wanders on at the beginning, the end and halfway through, as some kind of symbol of lost innocence and/or future hope. He gets to sing Somewhere, a song that reinforces its lyricist's contention that it should have stayed an instrumental. The show isn't already sentimental enough? With its dances, West Side Story still looks like a great musical. When, one copyright-expired day, it has to do without them, it may turn out to be not even good. - West Side Story plays in repertory until Oct. 31. Call 1-800-567-1600 or visit stratfordfestival.cafor tickets and information
