2009-06-11-not-quite-the-sum-of-its-part:
Julius Caesar

Avon Theatre, Stratford, Ont.

Maybe in the long historical view, the murder of Julius Caesar in the Roman Capitol can be seen as one of those funny things that happened on the way to the Forum. Maybe that's why the Stratford Festival has programmed both the musical and Shakespeare's play in the same season and in the same theatre. Otherwise, it might seem perverse of Stratford to place so public and declamatory a piece on the Avon stage, flat and enclosed even by proscenium standards, rather than on the open epic platform of the Festival Theatre itself.

As things turn out, it is perverse. James Macdonald's production delivers the play only in fits and starts, the fragments scattered across David Boechler's first-act set, which is mostly composed of the kind of steps you find leading up to the entrance of museums. It may be meant to supply grandeur, but it just looks cluttered and murky. Post-intermission, when the story moves away from Rome and towards the battlefield, the structure has been reduced to rubble. This must be one of the few productions of Caesar whose second half looks better than its first. Not that much better, though: This is a modern-dress production, and when we get to the battles they seem like the poor relations of those in this season's Macbeth. The personal and political conflicts in this Caesar seem no more urgent with the actors in suits and uniforms than if they were decked out in togas. Maybe less.

This is especially frustrating considering the calibre of the leading performances. The main problem with producing Caesar today is that of finding three actors with the brains, chops and charisma to carry off the co-equal roles of Brutus, Cassius and Antony. A fourth to play Caesar himself isn't as necessary, but is certainly nice. It hardly ever happens, but this time it does. Ben Carlson captures all the ambiguities of Brutus, the "honourable murderer" who kills to preserve a republic and ends by enabling an empire. Once primed, he's decisive (and incisive), but makes all the wrong decisions (and incisions). Carlson makes him priggish, certainly, but not pompous. He addresses the Roman crowd with the passionate faith in logic of a Barack Obama: He gets away with it, too, until his opponent, Antony, turns out to have the manipulative skills of a talk-show host.

The quarrel's a great autonomous scene, but there's a gap in the way it's set up that the production doesn't manage to fill. It presupposes a personal bond between the two men that the play never has time to set up; they're too busy plotting. Tom Rooney's Cassius is a feverish, vulnerable compound of opportunism and conviction; it's a less complete performance than Carlson's, technically and psychologically, but I applaud an actor intelligent enough to say "we petty men," rather then "we petty men." Jonathan Goad has a disconcerting habit of shouting, even when he's on his own, but otherwise his Antony is the perfect popular orator: the more dangerous because he believes his own stuff. Geraint Wyn-Davies' Caesar, as vain as he's powerful, is a great enigma, which is a compliment.

However, the fine individual performances don't cohere into relationships; the actors keep having to jump guns. Some cuts get in their way; so do some awkward choices. The veiled antagonism, brilliantly taut in the text, between the too-confident Antony and the coming man Octavius (one of the great small roles) is muffed. The crowd that becomes a mob isn't believable in either mood or from any period, for the forum orations they're placed among us, ad-libbing in our ears but with their real, crucial reactions out of focus. There's a new character billed as Soothsayer's Girlfriend, rather a specialized job description and one she doesn't seem to take very seriously since she's away from her partner, a cripple in a go-cart, in his scene of greatest need. More importantly, his lowly position means that when he gives Caesar his straight-up tip about the ides of March, the two can't make eye contact. So another key moment goes. The play remains locked behind its picture frame. Very flat, the Avon. - Julius Caesar is in repertory until Oct. 31. Call 1-800-567- 1600 or visit stratfordfestival.cafor more information.
2009-06-13-perhaps-edgar-allan-should-be:
Luminato is celebrating the bicentennial of Edgar Allan Poe with two separate productions. One of them, unsurprisingly entitled Nevermore, Ive yet to see, though I hear good things about it. The one I have seen, also good on its own terms, is A Poe Cabaret, and it's exactly what it says it is. Two shows in one festival strikes me as excessive, whatever the birthday, but then I've never found Poes combination of Gothic horror and romantic sickliness very appealing. It seems to fit the Zeitgeist, as it seems to have fitted most others.

The show is subtitled A Dream within a Dream. The outer dream is presided over by Mike Ross, as composer, singer, musician, reciter and host in a clown suit: striped-shirted, check-trousered, white-faced. He also devised the evening in collaboration with Lorenzo Savoini, best known as a designer but here functioning also as a very sharp director.

Moving among the audience, Ross discovers, seated at a table, a svelte and smart Patricia OCallaghan, whom he draws into joining him on stage and whose appearance and demeanour get less demure, though no less incisive, as the evening progresses. She's a superbly pointed, technically dazzling cabaret singer. He's a contrastingly eccentric vocalist, who favours jangling tones and has an individual line in wide-eyed menace. Separately and together, they sing Rosss settings of Poe poems (a Poepourri?), principally to string-quartet accompaniment. At one point, they join forces on a Weimar waltz. Poe, the show seems to be saying, was not of his age but of one particular later time; the evenings recorded warm-up music is ironically cheerful '20s jazz.

Well, though they do it, I doubt the effectiveness of setting poems, which already have their own rhythm, to music. It's like putting one melody-line on top of another. Even speaking a poem over music here proves hazardous. The inner dream -- the part of the show not directly involving Ross and OCallaghan--includes Tom Allen giving a rather rushed and inexpressive recitation of The Raven, with musical interjections from harpist Lori Gemmell and The Penderecki String Quartet (the evenings permanent backup group). They just get in one another's way.

Admittedly, nobody will ever be able to compete with Homer Simpson's performance of this perennial party piece, but I was never able to take it seriously even before he got to it. Its too obvious that the poet only gave his lost ladylove the unlikely name of Lenore for the sake of the rhyme, and every time it comes round I chuckle. The Masque of the Red Death is the inspiration for Conte Fantastique, a long-neglected instrumental composition by Andre Caplet, which the Pendereckians resurrect; lines from the story precede and succeed it, and OCallaghan walks across the stage in the middle of it, personifying the Red Death (at least that's the colour she's wearing), but any more precise correspondence is confined to both pieces sounding sinister.

The evenings most resounding success is sung prose: The Tell-Tale Heart (another piece with Simpsons connections; it helped rob Lisa of her diorama prize) is performed with virtuoso range and control by Sean Robert Clark. Its the story of a mad killer protesting his sanity; the music, composed and directed by Lance Horne, mocks and echoes him all the way. This is music giving new form to words, rather than just going along with them.

From Poe to Breau: or, Brault on Breau. 5 O'Clock Bells, named after an album, is a one-man show by Pierre Brault about Lenny Breau, the phenomenal Canadian guitarist who came out of country into jazz -- without, apparently, much encouragement from his parents. (They don't know who Oscar Peterson is. Isnt that a crime in Canada?)

As depicted here, Lennys dad, a country singer called Lonesome Pine, let the boy into the family act as a novelty attraction and was distressed when he started hearing bop chords behind his vocals. ( "One flat fifth and I'll knock you down.") Pine was already having family problems, with his wife turning out to be a more popular and accomplished singer than himself. Eventually, it seems, he drank himself to death. Lenny, naturally, inherited his addiction problems, though, also naturally, with him it was drugs. His mother begins and ends the story, waiting for him to come home. Behind her on a screen we see what appears to be a man falling to earth but turns out to be a body at the bottom of a pool, Sunset Boulevard style.

The production comes from the Sleeping Dog Theatre, Ottawa. Brian Quirt directs stylishly and (how else?) economically, and Brault of course plays all parts, male and female, stepping brightly from one to the next. The famous people include Chet Atkins, the Nashville king who on hearing Lenny declares himself to be now only the second greatest guitarist in the world, and our own Don Francks, rather reductively portrayed

as a hipster Sinatra wannabe. There's also Lennys teenage sweetheart and first wife, and Jewel, the Christian singer who seems really to have done for him.

The only person for whom Brault fails to find a distinctive voice is Lenny himself, whose talk is kept to a minimum. Offstage snatches of his playing dont really compensate. He never rises above the familiar figure of the doomed jazz musician, exploiting the people who love him as regularly as the business exploits him. It's like The Chet Baker Project of a few years back -- like this one, the work of a fan trying to find the key to why the music moved him. Brault's piece is better but, like most plays about musicians, especially jazz musicians, it fails to find an equivalent for its subjects verbal shorthand. Its like plays with phone calls; people keep telling Lenny things he already knows or repeating back, for our benefit, what we presume he's just told them. It's biographically interesting but, like most fan literature, its stuck on the outside looking in.

For all their merits, both these shows seem slight for a festival with Luminatos pretensions. Today, however, I'm bound for Robert Lepage's nine-hour Lipsynch which should be as much size as anybody needs.

- A Poe Cabaret played at Buddies in Bad Times Theatre; 5 O'Clock Bells closes tonight at the Berkeley Street Theatre Downstairs .
2009-06-20-in-the-end-luminato-did-get-a:
Robert Lepage is a guy who takes his time. It's not just that he goes in for marathon productions. By some standards, they arent even all that marathon. The Royal Shakespeare Companys recurring history-play cycles have kept audiences in their seats from 10 in the morning to 10 at night; so has Tom Stoppard's The Coast of Utopia. Compared to that, the nine hours of Lepage's Lipsynch, the theatrical centrepiece of this years Luminato festival, might count as chicken-feed. Within them, though, he takes extraordinary hypnotic chances.

Theres one right at the start. The show begins with a woman standing, in front of curtains and on a foreshortened stage, singing, beautifully. She is, we subsequently discover, an opera and concert performer, as is the actress playing her. The frame disappears and we're on a plane, the most convincing I have ever seen on a stage, partly because it's night and for some time nothing seems to be happening. Then something does; a woman collapses and, despite the crews best efforts, dies. Its all very discreet. Meanwhile, a baby cries.

Lepage can stage some things so well, you wonder why anyone else bothers. Another example from much later in the day, again creating high drama out of apparent banality: A woman, working as a caregiver in a London flat, sings along with -- yes, lip-synchs -- a Burt Bacharach song that's coming off the radio: something that anyone might do, but here rendered so naturally, so believably, you feel you know the woman even though she's yet to say a word.

So, whats the connection between the woman in the flat and the baby on the plane? Follow carefully: Sarah, the caregiver, is an ex-prostitute who was abused by her brother, now a BBC newsreader, when they were both in foster care. He grew up with unsavoury sexual tastes, bordering on pedophilia, and one of his victims was a 17-year-old Nicaraguan girl, forced into white slavery in Hamburg. She was the woman we saw die in the opening scene; rescued by a Canadian investigator, she was on a flight to Montreal. The baby was hers, fathered by the BBC guy.

Ive picked two moments more or less at random, but almost any two would do. Somehow or other, everything ties in. The tying is done, I must say, with pieces of string that threaten to snap under the sheer weight of coincidence. The show is avowedly less concerned with unity of plot than unity of theme: "voice, speech and language, which Lepage tells us in a program note are three very distinct and totally different things." Well, maybe. Anyway, every scene involves at least one of them. But then what scene in any play wouldn't? The idea is far too generalized and all-embracing to mean very much

It does get some ingenious applications. The opera singer Ada, who's German, was also on the flight and she ended up adopting the child. (She must have had enviable skills at dealing with bureaucracy.) They moved to London; theres a scene on the Tube thats as technically simple and transfixingly believable as the one on the plane; cars are the only mode of transport that give Lepage trouble, bringing him out in fits of the cutes. The boy, Jeremy, develops his own vocal talents, turning to rock; tiring of music, he goes into movies (another virtuoso sequence), making a picture about his birth-mother, about whom he's been fed inadequate information. Meanwhile, Ada hooks up with Thomas, a German brain surgeon who leaves her for Marie, a Canadian jazz singer whose life (and voice) he has saved. Marie has a sister, Michelle, who helps others find their voices through reading and writing poetry. This nine-hour play has nine principal characters, each given their own named sequence, with its own visual identity. Michelle's, summoning a snowbound town behind glass walls, is one of the finest; as is the performance of Lise Castonguay, who gets off one furious and funny tirade.

Other episodes are less successful; Sarahs story turns into a routine procedural, and so, even more, does its sequel, involving a Scottish detective called Jackson (somehow, the Scottishness seems very TV) with, for themes sake, an estranged French wife. Even weaker are the scenes for Sebastian, a Spanish sound engineer, which are pointless farce. Equally, some things are stunning. The invalid in Sarah's care is a speech-therapist, whom we've met in an earlier scene in which the actor (Im not sure who) does an uncanny job of lip-synching to an authentic filmed interview. Well, either that or were hearing real speech acted, in all its imperfections, as we've never heard it before. There's a very moving moment when Marie finds within herself the voice of her dead father: an epiphany that follows a lengthy period of boredom. When Jeremys mother, Lupe, finally gets to tell her own story, its shocking, but it doesn't tell us anything we don't know from documentaries. The themes of sexual abuse and of relations between siblings seem at least as central as anything else, but they arent often personalized. And if its all about memory, well what isn't?

The multinational, impeccably accented cast includes Rick Miller, very lively as Jeremy; and as Ada. Rebecca Blankenship, whose singing is as vibrant as her acting is subdued, though the latter somehow adds to the reality of it all: for a play about speech, this one has a high quotient of inaudibility, but maybe that's ironic. The actors are also the writers, along with Lepage and a dramaturge. The phenomenal sets and lighting are by Jean Hazel and Etienne Boucher. Look at the stage at almost any moment and you'll see a masterwork, but not a masterpiece.
2009-06-22-edie-does-it-with-nurse-jacki:
Edie Falco gets to say "previously on Nurse Jackie" at the start of every episode, after the first one. That seems to have become TV series stars' prerogative on every show since Kiefer Sutherland paved the way on 24. Some shows, though, take more naturally to previouslies than others. The ones on Nurse Jackie seem a little forced, because this series -- a cross between a procedural drama and a sitcom -- doesn't have much of a storyline. So instead of filling us in on plot, the pre-credit flashbacks have to highlight whichever psychological tics the characters will be displaying in the half-hour ahead. I've now screened the first six episodes (I'm hooked, but that's all I could get from my supplier) and I've already lost count of the number of times I've seen Peter Facinelli as the brash but insecure young Dr. Cooper grab Nurse Jackie's breast -- the titular tit, perhaps --and excuse it as a physical equivalent of Tourette's syndrome. So who's he going to semi-assault this week?

I am, of course, pleased to hear Falco's voice saying anything. She's my favourite American actress, and her performance here only confirms that. Though nobody's ever going to forget that she was Carmela Soprano, the role hasn't haunted her the way that the role of Tony has haunted James Gandolfini. There are things she brings to all her roles: a crooked, occasionally dopey smile, at once tolerant and world-weary, and the mindset that goes with it. In this one, she oddly reminds me of Jon Stewart, looking aghast at something especially stupid on the news: same gestures even, as of denial through humour. A crucial difference between her Carmela and her Jackie is that Carmela had to constantly deny her own considerable intelligence. There were things she couldn't afford to admit or to think about. Jackie--in her professional life, at least --has no illusions about anything.

Jackie Peyton is a senior nurse in the ER unit at a big New York hospital, a job in which, as she tells an eager trainee, you are always meeting people on the worst day of their lives. She has a bad back. "What," she voice-overed, (a device that seems, unfortunately, to have been dropped since the pilot) "do you call a nurse with back pain? Unemployed." So she keeps it a secret and sneaks medication for it -- and, of course, has to keep that a secret, too.

A medical show that concentrates on nurses rather than doctors has a chance to strip off the glamour, and that's the obvious intention of this one. "Doctors diagnose," Jackie says, "we heal," and she functions as an unsanctioned and unsentimental patients' advocate, cutting every piece of red tape she can get away with. So she has contempt for Dr. Cooper, wet behind the ears, whose first action on the show is to let a patient die, and whose war-whoops around the ward when he does get something right strain credulity even on a TV show. Her best friend, though, is another doctor, Eleanor O'Hara, whose name may be Irish but whose manner is wonderfully, offhandedly English. She's played by Eve Best, a major player in the British theatre, and one of the treats of the show is watching two towering actresses (Best is very tall) striking sparks off one another. "You do care, really," Jackie says; "No," Eleanor says cheerfully. "Don't think so." She's treating Jackie to a four-star meal at the time, something she seems to do on a regular basis. She's also a shopaholic. Jackie seems surprisingly unresentful of the financial gulf between them; also, Eleanor needs her. She calls for "Jacks" whenever a case threatens to turn emotional.

Other regulars include Mohammed (Haaz Sleiman), a male nurse who has yet to transcend the role of the heroine's gay confidant; Mrs. Akalaitis (Anna Deavere Smith), a battleaxe supervisor who's probably well observed but whose appearances I find myself dreading as much as the other characters do; and Zoey (Merritt Wever) the trainee, who refers to herself as Jackie's "protege" and is lovely. And there's Eddie, the hospital pharmacist, who slips Jackie her drugs and is also her lover, or perhaps more precisely her f---buddy, every day at noon, sharp. Eddie is played by the protean Paul Schulze, a CTU boss on 24, a hobo on Mad Men and -- of most immediate relevance -- Father Phil, the priest Carmela unavailingly fancied on The Sopranos. Good to see them consummating that passion at last.

What Eddie doesn't know -- what, apparently and incredibly, almost nobody at the hospital knows -- is that Jackie is married. We didn't know it until the last moments of the pilot when we were introduced, the surprises sprung in careful sequence, first to Jackie's two little girls, then to her husband. He seems very nice. What developing plot there is centres on their elder daughter being diagnosed with depression, brought on by watching the news and (we assume) by her mother's job. One other thing Jackie shares with Carmela: she's a Catholic, theoretically lapsed but still capable, in the pilot, of quoting Augustine ( "make me good but not yet") and also T. S. Eliot, taught to her by the nuns. This is another angle the show seems, sadly, to have dropped. And there still hasn't been another moment to match the one at the pilot's end when Jackie, having watched a bike messenger die on the table, advised another one to take care, got sworn at and promptly punctured his tire. That was Jackie in one enchanting nutshell.

I guess "procedurals" are true to life; most work-lives are repetitive which, in TV terms, means reassuring. It's still depressing to see cable TV retreating into this territory, away from the long-form serial and the scarce-remembered single play. That's the dark view. The light is to compare this show to the medical soaps on the networks. It knocks them into oblivion. Unlike House, it doesn't wallow in its protagonist's adorable misanthropy. Like Jackie, it has a job to do and -- in a smart, funny and sexy way --gets on with it. - Nurse Jackie airs Monday at 10 p. m. on The Movie Network and Movie Central.
2009-06-22-matriarchal-glue-is-only-so-s:
THEATRE REVIEW

Awake and Sing!

Young Centre for the Performing Arts, Toronto

Clifford Odets' Depression classic Awake and Sing!, revived by Soulpepper, is an odd duck: a political play whose conflicts are played out in purely domestic terms. In theory, that might be the best of both worlds -- we like to be made aware of wider issues, but we dont want to have polemic stuffed down our throats. In practice, theres a disconnect.

The play is set in the Bronx apartment of a poor Jewish family, the Bergers. Grandfather Jacob, from the old country (unspecified, but presumably Central European) is a convinced Marxist who lectures his daughter, Bessie, her husband, Myron, their two children and everyone else within earshot on the desirability of a life that isn't, in his recurring phrase, printed on dollar bills. And he does get through to the youngest generation. By the end, under his indirect tutelage, granddaughter Hennie has left her husband and baby for a new life with previous admirer Moe, a one-legged bootlegger who's also the lodger. Her brother Ralph declines to follow his love, preferring to stay and fight the good fight. These two paths to happiness, both probably doomed, would seem to cancel one another out. Anyway, some revolution.

In 1935, when Odets play was premiered by the pioneering Group Theatre, it probably added up better. Times were terrible, and audiences could extrapolate. (Yes, theyre getting terrible now, too, but "timeliness" can only take you so far. About two minutes into an evening, by my count.) Also, the play had a secret weapon. It was the first play to put working-class Jews on the American stage, and take them on their own terms. In this respect, it anticipates or parallels Lorraine Hansberry's A Raisin in the Sun which, 25 years later, did the same for American blacks, and which Soulpepper triumphantly staged last year. I would have expected Awake and Sing! to have the same impact, but it doesn't. Raisin has a firmer grasp of dramatic cause and effect, in terms of both plot and environment. Its characters predicament was intimately bound up with their being black. The Bergers has little to do with their being Jewish; anti-Semitism(amazingly, considering what was going on at the time) is hardly mentioned. They could as easily be poor Gentiles. Except, of course, that they wouldn't talk so entertainingly. Odets' dialogue, if not as consistently rich as its sometimes held to be, is what has kept the play afloat.

The current actors do well by it: Few of them are Jewish, at least as far as Im aware, but they're nearly all idiomatically fine. And yet, six years ago, there was a scratch production of this play in Toronto, with a mostly inadequate cast. I wrote at the time that it made me want to see the play done by someone else: the Shaw Festival or, so help me, Soulpepper. Be careful what you wish for, I guess, as with a first-rate director and actors, I'm still dissatisfied. Line by line, scene by scene, performance by performance, Miles Potters production, on a suitably brown set by Peter Hartwell, is impeccably sensitive, impeccably lucid; everybody responds intelligently to everybody else. But the evening crumbles away. The play isnt big on plot, but it does feature some far-fetched developments that the production can't make convincing or even very relevant.

The family is held together, and the play wants to be, by Bessie, a caring tyrant of a matriarch. She bullies her pregnant daughter into marriage, refuses to let her son's shiksa girlfriend in the house (which, unity of place and theatrical economics being what they are, means we never meet her) and heads off any disagreement at the pass. Nancy Palk plays her, in the first part of the evening, superbly: earthy, commanding, sensitive in her own way, on top but never over it. In the second half, handed a big bitter speech of self-justifying self-denial ( "I bought a new dress every week? A lover I kept?") she weakens, sacrificing anger for sentimentality and downplaying her scene of greatest vindictiveness. But her dwindling is partly the plays fault; it runs out of things for her to do. The big decisions are made behind her back, indeed after her last exit. She ought to be there.

Derek Boyes seems whimsically out of place as her perennially defeated husband, substituting a Celtic smile for a Yiddish shrug. William Webster might profitably be more whimsical as Jacob, who retreats by playing Caruso records, but he does the secular-prophet bit imposingly well. A shame that he has to make his greatest contribution to the plot from offstage. Michael Hanrahan, with a silk scarf wrapped around his vocal chords, is absolutely right as the familys comparatively rich Uncle Morty, and Ari Cohen righter than right as Moe whose amputation on the last day of the war made him a cynic, a pacifist and--as it transpires -- an unlikely do-gooder. The young people are very impressive: Jonathan Gould quivering with life as the irresolute Ralph, Sarah Wilson hard as nails as Hennie and Matthew Edison is lovely as the poor schmuck tricked into giving Hennie's child a father. It would be hard, and probably wrong, to play the last life-affirming moments for irony. But taken straight they seem wished for, tacked-on. Play and production are awake, no question, but they don't sing. - Awake and Sing! runs through July 31 at the Young Centre for the Performing Arts. 2009-06-25-the-importance-of-reading-osc:
Brian Bedford's intelligence and skill, the affability of his manner and the sharpness of his wit, should be familiar by now. But they're so exceptional, while seeming so deceptively easy, that they take you by surprise every time. It may be that we don't take them for granted because he doesn't; he's on his mettle every time, super-relaxed but never complacent. Recently, too, he's shown an enriching new quality, one that I don't remember being much evident in his earlier work: compassion. It was movingly evident in his King Lear a couple of years ago, and it shines out in his solo performance Ever Yours, Oscar, an assemblage of the letters of Oscar Wilde.

One in particular shows a side of its subject as well as its performer with which we haven't been too familiar: social concern. It's a letter to a newspaper, written after Wilde's release from Reading Gaol. It's a response to a report of the dismissal of a warder in the same prisonfor having slippeda sweet biscuit to a hungry child prisoner. It moves outwards from there to denounce the iniquity of locking up children of 14 and younger, let alone placing them in solitary confinement and feeding them a diet guaranteed to make them ill. It's very detailed, very measured and very contained. There's obviously anger underneath, but it's phrased as humane bewilderment. (Listen to Bedford as he painstakingly contrasts a child's uncomprehending attitude to being punished by "the system" with an adult's.) It's also, in contrast to some of what we thought we knew about Wilde, selfless. He doesn't complain about his own treatment at the hands of the Reading Gaolers; he goes out of his way to describe some of them as humane. They too are victims of the system. It's worth remembering, though neither the linking material nor Bedford's passionately reasonable delivery stresses the point, that Wilde himself was sick at the time he wrote the letter. He didn't have to take the time.

If that is the show's emotional high point, its comic counterpart is a letter sent by an Oscar on his uppers to the actor/manager George Alexander, asking for an advance on a new play that was to become The Importance of Being Earnest. He supplies a plot outline which, it's suggested in the introduction, he probably made up as he went along, and it's fascinating to hear how much was preserved from this improvization and how much altered or enlarged. There is, shockingly, no Ernest and hence no thematic earnestness in this version, but there is a Prism: also, the delightful last-minute suggestion that a clergyman should be brought in as her partner. Of course you have to know The Importance fairly well to get the underlying joke, but for this year's Stratford audience that shouldn't be a problem. See Bedford in a dress as Lady Bracknell on other nights, and in a suit as himself here.

Ever Yours, Oscar has been devised by Peter Wylde; Bedford directs himself. It doesn't pretend to be a play, and it's fragmentary even as a recital. Bedford reads or speaks at a music stand, placed about three quarters of the way upstage (anyone sitting behind in this three-handed space will have only his back to look at) with a large portrait of Wilde hanging on the back wall. In between

epistles, he delivers snippets of basic biography. The Sturm und Drang of Wilde's life are given bare-bones treatment; we hear very little of, or to, Bosie, though what we do hear makes him sound more appalling than ever. There's nothing from the anguished De Profundis, technically a letter but hardly an informal one. Basically, the show gives us sidelights, mainly delightful ones; ranging from the young Oscar admonishing his mother on what to send him at prep school to the enfant terrible Oscar on his lecture tour of the United States, instructing silver miners on the subject of modern art. (They hated the art, loved the artist -- i. e. him.) In short --and it is short -- this is not a momentous evening or, preferably, afternoon. But it offers insights, and one of our very finest actors being very fine. - Ever Yours, Oscar is in repertory through Aug. 29. Visit stratfordfestival.caor call 1-800-567-1600 for tickets and information.
2009-06-26-oh-mummy-dearest:
LOOT

Young Centre for the Performing Arts

---

Soulpepper's artistic director says in his program greeting that the two plays his company is currently alternating "couldn't be more different." He's right, in that Clifford Odets' Awake and Sing! and Joe Orton's Loot belong to different worlds, one a socially-conscious clarion call from the American 1930s, the other a disconcertingly cheerful black farce from the British 1960s. One preaches hope, the other offers a choice between despair and acceptance. Odets can sometimes seem confused or at least ambiguous; Orton's anarchic vision is uncompromising and undeviating. But the two plays do have something in common: both were trailblazers in their time that now look less than they've been cracked up to be. And both have been given productions -- one sensitive, the other smooth -- whose merits can't disguise the deficiencies and may even accentuate them.

Jim Warren's production of Loot is buoyed up by two splendid performances. One of them is by Oliver Dennis, who has a habit of playing uninviting roles and discovering things in them that previous actors may never have thought existed. He plays Mr. McLeavy, an ultra-respectable citizen who would regard "law-abiding" as the highest compliment in the English language. In other words, or at least in Orton's words, he's a dupe, a fool and a predestined victim. Mr. McLeavy is in the process of burying his wife, a process hampered by his son's being in league, and in love, with a young local undertaker who doubles as a bank robber. The two hide their latest swag in Mrs. McLeavy's coffin, having first removed the corpse, trussed it up and hidden it -- well, ina successionof locations, one of the rules of farce being that incriminating evidence is always about to be discovered and has to be kept on the move. Most of this, of course, is unknown to the bereaved husband until far too late. In the meantime he finds himself obliged to make a statement to the authorities on what has turned out to be a remarkably ill-fated journey to the church, and slips immediately into the appropriate official mode. The collision of the pseudo-literate with the absurd is Orton at his best. It's also remarkably difficult to perform. Dennis, earnestly informative and revelling in the opportunity to be of assistance, had me in hysterics from the start of his oration ( "We set off in high spirits") to its end. He also brilliantly defines the point at which respectability crosses over into vindictiveness, while his affection for his late wife and reluctance to incriminate his son would, in any other play, be touching. Orton, however, didn't do touching, and Dennis is fastidious about not doing it either. Which, in so likeable an actor, is integrity of heroic proportions.

Mr. McLeavy is a devout Catholic. A lot of the play's jokes are concerned with this, and they mostly fall flat. The assumption seems to be that the Catholic Church is the most sacred of cows and mocking it the ultimate taboo. That isn't the case now, and I doubt if it was then. McLeavy has to have a belief-system to make the play work, and he probably would be religious, but the horse doesn't have to be flogged to death. His concomitant trust in secular authority counts dramatically for far more, and here the play packs a punch that still lands. Michael Hanrahan, in the evening's other exhilarating performance, plays Police Inspector Truscott, who arrives in the McLeavy abode claiming to be from the water board and proceeds to abuse all the rules we might fondly have believed would govern either organization. The verbal association with waterboarding seems almost prophetic, and you may find yourself thanking heaven, or whatever, that Truscott came before Tasers. But he does pretty well without them. "Under any other political system," he says while interrogating young Hal McLeavy, "I'd have you on the floor in tears," to which the hapless Hal accurately replies "you've got me on the floor in tears." Orton had only one joke -- the saying of outrageous things with a straight face --but with Truscott, who bends all regulations without fear of self-contradiction and whose brutality and corruption are matched by his ineptitude as a sleuth, he hit gold. Hanrahan, comic energy under ferocious control, does the same.

Even while being brutalized, neither Hal nor his partner Dennis seems much afraid of being found out. That's a problem with Orton as a farceur; in his world, where everything's amoral, there's no threat. Matthew Edison's Hal (a pretty contrast with his shy role in Awake and Sing!) and Jonathan Watton's Dennis are good without really being convincing, certainly not as a couple. They do, though, deliver their lines with wit and despatch. In fact the only player who fails in this regard is Nicole Underhay, who plays a buxom nurse (also Catholic) anxious to add the widowed Mr. McLeavy to her already impressive list of mysteriously deceased husbands; she has the right seaside-postcard profile but she labours the epigrams, thereby slowing the proceedings considerably.

Neither the play nor its author are dismissible; Orton, unlike the self-satisfied rebels of London's Royal Court, was a real subversive, a working-class gay man who'd done time and ended up being bludgeoned to death by his lover. He had a genuine outsider's vision, one most completely and resourcefully expressed in his next and last play What the Butler Saw. Loot works perfectly on its own terms, but they're narrow terms. One personal complaint. When Truscott discovers Mrs. McLeavy's preserved corpse he asks, "whose mummy is this?" to which Hal replies, truthfully but without thinking, "mine." I always thought that was the funniest line in the play. It isn't here; the timing is off. But that doesn't happen often. - Loot is in repertory at the Young Centre through Aug. 1. Call 416-866-8666 for tickets and information.

2009-06-27-the-play-is-the-thing-not-art:
This is the 30th year of Toronto theatre's Dora Awards, and a celebratory book is being published. One winner from each year reminisces about what a thrill it was (I especially relished Daniel Brooks comment on awards ceremonies in general, which I roughly paraphrase as "theyre all pale imitations of the Oscars") and there's an overview of how great it's all been in promoting the profile of the community (I also paraphrase, but not by much). Nobody grapples with the recurrent complaints about eccentric choices of winners and nominees, but you wouldnt expect them to.

As for this season, the 2008-09 one: Im struck, looking back on its second half (i. e. this year) by how many of the most interesting shows were Doraineligible, either because they were revivals of previous productions or because they were only semi-professional or because they didn't run long enough: City of Wine, Seven Jewish Children, the revival of The Last Days of Judas Iscariot, the revival of Kristen Thomson's I Claudia ...

Hang on: It turns out I Claudia is eligible after all. Its been nominated for outstanding production of a play and also for outstanding direction. The first might just scrape by on a technicality since the play is, as they say, under new management: Crows Theatre instead of Tarragon. But the director is the same Chris Abraham as before; and if he's allowed a second kick at the same can, then why not Thomson herself, not as author (a play can't be new twice), but as actress? And what about the stunning replacement performances in Judas Iscariot-- by Morris Panych, Ted Dykstra and others? Replacements dont count? Then why is Jeff Madden up there (I dont doubt he deserves it) for his takeover job in Jersey Boys? The head, as ever, spins.

As it happens, I think Thomson's been robbed: not over I Claudia, which, much as I love it, shouldn't be there at all, but over The Patient Hour, which, though flawed, was the most interesting new play of the year. Of those plays that are nominated, Id have a hard job choosing between Andrew Moodies Toronto the Good (messy but compelling) and Joan MacLeod's Another Home Invasion (flawless but a monologue). The smart money, though, must be on Agokwe, a play I didn't see. It must have been spectacular because its gathered nominations for its author, leading actor (same man: Waawaate Fobister), producer, director, and set, costume, lighting and sound designers.

In the best-actor stakes, Diego Matamoros has been nominated (as he nearly always is and deserves to be) for Travesties. I thought, when I saw it for the second time at the last matinee, that this Soulpepper show was the most enjoyable production of the season. But I didnt think it the first time, so I can't really complain at its exclusion. Otherwise, the season's three stand-out events were Company Theatres Festen and Soulpeppers A Raisin in the Sun and The Way of the World. The last, which should have won nominations for its director (Peter Hinton) and at least three of its actors, has been completely shut out. The others are well-represented, with Philip Riccio's best-actor nod symbolizing, I imagine, the whole superb ensemble. This may be the place to register my bemusement at the nomination of Hrant Alianak, certainly a worthy pillar of the community, for giving one of the less-bad performances in the atrociously acted House of Many Tongues -- this in a year when Eric Peterson has been overlooked twice. I'd hate to choose between Jason Byrnes direction of Festen and Weyni Mengeshas of Raisin, but I'd probably go for Mengesha. And I'd certainly go for Alison Sealy-Smith in Raisin as best actress; this was a self-transforming performance.

Tastes differ, and mine are as eccentric as anyone elses, but one point on which all seem to agree, except the Dora people themselves, is that its lunacy to cram all the supporting performances -- play and musical, male and female--into one category. If there's a rational reason for this, could it please be made public? This year, there are five performances nominated, all by women. (Jordan Pettle in Travesties, anyone? Todd Thomson in The Patient Hour?) One actress, Raven Dauda, is running against herself, for a good performance in Miss Julie: Freedom Summer and a shallow one in Doubt. I'd like Brenda Robins to win for Ring Round the Moon, but Im not holding my breath. As for musicals: Jersey Boys will probably win, and I shant repine if it does, but I also carry a small banner for A New Brain, and especially for Daryl Cloran's direction of it. Elicia MacKenzie ( The Sound of Music) will undoubtedly romp home for solving the problem called Maria, twice. In the independent (i. e. smaller theatre) division, David Ferry is another one running against himself for best actor, and he is indeed twice worthy. All the same, I think that R. H. Thomson, in one of the same plays, has the edge. Best independent actress is split between three superb performances, one good one, and one that was terrible; gallantry forbids me from being more specific. Best independent play should be Anton Piatigorsky's Eternal Hydra, even though I didn't enjoy it much. But The Gladstone Variations, which took place over several ingeniously synchronized evenings in the eponymous hotel, deserves the palm for best production just for, so to speak, showing up.

2009-07-02-those-rollicking-romans:
If Stephen Sondheim had written nothing else, he would still deserve canonization for three lines in Comedy Tonight, the scene-setting and tone-setting number of A Funny Thing Happened on the Way to the Forum:

Goodness and badness, Man in his madness, This time it all turns out all right!

That's as conciseandhumane a definition of classic comedy as you could find. It not only stimulates the smile-muscles; it lifts the heart. So does the whole song, a catalogue of farcical types ( "tumblers! grumblers! fumblers! bumblers!") and farcical action, all of which we get to see in furious action in the show that follows. The song is reprised, of course, at the finale, when everything's been sorted out, with the combination of improbability and strict logic that's the hallmark of farce, and a golden glow suffuses the theatre. It's a glow that doesn't need to be disturbed by the threat of an earthquake, however momentary. But that's what happens here. It's an emblem of the way in which Des McAnuff's generally enjoyable Stratford production goes periodically off the rails.

It works when it trusts the actors and, through them, the text. It's a text worth trusting, assembled with diabolical craftsmanship by Burt Shevelove and Larry Gelbart from a handful of the plays written in the second century BCE by the Roman dramatist Plautus, whom Sondheim has described as "the guy who invented comedy." (More exactly, he was the guy who invented situation comedy.) Then add in Sondheim's music and lyrics, which are unfailingly delightful. Take, for example, Everybody Ought To Have a Maid, the trippingly lascivious soft-shoe performed by a gradually accumulating quartet made up of Senex, a gamely lecherous old man; his slave Pesudolus, whose desire to win his freedom helps drive the plot (Plautus may not have been a liberal, but his adaptors are); Hysterium, another slave, with a low panic-threshold; and Lycus, the brothel-keeper

next door. This goes right and wrong. I thought at first that McAnuff and Wayne Cilento (choreographer and co-stager) were killing it by having the actors exchange lengthy conspiratorial whispers between stanzas. My mistake: It makes it all the funnier when the music starts up again. But they do kill or at least wound it when Lycus' emporium revolves during the last chorus, and the courtesans arrayed within grab a piece of the lyric. It's the wrong kind of incongruous; this is a song with a strictly male point of view. It's also meant to be a showcase for those four comedians. It's between them and us. Nobody should get in the way.

Now, Pseudolus as prologue does promise to use "every device we know in our efforts to divert you" (Zero Mostel, the first Pseudolus, made it sound more like a threat) and probably Plautus himself would have used modern scenic technology if he'd had it. But whenever this production throws in a scenic gag -- when, for example, the breasts light up on the statues of Muses that flank John Arnone's set -- well, it doesn't always hinder but it never actually helps. Admittedly, there's a casting problem with this show. Its authors described it as "a scenario for vaudevillians," and it's a tribute not just to old Roman comedy but to old American. (My favourite exchange: "You want a soothsayer?" "How did you know that?" "I'd be a fine

soothsayer if I didn't." They should interpolate that in Julius Caesar.) This crosstalk clowning tradition was coming to an end in 1962, when the show premiered, and it's died out now. These days, we have to make do with mere actors.

Some actors, of course, can leap the gap. Stephen Ouimette is one; his Hysterium is comic genius. Scarcely less hilarious are the young lovers, Mike Nadajewski and Chilina Kennedy, he endearingly immature, she provokingly virginal. (Yes, she's a courtesan. But she's on special order.) Brian Tree is pleasingly befuddled as Erronius, checking in periodically while running seven times around the seven hills of Rome, and if Randy Hughson is somewhat junior for Senex, whose name means "old man," he compensates with beaming crispness.

Hughson and Ouimette get their laughs cleanly on the lines. Bruce Dow, in the star role of Pseudolus, acts fussily around his; he only comes into focus when he duets with Ouimette on the reprise of Lovely, the comic love-duet (already a hoot when the young 'uns do it). Most spectacularly miscalculated is Dan Chameroy's Miles Gloriosus ( "braggart soldier") who should be impregnably self-satisfied and terrifying, but is here made of jelly. But the actor hardly stands a chance in a production that has a single chariot wheel careening across the stage before his entrance, thus undercutting his immortal first line, "Stand aside, everyone! I take large steps!" Lycus is an underwritten role but Cliff Saunders' decision to play him as an epicene eccentric rather than a mercenary man of business is not a happy one. His non-speaking merchandise includes regular Stratford adornment Sara Topham, who may not be playing Medea later this week, as the song says, but was once a memorable Cassandra, and is obviously having a ball here. They've cut Pretty Little Picture, which is unforgivable, but they're not the first. The show remains irresistible. It all turns out all right. It has to. - A Funny Thing Happened on the Way to the Forum is in repertory through Nov. 1. Call 1-800-567-1600 or visit stratfordfestival.cafor tickets and information.

2009-07-04-what-happened-after-they-went:
David French tells us that he wrote Of the Fields, Lately (1973) because audiences kept asking him what happened later to the characters of his previous play Leaving Home (1972). The answer seems to be: the same, only more so. Not in terms of volume -- Of the Fields is a shorter, sparer, more concentrated play than its predecessor --but of intensity.

Leaving Home introduced us to the Mercer family, origins in Newfoundland, now living in Toronto. Principally they were Jacob, a carpenter; Mary, his wife; and Ben, their university-age son. Ben was the one who left home, ostensibly to live with his just-married brother, and to the great displeasure of his father. It was made plain, though, that Jacob would have been equally displeased had Ben stayed. He could be displeased at anything; love fought with resentment, the education-gap fused with the generation-gap, to produce a wound that never ceased to fester.

Soulpepper, which revived the earlier play two years ago, has now added the later one, with Ted Dykstra again directing and with the same actors playing the Mercers. About five years have passed (it's 1961) and Ben, having moved even further away -- to Saskatchewan, in fact -- has returned. The immediate reason is that Mary's sister Dot has died, and Ben is back for the funeral, though we're told they were never close. (An oddity: Dot was never mentioned in the preceding play. Another oddity: Ben's brother Billy and his ill-omened marriage are equally absent from this one. In a play concerned with family recriminations, that's strange.) It seems, though, that Ben's real purpose is to try and mend fences with his dad. Fate seems to present him with the perfect opportunity. Jacob is ill, too ill to work, though he angrily refuses to acknowledge it. Ben could move back in, get a job, pay the bills. Jacob, as might be expected, is partly delighted to have his son back, partly incensed. Jacob is an expert at denial, and what he denies most is his own mortality. Or as the ever-anxious Mary puts it, rather too explicitly for dramatic comfort, "He can battle all he wants; we're all up against the same enemy: time."

The play is bookended by Ben's reminiscence of the day his father paid an unprecedented visit to his school baseball game, and of how he, aged 12, was too ashamed and embarrassed to acknowledge him: a memory that has gnawed, unspoken, at both of them ever since. It's a fine speech, delivered here by Jeff Lillico with both subtlety and force, and it's obviously meant to underpin the play -- "the emotional cornerstone" as Ben says "of the wall between us." But it doesn't work that way. The play has nothing more to tell us about fathers and sons, or about this father and this son, than we had already learned from the first one. In autobiographical plays, which these confessedly are, the author's surrogate usually comes off as the most shadowy figure, and Ben, despite his actor's best efforts, remains a plot device with a bit of back-story about his life away thrown in towards the end.

The real interest lies with the older generation. It is, perhaps surprisingly in a play written by a man in his early thirties, an elegiac piece. Jacob and Mary, with loss hanging over them, are juxtaposed with Dot's widower Wiff, who is Jacob's fellow-worker, fellow-Newfie and enthusiastic fellow-drinker. In fact he never made it to his wife's deathbed, having stopped to take a drop first and then another drop. He had reasons for this, which are revealed in a funny affecting speech that's closely followed by another telling how he returned home to find Dot, in effect, haunting it. So he comes to the Mercers for refuge, rather like the old couple in Edward Albee's A Delicate Balance (though for reasons that are easier to follow). If anything, we learn more about Wiff and Dot's marriage than we do about Jacob and Mary's, but then of course, with only one survivor, the situation is less complicated. Anyway, Eric Peterson makes a three-dimensional person, both crafty and concerned, of a character who starts out looking like comic relief, with his vows of abstinence repeatedly made and as repeatedly broken. Part of the evening's pleasure of course is to see him square off against that other veteran Kenneth Welsh: Peterson's Wiff dry (considering he's an alcoholic) and contained, Welsh's Jacob explosive, juicy and hurt. Both are wounded men, but where one can acknowledge hurts both given and received, the other can only lash out. Welsh's performance is the same one he gave in Leaving Home (except that the accent's laid on less thick) but so it should be; his brief spurts of joy, when he feels his son actually loves him, are of course very moving. As Mary, Diane D'Aquila starts the play ironing endless shirts --a perfect image--and she goes on to be properly anguished and enduring, though she's also too ready to be aggressively aggrieved and seems upscale for the company she's married into. French continued the Mercer saga in Salt-Water Moon, which took us back to Jacob and Mary's courtship (Soulpepper, scrambling the chronology even further, revived this play in between the two others, with Lillico playing his own father as a young man) but, with all allowances for the ravages of time, I can't relate the two people we met then to the two we see now. And though I can appreciate the older Jacob's constant harking-back to his old haunts and friends, the theme of geographical displacement seems to me more taken for granted than explored. These are good Canadian plays that still stand up, certainly in productions as good as Dykstra's. I've still to be persuaded that they're universal classics. - Of the Fields, Lately plays through July 30 at the Young Centre for the Performing Arts. 2009-07-08-scent-of-excess:
One of the callers whose comments appeared at the bottom of Much Music's screen during the Michael Jackson memorial was speculating on who would be the first on-stage mourner to break down in tears.

"My money's on Jennifer Hudson, God bless her" the message said. She (I have a feeling it was a she) would have lost that money because Ms. Hudson didn't break down, for which God may bless her even more. The first tears I noticed were shed by Brooke Shields, who may have earned them by making Mr. Jackson sound more like a human being than did any of her fellow celebrities. Their friendship, she said, stemmed from their both having been child-stars; he started when he was three but she, having made her debut at eleven months, was in the unique position of being able to accuse him of being a slacker. "We had contests" she said "to see who could make the other laugh more."

It was reassuring, in the midst of tributes that painted Mr. Jackson as everything from an icon to a martyr, to hear that he could laugh. She spoiled it a bit by revealing that his favourite song wasn't one of his own numbers but the old Charlie Chaplin tearjerker Smile ( "though your heart is breaking"), a choice that even I, a pre-rock person, find suspect. It was probably the sentiments rather than the music that he was reacting to. Marlon Jackson then proceeded to sing it, without changing my mind.

The event itself, considering what it might have been, was remarkably dignified. It struck its most moving note at the beginning, with the surviving Jackson brothers bearing the flower-draped coffin, and never noticeably descended from it thereafter. But the scent of excess could never really be dispelled, less from what happened inside the auditorium than from the reaction outside: sometimes hundreds (and probably thousands) of miles outside.

In the Toronto streets, a presenter gushed about "the most talented people on the planet, in the universe, paying tribute to the most talented person in the history of music." I think we can put the bit about the universe down to over-excitement, but it would be interesting to know when people started thinking it more impressive to talk about "the planet" rather than simply "the world." I guess it sounds more grandiose, even spiritual.

Even those who believe "the history of music" only dates back 50 years may have found that "most talented person" claim for Mr. Jackson a bit excessive. And if you do go back further: well, roll over not just Beethoven, but Bach, Mozart, Louis Armstrong, Frank Sinatra and one or two others. The rhetoric inside the hall could get overheated as well. Even Berry Gordy, the boss of Motown, having begun with a persuasive estimate of Mr. Jackson's on-stage metamorphosis from shy boy to "kill-or-be-killed" performer who "loved it all, every moment," escalated to saying "King of Pop wasn't big enough for him; he was the greatest entertainer that ever lived." This estimate, patently unprovable since there were centuries of entertainers of whom we have no record, provoked the first standing ovation of the occasion.

The less we remember history the more we feel compelled to invent it, and to inflate ourselves. Al Sharpton ( "Michael taught the world how to love") seemed to be claiming that his breaking of racial barriers made possible the acceptance of both Oprah and Obama, though even if we confine the roll-call to show business, Mr. Jackson was part of a continuum that included Armstrong, Duke Ellington, Ray Charles, Aretha Franklin and (his predecessor as song-and-dance man and infant prodigy) Sammy Davis Jr, all of whom, coming earlier, had more barriers to break.

The hype--a word that has come to mean merely "publicity" but is short, after all, for hyperbole -- has other progenitors. Does Stevie Wonder know that with his "we need Michael here with us, God must have needed him more" he was echoing the 1920s Tin Pan Alleyman who wrote "they needed a songbird in heaven so God took Caruso away?"

Probably it is only technology that makes today's grief-orgies seem more excessive than those of earlier periods. Sorrow swept America when George Gershwin died at 37, but it couldn't be transmitted as well. There needs to be a perception of youth and/or vulnerability; Sinatra, an immeasurably more distinctive singer, would have had to keel over in his bobbysox days to provoke comparable lamentation.

Mr. Jackson was technically middle-aged when he died, but his absence from the performing limelight, and his peculiar persona, kept him young in people's minds. Prince of Pop he may have been, but he had to vacate the throne to be proclaimed King. robert.cushman@ nationalpost.com

2009-07-09-movin-on-up-hbo-proves-itself:
As Ray Drecker's wife Jessica drives away, out of their marriage though not quite out of his life, she screams at him through the open car window: You used to be beautiful and athletic and talented and smart and popular and hung." (Her mothers in the car, too, but Jessica seems uninhibited, at least about this.) "What am I now? Ray asks. Now," she says, "youre just hung. Ray ponders this and -- to cut a long pilot episode short -- decides that if he now has only one marketable asset, he may as well market it.

Ray's terrible luck is to have a mid-life crisis at the same time that his country, and especially his city, are having an economic one. Ray is a high-school basketball coach and history teacher living in Detroit. One of the strengths of the show's pilot -- which, breaking the usual rule, is the best of its first four episodes -- is the way in which it fills in the civic background. We see car wreckage, stadium wreckage. We also, coming in closer, see Rays own home-wreckage. After the divorce, Ray moves into his dead parents lakeside house, now heavily mortgaged due to Ray's gullible trust in the subprime market. Really, the best thing to happen to it from his point of view would be for it to burn down. Which it does, due to faulty and overloaded wiring, but unfortunately Ray has been equally careless about keeping up the insurance. Pending the house's reconstruction, which he cant afford, he takes to living in a tent at the waters edge. This costs him his twin son and daughter, whose earlier decision to live with him had been the one bright spot on his horizon. The kids have to move in with their mom and her new man, a doctor. He saves lives!" she says proudly. "Honey, says Ray, his voice dripping equally with weariness and scorn, he's a dermatologist." I didn't spot it myself, but experts tell me that this joke has already been used on Seinfeld, though that show typically upped the ante by revealing that the doc in question had in fact saved at least one person from skin cancer.

To top everything, Rays team is losing every game and he fears being fired as a result. In desperation he takes off to a you-can-be-whatever-you-want motivational workshop where hes told, unsurprisingly, to follow his dream. Trouble is, he doesn't at present have one. But another attendee gives him an idea. She's Tanya, a poet currently working as an editorial temp, an employment Hell from which she hopes to escape by baking cakes and placing her poems inside them. As we learn in a flashback she and Ray have met before, and it ended up in bed, where she was vocally

impressed by the size of his equipment but dismayed by the discourteous speed with which he removed it, along with the rest of himself. Anyway, this and a repeat encounter, which plays out almost identically, leads circuitously to Rays decision to sell his services to deprived ladies, with Tanya as his agent.

All this is set up in the first hour-long instalment. This has been criticized as overlong, but in fact its leisureliness is the best thing about it. Slow is sitcoms new speed, and this episode, generous with scene-setting and character quirks, handled it well. There's a problem with Ray himself. Richard Jane, who plays him, is a solid actor but not overly charming or charismatic; he reminds me of Tim Allen, the bleary over-the-hill Allen of Galaxy Quest, but without the built-in character association (and, face it, the super script) that made that performance funny. Jane Allen is a definite asset as the super-conscientious Tanya, standing in the street right outside her own house loudly protesting, "I'm an excellent pimp! Well, yes, its hard out there. Youd think she might prefer old-fashioned words like madam" or even "bawd, her being a poet and all. Ray himself wrestles with his job description; in his mind he goes from whore" to "male prostitute to, at my last count and after an encounter apparently gratifying to both parties, gigolo."

The question raised by Episodes 2, 3 and 4 is can they, so to speak, keep it up? Can they make a whole series out of an idea that Flight of the Conchords once got through in half an hour, including songs? Do they want it be shocking? Do they want it to be wryly compassionate social commentary? I'm not saying it couldn't be both, but at the moment the Hung jury is out. Theyve had to devise complications to delay or derail Rays professional assignations, and already they're beginning to seem routine or contrived. In other respects, though, the initial careful spadework is paying off. Plotlines are intersecting more neatly and ambitiously than is usual in sitcoms. Ray's teenage kids are refreshingly unglamorized, in their exasperated loyalty to one another and their plain exasperation with their elders. Ray also has a promising conflict going with his upscale lawyer neighbour, who objects to living next to two burned-out ruins -- i. e. the house and its owner, the latter of whom has taken to urinating in Lake Michigan, which most surely has seen worse. I think it could be good for a season. Im not sure, to invoke a production with a similar background and a similar premise, that it could ever go the Full Monty, but then Im not convinced that The Full Monty ever went it, either. - Hung airs Sunday nights at 10 p. m. on HBO Canada.

2009-07-10-hokey-pocus-series-about-king:
Two weeks in, and Merlin is settling into a pattern. Somebody arrives at the court of King Uther, father of the once and future King Arthur, with murderous intent backed up by supernatural powers. These evil plans are foiled by Merlin, the boy who puts the sauce into sorcery; he's a gauche but game young man, currently hanging around the castle as a physician's assistant. Merlin has his own superior magical skills, demonstrated by his ability to knock things over without touching them, which he has to disguise because it would be death to reveal them. In Episode 1, he defeated a celebrity singer whose performance put the whole courtly audience to sleep. Well, we've all been to shows like that. This chanteuse, though, went further than most, by enveloping her fans in cobwebs. She then tried to stick a blade into the heir-apparent, at which point Merlin, who had kept his ears prudently covered throughout the siren's song, sprang into action and saved Arthur's life. This was very sporting of him since the prince, a bully with an outsized sense of entitlement, had been treating him appallingly. Merlin's reward for his good deed has been a job as Arthur's personal servant: a mixed blessing if ever there was one.

Still, some kind of respect and even affection has sprung up between the two young men, and in Episode 2 Merlin saved Arthur's life again. This time he stopped him being treacherously killed in a tournament by somebody called Knight Valiant, whose shield incorporated a brood of snakes, programmed to spout venom on command. And the pellet with the poison's in the vessel with the pestle.

You don't have to be a student of Sir Thomas Malory to detect some revisionism here. We aren't used to Arthur and Merlin being chums and contemporaries, and certainly not to Arthur growing up at his father's court. In the received versions he's spirited away -- actually by Merlin -- to grow up in humble surroundings, and eventually to prove his parentage and his right to the throne by performing feats unattainable by anyone else. If this new series intends to work in the sword-in-the-stone stuff, I can't see how it hopes to go about it. There's a serving-wench on hand who takes a shine to young Merlin and whose specialized knowledge -- she's a blacksmith's daughter -- comes in very handy for instructing him in which bits of a knight's armour go where. She's called Guinevere, "but most people call me Gwen," and if names, even shortened ones, mean anything, Merlin is headed for a broken heart; though it's hard to see this cub-like Arthur falling for a lady's maid or his even more snobbish father allowing the match. Though of course, dad may be gone by then; he seems pretty lifeless already.

Speaking of names, the series began with the decapitation of a convicted magician who identified himself, in his last headed moment, as Thomas James Collins. This would certainly have jarred with Malory, whose characters, when they had them at all, sported surnames like Pendragon and du Lac. Merlin, by the way, identifies as a warlock rather than a wizard; though I can't fathom what brand of political correctness has dictated the dropping of the familiar title "sir" in favour of Knight Valiant and, obviously looming somewhere in the series' future, Knight Launcelot.

There's not much point in complaining about anachronisms. Malory's Morte d'Arthur, which has conditioned all subsequent treatments of the Arthurian legends, was itself outrageously anachronistic, the imposition of a medieval Christian world view on a figure who, if he existed at all, would have been an early British chieftain and probably pagan. Malory did, though, write great if stilted prose, and most subsequent modernisers have at least attempted a certain stylishness. The text of Merlin, a British series with four credited writers, seems to have been created by authors with tin ears for delivery by actors with cloth larynxes. It aims at jauntiness and misses. "We can't let Valiant get away with it" urges Merlin, urgently, to which Arthur thoughtfully replies "I don't like the guy, but that doesn't mean he's cheating." It would be one thing if they were trying to have fun with the story (I think, longingly, of the very old Robin Hood series with Richard Greene) but they seem to think they're doing it a favour.

From time to time we leave the toy turrets of Spamalot -- sorry, Camelot -- to descend with Merlin into the bowels of the castle, which are very deep indeed and reached by a series of perilous steps left over from an Indiana Jones movie. Here dwells the Great Dragon, who's the only one of his breed left alive by the fanatically ant-magical Uther and who, unlike anyone else in the show, talks as if he might have read a book, though not perhaps a good one. "Just give me a straight answer," begs Merlin, but nobody ever got one of those from an oracle. Bodeful pronouncements apart, the Great Dragon, flapping his wings as he descends from nowhere in particular (his captors have given him a lot of Lebensraum), seems rather gentle, even cuddly. He also does voice-overs, announcing at the start of each episode that "no young man, no matter how great, can know his destiny." It's John Hurt's voice that he uses. The show's only other contact with thespian distinction is the anxious presence of Richard Wilson as the court doctor, Merlin's protector, who alternately marvels at the boy wonder and tells him to clean up his room. Angel Coulby is an appealingly spunky Guinevere; Colin Morgan's Merlin and Bradley James' Arthur are well-intentioned young men, similar except that one wears a smock and a smile, the other chain-mail and a scowl.

Well, Rome-- the TV show, I mean-- wasn't built in a day. It took a whole season to progress from camp to something both serious and funny. So maybe Merlin will do the same. At the moment, though, it's jokey without the wit to know that it's a joke. - Merlin airs Sunday at 8 p. m. on CTV and NBC.

2009-07-11-french-farce-meets-bonnie-and:
Moliere's The Sicilian isn't quite the oldest play in this year's Toronto Fringe Festival; there's a production of Aristophanes' Lysistrata that has it beat by several centuries and change. But as classics go, it's one of the rarest; it also turns out --and not just because of its scarcityvalue-- to be one of the freshest.

A one-act farce, The Sicilian is one of its author's comedie-ballets; a proto-musical that can accommodate as much song-and-dance as a production cares to give it. This production at the Factory Mainspace by a company seemingly without a name, cares a lot, with results that are eccentrically delightful. The story takes aim at one of the self-tormenting Moliere's favourite targets: the jealous husband or guardian whose efforts to keep his charge away from eligible younger men only succeeds in throwing her into their arms. In this case, the unfortunate man is the Sicilian of the title, Don Pedro (a Mafia don? In the 17th century?), so possibly jealous by nationality as well as nature. He's played by Brandon McGibbon, best known for roles as pale young men in new plays and musicals, here displaying vocal and psychological weight previously unexplored, plus a wonderfully comic ability to turn volcanic rages on and off. Trish Lindstrom plays his intended, rather too aggressively; Seann Gallagher, pleasantly loutish, is the successful wooer, French and hence an object of suspicion. But everyone's a foreigner, since the action's set in Spain. This enables play and production to draw on the tradition of native buskers hired to soften ladies on their balconies or in their boudoirs; the cast includes a pair of musicians (Isaac Haig, also the composer, and Sarah Joy Bennett) who play and sing with the kind of purposeful inaccuracy that requires high technical skill to bring off. Amy Wright's choreography, which does a lot to speed the show along, has been executed on the same principle. Joanna Yu contributes bright sets and costumes. Nicolas Billon wrote the neat translation/adaptation, and probably had the idea in the first place. The first-rate direction is by Lee Wilson.

Adam Brazier, one of our leading young actors, steps into directing with Nebraska (Frangipani Productions, Passe Muraille), which tells the story of Charlie Starkweather and Caril-Ann Fugate, a 1950s Bonnie and Clyde. The show has a country-rock score credited to four different composers, one of whom, Kevin McGarry, also wrote the book and presumably the lyrics, besides appearing as Charlie. It's a helpful score, atmospherically and to some extent psychologically, if you can forgive a line about "our killing and kissing spree" that might have fallen off a movie poster. The script, though, carries most of the dramatic weight, and it very effectively sketches the forces that draw its no-hope couple together: he a garbage collector scorned since childhood, she a standard victim of paternal abuse, asking of her new beloved that he buy her a Chinese panda bear to prove his love. He finds a toy one in a store ( "Made in China" he proudly points out) and kills the storekeeper to get it. And so it starts, the robbing coming in a poor second to the killing as a source of erotic excitement. Soon they're world-famous, at least in Nebraska. It's hardly a new insight that murder is the most effective way for America's dispossessed to get famous and get even, and this show runs the risk of monotony from about half-way through. It recovers itself, with an extended scene of a house-jacking in which tensions keep building and roles reversing. The end, though forecast in the beginning, is inconclusive; Caril-Ann peels off from Charlie and it hardly registers. For the most part, though, Brazier's direction is adroit and sensitive. McGarry and Lindsey Frazier give fine blanched performances as the gun-happy couple; a third castmember, Geoffrey Tyler, is only less effective because his role as narrator and all-purpose support has been none too clearly worked out.

I've been hanging with the heavy-hitters of this year's Fringe. However, the most advance-noticed production I've seen is also the most disappointing. This is Red Machine Part 1, presented by a cadre of up, coming and almost-there practitioners calling themselves The Room (Lower Ossington Theatre). It's supposedly a dramatization of the workings of different parts of the human brain; what we're offered as work-in-progress is a triple bill of plays "inspired by the hippocampus, the primary motor cortex and the temporal lobe." On the assumption that we're seeing them in that order, I'd say the hippocampus rules. The first piece, written by Brendan Gall and called First and Last is a set of Pinter/ Kafka mind-games, wittily written and well played by John Gilbert as a taunting old man and James Cade as a tortured young one. Gilbert is especially fine, proving yet again that a mature actor can take anything his juniors can write for him, often better than they can. The subsequent pieces, by Erin Shields (whose We Were Birds I greatly admired last year) and Michael Rubenfeld, left me agonizingly hostile. Shields' Missing Jesus Church is effectively a monologue, bound up (literally) in masochistic religious imagery; religion persists into the title at least of Rubenfeld's A Tribute to Joseph Smith, though if the founder of Mormonism is actually mentioned, I missed him. The show's technical standards are very high, but somehow that makes it worse.
