2009-07-16-a-grit-free-gathering:
Perhaps the key line in Michel Tremblay's Albertine in Five Times is "I wish I'd never been like you." It's more than a figure of speech, being as how it's addressed by Albertine at age 50 to Albertine at age 40. These two share the stage with Albertines at 30, 60 and 70. Just to spell it out, we are beholding, simultaneously, the same Montreal woman at five stages of her life, from 1942 to 1982, the last date doing duty for the present since '82 is just two years before the play was first produced. Another way of putting it is that Albertine at 70, newly settled in a retirement home, is looking back at, and interrogating, her younger selves.

It's been a see-saw kind of existence. Roughly speaking, 50 and 70 have reached plateaux of acceptance and even happiness, while 30, 40 and 60 are locked into various flavours of bitterness and rage. The causes include lifelong poverty, a smothering mother, a husband who quickly absented himself and a mentally handicapped son and a daughter, Therese, who made an even less fortunate marriage choice than her mother and went downhill from there. Albertine calls her a whore, and seems to have been doing so ever since the girl was 11 and allowed herself to be approached by a grown man -- the very man, it turns out, whom she married 10 years later. Albertine (at 30) had been so enraged by her daughter's earlier behaviour with this man that she beat her, uncontrollably; the memory of this has left her consumed with guilt, reinforced by Therese's early, sordid and probably violent death.

When not blaming Therese, Albertine (at least in most of her incarnations) blames men, of whom she seems to have encountered a small and possibly unrepresentative sample. That at least is the opinion of her sister Madeleine, the play's one remaining character, who keeps talking about her own happy marriage. Albertine resents this, possibly because Madeleine's husband was a former beau of her own. That isn't mentioned in this play, but it was revealed in the later-written prequel Past Perfect, which presents Albertine at 20 as a raging and unrepentant narcissist. There's rather more to be said for the five-fold Albertine we meet here, including occasional signs of a sense of humour, but not as much as the play itself seems to think. It may have Canadianclassic status, but it's built on an unsustainable gimmick.

It pretends that we are totally distinct people at different stages of our lives. In fact, other than physically, most people don't change; that's usually their problem. Marking the distinctions off in decades makes them seem especially arbitrary. Even if we grant that the idea is intended as a conceit, a way of juxtaposing different chapters of a person's biography, it still presents a huge casting problem, one that the Shaw Festival's revival hasn't solved. We have to believe that the five actresses are playing aspects of the same person. I didn't. I couldn't see Patricia Hamilton, who plays the oldest Albertine, as the sum of the other four parts.

The lady that Hamilton presents is too much the serene gentlewoman to have demons, or even to have come from the same background as the others. It's especially hard to see how she got to where she is from where Albertine at 60 was; her we meet hunched over her resentments and sustained by tranquilizers, but despite being handed the surefire appeal of misanthropy, Wendy Thatcher's performance obstinately refuses to come into focus.

As the two youngest points of the pentagon, Marla McLean and Jenny L. Wright are mostly planted upstage and fade accordingly into the background; McLean, too, seems surprisingly un-leathery for someone who's seen the troubles she knows. Mary Haney commands the most attention as the middle Albertine, who has found a precarious independence working in a restaurant, whose patrons come for miles to sample her tomato sandwiches; her ode to her own job satisfaction is as mouth-watering as the sandwiches but it still comes over as a set-piece.

Not a monologue, not a conventional drama, the play combines the disadvantages of both forms; we never get right inside Albertine's head, or right outside it either. The play suffers from a sense of entitlement, not so much the character's as the author's. Tremblay had written about Albertine before and would again, and there is a sense that we had better care about her because she's a talismanic cultural figure. It's reinforced in this production, which offers little evidence of the Tremblay grit we keep hearing about; any demotic power has vanished in Linda Gaboriau's translation. Its literary air especially afflicts Nicola Correia-Damude, who, as Madeleine must have one of the least rewarding roles ever written; it's trying enough playing confidante to one heroine, but Correia-Damude has five bending her ear while complaining of her eternal sweetness. The production adds its own layers of gentility with Teresa Przybylski's wispy sets and especially with Marc Desormeaux's enervating and omnipresent incidental music that casts a sentimental glaze over anything. Though in a play that ends with all five Albertines reaching for, or at least towards, the moon (because "she's alone too") sentimentality must be hard to avoid. - Albertine in Five Times is in repertory through Oct. 10. For tickets and information visit shawfest.comor call 1-800-511-SHAW.

2009-07-17-diabolic-morality:
This year, Shaw at the Shaw means history plays. The festival has two of them in the bill, from opposite ends of the Shavian canon and in totally different modes. From near the end of his playwriting career we have In Good King Charles's Golden Days, which is as discursive as a play can get without falling apart, and from near the beginning we have The Devil's Disciple, which may be the most plot-driven thing he ever wrote. It is in fact an unabashed melodrama, and a good one.

It's not quite as unabashed as all that. Shaw rides the conventions pretty hard; a ne'er-do-well son and a pious mother, surprise revelations at the reading of a will, a wrongful arrest and a man nobly taking another's place on the scaffold, a woman torn between love and loyalty and her unsureness of which is which, a court martial and a last-minute rescue, all yield their traditional quotas of suspense and satisfaction. His setting is the U. S. war of independence, and his hero, the splendidly named Dick Dudgeon, is a serious rebel with a political agenda; he doesn't, unlike his possible inspiration Sydney Carton from A Tale of Two Cities, court martyrdom for purely personal reasons, though his rival's wife would like to think he does.

Dick is taking tea with the young and respectable Mrs. Judith Anderson, when the British army drops by to arrest her middle-aged and even more respectable husband, the local minister; they want, as Dick himself had foreseen, to make an example of the solidest citizen available. Dick lets himself be taken by mistake because, he says, he couldn't bring himself to take his head out of a noose and put another man's in. It's a question of nature rather than moral code. Nevertheless Dick has a code, or says he does. He goes on at great length in the first act about being "the devil's disciple," in opposition to the Christian code espoused by his mother, a puritanical monster whose first and only command is joylessness. Still, however much this production's program note (by the redoubtable Ann Saddlemyer) goes on about Shaw's "attraction to the diabolonian" and his debt to Bunyan and Blake, it's hard to see young Dick as more than the conventional good-hearted scapegrace. And, in fact, we hear less and less of his diabolic principles as the story goes on.

The play's last scene builds up to an execution; Tadeusz Bradecki's production begins with one, unscripted but much spoken of later. The officiating soldiers then step out of the frame, to speak some of Shaw's stage directions and to offer their own commentary on how refugees from the play's New Hampshire came to settle in the very Niagara-on-the-Lake in which we are sitting. Peter Hartwell's set, in which gallowstrees rear up behind the script's timbered interiors, provides another kind of frame. Within it is good storytelling, and more emotional and pyschological interest than you might expect. Much of the latter is due to Fiona Byrne's very fine performance of Judith; her well-bred detestation of the reprobate Dick is strong as well as demure, with no hint of caricature. Evan Buliung is Dick, playing with the dash and swagger and breezy common sense necessary to drive both the play and the character along, though sometimes slowing them with unnecessary vocal and physical curlicues. Peter Krantz gives a decent account of the minister with the soul of a soldier, though he lacks both weight and age. The end in which the two men exchange vocations doesn't convince, but then it never does; the play hasn't made us believe much in either in the first place.

We do believe, with a couple of lapses, in Donna Belleville's implacable self-pity as Mrs. Low Dudgeon, and are taken by surprise--at least I was -- by Jim Mezon as the British General Burgoyne, a Shavian fellow spirit who accordingly gets more good lines even than the devil, let alone his disciple. He may have the best set of sardonic one-liners in dramatic literature; Mezon goes beyond them, indeed even sacrifices a few laughs, to create a desperately world-weary man behind the mask.

Bradecki, a regular visitor from Poland, is one of the Shaw Festival's most imaginative regular directors. I have sadly to mark the passing of another, this one a resident. Neil Munro, who died on Monday, directed Man and Superman, The Petrified Forest, You Can't Take It with You, The Circle, Rosmersholm and the complete works of Granville Barker -- a long line of the best Shaw shows I remember. He was also responsible for a few of the worst, but the two things go together. He had an exceptional command of visual imagery always keyed to the play in hand, or at least to his conception of it, but he never sacrificed ating to environment. He was a rare bird, a loss not just to the Shaw but to the entire Canadian theatre. - The Devil's Disciple is in repertory through October. Visit shawfest.comor call 1-800-511-SHAW for tickets and information.

2009-07-18-mum-s-the-word-at-dream-in-hi:
Shipwrecks are not the easiest things to stage in open-air theatres, especially when the night is still young and lighting effects are minimal, so it's understandable that this year's Dream in High Park offers us The Tempest without the tempest. Well, not absolutely without. What happens at the beginning of Sue Miner's production is this: The spirit Ariel arrives, does some arm-waving and a storm starts. There's no distinguishable dialogue, but we see a couple of actors tumbling acrobatically andaristocratically down the auditorium steps. Then Ariel produces a model ship, which is passed among the audience, who handle it gingerly before it ends up onstage and is brusquely dispatched down a trap door. Actors appear onstage, waving blue cloths as it disappears. If we can't have the scene the author wrote, this is an effective and imaginative substitute. Meanwhile, the storm's sound-track issues with fearful effect from both sides of the theatre's sound system. Amplification in Shakespeare is an abomination, but at this point the speakers earn their keep. They will do so again later when the castaway Ferdinand has his senses further confused by hearing Ariel's song relayed in stereo on alternating channels. This softens him up for falling in love with Miranda, to the well-concealed glee of her mother, Prospera.

You read that right. Prospero in this production is a woman. It doesn't work out too badly: certainly better than the similar sex-change performed on Shylock in Merchant of Venice a few years back. That play pretended a Jewish mother is identical to a Jewish father, an unwise assumption. But perhaps magicians can be unisex; Karen Robinson's Prospera is, within certain limits, a fine performance, rising to compelling heights of anger and disillusion in the revels-ending speech, and sounding a distinctive note of wistful renunciation when she surrenders her supernatural powers. In more personal relationships, she seems a very nice woman. Even before the storm breaks, we're treated to a glimpse of her and Miranda at peace on their island. There's fondness in her description of the infant Miranda as "a cherubim"; and if the child, in Taylor Trowbridge's performance, hasn't quite grown up angelic, she's certainly a fresh and captivating young woman, matched with an eager Ferdinand (Patrick Kwok-Choon), who charmingly says his first words to her ve-ry slow-ly, on the reasonable assumption that they're unlikely to speak the same language.

All the same, something is missing, something best described as iron. In the end, the mother-daughter dynamic isn't the same as father-daughter, and there are tensions in the play that go by the board. The production seems committed to an all-girls-together aesthetic that ends up sentimentalizing it. Miranda is allowed to join Prospera for the epilogue, a solitary speech if ever there was one, and Audrey Dwyer's Ariel shows less resentment of her captivity and less fear of its renewal than any other on record. Her one gesture of defiance gets from Prospera an arch "how now, moody?" in tones that seem borrowed from Maggie Smith. Even Caliban seems affected by the good humour; Ron Kennell gives a skilled performance, but one that's low on malice. This is strange because you'd think that Caliban, deprived of his own mother, would feel more oppressed by a female conqueror than by a male one. The production proceeds on the assumption that you can alter one part of a play's chemistry --gender, race, time frame -- and carry on with the rest as if nothing had happened.

This doesn't affect the clown scenes, which are unusually good, with Mark Crawford's Trinculo dignified as well as craven and Jason Gray's Stephano growing in self-importance by the moment. They're a very believable pair of drunks, while Caliban and Trinculo, sharing a cloak, make a great pantomime horse. The cutting of the first scene makes the courtiers' roles seem thinner than ever, but the actors fight back with Robert Dodds' king as credibly conscious-stricken as any I've seen. There's some gender-alteration here, too, and it works well with Liz Gordon's Gonzala. The supposed ace, though, is that Prospera's usurping sibling is also a woman: a juicy idea, except that the two never meet till the last scene, during which the evil Antonia is almost silent. The sisters are reduced to throwing glances at one another, and in fact Tracy Ferencz's Antonia does project a powerful image of unredemption. In the earlier scene in which she tempts Sebastian (Karl Ang) to regicide, the production underplays its hand; the two are shown as already being lovers, though it would be more effective to have the sexual and political seductions play out simultaneously. Economics mean that most of the spirits' masque has to go, but that's hardly a loss; what magic we do see is inventive. This is a lightweight production but it isn't dumb. It's the best Dream anyone has had in High Park in years. - The Tempest runs through Sept. 6 at the Dream in High Park. Call 416-368-3110 for details.
2009-07-21-inside-the-actors-egos:
STAR CHAMBER

Royal George Theatre, Niagara-on-the-Lake, Ont.

---

The Shaw Festival, which over three evenings is mounting all nine of the one-act plays that make up Noel Coward's Tonight at 8:30, is also throwing in a lunchtime supplement. This is Star Chamber, a play written to be part of the original 1936 cycle but only performed then at a single matinee. The Shaw production seems to be its first outing since then.

It's a slight but entertaining piece that, in Kate Lynch's vivacious and good-looking production, comes over as one in-joke piled on top of another. A collection of West End stars and starlets gather together on the stage of a London theatre to fulfill their obligations as committee members of a retirement home for aged actresses. They are all devoted to the cause but their competing egos, added to their late arrivals and early departures when called for anything that isn't a rehearsal or a performance, greatly delay the meeting's getting started and keep derailing it when it does. The original audience presumably enjoyed watching popular performers lampooning themselves or other popular performers. The Shaw audience, certainly at the premiere, gets a comparable kick out of seeing some of its own favourite actors acting actors.

Double incest apart, the play's drawback is that the frustration felt by some of the committee members at the refusal of the proceedings to proceed can't help communicating itself to the audience. We too, once we've realized there isn't going to be a plot, would like them at least to get on with the meeting. Our representative onstage is the home's secretary, a stage-struck civilian on whom Guy Bannerman bestows a nice blend of the businesslike and bewildered; his is really the star performance though the program, which seems to have internalized the characters' own scale of values, denies him star-billing while according it to every one of the luvvies: a word that I hate but one that Coward really does seem to have gone out of his way to justify. Evan Buliung is in excellent form as Julian Breed, a matinee idol with a distinctive line in crisp narcissism. This wasn't, as might have been expected, Coward's own role; he played Johnny Bolton, a genial but unstoppably anecdotal comedian successful enough to own the theatre that houses the meeting and played here, with dead-on geniality and an irresistible waddle, by Neil Barclay.

The female stars in the chamber outnumber the males, while working hard to outsmart one another. Sharry Flett, who seldom gets a smart part, compensates delightfully as Violet Vibart, quick on the drawl and brandishing a stylish cigarette. Costumes have been slyly updated, though the text hasn't, to suggest that these types are eternal. It certainly seems so with Fiona Byrne as committee president Xenia James, an overflowing fountain of heartfelt gush who here comports herself like a blond Barbra Streisand. She's accompanied by a large and beautiful dog who may, in theatrical terms, be the greatest Dane since Hamlet. This is the only play known to me in which someone talks about the inadvisability of sharing a stage with an animal while actually doing so. There's a child too, though an invisible one, brought along in a pram by Jenny L. Wright as a proud and indignant champion of working motherhood, a subject that her fellow actresses seem to find vaguely distasteful. Peter Krantz plays a stage manager whose laconic bearing suggests that he has seen them all come and can hardly wait to see them all go.

The play keeps satire and sentiment running neatly in tandem, mocking its characters' self-aggrandizement while respecting their sincerity. In doing so, it foreshadows one of Coward's last and most heartfelt plays, Waiting in the Wings, which is set in just such an institution as the one these people are supporting and of which, as they remark with a mock-Dickensian relish that hides a real chill, they may one day stand in need themselves. Lynch rounds things off with a musical coda, a Coward singalong that includes a startlingly anachronistic arrangement of World Weary; the lyric's line about being "tired of all those Jumping Jacks" would be very apposite here, if we could hear it. Throwing this sequence in at all is probably a sign of desperation, an acknowledgment that the play -- really a sketch -- hasn't gone anywhere. But it's fun and well-staged, and Buliung's feigned reluctance before launching into a breakneck Mad Dogs and Englishmen is a treat. - Star Chamber plays in repertory through Oct. 11. 2009-07-23-a-triumvirate-of-music-and-ma:
PLAY, ORCHESTRA, PLAY

Royal George Theatre, Niagara-on-the-Lake

---

The umbrella title Play, Orchestra, Play shelters three of Noel Coward's Tonight at 8:30 oneacters, all with musical connections. The middle piece includes a character who torments her family by practising the piano, badly. The plays on either side of it are outright mini-musicals. The evening's principal connecting thread, however, is that all three playlets depict marriages, none of them happy.

The first couple up are the seedy British music-hall duo Red Peppers, the title of the play being also the name of their act: a song, dance and crosstalk routine that may, as the male Pepper proudly says, have been good enough for his father (and probably for his father before him), but is looking and sounding decidedly archaic in the brave new talkie-infested world of 1936. So the Peppers are reduced to playing the provinces, and nowhere near the top of the bill either.

In between musical performances, we spend time in the Peppers' dressing room listening to them bicker with one another, with the conductor (trouble over tempo), the manager (trouble over billing) and a senior actress with classical pretensions (trouble). The play is more about flavour than action, a nostalgic but mercilessly clear-eyed look at a dying theatrical world Coward himself had long since left behind. Christopher Newton's production imposes more shape on it than some I have seen, marking off very clearly the point at which our two troupers sink their differences and close ranks against the outside world. I had trouble buying Jay Turvey as a leathery veteran of the halls, but he and Patty Jamieson expertly calibrate their bitter rows and unspoken reconciliations, while Steven Sutcliffe offers an original view of the manager as an insolent sycophant, half toady, half toad.

The second play, Fumed Oak, takes Coward back to another world he had escaped but obviously still had nightmares about: that of stifling lower-middle-class respectability. Henry Gow, retail employee, sits meek and silent in his South London home where the first thing he hears every morning is his wife and her mother nagging one another. They nag, or ignore him too, and Mrs. Gow also nags their daughter (the amateur pianist), though her mother prefers to compete by buying the kid sweets. Finally Henry speaks, and once he's started he doesn't stop.

The play's entire second half is his tirade as he tells the assorted females what he thinks of them, how he was trapped into marriage and how he is now going to get out of it. Tears and threats are in vain, and when his mother-in-law insults him he slaps her, provoking an intake of breath from the auditorium but no noticeable protest. Sutcliffe, stewing behind his specs and then exploding through them, is a gloriously turning worm who has the audience spellbound. Jamieson, in a rare nonmusical role, is a thoroughly believable spouse; and Wendy Thatcher and Robin Evans Willis bring the oldest and youngest generations to horrific life. The play is snobbish, misogynist, one-sided and undoubtedly expresses deep, and deeply discreditable, impulses in its author. I loved it.

I was less transported by the third piece, Shadow Play, though it's potentially the most interesting of the trio and certainly the most advanced. In fact, it feels experimental even now. Victoria Gayforth, half of a troubled society marriage, comes home from seeing a musical comedy and dreams the nightmare of her own life, interspersed with memories of a happier past. The songs that invade her mind include two of Coward's best: Play, Orchestra, Play itself, frantically driven, and the truly haunting You Were There. This is Coward dealing not with worlds he'd left but with the one he now belonged to. And that, I think, is the trouble; he doesn't have to work at the background.

Victoria's problems are taken to be automatically interesting.

Despite all that Julie Martell does for her, she doesn't take on any individual life. And the staging, though expert in its own right, is too much. Newton and his designer, Cameron Porteous, make great use of projections; entertainingly in the first play and with bleak wit in the second. In the third, though, they go wild with them, providing a filmed backdrop for every scene. If someone mentions a Venetian honeymoon, we see gondolas. It's overkill; and has the perverse effect of damming up the play's fluidity rather than releasing it. Add everything up, though, and this is a fine and various evening. - Play, Orchestra, Play is in repertory through Oct. 31. Call 1-800-511-SHAW or visit shawfest.comfor tickets and information.

2009-07-25-a-sister-who-s-doing-it-by-he:
There is, despite is title and its being a rock musical, no nudity in bare. The bareness depicted is all emotional, or at least purports to be, and is flourished in our faces as insistently as any naked bodies might be. The show was first staged in Los Angeles in 2000 and was done off-Broadway in 2004. Its Canadian premiere is the work of a new group called WaterEdge Productions, whose credentials are, at most, semi-professional. Most of the cast are present or recent students. They nearly all sing well, and a couple of them have strong stage presence. It isn't the performances that make the evening unbearable. It's the material.

Bare takes adolescent self-pity and self-importance to levels previously unsounded even by rock musicals; it's like the least tolerable parts of Rent and Spring Awakening rubbed together and going on forever. It isn't that the characters don't have reason to feel sorry for themselves; it's that their agonies are presented without wit, perspective or context. The boys and girls, hormones raging, are students at a Catholic boarding-school. The central love-interest is between Peter and Spencer. Peter is basically cool with being gay, except that he worries about what his mother will think. Spencer is a lot more conflicted, especially when he gets involved with Ivy, who is, according to who's singing about her, the cutest girl around or the school slut. Also suffering big-time are Spencer's sister Nadie, a self-described "Plain Jane Flat Ass" (or so says the list of musical numbers; I thought while she was singing that the words were "bad ass," which would make her more interesting), who's jealous of Ivy's looks; and Matt, who fancies Ivy, therefore hates Spencer, and takes it out on Peter. The show keeps shifting focus among this quintet, eventually producing a suicide, though not from the character of whom you might most have expected it. This leads the survivors to arraign the religious authorities for their lack of understanding, and indeed the show presents itself as a struggle between youthful rebellion and institutional repression. But it won't wash, because the church hierarchy is hardly present. The kids are left to their own devices, dramatically and, as far as we can tell, socially. They do drugs and have sex without feeling any noticeable pressure except peer-pressure; even gay-bashing is the sole province of the jealous Matt, who apologizes afterwards. An uncomprehending Father Confessor is wheeled on from time to time, but the staff member we see most of is a hearty black nun, who tells Peter that she understands gay males because she's been around so many priests. This is much the funniest line in the show, but the topics it suggests are not pursued. The show starts with a rather powerful chorale, paradoxically entitled Epiphany, but this, too, is a trail that's never followed

The nun, Sister Chantelle, is much the most engaging character around. She directs the school play, Romeo and Juliet, in which Spencer plays Romeo despite an initial reluctance to audition since he's more of a jock than a thesp (shades of High School Musical, one of this show's less culturally respectable antecedents). Ivy, of course, is Juliet; Peter, Mercutio; Matt, Tybalt; and Nadie, the Nurse, for which she seems ungrateful, considering what a great part it is. The entire cast sing the opening chorus, causing the Sister to say at rehearsal "that note's a C-natural; there ain't nothing natural about what you're singing."

She could have been describing bare's entire score. This is one of those almost through-sung jobs, and though some of Damon Intrabartolo's tunes are pretty, Jon Hartmere's lyrics are the usual agonizing mock-ups. Trying to be conversational, they end up clunky and literal-minded. None of the words sit easily on the music. We get an endless procession of solos in which the characters solemnly spell out their feelings, without ambiguity, without subtext, without movement, and therefore without drama. Though, of course, it's hard to be sure about subtext, when you can't hear much of the text. Even the R&J excerpts are sung, though, prologue apart, they don't seem to be doing it as a musical. The authors do throw in a few spoken lines of their own and, compared to the score, they sound like miracles of point and economy. Hartmere is also one of those lyricists who don't know what a rhyme is. I know that the above description would fit most rock musicals, but this happens to be the one I've just sat through.

Brian Gregory-Waters' production happens up, down and across a broad flight of steps, behind which hang stained-glass windows and a crucifix, to suggest the context that the show doesn't. Down in the hole between the structure and the backing sit the musicians; at least I assume the conductor, whom we do see, is waving that stick at someone. Having the band onstage is no novelty, but this may be the first ever onstage orchestra pit. Nichola Lawrence sings mightily as Sister Chantelle. Her role includes a dream-appearance as the Virgin Mary, here a Motown chanteuse with two back-up girls; she brings down the house, as black divas with powerful voices nearly always do, but she deserves it. She also gets to speak a sizeable proportion of the show's sparse dialogue; her bio says she's never acted before but she seems to be a natural.

- Bare runs through Aug. 1 at Hart House Theatre. For ticket information, call 416-978-8849 .

2009-07-31-i-dream-of-durham-season-2-in:
No one can say that Durham County didnt give fair warning. Its first season began with a peeping Tom, in a peaceful woodland setting, witnessing the rape and murder of two schoolgirls. The voyeur went on to perform a couple of copycat killings of his own. We watched him; the show was in no way a whodunnit. By the halfway mark his guilt was also clear to the drama's protagonist, Mike Sweeney, a cop who, were he or the show given to lightheartedness, might reasonably have described the killer, Ray Prager, as his friendly neighbourhood psychopath, since they lived next door to one another. The showdown came when Ray staked out Mike's teenage daughter Sadie as his next victim. Mike arrived in time to rescue her, but it was Sadie who fired the gunshot that put Ray out of action without taking his life.

This was a disturbing production about disturbed people. It was stylish, brooding, left many questions open and made no emotional or narrative concessions. Among Canadian crime-dramas, it was the most intelligent since Intelligence. The publicity for the shows second season, now halfway through its six-episode run, has likened it to the best American cable series. Ive no wish to be unpatriotic but that's going too far. Durham County is intense, but nobody could call it rich. Probably the HBO series it most resembles -- in being domestic rather than panoramic -- is Six Feet Under: my least favourite of the bunch, but it did have a sense of humour. Durham County, mining a narrow seam, comes over as gratuitously creepy.

Or so I thought about Season 1. Season 2's story grabs me more and so do its characters, both new and continuing. Its something very rare in television: a genuine sequel. Most returning series merely rearrange the same old pieces on the same old board. But Durham County ended its first round with plenty of unfinished business, which the second is duly moving forward. Season 1 depended far too much on the relationship between Mike and Ray, boyhood friends as well as present neighbours, and on Rays reiterated claim that he

and Mike were really brothers under the skin: a proposition not nearly as fascinating as either Ray or the show seemed to think it was.

In Season 2, Ray is awaiting trial; he still exercises a malign influence on Mike and especially on Sadie, but he does it in short bursts and from a distance, which is far more effective. There's a new actor, Romano Orzari, playing Ray this season; the show's obsessive use of dreams, usually nightmares, and flashback means that he and his predecessor, Justin Louis, sometimes turn up in the same episode. Meanwhile Hugh Dillons shaven-headed, bat-eared Mike continues to be loaded with issues; he may not be a killer but he can be frighteningly violent. Dillon does a good three-way stretch between thug, father and sleuth, and a two-way as unfaithful but caring -- or maybe just guilty -- spouse.

He has, this time, a worthier antagonist, whos also his lover: Dr. Pen Verity (Michelle Forbes, TV's ubiquitous Lady Macbeth-in-waiting), a forensic psychiatrist whose young daughter drowned and who holds on to her son with what her estranged husband (the excellent Geordie Johnson) holds to be dangerous possessiveness. Pen is a consummate liar, and also a consummate fantasist, with a death wish for herself and others. This makes her a twin to Ray, and even more dangerous.

In some ways the central character is Sadie, herself a resourceful amateur detective with professional aspirations (Mike thinks she's better than he is), still traumatized by the assault, tortured when she starts doubting her dad and, just to round things off, wrestling with the assailants son being her boyfriend. Laurence Leboeuf is first-rate in the role of Sadie, as is Helene Joy, in the comparatively placid role of her mother.

With the exception of one goodcop(most sympathetically played by Patrick Labbe), Laurie Finstad Knizhniks script seems to regard the entire male sex as actual or incipient gangbangers; the female villain at least has a ghastly past to excuse her. It's a shock, of the wrong kind, when the plot suddenly turns out to be governed by events that happened 20 years ago; it plays like desperation. Conversely, key elements from Season 1 seem to have been forgotten: Nobody appears concerned to track down the original double murderer, and no one mentions that Ray's first victim was Mike's almost-lover. Some ambiguities are rewarding; others seem merely tight-lipped. But I'm sucked in.

- Durham County airs Mondays at 9 p. m. on The Movie Network.

2009-08-01-daylight-come-and-we-want-ano:
Based on a 1972 movie that the program calls "one of the first cult films" (though there've been cults almost as long as there've been movies), The Harder They Come is an enlivening musical with some boring bits. Structurally, it ain't nothin' but a house party, which puts it in the tradition of such other shows from the Theatre Royal, Stratford East -- East London, that is --as Five Guys Named Moe, the Louis Jordan anthology. This show is a Jimmy Cliff anthology, with the same good-time feel, but also with a lot more plot and a darker overlay. The elements don't always fuse.

The party here is a wake, held in memory of its hero, Ivan, whose story is told to us in, you guessed, flashback. Ivan, the role played by Cliff in the movie, is accordingly a reggae singer, who comes to town, gets work with a preacher, joins his choir and attracts the attention of the listening world, in general, and the preacher's ward, in particular. He elopes with her, on the preacher's bike, and auditions for a record producer, who represents the sleazy side of the music business; the show doubts there's any other. He strikes out on his own, incurring a lot of hardship. Asked to name his record label, he lights on "Rhygin," meaning "wild," which was the nickname of Ivanhoe Martin, a popular outlaw with whom our Ivan identifies and with whom the show identifies him. This historical Ivan was killed in a firefight with the police in 1948; our fictitious one operates in, presumably, the '70s. Superimposing one story on the other doesn't work; by all accounts (well, by Pauline Kael's account), it didn't in the film either. The show tries to annex the old Ivan's Robin Hood reputation, but it's rather a long road to travel from being swindled by a record company to shooting sprees with cops. Perry Henzell, adapting his own film script, tries to bridge the gap by showing the record mogul in league with, if not in control of, the corrupt police, who in turn are hand-in-glove with the marijuana trade at which Ivan, in desperate need of bread, also tries his hand. But it feels forced, and confusion overtakes the long stretches of the second act that pass between numbers. The heavy Jamaican patois helps make these incomprehensible for the uninitiated.

Though, it also helps the overall feeling of authenticity. In its grafting of pre-existing pop songs onto a story-line, the show resembles Mamma Mia, except that its songs have backbone and its story relates to something real. These songs belong to these people, even though their dramatic relevance is generally confined to their titles, with the title number becoming a metaphor for getting up and fighting. The best musical-dramatic sequence resurrects dear old Day-O, the Banana Boat Song, performed on the docks with the bananas a sly metaphor for weed. The villainous police chief sings Pressure Point many times as cue for a bit of audience participation: standard in British shows of this kind, but reducing his menace potential.

Directed by Dawn Reid and Kerry Michael, the show feels laid-back and uncluttered, helped by a cool and simple set from the great British designer Ultz and lighting by Jo Joelson in highly atmospheric shades of red. Jackie Guy's choreography uses simple formations to intoxicating effect, especially when Rolan Bell's Ivan, with his elastic legs and sunshine personality, is at the centre of them. The best individual singing comes from Lain Gray as his buddy and protector. The long reprise finale is a blast, and an indication of where the show's heart, and certainly its soul, really reside.

Another show with some songs (old-fashioned but nice) is The Menaechmus Twins, one of whose characters, a Roman slave, at one point makes as if about to sing about being free but then stops himself, as if he doesn't want to go into competition with Stephen Sondheim. This makes sense, as this play is by Plautus, whose ancient Roman comedies inspired A Funny Thing Happened on the Way to the Forum, though it's one that Forum didn't use. It did, though, inspire Shakespeare, whose Comedy of Errors added some sentiment and an extra pair of lookalikes. You may wonder if he really improved it much, since this open-air production is a total delight in its own right. Plautus at least explains why his long-separated twins should have the same first name, which is more than Shakespeare did. He also provided a tidier expository prologue, which the uncredited translation (in which someone "fills a fine freighter full of ... freight") gleefully exploits; as does Melee Hutton's production, brazenly presenting us with supposedly identical twins who are, at most, of about the same height. Wayne Ward gives a wonderfully self-satisfied account of the dark-haired married one, who finds himself excluded ( "I'm the most shuttest-out man alive") by wife and mistress, both of them played, as in some Freudian nightmare and deliciously, by the same actress, Sarah Evans. His fair-haired bachelor sibling is Ryan Hollyman, who plays on one flustered note but holds it well. Adrian Proszowski as one brother's servant and Jeffrey R. Smith as the other's parasite are towers of supporting strength. There is a basic two-door set, neatly used, and no need of lighting, since the show starts at 6 p. m. and is over at 7:20. It's early, short, hilarious and you pay what you can. The best theatrical deal in town. - The Harder They Come runs through Aug. 23 at the Canon Theatre. Call 416-872-1212 for ticket and schedule details. The Menaechmus Twins runs in Withrow Park through Aug. 9. Visit theatreworksproductions.comfor more information.

2009-08-08-to-love-is-to-hate-and-to-hat:
Today, if you've got up early enough, you can see an all-day performance, spread across the Shaw Festival's three stages, of the 10 one-act plays that make up Noel Coward's Tonight at 8:30. Or, as they might have subtitled it on this occasion, This Morning at 9:30. Theatrical marathons tend to be their own reward, though this one won't have the customary insurance of a continuous narrative. The plays may have been written for the same performers, principally Coward himself and Gertrude Lawrence, but each concerns a different bunch of people.

Meanwhile, for those who like to take their pleasures less intensively, the Shaw has completed its staging of the cycle with Ways of the Heart, a triple bill whose portmanteau title has been assembled from its first play, The Astonished Heart, and its last, Ways and Means. The name of the middle one, Family Album, couldn't be fitted in. ( Family Ways, perhaps?) Blair Williams, who made a spectacular directorial debut with The President last season, now gives smart and confident productions of all three.

On The Astonished Heart he bestows a hard glitter that is positively Pinteresque. This suits, since Coward, rather to his own surprise, was a Pinter fan, and Pinter returned the compliment. "I'm on Pinter's wavelength, no doubt of it," Coward wrote in his diary after seeing the first production of The Caretaker -- a moving gesture of recognition across the theatrical generation gap. The two playwrights shared a cauterizing view of human relations and a taste for apparently simple dialogue that masks as much as it reveals. Like Pinter's Betrayal, The Astonished Heart is a play about adultery that plays tricks with time. Those in the Coward play are comparatively primitive -- they consist of framing the play so that the main action is a flashback -- but they provide an effective perspective.

Christian is a psychiatrist, Barbara his wife, and Lenora his mistress. Barbara knows what's going on but tolerates, even encourages it, intent on preserving a marriage that's become companionship. That doesn't stop her being worried, and even hurt. Christian and Lenora, meanwhile, have an infinite capacity for wounding one another; neither can be as uncaring as they would like. The needs of each for the other are never in sync; the balance of dependency is shifting and, eventually, fatal. Unusually for Coward, the play presents passion that is neither heightened into melodrama nor defused into farce. Its lovers are the sophisticated counterweight to the repressed brief encounters of Still Life, from elsewhere in the cycle. As was once said of his friend and disciple Terence Rattigan, Coward shows in one play that love unbridled is a destroyer and, in the other, that love bridled is a destroyer. Laurie Paton gets straight to the sheltered heart of the concerned and comfortable Barbara, as does Claire Jullien, a veritable Hitchcock blond, to the more demonstrative heart of Lenora, an elegant agonizer and the cause of greater agonizing. Christian's heart proves the most astonished of all, but David Jansen hovers around its periphery; 1930s suavity doesn't seem to be his thing, and he lacks the professional assurance of a fashionable physician who conducts his affairs as if they were consultations and is shattered when, psychologically speaking, someone sends him the bill. The play ranks with Fumed Oak as one of the surprise discoveries of the season.

Coward's verbal economy isn't always matched, in these plays anyway, by structural economy. The Astonished Heart has a last scene that's symmetrically necessary but redundant as narrative. It goes on after it's made its point, while the other two plays take forever to get to theirs. Family Album, the only one of the trio I've seen before, is here the most disconcerting. It shows us a Victorian family in mourning, discovering a music box among the mementoes and breaking into song accordingly. Gradually, it's revealed that the deceased was a tyrant they're glad to be rid of. I remembered it as a dainty if ironic period piece; Williams directs it for broad farce, at which his cast are unevenly adept. All, however, is validated when Michael Ball, in a heavenly release from avuncular roles, shuffles on as a butler who looks like Quasimodo blessed with a shock of golden hair. His demented loyalty, as someone says, lightens up a pale room. The paleness extends to the actors' faces, set off, in Paton's authoritative case, by eyes red-rimmed from conscientious weeping.

Sue LePage provides a simple but handsome set of sets, which are now spectacularly changed by the cast who simultaneously divert us by singing Any Little Fish (which seems to be the season's theme song), culminating in the descent of a bed, with Jansen and Jullien inside it, in blue pajamas. We're now in Ways and Means, in which they play a married couple of spongers who've outstayed their welcome on the Cote d'Azur. As in the first play, she's completely and, in this case, hilariously, on top of the style, while he has to struggle, though he's certainly struggling in the right direction. The play's first half restates the situation at a length made more tedious by clumsy supporting performances, with Jenny Young being a riveting exception as a guttural adventuress of uncertain extraction. Things buck up splendidly with the arrival of a burglar ex machina who knows his place (Patrick McManus, delightfully deferential) and helps the hero and heroine regain theirs. Morally, it's an unimproving tale; theatrically, it improves all the way. The complete project doesn't rank as a major revelation, but all the plays in it have shown themselves worth doing and most -- not all--have been well done.

2009-08-11-an-overstuffed-couch-our-tv-c:
I was quite shocked the first time I saw Johnny Carson. Shocked and frustrated. I was visiting the U. S. from Britain, where I had become accustomed to TV interview shows in which the host not only asked the guest questions but seemed interested in hearing the answers. Some of these conversations even lasted for longer than five minutes. Carson couldn't let an exchange get underway without derailing it with a gag. This, we were never allowed to forget, was his show, and nobody else was going to be allowed to usurp the centre of attention. The fact that underneath it all he was probably very intelligent only made it worse.

In the long years since then, of course, things on the late-night talk-show front have only gotten worse. At least Carson was dapper, in the way he spoke as well as the way he looked. Conan O'Brien, the newish incumbent on NBC's Tonight Show, seems to want to make a style out of being flustered; his claim to maturity is that he doesn't look a day under 23. The trouble is, the nervousness seems genuine: understandably since his predecessor, Jay Leno, is about to come back with a heavily publicized new show of his own that, we're promised, will focus on comedy rather than interviews. This seems sensible of Leno; in the days when he used to be Carson's regular stand-in, he was funnier than Carson, perhaps because he had stuff to prove. That disappeared when he himself assumed the Tonight Show mantle; the format took over and he became just another host. It's mandatory to get a comedian to front these shows, so the presumption is that he has to try to be funny, but you can never get a really great comedian, because they have better things to do.

Meanwhile the conventions have petrified. O'Brien has revived the clasped-hand gesture of benison that was Carson's trademark, but it's unclear whether he means it as homage, satire or propitiatory offering. He also has a sidekick on the Ed McMahon model -- Andy Richter -- though the guy has almost nothing to do. And he has the obligatory cackling bandleader. The role of the musical help has diminished on these shows, since the visiting rock acts tend to provide their own accompaniment. Of course it's nice to see live musicians holding down a steady job in these hard and increasingly mechanized times, but their talents seem to be wasted on blowing fanfares and laughing, in a scattered and sporadic sort of way at the host's jokes, as if the studio audience weren't trusted to be sycophantic enough. The idea of the bandleader as comedian probably dates back to radio days, when Phil Harris did it on the Jack Benny show; it's meant, I suppose, to emphasize the informality of what are, in fact, stiflingly formal proceedings.

You get the monologue, in which the host hearkens back to his stand-up roots. It's difficult to get good material five nights a week, so the style is to make the unfunniness the point. O'Brien falls back on this, and David Letterman on the CBS Late Show is of course the past master of it. He certainly wears the best-tailored suits. I've always found the style-- so "ironic" that you lose track of what it's being ironic about -- extremely irritating; and now that everybody else has adopted it as a fallback, the best to be said for Letterman is that he got there first. There are usually a few political gags -- more of them since The Daily Show started providing competition on cable -- but they're just name-dropping. They fall victim to the overall attitude that nothing really matters and nothing is important. The lesson of The Daily Show is that you have to mean it.

On to the interviews, which have given up any pretense of being more than plugs for movies. If the performer is only an actor, then the chat will be short. If he or she (usually he) is a comedian, then host and guest will have some common ground and the audience gets to enjoy them buttering one another up. It's all-purpose fawning, the show business boys' club, which often seems what the whole world has been reduced to. There is, of course, a lot of convergence on the circuit. Last week you could probably have seen most of Funny People simply by checking out the clips on the chat show. Judd Apatow, guesting on Jimmy Fallon, was quite entertaining about the protocols of going from show to show: You start your day on Howard Stern, doing penis jokes; you end it on The Daily Show, doing political penis jokes.

Fallon, coming on after O'Brien, is supposed to provide an antidote but in fact offers the mixture exactly as before, though without O'Brien's residual charm. The other Jimmy, Kimmel on ABC, is no more likeable but sharper. One night last week he offered a parody on Paris Hilton's search for a New BFF; I didn't even know such a show existed (though I'm not surprised) but I'm not sure he nailed it. Sitting on a throne or lounging on a chaise, he had showbiz narcissism down cold.

The best commentary on that subject, though, comes from the one guy for whom it's worth staying up late (or, in his case, late late) Craig Ferguson. His Scottishness is a tonic in itself; so are his self-deprecating whoops, which he exercised last Tuesday when recounting the experience of recording his own autobiography as an Audiobook ( "I thought, this is a very long book") and anticipating listening to the result while re-reading the book and looking in the mirror. "I've just given myself a bad review for my book--good, I deserve it, smug bastard that I am." Coming on after Letterman, he does seem an antidote, operating on a set that seems to be identical except that he's the only person on it and the view through the windows behind him is not appetizing. He talked about someone who'd sued the network for $40-million: "If CBS had that kind of money, they wouldn't have an emigre host on a talk show. If they had 40 -- dollars, not millions -- they could fix the windows." He's shamelessly literate, sounds as if he means what he says, and his mea culpa about his past alcoholism is a classic, painful and hilarious. (Watch it on YouTube.) He postpones the interview until the last possible moment, and when it does arrive -- on this episode it was with Tony Shalhoub -- it's substantial if not searching. The rumour is that he's being groomed to be the next Letterman. Personally, I don't think he could do it. That's a compliment. - The Tonight Show with Conan O'Brien airs weeknights at 11:35 p. m. on NBC and A; The Late Show with David Letterman at 11:35 p. m. on CBS and OMNI; Late Night with Jimmy Fallon at 12:35 a. m. on NBC and A; Jimmy Kimmel Live at 12:05 a. m. on ABC and Citytv; The Late Late Show with Craig Ferguson at 12:35 a. m. on CBS and CHCH; The Jay Leno Show debuts Sept. 14 at 10 p. m. on NBC and Citytv.

2009-08-14-parochialist-friendly-canadia:
BILLY BISHOP GOES TO WAR

Young Centre for the Performing Arts

---

Here is one Canadian classic that deserves the title. Make that two Canadian classics: the play itself, written 30 years ago by John Gray in collaboration with Eric Peterson, and Peterson himself, reprising its title role. Since Billy Bishop Goes to War tells the story of Canada's First World War flying ace in his own words, which include a lot of reported conversations, he gets to play a lot of other people as well. As before he shares the stage with Gray, who delivers the odd spoken word but mostly confines himself to sitting at the piano playing and singing his own musical score, with Peterson joining in on the vocals. My impression is that Gray now does more of the singing, and Peterson less, than used to be the case but I wouldn't swear to it. Since that Soulpepper revival has been directed, with exemplary tact and imagination, by Ted Dykstra, it's tempting to think of it as One Piano, Four Hands.

I've only seen the piece once before, when it visited London in 1981 and when I didn't like it much: Blame it on my youth and, I guess, my parochialism. I didn't know Canada and, though I think I appreciated his energy and virtuosity, I didn't know Peterson; I now have an investment in both. Here, he's in robe and pajamas, as the older Billy remembering his youth, which lends a piquant edge to one of its climactic sequences in which he goes on a mission, also in pajamas under his flying-gear. Billy, as presented here, is a dead-end kid who joins up without quite knowing why. As the play's recurring theme song puts it "We were off to fight the Hun / We would shoot him with a gun ..." I used to resent the redundancy of that lyric, but its naivete, and the simplicity of the tune that accompanies it, now seemss appropriate. Billy, at this point, is naive, like so many young men who went to that war, both British and Canadian. "We were off to fight the Hun / And it looked like lots of fun." For him, it does turn out to be fun, though it takes time. Having, rather to his surprise, landed a cavalry command, he finds his hopes and prospects sinking in the mud of the trenches. Then he sees a plane landing. He talks himself into a position as a cockpit observer, and from there it's a quick progression to being a pilot.

"Somehow it didn't seem like war at all ..." It soon does, especially if you think of war

as a matter of survival. It's kill or be killed, and Billy proves incredibly adept at blowing enemy pilots out of the sky; in fact he racks up a record score, for which he receives multiple medals. He does this without ever seeming especially bloodthirsty, though he does develop an intense competitive streak. We never really know how he feels about it all; he writes letters home but they don't go into broader issues. We hear the British higher-ups making jokes about "colonials," and we see him being praised and patronised by the upper crust, but Billy's own opinions about being a North American embroiled in a European conflict are not explored. He isn't introspective.

This limits the play in some regards -- you leave with the odd feeling that you never really got to know the hero

-- but it also frees it from any temptation to preach. The ironies are there, built into the story, and we can make of them what we may. The closest the show comes to driving them home is in a fierce cabaret song, with an angular melody, about those who don't make it, performed in the style of a French chanteuse. Peterson does this with ferocious delicacy, and a bizarre physical daintiness. He moves beautifully throughout; his whole performance is a dance.

Among his other impersonations, I especially enjoyed his air ministry recruiting wallah, who has the voice, the praying-mantis eyes and the gleefully rubbing hands of an English Montgomery Burns. Gray also does his share of expert mimicry, both as singer and composer; there's one song in which he sounds, whether by accident or design, like a dead vocal ringer for Randy Newman. Camellia Koo has designed a simple objet-trouve kind of set; projections are held in reserve until the last moment and are the more effective for it. Peterson himself remains a sharp-eyed scamp underneath it all, a jewel in a cock-eyed Canadian crown. He adds, in himself, a layer to the evening, something and someone to cheer for. - Billy Bishop Goes to War runs until Aug. 29. Call 416-866-8666 or visit soulpepper.cafor tickets and information.

2009-08-15-epics-and-nude-models-and-imp:
The hit of last year's Summerworks festival was If We Were Birds, Erin Shields' dramatization of the myth of Philomel. Shes followed it this year with another play based in legend, The Epic of Gilgamesh (up until the part where Enkidu dies), which roguish title may presuppose a more intimate knowledge of Sumerian epic than many of us are likely to possess. Also, the fact that it is an epic -- meaning, one damn thing after another -- makes the source less amenable to drama than the Philomel story, which has a natural arc plus a gift of a metaphor. Gilgamesh is a hero king, very conscious of both his heroism and his kingship. He demands a lot of his people, whom he treats as his personal press gang, whether in battle or in the building of a tall and shaky tower to the citys, and his own, greater glory. He has a terrible attitude towards women, on whom he routinely exercises whatever is the Sumerian for droit de seigneur, and he's very bad for the environment.

This is no modern imposition. The original is ambiguous about its protagonist, whom it presents as a force of nature, noble but worrying. Shields takes this built-in irony and tilts it towards satire. Her writing has both wit and weight --colloquial one moment, incantatory the next -- and it always holds the stage. The story, though, doesn't, and the contemporary parallels are too obvious to be interesting. One of Gilgameshs angrier ladies journeys to the forest, where she seduces Enkidu, the wild man, whom she brings back to town hoping that hell topple the tyrant. But the two warriors, after the obligatory trial of strength, get on like a palace on fire; despite some minor differences --Gilgamesh wants to show Enkidu his music system, while Enkidu would prefer a brisk run around the city walls -- they become best buddies. Enkidu emerges as a moderating influence, but static characters having adventures aren't enough to make a play. Gideon Arthurs' production is very impressive; Frank OConnells Gilgamesh, with the eyes of a fanatic (specifically a fitness fanatic) and hitting just the right balance between spoiled boy and dangerous man, heads an excellent cast.

Shields also figures in Summerworks as co-author and co-performer of Montparnasse, in which she displays a roguish stage presence and a delectable body. The latter is worth mentioning, indeed cannot be ignored, since she delivers the play's first speech while reclining on a sofa and totally nude, a state to which she frequently returns. There's nothing gratuitous about this; she plays Margaret, an ex-pat model in the Paris of the 1920s where, it seems, a girl could hardly move without meeting and being propositioned by an artist (usually French) or a writer (usually American). Soutine, Modigliani, Hemingway, Joyce, Man Ray and Sylvia Beach all figure, and are briefly impersonated in these memoirs of two young ladies, of whom the other, Amelia, has come to town in order to paint on her own account but takes to modelling on her own account. So she strips, too, but later and more selfconsciously. She still proves successful enough, in a more specialized way, to arouse her friends jealousy, and when Amelia paints Margarets portrait, the possessive sparks really fly: which of them owns it, aesthetically and otherwise? This question has been posed before (in two musicals, for a start: Sunday in the Park with George and, less obviously, City of Angels) but it's done here sharply, amusingly, and even poignantly. Shields does her vocal quick changes well, but, as a performer rather than an actress, skates over them. Her partner, Maev Beaty, not only grabs immediate hold of each character, but nails and holds every one, while in her principal role she's astonishing, suffusing the theatre with her shyness, confidence, happiness and pain. Andrea Donaldsons direction is terrific, and I had the best time.

I had another good one at The Middle Place, which has been assembled by Andrew Kushnir from videoed interviews at an Etobicoke homeless shelter. Interestingly, the five actors read the transcripts but didnt see the footage, so they had to create rather than impersonate. The results, under Alan Dilworth's direction, are remarkable, both imaginative and respectful: factually-based but more than dramatized social work. Paul Dunn takes Kushnir's place as interviewer, and is thus an actor playing an actor; from the others we have more instant role-changing. Akosua Amo-Adem has massive, though quite different, presence, as both administrator and inmate; Kevin Walker is scarcely less compelling as a thin, shaky, prospective father. The whole is disturbing but not depressing.

For a topping-off Summerworks experience, I recommend Impromptu Splendour, at which three Second City alumni exercise their improvisational chops on parodying a given playwright, whose name is pulled from a hat by a previous audience. At the show I saw, the subject was David Mamet, and though they had time to prepare the essentials -- an office setting, much double-crossing, even more profanity -- they still had to include motifs suggested on the night. Made up or prepared, the results were a scream, with an accuracy that at times approached the poetic. Matt Baram and Ron Pedersen were perfect, and if Naomi Snieckus seemed less so -- well, nobody said that Mamet was any place for women. - Summerworks closes tomorrow. Visit summerworks.cafor details.
2009-08-18-the-brits-have-landed-mad-men:
Canadians used to be able to watch Mad Men on CTV. That arrangement has now lapsed, so unless you have a highly specialized cable package (I'm with Bell, and they don't offer it), you'll have to download the new third season from iTunes. This means a brilliantly written show with a sophisticated visual style has to be squinted at on tiny computer screens with muddy sound. The arrangement also, of course, discourages communal viewing, though this is one show that you actually want to share. Truly, civilization as we thought we knew it is coming to an end.

Which is how the characters on the show itself often seem to be feeling. The Season 3 premiere, which aired on Sunday night, was still feeling its way back, at least compared to what's been promised in all the advance publicity. We've been told that the boys and girls at the Sterling Cooper ad agency will be increasingly discombobulated by the advance of the 1960s. Not too much of that so far, though I thought I noticed one speck of prophetic irony. The firm, you may remember from the end of Season 2, has been taken over by a bigger concern from Britain, and this week the new bosses briskly disposed of a third of the New York workforce. The old head of accounts went down, not gracefully. "You're the dying empire," he told his tormentors. "We're the future." It's 1963, and it's impossible not to hear the bells of the British Invasion tolling in the near distance.

The invading Brits' subsequent behaviour was no more endearing. On the divide-and-conquer principle, they appointed two replacement heads of accounts, leaving each to believe for a time that he was the sole anointed, before humiliating them both at a meeting with a casual announcement of the true state of affairs. One of them was our old and endearingly wormy friend Pete Campbell, and this isn't going to do anything for his already troubled marriage. The younger and slimier Brit is a dead ringer for Pete, and I still haven't decided whether this is careless casting or inspired. I think I'd be happier with it if the audio on my laptop allowed me to make out their accents.

"There's no such thing as London Fog," the big English cheese instructed the remnants of Sterling Cooper's ancient regime; it was a purely chemical phenomenon, not a meteorological one, and Charles Dickens got it wrong even if he turned out a great piece of prose in the process. The reason this cropped up is that the clients the guys were buttering up this week were

the (American) raincoat manufacturers of that brand. Don Draper and Sal the Closeted Designer were sent out of town to reassure them, a task at which Don is spectacularly good, and to discourage them from diversifying. "There will be fat years and there will be lean years" said Don, "but it's going to rain." Back at their hotel Don almost got it on with a forward but coy air hostess, with whom he clinched the deal by telling her it was his birthday. This may even have been true; as a man with a double identity, he must have birthdays to spare. They were disturbed by a fire alarm, and while scuttling down the escape, Don was able to observe Sal similarly interrupted with a young male member of staff. Hard to believe that Don hadn't at least suspected Sal's orientation before this but, Don being as canny and close as he's sophisticated, Sal's secret is safe with him. Don himself is back with his wife, who is newly pregnant, and-- the odd flight attendant aside -- he seems to be making an effort. Back at Sterling Cooper HQ, both Sterling and Cooper are, shamelessly and mercifully, unchanged. We saw disappointingly little of Joan this week and even less of Peggy but, on past form, Peggy is likely to lay low for episodes at a time and then suddenly take centre-screen -- which, of course, is how the character goes through life. All the acting is as good as ever and so, on this showing, are the scripts. Mad Men effortlessly resumes its place at the very top of the heap. I just wish it could have resumed it a little more accessibly. Maybe the producers think Canada's part of the dying empire as well. They should heed their own wake-up call. Or at least be a little more polite. - Mad Men airs Sundays at 10 p. m. on AMC; Canadian customers without the cable channel can download the show on a per-episode basis from iTunes.

2009-08-22-why-would-one-refuse-a-chance:
A solid production despite dying art form The Shaw Festival now has a fourth stage, bringing it level with Stratford. Jackie Maxwell, director of both the festival and the inaugural studio production, says in the program that the new space, in back of the main house, is to be devoted to post-Shavian work that's part of a continuum of provocative, subversive playwrighting by "writers [who] continue to question the status quo." That would include all serious, and many non-serious, plays, since, without a status quo to challenge, dramatists would have nothing to be dramatic about.

Maxwell appends a shopping list of contemporary candidates that oddly omits Tom Stoppard, whose devotion to wit and ideas makes him the most obviously Shavian of contemporary playwrights, and whose The Invention of Love, which has been begging for production for 10 years now, already sits bang in the middle of the Shaws previous mandate. The studio has started with The Entertainer by John Osborne who, as playfully admitted in the program, was a vociferous anti-Shavian, denouncing the sages plays as fraudulent, inept ...posturing wind and rubbish. Imagine an Osborne Festival at which his plays were endlessly recycled. It would be hell.

In a better world, Osborne's career would have ended with Inadmissible Evidence in the mid 1960s. In a perfect one, it would probably have stopped a decade earlier with Look Back in Anger, the bombshell debut that thrust him into a position as generational spokesman that he'd never asked for and that he spent the rest of his life trying either to live up to or to live down. The Entertainer was his follow-up play and it shows him imposing a schematic pattern on an English music-hall family at the time of Suez. Music hall, as demonstrated this year at the Shaw, took a long time dying; its already in the throes in Cowards Red Peppers, written 20 years earlier. Archie Rice, protagonist and archetype, is a cankered and self-hating philanderer and comic, fronting a seaside nudie show. His father, once a top-liner, hankers for Edwardian glories when Britannia ruled. Archie's son and daughter represent Youth, disaffected by definition. Another son, offstage, is killed in the war.

The play alternates between Archie's on-stage routines and his fractious home life. You expect the usual Osborne mix: compelling solos, tedious ensembles. In Maxwells production, a good one, these preconceptions are up-ended. The scenes in the Rice family digs are at least as charged as those in the theatre; more important, the two worlds progressively merge. Peter Hartwells set design has much to do with this. The audience sits in two opposing banks looking down on the actors. There are two music hall stages, one at each end of the room, and the domestic scenes happen in the middle. We never quite know where we are; there's a nightmare element that's very helpful. The space doesnt permit an orchestra pit, so Archies accompaniment comes from an on-stage pianist. This makes his act seem more cabaret than music hall, and indeed Benedict Campbell's Archie, square, brusque and insulting, has a strong whiff of German nightclub. This is disconcerting at first, but it becomes its own creation. His life becomes a comment on his act rather than, as you might expect, the other way around.

Besides, Osborne's music hall pastiche isnt very good. The last-ditch attitudes (racist, sexist, you name it) may be authentic enough, but theyd never have been as in your face and devoid of lilt as they are here. The songs ( Thank God I'm Normal) are especially atrocious. Nor do we ever find out why Archie became a comedian; he has no love for it, and no need: He had an expensive education, one that permitted his brother (shades of Death of a Salesman) to become a successful lawyer. What did his dad make of it? There's no trace of the halls in David Schurmanns pained gentlemanly performance, but he, too, comes to fiery life when the family starts looking in all possible directions in anger. Real demons are let loose, at racking but very believable length. As Phoebe, Archies sozzled, nervous and incorrigibly loving wife, Corinne Koslo is sublime; when she sings The Boy in the Gallery it's like the stoned Mary Tyrone in Long Day's Journey recalling when she was happy for a time. Krista Colosimo and Ken James Stewart are respectively clenched and quirky as the juniors, faltering only when they force emotion: an endemic disease among young actors that Maxwell, like many directors, seems disinclined to stamp out. In minor roles, Graeme Somerville and especially Ric Reid strike virtuous blows for the ensemble spirit.

Ive never believed in Archies channelling of a black gospel singer when he hears of his son's death. It's too set up. I dont even know if were meant to believe it. Hounded by the taxman, Archie refuses the chance of escape to Canada because "you can't get draught Bass in Toronto." Some things change.

-In repertory through Sept. 20. Call 1-800-511-SHAW for ticket information.
2009-08-28-seasonal-affect-in-order:
THEATRE REVIEW

A Midsummer Night's Dream

Festival Theatre, Stratford

---

One of the joys of Stratford's latest Midsummer Night's Dream is seeing Geraint Wyn Davies play a Shakespearean role in which he remains alive into the second act. In the past two years he's given superb performances of Polonius, Duncan and Julius Caesar, all of whom get brutally dispatched before the intermission. In Dream he is, enchantingly, Bottom the weaver who, even after committing suicide as Pyramus in the play-within-the-play, rises triumphantly from the ground to reassure the spectators.

Before that, of course, he's serenely weathered temporary transmogrification into an ass. Sweet serenity is the note of Wyn Davies' performance, open-faced, open-hearted and played, in accordance with the actor's name and ancestry, with a magically melodious Welsh lilt; he really can roar you as gently as any sucking dove. The mechanicals' play is clearly the opportunity he's been awaiting for all his life; he delivers tremendous impromptu auditions for Pyramus and Thisbe and the Lion, and when denied the opportunity to play all three goes into a sulk so tremendous yet so devoid of malice that it's no wonder his friends all rally round to woo him back. The great clown scenes in this production aren't the usual set pieces of play and rehearsal, but this first meeting and the reunion when Bottom returns from the forest, in which the joy and wonder amount to an epiphany. There's inspired teamwork from the gang, with a Quince (Michael Spencer-Davis) whose glasses and moustache suggest high office in the Athenian Carpenters' Union and a Flute (Skye Brandon) who lights up with smug relief at the news that he's not the only man who'll have to play a woman.

I've never seen a better performance of Bottom than Wyn Davies', and when it comes to his meeting with the fairies, I've never seen one as good, especially in his compassion for the ill-fated family of Master Mustardseed. His disguise includes the asinine equivalent of buck teeth through which he projects a confident bashfulness: assurance and modesty in divine equipoise. When Titania throws herself at him, he's surprised but not shaken. His great awakening speech is radiant; you'd be tempted to call him a holy fool if he weren't, underneath it all, so grounded and sensible.

The lovers' scenes in David Grindley's production (he's this year's British import) aren't as consistently wonderful as this, but they have comparable comic flair and the same keen

nose for buried treasure in the text. Laura Condlln's Helena, long-limbed and besotted, goes optimistically down on all fours when comparing herself to a spaniel; she also has a knockout ad lib in response to the question "where is Demetrius?" The young men (Bruce Godfree and Ian Lake) mount a spirited contest in caddishness.

The early scenes are played on Stratford's original Tanya Moiseiwitsch set, reminding us of its unrivalled clarity and efficiency as a Shakespearean springboard. It implodes when we reach the forest, which is represented as a brutalist jungle gym, and it stays imploded until we get back to Athens. There's a corresponding mix of periods in the costumes; the mortals are from the 1950s, on the fearful verge of the permissive society, while the immortals are at least 20 years ahead of them (which I guess is a fairy privilege) being a collection of goths and punk rockers. They do a lot of slithering and a fair bit of climbing. The music's eclectic too; it starts and ends with big-band swing; in between it's ugly, even by punk standards.

Dion Johnstone's Oberon struts and poses like Michael Jackson; now, was this the production's starting point or a topical addition? Yanna Mc-Intosh's Titania is compelling in sections, among them the lament for her friend who died "of being mortal" and her bulletin on climate change, which for once gets reflected in the staging; there's snow this midsummer night. Tom Rooney's Puck casts an even more potent spell when he warns about the lost souls of ghostly suicides; elsewhere, an original performance seems trapped within its pop carapace. As for the mortal monarchs: Timothy D. Stickney is an urbane Theseus, but the production goes for the fashionable idea about Hippolyta being reluctant to marry him. This means as usual that the actress has to tie herself in knots trying to inject hostility into a speech that's plainly a celebration, and then has to stand around miming a mental journey that never gets mentioned in the text. The production then perversely underplays the couple's really important conflict: their differing views on imagination, which is only what the play's about. Still, the final coming together of all the different worlds is beautifully done, justifying a finale ultimo in which the entire cast breaks into wild celebratory dance. With effects like that, the show is a crowd-pleaser. But it's pleasing on deeper levels as well. - A Midsummer Night's Dream is in repertory through Oct. 30. Call 1-800-567-1600 or visit stratfordfestival.cafor tickets and information.
