2009-08-29-a-midsummer-night-s-terror-wo:
THEATRE

Kenneth Tynan once described Jean Racine's Phedre as a disappointing sequel to A Midsummer Nights Dream." I wouldnt necessarily endorse the adjective (and he himself went on to withdraw it) but the presence of both plays at this year's Stratford Festival gives us a unique opportunity to follow the story through and to reflect on the unreliability of happy endings. Shakespeare's Dream concludes with the king and queen of the fairies blessing the bridal bed of Theseus, Duke of Athens and Hippolyta, Queen of the Amazons: "And the issue there create/Ever shall be fortunate. Boy, were they wrong.

By the time Racine takes over, Hippolyta is dead; Theseus, promoted to King by tragic convention, has married again; and Hippolytus, the issue they created, has grown to a young manhood that is to prove spectacularly unfortunate. Phedre, his stepmother, falls violently in lust with him; devastated by an unrequited passion that counts as incestuous, she confides only in her nurse, Oenone, who tries to protect her by going to Theseus and accusing Hippolytus of trying to rape his wife. Theseus, seeking vengeance, calls in a favour from Neptune, god of the ocean, who obliges by sending in a sea monster. (This is one supernatural being who delivers.) Hippolytus meets a grisly end. Phedre, crushed by layer upon layer of shame, kills herself. Theseus survives, stricken.

If the problem with the Dream is that we know it too well, the trouble with Phedre, at least in English, is that we dont know it at all. Even if weve seen it a few times, we don't know it. It looms, perceptibly great, but locked within a baroque fortress composed of structure and style. In classic French tragedy, this one above all, everybody is trapped. Racine doesn't deny free will but he shows it helpless against circumstance. Theres a situation; theres an initial action, invariably misguided; and what follows is unstoppable. The famous unities of time and place allow no opportunities of escape, and the spare, swift couplets of the text create their own prison. Every rhyme draws another bolt. Rhyme in English only works for comedy (at least that's the consensus; I'm not entirely convinced), and Timberlake Wertenbakers new translation eschews it; it also shortens the French twelve-beat line, which certainly wouldnt work in English, into good old English pentameters. Her version is clear and alive, but it lets too much air in.

The Stratford production is the culmination of two years of workshops, here and at the American Conservatory Theater in San Francisco, under the leadership of Carey Perloff, the ACT's artistic director. Her production, like its text, is intelligent and economical, but it reaches its end leaving its audience unscathed; whatever we were meant to feel of pity or terror -- and one crushing moment would be enough -- has somehow leaked away. The costumes come from the time of Louis XIV, when the play was written; this makes a kind of sense, suggesting a monumental propriety just waiting to be outraged, but the heavy clothes weigh the actors down, and it leaves the audience at two removes from the story. It would probably work in French. In English, we'd settle for tunics.

I was looking keenly forward to Seana McKennas Phedre; she holds the Canadian patent on Greek tragedy, and no actress in the land can suffer more powerfully. She starts off all right with the traditional gaunt Phedre entrance, clutching at walls. But shes naturally a fighter, as witness her Medea, a role she took to the brink of comedy. She's at her best as Phedre when acridly taunting the goddess who's destroying her ( well, Venus, are you happy with my shame?"), or when threateningly shaking her Medusa locks, or when envisioning her father, Minos, god of the dead, consigning her to eternal damnation; Racine had a pitiless eye for the right myth. But these are isolated flashes. There isnt much fight left in Phedre, and there isnt really any laughter. She may be the only tragic protagonist who starts devastated: well, Hamlet perhaps, but he climbs out of his pit. Phedre sinks deeper into hers, and I'm not sure it's a congenial place for McKenna to be.

Tom McCamus makes an unconventionally reasonable Theseus, one who has to be goaded into fury: a defensible choice but contributing to the general lack of voltage. Sean Arbuckle, too, makes surprisingly little of his horrific messenger speech, generally a showstopper in any language.

The best performances come from the characters whose temperaments, if not their fates, are the least extreme: Jonathan Goads buffeted, well-meaning Hippolytus, Roberta Maxwells Oenone, and Claire Lautier's Aricie, Phedre's rival in both love and politics. Shes Racines invention; he draws his nets very tight. David Lang has composed discreetly haunting cello music that might, for once, be used less sparingly; having it underscore Theseus' call to the god might help move us to another level. It's a level that the production and its central performance may yet reach. I'd see it again.

- Phedre is in repertory at the Tom Patterson Theatre, Stratford, through Oct. 3. 1-800-567-1600

2009-08-29-reasons-for-the-four-seasons-:
(From the National Post, September 2, 2009) Jersey Boys' book writer Rick Elice's name was spelled incorrectly in Saturday's Weekend Post. 

Bob Gaudio was in Toronto last week for the first-anniversary gala performance of Jersey Boys, the musical based on the lives and songs of The Four Seasons. Gaudio was the Season who wrote the songs and the one who, if the show is to be believed, was the most diffident about performing them. I met him at his hotel that was, naturally, the Four Seasons.

According to Gaudio, the show is to be believed. "I was a more than reluctant performer. Who says you have to go out on the road and perform?" Beyond that, Jersey Boys isn't some outsiders' attempt to cash in on the fame and music of a legendary group. "It was homegrown; it was our idea," More specifically, it was the idea of the two most iconic of the original Seasons: Gaudio himself and lead singer and falsetto extraordinaire Frankie Valli. They had had "lots of TV offers," but the theatre beckoned, certainly for Gaudio himself: "Frankie and I thought, 'If we do a TV movie, it's a quick run and then it's over; we'll give the theatre a shot.' So we started to go back, to open doors."

Somewhere in the course of their door-opening, Gaudio saw Smokey Joe's Cafe, the roof-raising show based on the songs of Jerry Leiber and Mike Stoller, and thought, "Wow, look at that audience reception." That show was a revue with no connecting story. Then, even more successfully, came Mamma Mia!, which hung ABBA's hit songs on a newly invented storyline to which they had no particular connection. "I thought, well, where do we go from here? Well ... biography. When Rick and Marshall got involved, they jumped all over it." Rick Ellice and Marshall Brickman (the latter best-known as Woody Allen's screenwriting collaborator) were the show's book-writers. Des McAnuff, the show's director, now of the Stratford Festival, had a similar reaction. He's said that he had little interest in directing "another jukebox musical," but according to Gaudio, "his eyes lit up when he heard the backstory."

So, it seems, did the audience's. In October 2004, when the show opened at the La Jolla Playhouse in San Diego, where McAnuff was artistic director, Gaudio and Valli sat there "very apprehensive; how would a show about little old New York go down in Beach Boy territory?" It was perhaps a little late historically to worry about that; after all, nobody supposes that a show about the Beatles would only be of interest to people from Liverpool. Still, "we had mixed emotions about how it would all be dealt with. We had this upscale $300,000 audience. But it was stunning. We said, almost in unison: 'If this ever gets to New York...' "

Which, of course, it did. And it's still there. It does appeal to local pride; when I saw it in New York, the audience was full of present-day Jersey boys and girls, and their parents and grandparents, plus Valli himself, which delayed proceedings somewhat. But obviously the attraction goes far beyond that, as witness the success in Toronto, in London and all over the world. Gaudio says that keeping up with it and keeping an eye on it "is consuming most of my life." (He'd just got back from Australia.) So what are they responding to? According to Gaudio "at least 50% of the success is due to the staging, the story and how it's crafted."

At this point, Rick Ellice, one of the two men who crafted it, walked into the bar and joined the conversation. Gaudio, in his sixties, is tall, quiet-spoken and rather scholarly. Ellice, decades younger, is far more Manhattan and considerably more flamboyant. But he corroborated Gaudio. "We couldn't do Mamma Mia! Someone had already done Mamma Mia!. I thought I could do a turn for my friend Marshall Brickman to write it with me. I said 'Marshall, you wanna write a Broadway musical?' Marshall said 'no'. I said 'Marshall, it's about Frankie Valli and the Four Seasons.' " This apparently changed Marshall's mind. Ellice: "It's such a ripping yarn. That they led the lives they led. We were very lucky to have stepped in as good listeners."

And, Gaudio insists, they did lead those lives. Or at least "I'll go along with Frankie. He thinks it's 90% to 95% accurate --not chronologically perhaps, but most moments are the real deal." Even the things that seem too good to be true, like a teenage Joe Pesci being around as a gofer when the boys were scrabbling in Jersey, actually happened. And Gaudio writing their breakthrough hit Sherry 15 minutes before rehearsal -- that's true, too.

It's the breakthrough song in the show as well: The moment when the audience gets to hear what it came to hear and goes wild. But, as Ellice says about the show in general, there's no false drama attached to it: "Nobody sings 'oh Sherry baby' to a girl named Sherry." What it is, as Gaudio says, is an enormous release of tension: "You draw back a slingshot and, 45 minutes into the show, you finally release it. The audience shares in that reality." Part of that reality, as the show now stands, is the accuracy with which the actors mimic the sound and even the look of the original group, and especially the phenomenal Valli. Apparently, though, this wasn't the case in La Jolla where the actor, though talented, was far from a Valli soundalike: The scene still took off. These days, though, they insist on verisimilitude; "Frankie candidates have to go to Camp Castelluccio," Francesco Castelluccio being Frankie's real name.

I have a favourite theory about the Four Seasons' establishing hits, Sherry and the even better Big Girls Don't Cry, which is that with the extreme and abrupt contrasts between their high highs and low lows, they're funny. Well, that's how they sounded to my generation in London, where we couldn't have cared whether they came from New Jersey or New York or New Orleans. I tried my theory out on Gaudio, but he wasn't having it. Well, he did admit that "some of our songs have been quite humorous," and he did admit that the bass voice owed something to the cartoon sound of Yogi Bear, who at the time was even more popular than Sherry. But, he says, "we don't allow parodies of any kind. We wouldn't want to make light of songs that have moved people." And, obviously, are moving them still. - Jersey Boys is onstage now at the Toronto Centre for the Arts. For tickets and show-times, visit dancaptickets.comor call 416-644-3665.
2009-09-03-everything-old-is-new-again:
There are three Canadian plays in Stratford's studio season: one old, one new, one newish.

The new one is The Trespassers, written and directed by Morris Panych. The title possibly has all sorts of metaphorical significance, but on the literal level it refers to the regular excursions of Lowell, aged 15, and his grandfather Hardy into a neighbouring orchard, where they climb trees and steal peaches from the absentee owner. Gluttony apart, they do this because Hardy believes that property is theft, and is passing on his convictions to his grandson. Lowell is believed, though not by Hardy, to be suffering from some kind of emotional disorder; he certainly has a very short and angry fuse. Hardy is also teaching him how to bluff, at poker and other things. He tells the boy, "there's something in between lying and not lying; it's called a story," which is one of those nice-sounding lines with less to it than meets the ear.

The first act is mostly charming and, this being Panych, funny. The second occasionally verges on being moving, turning as it does on Hardy's imminent death from cancer. This adds assisted suicide to the play's concerns, with the characters lining up pretty much as you'd expect. But the various plot strands don't fertilize one another. The central issue is presumably Lowell's coming of age, but all we know of him is that he shouts a lot. That isn't a criticism of Noah Reid's performance; it's what's required and he does it well. He's surrounded by three of the best; none of them is much extended but Joseph Ziegler is a cunning delight; Lucy Peacock overflows with hardscrabble warmth, maybe more than the play can hold; and Kelli Fox conveys love by way of censoriousness.

Like The Trespassers, Rice Boy features a pubescent protagonist, tree-climbing, ladders and an unfulfilled title. The boy is Tommy, 12-years-old and of Indian parentage, living in the Kitchener-Waterloo area. Most of the play, though, takes place in India where, six months before the Canadian action, Tommy and his father had been visiting the family. Sunil Kuruvilla has, by his own account, much tightened his play since its 2001 production at Can-Stage. But he's also weakened it, since the Indian scenes now

so outweigh the Canadian that the play's fulcrum -- Tommy's sense of not belonging in either place -- has disintegrated. All that seems clear is that he has the Worst. Dad. Ever, whose self-pity, neglect and occasional downright cruelty can only partly be excused by his wife having recently drowned. Tommy's grandfather suffered a similar loss; his auntie is cuckolding his uncle with the local doctor; the family's servant girl has an off-and-on-thing with her husband the fish seller; and Tommy gets badly smitten with his imperious paraplegic cousin Tina, destined for an arranged marriage. Here too, a lot goes on but nothing truly happens. Sanjay Talwar and Deena Aziz reprise their original roles, and a good cast also includes Araya Mengesha (as Tommy), Raoul Bhaneja, Anita Majumdar, Sam Moses, Asha Vijayasingham and Anand Rajaram, who has a split-second opportunity to show he's an inspired clown and takes it.

Zastrozzi, directed by Jennifer Tarver, is the best time I've ever had at a George F. Walker play, dislodging Panych's Shaw Festival production of Nothing Sacred. Both these works, jokey literary extravaganzas in half-imaginary landscapes, sidestep the credibility problems that afflict Walker's plays set inpresentday Toronto. Zastrozzi is a jaundiced 20th-century lampoon of the romantic 19th-century vision of sanguinary 17th-century Italy: a Revenger's Comedy in which philosophy rules, and kills. Tarver's production impresses from its first moment: a monologue, scared and scary for Oliver Becker as a befuddled Renaissance thug who looks and sounds like Tony Soprano in reduced circumstances. Zastrozzi, "master of discipline," is the ultimate practical critic, pursuing a homicidal vendetta against bad artists; in Rick Roberts's performance, he's a sinner as impregnable as any saint. His particular prey, brilliantly twittered by Andrew Shaver, is Verezzi, a weak-minded painter who also stands accused of killing Zastrozzi's mother. How and why are never quite revealed; and strangely, when the two antagonists come finally face to face (over a heap of corpses), the matter is never mentioned. The play goes down a lot of blind alleys, narrative and intellectual. You can't, in the end, take it seriously; but you can relish it as a young man's high-style high-wire act. The best performance of all, and much his best at Stratford, is John Vickery's as Verezzi's unshakably conscientious guardian, a cropped black wig surmounting a face that's a white mask of determination and despair. - The Trespassers is in repertory through Oct. 4; Rice Boy and Zastrozzi through Oct. 3. Call 1-800-567-1600 or visit stratfordfestival.cafor tickets and information.

2009-09-04-this-ain-t-baltimore-cbc-s-gu:
Some TV shows riff off real-life events. Some riff off other TV shows. Guns, though gripping on its own account, does both. This two-part, four-hour drama from CBC begins with the death of a young girl, felled by a stray bullet in a gang shootout at the intersection of Yonge and Gould Streets in downtown Toronto. It's where 15-year-old Jane Creba was killed in similar circumstances in 2005. "The authenticity of the location," says a press release, "was therefore of tantamount importance." Is that the same as what used to be called "paramount importance"? It sounds paramount to illiteracy.

More importantly, the show should be able to register its disgust at random violence on city streets without modelling itself so closely on a real and recent case. This isn't a documentary. The creators (writer-producer Jennifer Holness and writer-director Sudz Sutherland) have upped the horrific ante, making the victim a six-year old. Her death naturally leads to public outcry, and to a determination at City Hall to get guns off the streets, or at least to be seen to be doing so.

The police, of course, would be only too glad to see it happen. Their main stumbling-block is Paul Duguid (a surprisingly boyish Colm Feore), a well-connected arms dealer who supplements his substantial legitimate income by selling illegally to foreign governments. (His main client for the story's purposes is Honduras, which seems almost too topical, though the mini-series was filmed in 2007.) He has so far proved untouchable but he has a son, Bobby, who could be described with perfect appropriateness as a loose cannon. He smuggles guns in from the United States, for street gang use. In need of a mule, he enlists his girlfriend Frances, who's played by Elisha Cuthbert, renewing her Canadian cred. Her presence (and Feore's too, come to think of it) naturally turns thoughts to 24, and to one of its primary lessons, which is, when in need of help in a tight spot, never turn to Elisha Cuthbert. Her Frances is as accident-prone -- and also, to be fair, as plucky -- as her Kim Bauer. She even has a scene in jail, this time wearing an orange jumpsuit.

Paul's agent-provocateur tactics are also close to those of one of the villains in the last round of 24, but the American show that this one most closely resembles -- whether through accident or imitation -- is The Wire. Here, too, we have a panoramic view of a city, taking in the streets, the police, the politicians, the money (lots of party scenes in Rosedale), the schools, the strip clubs and even a newspaper office. Though, of course, this show's two nights hardly afford the scope of The Wire's five years, and there's a lot that feels skimpy and rushed.

Bobby (Gregory Smith) is remarkably similar to the crazy son of the dock union boss in The Wire's second season, if with far more disposable income. And there are two matched pairs of pivotal characters who are very Wiry. We have two cops: Rick (Shawn Doyle) who's white and his partner Ford (Lyriq Bent) who's black, working in a semi-fictitious Weapons Enforcement Unit. We have two young guys from the projects, running guns rather than dealing drugs: Conrad (Cle Bennett) who wants to get on, and Derek (K. C. Collins) who wants to get out. All four men have fraught home-lives, three with their wives or girlfriends, Derek with his kid sister. (He tells her they're going away West. "West to Mississauga?" she queries. "West to Vancouver," he replies). The similarities to The Wire extend to a snitch being murdered in prison with the crime passed off as a suicide, and even to the unexpected playing of a Billie Holiday record -- well, it's Nina Simone, but she's singing Holiday's Don't Explain.

Guns has nothing of The Wire's tragic sense. It has much the same worldview -- much is rigged, some bad guys get away, but a modicum of justice gets done--and it even has the courage to kill off sympathetic characters, but it doesn't go the distance. Its veneer is tough but its centre is soft. It also crams too much in; the bereaved parents mount a "take back our streets" campaign that adds nothing to the story, and is awkwardly written besides.

In fact, most of the script above street-level sounds contrived: It's painful to watch old stagers like Feore and Jim Mezon exchanging would-be smart dialogue that plays like jumped-up exposition. The domestic stuff, too, is mostly cardboard, and the authors like to involve us with their characters by having them talk to themselves out loud, a device I thought TV had outgrown. However, Doyle, Bent, Collins, Bennett and Smithall giveexcellent performances, and their scenes sound real. Interrogation sequences are especially good -- the cops seem as likely to crack under pressure as the crooks -- and the basic thriller stuff is exciting, as well as morally grounded. It's good to hear a top policeman pointing out that the gun registry helps. Maybe there will be a spinoff. Weapons Enforcement Unit might have the same legs as its big brothers Counter Terrorist and Major Crimes. There have been worse ideas.

- Guns airs Sunday and Monday at 8 p.m. on CBC.

2009-09-05-matzo-balls-goulash-with-a-bo:
Sholem Aleichem. That isn't meant as a greeting but as an acknowledgment of one of few observable patterns in Toronto theatre this quarter. The Harold Green Jewish Theatre is bringing us, for one week only, Sholem Aleichem: Laughter Through Tears, a one-man show about the great Yiddish storyteller, featuring the actor and folk-singer Theodore Bikel. These days, anyone with a career thats lasted a decade gets to be called a veteran, but Bikel deserves the term if anyone does. Back in 1959 on Broadway, he was the original Captain Von Trapp in The Sound of Music. And 10 years before that, he was starring in London in Peter Ustinovs The Love of Four Colonels; he was the Russian colonel. He's also played the King of Siam in The King and I. He must be the Anglophone theatre's leading cosmopolitan. Hard on his heels, and more elaborately, comes Fiddler on the Roof (at the Canon, courtesy Mirvish Productions), the classic musicalization of Aleichems greatest hits. This is one of those farewell tours, bringing back Topol in the role he played in the movie and, before that, in London. Topol, who is of course Israeli, first saw the show in his home country, where he was heard to say, "If it works here, the least Jewish country in the world, itll work anywhere."

From matzo ball soup to goulash. Soulpepper, whose very name has a flavour of paprika, has long had a Hungarian connection, courtesy of their regular guest director Laszlo Marton, and this year they've doubled it. Hot on the heels of Marton's production of The Guardsman, they bring us a Hungarian play that for once isnt by Ferenc Molnar. Another Laszlo, Miklos Laszlo, wrote Parfumerie, which is known over here through a number of variously free adaptations: the movies The Shop Around the Corner and Youve Got Mail, the movie musical In the Good Old Summertime, the beloved stage musical She Loves Me. But who among us has ever seen the play? Before this, Soulpepper makes its first venture into Greek tragedy, or at least into the vicinity of Greek tragedy. In place of a scheduled homegrown adaptation of Sophocles' Antigone, they're presenting Jean Anouilhs Second World War play on the same theme, in which the heroines resistance is code for France's. Since Anouilh hewed close to Sophocles' plot and characters, the cast, headed by Liisa Repo-Martell and R. H. Thomson, remains the same.

Among more recent imported plays, the most eagerly awaited must be Tom Stoppards Rock n' Roll (co-production by CanStage and the Edmonton Citadel) in which, with vintage Stoppardian eclecticism, Pink Floyd meets the Velvet Revolution. Also highly rated from Britain, though less glossy, CanStage in collaboration with Nightwood, brings us That Face by Polly Stenham, about a mother named Martha, hooked on booze and drugs, which puts her one addiction ahead of her namesake in Who's Afraid of Virginia Woolf. From New York and, before that, Chicago, comes Tracy Letts very long August: Osage County, toting the raves and prizes that settle around one Broadway play per season. A touring cast is headed by Estelle Parsons, who at 81 is going very strong. The Mirvishes biggest gun, though, has to be The Boys in the Photograph, an atypically gritty Andrew Lloyd Webber musical formerly known as The Beautiful Game, i. e. soccer.

A presumably more modest musical is Mimi or A Poisoners' Comedy, composed by Allen Cole, directed by Alisa Palmer, and staged at the Tarragon, the same combination that gave us Anything That Moves, which, whatever people may tell you about The Drowsy Chaperone, was the best Canadian musical in years. For non-musical stuff, the Tarragon is currently enlisting shows from other cities. From the lively Edmonton Fringe, via Calgary's Alberta Theatre Projects, theres the Bent Out of Shape company in The Drowning Girls. From the RCA Theatre Company, St. Johns, N. L., but directed by the Tarragon's own Richard Rose, comes Rocking the Cradle, freely adapted from Federico Garcia Lorca's Yerma, a play that seems to invite adaptation: anything to stop it being done straight. The Factory, home of the Canadian playwright, offers accommodation to two of them: Brad Fraser directs his own True Love Lies, already seen in the U. K. and advertised as "a searing comedy exposing a modern family and their long-held secrets" (bet youve never seen one of those before); Michel-Marc Bouchard is represented by The Madonna Painter, an exquisite parable about the 1918 Spanish flu epidemic, "comic and cataclysmic." Well, it would be. Theatre Passe Muraille keeps a lower profile with, for one week apiece, Bash, a gay hip-hop musical, and a remount of Letters to My Grandma, by and with the gifted Anusree Roy, and with its script, one hopes, beefed up. Canadian classic department: CanStage revives Morris Panychs 7 Stories, about a suicidal man (Peter Anderson) standing atop a building with seven storeys. Add it all up, and there's not one new non-musical Canadian play that hasn't already been seen somewhere else. Are we turning into New York?

In Ottawa, the NACs English theatre, under Peter Hinton, announces a surprisingly conventional program: The Drowsy Chaperone, Jacob Two-Two, A Christmas Carol. The last, however, has the great Stephen Ouimette as Scrooge and a stunning supportingcast (DianeDAquila, Geordie Johnson, Tanja Jacobs and on and on) drawn from the theatre's new Acting Company. With this in mind, the season's highlight may well be The Ark, a one-night investigation of ancient Greek theatre that should bear later fruit. Back in Metroland, the Canadian Opera Company has two new productions with imposing staging credits: Madama Butterfly is directed by Brian Macdonald and designed by Susan Benson, legendary collaborators at Stratford on another Japanese extravaganza The Mikado. The Nightingale and Other Short Fables, a multiple bill, marks the return to the COC of Robert Lepage: a mouth-watering event.

2009-09-12-the-finest-guardsman-i-ve-eve:
In one of those glamorous continental opera boxes, sumptuously equipped for everything except watching opera, a Hungarian Hussar pays court to a married woman who happens to be an actress. Her husband, naturally, is an actor, supposedly out of town somewhere playing Cyrano. Nandor, the actor, is madly jealous of Ilona, the actress, who has a reputation for growing bored and unfaithful after six months, which is the precise time they've been married. So he decides to test her by making love to her in disguise; he, huzza, is the hussar. She, though professing herself flattered, at first spurns his suit (he's wearing a gold-barred uniform straight out of Mittel-European musical comedy); later, though, she shows distinct signs of yielding. This leaves him in a perfect frenzy of mixed emotions. Her, too.

The play is The Guardsman, written in 1910 by Ferenc Molnar and now directed for Soulpepper by Laszlo Marton, the company's own semi-resident Hungarian. That's the same combination that 10 years ago gave us a signature production of The Play's the Thing, another piece in which professional role-players find their lives forced into imitating their art.

The Guardsman is almost equally scintillating but cuts deeper, certainly in this version, which is the best I've seen (and that includes one at Stratford with Maggie Smith and Brian Bedford). Of course, on the surface it's incredible that a wife, especially one who's professionally accustomed to seeing her spouse in fancy dress, shouldn't see right through his charade. In fact, though, there's a good chance that she does; certainly she, when all is revealed, would like him to think so. But neither he nor we can ever be sure. And if she does know, is she playing along to spare his feelings or to teach him a lesson? He, meanwhile, is impaled on the horns of what I suppose has to be called a trilemma. As her husband, he wants her to stay virtuous; as her would-be seducer, he can't help wanting her to succumb; and as an actor, he has a vested emotional interest in carrying off his impersonation, whatever the outcome. The great achievement of Marton's production is that it keeps all these possibilities constantly, and teasingly, in play, and manages to reconcile several different styles in doing so.

The performance slips smoothly from agony to ecstasy; from high comedy to broad farce, mental and physical, and back again; which is what the play does, and what real life does. At one point, wife and lover ponder the possibility of the husband returning unexpectedly, knowing full well that in farce, as has often been pointed out, nobody ever returns expectedly. Except that in this case, at least one party knows that he will. The play's climax, though far from its resolution, is Nandor's slow deliberate re-assumption of his disguise: a sort of striptease in reverse. Underlying everything is a quicksand feeling of erotic uncertainty that looks forward both to the self-cancelling husband-lover of Irma la Douce and the marital fantasy of Pinter's The Lover.

The play starts with Nandor and Ilona at home, he very snappy, she seemingly and infuriatingly unperturbed: "If you knew," she says, "how little I was suffering, you wouldn't be so happy" -- one of several impeccably delivered lines that reveal a wit in Frank Marcus' translation that I would never have suspected. She sits at the piano, dreamily playing Chopin, which he takes as a very bad sign; he seethes, suffers and schemes. Nandor off duty is, in Albert Schultz's performance, a grumpy, vulnerable matinee idol, unused to domesticity and unsettled by it. In his guardsman gear, he's the complete opposite: gallant in get-up but shy, soft-spoken, socially out of his depth, painfully -- and, in the circumstances ironically-- sincere. Which is a surprise but, on consideration, logical: Nandor's masquerade allows him to express a gentleness that he otherwise keeps bottled up; it's fantasy on more than one level.

One thing that unites his personae is that both have the air of a small boy, apt to sulk in a corner; Schultz, apart from being expertly witty, keeps all the elements fizzing. Kristen Thomson's natural mode, casual and contemporary, doesn't sort too well with the brittle Ilona of the drawing-room, and verbal slips on the first night signalled discomfort. But in the opera-box-as-boudoir she's on the way to being enchanting, a coquette with a serious core, playing a game that only she--perhaps --fully understands. An actor, she emphatically informs her uniformed admirer, can be intelligent but not very intelligent. Whether the same goes for actresses, she isn't saying.

There's a third leading character who's said to be a critic by trade but spends his time hanging out with the stars and receiving their confidences; the job has certainly gone downhill in the last century or so. Diego Matamoros' role is similar to the one he had in The Play's the Thing, but this one's been removed from the controlling centre to the suffering sidelines. Anyway, in an evening where metatheatrics are already running riot, it's a pleasure to watch another instalment in the long-running, and constantly shifting, Schultz-Matamoros double act; no two actors play better together. A good supporting cast includes Dawn Greenhalgh as Ilona's dresser turned surrogate-mother (and Nandor's newly acquired and fearsome mother-in-law); Michael Simpson as an obsequious debt-collector who can be bought off with complimentary tickets; and Jennifer Phipps as an usherette who conveys, mostly in silence, that she knows exactly what she's worth and won't take a pfennig less. Camellia Koo's sets and Judith Bowden's costumes redeem the reputation of chocolate-box design: apt for a play with a sweet surface and a hard centre. - The Guardsman is in repertory at the Young Centre through Oct. 24. 2009-09-17-desperate-but-not-serious-fri:
The first season of Fringe ended with our heroine Olivia of the FBI (Anna Torv) gaining entry to an alternate universe, one apparently reached via the elevator of a Manhattan hotel. Here, she finally got to meet William Bell, the man she's been chasing ever since Episode 1. Bell is the head of Massive Dymamic, one of those companies familiar in TV series that own and control all the resources in the world except one or two left over for general consumption. He turned out to be Leonard Nimoy, a development that seems to have surprised some commentators: inexplicably, since Nimoys name was right up there in the opening credits, and who else would he have been playing? He doesnt wear his Spock ears in this role, but he still has squatter's rights to anything on TV that's extraterrestrial. Id rank his cameo appearance on ringe as one of the shows periodic lurches into low camp.

This may count as a negative spoiler, but I have to tell you: Nimoy does not reappear in the opening episode of Fringe's second season. What happens is that Olivia is dragged back, and we along with her, through one of those rips in the space-time continuum that are omnipresent on this show and that I don't pretend to understand. Last time, while driving to her appointment with destiny, Olivia narrowly avoided a collision with another motorist. That, we may innocently have thought at the time, is how it goes in New York. Now it seems she didnt avoid it at all. She is propelled, in a severe state of disrepair, right out of what seemed to be her empty car, and rushed to hospital, where she spends the rest of the episode in bed, hooked up to stuff, while her colleagues fear for her life: naively, as she still has star billing. Not that death is the worst thing, or even the final thing, that can happen to a person on this show. Anyway, bedrest seems to do wonders for Olivias temper. She's nicer to people than she's been in months -- though she does yell at a friend to go get that bitch when faced with an unsympathetic nurse.

Otherwise, things on Fringe are much as they were, which is, as someone once said of Austro-Hungarian politics, desperate without being serious. Wherever we go, we get our bearings from free-standing place names, spelled out in graven letters that seem to belong on Mount Rushmore. (I like them. Theyre very helpful.) At one point, Joshua Jackson as young genius Peter Bishop, aptly described on the first-season DVD box as "sardonic and roguish," fills Olivia in about their latest nemesis a shape-changing soldier from another universe, and breaks off to ask, roguishly if not sardonically, "Do you think it says something that I can say that without either of us thinking Im crazy?" Well, it says something about the show. Peter, like Olivia, works for a semi-official occult-crimes unit, based in Boston and investigating what it calls "the pattern." As Peter complains to his boss, every week they discover some bizarre manifestation involving the deaths of from one to a hundred people, every time they cut it off at the pass, and every next time it happens all over again. It's called being in a procedural. When, Peter asks, are they really going to do something? Be careful what you wish for, son. His chief, though, has his own problems, dividing his time between barking at his subordinates and defending the operation against the higher-ups who want to close it down. He's played by Lance Reddick who seems to be parodying, one hopes intentionally, his own performance on The Wire. But until someone casts him as something other than a beleaguered upstanding cop, I guess well never know.

Fringes pilot was shot in Toronto, with the Boston freeway played by the Gardiner, and U of T realizing what may have been a lifetime dream by standing in for Harvard. Since being picked up, the show has been able to stay closer to home: maybe in Boston itself, for all I know. Harvard gets into the act because it's where Peter's dad Dr. Walter Bishop, whos even more of a genius than his son, used to have his lab before they locked him in a mental institution. Hes out now, and back in the lab, because he's a nice man, with a sweet tooth and endearing memory lapses, and they need him. Every evil manifestation that gets loosed upon the world can be traced to his old experiments, so he's the only man who can put them right. Hes delightfully played by John Noble, and he and Jackson have a great exasperation-affection double act going. Also inhabiting the lab are a cop called Astrid, who never seems to be allowed out, and a cow called Jean. Jean was requisitioned because of her species genetic similarity to humans. Nobody's ever used her for anything, at least not in any episode I've seen, but shes good for one cute cutaway shot per show. Blair Brown plays the acting head of Massive Dynamic who seems villainous but may not be; she admits to a bionic arm but looks and sounds bionic all over.

Fringe often plays like Ghostbusters or Men in Black without the laughs. Really good shows have comedy in their texture; this one just turns it on and off, and at that its seldom more than whimsy. More surprisingly, it lacks suspense; it holds you, but not on the edge of your seat. That's the penalty of opting for disposable plotlines rather than an ongoing story. But that may be about to change. This season premiere ends with a reversal involving a much-loved regular character. That has to have long-range implications: In one world or another. - The season premiere of Fringe airs tonight at 9 p. m. on A channel and Fox.

2009-09-19-delving-deeper-into-the-heart:
The question posed by Goodness is what is the proper response to a genocide. Is it impersonal justice or personal vengeance? Most people, looking at it from the outside, would opt for the former, and Michael Redhill's play really does nothing to alter that conclusion. But he does let us see, and more importantly feel, that for a survivor the issue may not be that simple. Or that it might be all too simple, especially when the perpetrator at hand may be about to escape.

The play gets to this point by a circuitous route. Its central character is its author, or at least a writer with its author's name. "I'm being played tonight by Gord Rand", he tells us, "you'll be in good hands with Gord." I bet he says that to all the actors, or has all the actors say it for him. Jordan Pettle said it, when Volcano Theatre first did the play in 2005. It was true then, and it's even truer in Volcano's current revival, which follows on a triumphal progress through Edinburgh and New York. In Rand's hands we have a portrait of a physically and psychologically dishevelled man, trying to reconcile his beliefs with his emotions, and facing up to events he has read and thought about but with whose human consequences he has never before been brought face to face.

He knows about vengeful feelings; he has them himself, towards his wife and the best friend for whom she left him. This hardly seems an issue on the same scale as mass murder, and I can't believe that the real Redhill thinks it is, whatever may have happened in his own marriage; but the stage Michael does keep bringing it up. Its immediate effect was to send him to Poland, where his Jewish great-grandparents and their family were slaughtered by the Einsatzgruppen. He finds that the present-day Poles aren't interested; to them, it's just history. Stopping off in London on his way home, he meets a strange man who directs him to a strange woman. Her name is Althea, and there was a more recent genocide in her country; her family was among the victims. Later, one of the principal instigators was put on trial, and she was the prison guard. As she tells the story, her younger self acts it out, along with the accused, his daughter, and the prosecutor. And our author-surrogate gets more appalled and more confused.

The prisoner, Matthias Todd, has evaded prosecution on the main issue; he's being tried instead for a single killing, which he represents as a crime of passion, prompting a certain shamefaced empathy from Michael. That's insofar as Todd professes anything at all, since he claims to be suffering from Alzheimer's, or his daughter passionately claims it for him. The prosecutor is just as passionately determined to break these defences down. Michael's liberal principles are additionally battered when he's asked how he'd deal with his own Nazi spectre if it rose up before him; which, in a powerful hypothetical scene, it does.

The site of the crimes for which Todd stands trial is left unspecified; it might have been African, it might have been European. Cross-cultural music (live and superb) and cross-cultural casting keep the issue in doubt. This vagueness bothers me less now than it did four years ago, except when characters start batting around the numbers killed; if they can be bothered about specific numbers, then why not about specific places? There have been some textual cuts, but most of what's best about the writing then was there before; as when Michael asks of the atrocities in Althea's country "were there camps?" and she replies "no; they spared themselves that expense." Ross Manson's direction, though, is much sharpened, partly by being presented on a three-sided stage, with the actors rising like witnesses from the front rows of the house. The climactic sequence, in which all the personal and political issues collide and explode, has grown enormously in tension. As well as Rand, there are vivid performances from Layne Coleman as the artfully pitiful Todd and from J.D. Nicholsen as his implacable inquisitor. The women do less well: as old Althea, Lili Francks plays with a self-righteous stridency that diminishes what should be the most searing speech in the play; as young Althea, Tara Hughes can be strong but is too often merely sullen; and Amy Rutherford as the daughter supplies little except a look of haunting heartbreak at the final tableau. And though the play often transcends its own cleverness, it can't finally surmount it. The heart of darkness remains stubbornly, and perhaps inevitably, unreachable. However, they're taking it next to Rwanda (disgracefully, without proper Canadian support) and there, if anywhere, will be an audience qualified to judge.

- Goodness plays through Sept. 27 at Theatre Centre. Call 416-538-0988 for ticket information.
2009-09-19-do-we-really-want-a-seinfeld-:
It's ancient history now, but I've always thought that the finale of Seinfeld was underrated. I don't think it quite worked, and it certainly shouldn't have taken two hours, but it wasn't the cop-out that it was accused of being. It ended, you may recall, with the four central characters being lectured by a judge on their anti-social behaviour and sent down accordingly. After years of making us laugh at, and sympathize with, the quartet's irresponsibility, the show seemed to be turning around and condemning it. Steady on: The courtroom was filled with the stars' friends, relatives, ex-lovers and former victims, all dissociating themselves as speedily and sanctimoniously as possible. If they were respectable society, you could have it. The laugh -- the show's laugh -- was on them. Our heroes -- well, three heroes and one heroine -- may have ended up behind bars but they were happily, and rightly, unrepentant.

Well, that's how I saw it, and Larry David agrees with me. David, of course, wrote the show in collaboration with Jerry Seinfeld, and is often credited with being the brains and the sensibility behind it. Since then, also of course, he has had his own show Curb Your Enthusiasm in which he incarnates in his own person all the homely vices that previously had to be split four ways. I bring this up now because, as has been amply advertised, the new seventh season of Curb Your Enthusiasm revolves around the question of a Seinfeld reunion. And when Larry tries to get Jerry interested in the idea, one of Jerry's responses is that it might at least make people forget that awful finale. To which Larry says that he doesn't think it was awful at all.

Curb your enthusiasm. The Seinfeld connection doesn't crop up until the third episode. The first two find Larry behaving in the self-serving manner we have come to love and identify with. His new girlfriend Loretta has been diagnosed with possible cancer (she looks perfectly healthy; the show isn't that brave), and Larry is trying to get out of the relationship before a final diagnosis comes through and leaves him looking an irredeemable heel. The second show, which is entitled "Vehicular Fellatio," also incorporates a running gag about guys who appear to be getting blow jobs in their cars from wives or girlfriends, and how Larry keeps jumping to wrong conclusions, or at least to the right conclusions at the wrong moment. The publicity describes his character as "brutally honest," but I don't think he'd lay claim to that kind of courage. More often he's just tactless.

So, flashing forward a couple of weeks: Larry meets with a network chief (very convincingly young and smarmy) who desperately wants a Seinfeld reunion show. Larry refuses on the grounds that reunion shows are lame. This of course is double bluff-- the show's, not the character's -- designed to set up a reunion that we will accept as not being lame, as if the accusation could be deflected by being admitted. Or that we will enjoy its lameness, as good post-modernist fun. Or that just seeing the foursome reunited will be pleasure in itself, regardless, in thinking which they may well have a point. Anyway, back in the plot, Larry's objections are overcome by the realization that he may be able to cast his estranged wife (Cheryl Hines) as Jerry's new girlfriend, and hence get her back. Suspense and frustration (the same thing, really) ensue because Jerry, having bought the idea, sees Meg Ryan in the girlfriend role. And the cliffhanger, plus the chance for a star cameo, is that she wants to do it. So the reunion story still has some way to go. Word is that it will be threaded through the rest of the season.

So is it lame? So far it is, fairly. We see Larry talking with all the principals, which means we have to get used to seeing Jason Alexander, Julia Louis-Dreyfus and Michael Kramer addressed by their real names rather than as George, Elaine and Kramer. Of them all, Alexander comes off the best, because he's the best actor; he makes himself into a character, one who's disconcertingly self-possessed. By contrast Jerry is, for a stand-up guy, surprisingly awkward at playing himself.

Also, the reunion idea invites awkward comparisons. Seinfeld still seems, in re-runs, amazingly fresh, canned laughter notwithstanding. It is, after all, the only TV comedy to boast four first-rate characters. Few episodes of Curb withstand a second viewing; their improvisatory style, however winning in itself, becomes very slender, and Larry is essentially on his own; that his best friend's his agent seems only too likely. And maybe even misanthropy has its limits. Larry is selfish, cowardly, stingy, envious, obsessed with sex and status: all the qualities one loves and identifies with. And he's honest about them, at least by comparison with the people he mixes with. But there is a limit to what you can do with them, especially when the protagonist doesn't need to work another day in his life. David is said to have based George on himself, and here he's a George who's rich and successful, which is sort of a contradiction in terms. The show gets by with it, but at a cost. My favourite-ever Seinfeld moment had Alexander-as-George being asked how he lived with himself and replying "it isn't easy." David-as-George has no one to ask him that question, and no need to reply to it. Nobody's going to send him to jail, even in a series of finale. Larry is George without shame, and so without a vital spark. Curb Your Enthusiasm is a paradox: comedy of embarrassment featuring a man who can't be embarrassed. - Curb Your Enthusiasm, Season 7, debuts tomorrow at 9 p. m. ET on HBO Canada.

2009-09-21-mcmurphy-with-a-broken-heart-:
The new season of House starts with the protagonist in a new environment. This is all to the good as the formula of the show as it stood --House does snark, House does miracle cure -- was getting very tired. So of course was he. So here he is, having finally admitted he has problems beyond his gammy leg, checked into Mayfield Psychiatric Hospital and, needless to say hating it.

House's trump card remains Hugh Lauries performance in the title role, one that he now inhabits down to the last pore. (And of course this is one actor who doesnt have to fear either typecasting or total eclipse, once his iconic role has run its course. It's so far removed from everything he'd done previously that all he has to do is drop his totally convincing American accent and return to his roots.) According to expert medical opinion, Dr. House never had problems other than narcissism and anti-social behaviour;" well, that and OD-ing on his Vicodin. So he wants to get better and get back to his old job. Only he doesnt want to play along. "Ill miss you, he tells the staff and fellow inmates soon after arriving. In fact, I want to start missing you as soon as possible."

This ambition is at odds, of course, with his aversion to treatment of any kind. He takes badly to one-on-one sessions with a sympathetic senior shrink (massively played by Andre Braugher) and even worse, as you'd expect, to group sessions with his fellow patients: a feelgood environment from which every sarcastic, superior cell in his body recoils. Knowing the system, he tries to beat it from within. He avoids taking his medication and becomes a champion of patients' rights. For much of its two-hour length, this season premiere plays like an upbeat version of One Flew Over the Cuckoos Nest. And as long as it stays that way, its fine.

Thus, House recruits his roommate, a manic depressive rapper with an exaggerated belief in improvisation, as an ally. He successfully challenges table tennis rules that prohibit paddles and a net; even the man in charge admits he's right about that one. Perhaps less public-spiritedly, he encourages a patient with a superhero delusion in the belief that he can fly. It gets hard, even for House himself, to decide how much he's doing for himself and how much for other people; he is after all a doctor, with professional instincts.

Somewhere along the way, he gets his heart broken, or discovers for the first time that he has a heart to break. But much as we may be touched by his progress, it coincides with a wholesale surrender to mush. House has always had its own delusions, chiefly that having a misanthropic hero makes it more than another hospital soap. It belongs to the sizable group of network shows whose ambitions towards seriousness are constantly being shown up by whats happening on cable. This episode of House is up against In Treatment which, in its second season anyway, makes Houses stab at the symbiotic patient-psychiatrist relationship look soupy and superficial. There's no real pain here, just gestures, heavily underlined. In its second half, this episode reverses the Cuckoo's Nest pattern; there are no Nurse Ratcheds to rebel against, and the ideal is to take your meds and like it. In realistic terms, this is probably an advance; 1970s sentimentality about mental illness is something we can do without.

But this is TV, so any stab at maturity comes wrapped in compromise. It isnt enough that House helps to bring about simultaneous breakthroughs in the conditions of two of his fellow patients; there has to be inspirational music playing on the soundtrack. Not to get too specific, but at the end of the show, House is wearing a sweater with a smiley-face on it. Well, presumably, hes a better person for it, and perhaps when he gets back to his old stomping-grounds his show will be a different show. There's at least the potential for it. We shouldn't despair, but neither should we hold our breath. - The season premiere of House airs tonight at 8 p.m. on Global.

2009-09-21-nothing-to-fear-here:
THEATRE REVIEW

Who's Afraid of Virginia Woolf ?

Young Centre for the Performing Arts

It's common knowledge, verging on folklore, that Edward Albee's Who's Afraid of Virginia Woolf ? begins with George and Martha, history professor and wife, surname unknown, returning home in the small hours from a faculty party; and with Martha surveying their living room and exclaiming "what a dump!" She's quoting Bette Davis from a movie and in most productions, including the tremendous new one from Soulpepper, she does a Davis imitation. Nancy Palk's Martha, however, doesn't leave her mimicry there. She is a fountain of quick-change voices -- taunting, teasing, commanding -- until she finds her own voice, the one that underlies them all, which is lost and terrified.

This vocal virtuosity proves liberating for the play, the character and for the actress who gives the performance of her career. Make that the loud performance of her career; she's been very fine in quiet, caring roles such as the mother in Our Town. In more extrovert or domineering roles, she's sometimes seemed effortful. But here everything flows as freely as the booze the characters never stop downing, and at full throttle. Palk, playing one of American drama's great wisecrackers, is more confidently funny than ever before:Whiplash sarcastic at one moment, lankily languid -- sometimes self-mockingly,

sometimes not -- the next. Her bite and buoyancy help make her attractive; for once, when immersed in Albee's extended marital bloodbath, one sides, at least initially, with Martha rather than George, who usually attracts sympathy just for the amount he has to put up with. Their reciprocal baiting reaches its height, or its depths, when Martha ostentatiously makes out with Nick, the young chemistry professor who's been invited over with his wife, Honey, for an early morning of after-party partying. George's reaction is to bury his nose in a book, his imperturbability carefully calibrated, in Diego Matamoros' performance, to inflict maximum hurt.

The turning point, at the start of the third and last act, is a soliloquy for Martha that's not so much post-coital as noncoital, Nick having proved a disappointment. This is her cue to begin a harrowing downward spiral, for her and George (a team, whatever else) to reform ranks, and for him to take over. Up till now, Matamoros has been the irresistibly cool counter-puncher to her red-hot hammer-blows; he's also been the picture of a defeated man, "one of the biggest bogs in the history department" whose elegantly wielded words are his only remaining weapon. He now becomes both his wife's scourge and her salvation. The issue here is his demolition of a lie: This childless couple's imaginary son. I have always found both this fantasy and its destruction too cut-and-dried to be convincing but here it is, at least, very powerful. Albee subtitled this act The Exorcism, and for once it does have that ceremonial quality: a necessary rite that in Matamoros' hands starts cruel and finishes compassionate. One of its effects is to drive the intruders from the house (another exorcism). George and Martha are left together in an ending that can seem sentimental ( "Who's afraid of Virginia Woolf ?" "I am, I am.") but is here very moving, with the two actors -- old colleagues after all, but seldom teamed before--attaining a rare degree of communion.

The play juxtaposes, and exposes, two barren marriages. While George and Martha delight in stripping their marital scars in company, Nick and Honey have theirs dragged, cajoled or threatened out of them -- and they're at least equally grievous. As Nick, envied and mocked by George as the wave of the scientific future, Tim Campbell is perfect: broad-shouldered, self-satisfied, his limited sympathies subsiding as his insecurities increase. The recurring description of Diana Donnelly's Honey as "slim-hipped" here seems like just another of the characters' games but she beautifully registers the trophy bride's progress from delicious shock to shock absolute. Fine as all four performances are individually, the real prize of Diana Leblanc's production is the phenomenal degree of contact between them. There is never a moment at which either action or reaction goes slack, and both the pacing and the placing are impeccable. Astrid Janson's gaunt, precipitous set is a suitably gladiatorial arena, with a couple of oddities. The books are mostly painted, suggesting that even the household's literacy is suspect, and the shelves are adorned with pictures of George and Martha's namesakes, the Washingtons: Is this the production getting cute or are the characters? I still have doubts as to whether the play signifies much beyond its very enjoyable self. But that self is substantial: dialogue that stings, action that builds, characters who've become archetypes and -- it now appears -- compassion. In its 11 years, Soulpepper has given us any number of good productions and a handful of great ones. This is one of the greats. - Who's Afraid of Virginia Woolf ? is in repertory through Oct. 24 at the Young Centre. For tickets and information visit soulpepper.caor call 416-866-8666. robert.cushman@hotmail.com

2009-09-25-brooding-in-brooklyn-bored-to:
There was a nifty bit of free association at the start of the first episode of Bored to Death. Jonathan, the protagonist, was in the graphic process of losing his girlfriend. A moving van was taking their bed away, and her with it. Despondent in his newly solitary Brooklyn apartment he spied, in a pile of books littering the floor, Raymond Chandler's Farewell My Lovely. Ouch, he doubtless thought, and we with him. But it didn't end there. Jonathan had apparently nursed a secret ambition to be Philip Marlowe, and next thing we knew he was at his computer, placing an ad on Craigslist, offering his services as a private detective: "unlicensed," he was honest enough to point out. Whether this admission made it legal on something about which his friends, and especially his friendly neighbourhood police officers, turn out to have their doubts.

New and desperate career paths seem to be the new staple of TV shows. We've had the hero of Hung, branching out as a male prostitute, and the two heroes of Flight of the Conchords. Bored to Death isn't as consistently hilarious as Flight of the Conchords, but it's still the funniest thing to come along since. Jonathan differs from his predecessors in that he isn't doing it for the money. He already has a job, working for a glossy magazine editor, played by Ted Danson. Beyond this, he's the author of one apparently successful novel. In this he resembles his author and first-and-last-namesake Jonathan Ames. Jason Schwartzman fits the part perfectly.

When Jonathan's beloved dumps him, the heavy labour is carried out by a company called Moishe's Moving. It's staffed by Israelis, and Jonathan expresses surprise at seeing them engaged in heavy manual labour. "What are you," they ask, "another self-hating New York Jew?" "Guess I am," Jonathan

says with one of the gentle (obviously not Gentile) sighs, that we will soon recognize as being his default mode of expression. Jonathan is in fact an updated Woody Allen, prone to self-diagnoses like "I'm not good with anger; I go straight to depression." He's less intellectually prickly than Woody, and less indiscriminately libidinous; in fact he seems to be a one-woman man. A running theme of the first three episodes, and presumably of those beyond, is his attempt to win back his ex.

Jonathan is contrasted with his unkempt and burly friend Ray (Zach Galifianakis), whose lady, a vegan environmentalist, hasn't left him but whom Ray seems to think may as well have done. She's withholding intimacy until he cleans up his slovenly act, which seems like one of the grand-daddies of all lost causes. Jonathan's scenes with Ray are among the joys of the show so far. When we finally meet her in the third episode, Ray's girlfriend, so overwhelmingly caring she freezes the blood, turns out to be very funny as well.

I haven't said much about Jonathan's private-eye activities, because I don't think they work very well. For the comedy, that is -- obviously they don't work well for Jonathan himself, as that's meant to be the point. He does get a surprising number of cases, but it's probably no coincidence that much the best of the initial trio is Episode 3, in which the detective activities are mentioned but not shown. This is also the episode that makes full use of Danson, playing a full-blown Manhattan neurotic who, immediately after describing an ex-wife as "the most orgasmic woman I've ever met," encounters her at a party on the arm of his successor. He's miffed, reasonably, since she looks like Glenn Close while the man who's dispossessed him looks, and behaves, like Oscar Levant. Danson also says --incredibly, since he himself looks taller and more impressively white-maned than ever -- that he envies Jim Jarmusch for his good hair. Jarmusch plays himself and gets to spend one entire scene biking around what seems to be his personal gym; he's interested in having Jonathan revise the script of his next movie and tells him, "You must really suffer from the dark clarity of your vision." (He's read Jonathan's book.) As if that wasn't enough, Jonathan has also to subject himself to a psychotherapist who's said to fancy himself "the Carl Jung of Brooklyn." The shrink dismisses every one of Jonathan's problems with a brisk hand-clap and tells him that, "People don't change. We simply become more compatible with our core misery." This is a patchy show, but the best patches are princely. - Bored to Death airs Sunday at 9:30 p. m. on HBO Canada.

2009-09-26-antigone-vs-the-world-but-thi:
Jean Anouilh wrote Antigone in code. His version of the Sophoclean tragedy about the princess who defied temporal authority in the name of an ancestral morality was premiered in 1944 in occupied France. It could hardly not be seen as a parable of resistance to the Nazis. To protect himself, and probably in accordance with a dramatic instinct to balance the scales, Anouilh allowed his tyrant-figure a very good case. Creon, king of post-Oedipal Thebes, has declared that the body of Polynices, one of Oedipus' sons, be left unburied. Polynices and his brother Eteocles had killed one another in battle, and since Polynices was attacking Thebes at the time and Eteocles was notionally defending it, the latter got the funeral honours and the former got the dogs and vultures. Greek mythology held that the souls of those left unburied would wander in misery ever after. Antigone, the brothers sister, is determined to prevent this, and steals out to sprinkle some earth on the corpse. Shes caught, and brought before Creon. Their confrontation is the heart, soul and pulse of the play.

Anouilh's Creon is no Nazi; he is, at worst, a Vichy bureaucrat, trying to make the best of a very bad job. People always claim that the original Sophocles play holds the balance equally between Antigone and Creon, but I've never been able to see it; Sophocles seems to me to be on Antigones side from first to last; his Creon is both blinkered and cruel. Anouilhs Creon takes an avuncular tack, telling Antigone to go back to bed and let him cover up her job of pious covering. She isn't having it. So he tries logical argument. He points out the futility and cynicism of the traditional funeral ceremonies. He says, very believably, that both the brothers were scoundrels who broke their father's heart and that he doesnt even know which body was which; he simply buried the more presentable one. Antigone is convinced. But then Creon overplays his hand, welcoming her to the real world of accommodation and compromise. Antigone is revolted.

The new Soulpepper production uses the 60-year-old English translation by Lewis Galantiere but seems to have worked it over in rehearsal. (The original plan was for the company to do its own version of the Greek play, rather than Anouilhs.) Soulpepper, under Chris Abraham's direction, has roughened, shortened, sharpened (at least in theory) and, I think, weakened it.

This Antigone pours scorn on Creon's idea of life and opts for death -- for its own sake, apparently. Its Antigone as jihadist, though as suicide-burier rather than suicide-bomber. This accentuates a fatal flaw in Anouilhs play. The original French audience might have made a mental leap, identifying the heroine's defiance with that of their own fighters against hopeless odds. Today, though, we're left with a character whos been stripped of the religious convictions that motivated her ancient prototype and who protests, as somebody once memorably put it, "just because." This doesnt stop the play from being a riveting case study, but it doesn't make it a tragedy. Which wouldn't matter if Anouilh, through the mouth of his one-man Chorus, didnt keep insisting that it is.

Creon wins. He certainly does here, in a magisterially careworn performance by R.H. Thomson, whos found a place at which wit and weariness meet. If the play is a tragedy, it's his (and Anouilh certainly allows for this); he has flawed beliefs, which he articulates, on which he acts and for which he suffers. Liisa Repo-Martell's Antigone -- bewitched, bothered and bedraggled -- makes him a compelling adversary; their incompatibility registers very strongly. Shes moving, too, when she confronts her end. But shes vocally muffled, a fault that afflicts the whole production up until the big duet.

Lorenzo Savoini's stern panelled set and abrasive lighting give the show a promising shell, though the wall of surveillance screens is already a cliche. We're always being told that video on stage is necessary to make young audiences feel at home, but I think its more a matter of letting the grown-ups play with the kids toys. Perhaps in the hope of engendering tension or at least suggesting doom, nearly everyone speaks in a fast monotone. This irons out the naturalistic character detail that's one of the playwright's strongest suits. Maggie Huculaks nurse, who should be the voice of worried normality, is here a neurotic scold, while Claire Calnan, as Antigones glamorous sister Ismene, is allowed no personality at all. (Her name gets a French pronunciation while everyone else's is done English. There's a similar confusion in Stratfords Phedre. It should be one thing or the other.)

The best of the supporting per-formances are Jeff Lillicos everyman guard, though even he gets a bit flattened out, and Jordan Pettle's Haemon, boyishly crushed between being Creon's son and Antigones betrothed. David Storchs chorus veers between being a commanding ironist and an unaccountable pixie. The production obviously knows what it's about, but for too much of the time, barring Thomson's performance and all who sail with or against him, it isn't about the play. - Antigone runs through Oct. 17 at the Young Centre for the Performing Arts. 2009-09-28-choose-your-own-regal-adventu:
King Henry VIII is busting out all over. The Tudors returns for a third season, kicking off with Bluff King Hal's third marriage. At this rate the show has guaranteed itself a six-year run; maybe more if it justifies its title and gives us the rest of the dynasty. It's about time Henry's daughter Bloody Mary had her own TV show. Meanwhile, TVO brings us a four-part documentary from Britain's Channel 4 entitled Henry VIII: Mind of a Tyrant. And it could be coincidence that these two programs are reaching our screens simultaneously, but then there could also be a tooth fairy. Both shows demonstrate the resilience of the more colourful periods of English history in the face of all that supposed creativity can do to them.

"Five hundred years ago," says an unctuous voice at the start of TVO's offering, "an 18-year old boy sat in this chair in Westminster Abbey to be crowned king of England." Well, why should that be so incredible? The speaker, who's also taking up most of the screen, is Dr. David Starkey, a British historian who, like many experts, knows his stuff better than he can deliver it. Admittedly, once past that opening sentence, he lets up a bit on the gobsmacked italics, but what he goes on to say is pretty jaw-dropping. Henry, he tells us in monkishly shocked tones, "would grow up to become the most infamous monarch in history." More infamous than Nero? Genghis Khan? Ivan the Terrible? Even if you stick to English history there are some strong contenders in the royal infamy stakes, especially considering that Starkey himself cleaves to the traditional notion that it was Richard III who murdered the Princes in the Tower. He's on stronger ground when, sharing the screen with one of the Holbein portraits, he describes Henry as "the only king whose shape you remember," standing with his own hand on his hip to demonstrate.

The fact is that, though Henry was responsible for his own share of torture and bloodshed, it wasn't exceptional by the standards of his time. His real claims to notoriety are his appearance, as mediated by Holbein and Charles Laughton, and his six wives: circumstances that, taken together, have inspired as much titillated affection as revulsion. Starkey's mission, to judge from his first two instalments, is to lament Henry's tragic fall; to rehabilitate him before re-demonizing him. He gives us a young Henry devoted to his mother (who died in childbirth when he was still a boy), dubbed for dynastic reasons a Knight of the Bath, and one who "would always think of himself as a chivalrous knight." This involved some picturesque wars against France, undertaken mainly at the behest of the Pope, who subsequently thought better of the idea. Presumably Henry's resentment of this was a delayed factor in the Protestant Reformation.

Henry's story, says Starkey, is "the best and bloodiest royal soap opera of them all," and The Tudors is back to agree with him. "Best," though, is pushing it a bit; in fact, a lot. The show may be sticking closer to the facts than it used to, but the writing remains as crass and rib-nudging as ever. This, the previouslies remind us, is the production in which Henry once said "I so much want a new beginning -- a Renaissance" and went on to promise, "I will make such a Reformation in this kingdom that it will be remembered forever." Season 3's first episode shows us all this Reforming taking place, in the form of the cynical and extremely lucrative sacking of the monasteries, leading in turn to the northern rebellion known as the Pilgrimage of Grace.

The TV series Henry VIII, a mere six years ago, dramatized these events with a force and intelligence that The Tudors shows few signs of emulating. It also had the advantage of Ray Winstone's Cockney Henry, which imposed itself through sheer gusto. The acting in The Tudors, hemmed in by its cliche-ridden script, is pinched and suburban, showing among other things why most British classical acting is now outclassed by Canadian. (The Tudors is, bizarrely, a Canadian co-production, but there's almost no sign of that on the screen.) Jonathan Rhys-Meyers gives us a still-young Henry who seems to be anticipating his older self as promised by Starkey: a hysterical and calculating neurotic. He isn't remotely bloated yet; maybe that'll come by the time he hooks up with Catherine Parr, but lacking the famous "shape," Henry seems not only a physical but a spiritual shadow of himself. He isn't much fun. The show seems to pride itself on being idiomatically hip, but its accoutrements are relentlessly old fashioned. There's much terpsichorean hey-nonnynonnying; churchmen at parties snigger in corners; shepherds pose with their flocks while holding their crooks at picturesque angles. Violence, nudity and sexuality are promised and delivered: the nudity anyway. This is TV drama after all, and a naked woman is a naked woman, whatever style of costume she isn't wearing. - Henry VIII: Mind of a Tyrant airs tonight at 10 p.m. on TVO. The Tudors returns for a third season on Wednesday at 9 p.m. on CBC.

2009-09-29-don-t-throw-the-book-at-them:
THE BOYS IN THE PHOTOGRAPH

Royal Alexandra Theatre

---

It's amazing how much better Andrew Lloyd Webber's music sounds when you don't have to spend the whole evening listening to it. The Boys in the Photograph (Mirvish Productions via the Manitoba Theatre Centre) is a re-working of The Beautiful Game, which was staged in London in 2000. The game is soccer; the boys are a teenage Catholic team in the ravaged Belfast of 1969. This makes it the first Webber musical, with the possible exception of Evita, not to be set in some kind of fairyland. Most of his shows have had a stateless sound; there are a couple of ballads in this one that felt as if they'd been written before, but most of the music gains enormously, in flavour and in backbone, from being rooted in a real place at a real dire time. It gains even more from not having to do all the work; this is a book musical with dialogue, not one of those pretend-operas in which the story gets told mainly through droning recitative. The result is the freshest Lloyd Webber score since ... well, probably since Joseph and the Amazing Technicolor Dreamcoat.

The built-in hazard of a book musical, though, is that it has to have a book; and the one that Ben Elton has written and directed has enough holes to admit a whole fleet of British Army tanks. It does one important thing right; it resists the temptation to make the show a Protestant-Catholic Romeo and Juliet story. The principal lovers here come from the same side of the tracks. He is John, the team's star player with professional potential and no strong political feelings; she is Mary, a peace activist. Brutality and deception, from both factions, put their relationship under siege; John is framed, and does time in Long Kesh prison, from which he emerges the fanatic he had previously refused to be: an irony at least as potent now as then.

The show never downplays the grimness of the situation, but it can't find a consistent way of presenting it. That's not just because it now, in an effort to reverse its comparative failure in London, has a happy ending. This feels tacked on, but it might be excused as being in tune with a newly hopeful

Northern Ireland. But both the tone and the structure are unfocused, split between gag-writing and platitude-spouting.

If Elton's book-writing is amateurish, his lyrics are dreadful: "Football is the only reason/God Almighty gave us feet": Those are good lines, but they wave forlornly from a muddy field of formlessness, rhymelessness, and -- worst of all -- pointlessness. The songs never tell us anything we don't already know, either as action or commentary. In the second act, you dread the sound of the orchestra starting up because you know that the story, which has gathered some steam, is going to be stopped in its tracks for yet another stentorian meditation on how terrible sectarian warfare is and how we should all love one another. It's even worse when the band doesn't play. Erica Peck as Mary has to preach the score's climactic sermon a capella, meaning the music has no chance of drowning out the words; I was embarrassed, not by her but for her. When the lyrics do take a stab at developing story and character, you wish they wouldn't. As a writer, Elton likes to end a scene with a punchline; as a director, he leaves his actors to slink off after the punch has landed. The staging of more literal violence is remarkably unthreatening. The show begins with rival gangs dancing their antagonism on the streets. This can hardly help recalling West Side Story, though I'm not sure if Tracey Flye's choreography counts as imitation or parody. The production in general looks drab and trundling.

After all of which, it's awkward to have to admit that the show is always involving and ultimately moving. Credit goes to the history, to the music and to the fact that the creators, however much they fumble, do seem genuinely involved with the subject. The cast helps, too: Richard Harte, Brandon McGibbon, Tracy Dawson and Jacquelyn French give pungent if oddly uneasy accounts of team players and team fans, while Richard McMillan as priestly team coach takes some stock jokes and good intentions and makes a man of them. But it's John and Mary who really lump our throats by letting us partake in their growing up. Tony LePage is lithe, sympathetic and, when bitterness is called for, powerful. Peck is superb, confirming what she promised in We Will Rock You: that she's a first-rate theatre singer who's also a charming and economical actress, forceful without forcing and capable of projecting a passionate moral strength. It's a strangely admirable show. Let me put it like this: It's often dumb, but it's not stupid. - The Boys in the Photograph is at the Royal Alexandra Theatre until Nov. 1. For tickets and information call 416-872-1212 or visit mirvish.com.
