2009-10-03-the-emancipation-of-this-mimi:
The delight of Mimi, or A Poisoners Comedy, an elegant musical about group sex and mass murder in 18th-century Paris, is that its written by people who know how. That makes it a phenomenon among new musicals, Canadian or other. I feel this especially keenly, since I saw this show the night after seeing The Boys in the Photograph, whose achievements don't include the successful use of song to advance plot or explore character. Every number in Mimi does one or the other of those things, and many of them do both. What's more, they all do it with wit, occasionally of the laugh-out-loud variety. I cant remember a Canadian musical whose verbal standards were as consistently high.

What makes this all the more amazing is that, of the three credited lyricists, only one has any previous track record in musical writing. This is Allen Cole, who is also the composer, one of the most expert and prolific we have, and here doing some of his most inventive and melodious work. His partners, who also wrote the shows book, are Melody A. Johnson and Rick Roberts, both best known as actors and especially as stylish comic actors; Roberts is also a playwright, though none of his plays has been as good as this. Johnson is a former Second City performer and therefore writer, but I wouldn't be able to pick any of her stuff there out of a lineup. The writing in Mimi, though, has a determined zaniness of a kind that I associate with her work as an actress, and that is obviously infectious.

The evening starts with four young, or youngish, people frolicking on a bed: Mimi herself, more formally the Marquise de Brinvilliers; her somewhat ineffectual husband, who's Brinny for short; her lover, a promising fellow from the provinces, name of St. Croix; and Francoise, the obligatory and obliging maid. Their fun is interrupted by Mimis father, who disapproves and who holds the purse-strings. He imposes a monastic role on the household, and dispatches St. Croix to prison where he meets, and takes instruction from, an accomplished Italian poisoner. On his release, he imparts his new knowledge to his beloved who, after practising successfully on a blind and limbless beggar, uses it to dispose of her inconvenient parent. She serves him pigeon pie, her late mothers favourite recipe but with an added ingredient. She finds this very satisfying. Husband and maid are in on the plot as well, and the four of them embark on a killing spree.

The show is based on real events, unlike Stephen Sondheim's musical murderfest, Sweeney Todd, which is based on urban myth. The ironic jauntiness that's an occasional colour in that scores palette is here spread over most of the piece, mixed in with a kind of cankered innocence; its as if Sondheim had elected to write Sweeney in the style of A Funny Thing Happened on the Way to the Forum. In both Sweeney and Mimi, pies figure prominently, though at opposite ends of the homicidal process; in Mimi they're the cause of death, in Sweeney they're the result. Unless, of course, youre a pigeon. Dead pigeons in this show are constant causes of compassion, expressed in some of Coles most daintily unsettling music. Mimi herself, when forced into it, finds the role of good and charitable woman almost as erotically exciting as that of murderess. How lucky for her that she can be both at once.

I've never seen a show on the main Tarragon stage that gave me more pleasure than this one. Still, it does have flaws, and one is that, though it keeps signalling that it's going to dig deep into its heroines psychology, it never actually does. Even the statistical extent of her villainy is obscured. Though some of the shows characters (including Louis XIV, here seen riding a literal hobby-horse) talk as if there were indiscriminate killers on the loose, as historically there were, the verifiable murder count stops at four. Mimi's mother makes ghostly appearances, and the show seems to be building to a resolution of this relationship, but it doesn't arrive. This does prevent Trish Lindstrom from delivering a progressively impressive central performance; flirtatious, petulant, demonic and terrorized by turns, shes a musical-comic Lady Macbeth.

Alisa Palmers production makes fine use of Camellia Koo's magical mirrored set and of Matjash Mrozewski's choreography, which starts with an orgy and then gets sexier. The tone sometimes gets too giggly, especially with Martin Juliens Brinny, though he redeems himself with funny and touching dignity when fate catches up with him. Paul Braunstein is an entertaining master poisoner and Ron Pedersen a very apt pupil, especially when he makes a sung confession that, for undisclosable reasons, is one of the neatest things in the show. Victor A. Young underplays the puritanical dad, but is delightfully ponderous as one of the authors happiest inventions, a softhearted detective who hates being good at his work. Tamara Bernier Evans does a resounding double as mother and maid, the latter of whom gets to sing that her "salad days are almost tossed," a verbal twist I didn't see coming. The rhymes are similarly surprising, both in their accuracy, which is almost 100%, and in their inventiveness. You could kick yourself at the memory of ever having settled for anything less. Or you could kick other lyricists, which might be more satisfying. I bet Mimi would approve. - Mimi runs through Oct. 25 at the Tarragon Theatre. For ticket information, visit tarragontheatre.com.

2009-10-05-the-sound-of-the-fury:
THEATRE REVIEW

ROCK N' ROLL

Bluma Appel Theatre, Toronto

Fiona Reid has two magnificent moments in Rock 'n Roll, and shes a different character in each. Tom Stoppard's play covers a lot of ground, moving in time from 1968 to 1990, and shifting in space between an English professor's Cambridge house and a Czech dissidents Prague apartment. In Act One, Reid, as the professors wife, cries out that her body, ravaged by cancer, still houses the same spirit, the same desires, the same capacity to love and need to be loved. It's a heart-stopping sequence. In Act Two she's her former characters grown-up daughter, responding to an old admirers overdue overtures almost before he can make them. The wit and wisdom, simplicity and generosity, are overwhelming. Please: Stratford, Soulpepper, somebody cast our greatest comedienne as a Restoration heroine or as Beatrice in Much Ado About Nothing before time runs out on all of us.

The two scenes exemplify what the play is meant to be about. It's the plea of its author, himself an Anglo-Czech, for politics, not just socialism, with a human face. And the symbol for that, played out rather frivolously in England and with mortal seriousness in what was then called Czechoslovakia, is the music that gives the play its title and its linking soundtrack. As usual with Stoppard, the argument is both quizzical and passionate. There are people who think this his best play; I'm not among them, though I agree that second-rate Stoppard is better than first-rate almost anyone else. The recurring complaint that his plays are all mind, no heart, has always seemed to me to be rubbish. Paradoxically, though, the plays of which it seems most nearly true are the two, this one and The Real Thing, in which hes ostensibly closest to wearing his heart on this sleeve: in this case, a record-sleeve. What usually makes the disparate elements cohere in Stoppard is his humour, but Rock n' Roll is his least funny play. The parts never came together in Trevor Nunn's London-New York production, and theyre even further apart in this Toronto-Edmonton co-production, directed by Donna Feore.

Both of Reids characters --Eleanor, a classics teacher trying passionately and impatiently to impart the truth of Sappho's love-poetry, and Esme, her ex-hippie offspring -- are sideline observers. One thing Esme observes, peering over the garden wall, is an apparition that might be the god Pan, or might also be Syd Barrrett, troubled hero of Pink Floyd who, after the band cast him out, did indeed retire to a reclusive existence in Cambridge (history has always had a way of playing into Stoppard's hands). Esme passes on her enthusiasm, plus a few albums,

to Jan, an Anglophile rock-loving Czech who returns home for the short-lived Prague spring and whose heroes are the Plastic People of the Universe, a home-grown group persecuted despite being apolitical. Or persecuted because theyre apolitical, long hair representing an existential threat that can be cut but not tamed. Shaun Smyth is very fine as Jan, especially in his later, soberer years when, forcibly cropped himself, he comes to realize that engagement has a point.

Sometimes, though not often, he succumbs to this productions fatal weakness: acting so intent on demonstrating the characters' passions that it never makes clear what they're being passionate about. This unfocused emoting runs riot in the supporting cast who range, with the exception of Cyrus Lane as Jans more committed friend, from the anonymous to the atrocious. It also affects the third leading actor, Kenneth Welsh, who plays Eleanors husband Max, an old-school Communist who never left the party. Welsh looks, moves and sounds like the right kind of jaundiced English academic, but he hardly connects with the man's thoughts nor, accordingly, with his feelings. Max, who starts by saying that he's "kicked in the guts by nine-tenths of anything you can tell me about Soviet Russia" is probably, in isolation, the richest character in the piece; Stoppard, his political opponent, has written him with great magnanimity, as a man wrong about communism but right about nearly everything else. Welsh gets his anguished love for his wife, but his political pain stops short at irritability, and his ruminations on the decline of his own country lack weight. This is partly the fault of the play, which is sketchier in Cambridge than it is in Prague, accentuated by the production which places some crucial debates far back and out of reach.

Michael Gianfrescos sets give us two lots of painted bookshelves, especially unhelpful in Prague where theyre supposed to house Jan's LPs; these remain undisturbed even after the secret police have paid a supposedly devastating visit. The scenes of crackdown are altogether lacking in threat. That leaves the music which, even to a rock skeptic like me, is invigorating, as well as cunningly selected for thematic relevance (some wag has suggested a soundtrack album, which is a very good idea) though it does play down rock's more aggressive side. Its peace and lover, brother, even now. The play ends with the Rolling Stones playing a breakthrough concert in the Czech capital. Jan and Esme are present. Max isnt, though his opinions on the validity of a visiting millionaire pop group as a symbol of liberation might be very interesting. - Rock 'n' Roll is at the Bluma Appel Theatre in Toronto through Oct. 24. 2009-10-08-scottish-theatre-actor-adopte:
Note: Obituary of Douglas Campbell .

In 2001 the Stratford Festival, making its way chronologically through Shakespeare's history plays, arrived at the two parts of Henry IV. The year before, I had asked Richard Monette, Stratford's artistic director, whom he had down to play Falstaff, and he said "Douglas Campbell." I'm ashamed to say that my face fell a little. Wasn't this casting a little predictable? Hadn't Campbell already played the fat knight at Stratford many times, in The Merry Wives of Windsor as well as in the Henries? Actually, Monette informed me, Campbell had indeed played the Falstaff of Part One several times, but he had never before tackled Part Two.

Anyway, if I had been expecting something hackneyed or casual from Campbell's performance, I couldn't have been more wrong. The Scottish-born actor, who died on Tuesday in a Montreal hospital at the age of 87, had come to Canada from Britain for the very first Stratford season in 1953, and had stayed to become, fiercely and loyally, part of the festival and part of the country. Falstaff turned out to be his Stratford performance, and his rich, rumbustious contemplative voice and personality lit up the role. There's a moment in the tavern scene in Part One when Falstaff has to talk himself out of the charge of having run away from a disguised Prince Hal. "By the lord," he says "I knew him as well as he that made ye." A barefaced and outrageous lie, it's always cited in the textbooks as one of the great Shakespearean comic moments. Campbell is the only actor I have ever known who actually made it funny. He took full physical, vocal and spiritual possession of it, and he timed it impeccably. It was the perfect marriage of freshness and experience.

He came of a great tradition. He had also married into it, and he helped perpetuate it: His first wife, Ann Casson, was the daughter of one of one of England's greatest actresses, Sybil Thorndike, and their son Benedict is himself now one of Canada's leading actors. By his mid-thirties, when he first came here, Campbell had played leading roles at the Old Vic in London, including Othello. This was a part he repeated at Stratford in 1959; he had respectful rather than ecstatic notices, but Martha

Henry, who saw his performance three years before making her own Stratford debut, remembers it as being great. She added that he was also a great Hotspur -- in one production of Henry IV in which he didn't play Falstaff -- and he must indeed have had just the right fire-breathing quality. Another leading Stratford actress, Seana McKenna, has similar memories of his King Lear: "I've seen many Lears," she told me yesterday, "but his is the voice I always hear."

She heard it quite a lot at the time, because she was his Cordelia, in a production that went on an extended tour after its Stratford run; " Lear for a year," she calls it, and she recalled how complimented she felt when John Hirsch, the director, cast her, saying that she was "a chip off the old block." In fact, she played Campbell's daughter in three separate plays. "He was," she said, "a great spirit. It's tempting to say he was larger than life, but he was life. He was passionate and fierce; opinionated, loving and stubborn. He was unabashed. He was a man of the theatre, he breathed it, he acted it."

Full-throatedandfull-blooded both on and off the stage -- he was an ardent socialist -- he seems, too, to have been very practical and unpretentious about his career. "He went where the work was. It was typical of him to have moved to a new city -- Montreal -- in his eighties." McKenna also reminded me that in Vancouver, the Bard on the Beach theatre has named one of its two auditoria after him. And, she added, "he gave great bear hugs."

Tyrone Guthrie, the festival's first director, must have brought Campbell to Stratford in part because he sensed that they shared the same pioneer spirit. He was, initially, in all the great comic roles, but by his third season he was also playing Oedipus. He also directed: I remember, from his later years, a production of The Alchemist that was frankly nonsensical, and one of The Country Wife that was brilliant, hardheaded and hilarious. That powerful voice could also be used for singing; he was a fine Doolittle in My Fair Lady, and offstage -- just -- I remember hearing the voice ringing out in the ritual pre-performance singing of O Canada at the Tom Patterson. When he adopted a country, he really adopted it. There was probably a period, at Stratford and elsewhere, when his full-blooded style seemed old-fashioned. Later it came to seem timeless -- a quality much-needed and, when it isn't there, much-missed. It was in full flower the last time I saw him onstage, about five years ago, in Hamlet, at the National Arts Centre in Ottawa. He was the First Player: perfect casting.

2009-10-10-familial-relations-fodder-for:
The new Toronto theatre season has got off to a remarkably good start all around. There's a delightful small musical, Mimi, and a flawed but affecting big one, The Boys in the Photograph. There are three productions at Soulpepper: one great, one good, one ... interesting. There's Stoppard at CanStage. And there's True Love Lies, a new comedy by Brad Fraser that may be his best play yet.

Its title may remind you of the more unwieldy one with which its author first grabbed attention, Unidentified Human Remains and the True Nature of Love, and the two plays have characters in common. David McMillan, raffish protagonist of the earlier piece, is now a restaurateur. His former lover, a respectable citizen named Kane, is now married to a woman called Carolyn. They have a media business plus two children. Daughter Madison, 21, is aggressively sexually active, and aggressive about most other things as well; her younger brother, Royce, is more or less the opposite, spending hours looking at porn on the computer but defining himself, through a desperation that colours his entire existence, as asexual. Madison applies, all unknowing, for a job at David's eatery, and the interview goes swimmingly until he realizes who her father is. She returns home for a row around the family dinner table, in the course of which Kane's past gets revealed. The younger generation is appalled, if not by the relationship then by having it come so close to home ( "it's bad enough having a father who's creative and artistic, without discovering he's gay as well"). Carolyn, troubled but intrigued, takes the emancipated course of a woman faced with a possible rival; she has Kane invite David over for dinner.

If you find this last development hard to accept, you're in good company; David himself can hardly believe it and has grave misgivings about accepting. He does, though; and the gathering, despite everybody's best intentions except perhaps Royce's, is a social disaster. It does result, however, in Madison, through some polite blackmail, getting the job chez David, a position from which she can realize her transparent ambition of throwing herself at him. Royce has similar intentions, though not for the reasons you might think. When he and David have their confrontation it's shocking, but it isn't played for shock value: a mark of maturity that's characteristic of the play as a whole. Meanwhile, Carolyn, initially a willing partner in a marriage based (as the play caustically, but not cruelly, implies most are) on "insecurity, co-dependency and fear," sets about tentatively liberating himself. David, who has his own personal and financial problems lurking somewhere in the background, finds himself in the unsought role of family counsellor: a function that he discharges, in David W. Keeley's performance, with a magnetic mixture of weariness, tolerance and grace.

The play, which unfolds with admirable logic as well as being line-byline funny, has been given a very zippy production by its author. The action moves back and forth between eating places; and Britta Gerecke's functional single set makes all the scenes seem at home, the restaurant doubling easily and without confusion as family kitchen and dining room. Writing and performance probe the pain and, even more, the doubt, beneath the bright surface, without ever becoming self-consciously dark. Ashley Wright's Kane has the harassed look of a sitcom dad with blood-pressure problems, but his nervous reaching out to family and former partner is still believable. So are the well-meaning discomforts of Julie Stewart's Rose, the unnerving assurance of Susanna Fournier's Madison, and the terrors, both given and received, of Andrew Craig's Royce. The last word of the title is interestingly ambiguous; is it a noun or a verb? The latter would be the more interesting, with the play itself providing a rider: Love, it is suggested, does lie, sometimes and justifiably; but it doesn't have to do it all the time. The closing scene combines the attractions of inevitability and a question mark -- the neatest of the play's neat tricks.

Maintaining my unaccustomed Pollyanna mode I have to report that the new Second City revue Shut Up and Show us Your Tweets is one of this troupe's best, though not the best. Its attractions include a sketch about a married couple, separated by her travelling for her job, who try some self-conscious phone sex but keep getting sidetracked by memories of domesticity; a man's frantic call to a sadistically unhelpful computer help-line, proving that old jokes can be the best, especially if they tap familiar agonies; and a step-by-step historical retrospective on the ancient theme of "there goes the neighbourhood," allowing the cast to show off their prowess at accents and ethnic walks. The superb Darryl Hinds introduces this as "white people doing stereotypes" but does not participate himself; his personalized air of incredulous detachment, paraphrasable as "lord, what fools these Caucasians be" is given free and delightful rein elsewhere. Stabs at political satire feel dutiful, as usual; though there is a number depicting an American health-care town-hall meeting that spirals into a riotous identity of its own, each protester's absurdity feeding on the one before. Reid Janisse's patience as the man on the platform is ennobling to behold. Rob Baker, another in the cast of six, is older than the average Second Citizen, or maybe just looks it. Sandy Jobin-Bevans directs, smoothly; the designer, as always, here (and most of the time, everywhere else), is Camellia Koo. The show's first half is better than its second, but that's forgivable.

- True Love Lies runs through Nov. 1 at the Factory Theatre. Call 416-504-9971 for show times and ticket information; Shut Up and Show Us Your Tweets runs indefinitely at Second City. Call 416-343-0011 for details.

2009-10-16-yiddish-history-told-with-his:
Theodore Bikel, actor and musician, has an easy, comfortable way of belonging on a stage that I haven't seen equalled since the death of William Hutt. At the age of 85, he has of course had time to develop it. Early in his career, he appeared in London with Peter Ustinov, and some of Ustinov's confiding jocularity may well have stayed with him. In his tribute to the Russian-Yiddish humourist and storyteller who re-named himself Sholom Aleichem, Bikel envelops the audience in a casual, non-pressuring bear hug.

Supported by a pianist and an accordionist, Bikel appears before us in three principal guises: as himself, fan and preservationist of Yiddish literature; as Aleichem, shrugging chronicler of the shtetl, who ended his days in New York; and as Aleichem's most celebrated creation, Tevye the dairyman. Tevye is now of course best known as the hero of Fiddler on the Roof, a role Bikel has played thousands of times, as a projection in the preamble bears witness. At the opposite end of the evening, he has Aleichem lamenting the unlikelihood of getting a play about Tevye put on in the declining (he says) New York Yiddish theatre of the 1910s; I think we can take it that these are the author's authentic words. We can also be pretty sure that when he goes to envision the possibility of a singing and dancing Tevye in the distant future, his impersonator is putting cute words in his mouth.

Still, Bikel manages to maintain his dignity while doing it, and when he gets around to portraying Tevye himself, he quickly banishes any suspicion that he may be about to break into If I Were a Rich Man. He gives us the Tevye we're used to, bending God's ear with respectful grumbles, but he paints a darker picture than we get from the musical. We find out what actually happened to the tailor Motel Kamzoil and what became of the marriage plans of Tevye's two youngest daughters, and none of it is pretty. We also hear, via the author's own bitter thoughts from a refuge in Switzerland, how much more there was to a pogrom than some carefully choreographed furniture-smashing.

Running just longer than an hour and a half, this is a scattershot entertainment. There are some songs, in excellent English translations by Bikel himself. There are random glimpses of shtetl boyhood, involving a rabbi who would as soon beat a student as teach him and a best friend with a marked resemblance to Huck Finn; indeed, we're told that Sholom Aleichem and Mark Twain regarded one another as kindred spirits. The show only partly lives up to its subtitle. There is laughter, certainly, and there's the occcasional sigh, but the tears have to be taken as read. - Sholom Aleichem continues to Oct. 18. 2009-10-17-frontier-frights-the-mill-s-h:
The Theatrefront company are known for going off to foreign parts and assembling plays about those parts when they get back. An investigative trip to Bosnia resulted in Return (The Sarajevo Project) and one to South Africa gave us Ubuntu (The Cape Town Project). For their latest show, they've been exploring closer to their own backyard, in space if not in time. The Mill, set in northern Ontario, is their Canadian project. So far, it's a winner.

I have to say "so far" because The Mill is a cycle of four plays, of which only the first two have yet been unveiled. Part I: Now We Are Brody takes place in the 1850s. Part II: The Huron Bride is set 20 years earlier, and I apologize in advance for any confusion. Both plays have the same timbered setting: the eponymous sawmill (brilliantly realized by Theatrefront's designer Gillian Gallow), whose accoutrements include a forbidding staircase; some even more perilous floorboards with ghastly secrets underneath; and, but of course, a supremely horrific circular saw on whose teeth several characters come to grief, one of them before our very eyes.

You'll have gathered that The Mill is a horror story. It may even have invented a new genre, Pioneer Gothic: one that Part I, written by Matthew MacFadzean, seems content to explore and exploit for its own sake. Charlotte MacGonigal, a young lady of neurasthenic tendencies but with a very strong will, comes to take possession of the mill, bequeathed to her by her father. She is not, on the whole, welcomed. The surrounding community, once called Jameston after James MacGonigal who built the mill, wants to forget the recent past and has renamed itself Brody, hence the unlikely title. The things they want to forget are summed up by the figure of Lyca, a white-clad girl who literally haunts the place. Outside are all manner of terrors: wolves, Indians, other settlers and unremittingly awful weather. Equally menacing is Charlotte's husband, a maniacally possessive preacher who's tracked her down and is disinclined to leave without her.

Some of this show's best scenes are silent; they depict Charlotte's early days in her new home, each day ticked off in a surtitle, subsisting mainly on tourtieres dropped off by a friendly Frenchman. (She can hardly have expected this. So how had she planned to survive?) The dialogue, when company finally comes a-calling, can be awkward; characters are at one another's throats before they've been properly introduced, either to one another or to us, and there are anachronisms that are jarring without being funny. But nobody could say that the proceedings aren't scary.

They don't, though, as much as hint at any overarching statement about Canadian history or Canadian identity. (For that matter, Theatrefront's previous two shows weren't as enlightening about Capetown and Sarajevo as they must have meant to be.) This is partially redressed by Part II, written by Hannah Moscovitch. It has a prologue in which a helpful modern archeologist (Richard Greenblatt, luxury casting in a cameo role) instructs his students on the advisability of consulting the indigenous population before digging. The play proper bears this lesson out. We meet James MacGonigal himself, fanatically proud of his mill, which he built on Native bones, pretty much literally. He has imported Hazel Sheehan, a distant cousin (all the way from Liverpool, in fact) to mind the store; after a series of encounters, fraught sexually and otherwise, he marries her. But she isn't his first bride; that was the Native woman of the title who haunts the play and the place as, again, does the eerie Lyca, who's alive at this point though not always so you'd notice. Coming after MacFadzean, Moscovitch has the task, conceivably the simpler one, of explaining his mysteries while planting a few of her own. The style and the setting are different from anything she's tackled before, and she copes beautifully. A striking thing about this writer is her sheer competence; she does all the things one should be able to take for granted but rarely can: draw characters, tell stories, write dialogue -- and not just monologue, which is the suspicion that has dogged her previous work. An ecological fable that might have been awfully heavy-handed is related with dexterity and even wit. A brief digression on raccoons should make any urban audience feel in touch with its rural roots.

The productions -- Part I directed by Daryl Cloran, Part II by Christian Barry -- are outright superb, with scarifying sound by Richard Feren and lighting by Andrea Lundy that, especially in the second play, explores new dimensions of the crepuscular. Both scripts make extravagant demands on special effects, all of them--in the tiny Tank House theatre -- flawlessly met; in Part I a couple of actors levitate. Michelle Monteith plays both Charlotte and Hazel, the two young wives put mercilessly through the Mill, and delivers brilliantly contrasted studies in terrorized persistence: one intruder who inherits her demons, one who meets them fresh. Each has a husband from hell, played with appropriate intensity if insufficient weight by Ryan Hollyman. Three characters appear in both plays: Holly Lewis is an indomitably fragile Lyca; Eric Goulem lays on the Gallic relish, rather excessively; and Maeve Beaty is a serially intrusive biddy. She, too, can overdo the eccentricity; but it's hard to resist her sharpness of line, especially when standing and moving at impossible angles, and her whiplash verbal timing. She and Monteith, with complementary styles and personalities, are extraordinarily present actresses, and having them onstage together is a treat on its own.

-In repertory through Oct. 24. For showtimes and ticket information, call 416-866-8666.

2009-10-21-wry-school-musical-the-cast-c:
You have to love a show that can send up its own plot synopses. This week's episode of Glee starts with the customary brisk rundown of the story so far. Its exceptionally brisk, finishing off with a cheery and thats what you missed." That isn't quite all. We get some additional narration from the show's two major antagonists. The viperous Sue Sylvester, coach of the high-school cheerleading team known as the Cheerios, reminds us of how much she loathes Will Schuester, director of the school glee club, and of how she intends to take him down. Will, formerly mild-mannered but now beginning to fight back, realizes that "Sues turned me into her and adds, aghast, look at us, were even fighting in our voice-overs."

So the great thing about Glee is that it doesn't take itself seriously, or at least not often. It's that rare if not unprecedented thing: a serial musical comedy. The music of course comes from the glee club itself, a concept that seems to have advanced considerably from the days when club members just stood in rows and came out with barber-shop harmonies enlarged to choral proportions. These kids do numbers. They have an eclectic repertoire, from show tunes to soul, by way of Avril Lavigne and Motown. The songs comment on the action rather than flowing spontaneously out of it since, according to the shows creator, Ryan Murphy, its more realistic that way. That's an interesting view of realism. These characters may be performing because they're performers, but they have an enviable knack for going full-tilt into a routine, with full band accompaniment, without so much as allocating lines or selecting a key.

Glee reinforces the impression, fostered by all previous high-school sitcoms, that U. S. high schools are appalling institutions that place a fanatically high value on developing students self-esteem while creating a peer-pressured system guaranteed to destroy it. Anyway, Will divided his troops into two teams, male and female, for what he delightfully called "a glee-off. In the event, both sides killed. This wasnt surprising, as their high-energy performances were fuelled by decongestant pills supplied by Will's wife Terri, filling in as school nurse despite having had no medical training.

All this was part of a neat, and pretty much self-contained, storyline involving an attraction between Will and Emma, the school guidance counsellor. It was spotted by Cheerio Sue, who set out to destroy it. This wasn't strictly part of her anti-glee campaign; she just likes destroying things. She told Terri and suggested that, in order to keep a closer eye on her husband, she take the nursing job. A split-second flashback informed us that Sue had already disposed of the posts previous occupant: bodily.

Im not accusing anyone of being misogynist, but I have to say that the females on this show are all monsters. Terri (Jessalyn Gilsig) is a control-freak whose pregnancy has turned out to be hysterical, a fact she's hiding from her husband. Emma (Jayma Mays) is a germophobe who's accepted a proposal from a sad-sack football coach on condition that he keep well away from her after theyre married. Of the kids, Quinn (Dianne Agron), the cheerleaders leader, acts the spoiled prima donna both on the field and in the glee club. Yes, she's a double agent, which she confirms by being a) head of the celibacy club, and b) pregnant and not hysterically, at least not in that sense.

Jane Lynch's Sue, of course, with her scheming and her materialism and her sickly-sweet late-night spot on local TV, is off the charts for malevolence. Shes got herself appointed codirector of the glee club, and this week shes reinventing Will's strategy of divide-and-encourage as one of divide-and-destroy. Trying to cream off the best of Will's talent, she briskly calls them out as follows: gay kid, Asian, other Asian, Aretha."

For some reason, she neglects to name-check the paraplegic. You can have too much of a bad thing, and Sue can become not someone you love to hate but someone you just hate. This does allow Matthew Morrison as Will to be likeable without having to work too hard at it. Besides, the writers usually manage to rescue Sue by handing her the very poetry of anti-Will hypocrisy: "Sue Sylvesters rainbow tent will gladly protect you from his storm of racism. The kids arent impressed. The show is post-multicultural; it knows that everyone's a minority. Sure I'm a proud black woman," says Aretha-I-mean-Amber (Mercedes Jones), "but there's more to me than that. If we want to hear mom and dad fight," says one boy as Sue and Will square off at rehearsal, "we could stay home -- those of us who still have two parents. Every so often Glee gets glancingly serious, but so far it hasn't been soggy. Most of the time it is indeed gleeful. It can also, as befits a show about school, be educational. Did you know that after dentists, obstetricians have the highest rate of suicide among medical practitioners"? I heard it on TV.

- Glee airs on Wednesdays at 9 p. m. on Global and Fox.

2009-10-23-and-now-for-something-complet:
Its been 40 years since Monty Python's Flying Circus made its debut on BBC Television, and the anniversary's being marked by a celebratory chronicle entitled Monty Python:Almost the Truth (The Lawyers Cut), the story of six men told in six parts. The first episode covers Python pre-history. The next two are devoted to the four seasons of the TV show itself. The remaining three deal, one apiece, with the movies: Holy Grail, Life of Brian, Meaning of Life. The last one also finds space for the groups subsequent activities, though it restricts itself to those with Python relevance; Spamalot is in, Fawlty Towers is out. In other words -- words to which the Pythons themselves would probably offer cheerful assent -- it shows them cashing in on their legend.

In the show proper, the five surviving, talking-to-camera Pythons -- John Cleese, Terry Gilliam, Eric Idle, Terry Jones, Michael Palin -- go in for much whimsical dissing of themselves and one another, most of it more tolerant than barbed; Cleese, very elder-statesmanlike, says that they were never especially close as people anyway. It sounds as if, whatever the admitted disagreements and resentments, they've mellowed. They've certainly had time. Its been 26 years since the last full Python collaboration, Monty Pythons The Meaning of Life. In all that time the TV shows, the films, the songs, the catchphrases have never gone away. The best Flying Circus acts are sheer joy, the most inventive comedy ever seen on TV.

They came from rich soil. Python was the creation of young men in their twenties, five of whom grew up in postwar Britain and went to Oxford or Cambridge -- which makes Gilliam, the lone American, seem rather out-of-place in the opening reminiscences. The others lived through, and were heavily influenced by, the great age of British radio comedy, culminating in the inspired surrealism of The Goon Show. The more explicit kind broke out in the early '60s, initially in the theatre with Beyond the Fringe, from the preceding Oxbridge generation. For the first time, jokes -- heavenly, devastating ones -- were being made about actual politicians, and about the whole of British society, on a public stage.

The Python battened on the satire boom, but also reacted against it. The team came together through what seems to have been a typical BBC fit of creative absent-mindedness, and indeed the whole Python story, from influences to accomplishments, is one of the glories of public broadcasting. Outrageously literate, the Pythons fit into an English tradition of structured anarchy that stretches back from the Goons to Lewis Carroll, reflected too in Gilliam's savage animations, whose habit of trampling a sketch literally underfoot contributed materially to Pythons greatest formal innovation, the abolition of the punchline. Stage revue, what remains of it, has never found a way of doing this and suffers accordingly. Above all, the Pythons upheld the principle that sustains nearly all comedy: that authority is inherently ridiculous.

They knew about authority since, as sons of the lower middle-class, they had all grown up just outside it; Cleese, in particular, looks like an Establishment candidate gone off the rails. So does Graham Chapman, whose early death from cancer labels him the ex-Python and who is represented here in clips from earlier interviews. Inevitably the show becomes in large part a tribute to him. The others all concur that he was the best actor, a natural leading man, and the clips from The Holy Grail and Life of Brian prove them right.

Later generations of British comics pay tribute to the Python influence, and agree on the absence of anything comparable since; among this bunch Steve Coogan seems especially smart and Russell Brand like something that might have been invented by Sacha Baron Cohen. As with The Beatles, transatlantic reactions are even more effusive than the homegrown ones, perhaps because the Americans could regard them as exotic, visitors from a comedic outer space. The information is this documentary is fascinating, and nicely balanced between the personal and the technical.

I would have liked to know how Cleese, whose low boredom threshold led him to bow out of the final TV series (which suffered for it) was lured back for the films. Perhaps theres a clue in his statement that telling a story in 90 minutes is the most exciting thing in show business," and his consequent criticism of The Meaning of Life as a reversion to the sketch-comedy they'd outgrown. (Of course he went on to create Fawlty Towers, the greatest of sitcoms as Flying Circus is the greatest of sketch shows.) Even Jones, who directed Meaning of Life, admits that there was "no consensus about what the movie was going to be" and it shows. But you'll end up wanting to watch the whole Python oeuvre over again, dodgy bits included. - Monty Python: Almost the Truth (The Lawyer's Cut) premieres Saturday on Bravo! at 9 p.m.

2009-10-24-drowning-girls-is-wicked-and-:
Two studio-sized shows, all scoring higher on presentation than on content.

The Drowning Girls started in 1991 at the Edmonton Fringe, and the play has been in heavy rotation ever since, picking up several awards on its travels. It's the story of an English serial-murder case of the 19th century. Three women in succession were found dead in their respective baths shortly after getting married. Each, after a prolonged period of singleness, had wed the same man, one George Joseph Smith who, using a different name on each occasion, had drowned them, pocketing the modest sums of money they had brought with them and the larger sums for which he had had them insured. He got away with passing their deaths off as accidental until the mother of one victim read a newspaper account of the death of another. Smith was tried, hanged and attained nationwide notoriety as "the Brides in the Bath Murderer."

The brides and their baths supply Charlie Tomlinson's production with its central image, strikingly realized. Bretta Gerecke, responsible for the resourceful kitchen-and-dining-room set of True Love Lies, now gives us an epic bathroom: three full-length tubs, resplendent on a black floor, each with a functioning shower and filled with what one hopes is warm water. The design proves to be a constant source of arresting effects. The three murderees arise in succession and commiserate with one another. They then proceed to act out their stories, which of course have much in common.

Tomlinson wrote the script in collaboration with Beth Graham and Daniela Vlaskalic who also make up the cast along with Natascha Girgis. The writing's at its best in its earlier, more abstract phases. When the narrative takes over, it becomes repetitive. The first story takes forever to tell, while one realizes, with an appropriately sinking feeling, that there are still two more to go. We are given a thumbnail biography of Smith himself; it seems he was abused before becoming an abuser, but that's hardly revelatory. Vlaskalic has some poignant, trusting moments as his first prey; Girgis is very sharp and economical as his last -- she seems too smart and mature to succumb but her very loneliness betrays her. Girgis is also the best at supplying instant cameos, including a delightful one of a local gossip. But it's hard to see the play's purpose beyond dispensing historical information. It's apparent that it's trying to go beyond mere victimology; at the end, the three rise from their onstage watery graves to pronounce Smith guilty. This seems superfluous, as a judge and jury have already reached the same conclusion and made it part of Victorian mythology. Last time I checked, the Brides in the Bath Murderer, in waxwork form, was still on show in the Chamber of Horrors at Madame Tussaud's.

Then there are the heroes of Bash'd, billed as a gay rap opera. In this twohander (another import from Edmonton, this time via off-Broadway), Chris Craddock and Nathan Cuckow play TBag and Feminem, hip-hoppers with angels' wings. They tell of Jack and Dillon, a Toronto couple whose happiness was destroyed when Jack was all but killed by gay-bashers and Dillon tried to avenge him. Jack's the urban sophisticate raised by a gay couple, Dillon's the small-town boy whose dad is a redneck (but eventually sees the light). It is, avowedly, a Romeo and Juliet story; the parallels are especially acute when the lovers first meet at a club, and when Dillon falls into tragedy when trying to defend Jack. My companion, who knows far more about rap than I do, thought the beats monotonous, but most of it worked for me. Rhyme, whether in rap or Racine, is a treacherous medium for drama, but it can have clinching force when properly handled; the rhymes in this show only get sticky when the show gets preachy. It tells us, too often, that it's reclaiming a traditionally homophobic form, when it's best at just getting on and doing it. As performers, Craddock and Cuckow are impressively energetic, hurling themselves around vocally and physically without missing, you guessed it, a beat.

- The Drowning Girls runs through Nov. 15 at the Tarragon Extra Space. Call 416-531-1827 for ticket information. Bash'd runs through Oct. 31 at Theatre Passe Muraille. Call 416-504-7529 for more information.

2009-10-31-the-threads-tighten-all-aroun:
Site-specific theatre comes in two flavours: stationary and Queen In the first kind, the audience is ushered into a space that bears some similarity to the setting of the play -- dingy hotel rooms are a favourite -- and simply sits there watching the play unfold at unusually close quarters. In the second, which these days seems to be the more prevalent, the site in question is a whole building, in which the actors move from room to room with the spectators in dutiful pursuit. The latest of these magical mystery tours is The Turn of the Screw, an adaptation of the Henry James ghost-novella, currently haunting the stately Campbell House at the corner of University. and much

It isn't as logistically complex as, say, Tamara, the forms primary exhibit from some 30 years ago, which derived House of its effect from having different scenes unfolding simultaneously in different rooms. We had to admire the organizers cleverness in keeping their divergent narrative lines from bumping into one another on the stairs; as we did again last year in The Gladstone Variations. The Turn of the Screw is a single tale with only two performers, one of them playing several roles, and everything depends on their skill, and that of the production team, in ratcheting up the tension in a series of confined spaces. They win some, they lose some.

The story is the famous one of an unnamed young governess, late Victorian period, on her first assignment. Her employer, who is both personally and geographically remote, sends her to a house outside of London to look after his orphaned niece and nephew, both of whom are said to look angelic. Flora, the girl, is already in residence, and is shortly joined by her elder brother Miles, expelled from boarding school for behaviour apparently too unspeakable to be described. From Mrs. Grose, the obligingly informative housekeeper, the governess learns of her predecessor, a Miss Jessel, and the groom, the satanic Peter Quint, both now dead but formerly lovers, the details of their liaison also too horrible to be discussed. Miles and Flora, it seems, were their go-betweens, and even in death the guilty and now ghostly couple won't leave them be. The governess, herself the child of a stark and oppressive home with romantic notions derived from reading Jane Eyre, does passionate, even hysterical, battle for the children's bodies and their souls.

Jeffrey Hatchers dramatization calls for a neutral set with minimal furnishings. In accordance with the First Fashionable Law of Creative Direction, which decrees that a play be made either more or less cluttered than its author intended, Vikki Andersons production (for the DVxT company) gives it the kind of naturalistic trappings only available when a room is played by an actual room. Or in this case, by a succession of rooms. Some of this works handsomely. The entrance hall of Campbell me has a sweeping, winding staircase on which actors can cower in terror or cling for comfort to maximum visual effect. The various bedrooms and sitting rooms do their atmospheric bits as well, and John Gzowski has contrived an alarmingly spooky sound-score. But it all gets dissipated whenever a scene ends and we all troop out, transformed from voyeurs to tourists. The fact that we are made very aware of our fellow audience members doesn't hurt much. It isn't as if we can tune them out even in conventional theatres, and in fact their presence is less intrusive in a peripatetic production like this one than in a one-room-only show, where an implicit claim to absolute realism is negated by the presence of a bunch of people wondering whether they should be pretending not to be there. What does get disturbed here, especially in the later scenes, is the rhythm.

The mores the pity, because by this stage the actors are doing an excellent job of terrifying us and one another. Clinton Walker narrates, or at least tops-and-tails, and also plays the absentee uncle, overdoing the vague menace; but his most prominent roles are the housekeeper and the boy. For the former, he intermittently dons an apron (his only costume change) while sliding between prim caricature and genuine feeling; as Miles, hes truly uncanny, sullen and winning and terrorized, a credible boy in the grip of the unthinkable. (Nobody plays Flora who, traumatized into silence, is here invisible as well.) Christine Horne, who earlier this year was a numbingly monotonous Miss Julie, is transformed as the governess; facially and vocally, she transmits rapid shifts of feeling that bear scrutiny in the closest of close-ups. Her delicacy is matched by the force with which she faces disaster and the speed with which she hurtles towards it. The arcane precision of James's language always drives me up the wall, and neither actor can convince location, that this is how anybody, except perhaps James himself, ever actually talked, but they do manage to turn the words, bloodless as they are, into weapons. Horne's performance, for all its nervous energy, gives little support to the idea that the phantoms are merely the projections of the heroines own suppressed passions; shes too sure of herself for that, and Miles' torments are too real. But it's something to think about afterwards.

- The Turn of the Screw plays through Nov. 7 at the Campbell House Museum. For ticket information, call 416-504-3898.

2009-11-05-get-into-the-goo:
THEATRE REVIEW

THE TOXIC AVENGER MUSICAL

The Music Hall, Toronto

I greatly enjoyed the first five minutes of The Toxic Avenger Musical. Maybe the first 10 minutes. This show, about a New Jersey town to which Manhattan exports all its nuclear and other waste, starts with one of its five performers advancing bravely toward us to sing the opening number, and finding his first note collapsing into a cough. That's funny. The number itself, when he and his colleagues are able to embark on it, is funny, too. Its an over-the-top anthem about the town of Tromaville and how anyone fixing on staying alive would be well advised to give it the old go-by.

The music for The Toxic Avenger Musical is by David Bryan (of Bon Jovi), the book is by Joe DiPietro (I Love You, Youre Perfect, Now Change), and the two of them collaborated on the lyrics. The music is characterless clatter but the best of the lyrics, thanks I suspect to DiPietro's old-school show-smarts, bring off something otherwise unknown in rock-based musicals, by being a) decipherable and b) good. Its only predecessor in that regard has been Little Shop of Horrors, a show to which it stands indebted in other matters as well. Little Shop pioneered the fashion for basing musicals on junk movies. The new show also resembles Little Shop in giving us a pacific virginal nerd of a hero and a coy, well-used heroine who respects his values and his character but is slow to respond to him physically. In this case, the boy is Melvin Ferd the Third, who wants to clean up his polluted town without hurting anyone, and the girl is Sarah, a blind librarian.

This curious combination of qualities is due to the evil lady Mayor, who heads the corporation that's poisoning Tromaville and has cuningly placed the records of her misdeeds in the custody of someone who cant read them. But Melvin gets his hands on the evidence, and unwisely confronts the Mayor, who has two of her goons drop him into a vat of exceptionally toxic goo. He emerges from it a foot taller, green all over, possessed of superhuman powers, and not shy about using them. (He does tend to be sorry afterwards.)

From the moment of his transformation, the show, which up until now has remained fairly sprightly, takes a nosedive. It begins, perhaps in accordance with its environmental principles, endlessly recycling itself.

It recycles other musicals as well. The Mayor might have stepped out of Sondheims

Anyone Can Whistle (everyone hates her, yes, yes, being the Mayoress, yes) while the frustrated Melvin's more indiscriminate rampages give him a definite resemblance to Sweeney Todd, if without the same complexity of motivation. Its attempts at political and theatrical satire make it seem like a less sophisticated Urinetown. Like a depressing number of other recent musicals, it gives itself the airs of satire without ever taking the smirk off its face long enough to establish anything to be satiric about.

John Rando, who directed Urinetown with such efficiency and imagination, settles here for efficiency. He doesn't manage to turn low-rent into a style. He has an excellent cast. Evan Alexander Smith is endearingly earnest as Melvin, though he can hardly help being monotonous as his toxic doppelganger (Toxie for short). Brittany Gray flutters her lashes and her vocal cords in classic style as Sarah. She functions far more efficiently outside her home than in it. The show isnt into explaining this; it just wants the laughs. Some of these are bracingly tasteless, with great cruel lines like, If blind people didnt love ugly people, then who would?" But it then retreats with a number called All Men are Freaks, which strikes me as a cop-out.

Louise Pitre doubles as the Mayor and Melvin's mother, who is stock Jewish though she doesn't seem to have passed it on to her son. At one point, the two ladies sing a hate-duet which, the score having taken a nosedive along with the script, is entitled (and mainly consists of) Bitch/Slut/Liar/Whore. The intended panache of this quick-change act is negated by the use of doubles. Pitre also plays a nun, for reasons to do with little except camp; she's both resonant and resilient, though at this stage of her game she should surely have better things to do with her time. All other roles are divided between Darren A. Herbert and Jamie McKnight, billed respectively as Black Dude and White Dude.

The show lays great stress on its Jersey setting but the Toronto audience is indulged with references to Tim Hortons and the Don River. How dumb do they think we are? (Don't answer that.) And maybe the production exemplifies its own environmental thesis. This gets imported from New York while our own, insanely funny, An Inconvenient Musical languishes in neglect. - The Toxic Avenger Musical runs until Jan. 3. Ishould have sent you to boarding school" (or words to that effect) says Hugh, whos something successful in high finance, to his teenage son, Henry, who at that moment, and not altogether by his own choice, is wearing one of his mother's dresses. Hugh's words are weighed down with old irony since Henrys sister, Mia, has been sent to a boarding school, and weve already seen her there, assisting in the torture of a younger girl, apparently as part of an initiation ceremony. Henry isn't even in day school anymore, having dropped out to look after his mother, Martha, a pill-popping alcoholic mental case. Hugh hasn't been around to help, having taken off for points East and an Asian girlfriend.

This happy family is the subject of That Face, a prize-winning play by the then 19-year-old British writer Polly Stenham. In its Canadian premiere, from Nightwood Theatre, it comes over as a talented work but not an achieved one, tense and sparky in much of its dialogue but lopsided in construction. The torture scene at the beginning turns out to have no purpose beyond getting the play off to an arresting start. It begs questions: If this initiation is traditional practice, did Mia herself once undergo it and, if so, how did it affect her? Her partner-in-crime is briefly pressed into service as Henrys first girlfriend, thereby bringing out all the helpless possessiveness in his mother, and both girls may be meant to illustrate a pervasive callousness in privileged British youth: not that recent cases in Canada have given us any reason to feel superior. But the plot and character points could have been made in other, more economical ways.

Its the relationship between sick mother and caregiving son that turns out to be the play's main concern. We first discover them, the morning after one of Martha's binges, Henry sprawled across the foot of her bed. It looks for the longest time as if we have incest on our hands but this turns out to be a false trail. Technically, that is; Martha, who puts the "mother in smother," is happy to believe that Henrys gay, since it robs her of the threat of female competition. Meanwhile, Mia, whos long given up on Martha but loves Henry, stalks the outskirts of the play, giving off alternating signals of cruelty and compassion. Suspense hinges on whether Martha will go voluntarily into care or whether she'll be consigned there by Hugh, a cold but, in the circumstances, forgive-able fish.

Kelly Thornton's production is choppy, both physically and psychologically; the evenings pitted with the blank spots that actors feel compelled to fill with unfocused emoting. Sonja Smits has attracted a hailstorm of abuse but in fact her performance is the best in the play, admirably exposing Marthas imperiousness, vulnerability and the shaky sense of entitlement that sustains her until her final collapse. Nigel Bennett also seems at home, faithfully rendering Hugh as self-satisfied philistine, until breaking out with the play's most resonant moment: his terse admission that Henry is "a good boy, with bad parents. As Mia, Bethany Jillard plays another in her line of hair-trigger adolescents, but too often falls back on playing the (supposed) style rather than the character. Kristopher Turner has a fearsome task as Henry, and he doesn't really get into it until his scenes away from his mother, which allow him to be mercurial. The plays main problem: It keeps re-stating the same situation with a horror-struck look on its face and an almost total absence of humour.

That Face, downstairs at Berkeley Street, is part of Nightwoods 4x4 season, dedicated to showcasing female directors. Another of them, Weyni Mengesha, has done a triumphant job one floor up on Yellowman, an American play by Dael Orlandersmith about colour prejudice between blacks. We meet Alma and Eugene, who grew up together in South Carolina; she's Gullah-Geechie, dark-skinned; he's light, high-yellow." They both come of mixed parents; they develop from best friends to lovers; they face hatred within and without their own families, and one of them succumbs to it. The play is written as their parallel monologues; a "fluidity in the landscape, mentioned in the very first line, infects the writing and, even more, the performances, by Dean Marshall and Odena, which are just about perfect: always spontaneous but never out of control (well, Marshall may force the odd note), winning, funny, moving. Nothing sounds or feels literary," though the narrative method has its limits: the pole-axing climax lacks the inevitability it might have if we saw it rather than heard about it. But thats a very minor flaw. Yellowman is a co-production by Nightwood and Obsidian, and its the best thing I've seen from either company. Unmissable.

- That Face runs through Nov. 21; Yellowman runs through Nov. 14; both at Berkeley Street Theatre. For tickets, call 416-955-0101.

THEATRE REVIEW

AUGUST: OSAGE COUNTY

Canon Theatre, Toronto

Tracy Letts' August: Osage County has been acclaimed as the best American play of its decade. (Broadway, in defiance of statistics, throws up one of these every season.) What it actually is, at a running time of three-and-a-half hours, is a Gothic soap with pretensions.

The title, curt with rumblings of summer thunder, seems designed to bestow an ominous significance on an otherwise arbitrary sequence of family explosions. The time turns out to be irrelevant and the place hardly less so. The month is mentioned, I think, just once in the play itself, though we do gather that its very hot out and in (and the plays matriarch doesn't hold with air conditioning). Sausage County, as I can't help thinking of it, isnt name-checked at all, though the program tells us that its located in Oklahoma, about 24 minutes from Tulsa. There is some talk about the isolating nature of life on the plains, and there is one especially meretricious scene in which two of the characters get uppity and talk as if

they were some kind of metaphor for America, but mainly we have to take them for what they are.

They are the family of Beverly and Violet Weston. Beverly is a university teacher and once-acclaimed poet who spends the first scene drinking and maundering about T.S. Eliot. The acting in this touring production is generally better than that of the take-over cast I saw in New York, but I have to make an exception for Bev, who bestows a winking self-satisfied emphasis on the close of his every line. The only thing that made the scene bearable for me was knowing that at the end of it he'd be going away and not coming back. He drowns himself in the nearby river.

Violet faces widowhood through a blur, caused by galloping pill addiction. At other times, though still under the influence, she can be blisteringly clear, candid and cruel: in her own words, a truth-teller. In Estelle Parsons' performance, and indeed in Letts writing, she does this very well; Violet is a woman for whom attack is just another means of evasion, and Parsons is in total command of both the character and her carapace. Its a swinging, swingeing performance; and just to see her bounce or creep up and down the steps of a three-storey set is a treat. (The fact that she's 81 shouldn't, strictly speaking, influence our admiration, but of course it does.)

The brunt of Violets truthtelling is born by her three daughters. Oldest sister Barbara has also married a professor, and theyve brought their daughter along; Barbara's reeling bitterly from her husband's infidelity with a student. Middle sister Ivy, whos stayed home, is grabbing for what seems her last chance of happiness. Youngest sister Karen arrives for the funeral towing a thrice-wed fiance whom everybody else knows to be trouble. Theres also Violet's own down-home sister Mattie Fae, with whom she seems to have astonishingly little in common; her atypically good-natured husband Charlie; and their son, who's believed to be dim-witted and is known as Little Charlie. Big Charlie introduces us to Little Charlie in a short scene that may be the best in the play and is certainly the tenderest.

Letts can do other things as well. He can deliver melodramatic revelations when and how you least expect them. Theres one in the last act thats a humdinger: not the thing itself but the way it's sprung. He needs this talent because his method is to hop from one shock-horror episode, past or present, to another. You've had enough of Violet and her drug habit? Well, heres an older man hitting on a teenager, to take your mind off it. And, hey, how about some incest? And more unhappy marriages than you could shake a cocktail at. The trouble with all this is that it has no foundation. Theres occasional talk about Beverly's and Violet's marriage but no clear sense of what it was like; hence, no reason to care about them or, by extension, about anybody else. Maybe it is all meant to be about the locale. Or the month.

Theres humour, though less than the show or its first-night audience might like to think. Anna D. Shapiros production seems to have coarsened on the road, and to be aimed at people who think it shockingly funny to hear mature actresses using four-letter words. Most of the cast give in at some time or other; even Shannon Cochran, who otherwise dispenses a fastidious brand of swaggering self-hatred as Barbara, goes for an easy laugh at the second-act curtain. (She gets it; the public appetite for bad acting seems inexhaustible.) There's one character I haven't mentioned: a Cheyenne housekeeper (DeLanna Studi) who spends the first scene giving comfort to Beverly, the last giving it to Violet, and in between proves a very good cook and a great defender of virtue. Even the toughest American plays can wind up sentimental, and the final curtain of this one finds Violet the hitherto-untouchable curled up in the lap of the Indian (her word, though the others try to persuade her it's "Native American"). Perhaps this is a metaphor for America. Or it could just be a gimmick. - August: Osage County runs until Nov. 15. Two popular preconceptions about Newfoundland are that it's devoted to folk music and that it has a lot of bad weather. Both are reinforced from the very first moment of Rocking the Cradle. Storm clouds play on a transparent scrim curtain while, behind, the entire cast whoops it up in dance and, a little later, song.

They are celebrating the wedding of Joan and Vince, which takes place, as does the entire play, in what the program identifies as "an isolated outpost, accessible only by water." It's December, 1962. Five years later, to the month, Joan and Vince are still married but are also childless, a situation that makes them unique in their community. Joan is first philosophical about this, then puzzled, then angry and at last bitterly enraged. Vince isn't bothered. That's an understatement. He's aggressively indifferent.

Rocking the Cradle, a visiting production by the RCA Theatre Company of St. John's, is a free adaptation by Des Walsh, a Newfoundland poet and playwright, of the Spanish play Yerma by Federico Garcia Lorca, also a poet and playwright. Lorca's heroine, whose name actually means "barren," is in the same biological and sociological predicament as Walsh's, though of course she lives in a hot climate rather than a cold one. (An analogous disregard for climate change was demonstrated a few years ago by the Shaw Festival when it mounted another Lorca play, The House of Bernarda Alba, and entrusted it to a director from Poland.) The thinking seems to be that one enclosed community is as good as another. It doesn't work.

I'm not crazy about the original Yerma, either; I suspect that the exoticism (to us) of Lorca's plays may give them a freer pass than they deserve. Still, I'm willing to pay lip-service to the power of their Andalusian atmospherics, and I know that the right actress and/or director can make Yerma a study in tragic obsession to rival Phedre. But what seems single-minded and inexorable in Lorca here becomes merely repetitive. Joan has a series of meetings with her mother, who's more belligerent than understanding; and a concomitant series with a cheerful, and continually pregnant, best friend. She also conducts an inconclusive flirtation with the man she should have married, who eventually leaves for Toronto. The shrinking of the community, and its absorption into the outside world, occasionally threatens to become a sub-theme but never quite makes it. Vince himself is scarily insular; he sees no reason why Joan should even leave the house, despite his refusal to furnish her with any cause to stay inside it. Their marriage is profoundly dysfunctional, sexually and otherwise (some girl talk between Joan and her friends fills us in on some of the details); it's also dysfunctional dramatically, in that Vince doesn't appear much and says little when he does. It might be satisfying to see the situation explode, except that it all happens too suddenly. Having proceeded at an amble, the play finishes at a rush.

The writing is varied at one extreme by an occasional burst of willed metaphor and at the other by what sounds like self-parody that left me nostalgic for the Newfie newscasters on The Royal Canadian Air Farce. This reaches an extreme in the songs. All the characters except Vince (who doesn't have soul) break at the slightest provocation into folk-ballads that they seem to know off by heart. This isn't something that people often do in real life -- not even, I'll bet, in Newfoundland -- and Richard Rose's production totally fails to find a convention for it. (Rose is the artistic director of the Tarragon Theatre, which presumably explains the arrival on that house's main stage of a play underequipped for the exposure.) One of the wisest pronouncements on the theatre I've ever read states that if a production doesn't establish a style, "it automatically slithers into realism," and that's what happens here. Actors are left to sing whole songs at one another, or to react to them, as if they constituted normal dialogue. The fact that they're often out of tune may indeed be realistic, but it isn't helpful; one longs for moody accompaniment to help them through it. (It helps Lorca's plays to no end.) The odd attempt at imagistic staging misfires, too. Bolts of silk are unrolled and waved about to symbolize a storm. It's a tired device; worse than that, it doesn't connect with anything else in the production, unless you count a pervasive uncertainty about whether we're inside the house or out of it.

Ruth Lawrence begins solidly as Joan but, as the character progressively loses it, so does the actress. Darryl Avalon Hopkins is sullen as Vince, which seems to be what's required; he appears at a final Christmas party drunk and wearing a dress. If the play and production are trying here for a carnival dimension, they've left it a little late. Greg King and Didi Gil-lard-Rowlings have some charm and humour respectively. The rest are slapdash or worse.

- Rocking the Cradle plays through Dec. 13 at the Tarragon Theatre. For ticket information, call 416-531-1827.

THEATRE REVIEW

7 STORIES

BLUMA APPEL THEATRE, TORONTO

I have to confess to one tiny disappointment over 7 Stories, bred of my own mistaken expectations. I had never seen Morris Panych's 20-year-old play before, but I knew that it was about a man contemplating suicide by throwing himself off a high building; and I had assumed that the punning title meant that, as he plummeted from the seventh floor, we would see vignettes that involved the people residing on each level he passed. It seems, though, that even the Panych panache -- not to mention that of his designer Ken MacDonald and the current director Dean Paul Gibson -- wasn't up to presenting that picture of continuous precipitation intermittently frozen. And it probably wouldn't have made sense anyway.

I had also heard that this was Panych's best play; and that is something that, after seeing this exhilarating revival, I am in no mood to dispute. Its characters in fact share that seventh level, the protagonist -- known to us and the program as The Man -- teetering spectacularly on the ledge's edge, the others appearing at, naturally, seven windows, and one or two of them even joining him outside. Very few of them think to inquire what he's doing out there; they're all too preoccupied with their own lives, most of which are at least as desperate as his, even if they themselves don't realize it. At least, he knows he's unhappy; he also seems to be humane, and his humanity progressively interferes with his resolve. The first interruption comes from a man who seems intent on murdering his girlfriend, though it turns out that it's all a game and she can give as good as she gets. Next door, or next window, lives a paranoid psychiatrist in pajamas, who has no sympathy for or curiosity about his neighbours, though he deplores the noise. Even making allowances for the tromp l'oeil nature of Mac-Donald's set -- an awesomely tilting edifice surrounded by fluffy clouds -- these must be very narrow apartments.

At the opposite end lives an unsuccessful actor about to seal his vocation by marrying a rich woman under an assumed identity, which he will then have to maintain for life. Somewhere in the middle is a party that nobody's enjoying. And, by way of comparative comfort, the last person The Man encounters is a 100-year old woman, tended by an abrasive nurse who can't wait for her to die. All of which -- I don't think I'm giving much away here -- leads our hero to the conclusion that, as Dorothy Parker almost and immortally said, he might as well live.

In the age of Facebook, a 20-year-old line about a man with 940 friends, none of whom he actually likes, sounds uncannily prophetic; but of course it only puts a number on a situation that's existed ever since people started invented social gatherings. In fact the play's philosophy isn't the most original or attractive thing about it. What really counts is the tang and the snap of it all: also a sense of being plugged into a style and culture beyond Canada. Some of the opening scenes play, in Gibson's crackling production, like vintage American farce; some of the later, more whimsical ones, are positively Parisian.

The Man's urge to self-destruction comes from self-constriction; in his black suit, black shoes, black bowler (he has, he says dolefully, any number of duplicate outfits at home) he's a civil servant painted by Magritte. Everybody else in the cunningly costumed production looks very colourful, for all the good it does them. Peter Anderson, as we know from his performance in The Overcoat, is a virtuoso at physical acting; slipping and flailing in his opening moments here he looks close to landing in our laps; if we don't feel his pain, we can feel his vertigo. It's quite a shock to find that he can also talk, and do it well. His desperation comes over as more thought than felt, but I suspect that's the play.

Four actors share the other roles, all of them with guns blazing. Christopher Hunt is the most extrovert of all as, ironically, the crybaby shrink, constantly ducking beneath his lintel. Rebecca Northan is invigoratingly sharp and smart; Damien Atkins dazzles in three roles, two of them unlike any I have seen him play before. Melody A. Johnson pushes a bit too hard in her earlier incarnations; attack is not her natural mode. But she makes up for it a millionfold as the centenarian, first glimpsed bobbing enchantingly around in the recesses of her room, then emerging for an enchanting duet with Anderson that she plays with unnervingly calm assurance and with timing of almost unholy perfection. This is a very funny play, even by Panych's standards, but this scene had me literally breathless with delight. Johnson has a speech about the Louvre that's a miracle. - 7 Stories continues to Dec. 5. Call 416-368-3110 for ticket information.
