Today is the centenary of the birth of Johnny Mercer who wrote the lyrics to Come Rain or Come Shine, I'm Old Fashioned, Skylark, Too Marvelous for Words, Moon River and Jeepers Creepers. Those happen to be the six songs whose sheet-music title-pages are reproduced on the back cover of his newly-published collected lyrics, but in itself it's an arbitrary list. One could just as easily cite Blues in the Night, That Old Black Magic, One for My Baby, Autumn Leaves, Something's Gotta Give and On the Atchison, Topeka and the Santa Fe. It would probably be possible to compile another half-dozen half-dozens without exhausting the catalogue of Mercer songs that are still at least moderately well-known. Throw in all the buried treasures and coterie classics and the resulting list would cover this page. And he was only 66 when he died: in 1976, of a brain tumour.

The Complete Lyrics of Johnny Mercer (Knopf ) runs to more than 1,200 songs. It also lists 230 composing collaborators, probably a record for any lyricist. The dozen songs named above include four with music by Harold Arlen, Mercer's greatest and most compatible partner; one by Jerome Kern, the dean of American popular song; one by Hoagy Carmichael, Mercer's fellow ruralist; one each by Harry Warren and Richard Whiting, masters of the Hollywood musical; one by that johnny-come-lately, Henry Mancini; one translation from the French; and one tune composed by Mercer himself (the insouciant Something's Gotta Give, his finest effort as a melodist). He wrote, in fact, with almost everybody. If one man sums up the Golden Age of American Popular Song it's Mercer. He covered all the bases. He wrote Broadway shows, though not many of them; he originally wanted to be an actor, but the theatre wasn't his metier. Rather, he was the genius of the one-shot song; he wrote hundreds of individual pop songs. In the same vein he wrote for movies, dozens of them. He founded Capitol Records. He was deep into jazz, especially Dixieland and swing, and put witty or evocative or celebratory words to instrumentals. He was part of the big-band era, not just as a writer but as a very good singer. Indeed he was the best of all singer-songwriters, ranking with Fred Astaire and Louis Armstrong among the great vocalists who are most famous for doing something else.

A Turner Classic Movies documentary produced by Clint Eastwood and entitled Johnny Mercer: The Dream's on Me (it's on tonight) is most valuable for the clips it includes of Mercer singing and, charmingly and wittily, talking. Somebody could compile a great TV show or DVD simply by stringing together all the appearances he ever made on TV specials and just letting them roll; in the documentary they're invariably and frustratingly truncated. (It also suffers from a neurotic compulsion to illustrate everybody, no matter how fleetingly they're mentioned.) But it covers an impressive amount of ground; you see Astaire's hard-driving movie performance of One for My Baby and doubt that anybody could do the song better, then you see a youngish Sinatra sinking deep into its melancholy bravado and realize that somebody could. And it brings out the things that made Mercer an anomaly among his colleagues: his double life as a performer and the fact that he, like Carmichael, was a Southerner in a predominantly New York Jewish profession.

It leaves untouched the great paradox of his talent: that, if he hadn't been a great lyricist, he might not even have been a good one. Like his peers, he wrote mainly love songs. Unlike them, he had nothing individual to say on the subject. Cole Porter was steamily intense about love, Lorenz Hart painfully self-mocking, Ira Gershwin humorously above it all. Mercer was content to take the standard Tin Pan Alley tropes of dreams and stars and moonshine and endlessly re-shuffle them. The results should have been hack-work. In fact they were inspired. At some level, he probably believed in the sentiments, but really what he loved was words: how they sounded, what they evoked. From When the World Was Young (another of his adaptations from the French): Ah the apple trees Where at garden teas Jack o'lanterns hung. Fashions of the day Vests of applique Dresses of shantung...

"Jack o'lanterns...shantung": you feel the images on your tongue. Quoting those lines gives me special pleasure, since they're left out of the not-quite-Complete Lyrics, a handsome and invaluable volume disfigured by typos and omissions. Mercer's oeuvre is so scattered that it must have been a nightmare to collate, but they should have listened more carefully to the additions and variations in his own recordings, which hold the great truth about him: He was possessed by words.

Especially long ones that propelled rhythms and surprised with rhymes. How about, in the ironically-titled Too Marvelous for Words: "The sweetest words in Keats' and Shelley's lyrics/Aren't sweet enough to be your panegyrics." Mercer was once asked if he and his contemporaries hadn't been in a rut, constantly reworking the one theme of romantic love. He replied "I think we were in a rut, but ours was a more attractive rut." He was right on both counts.

Still there are times when one wishes he would escape the temptation to turn every song into a love-song, as in Whistling Away the Dark where the initial detailed image of a frightened child on his way home from school turns out to be a metaphor for lonely lovers.

It does though exemplify a recurring theme in Mercer's work, one that obviously was personal, and connected to his Georgia roots: a nostalgia -sometimes tender, sometimes scary -for half-remembered childhood things. Its apotheosis of course is Moon River, a song whose familiarity (plus some sugary arrangements) has obscured how brilliant it really is: not just the famous "huckleberry friend" line but the gentle "there's such a lot of world to see", words that linger, implying more than they say.

There's mystery, though never obscurity, in many of his best songs; in One for My Baby, we never discover what the heartbroken drinker's story really is, and we don't need to. Mercer himself was by all accounts a mean drunk, though irreproachably kind and courteous when sober.

The sadness that surfaces in his later lyrics also illuminates his later singing; as a young man he'd limited himself to rhythm and comedy songs (he could be very funny, both as writer and performer) but in the 1970s he trusted himself with ballads, which he sang with a mellow wistfulness that was very moving. What a legacy. What a man.

Jean-Paul Sartre's Huis Clos is a great image masquerading as a great play. It's been that way for 60 years now. It shows us three dead people condemned to spend eternity in one another's company, an inferno that has no need of fire, or of whips and thumbscrews. Its world-famous conclusion is "hell is other people." (Well, if you put it like that, yes.) The untranslatable title -- it refers to the vacation period when all the French law-courts are closed -- is most commonly rendered in English as No Exit, and that's the label on the version brought to Toronto by Nightwood Theatre as part of its 4x4 female directors' season. Other adaptations have used other, equally apposite names: Vicious Circle is one, and another is In Camera, which if it were adopted by Kim Collier's production, would count as a wonderful adventitious pun. As Collier has staged it, the play's a movie.

Her "live-cinematic interpretation of Sartre's play" comes to us from The Virtual Stage & Electric Company in Vancouver, to whom welcome. Visually, it's stunning. The bulk of the play is projected on a wide cinema screen, split three ways. Within each, the camera angles keep changing. In front of the screen, on what is customarily known as the stage, is a set representing the lobby of an ancient hotel, piled with the debris of former glamour. This is the domain of the play's fourth character, the hotel valet who escorts the deceased to their new permanent residence. We see him at the start, pushing and pulling the first arrival to a place he has no desire to go. He's finally deposited, as later are his companions, in a side room, where they're left to get on with their acting. All we, the audience, can see of the room is what the cameras choose to show us (though we are allowed to inspect it afterwards, occasioning much impressed head-shaking at the ingenuity of it all). What we see has the look of film, but it's being created as we watch by people in the same building. The movie's a play.

There are two principal devices at work in this production, one technical, the other textual; and the technical is far the stronger. The textual concerns the valet, who's now present throughout, keeping mainly in his own domain, and who has new lines that the actor, Jonathon Young, has written himself. We gather that he doesn't much like his job; he makes constant phone calls to his uncle (who may be God or the Devil or whoever) asking when this damnation business is going to end. Meanwhile, he amuses himself by climbing on furniture, mocking the gestures and attitudes of his captives, holding up placards to involve the audience in the game, and generally carrying on like the master of ceremonies in Cabaret. This is diverting to begin with, but it gets monotonous very fast.

The three lost souls are far more compelling. They are Cradeau, a supposedly fearless crusading journalist whose past as a Nazi collaborator isn't even the most damnable thing about him; Inez, a lesbian secretary; and Estelle, rapacious high-society blond. They have, they come to realize, been specially selected to get on one another's nerves. Inez, an expert at detecting weak spots, taunts Cradeau incessantly for his cowardice, the one thing he can't bear to admit. (He cares extravagantly what other people think about him, and the management has thoughtfully provided him with a video link to the conversations of his surviving colleagues.) Estelle, desperate for admiration, tries to seduce Cradeau, who would be happy to oblige but can't with Inez watching. And she can't be disposed of. The damned in Sartre still have bodies and bodily desires, but they cannot be killed. That's been done already.

Probably, given enough time, any three people could torment each other as effectively, but the devils at the end of the phone seem to want quick results. It does mean though that, dramatically speaking, there is something arbitrary about the whole set-up, reinforced by Sartre's inability to bring his dead characters to life. There's nothing especially compelling about their earthly biographies, or about how they're revealed to us, and the ways in which they torture one another are surprisingly limited. But if the play can't develop its conception, except to a pre-ordained philosophic conclusion, the conception itself is genius. And it's in illustrating it, drilling into it, that Collier's production is at its strongest. We are watching the actors, most of the time, in giant unforgiving close-up, and they respond with performances that are ingrained and unflinching. Andy Thompson's vulpine Cradeau tends to generalize, but the women are fiercely specific, Laara Sadiq's bruised incisiveness as Inez balancing the elegant meltdown of Lucia Frangione's Estelle. The triple screen isolates them, and accentuates the moments when one crosses into another's territory. Just occasionally an aerial surveillance shot shows us the whole room, an oppressively ornate Second Empire chamber, with heavy ornaments that can't be lifted and a door that mostly won't open (and when it does, doesn't lead anywhere you'd dare to go). Hell is also other furniture; and the sight of the three of them marooned there is far more powerful than in the sustained long-shot of a conventional staging. See them in hell. - No Exit closes tonight at Buddies in Bad Times Theatre. For ticket information, call 416-955-0101.

2009-11-23-the-versions-mary:
THEATRE REVIEW

THE MADONNA PAINTER

Factory Theatre, Toronto

Michel Marc Bouchard's The Madonna Painter is the latest carrier of a virulent strain of drama originating in Quebec. If that image is over the top, so is the play. It also seems apt since the play is set during a flu epidemic, though the topicality of that is of course fortuitous; in its French version, the play has been around since 2002. Previous prize-winning incubators of the genre are Woujdi Mouawad's Scorched and Bouchard's own The Coronation Voyage, plays in which the author takes a metaphor and beats us over the head with it. They all give us drama aspiring to the condition of fable, which sounds all right except that what we actually get is attitude and gesture, devoid of human content.

All these plays have their moments, and The Madonna Painter begins with three of them. We are in an isolated Quebec village in the last days of the First World War. Peace is on the way and so is the flu -- the dreaded Spanish variety. To ward it off, the new young parish priest envisions a fresco for his church, a Madonna triptych; his reasoning may seem peculiar but we can at least believe in his bright-eyed idealism, as reflected in an opening monologue.

After this we meet some of the local young women, all of whom, as is customary in Catholic communities or at least in plays about Catholic communities, are named Mary. Mary Louise is a laundry maid who can tell, by examining sheets, everything about the people who've been sleeping in them and who delivers a vivid speech about it. Mary Frances and Mary Anne are taking a walk when they see a naked man emerging from a stream. At least Mary Frances sees him; Mary Anne, who's never seen a naked man, closes her eyes while Mary Frances describes a terrible shape-changing monster. It's an amusing scene -- the only bit of fluent interaction in the play -- but Mary Anne, incredibly, goes through the rest of the play disabused of her mistake. Because her author needs her to. She projects her obsession onto the priest, whom she guiltily fancies, with horrific results. Most of the characters, in fact, are obsessives, which is a good way of writing farce. Bouchard does write the odd intentionally funny line (there's a real roof-raiser about a pregnant Madonna) but his mind is generally on higher things.

With financial input from the town doctor, a sardonic fellow who looks on people as incipient corpses, the priest engages a painter, an Italian. All the Maries in town line up to be his model; for some unexplained reason they recite for him, as if they were auditioning for a play. He chooses Mary of the Secrets, so named because she's been poaching on the preserves of both doctor and priest by ministering to the dying and hearing their unauthorized confessions. The painter seduces her (an event that does not go undetected by Mary the Sheet-Sniffer) and, just like an artist, tires of her soon after, with consequences for her life and his work.

There's a coupling scene in which one partner climaxes while feverishly reciting previous life experiences. It's true of course that people having sex aren't always concentrating on the person they're having it with, but I didn't believe that I was being told anything truthful about this character in this situation. I merely heard a playwright trying very hard for an effect. I didn't believe there was or had been a war on, however far away, or that these people had been touched by it. I didn't believe in the flu, even when one of the inhabitants caught and died of it. It's all words, words, words.

The style's side effects include recurrent outbreaks of whiny or rhetorical acting. In Eda Holmes' production, only two actors are immune. One is Juan Chioran, who as the painter is required to speak Italian and to sing, both of which he does with great melodiousness, but who is equally cool and commanding when talking in English. The other, in a tougher part and with less experience to draw on, is Marc Bendavid whose troubled, passionate naivete as the priest is the evening's driving force, He doesn't bring off the end when, having suffered a dire transformation, he has to persuade us that something has actually happened, but I doubt if anyone could. The normally luminous Jenny Young is bafflingly uneven as Mary of the Secrets, sometimes in command, sometimes just shouting. As the physician, Brian Dooley hardly gets beyond gruff rudeness, though I think he's meant to be a cynical teller of unwelcome truths. Nicola Correia-Damude begins arrestingly as Mary of the Sheets, but then finds nowhere to go; ditto Miranda Edwards' Mary Frances who gets very sulky. As the deluded Mary Anne, a key role judging from her position in the curtain call, Shannon Taylor has some piercing moments but mostly picks her way through her words as if they were a minefield. If I haven't engaged with the play's deeper themes (faith, art, etc.) that's because I can't detect where they are. And to be honest, I don't care. - The Madonna Painter runs until Dec. 13. Call 416-504-4060 or visit factorytheatre.cafor tickets and information. robert.cushman@hotmail.com

MY MOTHERS LESBIAN JEWISH WICCAN WEDDING

Panasonic Theatre

THE PRINCESS AND THE HANDMAIDEN

Lorraine Kimsa Theatre for Young People ---

Following Menopause Out Loud into the Panasonic, My Mothers Lesbian Jewish Wiccan Wedding, though a dozen times the better show, is drawing and pleasing the crowds for very much the same reason. It allows its audiences to rejoice collectively in the acceptance of subjects previously considered unmentionable. In the new show, the hot topic is of course gay marriage and its legalization, and we all get to feel happily enlightened. That's a good thing, by the way.

My Mother's etc., a transferred hit from the Toronto Fringe, is a musical written by David Hein and his wife, Irene Carl Sankoff. They both appear in it, Hein leading the band and apparently playing himself. This is the story, suitably adorned, of him and his own mother. When we first meet them, in 1990, mom, whose name is Claire, is a divorced Saskatchewan psychologist about to move to Ottawa; David initially stays behind with his dad, another shrink. (He blames or credits this upbringing for his having grown up to write musicals.) Claire meets her first same-sex lover and decides its for life; she comes out to David, whos cool with it. And since theirs is the show's central relationship, the story, about a third of the way through the evening, is over; all the rest is anecdote.

To put it another way, the first three words of the title are the important ones. If you thought the remainder sounded catchpenny-cute, you were right. The Jewishness is Claire's; she embraces it late in the proceedings, too late for it to contribute anything. The Wiccan is her partner Jane, whose beliefs are depicted at greater length but in hardly more depth. The wedding takes up only a little time at the end because it isnt that kind of schmaltzy show. Its another kind of schmaltzy show.

The cast is good, with Hein a charmingly casual actor-singer-narrator and Lisa Horner's Claire smart and vulnerable, like a singing Edie Falco. They get a real glow going. Andrew Lamb's direction neatly fills the space but not the time, which of course has expanded since the Fringe. (And by many accounts, it was stretched even there.) Heins lyrics have self-fulfilling titles like Oh! My Moms a Lesbian! and Never Take Your Lesbian Moms to Hooters; and his countryfied music doesn't spring many surprises either.

Which makes it a marked contrast to Leslie Arden's score for The Princess and the Handmaiden, whose melodies and harmonies stimulate, beguile and delight from the very first bars.

Not for the first time, the Lorraine Kimsa Theatre for Young People offers the most grown-up musical in Toronto, without being in any way above the heads of its target audience. (This is officially rated as from 5 to 16, but the receptive house I saw it with was very much skewed to the lower end of that demographic.)

The Princess of the title is sent by her miracle-doctor mother to cure the illness of a neighbouring king; with her, not too willingly, goes the Handmaiden whom she has been patronizing and maybe exploiting for years. Halfway through the obligatory forest, the Handmaiden appropriates the Princesss clothes, horse, magic medicine and even more magical lucky charm, and rides off to impersonate her. The Princess is left to her fate, which turns out to be a kind but crippled young shepherd. The musicals source is The Goose Girl, by the Brothers Grimm; this adaptation doesn't have geese, but there is a chorus of sheep who baa in Scots accents.

Arden wrote the book as well as the score, and she moves from speech to song and back again with exemplary ease. Her lyrics, though better than most people's, are a notch below her music, and one number gets bogged down in exposition that might be better handled by dialogue. (Every one of her shows seems to contain one song that doesnt belong.)

A graver flaw is that both the Princesss high-handedness and the Handmaiden's grievances and misgivings are underwritten; they are unalterably heroine and villainess, in accordance with the ancient class-prejudices of fairyland. But the show touches the deep narrative and emotional chords that are only reachable through fairy tale, from King Lear to Into the Woods. The latter is an obvious reference for Arden, whose music has a richness and astringency that recall Sondheim without sounding derivative. She also throws in a devastating parody of the I Dreamed a Dream theatrical power-ballad; it's called This Is Your Destiny with destiny turning out to be an appropriately, and literally, cardboard Prince. Allen MacInniss production captures all the wit and charm of the writing, and the cast is so uniformly fine that the simplest thing is just to list them: Regan Thiel (a magical Princess), Tracy Michailidis (a tart Handmaiden), Jonathan Tan (a sweet shepherd), Sharron Matthews (a crisp and disciplined Narrator), George Masswohl, Karen Wood, Susan Henley, Andrew Stelmack, Larry Manell and Julain Molnar. Arden has written a musical based on Much Ado About Nothing. Its time we saw it.

- My Mother's Lesbian Jewish Wiccan Wedding opened Nov. 7 and runs until Jan. 3, 2010. Call 416-872-1212 for tickets and information. The Princess and the Handmaiden runs through Dec. 30. Call 416-822-2222 for tickets and information.

2009-11-27-in-the-company-of-the-world-s:
STUFF HAPPENS

Royal Alexandra Theatre, Toronto

---

Studio 180's production of Stuff Happens survives transfer to the big house with impact intact, force and lucidity undiminished. There are two major cast changes, both with a clarifying effect. Michael Healey plays George W. Bush, going easy on the impersonator mannerisms while supplying a few of his own, mainly in the sphere of dangerous thick-browed affability. Healey's Bush, infuriatingly if courteously opaque to all who have to deal with him, emerges here as shrewder and more controlling than his predecessor's: an expert at letting himself be talked into courses on which he's already decided while neutering opposition. Whatever else he may be, this Dubya's no fool.

Karen Robinson's Condoleeza Rice is a complementary study in deviousness, hard-shelled as well as hard-centred, putting up walls where her boss prefers to smile deceptively through windows. Robinson has a megaphonic delivery that can sometimes be disconcerting, but her impersonality -- a kind of loud self-effacement -- explains why her opponents and questioners never stand a chance. She is her job; and they can't get through that.

David Hare's play traces the build-up to the Iraq War, from 9/11 to the parachuted president's premature announcement of victory, with some pungent last words on how wrong things have gone since. The focus is mainly on the U.S. inner circle, with side-trips to the UN and to a harried Tony Blair and team in London. I'm one of those who believes Hare to be more naturally a journalist than a playwright, but a journalist with a strong sense of theatrical effect. So this play, in which history supplies the plot and he supplies (most of ) the dialogue, finds him on his strongest ground. He supplies an immense amount of information, at high but digestible speed, while shaping a gripping and persuasive main action that's mainly a series of cabinet battles, official and otherwise. Joel Greenberg's staging is a shifting parade of suits in chairs. The chairs are the office kind, on wheels. They can be arrayed in triple formation to suggest a press briefing at the White House, then turned in an instant to face across the Atlantic for question time in the House of Commons.

The play's good guy, or its nearest equivalent, is Colin Powell, who goes through the action feeling the ground slipping beneath his feet while trying to persuade himself that it isn't. The sense of his arguments sometimes get swamped, in Nigel Shawn Williams' performance, by undirected emotion. But he presents a powerful, sympathetic figure whose final volte-face is almost comprehensible; he's been ground down. Andrew Gillies offers an equally winning, and more controlled, Tony Blair, a blend of career politician and career pedant. (As vocal impersonation, his performance is rather flattering.) I'd remembered the attack dogs, Donald Rumsfeld and Dick Cheney, as having more stage time than they actually do: a tribute to them that they make such vivid impressions so quickly. David Fox's Rumsfeld moves and speaks in snake-like parabolas, pulling out paradoxes like a triumphant professor. Hardee T. Lineham's Cheney, by contrast, is a blunt instrument, leading with his bullet head. The supporting roles include a memorably imperturbable Hans Blix from Guy Bannerman.

As before, I was much struck by the last speech, spoken by an Iraqi exile (Sam Kalileh), which has the effect of turning the rest of the play on its head. His is virtually the only voice we hear from the land that everyone else has merely been talking about, and what he offers is a lament for a country crucified (his word) both by its rulers and by the invaders. It balances an introductory tirade from an American journalist (Paul Essiembre) who says, if I may recycle my earlier review, that a dictator was removed, and that arguing about the character and motives of those who removed him -- which is what the play itself proceeds to do -- is moralizing self-indulgence. These two speeches, from opposite political perspectives, cast an ironic light on what goes between them that must have been intended, but not perhaps in quite the way that it actually plays out. There's a sense in which the play ends just when it's getting really interesting; and events since last March when this production first appeared, let alone since 2004 when the play opened in London, have distanced it still further. It's a history play now in more ways than one. But the history's exciting, and its consequences aren't going away.

- Stuff Happens opened Nov. 14 and runs until Dec. 23. Call 416-872-1212 or visit mirvish.comfor tickets and information.

2009-11-28-we-d-go-mad-too-if-we-were-in:
Gord Rand's Hamlet doesnt merely contemplate suicide in "to be or not to be"; he also, which may be a first, has a crack at committing it. Halfway through the speech he puts a plastic bag on his head, fastens it with duct-tape, and awaits asphyxiation. He pulls out of course -- of the bag and the deed--and resumes soliloquizing. I think it would make more sense if hed defied the rule against self-slaughter before saying perchance to dream instead of just after, but in all other respects he gets away with it. The speech has been re-positioned to show us Hamlet at his lowest ebb; it comes, in this production, just after he's mistakenly killed Polonius, been roughed up by the king and banished to England, and is only wearing underpants. And it looks as if he's had to be forced into putting those on, having spent some time daubing his naked body with his victims blood. Most Hamlets show some passing remorse at having murdered the wrong man. Not this one.

As well as changing the running order, Necessary Angels production has cut about half of the received text of Hamlet and made what remains as bleak and violent as possible. If that makes it sound cheap, it isn't. In its way it's as exciting and compelling as last years landmark production at Stratford, though its way isnt as satisfying. It also doesn't quite square with the declared intention of its Scottish director, Graham McLaren, of giving his actors, and hence his audience, as much freedom as possible. Like such gifted British directors as Mike Alfreds and Jason Byrne, he doesn't impose blocking; the actors can wander off and on as the mood and the situation take them. But that freedom must be limited when exercised within a frame as rigid as the one McLaren has provided. The cuts and transpositions make a statement in themselves; so does the set (designed by the director), which is one room, containing a table strewn with the remains of a banquet at which the main drink seems to have been Coke, plus some cheap if versatile chairs. "Thrift, thrift, Horatio," says Hamlet of the rapid transition from his fathers funeral to his mothers wedding, and he's so right. From the look of things, this royal family can't even afford help. Also, the show must have settled on a tone quite early on, since for months the press department has been sending out releases about how its seething with amorality. Im not sure what that means, or why it's supposed to be such a good thing, and I don't think its true of the characters, most of whom have moral codes, even if they transgress them. But its probably reflected in the production's rule of behaviour, which seems to be:When in doubt, hit someone.

So, why's it good? Its good in the basic way that any Shakespeare production needs to be; with a creme-de-la-creme cast, it makes compelling sense of the words and forges strong and complex relationships through them. Besides this, it has an identity, consistent and inventive. Much is startling but little feels imposed, at least until the end. The Hamlet we know is four acts of cat-and-mouse plus one of mayhem, and youd think this production's temper would best suit the latter, but it doesn't work out that way. That fifth act has a lot of plotting, indeed a lot of plot, and the show has to slow awkwardly down to accommodate it. Also, it has to cheat on its location convention, with Ophelia implausibly buried in the dining hall. The lack of a graveyard (alas, poor Yorick; hes gone, Horatio) hobbles Rands Hamlet who's denied his new philosophic self, but still has to act as if it existed.

His is still a fine searching performance, from one of the least pin-downable actors I know: I always admire him and never recognize him. He must be well past his twenties, but he's still totally convincing as a lean teasing punk of a prince, intellectually mature, emotionally at ground zero. This version starts with the "solid flesh" soliloquy, and Rand explores every nihilistic nuance of it. Later, he suffers, teases and taunts. "I did love you once" he tells Tara Nicodemos eager-to-please Ophelia, brutally; no wonder she goes mad. All right, maybe he is amoral. Benedict Campbells Claudius isn't; he's a dangerous, haunted ruler who surprises himself in the prayer scene. Laura de Carterets Gertrude catches the destructive balance between concerned mother and besotted wife; she dons a Marilyn Monroe wig and Claudius a gorilla mask to play adult (so to speak) games under the table. Eric Petersons Polonius is short-breathed for Shakespeare, but still furnishes a highly original Polonius, a Peeping Tom sadist at home and an officious sycophant at court. Then there are Steven McCarthy's limping scholar Horatio, Christopher Morris's fire-breathing Laertes, Robert Persichini's self-pitying Ghost and orotund Player, and -- in the new portmanteau role of Guildencrantz (as opposed to Rosenstern) -- Gray Powell, who for once suggests a previous warm relationship with Hamlet that gets shattered on the rocks of Elsinore. Tom Stoppard would be proud of him.

- Hamlet closes tomorrow at the Enwave Theatre, Queens Quay. Call 416-973-4000 for details.

2009-12-04-saved-by-the-accents-beatles-:
They looked so innoc ent back in 1962. Well, maybe not innocent, but fresh and fly and unspoiled. They sat politely around tables, drank cups of tea, smoked cigarettes (everyone did then) and -- at least when posing for the press -- wore jackets and ties. So did George Martin, their studio producer, the universally acknowledged fifth Beatle. Martin was still wearing a tie seven years later at the time of Abbey Road, (the album not the studio), while John, Paul, Ringo and the other George had progressed through the fashions of Carnaby Street, Haight-Ashbury, India and showbiz plutocracy.

Martin remained the school teacher, in appearance and in role, teased and respected by the smart boys in the class. "I thought they were nice boys" he says guardedly of his first encounters with them."

"I don't think he was that convinced about our musical ability" says one of the nice boys, probably John, "but he liked the way we had about us." Didn't we all.

These quotes are taken from The Beatles on Record, a documentary that purports to be "an intimate glimpse of the creative process behind their musical masterpieces" but is in fact a glorified promo for the new re-mastered versions of the original albums. It's "narrated entirely by John Lennon, Paul McCartney, George Harrison, Ringo Starr and Sir George Martin." This turns out to mean that bits from pre-existing interviews have been cobbled together to make a commentary track. Occasionally -- very occasionally -- someone talks to camera. John Lennon even gets name-checked by a caption. Otherwise, you're on your own as to which of them is talking and, especially early on, it can get very confusing. According to the publicity, the narrative "features never-before-heard outtakes of studio chat from the band's first recording sessions at the infamous Abbey Road studios." I'm not sure what those studios have done to deserve their infamy; most likely, this is yet another example of someone thinking the word means the precise opposite of its actual meaning. As for the studio chat ( "George is tuning up!") one tries one's best to pretend that it's scintillating or revealing or both, but if it wasn't for the Liverpool accents, it would be neither.

Visually, the show consists mainly of footage of the boys in studio, or purportedly in studio, much of it stills. And we do get to hear snatches of most of the songs, from Love Me Do all the way through to The End.

Still, there's some charm and there's nostalgia value. Where it comes will depend on your age and your perspective. For me -- more now than at the time -- the magical Beatle years were the first ones. The first records came out when I was in my last years at high school in London, when we were delighted to hear a pop group who sang as well as played. After Please Please Me, their second single and first monster hit, and the LP that was named after it, theirs became the only records you ever heard at parties, displacing those of Buddy Holly.

I always felt the Beatles' finest moment was John's remark when they played at the Royal Variety Performance: "Those of you upstairs, applaud; the rest, rattle your jewellery." It wasn't exactly revolutionary, but it was subversive: of the canons of showbusiness as much as of society. It's hard to imagine an American performer saying anything like that in the White House, or in the even more sacred precincts of the Academy Awards. It was in fact pure music-hall.

The Beatles' initial musical energy may have been borrowed American, but their joint personality was pure British. No wonder they went on to conquer America; the Yanks could never have heard a combination at once so refreshingly familiar and so devastatingly strange. (And still, at that stage, cuddly.)

Back home, once the first patriotic thrill had worn off, we began to feel that we'd lost them. Still, as the '60s progressed and became "the '60s," it was impossible, however much or little of a fan you were, not to feel simply glad the Beatles existed. And their breakup, however much it may have been heralded, was a real shock. They seemed, as an entity, so providentially well-matched and well-rounded. You knew that, individually, they were never going to amount to anything as good. And you were right.

The Beatles on Record can't help capturing some of all that, except for the last part; it all but ignores internecine tensions and it stops when the group does. It does contain some nuggets, some less familiar than others. There's what amounts to an early music video for I Feel Fine: John, Paul and George on guitars and Ringo on exercise bike. There's John, soon after that, saying that "We'd never heard of anything in rock 'n' roll lasting more than two years" and George expressing a modest hope that they'd survive for four. There's Paul saying they quit touring because, "We can't develop where no one can hear us." There's John saying, mercifully, that I Am the Walrus was "not that serious."

And most of all there's the unflappable Martin, who's really this program's central figure, patiently insisting on re-takes while admitting that by Revolver " They'd started telling me what they'd want." In the interests of musical communication he learned to play the guitar while they learned piano, and "they learned to play the piano better than I got to play the guitar." After what he plainly regards as the disastrous self-indulgence of Let It Be, he was surprised to get a call from Paul saying, "We're going to do another record -- do you want to produce it?" Martin said, "Only if you let me produce it." Which they did; and so all five came back, literally and figuratively, to Abbey Road. It made a nice ending. It still does.

- The Beatles on Record airs tonight on CTV at 10 p.m.

2009-12-05-fated-lovers-in-aisle-three-c:
For Parfumerie, Ken MacDonald has designed the most appetizing set ever to adorn a Soulpepper production. It's scrumptious -- truly scrumptious, in fact. Its also businesslike, giving its actors space to manoeuvre and a helpful, believable environment in which to exist. This suits, since Parfumerie is set in a shop, one that mainly dispenses beauty products; and though it is most obviously a romantic comedy, its as much concerned with the day-to-day survival of the store as with the affairs of its employees' hearts. It's sweet, but with a tang.

Morris Panychs witty and charming production is the theatrical definition of a gift that keeps on giving. This, as it happens, is something that Miklos Laszlos play seems to have been doing since its Budapest premiere in 1937. Its author moved to America the following year, making him one among what have been called Hollywood's resident Hungarians." The play, though neglected in its original form, has given birth to two movies ( The Shop around the Corner, You've Got Mail), one musical ( She Loves Me) and one movie musical ( In the Good Old Summertime). Finally, we get to see the play itself, which in this English version by Adam Pettle and Brenda Robins, turns out to be as good as any of its derivatives and better than some.

Its the old Much Ado About Nothing story of two people who are obviously destined to be together but in the meantime cant stand one another. This time they're clerks in the store. He is George, very organized and snippy about it, and she's Rosie, disorganized and defensive about it, hence equally snippy. Both are lonely; both, for more than a year, have been engaged in passionate correspondence with an admirer they intend soon to meet. This, of course, is the old device that Youve Got Mail found to be electronically new again. Its greatly to the author's credit that he doesn't play it for any more suspense than its worth; we guess the truth early on, only a moment before he reveals it. George guesses it, too; and some of the plays delight comes from his attempts to juggle his own knowledge and remorse with Rosie's lack of them.

Part of the cunning is that, for a considerable time, the subordinates' story is itself subordinated to that of their boss. Mr. Hammerschmidt, a hitherto benevolent dictator, is tormented by the ( justified) suspicion that his wife is unfaithful. So he takes it out on his staff, and Joseph Zieglers biting fury at this point, as of a Scrooge whos regressed, is a wonderfully smouldering display. It's all show of course; and Ziegler, with a great actor's ability to convey volumes in a moment, can break your heart with the way he walks towards a telephone, girding himself for bad news. This good father -- which is what old man Hammerschmidt turns out metaphorically to be -- is a performance to rank with his bad dad in A Whistle in the Dark.

His drama reaches an early peak, but continues as a ground bass to the duet of Oliver Dennis and Patricia Fagan as the mail-matched lovers, neither of them glamourizing or sentimentalizing their characters but each becoming more endearing by the moment. Its an interesting counterpoint, Dennis agonizing as Fagan melts. Their final moment of mutual recognition is a beautiful contrivance, the more satisfying because of the transparency with which its engineered.

If I wanted to hunt for faults, I could say that Michael Simpson's anxious senior clerk, who never saw a troubled water he didn't want to oil, could afford a little variation in his harried benevolence; and that Jeff Lillicos ultra-keen messenger boy could tone down some of his exuberance, especially after he too gets a chance to boss someone around. But these are minor blemishes on performances that bring their characters to vibrant life. Lillico vibrates with especial virtuosity, and his development as Zieglers surrogate son is one of the show's treats. Kevin Bundy delivers a suave outline of the establishment's resident cad and Maev Beaty an entertaining one of its aspiring flirt, both roles that get abruptly cut off when apparently approaching their prime. She Loves Me did rather better by them by giving each a showpiece farewell number; in general though, one of the joys of encountering the play lies in discovering how closely the musical, which is one of the best, clings to its source, and how right that was. Several of the staff double as customers, a role in which Beaty is especially sharp. The retail routine hums with life, and also with taste; Panychs staging has all of his choreographic inventiveness and none of his excess. It also has a lovely tone; I never knew he had such beatitude in him, though, on reflection, I should have guessed. Brenda Robins plays the stores cashier, who appears to be keeping an eagle eye from behind her register on both the day's takings and her own script, and William Webster turns up in three roles, among them a solicitous private detective who, after destroying his employer's happiness, does everything but wish him a merry Christmas. I should have said that the play takes place during the holiday build-up, thereby adding to the stresses on all concerned. And of course, if Soulpepper is looking for an ideal alternative to its bi-annual revival of A Christmas Carol, here it is.

- Parfumerie runs through Dec. 24 at the Young Centre. Call 416-866-8666 for showtimes and ticket information.

2009-12-07-the-celebrity-spin:
THEATRE REVIEW

ORSONS SHADOW

Theatre Passe Muraille, Toronto

In 1960, Laurence Olivier appeared at the Royal Court Theatre in London in Rhinoceros, a play by Eugene Ionesco, directed by Orson Welles. Hows that for a lineup. Add to it that Olivier's leading lady was Joan Plowright, his imminently future wife. This confluence of personalities is the subject of Orson's Shadow, a play by Austin Pendleton who is, in rough order of distinction, an American actor, director and playwright.

Ive an interest to declare. I could be the only person in this plays Toronto audience who saw that production of Rhinoceros, though not at the Court; I caught the subsequent West End run, with Plowright's role taken over by the then-lesser-known Maggie Smith. It was the first time I ever saw Olivier onstage, and the main thing I remember of his performance is its beguiling and, I later discovered, atypical unassumingness; he was playing a shy man and didn't care who knew it. Of Welles production I remember little, though I recall that it was widely criticized for being tricksy and heavy-handed. So I have my own reasons for finding Orsons Shadow fascinating. I imagine, though, that my fascination will be shared by any who have heard of and care about these people, though even they will have to make allowances. This is a play by the stage-struck for the stagestruck, and there are some odd things about it, starting with the title.

I don't know what it means. Is Orson's shadow Welles himself, who at this stage was widely held to be the mere ghost of the boy-genius who directed Citizen Kane? Not corporeally of course; when we first meet this plays Welles, hes just come offstage from playing Falstaff, without padding. Is everyone in the play meant to be in Orson's shadow? That doesn't make sense, since he isnt the central figure; nobody is. Maybe its meant to refer to the remaining leading character, who is Kenneth Tynan, British theatre critic, master stylist and hero-worshipper. Probably his two greatest heroes were Welles and Olivier, and this play presents Tynan as the catalyst who made this production possible. In the first scene, he visits Welles in a Dublin theatre and nervously castigates him for wasting his talents on a cobbled version of Shakespeare. (It's Chimes at Midnight, the compressed Henry IV that afterward became Welles' last near-masterpiece of a movie.) Tynan mentions that Olivier is looking for a director for Rhinoceros, and offers to suggest Welles. Welles, who has issues with Olivier, grudgingly agrees. So off hops Tynan to London, to make the proposition which Olivier, equally grudgingly and insecurely, accepts, with some prompting from the soon-to-be Lady Olivier. Tynan has his own agenda; he wants to be Oliviers dramaturg when Olivier becomes director of the new National Theatre.

Little of this holds water historically. In 1959, when these conversations are set, the National was four years in the future; nobody knew who its director would be or even if it would happen. Tynan did indeed buck for, and obtained, the National Theatre job but not until 1962, immediately after giving Olivier a notoriously bad review. He would have had nothing to do with setting up Rhinceros, a play he disliked; he already knew Olivier and his previous crazy-but-beautiful wife Vivien Leigh quite well, though the play presents him as a stuttering stranger to them; and he certainly wouldnt have hung around rehearsals as he does here. If he had done that, he wouldn't have reviewed the show, which he later did; like me, he saw the transfer. He defended Welles, said Olivier was great but wasting his time, and panned the play, condemning its satire on all varieties of conformity for not being politically specific enough. Tynan was the greatest of theatre critics, but sometimes he wore blinkers.

Does all this matter? It does because the play depends on celebrity appeal; it works in quotes and anecdotes from all over its characters' lives, but even at the level of gossip it ought to get its facts right. Its not as if theres any universal meaning here. I suppose the play may be said to be about self-destructiveness, with Welles eating and Tynan smoking

their respective ways to premature death. But that doesn't wash for Olivier, who may eventually have been laid low by his workload at the National but is here presented as a survivor, feigning humility but afraid only of his not-quite-ex wife.

Pendleton knows, though, what makes theatre and theatricals tick; and if his two set-up scenes drag a bit, the rehearsal that makes up the second act has a persuasive swing and crackle that Rona Waddington's production captures very well. The performances start from accurate impersonation and move outwards. Steve Ross Welles is physically and vocally massive, with a quicksilver turn of wit. As Tynan, Christopher Stanton hints at the brilliance while capturing the insecurity that can nag at a man in the presence of those he most admires. Paul Eves Olivier is maybe the cleverest, an obsequious pussycat in the face of his genius director but knowing exactly how to work any room. (He tells Tynan he can have the dramaturg job but only on the undertstanding that every recommendation he makes will be disregarded. Legend has it that that is what actually happened.) Janet Porter, though she makes no attempt at Plowright's throaty north-country accent, makes her a warm and supportive presence, and Geoff Scovell is perky as Welles' apocryphal Irish assistant who surprisingly gets away with calling Olivier Larry. The only false note comes from Camilla Scott, who plays Vivien Leigh as just any old West Ender isnstead of what she was: an exotically unplaceable wits ender.

- Orsons Shadow runs until Dec. 12. Call 416-504-7529 for tickets and information.

Ross Petty and his gang should immediately be put in charge of all TV commercials. Twice in Robin Hood, this year's Petty "family musical," as its creators describe it -- or pantomime, as the rest of us describe it -- a screen is lowered, and the show treats us to a few words from or about its sponsors. Each has its product lauded in a brief film clip, performed by the stage cast in their stage characters, and each so funny and so well-done that one quite forgets that it's an advertisement. I especially enjoyed the plug for Tim Hortons, which involves Jessica Holmes as the Queen of the Forest and Dan Chameroy as someone called Nurse Plumbum, stirring up viciously competitive toil and trouble over their double-doubles.

Now, of course not every theatre can give thanks for corporate help in this unbuttoned manner, though it might be fun if one or two of them did. The far-from-unspoken rule of a panto is that anything goes, and the ads are just the most blatant example of the ways in which Robin Hood pokes holes in the story it is theoretically telling.

They are also, I am inclined to think, the most enjoyable; their outrageousness is thoroughbred. Some of the rest comes off a bit apologetic. This Robin Hood is a reasonably entertaining entertainment, but it isn't one of the team's best. (As far as I remember -- and they do tend to blur together in the mind -- it's less good than the last one with this title.) Unlike, say, Cinderella, Robin Hood doesn't have a single recognizable story for a comedy writer to bounce off. He's just a cluster of legends, with a few permanent signposts. One of these, of course, is Maid Marian, of whom Chris Earle's script takes a revisionist view. She's a bossy environmentalist, bent on preserving Sherwood Forest from despoilers, while misguidedly respectful of her guardian, the Sheriff of Nottingham, who is of course the despoiler-in-chief, and suspicious of her outlaw-admirer whom she initially finds to be frivolous and far too full of himself. (She has a point.)

Neither the eco-friendly theme nor the love story develops much impetus. One doesn't expect a family musical (it's actually billed as The EnvironMENTAL Family Musical) to be as integrated as West Side Story, but if you're going to deconstruct something, it helps to have a structure there first. This one lurches from one scene to another, mostly helped by its gags, mostly hindered by its songs. These are a mix of rock, rap, contempo pop and Michael Jackson: all of them genres with a built-in disinclination to tell anybody's story but their own.

They're dragged in on the thinnest of pretexts; Marian, having been smitten by Robin, wanders about the stage singing Desperado, which should give you an idea. Admittedly, pantos have always interpolated the songs of whatever day it was, but I don't remember them doing it quite like this. Desperadoes indeed: the show's creators seem desperate to reassure the kids, not to mention themselves, that they're up to date. It feels, to be frank, like pandering.

All right, I'll stop being solemn. Ted Dykstra's production boasts three first-rate comic turns. Best of them is Holmes, who starts the show doing a riotously irrelevant lampoon of Celine Dion (it doesn't technically interrupt the story because the story hasn't even started) and then switches to her Fairy Queen role, which she discharges with a devastatingly snappish lisp. Next is Petty, whose Sheriff is the mixture as before, and more richly self-referential than ever; producers may sometimes be villains, but this one actually gets to tell his employees "if I leave the theatre, none of you lot will work again." Finally there's Chameroy whose man-hungry nurse is a most delicate creation, even if it does consist solely of jokes about her being a man-hungry nurse.

On the subject of repeated jokes: no show needs two references to Tiger Woods, and the one Chameroy gets is a lot better than the one Petty gets. Of the romantic supports: Eva Avila, former Canadian Idol, shows as Maid Marian that she knows her way about a stage, and Jeff Irving is a cheerful Robin. And then there are the Musically Merry Men: in the words of a song unfortunately not from the show but that I've just discovered and would like to share: "They laughed, they loved, they fought, they drank/They jumped a lot of fences/They robbed the rich, gave to the poor/Except what they kept for expenses."

The current representative selection includes Jaz Sealey whose Li'l Sean John is a hulking and magnetic rapper, and Yvan Pedneault whose Jacques le Rock (try finding him in the source material) is a full-throated chansonnier, though he has less good material than he had in We Will Rock You. That's a phrase I never thought I'd write.

- Robin Hood plays at the Elgin Theatre until Jan. 3, 2010. Call 416-872-5555 for information.

2009-12-12-civil-elegies-a-good-bite-but:
The dauntingly versatile Mike Ross figures in Soulpepper's Civil Elegies as actor, singer, pianist, composer and original begetter. The show grew from his enthusiasm for the work of Dennis Lee whose long poem of 1968 furnishes it with its title and much of its text. Ross recites it, or most of it, interspersing it with his own musical settings of Lee's comparatively lighter verse, the stuff that rhymes. These take very well to song form, and Ross has supplied them with plangent downbeat melodies that sometimes recall Tom Waits (Randy Newman, his other cited influence, not so much) though vocally he suggests a more melodious Bob Dylan, 1960s vintage, a sly and throaty prophet.

His unseen collaborators are Albert Schultz, who directs, and Lorenzo Savoini, credited as co-creator and designer. Old photographs of Toronto are projected onto a brick wall whose still-visible contours can make even a simple streetcar look ominous. There's also, more playfully, a video feed showing us what Ross's hands, when not hitting the keys, are getting up to on top of the piano; they're doing unexpectedly creative things with coffee and doughnuts. All this adds to his already considerable charm as a performer, which in turn leavens material whose nearest approach to optimism often seems to be a bruised wistfulness.

Civil Elegies the poem presents a young bard sitting in Nathan Phillips Square, meditating on a Canada whose colonized and colonizing past and compromised and compromising present have infected and dehumanized the cityscape. Forty years on, your thoughts may stray to Afghanistan and Dundas Square. Poem and songs reinforce one another's themes. "Skyscraper, skyscraper, scrape me some sky," sings the evening's first line, echoing a number from Fiddler on the Roof. The Americans want the country, says another song, "for a backyard barbecue." A rueful paean to William Lyon Mackenzie, entitled 1838, dovetails with an Elegy commemorating "the first spontaneous mutual retreat in the history of warfare." The most cheerful piece, celebrating the defeat of the Spadina expressway, could maybe use a more triumphalist setting than Ross has given it, if only for contrast. The components of Lee's vision sometimes seems strained, but it's a powerful one, especially when it turns to the failures of love.

For all the talent on display, the show doesn't satisfy. There's a monumental bitterness to some of the poems that Ross, lucidly though he delivers them, doesn't -- or doesn't yet --have in him; Lee may have been only 28 when he wrote them but one thing they don't feel is young. And there's the simple question of form. Most poetry since 1900 can be read aloud but it can't easily be listened to aloud; the words go by too fast and too knotted. Or, either the text is too dense or I am.

Kudos, I guess, to Rep 21, an outcrop of Canadore College in North Bay, for bringing us Martin Mc-Donagh's The Lieutenant of Inishmore. Shame on our more established theatres for leaving the Toronto premiere of a major piece by a major playwright to a barely professional company who have done it very badly. The play is a cruel Irish farce about terrorism. The title character, a splinter of a splinter-group from the IRA, takes time off from torturing a drug dealer to wreak horrible vengeance on the villagers --one of them his own father -- who have killed his cherished pet cat. Another faction lies in wait for him, and an aspiring gun moll completes the pattern. The action is a thoroughgoing reductio ad absurdum, but the casual attitude towards horrors seems glib and the tensions don't hold. Here, they don't stand a chance. I suppose it's reassuring that the one actor with an Equity card (Benjamin Clost) is the only one with any style, presence or timing; in a play where everyone's trigger happy, one dreads his disappearing too early. The rest are hung out to dry in a production (by Rod Carley) with no apparent sensitivity to tone or pace.

We mourn the death of Goldie Semple, a coruscating actress whose performances in The Royal Family and The Cassilis Engagement were among the Shaw Festival's finest.

- Civil Elegies runs through Dec. 24 at the Young Centre (416-866-8666); The Lieutenant of Inishmore closes tonight at the Berkeley Street Theatre. (416-363-3110).

Something is wrong with Fiddler on the Roof from the moment that Harvey Fierstein opens his mouth, which is very unfortunate since it's virtually the first thing that happens in the show. Fierstein, who has taken over the role of Tevye from an ailing Chaim Topol in what was meant to be Topol's farewell tour, has already played it on Broadway and I was looking forward to seeing him; he seemed, frankly, the more interesting prospect. He has at least the right imposing height for the role of the patriarchal milkman who chats to God, while his voice maybe the deepest and grittiest known to man. But gravel, it seems, does not necessarily equal gravitas. Tevye is a religious Jew in a Russian shtetl, and the father of five daughters. He has to cope with the marriages of the three eldest to progressively less desirable (because more progressive) suitors and, eventually, with the expulsion of himself and all his co-religionists from the village in which their families have lived for centuries. That's a lot to endure, but Tevye is a great and humorous endurer. Fierstein plays him as a lightweight fusspot to whom nothing matters.

I don't think he's doing that on purpose; he's a good actor who knows what's required and is trying to provide it. But, at every point, his delivery and demeanour betray him. He isn't even a teddy bear; he's a big baby. His oldest daughter marries a poor tailor, his second a revolutionary, his third a Gentile, all of them of course without traditional benefit of matchmaker. The "Tradition!" of which the opening number sings so defiantly is largely abandoned as the show proceeds, leaving only the irreducible minimum everybody needs. All three girls are terrified of telling their father, in a series of encounters that grows steadily less amusing; here none of them seems to have anything to be afraid of, and we have nothing to respond to.

Fierstein doesn't have much of a singing voice, but that isn't the problem; neither did Zero Mostel, the terrifying clown who created the role. Far more serious is that he doesn't have an authentically comic voice. He establishes no rapport with his deity, his neighbours or his audience; he doesn't have much confidence to take us into, and he increasingly falls back on a deprecatory squeak to indicate annoyance. He actually does better with the emotional scenes, partly because in this respect the show itself is absolutely impregnable. The most moving scene is the one he shares with Hodel (Jamie Davis), as she waits for the train that will take her to join her imprisoned husband in Siberia; I have never been surer, when she says, "Papa, God knows when we shall meet again," that they never will and that both of them know it. Her marriageable sisters (Rena Strober and Deborah Grausman) are charming as well, and the Matchmaker trio, with a broom as their silent partner, is a delight.

This musical's book (by Joseph Stein) is a marvel in the way it reels out its overlapping plot lines, then gathers them up in a quietly shattering climax. Sheldon Harnick's lyrics have the simplicity of great craft, and Jerry Bock's music (notably the Sabbath Prayer and Sunrise, Sunset) seems richer every time you hear it. Sammy Dallas Bayes's production provides a nondescript but unobjectionable surround for the enduring greatness of Jerome Robbins' choreography, which is even better because it's more centred than his work on West Side Story -- though paradoxically, if we had to lose his dances, Fiddler would stand the better chance of surviving without them. In Fiddler, it isn't just a matter of steps; it's what goes on through, behind and around them. It's the processional joining of hands in the opening number. It's the three Chagallian musicians popping up behind the bed in Tevye's dream. It's the Cossack intrusion in To Life that starts as challenge and becomes celebration. It's the bright costumes of the wedding guests, and those same guests watching the solemn, immortal Bottle Dance. It's the way the wedding itself, a distillation of tradition, is followed by its defiance as men and women start dancing together and the incredible detailed way in which that number builds. It's the brief heartbreak dance as Tevye tries to banish the memory of the one daughter he can't forgive. It's the downbeat ending, and the curtain-call that follows it.

The part of Golde, Tevye's formidable wife, is a surprisingly unrewarding one, but Susan Cella gets more out of it than most by pushing less. Yente the matchmaker is a role that seems to bring out the worst in whoever plays it, but Mary Stout's performance hits new lows of ethnic pandering. David Brummel is endearing as Lazar Wolf, the butcher deprived of a bride; the two young Jewish wooers are competent but unexciting. The show (not just this production) soft-pedals the Gentile atrocities, so maybe it's karma that the Gentiles themselves, or the two with any prominence, are atrociously acted. None of this production's performances will challenge any-one's memories of the 10-year-old Stratford production, and Fierstein's Tevye doesn't belong in the same universe as Brent Carver's. But the show conquers; it's the most moving musical ever written, and I long ago gave up believing that it's in any way sentimental. Les Mis is sentimental. Spring Awakening is sentimental. Fiddler is tough.

- Fiddler on the Roof runs through Jan. 10 at the Canon Theatre. For tickets, call 416-872-1212.

2009-12-22-science-is-obvious-after-it-s:
Jim Al-Khalilli begins Science and Islam, a three-part BBC series on TVO, gazing down from a balcony on a view of mosques and minarets. He's a scientist, who was born in Baghdad and whose family left Iraq when Saddam Hussein came to power; he's now a professor of physics at Surrey University. He sounds, and admits to being, thoroughly Westernized, but the series he presents is born of what he calls "a nagging feeling" that he needed to re-examine his roots and find a connection between them and his present existence. He "can no longer visit Baghdad because of recent events" but his quest takes him through Syria, Iran and North Africa. He's a model TV explorer, very winning and unaffected.

His subject is the Golden Age of Islamic culture and discovery, between the 9th and 12th centuries: a renaissance that preceded the Western one by some 300 years. We know, and probably take for granted, that we owe our system of numbering to it. Al-Khalilli asks us to consider just how revolutionary was this idea of using 10 numerical symbols. It was developed, he tells us, by Indian mathematicians in the 6th century AD; a century later the Arabs took it further by inventing the decimal point, thus making modern math possible: "like all great science it's blindingly obvious after it's been discovered." He asks to imagine doing long multiplication using Roman numerals. ( "It can be done, but it's clunky.")

"Arabic language," he says "hasn't changed much in 700 years." We're reminded that algebra, algorithms and alkali are all Arabic words, and that the first -- with which Al-Kalilli is especially fascinated and that he makes especially fascinating -- underpins modern physics. He talks to current Arab scientists and historians, and refers to his British colleagues for corroboration. He also follows the power and the money.

At its height, the Islamic empire was the largest, and hence the richest, in the world. For scientists "there's nothing like a large chunk of money to focus the mind," and the Caliphs and ruling elites were great dispensers of grants. They were also great bibliophiles. "Bringing books to the Caliph for his library could be very lucrative;" there was one who would reward the bearer of a rare book by giving him its weight in gold. (It must have been like an Oprah endorsement.) There was a passionate desire for preservation; the burning of the great library of Alexandria had bequeathed "the ever-present possibility of total loss." Many of these books were classical Greek and Roman texts; so arose the immensely influential Translation Movement which, rendering these texts into Arabic, seems to have anticipated the re-awakening of European humanism by several centuries. The reclaiming of ancient knowledge fed into new Arab science, especially in medicine, which in turn was hugely influential.

"Up until the 19th century," says a medical historian, "Western medicine was built to a large extent on the work of Islamic physicians." They in turn were based on the ancient Greeks, especially on Galen and his "theory of humours" which held that four bodily fluids governed the human mind and body. Anyone who has read an Elizabethan play will have come across this dodgy, if comically fruitful, idea; and will wonder if the two cultures discovered Galen independently of one another, or whether we got it from them. Like much else, it has of course been discredited. The program's verdict on Islamic medicine is that "they took for granted much we know to be nonsense, but their desire to deal with the subject logically and systematically is admirable."

Or, as Al-Khalilli puts it, "the scientific method was discovered by medieval Islam." Perhaps the most startling development of all concerns cartography and its consequences. A Caliph in 813 was "obsessed with measurements -- map-making," not surprisingly in view of the amount of territory he had to measure. Also, devout Muslims, spread all over the empire, "needed to know where Mecca was." Working out the precise directions in which they should be looking led geographers to measuring the earth's circumference, and getting a result (40,000 kilometres) very close to the right answer. Al-Khalilli doesn't make much of that word "circumference" but it pulled me up short. You mean they knew, way back then, that the world was round?

Among the scientists' other accomplishments were the anticipation, if not quite the invention, of the periodic table, the use of petroleum in weaponry, and, as one scholar puts it, "the whole idea of the chemical-industrial lab." They also, it seems, invented soap. And a visit to a modern Cairo bazaar produces a pair of carrier pigeons, whose ancestors were "a sort of medieval Telex." One thing that isn't addressed, at least not in the first two programs, is how and why it all stopped: why Islam turned in on itself, why riches stopped promoting knowledge and why -- in effect -- the Translation Movement went into reverse. What we do get is a stunning inventory, accessibly described and narrated: popular education at its best.

-Part Two of Science and Islam airs tonight at 10 p.m. on TVO. Part Three airs Tuesday, Dec. 22 at 10 p.m.

2009-12-26-it-was-a-golden-decade-if-you: I note two trends, though it's probably demeaning to call them that. They're achievements. 1. The TV novel. Not as in the BBC Classic/Masterpiece Theatre model, but as in great original creations: The Sopranos, The Wire, Deadwood and probably Mad Men, though the fat lady hasn't sung yet. This form may already have crested, but it was magnificent while it lasted. 2. The comedy news show. Forty-five years on, U.S. TV has caught up with where British TV was in the early '60s when David Frost and That Was the Week That Was were credited with bringing down the Macmillan government. This is unlikely but they certainly captured a mood, just as Jon Stewart and Stephen Colbert have done. Some complain that viewers are treating Stewart and Colbert, especially Stewart, as their primary news sources; that, too, is unlikely - you have to know the background in order to get the jokes - but even if that were the case, it wouldn't be terrible. Comedy depends on the telling of truths, and if these two men have become the most trusted commentators on TV, it's because they're the most intelligent. (Also because all the others are so pompous.) Stewart, in the best of his interviews, has broken the mould for both TV comedy and TV politics by asking questions as if he actually wants to know the answers. It's understandable that Christopher Hitchens and Rex Murphy have been having a go at him; it must be galling to see someone expressing opinions you disagree with and being funnier than you are while doing it.

These are the theatrical high-points of 2009: The Last Days of Judas Iscariot. Stratfords Three Sisters and The Importance of Being Earnest. Soulpepper's Travesties and Who's Afraid of Virginia Woolf. Robert Lepages day-long Lipsynch, more as an event than as a finished whole, though its best moments were heart-stopping. Lepages The Nightingale for the Canadian Opera, and the same company's Madama Butterfly. (Leave it to opera to produce the year's greatest visual treats.) CanStages revival of Morris Panychs 7 Stories, if only for Melody Johnson's breathtakingly funny performance in its last scene.

None of those, it has to be confessed, is a new Canadian play. Lipsynch doesn't quite count; all the others are old and/or foreign (and among the latter, Judas was a revival even as a production). Brad Frasers True Love Lies would come nearest to making the cut; other contenders were Kristen Thomsons The Patient Hour, Michael Healey's Generous, and, with a few more misgivings, Andrew Moodie's Toronto the Good and Panychs The Trespassers, a departure for him if not an entirely satisfying one. Add in two delightful home-grown musicals, Mimi and The Princess and the Handmaiden.

That list may not seem like much, but it isnt disgraceful and it certainly isn't unusual. Since the year's end is also the decades, Ive tried reckoning up the plays that delighted me when I first saw them and -- a stiffer test -- when I remember them. It's another short list. Thomson's I Claudia is on it, of course, even with the proviso that its sui generis, the impact of its writing inextricably linked to that of its performance -- by, of course, its author. Like Healeys The Drawer Boy, it has set impossible standards for its author's subsequent work; that kind of surprise lightning rarely strikes twice. Healey's Plan B probably belongs there; John Mightons Half Life certainly does. So do Florence Gibsons Belle, Claudia Dey's Trout Stanley and nearly everything by Hannah Moscovitch, especially East of Berlin and The Russian Play; one of the more perplexing myths of our time is the one that holds that plays by women are not getting produced.

Another is the one that suggests the paucity of good new plays is some sort of ahistorical scandal. The implication is always that there ought to be more of them and that it must be someone's fault that there arent. Against this, I would like to quote three theatrical sages. One of them is Sean OCasey, who said, with devastating simplicity at the end of a long career in which his triumphs were outnumbered by his failures, It is a hard, hard thing to write a good play." Another is Peter Hall, who wrote that a decade that produces two really good plays is lucky. The third is Max Stafford-Clark, director of Britain's pioneering Joint Stock group, who lamented that his group's success with the R&D method of developing plays had given rise to the verb "to workshop, meaning a way in which limping plays are helped on to the stage." When a play fails in Toronto, somebody is sure to say that it hadnt been workshopped enough. Its likelier to have been workshopped too much, to the point where all concerned have a vested interest in getting it on somehow. This partly accounts for all the productions that think all you need is an Issue, and that seem to have confused drama with social work.

It is true that nearly all the plays we see are physically and imaginatively small. (That's one reason Judas Iscariot, which was neither, felt so liberating.) Economic pressures have combined with the influence of TV to make our writers rein themselves instinctively in. In reaction, exaggerated praise gets heaped on shows that seem at least to have Big Themes; plays like those of Wajdi Mouawad or Michel Marc Bouchard or (lest anyone think I'm prejudiced against Quebec writers) The Danish Play: plays that bend their characters out of shape or hardly bother to create them in the first place. If youre looking for a good epic then try a real one: the multi-part City of Wine; or Peter Hintons Swanne trilogy at Stratford, uneven, of course, but exhilarating, especially as staged by its author. Hinton, to slightly change the subject, is our most consistently (and constructively) imaginative director. Ottawa, where he now runs the English theatrical wing of the National Arts Centre, is fortunate to have him; but one wonders why Stratford and Soulpepper, for whom he staged superb productions of, respectively, The Duchess of Malfi and The Way of the World, have let him go. Equally perplexing is the loss to Stratford, under the new regime, of the quieter talent of Miles Potter whose track record from Romeo and Juliet to Orpheus Descending was impeccable.

Regime change at the Shaw Festival these last few years has had few perceptible effects; this past season has been good but not great, with its flagship project (the Noel Coward cycle) not being its best. Stratford's Hamlet in 2008 seemed to inaugurate a new Shakespearean era of being both thorough and inventive but it hasn't been sustained; this years Midsummer Nights Dream had the year's great Shakespearean performance in Geraint Wyn Davies' Bottom and was interesting in other ways, but other productions of the house playwright have actually been a retreat from previous standards. The companys stronger than ever but it isnt always well used. Last year's Fuente Ovejuna and this year's Bartholomew Fair signalled a welcome commitment to expanding the repertoire, though it seems as if next years nearest approach to a non-Shakespearean classic will be Peter Pan. Soulpepper is the decades greatest and justified success story, and this year has confirmed the value of two of its less trumpeted assets: its permanent floating ensemble and the unique attractiveness (in Toronto theatre) of its premises. These make it a nice place to visit, though shows like Glengarry Glen Ross, Billy Bishop Goes to War and the Christmas treat of Parfumerie don't hurt, either.

2009-12-26-s-take-it-was-a-golden-decade:
I note two trends, though it's probably demeaning to call them that. They're achievements. 1. The TV novel. Not as in the BBC Classic/Masterpiece Theatre model, but as in great original creations: The Sopranos, The Wire, Deadwood and probably Mad Men, though the fat lady hasn't sung yet. This form may already have crested, but it was magnificent while it lasted. 2. The comedy news show. Forty-five years on, U.S.TVhas caught up with where British TV was in the early '60s when David Frost and That Was the Week That Was were credited with bringing down the Macmillan government. This is unlikely but they certainly captured a mood, just as Jon Stewart and Stephen Colbert have done. Some complain that viewers are treating Stewart and Colbert, especially Stewart, as their primary news sources; that, too, is unlikely -- you have to know the background in order to get the jokes -- but even if that were the case, it wouldn't be terrible. Comedy depends on the telling of truths, and if these two men have become the most trusted commentators on TV, it's because they're the most intelligent. (Also because all the others are so pompous.) Stewart, in the best of his interviews, has broken the mould for both TV comedy and TV politics by asking questions as if he actually wants to know the answers. It's understandable that Christopher Hitchens and Rex Murphy have been having a go at him; it must be galling to see someone expressing opinions you disagree with and being funnier than you are while doing it.
