2009-12-29-why-you-should-care-about-say:
According to a recent article in The New York Times, the apostrophe is an endangered species. Its probably true, but I don't know that I care very much. Or: Its probably true, but I dont know that I care very much. However, as long as apostrophes are around, they should be used right. You can probably see where I'm going with this one. Im going towards its" and "its, and the appalling tendency -- though naturally not by respectable newspapers -- to confuse them. It's appalling not because it's an affront to style, but because its an affront to sense and logic. (Though of course its on sense and logic that good style is based.) The apostrophe, as we all know, signifies an elision; it's" stands in for "it is. There's no need for an apostrophe, and therefore no place, when its" is possessive.

Confusingly, and yes illogically, we do use the apostrophe in other possessive cases. We speak or write of "Henrys hat. That is an elision; its short for Henry his hat," which is what our comparatively remote ancestors would have written. And said, too, probably, but you can bet that they stopped saying it before they stopped writing it. Writing fell into line to reflect speech, which is how things should be. But inserting an apostrophe into "its has no bearing on how anyone pronounces anything. The word sounds the same either way. The admitted inconsistency between the two possessives, its" and "Henry's, may be a good reason for letting the apostrophe die unmourned. Bernard Shaw, starting more than 100 years ago, made a point of doing without those jumped-up commas; he would certainly have written Henrys hat" -- probably did in Pygmalion -- and his prose was superb. Shaw wanted to kill the apostrophe by ignoring it; we, paradoxically, may be hastening its demise by shoving it where it doesn't belong. My guess is that the practice started with blithe ignorance and spread through earnest imitation. Thats how bad style gets around.

Even more infamous things have been done to English in this decade. One of them is the use of the word "infamous. It used to be the opposite of famous"; now it increasingly turns up as something between a synonym and a superlative. So a word we need is turned into one we dont. And people don't know they're doing it; they merely assume that a slightly longer word will be more impressive. The adjective for that is "pretentious.

Another might be cloth-eared." That, anyway, is what comes to my mind when, in another example, I hear people say that they could care less. The phrase means of course that they do care, but that isnt what they mean it to mean. They believe, in defiance of anything they may have been taught about negatives and double negatives, that its equivalent to saying they couldn't care less; which is plainly ridiculous. I've heard this usage defended as being ironic, like saying "I should worry to mean that you dont. The problem with that is that when people say I should worry" they accompany it with a shrug, physical or vocal. Ive never heard anyone say "I could care less ironically. They always say it aggressively. It merely proves that you can be as pretentious by dropping a syllable as by adding one.

And what gets into all the otherwise irreproachable people who tell you that something either beautiful or terrible is happening to my partner and I?" They would never dream of saying that it's "happening to I. But you don't change an object to a subject simply by sticking a few more words in front of it. In theory, its no worse than using me" as a subject -- as in "me and my gang can beat up you and your gang -- but that older solecism is at least forceful. The new one is just flabby.

Yes, I know, language changes, and should. And slang enriches, more often than it debases. That last sentence is the fourth in this article that Ive begun with the word and," something that my schoolteachers forbade me to do even once, and about which I remain completely unrepentant. Elisions, too, other than in dialogue, would have been barred from serious print 50 years ago; now, as you'll have noticed, I can't do without them. But the usages Ive been attacking arent slangy; they're shabby-genteel. Grammar exists for clarity, not the other way about, but these aren't creative attacks on grammar; theyre misguided attempts to seem more grammatical, a linguistic equivalent of political correctness. They dont subvert syntax; they merely misunderstand it.

We're becoming mealy-mouthed. Some blame it on the digital revolution -- all that blogging and texting and twittering, though I'm more inclined to believe the opposing argument, which is that people are writing again, maybe more than ever before, and that that's a good thing. Of course there's more bad writing than good; there always has been. The only difference is that both bad and good are now more visible. And sometimes the bad fades away. Twenty years ago, we were rightly alarmed at the constant misuse of the word "hopefully." Now it seems to have disappeared. Its over; hopefully.
2009-12-30-believe-it-or-not-musical-the:
Further to the decline of literacy: commercially successful musicals of the past decade have fallen into three categories:

-Jukebox musicals (no, I dont like the phrase either), meaning assemblages of preexisting pop hits, with no inherent dramatic presence.

-Slavish adaptations of pre-sold properties, not all of them movies (though they're the most offensive, because they allow the least alteration). The giveaway is that they never change the title.

Musicals, like opera and Shakespeare, have always thrived on adaptation, but just as Shakespeare wrote As You Like It, not Rosalynde: The Comedie, so Lerner and Loewe wrote My Fair Lady, not Pygmalion: The Musical. (I seem to have that play on the brain.)

-Worse than either of the above, which are at least up-front about their intentions: musicals that treat the mere idea of doing a musical as an outrageous giggle in itself. When everything's a parody, whats left to be funny about? Oh Irony, what crimes are committed in thy name.

These categories sometimes overlap, though in all honesty I cant think of a show that falls into all three of them. Probably Mamma Mia! comes closest.

This doesn't mean that intelligent, musically adventurous, and even witty shows aren't being written. Just don't expect to see them on a big stage.
2010-01-02-praise-for-the-year-s-best-pe:
Goldie Semple, whose death darkened the end of the year, went out on a high professional note. In Brief Encounters, the first of the Shaw Festival's trio of Noel Coward triple bills, she unveiled her own triptych of comic vignettes, culminating in a gloriously unbuttoned drunk in Hands across the Sea. Ive been asking some of her peers about her. Lucy Peacock, who names Semple as a mentor (they joined the main Stratford company together in 1987, though Semple was eight years the older) confirmed that she loved being wicked on stage ... she had a sparkle and a wit," and says that her Cleopatra, which I never saw, was "fantastic. ...I remember her in this huge play on this seemingly huge stage, and absolutely filling it -- the complexity she had and the full-stage commitment.

Complexity," expressed through grace and wit, is what distinguishes the two Semple performances, both at Shaw, that I most treasure: her uneasily retired actress in The Royal Family and her uneasily scheming mother in The Cassilis Engagement, both triumphant explorations of mixed motives. In the latter play, she was a fastidious society woman descending to unimaginable depths to prevent her son from making a declasse marriage; snobbery, shame, and ruthless determination performed an intricate dance through the evening. In The Royal Family, she had a matchless comic scene on the telephone, her words proclaiming her intention to give up stardom for domesticity, her body language revealing, hilariously, the precise opposite. Martha Henry, who directed that production, says, "You couldnt shirk in the same rehearsal hall as Goldie. She wanted to be very clear about exactly what I was asking of her -- and why -- but once you explained what you wanted, she bent over backwards to give it to you, and always went further than you could ever have imagined. She would take a piece of direction and (sometimes, literally) fly with it. Her immense sense of humour and fun always caught me by surprise-- you never really expected this beautiful, glamorous woman to be so wildly funny.

There were times, speaking for myself, when her star quality seemed to be operating at some distance from the character she was playing (Coward's Easy Virtue) or when (as with the pile-driving protagonist of The Matchmaker) she was simply miscast. Against that, I recall her being very moving as the bereaved Constance in a Stratford King John, and both moving and enchanting as Desiree in last year's Shaw production of A Little Night Music, in which her singing of Send in the Clowns seems, of course, even more touching in retrospect than it did at the time. Jennifer Phipps, who acted with her at both festivals, recalls how, when she herself was suffering from damaged hips that were cutting me off from the rest of the world, Goldie brought the community back to me. ... She was a very good community person" -- a description echoed, almost exactly, by everyone I spoke to -- and applied to her life both inside and outside the theatre, where her kindness and concern were legendary. All, too, were unanimous that, having fought cancer for years, she seemed indestructible, making her death an even greater shock.

Two of the actresses who talked to me about Semple were involved in the theatrical event of the departed year that touched me most deeply, Stratfords Three Sisters, directed by Henry and with Peacock heading a superbly unified ensemble. Continuing further, a brief catalogue of some of the years other outstanding acting. I named Geraint Wyn Davies' Bottom last week as the year's best Shakespeare; hed already been a fine Duncan and Julius Caesar, a set of performances that make his return to Canadian theatre the most satisfying of recent comebacks. Runner-up Shakespearean was Gord Rands abbreviated Hamlet; this unclassifiable actor was also good in Goodness. The Hamlet production had many provocative things, not least Eric Peterson's Polonius, vocally limited but still transfixingly nasty. This was Peterson's year, mainly at Soulpepper where he flew solo in Billy Bishop Goes to War (another triumphant return) and was part of another fine ensemble in Glengarry Glen Ross. Melody Johnson had a wild comedy time: She directed a good Second City revue; she co-wrote Mimi, the years best new musical; and as an actress she was dottily dignified and superbly funny in 7 Stories. Joseph Ziegler brought off an even rarer trifecta by working with all three major classical companies: acting at Stratford, directing at Shaw, and doing both at Soulpepper --all good stuff, with his performance in Parfumerie taking the palm. Nancy Palk surpassed herself in Whos Afraid of Virginia Woolf, a show that was faultlessly acted throughout with Tim Campbell being absolutely perfect. Other great teams were those in Stratford's Importance of Being Earnest and BirdLand's Trial of Judas Iscariot, with Ted Dykstra and an irresistibly squealing Morris Panych, among many others, joining Diego Matamoross smooth and terrifying Satan. Matamoros was neither smooth nor terrifying in Travesties, merely enchanting. Hardee Lineham in Blackbird was disturbingly good. Erica Peck in The Boys in the Photograph and Chilina Kennedy in West Side Story gave fine musical and dramatic performances. Jim Mezon broke new and pungent ground in A Moon for the Misbegotten, and Benedict Campbell gave a new but convincing take on Archie Rice in The Entertainer with sublime assistance from Corinne Koslo. Fiona Reid gave two magical performances in Rock n' Roll and Shaun Smyth a very good one. In a year of one-person plays, Nicola Lipman was virtuoso in Another Home Invasion (a play that I should have listed last week among the year's best). Michael Hanrahan and Oliver Dennis were magisterial in an uneven Loot, and Dennis went on to delight us in Parfumerie in a rare romantic lead. The list is incomplete. But in a year that deprived us of Neil Munro and Douglas Campbell as well as Goldie Semple and with the loss of William Hutt and Richard Monette still fresh in memory, it's consoling and, in its way, inspiring.

2010-01-08-homer-s-where-the-heart-isn-t:
This is the 20th year of The Simpsons so some celebration is called for, something perhaps on the order of the recent multi-part epic commemorating Monty Python.

But what we actually get is The Simpsons 20th Anniversary Special: In 3-D! On Ice!, a mingy single program, whose "executive producer, writer and director" Morgan Spurlock is also its presenter, and who strolls through it in the apparent belief that it's about him.

There aren't many clips, although those there are--mainly drawn from The Simpsons' earlier, greater years -- are joyful. Otherwise the prevailing note is unfocused sycophancy; the program takes The Simpsons' greatness as a given without ever, except in the most superficial way, asking what it consists of. It's way behind the show itself, which has always been as good at mocking itself as at mocking everything else. It marked a previous anniversary with its own retrospective, presided over by the oleaginous omnipresent actor Troy ( "You may remember me from such previous infomercials as ...") McClure. He asked, rhetorically, "Who knows what further wacky antics these characters will get up to until the show becomes unprofitable?"

That day, the special makes very clear, has yet to dawn. Merchandising tie-ins alone would keep The Simpsons in profit. This fact has also been unblushingly acknowledged in the show itself, with Bart in particular always ready to comment on the extreme tackiness of the products involved.

There are interviews with writers, actors and executives; Matt Groening, who started it all, comes over as furry and friendly. A reel of outtakes, enclosed with the press screener, reveals however that some of the best material wasn't used. One is the declaration of Nancy Cartwright, voice of Bart, that -- what with short hours, great material, good company and (one assumes) never-ending residuals -- she has "the best job in America." All the actors emphasize the importance of the animation being fitted to their voice-tracks rather than the other way around: a vital fact about the comic strength of The Simpsons, and one that the finished film doesn't mention, let alone explore. Dan Castellanata, who as Homer is the greatest voice of all, appears in both the accepted and rejected footage hidden behind dark glasses, as if to deny himself any independent existence.

Castellanata is also the voice of Mayor Quimby and Krusty the Klown who, though it's a tough call, may be the most venal characters in Springfield. We learn from Groening that Krusty is based on Rusty Nails, a real clown from his own childhood who wasn't venal at all.

That's nice. Spurlock gets to travel to Scotland to investigate whether Groundskeeper Willie hails from Glasgow or Aberdeen. Some of the best characters, though, go completely unmentioned: the divinely incompetent Police Chief Wiggum, for example, not to mention those magnificently haughty extra-terrestrials Kang and Kodos. The Halloween episodes, which are their preserve, aren't mentioned either. So with the show's superb musical sequences: Moby chooses Homer's Mr. Plow song as his favourite Simpsons number, which, given the existence of the "Oh Streetcar" episode, is pathetic.

The Simpsons is subversive, like all good comedy, but it isn't anarchic. It has structure. This distinguishes it from its imitators which start from the premise that there aren't any rules and so deny themselves the fun of breaking them.

There is some pretense at showing opposition to The Simpsons, but it's very tame: some risible protests from the Catholic League, and the well-worn sight of the first president Bush enjoining American families to be more like The Waltons and less like The Simpsons. A forlorn hope, George: All families are more like The Simpsons than they are like The Waltons. More amusingly, the head of the Nuclear Energy Institute complains, in a resigned sort of way, that "most people learn about nuclear energy from The Simpsons." (He's probably right.)

The one really damning criticism gets laughed off; I refer to the fact that, in the second of its two decades if not for longer, the show has gone terribly downhill.

The Simpsons took about two years to find its legs --and, especially in Homer's case, its voice. Its next four or five years were perfect, infinitely quotable and limitlessly rewatchable. Anything after that is depressing. The show used to pack every minute with jokes, verbal and visual, all of them pertinent, all of them inspired. Also, it never let up on its narrative. Now it's flabby.

What's billed as "the landmark 450th episode" also airs on Sunday, and it's a case in point. It starts well enough; the pre-credit sequence is up to legendary standards, and the main plot-line seems promising. Krusty's sponsors insist on him hiring a co-host, a sugary Julie Andrews update called Princess Penelope. The little girls love her, everyone else hates her, especially Krusty himself, until he has a change of heart, from which point things get soggy.

As for the Simpsons themselves: Marge is practically invisible, Bart and Lisa go through motions and Homer is confined to a limp sub-plot, about being lured away to a rival nuclear plant, which has no satiric point and is wrapped up with insulting casualness. The two plots barely nudge each other's elbows, a terrible decline for a show that was once an ongoing triumph of architectural elegance. If we're meant to be celebrating a Simpsons milestone, shouldn't the Simpsons be at the centre of it? For all the teeming life of Springfield, the show's strength has always been that it's a family entertainment. That and the fact that Homer -- as every man will guiltily admit --is Everyman.

- The Simpsons 20th Anniversary Special: In 3-D! On Ice! airs on Sunday at 8:30 p.m. on Global; a new, regular episode airs at 8 p.m.
2010-01-09-battle-lines-drawn-the-themes:
War and peace. Theres nothing novel about those as dramatic subjects, nor is there much new about the fact that, of the two, war provides the better copy. The first theatrical quarter of 2010 certainly looks set to confirm that. War is topical, of course. But then it always is.

Soulpepper is in an especially bellicose mood, with two productions -- both musicals of a kind -- set in that recurring theatrical reference-point for all armed conflicts, the catastrophe of 1914-18. (Think, for a start, of all the Shakespeare productions that have been set there.) Eric Peterson returns as the Canadian air-ace in Billy Bishop Goes to War (Jan. 22 to Feb. 27), a showpiece that he's been performing for upwards of 30 years now, and that seemed funnier and more affecting than ever when he revived it last year.

This solo-focused piece is paired with the panorama of Oh What a Lovely War (Mar. 11 to April 10), in which the history of the First World War is relayed through skits, statistics and, most memorably, music-hall songs. The show was the creation, in 1963, of Theatre Workshop, the aesthetically and politically radical company that operated mainly out of the Theatre Royal in Stratford, East London -- itself a house with the atmosphere of a converted music hall. It was, to choose my words carefully, the most powerful emotional experience I have ever had in a theatre. The juxtapostion of the cheery, increasingly sardonic music with the brute facts of the carnage, enumerated in the neon equivalent of tickertape, was overwhelming. The comic effect was slightly diluted when the show moved to the West End, but the sadness and the anger remained. (The movie version diluted everything.)

An acknowledged if peculiar classic, Lovely War has had few major revivals, perhaps because it was so much the creation of its original director, Joan Littlewood, and her cherished band of off-beat performers. Littlewood is said to have denied Britain's National Theatre permission to do the show on the grounds that they hadnt yet earned the right to do it. Albert Schultzs revival, with Marek Norman as musical director, should at least have the ensemble basics; two Soulpepper stalwarts, Oliver Dennis and Michael Hanrahan, appear in a cast otherwise recruited from the company's academy, whose members have a disconcerting habit of being gifted musicians as well as actors.

The war play of all 20th-century war plays, though, must be Bertolt Brecht's Mother Courage, another play associated with an ensemble (Brechts own Berliner one, which mounted it after the Second World War though it had been written during) and one that certainly influenced Theatre Workshop, which had staged it with Littlewood herself playing the leading role -- not, by all accounts, very well. Brechts plays, which used to be inescapable, have fallen out of fashion; the only ones that get done in Canada are -- for obvious reasons -- the musicals, The Threepenny Opera and Happy End. But even if the play has been seldom seen, Mother Courage herself, the camp-follower blindsided by her devotion to war and its profits, has remained an archetypal figure. The English company at the Canadian Arts Centre gives Ottawa audiences a chance to renew her acquaintance (Jan. 12 to 30) in, appetizingly, a new adaptation and production by Peter Hinton, the company's artistic director, that seems unlikely to be tethered to Brechtian tradition or theory. For one thing, it features music by Kurt Weill, which Brecht's own productions certainly never did. It features the NACs newly recruited 40th Anniversary English Theatre Acting Company, which one hopes will be able to stay together. Tanja Jacobs plays the lead, and her colleagues include at least two actors too long absent from our stages, Geordie Johnson and Waneta Storms. Also noteworthy: The assistant director is Stephen Ouimette (Scrooge in the NACs Christmas Carol), who, apart from being one of our best actors, directed Stratford's fine Timon of Athens a few years ago.

As for peace, or at least virtue: Michael Healey's new play (at the Tarragon till Feb. 7, then at the Citadel, Edmonton, Feb. 20 to March 16) is called Courageous, and -- following on his generous Generous -- its the second in what promises to be a cycle of plays named after hopeful adjectives. And in fact, though no one would call Healey a Pollyanna, his plays do tend to be more hopeful than most; the phenomenal success of The Drawer Boy is due in part at least to the human bond it celebrates. The new play deals, says the Toronto press release, with gay marriage, religious freedom, and liberal [it seems to be a small l"] immigration policy" all stemming from a chance meeting in City Hall. The Edmonton release, more broadly philosophical, says it deals with the gulf between "perfect ideals and imperfect humans," which is a good working definition of comedy. Its always about frailty. Healey breaks with his previous custom by acting in the play; he continues his custom of entrusting each of his plays to a different director. This time, it's Richard Rose.

Courageous exemplifies another, possibly less momentous trend: plays with oracular one-word titles. The Tarragon's other upcoming shows are Hush (in which, apparently, a thrilling mystery takes us to the core of our consciousness) by Rosa Laborde, author of Leo (Extra Space, Feb. 9 to March 21); and Communion, written and directed by Daniel MacIvor (Feb. 23 to April 4). The two have starting points that sound oddly similar, or at least female characters who do; in Hush, "Lily wakes up screaming, again," while in Communion, Lida has a secret; when her psychotherapist does the unthinkable and offers concrete advice (good one) "Lida acts on it."

Opera, of course, has always gone in for one-word titles though, since its probably the ultimate star-vehicle form, the words generally denote people rather than abstractions. The Canadian Opera Company is offering two favourites: Carmen (Jan. 27 to Feb. 27) and Otello (Feb. 3 to Feb. 28). Less familiar titles ( Maria Stuarda, Idomeneo) are held in reserve till later in the season.

One other much-anticipated opening is Cloud 9 (Panasonic, Jan. 19 to Feb. 21), Mirvish Productions annual venture into comparatively high culture. Like Oh What a Lovely War, this is a British play, honoured as a modern classic more in the breach than the observance. (It probably made more of an initial impact in New York than it did in London.) It's the Caryl Churchill play that came before Top Girls, and it anticipates that play in its fracturing of time and in its gender bending; Act 1 is set in Victoria's England, or in its African colonies, Act 2 in Margaret Thatcher's, and the more things change ... well, you get the idea. Alisa Palmer directs, following her successful Top Girls. Her cast bears witness to the fact that the winter, in between festivals, is the best time to cast a top-level Toronto play; everyone's available. Those assembled here include Evan Buliung, Ben Carlson, Juan Chioran and Blair Williams. One of them, if memory serves, gets to play a little girl, complete with skipping rope. The actor who did it originally, Antony Sher, got a knighthood.

2010-01-09-connecting-the-dots-in-this-p:
Try this for a paradoxical situation. A male justice of the peace, Catholic and openly gay, is asked to marry another male gay couple, and refuses on religious grounds. Immediately before this, we've seen him presiding over the union of a heterosexual couple, barely past adolescence, whose chances of happiness seem very fragile indeed.

Those are the starting points of Courageous, Michael Healey's new play. Having set them up, he divides the rest of the action into two apparently independent halves. Act One follows the gay relationships and is very good. Act Two concerns the straights, and is even better. The acts are written in different styles, the first, a conventionally realistic Shavian debate, the second, presentational with one character stepping repeatedly out of the action and even playing with the audience -- which by now, of course, is equally conventional. Both work, the question is, how well do they hang together? The answer is, I'm not sure. Ask me again in a year's time. For now, I'm prepared to settle for the wit and passion of Healey's writing, especially as delivered in a first-rate production with acting that is almost unwaveringly superb.

Act One. One of the rebuffed would-be spouses, who happens to be a lawyer, insists that his hard-won Charter rights have been infringed and complains to the Ontario Human Rights Commission. We don't see the tribunal in process, but we do see a waiting-room confrontation between Brian, the very belligerent lawyer, and Tom, the mild-mannered JP, who proves, when goaded, to be equally passionate about his own convictions, however irrational and even self-harming they may seem. Nobody wins in this scene; alternatively, they both do. Meanwhile, Tom's lover, Arthur, an apparently imperturbable Sudanese businessman, endeavours to plead his case by chatting up Brian's contrastingly nervous partner Martin, and ends up seducing him. Further wrinkle: Arthur threatens to leave Tom unless they marry, the one thing Tom, agonized but consistent, will not, cannot do.

Act Two. "That was rough," says Todd, with special reference to Tom who seems to have lost everything. Todd is the guy who got married at the top of the play and who, immediately after the intermission, announces himself as our narrator for the rest of it. He's feckless --his lifelong philosophy, repeatedly proclaimed, is "what the f--k" -- and, at crucial moments from wedding to job interviews, tieless. His marriage almost got derailed when Tammy, his bride, discovered that Lisa, her maid of honour had given him a blow job the night before. Lisa nevertheless remains in their life, because they both need a friend. With Tammy having given birth and sinking into depression, and with eviction threatened, Todd goes to work, loading bottles of Fresca onto trucks. He has a friend, neighbour and co-worker named George, a Somali refugee, who soon outpaces him in all three departments. George also turns out to be religious, as is their boss (who's also an alcoholic: one more element than the play can use). Slowly and resentfully, though certainly with humour, Todd recognizes that he isn't the centre of the universe, even if he is the narrator.

The dots are all there, begging to be connected, even if the play, for better or worse, refuses to do it for us. Tom, in the first half, and George, in the second, leave the impression that the author -- I speak without personal knowledge--isn't religious but rather wishes he was. Certainly, he respects people who are, but then he seems to respect everybody; though Brian, pressing for a speedy marriage because a delay will upset his plans for lunch, is rather a hard case. He's the one character who doesn't seem driven by love (and whom we never see, at any length, with his lover). Politically, the play is an explicit plea for tolerance; for preserving the values that might make people like George want to move here. Healey writes plays for Canada like nobody else does; he's also, as a playwright, almost unfairly fair. Todd expresses passing shock when he finds himself the victim, and George the beneficiary, of affirmative action; the moment gets a laugh but it isn't pressed, and Todd, whatever his other faults, is nobody's racist. We have two African characters; a poor one who learns English preternaturally fast, and a rich one who revels in his own super-literate command of it. Arthur rocks the theatre by saying that people think he's nice because he doesn't -- sorry, does not -- use contractions. Maurice Dean Wint plays both black roles, endowing them with distinct varieties of preternatural poise.

And here begins the roll call. Patrick Galligan plays Brian with a fire-and-ice ferocity I've never seen in him before. Tom Barnett has a few wavery moments as Tom but is funny and moving when roused to rage and plain moving when abandoned to sorrow. As Todd, Brandon McGibbon takes complete control of character, stage and audience. Erin MacKinnon as Tammy is fine when angry and finer when lost. Lisa, the sketchiest role, is nicely filled out by Melissa MacPherson. Tom Rooney plays both Doug and the soft-drinks dispenser, and conveys miraculous amounts by the most economical of means. Richard Rose directs with infallible clarity, delicacy and force; on David Boechler's bare, triangular set, every moment is charged with energy. The human connections, if not the philosphical ones, are always crystal clear. Anyway, with this play on its main stage and East of Berlin on its third go-round in the Extra Space, the Tarragon can boast of having the two best new plays in ages under one roof.

- Courageous runs through Feb. 7 at the Tarragon Theatre. Call 416-531-1827 for ticket information.

2010-01-15-the-trials-of-triage-and-love:
Vincent Lam's Bloodletting & Miraculous Cures is a collection of short stories about young doctors. We glimpse them at various stages from their undergraduate days, applying to get into medical school, to their first years in practise at a Toronto hospital. The operative word is "glimpse;" the book is a series of vignettes, presented in approximate chronological order, sometimes told in the first person though not always the same first person, some of them focusing on particular cases, others more concerned with the relationships between the principal characters. There's a triangle involving Fitz and Ming, whom we meet as students in Ottawa and who become lovers, and Chen who, like Ming, comes from a Chinese family and who displaces Fitz in her affections when she, with better grades than her boyfriend, moves to Toronto a year ahead of him.

Fragmentary in structure, the stories are also very uneven in quality. Some of them come to life through the quirks or psychoses of the patients, but of the doctors Ming comes over as merely cold and manipulative while Chen is a presumably well-meaning blank. Fitz is the most fully drawn, and his self-tormenting attempts to cling to Ming are painfully believable.

The TV mini-series drawn from the book pretty much maintains this character balance. Ming (Mayko Nguyen) is a bit more likeable in the flesh than she is on the page, partly through the addition of a storyline that's only hinted at in the book. Chen (Byron Mann) remains flat, but Fitz (Shawn Ashmore) is magnetic, an alcoholic running on self-deprecation on the edge of self-hatred.

Jason Sherman, the adapter, has had to pull this trio consistently into the centre of the narrative, while reorganizing much of it and inventing the rest. He's done this by starting where the source material leaves off and then doubling back. In the book, Fitz leaves the hospital for a job with a private plane company that ferries insured travellers back to Canada when they've been taken ill abroad. The TV version finds him delivering a patient to his old haunt, Mercy Hospital (played very convincingly by St. Mike's, Toronto, at least for exterior scenes) and bullied into getting his

old job back by a no-nonsense triage nurse (an invigorating performance by Alison Sealy-Smith). This is awkward because he's previously agreed to act as sperm donor for the child whom Ming and Chen are unable to have. Fitz aptly describes this situation (invented for television) as "f--ked up." It's also extremely implausible; why would they choose him? Doubtless much will be revealed but at the moment -- I've watched four of the series' eight episodes -- I'm having difficulty reconciling what we're told in Part One with something that happens in Part Four. But maybe I've got the timelines scrambled.

That would be easy to do, because in showing us what has gone before, the script goes in for flashbacks, flashbacks within flashbacks and fantasies within flashbacks within flashbacks. These various levels aren't quite as confusing as they may sound, and some of the fantasies are very effective. There may even, if you've read the book, be yet another level, as you try to reconcile the differing chronologies of the two fictions.

The book's penultimate chapter finds Chen and Fitz as SARS patients in neighbouring isolation cubicles. The scene is cryptically flagged in an early episode, but I would guess that TV too is saving it up for near the end. In the meantime, Sherman has been clever about reassembling, and sometimes reassigning, the individual cases that dot the original. Fitz has appropriated one of the best from the book's Dr. Sri, who on TV has been relegated to supporting-player status, though the incident plays less disturbingly than it reads. So, too, does one of Fitz's lowest moments when, post breakup, he lets himself into Ming's apartment and then has to beat a humiliated retreat. In other scenes Sherman improves on Lam's flat dialogue, and he has some nice inventions of his own, including a sweet scene in which Ming, longing for motherhood, finds herself presiding over the birth of triplets. Ming and Fitz also get to meet cute -- or, in this case, re-meet cute -- in good movie tradition.

In less agreeable Hollywod style, Ming's sneering cousin Karl has been turned into a gloating monster. Apparently the story needs a villain. But in supplying one the show pushes itself further in the direction it was probably always fated to go: that of medical soap opera, with heavy musical underlining, in which we're expected to place exaggerated value on the protagonists' emotional states, simply because they're doctors.

It isn't as enervatingly glossy and antiseptic as House or Grey's Anatomy (or as it's known in my neck of the woods, Desperate Housemen) -- it's Canadian, after all -- but it isn't as much fun as Nurse Jackie. Or even, by virtue of that show's central character, as gritty.

- Bloodletting & Miraculous Cures airs Sundays at 8 p.m. on HBO Canada.

2010-01-16-on-day-8-jack-merely-has-to-t:
The last time Jack Bauer enjoyed a happy moment with his family was way back in prehistory. We saw him, at the start of the first season, playing chess with his teenage daughter, Kim. Next thing we knew, Kim was out the door, then abducted, and Jack's descent into hell began. Many traumas later, Kim has a daughter of her own, who looks to be about four. The eighth season of 24 starts tomorrow with Jack, all gentle and crinkly, babysitting her; they're watching cartoons together and apparently having a great time. This cannot bode well. All I can say is, they better not kidnap that kid.

I don't think anyone will. But you never know to what depths people will descend on this show. This season, the bad guys are trying to derail a historic nuclear-inspection agreement between the U.S. and a Middle Eastern country (unnamed, but identifiable as Iran-in-your-dreams) by assassinating that country's president. There's something almost comforting about this. 24 began with an attempt on the life of a presidential candidate and it's good to see the show getting back to first principles after years and years of trying to top itself in the mass-destruction stakes.

24 is endearingly shameless about recycling its familiar tropes, but this time it's making them seem tolerably fresh. As always since Season 2, we have a weary, disillusioned Jack determined to stay away from his old counterterrorist existence; he wants to be with his family -- with Kim, with her daughter (named after Jack's wife, Teri, still mourned) and with Kim's latest and rather amorphous partner, Stephen. Once again, trouble comes knocking at his door (literally, this time); but, for once, it's Kim who persuades her dad to fight the good, or at least less compromised, fight. ( "You couldn't live with yourself if you didn't.")

This time around, Kiefer Sutherland looks older. A lot older. It becomes him, though. He still gets to use the patented Jack Bauer interrogation technique -- asking a question and immediately repeating it as a shout -- and to say "stay with me" to a guy who's bleeding to death on him. And that's just in the first two episodes.

The faux-Iranian head of state is played by Anil Kapoor, from Slumdog Millionaire, on the well-established principle that one exotic ethnicity is as good as another; actually, it's good to see him. He has a smooth brother and aide (as statesmen on this show so often do) and the two of them converse in Fluent Exposition.

I've carped before at 24' s habit of assuming a complexity in Jack Bauer that has never actually been demonstrated. This time there may be hope; Sutherland conveys a believable world-weariness even in the action scenes. One actually roots for him to find peace and go join Kim and the family back in L.A. -- though why he should want to live there, considering the memories the place must hold for him, Jack only knows. Maybe he'll get through this time without torturing anybody. In the meantime, the suspense stays tense. Maybe I relax my standards for this show, but it can still have me on the edge of my seat.

- 24' s two-part season debut airs tomorrow at 9 p.m. ET/PT on Global.
2010-01-16-what-s-a-girl-to-do-when-boys:
The Next Stage Theatre Festival provides additional exposure for groups that have attracted attention at the Toronto and other fringes. Ive seen three of this year's shows.

The Red Queen Effect (Seventh Stage Theatre Productions) takes its title from the famous advice offered to Alice by the spiky imperious monarch in Through the Looking Glass: "Here it takes all the running you can do to stay in one place." The show's protagonist is called Alice, and she comes before us with the authentic straight-haired look of the John Tenniel drawings and with the determination with which Lewis Carroll endowed his heroine, though neither she nor anyone else has the wit that Carroll bestowed on everybody.

Alice works in a financial company; shes the new girl, indeed the only female in sight apart from the bosss unsympathetic second-in-command. A Red Queen figure, speaking in execrable rhyming couplets (why do people think these are so easy to write?) tells us that life in the finance business is like moving on a chessboard. Alice's immediate and very patronizing superior is compared to Humpty Dumpty, mainly because he suffers a great fall; there's very little resemblance earlier on. That about does it for the literary references. And in fact this Alice doesnt stay in the same place; she rises, through her own hard work and intelligence, arousing first the resentment and then the enforced acceptance of her male colleagues.

The show, devised by the ensemble, develops in Kelly Straughans production as a mixture of dialogue and dance. Its best scene, by far, comes when a visiting tycoon surprises Monica Dottor's Alice working late; looking to make a deal with her employers, he ends up offering her the chance to broker it. (He probably fancies her as well.) For this encounter, the script, which has previously been straining every nerve to be paradoxical, relaxes into actual conversation and allows the actors to do the same. Nicholas Campbell's intruder, in particular, lifts the proceedings to a whole new level of distinction. The only other actor to come near it is Dylan Scott Smith as the incumbent CEO, nervous but ruthless. Other leading performances are terrible. The remaining players (six of them) make up a male chorus line, executing jerky ballets of masculine conformity that are neat the first time and tiresome thereafter. Theres also a confusion of satiric aim. We spend the show rooting for Alice to crash through the glass ceiling (shes less like Alice than like Peggy in Mad Men); when she does it, the show turns around to tell us -- shades of Top Girls -- that she's become part of what she should be hating. They've left it a little late to change the subject.

Gas (jsquared. theatre) is another dance of splintering male camaraderie, though with choreography more verbal than physical, but again with a woman joining and beating the boys at their own game. Written and directed by Jason Maghanoy, it shows five U.S. soldiers guarding gasoline supplies in Iraq and torn apart -- both individually and as a group -- by their split reactions to a single violent incident. Writing and performance are at their best early on, exploring the squads bravado, their learned hardness, their hopes and fears and homesickness. There are two apparently separate plot lines that converge, too neatly to be believed. Increasingly, its the bravado that takes over; the actors, not just the characters, get high on style. The dialogue becomes literary-tough, and the performances take on the same distanced, fake-intense quality. It's effective, but diminishingly so, and only in a generalized way. And though they've obviously worked very hard at being authentic, theres still something second-hand about it, a sense of playing at soldiers. Its as if a Canadian theatre company, while implicitly condemning the American presence in Iraq, also envied it: not the experience itself, but the theatricality of it.

The best Next Stage show I saw was Quite Frankly (Screwed & Clued), though it seemed at first that it was going to be awful. It's a one-man piece, whose author/performer, Justin Sage-Passant, is a British-born performer who's been over here for several years but still has his native rhythms down pat. (His director, Jonno Katz, is Australian.)

The patness is initially a problem. Playing an inhibited, mother-ridden 33-year-old man in an English provincial town, Sage-Passant is adept at hitting off the other, rowdier people with whom his hero comes in contact, but he does them, one especially, at self-indulgent length. A digression on how to get served at a bar (the only place in England where people dont queue up, instead forming what customers and servers recognize alike as "a virtual queue") is funny, and absolutely accurate, but it belongs in a magazine piece rather than a play; it doesnt help the story. The central figure, holding himself at a clenched, skewed angle, comes gradually to life though, as a human, imprisoned in gentility, rather than a caricature. He's been humiliated since childhood and his mother, now incontinent and largely helpless, has been the prime agent and abettor of this. But she's all he has, and vice versa, and his acceptance of this finally gives him a kind of dignity. The performance is carefully shaped to this peak, and attains it.

- The Next Stage Festival ends tomorrow at the Factory Theatre (Main and Studio Spaces). For showtimes and ticket information, call 416-966-1062 or visit fringetoronto.com.

2010-01-19-the-brat-act-buble-still-has-:
M ichael Buble, answering a question from the audience, expresses huge admiration for Elvis Presley because, somewhere inside himself, "he realized all the screaming wasn't real; hed mastered self-deprecation." Elvis, of course, had a self -- and a position at the very top of the hill -- to be deprecating about. He didnt have to work at it. Buble, still a newcomer, has to work very hard, both at being a hyperactive performer and being ironic about it in between numbers. It's very early for him to start sending himself up: early in his career and early in tonight's TV show. In Michael Buble at the Concert Hall (taped at the Masonic Temple, Toronto) he starts in on the roguish Q&A after having sung a mere two numbers.

Those two opening songs, All of Me and Georgia on My Mind, happen to be the two on the program closest to what are usually known as standards. All of Me was a favourite starter for Sinatra himself, and Buble does it in Sinatra style, at Sinatra tempo, and with Sinatra lyric-changes: "Cant you see Im just a mess without you." And so with the next tune: Georgia, I said Georgia, he interpolates, just like Ray Charles said Georgia. It seems to me that, if you want to breathe new life into old repertoire, it would help to go back to the original texts, rather than thoughtlessly reproducing what other singers have definitively done with them. Influence is one thing, imitation is another.

Original interpretation, though, isn't what bubbly Buble is about. He's one of a crop of neo-crooners, male and female, who are credited with rescuing the Great American Songbook from neglect, even though scores of jazz and cabaret performers have been exploring it for decades with far greater imagination and dedication: singers like Daryl Sherman, Wesla Whitfield, Eric Comstock, Justin Hayford. (Yes, I know you havent heard of any of them. Thats my point.) His initial success seems to have landed him with an identity problem. He's intelligent enough to know that being a "Sinatra knock-off" (his words) lays him open to mockery, so he tries to get in first. He does all his own announcements, even the ones promising that he'll be back with untold goodies after the commercial break. The idea is that he plays at being arrogant, while trying to disarm us by admitting it. Asked why he chose his career, he says frankly that he did it to get laid, then says that, of course, the official pious answer would be that he felt blessed to be able to carry on the legacy of my idols. This ought to come over as a welcome refusal of showbiz sanctimony, like Ricky Gervais hosting the Golden Globes, but the smile with which he accompanies it is suspiciously sickly.

Thats about the last we hear of his idols, or of their legacy. He does invoke Dean Martin before going into Youre Nobody Till Somebody Loves You, a lyric from whose sentiments he disassociates himself before starting (as well he might); as he does it, it's very Vegas but doesn't actually swing. Otherwise, he mainly sings his own compositions, for which he goes very pious, even while kicking his legs. He does a lot of that, also a lot of knee-bends, and his suit is very shiny. The kinetics, though, never seem to have much to do with what hes actually singing. At the end, he thanks us for accompanying him on this "journey": rather a grandiose term, surely, for a half-hours worth of performance. As it happens, though, the last stage of the trip is the best. His closer is Save the Last Dance for Me, a song nicely poised in date and quality between the classics to which he can't do justice and his own soppy originals. He gives it the right lightness of touch, and it can use both his moves and his urge to mingle with an adoring female audience. He may be shaping up less as the next Sinatra, or even the next Bobby Darin (not enough edge), than as the next Engelbert Humperdinck, but I'd take his last dance over Engelberts last waltz, any time.

- Michael Buble at the Concert Hall airs tonight at 10 p.m. on Bravo!

2010-01-23-poetry-of-personal-hells-has-:
All roads lead to Shakespeare. It's still a shock to find him signposting a pair of journeys as painful as those chronicled in Judith Thompson's Such Creatures, a play that juxtaposes two parallel monologues. One concerns Blandy, a Toronto teen who's been bounced from mother to father to school to foster home to street, and who is now facing a murderous girl gang who think she has disrespected them. At some point in her past she was one of three Hamlets in a school production, and though she at first rebelled against the idea, she found the lines speaking both to and for her. She came in on the closet scene with the queen (this must mean she got to do about half the play), which reminded her of all her rows with her mother and her mother's boyfriends; while the Ghost made her think of her own absentee dad. At some point, too, Blandy and her mom consulted a psychic whose unsatisfactory prophecies she dismissed with a withering "we defy augury." This, though the chronology is scrambled, presumably happened after her success as the great Dane.

In tandem with her, we have Sorele, an Auschwitz survivor, sent there as a young girl from Warsaw, where she had recently triumphed as Miranda in The Tempest. Shakespeare's words keep tripping off her tongue, too; at one point in her ordeal she even heard another inmate addressing her in the voice of Prospero -- in English apparently, with cultural cachet intact, though logic suggests that she would have played it in Polish or maybe Yiddish. Miranda's "brave new world" speech gives the play its title, though Sorele comes to feel that she and her companions were more like Caliban -- robbed of their identities, treated like brutes. Now, dying of cancer (nobody ever accused Thompson of being extravagantly cheerful), she's returned to the camp to settle her mental accounts.

Everybody thinks, and is entitled to think, that their own personal hell is the worst ever. But when two of them are placed side by side on the same stage, comparisons are inevitable; and to equate the Toronto streets with the death camps is frivolous going on obscene. It's the more uncomfortable because the Canadian story is probably better written, and certainly better acted, than the European one. Michaela Washburn feeds gutsily and wittily off the streetwise girl-talk that Thompson has provided for Blandy; I can't vouch for or against its authenticity but it certainly has flavour. (Blandy says that when she's drunk she feels extra, and initially dismisses being in a play as "too gay," by which she doesn't mean gay.)

Over in the other half of the evening, Maria Vacratsis tries hard to naturalize Sorele's storytelling, but the more she tries to break it up with pauses and underlinings, the more literary and artificial it sounds. She also, in Brian Quirt's production, has to deliver her first speech from a seat in the audience, making her, at least from my section of Theatre Passe Muraille's backspace, invisible; the same disregard for this tiny house's peculiar sightlines afflicts the closing tableau, a sort of defiant Pieta that finally brings the two characters together. Defiance is what's supposed to link them. Sorele was involved in the rebellion that destroyed one of the Auschwitz crematoria, a story that Thompson unreels with an adroit sense of how to give and withhold information. She's also very efficient and, of course, effective at parcelling out the unceasing horrors. But the competence of the writing only makes its structure more offensive; when Blandy's voice is suddenly conscripted as that of a doomed prisoner, it cheapens both stories. Sorele is also given a couple of lines linking Auschwitz to Palestine, as in "the persecuted becomes the persecutor." This is the kind of glib equivalence of which Caryl Churchill's 7 Jewish Children was unjustly accused. Churchill, with extraordinary economy, took us inside the situation. Thompson has an omniscient narrator gesture at it.

La Comunion, written and directed by Beatriz Pizano, exposes a less familiar set of atrocities: the use of child soldiers by both sides, guerrillas and paramilitaries, in the endless conflict in Colombia. This is special-case theatre, in which the impact of the subject matter has to battle the earnest clumsiness with which it's presented. Long by current standards, it yet seems to end when it's still getting started. A guerrilla who was recruited at 11 and whose four years of travails we've been following in detail, escapes to Canada from where she manages to secure the release of a prize hostage. Just like that.

- Such Creatures runs through Feb. 6 at Theatre Passe Muraille Backspace. For show time and ticket information, call 416-504-7529. La Comunion runs through Jan. 31 at Buddies in Bad Times. For ticket information, call 416-975-8555.
2010-01-29-some-pat-answers-cleopatra-do:
It seems that Bernard Shaw, in his Caesar and Cleopatra, didn't tell the whole truth about Caesar and Cleopatra. Well, we guessed that up to a point; few can have believed that the real Caesar was the sexless superman and cryptopacifist of the playwright's self-identifying dreams. It now appears, though, that GBS even got the facts of his star couple's first meeting wrong. In the play, it's not until they are already well acquainted that Cleopatra has herself delivered to Caesar rolled up in a carpet. In history, it's how she got in to see him in the first place. Least that's what Plutarch says.

It's also what Cleopatra: Portrait of a Killer says. This BBC documentary is part archeological detective story, part bargain-basement classic epic. Its starting-point is the discovery, 80 years ago, of a buried body believed to be that of Cleopatra's sister Arsinoe, described in the narration as "the only member of Cleopatra's family we have the remains of." The burial-site was in Ephesus, in what is now Turkey; and the reason Arsinoe ended up so far from her Egyptian home is that, after her sister had become queen courtesy of the invading Romans, she had been banished there. Initially, she had been taken to Rome as part of Caesar's triumph but, unusually for such captives, her life had been spared. Her two brothers, both named Ptolemy and both in succession married to her, hadn't been so lucky; their sister-bride didn't want any rivals in the family. Either Arsinoe benefited from Caesar's famous clemency or (this program suggests) sacrificing a frightened teenage girl would have looked bad even to a Roman crowd. So long as Caesar remained alive, Arsinoe was safe. After his assassination, and especially after Cleopatra hooked up with the less scrupulous Mark Antony, she was dead meat.

All this is history, and it's unclear why this TV show is presenting it as some kind of shocking revelation. The precise details of Arsinoe's murder may be unclear, but nobody can doubt that she would have been disposed of like this, or that Cleopatra would have been behind it. We've always known she was ruthless. Nor are her marriages to her brothers anything remarkable; these incestuous unions were standard practice among the Pharaohs. The show wants to destroy a "romantic illusion" that no one actually has. Eager to dish what it seems to believe is fresh dirt, it suffers from a bad case of split focus. It wants to be about Cleopatra, but the only "portrait" it paints is that of her sister.

The only mystery surrounds the body itself: whether it's that of Arsinoe or of some other woman buried in Ephesus around the same time. The tomb's decoration, based on the Pharos lighthouse in Alexandria that was one of the ancient world's seven wonders, suggests that the corpse must have been Egyptian. An Austrian archeologist and an English historian join forces to identify the skull and bones more precisely, and they build a conclusive case that they are indeed those of Arsinoe. They even manage a forensic reconstruction of her face: the closest thing to a snapshot of Cleo herself that we are ever likely to behold. They also manage to establish that Arsinoe, and hence Cleopatra herself, were of part-African descent; though even here they've been anticipated by the professional theatre, which has been casting black actresses as Cleopatra (in both Shaw and Shakespeare) for years now. The show also seems dubious that mere scholarship will hold its audience. It's punctuated by melodramatic music, to (literally) drum up suspense. A standard mid-Atlantic narrating voice (belonging to Colin Stinton, an American actor based in London) makes portentous promises about "the killler, the victim, and why she died:" cue percussive music and commercial break.

The principals are regularly seen in ruminative close-up; at other times guys in tunics and breastplates march across the screen, pretending to be the Roman army. Nobody, of course ever says anything, though Arsinoe at the point of death is allowed a scream, which may have necessitated the striking of a separate contract. This undramatic "dramatization" looks, as always, ludicrous. The bits that don't look like rejects from Rome look like inserts from Indiana Jones, but at least there's some reason for them. People digging may not be the most telegenic of subjects, but they are what the program is meant to be about.

- Cleopatra: Portrait of a Killer premieres Sunday at 9 p.m. ET on Discovery Channel.

2010-01-30-love-is-a-battlefield-megan-f:
Caryl Churchill's Cloud 9, first seen in 1979 and now mounted by Mirvish with a tremendous cast, anticipates her slightly later Top Girls in its themes and schemes. Its first act is set in British Africa in 1880. Its second takes us to London a century after, but for the characters, as the program puts it with unimprovable succinctness, "it is only 25 years later." Philosophically translated, this means that they, and society in general, should have had time to shed their Victorian hang-ups, but havent.

A few Act One figures make ghostly appearances in Act Two, but only three survive alive; and of these, one, a little girl patriotically christened Victoria, appears in childhood only as a rag doll (and is tossed around with comparable abandon). Her brother, Edward, is very possessive about the dolls own doll, and is played -- in the first act but not the second -- by a woman. This discontinuity is itself continuous; Betty, the children's mother, is a man before the intermission and a woman after. The gender-bending makes a pertinent point about fluid sexual identities, but it mostly registers as good theatrical fun.

It certainly does in Alisa Palmer's production whose first half hits, clear and strong and precise, every mark in a very witty script. In this outpost of the empire, both the natives and the imperialists are restless. Clive, head of the family, is lecherously involved with a fearless neighbour, a Mrs. Saunders. Betty has a passionate thing for Harry Bagley, an explorer who might have stepped out of Boys Own Paper, and who is indeed primarily interested in boys, especially Edward. (Edward reciprocates.) Harry nevertheless ends up married to Ellen, the governess, who would be a lesbian, especially with Betty, if she knew how. Clive urges wedlock on Harry, as an atonement for his sin. "It isnt a sin," says Harry, gaining our enlightened approval and then promptly losing it by sobbing its a disease, an instant reverse that shows Churchill at her quick-witted sharp-edged best. Also encamped is Maud, Betty's dragon mother, ostensibly visiting though as Betty shyly admits, "I think she's living with us." The group is completed by Joshua, the ostensibly and ostentatiously faithful black servant, disowning his own people while making himself available in any capacity his masters may require of him. These permutations are executed in brisk cartoon style and, apart from lingering doubts about the Victorians being an easy target, they are very satisfying.

The doubts linger longer in Act Two, which is set in a London park and now seems more dated than its fantastical predecessor. Victoria, discontentedly married, and her aggressive lesbian friend Lin, watch over their unruly children (one again unseen, and without even a doll to represent him). Edward has grown up gay, and very gentle, with a regular and very promiscuous partner named Gerry. Betty, since her husbands demise, has discovered masturbation and gives a monologue; she is not, even giving all possible hostages to magic realism, remotely recognizable as the same person, which throws the plays whole strategy in question. There's a limit to how much you can change style and preserve content. The play's title, and its title song, refer to a sexual nirvana which Edward, Victoria and Lin try to reach through establishing a) a menage and b) an orgy. The latter leaves them looking silly, which may be the intention, and the play looking scrappy, which probably isnt. The modern setting, and Churchills command of dialogue, set up expectations of believability that are neither fulfilled nor compensated for. The colonialist theme is mostly abandoned, apart from one bit about Belfast, which now seems, if you'll pardon the expression, dragged in.

But these actors. If there's a first among equals its Megan Follows, bringing off multiple quick changes as governess and adventuress, and then tripling up as sharp-tongued Lin. Ben Carlson finds chilly hidden depths in Joshua, the only first-act character granted an inner life; the others have secrets, which is different. Hes equally commanding as rough-trade Gerry. Evan Buliung is the tallest but most enchanting of expatriate ladies as first-act Betty and a sweet-natured second-act Edward. Yanna McIntosh, bustle in the ascendant, is a resoundingly epigrammatic grand-matriarch, and an even better thoughtful Victoria. Blair Williams, as her husband and as handsome Harry, provides two studies in sexual bafflement. Ann-Marie Mac-Donald, more revue performer than actress, is delightful as child Edward but damagingly far from believability as grown-up Betty whom she makes a comic turn. David Jansen by contrast, is a splendidly brisk cove as Clive; but his sullen little girl left me nostalgic for the delicate skipping of Antony Sher, one of my two abiding memories of the play's first production. My other is of its ending, a musical dying fall for which Palmer's staging substitutes an abrupt full stop.

- Cloud 9 runs through Feb. 21 at the Panasonic Theatre. Visit mirvish.comor call 416-872-1212 for show times and ticket information.
2010-02-02-a-moveable-piece:
The Thistle Project is a company avowedly dedicated to adapting "non-theatrical sources to the stage." Peer Gynt, Ibsen's sprawling comic epic, may just about qualify; Ibsen didn't intend his poem -- a sprawling comic epic -- to be staged, at least not initially. All the same, it's long since become part of the theatrical repertoire; it's the work of a master playwright and is in five-act dramatic form, with dialogue and characters and a story and stuff, so it can hardly help being a play. In fact, it's a great play: the greatest, I think, outside of Shakespeare.

It does present practical problems. Performed as written it would take at least four hours and a cast of thousands. The Thistle's adaptation lasts just over 90 minutes and has a cast of two. Susan Coyne plays Peer, the 19th-century Norwegian dreamer whose turbulent peasant youth gives way to a prosperous expatriate middle age and who eventually returns home to face death and -- the one thing he has always evaded -- disillusion. Matthew Romantini plays everyone else, from Peer's exasperated but fiercely protective mother to the Button-Moulder, sent to melt down Peer's soul in his casting ladle and then recycle it, on the grounds that he has never been whole-hearted enough to qualify for either heaven or hell.

The Thistle's other advertised principle is the use of "space and the body." The space around which Erika Batdorf, the director, moves her two actors' bodies is that of Holy Trinity Church, just behind Toronto's Eaton Centre. During Peer's youth, when he's climbing up mountains and invading the kingdom of the trolls, we follow him around, promenade-style. When he advances into his more sedentary years, we too are allowed to sit down (on benches) and watch him. Much of Batdorf's staging is brilliant; she makes imposing use of the site's built-in resources of lighting and sound (Richard Feren composed the music, Tom Kerr plays it) and inventive use of a few simple recurring props and masks. She also continually finds new and surprising ways to introduce the characters. Romantini, whose background is in dance, is as likely to appear beneath our feet as before our eyes, and his multiple performance -- switching roles and sexes by the mere donning or doffing of a shawl -- is unfussily spectacular; he can raise or chill the temperature without raising his voice. He seldom has to play more than one role at a time, but when he does, he's fully up to it; one scene has him faultlessly alternating poses and accents as a trio of gentleman tourists. His Button-Moulder, courteous and implacable, could well be definitive.

Coyne's Peer is unlikely to be, and not just for reasons of gender, but it has a lot going for it. Her emergence as a writer (notably with Slings and Arrows) has coincided with her new maturity as a character actress (notably in Slings and Arrows). She has great shy charm, and charm is part of what makes Peer, especially in his youth, tick; he gets away with everything short of murder. She is fine, too, in Peer's most moving scenes. Even better is the biting satire she brings to the middle-aged Peer's gospel of success. "Being oneself " is Peer's obsession and the play's; as a middle-aged slave trader who's salved his conscience by simultaneously exporting missionaries, he preaches a entrepreneurial creed of self-sufficiency that denies all social bonds and all responsibilities. It's very topical and practically prophetic. It's also what leads him to the casting ladle.

The performance falls short in Peer's final despair and, throughout, in his swagger. What first strikes anyone in reading the play is its humour, which hardly stops; in this production -- as, to be fair, in almost every one I've seen -- it largely evaporates. The spartan staging contributes to this; so does the unfriendly church acoustic and the text itself, credited to Batdorf "with the company" and probably patched together from existing translations. The original isn't just in verse, it's in rhyme; and I'm convinced, for it to work in English, someone needs to do for Ibsen what Richard Wilbur and Tony Harrison have done for Moliere: restore the clinching force and the sheer fun, of couplets. Without it, the piece seems pinched. It also, what with all the cutting and doubling, can't help being confusing; for all the virtuosity in display, I doubt if anyone without prior knowledge of the text could always figure out what was going on or between whom. I couldn't tell at the end whether Romantini was playing the Button Moulder or Solveig or both at once. Here I suspect the production lost its nerve. It couldn't face up to the possibility of Peer being saved by the love of a good woman or countenance the idea of her doing such a thing. But it wouldn't be sentimental; Peer still has to face the Button-Moulder --and it brings back the mother-motif full force. The play's a comedy, and it ends with the hero getting the girl, albeit in peculiar circumstances. This isn't, then, the ideal way to do Peer Gynt; but we seldom see it done in any way at all, and on its own terms this attempt is remarkable.

- Peer Gynt runs until Feb. 21. Call 416-536-6468 ext. 40 for more information.

2010-02-06-intimate-intensity-mandy-pati:
According to Patti Lu-Pone, a very smart booker approached her agent and said: "We have Mandy, how about Patti?" According to Mandy Patinkin (I spoke to them separately, in two different calls), someone a few years ago said, We have this new theatre in Dallas, we have Patti, how about Mandy? However it happened, this was the start of Patti and Mandy, the show that they have been doing together "on and off for about three or four years," across the United States and in Australia and New Zealand, and that they are about to bring to Toronto.

Its a reunion. Thirty years ago, LuPone played the title role in the Broadway production of Evita, with Patinkin playing Che. She was a known musical performer, even star, at the time; he wasn't. He thought of himself as an actor, not a singer; still does in fact: I'm an actor; sometimes the words I act are set to music. When his agent, after the Evita auditions, called and told him hed got the part, "I didnt know what part."

The two of them hadn't worked together since, but they'd stayed in touch. When the idea came of doing an evening of songs together, they were adamant that it wouldnt be just an evening of songs. Patinkin had always those shows where one performer comes out and does his stuff, then the other comes on and does hers, and they only meet for some token duets at the finale. So they put together a program of, in LuPones words, showtunes that tell a story. A love story, naturally, because what else would you do with showtunes?

It was Patinkin who did most of the putting-together. LuPone didn't have the time or, one suspects, the inclination. According to Patinkin she said, presumably in her gum-chewing voice, "go ahead, doll." When the two of them got together they started, as she says, tweaking the lineup: a lineup that ranges from I Really Can't Stay (a. k.a. Baby, Its Cold Outside) to Everybody Says Dont, the latter an aggressive song from the Stephen Sondheim cult flop Anyone Can Whistle. There is quite a lot of Sondheim in the show, as you might expect. Both performers are widely associated with his work, though in fact Patinkin has only appeared in one of his musicals (he created the title role in Sunday in the Park with George, and had to search his memory to confirm that really was the only one) and LuPone in one-and-a-half, both revivals: She was Mrs. Lovett in Sweeney Todd and Rose in Gypsy, for which Sondheim wrote the lyrics. Patinkin says of his association with Sondheim that "for me, he's William Shakespeare. They both have an uncanny sense of human nature -- I think they both work from elements of darkness that they illuminate for us." Given both writers' unerring capacity for finding the right words, that isnt an extravagant assessment.

Theres also a lot of Rodgers and Hammerstein. We start with South Pacific," Lu-Pone says, "and end with the Bench Scene from Carousel -- that's the big love scene built around If I Loved You. Occasionally in the show, one or other of them is alone onstage, but mostly even if it's just one of them doing the singing, the other is right there reacting. Patinkin calls it the story of two souls"; also, less grandiloquently, "a balls-out entertaining evening, thats nothing but fun, though he also adds we dont tell jokes -- we're not comics, we're actors." They also dance a bit: Ann Reinking has contributed what Patinkin calls "age-appropriate choreography.

Patinkin is known as an intense actor and especially singer, both in his love-it-or-hate-it performing style and in the volume and variety of work he takes on. Patinkin was in New Haven when I called, working on a new play called Compulsion, which takes its title from the American novel by Meyer Levin that was based on the Leopold and Loeb murder case. It isnt, though, based on the book; its the story of Levin's fight to get his adaptation of Anne Frank's diary onto the stage and of the plagiarism suit he launched against the authors whose version was used. (He even sued Otto Frank.) Patinkin plays the Levin character; asked if he thought the affair had destroyed Levins life, he first said that it did, then thought and amended it to it defined his life; it didnt destroy it." The show opened at the Yale Repertory Theatre last week, then was put on hold for a week so Patinkin and LuPone could fulfill their Toronto commitment. Later this year Patinkin will be re-united with Hal Prince, who directed him in Evita, for a new musical called Paradise Found. He plays the Shah's Grand Eunuch though it isn't an Oriental story; its set in Vienna, which explains why it uses music by Johann Strauss II, fitted with lyrics by the greatly underrated Ellen Fitzhugh, and with a book by the American playwright Richard Nelson. Susan Stroman co-directs with Prince, and the cast includes a half-dozen other Broadway luminaries. It opens in New Yorks favourite new try-out place, London.

LuPone is also known as an intense performer, and I asked her whether this accounted for the onstage chemistry between them. She says no ( "I have equal chemistry with Boyd Gaines, and he's very laid-back), but that Mandy and I have a combination onstage of sexual energy, personal energy, work energy. You can intellectualize but ... it's just our chemistry." She, too, sees herself as "primarily as an actor, led by lyrics, and adds that shes actually done more plays than musicals. Which is surprising but, as she also says, musicals have a higher profile." Patinkins take on their collaboration is that "it completely rests on our pleasure in each other, our love for each other; if you like being onstage, it doesn't get better than doing it with Patti. Which would be the best possible place to end, if it weren't trumped by Lu-Pone's definition of theatrical spontaneity: Theatre is an accident waiting to happen."

- An Evening With Patti Lu-Pone & Mandy Patinkin plays Tuesday through Sunday at the Royal Alexandra Theatre in Toronto. Call 416-872-1212 or visit mirvish.comfor tickets.
