2010-02-06-light-in-the-piazza-ideal-for:
An overture in a musical is a rare thing these days. The Light in the Piazza had me in its corner from the first notes played by a quintet, with a harp predominant, from behind a scrim. The opening theme they offer is a ravishing one, heralding a score and a show that turn out to be uncommonly beautiful and peculiarly moving.

It's peculiar in two senses: scarcity and strangeness. Honestly romantic musicals, of which this is one, are an endangered species, and this show, which ran for about a year in New York, tells an unusual and theoretically difficult tale. The Light in the Piazza, music and lyrics by Adam Guettel, is based on a New Yorker short story (by Elizabeth Spencer) that afterwards became a novel. Margaret, middle aged and middle American, comes to Florence where she spent her honeymoon, with her daughter Clara in tow. Clara is in her mid-twenties but her mental development, for guilt-inducing reasons, stopped short when she was 12; her physical and emotional development obviously didn't and neither, it becomes clear, did her perceptions. They meet Fabrizio, aged 20; he falls heavily for Clara, as she for him, even wants to marry her. His family offer few objections, but then they don't know the whole truth about Clara, and Margaret can never quite manage to tell them.

The unfolding of this story is remarkably un-queasy. It is, though, creatively disturbing, because not only does the audience not know what's going to happen, it doesn't know what it wants to happen. We have our own prejudices to overcome. The emotional effect isn't always due to the songs; Craig Lucas's book is exceptionally skilful and discreet. In Robert McQueen's very fine production for Acting Up Stage, one of the most powerful scenes involves Jacquelyn French as Clara simply rushing distraught about the stage; another has her, lost and frightened in a strange city, accosting strangers and reciting her name and address, the safety code her mother obviously taught her.

The New York production was by all accounts a visual feast. This one isn't quite that, but it has a good spare look, and it makes us listen. Guettel's music, flavouring and pervading the evening as in a chamber opera, is alternately bracing and sensual. The Italian characters sing mainly in Italian (this isn't confusing) and are joyous and full-throated, even when cynical; Jeff Lillico's Fabrizio, ardent and naive, and Juan Chioran as his witty and worldly father are beyond good, while Christina Gordon, Tracy Michailidis and Michael Torontow supply some darker sidelights as their relatives (of whom one would like to know more than the show tells us). The two American ladies, let loose in their and most other people's dream country, have numbers that veer between spiky and abandoned, with something of Richard Rodgers (Guettel's grandfather) and something of Stephen Sondheim (Guettel's mentor). The only song that misfires is the title number; the most conventional item in the score, it seems to be trying strenuously to justify a title, and an image of happiness, bequeathed by its source. The major love duet, Say It Somehow, is musically a marvel, though its lyrics ( "I hear the sound of wrap your arms around me") seem to have lost touch with what these two young people might actually be saying. It's like they've been listening to too many love songs (and Fabrizio's English, I must say, seems to improve spectacularly over a very short period.) Elsewhere, Guettel's words, if not the equal of his melodies, are intelligent and aware.

There's a crucial shortfall in the presentation of Margaret. This is really her story, though at one remove; her own marriage is decomposing, and she's torn between rejecting it, reliving it through her daughter and simply letting Clara, after all these years, go her own way. (She also seems to be nourishing a crush on Fabrizio's papa.) It's through her eyes that we're meant to see the conditional quality of happy endings. It's all there in outline, but not really fleshed out; and Patty Jamieson, though acting and singing well enough, cannot take us deep enough inside the woman for us to believe in some very abrupt transitions. Too much of her is shell. All the same, I haven't witnessed a standing ovation so heartfelt and deserved since the Shaw Festival's The President. That show overwhelmed us with laughter; this one does it with unsentimental tears. Guettel may not be the future of Broadway, things being as they are, but he ought to be.

From the near-sublime to the indisputably ridiculous: Little House on the Prairie, based as it is on a popular series of books that became a television series, seems to be America's answer to Anne of Green Gables, only less gritty. Set in pioneer South Dakota, it doesn't even work on its own tear-jerking terms; we can't be moved by the simple fact of a girl going blind because the show insists on singing inspirational songs about it. For rural flavour, the music strains after Aaron Copland and the dancing after Agnes de Mille. Melissa Gilbert, famous for having played Laura the tomboy heroine on TV, reappears as her mother, for no other discernible reason. Kevin Massey stands out as the love interest of the present Laura (Kara Lindsay, pretty good considering); they have a quirkily shaped second-act duet that seems to have fallen out of a better show. It even hints, briefly, at some sustained narrative interest. Otherwise, it's just one tarnation thing after another, so unspeakably saccharine that for long stretches I could hardly look at the stage.

- The Light in the Piazza runs through Feb. 21 at the Berkeley Street Theatre Downstairs. For details, call 416-368- 3110. Little House on the Prairie runs through Feb. 28 at the Canon Theatre. For more information, visit mirvish.comor call 416-872-1212.

2010-02-13-merrily-they-roll-along:
It looks at the start as if An Evening with Patti LuPone and Mandy Patinkin is going to consist of two Broadway stars singing Broadway songs, strung together to tell a single story. That turns out to be a false trail. What we get instead are groups of songs, each group telling a separate story, plus a few numbers that seem to be there for their own or their performers' sakes.

Its clear, looking back, that we were warned. They start off with Another Hundred People, Stephen Sondheims ode to urban angst. We then move into what seems to be the entire opening scene of South Pacific, which obviously isn't urban. LuPone slips right inside the skin of Nurse Nellie Forbush from Little Rock, Ark.; Patinkin gives a louring performance, both physically and vocally, of Emile de Becque (here described as "a cultured man" rather than "a cultured Frenchman," though it's hard to believe that Patinkin would have trouble with the accent); between them they get through A Cockeyed Optimist, the Twin Soliloquies, Some Enchanted Evening -- practically the whole bit. And since it ends with Emile proposing to Nellie, its not too much of a stretch to see them, though apparently with their names changed, whisked back to Sondheim-land for LuPone to give a flawlessly tongue-twisted account of the neurotic bride from Company who is so not getting married today. This is unexpectedly interspersed with Patinkin singing the super-ardent Loving You, from the same composers Passion. The two songs undercut one another beautifully: a case of Mutually Assured Deconstruction.

But then they go off on another tack altogether: back, it seems, to being singles. The songs continue to be artfully woven together; they're also good and enterprising choices in themselves. We get the only fast version of Baby It's Cold Outside Ive ever heard; a trio of first-rate Jerome Kerns; some prime cuts of Kander and Ebb; and Murray Grands neglected April in Fairbanks, which with the two frozen thesps propelling themselves around the stage on office chairs, is funny if not as hysterically so as the first-night audience seemed to think. (Ann Reinking did the show's amusingly sedate choreography.) There's also a large helping of Sondheims Merrily We Roll Along whose only fault is that it doesnt roll along long enough. I would happily have heard them do the entire score. As it is, the section finishes with Franklin Shepard Inc., a hysterically virtuoso number that finds Patinkin on his most compatible ground. He likes being virtuoso and he seems to like being hysterical.

I was getting to that. Both he and LuPone are known as mannered performers, but she seems to have put her mannerisms on hold, along with her sometimes mushy diction and her brassiness. Here she's precise and economical and, very often, achingly vulnerable: in Like It Was (incredible), In Buddy's Eyes and the aptly named A Quiet Thing. Patinkins fabled falsetto is matched by a lower register thats even more startling, but between the two, the actual songs -- their emotions and their thought-processes -- get mashed. He performs them to death. He switches speeds recklessly and, though he could obviously hit any note he chooses, underlines key points by speaking them. This is self-defeating; the glory of Sondheim's lyrics in particular is that they're impeccably colloquial within a strict musical form. Anyone can talk conversationally. Patinkin, an intelligent and sophisticated actor (he directed the show and, with pianist Paul Ford, put it together), insists on turning himself into a ham.

Just before and just after the intermission, the performers jump track and do Greatest Hits. LuPone, Broadways first Evita, sings Dont Cry for Me, Argentina. The fans scream, but it's a terrible song out of context. In context, it has a saving irony, set up as it is by it's anti-song Oh What a Circus, which Patinkin, Broadways first Che, could sing here but doesnt. LuPone's Everything's Coming Up Roses also plays over-intense, divorced from the revival of Gypsy that gave it birth. Patinkins finest Broadway hour was Sunday in the Park with George, but that shows Finishing the Hat was probably thought too rarified; instead he does Buddy's Blues, which he first assassinated in a concert performance of Follies and which he makes as agonizingly meaningless now as he did then.

But redemption awaits. The final sequence of the show returns to Rodgers and Hammerstein with the magnificent Bench Scene from Carousel. Lu-Pone, heart-stoppingly still and sure, transforms herself into the young Julie Jordan; though Patinkin, who's actually younger, looks and sounds more like her father than her lover --OK for South Pacific but creepy here. However the scene, one of the hottest in musicals, remains magic. Doing still more of Carousel counts, I think, as gilding the lily; it seems for a terrifying moment as if Patinkin might be embarking on the entire Soliloquy. But he doesnt; he does Youll Never Walk Alone, which usually reduces me to a blubbering wreck and did so again. Then there's the encore, bringing Irving Berlin's contrapuntal classic Youre Just in Love and Coffee in a Cardboard Cup, a Patinkin standby that sounds even better when the two of them are going at it in fast and furious unison. And then theres the encore to the encore when, with the house lights up and the mikes off, they sing a standard apiece. Tony Bennett does the unplugged thing at the end of his shows, but they go him one better by being not only unamplified but a capella. You've got to love that. And maybe they do it every performance but it felt spontaneous on Tuesday night.

- An Evening with Patti LuPone and Mandy Patinkin ends tomorrow. Call 416-872-1212 or visit mirvish.comfor more information.

2010-02-17-a-killer-musical-show:
ASSASSINS

Theatre Centre, Toronto

---

One of the new joys of Toronto theatre is the abundance of independent companies, working to the highest standards: Company Theatre, Studio 180, Acting Up Stage and BirdLand Theatre, whose first couple of shows were shaky but who broke through magnificently with The Last Days of Judas Iscariot. They have now (in a joint venture with Barrie's Talk Is Free Theatre) mounted a production of the Stephen Sondheim-John Weidman musical Assassins that hits the same exhilarating mark.

Assassins is a show that alternately seduces and shocks, a pattern that's set within the first two minutes. In an especially dilapidated fairground, the proprietor of a shooting-gallery makes his pitch with a soothing, insidious tune: "Hey, pal -- feelin' blue? ... Hey pal -- I mean you. ... C'mere and kill a President." It's a funny line that blows up in your face. In both tone and meaning, it sums up the show. One of the clients who comes to the booth is actually called Booth. The show mixes and matches the stories of nine people who tried to kill the President of the United States including four who succeeded. It takes us from John Wilkes Booth to Lee Harvey Oswald ( "why" someone asks "do all these rednecks have three names?") and beyond. They aren't presented chronologically; they rub shoulders as in some carnival version of the Bar at the End of the World, goading and mocking and encouraging one another. The final scene finds Oswald in the Texas Book Depository, with the others past and future persuading him to shoot JFK rather than shooting himself. It'll make him famous. Look at Brutus. Look at Booth.

Booth, killing Lincoln to avenge the honour of the South, is the only one with a discernible agenda and a specific target. The others are desperate people, beaten-down or deprived or merely crazy, failures in a society that worships and promises success, lashing out at the most prominent symbol available. Each gets his or her own scene, own song. Some are moving, like Leon Czolgosz, the starving immigrant factory worker who killed Mc-Kinley. Some are farcical, like Squeaky Fromme and Sara Jane Moore, failing to kill Gerald Ford. The show's analysis of what drove them isn't especially original, and it may not even be especially profound, but it has the virtue of being true. Given America's current mood, it seems prophetically scary. (The show was first staged in 1990.) It does run the risk of monotony, but just as you think the show may be repeating itself, it explodes. A tempter-character billed as the Balladeer sings about the land of opportunity ( "the usherette's a rock star ... the mailman won the lottery"); the others respond with "but it's never gonna happen, is it?" and go into the most un-Broadway number ever written by a Broadway composer. ( Assassins didn't actually reach Broadway until 2004, and it didn't run then.) Most show tunes, most musicals, reiterate the promises. This one tramples them under its feet. And it doesn't pretend to feel virtuously good about it, either, though it's immensely enjoyable as a song. The commitment of the actors doing it is thrilling in itself.

Like Judas Iscariot, Adam Brazier's superbly lucid production offers one great individual performance after another, coalescing into an ensemble. Many of the actors double as musicians: a currently popular device but one that makes particular sense here, where they're all part of the carnival troupe, and where their instrumental contributions are an exciting part of the staging.

Weidman's book is the equal, in content and structure, as Sondheim's score, a miniature cavalcade of pastiche Americana, but all infused with an individual voice, from the strumming Ballad of Booth through the lulling, brooding Gun Song ( "all you have to do is move your little finger") to the 1970s throbber Unworthy of Your Love in which John Hinckley and Squeaky Fromme pledge devotion to photographs of Jodie Foster and Charles Manson respectively.

The cast, as you may have gathered, is superlative. Graham Abbey, in a Santa Claus suit, has a mesmerizing high-definition soliloquy as Samuel Byck, taping a message to Leonard Bernstein about his plan to fly a 747 into Nixon's White House while adjuring him to write more love songs. (He hums bits of the Bernstein-Sondheim West Side Story to illustrate. He also eats a banana. Is this Byck's Last Tape?) Mike Ross, in his finest performance yet, is heartbreakingly lost as Czolgosz, and Steve Ross boisterously unsinkable as Charles Guiteau; the two Rosses have a great brief scene together. Paul McQuillan has enormous Dixie style and command as Booth; Christopher Stanton is all pent-up boyish frustration as Hinckley; and Trish Lindstrom's Squeaky, a crop-haired bouncing automaton, makes a hilarious double-act with Eliza-Jane Scott's fretful housewife of a Sara Jane.

Then there are Jay Davis' Zangara, comprised of stomach cramps and an Italian accent; Martin Julien's proprietor, creepily grinning if vocally underpowered; and Geoffrey Tyler's chirpy Balladeer morphing ironically into the desperate Oswald. Reza Jacobs' musical direction is impeccable; Beth Kates' set design has the shooting-stall doing ingenious duty as a scaffold and an execution chamber. As no choreographer is credited, Brazier and the actors must have worked up the steps themselves; they are mainly furious stomps, and perfectly appropriate. The show is the apotheosis of Sondheim's long line of songs for the dispossessed, from Gee Officer Krupke to Sweeney Todd. It's our equivalent of Brecht and Weill, but better; it doesn't sit around, congratulating itself on its own cynicism. It doesn't condone its characters; what it does, far more disturbingly, is understand them.

- Runs through Feb. 20. Visit totix.cafor tickets.
2010-02-19-marriage-of-compliance:
YICHUD (SECLUSION)

Theatre Passe Muraille, Toronto

---

The main space at Theatre Passe Muraille has been transformed into an orthodox synagogue. There's even a Hebrew inscription over the door whose English translation is "without walls," this being the equivalent of the theatre's own name. (I confess: I had to have this pointed out and explained to me.)

Within those non-existent walls, there's a wedding going on. Arrive in good time, and you can watch, even join in, the pre-ceremonial dancing and singing. We are here to celebrate, boisterously, the marriage of Rachel and Chaim.

Well, we aren't really. Yichud (Seclusion) is a play. There is a meta-dramatic kick to it, though, since the actors playing the couple, Julie Tepperman and Aaron Willis, are husband and wife in real life. And just to make art's imitation of life imitating art even more intense, Tepperman wrote the play and Willis directs it. Mazel tov to both of them, as they've done spirited and intelligent jobs, though the writing at least is fragmented -- which, up to a point, was probably the intention.

There is a large -- and by today's straitened standards, a phenomenal -- ensemble, plus a klezmer band, but only six speaking characters. They come in pairs. Apart from Rachel and Chaim, we have her parents and his brothers. Relations within each of the latter couples are strained, and this puts extra pressure on the newlyweds. Theirs in an arranged marriage, and their few dates have been chaperoned. So when, immediately after being officially pronounced man and wife, they are sequestered in the yichud room it's the first time they've been alone together. They've grown up in a North Toronto enclave that seems rather less liberal than the viilage in Fiddler on the Roof, and indeed it's often hard not to be reminded of that show, especially in the staging of the post-nuptial celebrations (though there is, alas, no Bottle Dance). The play is savvy enough to acknowledge the resemblance; bride and groom break into a gently self-mocking rendition of Miracle of Miracles, that proves more touching out of context than it has ever been inside it.

Outside the isolation booth, the in-laws conduct their own duologues, bringing to the boil tensions that have been simmering throughout. Rachel's mother, Malka, has been waiting until the wedding is over before walking out on her own marriage, and she resents her daughter for delaying the moment by insisting on an education and a career. Her husband Mordechai acknowledges that he's been a selfish lover, and has contacted a Torah sex-therapy site for advice. He presents Malka with a numbered list of proposals; she is, smoulderingly, not impressed. Diane Flacks plays Malka and Richard Greenblatt plays Mordechai. He is especially funny when telling the guests a long Talmudic joke whose sexist implications come back, in

the audience's minds at least, to haunt him. She turns on a dime to lacerating effect.

Chaim's elder brothers, Menachem and Ephraim, are both yeshiva teachers. Ephraim (Jordan Pettle) has done better at it; he has a job in New York and Menachem (Michael Rubenfeld) resents it. ( "How's Brooklyn?" Menachem asks. "How's Thornhill?" Ephraim replies.) We first meet them, in the only substantial scene that isn't a duologue, giving their shy and sheltered sibling some highly suspect marital advice. Their gloves come off later, when Ephraim tells how he's incurred the displeasure of his employing rabbi, who's also his father-in-law, by standing up to him over the threatened dismissal of a gay student. Menachem is shocked that Ephraim should have jeopardized the advantages of which he himself is jealous, and tells him he should have toed the line. Ephraim wants to "cure" the student, which seems naive of him; still, there's no doubt that he wins this round, though Jordan Pettle's being an exceptionally sympathetic actor may have something to do with this.

Meanwhile, back in the seclusion zone. Chaim, under the impression that this is where the marriage actually gets consummated, wrestles with Menachem's supposedly Biblical instructions about doing it through a hole in a sheet. I laughed, I admit, like a drain over the uncertainties about how big the hole should be. It gives Chaim and Rachel something to laugh at, too, and it could be the start of a good marriage; we want it to be, since Tepperman is attractively sparky and Willis delightfully earnest. (I'm talking, of course, about their onstage personae, though I'm sure they're very nice off as well.)

I guess most courtship rituals are bizarre, and none come with guarantees of happy endings; still, to these secular Jewish eyes, many of the rules and prohibitions related here seem ridiculous, and some of them barbaric. Rachel seems to endorse this when she suggests that maybe some customs should have been left in the ghettoes of the Middle Ages, and she isn't just talking about holes in sheets. So the play comes over as an attack on ultra-orthodox Judaism, even though it was obviously aiming at something more nuanced; which is why I call it fragmented. Moment by moment, though, it's well written and excellently acted. It's also beautifully staged, on both levels and in all corners of the Passe Muraille auditorium: much credit to Beth Kates, the newly ubiquitous designer also responsible for the modestly environmental set for Assassins and the striking abstract background for Such Creatures. Credit, too, to Passe Muraille for saving the day: Yichud was originally to be co-produced by the Harold Green Jewish Theatre, who pulled out; though a show like this one -- joyous and critical and indigenous -- is surely just what they should be doing. Though if they prefer to mount pre-tested American plays whose authors just happen to be Jews, that I suppose is their business.

- Yichud (Seclusion) runs at Theatre Passe Muraille until Feb. 27. Visit passemuraille. on.caor call 416-504-7529 for more information.

We have a show entitled Once and for all we're gonna tell you who we are so shut up and listen. We also have another show called Hush, which is a much shorter way of saying the same thing. Both focus on characters who are under voting age.

Rosa Laborde's Hush seems to have taken its title from lullabies. Its first line is "I dreamt about you last night." Its second is "people used to think that dreams are a second world and that's what led to the invention of a soul and ghosts and gods." The play seems to inhabit that second world; it presents itself as a series of interlocking dreams.

The dreamers are Harlem, a dentist (his name derives from Dutch ancestry, not from blackness), and his 12-year-old motherless daughter, Lily. They are half the cast. The others are Andre, Harlem's colleague (who is black), and Talia, a lady with whom Harlem appears to be having a relationship. Andre, though perfectly amiable in his everyday life, doubles in Lily's nightmares as a sacrificial priest intent on slaughtering her favourite teddy bear. Lily claims that she never dreams, but Harlem knows that everyone does; her nightmares naturally become his as well. Lily sorely misses the mother she never knew, and acts up at home and at school. The only person she seems able to connect with or confide in is Andre. Harlem ceaselessly intellectualizes (he's the one who advances the "second world" theory) and it puts up barriers between them. Though a convinced carnivore himself, at one meal, he tries the experiment of feeding Lily tofu, which only arouses her disgust. Here he seems to be reflecting the vegetarian influence of Talia, who also comments unfavourably on his keeping a jar of his baby teeth beside his bed. She leaves elegantly phrased messages on Harlem's answering machine, asking him why he hasn't called.

Elegant phrasing is a feature of Laborde's writing here; her people communicate in pithy, electrically charged sentences. A rejoinder at the end of one scene frequently doubles as a punning introduction to the next: a device that seems witty at some points and a mere nervous tic at others. We're kept guessing about what's dream, what's real, what's present, what's past. There's a tantalizing hole in the play's pattern of relationships; exactly half-way through it gets filled in. When the play loses its mystery, it also -- a not uncommon occurrence -- loosens its hold. We aren't meant to take the whole play as a dream(or if we are, I lose interest), but there's one plot development that on any realistic level is, to employ the play's own brand of imagery, almost impossible to swallow. The father-daughter relationship at the heart of the play is well observed and/or imagined, but it comes with a lot of fancy baggage. Richard Rose's production is first-rate, not an ounce of flab upon it, scenic or emotional. The acting, yet again, is super. Graeme Somerville's performance lands him in the front rank; his Harlem coats a furrowed brow and mind with a smiling gloss that may be of immense professional help. Vivien Endicott-Douglas has all the pain and fight and resilience of contemporary pre-adolescence. Conrad Coates radiates reasoned, quizzical concern as Andre, and Tara Rosling would haunt anybody's dreams. Laborde's previous play, Leo, was full of promise and, in style and technique if not in substance, her new one delivers. I was impressed, but I never cared.

"Dad," says Lily at the end, "we've entered the teen years. Could be rocky." She must have seen Once and for all..., which has been brought to World Stage from Belgium by Ontoerend Goed & Kopergietery & Richard Jordan Productions Ltd., credits almost as long as the title. It has been assembled and ferociously ordered by its director Alexander Devriendt from the improvisations of its 13 performers, aged 14 to 18, on the theme of teenage rebellion. Or just teenagedness. What comes across is that adolescence -- a word of which they're fond on the rare occasions when they get to use words -- is a state in which you alternate between having fun and getting mad at everyone, including yourself. Just what it's always been in fact: All that changes is the soundtrack and maybe the access to drugs. One of the cast as good as admits it. After announcing to her (invisible) parents her intention of disobeying everything they tell her, she says, "Everything has been done before; but not by me, not now." True enough, but she doesn't admit the corollary, which is that for us to care about something so commonplace happening to her, we would have to know something about her, and we don't. Or about any of them; they display more individuality in their program bios than on stage. As cliches go, though, this one is forcefully presented; the group alternately burn up the place with energy or cool it with their sullen bewilderment when the energy subsides. It's mainly a series of party scenes with recurring images, the most prominent being a couple heading together into the erotic privacy of a black garbage bag. Like Hush it presents itself as a dream, but a much noisier one. It runs about an hour; Hush goes about an hour and a half.

- Hush runs through March 21 at the Tarragon Theatre. Call 416-531-1827 or visit tarragontheatre.comfor more information. Once and for all... closes tonight at the Enwave Theatre. Call 416-973-4000 for ticket information.

2010-02-26-the-kindness-of-strangers:
The Brigantine Room at Harbourfront Centre, generally a sober site for authorial readings or for devout question-and-answer sessions with Margaret Atwood, has been transformed into a cabaret. The patrons still sit at tables, but instead of merely sipping water, they can gorge on popcorn (free) and alcoholic beverages (not). They may also notice -- indeed they can hardly fail to -- a lady with a ripe French accent and a clown's red nose circulating among them, pre-show, and inquiring after their well-being. She turns out to be Rebecca Northan, originator and performer of Blind Date, which premiered at last year's World Stage festival, and has returned for this year's by popular demand and, if Tuesday's sold-out first night is any gauge, to popular approval. For the duration of the evening, she will be known as Mimi.

The performance proper finds Mimi onstage, at a table of her own, awaiting a prearranged companion for the evening who after two hours (she tells us) has proved a no-show. ( "We haven't even met and already he's insulting me.") So she seeks a substitute, and finds one among the audience. On Tuesday it was Scott, a cartoonist. He became in effect her costar, and he was very good.

"This is not" said Northan at the curtain-call, "a one-woman show." She can say that again (and probably does). The people she was paying tribute to at the time were the techies (who have to do their own improvisation), the ushers and a couple of supporting actors, one of whom gets to do a hilarious silent bit as an undertipped waiter. But her greatest debt was to Scott. All unrehearsed, he had to act out with her a story that took them from first date to going back to her place, and then on to marriage, pregnancy and even delivery. Game guy.

Scott emerged as sweet, funny and intelligent with some very quick come-backs. Expounding on her own mixed feelings about children, Mimi asked him what he does when, in the course of his work, he comes across children he doesn't like. "I draw them faster" he said. Either partner has the right to call a temporary halt to the action and retire to the side of the stage for a time out. "I wish" said Scott, on being told about this, "that life was like that." Right on. He called for one of these times out when Mimi started asking him about his ex-girlfriend who, it turned out, had come to the show with him. Should he act, he asked, as if he were aware or unaware of her presence in the audience? This raised all kinds of questions about the nature of theatre and the relation of fact and fantasy; and it seemed to me that Northan, protected by her persona, was rather flippant and evasive about answering them. I don't know how much the show varies from partner to partner; I would guess that Northan has a number of set routines and tries to steer the action toward them. But she still has to roll with a variety of punches.

An experienced Second City performer, she is a smart improviser. The show is enjoyable, but it's also rather unlikeable. Tina Rasmussen, World Stage's artistic director, says in a program note that Blind Date owes its success to "our desire to see people being real onstage." This strikes me as crazy. Scott and his fellows at other performances may be real; they don't have any choice. But Northan isn't; at least, I doubt that she goes through her offstage life with a red nose and a fake accent. Besides this, she has prepared, and she comes with a set of skills.

Two other entertainments passed through my mind while watching this one. One was the recent visit of Patti LuPone and Mandy Patinkin at which the closing ovation seemed to signify not just appreciation for a job well done but gratitude to such superior beings for doing us the honour of coming us. This struck me as a demeaning reversal of the proper order of things. After all, they were our employees; we (well, not me personally but some of us) had paid for our tickets. The other, humbler enterprise, was the Mysteriously Yours dinner theatre, whose presiding genius Jean Daigle invariably harangues and involves the audience in a Hercule Poirot accent remarkably lie Mimi's. The pattern of his shows is similar as well, from the pre-performance mingle-and-greet to the final adjuration to tell our friends if we liked the show and to shut up if we haven't. That's an old line of course, and the cheerful way in which Daigle & Co always deliver it is a virtual acknowledgment of its corniness. At the end of Blind Date it sounds more like a command.

- Blind Date continues at Harbourfront Centre to March 6. Call 416-973-4000 for details.

'Padom ... padom...padom ... dom ... dom ... dom." Those, as far as I can capture them, are the words repeated, many times, by the three female performers of Future Folk at the start of the show. I don't know what they mean, probably nothing that could be literally translated, but while uttering them, they weave a slow, hypnotic and, as far as I can tell, joyous series of dance movements. It's probably about solidarity.

The three actresses -- Karen Ancheta, Aura Carcueva and Catherine Hernandez -- wrote the show in collaboration with Romeo Candido, who's also the composer. There doesn't seem to be a director, though the production has made it to the stage in very good shape. It's part dance, part drama, part documentary and strong in all departments. In the opening sequence, the dancers are wreathed in what appear to be voluminous shawls. They are, as it turns out, voluminous enough to double as sleeping bags. They are the only props.

The show is about the experiences of Filipino nannies working in Canada. Most of these experiences seem to be unhappy ones. A program note says that "Canada's Live-In Caregiver Program is an important one," but the production expresses serious reservations about the live-in part, which it sees as an open invitation to exploitation. Anyway, it's hard not to be bothered by the paradox of women separated by oceans from their own children while looking after other people's. Paradox, in fact, is a gentle way of putting it. There are moving scenes here, the more heartbreaking for being largely played for comedy, of the nannies phoning home to their own large families, dealing with birthday requests, inquiring after absentee husbands. Still, the government and system most at fault here are not Canada's but the Philippines' own, running on the cheap exported labour of women whose greatest dream is to earn citizenship somewhere else. That's harder to dramatize, though.

On a case-by-case basis, too, the Canadian families who do treat their Filipino nannies with respect might be harder to make theatrically interesting than those who don't. None of the employers actually appear in the play; we only hear about them. One fairly harrowing scene shows a nanny having presumably coerced sex with the man of the house while thinking desperately about her own family, and then being upbraided by the wife on the lines of "this is how you show your gratitude for us taking you into our home." Most of it, though, isn't that stark. We start by thinking that the three performers will be spending all evening as a fluid, generalized collective, but they soon take on individual identities. The prevailing note, as they battle with inhuman schedules and immigration red tape, is of shared and mostly cheerful stoicism.

Where the show falls down is in focusing on a fourth, offstage character: a nanny named Grace who attracts all the bad fortune and treatment the other three manage, at least, to live with. The play turns into a tribute, or an offering to her; but it's hard to be moved by someone we haven't met, especially when she's clearly a symbol rather than a person. Otherwise, no complaints: The show unfolds with delicacy, considerable virtuosity and a passion that's more effective for being understated. It's the work of the Sulong Theatre Collective. As Pete Seeger and the gang once very nearly sang: Sulong, it's been good to know yuh.

In the reporting of this year's Governor General's Awards, the name of Robin Phillips, perhaps because he's neither a pop musician nor from Quebec, has been rather neglected. It's also true that his most famous achievements, as director of the Stratford Festival from 1975 to 1980, are now in what must seem to some the distant past. And so all the more reason for pointing out that his lifetime achievement award is long overdue. Phillips probably had a greater influence on the festival's image than any director since its founder, Tyrone Guthrie. He increased its sheer scale and volume of productions; more importantly, he gave it his own personal style, in which sensitivity to text and actors combined with extraordinary visual flair. There are moments from his 1977 production of A Midsummer Night's Dream whose magic still reverberates in my mind, even though I didn't much care for the production as a whole. His Richard III, the same year, with Brian Bedford and an unbelievably believable battle, remains one of the two or three best Shakespeares I have seen on the Festival stage; though his Measure for Measure two years before was, by many accounts, even better. He had a second lease at Stratford when, during John Neville's regime, he directed a young company whose productions had a 100% strike rate of success. Its members became the nucleus of Soulpepper whose first two productions Phillips also directed; the first of them, Don Carlos, set a high standard that the company has sometimes equalled but never surpassed. Not all of his productions have been easy to love -- I once wrote of his Stratford comedies of the later '70s that they seemed to be coming off an especially elegant conveyor belt --but it's been very rare for them to lack distinction; arriving late for his last-to-date Stratford production ( King John, 1993) I was struck full in the face by the quality of it, even before I'd had time to get my bearings. He has not, by general agreement, been the easiest person, but those who bear the scars of working with him are also often among his greatest fans. I was on the preliminary committee for the G-G's Awards two years ago, and the sheaf of testimonials in his favour, from some of our greatest talents, was extraordinary. He didn't make it to the shortlist then. I'm glad that the decision makers have finally seen the light.

- Future Folk runs through March 13 at Theatre Passe Muraille Backspace. Visit passemuraille.on.cafor details.

Tonight, CTV unwraps two new comedy shows that, while not exactly spinoffs of Corner Gas, trade in the same kind of gentle urban-folksy humour. An American sitcom, even one as sophisticated as Seinfeld, virtually screams at you "aren't these people crazy?" A Canadian sitcom is likelier to roll its eyes and ask you to identify with its people while suggesting that they are, really, rather odd. Both Hiccups and Dan for Mayor look, on the strength of their first episodes, mildly promising, with an emphasis on the adverb.

Both are set in larger communities than that of Corner Gas, though the size, nature and even the region of the towns in question has so far been left vague. Both, as is typical of a current sitcom as it scrambles for new subject matter, have unlikely premises that leave

you sceptical of their capacity for development. Or rather perhaps of their capacity for repetition, as the plague of episodic television, comic or dramatic, is that it has to tell the same story every week.

Hiccups is the show with the stronger links to Corner Gas; even the title suggests a kind of word association. More importantly, the man behind it, as writer and originator, and in front of it, as a principal performer, is Brent Butt. He plays Stan, a self-appointed "life coach" who, when we meet him, has spent six poverty-stricken months waiting for someone to drop by his office and ask to have their existence straightened out. Finally, someone does. This person is Millie, who writes children's books and does very well at it; her most famous creations are called the Grumpaloos, and she's something of a grumpaloo herself. She's a diminutive lady with a big heart and a short fuse, or as Stan professionally puts it, she's an over-reactionist. Nancy Robertson, also of Corner Gas, portrays her.

I've probably strayed into spoiler territory, as Millie's profession and her success at it are only revealed at the end of the half-hour. But I can't see any way of discussing the show without revealing it. It may even be that we were meant to twig early on that the bossy lady (Laura Soltis), in whose office Millie seems to occupy some barely tolerated menial position, is actually her publisher, who has every reason to put up with her. We find too that that staple of workplace comedy, the smooth and unsquashable office Lothario (David Ingram), doesn't belong on the premises at all; he's Millie's agent.

These people, plus a couple of others, are obviously going to be shaken up into various formations in the weeks ahead. I'd like to say I can't wait, but I can. The real problem is that, though Butt is charmingly frazzled and understated as Stan, he isn't the lead. Millie is, and she belongs to that large class of fictional characters whose eccentricities aren't nearly as endearing as their creators think they are. It's fun when she's kept waiting in a coffee-shop line-up, as we all have been, and makes a scene about it, as we all haven't but would like to do. It's merely irritating when a carton of milk explodes all over her, and she hops in a taxi to complain to the manufacturers in person.

Nor, though it tries hard, does the show ever make credible that someone as prosperous as she should seek the services of a small-time operator like Stan. Robertson brings gumption to the proceedings, but to win us over she'd need the comic genius of Nancy Walker -- whom she resembles and who could well have done it if the show were transported back 40 years and set in New York. Presumably, given Millie's success level, the setting is meant to be metropolitan but nothing, inside or outside Joyce's office, suggests it.

Dan for Mayor is, on the face of it, even farther-fetched. Dan (Fred Ewanuick), a barman at a fairly scruffy tavern, decides to run for mayor of his hometown of Wessex (impersonated by Kitchener, Ont.), even though the incumbent has never had to face a rival candidate in living memory. Fred's most prized possessiom is a Pac-Man video game. His ex-girlfriend (Mary Ashton) is about to marry someone else. Dan's ambitions are nearly derailed at the start, when he can't come up with the $1,000 registration fee, but stuff duly happens. His best buddy Jeff (Paul Bates) runs a print shop, which qualifies him to be Dan's campaign manager. Dan also gets ambiguous support from his employer (a more than usually hirsute David Ferry); some real-life mayors, including David Miller, are slated to make cameo appearances, though not necessarily as themselves. An unexpected plot development, shot with gleefully brutal economy, leaves Dan suddenly in with a chance. This, at the 29th minute of the half hour, potentially raises the show's entire game. Could we be about to see a sitcom with suspense? Even with a plot? The general air of harmless whimsy could well put paid to that but, like Dan himself, we can dream.

- Hiccups premieres tonight at 8 p.m., followed by Dan for Mayor at 8:30 p.m., on CTV.

Daniel MacIvor's Communion is, undeniably, a spellbinder. MacIvor's plays usually are these days, whether directed by Daniel Brooks or, as on this occasion, by the author himself. Here he delivers a clean-lined, meticulously staged and outstandingly well-acted production that squeezes all the tension and all the humour from a text that comes equipped with bags of the former and a reasonable supply of the latter. A show can often be judged by the quality of silence it provokes in the house; this one had its first-night audience taut and engrossed. Moment to moment, it compels attention. When it's over, however --or before that, as it begins to wind down -- you may wonder how much you are being left with.

Communion has three scenes and three characters; also three chairs, which are lined up handsomely in a row for our inspection as we take our own seats. When the play begins, this egalitarian arrangement gives way to a naturalistic arrangement of furniture that looks less formal but is actually more so. Where a person sits, and in relation to whom, becomes an index of power, just as it does in real life, especially in such confrontational situations as medical appointments and, especially, therapy sessions. Two such sessions bookend the action of MacIvor's play; sandwiched between them is an even less comfortable confrontation in a hotel room between a mother, Leda, and a daughter, Ann. It's the first time they've seen one another in eight months. Leda's husband has left her for another woman, and Ann has been living with them. She's also become a belligerent born-again Christian, having previously done time for attacking an abortion clinic. Leda and Ann have drastic news to impart to one another.

Her personal predicament, and her relationship or lack of it with her daughter, are what have driven Leda to see a psychiatrist, whose name is Carolyn and who has issues of her own, as who in her line doesn't? Even if you start without them, which is unlikely, you are likely to acquire them on the job; Carolyn certainly seems to, landed as she is with patients who keep questioning what possible help she can be to them, while lambasting her for her refusal to tell them what's wrong with them or what to do about it. The things, in fact, that drive any patient mad about any shrink, and presumably vice versa. (And can sometimes drive audiences mad about playwrights.) Besides this, it seems that Carolyn is having problems with her own (female) partner, though she doesn't say very much about them. This, of course, is her personal and professional right, but it makes her unsatisfying as a dramatic character. Leda, by contrast, is very forthcoming about her problems, though neither she nor the play does much more than re-state them. Ann is a problem every time she opens her mouth, though sublimely unaware of it. "Everything's not black and white," says Leda, provoked by her daughter's religious certainties. "Yes, it is," says Ann. Well, that's that then. But the question of how Ann reached this stage of undentable satisfaction is left unbroached. She even manages to disturb the quiet in the auditorium. "Women should raise their children and obey their husbands" she tells her mother, and the shock in the house was audible. I'll swear that if she'd proudly proclaimed that she was a serial killer, they'd have taken it without a murmur

The dialogue crackles, and the play bristles with small points of contact, personal and structural. A box of tissues, withheld in Scene 1, becomes a major statement when proffered in Scene 3. Kimberly Purtell, best known as a lighting wizard, is here the set designer as well, supplying a trio of starkly helpful interlocking environments. The three actresses get plenty of ammo, which they discharge with exhilarating accuracy. Only with Caroline Gillis's Leda does a gap open up between the performer and the performed, but then there's already a gap in the role itself. Leda with daughter is so much more measured and less distraught than Leda with doctor that it's hard to believe she's the same woman. (Interestingly, and maybe intentionally, Ann of Scene 2 is more like Leda of Scene 1 than Leda of Scene 2 is.) She's also the victim of some fancy writing; in a production that's a masterpiece of behavioural naturalism, with every movement of hands on laps making a statement, her long image-crammed speeches ring false. Athena Lamarre's Ann, by contrast, has few problems of credibility and none of consistency; hers is a one-note role but it's a very entertaining note. Ann has no self-censoring mechanism, and this kind of forthrightness, a pain in real life, feels irresponsibly liberating at a safe distance. As Carolyn, Sarah Dodd offers the best of both worlds, vocational restraint underpinned by private passion. She almost justifies her emerging position as the play's protagonist. She stakes this claim at the outset, with an opening soliloquy about doubt and loneliness and "the light behind the door." This motif also figures in a recurring dream of Leda's, but the light is more mystifying than illuminating. The play's closing gesture of hope seems similarly facile. It may be true, it may be false; we don't know enough to tell.TV's In Treatment was more detailed and informative about the therapist-patient relationship and its ramifications, as well as more moving and less pretentious; so, come to that, were the Dr. Melfi scenes in The Sopranos. It's false piety to praise the theatre for doing what television has already done better. - Communion runs through March 2 at the Tarragon Theatre. Call 416- 531-1827 or visit tarragontheatre.comfor ticket information.

2010-03-08-a-wild-and-crazy-guy-a-mild-a:
Some people can do self-deprecation. Some can't. Some can do ironic self-praise, and keep it ironic and therefore charming. Some merely come off smug, or at best clueless. Steve Carell and Cameron Diaz, presenting this year's Oscar for best animated picture, told us how beautiful they were; he made it seem funny, she didn't. But then he has the comedy background; all she had was the fact that she actually is beautiful. Anyway she wasn't unduly strained by announcing the winning title, which was Up.

Oscar-giving actors have always come in pairs and they have, with rare exceptions, proved awful at playing themselves in public. (The flatulent material they're generally given doesn't help, of course.) Oscar hosts have generally been solo acts, but this year the powers that be decided to go for a double. Steve Martin, who's experienced at this kind of thing, was partnered with Alec Baldwin, who isn't.

Well, it was an idea. It seemed planned as a homage to great double-acts past: Hope and Crosby, Astaire and Rogers, Burton and Taylor. What? No, straight up, Dick and Liz were among those hymned in an opening number, alternately star-struck and smutty, delivered, somewhat off-key, by Neil Patrick Harris. He did so, with dancing girls, against a blue Art Deco set. It was the kind of number that really needed Cole Porter to write the lyrics, but he was unfortunately unavailable. It also pointed up the double bind in which the Academy Awards increasingly find themselves. They're torn between making fun of the whole event and the knowledge that if they go too far, there won't be an event.

"I wrote that speech for him," said Martin, presumably off the cuff, after an especially tear-drenched acceptance speech for best adapted screenplay. Earlier on, surveying the audience, he'd said "over here is the Inglourious Basterds section, and over here are the guys who made the movie." It may not read like much, but it was funny when he said it. That's his gift, abetted by the fact that he's never quite been a major movie star, and so can plausibly pose as a WASP-ish outsider. His delivery was weightless but priceless. Baldwin, by contrast, was heavy. We were rooting for him; we wanted him to make a transition comparable to the one he made in 30 Rock. (He did, in fact, pay tribute to Tina Fey for revitalizing his career. She was part of a fascinating duo with Robert Downey Jr., and was comedically on top of things. With Downey, you can never tell.) Baldwin, on present evidence, can do sitcom but not stand-up But once past the embarrassing song-and-dance at the top, the show looked like settling down. The clips were longer than usual and this, oddly enough, speeded things along. They actually told you something about the movies.

2010-03-09-academy-rewards-film-s-bigges:
Canadas own and native sons bookended Oscar night, and both were required to play the good loser. Christopher Plummer, in the evenings first prize-giving, lost to Christoph Waltz as best supporting actor. Plummer himself had predicted he wouldn't win, and personally I think he was up for the wrong performance: for his dying-by-inches Tolstoy in The Last Station rather than for his delightful display in the far more entertaining -- and indeed imaginative -- Imaginarium of Doctor Parnassus. Anyway, he looked very gracious and amused whenever the camera caught him, as it did frequently throughout the evening.

James Cameron, when the camera caught him, looked grumpy, as if he had heard enough jokes about Avatar to last him several lifetimes. But he rallied at the end, embracing and applauding his ex-wife Kathryn Bigelow when she bested him not only for best director, which was sort of expected, but for best picture.

People have been saying for ages that Bigelow's The Hurt Locker was the only movie with a chance against Avatar. This isnt fair; Up in the Air, which scored no wins, was a better film than either; so was A Serious Man, shut out even from the nominations. But The Hurt Locker is a strong war picture that only falls apart toward the end when its characters start saying what it all means. Clearly it deserved to beat Avatar.

I say this with complete confidence despite not having seen Avatar. Or perhaps because of not having seen Avatar. Oscar night is one of the last bastions of permissible prejudice. I now know for sure that I dont want to see Precious; any movie whose participants break down in tears when accepting their prizes goes straight to the bottom of my to-do list. I do want to see Jeff Bridges in Crazy Heart, but then I always did. I like Bridges anyway, and on Sunday night he was Plummer's only competition in the leonine stakes. The only thing that might have put me off him was his actual acceptance speech which, on a generally tight night, was folksy and rambling. Stop saying "man," man.

Still, I liked the idea of having each of the anointed 10 saluted in advance by a former co-star. None of them were embarrassing, and Tim Robbins' roasting Morgan Freeman was even funny. Funniest turn of all, though, was Ben Stiller announcing the make-up awards with his face and, for all I know, the rest of him painted Avatar blue. And not failing to point out that Avatar wasnt up for a makeup award. Maybe hes bucking for a future host gig; they could do worse. Having James Taylor singing In My Life during the obits was a bad idea; having anyone singing anything at that point would be, but this choice took the cake. A mini-documentary telling us what sound editors actually do was helpful. Indeed the whole show seemed, more than usual, to have something to do with film. Hence, perhaps, the retro feel of the staging and music, though some of the golden oldies on the soundtrack seemed chosen at random: As Time Goes By will fit any occasion, but Moon River? The dance sequence was spectacular, if hard to connect to the films it was meant to evoke. Randy Newman, always the bridesmaid, again proved himself (twice, in fact) the only class songwriter left in Hollywood.

Sandra Bullock's dress was accurately described by one of the red carpet experts as looking like an Oscar; which means that, if she hadn't won, she could have gone happily home with herself. Increasing the best picture slate to 10 had surprisingly little impact, except at the end when a rushed Tom Hanks, perhaps fearful of turning into a pumpkin, had no time to list them all before midnight and the big prize. (Hands up, anyone who could have named them.)

Sacha Baron Cohens name had been mentioned as a possible presenter, and that really might have broken the mould: not because hes irreverent, though I'd love to see him do it as Ali G, but because he isn't American. That, I think, would be a first. American hosts have to pretend to be mocking the system, but we know theyre faking it; British or indeed Canadian performers wouldnt have that problem. That said, team Steve 'n' Alec did a fine job. I was grudging about Baldwin in yesterdays paper, but at that point I hadnt seen the whole show. He was given the last word, took it, and ran.

2010-03-12-to-serve-and-protect-the-poli:
'Together" says Frank Leo, newly elected president of the police union, "we own this city." The city is unnamed, but looks very much like Toronto; and when Frank says "we," he appears to mean not the population at large but just him and his fellow cops. It is not a very reassuring message; but The Bridge, the new CTV drama series of which Frank is the central figure, seems disinclined to question it. It may be the first ever right-wing pro-union show.

That's probably the newest thing about it. It's being promoted as depicting police as real people with their own lives, and as taking on issues of corruption within and around the department; but it's hard to think of a recent cop show that hasn't tried to do such things. Publicists were probably making similar claims back in the days of Dragnet.

A decade or so ago, there was a brilliant British series, shown over here as Inside the Line, whose protagonist had an extremely colourful private life

and whose main job as a cop was investigating other cops. Here, admittedly, he differs from Frank, whose energies are largely devoted to opposing the investigation of other cops. He's concerned with rooting out individual bad apples but they have to be very bad indeed: An officer, for example, who's using his uniform to steal money from drug dealers. And even his main offence is that he's threatened the lives of other police.

Frank's real enemies are the brass, i.e. the departmental chiefs, and what might be called the super-brass: the bureaucrats and politicians who spread distrust of the guys on the beat. What makes him froth at the mouth is the sight of the men from the Criminal Investigation Unit, officious busybodies who arrive to ask annoying questions whenever somebody, say, dies in police custody.

The Bridge's executive producer is Craig Bromell, former police officer, president of the Toronto Police Association and radio host: so, two-thirds of Frank's own trajectory. As union president, he was famous for his vociferous opposition to any outside attempts to police the police. Whatever the politics of this, it makes for thin -- because it's one-sided -- drama.

It's probably unfair to compare The Bridge to The Wire (it may be unfair to compare any TV show to The Wire) but it's inescapable. Both shows centre on loose-canon rank-and-file detectives who take a principled stand against their superiors, who in turn devote themselves to making the hero's life miserable. Frank leads a revolt to secure a proper police funeral for an officer who's committed suicide. He succeeds, and is elected union boss on the strength of it, but the brass will never forgive him.

The Wire's Jimmy McNulty ran into similar problems when trying to expose the gang bosses of Baltimore; and his opponents, both within and without the force, were at least as unscrupulous as Frank's. But they were also more human and more detailed, capable of surprising moments of decency; which in turn made Jimmy himself, a far more flawed character than Frank, more sympathetic because he was more real. They were also part of a wider civic picture.

It's early days, of course, but so far The Bridge shows no signs of going there. Its villains are one-dimensional; there's a female deputy chief who's a monster of charmless (and clueless) vindictiveness, while the CIU men are filmed, and musically accompanied, like Gestapo interrogators. There are top cops with political ambitions, whom we rarely meet, and there's a do-gooding demagogue whom Frank demands be robbed of his "bully pulpit" and whom we've yet to meet at all. The writing (by Alan Di Fiore, of DaVinci's Inquest) and the performances, led by Aaron Douglas's square-jawed Frank, are vigorous enough, but they've yet to display any depth or texture. This even goes for Michael Murphy, who plays a police chief with ambiguous sympathies, i.e. he's playing both sides against the middle. Amusingly, when he and Frank have secret meetings in cars, each of them, unknown to the other, records the conversation. I think we can guess which of them, in a future episode, will resort to selective quotation.

One of Frank's colleagues tells him that, though notionally a civilian, he still thinks and acts like a detective. This could be the show's salvation; on the strength of tonight's episode it's beginning to function as another police procedural, of reasonable speed and grittiness. Frank has two sidekicks: his former patrol partner and union-rep predecessor, who's less impulsive than he is, and a lawyer who's also his girlfriend: another McNulty resemblance, though here too the love interest suffers in the comparison. Frank says, and the show's publicity backs him up, that he wants to clean up the city, not just the police department, "from top to bottom." So far, though the non-criminal civilians -- the people he is sworn to serve and protect, the ones on whose behalf the show asks us to protect him -- have been conspicuous by their absence.

- The Bridge airs tonight at 10 p.m. on CTV.

2010-03-13-friendship-s-great-divide-isn:
I owe the Harold Green Jewish Theatre an apology. A few weeks ago I admonished them for neglecting Jewish Canadian plays like Yichud, a show out of which they pulled, in favour of pre-tested Jewish American ones. They've now removed the rug from under me, and in very short order, too. Their new production, Talk, is unquestionably a Jewish Canadian play. It isnt an especially good one, but you cant have everything.

It isn't especially bad either: just humdrum, respectably intelligent, and made palatable by its actors. Michael Nathanson's play suffers from a self-defeating format. Its title is an accurate reflection of its theme, but also of its plot and, for want of a better word, its action. Two old friends re-unite in a bar in Winnipeg, which is where the play was first staged. Josh is Jewish, Gordon isnt; though for some reason, I assumed at the start that he was, and I still think that the play might be more interesting if he had been. Gordon has been living in Europe, mainly in London: the good London, as Josh puts it, as opposed to the one in Ontario. Gordon has got engaged to a French girl, Clothilde, and he has brought her along so that Josh can meet her; she has, however, left the stage before we arrive. But while she was there, she seriously raised Joshs hackles by announcing that the scarf she was wearing was bought in Palestine. Josh counts himself a liberal, but as far as he's concerned "Palestine" is a place that never existed and doesn't now, and any reference to it is tantamount to anti-Semitism. Gordon, from what we can gather, has been apolitical most of his life, but lately he has taken to going on anti-Zionist protests. This is why I think there might have been more at stake if he, too, were a Jew. Anyway, from that one moment of dissension -- that one word, in fact -- the friendship begins to unravel as if it too were a piece of fabric.

Nobody expects a playwright to solve the problems of the Middle East, or even to have anything new to say about them; and Josh and Gordon do little more here than restate standard positions. (Its mournfully true that, though the play was first produced in 2007, the author probably hasnt had to change a word.) But that isn't what's principally on the plays mind. Its about the course of friendship and the dynamics of doubt. Josh and Gordon don't just talk to one another; they talk to us, or at least they talk to themselves with us overhearing. Each of them is continually second-guessing what he has just said, or seeking for subtext in what the other has just said. In Ted Dykstra's production -- and, I assume, in the play as written--each of these mini-monologues is accompanied by a spotlight: a device that irritated me at first but that I accepted as the play proceeded.

This may not be primarily a political play, but the politics get in the authors and the audiences way as surely as they do in Josh's and Gordon's. The pretext lacks context: If Josh, as he says, believes in a two-state solution, then why should the mere mention of the word "Palestine" rile him so much? Perhaps it depends on the exact locality in which Gordons fiancee made her purchase. If she was referring to Gaza, I think Josh might have lived with it; if it was Tel Aviv, then, yes, we have a problem. Its exacerbated when Gordon lets slip that his new activism is due to the influence of Clothilde. She looms so large in the conversation that we want to meet her. But of course we can't.

As the boys' night out collapses in what appears to be terminal rupture, Josh starts constructing what, if this were history, would be called a counter-factual: a counter-fictional, perhaps. Suppose Clothilde hadnt dropped that bait, or suppose he hadnt risen to it? He imagines himself going to France, to be Gordon's best man, and feeling out of place. Apparently, the end result would be the same, only it would take longer. We are left to mourn a relationship that we never really believed in anyway. Gordon, who gets to talk more as the play goes on, starts recapping their shared youthful experiences, but none of them are especially compelling. You can't establish that two people are friends just by having them assert it over and over: It may even be counterproductive, in art as in life.

Dykstra delivers a good yeasty production, though the rostra at either side of Steve Lucass set seem unnecessary, used too little and too late. Both Michael Rubenfeld and Kevin Bundy give excellent performances, with Rubenfelds Josh benefiting from having the more volatile, not to say voluble, role. The character conforms to at least one Jewish stereotype; he has all the funniest lines. Bundy has to play straight man, a task he undertakes with grace and some subtlety; a polite stick to begin with, he gradually reveals that insecurities and resentments seethe within him as well. The author may be saying, though I doubt it, that any friendship between Jew and Gentile is foredoomed; he may, more mournfully, be acknowledging that most friends grow apart. In which case, Josh and Gordon don't need the Middle East to separate them; time and the Atlantic Ocean will take care of it. They will probably send emails.

- Talk runs through March 20 at the Jane Mallett Theatre. For more information, call 416-366-7723 or visit hgjewishtheatre.com.

2010-03-17-art-does-history:
Joel Greenberg's Studio 180 is our foremost practitioner of what is generally known as "documentary theatre." Its two best productions have been The Laramie Project, which was pretty much a documentary, reconstructing the murder of Matthew Shepard and its aftermath through the recorded words of the actual participants; and Stuff Happens, in which most of the words were made up, but in which the characters -- American and British politicians in the run-up to the Iraq war -- were both actual and persuasive. Studio 180's new show, The Overwhelming, is also a run-up piece, and the events it runs up to, the Rwandan massacres, are even more appalling; but this time the characters are fictitious. And one sits through it asking a question that may be unfairly prompted by the memory of Studio 180's previous shows, but is inescapable nonetheless: Why am I supposed to care about these made-up people when a real and recent atrocity, taking countless real lives, is just waiting to happen?

It might be easier if the characters in J.T. Rogers' play, written by an American but first staged by the National Theatre in London, came across as people, rather than representative mouthpieces and well-intentionedreactors. Chiefamong the latter is Jack Exley, a U.S. political science academic who comes to the Rwandan capital Kigali in 1994 to research a book he hopes will gain him

tenure. Specifically, he wants to meet up with Joseph Gasana, an old Rwandan friend, now working as a doctor. Joseph is a Tutsi, and he's gone missing. Jack's attempts to track him down -- via the police, the UN, his own embassy -- are met with stonewalling or outright hostility. With him are Linda, his second wife and a writer, and Geoffrey, his teenaged son from his first marriage. There's some stepson-stepmom tension between these two (Geoffrey all but says "you're not the boss of me") that contributes nothing to the play, either personally or politically, but is emblematic of the soap-opera level on which the playwright feels obliged to operate.

It isn't all as bad as that. All three members of the Exley family seem remarkably naive, but their explorations of the society in which they find themselves means they're always asking questions, and sometimes getting interesting answers. Linda, while remaining sympathetic to the plight of her husband's friend, lends an increasingly sympathetic ear to some smooth Hutu propaganda. She wants a story; Geoffrey wants sex, which he finds courtesy of a friendly Tutsi prostitute. His reluctance to use a condom in a disease-ridden country is set up as a plot point, but never pursued. The relationship culminates in the first (offstage) outbreak of full-out horror, but it's questionable whether we need a whole laborious subplot to get us there. It's as if the reactions of these innocents abroad were more important than the events themselves.

Sometimes, the play finds a pithy and powerful way of relaying the news. A diplomat asks Jack the blunt rhetorical question of whether any country, in the history of the world, has based its foreign policy on "the right thing to do." It's a moment that, on the first night, stirred the audience to uneasy laughter. Foreign or indigenous, the parties on the ground engage in an elaborate routine of buck-passing. It's clear that, given a shift in dynamics, the Hutu might as easily have been victims and the Tutsi killers; and that their tribal differences were invented and exploited by their Belgian conquerors. The French, the Americans, the beleaguered UN peacekeepers. All have their plausible reasons for refusing to intervene. Nobody's to blame or, to put it another way, everybody is. But didn't we know that already?

Greenberg's production is swift and efficient, though he hasn't found a distinctive visual style here, as he did for Stuff Happens, with its serried rows of mobile chairs. He settles here for everyone democratically moving the furniture around, as demonstrated in just about every play we see. David Storch holds the centre as Jack, though his exaggerated nervousness and bizarre all-purpose academic accent can strain both patience and belief. Some other performances are muddy, swallowed up in the bare brick-backed expanses of Michael Gianfrancesco's tandoori-red set. In the service of appearing hard-bitten, Hardee T. Lineham as an American resident gnashes and mashes most of what he says, including some important information. Brendan McMurtry-Howlett is suitably fresh as young Geoff. Nigel Shawn Williams makes, as usual, a weighty and sympathetic impression as Joseph, whom we first meet through his idealistic letters to Jack but who, when he finally appears, turns out to have his own share of ambiguities. He also plays various non-speaking servants, a telling way of linking Joseph's plight to those of compatriots less articulate than he is.

Eventually Jack, who has spent the play trying always to say and do the right thing, finds his principles tested when the conflict comes literally to his own door. It's nerve-rending, as it should be. But everything leading up to it is underwhelming.

- The Overwhelming runs until April 3. Visit canadianstage.comor call 416-368-3110 for tickets and information.

2010-03-20-bleak-beautiful-in-need-of-ba:
The Soulpepper production of Oh What Lovely War picks up steam when it pulls into Waterloo station -- 1914 is approaching its end, and the first British troops from the First World War are returning home, some wounded, some blind and some on stretchers. They're singing that grandly disgruntled traditional chanty were here because were here. Transport is available for officers, but no arrangements have been made for other ranks; eventually some lorry drivers offer to ferry them to hospital on their lunch-hour. From there we proceed to the famous Christmas Eve truce in the trenches; the British and German troops exchanging carols ancient and profane, and lobbing eatables at one another in place of shells. The effect is at once heartwarming and heartbreaking: like the Waterloo scene, only more so. This is almost the end of the show's first half, but the momentum is pretty much maintained through the second. It's a story told in sorrow and in anger, and it provokes both feelings in its audience.

It still isnt quite what it might be; or, to declare my own prejudice, what it was. Lovely War is a musical/scrapbook/ documentary in which mostly cheerful songs are juxtaposed with mountingly horrendous casualty figures. A bewildering number of writers and creators are acknowledged in the program, but the show is basically based on a BBC feature by Charles Chilton, a great radio producer who was a master at rendering history by song; and then given inspired stage form by Joan Littlewood and her Theatre Workshop troupe. That was in 1963, and I saw it at the companys theatre in East London. It was incredibly funny, incredibly moving: one of the three or four formative theatrical experiences of my then-young life. The Soulpepper revival, the first I've seen, is good but not great. It falls short in two apparently contrasting directions: It's too bleak, and its too beautiful.

The shows framework is that of a seaside pierrot show. It starts upbeat, in an attitude of patriotic certainty, one that gets progressively blown to bits. In this trajectory it resembles Cabaret, a show much influenced by this one; at least it resembles Cabaret before Sam Mendes decided to make it dark from the get-go. Albert Schultz does the same thing with Lovely War; the stage has the traditionally comforting curtains and footlights, but visible behind them is a threatening brick wall. There ain't much warmth. Proceedings start with a mordant overture that gives away too much, musically and dramatically. The score divides, broadly speaking, into two: rousing music-hall numbers, recruiting pamphlets in song, in the first half; stoical disillusioned barrack-room ballads in the second. Here, the latter work better than the former. The cast is largely composed of members of the Soulpepper academy, and the boys at the front, young men playing raw young men, take more naturally to their posting than the theatrical seductresses who send them on their way.

Here's where the beauty part comes in. As I remember it, the Theatre Workshop cast included just one trained singer plus a lot of actors who could "put over a number." The academy actors are intensely musical; they all play instruments and, under Marek Normans expert direction, they execute intricate vocal harmonies. This is especially evident in a wonderfully grotesque chapel scene, in which the troops interrupt the padres platitudes with their own mocking lyrics to the old hymns. Originally, the show's emotional highlight was a despairing nurse's singing of Keep the Home Fires Burning, evoking tears and rage together. Here its just another song, one partly defused by having been instrumentally forecast, twice.

Some things work better than Id remembered, notably a revue-sketch meeting of international profiteers on the grouse moors. There's a stunning staging of the title song in which four pianos, each with its own pianist, are strung diagonally across the stage. Assorted detritus cunningly suggests the trenches, though it does cramp what should be a devastating last scene: French soldiers advancing "like lambs to the slaughter," baa-ing defiantly at the audience.

Two Soulpepper vets do lovely work: Michael Hanrahan, switching between a dainty, raunchy MCand a bullheaded Field Marshal Haig, and Oliver Dennis in a dizzying succession of roles, but happiest in the exploiter-and-officer class. Mike Ross alternates beguiling cheeriness with haunting blankness, and Ins Choi tosses off an array of accents. There is plenty to be pleased and stirred by, especially for those unburdened by memories.

- Oh What a Lovely War runs through April 10 at the Young Centre. Call 416-866-8666 or visit soulpepper.cafor details.
