2010-03-22-our-ladies-of-grace-tara-and-:
The two best comedic series of recent years are back: back, to back, in fact. Actually I hate that word "comedic" -- I can't see what was wrong with good old unpretentious "comic" -- but it's clear that neither Nurse Jackie nor United States of Tara can be called a sitcom in the traditional sense. Tara is the closer of the two to the old model; it has the traditional family setting, even if the protagonist's multiple-personality disorder means that the family itself is far from traditional, but both shows break the mould in being about development rather than stasis. No episode of I Love Lucy or Seinfeld ever had to start with a recap of the story so far. Perhaps the decisive difference is that both Jackie and Tara have children; and the ineluctable fact of their growing up immediately imposes a new and urgent dimension.

There is, of course, repetition in these shows. Each set up its framework of character and situation at the outset, and has adhered to it. "Previously on ..." at the start of both new seasons means, in large part, going back to the very first episodes. Nurse Jackie, which gets off to the more bracing new beginning, finds its title character as capable as ever and even more strung out. "Why do all the things that are good for you make you feel so bad?" asks her gay orderly friend Thor during one of their recurrent meetings in the hospital chapel, to which Jackie replies "I hear you." The amount of pain, regret and acceptance mined by Edie Falco from those three little words is extraordinary.

What's haunting her most at the moment is the situation of Eddie, her ex-pharmacist/ ex-lover, dumped by both Jackie and the hospital but still very much around. He's taken to hanging out at the bar where Jackie's husband Kevin works, trying to experience her vicariously.

Kevin is, for me, one of the less convincing characters. I am, conversely, one of the few who finds the friendship between Jackie and the English Dr. O'Hara thoroughly believable, if only because Falco and Eve Best play so irresistibly together. Young nurse Zoey is coming along well too; next week's instalment finds her coping admirably with a local schizophrenic who calls himself God, because that's who he thinks he is, and who has to be coaxed through a crisis of self-disbelief.

Jackie's own religious beliefs are an impotant part of her personal mix; when the favourite

painting of the Virgin to which she gravitates in her off-moments is bruised by gunfire (this is an inner-city hospital) she calls out, with indignation but no particular surprise, "she's a mother." Her pill-popping is as compulsive as ever, mined for humour of various degrees of darkness.

Falco excels at presenting a woman who's personally vulnerable and professionally invincible. Tonight's episode shows her expertly manipulating an insurance company that's trying to default on covering a desperate patient. It gets you thinking that the best thing for American healthcare would be to put Jackie in charge of it. But she isn't infallible, and next week shows her, for once, coming off worst in one of her conflicts with the infuriating Dr. Cooper. His habit of hitting on her despite all discouragements is one tired device the show might be better without, but his larger combination of extreme arrogance with extreme insecurity can produce comic gold.

More deeply haunting is the sight of Grace, Jackie's anxiety-stricken little girl, offering to put her allowance towards the latest model smoke detector, because she's afraid of the house burning down. Speaking of houses: As a hospital series, Nurse Jackie has House beat right down the line, beginning with their protagonists' respective bedside manners. One is rude, the other just practical. Apart from being funny, Nurse Jackie may be the only believable medical series in the history of television.

Comparisons for Tara are harder to come by. At the moment, it seems in greater danger of becoming formulaic. Tara and Max's two children are each striking out on their own paths: daughter Kate gets a job with a collection agency, which seems to suit her acquisitive nature, while school-age son Marshall is struggling with his sexuality. That is, he's been adopted by the cafeteria gayble (gay table) whose presiding figure is an aggressive proselytiser, but is getting suspiciously comfortable with a girl who sits there too because she is, in her own description, gay-friendly. Go Marshall, whichever way you decide to go.

Tara's sister Charmaine remains more interesting for the actress who plays her (Rosemarie DeWitt) than for anything she actually does. The central situation has been put, to a certain extent, on hold, with Tara on her meds and, hence, off her alters. However, a suicide in the house next door gets to her, and her biker-dude persona takes possession of her body and also, in another sense, of the body of a neighbouring barmaid. There's a lot of sex on this show, one way or another. It's everyone's fantasy suburbia.

Well, maybe not everyone's. Alice, Tara's prim housweife identity, would have something to say about it and, I hope, soon will. The dialogue still zings, the style remains attractively cool, and Toni Collette is still irresistible.

These two sagas of conscientious, drug-dependent wives and mothers must rank as twin fables for our times. And cable is finally doing for comedy what it has previously done for drama. It's brought the two genres closer together, while still allowing each a separate identity.

- Season 2 of Nurse Jackie premieres tonight at 10 p.m.; Season 2 of United States of Tara premieres tonight at 10:30, both on The Movie Network.

2010-03-23-it-s-a-lively-show:
YOUNG FRANKENSTEIN

Princess of Wales Theatre, Toronto

---

There's a light shining over at the Frankenstein place: another one. Like The Rocky Horror Show, Mel Brooks' Young Frankenstein is a manic, campy musical that takes off from the most revered of all sci-fihorror stories, holding the reverence but with a double-order of sex on the side. This time, though, the ambience and especially the music are more glitz than grunge, and the sex is strictly hetero.

A more obvious comparison of course is with Brooks' previous musical The Producers. They're both transformations and extensions of their creator's canonical movies. The Producers was a huge Broadway success; Young Frankenstein has been a mild Broadway failure. The newer show is in fact a fair amount of fun--just as well considering how hard it works at it -- but three things conspire against it. One is the inescapable deja-vuishness of the whole enterprise. Second is that Brooks' whole shtick is to reduce everything to showbiz: a natural fit for The Producers, which is about showbiz, but with no particular relevance here. Third, and closely allied to the second: The Producers had a dramatic pulse. Its protagonists desperately needed to put on their terrible show, and their drives drove the story. Young Frankenstein is half-over before it even has a story.

For those who don't know, the famous Dr. Frankenstein is dead, and his Transylvanian castle, with all its appurtenances, has been inherited by his grandson Frederick FrahnkenSteen, as he insists on being pronounced. Frederick is a celebrated brain-doctor working in New York at the Johns, Miriam and Anthony Hopkins Hospital. The time is the 1930s, a factor that determines the show's musical and choreographic style. Even when the show's action moves back to mythical Europe, its Art Deco heart belongs to Fred Astaire and Busby Berkeley.

As lyricist and composer, Brooks ladles out the same generic pastiche as in The Producers, but to far less purpose. I yield to none in my nostalgia for vintage musical comedy, and I confess to being a sucker for dialogue lines like "Pardon me, boy, is this the Transylvania choo-choo?," but Brooks isn't aiming here at sustained parody or satiric commentary; he's just writing the kind of tunes that other people have already written better. As if to prove the point, this show, like The Producers, brings over one song from its mainly non-musical original.

Instead of Springtime for Hitler, Brooks' own and relevant, we have Puttin' on the Ritz, Irving Berlin at his best, putting to shame everything else in the score.

Frederick at first wants no part of the Frankenstein legacy, but his ghostly granddad, accompanied by other ancestral spectres, prevails on him to change his mind: an idea borrowed from, or at least anticipated by, Gilbert and Sullivan. So he creates his own monster, a hulk with some charm but, owing to a grave error (actually a grave-robbing error) on the part of Frederick's humpbacked henchman Igor, of very little brain. The local yokels, NIMBYists to a person, go after the doctor and his creation with pitchforks. This being a Brooks show, the hero has his pick of available blonds. One, a local wench, closely resembles Ulla from The Producers, though with a lesser class of material; the kind she does have suggests that Brooks might have adapted Berlin still further and given her a number called Puttin' on the Tits. Frederick's other lady, a holdover from his New York days, is an untouchable tease, at least until she meets the monster of her dreams; she gives in fact a new meaning to the phrase "vamp till ready."

Susan Stroman's staging, and especially her choreography, put a high gloss on what is basically the old burlesque mix of leers and laughs. Some of the laughs, in Brooks' and Thomas Meehan's book, are good, and the sheer volume of them, good or bad, batters you into a sort of submission. Roger Bart's Frederick, the one remaining Broadway principal in this touring company, provides a valuable point of rest: His basic style is beamish and manic, but he can turn it on and off like a tap. He also resembles Danny Kaye, especially in a tongue-twisting introductory number about The Brain. His creation is played, most endearingly, by Shuler Hensley. Brad Oscar knocks himself out playing a blind hermit as Al Jolson in whiteface; Cory English, whose accent matches his name, is a cottage of strength as Igor; and I guess that Joanna Glushak is funny as the late Doktor's Dietrichian housekeeper; though I also guess that her catchphrase, "He Vas My Boyfriend," did better spoken in the movie than sung here.

Brooks' lyrics, indeed, are very disappointing, though there's a surprisingly pleasant ballad called Listen to Your Heart. The designers are Broadway royalty; Robin Wagner's sets aren't his best, but William Ivey Long's costumes take a witty trip into the world of lederhosen und Gewurtztraminer. The bodywork gleams. But the machine doesn't have an engine.

- Young Frankenstein runs until April 18 at the Princess of Wales Theatre. Visit mirvish.comfor tickets.

Just closed at the Jane Mallet Theatre in the St. Lawrence Centre: Talk, a two-character play in which a friendship is compromised by the mention of the word "Palestine." Just opened at the Bluma Appel Theatre in the St. Lawrence Centre: Art, a three-character play in which a friendship is compromised by the mention of the word "art." For a few days, two shows on essentially the same theme coexisted under the same roof, the similarities enhanced by the fact that both are conversation pieces in which -- in these productions at least -- spotlights isolate the speakers when they switch from dialogue to monologue.

Yasmina Reza's Art is a widely produced play, a hit in Paris, London and New York and probably qualifying by now as a modern classic, while Talk is a newish piece by a little-known Canadian playwright. I don't want to use the former to bash the latter but I will say that Art wins by miles on sheer flexibility. Having three characters instead of two immediately makes it static rather than dynamic. It also has a subject -- or rather a metaphor -- that allows those characters to duck, weave and reveal themselves.

The start of Art comes when Serge, a dermatologist, spends thousands of francs on a painting: an all-white canvas that may, depending on who's looking at it, have a couple of white lines on it. This purchase arouses not just the mockery but the anger of his friend Marc, an engineer of conservative aesthetic views who distrusts just about anything that could be called "modern art" and becomes positively apoplectic at the mention of the word "deconstruction." (Bear in mind that the play is now at least 15 years old. Nothing dates faster than modernism. Except of course postmodernism.) Marc, who regarded himself as Serge's mentor, now feels personally betrayed.

Serge is married, Marc divorced. The play's third party is Yvan, who once worked in textiles, is now in stationery, and is about to get married himself. He isn't very happy about any of these things, and his situation is made worse by the fact that his two friends, on whom he is emotionally dependent, are now at loggerheads. He doesn't know which to side with and, trying to please both, inevitably ends up pleasing neither. But this worm can still turn, though he does himself a mild physical injury in the protest. He obviously doesn't care much about the painting either way, but even for Marc and Serge it becomes less text than pretext. The three men fall to badmouthing one another's spouses -- past, present or prospective -- but even that's a diversion; the rifts that are now revealed were always incipiently there. The men manage to patch up their differences or, more exactly, to paper them over, but it's clear that this only works through a process of willed self-deception.

Art isn't about art, but it is art, of a kind: Like Serge's painting, it's a plain surface on which we can project our own interpretations. It isn't deep, but it's smooth, as its characters group and regroup, each reflexively fighting his own corner.

Morris Panych's production isn't the most emotional I've seen, but it is the funniest, triumphantly so in the case of Evan Buliung's unconscionably uncomfortable and perpetually pleading Yvan. His long-winding wound-up complaint about the impossibility of wording a wedding invitation to please every member of both families always brings down the house; here it stops the show as well, the first speech to get mid-scene applause since Ben Carlson's great tirade in Man and Superman. He's as good, if less spectacular, when retailing gnomic advice from his shrink about the perils of letting yourself be defined by other people: counsel of which the entire trio stand in need, and on which none of them can act.

The only flaw in Buliung's performance, a venial one, is that he seems too young to have been the lifelong buddy of the other two. Peter Donaldson lays on Marc's vulnerability at the expense of his presumed vulnerability, but his presence is undoubtedly felt. Colin Mochrie, the quietest of the three, is a formidably placid and then surgingly indignant Serge. Panych's use of between-scenes video, showing the guys shuttlingbetweenoneanother's residences, hardly seems necessary; but once they've arrived he places them to maximum comic and dramatic effect, on and around the Le Corbusier furniture that they unavoidably have in common. Ken Macdonald's set design still allows them some measure of individuality through the light fixtures in the ceiling and, of course, the pictures on the walls. And the videos do remind us that we're in Paris: the only place in the world where people dispute with the same passion, the same flippancy, and virtually in the same breath, on the meaning of life and where they're going for dinner.

- Art runs until April 10. Call 416-368-3110 for tickets.

As the late Spike Milligan used to sing: "I talk to the trees, that's why they put me away." The Tank House, one of the smaller performance spaces in the Young Centre, has The Woods, the third part of the planned tetralogy known as The Mill. The main stage at Theatre Passe Muraille has Birnam Wood, a movement-based piece (which doesn't mean it's mimed or danced) with Shakespearean antecedents. Both feature actors pretending to be trees, but neither to the extent that you might expect. In fact, for large stretches of both, you can't see the wood for the plays. Which may be as it should be.

J.R.R. Tolkien got very angry at Shakespeare for cheapening the potent idea of a mobile forest attacking a castle by making the trees a front for a gang of mere humans. His militant Ents in The Lord of the Rings were his demonstration of how the thing should have been done. Birnam Wood, conceived and directed by Allyson McMackon for her Theatre Rusticle company, has at least one moment whose sentiments seem to echo Tolkien's: One of the six actors, Hume Baugh, asked if the camouflaged soldiers advancing on Dunsinane really looked like a wood, says that, no, they just looked like people holding broken branches in front of them. His character is announced in the program as "Tree of Dreams -A King," and he does indeed have an arboreal circlet on his head. He's mostly a gentle presence, though there's one sequence in which he plays the warrior, and, having despatched his opponents, returns to a victory party singing "when Johnny comes marching home." His fellow celebrants aren't impressed. The sequence seems to be the show's pacifist response to the account in Macbeth of the hero's meeting the Norwegian invader and unseaming him from the nave to the chaps: Not, it is hinted here, a very nice way to behave. Similarly, we have a scene that seems to be recreating the murder of Duncan, from Duncan's point of view; we are made to feel what it must have been like to have been on the receiving end of that bloody dagger.

Few of these Macbeth motifs have much to do with Birnam Wood itself, though there's an arboreal setting with an especially impressive black-and-white floor-cloth that extends, in Lindsay Anne Black's design, to the very verge of a foreshortened auditorium. Perhaps the idea is that Shakespeare's whole play is a forest, and they have extracted a few limbs from it. There were plenty of times when I couldn't make root or branch of what was going on, but a dominant theme seems to be relations between the sexes, as extrapolated from the dysfunctional relationship of the Macbeths themselves. The problem is that, though the various sequences are fluently staged and executed, they don't cohere very well, while the underlying view of love and war comes across as finger-wagging. Also, some of the more flirtatious episodes seem more suited to another Shakespearean wood, the one near Athens.

Maev Beaty, playing "Tree of Dreams -Critters" (I don't know what that means, either) has a piercing scene in which she oscillates between pleading for a man's attention and enumerating all the domestic things she has done for him. One of our best younger actresses, she has sometimes come on too comically strong; here, she's both disciplined and delicate. She's also been through both earlier instalments of The Mill, though she is, of course, absent from the new one. The Woods does involve a chorus of actors playing oracular trees, whom neither Tara Beagan's writing nor Sarah Garton Stanley's direction can prevent from seeming as absurd as the king's comment in Birnam Wood might suggest. They are, however, peripheral. The central action is absorbing. In this play, set centuries before Parts One and Two, we learn the origin of the buried bones (buried even before the play begins) that were to exert such

a baleful influence. In 1640, before the Mill was even a mill, its future site is occupied by a First Nations woman and her daughter whom she has taught, with good reason, to hate and fear the white man. Their equilibrium is disturbed when an actual white man, an ethnographer who's got lost, almost literally stumbles upon them. Gradually -- very gradually -- an attraction develops between mother and intruder, one that Ryan Hollyman and Michelle Latimer present with a delicate tragicomic awareness; Hollyman is especially delightful as a man half-fearful for his life, half-afraid to believe his luck. He describes the daughter as "a weird child"; Holly Lewis, who has specialized in this cycle at presenting weird children, does her fullest work yet as a girl in whom tribal and filial resentments come combustibly together. The four remaining members of a strong ensemble double as talking trees and French colonizers on stilts; neither gives them much chance at subtlety, though Michelle Monteith gets an amazing amount of graciousness from the ethnographer's wife. At three-quarters done, The Mill still doesn't add up to the statement about Canada that seems to have been intended, and this segment is shorter than its predecessors on Gothic thrills. But it's the best, so far, on concentrated human content.

- Birnam Wood closes tonight at Theatre Passe Muraille (416-368-3110); The Woods runs through April 3 at the Young Centre (416-866-8666)

For as long as I can remember, Second City's revues have taken place on inoffensive sets mainly composed of doors. The new one does away with all that. Second City for Mayor demonstrates its commitment to urban renewal by erecting a new multi-levelled set composed of fire-escapes and catwalks. The design, by Camellia Koo, gives new opportunities for inventive staging, of which Melody A. Johnson's direction takes full advantage. Especially good are the transitions from one sketch to the next, with Steve Del Balso's lighting bathing the stage each time in something rich and fairly strange. This may be the most stylish Second City show ever.

It is not, however, the funniest. Some things are very good, and there's an unaccustomed consistency of tone, but overall standards of both writing and performance are down from the last few shows. What gives it unity, apart from its visual excellence, is a mordancy about Toronto that has been an intermittent theme before but that here takes over. Even the title has a purposeful air about it. These comic candidates call their constituency "city town," and it even seems to have its own superhero, the Blue Falcon, who looks not unlike Adam Giambrone, with skeletons falling out of wherever it is he keeps his cape. (He more or less says that he has better things to do than save his fellow-citizens from themselves. They more or less say that they have better things to do than to be saved.) There's a scene in a hard-core gym, terrifyingly calling itself the lifelike name Extreme Fitness, where clients are given new names that combine natural disasters with elements from the periodic table. (Hello, Iron Famine.) The idea is repeated rather than developed, but visually, with all those levels coming into their own as things to hang bodies from, it's a scream.

The design reflects the fact that most of the show is set, if not outdoors, then in public spaces, even when the subjects treated are basically domestic. Befuddled, sleep-deprived new fathers huddle for mutual commiseration in -- where else? -- Shoppers Drug Mart. Even the mandatory dating-sketch has a new spin on it: An operative from eHarmony has been sent to discover firsthand why one of their less successful clients ( "we call you the black hole") scares off all the men they fix her up with; it turns out to have something to do with the falcon that perches on her wrist, and that we are told about but, alas, never see. There is one family-values item, but it, too, is a little off the beaten track; mom and dad are shocked to find their daughter sexting, and even more shocked by how mild it is compared with what they used to get up to. But this again is just one joke -- all right, one-and-a-half jokes--repeated.

Two numbers do break new ground. One of them is an encounter between an ex-Guantanamo inmate, now running a Coffee Time, and one of his former tormentors. This may be the blackest revue sketch since Beyond the Fringe took on capital punishment; and unlike that one, it manages to work as comedy, superficially bland but dangerous. The other is an old-time hootenanny, on the theme of countries you probably wouldn't want to live in: titled It Could Be Worse. As to which countries those might be, Reid Janisse takes suggestions from the audience, some of them less expected than others. He probably has some lyrics prepared, but, spontaneous or not, you have to respect a man who, asked to sing about Iran, can come up in perfect rhyme and metre with a line about a place whose name is the past tense of "I run." This is an historic occasion -- the first time I have ever laughed out loud at a Second City song. Music has not generally been this organization's strongest suit.

Janisse, the most seasoned and familiar of the performers, is admirably crisp and exact throughout: not so much the evening's star (it doesn't have one) as its tent-pole, holding the whole edifice up. Adam Cawley is lanky, fresh-faced and underneath it all (he's the Falcon), lethal. Caitlin Howden has a virtuoso bit, especially well staged, glorifying the human hand, and a dead-on portrayal of a kindergarten teacher dedicated to squashing her students' dreams just as her own were squashed. Rob Baker, playing politicians and other loudmouths, meets them rather too enthusiastically on their own terms; he's more restrained and more effective, oddly enough, in the complimentary improv section that follows the main performance -- at least, he was the night I went. (Funnily enough, the improv in general seemed more structured than some of the rehearsed stuff that preceded it. Could it be...? Oh no, perish the thought.) Dale Boyer and Kris Siddiqi complete the company. In Second City tradition, motifs from earlier scenes recur in later ones, but this time there's even an attempt to tie them all together at the finale. One perpetual failing remains: Johnson certainly knows how, visually, to frame a sketch's ending but nobody, it seems, knows how to write it. I blame television.

robert.cushman@nationalpost.com

2010-04-07-the-maritime-divide:
A BOY CALLED NEWFOUNDLAND

Tarragon Theatre Extra Space, Toronto

The play is called A Boy Called Newfoundland and this is the set-up: Bill Willow and his wife Marianne live with their son and two daughters in what the program, reinforcing the tone established by the title, identifies as "a Nintendo-blue house at the top of a Maritime hill." From these premises they edit and distribute a newspaper called the Romantic Times. Whether this is a weekly, a monthly or a twice-a-yearly is left unclear but, even factoring out the Internet and the recession, it sounds like an uncommercial proposition. Bill Willow seems to have come to this conclusion himself, as he has vanished from the scene, leaving a hole in his family's lives, and also in the front page of their upcoming edition.

The three children are all in their teens. Arley-Rose is blond, and dating a divinity student named Hadley; they eventually marry. Brigid is brunette and a frenetic cut-up, initially devoted to making her younger brother's life a misery but eventually revealed to be in love with him. And playing Cinderella to his two sisters is the boy called Newfoundland himself, so-named because his parents were vacationing there when he was conceived. He is a shy but amiable 14-year-old, constantly inventing tunes on a portable keyboard. Marianne Willow wants to bring her son out of himself, but isn't sure how. A possibly encouraging sign is that he is conducting a telephonic relationship with a Quebec girl whom he once met at a French camp. They converse by exchanging lyrics from pop songs of the non-rock persuasion. This explains why, though the time is "the present," the air is filled with sounds from the '50s and early '60s. Arley-Rose and Brigid set off in their mother's car to find their father whom they locate ice-fishing in the far north. Later on, Flounder makes the same pilgrimage, but Bill Willow remains reluctant to return to a household that likes to keep its Christmas lights on for most of the year.

Graeme Gillis, the author, is not aiming at literal plausibility. Emotional plausibility is another matter and he does get that in isolated exchanges, plus a measure of charm and a streak of humour. What he doesn't do is build and develop. We're told, repeatedly, about Arley-Rose's dalliance with Hadley, but we don't even meet the guy until late in the first act, and then it's for a scene with Newfoundland; the two young fellas start playing video games together. This apparently does wonders for both of them, but it's never explained how. When Hadley proposes (to Arley, that is) it's the best scene in the play, no contest, but it could as well be an isolated sketch. Most damagingly, the spine of the play is supposed to be the sentimental education of its title character but it's just one thread among many. We're asked by the end to believe that he's grown but we haven't seen or felt it happen. We don't know if he's re-asserting the values of the Romantic Times or, really, what those values might be.

The last thing this play needs is an extra layer of whimsy, but in Ashlie Corcoran's production for Theatre Smash, that's what it gets. The action is sliced and diced across a set (by Robin Fisher) consisting of a wide set of multi-coloured steps; a protruding bit at the top looks like the fin of an uncommonly gaudy shark. Holes open up on different levels, to show the girls recklessly driving or Bill fishing, but the general effect is to keep the characters even further from getting to grips with one another or with recognizable reality.

Martin Happer's performance as Hadley is the most solid and also the funniest. Patrick Kwok-Choon, a hitherto uneven actor (promising in The Tempest, dreadful in Rock 'n' Roll), redeems the promise in a sweet performance as Newfoundland. As the sisters, Lara Jean Chorostecki and Natasha Greenblatt start out over the top but pull back very satisfactorily as the evening progresses. Layne Coleman and Martha Burns are the elder Willows, he pleasantly stoic, she alternately flighty and concerned, and more starved of motivation than anyone else on the stage. The play points toward a resolving scene between them and then withholds it. The production can't make a virtue of this; indeed, both acts conclude with the audeience going "Huh?" Vivien Endicott Douglas plays the hero's long-distance love, whose occasional appearances in a remote alcove sum up all that's gone wrong in both script and direction.

- A Boy Called Newfoundland runs until April 11. Visit theatresmash.comfor tickets and more information.

2010-04-10-jazz-baptism-after-his-elegy-:
First thing you see on Treme is a title, on a black screen, that says "three months after." David Simon's new series is set in New Orleans, so there's no need to ask "three months after what?" The show is about people getting their lives and their city together in the wake of Hurricane Katrina, and in the first episode they seem, for the most part, to be making a good and hopeful job of it. The episode ends with a funeral procession -- not for anyone we know--and, as we've always been told about such events, it's a joyous, jumping occasion: also a businesslike one, as many of the show's characters are musicians. You end up thinking that if Simon's The Wire, set in Baltimore, was an elegy for a city, Treme is a celebration.

That, though, is just Episode 1. The next two instalments reveal that things aren't that simple. Nor were they, indeed, on The Wire, at least some of whose characters were survivors. A difference between the two shows is that on The Wire, hope, however often dashed, was the prerogative of the young. Here it stretches across the generations, largely buoyed by the music. We've all heard of the French Quarter of New Orleans, but the Treme is a different district, shabbier and less celebrated but claimed as the true birthplace of jazz. Simon and Eric Overmeyer, his chief collaborator as writer and executive producer, planned it in part as a tribute to the music; I suspect that by the time the season is over it will have done more for jazz, and made better dramatic use of it, than anything in the history of television. As in The Wire, and indeed in all the best HBO shows, the music is come by honestly. It's always there as part of the story. There's no manipulative underscoring. The first tumultuous scene shows musicians assembling for a parade, one trombonist short. Then the missing man arrives: Antoine Batiste, bulky and broke, haggling with the taxi driver who brought him. This becomes a running gag; Antoine takes three cabs in the course of the hour, and he's always arguing about being overcharged. Wendell Pierce plays him with the same world-weary ebullience he brought to Bunk in The Wire, though his heartbreak look, when deprived of both his 'bone and his livelihood, is something that the earlier show never required of him.

Antoine takes his place in the second-line parade, playing, marching, chanting with the others "I feel like funkin' it up." The sequence is superbly staged and shot by the episode's director, Agnieszka Holland. It's defiance, recognized as such by a bespectacled, and currently naked, young man watching from a window. "It is," he says, "the first second-line since the storm." He is Davis (Steve Zahn), the kind of white boy who's more deeply, or at least more selfconsciously, into black culture than most blacks. A manic, self-destructive fixer, fired successively from jobs as a radio DJ and a hotel desk-clerk (he looks hilariously smart in a tie), he gives the show a lot of energy. Watching him disenchantedly from bed is his sometime girlfriend Janette (Kim Dickens, in a role not dissimilar to her Joanie in Deadwood), a restauranteuse who's having difficulty meeting her bills. Nobody says anything about the flood until, suddenly, we find ourselves watching Creighton Bernette, a Falstaffian English professor, being interviewed at the canal-side by an oddly unsympathetic BBC man and excoriating governmental neglect for decades before the disaster. We relish his wit and his passion, but what we enjoy most of all is the fact that he's played by John Goodman. The best acting duet in the first three episodes comes when Goodman's irony bumps up against Zahn's frenzy. It's like jazz.

Creighton's wife, Toni (Melissa Leo, alternately charming and splenetically frazzled) is a civil-rights attorney, and the nearest thing to a unifying character, since just about everyone in the cast needs her services; Episode 3 finds her, time after time, bailing victims out of jail; the recurring motif of part 2 is people asking their parents to bail them out of debt. Toni is trying to locate the brother of Antoine's ex-wife, LaDonna (Khandi Alexander) who vanished from a prison when the apocalypse came; she meets official intransigence that may have been exacerbated by recent events but was obviously always there; here the show is at its most Wire-ish. We also meet a pair of street musicians, one of them played by Lucia Micarelli, a professional violinist who turns out to be a bewitching screen presence and a natural actress. Finally, there is Albert, a building contractor who's also a part-time musician and head of a tribe of Mardi Gras Indians, a singular black New Orleans institution. Clarke Peters, the laid-back Lester of The Wire, is here almost equally compelling in a completely different mode; ferociously dedicated to re-building his house and re-uniting his tribe, he screws up his face in obdurate determination, and has frightening reserves of violence. When he puts on his feathers, whooping and summoning, he's extraordinary. He has a son, Delmond (Rob Brown), a saxophonist who has moved to New York to play bop, reminding us that there's a world, including a jazz world, outside New Orleans, but who can't escape tradition.

Is it as good as The Wire? Not quite or not yet. Baltimore was representative while New Orleans is singular; so it's harder to identify. The Wire, a cop-and-crime show however much it ramified, had built-in narrative drive; Treme ambles. There is, to be frank, something soapy in the measured way it keeps moving from one storyline to another, with no dominant character or theme, though the latter may well emerge. It's rich, and it teems, and there is, naturally and omnipresently, the music. This is a milieu in which even the strippers perform to live accompaniment. Some star players (Allen Toussaint, Dr. John) appear as themselves, without seeming cheap; Elvis Costello adds to his already Alpine credibility just in the way he gazes from beneath his fedora at the resident guys in a club. The same respect that the show pays to the music, it also grants its viewers and itself. I don't think I've heard the word "Katrina" spoken, but it does appear on the screen, at the end of Episode 3. A bus, advertising Katrina Tours, pulls up in the Treme, disrupting another funeral procession--and this time we do know the corpse; we saw it discovered, rotting, in one of the devastated houses. The mourners angrily send the bus on its way, and even the driver acknowledges the impropriety. The procession re-forms, but this time we don't accompany it. It's a sign that the show, too, is moving on.

- Treme debuts tomorrow night at 10 p.m. ET/MT on HBO Canada.

Black & White Photo: Paul Schiraldi, Hbo / Michiel Huisman and Lucia Micarelli in Treme. In contrast to The Wire's narrative drive, this show ambles.; Caption:
2010-04-10-the-ties-that-bind-are-beyond:
Factory Theatre's Performance Spring is a festival of new works, many of them re-runs of pieces that have already had exposure in a variety of venues elsewhere. For example, Where the Blood Mixes, the current incumbent, started as a co-production by the Vancouver Playhouse and Victoria's Belfry Theatre. It was previously mounted in Toronto in 2008 by the Luminato festival, which must, on the evidence presented here, have been out of its mind.

Kevin Loring's play is rooted in a subject that could hardly be more painful or, at this moment, more topical: the abuse of aboriginal children in residential schools. There is a short speech bluntly describing the kind of thing that went on, and a longer one describing the continuing effects on a whole community of victims when they become adults. These are powerful, the first of them chilling, the second chilling and thought-provoking and guilt-inducing. But the dramatic structure that supposedly supports them is clumsy and dilatory. The same goes for the direction and much of the acting, but the problems the play presents may be insuperable.

We meet Floyd and Mooch, two middle-aged men, lifelong friends and sparring partners, in a B.C. bar of which they seem to be the only patrons. Floyd is avoiding the solitude of home, Mooch is avoiding his girlfriend, who objects, violently if understandably, to his habitual embezzlement of the housekeeping money. Mooch seems at first to be a half-wit, but is later revealed to be merely not especially bright, and shamefacedly aware of it; he does develop a certain poignance. Floyd is morose, oppressed by the long-ago death of his wife and the loss of his daughter Christine, who was taken off into adoption when he proved unable to care for her; though the flashbacks we see of their life together don't look all that bad. Anyway, though the play hardly makes a point of it, we have two generations forcibly estranged from their families, since Floyd and his wife and Mooch and his girlfriend all went through the residential experience and were permanently scarred by it. In Christine's case, the uprooting doesn't seem to have worked out too badly, but this, of course, only increases Floyd's sense of shame. When Christine comes back to find him, he's afraid to meet her. That's believable. But in order to establish this alienation, the play spends most of its length on interminable scenes of Floyd and Mooch interacting, in the bar and on salmon-fishing trips at the confluence of the Fraser and Thompson rivers. There's a lot of watery lyricism, and at one point Christine, who's been hovering as a choral presence, appears as a fish. If that's the kind of thing you like, that's the kind of thing you like.

Glynis Leyshon's production hardly puts a foot right. Transitions between scenes are awkward, and even within scenes actors are frequently left gaping into space. Robert Lewis' blue-tinged twin-levelled set conveys no atmosphere of either river or tavern, though there's some compensation in the latter department from Tom McBeath's discreet, cordial performance as the barman. A musician (Jason Burnstick) plays folk-and-blues guitar, and nobody seems quite certain whether he's meant to be there or not. At one point, he abruptly joins the main action-- perhaps because it's felt that more bodies are called for -- and then as abruptly departs it. His underscoring of much of the dialogue has the same effect that this device has in movies and on network TV: It absolves the actors of the responsibility of acting. The music also makes them look as if they're about to go into a number, although none of them actually does so. I tell a lie; one of them does an impromptu parody of Heartbreak Hotel, but the instrumental backing means it doesn't sound impromptu. It sets up a convention that is never followed through.

Most damagingly, there's little flow or contact between the performers; they talk and then they stop. That the characters have trouble communicating doesn't mean that the actors should. Both leads are monotonous, with Ben Cardinal making little more of Mooch than a comic turn, and Billy Merasty playing Floyd with a heavy hand and an appallingly limited range of expression. The women are uneven, which in this context is almost a compliment. As June, Mooch's madam, Margo Kane is a stock harridan when berating her mate, but surprisingly real when given the task of unfolding the play's backstory and expounding its theme, the two being identical. Kim Harvey's Christine is fresh and strong, except when resorting to generalized teariness near the end. The two ladies share what is, the author being also an actor, the play's best in-joke. Christine says that she's an artist, specializing in "spoken word"; the term baffles June, as it's always baffled me. (Most plays are made up of spoken words). I also liked the unifying motif of smell; people are constantly being judged by their odours, pleasant or otherwise. Many of these of course are alcoholic. The play apparently started as a bar-room duet for the two guys, and sprouted from there. This may explain why the abuse-theme emerges as a kind of topdressing, while making everything else seem like a waste of time.

- Where the Blood Mixes plays at the Factory Theatre through April 18. Call 416-504-9971 or visit factorytheatre.cafor details.

2010-04-16-some-serious-comedy:
The George Brown College Theatre School is taking us back to the 1950s: the early '50s, before the drama was upended by Beckett and John Osborne and the other cats. It's an instructive journey, and an entertaining one.

The school's graduating class is presenting, in repertory, Clerambard, by the virtually forgotten French author Marcel Ayme, and Cock-a-Doodle Dandy, one of the later and lesser-known works of the Irish maestro Sean O'Casey. The two plays have a lot in common. They're both serious comedies. They're both fantasies, of a literary bent. They both have sex on the brain, the French one more earthily and imaginatively than the Irish. They're both pastorals: the generic term for satiric works with settings somewhere between the rural and the mythical. They are both attacks on the Catholic church, Ayme's a light-fingered insider's job, O'Casey's the virulent outpouring of a Protestant-turned-atheist, for whom the religious hierarchy represented everything he most hated about his native land.

The title character of Clerambard is a deeply impoverished provincial nobleman, working the fingers of his wife, son and mother-in-law to the bone in order to hang on to his title and his chateau. His favourite off-duty pastime is strangling cats and dogs. One day he has a vision of St. Francis of Assissi, together with the revelation that one of his canine victims is mysteriously still alive.

This causes a 180-degree turn in his behaviour, like Timon of Athens in reverse; he switches from aggressive misanthropy to self-abasing benevolence. He vows poverty, no great stretch really, and tries to marry his son off to the local prostitute: again no big deal since the repressed youth has been fantasizing about her since he was 12. It doesn't, though, sit too well with the womenfolk who, in an unconscious echo of Gilbert and Sullivan, want him to marry the ugliest of a rich attorney's ugly daughters; the lawyer himself is one of the working-girl's regular clients, with the expected farcical results, though with unexpected side effects. (The legal family seem, in the George Brown production, to come from the famous French province of Alabama. It sort of works.)

The count discovers that the resurrected dog was a mistake but, in a brilliant twist, this only confirms him in his new course: When you know you're right, who needs miracles? The entire cast gets one anyway; they all have a heavenly vision, the only one who can't see it being the parish priest. His excuse is that he's lost his glasses, but we know better. He's the symbol of blinkered conformity, answering only to his bishop and, through him, to respectable society.

The O'Casey play also features an other-worldly visitation, in this case from a fertility symbol in the shape of an enormous cock. (As a revered English critic wrote when the play was done in London, I trust I make myself clear.)

The nicer people in the community make much of the bird, the nastier ones excoriate him as an emissary of flesh and the devil, and a few characters are stuck in the mushy middle. Chief among these are a typical O'Casey pair of timorous yarn-spinning drinking buddies, one of whom, unusually, has a job, while the other, name of Michael Mathruan, has a house, in front of which the play happens. Both fellas have moments of rooster-induced generosity, but slip back into their old ways of cheating one another while exploiting and abusing their womenfolk.

In the latter pursuit, they're much encouraged by one Father Domineer (O'Casey isn't being subtle), who regards dancing as an abomination and females as domestically necessary evils. Michael's wife, daughter and even his Irish equivalent of a saucy French maid abandon him for cursed heathen climes, such as England-- which is where O'Casey himself had been since circa 1930. When he lived in Ireland, he wrote great realistic plays about his own Dublin; after he fled, he wrote embittered fables about imaginary villages. When the priest is defied by a local labourer, he literally strikes the man dead, and gets away with it. Things can't have been that bad, even though we're learning that in some respects they were worse.

These student performances of stylistically alien texts are, as you'd expect, uneven but they're never boring. Gina Wilkinson's Ayme production has the advantage in speed, Todd Hammond's O'Casey in tone and rhythm, though the cock himself doesn't make the choreographic impact he probably should.

Clerambard has a great opening tableau, the count's family slaving away at their sewing machines. Later, the actors tend to hug rather than use the furniture; they fare better when the stage is fairly clear, as it also is throughout the O'Casey. There are 16 actors, all of them in both plays.

They are generally most comfortable, playing people their own age. In Clerambard Jonathan Brass's itchy-twitchy Vicomte is outstanding, closely followed by Kate Ross's warmly pragmatic sex worker. As the comte de Clerambard, Alex Dault is forgivably taxed by a role that really needs Christopher Plummer, but he does very well in Ireland as the domineering Domineer.

The age barrier seems to count for less in Cock-a-Doodle Dandy, and Andy Trithardt as Michael bursts wittily and authoritatively through it. There's one vital element these plays and productions share; they remind us of the lost theatrical art of confident storytelling. I really wanted to know what happened next.

- Cock-a-Doodle Dandy continues to April 22, and Clerambard to April 23 at the Young Centre for the Performing Arts. For tickets, call 416-866-8666.

2010-04-17-people-are-strange-but-that-s:
Sky Gilbert's new play Reconciliation is the latest variation on the old theme of the town mouse and the country mouse. This time the mice are siblings. Some details are vague, but Blake lives in rural Ontario, and it's in his farmhouse that the play is set. His brother Jared is visiting from the city; I don't recall Toronto being mentioned by name, but it must be the place, since Jared wants to use their paternal inheritance to invest in a condo in the Trump Tower, something with which Blake is decidedly not cool.

They have other points of disagreement. Blake operates a steam-shovel at a gravel pit; he defends this as being constructive work, on the grounds that the dirt on the end of his shovel is in a different place at the end of his shift than it was at the beginning, but Jared is not impressed -- scornful in fact. But Blake is equally contemptuous of Jared's job, which is teaching language theory to students who will be able to do nothing with it except become language-theory teachers themselves. And so ad infinitum or, in Blake's judgment, nauseam. Again, no names are given, but my hunch is that Jared works at Ryerson. Jared disapproves of Blake's sex life, which consists of going out one or two nights a week for encounters with men he hopes never to see again. Blake mocks Jared for being pussy-whipped by a girlfriend who only allows him to see her at weekends, and for less than the full 48 hours at that. In sum, we learn more about Blake's lifestyle than we do about Jared's; he is the home team after all. We hear that Blake has only the most basic of TV services, and just one set of DVDs: Star Trek, which he watches incessantly because, he says, it deals with "eternal values," good and evil. He also has a pair of pet emus in his shed. Jared shudders at Star Trek, and initially at the emus as well, but the latter he eventually comes to find rather sweet.

Blake also arouses Jared's mockery, not unmixed with panic, by claiming to have conversations with their dead father. But it's the truth. Just after the intermission -- I don't think the play should have one, but there it is -- the Ghost of Dad (that's his billing) appears on the top floor of Andy Moro's split-level set, and listens to Blake's account of the rows he and his brother have been having. Dad's considered opinion is that they should cut it out. Apart from a few generally agreed rules of decent human conduct, there are no rights or wrongs. His sons should stop painting themselves into corners, give up on being judgmental, live and let live.

I couldn't agree more. But I'm not sure why we have to spend a whole evening finding this out. You have, not for the first time, to consult the program notes rather than the play itself to discover the intended wider significance. "City folk and country folk" says the oracle, "symbolize, through this specific case study, the diversity of Canadians." That's a stretch. We have two characters with differences; if they didn't have differences, there couldn't be any play. But the mere fact that these two Jacks-in-a-box are a Jack-in-the-country and a Jack-in-town doesn't make them emblematic of Canada, any more than the fact that one of them is gay and the other straight. If one of them were a woman, and the other a man, that wouldn't prove anything either. If they have different values, these aren't probed very deeply. All we have are a few fraternal grudges, spread very thin. Gilbert writes, as usual, fluent dialogue with the rare quality of sounding like believable conversation, but this time the exchanges are repetitious and, by the end, quite agonizingly tedious.

As far as performance goes, Jason Cadieux (Blake) and Wes Berger (Jared) bring the siblings' quibblings to three-dimensional life, though, at the preview I saw, Berger's score went down to two-and-a-half in his more vengeful and hysterical moments, which were both overdrawn and underpowered. Otherwise, the two play a convincing, shifting counterpoint of surliness and need. Dad is a ghostly presence indeed, but he only has one scene. Gilbert's direction, again as usual, is excellent in the easy way it cushions the actors and frames the dialogue: old-fashioned virtues but then Gilbert, for all his professions of outrageousness, is as traditional a theatre artist as we have. I'm repeating myself in saying this, but then so is he.

- Reconciliation runs through April 25 at Buddies in Bad Times. Visit artsexy.cafor ticket information.

2010-04-21-keeping-it-very-real:
The first time I saw Daniel MacIvor perform one of his self-penned one-man shows, I was knocked out by his vocal and physical virtuosity, by his tight control of the same, and by the equally precise and frequently scary array of light-and-sound effects with which Daniel Brooks' production surrounded him. Subsequent encounters found me still impressed but left me increasingly unsatisfied. All that technique was adorning sinister urban fables that didn't amount to much beyond "look at all the lonely people." A couple of years ago, MacIvor forswore solo performance and dissolved his company, da da kamera. Now, under the aegis of Brooks' company, Necessary Angel, he's back in solitary, having renounced his renunciation.

This Is What Happens Next, a title for whose relevance see above, differs from its predecessors in being the only one in which MacIvor appears initially as himself. He comes onstage with nice unexpectedness, through the auditorium, clutching a Starbucks cup and claiming to have been delayed by the demanding customers of an inexpert barista. It's good stand-up stuff that keeps promising to be more sidesplitting than it actually is. It's also dynamited a little later on, by the performer's pouring scorn on the idea that his opening routine could possibly have been either truthful or spontaneous. The admission hardly needs making but it's there as an early warning example of the second-guessing -- or, in technospeak, deconstruction --that typifies the evening.

MacIvor tells us a story, through the mouths of its various participants. First off, we meet Warren, who's recently come through a gay divorce and is off to reclaim some belongings -- including, he stresses, a John Denver album--from the home of his ex. This apparently is a reflection of MacIvor's own recent marital history, which I had probably heard about but had forgotten. Really, it shouldn't matter whether you knew about it or not. But the show keeps nudging us that it does matter, and then backing away again.

One thing leads to another, sort of. Warren mentions a possible appointment with his friend and lawyer Susan, one tough broad with two problem daughters. We meet Susan, though not her daughters, and find that if Warren breaks their date then she can keep one with Erin/Aaron, a semitransgendered astrologer who in turn tells us about his/her seven-year-old nephew Kevin, whom we eventually meet too but not before we've encountered his alcoholic father. We've been given early warning about Kevin really being the centre of things; we've been told that the author's experience figures here as well. Semi-autobiography keeps shuffling its feet and hedging its bets. Why should we care?

In between impersonations, MacIvor reverts to being himself, or as much of a self as anybody can be onstage or indeed off it; his persona is, obviously, another construct. He tells us of another character, called Will. This is a name young Kevin bestows on a giant who figures in his fantasies as a substitute for his dad. He's also The Will, as described by Schopenhauer who gets mentioned anecdotally, but doesn't appear, though he's the one person involved about whom I wanted to hear more.

Anyway, my impression is that the play is MacIvor's attempt to escape his own Will, the one that dictated the dark-glassed plays of his past, by giving us something personal and optimistic. But of course the Will will have its way. The story that gets told has a shock-horror conclusion, though it's one that, despite a child being involved, fails either to shock or to horrify. Set up as accidental but inevitable, it simply feels contrived. And that's even before the rug gets pulled from under it by a couple of alternative endings. But we know that narrators are unreliable and fictions fictitious. What's more, we always have. Breaking the fourth wall can be fun, but there's no point in getting solemn about it; nobody believed in it in the first place.

I found myself remembering The Blonde, the Brunette and the Vengeful Redhead, the Australian play of intersecting monologues that Lucy Peacock performed at Stratford a few years ago: a more conventional piece, but a far more satisfying one. That goes for performance as well as script. Peacock played people; MacIvor plays rhythms, and they aren't that various. He can be very impressive, especially when switching between tones in a fast furious staccato with his head moving in sympathy like a demented tennis umpire, and underneath it all he's likeable. But all he has to say is that he has nothing to say, which he says repeatedly. The show relies heavily on the audience's regard for its creators' previous work. It isn't a case of the emperor having no clothes, but his wardrobe does seem limited.

- This Is What Happens Next runs until May 8. Call 416-368-3110 or visit canadianstage.comfor more information.

2010-04-24-when-ancient-myth-meets-moder:
This is the story of Philomela, as told by the Roman poet Ovid. Philomela was the daughter of Pandion, King of Athens. Her father married off her sister Procne to his ally and vassal Tereus, King of Thrace. At Procne's request Tereus sailed to Athens to bring Philomela on a visit; on the voyage, he lusted after her and, on their arrival, took her to a cabin where he raped her. To prevent her telling, he cut her tongue out. She still, however, had the use of her hands, and with them she wove a tapestry that informed Procne of her fate. The sisters took a grisly revenge on Tereus, one involving his and Procne's young son. Not to give too much away but when Shakespeare's horror-comic protagonist Titus Andronicus proclaimed "Worse than Philomel you used my daughter, And worse than Procne will I be revenged" he was setting the bar very high. At retribution's climax, Procne, Philomela and Tereus were all changed by the gods into birds, Philomela most famously into a nightingale, thus qualifying for a triple in Ovid's magnum opus The Metamorphoses.

Their transformation also provides the title and governing image for Erin Shields' startlingly fine play If We Were Birds. Much of it is a straightforward retelling of the myth in barely noticeable verse: easy conversational exchanges that are alternately stark and playful. But it also opens the story up to wider, later vistas. As befits a Greek tragedy it has a chorus: six women, enslaved by one king or the other. They tell their own stories, of capture and violation; and as one talks of soldiers gang-raping her in her home ( "My husband refuses to see me. It was a lot for him, poor thing"), and another mentions internment-camps, it becomes clear that they also represent the victims of contemporary atrocities, from Bosnia to Rwanda and beyond. This is remarkably unforced, ancient myth and modern reality illuminating one another, as they're always supposed to but very rarely do. A powerful link is established between military and sexual enforcement. The legendary women are able to strike back in ways unavailable to those of the present day, but then they do have the advantage of being princesses.

The parallels strike less hard in Alan Dilworth's current production than when he first directed the play, with an almost identical cast, at Summerworks two years ago. I can't claim total recall of the original, but my impression is that rewriting, elongation and the move to a more formal venue have diluted the impact a little. But only a little. It's no longer the surprise that it was to find a newish playwright writing so extraordinarily well, but at least two of her scenes seem to me to touch greatness. Both are domestic episodes that forecast or reflect the central horrors, and both are superbly staged. One finds the two sisters sharing a bath, comparing their respective records for staying underwater and comparing what they're discovering about their own bodies and what they've heard about men's: specifically about the respective "fleshy utensils" flopping between each gender's legs. It's both more charming and more ominous than I've made it sound. The other finds old king Pandion, sick and senile but possessive as ever, berating his slave-women as if each of them were the daughter whom he simultaneously laments as having drowned. Author, actors and director combine, here and elsewhere, to freeze characters in the moment while keeping them flesh and blood and troubling: in fact, to make them mythic. David Fox's Pandion, pettish, gloating and obsessed with the grisly technicalities of far-off conflicts, suggests his Donald Rumsfeld (in Stuff Happens) translated to a grander sphere. Tara Rosling, in an astonishing elemental performance, captures Philomela as in a set of snapshots. First comes girlish awareness, rendered completely without self-consciousness; then, imperious naivete, demanding her attendants' experiences ( "speak or I won't give you any lunch"); then, half-aware young womanhood; then horrified resistance and recrimination; then mute, vindictive fury (in both senses of the word). The ineradicable memory of the girl makes what happens to the woman all the more appalling. Philippa Domville's Procne goes, in her best performance to date, a more sophisticated version of the same route. Geoffrey Pounsett's Tereus doesn't have the same iconic effect, but his role doesn't allow it; he's sweatily, uncomfortably human, a decent enough chap, in his own estimation at least, when not terrorizing people and blaming it on his "blood." This, one of the play's key words, informs the spasms of red that periodically splash across Jung-Hye Kim's mostly white set, and which Dilworth's staging brilliantly orchestrates. The chorus now includes a couple of older women, Karen Robinson and Barbara Gordon, the latter peering and squinting at the action as one who has seen the worst and only expects more of it.

The least satisfying part of the text, oddly, is the stuff about the birds. It doesn't fly. The Greeks, never too obsessed with moralizing, seem to have regarded such last-minute transmutations as a kind of escape: a celestial washing of the hands. Shields wants it to be the opposite; however much they flap their wings, these women can never forget their experiences, nor indeed can their oppressors. But I don't see that she needs the image to make the point. There's a touch of preciousness about it, the kind that, magnified, made her Epic of Gilgamesh (last year's Summerworks) a fable thrashing about for a meaning and her contribution to Red Machine (last year's Fringe) almost unbearable. This play, though, surmounts it. It tells a story -- cleanly, hauntingly, thrillingly, wittily -- and makes it reverberate. Its presence at the Tarragon crowns what must be this theatre's best season ever.

- If We Were Birds runs through May 23 at the Tarragon Theatre. For tickets, visit tarragontheatre.com.

2010-04-26-freefalling-gravity-makes-lig:
Robert Louis Stevenson wrote a sequence of short stories called The Suicide Club about an organization of people bent on doing themselves in, and about the heroic detective -- a European prince in private life -- who stops them. The stories have been adapted, with varying degrees of freedom, many times. The new TV series Gravity is, knowingly or not, the latest variation on the theme.

The suicide club it presents has aims the very reverse of Stevenson's. It's a court-ordered support group for people who have tried and failed to kill themselves: a sort of Suicides Anonymous, aimed of course at discouraging them from trying it again. In the opening sequencetwoprincipalcharacters are seen qualifying for membership. Robert Collingsworth (Ivan Sergei), a New York ophthalmologist grieving the death of his wife, drives off the edge of a cliff, to which he has been meticulously guided by GPS. There must, though, be a mercy clause built into the system, because he takes a nose dive into the pool of a gay cruise ship, whose clientele are none too pleased at having their space invaded.

Meanwhile, Lily (Krysten Ritter), who also works in the healing industry but at a less prestigious level ( "I sell makeup at a department store; I change lives," she says repeatedly), tries to off herself with, as far as I could make out, chocolate cake chased with codeine. She's rushed to hospital in time, her near-death experience involving falling in love with a non-suicidal fellow patient who seems to be a minor criminal. So at least says the policeman who spies on her, and seems to have been appointed, or to have appointed himself, her caseworker. He's as seedy and possibly disturbed as Stevenson's princely sleuth was elegant and efficient. He's played by Eric Schaeffer, whose other credits on the show include writer, director and producer. It is, I think we can assume, his baby.

It's a mongrel. The promotional material calls it a "dramedy:" a literally unspeakable word signifying a misbegotten thing. Comedy and drama can of course be combined to rich effect, as much of the best TV, current and recent, can testify. But, as any many suicide survivors could also testify, it can be hard to get the dosage right. Like a lesser Six Feet Under, itself my least favourite of the major HBO shows, Gravity, which might be subtitled "or levity," alternates rather than combines, resulting in drama that keeps undermining itself and comedy that's not so much dark as queasy. Robert's predicament is set up for laughs, Lily's for chills. Nevertheless, the two of them, right after their very first group encounter, become an item. Or at least they get it on, right there in the street. This leads to the most entertaining scene in either of the first two episodes. Robert's a Catholic, and his lapse sends him hurrying to confession. The officiating priest doesn't see how it can be adultery, given that Robert no longer has a wife, and is bored with the conversation anyway; he'd rather be placing bets over his iPhone. His message is less "go and sin no more," than, "get a life, preferably sexual." This is certainly the funniest confessional scene I've ever seen. It also features the most Jewish-sounding of Catholic priests. He's played, in what sadly seems to be a one-off guest appearance, by Robert Klein, who comes honestly by both the comedy and the Jewishness.

The group itself is presided over, and out-acted by, Ving Rhames as a former baseball player in a wheelchair. He will doubtless get even more commanding in the weeks ahead. The other members include a former model and apprentice cougar (Rachel Hunter) who is obviously being set up for future development; and a housewife (Robyn Cohen) whose problem, in stark contrast to those of her fellows, is that her life is too perfect. She gets a lot of attention in Episode 2 but doesn't really justify it. Robert has issues with his mother; Lily with her father, whom it's possible she misjudges. Gravity isn't terrible; I'm not actively opposed to finding out what happens to its characters. But I can't say I care much either.

- Gravity airs tonight at 9:30 p.m. on The Movie Network.

2010-05-01-a-play-within-a-play-within-a:
Last week, I saw the British National Theatre production of Alan Bennett's play The Habit of Art, directed by Nicholas Hytner and starring Richard Griffiths. I am tempted to call it the best time I've had in the theatre since seeing the same team's collaboration on the Broadway transfer of The History Boys. Except that I wasn't having it in the theatre, or at least not in the same theatre that the actors were in. I was at SilverCity in midtown Toronto, one of the Cineplex outlets across North America to be receiving the latest offering in the series known as NT Live. I was vicariously experiencing what must, if I have the time difference right, have been a midnight matinee at the National. Just to make the theatrical experience even more meta, The Habit of Art is actually set in a theatre. And not just any theatre. The conceit, hinted by sly in-jokes at the start and made explicit in a major speech at the end, is that we are witnessing the rehearsal of a play in the National Theatre itself. The play they're rehearsing is about a late-life meeting between two English cultural heroes, W.H. Auden, poet, and Benjamin Britten, composer. The rehearsal is marked by all the battered camaraderie, farcical misunderstandings and bruised but resilient egos that theatrical preparation is heir to.

The National has done four of these simultaneous transmissions so far, with more on the way. I've seen two, the first being Phedre, a different but almost equally successful proposition. Many of the supposed distinctions between stage, film and television acting melt away, though the audible (and occasionally visual) presence of a live audience provides an overall perspective. This isn't the film-of-the-show (always a dilution, as the movie of The History Boys, even with all the original personnel, handily demonstrates) but neither is it a static recording of the play. The cameras move, probe and explore; wide shots establish the full stage picture, close-ups reveal how inward and detailed the best stage acting can be, even when its immediate destination is a large auditorium. Though a residual theatrical piety makes me wish I had been there in person, the only thing I really missed was the opportunity to applaud. Doing so, when you aren't in the same room as the actors, still feels silly.

The play is less than the sum of its mostly brilliant parts, though its title, a phrase of Auden's own, gives it a kind of unity. "Art" is something an artist does, by compulsion that's part psychological, part economic and eventually unshakable. This applies to Auden, to Britten and to the people we see trying to put on a play about them. Griffiths plays the actor who plays Auden, who worries publicly about not looking the part (much too tubby, and needing an uncomfortable mask to suggest the aging poet's tram-lined face) and privately about learning the lines. Auden is shown returning to Oxford after his long exile in America, and sought out by Britten who wants his advice about the opera he's trying to write: Death in Venice. The meeting is imaginary, but in much earlier years, the two men had really been friends, and had even collaborated; Auden had been Britten's librettist. He very much wants "Benjy" to ask him again, but Benjy isn't buying. It's a searching, touching scene, a clash of values, styles and personalities; both men are gay, and the raffish poet wants the uptight composer to come out -- in his music, if not in his life. In truth, everyone in Britain knew about Britten, but they didn't ask and he didn't tell.

Also in attendance is Humphrey Carpenter, who in later life wrote biographies of both men. For now though, he's just a budding journalist who's come to interview Auden in his grotesquely untidy lodging, but who gets mistaken for a sex-worker whom the professor of poetry has ordered up by phone, occasioning the deathless line "I'm not a rent-boy, I'm from the BBC." When the real rent-boy turns up, he's impressed by the culture around him, but only up to a point; he ends the play-within-the-play with a speech on behalf of all those who haven't acquired the habit of art and are ignored by those who have. This seems belated and dragged in, though his fictional author claims that he's merely riffing on The Sea and the Mirror, Auden's own riff on The Tempest, which gives the last very ornate words to Caliban.

His real author, Bennett, presumably agrees, though maybe he's just having fun. He certainly provides lots of it. Travesties meets Noises Off, with results that may be even more hilarious than either. Comic writers are supposed to slacken with age, but Bennett at 75 remains funny like nobody else, generous and forgiving but always surprising and scalpel-sharp. Griffiths, the world's most complicated teddy bear, has become his ideal mouthpiece. Alex Jennings' pettish Britten is equally fine, with both men scrupulously distinguishing between their on-and-off stage personae. Frances de la Tour, the voice of reason and tolerance, as she was in The History Boys, gives a perfect performance of the perfect stage manager. Bennett apparently devised the backstage framework as a painless way of feeding the audience information, but it's grown into irresistible comedy on its own account. Hytner's production is flawless; it restored my battered faith in high-end British theatre. Short of a plane ticket, this series is the ideal way to experience it, the best of most worlds. Next up, in June, and currently packing them in on the South Bank: London Assurance. Which might be a good overall title.
