2010-05-21-productions-hands-on-and-off-:
The hottest tip for this season's best new play Tony Award is John Logans Red (Golden Theatre, New York), a two-hander in which the principal hand, and voice, is the painter Mark Rothko. Plays about art and/or artists get brownie points on Broadway, especially if theyve been imported from England. Red originated at the Donmar Warehouse in London, though its author is American. Logan's most prominent credits are the screenscripts for Gladiator, The Aviator and also for Sweeney Todd, which prompts me, especially in this Sondheim celebration year, to think of his painter play as Sunday in the Park with Mark.

Red is a discussion about art, or rather a series of tirades about it, directed by Rothko at the aspiring young painter whom he's taken on as an assistant, meaning a glorified gofer. On no account must he expect to do any actual painting; the most he can hope is to help apply the primer. And we do indeed get to see the two men furiously lathering a previously blank canvas with the heros favourite eponymous colour, thereby earning the rapturous applause that audiences always bestow on actors for performing strenuous real-life feats that they never expected to see on a stage. It also, I suppose, makes a point about art being work.

Theres one legitimately great moment. Rothko tells of someone passing his house and saying, "Hey, all those Rothkos: I wonder who owns them." It's the 1950s and he's getting hot, after years in the cold. Some of his preachments are interesting and all of them are vigorous. But theyre generic. He could be any self-centred practitioner letting off steam. He lauds his own work, expresses qualified admiration for some of his peers (hes guardedly OK with Jackson Pollock), and pours scorn on his juniors, Andy Warhol and the pop art generation, whom he accuses of giving in to commercialism rather than standing tall against it. (All artists, he says, in a predictable but still funny line, should be poor, except me.) The dramatic fulcrum is Rothko's real-life commission from New York's Four Seasons restaurant, a deal on which he reneges when he visits the place and realizes that, however uncompromising, his art doesnt stand a chance of disturbing the diners.

Late in the play, Ken the assistant, in a welcome bit of worm-turning, points out that his boss has never once asked him anything about himself -- he might be single, married, straight or gay. But the same accusation could be levelled against the play itself. I learned from Simon Schamas program note that Rothko's trip to the Four Seasons was made in the company of his second wife; the play never lets on that he had a second wife, or indeed a first one, or any children. It grants him no humanity, only opinions. The show has earned additional Tony nominations, deserved, for its director (Michael Grandage),

its designer (Christopher Oram's studio set is a stripped down battleground) and both its actors; Eddie Redmayne is a keen Ken and Alfred Molina a Rothko of high energy and even higher definition.

A Tony-nominated performance as laid-back as Molinas is aggressive is given by Christopher Walken as a man who years ago was forcibly deprived of one hand by a locomotive careening down the railroad track to which he had been playfully bound by a small gang in Spokane, Wash. (Well, thats his story. There are some holes in it.) The play is actually called A Behanding in Spokane (Gerald Schoenfeld Theatre) and it's the work of Martin McDonagh, who has transposed to an American setting the same tone of grisly flipness that characterizes his comparably titled Irish plays ( A Skull in Connemara, The Lieutenant of Inishmore). What he has left behind is the socio-political colouring and the narrative skill. Walken's character is on a lifelong country-wide search to recover his severed appendage, a quest that inevitably makes him a target for all kinds of con-artists. He doesnt take this kindly, and at one point he has two of his would-be exploiters handcuffed in a motel room that he has primed to blow up; inexplicably, they dont call for help, even though they have access to a phone and at one point even take a call -- from, oh the cuteness, their captor's aged mother.

Walken, who started his career as a song-and-dance man, glides through his role, both physically and vocally; he's always graceful, often terrifying (like an accident-prone version of Javier Bardem in No Country for Old Men), sometimes hilarious, and once -- in a spasm of self-doubt thats the plays finest moment -- both baffled and piteous.

Sam Rockwell impishly plays a bellboy-ex-machina, and Anthony Mackie ( The Hurt Locker) is one of the two tricked tricksters, both of whom are black. This has prompted accusations of racism from a New Yorker reviewer who professes to have no problem with MacDonagh's uniformly unflattering portrayals of the Irish. What's really troubling is that its MacDonagh himself, one of the few real playwrights around, who seems to have lost a hand, or at least to be writing with one tied behind his back.

The best dramatic evening I had in New York was at a two-year-old revival of a 70-year-old play. I never expected to see a better production of Thornton Wilders Our Town than Soulpepper's in Toronto, but David Cromer's acclaimed off-Broadway staging is as good, and different.

At the Barrow Street Theatre, which has the feel and dimensions of a community hall, Wilders prescribed simplicity of setting is taken to extremes: just two small tables and some chairs with the audience on three sides. The narrating Stage Manger (Michael Shannon) passes among us in a performance of virtuoso unassumingness, and a vanished society, narrow in its horizons but rich in feeling, comes movingly to life. The final graveyard scene is especially fine, crowned when the just-buried Emily is granted her one day back on Earth; a white curtain parts, disclosing the sights, sounds and smells of a real kitchen. Besides being a great coup de theatre in its own right, this ironically honours the plays own conventions. The play rejects naturalistic scenery, in the pursuit of truth; the production restores it--in the one scene that's pure fantasy.

Black & White Photo: Sara Krulwich, The New York Times / "More cowbell? What are you talking about? I'm trying to act baffled and piteous here!" Christopher Walken on Broadway.; Caption:
2010-05-22-a-fear-of-death-and-what-come:
John Patrick Shanleys play Wheres My Money? is a dark comedy of Manhattan manners, befitting the screenwriter of Moonstruck. Shanley is also the author of Doubt, one of those pseudo-serious dramas beloved of both Broadway and Hollywood, but the present piece is far more entertaining, and also more searching.

It's constructed somewhat on the model of Arthur Schnitzler's La Ronde, though only somewhat. Its a succession of duologues in which a character from one scene will be paired with a different partner in the next. It does not, however, adhere to this pattern with the same geometric purity as its predecessor. A couple of the couples get to play return matches, and a few scenes even involve a third party, though admittedly under peculiar circumstances: To make no bones about it, the third person is always a ghost. The difference that makes all the difference is that most of Schnitzlers scenes depict one-night stands while Shanley's characters are all -- I nearly said trapped but anyway, all in relationships.

It goes like this. In Scene One, Celeste, a deeply unsuccessful actress, confides in her friend Natalie about the two men in her life: her loser druggie boyfriend and her older S&M lover. Natalie tells her, very emphatically, to get a life, preferably one like her own: She married a lawyer. However, that marriage, when we follow Natalie home, turns out to have its own problems, mainly of non-communication. Natalie's husband, Henry, takes those problems to the office; he confides in his boss, Sidney, whose experience of wedlock is even bleaker than his own, but who is taking traditional means of escaping from it. He expounds on these, at frequently hilarious length: Monogamy," he says in what may not be the plays best line but is certainly its most quotable, "is like a 40-watt bulb; it works, but its not enough." We follow him home, too, and find his wife, Marcia Marie, seething equally with resentment and possessiveness. Theirs is a love-hate relationship, like all those in the play, but it's important to note that in all of them the love exists. Sidney and Natalie are the characters who get the most stage time, and each of them is haunted, literally, by the ghost of a dead lover. Tommy, Natalie's ex, makes threatening appearances from beyond, demanding repayment of $3,000 -- her price for leaving poor him and marrying rich Henry. Just about everyone in the play claims to have been financially shafted by his or her partner, hence the title. This theme, though, is not well integrated into the rest of the play, and David Ferrys production (for Alley Co-op) cannot bridge the gap. Ferry is our most undervalued director, but this is not his best work.

He deals well with the spookiness, bringing the cast before us in separate columns of eerie light, singing. When he repeats the effect at the end, though, it effectively defuses the authors own denouement. The performances, meanwhile, have largely failed to connect. The play's structure sets its own acting problems. We are all, to some extent, different people, depending on whom we're talking to, so most of these characters have two personalities. The trick is to make each of them add up to a person, and the only actor who really brings this off is Ingrid Rae Doucet as the woebegone Celeste. But then she doesnt have anything to reconcile; having made the first scene work superbly, she all but disappears -- for which, I have to say, she has a first-class alibi. None of the others seem to have quite the skills. Michael Kash brings Catskill-comic bravado to Sidney, but lacks weight. John Clelands Henry is amorphous, Mary Francis Moore's Marcia Marie biting in her bitterness but unvaried, while as Natalie, the closest thing to a central figure, Anna Hardwick delivers an excessive amount of vocal finger-wagging.

From duologues to monologues. La Sagouine gathers five of them, the reminiscences of an Acadian floor-scrubber and fisherman's wife as imagined, originally for radio, by Antonine Maillet and as performed, for almost 40 years, by the now octogenarian Viola Leger, who has taken such complete possession of them that its impossible to imagine anyone else doing them, or her playing anybody else. Though Im assured, on excellent authority, that she most certainly can. The writing is weakest when anecdotal, strongest when reflective to the point of being metaphysical. La Saguoine reflects, like Hamlet but more cheerfully, on why she should fear death, or something after it, when it could hardly be worse than her own hardest of hard-scrabble lives. She muses on how unfair it is that, when the doctors tell you that you've got something, it's you and not they who have to live with it. She looks back nostalgically on the war, as the best thing to have happened since the Depression; they were the only times when the government felt obliged to do something for you. And she welcomes spring and does indeed seem, quite unsentimentally, transfigured by it. The cracks in her face light up. Shod in plimsolls (Act One) or boots (Act Two), her defining gesture a stern strong shake of the head, Leger summons both a harshly particular way of life and a universal spirit of transcendence.

- Where's My Money? runs through May 30 at the Pia Bouman Studio Theatre. Call 416-504-7529 for more information. La Sagouine runs through May 29 in English (June 5 in French) at the Berkeley Street Theatre Downstairs. Call 416-368-3110 for details.

2010-05-26-bye-bye-bauer-after-eight-sea:
'If only I'd listened to you, Jack" said soon-to-be-ex-President Taylor in the closing moments of the closing episode of the closing season of 24, "things wouldn't have turned out like this." It could have been the motto of the entire show, or at least of the last seven of its eight seasons. As I remember it, the Jack Bauer of Day 1 was a super-shrewd action hero with unbeatable martial and physical skills, but he wasn't omniscient. Subsequently, though, he developed the ability to see around corners. This season, in particular, has shown him constantly able to see through his opponents' schemes, almost before they launch them. They set traps for him, he gives every appearance of walking into them, and then he escapes because he can read their minds.

I shouldn't be using the present tense. The game is over; even if, as half-promised, there's going to be a movie, it's over. 24 needs its long haul, and it has made excellent use of it. The show has taken the manufacturing of televised tension to new levels, of both intensity and durability. The last season, happily, has been one of the best, and its sign-off was a treat. Jack, escaping summary execution for the umpteenth time, was allowed a tearful farewell, appropriately via long-distance hookup, with Chloe. "I never thought," said Jack, with uncharacteristic emotion, "when you first came to CTU, that it was you who'd end up watching my back." Fans had been pining for a moment like that: An acknowledgment that the two loved one another but were not in love.

Like every previous head of CTU, Chloe had found herself trying to rein Jack in. Unlike them, she had succeeded: she managed to dissuade him from shooting the Russian President. President Suvarov was in New York to ink a peace treaty whose other signatories were the United States and a fictitious but recognizable Islamic country known as the IRK. U.S. President Allison Taylor desperately wanted this agreement; so, in the face of violent internal opposition, did IRK President Omar Hassan. The Russians didn't, and Suvarov had Hassan assassinated. However slimy ex-President Logan had the dirt on Suvarov, and blackmailed him back to the conference table, in hopes of refurbishing his own reputation. President Taylor, passionately committed to the peace process, went along with this, even after learning the truth about Hassan's death. But the Russians had also taken out Jack's girlfriend Renee, who knew too much. That did it. Jack got through to Taylor's better nature, and the treaty died. The irony, unnoticed by Jack and also apparently by the show itself, is that, so far from this being a defeat for Suvarov, it meant he got exactly what he'd wanted. But maybe he'd forgotten.

Taylor's conscience was stirred, with more intentional irony, by hearing Jack's self-videotaped valediction in which he declared that no worthwhile peace could be based on lies and murder. This foray into international morality was a new departure for our protagonist. It's part, obviously, of the show's determination to pass him off as a tragic hero. A tragic hero needs self-awareness, and neither Jack's character nor the show's format has allowed for that. His friends have talked of Renee's death sending him "to the dark side" but he really doesn't seem to have changed much. If anything, he's tortured fewer people this season than previously, though his evisceration of Renee's killer was admittedly a showpiece.

Occasionally, someone asked Jack who gave him the right to be judge, jury and executioner. The answer is, we did; we shared those functions with him. We were entitled, because we always knew the facts. It's one of the differences between this show and real life. Another is that in the real world, political processes are unlikely to be halted on moral grounds. And if that process is a peace settlement, the real world may even be right.

If the season has had a tragic figure, it's been Cherry Jones' self-compromising President Taylor, faced with impossible choices. Her performance, and Gregory Itzin's face-screwing Logan, have been welcome injections of class acting. Kiefer Sutherland's performance one takes, unfairly, for granted; but try imagining the show without him. As Chloe, Mary Lynn Rajskub remained splendid, and could still be hilariously sour.

Annie Wersching's death as Renee was enough in itself to refute Jonathan Kay's assertion in these pages that the also-late Lost is the only TV show in which bad things have been allowed to happen to good people. 24 has been slaughtering its innocents since its inception. And that's without getting into cable TV, in which sympathetic characters are devastated or despatched on a regular basis. It's called serious drama. 24 has never been that, though it has expertly scratched some contemporary itches. Its first season remains its best: the only one which seemed plausibly to be unfolding within a single day. It also gave us Jack himself at his most believable, even without soul-searching. He never really developed after that, whatever his creators may have told themselves. And people never did learn to trust him. But if they had, there wouldn't have been a show. And we would have missed something. I'll miss it now.

2010-05-29-finding-strength-in-weaknesse:
Oscar Wilde's An Ideal Husband opened in London in 1895, months before his last and most lasting play The Importance of Being Earnest. So it might be categorized as "late transitional" -- Wilde's final attempt to graft traditional society melodrama onto his own unique creation, the farce of manners, before letting the latter genre take over completely, thereby creating a masterpiece. You can see it coming in An Ideal Husband in the scenes in which Viscount Goring, young man-about-town, presses his suit on Miss Mabel Chiltern, who has no intention of refusing him but wants him to work at it. Then they have to convince their relatives, who aren't monsters. It's as if the courtship of Algy Moncrieff and Cecily Cardew were to happen in a world with repercussions

It can be quite a relief to meet Wilde characters who, while funny, are more than walking epigrams. There were even moments, during the Shaw Festival's production, when I found myself heretically thinking that An Ideal Husband wears better then The Importance, though that may well be because we don't have to see it as often. Not that it's that much of a rarity. This is the play's third major Ontario staging in a decade.

It's also the best. Jackie Maxwell's production has both wit and passion, though it delivers them in imperfect quantities. The plot is ignited by a Mrs. Cheveley, an archetypal late-Victorian adventuress whose flamboyantly dubious past entails our never learning anything about Mr. Cheveley. She returns to London, from profitable exile in Vienna, to reveal herself as Europe's most glamorous lobbyist. She wants Sir Robert Chiltern, a notoriously honourable British MP, to come out in favour of a canal-building scheme that they both know to be deeply corrupt. Sir Robert's one weak spot is that, at the very start of his career, he engaged in a not dissimilar spot of insider trading, and Mrs. C. has the goods on him. Besides, it's personal: She and Lady Chiltern were at school together; they despised one another then and they do so now. Lady Chiltern has an even higher moral code than her husband; they place one another on pedestals, and Mrs. Cheveley would like nothing more than to knock them off.

The play's wild (or Wilde) card, the one character to travel freely between plot lines and dialogue styles and moral codes, is the debonair Lord Goring, Robert's best friend and putative brother-in-law, and -- for about five minutes, long ago -- Mrs. Cheveley's fiance. He's in a good position to defeat her blackmailing schemes. He's also, and more interestingly, ideally equipped to dissuade each of the married Chilterns from being their own, and one another's, best-intentioned worst enemies. The last act is a minor triumph of interlocking ironies as the characters are brought to realize not just that in their union there is strength, but that part of that strength lies in acknowledging and accepting weaknesses.

The play's continued political and moral pertinence hardly needs underlining, but it gets some anyway. The avowed aim of Maxwell and her designers is to respect the play's period setting but "twist it ever so slightly." This just about works, especially in the nerve-jangling sound score that John Gzowski has cooked up. Judith Bowden turns the Chilterns' drawing-room, where most of the action takes place, into a vast balustraded whispering gallery, which seems apt in a play that largely hinges on gossip and the dread thereof. Her costumes are, well, eclectically creative. Moya O'Connell's Mrs. Cheveley, a classic scarlet woman at her first appearance, is even greater, later, in green. Steven Sutcliffe's Lord Goring seems to be sporting some kind of apron underneath his frock coat. The two of them play their great confrontation superbly; there is, unusually, a feeling that there was once a strong sexual connection between them, and that it still holds. Both performances can stray into the wrong kind of anachronism. Sutcliffe in particular sometimes indulges in the kind of special pleading that's the bane of all but our best actors: Especially perplexing since he is one of our best actors. Mostly though, he personifies the play's meaning and its attraction: dandyism as a moral force.

Patrick Galligan seemed, in prospect, almost too well cast as the upright Robert. His recent role in Courageous, though, gave him a welcome break from being noble, and the iron injection obviously took; his performance here is equally powerful in self-assertion, self-defence and self-flagellation. He finds the passion in priggishness. As his lady, Catherine McGregor unfortunately finds only the priggishness. When she berates or exhorts her husband, she seems to be striking attitudes rather than making her own kind of love. You wonder whether their marriage is really worth saving.

The minor aristos, presumably meant to set the social tone, are mostly dowdy, with Ali Momen's Vicomte de Nanjac a briefly sparkling exception. Marla McLean makes a pleasing bobbing-cork impression as the future Viscountess Goring, while as her putative papa-in-law, Lorne Kennedy mines every laugh from a role that's studded with them, though without gluing them together into a person. He's also the voice of the political establishment; when Sir Robert unexpectedly gains political capital from doing the right thing, he welcomes him as a new rising star who'll help keep the radicals out. One hopes that, at moments like this, Wilde's tongue was in his cheek, especially as 1895 was to be the year of his own downfall. There was no Lord Goring to rescue him, making it especially ironic that the character is generally taken to be a self-portrait. I recant my heresy: An Ideal Husband is wish fulfilment; it offers hostages to morality. It's the escapist Importance that takes no prisoners.

- An Ideal Husband runs through Oct. 31 at the Festival Theatre, Niagara-on-the- Lake. Call 1-800-511-SHAW or visit shawfest.comfor details.
2010-06-05-what-good-is-reality-anyway-s:
The two best productions in an impressive opening week at the Shaw Festival are of Chekhov's The Cherry Orchard and Mary Chase's Harvey, both of them domestic comedies, staffed by obsessives. They are also both about the urge to escape reality, an impulse that, in defiance of their cultures' respective reputations for dreaminess and practicality, the Russian writer deplores and the American enthusiastically endorses.

The Cherry Orchard is directed by Jason Byrne, the Irishman celebrated in Toronto for his productions of Festen and A Whistle in the Dark; his compatriot Tom Murphy, author of the former play, provided the easy-flowing adaptation of this one. Like those other shows, this one unrolls freely but compulsively. It starts with a perfect evocation of the half-awake early morning as Lopakhin, the peasant turned profiteer, and Dunyasha, the sentimental maid, await the return from Paris of Madame Ranyevskaya and her abbreviated retinue. The second-act prelude is similarly evocative: The domestics' criss-cross patterns of loneliness and flirtation, at once aimless and desperate, are as compellingly executed as any I recall. Much the same is true of the mopped-brow partying that starts the third act, and of the hurried, empty packing-up that starts the last one. The final dying fall, Al Kozlik's superannuated Firs, alone and forgotten in the deserted house, is equally haunting, equally precise and unstressed.

Within these multiple frames is a production that seems to have no specific agenda except to render every moment as truthful and spontaneous as possible. It doesn't beg us to laugh or to grieve at its characters; their saving grace as people is that they can do those things for themselves, often simultaneously. Laurie Paton's Ranyevskaya is a mix of soft-hearted and hard-headed; she knows what she is doing to herself, and to those around her. The only thing I can fault her for is an apparent absence of anxiety as she waits for news of the auction of her estate; she may not care as much as she claims about the fate of the cherry orchard, but she should care something. Jim Mezon may never have done anything better than his gravely ridiculous Gayev, the self-proclaimed "man of the '80s" trying to find himself a place in a new and hostile world. His ode to the family bookcase is exquisite, though delivered from a corner that, from my seat at the side of the house, rendered him almost invisible. However, Byrne doesn't believe in set blocking, so at other performances he may well declaim it from centre stage. The tearful farewells of this brother and sister, consumed with too-lateness, will be deeply affecting, wherever they play it. Benedict Campbell is extraordinary in Lopakhin's falling-down-drunk account of how he bought the orchard, pride and shame erupting from him in alternating violent spasms; it's the culmination of the love and resentment that he feels towards his exasperating genteel neighbours. Gord Rand's emaciated Trofimov, the perpetual student and apprentice revolutionary, is his perfect foil and perfect goad; a mellower sequel to these actors' recent confrontation as Hamlet and Claudius. Severn Thompson does fine pent-up emotion as Varya, Neil Barclay is irresistibly shameless as the Micawberish Pishchik and the servants, as I've hinted, are excellent. Julie Martell's Dunyasha is the most finished among them, but Mark Uhre gets at the springs behind the valet's callousness, and Gabrielle Jones is strikingly bold as the circus-bred German governess. She is hardly the play's central character but, with her conjuring tricks and her fear of destitution, she may be its emblematic one.

Harvey, the 1944 hit, emerges here as a good play, suspenseful and hilarious, not just a star-encrusted legend. Elwood P. Dowd, Denver's most lovable drunk, calls his invisible six-foot rabbit companion Harvey because he'd never known anyone of the name and therefore "had such high hopes for it." James Stewart, re-creating his Elwood in London, sounded depths of hopeful melancholy with that line that Peter Krantz at Niagara cannot reach. Stewart, though, never succeeded in making me see Harvey for myself, while Krantz, in Joseph Ziegler's lovely production, succeeds completely. Elwood is a one-note role; Krantz hits his note--sweet undentable wistfulness -- exactly, and sustains it impeccably. The real motor here, though, is Mary Haney as Elwood's sister, driven to her own kind of distraction -- some farcical, some dead serious -- by her brother and by the psychiatrists to whom she commits him. Just the way she says "festooned" in an opening phone conversation brings the house down; she also has it on tenterhooks at the end as she battles herself on whether to do the right thing. Also sublime are a brace of shrinks: Norman Browning's senior clinician, haughty and haunted; and Gray Powell, a precision instrument of an actor, as his unluckily confident junior. Diana Donnelly is pleasing as an adoring nurse. This is a huggable production that never quite lets you forget that this (like Blithe Spirit) is one of those wartime plays that Never Mentions the War but is still soaked in it. Both these Shaw shows have fine sets. Peter Hartwell's for the Chekhov is spare and suggestive; Sue LePage supplies for the Chase one of those comfy American drawing rooms you would swear the festival keeps in storage, except that this one can turn quite spectacularly into the shapeliest of sanatoria.

- The Cherry Orchard is in repertory through Oct. 2 at the Court House Theatre, Niagara-on-the-Lake; Harvey through Oct. 31 at the Royal George Theatre. Call 1-800-511-SHAW or visit shawfest.comfor details.

2010-06-09-all-together-now:
AS YOU LIKE IT

Festival Theatre, Stratford

---

Des McAnuff's production of As You Like It is the best thing he has done at Stratford, by miles. It's visually glowing, musical in manners both riotous and subtle, mines nearly all the humour in the text plus some from outside, and is finally very moving. The play is a clear-eyed celebration of love and marriage, and the test of a production's success is whether it can inspire both happiness and awe when the four couples are united at the close. This one brings it off triumphantly.

It also highlights the play's headlong mix of conventions and, in so doing, reconciles them. This is a production set in, though mercifully not "about" the 1920s. Debra Hanson's desings for the Forest of Arden draw on a surrealist palette to depict the script's all-purpose Arcadia in which storybook lions may not lie down with lambs but do co-exist with realistically tended sheep. Motifs out of Dali or Magritte drop from the flies, though the green beneath them, dazzlingly lit by Michael Walton, is surprisingly uncluttered; there are no trees to get in the way of the wood. Before we get there, we're in a court ruled by a usurping Duke who's an apprentice Hitler. There are some excesses here: Duke Frederick may be a neurotic tyrant, but it's a cliche to have him kill or beat up everybody who comes before him (I'm still trying to work out the identity of one of his victims); while the initial grappling of Orlando and his big bad brother is so prolonged that the official wrestling match in the next scene is an anti-climax.

A play that's mostly mood rather than narrative is hurt by having two intermissions. And I strongly object to having old Adam, just before the first break, drop dead from faithful exhaustion, while those around heartlessly get on with singing, "Blow, blow, thou winter wind." It may be a cynical song, but it doesn't work as a requiem. Most of the song settings, though, are delightfully jazzy (they're by Justin Ellington, himself related to a Duke), culminating in an irresistible treatment of that prototypical pop number "It was a lover and his lass." Other music is by Michael Roth; as in his Romeo and Juliet, McAnuff underscores the moments at which people fall in love, but this time he does it with delicacy.

Most of all, this Arden is a forest of good performances. Andrea Runge's Rosalind is a Bloomsbury painter (the unfortunate Touchstone has to lug her easel on his back, along with sundry suitcases), and her interpretation is as yet more of a sketch than a finished portrait, stronger on wit, which could still be sharper, than on ardour.

Thegreatlove-lessontoOrlando is still a shadow of what it might be. But she's astringent, responsive to moods, lovely when she declares the fathom-depth of her love, and--the acid test of a Rosalind -- she earns the right to speak the Epilogue. Like nearly everyone in this show, she makes the words leap off the stage. Of her two foils, Cara Ricketts is an aptly deflationary Celia, alternately tickled and shocked by her cousin's gender-bending excesses, while Paul Nolan's Orlando, his first non-musical role, is quite the revelation.

Brent Carver, in a Magrittean bowler hat, is not the most amusingJaquesIhaveseen, and his diction can carry casualness to the point of sloppiness, but he may be the most painful and authentic loner; his self-exile at the end is inevitable and makes you feel both with and for him. Ben Carlson's Touchstone suffers in his first scene from there being no 20th-century equivalent of a uniformed court jester, but once in the forest he blossoms as a sensual, sardonic commentator on everything including himself, not to mention an enthusiastic impromptu bassist. He too has a couple of fine foils: Lucy Peacock's enchantingly moonstruck Audrey and Randy Hughson's imperturbable herdsman Corin.

The philosophical debate of shepherd and clown is prefaced by offstage baa-ing, which is funny and apt, and interrupted by much more of it, which isn't. The younger shepherd Silvius is exceptionally well played, for both comedy and pathos, by Ian Lake, who is in turn well partnered by Dalal Badr's Phebe, vain but with a brain. Mike Shara's Oliver is better at redemption than at rage; good at both is Tom Rooney, who doubles the Dukes, showing the odd spark of frustrated affection as Frederick, while playing his banished brother for warmth rather than preachiness. Brian Tree's Adam, while alive, is a smashing serio-comic retainer, lifting very large stones and carrying them very short distances, while Dan Chameroy's rustic William is bewitchingly bothered and bewildered. In fact, this company has never functioned better; the most anonymous roles are likely to be lit up by established names (Sean Arbuckle) or unknown ones (Jonathan Purdon).

I come back to that ending. When Rosalind reappears in her woman's clothes, she's ushered in by Hymen, the god of marriage. In some productions he's a forester dressed up; here he's played (by Roy Lewis) as the real deal. The rustic pastor (Victor Ertmannis) who'd thought to perform the rites recognizes he's been out-ranked, and falls to his knees. It's a small moment but transcendent. A little later the Duke calls for a dance to close proceedings. It's nice, and you expect to go on for ever, but it's cut short. Someone has discovered tact, and it's a blessing.

- As You Like It runs through Oct. 31. For tickets and more information, visit stratfordfestival.ca.

2010-06-12-she-s-their-fire-at-their-des:
History books may record this as the Shaw Festival's Clare Boothe Luce season. Luce, New York society beacon and journalist (edited Vanity Fair, married into Time-Life) is mentioned in One Touch of Venus as a symbol of style and wealth and smartness, and is author of The Women, a play that both skewers and worships the same qualities.

One Touch of Venus is a 1943 musical assembled by the heady team of Kurt Weill (music), Ogden Nash (book and lyrics), and S.J. Perelman (book). It's based on a Victorian English comic novel, The Tinted Venus, in which a statue of the goddess comes to life and wreaks havoc. The musical updates and transports it. The Anatolian Venus is brought to Manhattan by Whitelaw Savory, a super-rich art expert who sees it both as an investment and as a reminder of a girl whom he once loved and lost. The statue is accidentally reanimated by Rodney Hatch, a shy young barber on whom she immediately sets her sights, sights that he speedily comes to enjoy. And whats more, shes got arms.

This is a post-Oklahoma! musical, though so immediately post (they opened the same year) that the narrative revolution had hardly had time to take. Some of the show is story-driven, some is haphazard; it opens, for example, with an arbitrary, not to say philistine, number about the faddishness of modern art. Much of the action is a chase: Savory and his goons in vengeful pursuit of the barber and his divine doxy, with additional input from Rodney's bullying fiancee, her yet more monstrous mother and some late-arriving Turkish guerrillas. It's a thin but frantic story, sometimes funny, occasionally touching, the latter quality much enhanced by the best of Weills music. This is the most "Broadway" of his American scores, and some of it is stuff that Cole Porter could have done better, but it also boasts such a driving, jagged tune as Venus perplexed I'm a Stranger Here Myself, and the great ballad duet Speak Low, Shakespearean in its title, its imagery and its compression. Nash, the laureate of comic verse, was paradoxically best as a lyricist when writing love songs. Speak Low deepens the evening, or should; the approach to it at the Shaw is strangely giggly.

Most of Eda Holmes' production is delightful, especially in its evocation, via Camellia Koos sets and act drops, of wartime New York: something that the original audiences must have taken for granted but is helpful to us. Ryan deSouzas musical direction is excellent, as is Michael Lichtefeld's choreography, especially in the show's two satirical ballets. The one major problem, the one that has always dogged this show, is how to cast the goddess of love. Robin Evans Willis, whos a bit too young for divinity, plays her as a self-conscious seductress, and comes off coy. Venus wouldnt have to act sexy; she is sex. There must be subtler ways of showing a woman's feelings for a man than the current Shaw practice (it happens in Harvey, too) of having her rub herself up against him. Kyle Blair's Rodney -- half eager-beaver, half nerd -- is spot-on. Mark Uhre doesnt have the mileage for Savory, but he sings beautifully, especially in a yearning ballad that has nothing to do with the rest of his character. The toughs are very sharply played by Jay Turvey and Neil Barclay, whom the authors of Guys and Dolls must have foreseen when they wrote Sit Down, Youre Rockin' the Boat. Julie Martell and Gabrielle Jones play the barber's thwarted in-laws as arrant grotesques, which is perfectly fine. The most commanding performance of all comes from Deborah Hay as Savorys sharp-tongued secretary who informs us in show-stopping song that "one way to be very wealthy / Is to be very, very rich."

She carries the same message, along with the rest of the large all-female cast, in The Women. She also, in both shows, adheres to the Niagara convention by which all American women below a certain social level -- and sometimes, as in Hays two roles, above it -- are presumed to sound like gangsters' adenoidal molls. The Women elaborately depicts a rarefied slice of the inter-war Big Apple in which wives take their husbands' infidelities for granted, and compensate with shopping, card games, workouts and, in extreme circumstances, divorce; one scene takes us to Reno where, were told, the actual residents seldom use the facilities. Its a sharp moment in a generally flabby script. Mainly we follow the story of Mary, the solitary innocent in the pack, who finally learns to sharpen her nails and reclaim her spouse from the gold-digger by whom he's been appropriated. It's a long journey to nothing very much. Jenny Young as Mary and Moya OConnell as her antagonist give recognizably human performances, along with Kelli Fox, whose voice cuts like a knife through a blur of an opening scene, placed so far upstage that the complicated task of establishing the characters becomes impossible. The other rich bitches are caricatures, Wendy Thatcher being the most entertaining. The lower orders double, treble and quadruple like rabbits, throwing up believable performances from Melanie Phillipson as an Irish maid and Patty Jamieson as several people. Theres a submerged class-war in the play, but in Alisa Palmer's production, it's mostly fought in the wrong way. A society dame complains from her hospital bed about the inconveniencies of her latest childbirth; a nurse tells her grimly how bad pregnancy can be for poor people. It's acted here as a tantrum meeting a lecture. The main attraction is watching the massive components of William Schmuck's set form and reform; sometimes, as in a deluxe bathroom scene, the finished product looks witty. Mostly, it just looks expensive.

- One Touch of Venus is in repertory until Oct. 10; The Women until Oct. 9. Call 1-800-511-SHAW or visit shawfest.comfor more information.

2010-06-18-play-by-the-colonial-rule:
THE AFRICA TRILOGY

Fleck Dance Theatre, Toronto

---

Everybody wants a piece of Africa. The old colonial theme is also, more subtly diffused, the unifying theme of The Africa Trilogy, staged at this year's Luminato festival by Toronto's Volcano Theatre, which has gathered an impressively multinational creative team. All three of the evening's plays centre around an African girl or young woman whom the other characters need for their own validation. Some of those laying claim are other Africans.

In the middle play, though, which is also the best, all the people we actually meet are European. Peggy Pickit Sees the Face of God, written by Roland Schimmelpfennig, who as you might have guessed is German, and directed by Liesl Tommy, who is South African-American, is set in what might well, for present purposes, be Toronto. There are four characters, married couples, all of them doctors. Carol and Martin have returned from four years of working in an unnamed African country; their old friends Frank and Liz have invited them over for dinner. Frank and Liz would like to have gone to Africa too, but feel that, having a young daughter, they really couldn't. This prompts their guests to point out, acidly, that there are children in Africa too. It's the first drop of acid in a play that ends up suffused in it. There are scars and chasms in both marriages, and the reunion lays them bare. The domestic bourgeois battlefield isn't exactly new territory for drama, but this one explores it sharply, economically and without patronizing anybody.

It seems for a time that the African element is almost incidental, and that the play might work better in isolation than as one third of a whole. I'm actually not convinced that that isn't the case, but the suspicion that Carol and Martin could have gone anywhere with the same dramatic results does gradually melt away. While in Africa, the two expats virtually adopted a sick girl; now, for reasons that are hinted at but never fully explained, they've returned in a hurry, without her. Frank is jovially unconcerned by this, as by most things, but Liz is appalled, for an inextricable variety of reasons. She's a concerned, if absentee, humanitarian; but she's also immediately concerned with the effect on her own daughter, who has lost a pen pal, and on whose behalf she has bought a doll, for a girl who is now probably dead. That's what the title refers to.

The play uses a stop-time device; periodically, the scene freezes, and is then replayed, with additional information providing a different perspective. (Perspectives are very much what this play's about, reflected -- the perfect word -- on a screen doubling as a mirror. The entire trilogy is very video-conscious.)

The actors, in a superbly rigorous production, are constantly required to switch tone, from polite conviviality to undercover bitterness, until the barriers drop and the moods converge. This is particularly true of the women, with Jane Spidell's Liz moving inexorably towards hysteria and Maeve Beaty's Carol turning brilliantly on a whole march of dimes. Tony Nappo plays Frank, and Trey Lyford, an American actor, plays Martin, balding and unsettlingly amiable, who halfway through steps outside the frame to narrate a fable about the sources and expectations of aid. At the time it seems gratuitous; later it reverberates, as the centre of the whole trilogy.

In the preceding play, Close Your Eye, written by Binyavanga Wainaina, a Kenyan, but set in Nigeria, the pivotal figure is Beka, daughter of a revered, and murdered, activist. Shiningly played by Dienye Waboso, she is courted, professionally speaking, by a Lagos computer entrepreneur, and more intimately and from a distance by Doreen, a compassion merchant (no slight intended) who lives in Toronto and with whom Beka maintains a lively electronic correspondence (if the Doras were to introduce a category for best Skyped performance, Karen Robinson's Doreen would be a worthy recipient). Ross Manson, Volcano's artistic director, handles this play himself, and delivers a production stronger on musical and technological bravura than on narrative development.

After one play with an all-black cast and one with an all-white one, integration arrives with Glo, unhappily the weakest of the three. Written by Christina Anderson (American) and directed by Josette Bushell-Mingo (British-Swedish) this, like Close Your Eye, has a heroine bemused by the attention she's attracting. She's Lydia, a Kenyan attending a diversity conference in New York on the strength of having written a book. She's besieged by her British sponsor; by a couple of start-up business partners, one black, one white and trying to impress with what Dame Edna Everage called "that meaningless word, infrastructure;" and, via phone calls that never connect, by her troubled brother back home. The situation keeps being restated, and the staging is dour and portentous. Dorothy A. Atabong is a sensible, sympathetic Lydia, and two of the Peggy Pickit cast reappear: Lyford, unrecognizable, as a would-be smooth operator, and Beaty, recognisable, though with an English accent that could fool Professor Higgins.

- The Africa Trilogy runs until Sunday. For tickets, visit luminato.com.

2010-06-19-start-to-finish-this-is-an-in:
I have a couple of pedantic reservations about Stratford's smashing production of Kiss Me, Kate, and I'll get them out of the way at the start. First: The interpolation, from another Cole Porter score altogether, of From This Moment On does nothing for the show, and the character who sings it shouldn't be singing at all, as he's the one civilian in a backstage/ onstage musical otherwise peopled by theatre folk going, mostly frantically, about their business. (This is no reflection on the actor, Kristian Truelsen; he's excellent.) Second: Director John Doyle has had the idea of using the chorus characters, actors or stage hands or both, as a more classical kind of chorus, live sounding boards for the principals' songs, and it mostly works brilliantly. But he overplays his hand when he lets them share the stage with soubrette Lois Lane for her gold-digging classic Always True to You in My Fashion, which should be strictly between her and her boyfriend-in-waiting. He's also cut about half the song, including its best stanza, the two decisions depriving Chilina Kennedy, who plays Lois, of a full-blooded chance to stop the show.

On the other hand, she has been stopping it all evening. Kennedy is a tornado dancer, a dynamite singer with a voice as true as powerful, and a lithe and delectable looker. She's also an actress, able to take a role to its limits. She runs here with the idea of Lois as a nightclub singer, eager to prove herself in a Shakespearean musical based on The Taming of the Shrew but unable to shed old habits. Lois's blank-verse line readings are best described as enthusiastic; likewise her vamping of the audience. Mike Jackson matches her as Bill, her amatory and professional partner, a champion hoofer who has a slightly more refined version of the same thespian problem. The two of them also manage to build a relationship, ultimately a touching one, from a minimum of material. This is part of the triumph of Doyle's production, the only one I've seen to make Porter's score seem like a score, rather than a collection of great individual songs. He knows which, like Why Can't You Behave, can be finessed to advance story and character; which, like Too Darn Hot, must be given extended and irresistible rein in their own right; and which, like the glorious So in Love, can do both. The reappraisal starts at the top. This Kiss Me, Kate is not only a show within a show; it's also a show within a dream, maybe owing something to the Christopher Sly framing scenes in Shrew itself. The normally rumbustious Another Op'nin, Another Show is here bemused and reflective (and it actually comes before the overture); the production's ending I wouldn't want to give away, except to say that it's magic and a perfect match.

Which reminds me: the leads. Juan Chioran plays Fred Graham, the egomaniacal actor-manager who both directs and acts Petruchio, and Monique Lund is his ex-wife Lilli Vanessi, lured back from a dubiously successful stint in Hollywood to play Kate, and finding herself stuck in an unusually trying tryout in Baltimore. Of course they squabble, enflamed by all kinds of jealousy; of course they will get back together again. The process is here surprisingly detailed, and even moving, with the interplay of their on-and offstage roles more vividly realized than I would have thought possible. If a few vital pages of the relationship seem to have gone missing at the end, that must be blamed on the book (by Sam and Bella Spewack), which is funny but fragmentary. Chioran, an obviously fine Petruchio in any context, is witty and commanding, but also unobtrusively sensitive, though his singing, while resonant, is not as supple and exploratory as his acting. Lund, who has a powerhouse voice, also seems to be a very good sport; I'm not sure that she too needs to vamp the audience (maybe Lilli is being competitive) but nobody could fail to love her spectacularly furtive exit, flat on her back, all the way down the Festival stage's front steps. It's good to see those in use again, and indeed David Farley's designs make excellent use of the space, leaving it uncluttered for the backstage scenes while giving us a spectacular and hilarious slant on Mr. Graham's interpretation of The Taming of the Shrew. He appears to have been ahead of his time in some respects, such as using actors as mobile scenery, though his taste in costumes might have been considered garish even in 1948. His production, as we behold it, is in a state of severe accident-proneness, not all of it due to histrionic temperament or novitiate ineptitude; a door frame makes a memorable appearance with the side marked "Interior" pointed proudly towards the audience. It's also used to great effect by the two gangsters who, through a slight case of mistaken identity, turn up to collect a debt of honour from Fred and will not be dissuaded. Theirs are infallible roles, taken to incomparable heights by Steve Ross (burly and menacing) and Cliff Saunders (slight and even more menacing). Their 11-o'clock injunction to Brush Up Your Shakespeare, with multiple built-in encores is, as expected, sublime, an old-time waltz for mugs, for which choreographer Tracey Flye has devised dainty stepping as great in its way as the full-blooded routine with which she galvanizes Too Darn Hot. Yes, I know I said that civilians in this show shouldn't sing; the point, maybe the show's main point, is that by the time the two guys do this number they, too, have been thoroughly caught up in the dream. They've even been given walk-on roles. Start to finish, this is an intoxicating show, up there among Stratford musicals with Fiddler on the Roof and My One and Only. Or, as one of Mr. Graham's underworld visitors puts it, having caught part of the first act, "It's entertaining, vivacious and calculated to please the discriminating theatregoer. You may quote me."

- Kiss Me, Kate is in repertory at the Festival Theatre, Stratford through Oct. 30. Call 1-800-567-1600 or visit stratfordfestival.cafor details.

2010-06-24-forgive-and-regret:
Nothing in world drama can move an audience in quite the same way as the last scene of The Winter's Tale. The statue of Hermione, the supposedly dead queen of Sicilia, descends from its pedestal and turns out to be the real and living woman, kept in seclusion for 16 years. She embraces her daughter Perdita, torn from her at birth and also left to die, and her husband Leontes, whose sudden irrational jealousy had set the whole seemingly tragic chain of events in motion all those years before. The sequence of resurrection and reunion touches deep chords; it can, for no clearly explicable reason, send shivers down the spine in even the crummiest production. In a good one, like that at Stratford, it also brings tears; Marti Maraden, the director, unfolds the scene at full strength, with a stageful of rapt spectators to reflect the audience's wonder, and then, with exemplary tact, extends it. The king gets the last line -- it's part of his job description -- and Leontes's here is "Hastily lead away," but he disobeys his own instruction. He and Hermione remain onstage, perhaps on the verge of an embrace, but only on the verge. For all the forgiveness, their relationship still hangs in the air as the lights fade.

Leontes's jealousy began when his wife succeeded where he had failed, in persuading his boyhood friend, King Polixenes of Bohemia, to prolong what was already a nine-month visit. Granted what is obviously a deep-rooted insecurity ( "at my request he would not"), it's possible to enter Leontes's mind and to hear with his ears what, to Hermione and Polixenes, are routine polite endearments. The disjunction between the reality and his perception produces some of the toughest, most fevered verse in Shakespeare, one poisonous image hurtling after another in a parody of logic. Ben Carlson, an actor of supreme lucidity, is especially good at the barriers this king erects against the reasoned arguments of his courtiers, not one of whom supports him though they all obey him. Powerful though this is, the turning point of the performance is Leontes's own, when he recognizes his error and his world collapses. (He loses his wife and his young son; the latter he never gets back, which takes the play almost beyond the bounds of tragicomedy.)

The subsequent scenes of penitence and atonement are intently, beautifully done. Equally commanding, in a role as straightforward as the king's is tortured, is Seana Mc-Kenna's Paulina, by turns his accuser, conscience, and consolation; she is, in all senses, a blast. She's also funny. These two performances are matched by Yanna McIntosh's Hermione, the best Shakespearean performance she has given. This queen lives up to all the praise the other characters heap on her; her passion and dignity when on trial are, save for one momentary descent into self-pity, superb, and her return to life is as heart-stirring as theatre gets.

This is an ensemble play, and the 16-year flash-forward to the sea-coast of Bohemia unleashes another clutch of fine performances. These start with Brian Tree's Old Shepherd, who doesn't so much utter his lines as graze on them like his sheep, and with Mike Shara, enchantingly blithe and trusting as his son; and culminate in Tom Rooney's shape-shifting Autolycus, tuneful, biting, and on great confidential terms with his hearers both on-and offstage. The production sometimes loses focus at the sheep-shearing revels; the nature-versus-nurture debate between Polixenes and Perdita is hard to follow, being played as if it were a personal feud rather than a philosophical debate. Dan Chameroy's Polixenes is otherwise excellent, both as victim and tyrant, and Cara Ricketts' Perdita is enchanting except when trying too hard to be. She's bewitching when, escorted by Ian Lake's eloquent Florizel, she returns to her father's court in a dazzling gold dress; the Turkish fashions that the designer, John Pennoyer, has dreamed up for the Bohemians in their rural state are rather less becoming. Randy Hughson is unfailingly good-humoured in a double role. As the unfortunate Antigonus he's sequentially victimized by his king, his wife and by this production's spectacular Bear, which contains two actors even before it swallows him. He then does a turn as Time, the chorus, and I mean a turn; he's suspended high up in a harness, in whose clutches he revolves a full 360 degrees, twice, remaining beamingly imperturbable throughout. It's as if he's daring us not to believe; which is precisely what The Winter's Tale is about.

Some of the same themes -- art, time, children -- are quietly, impressively woven in Anthony Black's play Homage, which was brought to Luminato by the 2b company from Halifax, and deserves to be seen wherever it appears. Instead of a statue that comes to life, we have a sculpture that's dismantles: offstage but still with resonance. The story, based fairly closely on real events, raises issues of creative and civic responsibility, fairly and passionately. Christian Barry's production contains ripe, unforced performances from Jerry Franken as a late-life sculptor determinedly making up for lost years and, especially, from Barbara Gordon as his wife, who in both her encouragement and upbraidings is something of a Paulina in her own right.

- The Winter's Tale is in repertory through Sept. 25. Call 1-800-567-1600 for ticket information.

2010-06-26-navigating-the-nominations-ou:
For hardened Dora explorers, awards night 2010 could be an unusually beatific occasion, as befits the prize-giving at the end of an unusually good Toronto season. There are, as always, quibbles and questions over what has been nominated, and there will doubtless be more over what actually wins, but it's comforting to look at the key category -- general theatre division, outstanding production -- and realize that all five of the designated shows have a right to be there. They are: Soulpepper's Parfumerie, Tarragon's If We Were Birds and Courageous, Necessary Angel's Hamlet and Canadian Stage's 7 Stories. Since this category really means best all-around show, it should follow that the nominees will turn up in other slots as well. And so they have, apart from 7 Stories, which, if the Dora judges are to be trusted, arrived at its eminence without any of its participants having done anything individually remarkable. This is obviously nonsense, but at least Morris Panych, who wrote 7 Stories and directed Parfumerie, can take comfort in being up there twice, at least in spirit.

7 Stories, being a revival, could not of course qualify for outstanding new play. Erin Shields' If We Were Birds and Michael Healey's Courageous could, and have; and I expect them to duke it out. The only possible contender, Brad Fraser's True Love Lies, is deemed ineligible on a technicality (it's already been done elsewhere), and the nominations for Judith Thompson's Such Creatures and Anusree Roy's Letters to My Grandma (respectively skewed and skeletal) ought to be jokes, though they probably aren't. George Walker's And So It Goes is a surprise omission -- doesn't sentiment mean anything anymore? The Shields and Healey plays are both very strong, but I expect the former to win since a) its tragic fusion of classic myth and modern reality make it a more unusual kind of play, and b) its author is a comparative newcomer. In fact, I expect, and indeed hope, that If We Were Birds will sweep the board in every category it's up for.

I loved Parfumerie, which is just as well, as they'll probably be reviving it every other Christmas. All the same, if I'd had to choose an outstanding Soulpepper production it would have been Who's Afraid of Virginia Woolf; the Doras' snubbing of Diana Leblanc (direction), Tim Campbell (supporting performance) and above all of Nancy Palk (actress) is, to put it nicely, incomprehensible. Diego Matamoros is up for best actor, and he was fine, though his un-nominated performance in Faith Healer was finer. And finest of all, though not eligible for perfectly legitimate reasons, was his solo version of Jorge Luis Borges' The Aleph; watch out for it in the future.

In fact, the best actor award will go, almost beyond a doubt, to Eric Peterson in Billy Bishop Goes to War, one of those occasions on which sentiment and actual achievement beautifully combine. Viola Leger in La Sagouine was another such instance, but she, most surprisingly, has been ignored. Tara Rosling, in If We Were Birds, should romp off, though that may not be the appropriate phrase, with best actress; she was stunning, and besides, what should have been her strongest competition -- Fiona Reid in Rock 'n' Roll, Palk (see above) -- has been ignored. Meanwhile, the actresses who played Gertrude and Ophelia in Hamlet have been nominated, though neither could ever be a leading role, however radical the adaptation. And Hamlet himself, Gord Rand, has been slighted, though without his uncanny performance the production couldn't have succeeded as well as it did. Rand has been nominated, in the independent section, for his performance in Goodness, and I hope he gets it; this has been his breakthrough year.

The Dora people continue their stubborn (again I'm being polite) custom of lumping together male/female/ dramatic/musical "featured" (i. e. supporting) performances in one category, and have compounded it by lumping in something called "ensemble." This is a cop-out, and anyway the two finest ensembles of the season haven't been honoured. I refer to those in Assassins and Top Girls; the latter, probably because it was a Mirvish (i. e. commercial) production, might as well not have existed, as far as the Doras are concerned. Anyway, Peterson is in that category, too, twice, and more power to him; but it should, and will, go to Maurice Dean Wint in Courageous. The sublime "featured" perf of the year, though, was completely ignored; I refer to Melody Johnson in 7 Stories. They got something against women, all of a sudden? Actually Johnson is sort of there, as director of Second City for Mayor, one of the "ensemble" nominees, though it was actually the less good of Second City's two shows. Johnson is also co-author of Mimi, which, unless some opera gets in the way, should split the vote for best musical with Leslie Arden's The Princess and the Handmaiden, my own vote going --slightly--to the latter. Mimi is also up for best musical production, which is different, along with Assassins and Light in the Piazza; there's riches, seriously. The Toxic Avenger Musical is also nominated but, to adapt John O'Hara, you don't have to believe it if you don't want to.

There's now a separate musical theatre division though it overlaps confusingly with the general one. Thus Adam Brazier ( Assassins) is up for best general director, and though all five contestants are more than worthy, he is the only one who should have a prayer over Alan Dilworth ( If We Were Birds). The year's best musical performance, Erica Peck's in The Boys in the Photograph, hasn't been anointed; of those who have, I'd go for Jacquelyn French ( Light in the Piazza). I have, for once, seen all five nominees for independent production; I'd plump for The Mill. (And, please, for its designer, Gillian Gallow.) Best touring production should probably go to The Walworth Farce, which I didn't see but wish I had. No nominations at all for August: Osage County; I'm surprised, but relieved.
2010-06-28-how-popular-are-the-populists:
PETER PAN, EVITA & JACQUES BREL IS ALIVE AND WELL AND LIVING IN PARIS

Stratford Shakespeare Festival

---

To be sung to the tune, if you know it, of Bobby and Jackie and Jack, the pastiche revue number about the Kennedys, from Merrily We Roll Along: There's Peter, Evita, and Jacques:

The final three cards in the pack.

One is the boy with a magic touch,

And one's a dictatress who spent too much,

And one wrote a song that's about the Dutch -

That's Jacky and Eva and Pete:

One flying, one dying, one beat.

Tim Carroll's production of J.M. Barrie's Peter Pan is just about perfect. It's spectacular without being overpowering, tender without being cloying (a feat with this play), insidiously disturbing without getting in anyone's face. It's also expensive without being profligate; every cent looks well spent. Carolyn M. Smith's sets take us from a spacious-but-cozy Edwardian nursery to a Neverland whose every detail is playfully evoked -- Barrie, like Shakespeare dreaming up the Forest of Arden, wrote an adventure playground that left nothing out.

The casting is unbeatable. Michael Therriault's Peter is boyhood personified: all charm, all brashness, all conceit, with just enough empathy to feel lonely. He is ever so friendly, makes whimsy seem practical, and is scarily unreachable. The production's final image, showing him outside the forever-barred nursery window, is the logical culmination of the performance as well as of the story, the more haunting for not being forced. All the children's roles are played by adults, all of whom seem to having a roaringly good but perfectly disciplined time. Sara Topham may have found her ideal role as Wendy, whom she makes enchantingly bossy and more self-aware by the moment, while Paul Dunn, has certainly found his as the touchy adolescent John; he's a man playing a boy playing a man. Stacie Steadman rounds out the Darling siblings as a piping Michael, proudly possessive of his teddy bear. The Lost Boys are as distinctive as the parented ones, with Shane Carty a stand-out as Slightly.

The pirates are, except in their costume and makeup, less colourful than the kids, maybe because they're written that way; Barrie seems to have spent more energy on describing them than on dramatising them. Tom McCamus, like every other actor I have seen in the role, fails to solve the conundrum of Hook, which is that he's spoken of as frightening but written as almost entirely comic. His death, flinging himself into the jaws of the croc-with-the-clock, seems to come out of nowhere. McCamus still makes a fine fop of him, but the real delight comes from his other role as narrator: Barrie himself, trying out the stage directions and experimenting with different versions of a text with many variants. It's been done before, but never to this extent or with this finesse.

The attendant bestiary includes the longest, meanest, crocodile you'll ever see, not to mention the best motivated; we know what makes him tick. The director, who's British, has a lot of Shakespeare in his resume; Stratford must bring him back.

It's been a fine batch of Festival openings; if the remaining two shows let down the side a bit, that's mainly because of the material. Not quite so much with Evita: Andrew Lloyd Webber isn't the musical Antichrist and this may be his best score. Tim Rice's lyrics, especially in the opening Oh What a Circus make intelligent satiric points, though his words don't usually sit well on the music; some of his jokes would sound funnier spoken, which is a working definition of bad lyric-writing. Also, his Che's initial indictment of his Eva ( "she did nothing for years") turns out to be, dramatically speaking, all too true; once she's bed-hopped her way to the top, she subsides into inaction, until it's time for her to expire. The show sometimes assumes she's done stuff, but that's not the same thing. It's all very static.

Gary Griffin's production is handsomely staged, and as lucid as possible, and Chilina Kennedy does something unprecedented in rock musicals: she doesn't act the style, she acts the character. Instead of all-purpose brass, she offers vulnerability, believable in the early scenes and invaluable in the later ones. Juan Chioran does everything possible and more than most for Peron, and Josh Young is a decently charismatic Che. Josie Marasco is the discarded Mistress who exists solely to sing another Another Suitcase in Another Hall, a rotten song that serves no purpose. So Pan, Mrs. Peron, and Brel: From Heaven, through Limbo, to...

Well, you get the point. The mendaciously titled Jacques Brel Is Alive and Well and Living in Paris has always been one of my least favourite shows, and it remains so even in Stafford Arima's unusually inventive production. Brel wrote monotonous melodies, that fake emotion by getting progressively faster and faster -- and, as sung by the two ladies in the cast, Jewelle Blackman and Nathalie Nadon, louder and louder.

Thewords, theEnglishwords anyway, are awful; the few sung in French go with more of a swing, but the translations, by Eric Blau and Mort Shuman, are best described in the tag-line of their lyric for Jackie: "Completely cute, cute in a stupid-arse way." That song itself doesn't seem to know what it's about from one sentence to the next; it's incoherence masquerading as profundity. Brent Carver sings with devout intensity, but the evening belongs to Mike Nadajewski, who appears to have nabbed all the best material, including one song ( Next, about an army recruit lining up for STD treatment after a first encounter) that even I liked. He has ferocity and he has humour. Double, even triple, commendation for Rick Fox, musical director for Evita, musical supervisor and arranger for Brel: this Fox knows many things.

- Peter Pan is in repertory through Oct. 31; Evita through Nov. 6; Jacques Brel Is Alive and Well and Living in Paris through Sept. 25.

2010-06-29-prosperous-the-tempest-become:
THE TEMPEST

Festival Theatre, Stratford

---

Stratford's new production of The Tempest is, for its first 40 minutes, terrific. After a shipwreck scene that's both exciting and comprehensible, Christopher Plummer takes the stage as Prospero to tell his daughter Miranda, and us, the backstory. He does it superbly, switching back and forth with quicksilver brilliance between present tenderness and past pain, sometimes merging them so that the past itself seems present. He relives every detail, and makes us live it too; when he speaks of the brother who betrayed and banished him, both his anger and his anguish are searing hot.

The subsequent scene with an uncanny, and uncannily effective, Ariel maintains both the pressure and the delight; the parallel encounter with a nondescript Caliban lowers them without, at this point, doing serious damage. Then comes the love-at-first-sight meeting of Miranda and the castaway Ferdinand: very nice, until Ferdinand attempts to draw his sword, only to find it not, as in most productions, glued to its scabbard but waving helplessly in the air on invisible strings. And it's at this point that things start to come apart. Instead of a fearsome magician imposing himself by force of will as much as art, Prospero becomes a children's conjuror, playing twinkling party tricks. Worse, both Ferdinand and Miranda seem to be in on the joke, both here and later; they say they're scared of him but it's never believable. Bang goes one of the prime sources of tension in a play that needs all it can get.

The Tempest is a play that's indisputably great without being, by most conventional criteria, good. Its protagonist is all-important but he's mostly absent during the middle section; then, when he returns, he hardly lets anybody else get a word in. His supernatural powers give him complete external control; the only suspense lies within -- is he going to opt for forgiveness or revenge? Plummer plays the moment of choice with the expected authority; he holds a magisterial, agonized pause. But for the decision to reverberate beyond the moment, we have to believe in the world in which it's made and the people who are the objects of it. The work of establishing those characters has to be done in the play's first half; in the second, they don't stand a chance. In this production, most of them are lay-figures. The evening becomes less and less a play, and more and more the Christopher Plummer show. As such, it's well worth seeing, and hearing. Plummer has virtuoso command of the verse, and Prospero's farewell to his art is a vocal symphony. He can also be endearingly self-deprecating.

Des McAnuff's production certainly keeps him hopping. This Prospero is liable to appear unexpectedly in any corner of his island; in the mock-banquet scene he arises suddenly through a trap-door though, as at this point he's supposed to be invisible, I'm not sure whom he's trying to impress. There's much about McAnuff's direction that I liked; he makes line-by-line sense of the text, something for which he sometimes gets insufficient credit, and he knits the plot threads together by showing us Prospero's victims groping their way around the isle, though perhaps they should look more in acute distress and less as if they were on a nice hike.

Robert Brill's mostly bare set incorporates a revolve that's well used, and a boat that's delightfully used, not least when Julyana Soelistya's tiny Ariel, an apparent refugee from the Blue Man Group, pops up in the corner of it. In fact, nearly everything in, and around, this performance is magical, including her singing of Michael Roth's lovely songs. She's pert and truly unearthly, and yet with a yearning connection to humanity. Her "do you love me master, no?" is moving, and movingly reciprocated. In fact this new father-daughter relationship rather displaces the play's official one.

Trish Lindstrom's homeschooled Miranda has perfect rapport with Plummer in their first scene, but neither she nor Gareth Potter's Ferdinand, doing some phallic business with an impossibly long log, seem able to regard the play's and Prospero's emphasis on chastity as anything more than a giggle. Perhaps we can't play these scenes anymore, but the joke could be on us. Besides, Prospero has seen his daughter almost raped; he's entitled to be neurotic about it.

Prospero and Ariel apart, the stand-out performance is Geraint Wyn Davies' Stephano, which starts with the sozzled Welsh charm of his Bottom and builds into a grotesquely frightening mock-king. He carries the clown scenes almost single-handedly, since Bruce Dow's Trinculo is wearisome camp and Dion Johnstone's Caliban, apart from a nice reading of "the isle is full of noises," almost nonexistent. Caliban may be a noble savage or a savage savage or, and preferably, both, but he shouldn't be bland. He and Prospero have a "moment" at the end, and Prospero has another when he and his brother exchange baleful looks; both are correct, but neither comes out of anything. The courtiers are in Jacobean dress, which makes a nice change, but they never emerge from their elegant shells. Alonso's torment and repentance, Sebastian's vacillation, Antonio's unregeneracy: the actors go through the motions, but never bring them to life. And unless I was nodding off, Gonzalo's benediction, a rare last-act opportunity to see the story from someone else's perspective, has been cut. Also surprisingly truncated is the wedding masque: Three built-up goddesses who display minimal interest in what they're saying, and no dancing. Not much of an engagement present, considering Prospero's, and Stratford's, resources. It also takes some of the edge off what may be Plummer's finest, silent moment: the metaphysical headache, as if his brain were about to split, that precedes the tempered bitterness of his "revels now are ended" speech. This is telepathic acting, and very impressive. But it isn't part of a complete whole.

- The Tempest continues through Sept. 12. Call 1-800-567-1600 for ticket information.

2010-07-03-kiss-and-ride-shakespeare-s-t:
This year's Dream in High Park is set in an Italian railway station: an airy, attractive structure that, for once, sets off the surrounding parkland instead of obliterating it. The deal, as far as I could follow it, is that a bunch of actors are persuaded to perform a play while waiting for their connection. In the words, more or less, of Kiss Me, Kate: A troupe of strolling players are they, and I wouldn't be surprised if they'd opened in Venice.

Certainly, they're now playing Verona; and since that's their current station, in life and in art, the play they just happen to have on tap, in their memories and their costume-hamper, is Romeo and Juliet. They play it in English, but since the travel announcements by which they are occasionally interrupted are still in Italian, their unseen fellow passengers must be mystified.

The show these buskers do right there is rough, uneven, occasionally piercingly good, and very fast. In Vikki Anderson's production, the famous "two hours' traffic", still mentioned in the prologue, comes out at a brisk 90 minutes -- though, of course, the line may now refer to the unpredictability of Italian trains. The text has been cut to the bone, but I can't say I minded; in fact, and especially on an unseasonably cold first night, I was grateful.

The play still makes perfect sense. It makes especial sense here with the young lovers themselves, who take the time-honoured truth that she quickly matures and he almost doesn't, and make it fresh. Jeff Irving's Romeo is a passionate sulker, whose moods, sincerely felt, take him through masochistic infatuation, real love, a vengeful duel and suicide. He's unsparingly good in his tantrums after banishment, when Romeo, with all the egotism of adolescence, really does believe himself the hardest-done-by guy in the history of the world.

Christine Horne's Juliet starts out cool and a bit mischievous, theoretically willing to consider an arranged marriage; and in the balcony scene, which both actors play with a delightful blend of passion and laughter, she remains in intelligent control of the situation. (The station comes equipped with an actual balcony, but it isn't exactly unscalable. In fact, if Romeo weren't such a gentleman, he could run right up the stairs.) Horne can't manage the surrender to Juliet's more desperate extremes, but she does meet the challenge of both her fake death and her real one. This couple does a lot of kissing-- from the ball, where they definitely exceed Renaissance rules for behaviour in public places, all the way to the tomb, where the editing allows her to wake up before he's quite popped off. Friar Lawrence (played by a woman, Caroline Gillis) is unwise to leave them alone before marriage as long as he does.

A scene that's very well done, and that I've barely noticed in other productions, is the one in which Paris (Peter N. Bailey) clumsily flirts with a Juliet who just wants to be left alone with her ghostly father so that he can advise her on how to avoid becoming a ghostly wife. Jamie Robinson's Tybalt is a killer, in every sense, and Ron Kennell a remarkably restrained Nurse, which is disconcerting at first but pays excellent dividends later on. This sober nanny holds back the good news about Romeo's eligibility until the last moment, thereby driving Juliet into a similarly undemonstrative but very effective frenzy; while her equally prosaic advice to go ahead and marry Paris drives, as it should, the last nail into the heroine's innocence. The Nurse's subsequent grief over her charge's supposed end, is equally underplayed and equally effective. Lisa Berry plays the Station Master who inaugurates the action and then takes part in it, notably as a funny servant; the director's concept doesn't make much sense but it's what goes on inside it that's important. I wish them warmth.
