2010-07-10-if-broadway-loves-you-we-will:
Soulpepper's ongoing voyage through the plays of David French has now arrived at Jitters, the 1979 piece in which the author poked fun at the burgeoning Toronto independent theatre movement of which he himself was an important part. The title refers to the different varieties of nervous terror experienced by everyone in the business of putting on a play (and in most other businesses). In a Toronto theatre not unlike French's old stamping ground, the Tarragon, a new play is being mounted under all the usual pressures, plus some additional ones caused by the promised presence of a Broadway producer.

The play is part farce, part satirical commentary on the Canadian theatre and its insecurities, and its misfortune is that both halves of its split personality have been eclipsed by later events. It opened a few years before Michael Frayn's Noises Off, the most inventive of backstage farces, and one that never feels like an in-joke. The comic anatomy of Canadian theatre was performed more expansively, more incisively and more affectionately by Slings and Arrows. In Jitters, the farcical part is the better, or so it seems in Ted Dykstra's Soulpepper production. The second and best of its three acts takes us to just before curtain-up on opening night. It's an occasion plagued by actors who go missing, arrive late and drunk, or get locked in the bathroom. Much of the burden of this falls on the author, who, since he knows all the lines and was once an actor, may have to go on himself. A nervous creature at the best of times, he is now petrified, although there is obviously a part of him that would really love to do it. He's presumably a French self-portrait, though Mike Ross's performance sports both the spectacles and the mannerisms of a Canadian actor-dramatist of more recent vintage. Whoever he is, Ross builds him up beautifully in all his fretful, accommodating passive-aggressiveness, finishing him off in a sustained cadenza of physical comedy as he throws himself in and out of an ill-fitting costume, according to the fluctuating condition of the man he's supposed to be replacing.

Unfortunately, when we come back after the intermission, all this exciting stuff might just as well not have happened. The play switches gears and goes back to what really seems to be on its mind, which is the Canadian theatre's psychological dependence on the approval of America. We have a leading lady who has returned to Toronto after achieving some measure of success in New York, and who is responsible for Broadway taking an interest. We have a leading man who proudly parades his indifference to such temptations but is obviously a prey to bitter doubts. "Where but in Canada" he asks in the play's most widely quoted line "can you be a top-notch actor all your life and still die broke and anonymous?" (Answer: A lot of places. Including America.) C. David Johnson's performance is admirably huffy; Diane D'Aquila is more effective in the diva's vulnerability than in her imperiousness. Maybe it's because we've just seen Kiss Me Kate; maybe it's because Johnson and D'Aquila were once husband and wife; but there seems to be more history between these characters than the play ever gets round to exploring. Their hostility fuels much of the action, but it's hard to believe that it's just a matter of differing world views. In the weak third act, they, like the play, seem to be repeating themselves. There's a line about all Canadian actors measuring themselves against Christopher Plummer that gets as big and as rueful a laugh now as it presumably did 30 years ago, so the national complex about making it, or not making it, somewhere else still persists. But it isn't that pervasive, and this play really runs it into the ground.

As self-satire, it's pretty skimpy. The play that's being rehearsed bears the blessed title of The Care and Treatment of Roses, and it seems to be in the vein of French's own Newfoundland family dramas; but we only see one rudimentary scene from it, twice. He does, though, offer a wicked parody of a really starchy theatre review. The director is seriously under-characterized, and Kevin Bundy doesn't manage to give him much personality. Jordan Pettle's prissy dictator of a stage manager has a lot of personality. Oliver Dennis is very funny as a hypochondriacal actor, though this is one of his reliable performances rather than one of his inspired ones; Sarah Wilson is a delight as an ASM. After a sluggish start, and before stasis sets in, there is a steady stream of theatrical disaster-jokes, so the evening is pleasant. But it's fuzzy.

- Jitters runs through July 24 at the Young Centre. Call 416-866-8666 or visit soulpepper. ca for details.

Color Photo: Cylla Von Tiedemann / Diane D'Aquila and Kevin Bundy take a moment to calm their nerves in Jitters.; Caption:
2010-07-13-objection-overruled:
LEGALLY BLONDE THE MUSICAL

Princess of Wales Theatre, Toronto

---

I have an instinctive hostility to any show entitled Whatever: The Musical but in this case I have to relax it. It may well be my good fortune that I never saw the movie, but having now beheld the stage version, I am unable to imagine Legally Blonde as anything but a musical. It's a good one too: silly and sensible in about the right proportions.

For any fellow ignorami out there: Legally Blonde tells of pink-clad golden-locked Elle Woods, Californian major in fashion merchandise who at curtain-rise is all set to get married to the boy of her dreams, to her own deep satisfaction and the squealing delight of her chorus-load of girlfriends. But instead of a proposal she gets a rejection: Her prospective fiance -- whose name, Warner Huntington III, pretty much sums him up -- tells her that he is off to Harvard Law School and is dumping her for someone more befitting his wealth and social standing. Elle is undaunted. She's already demonstrated her educational attainments by sending back a dress she knows at a glance to be last year's model. Now, assisted by a high LSAT score attained in double-quick time (and also by her father's money), she follows Warner to Harvard Law, hoping to win him back. Why she should want to is a question the show never quite answers; one of my lasting regrets is that she doesn't just slug the guy halfway through the first act. To be honest, she hasn't even done it by the end of the second, though she has seen the light in other ways.

Still blond, and still pink right down to her laptop, Elle is at first a laughingstock in class, but she proves to have a quick mind plus an intuitive sense of justice and how to attain it. The feared Professor Callahan, notorious for humiliating vulnerable students, invites her to join his team of interns, where she helps win an apparently unwinnable murder defence case. She also finds love.

The story is a little like Erin Brockovitch Lite. It might also be called the photo-negative of Wicked, in that it shows that a rich and beautiful girl can overcome her disadvantages as effectively as a poor and plain one. And, I have to say, with a lot less whining.

The music and lyrics are by Laurence O'Keefe and Nell Benjamin, a husband-and-wife team whose male half was previously responsible for the underrated score of Bat Boy The Musical. (I should know; I was one of those who underrated it.) Their pop-flavoured tunes here are cheerful rather than distinguished, but their lyrics are excellent, technically and dramatically. The opening Omigod You Guys perfectly captures the overheated enthusiasm of privileged female West Coast youth. Chip on My Shoulder is a pungent, narrative-propelling number begun by Emmett, the prof's up-from-poverty top student and Elle's guide, philosopher and predestined more-than-friend, and subsequently taken up by nearly everybody else.

The show's first half works, delightfully, as a cartoon. The second half sometimes deviates into unwelcome solemnity, with the obligatory inspirational title number. But it mostly keeps its temper, not to mention its tempo.

As for the cast: Becky Gulsvig's Elle is bright and charming, in a standardized kind of way, while Natalie Jay Johnson is comparably cookie-cut as her man-handled hairdresser buddy giving off indistinguishable squeaks of joy and frustration. Both ladies have pet dogs, one of whom can yelp on cue. The greatest individuality, though, comes from the male humans. D. B Bonds' Emmett is an offbeat hero for whom one can genuinely root, while Jeff McLean's Warren is an antihero whom one can cheerfully despise while still enjoying his singing voice. The most vivid of all, though, from his first impregnable entrance and first ringing note, is Michael Rupert's Professor; this performer, once the male ingenue of his Broadway generation, has matured into a singing Alec Baldwin, sneering magnetically. He later declines into outright villainy, which the show may think sharpens its satiric point but actually blunts it; the things Callahan represents are too insidious to be passed off as melodrama. This isn't a dyspeptic show like Urinetown, but it has a brain. When a lyric mentions Thomas Hobbes, you can believe that somebody has read him.

- Legally Blonde The Musical runs until Aug. 8. For tickets, call 416-872-1212 or visit mirvish. com.

A MONTH IN THE COUNTRY

Young Centre for the Performing Arts, Toronto

---

A wise man once said that the tragedy in an Ibsen play is that nothing proves to be what it seems, while the tragedy in a Chekhov play is that everything does. Chekhov's compatriot Ivan Turgenev was on to this before him, and Laszlo Marton's fascinating Soulpepper production of A Month in the Country, Turgenev's one major play, drives the point home in its final image. On one side of the stage Natalya Petrovna, bored wife of a landowner, reclining in a chair; on the other, an assortment of friends, relatives and dependants playing cards.

The play starts that way too, though there are some differences in personnel. By the end, as in Three Sisters or Uncle Vanya, various people have departed, taking some life and hope with them. Natalya's situation hasn't changed, but it's been stripped. When we first met her, she was frustrated; now she's drained and desperate. And, in a play that's as much comedy as tragedy, it's largely her own fault. She's been playing with people's lives.

The most important man in her own life has been not her affectionately oblivious husband but her long-standing platonic admirer Rakitin. Into this mix has come Belyayev, a new young tutor for Natalya's son, and still more or less a boy himself. He attracts every woman in the household, including Natalya's ward, Vera. Jealousy almost drives Natalya to marry the girl off to a grotesque suitor, and though she pulls back, damage has been done. In fact Belyayev, no Casanova, nurses what he considers a hopeless passion for Natalya herself, and the revelation throws everyone into confusion. Natalya makes her own, technically unstained bed, but everyone else's good intentions help arrange the bedding.

Turgenev was a greater novelist than playwright, and some things about the play are lax; minor characters flash in and out rather than, as in Chekhov, being held in suspension to reflect the central relationships, though that's clearly the intention. The relationships themselves are developed at leisure and resolved in haste, often without the satisfaction either of an explosion or a dying fall. But along with this goes a vaudevillean freedom unexpected in a drawing-room play; one scene climaxes in a song (scripted) and a bit of a dance (not). Marton's production uses a sparky new adaptation by himself and Susan Coyne, and a setting (by Andrei Both) that could be indoors or out or both at once. A similar ambiguity pervades the time-frame; the dialogue still denotes mid-19th-century Russia, but Rakitin is dressed like a 1930s boulevardier, while the props include a car, a radio and a skateboard, ridden effortlessly by Belyayev and very gingerly indeed by Rakitin -- an effect that in itself is enough to justify the anachronisms. The multiple focus brings us close to the characters pyschologically while still respecting the society from which they spring.

Once again in a Marton production, the characters are driven to physical extremes that are startling but completely appropriate. There is one of the director's trademark thunderstorms, and people get drenched in other ways too. If the production, like the play, remains fine but frustrating it's because it doesn't solve the problem of why we're supposed to care about the heroine. A few years ago, in a far freer adaptation at the Shaw Festival, Fiona Byrne gave a performance of the role that was both sympathetic and unsparing. This time she seems to be playing it scene by scene: honestly and attractively but without ever finding the key. Not at least until that last tableau, the production's own invention, that finds her catatonic, fanned by a wind-machine invented by her solicitous spouse. (In the original he was working on a thresher.)

Diego Matamoros, who opens the proceedings bending over Natalya in a pose at once predatory and protective, plays an urbane, self-mocking and self-torturing Rakitin; his observant spirit pervades the play, as it should -- Turgenev had been there himself. Joseph Ziegler is outrageously believable as the local doctor who exploits the gentry as bitterly and hilariously as they unthinkingly patronize him. One of the production's pleasures is that it allows these two actors, than whom we have none better, to square off against each other--for the first time, I think. Another is that it lets Ziegler and his wife Nancy Palk, as a beanpole ladies' companion yearning for escape, play a wonderfully unromantic proposal scene, that's here even more of a delight than usual. Jeff Lillico gets both the brashness and the shyness of Belyaev ringingly right, and Tal Gottfried's Vera grows rapidly and impressively from slip of a schoolgirl to disillusioned woman. As Natalya's husband, nobly overcoming his jealousy of the wrong man, David Storch is a full-blooded treat. It's even more of a treat, and a relief, to see Soulpepper tackling a big play again.

- A Month in the Country runs to Aug. 7. Visit soulpepper. ca or call 416-866-8666 for tickets and more information.

2010-07-17-medical-muddle:
The Shaw Festival this year has taken its sweet time getting around to doing Shaw, but it's been worth the wait. Morris Panych's production of The Doctor's Dilemma is as funny as this play, with its perambulating chorus of physicians, each obsessed with his own miracle procedure, usually is. It also carries an emotional clout that isn't usual at all. Following on his charming mellow Parfumerie at Soulpepper, it suggests that Panych is reaching a new maturity as a director.

Shaw called The Doctor's Dilemma a tragedy, but, as the man who pointed out that "life doesn't cease to be funny when someone dies any more than it ceases to be serious when someone laughs," he was at least half-kidding. Someone does die in this play, and mortality hovers over all of it, often to comic, or at least satiric, effect. Mentioning death, says one of the corps of beknighted, and benighted, specialists, is "a dastardly advantage to take of a medical man." The dilemma of the title is the one faced by the newly ennobled Sir Colenso Ridgeon, who has discovered a cure for TB at a time when it was a killer. His clinic is full but he agrees to squeeze in one extra patient, the genius young painter Louis Dubedat, whose case has been pleaded by his bewitching wife, Jennifer. Two snags emerge: Dr. Blenkinsop, an old classmate of Ridgeon's, now a penurious GP, turns out to be another sufferer, while Dubedat turns out to be, by the doctors' respectable lights, a rat; he cheats on his wife and also on anyone whom he can persuade to write him a cheque. So Ridgeon, in a play set 40 years before England gained a national health service, has to choose between saving a talented scoundrel and a virtuous mediocrity. The issue is complicated by his having fallen in love with Mrs. Dubedat, and hence having a vested interest in seeing her widowed. This may weaken the play as pure Socratic debate, but enriches it -- in fact makes it possible--as drama.

Ridgeon's motives aren't all dis-honourable, and Patrick Galligan does a good job of portraying a sheltered man who's grown up believing in his own decency without ever having it put to the test. He and Krista Colosimo as Jennifer play chillingly off one another in the play's sardonic epilogue, while earlier on she's burningly believable in her protective love for Louis, both in and out of his presence. Dubedat charms the doctors too, initially, though Jonathan Gould makes him too obvious a snake for this to be credible; he's more effective, though still casually anachronistic, when running insouciant rings round them later, and is very good at dying, in their embarrassed presence, in his own studio.

The most powerful moments of all come from Ric Reid, one of the Shaw's best and most taken-for-granted actors, as the penurious Blenkinsop, proudly refusing to sponge on his friends (as opposed to Dubedat who'll sponge on anyone). The friends themselves are a grand collection, with Michael Ball courteously implacable as the voice of conscience, the sage who's seen medical fashions come and go, and Patrick McManus, an appropriately incisive surgeon. The medic to whose tender but unskilled mercies Dubedat is consigned is Sir Ralph Bloomfield Bonington, consultant to rich families, with his mellifluous bedside manner and his unvarying determination to "stimulate the phagocytes." (A phrase that became proverbial; at least, my mother used to quote it.) Thom Marriott savours the role like the rich plum it is, though he short-changes the patchwork of Shakespearean misquotations with which BB salutes his patient's death; it should be so ludicrous it's moving, but here it stops at ludicrous. A couple of minor roles are misjudged, as well as being assigned to actors too young for them, but there's a notable small performance, poignant without being mawkish, by Cherissa Richards as one of Dubedat's discarded loves. Ken MacDonald's set designs feature giant X-rays at Ridgeon's place and a giant paint-brush suspended over Dubedat's; medical and artistic images merge until we arrive at Louis' posthumous exhibition, which consists entirely of portraits of the play's doctors. The doctor's dilemma becomes the artist's revenge.

One of Shaw's doctors gets a laugh by claiming a friendship with his fellow-playwright J.M. Barrie, for whom this is proving to be quite a year. Stratford has his Peter Pan, and the Shaw has uncovered a one-act gem called Half an Hour. The title refers to the time-frame in which a society lady may or may not put her life back together. She's walked out on her husband, after the latest of many rows, but her plans for escape go cruelly awry. Like Peter Pan, this production gives us Barrie as quizzical narrator, utilizing his own irresistibly garrulous stage-directions, which make Shaw's seem laconic; Michael Ball, perfect again, does the honours and also throws in one of his sublimely offended butlers. A program note suggests that the lady's a bitch, but Diana Donnelly plays her sympathetically and very involvingly; it's her best work yet. She has two fine foils in Gord Rand as her broken lifeline and Peter Millard as yet another doctor: one who enters the play as a mere functionary and by the end has become inexorable Fate, weighing its options. Gina Wilkinson's production squeezes the tension very tight, and makes highly imaginative use of dust sheets and a trap door. Deadline plays -- think of The President -- seem to suit the Shaw at lunchtime very well; they go like clockwork.

- The Doctor's Dilemma is in repertory at the Festival Theatre, Niagara-on-the-Lake, through Oct. 30; Half an Hour at the Royal George Theatre through Oct. 9. Call 1-800-511-SHAW or visit shawfest. com for details.
2010-07-21-the-act-you-ve-known-for-all-:
RAIN

Canon Theatre, Toronto

---

The band called Rain, who perform the show called Rain, started out in southern California in the 1970s playing Beatles covers, which is what they still do. Of course, few groups, musical or other, retain the same personnel over 30 years or more, so the guys currently playing the Canon Theatre in Toronto are a cover band of a cover band.

What they offer is basically a concert, but they're playing in a theatre and there are some gestures towards drama, or at least narrative, in the show they put on. They start with a video montage illustrating the cultural scene pre-Beatles, roughly from Bill Haley and Rock Around the Clock to the Kennedy assassination. It's strictly the American cultural scene: England, and the culture from which the Beatles actually sprang, apparently didn't exist until the lads waved their way down the aircraft steps on their first trans-Atlantic trip. Then we're into their appearance on The Ed Sullivan Show with Ed himself, amiably grotesque as he sways on his heels, looking and sounding as if he wasn't sure what was about to hit him but thought it could probably be contained. And then, finally, the lights go up on the stage itself to reveal our four Beatles simulacra, dressed, wigged and positioned exactly like their models in their early-mid-'60s incarnation, and giving out with a succession of their first and most immediately likeable hits.

They do a decent imitation, especially of the harmonies, and they look, at least from the middle distance, very convincing. At least three of them do; Steve Landes' John looks as if his moptop has to be kidding. In compensation later on in the show, when there's some talking, he sounds the most believably Liverpudlian of the bunch. Joey Curatolo, who as Paul gets to do most of the emcee-ing when it's called for, comes off as a mid-American chat-show host. Ralph Castelli as Ringo thrashes around enthusiastically, probably with more fireworks than the original, and Joe Bithorn as George fades into the middle, as George himself tended to do. None of them has much bite or personality as an individual singer, so once the first wave of nostalgia has subsided, the songs stop sounding very interesting.

I've never understood the appeal of watching one performer spend an entire evening imitating the repertoire, sound and mannerisms of another performer when the originals are freely, if now only mechanically, available. There is, I concede, a little more point to the exercise when it's celebrating a collective rather than an individual, but only a little. It would be different if the show were providing some kind of context or commentary but Rain barely attempts this; it makes Jersey Boys look like high art. It's also disconcerting that, though they have made every effort to look and sound like the Beatles, they sometimes step out of character, speaking of them in a reverential third person. It may sound like honesty, but it comes off more like damage-control. Even more confusingly, they're still using their Beatle speaking voices and personalities even when talking as themselves. What they talk about, mainly, is how happy they are to be back in Toronto; they also beg for audience participation, rather than simply earning it. It's middle-of-the-road pandering, and one hopes that it would have made The Beatles themselves cringe.

The show proceeds on its vaguely chronological way, reaching Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band by intermission. For this section, Rain are togged out in carnival costumes from the album sleeve. The Beatles themselves, having already given up live performance, never had to look this silly, and it doesn't do much for the songs. Nor does the necessity of reproducing the studio sound in live conditions, something else the originals were spared. The mix here is bleary, drowning out the words without providing a compensating ambience; A Day in the Life sounds toothless. Act Two starts with a peace-and-love sequence that lacks conviction but can't bring itself to be ironic either. It's just nostalgia. And then the story's more or less over, since this show certainly isn't going to deal with the band's break-up. All the rest is singalong, with Hey Jude a rather uninspiring climax. Some of the best Lennon-McCartney songs have been overlooked on the way through; the Revolver album is a particular casualty, represented only by Eleanor Rigby; For No One and Here, There and Everywhere -- their two best, I think -- are nowhere to be heard. The side-show visuals continue, but more as distraction than illustration; the graphics are imitation Terry Gilliam without the sidestepping wit; they go, always, for the obvious. Americans seem never to have understood the Beatles' humour. They owed as much to British music-hall as to American rhythm and blues. Rain is more like seaside variety.

- Rain: A Tribute to The Beatles is on through Aug. 1; visit mirvish. com or call 1-800-461-3333 for tickets and more information.

2010-07-22-this-had-better-be-good:
The fourth season of Mad Men kicks off this Sunday on AMC, and we're taking a week-long look at the show that has brought sharp suits, casual sexism and drinking at work back to the office, if only as subjects for water-cooler conversation. Today, Robert Cushman on the high expectations that Season Three left us with.

The last season of Mad Men ended on an uncharacteristically up note. The top guys at the Sterling Cooper ad agency decided to resist being sold to a new owner by the British concern that had taken them over the season before, and to strike out on their own. A buccaneering spirit was abroad in the season finale as our hero Don Draper egged on Sterling and Cooper, a.k.a. Roger and Bertram, to abandon their gold-plated retirement schemes and start again from something like scratch. They even persuaded their English overseer Lane Pryce to thumb his nose at London and join them. They enlisted Peggy Olson, the super-talented copywriter with the secretive smile, and Pete Campbell, the oddly endearing worm of an accounts manager. For administrative assistance Roger placed a call, thunderously applauded by all regular viewers, to Joan, his busty ex-mistress and office manager, currently languishing in a hopeless marriage; he knew that she'd be the exact person to organize the midnight flit and to tell everybody where to locate the files they wished to loot. Welcome to Sterling Cooper Draper Pryce, new home of all the SC personnel we actually cared about, plus Harry Crane.

Well, not quite. Nobody thought of rehiring Sal, the closeted gay art director fired for resisting the advances of the son of the boss of Lucky Strike. Since that account is one of the new firm's biggest assets, it seems doubtful that we'll ever see Sal again. And even discounting him, the finale wasn't all rosy. As Don's career burgeoned, so his marriage collapsed. Good though Don has always been at compartmentalizing, he must have been struck by the coincidence of having to find two new homes at the same time.

The parallel telling of the business and domestic stories has always been one of the prime strengths of Mad Men, and never more than in the past season. After two years, the show had to outgrow its period appeal, basically the thrill of registering how a time as chronologically near to us as the early 1960s could seem so sociologically far. The references to actual political events sometimes seemed dragged in.

The Drapers' marital breakupwasamongthe rawest things in TV drama, on a par with the one in The Sopranos. The last straw for Betty wasn't one of Don's multiple infidelities; it was her discovery that he, the scarred remnant of a Depression childhood, had taken another man's name and identity to give himself a passport into a more prosperous world.

JonHamm'ssuperblysmooth performance took on new depths, as his face, voice and shoulders went into a slump befitting a man unsure of whether he exists; while January Jones continued her remarkable portrayal of a woman awoken from a different variety of mental and emotional sleepwalk.

Obviously there are going to be more threatening breakers ahead for the new Sterling Cooper. There could hardly be a show if there weren't; and even in real life, the euphoria of a new enterprise is bound to fade.

Not to mention that the youthful idealists of the new set-up are for the most part middle-aged and up. When we left them they were working out of a hotel suite; just see how they behave when they get a real office.

Also, The Beatles are coming and the '60s are about to become the '60s, even on Madison Avenue. Or especially on Madison Avenue. In the meantime, word from the spoilers is that Don will find playing the field when single harder than when married. Nor does Betty's new romantic arrangement, with a stuffy aide to Governor Rockefeller, look that promising; her three children are going to hate their new stepdad. Betty was never a good mother, anyway; her response to any problem with the kids has been to tell them to "go play" and Don's claim that they'd be better off with him was probably justified. The scene where he and Betty told the kids about the divorce was a legitimate heartbreaker.

I have high hopes for Season Four. But it has a very hard act to follow.

-The season premiere of Mad Men airs Sunday at 10 p.m. on AMC.

2010-07-24-trials-tribulations-and-the-t:
Bernard Shaw set just one major play in his native Ireland, and the split loyalties he must have felt between that country and his adopted England are reflected in its guarded, off-centre title. John Bulls Other Island is an untidy piece, suggesting that Shaw was cramming into it all he ever felt about Ireland, regardless of its immediate relevance. Not coincidentally, its also, or so it seems in Christopher Newton's production at the Shaw Festival, his angriest play. It contains at least two transfixing eruptions, one of them emanating from a minor character and one from a major.

The minor one is Hodson, a valet in the employ of the Englishman Tom Broadbent who, with his Irish business partner Larry Doyle, embarks on a trip to Larry's old home town of Roscullen. Hodson, accompanying them, is all deference until he finds himself alone with a native Roscullener, indulging in the familiar local custom of bemoaning the luck of the Irish. At which point Hodson loses it; dropping his vocational toffs accent for his native cockney, he tells his companion that until hes experienced London poverty, he doesn't know what suffering is. The switch from gentleman's gentleman to workers worker is blistering, especially as executed here by David Schurmann, who is himself, under normal casting circumstances, the most gentlemanly of the Festivals actors. You can feel the release.

Not that the play denies the Irish their grievances. Its justly celebrated last scene confronts Broadbent and Doyle, who are in the development game and intend to play it in Roscullen, with Peter Keegan, a defrocked priest whom the locals still persist in calling father and who is something of a Hibernian St. Francis; we first meet him communing with a grasshopper, and he is later moved to passionate indignation over the fate of a pig whom he calls "our brother." He also speaks of the Earth as Hell. He knows exactly what the visitors, with their grandiose schemes for hotels and golf courses, are up to, and his excoriating summary of it is the evening's second fit of transcendent rage. He then proceeds to a vision of Ireland as a country where the State is the Church and the Church the people and of the world as "a godhead in which all life is human and all humanity divine." Among lapsed Catholics, he's on a plane of his own, and he inspires his author to a visionary prose unique in his work. Jim Mezon, who can do marvels with quietness, plays him as fiercely gentle, a tormented soul physically and spiritually apart, and also funny. This, after his work in A Moon for the Misbegotten and The Cherry Orchard, completes a triptych of performances alike only in -- and I try to use the word sparingly--greatness.

Keegan may get the glory but the plays heavy lifting is done by Tom and Larry, whose approaches to Ireland are, respectively, enchanted and embittered. Benedict Campbell and Graeme Somerville give strong anchoring performances in the roles, though both are unduly self-conscious. Somerville goes into periodic vocal trances, as if Doyle were turning his sarcastic lyricism on and off like a tap; Campbell suggests not only that he sees through Broadbent, whos as bouncingly and bone-headedly and victoriously English as only a Shavian Englishman can be, but that Broadbent sees through himself. Which is going a bit far.

Among the native prizes Broadbent carries off is Nora, the local heiress and an old love of Larry's, whom Severn Thompson plays with enchanting romantic circumspection. Thom Marriott stands tall among her neighbours as a bigoted priest, frocked, whom Sean O'Casey might have drawn. OCasey might also have got more uproarious fun than Shaw does from the fate of the pig, taken for a disastrous ride in Broadbents car, though he, too, would probably have left us wanting to see it for ourselves rather than just hearing about it. Mary Haney provides an upright centre to a fine bunch of town rowdies, debating their country's future while obsessing over their own feuds; they include Guy Bannerman, Patrick McManus, Jonathan Widdifield as a terrified youth, and Ric Reid as two identical stage Irishmen named Haffigan, the first one mocked as a fake, the other presented as the genuine article: Shaw could be shameless. He was also, unmistakably, an urban Irishman patronizing the peasantry. But he had a tragic sense, and though the play was written and set a decade before the official Troubles, it's still troubling enough. Structurally and emotionally its all over the map, but the map has the authors blood on it.

Another deracinated Celt is on view in Do Not Go Gentle, an ambiguous celebration of Dylan Thomas, apparently set in Purgatory and performed by Geraint Wyn Davies, another actor who has, in the last few Stratford seasons, blossomed extraordinarily. He does finely by the staple Thomas poems, especially the titular exhortation to his dying father, which here concludes the first half and seems directed more at himself. The relation to his father isn't very central; indeed there's little discernible focus to the piece, which was concocted by another fine Welsh-Canadian actor, the late Leon Pownall. Wyn Davies presents Thomas, with considerable charm, as rather a bashful boyo, despite his boasted amatory and alcoholic prowess. He also recites a lot of Shakespeare, with whom Thomas, on slender biographic evidence, is said to have felt a lifelong and of course hopeless rivalry: especially hopeless in this context, since Shakespeares stuff, unlike Thomass, was actually written for the theatre. He gets to do "fear no more the heat o' the sun" as an 11 o'clock number: Beautiful, of course, but it leaves the supposed subject of the evening definitively upstaged.

- John Bull's Other Island is in repertory through Oct. 9 at the Court House Theatre, Niagara-on-the-Lake. For tickets, call 1-800-511-SHAW or visit shawfest. com; Do Not Go Gentle is in repertory through Aug. 22 at the Studio Theatre, Stratford. For tickets, call 1-800-567-1600 or visit stratfordfestival. ca.
2010-07-31-you-re-going-to-want-to-sit-d:
Five ladies, all clad in fashionably inescapable black, sit in a row onstage and read statements written by other ladies about the emotional crises in their lives and the articles of clothing with which they associate them. The fact that none of the actresses has to learn any lines cuts down on rehearsal time, and makes the gig attractive to well-known performers who are between other engagements. Love, Loss, and What I Wore ranks in this proliferating semi-theatrical genre somewhere between Love Letters and -- given its gynocentricity -- a more inhibited version of The Vagina Monologues.

The show has its origin in an autobiographical book by American writer Ilene Beckerman. Two other American writers, Nora and Delia Ephron, have buffed it up by soliciting testimonials from acquaintances, and intercutting them. There cant be any plot, but the evening is subdivided by categories, each announced by one of the performers. Someone will say "the training bra"; and everyone onstage -- not to mention a sizeable proportion of the audience -- snaps to nostalgic attention. Its an evening of anecdote, lasting nearly two hours without intermission, and dread attends the mention of each new garment, as it means that the proceedings are about to be dragged out even further. They do, to be fair, make some amusing capital out of this at the final curtain.

For a boring show, it can be quite entertaining. The performers are all good and some of them are famous. Louise Pitre deals with the original Beckerman material, and I'd call her the standout if she didn't spend the entire show sitting down. She is stationed a little apart from the others, and more or less conducts them. She turns over drawings of dresses on an easel, and even gets to draw one herself. Textually, she delivers with exemplary tact and wit, never missing a wry comic point but never underlining one, either. Pitre is best known of course as a musical performer, but Im not trying to be back-handed when I say that Ive liked her best in shows -- this one and The Last Days of Judas Iscariot -- in which she's only talked. (Well, that's a bit hasty; I loved her in Annie Get Your Gun.) There are two opposed traps inherent in the rehearsed-reading format -- dry recitation and frenetic vocal colouring -- and Pitre, alone in this company, evades them both.

Shes helped by being cast, if not as a consistent character, then at least as a consistent voice. All the others have to do turns, and they all at some point overdo or underdo. This applies even to Andrea Martin, the most experienced stand-up comedienne of them all; she takes time to find a comfort level, though once she does shes razor-sharp, especially in a diatribe about purses or in a vengeful obituary for a husband who is, unpardonably, still alive. The latter is one of several occasions in which the script seems to want to break free from its own professed subject, or at least its own professed metaphor. Sharron Matthews has some fun with the frustrations of shopping. Paula Brancati has some nice wry moments. Mary Walsh has a couple of set-pieces; one, about choosing a bra after a mastectomy, is obviously meant to be the evening's gesture towards depth, and it does contain the script's most startlingly funny line, but shes really more memorable in grumpier mode, describing how to dress for accessibility on a prison visit while still getting past the guards. Occasionally, the players get to interact; some early exchanges about sartorially rebellious teenagers get the laughter of recognition: from women, obviously, but also from any man whos had a daughter, a sister or, come to that, a mother. But mostly, the show seems to be congratulating itself on its own superficiality; it takes for granted that all women are obsessed with their wardrobes, and never even asks why. Whenever it seems to be reaching out to something wider, it crawls back into its closet. The real costume it wears is a straitjacket.

It's closed now, but I'd like to record that in a recent show at, but not by, Second City, an actor playing Stephen Harper got up and said "shows with The Musical in the title are always terrible," suggesting that, whatever his future as a prime minister, he might make a hell of a theatre critic. Unhappily, the show in which he made this declaration was called Stephen Harper: The Musical, and it demonstrated that you can't escape a curse simply by acknowledging it. It showed the PM being persuaded to boost his popularity ratings by becoming the subject of a Broadway show, also called Stephen Harper: The Musical, a double structure that brought off the remarkable feat of being thin and confusing at the same time. Its closing number was called Nothing Rhymes with Canada; that may be true, but it still doesn't excuse setting the word so that the accent falls on the last syllable. There was a good joke about the Tories being hoisted on their own arts-cutting petard, and the performers were mostly all right. Mr. Harper himself emerged as a put-upon patsy which may, at least on a Toronto stage, be a first.

- Love, Loss, and What I Wore plays through Sept. 4 at the Panasonic Theatre. For more information, call 416-872-1212 or visit lovelossonstage. ca.

2010-08-07-his-was-an-age-of-kings-remem:
In 1960, there was a BBC television series, unthinkable in today's climate, called An Age of Kings. It was a 15-part serial, drawn from Shakespeares chronological sequence of English history plays: from Richard II to Richard III with three Henries in between. They were screened at fortnightly intervals: too long a gap, but necessary because each complex instalment was transmitted live. They were recorded on transmission, of course, and shown worldwide; and theyre now available as a box set on DVD. Seeing them again has been a treat and a revelation. The revelation lies in the sheer intelligence and capability of everybody concerned. There was a core company of about 20 young actors, who could feel their way around a Shakespearean text with a confidence that today would also be unthinkable. Among the ensemble are a few future stars: Judi Dench an enchanting French princess in Henry V; Sean Connery amazingly good as Hotspur; Eileen Atkins embodying the malignant Elizabethan view of Joan of Arc. And kicking the whole thing off as a mellifluous Richard II, there's David William.

William, who later moved to Canada and who died last week, is best known here as a director; he did many productions at Stratford, and was the festival's artistic director from 1990 to 1993. His regime came between those of John Neville (another golden-voiced English actor)and Richard Monette. In fact, he maintained a threefold identity as director, actor and scholar. His essay on The Tempest, a "preface" in the style of an earlier triple threat Harley Granville-Barker and published in that same Age of Kings year of 1960, is one of the best things written about that play. He described it, most succinctly, as the noblest of the revenge plays.

His acting and directing were often thought of as scholarly as well. An Oxford graduate, he had started his career in small roles at the Old Vic and rapidly gained a reputation for his verse-speaking. He was known, too, as an intellectual dandy, and this may well have influenced his casting as Richard II. His Richard certainly gave the impression of being in love with his own voice, but thats legitimate for the character. He ascended, as Richard should, to the status of minor prophet: unworthy perhaps as a man but still the vessel for a curse that it takes seven more blood-soaked plays to expiate.

Richard II was a favourite play for William; he directed it, meticulously if unexcitingly, at the National Theatre in 1972. His directing career had really taken off 10 years previously when he revivified Londons Open Air Theatre in Regent's Park, a place that no one had taken seriously in ages. He started with a delightful Midsummer Night's Dream (in which he, typically, played Oberon) and followed it with a Loves Labours Lost whose reviews were orgasmic; the late Bernard Levin wrote that the pleasure it gave him could only be compared to sexual pleasure.

None of his work in Canada, where he first worked in 1966, aroused responses that heightened. In fact, of the three Stratford productions of his that I saw, two were boring. One was a Romeo and Juliet, with two future Stratford ADs, Monette and Marti Maraden, as the lovers, and with a built-up multi-levelled set that practically screamed 1950s. The other was T.S. Eliot's Murder in the Cathedral, a piece of High Church martyrology that only he would have programmed; though, as he pointed out to me, it did very well at the box office, suggesting that some spiritual cravings were indeed being served. The Stratford production of his that I enjoyed was the robust Elizabethan comedy The Shoemaker's Holiday, a play that hed previously directed with great success in London. And for all his ascetic image, comedy may have been where he was happiest. As often happens he was far less of a purist, certainly far less of a puritan, in practice than in theory. He directed Troilus and Cressida, as part of a Stratford "war" season in 1987, as if the words conservative and "academic" had been hurled in his direction just once too often, and he was determined to disprove them. He was roundly damned for doing so but, judging from those same reviews, most of his supposedly outrageous inventions were perfectly in keeping with an outrageous text.

His less controversial Stratford work, over a period of three decades, included a mellow Twelfth Night, with Monette and Martha Henry as visually persuasive twins; and highly praised versions of The Winters Tale and Ben Jonson's scabrous Volpone. Jonson suited him; my favourite acting role of his was Ananias, the scruffy Puritan fanatic in The Alchemist whom he played, with quivering shoulders and a Cockney accent, twice: on television, directed like An Age of Kings by Peter Dews, and on stage in a riotous modern-dress production by the man I suspect was his idol, Tyrone Guthrie -- a great show, and William more or less stole it. As Stratford's chief, he was hardly in political-theatrical fashion but he was, in his own way, adventurous. He once wrote scathingly of "our suburban concern with relevance, " but along with Racine and Euripides, he championed Canadian plays, especially those of Michel Tremblay, whom he programmed in three successive seasons. He also, for better or worse, helped institutionalize the Stratford musical.

A few years ago, he came out of semi-retirement to play Boyet, the senior courtier, in Maraden's production of Love's Labour's, and was elegant as ever. He was never in the theatrical mainstream, not in Canada, and certainly not in Britain. A supposed revolution in Shakespearean acting took place in the 1960s, emphasizing irony and intellect; he certainly had both those qualities but he was too old-school to be really part of it. He was though, a late flowering of the tradition whose know-how made that revolution possible; and his presence in An Age of Kings puts it on permanent record.

2010-08-07-stages-of-the-air-the-cbc-dec:
I love radio drama. I've enjoyed working in it and -as a post-war child in England -I practically grew up listening to it. I doubt if thats possible for anyone now, even in the U.K. In Canada, where for years CBC ranked second only to the BBC in the production of audio plays, it certainly isnt. Chris Boyce, CBC Radio programming director, acknowledges that audiences fell in the 1990s, due mainly, he says, to inappropriate scheduling. Now they've figured out when people are likeliest to listen: 11:30 p.m. Thursday evenings with a repeat on Friday mornings. It's still only one slot, but Boyce says they are "constantly developing stuff" to fill it. What that stuff is, we may have to wait until 2011 to discover. For the present, Canadian radio drama consists of just two series: Afghanada and Backbencher.

Afghanada has been CBCs flagship drama production for four years now; at the moment, indeed, its the only one to be found on air. The last season--the fourth--is being re-run through the summer, with a fifth announced for the fall. It's the ongoing saga of Canadian soldiers -- three in particular -- serving in Kandahar. I've always found the title a little unfortunate; it suggests a satirical comedy, a vein that might be hard to sustain over so long a period, and anyway isnt being attempted. Afghanada certainly has its humorous moments, but its closer to The Hurt Locker than it is to MAS H.

It was originally the joint project of four playwrights: Andrew Moodie, Greg Nelson, Adam Pettle and Jason Sherman. Nelson and Pettle are still regular writers on the show, usually in collaboration, but the stable has broadened to include many others. As with most long-running shows, though, on radio or TV, you'd be hard-pressed to detect anybody's individual style; Hannah Moscovitch wrote one of last seasons episodes, but I wouldnt have known unless I'd been told. The regular characters, since the show's inception, have been Patricia Kinsella, known mysteriously but endearingly as Coach, who over the years has risen from corporal to sergeant, and the two private soldiers under her command, Chucky Manson and Dean Donaldson. (Theres usually a third as well, but hes varied from season to season.) Kinsella is played, excellently, by Jenny Young, as troubled but determined. Chucky (Billy MacLellan) is the cut-up of the trio, a winsome Newfoundlander whose accent sometimes sounds too much to be true, but is probably authentic. Dean (Paul Fauteux) is the morose, sardonic one. One scene found Chucky avidly clucking over family videos sent from home, and Dean commenting "there's nothing worse than listening to people listening to things." In radio terms, that's almost meta-dramatic.

Afghanada is billed as a grunts eye view of the conflict and its kept true to that. I suspect that if you polled the show's creative staff on what they thought about Canada's presence in Afghanistan, they would

say that we should get out yesterday. In an early episode Chucky wonderered aloud about what good they could possibly be doing; a recent one found Kinsella arguing with a NATO superior, who wanted to burn a village for security reasons, that "were here to protect these people, not to destroy their homes." For the most part, though, the program is determinedly apolitical; its about getting through each day, keeping yourself and your buddies alive.

It's well done, though my sense (I haven't heard every episode of every season) is that its beginning to repeat itself. But then war is repetitive. The shows better when it's concentrating on character interaction rather than on firefights, which just come off confusing. Its main formal characteristic is that each episode is narrated by a principal character, not in retrospect but as the events are happening: stream-of-consciousness in fact, though tightly controlled. Originally this function was rotated among the three regulars, but guest characters have increasingly been allowed to join in as well: a journalist captured by bad guys (usually meaning Taliban but on this occasion warlords), a soldier who carries his son's action figure as a mascot and is invalided home after his legs have been blown off. (A season typically proceeds in three-episode arcs, and this was one of the more sentimental ones: not the subject, the treatment.) The narration constitutes a frank acknowledgment of radios main problem: the need to explain everything. I love radio drama -- I grew up on it -- but I have to admit that it has little room for subtext; Chekhov on radio sounds like aimless talk. The narration on Afghanada can sound literary, the dialogue self-consciously tough but not--this is the CBC after all--quite tough enough. If soldiers are going to say "freaking" all the time, better perhaps they shouldnt swear at all.

If Afghanada makes a serious attempt to overcome cliche, then Backbencher, CBC's other drama series, enthusiastically surrenders to it. This show, back next January for a second season, is about an ex-paramedic from Nova Scotia who becomes Canada's first MP with a nose ring. (Much is made of the nose ring.) Its announced in the opening credits as one womans journey through the snakepit of Canadian politics, and the writing that follows is on the same level of subtlety and sophistication. It's the kind of show in which the dialogue laboriously describes the characters immediately before they appear. Tactful acting and direction might mitigate this kind of thing, but the actors here seem to be wallowing in it; the production also goes in for portentous fades where Afghanada prefers the quick cut. Wendy Lill, the principal author, is an ex-MP herself, and for all I know her portrait of Ottawa is more factually authentic than Afghanada's of Afghanistan. It still sounds like soap opera.

Thats true, to some degree, for most drama series, whether on radio or TV. Whats become almost extinct in both media is the individual one-off play. Boyce says that CBC radio is commissioning some of these, so we'll see. He's right, surely, in saying that drama is the best of all forms for life beyond its scheduled transmission, whether as podcast, download, podcast or CD box set. "We're going" he says "through a bit of a revival." I hope.

2010-08-12-selves-evolved:
Last week marked the beginning of SummerWorks, Toronto's indie theatre and arts festival, which is presenting performances on various stages throughout the city.

The oldest play on view this year, by two and a half millennia, is also, of those I've seen, the most exciting. Euripides' Iphigenia at Aulis (at the Factory Mainspace theatre) was his last play, its chosen myth being that of the princess sacrificed by her father Agamemnon, the Greek general, so that the winds might change and the Greek fleet sail for Troy. Euripides' method, as usual, is to ask how real people would have behaved, given the extreme circumstances dictated by the legend. Their reactions here are humanly inconsistent. Agamemnon vacillates between paternal horror and professional pride; his prestige, as his wife Clytemnestra bitterly points out, is at stake. His brother Menelaus, husband of Helen, for whose sake the whole expedition is being undertaken, is unexpectedly ambiguous as well. Iphigenia is lured to the Greek harbour at Aulis on a promise of marriage to the hero Achilles; he knows nothing about it, and is furious when he finds out. He vows to defend Iphigenia, but it seems that he too is motivated as much by amour-propre as by compassion.

The heroine herself seems to resolve the situation by opting for martyrdom in the national interest. This is genuinely moving, but over the whole play hangs the image -- as potent in Euripides' own time as in ours--of young lives being wasted in a dubious struggle initiated by their elders. Alan Dilworth follows his fine production of the faux-Greek tragedy If We Were Birds with an equally powerful staging of the real thing. The text (Nicolas Billon's adaptation of a translation by Roger Beck) occasionally goes for easy laughs, and it certainly shouldn't say "flaunt" when it means "flout," but it's mostly primed for irony: the real, dark thing, not the giggly modern substitute. The tensions between the characters are brilliantly realized; and though individual performances vary in quality, everybody on the white-clad team gets the tone right.

The bar is set by David Fox as Agamemnon's old servant and personified conscience: superbly human in speech, magnificent when he just sits in silence at the side of the stage, which he does for much of the play. Stephen Bogaert is a persuasively riven Agamemnon, and Sarah Orenstein grows steadily in vengeful stature as Clytemnestra, whose grievances include having had her child by a previous marriage ripped from her arms and killed by her current spouse. That useful bit of the myth is ignored in other surviving tragedies, but a more general piece of knowledge haunts the play without needing to be mentioned: the fact that when Agamemnon returns to his wife after 10 years, she will kill him. Greek mythology was a forcefield that the playwrights could darken or illuminate at will, greatly to their benefit. The chorus is stationed among us in the auditorium, thus fulfilling their proper function, as a funnel between us and the action, even though reduced to three and deprived of most of their lines. The text of this play is much in dispute, the doubtful passages include a surprise ending that this version retains but over which it casts a mordant pall. The closing sections of this production are drainingly powerful, the real Athenian McCoy.

A lighter-hearted venture into a more recent past is Or (also at the Factory Mainspace theatre), whose central figure is Aphra Behn, England's first professional female playwright and one of the most entertaining if neglected authors of Restoration comedy. To support her writing habit, she also worked as a spy; this American play, by Liz Duffy Adams, finds her first in a debtors' prison, from which she's sprung by King Charles II himself, who appreciates both of her talents and her body as well. This scene, in Kelly Straughan's, is dark and cramped in more than its setting, but things liven up considerably when we move to Aphra's apartment where she juggles careers, storylines, theatrical metaphors and lovers of both sexes. Sophie Goulet gives her a warm presence that's both amused and amusing, and Damien Atkins executes an awesome series of sartorial and psychological quick-changes as the womanizing monarch, a cringing secret agent and, most delightful of all, Lady Davenant, the polite but demanding manageress of London's principal playhouse, who doesn't like plays with double titles, even if Shakespeare did it. Hence this play's title, though it's also meant to signify ambiguity in general. The titles of at least two of Behn's own plays make their way artfully into the dialogue, the kind of thing for which I am a sucker.

Another triple, if not more, threat: Johnnie Walker, who plays three roles in his own play Redheaded Stepchild (at the Factory Studio theatre). This solo piece, astutely directed by Morgan Norwich, is about a loner of a boy who has both of the title's characteristics, and so gets bullied. The play has a more elaborate structure than it needs, and it owes something to I, Claudia, both in subject and in its hero's pleadingly indignant tone, but it's funny and a bit harrowing; Walker's writing is good and his performance just about flawless.

Melody A. Johnson, author-performer of Miss Caledonia (Factory Studio) does better in the latter role than the former. Drawn from life, though not her own life, this piece about a farm girl finding realization through entering beauty pageants, is a pedestrian treatment of a commonplace theme. "Commonplace" isn't usually what Johnson, a great eccentric comedienne, is about, so it seems a waste, but she's irresistible at the end, singing "I've been everywhere, man" at tongue-twisting speed while twirling a baton at similar velocity. The end is calculatedly heartwarming; the calculation works.

- SummerWorks runs until Sunday. Visit summerworks. ca for tickets and information.
2010-08-13-glacial-case-rubicon-is-a-slo:
We are now two weeks into Rubicon, three if you count a preliminary instalment that aired a week before the official premiere, and so may be regarded as an optional extra (Episode Minus One). Rubicon seems to be a spy show, though both its story and its characters are so heavily draped in mystery that it's difficult to tell what anyone involved is up to. It does take place, more or less undoubtedly, in the New York HQ of something called the American Policy Institute, where some unglamorous, and probably underpaid, figuresareresearching the movements and motives of people who have been detected doing questionable things in foreign parts. Conversations among the employees are glacial, meaning that they're both slow and icy. It's like 24 slowed down to the methodical pace and down-at-heel ambience of John Le Carre, with an atmospheric dash of The Prisoner and the possible philosophical blessing of Franz Kafka. The air of stealth and subterfuge, with heavy musical underlining, is plainly intended to be hypnotic. I think it succeeds, but I don't deny that it can also be frustrating.

Our hero is Will (James Badge Dale, looking tense and inquisitive), who starts as a mid-level functionary at Inscrutable Investigations Inc, but is promoted when David, his superior, mentor and friend is killed in a train crash. You need to have watched the prologue episode to have clapped eyes on David when alive; on the other hand, he may return, since before boarding the train he deposited his car in Parking Space 13, and Will knows how unlikely it is that David, a highly superstitious man, would have done such a thing. He thinks that David was trying to tell him something. David has also made Will a present of his motorcycle which Will, short of space, keeps in his kitchen. When he disassembles the bike, he discovers clues and a gun, the latter of which should come in especially useful if the show, which sems to have taken a vow of onscreen non-violence, ever allows him to use it.

Will, in his new position, presides over a disconsolate team of three. There's Miles, youngish and mildly bearded, who worries a lot about riots in Nigeria, and can't get anyone else to take an interest in them. There's Tanya, whom somebody suspects of being an alcoholic and, who as the only woman on the team, has the responsibility of bringing the doughnuts. (Yes, I know.) There's Grant, who's very particular about his doughnuts, and who gets teased over whether his namesake, Ulysses S., was one of the five worst presidents in U.S. history or only one of the 10. Grant is both prickly and pompous, and wears a shirt and tie. All the others dress casual, including Will, who is upbraided for it when his immediate boss, who is unpleasant, takes him to meet his ultimate boss, who

is comparatively polite and so probably untrustworthy. The Big Boss asks Will and his team to look into the activities of a German called George ( "not even Georg," laments Grant), and they spend much time looking at footage of him going through airport security.

They can't find much out about him, except that his financial records suggest that he's impeccable to the point of sanctity. At other times, they seem to be looking into Hezbollah's acquisition of former Soviet missiles, and the travel plans of David Cameron; they're nothing if not up-to-the-minute except that they seem to live in a pre-computerized age: when they talk about "files" they mean the heavy, bulging manila kind. Will, I should have mentioned, lost a wife and child on 9/11, so his cheerlessness is more than excusable.

Meanwhile, in another part of the plot entirely, there's Miranda Richardson, playing the wife of a recently deceased rich man who has left her a townhouse of whose existence she was previously unaware. She's suspicious, especially when she goes to look at it and find it contains a copy of a novel by Graham Greene. "He hated Graham Greene" she protests, apparently pondering whether literary infidelity might be grounds for posthumous divorce. She also finds a four leaf clover, which isn't as lucky as might sound. Because the only link so far between her and the rest of the show is that a 4LC (dandy acronym, don't you think?) seems to be the motif of a secret cabal of posh gents who may be responsible for David's death, or for his not being dead. Dead or alive, David has a jumpy son who wants Will to return his dad's motorbike. Will also has a secretary, Maggie, who wants to be his love interest but is being forced to spy on him and his team as well.

And if Will thinks he's being followed, he's right. He's already detected one stalker, who turns out to be nothing but an FBI man doing clearance in his clearance. He doesn't know about two other guys, who seem to want him dead, or to be working for someone who does. He also finds secret codes in newspaper crossword puzzles, and takes them to a wise old cryptographer; he's played, I'm happy to note, by Isiah Whitlock Jr, who was Clay Davis on The Wire.

I suppose it will all come together. The show has an infuriating air of knowing what it's doing, even while refusing to tell us. Just one thing: If there turns out to be another of those world conspiracies, like all the other TV shows have, then I want to know what its goals are, how it's financed, and just who's in on it: no more chickening out. As for the title: It sounds pleasantly ominous, but I've yet to notice any reference to the river or to anyone crossing it, literally or otherwise. It may of course be a pun, given the tricksiness of everything. And I am beginning to think of Will, a good fellow in an impenetrable maze, as Cubik's Rube.

- Rubicon airs on Sundays at 9 p.m. on AMC.

2010-08-14-love-in-the-time-of-victrola-:
A quick rundown on the plot of The Two Gentlemen of Verona, possibly Shakespeare's earliest comedy and almost certainly his weakest: The two gents are Valentine, who laughs at love, and Proteus, who sighs about it, and sighs especially for Julia, who sighs and loves right back. Valentine goes off to Milan, where he promptly falls for Silvia, the Duke's daughter, who reciprocates. Proteus joins him there and also falls for Silvia, so heavily that he forgets Julia and gets Valentine exiled, which doesn't do him any good with Silvia. Valentine is waylaid by outlaws, who make him their captain. Julia follows Proteus to Milan, disguised as a page. It all comes right in the end, sort of.

Some years ago there was a celebrated production by the Royal Shakespeare Company that set the play in the 1930s and broke it up with songs by Gershwin and Porter. It was, by all accounts, delightful. Dean Gabourie's new production, the first (and overdue) Shakespeare in the Stratford Studio, is set some 20 years earlier, in the Victrola age when pop songs, though rousing, were less sophisticated; it's also the age of silent movies, disjointed clips from which are projected before the action gets started. When it does, we find that both Julia in Verona and Silvia in Milan are actresses, and that Valentine and Proteus are stage-door johnnies, though when they first appear it seems that they too may be in the business, as they look and behave like a couple of off-duty song-and-dance men. It seems likelier, though, that they're just two guys who like to dress in matching blazers and boaters. Thurio, Silvia's hopeless and hapless suitor, is also an actor; he plays Othello to her Desdemona on variety bills, leaving her as unimpressed with his performance onstage as off. It's all very confusing, especially socially. I suppose it isn't impossible for a duke to have an actress for a daughter, but it seems odd that nobody remarks on it. You get the impression that they would like to have made him a theatre manager, but couldn't square it with the text. Nor does the theatricality, which includes a mirthless Keystone Kops chase, work on its own account. It's meant to be jolly good fun, but it obstinately refuses to take off.

Within this misshapen frame are a couple of good scenes and one interesting performance. The scenes include one in which Proteus finds the banished Valentine moping on top of a flight of library steps (the high-point of Lorenzo Savoini's design) and is visibly torn between triumph and conscience; and one in which the disguised Julia is forced to bear a love-letter to her rival Silvia. Both these encounters involve mixed feelings, and they bear out the production's declared intent (if you believe what you read in program notes) to bring out the comedy's darker or ironic side. All the more amazing, then, that it should shy away when it reaches the most notorious, and most troubling, crux in the play. Get this: Silvia is captured by the outlaws, Proteus rescues her and then threatens to rape her, Valentine steps in, Proteus says sorry, and Valentine, much moved, hands over his love: "All that was mine in Silvia I give thee." Now this might be a satire on Renaissance ideals of male friendship; it might be a seriously intended example of it. Either way, it's a problem, especially in a quasi-modern setting. At Stratford, the line is spoken but the production shuffles by the moment as if it didn't exist.

The notable performance is Gareth Potter's baby-faced Proteus, who passes with seeming ingenuousness from one deceit to the next, sincere in the belief that far more things are fair in love than anyone would dare to try in war. Of the others in the central quartet, Dion Johnstone's Valentine is cheery; Sophia Walker does her most flexible work yet as Julia, especially in her boy's get-up; and Claire Lautier's Silvia plays the prima donna well but without ever unbending. All three, in a commendable endeavour to get their meaning across, tend to italicize every other word.

There are pleasing cameos from Andrew Gillies as a painstakingly proper English manservant, Wayne Best as his huffy employer, and Stephen Russell as an elderly knight vowed to chastity with, his eyebrows tell us, occasional lapses. This leaves the play's two clowns. Speed, Valentine's servant, is a wisecracker whose jokes Bruce Dow, perhaps forgivably, fails to resuscitate. Launce, Proteus's fellow, is a far richer role, and traditionally the play's salvation. He speaks droll, earthy prose, and he has a dog. Robert Persichini is the victim both of a partner who's a scene-stealer even by canine standards and of a concept that presents his monologues as conscious vaudeville routines, rather than as human outpourings that happen to be addressed to an audience. Also, he is in himself a dour comedian, which in theory should help with Launce's tales of woe but in practice cancels them out. He's very good, though, at registering silent disgust with his master. The production's ultimate message is that Launce's love for his four-footed friend surpasses anything felt, in love or friendship, by his supposed betters. It's a reasonable point, nicely made at first, but it then gets overstressed with Launce giving the finger to the happy-enders while they give out with A Good Man Is Hard To Find. Talking of interpolations: one of Launce's speeches has been lifted wholesale from The Comedy of Errors, making this the first Shakespeare production I remember to include lengthy passages from two of its author's other works. At least Errors, unlike Othello, is another early play. It still seems like a gesture of defeat.

- The Two Gentlemen of Verona is in repertory through Sept. 19 at the Studio Theatre, Stratford. Call 1-800-567-1600 or visit stratfordfestival. ca for details.
2010-08-19-love-loss-and-tensions-washed:
SOUTH PACIFIC

The Four Seasons Centre for the Performing Arts, Toronto

---

Nellie Forbush, the heroine of Rodgers and Hammerstein's South Pacific, comes from Little Rock, Ark. Mary Martin, who created the role back in 1949 came, famously, from Texas. So does Carmen Cusack who, in the wonderful production that's just arrived in Toronto, gives a performance of Nellie that I doubt Martin herself could have equalled and on which I cannot believe that anybody could improve.

Nellie is a U.S. navy nurse, stationed in the south seas during the Second World War, who falls in love with a middle-aged French planter, Emile de Becque. She overcomes her initial qualms about the differences between them, only to recoil when she discovers that he has two children from an earlier marriage to a Polynesian woman, now deceased. She can accept that her beloved once killed a man, hence his exile; she can't, until sorely tested, overcome the racial indoctrination that comes with being a little girl from Little Rock. It seems prophetic that Nellie should hail from the town that, only a few years after the show's premiere, would be the site of one of the first battles over segregation. The triumph of Cusack's performance is how firmly it's rooted and how naturally it blossoms. Her accent, for a start, is impregnable, summoning a whole background and a whole cast of mind. She's both guarded and generous, cautious and headstrong, graceful and gawky, and when she runs up against her own limitations, she's as appalled by them as anyone; note how she has to bring herself to utter

the word "coloured." She makes you share her delight at washing that man right out of her hair and her deeper joy when she accepts him, just one song later, as a wonderful guy. You laugh with her, and cry both with and for her. South Pacific is, of course, a show designed to draw tears, but it doesn't win them cheaply. The show both begins and ends, especially in this production, with remarkable economy and tact. Jason Howard's Emile is rather stiffly acted, as this role written for an opera singer nearly always is, but he is honest

and earns his part in the finale.

Questions of race haunt the entire show, but there's only one song that directly confronts it: The self-hating You've Got to Be Carefully Taught, sung by the Philadelphia-born, Princeton-bred Lt. Joe Cable (Anderson Davis, strong and surprisingly complex) after refusing to marry the island girl Liat. In Bartlett Sher's production the message is as much in the staging as in the lyric. It's watched by six sailors, three black, three white, each trio on its own side of the stage. As the song proceeds, the three white guys peel off the stage in silent protest; they might be standing in for the audiences for whose benefit this song had to be cut when the show first toured in the South.

This is a touring version of a revival originally staged at New York's Lincoln Center, but nothing about it feels second-hand or second-rate. Every number here is not only beautifully sung but thoroughly acted; Cusack's blithe exploration of A Cockeyed Optimist sets the standard right at the start. The only disappointing number is the concert-party special Honeybun: significantly the only one that isn't part of the narrative. The revelation of Sher's direction is the quality of Hammerstein's and Joshua Logan's book--not only in the development and interaction of the love stories but in the itchy atmospherics of servicemen waiting on the edge of global conflict. There's an epic quality about the closing scenes in which they leave their island for actual combat. South Pacific is the great liberal musical, and this production honours its triple place in history: in its own time, in the time it depicts, and in ours.

- South Pacific runs until Sept. 5. Visit dancaptickets. com for more information.
