The Marquise de Merteuil to the Vicomte de Valmont, Stratford, Canada, August 2010

Well, my dear Vicomte, how very pleasant and unexpected to see you again. And at the theatre, too. Of course, at the Paris Opera, one had better things to do than to pay attention to the cavortings on the stage. How the world has declined in--what is it? -- 230 years. Nor did I expect to find myself watching any kind of entertainment in a small town of which I had never heard, in a country which I remember, insofar as I remember it at all, being called something else entirely. Imagine, too, my perplexed delight at finding the entertainment which they call Dangerous Liaisons --and to which, I must confess, I paid rapt attention--actually had me as its principal character, and you in what, I believe, is known as a featured role. I knew, of course, that soon after our earthly departures, that artillery-officer fellow Choderlos de Laclos had had the effrontery to publish our correspondence, and that of some of our more intimate acquaintances, and that ever since the world has taken his volume to be a novel, fictions made up of letters having been the fashion at the time. As if any part-time scribbler could invent us. Or me, at any rate. Still, there is his book transformed into a play, and there are you, the self-proclaimed libertine, elaborately seducing that arch prude Madame de Tourvel, the judge's wife; while also performing the more banal task of ruining that pert little idiot of a convent-girl, Cecile de Volanges. The latter, of course, undertaken at my behest, since I wished to avenge myself on one of my former lovers, who was to marry the little chit and to find her, on their wedding night, less or perhaps more than he would have wished. I confess, Vicomte, that you undertook her education very thoroughly, as is most delightfully and graphically conveyed in this theatrical adaptation. Well, I always knew how to pull your strings. Tell me, by what charitable dispensation were you released to see this play from wherever it is you are spending eternity? It can scarcely have been for good behaviour.

The Vicomte de Valmont to the Marquise de Merteuil, Same Place, Same Time

I might ask the same of you, Madame, and with the same impudent proviso. I confess that my earthly career was that of an impenitent and incorrigible rake, but I could never presume to compete with you in hypocrisy. However, my visit is easily explained. I have a permanent dispensation to check out, as they say, every new representation of our adventures, and there have been many. Since it is actually I who am the protagonist of this drama, and you the mere accessory, I have what are known as bragging rights. I even attended the premiere of the present drama, a quarter-century ago, at another town called Stratford, in England. I do not think that the language furnished by the British playwright Christopher Hampton approaches our own levels of style and raillery, but I must commend the skill with which he has fashioned M. Laclos' epistolary compilation into a series of dialogue scenes of accelerating excitement. It can have been no easy task. The play was billed then as Les Liaisons Dangereuses -- I cannot fathom why it has been altered in what I am told is a bilingual country -- and it was staged in a small cabin, barely a theatre at all. In mounting it upon a large platform the present metteur- en-scene, who goes by the exotic name of Ethan MacSweeny, has had both to coarsen and to over-decorate it. He begins his production by elevating a large chandelier from the floor to the ceiling, something I am positive has been done before. However, I have nothing but praise for the way in which I am portrayed by the actor Tom McCamus, who conveys all my irresistible humour and charm, together with my destructive ennui and my ambiguity of feeling. Did I actually love the prude Tourvel? Even I cannot tell. The actress Sara Topham lacks something of the inner radiance that first provoked me, but her surrender and decline are movingly enacted. Bethany Jillard is likewise a pleasure as Cecile. I do not recall her admirer Danceny as being altogether the booby embodied by Michael Therriault but he is certainly amusing; as, in a discreetly insolent way, is Paul Dunn as my valet. As my octogenarian aunt, Martha Henry, exudes both wit and charity while being, by the bye, the only person in the company who is actually too young for her role. As for the representation of yourself, I leave the verdict to you, only cautioning you that the player in question, Seana McKenna, is one of the most highly regarded in our former colony.

Merteuil to Valmont Justly so, I could tell. But she misses the mischief with which I always tempered my malice and which made my wiles so much the more deadly. Nor would I ever have appeared in so sombre a dress and wig. Indeed, the whole enterprise is excessively solemn. Why, in the last scene, the portentously ironic references to the 1780s and '90s, followed by the trundling on of a guillotine, when in truth we were all safely dead or in exile by the time of the Terror?.

V toM

Ah yes, the Jacobin curse of political correctness. The English production was equally judgmental at the close, though it confined itself to the mere sound of a descending blade. As I wafted my way out of the Canadian playhouse, I brushed up against one of the local scribblers and managed to decipher what he, with typical reviewer's malice, had scrawled in his notebook: "This has the trappings of a major production. It also has some of the substance. But not enough."

- Dangerous Liaisons is in repertory at the Festival Theatre, Stratford, through Oct. 30. Call 1-800-567-1600 or visit stratfordfestival. ca for details.
2010-08-24-full-of-irish-snide:
How Now Mrs. Brown Cow!

Canon Theatre, Toronto

---

Pre-show announcements, concerning cellphones and such, are notoriously boring, or, if comically intended, notoriously embarrassing. But now, as we settle in for How Now Mrs. Brown Cow!, there's an exception. A voice, purportedly female, instructs us on the theatre's safety regulations and especially on what steps to take in the event of a fire: "F--kin' big ones." It's explosively funny, and so is much of the show that follows. I have a feeling that the more I describe it, the less good I will make it sound, but trust me.

The voice, and this isn't a surprise, is that of Brendan O'Carroll, the entertainment's star, author and director. He appears as Mrs. Agnes Brown of Dublin, the sexagenarian widowed mother of five or six grown children. (Sorry to be so vague, but the program quotes one figure while the play shows another. Maybe this is another of those jokes about careless Catholics.) The play, as O'Carroll disarmingly tells us at the curtain call, is the fifth in a trilogy; being as prolific as Mrs. Brown herself he promises a sixth, to be entitled I Know a Bandwagon When I See One. Now, we're not in the land of well-made drama here. The four preceding instalments may conceivably have been closer-knit, but this one plays like a bunch of sitcom episodes placed end to end.

This is not unexpected, as Mrs. Brown started out as a sitcom character on Irish radio, and the plays are spinoffs. It's old-fashioned sitcom, at that: the kind that revolves around a star comedian given free rein and surrounded by stooges. If it were on TV, it would have a laugh track. Mrs. Brown is a self-absorbed, foul-mouthed matriarch whose favourite word, when she doesn't feel like using the stronger alternative, is "feck." (On what system she chooses between them is a mystery.) She also makes many cups of tea. Her family lives in fear of her, but admit that only she could have kept them together. This dynamic is just about credible, and it keeps the show similarly afloat. Agnes has her own share of neuroses and vulnerabilities; we're told, in a rare example of someone else getting a good line, that when one of her sons came out of the closet, she retreated into a cupboard. The only one of the clan who doesn't regard her with awed affection is her white-haired dad (Dermot O'Neill), of whom her treatment verges on elder abuse and who spends most of the play praying that something terrible will happen to her. He almost gets his wish when she has to lean perilously over a banister to hang a star on an inaccessible Christmas tree. It's the evening's sustained peak of physical comedy.

Less effective is a scene in which she jerks about the stage after

accidentally tasering herself, mercilessly prolonging what should have been a one-off gag. There are several story-lines, running in attenuated tandem, including one about a son who may or may not be coming home for Christmas and another about the younger Browns believing, on tenuous evidence, that one of them may have been adopted.

But the evening is not about plot. It's about a lot of hilarious one-liners, and about O'Carroll's own effrontery. He steps outrageously out of the frame, while still maintaining a grasp on the character. Where Dame Edna Everage (a richer creation) victimizes the audience, O'Carroll victimizes his fellow actors. He's always throwing them off with what we must presume to be ad-libs; you'd think they'd be hardened by now, but I've never seen so many performers breaking up on a professional stage. He doesn't stop at verbal interpolations; on the first night the actor playing the gay son's partner was treated to a succession of slaps, right on his face mic. Trying repeatedly to get his lines out, he was asked, "Are you trying to make a small part bigger?" The audience, myself included, loved it.

I especially enjoyed O'Carroll's miming of a tape-rewind to give a cast member a second chance at a line that came out wrong the first time. Life and art intersect here, as O'Carroll overpowers his 10 colleagues the way Agnes overpowers her family. Like the old-time actor-managers who used to surround themselves with inferior talents and keep them out of the limelight, he permits a modicum of competition from his wife (Jennifer Gibney, playing his daughter) and none from anyone else.

The pace, on the few occasions when the star is offstage, is funereally slow, since no one else seems able to pick up a cue. The tough talk periodically gives way to syrupy sentimentality, including a very canned-sounding rendition of Silent Night, and there's a surprise ending that can be seen coming a mile off. If you're wondering about the title, it's only explained at the last minute, and when it is you may wish you'd never asked. There are, in short, any number of faults to be found with the show, and none of them matter. O'Carroll keeps pulling the rug from under everyone's feet, and we all fall happily down.

Two shows you are strongly advised to catch this week, while stocks last. Window on Toronto, a Soulpepper Lab Series production at the Young Centre for the Performing Arts, devised and performed by the company's academy and directed by Laszlo Marton, is sheerest magic. I cannot properly review the open-air Hamlet at Newmarket's Resurgence Theatre, since when I saw it an electrical failure caused the first half to be played with makeshift lighting, while rain stopped the second half from being played at all. I saw enough to determine that Lee Wilson's direction is highly intelligent, that the wonderful parkland setting is brilliantly used, and that Graham Abbey is an affecting, seething Hamlet whose nunnery scene with Jane Spence's Ophelia is the most searching, from both parties, that I have ever encountered.

- How Now Mrs. Brown Cow! runs until Sept. 4. For tickets, call 416-872-1212 or visit mirvish. com.

2010-08-28-when-light-verse-becomes-too-:
Iused to hate Serious Money. I mean the play. I'm not in love with it now, though my objections have nothing to do with what it has to say. Caryl Churchill's play, first staged in London in 1987 but only now receiving its professional Canadian premiere, is billed as "a city comedy," and it deals with financial trading, insider and otherwise, in the ferocious wake of Britain's Big Bang, less explosively known as deregulation. Topical in its day, it seems positively prophetic now. It concludes with its banker-protagonist, an ex-pat American, looking forward to "five more glorious years" of Thatcherism, which he adds are "handy though not essential, because it would take far more than Labour to stop us." He also says "sure, this is a dangerous system and it could crash any minute", though he adds that he confines his intimations of Armageddon to "just before breakfast." No, the problem isn't the message, it's the medium.

The play is mostly in verse, and when I first saw it I growled that it was an attempt to write in rhyming couplets by someone who hadn't a clue. That was unfair. Couplets indeed predominate, but Churchill varies them with quatrains, unrhymed verse and the occasional chunk of prose -- all adroitly done. The rhymes themselves are good, even in the two-liners; "pay for it" goes very smartly with "favourite", though it might go even better if it didn't crop up twice in as many minutes. It's the lengths to which she has to go to get to the rhymes that torture the ears. I mean "lengths" literally. She uses uneven lines of the kind that Ogden Nash made intentionally funny and William McGonagall made unintentionally hilarious. She also pads shamelessly. Somebody asks to be treated not only with "respect," which is where the line should end, but with "bonhomie" (rhymes with "economy"). Rhyming couplets fastidiously used can be wonderfully sharp comic weapons, as witness the Moliere translations of Richard Wilbur and Tony Harrison. Carelessly, they become point-blunting doggerel. Which is what happens here. A play that fancies itself as wielding a scalpel is actually brandishing a blunderbuss.

There is, to be fair, more to it; Churchill says she used verse to capture the energy of getting indescribably rich unimaginably quick. And here she does succeed. She tells a tangled tale that's centred in Britain but also takes in North and South America. At its centre is a young dealer who dies when about to be investigated; it could be suicide, it could be murder. He's a son of old money who's been making a fortune in new; and the play partly depicts a greedy, corrupt old-boy network displaced by a greedy, corrupt new-boy-and-girl network. There are no heroes here, and few visible victims, though we do occasionally hear of lives being ruined on a massive scale as the deals go through. There's no emotional investment for the audience. Everything depends on our being caught up in the story.

Churchill doesn't make that easy. We take for granted that the financial dealings will be impenetrable; it's almost part of their charm. I couldn't work out what the one character who ends up going to jail had actually done, but maybe that, too, is the point. The timeline is equally confusing; just when you think you're safely in the present, they throw another flashback at you. Style and story together need expert handling. In Eda Holmes' production, they come over loud but not clear. The Studio Theatre's acoustics seem largely to blame; The Entertainer, last year, had upholstery to soak up the sound, but this time the words get swallowed. The older players, predictably, cope best: Anthony Bekenn as a Brummie whistle-blower of mysterious motivation, Steven Sutcliffe in a variety of roles including an industrialist who's targeted by a take-over and, typical of the play, is as great a weasel as those who want to swallow him. Less distinct but still distinctive are David Schurmann as an old-school stockbroker and Graeme Somerville as a snarling corporate raider. Apart from Ali Momen, who supplies an oddly likeable centre as the guy from the Yank bank, the younger ones simply don't have the chops, at least not as individuals. As a group, they contribute energy, notably in two songs that conclude each of the acts, with lyrics (by Ian Dury) that really know about verse-rhythms. The first, depicting the activity on a trading floor, consists mainly of four-letter words. If the Shaw's intention was to outrage the bourgeoisie, they may have succeeded. Some rows of seats were conspicuously empty after the first-night interval.

The Age of Arousal, Linda Griffiths' fantasia about feminism around the turn of the last century, gets a more stylish production (from Jackie Maxwell) than it received at the Factory a few years ago. There's an especially beguiling ballet for typewriters: both the newfangled machines themselves and the women who use them to assault a previously male secretarial preserve. If the play runs out of steam in its second half, it's because its characters are less people in a story than figures in a pattern. Two of them, though, get exceptional performances: from Kelli Fox, again demonstrating her capacity for turning individual grievance into torrential emotional force, and from Sharry Flett as her sister who finds a comparable fervour in shocked shyness. As the veteran suffragette who takes them in and oversees the arousal, educational and sexual, Donna Belleville lacks the eccentric authority Claire Coulter brought to the role, while Jenny Young as her rebellious protegee spells out her part rather than embodying it.

- Serious Money plays through Sept. 12 at the Studio Theatre, Niagara-on-the-Lake; Age of Arousal at the Court House Theatre (1-800-511-SHAW).
2010-08-31-serving-the-servant:
WHAT THE BUTLER SAW

Young Centre for the Performing Arts, Toronto

---

The title What the Butler Saw refers to a peepshow machine that used to be found on British seaside piers. Customers could insert a coin and see pictures of high-born ladies and gentlemen enjoying themselves and one another in variously titillating poses. Joe Orton's 1969 play, his last, makes the audience the butler. We gaze at the antics of a more modern kind of English aristocracy, drawn from the professional and governmental classes.

The setting is a mental hospital, or as most of the characters unabashedly refer to it, a madhouse. The arch voyeur, watching the farcical proceedings in gleeful disbelief, is Orton himself, the young playwright famously dubbed "the Oscar Wilde of the welfare state:" a Wilde whose Bosie, apparently jealous of his lover's success, bludgeoned him to death, before taking his own life. The play, accordingly, reached the stage in a posthumous unrevised state, the source of some of its charm and some of its untidiness.

Dr. Prentice, the clinic's head head-shrinker, inaugurates the action by instructing Geraldine, a phenomenally innocent secretarial applicant, to take her clothes off for a medical examination. No sooner does he have her where he wants her (on his couch, behind a curtain) than he's interrupted by his wife, who's arrived in a comparable state of undress, having survived an attempted rape by a page boy at a local hotel.

Much swapping of clothing ensues at, as befits a farce, an increasingly frantic rate. Two more intruders raise the stakes. One is a police sergeant, investigating the disappearance of the private parts of a statue of Sir Winston Churchill. The other is Dr. Rance, whose opening line is "I represent Her Majesty's government -- your immediate superiors in madness" and who proceeds to take what passes for control. The play's epigraph, drawn from Jacobean tragedy, is "surely we are all mad people, and those we take for mad are not."

The play accordingly takes shots at the official pieties of medicine, the law and the civil service. But it's more deeply and personally subversive than that. All the sex described or attempted in the play is straight, but Orton clearly regards all such relationships as both a joke and a fraud. What he's actually saying is "surely we are all gay people and those we take for straight are fooling themselves."

"I'ma heterosexual" protests Dr. Prentice, to which Dr. Rance replies, "I wish you wouldn't keep using these Chaucerian words; it's very confusing." He's equally capable, mind you, of upholding orthodox morality, if his author can get a joke out of it; the play's greatest weakness is its inability to see beyond the next epigram. But it builds a funny and incipiently frightening world. It is, for its time and place, the ultimate outsider's play; Orton, aggressively uncloseted and with a prison record (for defacing library books, which seems deliciously English) was not so much the Oscar Wilde as the Jean Genet of the welfare state--though a Genet with a sense of humour, which makes all the difference.

Jim Warren's Soulpepper production is very lucid, which in this play is both a virtue and a vice. He sets the action and the characters up very neatly, and he does a fine job on the phantasmagoric finale, which finds most of the characters bloodied, drugged and transvestite (the policeman descending a rope-ladder in an off-the-shoulder leopard-skin dress) while Sir Winston's now-discovered portions are waved proudly aloft. There's also a multiple, and conceivably incestuous family reunion, in which comedy itself gets parodied. Warren gets the Orton tone more consistently than in last year's Loot, but not the tempo; in the middle of the play, when the pressure should be on, things get very slow.

There is one triumphant performance: Graham Harley, resisting all temptation to play for eccentricity, makes Rance the ultimate civil servant. A moustached mole, impervious to argument and smug with power, he rolls out his terrifying pronouncements like points on a memo. Meanwhile, his eyes dance with ambition and self-satisfaction. Harley has both the style and the character down to perfection, which includes making some of Orton's less polished phrases sound natural if not witty.

Brandon McGibbon's page is admirable, Nicole Underhay's shaken secretary is admirable cubed. Oliver Dennis is his sterling self as the copper, particularly good at registering silent bafflement shading into indignation; he doesn't manage, though, to rescue a long speech that must be the most inert thing Orton ever wrote. (Dennis made magic with a similar aria in Loot, but this time the task was probably impossible.)

Brenda Robins' Mrs. Prentice is excessively brittle and unyielding, but then she is being asked to play a frigid nymphomaniac, depending on which laugh her author is after at any given moment.

Blair Williams as her husband exemplifies the good and the bad in the production. He makes a dapper first impression, establishing the doctor's professional assurance and personal frustration. But when frustration becomes desperation, he remains strangely imperturbable. This is damaging, since he's the character who keeps trying to put things right while getting them even more wrong. To put it another way, he's the farce. It's doubly surprising since Williams is an accomplished comedian who also showed, as director of The President, that he knows all there is to know about theatrical frenzy and farce's eternal race against time.

- What the Butler Saw runs until Sept. 18. For tickets, call 416-866-8666 or visit young-centre. ca.

Theatre impresario David Mirvish announced on Monday that Theatre Museum Canada will finally have a permanent home in a new development at 355 King St. W., in the heart of Torontos Mirvish-controlled theatre district.

Planning is underway for a museum of 900 square metres that will include space for exhibits, presentation and theatrical programming.

Up until now the museum, which was registered as a charity in 1991 by its founding chairman, veteran theatre critic Herbert Whittaker, has led a nomadic existence, mounting exhibits at the Elgin and Wintergarden Theatre Centre, the Toronto Reference Library and other places.

Its programs have included Backstage, a series of educational theatre discussions, and an online history project, the Legend Library, in which R. H. Thomson has interviewed such seminal theatrical figures as William Hutt, Martha Henry and Paul Thompson. (The videos can be found at TheatreMuseumCanada. ca.)

The new museum was announced at a celebration in the Toronto home of board member Nona Macdonald Heaslip. Honorary patron Christopher Plummer sent a message proclaiming "God bless David Mirvish, everyone responsible and 'all who sail in her' for magically evoking this major miracle."

2010-09-02-doctor-estranged-love:
DOC

Young Centre for the Performing Arts, Toronto

---

The best scenes of Doc are also the best to have appeared in Soulepper's entire season of Canadian collectables. (They must be collectables because they've been published in collections.)

In Diana Leblanc's finely acted production of Sharon Pollock's 1984 play, R.H. Thomson plays the doc of the title, whose name is Ev. Ev, a character based on the author's father, is a family physician whose own family is the first casualty of his devotion to his work.

The play is a memory piece, juggling periods, and Thomson switches with absolute authority between at least three incarnations: passionate young visionary, dedicated but weary professional, aging grouch, all united by a bracing sharpness of tongue and mind and a crippling incapacity for expressing tenderness, or even perhaps for feeling it. For Ev, charity ends at home.

He's a budding specialist, diverted into general practice, presumably in Pollock's own province of New Brunswick, though I don't remember hearing it specified. He fights fiercely and profanely to improve the local health facilities, and ends up with a hospital named after him. His concern for his patients is passionate and personal; he's forever leaving home at unsocial hours to make house calls.

You may wonder whether the play has to show quite so many times that Ev is a raging workaholic who neglects his wife and children, but Ev's drive is unrelenting, so it figures that the scenes depicting him should be unrelenting as well.

In order to attend an old patient's son who's fallen under a thresher, he absents himself from the birth of his own son. It's monstrous, but he does have his own kind of point. Anyway, you can't argue with him. No one can.

The chief casualty is of course his wife, Bob (actual name, Eloise Roberts). When they first met, she was a feisty and, by her own believable account, super-competent nurse. After their marriage, and for reasons that are never completely explained, he forbade her to work. (He says that having her in his operating theatre would create conflict, but that doesn't account for why he won't let her work anywhere else.) So she vegetates, neglects her two children, or so her husband says, and becomes an alcoholic. Jane Spidell gives a harrowing, emotionally naked performance as Bob, grabbing your attention with her throaty vocal attack and pinioning it with an unsparing descent through anger, loss and despair.

For solace, strictly psychological, Bob turns to Oscar, Ev's lifelong friend, who has drifted into doctoring and whom Ev uses, with mostly unthinking patronage, to pick up his own slack. Oscar is a go-along smiler who can be pushed too far, and Derek Boyes captures both sides of him admirably. He is, of course, in love with Bob, though Ev won't even pay him the compliment of being jealous. Bob, though, is good and jealous of Ev's office nurse Valma on whom he is completely reliant, both at work and, in extreme circumstances, at home. This, too, is a platonic relationship, though Bob understandably doesn't believe it. We get quite a picture of Valma, considering that she doesn't actually appear, the play being not a triangle but a quadrilateral with one invisible side.

There are, though, two other characters -- or rather two other roles, since the author has written herself into the play in two separate guises: as Catherine, a woman in her thirties, and as Katie, who is Catherine entering her teens.

This is where the play stops being good. It's framed as Catherine's return to see her dad, after years of semi-estrangement that she's spent being a writer; but their relationship, and Catherine's whole persona, remain shadowy. The play's admirers enthuse about how its fluid structure permits Catherine and Katie to address one another across the years. But they have remarkably little of interest to say, and the play would work as well if there were only one of them. (For a witty and moving use of this elder-meets-younger device, see -- if we're ever allowed to see it -- Tom Stoppard's The Invention of Love.)

Hannah Gross makes a singularly assured debut as Katie, and Carmen Grant does what she can with the ungrateful role of her older ego. Ev's mother committed suicide, and this is also meant to hang more significantly over the evening than it actually does. In trying to give these matters greater weight, Leblanc makes the play's last scene overly sentimental and its first one overly portentous. The show begins with the characters picturesquely posed on Astrid Janson's set, a perspex structure punched with actor-sized holes, and presumably meant as a metaphor for memory; it looks impressive, but it's hard initially to make out who's who and what they're talking about. Once they start getting to grips with one another, the production itself gets a grip and it's a fierce one.

- Doc runs until Sept. 18. For tickets, call 416-866-8666 or visit youngcentre. ca.

2010-09-04-macis-back-yet-another-musica:
George F. Walkers new musical -- you read that right -- includes a song whose refrain goes everybody wants what someone else has got." Walker isnt the best lyricist in the world, but he isn't the worst either, and that line makes a good point. It applies to the show itself, which is called King of Thieves and which is trying to catch some of the reflected glory from the 18th century's greatest hit The Beggars Opera and from its offshoots, some of which are by very gifted people. (Anyone on for a revival of Beggars Holiday, by Duke Ellington and John Latouche? Thought not.) Jennifer Tarver, Walker's Stratford director, writes in her program note that the story was "immortalized in the great Brecht-Weill composition The Threepenny Opera. Some people would say that John Gay had already done a pretty good job of immortalizing it back in 1728, but Walker's piece does indeed owe most to the Brecht. It takes off, really, from one of that shows most famous lines: What is the crime of robbing a bank compared to the crime of founding a bank?"

It also takes off from the fantasy-American setting beloved of Brecht and Weill in their other works: another case of wanting what someone else has got. Were in New York, mainly in a nightclub, in the 1920s; and if you don't believe we're on the eve of Depression, the show has a trio of bankers who can see it coming and are planning to use it to get even richer. Topical, huh? The opening and closing numbers suggest that this super-scam is what the show is about, but in between both the plot and the plotters get lost, obscured by a parade of double, triple and maybe even quadruple crosses on the parts of everyone else.

Walkers king of thieves is called, unsurprisingly, Mac; and his story more or less picks up where those of Gays Captain Macheath and Brecht's Mack the Knife left off. Mac is out of jail and married to his Polly; and his in-laws, the Peachums, still don't approve. Theyd like to do him in, but theyre up against FBI chief Brown who wants to use Mac as an anti-trust mole, to which end he puts him into a disguise (an Italian accent and a moustache) that even a banker could see through and eventually does. Brown, by the way, is not a nice man. Macsort of is, at least compared to those around him; looking up close at the rich, and then at the poor, he decides to turn Robin Hood. Or that's what he says; but, apart from taking a beggar off the streets and turning him into a house-breaker, he doesn't do much about it. Nor is it very clear what he could do. His starring role is paper thin, and Evan Buliung cant do much more with it than look cool and hope for better things.

The theme is much the same as that of Serious Money; both, coincidentally, opened in the same week, in studio productions at our major festivals, and with spartan but suggestive sets designed by Peter Hartwell. Im not the greatest fan of the Caryl Churchill play, but it does tell its story forcefully; while Walker's piece is one of those in which there's too much going on and not enough happening. A mostly excellent cast grabs what it can. Laura Condollns viperish Polly proves much tougher than her old man; she also does the best singing. Her parents are rollickingly played, Jay Brazeaus mountainous Peachum being a fence capacious enough for anyone to sit on, and Nora McLellan's Mrs. P an enthusiastic murderess with an incisive style and a stripping fetish. Nigel Bennett plays a chilling, authoritative cop, a type that isn't new to him; he also gets to play a scene in womans underwear, which probably is. (And he doesnt lose his authority.) The bankers, when allowed to take the stage, are a fine sneering crew, with Shane Carty as the regulation weakling, and Sandy Winsby and Scott A. Hurst as his conscienceless cronies. Sean Cullen plays a club-owner/narrator, because in this kind of show there's always a club-owner narrator. There's always a spiky jazz score, too, which John Roby duly supplies, though his pastiche falls short of John Kanders in Chicago, which itself falls short of the real thing. Tarvers production is swift and tidy, though she must take some of the blame for two act-endings which, considered either as play or as musical, are extraordinarily feeble. There's liveliness and vivacity in Walker's writing but its squandered on a useless conceit. We dont need another Beggar's Opera rip-off in a neverland setting. Maybe he should have been encouraged to place the same subject-matter in today's Canada.

Yesterdays Canada, Quebec division, gets loving attention in For the Pleasure of Seeing Her Again, Michel Tremblays recollection of conversations, from young boyhood to young manhood, with his mother. It's from her, plainly, that he got his dramatic imagination; she was a dominating fantasist who never lost, or ran out of, an argument. Lucy Peacock scores an unquestionable triumph in the role, even managing to get a French lilt into the English text. She does, though, let the woman's wilder flights run away with her; shes best, and most varied, when quieter: musing on whether the actors she sees on TV ever think about her, or, in an unutterably moving last scene, still tough but dying of cancer. Tom Rooney is subtly superb as the storyteller/antagonist, making flawless osmotic distinction between his ages without, apparently, moving a muscle. The play says less about the power of theatre than it thinks it does, so its beginning and end seem unwarrantably cute. But not, in Chris Abrahams production, offensively. It's the kind of minor play to which a major playwright earns the right.

- King of Thieves is in repertory through Sept. 18 at the Studio Theatre, Stratford; For the Pleasure of Seeing Her Again through Oct. 2 at the Tom Patterson Theatre. Call 1-800-567-1600 or visit stratfordfestival. ca for more information.

Brace yourselves: The new revue at Second City doesn't have a single dud number. That's not all it doesn't have. It doesn't have a title that's a weak attempt at a topical pun. The show is called Something Wicked Awesome This Way Comes; and though that may be a jaw-breaker, it's an apt description of the show itself, which despite the implicit disclaimer, has more -- and more pungent -- political satire in it than any Second City show I remember. Not only that, it has a shape. It's standard practice at this house for characters from an early sketch to make surprise appearances in a later one, but I don't recall any show whose closing number managed to tie together as many previous themes as this one does. It has us surrounded.

Which is what the first number is about. It's a riff on the G20 summit that involves police corralling progressively smaller sections of the

audience until they're finally concentrating their attentions on just one man. (At least it was a man the night I went. His name was Doug. He was a sport.) Meanwhile they shout bizarre commands at one another, and at the public: "Please go back to the suburbs!" "Pay your mortgage!"

The show can cut surprisingly deep. An early number finds a couple, tired of the restrictions that come with being parents, attempting to unload their offspring on the folks next door, and getting a bleak response, not just about parenthood but about the whole family contract. ( "He's going to leave you, or die first -- he's a man.") Much later, two guys, who thought they were having a friendly discussion, find themselves arguing about the Middle East: a subject on which it's almost impossible to say anything without giving mortal offence to someone. Simultaneously invigorated and appalled by the taboos they're breaking, they chase one another around the auditorium -- and, at one point, into the street outside -- yelling "We're talking about Israel!" En route, as it happens, they get off some very handy capsule versions of the basic arguments on both sides. The fact that they do it at the top of their respective lungs seems thoroughly appropriate.

The most sustained piece is a press conference conducted by somebody ministerial with some kind of responsibility for the environment, speedily deflecting unwelcome inquiries by answering them in French, a language of which she's nimbly capable of professing ignorance when it's the one in which the question happens to be asked. This is a smashing spiralling scene in which the supporting cast keep switching between journalistic identities and all available parts of the theatre. (Helen Thomas, seeking new Canadian pastures, pops up in the balcony, peeved at her lack of access.) This is at once the sanest and the zaniest item--the saniest, perhaps -- of the evening. A subsequent, more sober kind of protracted craziness finds everybody forgetting there's a war on, including those who are fighting it.

On more domestic fronts, the obligatory dating sketch takes approach-avoidance to diabolical new levels of consistency and ingenuity. Another item turns relationships into a video game, while yet another finds kids packing for the cottage, i.e. cramming all their Nintendo games into a suitcase. (An impatient mother threatens to punish them by playing Diana Krall records.) There is indeed a lot of stuff involving gadgetry of one kind or another: Backseat driving takes on a new dimension when the person doing it is a grinning menace, trying out all the apps on his iPhone.

The show is anchored by two performing vets, Rob Baker and Adam Cawley, doing their most authoritative work yet. Baker's basic persona is that of the flabby bully, Cawley's is the skeptical, well-meaning everyman -- you see them at their purest as the Israel disputants -- but they find many variations within those parameters. The third male in the cast, Kris Siddiqi, has comparatively little to do, and the same goes for the female newcomer, Inessa Frantowski. The two longer-standing women are fine, Dale Boyer doing a bang-up job of outflanking opposition as the ministerial lady, and Caitlin Howden handling the one musical number, a song that begins as a wan, earnest Joni Mitchell parody and gradually expands into a just-about-everything parody. It's called Words, a title whose universal application is nicely, even beautifully, confirmed at the finale. Chris Earle, the director, has marshalled an evening with a brain, a heart, and--stop me before I get to Oz -- an identity. Some Second City revues may have had more individually hysterical moments, but overall this is the best since the halcyon shows of the '70s and '80s. And on those, since I only witnessed them as a tourist, my memories could be rose-coloured.

- Something Wicked Awesome This Way Comes runs indefinitely at Second City. Call 416-343-0011 or visit secondcity. com for ticket information.

2010-09-18-fumbling-towards-ecstasy-or-s:
There is, despite its title, nothing arboreal about Through the Leaves. The leaves in question are the pages of a diary kept by Martha, one of the play's two characters. Martha is the owner and proprietress of a Bavarian butcher's store or, since she specializes, offal emporium. In her early fifties and unmarried, she starts a relationship with Otto, a factory worker for whom the word "sexist" might have been invented. Younger than her, though not by much, he behaves as though middle age were a pitiable condition peculiar to women. He exploits Martha, sexually and otherwise, and absents himself from her life and her bed for long, unexplained periods, but despite his best or worst efforts, it wouldn't be true to say that he humiliates her. It may be a close call, but the one thing he cannot violate is her intelligence.

The play dates from 1981. Franz Xaver Kroetz, who wrote it, first became famous in the 1980s for a stark series of plays about contemporary German peasantry. (One of them, Stallerhof, is a masterpiece.) They too depicted people grabbing at love, or at least sex, or at least human contact, in circumstances that make those depicted in Through the Leaves seem positively idyllic. At least this one takes place indoors, in Martha's shop and its attached living quarters. (There's a bedroom upstairs, but we never visit it; and Otto doesn't seem too keen on going there either.) It's quite comfortable, as Martha is running a fairly successful business. It's one of the things about her that Otto resents. Another is her beloved dog, whose yapping at intimate moments puts him off his stride. Remembering the well-known Chekhov doctrine -- "never bring a gun onstage unless you intend to use it" -- you may well shudder when Otto, given the run of Martha's premises, starts brandishing a meat cleaver.

The play is brought to us by Company Theatre, in a debut production by Philip Riccio, one of their two artistic directors. More modest in scale and range than this group's previous triumphs, Festen and A Whistle in the Dark, it's up to the same standards of detail and intensity. On Martha's and Otto's first date, or at least the first time she invites Otto over, she feeds him caviar, which he greets with something between suspicion and contempt. That sets the tone. She's always making gestures, or making allowances, without quite succeeding in fooling herself. Maria Vacratsis, in a performance that's at once full-bodied and self-effacing, keeps the balance superbly. We feel for her, but we never despair for her. "Where did it all go wrong?" she asks in her diary, of a liaison that, as far as we can tell, never went right. Those diary entries link the play. She reads them to us at the beginning, at the end, and between the scenes, complete with punctuation: "open brackets ... exclamation marks...close brackets." That semi-comic device helps distance them without, in any sense, alienating us. One of the achievements of the play and of the performance is that, though we are told the story in Martha's words, we don't have to see it through her eyes. We can realize, intellectually, that losing Otto would be the best thing that could happen to her -- so, at some level, does she -- but we can feel the toll it would take. When Vacratsis refers to "my Otto" it sometimes sounds as if she's talking about a car, but otherwise she's perfect.

She isn't, thankfully, a victim. It's likelier that he is: not of her, but of a social and sexual code that's left him adrift in a changing world. Nicholas Campbell's performance, equallyunsparing in its own way, never courts sympathy, but makes us vividly aware of the pressures on Otto, bragging of past and present sexual successes that probably don't exist. When Martha wants to go to a costume ball, he insists on paying for the tickets, because that's what the man does, and then grumbles about the whole experience. Having paid that token debt to chivalry, he settles down to battening off his lady-friend, resenting her offer of a job, accepting her bed and board without actually committing to them, mocking her aging body while availing himself of it, though not as often, and certainly not as tenderly, as she would like. Play and production make painfully clear that, physically and emotionally she wants him more than he wants her, and that they both lose by it. There's one explicit sex scene in the play, and it's crude but clothed: indeed, crude because clothed. Here the production contrasts with one in London a few years ago that did have nudity, and also had Simon Callow as Otto: aggressively miscast in a working-class role and compensating with studied brutality and a touch of the grotesque. That gave the play more suspense than it has here, but less inexorability. Here things work out, in terms of emotion if not of incident, as you know they'll have to.

John Thompson has designed a brightly lit set in which the clinical butcher's store at the back provides a striking ironic counterpoint to the spar-tan domestic chintz that occupies what's left. There's something tragic in the air here, at least in textbook terms: a lot of pity, a little terror and no sentimentality. (Martha can be sentimental, but the play isn't; besides, she sees through herself.) The play's view of life may be offal, but it's red meat.

- Until Oct. 3 at the Tarragon. Call 416-531-1827 or visit tarragontheatre.comfor tickets. robert.cushman@hotmail.com

2010-09-22-vaudeville-meets-vegas:
There are two obvious ways in which Banana Shpeel differs from all the previous Cirque du Soleil shows that have been seen in Toronto. One is that it's staged in a theatre rather than a tent. The other is that it has dialogue, lots of it, that can be both heard and understood. These are not good things.

There have been spoken words in previous Cirque shows, but they have generally sounded like gibberish, either because of big top acoustics or because they actually have been gibberish. There have also been rudimentary plotlines that were difficult to follow but usually seemed to involve someone being captured or placed under a spell or both, and finally rescued and redeemed. Clowns figured intermittently, as supplementary goodies or baddies or just as relief. This time, though, there's a story that crowds everything else offstage and has clowns at the centre of it. Three tiers of buffoon are involved. At the top there's Marty Schmelky, the showman whose show this supposedly is. He's a short man in a flecked, shiny green jacket, which gives him the air of an ambulant pistachio ice cream with mint chocolate chips. Like so many legendary showmen and/or circus ringmasters, he's a tyrant and shouts at everybody. In the course of the evening he reforms, then re-reforms, and finally has an epiphany involving Paris, a city the mention of whose name has been driving him to distraction all evening. We're meant to wonder why this is, and we don't. Whether acting nasty or nice, Marty is an obnoxious presence, and our resentment of him rubs off on Danny Rutigliano, the perfectly efficient and doubtless amiable actor who plays him. He has a tall, beaky female foil, in the person of Shereen Hickman, who would probably be hilarious with better material.

Their seconds-in-command are two vocational clowns, one (Wayne Wilson) irresponsible, the other (Daniel Passer) officious -- the classic duo -- and both, through no identifiable fault of their own, clogging up the evening. They have even more text to carry than Marty and even less character.

Finally, there are three zanies who erupt onto the stage from the auditorium as part of a supposed talent contest and refuse to vacate it. These guys are really good, each of them specializing in a different variety of smile. There is Gordon White, a familiar Cirque figure, self-announced as "the oldest mime in the world" and exploring new horizons of happy, hopeful decrepitude. There's Patrick de Valette, a lank-haired "modern dancer" with a devilish, unconquerable grin. And there's Claudio Carneiro, a smirking gigolo who does a protracted silent number that's the best thing of the night and depicts him going out for dinner and a drive with a young lady selected from the audience. Though if his date on the press night wasn't a plant, she must have had quite amazing skills of instant adaptation.

Talented though they are, the intruders get nothing but grief from Marty, who carries on as if they were the lunatics taking over the asylum. In a way, he's right. But what he doesn't acknowledge -- and what the show itself, written and directed by David Shiner, catastrophically fails to realize -- is that Marty himself is part of the problem, indeed its biggest symptom.

This "vaudeville with a twist," as it calls itself, is all frame and no picture. Traditionally, people have gone to the circus to be thrilled by the sight of performers in peril, in danger of either being eaten alive by wild animals or falling to the ground from immense heights. Cirque's humane instincts have always eliminated the first possibility, and the dimensions of their current playing space put paid to the second. There can be no tightropes or trapezes at the Canon. Indeed there are few specialty acts of any kind. What we are offered, when the clowns kindly leave the stage, is an underpopulated third-rate variety show. There are two helpings of fast but unexceptional tap dancing. There are showgirls. There are two jugglers: a lady (Vanessa Alvarez) who does it, impressively, with her feet; and a gentleman (Tuan Le) who, more traditionally but even more impressively, uses his hands. For some reason these fine but not dissimilar acts are placed close together in the first act. The show can't even leave its best talents alone to dazzle us. It clutters the stage with lesser performers, either looking on in dumb admiration or executing paler versions of the main event.

What the production most signally lacks is the one quality that Cirque du Soleil could always, even at its most maddeningly pretentious, be counted on to provide: beauty. Perhaps it was inevitable that in going to Vegas, Cirque would also go Vegas. Here it's gone cut-price Vegas, the worst of all worlds.

- Banana Shpeel runs until Oct. 10. For tickets and more information, call 416-872-1212 or visit mirvish.com. robert.cushman@hotmail.com

2010-09-25-the-joys-and-terrors-of-time-:
Some thinkers in the 18th century conceived of the universe as a gigantic timepiece, and God as the mechanic in charge. In his play The Clockmaker, Stephen Massicotte takes off from this idea, to produce something that starts out irritating and ends up impressive.

Perhaps in homage to his philosophical heritage, Massicotte has given his play a Germanic setting and ambience. His central character is called Heinrich Mann, though with no apparent reference to Thomas Mann's equally smart brother, and is, as advertised, a timid but expert maker and refurbisher of clocks. When we first meet him he's been summoned to a government office for a meeting that it would be nice, but impossible, to avoid describing as Kafkaesque. His interviewer goes by the name of Monsieur Pierre, which makes the continental waters even muddier, and he starts out modestly enough, wrongfooting Heinrich over how he feels about the chair he's sitting in and having him fill in apparently meaningless forms that are duly consigned to the filing cabinet. That's just at the first appointment. At the second, he escalates the treatment, informing our hero that he is under surveillance for crimes he has not yet committed but might in the future. He even, with unusual liberality, suggests what these crimes might be. One is murder. Another is adultery.

These strike a couple of fearful chords with Heinrich, since he's recently encountered a new customer: from all appearances, his only customer. This is Frieda, a young woman with a badly damaged clock that should be either repaired or abandoned, and a marriage answering to the same description. Between the virginal Heinrich and the worldlier but terrorized Frieda, an understanding begins to take shape.

So far, so average. The interrogation scenes seem derivative, the incipiently romantic ones sweet but also -- to use the appropriate timepiece term -- second-hand. Then the play starts to gain traction. We follow Frieda home and behold her abusive husband, Adolphus, who alternates between beating physically up on her and mentally up on himself, the two kinds of violence being equally abrupt and almost equally alarming. There's even a scene in which Heinrich, empowered by love, confronts Adolphus, only to learn the sad truth that, whatever the story books may say, when you stand up to bullies, they do not invariably run away. Meanwhile--and I do mean meanwhile--there has been a separate series of scenes between Heinrich and Frieda, that seem to be taking place either in dreams or in an alternate universe. In these, Frieda prefers to be called Anna and is on her way home bearing a loaf of bread. (Heinrich, however, has not turned into a baker.) They show no awareness of their other encounters, and besides, the weather's different. But they are recognizably the same people, with much that was unspoken between them in their workaday lives coming joyfully into the open. They even make their way to the site of Heinrich's bureaucratic torments; this enables the play's designer to pull off a minor coup, and the playwright a major one. The office turns out to be housed in a clock tower, which, of course, finds Heinrich on his home ground. The play approaches its climax amidst a joyous clanging of symbols.

The double time scheme, or whatever it is, passes from being baffling-going-on-infuriating to being satisfying and even enlightening. Time, for a moment, stands still, and the play becomes a meditation on the joys and terrors of remembering things. (Most "time" plays are in fact "memory" plays.) Both Heinrich and Frieda have to decide how much future torment is worth the memory of past happiness, and we share their dilemma because we have come to care about them. I don't want to give away the ending, if only because I'm not sure I understand it, but on the way we have a slant on the afterlife, which may owe something to Bernard Shaw (the Don Juan in Hell scene in Man and Superman) and Thornton Wilder (the graveyard scene in Our Town) but is still quirky and individual. The moral might be that no one has the right to play God, including God.

The play was first staged at the Alberta PlayRites festival, and has been remounted here, very well, by its Calgary director, Bob White, who has given it weight while -- mostly -- avoiding heaviness. Christian Goutsis repeats his original role as Heinrich; he's initially charming and ultimately touching, but he does keep hitting the same piping note between times. The other actors are Toronto regulars. Damien Atkins is a suave functionary, at his best when admitting to unaccustomed discomfiture. The remaining two performances are stellar. Kevin Bundy, not an actor I usually associate with menace, has tremendous presence as Adolphus, whether letting himself go or holding himself in, as he does in a long sequence of silent motionless bewilderment at the end. As Frieda/ Anna, Claire Calnan is magnificently strong and clear in every moment, authoritative as an actress even when her character is jelly. Scott Reid's set is dominated by an imposing archway that gives it the air of a vintage railway station; but it's also remarkably versatile. A good start to the Tarragon's new season (especially with Through the Leaves playing concurrently in the Extra Space) and to Toronto's.

- The Clockmaker runs through Oct. 24 at the Tarragon Theatre. For more information, call 416-531-1827 or visit tarragontheatre.com. robert.cushman@hotmail.com

2010-09-29-marital-twist:
The opening line of Fernando Krapp Wrote Me This Letter is "Fernando Krapp wrote me this letter." It's a splendidly declarative beginning, not just for this play but for the new regime at Canadian Stage that it inaugurates. If the choice of script is a bracing departure from the previous management's staple menu of Broadway and off-Broadway naturalism, then so too is the manner of its presentation. The width and depth of the Bluma Appel stage have sometimes seemed an embarrassment; this debut production by the theatre's director Matthew Jocelyn glories in them. Staging and acting are extravagant, and yet ferociously disciplined.

It's a cosmopolitan style for a cosmopolitan piece. The play is a retelling by the German playwright Tankred Dorst of a story he found in a Spanish novella by Miguel de Unamuno. (The book dates from 1920, the play from 1992.) Fernando Krapp is an inordinately rich man; he can buy anything he wants, and what he wants is Julia, the most beautiful girl in what seems still to be a Spanish vicinity.

It's she who delivers the titular line, and she's furious about it. How dare he? Still, she accepts his proposal, and with it the proposition that beauty and wealth belong together. Call it a mix of practicality and arousal. Fernando and Julia settle down to a life replete with every comfort; as if to illustrate, a bearskin, with head still attached, descends from above and obligingly arranges itself into a rug.

It's one of two key furnishings. The other is a couch, on which Julia receives admiring visits from an impoverished local Count. The Count, who seems to suffer from a peculiarly refined strain of what D.H. Lawrence called sex in the head, pours out his adoration but seems disinclined to do anything about it. It isn't clear that Julia would want him to, but she is put out by

her husband's refusal to be perturbed. She wants him to be like Othello. I recall a school edition of the Shakespeare play, whose title page bore a quotation from Pushkin: "Othello wasn't jealous, he was trusting." I'd question that, but it's certainly true that Fernando isn't jealous, he's supremely confident -- of himself and his power. The idea that a pipsqueak like the Count -- a poor pipsqueak -- could be any kind of threat to him, is self-evidently ridiculous. He finds it equally ludicrous that Julia could resent his own goings-on with the female servants; he's Fernando Krapp, he can do as he wants, and that isn't what their marriage is supposed to be about. But if his libido can't be threatened, his sense of ownership can. When he believes, or professes to believe, that Julia has indeed succumbed, he summons the Count, terrifies and humiliates him. Later on, ostensibly oozing friendship and forgiveness, he terrorizes him all over again. The Count, obediently taking tea on the selfsame couch, literally turns cartwheels in his efforts to distance himself.

In a program note, Jocelyn invokes the Theatre of the Absurd, which I don't think is very helpful. (It seldom is.) Dorst's play is more socially, and even geographically, specific than anything in Ionesco or Beckett, though I suppose

you could think of Fernando's prolonged assault on Julia as Krapp's Last Rape. It's an assault that sends her for a time into a mental hospital. (Fernando has a couple of tame psychiatrists.) Her confusion about the facts is shared, on a less desperate plane, by the audience. The play's long title has a subtitle: An Attempt at the Truth. It's a quest that's both hopeless and essential. It seems, from what we've been shown, logistically unlikely that Julia and the Count should have had an affair. But you never know. Even Fernando doesn't know; and, unexpectedly and even movingly, the play explores the depths of his unknowing-ness. There's one thing that even the most powerful man in the world can't conquer. Tamburlaine the Great found that out. So does his modern equivalent.

The unpitying void of the stage is occupied, not filled, by Astrid Janson's ingenious revolving set, which has memories of old Castile secreted around its doors and window frames. Jocelyn, a professed Europhile, has translated the play himself, with a cunning, unsettling blend of the colloquial and the ornate; as a director, he has secured from his actors performances of remarkable physical and emotional boldness. In Ngozi Paul's Julia, the boldness sometimes tips over into coarseness, but she looks the part and is very fine in the play's last stretches, as bewildered victim and enforcedly elegant chatelaine. Ashley Wright captures Fernando in all his ineffable impregnability; portly and probably sweaty in a white suit, he's a man who doesn't have to care about appearances; he simply is and simply has.

Ryan Hollyman is piteously confused, and hilariously acrobatic, as the Count. Walter Borden completes the cast as Julia's father who, after vociferously encouraging her to sell herself, is consigned to benign contented silence, either pushing his grandchild's pram or, in a particularly delightful intrusion on a scene of high drama, twirling a yo-yo. The production's last image is of roses falling onto a garden wall. Like the plague of frogs in Magnolia, of which it's a gentler equivalent, it makes no factual sense, and it seems absolutely right.

- Fenando Krapp Wrote Me This Letter runs until Oct. 16 at Bluma Appel Theatre. Call 416-368-3110 or visit canadianstage.comfor tickets. robert.cushman@hotmail.com

2010-10-02-the-highly-strung-life-of-a-m:
Ronnie Burkett is one of our best actors. He's also a considerable playwright. He can sing too. And, oh yes, he also does puppets.

His new show Billy Twinkle (new to Toronto, that is; he's been touring it for the last two years) shows him in his finest form as a performer, but a little below that as a writer. It's full of brilliant scenes, but the thread that connects them frays a bit. It's the first Burkett show I've seen in which he himself, rather than one of his marionettes, plays the central role. There's probably some autobiography attached, though the story seems to owe more to its creator's worst nightmares than to his actual achievements. Billy Twinkle is a puppeteer, who when we meet him is clinging to a fairly debased rung in the professional hierarchy. He's working cruise ships, and Burkett starts the proceedings with a wonderfully smarmy rendition of his act. Technically, it's a good act -- it features a stripper-on-strings whose peeling is orchestrated with the maestro's usual breathtaking finesse -- but Billy isn't happy. He despises his audience, and treats us to an interior monologue about them. We then discover, as does he, that it wasn't as interior as he thought; he was overheard, and he's fired. He contemplates a conveniently located watery grave, quoting liberally from "to be or not to be" as he does so, but is dissuaded by the apparition of Sid Diamond, a former mentor whose stock-in-trade was puppet Shakespeare, and who finds Billy unworthy of his legacy. Sid, unusually for a Burkett character, is a glove puppet. He whisks Billy away to a miniature stage-upon-a-stage, on which unfolds the story of Billy's life. This means that we get to watch marionettes being operated by other marionettes: a split-level of virtuosity remarkable even for Burkett.

There are a few things wrong with this scenario. One is that there's too much, and too repetitive, cross-talk between Billy and the ghostly Sid. (The so-to-speak live, flashback Sid is another matter entirely.) Another is the matter of Billy's decline. The play's subtitle -- every play these days seems to have one--is Requiem for a Golden Boy. The implication is that Billy was a prodigy, who sold his soul to the cruise ships. He's signed up by a shady-looking-and-sounding manager, but the nature of the deal, and its implications, are skated over. It isn't clear what else Sid, or Burkett, or anybody else, expected him to do. Not everybody can be Ronnie Burkett, even if they're being played by Ronnie Burkett. Finally, though less importantly, the shipboard setting lovingly designed by Burkett himself -- he does that, too -- isn't used much as location or, up until the very end, as metaphor.

The biographical voyage itself, though, is treasure-stuffed. The scenes depicting Billy's Saskatchewan childhood are joys. He's shy but obsessed, with a busy mother and an indulgent father who confesses to ineptitude at building his son a toy theatre ( "I'm not like other dads ... I'm a pharmacist") but still enables his attendance at a puppet convention in Detroit. Here, and on subsequent visits, Billy meets several varieties of his fate. He introduces himself to Syd, who's impressed despite himself by the boy's cheek and determination. He encounters Benjy, a contemporary with avant-garde ambitions who comes to regard Billy as a marionettists' Messiah. He is seduced by an older man. The gay theme is almost as important as the puppetry one, starting with Billy's mom's friendship with a sales-rep colleague whom his dad describes as "bohemian." Back in Moose Jaw, Billy takes singing lessons from a Scots lady of mature years, who is at first shocked by his desire to do a red-hot mama number, but who throws herself enthusiastically into it on learning that the puppet, not the puppeteer, will be wearing the frock. The neat pastiche songwriting, here and elsewhere, is by John Alcorn.

As Billy Twinkle's Stars in Miniature expand in scope, so the shadows lengthen. Gawky, eager young figures give way to shuffling older ones, with the dolls representing Billy himself becoming progressively stiffer and more corpulent. Characters not currently in use sway visibly as they hang on their strings at the side: a fine, ghostly effect in itself. An evangelist puppeteer, with Jesus as her puppet, does an act that Billy finds at once ludicrous and disturbing, though his reaction might carry more weight if the show had touched any religious themes previously. (Billy does say that his family were Mennonites.) As far as secular religion goes, Sid's last hurrah is a beautiful Romeo and Juliet scene; Billy's lowest ebb, at least as Sid sees it, is a debased take on The Taming of the Shrew. Burkett adds Shakespearean verse-speaking to his accomplishments, culminating, as Billy returns to his nautical roots, in a reading of Prospero's epilogue totally different from, but bearing comparison with, that of Christopher Plummer -- echoes of whose tones I thought I caught in the portrayal of Sid. Burkett isn't a golden boy, but one of our theatre's golden men. His show may conceivably be some kind of an exorcism, but he's in no need of a requiem.

- Billy Twinkle runs until Oct. 24. Call 416-504-9971 or visit factorytheatre.cafor ticket information. robert.cushman@hotmail.com

2010-10-06-it-s-ok-to-have-stage-fright:
I was in London when Sarah Kane's play Blasted opened there in 1995, but felt too squeamish to go see it. It was denounced by most reviewers as being pointlessly, even pornographically, violent; praised, notably by other playwrights, as an imaginative portrayal of the way things actually are. As generally happens when the critical morality cops come out against a play (Ibsen's Ghosts, Edward Bond's Saved) history has ruled against them.

I still wouldn't blame anyone who couldn't face seeing it, and there were times when I averted my own eyes. But the play, finally receiving its Englishlanguage Canadian premiere in a superb production at Buddies in Bad Times, is a remarkable experience.

It starts with sexualized aggression on a small scale that's both psychologically and geographically specific; then explodes--literally--into global atrocity that comes, apparently, from nowhere. Ian, a middle-aged journalist, has brought Cate, a much younger woman from London, to a hotel room in his home town of Leeds. They have had a previous relationship, though how bright that old flame actually burned is open to question. Ian is drinking and smoking himself to death. Cate has sporadic fits; Ian, at least once, calls her "a retard," which is a fair example of the way he usually talks, especially on the subject of immigrants and other foreigners.

Ian of course wants to get Cate into bed, and that would seem indeed to be part of the deal. But she's resistant; and though what eventually happens may not technically qualify as rape, it leaves her bruised and resentful. Ian, by the way, is no monster; every advance is balanced by a shamed retreat, and he spends more time comforting Cate than threatening her. The acting of this duo, with all their shifts and gradations of feeling, is beyond praise. I couldn't quite believe in David Ferry's accent as native to Wales (where Ian was born) or Yorkshire (where he lives) but the man's belligerence and his hopelessness are there before us as living facts. So is the unreachableness of Michelle Monteith's Cate, at once full-blooded and detached ; the way she jumps up and down on an unwontedly luxurious bed is a perfect, joyous foil to the horrors to come.

They come with the irruption into the literally blasted room of an alien soldier (Dylan Smith, powerful if excessively indistinct) who announces that the town has been taken over, war brought home. It comes home to Ian in the form of anal rape, blinding, starvation and eventual cannibalism: scenes that are graphic, but not gloated over. Cate, who has mysteriously escaped, returns carrying a baby that she wants to take care of but has no idea how to. The British director, Dominic Dromgoole, an admirer of Kane's, has described her as a fine writer rather than a natural playwright. I'd agree, if it weren't for the initial scenes between Ian and Cate--the bulk of the play -- which are models of economy, of creating a relationship through hints and actions.

Where the play falls down is in its explicit attempts to tie its parts together. The soldier accuses Ian, who files tabloid stories about sex crimes abroad so long as they've happened to British holiday-makers, of ignoring far worse, more distant things. This must have seemed flimsy then, and it's flimsier now, when atrocities of all kinds get extensive coverage. What works better is the suggestion that Ian with Cate, and the soldier with Ian, are both avenging wrongs done to them: an endless cycle of reprisal.

Everything in Brendan Healy's production is brilliantly timed and brilliantly staged. He starts the evening with a pointless piece of audience-baiting that has us entering the theatre through the back door and in groups, and ends with Gene Kelly's recording of Singin' in the Rain: a monstrously heavy-handed attempt at irony, and A Clockwork Orange did it already. In between though, his direction is perfect: detailed, unhurried, ruthless and compassionate. Julie Fox's set, a white box that's the essence of every soullessly pristine hotel bedroom, is enclosed by a descending shutter that slams open and shut in a series of short, sharp shocks. If that isn't enough to scare the life out of you, Richard Feren's sound and Kimberly Purtell's lighting are there to finish the job.

- Blasted runs through Oct. 17 at Buddies in Bad Times Theatre. Call 416-975-8555 for tickets.

2010-10-07-if-west-side-story-had-a-tram:
The reopening attraction at the Sony Centre (formerly the Hummingbird, pre-formerly the O'Keefe, and frankly not looking startlingly different after its latest makeover) climaxes in the most exhilarating trampoline act you have ever seen. One of the wildest things about it is the fact that the trampoline itself is sunken, and hence out of sight. So there are all these bodies bouncing high in the air, apparently from nowhere. It's like whatever the opposite may be of free fall.

And I do mean to say "all these bodies:" There are 17 named performers in iD, a production from the Montealbased Cirque Eloize, and -- though it seems like more -- there are six of them on the trampoline or, as the program calls it, Trampowall. And there's another thing: The set for this production, designed by Robert Massicotte, is a cityscape, whose walls--especially in this number -- are lavishly washed with video projections. When the human projectiles grab onto the wall in passing, as they often do, it's as if they're seeking support from something insubstantial. It really looks death-defying.

Unlike some other cirques one might mention, Cirque Eloize -- in this show at least--doesn't offer much in the way of a storyline. It's more like a tone-poem, in which urban alienation gets conquered, repeatedly, by the power of positive acrobatics. A number will typically start with one performer grabbing aggressively at another, both looking as if they're ready to rumble. But before you know it they're in harmony, though with a competitive edge still remaining. The more traditional acts tend to be the less exciting. The juggling can't really compare with what the du Soleil bunch are offering a few blocks up Yonge Street, and even the famed lady (Josieanne Levasseur) with, or in, a hoop -- virtually the show's logo--isn't all that hot. The show's signature performer may be its trick cyclist (Thibaut Philippe), whose bike is vertical at least as often and it's horizontal, and who has a nice line in leaping it from ledge to ledge. When confined to street-level, he specializes in jumping over prone bodies, including one belonging to an intrepid member of the audience (who, to the best of my belief, was not a plant).

This is a dance show as much as it's a circus, though the really thrilling aspect of Jeannot Painchaud's production is the way in which the two forms blend. That and the sense of place, especially when the scene is set down in the docks. Rival groups confront one another though, as already noted, the confrontations tend to be short-lived; togetherness keeps breaking through. It's probably impossible to evoke any kind of youth-gang warfare onstage without waking echoes of West Side Story, and this show duly wakes them. When the dancing breaks out, though, it's very different. The choreographic style is hip hop, raised to a higher power. It seems spotty to begin with, but it gradually takes over. An environment that initially seems something either to oppose or to conquer becomes something to accept, celebrate and feel part of. The Trampowall, which seems to engage the entire company even if it factually doesn't, seals the deal. The evening starts out tepid and ends up supercharged.

- iD runs until Oct. 9. For tickets, call 416-870-8000 or visit ticketmaster.ca. robert.cushman@hotmail.com
