2010-10-09-it-s-mind-over-meta-hard-time:
The puppets are taking over. They're everywhere. They'll soon be pulling all our strings. There are, though, no strings on Hard Times, the newest and most ambitious show from Puppetmongers. The dolls in their adaptation of the Dickens novel are, in a departure for this troupe, glove puppets. They are supplemented by other devices; there is much use of silhouette and shadow-play, and the three human performers also appear in their own persons, full length and generally wearing masks. Much has had to be cut of course, even from Dickens' shortest and severest novel, but Chris Earle's adaptation and direction manage to present a remarkably complete account of its setting, ethos and principal characters.

Some of these characters are passed, vocally as well as physically, from one performer to another, and even from one convention to another. The puppetmongers themselves, David and Ann Holmes, make up two-thirds of the cast, and as actors they have their limitations. David's range seems confined to geniality, though this comes in very handy for the role of Mr. Sleary, the circus manager (here deprived of his lisp) who represents the forces of generosity and imagination that Dickens opposes to the pitiless aridity of utilitarian philosophy and the downright inhumanity of the Manchester mills and factories that are its practical expression. Ann seems to have no range at all; her delivery is, perhaps appropriately, wooden, and on the first night she often seemed uncertain of her lines. Non-acting is preferable, though, to bad acting; and the neutrality of her performance actually pays off in the central role of school superintendent Gradgrind, arch-advocate of Fact and arch-enemy of Fiction, whose principles stunt the emotional growth of his own children and who becomes a tragic figure because of it. An uninflected rendition of a studiedly dispassionate man balances out and is moving. Anand Rajaram, who has plenty of acting and comedy credits in his resume, overdoes the role of Gradgrind's crony Bounderby, the fraudulently self-made mill owner, who emerges as a mouthful of north-country vowels with hardly a consonant to be heard. But he compensates with brilliant portrayals of James Harthouse, the languid cad who finds himself in Parliament without the faintest notion why, and of Stephen Blackpool, the honest illiterate mill-hand who finds everything "a muddle" and who is indeed crushed between millstones: between his mates, who shun him when he refuses to join a strike, and Bounderby, who fires him anyway. Stephen's tangled love life has been sternly excised, and he emerges here as a genuine working-class hero, rather than the cardboard martyr he is in the book.

All these characters are among the walking masked. The younger Gradgrinds and Sissy Jupe, the circus orphan taken in as the Gradgrind maid and eventual moral conscience, are handpuppets who amusingly sprout extra inches before our eyes as they enter adolescence. Puppet as she is, Louisa, married lovelessly off to Bounderby, becomes a searching study in emotional blight; you feel she's lucky to get out of the story alive. Bounderby's genteel housekeeper Mrs. Sparsit sadistically imagines Louisa falling down a staircase of disillusion, and the image is here brought before us as a shadow-play upon a screen. The same device is briefly used to evoke a parliamentary meeting: one of the few moments at which Earle overplays the story's obvious, and devastating, contemporary relevance. Another is the provision of Mr. Sleary with-- rather too appropriately -- a ventriloquist's dummy to voice the subversive sentiments that Dickens himself inconveniently left unspoken. His method, a far more effective and imaginative one, was to let his enemies condemn themselves out of their own mouths, as in Bounderby's definition of his workers' ambition to be paid a decent wage as a desire to ride in a coach-and-four and be fed on turtle soup. (He dismisses Stephen -- in two senses -- as "another of the turtle-soupers.") It's also odd that Earle has the novel's subdivisions -- Part One: Sowing; Part Two, Reaping -- inscribed upon the stage but leaves out Part Three: Garnering, especially as the harvesting process is so powerfully presented. Dickens' central and recurrent insight, the equation of philistinism and oppression, comes over beautifully. The show takes time to get going, but once it's established its terms, it works wonderfully. And Earle, with this and the current Second City revue, has two of the best shows in Toronto to his credit.

Dickens could have taught some moderns a few things about political satire. Ali and Ali, who gave us a terrific show about reactions to terrorism some seasons ago, return with Ali and Ali: The Deportation Hearings, in which our two Middle Eastern comedians undergo the process described in the title. It's a dogged performance that carries on as if there has to be something funny here somewhere but never locates it. Since the Alis are interrupted in the course of presenting their own self-confessedly awful show about a President Osbama, there's a lot of meta-joking, the highlight being the anguished comment of Paul Sun-Hyung Lee ( "our added Mongolian") that they should have hired a fight-captain. He deserves better material. So really do the Alis themselves, Guillermo Verdecchia and Marcus Youssef, though sympathy is limited by the fact that they wrote the show with Camyar Chai (and Verdecchia directed it). Completing the cast as an investigating Mountie is Anita Majumdar, uncomfortably out of her element. The show gets good when it gets serious, but this happens very briefly and very near the end.

[title of show] is what two musical-theatre creators and their two actor-friends entered on a festival application form when asked for the title of their show. The finished piece depicts the evolution of a musical from those festival beginnings to the Vineyard Theatre, off-Broadway, to the Lyceum Theatre, on it. This is the exact trajectory pursued by the show about the show; it's all, again, very meta, and it's fun to imagine the frantic re-writing and re-existing that must have gone on as art and life panted to keep up with one another. There's fun, too, in the four performances of Angelwalk Theatre's Toronto production and in Tim French's neat direction. But without the original creators playing themselves, and with an uninvolving book and an undistinguished score, the show seems like pointless camp: narcissism at one remove.

- Hard Times runs through Oct. 16 at Theatre Passe Muraille Backspace; 416-504-7529, passemuraille.on.ca. Ali & Ali: The Deportation Hearings through Oct. 17 at the Factory Studio; 416-504-9971, factorytheatre.ca. [title of show] through Oct. 10 at Toronto Centre for the Arts; 416-872-1111, tocentre.com. robert.cushman@hotmail.com
2010-10-13-the-ballad-of-ol-blue-eyes-am:
There were three stories being told by turns in last Wednesdays premiere instalment of Michael Feinsteins American Songbook and they kept treading on one another's toes. One was a celebration of the career of Feinstein himself: The New York cabaret performer made spectacularly good, singing songs from the Golden Age of popular song, a.k.a. the pre-rock era, to sold-out concert audiences all over the U.S. and beyond. The second was a history of that music as it was performed in the 1950s, when most of the canonical songs had been written but when, thanks to them new-fangled long-playing records, more of them were being more widely heard than ever before. Finally, and most interestingly, there was an account of Feinstein's own activities as a collector and curator of this music. This last subject, combined with either of the other two, might have made a coherent program. The three together were too much and not enough.

The shows most powerful moment was a shot of Feinstein looking down on a Los Angeles freeway beneath which, he told us, MGM had buried troves of musical material, turning irreplaceable history into landfill. He looked and sounded genuinely angry: bracingly so, for a performer whose usual public persona is all smiles. Id like to think that it was PBS, rather than Feinstein himself, who was responsible for so much of the rest of the show being devoted to a worshipful portrait of the star on the road, seen largely through the eyes of his companions and manager. His travels and travails (jetlag, malfunctioning microphones) didn't seem much different from those of any other performer. (Though, did my eyes deceive me, or does he have a private plane?) I suspect that it's the same conventional TV demand for instant accessibility that has led Feinstein to tell the historical part of his story backwards; this episode is being followed by others concentrating on the 1940s and 1930s. So he had, for example, to spend time bringing us up to speed on who Cole Porter was, rather than letting that information emerge naturally, in chronological sequence.

The initial episode was called "Putting on the Tailfins." This, it was explained, being a metaphor for how Frank Sinatra updated the wartime and pre-war songs to the jet age: He burrowed into the lyrics while supercharging the rhythms. There was a lot about Sinatra, rather at the expense of other singers. Feinstein did pay passing tribute to his old friend Rosemary Clooney, whom he described as the greatest female singer of the 20th century. I happen to agree, but its an unorthodox opinion and one not really supported by the cheery 1950s footage of her that was on display; Clooney didnt become a great singer until the 1970s (when she was long past being a pop star).There was, amazingly, no mention of Ella Fitzgerald, whose succession of Songbook albums probably did even more to codify the repertoire than Sinatra's more personalized collections. What Feinstein didn't have time for was to explain in any detail what makes the songs good, or how Porter differs from Gershwin. I would guess that everybody was nervous of this turning into a music appreciation class--though thats exactly what public television should be presenting.

The Sinatra emphasis, however, dovetailed--or tailfinned -- with the current focus of Feinsteins career; he has a recent album called The Sinatra Project. He applies the Sinatra-Nelson Riddle sound to songs like Begin the Beguine that the collaborators might have done themselves but didn't. He also does songs from the actual Sinatra repertoire; he disclaims imitation, but it's hard to hear anything else when he sings Come Fly with Me, complete with original arrangement. Its ironic, since some 12 years ago Feinstein wrote a good semi-autobiographical book called Nice Work if You Can Get It in which he professed himself anything but a Sinatra devotee; he admired the voice and the technique but deplored the persona and the musical and lyrical liberties. It would be interesting to know how and when the conversion happened. Whatever: Feinstein makes a more convincing, less callow Sinatra stylist than, say, Michael Buble (the film even shoots him at Sinatra angles) and is altogether a more polished singer and showman than when he started out as a singer-pianist with a little-boy-lost approach to ballads. What does seem to have disappeared is the sly joy that this former archivist to Ira Gershwin used to take in introducing his audiences to unfamiliar lyrics to familiar songs. FromS Wonderful: "But say, what's all this dizziness?/ I thought that I came here on busi-ness."

That's as a performer. In his other life, he retains all his zeal for collecting and preserving, with greatly enhanced resources for pursuing it. We see him, in mask and gloves, sorting through the garbage of a deceased composer/arranger, or carting away boxes of sheet-music from a big-band singers bemused widow. Thats probably his most valuable work and it's where the program scores. He seems to have grown more eclectic with the years; the boy who grew up fixated on Gershwin when his friends were listening to The Beatles now celebrates not only Frank but Elvis -- to whom no disrespect, but he doesn't belong to the same tradition. Saluting him makes the program even more diffuse. Maybe, as it retreats further into the past in its remaining episodes, it will become more focused, less self-indulgent. I'll hold my breath.

- Michael Feinstein's American Songbook screens tonight at 8 p.m. on PBS. Visit pbs.orgfor details. rcushman01@gmail.com
2010-10-16-sisters-doing-it-to-themselve:
So far, this has been an exceptional new Toronto season. The Clockmaker, Billy Twinkle, Fernando Krapp, Through the Leaves, Blasted, Hard Times, plus Second City and Cirque Eloize, all within a month. There have been letdowns, too, of course, some of them severe. Though not a disaster, The New Electric Ballroom has, surprisingly, to be ranked among the disappointments.

The surprise stems from the fact that it is an Irish play, presented by a Canadian company, the weirdly named MackenzieRo, that specializes in such; and Irish drama, what with Martin McDonagh and Conor McPherson, has been riding high this last decade or so. Enda Walsh, the author of The New Electric Ballroom, has come in on a more recent wave; his play The Walworth Farce won high praise here when an actual Irish company brought it to World Stage, and I regret having missed it. This new one, though, despite some fine acting, seems cramped, mannered and contrived.

It starts with a woman standing with her back to us at a coastal cottage sink, delivering a high-velocity tirade whose only discernible specifics are that it sounds extremely bitter and makes recurrent use of the word "fish." It turns out that she is called Breda, and is the oldest of three sisters, all of whom are present on stage as the play begins and indeed never leave it. The others are named Ada and Clara: that's ABC, though the alphabetical order is teasingly different from their order of birth; Ada, who's pushing 40, is the youngest. She's also the only one who ever goes out; she works at a fish cannery. Fish is, so to speak, in the air: a recurring topic of conversation in the house (see above), the presumed economic mainstay of the surrounding community and the occasion for the only visits the sisters receive. These are from Patsy, a bashful youngish chap, who delivers the stuff on what seems to be a daily basis and lives in hopes of being asked to come in and sit down.

Breda and Clara haven't stepped outside the house in 40 years; not since they visited the New Electric Ballroom and were cruelly let down, both on the same night and both by the same guy: a local heartthrob of a singer, name of Doyle, who proved, like so many others, to be less of a charmer offstage than on. This means that they have had most of Ada's lifetime to warn her against men, which they have done by dressing up in their finery and ritually re-enacting the traumatic evening. We see them at it, and at some length. But either the warnings haven't taken or they're beginning to wear off. Ada is beginning to yearn for something else, and she thinks it might be Patsy. He thinks so, too, and finally invited to stop for tea, goes into an extended reverie of his own, complete with musical interlude. Maybe this strikes altogether too close to home; anyway it doesn't turn out to be the brightest of ideas. Like much of the play, it leaves the audience--this member of it, anyway -- asking "What exactly is going on?" and "Why should I care?" (Answer to both: I don't know.)

It's always tempting, when confronted by three theatrical sisters, to invoke Chekhov, but it doesn't seem too apposite here. Compared with his siblings, these three are zombies, who don't even want to go to Moscow, or Dublin, or anywhere. They bear more of a resemblance, and not just because they're Irish, to the wailing women of J.M. Synge's Riders to the Sea, or to their Hispanic cousins in Garcia Lorca's The House of Bernarda Alba, one of whom tried to break out from behind the shutters with tragic results. Or, coming back to the oul' country, they're like the enraged daughter of McDonagh's The Beauty Queen of Leenane, split and diluted three ways. Lorca's and McDonagh's heroines had a tyrannical mother to rebel against; Walsh's sisters are doing it, very efficiently, to themselves. In fact, the play is a, presumably unconscious, riff on Cinderella; the Ugly Sisters go to the ball, are disillusioned by the Prince, and take an especially cruel revenge on Cinders by warning her against following in their own dance-steps. And she believes them. And when she does meet Prince Charming, he smells of fish.

Stranger things have happened, and Walsh probably does have a personal vision. But he releases it here in an endless stream of words, words, words: some of them evocative, some funny (Patsy has a beaut of a line about haddock), but cumulatively numbing. To make one last Irish comparison, the play's conception of life as an endless loop of reminiscence makes Samuel Beckett ( Krapp's Last Tape especially) seem like stern, character-driven social realism. The characters here are just mouthpieces. Some of them, as played here, are very good mouthpieces. Rosemarie Dunsmore as Breda holds on to the mean ferocity she unleashes at the beginning, while thankfully letting up on the speed, while as the more pliable Clara, Sarah Dodd is quite spectacular, spinning her own memoir from hope to heartbreak and reliving every moment of it, while also keeping going a nice running gag about cake. She does suffer, in Autumn Smith's production, from having to give much of her performance in a low chair placed far downstage; it often looks, from the restrictive sightlines of the Tarragon Extra Space, as if she's left the stage, which would seem to contradict the play's point. But the two senior sisters' frozen faces at the end -- Dunsmore's a gorgon mask, Dodd's a doughy smile -- is quite a picture. Cathy Murphy's Ada doesn't have comparable definition, but Christopher Stanton's Patsy is a winning kind of loser; when he's left hovering, we share in his discomfort. Which I suppose is the intention; but a play that leaves its audience frustrated rather than moved has missed its aim. Like most plays these days, this one is short; like too many, it feels long.

- The New Electric Ballroom plays through Oct. 24 at the Tarragon Extra Space. Call 416-531-1827 or visit tarragontheatre.comfor tickets robert.cushman@hotmail.com

2010-10-18-an-afterlife-less-ordinary:
THEATRE REVIEW

Soulseek

Walter Centre, Toronto

Zorana Kydd, the power behind BirdLand Theatre, has put us all in her debt as the producer of two of the most exciting shows seen in Toronto in recent years ( Assassins and The Last Days of Judas Iscariot) and of another ( The Pillowman) that was substantial, if not quite in the same league. But there is another side to the ledger, dating back to Bird-Lands first two productions, which were of noted if not especially notable American plays ( The Ride Down Mount Morgan, Frankie and Johnny in the Clair de Lune), both of which featured Kydd as an actress, in roles for which she was under-equipped.

Those memories, much magnified, have now come back to haunt us in Ognen Georgievski's Soulseek, a new play in which Kydd once again stars and which seems to have been written especially for her. It's one of those occasions in which text and performance keep luring one another down into new circles of unhappiness.

That image was probably suggested to me by the play itself, which takes place in the underworld. Kydd plays an actress whose husband has died of cancer. She has either committed or is contemplating suicide, with the second possibility meaning that every-things a hallucination, which is by no means unlikely.

On arriving at the crossroads of the afterlife, shes greeted by Morpheus, best-known as the Greek god of sleep and still in the soporific business. ( I'm Morpheus he says, "I give you morphine." Well, that's etymologically fair enough.) His duties, though, seem to have extended to being Kydds guide through her posthumous existence; mixing mythologies, he plays Virgil to her Dante. For a slumber merchant hes very voluble and, in a performance by Andre Sills stronger on force than lucidity, very loud. Also snippy: He tells his charge, apparently speaking for the whole hellish and heavenly hierarchy, that he doesn't much like the arts. Nor does he think that she was very good at them. It seems that the traumatic event of her professional life was appearing in a production of The Tempest and blanking out on an important speech. As far as I could tell (neither actor is very distinct) she was playing Miranda, but the speech that gets quoted -- actually misquoted, twice -- is one of Prospero's: our revels now are ended no less. The humiliation apparently sent her fleeing into reality TV.

The play seems to be making up its own iconography as it goes along. Projected titles inform us that we have moved from one stage of the protagonists journey to the next, but its impossible to distinguish any progression or even any distinction, given that both script and performance have the texture of sludge, faintly leavened with whimsy. As much as she talks, we never learn enough about Kydd's character or her predicament to figure out why we're supposed to be interested. And at the risk of sounding xenophobic: Her Serbian accent doesnt do anything for her expressiveness.

What comes over is not pretentiousness, since one cant make out what the pretensions might be, so much as self-importance. A television news-reader brings reports of seismic ructions in the nether regions, but whether these are connected with Kydd's presence or just a coincidence is something else left undefined.

Talking of ferrymen: David Ferry is in the play too, sort of. His name in the program threw me a bit, since I didn't think that even an actor of his talent and energy could appear here while still giving his devastating performance of what King Lear called "unaccommodated man" in Blasted. Turns out hes only here on video, speaking presumably wise and comforting words as the heroines deceased partner. That means he's currently in two plays during which, though for rather different reasons, I sometimes found it hard to look at the stage. Even dead and phoning it in, he gives the liveliest performance in this one. Also technically, or technologically, present is Janet Porter as the TV anchor, who resembles Samantha Bee on an off-night. The video and audio effects, plus Camilla Koo's set, are the most striking things about Stefan Dzeparoski's production. Of the live human action he cannot, or at any rate does not, make any sense.

- Soulseek runs until Oct. 23 at the Walmer Centre, 188 Lowther Ave., Toronto. Visit artsboxoffice.caor call 416-504- 7529 for details. robert.cushman@hotmail.com

2010-10-19-office-case-mad-men-wraps-up-:
The play-out music for the season finale of Mad Men was Sonny and Cher's glutinous 1965 hit I Got You Babe. That tied in very nicely with what Don Draper said, early in the episode, about teenagers being sentimental: "Have you heard their music?" He was talking to the bigwigs of the American Cancer Society, pitching about a possible campaign to keep teenagers from smoking. Which, on Don's return to the office, allowed Roger to get off a casual one-liner awesome even by his standards: "Did you get cancer?"

And with everyone at Sterling Cooper Draper Pryce smoking as much as ever, Roger's joke could be blackly funnier than he meant it to be.

Like any long-running drama with depth to it, Mad Men is an echo chamber. That's true over the series as a whole, and within individual episodes. A few weeks ago, Roger told Joan, carrying his baby, that if she wanted to go ahead and have it, her husband, Greg, stationed in Vietnam, would never know; plenty of GIs in the Second World War had consented to be fooled the same way. This season damn near concluded with Joan telling Greg over the phone how nicely her pregnancy was progressing and him lacking it up. That she hadn't in fact had an abortion was one of the most satisfying revelations of the season. Not morally satisfying, necessarily, but dramatically: it was both surprising and believable. It also means that Joan, generally one of the more honest characters, is going to sail into the next season living a lie. Chances are that Roger's urbanity will take a hit as well.

A closer internal rhyme: Don is bequeathed the engagement ring of the real Don Draper, the dead man whose identity he stole and whose wife he came to love, with the injunction "you shouldn't play around with this." And he uses it to propose to Megan, the secretary he hardly knows, which is playing around on a grand scale. Judging from the traffic online, this last narrative development has made the episode the most hated thing on television since the ending of The Sopranos. It's been denounced as soap opera.

There probably is something of soap opera in Mad Men, in the sense that we get involved with the characters as if they were real people, and start handicapping their futures. Real soap, though, depends on shock and predictability, as opposed to logic and surprise; it also wants you to love or hate everybody. Mad Men is being condemned for not being soap-opera enough: for Don not behaving as people would like him to behave. He has continually taken one step forward and then the same step back, and now he's done it again. Having told his previous lover some of the truth about himself, he's retreated into renewed cover-up. If Jon Hamm's performance in the proposal scene seemed, for once, less than convincing, it's because Don was hardly convincing himself; he was behaving, in fact, like a sentimental teenager. The season's closing image found him waking up next to his fiancee and looking longingly through a window. That engagement may not even make it to the altar.

Don's a fitting leader for a cast of characters who cheat -- themselves mainly -- and suffer and survive. (Some viewers were betting on whether Roger would commit suicide by the end of the season. He's still there.) The actual business of advertising has mostly faded into the background, along with the '60s historical bulletins, and the show is the better for it. This season, the best ever, was at its weakest in a caper episode, in which plot displaced character. Its best scenes have been the brief one of Joan at the abortion clinic, a miracle of economy and subtext; and, longer but equally suggestive, the long alcohol-fuelled rapprochement of Don and Peggy, the heroine and the anti-hero, the professional equals who, in a better world or perhaps an alternate universe, would be made for one another. Even in this one, they both know it, and that unacknowledged ache, breaking surface at long, judiciously spaced intervals, is the show's secret motor, the prime example of what makes it good. Soap wouldn't know from subtext.

2010-10-21-that-many-apples-a-day-may-re:
It's no great surprise that The List, by Jennifer (fated to be known as "no relation") Tremblay, should have won a Governor General's Award before even being staged. The play is a monologue, and monologues read better, or at least easier, than texts with a multiplicity of voices. It deals with, or at least invokes, serious-sounding subjects like loneliness and alienation. It is, in fact, competently written. It is also, in its Englishlanguage premiere -- a joint venture by CanadianStage and Nightwood Theatre -- competently presented. It still seems pointless. Or, funnily enough, listless.

I don't mean the play itself has no point. I mean there is no particular reward for the audience in sitting through it. A character billed as The Woman confronts us from her kitchen. She's a wife, and the mother of three, who has moved from the city to the country in the mistaken belief that this would let her spend more time with her husband. She didn't count on his having to commute. So she stays home and cooks and keeps house and tends to her children; she also makes, and compulsively recites, lists of all the tasks that this entails. She looks down on her bumpkin neighbours, and for that reason hardly ever leaves the house.

The one time she did, somebody got under her guard: another wife and mother, named Caroline, whose life and home were as messy as The Woman's are neurotically neat. They became unlikely friends. Caroline became ill, and asked The Woman to do something for her and put it on her list. The Woman, it seems, obliged with the list-making part but never got around to the doing. Caroline died in hospital. The Woman can't shake -- doesn't seem to want to shake -- the feeling that it was her fault.

So this might be a play about a broken trust (file under Guilt) or it might be about domestic self-exploitation (file under Control-Freakiness and Agoraphobia). Obviously it wants to be about both. But the causal link between The Woman's forgetfulness and Caroline's death is of the thinnest, so we merely wonder why the protagonist is beating up on herself and on us.

Thin, too, is the connection between this and the rest of the play. There is some grim humour to be found in The Woman's repeated recitation of her daily agenda, and Allegra Fulton, whose performance is technically flawless, expertly mines it. She does the same for the painful suspense, and even more painful certainty, surrounding the discovery and the aftermath of Caroline's death.

The play makes an efficient enough job of the nuts-and-bolts narrative. There are some puzzling things, though, about Kelly Thornton's production. The gleaming kitchen that Denyse Karn has designed is enviably, even superhumanly, scrapless and spotless. Nothing disturbs its purity but apples, which The Woman is mechanically slicing at curtain-rise. At a later point, she opens the fridge to disclose more apples, rows and rows of them. And that's all, apart from a profusion of identical jars, also in rows, that may very well contain apple sauce. If this display is to be taken literally, it suggests that The Woman's family is in imminent danger of succumbing to malnutrition: which would seem at odds with everything else in the play. Or maybe it's meant to be symbolic, an image for the monotony and repetition of her life. There seem here to be at least three possible interpretations of the old adage about a woman's work never being done.

Or The Woman's work. Calling her that reads, as such labels always do, like an attempt to blackmail the audience into feeling guilty about her situation, while absolving the author of the responsibility to get specific. It also feels like cheating: She can hardly be Everywoman if she has a friend who actually has a name; and if Caroline could get christened, then why couldn't she?

The program reveals that the author is working on a sequel -- something to which playwrights called Tremblay seem especially prone -- that will show her heroine in later life. It's to be called The Merry-go-round, and I can't say that my heart is racing. It's hard to get excited over the further adventures of somebody to whom you haven't been introduced in the first place.

- The List runs until Nov. 6. For tickets, call 416-368-3110 or visit canadianstage.com. robert.cushman@hotmail.com

2010-10-23-home-is-where-the-heart-break:
Joseph Ziegler is a heroic actor, and also a hugely sympathetic one: not such a common combination. This makes his Willy Loman in Soulpepper's Death of a Salesman (which I saw at a preview) an overpowering experience. He was already burrowing into my heart in his first scene; he had broken it, but also lifted it, long before his last.

That first scene, which shows Willy the travelling sales rep returning to his Brooklyn home in the small hours, having suffered a panic attack on the road, is played, in Albert Schultz's production, very quietly. Willy is dog-tired, his wife, Linda, is consumed with anxiety but trying her considerable best to be supportive, and both of them are trying not to wake their two grown sons in the bedroom upstairs. Even with his voltage down, his hair grey, and his body in an unaccustomed state of slump, Ziegler has bounce. Willy, as Arthur Miller drew him, is above all else a volatile creature; he keeps turning on the same dime. When we meet him, he's trying to keep desperation at bay, mostly by denial. But the play's flashbacks reveal that he's always been like that. An optimist by culture and profession, he's always feared that he might be missing out, even when he and his family were at their happiest. (This seems, counting back from the play's 1949 date stamp, to have been during the Depression. It's in the postwar boom that their world falls apart.) Some of Willy's mood swings are almost funny; one moment he's admonishing his son Biff to act serious in a job interview, the next he's advising him to crack a few jokes. Ziegler plays each moment to the hilt, lingering on none. Most moving perhaps is his rock-bottom humiliation when his boss, Howard ( "business is business") fires him; most powerful is the wrath he turns on his sons in their subsequent meeting at a restaurant; most terrible is the joy that suffuses him when, screening out everything the boy has actually said, he takes refuge in the love that shines through Biff's anger. It's a joy that leads him to commit suicide for the sake of the insurance. Well, not just for that: Miller himself said that Willy's motives were inextricably mixed, and some of the play's stature comes from making all the options both tangible and tantalizing.

It connects with economic tensions that are persistent, certainly now, and family tensions, especially father-son tensions, that are eternal. Nancy Palk has all the gentleness and all the fury of Linda, who's both appalled onlooker and tortured participant; high among this production's moments of electrifying rages is her "then make Charley your father, Biff" delivered from the door of the totemic family refrigerator. She also, through beauifully sharp timing, gets one perfectly appropriate laugh that I've never heard in this play before. Ari Cohen's Biff, the least defined character as written, comes superbly into focus when we scroll back to his crucial moment of disillusion with his dad; he's a heartbroken boy who gives birth to the passionate shell of a man that explodes in the concluding scenes. Tim Campbell's Happy, all set to follow in his father's footsteps, is an all-American glamour boy to rank with the one he gave us in Who's Afraid of Virginia Woolf ?, though I don't think the production needs to give him its final moment; the point's been made, and the play isn't about Happy. Michael Hanrahan breathes Brooklyn as Charley, the charitably ironic neighbour. Soulpepper academicians fill out the cast to great effect: Gregory Prest as Bernard, graduating from geekhood to sober young maturity; Brendan Wall as Howard, embarrassed but impervious; Ins Choi as Stanley the waiter, wishing he was dead; and Raquel Duffy as the woman from Willy's past, first glimpsed as a ghost in a mirror. The only flaws in Schultz's direction are visual; Lorenzo Savoini's set crams two levels into one, promotes traffic problems, and forces the epilogue into a straight line. Otherwise, acting and

production are rock-solid, with Ziegler's Willy a triumph of character acting, raised to the highest power.

There's another fine American family, but rising rather than falling, in Soulpepper's other space, which now houses A Raisin in the Sun, revived from two years ago. The creaks in Lorraine Hansberry's play are more noticeable the second time around, but so are its strengths and those of Weyni Mengesha's production. The one major newcomer is Bahia Watson who makes the aspiring doctor-daughter both sweetly capricious and bracingly bright; the play has nearly as much to do with gender issues as with racial ones. Charles Officer's Walter Lee now smoulders as powerfully as he explodes; Abena Malika as his wife movingly suffers and passionately protests; and, dominating all as the matriarch with the South still in her, Alison Sealy-Smith continues to amaze with vocal and emotional depths beyond any she has previously sounded. This play, in this production, doesn't break our hearts; in a way that's neither shameless nor shameful, it warms them.

- Death of a Salesman and A Raisin in the Sun run through Nov. 13 at the Young Centre for the Performing Arts. Call 416-866-8666 or visit soulpepper.cafor ticket information. robert.cushman@hotmail.com

2010-10-26-meta-metamorphoses:
THE ANDERSEN PROJECT

Bluma Appel Theatre, Toronto

---

Robert Lepage, the French-Canadian theatrical magician, was commissioned by the Danish government to create a show about their country's favourite literary son, Hans Christian Andersen. Uncertain of how to approach the subject, he hit on building it around the character of a French-Canadian artist, commissioned to create a show about the selfsame writer, and uncertain of how to approach it. The result is a consummate piece of stagecraft, whose only flaw is that it never quite connects with its ostensible subject. Rather, it dances around it. But it's an intoxicating dance.

The joy of Lepage's work is that it manages to be both high-tech and actor-based. In terms of performance, The Andersen Project is a one man show, the one man being Yves Jacques, who plays three principal roles, and is as impressive at embodying each of them as he is dazzling at switching between them. Like his director, he projects a kind of insouciant shyness, daring you to believe what he is bringing off and never breaking a sweat while doing it. All three of his characters are in some way beleagured. Frederic, the commissioned writer, is a rock lyricist who's never sure why he was given the job in the first place. The finished piece is to be presented at the Paris Opera, and he comes to the city of lights to work on it. There's an odd similarity here to the hysterically unhistorical Danny Kaye movie in which the storyteller -- he's Hans Christian Andersen; Andersen, that's he -- comes to wonderful Copenhagen and gets his heart broken. There's a more intentional link to one of Andersen's own lesser-known stories, The Dryad, in which a tree-nymph sacrifices all for one day in Paris. This is the story on which Frederic, to the bemusement of his patrons, chooses to base his own homage. The dryad's tale is spread out across the evening, told to us in charming, wistful increments, as a cross between a puppet show and an animated cartoon. But much of the time it's forgotten about, and it never seems all that relevant when it's remembered.

Lepage seems more interested in Andersen's own biography, and especially in his sexuality or lack of it. He seems to have been, for practical purposes, asexual; but that doesn't mean that he doesn't have pangs. These are reflected in the play's own characters, at least two of whom are having trouble with their love lives. Frederic has broken up with his girlfriend back in Montreal, and obviously regrets it. He spends a lot of time on the phone with her, and finally has a rude if not unexpected awakening. At the same time, he's being double-talked and double-crossed by Arnaud, the Parisian opera director, who has his own betrayal problems. A flat-sharing arrangement has deposited Frederic in an apartment above a peep-show emporium, and when Arnaud calls on him for meetings, he finds the location reawakening instincts that he has struggled to suppress and that are derailing his marriage. We also meet, after a fashion, the peep show's janitor, a Moroccan immigrant who has to mop up after people like Arnaud. Though we aren't privy to his inner life, it's a fair bet that he, too, has his frustrations; and we see him expressing them through his secret life as a subway graffiti artist. (Enchantingly staged, by the way.) The nearest thing we see to a loving relationship, though it too seems somewhat one-sided, is between Frederic and the bitch -- I mean that literally -- whom he has inherited along with the apartment. At one point he takes her to a dog psychiatrist, though she seems very free from hang-ups. As Frederic rather bitterly says, how come he never gets laid when she does all the time?

Jacques plays all his roles, silent or voluble, with equal virtuosity; Arnaud, when he gets going, is a nonstop talker; he starts the show hilariously by apologizing for a cancelled performance of La boheme (it's been struck by a strike) and later delivers a breakneck broken-English oration whose impact may even have been increased by the fact that I couldn't understand a word of it. Around him, Lepage builds an extraordinary -- but never overpowering -- production, in which the actor becomes part of the desiogn without ever being swamped by it. No director uses projections this inventively or -- pardoxically -- this unobtrusively, to the point where you can hardly tell where they leave off and the more solid scenery starts. He can whisk us, magically but also very simply, on a subway train (he's always been great at transportation); he can take delight the in the old-fashioned drapes of an opera house; he can find magic in the grim line of cubicles at a porno theatre. Intellectually, The Andersen Project may not add up. Theatrically, all its parts make a perfect fit.

- The Andersen Project runs to Oct. 30. Visit canadianstage.comor call 416-368-3110 for tickets and information. robert.cushman@hotmail.com

2010-10-29-brawn-broads-booze-boardwalk-:
You should have seen the Atlantic Ocean in the old days.

Burt Lancaster, delivering one of my favourite lines from one of my favourite films, Atlantic City, directed by Louis Malle and written by John Guare. Boardwalk Empire shows us the Atlantic Ocean, and the slice of New Jersey adjoining it, as it was in the old days of the 1920s: Prohibition days, which were at least some of the days that Lancaster's character, an ex-gangster, would have been referring to. And the ocean does indeed look good, as does the city: good and bad perhaps. Boardwalk Empire itself looked, in anticipation, almost too good.

It's a lavish, teeming, near mythic period setting that television has left almost untouched since the 1960s, which gave us an entertaining but generic music-drama series called, inevitably, The Roaring Twenties. Booze and jazz and some very famous gangsters. Terence Winter, of The Sopranos, as head writer, Steve Buscemi in the leading role, and Martin Scorsese as executive producer and even as director. He did in fact direct the pilot, which in its expansiveness and its expensiveness was like a scaled down Scorsese movie. The lavishness has persisted in subsequent episodes, though the breathtaking visual style has diminished; the last we saw of it was in a panoramic descending shot of a mobsters funeral at the start of Episode 2. But if the spectacle has diminished, the drama has sharpened.

Winters writing in the first episode was surprisingly flat-footed and over-explicit, perhaps due to the necessity of establishing everybody. A racketeers' summit, Atlantic City hosting delegates from New York and Chicago, had the participants making, in Max Beerbohm's phrase, remarks highly characteristic of themselves," and still didnt manage to clarify who was who and what they wanted. A climactic shootout was confusing at its beginning, intentionally, and at its end, probably not. Later scripts have seldom reached a Sopranos level of wit and complexity (or that of Mad Men or Deadwood or The Wire) but they have become increasingly compelling.

Everything turned around on St. Patricks Day. Buscemi's character, Nucky Thompson, is the treasurer of Atlantic City, and at the centre of every money-making operation in town. He's also Irish-American, and Episode 5 of a 12-week season (were currently at the exact halfway mark) showed him partying with his compatriots, or at least with the rich and powerful among them.

It isnt a task he relishes -- neither sentiment nor patriotism are high among his priorities -- but he knows what has to be done and he's very good at doing it. The show paints a broad canvas, but it also knows that one of the benefits of spaciousness is that you don't have to include all the elements every time.

So it lingered on the celebratory banquet, the booze and the blarney freely flowing, followed by fisticuffs, and all topped off with a raid by the Feds, itself the culmination of another carefully developed plot thread.

Meanwhile in Chicago, Nuckys former protege Jimmy Darmody (Michael Pitt) was taking playful knocks about his own Irish ancestry from his new Italian buddy, the still up-and-coming Al Capone. Capones boss was engaged in turf warfare with Chicago's own Irish gang, who celebrated less playfully by cutting up the face of Jimmy's prostitute girlfriend, who subsequently shot herself. Which led in Episode 6 to a bloody coup by the Italians, mastermindedbyJimmywhose backgroundincludesPrinceton, for brains, and the First World War, for killing. He told Nucky early on that hed been deadened inside by the things hed seen in France, which struck me as unpersuasively self-conscious writing. But Jimmy, and Pitt's performance, are coming on, no question.

Buscemi is fascinating, though as anti-heroes go, he may be too little anti and too much hero. We hear about him doing terrible things, but what we actually see is him being clever, charming and racially unprejudiced. He had two great lines in the first episode, both impeccably delivered. One, to an underling who failed to understand "A rose by any other name, was Read a f--king book;" the other, to a lady who'd promised to name her own son Enoch, was, "You couldnt be so cruel." The lady, who has read plenty of books, is Margaret (Kelly Macdonald), a first-generation Irish immigrant and temperance advocate, whos a political challenge to Nucky and also an erotic one. She's the most compelling character on the show, and theirs is the relationship that ultimately drives it. They sealed their deal at the close of St. Patrick's Day, rounding off that episode very satisfyingly but still leaving plenty of room for complications. One of them is Lucy, Nuckys resident mistress, who throws her body at him like a weapon, which he finds exhausting but hard to resist. More nookie for Nucky.

Margaret is also a lust object for Van Halen (Michael Shannon), the prohibition enforcer whose zeal for his job approaches mania, some of it homicidal. Equally powerful are Michael Stuhlbargs implacable New York boss Arnold Rothstein and Stephen Graham's Capone, deglamourized as a brutally cocky punk but also humanized as the father of a deaf son.

There's more, including a team of midget boxers; the show is spinning enough plates, and skillfully enough, to ensure a second season. It makes a pair with Treme, this years other entry in the HBO major series stakes: both about real-life mythical cities, Treme stronger on texture, Boardwalk on narrative drive, and neither as yet combining those qualities in the way of cables very best.

Both shows, however, surpass all the competition in their music. Boardwalk's score, mixing new and vintage performances, is supervised by a musician, Vince Giordano, who really knows this stuff. One very impressive point: The show begins in 1920, the year the U.S. went dry, and all the songs heard on the soundtrack or in the action were written in that year or earlier, no cheating. There's been one lapse: Last week's episode included A Good Man Is Hard to Find, which my reference books date in 1927. Thematically, though, it could hardly be more appropriate.

- Boardwalk Empire airs Sundays at 9 p.m. on HBO Canada.

2010-10-30-to-woop-woop-and-beyond-prisc:
As you may have heard, Priscilla Queen of the Desert doesn't have a title character, it has a title bus. In this vehicle three Australian drag queens, Tick, Bernadette and Felicia, make their way from Sydney, where they live, to Alice Springs, where they have a booking. It's also where Tick, who's having a Cage aux Folles type of storyline, hopes to be reunited with his son, though in this case, the son is not a young adult but an adoring six-year-old.

It's a long way from Sydney to Alice -- 3,000 kilometres according to the program -- and there's not a lot that a stage show, as opposed to the movie that Priscilla originally was, can do to show us the variations in the territory between. The authors, Stephan Elliott and Allan Scott (adapting their own screenplay), settle for showing us signposts bearing such outlandish, or outbackish, names as Broken Hill, Woop Woop (invented) and Coober Pedy (real) and having the characters make jokes about them. Three times, our odd triple get off the bus to patronize a local bar and three times they hit trouble. The level of hostility they encounter, and the strength of their reaction to it, increases each time. At one point the bus gets defaced by hillbilly gay bashers, and has to be spray-painted new. A musical has to pass the time somehow. Still, all this stopping and bar-hopping gets to feel repetitive.

That the show stays triumphantly on the road is due to performances that are excellent, costumes that are splendiferous and musical numbers that are, if nothing else, lively. The production, already a big success in Australia and Britain, is trying out in Toronto prior to Broadway, and its cast is mainly American, with a couple of token Canadians and one hold-over from down under. (The script is full of lines like that but not nearly as mild.) The Aussie is Tony Sheldon, and he's here because he is, in all probability, irreplaceable. He plays Bernadette, a post-op transsexual whose glory days as headliner in a troupe called Les Girls are now far in the past, and who, at the start, is about to bury her--pronouns are tricky in this context -- late, or latest, stud. She's brave and sharp-tongued and vulnerable, a king of queens, and in the course of the journey she finds true love. Sheldon plays her with superb comic and pathetic timing, has one great spoken moment of surprise basso profundo and goes through his numbers with physical and vocal panache, shot through with delicacy. This is his show.

It comes damn near being Will Swenson's as well. He plays Tick, the so-to-speak straight man of the group; he too is both a flamboyant musical performer and a strong, sensitive and sensible actor. Against all odds (and the production, towards the end, stacks them pretty high), he establishes his love for his son as moving and unsentimental. Nick Adams, the final member of the star trio, suffers from the fact that Felicia, real name Adam and with the pop version of a Madonna complex, is in his unrelenting bitchiness nearly as irritating as the other two keep saying he is, but he's technically fine and he gets his touching moments, too. Near-equal billing goes, deservedly, to C. David Johnson as a gruff but tender mechanic whom they encounter in the desert, just when they and the show need him the most, and who is bowled over at meeting a former Les Girl. On the first night Johnson, one of Canada's own, endeared himself even further by the unflappable way in which he greeted a malfunctioning piece of scenery that effectively truncated his one and only song while bringing the whole event to a temporary halt. Way to get the audience on your side, show: seriously. The only other homeboy on the team is the redoubtable Thom Allison, so underused that I failed even to spot him.

This is a jukebox musical, using pre-existing songs. There's no good reason for this but, considering what most new scores are like these days, especially for shows like this, it may not be such a bad decision. It even includes one real song, A Fine Romance, lip-sunk by Sheldon, reprised by Johnson, together with a few almosts, like I Say a Little Prayer and the shamelessly irresistible I Will Survive, here rather cheekily used to send the audience on its way. The rest is mostly disco and sub-disco. There's a great moment when Tick sings "someone left the cake out in the rain" which someone has in fact just done, though it's spoiled when he proceeds to do MacArthur Park in what seems like its entirety. Admittedly, he does it accompanied by a chorus dressed as cupcakes, which is something to see. So are all of Tim Chappel's and Lizzy Gardiner's costumes, which range from giant Motown mock-ups via animated paintbrushes to a cross-section of Australian wildlife. Simon Phillips' production may not always be tasteful but it's certainly spectacular. It's also good-hearted. The program lists what may be a record number of producers, from Bette Midler to David Mirvish, with 18 people or entities in between. They obviously took their duties seriously. Or, as C. David observed during that opening-night snafu, "they spent a lot of money on the bus."

- To Jan. 2 at Princess of Wales Theatre. For tickets, visit mirvish.comor call 416-872-1212.

2010-11-05-best-judged-by-its-cover:
As befits a show about a photographer, Studies in Motion looks very good. Its subject is the life and work of Eadweard Muybridge, who in the late 19th century used multiple cameras, placed strategically along a route, to capture the movement of human and other bodies. You might say he invented the motion picture, and when the actual movies came along, he was their forebear.

Kim Collier, who this week was awarded the Siminovitch Prize for direction, begins her production with an extended, invigorating demonstration sequence. An ensemble of 11 actors run, walk, skip, jump and tumble across the stage in dizzying, seemingly endless succession. It's hypnotic because of the skill and endurance involved; also because it's distanced. This turns out be typical; we peer at much of the show through a scrim, while watching the actors disport themselves on a set laid out like a grid. Crystal Pite is the choreographer and Robert Gardiner the set, lighting and video designer. It's hard to be surprised any more by the things projections can do, but it's still possible to be impressed, and the work of this team is exceptionally impressive.

The production comes from the Electric Company Theatre of Vancouver, which originated it in 2006 and revived it in 2009. The present touring incarnation, which I saw at a preview in Edmonton, is headed to Canadian Stage in Toronto. As performance art it's fine, if inevitably monotonous; how many times do you want to watch the same performers propelling themselves across the same area? It would help of course if we knew and cared about the people concerned, but that's where Studies in Motion falls down. It isn't just a show, it's a play; and a badly written one.

Kevin Kerr's script is subtitled The Hauntings of Eadweard Muybridge, though apart from presenting some of its events in the wrong order, it's less imaginative than that might suggest. We first see the protagonist falling foul of Britain's Royal Society, whose members patronizingly inform him that they "keep abreast" of new scientific developments, and slap themselves on their chests to emphasize the point. (That's about as witty as the evening gets.) He finds a home for his research at the University of Pennsylvania and, though he runs up against the regulation amount of bureaucratic interference, he does manage to carry much of his

project through. In his dealings with his volunteer subjects he can amusingly anticipate some of the frustrations of later pioneers of spectacle, especially in the perennial problems associated with getting actors to act natural. Or in this case to walk natural. Otherwise all we learn about him is that he's a fanatical martinet with a beard, and that his first name, despite its alarming spelling, is pronounced just like that of any other Edward.

As for his private life, we see most of that in flashback, though it's a confusingly long time before the chronology becomes clear. Muybridge was married, and his devotion to his work, plus your standard genius' indifference to other people's feelings, led him to neglect his wife. So she took up with a smooth-talking cad introduced as "the theatre critic of the Post" (I give you my word), a position apparently so remunerative that its occupant could afford to pay an even lowlier hack to do the actual reviewing part for him. Carnage ensued; and when Muybridge describes the details (at his trial, and I'm not giving any more away than can be deduced from the program notes) he seems mostly concerned with the different types of physical movement that were involved. Either we're asked to believe that this gave him the inspiration for his life's work or, more likely, it's a painfully arch attempt to tie the play's strands together. Back in the present tense, Muybridge and his routine are periodically disturbed by messages about a boy at an orphanage. These aren't nearly as suspenseful as seems to have been intended -- in fact, we forget about them -- but they do lead to a final meeting that's much the best written scene in the play; it has some delicacy to it, and allows the protagonist to appear as something other than a tyrannical nonentity.

Otherwise it's scissors and paste, picturesquely presented. Muybridge's preference for photographing nude bodies, of both sexes, brings down the threat of censorship, which is elaborately built up and then abruptly and inexplicably dropped. (Whatever happened, happens in the intermission.) A Muybridge assistant, who obviously adores him, spends most of the play resisting the idea of posing naked herself, but finally agrees to do it. A friend who has no such inhibitions has an amusing scene in which she has to keep donning and doffing her robe due to a prolonged technical hitch. Andrew Wheeler's acting in the title role consists of deploying a deep voice to match his facial hair. The rest of the cast do all that is required of them, and are probably capable of more; when somebody, in a scene set in a theatre, says "let's pretend we're real actors," it sounds like a very good idea. For all its visual sheen, the production is strangely sullen. And the play belies its title; it's essentially static .

- Studies in Motion runs until Nov. 14 at Edmonton's Citadel Theatre. For more information, call 780-425-1820. The production runs from Nov. 22 to Dec. 18 at Toronto's Bluma Appel Theatre. For more information, visit canadianstage.com. robert.cushman@hotmail.com

The two title characters in Lenin's Embalmers are Vladimir Vorobiov, a prickly genius, and Boris Zbarsky, a twisty politician, though political by instinct rather than profession. They are, and historically were, the two scientists charged with the duty of keeping the body of the deceased leader of the Russian Revolution free from rot and fit for public view: not for just an hour, not for just a day, not for just a year, but always. This was a tall, indeed unprecedented order, but they met it. And, life being what it is, they suffered for it later.

Vern Thiessen's play about them starts with a joke about the Gulag. It then gives us Lenin dying, Stalin and Trotsky staking their claims, Stalin winning, and Trotsky fleeing,

all at farcical speed. This is in accordance with the established tradition, which I cannot logically defend but intuitively support, that stories about Stalinism can be funny in a way that stories about Nazism can't. (Yes, there's The Producers, but that's set a long time after the fact.) Stalin wants to preserve Lenin's legend in order to shore up his own. This will not be news to students of the period, though they might be surprised by the play's insistence that Trotsky got ice-picked while Lenin was still fresh in his grave. Or would have been, under normal circumstances.

Both Vladimir (not Lenin, the other one) and Boris were Jews, which accounts for their play being presented by the Harold Green Jewish Theatre Company. It also gives an extra edge to Stalin's animus towards them, though that isn't much explored, and it's not as if Stalin's animuses (is that a word?) ever took much encouraging anyway. For a time, he seems genial towards the embalmers, even pinning medals on them; then he turns, apparently because a drunken Vladimir has kissed him on the mouth while being decorated. He asks to see their files, which is tantamount to a death sentence.

So the play's a cartoon, an intended black farce. But it's jokey without being witty, and its development becomes an exercise in automatic writing. There are these techniques, there's this predestined historical ending (foreseeable even without foreknowledge), and the characters move along on tram tracks. There's a cross-talking pair of secret policemen, who fill in as other supernumeraries. There are three women all called Nadya, a point the play with incorrigible waggishness points out, one of whom keeps talking about her lovers, and who predictably betrays her main squeeze in ways that go beyond the sexual; another of the Nadyas is equally predictably loyal to hers. (Mrs. Lenin is the third Nadya.) The embalmers themselves fight, reconcile and fight again.

The play tells us nothing about the period, or about life in a terror state, that we haven't been told before. The only revelations concern the technical details of the embalming, a process that we see the duo actually carrying out in an ingenious if protracted mime sequence at the end of the first act. Otherwise Geoffrey Brumlik's production appears to be doing what the script asks of it, which is to be clownish and blatant and out front, though some of the supporting cast do this with less finesse than would seem desirable. There is a bit of tension, and even surprise, in the later stages; Vladimir's an ex-Tsarist and Boris an ex-Marxist, and we wonder which of the two will crack and inform on the other first. (The Cheka's techniques seem unhistorically mild, but that's probably part of the joke.) Hardee Lineham, an underused actor who emerges periodically from the shadows to give another excellent performance, gives one of them as Vladimir, angry and entitled, though he's more powerful sober than he is drunk. Martin Julien has less definition as Boris. Janine Theriault plays all the Nadias, and seems most comfortable as the shyest one. If ever an actor was born to play Stalin (I mean that as a compliment) it's the great David Fox, and he sort of delivers here; all the same, he's hemmed in by writing that mainly has him coming on and ordering people's deaths, apparently because it's expected of him. That he does it with an overlay of casual bumbling is obviously meant to add to the horror. It doesn't.

- Lenin's Embalmers runs through Nov. 21 at the Al Green Theatre. Visit stlc.comor call 416-366-7723 for ticket and show time information. robert.cushman@hotmail.com

2010-11-09-war-peace-and-the-caricatures:
THE GREAT WAR

Cameron House, Toronto

---

The First World War keeps on being fought. Soulpepper has revisited it twice this year, with Oh What A Lovely War and with Billy Bishop (who will be going to war again next year). Video Cabaret, working its way through its mordant comic-strip history of Canada, have now reached 1914-18 for the second time. Or really the third, since The Great War, first staged by Video-Cab in 1993, was revived earlier this year and was such a success that it's now been re-revived.

The success is deserved. I've been known to carp at VideoCab's reliance on caricature, not because I doubt its skill or even its accuracy, but because an evening of sneering and sniggering can, and sometimes has, become monotonous. This instalment begins as if it might tempt that same old law of diminishing returns, but it bucks it. The basic technique is the same: seven unbelievably quick-changing actors in a succession of brief black-out sketches. But the subject-matter, and the concentrated time frame it inhabits, give the production a unity that some of its predecessors have lacked. Michael Hollingsworth's direction is as pointed and inventive as ever, Andy Moro's lighting as devastatingly precise, Astrid Janson and Sarah Armstrong's costumes as over-the-top gorgeous. And Hollingsworth's script may be his best ever. It's certainly, in my experience, the most layered.

It starts on the Canadian home front. The Duke of Connaught, Governor General of Canada, surveys the coming carnage from the privileged point of view of everybody's uncle. England's king, Russia's emperor, Germany's kaiser: they're all his relatives. Sobering to realize that all those lives were sacrificed in Europe's last dynastic struggle -- "a family quarrel" as the Duke blithely observes. The Duke's Duchess is German, and makes no secret of her sympathies. In fact, her role consists of chanting "Deutschland! Deutschland!" in an aggressively manic way that eventually leads to her being discreetly deported; I was bothered at the time by characterization that seemed simplistic even by VidCab standards but, on reflection, maybe not. Canada does its colonial duty, under the auspices of Prime Minister Sir Robert Borden, while Henri Bourassa does his apoplectic best to keep Quebec out of it. Everybody acts (I'm referring to the characters, not the performers) self-centredly, and many of them appallingly: par for this particular course.

And we meet the private soldiers who suffer for their superiors' mistakes and who are presented, also as expected, with far greater sympathy. What distinguishes this production, however, is that there's a middle ground. It's occupied by two young officers who start out rivals for the same woman and who then, after she's chosen one of them, are comrades at Ypres, Vimy, Passchendaele and Amiens. One (Paul Braunstein) loses his previously permanent smile when he gets his face blown off. The other (MacFyfe, who also, and in complete contrast, plays the Germanophile Duchess) starts out as a sardonic commentator and becomes steadily more so. Both these performances punch above VidCab's usual moral weight. And so, but even more so, does Rick Campbell as the Canadian commander Sir Arthur Currie, trying to preserve his and his country's dignity while sending his men to the slaughter at the behest of a succession of incompetent and vainglorious British generals. When peace finally comes, he finds the colonies' contribution relegated to an official footnote. A new Canada stirs: a point touched on in Billy Bishop but explored more suggestively here.

The other ranks are represented, poignantly but unsentimentally, by Johnnie (Dylan Roberts) who loves his mother and ends up crying for her while crucified, and Dave (Anand Rajaram), a sweet-natured boy from the farm who, after being shell-shocked, turns into a killing machine. Rajaram's other roles include Sam Hughes, a war minister who's not only outstandingly clueless but outstandingly neckless; he's built like a playing card. This actor's versatility was established in his Second City days, but this may be the first time he's been allowed to go through an evening without playing anybody who could conceivably be Asian; he does the whole show in white-face. But then so do all the other actors; it's part of the style.

Also a part of the style is an almost total absence of scenery, there being neither the time nor the space. We do get a single glimpse of barbed wire, and it may be the most memorable image in any Video Cabaret show. Terrifying too are the anonymous gas-masked, almost science-fiction figures, wreathed in smoke, who fall upon the empire troops from behind. Back home, a couple of scenes in a munitions factory contrast the heedless relief a war-wife feels when the dreaded telegram is for someone else with the heart-rending collapse when it's for her. As in Oh What a Lovely War, the evening gets more powerful as the casualty figures get more overwhelming, though on the one occasion on which it strays into that show's territory (a rendition of Pack Up Your Troubles) it suffers in the comparison. Otherwise, it's nearly as powerful. The difference between this and some other plays in the cycle is the difference between making a joke and making a point.

- The Great War is at the Cameron House for a limited run. Visit videocab.comor call 416-703-1725 for more information. robert.cushman@hotmail.com

2010-11-13-vivid-take-on-true-events-sea:
Seana McKenna is wonderful. That's almost a given. Her solo performance in The Year of Magical Thinking is a super-intelligent, beautifully controlled account of a woman who prided herself on both her intelligence and her control, and who lost the latter but not the former when confronted by events that, for sanity's sake, she would previously have thought unthinkable. There are very few moments of emotional breakdown in McKenna's performance. When they do occur, they are, of course, all the more lacerating.

Which is all very well, but the play is Joan Didion's adaptation of her own book about an appalling period in her life. First, her married daughter, Quintana, went into a mysterious coma. Then her husband, John Gregory Dunne, like her a writer, suffered a massive heart attack while sitting right there at the dinner table, and died soon after being admitted to hospital. Then her daughter, who had come out of her coma, was stricken again; and she, too, died in hospital. This last event happened after the writing of the book -- just before its publication, in fact--so the play can't strictly be described as a dramatization of the non-dramatic text. And, in fact, it doesn't play like one, but for other reasons, it's more like a very animated recitation. The material hasn't been transformed or reimagined.

The title refers to a coping strategy. Didion finds herself, after her husband's death, imagining that he has simply gone away: to Europe, where the couple spent many happy times. (We're told about them in some detail.) Quintana, in the period between her recovery and her relapse, indulged -- by coincidence, not collusion -- in the same fantasy. "Magical thinking" Didion tells us, "requires thinking 'if.' " It sounds very much like the bargaining stage of the classical grieving progression.

It's a progression that the protagonist has undergone by the time she sets foot on the stage. That's a constant problem with monologues, especially those with a biographical source. It's very hard to make anything external happen, so the action has to take place inside the character. She has to discover something about herself while we watch. In this case, as in many others, the discovery has already happened. She simply tells us about it.

She does it vividly. I've only read extracts from the book, but taken with what I've read of her journalism, I can readily believe it's an elegant, accomplished piece of work, mordantly witty, spare but unsparing. It's a New Yorker level of writing, but different from what would usually appear in that magazine in that the writer is reporting on her own tragedies rather than somebody else's. It's very civilized, though in this instance part of its effect is to show us how thin a protection civilization can be. Fate can strike as mercilessly in Manhattan or Malibu -- Didion's two main points of reference -- as anywhere else. (Though I have to say that the famous names that constitute the author's social circle have a more distancing effect than may have been intended.) McKenna's brains and taste are a close match for those of the text. Maybe too close: some friction, rather than duplication, might actually be welcome. On the carefully chosen occasions on which she unleashes her feral tragedienne's strength, she does bring us closer to the experience of desolation than we might get to by simply reading it for ourselves. These moments, though, are necessarily few, and McKenna is both too sensitive and too technically skilled to overuse them.

Maybe her most powerful moment of all is her first. After holding a long pause (possibly longer on the first night, as she had to wait for the passing of one of the trains that regularly disturb the tensest moments at the Tarragon), she tells us she is about to describe something we are all going to go through. If we don't want to believe it, well, neither did she. We feel disturbed, as intended; we also feel vaguely guilty. I don't think there's any pretence that what we are about to hear will make us feel better in our own turn. The highest, and the most shocking comic moment comes when Didion demands that the TV be turned off in her comatose daughter's hospital room, so that she may not learn of her father's death by hearing it on CNN. She returns to find a sign that reads "Keep TV Off: Dad Dead." Or did she, she wonders, dream that? That is a scene worth sharing with a live audience; it's always best to laugh in company, however ruefully. Michael Shamata's direction and John Ferguson's dark design give the evening some discreet visual interest. But the evening remains a demonstration, not a drama.

- Until Dec. 12 at the Tarragon Theatre. Call 416-531-1827 or visit tarragontheatre.comfor ticket information. robert.cushman@hotmail.com

2010-11-17-love-squared:
WIDE AWAKE HEARTS

Tarragon Extra Space, Toronto

---

OK, let's get alphabetical. Meet A, B, C and D. A is a screenwriter. B is A's wife, an actress who's appearing in his latest independent movie. C is A's oldest friend, an actor who's also in the movie, in which he gets to play steamy seduction scenes with B. D is a film editor, and an old flame of C's, a flame that may or may not still be burning. The four of them are the characters in Brendan Gall's new play Wide Awake Hearts. They are played by --reading from A to D--Gord Rand, Lesley Faulkner, Raoul Bhaneja and Maev Beaty, all of whose performances are alive and quivering.

The highest quiver quotient is scored by Rand, who starts the evening with a long speech about a child actor who messed up on every rehearsal but was perfect on the take. It's an entertaining way of filling us in on what the characters do for a living, but its broader thematic relevance is not immediately apparent. (Nor, as things turn out, is it ultimately apparent.) Rand and Faulkner have invited Bhaneja over for dinner, and they now invite him to stay: a step up from the chain motel on which he has previously been billeted. Next thing we know, Bhaneja and Faulkner are getting it on together. Only it turns out they aren't really; they're merely performing a scene from Rand's script. But then why should Rand have put them in that position, given that he's obviously insecure, both personally and professionally, and seems to have his real-life suspicions in the first place? It's hard to care about the characters as individuals, what with them having letters as well as names, so maybe the play is making a general statement about all writers being manipulative masochists. Well, I've heard less persuasive things.

Tom Stoppard's The Real Thing also begins with an infidelity scene that turns out to be an extract from a play written by one of the characters in the main action. After that trick opening, however, Stoppard dropped the device and got down to business. Gall stays on the life vs. art, reality vs. illusion kick, which proves, yet again, to be not nearly as fascinating as its author thinks it is. Also, Stoppard's players-within-the-play turned out to be in a situation at stimulating right angles to their factual existence, whereas in Gall's play the fantasy is a mere mirror of the reality, even if a distorting one. Wife and putative lover go on misbehaving, and the author never quite gives up on the possibility that it's actually happening. Neither do the two other characters, who are jealous and who treat the possibly guilty couple to angry pieces of their own minds. Rand is especially prone to upbraiding Bhaneja for betraying their friendship; Bhaneja also gets it from both Faulkner and Beaty for being a compulsive, immature womanizer, something he doesn't feel inclined to dispute.

Some of these exchanges are elegantly funny -- those good performances didn't come from nowhere -- and some are acute. There's an especially thoughtful bit about whether we feel ourselves to be "in love" only because it's something we've seen on the screen. (Or read about in books. There's a school of thought that believes romantic love to be something that was invented by the troubadours in the Middle Ages.) The characters all talk movie-smart, and when one of them tells another off for doing this, he does so in words that are equally movie-smart. This attempt to disarm by double bluff is the moment at which it becomes impossible to take the play seriously. And once that happens, it turns tiresome.

Each of the performers gets a monologue. My favourite was Bhaneja's, apparently delivered in a confessional booth, in which he pleads cheerfully guilty to having broken all the major Commandments, plus a few others. ( "I have eaten meat on Sunday -- and enjoyed it; I have worked on Sunday -- and received overtime pay.") Rand, having got the play off to a flying start, continues to inject it with nervous adrenalin, though he does end up repeating some of his effects. He is unexpectedly absent from the play's last section, but maybe his early departure is meant to balance Beaty's late arrival, which has the combined impact of a cold shower and an electric shock. Poised and furious, she blasts Bhaneja for betraying her, Faulkner for letting him, and Rand for hiring her so that she'd find out. She is masterful too in the play's last soliloquy, in which she ( "a mere cutter") lectures on the practical problems and responsibilities of her craft, not to mention its metaphorical significance. She's disappointingly conventional, though, in the jealousy scenes that come in between.

Gina Wilkinson delivers a fast production with one unfortunate side effect; the play's habit of having the first line of a scene echo or contradict the last line of the one before becomes an irritating mannerism. For all his pretensions, what we hear and see of Rand's movie script resembles a weepie from the 1940s; Lorenzo Savoini's set and Bonnie Beecher's lighting are moodily helpful in establishing this. The play is a step back from Gall's previous Tarragon piece, Alias Godot, which was also tricksy and allusive, but with a wider range and more verbal and structural wit. And its characters weren't theatricals. Wide Awake Hearts reinforces my suspicion that, except for musicals and really funny farces, plays about plays, in which I include plays about movies, are a snare and a delusion.

- Wide Awake Hearts runs until Dec. 12. at Toronto's Tarragon Theatre. Visit tarragontheatre.comor call 416-531-1827 for tickets and information.
