2010-11-19-swingin-and-nearly-16:
THE CURE FOR EVERYTHING

Theatre Passe Muraille Backspace, Toronto

---

We start with Maja Ardal, standing in a corner upstage with her back to us, shaking her hips to The Hippy Hippy Shake by The Swinging Blue Jeans, an early 1960s group who have not crossed my mind, or I would imagine many other people's, in a very long time. The Cure for Everything is the sequel to Ardal's previous solo show, You Fancy Yourself, another chapter in her semi-autobiographical saga about growing up awkward in Edinburgh. It's very skilled, very charming and very slight.

It's also rather approximate about chronology. Elsa, Ardal's presumed alter ego, is shown as being hippy-happy-hypnotized by that song, a British hit in December 1963, while simultaneously being traumatized by the Cuban missile crisis, which happened a full year earlier. Just thought I'd mention it. Elsa, generally regarded as an oddball, has gained unaccustomed credibility by being the first girl at her school to wear Beatles tights. If we're to take the Cuban missile date as our benchmark, this would put her very much ahead of the curve, since Beatlemania hadn't really broken then.

She's precocious in other ways, too. The possibility of a nuclear holocaust, which keeps her immigrant parents glued to the TV set in the kitchen and pretty much neglecting her, spurs her to catch up with all the things she hasn't yet done in her life, primarily getting drunk and losing her virginity. Elsa is 15; and in the Britain of 1962, or even 1963, her innocence at that age, in those matters, would not have been all that exceptional. (Though I suppose things may have been different in Scotland from what they were in England.) Anyway, she sets about filling in the gaps, with the assistance of her new and very unexpected best friend Sheena, generally regarded as the most dazzling and desirable girl in the school, but gradually revealed to be in a far sadder state than Elsa herself.

Elsa's relationship with Sheena is one of the play's poles. The other is the background political threat. In between there are Elsa's Saturday job in a butcher's shop (greeted by Sheena with the '60s equivalent of "ew, gross"); and Elsa's worship-from-afar of Sheena's male equivalent Brian Baxter who is similarly revealed, in the most touching moment in the play, to be less than he might appear. There is also music. Elsa, revealed in the previous play as the best singer in the school, is selected by an appreciative teacher to play the French horn in the school orchestra; it is, he points out, the most difficult instrument, befitting a natural musician like herself. This gets her further grief from the bullies, all brandishing their graceful easy flutes, but what starts as a ground-bass ends as an epiphany.

All these strands are neatly tied together, but they don't make as rich a mix as we had in You Fancy Yourself, a lumpier play but one with more texture and sounding greater emotional depths. This one is linear and simple. It's delightfully performed. Under Mary Francis Moore's direction, Ardal makes Elsa live as both anguished adolescent protagonist and wide-eyed adolescent narrator. She also nicely sketches in the other characters, doing canny instant switches from Elsa's pawky Caledonian to Sheena's throaty tones, somewhere between finishing school and BBC, and then to the shy and wholly unexpected tones of the longed-for Brian. I'm not sure what the play's title means, but I note that Elsa's peers no longer accuse her of fancying herself, even though she, and certainly her interpreter, has a right to. Elsa is still insecure, but there's been progress.

- The Cure for Everything runs until Dec. 4 at Toronto's Theatre Passe Muraille Backspace. For more information, visit passemuraille.on.caor call 416-504-7529.

Shows about photographers seem to be all the rage in Vancouver. The Electric Theatre Company has the acclaimed (though not by me) Studies in Motion, soon to arrive in Toronto, care of Canadian-Stage. In the meantime, World Stage brings us a less-heralded work from the same city's Boca del Lupo group, one bluntly entitled Photog.

Studies in Motion has a cast of thousands and is aggressively hi-tech in its presentation. Photog is essentially a one-man show, and though it certainly mixes its media, its techniques are comparatively modest. Studies in Motion derives from the life and work of a real, though long dead, camera man. Photog concerns one who would be alive if he were real. It's subtitled "an imaginary look at the uncompromising life of Thomas Smith," and it would be quite possible to reverse those adjectives: to call the life imaginary and the look uncompromising. The imaginary Smith is a composite figure, a combat photographer whose story has been pieced together through interviews conducted by the show's creators on a trip to Brooklyn, which apparently is where guys in the trade hole up in between assignments.

We meet Thomas in his own Brooklyn apartment, from which he is about to be evicted: not for nonpayment of rent or anything but because his building is about to be pulled down in favour of a luxury condo. (The program makes more of a point about this than the play does.) While he fends off the landlords and cops who are knocking on his door, he rifles through his memories, which, of course, mainly means going through his pictures. Being a composite, Thomas has seen service in most of the world's worst trouble-spots: Liberia, Haiti, Afghanistan, Iraq, Ivory Coast. His professional souvenirs are displayed on the big screen that constitutes the set's back wall, searing his mind and, at least in intention, the audience's comfortable consciences.

The show can truthfully call itself uncompromising. It doesn't flinch from showing us pictures of devastation, or from having its protagonist describe atrocities that he has witnessed, recorded or feared. But uncompromising isn't the same as successful or well-planned. The enclosing scenario just seems contrived. It's difficult to see that a middle-class New Yorker's enforced departure from his home ranks anywhere on the same scale of suffering as massacres and starvation in Africa and the Middle East. I have a terrible feeling that it's meant to be a metaphor: that Thomas the truth-teller, having fallen foul of tyrannical regimes abroad, is now being dispossessed by more politely repressive forces at home. I hope I'm wrong.

Thomas begins the proceedings by recalling the old adage about a person's life passing before his eyes at the moment of death; and though he doesn't seem to be dying himself, he has seen enough other people do it, and has been in mortal peril often enough himself, for the feeling to be justifiable. Some of his memories stem from his childhood; he tells us that he chose his career because, at the age of 12, he already found things slipping away from him and wanted to preserve them. Now he is, plainly, at the end of his tether, and not just because of his imminent eviction. He has seen too much. Jay Dodge, who wrote the script, also plays the role; he has an appealingly gentle stage presence but not much range, so his overall agony doesn't count for much. He is best when soberly recounting the gradations of fear experienced by troops on a bomb-strewn road, or when telling a cohesive story, as when he relates an escape from near-certain death during the Ivory Coast civil war. The pictures can be powerful, too, though less than you might expect. The most haunting is shown to us early on, a shot of an Iraqi girl with frightened eyes.

Dodge spends two separate sections hoist aloft in a harness, describing experiences airborne or equestrian. These might be more effective if we couldn't see the stage-hand pulling on his ropes; it may count as full disclosure, but honesty isn't always the best policy. Most of the projections, in Sherry Yoon's production, are straightforward, though there's one snazzy sequence in which a photograph is overlaid with a functioning video. There's another in which an image gets draped all over Thomas's one armchair. His unwelcome callers are glimpsed on the screen in close-up, framed in a keyhole, which is not exactly original but is still menacing. Further menace, and other atmospherics, are supplied by a musician, Pietro Amato, doubling on keyboards and French horn (the second French horn to figure in a play this week). At one point, we get a shot of the Enwave theatre lobby itself. Since Thomas at this point is arraigning Western society for its indifference to the troubles he's seen, the effect is to include the audience in the indictment. But if we're at fault for watching something as bourgeois as theatre, isn't the Boca del Lupo company equally at fault for offering it to us? Indeed, isn't Thomas himself, for all his devotion to bearing witness, also part of the system? After all, he's doing it for a living (as he reminds us) and he could get out, close call though it may sometimes have been. If his martyr status is deserved, the play hasn't justified it to us. His war mementoes are turned into pretty pictures. I know that's not what they're meant to be, but that's theatre for you.

- Photog closes tonight at the Enwave Theatre, Harbourfront Centre. For ticket information, call 416-973-4600 or visit harbourfrontcentre.com. robert.cushman@hotmail.com

2010-11-24-see-three-flings:
BETHUNE IMAGINED

Factory Theatre, Toronto

---

Ken Gass' Bethune Imagined imagines the celebrated doctor and political activist in Montreal in 1936. He's considering going off to fight in the Spanish Civil War. In the meantime, he amuses himself by drinking heavily, railing at the medical establishment while touting his own surgical prowess, organizing a children's art workshop, and dallying with a troika of admiring women. It's the last activity that takes up most of the play's time, and supplies most of its interest.

All three ladies have their moment, hence the play does too. But they are moments without momentum. Norman Bethune, known to his female friends as Beth, does take off to join the anti-Franco loyalists at the end of the play, but he might equally well have done so at the beginning. It's hard to see that his amatory exercises have done anything to change his mind. Indeed, it's hard to get into his mind at all. He talks, but his passions, sexual and otherwise, seem interchangeable and indistinguishable. At one point he takes off into a piece of political oratory, for which he's spotlit like a bullfighter in an arena: an incongruous device in a play and production (the author's own) whose style is otherwise routine naturalism. This applies even to a later, and livelier, homage to Hispanic culture in which the characters extol the virtues of flamenco dancing while trying a bit of it.

First flame on stage is Marian Dale Scott, a talented painter with whom Beth had one night of passion -- consummated or not is hard to determine -- on the ocean, years ago; both of them wish at different times to reignite it but never, unfortunately,

at the same time. Marian is Norman's conscience, insofar as he has one. She is followed by Margaret Day, a 22-year-old political acolyte, who offers him her virginity, which he accepts. He gets her pregnant, and she asks him to perform the abortion; again he grants her wish. Marian shares Norman's artistic interests, but is indifferent to his politics; with Margaret it's the reverse. No wonder he needs both of them. Finally, meaning in the second act, we meet Frances Penney, the former Mrs. Bethune, who is over him but not through with him. (Or possibly the other way around.) She is a twinkling, practical soul, who is probably the only one who really understands him. This gives the play a surprising resemblance to Noel Coward's Present Laughter, and as in that play it's the former wife manages to get her ex packed and on board the boat he has to catch.

Advanced soul that he is, Norman has no problems with the three of them knowing about, and even meeting, one

another. Indeed Marian and Margaret, after a few understandably awkward moments (one of them has found him in bed with the other) get on like a house on fire, even collaborating on Norman's art-teaching project. When Frances arrives, they turn out to have a lot in common with her too: All find Norman both exasperating and irresistible, and are very happy to discuss it. It's a middle-aged man's dream; three attractive women arrive at his place in succession, and each of them either starts taking her clothes off or talks as if she might.

Some of the talk is entertaining, even informative, but the total effect is -- in more than one sense -- of vamping till ready. We are obviously meant to see Bethune as a force of nature to whom all must be forgiven, because he's on the right side politically and approaches everything in his life, if not with passion, then at least with gusto. Here this boils down to obstinate shamelessnes; if that's meant to amount to magnetism, the writing doesn't explain it and Ron White's energetic performance doesn't supply it. Marian has the most interesting trajectory -- to put it another way, we're never sure how she feels about Norman, and neither is she--and Irene Poole plays her intelligently, if sometimes excessively, on her nerves. Sascha Cole plays newbie Margaret with appropriate bluntness, and as Frances, Fiona Byrne brings onto the scene a welcome Scots practicality, and an even more welcome Scots mischief. But if Bethune has been imagined, the imagination seems to have been extremely selective. The play leaves you wanting to know more about him, not because it's made him fascinating but because it hasn't.

- Bethune Imagined runs until Dec. 12. Call 416-504-9971 or visit factorytheatre.cafor more information.

A couple of caveats. I gave a talk on Noel Coward and Blithe Spirit immediately before seeing a performance of the new production at the Segal Centre, which I don't think counts as a conflict of interest, but still had better be declared. More importantly, the performance I saw was the first preview -- a matinee at that -- at which the show was plainly still finding its feet.

The surest feet it found belonged to Blair Williams and Kelli Fox as Charles and Ruth Condomine. Theirs are the least showy of the principal roles but -- even more than in the Soulpepper revival a few years ago -- their relationship here underpins the whole play. Charles is the novelist who, for research purposes, arranges a seance in his English country home and finds that Madame Arcati, the local medium, has inadvertently conjured up the spirit of his dead wife, Elvira. Ruth is his current wife, who has always been vaguely jealous of Elvira's memory, and has a lot more cause when her equally jealous rival actually materializes. Charles professes to have been worn out by Elvira's passionate playfulness and to have greeted Ruth's comparative placidity with relief.

Outwardly, Charles and Ruth have a good, companionable marriage. Underneath, a bored resentment seethes. For the first two of the play's three acts, Williams and Fox, expert barbed comedians, cruise the polite surface and dip toes into the embittered depths with equal adroitness. Williams, one of our smoothest stage sophisticates but with a gift for suggesting trouble within, plays host to the audience as well as the characters; it's through his eyes that we see the play. If his grip slackens in the last of the three acts, that's because he doesn't in fact have much to hold on to. It's hard to disagree with John Gielgud's criticism that the play spins out a good comic idea beyond a reasonable length.

Charles isn't one of the more individualized of Coward's comic heroes; he's the quarrelsome Elyot of Private Lives and the suave beleagured Garry of Present Laughter, mixed and diluted. Ruth is absent from most of the last act, only reappearing (this would be a spoiler alert, if the play weren't so well known) in the evening's second ghostly form, a device that should double the farcical effect but actually succeeds in halving it. Charles ends by bidding a not-very-fond farewell to both his exes, plus all the previous demanding women in his life from his mother onwards; this burst of unregenerate misogyny might be quite bracing (as it is in Coward's one-act Fumed Oak) if only the characters and the situation hadn't already outstayed their welcome.

The repetition is emphasized by the slack pace of Marti Maraden's production, though it may very well have tightened up by now. When I saw her, Clare Coulter's Madame Arcati was effective only by fits and starts. Coulter excels at playing people who live strictly by their own rules, and her blend of dottiness and practicality would seem to be ideal for what is, by far, the most distinctive role in the play. But what should have been a seamless blend of hearty and wispy was still jerky. Gemma James-Smith has an unusual take on Elvira, whom she presents as upstart guttersnipe rather than throaty socialite. This seems to be playing not so much against the text as against the context. In fairness, I've yet to see an Elvira who justifies the claims that the play implicitly makes for her; as with some other screwball heroines, we have to take her enchantress qualities on trust. In this production, she does actually look like a refugee from Restoration comedy, as she returns from the dead wearing a voluminous blond wig. This seems to be regulation gear in the beyond as the revenante Ruth also sports one, though on Fox, one of nature's brunettes, it doesn't look so good.

Diana Donnelly gives a spirited (to put it mildly) account of the maid Edith who, it turns out, has inadvertently caused all the trouble; she's excellent when terrorized into taking the rap for it. Every time I see the play I hope to understand how Edith, who never even knew Elvira, could have been responsible for her re-appearance, but I never do. The set, by John C. Dinning, is wonderfully spacious and detailed, providing a fine environment for actors while summoning up both the comfortable place and the distinctly uncomfortable time: provincial England in the middle of the Second World War -- a fact that, in this comedy about death, is never mentioned but always present.

- Blithe Spirit runs at Montreal's Segal Centre until Dec. 12. For tickets and information, visit segalcentre.orgor call 514-739-9340.

Anusree Roy's previous plays have been monologues -- one good, one not so much -- that she has performed herself. In Roshni, her new one, she splits a couple of differences. There are two characters, one of whom she plays herself. The play, though short, has some dead patches, but it starts out engaging and ends up very affecting.

It concerns two 12-year-olds (though here they look more like late teenagers), each hustling a perilous and penurious living at a railway station in Calcutta. Chumki, the girl, polishes boots; King Kumar, the boy, sells tea. ( "Will that be regular or special?") He dreams of being a Bollywood star; she, blind from the measles, dreams of regaining her sight. Their paths crossed by accident but, since then and until now, they have always been there for one another.

Each thinks that he or she has found a way out: an escape from sleeping on trains, and being kicked awake by the guards. Chumki talks of an unspecified Boss Man who, if she can raise the money, can arrange for an operation that will cure her. King Kumar has an uncle in Mumbai who claims to know someone who knows someone who, if he can raise the money, will get him a job as a movie extra, after which the sky will be the limit. Twice, we watch the boy talking, on a very unreliable telephone line, to the uncle whose circumstances seem to keep changing and whose financial demands keep increasing.

We also spend time watching the couple at work, sometimes individually, sometimes backing one another up. They supplement their earnings by picking the occasional pocket, for which it's impossible to blame them. Seeing them do all this is interesting to begin with, repetitive later on: not, of course, as hideously repetitive as it would be for the real people concerned, but this is the theatre. The play's middle stretches are brightest when musical. To charm more money from her customers, Chumki sings; her strenuous off-key My Heart Must Go On leaves Celine Dion grovelling in the dust, and she does Humpty Dumpty as an encore. (Both English songs, she announces proudly.) Sometimes, King Kumar joins her for a snappy dance routine.

For all this, their friendship is fracturing. Both of them are chasing the same finite supply of cash, and though this might not have mattered when their needs were less, now they're desperate. Under pressure, each starts to point out to the other what the audience has always known: Their dreams are doomed. King Kumar's uncle is a swindler, and the boy has no chance of becoming a slumdog millionaire: not the millionaire part anyway. Chumki's Boss Man is likewise a crook. Almost the most moving moment in the play is King Kumar's cruelly truthful declaration that the doctor, even if he exists, could never cure her because her blindness is incurable. It's topped, though, by Chumki's cry: "I am only wanting the money to see you;" true or not, it's the most devastating line in any play this year.

Thomas Morgan Jones' production squanders some energy; the actors shout too much, whether at one another or at invisible passersby. Byron Abalos is frenetic almost from the get-go; he's far more effective when he quiets down for his chats with his uncle, trying furiously to fool himself, and best of all when he comes into a sad, almost tragic maturity at the end. Roy herself is more controlled, increasingly beguiling, and finally, heartbreaking.

- Roshni runs through Dec. 11 at Theatre Passe Muraille, 416-504-7529.

Stephen Sondheim's Finishing the Hat surrounds his complete lyrics with commentary (on his own work and lyric-writing in general) thats as witty, graceful and perceptive as the songs themselves. In the same category of books even better than Id dared hope: Will Friedwald's Biographical Guide to the Great Jazz and Pop Singers offers essay-length appreciations of American Songbook performers, blessedly free of snobbery (though not of omissions). I'll be reading it well into 2011, and consulting it indefinitely thereafter.

THE SILICONE DIARIES

Buddies in Bad Times Theatre, Toronto

---

I've never seen as many people leave the theatre during a performance as I did at the reopening of The Silicone Diaries. (The show, a hit in Buddies in Bad Times' cabaret room last season, is back for a run in the main space.) Their discomfort was, I'm fairly sure, physical rather than aesthetic, since the performance itself is a remarkable one. It's a transsexual's detailed account of her journey from a male body to a female one, and it includes extensive film footage of plastic surgery, both bodily and facial, as well as extensive verbal descriptions. The protagonist's trajectory was, in a sense, reversed by those in the audience who took early retirement: in the show's first half, the evacuees were women, in the second, as the story threatened to cut closer to home, so to speak, they were men.

Nina Arsenault, who lived the story and is now telling it, was very understanding. "It's intense," she said sympathetically, in the wake of one especially distressed patron who was actually throwing up as she exited. I confess to averting my own eyes from some of the procedures on the screen. The procedure on the stage is another matter. This is a show about self-fashioning that's also an example of it.

Over the years, Arsenault has turned herself not only into a woman but into a very accomplished performer. With sympathetic direction by Brendan Healy, she plays with great physical grace, never more so than in a late and very amusing section when, delicate feet furiously turning, she mimes her progress on an exercise bike. Her petite pedal extremities (thank you, Fats Waller) round off a tall body, sheathed in a strapless, see-through dress, possibly made out of latex. Vocally, she has only one tone but great command of phrasing. She has written herself some long twisting sentences, which she navigates with extreme elegance and unfailing wit.

First she takes us back to the formative experience of her life when, as a five-year-old boy from an Ontario trailer park, she was entranced by the sight of a mannequin in a chain store. (This may be the only time, in art or in life, in which the words "a Zellers employee" have been uttered in tones of rapt enchantment.) Her life becomes a quest to look, to be, that beautiful, that immune. With a brain that gets her through college and into a teaching assistantship, she moonlights in a porn parlour, still physically a man but communicating online as a woman; so she did have early practice as a performer, if of a rather specialized kind. She's very good at it; a couple of grateful long-distance clients stake her to her first trip to the U.S., for the first of many, many additions and subtractions. She becomes a passive virtuoso of the operating table, and she meets others similarly dedicated, including one who eventually becomes a cosmetic martyr.

The show's serio-comic highlight is Arsenault's account of an evening at a Toronto nightclub where she sets her sights on Tommy Lee. As a six-foot expansively (not to say expensively) sculpted blond, she naturally attracts his attention. And he compels hers, not just by being a rock star trailing hundreds of reputed conquests, but as the ex-husband of Pamela Anderson, who seems to be Arsenault's role model; though of course Anderson started off with more advantages, or at least fewer handicaps. It all goes very well until Lee's entourage clue him in that all is not quite what it seems, though both parties manage to retire with their dignities at least outwardly intact.

Arsenault's Pamela Anderson project, though, raises questions, with which the play's last scene attempts, not altogether successfully, to grapple. On the one hand, we seem meant to admire her as someone who has, to an extraordinary degree, taken control of her own destiny. On the other, we're always being told how pernicious it is that women should be pressured to buy into a commercial ideal of beauty, and this seems to be what Arsenault has done, in spades; the fact that she started on the other side of the fence gets her all kinds of added marks for effort but doesn't really alter the equation. In fact it illustrates it, in starkest relief. So it's unclear whether it's tragic or ironic that Arsenault, who's treated her body as an ongoing work of art, should turn out, inevitably, to have been working in a perishable medium.

There's a stunning moment at which she takes off her wig and turns out to have realized her ambition; she looks, in that second, as much like a mannequin as anyone ever could. But of course she also wants to be a person, and still wants to be a beautiful one, though she starts talking about inner beauty and takes more conventional steps (thus, the exercise bike) to preserve the outer kind. Well, we all grow old, and the air of special pleading, not to say self-piety, that overtakes the play at the end doesn't feel earned. The applause, however, does. The production has stylish visuals, designed by Trevor Schwellnus, and sound by the ubiquitous Richard Feren, which, if anyone else had done it, would be exceptional.

- The Silicone Diaries runs until Dec. 11. For tickets, call 416-975-8555 or visit totix.ca.

Frog and Toad are great friends, but the amount of time they can spend together in a given year is limited by the fact that they spend nearly half of it hibernating. A Year with Frog and Toad, the charming American musical imported to the Lorraine Kimsa Theatre for Young People, takes their relationship from its spring re-awakening (to adapt a title already taken) to its winter hiatus.

I don't know the Arnold Lobel books on which the show is based, but I did grow up on The Wind in the Willows, with which these stories seem to have a considerable affinity. Theres no frog that I recall in the Kenneth Grahame book, but his Mr. Toad does have some points of contact with this one, mainly a touching self-consciousness; they both care what the world thinks about them, though this manifested itself in the older Toad as vanity and bravado, and in this one as shyness. The Frog-Toad relationship here seems to owe something to Grahames Rat and Mole, one of them protective, the other vulnerable; though Grahame's riparian rodents switched roles more adventurously than Lobel's woodland amphibians do.

Anyway, Frog and Toad live next door to one another, and the show begins with Frog preparing to give Toad his annual wake-up call. He knows his friends limitations ( hes not so good at sports / and of course, he has those warts") but loves him anyway. When he calls round chez Toad with the news that it's April, the reply he gets is not too encouraging ( "Come back when it's May), though if ever I saw audience empathy, I got it from the massed five-to-10-year-olds watching this production. It went double as Toad re-snuggled himself beneath the covers, and triple when, in a further fit of defiance, he smashed his alarm clock. This particular plot development enables Toad to be late for every subsequent date he makes in the show, on the grounds that he has no means of telling the time. Frogs reaction, mostly, is a tolerant smile. Though, when the shows second winter comes around, it does look as if he's about to spend it camping out at Toad's place rather than back in his own bed. Seems hes not about to take any more chances.

Louise Pitre plays Toad, and she is enchanting. The further she gets from the belting persona with which she first established herself, the better she becomes. This Toad is a worrier, who needs constant re-assurance. He gets scared when he finds himself all alone on a downward-hurtling sled. (Well, who wouldnt?) He gets embarrassed when he goes swimming, because he fears that he looks silly in a bathing suit -- and the supporting characters, mainly birds and turtles, agree that he does, in chorus. (I must say I was expecting a more encouraging pay-off to this number.) He also, in a moment that Pitre makes especially touching, gets sad at 10 o'clock every morning, because that's the time when the mail gets delivered. Or, in his case, doesnt: a revelation that goes straight to Frogs heart. The role of Frog was originally intended for Denis Simpson, who died just before rehearsals were about to start. Allen MacInnis, director of the show (and of the theatre) took over, and gives a very judicious and sympathetic performance. He sings well, too.

The show ran on Broadway and got a Tony nomination. This is surprising, since in scale and style it's very off-Broadway. The music by Robert Reale and the lyrics (by Willie Reale, who also wrote the book) are in the deceptively simple, actually sophisticated, style, jolly with melancholy undercurrents, that's been standard in those parts at least since The Fantasticks. Todays kids are unlikely to have heard much like it at home, but maybe it will be a civilizing influence. Some numbers do go on too long, as do some passages of script. The structure doesnt allow for much narrative development. It does, though, make intelligent use of repetition, in the shape of gags that don't so much run as amble. One of these involves snail mail, literally; Kevin Dennis gets to sing, proudly and delightfully, a recurring country song ( I'm the snail with the mail") about how incredibly, conscientiously fast hes going, a joke thats kept going through the show and even, in a cleverly understated touch, beyond. Jennifer Villaverde and Cara Hunter complete the cast as a variety of creatures, some of them with a mean streak that proves refreshing in a show that might otherwise overdose on sweetness and light. Diane Leah's musical direction, with herself at the piano and Tom Jestadt on drums, is first-rate. Robin Fisher's set and costumes, lit by Lesley Wilkinson, are beguilingly vernal. It may or may not be easy being green, but the results are certainly good to watch. A show that hinges on, and illustrates, the turn of the seasons connects to the roots of storytelling.

- A Year with Frog and Toad runs through Dec. 30 at the Lorraine Kimsa Theatre for Young People. Call 416-862-2222 or visit lktyp.cafor more information. robert.cushman@hotmail.com

THEATRE REVIEW

Beauty and the Beast

Elgin Theatre, Toronto

In their ceaseless quest for new but old source-material, Ross Petty's family musicals -- British Christmas pantomimes, slightly Canadianized -- have reached Beauty and the Beast. I've never known this tale to be used before as panto material. Previous authors must have thought it wouldn't work. The current version suggests that they were right.

The writers, Lorna Wright and Nicholas Hune-Brown, have detached the story so far from its original moorings that it doesn't even qualify as parody. It does have a Beauty: a village maiden who, in deference to the Disney movie, is called Bella. It does have a Beast, sort of, but he's a wannabe Beast, as opposed to the original who was very much a don't-wannabe Beast. This guy is a bashful, awkward Prince named Zack, who is ineffectually practising to be a mean ol' rock star so that Bella will notice him, though in fact she's quite prepared to love him for his nerdy self. It takes a full half-hour for the show to set up even this much of a situation, and it has no idea where to go from there. The Prince does get to be a Beast through the wiles of a nefarious magician who wants the kingdom for himself (and is played, of course, by Petty himself ); but it's a half-hearted kind of transformation. By way of a twist, Beauty becomes a bit of a beast herself, courtesy of the villain's villainous iScroll, a device whose apps function and malfunction with baffling irregularity, even when backed up by their owner's most malevolent snarl. There's nothing here of Beauty tending to the Beast and recognizing his better qualities, on account of she's already done that before the story even starts. But if you remove that element there really is nothing left, nothing even to make fun of. First law of comedy: set up your target before trying to knock it down. Wright and Hune-Brown are best known as the authors of Lord of the Rings: The Musical: The Musical!, a show on whose quality I cannot comment because I never saw it, but whose nature seems pretty clearly indicated by its title. This Beauty and the Beast comes with a prologue in which performers audition hopeless ideas for family musicals. It's travesty

at one remove: not so much a genre as a disease.

The show does have another quarry in its sights. Petty's character is called Baron Barnum von Cowell, and the show spends as much time, and rather more energy, spoofing the American/ Canadian Idol thing as it does on its ostensible subject. Bella is played by Melissa O'Neil, a former Idol herself. The Baron has a nasty singing protege called Buskin Beaver; he also manages to lure away Bella's faithful sheep (are we in the right story?) and rebrand her as Lady Baa Baa. Goodies and baddies finally face off in a battle of the bands, an idea that's turned up at this address at least once before. The amount of humour the production doesn't manage to extract from all this is amazing. The underlying conviction that kids can't be made to care about anything beyond TV, pop music and computer games is depressing.

Petty himself goes through his usual routine (villain as smarmy narcissist, with a dash of hysterical paranoia) with his usual aplomb, but his material gives way beneath him, and I suspect he knows it. This isn't one of the boss's years for going into drag; that chore is bequeathed to Scott Thompson, who plays Bella's man-crazy aunt (in this kind of show, there's no other kind) and who doesn't even pretend that his lines are funny. The ultra-reliable Eddie Glen, playing one of Zach's two sidekicks/bandmates, makes an effort in that direction but is defeated; Jake Simons, mustachioed, Hispanified and playing the other (who plays the guitar) fares even worse.

Jake Epstein's gormless Zack does have a spark, and his shy courtship with Bella in the castle library -- two bookworms in their natural habitat -- is one of the show's candidates for Redeeming Feature. Another -- actually the only other -- is the standard and staging of the musical numbers (choreographer Tracey Flye, musical director Mark Camilleri). When the music isn't playing, Ted Dykstra's direction just gives in and slouches. Am I taking a children's show too seriously? I don't think so. For one thing, many of the names that get dropped in place of jokes are there for the grown-ups. (Des McAnuff? Christopher Plummer? Or -- not named but pictured -- Rob Ford?) For another, the kids deserve far better and there are at least two other seasonal shows in town that give it to them. As, in years gone by, Petty himself has done. His shows have fluctuated wildly in quality, but this one is the worst. Oh no, it isn't? Oh yes, it is.

- Beauty and the Beast runs at Toronto's Elgin Theatre until Jan. 2. For more information, visit rosspetty.comor call 416-872-5555. robert.cushman@sympatico.ca

On its fifth go-round -- two at the old address, three at the new one -- the Soulpepper version of A Christmas Carol is as good as ever, and possibly better.

If God -- or the composite spirit of Christmas--is in the details, then this show is multiply blessed. The moments of delight pile up. The solitary bulb, burning on stage at the beginning, that John Jarvis, the narrator, identifies as a ghost-light, traditionally designed to keep spirits at bay, and then removes because tonight he wants them to be present; the long white tablecloth that gets magically whisked from position and hangs briefly in the air like a furled banner; the momentary sight of a scimitar-flashing Ali Baba, summoned from a story-book; the giant clock-face projected on to the stage floor on which Joseph Ziegler's Scrooge checks the minutes before the arrival of his next spectral visitor; the multiplicity of smiles that cross the face of Oliver Denniss Bob Cratchit, especially the amazed one that suffuses it when he takes in his employers transformation.

Ziegler, Jarvis and Dennis have all been with this production since its first Toronto appearance in 2001, and all three are joys to re-encounter. Ziegler has always been irresistible in the delirious caperings that attend his conversion, but his delineation of the earlier grimmer Scrooge has grown richer, sharper and deeper over the years. I tend to agree with Dickens' biographer Edgar Johnson who wrote that a character who declares that anyone who wishes another a merry Christmas should be buried with a sprig of holly through his heart cannot be taken altogether seriously as a misanthrope; he's protesting too much and too imaginatively. But an actor has to play it like he means it; and in his early dealings with his incorrigibly cheerful nephew, with Cratchit, and with the gentleman who comes to ask for charitable contributions (there used to be two of them, now its just one, ah the cruel times we live in), Ziegler displays an iron economy worthy of the miser himself. His melting begins early, but it was crafty of Dickens--and beautifully preserved in Michael Shamatas in-the-round direction of his own adaptation -that his armour is first pierced by a kind of retrospective self-pity. He sees his childhood self at school, alone and abandoned when everyone else has gone home for the holidays, and the sight of the solitary boy goes to his heart as it does to ours. We can also appreciate his love for his sister, and sense that her early death helped make him what he bitterly became. Counting back, we can see how his early abandonment led him to focus his misanthropy on the idea of Christmas, despite his more positive experiences of the season during his apprenticeship with the Fezziwigs. I confess that these celebratory scenes, which involve much scampering up and down a step-ladder, have always struck me as the only weak spot in the show; in fact they bring out the unregenerate Scrooge in me. It's impossible though, not to be charmed by the poignant, hypnotized dance-steps that Ziegler tries out with the girl of his dreams (a bewitching Sarah Wilson) after he's watched her dancing with his younger self (Matthew Edison, who doubles as the nephew). And its very moving to behold him beholding that same younger Scrooge rejecting that same girl, while beseeching him to say something different, something that will change everything. At moments like this, A Christmas Carol becomes not just a moral fable but a universal human tragedy, about time irrevocably lost. It goes on, of course, to show the possibility of some future time being redeemed. Still, however happy the ending (and in this performance, its contagiously so), the awareness of past waste never goes away. Ziegler, an actor equally capable of iron and of gentleness and with a magical wit that binds the two together, gets both ends of Scrooge, and the developing middle, to perfection.

Bob Cratchit is a simpler soul, though hardly less of a challenge to act; Dennis, supremely well cast, moves us in all his gradations of grief and joy, without becoming mawkish in any of them. The production as a whole is a triumph of storytelling; Shamata is especially faithful, and especially inventive, in his handling of the succession of street-scenes with Scrooge moving through the crowds and being first aggressive and resentful, then wracked and fearful, and finally boyish and exultant. John Ferguson's sets are resourceful and suggestive, Alan Brodie's lighting superbly moody and evocative. Jarvis presides as Marleys ghost and as all three spirits, powerful as all of them though sometimes overplaying both the sternness and the jollity. In truth, just about everyone in the cast, Ziegler and Dennis excepted, overdoes things at some point. But this hardly gets in the way of the message; the apparition of Ignorance and Want, the twin childish figures who are Christmas Presents surprise Christmas present, remains another of the great moments. I remember feeling a little unease when I first saw this production; after partaking in a powerful lesson on charity, that left us with a virtuous glow, we were given no chance to do anything about it. Or that's what I thought until the curtain-call, when we were asked to put donations into baskets held in the lobby by "young Crachits": Ziegler's phrase in his curtain-speech for what has now become a tradition. If it sounds simple, it is; if it sounds sentimental, it isn't. This show, both in the auditorium and immediately outside, represents Soulpepper at its best, practicing what it preaches.

- A Christmas Carol runs through Dec. 24 at the Young Centre, 416-866-8666.

2010-12-21-plummer-a-good-two-fisted-dri:
'It's an octogenarians' festival." So says Christopher Plummer, an extraordinarily dapper, elegant, spry and courteous 81, while taking tea in the Four Seasons' Studio Cafe. He's about to open -- or re-open -- in Barrymore, the sort of solo play (there are two actors, but the other one spends all his time just offstage) that he originally played at Stratford in 1996 and subsequently took to New York and Toronto. His "very astute" director, Gene Saks, who among other things has been encouraging him "to talk to the audience more" is 89; the author, William Luce, a youth of 79, has also been "very good, realistic; he's cut a lot of unnecessary things."

Saving, or maximizing, time has become a priority for Plummer. "When you get to my age, you're in a terrible hurry. You ask yourself, 'Why am I doing this, going backwards?'My only regret about the original was not having done it in London."

He's found some other reasons. "It's much more touching than when we did it before. The minute we started, I got excited about doing it." And there are also more practical reasons: "There's the promise of putting it on screen. And in the theatre, it's just a five-week run, five performances a week: no more."

And, of course, there are the reasons that first drew him to the play and the character, 14 years ago. John Barrymore, the pre-eminent American theatre actor of the first half of the 20th century, was a formative influence on Plummer himself. "I was 14 when I read Gene Fowler's biography. I swore to emulate him, this wonderful bon vivant. So I blame Jack Barrymore. I'm disappointed that I never saw him in his prime. None of his films do him justice. Except Twentieth Century [in which Barrymore plays an egomaniacal actor-manager, clawing his way back to the top]; that was really him."

There's also The Show of Shows, the 1929 omnibus picture in which Warner Bros., like all the other studios, cashed in on the birth of the talkies by displaying all the performers on its roster who could actually make a sound. Barrymore's contribution was a Richard III soliloquy (actually taken from the prequel, Henry VI Part 3), which he delivered standing triumphantly atop a heap of fresh corpses. (The play Barrymore revolves around the alcoholic actor's apocryphal attempt to revive his career by playing Richard.) Plummer pronounces it "some of it terrific, some not so good. There's a mystery surrounding him still. He had the ideal look for Hamlet, the ideal manliness for Hamlet. He was princely and handsome, not a pretty boy. He must have driven all the girls wild -- all the boys, too. And he had a wonderful humour." (Humour is one of the qualities that Michael Langham, the director who brought Plummer to Stratford in the 1950s, singles out among those that make him a natural classical star.) "And of course Barrymore didn't have much competition. There weren't many great classical actors in America then. And he didn't sound old-fashioned, not from the age of Henry Irving or Forbes-Robertson." At this point, he pauses to deliver a hilarious impersonation, based on an old recording, of Johnston Forbes-Robertson, the Edwardian heroic actor for whom Bernard Shaw wrote one of Plummer's own recent successes, Caesar and Cleopatra, and who, I have to confess, I had never imagined sounding quite so Scottish.

Plummer in the past has named Barrymore as the inspiration for his own thespian generation of "good two-fisted drinkers," though you have only to inspect his own recent resume to realize that he has been spared the Barrymore self-destructiveness. He's always claimed that he likes food too much to be a really dedicated drinker. Especially now: "You need fodder during rehearsals. I've been getting fatter and fatter in Toronto." (I can't say it shows.) He's also had to interrupt rehearsals by commuting to Stockholm ( "Canada and Sweden look exactly alike--no light at three o'clock." Our conversation, I should make clear, occurred before the recent bombing) where he's filming the second part of the Dragon Tattoo trilogy, English-speaking version. "Ours will look more beautiful--I play the patriarch of a huge and ghastly family.

He's the only nice person in the whole friggin' thing." His film career has of course moved into its highest gear, since his performance in The Insider, though apparently it didn't feel like a breakthrough while he was doing it and "trying to get through 40 takes; I had to tell Michael Mann, the director 'I can't do it differently, I won't be Mike Wallace anymore.' " Then this year there was his proto-Prospero in Terry Gilliam's The Imaginarium of Dr. Parnassus, which he loved doing though he thinks that Gilliam should get himself a writer, and his first Oscar nomination, for playing Tolstoy in The Last Station. He and his co-star Helen Mirren were each limbering up for their own attempts at Prospero (or in her case, Prospera) in stage or film versions of The Tempest; they used to tease one another about it. Now he'd like to try some gender-switching himself. He amazed me, because it's not a play anybody thinks about anymore, by saying he'd like to play the title role in Jean Giraudoux' The Madwoman of Chaillot. Sounds like a great idea; we're unlikely to see the play any other way and it could be very timely. (Arthur Miller once called it the most outspoken attack on exploitation he'd ever read.) He downplays rumours that he might be playing James Tyrone in a revival of Long Day's Journey into Night: "I want to have more fun than that at my age. Though if somebody like Meryl Streep would play opposite me ..." What he really wants to do now is "an outrageous comedy. I wish they were writing them now. They only play TV comedies." To spend an hour in his company is to wish to see that sense of fun, and that charm, fully unleashed.

HOW THE GRINCH STOLE CHRISTMAS! THE MUSICAL

Sony Centre, Toronto

---

Literature's doughtiest Warriors Against Christmas are out in force on Toronto's stages this year. Charles Dickens' Scrooge is making his biannual return to the Young Centre, while over at that other Centre currently known as Sony, Dr. Seuss' Grinch is meeting his pre-destined fate as the subject of a holiday musical.

A Christmas Carol is a great show, How the Grinch Stole Christmas! The Musical is a terrible one; and in both cases, the causes lie about equally with the original material and with how it's been put on the stage. The two stories are of course identical: misanthrope hates Christmas, does his best to spoil it for everyone, is made to see the error of his ways and ends up as a kind of super-Santa. The difference, apart from the fact that Dickens got there first, is that one provides a social and psychological context, while the other exists in a self-created void. That is its right as a fantasy, but it doesn't give theatrical adaptors, or indeed audiences, much to work with. So they have to pad. The original Seuss poem takes about five minutes to read; double that, perhaps, if you're doing it aloud, and add in a few more to savour the illustrations. It's already been blown up into a TV cartoon special. It now has to be further inflated to 90 minutes of stage time, which is a problem.

The solution adopted by Timothy Mason (book and lyrics) and Mel Marvin (music) is to take what was already sugary and sweeten it. The Grinch's dog Max, barely mentioned in the original, is promoted to a mixture of sidekick and conscience: a sort of canine Jiminy Cricket. Max's later self narrates the story, in a suitably hangdog fashion, and there are times when both are onstage simultaneously, castigating the Grinch for his Grinchiness. But then this is a musical whose last seven numbers are all reprises; it has no qualms about repeating itself. The Grinch, looking down from his Mount Crumpit fastness, sings a song about how much he detests the Whos and their incorrigible Christmas cheeriness; the scene then shifts to Whoville itself, whose inhabitants prove the Grinch's point by going through exactly the same number, with nothing changed except the tone of voice and the pronouns.

As may be evident, I'm no great fan of Seuss in general, or of this poem in particular. What the original does have going for it -- the swing of the verse and some of the rhymes -- gets lost amid the clumsier couplets added here, both spoken and sung. The interpolation, from the TV version, of You're a Mean One, Mr. Grinch, with Seuss's own lyrics, turns out not to be the expected bright spot; it's an awful, laboured song. Musically it's inferior to the new stuff, though I might be influenced here by memories of a lovely show called Tintypes, which has a score assembled, though not written, by this musical's composer.

Talking of pedigree here, How the Grinch ... was originally directed by Jack O'Brien, who's American theatre royalty, though how long it's been since he saw it, I couldn't say. I doubt, though, that it ever ranked among his most distinguished work. The Grinch himself has quite the resume, too; he's Stefan Karl, whose record in Reykjavik, from Cyrano to Singin' in the Rain, suggests Iceland's answer to Colm Feore. Good place for the Grinch to come from, really, and Karl plays him with enthusiastic grittiness, cresting in a shameless audience-baiting solo called One of a Kind. It makes no sense of course: when Mr. Burns, on The Simpsons, does a comparable hat-and-cane routine, it's because he's a social monster who wants applause; the Grinch is anti-social and only wants to be left alone. Anyway Karl looks the part, or at least he has a good green costume. His best moment on the first night came near the end, when he traded jibes with small members of the audience who were stubbornly refusing to say what was expected of them. For one blissful minute of a pre-packaged production, spontaneity reigned.

- How the Grinch Stole Christmas! The Musical runs until Dec. 30. Visit sonycentre.cafor more information. robert.cushman@hotmail.com

2010-12-23-remembering-domini-blythe:
In 1984, visiting Canada from England, I caught a Stratford Festival production of Molieres Tartuffe, directed by John Hirsch. It was splendid all around, but in one scene it touched greatness: the attempted seduction by Brian Bedford's Puritan hypocrite of Elmire, the married woman into whose house he had insinuated himself. She was played by Domini Blythe.

I had seen spectacular things at Stratford on previous trips, but this was in a different class of intimacy and concentration; never before had I known the Festival theatre, with its epic stage and auditorium, to be so transfixed by a domestic encounter. Elmire is playing a double game in this scene, leading her tempter on so that her husband, concealed under the table, will see him for what he is. Blythe, in her late thirties at the time, blended the eroticism, the uncertainty and the underlying purpose with a superb sense of comic tension. Her duet with Bedford (Douglas Campbell, in furious hiding, making a third) was, in terms of contact and concentration, the most breathtaking acting I had seen at Stratford up to that time and nothing has surpassed it since.

Domini Blythe, who died last week of throat cancer at the age of 63, was one of the most loved actresses in the Canadian theatre. To meet her was to be enchanted by the beautiful face and honeyed voice that adorned her acting. To get to know her was to be knocked out all over again, by both her toughness and her gentleness: by her honesty, her forthrightness, her sense of fun, and her ability to make whoever she was talking to feel like the most important person in the world. Peter Hinton, who wrote and directed the one-woman play Fanny Kemble that was her last Stratford appearance, speaks of her genuine curiosity about other people. She cared so much about the young people in the company, about passing on her knowledge and expertise.

She was born into a British theatrical family, and she began her career there. She was in the original London cast of the famous erotic revue Oh! Calcutta!; I must have seen her in it, though I regret that I have no specific memories. She must have made an impression, though, on Kenneth Tynan, who created the show; in one of his posthumously published letters he wrote that she was one of only two actors in the cast whose performance sustained over the run. The other was a Canadian: Richard Monette, in fact, who, when he returned to Canada, and ultimately to Stratford, brought her with him. For several years, they lived together. I have a fond memory of Richard, years after they had split up and he was running the Festival, standing on the Stratford sidewalk during the intermission of Private Lives, and telling Domini how much the tempestuous relationship in the play reminded him of their own. They remained devoted to one another, and fiercely loyal.

She joined the Stratford company in 1976.The following year she had her first major role there, and one of her few failures: an oddly passionless Miss Julie (a role and a play that have defeated many people). In 1979 she was Rosaline, the dark lady of Love's Labours Lost. Martha Henry, who played the Princess of France, recalls that, "Robin would get all the rest of us into the house to watch Domini and then try to get us to do that!' I could indeed see what 'that was but couldnt for the life of me do it. She had the ability to join the word to the thought

absolutely seamlessly so that the two things were one -- so that there was never a schism in her characters -- they were always absolutely authentic."

In the early '80s she returned to Britain for a couple of years, acting with the Royal Shakespeare Company and more than holding her own. I remember her as an indignant Elizabeth to Alan Howard's Richard III. Even better was her performance of the title role in the Jacobean rarity The Maid's Tragedy. Back at the Canadian Stratford, she moved gracefully and wittily into character roles, playing a deliciously amused lady-in-waiting in Henry V, an imperious Maria in Twelfth Night and a primly provocative Prism in The Importance of Being Earnest. Her solo Fanny Kemble was a long-cherished project; according to Hinton, "she loved the rigour of a woman who fought for her political and literary and social and professional life."

She was forging a new career in Montreal, where she lived with her husband, when illness struck. Her brother Ben, who came from London to be with her in her last days, says that she faced death with peace and acceptance and even with happiness. All the same, losing one who still had so much to give seems cruel. She was lovely.

2010-12-24-cute-overload:
Just like everybody ought to have a maid, everybody ought to have a favourite number in A Funny Thing Happened on the Way to the Forum. It's a tough decision, given the delights of Stephen Sondheims score, but mine has always, in fact, been Everybody Ought To Have a Maid. This elegantly lascivious celebration -- a cumulative quartet that adds a performer with every refrain -- is almost guaranteed to delight. It did so in last years Stratford production, but in that production's transfer to the Canon, it doesn't so much stop the show as stop it dead. The whispering game thats been inserted between each chorus, and that used to build tension by delaying it, has now swollen to destructive proportions. Im no metronome, but the actual musical tempo seems to have

slackened disastrously, too; while the opening up of the number to include the corps of courtesans is now, more than ever, the height of unnecessary. The number has nothing to do with them. It's about four low comedians -- four dirty youngish-to-old men -- connecting and conniving with the audience. That, in various formations, is how this Broadway tribute, both to old Roman comedy and old American burlesque, is meant to work. Even when, as in this case, a number is irrelevant to the plot, it's planned, delightful irrelevance. The show is a brilliantly economical piece of work. The last thing it needs is bloat. It gets a lot of it here.

Des McAnuffs production, as at Stratford, works when it trusts the material and doesnt when it doesn't, but the level of trust seems to have declined precipitously. Two actors now alternate in the leading role of Pseudolus, the slave who undertakes to unite his young master to the virginal courtesan next door, in exchange for his own freedom. I saw Sean Cullen, who at Stratford took over from Bruce Dow when Dow became ill, and who by and large looks better than he sounds. Pseudolus drives the plot, coming up with a new scheme every minute; and whether he's doing it for fun (as in Plautus, the Roman source) or for liberty (as in Burt Shevelove and Larry Gelbart, the American adaptors), he needs urgency. Cullen doesnt have it, or much connection with the other actors or the very funny text, so the show drags and dawdles. What he does, by way of an assumed speech impediment and a muffler, to the scripts most inspired exchange ( You asked for a soothsayer? "How did you know that?" "I'd be a fine soothsayer if I didn't") deserves condign punishment: maybe, as Pseudolus himself suggests in another context, being trampled to death by a female water-buffalo in heat. On the other hand -- and feet, and the rest of him -- he wears a Roman tunic as to the manner born, or enslaved, and physically he can be inspired. One applauded his elaborate mime of pretended death even while wishing it to be over so we could get back to the show. Hes a nimble dancer, too; his dainty stepping in Free (a number thats Wayne Cilento's best contribution as choreographer) is delightful.

He shares the routine with Mike Nadajewski who plays Hero, the hero, opposite the equally enchanting Philia of Chilina Kennedy. These two -- he gauche and gobsmacked, she dumb and demure -- apart from being terrific singers, came close last year to being funnier than any of the designated comics. This year they truly are, partly owing to the absence of Stephen Ouimette, a genius clown. He's been replaced as Hysterium-slave-of-slaves by Steven Sutcliffe whos a very good actor, which isnt quite the same thing. He's also, at the risk of offending previous Hysteria, too good looking for the role; when he's forced into drag in the second act, theres nothing grotesque about it, hence nothing very hilarious. Randy Hughson as old man Senex is efficient and endearing, if not ideally cast; Brian Tree as other-old-man Erronius is ideally cast, and his seven increasingly exhausted circuits around the seven hills of Rome punctuate the action with the charming unexpectedness thats expected of them. Cliff Saunders' Lycus, buyer and seller of the flesh of beautiful women (for those of you who have no interest in pirates), wafts through the action, more inexplicably than ever; he's supposed to be a grasping merchant, not some kind of sprite. Dan Chameroys Miles Gloriosus is still undercut by the productions determination to make him look a fool before he can do it for himself, but he fights back more authoritatively than before. He's also the first Miles I've seen young enough to be almost credible as Philias twin. Damn, Ive given away the denouement, but I don't think you'll hold it against me. And, to be both fair and honest, this production is the first in which Ive been able to follow all the twists, involving the transfer of a ring from one finger to another to another, that makes the revelations possible. John Arnones set does all kinds of cute things, none of them necessary or even helpful. Forum is a farce, one of the best, and farces aren't meant to do cute. They're meant to mean business.

- A Funny Thing Happened on the Way to the Forum runs through Jan. 16 at the Canon Theatre. Visit mirvish.comor call 416-872-1212 for ticket information. robert.cushman@hotmail.com

2010-12-31-courageous-assassins-and-fern:
A few trends, some of them interlocking, from the departing theatrical year, in and around Toronto.

Desperation/Disintegration As they sang in Assassins: "Everybody has the right to be happy/even if at times they go to extremes." I can't remember a year in which there were so many powerful performances of characters driven to such extremities, physical and/or psychological. Two of these occurred in Buddies in Bad Times' production of Blasted, the British play by the suicidal young writer Sarah Kane, about all kinds of apocalypse. Michelle Monteith played a young woman in a self-protective shell, going in and out of fits. She's an uncanny actress. David Ferry is a very canny actor, who let his defences totally down as a fearful, predatory man whose later turmoils included being brutally blinded. There were profounder echoes of King Lear when Ferry presented us, naked and fearful, with what Lear recognized as "unaccommodated man," still preserving a kind of dignity. Jane Spidell went hauntingly mad, after a soigne start, in two different plays: Soulpepper's Doc and Peggy Pickit Sees The Face of God, the latter the central and much the most impressive panel of World Stage's Africa Trilogy. As the sequentially trusting, violated and vengeful Philomela of If We Were Birds, Tara Rosling was astonishingly present in all her moods. Jacquelyn French wrung tears, without begging for them, in The Light in the Piazza. Anusree Roy was devastating at the end of her own play Roshni (a duologue twice as good as her earlier monologues). Mike Ross, breaking new ground, had a virtuoso farcical melt-down in Jitters. Earlier he had been one of that corps of Assassins, who, with perfect musical and dramatic control, lost it, individually and as a collective. Graham Abbey was especially wonderful. Another National Anthem was the greatest musical number of the year.

Germans Nobody has bothered much with Teutonic drama, since they stopped doing Brecht. This year, it made a rewarding comeback. The aforementioned Peggy Pickit was the work of the divinely-named Roland Schimmelpfennig; it revitalized the middle-class domestic-battleground format by giving it a global context. It was given a superb production, directed by Liesl Tommy, from South Africa via the U.S.A. Franz Xaver Kroetz's Through the Leaves, which finds the lyrical in the prosaic, was finely done by Company Theatre, Philip Riccio directing. Maria Vacratsis' performance, perfect, showed us a woman surmounting desperation; Nicholas Campbell's vied with Ferry's in the broken-machismo stakes. (Good year for Campbell; he stood out in The Red Queen Effect, a show otherwise dismal.) Matthew Jocelyn's regime at CanadianStage got off to a brilliant start with Fernando Krapp Wrote Me This Letter, which also had notable extreme performances from Ashley Wright (extremely unpuncturable, until the end) and Ryan Hollyman (extremely physical, especially when terrified). All these plays had size, scope and imagination. And any games they played were serious, not silly. It strikes me that in this they resembled the best Canadian play, Michael Healey's Courageous, which arrived at the beginning of the year; only a couple of plays ( If We Were Birds, The Clockmaker, both also at the Tarragon) arrived to challenge it.

Mention of games brings me to Meta "Shows with The Musical in the title are always terrible." Those words of wisdom are from something called Stephen Harper The Musical, which unfortunately proved them true. So, on a much larger scale, did Rock of Ages, which didn't have the subtitle but behaved as if it did; it was a spoof of a spoof. So was Young Frankenstein. So was Legally Blonde The Musical and, probably, Priscilla Queen of the Desert, though those last two, to be honest, were fun. The meta trend may be spreading to more august addresses. Stratford's production of Shakespeare's weakest comedy might have been subtitled The Two Gentlemen of Verona The Play.

Miranda Two plays -- Judith Thompson's Such Creatures and Zorana Kydd's Soulseek-- involved characters with unreliable memories of having played the heroine in The Tempest. More meta, I guess. The real deal turned up at Stratford, in what was essentially the Christopher Plummer show, in which he magisterially acted both through and around the words.

Festivals Stratford's company was unevenly divided. The Tempest was essentially Plummer, plus Julyana Soelistya's extraordinary Ariel, diminutive and blue-bleached. The Winter's Tale (plain) and As You Like It (fancy) were more solidly cast and performed, all down the line. The season's best shows: Kiss Me Kate ( Brush up Your Shakespeare was the year's second best number) and, leaving nothing to be desired, Peter Pan. The Shaw similarly did well by its patron saint, but even better by others, with Harvey and The Cherry Orchard; Jim Mezon proved himself a great actor in the latter, and re-proved it in John Bull's Other Island. Most worrying trend: the retreat, at Stratford and Soulpepper, from un-obvious classics --other than Soulpepper's A Month in the Country, another case, in Laszlo Marton's production, of actors going rewardingly to extremes. Soulpepper also had a series of lab productions that weren't available for review but, I can now reveal, were among the year's highlights. One was an experimental Cherry Orchard, cut down to its major characters, one of whom -- Brendan Gall's Lopakhin -- was the best I've ever seen. The others, Diego Matamoros' solo version of Borges' The Aleph and the academy's bewitching Window on Toronto, will be back next year, in the main bill.

2011-01-03-having-a-laugh-insecurity-and:
I nSecurity (CBC), whose title is its best joke, starts with an Ottawa-based team of agents debating whether the code name of their most intrepid member is Goldilocks or Mama Bear, and finally giving up on the idea altogether. That just about sets the tone. They then fail to rescue her from her current daredevil assignment.

These operatives--there are six of them--belong to a mercifully fictitious National Intelligence and Security Agency (NISA) and judging from the first two episodes, the only reason any of them are still alive and employed is that their opponents are even more insecure and unintelligent than they are. The idea, I guess, is to satirize the equally implausible inhabitants of the 24 universe: those supermen and women, goodies and baddies alike, whose martial skills are only equalled by their deductive prowess, and whose computers never malfunction. We'd all like to take them down a peg, and the idea might make a good half-hour spoof. I question whether its going to make 13 of them.

Leading the pack, if only by virtue of being marginally more competent than her fellows, is Alex(Natalie Lisinska), a blonde spitfire who can really kick ass, and quite frequently kicks the right one. Claude (Remy Girard, from numerous Denys Arcand movies) also has some authority, chiefly as a lethargic, roly-poly whipper-up of souffles, to be consumed during stake-outs. Some of his colleagues feel that such haute cuisine lowers their status as tough guys and would prefer to order in pizza; but they greedily consume Claudes creations nonetheless. Then we have Peter (William deVry), top guy on the official food chain, and the obligatory self-appointed office Lothario; Jojo (Grace Lynn Kung) who's brusque and Asian; N'udu (Richard Yearwood) whos violent and African; and Burt (Matthew MacFadzean) who really, really fancies himself.

The show is officially described as character-driven comedy, a claim that rests somewhere between ambitious and delusional. Episode 1 has the gang trying to bust a uranium-smugglingoutfit(Saskatchewan to Tehran); the big giggle is that, when Alex gets captured, the doctor assigned to torture her is someone she knew in high school, and a wimp to boot (which Alex pretty much does). In Episode 2, which is marginally better, they infiltrate a Russian group who have stolen the plans to Canadas incredibly secret nuclear submarine, but whose efficiency is weakened by their propensity for having sex on the job: with Alex or Peter or one another. NISA's own secret weapon is that our clean half-dozen always seem to operate in three groups of two apiece, so that there's generally one couple left to ride to the rescue of the others. Well, that and dumb luck, in the shape of dumb opponents. Thats the problem.

Even the wildest crime-spoofs generally incorporate some real threat. So far, InSecurity has none.

Episodes (TMN) has more going for it in that, rather than satirizing a fantasy genre, it satirizes the making of TV itself; so it has more connection with real life, if only with a very rarefied section of it. Its starting point is the process by which smart British comedy shows are bought by American companies, rewritten, re-shot and destroyed: as in Fawlty Towers, Coupling, The Office -- well, perhaps not The Office.

So: in what is, fittingly, a U.K.-U. S. co-production, we have Sean Lincoln (Stephen Mangan) and his wife Beverly (Tamsin Greig), authors of a BAFTA-award winning show called Lymans Boys, set in an exclusive academy, which attracts the fervent admiration of Merc Lepidus (John Pankow), even though, it transpires, he hasn't seen it. Someone who has says it reminds him of The History Boys, a charge Sean and Beverly hotly deny, even though their principal character, who's also the schools principal, is supposedly played by an actor who strongly resembles The History Boys Richard Griffiths: not surprisingly since Griffiths himself acts the actor.

The high point of Episode 1 of Episodes is Griffiths' U.S. audition for a role he thought he'd made his own, and his philosophical acceptance of Mercs discovery that "hes -- I can't quite put my finger on it -- too British." So they call in Matt Le-Blanc -- the real Matt LeBlanc -- who, as is obvious to everybody including himself, is totally wrong for the role. At least he is until the authors are part charmed, part blackmailed, into re-conceiving the character as an all-American hockey coach. (New title: Pucks.)

There are plenty of things to object to here. Hollywood philistinism is a barn-door of a target, already riddled with bullets, and Merc's grossness is, well, gross; he greets his new British subjects with a different fake-British accent every week, and it makes your skin crawl. Sean and Beverly in Beverly Hills arent in themselves all that magnetic, though Greigs sharpness (she's like a cut-rate Emma Thompson) registers more strongly than Mangan's tousled amiability. Theres a tiresome running gag in which theyre never recognized by the guard at their luxury compound, who seems to work a 24-hour shift. However, the voice that says "front door ajar" every time they open it did crack me up, and our sightings of the studio's head of comedy are hilarious; she's the most unsmiling woman you saw in your life, and thoroughly credible.

Above all, and perhaps surprisingly, theres LeBlanc himself, whos become the Gen X Dean Martin: a master of amiable self-satire. There's some texture both to the writing and acting of his role; he alternates between boorish and sensible. He seems, all told, to be the only member of the Friends ensemble currently doing honest work. ( Friends' David Crane is one of Episodes' creators.) Both these shows try hard to seem laid-back. Episodes shows that relaxation is easier with a real subject to lay back on.
