2011-01-04-actress-was-forceful-and-viva:
The end of last year was darkened by the death, shockingly early and sudden, of Gina Wilkinson. Wilkinson, who was 50 and seemed younger, had a triple career as actress, playwright and director. Her acting was typically, as she was herself, forceful and vivacious, a combination that served her well in Shakespearean comedy; I remember her most as Beatrice in Much Ado About Nothing, and especially as Rosaline in Loves Labour's Lost, both of them at the much-missed Festival of Classics in Oakville', Ont.s Coronation Park.

She wrote two adventurous plays with lively, speakable scripts: My Mothers Feet and Whistle Me Home, the latter a monologue in a bath, brilliantly performed by Tom Rooney. (Wilkinson and Rooney had been partners for the past 10 years; they had long planned to marry, and in fact did so shortly before her death, in the hospital.) But it was as a director that she seemed likely to make her greatest mark. Indeed she was already doing so.

After making her debut on the Toronto Fringe in 1997, she worked her way up at theatres all over the country (plus one in Germany), and had a decisive

breakthrough with her Shaw Festival production of Born Yesterday in 2009. She took this over at short notice, and demonstrated complete command of the Festival's daunting main stage. The following season her lunchtime production of J.M. Barrie's Half an Hour was less spectacular but at least equally impressive, and she was due to return to the Shaw this season to direct Candida.

Last year she had two very different shows on at the Young Centre in Toronto; Marcel Aymes Clerambard (for George Brown Theatre School), a French classic in the literary-whimsical tradition by which she professed herself amiably bemused, and for Soulpepper, Brian Friels Faith Healer. She was in Winnipeg in November, directing another Irish play, Conor McPherson's The Seafarer, for the Manitoba Theatre Centre, when she received a diagnosis of cervical cancer. If ever an artist was cut off in her prime, she was.
2011-01-06-antebelt-em-out-loud:
What we have here is a delayed Canadian premiere. Parade was originally commissioned by Livent Inc., who workshopped it in Toronto, a dozen years ago. Livent then produced it in New York, but the company imploded and the production was seen no more. The show now returns to where it started in a joint production by Acting Up Stage, who specialize in musicals, and Studio 180, who specialize in plays on public themes. Parade being a musical on public themes, the combination ought to be ideal, in the event the show remains what it always was: interesting, ambitious and flawed.

The main problem is that, in trying to tell two stories, Parade shortchanges both. The subject is the case of Leo Frank, an American Jew from the Northern states who settled in Atlanta, Ga., and who in 1913 was tried and found guilty of the murder of a 13-year-old girl, Mary Phagan, who worked in the Atlanta pencil factory at which he was the supervisor. It's clear that Frank was railroaded, the victim of a xenophobic culture still licking its wounds from the Civil War. The show's first act takes us as far as the trial. The second is mainly concerned with Frank's efforts, and especially those of his wife, Lucille, to appeal the verdict. The marriage of Leo and Lucille, who come closer

in adversity than they had ever been before, is one of the two stories. The other is that of the town itself, and by extension of the whole Southern consciousness. In theory, of course, the two narratives should be one. In practice, it feels as if they're alternating.

Leo, in particular, seems alienated from the action, and not just because he spends most of it in jail. He's sketched in for us, but only sketched, as a pettish, repressed man whose demeanour attracts as much suspicion as his religion. He also has the perennial problem of victims in drama: Because he doesn't get to do anything, it's easier to feel sorry for him than to feel moved or involved.

TheFranks'relationshipgetsfuller treatment from Jason Robert Brown's score than it does from Alfred Uhry's script; the couple have a propulsively hopeful duet, and then a serenely rhapsodic one, to both of which Michael Therriault and Tracy Michailidis bring the requisite urgency if not the hoped-for glow. Therriault excellently depicts the buttoned-up Leo of the beginning (this, after The Producers, is his second musical role as a nebbish called Leo) but he doesn't get much chance to take it further, and his growth in courage and dignity is stated rather than explored. His final moment of heroism comes out of nowhere. Michailidis has a more active role, but she's done in, at least in part, by the authors' second thoughts, which strike me as unwise.

The script performed here is one reworked by Uhry and Brown for a London production at the Donmar Warehouse. It streamlines the second act, most of which revolves around Lucille's successful attempt to get Georgia's governor to reopen her husband's case, which he had previously regarded with urbane disinterest. He's potentially the most interesting character in the piece, a man conflictedly doing right being always more compelling than one who's being done wrong, and the scenes in which he cross-examines the various perjured witnesses are the most exciting in the show. But the complexities of his relationship with the case and with Lucille have been ironed out.

Gone are any hints of flirtatiousness, including his escorting her to a state house ball. Gone are the conscience-stricken second thoughts of the judge at Leo's trial. Jay Turvey plays the governor sympathetically, but the reduced circumstances are unfair to him, to the story and to the audience. Also to George Masswohl who is twice wasted: as the judge and as an emblematic Old Soldier who appears at the beginning and the end as a representative of the embittered Confederacy, but has no existence in between, as man or symbol.

This brings us to the show's second weakness: its failure, certainly in this production, to do justice to injustice, both inside and outside the courtroom. Brown has musicalized the trial itself resourcefully, but without capturing the full outrageous scope of the proceedings; as often, you learn more about these from the program than from the play. You find, for example, that the viciously anti-Semitic demagogue played by Mark Uhre was actually a newspaper editor; he seems here to be a deranged evangelist. Joel Greenberg is usually a good director of political drama (and of lynching dramas, cf. The Laramie Project), but the manoeuvrings in and around the governor's mansion hardly register.

Paul Sportelli's musical direction is especially taut here; so is Daren A. Herbert whose double performance as a terrified janitor and a contemptuous convict is the strongest of the night. He shares with Alana Hibbert a rousing second-act opener in which two black Atlantans get to exult that, for once in the South, another minority group is getting it. It's one of too few occasions on which the piece takes us inside the thoughts of the community it's depicting.

Meanwhile, the plain staging shortchanges the imagery implicit in the title. The murder takes place on Memorial Day (described by Frank as a typical Southern notion -- glorifying a defeat) and two more Memorial Day parades come and go before the drama is done. This doesn't quite unify the action, but it strengthens it. Parade needs that strength. Its subject-matter is hardly grimmer than that of Sweeney Todd, Assassins or Cabaret, but those shows leave you with irony or tragedy or both. Feeling drained is good; feeling depressed isn't.

- Parade runs until Jan. 22. Call 416-368-3110 or visit canadianstage.comfor more information. robert.cushman@hotmail.com

2011-01-08-the-case-against-anger-manage:
Charlotte Dean, who consistently designs the most elegant sets and costumes around, has outdone herself in Tarragon's production of The Misanthrope. The action takes place in a seductively curved white and cerise apartment, the col-ours of the walls and furnishings finding echoes in the actors' clothes. In the last scene they sport periwigs the colour of pink grapefruit, each shaped slightly differently from the others. This is an updated production of Moliere's comedy but the finale finds the characters partying in fancy dress, in knowing homage to their 17th-century prototypes. Martin Crimp's 1996 translation, like the people who inhabit it, is nothing if not knowing.

It actually calls itself a "version." It keeps the original's shape and action, and much of its dialogue, but it changes the locale to London, and diverges in several other respects. Alceste, the title character and the only one to retain his former name, is now a permanently disgruntled dramatist. "Surely as a playwright you're aware," says his friend John, formerly Philinte, "of sounding like something straight out of Moliere;" to which Alceste aptly replies, "Jesus Christ, you think you're so clever." Celimene, the fashion-conscious coquette to whom he is agonizingly enslaved, is Jennifer, an American movie star; it's in her hotel suite that the action unfolds. The marquesses who attend her are now her agent and a blue-blooded and terminally vain English actor. Moliere's Oronte, the influential courtier who unwisely solicits Alceste's opinion of his poem, is now a theatre critic with delusions of creativity.

Crimp's couplets aren't equal to those of Richard Wilbur (whose translation is being done at Stratford this year) or of Tony Harrison (whose translation was done in Toronto a couple of years back in an arresting production by Bertolt Brecht's granddaughter). At one point he even rhymes "paracetamol" with "acceptable," which certainly isn't acceptable, though it does provoke a derisive reply from Alceste, who's more critical than any critic. "Nothing's more effete," he says, "than the moral contortions of the self-proclaimed elite," and that certainly strikes home, not least because, in some ways, it can apply to him as well. Crimp's is a racy, punchy text that succeeds superbly in creating a world. Admittedly, it's a more trivial world than Moliere himself created; he, as actor-playwright-manager, was as much a showbiz creature as anyone, but as a satirist he took on bigger targets. His Alceste antagonized a man who might have had him sent to the Bastille; Crimp's risks only gossip and bad reviews. But the trivialization is itself a part of the point, and Richard Rose's production gets it dazzlingly across.

He has a magnificent Alceste in Stuart Hughes who gives the performance of his life: surly and magnetic not by turns but simultaneously. He's a 1950s rebel -- John Osborne's Jimmy Porter or Kingsley Amis' Jim Dixon--thrown into a glib 1990s society that likes to think of itself as "post-modern": a provincial among the metropolitans (accents and manners throughout are spot-on) and angrier than ever. What distinguishes him from some others is that his anger isn't a pose; it's also, for the most part, justified, even if out of proportion to most of its targets. And of course when it comes to the woman he loves, he can't follow through; he rages but he relents. When he seems to be treating her the same way he treats his enemies, monotony momentarily threatens, but by the end we can see that his romantic obsession is just another side of the same unalterable man. Hughes keeps the vitriol and the vulnerability going full-strength; he's impossible, and underneath it all a good and even likeable man. You can see why Patrick Galligan's pliable, affable (and admirably acted) John wants to leave the party and talk him around, though in this version he's soon dissuaded.

The production doesn't go to the cynical extremes of some others. Even so, its revelation -- Hughes apart -- is the radical transformation of Alceste's other confidante, who loves him but isn't going to wait around forever, into a reporter for whom no confidences are sacred, and whose revelations precipitate the denouement. This gives the play something it's never had before, narrative suspense; it also gives Michelle Giroux, whom Stratford was mad to lose, the opportunity for a devastatingly observed and delivered performance of an iPad tapping scribe, nasally languid behind her big black specs. David Storch is equally delightful as a critic in tight pants, insinuating himself obsequiously through doorways and leaping beseechingly over couches -- the latter a habit that Alceste amusingly picks up -- before turning nasty. (He's called Covington, a name that's a hybrid of two current London reviewers. I obviously got out just in time.) Brandon McGibbon and Julian Richings are suitably vulpine hangers-on, and Maria Ricossa makes something, though nothing definite enough, of a role that never seems to come out right: a jealous prude who has here been transformed into Jennifer's jealous acting teacher. Andrea Runge plays Jennifer, and seems, visually and verbally, to be trying much too hard. The score (Mike Ross and Nicole Bellamy) gives 20th-century tunes a 17th-century gloss: as in, Don't Knock Baroque. There's an equivalent visual joke in the way the actors treat the fourth wall. At first you think they're addressing the audience, old comedy style; then you realize they're preening in front of an invisible mirror: all of them, Alceste included. Everyone is sick of self-love, misanthropes included.

- The Misanthrope runs through Feb. 6 at the Tarragon Theatre. Call 416- 531-1827 or visit tarragontheatre.comfor more information. robert.cushman@hotmail.com

2011-01-12-bullets-over-broadway:
ASSASSINS

The Theatre Centre, Toronto

---

'All you have to do is move your little finger, move your little finger and -- you can change the world.'

The Toronto revival of Assassins opened to the press on the day of the Tucson massacre, making a show that already seemed scarily prophetic horribly immediate. All the elements that seem to have been in play on Saturday in Arizona, and then some, are given dramatic form in John Weidman's book and Stephen Sondheim's music and lyrics. The sense of grievance, justified or otherwise. The almost mythological fixation on a scapegoat. The personal craziness enflamed by an apocalyptic political culture -- by a rhetoric of destructiveness that has always been with us, from both sides, but now has a more sophisticated media system than ever before to amplify it. The sense -- indelibly conveyed in the show's climactic number, Another National Anthem -- of being left out, of being cast as a failure in what's supposed to be the American success story and of realizing that, whatever the promises, "it's never gonna happen, is it?" Easy access to guns doesn't hurt either.

As The Gun Song, quoted above, goes on to say, "when you've a gun -- everybody pays attention." It's crooned, in beautiful lullaby harmony, by three killers of U.S. presidents: Leon Czolgosz who shot Mc-Kinley, Charles Guiteau who shot Garfield and John Wilkes Booth for whom no identification is necessary, which is part of the show's point. There are six other principal characters, each of whom tried to assassinate the president of his or her day. Five of them failed. The sixth is Lee Harvey Oswald.

Even without the fresh context, the remount of Assassins, as jointly produced by Birdland and Talk Is Free, would be a stupendous evening. It was the best thing to happen in the Toronto theatre last year and it's every bit as good on its return. Adam Brazier's production is an ensemble triumph, with the added kick that the ensemble is made up of star performances. That's part of the reason that Another National Anthem is so shattering. It's a chorus number that ends with everybody singing the same words, stomping the same steps. (Cheers by the way to Linda Garneau, the choreographer, whose contribution I failed to recognize last time.) Their impact as a collective is intense enough; it's multiplied as you glance from one to the next and realize that each is coming from the same individual place that's been so powerfully established earlier. I don't think I've encountered anything quite like it before in a musical.

Along with the shooters themselves, there are two other characters present: a carnival proprietor, taunting them into greater despair, and a Balladeer who does the same thing by dangling false hopes in front of them. They turn on him, and in effect make him one of themselves. He becomes Oswald, the only assassin we haven't met yet, persuaded to kill the president instead of killing himself, and so earn a place in a historical line that even he has heard of. "Brutus assassinated Caesar -- what? -- 2,000 years ago" says Booth, the tempter, "and here's a high school dropout with a $1.25 an hour job in Dallas, Texas, who knows who

he was. And they say fame is fleeting." Weidman's writing is as weighty as anything in the American theatre, musical or dramatic, in the past 20 years. It's stark and ironic and often very funny. But it's never giggly or demeaning or smug; it restores the tarnished honour of black comedy.

PaulMcQuillan'sBooth, with his flashing eye and patrician drawl and exquisite singing, is even more imposing than before; likewise, in a different key, Steve Ross's self-inflating Guiteau, cakewalking his way to the gallows. Graham Abbey's Samuel Byck, paranoia in a Santa suit and a toy car, was hardly susceptible of improvement; his monologue, in which pleasantry gets increasingly soaked in hate, remains a marvel of both phrasing and feeling. Geoffrey Tyler's Oswald and Christopher Stanton's John Hinckley are fine fragments of social and psychological wreckage. Newcomers include Alex Fiddes' haunting Czolgosz; Lisa Horner's Sara Jane Moore, hilarious hippie housewife; and Whitney Ross-Barris, who movingly sings Something Just Broke, the show's nearest approach to an epiphany.

Actors double as instrumentalists, the reed section making especially witty fleeting appearances in Unworthy of Your Love, a '70s country ballad more poignantly sappy than the real thing, sung by Hinckley and Squeaky Fromme to an absent Jodie Foster and Charles Manson respectively. Sondheim has furnished one of his most apparently forbidding subjects with one of his most ingratiating and accessible scores, one whose journey through Americana may even surpass Follies as pastiche composition with a steely double edge. The show ranks among Sondheim's masterpieces, alongside its immediate predecessor Into the Woods. Two very different approaches to that most abused of words and subjects, community.

- Assassins runs until Jan. 23 at the Theatre Centre in Toronto. Call 416-504-7529 or visit theatrecentre.org. robert.cushman@sympatico.ca

2011-01-12-totally-believable-as-the-war:
I seem to be spending too much of my time writing memorials and obituaries. As well as Domini Blythe and Gina Wilkinson, Canadian theatre recently lost the witty and urbane Graham Harley, probably most familiar as one of the two thesps whose waspish song parodies heralded each episode of Slings and Arrows; and now we're mourning Peter Donaldson, who died last week at the age of 57 and whose death leaves perhaps the most glaring of all the holes in the fabric.

Donaldson was the heir apparent. He spent most of his career at Stratford; and though there are other remarkable Canadian actors of his generation, there were none who seemed so obviously destined for the great Shakespearean roles: to be the next William Hutt or Christopher Plummer or both.

Craggy" was the adjective that came to mind in connection with Donaldson; his voice, his face. So when he crumbled onstage, the impact was powerful. It certainly was in the two great tragic roles he played at Stratford: Timon of Athens, in which he went magnetically from prodigal to misanthrope; and Antony in Antony and Cleopatra, in which he played the heros masochistic joy in self-abasement. Lucy Peacock, who acted opposite him in many plays (though not that one), recalls that he was "totally believable as the warrior."

He was also a superb comedian (and married to a great comedienne, Sheila McCarthy), who excelled at portraying an impregnable, off-hand eccentricity. It made him, three years ago in what turned out to be his last Stratford season, a practically definitive Don Armado in Loves Labour's Lost.

His career, though, wasn't all Stratford. He was rehearsing Glengarry Glen Ross for Soulpepper when he received his cancer diagnosis. In Glengarry, he was unflinchingly nasty as the most vicious of David Mamets dog-eating salesmen. And he was explosive again in George Walkers And So It Goes, a role that exploited his gift for sardonic twinkle. If there had to be an epiphany, it wasn't a bad one.

2011-01-15-at-least-the-bird-s-titular-f:
Noel Coward once wrote of The Seagull, or it may have been The Wild Duck, that he hated plays in which there was a stuffed bird sitting on the bookcase shrieking "I'm the title! I'm the title!" The bird in The Bird is also stuffed and even more irritating. At least Ibsen and Chekhov gave us wildfowl who served a specific purpose in the lives of their plays' fully developed heroines. In Sonja Mills' new play, the significance is spread around and hopelessly diluted. In prosaic terms, the bird owes its presence, and its present stuffed state, to the fact that one of the characters is a taxidermist, half of a lesbian couple who live high up in a luxurious-looking Toronto condo. They're throwing a party whose action makes it "finally clear that we, all of us, are no better off than a bird who has hopelessly smashed into the 40th floor window of a skyscraper, unaware there was any obstacle in its path at all." That's even though some of us live in nice spaces and have good jobs.

The quotation above comes from a plot-and-theme synopsis that was issued to the critics and for which I am profoundly grateful, since I certainly couldn't have worked any of it out -- the thematic part anyway -- on my own. Ordinary punters presumably have to do without, though they can read a program note in which the producing company, Union State Theatre, announces that its mandate (from whom?) is to present work "which integrates text with movement." I thought that was what all productions try to do, unless they're either mime or stationary recitations. I did notice a certain awkwardness in some of the blocking, but I'd put it down to the director, Ruth Madoc-Jones, being defeated by some of her author's more improbable contrivances regarding entrances and exits. But I now see that it was a conscious stylistic choice, and that the show has a "movement director," Clare Preuss, to prove it. (And on the subject of programs, what's wrong with the good old tradition of listing the characters' names on the main page alongside those of the actors, rather than having the audience hunt through the cast bios to discover who's playing whom?)

Even with two directors, The Bird is the worst-acted play to have arrived on a Toronto stage in a long time (and, no, I'm not forgetting Soulseek). I spent some time wondering whether the script might have sounded more credible if the players had delivered it with a bit more naturalness and a lot more nuance, or if they were forced into strident artificiality by a text that consists entirely of people bitching. Quite possibly all concerned got helplessly locked into the same spiral. Anyway, Mia the bird-stuffer lives with Kate who's in marketing, and they've invited Kate's new assistant, Petula, a.k.a. Petty, over for drinks and chat. Petty brings her husband, Gord, and also her brother, Boo, and his wife, Donna. All these pairings are acutely dysfunctional, both intra-and extra-murally. Kate suspects that Petty in fact may be Mia's new pet. Donna is acidly, and continuously, contemptuous of Boo, who's in turn convinced that she's out every night cheating on him, quite possibly with Gord. It doesn't even stop at sex. Boo is a bank manager, and Kate one of his customers, each complaining that the other has been extremely rude. This disclosure drives Boo to tears and Kate to a level of abrasiveness that may be even higher than the one she started the play with, though it's hard to tell. There's a seventh character, Mia's heavily pregnant sister, Spencer, who seems to be there mainly so the others can discuss the pros and cons of smoking (either tobacco or weed) in her presence; just for a laugh, she herself is the heaviest puffer of them all. When all other avenues have been exhausted, the play throws in some remembered incest. To be fair, August: Osage County employed the same scattershot approach and it got a Pulitzer. But at least it had some wit, and characters with a modicum of depth. The people here are dummies, set up merely to knock one another down. Towards the end, there's some attempt to broaden the focus. Boo complains that because he's a banker, everyone blames him for the recession, whereas marketers like Kate, pushing useless goods, are equally responsible. My impression is most people at the moment hate both professions equally, and the play possibly agrees. It seems to want to implicate all the other characters as well, selfish things that they are. It also seems to want us to feel sorry for them, without giving them enough humanity to warrant either reaction. Throw in a few lines about the economy, and you get marks for sociological concern. Add a symbolic dead bird, and you also get credit for compassion and poetic imagery. It's a fair summation of what's wrong with Canadian playwriting.

To be fair, again, Mills' previous, and slightly better, work The Danish Play seemed to me equally forced and artificial, but everyone else loved it; it got raves and awards and revivals and everything. There, too, unnatural writing seemed to breed unnatural acting; it had one good performance (and not the one that won the raves and awards). I don't see any of the present team romping home with Doras, but again, what do I know? Astrid Van Wieren gives the keynote loud performance as Kate; it isn't so much that she's worse than the others, it's just that there's more of her. The most tolerable is Bruce Hunter as Boo, perhaps because he gets to show some variety. Before he becomes hateful, he's allowed to be pitiable; he keeps saying he wants to kill himself, and it's hard to resist that. But, really, it's for the birds.

- The Bird runs through Jan. 30 at Buddies in Bad Times Theatre. Call 416-975-8555 or visit buddiesinbadtimes.comfor more information. robert.cushman@hotmail.com

2011-01-18-he-mined-the-energy-in-the-te:
Note: Obituary of Michael Langham.

Michael Langham, who died this past weekend in England at the age of 91, was the second artistic director of the Stratford Festival. He ran it from 1956 to 1967, and returned many times later as a guest. He was, with the single exception of Trevor Nunn, the most consistently inspired Shakespearean director whose work I have known. There's remarkable unanimity among those who worked with him about what he actually did. Brian Bedford summed it up perfectly: "He mined the energy in the text."

Bedford, who was in half a dozen of Langhams later productions at Stratford and elsewhere, also says he made every second of the play important. He had a strong opinion about how it should come out of the actor. Like a dog with a bone he wouldnt let ago. According to Diego Matamoros, a member of Langham's young company at Stratford in the '80s, "he understood what each character did in the play; how the story got told." Martha Henry, whose Stratford career began under Langhams auspices in 1962, says, He knew the play better than anyone. ... He was demanding but not rigid. You felt that hed actually known Shakespeare and walked hand-in-hand with him. And Michael Bawtree, his dramaturge at Stratford and later the director of the Atlantic Theatre Festival in Wolfville with Langham as his associate and eminence grise: "He had an incredible eye for the psychological implications of language ... an instinct for looking behind the words." I'd say, as an audience, that he made the text reverberate.

Langham was British, born in 1919, and the formative experience of his life came when he was serving during the Second World War. He was captured, and -- almost as a survival tactic -- started directing plays cast from his fellow POWs. This military beginning must have made him fearless.

He emerged with a commitment to spartan aesthetics and community service that was expanded, but not fundamentally altered, when he met his mentor, the flamboyant genius Tyrone Guthrie, who groomed him at the Old Vic in London and then appointed him his successor at Stratford. Langham's first season was the last in the Stratford tent, and included a triumphant Henry V, marking the festival debut of the 26-year-old Christopher Plummer, inaugurating a long collaboration. Plummer has said that he literally owes Langham his career: "Without his talent, taste, intellect and wit, God knows where I might have gone with my life."

Langham himself, after his Stratford reign, went to the Guthrie Theatre at Minneapolis, to the La Jolla Playhouse in San Diego and to running the acting program at the Juilliard School in New York. He did some of his finest work in Wolfville, much of it in collaboration with his wife, the actress and director Helen Burns (who survives him).

Stratford now has a directors training program named after Langham, and there was always hope that he would return to the festival. He was talking of directing Hamlet, which he felt he'd never got right, and of returning to The Merchant of Venice. The sharpness and the mental energy, as I and others discovered in phone and other conversations in the last couple of years, remained unblunted and undimmed. He was past 90, and still had much to give us.

2011-01-19-clown-on-the-farm:
WINGFIELD: LOST & FOUND

Panasonic Theatre, Toronto

---

A t the beginning of Wingfield: Lost & Found, Walt Wingfield's herd of cows wanders off. In this, the seventh play of the Wingfield series, Walt, stockbroker-turned-farmer, is still writing rueful, humorous letters to the editor of a local paper, detailing his adventures and misadventures in Persephone township. The cow-catching, or at least cow-hunting, episode is something of a teaser, in that it has nothing to do, in plot terms, with the rest of the piece. In thematic terms, it's very relevant; see the title. It's also very funny. The unpractised efforts of Walt and assorted friends, neighbours and relations to maintain contact via texting are especially hilarious.

This Wingfield play, like all the others, is written by Dan Needles, directed by Douglas Beattie and acted, all on his own, by Rod Beattie, whose timing, sympathy and vocal versatility remain immaculate. This one is about a drought. Walt's well dries up, which is bad enough, and it seems to be connected to all the other wells around, which is obviously worse. He doesn't know where on his property to start drilling for water, and the cheerfully malevolent firm of professional diggers who charge him $8,000 per failed excavation are no help. Somebody suggests calling in the water-diviners or, as they're known locally, water-witches. Walt, who has been around Persephone long enough to know when to keep his skepticism in check, interviews three of them, this despite the warning of Maggie, his enchantingly soft-voiced and sensible wife, that three witches have been known to signal tragedy.

In fact the real true witch has been around all the time,

and everybody knows it. This is Delbert, the estranged father of Walt's dairy-farming neighbour Don, who seems to have lost his touch: both for finding water and playing the piano. How he regains these things, and how all kinds of metaphorical fences are mended, is the matter of the play. The losses include Walt's anniversary present to Maggie. The resolution of this comes right at the end of the play, and is thoroughly predictable -- the kind of pleasing predictability that makes the theatre, if not the world, go round. On its own it would be sentimental; as part of a pattern it feels both right and rewarding.

One piece of the pattern, involving the linguistic and bureaucratic problems of emailing money to Italy, feels like padding; and the overarching threat to he community from a water-bottling company doesn't register as strongly as seems intended. But the writing Beattie keeps the central tension going, while throwing in wry details, such as Walt's mathematical demonstration that his carbon footprint in the country is orders of magnitude heavier than ever it was in the country. The acting Beattie switches from one role to another, and then another, and then back, with his usual unassuming knife-edge virtuosity. Old Delbert, slow and deliberate, is a weighty new creation; Walt's brother-in-law Freddie remains the most entertaining of the familiar ones. (He's an oracular stammerer: a brilliant device.) We discover, once again, that we could listen to Walt and company till the cows come home.

The ensemble work in Ash is as good as the ensemble work in Assassins. In this, the fourth and last play in the Theatrefront cycle known as The Mill, we shift from a haunted past to a post-apocalyptic, or maybe just apocalyptic, future. We are still in the mill, which seems to be the safest place to be. The world outside is covered in the ash of the title, the result of some unspecified disaster that might be nuclear or ecological or, very likely, both. Inside, five young adults huddle together, hoarding and dividing their painfully meagre rations; and their interaction, under Vikki Anderson's pitch-perfect direction, fills up much of the play.

The five are known, at least in their current habitat, as Beaver (Maev Beaty), Rabbit (Frank Cox O'Connell), Bear (Eric Goulem), Fox (Ryan Hollyman) and Bird (Michelle Monteith), and the collective rhythm of their performance is remarkable. They seem telepathically linked. Individually, they're all excellent, though two stand out: O'Connell, gangling and embarrassed as the one with the most detailed memories of a former life, and the miraculous Monteith as the de facto den mother, who cooks and parcels out the provisions and who, from our first sight of her, is obviously on track to be a real mother. Monteith gives extraordinarily centred performances of women at physical and mental extremes, and what she does here, especially in scenes concerning childbirth, is uncanny.

The actors in The Mill have remained constant, but each episode has had a different author and director. Ash is written by Damien Atkins, who tells an exciting story, while making his way through a landscape previously charted by William Golding, Cormac McCarthy and, closer to home and surprisingly, Judith Thompson; some tense and tender scenes towards the end recall Crackwalker. Before we get there, stocks grow low, jealousies grow high, anger flares and violence erupts. Atkins writes dialogue and action that his actors can feed on. Where he's less successful is in linking this final instalment to those that have gone before. The three episodes that preceded the current Great Leap Forward, traced the story of the eponymous lumber mill backwards from 1854 to 1636. We found that it was built on what was previously Wendat land, and that its subsequent history was one of rape, both physical and territorial, and of some especially grisly deaths. ( Saw, meet Mill.) Presiding over the whole saga was the spirit of Lyca, a girl half-Huron and half-European, whose own mother and grandmother had been violated and who was killed by the then-current mill-owner in 1834; since, at that point, she was already 200 years old, it's hardly surprising that, though dead, she refused to lie down. She was already out for revenge and, in the current play, she still is, egged on by her mother, played very effectively as a hologram (by Michelle Latimer, reprising a role she formerly did as flesh and blood). However, given the extreme external circumstances, Lyca's intervention here seems hardly necessary. One complicating factor is that we don't know whether the whole world has been devastated, or just Canada, or just the neighbourhood. The two fables, those inside and outside the mill, don't exactly cancel one another out, but they do tend to crowd.

Rather mysteriously, Lyca, who's embodied in the other three plays by the dangerously ethereal Holly Lewis, is played in this one by Natasha Greenblatt, who's almost equally haunting but not quite. The actress's father, Richard Greenblatt, appears as a character actually called Father; it's he who has taken in the five young'uns, given them their new furry and feathery names, and generally infantilized them: for their own good, he says, but also for his own ends. For much of the play, he's absent, foraging. When he returns, it's to tell his instant family to stay indoors, as the world outside is even bleaker than they'd imagined; as, in these plays, it generally has been. Indeed, the fine line between protection and exploitation has been one of The Mill's recurring themes. Anyway, he also lights the fuse that leads to the play's sequence of explosions. Hollyman, who has glowered and grumbled throughout, turns up the threat: an interesting change of pace for an actor I generally associate with gentleness. Goulem, in his best performance of the cycle, keeps springing surprises. Beaty surprises, too, though some of her changes of front seem to come out of nowhere.

There is less Grand Guignol in this play than in its predecessors, but Anderson's production maintains the same, literally awesome, technical standards: in Gillian Gallow's brooding set, Richard Feren's scary sonics, and especially in Andrea Lundy's lighting. One trivial note: The mill has a precious stream of pure water running beneath it, just like the one in Wingfield Lost and Found, which opened in Toronto a couple of nights earlier. A less trivial note: I'm not sure that the overall tale of exploitation and expiation works as a foundational Canadian myth, which seems to have been the intention. But then I've only been here 20 years. Anyway, all four plays are now running in repertory and open for inspection -- on Mill Street.

- The Mill runs in repertory through Jan. 29 at the Young Centre. Call 416- 866-8666 or visit youngcentre.cafor ticket information. robert.cushman@hotmail.com

In Ruined, form and content are at war and content wins. Lynn Nottage's play is set in what it hurts to call the Democratic Republic of Congo, and its constructed on the naturalistic Broadway model: well-made except for some loose ends. But its subject is endless civil war with the issues hopelessly muddied and with nearly everyone an actual or potential victim. The women, of course, suffer the most. Its their agony that stays with you, rather than the specific story the author has chosen to tell.

The title refers to the state of a woman's body after months of being used as a soldiers' sex slave. (The forces may be government or rebel; from a civilians point of view, theyre interchangeable.) It can also serve as a metaphor for the whole country. By the end of the play it's attached itself -- in one of several moments that are short-term effective and long-term inconclusive--to the central character, who's known as Mama Nadi and who is a kind of stationary Mother Courage. Where Bertolt Brechts protagonist pulled a food wagon, Nottages runs a bar and brothel. Theoretically, it's a conflict-free zone; both sides are welcome, both have to lay down their weapons before being served. But, of course, things don't always work out that neatly or that safely. Like Mother Courage, Mama Nadi has a persistent male admirer and even the chance of marriage. Unlike her, she has no children of her own and--this being an American play -- a heart of gold beneath the businesslike exterior. Brechts Mama was complicit in the system that oppressed her; her compulsive haggling led to the death of her own son. Theres a comparable scene in Nottage's play, but here the shuffling has been displaced onto another character. And where Mother Courage went on hauling her wagon regardless, Mama Nadi -- this being also a Pulitzer-winning American play -- gets a redemptive coda that seems to have been tacked on from some other script.

There are, we're told, 10 girls in Mamas establishment but, for obvious if frustrating economic reasons, we only meet three of them. Theres Josephine, already in residence when we get there, and two who are brought in during the first scene by Christian, a long-standing friend and business associate of Mama's. One of these is his niece Sophie, raped by a bayonet and hence "ruined"; the other, Salima, though technically spared that state, may have suffered even worse. As she already has a full house Mama refuses to take them, but soon (see heart of gold, above) she relents. Sophie, who's educated, becomes her resident singer, her bookkeeper and her favourite; she is, in one of the plays most moving threads, desperately saving up for a curative operation. Salima, after escaping from months of servitude chained to a tree, was cast out by her husband; Mama protects her, too, when he comes looking for her. This, through a neat telescoping of plot lines, gets Mama into serious trouble with the army, but its another action that's set up and not followed through. Horror is defused by a "powerful" speech in which one of the characters turns herself into a metaphor. This supposedly shames all the others. If only.

Mama is terrifically played by Yanna McIntosh whose only conceivable flaw is that it's almost impossible to think ill of her. We know shes going to do the right thing, because shes Yanna McIntosh. In her actual performance, though, she never gives a sentimental inch; she's flinty and earthy and even her most generous moments have an appropriate air of grudge about them. She's also brilliantly expressive with the African accent, which isnt her own. The only other performance that approaches her level of reality is Sabryn Rocks Sophie, not so much when she speaks as in the way, wounded and distant, she moves among the men in the bar. She sings affectingly, too, though Philip Akin's direction seems uncertain whether to treat her songs as action or as commentary. The production (a joint venture by Obsidian and Nightwood) is sympathetic but slow; it moves haltingly from one scene to another, and though it builds tension it never squeezes it. It's weakest in the crucial scene in which Marci T. Houses jaunty, jealous Josephine listens to the stories of her two new companions. Each of the actresses seems to be in her own world. Salimas narrative can hardly help being harrowing, and in Sophia Walker's performance it duly harrows. But it would do so even more if she actually looked at the person she was talking to, and if she didn't keep pausing for effect like a character in a play.

Sterling Jarvis is quietly, sometimes too quietly, delightful as Uncle Christian, though he too suffers from his authors reluctance to follow a theme through. Hes a teetotaller, because he knows from experience what happens when he isn't; then, in a reasonably tense scene, he is, almost literally, driven to drink by a hulking suspicious general (Andre Sills). Thereafter, he drinks like a fish, but the play never capitalizes on the connection. He might as well be three different people. It's an OK play in an OK production, with one more than OK performance. The reality dwarfs it; but it also gives it power.

- Ruined runs through Feb. 12 at the Berkeley Street Theatre. Call 416-368-3110 or visit nightwoodtheatre.netfor more information. robert.cushman@hotmail.com

Christopher Plummer in Barrymore doesn't put a foot wrong. That's the literal as well as the metaphorical truth. As Plummer portrays him, in what is virtually a one-man show, John Barrymore, the great American actor and lush, was also no end of a twinkle toes. He also sang very well, and though he was 59 in 1942, the year in which William Luce's play is set, he kept right up to date with the popular songs of the day. He comes before us hauling a drinks trolley while giving out with I Got a Gal in Kalamazoo, and moving about as gracefully and roguishly as a man in that position possibly could. Later on there will be more singing, all unaccompanied and impeccable, and even some dancing, likewise delightful.

There's also quite a lot of Shakespeare. The year 1942 was also the year of Barrymore's death, and the conceit of the play is that Jack, as he was commonly known, is making a last-minute attempt to reclaim his reputation as a classical actor, tarnished after long years spent degrading it in the movies while succumbing to the ravages of alcohol and alimony. His past includes legendary performances in two Shakespearean roles, Hamlet and Richard III, and he's making a desperate bid to revive the second of these, though the evening also includes numerous quotations from the first. (Plummer, who himself has played both of the roles in his time, strikes an especially fine yearning note on Hamlet's "what a piece of work is a man.")

Barrymore has rented a theatre, just like the one we're in, in order to go over Richard's lines, and hired a prompter to get him through them. In the first act his talent for digression, fuelled by his own rampant insecurities, prevents him getting much further than "now is the winter of our discontent," and he needs help even with that. After the intermission he jumps, unexplained, straight to the battle of Bosworth and "my kingdom for a horse." Having done the first half in civvies, he has now acquired a crown, a hump, a makeshift throne and a very tatty Plantagenet costume. I don't remember these accoutrements from when Plummer in Barrymore first came to town, 10 years ago, but whatever, they're a welcome change of visual pace, and Plummer plays the seedy comedy of them to the self-satirizing hilt.

There are various conventions available to first-person plays, especially first-person plays about entertainers, and this one switches unblushingly between them. Barrymore

talks to the prompter, who's kept in the wings throughout; he talks to himself; and he sometimes seems to be talking directly to us. (He even mentions us.) The main problem with Luce's script, though, is not that it's shameless but that it's shapeless. It has one moment that ought to be pivotal: Barrymore says piteously that he was once a good Richard, to which the prompter (the invisibly admirable John Plumpis) sternly and indeed promptly replies, "No, you were a great Richard." This would seem to be the cue for Jack to jack it up, and recover his former glories, or alternatively to jack it in, and surrender to desolation. In fact he just goes on favouring us with his reminiscences. The point, perhaps, is that he's unsalvageable, but he's no more or less so at the evening's end than he was at its beginning, which is dramatically unsatisfying. He doesn't learn or acknowledge anything that he doesn't already know and neither, anecdotes apart, do we.

That's not to deny that the anecdotes can be very entertaining, especially as retailed by Plummer with infallible wit, cheek and timing. He recites limericks, about drink or women. He tells showbiz stories, some of which -- like the famous Sam Goldwyn one about turning lesbians into Americans -- have been dragged in from the common store. He boasts about his alcoholic capacity and his marital incapacity: four wives, all aspiring actresses, all the occasion of barbed one-liners (though Elaine Barrie, the last and most notorious Mrs. Barrymore, gets off remarkably unscathed). He talks about his comparatively late awakening to serious theatrical ambition, about his daunting actor father and his daunting actor siblings: Lionel, who revelled in ham and Hollywood, and Ethel, who stuck sternly to the theatre.

Plummer knits the whole together into a portrait of rueful bravado. There's a powerful extra ingredient in the contrast between the subject, self-wasted at 59, and his impersonator, some 20 years older and in his prime, in fact probably better than ever. It was all the more poignant for those of us who came directly to it from the memorial celebration of Peter Donaldson, who was Plummer's natural successor among Canadian Shakespeareans and who died even younger than Barrymore; clips of Plummer and Donaldson together in Stratford's Caesar and Cleopatra took on extraordinary resonance.

What Plummer offers us in Barrymore isn't great acting; the material doesn't allow it. But it's the irresistible work of a star who's also a craftsman. He pays implicit tribute to Barrymore as both man and legend, makes us like him, lets us see flickers of past genius amid a roaring fire of congeniality. He's super-enjoyable.

- Barrymore runs until March 9. For tickets, call 416-872-5555 or visit ticketmaster.ca. robert.cushman@hotmail.com

Anton Piatigorsky's Eternal Hydra may not actually be immortal but it's certainly proving to be durable. It was first seen as a one-act play in Stratford in 2002; it resurfaced in 2009, much enriched and expanded, in a production by Crow's Theatre at Buddies in Bad Times; and that revival is now itself revived at the Factory. The Hydra of Greek mythology had heads, some say a hundred of them; the play inspired by it has legs, legs that grow in style and strength with each excursion.

The play, actual, is named after a book, imaginary. Piatigorsky's fictitious novelist Gordias Carbuncle was, like the James Joyce of whom he cannot help but remind us, an Irishman who lived in Paris; he was also Jewish, like Joyce's most famous creation, Leopold Bloom, an Irishman who stayed in Dublin. ( "Why," asks Gordias, rhetorically and hilariously, "do you think I left?") His magnum opus was Eternal Hydra, a novel of a hundred chapters, each written in a different narrative voice. When he died, though, he had only completed 99 of them, which might be considered fortunate, since the mythical Hydra needed to keep just one of its heads unsevered in order to survive. The manuscript, long thought lost, was at length retrieved by Vivian Ezra, an English-born American-based academic, whose special subject is Carbuncle; indeed she's so obsessed with him that she believes him to have taken up residence not just in her head but in her apartment. They talk together and pay calls together.

One of their destinations is the New York office of Gordias' old publisher, whose son now runs the business and is more skeptical of the rediscovered masterwork than his dad might have been. ( "I know it's a masterpiece," says junior, "but is it any good?") He makes a deal with Vivian; he'll publish Eternal Hydra but only in tandem with a novel by one of his protegees, a young woman named Pauline Newberry, that's set in interwar literary Paris with Carbuncle as one of the major characters. Vivian protests that Pauline's portrait is a travesty, but she has no choice but to go along; Gordias, or his ghost, is most insistent that she should. Through the pages of Carbuncle's rather discreditable diary, also in Vivian's possession, we travel back to his expatriate life. We see him deflecting his publisher's erotic, though not his financial, advances; we see him in turn making advances to women whom he wants to use physically and/ or imaginatively. And, finally, we hear a chapter of his book. It's the story of a young black woman in post-Civil War Louisiana, a gifted shoemaker but illiterate, taught to read by her white employer, caught up in the struggle for black (male) suffrage and in the riots that accompanied it. She lives to hear the state's new progressive governor make a speech in which she can hear her own voice. He may have appropriated it. But then, by making him and other whites characters in her narrative, she may have appropriated them. And Carbuncle, who has put their story in his own book with who knows what changes, has appropriated the lot of them. It's not a question of this being good or bad. It's that in literature, as in any other form -- and most especially in drama--it's inevitable.

I confess to having previously underestimated the grace, fun and emotional power of this play. "Appropriation of voice" may sound like a dry dramatic subject, but its deployment here is dynamic, ever-changing: Hydra-headed in fact. It's also witty and light-handed, with a cunning use of recurring verbal motifs -- that of Hercules, for example, whose second labour, in training for the really hard stuff, was to decapitate the monster for good and all. Some of my new-found enlightenment may be attributed to the maturing of Chris Abraham's production; good before, it's superb now. Physically, it sits far better on the Factory stage than it did at Buddies. John Thompson's set, a starkly elegant arrangement of chairs and table on a sloping floor, seemed oppressive before; now, with more height to play with and imaginatively lit by its designer, it's liberating. Each of the actors plays two or more roles, which may be Hydratic in itself. The major theme is sounded from the start in Liisa Repo-Martell's magnificent Vivien, the very archetype of the star-struck academic, whose voice and mannerisms, whether or not the actress knows it, bear a close resemblance to those of a current and prominent English biographer and critic. The alternation of personal diffidence and professional possessiveness is perfectly hit off. She has one particularly fine speech, delineating the limits of the scholar's world, that combines both qualities. Sam Malkin repeats his genial triple of father, son and southern gentleman, and David Ferry is again an irresistibly grizzled and sozzled Carbuncle. Cara Ricketts, the one newcomer, starts with a magnetically cool outline of the rising star Pauline and finishes by digging deep into the Louisiana story, a solo turn that's all the more moving for being so stoic, all the more vibrant for being so restrained. It's still a shock to find that her story ends the play, without returning us to the people we came in with; but a) it would be an impossible act to follow, and b) incompleteness is built into the subject. Unless you're Hercules, the Hydra's heads are innumerable. Two years ago, Eternal Hydra won the Dora for best play, independent theatre division. This probably disqualifies it from winning this year in the general theatre category to which it's been promoted. That could be fortunate for the competition, which so far this season has been non-existent.

- Eternal Hydra runs through Feb. 13 at the Factory Theatre. Call 416-504- 9971 or visit factorytheatre.cafor ticket information. robert.cushman@hotmail.com

OLEANNA

Young Centre for the Performing Arts, Toronto

---

Twenty years after its premiere, David Mamet's Oleanna can still have an audience literally gasping. It certainly does so in the production that kicks off Soulpepper's American year. Not that it's been officially announced as such, but it's hard to see how else to describe a season that includes Mamet, Miller, Wilder, Williams, Simon, Saroyan and The Fantasticks.

Laszlo Marton's production of Oleanna is powerful, accomplished and unbalanced -- the last being a quality that isn't nearly as inherent in the play as popular mythology might suggest. There are two characters: John, a university professor on the verge of tenure, and Carol, one of his students. There are three scenes, all of them set in John's office.

In the first scene, Carol arrives to protest a failing grade that -- judging from the one sentence we hear of her paper --she deserves. Her complaint is that she doesn't understand: what John says in class, what he's saying now, and what's in the books. He offers to scrub her grade, start again, and give her some private tuition. He also makes the mistake of putting a comforting hand on her shoulder. Next thing he knows, he's being accused of sexual harassment. In the second scene, he asks her to withdraw her complaint to the tenure committee. Things get worse. The committee makes its decision. In the couple's last interview -- the only one that, in this production, takes place with the door closed --all hell breaks loose.

The visceral reaction the play evokes has to do with the apparent unfairness of it all. Carol gets very articulate. Terms like "rape" get thrown around in a context to which they do not, if words mean anything, apply. As John, Diego Matamoros brings him superbly to life, tying himself in a tighter knot, the harder he tries to make himself clear. John spends a lot of time on the phone, negotiating the purchase of a house befitting his new station. Believable telephone conversations are among the rarest things in drama, but Matamoros actually persuades us that there are real people on the other end of the line.

With fiendish persistence, Mamet uses the constantly ringing phone to advance the plot and to delay understanding between the characters. The tension here is raised very high, with Sarah Wilson giving an equally fine performance as Carol. As a matter of fact, she gives two equally fine performances. The usual knock against this play is that the mousy student of the first scene is unrecognizable as the aggressive spokewoman of the rest. I've never believed this; it seems to me that Carol starts as a blank slate who then gets written on. Wilson, though, pushes the contrast to extremes.

First, she's a bewildered naif, whose breakdown is truly alarming. Then, she's an impervious, unyielding, sternly spoken, self-appointed symbol. What gets lost, though, is that Carol actually has a case: a general if not, in this grotesque instance, a particular one. When she talks about the disadvantages and humiliations that she's had to overcome to get here, there's no reason not to believe her. And she's dead on when she criticizes John's privileged pride in his "maverick" status.

The irony, in a play that's loaded with them, is that she, the apparent revolutionary, is the conservative one. She doesn't want to hear the education system mocked, because she has too much invested in it. She attacks John for misusing his "power," and proves her point by abusing her own, thereby provoking those audience gasps. She goads him too far, and in his response he effectively destroys his own life.

It's a wonderful ending, but three things conspire against it here. First, there has never been any previous sexual tension. I don't mean that John actually has designs on Carol, but when he says he wouldn't touch her with a 10-foot pole, we should at least feel that he's protesting too much. Second, Teresa Przybylski's stark, white set starts doing crazy things meant to illustrate the denouement but comes close to destroying it. Third, and minor: John in his fury uses the phrase "political correctness," which may be meant to show him again resorting to cliche but sounds more like the author doing it. He writes a mesmerizing play, and then puts a bumper sticker on it.

- Oleanna plays at the Young Centre in Toronto until March 5. For tickets, visit young-centre.caor call 416-866-8666. robert.cushman@hotmail.com

THEATRE REVIEW

Highway 63: The Fort MacShow

Theatre Passe Muraille Backspace, Toronto

---

"Be light" are the last words spoken, and the creators of Highway 63: The Fort Mac Show have taken them to heart. This very entertaining piece in a slice of old-style drama-doc theatre, the kind in which a group of writers and performers, or most often writer-performers, descend on a particular community, hang around, ask questions and serve up the answers and observations in a free-wheeling script that has been worked out and improvised in rehearsal. On this occasion, the territory under inspection is Fort McMurray, industry centre of Alberta's oil sands. Or tar sands. Or, as the show insists is the label with the least baggage attached, bitumen sands.

Of the three performers, two -- Georgina Beaty and Jonathan Seinen -- are Albertans themselves, while the third, Greg Gale, is from Newfoundland. They are young, funny, energetic and versatile;

at least each of them manages to switch quickly and with conviction between a variety of roles with no changes of costume, unless you count Seinen taking his glasses on and off. They provide amusing sketches involving schoolrooms and council meetings, but these are sideshows. There's a sustained narrative thread going through the evening, and it takes up most of the time.

It involves Steve (Seinen), a shy reclamation scientist, and Chad (Gale), a brash, self-confident Newfie oil worker. They share a flat, and one day when out grocery shopping they encounter Mary (Beaty), whom Steve, with encouragement from Chad, tries ineffectually to pick up. They meet her again at a bar, and this time Steve lucks out. He even gets her to come home with him, but at the last minute loses his nerve and heads for bed, leaving her alone with Chad, with expected results. The reason seems to be that Steve is gay, though closeted; an inset scene shows him placing an ad on Craigslist, in quest of a first-time male partner; I say "seems" because it's never mentioned again and it's quite possible, given the show's conventions, that Seinen at this point is playing someone else entirely, perhaps as a cameo designed to show off the varied social opportunities available in Fort Mac.

Mary works as a tour guide, but is about to move to Toronto to study dance. One thing the show keeps insisting on is that everybody who lives in Fort McMurray has either moved there from somewhere else, or is going to leave. Hence, I suppose, the main title; otherwise inexplicable since nothing here actually happens on the highway. Despite all this transience, the show keeps insisting that Fort Macis a nice and underrated place to live and, in its overall cheerfulness, it pretty much makes its point.

Tensions develop in the Chad-Mary story, due to their differing ideas about the possibility of a long-term relationship; and they finally explode in a presumably symbolic episode in which Mary's conservationist ideas, fostered by Steve, come into conflict with Chad's cheerful lack of them. At least I think that's what's going on; it's all rather murky, visually and otherwise. The general effect is of the creators' belated determination to wring some local relevance from a plotline that has been chuggingly happily along on its own terms, and that mostly could have happened anywhere. In its praiseworthy determination not to preach, the show almost avoids raising any issues at all, and certainly avoids dramatizing them. Basic information is dispensed in the first scene, and there's a shrugging attempt at synthesis in the last, but mostly the script, though full of nice one-liners and aphorisms, seems pleasant but slight. Every so often it steps outside itself and becomes, explicitly, about a bunch of actors researching a play about Fort McMurray.

The neat and speedy production is by Charlotte Corbeil-Coleman, with unspecified inspirational input from her father Layne Coleman, a veteran of Canada's theatrical documentary movement and the past artistic director of Theatre Passe Muraille, which co-produces the show with a new group, Architect Theatre.

The last substantial speech, delivered by Gale in a droll drawl, is a shaggy-dog story. It starts with a promise of ecological relevance but ends as a (very good) joke about marriage and, ultimately, about acting. Which in turn leads to the well-heed admonition, presented as Fort Mac's gift to the rest of us, which is how they go out and where I came in.

The title Divisadero ostensibly derives from a street in San Francisco that, in the current theatre version, is mentioned just once. The show's official title is Divisadero: a Performance, a description both apt and honest. Michael Ondaatje's novel has been adapted for the stage -- there it is, or bits of it, up there -- but it hasn't been dramatized. The result is not, in any traditional sense, a play. But it is a performance, quite an impressive one, and it's also a set of performances: some of them excellent and one of them exceptional.

That would be Maggie Huculak, who stands at a microphone and talks to us in the person of a mature woman named Anna, telling what happened in her youth; and does it so carefully and yet so fluently that, when she slips back into her past persona, you never hear or feel the joins. Anna grew up motherless on a farm in California along with two adopted siblings, Claire and Coop. When she was 16, she and Coop became lovers, which made Claire jealous (partly due to Coop's endearing habit of mixing up the girls' names) and their dad, when he found the two lovebirds together, furious. Coop, after being savagely beaten, fled. Anna, at the first opportunity, took off, too, and never went home.

I confess: I've read about the novel, but I've never read it. I can see the merits of Ondaatje's meticulously parcelled prose, but I can't get through it. (And on The English Patient, which I did get through -- in both media -- I'm with Elaine.) I therefore cannot say how much of the script, which Ondaatje worked up in rehearsal with the actors and director, comes directly off the printed page and how much, if any, is fresh. It all sounds of a piece, and though the accumulation of detail might have been expected to die in the theatre, it actually works well. It certainly does when spoken by Huculak, who makes the cadences her own and is only rarely self-indulgent with them. Tall and still, she's superb both as actress and storyteller.

She carries most of the weight in the first part of the first act, though some of it is shouldered by Liane Balaban, whose Claire is more effortful but effective. (Her strongest work comes later.) Just when all the highly wrought lyricism threatens to become too much, Daniel Brooks's Necessary Angel production invigoratingly changes pace. Lights brighten, mics disappear, a vestigial supply of furniture gets shifted, and Tom McCamus rolls on, wry and rambunctious, as a gambler ( "born in Rochester -- for my sins") to tell us how he used to hang out at Lake Tahoe with a gang of cronies including the Dauphin (so named because he was once caught reading a French novel) and Coop. Coop, we learn, had matured into a champion card-shark who had to leave town--again -- after outsmarting an unforgiving evangelical. McCamus, unlike his narrating predecessors, gets to move around while talking, and his intricate depictions of an endless series of poker games are virtuoso feats of delivery, not to mention of memory. It's a juicy turn, flanked by two other performances from the same actor in sterner, plainer mode. We've already seen him, briefly, as the vengeful father by whom Coop was beaten up; we will next see him, again briefly, as a Nevada operator by whom Coop is also beaten up, worse.

If this were a play, Coop would be its protagonist, since he's the one who does things and to whom things happen. As it is, he does the least talking but is still the centre of everybody else's attention. And here's a problem, because he's played by Justin John Rutledge; and if Balaban, a film and TV actress, has never acted on stage before, Rutledge has never acted anywhere before, and it shows. He isn't a disgrace, he's intelligent, he has a pleasant presence, but it's presence without definition. His Coop seems too nice a guy to get into the trouble he gets into. It's funny, because he's the reason the show exists. Ondaatje saw him in concert, and thought his singing and song-writing would be a perfect match for the book if ever it were put on stage. Oddly, the singing and strumming Rutledge actually does in the show isn't particularly helpful. It contributes a vague sense of Western place but nothing more. Indeed, the most electrifying musical sequence in the show is a song that Rutledge didn't write and doesn't sing; it's London Calling, given a despairing, discordant (though with a song by the Clash, how can you tell?) near-suicidal rendition by Amy Rutherford as a woman sent to lure Coop to his doom and hating herself for it. She's good and biting when she talks, too.

The play this staged Divisadero most resembles is probably Brian Friel's Faith Healer; but though that, too, is a series of monologues, they're speeches that offer us divergent views of a situation. So there's a kind of conflict there. Here it's just someone talking when someone else leaves off, a sequence of soliloquies. That makes Brooks, a past master at staging one-man shows, its ideal director; his inventiveness here is as stylish and as fiercely disciplined as usual; John Thompson has designed another of his spare platforms and Andrea Lundy does the lighting. I've read enough crib-notes to know that the book has an entire second half, set in Europe, that's omitted here. All that remains -- I guess -- is Anna's final announcement that she became a writer, as if that were somehow the point of the whole thing. Huculak can make it sound like a benison, but even she can't avoid the unspoken response "so what?" With all that she, McCamus, Rutherford and the others can do for them, none of the characters here are more than the sum of their words.

- Divisadero runs through Feb. 20 at Theatre Passe Muraille. Call 416-504- 7529 or visit passemuraille.on.cafor ticket information. robert.cushman@hotmail.com

SAINT CARMEN OF THE MAIN

Bluma Appel Theatre, Toronto

---

I would love to see Peter Hinton direct a real Greek tragedy. For the moment, we have his production of Michel Tremblay's Saint Carmen of the Main, a 35-year-old play acknowledged by everyone, including its author, to be constructed on the Athenian model. Hinton's revival is a joint venture of Canadian Stage and the National Arts Centre.

The curtain rises -- and for once in the institutional theatre there actually is a curtain and it does actually rise, slowly as if to savour the moment -- to reveal 11 pairs of red shoes, some of them platform-soled to approximate the old Greek tragic buskins. It rises higher, to show the shoes surmounted by equally garish red dresses. Wearing them are a line of prostitutes from the Main, the poorest corner of Montreal, among them an indeterminate number of transvestites. They are the chorus, and their speaking, both individually and in unison, is impressive. They have two leaders: Karen Robinson, strident but compelling, and Robert Persichini, marvellous as a tender-hearted hulk. Leaders and followers together bring off the evening's most stirring sequence, a heartfelt ode on how Carmen's singing has brought meaning to their lives.

I've got ahead of myself. The Carmen who's canonized in the play's title is what was known in those old hyphenated days as a country-and-western singer. She grew up on the Main and, having achieved success in the local clubs, took off to Nashville to study at the source. While there, she had a revelation: She no longer wanted to sing the old favourites, she wanted to perform her own material, which would honour and celebrate her old exploited friends of the streets. They start the play, though as yet they know nothing of her transformation, by heralding her return; apparently she's made the sun shine like it never has before. This makes them resemble less a Greek chorus than a Broadway one, the kind that in shows such as Hello, Dolly! and Mame insist the star is wonderful because she's the star, without providing any other evidence. And that's pretty much how the play proceeds. As in a Greek tragedy, though generally not in a Broadway musical, the exciting stuff tends to happen offstage, and that includes the show that Carmen gives to unveil the new her. We get the reaction, affecting as noted, but the action we have to take on trust. Laara Sadiq, standing out from the scarlet crowd in sacrificial white, is believable when Carmen describes the awe she felt on arriving in the country-music capital, but in her prevailing moods of triumph and defiance, she aims at forceful but winds up with forced.

The defiance is aimed largely at Maurice (Jean Leclerc), her manager/pimp, himself in thrall to a more powerful manager/ pimpknownasToothpick. Carmen's evolution into yet another preachy and pretentious singer-songwriter is greeted by the bosses as a challenge to the established order that will give downtrodden hookers ideas above their station. The scene in which Carmen and Maurice thrash these things out is interminable; neither actor has the guns. Joey Tremblay, though, has considerable slinky power as Toothpick, and he does well by the play's climactic messenger speech. The two rats contribute to the production's variegated colour scheme by wearing identical black suits and white shirts, a fashion choice they share with Harelip, Carmen's fiercely loyal lesbian dresser and Exhibit A in her campaign to dignify the masses. Diane D'Aquila, physically unrecognizable and vocally unforgettable, makes of Harelip an underdog with bite; when she's on, the play flies.

Eo Sharp's red set adds to the hieratic effect. It's possible Hinton has squeezed some everyday life out of the play by stylizing it so emphatically, but given the material he seems to have made the right choice, even if not all his executants are up to the task. The Greek echoes are the play's most interesting feature; when Carmen,

against all advice, goes off to take a shower, there is an echo of Agamemnon in The Oresteia, crossing the red carpet to his doom.

There is, though, one final gaffe. Carmen has a female nemesis maybe deadlier than the males; this is Gloria, a retired star singer who specializes in Latin American, and who was Carmen's patron until the young woman started acting uncommercial. Jackie Richardson makes a glorious Gloria, prowling the stage in lazy circles, walking rings around the competition. We don't hear Carmen sing, but we do hear Gloria, making her comeback in a big number at the end of the play, which, given the play's own pro-Carmen logic, ought to be terrible. So the production wants us to believe that Richardson is singing badly, which is not going to happen. Alternatively, it just wants a slam-bang finish, and in the circumstances, who can blame it? The received opinion is that Tremblay is the great Canadian playwright, but as one revival succeeds another, my doubts increase.

- Runs until March 5. For tickets, call 416-368-3110 or visit canadianstage.com. robert.cushman@hotmail.com
