THEATRE REVIEW

Royal Alexandra Theatre, Toronto

Here we have the Canadian premiere, in a visiting British production, of a U.S. musical, based on a very English novel by a writer, Frances Hodgson Burnett, who was indeed English but who wrote the book in Tennessee, where she lived most of her life. Just to make things more confusing, the story is mostly set in a house on the Yorkshire moors but has a prologue in India, a locality that keeps reasserting itself in the characters' nightmares and the shows creators wildest dreams.

The heroine, Mary Lennox, is a 10-year-old child of the British raj, whose entire family has perished in a cholera epidemic. She's adopted, or at least taken in, by her uncle Archibald, who has also suffered a loss: the death of his beloved wife, Lily, sister of Mary's mother. This, and his self-consciousness about his humped back, have made him very remote; he spends a lot of time travelling and when at home, though he means Mary no harm, he wishes to see as little of her as possible; she reminds him too much of the late Lily, especially around the eyes. He shares this ocular fixation, and even a song on the subject, with his brother, a doctor, who also loved Lily and is a semi-scoundrel; that is, he wants possession of Misslethwaite Manor, Archies country seat, and is willing to sacrifice everyone, including Mary, to get it. But mindful perhaps of his professional oath, he tries to persuade himself that he is doing the right physicianly thing. In other words, hes a Hippocratic hypocrite.

Archie has a bedridden son, Colin, whom he can hardly bear to look on (care of memories of dead mother) and whom his brother tries to keep out of sight as well. But Mary, who's both nosey and bossy, wanders into Colin's room and, after an initial round of mutual youthful insults, sets about making him well, or rather proving he was never ill in the first place. She does this by getting him out into the open air, and especially by introducing him to his mothers garden.

Growing things from the ground is Marys chief pleasure, and she gains access to Lily's own beloved orchard, long locked up by her grieving husband, but still faithfully tended by her old gardener. Mary's own horticultural mentors are Martha the housemaid, and especially Marthas green-fingered brother Dickon. Together they represent life, as opposed to the creeping deadliness of the grown-up world indoors. Pauline Kael once wrote that its almost impossible not to be moved by the sight of a sick child, and by the same token it's even harder not

to respond to a child's restoration to health. The end of this show leaves the throat duly lumped. But it takes a long and anguished time to get there.

First, theres the Gothic overload of Marsha Normans script, which seems to draw on the Brontes as much as on Burnett. This can be unwittingly funny; the Misslethwaite housekeeper's description of the sound the Yorkshire wind makes -- "we call it wuthering"-- is a rare moment of high literary camp. Then there's the Asian overload of Anna Linstrums production; on the slightest provocation, the stage is filled with ghostly Indian figures from Marys past. It illustrates very little and explains less. It also clutters up a stage that is already in an unnerving state of permanent revolve; you can see why Archie would want to get away from a house whose walls refuse to stand still. Well, that and the fact that his late wife keeps haunting it in flashbacks. There's Lucy Simon's score, which is appealing and original in its folksier moments but deadening in its more frequent moods of neo-Broadway bombast; as usual, the worst song -- the brothers duet of competitive agonizing -- gets the loudest applause, perhaps because its so loud itself. And there's the acting.

Mary is asked at one point whether she's always so rude and so loud, and the answer must be: usually, yes. Of course shes been through a lot, and must have been terribly spoiled in India, but some modulation might be in order; and its probably the director, rather than the perfectly competent young actress (Ellie Coldicutt at the performance I saw) who's to blame for its absence.

Similarly with Gene Goodman's Colin, whom one certainly wants to get well and who can be touching. Martha (Lauren Hood) and Dickon (Jos Slovick) are pleasant if indistinct. Caspar Phillipson works himself up to a fearful pitch as Archibald, and is very coy about letting us get a look at his hump; Graham Bickley ignores any hints of ambiguity in the doctor in favour of cardboard mutton-chop villainy. Bickley was last seen on this street in The Pajama Game, in which he was very good, but of course thats a much livelier show.

The performer with the most impressive resume is Siobhan Redmond, best known in these parts from the fine TV cop series Between the Line, and here wastefully cast as the housekeeper; she pounces when the occasional good line comes her way, but its very occasional. I realized how accustomed we've become in Canada to seeing musicals that are well acted; I found myself thinking that our local talent might even have handled the accents better.

- The Secret Garden plays at the Royal Alexandra Theatre in Toronto until March 20. For tickets, visit mirvish.comor call 1-800-461-3333. robert. cushman@hotmail.com

Auditions, says Martha Burns, probably speaking for most actors, are not my favourite thing. But when you don't have to learn lines for them, it's a plus." She was speaking of her tryout for Penelope Buitenhuis A Wake, an improvised film cast, naturally, from improvisatory auditions. The candidates were given an outline of the intended story, situation and of their own characters. The punning title refers to a gathering in memory of a Hungarian-born Canadian theatre director named Gabor Zazlov, recently felled by a heart attack. Burns part (yes, she got it) is that of the director's patron and principal fundraiser. This makes her one of the few actors in the picture not playing an actor.

Other roles cut closer to the professional bone. Graham Abbey, for example, plays "an actor with classical rep experience, whose mentor had died and who had gone off to do a cop series on TV. This parallels Abbey's own track record: a leading player at the Stratford Festival who then became a TV regular on The Border. At one point his character owns up to having appeared in a Hollywood film called Revenge of the Snow Yeti, though Abbeys at pains to make clear this title does not derive from his own experience.

Gabor, the genius-tyrant of A Wake, is playing what seems to be a posthumous practical joke, gathering together the people who used to work for him so that they can pick at one anothers scars. The process involves having them do an impromptu performance of Hamlet, the play he could never get on. His wife films these proceedings, and also installs a camera in the powder room, to which each of the participants can record his or her own reminiscences of the great man, For Abbey, this produced another art-imitating -life moment, since shortly before filming his own bathroom soliloquy he'd received news that one of his real-life mentors, the theatre director John Wood, had suffered a heart attack (from which, happily, he recovered).

Like the guests at the party, the actors in A Wake spend a lot of time waiting for their next confrontation, in Abbey's words holed up in the basement of a home in Guelph" -- actually a snowbound farmhouse whose owners, Burns says, couldnt have been more hospitable."

Unlike in a Mike Leigh film, where the actors perform a written script, derived from an extended period of improvisation in rehearsal, this team were allowed to make lines up on camera. Rehearsal time had been short and there was only about a week for the actual filming. Even here the amount of spontaneity had to be limited, at least in the big group scenes; otherwise, Abbey says, the cameramen would go nuts.

Burns says that it "gave you a different kind of energy -- it was a big task to lose your self-consciousness. There was the adrenalin of what can you do in that span of time. It was amazing to me that Penelope had complete stories when it was finished." Buitenhuis certainly approached the project with the right combination of credentials: from horror films such as Killer Bees to the improvised TV comedy of Train 48.

Gabor himself, whom we meet in a brief prologue, is played by Nicholas Campbell, who was in his own words "an afterthought -- I

came in after theyd shot most of the movie. I had a day to

come up with the accent. There were fights and

everything going on when I got there. But

I've known Penny for years; she always struck me as someone who would get things done on her own."

- A Wake opens in Toronto, Montreal

and Ottawa on Feb. 18.

2011-02-18-the-man-comes-around-again:
Johnny Cash led, to put it mildly, an eventful life. Very little of it gets in The Man in Black, the self-proclaimed "tribute" show that's just rolled into town starring Shawn Barker, who's making a career out of it. When he sings Folsom Prison Blues (the second song in) and I Got Stripes (two songs later) you would imagine there might be some theatrical mileage in mentioning Cash's own frequent brushes with the law -- even, if Wikipedia be my witness, he never did real time himself. At the least, there might be some reference to the iconic status of his Folsom and San Quentin concerts within his own career. He wasn't just playing another couple of gigs. He had reasons, passionately felt, for being there.

The Man in Black is in fact just another concert playing at being a theatre piece. Its director, Kurt Brown, also gets a credit as writer, though it's hard to believe he stayed up late many nights to come up with this script. There's also the perennial puzzler of why we should want to see somebody spending an entire evening singing somebody else's songs, without putting them into any kind of context, when the originals are still readily available. That said, the show is better than many of its kind, much better certainly than the Beatles show Rain that paid us a visit last year; though it does suffer from the same uncertainty over who we are meant to believe is actually singing to us.

For most of the evening, Barker insists that he's Cash; toward the end, after he's offered the ritual thanks to his back-up musicians, one of them, without any change in staging conventions, asks for a round of applause for him under his own name. That's not the only example of having it both ways. The show's conceit is that we're seeing Cash in his prime, but in a program that includes some songs from the very end of his career. Well, all right, we'll suspend disbelief. But we're also told that his two lady back-up singers will be standing in for his wife and sometime duet partner June Carter who can't be there on account of she's dead. In fact she died only a short time before he did. What does that do to the chronology?

Barker is a performer of considerable authority, and physically and vocally he makes a very convincing Cash. (But what, one wonders, is he going to do for an encore?) He might make an even more convincing Elvis; in fact it seems that he was a Presley imitator at the time he was tapped to become a Cash imitator. The one aspect of Cash he doesn't even try to capture is the man in black's cavalier attitude toward singing in tune. Even on A Boy Named Sue he remains obstinately on key. But then singing off it, on purpose, is one of the hardest things to do. He chats the audience up between songs with reasonably charming self-deprecation, and he does manage to sneak some of the man's demons in through the show's back door.

The script confines biographical detail to descriptions of his first and last recording sessions, but something of his feeling for, and championing of, the dispossessed comes through in the prison songs. There's even more in The Ballad of Ira Hayes, the bitter commemoration of a native American war hero, and there's the most of all in The Man in Black itself. We get a sense of what makes Cash, even to a country-music agnostic like me, one of the most powerful and attractive figures in popular song.

There's also the fact that, unlike so many Nashville heroes and heroines, he never whined, either in his songs or in how he sung them. One of the best sections here, and another that subliminally tells you something about the man, is a rip-roaring gospel medley, in which the back-up ladies (Michelle Berting and Blair Irwin, both locally recruited) also do themselves proud; as they also do when duetting with the star on Jackson and If I Were a Carpenter. The latter, which I've never associated with Cash, sounds much more attractive here than it ever did as a solo.

The show never tells us anything about its protagonist's scarred upbringing, and it keeps very quiet about his drug busts, though it does end, in a rather coy fashion, with Cocaine Blues. (They try to pass it off as an impromptu encore, though in fact it's listed right there in the program.) The musicians, led by guitarist Mike Burns, are scorchers. For what it is, this show is all right. It also leaves all the room in the world for a real musical written about Cash, one that links the man to the music and that would belong in a theatre, not -- as this production spiritually does -- in a bar.

2011-02-19-fathers-know-best-well-not-al:
With their production of The Fantasticks, Soulpepper are in charming and benevolent mode, a mode they do well and often. This is the modest musical that made a modest start, off-Broadway in 1960, and then ran there for 50 years, which was not quite long enough for me to have got around to seeing it. I cannot say that seeing it now is a revelation; the show's qualities are well known, as are many of the songs. It's still fascinating, and mostly delightful, to see how they play out.

The Fantasticks gives us Romeo and Juliet in spite of themselves, twice. It's based on The Romanticks, a 19th-century bonbon by Edmond Rostand ( Cyrano de Bergerac), that's set in the familiar sweet-and-sour pastoral landscape of French classic comedy, but given what was then a modern tweak. The musical changes the locale to a non-specific rural America, but keeps the play's central conceit. This is that the fathers of the young couple are all in favour, but determine to put obstacles in their way, so that their children may have the pleasure feeling star-crossed and defying their elders. As far as we can see, the boy, Matt, and the girl, Luisa, were going to fall in love anyway, but their fathers, who are next-door neighbours, have built a wall between their properties, just to make sure. This is less like Romeo and Juliet than like Pyramus and Thisbe, while the old-time locale, use-your-imagination setting and presence of a hospitable narrator, also seem to look forward to Our Town -- especially as both that play and A Midsummer Night's Dream are on this year's Soulpepper schedule. The scheme involves arranging a fake abduction of Luisa, so that Matt may thwart it. To this end, the seniors engage a professional abductor, known as El Gallo, who in turn engages a couple of strolling actors. By intermission, everything has worked out very nicely. In the second half, it all starts to unravel. This, in addition to the other analogues, makes the show a precursor of Into the Woods; it shows what happens after happily ever after. There's also a resemblance between these young romanticks, at least in the first stage of their relationship, and the amorous dimwits of A Funny Thing Happened on the Way to the Forum. And I wonder if the young Tom Stoppard ever saw The Fantasticks; its thespians-for-hire, emerging from a property hamper and complaining about having fallen on hard times and offering death scenes as their specialty, look like ancestors of the itinerant players of Rosencrantz and Guildenstern Are Dead.

Harvey Schmidt, the composer, and Tom Jones, librettist and lyricist, are charter members of the last great generation of American musical theatre writers; and they may -- Schmidt may, anyway -- be the most purely melodious. The score's most famous number, Try To Remember, is of course impossible to forget, but it's rivalled as a standard, and surpassed as a song, by the beautiful Soon It's Gonna Rain. The songs that register most strongly, though, are I Can See It, which surges, and It Was You, which rapturously heals. These both occur in the second act, which needs them. The first half preserves a perfect balance of innocence and experience. The second, which departs more from the original, sets out to prove that you need to suffer before you can truly love; or, as the song has it, "without a hurt, the heart is hollow." As wisdom that's unexceptionable, but in acting it out, the show turns schematic. Not only the lovers but their fathers start squabbling. The actors return in the guise of pirates, though they may just be doubling; anyway this time they abduct Matt instead of Luisa, and they do it for real. Though how much of his misadventures with them are meant to be real, and how much is fantasy, is uncertain; at least, I couldn't follow it. The action begins to feel forced, though the music and the production eventually bring it to a satisfying conclusion.

Under Joseph Ziegler's direction, the performers are tender and funny and hardly ever sentimental. Albert Schultz as narrator gives the musical version of his Our Town performance, soothing and understanding; as El Gallo, he's a flamboyant but vulnerable swashbuckler, who had me puzzled as to which moustachioed Hollywood hero he most resembled. The lovers, I guess, could be more full-throated; Jeff Lillico's singing sounds oddly less assured here than it did in Light in the Piazza, which I would imagine to be the more testing score. But he gets the mixture of doubt and ardour exactly right, just as Krystin Pellerin's Luisa bewitchingly balances the demure and the determined. Michael Hanrahan and William Webster as the two not-so-heavy fathers, both devout gardeners more jealous of their vegetables than of their offspring, provide expectedly endearing duets, vocal and otherwise. The real show-stopping performance, though, comes in a non-musical role; this is Oliver Dennis' old tragedian, wispy-haired and down-at-heel, parading past glories and mixed-up Shakespearean soliloquies. In a show whose humour mostly provokes gentle smiles, he sets off uproarious belly laughs, but without disturbing the delicate equilibrium. He's ably seconded by Michael Simpson, got up as a squaw in case there should be call for one. (There is). The original harp-and-piano score is impeccably played, onstage, by Erica Goodman and musical director Paul Sportelli, whose appearance, beneath a battered hat and with his back turned stubbornly to us throughout, is fantastick in itself.

- To March 24 at the Yonge Centre for the Perfoming Arts. Visit soulpepper.caor call 416- 866-8666 for details.

2011-02-22-shelter-from-the-norm:
The onstage methods of The Middle Place could hardly be simpler. The impact is very powerful, and also surprisingly complex.

Set in a homeless youth shelter in Etobicoke, it's "verbatim theatre," a new name for a form of documentary drama that's been with us for a long time now, but is here distilled to what is likely to be its purest form. How pure that actually is, we are never likely to know.

The script of The Middle Place derives entirely from filmed interviews conducted on-site, with inmates and staff. But of course, even if none of the words have been changed, they must still have been selected and edited. And they aren't being spoken by the subjects themselves; they're being delivered to us by actors who, however talented and dedicated they are (and some of the performances here are remarkable), cannot help but have their own agendas. The very fact that four out of the five of them play multiple roles means that we spend some of our time admiring their virtuosity. Alan Dilworth's direction, though technically spartan, is precisely calculated for maximum theatrical effect.

The above, by the way, is compliment rather than complaint. The Middle Place started when Project: Humanity, an artists' group focused on community projects, commissioned Andrew Kushnir, an actor and writer, to write a play for Youth Without Shelter, a Rexdale centre where they had already run some drama workshops. Kushnir decided that the centre's inhabitants had more to tell him than he had to tell them. Hence the interviews and hence, later, the play, which itself has gone through a long gestation process.

It was staged, triumphantly, at SummerWorks 2009. It's now returned for a double run: at Theatre Passe Muraille at the end of last year and at Canadian Stage now. It's the first example known to me of a co-production by two companies within the same city. I'm all in favour of good work being given the most exposure possible, but I can't avoid the feeling that both of these theatres attract essentially the same audience.

Dilworth's program note contains the following fascinating-- actually mind-blowing-- information: "Neither I nor the actors listened to or watched any of the audience footage." So, coming back to "purity:" we're getting something that's impure as documentary but thoroughly pure as theatre, interpretation rather than impersonation. It's a choice that obviously respects the actors and more subtly respects the people they're playing, which in combination means that it respects the audience.

In truth, one of the actors must be thoroughly familiar with the footage, since Kushnir appears as himself, mainly in the auditorium and behind our backs. His four colleagues -- Akosua Amo-Adem, Antonio Cayonne, Jessica Greenberg, Kevin Walker--stand on a tilted white disc (lit brightly, sometimes cruelly, by Kimberly Purtell) that covers most of the stage. They step off it, and to its side, when playing members of staff, in which roles they communicate an overall sense of careworn optimism. They make you feel that, considering the alternatives, the middle place isn't such a terrible place to be.

When they step back into the ring, their perspective changes. None of their clients actually challenges the shelter's implicit claim to be preferable to some others; some of them even project a determined cheerfulness, whose very relentlessness seems suspect and is usually the product of drugs or mental illness are both. The comment, though, that resonates the strongest comes from Amo-Adem as the most articulate and also the most belligerent of the inmates, and is to the effect that once you've entered the shelter you're already in a pit from which it can be almost impossible to climb out.

Her performance, which was overwhelming at SummerWorks, has lost a little in vocal focus in its new and more sprawling surroundings, but she remains spot-on as the shelter's equally articulate and forceful director. The common ground between the two roles reinforces the sense of there-but-for-the-grace-of-godliness that permeates the play, and occasionally gets explicit statement.

The most haunting performance is Walker's, playing a variety of disturbed young men with bleached-out voices, one of them looking forward with unnerving serenity to impending fatherhood. Nearly as unsettling in its own way is Greenberg's aggressive cheerfulness as the self-named Nevaeh. That's "heaven" backwards; another character chooses to be identified as Brussels Sprout.

Most of them are aggressive-defensive, towards their interviewer and, in the stories they tell about shelter life, toward one another. It can sometimes be hard to distinguish which of his or her allotted roles a given actor is playing, but they all do justice to the vigour and wit of the lines with which their impromptu authors have blessed them. The way these kids talk can give you hope. Like them, the play makes painfully but not depressingly clear, we need it.

- The Middle Place runs until March 12. For tickets, call 416-368-3110 or visit canadianstage.com. robert.cushman@hotmail.com

THEATRE REVIEW

Sandra Shamas's Wit's End III: Love Life

Winter Garden Theatre,

The first thing to know about Sandra Shamas' Love Life is that it isn't about her love life. The title is an admonition, not a description. Thankfully, though, it isn't until the last section of the show that we get to the uplift. That is, unless you count an earlier and very funny section about the quest for a post-menopausal bra.

Puberty and menopause are the show's main concerns, and Shamas is funny about both of them. She is very skilled verbally and, uncommonly among stand-up comics, visually; she can contort her body at some quite remarkable angles. Refreshingly, she does not roam the stage haranguing us through a hand-mic; though this admittedly is something that male comedians are likelier to do than females anyway.

Her comedy, like comedy through the ages, is largely concerned with the infirmities of the flesh, especially as it ages, and its attendant social and psychological embarrassments. She doesn't sound angry about it; her predominant tone is something between accepting and regretful. She's friendly, making sure we're all present and comfortable before she gets started. ("Are we all in?" she enquires solicitously, adding, "It's a question we girls ask." It's also an atypical line in a largely asexual show.)

She also compliments us on our memories, to which she self-deprecatingly compares her own. Christopher Plummer, she reminds us, is playing downstage in Barrymore, and if he at his age can remember all those words about someone else's life then the least she can do at hers is remember all the words about her own. She doesn't seem too confident that she will. And though this may just be schtick, it did actually take practical effect on the first night. She began her second act by informing us that she had forgotten an important segment of the first, and that she would do it for us now. Being a natural and accomplished chatter-upper, she got away with it, but it accentuated what is already an imbalance in the show. The first half is short, though presumably not always that short, and sweet. The second does go on.

She begins the story proper by taking us back to when she 11 and was shown, along with all the other girls in the class, what seems to have been a frightening and not terribly helpful film called Now You're a Woman -narrated, as she pointedly points out, by a man. She adds, even more pointedly, that the film wasn't shown to the boys, with the result (I paraphrase) that they've been playing catch-up ever since. Later, when she gets around to menopause, she suggests a possible sequel entitled Now You're a Hag. Not that she herself looks or acts in the least haggish. In her fifties, she seems sleek and handsome and comfortable. She hasn't dyed her hair, though she tells us she once considered henna: "It's so festive." That seems to be a favourite word.

The show itself becomes less festive as it proceeds, though that probably isn't its intention. Men, perhaps as a consequence of their early educational deprivation, figure only marginally, though she does reach out by including a lengthy digression on Cialis, and the improbability of its being advertised in the afternoons during Oprah. Much of the second act, though, is about life on the farm.

The show is the concluding part of Shamas' Wit's End trilogy, Wit's End being the name she's given to her reallife rural retreat. All those Wingfield plays are there to remind us that farming can be funny, but of course they're all fictitious. Shamas, waxing autobiographical, doesn't get too much comic mileage out of butternut squash. But that may not be her intention. She seems more concerned to provide examples of how she does in fact Love Life. It gets rather cloying; and, after the sharper stuff at the beginning, like a short-changing of her talents.

Still, she remains likeable. She rounds everything off with a pun about moving from her summer garden to the Winter Garden, and then she's gone, not to return, her end as unceremonious as her beginning. I've never seen a solo performer do less of what is known in the trade as "milking." But then, she isn't a dairy farmer.

- Runs to March 13 at Toronto's Winter Garden Theatre. For tickets, call 4168725555 or visit sandrashamas. com.

Soulpepper's A Midsummer Night's Dream contains one scene that's better done than in any other production I've seen. It comes after the big four-way lovers' quarrel. To stop the two men, Lysander and Demetrius, from killing one another, Oberon, king of the fairies, orders Puck to fog up the Athenian wood so that they'll get lost and pass out. This midsummer's night has already been less vernal and more nocturnal than any other Dream I recall; in this realm, Oberon's sovereignty is signified by his possession of a magic wand with a flashlight at each end. The production boasts a corps of actors who may at any moment be drafted to play fairies or trees or bushes or fairies pretending to be trees or bushes. Puck now marshals these forces in sinister shifting formations that obstruct and baffle the young men while making their predicament perfectly clear to us. We feel for and with them.

They deserve it. In this production not only do the two guys outshine their girls, which is practically unheard of, but they also emerge as the most vital characters in the entire piece, which is absolutely unheard of. Mike Ross is a preppy Lysander who presents himself sullenly, hands in pockets, at the Athenian court, before blossoming as a wide-eyed, buttermouthed amateur Lothario in the forest. Brendan Wall is a frustrated jock of a Demetrius, increasingly incensed at what a cad he's becoming. Opposite in temper, they're alike in their quicksilver communication of what they're saying, thinking and feeling, a quality mostly absent from Abena Malika's Hermia, who is over emphatic, and Karen Rae's Helena, who's the reverse. Ross, whose various talents seem to include bringing unpromising Shakespearean young men to life (he was a notable Oliver is As You Like It), was also responsible for the production's sound score, which manages to be both omnipresent and unobtrusive. And he may have had an additional influence on the show as a whole, since a cryptic program note credits him and the Soulpepper Academy (whose alumni make up most of the cast) with workshopping the production's "conceptual development."

I'm not sure, though, just what that concept has developed. Maybe it's making Puck and the fairies the controlling element in the play, at least in theory, by bringing them on as prologue as well as epilogue. Maybe it's their use as mobile scenery, which works beautifully some of the time and is just distracting at others. Maybe it's the "nothing up our sleeves" approach that this production, echoing the legendary Peter Brook one, takes to the supernatural. But that's no big deal, since this play, unlike The Tempest, doesn't call for magic tricks; three characters get eye drops and one gets a donkey's head, hardly effects requiring a Houdini level of prestidigitation. Rick Roberts' production is, in fact, uneven, though that's hardly a damning adjective to hurl at someone who, unless his bio is leaving stuff out, has never directed Shakespeare before and has only directed a couple of things by anyone else. Ken MacKenzie's spare set features a translucent screen behind which appear some lovely images, including a breathtaking one of Titania (the program spells her Tatania but I'll ignore that) stretched out asleep in her bower.

As usual, Oberon and Titania are doubled with the earthly rulers Theseus and Hippolyta, and this time it's the mortal half of the equation that proves more interesting. If there's a link, it's that in both kingdoms the woman challenges the man; in the palace she wins and in the wood she loses. Trish Lindstrom is not, mercifully, one of your sulky Hippolytas; in her first lines, she throws down an erotic gauntlet that Ins Choi's affable Theseus is slow to retrieve. She later strikes a blow for something or other by taking it upon herself to forgive the lovers, thereby overbearing the will not only of heavy-father Egeus, who would prefer honour killing, but of Theseus himself, to whom the speech textually belongs. Neither actor is as compelling in fairyland, with Choi's Oberon too monotonously the Demon King and Lindstrom almost obscured by the staging. Gregory Prest does very well as Puck, a Pan-like figure with a sympathy deficit, whose demands for attention include bemusing slides into a Russian accent. (I suspect an Academy in-joke.) But Titania's encounter with the translated Bottom can never have gone for less, mainly because this Bottom has nothing to be translated from.

After playing a magnificently down-at-heel professional actor in The Fantasticks, Oliver Dennis falls unexpectedly foul of the greatest of all amateurs. I didn't think it was possible for Dennis to be miscast, but Bottom's blithe self-assurance isn't in him. When he meets Peaseblossom, Cobweb and co. (played by tiny puppets, which is a cop-out), he seems intimidated by them, playing against the text and getting nothing in return. The clown scenes, though staffed by company vets, crumble around him. There are some nice bits, when we get to Pyramus and Thisbe: Michael Hanrahan's sorely tried Quince, miffed at being denied his epilogue, Michael Simpson's Thisbe, discovering his inner diva, and John Jarvis' indignant battered Wall. William Webster plays a wheel-chaired narcoleptic Lion, and he also delivers by orthodox standards -indeed by any standards -the evening's most authoritative verse-speaking in the monstrously thankless role of Egeus.

Though he may be challenged there by Jason Rothery, who as Philostrate seems to be channelling John Hodgman. The finale, with Puck in the ascendant, is beautifully done, and in sending us home happy it keeps the play's most important promise.

2011-03-02-hammering-it-home:
Theres a heart-stopping moment early in South Pacific when Carmen Cusack, as Ensign Nellie Forbush, sings one of the Twin Soliloquies in which she and the middle-aged planter Emile de Becque guardedly express their awakening feelings for one another. He's a cultured Frenchman, Nellie sings. "I'm a little hick." In the preceding dialogue, shes already laughingly used the word hick to describe herself; now it comes back to haunt her, and her hesitation before singing it and the determined emphasis with which she eventually does, speak subtle volumes.

Cusacks performance as Knucklehead (and also, in this production, Touslehead) Nellie, is one of the best I've seen in a musical: forthright, puzzled -and to an amazing extent in this genre -quiet. Nellie is the Second World War army nurse from Little Rock, Ark., who can cope with differences in age and education, and even with her lover's admission that hes killed a man, but not with the discovery that the two enchanting Polynesian children in his house are actually his. Her deliberate (as in slow and thoughtful) Southern accent helps a lot; you feel the battle between her inherited prejudices and her shame at making what she knows to be the wrong decision. It helps, too, that the shows book is tactful enough to excuse her from making any kind of reasoned declaration; she would have been too embarrassed. In another mood, her full-out singing and goofy dancing when she proclaims her love for a wonderful guy are wonderful themselves; anyone would melt. And her own melting, when she meets a girl from the other part of the plot who's in a state analogous to her own but worse, is another example of tact in writing and performance producing something powerfully and legitimately moving.

Bartlett Sher's very fine production is now on its second tour of duty in Toronto. Visually and musically, its as good as ever; dramatically, its even better. The part of Emile, previously played by Jason Howard, who sang well but acted stiffly, has been assumed (until March 8 when Howard returns) by David Pittsinger, who is swell in both departments. He can't quite compensate for the sketchy writing in Emile's plea of justifiable homicide but hes persuasive when uttering his outsiders credo to the U.S. Forces ("I know what you're against -what are you for?") and he even manages to make something heartfelt out of This Nearly Was Mine, an outrageously redundant song with all the earmarks of having been written to honour the leading man's contract.

Conviction and determination stamp nearly all the performances, notably Jodi Kimuras Bloody Mary, who rises far above her characters traditional role of exotic comic relief. She's a crafty chancer, fighting for her own and her child's survival. Early on in the show the marines teach her the phrase stingy bastard and she uses it constantly thereafter; it escalates from a joke to a bargaining tool to a heartbroken angry rebuke hurled at the faithless Lieutenant Cable (another guilty victim of his own prejudice). Earlier on weve seen her trying to seduce him on her daughters behalf even while knowing that he's slipping away. You may never have thought of Happy Talk as a song of desperation, but once you've heard this performance you may never think of it any other way. Luther Billis, Marys American counterpart, is given a new shine by Timothy Gulan, his eye constantly cocked and with a sensitive streak, traceable to his being hopelessly in love with Nellie. Hes the comic and she's the leading lady; romantic barriers don't get more insuperable than that.

Aaron Ramey, the new Joe Cable, is ardent and tortured enough in his love scenes but disappointingly wooden at marine HQ. These are the least convincing scenes in the show; some of the fault may be in the writing, but these are the only spots in the show where Shers actors seem content to play the stereotypes rather than to burrow beneath them. The Thanksgiving Follies sequence, though, seems to have improved, not only in the cheerfully tacky numbers themselves but in the tension of what goes on around and behind the stage, as everyones lives unravel in a contrast that's almost Chekhovian.

Despite all the obvious simplifications, there is a sense in this show of what life in the real Pacific theatre might have been like. It's always been my least favourite of the big four Richard Rodgers-Oscar Hammerstein musicals, but this revival makes a hell of a case for it. The sheer assurance of the piece, and the way it justifies that assurance, makes much of subsequent Broadway look like a joke. Note how it paints a broad canvas but begins and ends in domesticity. It comes from a time when liberal pieties could have the force of a manifesto. Another writer, a victim of McCarthyism whom Hammerstein befriended, said at his death, "The man was my friend; I liked the world a lot better when he was in it." Too right.

-- South Pacific runs until April 10. For tickets, call 416-644-3665 or visit dancaptickets.com.

THEATRE REVIEW

Billy Elliot The Musical Canon Theatre, Toronto

The signal achievement of Billy Elliot The Musical is to be even phonier than the movie it's based on.

Like the film, the show tells the story of an 11-year-old boy from a mining village in the North of England who wants to be a ballet dancer. His father is bitterly opposed to such a cityfied and sissified idea, because this is how Northcountry working men are expected to behave in popular fiction. He then undergoes an even more arbitrary conversion and becomes staunchly supportive. The background is the epic miners' strike of 1984-85, but we're given no reason to believe that Billy's dad and his even more virulent older brother would have reacted to him any differently if they'd still been happily employed. In fact, we're well into the second act before the personal and political stories make any contact at all. The strike at least gave the film some grounding in reality. In the stage version it's a decoration, to be alternately displayed and forgotten.

The obvious reason for making the story into a musical is the presence of dancing. It's also the greatest trap, and the show falls right into it, over and over again. Actually it's less a show about Billy than about whoever happens to be playing him; and there's no doubt that Cesar Corrales, who played him on the first night in Toronto, is a prodigy. (So, I dare say, are the three other kids who will be alternating with him during the run.) He acts appealingly, sings well and dances like one both possessed and selfpossessed. He also, for a 14year-old Canadian from a Mexican-Cuban background, copes amazingly well with the Geordie accent; He isn't always quite clear, but all around him more experienced players are having the same problem. He deserved the cheers he got at the curtain. The show, though, isn't content to wait that long. I've never seen a musical in which the performers get to take so many calls at the end of numbers.

Billy's life changes when he blunders into what is otherwise an all-girls' dancing lesson and finds, like the young man in A Chorus Line who crashed his sister's dance class, that he can do that. The story's whole basis is that he's the only person in town who can, and it might have been interesting if the show had run with that. But in this one, everybody dances, including the miners and the police who are sent in to break the strike. The coppers, doing their time-honoured knees-bend moves amid industrial unrest, might be called The Full Monty Python. And they're meant to be a threat. There's an especially dumb number, ironically entitled Solidarity, in which the worlds choreographically collide, with the schoolgirls crawling over the coppers' laps. It makes no sense of any kind.

There's a much better number in which Billy, at the height of his frustration, hurls himself against the cops' riot-shields. It, too, recalls A Chorus Line -The Music and the Mirror to be exact -and it's the one time that Peter Darling's choreography surpasses its model. But it isn't as if it's the police who are thwarting Billy's ambitions. Good dancing meets catchpenny thinking.

The show has the same author (Lee Hall) and director (Stephen Daldry) as the film, and together they've embraced every possible cliche. It isn't enough for Billy's mother to be dead; she has to keep coming back to him in dreams. His forgetful gran is a kitchen-comedy caricature. There's equal-opportunity stereotyping; the posh Southerners who greet Billy when he goes to London to audition for the Royal Ballet are ludicrously toffee-voiced. Back home, Billy's cross-dressing chum Michael involves him in a drag number in which they're joined by a stage full of huge ambulant frocks. Welcome to Broadway. So Michael's a dancer, too? A big guy with Afro horns in on one of Billy's dance lessons, though he's supposed to be playing iano. In an honestly frivolous musical, such inconsistencies could be fun. But this one has pretensions.

It pretends, for example, to be about ballet, though the most energetic number is called Born to Boogie and much of the other dancing is tap. There's one major exception: Billy imagines performing the pas de deux from Swan Lake, partnered by the dancer he hopes to become. This involves him dancing the girl's part, which you would think might confirm his dad's worst suspicions. In fact, it immediately precedes his change of heart. Now wait a minute: a man is motivated by his son's dream sequence? And wait another minute: Corrales' dancing is yearningly superb but what really brings down the house is the sight of him flying on wires: a mechanical effect having nothing to do with dance. And wait a third minute: much of the power of this scene is due to having the Tchaikovsky music piped in, which rather takes the shine off the show's official credit "music by Elton John." Shine happens to be the name of the score's big song; at least it's the one they reprise at the curtain call, though I had already forgotten hearing it before. John's music throughout is inoffensive (no power ballads) and thoroughly unexciting; Hall's lyrics are hard to judge, since they're mostly inaudible, but they don't seem to be forwarding plot or character.

The show has an uplifting story, a child hero and a presold title; no surprise that it's swept the world and that the first-night standing ovation was tumultuous. It has a good cast, too; Kate Hennig is outstanding as Billy's sweet-andsour dance teacher and surrogate mum, Armand Schultz and Patrick Mulvey are solid as his family, and the kids are more than all right. There are some legitimate goosebumps when the striking miners, plus one scab, rally round to raise the money for Billy to go to London, the father-son dynamic strikes some nice chords, and there's an occasional reminder of what life will be like for those in the village who, as Billy's brother bitterly puts it, aren't dancers. But none of this is done with music. It could be the right time for a stirring musical about a strike, but this one just goes through the motions. The extended curtain call finds the whole cast in tutus. So they are all dancers after all. Anything for a happy ending.

? For tickets, call 416-872-1212 or visit mirvish.com.

2011-03-05-a-canadian-stagehand-s-evalua:
In its upcoming season, Canadian Stage will be shifting from plays with long titles to plays with short ones. I'm only half-kidding. Matthew Jocelyn, the company's artistic director, began his regime last fall with his own production of Fernando Krapp Wrote Me This Letter: An Attempt at the Truth, and his inaugural season is about to wind up with The Cosmonaut's Last Message to the Woman He Once Loved in the Former Soviet Union. In between we have had Studies in Motion: The Hauntings of Eadweard Muybridge and -just about making the verbiage cut -Saint Carmen of the Main. Next season reverts to previous CanStage practice by including Red.

So, I asked Jocelyn over a cup of tea this week, did this mark a major turn-around in his brave new policy? Red, a recent Broadway success, is in a tradition of American plays with monosyllabic titles -Wit, Proof, Doubt -and self-evidently "important" subjects that have arrived on the stage of the Bluma Appel bearing Pulitzers and/or Tonys. Red, whose principal character is the American painter Mark Rothko, is about Art (which as it happens was the title of another ancien-regime playchoice). So, will our seeing Red signify not just a reversion but a retreat?

Jocelyn says not. "It's a brilliant play, and there will be no reverting." He adds that the play, which is set in Rothko's studio, is a perfect fit for Kim Collier, the Vancouver-based artist who directs it and whose productions of Studies in Motion and No Exit have demonstrated a remarkable and sometimes stunning visual imagination if, I would say, a less impressive judgment in choice of texts. Collier joins Canadian Stage full time next season as an associate director, and she typifies the kind of artist on whom Jocelyn pins his hopes and his policy: outside the Toronto mainstream, aesthetically and geographically, and devoted to the breaking down of barriers between drama, music, dance and technology.

He's an outsider himself. Now aged 53, and Canadian born and bred, he was a darkhorse candidate for his current position, having spent most of his career directing drama and opera in Europe. He was hired, he says, "with a very clear mandate to create an arts centre, to show the very best of Canadian artists in the context of the performing arts of North America. We're looking at a range of great Canadians at work, and working out the best place for them. This is a very sophisticated, wealthy, international city. But it also represents both a crest and a trough of sophistication. There isn't a tradition of curiosity. People haven't been taught to be curious about the unknown." He defines his mission as being about creating "zones of discovery as opposed to comfort and reassurance."

Bearing in mind that one person's discovery can be another's reassurance (and, in the immortal words of Tom Stoppard, that the audience doesn't owe the theatre anything, I'd say that so far Jocelyn has succeeded about 50% of the time, which is a very respectable score. Counting productions that Canadian Stage has either originated or hosted, either at the Bluma or in the smaller premises at Berkeley Street, the successes would include Fernando Krapp (though it met with some surprising opposition from the theatrical establishment), Robert Lepage's The Andersen Project and the current offering The Middle Place. Studies in Motion and Saint Carmen seem to me, at best, triumphs of style over content.

The Lepage show did best at the box office, not surprisingly in view not only of its attractiveness but of its creator's reputation. It's hardly news that Lepage mixes media better than anyone, but it's still an event when his work reaches Toronto. Of the shows announced for next season, I'm especially interested by Martin Crimp's Cruel and Tender, because of its author and because it marks Atom Egoyan's virtual debut as a director of drama; by Jocelyn's own production of Marivaux's The Game of Love and Chance, because it's the most celebrated play of a perennially neglected classic playwright, and because it's been newly translated by Nicolas Billon, who two years ago did a bang-up job on Moliere's The Sicilian; and by a German play The Test, because it reunites director Jason Byrne, actor Eric Peterson, and Company Theatre, jointly responsible for the remarkable Festen a few years ago.

Company Theatre, who have a sparse but superlative track record and an indefinable identity, begin with this production a residency, or co-partnership, with Canadian Stage which, Jocelyn says, "could make the biggest difference with them; it could help them consolidate." He seems to be limiting himself to one production a year. "I'm not obsessive about directing. I love it. I'd be emotionally wizened if I didn't do it. But if I did it nine months of the year, it wouldn't be good. This theatre is not about me." It is, though, about his taste, and so far I'd trust that.

Brothel #9 Factory Theatre, Toronto

The steady advance of Anusree Roy must rank among the most heartening forward marches of recent years. As actress and as playwright, she keeps doubling up on her own accomplishments. She first grabbed our attention with a delightful solo piece, Pyaasa.

Admittedly, she followed that up with a less delightful solo piece, Letters to My Grandma, but she compensated for it with a smart twohander, Roshni. And now comes Brothel #9, which is an even smarter four-hander, a fully fashioned full-length drama, complete with intermission. The bigger she gets, the better she gets. At this mathematical rate, she might, within a couple of years, give us an epic.

Brothel #9 is set in Calcutta, and as you might expect from its off-hand title, which combines the stark and the casual, it's about sexual trafficking. Rekha, a young vil-lage woman, arrives in the city thinking she has a job at a light-bulb factory, arranged for her by her brother-in-law. She finds instead that he has sold her as a prostitute. Her owner/employer is a man named Birbal. Jamuna, an indeterminately older woman, is the brothels senior attraction, cook, bottle-washer (fairly literally) and de facto madam.

Having pleaded with both of them, piteously and unavailingly, to release her, she turns with relief to a police officer, Salaudin, and finds -to the surprise of no one but herself -that hes one of the establishment's regulars, on the take and with first call on new merchandise. Salaudin's defloration of Rekha is unseen but very much heard; she emerges from it, staggering and apparently broken. She does not, however, fall apart. Determined to regain her freedom, she starts saving for it.

In addition to the four named characters, the cast includes a succession of anonymous men, skulking through the brothel door with varying degrees of furtiveness and bravado, and Rekhas door is, with increasing frequency, the one they make for.

The play tells a fairly simple, even melodramatic story, though its twists are both credible enough and adroit enough to keep us glued to the edges of our seats. It isnt often that a new play has us genuinely keyed up about what's going to happen next. There's an even more compelling set of interior actions, stemming from the fact that the power-relations within the quartet keep changing.

There is a solid sense, in Nigel Shawn Williams excellent production, of real lives being lived, real things being said: texture as well as text. The most obvious progression is Rekhas, from innocence to toughness, and Pamela Sinha makes both ends of the journey equally affecting. You could call her journey "empowering," but the play doesn't go in for words like that (or "journey," for that matter). It makes a big statement but, unlike the somewhat similar Ruined, which represents the Broadway idea of seriousness, it doesn't make big statements. Its also far better constructed, though like Ruined, it does leave you wondering whether the brothel is understaffed or the theatre is just underfunded.

Roy, who continues to write juicy roles for herself and to play them juicily, is Jamuna, whose whole existence is conflict. Shes capable of kindness, so long as she doesn't feel threatened, but she feels threatened most of the time. In the course of the play, Rekha gets pregnant, which makes Jamuna jealous on any number of levels. She fears loss of status; she also fears the loss of Salaudin, who's increasingly attracted to Rekha and whom she thinks to be, in a sense, hers.

The play, which manages to be unsentimentally hopeful, has a strong vein of equally unsentimental humour, and Roy mines most of it, which seems fair as she deposited it in the first place.

Sanjay Talwar, whose forte is playing weak authority figures, adds to their number as Salaudin, desperate to believe himself a good guy, and inclined to prove it by being generous with money; theres something pleasantly circular about how he effectively bribes the women whose other exploiters have bribed him. His developing feelings for Rekha seem genuine; but he is also, unsurprisingly, married.

The brutal Birbal, too, has a wife whos sick, in a village; his position on the totem-pole is compromised by the fact that most of what he earns goes to her.

Ash Knight's performance is the least defined of the four (also, to Western ears, the hardest initially to understand, though all four present us with that problem), but he fits aptly into the play's shifting cycle of dependencies.

There's a real dramatic world for the actors to fill; they are not forced, as actors so often are, to devote their energies to papering over the cracks. The people in this play are in flux, as people generally are, and the performers give us changes we can believe in.

Speaking of gifts, the Factory has already, with Eternal Hydra, made us a present of the best, almost-new play of the season. They now offer us the best really new one.

- Brothel #9 plays until March 27 at Toronto's Factory Theatre. For tickets call 416-504-9971.

THEATRE REVIEW

Are You Okay

Factory Studio Theatre,

Toronto

In Are You Okay Michael Healey talks and walks around the edges of the stage while Peggy Baker dances in the middle of it. It's a very satisfying, if occasionally puzzling, combination. The absence of a question mark from the title presumably means that no answer is required or expected. So I guess you could call this a rhetorical show.

Its gentle but searching rhetoric. Healey, whose contribution inevitably absorbs much of the attention of verbal animals like me, takes us through a day in the life. He lives, he says, at Queen and Ossington ("a terrible place to be if youre over 26"), and has a writer-in-residence's office at the Tarragon theatre, which is roughly at Bloor and Bathurst. Every day, he tells us -and I guess we have to believe him -he walks from home to office and back again. That's quite a schlep, especially for someone who admits to having trouble even getting out of the house, but I was with him, mentally, every step of the way. At least, I was with him on the way there; I especially enjoyed his cynical sojourn on College. The route back, though, sounded suspiciously circuitous to me. (What was he doing over on Jarvis?)

His walking thoughts arent all about local topography. Some of them are about the meaning of life, and theyre very persuasive. He ponders the distinct possibility that insights he thought he got from Wittgenstein might really have come from Dr. Phil, and worries about the likelihood that someone might find out. He compares his own sense of purpose -unfavourably, I think -to that of a monk making his way through a labyrinth in the courtyard of Chartres cathedral.

Healey's writing in this piece is as good as anything he's done, while his acting is his best ever. He always seems to be playing himself, whatever the role, and here hes spared the pretence that hes playing anyone else. He comes before us as a clear-but-baggyeyed philosopher, improvising his way through his own secular maze of good intentions and mixed accomplishments. He's very confident about his own hesitations. He looks and sounds the right age and attitude to be having a mid-life crisis, but he spurns the idea in favour of something far more interesting: a life crisis. Vocally, physically and mentally, he worries at things.

And while he worries about time running out, Baker demonstrates what great use she's making of her own. Healeys in his 40s, shes in her 50s; in terms of career expentancy, as between dancers and actors and/or writers, the gap is far wider. But she doesn't seem to be pining about it. There isn't, as far as I could tell, much direct correlation between what hes saying and what shes doing, though there's a rare moment of contact when he arrives at his office door and she virtually pushes him through it. That should learn him. If he frets about repetition, she appears to accept and even celebrate it. There's a recurring action in her dance, a bending and stretching, that suggests a visual ode to repetitive strain injury, except that where shes concerned there doesnt seem to be any strain. She's in great trim. Near the end of the show, Healey clears off the stage and she gets solo time, which she uses to communicate exultation. Or maybe the exultation is ours in seeing such grace, such discipline, such victory.

Healey starts the proceedings by introducing himself and everyone else connected. His own biographical details are correct, at least to my knowledge, except that he throws in a short riff about his own award-winning career in modern dance. This is an obvious fiction, possibly designed to clue us in that his later revelations may not be strictly factual either. He may not even walk to work. Not that that would invalidate the show. Among the others to whom he pays deserved tribute are Rebecca Picherack who did the lighting; Andrea Lundy who for once didn't, but is the production manager; Debashis Sinha who does the music; and Daniel Brooks, the director, whose production is yet another of his perfectly tuned precision instruments. The thing's a jewel.

- Are You Okay runs until March 13. For tickets, call 416-504-9971 or visit factorytheatre.ca.

If I were looking for some kind of unifying theme in Second City's latest revue, I'd say that most of the sketches concern dysfunctional relationships. But then most comedy is about dysfunctional relationships. So I won't look. Anyway This Party's a Riot! doesn't quite live up to its name, and is less good than its immediate predecessor, partly because it's not as striking visually, partly because its horizons are more limited.

Something Wicked Awesome This Way Comes, the previous go-round, recognized that politics might be good for something more than an irrelevant show title. (Although, admittedly, it's hard not to sympathize with the current team's quoted opinion that jokes about Toronto Mayor Rob Ford would be too easy and therefore not funny.) This one gets us firmly back in the living room, the bedroom, the office, the family car and Starbucks. It should appeal to anyone who has ever wanted to shoot a barista. It's a very good night out for other reasons, too. For instance:

The car scene A complacent boomer reminisces with infuriating smugness about the '60s while his son bitterly complains about dad's failure to die, or at least retire, thereby freeing the younger generation to get a job and pay off its student loan. Turns out they're on their way to the old people's home to pick up grandpa whom they've both treated appallingly, and who in a mumbling but humbling sort of way (shades of The Simpsons) lets them know it.

This scene comes early in the show and is probably the best thing in it. In its casual way, it draws blood. It's also a great showcase for the three men in the cast: Bob Baker (a big baby who can really boom) outrageously preening, Adam Cawley indignantly smouldering and Kris Siddiqi furiously muttering.

The office scene Might also be called the suggestions box scene. Several funny things happen, but none funnier than Dale Boyer standing pained and completely silent at the side of the stage while everybody else is sitting down. The relevant suggestion is that the office needs more chairs. It's nixed.

The other office scene This is dominated by Inessa Frantowski, a newcomer, lamenting the fact that she has to come to work every day. Also that she has to decide which weather-appropriate clothes to wear. We hear you, sister, and your existential angst.

This is one of two numbers in the evening that have something resembling a good punchline. The other one I won't spoil for you, except to say that it rounds off not only its own first scene, but the entire first half.

The club scene Two adolescent dudes jerk their carcasses about, more or less to the music, while boasting about all the chicks they expect to pick up here at the hub of the nightlife universe. ("It was worth the drive from Woodbridge.")

Cawley and Siddiqi are hilariously clueless here, especially the tall, thin Cawley showing off his post-workout physique. I suppose this may be the title number.

The hospital scene Carly Heffernan, as an oblivious nurse, tells her troubles to a patient who is comatose and wishes, to judge from his electronically amplified thoughts, that she were, too. This one gets quite dark.

The divorce scene A bewildered teenager (Cawley again; he's really the star this time), already traumatized by his parents' split, has to cope with the fact that his stepdad, with whom he's just decided to bond, is about to become his ex-stepdad. There are further complications, reminding me at least of the old calypso about "shame and scandal in the family."

The gesture at world affairs scene, doubling as the computer scene Actually, this isn't all that great, but the idea carries it. Middle Eastern revolutionaries, empowered by the Internet, are too glued to their screens to get up and take part in anything.

The school scene This touches on the multiculturalism debate, and occasions the best (and most truly political) line in the show: "I have no clue what it means to be a Canadian but I'm pissed off when people aren't."

There are also the zombie scene, the threesome scene, the compulsive-hoarder scene and a very good mistaken pickup scene. And there's the fact that the show doesn't know how to conclude, and decides to end it all with an improvisation that will (one hopes) vary from night to night but refused to take at the premiere. Of course, they could improvise still further and ditch the idea. In an earlier attempt to involve the audience, they also pulled CBC's Jian Ghomeshi up onstage, but I don't suppose that he'll be there every night. The show was directed by Bruce Pirrie.

? This Party's a Riot! has an indefinite run. For tickets, call 416-343-0011 or visit secondcity.com.

I seem to remember that when How Now Mrs. Brown Cow played here last year Brendan O'Carroll - its star, author, director and reason for being - told us in an uproarious curtain speech that he and his gang would be back this February with another instalment of what he cheekily described as their "five-part trilogy. He said he knew this because David Mirvish had promised him that it would be a cold day in February before he was ever allowed on a Mirvish stage again. Hes back again now with the threatened sequel, which is called Good Mourning Mrs. Brown. And hes behind his promised time, although in fairness this March certainly feels like February. Anyway, I hardly have the right to complain as I was late on the first night myself, for which I too blame the weather.

I wasn't all that late. I was in time for the play proper, if proper is the word. But I did miss the opening announcement in which O'Carroll told us just what to do with our cellphones and which last year had disposed me to love the show even before it got started. Id be very surprised if there wasnt such a prelude this year as well, since the format repeats that of its predecessor in every other respect. Maybe, if I had been thus softened up, I would have enjoyed myself as much this time as last. As it is, I have to profess myself disappointed and, in view of my previous enthusiasm, more than a little shamefaced.

If I, too, may repeat myself: O'Carroll plays Mrs. Agnes Brown, a Dublin widow who rules her family with a rod of iron and a tongue of salt. It's all a bit hard to keep track of, but she has an older unmarried daughter and two sons, one gay and partnered, one married and straight: sexually anyway. All these, plus the married sons wife, live under her roof. Theres another daughter, married, who fades out of this particular play and whose only function when in it seems to be to permit her mother to refer to her in-laws out in Donegal as sheepshaggers." Another of her favourite words is "feck; it, or its derivatives or their stronger Anglo-Saxon equivalents, crop up in just about every other line she utters. (Here she is admittedly in good cultural company; Canadian Stage's next season includes a compilation entitled Beckett, Feck It!) She's 9/10 prurient, 1/10 puritanical: a not-unheard-of combination, but one that seems to operate here according to which aspect is going to get the next laugh.

Also on the premises is Mrs. Browns nonagenerian father-in-law, on whom she inflicts unceasing verbal abuse and sometimes, in a slapstick sort of way, physical abuse as well. There was an odd resonant moment in the Brown Cow play when Grandad (Dermot ONeill in a flaxen floppy wig that must have been abandoned the day that the circus left town) turned to a family member and simply said, Help me." It went nowhere, but there were hopes, dashed, that this time it might. The family decides to stage a mock funeral so that the old man, who hasn't heard a nice word said to or about him in decades, may hear his own eulogy. This is the main storyline. At least it's what the title is about.

There are other bits of plot alternating through the evening. Theres the tribulations of Father Quinn, who is losing his vocation on account of his flock being lured away by evangelicals. This leads to the unprecedented spectacle of two Jehovahs Witnesses (well, actually they're Mormons) who, once they've met Mrs. Brown, cant wait to get their feet outside the door. There are the tribulations of brainy daughter Cathy, a psychologist, whos dating a copper. There's the saga of daughter-in-law Maria who may or may not be having twins. There's her husband Brendan, a former safe-cracker, being lured back to his life of crime by a loony confederate.

At one point, when Mrs. Brown is uncharacteristically offstage, theres a rather touching little scene in which Grandad gives Brendan some good advice. Then the matriarch barges back in and spoils it. At this point I decided that I didnt really like Mrs. Brown. And my annoyance at her habit of hogging every conversation spilled over onto her creator's habit -well, it's really a cross between a professional obligation and a compulsion -of hogging the stage, good at it though he undoubtedly is. Ironically, part of the trouble may be that, underneath all the gags, Mrs. Brown is quite a believable character, though not a very attractive one. When Cathy (Jennifer Gibney, whos Mrs. OCarroll in private life) accuses her mom of ruining her life, it's a textbook mother-daughter conflict.

There was a scene just like it in the previous play. Like all sitcoms, this one repeats and recycles, in technique as well as subject matter. Once again, in a deadeningly overamplified production, a supporting actor gets rebuked when her mic goes off. Once again O'Carroll suggests doing an instant recap when someone else gets a line wrong. Once again -many times again -the other actors break up at the stars supposed ad-libs. I almost believed in this last time, but its now impossible not to notice that it's always the actors playing the gay couple who get hysterics and that they always regain their composure with miraculous ease. The supporting acting does seem, with one terrible exception, to have improved, but the material has deteriorated, though O'Carrolls timing of the odd good lines remains impressive. (He has less physical comedy than before, though he still makes innumerable cups of tea.) Maybe this lightning just cannot strike twice. Even with three parts still to come, it seems safe to say that when youve seen one Mrs. Brown play you've seen them all. It's probably worth seeing one though.

Good Mourning Mrs. Brown runs at the Princess of Wales Theatre through March 19. Call 416-872-1212 or visit mirvish.com for ticket information.

THEATRE REVIEW

More Fine Girls

Tarragon Theatre, Toronto

My memories of the 1995 Theatre Columbus hit The Attic, the Pearls and Three Fine Girls are rather dim, though I do recall that arriving late in the run I couldn't see what all the fuss had been about. The show seemed, to put it charitably, slight. That, though, would place it several steps above its new sequel More Fine Girls, which is dire.

The three fine girls are three sisters whose surname is Fine (which sounds Jewish though we're led to believe they aren't) and whose first names are Jojo, Jelly and Jayne: an arrangement that should have led them to hate their parents more than they actually do. Not that they don't have their issues. They are the creations of Martha Ross, Leah Cherniak and AnnMarie MacDonald, who wrote and played them the first time around, and who now, as then, share authorship credit with Jennifer Brewin, Theatre Columbus's new artistic director, and with Alisa Palmer, director of the actual shows.

The first play found the three Fines on the top floor of the old family home, acting out memories from childhood and later, while their father's funeral happened downstairs. The new play balances its predecessor to the extent that it ends up in the same house, but with the revelations occurring in the basement. And if part one had an overload of whimsy, this one has nothing but.

It's aimed, obviously, at audiences eager to discover what happened to the characters in later life, rather than at those like me who had completely forgotten what happened to them earlier. However, research reminds me that Jojo was a theatrical academic, Jelly an artist and Jayne a high-flying exec. Fifteen-odd years later, Jojo and Jelly are still in the same lines of work, but Jayne has come down with a severe case of back-to-nature and has retired to a farm. Jojo and Jayne each keep expressing anxiety about the other's love life, or lack of it, and as much as they try to sound well-intentioned, they end up sounding schadenfreudian. They have similar, though greater, worries about Jelly who has inherited the house. She's turned it into an outsize art installation and hopes, as a birthday present to her daughter whose name is Jessie (of course), to levitate it. There are chairs and tables hanging on the walls of Judith Bowden's set, which turns out to be not a metaphor but a naturalistic depiction of how Jelly has done the place up.

The whole performance aims at being engagingly offthe-wall, but other than scenically, it doesn't have any wall to be off. It's weightless and aimless, a play with no moorings, just a series of gags loosely tied to presumed emotional baggage that nobody gets around to unpacking. Jojo, whose professional tic is to drop the names of major modern playwrights, demonstrates terminal chutzpah by remarking that Chekhov at least gave his three sisters somewhere to sit down. He also of course gave them relationships, passions and motivations, but Jojo is tactful enough not to mention it. She and her siblings do get to sit down together in one scene, set in a restaurant where they frustratingly fail to order anything: a frustration that the audience finds it all too easy to share. The only other emotions to make themselves properly felt are Jelly's annoyance at her sisters for invading her space and her fervent wish that they would go away.

Part of the reason for siding with Jelly rather than with either of the others is the way that Severn Thompson plays her; or perhaps just the fact that Thompson plays her. She is, to put it brutally, the only person onstage who can act: the only one, that is, who delivers her lines as if they were actually addressed to someone and who grasps that, even in the role of an eccentric artist who claims contact with extraterrestrial forces, underplaying can be a viable option. Thompson came late into the cast when Cherniak left it for what are described as "personal reasons." That, though it may be a breach of critical protocol to mention it, sounds suspicious; it suggests she had realized that there was no there there.

Anyway, Thompson, though playing in a different mode from her colleagues, manages to mesh with them perfectly in matters of narrative and timing, which is admirable. The other two are not actors but performers, at least MacDonald is. I remember thinking that she was much the best thing in The Attic, but her wide-eyed, jolly-hockey-sticks, hyper act has worn very thin. I will admit, though, that she's very funny when placing a call to Ikea and having to deal with their automated operator; we've all been there. (I mean to the operator, not to Ikea, though on second thought and since we're at the Tarragon .) Ross just wafts, all over the stage. Though she, too, has her empathetic moment when she reveals that, even though he's been her bread and butter, she hates Brecht. Like an AA confessional, it should do both speaker and listeners a power of good.

More Fine Girls runs until April 3. For tickets, call 416-531-1827 or visit tarragontheatre.com.
