For the second time in one week we have a new play that revolves around three sisters, and that invokes Chekhov in doing so. Though in Marie Clements' Tombs of the Vanishing Indian (a Native Earth Performing Arts production) the invoking is done in the program rather than, as cheekily in More Fine Girls, in the script itself. Unlike the Fine sisters, or indeed the Chekhov sisters, the Native American sisters in Clements' play haven't grown up together. They were separated in childhood and, as in a folk tale, all turn up in the same place years later. Unlike in a folk tale, their proximity doesn't result in their paths actually crossing; not at least on any realistic level. Spiritually, they may still be family; practically, not a chance.

They inhabit a political-psychological-symbolical drama whose powerful qualities are sidelined by diffuse construction and flat performance. Line by line, even scene by scene, it's often very well written. One of the most powerful scenes, and also one of the briefest, is the first, in which the girls' mother is gunned down by state troopers (at least I think that's what they are) who she fears have come to take her children from her: an anxiety well-rooted in both personal and tribal history. After her death the girls were placed in foster homes, and now (which for the play's purposes is circa 1975) we find them all in Los Angeles, in widely differing circumstances. Jessie is a doctor, Miranda is an aspiring actress and Janey is troubled, apparently vagrant, and convinced that she's killed a baby she may never actually have had. (The names aren't quite as insistently alliterative as those of the Fine girls, but close.) Each of the three is linked with a white man who has, for reasons affectionate and/or voyeuristic, a thing about Indians. For Janey, it's a friendly detective with anthropological interests. For Jessie, it's her husband, also a doctor, with whom she runs an inner-city clinic. Miranda's sparring partner is a washed-up movie director, at work on what promises to be a very minor Western -as, by the 1970s, most Westerns were. Miranda has been unadventurously cast as an Indian maiden, required to utter a line that she reads as "I'm dying; it is a good day to die, as usual," words of which she proceeds to make fine ironic hay. This arouses both the ire and the interest of the director who, we subsequently learn, has never got over playing cowboys and Indians as a kid. Their scenes together are the sparkiest and the most entertaining in the play, at least until they turn selfconsciously nasty.

There's fine writing in another vein, in the sisters' memory of their journey with their mother in a bus "with a dog on the side," along the traditional hopeful road from Oklahoma to California. Each of them in turn recounts the same incident, the words changing only slightly according to perspective. It does more than anything else to give the play some kind of poetic unity. Far less successful are the periodic appearances, in a recessed compartment high up on the stage, of a woman who offers obscurely encouraging exhortations and who might, at any given moment, be the ghost either of the mother or of a semi-legendary Indian woman who lost a child more than a century earlier. The program, which calls her The Lone Woman, provides more information about her than the play ever does. To add to the confusion, the same actress (Michelle St. John) also plays a succession of patients at Jessie's clinic whose reality status is also in question. Jessie's story, like Miranda's and also like Janey's, starts strong and ends up misty and overwrought ...

The play's constant shifts between levels, both psychic and physical, are more or less ignored in Yvette Nolan's production, which on an unfriendly set, takes everything pretty much as it comes. Performers, male ones especially, are left stranded on the edges of scenes in which they don't belong. The overall impression is of actors wandering through fog, guided only by their own survival skills. Falen Johnson's Miranda comes off best among the sisters, the feistiest performer handed the feistiest material; David Storch partners her wittily in their earlier scenes and rather desperately in their later ones. (Storch is an actor frequently attacked for extravagance. I've never understood this; he's usually seemed to me both funny and centred: indeed, funny because of being centred. But he may have met his match here.) PJ Prudat's Janey presses hard on the panic button, which seems to be what's required of her; Martin Julien, as a rumpled representative of L.A. Law, provides her with a sympathetic restraining influence. As Jessie, Nicole Joy-Fraser starts composed but goes out on an emotional limb that's increasingly unsupported: by the writing, by her own resources or by the stiff performance of her spouse (Keith Barker). It turns out that he, to her horror, has been running what's basically an Indian-sterilization operation: as mandated by a now-discredited official policy. This is at the heart of the play, and if I'm late in mentioning it, then so is the author. It links Jessie's story with Janey's (I'm not so sure about Miranda's) but dramaturgically it's stuck in its own little corner. As are too many parts of the play. The evening may aspire to be a universal lament but it comes off as more of a lopsided case study.

Tombs of the Vanishing Indian runs through March 27 at Buddies in Bad Times Theatre. Visit buddiesinbadtimes.com or call 416-975-8555 for ticket information.

THE TIME OF YOUR LIFE

Young Centre for the Performing Arts, Toronto

I had one of the times of my life at The Time of Your Life when Soulpepper first revived it three years ago. I had an even better time now that they have revived their revival.

William Saroyan's 1939 play is set in a San Francisco honkytonk saloon populated, like most of the great theatrical bar rooms, by a collection of drunks and dreamers. (The latter, surprisingly, outnumber the former. Compare it with the play's monumental anti-type, Eugene O'Neill's The Iceman Cometh, in which the two categories are almost synonymous.)

Albert Schultz's impeccably rhythmed production unfolds on Lorenzo Savoini's genre-defining set, between a series of fixed points. Upstage is the bar, where Nick, the owner, dispenses alcohol and a humorous tolerant brand of authority; Derek Boyes' genial performance in this role has strengthened over the years, and his momentary embrace of his young daughter (Alyson MacFarlane) is now a piercing emotional highlight, suggesting a world elsewhere.

Downstage right is a pin table to which a fanatical player (Ins Choi) devotes almost the entire length of the play. On the wall stage left is a phone, the conduit to many of the characters' hopes and despairs. And downstage from there sits Joe, who drinks only Champagne, because he can afford it, and who benevolently arranges some of the other characters' destinies, because he can afford that, too.

JosephZiegler'sperformance of his namesake is the magnetic, magnificent centre from which everything else radiates. Joe has made a pile in some unspecified business, which he says involved stealing, "and not from the rich," like all legalized money-making. We also learn that he never married or had a family, though he can imagine both. Ziegler's performance is the embodiment of still waters running deep; it summons the memory of great pain, both suffered and inflicted, and the desire to atone for it.

Particularly delightful is his relationship with his gofer Tom -a perfect performance by Kevin Bundy, naive and enthusiastic and on the edge of goofy -whom he sends out to buy toys and newspapers, and with whom he indulges in a gum-chewing contest, gleefully presided over by Stuart Hughes as a self-proclaimed old frontiersman, some of whose tall tales may even be true.

This scene, extraordinary enough in its own right, also helps forward Tom's blushingly ardent courtship of Kitty Duvall, a streetwalker who may or may not have a heart of gold but who does have the traditional supply of life-support illusions. Her name may be one of them. Karen Rae's Kitty is too much stolid, too little vulnerable; all the same a scene in her apartment, in which the play breaks its own implicit commitment to unity of place, turns out to be one of the best things in the production: tense and affectionate and beautifully inserted in its own pool of light.

The transition is also eased into by having Denzel Sinclaire, a fine singer-pianist in the Nat Cole vein, preface it with a dreamy rendition of Little Girl Blue. His actual character, very well played, is a dishwasher whose talent gets him promoted to inhouse entertainer and whose ill-treatment helps precipitate the denouement. Partnering him is Jeff Lillico as a hopeful -indeed, super-optimistic -hoofer-comedian whom the play declares to be both brilliant and terrible. His dancing brings down the house; his monologues provoke Oliver Dennis to advance on him with handcuffs.

Dennis plays an intermittently introspective cop who finds he has less in common with his buddies than with the old school pal whose longshoreman's strike he is supposed to be breaking, and to whom Brendan Wall gives a powerful supply of baffled bitterness. Gregory Prest is delightfully confused as the play's second hopeful wooer (mainly via that phone) whose true love (Krystin Pellerin) finds herself tearfully confronting the likelihood that she'll lose him in the coming war: still two years off if you were American, but the play knows.

Nearly everyone in this play is nice; even a snobbish society gentleman (John Jarvis) resentfully indulging his slumming wife (Brenda Robins) has his moment of protesting at cruelty. The necessary devil. unredeemed and irredeemable, is Blick from the vice squad, to whose nastiness Michael Simpson, in a startlingly improved performance, now brings complete conviction. A friend on the way out told me, rightly, that I should mention every performance; there isn't space but I should squeeze in William Webster's drunk with his reverberating rhetorical questions ("This is a free country, ain't it?"), Mike Ross, a mournfully oracular fixture at the bar ("no foundation, all the way down"), and Lyndon Hanrahan as a newsboy who breaks into When Irish Eyes Are Smiling and whom Nick, atypically, won't hire.

Everyone gets a chance, one of the defining joys of this kind of play and this kind of production. Saroyan's greatest subsequent success seems to have been writing the lyrics for Come on-a My House, the novelty song that made Rosemary Clooney a star but that she practically had to be forced to record. In this play, though, he managed somehow to be both wide-eyed and clear-eyed. It gives feel-good drama a good name.

- For tickets, call 4168668666 or visit soulpepper.ca.

2011-03-25-unfolds-into-six-pieces:
PAPER SERIES

Young Centre for the Performing Arts, Toronto

In David Yee's Paper Series, presented by Cahoots Theatre Company, six actors perform six short plays, all in the space of an hour and a half. The segments vary in tone and tempo, but all are at least a bit funny and at least a bit sad. Some of them are a lot of both. Each actor gets to be the protagonist/narrator of one piece, with the others lending sharp, disciplined support as required. Acting, writing and Nina Lee Aquinos direction are all first-rate.

As for what links the playlets to one another and to the overall title: They are called, in order of appearance, Paper Burns, Paper Cuts, Paper Dolls, Paper Tears, Paper Folds and Paper Route. (Alas, no Paper Moons or Paper Tigers.) You have to consult the actors bios to discover these subheadings; most of them are incipient puns, as are the characters' names.

We start with Baht (Marjorie Chan), a schoolgirl chastised by her father for forging his signature on a sick note: not for doing it, but for doing it badly. Forgery is his own game, and he teaches his skills to his daughter, but not well enough; his bullet-ridden demise lands her in trouble with the Russian mob, who are unimpressed with the quality of her bank notes; she can burn paper but paper burns her. The action moves swiftly and internationally, getting us off to a breezy start. Entertaining though it is, however, it seems in retrospect the weakest part of the evening.

We shift into high gear as Hope (Rosa Laborde) tries, hopefully, to write a Dear John letter to a partner whose name happens, ridiculously, to be John. Trying to dump him, she begins listing all the things about him she can no longer stand, but discards the letter as too cruel; this paper cuts too deep. She tries a succession of softer messages, and with each she gives us a clearer and wittier view of the relationship itself. This is lovely writing and lovely acting.

Lovely, too, is Mutt (Rebecca Applebaum), who in her fifth or sixth foster home, comforts herself by making paper cutouts of her Scottish father and Asian mother, and imagines them loving her while gently bickering among themselves.

In a cast equally divided by gender, the three women all get to strut their solo stuff before the three men, which is unexpected but unimportant. First up among the guys is Wisdom (Lorenzo Garcia), a waiter in a Chinese restaurant, whose fed-upness with a loutish customer incites him to write the man and his date fortune cookie mottos that effectively ruin their plans for the evening. The idea catches on, and soon customers are flocking to the place, not to consume the cuisine but to sample Wisdom's wisdom. Brilliantly set up, the story rises to a climax of mayhem that feels forced as narrative, but is hilariously staged. The section, too, has a very good deflationary punchline, as indeed do most of the sections. (David Yee, Second City needs you.)

The paper that folds is an origami swan that Symbol (Byron Abalos) presents to his suddenly ex-girlfriend as a memento of their relationship. This fifth episode in the series suffers from being a photo-negative of episode two, but like its predecessor, its full of bittersweet insights into the pleasures and pitfalls of coupledom.

Finally, and most memorably, we meet Isaac (Kawa Auda), whose route is the one he follows as a Toronto taxi driver and whose paper, which he keeps in his cab, is the certificate he received on completing his medical studies in India. Hes one of a knot of immigrant taxi jockeys with no outlet for their real skills. Finally, they get a chance to put their training into practice. Triumph is shot through with bitterness, or maybe it's the other way about.

Laborde and Auda give the standout performances, but all half-dozen are fine, not just in their solos but in their supporting interjections. In an exceptionally light and fluid production, they bob invigoratingly up from the sidelines as thickvoiced Slavic gangsters, as the orphaned Mutt's pungently accented parents, as an infuriatingly yowling cat, as cocksure discomfited restaurant patrons. They also go into full-company kung-fu or Bollywood routines.

The paper, meanwhile, lives up to its title billing, filling an already-white stage (Camellia Koo, designer) like a snowstorm, as each new sheaf of it is discarded. Yee, already known as an excellent actor, received award nominations for his play Lady in the Red Dress. I missed it, but I'll take it on trust and say that this new collection establishes him among Canada's more-thanpromising playwrights. There it is, on paper.

- Paper Series runs until April 9. For tickets, call 4168668666 or visit youngcentre.ca.
2011-03-26-of-models-muses-and-mistresse:
The theme and subject of Montparnasse is female nudity, and its most obvious attraction, though it has many others, is that it features two beautiful and talented women -the talent being part of the beauty -who spend a substantial portion of it with their clothes off.

Maev Beaty, best known as an actress, and Erin Shields, best known as a playwright, wrote this play together and play all the roles, the chief ones being an artist and a model. The scene is Paris in the 1920s. Shields is Margaret, a young expat from Toronto who, after a brief period working in a sausage factory, opts for the more fulfilling and certainly more exciting job of posing for painters. She finds it both physically and psychologically liberating. Beaty is Amelia, her more reserved friend from back home, who takes a ship to join her. Amelia envisions a career on the other side of the easel, but that takes time as well as talent. Both women have amusing monologues in which they count off the things they have learned about Paris, such as the difficulty of finding your best friend's lodging when you dont have the right address and the greater hardship of earning a living. Margaret, overbooked, suggests Amelia take over one of her modelling assignments. Amelia protests that she couldnt possibly, but necessity overrules, and she soon finds herself as much in demand as her friend if not more so. Success as a model doesn't necessarily lead to success as an artist, but she does get to meet some interesting people.

Natives or tourists, the famous Parisian painters of the '20s dont include any women. Montparnasse doesnt really get into the question of why this was the case, but it does leave it hanging intriguingly in the air. It's far more forthcoming on the relationship of painter and subject. It's inevitable, by the laws of drama if not of life, that Margaret will end up posing for Amelia when the latter gets a shot at a major exhibition. The resultant portrait is a stunner, or so were told (we never, of course, get to see it), but it brings to boiling point all the tensions and jealousies -personal, professional, sexual -that unavoidably simmer when two highly charged people in the same line of work share living quarters. Margaret likes to go to wild parties and bring people home; Amelia likes -needs -to use the same small space as her studio. Margaret claims the portrait wouldnt exist without her and that, morally if not legally, it's as much hers as Amelia's. Amelia, like artists through the ages, doesnt see it that way. And the play leaves us with a bittersweet question: If a work of art continues to find an audience, what actually survives, the subject or the object? (Mr. Keats, your Grecian urns agent is calling.)

On a chattier level, Montparnasse functions as a quick guide to la vie de Boheme, post-war, pre-crash. Our imaginary heroines get to meet, and at the very least greet, their real-life heroes. It could be argued that when Margaret changed careers she went from one meat market to another; and indeed one of her lover-employers is Chaim Soutine, who sends her out to buy the bovine carcasses he paints. Amelia becomes the muse, model and mistress of Fernand Leger, to whom she offers expert advice on where to position his subjects. But what, after her first modelling experience, brings her further out of her shell is an affair with Sylvia Beach, proprietress of the legendary bookstore Shakespeare and Company. The French Mount Parnassus naturally has writers as well as painters nestling on its slopes; James Joyce, Sylvia's particular protege, makes a fleeting appearance, and Henry Miller makes a less fleeting and rather riotous one. At its pyrotechnic highpoint, the show cross-cuts between two social gatherings, showing us Amelia briefly feted by the acclaimed and artistic, and Margaret drowning her resentments with the louche and the lively. The transitions are done at dizzying speed, the two performers in multiple impersonations daring us to keep up. It's here that the differences between them come most fully into relief. Shields is emphatically there, glorying in Amelia, right from the nude soliloquy that, in opening the play, both charms and disarms. (And if you want to observe exactly how an actress breathes, youll never have a better chance.) She is more slapdash in her other roles. Beaty is more elusive: a lightning caricaturist, sharp and supple, who also digs deep and true into her main assignment. Unlike Margaret, Amelia develops, and Beaty fills in her whole progress. She can also, in delivering a sobering epilogue, step out of her role without abandoning it. She doesnt quite recapture the astonishing concentration of shyness with which she first appeared outside her friend's door when the play was done at Summerworks two years ago. In other respects too, as often happens when fringe shows get promoted, Andrea Donaldson's production has lost in impact what it's gained in elaboration. A crucial scene, the destruction of a painting was more wrenching when more simply done. It still works though, as does the whole piece. A play celebrates another art form and in doing so glorifies its own.

? Montparnasse runs through April 12 at Theatre Passe Muraille. Call 416-504-7529 or visit passemuraille. on.ca for ticket information.

2011-03-31-the-creature-featured:
THEATRE REVIEW

FRANKENSTEIN

National Theatre Live

Man, look in the mirror. Behold a Monster. In the British National Theatre production of Frankenstein, two young actors alternate in the roles of the eponymous scientist and his scarifying creation. Two weeks ago, courtesy of National Theatre Live, audiences in movie theatres worldwide had the chance to see Benedict Cumberbatch and Jonny Lee Miller as creature and creator respectively. Thursday, in the production's second international transmission, the roles will be reversed.

The production, which has been generally and for the most part justifiably acclaimed, marks the return to theatre direction for Danny Boyle. The adaptation is the work of the British playwright Nick Dear. They are rightly proud of having given Frankensteins monster his voice back. Most movie versions have presented him as a grunting, lumbering ogre. In Mary Shelleys original novel, though, he is intelligent, highly articulate and even, no thanks to Victor Frankenstein whose responsibility it might reasonably have been, literate.

In both the novel and the play, Victor, disgusted at the ugliness of what he has wrought, turns his back on it and leaves it to wander through GermanyandSwitzerlandfending for itself. It discovers three impoverished French swells in a hut, and through a combination of lip-reading and deduction, learns their language.

In the book, this is accomplished through a prolonged period of observation on the part of the monster. As a theatrical device, this could be limiting, so the Creature, to give him his program billing, is granted a prolonged relationship with the aged head of the house who, being blind, can't be physically revolted by him, and who gives him a crash course in Plutarch, Goethe and Paradise Lost.

As a created being, the Creature finds a kindred spirit in Adam; as an outcast, he identifies, far more strongly, with Satan. When he finally tracks down his own maker in his Genevan retreat, he's able to pose the pointed questions that man has always wanted to ask of God: If you constructed me -- and in your own image at that -- how can anything be my fault, and why am I suffering? And Shelley sees to it that Frankensteins answers are as evasive and unsatisfactory as religions have always been.

It's in bringing this debate and its attendant metaphor home that this version is at its strongest. The actual text isn't that wonderful. Some of it is authentic Shelley, which when spoken sounds stiff; the rest, meaning the most, is pastiche Dear, an uneasy compromise between ancient and modern. Theres nothing that good acting couldnt successfully navigate; but the standard of supporting acting here is far below what used to be the norm at the National. The lower orders drag out all the old rustic cliches; the nobility are dull or, in the case of Frankenstein pere, unforgivably bad. The only exceptions are Karl Johnson as the sightless tutor and Naomie Harris as the literal bride of Frankenstein, who comes to a nasty end on her nuptial night: the result of the Creature's taking revenge for Victor's welshing on his promise to provide him with a lady Creature to ease his terrible loneliness.

The monsters pain is palpable, and gets us on his side throughout. So what if he burns his benefactors in their beds, murders Victors kid brother and rapes Elizabeth, who's been anachronistically kind to him, before killing her? Cumberbatch achieves a looming, slow-moving, painfully eloquent triumph. So, by all accounts, does Miller, his alternate; though their movement director and make-up artists must surely share some credit.

The title character, at least as Miller plays him, is reduced to minor-character status, and overdone like the rest. When man and monster have their great confrontation, the monster is all focused anger and anguish; the man merely rants. Just in terms of stage time, the adaptation gives the Creature a head start over the Doctor, who never really catches up.

Technically and sonically Boyle's production is very impressive, although seeing it at second hand, so to speak, we find ourselves watching the effects for their own sakes rather than for their results; as was not the case on other, simpler, National Theatre Live occasions. It's tempting to compare the central duo to a Germanic Prospero and Caliban, but they come off here more like Othello and Iago: partners in crime, indissolubly knit. And they follow one another to the extremes. Like the novel, the play drives through to a finale in the Arctic wastes, and it summons them up with comparable intensity; though its new open-ended ending is more frustrating than stimulating. In this matter, Mary knew best.

- Danny Boyle's National Theatre production of Frankenstein screens March 31 at various Cineplex theatres across the country. For ticket information and showtimes, visit cineplex.com. robert.cushman@hotmail.com

2011-04-01-pope-on-the-ropes-the-borgias:
Some things look too good to be true, or too attractive to come out right. Boardwalk Empire was one of them: all that booze, all that dancing, all those gangsters, all those 1920s fashions, all that Atlantic City, all that sex. The Borgias is another: all that poison, all those brawls and banquets, all those corrupt cardinals and guzzling grandees, all those Renaissance frocks, all that Rome, all that sex.

Boardwalk Empire, after a disappointing start, did eventually pull itself up by its bootstraps and become an approximation of what wed hoped it would be. The Borgias, which has the cords of innumerable ecclesiastical robes on which to elevate itself, may manage a similar improvement over the season. Judging, though, from its double-length series premiere and conventionally proportioned second episode, I can't say I'm hopeful.

Like Boardwalk Empire, which had Martin Scorsese among its producers, The Borgias has a famous film director in its corner. The show is Neil Jordans baby. Like Scorsese, he directed the first episode. Unlike Scorsese, he also wrote it, and the eight that follow it. His direction here is standard TV historical, very solemn and scenic; so, and rather more damagingly, is his writing. The smarts of The Crying Game are nowhere to be heard.

The show is advertised as the story of the original crime family and were meant to think of the Borgias, whose patriarch bribed and intrigued his way to the papal chair, as ancestors of the Corleones and the Sopranos. Those families' writers, though, were spared any stylistic battles between ancient and modern; they made the current vernacular poetic. The Borgias, ploddingly prosaic, tries instead to creep us out by telling us, over and over again, how recognizably evil these 15th-century priests and nobles were. And, look, they had sex, too.

We start, in 1492 (now, there's a year) with Pope Innocent VIII on his deathbed, lamenting that neither he nor the church he represents have lived up to his chosen name. Lurking round a pillar is Jeremy Irons as Cardinal Rodrigo Borgia; skulking round another pillar is Colm Feore as his arch-enemy Cardinal Della Rovere, whos nasty but incorruptible; and peering round a third is seasonpremiere guest star Derek Jacobi. He plays a cardinal more venerable than the others but no more trustworthy.

Borgia, a Spaniard, is an outsider in Rome and hated for it; he also, despite his vows, has fathered two grown sons, Cesare and Juan, and a growing daughter, the laterto-be-celebrated Lucrezia. But then, as one of his fellow cardinals, says, "Let he who is without children cast the first stone." (That, by the way, is as good as the dialogue gets.)

Irons, whos the best reason for watching the show, excels at the silky, ambiguous pronouncement, and at conveying, through pouchy cheeks and darting eyes, that he's burning with three conflicting emotions at the same time. When Irons is on fire, he glows. He hasn't, though, communicated that heat to the rest of the family. His sons (Francois Arnaud and David Oakes) are indistinguishable, despite one being a priest and the other a soldier; and with Lucrezia (Holliday Grainger) its too soon to tell. She may grow up to justify her, possibly spurious, reputation as the most lethal of the Borgias, but at the moment she seems no more than spoiled, though with an unhealthy attachment to her priestly brother Cesare. The old combination: incest and incense.

Theres also the usual complement of degenerate princelings, including the stone-deaf king of Naples and his mincing son. But nobody comes to life, though Sean Harris tries hard as a dedicated assassin who knows the value of hanging out with cooks.

It must all, what with sets and costumes and extras, have cost bundles; and I may go on watching, from a residual interest in the subject and in some of the actors. Joanne Whalley, for example, plays the ex-mistress, and I'm intrigued by the prospect of Steven Berkoff, who was once TV's best Hitler, as the blistering friar Savonarola, who cast all vanities into the fire and was finally cast there himself. But really, if you want literate and involving drama on a Sunday night, best to stick with A&E's Breakout Kings.

The Borgias premeries April 3 at 10 p.m. on Bravo!

Showtime / Jeremy Irons is the best reason for watching The Borgias, and not just because he looks so great in that excellent hat.;; Caption:
2011-04-02-the-gulag-the-blacklist-from-:
The brief opening scene of After Akhmatova, a scene discreet and powerful in equal measure, shows two women reciting lines of a poem back and forth to one another, so that they may commit it to memory. When this has been accomplished they burn the paper on which the poem was written. One of the women is the Russian poet Anna Akhmatova, the other is a friend. The poem is Requiem, composed by Akhmatova at the height of the Stalinist terror, as testimony to the sufferings of her son Lev Gumilyov, who, when she wrote it, had just begun what was to be an 18year sojourn in the Gulag, and of all the others who shared his fate.

Kate Cayley's play, which is fascinating if not quite satisfying, shifts between the 1930s and the 1960s. Lev was released in 1963; his mother died three years later, by which time she had become an international celebrity. Two years after that, a brighteyed American academic named Alan Taylor arrives in Leningrad to interview Lev, and is surprised not to find the mother-revering, Communisthating figure he had expected. According to Lev, Anna had been a cold, neglectful parent; after divorcing his father (executed under Lenin), she had left him with her mother-in-law. When he finally moved in with Anna, he had to sleep in the hall. She had, in fact, more compassion for humanity in general than for the humanity at hand: a charge that Anna, back in the '30s, does not deny.

Lev's political position is harder to work out. Maybe his "rehabilitation" actually took; maybe, in a postStalinist but still Communist Russia, he's keeping his head down; maybe his experiences have soured him on all ideological positions. He certainly takes great sour pleasure in debunking the American's humanist idealism. Undoubtedly he has earned his bitterness, something that Eric Goulem, who plays him, conveys fullforce. Gaunt and mocking, he looks and initially sounds exactly right. But, as he goes on, his performance hardens into a machine-gun monotony, unvaried even in the flashbacks to his 20-years younger self.

The heart of the play is in the debates, increasingly keyed up, between Lev and Alan, a role that finally gives Paul Dunn the chance to play a grown-up; he even has a beard. He's still boyish; Alan, who comes bearing a tape recorder, has some growing up to do. His default position, presented by Dunn with brilliantly articulated back-to-the-wall lucidity, is that, yes, Anna failed Lev personally, but that she did something more important by creating art that will fix and outlast the entire period, and to which Stalin himself will be "merely a footnote." Nice, but I have my doubts; the evil that men do has a habit of living after them.

I suspect the author's intellectual sympathies are with Alan and her emotional with Lev who forces Alan, and us with him, into seeing the arrests and interrogations through his eyes. There are some clever strokes of theatre here, but the discusssion never quite connects with Anna herself or with the dramatic scenes from the terror, excellent though these are in their own right. In Alan Dilworth's stark, tactful production we feel the hunger, the cold and the fear. Sarah Orenstein has the full measure of Anna's flinty far-sightedness and emotional myopia, while as her fellow poet and her son's fellow victim Osip Mandelstam, Richard McMillan, one of our finest actors, gives one of his finest performances. In his early appearances, as a gentle mentor, he's pure secular Russian saint; his final scene in which his wife quietly feeds him an egg before he's dragged off by the police, is extraordinarily moving. Caroline Gillis, who plays the wife, is also fine as the old woman, lined up outside a prison in hopeless hope of glimpsing her own son, who inspires Akhmatova to write Requiem. Claire Calnan seems wasted as Anna's confidante, but it's nice to have her around.

From A to Z: after After Akhmatova, Zero Hour. This is a one-man show, written and performed by American actor Jim Brochu, brought in by the Harold Green Theatre, about Zero Mostel, actor, comedian, painter (his favourite pursuit), "giant talent and giant pain in the ass" (I quote, though not from the play). He was also a victim of the 1950s blacklist, which if hardly comparable to the Gulag, was an atrocity real enough and stupid enough in its own right. The late Jack Gilford, Mostel's friend and fellow victim, once told me how it felt to face the Un-American Activities Committee: "They wanted you dead." He also told me how it felt to share a stage with Zero himself, after Mostel had secured him a role in his own comeback show A Funny Thing Happened on the Way to the Forum. It was a different kind of persecution: "I thought, if he's doing this to me when I'm his friend, how would he treat me if I was his enemy?" (I suggested that if they'd been enemies, Zero would have left him alone. Jack seemed to think there was something in that.) In short, Mostel was hardly just a teddy bear with a paintbrush; Brochu compromises at making him amiably rude. The show has many of the familiar faults of its genre. It has the needless framework of an imaginary interview with an invisible journalist. It drags stuff in (Billie Holiday's appearance with Zero on a nightclub bill is mentioned, just so we can hear a soundbite from one of her records) and it leaves stuff out; Zero's disowning by his parents when he married a Gentile is mentioned, then forgotten until needed for tearjerking purposes. Jerome Robbins' future status as an informer is given away too early, and though we're told that Mostel hated making The Producers, we're never told why. There are, though, some very good jokes, whether or not they're authentic Zero; I especially liked the one about the Hasidic rabbi and the parrot, and I laughed aloud at the revelation that the Torah allows us to eat pork and shellfish "only in Chinese restaurants." And, as well as perfectly reproducing Mostel's physical and vocal bulk, Brochu does deliver a performance that stands in its own right. He may be trying on another man's suit, but he isn't just hanging on to his coattails.

After Akhmatova runs through May 1 at the Tarragon Extra Space. Call 416-531-1827 or visit tarragontheatre.com for details; Zero Hour runs through April 16 at the Al Green Theatre. Call 416-366-7723 or visit stlc.com for more information.

2011-04-05-fright-radio-theatre-review-t:
The Art of Time Ensemble starts with music and doesn't stop. Its contribution to this year's World Stage season was a doubleheader of music and drama: the first half a concert, the second a play.

It was first planned, as the ensemble's director and conductor Andrew Burashko informed us, as a centenary tribute to the American composer Bernard Herrmann, best known for his classic movie scores. Herrmann worked with Orson Welles in his infant prodigy days; he was the musical director for Welles' New York radio shows before taking off with him to Hollywood. It seemed a reasonable assumption, then, that Herrmann had composed the music for Welles' most notorious radio project: the 1938 adaptation of H.G. Wells' The War of the Worlds that sent New Yorkers and New Jerseyites screaming out of their homes, convinced that the Martians were coming for them. Or so the legend goes.

Unfortunately, Herrmann's participation as composer proved on examination to be another legend. He did indeed conduct the CBS orchestra on the show, but it was playing other people's tunes. The Art of Time musicians did the same in the evening's second half, which was a re-enactment of the original script, read and performed by three actors in a mock-up of a radio studio.

It was preceded by a more formal composer tribute. The fearsome number of consonants in Herrmann's name seems to have been exceeded only by the quantity of famous films for which he provided scary scores; he was Hitchcock's favourite composer as well as Welles'. Dan Parr assembled some 20 of these themes into a composition entitled Herrmannthology, which the orchestra played while we watched a seamlessly synchronized montage of corresponding clips.

Back from our drinks for the main event, we discovered Nicholas Campbell as a grizzled seen-it-all actor, Marc Bendavid as a young eager-toplease actor and Don McKellar, whose name was Orson Welles. McKellar, Canadian drama's go-to guy for playing egomaniacal directors, presented this one as a self-satisfied prankster who devoted as much energy to strolling around the set exchanging gleeful winks with his collaborators as he did to his official duties of acting, announcing and seat-ofthe-pants directing -which, in this context, bore a marked resemblance to conducting.

In 1938, radio drama was done live, and McKellar left us in no doubt that Welles really dug the power involved. As is well known, Welles' War of the Worlds told the story as a succession of news bulletins, as if the invasion by aliens were happening then and (if you lived in New Jersey) there. To preserve the illusion, the announcer kept returning the audience to "our scheduled programming," which consisted of ballroom music, performed by "Ramon Raquello and his orchestra," who were impersonated by the Herrmann herd (herrd?), who were impersonated by the Burashko bunch.

Question: Was the original audience really fooled, accustomed as they must have been to tuning in every week at this time to hear Welles' Mercury Theatre of the Air? Didn't they find it suspiciously coincidental that the tunes selected by Senor Raquello -Stardust, I'm Always Chasing Rainbows -all had extraterrestrial connotations? Even taking the legend at face value, one obvious thing missing from the meticulous re-enactment onstage was a counterpoint narrative about the audience response.

Another thing was the efforts of the CBS brass to get Welles to come clean while the show was on the air and his refusal to oblige. These after all, rather than the show itself, are what have fascinated people down the decades and why we turned up for it now. We did get some inkling of it from Campbell's restrained, wearied rendition of the scientist, and narrating survivor, Professor Pierson, making us suspend two distinct levels of disbelief.

Welles apparently played this role himself, but McKellar principally confined himself to looking devilishly pleased at wreaking all that havoc. Or maybe he just enjoyed playing with all those toys. He certainly had a marvellous collaborator in the show's fourth performer, and real star, John Gzowski. Usually just an invisible name in the program, affixed to a sound-design credit, Gzowski obviously relished his time in full view, surrounded by a battery of homemade devices for answering every challenge the script could throw at him and delighting in employing them. When I was at the BBC, eons ago, the official description for this job was "spot effects." Gzowski has the grander title of "foley artist." But he deserves it.

2011-04-09-the-pains-and-privilege-of-fr:
Isaw Lost Voices at a students matinee, which was probably the best way to see it. Ed Roy's play is the kind that takes an issue, and then attempts to build a drama around it. In this case, the subject is the plight of child refugees. Two early teenagers -a girl from India, a boy from Pakistan -arrive, separately and unaccompanied, at Pearson airport, where the authorities have to decide what to do with them. The emotional stakes are high enough, and the narrative tension strong enough, for the students -schoolkids actually -who comprised the audience to have sat quiet and attentive. I was held myself.

However, Topological Theatre, which presents the production, is not primarily a young people's company -at least it makes no claims to be -and if the show is judged as a fleshedout drama for grown-ups, then big holes start appearing. The play might actually do better as a documentary piece that concentrated on the fleeing kids. In fact, it devotes as much time to the Canadian childrens aid workers who are handling their cases, and who have their own problems. Its obviously intended that the two strands will enrich one another, and there are occasional moments when this kind of dramatic cross-fertilization does seem about to happen. Mostly though, the stories just get in one another's way. Each prevents the other from being explored at anything but the most rudimentary level.

The youngsters are Nabeela, whose abusive father has sold her to a trafficker who has a buyer for her in Canada, and Wakeed, who is fleeing from the Taliban after they have burned a school with his two sisters inside it. The officials investigating them are Terri, a veteran in the field who's experiencing burnout, and Phil, whos just off his training course and whom Terri is supposed to be mentoring, something for which she warns him at the start she has neither the time nor the patience. Terri gives Phil a very hard time, something for which he thanks her in the end, though its not very clear why.

For the most part, Terri deals with Nabeela and Phil with Wakeed; whether the gender alignment is deliberate or coincidental is something else that remains unclear. Their tasks are made harder by the fact that initially neither of their clients will say a word; their interviewers aren't even sure they understand English, though the audience has reason to think otherwise. We've heard their inner monologues addressed to the more sympathetic of the folks back home (Nabeelas mother, both of Wakeeds parents), and these have all been in English. These may, of course, have been translated for our benefit, but it's still obvious that the characters are going to have to find some words if the play is to proceed. In fact, their initial silence -part caution, part trauma -doesn't strain credibility; what does is the extent of their bilingual facility once their lost voices are found. With Wakeed it all starts with the word pizza; Terri has told Phil that everybody likes pizza, and it may be the soundest advice she gives him. Wakeed even likes it for breakfast, which takes Phil aback.

Nabeela learned English by running errands for an Englishwoman, Wakeed by fraternizing with a Canadian army sergeant, in scenes that suggest some future CBC radio series called Pakistanada. (The plays view of the Canadian military mission seems to be that its a good idea that doesn't work.) The details surrounding Nabeela's arrival in Toronto are murky. She is said to have been accompanied by a mysterious "uncle" who then deserted her; in which case, how was the transaction supposed to work? Both have mixed feelings about remaining in Canada: Nabeela fears for her younger sisters left to her fathers mercies, Wakeed fears for his "honour." Their background scenes are written in flat, stock terms but their situations, and all the other blighted childhoods that they represent, are strong enough to involve us, just as, despite all professional protocol, they involve Phil and Terri.

Those two, however, do not have their charges built-in dramatic advantages. We learn that Phil is a son of privilege, trying to compensate; we learn what motivated Terri's choice of profession (and it turns out to be the biggest cliche in the whole play). The two of them lecture one another on their respective failings, without convincing us that these exist for any other reason than to fill out the play. The pressures on them, ferociously overworked and under-supported as they are, arouse our concern; they themselves don't. Its neat that they both should achieve a breakthrough when they temporarily swap cases; its frustrating, to put it very mildly, that the resolution of both those cases should take place offstage. Sarena Parmar and Owais Lightwala give sympathetic performances as the young refugees. So, as far as the play allows, do Soo Garay and Shaun McComb as their elders; if Garay's flights off the handle sometimes seem forced, that's probably unavoidable. Both actors also play the older characters in the flashbacks, more earnestly than persuasively. Its perhaps in recognition of their awkwardness that the author, whos also his own director, keeps most of these scenes to the side of the stage half-hidden behind curtains. The centre, meanwhile, stays bare: an apt if unintended metaphor for the play itself. Still, it isn't pretentious.

- Lost Voices runs through April 17 at Theatre Centre. Call 416-538-0988 or visit theatrecentre.org for details.

Jim Lefrancois / Owais Lightwala and Sarena Parmar in Ed Roy's Lost Voices.;; Caption:
2011-04-13-mortality-play:
OUR CLASS

Berkeley Street Theatre, Toronto

There are 10 actors in the cast of Studio 180's Our Class, and the play begins with them all sitting in rows, as if in a schoolroom, making grotesque faces and a lot of noise. The year is 1925, and the characters are young children, growing up together in a village in Poland. Five of them are Polish; the other five are Polish, too, but as history progresses -and the play takes us practically up to the present day -their national identity, along in many cases with their lives, gets stripped from them.

This exceptionally powerful and also remarkably thoughtful play has already been seen in England but not in Poland, though its the work of a Polish playwright, Tadeusz Slobodzianek. (The translation is by Ryan Craig.) Its based on an atrocity that took place in the village of Jedwabne in 1941; maybe 1,000 Jews were herded into a barn by their Christian compatriots and burned to death. The precise number of victims is in dispute, a point the play acknowledges in passing, but even if it were only" a few hundred, and "only some local Poles participated (as claimed last week in a stomach-turning press release by the Canadian Polish Congress) it would still be a major crime. And though it wouldn't have happened if there hadn't been a Nazi occupation, we are still faced with the recurring spectacle of neighbours turning on neighbours or merely turning away.

The villages name isnt actually mentioned, which normally would prejudice me against the play (repeat after me: You can only reach the universal through the specific") but here seems justified. The national and historical colouring is detailed enough, and the characters, though thoroughly individualized, aren't documented people. They are figures in a pattern, or maybe ingredients in a crucible: boys and girls, later men and women who, whatever they do to one another or suffer from one another, remain linked throughout their lives and even beyond.

The play's first act shows childhood unity fractured by social and sexual rivalries and jealousies, by the toxic blend of religion and nationalism, and most of all by the succeeding traumas of Russian and German invasion. The march to terror, through resistance and collaboration and betrayal, seems relentlessly logical. The second act takes us past the conflagration. Two survivors get protected by, and even married to, ex-classmates, who in later years are honoured as Righteous Gentiles: One of them likes the idea, the other resents it. The marriages have turned out mixed in more senses than one. One escapee gets to return, and to investigate the massacre, proving himself as enthusiastic an interrogator as his former tormentors.

Technically, the play is a remarkable achievement. It manages to tell its entire story through its 10 representative characters, with no recourse to small-part doubling or to lengthy expository monologues. Joel Greenbergs production shows Studio 180 at its semi-documentary best: speedy, rigorous, humane. Chairs are again the only furnishings; the actors line up at the back of the stage as each passes out of life, though not out of their fellows consciousness.

Fine individual performances include: Michael Rubenfeld's expatriate rabbi, with his virtuoso delivery of two long roll calls of his relatives' names, one a shattering memorial, the other a joyous celebration; Alex Poch-Goldin, whose progression from fugitive to torturer echoes the role he played in Scorched; Mark McGrinder, awkwardly blundering in and out of a kind of heroism; Ryan Hollyman and David Beazely, symbiotically linked as killer and victim; and Jonathan Goad, whose face in the opening tableau is the most hideously contorted of all, prefiguring the mental contortions he will later execute in order to feel good about himself.

Apart from Amy Rutherfords touching sacrificial offering, the women in Our Class are mostly outclassed by the men; Kimwun Perehinec is shrill and Jessica Greenberg shriller. Not everybody in this play dies a violent death, but disappointment, disengagement or just the cruel infirmities of old age await the others. The plays ultimate theme, whether or not it knows it, may simply be mortality. It's sweeping enough and sympathetic enough to be up to the task.

? Our Class runs until April 30. For tickets, call 416-368-3110 or visit canadianstage.com.

A play can be the victim of its own publicity. Or just of its own title. Some first-night audience members at Ghost Stories sounded like they didnt know whether to laugh or scream. They tried doing both, sometimes simultaneously, but seemed very selfconscious about it. As audiences in such circumstances invariably do: see any production of The Rocky Horror Show. This though was worse. There was nothing about the evening at the Panasonic to justify any reaction more violent than the occasional sigh or giggle at the feebleness of it all, plus perhaps the odd murmur of wonderment at what might have happened to a show that crossed the Atlantic with glowing credentials.

Ghost Stories is the joint product of two respected British companies (Lyric Hammersmith, in West London, and the combined Everyman and Playhouse theatres in Liverpool) and it got excellent notices on its own ground. It has a script by two successful British writers, Jeremy Dyson and Andy Nyman, who have co-directed it with Sean Holmes, whose record includes some good work with the Royal Shakespeare Company.

This is the set-up. A man announcing himself as Philip Goodman, professor of parapsychology, gives an illustrated lecture on supra-normal phenomena and the people ("percipients") who claim to have witnessed or experienced or been terrified by them. The professor professes himself skeptical but open to conviction. He replays interviews with three of these percipients, whose stories are acted out in front of us, all of them involving ghoulies and ghosties and (especially) things that go bump in the night. There is a night watchman, spooked by mannequins at the deserted factory he guards and especially by one resembling the brain-damaged daughter whom hes never visited. There's a teenager, out driving his parents' car without a licence, who runs someone over and is, naturally, and perhaps supernaturally, traumatized. And theres an ostentatiously prosperous businessman haunted by his wife who died in childbirth. These peoples guilt-problems, however, have nothing on those experienced, and long repressed, by Prof. Goodman himself, who turns out, in a series of selfcancelling twists, to be the effective subject of his own experiment.

The script has been riddled, for export purposes, with artificial Canadian references patronizing to both the actors (can't they do British accents?) and the audience (are we that insular?). The awkwardness infects the performances, especially that of Jason Blicker, who plays the professor with the air of a man who'd rather be anywhere else. Admittedly, the guy has things to hide, but the actors unease seems way beyond the call of character. Jack Langedijk and David Reale arent bad as his first two exhibits, and Darrin Baker as the yuppie third has moments of being positively good. Each of their anecdotes concludes with something materializing with a loud plop, though without remaining long enough for us to feel anything except frustrated. It took three directors to stage this? Our homegrown cycle The Mill managed to be far scarier with fewer resources, and threw in some substance as well. In short, Ghost Stories is nothing to lose sleep over.

Thornton Wilder's Our Town is also something of a ghost story, with its last act set in a graveyard whose inhabitants either pity or are indifferent to those left behind, and whose most recent arrival is allowed to relive a day from her past. She speedily flees back to the cemetery, not so much a ghost as aghast, at how precious every moment of life seems when you know how briefly it lasts.

The implication, that this knowledge would be intolerable if the living actually had to live with it, has always seemed flimsy to me in the past, but now in the fourth run of Joseph Ziegler's much-loved Soulpepper production, it fully strikes home. Some of this may be due to the arrival of Krystin Pellerin in the role of Emily, the wife who died young and whose adolescence, engagement and wedding we have already witnessed. Radiant, she has already established Emily as someone for whom every thought, word and feeling has a value, so her posthumous devastation is devastating.

The chorus of the longer dead is also polyphonically finer than ever: Nancy Palk serene though hurting, William Webster bitter through hurting, Brenda Robins, Diego Matamoros, a near-invisible Kevin Bundy. The more often you see this play, knowing whats to come, the more moving it is, especially when most of the faces are so familiar. The gentle Palk and astringent Jane Spidell have refined the contrast between their neighbour-mothers, Jeff Lillico plays by my count his third enchanting courtship of Pellerin, and among a fine corps of children, Dominique Matamoros exhibits a presumably hereditary gift of presence and timing. Albert Schultz now practically is the Stage Manager.

What Ive previously described as Soulpepper's feel-good factor can have its sentimental downside, but so far this year -in The Fantasticks, The Time of Your Life and here -it's been at its humane and welcoming best. Two footnotes: In the smaller space next door, the George Brown school is presenting Wilders other major play, The Skin of Our Teeth: a rich educational opportunity (and also, perhaps, a missed marketing opportunity). The Polish holocaust play Our Class has, perhaps surprisingly, more in common with Our Town than a possessive pronoun: Theyre both microcosmic plays, reaching outwards. And a correction: Contrary to what I wrote in my review, Our Class has been produced in Poland (at Teatr Na Woli in Warsaw, where it's still running) though after its world premiere at the National Theatre in London.

- Ghost Stories runs through May 29 at the Panasonic Theatre; Our Town is in repertory at the Young Centre for the Performing Arts, 416-866-0666.

Mirvish Productions / Jack Langedijk shares his supernatural encounter in Ghost Stories.;; Caption:
2011-04-21-new-orleans-is-thinking-treme:
If Treme were any other TV series, its first season would have consisted of a web of interrelated narratives, all forcibly resolved when Katrina struck in the season finale. Sort of like The Last Days of Pompeii.

In fact, of course, Treme began post-hurricane, to show the people of New Orleans trying to get their lives together in the aftermath. There was an unexpected flashback to the disaster, and it did come in the first seasons last episode, to answer some questions that wed had no particular interest in asking. The show had a rhythm all its own. Composed of short scenes, rapidly intercut, it yet managed to feel laid-back. Credit the setting, the wit and style and underlying passion of the writing, and above all the music.

The second season looks like being the same mixture as before. We pick up eight months after we left off, and -with one obvious exception -all the previous regulars are still in place, though not all of them are still in town. The absentee is of course John Goodman's university teacher, who last year threw himself off the ferry for reasons that never became very clear; it was not as if he was any more depressed at the end of the season than he'd been throughout. His onscreen family miss him in their different ways; his teenage daughter, never the most engaging cast member, is now in a state of permanent mope, while his charmingly frazzled lawyer wife Toni (Melissa Leo) is throwing herself still more into her work. Once again shes called upon to discover the truth about a Katrina death, in the face of bureaucratic obstacles ranging from intransigence to inertia.

Theres one major new arrival: a go-getter all set to cash in on the reconstruction projects; his ears prick up at mention of Bobby Jindal. He also gives rise to some unwontedly explanatory writing. In his favour, he does want to explore the city's music, which bulks even larger and less classifiable than it did before. "Gumbo ya ya -it means everyone talks at once," says DJ Davis (Steve Zahn), introducing his girlfriend to a rap act with a traditional jazz backing.

His lady, a virtuoso of versatility herself, is the beauteous Annie, played by Lucia Micarelli, who must surely be the most bewitching actresssinger-violinist ever and, with Goodman gone, the show's true star.

Her chops just get better and better, says Sonny (Michiel Huisman), her former partner now reduced to playing street-piano as a solo act, and hes right. She and Zahn are quite a couple. Her appearance at his rich familys Thanksgiving dinner is a comic highlight, playing out in a way that stupefies Davis and satisfies us. Davis's playlists are still getting him in trouble with his station manager, but he's trying hard at home. "Youve cleaned up for me, Davis" says Annie, returning wide-eyed from a tour. Daviss idea of cleaning up is to throw a sinkfull of dirty dishes straight into the garbage, but it obviously works short-term.

The season's second episode finds no less than three of the characters trying to form their own bands, while LaDonna (Khandi Alexander) is thinking of having live music in her bar. Even her ex, Antoine (the wonderful Wendell Pierce, underused these first two weeks), has grown tired of being a sideman. Albert (Clarke Peters) is devoting himself, for the second season running, to renovating a former dwelling, and seems suspiciously uninterested in reuniting his Mardi Gras Indian band. His son Delmond (Rob Brown) is apparently commuting between New Orleans and New York where he's making a living, or what passes for one in modern jazz circles, as a trumpeter. Its typical of the show that it trusts us to know what city were in without benefit of captions.

Also in the Big Apple is Janette (Kim Dickens) who, after the failure of her own restaurant back home, is working in the kitchen of a sadistic prima donna of a chef. Slow down he tells her, when dissatisfied with her salmon "listen to your fish." Her N.Y. colleagues seems as dismissive of N.O. cuisine as Delmond's are of its music, and she's bound to be on the plane back soon. Again, in any other show, it would have happened by the end of the first episode. This one takes its time.

There is a slight change in overall tempo. The initial sense of crisis has dulled; survival is less of a battle, more of a grind. As befits a show from David Simon, creator of The Wire, this season is widening its lens, to take a closer look at the devastated schools and at the overstretched police. Let Bourbon Street be Bourbon Street, says Tonis favourite officer, advising his detectives on not running people in for indecent exposure unless theyre actually having sex on the street. Tolerance, he tells them, is "one thing we're famous for -I mean famous, not infamous." Nice to find that someone still knows the difference.

Treme's mental habitat is more whirlpool than river, and the lack of obvious forward motion can be disconcerting. But the rewards are rich. The premiere title is "Accentuate the Positive." That song is sung, beautifully, during the action and its hopeful; and again over the closing credits, where it feels ironic but still uplifting. Theres no other current TV drama of this distinction, and the music always intoxicates.

- Treme's second season premieres on April 24 at 10 p.m. on HBO Canada.

2011-04-23-disrupting-the-spectacle-the-:
Sky Gilbert sometimes seems to me like the gay Steven Berkoff. Berkoff is the aggressive British actor-playwright-director who has done powerful work in all three departments but devotes much of his energy to proclaiming how wonderful his own work is and how worthless is that of everybody else. Gilbert is a more engaging figure, but his productions for his Cabaret Company always come adorned with a manifesto informing us that what we are about to see is something radically subversive that goes beyond conventional categories like "literature" and "drama." What we actually do see invariably falls into the long-established category of discussion drama, and is as "literary" as anything by Bernard Shaw or Tom Stoppard.

I drop those names because Gilbert himself does, in the course of his new play, The Situationists. He has his actors step out of frame to refer scornfully to playwrights like those two who, by his account, flatter their audiences by tossing ideas around and telling us what to think about them. The implication -actually it's more of a statement -is that this play is above all that. In fact, Stoppard usually leaves you in doubt about what to believe; Shaw was more dogmatic, perhaps, but he was also too incorrigibly mischievous to refrain from periodically dynamiting his own side. And though Gilbert's best plays can be funny (Bad Acting was very funny), Stoppard and Shaw are consistently funnier.

The Situationists isn't one of Gilbert's best plays, though it's possible to see why its subject attracted him. The Situationists were a group of armchair revolutionaries, largely French, who believed that a consumer society could be changed if people were made aware, by histrionic methods, of just what, practically and ideologically, they were consuming. They called it "disrupting the spectacle," though of course they would have had to create another spectacle to do it. And they did have some success. They are credited, not just by themselves, as a prime influence on the Paris uprisings of 1968. They may even have inspired my alltime favourite political slogan: "Je suis Marxiste, tendance Groucho."

The spirit of '68 lingers, but it was still a long time ago. The characters in Gilbert's play want to revive it, in Canada, now. We meet Jacques, a philosophy professor, and Lise, his student who reveres his ideas but can get pretty impatient with him personally. (Though, occasionally, it seems that her feelings may be the other way around.) Jacques, obviously and perhaps in deference to the movement's history, is French. And I don't mean French-Canadian. Gavin Crawford plays him with a spindly gait and an even spindlier accent. He is, for much of the play's first half, incomprehensible, especially given the author's decision to stage his play on an oblong strip down the middle of the auditorium. Your chances of understanding the professor are greatly affected by whether you're sitting on the side that he happens to be facing. Haley McGee, who plays Lise, practically runs the first act by virtue of being loud and clear and very forceful. The fact that the play features a male professor and a female student has caused the play to be announced as a parody of David Mamet's Oleanna, which suggests that some people have a very low threshold for what constitutes parody.

Rightly sensing that, left to himself, Jacques will never get anything done, Lise insists they enlist Yvon, a dropout student even more aggressive than she is, with anarchist views and exhibitionist talents. He is also a compulsive contrarian, expressing opinions on recycling that may coincide with the author's own, and on AIDS that certainly do. He's also very Gilbertian in seeing sex in everything, and in this company he may well be right. Jacques and Lise, of course, deny being attracted to him or to one another. Nevertheless, by the play's end, each of the three characters will have had an onstage orgasm.

It isn't clear whether Yvon, played by Gil Garratt on alternating notes of sneer and threat, is attacking the hypocrisy of ideologues in general or of Situationists in particular. But his methods do undeniably perk the play up: not the seductions themselves but their aftermath, in which intersecting jealousies finally bring the three-handed debates to some kind of comic life. As they advance their own plans for disrupting the Canadian spectacle -say, by planting gay or pretend-gay candidates in either of the major parties and then outing them -one thing begins to dawn on them: It ain't gonna work. It would take too long and probably nobody would notice anyway. The play also gets clearer because Jacques' accent gets lighter; and as Yvon remarks on this, we know that it's not due to the actor being careless. Indeed, his performance begins to acquire some subtlety, and we wonder if Jacques is about to be revealed as an ethnic fraud as well. The play, though, stops before that can happen. Or rather it jumps tracks. The house lights go up; and Gilbert starts disrupting his own spectacle. Only he doesn't do it very thoroughly, because though the audience is exposed, the actors are given the unfair advantage of remaining in character, Jacques' accent included. It's here that the play name-checks Shaw and Stoppard. It's also here that the actors enjoin any reviewers to refrain from giving away the final twist. So I won't, except to say that Gilbert had me fooled for a couple of minutes, and that it was only good professional acting (actually the best in the evening) that gave his game away. Probably The Situationists is trying to be more situationist than the Situationists, while simultaneously telling us that in an age where meta-theatrics are the norm, it's a non-starter of a technique. Jacques might call this having your gateau and eating it. It happens a lot in the theatre.

? The Situationists closes April 24 at Buddies in Bad Times Theatre. Visit buddiesinbadtimes.com or call 416975-8555 for details.

David Hawe / Haley McGee as Lise, Gavin Crawford as Jacques and Gil Garratt as Yvon.;; Caption:
2011-04-26-a-true-story-stripped-down:
THEATRE REVIEW

Calendar Girls Royal Alexandra Theatre, Toronto

Here comes another idea masquerading as a play. And in this case, it was somebody else's idea.

Calendar Girls derives from the well-known story of a group of mature members of a women's institute in the north of England who decided to pose sort of nude for a calendar, in order to raise money for a new visitors' sofa in the hospital where the husband of one of them had recently died of leukemia. Their initiative paid off beyond their wildest dreams, bringing in thousands of pounds for cancer research. It also gave rise to a successful movie, which in turn became a West End play though, possibly due to a Titanic act of selfdenial on someone's part, not a musical. Not yet, anyway. In the meantime, the play, which has now arrived in a Canadian production, does manage to squeeze in a few songs. These are pretty much padding, but then so is most of the play.

Writing that can pass on the screen can seem very exposed on a stage; and though I never saw the film, my impression is that Tim French, who has adapted his own film script, has made few allowances for this. All his play has to offer is the basic situation, and the goodwill that naturally attends it. The facts have presumably been fictionalized. They've certainly been pared down; there are only six ladies in the group, posing for a month apiece; how the other half waved is never explained.

The premature widow is named Annie; her bossy best friend, who originates the scheme, is called Chris. The others are Jessie, a retired schoolteacher; Cora, who sings and plays the piano; Celia, who ranks as the sex symbol of the troupe by virtue of having in her youth been photographed topless on a Harley-Davidson; and Ruth, who acts dowdy and repressed.

The actual photo shoot takes place at the end of the first act. After that, the play has nowhere to go. There are murmurs of puritanical objections from the community but they fizzle out as soon as mentioned. To fill out the time before we go home, the play has to give each of its central sextet a manufactured back story.

Marti Maraden's Toronto staging doesn't do much to fill out the gaps. It's the play's fault that what should be the crucial scene, the one in which Chris sells the grieving Annie on her idea, hasn't been written. But it's the production's fault that when the two of them confront their friends with it, the moment simply glides by. Even more, the real-life selling point has been blunted. These ama-teur pin-ups were respectable women "of a certain age." The actresses who have been cast here may be age-appropriate on paper, but few of them look it. The story is cut adrift from whatever realistic moorings it may once have had.

Given all that, there's some OK acting going on. Barbara Gordon takes the honours as the acid-tongued teacher. Fiona Highet is a watchful, touching presence as Annie; Fiona Reid enjoys Chris's wisecracks, as do we. Kathryn Akin brings warmth, if no great sense of character, to musical Cora, and Terri Cherniack's Ruth develops rather impressively from caricature to feeling person. Jane Spence, though, really does seem too young to be in this group and compensates by playing with a coarseness surprising in an actress I've previously admired in roles ranging from Ophelia to Ben Affleck.

There are men present, too. Dan Lett graphically depicts John's all-too-rapid decline, and Gordon Tanner hovers amusingly between delight and embarrassment as the designated cameraman. Robert Jones' sets, from the U.K. production, are unhelpfully skimpy. On which subject, whatever the posters may be trying to suggest, there's even less actual nudity in this show than there was in The Full Monty. Coming more up to date: after Billy Elliot and Ghost Stories, Calendar Girls makes Mirvish Productions' third British turkey in a row.

Calendar Girls runs until May 28. For tickets, call 416872-1212 or visit mirvish.com.

THEATRE REVIEW

The Cosmonaut's Last Message to the Woman He Once Loved in the Former Soviet Union Bluma Appel Theatre, Toronto

An especially fine scene in The Cosmonaut's Last Message . (we can call it Cosmo for short) involves Vivienne, a Scots speech therapist, and her neighbour Claire, a policewoman. Earlier, we've seen them together socially, as awkward new acquaintances, but this is official. Vivienne's husband Keith, a civil servant, has disappeared, leaving only a neatly folded bundle of clothes by the side of the ocean. Maybe he's drowned; maybe he's pretending. Although as Claire rather tactlessly reminds Vivienne, "one way of seeming dead is to be dead."

Claire also says "Nobody knows him, Viv. That's the awful thing." David Greig's brilliantly woven play, first staged in Britain in 1999, is about not knowing people, and about the forcible efforts, frustrated and frustrating, to get through to them.

One thing we know about Keith that Vivienne doesn't is that on his trips to London, he's been seeing a Russian stripper by the name of Nastasja. "The impossibility of communication" has been a staple of playwrights at least since Chekhov, but Greig's play is the first I know to make it the explicit subject, rather than something to be inferred. Another thing we know about Nastasja is that she is the daughter of a cosmonaut, the partner of the one referred to in the title.

The two of them have been circling the Earth for 12 years, unaware that the Soviet Union that sent them has become former. The object, apparently, was to determine how long they could survive such isolation without going crazy, and it's surprising they've lasted as long as they have. In fact, both men have women on their minds whom they loved; for one it's his daughter, for the other it's an almost-girlfriend with whom he missed his chance by not knowing what to say. We undoubtedly meet the daughter down below; we may very well meet the girlfriend.

The irony in Cosmo, satisfying for us if not for the characters, is that in a play about not connecting, everything connects. One of the cosmonauts is trying to make radio contact with Earth; he only succeeds in ruining the reception on Keith's and Vivienne's TV set. A later attempt is misinterpreted by a scientist who believes in aliens. This man, Bernard, has previously suffered a stroke; Vivienne, because of her work, recognizes the symptoms. She's there because she's following the one clue left by her husband: a Cezanne painting imprinted on his tie. Unfortunately, neither she nor Bernard speak a word of the other's language, barring the odd international phrase like Star Trek. When they hover on the brink of a love scene, it's very moving.

Each of Cosmo's six actors plays two roles: very apt for a play in which everything doubles and everything echoes. There's barely a line that doesn't reverberate somewhere else.

Jennifer Tarver's production, unfortunately, doesn't do the play full justice. On the unforgiving Bluma stage it, too, feels lost in space; as the action moves from country to country, and from terrestrial to extraterrestrial, the production seems to trundle after it.

The acting is very uneven, notably in the matter of accents. Some are at least approximately appropriate; others don't even sound like they're trying. Fiona Byrne's Vivienne, first sheltered and then shattered, is linguistically and emotionally pitchperfect; and she finds a fierce contrast in Sylvia, Nastasja's dogged friend and self-appointed protector.

Sarah Wilson does similarly fine dual delivery as Nastasja, speaking largely in what a lobby warning calls "mature language," though it might be more accurately described as immature language. Raoul Bhaneja combines a succession of cynical barmen with a powerful but vestigially vulnerable Erik. David Jansen hardly differentiates his Keith from his Bernard, though he seems better suited to the former.

The spacemen, too, fall flat with Tony Nappo and Tom Barnett almost indistinguishable, not so much physically as psychologically. There's a desperate playfulness here that the production misses.

The play comes through, though, wittily and even poetically. After all the jumped-up soap operas trying to pass themselves off as serious drama, this is the real thing.

? Cosmo runs until May 14. For tickets, call 416-368-3110 or visit canadian stage.com.
