2011-04-30-the-beasts-of-burden-forests-:
Critics making their way out of Wajdi Mouawad's Forests were presented with a family tree of the characters' tangled relationships over two continents and several generations. We were told that being given this information earlier would have spoiled the surprise. I find it hard to take seriously a play whose ultimate effect depends on genealogical suspense, but that may not matter as the author takes it seriously enough for both of us.

So, what's the big idea? It seems to be about memory, or perhaps historical awareness. The play, a companion but not a sequel to Mouawad's highly praised Scorched, begins in Montreal with Aimee, an expectant mother, declaring that she doesn't know or care much about the Berlin Wall, which has recently fallen. "Our lives," she says, "must be pretty boring to care so much about other people's happiness!"Pretty soon she sees the error of her ways. She's diagnosed with brain cancer, with a bizarre genetic complication that means if her child lives she herself will shortly die. She decides against an abortion because that would mean adding to the number of women killed in the Montreal massacre. As it reaches back in time, and into Aimee's ancestry, the play also brings in the French resistance, the Holocaust and the Nazi connections of Alsace industrialists whose 19th-century employment practises had already verged on slave labour. (They supplied the transport to the death camps; for once the trains that roar past the Tarragon have a macabre effectiveness.) I criticized Scorched for its historical vagueness, but I guess I was wrong. Forests uses real events, whose horror is already of mythical proportions, as fodder for a rickety myth of its own. It involves, among other things, the idea that a known resistance fighter might have been spared by the Nazis, just because they didn't know she was Jewish. Halfway through the three-hour play I felt angry. By the end I just felt numb.

The first scene invokes an actual Greek myth, that of the House of Atreus whose members killed and even ate one another. The events of Forests, though, don't bear much relation to it except that, as someone once said of a Jacobean tragedy, the incest is sustained throughout. The play also makes even heavier use than Scorched of the "twin" metaphor. Interrogating her family past is Aimee's 16-year-old daughter Loup, who's been sent on one of Mouawad's maternally mandated treasure hunts. She isn't happy about it, but then she isn't happy about anything; she takes teenage resentment to new exhibitionist levels. Escorting her is a polite paleontologist whom she calls a "pantologist," this, like the malapropisms in Scorched, representing the play's ration of humour. Loup's unstoppable discoveries lead her, quite arbitrarily, to enlightenment, or at least to the right to deliver a cracker-barrel epilogue. She isn't the only person here with an animal name; the Alsatian branch, revolting against their inhuman inheritance, founded a zoo, in the play's only actual forest, and one of their progeny is known as Gerard the Boy Giraffe. Maybe it sounds better in French.

In fact, once past the first couple of scenes, hardly anybody in the play utters a believable word. Instead they go in for fake poetry. "She's as beautiful as the horizon," says a father of his newborn daughter, really straining for simile. A man rhapsodizes over his beloved's "you-ness." (Shame, it sounds as if he's calling her Eunice.) Or they go in for shameless exposition: "Don't forget," a son reminds his father, "that I am your company veterinarian." It can't all be the fault of the translation.

You can certainly give Mouawad points for energy and ingenuity, and the same goes for Richard Rose's production, which careers through the undergrowth at a tremendous lick. But it leaves in its wake some wretched acting, some of it from normally excellent actors. Vivien Endicott-Douglas is half an exception; she plays Loup's abrasiveness way beyond the hilt, but her calmer moments shine, if only in comparison. As her confidant, R.H. Thomson brings a pleasing ease to a long but sketchy role; the play pretends that it's established a relationship between the two of them but it hasn't. Jan Alexandra Smith delivers Aimee's opening speech very well; as her husband Alon Nashman, granted the only recognizable human emotions in sight, takes full sym-pathetic advantage of them. Terry Tweed plays a scarifying grandmother, while Matthew Edison does a remarkable job of riding the play's rhetoric rather than, like too many of his colleagues, drowning in it. If you want a play that really puts a human face on atrocity, or a whole gallery of faces, go see Our Class. If you want a play whose characters are the partners, not the puppets, of its metaphor, try The Cosmonaut's Last Message to the Woman He Once Loved in the Former Soviet Union.

- Forests runs through May 29 at the Tarragon Theatre. Call 416-531-1827 or visit tarragontheatre.com.

THEATRE REVIEW

Edward the Crazy Man Theatre Passe Muraille, Toronto

Workman Arts is a company whose initial aim was to use artistic creation as a form of therapy for mental illness. It started as a group of eight people: "individuals," to quote their own literature, with mental illness and limited theatre training.

Over the subsequent 20 years or so, both the size and the professionalism of the company have grown considerably. Edward the "Crazy Man" is one of their flagship productions. It's already been seen in Toronto at the Lorraine Kimsa Theatre for Young People (now, blessedly, to be known again as the Young Peoples Theatre). Its now being given a well-deserved showing to wider audiences at Passe Muraille and on tour.

Emil Sher's play, adapted from a book of the same name by Marie Day, is a portrait of a schizophrenic, and an examination of his relationship with some neighbouring children. Edward, played remarkably by John Cleland, is a homeless man pushing a shopping cart through the streets, laden with shiny things. He has a special fondness for hubcaps, some of which he pinches from 12year-old Charlie. Charlie is initially indignant but is later captivated when he sees how beautifully Edward has decorated them and displayed them on a back wall.

Before, he and his friends had alternately teased Edward and run away from him. Now Charlie forges a friendship with him. He even asks Edward home for supper, specifying to his mother that he likes cheese sandwiches. When the mother actually sets eyes on Edward she is of course both shocked and scared. This is despite her being a social activist when the objects of her concern are a little less close to home. As Charlie points out to her, Edward isn't a bike lane or a pool threatened with closure; hes a person.

Directed by Leah Cherniak, the play is very good as far as it goes, though, at least in narrative terms, it may not go far enough. Perhaps because its based on a book, it's a series of vignettes rather than a developing story. There is an attempt to shape the action towards a finale on Halloween but the characters stay on the same spots.

The two principals, though, are very well drawn, both in writing and performance. Cleland as Edward has found a disconcerting shuffling rhythm, both physically and mentally. He can be very sharp, he can be very absent; always he's in his own world, whose connection to everybody elses is unpredictable. Its a surprise when he turns up to supper on time; it's as much of a surprise when he leaves. Olaf Sham, a 30year-old, manages an equally impressive if less obviously spectacular transformation as Charlie. His home life has its own issues, and he might almost regard Edward as a surrogate father; there's a moment at which he seems as let down by his errant friend as a child might be by a forgetful parent.

Two other actors double as children and adults. Both are fine as Charlies friends and contemporaries, but Faeghan Williams may be too young to convince as his mother, whos an underdeveloped character as written; her fear and protectiveness are certainly credible, and the single-parent and son relationship is truthfully sketched in, but it's only sketched. Charles RevoredCouto has less familiar, more suggestive territory to work as Edward's brother Lewis who barred him from their house when he began fearing for his own wife and child. He retains some guilt and concern, just as Edward remains both resentful and devoted.

Here, writing and acting leave us wanting more in a good way. Two of the actors, it was revealed at a first night talk back, are mentalhealth patients themselves, and one of them is actually a schizophrenic in remission. The quality of their work here shows that a social good can also be an artistic good.

Runs until May 14. For tickets, call 416-504-7529 or visit artsboxoffice.ca.

2011-05-07-when-opera-is-more-than-simpl:
Both of the operas to have arrived in the Canadian Opera Company's repertoire over the past two weeks are comedies. Rossini's Cinderella (La Cenerentola) is a re-telling, in largely farcical terms, of the most famous fairy tale of them all. Richard Strauss's Ariadne auf Naxos is actually about comedy, and its intersection with tragedy. Both provide interesting sidelights on the theatrical world beyond the opera house: We do musical and nonmusical plays now, especially the classics, and on the whole tradition of the backstage play, and especially the backstage musical.

The COC's Cinderella impressed me as maybe the first comic opera I've ever seen that is actually funny. (It's also a musical feast, from the sumptuous overture onwards.) The production is one of those that has been bought in from abroad. Four other opera houses are involved but the prime mover is a Catalan director, Joan Font, who heads a multi-disciplinary company -a clown super-troupe, to judge by description, called Els Comediants. Members of this group are responsible for the show's design and choreography, both of which are delightful. The production's most obvious innovation is the addition to the cast of halfa-dozen mice. At least I, conditioned by Disney, took them to be mice; a rival faction holds that they are rats. Anyway the six long-tailed rodents act as Cinderella's sympathetic attendants, and also as all-purpose scene-shifters. They are most beguilingly danced, and they never (well, hardly ever) obscure the main action. It's worth a visit just to see them lined up in a row on the floor, their chins cradled in their paws, caught up in the conversation between the heroine and the opera's equivalent of her fairy godmother, who happens to be neither fairy nor female. Easier to miss, but lovely, is the mouse (or rat) who curls up and goes to sleep on a pillow thrown on the stage by Cinders' tyrannical impoverished stepfather, roused from slumber.

This is another gender reversal from the story we've grown up on. We expect a wicked stepmother. Rossini and his librettist go back to the original tale as told by Charles Perrault, a version not as grim as Grimm but still plenty tough enough. The ugly sisters could hardly be more snobbish or unpleasant, or their father, for a sign of whose affection Cinderella still movingly yearns, a more unscrupulous or more unfeeling social climber. The production has been criticized for making his scenes with Dandini, the prince's valet disguised as the prince, too slapstick, but I can't see how else they could or should be done. Brett Polegato's Dandini, revelling in the brief opportunity to be his boss's boss, is a clever valet who beats any Figaro I've seen, Rossini's or Mozart's.

Equally amusing is the staging of the huge chorus, the prince's retinue improbably invading the baron's house, and all nodding their heads in obsequious bureaucratic unison. They make a good satiric point, as does the staging of a ball in which the rats (or mice) are the waiters and Cinderella's family the only visible guests. The laughs throw into sharper relief the technical and emotional heights scaled by Elizabeth DeShong's coloratura Cinderella and the ambiguous ardour of Lawrence Brownlee's game-playing prince.

Only the suggestion at the end that the whole thing has been Cinderella's chimney-corner dream seems a bitter twist too far. We already know from Dandini's rueful admission of his real impoverished status that fairy tales don't usually come true; we don't need to have it rubbed in. There's no coach-and-pumpkin scene, but the set performs its own transformation -airy, magical and economical -from kitchen to palace. We've been hearing a lot recently about "European style" in the theatre; this clean-lined production is a triumphant example of it. Opera is often the crucible of theatrical production, and the COC veers regularly between old-fashioned and cutting-edge. Cinderella is the latter.

Ariadne auf Naxos falls between the two, as may befit a work that promises more stylistically than it delivers. There is a prologue, in which a rich capricious patron decrees that a tragic opera and a burlesque commedia shall be performed simultaneously. The opera people are appalled, the comedians cheerfully grit their teeth; the show goes on. The preceding proceedings, especially on this production's realistic backstage set, prefigure a long line of American musicals. Zerbinetta, the soubrette, realistic about sex while yearning for just one serious admirer, recalls the girl in Show Boat who sings about Life Upon the Wicked Stage, while the whole set-up, intermingling life and performance, suggests last year's dazzling Stratford production of Kiss Me Kate. And I've a suspicion that Cole Porter did both the romantic and the deflationary part better.

The opera proper concerns an abandoned heroine, Ariadne, determined on suicide but deflected by the arrival of the god Bacchus. Or, as Zerbinetta sardonically comments, by just another man. I'm not sure that she's doing more than underlining the obvious; after all, that would still have been the story even without the comedians' intrusions. Vulgarian that I am, I wanted the conflict between them to be more direct, and Zerbinetta's triumph to be more emphatic. I also wanted the opera's self-important young composer, who in the prologue seems quite smitten with Zerbinetta, to come back and admit defeat or perhaps -which would surely be a tragiccomic point -a shared half-victory.

The production's skimpy secondact set suggests that the invisible patron is a skinflint as well as a prankster. I'm not sure what to make of the fact that Ariadne's three Wagnerian attendants are funnier than the actual clowns, skilful though their performances are. Jane Archibald's Zerbinetta is more than skilful, physically as well as vocally; if she ever wants a change from opera, she could be an ace musical-comedy performer. She's one of a trio of superb Canadian female singers in this production, the others being Alice Coote, delightfully pompous in the travesti role of the composer, and Adrianne Pieczonka, who has now resumed the role of Ariadne; she was ill at the premiere but her understudy, Amber Wagner, performed with increasing confidence and ended in triumph.

The idea of the piece is wonderful, the execution patchy, though the librettist, Hugo von Hofmansthal, was a searching comic playwright in his own right, one whose plays are well worth investigating. I'd recommend The Deep Man.

? For ticket information on these shows, visit coc.ca or call 416-363-8231.

2011-05-10-train-of-thought:
THE RAILWAY CHILDREN

Roundhouse Theatre, Toronto

The star of The Railway Children is a genuine vintage locomotive, both engine and carriages, imported, like the show itself, from England. Knowing like all stars -and indeed like many other trains -how to make its audience wait, it husbands its appearances. Indeed it only makes two of them, if you don't count its personal curtain call. These come at the end of each act. The first one is thrilling, coming at a moment of potential disaster. The second is nice, but not quite as celebratory as both the storyline and the production mean it to be. We're travelling on a diminishing return ticket.

The Railway Children is a charming show with a built-in flaw. It's based on a classic children's novel, by the Edwardian writer E. Nesbit, which has, like many of its kind, an episodic structure. Three children and their mother are up-rooted from their cosy metropolitan existence when father is arrested and sent to prison on what, because he's such an obviously nice man, has to be a trumpedup charge. The children, two girls and a boy, aren't told exactly what's happened, but the audience is fed heavy hints. The family moves to a Yorkshire village; their house is near the railroad tracks, with which they become happily obsessed. They wave at all the trains and befriend the station master.

The story's most congenial medium for adaptation is the TV serial, which allows every episode its own episode, but this stage version has a lot going for it. It originated, fittingly enough, at the Theatre Royal, York; and had a successful London run at, even more fittingly, Waterloo Station. Its Toronto home is a specially constructed theatre, actually a large tent, on Bremner Boulevard between Skydome and the CN Tower, where retired Canadian steam-engines can make their English cousin feel at home. The audience sits on two sides of a platform, beneath which run rails to enable the visitor to make its spectacular appearances. Most of the action takes place around and between the big holes necessary to allow the train its space. This looks at first as if it is going to be confining, but in fact Damian Cruden's production uses the space resourcefully and at times beautifully. Joanna Scotcher's set and costume designs make major contributions, and Richard G. Jones' lighting is wonderfully atmospheric. So, up to a point, is Christopher Madin's music, the point being reached somewhere in the second act where it turns syrupy and manipulative.

Here, though, it may only be keeping pace with Mike Kenny's script, whose own limitations probably come with the territory. It has a good framing device; the three heroes, at some unspecified later date, recall how they became, and then ceased being, railway children. This gives a nice sense of reminiscence and regret, and it also permits the hiring of adult actors to play the central roles. In this production, that's certainly a blessing. As Roberta the burgeoning eldest, Natasha Greenblatt, thoughtful and concerned, puts a new gloss on the battered word "sensitive." As Phyllis, the youngest, Kate Besworth is unquenchable even when terrified. As Peter, squeezed between his sisters while trying precociously to lead, Harry Judge tends, in his own words, "to lay it on thick," but so does the character.

The adaptation tries conscientiously to give them, Phyllis in particular, a through-line, but it can't disguise the fact that, basically, the kids just do one good thing after another. They prevent a train wreck. They rescue a trapped boy from a tunnel, which scenically is exceptionally well evoked. They give succour to a nonEnglish-speaking passenger who turns out to be a dissident writer, escaped from Siberia, and whose initial reception by the local authorities makes you feel grateful that tasers hadn't yet been invented. Their mother, who in an autobiographical touch is supporting her family by writing herself, is very appreciative, but the man passes on out of their life, leaving no dramatic mark. They also overstep the bounds of middle-class manners by throwing their station master friend a birthday party, making him feel patronized. He does though forgive them later; Craig Warnock plays him warmly enough but without ever quite locating the character's centre. Marilla Wex, however, is right on target as the family's newly recruited housekeeper.

As the incidents mount up so, in the second half, do the coincidences, a character known as the Old Gentleman being pressed into quadruple service as a fairy godfather. Which reminds me: In a show that makes constant use of direct address, the audience gets told, more or less, to clap hands if it believes in returning fathers. This one, naturally, arrives by train: its second full-dress appearance. But the moment isn't quite the coup that must have been hoped. In the first place, father hasn't been much of a presence; he's been too busy playing other characters. In the second, we've already had the thrill of seeing the train, if only once. Not that there haven't been many other arrivals and departures -the show practically consists of them. But they've been represented by simple trucks, the theatrical rather than the locomotive kind. And they work so well that you begin to wonder whether we really need to see the real thing at all, which I admit is an ungrateful thought, and commercially counterproductive.

Anyway, there's a decent, benevolent feel to the production, as well as a lot of imagination, and the combination takes us way above the usual familyentertainment level. Make tracks for the Roundhouse. After all, the producers have.

2011-05-11-farklempt-footwear:
THEATRE REVIEW

Zadie's Shoes Factory Theatre, Toronto

Adam Pettle's Zadie's Shoes was first seen at the Factory in 2001, and was successful enough to be given a commercial run, in essentially the same production the following year. Two major stagings in the same city make it, by common definition, a Canadian classic. It's now received a third, wholly new production back at the theatre where it started. That should make it a Canadian masterpiece.

It isn't quite that. Despite some trims and rewrites, it remains what it always was: a richly enjoyable play with some holes in it. The current revival is co-directed by the author and his brother, Jordan Pettle, who appeared in the original in the leading role of Benjamin. Benjamin is TorontoJewish and a compulsive gambler, like his father and grandfather (or "zadie") before him; the latter also bequeathed the play its title by losing his shoes in a bet while en route to Canada from the old country. Benjamin is currently in deep hock, and is trying to get out of it by the traditional gambler's route of gambling some more. He snaffles some money from his gentile girlfriend Ruth (Patricia Fagan), a cancer patient. Benjamin genuinely loves Ruth, and of course he means to pay her back with enormous interest. She, naturally, doesn't see it that way.

Ready to try anything, Benjamin, for the first time since his bar mitzvah, wanders into a synagogue where he meets Eli, an old man who seems to know all about him. This may be because he has prophetic powers; it may also be that he's just wise in the ways of the world and especially in those of gambling addicts, since he's one himself.

I'd forgotten just how deep and funny the scenes between Ben and Eli actually are. Joe Cobden as Ben and Harry Neiken, a wonderful Eli, by turns encouraging and disparaging, make a classic double act. Pettle (Adam, not Jordan) writes the best Jewish dialogue of any Canadian playwright.

He doesn't, for better or worse, write it just for his Jewish characters. Ruth has two sisters, and the three of them indulge in the same kind of barbed, quick-fire banter. Ruth's sisters were the weakest link in the two earlier productions and, though they're better played now than on either previous occasion, they still are. Beth (Lisa Ryder) is a curling champion, fanatically preparing for her next contest; Lily (Shannon Perreault) is an allpurpose flake, swinging from one counterculture to the next. But because they come into the play a little late, they seem like distractions from the main issue, rather than enrichments of it.

The two central roles are very well taken. Cobden's Benjamin has as much charm as Pettle (Jordan, not Adam) and more stature and technical command. But it swings and roundabouts; his slitherings into temptation are less credible than his predecessor's, and the play's climax that much less powerful.

Jackie Chau's set is less atmospheric than the original's arrangement of bleachers, but more practical. Several of the cast are more familiar in Winnipeg, Calgary and Vancouver than they are here. There often seems to be an impenetrable wall between the theatres of East and West. We're all the richer for its being broken down.

- Runs until June 5. For tickets, call 416-504-9971 or visit factorytheatre.ca.

Jeremy Mimnagh, Factory Theatre / William MacDonald and Joe Cobden in Zadie's Shoes.;; Caption:
2011-05-14-a-gift-to-the-audience-window:
I was so delighted by Soulpepper's Window on Toronto when I first saw it that I rather dreaded seeing it again. The show started life last year as part of the companys lab series, exploratory productions mounted for just a few performances on one of the Young Centres smallest stages. I was afraid familiarity, plus the move to the centre's second-largest space, might dilute the magic. I was thoroughly, jubilantly wrong. This is the funniest, most enchanting theatrical concoction since . well, I honestly can't think of a comparison.

The window through which we are invited to look is the service-portal of a hot-dog truck in Nathan Phillips Square. The stalls proprietor, whose name is Jason -and whos played by Jason Patrick Rothery -begins the proceedings by opening up for business and then retreating to the front row of the auditorium, from which he proceeds to watch the action. We, of course, watch it with him, through a small square brightly lit aperture surrounded by darkness. It's like a puppet stage, except that the figures who appear on it, mostly from the waist up, are teemingly flesh and blood. They are played by six members of last year's Soulpepper academy plus a couple of newcomers. They appear, disappear and reappear at a staggering rate and in an equally exhilarating multiplicity of guises. At first it seems that we are going to be watching a day in the life. By the time the show has run its 45-minute course, we will have watched a year, one that, before our very eyes and in a vivid succession of weathers, brings birth, love, marriage and near-death.

Jason himself is the mostly still centre of this maelstrom; and Rothery is superbly imperturbable. Jasons customers dont just come to him for sausages on buns. Many of them, including those who've never met him before, treat him as a friend and confidant. They use his counter, and the space behind it, as a drop-off and pick-up point. One (Brendan Wall) leaves a guitar in storage, and gets very threatening when he learns that someone else has picked it up. (All right, you've been lucky this time is his gracious response, more or less, when his instrument reappears.) Actors, using their real names, pick up scripts, and are dashed to find theyre for The Hobbit. (Jason says consolingly that it was always going to be a small role.) Tourists ask for the Vatican and are told to turn right at the Colosseum. A recent immigrant, in search of a girlfriend, is warned against seeking her in the back pages of Now, but finds romance (and more) anyway; Ins Chois ingratiating performance of this Romeo-in-waiting is probably the show's star turn, buttressed by his more sinister appearances in other hats and, especially, shirts. Gregory Prest comes by, belligerently, on a bike. Andre Sills looms, hugely, once as a cut-out of himself. People ask for stuff Jason doesn't stock, and occasionally congratulate him on the stuff that he does. An old lady (Trish Lindstrom) asks, more than once, if Jason knew there used to be a corner store on his site. Somebody else asks him if hes looked out recently. He replies that its all he does.

Among the things he sees is the rest of the cast travelling diagonally up and down as if on an escalator; I can't account for this naturalistically, but it's a wonderful effect. I started laughing almost as soon as the show began, and hardly stopped until the end. Even at the sad bits I smiled, not, I think, because Im particularly callous, but out of sheer joy at a production that feels like a perfect, loving gift from actors to audience, and of course of the quick-fire technical brilliance of it all. The most recent production, come to think of it, that does compare is the Shaw Festivals The President (to be revived this season), another high-speed firework display bursting with humanity, if of a more jaundiced kind. Window on Toronto is the best possible advertisement for the city. And for hot dogs.

It's directed, perhaps unexpectedly, by Laszlo Marton, who's scarcely a Toronto resident, though Im told hes done similar shows on his home turf. (Window on Budapest?) It shares a bill with (re)Birth: E.E. Cummings in Song, which doesn't name a director, though the first question I asked when I caught its trial airing at the last-but-one Global cabaret festival was "Who staged this?" It's a beautiful-looking and beautiful-sounding piece in which 10 actor-musicians (eight of them doubling from the evenings other half) appear in charming, intricate formations within a white marquee. (Theres an acknowledgment to Brendan Healy, the more-than-promising director who was part of the year's academy intake and now runs Buddies in Bad Times.) They perform musical settings of Cummings poems, to a constantly varying instrumental lineup, which at one point includes two accordions, which is a lot. There are a couple of drawbacks. One is that there is no discernible shape or progression; we are adjured to let it all just wash over us but when words are involved, as opposed to just music or dance, we can't help looking for sense. The other is the words themselves; I have great tolerance for whimsical wordplay, but Cummings' variety rubs me the wrong way. Also, the music makes them hard to follow, as is often the case with verse originally intended for neither music nor theatre. The best number is the chronicle of a courtship and marriage: It has a story; it's sung by musical director and multi-instrumentalist Mike Ross at his piquant and grainy best; and its visuals include a heart-stopping embrace between a fully lit actor and a silhouette. Cummings comes on first in the double bill, Window second. I saw them at a preview, but no allowances were needed.

Sian Richards / Gregory Prest and Trish Lindstrom dance to Cummings.;; Caption:
2011-05-19-musical-meshugas:
TO LIFE

St. Lawrence Centre for the Arts, Toronto

The first act of To Life begins with the song of that name, from Fiddler on the Roof, and the second ends with it. Despite this symmetry, anyone trying to find an overall unity in this musical entertainment from the Harold Green Jewish Theatre Company risks turning their brain into a pretzel. Best to regard the evening as a double bill of two separate shows, linked only by a focus on the Jewish contribution to the American musical theatre, and by the presence in both of the same quartet of agile and melodious song-and-dancers.

Act One is concerned with four famous performers from the early decades of the 20th century: Eddie Cantor, Sophie Tucker, Fanny Brice and Al Jolson. Patrick Cook gets to approximate Cantor's appealing rhythmic bleat. Charlotte Moore, trailing the longest of red boas, does Tucker's red-hot basso mama routine, in accordance with the general image of Tucker as someone who can never have been young. Gabi Epstein gamely summons the ghost of Fanny Brice, while necessarily battling that of Barbra Streisand; her Second Hand Rose is actually faster and more economical than Streisand's. Shawn Wright brings weight and wit to a Jolson innocent of blackface and even, until near the end, of oratorical mannerisms. Each actor gets the establishing number for his or her character; afterwards, each legend's repertoire is up for grabs from the entire company. The performers and most of the material are good, so it's fun.

It might be even more fun if we were told more about, say, Jolson's egomania or Cantor's peppy liberalism, or about how their Jewishness informed their public personae. I guess it just isn't meant to be that kind of show. Cantor and Brice were comedians who sang, Tucker and Jolson were singers who clowned; so there's a welcome accent on comedy numbers, some of them done in welcome accents.

We also get the Spamalot number You Won't Succeed on Broadway (If You Don't Have Any Jews), done more enjoyably than in the original, with the cast gleefully pointing out that three-quarters of them are from the gentile percentile. In fact, Spamalot and other myths to the contrary, Jewish performers have not, after the heyday of Cantor and Co., run the American musical. (No, Ethel Merman wasn't Jewish and neither, obviously, was Mary Martin.)

Jewish writers are another matter, and the evening's second half is built around the songs they wrote for the book musicals of the '60s and early '70s: the last hurrah of the Rodgers and Hammerstein style. A few numbers, not all of them by Jerry Herman, show why the last hurrah was also the last gasp, but in general the standard is high. The songs have been arranged to tell a kind of story, and the idea works better than I would have expected.

It's a story of family, though not one particular family; or if it is, it involves a brother marrying a sister. The ambience is established in a fine sequence of songs from Jule Styne's London show Bar Mitzvah Boy. The general upliftingness sometimes makes you yearn for something mordant from Company or Follies, but the only real misstep is a group treatment of Maury Yeston's New Words, a song that loses its poignancy and point when it isn't done solo.

Conception and direction are by Avery Saltzman, and the excellent choreography is by Tim French. Mark Camilleri, the show's ace musical director, and Jeffrey Huard, who has been many other shows' ace musical director, provide two-piano accompaniment that ranges from admirable to dazzling.

? Runs until May 29. For tickets, visit stlc.com.

Rachel McCaig / To Life is a fun ode to the Jewish contribution to the American musical theatre.;; Caption:
2011-05-24-in-search-of-a-prince-soulpep:
Diego Matamoros, than whom Canada has no better actor, is the son of an El Salvador diplomat, and came to this country with his divorced mother at an early age. That much we know to be true. How much else we can believe of what he tells us in The Aleph is anybody's guess.

The Aleph, a one-man show that Matamoros created in collaboration with Daniel Brooks, is a devilish overlaying of what may or may not be his autobiography upon a story of the same name by Jorge Luis Borges. It starts with him telling us about an apocryphal Broadway production of Hamlet that had George Clooney as Claudius, Meryl Streep as Gertrude ( "with a Danish accent"), Sandra Bullock as Ophelia ( "horribly miscast") and Jim Carrey in a to-die-for cameo as Osric. All it lacked was a prince. After auditioning every young hopeful in town, they finally gave the part to a stooped, guttural 80-year-old actor who at his audition had miraculously transformed himself into Hamlet. Asked how he did it, he replied "that's actink."

Matamoros, who by this point has been doing some casually virtuoso actink himself, now drops that story and proceeds to tell us about a trip he took, as a shy post-adolescent, to Buenos Aires where his father was stationed. He talks about his father's womanizing, and about his own infatuation with his cousin's beautiful sports-car-driving fiancee who unexpectedly returned his feelings. Conquering his initial diffidence, he prolonged his stay and was rewarded. Returning a year later, he found that his beloved, soon after her marriage, had died of cancer. Still obsessed with her, he sought out her cousin Vittorio, a theatre director of monumental pretentiousness working on a production with the modest title of The Universe, and the subtitle of You in Verse, which seems to have consisted largely of an interminable monologue for himself. He allowed young Diego into rehearsals because, it turns out, he wanted to enlist his assistance in engaging another young Canadian actor named Colm Feore. Diego allowed that yes, he knew Colm, and had even acted with him at the Tom Patterson (this much is true; I've checked) but tactfully neglected to make the call. Anyway, it turned out that Vittorio had other plans for him. His theatre was about to be demolished and he wished

Matamoros to descend to its basement where was housed an Aleph: "one of the points in space that contains all space."

That's how it's described in Borges' tale, which was published in 1949 and whose hero and narrator is a man called Borges. His story duplicates Matamoros's in many respects. He, too, has a lost mourned love, and the two girls share a name: Beatriz. (The echoes of Dante are unlikely to be accidental.) The Borgesian Beatriz's cousin is not a director but an equally self-admiring poet, whose magnum opus is called The World. Both Borges and Matamoros are terrified when they realize that they've let a madman lock them up in a cellar. Both, to their amazement, behold the Aleph and see everything, simultaneously. Well, maybe not everything, but a lot of things, some of them connected with Beatriz. Both come to the conclusion that what they saw was not a true Aleph, though they are confident that such a thing exists. Borges' reasons, which are scholastic, are more convincing than Matamoros's, which are theatrical. On the other hand, because we hear them in real time rather than just read them, Matamoros's carry more emotional weight. His Aleph is a meditation on the sweet sorrow of romantic love and on the theatre, as well as a literary joke played on an author whose own stock-in-trade was literary jokes.

By coincidence or design, the Soulpepper repertoire contains another monologue with Argentinian connections, Guillermo Verdecchia's 20-year-old Fronteras Americanas. Verdecchia uses his own immigrant experience, from there to here, to plead in effect for a breaking-down of borders so that we can all get along as just Americans. I applaud the sentiment, though as an immigrant from Britain of Polish grandparentage, I felt somewhat left out; how about all being citizens of the world? I could certainly identify with Verdecchia's experience of feeling at home everywhere and nowhere. Some of his audience-baiting gambits, though, struck me as tendentious. He complains that American filmmakers depict Colombian (and, now, Mexican) drug lords as stereotypes while ignoring the fact that they can be quite philanthropic on the side. Well, yeah, you could say the same about the Koch brothers. He also lampoons the Distillery itself, as an example of the Saxon habit of selling things on what were once cultural sites; since the things that used to be made there were intended for sale, the moral difference escapes me. He alternates between two personae: his own, and a self-admitted Latin stereotype with three names. As the show progresses, you stop caring which is which. Some of it's funny: Verdecchia describes "white people dancing independently ... of the beat and the rhythm"; later he disarmingly admits that he himself "couldn't dance a tango to save my life." Much of the undercutting, though, just seems aimless, other than as a short cut to the next point-scoring. The end result is overbearing and underwhelming.

- The Aleph and Fronteras Americanas are in repertory at the Young Centre in Toronto. Call 416-866-8666 or visit soulpepper.cafor ticket information.
2011-05-28-of-heartbreakers-and-horsebac:
Bernard Shaw's Heartbreak House was written in, and set during, the First World War, though theres no mention of this in the play until the last 10 minutes, when the English country home in which its set is visited by an air raid. Two of the houseguests, a burglar and an industrialist, run for cover and get blown up. The others, residents and visitors alike, stand their ground and even turn up the lights to make things easier for the bombers. They survive this time, but the play ends with them fervently hoping for another raid tomorrow. There is, of course, a certain grandeur to their defiance; and this, coupled with the fact that they are by and large the most charming and amusing people in the play, usually means that we end up in their corner. Not so in the revival with which the Shaw Festival begins its 50th season. This time we see the ending as Shaw seems to have meant it: as an image of a useless, used-up ruling class embracing its own merited destruction. So, one up to Christopher Newton's production.

The house, which looks like a ship, belongs to the octogenarian Captain Shotover, for many years a mariner and now marinating -in rum and in a despairing philosophy. Learn your business as an Englishman" is his most famous pronouncement, the business being "navigation . neglect it and be damned. He's certain that all around him are damned, and he keeps a store of dynamite to blow up the human race when it goes too far." In his less oracular moments, hes an amiable, absentminded old codger, with two married daughters. In his preface, Shaw divides the British establishment into two categories: the Heartbreakers and the Horsebackers. Of the Shotover sisters Ariadne, whos married a colonial governor and who believes that the people who hunt are the only decent people, is definitely a Horsebacker; Hesione is a vocational Heartbreaker, who enchants every man she meets and whose husband, Hector Hushabye, enchants every woman. The distinction is clearer-cut in the preface than in the play since Ariadne, a.k.a. Lady Utterword, has her heartbreaking moments, too, being if anything a more determined, more cold-blooded flirt than her sister. The play, like many of Shaw's, is full of coruscating oneliners about marriage, though they seem loosely attached to the matters at hand. The second of the play's three acts ends with an exasperated Hector, enslaved to his own romantic image, cursing the world in general and women in particular. In this version, he begins the third act by repeating his imprecations, at which point Leslie Frankishs set obliges him. Its already earned applause by its combination of the domestic and nautical, setting most of the indoor action on a deck with billowing sails for curtains. It earns more by violently tilting, the deck becoming a patio, the perfect setting for the discursive nocturne that constitutes the play's last act. The house is full of electronic noises and this transformation occasions the most striking of them. Two up to Newton's production.

Add to this a batch of good performances and a couple of very effective scenes. But set against all these the lack of an overall rhythm, which raised in my mind all manner of doubts about a play I thought I loved. Its sometimes been described as a dream play; it can be a dream of a debate play. But if it splinters, youre left wondering how it was ever meant to fit together, and why an anatomy of society should devote so much time to its characters' love lives, especially when their emotions are more discussed than displayed. Much depends on Shotover himself. In his early scenes, Michael Ball is funny and endearing, as he wanders on and off delivering perfectly timed dismissals of people he obstinately refuses to recognize, one of them his own child. When challenged about his refusal to stick around whenever someone challenges him, the Captain blames it on his age: "I must go in and out. But going in and out isn't enough to get him through the last act, where hes stationary. His prophetic stature defines the plays; Shaw compared him to Lear, and it's at least true that of the play's three principal women, two are his biological daughters and the third a kind of surrogate. If Ball were to play Lear, I can imagine him bringing off a, well, heartbreaking reconciliation scene, but I find it harder to envisage him on either the throne or the heath.

Blair Williams Hector is splendid from start to finish, at once full-blooded and ironic. Others tend to ease into their roles. Patrick McManus, for example, as the gentle failed industrialist Mazzini Dunn; at first, with his curly hair and tilted nose, he looks like a cartoon of ineffectuality. He is ineffectual, but he also has his share of wisdom, and McManus makes this increasingly and ringingly apparent. Mazzini is also the only man who can resist the charms of Hesione Hushabye which, in Deborah Hays clear-eyed and warmthroated performance, are considerable. The scene in which she recoils from him recoiling from her is both the deepest and the most scintillating of the evening. Laurie Paton's Ariadne begins as a snobbish stereotype; when she finally gets to state her case, it's intolerable on one level and irresistible on another -a case of the she-devil having some of the best tunes. The same grace isnt afforded to Boss Mangan, the tycoon who has bankrupted Mazzini and many others while pretending to rescue them; he perishes while the Lady survives. And though he too is allowed a credo, its bumptious rather than assured; he even confesses that his riches are mainly fictitious. He's also out of his depth in this household, and of course, he falls hopelessly in love with Hesione; and his continuous confusions and humiliations can make him a perversely sympathetic figure. Benedict Campbell will have none of this; his Mangan displays no audible class differences from his hosts and is undeviatingly, sneeringly malignant. He also executes some magnificent twitches when awakened from a trance. The odd thing about Campbell's performance is that he commands the stage while hes on it but one forgets about him when he isnt: a fault perhaps of the production, but also of the play, which is so intent on exposing and undercutting the Boss that it removes him as a threat. Or maybe it just likes being paradoxical.

There's solid support from Patricia Hamilton as the brisk house help and Patrick Galligan as Randall the rotter," a character the play cuts down without bothering to build him up. William Vickers' heartbreak housebreaker would probably be more hilarious if less of a meal were made of his mock-repentance. Which leaves Robin Evans Willis in the pivotal role of Ellie: Mazzinis daughter, Mangans possible prey, Hesione's friend and the Captain's convert. She does very well, but without solving the roles tough if not insurmountable problem: Her progress, if any, is the plays. It's she whose heart is initially broken, by Hector, in a relationship talked about but hardly shown. All the subsequent talk of heartbreak remains just talk. Other things resonate: "What, asks Hector, of the bigger ship, this soul's prison we call England?" Now it could be Canada. Or the world. Two minor cavils: Newton surprisingly fails to make much of the play's lurch into rhymed verse at the end of Act 1 which, if boldly handled, can jerk us into another world. He also flouts the stage directions by not allowing Randall to play Keep the Home Fires Burning on his flute at the end. This may accord with his wish for a downbeat ending. But it's a loss.

- Heartbreak House is in repertory at the Festival Theatre, NiagaraontheLake, through Oct. 7. Call 18005117429 or visit shawfest.com for details.
2011-05-28-shards-of-the-bard:
BOOK REVIEW

How Shakespeare Changed Everything By Stephen Marche HarperCollins Canada 224 pp; $24.99

The humble starling is a major blight on North America, a brightly coloured pest that ruins crops, spreads disease and breeds at an unstoppable rate. And it's Shakespeare's fault.

This is one of the fascinating facts I learned from Stephen Marche's How Shakespeare Changed Everything. It seems that in the 19th century, Eugene Schiffelin, a New York pharmaceutical magnate devoted equally to Shakespeare and to birds, conceived the idea of introducing into America specimens of every fowl mentioned in the complete works. Shakespeare mentions starlings just once; indeed he seems to have been the first writer ever to mention them, as is detailed in another essay in the book, one devoted to the unparellelled number of words the English language owes to its greatest writer. ("Unparallelled," by the way, is another of them.) The starling turns up in Henry IV Part I, in a speech that Marche calls "forgettable," though I think it's pretty memorable; it's the one in which Hotspur threatens to train a starling to say "nothing but Mortimer" to a king who has good reason to fear the name. Anyway, in 1860 Schiffelin released 60 starlings into Central Park, and since then there's been no stopping them.

This is the clearest case of cause and effect that Marche adduces in a sprightly, erudite sampling of Shakespeare's influence on absolutely everything. Others have to be more speculative. Even the book's initial statement -"William Shakespeare was the most influential person who ever lived" -is open to question. Has he really been more influential than Jesus or Muhammad? Grant, though, that he's the most influential writer who's ever lived, worldwide, and that the influence, once past a certain point, has become a self-perpetuating mechanism. An actor wants to play Hamlet because every other actor has played Hamlet. Shakespeare gets quoted (and misquoted) all the time, even by people who've never read him, and that omnipresence affects the way we think, speak, behave and see one another. "There would be no Obama," Marche writes, "if there were not first Othello, just as there would be no Leonardo DiCaprio if there were not first Romeo."

I wonder. Marche is probably right to say Shakespeare "invented teenagers as we know them today"; the same point was made by Marjorie Garber in Shakespeare and Modern Culture, a book similar to Marche's in its arguments, though perhaps because it's the work of a professional academic, more strait-jacketed by them. DiCaprio's career was certainly jump-started by his playing Romeo, though of course it's perfectly possible he would have been a movie heartthrob if neither Shakespeare nor Romeo had ever existed; after all, the role didn't do much for Leonard Whiting (the previous film Romeo, if anyone remembers). Really, it's unknowable. Still, I'll give Marche DiCaprio. I'm far more skeptical about Obama. The thesis here, advanced in the book's first and flagship chapter, is that Shakespeare's black general eventually paved the way for a black president. The linchpin figure is Paul Robeson, whose successive and increasingly confident appearances as the Moor established him as an American culture hero. But there was far more than that to the Civil Rights movement, of which Obama is to date the ultimate beneficiary and the ultimate symbol. The canonical writer who did most to make him possible was probably not Shakespeare but Harriet Beecher Stowe. (Which doesn't make Obama an Uncle Tom, any more than he's an Othello.)

Marche complicates his argument by getting the play wrong. He says it's racist: "In the play's opening scene . Iago whips the city of Venice into a fury over Othello's elopement with Desdemona." No, he doesn't. The only person he whips up is Desdemona's father who, until his paternal pride was challenged, liked and respected Othello. As does everyone else in the play. When Lodovico, in the last speech, says, "The object poisons sight," he isn't, as Marche claims, referring to the spectacle of a (dead) black man embracing a (dead) white woman, he's describing three dead bodies on a bed, all of them the victims of Iago's villainy. Far from being racist, the play places racism as the refuge of people with their own agenda. The play Marche describes might have been written by Iago. Nor do I buy the idea that, according to Shakespeare, "Othello is a man whose inherent barbarism undoes his civilization." When Laurence Olivier played the role, he marked the moment of Othello's fall by tearing off the crucifix that he'd previously worn around his neck. It was a powerful moment, but there's absolutely no cue for it in the text. You might as well blame Leontes' jealousy in The Winter's Tale on his being Sicilian. (The Merchant of Venice is a more problematic case. Marche mostly avoids it, though he does bring forward two fascinating facts: The play, contrary to what you might expect, was banned in Nazi Germany; and it's always been very popular in Israel.)

Marche on Othello is doing what he, like Garber before him, recognizes has always been done with Shakespeare: quoting out of context for moral effect. He acknowledges that in Shakespeare "everybody finds what he or she is looking for, and I'm no exception." Not everybody is so frank. Just recently a columnist in this very newspaper quoted some lines from Julius Caesar that sound very noble and reflective in isolation, but are actually part of an incitement to mob violence. Even more amusingly, he attributed them to Macbeth. Not that Shakespeare's the only writer who can be misused in this way. Marche himself writes that George Orwell's vision of the future was "a boot stamping on a human face over and over." But that isn't Orwell speaking; it's his character O'Brien in 1984. Orwell crops up again, though less prominently than he should, in a chapter on Tolstoy's hatred of Shakespeare in general and King Lear in particular. Marche has little to add to Orwell's classic essay on the subject, but the chapter does occasion one of his happiest phrases, on Shakespeare's ability to cross borders: "He's better in English, but he's willing to negotiate."

And so it goes: rash generalizations balanced by elegant insights. Rightly, he links Shakespeare's frankness about sex to our own; wrongly, he asserts that all love poetry before Shakespearean had been Petrarchan idealism. In fact, Shakespeare's cheerful obscenity is also typical of his fellow playwrights, of his near-contemporary John Donne, and even of a gentle sonneteering predecessor like Sir Thomas Wyatt. And besides, the Shakespeare sonnet he actually quotes ("the expense of spirit in a waste of shame"), though certainly frank, is anything but celebratory. On the other hand, he can cut to the heart of what makes Shakespeare supreme: his "preternatural ability to match the sound of a word to its sense"; that "no one produces characters with more individuality of language than Shakespeare"; that he "violates the idea that life can be fully understood." And I could forgive anything for Marche's summary of Shakespeare the working playwright, indifferent to the printing of Hamlet: "He wasn't going to get paid whether it was good or bad, and besides he was in the middle of writing Macbeth."

- Robert Cushman is the National Post's theatre critic.

Note: .EDS: Edited by National Post.936 words

Some people think Cat on a Hot Tin Roof is Tennessee Williams' best play. As of this Shaw Festival revival, I'm one of them.

The play, as has often been noted, is eccentrically constructed. Its first act is basically a duet between Maggie, the title character, and her husband Brick. Or maybe a solo with brief interruptions, since Maggie, who earns her scalded feline status by being passionately frustrated, does most of the talking. She wants a child, preferably male, and Brick, a star athlete whose career ended when he hit the bottle, won't even sleep with her. Her motives are at least as much economic as sexual, since Brick's Big Daddy is, though he doesn't yet know it, dying of cancer, and is far likelier to leave his property - the biggest cotton plantation in the Mississippi Delta - to his unloved but philoprogenitive elder son Gooper than to the favoured but unproductive Brick.

Act Two is another duet: Brick and Big Daddy, a force of nature who, high on his mistaken belief that all that ails him is a li'l ol' spastic colon, doesn't care what he says or who he says it to. His immediate mission is to discover the nature of Brick's relationship with his sporting buddy Skipper, who committed suicide after a failed attempt to prove his manhood by going to bed with Maggie. Brick famously declares his disgust with the "mendacity" he sees all around him, to which Big Daddy replies that there's nothing he himself needs to be taught about that. The scene is a tremendous - and tremendously acted - display of punching and counter-punching, ducking and weaving, that climaxes with father and son shouting goaded unwelcome truths at one another. And Brick, though it doesn't give him much joy, may be said to win this round since what he reveals is scientific and incontrovertible while what he hears is psychological and deniable.

Act Three is a variation on that old staple, the reading of the will, with the twist that the deceased is still around. It is, for a change, an extended ensemble, though it centres on Big Daddy's Big Mama (not his mother, of course, but his wife) whose husband has said repeatedly that he can't stand her but who is still devoted to him and is in denial over his impending demise. At least it centres on her in the play as Williams first wrote it. Elia Kazan, his director, persuaded him to rewrite it; mainly, it seems, so as to include an encore scene for Big Daddy. The urge is understandable, and the revision has become standard; but I still wish Eda Holmes, the Shaw's director, had gone with the original Tennessee waltz.

I have no other reservations about her production, which is a continuous and exhilarating blast. Moya O'Connell's Maggie, sultry and driven, whips the first movement along; so, though as taciturn as she is voluble, does Gray Powell as the psychically and physically wounded Brick. His physical handicap stems from a hurdling accident sustained the previous evening while attempting, he says, to get himself back in shape. He's on crutches, and as he swings himself about on them, usually in the direction of the liquor cabinet, he just about defines the phrase "passive aggression." My feelings at the first intermission were, roughly, "This is magnificent. And Jim Mezon hasn't even come on yet."

When he does, he delivers on a scale that probably no other actor in Canada could match. His Big Daddy is, literally and metaphorically, a towering performance, a bald-headed Rabelaisian giant whose vocal and emotional power seems limitless. He's also delicate. A bullying misogynist he may be, but Big Daddy is the most sympathetic and even admirable person in the play: the creation of a playwright who seems to have consciously set out to write a great character and, damn it all, succeeded. He's been, in his own mind, to death and back; he's also, as he says, bummed all over the country, and the combination has taught him tolerance. He also wants desperately to reach his son who, in turn, is torn between wanting to reciprocate and to remain unreachable. As the father reaches out, the son lashes out; Powell's task, given less colourful ammunition, may well be the harder of the two and his achievement is equally fine.

His anger and bitterness can be elegantly ironic, and they continue to percolate through the final act, which is also where Corrine Koslo's Big Mama, terrified and obstinate, comes memorably into her own, and where O'Connell reasserts herself. Putting this central quartet into action, and building them a world, are the play's great achievements. It also finds a moment of sympathy for Patrick McManus's Gooper, understandably resentful of the love lavished on his football-hero brother and determined ("I'm not a corporate lawyer for nothing") to get even.

His wife Mae, greed incarnate, isn't allowed a case, but Nicole Underhay's unflagging performance lets us know she thinks she has one. Their brood of no- neck monsters is here reduced to two, which is a shame, but their birthday serenading of Big Daddy is authentically horrible. "No-neck monsters" is of course their unloving auntie Maggie's phrase for them; vivid though it is, one wishes she would vary it occasionally.

Holmes' actors have the authority and flexibility to use the Southern accent rather than, as sometimes happens, letting it use them. Williams' language here could never be described as stripped for action, but in this play it's brilliantly armoured for it.

In repertory until Oct. 23. For tickets, call 1-800-511-7429 or visit shawfest.com.

THEATRE REVIEW

The Merry Wives of Windsor

Festival Theatre, Stratford

Stratford this year begins operations with The Merry Wives of Windsor, which is set in a period somewhere between late Regency and early Pickwickian. In fact, Geraint Wyn Davies' rubicund Falstaff carries himself initially like Mr. Pickwick, which is disconcerting considering that Dickens protagonist is benevolent and virginal while Shakespeares is anything but. But he soon gets over it.

The choice of period, too, seems at first perverse, for a play whose main attraction is its homely, informed portrayal of Elizabethan small-town life. Something does get lost, but on its own terms Robert Perdziola's design proves attractive, unobtrusive and versatile.

As does Frank Galati's whole production, his Stratford Festival debut. Its blessedly unforced and perceptive nearly all the way through, and it makes excellent use of that princely, demanding stage. Its also very funny, at least some of the time. That it isn't more consistently so can to a large extent be blamed on the play itself, which takes the classic comic Rule of Three to the grim extreme of staging the same situation time after time and then after time.

Sir John Falstaff, cast adrift from his career in the history plays but still carrying the same weight and a portion of the same wit, pays avaricious court to two comfortable housewives, the mistresses Ford and Page. Very much not turned on, they lure him into a trio of assignations in which he is a) consigned to a laundry basket full of foul linen and tossed into the Thames; b) dressed up as an old woman, in which guise he is savagely beaten by Mistress Ford's jealous husband; and c) persuaded to show up in Windsor Forest at midnight, got up as the legendary Herne the Hunter, complete with horns, there to be pinched and tormented by a gang of local children pretending to be fairies.

Fool you thrice, what are we to make of you? The Falstaff of Henry IV also falls victim to practical jokes, but never to the same one even twice, and up until his last tragic mistake he always manages to talk his way out of things. This Falstaff gets resigned, in a way previously unheard of. The real problem, though, is not that the two Sir Johns are different animals -in fact they have quite a lot in common -but that this new one operates in so restricting a framework. His three sitcom episodes play themselves out in descending order of hilarity.

Theres a lot to enjoy, though, on the way down. Wyn Davies, apart from providing a very persuasive outline of an adventurer down on his uppers, fastens with lyrical relish on every flavourful line the script gives him; physically, hes richly and even subtly inventive. The buckbasket scene and its immediate consequences are masterfully handled by all concerned, especially Tom Rooney's Master Ford, the first in Shakespeare's self-tormenting line of imaginary cuckolds. I have seen Fords more hysterically funny than Rooneys (correction, Ive seen one -the late Ian Richardson), but his is still memorably masochistic, especially in his interactions with Falstaff's footbath and with an all too snug-fitting brandy glass. He also digs unusually deep and disturbingly into Ford's eagerness to believe the worst of his wife, to whom Lucy Peacock also gives some moments of troubled awareness to balance her irresistible delight in controlling the main farcical action.

These Fords have a real relationship going, and one feels an unaccustomed satisfaction at their reconciliation, plus severe misgivings at how long it will last. Their counterparts, the Pages, are less interesting. Laura Condlln doesnt have the authority, or indeed the experience, to be a worthy partner for Peacock; Tom McCamus does everything possible for her complacent spouse but there isnt much to do. He's at his best when playing the tyrannical father in one of the play's many subplots.

The most promising of these, the abortive duel between a timid Welsh parson and a bellicose French physician, is one of the productions few outright miscalculations. The situation is never made clear, and its further confused by making the supposedly terrified Sir Hugh (Andrew Gillies) as enthusiastic a fire-eater as his Gallic opponent (Nigel Bennett, explosively effective in his first scene but with nowhere to go thereafter). Given the play's reliance on dialect comedy, it's instructive that Doctor Caius insistence that sexual jealousy is not the fashion in France goes down a topical treat, while Falstaffs expostulations in the last scene about "that Welsh fairy" fall unaccustomedly flat, perhaps because he himself sounds the more authentically Welsh of the two.

Very good indeed -in fact my favourite in the cast -is James Blendick's Justice Shallow, a character even further removed than Falstaff from his chronicle-play prototype, played here as a tetchy squire, very much on his dignity and in rich, relaxed voice. Especially delightful is his exasperation at his young cousin Slender's hopeless idea of romantic courtship, the lad being played charmingly if with almost too much restraint by Christopher Prentice. The last woodland scene isnt as healingly festive as its trying to be, but it looks lovely, with Herne's Oak itself descending from nowhere to make a real gnarled picture.

- The Merry Wives of Windsor runs until Oct. 14. For tickets, call 1-800-567-1600 or visit stratfordfestival.ca.

2011-06-02-a-regal-affair:
THEATRE REVIEW

Camelot Festival Theatre, Stratford

Both of our major festivals this year are mounting famous musicals by Alan Jay Lerner and Frederick Loewe. Shaw has My Fair Lady, a show that always works and does so again, very nicely. Stratford has Camelot, a show that never works. Except that this time it does, magnificently.

Chief among its many glories is the King Arthur of Geraint Wyn Davies, an actor who seems, like Arthur's teacher Merlin, to be aging backwards. In the past few Stratford seasons we have seen him nudging greatness as Polonius, Bottom, Julius Caesar and, just the night before this one, Falstaff. He reaches it as Arthur, who starts the show boyish, shy and idealistic, and retains those qualities even as they become battered and embittered by tragic experience. And for this show, "tragic" is not too high-flown a word. It deals with hopeless choices.

In Lerners adaptation of T. H. Whites adaptation of Thomas Malory and his predecessors, Arthur, born into a world of war, conceives the ideas of peace and civic justice and, for a time, makes them work. Then Guinevere, his queen and confidante, and Lancelot, his best friend and champion knight, fall in love. Their passion may not be consummated (the show's ambiguous on the point) but Mordred, Arthur's illegitimate son and ambitious antitype, makes sure that it looks like it was. Guineveres condemned to death; Mordred gleefully points out Arthurs magnificent dilemma between law and love.

There are two major climaxes that Wyn Davies makes achingly real. At the end of Act 1, Arthur, recognizing the emotional facts on the ground, tries to argue himself into believing that everything will turn out for the best because everybody will behave well. At the end of the second, when they haven't and it hasn't, he prepares for his last battle and passionately enjoins a boy called Tom of Warwick (read, Tom Malory) to run away and keep the story of Camelot alive. This involves a reprise of the title song, miraculously transformed from cheerful jingle to desperate anthem.

Both these scenes are superbly written, and the finale, invoking failure and triumph and history and literature all at once, can bring a lump to the throat in even the crummiest productions. (Believe me, I know.) Whats exceptional about them here is theyre seamlessly connected to what has gone before, much of which is very funny. Arthur never believes himself clever, though he's always thinking things out; he has a gauche quickwittedness that Wyn Davies makes supremely winning. Lancelot, questioned about his martial prowess, says, "my skill comes from timing," and the same is true of Wyn Davies' Arthur. Lancelot adds that his "strength comes from purity," and that suits for this Arthur, too. You truly believe that hes a good man. It both warms and breaks the heart.

The tact and boldness of this performance are emblematic of Gary Griffins production, which solves every one of the show's problems. It digs beneath much arch and awkward writing to get at what's real. Arthurs eccentric buddy King Pellinore talks with a forced joviality that suggests very bad imitation Wodehouse; Brent Carver downplays the mannerisms in favour of grit, loyalty and genuine humour. He also plays a truly unearthly Merlin, and this doubling of Arthurs two advisers adds up to his finest performance in years.

Similarly, Mike Nadajewski softpedals the failed wordplay of Mordred's selfrevealing song, and plays it instead for a passionate, twisted delight in destructiveness.

Kaylee Harwood's Guinevere is plummy for my taste, but her relationship with Arthur rings true, and their duet of mutual consolation (What Do the Simple Folk Do?) is both amusing and revealing. Her relationship with Lancelot is more perplexing. Jonathan Winsby has a ringing voice and handsome presence, but its still hard to see why Guinevere should fixate for years on a man who starts (Cest Moi) as a self-glorifying buffoon and then turns into cardboard. All this pair seem to do is sing heavy ballads at one another (though one, mercifully, has been cut).

Camelot is in fact unique among classic musicals in having a book that's far more interesting than its score; it seems somehow appropriate that Loewe's best tune, Follow Me, should be sung by a character we barely see to one we are about to lose. Griffin and his choreographer Warren Carlyle excel, however, at making the songs tell the story, especially the big concerted numbers like The Jousts, a medieval Ascot Gavotte thats here more exciting than I would ever have thought possible, and the insanely expository Guinevere.

The Lusty Month of May is rescued from coyness to become a feast of movement and -courtesy of Maria Blumenfelds costumes -colour. Debra Hanson's sets speed, adorn and beautify the action without ever overpowering it. They include a magical forest and castle where dwells Lucy Peacock's deliciously languid Morgan le Fay, anachronistically hooked on chocolate. Theres an equally magical prologue in which we see Arthur growing up while Merlin -whats the word? -youthens, and that incorporates a real hawk, a vital part of the hero's education.

Maybe the show's time has come; what was once known as the Kennedy musical may now be the Obama musical. Anyway, Ive never heard of, and certainly never seen, a production of Camelot that came anywhere near matching this one.

- Camelot runs until Oct. 30 For tickets, call 1-800-567-1600 or visit stratfordfestival.ca.

2011-06-04-it-is-in-fact-quite-loverly-m:
The first thing to be said of the Shaw Festivals production of My Fair Lady is that it's a very good production of Pygmalion. That isn't the back-hander it might seem. A lot of Shaws play remains in the Lerner and Loewe musical, however trimmed and romanticized. The romance, in fact, was there all the time, just waiting to be brought forward - which is one reason the show is so strong; it establishes its own identity while respecting that of its source. In this revival, Deborah Hay as Eliza Doolittle and Benedict Campbell as Professor Higgins do especially well at exploring the penultimate stage of their relationship: when she declares her independence from him and he grudgingly admits to having become attached to her. Theres much backand-forth role reversal in this scene, and both actors explore and expose every moment of it. They do so, incidentally, more economically than would be possible in the play, which at the equivalent point has the two characters going round and round in repetitive circles.

Hay's Eliza is enchanting throughout, and a more credible denizen of the Covent Garden flower market than most. She gives very good, very funny and sensitive cockney, and her performance of Wouldn't It Be Loverly is, well, loverly; the staging involves her being pulled around in a barrow thats an impromptu carriage, from which she transmits a delightful mixture of pride and apprehension. Rather the same qualities infuse her first entry into the Higgins home asking for speech lessons; shes on her best behaviour and on her guard. There's a superb moment at which, battered by his brusqueness, she not only threatens to leave but makes, wounded, for the door. The lessons themselves could hardly be more amusing or more touching, and her timing and phrasing of the transplanted tea party scene (which Kenneth Tynan rightly called Shaw's peak of pure, as opposed to applied, comedy") are gorgeous. At the ball shes a vision, and she pretty much remains so. The musical Eliza is a terror of a role, especially for a nonBritish actress: Shes required to get two English accents exactly right as that's what the story's about, to act a full-blown Shavian heroine and, especially in the later stages, to soar in song like Julie Andrews. Hay doesnt quite bring off the last part; I Could Have Danced All Night and the climax of Without You are a bit of a strain. But shes a believable, irresistible woman and that's what counts. It's probably heretical but I loved her more in this role than I did in Born Yesterday.

Campbell breaks with the tradition established by Rex Harrison and followed by all subsequent Higginses by singing rather than talking almost every line of his songs. Ive often wondered what the melody line of Why Cant the English might be; now I know. The treatment reveals an unsuspected astringency in the music, and in no way weakens the wit of the lyrics. In fact, Campbell acts Higgins more pointedly in the songs than in some of the dialogue, where he tends to play the man's rudeness as calculated rather than automatic. He has, though, a fascinating look. He wears glasses almost throughout, which at first suggest scholastic gentleness but turn out to be a defence against feeling. The one and only time he takes them off is in the last section of I've Grown Accustomed to Her Face, his one and only love song; and its like a thunderclap of vulnerability. (He replaces them immediately afterwards: another kind of thunderclap.)

Molly Smiths production perpetuates some of the American musical's sentimental misconceptions about the English class system: that a professor of phonetics would live in a mansion with an entire brigade of liveried servants, and that London's lower orders would exist in a perpetual state of jolly costermongering that isnt even laid on for the benefit of the tourists. The first of these stereotypes is built inescapably into the show (though not the play); the second doesnt have to be. Nor does the musical need not one but two jolly cockney knees-ups. Neil Barclay, who as Alfred Doolittle is at the centre of them, certainly doesn't; he sings with point and gusto, dances with the delicacy of great bulk, and in speech conveys the less attractive aspects of Eliza's absentee dad without rubbing our faces in them.

Daniel Pelzigs choreography is actually most valuable not in the big concerted numbers but in the way it navigates the actors through the smaller ones. The Rain in Spain regains the joyous impact that this impromptu tango must have had in the far-off days when nobody knew it was coming. The Ascot Gavotte has gone Latin in less felicitous ways, since the female members of the Edwardian aristocracy seem from their headgear to be prophetically channelling Carmen Miranda. Another oddity of Judith Bowdens costuming is that Higgins, admittedly a social eccentric, appears to be attending the embassy ball in his very best dressing gown. At home he lives, courtesy of Ken MacDonald's sets, surrounded by giant symbolic bird cages, in addition to the tiny real one mandated by the text. It's a striking and not unhelpful environment, though the recurring projections of actual birds in flight seem excessive, at least in a production as otherwise straightforward as this one.

Theres gracious support from Sharry Fletts Mrs. Higgins, Patrick Galligan's Colonel Pickering and from Mark Uhre's Freddy, who sings his one song beautifully and is hardly called on to do much else. The show's vexed ending seems here not so much ambiguous as undecided. For the overwhelming majority of the time, though, this is a touching, intelligent and generally magical evening.

? My Fair Lady is in repertory through Oct. 30 at the Festival Theatre, Niagara-on-the-Lake. Call 18005117429 or visit shawfest.com for ticket information.
