2011-06-07-deities-dust-bowls:
THEATRE REVIEW

Jesus Christ Superstar & The Grapes of Wrath Avon Theatre, Stratford, Ont.

Regarding Jesus Christ Superstar: I don't know how to love it. But I can certainly admire what Des McAnuff has done with it, which is to bring shape, lucidity and narrative drive to what is at root a rock oratorio. Theres an explosive but disciplined theatricality to his direction here that taps right into the pulse of Andrew Lloyd Webbers music which in this, his first full-scale work, was powerfully theatrical, theatrical not being necessarily the same thing as dramatic.

Robert Brill has designed an apparently simple set, metallic and split-levelled, that proves very versatile, and eventually furnishes an amazing crucifixion. Paul Tazewell's costumes make the odd Biblical nod but mainly summon the 1960s youth movement that spawned the show and the contemporary Middle East. Howell Binkley's lighting is superb and Rick Foxs musical direction is powerhouse. The cast is across-theboard ideal. Paul Nolans Jesus played opening night with a bronchial infection that robbed him of notes, but the challenge may even have helped his intensity; anyway, he was flawlessly charismatic and unreadable. Chilina Kennedy is a touchingly devoted Mary Magdalene and Josh Young an electrically angry and baffled Judas. And so on and on, with special mention for Bruce Dow's Herod who, more Roman than the Romans, seems to be playing all the decadent emperors rolled into one.

It's interesting that this number, the closest thing in the score to a traditional show tune, should always go down so well. Apart from its entertainment value as a vaudeville strut, it gives Tim Rices lyrics a chance to stretch out and be funny. Elsewhere, the clenched musical rhythms enforce clenched, earnest words, lyrics that are prosaic without being conversational; the exchanges in the high priests scenes are especially painful. Banality, musical and verbal, of a higher-flown kind comes in the big ballad: the detachable hit (generically I Don't Know How to Cry for His Memory, Argentina) that is the worst thing in every early Webber score. Mary M's variant of it, apparently stemming from her prostitute past, is that shes baffled by Jesus refusal to fancy her. This keys into the show's binding idea, which is that everybody sees in the superstar whatever they want to see. It's a valid point, though it has the disadvantage of reducing the protagonist to a blank slate; even when he throws the money-changers out of the temple hes a strangely passive figure. It also means that the other figures are static, though Pilate is a possible exception.

Judas ought to be, especially if you accept Rices contention that he, Jesus and Mary make a romantic triangle; but that has the effect of cheapening the story without illuminating it. Judas' motivations may be more tangled than usual, but they're no more accessible, however hard the music pounds them. That goes for most of the show. Some bits seem to be there simply because theyre too famous to be left out. Maybe the Gospel story should only be told by someone whos passionate about it, whether for or against or torn between: like Stephen Adly Guirgis' The Last Days of Judas Iscariot, the work of a Catholic, however lapsed. For all the sound and the fury, the bells and the whistles, the agnostic superstar leaves the enigmatic story exactly where it found it. Unlike the more satisfying Camelot: the other musical being given a probably-definitive staging at Stratford this year.

Stratford can also boast two Biblically-soaked epics, the other being a stage version of John Steinbeck's Depression classic The Grapes of Wrath. This, too, is a mightily impressive production of a problematic text. Two scenes in particular burn themselves on the mind. In one, a character billed as Man Going Back (Robert King) gives a bitter account of just why hes returning to the dust bowl of Oklahoma from the supposed promised land of California, where the fruitpickin work certainly exists but where there are 10 hungry applicants for every piece of it. The other has a labour organizer (Tyrone Savage) passionately describing what this does to wages and how the law and the bosses react to any attempt to resist it. Both these actors, who do equally well in various other roles, are standouts in an already outstanding cast.

Their characters, though, are peripheral, and there's the rub with Frank Galati's adaptation; the commentary is more powerful than the main action. This concerns the Joad family, sharecroppers who, having lost their Oklahoma home, make that California trip, getting kicked on Route 66. They journey, some dozen of them to begin with, in an overloaded weather-beaten truck that itself makes a great visual statement. Antoni Cimolinos production is in fact full of remarkable scenes, culminating in the frantic building of trenches to stem a flood; though, given the sightlines at the Avon, its cruel to the audi-ence to have so many scenes of actors sitting on the floor.

Evan Buliung is riveting as Tom Joad, the hero in spite of himself, doggedly cresting wave after wave of disaster; Tom McCamus no less so as his de facto mentor, a selfdefrocked pastor who ends up preaching what the authorities take to be red revolution -i.e. social justice -though still in sacerdotal cadences.

There are lovely performances from Steve Ross as a simple-minded brother and Randy Hughson as an agonized uncle, drinking to anesthetize. But, as often in dramatized novels, the focus gets dispersed, not helped, by occasional inconsistent recourse to onstage narrators and by the all-too-consistent use of a folk-country trio who, by underlining the obvious, make the Depression more depressing than necessary.

Unlike the film, the play doesn' t end with Tom's freedom-fighting cri de coeur, but goes on to further miseries. This is morally admirable but dramatically risky; it means the most vital character leaves before the end. The actual end is a kind of pieta, finely and stoically acted by Wright and Kennedy and, as a harrowingly ageless and hopeless man, Dylan Trowbridge. Its moving, but not completely so, perhaps because the final gesture is Rose of Sharons and, for all that Kennedy does for her, we just haven't previously seen enough of her to really know her. That said, for a big production to end on a note of bleak endurance is rare indeed, and truthful. Even hopelessness, in the right context, can be hopeful

? Both shows run until Oct. 29. For tickets, call 1-800-567-1600 or visit stratfordfestival.ca.

2011-06-08-irish-pride-marital-divide:
THEATRE REVIEW

DRAMA AT INISH & CANDIDA

Court House Theatre; Royal George Theatre, Niagara-on-the-Lake

Heres what happens in Drama at Inish (subtitled A Comedy, so nobody gets the wrong idea). In the early 1930s, a touring theatrical company arrives to play a date in a small Irish town. The local idea of stage entertainment has usually been on the lighter side, circuses and such, but these strolling players offer sterner stuff: "serious plays -Russian plays and that sort of thing." Their Russian repertoire seems to lean more to tragic Tolstoy than, as wed nowadays expect, Chekhov; and they also administer a hefty dose of Scandinavian. They're positively bursting with Ibsen.

Lennox Robinson, who wrote the play and was a major force in Ireland's native dramatic flowering at the Abbey Theatre, is here paying affectionate and slightly self-mocking tribute to his own youthful awakening when an Ibsen troupe came to Dublin and changed his life. Their successors, in his own plays, change the lives of the citizens of Inish in surprisingly direct ways. They play to packed houses: a surprise in itself. The play is set in a hotel where the married couple, who are the companys managers and stars, are billeted. The proprietor is a jovial heavy-drinking fella; his sister, who does much of the work, is a spinster mourning her great lost romantic opportunity. Seeing the plays brings it all back to her. Others are even more drastically affected. The local MP, after seeing An Enemy of the People, goes so far as to flout party lines and vote his conscience. That, decides the community, is the last straw.

The play (Robinsons, not Ibsen's) has a great idea, which it develops agreeably but tamely. The structure and much of the tone are conventional domestic comedy. Too many of the exciting events happen offstage, and the correspondences between the townsfolk and the plays that influence them seem too cut-and-dried, too oneon-one, to be credible. However, in production, Drama at Inish acquires a joyous dimension beyond its plot. It comes from actors playing actors, and from other actors playing the supposedly ordinary people affected by them, especially when those actors are as good as the leads in Jackie Maxwell's Shaw Festival production. You never know which is the more theatrical. Ric Reids hotelier is a genial, peppery old party whose only drawback is his lengthy absence from the stage in the second half. Mary Haney, as in Harvey last year, grounds frustrated excitability in hard reality and then takes it to delirious heights that are a kind of greatness.

And then there are the visitors, wonderfully named Hector de la Mare and Constance Constantia. Thom Marriotts Hector is a grandiose, grandiloquent figure who always seems to be swishing an invisible cloak; I never quite did myself justice in melodrama, he says, melodramatically. But when he speaks about the new drama that has inspired him, he is both moved and moving. Corrine Koslo's Constance, looking daggers at the suggestion that she might like "a nice, creamy cup of tea," is flighty but also motherly. And their domestic concerns, as they confront unaccustomed success and customary penury, are at least as real as those on which they intrude.

The proceedings get positively Pirandellian (to invoke the one modern master who doesn't seem to figure in the de la Mare repertoire) when the couple are prevailed upon to audition the shy and humble hotel boots. To their amazement, he turns out to be good; "the spirit," says Hector, wonderingly and hauntingly, "bloweth where it listeth." Indeed, it bloweth all through Andrew Bunkers performance as the aspirant, both in and out of his day job. Hector warns him of the horrors and uncertainties of the actors life, and you agree with him; and then you remember that he and the boy he's talking to and everyone around them are actually living it. Less complex in its implications but equally delightful is Craig Pike's turn as the gauche son of the house, tempted to tragic extremities by the plays hes seen and the practically minded woman hes courting.

An exceptional opening week in Niagara is completed by Candida, usually one of my least favourite Shaw plays because it seems, in its sane, and economical and well-constructed way, like something somebody else might have written. Tadeusz Bradecki's production, however, gives it a hard comic edge and, even more rewardingly, a hard passionate edge.

Nigel Shawn Williams as Morell, the Christian Socialist East End preacher, is the most muscular of Christians. He probably doesn't have to speak quite as loudly to persuade us that Morell is over-fond of the sound of his own voice, but he makes the point, and when his intensity is funnelled into anguish over the possibility that he might lose his wife to another man, he is more real in the role than any actor I have known.

Its telling that Shaw, who must have agreed with Morell politically, was so merciless at pointing out his flaws. Hes comparably, though not quite equally, ruthless with his other alter ego and Morell's rival Marchbanks, the 19-year-old poet of preRaphaelite tendencies, whom Wade Bogert-O'Brien plays with a coltish enthusiasm thats touching rather then embarrassing. As Candida herself, who has significantly less stage time than either of her admirers, Claire Jullien is a sensible, capable sphinx.

This well-made plays cast list is symmetrically divided between three principals and three supports. Most aggressive of the latter is Krista Colosimo who, as Morell's unrequitedly adoring typist, shouts even louder and far more continuously than he does, either in self-defence or because it's catching. Graeme Somerville is contrastingly sly and winning as his equally worshipful curate. Somewhere between the two comes Norman Browning as Candidas boorish but funny dad, forever on the make. Another unresolved question around this plays heroine is how the apple fell so very far from the tree, or the chip from the old blockhead. There's certainly no similarity between their accents. Maybe, along with his sermonizing talents, Reverand Morell possessed some of the skills of Professor Henry Higgins, currently in practice just down the road.

? Drama at Inish runs until Oct. 1; Candida runs until Oct. 30. For tickets, call 1-800-511-7429 or visit shawfest.com.

2011-06-11-an-unwinnable-game-of-thrones:
Seana McKenna is formidable as Richard III

One of the abiding puzzles of Richard III is that, while few people in the play have any illusions about the hunchbacked schemer who's decimating them on his way to the throne, he still gets away with it. The other characters hardly cease insulting him ("bunchbacked toad" and so on) and they all know his murderous record, but they still go along with him, either for what they think they can get out of it or because they just don't take him seriously. Seana McKenna, striking a blow for gender-neutral casting by playing Richard at Stratford, shows why they should believe this and just how wrong they are.

There have been plenty of impish Richards played by men. McKenna goes further by playing him as an imp: a descendant of the personified Vice of the English morality plays to whom at one point he claims kinship. If McKenna's voice is higher than those of some Richards, her bodily stature is lower; she lops a few inches off her height by adopting a steep stoop to add to the character's other infirmities, and she may be setting new records in regard to size of hump and black lankness of hair. I don't know quite what the correct word is for the physical aura that McKenna brings to the role -neither "androgynous" nor "asexual" seem to fit the bill -but she does seem like a creature from another mode of being: someone whose contemporaries could quite easily accept as a combination court jester and court executioner, but whom they could never imagine wearing the crown. But then they don't know what we do.

Richard III is one of Shakespeare's earliest plays, and its protagonist buttonholes the audience in a conversational, self-revealing manner without precedent in world drama. He is, in the words of a Broadway song, the man who invented chutzpah; and he uses it on us as, in different ways, he uses it on everybody else. In other roles -Medea, for example -McKenna's humour has sometimes threatened to overstep the tragic mark, but in this one she has wit and danger in razor-sharp balance, bound together by pain. When this Richard says he isn't "shaped for sportive tricks" (we'd noticed), it's both a joke at his own expense and an expression of bottomless bitterness. Ruthlessness logically follows. Richard knows exactly how far to go when playing politics. Some of McKenna's effects have been done before -for example, the instant transition from the insouciant brutality of "chop off his head, man" to the genial retreat of "something we will determine" -but they're traditional for good reason. McKenna coruscates all the way to the throne, and continues to fascinate and increasingly to frighten, through Richard's desperate improvising as the walls start to fall in on him.

The performance only runs out of steam in the last movement on Bosworth Field, a decline it shares with Miles Potter's production and, to be frank, with the play itself. Richard's eve-of-battle terrors, after being visited by the ghosts of his victims, furnish a soliloquy different in kind from all the preceding ones. Instead of talking to us, he's talking to himself, and he doesn't seem to have the vocabulary; exhilarating naturalism gives way to turgid pattern-making. Very few actors in my experience have managed to animate that speech, though it's presumably meant to be the climax. Cutting deprives McKenna of the chance to rally herself by rallying the troops, but she does bring off an awesome "my kingdom for a horse." Unfortunately, the battle she's attempting to rejoin is being fought in slow motion, a very tired device. So is the idea of having Richard laid low by the ghosts (i.e. by his conscience, which he doesn't have), rather than by his actual adversary Richmond (Gareth Potter), who's here played, rather simplistically, as a St. George who doesn't even get to engage the dragon.

The production in general looks starved, on a nearly bare set by Peter Hartwell that might better have gone all the way to full emptiness. Potter's direction is at its sharpest in the last stages of Richard's rise to the throne and in its immediate aftermath. The relationship of Richard and Buckingham (an excellent Wayne Best, selling his soul and then cavilling at the price) is a fine game of protracted cat-and-mouse, ending in a trap whose snap you can practically hear. Their hoodwinking of the disoriented Lord Mayor (Shane Carty) and citizens is very funny and thoroughly believable. Other good if stylistically scattered performances include Michael Spencer-Davis's Clarence blithely incredulous that a noble like himself should be sent to the Tower; Nigel Bennett's Hastings; David Ferry's Edward IV ranting himself to death; Cyrus Lane's one-scene, one-speech Scrivener sensing the beginnings of a police state; Oliver Becker's roughneck Ratcliffe; and Sean Arbuckle's courtly Catesby, the last two providing a helpful contrast between Richard's thugs-in-chief.

Them's the men. Even apart from McKenna, the production boasts a monstrous regiment of talented women. Martha Henry is resonantly oracular as Margaret, the prophetic fury from the “Wars of the Roses”. Roberta Maxwell's Duchess of York, denouncing and disowning her misshapen son, delivers him a powerful coup de grace. Yanna McIntosh is a supple and passionate Elizabeth, especially electric in her ultimate duel of wits with Richard, though it isn't made clear enough that she wins it, marking the beginning of his end just as his earlier seduction of the Lady Anne marked the beginning of his beginning. Bethany Jillard doesn't face up to Richard with the vocal virtuosity of her more experienced sisters, but she spits at him very eloquently and, once conquered, suffers with grace. She's hauntingly present onstage when Richard plots her death, the most chilling sequence of the evening. "Was ever woman in this humour won?" asks Richard; and humour, in the modern sense, is part of his magic. Strength of mind and of will are more. Richard's enemies never know what hit them. It's to McKenna's credit neither, after a whole evening in his/her fascinating company, do we.

One of the abiding puzzles of Richard III is that, while few people in the play have any illusions about the hunchbacked schemer whos decimating them on his way to the throne, he still gets away with it. The other characters hardly cease insulting him (bunchbacked toad and so on) and they all know his murderous record, but they still go along with him, either for what they think they can get out of it or because they just don't take him seriously. Seana McKenna, striking a blow for gender-neutral casting by playing Richard at Stratford, shows why they should believe this and just how wrong they are.

There have been plenty of impish Richards played by men. McKenna goes further by playing him as an imp: a descendant of the personified Vice of the English morality plays to whom at one point he claims kinship. If McKenna's voice is higher than those of some Richards, her bodily stature is lower; she lops a few inches off her height by adopting a steep stoop to add to the characters other infirmities, and she may be setting new records in regard to size of hump and black lankness of hair. I dont know quite what the correct word is for the physical aura that McKenna brings to the role -neither "androgynous" nor asexual seem to fit the bill -but she does seem like a creature from another mode of being: someone whose contemporaries could quite easily accept as a combination court jester and court executioner, but whom they could never imagine wearing the crown. But then they don't know what we do.

Richard III is one of Shakespeare's earliest plays, and its protagonist buttonholes the audience in a conversational, self-revealing manner without precedent in world drama. He is, in the words of a Broadway song, the man who invented chutzpah; and he uses it on us as, in different ways, he uses it on everybody else. In other roles -Medea, for example -McKennas humour has sometimes threatened to overstep the tragic mark, but in this one she has wit and danger in razor-sharp balance, bound together by pain. When this Richard says he isnt "shaped for sportive tricks" (we'd noticed), it's both a joke at his own expense and an expression of bottomless bitterness. Ruthlessness logically follows. Richard knows exactly how far to go when playing politics. Some of McKennas effects have been done before -for example, the instant transition from the insouciant brutality of chop off his head, man to the genial retreat of "something we will determine" -but theyre traditional for good reason. McKenna coruscates all the way to the throne, and continues to fascinate and increasingly to frighten, through Richard's desperate improvising as the walls start to fall in on him.

The performance only runs out of steam in the last movement on Bosworth Field, a decline it shares with Miles Potter's production and, to be frank, with the play itself. Richards eve-of-battle terrors, after being visited by the ghosts of his victims, furnish a soliloquy different in kind from all the preceding ones. Instead of talking to us, hes talking to himself, and he doesn't seem to have the vocabulary; exhilarating naturalism gives way to turgid pattern-making. THEATRE REVIEW

One Thousand and One Nights The Joey & Toby Tanenbaum Opera Centre, Toronto

There are scenes in One Thousand and One Nights when we're watching a story within a story within a story within a story. (There may be even deeper ramifications but the human brain can only take so much.) The show, which is both exhilarating and exhausting, is a two-part, six-hour reduction of the massive volume commonly if erroneously known as the Arabian Nights. Its also the first theatrical production that Torontos Luminato has commissioned from scratch, in association with Dash Arts, the company run by the British director Tim Supple. The current show is performed in a mixture of English, French and Arabic, the last two with surtitles, by a company of 19 Arabic actors.

The story from which spring all the others is the worldfamous one of Shahrazad, who offered herself as bride to a king whose habit, after being betrayed by a former wife, was to take a virgin to his bed every night and behead her in the morning. Shahrazad, possessed of fabulous narrative skills, knew that she could keep herself alive by spinning the king a yarn too complex for one night and trusting in his desire to find out what happened next. And then next. Shahrazad invented the cliffhanger.

She starts the king off easy, with the tale of a fisherman who unwittingly releases an angry Jinn from a bottle and saves his own life by daring the demon to creep right back inside his prison. The story is charmingly acted out and we, like the king, are captivated. But that, says Shahrazad, is nothing compared to what happened to the porter who was the fisherman's brother; and we, irretrievably and inextricably, are off.

The porter, helping a lady home with her shopping, finds himself in the house of three beautiful sisters and their two bitches. (No, really, lady dogs.) In the course of a sportive night it is announced, in my favourite line of the entire entertainment, that there are three one-eyed Dervishes at the door. They are quickly followed by three merchants, all fully sighted. It becomes necessary for each of the visitors to explain what brought him there, and for each of their hostesses to explain why they prefer to live as they do, shunning men and marriage. Many of these stories involve people telling other stories. One of the visitors turns out to be the Caliph Haroun Al-Rashid in disguise and under his chairmanship the thing becomes a kind of cutting contest: Tell me a story funnier or more improbable than the one I've just heard, or take the consequences.

This progression, going full blast at the end of Part One, resumes immediately at the start of Part Two, but to lesser effect. This is largely because it is Part Two; we continue to be buffeted by one discrete narrative after another. For a couple of them, I simply tuned out, knowing that everything would be much the same when I tuned in again. Also, though Supples inventiveness and the charm and agility of his cast are considerable, they are not infinite; the show, staged on a three-sided platform, begins to repeat its effects. But theres also a change of tone.

These Arabian Nights aren't kids' stuff; no one told us before, for example, that the king raped Shahrazad before listening to her. The show is violent, more in report than in action, and very erotic, in ways both cruel and tender.

Theres still a lot to feast on, though, not least in the acting. Shahrazad (Houda Echouafni) is beguilingly expressive in Arabic, if stilted in English. Assad Bouab plays the captives captive audience, plus a succession of other disarmingly boyish potentates. Falah Ibrahim is ideally solid as the fisherman and many others, and Ramzi Choukair wins all our sympathies, and many laughs, as the porter, who eventually gets to play Sinbad the Sailor in a tale of burial alive that's the most darkly compelling part of the second instalment. And look, be grateful: We're getting in two nights what cost King Sharayah an additional 999. But of course he did get the girl as well.

? One Thousand and One Nights runs until June 19. For tickets, call 416-368-4849 or visit luminato.com.

THEATRE REVIEW

Women Fully Clothed: Older and Hotter

Royal Alexandra Theatre, Toronto

The four writing, performing and producing ladies who constitute Women Fully Clothed begin the evening (fully clothed) playing a team of stressed executives, working to horrendous deadline on some product whose specifications are difficult to grasp, since they all talk so very, very fast. But then between them they have a lot of their things on their minds: children's dental appointments, hot flashes, divorces, shared recipes, office gossip. This opening number sets a tone, a subject and a standard for the show. It's about the pressured modern woman, mainly middle-aged and middle-class; it's somewhat satirical, in an accepting kind of way; and it treads familiar comic ground with flair.

It's also, barring the very occasional solo song, a collection of group scenes. Not having seen WFC's first show I approached their second, Older and Hotter, under some misconceptions. I had expected, and rather dreaded, an evening of stand-up. What I found was an evening of sketch comedy: a single-sex Second City show minus the cabaret atmosphere, the tables and the nibbles, but with a higherthan-average standard of material. Robin Duke, Jayne Eastwood, Kathryn Greenwood and Teresa Pavlinek make up the quartette, and there are seldom less than three of them onstage at a time. Pavlinek, tall and dark, specializes in being lost and loopy; Greenwood is the youngest-looking and plays the characters who seem the most together, except when they aren't; Eastwood has an acerbic line in the blond and judgmental; and Duke, though in a recognizable tradition of obsessed and diminutive North American female clowns, has a fine madness all her own.

She is, for example, wonderfully mean and moody if not perhaps munificent, when sent to a school principal's office on a charge of bullying. It's a scene that, in a show that makes something of a fetish of hand-held technology, allows her to pull off the funniest cellphone gag I have ever seen. It is in fact my favourite moment in the entire show, and part of what is perhaps my favourite number; certainly it's the one that develops in the least predictable ways. It allows Pavlinek to play an aggrieved victim, at which she's very good, and Greenwood to act the unreasonably reasonable mediator, at which she's even better. Duke also convulses as a daytime TV anchor with a show about how to turn your divorce into trash (literally), with a sidelight on how to find a new husband to take it out. Nicely offbeat, too, is the saga of three Girl Guide leaders who lose their entire troupe, possibly because they've devoted too little time to teaching them woodcraft and too much to rehearsing them in songs from Annie, in hopes, as far as I could make out, of getting them a spot on Glee. Greenwood, a Girl Guide cookie in herself, is a memorably fraught Brown Owl, and the sight of Eastwood trying vainly to start a fire by rubbing things together, even while lighting up a cigarette, will probably stay with me.

All these scenes have satisfying shapes; the school one even manages to resurrect that almost-vanished species, the effective punchline. Other things fade out. Duke and Greenwood are a riot as a couple of competitively cranky seniors on a shopping trip to Target in Buffalo (Duke driving, while anticipating cataract surgery), but when they get halted at U.S. customs, the sketch, like the ladies themselves, has no place to go; first it twists in the wind, then it grinds to a stop. Another number that has the four clucking in counterpoint over the state of the planet while continuing to spend, spend, spend; it shows the team at their most Second City-fied, taking an obvious target (only this time it's Walmart, at least it starts that way) and driving it to an equally obvious conclusion.

This is the comedy of shared guilt, and even men in the audience can partake. Women Fully Clothed struck me at first as Women Over Miked, but by the end either the technicians had adjusted or I had. Most of what the show says hits a nerve, with the laughs ranging from rueful to uproarious. The stray musical interludes supply some of them, though they can't escape the curse of the comic song; they let off their key jokes early and then have to pad. As theatre vocalists, none of the four are likely to pose a threat to Louise Pitre, but they do well. And they come together very well when the show, right at its end, addresses the subject of children and what their post-Boomer parents have done for and to them, in a song that seems to be called Give Them Less: "We told them they could have it all, that couldn't hurt them could it? Now they have it all, but there's no place to put it." The rhyme isn't quite perfect; but then, as the show spends much of its time implicitly inquiring, what is? ? Runs until June 19. For tickets, visit mirvish.com.

The stage floor at the start of Tout Comme Elle is covered with ladies' shoes: 50 pairs of them. We know there are that many, because there are 50 actresses listed in the program, and the action proper commences with each and every one of them coming onstage and slipping into a pair. It's a drawn-out, dream-like sequence; and since the performers include a phenomenal number of Toronto's finest, it's possible to while away the time quite happily by trying to pick your own favourites out of the crowd.

You can go on doing this for most of the show's 90-minute length since, for all the scintillating individuals involved, Tout Comme Elle is a choral piece. It's Luminato's presentation of Necessary Angel's production of a piece that originated in Quebec in 2006. Brigitte Haentjens directed it, which must to a large extent mean that she choreographed it; Louise Dupre wrote the text; and Erin Moure wrote the English translation. The subject is mothers and daughters.

Everybody onstage is by definition a daughter, and there is one sequence in which each in turn identifies herself and her real-life mother by name. For much of the time, though, they speak and move and sing in unison, speaking alternately for both generations. Even when one detaches herself for a single sentence or paragraph, she seems to be speaking for the collective. Initially we get the daughters' perspective; there are evocations of gazing across the tea table at the woman who bore you, realizing that you hardly know her and she is beginning to lose all memory of you. There are guilty reflections on how seldom you go to visit and how glad you are to get away. In one logistically uncharacteristic sequence, the older and younger performers square off, one on one, and chant reproachful imprecations at one another. Rather more thoughtfully, when the daughters become mothers themselves, they find their tolerance of their daughters increasing incrementally. The show is a multiple reiteration of Oscar Wilde's famous dictum that all women become like their mothers and that's their tragedy, though it suggests -as Wilde of course implicitly did -that it's their comedy as well.

There are individual observations that strike forcefully home, but they never develop. We all know that the mother-daughter relationship can be fraught. Having it repeated 50-fold gives it a certain theatrical impressiveness, and the show's pictorial accomplishments give it even more; the cast, colourfully costumed by a designer billed as YSO, move around the stage in great sweeping arcs. But truisms can only come to life on the stage when stories and characters are fleshed out, and the format denies that any chance of happening. It even becomes a form of emotional blackmail: as in, this must be important because so many women are saying it at the same time. Denied emotional and intellectual sustenance, the mind starts brooding on some of the great metaphysical questions: Is Fiona Reid only going to get one speech? Can I really sit through a whole show and fail to recognize Kristen Thomson? The sheer quantity of talent involved actually gets frustrating: all these terrific actresses and they don't get a chance to act. Or even interact. There are a few times when somebody gets to stand out briefly from the throng. Diana Leblanc and Barbara Gordon make sharp impressions. (The joint presence of Reid, Gordon, Fiona Highet and Kyra Harper prompts the frivolous thought that Tout Comme Elle might be Calendar Girls-plus.) Another question that comes to mind is just why it's impossible to imagine a similar show about fathers and sons. It's nearly as hard to envisage one about fathers and daughters or mothers and sons.

About the closest the show gets to admitting the existence of the other gender is a massed rendition of I Saw Mommy Kissing Santa Claus, executed with great poker-faced charm. (Kudos, by the way, to Lily Ling, musical director.) The cast contains one actual mother-daughter pairing, in Anne Anglin and Severn Thompson. Anglin, who I think is the senior person present, gets to deliver a wonderfully deflationary last line that may well be worth the price of admission all on its own -though I'm not sure that you negate pretentiousness simply by disowning it. Trivia note that may not be all that trivial: What may be the earliest play we have -The Suppliants by Aeschylus -also features a chorus of 50 women; indeed they are, collectively, its central character, though not only was that play written by a man, but in ancient Athens all those women would have been played by men. So Tout Comme Elle may be going back not just to the roots of Western drama but to its fathers. It's Just Like Him.

Tout Come Elle closes tonight at the Bluma Appel Theatre. For ticket information, visit luminato.com or call 416-368-4849.

2011-06-25-the-dora-nominees-on-closer-i:
Next Monday sees the 32nd annual presentation of the Dora Awards. In past years, I've had malicious fun casting an eye over the nominees, wondering what could possibly explain who's been included and who's been left out, and hazarding guesses as to who would come out on top. This year, though, I'm writing from a glass house, as I'm one of the four daily critics who inaugurated our own Toronto theatre awards. We announced our results the same day as the Dora people announced their nominations, so there was no chance of either process influencing the other. But now, of course, if I or any of my colleagues castigate the Dora judges for their fallibility, they or anybody else are entitled to come right back at us. Myself, I think we made very good choices but then I would, wouldn't I?

As it happens, most of the recipients of the critics' awards are also up for Doras, so maybe there's more common ground between the critics and what is commonly known as "the industry" than we've often been led to believe. Where there isn't an overlap, it could often be due to a technicality. For example, the Toronto Theatre Critics Awards and the Doras have different criteria for what qualifies as a new play. We decided it could be any Canadian play new to the city, and we gave our prize to Stephen Massicotte's The Clockmaker, which had already been seen in Calgary. The Doras insist that the new play must be a world premiere, and they don't seem to worry about nationality; one of their five nominees for outstanding new play (they don't like the word "best") is Peggy Pickit Sees the Face of God by Roland Schimmelpfennig who is, believe it or not, German. It was a distinguished piece and I'd rate its chances very high, though it might be hampered by the fact that, as part of Luminato's Africa Trilogy, it was only one third of an evening. Also, it's up against Brothel #9, a show that probably stands this year's best cross-category chance of sweeping the board; its author, Anusree Roy, had two plays on this season as both author and actress.

The critics' choice for best production (or, as I like to think of it, best allaround thing) was The Middle Place, which didn't make the equivalent list at the Doras, but is up for new play; though it might be hampered there by the fact that its author, Andrew Kushnir, didn't so much write as edit and transcribe it. The transcriptions were riveting, but I'm inclined to think that we made the better category decision. The Doras' best production choices are The Railway Children (a surprise populist entry), Brothel #9 (what did I tell you?), The Africa Trilogy (ditto, though the two parts that weren't Peggy Pickit weren't a patch on the one that was), Ruined and Blasted. From that last pair of apocalyptic titles -indeed from the whole batch -my own pick would be Blasted, a ferociously powerful evening at Buddies in Bad Times. The one I think will win, for feel-good reasons, is Ruined.

The critics gave best actor prizes to performances in those last two plays, and both are strong Dora contenders, as well. In fact, David Ferry, whose scary ground-zero performance in Blasted was of a man both blasted and ruined, already has a well-deserved Dora this year: The special Barbara Hamilton for being (I paraphrase) a force for good in Toronto theatre. If he gets the best actor Dora as well, his mantelpiece will be groaning. His main competition will be -should be -Joseph Ziegler's heartbreaking Willy Loman in Soulpepper's Death of a Salesman. Maybe it's time to proclaim how blessed are Toronto in general and Soulpepper in particular to have both Ziegler and Diego Matamoros working consistently at the height of their or anyone else's powers. Matamoros is nominated, too, for his performance in Oleanna; he was brilliant, but the production wasn't enough liked for him to stand much of a chance. Yanna McIntosh in Ruined was the critics' best actress; of her Dora competitors I would root, fiercely, for Michelle Moneith's uncanny performance in Blasted, though this may be the most hotly contested category of all, what with Jane Spidell in Peggy Pickit and two performances -the author's and Pamela Sinha's -in Brothel #9. In which connection: It wasn't planned that way, but I'm personally pleased that no one production carried off more than one critics' award. Spread it around, I say.

It's a perennial complaint that the Doras, apparently for lack of sponsorship, always lump supporting (or "featured") performances in one category, be they male, female, musical or dramatic. This year's mixed bag includes Oliver Dennis, put forward for Jitters, in which he was indeed expertly jittery, rather than for The Fantasticks in which he was fantastic. All right, I'm being smug; we critics, flush with categories, gave him best supporting actor in a musical. We gave best actress in a musical to Louise Pitre in A Year with Frog and Toad, and here I hope the Doras do follow suit because hers was a selftransforming performance, and not just by virtue of being amphibian. We only, though, gave one design award, where the Doras seem to have dozens. Our choice, Studies in Motion, must be Dora-ineligible as it came from outer space, or at least from Vancouver. I'm glad at least that Charlotte Dean gets a costume nod for The Misanthrope, to my mind the year's most shut-out production; I'd happily have nodded at Richard Rose (director), Stuart Hughes (actor) and Michelle Monteith (supporting actress). I suppose they'll give best musical to Billy Elliot, though if you like 'em big Priscilla Queen of the Desert was a better show. There are four COC productions nominated in the opera division; I'd hate to have to choose between them, and I mean that in the nicest way.

? The 2011 Dora Awards are presented at the Bluma Appel Theatre on Monday.

2011-07-02-how-to-succeed-in-business-wh:
Among the credits in her program bio, one of the cast of 9 to 5 The Musical lists an appearance in Hair The Musical. Gee, I can't remember when Hair wasn't a musical. But maybe this nomenclature has become compulsory. It's got to the point where shows list themselves as The Musical even when they're spoofing the idea of shows listing themselves as The Musical.

Well alright, 9 to 5 The Musical, isn't a spoof, though its plenty derivative -battening, among other things, on its composer's name and image. It's the show of the film of the song, the song being of course Dolly Parton's hit number of the same title. That song, with its peppy and flavourful description of the office grind, always sounded like it might make a good opening number for a musical, and so it proves, though its effectiveness as scene-setting exposition is somewhat diluted by some standard strap-hanging, briefcasebrandishing choreography.

It does serve to introduce us to the three leading characters: Violet, the office manager, five years widowed; Judy, the office newbie, freshly divorced, from a heel; and Doralee, the pneumatic office eye-candy, a happily married Texan who bears a strong vocal and physical resemblance to Idon't-think-I-need-to-complete-thissentence.

The film wasn't a musical, but Parton has supplied a full-length original score for the stage version. I wouldn't exactly call it a good theatre score, but it does suggest that, given more of a source to write into, Parton might well come up with a very good one. Country music, being rooted in story and character, not to mention aural clarity, has a habit of working in the theatre in a way that rock usually doesn't; and Parton supplies some attractive tunes, matched to observant and even funny lyrics. One number, a duet between Violet and the junior accountant who's been laying hopeless siege to her, actually advances story and character. The actors are in a different place at the end of it than they were at the beginning, and we believe in the journey. That's the way theatre songs are supposed to work, but unfortunately it's an exception. More typical is the stentorian ballad sung by Judy, who started the evening shy but isn't any more, after she's discovered that she no longer needs her ex. However strenuously she sings it, and however overpowering the amplification, it doesn't tell us anything we don't already know.

I blame the book, written by Patricia Resnick, which is both skimpy and incredible; it does sort of own up to the incredibility but with more desperation than wit. It's 1979, which in consciousness-raising terms, and indeed in showbiz terms, is depicted as somewhere between How to Succeed in Business Without Really Trying and Mad Men. Assistants are still called secretaries, and the boss is a Mr. Hart, who is described at least four times (thrice in the show and once in the program) as "a sexist, egotistical, lying, hypocritical bigot." He's also an embezzler, something on which great store is set for much of the evening, but which turns out to be strangely irrelevant by the end. He patronizes Violet, who obviously does all the actual running of the office, denying her a long-promised promotion because, he says, guys prefer to do business with guys. He hits on Doralee, grossly and persistently, while rather inconsistently inviting his buddies into his office to admire her attributes. Judy doesn't like him much, either.

The three fantasize, each in her own way, on taking revenge; and it's here that the show, despite making a great pretense of being energetic, grinds to a halt. Each of their fantasies is sung, danced and acted out. So we watch the same situation staged three times; and none too inventively at that. And then, their fantasies come true, sort of. I'll spare you the full details, but they do include a protracted farcical interlude in a hospital that's quite agonizingly forced, as well as Mr. Hart's prolonged absence from work.

In his absence, the three heroines take over, and institute many lifechanging reforms, such as lunchbreaks. How they manage to do this is unexplained, given that Violet is the only one of them with any seniority, and one of the supposed mainsprings of the action is that she's been passed over, in favour of a toadying male creep whom seasoned musical buffs may recognize as the re-incarnation of Bud Frump. The authors have to banish him from the stage lest we ask awkward questions about why he hasn't taken over.

Jeff Calhoun's staging is standardissue second-rate Broadway, office furniture division, but this touring version has first-rate principal casting. Dee Hoty, a musical-theatre treasure these 20 years, is a Violet as tasteful and spirited and economical as the lady she plays, with just a dash of poignancy. Diana DeGarmo is a roof-raising Doralee, revealed at the end though never before to be herself a country chanteuse in training, and Mamie Parris does everything possible for Judy. (For the record, I saw the show in preview, though admittedly, the same day as the opening night.)

In its sexual politics, though, the show may not be quite as advanced as it thinks. Why does Violet, imagining herself as a future CEO, sing about being One of the Boys. (It isn't even an original title). And then there's Kristine Zbornik, a talented comedienne, who's been lumbered with the role of Roz, Hart's secretarial sycophant, who sings an embarrassing number about how much she adores him, and whose attempts at bumping-and-grinding are meant to be hilarious because she's so plain. And this in a show that claims to be empowering women. Parton herself appears via video-clip to reinforce the claim, and to begin and end the story: fittingly perhaps, given that even in absentia she's the chief selling point. They could call the show Hello Again, Dolly (The Musical), but it might not be legal.

- 9 to 5 The Musical runs through July 10 at the Toronto Centre for the Arts.

THE WINTER'S TALE

High Park Amphitheatre, Toronto

THE TEMPEST

Georgian Theatre, Barrie, Ont.

Ben Jonson, Shakespeare's friendly (or so we hope) rival among the great Jacobean playwrights, once wrote disdainfully of authors who "beget Tales, Tempests, and suchlike drolleries" and thereby "make Nature afraid." Both of those unnatural drolleries, the Tale and the Tempest, are here to offset the heat wave with their wintry narrative and stormy weather. The Tempest, a favourite summer play, this time proves the droller of the two, but also the weightier. The Winter's Tale, theoretically the braver choice, is also here the fluffier

It slides by, as plays have a habit of doing at the Dream in High Park, a space that offers all the scenic and acoustical disadvantages of open-air theatre and none of the attractions. (So it has trees. Nobody ever uses them and there's always a built-up set to obscure them.) Productions there vary from the anonymous to the obstinately wrong-headed.

Estelle Shook's production, which belongs in the first category, does get off to a good start, with the Sicilian family group -King Leontes, Queen Hermione and their young son -happily displayed for the brief moment before their world is destroyed. The instrument of destruction is Leontes's sudden self-generated jealousy, which David Janssen excellently portrays as a gnawing and obstinate sickness, refusing all physic; to himself he sounds reasonable. Kelly McIntosh is an eloquently wronged Hermione; Sicilia's two good counsellors comprise a Camillo (Jovanni Sy) of notable assurance and a Paulina (Nicole Robert) who confuses a moral force with a woman who shouts a lot.

The Winter's Tale is one of Shakespeare's longer plays; indeed one of its scenes, the Bohemian sheep-shearing, is the second longest in the canon. The cuts in this scampering 100-minute production include that scene's debate on nurture and nature; I know that's what the play is supposed to be about, but I can't say that I minded not hearing it this time around. The rural scenes here are most distinguished by George Masswohl's funny and touching Old Shepherd, efficiently seconded by Sean Dixon as his son and by John Blackwood as an unusually downbeat Autolycus. Jasmine Chen plays both Leontes's lost son and his lost-and-found daughter, and she has far more personality as the boy.

The scenes that are really hurt by the general foreshortening are the crowning episodes of forgiveness and reconciliations back in Sicilia. Here they don't seem to be crowning anything. The resurrection of Hermione is extraordinarily perfunctory and unmoving. The famous maneating bear (as in "exit, pursued by") is here a polar one; maybe he's enacting his own revenge play, as one of his deceased relatives has earlier appeared in the shape of a rug.

The Winter's Tale moves back and forth between countries, and has a 16-year time jump in its middle. Shakespeare, experimenting to the last, followed it up with The Tempest, which unfolds in a single location in real time. So we have one play that almost demands an intermission and in High Park doesn't get it, and another that at Barrie's Theatre by the Bay (operating in collegiate premises until its own new home is built) can do without but does get it anyway.

Brett Christopher has placed the break in his production very cunningly, as indeed he has placed nearly everything else. The set, consisting of trailing fronds, is a bit dispiriting, but there are compensatingly splendid costumes of Napoleonic cut. Robert Joy is an unconventional Prospero, a little nervous about his powers, always having to prove himself. I'm not sure how much of this is interpretation, and how much is just the actor's natural manner, but there's a questioning tone to almost everything he says.

When he recalls his past achievements, in his great renunciation speech, he almost can't believe them: to think he did all that. He's a different man when he puts his magic robe on; when he resumes his ducal garments he's amusingly conscious of just how long it's been. That dukedom means more to him than to most Prosperos; he speaks with wounded passion of "the gates of Milan" being breached by his enemies. He could use more iron to balance his charm, but he has a delightfully believable relationship, both playful and wary, with Miranda, who's played by his real-life daughter, Ruby Joy.

She's a determined lass, who not only offers to carry logs for her Ferdinand (Caden Douglas) but actually does so. Their love scene becomes a wood-bearing contest, pushed to the verge of slapstick and then retreating into an enchantment that is itself enchanting. There's the same tact, the same mix of inventiveness and sensitivity, in Ryan Hollyman's thick-voiced Caliban (he seems to share an accent with Dr. Frankenstein's creation), who waits until the very end of his "isle is full of noises" speech to break our hearts. His encounters with Trinculo (Scott Hurst) and Stephano (Kristian Bruun) are the funniest, truest and most volatile in ages.

The courtiers' scenes, too, are unusually compelling; Sheldon Davis' tempter Antonio exerts a palpable hold over Richard Alan Campbell's tempted Sebastian; John Dolan is a beneficent Gonzalo; and Michael Rawley's Alonso sounds more of the king's guilt and remorse than any actor I remember. Even the minor lord Adrian (Alex Dault) has a personality, plus a cushion for his master to sit on and a mobile tree-stump on which to put it. Ariel (Jennifer Toulmin) is, as she herself says, "pertly done," rather like Peter Pan, in the days when Peter was played by a woman, exulting in the cleverness of him/her. The most magical thing about her, though, is her singing, of exquisite new settings by Jonathan Monro.

Both she and Miranda show an unusual compassion for Caliban at the end. The production doesn't downplay the darkness en route but its conclusion is, by current standards, remarkably un-bitter. It makes a nice change. What this show has in spades that The Winter's Tale lacks is concentration: the sense that every moment counts and that each relates to the next. Even Jonson might have been charmed.

? The Winter's Tale runs until Sept. 4. For more information, visit canadianstage.com. The Tempest runs until July 16. For more information, visit theatrebythebay.com.

THEATRE REVIEW

Hugh Jackman in Concert

Princess of Wales Theatre, Toronto

The man has warmth, charm and bags of talent. But there's still something very forced and insubstantial about Hugh Jackman in Concert. It starts -well, actually it starts with the audience applauding the house lights just for going down. It's that kind of evening, that kind of house. But the performance proper begins with the star singing Oh, What a Beautiful Mornin', starting from the wings and carrying on with it as he enters.

This of course is how Curly sings the song at the start of Oklahoma!, and Curly is a role that Hugh Jackman has played at the National Theatre in London. But there's no suggestion that he's playing it here; the song is just an opening number, and rather a strange one to sing out of character at 8 p.m. It also gets interspersed with the singer buttonholing the audience, and saying how happy he is to be here: a little early in the game for that kind of schtick.

It turns out to be a selfreferential evening, with every song pegged to something in the actor's life story. The running gag, mostly submerged but sometimes acknowledged, is that here is a performer whose fans know him mostly as Wolverine in the X-Men movies, but who has also had a substantial career in musical theatre and is here to prove it. At one point he tells us that the studio bosses were worried about him doing this show because they want him to put on weight for the next instalment of the franchise, and singing and dancing, especially dancing, might make him lose it.

On this slender pretext he goes into an abbreviated version of I Won't Dance, followed by snippets of about a dozen other numbers on the same theme. They're all great songs, but he never gets to do justice to any of them. The medley format puts paid to that; well, that and the implausibility of the hook in the first place.

The whole show is snookered by that kind of thing. It's a double-bind: None of the songs seem to be there for their own sake, and the sakes for which they are there seem manufactured. Even when he sings the Soliloquy from Carousel (Billy Bigelow is another role he's actually played, in concert at Carnegie Hall), the performance is superficial; he gives a ringing account of the song's bravura climax, but on the way there's no change in feeling between the sections about his unborn son and those about his unborn daughter.

About the only song in the evening of which he takes personal possession is, weirdly enough, I Got Rhythm, done briefly as part of a tribute to old movie musicals. The autobiographical excuse for this is that when he was a kid he used to watch them every Saturday afternoon on Australian TV; the segment is introduced by a clip of the old 20th Century Fox logo. This, too, got inexplicable applause, though the moviepedant in me can't resist pointing out that none of the subsequent songs are from a Fox movie. They include Luck Be a Lady, which again gets short shrift, textually and emotionally, even though Sky Masterson is a role I would like to see Jackman play.

I'd like, for that matter, to have seen his Curly, and even his Peter Allen in The Boy from Oz, which he did on Broadway and which gets sizable representation here. He can't reproduce Allen's sly timing on his self-defining line ("For those of you who are wondering, is he or isn't he? Yes, I am Australian") but he manages a surprising transformation, just by changing into a lacy shirt and shimmering. He does well by Allen's songs, too, though none of them really stand up except for Quiet Please, There's a Lady on Stage, which gives us the triple tweak of Jackman paying tribute to Allen paying tribute to Judy Garland.

The spoken stuff includes the old bit of pulling a hapless male up from the audience to cavort with the dancing girls. (There are two in the show, plus an impressive big band.) On the first night the guy looked far from hapless, since he was Mirvish Productions' own John Karastamatis, who may be the coolest PR man in town. It's hard to believe this wasn't a set up, but it seemed spontaneous, and they kept it going for an impressively long time.

Jackman also says some funny things about Hollywood and some stirring ones about his home country, both its landscape and its population. In these he communicates real pride, real awe. But, but, but . what's Over the Rainbow doing there? Couldn't they find something more indigenous, or at least less familiar? Showbiz strikes again.

So there's the paradox. Quiet please, there's a grounded guy onstage, but he's swimming in glitz. It's probably the culture's fault, rather than Jackman's, that he's presented as a legend when he's too young to be one.

Anyway the real ones -Frank Sinatra, say, or Rosemary Clooney -don't trade on it; they didn't play their legends, they played off them. Jackman arrives without a built-in personal repertoire, and he hasn't managed to create one; it's all fragments. For an encore he did Mack the Knife, and it was a virtual cover of the Bobby Darin version. Is that how he wants us to remember him?

? Hugh Jackman in Concert runs until July 17. For tickets, call 416-872-1212 or visit mirvish.ca.

Ontario theatre is throwing Tennessee Williams a great 100th birthday party. On the heels of the Shaw Festival's Cat on a Hot Tin Roof, wonderful for its sustained firepower, Soulpepper gives us a production of The Glass Menagerie, no less wonderful for its sustained delicacy. The two productions have in common that they are both, on occasion, very funny. In Cat,the comedy serves momentarily to relax the tension. In Menagerie, it tightens it. The more we laugh, the closer we come to tears.

The Glass Menagerie, Williams' breakthrough play from 1944, is also his most overtly autobiographical. There are degrees, of course. Williams gives us a reminiscing narrator figure who's clearly a surrogate for the author, but his play still isn't as dependent as Eugene O'Neill's Long Day's Journey into Night on our knowledge that the author is writing about his own family. All the same, it's hard to believe that a situation at once so hard and so fragile as the one Williams conjures up could have been imagined by a playwright who wasn't drawing on his own experience.

To refresh memories of this memory play: The setting is a run-down apartment in 1930s St. Louis where live Amanda Wingfield, former Southern belle forever lamenting a luxurious plantation past that may or may not have existed as she remembers it, and her grown-up children Tom and Laura. Amanda married a telephone man who, as she says more than once, "fell in love with long distance" and hasn't been heard from in years. Tom supports the family by working in a warehouse, disappearing every night to the movies (or so he says) while practising on the side to be . well, to be Tennessee Williams. Laura is physically crippled, or at least has a bad limp; she's also, and perhaps consequently, emotionally crippled, shy to a point beyond the pathological. Amanda frets that her daughter has never had a gentleman caller, whereas she in her own youth was besieged by them (or so she says). Finally, Tom brings to dinner a colleague from the warehouse who also happens to be Laura's unspoken crush from high school days. When he meets her this time, he's nicer to her than anybody has ever been, which makes it all the more brutal when, through no real fault of his own, he has to let her down. Laura's hobby, her lifeline, has been her collection of tiny glass animals, her favourite of them all being a unicorn. We know, even if we've never seen the play before, that the mythical treasure is going to get smashed, taking Laura with it; waiting for it to happen is a source of exquisite tension.

There's less of the Southern Gothic in this play than in Williams' others; the language, though finely tuned and finely turned, sounds more natural than usual. It certainly does in Ted Dykstra's production, which doesn't have a slack moment and manages to be both tough and magnificently moving. It has a functional and atmospheric set by Patrick Clark, superb moody lighting by Lorenzo Savoini, and haunting music by Dykstra.

It also has actors who play off one another like co-operative virtuosi. The most surprising stroke of casting is the entrusting of Tom to Stuart Hughes, who must be about the same age as Nancy Palk, who plays his mother. It works, through Tom's role as self-admittedly unreliable storyteller. In this guise he's pretty much ageless, as well as being wry and witty and cracklingly sardonic to a degree I would not have believed possible in this play. So when he's playing his younger self, we accept him as a retrospective projection. Anyway, he's so good in these scenes, nobody's going to quibble. He's witty here, too, touchingly urgent in his concern for his sister (expressed at embarrassed second hand), and superb at charting the ebb and flow of his exasperation with his almost uniquely exasperating mother. This, I realize for the first time, is one of the richest mother-son relationships in world drama.

Like Cat, though less spectacularly, this is a play in which the characters take turns at centre stage. The first half is mostly Amanda's, and she's kaleidoscopic. She's the starry-eyed nostalgic, the passionately worried mother, the sweet-talking saleslady peddling subscriptions to a ladies' magazine while conscious of how far she's declined that she should have to be doing this, the overweeningly gracious hostess, the unreasonable matriarch blaming everybody (which usually means her son) for everything. She's a romantic tumbled into reality, knowing it for what it is even if she can't always cope with it. These qualities don't just alternate, they coexist; and Palk, operating at tremendous voltage and with a marvellous sense of shifting tempo, renders them as a seamless whole.

The second half chiefly belongs to Laura and her gentleman caller. Their long candlelit duologue may be infallible -at least, I've never seen it fail -but it could hardly be better done than it is here by Gemma James-Smith and Jeff Lillico. She's less physically ethereal than most Lauras, and more uncompromising in her neurosis (which here sounds partly catarrhal) but there's nothing in the text that contradicts that, and her final silent meltdown is a heartbreaker. Laura's real-life model spent most of her life institutionalized, and you can see it happening here. Lillico exactly captures his character's boyish enthusiasm, born of insecurity and thwarted hopes. With the best of intentions, he destroys Laura at least as surely as Stanley Kowalski, in Williams' next play, destroyed Blanche DuBois. Indeed, you might say that Williams created Blanche by combining Laura with Amanda.

There are cracks in the play; it's hard to believe Tom would have walked out on the broken Laura quite as abruptly as he says he did, and indeed their whole relationship, the subject of his valedictory speech, is underwritten in the play itself. Some of the social comment is overwritten; it's odd that this most domestic of Williams' plays should be the one to engage most explicitly with the world outside, and some of the attacks on '30s escapism and isolationism are facile and unfair; it's not as if America didn't have its own problems. But those are specks.

Writing about this production, I'm tearing up all over again. Happy 100th. Blow out your candles, Tennessee.

- The Glass Menagerie is in repertory through September at the Young Centre. Call 416-866-8666 or visit soulpepper.ca for ticket information.

Cylla Von Tiedemann / Gemma James-Smith is delicate and damaged in The Glass Menagerie.;; Caption:

THEATRE REVIEW

ON THE ROCKS

Court House Theatre,

Niagara-on-the-Lake, Ont.

The central character of George Bernard Shaws On the Rocks (1933) is Sir Arthur Chavender, the Liberal head of a British coalition government. Outside 10 Downing St. -and, we gather, throughout the country and indeed the world -huge numbers of the unemployed are out protesting. Well, it's 1933.

All Sir Arthur has to offer them, or anyone else, are affable bromidic speeches about the virtues of the family. In himself, he's a compassionate man and a conscientious worker. So its hardly surprising that hes rundown and depressed. At the urging of his wife, he takes himself off to a sanatorium, run by a mysterious lady who promises him that after two weeks of meditation "your dead mind will come to life." Prompted by a recent meeting with a delegation from London's povertystricken Isle of Cats (a facetious variant of the actual Isle of Dogs) he asks his secretary to pack him all the books you can find by a revolutionary German Jew named Harry Marks. She puts him right about the name.

That's Shaws Act 1. In his Act 2, the regenerated PM attempts to put through a program of wholesale nationalization. He gets initial support from surprising places: the police, the navy, the city and the landed aristocracy all decide theres something in it for them and are prepared to overlook as impracticable the parts that might work for the benefit of anybody else. Chavender only meets implacable opposition from the Conservative leader Sir Dexter Rightside and, extremes meeting, from the very proletarians who inspired him in the first place. They balk at the ideas of compulsory public service ("Slavery," moans Sir Dexter. Call it by its proper name) and a ban on strikes.

For what is only the play's second appearance at the Shaw Festival, and taking advantage of the expiration of Shavian copyright, Michael Healey has prepared a new adaptation. His boldest stroke is to reverse the order of the two acts. The advantage of this is to confront us at the outset with some of the juiciest issues and most explosive characters. The disadvantage is that what was once exposition is now back story, giving us information that at this point of the evening we are not too interested in hearing. More importantly, it removes Chavender himself from his place at the centre of the play; he's now just one voice among many. This is compounded by the casting of Peter Krantz, who has some nice winsome moments of hope and disappointment, but lacks the joviality and the sheer force of personality to convince as one of Shaws compulsive orator-politicians.

Hes also been deprived of what might have been his finest moment: Sir Arthur's acknowledgment that "I'm not the man for the job . and I shall hate the man who will carry it through for his cruelty and the desolation he will bring." This must be part of an attempt on Healeys part to save his deceased collaborators face: to clear him of any sympathy for fascism in the very year of Hitler's accession to power. (The left was attacking Shaw for this long before it occurred to the right to do so.) Healey's Sir Arthur explicitly declines to take Mein Kampf away with him on holiday, though Shaw was ahead of his adaptor in satirizing Sir Dexters threat to put his supporters on the streets in Union Jack shirts. But the suspicion still lingers, notably in the speeches of old Hipney, the veteran working-class delegate who has come to think democracy a sham and says "you cant frighten me with a word like dictator." Some critics have claimed that Shaw meant him as devil's advocate rather than author's mouthpiece but, certainly in Guy Bannermans gently persuasive performance, it doesnt play that way.

As Shavian pastiche, Healey's version is first-rate; you can't tell where one author leaves off and the other starts. It works both ways; a startlingly unShavian word like sexy turns out to be totally authentic. Some jokes have been reassigned, notably one about "the nationalization of women." (Neither Shaw nor Healey explains how thats supposed to work.)

As noted, the new text treats us immediately to some exuberant cartoon characters with strong political underpinnings, nearly all of them, under Joseph Zieglers direction, excellently acted. Steven Sutcliffe's hysterical (in both senses) Dexter is admirably counterpointed by Norman Browning's huffy First Lord of the Admiralty, rosyfaced and rosy-voiced.

Cherissa Richards Singhalese businesswoman lights up the stage when a racial epithet sets her off on a splendidly indignant tirade. Marla McLean, as one alderwoman Aloysia Brollikins, signally fails to do the same with her long speech, but is neat in her less demanding stretches. She and Martin Happer, as a sulky aristocratic revolutionary, form half the plays love interest, as they pair off with the junior Chavenders. There's supposed to be an ironic contrast here between Sir Arthur's paeans to the family and the mess his own is in; but Shaw didnt make it work and Healey cant do it for him.

The original play starts with the police threatening to break the heads of protesters and ends with a description of what sounds like kettling. Its main concerns are an intractable economic crisis and the thwarting of reform by special interests. It all seems, when you read it, blazingly topical. It has some of the same effect onstage but not as much, because the action, what there is of it, doesn't so much carry the ideas as buckle under them. That's true of both versions, though on consideration I prefer the original, ugly warts and all. The rewrite gives the final moment to Chavenders secretary. It doesnt mean much because, even though she's played by Mary Haney, we don't know anything about her. ? On the Rocks runs until Oct. 8. For tickets, call 1-800-511-7429 or visit shawfest.com.

THEATRE REVIEW

The Admirable Crichton Festival Theatre, Niagara-on-the-Lake

The two newest productions at the Shaw Festival are both of British plays about failed social experiments. In George Bernard Shaw's On the Rocks, a prime minister tries to ram through what he takes to be a populist agenda and is defeated by an unholy alliance of vested interests. In J.M. Barrie's The Admirable Crichton, the established order of masters and servants is upended when its representatives find themselves in drastically altered surroundings, only to be restored when they return to what is conventionally known as civilization.

Barrie introduces us to the earl of Loam, who believes in equality: at least he believes in it once a month, when he hosts a tea party at which his family and friends wait on the army of domestics who make their comfortable lives possible. Everybody except the earl himself finds this embarrassing: his three daughters, their respective suitors, the servants themselves and most of all the butler, the supremely competent Crichton. He believes there has to be a hierarchy in every situation and, living in England, seems quite content that it should be based on birth rather than ability. He does allow that in a different situation, different criteria might apply. And of course the laws of drama ensure this will be put to the test.

Off on a tropical cruise the household -earl, daughters, daughters' admirers, butler and the lowly maid known as Tweeny -finds itself cast away on a desert island. And of course, after a brief attempt at maintaining the customary niceties, it transpires that the wholly admirable Crichton is the only one with the brains and the experience to get things done. If it wasn't for him, they'd all perish, but with him in charge a flourishing little society evolves, complete with improvised modern conveniences. Crichton is its unquestioned monarch; everybody else calls him "the guv" and happily worships him. Then they all get rescued and everything reverts to what it was.

This is all very predictable. But predictability can be dramatically satisfying, especially when the story is essentially a fable, and so it is here. Also Barrie was canny enough to complicate his situation, and the complication he introduces is sex. Back home, Lady Mary, the oldest and possibly (though it's a tough call) the most snobbish of the Loam sisters, wouldn't have given Crichton the time of day, though she might possibly have demanded it of him. On the island, seeing the man he really is, she falls heavily for him, and he for her, even though he had conditionally promised himself to the stilladoring Tweeny. Crichton and Mary, with her father's blessing, are just about to get married (one of their fellow castaways is, providentially, a parson) when the rescue ship arrives.

Back home, the entire party is subjected to a drawing-room interrogation by a suspicious dowager, and it seems for a moment that the two nearlyweds may crack under the strain and confess a passion that still obviously exists. But they don't, and everybody proceeds to breathe easily, notably the supposedly egalitarian earl. It all leaves a pleasantly bitter taste in the mouth.

My only previous acquaintance with the play was in a 1950s movie version, with Kenneth More as Crichton, in which he paired off happily with Tweeny just before the final credits, as if love among the lower orders conquered all and this constituted a happy ending. It's a relief to find that Barrie himself wasn't about to let his audience off so lightly.

Morris Panych's Niagara production, though, has its own compromises to make. First, as now seems to be the convention among directors of Barrie, he has his actors recite the author's stage directions, which, being equal parts sugar and vinegar, are admittedly irresistible. Trouble is, the performers who deliver them, in what sounds like imitation cockney, don't do it very well. Attired and masked as the wild animals who make desert-island life so interesting, they seem to have been cast for their prowess in the musical numbers.

No, Barrie didn't actually write or prescribe any such numbers, but Panych gives us Irving Berlin's great but puzzlingly irrelevant Shakin' the Blues Away; De Sylva, Brown and Henderson's not-greatbut-good It All Depends on You; and some others that even I couldn't identify. The songs, and their staging, come from the 1920s, though the play itself is from 1902 and depicts a world whose assumptions were to be seriously shaken by the First World War. My own guess is that Panych found the play too slight to sustain an evening on the Shaw Festival's main stage and wanted to give us a more substantial run for our money. Up to a point he succeeds. There's certainly fun to be had. But it comes at the cost of a creeping, and eventually contagious, suspicion that the director doesn't absolutely trust the play.

Both pleasure and doubt reach their climax at the curtain call, when we get a reprise of the Berlin tune with the entire cast Charlestoning like crazy, and with Steven Sutcliffe's Crichton shedding his sedateness to shake a festive leg, while apparently trying out both his possible partners. Which, I guess, may count as ironic epilogue. Anyway, it's delightful to see Sutcliffe reverting to his musical-theatre past.

Up until this point, the most spectacular physical activity he's been permitted is to shimmer into a room, Jeeves-like. Whether knowing his first place, basking in his second or, in his third, allowing the briefest glimpse of what looks suspiciously like a breaking heart, Sutcliffe's butler is as splendidly imperturbable as his Tory leader in On the Rocks is splendidly perturbable.

David Schuurman, by contrast, progresses from worldweary duke in that play to world-bettering earl while exuding an identical sweet crinkled reasonableness.

Ken MacDonald's sets are beautiful -if, by his standards, unspectacular -but the isle is fuller of noises than it is of danger.

? The Admirable Crichton runs until Oct. 29. For tickets, call 1800-511-7429 or visit shawfest. com.
