THEATRE REVIEW

Wishful Drinking Royal Alexandra Theatre, Toronto

"I like to quote fictional characters," says Carrie Fisher, after citing Sherlock Holmes on the amount of information it's possible for one person to hold in his head, "because I'm something of a fictional character myself." I wish she'd gone into that a bit more. Wishful Drinking, an in-person memoir of Fisher's life as Hollywood child and bipolar adult, is a kind of psychological striptease. It's entertaining and revealing, but never quite enough of either.

Or it's like visiting someone, enjoying the house and appreciating the welcome, but never getting to know the hostess. Fisher's set does actually approximate a living room, furnished with mementoes of her past, including an R2-D2 or two: As she says herself, if we don't remember her as Princess Leia in Star Wars, then what are we doing there? Just to remind us, she appears before us in full bunnish Leia hairstyle, and with glitter dripping from her eyelashes. She's also singing: an ironic, Streisand-ish version of Happy Days Are Here Again, which she does pretty well; even, after a tantalizing pause in which we wonder whether she'll have to fake it, hitting the last high note. But then her parents were both singers.

We hear a lot about Eddie Fisher and Debbie Reynolds in the show's firstact.Theirphotos occupy the top left-hand corner on a board labelled Hollywood Inbreeding 101; Fisher (Carrie, that is) stands in front of it with a pointer, guiding us through the intricate saga of marriages, divorces and re-marriages. It goes on for rather longer than its stage-worthiness deserves; the mock-schoolteacher manner begins to grate. There are some fun bits, though. We learn that Papa Eddie, before his death, took up with "most of Chinatown" and that Mama still lives next door and phones regularly, gruffly announcing herself as "your mother, Debbie." Well, her daughter makes her sound gruff.

She obviously loved and loves her parents. All the same, we're left in no doubt that, however titillating it may seem in retrospect, it was a childhood certain to cause problems later. Although how much it contributed to Fisher's alcoholism, substance abuse and (conceivably) her mental illness is never examined in much detail. They just sort of happen.

The show abounds in missing links. We learn that young Carrie studied in London at the Central School of Speech and Drama. She does a very funny rundown of the tongue-twisting vocal exercises she learned there, and an even funnier riff on how they might have melded with the prose she was called upon to deliver as Leia.

How George Lucas came to think of her for the role, all untried as she was, is not revealed; but since she portrays Lucas as the ultimate sphinx, it could be that he never let on. Fisher pokes some scathing, if presumably affectionate, fun at the film and her role in it, without ever making the connection to what came after. She emerged, especially when she started writing, as more talented and intelligent than anyone had given her credit for. That must have been a blast. In this show, it's taken for granted.

Instead we hear about her marriages, especially the one to Paul Simon. And then there are the depths: "I've got prizes for mental illness," she tells us - adding "because I'm so good at it." She's actually very enlightening on what it feels like to be bipolar, without telling us very much about how and when it actually happened to her.

That's not the only double bluff. She ponders the possibility of her doing "a pandering, audience-pleasing show - like this one." That's cute, without actually being disarming. Her own audience-pleasing (or audience-baiting)tacticsinclude picking out spectators by name and repeatedly coming back to them, Edna Everage style.

The show's title is neat but a cheat. Compared with some of her other problems, Fisher's drinking is glossed over. There is, though, a double whammy of an ending. We see a projected headline paying tribute to "Bipolar Woman of the Year," with a subhead that seems to confirm all the star's most endearing self-doubts: "Carrie Fisher Runner Up." It's followed by another headline that I couldn't read, so transfixed was I by the masthead above it: News of the World. Was this a late addition? Fisher says, very soundly, that she hates being described as "a survivor." All the same, who's surviving now?

- Wishful Drinking runs until Aug. 21. For tickets, call 416872-1212 or visit mirvish.ca.

THEATRE REVIEW

Titus Andronicus Tom Patterson Theatre, Stratford

There are 24 named characters in the standard texts of Titus Andronicus, and by the end of the play, 14 of them are either dead or under sentence of same. Two of the deceased have, while alive, been raped or mutilated or both; another two, brothers, have been ground into paste and served up in a pie, to be consumed by their own mother. The play is the earliest-written of Shakespeare's Roman tragedies (it may even, though I personally doubt it, have been his earliest play of any kind) but it's the latest set. In fact, it's hardly historical at all, though it does seem to be taking place in the last years of the Empire, with Rome at war with the Goths who were eventually to overthrow it. From what the play shows us, Rome had it coming.

Darko Tresnjak's Stratford production actually manages to up the play's mortality rate. Shakespeare calls for a mere four killings in his concluding banquet scene. Tresnjak ends with a veritable orgy of arbitrary homicides, in which a hitherto blameless male child takes an enthusiastic part. This is one of the few false steps in a generally disciplined and exciting production. It runs counter to the spirit in which all the previous killings have been committed.

Every one of them has had a motive. Every murderer has considered himself (no woman directly sheds blood in this play) to be justified. There's a code. In breaching it, the production is probably trying to make a point, about violence being contagious. But that's something we hardly need to be told; doing it this way seems frivolous and selfcongratulatory. For much of the play, the house lights have been up, as if to confront us directly with the violence. But a production that aims to be that tough on the audience has to be equally tough on itself. And until we get to that finale, this one is.

The play begins with Titus, aged and honoured Roman general, returning victorious from a campaign in which he's lost 21 of his 25 sons. (Another three will shortly follow, one of them dispatched by Titus himself.) He's pulling a covered wagon that we assume contains his offspring's honoured corpses. But when the covers are pulled off we behold, in a tremendous coup that had me in the production's corner thenceforward, a cage in which cower, naked and afraid, the Gothic queen Tamora, her three sons and her black lover, Aaron the Moor.

Titus's surviving sons demand the eldest Goth prince as a sacrifice; he agrees, and seems genuinely surprised that Tamora should object. From then on she is, naturally, his mortal enemy; and when she catches the eye of the new Roman emperor Saturninus and marries him, she holds the aces. She encourages her two sons to ravish Titus' newly married daughter Lavinia and to cut off her hands and tongue to prevent her from either telling or writing who did it to her; and she has two of Titus's boys framed for the murder of Lavinia's husband. Hence, eventually, Titus's culinary revenge. And even though he struck the first blow, and the final blood count is about even, we do mostly sympathize with him, for several reasons. First, the story is told largely from his point of view. Second, we get to know and even like him and what remains of his household. Third, he's the victim of several dirty tricks and while he rages, mourns and goes a kind of mad, his enemies gloat, which is not endearing.

John Vickery is an actor whose best Stratford performances, in Zastrozzi and The Grapes of Wrath, have been outside of Shakespeare, and whose classical work has been uniformly stolid. But as Titus, he makes that stolidity work for him, presenting a man with limited horizons and an iron sense of duty who simply cannot understand what is being done to him. He's a Stoic driven beyond stoicism, a limited but logical mind crazed by illogical pressures, a plight in which the cankered quizzical humour that Vickery found in Zastrozzi comes in very useful and proves surprisingly moving.

Another happy surprise is the hitherto bland Dion Johnstone, giving a smooth and dangerous performance of Aaron, the play's unrepentant evil genius and a very cool dude, indeed. Neither of these actors sounds his character's fullest depths, but both are excellent.

Claire Lautier's Tamora is splendid when pleading for her son's life, and later when got up as a giant masked bat to impersonate the spirit of Revenge, but lightweight for what comes between; Amanda Lisman's Lavinia, by contrast, is disconcertingly matronly when inviolate but a wrenching vengeful apparition afterwards (which means for most of the play). David Ferry is urgent and sympathetic as Titus's civilian brother, the nearest thing the play affords to a nice guy; Sean Arbuckle shows as Saturninus how thoroughly Shakespeare anticipated Hollywood's idea of the Roman emperor as whimpering tyrant.

The director's program note claims that "this gruesome play . is also very funny and very beautiful." In fact, it isn't all that funny (compulsive Elizabethan wordplay doesn't count) and in practice and to his credit Tresnjak hasn't tried to make it so: which is one reason his imposed ending is so out of place. But the play's unflinchingness is beautiful, and beautifully illuminated (literally) when we are kept gazing for the longest time at an axe about to descend on a human hand and a man, for the noblest reasons, awaiting the blow.

Titus Andronicus plays in repertory until Sept. 24. For tickets, call 1-800-567-1600 or visit stratfordfestival.ca.

Back in the 1960s, there was a gently rocking musical based on Twelfth Night entitled Your Own Thing, which is a pretty fair translation of the original play's subtitle What You Will. More recently there was a Twelfth Night musical whose score was made up, attractively if for no other readily apparent reason, of Duke Ellington songs and that was called, in deference to Shakespeare's own opening line about the food of love, Play On. That line keeps resonating through Stratford's new Twelfth Night in which people, with good thematic cause, keep singing it. Des McAnuff's production, with a score by himself and Michael Roth, is virtually a musical itself, not unlike Your Own Thing in its cheerful eclecticism, aural and visual. I expected to find it, at most, a guilty pleasure. It turns out to be the best Shakespeare on the main Festival stage since Hamlet three years ago, and one of the most satisfying accounts of the play I've seen.

Shakespeare's romantic comedies are music soaked and music-driven anyway, like much of the greatest theatre since the Greeks; in fact, if you want to get historical about it, it's the non-musical drama that's the aberration.

McAnuff's also on authentically Shakespearean ground in opting for a mix of periods in set and costumes. In a program note, he calls this "postmodern," though I'd be more inclined to call it Pop Art, especially since this Duke Orsino seems to have engaged a Beatles cover band, Sergeant Pepper era, for his house musicians. (Or maybe he's rich enough to have hired the originals.)

There are two problems lying in wait for any staging of this play in modernish dress: Malvolio's crossgartering, and the sword fights. Both are brilliantly solved, the first through a lightning stroke it would be unfair to reveal, the second through some long-range planning. Olivia's household, as commandeered by Sir Toby Belch, resembles a sports compound; we see Toby and friends on the golf links, at the nets and in a sauna, so it's logical they should eventually get around to some fencing practice. These games are fun to watch in themselves; they're also used to point out the relationships of the people playing them. Which brings us to what's really memorable about this production. A cast made up of A-list actors is the norm at Stratford. What's less guaranteed is to find nearly all of them, right down to the First and Second Officers, giving A-list performances.

There are some excesses. Bringing on a spectral pop group (could this be the meaning of the term "ghostband"?) as back up for O Mistress Mine merely dilutes the rich chemistry that the scene's three designated characters have already established.

Sometimes, the music itself gets undercut. Ben Carlson sings a heartstopping first stanza of Come Away, Death; he sings a heart-stopping second stanza, too, but we're distracted by the appearance of an emblematic lover and lass striking illustrative poses.

Debra Hanson's costumes are spiffy, but the meaning of her basic set, a high and yawning maw, escapes me. Still, much of what happens beneath or before it is lovely, notably the arrival of Suzy Jane Hunt's shipwrecked Viola by rowboat through a sea of dry ice, as if cruising the catacombs of The Phantom of the Opera. Her "what country, friends, is this?" sounds the authentic note of wonder (and Timothy D. Stickney's answering sea captain maintains it); later on she's better at being heartsick than at being witty or commanding. She has, though, two ideal opposites. Mike Shara, taking a quantum leap as a Shakespearean actor, is a magnetic Orsino, luxuriating in romantic selftorture and, when thwarted, darkly prepared to torture others. Sara Topham's Olivia is a delightful poseuse, half aware of her own absurdity and with strong reserves of feeling just waiting to be aroused. She also establishes firm relationships, vexed or affectionate or both, with everyone under her roof.

That would include Carlson's Feste, the production's master of ceremonies: a sardonic loner with professional worries, scoring points off everybody with whom he comes in contact and mining fool's gold from the most recalcitrant lines. This textual and psychological nimbleness is a feature of the below-stairs scenes, with Brian Dennehy a gentleman sharper of a Toby who waits long (possibly too long) before baring his fangs, and Stephen Ouimette an ecstatic Sir Andrew, less vulnerably winsome than we're accustomed to (and than when Ouimette himself last played the role), but still endearing. It's telling that when Olivia says "let him be looked to," it's the hapless Andrew she means, not the drunken uncle of whom she's obviously washed her hands.

There's a strong hint that her exaggerated mourning is controlled by Tom Rooney's Malvolio, a discreetly officious steward whose letter scene almost crowns the play, showing us self-seduction by easy stages. In his later torments, this outstandingly inventive and economical actor walks a very fine line, unlikeable but sympathetic.

Juan Chioran makes an exceptional deal of the notoriously nondescript Fabian, here an apprentice majordomo who briefly perks up in song, perhaps due more to the actor's proclivities than the character's. Shane Carty and Michael Blake likewise do more than usual for Sebastian and Antonio.

The general busyness, including a cage on pulleys for Malvolio, sometimes threatens to swamp the play, but there's always, especially towards the end, a sharp moment to pull everything together. The bated-breath reunion of Viola and her brother; the last mutually vengeful encounter of Feste and Malvolio, their masks off; the final song, that's almost an epiphany. Our last sight of Rooney is an unlooked-for stunner; he'll be revenged on the whole pack of them.

Twelfth Night is in repertory through Oct. 28 at the Festival Theatre, Stratford. For ticket information, visit stratfordfestival.ca or call 1-800-567-1600.

THEATRE REVIEW

NEXT TO NORMAL

Four Seasons Centre for the Performing Arts, Toronto

The musical Next to Normal goes irretrievably down the tubes at the moment, early in Act One, when one of its characters, already a driving force in the action, is revealed to have been dead all along.

The character is Gabe, who died when he was a baby. His mother Diana, the show's central character, is a depressive; maybe bipolar, though we're cautioned that this can be a glib generalization that doesn't fit all cases. When we first meet her she's slipping into one of her bad periods, to the agonized dismay of her husband Dan and the resentful anger of their teenage daughter Natalie. A psychiatrist prescribes a cocktail of pills, which she tries for a time and then flushes down the toilet, encouraged by Gabe, whom at this point the audience believes to be alive. Later on, when we know he's dead, he reacts similarly but even more violently when another psychiatrist prescribes ECT. He's afraid that it will make Diana forget him.

There's the problem. If Gabe simply represented a voice in Diana's head, then we might accept his presence onstage as merely a device, however clunky. But he's given feelings and motivations of his own. And it isn't only Diana on whom he imposes them; he gets to confront his father as well, in a near-to-closing number that's touching on its own account but facile in its implications. If there are issues here, then why didn't the show confront them earlier? Most of the time, Gabe's influence on the musical's score, and on the show as a whole, is negative; his contributions veer between hysteria and New Agey sentimentality.

Which is a shame, because Next to Normal, which comes to us on its post-Broadway tour, obviously earns respect for its ambitions and, to some extent, for its achievements. After all, there are not many big musicals about mental illness, and there may well be even fewer about the travails of middle-class families; musicals traditionally end with a marriage rather than throwing us into the centre of one. If the roots of Diana's condition seem pat, its progress isn't, and the show ends realistically balanced between hope and despair. At least, its storyline does; musically it can't resist ending with one of those patented uplift numbers, this one with the giveaway title of Light.

The show's score actually sounds better on the cast album than it does in the theatre. That especially goes for Brian Yorkey's lyrics, which reach what is nowadays an unusually high level of intelligence and craftsmanship; the best song, catchily entitled My Psychopharmacologist and I, has Diana singing, "He knows my deepest secrets/ I know his .name." Barbs like this, though, are often drowned or blunted by the sound of shrillness; it's not so much that the words don't sit well on the music as that the music doesn't provide them with much of a saddle.

Tom Kitt's score, as orchestrated by Michael Starobin, has some beautiful lyrical passages; it also has a lot of unfocused pounding. After the decades that American theatre composers from Irving Berlin to Stephen Sondheim devoted to evolving a musical language that could reflect actual speechrhythms, it's frustrating to find the post-rock generations throwing it all away.

Yorkey also wrote the show's book, of which there isn't enough. This isn't quite a through-sung score, but it's near enough to one for the occasional spoken lines to fall on the ears like manna. Alice Ripley's performance of Diana is remarkable for its bravura honesty; her singing isn't always pretty, and some of her vowel sounds belong to her alone, but it's always musical and it always illuminates or expands the dramatic line. She originated the role in New York, and she at least is far more impressive live than on the CD, on which she sounds like anybody. But powerful as her singing is, she tells us more, and more trenchantly, about Alice's condition, when she's allowed to talk: so much so that I began to resent it when the music started up again.

Asa Somers' Dan is initially bland, but purposefully so; as he gradually discovers that even being ultra-supportive isn't always enough, he becomes moving. Natalie is a schematic character: a music major who seeks escape from the pressures at home in the disciplines of the classics, and is wooed and won by a boy who's more into jazz. Under his influence, and even beyond it, she experiments; just as Diana is going off her meds, Natalie gets into them.

Mother and daughter naturally have screaming duets. The parallel between the older and younger generations (two quiet men, two noisy women) is very forced. Anyway, Emma Hunton as Natalie does, efficiently, all that's required of her; likewise Preston Sadleir as the boyfriend, Curt Hansen as Gabe, and Jeremy Kushnier as a couple of shrinks. Michael Greif's production takes place on an overpowering threelevel set, perhaps to demonstrate how far apart these family members are, perhaps because even an unconventional Broadway musical is obliged to look big. Pre-Broadway it was apparently a chamber musical, and - visually, aurally and dramatically if not commercially - it would probably still work better that way.

? Next to Normal runs until July 30. For tickets, call 866950-7469 or visit dancaptickets.com.

THEATRE REVIEW

The Kreutzer Sonata

Young Centre for the Performing Arts, Toronto

This is Ted Dykstra's time. He is the director of all three of the plays in Soulpeppers current repertoire: the superb Glass Menagerie, the perennially successful Billy Bishop Goes to War, and now The Kreutzer Sonata, of which he is also the adapter and sole performer. In the latter role, his achievement is unimpeachable. He sits in an armchair, in the persona of an upper-class Russian from the late 19th century, and tells the story of how he murdered his wife. He tells of how he loved her and of how he became jealous of her relationship with a Frenchified fop with whom she played violin-and-piano duets. Music, he observes, fosters a dangerous intimacy between those who perform it; it also, he laments and proves, arouses dangerous emotions in those who listen to it. Like Richard II, Dykstras narrator might have cried, This music mads me, let it sound no more. So he stops it, dead.

All this, and more, Dykstra tells us in the course of just over an hour, without ever standing up. He's wearing a rather elegant dressing gown, and he has a few props: a glass of water, a Bible. (His character is very religious; he also keeps relevant documents between the pages.) His hand movements are studied, sparing and revealing; he uses them to make or underline points. The visual effect is enhanced by Lorenzo Savoini's fierce, concentrated lighting. Dysktras vocal delivery is virtuosic, generally suave and measured but breaking into an intensity that we can recognize as hysterical even though the character doesnt. He is a crazed man priding himself on his lucidity. It's a perfect performance.

The script may also be perfect in its own terms, but those terms are limited. The play is based on a novella by Tolstoy, that in turn takes its title from a composition by Beethoven. It's the principal piece that the narrators wife and her supposed lover play together, and whose sensuous first movement in particular drives the husband to frenzy. One of the most obvious differences between play and book is that were more than halfway through the latter before the sonata itself is even mentioned. In the play, we not only hear of it, but hear it, right from the start; it would be theatrically unthinkable for us not to.

The music becomes the play's theme, in more senses than one and in a way that isn't true of the novel, despite its title. Dykstra first performed his adaptation for the Art of Time ensemble, as half of a double bill of which the other half was a dance piece performed to the Beethoven music. And I suspect that it was more satisfying in that context than it is all on its own.

Theres more context in the book, too. The protagonist tells his tale to an anonymous narrator whom he encounters on a train and who has already heard other fellow-passengers expounding their views on women and on marriage: Some of them, to present-day ears, sound agreeably advanced, others fearsomely obscurantist. Dykstra can hardly be blamed for ditching this framework; indeed, nearly all his alterations are understandable and most of them were probably inevitable. They include getting rid of the characters account of his early life. In fact, his story begins about halfway through Tolstoy's. And this does have consequences, both visceral and intellectual.

Like his author, Tolstoy's hero led a wild brothelhaunting life in his youth and is now revolted by it; he belongs in the line of repentant sinners from St. Augustine to Malcolm Muggeridge who, having had their fun, are intent on denying it to everyone else. Although he still finds the temptations physically overwhelming, he finds sex, inside or outside marriage, spiritually and intellectually abhorrent, tolerable only when it produces children, and dubiously so even then. So what if the human race dies out? There are higher considerations than that.

Tolstoy wrote a "postface" (opposite of a preface) to insist that no, he wasnt kidding, those were his beliefs; though he did rather hedge his bets by admitting that, humanity being what it is, his ideals were unlikely to be realized. Being an artist as well as a theorist, he couldnt help complicating things in the actual story; there are too many layers for us to take the protagonist on trust. You do read him, though, disturbingly swayed by the hero's intensity while noticing how many of his positions - the horror of contraception, the idea of marriage as legalized prostitution - still recur at different points on the political map. Dysktra gives them passing mention, but mainly what he offers us is a straightforward story of jealousy and revenge, brought on by music, here standing in for the carnal temptations that Tolstoy found in absolutely everything.

There are some more minor alterations, notably in the matter of names. Tolstoy's protagonist Pozdnyshev is just Yuri to us; his wife gets a name, too: Sonya. And she now plays violin in the duets rather than, as might seem more natural in an amateur, piano. Maybe (I'm not being frivolous) Dysktra is trying to establish an independent identity for his own version. His text certainly seems to be his own paraphrase, and an effective one, rather than an adaptation of an existing translation. Like the story, he's at his most gripping in the account of the murder itself, which has a horrible inevitability to it. It also makes you wish that, for all his other skills, Dykstra would act more often.

- The Kreutzer Sonata runs until Aug. 11. For tickets, call 416-866-8666 or visit soulpepper.ca.

The Canopy Theatre Company's Lysistrata - The Sex Strike (their subtitle) is the most satisfying production of an Aristophanes play I have ever seen. That isn't quite the sweeping statement it may sound. I don't have many Aristophanic experiences to choose from since, despite his textbook status as the father of comedy, his plays aren't done very often, certainly not in English. And there's a very good reason for that, which is that they don't usually work. That doesn't mean that his reputation is undeserved or that some of his jokes don't continue to resound down the millennia. It means that his and his contemporaries' conception of what makes a comedy is completely different from ours, in a way that certainly isn't true of Greek tragedy. By our definitions his plays are hardly plays at all; they're more like topical revues. And it isn't the topicality that does them in; the themes most of them deal with - in Lysistrata's case, war and sex - are always topical, because they're eternal. It's the form. Aristophanes' plays are largely indifferent to plot and character, the things that for us are the motors of any kind of comedy lasting more than 10 minutes. Situation comedy only came in with his Greek successors and their Roman successors. And it's been around ever since.

Aristophanes wrote comedies of ideas (like Shaw's, but lower on human interest) and the one that kicks off Lysistrata is a corker that has become a Greek myth in its own right, thereby earning its author a place at the very top of the class. The women of Athens, led by the title character, swear off sex with their men until the men put an end to the war with Sparta that is tearing both cities, and the whole of Greece, apart. (And eventually did.) They persuade the women of Sparta to do the same, though how the ladies of both towns were able to meet up for their conference is one of those pesky naturalistic details Aristophanes preferred to not to get into. The idea is a great one, like Christianity and western civilization, and though the actual women of Athens never put it into practice, the Canopy Company's program includes a page of instances in which similar plans have worked in other situations. It's a great dramatic idea, too. The problem is, once you've stated it, what do you do with it? For much of its length, Lysistrata does surprisingly little.

It does advance alternate, or maybe parallel, strategies. As do the women themselves. With remarkable ease, they take over Athens' public buildings, Acropolis included. Token explanation: all the able-bodied men are away fighting, leaving only some senile governors and a few easily intimidated thugs. And it's in the political confrontation of complacent men and angry, intelligent women that this adaptation comes on strongest. It's actually an adaptation of an adaptation: A writer called Phil Wilmott has worked over a version that Britain's National Theatre commissioned in the 1970s from no less than Germaine Greer, then in the full flush of The Female Eunuch. It must have seemed like a slam-dunk combination, though, for whatever reason, the National never produced it. But, whoever did what, the current version is excellent, very stylish and speakable and playable, preserving the original structure but making it more coherent while decorating it in ways that are contemporary but still thoroughly in keeping. (The National may have expected a more rampantly feminist interpretation, but as a literature teacher Greer has always, from what I know of her, been insistent on fidelity.)

The scene here is a bath house, cheekily adorned with a sign reading Male Members Only. As the theme of sexual frustration is advanced, those members will become increasingly prominent, so to speak. For the moment, though, Lysistrata and her cohorts say nothing about keeping out of men's beds. They scorchingly attack the male establishment for its conduct of the war, and its patronizing treatment of women in general; and they score all around the clock. The aged senators, furious at having the holiest of masculine sanctums invaded and clad only in towels, keep condemning themselves out of their own mouths. They are further humiliated by a chorus of cleaning women who, in a touch of class consciousness not so evident in the original, put brooms and mops into their hands and tell them to get on with it.

The sex strike only appears in earnest later on, though not before some attempted backsliding from the ladies, who are getting horny themselves. "Women!" complains their exasperated leader in a line sadly omitted in this version, "it's no wonder they write tragedies about us." But she rallies the troops, and there's a set-piece scene in which one young wife teases her husband, home on leave, to the point of desperation and beyond. From here it's a short skip to a summit conference of Greek leaders, each more protuberant than the last, and the joyful outbreak of peace.

The company, an offshoot of Hart House, performs in its own little amphitheatre on Philosopher's Walk: a perfect-sounding location for Greek drama, though most summers they do Shakespeare. Andrea Wasserman's production is lively and excellently pointed, with a few rough edges. In a cast that's at most semiprofessional the best, or at least the most contained, performances come ironically from men: from Thomas Gough as the most intransigent of the senators and from Coner Hefferon as the most conciliatory. Among the women, including Claire Acott in the title role, there's more enthusiasm than finesse. Music is confined to recordings of '50s rock 'n' roll hits, which is probably a wise decision. The ending, after all that foreplay, is something of an anticlimax - unavoidably, given the nature of the play. But we can at least applaud the feeling behind it, and wish that Aristophanes' dream had actually come to pass.

- Lysistrata runs to Aug. 6 at Philosopher Walk's outdoor stage. For show times and ticket information, visit canopytheatre.ca.

Daniel Dimarco / Claire Acott as Lysistrata, leading the charge for a sex strike.;; Caption:

Tickets to shows at Toronto's Summerworks Festival, previously $10 apiece, will this year cost $15. That doesnt sound like much, but if you want to take full advantage of a festival containing upwards of 50 shows, of which you can catch four or five on any given day, then it mounts up. The reason for the increase is that this year Summerworks has been deprived of federal funding. Nobody knows the reason for certain, but last year the Prime Ministers office had castigated the festival for producing a play called Homegrown, which, it said, glorified terrorism. (It didn't.) This year the subsidy was withdrawn. What a coincidence.

There is an argument for not subsidizing the arts at all. I don't agree with it, but its an argument. But as long as subsidy exists, it seems reasonable to ask that it be given or removed for reasons more substantial than governmental pique. The official word is they have a lot of arts events to choose from. Right. So it seems a good idea to take track record into account. Summerworks record is excellent. Many of its shows, apart from being fun at the time, have gone on to enjoy much wider exposure; for example, The Middle Place, which won the 2010-11 Toronto Theatre Critics Award for best production and was nominated for a Dora for best play, started out at Summerworks, was subsequently staged by two major Toronto theatres, and was then taken on tour.

The festival's greatest individual success story may well be Hannah Moscovitch, whose place among our best playwrights stems from her exposure at Summerworks. She's had several scripts done there, most memorably The Russian Play. This year, she and her director and leading actress from that show are reuniting for what amounts to a victory lap. By special invitation (as opposed to the usual process of juried selection) theyre offering Little One (Passe Muraille Mainspace), described as a stylish little lullabynightmare" about two mutually adoring, and mutually destructive, adoptive siblings from one of the nicer parts of Ottawa. That might turn out to have all kinds of ramifications, but on the surface it sounds more domestic, less political, than most of Moscovitch. On the other hand, shes an expert at blending the two. Natasha Mytnowych directs, and Michelle Monteith plays the sister, with Joe Cobden, new to the team but admirable elsewhere, as the brother. Which one is little remains to be revealed.

From Hannah's turn to Hannah's Turn (Lower Ossington Theatre), where the Hannah is Arendt (Jewish), and the relationship is the one she had with Martin Heidegger (Nazi). Fascinating subject, however they treat it. Richard Sanger "created (does that mean wrote?) and directs it, and Severn Thompson, previous adornment of Shaw, Shakespeare and elsewhere, is in the cast.

Every year seems to bring a greater number of established practitioners at Summerworks. In that department, though, few shows this year can compete with White Rabbit, Red Rabbit (The Theatre Centre), an Iranian play presented jointly by the prestigious Volcano company and the even more prestigious Necessary Angel, and described (by them) as wild" and "utterly original. Its a oneperson play, and at a given performance the person might be Eric Peterson or Yanna McIntosh or Gord Rand or Natasha Greenblatt or Kawa Ada or (a new name to me) Tara Grammy. Each of them will perform it cold," i.e, they wont have seen a script beforehand. You'll notice a wide range of age, gender and ethnicity there so I think we can take it the play isn't strictly representational. "It dissects the experience of a whole generation, the publicity says. But which generation? The author, Nassim Soleimanpour, is 29, and the producers note, acidly, that he crafted [the play] in such a way that it can travel throughout the world - unlike himself." Heres the catch, for those who may be particular fans of any of the above actors; it isnt announced which will be performing when. So the audience attends cold as well. So much for the star system.

There are star playwrights as well. Sarah Ruhl, the rising American, is represented by Eurydice (Passe Muraille Mainspace), "a retelling of the Orpheus myth from his dead bride's point of view. I imagine she had quite a lot to say about it. This is produced and directed by Kristina Nicoll, whom I know best as an actress, though, come to think of it, I haven't seen her at it in the last few years. Derrick Chua, well-known Toronto theatrical entrepreneur, is billed as godfather," I assume, affectionately.

The versatile Christopher Stanton, a coming man as actor and sound designer, is author and director of Elora Gorge (Theatre Centre), that promises to be Gothic-scary. The title is geographic.

The festival's most intriguing title though may well be The Physical Ramifications of Attempted Global Domination (Passe Muraille Mainspace), which examines the psychosomatic ailments typified by Hitler, Napoleon and Pol Pot - though I'm not sure the last aimed at global domination. Anyway, serves them right.

Time was when you could spend a Summerworks afternoon and evening happily shuttling between Passe Muraille and Factory Theatre, which are just around a couple of corners from one another. Now there are regular venues further afield, though everything, including a few "sitespecific" productions, is in the general area of Queen and King West. Enjoy. And keep cool.

? Summerworks runs until Aug. 14. For ticket and show information, visit summerworks.ca.

THEATRE REVIEW

Maria Severa Court House Theatre, Niagara-on-the-Lake, Ont.

Maria Severa Onofriana sang the blues, in Portuguese. More exactly, she was an early exponent - some say the inventor - of the guitar-based form known as fado. She was born in Lisbon in 1820, and died 26 years later. She was also a prostitute and her mother owned a tavern in one of the city's more colourful neighbourhoods. Her lovers included the Count of Vimioso, aristocrat and bullfighter.

Those, which seem to be almost the only known facts about Maria, are faithfully incorporated in Maria Severa, the new musical at the Shaw Festival, with book, music and lyrics by Jay Turvey and Paul Sportelli. The music, the actual sound and flavour of fado is, by the authors' own account, what attracted them to their subject, and they communicate that attraction powerfully to the audience. The songs they've written for Maria herself, who's given a spitfire performance by Julie Martell, are melodically moody and rhythmically complex; a number that she shares with a street-walker friend, titled Bread and Butter, comes over like Portugal's answer to Brecht and Weill. Sometimes the score strays further afield, or maybe that should be closer to home; the ensemble number At the Bullfight, is high-end contemporary Broadway, and so, even more, is the beautiful love-duet I Can't Touch You with Words. The lyrics can be pungent, though they can also, too often, sound earnestly explanatory. The book is strong on atmosphere, short on story, and confusing on structure.

The main focus is on the doomed passion of Maria and her high-born matador, here called Armando, who first picks her up, or is picked up by her, when out slumming with his younger brother. They fall in love, to the fury of Armando's mother, who wants to repair the family fortunes by marrying him off to an heiress. (Though if he's such a star of the bullring, couldn't he repair them himself? But maybe sporting economics were different back then.) Clara, the young lady in question, is a rather subtly drawn character, a sheltered drawing-room pianist who is fascinated by Maria and her songs of love and social protest and who doesn't actually want to marry Armando. He therefore seems no end of a wimp for giving in to the maternal demands. For all that the actor, Mark Uhre, can do for him in the way of voice, presence and even wit, he's an unsatisfactory hero. And the show seems to realize this because towards the end it gives increasing attention to Carlos (Jeff Irving), Maria's accompanist and companion-since-childhood, who nurses a hopeless love for her. Carlos actually starts the show off as a narrator ("There is a song/There is a singer/There's a guitar/and there's a player"), and the switch from commentator to protagonist is hard to accommodate. If it's really all about Maria and Carlos, then why have we been spending so much time with Armando?

There are nine characters, and though the dialogue serves them well, the narrative runs out of things for them to do. That opening number has most of them saying in turn that "it was my fault."

"It" must refer to Maria's fate, but it's never quite stated what that was, which makes responsibility rather hard to apportion. (In actual fact, she died unromantically of tuberculosis.) Anyway, the guilt thing has been forgotten by the last number, even though in staging it's a mirror-image of the first. The second act features a succession of solo turns, for the cast members who haven't had one yet. One of them, for Maria's friend Jasmine (Saccha Dennis), works better on the cast CD than on the stage, even though it has a big dance component. It's a strong character piece in itself, but it's a distraction (and the preceding dialogue tells us in advance what it's going to say). Jenny L. Wright has been bringing down the house all evening as Maria's lovably caustic mama who, rather like Mama Brice in Funny Girl, fancies that she knows better than her daughter what the customers really want; giving her a number to prove it seems somehow anti-climactic. The only one of these songs that both relates to and advances the plot is The Money Tree, in which Clara (a lovely performance by Jacqueline Thair) describes her pretty, wealthy, cloistered and frustrated existence. It stops the show without even trying.

Sharry Flett, whom I never knew could sing, gives an icily commanding account of the kind of scheming matriarch whom you expect to encounter in the Shaw's non-musical repertoire, her deadest recent ringer being the mother in The Cassilis Engagement. Jonathan Gould plays her other son, a nasty bit of wastrel, and Neil Barclay is a kindly priest, blackmailed by the prospect of being sent to do missionary work in Paraguay and, for some reason, the only person with an accent. There are no weak performing links, and Martell's Maria is a triumph; musically and dramatically she burns up the stage. Jackie Maxwell's direction fits everything smoothly together, Eda Holmes has devised choreography that's alternately quirky and sinuous, and Judith Bowden's set is cleverly shaped to suggest a guitar. The show teaches one unlooked-for lesson: It's acceptable in opera for a character to sing while dying but in a musical - well, that's why musicals have books. More generally, this is a talented evening that hasn't decided whether to be a portrait or a whole canvas.

? In repertory until Sept. 23. Call 1-800-511-7429 or visit shawfest.com for tickets.

The "Palestinian Chicken" episode of Curb Your Enthusiasm, shown two Sundays ago, ended in a classic standoff. On one side of the screen, a group of Los Angeles Jews, protesting the opening of a Palestinian restaurant next door to a deli, this apparently being the Californian equivalent of a mosque at Ground Zero. On the other side, a group of Palestinians protesting the protest. And in the middle, Larry David, his allegiances hopelessly split, partly by his lust for Palestinian chicken, but more by his lust for a Palestinian chick, who had given him the best sex of his life and called him a dirty Jew while giving it. He had first attracted her attention by getting into a fight with a coreligionist who had tried to enter a similar restaurant while wearing a yarmulke. Larry, it seems, likes a little bit of trangressiveness but draws the line at outright provocation.

The appeal of Curb Your Enthusiasm is that it displays everybody in the worst possible light; it's the most misanthropic American comedy since, I should think, W.C. Fields. My own enthusiasm for it was severely curbed by the last season, which engineered a Seinfeld reunion while still insisting that it was a very bad idea (and proving it). The new series, though, is more than a return to form; it's the best ever. The "Palestinian Chicken" finale illustrates why. It's something of a political metaphor; it scales wonderful heights of bad taste; and it brilliantly pulls together all the themes and plot-threads of the preceding half-hour. Construction, despite the apparent casualness, is where the show is strongest. All the elements of each instalment pay off. There's a prize example coming up this Sunday. The ingredients include the putting-down and last rites of Larry's best friend's wife's dog; the greed of both Larry and friend for a particular brand of ice cream; Larry's own outrage at motorists who straddle two

parking spaces; the earnings of Lexus driving vets; and a vow of silence taken, for spiritual reasons, by a guy who's goaded to break it at the worst possible moment. Feydeau, the master of French farce, would have approved that last device.

It's tempting to call Larry the ultimate self-hating Jew, but I'm not sure that sticks. His social circle and his frame of reference are thoroughly Jewish, or Jewish-American (I doubt if Gentiles have any trouble understanding the show but I do wonder if they find it funny), but Larry doesn't have enough passion to hate, or love, anyone. What he's very good at is criticizing or despising. Here, of course, we often cheer him on. His attacks range from the petty (parking) to the devastatingly logical: As he says, a vow of silence is pretty meaningless when you still expect people to read your lips. It's common knowledge that David, when writing Seinfeld, based the character of George on himself, but George has the sympathetic safety net of being an all-around loser. Larry is rich and successful and he gets laid with implausible frequency, though of course the last quality may be a consequence of the first two. George sometimes insulted people on purpose, but mostly he did it by accident. Larry makes a point of it, is even (sometimes) applauded for it. It's his contribution to the social mix: speaking truth to powerlessness. As a performer, David is limited, but he does what he does -- or is what he is -- very well. And he retains his gift for inventing the phrases we never knew we needed. To George's "double dipping" (and Elaine's "sponge-worthy" and the whole crew's "master of your own domain") we can now add Larry's "chat and cut," meaning jumping the queue in a buffet line by latching on to an acquaintance. In Larry's world, such things are vital.

I especially recommend tuning in to HBO Canada on Sept. 4, when the scene is New York (Larry has fled there to avoid a charity event in L.A.) and the narrative involves a lost softball game, a scorned baseball player, a psychiatrist who doesn't mention names but one of his clients directed Star Wars, an aphrodisiac carseat, and Larry's boyhood encounter, socially and sexually traumatic, with an ice-cream van: the episode is called "Mister Softee." This one has a redemptive finale. Larry is not the one redeemed.

Black & White Photo: Doug Hyun / Hey, chin up, Larry David. After all these years, you're still as critical and funny as ever.;; Caption:

THEATRE REVIEW

TOPDOG/UNDERDOG

Studio Theatre, Niagara-on-the Lake, Ont.

The two characters in Topdog /Underdog, a prizewinning American play by Suzan-Lori Parks, are brothers, black, whose father named them Lincoln and Booth. This, according to Lincoln, was daddy's idea of a joke, though as the boys arent twins - Linc in fact is the elder by five years - he must have had a long-range sense of humour. A twisted one too: Short of calling them Cain and Abel, its hard to see how he could have done a better job of blighting their lives.

When we meet them, they're in their thirties and living in Booth's squalid one-room apartment. Booth has no vocation beyond shoplifting, at which hes an expert. Lincoln brings home what legitimate bacon there is, from a job impersonating his presidential namesake. He sits in an arcade, in top hat, frock coat, stuck-on beard and whiteface; and people pay money to shoot him. Once, though, he was a champion dealer in a three-card monte scam; he quit after a day when life on the street went violently wrong and one of his associates got shot. Booth itches to take his brothers former place in the game but, as Lincoln keeps telling him, he hasn't got the stuff; he lacks both the sleight-of-hand and the sleight-of-tongue. Lincoln was married, but his wife left him in the wake of his other troubles. Booth harbours a long-standing passion for a woman called Grace - amazing Grace - and claims to be making great progress with her, but it's pretty clear that most of his boasts are fantasy. He consoles himself with girlie mags, which he stacks under the one bed. Lincoln sleeps in a reclining chair. Despite this, and despite constant fluctuations in mood and fortune, he is, as he has always been, the top dog. Booth reacts with a smouldering blend of love and resentment.

The play is brilliantly written, in probably the best American dialogue for urban no-hopers since the David Mamet of American Buffalo. A program note makes even grander poetic claims for it, but in this Shaw Festival production it comes over as a naturalistic piece with a few bits left out. The missing parts include any clear statements about time and place. We dont know if its happening in New York or, say, Atlanta, which could make a difference, especially given the presidentialassassination motif. And though the idiom sounds very up-to-theminute, Booth's insistence that in order to get a woman Lincoln needs to get a phone - "the world's most revolutionary communication apparatus" - would seem to put us back in pre-Internet days.

Lincoln, defending the integrity of his day job, says that people like their history to be served up "in a certain way. They like it to unfold the way they folded it up." Both brothers are keenly aware - at least they mention it from time to time - of the bitter irony of a black man making a living by pretending to be a white one. (And not, though they dont explore it, not just any white man but a liberating president who was killed by a white supremacist, to whose spiritual descendants Linc may now be affording targetpractice.) Theres some amazing writing, too, some of it bitterly moving, in the brothers' reminiscences of their parents who left them, one at a time, when they were both still young, bequeathing them $500 apiece. Lincoln spent his inheritance, Booth has hoarded his, and who's to say which was the more provident? But its hard to draw the personal and political threads together, unless were meant to think that a black father has taken a crazy delight in dooming his sons to be even more disadvantaged than he was himself, playing a trick on both races at once. What we have is a drama of shifting domination and dependency, in the Harold Pinter tradition: as if the two brothers from The Caretaker were to be thrown onstage together, with no tramp to act as buffer. The play moves towards a pre-ordained ending, whose precise moment the author cunningly delays and diverts, giving us the shock of the expected when we least expect it.

It's very well acted. Kevin Hanchard's Booth is electric as an eel; Nigel Shawn Williams Lincoln is almost too weighty for the situation in which he finds himself, but the interplay between the two is flawless. Philip Akins direction is less funny than it could be, but I suspect that's due to the Shaw studio's logistics; the audience surrounds a surprisingly ample playing space on three sides, which somehow makes it seem diffuse rather than confined.

The festival has brought back Blair Williams lunchtime production of Ferenc Molnars The President, in which a New York tycoon turns a Communist taxi driver into a plutocrat in 60 minutes, real time; and it remains an intoxicating treat. Many roles have been recast but all fit perfectly into the play's and its protagonist's immaculately oiled machine. Julie Martell now plays the pregnant bride who makes it all necessary, and is lubriciously entertaining, if less subtly slutty than her predecessor Chilina Kennedy. (This role seems reserved for leading ladies from festival musicals.) Jeff Meadows repeats his wonderful turn as the made-over lunk; and Lorne Kennedy is again worldclass incomparable as the smoothtalking fast-thinking manipulator who makes it all happen. There is no better hour to be spent or time to be had, anywhere.

- Topdog/Underdog is in repertory until August 27, The President until Oct. 9.

Shaw Festival / Three guesses which brother this is.;; Caption:
2011-08-13-hannah-moscovitch-s-monologue:
Hannah Moscovitch's Little One (Summerworks, Theatre Passe Muraille) is about growing up with a sociopath. There's Claire, who as a sexually damaged four-year-old was rescued by an Ottawa couple with exemplary liberal principles, and there's Aaron, her adoptive elder brother, to whom their parents entrust much of the responsibility of looking after her, understanding her and forgiving her more outrageous actions. These include hurting Aaron physically and drowning his goldfish. When he's older, he acquires a more challenging pet, a kitten, who is the Little One of the title, and whose presence really seems, Claire being Claire, to be asking for trouble. Claire also develops a fixation on the people next door, a techie and his Vietnamese mail-order bride. She harbours dark suspicions about them and, disturbed though she is, she may not be wrong.

Claire begins the play by talking about this couple as though she were telling a story, the creepier for being understated. Then Aaron appears and starts telling his own story, which is also the story of the play. I sometimes worry about Moscovitch's reliance on monologue. But she writes uncommonly good ones, and Aaron's narrative is a riveting fusion of hurt, compassion, dread and humour. (His description of suburban Ottawa as the sound of a million people being quiet together is a classic.) The increasingly impressive Joe Cobden doesn't miss a beat or a transition of it. In his good intentions and his exasperation, he's very easy to relate to; and it's characteristic that his most moving moment should be about somebody else's feelings: his parents' tearful admission of guilt that they've neglected him in their efforts to do right by Claire.

Claire, by contrast and as Aaron comes to know only too well, is almost impossible to relate to. Michelle Monteith does unreachable better than anyone, and her performance here is expectedly and impeccably scary, the more so because even at her most capricious, she seems logical. Her finest moments, though, come at the very end when she is, for the only time, nakedly vulnerable; she also does childlike better than anyone. The play isn't exclusive monologue; the two actors have scenes together, mostly brief and psychologically or physically violent. Their last, delicate encounter is an exception, though as haunting a conclusion as it is, it leaves a few loose ends, especially concerning the neighbours.

One thing that connects the two households is music; Claire's and Aaron's mother teaches piano, the Vietnamese lady intermittently studies it. A 13-year-old pianist, Kaylie Lau, sits at the side of the stage punctuating the proceedings with Bach, and seeming in her own person to unite the girl we see and the one we only hear about. Natasha Mytnowych's production is as well orchestrated visually as verbally; Aaron talks to us from the light, Claire keeps irrupting from the dark, and from progressively scarier places.

My other Summerworks choices this year have been less happy. Hannah's Turn (Lower Ossington Theatre) at least offers a fine performance by Severn Thompson, who plays Hannah Arendt at two stages of her life, presented in alternating segments. She's an earnest young German-Jewish philosophy student, intellectually and physically seduced by Martin Heidegger before he became a Nazi; and she's her later self, famous and in America, questioning and haranguing a student of her own whose father was the only member of his family to survive the Holocaust. She's especially impressive in her grey-haired incarnation, as a careful thinker and, in what is after all her second language, talker. But the play itself (by Mark Migotti and Richard Sanger) is trite, taking the known facts and their most obvious ethical consequences and doing nothing with them, except perhaps to instruct us in some interesting niceties of concentration-camp slang. The love-passages of Hannah and Heidegger give us the student-teacher-seduction cliches without illuminating what he, in particular, subsequently became. Then, when they meet again postwar, she lectures him on the terrors of Nazism and his own insensitivity, neither of which are revelations. It doesn't help that Richard Clarkin plays the philosopher as an absentminded professor who hardly seems to believe his own ideas.

The Safe Word (Theatre Centre) is about love, or at least the current dating scene. Two new roommates dance around one another, she abrasively, he helplessly. An older, Russian, gay chess master looks on. The guy has a disturbing encounter with an emotionally older woman. The play stops. There is the occasional sharp line, as there tends to be when sex is the subject. The author is Nicolas Billon and the director Lee Wilson, both of whom have done better in the past. The overall nervelessness may partly be blamed on the weather. Maybe our theatre schools should institute a new class: How To Act Over Air-Conditioning.

The Physical Ramifications of Attempted Global Domination (Passe Muraille) brings together, for the first time on any stage, Napoleon Bonaparte, Adolf Hitler, Oliver Cromwell, Pol Pot, Idi Amin, Pancho Villa, Mao Tse Tung and Pope Pius XII, who seems a little out of place in this company, whatever you think of his war record, but is maybe standing in for popes through the ages. They're all played by women. They compete in a game show. Each boasts of his own atrocities while blaming the others for theirs. At the very end we hear about their respective illnesses. The performances are eight shades of awful.

The Summerworks festival continues until Aug. 14. For schedule and ticket information, visit summerworks.ca.

THEATRE REVIEW

The Homecoming

Avon Theatre, Stratford

In 1958, the British theatre critic Irving Wardle, later to become the revered reviewer for The Times, wrote an essay entitled "Comedy of Menace," in which he identified a group of playwrights devoted to raising laughs by raising chills, for purposes satirical, metaphysical or both. His prize exhibit was Harold Pinter, whose only full-length play at the time was The Birthday Party. In this play, he noted, menace, in itself a meretricious and easilymanufactured device, stands for something more substantial: Destiny.

Wardle did not, contrary to claims in the Stratford program, invent the "comedy of menace" label for Pinter's The Homecoming, which didnt come along until 1964, though it certainly is plenty comic and plenty menacing. Its a far tidier, more accomplished play than The Birthday Party, but it doesn't have the same sense of inevitability. Its characters are the playthings not of destiny but of their author's caprice. It ends up feeling forced and false.

Morally, this may be to the playwrights credit. The most acute comment on the play may have come from another playwright, Joe Orton, whose specialty was the comedy of bland outrageousness. Theres a very Ortonesque moment in The Homecoming when a character is felled by a heart attack and another character says what a shame that is because he'd been hoping the victim would drive him to the airport. It brings the house down, but it isn'tcredible. The trouble, according to Orton, is that he really believed people were that heartless but Harold doesnt. The line plays like imitation Orton. And so, more importantly, does the major plot development in which a father and two of his sons conspire to turn the wife of a third son into a call girl, to her acquiescence and that of her husband.

Its not that such a thing couldn't happen. It's not even that the play hasnt prepared the ground; its dropped all kinds of hints about the wife's previous life and present discontents, and it's positively revelled in depicting the men of the house as competitive misogynists. But it still seems to be happening because the author, against his natural grain, is willing it to happen. And yes, the menace is manufactured, though how easily only Pinter himself would know.

To be more specific: Were in the North London house of Max, a retired butcher; his brother Sam, a chauffeur; and Maxs sons Lenny, who we gradually gather is a pimp, and Joey, an aspiring boxer who, according to his dad, has now only two things to learn: how to defend himself and how to attack. In this household, not knowing those things is fatal; psychologically everyone in it, Max and Lenny especially, is always on the attack and had better know how to defend. The place has been womanless since the death of Max's wife, whose memory he alternately reveres and reviles; Max now does the cooking and this, plus a gammy leg, undermines his status.

Another British critic, the late Ronald Bryden, described the play, and Pinter's work in general, as a fight for territory; as a theory, this has the disadvantage that you could apply it to almost any play ever written, but it is fair to say that The Homecoming gives us the battle for stage space in its purest form, with Max as the wounded lion surrounded by ambitious cubs. The eldest of them, Teddy, got out and became a philosophy professor in America; he now returns with Ruth, his wife and mother of his own three sons. The family, whove never met Ruth before, greet her as Teddys whore. She, though, is a match for even the impenetrably street-smart Lenny: "you take this glass," she tells him during their major altercation and I'll take you. That line is, in its self-consciousness, the first false note in a hitherto pitch-perfect text. It's like imitation Pinter.

This chiselled, oracular tone dominated the first production of The Homecoming, and its become the recognized "Pinter style," though oddly enough Pinters acting in his own plays was nothing like it; he was wonderfully forceful and brutal, barrelling through with never a trademark pause in sight. He would have made a magnificent Max.

Jennifer Tarver's Stratford production is in the older, heavier tradition but strong and exact on its own terms. The nearest thing to a weak link is the Max of Brian Dennehy, who's physically too tall for the role and vocally too slight; he negotiates all the transitions from bullying to cringing without carrying absolute conviction at either extreme. Since the play literally begins and ends with Max, this matters.

Aaron Krohn is a brilliant Lenny, in absolute command of the flash, needling idiom, and Ian Lake an enchantingly vacant Joey. Stephen Ouimette makes a real flickering moral force of Sam who, like Petey in The Birthday Party, is the small disregarded voice of decency. Mike Shara, ineffectual rather than distant, softens Teddy who should probably be as callous as his siblings, but he does what he does very well. Cara Ricketts, handed the most opaque role in the play, makes Ruth a living woman, intelligent as well as beautiful, a believable lust-object for the men but more than a mystery object for the audience.

Leslie Frankish's costumes are spot-on, though Teddy's turtleneck does seem to be about to devour him; her set is big and brown and brooding, fittingly devoid of any feminine influence whatsoever. The Homecoming has been described as "the ultimate Pinter play," and so it is: with all the brilliance that implies, and all the limitations.

- In repertory until Oct. 30. For tickets, call 1-800-567-1600 or visit stratfordfestival.ca.

Cylla Von Tiedemann / Brian Dennehy battles for stage space with the cast of The Homecoming.;; Caption:

THEATRE REVIEW

The Misanthrope

Festival Theatre, Stratford

Hosanna

Studio Theatre, Stratford

Moliere wrote comedies about monomaniacs: misers, hypochondriacs, religious charlatans and their dupes, grotesquely possessive husbands. In all of these the audience is on the outside, laughing in; as is the author himself.

The Misanthrope, by general consent his greatest though possibly least funny play, is also about a monomaniac: Alceste, who believes in telling people to their faces exactly what he thinks of them and is willing to take the consequences. So far, so admirable; but Alceste has, as he himself admits, an Achilles heel. He's in love: with Celimene, a compulsive flirt who also believes in saying what she thinks about people, but only behind their backs and in sycophantic company.

He has another problem, too; he's inclined to glory in his own rudeness. The question of where honesty ends and vanity begins is a nice one, and the play makes no pretence of resolving it. That's true even on the level of plot; Alceste regularly threatens to depart to some desert place where he can be his uncompromising self, and at the end of this one he does indeed storm off with that apparent intention. But his friends - yes, he has friends - go after him. As in Twelfth Night, currently available on the same stage, they pursue him and entreat him to a peace, and maybe they'll have better luck than the Illyrians had with Malvolio. This seems like a situation that could go on for ever.

Plainly, Moliere had more invested in Alceste than in any of his other protagonists. It's not just that he played the role himself (as actor-manager, he always starred in his own shows); it's that his much younger wife played Celimene. Jealousy in this play goes deeper than in any of Moliere's others. It's as much intellectual as physical; Alceste fears that Celimene is mocking not just his devotion but his ideals.

The Stratford production, directed by David Grindley, has two great things going for it. One is its elegant simplicity. The old Festival Theatre stage, with its steps and balcony, has been restored, and as ever it provides a wonderful focus, especially for this formal comedy. Everyone seems to be in the right and meaningful place at the right time, and there's especially witty use of the upper level. The designer, John Lee Beatty, has draped the old Tanya Moiseiwitsch structure in gilt and gold, and Robin Fraser Paye has decked the actors out in handsome Louis XIV costumes.

The second treat is that, more than ever before in my experience, the play becomes an evenly matched love story for two people.

Ben Carlson's Alceste, as expected, wraps his tongue pointedly and wittily around the rhyming couplets of Richard Wilbur's translation. He's delightful in the moments in which Alceste makes an agonized try at being tactful. When the dam bursts and he lets fly he might, if anything, be more explosive than he is.

What really strikes home is the desperation with which he tries, in their last and remarkably moving scenes together, to prove to himself, and to make her prove, that Celimene is worthy of him. And what strikes equally hard is the refusal of Sara Topham's Celimene to grant the necessity of any such thing. She has her own corner to fight, and her own identity to protect. She may be a coquette but she's nobody's fool; her shallowness does not, so to speak, go very deep. There's a lovely moment at which she spreads the folds of her voluminous dress over a pouffe in front of her, and controls the scene from there. It's plain that these two love one another, and that they both lose.

As Celimene's prudish rival Arsinoe, too, often played as a mere frump, Kelli Fox, gives a delicious, velvet-clawed performance. Her command of the text rivals Carlson's, and their scene together is a joy. Peter Hutt, with threatening eyebrows, makes the courtier-poet Oronte a man whose wrath Alceste might have some reason to fear, which proves him a heroic critic indeed. As Philinte, the voice of moderation or hypocrisy depending on your point of view, Juan Chioran stops the show, or did on the first night, with his impersonation of Alceste before the courts, scaling heights of anger that actually exceed any displayed by the hero himself. As Eliante, his female counterpart, Martha Farrell is uneven; sometimes defeated by the script's technical demands, at others sailing right through them, but always believable as another prize worth winning.

The production is refreshingly uncynical about these two. This has been a vintage misanthropic year; Stratford's production isn't better than the one at Tarragon, which was really a different play, but it's as good.

Stratford has another play translated from the French, or at least the French-Canadian: Michel Tremblay's Hosanna, the saga of a disillusioned drag queen. Gareth Potter, shoulders heaving at moments of stress, gives a very good performance of the passionate Liz Taylor impersonator, though he doesn't muster the full venom for the role.

Oliver Becker is excellent as his biker boyfriend, and Weyni Mengesha's production is very well-paced, much the best of the four I've seen. So if I still felt, halfway through the second act, that I now knew as much about these characters as the author could tell me, I guess it must be the play's fault. (I've never understood the theories about the play being a metaphor for a Quebec with an identity crisis, but then I wasn't around at the time.)

Toward the end it gets very sentimental, falling back on having the couple say "I love you" as if it were a revelation. Meanwhile the idea that Hosanna can only become a real man by crossing crossdressing off his list now seems dubious; this is a play that Sky Gilbert might consider updating. Anyhow the production completes a good Stratford season, with several peaks and no clunkers.

- The Misanthrope is in repertory through Oct. 29; Hosanna through Sept. 24. For tickets, call 1-800-567-1600 or visit stratfordfestival.ca.

THEATRE REVIEW

Exit the King Young Centre for the Performing Arts, Toronto

Eugene Ionesco's Exit the King is a play that seems, provokingly, to have set out to be a masterpiece. Even more provokingly, it succeeds.

Ionesco, the supposed maestro of the Theatre of the Absurd (a gimcrack term used to bestow a false uniformity on many disparate playwrights, and one that he to his credit disliked) wrote the play in 1962 when serious illness brought him face to face with his own mortality. (He got better.) Solipsism, or maybe just narcissism, was an affliction not unknown to Ionesco; he once said that he could write about everybodys problems by writing about his own. But in this play he did create a universal fable. He covers the whole spectrum of a human beings attitude toward death. He takes in both the physical and the metaphysical. He makes it funny and he makes it moving. Soulpepper's new production does the same.

The play's method is to collapse time and to create a metaphor. King Berenger, Ionescos recurring little man/everyman figure but with a crown on, is informed at the beginning of the play that hell be dead at the end of it. That gives him two hours and 20 minutes, with intermission. At first he refuses to believe it; of course he's going to die some time, he knows that, but today? He tries to prove his continuing strength, but at every step his body betrays him. He even cries from his balcony for one of his subjects to exchange lives with him, but nobody answers. (The kingdom's severely depopulated anyway.)

His counsellors remind him that everybody dies; "nobody living has," he replies, which is quite a comeback really. He clings to every sensation, every taste. He cant decide whether he wants to be remembered or forgotten.

Berenger has been alive for 400 years, and king for most of them. His reign, apparently glorious to begin with, is now in ruins, as is his kingdom. The throne room, where the play is set, has an ever-widening crack in its wall and, at least in this production, a fearsome slope in its floor. As a dramatic device, Berengers kingship combines the symbolic (every man the centre of his own universe) and the satirical; indeed the state of Berenger's world, where the environment is really acting up, seems more topical now than when the play was written.

The precedent kings of whom he most reminds us are Canute and Lear. Like the former, he tries under pressure to stop nature in its tracks; like the latter, he comes to realize that he has neglected his poorer subjects. Talking to the maid-of-all-work who seems to constitute the palace's entire domestic staff, he inquires, solicitously and for the first time, into the details of her daily round. Unlike Lear, though, he feels sorrier for himself than for her; what really concerns him now is the memory of the stew she used to serve him. He clings especially to the wonder of carrots.

A play that starts by announcing the protagonists death and then devotes itself to showing it happen is unlikely to be a riot of suspense. The only comparable piece I can think of is the medieval morality Everyman, of which Exit the King is really the secular version; instead of admonishing us to make our peace with God, it tells us to let go of selfishness because, well, really, we wont have any choice. The only previous production of the Ionesco that I have seen was a starkly ceremonial one starring Alec Guin-ness, and it was very boring. Albert Schultz's production, which in this context is something of a revelation, uses a sparky new translation by Geoffrey Rush (who played it in Australia and on Broadway) and Neil Armfield, and is crammed with comic detail, outrageous but never gratuitous. His Berenger is Oliver Dennis, whose resume pre-Soulpepper includes clowning with Theatre Columbus.

Exit the King here starts with the king entering, crossing the stage, nose in air, trailing the very longest of trains; I half expected him to turn a couple of corners and appear again behind it. This most sympathetic of actors never plays for sympathy; he doesn't slight on the pettiness or the peevishness, and he is superb in the symphony of collapsing limbs. He is a very ordinary man, whose weaknesses are magnified by his position and who achieves grandeur by enforcedly transcending them; before then his unceasingly fluctuations, as he clings desperately and indignantly to life, are so consuming and so recognizable as to be suspenseful in themselves.

His subjects, pulling and pushing him both ways, accentuate the tension; all excellent, they are Brenda Robins as his imperious first wife; Karen Rae as his younger and coexistent second; William Webster as a doctor whos all brisk professional protocol; Trish Lindstrom as the universal slavey; and Derek Boyes, who relays the kings ricocheting moods as a series of public-service announcements. It's the cruellest characters, the older queen and the physician, who turn out to be the kindest; they're the ones who counsel Berenger to accept his death - Robins literally sees him through it - while Rae, whose seductiveness is a desperate kind of selfishness, has to leave the field defeated. Lorenzo Savoini's set is a triumph of dilapidation; you half-expect it to fall apart before your eyes.

- Exit the King runs until Sept. 9. For tickets, visit soulpepper.ca or call 416-866-8666.
