2011-08-20-hairdresser-confessions-da-ki:
When Trey Anthony's da Kink in My Hair was seen at the Princess of Wales Theatre six years ago it had a few musical numbers, and I wished that there might be more. I should have been more careful. The shows new staging at Harbourfront, produced by the author herself, now has 11 musical sequences by the program's count. It doesn't seem like a musical, more like a play with a lot of interruptions. The new production has its strengths, which include some of the music, but what was once a rough, uneven and invigorating piece now seems bloated in form and shrunken in content. da Kink has already had a spinoff, in the form of a mediocre TV series; in this version, it looks like a spinoff of itself.

The director is Michele Shay, who first staged the play at the NYU Tisch School for the Arts. Several recent Tisch graduates are in the current cast, along with a couple of comparably young Canadians. The setting, as before, is Novelettes hairdressing salon in Toronto. As well as being an expert stylist, Novelette functions as counsellor, confidante and mother confessor to her clientele, who are all female and nearly all black. Novelette believes the key to a woman's character lies in her hair, though the show states and restates the point rather than proving it, and she gives each customer brief advice or consolation, after each has divulged the details of her life. Some are happy, most aren't; even though the general tenor of the show is upbeat. Each vignette reaches us in the form of a monologue; or, in this production, a monologue followed by a song.

Whether through enforced economy or artistic choice, the actual life of the salon, its day-to-day bustle that was a strength of the play as originally staged by Weyni Mengesha, has virtually disappeared from this production. Theres a chair in the middle of the stage, and thats about it. Novelette herself (Alana BarrettAdkins) is reduced to the role of mistress of ceremonies, though a spirited one. The sense of group life is further diminished by the inexperience of the cast. The first thing to go in a nonprofessional or semi-professional production is usually - not always - timing: not necessarily the timing of individual lines or speeches but the rhythm, the ebb-and-flow, between actors. Which means the second thing to go is overall pace. Which is what happens here.

The monologues themselves vary greatly in effect, with the best moments involving the most pain. We have the evangelical mother (Naja S. Selby) whose boy was killed in a gang shoot-out in a parking lot, and who wonders where the police were; and the white woman from the American South (Jennifer Neales) whose family disowned her when she married a black man, and whose heart was broken afresh when, after a supposed reconciliation, they turned on her young son and she pretended not to notice. Both these performances pierce the heart; so, eventually, does the star TV actress (Teryl Brouillette) who found out who her friends weren't when she came out as a lesbian. Her story is weakened by some awkward audience participation involving her mother; on the other hand it does have the most effective musical sequel of any, composed by Michael McElroy, who's credited with half the score. (The other half is by Carol Maillard.)

The most piercing speech of all, as it was in the original, is that of the young Trinidadian girl who was overjoyed to be brought to Canada to join her mother, and who then found herself being abused by her stepfather. I never expected to find a performance in this role that rivalled that of dbi.young, but Thais Francis is equally moving, both in her initial joy and in her later shame and terror. Unfortunately shes subjected, like everyone in the cast only more so, to amplification that makes her sound as if her voice were coming from some place else. Presumably the face mics are there for the musical sections, but it's shameful to keep them on for the dialogue; the Enwave is not exactly a big theatre. It adds to the feeling that the songs and dances aren't earning their keep. (Theres already a musical about hair, and several about kinks.) Giving each character both a speech and a song makes the show feel repetitive; this, on top of the pacing problems already noted, makes it feel long. ? da Kink in My Hair runs through Aug. 21 at the Enwave Theatre, Harbourfront. Call 416-973-4000 or visit tickets.harbourfrontcentre.com for ticket information.

2011-08-23-doing-it-their-way:
THEATRE REVIEW

Come Fly Away

Four Seasons Centre for the Performing Arts, Toronto

Frank Sinatra never sang the words "come fly away." He did of course sing the words "come fly with me," at the beginning of the song of that name, closely followed by "come fly, let's fly away." But "come fly away," no. Which makes it odd that Twyla Tharp should have made that the title of her dance piece set to Sinatra songs. Maybe there's some arcane copyright reason. It's even odder in that Come Fly with Me itself is not one of the show's chosen songs. It points to a certain spirit of approximation, or compromise, or opportunism that does in fact permeate the entire entertainment. It's as if - excuse me while I mix some metaphors - the show were trying to hang itself from Sinatra's hatband without having earned hanging rights.

Fourteen dancers, comprising eight principals and an ensemble, perform Tharp's choreography to 24 Sinatra recordings, plus three instrumental ringers. The vocals have been surgically detached from their orchestral accompaniments; instead, and I guess preferably, a live band plays the original arrangements. The dancers and musicians are all excellent, and the singing, obviously, is magnificent. (Well, most of it is. I may be the only Sinatra-phile who has never much cared for his version of The Way You Look Tonight. And it's my favourite song.) It's Tharp's own contribution that's the letdown. Her staging amounts to 80 minutes of second-best Broadway.

She's also credited with "concept and book." The former may be the idea of setting dances to the songs. The latter is a bemusing term for a show with no spoken words, but perhaps it refers to the story, which is paper-thin. Four couples meet in a bar, and fall in and out of love or lust for the duration, their moods theoretically reflecting, or dictated by, whatever music happens to be playing. As a prologue we have Sinatra singing the verse to Stardust, setting a nostalgic bittersweet mood to which the show never returns. (There's no matching epilogue.)

Then the full lights go up and the company assembles in the watering hole, for a generic athletic opening number to the strains of Luck Be a Lady. That song, you may remember, was originally about gambling. There's no hint of that here; here, insofar as it's about anything beyond being an opening number, it's about getting lucky with a lady. Which, considered on its own, may be a legitimate stretch. It seems a shame, though, to take one of the few songs of the evening that isn't some kind of love song and turn it into one.

And that really is the problem, and it may explain why Tharp's work here is so far below the level of her previous dance-musical, Movin' Out. The musical material there, Billy Joel songs, was far less distinguished, but it did have wider-reaching subject matter; it gave her something to dramatize. Sinatra, most of the time, just sang love songs: happy love songs and sad love songs. He found marvellous distinguishing nuances in their lyrics, but it's hard to provide physical equivalents for them. The difference here between the subtlety of the sounds and the blatancy of the moves can be painful. Actually, it's worse than that.

I said that Sinatra sang sad love songs; and in fact, invigorating though his up-tempos can be, it was in the heartbreak ballads, sometimes called "suicide songs," that he did his greatest work. Come Fly Away includes just one of them, the iconic One for My Baby. Well, how do you illustrate that? Not the song itself - it started life, after all, as a driven specialty for Fred Astaire - but Sinatra's broken-voiced assumption of the solitary drinker, pouring his heart out to an unresponsive bartender. Tharp's solution is to have one of her couples do a slo-mo recap of the happier times the singer is presumably recalling. Meanwhile, on the other side of the stage, a waiter clears up for the night. The latter touch is appropriate and effective. All the same, it's tempting just to close your eyes and listen.

It may be telling - or maybe it's just carelessness - that some of the brighter Sinatra numbers, Witchcraft or You Make Me Feel So Young, are heard not in the singer's definitive 1950s performances but in his more blatant, less delicate remakes from the following decade. There is nothing spooky or teasing about the dance to Witchcraft; it's just another strenuously suggestive duo, in sub-Bob Fosse style. Humour is out, too; Sinatra's and Neal Hefti's Pick Yourself Up, with its cheeky delayed ending, loses its impact by being cut in half. Numbers such as Yes, Sir, That's My Baby and Let's Face the Music and Dance have little relation to what their lyrics are saying and less to how they're saying it. Even eroticism can pall.

That's hardly the performers' fault. Ashley Blair Fitzgerald, in particular, is endlessly sexy with gorgeous auburn hair, a body that seems to thrive on being thrown about Apache-style, and limber legs that wrap themselves provocatively, and often, around her partner. On Fly Me to the Moon, she really does seem about to take off into space. She and Anthony Burrell also shine on That's Life, not one of the Voice's finest hours but one in which Tharp finds genuine punchy inspiration. The corps en masse are also well served on Here's to the Losers, with its witty Marty Paich arrangement that keeps promising to turn into I Wish I Were in Love Again. (Now there's a song they might have included.) It's significant though that the strongest, most inventive dances are done to the non-vocal tracks, and that the best of them is to Dave Brubeck's Take Five, a song with no Sinatra connections whatever.

As if to compensate, the evening ends with the Chairman's two late-life hits, My Way, done at grim full length though it's a song loathed by every Sinatra fan I've ever known and also apparently by the man himself, and New York New York. These are presumably thrown in for easy identification as neither of them has any relevance to the story the show has purported to be telling. At the very end, courtesy of Donald Holder's fine lighting design, an outline of Sinatra's face appears in the empyrean, as if the show has been about him. It hasn't.

- Come Fly Away runs until Aug. 28. For tickets, call 416644-3665 or visit dancap.com.

2011-08-27-savage-whimsy-or-how-to-descr:
Judith Thompson's White Biting Dog begins with a depressed and divorced 31-year-old lawyer, who goes by the name of Cape Race, preparing to kill himself by jumping off the Bloor Street Viaduct. (The play dates from 1984, when this was a more practicable endeavour than it is now.) He's talked down, kind of, by a small dog whom the audience can neither see nor hear, and who informs him that he can save himself by saving his father. Father, whose name is Glidden, has been brought to the point of dissolution by his own depression. It isn't exactly a case of like father, like son, as Glidden's sadness has something winsome and quirky about it, while Cape is just desperately glum. Still reeling from his canine encounter, Cape encounters Pony, a former paramedic who now practises her healing arts in a shopping mall. Pony is also a medium whose control is a dog seemingly not unlike the one that appeared to Cape. Cape and Pony team up, to rescue Glidden by reuniting him with his absconded wife, Loamia. As luck would have it, she turns up at the family home that very night, accompanied by Pascal, her latest young stud. They need refuge because their own place has been torched by a meth addict.

If all that sounds weird, extreme and more than a little ridiculous: well, it is. It does have energy, and even a certain charm, at least in its earlier stages; and these qualities are very well captured in Nancy Palk's Soulpepper production, her debut as a director and, in terms of attack and actors' togetherness, an impressive one. It scores less well on quotidian believability, but that might not have been intended or even appropriate. All the same, Christina Poddubiuk's set does seem to have mortgaged any appearance of domesticity for the sake of providing an upper level for the first brief scene on the bridge. In the Thompson plays that I think I like best (Crackwalker or I Am Yours), the excesses spring from some defined social background. Here, they seem to be there for their own sake. I'd describe the play's tone as savage whimsy, with emphasis on the noun.

Cape's schemes for preserving his dad are murky, and very much made up on the fly, but we want them to succeed, if only because Glidden is played by Joseph Ziegler at his most commandingly endearing. Whether crawling about his house covered in earth or, at a hopeful moment, erect and tuxedoed, he's sympathetic without ever being squishy. Most moving is his realization that though he loves his wife, she doesn't love him, at least not carnally, which for her is what counts. Fiona Reid, who goes through most of the play in a slip, makes this blazingly clear in a performance glittering with wit and need, like a Tennessee Williams heroine gone north. Gregory Prest's Pascal is an appealing third side to the triangle, with a Mohawk hairdo and, initially, a hoarse mutter of a voice because, we are told, he despises the English language. In the second act, though, he talks like anyone else, which suggests the play has a fondness for short-term effects.

This is confirmed by a series of more or less erotic encounters - between Loamia and Pascal, Pascal and Cape, even Cape and Loamia - which are arresting in themselves but have no particular connection with how the characters behave before or after. The Loamia-Glidden relationship does hold and develop, but everything around it is just attitude. And that goes especially for Cape and Pony. Pony hardly stops talking, and Michaela Washburn can't muster the resources to prevent her saintly earth-motherliness from becoming tiresome. She claims that in making love to Cape she let "evil" enter into her, a crucial claim (or so I assume) that isn't credible. Mike Ross can do many things, including beating a terrific drum for Pony's seances, but embodying evil doesn't seem to be one of them. I admired his intensity and his watchfulness, the latter a quality much emphasized in the staging, without ever understanding just what dog was biting him. The name Cape Race, we are given to understand, is self-bestowed; his mother called him Sonny. Well, sometimes funny names work and sometimes they don't. I still have fond memories of Claudia Dey's Trout Stanley whose hero, questioned on that point, said simply "it's a fish name." If Dey hadn't given up writing plays she might rank with Michael Healey, John Mighton and Hannah Moscovitch among those who are producing work better than anything from the supposed Golden Age of Canadian drama.

From a play with a dog to its name but nowhere else, to a circus without animals. In other words, Cirque du Soleil is back in town with Totem, directed by Robert Lepage and announced as "the Odyssey of the Human Species" but not in chronological order. In other words, anything goes. But there is more continuity and sense of purpose than usual, and of course, some of the visuals are extraordinary. The basic setting is a turtle-shaped island, suffused with water without an actual drop being spilled; it's all done with projections. (Get this man to direct The Tempest.) Among the acts that show what humanity is capable of, I was especially dumbstruck by a quintet of lady unicyclists who balance on their heads what look like dim-sum baskets and who toss them from one to another with dazzling abandon, sometimes doing it back-handed. They top it off with teapots. There's also a twoman high-wire act that demonstrates the true meaning of trust. And there are animals. At least, there are performers in gorilla suits who ambush what looks like a team of chartered surveyors, one of whom turns really nasty when they try to stomp on his cellphone. They then strip off and perform acrobatics so intrepid that even the anthropoids applaud. The clowns are as tedious as ever, and the stunts in the second half are a bit disappointing, declining from the flatly impossible to the merely incredible; though there's still a bewitching male-female double act, on a trapeze: a graceful altercation for two real-looking people. My companion thought they represented Adam and Eve, and she could well be right. A figure clad in silver foil descends on a wire at the start to get the species started, and returns at intervals to pick up the odd chair. Furniture removal is the bane of many directors' lives, and this show may have found the perfect graceful solution.

- White Biting Dog runs until Oct. 1 at the Young Centre for the Performing Arts. Visit soulpepper.ca or call 416866-8666 for ticket information. Totem runs through Oct. 9 at the Grand Chapiteau, Port Lands. Visit cirquedusoleil. com or call 1-800-450-1480 for details.

2011-08-30-water-water-everywhere:
THEATRE REVIEW

When the Rain Stops Falling Studio Theatre, Niagara-on-the-Lake, Ont.

The year is 2039, and in Alice Springs, Australia, a dead fish falls from the sky. This is even odder than it might seem, because the man at whose feet it falls, whose name is Gabriel York, informs us that this kind of fish has been extinct for years. For him, the miracle couldn't have come at a better time, because it means hell now have some dinner for his son, whom hes about to meet for the first time in two decades.

Gabriel had walked out on his family as, in a way, had his father before him and, in another way, his father before him. Gabriel's father was also called Gabriel and his mother Gabrielle, which the couple themselves admit to be quite a coincidence. Andrew Bovell's When the Rain Stops Falling is composed of echoes and parallels, parents and children, husbands and wives. Its a tremendous play, and the Shaw Festival has given it a superb production.

The program tells us that Bovell belongs to a theatrical wave, distinguished among other things by characters who . acted like full-blooded Australians, that started to gather in the late 1960s. As an ignorant Pommie, I find this claim surprising; I do know that as far back as the 1950s there was a full-blooded Australian play called The Summer of the Seventeenth Doll that conquered the world. Besides, more than half the characters of When the Rain Stops Falling are English, either by birth or recent descent.

After its futuristic prologue, the play takes us back to London in 1959, and it keeps switching between years and countries. Its two female characters are each played by both a younger and an older actress. It presents a cats cradle of relationships, a mosaic of themes; and I'm more than usually reluctant to give away details of plot, because so much of its fascination depends not just on what is revealed but how and when.

We watch people discovering things and concealing things. We arrive at the realization, explicitly stated in the dialogue and honestly backed up by the action, that when they don't talk to one another its often not because they have nothing to say, but because they have too much. We watch them wrestling with appalling fears and guilts, their own or their parents or partners'. It's all, once youve latched on, surprisingly easy as well as satisfying to follow.

We also, as per the title, see and hear a lot of weather. Many entrances are made with umbrellas. The Australian drought seems by 2039 to have ended, to be succeeded by conditions even more cataclysmic. A recurrent flippant line in the dialogue is "there are people drowning in Bangladesh" (or East Pakistan, depending on the date); by the last scene, which returns us to the first, they actually are - and everywhere else, apparently. The play manages - and I wouldnt have thought it possible - to rhyme, without glibness, environmental catastrophes with human ones.

Shaw has paired its great choice of script with an ideal choice of director. Peter Hinton, picking up on the author's stage directions, stages the play around, and sometimes on, a great table, at once epic and domestic. The space that frames it is square, backed on Camellia Koo's set by movable, translucent screens. Kevin Lamottes lighting and Richard Ferens sound are magic, even for them.

What marks Hinton as a great director is that the performances and the images seem to have grown up together. The evening feels wonderful from the moment when Ric Reid, a fine taken-for-granted actor, launches into his opening monologue, in a play otherwise composed almost entirely of duologues, and mines all of its wryness, cragginess, bewilderment and pain.

There are a few performance flaws, and the play's central incident strains - not so much coincidence as the characters' recognition of it - a few inches too far. But this is a show that excites while you're watching it, and just keeps on resonating. It has to be revived or transferred or both. Shaw, like Stratford, has had an unusually good season and this belongs, with Cat on a Hot Tin Roof, at the very top of the rock.

- In repertory until Sept. 17. For tickets, call 1-800-511-7429 or visit shawfest.com.

David Cooper / "All I wanted was an umbrella, or at least a nice parka!" Ric Reid as Gabriel York in When the Rain Stops Falling.;; Caption:
2011-09-03-this-time-the-show-has-a-shap:
The new Second City revue Dreams Really Do Come True! (And Other Lies) is not one of the best. It is, for example, nowhere near as good as its immediate predecessor. Still, it has a few things going for it with which few of its forerunners have bothered. One of them is a title that actually has some relevance to the show. The opening number features the six performers writhing nightmarishly about in the half-light and, yes, telling one another about their impossible dreams. There's the one, for example, who wants to be a star but is told to forget it because this is Canada. Snappy, that.

The show also has a shape. At least, it keeps referring back to its initial idea and staging, though the linking bits that keep nudging us in this direction are painfully lame. The closing number reprises key moments from what has gone before, something that's been done in the past at Second City but never this thoroughly. Half of these supposed highlights I was quite happy to be reminded of; the other half I'd rather forget.

I'll start, as the show itself does, with the good stuff. First up after the prelude is the dating sketch. Every Second City revue has one, but this breaks new ground by being about a good date. A man and a woman, matched by eHarmony, complain about their previous partners having lacked the intelligence for which they had advertised and then find that not only can they both name-drop Nietzsche, but they both sound as if they've actually read him. It's like when Harry met Sally, only better because they both explosively feel it and neither of them is faking.

Then there's the technology sketch, this one being a laughterof-painful-recognition item about a mother grovelling to her blackmailing eight-year-old for help with the Facebook photo and the VCR. Elsewhere in the evening Nigel Downer, who plays the kid, is more impressive at physical comedy than verbal, and in this scene he does indeed do some spectacular rolling-around. But it's his unbelieving cries of "Mom, it's so EASY" (the last word extended to some 20 syllables) that really eat into the grown-up soul.

Best of all, both subtle and savage, is the Stephen Harper sketch. This finds the tall and very funny Alastair Forbes as the PM, reflexively congratulating the short and very funny Jason DeRosse on his heroism as a disabled Afghanistan vet, the two of them remaining at devastating crosspurposes over what it's all supposed to be for. (Most persuasive rationale: "It's to help Tim Hortons gain a foothold in a new market.")

All these come before the intermission, as does the one in which a suburban married couple is dismayed by the news that their two hip downtown lesbian friends are about to tie their own knot. Not, of course, that they themselves have anything against gay marriage: just against marriage. (And the suburbs.) This, too, is familiar territory, but at least it's covered with a fair amount of zing. In its second half, though, the show goes into a steep decline, with only a couple of treasures. One, very nicely staged, is about mounted police representing the kinder, gentler face of law enforcement because, after all, it's hard to arrest someone when you're on a horse. The other is about breastfeeding in a public place and boasts that rarest of rarities, a punchline.

Otherwise, the show relies, to a crutch-like extent, on audience participation. On the first night, one intrepid conscript proved fully capable of upstaging the professionals when pressed into service as a grunt in Vietnam. This number is, or was, quite good fun though you may question why the show is digging into ancient history, and ancient American history at that. Don't they know there's a war or two on now? But perhaps one number on Afghanistan was thought to be enough. Not much fun at all, though the cast tried hard to behave otherwise, was a long bit about a TV station whose ownership kept changing, according to suggestions from the house. So all right, those who pay the piper get to call the tune, but at this rate shouldn't they be paid them-selves? And couldn't they call better ones, or ones that yielded funnier results? The responses here proved that it's possible to be improvisational and mechanical at the same time. But then it can't be easy to come up with good instant jokes about the Abraham Lincoln channel.

Two-thirds of the cast are new to the main troupe: all three of the men, plus Ashley Cormeau who's been lumbered with the interlocutor's role but is otherwise clever. The female recidivists are Carly Heffernan, who's likewise agreeable, and Inessa Frantowski who, playing a far-too-available lady with an accent that may possibly be Russian, gets to importune a gentleman spectator in a scene of which the show seems to be unreasonably proud. At least, they keep reminding us of it. The direction, both the good and the selfindulgent, is by Kerry Griffin.

- Dreams Really Do Come True runs indefinitely at The Second City, 416-343-0011.

Once upon a time there were two brothers and their washed-up father. Or, in the corpus of Arthur Miller's plays, once upon several times. The Price, first staged in New York in 1968 and now revived in a very fine production by Soulpepper, has Miller revisiting the territory he had earlier marked out in All My Sons and, especially, Death of a Salesman. Only in this play the father is already dead. In his time he had been a big shot. Then came The Crash. Which is another departure for Miller. It's reasonable to assume that the dreams and fears of Joe Keller and Willy Loman were partly fuelled by their having lived through the Depression. But their plays never mention it. The Price never stops mentioning it.

Old man Franz's two boys are Walter, who got out of the family home and became a very successful surgeon, and Victor, who sacrificed his own scientific ambitions to look after their widowed dad and who became a cop. Victor is now wondering whether to take early retirement, maybe pursue his old dreams. Another part of his past is more surely about to disappear. The old building on whose top floor he and his father used to live is about to be demolished; the physical evidence of their existence there - everything from a harp to a fencing-foil - is up for sale. Victor has found a dealer in the phone book, one Gregory Solomon who claims to be 90 years old; we believe him, not that he doesn't look in great elderly shape, but because he's the kind of man who could, and does, make anything sound believable. Which doesn't make him a cheat. Waiting impatiently with Victor is his wife Esther, who longs for a more comfortable life than they have ever had and who, in the meantime, would like to get out to a movie. For both these reasons, she hopes that Solomon will hurry up and give them a good price. The title, needless to say, has other reverberations, as in: What does a man's life add up to, and what value can you put upon it? Most of the play's second half is a bitter debate between the brothers, who haven't met in 16 years, on precisely these matters.

The first half belongs, really, to the dealer, who is a virtuoso creation. Miller was not previously known for being funny but in this character, who makes us crack up practically every time he opens his mouth, he seems to be gloriously compensating for a lifetime of sobriety. Solomon's also a breakthrough in another, though related, way: He's the first explicitly Jewish-American character in any Miller play. To be sure, much of the salt in Miller's earlier work, as in much American writing, comes from its use of Jewish idioms, or just Jewish word order, but this is the first of his plays in which it's out in the open (though the Franzes themselves still seem to be passing). Solomon, we learn, has been through three wives (he later, chiding himself for his absent-mindedness, amends this to four), several countries and uncountable careers, including an early one as a circus acrobat. He also, having seen and done it all, functions as a moral barometre; he sizes up Victor's marriage at a glance, and whenever Victor and Walter say, or seem about to do, something truly unpardonable or irretrievable, he steps in. Or rather, he slumps back, as if about to have a heart attack, as indeed he may; at his time of life, should you expect any different? Even when he's technically offstage, he seems to be keeping tabs on what's going on. The part is a gift for any actor, but it's hard to imagine it better done than it is by David Fox who, like his character, is both cunning and honest: a secular holy fool. For an actor with so strong and idiosyncratic a presence, Fox is remarkably versatile; this performance, wizened and stooping, has nothing in common with his beaming farmer in The Drawer Boy or his vulpine Rumsfeld in Stuff Happens beyond their completeness.

He does not, however, steal the show, which under Diana Leblanc's direction, is beautifully measured. Michael Hanrahan's Victor, wearing his uniform like a slightly uncomfortable second skin, is to-the-bone believable, right from the play's silent overture in which he lovingly lifts the dust sheets from the attic furniture that Paula Wing's program note aptly describes as "imagined in luxurious detail by designer Phillip Silver." (I'm not sure that it's the program's job to do the critics' work for them, but thanks anyway, Paula.) Hanrahan is quiescent, tolerant, almost genial when dealing with the dealer, or even with his own semi-alcoholic wife whom Jane Spidell somewhat underplays, perhaps in tactful self-defence; when Canada's own Kate Reid created the role on Broadway, one ended up disliking the actress for the faults of the character. It's only when his brother appears that Hanrahan begins to explode; trying through long habit to rein his anger in, this Victor looks as if he may burst a blood vessel.

Walter's arrival is the play's firstact curtain, and Stuart Hughes, transformed in camel-hair coat and tortoise-shell glasses and slickeddown hair, makes it an event. The character is in fact a lifelong selftransformer, and he has a tempting offer or two for Victor. Meanwhile, he taunts him with having thrown away his life for a selfish old man who could have fended for himself. ("What was he? Exiled royalty?") There is admittedly something dramatically unsatisfying about all this: As one recrimination and revelation leads inexorably to another, it all begins to seem a little too neat. And of course the real protagonist, however artfully Leblanc focuses on his empty chair, isn't there. But the author plays fair; there's little doubt where his deepest sympathies lie, but both combatants are given a fair shake; all their accusations strike home and Hanrahan and Hughes make the contest devastating, the more so for the tantalizing hope that these brothers may somehow act brotherly.

"Spite, spite, is the word of your undoing!" Willy Loman shouted at his son, wrongly in that case. But it's right enough in this one. It isn't, though, the play's last word; that goes to the wisdom of Solomon. He also gets the last laugh: a living example of the play's humanity and also, for reasons it would be unfair to reveal, of its craftsmanship.

? The Price runs to Oct. 22 at the Young Centre for the Performing Arts. Visit soulpepper.ca or call 416-866-8666 for ticket information.

Im not sure whether it's due to thoughtlessness, ignorance or plain old cashing-in, but Camelot, television's latest stab at domesticating the King Arthur legends, shares a title with the celebrated musical on the same subject. The two treatments do not, on the evidence of the first two TV episodes, have much else in common; though they do share a conception of Arthur himself as a starry-eyed idealist intent on bringing not only order and chivalry but a democratic spirit to the realm.

In the musical, human nature, as expressed in both love and politics, gets tragically in the way. Its too early to say whether the new Arthur (Jamie Campbell Bower), who looks and behaves like a male ingenue of 16, will be faced with the same challenges as he matures, or even if he will mature at all. I will just say cautiously that if youre an Arthurian fan who's also in search of literate writing, imaginative production and threedimensional acting, you'd be better advised to buy tickets for this years Stratford festival.

Not that this material hasnt always been up for grabs. Its hero is a supposedly ancient British monarch whose canonical treatment - Thomas Malory's Morte d'Arthur - didnt come along until the 15th century. It was born anachronistic. The TV Camelot, like most of its predecessors, is set in a hybrid of post-Roman Britain and medieval no-mans-land.

It starts by hewing tolerably close to Malory. King Uther Pendragon falls down dead. Merlin (a skin-headed Joseph Fiennes), who seems to be a mixture of court doctor and visionary counsellor with just possibly a bit of sorcery on the side, rushes off to reclaim Uther's son Arthur whom he stole when he was a baby, to be brought safely up by gruff old Sir Ector.

Arthur shyly accepts his destiny, attended by his devoted foster-brother Kay, whom he subsequently makes marshal of the kingdom. This is a departure, since in Malory Arthur starts out as a bit of a Cinderella, with Kay as his bullying Ugly Brother, a disposition that he maintains even after his promotion. Making Kay a faceless good guy seems rather less interesting.

On the other hand, the witch-like Morgan le Fay (Eva Green, much given to flaunting herself, vocally and physically), who in most versions malevolently haunts the story's outskirts, has been pulled firmly into its centre. Shes Arthurs half-sister by his father's first wife, and very jealous, though with occasional redemptive moments. Morgan seems to have sold her soul to a wolf, who presumably represents yet darker powers, and she goes into convulsions that make her look like a character from True Blood. She allies herself, in and out of bed, with King Lot, a warlord (note the timely terminology) with no redeeming features at all.

It seems for a time that there's going to be no Excalibur in this version, but eventually Arthur climbs a cliff to dislodge what Merlin calls the sword of the gods as opposed to just having it handed to him by what Monty Python and the Holy Grail, for which I often felt nostalgic, called "some bint in a river." That description would do very well for this shows Guinevere; at least we first see her emerging from a seaside dip. Arthur sees her too, and they are playfully attracted to one another. Turns out, though, that shes betrothed to one of his loyalist followers, which plainly points to breakers ahead.

The knight's name is not, as you might expect, Lancelot (there's no one of that name in sight) but Leontes, which suggests a displaced riff on the jealous king from Shakespeares The Winters Tale.

In principle, there's nothing wrong with any of these variations. In practice, though, they seem to have been drawn from a grab bag of perioddrama cliches, and written by a committee of the tin-eared. The first line is King Uther, there's a visitor; she wont give her name and it doesnt improve. When it isn't flat, it's pompous: "Leave now and salvage your life," Morgan tells Arthur: what's wrong with save?

Maybe a few more Canadian actors might have helped; Canadians these days get more experience in the classics than British actors and do them at least as well. Camelot, like The Tudors, is a Canadian coproduction (CBC, no less) but you wouldn't know it.

Actually, for all my carping, I prefer it to The Tudors, not to mention The Borgias; it gets itself fewer airs. It starts with the customary blanket warning - or promise - regarding "nudity, sexuality, violence and coarse language," but as it proceeds, it tells us which of these appetizing ingredients will appear in a given segment. So, depending on our preferences, you can stay glued or wait until after the next commercial break.

? Camelot premieres Sept. 13 at 9 p.m. on CBC.

Cbc / Slightly sinister Merlin, check. Ineffectual Arthur, check. But does Camelot add up to fun?;; Caption:

THEATRE REVIEW

The Tale of a Town

Theatre Passe Muraille, Toronto

It isn't really accurate to say that The Tale of a Town happens at Theatre Passe Muraille. Taking its name literally, and perhaps reverting to its roots, TPM is here the embarkation point for a walkabout tour of the immediate surrounding area of Queen Street West, with an ultimate destination that's just a couple of blocks away, at least if you happen to be a crow. It's a mix of two kinds of theatre, promenade crossed with site-specific.

The audience gathers outside the theatre building, there to be greeted by a white-faced mime whose performance seems to be a commentary on the gentrification of the neighbourhood. (The accompanying song is Rise Up.) This turns out to be the merest prelude to the main event, though it does establish the theme. Our attention is rudely commandeered by an excitable lady in a fright wig (blond) and a fright dress (red) who will be our guide on the magical mystery tour. She talks in rhyming couplets whose main effect was to make me, for the first time in my life, nostalgic for the mime.

Lisa Marie DiLiberto is the lady doing the talking while leading the walking. She's the artistic director of Fixt Point, whose co-production this is, and is the show's principal creator and sole actress, though with some assistance from musicians and what the credits call "shadow play performers." She appears later in more agreeable guises than her first, but it's hard to forgive the initial impression.

Why do people think couplets are so easy to write? Perhaps they are, if you have no regard for scansion or even, on occasion, to what a strict critic might regard as rhyme. It's a tough discipline, which if the rules are obeyed can have great potential for wit. If they aren't, it has even greater potential for being excruciating. The latter being the case here, I'm not sure whether it's good or bad that the doggerel being screeched at us in the open air as we jostle for an advantageous position is often inaudible. We seem, though, to be asked to admire the transformation of what was once a bohemian neighbourhood, and to be asked to buy into it. ("Two years ago you had the foresight to surmise / Your new condo was going to rise.") Life colluding with art, we walk right past a brand-new Winners.

All this of course is "deeply ironic." Our destination, when we reach it, turns out to be the loft floor of a recently burnedout building, which for the purposes of the show is being advertised as the Champagne Flaming Feather Eco Boho Legend Lofts, ripe for conversion at astronomical prices. (For $610,000,000, says a projected legend on one of the walls, you get all the amenities, including two phone jacks.) And in fact, and presumably at far lesser expense, the production team has done a great job of converting it into a performance space. We keep being ushered in to scenic areas we hadn't realized existed, and the videos, props and sound effects mustered under Varrick Grimes' direction are impressive, both in themselves and in the precision with which they punctuate the narrative, which does exist, even though it comes to us in the form of retrospective monologue.

It's the self-told story of Jane, whom DiLiberto plays with comparative (and merciful) restraint, who for many years ran a vintage-clothing boutique on Queen West but had to close when her landlord, with many regrets left on her voice mail, sold her out. She reminisces about the good times, including her romance with a rockabilly musician who drugged himself to death. Well, maybe you had to be there.

The story takes a long time to come into focus, and at this distance the scene doesn't sound all that attractive, or all that missable. Extrapolate as you will, it hardly amounts to the tale of a whole town. The most resonant line in the show is Jane's admission that when she started her business, she herself must have been displacing someone else. That bit of perspective apart, the show's journey (the appropriate term for once) is from clumsy satire to high-tech sentimentality.

? The Tale of a Town runs until Oct. 9 at Theatre Passe Muraille. For tickets, call 4165047529 or visit passemuraille. on.ca.

2011-09-21-no-one-should-take-opinion-as:
Soulpepper's production of Arthur Miller's The Price received a standing ovation on its first night. These days that isn't such a rarity, anywhere you go. But the cheers and claps on this occasion were unusually prolonged, to the point that they took the cast and stage management by surprise; the actors staggered on for their last call with the house lights up, and looking uncertain whether to stay or go. The audience, of course, lapped up the confusion, laughed in delighted sympathy and clapped all the harder.

Among "the audience" I include myself. I thought the enthusiasm wholly justified, participated in it and subsequently wrote a rave. My colleagues (that's journo-speak for the other critics) mostly didn't, which surprised me. Never mind the demonstrations at the end: Hadn't they noticed how the audience was held and excited by the soul baring and illusion stripping, not to mention the humour, that had gone before? Apparently not. I was shocked.

Which was probably silly of me, and is certainly ironic, because I've been in the identical situation to those reviewers on numerous other occasions, grimly keeping my head while those around me were vociferously losing theirs. Just this year, there have been at least three occasions -- Billy Elliot, Hugh Jackman in Concert, Come Fly Away -- when I've returned a negative verdict, in the face of apparently universal delight in the audience, reflected almost (though not always quite) unanimously in the other reviews. The reaction I aroused was predominantly one of resentment. I have the emails to prove it.

I'm not complaining. I even sympathize; my own feelings in the case of The Price weren't that different. When somebody fails to appreciate something you yourself have deeply enjoyed, it's hard not to feel personally affronted. This isn't logical -- why should your own pleasure in something be lessened by somebody else failing to share it? -- but it's human. You may feel that your whole value system is under attack. The feeling can be especially acute when the person who disagrees is someone you love. Though that may not be relevant to this discussion; after all, as more than one playwright has inquired, who loves critics?

We do, though, get questioned on other grounds. All three of the shows on which I've recently been called out have been large-scale commercial musicals, and several of my correspondents have questioned my credentials for pronouncing on musical theatre at all. I don't know how to answer that, because I don't know what the appropriate credentials would be. (I've seen a lot of musicals, if that helps.) Obviously the only credential that counts for most people is that of agreeing with them. It's also true that music affects us even more viscerally than drama, so feelings about it are apt to be more passionately expressed. In addition, a big musical has a big publicity machine behind it, and though ideally this shouldn't affect audience response, in practice it does, especially if the show in question has been a hit elsewhere; now it's come among us and we want a piece of the action. Then, too, patrons may enter the theatre with a built-in devotion, say to Hugh Jackman as a performer or to Billy Elliot as an emotionally loaded subject. Musicals give us more opportunity to applaud -- in a real sense, to participate -- as the show proceeds. And the tickets cost. Audiences are, in every sense, invested. These feelings are, of course, accentuated on an opening night, when the pitch can be feverish and there are plenty of interested parties present. Though, in all fairness, this can apply just as much for a play at Stratford or Soulpepper or the Tarragon as for a musical at the Canon or the Royal Alex or the Princess of Wales. The involvement may be different in degree but not in kind.

An accusation that frequently gets hurled at critics is that we may be spoiling, not our correspondents' fun, but that of hypothetical future audiences whom we are discouraging from seeing the show. It's an interesting point but I don't think it's a very serious one. I doubt, truthfully, that any of us locals have that much power; Toronto isn't New York where The Times is supposedly all-powerful. (Supposedly, not actually, even before the arrival of the Internet and its multitude of bloggers.) That's healthy; Toronto doesn't have as many critical voices as London, but it has several, and between us we're likely to cover the spectrum of possible responses towards a given show. Nobody should take the opinion of a single critic as gospel. Not to mention that, if we take the accusation literally, a negative review of any show has the potential of limiting its audience. It can't just apply to shows that the complainant happens personally to like. I doubt if anyone wants each of us to give raves to everything, but that would be the logical conclusion. In the case of the shows I've mentioned, the implicit appeal -- often the explicit appeal -- is to the verdict of the cheering crowds. Well, if word of mouth means anything, that verdict will make itself heard beyond anything a critic might say. (As, in the case of Billy Elliot, it demonstrably has.) I've noticed too that, as years go by, shows tend to acquire a "critical reputation" that may have little to do with what the critics actually said. As Arthur Miller might have said, as one who suffered his share of critical ups and downs and continues to after his death, it's the Price.

2011-09-22-all-aboard-hinton-s-theatre-a:
Last weekend I caught the final performance of the Shaw Festival's When the Rain Stops Falling, directed by Peter Hinton, and enjoyed it even more than I had on the first night. This Australian fable of catastrophe and (possible) redemption, followed across two continents and four generations in terms both human and meteorological, has been staged with Hinton's signature qualities of imagination and sensitivity, and also with his ability to draw from his actors work that's both committed and combustible. At the curtain call some of the cast seemed close to tears, as if this were one show they didn't want to let get away.

The director himself wasn't there. He's in Fogo Island, "an incredible place" (his words) in the northwest corner of Newfoundland, working on the plays of Henrik Ibsen, which somehow seems an ideal match of material and locale. As he pointed out to me in a telephone conversation, with the single exception of A Doll's House, all of Ibsen's plays are set in rugged coastal communities. It is, he says, "an amazing place to investigate Ibsen."

Hinton, a gentle and softspoken man who was once an actor and is still a playwright, is artistic director of the English company at the National Arts Centre in Ottawa, and the Ibsen project is the fifth incarnation of an NAC institution known as "The Ark": a kind of annual three-week retreat in which a group of actors "research a period of theatre history or an author."

Previous arks have been devoted to Shakespeare and Greek tragedy. Part of the idea, according to Hinton, is to "put together a company that's half students from the National Theatre School and half professional actors. It makes for a kind of informal mentorship. It also reminds the professionals that all of us are students."

They research, they read and work on the plays, and they hear lectures. "We've had historians, scholars, novelists. This year we've a philosopher telling us about Hegel, Kierkegaard, Nietzsche."

There's a company of 35, one of whom is actually Norwegian. Discussing the problems of translating Norway's national playwright, Hinton remarked that "Ibsen wrote plays in a language that's no longer spoken, a Danish-Norwegian hybrid. Even in Norway nowadays they have to be translated" - which I confess was news to me.

"We'rereading14 plays,"Hinton says. That's starting with the two great verse-dramas, Brand and Peer Gynt, and moving on, as Ibsen himself purposefully did, to the more familiar prose plays, a 12-play progression that the dramatist, according to Hinton, saw as a complete cycle. They do indeed mark a steady progression, beginning in the social drama of Pillars of Society and ending in the near-mysticism of When We Dead Awaken.

All this activity culminates this Friday in what's described as "the summit" or, more jovially, as "a presentation of a bit of what we've encountered." There'll be scenes and lectures. And then what? How does it affect what happens next in Ottawa? It doesn't apparently have to be anything obvious: "We're not necessarily planning to do An Enemy of the People next year," Hinton says. Still, "it has influenced our programming"; the Shakespeare project led to an NAC production of Macbeth, the Brecht to Mother Courage, the medieval one to "our cycle of morality plays," and "the Greek work fed into Saint Carmen of the Main," the early Michel Tremblay play on a Greek model, which the NAC visited in Toronto last year.

Hinton also mentions his superb NAC/Soulpepper production of The Way of the World, though I can't quite see which ark that restoration comedy escaped from. Anyway, he sees the effects of these projects as being somewhat less tangible. "The ark has fed into the NAC work in a very profound way. Here there's less pressure, it's more about the process," he says. "It's a great way to get to know our new artists."

All the company members currently in Fogo will reunite in Ottawa. "We're employing 34 actors this season, so it will be large," he says. And permanent? "About 20 of them will be there for the entire season." And, befitting a National Arts Centre, "it's national because our actors come from all across the country."

It's hard not to see a fanciful link between Hinton's current and most recent projects: When the rain stops falling, it's good to have had an ark. (And Ibsen, challenging the moral complacencies of his own time, says that his aim was "to torpedo the ark.") The connection, though, as you might expect, goes deeper than wordplay.

Hinton's own major work as a playwright is the Victorian trilogy The Swanne, a comic epic staged over three years at the Stratford Festival, and as a director he exhibits and responds to a combination of delicacy and strength. When Jackie Maxwell at the Shaw brought him the Rain play he responded to its "range of ideas, and the scope of its dramatic form. It bridges the gap between the tragic, poetic, sacred and the very real world."

And of course there's the landscape and the weather. Andrew Bovell, the author, describes his play as "a fog that gradually clears," which is how Hinton's production works and what relates it, not just to other wild classics, but to us.

"There are Australian and Canadian similarities: in the relationship to the land, and the colonial ties to England," Hinton says. "And the humour, in a funny way. An Australian woman I know told me 'the Australian sensibility is sarcastic.' "

From Niagara to Fogo to Ottawa, by imaginative way of the fjords and the Outback, may not be so impossible a journey after all. And it's hard to think of anyone better qualified than Hinton to pilot the ark.

2011-09-24-feeling-superior-to-prudish-v:
Dr. Givings, New York physician circa 1880, turns on the newly installed electric light in his living room and wonders at the marvels Edison has wrought. His wife, Catherine, feels less jubilant about the invention; she misses the subtler, flickering illumination of candlelight. This isn't all she misses; shes a nursing mother whose milk is insufficient and who has to hire a wet-nurse to compensate. Shes frustrated in other ways, too, ways that she can't quite identify or at least can't quite describe. Meanwhile, in the next room, which is his consulting room, her husband treats the fashionable and predominantly female complaint of hysteria by applying to his patients another new electronic device, a vibrator. The patients react with shocked enjoyment, though they get over the shock part. Can I, one of them inquires, get one of these to use at home?

In the Next Room, subtitled the vibrator play, is the work of the much-lauded youngish American playwright Sarah Ruhl, and its being given its Canadian premiere at the Tarragon (in a co-production with the Royal Manitoba Theatre Centre). Its an engaging play, in an engaging production. But it doesn't really hang together. It plays as if the author had let her mind roam over a series of loosely associated ideas, and assumed they would cohere into a narrative. It has the structure of a story but the feel of a fantasia. It reaches, for example, a hopeful ending that's nice in itself but seems in context like wishful thinking.

Its also historically suspect, maybe not in scientific detail but in philosophical assumption. Dr. Givings is allowed to take credit for an improved device, a splendid Heath Robinson contraption in the current staging, called the Chattanooga Vibrator, ("Pardon me, boy, is this the Chattanooga Woo-Woo?"). It gets rapturous results from his principal patient, a Mrs. Daldry; and though the doctor likes to keep the two halves of his life and of his house separate, Mrs. Givings prevails on him to try it out on her. The two ladies compare mystified notes, and then describe their sensations to Elizabeth, the wetnurse, who happens to be black. She says the reactions sound similar to what the women would experience when having relations with their husbands. They dont know what she's talking about.

The implication is that Victorian women, or at least white middle-class Victorian women, had no idea there could be such a thing as a female orgasm. Which suggests that the decorous conventions of the 19th-century novel are an infallible index of what actually went on in the bedrooms of the time and that we should be congratulating ourselves on our enlightenment. It's as if the patronizing first act of Caryl Churchills Cloud Nine were to be played without its compensatory self-critical second. I doubt if this is what Ruhl actually intended, but she does seem to be going for the easy contemporary laugh.

Not that she cant be witty, both in dialogue and in situation. The web she spins also encompasses Leo, a young painter who speaks at rapturous and entertaining length about the sexual freedom he's encountered in Europe but is still inhibited at home; he becomes a rare male recipient of Dr. Givings' good vibrations. The doctors wife falls for him, prompting her husband to compare her to "that Mrs. Bovary." Leo, however, only has eyes for Elizabeth, whom he wishes to paint in the act of suckling. Elizabeth has recently buried her own child, but she has others, and her fecundity is implicitly contrasted with the barrenness of Mrs. Givings, who has but the one child, and Mrs. Daldry who has none at all, this probably being their neglectful husbands fault. They predictably develop a lesbian attraction, this giving them a theoretical kinship with Annie, the doctor's mature unmarried assistant. They also have a musical relationship, Mrs. D having a knack for inventing tunes and Mrs. G supplying the words. The patterning is ingenious, but it's never more than that since the characters remain puppets, smaller than life.

Richard Roses production is distinguished, as the text virtually dictates it must be, by David Boechlers boldly bisected set, full of elegantly exaggerated period detail, but it leaves the actors in sink-or-swim mode. David Storch's Dr. Givings is the most efficient swimmer; his character's name brings with it a panoply of double meanings - very giving in his work, very withholding in his personal life, well-meaning but blinkered in both - and Storchs performance is, as it should be, undeviatingly ambiguous. The doctors effect on his patients might be described as intermittently galvanic, and the same description might fit several of the performances.

If the play has a central character, it's the frustrated Catherine, gradually discovering the depths of that frustration; Trish Lindstrom has some startlingly powerful moments on the voyage, but she's less successful at making her situation seem, as is apparently also intended, funny. Melody A. Johnsons Mrs. Daldry, by contrast, is hilarious in her evocations of unexpected arousal (which happen to resemble closely a recent episode of Curb Your Enthusiasm) but even her powers of making eccentricity look normal are strained in her other scenes, maybe because shes meant to be your average Victorian and Johnson isn't your average anything. Jonathan Watton is in terrific control of Leo's first long speech, but rushes everything afterwards. Elizabeth Saunders is fine as Annie, unassailably patient with the patients. The palm goes, though, to Marci T. House who plays Elizabeth with a dignity and poise unmatched anywhere else in the cast. But then she's the only one who's given the chance.

? In the Next Room runs through Oct. 23 at the Tarragon Theatre

2011-09-27-a-canadian-in-paris:
THEATRE REVIEW

Private Lives

Royal Alexandra Theatre,

Toronto

Just to refresh memories: Elyot and Amanda used to be married. They fought all the time, so now, meaning at the beginning of Act 1, they're divorced. Theyve also remarried and, honeymooning with their new partners on the Riviera, they find themselves booked into adjacent rooms. Thrown together across their respective terraces they realize, inevitably, that they are still in love and they re-elope to, almost as inevitably, a flat in Paris. And there for the bulk of the play they remain, still loving, still fighting.

The play, of course, is Private Lives, Noel Cowards most concentrated report on the sex war. It comes to Toronto, en route for Broadway, in a production that's already been a success in London, with Kim Cattrall as Amanda. For the North American run, she's been joined by Paul Gross as Elyot, a combination that is tempting to describe as Sex and Arrows. That might not be such a bad summation of the play itself; though when it comes to weapons, Elyot and Amanda favour blunter instruments.

They start their new relationship fully aware of their past mistakes and determined not to repeat them. The audience knows these promises cant possibly be kept and waits, with varying degrees of schadenfreude, for them to be broken. That really is all the suspense the play has; and Richard Eyres production is at its best in mining it. There's enough giddy romance in the first act's evening air for us to wish the couple well; Coward even composed a song, Someday Ill Find You, to oil the reunions wheels. "Strange how potent cheap music is" as he famously and with shameless effrontery has Elyot remark.

Cattrall gets to sing it, twice, with more charm than accuracy, in which she probably resembles the first Amanda, Gertrude Lawrence. She may also resemble Lawrence in projecting a kind of guttersnipe sophistication. This suits Amanda, who is never as sure of herself as Elyot is, a quality that dramatically works to her advantage.

For all her bravado, physical and otherwise, Amanda seems the more vulnerable, not only to Elyot but to Victor, her discarded stodgy second, to whom she shows some sympathy, even tenderness. Which is more than Elyot ever does for his newer model, the tearful fribble Sybil.

The play's central scene, bringing the central couple from embraces to words to blows, is a tour-de-force of psychological warfare in which the dialogue is the plot (no wonder Coward liked Pinter), played out here in an unnervingly spacious Parisian pieda-terre whose furnishings amount to a lot of bed and very little board. The sex is there all right, and the regret, but the wit has mostly gone missing.

Coward's lines dont call for epigrammatic elegance, but they do need charged crispness. Cattralls delivery is often flustered, and she underrates the adjectives. Gross is effectively hushed rather than conventionally clipped, when assuring his newly rekindled old flame that her body holds no secrets for him, which is not only the character's key moment of erotic surrender but the play's. Hes admirably tactful, too, at delivering Elyots credo of heartfelt hedonism, which has the potential to be very embarrassing. These moments apart, he doesn't come into his own until the last act when fate, in the shape of their temporarily lawful spouses, catches up with the duo and has to be faced with a desperate insolence that gives the serene smile Gross has been wearing for most of the evening a whole new purpose in life.

Bad news though it may be for Elyot and Amanda, the arrival of Sybil and Victor is balm for the audience.

Anna Madeley, all pert sweetness when we first meet her, develops under pressure an aggressive shrillness that's as funny as its alarming. Simon Paisley Day, by contrast, gets more sympathetic as he goes on, his dogged devotion to the woman whos deserted him becoming rather touching.

Caroline Lena Olsson completes the cast as a haughty and cold-ridden French maid, breathing unhygienically over the brioches. I could not, though, however hard I tried, warm to the apartment that Rob Howell has designed for her to clean, an Art Deco jape, with ducks on the walls and goldfish in three tiers of bowls, and in its cavernous lack of coziness, enough in itself to drive Elyot and Amanda to blows.

I suppose it's possible the goldfish are a metaphor for their relationship, and I'll admit that they (the fish, that is) occasion a first-rate and unmetaphorical visual gag; some of the other physical comedy, though, is strained. I'll end with a non-spoiler and a question: The play concludes with Victor and Sybil at one another's throats, just like their exes. Is Coward trying to tell us that all relationships are like this? Or did he just want a nice symmetrical final curtain?

? Private Lives runs until Oct. 30. For tickets, visit mirvish. com.

2011-09-28-blasted-he-s-done-it-again:
THEATRE REVIEW

The Maids

Buddies in Bad Times Theatre, Toronto

Brendan Healys last-season production of Blasted, his opening shot as director of Buddies in Bad Times, left no doubt that hes got the goods. If any more proof were needed, it's available in his secondseason opener, the only production I have seen of Jean Genet's The Maids that comes close to making the play enjoyable. Make that the only production of any Genet play.

Like Blasted, The Maids has an overpoweringly effective setting, in this case a boudoir designed by Julie Fox in several shades of red and sumptuously lit by Kimberly Purtell. There may not actually be perfume in the air but the production definitely has an aroma. Also like Blasted, it has a cast of three: two who are onstage practically throughout, and a third who functions dramatically as an intruder, even though in this case its her house. After that, the tracks diverge.

The newcomer in Blasted brings violence graphically on to the stage; in The Maids, her arrival carries the threat of it but not, it turns out, the reality. In Blasted, Healys achievement was to present human behaviour in such detail that naturalism took on the quality of ritual. In The Maids, he takes a text that stakes everything on ritual and, in honouring that quality, makes it human.

The maids are Solange and Claire, middle-aged sisters locked in a love-hate relationship with the Madame who employs them and also, it seems, with one another. As the play begins, they are acting out a habitual charade, in which one of them puts on Madame's clothes and humiliates the other. This time it's Claire whos doing the dressing up, and just to make the game more interesting, shes addressing Solange as Claire. The logical end of the game would be that they kill Madame and that does seem to be the end toward which, in fantasy at least, they are working. Meanwhile, in what passes in Genet for the real world, the girls have framed Madame's lover on an embezzlement charge. Now they learn that he's out on bail, and likely to reveal everything; so the removal of Madame becomes an urgent necessity.

Genets drama is mesmeric or its nothing, and in the first long scene of this production, the spell is superbly cast. Diane D'Aquila's Solange, in particular, is a major achievement, limping around the stage with an aggressiveness born of long and painful habit and contemptuous of pity, kaleidoscopic in mood and cadence, but with a flinty undeviating economy of means. I hung on her every word even when I had ceased to care what those words might be.

The characters are female, but Genet was known to declare that he had written them for men (or boys) and indeed theyve been played that way. Healeys production breaks (as far as I know) new ground by splitting the difference, D'Aquila's Solange being partnered by the Claire of Ron Kennell, who does not seem to be doing a female impersonation; at least, he starts the play topless and he certainly doesnt have a womans breasts.

In his stage directions, Genet specified that the maids should be in their thirties and Madame even younger. I've yet to see a production realize that potentially interesting dynamic, but this one comes closer than most with Maria Ricossa playing Madame as a flighty chatelaine who obviously thinks she's young, and whose mindless patronizing of her domestics is as poisonously delightful as her declarations of undying loyalty to her fettered beloved.

Theres an element of suspense in her scene, though Genet was hardly a thriller writer. In fact, he was hardly a dramatist at all; his plays are essentially monologues, divided between a given number of mouthpieces. In this production the one idea - that social hierarchy is a matter of roleplaying, unjust but inescapable - is endlessly if fancifully reiterated. Which is why, even in a production as good as this one, using a translation as spry as Martin Crimps, it ends up boring. But still, on this occasion, hypnotic.

? The Maids runs until Oct. 9. For tickets, call 416-975-8555 or visit buddiesinbadtimes.com.

The most enjoyable Daniel MacIvor plays have usually been those in which he has appeared himself. This, in recent memory, has meant that they have been monologues. However, his new play, entitled His Greatness, gives us not just the acting but the interacting MacIvor, functioning - excellently - as one equal member of a cast of three. It's very refreshing.

As is the play itself. It's a more or less realistic piece whose structure and development are almost defiantly traditional. So is its subject; it belongs to the comparatively recent but still proliferating genre of the artist-and-amanuensis drama. Unlike most of its kind, however, it isn't just a biographical retrospective thinly disguised as a play. It tells a present-tense story, and it has that all-important third wheel.

The play is billed as "a potentially true story about the playwright Tennessee Williams" though he's never given that or any other name in the text. He's simply The Playwright, ailing and alcoholic and with his greatest successes far behind him. He's in a hotel in Vancouver, awaiting the premiere of his latest play (actually the revision of an old one) on the heels of its failure in London. The play's name isn't mentioned either but it has to be The Red Devil Battery Sign, which was done in just those circumstances at the Vancouver Playhouse in 1980. That production featured a young actor named Richard Donat who, 30 years later, is now appearing as the dramatist. Mac Ivor plays The Assistant, once the playwright's lover, now a combination of secretary, banker and nurse. Or Head Cook and BottomWiper. The play begins with the assistant, in what is obviously a familiar late-afternoon routine, awakening his patron from the effects of a drunken night spent insulting and/or trying to seduce the members of his Canadian production team.

Reminiscences and recriminations ensue, as does the playwright's decree that they cannot possibly attend that evening's first night together and that the assistant will have to find him a suitable escort. The assistant, not too plausibly given that discretion is supposed to be the object, picks out a young man who's actually a rent boy from Newfoundland. The young man, who claims optimistically to be 21, knows almost nothing about plays and absolutely nothing about this particular playwright, but the assistant briefs him on what to say (i.e. as little as possible) and how to behave. The instant protege, who had assumed he was there for just one thing or maybe two, coke being the second, sets about playing his new acquaintances off against one another, with some theoretical success.

That's pretty much the first act and it's very neat and racy if a touch hackneyed. The playwright, lolling around in his dressing gown while flicking a forked tongue at everyone within reach, comes over as The Man Who Came to Dinner with a Southern accent. In its first half, the play skates merrily over the themes of failure and humiliation; in its second, while keeping its lightness of touch, it highlights and explores them. First night applause had persuaded the playwright that he had a hit, his first in decades; the next morning's papers tell him different. The young man, still very much around, is cunningly used as a lightning rod. "Is that bad?" he asks of one critique that has used the word "fiasco"; he's informed that, compared to the only other review to hand, it's a rave.

The young man, played by Greg Gale with a blend of aggression and naivete, has some dogs of his own in this fight. He'd been thrilled by the play, it being only the second one he'd ever seen and him being the playwright's date; what's more, his previous dream of becoming a porn star has now been trumped by the playwright's promise to write him a vehicle (a word with which the young man has some trouble) of his own. The assistant, of course, has heard that one before.

The rich achievement of MacIvor's script, and of Ed Roy's production, is to put three fleshand-blood people onstage and to make us feel the situation, simultaneously, as it affects each one of them. The phrase "his greatness," a mocking honorific, gets applied to each of them in turn, in descending registers of sarcasm. Donat, playing, after all, a man he once knew, gives us a wounded, thrashing sea lion, equally desperate for pity and praise and nasal spray. The play cleverly echoes the reminiscing structure of The Glass Menagerie, and there are moments when the playwright, meeting a potentially kind stranger, comes on very much like Blanche DuBois in Streetcar. It's been a long time since either of those two triumphs, or even since The Night of the Iguana, but this is still the man who wrote them and who can never forget it. Neither, for better and worse, can anyone else. In the first act, the playwright gives a phone interview and insults the interviewer; in the second, we hear her radio review, which concentrates not on how bad the play is but on how wonderful its author used to be. That must hurt a lot. When the young man puts the familiar question, "Who are they to judge you?" any critic in the audience is likely to blench.

"You think it's easy to write a play?" laments the unbuttoned Tennessee fella (from St. Louis), earning from his very buttoned assistant the disdainful comeback, "As if you'd remember." But then the assistant, we learn, had once wanted to be an actor; which is all very meta, given that his creator and impersonator is actor and writer both. The assistant is seemingly trapped in his own endgame, always about to leave his employer who's confident that he'll always return. The play's last speech closes the theatrical gap still further; like a Shakespearean epilogue it places itself, gently but firmly, at the audience's mercy. Kimberly Purtell has designed and lit what must be the solidest and handsomest set ever erected at the Factory Studio, and the production is the debut offering of the Independent Artists Repertory Theatre, a group composed of this play's author, director, production manager and publicists.

? His Greatness runs through Oct. 23 at the Factory Studio Theatre. Call 416-504-9971 or visit factorytheatre.ca for schedules and ticket information.
