2011-10-04-musical-squares:
THEATRE REVIEW

Chess

Princess of Wales Theatre, Toronto

The best thing about Chess is its title. The worst is that the title has nothing to do with the rest of the show.

OK, that's an exaggeration. The storyline does involve a world chess championship match - two of them, in fact - and the musical begins with a company number outlining the history of the game, though the information is bewilderingly irrelevant to what follows and - this being a high-decibel, low-definition pop opera - is mostly incomprehensible anyway.

We then narrow down into a personal contest between an American chess master, Freddie Trumper, and a Russian, Anatoly Sergievsky, whose story is "inspired," as they say, by the encounter of Bobby Fischer and Boris Spassky. The twist here is that the American's coach or "second," Florence Vassy, tired of her principal's hysterical narcissism, falls for the Russian and he for her. In other words, it's the same old trite love story, and the contestants could just as well be playing Tiddlywinks. Or at least tennis.

Which seems a waste of a terrific metaphor. A checkerboard stage (which this show doesn't have) always looks good, and the game itself is the purest of power plays, the more powerful for being conducted under a code of chilly politeness. Chess, the game, is politics, or at least diplomacy. The musical does have this somewhere in mind. There is pressure on both players to throw the game, and in the first act - set in Italy - Freddie literally does so, hurling the pieces to the floor. Boris is pronounced world champion, and promptly defects, to England and to Florence.

A year later, in Bangkok, he defends his title against another Russian. Boris's wife, who wants him back; his country's government, which wants him back; and a TV company that wants ratings, all put the screws on him to lose the game and come home. The Russians also blackmail Florence, who's Hungarian, by promising to release her father who's being held in Moscow. The Americans, for their own nefarious reasons, are in bed with the Russians on this one. So it could be quite the game of chess, but it doesn't even get started till the second act, and the connections between microcosm and macrocosm are never pushed through in writing or staging.

The action takes place in 1979 and 1980 and the show, after being a record album, was first staged in London in 1986. The current production is also British and, like Private Lives next door, comes to Toronto en routetoNewYork.Thedirectorchoreographer, Craig Revel Horwood, makes a determined metaphorical effort by dressing up his chorus as chess pieces, black and white, individually denoted by rank (in the program anyway) and costume.

When, at the back of the stage, an actual game is in progress, the ensemble down at the front knock one another about, from which we may deduce that a piece has been taken. But that's as far as the idea goes. There's no sense of hierarchy among the chess persons, and most of the time the performers could be anyone. What is impressive about them is their ability, in a production conceived on the John Doyle model of actors-as-musicians, to sing, dance and provide the entire accompaniment all at the same time. Playing the violin while lying flat on your back is probably not a skill much taught in music schools, but these people really have it down.

And the music they play (by Benny Andersson and Bjorn Ulvaeus of ABBA) is demanding, though that isn't necessarily the same as good. The curse of the poprock-through-sung-musical is that it equates drama with noise. Internal conflict means a character screaming prepackaged feelings at the audience. External means two characters (seldom more) bellowing them at one another.

Admittedly, traditional musicals aren't always much better at the interpersonal relationships, but at least they have dialogue to help out. The lyrics here, plus the almost non-existent book, are by Tim Rice, whose considerable sense of humour (his program bio is the second best thing in the show) nearly always goes missing in his musicals. A semiclever couplet such as "have you an appointment with the consul/if not, his response'll be no" sticks out like a comparatively healthy thumb.

The general tone is starchy, though some overarching irony seems also intended; how else to explain the presence of the Arbiter (David Erik), a slinky referee-narrator figure who suggests the MC from Cabaret, starved of any function? Also somewhat in the Cabaret tradition is One Night in Bangkok, the original breakout hit number about how decadent the city's nightlife is. It has nothing to do with the rest of the show, which could be happening anywhere.

The other famous song, I Know Him so Well, duetted by Anatoly's wife and mistress, is perhaps the answer to Rice's earlier I Don't Know How to Love Him; the advance in knowledge may be admirable, but it can't make up for the fact that we don't know him at all. Or anyone, except perhaps Freddie (James Fox) whose childishness gives him a certain flavour and who has an interesting trajectory in the second act.

The end of the Cold War has removed some of the show's initial urgency, but historical drama is still a respectable genre, provided the people and the issues are clear. But here the characters are pawns, in an unintended sense, and the narrative impenetrable; as the inclusion of a detailed synopsis in the program virtually admits. Maybe they should go the whole operatic hog and add surtitles.

- Chess runs until Oct. 30. For tickets, call 1-800-461-3333 or visit mirvish.com.

2011-10-08-two-out-of-three-is-most-cert:
Ahearty welcome to Another Africa, which actually is the same Africa we saw last year at Luminato, only shorter. Shorter by a third, since what was previously The Africa Trilogy is now just a double bill, having shed what was generally agreed to be its weakest component.

The strongest, entitled Peggy Pickit Sees the Face of God, remains the strongest, though it may suffer a bit from having only one play rather than two to be better than. Its an unusually compelling piece, given a superbly stringent production. The author, Roland Schimmelpfennig, uses competing and overlapping perspectives in a manner that is, as far as I know, unique. We have two married couples, Carol and Martin, Frank and Liz, all of them past or present medical professionals. Carol and Martin have returned from a few years working in an unnamed African village, and are obviously burnt out. Frank and Liz have stayed home (this location also unspecified though it could easily be Toronto), and they are in a state of burnout, too, though one thats slightly less obvious.

Frank and Liz have invited their old friends over for a reunion dinner. First thing we hear is Frank's confession that the whole evening was a disaster, which makes the rest of the play a flashback. The next thing we see is the two women slapping one another's faces: a flash-forward within the flashback. We watch the main action knowing the slaps are going to happen and waiting to find out exactly when and why, which is suspenseful enough in itself. Only there isnt a why, exactly. The timeslips keep happening. To put it another way: The plays tape keeps running forward, but every so often it stops, freezes frame for a moment, rewinds, and then plays again. During the freezes we hear, briefly, the thoughts or reactions of one or other of the characters. When the action resumes and repeats we, with more information at our disposal, view it differently. This isn't pretentious, and it isn't confusing.

It is like Whos Afraid of Virginia Woolf?, only compressed and turned inside out, since in this case the couples meet as equals. Offstage children bulk large in the conversation, but in this play theyre real. Frank and Liz have a daughter, Carol and Martin virtually adopted a village girl but have left her behind, probably to die. Liz is aghast, since the two girls had been pen pals; what, she asks in what may be the most highly charged line in the play, is she going to tell her daughter? Standing in for the two children onstage are a pair of dolls, their presents to one another. The European doll is the matchstick-thin Peggy Pickit; the African doll has a camera hidden inside it, whose viewpoint is conveyed to the audience via projections. Hence the title, which does seem pretentious, or at least unearned.

Second time around, in fact, the play is more impressive for its technical virtuosity (by which I don't mean the projections) than for anything it tells us about Africa, or even about white reactions to Africa. It tells us more, quite intentionally, about liberal guilt, a subject on which it's trenchant if not exactly revelatory, and which it also of course exemplifies. Frank and Liz by their own account (or at least by Lizs account) would have liked to go to Africa too, but of course family responsibilities kept them home. Carol and Martin (especially Carol) rebut their friends more facile assumptions about a situation of which they know nothing, but they are obviously carrying their own wounds; the possibility that one or both of them may have contracted AIDS looms larger on a second viewing than it did on a first. Both marriages are festering (as what marriages in plays are not), and it's exciting to watch and hear the scabs come off: The German author writes sharp, resonant, sometimes witty English dialogue.

Under Leisl Tommy's direction, which is both pitch-and pace-perfect, the two women give especially fine performances. Kristen Thomsons Liz moves from a precarious comfort zone to total meltdown; Maev Beatys Carol is on crisis alert from the start, but with a top dressing of poise; and both of them can explode, or implode, at an instant's notice and with frightening conviction. The men are less well served; Tony Nappo overdoes Frank's insensitivity, which is already exaggerated as written, though it does give rise to Lizs memorable accusation that hes only present physically - if that. He has the play's last line, which seems not so much a clincher as thunderingly obvious. But there's a lot to enjoy before we get there.

Embedded in Peggy Pickit is a fable, delivered shyly but craftily by Tom Barnett as Martin, about paternalism. Theoretically detachable, it centred the whole trilogy, when it was a trilogy. Now, it seems out on a limb. The preceding play, Shine Your Eye by the Kenyan Binyavanga Wainaina, does tell us more about Africa, if only because its set there, though its a lesser piece in every other way. We're in Lagos, at the epicentre of one of those email scam operations. Here works Gbene (winningly played by Dienye Waboso), a high-flying young geek whose downtime is spent in Skyped correspondence with a Toronto-based lesbian who'd like her to pay a visit; this, even more than Peggy Pickit, is a highly techno-savvy production. One reason everybody wants a piece of Gbene is that she's the daughter of a martyred freedom fighter. The converging pressures eventually lead her to what appears to be a kind of virtual self-immolation; I say "appears" because the process is, surprisingly, harder to follow this time than last. Lucky Onyekachi Ejim is, literally, a towering presence as Gbene's boss, who sees his operation as payback for colonial exploitation, and Muoi Nene is his cheery subordinate, who celebrates graduating to a higher level of scamming by performing a hip-hop number - lively in itself but contributing to the overall impression that this is less a play than a series of devices with a couple of good points to make.

The North American-based play is directed by a South African, and the African one by a Canadian, Ross Manson, whose Volcano company originated the entire project, making an elegant symmetry, ? Another Africa runs through Oct. 22 at the Bluma Appel Theatre

John Lauener / Milton Barnes and Dienye Waboso in Shine Your Eye, Another Africa.;; Caption:
2011-10-11-looking-the-part:
THEATRE REVIEW

The Ugly One

Tarragon Theatre, Toronto

Sex, Religion & Other Hang-Ups

Theatre Passe Muraille, Toronto

There's an old comedy routine in which a man who has lost his memory is returned by the authorities to the bosom of his family. "Is it really true," his wife asks, on her way up to bed, "that it's as if you'd never met me before?" He confirms that it is. "Hmm," she says - it's all in the timing - "don't be too long, will you dear?"

I thought of this while watching The Ugly One, whose protagonist undergoes radical facial reconstruction, with results that have a similar aphrodisiac effect, not just on his wife but on every woman he meets. Men go for him, too; either they want him or they want to be him.

Our hero's name is Lette, and he's probably German; anyway he's the creation of a German playwright, Marius von Mayenburg. Lette is a well-regarded inventor who's shocked when his boss informs him that the trade show presentation of his latest brilliant creation is to be entrusted to a smarmy young subordinate. Lette himself is apparently too villainously ugly to be allowed out in public; his spouse confirms that this is indeed the case, and that she's only been able to love him by steadfastly refraining from looking him in the eye.

Lette takes himself off to a plastic surgeon, who regards him as the biggest challenge he's ever had but manages to turn him into something transcendently beautiful. Lette's life changes. He becomes first choice not just for his own presentation, but for everybody else's. Women throw themselves at him, notably a widowed CEO who is 73 but, thanks to repeated procedures of her own, doesn't look it. Unhappily for Lette, the surgeon realizes that he can perform the same operation on literally anybody else, with identical results. The world is soon full of Lette look-alikes; and the original's stock falls as rapidly as it had risen. It doesn't help that, in his new-found arrogance, he's been pricing himself out of an increasingly crowded market.

The play keeps up the same tone of deadpan extravagance all the way through, but in other respects it's uneven. Its premise is, even for a dramatic fable, unbelievable. I hate to be so literal, but if Lette really is, as everybody else keeps insisting, the worst-favoured thing since the Elephant Man, wouldn't somebody have told him already? I mean, people aren't that nice. Structurally, the evening begins with a bang. It then gets to feeling obvious, telling us over and over that we live in a beauty-obsessed society, as if this were news. Later, as the multiplying paradoxes of Lette's situation affect everyone around him, it becomes really interesting and inventive. Finally, it overplays its hand, its last development being too clever for its own good, or at least for mine. The pluses, all told, beat out the minuses.

Ashlie Corcoran's production, for Theatre Smash, is brisk and sharp; much of it, like When the Rain Stops Falling but to less poetic effect, is performed on top of a table and in a confined space.

Lette is played by David Jansen, who is neither the handsomest man in the world nor the ugliest but manages, without benefit of makeup, to convey how it feels to be both; from the audience's perspective the character's degree of likeability varies in inverse proportion to his imagined looks, and Jansen grades this process acutely.

Three other actors divide all the other roles between them; and, in another example of too-cleverness, the characters portrayed by each one have the same name. Thus, the wife, the boss lady and the surgeon's nurse are all called Fanny; maybe it's this uniformity that causes Naomi Wright to make each of them aggressively unpleasant. Hardee T. Lineham doubles surgeon and industrialist with sabre-toothed attack but also with excessive jerkiness, even given that both of them are jerks. Jesse Aaron Dwyre completes the company as Lette's upstart rival and rich Fanny's mother-loving and mother-smothered son.

I was reminded of Eugene Ionesco's Rhinoceros, which satirized conformity by having everyone turn into rhinos. Here everyone opts to become very lovely instead of very ugly, but the message is the same. At one hour and five minutes, though, von Mayenburg delivers it more economically.

Sex, Religion & Other Hang-Ups, a one-man play - really an extended stand-up comedy act - by James Gangl, is also about a guy becoming more attractive. Avowedly autobiographical, it tells of how the gangling Gangl finally got his break both as an actor and as a lover.

The professional breakthrough came when he got the part of Buddy No. 1 in a Coors Light commercial. The personal came when, at a comparatively advanced age, he lost his virginity - or, as he puts it, neatly tying the two themes together, got his union card - after a doomed romance with the girl of his dreams, who'd appeared in the same commercial as Bunny No. 3. His failure to score with her he puts down to a Catholic upbringing taken too earnestly to heart.

Some of this is very funny, most of it is charming, and nearly all of it feels truthful. It proves once again that the great thing about sexual confidence is that it does wonders for your sexual confidence.

? The Ugly One runs until Oct. 16. For tickets, call 4165311827 or visit tarragontheatre. com; Sex, Religion & Other Hang-Ups runs until Oct. 22. For tickets, call 416-504-7529 or visit passemuraille.on.ca.

Note: Obituary of DR. Robert Buckman

Robert Buckman, doctor and comedian, divided his life between making people well and making them laugh. Sometimes he did both at the same time. Its hard to think of a life more productively or benevolently lived. It's also hard to conceive of a better, kinder or funnier friend.

It isn't strictly true, perhaps, to say that he always made people well. He worked in a field - oncology - in which that often isnt possible. But, by the general testimony of both patients and colleagues, he always made them feel better. He was a pioneer in the neglected art of helping doctors to talk, honestly and sympathetically, to patients. The sympathy part was probably helped by his being ill himself for much of his life. But having known him for even longer than that - we both grew up in London, went to the same university, and emigrated to Canada at around the same time - Im sure that those qualities were there from the start.

He belonged to a distinguished English line of funny doctors of whom the most famous is probably Jonathan Miller; unlike Miller he remained a practising physician and a practising performer throughout his career. Like Miller and others, he first came to notice as a member of the Cambridge University Footlights. He arrived in Cambridge a year after I left, but I heard about him through mutual friends, and I saw him in a Footlights revue on the Edinburgh festival fringe.

Later I heard him as a DJ on BBC radio while he was working his way through London medical school. He formed a comedy partnership with another doctor, Chris Beetles, and the first time we really met was when I went to see Beetles and Buckman in a cabaret booking at Quaglino's restaurant in the West End. Except that I didn't see them, or not both of them; Beetles was off sick, and Buckman performed, hilariously, with a cardboard cut-out of his partner. I was able to write afterwards that Id seen an intelligent, original stand-up comic.

Much of the humour was medically related, and the duo went on to a TV series in similar vein which they called The Pink Medicine Show. This involved, among other things, Rob lecturing on the Ascent of Man: Some specimens learned to stand erect and became homo sapiens; others crawled on their hands and knees and became estate agents.

There was also a thighslapping song-and-dance routine entitled "Medical Men" ("and thats how they discovered schizophrenia"); and I also recall B&B, at an Amnesty International benefit, performing a Cossack dance in the background of the legendary John Cleese-Michael Palin exparrot sketch. He convulsed audiences (and guests in his living room) with a story of how, as a junior doctor, he had to deliver the baby of a woman who spoke no English, showering her with encouraging phrases erratically gleaned from a Berlitz phrasebook. And he was writing comic columns and collecting them in books.

All this time, he was advancing as a cancer specialist and researcher, which is what brought him to Toronto, as a consultant first at Sunnybrook and then at Princess Margaret. By then he had mostly abandoned formal performing, but his comic talents were irrepressible - I doubt that he ever tried to repress them - and he was in constant demand as a radio and TV pundit and as an afterdinner speaker.

He taught and lectured all over the world. He made a highly praised series of instructional videos with Cleese, and was at work on another series with another Python, Terry Jones; he was returning from shooting from one of these in England when he died, on a plane, at the appallingly early age of 63.

He was also at work on a novel. At his death, he had published 14 books, including a tongue-in-cheek autobiography (title I'm Not Dead Yet) and several devoted to what must have been his greatest cause: demystifying and, as far as possible, de-terrorizing illness. This concern stretched far beyond his own practice and his own specialty.

If I or any member of my family had a health problem, we always knew we could call him, wherever he might be (and he was always travelling), talk to him and count on a sympathetic, serious, compassionate and unsentimental response. I know there must be many others who relied on him in the same way.

The greatest loss of course is to his wonderful family. More selfishly, I still can't believe that I shall never again pick up the phone to hear one of his quizzical, funny-voiced greetings. He is, in so many ways, irreplaceable. He led a rich and loving life, and he led it by example, suffering from two potentially crippling conditions in succession and refusing to be limited by them.

His last major book was called Cancer Is a Word, Not a Sentence; and that title in its concern and practicality and its humour is quintessential Rob.

Nathan Denette, National Post Files / Dr. Robert Buckman managed to juggle medicine, comedy and writing at the same time.;; Caption:
2011-10-15-of-sexy-fruit-and-string-quar:
The Art of Time ensemble likes to merge all kinds of performing disciplines, sometimes throwing in some non-performing ones as well. Canadian Stage is giving its Berkeley Street platform to the ensemble's latest project I Send You This Cadmium Red, a double bill of which the first part is interesting and the second - which gives the evening its name - fascinating.

The unifying factor is the enthusiasm of Andrew Burashko, Art of Time's artistic and musical director, for the work of the British composer, whose music he describes as classical (I'm not sure that word means much anymore, but we know what he's saying) with a touch of jazz. The production takes two Bryars compositions, both of which appeared on CDs with spoken or sung components, and adds visuals to them. Burashko introduces the evening himself, and he's very informative, but I think he should either speak louder or invest in a microphone.

The first half is a revival of a preexisting piece, a ballet entitled Soudain l'Hiver Dernier, choreographed by James Kudelka and set to Bryars' music. The music itself was a response to a vocal performance: a four-line hymn, Jesus' Blood Never Failed Me Yet, sung unaccompanied and with no pretentions to technical accomplishment by an old man. This song is endlessly looped, while a string quintet provides its own instrumental commentary.

I suspect that if I heard it on disc the monotony would drive me mad, but here, of course, there's another element. Two dancers, Michael Sean Marye and Luke Garwood, perform a slow pas de deux of trust and dependence.

As for the singing - a continuous devout drone, dubbed in from the original disc, while Art of Time's own musicians provide live backing - I found that I was tuning it in and out; it took me time to accept that it wasn't gong to stop and wasn't going to develop, and I began to resent it. Gradually, though, I came to accept it as a necessary background that finally fused with the emotional effect of the dance. They illustrated one another. Oddly enough, considering that it was the initial spur for the whole show, it was Bryars' minimalist music that got squeezed out of the equation, at least in my consciousness. Intellectually, I knew that it was vital, but in practice it was one element too many for me to respond to.

I felt somewhat the same in the early stages of I Send You This Cadmium Red itself, but the feeling rapidly vanished. The musical piece (originally commissioned by BBC radio) that inspired this section was itself inspired by an exchange of letters between two British painters: one, John Berger, octogenarian and living in Paris; the other, John Christie, some 20 years younger and still at home. Christie is also a filmmaker and Berger one of the world's great art critics and art explainers. The title is the first line of a letter sent by Christie to Berger, extolling the glories and associations of a particular shade of red and enclosing a sample of it. This sparks off a long epistolary conversation in which they delightedly explore the properties of other shades and then of other colours.

This staged version, directed by Daniel Brooks, gives us two actors to recite the letters ("recite" is an unhappily lifeless word for what they do, but they mercifully don't "act" them) and two screens across which the colours they discuss appear, dazzle and dance. Julian Richings plays Berger and is wonderfully urgent yet relaxed; one of the hardest things for an actor to do is make a literary text, which these letters, however informal, have to be, and make it sound natural, conversational, without ever forcing or self-consciously dramatizing - and Richings brings it off perfectly. (Having music behind him probably helps; the onus isn't all on him.) John Fitzgerald Jay, an actor too seldom seen (in these parts, anyway) is Christie, patiently stoking Berger's fire. Among other things, we get a celebration of friendship. We hear of Christie's wife and of their new baby daughter of whom they are, obviously, joyously proud; the wife's name is Genevieve, and it's amusing to hear how Berger always gives the name its French pronunciation and Christie the English.

Among the things we learn from their back-and-forth is that yellow is the only colour that positively demands a form (though saffron, if I got it right, may be an exception); that blue, not just the blues, must have inspired and intoxicated Charlie Parker; and that, at least according to Berger, blueberries are the only kind of blue that is really sexy.

We're in on a kind of quest, which the music and the projections help make witty, urgent and eventually ecstatic. It made me wish that I could see the world, or at least see colours, as painters do. "Colour, and our need of colour," says Richings at the conclusion, as magisterially and yet as humbly as if it were a truth newly revealed, "is everywhere."

? I Send You This Cadmium Red runs through Oct. 22 at the Berkeley Street Theatre. Visit canadianstage. com or call 416-368-3110.

John Lauener / Michael Sean Marye and Luke Garwood in I Send You This Cadmium Red.;; Caption:
2011-10-19-bemusing-my-religion:
THEATRE REVIEW

GHOSTS

Yonge Centre for the Performing Arts

In Ibsens Norway, weather is a metaphor for fate, and in Morris Panychs Soulpepper production of Ghosts the rain that pelts down outside the Alving home at the beginning of the play is practically a character in its own right.

Ken MacDonald has designed one of his finest sets, a wide-windowed antechamber furnished with all the regulation Ibsen trappings - chairs, tables, sofas and, most vitally, books - but here arranged to be stylish rather than cluttered. Alan Brodie's lighting is superb, especially in its summoning of the sun that rises at the end, herald and symbol of the worst catastrophe in a day and night that have been full of them.

Within this frame is a good, not great, production that holds its fire until the conclusion: the revelation that Oswald Alving, the young artist home from Paris, is sinking into the last stages of the brain-softening syphilis that he inherited from his father, the late and locally revered Captain. Beside him stands his mother, whom he has besought to end his life rather than leaving him to endure it as a vegetable. So assisted suicide is one still pressing issue the play raises, one more taboo it breaches.

Mentioning venereal disease now seems the least of these, even though it's what ostensibly (and ostentatiously) most shocked the 19thcentury critics. They were perturbed, too, by the plays apparent willingness to wink at the possibility of brotherand-sister incest. Underlying all the disquiet is the plays questioning, embodied in Mrs. Alving herself, of all the conventional moral and religious codes.

Long ago, she fled her debauched husband's home and sought counsel of her priest, Pastor Manders, whom she had loved and who was attracted to her as well. Doubly scared, he told her to go back to her duty, and the two have not met again until now, when they've come together to arrange the opening of the Captain Alving orphanage, a monument to a lie.

It used to be all too easy to play the pastor, with his provincialism and his prejudices and his consuming fear of what respectable people will think (and his horror of nonrespectable people thinking at all) as a figure of fun or just as a tiresome bore. The resurgence of the religious right has made him seem far more realistic a threat; the temptation now is to play him as a monster.

Joseph Ziegler avoids both extremes; hes conscientious, reflexively blinkered, and vulnerable, still shrinking away when Mrs. Alving lays a hand on his arm. (We arent told what his life was like after he rejected her, but it seems likely that he never married.) Nancy Palk's Mrs. Alving, surveying him from a handsome height (Dana Osborne has costumed her beautifully), seems to have seen right through him from the play's beginning, and through everything he represents. This makes for some exciting moments; when the pastor remarks on the "advanced" literature she seems to be reading (and that hes read about in the newspapers) and when he recommends Scripture as an antidote, Mrs. A replies, in Panychs own zippy new rendering, "the Bible; there's a book": a more spiritedly scornful response than I recall hearing in any previous translation. Instead of progressively shedding illusions as the play proceeds, this Mrs. Alving seems to be free of most of them from the start; interestingly, she seems vindicated rather than upset when the orphanage burns down, uninsured since the pastor felt that to do otherwise would suggest insufficient trust in God. (A creak in the plot: It all happens so quickly there wouldn't have been time to take out a policy anyway.)

The downside of the interpretation is that Palk has to spend much of her time being angry with Manders, and runs out of fresh ways to do it. Instead of being the culmination of a protracted unmasking, her last scene with Oswald becomes a new and separate drama, though its one that she plays magnificently, as does Gregory Prest, who from the start has been a charismatic figure, with a shaky bravado fuelled by the terrified awareness of his own mortality.

This scene faces its heroine with the one duty she has no wish to deny - motherhood - and with a horrifying uncertainty as to what, in these circumstances, that duty should be. Its where all the ghosts - spiritual, intellectual, physical - catch up with her and with us. It blazes; much of what has gone before is, presumably by intention, muted, sometimes to the point of inaudibility.

Especially subdued, though with differing results, are Diego Matamoros as Engstrand, the crippled and crafty carpenter, and Michelle Monteith as the maid Regina. Matamoros offers an engaging sketch, but no more; the scene in which he sanctimoniously and successfully blackmails the pastor lacks menace and, surprisingly from these actors and this director, humour. Monteith is the discreetest of domestics, obsequiously so until events enable her to speak for herself. This actress excels at presenting a calm exterior and then digging beneath it; she does it, in simpler and sunnier fashion, as one of the dolly birds in Soulpepper's restaging of The Odd Couple, and she does it here, sounding depths that are freezing. This is a production strong on tension, less on texture.

? Ghosts runs in repertory until Nov. 18. For tickets, call 416-203-6264 or visit soulpepper.ca.

Soulpepper / Joseph Ziegler, left, avoids the temptation to play the pastor as a monster. Good for him.;; Caption:
2011-10-22-pain-and-some-self-indulgence:
For eight years now, Joel Greenberg's Theatre 180 has been bringing us plays on urgent public subjects. They have divided into the documentary or quasi-documentary (The Laramie Project, Stuff Happens, Our Class) and the more conventionally fictionalized. It's telling that the former category has excelled the latter, not only in polemical impact but in human complexity. The Normal Heart, the most famous of all plays about AIDS, belongs in the second group and is very much a case in point.

There's a sense in which Larry Kramer's play may be said to straddle the line between the two camps. It uses real-life characters, but gives them made-up names; the originals are all individually identified in the author's program note for this revival, and one of them is Kramer himself, here called Ned Weeks. Ned is a gay journalist, living and working in New York in the early 1980s when AIDS first hits. He's also one of the first people - the play sometimes makes it seem that he's the only one - to realize that it's a virus that is being sexually transmitted. This, and his passionate campaigning about it, earns him hatred on two fronts. He makes himself unpopular with the straight world, especially the straight political world, which would rather ignore the issue altogether. More woundingly, and something that occupies most of the play's attention, he antagonizes other gays, who feel that they have only just achieved sexual freedom, and who equate liberation with promiscuity. At least some of them do; others are still nervous about coming out. Doing battle on all these fronts, Ned emerges as a beleaguered crusader. He is in fact the hero of his own play, and that's a problem.

The Normal Heart took New York by storm when it was first produced, a theatrical equivalent of Kramer's own off-stage work as an activist. Some of that pain and passion still registers. But it also seems self-indulgent, probably more so than it would if it were more frankly autobiographical and less tied to Broadway tradition. The opening scenes, trying to present the first facts on the ground through the medium of normal dramatic exposition, are full of cardboard characters speaking cardboard lines and receiving, in Greenberg's production, mainly cardboard performances. Both play and production get better as they go on, partly because the story becomes inescapably grimmer and more harrowing, partly because Kramer, like an American John Osborne, seems to have a greater talent for monologue than for dialogue. Most of these tirades go, obviously, to Ned, but others get a turn, too, and the actors rise to the opportunities.

Jonathan Wilson gives an unflagging and compelling performance as Ned himself, scrappy in the best pugnacious sense; the fact that he's physically slight adds if anything to the effect; he's a bantam up against a battalion of Goliaths. The writing, though, is scrappy by a less complimentary definition: elementary and diffuse. The author tries conscientiously to complicate things by having his surrogate admit to being tactless and confrontational, but these are gestures; in essence, Ned is always right. He's also very repetitious; I lost count of the number of times he upbraids a cautious colleague for not living up to his daredevil past as a Green Beret. Certainly we feel for Ned when his intransigence leads to his being effectively ousted from the movement he did more than anyone to create. That's good personal and political theatre. Less so are the attempts to provide Ned, as a good protagonist, with relationships. He has a lover, who dies: horrifyingly and movingly, though no more so than would be the case if he and Ned had no personal involvement. Ned also has a brother, a lawyer, who seems to be standing in for that section of straight society that's sympathetic but uncomprehending (it seems almost too good that the actor who plays him is named John Bourgeois); the production's last image suggests that the fraternal relationship is the central one in the play, though there's very little to justify it.

Brother and lover share a scene, with Ned not present; and it's almost the best in the play. He's also absent from the very best, which is played from opposite corners of a quadrilateral stage, and in which the despairing polio-stricken doctor who first suspected the nature of AIDS and is trying to treat it with pitiful resources, gets a generally hostile response from a medical executive. The latter is played by Mark McGrinder, who has earlier appeared as a similarly unhelpful man from the mayor's office; I thought for a while that they were the same character, and in essence they probably are. Sarah Orenstein is the doctor and the scene affords her one of the play's great outbursts, which she delivers with ferocious intensity, spreading the stage floor with detritus, which, in the evening's chief image, accumulates thereafter. Quieter, but at least as lacerating, is the breakdown speech of Ryan Kelly as an activist cracking under professional pressure and both personal and institutional cruelty. Paul Essiembre traces, with some subtlety, the evolution Will's principal collaborator into his prime antagonist, and Jonathan Seinen brings light and shade, in that order, to a male Southern belle who emerges as a responsible peacemaker.

Caught up in its own moment, the play now seems to leave a lot out. There's the barest mention of infections in Africa or anywhere else outside America or even outside New York; or of heterosexual cases; or of transmission through drug use; or of the helpfulness of condoms. Most of these are covered, admittedly with the benefit of 30 years' hindsight, in Kramer's program note which, in its angry accounting of how little has actually changed, is more challenging and more powerful than his play.

? The Normal Heart runs through Nov. 6 at Buddies in Bad Times Theatre, 416-975-8555.

John Karastamatis, Studio 180 / Sarah Orenstein and a compelling, unflagging Jonathan Wilson.;; Caption:
2011-10-26-death-of-a-game-plan-if-soulp:
Soulpepper's 2012 season, its 15th, will contain a dozen shows. Two of these are revivals from previous years: Death of a Salesman, from 2010, and the perennial A Christmas Carol. Another is described as a "revisit": Daniel Brooks, who directed Samuel Beckett's Endgame back in the company's second season, is returning to it in what's announced as an entirely new production; I'm not sure how many different ways there can be of staging Endgame, but Brooks, whose previous production was a triumph, has certainly earned the right.

The new offerings include two Canadian plays: one, Lee MacDougall's High Life, about 20 years old, and the other - Kim's Convenience by Ins Choi, a former member of Soulpepper's acting academy - brand new, at least if you don't count a successful airing at this year's Toronto Fringe. There's also an English play from the 1970s, Home by David Storey, and an against-the-grain Soviet Russian work, Mikhail Bulgakov's The Royal Comedians, also known in English as Moliere and in fact about him. The balance of the season comprises, in order of composition, Kaufman and Hart's You Can't Take It with You, Eugene O'Neill's Long Day's Journey into Night, Arthur Miller's The Crucible, Neil Simon's The Sunshine Boys and David Mamet's Speed the Plow. Add the revived Salesman to those five and you have, next year as this, a predominantly American repertoire.

When I remarked on this in a telephone conversation with Soulpepper's artistic director Albert Schultz, he denied there was any particular plan about this and even seemed a bit surprised. I think I can see a rationale, one not limited to this company. There isn't, or at least there isn't yet, a Canadian canon, but there is an American one, composed of substantial modern plays that have name recognition and are more immediately accessible to both actors and audiences than the classics of Britain and Europe.

Long Day's Journey, by common consent the great American play, will have Nancy Palk and Joseph Ziegler in roles for which they have looked ideal for some years now, and will be directed by Diana Leblanc, whose legendary Stratford production of the same play looms in memory as something between a shining beacon and a hard act to follow. At the other extreme, though, I do rather relish the prospect of Kenneth Welsh and Eric Peterson as the Sunshine Boys, but I can't help feeling that one Neil Simon play, The Odd Couple, is enough. (Or, since it's been revived this year, more than enough.) We're talking after all about the company that first burst on us with Schiller's Don Carlos and whose signature production in my estimation (and, I discovered, in Schultz's as well) remains Chekhov's Platonov. Both were not just rediscoveries but revelations. This year's Soulpepper lineup has included just two plays from before 1900, A Midsummer Night's Dream and Ghosts, neither of them exactly rarities. Next year's doesn't have any.

Part of the problem, of course, is economic. The Soulpepper box office has never done well with Shakespeare; Schultz attributes this to Stratford being so close. Given the centrality of Shakespeare, I don't think it's healthy for Stratford or anyone else to have exclusive rights, but I see what he means. "If they're not going to come to see us doing Shakespeare, would they come to see us doing Middleton?" Schultz says, with reference to the rest of Elizabethan and Jacobean drama.

Maybe the only way to find out is to try; but, as he says, that could be expensive. Like nearly all plays written before the 20th century, indeed like most before the Second World War, these plays have a lot of characters. Soulpepper, by the way, this year and next, bunches its largest-cast plays together, which is a sensible use of resources.

More troubling, I think, is a second reason Schultz adduces: that the classics, as traditionally defined, are not the plays about which "the company" (defined as "a core of about 25 actors and directors," starting with the 12 founding members) "are coming to me and saying, 'I want to do this.' " The problem with that is it can be self-perpetuating; both artists and audiences lose touch with what's out there. If Soulpepper isn't going to expand our horizons, then who in Toronto will?

Maybe at this point I should bite my computer. When the 2011 season was announced, I looked at the list and thought the plays disappointingly small: physically and, for the most part, spiritually. I still miss the masterpieces, but in practice, and on a one-by-one basis, most of the new shows have been good and a couple (The Glass Menagerie, The Price) have been exceptional.

We also had a second chance to see The Time of Your Life, which should be everybody's favourite. It was one of four revivals, and the beginning of a plan to start an ongoing rolling repertoire, on the European model. I thought it was a great idea, on both artistic and commercial grounds; a show should be kept alive as long as people want to see it, while the flow of new productions should keep the old ones from going stale. But Schultz's team discovered that "you can't possibly keep the machine going; Toronto isn't Budapest" - people don't go to the theatre in the same numbers and with the same devotion, certainly not in a recession.

This year's most popular production has been The Fantasticks, but it isn't coming back; apparently it exhausted its audience. Also, scheduling became a headache, and patrons got confused.

"In a perfect world" says Schultz, "we'd keep Death of a Salesman in rep for two years." As a next best thing, it will be sharing summer and fall with four other plays in two theatres, the precise allocation of the last three weeks to be announced, depending on how Salesman fares against The Crucible. That sounds good, not least for the Arthur Miller estate; still, if the modification of the rolling rep ideal is logistically and financially understandable, it is also a pity, though a lesser one than the reining-in of the repertoire.

Soulpepper began with a season of two plays in rented premises. Now they do a dozen a year in their own complex. The more you do, the more misfires you're likely to have; besides, you can't be brand new forever. On the other side, productivity has its own excitement; and we have, uniquely in North America, a year-round rep with several of the country's best actors on tap, some of them for 15 years straight. It's a trade-off worth making. If, that is, the company can avoid sacrificing its soul and diluting the pepper.

Tyler Anderson, National Post Files / "If they're not going to come to see us doing Shakespeare, would they come to see us doing Middleton?" Albert Schultz, Soulpepper's artistic director, says of the 2012 season, which includes just two plays from before 1900.;; Caption:
2011-10-27-dance-dance-revolution:
THEATRE REVIEW

Fela! Canon Theatre, Toronto

Here is a production with a large cast but only one real character; at its heart, in fact, a one-man show. It's an audience-pleasing, even audiencebaiting, piece of work that can also land hard political punches. It's been a success on Broadway and at Britain's National Theatre, in that order, which is the reverse of the usual one.

It's a vibrant show - visually, choreographically and especially musically - that can lurch into quite lengthy periods of boredom. It has a story to tell, which it seems passionate about but of which it also sometimes loses track. Fela!, in fact, is one paradoxical entertainment.

Fela is Fela Kuti, the Nigerian musician and activist, and the show is his biography. Or maybe that should be autobiography. We are supposedly in Kuti's Lagos club The Shrine, on what we are told is its last night. He's about to leave the country, following a murderous raid by the government. (At least I think that's the sequence of events. It can be confusing.) Kuti is played by Sahr Ngaujah, who is extraordinary; he sings, dances, delivers long sharp-edged stand-up comedy routines with perfect timing and seamless command, and plays the saxophone; it's conceivable that he's only miming the last accomplishment, but I don't want to think so.

He tells us the story of his life, growing up in a middleclass family with an inspiring and politically fervent mother. Already immersed in music, he goes to study in London in the late 1950s; the British jazz and blues names he drops at this point (Tubby Hayes, Joe Harriott, Cyril Davies) reveals it is the rare bio-musical that has bothered to get its facts right; there's also a five-second clip of Frank Sinatra, from whom Kuti seems to have de-rived some of his cool, that's a more effective tribute than the whole of Fly Away with Me.

He begins to develop his own style, which he describes as a mixture of jazz and highlife; it's an intoxicating sound that gets the evening off to a great start. There's a lengthy onstage overture, before the lights even go down and the actors assemble, with captivating work from trumpet and, as I guess you'd expect, drums. It's a tribute to the production, and especially to Ngaujah, that they can keep that momentum going when the play proper begins.

Returning to Africa, Kuti gets both funkier (both enraged and inspired by a local James Brown imitator) and more traditional, forging the style that becomes Afrobeat. It lends itself to the jokes and rants that become his spe-

cialty and that sound increasingly like rap, only musical. He also visits the U.S. where he meets Sandra, his second wife. They do some reciprocal consciousness-raising; she teaches him about Black Power, he teaches her about the abuse of it, in a country that's exchanged the shackles of colonialism for those of corrupt generals and international oil. Raging against these entities is to consume much of the second half of his life and of the show.

Sandra appears as a character, with a couple of scenes, rudimentary ones. This is a breach of the show's prevailing convention, and not a very happy one. The script, written by Jim Lewis and Bill T. Jones, mostly lets Fela tell his own tale, with sung and danced support from a 20-strong ensemble. Jones, whose choreography was the best thing about Spring Awakening, scores again here with hard-and-fast dances that fuse traditional African with very contemporary American.

As author-director, though, he lets some of the narrative slip through his fingers. We experience the music (nearly all the score is authentic), we trust the show's evocation of Kuti as a performer, but we only hear in general terms what he was for and against. We do discover that he later took 12 wives at once, something of which the show wants us both to disapprove and to be amused by, but we never discover what Sandra thought about this or even if she were still around. We note that Kuti does tend to bully people, audience included, though he claims it's for their own good.

There are some powerful evocations of police brutality; one comic-grotesque, another overwhelmingly brusque and factual, when there's an allout raid on Kuti's compound. (He seems almost to have set up a state within the state.) This includes the murder of his mother, thrown from a second-storey window. Up to now she's been a figure more talked about than seen, unless you count her everpresent picture hanging upstage left.

Now Kuti undertakes an extremely protracted journey into the spirit world, to seek her counsel; should he stay or should he go? She tells him in what, despite Melanie Marshall's searing singing of it, is unmistakably a Broadwayinspirational number, the show's only song to be written by someone other than the protagonist.

The protagonist's later life is only relayed in surtitles at the curtain call; and even they don't mention the possibility that his death was AIDSrelated. Still, this is a show far out of the norm, in music, setting (Marina Draghici's design features a catwalk and presumably traditional abstract icons), real feelings, and a genuine star performance.

? Fela! runs until Nov. 6. For tickets, call 416-872-1212 or visit mirvish.com

2011-10-29-cuts-from-a-knife-circumcise-:
Bearing a title that may well be the least enticing come-on in the history of show business, Circumcise Me, presented by the Harold Green Jewish Theatre, turns out not to be the kosher alternative to either Puppetry of the Penis or The Vagina Monologues. It isn't as frivolous as the first or as partisan as the second. Its a moderately likeable monologue in which a writerperformer called Yisrael Campbell tells us of his conversion from Catholicism to Judaism, a journey that I would guess is more frequently taken in the opposite direction.

Obviously Yisrael is not the name the protagonist was given at birth. He was originally called Christopher, a name that an Israeli rabbi told him - quite late on in the conversion process, apparently - it might be tactful to change. He grew up in Philadelphia where, he tells us, he became an alcoholic at the age of nine. Theres an implication it was partly to purge these early excesses that he turned to a different religion than the one in which he was raised. (His mother, he says, was briefly a nun. His aunt became and remained one. She was also a mental patient. Apparently there are mental institutions especially for nuns. Fascinating.) It's a major shortcoming of the show, though, that the author never delves very deeply into his own motives or mental processes. He tells us that his interest in Judaism was first sparked when a girlfriend gave him a copy of Exodus: the Leon Uris book, not the Old Testament one. He makes a joke of having been so influenced by a not-good novel that became a worse movie (starring Paul Newman, he says, as if this somehow compounded the crime) but he never offers a more sustained explanation.

In fact, it seems he underwent conversion in three stages, moving from Reform to Conservative to Orthodox, and undergoing two adult circumcisions in the process (that's on top of a non-religious one he received as an infant but that unhappily wasnt considered sufficient) and two ritual baths, one of them in deluxe circumstances in California, the other less sybaritically in Tel Aviv. He now lives full time in Israel, having originally committed to a couple of years there to qualify for full orthodoxy. Having attained it, he has gone, to use a most inappropriate metaphor, the whole hog, and appears before us clad in what he himself calls (having, he proudly notes, spent just two days in Toronto) the full Bathurst-and-Lawrence. It looks good on him, and he sounds good in it.

What he doesnt tell us is how, either in America or in Israel, he supported himself. You have to consult his program bio to discover he is a trained actor and comedian. The acting part shows, in his confidence and authority onstage, and I'm sure the stand-up experience helps there, too. This is despite the fact he isn't all that funny, though its a saving grace that he doesnt carry on as if he thinks he is. He does have one great line that, despite overwhelming temptation, I will refrain from quoting; I'll merely say that it has to do with handicapped parking permits and the healing qualities of the sidewalks of Jerusalem. I suspect, too, that he somehow inherited a Jewish cast of humour from his lapsed Catholic dad who, when declining to attend his son's first conversion, said hed wait 13 years and come to the bar mitzvah. The program also tells us Campbell belongs to "a group of comedians bringing awareness to the Palestinian-Israeli conflict and seeking peace through comedy." Id like to have heard something about that in the show, which all but skates over the complexities of the situation. It does include an account of how it feels in the aftermath of a bombing to wonder how many of your friends may have died: powerful in itself, but not very well connected to the main theme. Rather more blatantly dragged in is a protracted account of how his life was instantly changed when he became a father. You don't have to be Jewish or Catholic or both or neither to feel that; you just have to be human. This is, by its author's own now inaccurate description, "an off-Broadway show," with an American director, Sam Gold, whose listed credits are very interesting; his production here is barebones but hardly needs to be anything else

At the opposite extreme: The most visually and conceptually exciting theatre in Toronto has been happening, not for the first time, at the Canadian Opera Company. Its production of Gluck's Iphigenia in Tauris, in its compression and concentration, cut to the merciless heart of concentration and compression. Its Rigoletto was set in a plush 19thcentury men's club, brilliantly created by the great Canadian designer Michael Levine. The program notes claimed that this was a comment on the patriarchal society in which the story is set, but it was selling itself short; what we saw was a privileged group ganging up on all outsiders, including the crippled clowning protagonist; which is what the Verdi work is all about. (The singing in both productions was great, too, but you expect that.) ? Circumcise Me runs through Nov. 6 at the Jane Mallett Theatre. For showtimes and ticket information visit hgjewishtheatre.com or call 416-366-7723.

2011-11-02-a-vital-recital:
THEATRE REVIEW

2 Pianos, 4 Hands

Panasonic Theatre, Toronto

Having seen 2 Pianos, 4 Hands three times across the years (that'd be six pianos, 12 hands), I have to report that it seems better, and even fresher, than ever. It was in 1996 that Ted Dykstra and Richard Greenblatt first launched their unclassifiable musical-dramaticalconfessional entertainment upon the world, and this is its Positively Definitely Final Appearance, at least until the next time.

The show arose from a coincidence: the discovery on the part of two prolific actorauthor-directors that each of them in his boyhood had aspirations to be a concert pianist, dreams they were forced to abandon in their late teens. At least that's what happens to the two guys they play here, whom we presume to be self-portraits since one of them is called Teddy while the other is variously addressed as Ritchie, Rich or - when some authority figure wishes to read him the riot act - Richard.

It's probably best regarded, in musical terms, as an autobiographical fantasia. Not everything in the show matches up with the facts; we know, from the program if nowhere else, that Dykstra grew up in Alberta and Greenblatt in Quebec, so they are unlikely to have been, as the show insists they were, duet partners in a junior Kiwanis Club competition, which required them (one piano, two hands) to take one part each of In the Hall of the Mountain King and at which one of them completely froze to the fury of the other. However, watching Dykstra catatonic with terror and Greenblatt purple with anger is enough to make you feel that it certainly should have happened. And maybe it really did, at least to one of them.

I had forgotten how much of the show is about humiliation, and how hilarious they make it seem. In the twin climactic scenes, each of our heroes, now both aged 17, auditions for a conservatory, one classical, one jazz. Both get rejected, Dykstra as the classical applicant being told by a memorably angry Greenblatt that he has all the necessary talent and none of the discipline.

Dykstra's crumpled face as he hears the judgment should speak to anybody's crushed adolescent dreams. He then switches to become the drawlingly laid-back jazz professor, crushingly contemptuous of the youthful Greenblatt's claims to have recently acquired soul; "Where," he asks "do you classical guys get off?" In an evening that's quite fanatical about its symmetry, it's notable that both masters claim to have heard 13-yearolds who play better than these self-confident young bucks.

But then these encounters are just the culmination of a series of bruising encounters with the outside world: with piano teachers whose methods are diametrically opposed; with parents who bully, bribe or blackmail their sons into practising and then in later years turn on them for practising too much; with belligerent drunks in bars who ask to hear Piano Man just after the pianist has played it. A motif from Teddy's career will recur in Ritchie's; ultimately the two are one. The cameo roles in which each plays off against the other's principal portrayal are shared out with, as far as I could tell, scrupulous fairness and are etched with revue-sketch sharpness.

They sometimes seem to be fudging the time scheme; I doubt that cordless phones were much in evidence when these fellows were teenagers, though I have to admit that Dykstra looks mysteriously younger now than he did 10 years ago.

The question remains, too, whether their formative years were as wholly given over to music as they claim or whether they didn't devote some of the time to, say, acting. Or did they have road-to-Damascus conversions at precisely the same age? If their current careers strike them as second-best, well, we should all have such second-bests. I mean, look at them now. So how do you get to the Panasonic? Don't practise. Not that their piano chops seem all that rusty.

Their final claim to be, at the least, two of the best players in the neighbourhood is more than vindicated by their sign-off performance of a Bach concerto, with Sheep May Safely Graze as an even better encore. They co-directed the show themselves, and it flows beautifully and wittily. It's pleasant that what seems to have started as a jeu d'esprit has turned out to be one of the sturdiest of Canadian plays. And, even at a third viewing, one of the funniest.

? 2 Pianos, 4 Hands runs until Nov. 20. For tickets, call 416872-1212 or visit mirvish.com.

2011-11-03-oxford-in-love-a-new-movie-re:
So what I want to know is: Who wrote the tavern scenes?

Controversies about the authorship of the works published under the name of William Shakespeare always start from the sceptics conviction that no unlettered actor could possibly have acquired such an intimate knowledge of political affairs, and high life generally, as appears in the plays, or have possessed the classical education needed to read up on the source material. It seems to underpin the new movie Anonymous, which takes up the theory that the real author was Edward de Vere, the 17th Earl of Oxford.

I say "seems" because the authorship question gets shunted to the side in the film, which is far more concerned with defacing another cherished historical image, that of England's Virgin Queen. The Elizabeth I of Anonymous enjoys a promiscuous private life and has apparently given secret birth to about half the young noblemen in the queendom.

It's a fun frolic, and Vanessa Redgrave is quite wonderful as Elizabeth, maybe even better than Judi Dench in Shakespeare in Love. Though the earlier film is even more fun and, since it cheerfully acknowledges its own anachronisms, far more worth taking seriously. Its especially moving and persuasive when it shows the first audience of Romeo and Juliet stunned for a moment and then cheering and applauding as if theyd never seen anything like it. Which, if you look at the plays written before it, they wouldn't have.

There's nothing that convincing in Anonymous, which is partly Oxford in Love, since the earl is presented as one of the queens old flames. In the real world, hes proven to be the most durable pretender to the Shakespearean throne, though there have been plenty of others. The late Samuel Schoenbaum, redoubtable Shakespearean scholar and biographer, once wrote that he couldn't take a holiday without fellow travellers approaching him and asking him what he thought about the real author being Francis Bacon. It was the one thing about the plays of which everybody seemed to have heard.

In the 1950s, an American named Calvin Hoffman mounted a vigorous campaign to prove that Shakespeare's fellow playwright Christopher Marlowe had survived his supposed death in a tavern brawl and had ghosted the plays from a European hide-out. Hoffman even got permission to open the tomb of one of Marlowes patrons, hoping to find the Shakespearean manuscripts in there. Richard Burton, guesting on a radio comedy show at the time, quipped that the host comics ambition to be a classical actor was enough to make Shakespeare turn in Marlowe's grave. And people knew what he meant. Those were the days.

Anonymous begins with another distinguished actor, Derek Jacobi, conceivably playing himself, intoning on how suspicious it is that nobody has ever discovered the manuscript of a Shakespeare play bearing Shakespeare's signature. Hes right about that. Nobody has ever found a Shakespearean manuscript, in a tomb or out of it. But that doesnt mean anything, because we don't have the manuscripts of other Elizabethan and Jacobean dramatists either. They can't all have been frauds or frontmen. The Jacobi prologue goes on to say that Shakespeares father was illiterate, and so were his daughters. That hardly proves that he himself was, and in fact Anonymous goes on to cover its flank by admitting that, as an actor, Shakespeare could hardly have learned his lines if he couldnt read. In fact, if he went to the Stratford-on-Avon grammar school, as we have no reason to believe he didn't, he would have received a rigorous if narrow education, especially in Latin.

He didn't go to university; we do know that. And his immediate predecessors, the mostly self-destructive group of writers known as the University Wits, knew it too, and resented it; one of them, Robert Greene, wrote a deathbed denunciation of the "upstart crow, beautified with our feathers" who fancied himself the only Shake-scene in a country. But then Ben Jonson (who plays an especially implausible role in Anonymous) didnt go to university either, had in fact less formal education than Shakespeare, but he still wrote the most aggressively erudite plays of the age. It would be easy to point to other formidable theatrical auto-didacts, from Bernard Shaw to Tom Stoppard and Edward Bond. How did they find out what they needed to find out? They read, they listened, they imagined, they invented. And so, obviously, did Shakespeare. Anti-Stratfordians love to say, for example, that only a well-heeled traveller could have known all the details about Italy that appear in the comedies. But he only had to ask.

And he would have known the right people. Anonymous, presumably on the principle that if youre going to deface a literary monument you may as well do a thorough job of it, presents him as a graceless oaf who murders Marlowe to stop him from blabbing and cutting off the supply of Oxford's hush-money. In fact he was a highly successful actor-manager, at a time when all theatres were obliged by law to have aristocratic patronage. His company was the Lord Chamberlain's Men, later the Kings Men. He would have seen at first hand how noblemen talked and behaved. So, by the way, would all his colleagues. John Websters two great tragedies, The White Devil and The Duchess of Malfi, are every bit as courtly and "political" and learned and Italianate as any of Shakespeare's, and we know far less about his life than we do about Shakespeare's, but nobody goes about claiming his plays for Oxford or any other contemporary toff. But then of course he isnt as prime a piece of cultural real-estate as Shakespeare.

Its not as if Shakespeare's English and Roman histories are full of arcane information, accessible only to scholars or diplomats. Rather, they suggest an author who had read the chronicles, been fired by their stories, and set about asking himself how real men and women would talk and behave in such situations, putting himself inside his characters' heads as if he were - I dont know, some kind of actor. For performers of the calibre of Jacobi or Mark Rylance to join the deniers, both in and out of the movie, is a particularly galling kind of trahison des clercs.

Of course, you dont have to be an actor to write great plays, but it certainly helps to have knocked about the theatre a bit. (How could Oxford or any of the other courtly contenders have attended rehearsals? It would have blown their cover.) The author of the Shakespeare plays must have knocked about other low places as well, which brings me back to my opening question. Not every Shakespeare scene takes place in a palace. The ones that bear the plainest marks of personal experience and, being in prose rather than verse, the plainest marks of reported speech, happen on the streets, in pubs, in brothels (OK, the nobility probably knew something about those), in police courts, among thieves and whores and bar staff and cashiered soldiers. When they're set out of town they deal, realistically, with artisans and rural labourers and country constables: Exactly the kind of people among whom the Warwickshire Shakespeare would have grown up. The orchard scenes in Henry IV, set in the neighbouring county of Gloucestershire, are extraordinary pieces of naturalistic writing. I don't think a sheltered earl could have written them. I dont think hed have known where to start. (I can't resist mentioning here the one sceptic who came at the authorship question from the opposite direction, Charlie Chaplin. He thought the plays could only have been written by someone of humbler origin than Shakespeare, someone like himself.)

Even given the talent, which there's no evidence he possessed, its hard to conceive of some noble amateur writing all those plays in secret: A couple perhaps, as an exercise, but 37? And why wouldnt he at least have put his name to the narrative poems, to which no social stigma would have been attached? He must also, since he died before several of the greatest were produced, have stockpiled them, which would necessitate a rate of composition even more staggering than Shakespeare's own.

I'll give the doubters one thing. Shakespeare spent his last years in retirement at Stratford, not writing anything. Its hard to think of any comparable artist who simply stopped producing. But maybe he just thought hed done his job, and saw no need to go on doing it. It's almost impossible to imagine the man who could have written those plays. But one thing about him seems clear, though it's the one that seems to infuriate a lot of people. He was a professional.
