2011-11-04-down-on-his-nuck-tough-times-:
Acorner was turned in the first season of Boardwalk Empire when we were introduced to Richard Harrow. Harrow is an ex-soldier who had half his face blown off in the First World War. He now wears a half-mask and is naturally shy about it, especially around women. He must also have lost half his vocal cords, and speaks in a gentle croak, which makes him, in Jack Huston's performance, very sympathetic.

We're now into the second season of the acclaimed HBO drama, with Richard the devoted henchman of Jimmy (Michael Pitt), the young man who would be boss of Atlantic City and who once, in Chicago, helped him to get laid. Two weeks ago Richard almost committed suicide - on Remembrance Day, poignantly enough - but, to every viewer's relief, was distracted when a dog ran off with his mask. Richard is also an expert sharpshooter, and in that same episode he reasserted his loyalty to Jimmy by tracking down a pompous big shot who had disrespected him and, wait for it, scalping him. In a way this was poetic justice since the victim (played incidentally by the distinguished Canadian actor Richard Easton) liked to boast about how he had helped massacre the Sioux.

Harrow's two faces are emblematic of Boardwalk Empire, a show that has improved immeasurably now that the grunt work of establishing the characters and filling us in on the Prohibition era has been completed. Most people in it are ambiguous, as all good dramatic characters are. Most complicated of all is Nucky Thompson, the elegantly corrupt city treasurer who, in all senses, runs the show.

Steve Buscemi, slight and precise, wasn't obvious casting for this more or less historical character, as was admitted from the outset by the series' creators; obvious casting, they said, would have been James Gandolfini, though we must be glad for everybody's sake, including Gandolfini's, that it didn't come to pass; the echoes of The Sopranos, in a show from the same creative stable, would have been too deafening.

Buscemi doesn't have Gandolfini's heft, or his pudgy intimations of a lingering vulnerability, and Nucky, perhaps because he's tied to his reallife origins, doesn't have the complexity of Tony, who remains the definitive TV antihero. But the producers also prophesied that by the end of the first season we would be unable to imagine anyone else but Buscemi in the role, and he's proved them right. In a way he's Tony in reverse. We were always surprised by Tony's better impulses; we're always shocked by Nucky's worst ones. Because of his wit and his intelligence, and what seems to be a genuine reluctance to hurt more people than is absolutely necessary, we forgive him a lot.

When we first met Nucky he was on top, which naturally means that his position has since been challenged at every turn. Last Sunday's episode found him facing three separate challenges. His plan for evading charges of electionrigging began to crumble; Jimmy made his strongest bid yet to take over Nucky's bootlegging empire; and, though Nucky doesn't know it yet, his Irish live-in love Margaret is beginning to let her thoughts stray in the direction of a young hit man from the same old country. She revealed this under seal of the confessional, a motif that does seem like a retread from The Sopranos; despite Kelly Macdonald's vibrant performance, her relationship with her priest hardly compares to Carmela's with Father Paul.

However the religious angle does connect with the character of Agent Van Alden (the riveting Michael Shannon), the fanatical prohibition agent undone by his own uptightness. He and Nucky, who hardly ever meet, are emerging as the show's opposite poles, and the most recent episode was built on the contrast. In a show marked by its pointed transitions we kept switching between them, with Van Alden impaled on a few dilemmas of his own.

There was the delirious subordinate whom he feared was about to reveal his guiltiest secret, and there was the secret herself: Lucy the exshowgirl, his one moral lapse who also happens to be part of Nucky's more colourful past. Last week, in one of the more wrenching scenes of a violent show, we practically watched her giving birth - all by herself, as she later proudly announced to Van Alden. He still can't catch a break; he'd planned, he says, to give the baby to his own childless wife who, when she arrived unexpectedly at the bedside, was not amused.

Paz de la Huerta's Lucy, a discouragingly whiny character in the first season, has become both interesting and moving. Confined for her pregnancy she was visited by the great Eddie Cantor (a fine imitation, incidentally), who told of a Broadway show that she yearned to try out for, though it hardly needed Van Alden to point out that her condition made this unlikely. (Her incredulity at his ignorance about the theatre, and especially of what a script might be, was among the show's most delectable moments.) The musical in question was called A Dangerous Maid, which, apart from being a neat handle for Lucy herself, is the title of an actual show, an early effort by the Gershwins. It closed out of town, which suggests that Lucy was well out of it. But it's a pleasing example of how thoroughly Boardwalk Empire does its homework.

This also shows, of course, in its parade of famous gangsters. We have vivid portrayals of Al Capone (typically humanized by having a disadvantaged son) and Lucky Luciano, both still underlings on the way up; and it's always a pleasure to meet Michael Stuhlbarg's Arnold Rothstein, who beats even Nucky in the fastidiousness department. Waxey Gordon has just put in an appearance, and Dutch Schultz can surely not be far behind.

One problem the show does face, common to all drama series with ambitions, is that of where it thinks it's going. They never know how long they have. The Wire is the only one to announce a five-year arc and then stick to it, with gratifying results. The Sopranos got extended, and distended. Deadwood, by contrast, is an example of a masterpiece cut off in its prime, leaving its devotees permanently frustrated. It's hard to tell whether Boardwalk Empire has a shape in mind. Its texture is rich enough for us to hope that it has. Nucky's historical prototype ended up in jail. Will time and the networks allow that to happen?

? Boardwalk Empire airs Sundays at 9 p.m. on HBO Canada.

Hbo / James Gandolfini would have been a more obvious choice than Steve Buscemi, pictured, to play Atlantic City's corrupt treasurer Nucky Thompson in HBO's Boardwalk Empire, but now it's hard to imagine anyone else in the role.;; Caption:
2011-11-05-in-the-company-of-strangers-f:
Two small Toronto theatre groups are mounting plays by modern European masters whose work is more often read about than seen. The more recondite of the two is Max Frisch whose plays were very big circa 1960 but have not, at least in their English translations, been staged much since. He was a German-Swiss playwright and novelist and like his contemporary and compatriot Friedrich Durrenmatt, he wrote taut cockeyed political parables, situated somewhere between Bertolt Brecht and Eugene Ionesco. Fireraisers, which isn't his most ambitious play but may be his neatest and most approachable, is being staged by the Red Light District company or, as they roguishly put it, by their Fire Safety Initiative.

The plays original title was Biedermann and the Fire Raisers, and that title isnt the only thing that's now been tweaked and compressed. It's a cautionary tale about complacency and psychological blackmail. In an unnamed city thats experiencing a wave of arson, two confidence tricksters - one rough, one smooth - strong-arm and sweet-talk their way into a prosperous bourgeois home, Gottlieb Bierdermann proprietor.

In the current version, updated and transplanted to the time and place of smoke detectors and chrysotile asbestos, Gottlieb has become Gillian Biedermann, a svelte female CEO with chrysotile connections, who recently fired (pun unintended but apposite) a creative employee who subsequently committed suicide. Schmitz, the orphaned circus strongman who intimidates Biedermann into giving him food, wine and a bed for the night, has also changed gender and is a female wrestler, not only foster-homed but homeless. Schmitzs buddy Eisenring remains much the same, blithely vouchsafing that he has just got out of prison. The pair take up residence in the Biedermann garage, filling it with flammable material, secure in the knowledge that, having once admitted them, their host will go to any lengths not to see what's in front of her face. The original Biedermann had an onstage wife even more readily guilttripped than himself, the new one has an offstage husband named Robert of, we are repeatedly told, a nervous disposition. Many of the wife's former lines have been appropriated by a maid hired to help care for Robert. At least thats what the program says; Im glad it does because otherwise I'd never have guessed.

Frisch, grappling with Switzerland's ambiguous wartime record, seems to have intended his play as a commentary on the resistible rise of Nazi Germany. It plays here as a generalized and rather protracted satire on human gullibility. There is a chorus of firemen, who utter fateful warnings; they keep saying "woe, woe," prompting Herr Beidermann as he then was to request them, in a line unhappily cut in the current version, to stop being so defeatist. Like their Greek antecedents, they know whats going to happen but are powerless to stop it. In this production theyre reduced to two who appear, rather wittily, within an alcove that may represent a TV screen or just the outside world. In addition to their original text, they spout antincendiary warnings taken from contemporary public announcements. Obviously we're meant to think of Canada now, but it's unclear whether were being warned against too much surveillance or too little.

The shows best things come straight from Frisch's play-as-written: the cat-and-mouse game between Biedermann and his/her self-invited guests. But much of this has been dulled in Lauren Gillis' production, which hardly matches up to the dynamic re-working of The Misanthrope that was my previous Red Light experience. Marcel Dragonieri, who was superb in that, is similarly imposing here as half the chorus, plus the plaintive voice of Robert, and Justin Miller hits the right audacious note as the cool ex-con. Briana Templeton holds the centre pretty well as Gillian; you can sense her defences crumbling. But the overall effect is both slow and slapdash.

Adam Seeligs Like the First Time is announced as "modelled on a play by Nobel prize winner Luigi Pirandello"; how closely modelled I couldnt say, but the characters all have Italian names and the script certainly exhibits the Pirandellian obsession with the fluidity of identity. We are, his plays assert, whatever other people take us to be, which means we can be trapped in several personas simultaneously. This play gives us a woman - known variously as Fulvia, Flora and Francesca, according to which of the men in her life is in it at the time - who, after a long time running wild, returns to the bosom of her family, posing as her husband's second wife, unrecognized by her now-teenage daughter, which is plausible, and also by her mother, which isn't. At least it isnt in Seeligs production, which takes most of the play with plodding earnestness, making it seem like screechy melodrama.

Unlike Red Light, Seelig's One Little Goat company employs Equity actors, but the performances here are even more plodding and tentative than those in Fireraisers. The one actor with spark is Dov Mickelson, who starts the play off as an ex-lover of the heroine's, prepared to leave and maybe even kill his own wife to be with her. So locked is he in his obsession, that he fails to notice that his beloved has suspended herself with a scarf round her neck and may be attempting suicide.

If the other actors reached his level of wit and intensity, the play might make sense. As it was, it left me wishing again that some Canadian company would take on Pirandello's Right You Are If You Think So, a more scintillating examination of the madonnawhore complex that was recently staged in London under the unanswerable title Absolutely Perhaps. Pirandello's admirers always claim that he was a great but untranslatable comic writer. That production disproved the second part of that assessment while triumphantly proving the first.

THEATRE REVIEW

The Sankofa Trilogy

Taragon Extra Space, Toronto

Her performance in the original production of 'da Kink in My Hair made it clear that d'bi. young, as she was then billed, was an intense and magnetic actress, who could be remarkably moving. She seemed so at one with her role, which was essentially a monologue, that one suspected her of having written it herself. Apparently she didn't, but a little later, in her solo play blood.claat and renaming herself d'bi.young anitafrika, she showed that she was also a writer and a compelling one. She also, playing several characters with pinpoint accuracy, proved to be both versatile and, something she hadn't had cause to demonstrate before, extremely funny.

blood.klaat has turned out to be the first of three linked plays, centring on three generations of Jamaican women, and collectively known as The Sankofa Trilogy. In benu, which I haven't seen, she played the daughter of her original protagonist; and now in word! sound! powah!, she's the granddaughter. (All three plays are being done in repertory, with the newest one getting the lioness's share of performances.) The emotional impact of the third play isn't as great as that of the first, but the writing is wittier. And from being merely an impressive performer, young has become an astonishing one.

In word! sound! powah! Benu Sankofa, the central character, is a drama student and aspiring dub poet, which makes her seem a younger version of the author herself. At the play's beginning, she's being interrogated, which largely means being brutally smacked, by a police constable, for being involved with a group called Poets in Solidarity. We flash back from there. There's an election in process, with two parties running; they are the PNP and the JLP and it's presumably intentional that they are virtually indistinguishable. young, who of course plays everybody, has the most fun with the PNP, they being the incumbents and running on the stirring platform, "We will continue to promise to invest in employment."

The solidarity poets themselves are more sympathetically portrayed, especially Peaches, a single mother, and Stamma, who stammers, at least when talking; he finds his voice in song (or, more accurately, chant). Their leader, Bobus, likes to refer to himself as "the Robin Hood of poets," and he does it often enough and vaingloriously enough to make it hard for us to take him as seriously as he takes himself and as the play seems to want him to take us. It's hard, too, to place as much weight as the show would like on Benu's past and present relationship with her grandmother. As a text, the piece doesn't quite add up; and toward its end it gets confusing.

This, though, seems like quibbling in the face of young's lightning transitions from one character to the next, and of the precision with which she delineates every one of them. She can offer a savage cartoon of a bully, an affectionate swaggering sketch of a poseur (several of these), a full-blown painting of a heroine who can be fearful or triumphant. Indeed one of the play's great qualities is that Benu herself, who might easily have been a narrating cipher, comes so fully to life.

Many of the characters like to buttonhole the people they're addressing, but it's Benu, finding herself as writer and performer, who engages the audience most boldly and most warmly. This, not coincidentally, is one of young's own great strengths; she's the rare performer who, when she makes one-on-one contact, can make the recipient smile rather than cringe. This seems to apply not just to the people in the auditorium but to her three musicians, all excellent in their own right. When she talks she's moving, hilarious, beguiling. When song and dance come into the mix, she's electric.

- The Sankofa Trilogy plays until Dec. 4 at the Tarragon Extra Space. For tickets, call 4165311827 or visit tarragontheatre. com.

THEATRE REVIEW

Mary Poppins Princess of Wales Theatre, Toronto

It's a shock, if you come to the original Mary Poppins stories after seeing the movie, to realize just how stern and unyielding the central character is.

She hardly says a nice word to anybody. If she's more palatable on film, it's not just because of the sugar that the Disney people applied by the now proverbial spoonful; that could have turned out even more distasteful. It's because the central performance managed to preserve some of the tartness along with the sweetness, and to combine absolute assurance with a self-awareness that stopped just short of self-mockery. To bring that off it's probably necessary to be Julie Andrews. Failing that, it helps to be English.

In the stage version that has come to Toronto after great success in London and New York (in both of which it's still running) Mary Poppins is played by Rachel Wallace, an American performer who sings nicely but most of whose acting energies seem to be focused on getting the accent right, with special emphasis on exaggeratedly rounded vowels.

Admittedly, some of the textual and musical additions make things hard for her. When the nanny in the movie serenely informs her two young charges that she's practically perfect in every way, it's unanswerable; when, as here, she does a whole selfcongratulatory number about it, it's insufferable. That isn't the actress's fault, but there isn't much charm or humour in her performance; and what with two children (Camden Angelis and Dakota Ruiz) who are having their own enunciation problems, plus an abrasive sound system, the show - which I enjoyed when I saw it in London - turns into one of the shrillest musicals I have heard.

One minor piece of collateral damage is the character of Miss Andrew, the anti-nanny who appears in the second act when the heroine has flown off somewhere, and threatens to blight the lives of the Banks children as she blighted that of their father before them. Miss Andrew's chief weapon, as brandished by a powerful performer called Q. Smith, is her ability to hold high, loud closing notes for a long time; but as we've already been vocally belaboured for half an evening, this doesn't constitute quite the climax that it might. More damagingly, playing her as a cartoon Wicked Witch of the West works against what's best in the show, the serious treatment of the parents.

In this revisionist version (book by Julian Fellowes), Mrs. Banks is no longer a suffragette neglectful of her offspring - that would now seem politically incorrect, and I'd probably find it offensive myself - but a loving, harassed mother who misses her former life as an actress. He's a banker who, because of his upbringing, doesn't know how to relate to his children but, because of Mary Poppins, learns. He also gets into professional trouble by giving a loan to a client who wants to invest in people while turning down one who wants to invest in what sound suspiciously like unsecured derivatives. (This show, which opened in 2004, was ahead of its time.)

It's pleasing to report that all the best performances in this touring production are given by Canadians; and none are better than Laird Mackintosh and Blythe Wilson who play the Bankses. She sings like a dream, with brains as well as pipes; he's lump-in-throat moving as he reaches out, especially to his son, and even gets a chance to caper a bit. Other legitimate sources of local pride are Valerie Boyle, ferociously funny as the family cook; Janet MacEwen, who sings a beautiful Feed the Birds; and, most prominently, Nicolas Dromard as Bert, the show's master of ceremonies, the virginal Mary's unrequited and understated love interest and - at one point - everybody's human fly. That is, he climbs right up one side of the proscenium, crawls upsidedown along the top, and climbs back down again, remarking as he goes "this is harder than it looks." Wires or no wires, it's a feat worthy of a sustained ovation, which the production mysteriously denies him by carrying right along.

Richard Eyre's direction is best when most dramatically or comedically human. At showbusiness level it's an efficient reordering of familiar ingredients. Like all musicals set in Edwardian London it resembles My Fair Lady, but at various points it also recalls Peter Pan, Wicked (or would that be The Wiz?) and even the Nutcracker Suite.

The choreography, by the famous Matthew Bourne, is surprisingly run-of-the-mill, though the chimney-sweeps' chorus, a.k.a. Step in Time, breaks down defences by sheer energy and insistence, and also bleeds entertainingly into the scene that follows.

That brings us to the score, which is half from the movie, and half new. It comes hard to admit that songs with titles like Chim Chim Cher-ee and Supercal - well, you know the rest - are good songs, but in fact they are: very infectious and celebratory. They do not, however, advance plot or character, or pretend to; so the grunt work has to be done by the new stuff, supplied by George Stiles and Anthony Drewe. They are conscientious, not much more, except perhaps for Being Mrs. Banks, sung by Mrs. Banks.

Bob Crowley's sets are enjoyably mobile, solidly atmospheric whether domestic or arboreal and - when we get to Mr. Banks' bank - positively Gorey. There is of course flying, with an umbrella, and a jolly good thing, too. And if you're going to reach for the roof, then the mountainous Princess of Wales is the ideal theatre in which to do it.

- Mary Poppins runs until Jan. 8. For tickets, call 416-872-1212 or visit mirvish.com.

THEATRE REVIEW

The Life and Times of Mackenzie King Cameron House, Toronto

The Rez Sisters Factory Theatre, Toronto

The latest episode in Video Cabaret's staged comic strip of Canadian history is not quite as good as its predecessor, The Great War, but it still makes a smashing evening, with the usual complement of dazzling quick changes of both costume and character, magnificently exaggerated wigs and costumes, pinpoint lighting and spectacular action on a tiny stage.

The Life and Times of Mackenzie King is as much about the times as the life. Its a high-speed tour of the roaring 20s and the hungry '30s. The title character is portrayed by Paul Braunstein, on a beguiling note of cankered winsomeness, as a mother's boy whose mother happens to be dead, but who compensates by contacting her spirit and consorting with a highly supportive married lady while her husband dances attendance and delivers messages. Hes in office for much of the first act, out of it for most of the second, but were always glad to see him, and though Michael Hollingsworth's script and direction do their conscientious best to keep him in play, he does have to do a lot of hopeful hopping on the sidelines.

His conservative opponents, though, provide plenty of malicious entertainment, with Rick Alan Campbell's Arthur Meighen shooting himself in the foot as he wonders why vacating the throne doesnt make you the power behind it, and Jacob Jamess R.B. Bennett gleefully and gluttonously grinding the faces of the poor beneath the famous iron heel. Although I was surprised to see his eyes lighting up at the thought of concentration camps on the German model, a full three years before the Nazis came to power.

It may be a less serious anachronism, but I also felt that when the gangster Al (Greg Campbell) professes himself so happy that he can't even remember the lyrics of Top Hat, White Tie and Tails, the real reason might be that they hadn't been written yet. Hes part of the shows other half, which deals with the people who aren't in the history books, and part of his function is to remind us that prohibition and racketeering were games that Canadians could join in, too.

The prohibition stuff, though, takes up too much of the first act, thereby having an unfortunate knock-on effect on the second, which gets to feel longer than it actually is.

One of the triumphs of The Great War was that it managed to be humanly affecting (a new quality for VideoCab) while still maintaining its satiric edge. It brings off something of the same with Joe Slomkowski, its all-purpose oppressed worker and indomitable anti-Fascist, but this time it can't avoid a generic sentimentality. Joe (well played by Mac Fyfe), gets his head broke, volunteers for one of Bennetts work camps before leading a revolt there, and finally takes himself off to the Spanish Civil War. Like his spiritual cousin in The Grapes of Wrath, hes everywhere.

Meantime the title character, back in power, is getting starry-eyed about Hitler, proving Hollinsgworth's indisputable point that you can't trust anyone. At the end, and in a startlingly effective break with the prevailing staging conventions, King gets a vision of the carnage to come; it terrifies him while whetting our appetite for the next instalment, which of course will be the Second World War. Tomson Highways 20-year-old play The Rez Sisters owes an acknowledged debt to Michel Tremblays Les Belles Soeurs. It also recalls another sister play, the one about the three who longed to go to Moscow. Highway's characters, living on a native reserve, yearn to go to Toronto to participate in the biggest bingo in the world," and they actually get there, prompting the suspicion that Chekhov's siblings didnt know when they were well off.

The play stands up pretty well, especially in its sharp evocation of the conditions the women are relying on their bingo winnings to alleviate; one of them dreams of paving the streets and thereby setting off an economic revival. The seven female characters arent all literal sisters; in fact their precise relationships, in Ken Gass's production, remain blurry throughout.

The casting is ethnically diverse: a perfectly fine idea given that this isn't one of those plays (from Othello to A Raisin in the Sun) that depend on identifiable racial differences. It does mean, though, that the sense of community has to be established through acting alone and this production is too unfocused, visually and verbally, for that to happen.

We get a series of disconnected vignettes, some clearer than others, though only one actress, Jean Yoon, manages to build a character with a clear relationship to everyone else; the others - notably Kyra Harper yearning for a fully functioning toilet - flourish only in monologues.

One scene, on a very oddly shaped bus, does manage to create a mood. Against that, set the treatment of Nanabush (Billy Merasty), an allpurpose spirit, who hovers around in a manner that's not so much mysterious as inexplicable.

- The Life and Times of Mackenzie King runs until Nov. 27; The Rez Sisters until Dec. 11. For tickets, visit videocab.com and factorytheatre.ca.

Note: .1,104 words with 194 in optional trims

John Neville was a maverick with a golden voice: a combination that made him a major theatrical force, first in England and then in Canada. It was the voice, allied to matinee-idol good looks, that first brought him to prominence in London. He was a member of the Old Vic company from 1953 to 1958, a period in which the Vic worked its way though all the plays of Shakespeare. Neville progressed from playing Fortinbras in the first season, to Hamlet in the last, taking most of the major juvenile roles, with a few wilder parts thrown in. He acquired quite a fan base, including a notoriously vocal contingent of teenage girls in the gallery.

The five-year plan was a major part of my own education. I entered high school in London during this time, and must have seen more than half of the plays. My first sighting of Neville was as Orlando in As You Like It, a role in which I seem to remember him displaying more voice than personality. (I may have been distracted by his Rosalind, Virginia McKenna, the most beautiful sight my 11-year-old eyes had yet beheld.)

It soon became obvious, however, that there was more to Neville than a pretty larynx; his Mark Antony in Julius Caesar was as cynical as he was eloquent. He kept his end up as Troilus, effectively the straight man in Tyrone Guthrie's riotous Edwardian production of Troilus and Cressida, and his Hamlet proved touching, intelligent and unsentimental. His Ophelia was an actress straight out of drama school named Judi Dench, whose career was to intersect with his on many future occasions. But the performance from this period that I remember most fondly was his Sir Andrew Aguecheek in Twelfth Night, whose folly had a delicate innocence about it that I have never seen equalled.

He always claimed that character roles, when he could get them, were what he most enjoyed. He was a Londoner, who relished the opportunity to use the accent he had grown up with. It was Neville, before Michael Caine, who first showed us what Alfie was all about. In 1963, in the stage version of what had first been a radio play, he was a beguiling rogue who, in a role full of direct address, delighted in engaging and bantering with the audience.

He bought a similar zest to acting in musicals. But there were other boundaries he was interested in breaking. Like many actors, he would talk about the neglected role of the actor in shaping theatrical policy, and the necessity of bringing the theatre to the people, and vice versa. Unlike many actors, at least at that time, he did something about it. He started directing plays, beginning with a competent Henry V at the Vic. Then, in the mid-'60s, he became one of three artistic directors at the new Nottingham Playhouse (Peter Ustinov was one of the others). The triumvirate broke up, as triumvirates tend to, and Neville was left in sole charge. His regime was strikingly successful, in staging old plays, encouraging new ones, and reaching out to the community.

It also recharged him as an actor. The role that had made him a star at the Vic was Richard II; he repeated it at Nottingham in a performance that Richard Eyre, who was later to have his own distinguished and adventurous regime at the Playhouse, but was then a beginning director in nearby Leicester, has described as "still one of the best Shakespearean performances I've ever seen. John was tall, aquiline, a natural aristocrat with feline grace who disguised well the roaring boy underneath." Learning of Neville's death, Eyre emailed me: "I'm very, very sad. . . . I was very fond of him." Neville had given him some of his own early breaks, and, many years later, when Eyre was running the National Theatre, he had cast Neville as Sir Peter in The School for Scandal.

It was one of Neville's rare British stage appearances in the latter part of his career. The excitement of Nottingham seems to have disenchanted him with London and, eventually, with Britain. In 1971, he was invited to Ottawa to direct a guest production of The Rivals, and essentially, he never went back. He became a Canadian citizen, and artistic director of, in turn, the Edmonton Citadel and the Halifax Neptune. He revitalized them both artistically and economically. In 1986, he took over the Stratford Festival, which he ran for four years; this theatre, too, he took out of the red.

The move to Stratford may have seemed predestined, but it wasn't inevitable. He'd been invited before, and had refused. Still a star, he had remained outside the Canadian establishment, as he had outside the English. (He was also on, to put it mildly, unfriendly terms with his immediate Stratford predecessor, John Hirsch, another theatrical rebel but of a different stamp.) Neville's Stratford programming was initially adventurous - all the late Shakespeare plays in one season - though, as often happens, it got progressively safer (The Merchant of Venice and A Midsummer Night's Dream in one year). He also virtually began the festival's commitment to, and eventual reliance on, American musicals; he played Higgins in My Fair Lady, and seemed to be having a lot of fun. His wasn't one of Stratford's highest-profile regimes, but it was a good one.

Since then, he'd been most visible in films (The Adventures of Baron Munchausen) and TV (The X-Files). Perhaps his most notable theatrical contribution in recent years was to organize The Ibsen Project, rehearsed readings in Toronto of the last three Ibsen plays, two of which he directed or co-directed, and in one of which he acted. These were exciting and made one want to see the plays in full-scale productions, something for which we're still waiting.

He was, I think, a great director of theatres rather than of plays, though I do remember a good Three Sisters at Stratford. As an actor, he could sometimes rely overmuch on those resonant and melodious tones; I felt, though I was in a minority, that this was the case with his mournful Don Armado in a Stratford Love's Labour's Lost. But when his mind and his sense of humour were fully engaged, he could be remarkable.

His career was unusual, maybe unique, not least in the way it split into two halves and between two countries - each, it seemed, largely unaware of his achievements in the other. I feel lucky to have witnessed some of both, and to have seen a man so devoted to putting his talent where his ideals were.

National Post

THEATRE REVIEW

The Addams Family

Toronto Centre for the Arts

There seems to be a consensus that the touring production of The Addams Family works better than the one that opened on Broadway last year (and will shortly be closing). As the closest I've come to the original is hearing the cast CD, I can't make comparisons, beyond noting there have certainly been changes in the score, and probably in the book.

The show that's touched down in Toronto is "supervised" by the illustrious Jerry Zaks, who was merely credited as "creative consultant" in New York, and it's a slick piece of goods, scenically and choreographically. The performances are fine, too. But it still isn't a good musical, and I doubt that it ever could be.

The insurmountable flaw is that the authors have taken something static and tried to make it move. The cartoonist Charles Addams invented his ghoulish namesakes in a long series of drawings in The New Yorker: Not even a cartoon strip, just a succession of creepily funny one-offs depicting a clan that had turned conventional moral values upside down, prizing death over life and laughing where others would shudder.

It's hard to write a story about them without falsifying them, especially if you don't want to rock any boats. (Yes, I know they were made into a successful TV series and two movies. So?) The musical's solution is to pit the Addam-ses against a straitlaced family from Ohio, which, despite there being 49 alternatives, is the state that musicals - see Wonderful Town and Bye Bye Birdie - always seem to pick on as emblematic of small town, small world America.

In this case the Ohioans, if that's the word, are Mr. and Mrs. Beineke, whose son Lucas has fallen in requited love with the Addams daughter Wednesday. They met in Central Park, which is where the Addamses, due to zoning laws established in the 15th century (by the Queen of Spain) have their spooky abode.

The lovers are nervous as to what their families may make of one another, but the Beinekes get invited to dinner anyway, dinner being one of those theatrical Last Sup-per affairs in which everyone sits on the same side of the table. In accordance with a Broadway trope that stretches, at the very least, from You Can't Take It with You to La Cage aux Folles, the eccentric family has vital life lessons to teach the visitors, being not only better-adjusted than they are but nicer, too.

You get that? The Addam-ses are nice. Papa Gomez (the show makes a great point of his Hispanic lineage) is over-flowing with what looks suspiciously like the milk of human kindness, wanting only the best for his daughter; he's like Tevye with castanets. He offends his wife Morticia, a thoroughly desirable wraith with what her husband aptly describes as "a neck line that stretches all the way down to Venezuela," by keeping from her the news that the young folks want to get married, maybe because it's so obvious that it hardly seems worth talking about.

Other pieces of narrative desperation include a hurricane that arrives at the end of Act One to keep everyone indoors but seems to have thoroughly dissipated by the start of Act Two, and a young heroine whose attitude to her betrothed seems to change from moment to moment according to the writers' whims. There's the standard strangled-voiced Gothic retainer; Mr. Beineke takes it as evidence of the Addams' oddity that they have a zombie for a butler; it's surely more uncommon that they have a butler at all. There is also a loony grandma, who's rather entertaining; an enthusiastically masochistic little boy; and an especially annoying uncle who's in love with the moon. You wouldn't expect the Addamses to stand for this last bit of sentimental whimsy, but they seem to lap it up, which is more than I could.

The book (by Marshall Brickman and Rick Ellice) has some funny lines, but not enough to stop the plot from yawning. Mandated tango rhythms apart, it's hard to decide whether An-drew Lippa's music is meant to be pastiche or just old-fashioned; much of it sounds like a lesser Jule Styne score from the '60s, which, admittedly, there are worse things. His lyrics are neat, in a rather mechanical way; putting macabre sentiments to jaunty tunes is by now hardly a new idea, but Ma and Pa Addams do have a duet (Live Before We Die) that can stand on its own melodic feet.

Douglas Sills makes a delightful Gomez, better I would guess than Nathan Lane's original since Sills, feasting on the Latin, has had to invent his own sweetly extravagant persona whereas Lane sounds as if he's just doing his usual. As Morticia, Sara Gettelfinger looks stunning but feels wasted; I imagine that Bebe Neuwirth on Broadway was even more so, both ways.

Two other musical vets are landed with the elder Beinekes, who are the wrong kinds of caricature. Crista Moore, as Mrs. Frustrated, at least gets a showpiece opportunity to let it all hang out. Martin Vidnovic, as Mr. In-sensitive, gets nothing. This may be part of what I deduce from the CD synopsis to have been a general softening up. It also suggests that there was once a sound structural reason for the chorus of Addams ancestors to have emerged from their tombs. Now, they're just bony background, though well disported in Sergio Trujillo's choreography and in the set and costume designs of Julian Crouch and Phelim McDermott.

These latter two were the show's original directors; and I wonder if their vision may not have been darker, perhaps closer to Charles Ad-dams, than the giggly merry-making that's being served up in his name here.

- The Addams Family runs until Nov. 27. For tickets, call 1-866-950-7469 or visit dan-capticket.com.

Hannah Moscovitchs The Childrens Republic stakes out its ground very clearly. Literally, too: When the audience enters the theatre it sees the words Warsaw 1939" written on the stage floor. When it returns after the intermission, the words have changed to "Warsaw 1942. Since the principal setting is a Jewish orphanage, we know what we're in for. The orphans themselves begin the second act by chalking on a wall the new restrictions that confine them to the ghetto. They then partially deface them, in a silent sequence infused equally with desperation and defiance.

The play, a joint commission of Tarragon and the Harold Green Jewish Theatre Company, is in part a celebration of and memorial to Dr. Janusz Korczak, who ran the orphanage and was a pioneer in the advocacy of children's rights, physical and moral. In one of the earliest scenes, he holds a microphone against the chest of one of his charges and announces to unseen auditors this is how a childs heart sounds in the presence of adults" -- a wonderful line that I hastened to write down, only to discover that it had been printed in the program, twice. Hardly less resonant is Korczaks rationale for transforming himself from physician to pedagogue: "You can't cure poverty with Aspirin.

These may be direct quotes from source -- Moscovitch admits to lifting a few -- but that would just prove she knows how to borrow as well as how to write and construct. She retains the rare ability to sketch large historical subjects on small domestic canvases, without cheapening the first or inflating the second. This is the best new Canadian play in a longish time. But it's also second-tier Moscovitch in which the authors scheme, like her heros if less tragically, gets derailed by history.

The first half of the play is mostly about children's autonomy. Korczak sets up a children's court" in which the orphans settle their own disputes by putting one another on trial and then rendering judgment. But once the Germans have invaded, these things become moot. Life in the ghetto becomes about survival; Korczaks children are in a prison within a prison, forbidden the streets for fear that they would be traumatized, or worse, by what theyd find there. One boy, a troublemaker from the start and deeply troubled, breaks out, in all senses. He's perhaps more autonomous than Korczak would like; they're equally self-willed but the relationship is reiterated rather than explored. The play is tough but sparing in its depiction of the approaching Holocaust; of course, the audience can fill in most of the blanks. The odd result is that the second act is more exciting than the first but less interesting. The author also permits herself a note of uplift at the end that feels both uncharacteristic and unearned.

The play is moving and compelling, and Alisa Palmer has given it a tense and sensitive production, though she cant prevent the first half, made up of short scenes, from seeming choppy; the second benefits from having fewer transitions. Peter Hutt, valued veteran of Shaw and Stratford, has a rare chance at a leading role and takes it beautifully, showing Korczak as a man keeping despair at bay while radiating intellectual passion and practical concern. As his assistant, Kelli Fox has to alternate between nagging and supporting him; she does both forcefully but there are times when she seems to be stating the obvious rather too obviously. Mark Correia as the rebel heads a striking selection of orphans whose other members are Elliott Larson (touchingly tremulous), Katie Frances Cohen and Emma Burke-Kleinman. Theres also a delicate performance by Amy Rutherford as a genteel schoolteacher who, both in what we see and hear of her, embodies the terror of the times.

- The Children's Republic runs through Dec. 18 at the Tarragon Theatre. Visit tarragontheatre.comor call 416-531- 1827 for more information. robert.cushman@hotmail.com

THEATRE REVIEW

Ride the Cyclone Theatre Passe Muraille, Toronto

No question that for verve, imagination and an unflaggingly high level of performance, Ride the Cyclone, a small-sized musical, puts bigger shows to shame.

It also represents an interesting confluence of forces. It's the creation of the Atomic Vaudeville company from Victoria; in Toronto it was the hit of last years Summerworks festival; and its now returned as a co-production by Theatre Passe Muraille, one of the city's oldest established alternative theatres with no particular track record in musicals, and Acting Up Stage, who do nothing but musicals, usually off-the-wall ones that originated in the United States. So it's a step forward for everyone concerned.

That said, I have my reservations, which are about the presentation being superior to the material. Jacob Richmond, who wrote the script, was the author of Atomic Vaudevilles Legoland, a satire that was often crazily funny but had a rickety structure. The same is true of Ride the Cyclone.

Set in the fictitious town of Uranium, Sask., it concerns six teenage members of the high school glee club who went for a ride on the eponymous local roller coaster and were killed when it malfunctioned. When we meet them, theyre holding a posthumous convocation to reflect on their so-called lives. Each contributes a monologue followed by a song, which evolves into a production number in which all the others enthusiastically, if mostly sardonically, join. It's like Glee with claws.

Their self-appointed leader, in death as in life, is Ocean O'Connell Rosenberg (Rielle Braid), half-Catholic, half Jewish, who channelled her mixed feelings about her mixed parentage into becoming a take-no-prisoners debating champ. Then there are Noel (Kholby Wardell), who has/had fantasies of being a Parisian sex-object; Ricky (Elliott Loran), a blank nerd whose secret life centred on being a superhero; Misha (Matthew Coulson), an immigrant from Ukraine whose old hometown was devastated by the uranium that gave his new hometown its name; and Jane Doe (Sarah Pelzer), so named because nobody knew who she was or, since her head was cut off and no one can find it, ever will. Last, and maybe least in the others estimation, is Constance (Kelly Hudson), a bespectacled girl who is embarrassed at being the only one who actually loves Uranium, a ghost town the others couldnt wait to leave.

Their set-up speeches are, without exception, hilarious. The lyrics, on which Richmond collaborated with Brooke Maxwell, are less good, though some of this may be blamed on an indistinct sound system and on accompaniment that is sparse but loud.

The show also has a complicated set-up. Jane Doe, whose plot line is implausible even in this context, is thrust to the front too early, so we wonder if she belongs in some other story. We've already met a super-narrator, The Amazing Karnak, a mechanical fairground fortune teller who, naturally, knew what was going to happen but didn't say and now feels guilty.

Karnak, though played by a presumably pre-recorded voice, is a delight, so much that I felt rather cheated that the show wasnt actually about him. He does however provide some justification for the title, which is otherwise catchy but irrelevant.

All the performances are smashing but Hudsons is the standout, as riotous as the others but poignant in a more grounded way. She has the best song and she rocks the house with it. She also has the last laugh, since it turns out that just before the fatal ride she lost her virginity, which is more than any of her more glamorous colleagues seem to have achieved.

The direction, by Richmond and Brett Small, gets the show resoundingly across. I saw it from the end of the front row, which, sightlines being what they are, may have skewed my perspective and soured my reaction. Anyway, it's already a super hit and on its way to becoming a cult. Or maybe vice versa.

- Ride the Cyclone runs until Dec. 3 (for now). For tickets, visit passemuraille.on.ca.

2011-11-26-from-russia-about-love-do-you:
The new Mady Centre for the Performing Arts in Barrie incorporates a black-box theatre that is to be home for the enterprising and previously peripatetic Talk Is Free company. The opening production is one of those shows in which the performance outclasses the material.

Do You Turn Somersaults?, a line that turns up twice in the actual dialogue, is the whimsical title newly bestowed on a Russian two-hander originally called Old-Fashioned Comedy and written in 1975. In historical context, that former name was itself something of an act of defiance. Aleksei Arbuzov, the author, may have been the theatrical personification of the Soviet thaw; his plays, at least the ones I know about, draw on recent Russian history without being overtly, or even covertly, political. One of them, The Promise, was quite a hit in the West in the 1960s.

Soviet Russian drama is generally reckoned a dead zone, governed by officially mandated simplicities. Arbuzov seems to have rebelled against that while falling into a simple-mindedness of his own. What's especially startling, and eventually stultifying, is that everything about it is there on the surface. Thats not to say that the characters dont keep secrets from one another; they do, or there could hardly be a play. But they reveal them, explicitly and at times that are both personally and dramatically convenient. What's remarkable is that they don't seem to be keeping any secrets from themselves. This, amazingly from a compatriot of Chekhov, is a play totally innocent of subtext. And it makes you realize how much even the most insubstantial modern plays depend on the ambiguous and the unspoken. Without them, things seem very flat; though in this case some of the flatness may be due to a pedestrian translation.

It does though provide a platform for an outstanding couple of actors. "Do you turn somersaults?" is a question asked by Rodion Nikolayevich, medical officer at a sanatorium, to Lidya Vasilyevna, an unruly patient who claims to be a circus performer. Later it transpires that, though she has been an actress in the past, her circus role is in the box office. Shes an eccentric and demanding lady who gets under Rodions skin; he's a conscientious and imperturbable man who gets under hers. But of course, as time goes on and they keep bumping into one another inside and outside the institution, they grow to like one another. Both are late middle-aged people with past marital scars that need healing. It's fairly obvious where this is heading, the only real suspense being whether time will catch up with them before romance does. But the advances, withdrawals and revelations are grist for the players. Lucy Peacock overdoes the imperiousness of her first scene, the more perplexingly in that its a quality that never reappears. She has, in effect, to start over; once she does, she gives a glowing performance thats brusque and funny; moving when dismissing her own pain and even more so when contemplating her partner's. Geordie Johnson finds the right weary, humorous tone from the start, and never loses it. He's especially delightful in a shameless but enjoyable scene in which he recalls, and demonstrates, how he used to dance the shimmy and even the Charleston. (Amazing that steps so complicated could ever have been dance-floor favourites. How civilization has declined.) More potently nostalgic, though, are both characters' reminiscences of how they got through the war: a genuine insight into the experiences of ordinary people in a catastrophic piece. The production far outclasses one I saw in a former life in London; the Royal Shakespeare Company did it on one of its main stages, under the title Old World, and despite having no less than Peggy Ashcroft and Anthony Quayle as its cast, it was dead on arrival. A small space lets it breathe more. Marti Maraden's staging is visually drab beyond the call of economy, but she places one scene beautifully: Peacock sits behind Johnson on a bench and her face, tilted to the side, drinks in everything he has to tell her.

? Do You Turn Somersaults? closes today at the Mady Centre for the Performing Arts, Barrie. Visit tift.ca or call 705-792-1949 for ticket information.
2011-11-27-theatrical-maverick-with-a-go:
John Neville, who died Nov. 19 at the age of 86, was a maverick with a golden voice, a combination that made him a major theatrical force, first in England and then in Canada.

It was the voice, allied to matinee-idol good looks, that first brought him to prominence in London. He was a member of the Old Vic company from 1953 to 1958, a period in which the Vic worked its way through all the plays of Shakespeare. Neville progressed from playing Fortinbras in the first season to Hamlet in the last, taking most of the major juvenile roles, with a few wilder parts thrown in. He acquired quite a fan base, including a notoriously vocal contingent of teenage girls in the gallery.

The five-year plan was a major part of my own education. I entered high school in London during this time, and must have seen more than half of the plays. My first sighting of Neville was as Orlando in As You Like It, a role in which I seem to remember him displaying more voice than personality. (I may have been distracted by his Rosalind, Virginia McKenna, the most beautiful sight my 11-year-old eyes had yet beheld.)

It soon became obvious, however, that there was more to Neville than a pretty larynx; his Mark Antony in Julius Caesar was as cynical as he was eloquent. He kept his end up as Troilus, effectively the straight man in Tyrone Guthrie's riotous Edwardian production of Troilus and Cressida, and his Hamlet proved touching, intelligent and unsentimental. His Ophelia was an actress straight out of drama school named Judi Dench, whose career was to intersect with his on many future occasions. But the performance from this period that I remember most fondly was his Sir Andrew Aguecheek in Twelfth Night, whose folly had a delicate innocence about it that I have never seen equalled.

He always claimed that character roles, when he could get them, were what he most enjoyed. He was a Londoner, who relished the opportunity to use the accent he had grown up with. It was Neville, before Michael Caine, who first showed us what Alfie was all about. In 1963, in the stage version of what had first been a radio play, he was a beguiling rogue who, in a role full of direct address, delighted in engaging and bantering with the audience.

He bought a similar zest to acting in musicals. But there were other boundaries he was interested in breaking. Like many actors, he would talk about the neglected role of the actor in shaping theatrical policy, and the necessity of bringing the theatre to the people, and vice versa. Unlike many actors, at least at that time, he did something about it. He started directing plays, beginning with a competent Henry V at the Vic. Then, in the mid-60s, he became one of three artistic directors at the new Nottingham Playhouse (Peter Ustinov was one of the others). The triumvirate broke up, as triumvirates tend to, and Neville was left in sole charge. His regime was strikingly successful in staging old plays, encouraging new ones and reaching out to the community.

It also recharged him as an actor. The role that had made him a star at the Vic was Richard II; he repeated it at Nottingham in a performance that Richard Eyre, who was later to have his own distinguished and adventurous regime at the Playhouse, but was then a beginning director in nearby Leicester, has described as still one of the best Shakespearean performances Ive ever seen. John was tall, aquiline, a natural aristocrat with feline grace who disguised well the roaring boy underneath." Learning of Neville's death, Eyre emailed me: "I'm very, very sad ... I was very fond of him. Neville had given him some of his own early breaks, and, many years later, when Eyre was running the National Theatre, he had cast Neville as Sir Peter in The School for Scandal.

It was one of Nevilles rare British stage appearances in the latter part of his career. The excitement of Nottingham seems to have disenchanted him with London and, eventually, with Britain. In 1971, he was invited to Ottawa to direct a guest production of The Rivals, and essentially, he never went back. He became a Canadian citizen, and artistic director of, in turn, the Edmonton Citadel and the Halifax Neptune. He revitalized them both artistically and economically. In 1986, he took over the Stratford Festival, which he ran for four years; this theatre, too, he took out of the red.

The move to Stratford may have seemed predestined, but it wasnt inevitable. He'd been invited before, and had refused. Still a star, he had remained outside the Canadian establishment, as he had outside the English. (He was also on, to put it mildly, unfriendly terms with his immediate Stratford predecessor, John Hirsch, another theatrical rebel but of a different stamp.) Neville's Stratford programming was initially adventurous - all the late Shakespeare plays in one season - though, as often happens, it got progressively safer (The Merchant of Venice and A Midsummer Nights Dream in one year). He also virtually began the festivals commitment to, and eventual reliance on, American musicals; he played Higgins in My Fair Lady, and seemed to be having a lot of fun. His wasn't one of Stratford's highest-profile regimes, but it was a good one.

Since then, hed been most visible in films (the title role in The Adventures of Baron Munchausen) and TV (the wellmanicured man" in The X-Files). Perhaps his most notable theatrical contribution in recent years was to organize The Ibsen Project, rehearsed readings in Toronto of the last three Ibsen plays, two of which he directed or co-directed, and in one of which he acted. These were exciting and made one want to see the plays in full-scale productions, something for which were still waiting.

He was, I think, a great director of theatres rather than of plays, though I do remember a good Three Sisters at Stratford. As an actor, he could sometimes rely overmuch on those resonant and melodious tones; I felt, though I was in a minority, that this was the case with his mournful Don Armado in a Stratford Love's Labour's Lost. But when his mind and his sense of humour were fully engaged, he could be remarkable.

Neville suffered from Alzheimer's, to which he succumbed at Wellesley Central Place in Toronto. His family held a private service this week, with a public memorial to be announced in the new year.

His career was unusual, maybe unique, not least in the way it split into two halves and between two countries - each, it seemed, largely unaware of his achievements in the other. I feel lucky to have witnessed some of both, and to have seen a man so devoted to putting his talent where his ideals were.

2011-11-29-a-frank-canvas:
THEATRE REVIEW

Red

Bluma Appel Theatre, Toronto

Jim Mezon, in the past three seasons at the Shaw Festival, has shown himself a great actor, perhaps most notably as Big Daddy in Cat on a Hot Tin Roof. That performance was a brilliant display of nonstop, highly focused vocal and physical energy, and it should have made him ideal casting for the role of Mark Rothko in Red.

John Logan's play presents Rothko, New Yorks high priest of abstract expressionism, as a hectoring loudmouth who hardly stops glorifying himself, denigrating his competitors and preaching about art. Although both the author and the character are American, the play started in England, where it was an acting triumph for Alfred Molina, whose performance had whirlwind speed and volcanic strength.

I had expected Mezon to offer something on the same lines. In fact he tries, initially at least, something quieter and more contemplative. This is another mode hes very good at, and for a time it works. Our first sight of him is memorable, gazing out from the tip of a stage that's been angled to point at the audience. He's lost, it seems, in contemplation of the canvases on which he is presently at work. Hes disturbed by the entrance of the only other character, his new young assistant, who stretches out a hand that his employer pointedly ignores. That sets the tone for their subsequent relationship.

Its the 1950s, and what plot there is concerns Rothko's commission to paint a set of murals for the new and swank Four Seasons restaurant in the Seagram Building. As the job and play proceed, so Rothko's pronouncements get angrier and louder and Mezon is forced to shout. This he can certainly do, but it all sounds hollow and unmodulated, apart from one passage. This is Rothkos account of a visit to the Four Seasons, which left him horrified by the place, the patrons and even the menu, convinced that his work would be ignored by the people whose complacency its intended to puncture.

As writing, this is very suspect, but at least it's about an actual place and actual people and Mezon can make his passion specific, just as it was in his astonishing confrontation with his son in Cat.

The play is one of those middlebrow American prizewinners with monosyllabic titles that are thought to be profound because they take on, or at least mention, big subjects. They were a staple of the previous regime at Canadian Stage, but the new one was thought to have left them behind.

As an earnest of progress, the production has been entrusted to Kim Collier, an innovative director who must have seemed a logical fit for a play about an innovative painter. In fact, there's a severe limit to what she can do with whats essentially a talk piece. A curved wall slides apart to reveal David Boechlers big, bare and impressive studio set, on which objects from paint cans to cartons of Chinese takeout make powerful visual statements.

Less happy is having the lighting turn yellow when somebody mentions "golden ambition" and the introduction of a slide show of pop art where an intermission used to be.

The acting, meanwhile, could use more light and shade. David Coomber certainly holds his own as the sorcerer's apprentice but he's too unvariedly fresh-voiced as well as fresh-faced.

Meanwhile, the production has muffed what in New York was the plays highpoint: the two men furiously priming a canvas with the colour thats the play's title and the character's lodestar. Its meant to be orgasmic; Rothko even lights a cigarette afterwards. Here, its over too soon and there isn't enough passion leading up to it.

By coincidence or design this is Canadian Stage's second meditation this season on that same colour and its infinite varieties. I Send You This Cadmium Red, using artists' actual words, was more modest, more informative, and more moving.

? Red runs until Dec. 17. For tickets, call 416-368-3110 or visit canadianstage.com.

2011-12-01-a-tribute-to-canada-s-greates:
One of the first and best Canadian productions I ever saw was The Dybbuk, directed by John Hirsch. It was in 1974, at the St. Lawrence Centre in Toronto, though it had originated at the Manitoba Theatre Centre, of which Hirsch was the artistic director and effectively the creator.

I don't remember much about the acting, except perhaps for Marilyn Lightstones performance, but I do recall the intensity of it all, the atmospherics, the extraordinary visual and vocal evocation of the vanished world of Russian shtetl culture, centred around the synagogue. It was a world of great terrors and great warmth. It was in part a tribute to Hirschs own roots, from which he had been forcibly and horrifically torn by the Second World War, and also perhaps to his own temperament. He was also a man who experienced great terrors and great joys, and who both shared and inspired them, on and off the stage.

He used to say that he was a member of four mafias: Hungarian, Jewish, homosexual and Winnipeg." I owe that quotation to a new biography entitled A Fiery Soul: The Life and Theatrical Times of John Hirsch, by Fraidie Martz and Andrew Wilson. The rather fanciful title comes from a poem by John Dryden; the book itself does a good, if sometimes too breathlessly catalogued job of chronicling both the life and the work and relating one to the other.

Hirsch died from AIDS in 1989. Seana McKenna, who was directed by him as a young actress after having failed her first audition with him, spoke - enchantingly, hilariously and without notes - about both experiences at a book launch in Toronto this past week. She also remarked that a whole generation of Canadian theatre people, some of them already quite influential, must now have grown up without knowing who he was or what he accomplished. That is unfortunate because his talents were remarkable, his influence vital and his personality unique.

What is clear from the book is that, from the perspective of the Canadian theatre as a whole, his greatest achievements were in Winnipeg. The MTC, whose origins were in amateur theatre and which he, greatly assisted by the still-feisty Tom Hendry, brilliantly transformed during the 1950s into a wholly professional one, inspired the entire regional theatre movement. That makes its creation second in importance only to that of the Stratford Festival.

That Hirsch found himself in Winnipeg at all was something of an accident. He was a Holocaust survivor, who had grown up in Budapest with a heritage that was mostly Jewish but partly Catholic, both strands vital to his later work. None of his family outlived the war, and he did so mainly by scavenging. Given the chance to emigrate to Canada - he happened to be standing in the right visa line on the right day - he chose Winnipeg over Halifax or Vancouver because it seemed safer to be in the middle.

The household on which he was billeted expected to have him for a couple of weeks but got him for life. Nothing in the biography is more touching or telling than his continued loyalty to his adoptive mother and sister whom he continued to phone every week of his life and whom he visited every chance he got. With them, he found the home he had lost.

By the time of The Dybbuk, he was an internationally known director, working regularly in New York. As an occasional visitor to Canada, I didn't see his work again until 1980 when he directed A Funny Thing Happened on the Way to the Forum, a highly praised production that I didn't much enjoy; all the same, I liked the fact that hed done it. He was a gleeful polymath, as ready to mount a musical, or even a cabaret, as a classic.

In 1981, in the wake of a notorious debacle over the post-Robin Phillips succession, he took over Stratford: a stormy regime launched at a stormy time. He was not, it seems, very happy there, any more than he had been when running CBCs TV drama department, though he did fine work in both places. His 1983 Stratford Tartuffe, overlooked in the book, was exceptionally fine, very tense and intelligent; so, despite some critical damning, was his As You Like It. But he did leave the place in the red.

He's most celebrated as a director of Chekhov; his Three Sisters, in Phillips' regime, is legendary. In fact, he only directed two of the plays in Canada, plus an unhappy attempt at The Seagull for the Habimah Theatre in Tel Aviv; his only attempt at directing in a language he didnt speak.

He could be cruel to actors, though to his credit his bullying seems to have been hot not cold, impulsive not calculated. And the victims seem to have forgiven him. At the launch, Alon Nashman gave us a riotous taste of a one-man play about Hirsch that hell be performing at Stratford next year. (Although I have to say that he looks less like Hirsch than I do.)

By the time I moved to Canada in 1986, Hirsch's career was largely over: something I regret for my own selfish sake, and for the country's because he has yet to be replaced. There are directors who are his partial heirs: Peter Hinton and Morris Panych come to mind, and our leading Chekhovian in recent years has been another Hungarian, Laszlo Marton; all of them more equable characters than he was. But theres nobody who combines his pictorial flair, his intellectual reach, and - perhaps luckily - his tragic inheritance. So far, hes Canada's greatest director.

? A Fiery Soul: The Life and Theatrical Times of John Hirsch by Fraidie Martz and Andrew Wilson ($22) is available from Vehicule Press.

2011-12-06-we-re-not-in-oz-any-more:
(From the National Post, December 7, 2011) Tickets for The Wizard of Oz can be purchased by calling 1-855-599-9090. An incorrect number appeared in Tuesdays Arts & Life.

THEATRE REVIEW

The Wizard of Oz Elgin Theatre, Toronto

Ross Pettys latest holiday extravaganza - or wickedly wacky family musical - is the best in several years. The good things start with the choice of material. The Wizard of Oz is a famous fairy tale, but one that has never been on pantomime's usual source list. Unlike, say, the tangle of Robin Hood stories, it has a solid structure that can be messed around while still standing up straight. The show gives official credit to L. Frank Baum's original story, but it also pays surreptitious homage to the Judy Garland movie, that being the version that everybody knows. In fact, it gets the best of both worlds.

Speaking of worlds: in this incarnation we arent in Kansas anymore, even at the start. This script, "adapted" by Lorna Wright and Nicholas HuneBrown, gives us a skateboarding Dorothy from present-day Toronto, a self-possessed teen clearly unfazed by witches or wizards, not to mention lions or tigers or bears. The urban landscape she inhabits, neatly depicted or projected by designers Beth Kates and Ben Chaisson, comes complete with streetcars that pass in the background with implausible frequency. I could happily have spent more time there. Plot requires though that we get speedily whirlwinded off to an Oz that takes its name seriously, being populated by Aussies, a gyrating gesticulating crew of outback yokels, whom the Wicked Witch of the West dismisses, not too unjustly, as a bunch of ethnic stereotypes.

Some things are familiar: Dorothy still has her dog, who is granted an endearing amount of stage time. Others have changed: She now also has a love interest in the shape of the Tin Man, though, for reasons best not gone into, he isnt a tin man when they meet. Although he does feel in need of a heart, which is where she comes in.

The Scarecrow and the Cowardly Lion remain much as we have always known them, except they are already buddies rather than picking one another up on the yellow brick road. The writers do a good job of reconciling the old with the new, though they run out of steam toward the end.

This apart, Tracey Flye's direction keeps things moving briskly and imaginatively, with a nice degree of self-mockery. A curiosity is that, though she's best known as a choreographer, she didnt do the dances here; theyre the work of Marc Kimelman, and they're excellent.

The show's greatest asset, though, is its cast, which is crammed with some of the citys best musical comedians. A funkier, spunkier, less cloying Cinderella - sorry, Dorothy - than Elicia Mackenzie could hardly be imagined; or a more charmingly metallic Romeo than Yvan Pedneault, who sings strong and acts shy; while his buddies, all Antipodean miners, sing about being macho men, he keeps a psychological distance.

Kyle Blair is a winsome Scarecrow, and Steve Ross the most ideally suited Lion since Bert Lahr. Jessica Holmes plays a well-intentioned if absentminded fairy named Splenda, who has a double function: in panto terms shes the traditional fairy godmother, setting the story up and keeping a benevolent eye on it; in the Oz universe, she's a delightfully lisping parody of the good witch Glinda, who was the one insufferable element of the classic MGM movie. She bridges both worlds by addressing the audience as her Munchkins, and getting away with it.

If anything, there is more talent on this stage than the show knows how to use. As the wizard, who always seems as much a fraud as a title character as he is a wizard, Eddie Glen has nothing to do in the first half and hardly anything in the second.

In accordance with recent Petty tradition, we have not one but two man-crazy dames. As the Witch, there's the boss himself, having his usual good time taunting us for not hissing him loud enough, though Im not sure his heart is still in it. As Dorothys guardian Plumbum, we have Dan Chameroy, also recycling.

The interpolated pop songs contribute to the fun feel, though they aren't likely to vex the ghosts of Harold Arlen and Yip Harburg, which may already be sufficiently vexed at having their film score padded out on the current London stage with additional numbers by Andrew Lloyd Webber.

Meanwhile, in Toronto we have one other wrinkle they couldn't have anticipated. Everyones glad she took such a crowning, Harburg wrote of the grisly fate of the Wicked Witch of the East, "getting hit by a house is even worse than drowning." He never dreamed that, courtesy of Dame Plumbum, it would be an outhouse.

- The Wizard of Oz runs until Jan. 6. For tickets, call 8664477849 or visit rosspetty.com.

2011-12-14-on-rhythm-the-blues-memphis-h:
An intriguing thing about Memphis is that it seldom mentions the words "rock 'n' roll." It's noteworthy, because the birth of that music is what the show is supposed to be about. As far as I can tell, the phrase doesn't even crop up until the second act. A New York record producer, memorably small and smarmy, comes to the eponymous city some time in the mid-1950s and informs some black musicians, who thought they were playing rhythm and blues, that R&R -- the stuff he puts out for white kids -- is just R&B "sped up." The musicians look as if they're about to contest the point, but opt for a quiet and conceivably more prosperous life instead.

Memphis is a better show than I'd expected and a less good one than I hoped. It takes some bold steps and then shuffles back on them. It ends with a celebratory number called Steal Your Rock 'n' Roll (as in "don't let them ...") suggesting that the show and the characters have bought into the Man's values and vocabulary. In which case, why were they shown implicitly questioning them?

The central character of Memphis is a young, poor, white enthusiast of black music named Huey Calhoun, loosely based on the real Memphis disc jockey Dewey Phillips. (Huey, Dewey, where's Louie?) Though unable to read a script or anything else, Huey -- through a combination of performer's instinct, musical passion and sheer wheedling energy -- becomes the city's top DJ, the first to hook a young white audience on black music. He even gets his own TV show, Huey's Rhythm and Blues Cavalcade. (Note the title.) He also falls in love with Felicia, the singer at the basement club where he first got hooked. Felicia's brother, who runs the club and carries his own (literal) scars, is suspicious of Huey and scared at the thought of an interracial romance. That's nothing to the reaction of sections of the white population. Huey gets attacked; Felicia gets beaten.

Taking a stand against the racism of 50 years ago may not be especially daring, but Memphis (book by Joe DiPietro) does it with tact and force. It also takes a refreshingly tangy approach to its central couple. Huey, indelibly embodied by Bryan Fenkart, is nobody's hunky crusader; he's snaky, in voice, gesture, gait and, to some extent, behaviour. He's gutsy and his values are good, but once success strikes, he goes from being nervy, graceless and socially inept to being arrogant, graceless and socially inept. He pretty much digs his own grave by doing the right thing at the wrong moment. (Added source of suspense: Will the show itself sell out by resolving the love plot too easily? I'm not telling.) Felicia Boswell, playing her namesake, doesn't get to be so individual, but she's attractively sharp-tongued, and her singing stops the show. Though, as is par for the course these days, she stops it the coldest with the worst song; the program reveals that it's called Colored Woman, but other specifics are unavailable, so incomprehensibly does she blast it. I'm not blaming her; it's what the form and the fans demand. But, whatever they think, it ain't drama.

Which is a shame, because a surprising amount of the score is -- especially the parts with a comic edge. The music is by David Bryan, of Bon Jovi (he also collaborated with DiPietro on the lyrics). Unexpectedly, given those pop credentials, the character numbers, with good shapes and rhymes, are better than the onstage recreations, which are yardgoods stuff and make the show feel like the first jukebox musical to be stacked with newly written songs.

Christopher Ashley's production keeps score and story driving, much helped by the ubiquitous Sergio Trujillo (this is his third show to reach Toronto this year) whose choreography puts familiar moves into invigorating patterns. There are notable supporting performances from Will Mann as a cheerfully versatile janitor; William Parry as a radio station boss, cheerfully adjusting his values to suit the market; and Julie Johnson as Huey's widowed mom who comes on like Ethel Merman channelling Mahalia Jackson.

That last requires a bit of explaining. Initially as prejudiced as anyone else on her side of the tracks against the idea of her boy hanging out with a coloured girl, mama is nonetheless stirred by the sound of a black choir; and the show does an admirable job of showing how two musical traditions, country and gospel, can find common ground. Once Huey has bought her a new house and a new coat, she really lets loose and lays some soulful, roof-raising advice on him. It turns out, though, that it was the wrong advice, which retrospectively takes the shine off things and underlines the show's willingness to sacrifice everything for short-term effect. We've already had an astonishingly cheap moment in which a character, previously traumatized into silence, finds his voice: not just his speaking but his singing voice, in a scene that was actually moving until they got manipulative with it. And then there's that closing number, whose semantic problems are compounded by a structural one. This is musical about music but with a central character who isn't a singer. The actor can certainly sing, and as long he does it in character, in plot numbers, it's acceptable. But the finale brings him into a performance context; his sweetheart, who seems to have jumped into the Motown era of the next decade, is in concert, and there he is, part of it. The calculation is that the audience won't care, as long as they get a big finish with rock 'n' roll in the title. The dumbing down of the American musical continues, the sadder for happening in a show that for so much of the time is intelligent.

- Memphis runs through Dec. 24 at the Toronto Centre for the Arts. For more information, visit dancaptickets.comor call 416-644-3665. robert.cushman@hotmail.com
