THEATRE REVIEW

Dying City

Toronto Free Gallery

Parfumerie

Young Centre for the Performing Arts, Toronto

The best play in Toronto can be found in the back room of a small art gallery at Bloor and Lansdowne.

Christopher Shinn is an American playwright whose work is beginning to make inroads in Canada. Dying City had a prestigious Manhattan premiere at Lincoln Center though - not uniquely - it had to be staged in Britain before any producer in its homeland would take a chance on it. Its title is ambiguous or, to put it more invitingly, double-edged. It's used at one point to refer to Baghdad; it could equally well mean New York, which is where the action takes place and which here is still in the shadow, vividly summoned, of 9/11.

We're in the apartment of Kelly, a widowed therapist, who receives a surprise visit from her brother-in-law, a gay actor named Peter. It's especially surprising because a) despite her bereavement, she hasn't seen or heard from him in ages and b) the evening is still young and he's supposed to be on stage in a production of Long Day's Journey into Night, which normally takes quite a long time.

Peter has interesting reasons for taking early retirement from the world of Eugene O'Neill but they aren't the main points at issue. Kelly's husband and Peter's twin brother, Craig, was killed, in exceptionally absurd circumstances, in Iraq. Craig was an English major who put a promising academic career on hold in order to enlist. Just why he did it is an unanswered, perhaps unanswerable, question. There are all kinds of possibilities.

So there are in Peter's relationship with Craig, and in Craig's relationship with Kelly, and in Kelly's relationship with Peter. The play switches between two time frames. In the present tense, Peter vanishes into an offstage bathroom to be replaced a moment later by Craig, taking us back to the night of his final departure. The twins are of course played by the same actor; in this production he's Sergio Di Zio, who alternates two fully realized performances without ever letting one overflow into the other. The quick, and fairly basic, changes of costume matter less than the contrasts in voice, stance, manner and personality.

Craig is forceful, unyielding and at the end of his tether, certainly in his marriage; he's also terminally impatient with his brother, who seems to be juggling partners. Peter, by contrast, seems terribly open - as Di Zio plays him, the confidences seem to spill out of him uncontrollably - but he's holding plenty back, some of it to be revealed at the most hurtful moment possible. Clearly, he adored his late brother and also resented him; the mixed feelings were mutual and, in Peter's case, continuing. Peter also, as you might expect and in his own way, loves Kelly. She's in no state to love anyone.

Lesley Faulkner, who plays her, has probably the harder task; she spends as much time reacting as acting, and carries a load of pain that is only gradually revealed to us. At times it seems to be the actress rather than the character who's impassive; she doesn't come into her own until she's able to unleash some anger, at which points, both past and present, she's very powerful.

In 80 minutes' playing time, the play brings its relationships fully to life, including the one between two people who, for obvious reasons, can never meet. It also summons a whole world, both material and intellectual, beyond the room, the political playing itself out through the personal; it's especially interesting to be reminded how feelings and opinions changed about Iraq. It does all this in dialogue that's never forced and sometimes funny. It's a relief to encounter an American play that isn't soft-centred, emotionally or intellectually Peter Pasyk's direction, on a tiny stage, is first-rate, physically and tonally.

I should, though, qualify my opening sentence; Dying City is the best new play in Toronto. The best allaround, certainly the biggest treat, is Soulpepper's Parfumerie, which has returned with even more wit, point and unsentimental tenderness than it showed two years ago. If your heart has cold cockles, this is where to have them warmed.

? Dying City runs until Dec. 17. For tickets, visit dyingcity.com. Parfumerie runs until Dec. 31. For tickets, visit soulpepper.ca.

The movie franchise may have run its course but Harry Potter and his almost-nemesis Severus Snape continue to confront one another, though for a limited time and only along one New York street.

At the Al Hirschfeld Theatre Daniel Radcliffe stars in a revival of the classic musical How to Succeed in Business Without Really Trying. At the Golden Theatre, one block down on West 45th, Alan Rickman has the dominating role in a new play, Seminar. Each of those two actors, it's safe to say, is his shows principal selling point. And both are very good in their roles, though Radcliffes success is the more unexpected of the two.

It's remarkable to find a British actor, barely into adulthood and with limited stage experience, taking such complete command of a big Broadway musical. Not only does he sing and dance with captivating enthusiasm, he is the only member of the cast to get the show's comic-satirical style right. Almost everybody else overplays or underlines or both.

As J. Pierpont Finch, conniving his way up from window washer to chairman of the board at World Wide Wickets Inc., Radcliffe draws a deft, smiley bow-tied outline that he can both inhabit and comment on. His Finch is outrageously, boyishly earnest, daring anyone to doubt him.

Rob Ashfords choreography is altogether uneven; many of the routines are crass and coarse, making you long for the resurrection of Bob Fosse. But there are two wonderful numbers. The first, Grand Old Ivy, spoofing college rah-rah, pits the diminutive Radcliffe against his boss, John Larroquette, whos approximately twice his height and at one point steps right over him. The stature-differential is more spectacularly exploited in the eleven o'clock rouser, Brotherhood of Man, a barbed paean to corporate togetherness in which everybody towers over Radcliffe, who still seems to be both leading and relishing the dance; he's obviously hardworking but without seeming effortful.

A compartmentalized set tries for satire and succeeds at being ugly and constricting, but Frank Loessers snazzy tunes and incomparably funny lyrics are a wonderful reminder of the days when people expected Broadway to be smart.

In Theresa Rebecks play Seminar, Rickman plays Leonard, a once-famous novelist teaching a private writing course to a quartet of twentysomethings. The man is patronizing, vituperative and unshakably aggressive, but this is gradually revealed to be a mask for self-hatred and - of course - passionate devotion to literature. Rickman is masterful with the snark, and in beautiful control of his aria of self-revelation.

Indeed all the actors are good, especially Lily Rabe and Hamish Linklater as the most gifted of the students, at least if we are to believe Leonard's instant judgments; he seems to be a phenomenal speedreader. He has to be, to stop the audience getting bored, but the device contributes to an overall impression of glibness. It's one of those instantly entertaining but quickly forgettable American plays that toy with ostensibly serious subjects.

The biggest hit on Broadway is, of course, The Book of Mormon (Eugene ONeill Theatre) and deservedly. Its become famous for its profanity, which in truth is fairly mild. The real and pleasant surprise is that, apart from being hilarious and well-performed and a true non-adapted original in an age where most musicals are conscienceless recyclings of pre-sold properties, it's about something.

Two recently graduated Mormon missionaries are sent on their probationary assignment to a village in Uganda, which of course has its own problems and couldn't be less interested; nevertheless the boys achieve something. It may not be realistically believable but as somebody says, in one of the shows finest moments, its a metaphor." The two young Elders are a highachieving favourite son, given a virtuoso straight-arrow performance by Andrew Rannells, and a plump and gormless acolyte, an accumulation of giggles and malapropisms that Josh Gad somehow stops from being irritating.

Book and score are by Trey Parker and Matt Stone (of South Park) and Robert Lopez (of Avenue Q); musically and lyrically, the three of them together don't add up to one third of a Frank Loesser; but apart from an interminably campy item set in hell, the songs do their work.

The show manages to make jokes about warlords and poverty and disease without making light of them. That's an achievement. It also pays tribute to traditional Broadway without being patronizing or parasitic.

A crowning attraction is the presence of Nikki M. James, Stratfords Juliet and Cleopatra of three years ago, as the sweetest, toughest, and most delectable of heroines.

Handout / The pleasant surprise with The Book of Mormon is that its about something. That and it's hilarious.;; Caption:
2011-12-22-gone-broadway-where-to-go-and:
The 1965 musical On a Clear Day You Can See Forever is rightly revered for its score; Burton Lanes music is glorious and Alan Jay Lerner's lyrics, though uneven like all his work, include some of his best. The book, though, is generally agreed - not least by Lerner himself, who wrote it - to have been a mess.

It concerns reincarnation, ESP, hypnotism and psychiatry, all of them among the author's own obsessions at the time. Its heroine was a greenfingered kook, appropriately named Daisy, with a smoking habit that led her to consult a shrink, one Mark Bruckner, who discovered that she had existed in a former life as an English regency heiress. He fell in love with her, in both her incarnations.

In the recently opened, and rather unexpected, Broadway revival (at the St. James Theatre) much has been changed. The shows present-tense period has been updated to the 1970s, whose fashions here look even more hideous than they actually were; and Daisy has become David, a gay florist. His previous self, though, is still a woman: a 1940s big band singer named Melinda. (The name could hardly be changed as its also the title of one of the most bewitching songs.) Mark, a widower, again falls for Melinda though not, he is at somewhat awkward pains to reassure us, for David.

To the extent that the original show worked at all, it seems to have worked as a vehicle for its leading lady, Barbara Harris. Bisecting, or bisexualizing, her double role deprives the show of its main motor, while making Mark the protagonist by default. That, the default part anyway, seems an apt description of Harry Connick, Jr., the production's marquee attraction, who is either not much of an actor or too embarrassed by his character's situation to try.

Hes a friendly stage presence, though, and his noncommittedness has an appeal of its own. As a singer he sounds more like Frank Sinatra than ever, which is fine in itself but doesnt blend well with the more traditional musicaltheatre attack of his fellows.

David Turner as David, alternating between flounces and hysterics, is probably obeying director's orders; Jessie Mueller performs very well as his alter or earlier ego, without quite justifying the script's insistence that Melinda could have been the second coming of Billie Holiday, Judy Garland and Ella Fitzgerald all at the same time. (The world would never know, because she died in a mysterious plane crash, just like Glenn Miller, who makes an appearance under a slightly altered name.)

The original stage score has been augmented with additional songs supplied by Lerner and Lane for the movie version, and with significant others from their earlier film musical Royal Wedding. Ironically, the numbers from the latter source often fit better into the rejigged book than those from the authentic Clear Day. There is a fascination in seeing which song will turn up next, and how; and for the first half-hour or so the show does look as if it might actually work.

The ending, too, is rather touching; we finally get to hear the title song and Connick does it very affectingly. Peter Parnells adaptation was commissioned and staged by Michael Mayer, director of Spring Awakening among other things, and its been designed, in psychedelic headache style, by Christine Jones. The sum is a disaster but not a disgrace. Anyone who collects golden age musicals should see it.

They will certainly want to see the latest revival of Follies (Marriott Marquis), a show whose first production, in 1971, is a legend difficult - or, given economic and other constraints, impossible - to live up to. It's equally impossible not to try. Stephen Sondheim's score - half of it pastiche with a sting, the other half elegant contemporary with an even greater sting - remains a tour de force; the lyrics may well be the best collection that he, or anyone else, has ever written for a single show. But without the magnificent fusion of the original Hal Prince-Michael Bennett staging, plus the unbeatable original cast, the central metaphor, tracing the human follies of the present, to the Ziegfeld Follies of the past, tends to fall apart.

The central quartet, vainly trying to obliterate their youthful mistakes but doomed to relive them, comprises Bernadette Peters, vocally ravaged at the performance I saw but still very moving; Ron Raines, correct but stolid; Danny Burstein, superb; and Jan Maxwell, who has won plaudits and awards as the super-sophisticated Phyllis but seemed to me to be having too good a time. The other three all have their meltdowns; why doesnt she?

Eric Schaeffers direction is lucid without being inspired; and it shirks the full darkness of the ending. In fact its most poignant moments come at the beginning, as the showgirl veterans assemble at their reunion, and exchange the fond embraces of incredulous recognition. Reencountering the show itself, 40 years on, yields something of the same sensation. Not only has Follies become its own myth, it's become part of its own subject.

RelativelySpeaking(Brooks Atkinson Theatre) is a triple bill of one-acts by famous cutups: Ethan Coen, whose opener is unspeakably bad; Woody Allen, whose closer might be called speakably bad, meaning that even its good jokes are tired; and Elaine May, whose middle piece is brilliant. Its title is George Is Dead. He was also very rich, and his death has left his widow, who's never had to do a thing for herself, dependent on a childhood acquaintance, whose own marriage is in vividly depicted trouble but who cant prevent herself from trying to help.

The play is a study of entitlement, financial and emotional, and hence both topical and eternal. Its farcical realism, superbly sustained up to but not including the very last moment. It's perfectly performed by Marlo Thomas, woman as grown-up child, and Lisa Emery, weary with maturity. This play needs to be rescued from its surroundings; May must have written something else it could be paired with.

A final New York holiday recommendation: Up until New Year's Eve, you can see Barbara Cook and Michael Feinstein performing together in Feinsteins own cabaret room at the Regency Hotel. The mutual congratulations are laid on too thick, though they do manage to sound surprisingly spontaneous, but the songs are the things.

Feinstein has acquired vocal weight over the years, certainly as a rhythm singer; Cook is less stunning than when performing solo last year in Toronto, but at 80plus, shes still the singing actress beyond compare, sacrificing neither half of the equation to the other. They end, though this will presumably change next week, with White Christmas; and for once it's a pleasure rather than an embarrassment to sing along.

Sara Krulwich, The New York Times / On a Clear Day You Can See Forever - this time with Harry Connick, Jr., a sex change and bell-bottoms.;; Caption:
2011-12-24-pastiche-without-purpose-hair:
The received wisdom on Hair is that it has great music and a terrible script. I wonder. Galt MacDermot's score must be the most copious ever written for a musical - the program lists 41 separate songs, in a show that isnt even throughsung - and most of the tunes have attractive hooks. The majority, though, fail to develop - Good Morning Starshine, which has a surprising but logical middle, is an exception - so they end up irritatingly weightless, whether as theatre or as pop. Theres also, especially considering the show's implicit claim to represent the youth movement of the 1960s, something curiously uncommitted about them; they feel like pastiche without purpose. It's a fragmentary score, only with an exceptional number of fragments.

The lyrics, by Gerome Ragni and James Rado, are similarly shapeless, rarely deigning to come to anything as conventional as a point. Again, there are exceptions: Frank Mills is one, and What a Piece of Work is another, though with that of course they had some august assistance. Pity the writer whos hailed as a pioneer: Just as John Osborne, after the success of Look Back in Anger, was lumbered with being the revolutionary saviour of the British theatre when he was in fact rather old-fashioned, so the authors of Hair were thought to have overturned the traditional musical and were expected to go on overturning it. In fact, their subsequent shows were major flops, and MacDermot, at least, seems to have been miscast. Hair billed itself - still bills itself - as "the American Tribal Love-Rock Musical (how many trendy bases can you cover in one subtitle?) but its doubtful that he was a rock composer. His roots were in jazz and swing - he composed African Waltz, theme of the Johnny Dankworth orchestra and a better tune than anything in Hair - and his best theatre score, for The Human Comedy, was persuasive big band 1940s.

There is, however, more to the book of Hair, also by Ragni and Rado, than previous stagings, including the original, have suggested. There is, for example, humour. That's one of the revelations of Diane Paulus' production, which comes to us on its postBroadway tour. Its visually and sonically vibrant; you can actually hear the words, not just because of technological advances but because the actors deliver them with both feeling and timing. The cast seem happily unselfconscious about enacting their parents revolution, and they make the most of what story there is.

It concerns, you may remember, the forcible enlisting of Claude, gentle member of a community of Central Park drop-outs. His parents, especially his dad, are all in favour of his going to Vietnam and proving himself a man; his friends want him to burn his draft card as a gesture, and then escape to Canada as a practicality. The friends include Jeanie (Aleque Reid) who, being both pregnant and ecologically conscious, might be described as an earth-mother-tobe; Sheila (Sara King), the clearest thinker of the group if you discount her claim to have seen the Pentagon levitate; and Berger, an all-purpose anarchic prankster. They're all well played, and if Steel Burkhardt as Berger comes over as insufferably smug and smirky, that probably means he's doing a faithful job. Claude was played, when I caught the show, by William Joseph Lewis, an understudy whose performance, vulnerable and unknowable, I cannot imagine being bettered.

All these characters, and several others, are engaged in an overlapping ritual - literally, at one point - of love and lust, but none of these emotional or physical entanglements are explored in any depth. Neither is anything else. The girl who sings about Frank Mills never mentions him again, and even Claudes predicament is ignored for lengthy periods; though it does give rise to a secondact dream (or nightmare) sequence thats here more intelligently and comprehensibly presented than ever before. Another surprise is the weight given to the show's elders. What do you want to be, besides dishevelled?" asks Claude's mother (Liz Baltes) and its the best line in the show, not because we agree with it but because its smartly turned. Her partner (Will Blum) turns up as another, more tolerant adult, in an initially funny scene that can't resist an extra twist.

The show wants to be - is neurotically afraid of not being - too hip for the house. It makes a great display of tearing down the fourth wall, but it wants us to cry over Claude. All the rushing down the aisles and inviting the audience onstage for a post-show dance that may have felt liberating when the show was new, now just looks like something that every show does when it runs out of ideas. And maybe it was never all that spontaneous. It's worth consulting William Goldmans book The Season in which he contrasts the shows off-Broadway premiere, when it did seem fresh and even brave, with its Broadway makeover, which arrived when the end of the war was already in sight and which has perforce been the source of all subsequent revivals. He also contrasts the predictably shocked responses of the more conservative critics with the far more vitriolic comments of an underground paper whose reviewer actually knew the scene the show was supposed to be depicting. He accused the producers of turning it into a kind of hippie theme park. It still feels like that, even in a production as good as Paulus's, only with 40 years of nostalgia thrown in.

? Hair runs through Dec. 31 at the Royal Alexandra Theatre. For ticket information, visit mirvish.com or call 416 872-1212.

Joan Marcus / From left, Lawrence Stallings, Steel Burkhardt and Matt De Angelis.;; Caption:

THEATRE REVIEW

Quidam

Ricoh Coliseum, Toronto

Cirque du Soleil's Quidam is one of its earlier productions, dating back 15 years or so. It's been revived for a tour, whose Toronto date is the Ricoh Coliseum, an arena that proves unexpectedly cozier than the very big top under which the Circus of the Sun usually shines.

According to a program that's short on information though long on pictures and even longer on price, Quidam means "a nameless passerby, a solitary figure - a person who lives lost among the crowd in all-too-anonymous society." I'm not sure whether that makes him a good or a bad thing.

Anyway, in this show, if he's the character I think he is, he's not only nameless but faceless, indeed headless; between his hat and his coat there's nothing but empty space: not perhaps the show's most spectacular effect but certainly a striking one. He rescues a young girl who's being ignored by her conventionally conventional parents, and leads her, to nobody's surprise, into a wonderland of acrobats, jugglers and clowns.

They, too, are anonymous, unless you're prepared to grapple with some very small print, but they're certainly colourful and, as usual at Cirque, their accomplishments can be incredible. They have skills that most people don't, though I find the implication that this makes them superior beings - superior at least to the heroine's mom and dad - very suspect. Chances are that when they take off the makeup and go home, their lives are as boring as anyone else's.

Circuses are formulaic, almost by definition, and I've never found Cirque du Soleil's attempts to elevate its own brand by applying some kind of mystical narrative thread to be very persuasive. It isn't here, but at least the Quidam story is simpler than most, and the title figure does make a magical reappearance to round things off at the end of the show, though for most of the time it's not just his head that's been invisible.

Quidam has other special attractions, both sonic and scenic. The music in Cirque shows is always good, but here it buoys the spectacle up to an exceptional, even hypnotic, extent. Everything that happens happens in rhythm. Meanwhile, the set features five girders just below the roof, each bending in an arc, and each equipped with a mobile block than can move toward or away from the audience. From each block there hangs a wire, and from each wire there can hang a performer. A quintet of them, with attendants, are as graceful as they are death-defying.

Jugglers toss vessels from one to another, at increasingly impossible angles and velocities. (Cirque, always marketconscious, sells miniature versions of these missiles at intermission. Patrons probably shouldn't try them at home.) An exceptionally beautiful act, devoid of props and trappings, consists of two bodies, one male and one female, supporting and balancing one another at increasingly improbable angles. Other, less rarefied performers skip rope, or roll and spin within what is apparently known as a German wheel. A late act takes apache or adagio dancing - the kind in which a woman gets flung around from one man to another - to surreal heights, with the emphasis on the noun: A small girl, though she might conceivably be a small woman, is thrown, with nonchalant expertise, into the arms of a man who has two other men in vertical formation beneath him.

All this, though breathtaking, is the kind of thing you expect from Cirque. More of a surprise is a clown who's actually funny, one who specializ-es in creative audience participation. In the first half, he inveigles a female customer into an imaginary car and makes more or less imaginary advances. In the second, he gets four punters to go through the motions of making a silent movie, the kind in which a pair of lovebirds are surprised by the lady's husband. To these three impromptu actors, he adds an impromptu clapper-boy.

The comic himself is ceaselessly inventive, while the draftees prove themselves (at least when I went) to be more than just good sports. They don't just enter into the spirit of the thing; they get possessed by it. Maybe this counts as an extension of the main theme; the clown draws civilians into an unexpected realm, like an earthier and more enjoyable version of the mysterious Quidam himself.

Quidam runs at Toronto's Ricoh Coliseum until Dec. 30 before moving on to performances in Oshawa and Windsor in January. For tickets, visit cirquedusoleil.com.

John Mahoney, Postmedia News / Whether that wheel is German or not, from the look on this clown's face, we're guessing that's not how it's supposed to roll.;; Caption:
2011-12-31-the-best-of-the-year-in-holes:
This was the year of plays from away. Canadian playwrights were either absent or below their best form. The most impressive new play of the year was Australian; the runners-up were German, British and Polish. Let's look at them, and the companies that brought them to us.

The Aussie one Andrew Bovell's When the Rain Stops Falling, the one from Down Under and the unexpected crown of an exceptional Shaw Festival, ranged boldly free in time and space while keeping tight control of story and theme, and examining its characters with what I can best describe as ruthless compassion. The same discipline and imagination distinguished Peter Hinton's production; from a fine cast, I'm most haunted by Ric Reid, whose long opening speech had me in his and the play's corner from its first line, and Graeme Somerville, as an apparently nice man destroyed by shame. The Shaw also gave us a monumental Cat on a Hot Tin Roof; Eda Holmes' production had a dream cast, with Jim Mezon as, vocally and emotionally, the biggest of Big Daddies and Gray Powell craftily counterpunching as Brick. Their long second-act confrontation was the duet of the year. The rediscovered Drama at Inish proved another actors' delight, with Thom Marriott melodramatically announcing that he wasn't at his best in melodrama, and Corinne Koslo as his devoted co-star and spouse. Marriott also shone as the police chief in On the Rocks, a lesser-known play by Shaw himself, "adapted" by Michael Healey - a new policy, apparently, and not a good one. It makes a production look like an apology. I'm not, though, as bothered as perhaps I should be by the festival's decision to confine its patron's plays to its smaller stages next year; if they dropped them altogether, that would be a problem. Of this year's Shavian shows, the best was the small-house Candida, with Somerville again exceptional, this time in a minor role. Of course, My Fair Lady might well count as Shaw, and was a delight anyway.

The German one The Test by Lukas Barfuss, a Company Theatre production by Jason Byrne whose direction, though by all accounts allowing the actors a lot of freedom, always comes off as exceptionally rigorous. In this study of inheritance, dynastic and political, Philip Riccio as a modern Iago struck chillingly to the soul of soullessness: a remarkable performance. Company Theatre, who have a spare but virtually unblemished record, here inagurated a new relationship with Canadian Stage. Which brings me to -

The British one David Greig's The Cosmonaut's Last Message to the Woman He Once Loved in the Former Soviet Union, a brilliant play though the production didn't do justice to its playfulness or the interlocking of its themes. Matthew Jocelyn's brave - and necessary - cosmopolitan policy at CanStage also brought us I Send You This Cadmium Red, a wonderfully casual meditation on art in which Julian Richings as John Berger gave one of the year's tenderest performances (it certainly showed up the similarly titled but artistically regressive Red) and brought back Another Africa, formerly The Africa Trilogy.

The Polish one Our Class, Tadeusz Slobodzianek's remarkably evenhanded examination of the Jedwabne massacre and its prolonged aftermath. Technically, this set of counterpointed reminiscences was unpretentiously daring; and it never once cheated. It showed Studio 180 at its semi-documentary best; as opposed to its revival of The Normal Heart, the seminal AIDS play, which mainly seemed worthy.

Most surprising actor of the year Stuart Hughes, who in Tarragon's modernish-dress The Misanthrope showed a new talent for sustained bravura, reinforced in at least one marvellous tirade in Soulepper's The Glass Menagerie, a moving production (Tennessee Williams had a good centenary) with a gloriously mercurial Nancy Palk. Hughes transformed himself again in The Price, also a Soulpepper peak. Otherwise their best were The Fantasticks, with Oliver Dennis' down-at-heel show stealer, and a slew of remounts, a policy that I wish could be continued: shows like The Time of Your Life, Window on Toronto and Parfumerie should always be available.

Stratford's Broadway-bound Jesus Christ Superstar was as good as that show is ever going to get. Still, its best musicals were Camelot, in which a flawed but beautiful show finally worked, and Twelfth Night, in which the songs - unlike those in the Shaw's The Admirable Crichton - are actually part of the text and which also happened to be a splendidly acted version of the play. Titus Andronicus was an exciting production; Seana McKenna's impish Richard III an insolently persuasive performance; The Grapes of Wrath an impressively unsparing staging; and The Little Years a decent newish play.

Most perplexing theatre Buddies in Bad Times, which hosted some dismal guest productions but whose own flagship show, The Maids, was superb (and I don't even like the play). Diane D'Aquila was transfixing, as she'd already been in CanStage's Saint Carmen of the Main.

Best Canadian script That may well have been Michael Healey's Are You Okay, if only for its resonant line about the remote chance of doing something "slightly better than awful"; he meant morally, but it works for art as well. I feel mean enough to mention Hallaj, an evening of melodramatic earnestness that - in writing, acting and direction - was one cliche after another. Some people liked it. Ride the Cyclone was terrifically staged and performed (especially by Kelly Hudson) but its numbers went on long after they'd made their points.

Commercial managements persisted in their belief that anything with a Broadway sticker on it is automatically doing us a favour. Conversely, some of the best things happened in holes and corners: David Yee's imaginative Paper Series, Brett Christopher's Barrie production of The Tempest, Dying City, which suggested that, despite all evidence to the contrary, good plays can still come out of America. There were some welcome returns: Assassins, Montparnasse and Two Pianos, Four Hands,which I hadn't remembered as being so funny.

David Hou / Camelot: One of Stratford's best musicals of the year, says our critic.;; Caption:
2012-01-03-welcome-to-a-musical-kind-of-:
THEATRE REVIEW

American Idiot

Toronto Centre for the Arts

The title American Idiot almost invites its own rejoinder, something about sound and fury and what it signifies. To be fair, the shows authors are probably smart enough to have seen that coming. To be further fair, the production does signify something, and something important. It signifies a generation's impotent rage. That much comes over loud and clear. Loud, anyway.

It signifies, but it doesn't illuminate. Officially entitled Green Days American Idiot, it represents both a nadir (so far; things can always get worse) and a culmination for the rock musical. It takes an album of minimal dramatic content, and diffuses that content even more by splitting its story three ways. We have Johnny, living a frustrated teen-or-twenty-something life in the suburbs of whats bitingly identified as Jingletown, U.S.A., and then moving to the city where things feel even worse.

He has two mates: Tunny, whose despair leads him to enlist for war, presumably in Iraq, from which he returns an amputee; and Will, who decides at the last moment to stay home because he's got his girlfriend pregnant. Will, who doesn't seem to have any, is the ultimate couch potato, staying in that position for the entire evening.

Different things may happen to these guys, but theyre still interchangeable blanks. The writing gives them no chance to be anything else. The music, credited to Green Day en masse, is mainly a series of indistinguishable ear-splitters, sometimes throwing off a stabbing or appetizing melodic phrase but never developing any of them. Interspersed are a few gentler tunes; the most appealing, Last Night on Earth, sounds, intentionally or not, like a pastiche of a 50s teenage ballad.

As always the music drowns out the words; though on examination, they don't add much. Billie Joe Armstrong's lyrics work best through simple repetition, as in, I dont care if you dont care," reiterated as a bonding ritual between the three heroes. Anything more ambitious is defeated by a mixture of pretentiousness and technical incompetence, two things that tend to go together; a lyricist who doesn't know where the stress falls on the word "today or how it should sit on the music is unlikely to have anything interesting to say on weightier matters. Let's not even get into the question of rhyme; why use it, if youre not prepared to do it right? Anyway the overall result is of portentous vagueness: OK for a rock concert, but fatal for a show with narrative intentions.

Example: Sept. 11 is never mentioned, but is presumed to hang over the action. So I guess the group lament Wake Me Up When September Ends is supposed to have historical resonance, rather than just being the latest in a long line of wistful September songs. Its defeated, though, by the rock lyric's traditional inability to hold a thought or an image from one line to the next. Further example: Johnny calls himself, and goes on calling himself, the Jesus of Suburbia. The show seems to agree, or at least makes a very big deal of it. On what grounds? He's no kind of preacher, no kind of teacher. Its the latest manifestation of the messianic complex rock has had since the 60s. But Johnny isn't the messiah; he's just a very sulky boy.

He does have a tempter: an apparent emanation of himself called St. Jimmy who, as befits a musical Mephistopheles, likes to make sashaying, head-tossing entrances down a fire escape. He turns Johnny on to heroin and off his girlfriend, affectionately known as What-sername, with whom he had earlier seemed truly smitten.

The performers do what they do, and do it well; I cant write about them individually because none of them is allowed to show any personality. The best part of the production is Steven Hoggetts choreography, which is practically continuous and which finds an expressiveness in brute force for which the rest of the show seems to be straining.

Otherwise, the most notable feature of Michael Mayer's production is its use of multiple video screens: I counted 33 (I needed the distraction) and I bet I missed a few. These are used for atmospheric and commentative purposes: as in, when the lyrics mention the 7-Eleven, a 7-Eleven sign pops up on the screens. For a show that rails, from its second line on, against the media," this one seems awfully proud of its own technology. But maybe this is all very subtle and self-reflexive point. Maybe the show is saying that Johnny's protest is not only pointless, but deserves to be.

Underneath he seems to be a nice old-fashioned boy; he sends postcards home, for Gods sake. Not emails, postcards. The funniest of the few spoken lines concerns not robbing a convenience store. And Johnny ends up back where he belongs, reunited with his friends. Regrets, he has a few; but if theres irony here, it's very hard to detect.

We have, who'da thunk it, an endorsement of Norman Rockwell's America: an anti-youth musical. It makes a change. But for it to be interesting, we would first have to care.

- American Idiot runs until Jan. 15 at the Toronto Centre for the Arts. For tickets, call 1-866-950-7469 or visit dancaptickets.com.

2012-01-07-the-mechanics-of-relationship:
Next Stage, based at the Factory Theatre, is an extension of Torontos Fringe Festival: an opportunity for Fringe companies to re-mount favoured productions in slightly less frenzied circumstances. For at least one of this years shows, the promotion (in both senses) is thoroughly justified.

LoveSexMoney, written and directed by Kit Sandler, is presented by Theatre Brouhaha, an outfit whose mission statement makes the usual inflated claims about treading boldly where no company has dared to go before. In fact, it's a play constructed on a model patented by that most commercial of dramatists, Neil Simon. Like his Plaza Suite, and its less successful successor California Suite, it's a sequence of three episodes all set in the same hotel room. (Which never gets re-decorated; theres scenic economy for you.) Theres nothing wrong with using a popular model; what's right is that Sandler has invigorated the formula with wit, invention and feeling. It's a heartening debut.

Her play differs from Simons in providing a narrative link between its scenes - characters from one reappear in the next. The jumping-off point is the famous Nevada news item about the 22-year-old student who auctioned off her virginity via radio and the Internet. The first scene here asks how the buyer and the seller, whos also the sold, might feel and behave when such a transaction came to fruition. Olivia, who's in college like her prototype (though not, apparently, in women's studies) seems to be going for thousands rather than millions - this is Canada - and has even turned down the highest bidder in favour of Simon, a middle-aged lawyer who must have seemed nonscary and in fact is. He books a room in what we subsequently discover is the Four Seasons and arrives bearing gifts. This disconcerts the waiting Olivia who had arranged herself in what she took to be an acquiescent position on the bed, and now has to get up to answer a stubbornly uncooperative door.

That door is a gag that keeps running through the evening, and earns its keep. Theres also a hilarious sequence, not repeated, about your typical hotel rooms baffling system of lamps and switches. Much of the play functions as sex farce with serious underpinnings. Olivia doesn't seem to be trying to make a political point; her motives are more personal. She wants the money, sure; she also seems to feel that, since defloration is bound to be a painful process, she may as well get something out of it. Simon wants her to get some pleasure out of it, even though this hardly falls within the terms of the contract, since a) he's a nice enough guy and b) his masculine pride is involved. Olivia wants to keep her sex life separate from her love life. As soon as they start talking, human complications are bound to arise. And of course they do talk, a process propelled by Simons placing a courtly order with room service and by a subsequent knock on the door.

The second scene, six years later, revolves around Jim, an ex-boyfriend of Olivias who can't stop reproaching himself for his reaction to her earlier behaviour, though I can't see why he should have to. Anyway, now rich and successful himself, he goes in for his own form of extravagant sex shopping. He has delivered, to the very same room, a life-size, completely obedient robotic sex toy who looks exactly like Olivia and may well be Olivia; the ambiguity is cunningly sustained, though in the end, its more tantalizing than helpful. Finally, we have a perverse tryst fuelled by alcohol and understandably mutual distaste, between two of Jims co-workers: Sandra, another ex, who left him in a strident if understandable huff, and Marcus, a self-anointed stud. Their joint unlikeability works against the scene; but they too get humanized, in part by the introduction of another toy, a mechanical arm that arouses all kinds of lubricious thoughts in Marcus and the audience, but that Sandra uses as a chaste source of comfort and consolation.

The linking conceit, that commerce and technology have made relationships more mechanical than ever before, is strained and unproven. If anything, the play shows the opposite: emotions breaking through. You might say that the first scene is the Money scene, the second gives us the Love and the third is Sex; but it's overlaps that count. The performances are excellent, with Gwenlyn Cumyn finding the robot in the woman and vice versa, and Scott Clarkson and Daniel Pagett as the two self-doubting men in her lives. Len Silvini and Brooke Morgan have tougher rows to hoe, but emerge from them with credit. The laughter, if not continuous, is frequent, sometimes uproarious, and never demeaning.

Tomasso's Party, by Jules Lewis, starts almost like a continuation of the above, with a woman in bed and a man admiring a stray part of her body. Its downhill from there, though. We have Hugo and Madeleine, who may be married but probably arent. They've been invited to Tomasso's party, Tomasso being Madeleines boss of whom Hugo is jealous despite insisting, repeatedly, that he must be gay. Most of the play consists of Hugo, who has a self-pitying knack for rendering compliments as insults, haranguing Madeleine, whose mouth reminds him of a Mexican porn star; her ankles, she tells us in one of her own contrastingly brief speeches, remind Tomasso of Jennifer Lopez. The inherent monotony is compounded in Nigel Shawn Williams production (for Rooftop Creations) by having Simon Bracken deliver Hugo's outpourings in a clenched and spiteful whine. Leah Doz's Madeleine, lying with her back to us throughout, benefits from the contrast. The most discernible influence is Pinter - the chronically insecure man, the sphinx-like woman, the offstage amorous threat - with some psychological grounding without the wit or the danger. Both plays are in the Factory Studio.

? For details and ticket information, visit fringetoronto.com.

2012-01-10-all-they-need-is-love:
THEATRE REVIEW

Next Stage Theatre Festival Factory Theatre, Toronto

This years Next Stage Theatre Festival, spread across three spaces at the Factory Theatre, is a festival of love. Four shows, out of a lineup of 10, have that word or a derivative of it in their titles, and of course it crops up as a subject in several more. Last week I wrote about a couple of these love stories that were, in two senses, straight: heterosexual and non-musical. Today we have some that are gay, with songs.

Living with Henry, a musical by Christopher Wilson, is about living with HIV. Henry, despite a pointless trick opening that leaves the audience confused for the next 10 minutes, is not the sufferer; he's a personification of the virus - they have the same initials - and he leers around the stage, alternately taunting and encouraging the real protagonist, Michael. It's a clumsy device that underlines the shows main failing; it lurches from one scene to the next, grabbing at instant emotional effects without establishing any kind of centre.

Illness of any kind is a perilous subject for a play, let alone a musical, because it turns the central character into a victim; you can feel for him but not with him. Michael, played as resourcefully as possible by Ryan Kelly, keeps saying that he doesnt want to be defined by his condition, but the show automatically defines him that way, despite showing him with two successive live-in partners, the first dangerously feckless, the second angelically supportive.

Other prominent characters are Michael's best female friend and his mother, who greets his diagnosis with amazing composure (most moms freak when their offspring so much as sneeze) but otherwise acts and reacts totally on cue. So does everyone; the script never brings the characters to any kind of spontaneous life and the songs, with pedestrian lyrics and anemic soft-rock music, keep labouring the obvious. There are maybe two moments at which singing and staging make a point more powerfully than dialogue could: Michael's realization that hes infected and the conclusion of a bathhouse tango at which hes left alone. Otherwise there seems no reason for this piece to be a musical.

In Loving the Stranger or How to Recognize an Invert, Hume Baugh gives a remarkable performance as Peter Flinsch, an artist who grew up in Germany in the 1930s, joined the Hitler Youth and the army because he had no choice, and was court-martialled and imprisoned for kissing another man. As a soldier he was spared the worst the Nazis could do to gays, and after the war he emigrated to Canada.

His story, as told in interviews with this show's authordirector Alistair Newton, is the backbone of what aspires to be a political-historical cabaret; and Baugh's performance is notable for avoiding all the usual pitfalls of the actor as raisonneur: He neither under-acts nor overstresses. With Flinsch (who died in 2010) as quiet and thoughtful linchpin, noting the remarkable advances made in his long lifetime, the production juxtaposes Germany in the first half of the 20th century with North America now.

From the former, we have some sinister pseudo-scientific documents, one of which gives the show its subtitle, contrasted with some startlingly outspoken 1920s gay anthems composed by Mischa Spoliansky, who later wrote music for very mainstream British movies. From the latter we have Proposition 8 and a family values speech by Stephen Harper, after which we get a rendition of Deutschland Uber Alles. Thats a pretty silly connection, unless you believe that Canada is planning world domination.

The show, like many before it, latches enviously on to the mythical spirit of Berlin cabaret. Gosh, wasnt it decadent? Gee, wasn't it political? It's a legend that these days owes less to the actual German repertoire than to the Kander and Ebb musical Cabaret, especially in its recent and more hysterical revivals. True to form this show ends by hitching a ride with Cabarets title song, performed with a genderaltered lyric. A reverse stereotype is still a stereotype.

Theres more of the same in Love Is a Poverty You Can Sell, a cabaret homage to the music and musical influence of Kurt Weill, that's hosted by a giggly duo who might be Cabaret's emcee amoebically split. Apart from being strenuously unfunny, they take up time that could easily be occupied by a couple more songs. Thats an issue, since the half-hour show is a cut-down version of a provocative musical idea.

Weills inheritors turn out to include not only Kander and Ebb but Sondheim, whose Sweeney Todd emerges as a cousin in cutlery to Mack the Knife. The performers are mostly too callow and insecure for the material but there is a lovely duet version of September Song, from Weill's Broadway period, its message running serenely counter to the narrators' description of love as "the lack of a healthy solitude."

Thats a definition that would be hotly contested by the heroine of Modern Love, a glorious show written and performed by Jessica Moss. She doesnt find solitude healthy; she finds it debilitating. With 660 friends on Facebook and none anywhere else she despairs of finding a connection. Only occasionally overdoing the franticness, Moss or her alter ego navigates herself and us through the wilderness of online dating, or online anything, including a bait-and-switch cyber dialogue with one Charlie Brown, who seems to be a good man. She herself signs in as Funny Girl; and though both names would surely be already taken, she more than justifies her own, in technique and observation and thoroughgoing appeal.

It is of course impossible, despite her confessed pudginess, to believe that she can't get a date. An unassailable theatrical truth is that anyone who can hold an audience on her own for five minutes, let alone 60, is by definition attractive.

The Next Stage Festival runs until Jan. 15. For more information, visit fringetoronto.com.

Robert Lepage's The Blue Dragon is a quiet knockout: seductively gentle even when making noise and flashing lights. It's been publicized as a mixed-media show, which in the most literal sense is accurate. The production employs a lot of projections, and a certain amount of film footage. Its stage, or parts of it, moves gracefully up and down or from side to side, music and dance are gainfully employed, and the lighting and sound effects are so exquisitely timed and calibrated as to constitute new media in themselves. None of the hi-tech, though, seems overbearing or there for its own sake. As in all Lepage's best work it's at the service of story and character. It may seem counterintuitive to say so but his is an actor's theatre.

The narrative here is not, perhaps, the strongest in the world, though I suspect I would find it more substantial if I had seen Lepage's Dragon Trilogy to which it forms a sequel or pendent. That work ended with its protagonist, Pierre Lamontagne, departing Canada for China, which is where we find him, 20 years on, running an arts centre in Shanghai. He's visited by Claire Foret, a highly successful and heavy-drinking advertising executive, with whom he shares a romantic past. Facing professional obsolescence (she says her younger male colleagues look at her "as if I were a black-and-white TV"), Claire has come to China desperate to adopt a baby. Both she and Pierre trained as artists, though Pierre now devotes himself to exhibiting others' work. His current protege, also his current lover, is a gifted young woman named Xiao Ling, who becomes unwillingly pregnant. Combine her circumstances with Claire's and you might seem to have an excellent case for surrogate motherhood. People, however, are not that predictable.

The text, by Lepage and Marie Michaud, switches between English, French and Chinese, the last two being surtitled; it's laconic but capable of being powerful or funny or both. Michaud plays Claire, a generally tight-lipped performance that periodically explodes into bitter self-mockery. Henri Chasse's Pierre is gentle and relaxed, maybe too much of both for the man's own gnawing sense of failure and growing sense of responsibility. He's at his best when talking directly to us, on the subject of Chinese calligraphy, whose lines and symbols inform much of the show's own suggestive visual style. He tells us that he used to haunt tattoo parlours as other Westerners might bars or brothels, and it's in one of them that he first met Xiao Ling - she inscribed on him the blue dragon of the title, which is illustrated but never explicitly mentioned. Tattoos, we also learn, used to be forbidden in China except as a form of punishment; now they're a business. So Xiao Ling herself is an emblem, and a conflicted one, of the country's transformation. This seems to be the burden of the dances that she performs, one at each end of the show; they're semi-traditional, graceful but angry. Tai Wei Foo, who plays her and is also the choreographer, is a dancer making her acting debut; and hers is the best performance of the three, especially impressive in eruptions of feeling that seem to come out of nowhere but are, on examination, securely grounded. Hers is the most dynamic part of an action that might, at the risk of conflating Asian cultures, be subtitled The Revenge of Madam Butterfly.

Xiao Ling's own art is based in self-portraiture; it's one of the most haunting ironies in a script and staging suffused with verbal and visual echoes that she finds herself at one point working at a "copyist fair" where the favoured subject is Van Gogh's most familiar picture of himself. The stage steadily fills with projections of this image, in the evening's most magical and most mordant effect.

It has plenty of competition. Lepage continues his fascination with transport. We get an opening scene on a plane, Claire returning to her seat with drink in hand; an illuminated miniature train snaking its way across the back of the stage; a mobile bar, with drinks daintily displayed, that seems to be chasing its own tail; and numerous trips on bicycles, in vignettes ranging from lyrical to satirical. Claire and Xiao Ling, on their way to see the pandas in the zoo, wear masks; Pierre, in similar situations, seems less concerned by the air quality in Shanghai but does worry about the drinking water. His own apartment and gallery are threatened with demolition by developers; meanwhile international negotiations over threatened cuddly species are described as "pandaplomacy." None of this adds up to a profound examination of the new Chinese capitalism, or to its relationship with Canada, but it does set off some suggestive signals.

Some of the most potent effects are the simplest: a still-clothed couple in silhouette, about to make love; the offstage shrieking of a kettle. Michel Gauthier's set starts as a plain split-level affair; towards the end of the play it magically compartmentalizes, for short and silent scenes that might be dreams or flashbacks. The final sequence, set with impeccable logic in an airport, is surpassingly witty; it has you looking wryly back on all that has gone before and discovering that - to misquote a favourite songlyric - everything is possible and everything makes sense.

- The Blue Dragon runs through Feb. 19 at the Royal Alexandra Theatre. Visit mirvish.com or call 416-872-1212 for ticket information.

2012-01-17-ladies-of-hades:
THEATRE REVIEW

The Penelopiad

Buddies in Bad Times Theatre, Toronto

It is to marvel: A few years ago, and with much fanfare, a stage version of Margaret Atwood's The Penelopiad was jointly mounted by our National Arts Centre and Britain's Royal Shakespeare Company and proved stodgy and dull. Nightwood Theatre now addresses the same material and comes up with a show that's vibrant, moving and darkly, explosively funny.

Some of the difference can be traced to the adaptation, which is credited to Atwood alone, and which seems to hew closer to the letter of her original than did its predecessor. It certainly makes a better job of preserving the spirit. Atwood's novella was her commissioned response to The Odyssey: the Homeric epic retold from the point of view of the wandering hero's wife, Penelope, who remained chastely and patiently in their Ithacan palace during the 10 years her husband was away besieging Troy and the further 10 years it took him to get back home again. The chastity, in Atwood's version, is a point left moot; the patience definitely gets frayed. The dramatic time is the present, sort of.

Penelope, dead for millennia, tells us her story from the underworld. She recalls her girlhood, as the offspring of a king and a water nymph; and how she, a shy but observant adolescent, was married off to the man who won her in a footrace, despite having short legs. As mythical marriages go, it wasn't a bad one; Odysseus, Penelope appreciatively notes, was quite the communicator, at least when he was around.

The key event, though, is something that happened on his return home, disguised as a beggar. First, with the aid of a bow that only he could draw, he disposed of the hundred riotous suitors who'd been courting his wife and despoiling the kingdom. Then he ordered the hanging of a dozen palace maids who'd been sleeping with the intruders. Homer doesn't seem to have been bothered by this, but later generations have naturally been shocked. And so, it turns out, was Penelope. The maids - all slaves, of course - were only fraternizing with the suitors in the first place because she'd asked them to be her eyes and ears among them. The suitors, also of course, took brutal advantage. Now, in the afterlife, the maids' shades remain vexed; they will never stick around to talk to Penelope. Neither, wanderlust being apparently impervious to mortality, will Odysseus.

The all-female cast of 13 comprises Penelope and a chorus who step out to play everybody else, male and female. It's down to Megan Follows to set the tone as Penelope, and she sets and maintains it in a performance of exemplary grace and intelligence. Reversing tradition by entering in a puff of smoke (dry ice has seldom been more impressively employed), she addresses us as a woman who never stopped learning from experience and, even posthumously, is still doing so. Wryly, she summons up her own past innocence, suggesting that her early bemusement was even then tempered by an ironic awareness of her own situation. It seems that she could always see through Odysseus, even while loving him. When he goes away she learns to govern because, as she says, she had to; and we never doubt her capacity.

Follows' technical achievement alone is remarkable; in a packed witty text, not a line or a point gets past her. She was still surprising me into laughter, right up till the end. As sharp as her humour, and as fastidiously conveyed, is her pain; especially when coloured with guilt as, having been off-stage when it happened, she hears of the fate of the maids. She also looks lovely throughout. This might be called a post-tragic performance, bearably wounded, eternally quizzical.

It's an ineradicable flaw in the piece that, though the maids are crucial, we don't get to know them, collectively or individually, till the second half: an improvement on the previous production where we never got to know them at all. The ladies of Hades include some major talents, some of them - Maev Beaty, Tara Rosling, Sarah Dodd - underused, at least as soloists.

Of those who do get chances, Kelli Fox's bantam Odysseus is a wonderfully brisk and chipper opportunist, considerate in short bursts. Pamela Sinha supplies some devastating punctuation as the unforgivably bewitching Helen whose looks, her cousin Penelope hears with satisfaction, Finally begin to decay; Bahia Watson is a delight as her son Telemachus who brings her that news; Cara Gee has a piercing speech as the first of the maids to be despoiled; and Pat Hamilton is a riot as the Odysseus family nurse, doing the patriarchy's work for it. (She takes special delight in relating that the girls sacrificed were the youngest and most beautiful.)

The ensemble functions beautifully together under Kelly Thornton's direction; even the dances, choreographed by Monica Dottor, are both decorative and helpful. The composer, Suba Sankaran, supplies a rollicking sea shanty to take care of Odysseus's wayfarings, from Cyclops to Circe. The only false visual note is struck by some peculiar headgear and near-headgear; the suitors seem to have antlers growing out of their shoulders. Otherwise the production, lit by Kimberly Purtell looks, as it sounds, a treat. With this and Robert Lepage's The Blue Dragon in a single week, the year is off to a wonderful start.

- The Penelopiad runs until Jan. 29. For tickets and info visit buddiesinbadtimes.com.

2012-01-21-just-the-right-amount-of-cook:
This is the year of the dragon, or so the flyers tell me, and Toronto theatre is getting with the program by becoming a dragons' den. Hot - actually, rather cool - on the tail of Robert Lepages blue one comes The Golden Dragon, by Canadas and the world's new favourite German playwright Roland Schimmelpfennig.

The title of the play is also the name of what is described - many times - as "a Chinese-Vietnamese-Thai restaurant," in, above and around which the action takes place. The printed cast list comprises A Man Over Sixty (David Fox), A Woman Over Sixty (Lili Francks), A Man (Tony Nappo), A Young Woman (Anusree Roy) and A Young Man (David Yee). It rapidly becomes clear that these labels refer not to the characters but to the actors, each of whom plays many roles of many kinds. Ross Manson's production tips its hand from the beginning when, looking us straight in the eye and with a twinkle in its own, it introduces them as the Asian members of the restaurants kitchen staff. Yee is the only one of the five who looks even remotely like the relevant kind of Asian; and so the rest of the show goes. Occasionally, to keep us on our toes, a performer will appear as a character of his or her own age, race or gender, but those are rare exceptions. You may never, for example, have expected to see Fox apply his mature, weighty presence and silvery technique to the role of a blond flight attendant whose boyfriend calls her his Barbie, but he does, and its not just a hoot but a touching and persuasive hoot.

The stewardess, whose more formal name is Eva and whose accent is the only hint that the action may be taking place in the author's homeland, is dining at the Golden Dragon with a colleague who discovers something nasty in her lemongrass soup. Rather mysteriously, she fails to send it back, though the mystery is somewhat mitigated later on. Meanwhile, in the kitchen, a more desperate drama is unfolding. The youngest employee, recently arrived from China in search of work and a vanished sister, has an agonizing toothache. Since he's an illegal, professional help is out of the question, so a co-worker, calling himself the boys uncle, performs some emergency dentistry, with grim and far-reaching results. The rest of the staff helps out, mainly by holding the patients mouth open and pouring vodka into it, while still managing to take and fill a succession of complicated orders, showing that fusion can beat confusion.

On other floors of the same building, relationships are fraying or falling apart. A grandfather hears from his granddaughter that he's about to become a great-grandfather. A wife walks out on her husband, who does not take it well. He takes alcoholic refuge in the ultra-convenient convenience store next door, and later in its owner's apartment. Threaded through all the other storylines is the fable of an unfortunate Cricket who throws herself on the mercy of a more provident Ant and finds that the price of sustenance is becoming a sex slave. Here, the actors take a further step by crossing species lines, although ... well, I wont give anything away.

The kaleidoscopic method is its own reward, especially in terms of virtuosity of performance; the occasional wig or apron helps out the changes but theyre mostly done by sheer skill and imagination. Teresa Przybylski's set works the same way; it's a long flat platform, with the audience on both sides, that can function either as the kitchen counter or just as a floor. But the method also invites its own penalty; once the surprise has worn off, it can seem glib and superficial. In a way the play does for, or to, Asia what Schimmelpfennigs Peggy Pickit Sees the Face of God did for Africa; it juxtaposes us with them, comfort with misery, except that this time its about them coming among us, rather than vice versa. It doesn't have the close psychological warfare of Peggy Pickit or the black humour. On the other hand, it does build as the other play doesn't. In the middle, I was losing patience with the constant changes of focus, with the implied but unspecified guilt trip, and with some flights of fancy that seemed merely whimsical. Id count among those the mock-ceremonial use of the restaurants carpet, emblazoned with the titular image. But then, startlingly, the play pulls some - not all - of its threads together, to make some shattering connections, some of them spelled out, others not. There are also, which there weren't in Peggy Pickit, traces of compassion.

If I found myself blowing hot and cold about this dragon's text, I have no reservations about the performances or Mansons orchestration of them. Yee has a bewitching hurt delicacy as, among others, the grandfather and the cricket. Roy brings to both the agonized kitchen boy and the swaggering Barbie-fancier (he uses a more forceful word) the same mercurial authority with which she has acted in her own plays. Francks is gnarled and mean as the ant and the storeman, and all clucking concern as a senior cook. Fox doubles up on his Teutonic air hostess by acting his age as the impromptu tooth surgeon. Nappo, very affable, is the nearest thing to a master of ceremonies, or maybe mistress, since his principal role is that of Evas fellow diner who, swallowing her suspicions along with her soup, emerges, rather arbitrarily, as the nearest thing to a philosophical voice. The play's achievement doesn't quite match its audacity, but it's close.

- The Golden Dragon runs through Feb. 19 at the Tarragon Theatre. Call 416-531-1827 or visit tarragontheatre. com for ticket information.

2012-01-24-depth-of-a-salesman:
THEATRE REVIEW

Kim's Convenience, Other People

Young Centre for the Performing Arts, Toronto

If you're going for realism, go for it. Ken MacKenzie's set for Kim's Convenience is a wonder of verisimilitude: a Regent Park variety store brought to the stage in such amazing detail that it seems to have been not so much designed as reassembled. Ins Choi's play, adopted by Soulpepper after a triumphant debut at last year's Toronto Fringe, has been given the best imaginable relaunching pad, and deserves it.

I didn't see the Fringe production, which Choi directed and in which he also acted, along with four colleagues of whom all but one have come along for the remount. There is now a new director, Weyni Mengesha, whose production makes a fine and fitting twin to her earlier staging of 'Da Kink in My Hair; both put a believable slice of multi-ethnic Toronto onstage and keep faith with it.

Kim's Convenience may be the better play; it's certainly the more cohesive. It makes a further pair with Soulpepper's own magically realistic Window on Toronto, a group creation in which Choi was one of the group, while also maintaining the company's Parfumerie tradition of doing heartwarming shows about retail. In a wider theatrical context, it's a pleasant coincidence that this production opened the night after The Golden Dragon, which is set in a fusion restaurant that's one-third Korean. The principal characters of Kim's Convenience, the family members who own and run and mind the store, are firstgeneration immigrants from that country, and their children. In the words, or almost, of I'm Still Here, we career from Korea to Korea.

Mr. Kim himself, patriarch and protagonist, has enforcedly careered from one job to another. In his birth country he was a teacher; and he runs his shop, and his family when they let him, with a fierce educator's pride. He's brought with him an encyclopedic knowledge of his national history and an ingrained hatred of the Japanese, one that leads him to call 911 to report illegal parking if the offending vehicle happens to be a Honda.

He and his wife have a grown son and daughter. The daughter, 30 and still living at home, is a photographer - not the profession her father would have chosen for her - who resents any encroachments on her independence and especially resents her father's suggestion that she should take over the store. Her brother is a graver disappointment, a brilliant student who got into drugs and then into prison; he now works for a car rental company, hating the fact that his clients can drive away while he has to take the TTC.

The neighbourhood is gentrifying, and Kim receives a generous offer to buy him out. He refuses; his customers, he says, depend on him and he couldn't desert them. Plain to us is that, domestically and professionally, he depends on them. The store is his identity.

In some ways the play is a lighter-hearted Death of a Salesman, one in which gulfs between the generations are wide but bridgeable. It also, as people come and go, has some elements of soap opera and some of sitcom; it could be accused of sacrificing truth to reconciliation. But the comedy is funny, and the emotions genuine, and at its best, the play combines the two.

There's a terrific scene in which father and daughter furiously tally up what, both emotionally and financially, they owe one another. A flashback in which Mr. and Mrs. Kim try to settle on a name for their new business that hasn't already been used on some other street corner is tender and poignant and handed me the biggest single laugh I've had in a theatre in ages.

All these elements are incarnate in Paul Sun-Hyung Lee's Kim, a massive creation, cunning and vulnerable. Stoutly built, he's a martial arts expert (who meets some serious competition) and a smart operator who is unshakably proud of his ability to recognize a shoplifter at 40 paces. He can vary the thickness of his accent according to whom he wants to mystify; he can also surrender, almost unconditionally, when his parental heart is touched. He made me laugh and he made me cry; and you can't ask for more than that.

Esther Jun, as his offspring and chief antagonist, is too unmodulated in her abrasiveness, but nicely melts when she finds love with a passing cop. Jean Yoon is so gently persuasive a wife and mother that I wish she had more to do and that more of it were in English. Choi has written himself the least rewarding role as the son, who tends to speak in set pieces, but he plays it very well. We meet four of Kim's customers, all of them black and all of them played by Cle Bennett, who transforms himself so completely that it was only at the third go-round that I realized he was the same actor.

A less hopeful but equally riveting slice of life in another city is provided in Christopher Shinn's Other People, an independent production under the same roof (in the small Tank House).

The principal characters are two aspiring artists and one who's seemingly made it, all sharing a house in New York's East Village around Christmas and New Year - not unlike the characters in Rent, a show one of them explicitly indicts for its sentimentality. I'm not sure the play can quite escape the same charge of putting its characters on view for the delectation of outsiders, but it certainly doesn't go easy on them, and it doesn't objectify them.

All three find a possible partner at some point; only one - a reformed junkie whose replacement addiction is God - is in that partnered state at the end, and you rather wish he wasn't. Under the direction of Aaron Willis, a cast that's mainly new to me (Tatiana Maslany, Ben Lewis, Indrit Kasapi, Mike McPhaden, Brendan McMurtryHowlett, Richard Lee) performs with flawless tonal and emotional accuracy.

This early Shinn play confirms my impression that he's the most interesting American playwright to appear since Stephen Adly Guirgis, himself the best since David Mamet.

? Kim's Convenience runs until Feb. 11. For tickets, call 416-866-8666 or visit soulpepper.ca. Other People runs until Jan. 28. For tickets, visit youngcentre.ca.

THEATRE REVIEW

Caroline, or Change Berkeley Street Theatre, Toronto

I have lost count of the American shows that someone or other has hailed as "the first great musical of the 21st century." They include - and please don't laugh - Spring Awakening, The Producers, Avenue Q, American Idiot, Next to Normal and Caroline, or Change. The last - book and lyrics by Tony Kushner, music by Jeanine Tesori - is the one with a serious claim: the most exciting, the most moving, simply the most.

So it certainly seems in the show's Canadian premiere, a triumphant joint production by Acting Up Stage and Obsidian. Caroline is a black maid, working for a white Jewish family in Louisiana in 1963. "Change" refers both to the political transformation that's about to overtake the country, and to the coins that Noah, the eight-year-old son of the household, has an incorrigible habit of leaving in his pants pocket.

Noah is traumatized by his mother's death from cancer and by his father's second marriage; the stepmother is a New Yorker named Rose, who is often flummoxed by her new surroundings but wants to do right by them. To teach Noah providence and tidiness, she tells Caroline, who has always been scrupulous about returning his coins when she finds them in the laundry, that from now on she may keep them. Caroline resents the implied charity, but working a six-day week for $30 and with three children to feed, clothe and medicate, she's hardly in a position to refuse.

Out of their individual deprivations, Noah and Caroline have formed a bond; at least, she lets him light her cigarettes, which is a big thrill.

Somewhere in the first act, the president is assassinated. This galvanizes everyone, or at least makes them think. Caroline muses, in remarkably nuanced song, about JFK having at least had good intentions. On civil rights, as on most other things, she's an angry stoic. She has an older son in Vietnam, and her vision of the future stretches to being able to read a map so she can find out just where that is.

Arlene Duncan, playing her, manages at this point as at many others to make limited horizons seem radiant. Her teenage daughter is far more militant, though, as a Martin Luther King supporter, not militant enough to suit Rose's father, who comes to visit for Hanukkah. He's an unreconstructed 1930s radical who might have been one of the good guys in a Marc Blitzstein agitprop musical.

Granddad also performs the narrative function of making Noah a present of a $20 bill, which he leaves in the laundry. This occasions a delicious musical sequence in which he counts off the hours till he can get home from school and rescue his riches. More significantly, it precipitates a bitter battle between Noah and Caroline in which both say unforgivable things.

The show keeps the personal, the political and the grey areas in between in almost perfect balance. There's very little dialogue; the score carries the narrative and the ideas, and the sophisticated results make all the bloated humourless pop operas look sick.

I haven't been the greatest fan of Kushner's plays; the two-part Angels in America struck me as a good small piece about Roy Cohn unmercifully distended. But his actual writing gifts have never been in doubt, and he turns out to be a very good lyricist. He knows what rhymes are, and what they're good for; he's conversational without being banal; he writes to character, action and themes; and he's off-handedly funny, notably in a couplet about lighting the Menorah, though it isn't in the Torah.

There's blues and there's gospel. Supposedly soulful roof-raising anthems have been ruining the musical ever since Jennifer Holliday told the world she wasn't going at the first-act curtain of Dreamgirls; Duncan, who superbly conveys both Caroline's pride and her hurt, redeems their honour and their relevance here. And she does it unplugged, and to invisible accompaniment. Reza Jacobs' musical direction is immaculate, suggesting an awesome and justified degree of trust between his offstage five-piece band and the cast.

There are some flaws, though. A commentative trio modelled on the Supremes is a device that has been done to death in other shows and that this one can't make fresh. It's impossible to tell that the other anonymous singers who appear in the basement are meant to be the voices of the appliances or that the messenger of Kennedy's death is meant to be a bus rather than its driver.

Otherwise Robert McQueen, who directed Acting Up Stage's beautiful Light in the Piazza, moves masterfully between the various levels, physical and thematic, with crucial assistance from Tim French's choreography and Kimberly Purtell's lighting.

Michael Levinson's Noah is a phenomenal child performance and Deborah Hay's Rose a dazzling grown-up one, a devastatingly well-observed portrayal of a woman striving for brisk cheerfulness while actually at her wits' end. There is also blazing work from Alana Hibbert as Caroline's skeptical friend and from Sabryn Rock as the activist daughter whose closing number is the show's nearest approach to traditional musicaltheatre affirmation. It's also a significant departure from tradition since you would expect the mother, the central figure, to have the last word.

The double title may be more than a cute excuse for a pun. It may be about choice.

- Caroline, or Change runs until Feb. 12. For tickets, call 416-368-3110 or visit actingupstage.com.
