I am far too cautious to proclaim a new theatrical Golden Age, but I confidently announce that this has been a Golden Fortnight. The past two weeks have brought onto Toronto stages The Blue Dragon, The Penelopiad, The Golden Dragon, Kim's Convenience, Other People and Caroline or Change: each in its way a triumph. And now, to round things off, we have Penny Plain, the latest from master puppeteer Ronnie Burkett and his Theatre of Marionettes.

At the risk of bursting my own bubble, I have to say that as a whole Penny Plain does not reach the exalted level of the shows listed above, or indeed of some of Burkett's earlier work, though it does in flashes. Burkett isn't just a virtuoso puller of strings; he's a fine actor and a considerable playwright. A first response to his new piece is that the puppetry is the least of it, though that may be because we have come to take his skills for granted. Once again, he has created an array of extraordinarily lifelike miniature figures, whom he can guide through the subtlest of movements and expressions. Once again, when they aren't performing scenes - usually in twos - they hang from their wires at the back of the set, a haunting image in itself. This time, though, they don't go in for, say, the incredible musical interludes of Burkett's previous show, Billy Twinkle. Such trickeration would likely be out of place in the present narrative circumstances, which are grim.

Penny Plain herself is one of Burkett's frail but indomitable old ladies: a blind octogenarian who keeps a boarding house. Outside, it's all-purpose Armageddon; every economic and environmental disaster has materialized at the same time. Banks are sinking, and so are countries. A virulent new strain of flu rages uncheckably across the world, killing millions. In Australia, kangaroos are eating people (and, one hopes, depositing the leftovers tidily in their pockets). In a development that ingeniously wraps three contemporary nightmares in one package, the U.S. is part-paying its national debt by shipping fertile young women to China, which needs them having depleted its own female population through selective abortion. This information and more is brought to us in a series of newsflashes, recorded by guest voices; one of them, especially welcome since we no longer get to hear on it on the real radio, is that of Andy Barrie.

Indoors, Penny sits neatly on one of two straight-backed chairs. Sitting on the other, in a matching upright position, is Geoffrey, her guide dog and companion. Geoffrey talks with an attitude that suggests a crossbreed of Family Guy's Brian and Wallace's Gromit. Penny has always treated Geoffrey as a human being, but now he wants to leave and live among his own kind. This is obviously rash. It's a dog-eat-dog world out there; and that's the least of it.

Penny advertises for a replacement canine companion and, after auditioning a couple of extremely unsuitable applicants, settles on one who insists that she's a dog though everybody else, including the audience, can see that she's a girl. "Everybody" here doesn't of course include Penny, who every time somebody asks her, usually metaphorically, to see something replies that she can't: an all-purpose line that bears repetition surprisingly well. The newcomer's name is Tuppence. As in Penny Plain, Tuppence Coloured, though if there's anything more to this than an unspoken private joke, then I'm the one who can't see it.

We also meet Penny's lodgers, of whom the most cheerful is a bank manager who greets the end of things by indulging what must be a long suppressed taste for cross-dressing. There's Queenie, a mean and incontinent old woman with a walker, Burkett's manipulation of the latter device being an especially insouciant example of the taken-for-granted skills referenced above. There's her even meaner daughter Jubilee, an editor (she says) who stabs people with her red pencil when they annoy her by talking too loudly on their cellphones (we hear you, lady) or otherwise making noise; her murderousness is in line with the terminal state of the world, but the impression is that she's always been that way. There are the Titties, a highly sexed evangelical couple from the southern States who take refuge in Penny's basement while happily awaiting the Last Judgment and who are caricatures even by puppet standards.

Perhaps most important, and maybe a tip of the hat from one great puppeteer to another, there is the famous Gepetto, maker and father of Pinocchio, who has somehow fetched up in 21st-century Canada. To him there comes Evelyn, an unhappily childless woman who wants him to build another doll that will turn into a real boy. After much persuasion, he agrees but the resultant creation is shockingly far from what she had expected. It is, Gepetto says, a child fit for the world you have created, though by "you" he'd better not mean Evelyn personally. Anyway, one of our last sights is of Evelyn cradling her new infant. This could be an image of horror or of hope. It works either way.

The only thing that seems to be blooming in this blighted world is Penny's garden, and she calls Evelyn "Eve." So maybe we have a fable of regeneration; the last sections of the play are in fact quite beautiful. But they can't compensate for too many arid passages earlier on. The fact is that what's going on inside the house is dwarfed by what we're told is going on outside, and I frequently found myself wishing that the characters would stop chattering and let us hear more short and snappy bulletins from the front. Penny is an endearing creation, though with nowhere much to go dramatically. The others are, well, puppets. They've been given a fine setting, a stained-glass colonnade, designed by Burkett himself, who also did the costumes. There's a sweet-naturedness that shines even through his darkest imaginings. He is, to state the obvious, a major talent. But this isn't, though it seems intended to be, one of his major works.

- Penny Plain runs through Feb. 26 at the Factory Theatre. Call 416-504-9971 or visit factorytheatre.ca for details.

THEATRE REVIEW

Cruel and Tender

Bluma Appel Theatre, Toronto

Martin Crimp is a reasonably hot British playwright. Atom Egoyan is an extremely hot Canadian filmmaker who has also directed at least one fine opera production, the COC's Die Walkure. Arsinee Khanjian's reputation as an actress is practically on fire. Canadian Stage has brought them all together, with considerable fanfare, and the results are atrocious.

Cruel and Tender, which is more the former than the latter and inspires similar feelings in return, is based on the Greek tragedy The Women of Trachis, possibly the least familiar of Sophocles' surviving seven. The original concerns Deianira, the stay-athome wife of Heracles who, having completed his 12 famous labours, has been off having other adventures. One of these has been the sacking of a city, whose princess he covets; he has sent her on ahead, hoping to pass her off as one of a convoy of slaves. Deianira finds out and, to regain her husband's affections, sends him a robe dipped in what she believes to be a love potion but is actually a poison. On discovering what she's done, she kills herself. Heracles, unable to remove the robe, comes home to die in agony.

Crimp has adapted, or appropriated, the story as part of the backlash against the backlash against 9/11. His contemporary Deianira is called Amelia; her husband, known simply as the General, is away in Africa pursuing the war on terror. Like his mythical prototype he has laid waste to a town in order to gain access to one of its young women, here named Laela, and he, too, has sent her on ahead, claiming that she and her little brother are refugees, as in a way they are.

Now, massacring for love may be standard behaviour for a mythical superhero but it isn't credible in a 21st-century commander; we have our own abuses but they aren't as narrowly personal as that. The play is trying to tell two incompatible stories and the strain shows, mainly in the form of padding. Bizarrely, Crimp has omitted the most compelling part of his source: the steps by which Deianira, maybe the earliest detective in world drama, realizes what she has done and that lead her, first to try and undo it, and then to suicide.

In this version, even the manner of the heroine's death remains obscure. Instead of logical emotional processes we get a lot of fancy talk about war that bears no relation to Amelia's specific circumstances. She seems to be trying to bond with her rival, a character whom Sophocles sensibly kept silent. It's like one of those French plays of the 1950s, also often based on the Greeks, in which abstractions trump feelings.

The wife has the first twothirds of the play and the husband the remainder; they never meet. Here the play is being true to its original in which, given the parsimonious conventions of ancient Athenian theatre, they would likely have been played by the same actor. But it feels frustrating even in Sophocles, and more so in Crimp. The General, when he finally gets his own turn to strut and fret, is a little more believable than his spouse, but not much. His dying delirium is full of scrambled imagery from the legends of his progenitor that seem like a last-minute attempt, on both his part and the author's, to grab some grandeur.

Speaking of which: Debra Hanson has designed the kind of set that looks impressive when the curtain rises (there is a curtain and it does rise) but then proceeds to eat the play. It's a vast white structure that seems to be half kitchen and half garage. It's also, literally, full of holes, with a lot of empty space on top, all allowing the sound to leak out. It accentuates the difficulties both of an acoustically tricky theatre and of a leading actress with clarity and projection problems. It does allow Egoyan to frame the occasional striking picture, notably the sight of a young boy alone on a promontory in the far corner of the stage, but that remoteness itself turns out to be symptomatic of a crabbed aloof production in which nobody connects with anyone else.

There are intermittent odd-ities such as a chandelier that goes on and off for no apparent reason and a microphone that gets passed from hand to hand like some kind of totem. I wished it might take longterm residence with Khanjian, whose Amelia is a vocal and emotional blur.

Daniel Kash's General has more presence but remains a stereotype of a bully. His death throes are shown to us in video close-up, which mainly suggests a director playing with toys.

A lot of supporting talent gets wasted. Jeff Lillico comes off best as the couple's son whom they keep using as a go-between; he in return treats them with dismay or disdain, thereby giving the audience somebody to root for. Brenda Robins gets off some tart zingers as Amelia's housekeeper, leader of a mini-chorus of domestics. Its other members, Sarah Wilson and Cara Ricketts, put that mic to use for some karaoke; they specialize in hopeful Billie Holiday impersonations but are decisively upstaged by Laela (Abena Malika), who can really do Billie and even sports the trademark gardenia. Nigel Shawn Williams as a shifty diplomat seems constantly on the verge of delivering a smooth performance but never gets beyond fits and starts.

The production may seem to fit in with Matthew Jocelyn's generally stimulating policy of promoting a "European" aesthetic at Canadian Stage. It doesn't. Misplaced grandiosity can happen anywhere.

Cruel and Tender runs until Feb. 12. For more information, visit canadianstage.com.

2012-02-04-the-marriage-plot-the-quest-f:
It's hard not to warm to a play whose author-director, who is also one half of the cast, greets you by name when you walk in and introduces you to his mother, who's the other half, and then proceeds to offer you a samosa. I'm not saying that any show that gives me this kind of welcome will automatically get a rave review. I'm just, as they say, saying.

A Brimful of Asha is about a family's desire to get their son married, preferably to someone of their selection, and about the son's obstinate preference for waiting until he's ready and has found someone for himself. The son, born 32 years ago in Canada to immigrant parents from India, is Ravi Jain, a professional theatrical here playing himself. His mother, similarly playing herself but making her first appearance on any stage, is Asha Jain. They have, in a small way, recreated their own kitchen in one corner of the Tarragon's Extra Space, or at least their own kitchen table. Asha sits at it; Ravi strolls or paces around it and, at one point, perches on it, for which impertinence his mother sternly rebukes him. She did this, when I saw the show, with such apparent spontaneity that I would like to believe it was a one-timeonly occurrence, but I have reason to believe that it wasn't.

While walking, Ravi talks. He tells us about a trip he took to India, some half-dozen years ago, principally to teach a theatre workshop in Calcutta, but also to travel around the country seeing new places, all his previous visits having been to his family's hometown of New Delhi. He was surprised, and more than a little disconcerted, to discover that his parents had planned their annual journey home to coincide with him. They had already, via the Internet, tracked down an eligible young lady in Bombay who would be just right for him. When he grudgingly agreed to meet her, he was alarmed to find his father insistent on travelling with him to perform the introductions. As it turned out, Ravi and his enforced date got on rather well, if only because she had no more interest in marrying him than he had in marrying her.

That, however, was not the end of it. It seems that, wherever he travelled, his extended family found means of throwing the two young people together. If it wasn't his family, it was hers. Often, it was both together: Ravi has stories to tell of gatherings in which tablesful of people discussed him and his career and marital prospects as if he wasn't there (and in a sense, since he could understand Hindi but not fluently speak it, he wasn't). And when his parents finally gave up on this particular girl, they found him another one of the same name.

Ravi recounts all this in a tone of aggrieved amusement. His co-star Asha meanwhile sits serenely and offers comments, most of them variations on the age-old question, one that seemingly crosses all cultural boundaries, "Why won't they listen to their mothers?" Her own marriage, she points out, was arranged, and it was also a happy one; still is, in fact. She makes a disarmingly good case, one to which even Ravi, as he tells us, was at one point inclined to give in. Or maybe he just felt beaten down; well actually, there was no maybe about it. In the end, though, they agree to differ. Or at least they agree enough to be here together, tonight and for a limited season.

It's a charming show, but it's also monotonous. Ravi's story necessarily consists of the same thing happening over and over again. More importantly, the dynamic between the two performers remains unchanged throughout. Asha's theatrical inexperience can also be a handicap, especially when it comes to audibility, though nobody could say she lacks for personality and, to be fair, raising her voice would go against the grain of her character. And she does prove capable of re-enacting a screaming phone conversation with her errant son, proving his own implicit claim that she is indeed a performing natural.

Visiting Mr. Green, presented by the Harold Green Jewish Theatre, touches on some similar themes and is also a two-hander for two generations, though in this case the representatives aren't relatives. Also in this case, the older performer is the furthest thing from a theatrical novice. He is, in fact, the 87-year-old Theodore Bikel, playing a character slightly younger than himself: an orthodox Jewish New Yorker, recently widowed and even more recently almost knocked down by a car while crossing the street. The errant motorist has been courtordered to spend every Thursday evening for the next six months calling on his near-victim and attending to his needs: a case of making the community service fit the crime. Bikel, as the visited Mr. Green, is a marvel to see and even more to hear, freshening the stockest of lines, situations and character traits. An arch-traditionalist who can be sharp or dense according to the author's requirements, he has barely cooked and never cleaned since his wife's death; their marriage was not an arranged one - they were both, like Ravi Jain, second-generation immigrants - but, at least by Mr. Green's own account, it was as happy as Asha's. Ross, the visitor, tidies up and brings kosher takeout. Mutual suspicion gradually gives way to mutual affection.

The play has two surprises to spring. The first, so unsurprising that it begs to be spoiled, is that Ross is gay. Since he is also Jewish, though secular, Mr. Green refuses to believe it (how long has he lived in New York?) and, again like Asha if for rather different reasons, tells him that he only has to find the right girl. Ross talks him through Sexual Tolerance 101, apparently for our benefit as much as Mr. Green's, though it's hard to conceive of any theatre audience that would need it, either now or in 1996 when Jeff Baron's play premiered. The date at least explains why Ross, a high-flyer with American Express, doesn't have a cellphone. Mr. Green's phone is rotary and disconnected, except that it does connect with the second surprise, which concerns Mr. Green's past and which I didn't see coming, though I kicked myself afterwards. The play then goes back to being predictable, up to and including the final curtain. For what it is, it's efficiently written; Aidan deSalaiz as Ross is good if a bit forced; and Bikel is as good and as unforced as any actor could possibly be. I have far more respect for A Brimful of Asha as a piece of theatre but I have to confess that I enjoyed Visiting Mr. Green more, or at least that it held my attention more easily. I am not proud of this.

A Brimful of Asha plays through Feb. 19 at the Tarragon Extra Space. Visit tarragontheatre.com or call 4165311827 for ticket information. Visiting Mr. Green plays through Feb. 18 at the Jane Mallet Theatre. For ticket details, visit stlc.com or call 416-366-7723.

2012-02-06-coriolanus-film-review:
Caius Martius, surnamed Coriolanus, would do terribly in a U.S. primary. In fact he’d do terribly in any democratic political process. He just doesn’t know how to make nice to people. Not only does he not know how to do it, he doesn’t want to do it. And he has no inhibitions about telling the people so. The Coriolanus who’s the title character of one of Shakespeare’s greatest and toughest plays can be accused of many things, but hypocrisy is not among them.

Coriolanus has never been a very popular play but it’s nearly always been a topical one. The new and very good movie version, directed by and starring Ralph Fiennes, is in modern dress, long an accepted practice in the theatre but fairly new to Shakespeare on film, or indeed on TV. It used to be assumed that a literal-minded audience, already having to cope with unfamiliar language, would just be confused if it issued from the mouths of people like themselves. There’s something in that; theatrical talk about making the plays “accessible” by scenically updating them can be very glib. The 1950s film of Julius Caesar, the one with Marlon Brando as Antony, showed that in one respect the screen could have a (literally) huge advantage over the stage, simply by showing us a crowd in the Forum hundreds, maybe thousands strong. But they all wore togas; I doubt if that play has much to gain from modern dress, on stage or screen. Caesar is about political issues, sure, but Coriolanus deals with political process: a process whose practice and psychology unites three eras: Rome’s, Shakespeare’s and ours. Fiennes makes both the civic and the military battles stunningly immediate.

The play Coriolanus begins with a demo. So does the movie. The citizens of Rome have taken to the streets, proclaiming that they’re starving and that the ruling patricians are hoarding grain. (We never do find out if the latter charge is true.) The man they blame is the war hero Martius, whose contempt for anyone lower born than himself is notorious and unconcealed, indeed flaunted. The riot, if that’s the word, looks like something you might see any night on the news, and the film cuts away to show us a video feed of it being watched with interest by Rome’s current enemy, the Volscians. An update appears at the bottom of the screen: “General Martius imposes martial law.”

John Logan’s screenplay has cut many lines from the play, and cleverly re-assigned many more, but it hasn’t added any, at least not spoken ones. That caption, though, is the movie’s own invention as are others like it. It also departs from the source in the message it carries. The Martius of the play does not have the power to impose martial law, and may not even have the will. He makes threatening noises but he is at heart indifferent to political power; it’s impossible, despite the alarming militaristic trappings, to label him a Fascist. Later on his friends and family will have him run for office, because that’s what war heroes do, but for his more practical fellow nobles he’s a figurehead, somebody to be admired and to be embarrassed by. One of them is his friend and surrogate father Menenius, whom the crowd describes, credulously, as “one who has always loved the people” and who now appears, also by TV remote, pouring oil, which is what he does best. Come the end of the picture Menenius will be unduly sentimentalised, but as played by Brian Cox he’s a wonderfully recognisable figure, at home in any club or committee room, and on good if spiky verbal terms with his left-wing opponents (also very recognisable) whom he characteristically addresses over his shoulder while enjoying a drink..

There’s one small cut in the first scene that’s unfortunate: the line in which the leader of the protest admits Martius’ outstanding war service but says that he did it “to please his mother.” This is the mainspring of the hero’s heroism and of his downfall, and it should be broached at the start. It would also prepare the ground for our first sight of the matriarch herself, Volumnia. Vanessa Redgrave plays her at this point with imperious cheerfulness, exulting in the wounds her son has received in previous campaigns and those he’s about to get in his next one.

Which is where we immediately find him, besieging the Volscian city of Corioles. And it’s here that both the medium and the modernity do their most transformative work. Actors on a stage can talk about sacking a city but, whether they’re wearing tunics or fatigues, it can all seem very distant, very abstract. Here we get to experience what it actually entails. We see the Roman troops blasting their way through actual streets; we see civilians, men and women, cowering in corners and Martius himself shooting them at point-blank range. I doubt the Martius we meet in the play would have done that – he has his own peculiar chivalric code – but it’s an issue that Shakespeare, with his stylized stage battles, didn’t have to confront. A movie doesn’t have that option, certainly not now. Fiennes does manage to retain the Elizabethan theatre tradition of single combat between the generals and, against all realistic odds, gets away with it. Martius and his Volscian counterpart Aufidius (Gerard Butler) are so locked into their hatred and jealousy of one another that it’s just about believable. Fiennes shot much of his picture in Bosnia, and the associations certainly help, but I suspect that these scenes could have transfixed us in any location.

It has been possible in the past to make a Shakespeare movie that glorified war, or at least the war effort. Like Laurence Olivier and Kenneth Branagh before him, Fiennes has made his film directing debut with a Shakespeare play in which he also acts, in a role that he’s already played on stage. For both Olivier and Branagh the film was Henry V, another war-piece that each interpreted according to the tenor of his times; for Olivier, in World War Two, it was a patriotic rallying-cry; for Branagh, post-Falklands, it was blood and guts and scepticism. Both went on to make films of Hamlet; and in a final turn of the screw, Branagh, having dogged the footsteps of Olivier’s career, has now actually played him in My Week with Marilyn: the least mannered of actors impersonating one of the most mannered, and not only bringing it off but getting an Oscar nomination for it. As it further happens both actors have been notable Coriolani on stage; Olivier’s, by all accounts, was one of his greatest performances. It seems he made the man likeable. Fiennes doesn’t, and probably couldn’t. He makes him instead perversely admirable, which is probably closer to the play’s truth.

The name Coriolanus is an honorific bestowed on Martius for having conquered Corioles. In one of Shakespeare’s (and Redgrave’s) nicest touches his mother, on his return to Rome, gives a half-proud half-shy smile at having to pronounce this new word. It also leads to his being invited by his fellow-patricians to run for the top job of Consul. The catch is that the election process means meeting the lower classes face to face, showing them his war-wounds, and asking for their literal and metaphorical “voices”. This he loathes doing; he has nothing but contempt for “the people” and has never disguised it. He’s also, despite his bravado, pathologically shy. Under pressure, he consents to go through the motions; but his distaste shows through, and he ends up being banished, by popular acclaim. Once again the movie takes an antique custom and makes it seem contemporary. It is after all only an extreme literal version of what politicians routinely do to solicit votes. Some of the arguments that in the text happen in the market-place are transferred to a TV studio. It’s too much of a clever thing when a real-life newscaster, playing himself, addresses his audience in blank verse, but otherwise these scenes too work with amazing naturalness, especially when a female citizen-pundit states the anti-Coriolanus case in the most earnestly reasonable of tones.

Making something contemporary isn’t the same as making it timeless. Coriolanus in the theatre is one of the very few plays that can capture the sensation of history on the move. The movie, with all its apparent technological advantages, doesn’t do that, partly because the text has been so streamlined. Coriolanus’ exile, with no judicial process, is credible in the play, where it’s the climax of a long inexorable process. In the movie, you wonder where the people-power has suddenly come from. Admittedly the protagonist makes it easier by taking matters into his own hands; telling the populace “I banish you” he turns his back on Rome and on Roman exceptionalism. “There is” he proclaims with terse and clinching eloquence “a world elsewhere.”

One of Fiennes’ finest moments in the film, this is also one of the few occasions on which he allows himself a long speech. Elsewhere he plays things very close to his chest. Perhaps he’s bowing to perceived necessity. Film and TV have always had a problem with Shakespeare’s language. One reason Cox’s performance works so well is that most of his role is in conversational prose; asked to speak rhetorical verse on screen, most actors’ instinct is to scale it down, aiming for a kind of naturalism that, given the size of the words, sounds very unnatural. The one performer here who rides right over that compromise is Redgrave. One reviewer has said that Redgrave, though a great actress, is not the greatest verse-speaker. Actually she’s a superb verse-speaker, able to preserve the shape and momentum of the lines while still making them sound real. Her role, the third-longest in the play, has been cut less than anyone else’s; which is sensible as the climax depends on letting her talk at length. Coriolanus, breaking what would once have been his ultimate taboo, has offered his services to the Volscians and they’re marching unstoppably on Rome, which knows it’s about to receive the same treatment that it inflicted on Corioles. Only his mother, who has guided his every step, can stop the human war-machine in his tracks. Why she should want to I’ve never quite understood (wouldn’t she be inclined to tell him to burn down the ungrateful city with her blessing?) but patriotism trumps maternity. She doesn’t do it alone; she has the support of the wife whom Martius calls his “gracious silence” whose influence is more believable in Jessica Chastain’s performance than in any other I have seen, and of their young son whose words and actions also makes more sense here than ever before. The turning-point of this very public drama is determined, ironically enough, by private affections. Volumnia’s victory is signalled by the most eloquent stage-direction in Shakespeare, followed by one of the most devastating lines. The direction is “he holds her by the hand, silent”; the line is “oh mother, mother what have you done?” The machine breaks. The greatest Coriolanus I’ve ever seen was Nicol Williamson, whose death was announced last week, and he uttered those words with a giant, wracking sob. He fell apart before our eyes and ears. Fiennes’ collapse isn’t on that massive scale but it’s wrenching enough.

Volumnia returns to Rome in triumph, though the film falls down in not showing us her awareness that in saving the city she has signed her son’s death-warrant. (Martha Henry, in two successive Stratford Festival productions, has brought this off superbly.) Coriolanus returns to the Volscians, to be murdered by his enemy-turned-ally Aufidius, who’s been awaiting just such an opportunity. He says he’s sorry afterwards, but the film predictably cuts this, just as much earlier it’s cut Martius’ surprisingly touching sympathy for a Volscian captive who’d once been kind to him and his characteristic and rather endearing failure to remember the man’s name.

Those are losses. Sympathy doesn’t equal sentimentality: certainly not in a play whose climax is a man’s surrender to human bonds he thought he had transcended. Sympathy is also, in Shakespeare, unpredictable and impartial. The citizens are fickle and easily manipulated; they’re also real men (and, in the film, women) with real grievances. Coriolanus’ views on the poor are to the right of Mitt Romney’s, but no-one could accuse him of playing politics; in fact his friends wish he could. The play has been claimed for both right and left, but it eludes both. All that, all the essentials, the film gets sternly and thrillingly right.
2012-02-06-making-a-show-of-it-smash-is-:
You do not, even in this age of revivals, expect a touted brand new musical to start with somebody singing Over the Rainbow. That, however, is how Smash begins. It isn't the only instance of false advertising in connection with this show. The advance clips have all made it look like a knock-off of Glee. In fact, it isn't like Glee at all: well, hardly at all. It's better.

It is - the publicity has been accurate about this - a series about the creation of an imaginary Broadway musical about Marilyn Monroe. It has subplots as well, but they sprout naturally, or mostly so, from the main theme, which is tenaciously, and even accurately, pursued. It's also very witty, with the sharpest script this side of Mad Men, and very fast. The scenes are mostly short. The first 20 minutes of the pilot introduce a host of interlinked characters with exemplary crispness.

And that first number is a tease. It's sung by Karen (Katharine McPhee), an aspirant actress who gets as far as "once in a lullaby" before she's cut off. It turns out she's auditioning for a jaded panel that hardly bothers to conceal its indifference. That's the biz, and Smash gets it right. Karen is ushered out, to be replaced by Ivy (Megan Hilty), a more seasoned young chorine who inquires, as provocatively as she knows how, "Do you want the ballad or the up-tempo?" Karen is trim and brunette, Ivy blowsy and blond. Ivy looks more like Monroe, but it's possible that Karen thinks more like her. By the end of the second episode, they'll be the contenders for the role.

The Marilyn musical isn't what they're up for when we first meet them. That show hasn't been conceived of yet, though it will be in the next scene. We meet the composerlyricist team of Tom (Christian Borle) and Julia (Debra Messing), who are allegedly modelled on Betty Comden and Adolph Green, the urbane Broadway and Hollywood legends who wrote Singin' in the Rain and much else, but who seem more like the current partnership of Stephen Flaherty and Lynn Ahrens, who wrote Ragtime. Tom's dangerously eager young assistant Ellis (Jaime Cepero) idly mentions Monroe as a great subject for a musical, a suggestion that will come back to bite everybody round about Episode 3. Tom and Julia pooh-pooh the idea, and then of course get possessed by it, despite the fact that, as somebody mentions, there's already been a musical about Monroe and it was a disaster. In real life, there have been two, and only one was a disaster. The other was merely a flop.

Julia's reluctance is partly connected to her marriage. She and her husband Frank (Broadway musical veteran Brian d'Arcy James, roguishly cast in what, unless things are to take a radical turn, is a non-musical role) are taking time out from their careers in order to pursue the adoption of a child from China, since that's where everything comes from these days. I'm not clear why they should both have to give up work to do this, but chances are that Frank's career as a science teacher is not what's been supporting their lifestyle.

Apart from one funny/harrowing scene involving a focus group, the adoption plot is the least successful part of the show, especially when it brings in the couple's biological son, who seems to have been waiting an awfully long time for his baby sister. (If they could have one kid of their own, why not another?) Tom and Julia have a hit show still running, with the admittedly terrible title of Heaven on Earth; we see a bit of it, and it looks for all the world like the closing number of A Chorus Line.

We meet two Brits. One is Dev (Raza Jaffrey), Karen's highly intelligent and supportive boyfriend, who has snagged himself a job in the mayor's office. The other is Derek (Jack Davenport), a hotshot director whom Tom loathes but who gets attached to the project anyway.

Theresa Rebeck, who conceived the series and wrote the first three episodes, is also the author of the current Broadway play Seminar, in which Alan Rickman plays a role similar enough to Derek to make you wonder which came first; both characters are manipulative, sneery, supposedly brilliant and great believers in the casting couch. Dev and Derek share an especially delightful scene of competitive one-upping, such as only Oxbridge graduates could indulge in.

Davenport and Borle share the acting honours so far. The only jarring performances come from Anjelica Huston, who seems somehow out of focus as the show's putative producer, and from Michael Cristofer, as her nasty estranged marital and professional partner. But I have a bias against that actor, on account of a terrible Pulitzer-winning play he once wrote called The Shadow Box. When Huston threw drinks in his face, as she does with the regularity of a running gag, I silently applauded.

Add McPhee to the standout performers, especially when she gets up on a karaoke stage and does a very un-karaoke rendition of Redneck Woman. Most of the songs, though, are new ones, ghosted so to speak for Tom and Julia by the Hairspray team of Marc Shaiman and Scott Wittman. Their putative score for Marilyn is schizophrenic; much of it is snazzily true to period but there's also the regulation "contemporary" boneless ballad.

The presentation's schizoid, too; rehearsal scenes will sometimes morph into fantasy visions of the finished product. That's fine, but they miss one of the oldest and best tricks in the book: the transition from piano accompaniment to full orchestra, guaranteed to tingle the spine. Here, there seems to be a full band in the rehearsal room, which is too much Glee for comfort or belief. And the show actually is believable, most of the time; it might be darker and racier if it were being done on cable, as was the original intention, but it wouldn't necessarily be better.

The numbers, too, are excellently staged and shot. The presiding director is Michael Mayer, a Broadway regular whose shows aren't my favourites but who certainly knows the territory. Steven Spielberg is the executive producer and apparently had the original idea.

The third episode concludes with an absolute charmer of a number for Monroe and Joe DiMaggio. It makes you wonder if someone is planning a stage spin-off, in the form of an actual Marilyn musical, and also what kind of song-and-dance they could have in store for Arthur Miller.

Karen is the more obviously sympathetic of the two heroines, but you get to appreciate Ivy's point of view as well; that's a real strength, and very handy given that anything can happen on a musical's long and tortuous road to Broadway. Smash deserves to be a smash; it's already, as far as I'm concerned, a date.

- Smash premieres Feb. 6 at 10 p.m. on CTV and NBC. The series also airs on Bravo! beginning Feb. 10 at 9 p.m.

2012-02-09-up-where-we-belong:
THEATRE REVIEW

In the Heights Toronto Centre for the Arts

A renowned U.S. director once made a distinction between "energy," which may be the most desirable of all theatrical qualities, and mere "energeticness," which isn't. The touring production of In the Heights that's arrived in Toronto is full of energeticness but the pace, tension, focus and, above all, the level of experience that might transform it into energy have largely gone missing.

In the Heights comes to us with a non-Equity cast, a worrying sign of the times, and it shows.

The audience is short-changed, and so is the material. In the Heights won the 2008 Tony for best Broadway musical and, unlike some other recipients, it deserved to. It also introduced a newish musical sound to Broadway and, again unlike some other shows, used it well.

The heights of the title are the Washington ones, up in Manhattan where the street numbers are in the high three figures. It's a largely Hispanic neighbourhood; to get there, as Usnavi, the show's protagonist and narrator tells us in his opening rap, "you must take the A train even farther than Harlem."

There's no way I'm going to resist a new musical that starts by invoking Duke Ellington, especially as it continues its scene-setting by informing us that, "Oh my God, it's gotten too darn hot like my man Cole Porter said."

Lin-Manuel Miranda, the debutant composer-lyricist who wrote the score and who also created the central role, is a resourceful talent who couples an ear for the life around him with a cockeyed respect for tradition; indeed, in terms of plot, the show may be too traditional.

In the Heights has been touted as a hip-hop musical but that idiom is pretty much confined to Usnavi's own commentative numbers where it belongs; even there it's more elastic and sophisticated, lyrically and especially musically, than your average rap: better-natured, too. Insistently urban though it may be, hip hop shares something with country music; they're both forms that I don't much enjoy outside the theatre but that can work very well within it: much better than rock because they supply something more than a wash of sound; they're specific, story-driven and character-driven. As is this score: soaked in salsa but not drowning in it.

Usnavi owns what in local parlance is a bodega but we'd probably call a convenience store. It stands centrestage; to its left there's a hairdressing salon, to its right a taxi dispatcher. Above and behind them yawns the George Washington bridge. For a current Toronto audience the set-up, minus the bridge, may seem somewhat familiar: the three businesses have parcelled out between them the various problems - rising rents, generational tensions, romantic attraction across cultural and racial divides, buy-out offers from outside the area - that in Kim's Convenience are all crammed into Kim's convenience.

The hairdressers (shades of another Toronto hit) are pulling up their roots and moving to the Bronx. Usnavi has a thing for Vanessa, one of their employees, but is too shy to do much about it. Nina, one of Vanessa's contemporaries, has made everybody proud by getting into Stanford, but has dropped out. Her reason: "I was working so hard to pay for the books, I didn't have time to read them."

Talking of books, that's maybe the most resonant line in the one that Quiara Alegria Hudes has written for this show. Nina's parents, who run the taxi company, are devastated; her dad's pride, in her and in himself, is especially hurt. Nina further upsets them by starting a relationship with Benny, their ambitious young despatcher, whom they distrust because he's black. Everybody dreams of winning the lottery. To top everything off it's the eve of July 4, which, patriotic considerations apart, accounts for the darn heat. Which in turn is accentuated when the electricity breaks down. As it metaphorically has in this production.

We're back in the line of American musicals set in enclosed communities: Porgy and Bess, Street Scene, Fiddler on the Roof. The resemblances to Fiddler are especially close, what with the narrating hero, the expository prologue, the threat of everybody having to pull up sticks, if for slightly less grievous reasons than those that caused the exodus from Anatevka.

In the Heights, though, isn't as good as Fiddler at spinning out its overlapping narratives. It's a shock, at the end of the first act and the start of the second, to find that we're supposed to have been centrally invested in the love of Benny and Nina; they've seemed like two supporting characters among several.

This, as already noted, is accentuated by the casting, or under-casting. These untried actors aren't necessarily untalented but they can't give one another the mutual support that might enable them all to blossom. To make matters worse, the original direction has been "recreated" by someone else, so it's like seeing and hearing the show through two layers of cotton wool: three if you count the sound system, which consistently obscures the lyrics.

This seems especially unfair to the tongue-twisting Usnavi, who on opening night wasn't even the listed touring performer but his understudy, Perry Young. In fact, though, he did very well: sweet and appealing if without the edge and the dynamism that Miranda himself, to judge from the CD and a promotional video, must have brought to the role.

Presilah Nunez has some sexy impact as Vanessa. Benjamin Perez obviously understands the anguish of Nina's father very well but doesn't have the weight, or maybe the age, to make us feel it. Even the dancing, of which there's a lot, suffers; Andy Blankenbuehler's choreography looks as if it ought to be exciting but the conviction isn't there. As Cole Porter said, we're down in the depths when we ought to be in the heights.

- In the Heights runs until Feb. 19 at the Toronto Centre for the Arts. For tickets, visit dancaptickets.com.

2012-02-11-man-vs-man-the-double-and-hug:
Time to order a double-double. The show called The Double is based on a Dostoevski novella of the same title, concerning one Yakov Petrovich Golyadkin. Or rather two Yakov Petrovich Golyadkins since the original owner of that name becomes convinced that he has a lookalike namesake who is usurping his job, his social position, his very life. Two highly accomplished actors play the two Golyadkins, one of them also impersonating all the other characters in the piece. There's a third performer, a musician who plays, of all inevitable instruments, the double bass. So make that a triple-double.

Let's start with the musician, because the show does. His name is Arif Mirabdolbaghi and as well as supplying atmospheric accompaniment in a protean range of styles, he also functions as narrator. He speaks his lines with a deadpan wit that is not uncommon among instrumentalists but is still, for somebody who apparently has never been in a play before, pretty impressive. He is also one of the production's reasons for being, as he's a Dostoveski fan who transmitted his enthusiasm for the story to Adam Paolozza who directed it and also plays the primary Golyadkin. Both Paolozza and his opposite acting number Viktor Lukawski are superb mimes, but don't let that scare you. Like their musician friend they also talk, very well and at greater length.

Yakov Petrovich, like so many heroes and anti-heroes in Tsarist Russian fiction, is a low-level government official, and thus oppressed and paranoid almost by definition. He seems to have been storing up negative feelings for years but his explicit troubles begin when he's walking home one night and catches a glimpse of someone who seems unsettlingly familiar. He takes his troubles to a doctor who seems to fancy himself a psychiatrist ahead of his time, and who is either no help at all or too helpful by half, depending on how you look at it.

Like anyone in a rigorously stratified society, Golyadkin clings desperately to what status he has. He has a manservant, whom he patronizes or insults, and he fancies himself a social lion, though the lady on whom he has set his heart and whose party he crashes barely recognizes him. The toughest blow to his pride, though, comes when he finds his doppelganger working in the same office and getting along far better with the boss than he himself has ever managed.

Obviously, or unless you're an extreme believer in coincidence, the protagonist's double is his own fevered projection of the man he would like to be. The point is wonderfully illustrated when Golyadkin I invites Golyadkin II back to his place and tries to make nice with him. The scene is played, with magnificent technical aplomb, as a ventriloquist's routine, Paolozza speaking all the lines while Lukawski's lips silently move and his body goes all floppy.

The adaptation is quite a free one; at least, I don't imagine that Dostoevski wrote the stand-up comedy routine that Paolozza delivers at the height of his distraction and that is, in every sense, hysterical. There's a cabaret atmosphere to the whole production, with audience members nearest the stage seated at tables. Lukawski switches between his multitude of roles with absolute clarity and precision; Paolozza within his one role responds in kind. All this comes to a head in a marvellous quick-change sequence that may owe something to the Marx Brothers' great mirror scene in Duck Soup; indeed the whole show might be taken as a sustained riff on that classic routine, with the sinister undertones brought to the surface. It's pure theatre, with none of the preciousness that term sometimes signifies and all of the exhilaration.

There's another double act in Hughie, Eugene O'Neill's late one-act play about a gambler who returns late and drunk to his flea-bag hotel and the night clerk on whom he unloads himself. David Ferry's production also throws in musicians - two of them this time, on piano and trumpet - to establish the pre-crash 1920s atmosphere. I'm not sure that either they or some other environmental techniques are necessary, and I had my doubts even when the play proper got going. But then the production played its ace.

No character called Hughie actually appears; that was the name of the night clerk's predecessor, the previous confidant of Erie the gambler, now dead and - by Erie's likely unreliable account - much mourned. His successor doesn't have much to say, but O'Neill's stage directions spell out what he's thinking.

That's all very interesting in print but it's not ordinarily much help to the audience or to the actor, whatever the latter's telepathic skills; but in this staging we get to read them, as surtitles behind the desk. They're mainly discontented and disconnected musings on the street sounds outside - the fire trucks that make the clerk fantasize about setting the whole of New York on fire, the garbage cans that he would like to bang much louder.

These thoughts, of a footsore man who can't wait for his shift to be over, give the actor, Laurence Dean Ifill, something to play off, a way to chart the reluctant interest he eventually takes in his guest's maunderings. They also benefit Michael Kash, whose vocal and emotional range initially seem too limited for Erie's yarn-spinning about his financial and sexual conquests, but who gradually eases his way into the man's terminal seediness.

There's a humour in this play, and a low-down grace of language, that aren't usually associated with O'Neill. It also helps that, thanks to Boardwalk Empire, the one thing about Erie that really intrigues the clerk - does he know Arnold Rothstein? - has taken on a renewed urgency. The two eventually connect as equals, and a play that could be just a solo with subdued accompaniment becomes a true duet.

? The Double runs through Feb. 19 at the Factory Studio. Call 416-504-9971 or visit factorytheatre.ca for details. Hughie runs through March 3 at Theatre Centre. Call 416-538-0988 or visit theatrecentre.org for details.

2012-02-17-stable-as-she-goes-horses-are:
I trust this isn't too much of a spoiler, but Episode 5 of Luck ends with a horse leaning its head out of its stable door and nuzzling a sleepy Dustin Hoffman, who's keeping watch outside. It's a lovely moment and it sets the seal on the show's development thus far. It's progressed, that is, from a show I wanted to like to one that I see some possibility of loving: a rich, dark human comedy. That episode doesn't reach the screen for another couple of weeks, and earlier instalments have tested many people's patience, including mine, but the wait is worth it.

Luck began with Hoffman, as millionairebusinessman-gambler-crook Ace Bernstein, getting out of jail after - he said - taking a three-year fall for somebody else's misdemeanors. He now intends, like a latter-day Count of Monte Cristo, to use his wealth and skills in a labyrinthine plot to get back at the guys who put him there, in particular one called Mike.

He also bought a racehorse; or at least, since being a felon apparently debars you from owning horses, he had his driver and confidant Gus (Dennis Farina) buy one on his behalf. It still isn't quite clear whether these two plans are connected. I started out assuming they were, and that Hoffman's horse was a Trojan one, but that end-of-episode image, along with a few things that happened earlier in the hour, suggested that he genuinely loves his horse. He could certainly stand some love in his life.

His more sinister game plan involves buying the Santa Anita racetrack in California, on and around which nearly all the action takes place, and expanding its activities to include a casino. The rationale (and I really can't follow this) is that horse racing is legal in the state, but gambling - other than presumably betting on horses - isn't: in which case, why would a casino be any more kosher for being situated on a track? Still, Ace seems to know what he's doing and Hoffman, playing a dapper man with a short fuse, certainly does. He's been a star now for nearly half a century, and he's still at the top of his game.

If his motivations, and even his dialogue, seemed obscure to begin with, they were crystalline compared to those of the rest of the cast. We have Nick Nolte, who hasn't been around as long as Hoffman but who

looks and sounds much older, playing the proud but mumbling owner of a prize horse with a noble but troubled ancestry (the horse's ancestry, that is). We have a quartet of self-styled "degenerates," each with a mental and/or physical disability of some kind; hanging around the track seems to be their life and, after winning big on an impenetrable system called a Pick Six, they've bought a horse of their own. It's hard to believe that this will end well.

There's an assortment of jockeys, male and female, most of them nervous most of the time. There's Joey (Richard Kind), a sweaty agent who represents at least two of the jockeys and has a bad stammer, which actually makes him easier to understand than some of his fellows. And there is Escalante (John Ortiz), a Peruvian trainer who may be wearing his extremely thick accent as a badge of defiance; he doesn't believe in making polite allowances for anyone. They all have to put up with him, though, because he's the best at what he does, and has nearly all the show's horses in his stable. This makes him, in structural terms, a unifying factor even though in most other ways he's a divisive one.

Asked by Ace how his horse is getting on, Gus replies, "What would I know? All four of his legs touched the ground." Apart from its admirable stylistic qualities, I warmed to this line because it suggested that Gus knows as little about horses as I do. In fact, I have difficulty telling the noble animals apart, and it's only around Episode 4 that the show has begun to make it easier for me.

David Milch, who created the show, writes - or he and the other writers in his, well, stable, write - the fruitiest dialogue on television, which makes you wonder why he has made so much of it so hard to hear. However, either they've adjusted the mix, or the actors are speaking up and slowing down, or my ears are getting attuned. Milch's Deadwood was no aural or narrative picnic either, to begin with, but I got addicted to it (and am still feeling the withdrawal symptoms). Deadwood, too, was a horse opera, i.e. a Western, though looking back I don't remember horses playing as crucial a role as they do here. And the horses are what bring the show together because they're what bring the characters together.

I've given up waiting for the various storylines to converge; instead they play off one another. The characters are figures in a pattern rather than spokes in a wheel. The track is not as compelling or interdependent a community as the town was in Deadwood, but it will serve. There's a desperation to it, both good and bad; we're made aware that it's a dwindling business, with the same few people turning up for every race. Chief among these obsessives, even after making their big score, are the four degenerates, who are becoming a fine set of comedians, crisscrossing egos trying to make common cause.

"I got three friends," says their leader, Marcus, "who I can hardly stand most of the time." Marcus (Kevin Dunn, terrific) is a paraplegic with heart and respiratory problems; his anger, even greater than Ace's, is alternately tolerated and resented by his buddies, one of whom has been distinctly heard to complain that "my mental adroitness is dulled by this constant negativity." A crooked security guard has told Marcus, less ornately, "Don't hold your breath - oh, I forgot, you can't." Karma being a bitch, this guy will also find himself in dire need of friends. While I'm quoting I can't resist Ace's advice to Gus, who has a habit, handy for exposition if for nothing else, of telling people what they already know: "If you can't advance the conversation, you're not required to talk."

Each episode naturally includes a race. One of the most exciting is in Episode 4, where the jockey we've been rooting for triumphs, despite covering most of the course in slow motion. This kind of trickery, like the constant use of extraneous music, is contrary to the best canons of cable drama, but the show gets away with it. In this episode we also get to meet Mike, who turns out to be English; maybe every Milch show needs its limey "c--ksucker."

In fact, he's Michael Gambon, who's massive, though he does seem to have come out of another show, maybe a Guy Ritchie movie or a Harold Pinter play which, come to think of it, is a thought. His meeting with Ace takes place on a boat, and is shot at appropriately queasy angles. In other circumstances Hoffman can wear a face of pure heartbreak. "As far as sexual activity and so forth," he tells Gus, "that ship sailed a long time ago." Nonetheless, he seems interested in a lady (Joan Allen) who's requesting his charitable contribution to a scheme for prison inmates to work with horses. This would connect with Ace on two levels, but that may just be coincidence.

Episode 5 lets us in on touching things concerning stuttering Joey's home life. It also finds Marcus having a checkup. His doctor asks, "Do you have anyone you can talk to?" Marcus thinks and says, "a horse." "That's not bad" says the doctor, thoughtfully. In this show's universe, that's an understatement. I think we're in luck.

? Luck airs Sundays at 9 p.m. on HBO Canada.

2012-02-18-when-harry-met-satire-potted-:
Fifteen years ago, TVOntario took its cameras into a Toronto school library in an attempt to find out what the children were reading. One 10-year-old girl spoke enthusiastically about a book she'd just received from her uncle in England, a book that was already very popular over there but had yet to be published anywhere else. It was about a boy called Harry Potter. "And who," the interviewer asked, in words destined never to be uttered again in a public forum, "is Harry Potter?"

I can vouch for the authenticity of this story, as the young lady in question was my daughter. So I can boast that, where North American Pottermania is concerned, my household was way ahead of the curve. My Potter credentials, though, pretty much end there; I never got around to reading any of the books, and I only saw the first half of the first movie. (It was on the VCR, as we called it in those days; I got called away and never returned.) However, the performers and producers of Potted Potter claim their show can be understood without any knowledge of the source material, and I can proclaim, from the full depths of my ignorance, that they're right.

Not, of course, that anyone can really remain ignorant of the Potter universe. When Daniel Clarkson and Jefferson Turner drop names like Voldemort and Dumbledore, they don't need to explain who those people are or what they stand for. Though, actually, they do. Their show, which is subtitled "The Unauthorized Harry Experience - A Parody by Dan and Jeff," presents itself as a 75-minute synopsis of all seven Potter volumes. It's Dan and Jeff themselves who need an introduction. So here it is: They are a couple of young British writerperformers who've been working this material up for several years now, and whose style of academic knockabout is fifth-generation Monty Python. It's also, and more fundamentally, in the venerable tradition of comic and stooge. In this case Dan, the taller, is the comedian and Jeff, the shorter, is the straight man. As usual, the seeming authority figure gets progressively undermined by the feckless zany to whom he is shackled for the duration.

Clarkson and Turner are especially close to the great British team of Morecambe and Wise, whose standard procedure on their TV shows was as follows. Ernie (that was Wise) would proudly announce that he'd written a play, based on some literary or historical theme and Eric (Morecambe) would proceed to ruin it. Similarly: Jeff is a self-proclaimed Potter expert, and this dramatized speed-read is his idea. He will also play Harry. Dan will play everybody else, despite the fact that he hasn't read any of the books. He has to play everybody else because he has taken the budget with which he was supposed to hire actors from the Stratford Festival and blown it all on what he promises Jeff will be a truly amazing dragon. To be fair to Dan, we do get to see the dragon. To be fair to Jeff ... no, it would take too long. Anyway, it finally dawns on Jeff that Dan is having all the fun and that Harry, in these reduced circumstances, is not much of a role, is in fact the straight guy to end them all. This is a history-making departure; never before have I known the sober half of a duo to act jealous of the fact that his partner is getting all the laughs. An ancient comic secret is being dragged into the open.

And indeed Clarkson, who has the air of innocent solicitude characteristic of havoc-wreaking clowns, can be very funny indeed. He's funniest, as is the show as a whole, when it gets furthest from its presumed premise: most of all when he takes charge of both stage and auditorium to involve the audience in a game of Quidditch. Some of what he does counts as Potter parody, as when he remarks of the rule concerning the Snitch (all new to me, of course, but they make it easy) that it renders the rest of the game completely pointless. But what's really fun is the glee he injects in some very traditional routines: dividing the house into competitive halves and getting two of the smallest spectators onstage as their representatives. He can be surprisingly, and refreshingly, impolite about all this, and he really does seem to be thinking on his feet.

The most striking of his instant impersonations is his Ron Weasley who sounds remarkably like Ali G. The duo gets surprising mileage out of an oft-repeated and extremely irritating prophecy of Dumbledore's and they do indeed provide a comprehensible, if not comprehensive, rundown of the books, with a sidelong glance at the movies' one-for-the-priceof-two rendition of one of them. All the same, there's a depressing air of cashing-in about the whole occasion. A joke that would be good for one revue sketch is made to serve for an entire show. It's a longish ride on somebody else's broomstick.

? Potted Potter runs until March 25 at the Panasonic Theatre. For ticket information, visit mirvish.com or call 416-872-1212.

Seabright Productions / Turner, left, as Harry and Clarkson as everyone else in Potted Potter.;; Caption:
2012-02-23-settling-scores:
THEATRE REVIEW

HIGH LIFE

Young Centre for the Performing Arts, Toronto

The high life enjoyed, if that's the word, by the four characters of Lee MacDougall's play is a chemical one. The quartet consists of hard-core addicts who feed their habits by committing petty crimes and have consequently spent a large part of their lives behind bars. Call them another gang that couldn't shoot straight, except when the shooting is being done with hypodermics.

The play premiered in Toronto in 1997 and was a great success. This, its first major revival, continues Soulpepper's line of Canadian classics and is the worthiest of the title. It isn't the deepest play ever written, or the one with the widest significance, but it's taut and tense and funny, complete in its own world and with no fat on it.

The author has updated it slightly; at least I'm fairly sure that the original could not have ended with the guys, eternal optimists, planning a new scam involving iPads.

Most of the play concerns a previous scheme masterminded, again if that's the word, by Dick, who likes to hang out at Narcotics Anonymous meetings recruiting fresh talent. His senior sidekick is Bug, who is rough and surly and very quick to take offence; he can shoot straight, which isn't always an asset.

An old friend and associate of theirs, Donny, has just about destroyed himself; he currently has half a kidney and little hope of a transplant. He says, not too convincingly, that he's now clean; he's also a delightfully gentle soul who supports himself by stealing nice ladies' bank cards and using them at ATMs, but tries always to return the cards afterward.

This game of Donny's is what gives Dick an idea for the big score, a carefully calibrated hit on multiple bank machines. To carry it out he needs a fourth player, the young and comparatively presentable Billy who can charm women, especially bank tellers. Billy has never done time, a circumstance that excites everyone's suspicion, especially Bug's. Dick has patiently to explain that this may just mean that Billy is to smart to have been caught.

The play's territory lies somewhere between Damon Runyon and David Mamet: less cute and more genuinely seedy than Runyon (who never acknowledged the existence of dope), but without the broader social ramifications of Mamet. It could be happening in any Canadian, or indeed American, city but its default setting may be Toronto.

All I could recall from the original production was that most of the play is set in a room but that the big scene takes place in a car. Other memories are hazy, which in a play that depends so much on narrative surprise is probably an advantage, but I have the impression that Stuart Hughes' Soulpepper production is better paced and balanced than its predecessor.

It certainly benefits from having four actors who have worked together in any number of contexts and who seem, in the precisely differentiated costumes designed for them by Lorenzo Savoini, to be having a blast as High Life's low-lifes.

Two of them give cast-iron performances: Michael Hanrahan, impregnably tough and dumb and blinkered as Bug, and Oliver Dennis whose Donny, replete with good intentions and conscientious objections, is a beautiful symphony of decomposition.

Mike Ross takes time to get inside Billy's overconfident skin but he comes into his own when working his magic on the unseen bank clerk and stays there for the duration.

Diego Matamoros as Dick is fine in the central scenes, controlling the operation with barely masked brutality, but in his string of one-on-one encounters he's surprisingly coarse and forced, with shouting and barking standing in for real authority. He's also the least convincing junkie of the four; the cravings of the others are palpable but he seems above it all.

If Dick is meant to be faking, the script gives little sign of it. It does, though, provide delightful insight into his former reign as king of the prison, in particular in the matter of selecting the films for movie night. Donny testifies that Dick drastically expanded the cinematic horizons of all the inmates. Dick himself, at moments of crisis, is apt to compare the situation to a Bergman movie. Here he may, and not for the only time, be kidding himself.

Things here just aren't that existential. Think Tarantino, Dick, and think yourself lucky at that.

- High Life runs until March 28. For tickets, visit soulpepper.ca.
