2012-02-25-field-of-dreams-seeds-an-impr:
The documentary play Seeds centres on the 2004 patent infringement case of Monsanto vs. Schmeiser. Monsanto, the bio-tech company, claimed that Percy Schmeiser, a Saskatchewan farmer, had in effect stolen a batch of seeds for their genetically modified canola plant, a seed resistant to their own brand of Roundup herbicide. (That's an awesomely symmetrical business model. You sell something, and then you sell something else to counteract it.) Schmeiser claimed that the seeds had found their way onto his 1,000-acre farm by accident, maybe blown there from a passing truck. After a long process, with many adjournments, the court found for Monsanto. The decision stuck in a lot of throats - nobody likes to see David crushed by Goliath - and the analogy, made by Schmeisers own supporters, gave the case an afterlife that includes this play.

Its author, Annabel Soutar, is herself one of the characters; the play is the narrative of her investigation, interview by interview. She was pregnant at the time, and this also feeds into the play, which periodically asks the question, what is life? Its suggestive, if not as strong a unifying theme as the author might wishfully have thought. As narrative, though, her script is both thoughtful and exciting; it makes the science fairly clear and the personal issues convincingly complex. The play has been masterfully staged by Chris Abraham. (The show is a co-production of Crow's Theatre, which Abraham directs, and Soutar's own Montreal company Porte Parole.) The design team has done superb work. Julie Fox designed the set, a deep wide space that looks initially like a lab but can take on any identity thats required. Richard Feren did the sound, Ana Capellutto the lighting and Elysha Poirier is responsible for the projections, which are exceptionally clear and helpful.

The play splits sharply into two halves. Act One ends with the initial trial verdict. Act Two shows Schmeiser emerging as a crusader, sounding alarm bells worldwide about the dangers of genetically modified foods. A Monsanto mouthpiece points out that this is not actually what the trial was about, and thats fair comment. It's also true that Schmeiser himself never mentioned it before, at least not in the play's hearing. Maybe he was some combination of victim, opportunist and self-publicist. That doesnt dispose of the validity of his concerns. He also has plenty to say about Monsantos continued harassment of him; about the treats, ranging from jackets to junkets, that they bestowed on his enemies; and on the inspection of his land by what he calls "the gene police."

Eric Peterson is dream casting for Schmeiser, cranky and scrappy. The guy's no innocent, as he keeps telling us he's an experienced politician, in fact an ex-mayor. Hes a believer, who knows how to frame his beliefs to advantage. He can be grand and he can be petty - witness the way he turns on his chief defender at the end. Petersons stumbles and hesitations when confronting the press or making a speech are dead on; it does seem to be the character who's stumbling rather than the actor, since in his domestic scenes he's perfectly fluent. As his quietly supportive wife, Tanja Jacobs delivers one of a whole series of fine lightning sketches; others include Monsantos steamrollering counsel and a thoughtful academic (Alex Ivanovici, Mariah Inger). Bruce Dinsmore and Cary Lawrence are all fine in multiple roles, and Liisa RepoMartell makes an involving playwrights stand-in, though having her double as the voice of the supreme court is confusing. The whole is one of the most impressive docu-dramas I've seen.

Confession of interest: The assistant director of Seeds is my son. Confession of further interest: Dani Girl, a musical born in America but premiered here, is produced by Talk Is Free Theatre, who also this week produced a reading of a play of my own, and it's directed by Richard Ouzounian, my opposite number at the Toronto Star. Its about a preteen girl and boy, sharing a terminal cancer ward. This is a brave subject for a musical, but its also a terrible one, especially as the chosen tone - starting with the forced joke of the title - is cute-fantastical, involving the kids' imaginary flight to heaven to ask God the question Why is cancer?, dramatically an even less fruitful inquiry than What is life?"

The show's book is better than its score though, frustratingly enough, it couldnt exist in this form without the score. Michael Koomans tunes, handling the fantasy, are lightweight, with one notable exception near the end; Christopher Dimond's script, handling more of the facts, gets a touching counterpart going between Dani girl and her companion, and a moving one between Dani and her mother. The latter partnership indeed tears your heart out, but then it would be hard for it not to. The performances are excellent, and very well co-ordinated. Gabi Epstein is crystal-bright as Dani; Jonathan Logan unforcedly endearing as her sci-fi obsessed companion; Amanda Leblanc steadfastly helpful as the mother; and Jeff Madden a fount of deep-focused energy as a succession of imaginary friends, even though most of them are profoundly irritating. It's in these figures that form meets subject and retires defeated. You can, of course, write a musical about anything. But you don't have to.

? Seeds runs through March 10 at the Young Centre for the Performing Arts. Visit youngcentre.ca or call 416-504-1666 for ticket information. Dani Girl runs through March 11 at Theatre Passe Muraille Backspace. Visit passemuraille.on.ca or call 4165047529 for tickets.

Susan Benoit / Dani Girl's Gabi Epstein and Jeff Madden.;; Caption:
2012-03-01-straight-from-its-mouth:
THEATRE REVIEW

War Horse

Princess of Wales Theatre, Toronto

The transforming moment in War Horse - transforming in every sense - comes about 20 minutes in. Joey, the title horse, changes before our eyes from foal to full-grown stallion. It would be unfair to reveal exactly how, but up until this point Joey has been a life-size skeletal puppet, visibly manipulated by three performers whom it is sometimes confusingly easy to mistake for characters in the story; stable hands perhaps?

The puppeteers are still in evidence when Joey grows up, but they're now so disposed that we can tune them out. For the rest of the evening we believe in Joey as an actual horse, even while remaining happily aware that he's a product of theatrical wizardry. The magic is manifold. The technical peak coincides with an emotional peak. And that synergy, of spectacle and feeling, keeps going throughout the show.

It makes a great evening out of a less-than-great script. The play is Nick Stafford's adaptation of Michael Morpurgo's novel, brought to the stage by the National Theatre of Great Britain in a production (by Marianne Elliott and Tom Morris) that's been restaged here (by Alex Sims) with a Canadian cast.

Joey is a natural-born hunter bought at auction by Ted Narracott, a drunken Devonshire farmer, mainly to spite his more successful brother Arthur. Ted's 16-year-old son Albert takes care of Joey and, under paternal pressure, trains him to pull a plough though he's clearly meant for nobler things. The year is 1914; when the First World War breaks out Ted sells Joey to the British Army. A heartbroken Albert lies about his age and enlists, in the hope of being reunited with his beloved steed. His quest, which gets us all the way to 1918, takes up the second half of the play.

A not-unexpected climax is quite shamelessly delayed, in both the long and the short term. There's a string of coincidences that seem to be pointing to an early reunion; but each of them is bypassed in favour of a protracted finale that plays every trick of suspense and remorselessly assaults every tear duct while uplifting every heart. Remorselessly but forgivably: It feels sentimental but, like the show as a whole, it doesn't feel untruthful. It's underpinned by an anger about war that is ages old and always new. The First World War remains the perfect crucible because it was both the last of the glamour wars and the first of the modern ones. In War Horse's terms, it was the war where cavalry charges met machine guns.

In a program note Morpurgo lists several inspirations for his novel. One he doesn't mention, but that must have been read by every English schoolchild of his (and my) generation, is Black Beauty, the fictitious autobiography of a Victorian horse, one who in a more domestic version of Joey's trajectory goes from country horse to cab horse and ends up reunited with his first stableboy. The stage version of War Horse drops the book's narrative voice; a talking horse would hardly strike the right theatrical note. Instead it gives us the perspectives of two theoretically opposed humans who in fact have a lot in common but who never meet.

There's Albert, and there's Friedrich, an enemy officer who, in Patrick Galligan's warm but somewhat wavering performance, is so good a German that he speaks with an English accent. He puts the captured Joey to work ferrying the wounded, thereby drawing unknowingly on the wonder horse's early training. There's another German, who seems more of a proto-Nazi but who still ends up cursing the war and asking Friedrich (and by implication, the play and the audience) why he can't care as much for the sufferings of humans as of horses.

The most affecting scene in the play makes us care for humans because they care for horses; in an episode apparently modelled on the famous 1914 Christmas Eve truce, one soldier from each side, both waving white flags but unable to speak one another's language, combine to rescue Joey from his impalement on barbed wire and then toss a coin to decide which will keep him. It's well written and, by Dylan Roberts and Richard McMillan, delightfully acted.

This is not, though, a show that much extends its actors, except perhaps physically. The obvious exception is Alex Furber, a newcomer whose Albert carries all before him (or in Joey's case, underneath him). He gets good support from Tamara Bernier Evans, alternately sharp and sweet as his mother; Brad Rudy, dogged or maybe just hang-dogged as his dad; and Patrick Kwok-Choon as his buddy in the trenches. But mostly this is a production kind of production, and a triumphant one.

It isn't just the puppeteering, wonderful though that is; the Handspring Puppet Company, from South Africa, bring to life a subsidiary horse called Topthorn plus a goose and the odd vulture, but of course it's Joey who's the king of their world. "Back legs of the horse" will from now on be a more honourable actor's credit than ever before.

In terms of staging techniques you might say that this is where Equus meets The Lion King, though there was nothing in The Lion King as shattering as this show's first evocation of the actual shock of battle. It's a confluence of design (Rae Smith), music (Adrian Sutton), lighting (Paule Constable) and, perhaps above all, projections (59 Productions) that are preternaturally stark, clear and economical.

To cite some comparable British theatrical epics: Nicholas Nickleby this ain't; it doesn't have the humanity or the humour. Oh! What a Lovely War it also ain't; it doesn't have the bite or the wit. But it has heart, and just enough mind and dazzle that's never merely an end in itself. It also cured me of any desire to see the film. I know that movies can do horses and battles. I also know - check out the prologue to Henry V - that the stage can't, not easily; which makes it all the more exciting when it does. War Horse gives manipulation - again in every sense - a very good name.

- For tickets, visit mirvish.com.

Mirvish / If nothing else, the stage version of War Horse gives a new sense of honour for actors credited with playing the tail end of a horse.;; Caption:
2012-03-03-say-terrible-things-apologize:
'If you didn't make allowances in this family, you'd go nuts." Those words, spoken by James Tyrone Jr. in Eugene O'Neill's Long Day's Journey into Night, could probably apply in some degree to any family anywhere, but Jamie's has to be accounted an extreme case. He's the self-hating, alcoholic wastrel son of a successful but pathologically stingy actor-manager father and a morphine-addicted mother who owes her condition to pain-medication administered to her after the birth of Jamie's younger brother Edmund. The long day in the life of the Tyrones is the one on which Mary, after a period of remission, relapses into hallucinatory oblivion, and on which Edmund, an aspiring writer with a tiring cough, learns that he has tuberculosis.

O'Neill himself was a consumptive, and the play, as much of the world knows, is barely disguised autobiography. Only the names have been changed, and a couple of those have merely been fudged; a third brother who died in infancy and was actually called Edmund is here referred to as Eugene, an exchange that would make a field day's journey for any psychoanalyst. The memory of that child is another of the curses hanging around the family's necks. Long Day's Journey is perhaps the most special of special case dramas. Part of its power to move derives from our awareness that the author was writing about himself, which seems rather unfair; but we respond also to the unsparingness of the drama, and in the end to its charity. O'Neill forgets nothing and, it seems to me, forgives everything.

In being so specific, he outlines a universal dance. Four people, inextricably locked together, say terrible things to one another, feel instantly ashamed, apologize, and then say them again. It's amazing the number of variations O'Neill can play on this single tune, but then the compulsiveness is the point. Nearly 20 years ago, Diana Leblanc directed a legendary production at Stratford that stressed the love between the characters as well as the pain. Her new production for Soulpepper takes the same tack; it doesn't unfold with the same seamless inevitability, but it's equally affecting. One of the play's key moments is James Sr.'s appeal to his wife when he starts to feel her slipping back: "Mary, won't you stop now?" Laurence Olivier at the Old Vic made it a great theatrical howl; maybe he was showing us Tyrone the actor playing for effect, but it sounded more as if he himself was. William Hutt made it a cry wrenched from the heart; even on a second viewing, it took you by world-rocking surprise. Joseph Ziegler accompanies it with a desperate embrace, and is less startling but even more moving. Ziegler showed in A Whistle in the Dark how superbly he could play a monstrous hypocrite of a father (transplanted Irish, too, like Tyrone); if he doesn't do the same here, that could be because Tyrone is not, in fact, a monster. He's a limited but loving man, whose good intentions are undercut by a tragic flaw that's also a running gag. He can't stop himself from crying poorhouse (literally), from measuring the whisky in the bottle (everybody in this play is a drinker, including the maid), from railing at his sons to switch off the lights; more darkly, his miserliness has caused him to stint on proper treatment for his wife and, incipiently, his son. He also knows it, though he has to be pressed into admitting it. Ziegler's performance has been criticized as insufficiently actorish and insufficiently Irish, but there's nothing in the text that suggests he should be either.

It's Mary whose accusations are the cruellest; even her apologies, as the drugs anaesthetize her, draw blood. Nancy Palk brilliantly charts her growing estrangement from reality, along with the retreat into her convent girlhood, a fantasy that by the final curtain has reached the stage of total immersion. It's unfortunate, though, that she has no staircase to descend for her final speech; she has to sidle on, which blunts the impact. The play, by the way, follows High Life as Soulpepper's second opening in one week involving morphine addiction, taking thematic programming to new levels of specialization. The two sons are terrifically played. Evan Buliung's Jamie has a tormented bravura that declares itself on its first appearance, and pays off wonderfully in his last-act return from an evening of sousing and whoring; vicious one moment, shamefaced the next, driving and driven throughout, he's a one-man summary of the entire play. Gregory Prest's watchful Edmund, by contrast, bides his time; he declares himself, both tolerant and triumphant, in the marvellous final scene where he trades bittersweet burnt-ember memories with his father and brother. As the maid, alternately solicitous and supercilious, Krystin Pellerin is, not for the first time, superb, which here includes being funny. The play is not a tragedy but a tragicomedy, and no less moving for that. I watched a goodly proportion of this production through tears.

I didn't cry at The Big Smoke, but I was both impressed and transfixed. This import features a British based Canadian-born performer, Amy Nostbakken, as a blocked young painter trapped in depression in both countries. Her solo performance, of a script written by herself and her director Nir Paldi (with acknowledgments to Anne Sexton, Virginia Woolf and Sylvia Plath, which should give you an idea) is mostly sung, a capella. This turns out to be an extraordinary vehicle for portraying a mind on the edge, with time out for instant portraits, mostly satiric, of less encumbered people encountered on the way down. Technically, the performance is a marvel; emotionally, it's a disturbance. It closes tomorrow, and is well worth grabbing.

? Long Day's Journey into Night plays in repertory at the Young Centre (416-866-8666); The Big Smoke plays at the Factory Studio (416-504-9971).

Michael Cooper / Watchful Gregory Prest, brilliant Nancy Palk and moving Joseph Ziegler.;; Caption:
2012-03-08-buying-the-farm:
FREE AS INJUNS

Buddies in Bad Times Theatre, Toronto

It's a jim-dandy farm, says the sheriff, fulfilling officialdoms customary theatrical task of surveying a scene of physical and psychological wreckage. "Wish I owned it." That line, unfortunately, does not come from Native Earths new production, Free as Injuns, but from Desire Under the Elms, the Eugene O'Neill play on which it is based.

Toronto is having an unaccustomed feast of O'Neill at the moment, what with Long Days Journey into Night at Soulpepper and Hughie at Theatre Centre. Desire is generally reckoned to be the best of ONeill's early plays -- "early" here being anything before the late twin peaks of Long Day's Journey and The Iceman Cometh -- and this adaptation makes one want to see a good production of it. Free as Injuns is far from being that production.

Fair enough: Its not trying to be. But Tara Beagans play borrows enough of the characters and structure of its original for us to be painfully aware of the gap. As in O'Neill we are on the farm of Ephraim Cabot, who has three sons, each by a different wife. He brings home yet another bride, a woman decades younger than himself named Abbie, or in this version simply Be. She catches the eye of Even (Eben in the original), youngest of the Cabot boys and sets about seducing him. He, after some early hesitation, responds with enthusiasm. Other considerations apart, he has a score to settle with his old man for the way in which he treated Even's late mother, with whose ghostly voice he periodically converses.

The source play is a hot brew of physical and territorial lusts, the latter trenchantly summarized in the clinching line quoted up top. This version stirs in a new element. Ephraim, who is white, has built his farm on Native American (or would that be Canadian?) land. He has compounded this act of dispossession by marrying and mistreating a succession of native women -- though one of them, judging by the looks of her son, may have been Asian. (Or is this colour-blind casting? You never know.)

This theme, though, is never actively realized in the text. It merely gives rise to some windy writing, with the occasional stab of genuine poetry, all bound together with more palatable passages of rougher stuff. This admittedly is the mixture ONeill himself favoured when he was straining for tragedy rather than achieving by mining his own past. He was, though, a lot better at storytelling.

The last half-hour or so of Free as Injuns circles endlessly around the same situation. Be has given birth. Ephraim thinks the child is his. Even knows better but is tormented by jealousy. The theory seems to be that the more they all agonize about it, the more that agony will transmit itself to the audience. It doesnt; or at least not in the way intended.

Ruth Madoc-Jones' production makes heavy weather of a heavy script. It's also erratically acted. Old Ephraim is one of those tyrannical patriarchs who are always hard to cast if neither Jim Mezon nor David Fox is available. Here we have Jerry Franken, Foxs old sparring partner from The Drawer Boy and elsewhere, whose performance occasions the kind of pain peculiar to the spectacle of a good actor doing his best with a role to which hes totally unsuited.

Ephraim mercilessly and habitually humiliates all three of his sons, and Franken is neither physically nor vocally imposing enough for us to believe that they, all strapping fellows, would let him get away with it. The stammer that he adopts to indicate failing powers only aggravates the situation.

PJ Prudat's Be mainly projects an effortful idea of sultriness, though James Cade does infuse some raw if intermittent passion into Eben. John Ng and Ash Knight as the other brothers are competent at what they're required to do, which is mainly to leer about the place, long after threatening to leave (which in O'Neill they do). They seem to have been kept on mainly for symbolic purposes; one of them goes around carrying a door frame, which everybody refers to as his gate.

In other respects the show looks good; Andy Moro's set transforms the Buddies main space, the most versatile in Toronto, into a kind of cockpit, lacking only a good fight.

2012-03-10-scarifying-ladies-and-talking:
On my left a green patio, on my right a yellow kitchen, each of them occupied by a woman dressed to match. Between them the facade of a house, picked out in blue with square black holes for windows. Above and around a dark sky decorated with fluffy white clouds, the contrast may be indicating that happiness is possible but may also be illusory.

Rose Cullis's play is called The Happy Woman, and taking into account the expected doses of irony, the decor is very appropriate. It's also very stylish, which befits a script that's accomplished, penetrating but somewhat frustrating. The title figure, though not exactly the central one (this is part of the frustration), is the yellow lady, Margaret, a widow who reveres the memory of her recently departed: a reverence not shared by others, notably her grown-up son and daughter. Barbara Gordon plays Margaret: providential casting since no actress is better, or even conceivably as good, at probing the horizons of the upper-middle-aged middlemiddle-class. Margaret is sunny without being silly, but she is only able to maintain her serene practicality by shutting out unwelcome facts.

Her polar opposite is her daughter Cassie, a barmaid and performance artist (not, she insists and despite her brother's insinuations, a stripper), who wears her heart not so much on her sleeve as on her entire body. As played by Maev Beaty, she's alight with wit, warmth, pain and anger; this actress's ability to take instant command of both stage and character has never been more electrically on display. Cassie is widely suspected of carrying on with the married man across the street, an allegation that shocks her mother though, where her daughter's demons are concerned, she doesn't know the half. In the play's showpiece scene, Cassie confronts Margaret with things that have been going on in her own life and under their own roof. Interestingly, Margaret is shocked but not outraged. Her composure cracks, but not irreparably.

The play is not, though, just about the two of them. There's Christian, Cassie's brother, whose wife Stasia is terrified that she is about to give birth to a monster and, after delivery, is convinced that she's done so. There's some scarifying writing here; scarifying acting, too, by Ingrid Rae Doucet. The remaining character is the woman in green, named (in the program, though mercifully seldom in the text) BellaDonna, and appropriately venomous. She, too, is perfectly played by Maria Vacratsis, sitting on her porch and commenting, with censorious prurience, on the impending end of the world and the assorted fecklessness of her neighbours. She may have a point, and she certainly seems to enjoy making it. She could be a happy woman, too. Indeed, the play's title might be generic, with an implied question mark on the end; Cassie may be en route to her own kind of happiness, and even Stasia gets some, at a price. There's a pattern here, but there isn't much of a climax and the strands are only loosely tied together. The link between all the women is Christian (the name presumably means something) but the play doesn't seem much interested in him, or in men generally. Martin Happer plays him strongly, but is principally confined to a note of vexed cheerfulness. Whatever: Kelly Thornton's production is the second consecutive triumph, following The Penelopiad, for her and for Nightwood Theatre, while the colour co-ordination of Denyse Karn's set and costumes takes in the smallest details. The play does haunt the mind, and may even invade your dreams. The work of a new playwright (to me, anyway), it stands out in a season that's been notably short on good new plays.

A comparable stand-out in its way is The Never Ending Story, adapted and directed by David S. Craig from the children's classic by Michael Ende. The adventure story itself is fine enough, centring on Adamo Ruggiero as an engaging boy-hero and featuring a throng of actors in multiple roles among whom Charlotte Moore is a sequential delight. But what really counts is the involvement of the bullied boy Bastian, played with wonderful freshness and conviction by Natasha Greenblatt, who steals the story from a mysterious bookstore and finds himself progressively drawn into it. It's an essay on imagination that only disappoints at the close; this never-ending story ends all too abruptly. Up until then, it's a resourcefully staged delight. It may not be as spectacular as War Horse, but it's every bit as stirring. And its horse talks.

The Happy Woman plays until March 24 at the Berkeley Street Theatre Downstairs. Visit nightwoodtheatre.net or call 416-368-3110 for details. The Never Ending Story runs until March 17. Visit youngpeoplestheatre.ca or call 416-862-2222 for more information.

2012-03-13-the-insider-deal-with-stratfo:
On Sunday it was announced that Antoni Cimolino will be the next artistic director of the Stratford Festival. This was not a surprise. What was surprising, or at least unexpected, is that his regime will commence next season. It had previously been thought that 2013 would be a transitional year with the current director, Des McAnuff, working alongside his successor and formally handing over at the end of the season.

In a speech on Saturday at Stratford's annual general meeting, McAnuff outlined the reasons for speeding up the process: Cimolino "is an insider. He doesn't require an extended period - the way an outsider would."

He expanded on this when I spoke with both men on the phone on Sunday: "Antoni, besides being politically very astute and creative, has what I call institutional memory."

Indeed Cimolino, who has been at Stratford for 25 years - first as an actor, then as both a director and an administrator - has a better claim than almost anyone else to having the Festival in his bones.

It's both a good and a threatening time to be taking over Canada's biggest institutional theatre. Stratford finished this past season with a surplus of just under $53,000, which is more than most theatres could claim but is still not that much money in the real world. It certainly pales in comparison to the million-dollar debt that has just led the Vancouver Playhouse to close its doors: an event that has shocked the whole tightly knit network of Canadian theatre. (See Page AL2 for more.)

McAnuff remarked that "our brilliant Chris Newton" who makes a long-overdue directorial debut at Stratford this year with Much Ado About Nothing, "grew up at the Playhouse. The main problem is the recession. A lot of institutions are in danger. There are things we probably would have done at Stratford if we'd been working together in flush times."

"A lot of care has been taken on every side with budgeting and so on," Cimolinoadded, "but then I'm sure Max [Reimer] in Vancouver has done the same. The lion's share of our revenue comes from the box office - which works well in good times, less well in bad. The whole level of support, both private and public, needs re-examining. Our donors have been amazing - but they've been inspired by the quality of our work."

Stratford's accumulated prestige - 60 years' worth - probably doesn't hurt either. Or, as Cimolino puts it, "we're standing on the shoulders of many artists before us."

Those artists would include Michael Langham and John Hirsch, the two earlier artistic directors whom McAnuff names as inspirations and who indirectly caused "the idea of this job to cross my mind way back when - in the late '70s, early '80s."

So when the job came up for McAnuff six years ago, "I didn't have a choice. I had to do it. I continue to enjoy every moment I've had at Stratford." And there is still, apparently, a "very exciting" though undisclosed project that he'll be doing there in 2013.

The biggest hit of his tenure has undoubtedly been his production of Jesus Christ Superstar, about to reopen in New York. Even if you find it ironic that a self-described Shakespeare festival should make its greatest splash with a revival of an Andrew Lloyd Webber musical, it's impossible not to feel a thrill of pride when McAnuff speaks of "28 Canadians creating beacons of light on 52nd Street."

"The company," Cimolino says, "is the great strength we have here. We perform Shakespeare like no other company in the world. I don't see the same skills in England or in New York."

I'd agree, and when you consider that every year in Toronto I see a dozen more actors who ought to be at Stratford, the only problem would seem to be that of finding roles for all the talent. Directors are another matter. Stratford in the past few years has employed some of our best younger directors, but not in Shakespeare. There are directors around who should be given the chance, at the Tom Patterson or in the Studio if not immediately on the main stage; some of them are training in the new Michael Langham workshop, which Cimolino cites as an example of "enhancement and growth" under McAnuff.

Cimolino himself has a solid record as a director of Shakespeare, stretching back to Stratford's last Twelfth Night. He also took Stratford on one of its too-rare excursions into the works of Shakespeare's contemporaries with a remarkably lucid account of Ben Jonson's Bartholomew Fair, and last year surpassed himself with an unsparing staging of The Grapes of Wrath.

His Calgary production of Lucy Prebble's Enron was, by all accounts, equally strong; which sonds like a good omen for a director who wants, he says, "to do new ambitious plays of a classic scope."

There's certainly room at Stratford for expanding the repertoire, old and new. The first thing Cimolino said when I asked him his plans for the future was that he was that he wanted to "continue and build our momentum in classics. The spoken word is at the heart of what we do."

2012-03-17-fighting-tradition-small-room:
Ihaven't been a great fan of Carole Frechettes plays; theyve seemed to me like tiny surfaces, obsessively polished. Her new one (new to Toronto, anyway; it premiered in Montreal in 2008) is small too, at least physically - its very title is The Small Room at the Top of the Stairs. Its reverberations, though, are immense: immense and unforced. It's a miniature masterpiece, and it comes to us in an astonishingly good production.

It's a contemporary variant of the Bluebeard legend, which may account for it possessing a narrative strength beyond any of Frechettes previous plays. Grace, our heroine, is a beautiful young woman who has married into the extreme 1%. Her husband Henry is an investment banker who tells her, I dont know how to create beauty, but I recognize it when I see it. He sees it in her and in the new 28-room house ("designed by the world's best architect, furnished by the world's best decorator") in which, following a whirlwind courtship, he has installed her. Henry has, of course, been married before: three times, though he doesnt care to talk about them. Also, of course, there is just one room among the 28, the attic of the plays title, that he forbids Grace to enter. And again, of course, Grace can't resist looking into it.

We find her, as the play begins, standing on the stairs outside the prohibited door, with her doubts and fears, and other people's voices, ringing in her ears. One voice is that of Henry, extravagantly protesting his love for her. Another is that of Joyce, her mother, gamely making do in her own mere five and a half rooms, overjoyed that her daughter has found wealth and happiness, especially wealth, and living for their weekly shopping trips together. And a third belongs to Anne, Graces older sister, a dedicated aid worker, who detests (her word) Graces values and her new lifestyle and the way she has always been her parents' favourite, but who loves her, in a rather patronizing way, nonetheless.

Henry, returning early from one of his many business trips, is furious - frighteningly so - to find that his wife has disobeyed his one command and entered the room. What she has found there is not to be revealed in a review, though it's fair to say that its not exactly what a reader of the original fairy tale might expect. As to what it means: There are various interpretations of that (there was vigorous debate in the lobby on the night I went) but clearly what Henry has kept locked in there represents everything he himself has had to lock out, everything he has had to banish from his mind and his existence in order to live the life he does. And everything that Grace has to decide whether to deny or admit. The play is a parable but an open-ended one.

Weyni Mengesha has given the play a hypnotic L-shaped staging, the audience on two sides at right angles to one another. (This must have been done before, but not often.) Astrid Jansons set is a shiny black floor. There is no practical staircase; the all-important steps are suggested by lights and white lines, enough to make Grace's succession of approaches and retreats into occasions of heart-stopping suspense. Thomas Ryder Payne's sound design takes a further toll on the nerves. Bonnie Beechers lighting is extraordinary; it creates a whole geography for the house to which the production meticulously adheres. It also creates a separate pinpointed world for each of the characters, whether theyre in the heroine's head, in the next room or - in Anne's case - on the other side of the world.

There is a jewelled precision to Frechettes writing here, certainly as transmitted through John Murrells translation. There's also considerable psychological complexity; the characters may be representative figures, often seen at one remove, but they spring to life in relationships that are subtly imagined and deftly drawn. The performances are very fine, collectively and individually. Nicole Underhay's amazing Grace starts as Goldilocks crossed with Cinderella. Spoiled from the cradle, even her growing compassion has a sense of entitlement about it. That doesnt make it any less moving; you feel for her and fear for her. Rick Roberts Henry is a dream suitor with a terrifying crack inside, all charm and solicitude, Champagne and roses, he can also unleash a sudden and ferocious anger that seems fundamentally directed at himself.

Sarah Dodd's Joyce gets a laugh, mainly at her own snobbery, almost every time she opens her mouth; hers must be the wittiest performance in Toronto. It's also a very human and surprisingly sympathetic one, of a mother fighting for what she perceives as her childs best interests that just happily coincide with her own. Claire Calnans Anne, by contrast, takes positions that the play intellectually endorses and emotionally doubts; with her meetings and her causes, she can seem as narrow as her mother and rather more selfish.

The people to whose desperate real-world problems she caustically compares Grace's privileged ones are represented onstage by Raquel Duffy as Jenny the maid, an immigrant of unspecified nationality who seems to have designs, if not on the master himself, then on his mansion, which she seems to be running singlehanded. She functions as a litmus test for everyone else onstage: Henry depends on her; Joyce bullies her; Anne never meets her but would probably regard her as a statistic; and Grace first condescends to her, then desperately tries to ingratiate herself with her, and condescends even more in doing so. She fits in with the play's themes, but not quite with its style; unlike the others, she seems to be standing for something rather than embodying it. The strength of the other characters, and of the whole play, is that they feel themselves to be figures in a traditional story and keep fighting it. We have the brilliant clarity of a fairy tale and the murky depths beneath it. There have been some great things in the Toronto theatre recently, but this is the best, the very best.

- The Small Room at the Top of the Stairs runs through April 8 at the Tarragon Theatre. Call 416-531-1827 or visit tarragontheatre.com for details.

2012-03-21-either-censored-cancelled-or-:
Three shocks have hit Canadian theatre recently. There was the abrupt closure of the Vancouver Playhouse, $1-million in the red; the announcement that the annual $100,000 Siminovitch Prize will be awarded for the last time; and the cancellation by Torontos Tarragon Theatre of Michael Healey's new play Proud because - according to the author - the theatre feared the play's portrayal of Canadas Prime Minister might result in a libel suit.

I would like to be able to construct a single grand narrative out of these events, but I cant. So, some individual thoughts instead.

Of the three, the Siminovitch termination is the least serious. According to Joseph Rotman, one of the award's founders, the prize was only intended to exist for 10 years; after that, the money would run out, though it does seem unfortunate this wasn't made clearer at the outset.

Its been given on a rotation system: a playwright one year, a director the next, a designer after that, and then back to square one. Its arguable that the cash could have been given to more people in smaller amounts over a longer period, but it wasn't public money and the donors were entitled to bestow it as they wished.

They obviously made a substantial difference to the lives of a certain number of practitioners: actually, to two a year. The award is given to an artist in mid-career who has to donate a quarter of it to a younger artist, a protege, of his or her choice. It's an investment in the future as well as a reward for past and present. Even so, its affected only a tiny number of people and its disappearance will make no difference to the theatre at large.

The disappearance of the Playhouse will, and not just in Vancouver. It was part of an informal network of Canadian civic theatres that feed into and off of one another. Sometimes these theatres act as co-producers; the Manitoba Theatre Centre currently houses a production of God of Carnage that was set to transfer to the Playhouse at the end of its run in Winnipeg.

Miles Potter, who directed God of Carnage and has worked across Canada as actor and director for 40 years, is surely right to refer to this network as "our unofficial national theatre." They are interdependent training-grounds for our younger actors and our best older actors return to them.

Any number of reasons have been suggested for the demise of the Playhouse: that it was profligate, that it was underfunded, that the city behaved more like a landlord than a patron. Its fundamental problem, one shared with most regional theatres, may have been a lack of identity.

Some former patrons have accused it of being too elitist in its programming, others of being too populist. Chances are both were right, depending on which week it was.

There is, by the same token, no such thing as a show that everybody would enjoy, even though people persist in talking about "the audience" as if it were a monolith. Tastes differ; and its suicidal, artistically and probably economically, to try to appeal to all of them. A theatre's job is to do work it believes in. Subsidy's job is to make that work available and affordable to the people who would enjoy it.

The Arts Council of Great Britain used to say that it didnt subsidize artists, it subsidized audiences, which is the right approach. If nobody comes under those circumstances, then its time for a regime change. A theatre is something to be used, by whoever can use it best.

Healey's Proud was given a public reading at Theatre Passe Muraille on Monday. I couldn't get in, and it would have been unethical for me to review it in any case. I did, though, read the scene that was printed in the Globe and Mail. An encounter, full of double meanings and misunderstandings, between Stephen Harper and a Tory backbencher, it seemed, out of context, to be funny on a revue sketch level.

If the rest of the play is like it, and if there were to be legal action, the Harper government would be passing up a golden opportunity to look like good sports. So far, we only have Healeys word that the fear of a libel suit is what got the play cancelled.

Richard Rose, Tarragons artistic director, has declined to comment. Maybe he thinks the play isn't good enough; Healey is one of our best playwrights, although he isn't infallible. But the play is the third of a trilogy whose previous instalments, Generous and Courageous, have been among Tarragons biggest recent successes. They would surely have wanted to complete the set, so any decline in quality must have been precipitous indeed.

As it is, it looks as if whatever theatre picks up the play is almost assured of a hit, if only from curiosity value. If there really has been political pressure at work, or just the fear of it, then thats a disgrace. There's a case to be made against subsidizing the arts at all; I don't agree with it but I recognize that it exists. But as long as there is subsidy, it has to be independent of the wishes and sensibilities of the government of the day. Otherwise, it's censorship by another name.

Besides, a sensible ruler has always recognized the value of publicly funded criticism, even if it stings, even if it comes wrapped as comedy. It's why kings had jesters.

/ Playwright Michael Healey;; Caption:
2012-03-24-swamp-dwelling-misanthrope-se:
As one of the few people in the world who never saw the movies, I am in no position to pronounce on how faithful Shrek the Musical is to its source. I have gathered that the first film was good and its two sequels weren't. To this extent, the fidelity is high. The stage show is based on that first movie, and its good, too: much better, to be frank, than Id expected.

I'm also sure, from asking around, that the show sticks close to the movie's story (ogre gets princess, after finding they have more in common than either expected) and moral (dont go persecuting people, or other creatures, just because theyre different). What the musical does have, obviously and thankfully, is a brand new score: brand new at least as of 2008, which is when the show opened on Broadway. The composer is Jeanine Tesori; and though her music here is hardly in the same class as her brilliant work in Caroline, or Change, it's a very bright and ingratiating collection of pop and theatre pastiches. David Lindsay-Abaire's lyrics, though not devoid of missteps, have a similar teasing quality; theyre especially fond of spreading a welcome rug and then pulling it out from under, as in the opening number where Shreks fond parents send their seven-year-old little ogre into a big bright beautiful world where "every dream comes true - but not for you." Lindsay-Abaire also wrote the book, which takes the same tack; it tells a fairy tale that it alternately celebrates and undermines.

Actually it tells, or at least alludes to, a lot of fairy tales, plus a few nursery rhymes; in that respect it's a more frivolous but also more earnest Into the Woods, crossed with Wicked and with just a dash of Beauty and the Beast. Obviously, it isn't as great as Into the Woods but its a lot better than Wicked; Beauty and the Beast, at least in its stage version, doesnt count. It's funny and fairly inventive and a bit touching. It's also very well staged and performed.

That last is a surprise, since this touring version has a non-Equity cast: the second in succession that Dancap has brought us. Cheapskate casting ruined In the Heights but this less challenging show stands up well. In fact, if I hadnt been told I wouldnt have known. It also helps that the sound balance is better; you can make out all the words except when the singers are screaming, as they rather too often are. In the title role, grown-up incarnation, Lukas Poost justifies all the sympathy that naturally accrues to a swamp-dwelling misanthrope with a raw Scots accent, thrown into incorrigibly cheerful allAmerican company. Liz Shivener is a bit of a treat as Princess Fiona, the spoiled romantic waiting in her tower for her rescuing prince of her dreams and getting petulantly bossy when he doesn't match her dreams; she may pre-empt the upcoming Veep by suggesting Julia Louis-Dreyfus impersonating Sarah Palin. Andre Jordan's talking Donkey is vocally and physically manic; hes also incredibly irritating but thats probably what's required. Shrek, his reluctant companion, puts it best: He's as chatty as a parrot / more annoying than a mime.

I had something of the same reaction to the villain of the piece, Lord Farquaad, who has banished all fairy-tale creatures from his kingdom because theyre not normal, which given that he himself is the son of one of the Seven Dwarfs and looks it, is a clear case of projection. (Were meant, obviously, to make the connection with right-wing homophobia.) Anyway, Merritt David Janes is fearsomely acrobatic in the role, a human puppet with a voice that's all giggle and squeak and a costume inherited from Laurence Olivier's Richard III - the shows references are nothing if not eclectic. I did grow weary of the Disneyland chorus of his victims, especially when they padded out the evening with a protest number, at once too serious and too silly, called Freak Flag. I did, though, warm to the eviction complaint of the Three Little Pigs that "zey blew our condos down." On the other hand having the Big Bad Wolf lament that they tore my cotton granny dress / and called me a hot n' tranny mess suggests that this supposed kids' show may not be quite sure of its audience, and also that it doesnt always know what a rhyme is. But on the third hand, the show has a Dragon, with a quartet of bedraggled victims who announce, irresistibly, that "she kept us around to sing back-up." Shes a flirtatious beast with fluttering eyelashes, manipulated by four visible puppeteers, which makes her, I guess, a War Dragon.

Out the Window is a documentary, every word transcribed and vouched for, written and directed by Liza Balkan, who in 2000 saw from her apartment, or thought she saw, four policemen beating up a mentally disturbed man who subsequently died. Act One is the trial, Act Two the inquest. In between is a scene, set confusingly later than both proceedings, in which Balkan lunches with a lawyer from each side and wonders whether her play will get her sued for libel; for some reason this is staged as a Last Supper with members of the audience filling in as guests. The play is better, and engrossing, when it sticks to the facts, or rather to the record, since the facts are in dispute and memory, including the author's own, is acknowledged to be erratic. Balkan tops and tails the show in her own person; in the main action she's played by Julie Tepperman, very well though she fades out of the action. The lawyers are composites, swingingly embodied by David Ferry and RH Thomson; Thomson in particular is quite amazingly natural. So, too, are the four actors who play the cops and who are liable to leave you with very mixed feelings indeed. Well worth catching, though you only have a day to do so. Another last-minute alert: Briefly on view at Theatre Passe Muraille (closing tomorrow) is The Vindication of Senyora Clito Mestres, a solo play performed by Dragana Varagic, who when she played it here some years ago, gave every indication of being a great actress.

Shrek the Musical plays through April 1 at Toronto Centre for the Arts. Call 416-644-3665 or visit tocentre.com for details. Out the Window closes tomorrow at Theatre Centre. Call 416-538-0988 or visit theatrecentre.org for details.

2012-03-27-bombay-plights:
THEATRE REVIEW

My Granny the Goldfish

Factory Theatre, Toronto

Death? Communication? exclaims the title character of My Granny the Goldfish. (She really is a granny, though she isnt any kind of fish and there seems no reason beyond authorial whimsy for saying that she is.) "These are themes! Why are we talking about themes?" It's a good question, but since it doesn't get asked until quite late in the second act, the only answer can be that the play is afraid of being thought pretentious and is attempting some last-minute damage control. It doesnt work. And, sadly, little else in the play works, either.

Anosh Iranis play is not in fact pretentious. Rather it's unpretentious to a fault, or way beyond. It's an empowerment drama sharing the stage with a sitcom. The sharing is literal. On one side of the stage theres a Vancouver hospital room occupied by Nico, a young business student from India whos also a self-confessed hypochondriac; he's found a lump and is awaiting the results of a biopsy. On the other, there are his parents in what all the characters still refer to as Bombay (the date is 2005); mom and dad are both alcoholics, and though they know their son is in hospital, they seem cheerfully unconcerned as to what might be the reason. The mother's mother, less irresponsible despite having a severe drinking problem of her own, flies to Canada and sets about teaching her grandson some life lessons.

The plays first-act climax is worth noting. Granny has been informed by Nicos doctor that the boy has cancer. She phones home, and the audience assumes she's going to tell his parents the terrible tidings. What she actually tells them is that Nico, who has confessed to a one-night fling with a Chinese nurse, is going to marry the girl. This news so appalls Nico's mother that she and her husband get on the next plane to their sons bedside. The state of his health would not, apparently, have been sufficient reason.

The psychological implausibilities here are only exceeded by the physical ones. Were asked to believe that a doctor would give a third party medical information still undisclosed to the patient himself. (The doctor seems remarkably cavalier about this violation of professional ethics. Later on in the play he does it again.) Also, though getting it on with your nurse is a common hospital fantasy, in real life it's apt to present certain difficulties, especially when the patient in pumped up with post-op morphine. The information about intra-Asian racism is interesting, but as it's presented solely as a series of gags, its hard to take it seriously as motivation.

Rosemary Dunsmores production has a few things going for it. One is the bright white hospital portion of John Thompson's set and lighting design. Another, once he gets past an introductory soliloquy that plays like failed stand-up, is the performance, at once full-bodied and restrained, of Kawa Ada as Nico. He's helped, I think, by being required to register exasperation with his parents and amused indulgence of his gran, both of them feelings well expressed in the writing and likely to be shared by the audience.

Granny herself is played by the Sri Lankan actress Yolande Bavan, whose presence intrigued me partly for nostalgic reasons. I remember her replacing Annie Ross in the legendary jazz vocal group formerly known as Lambert, Hendricks and Ross, and also for a less-publicized gig as a jazz DJ for the BBC. Her performance here suffers from an excuse of the cutes, but thats excusable given that shes playing one of those supposedly irresistible life-force characters: a woman who regards her daughter's alcoholism as pernicious but her own as endearing, and who waltzes around arranging people's destinies while showering them with philosophical advice.

Well, maybe not waltzing; she confides that "I wanted to be a tango dancer but my mother wouldnt let me," and does finally dance with her grandson in a kind of choreographic epiphany. Bavan manages to carry most of this off with grace while looking ageless; shes an aerating presence.

Back in Bombay, and later in Canada when Bombay gets there, things are a lot grimmer; the production takes crass and jerky writing and makes it crasser and jerkier. Veena Sood has apparently given up on any possibility of making the mother credible; she merely bashes through from one supposedly hilarious bit of insensible insensitivity to the next. As her husband, an unsuccessful bookie, Sanjay Talwar seems to be forlornly waiting for a chance to act believable, a chance that never arrives.

A lot of the action, in both locales, depends on unseen characters: the doctor, the nurse, Nico's hospital roommates, the inhabitants of the red-light district where he grew up and where his parents still live, and a woman who keeps showering his mother with wrong-number phone calls and eventually, of course, gets treated as a confidante. It isn't just sitcom, its old-fashioned sitcom in need of a laugh-track.

There are moments, in Nico himself and in some of his interaction with his granny, that hint at better things. But theyre swamped by everything else.

My Granny the Goldfish runs until April 15. For tickets, call 416-504-9971 or visit factorytheatre.ca.

2012-03-31-now-playing:
Tennessee Williams' Vieux Carre is one of his late plays, worked on over many years and first staged in 1977. It harks back both to the New Orleans setting of A Streetcar Named Desire and to the confessed (and confessional) autobiography of The Glass Menagerie. A young man, identified simply as the Writer, tells of his intellectual and sexual coming of age in a lastditch boarding house in the old citys French quarter at the end of the 1930s. Its an engaging play, though as the title tacitly acknowledges, stronger on atmosphere than on story.

The World Stage offering billed as The Wooster Group's Version of Tennessee Williams' Vieux Carre is the work of a New York experimental theatre company with a history almost as long and revered as Williams own. Textually, their show is far less of a deconstruction than might be expected. Most of the plays original lines are still there, and in the right order; maybe they all are, but it's hard to be sure as Elizabeth LeCompte's production seems to be going out of its way to obscure many of them. Perhaps in compensation we get some of the text twice; in the plays second half the lines appear on a screen as the actors are saying them, though you may have to cock your head quite painfully to read all of it. The idea is presumably to remind us that the Writer is in fact writing - that these people, real as they may once have been, are now his creations, speaking his words. Or alternatively that theyre speaking their own words and he's a very fast typist. It also exemplifies the belief, by now rather tired, that using video on stage is automatically new and exciting.

Screens and cameras figure prominently in the staging, which is otherwise adorned with hooks, pulleys and naked bed-frames representing beds. (Then again, this is anything but a deluxe establishment.) Visually it's striking, though like much conceptual theatre it makes its statement early and then has just to go on repeating it. The plays two important female roles are doubled, and so are two of its three important males.

The leading lady is Kate Valk, playing Mrs. Wire, the landlady, and Jane, the one woman among her guests. Mrs. Wire sleeps in the hallway the better to keep an eye on the lodgers. Shes mean, suspicious and bullying, but a softie underneath; like nearly everyone else in the play she's in thrall to a glamorized past, and she comes to look on the Writer as a surrogate son. As written, she's the idea of a memorable character rather than the thing itself; as acted shes even less, since many of her lines are muted or unintelligible and all of them are delivered in a flavourless monotone.

Valks other performance is also monotonous, but the tone's more interesting. Jane is one of Williams' faded and fated genteel ladies (a Yankee this time) tied to an insensitive stud. Verbally at least, she gives as good as she gets, though delivered with more force than resource her outbursts begin to pall. Maybe theres a style here, but bad acting done on purpose is still bad acting.

And, by the opposite token, good acting triumphs whatever the context: can indeed justify the context, as proved by this companys two main men. Scott Shepherd plays Tye, Jane's guy, and Nightingale, a tubercular self-prostituting painter (refrain: You should see my serious work) who invades the nervous Writer's room and helps him come out. I dont mean out of his room. To make sure we dont miss the point he's equipped with a stuck-on and sticking-out phallus. Maybe this, along with his faded magician's dressing-gown, is a tribute to the spirit of old comedy; anyway Shepherds performance is bold and strong and pitiful enough to get away with it.

As is his Tye, a strip-club bouncer who is insistently heterosexual (he insists, that is, that nobody can blow him for less than $100) and delivers, rivetingly, a speech on one of Williams favourite late themes, the tearing apart of a human being by a pack of dogs. Shepherd is miked, as is Ari Fliakos who plays the Writer, but to opposite effect. The electronics make Shepherd sound more immediate, Fliakos more impersonal, as befits a character whose primary function is to observe.

We are told, by him and by others, that he changes and develops, but the change is told, not shown, and Fliakos can hardly be blamed by failing to convey it. Some other characters, and much of the action, would be incomprehensible to anyone who'd never read or seen the play. The potentially haunting figures of two starving and scavenging old ladies are reduced to one actor, in drag and on video and barely visible or audible, while the less said about Nursie, Mrs. Wire's black help, the better. The Wooster Group are always worth seeing, and they obviously meant to honour Williams play, but their "version" may leave you wanting a, for want of a better word, straight production on the lines of Miles Potters Orpheus Descending. Sia, by Matthew Mackenzie, is set in Ghana, where a well-meaning Canadian is kidnapped and held to ransom by a Liberian refugee he, rather patronizingly, thought was his friend. His captor wants to prevent the testimony of a key witness at the warcrimes trial of the Butcher (i.e., presumably, Charles Taylor) of Liberia.

This seems far-fetched to begin with, and hardly less so when it's explained. It gives rise to some intense (or, less flatteringly, semi-hysterical) acting from Brendan McMurtryHowlett and Thomas Olajide as hostage and jailer. Olajide is calmer in scenes he shares with his idealistic kid sister, delightfully played by Jajube Mandiela, though it's confusingly uncertain until very late whether these scenes are flashbacks or whether the brother is leading a double life.

The play touches on the subject, always timely and currently topical (not the same thing) of child soldiers, and the resolution is momentarily powerful, but only that. And if, as seems possible, the intention is to finger the disparity between the worlds indifference to African suffering and its sympathy when its a Westerner who's in danger, then there's been a basic theatrical miscalculation.

In the situation were given, its the Canadian who's the victim. He's the one we cant help rooting for.

The Wooster Groups Version of Tennessee Williams' Vieux Carre closes tonight at the Fleck Dance Theatre, Harbourfront; Sia runs through April 15 at Factory Studio Theatre.

Franck Beloncle / Kate Valk and Scott Shepherd in the Wooster Group's Vieux Carre.;; Caption:

THEATRE REVIEWS

Ajax & Little Iliad

Enwave Theatre, Toronto

Was Spring

Tarragon Theatre, Toronto

Of the seven surviving tragedies of Sophocles, two deal with the Trojan War: Ajax, one of his earliest plays, and Philoctetes, one of his last. Both are newly pertinent today, at least according to, of all unexpected organizations, the U.S. Army. It has pressed both plays into service to help its soldiers deal with post-traumatic stress disorder. This has caught the attention of two Canadian theatre creators, Evan Webber and Frank Cox-OConnell, and their linked double bill, Ajax & Little Iliad, is the stimulating result. I saw it in Toronto, as part of World Stage last week; it's now going on to Vancouver and Banff, Alta.

We begin with the Little Iliad, the name given to a supposed lost Homeric sequel that covers the parts of the story left untold by the big Iliad, notably the bit about the Trojan horse. Leading up to this, and dramatized by Sophocles, is the tale of Philoctetes, a PTSD sufferer if ever there was one. He was a champion archer who on the approach to Troy was bitten by a serpent, leaving him with a suppurating wound that revolted all who came near him. His Grecian comrades abandoned him on the island of Lemnos.

Ten years later, with Troy still untaken, a prophecy revealed that they needed the power of his bow if ever they were to get the job done. So they sent the crafty Odysseus, who had counselled the marooning of Philoctetes in the first place, to repatriate the bow, with or without its owner. Also along is Neoptolemus, the idealistic son of the recently deceased Achilles, who, repudiating Odyssean trickery, makes an appeal to Philoctetes' better nature, or at least his patriotism. Philoctetes, understandably consumed with anger and bitterness, will have none of it, and it takes a last-minute appearance by the god Heracles (who promises him that if he goes to Troy hell be cured) to change his mind. This is a tragedy with a happy ending.

In the current version we meet Evan (Webber, naturally), a Toronto theatre person whos made Skype contact with Tom (Cox-O'Connell, obviously), an old buddy whom he hasn't seen in years and who is now in the Canadian military, about to leave for Afghanistan. Evan leads him through an impromptu re-enactment of the play, designed to question Toms willingness to go to war, as opposed to Philoctetes determination to stay out of it.

The shifting, sliding relationship between the two guys is cleverly written and delightfully played, and the technical realization is superb. We never see Tom in the flesh: just his face, a tiny image projected on to a doll (antique if not Greek) on Evan's desk. We still feel we've met him; and we get closer to both men, or to the contours of their conversation, by listening to them through headphones.

Our reactions to them - mine, anyway - are not what the authors may have intended, or indeed what I would have expected. Its the patriotic Tom who emerges as honest if confused and the pacifist Evan as manipulative: not so much of his friend as of his source. I have to confess to feeling protective of this material (for sentimental reasons: I once played Philoctetes in school), and though I concede that its up for grabs by anyone who cares to do the grabbing, I detected some fancy footwork here.

For example: When Evan, under pressure, agrees to let Odysseus state his case, it's a different case to the one Sophocles gave him. That case was based on realpolitik; this one is based on camaraderie, which actually makes it seem less honest. Odysseus, by the way, appears here under his more familiar Latin name of Ulysses, and Neoptolemus under his alternate label of Pyrrhus, which apart from rolling more easily off the tongue reminds us that this nice young man is also the merciless sacker of Troy whose acts are horrifically chronicled in the Player's speech in Hamlet. The show obviously wants us to make the connection; indeed Evan draws Toms attention to it.

Greek mythology comes with character complexity built in; its a tapestry with an unlimited number of panels, and each author - from Sophocles to these, his latest descendants - can choose which he wishes to highlight, and how.

Sophocles had a military career as well as a theatrical one, though I think our hosts may be exaggerating both his importance as a general and his incompetence. In their second half, Ajax, they appear, through a splendid piece of trompe l'oeil staging, as a couple of battleweary Athenian vets, attending the theatre to see what their commander has to say about war. We are told something, but hear virtually nothing, of the play itself, whose title character goes mad and kills first some sheep and then himself when his rival Odysseus, still duplicitous, is awarded the coveted armour of Achilles.

Contrary to what's claimed here, theres no tradition that this happened after the fall of Troy, or that Ajax himself was ever in the horse. Still, again, liberty of interpretation and all that. The shows point of view, however, is lost in the (frequently funny) cross-talk and in one piece of deconstruction too many. The real, i.e. paying or freeloading, audience are handed masks so that we can pretend to be the chorus, which also seems pointless. The principals are represented by midget puppets, moved around by the sound designer, Chris Stanton, who is also an accomplished actor and makes a surprise personal appearance. This could be a scholarly joke: Sophocles is celebrated for introducing a third actor to the Greek stage where his predecessors had never dared employ more than two. Anyway, Ajax is the only one of his plays that I had never seen in any form, so I am glad to have had this chance of collecting it, kind of.

The first 20 minutes or so of Danel MacIvor's Was Spring are wonderful. Clare Coulter appears as an elderly woman confined to some kind of institution; white-haired and imperious, radiating fear and assurance in equal proportions, she waxes nostalgic for the days when you could smoke in hospitals and expresses her profound disapproval of everybody and everything in her current existence. One thing she does not seem to be is sorry for herself.

Unfortunately her perfect monologue has to end, and she is joined by one middle-aged woman and one young one. The three are called Kitty, Kath and Kit. One clings desperately to the hope that they might be grandmother, mother and daughter, or maybe just three members of a namesake association, but as they serially reminisce about their suspiciously similar life experiences, the awful truth has to be faced: They are three aspects of the same person, and the play is the anglophone, though mercifully shorter, equivalent of Michel Tremblay's Albertine in Five Times.

A character split several ways inevitably arouses expectations; she is implicitly offered as Everywoman. KKK, though, seems to have had a rather specialized biography, chiefly consisting of an abusive boyfriend and an abusing daughter. Theres hardly enough of her to go around.

As each of her upbraids the others for what she was or will become, Coulter maintains the edge, devastatingly disapproving even when silent. Caroline Gillis gives a reading, competent but featureless; Jessica Moss, superb in her own play Modern Love, seems constrained in this one. There are some good lines, including a real heart-stopper about shy not being called painful for nothing. But mainly its another evening of people sitting around being lyrical.

Ajax & Little Iliad runs April 11-14 at the Anderson Street Space in Vancouver; Was Spring runs through May 6 at the Tarragon Extra Space.

2012-04-12-perturbed-in-the-suburbs:
THEATRE REVIEW

Clybourne Park

Berkeley Street Theatre

The first act of Clybourne Park takes place in an American suburban house of the 1950s, and it plays initially like a typical domestic comedy of that era.

There's Russ, the householder, deep in his armchair and in the National Geographic, and there's Bev, his wife, bustling around and amiably bickering with him over the location and pronunciation of foreign countries and whether people from Moscow can seriously expect to be called Muscovites. It's all reliably entertaining in the writing and, in this Canadian premiere, in the performance. Then, suddenly, Russ snaps, displaying feelings and using language unwelcome in the polite society of the time, and certainly in its polite drama. And after that explosive moment nothing in Bruce Norris's play or in this exceptional production from Studio 180 is the same again.

This is America 1959, post-Korea, pre-civil rights. Russ and Bev are about to leave. They've sold their house to a black family, the first ever to move into this prosperous Chicago neighbourhood. If that sounds theatrically familiar, it's meant to. The play, a Pulitzer Prize winner from its off-Broadway run and only now about to open on Broadway (making the Toronto production something of a scoop), takes off from a much earlier American success, Lorraine Hansberry's A Raisin in the Sun. It gives us the other side of the story, one as acidic as Hansberry's was hopeful.

It seems the reason the Raisin family was able to buy was that Russ and Bev were desperate to sell. There's been a tragedy in their family, and in their house. One of its effects has been to sour Russ on the vaunted "community" of his neighbours, whose reaction to the imminent invasion ranges from bland discomfort to active sabotage. The latter is the province of Karl, the one carry-over character from Raisin where we met him there trying to bribe the Younger family into cancelling their bid. We now see him on his home front preaching, with ever-increasing virulence, the virtues of polite apartheid (have you ever, he asks, seen a coloured person skiing?) and even trying to enlist the moral support of Russ and Bev's black maid and her prince of a husband.

As Russ, his fuzzy amiability giving way suddenly and irrevocably to wounded bottomless rage, Michael Healey gives what may well be the performance of his life. Likewise, I have never seen Maria Ricossa be as good as she is here, wedding style to substance as she shows Bev's initial flightiness maturing into an honest perplexity over why people with different complexions shouldn't live on the same street. (It's only with the best intentions that she's patronized the help, like her counterparts in Caroline, or Change, and indeed The Help.)

It's a shock to realize that Mark McGrinder's Karl is the same character that Diego Matamoros played in the Soulpepper production of Raisin; that weaselly politico is hardly recognizable in the enflamed hothead whom we encounter here. The scarier he gets, the funnier he is; and it isn't a comfortable kind of funny. His wife, played delightfully by Kimwun Perehinec, is deaf, and the play isn't afraid to get at least one huge belly laugh from that either. But it isn't a cheap laugh; it comes at a climax that's at once farcical and threatening, and it pushes the multiple tensions even higher.

They escalate further in the second act, set in the same house an exact half century later. There, it seems, went the Clybourne neighbourhood. This time it's a white couple who are moving in, with plans to tear the place down and build something grander, and a black couple, comfortably professional, who are protesting the encroaching gentrification. The two sides meet to negotiate, flanked by a pair of lawyers (cool satiric portraits, wittily filled out by Ricossa and Jeff Lillico).

We have, on the surface, come a long way, baby. There's no explicit racial or cultural divide; a man can reveal that he's gay without the heavens falling, or being expected to, and people chat as equals. They exchange vacation tips, and quiz one another about the capital of Morocco, thus reprising and amplifying the geographic patter from earlier; the act is full of echoes. Underneath, of course, things aren't so sweet.

Subversive humour becomes not just the play's medium but its subject. The meeting becomes a battle, one mainly fought from seated positions. Or rather, it's a game of "my grievance can beat your grievance" played through an escalating series of calculatedly outrageous jokes. The jokes become the structural equivalent of Chekhov's revolver: you show 'em, you'd better tell 'em. As the couples square off against one another, the rifts in both marriages open up; and the play becomes a brilliant display of cross-cutting revelations. It keeps topping itself, bitingly and hilariously.

It's also, under Joel Greenberg's direction, a brilliant feat of ensemble work: fine in the first act, superb in the second. The performances, all individually excellent, mesh perfectly, bouncing off one another with exhilarating precision. McGrinder and Perehinec play the embattled newcomers, he as overbearing an underdog as, pre-intermission, he was an over dog, she all squawk and self-preservation. Audrey Dwyer and Sterling Jarvis, who as the first act domestics were all strength and forbearance, now get to explore all the self-protectiveness the middle class is heir to, she svelte and increasingly edgy, he relaxed and good humoured until his last amazing moment.

Studio 180's nine-year track record breaks down into quasi-documentaries and the rest; this is the best of the rest, by far. It did leave me wondering how the play will fare in its reincarnation on Broadway, which prefers its serious drama preachy and soggy (Wit, Proof, Doubt, Red) or gothic and rambling (August Osage County) rather than in the form of comedy as tight and tough as this. Maybe the Pulitzer will do the trick; this is one of the few award-winning plays that actually deserves its prize. It's also, underneath its ruthless equal-opportunity satire, a haunted house play that genuinely haunts .

Clybourne Park runs until April 28 at the Berkeley Street Theatre in Toronto. For tickets, call 416-368-3110 or visit canadianstage.com.
