The program for Prisoner of Tehran carries the subtitle A True Story. That phrase sums up the play's claim to serious attention. The things it presents really happened. It also sums up whats wrong with it. Theres a bullying note about it: This is true so you'd better pay attention. It's special theatrical pleading.

The truthfulness of Marina Nemats book, on which the play is based, has in fact been challenged; I cant pronounce on that as I haven't read it, but her story as told here seems plausible enough, and I'm going to assume that its faithful to its source. Marina was a Christian girl in Iran, 16 years old when the Shah fell; at first a supporter of the revolution, she was bitterly if naively disappointed when the new system proved as cruel and repressive as the old. She was arrested, tortured, tried in absentia, condemned to death, reprieved just as the firing squad was taking aim, with her sentence commuted to life imprisonment. However, one of her interrogators fell in love with her and proposed marriage, threatening reprisals against her family if she refused. So she accepted, converting to Islam as part of the bargain. She was still confined to the notorious Evin prison (notorious under both regimes) but with privileges and with a chance of eventual liberty. Her husband raped her on their wedding night, but she liked his parents and came to have a grudging respect for him; at least, thats what the play seems to be saying. The last part, starting with the last-minute rescue, has a whiff of romance fiction about it but stranger things have happened.

The stage version has been adapted and directed by Maja Ardal, recently and justifiably acclaimed as author and performer of You Fancy Yourself, a theatrical memoir of her Scottish girlhood. Something of the same feeling, minus the wit, has crept into this play, and it doesn't feel appropriate. After her near execution, Marina was placed in a cell along with an unspecified but obviously substantial number of other women. She met some old friends there and made new ones. She even asked to be sent back there after her marriage. Female solidarity is one thing; all-girls-togetherness is another. Neither the dialogue nor the delivery make any allowance for cultural differences, or for the enormity of the stakes; we are told that terrible things are going on, but the atmosphere onstage is almost ludicrously cosy.

Earlier in her career Ardal was the artistic director of Toronto's Young Peoples Theatre, and the nannyish tone that I recall from her regime there (its disappeared under the current one) infects this production as well. Horrific things get mentioned, even get staged, but are never brought home. There is a senior prison official who, we are told, has it in for Marina; he has one scene, in which he utters B-movie villain threats, but his presence on-or offstage is never felt. The text is lightweight to the point of being giggly. Marina's present ordeals are juxtaposed with her memories of happier times, including trysts with a boy who's personally shy but politically passionate; the effect, as we jump from one time frame to the other, is to devalue both. The word "jump" is disconcertingly appropriate; especially in the earlier scenes, the actors never stop illustrating. When they arent doing strenuously helpful mime, theyre providing vocal sound effects. It's like sitting in on an evening's worth of dramaschool exercises.

A stark simplicity was probably the intention, but simplicity without strength becomes banality. It shows, inevitably, in the acting. Bahareh Yaraghi as Marina is impressive in her quieter moments, but is more often shrill than still. This kind of accusatory acting - it happens all over the place, not just here - may conceivably be the actors fault, but its more often the result of lax direction; bereft of context, the performer tries to pump in emotion. At least Yaraghi has the luxury of playing only one role. Two actors divide all the others between them. Maybe there's a way of making this look like a stylistic choice rather than an economic necessity, but the production hasn't found it; it robs the crowded cell scenes of any conviction. Razi Shawahdeh, playing the men, does a competent if unpolished job on most of them, but his various personae merge into one. The women, as played by Mirian Katrib, are uniformly bossy, even when theyre being oppressed. She does have sympathetic moments as the heroines understanding mother-inlaw (the most interesting character in the piece), and she also attracts sympathy, though for other reasons, when faced with the impossibly underwritten role of Marina's actual mother, which comes with a mad scene.

Nemat has said in interviews that her greatest trauma came after she and her parents had emigrated to Canada and she tried to make them understand what she had been through; but the play makes only the most cursory attempt to deal with that. It's writing by numbers. It's also do-gooding theatre. There's a lot of it about.

Prisoner of Tehran plays through April 28 at Theatre Passe Muraille. Visit passemuraille.on.ca or call 416-504-7529 for ticket information.

Victoria Scholes / Cell mates Razi Shawadeh and Bahareh Yaraghi star in Prisoner of Tehran.;; Caption:

Half a dozen years ago a Canadian author, Chris Turner, wrote a book called Planet Simpson, about the achievements and ramifications of the greatest of all TV cartoon shows. It was encyclopedic and enlightening, and as far as I was concerned there were only three things wrong with it.

One was that it insisted on referring to the inhabitants of Springfield as Springfieldianites. This is ridiculous; they might be Springfieldians or they might be Springflieldites, but they can't be a barbarous combination of the two. To say they are is to trespass against the show's own standards of literate perfection. Or rather what used to be its standards, since the book's second flaw is its euphemistic description of the show's steep decline (which has only got steeper since) as a "long plateau."

The author's third offence, and by far the most grievous, was to attribute to The Simpsons his own philistine ideas about musicals. He thought that by employing musicaltheatre parodies The Simpsons was exhibiting its contempt for, and superiority to, the form. The truth is of course the opposite; in the monorail number that pays tribute to Ya Got Trouble from The Music Man ("monorail - monorail - monorail!") or the sublime A Streetcar Named Marge episode could only have been created by someone with a deep affection for musicals and for the golden age of American popular song that gave birth to them. And no wonder: You have to know smart to do smart.

Further proof, at a couple of removes, came recently with the release of Music Is Better than Words, the pop vocal CD by Seth MacFarlane. MacFarlane is the Family Guy guy: that show's creator, producer, head writer and principal voice. Now, if The Simpsons was an expression of the rock and post-rock generations' contempt for the music that came before them, you would expect Family Guy to be even more so, because its anything for-a-gag construction is a betrayal of the stylistic consistency that makes - well, made - The Simpsons great. It also means that, hard though it tries and funny though it can sometimes be, Family Guy can never be as deeply subversive as The Simpsons, because it never bothers to define what it's satirizing. But then maybe its heart was never in satire anyway, at least if MacFarlane's heart can be found in his singing. He's come out as a vocalist in the Frank Sinatra tradition, and a superb one.

It's hard to think of sentiments less Family Guyish than "you couldn't buy a ticket to hear the first robin sing" from this disc's opening number, It's Anybody's Spring, delivered here with the kind of Bing Crosby insouciance that puts wit into whimsy. MacFarlane doesn't have the edge or the depth of Sinatra, and his phrasing can sometimes be stiff. In fact he sounds more like one of Sinatra's more populist disciples from the next generation, most of all probably like Steve Lawrence. He has great control, and intonation of enviable perfection.

The disc is a tribute not only to the songs and singers of the era but, very explicitly, to the arrangers who contributed so much to the great jazzpop vocal records of the 1950s. Unlike most singers who specialize in this material, MacFarlane can afford to hire a big orchestra of crack musicians, and part of the joy of this record is his joy in singing with them, the way in which he rides and crests the waves that they create.

He also - something else that distinguishes him from the rockers who've recently been jumping onto the big band wagon - has an adventurous choice of repertoire. He doesn't just recycle They Can't Take That Away from Me and The Way You Look Tonight. There are four songs here at most that would be generally recognized as standards, and only two associated with Sinatra himself: Johnny Mercer's Laura and Rodgers and Hart's It's Easy to Remember. The latter is the album's high point; Joel McNeely's orchestration recalls Gordon Jenkins in its symphonic sonority and Nelson Riddle in the cunning of its architecture, while MacFarlane brings off a breathtaking bravura ending that's both technically and textually superb.

MacFarlane does twice well by Rodgers, making Something Good (one of the songs added to The Sound of Music in its film version) both more tender and more thoughtful than I would have believed possible; the musing strings match his vocal. Talking of movies, the title song comes from It's Always Fair Weather, one of the best but most neglected of screen musicals. Gigi is hardly a forgotten film, but though I suppose I must have heard The Night They Invented Champagne sung out of context before, I certainly can't remember where or when.

A charmer of a song called Nine O'Clock I had to look up; it's from a 1950s stage musical, Take Me Along (based on Eugene O'Neill's Ah Wilderness); MacFarlane must have one hell of a record collection. There are a few flaws: Norah Jones, duetting on Two Sleepy People, sounds as if she's on a different record, and MacFarlane himself misses the humour of the lyric. But he compensates on The Sadder But Wiser Girl, another of those gloriously intricate patter songs from The Music Man, which he sings with exhilarating precision and acts with equally exhilarating abandon.

It makes an interesting contrast with, and complement to, the other major album in this vein to appear recently, Paul McCartney's Kisses on the Bottom. Both men recorded in Hollywood, in the Capitol studios where, we're told, MacFarlane sang into Sinatra's mic, while McCartney used Nat King Cole's. The contrast is apposite; there are some orchestral tracks on the McCartney record but the overall feel is of an informal small-combo date, the tradition that Cole himself came out of.

McCartney also doesn't aim for anything like MacFarlane's virtuosity; he has a modest, husky sound; though far more expressive and certainly more pleasing than the strangled croon with which Rod Stewart navigates these waters.

McCartney's choice of repertoire, like his performance, is cozier than MacFarlane's, but it generally avoids the obvious. I was delighted by the inclusion of More I Cannot Wish You, from Guys and Dolls. More familiar, but still largely ignored by the general run of retro singers, are Bye Bye Blackbird, complete with verse, and a couple of songs, including the sort-of title number, made famous by Fats Waller.

I'll bet that McCartney, like me, used to hear them every morning on the BBC's Housewives' Choice. It's ironic, of course, that the writers generally credited with supplanting the preceding tradition should turn out to be respectful of it and even part of it, but it makes sense; these were the songs they had to have grown up listening to and that they could hardly help absorbing.

The Simpsons' Matt Groening, born a decade later, seems to have avoided the musical bigotry of his own generation. For MacFarlane, 20 years younger still, it probably isn't even an issue. He simply heard music recorded before he was born, and fell in love with it. The love, however unexpected, shows.

Music Is Better than Words by Seth MacFarlane and a new deluxe edition of Paul McCartney's Kisses on the Bottom are both available from Universal Music.

There's an extraordinary scene in the second act of Oil and Water - extraordinary in a good way. A woman is washing down the body of a man who seems at the moment more dead than alive. The date is 1942; the place is the coast of Newfoundland, in the wake of a ferocious storm. The woman is Violet Pike, the unlettered wife of a miner. The man is Lanier Phillips, a sailor in the U.S. Navy, whose ship has just been wrecked. Violet and her neighbours have already cleaned off the oil-soaked bodies of Laniers fellow survivors, but his remains obstinately discoloured, or so they think. His first sign of life comes when he opens his eyes and his mouth, and gently informs them that it wont come off: he's black. He is the first black man they have ever seen. They are the first white people, either in the service or in his hometown of Atlanta, to treat him like a human being.

It's a true story. More importantly, it feels true - in this scene, anyway. Some of its impact comes from the patience, the determination, the quietness, with which Violet - a superbly gnarled and business-like performance by Petrina Bromley - carries out her task. The theatrical impact of careful, honest, determined work (as championed in the theories, if not the practice, of Bertolt Brecht), has seldom been more powerfully demonstrated. The quietness has a lot do with it; up till now, Jillian Keileys production has been very noisy, and not always helpfully so, and this scene gains immeasurably from the contrast. The unfussy intensity of Keileys staging and Bromley's performance casts a spell on the audience and also, it seems, on everyone else onstage - on her helpers, on the recipient of her ministrations, and even on those who aren't strictly part of the scene but are there as onlookers. At the back are two of Laniers fellow sailors, one drowned, one saved; to the side is his future self, telling the story to his young daughter.

Subsequent scenes are almost equally affecting, and for similar reasons. We see Lanier in contact with Violet, her husband, her nephew and a friend; theres a shy ease about the encounter, along with some spiky intimations of domestic conflict, that gain enormously from the feeling that nobody is trying to batter us into anything. The late sections of this show restore confidence in Keiley's high reputation, and in that of her St. John's company, Artistic Fraud, which presents it. They also raise high hopes for her new appointment as director of the English-language company at the National Arts Centre.

And not before time, because the first act of Robert Chafes play, at least as presented here, is a mess - a sincereandwell-intentionedmess,but thats not much consolation. Even presenting it in two acts seems unnecessary, since the total running time is only 90 minutes, and the intermission arrives so abruptly that what must have been meant as a cliff-hanger registers only as a question mark.

The structure is not so much complex as complicated. We have Lanier's life on board crosscut with the miners' and their families lives on land and underneath it: two kinds of exploitation plus the pouring of oil into already troubled waters. I could buy those as ideas, but they arent fleshed out and we don't get close to the people who are supposed to be embodying them. Part of the reason for that is that it's hard to hear them. The Newfie accents, or my provincial lack of exposure to them, may be partly to blame, but whats really troublesome is the music that the actors have to act against. The production claims to have found much common ground between Newfoundland folk tunes and American spirituals, and it may well be right because Andrew Lambs score, drawing on both, comes to feel like a constant homogenous wash, drowning everybody out long before we get to the actual drowning. The music isn't in itself bad, and it's very well sung. Indeed, when the healing process is capped by an a capella rendition of Balm in Gilead, its very stirring indeed, partly because it comes at the end of a long stretch of fine and unmediated dialogue.

There are still further layers. Young Lanier is haunted by the warning voice of his great-grandmother, an exslave, warning him against the dangers of land and of white people in general. The historical Lanier, transformed by his wartime experience, became a civil rights pioneer, and marched with Martin Luther King. When we meet him with his daughter, shes being bussed into a newly integrated school and is meeting the kind of racist violence we associate with, say, Little Rock in 1957. Only this is Boston in 1974, which is a shock. The connection is made, though, in the program rather than in the play. Indeed, it's only late in the action that it's made clear that the man at the side of the stage is recalling the events that are happening in the middle of it. So maybe its meant as a surprise. But I think youre better off knowing it. Otherwise, it's just confusing. Even with the knowledge, the introduction of the older Lanier does nothing to make the story more moving. It merely turns him into a plaster saint.

None of the other acting is on the level of Bromley's Violet, but Neema Bickersteths singing is powerful, Jeremiah Sparks patriarchal Lanier is dignified, and Ryan Allen as his younger self is very touching, especially after his rescue. Violet's menfolk (Jody Richardson and Mark Power) likewise come into their own when they're given characters to act and the space to act them in. On a set by Shawn Kerwin mainly composed of ladders, Keiley does surprisingly little to summon up the ship in its initial state, but the wreck itself is skilfully evoked. Probably you have to have the storm before you can appreciate the calm, but the balance here is out of whack.

Oil and Water runs through May 6 at the Factory Theatre. For ticket information, call 416-504-9971 or visit factorytheatre.ca.

THEATRE REVIEW

The Game of Love and Chance

Bluma Appel Theatre, Toronto

Pierre Marivaux's The Game of Love and Chance (1730) is situation comedy raised to its highest power. The situation is classic: A young woman, Silvia, whose father wants her to marry a young man whom she has never met, stipulates that she be allowed to check him out from a safe distance by changing places with her maid. The twist here is that her suitor, Dorante, has had the equivalent idea and comes a-calling disguised as his own valet. Think She Stoops to Conquer and then double it. Think, too, that Marivaux got there first, by 40 years.

Needless to say, the disguised young master and mistress fall for one another, as do the two disguised servants. Each member of the quartet believes that he or she has snagged a partner from the other side of the class barrier, and reacts with the appropriate amount of delight or dismay. The audience has to keep reminding itself which character is which and how much each knows about the person with whom he or she is interacting. It's a demanding and stimulating exercise in what the textbooks call "discrepancy of awareness" and it gives the play much of its kick. That kick is intensified when one of the lovers reveals his or her real identity to his or her partner (pardon my pronouns but it should be a surprise) and the favour is not reciprocated. The awareness becomes even more discrepant. Add in that Silvia's father (we never meet Dorante's) knows what's going on, as does her brother, and that both are having too much fun with the situation to allow anyone to call a halt.

Silvia's maid is named Lisette; Dorante's valet seems to have two names. He's referred to in the dialogue as Bourguignon, but in the program as Arlequino. That is, he's descended from the Harlequin figure of the Commedia dell'Arte, a phrase calculated to strike terror into the heart of anybody who has seen its effect on modern directors.

In Matthew Jocelyn's Canadian Stage production it signifies an hysterical, hyperkinetic style in which, especially among the lower orders, voices are high-pitched and bodies are twisted into pretzels. Jocelyn took a similar acrobatic approach in his production of Fernando Krapp and it worked there because the antics were kept under control and were keyed to what the people performing them might actually have been feeling. Krapp, paradoxically, was a modern play with no apparent Commedia connections. Marivaux does pay explicit homage to the old tradition, though I suspect that in his case it was more a matter of lip service and that he would have ditched the whole idea if it hadn't been in his contract. This production only works when it does the same: when, that is, it allows its characters to behave like human beings.

For some unaccountably snobbish reason, only the bosses are permitted this privilege. The servants act like wind-up dolls, mechanical in every sense, bombarding us with external and relentlessly unfunny effects. (For an instructive contrast, see the hilarious automaton scene in the Canadian Opera Company's excellent production of The Tales of Hoffman.) Apart from not being very entertaining in itself, this undercuts what's most interesting about the play.

The Game of Love and Chance, like Beaumarchais' The Marriage of Figaro before they turned it into a musical, is one of those pre-revolutionary French comedies that suggested servants might have emotional lives as interesting as those of their masters. The original audience, missing the point, laughed all the way to the guillotine, but we don't have to join them. We know that, by all social and theatrical rules, the play will end with the young people pairing off according to rank. When the valet dreams of marrying the heiress, it's funny, but it's also ironic and even poignant; or it could be, if he were allowed to be a real person. Marivaux's ending is more realistic than any wish-fulfilling democratic finale might be, but for that very reason it should carry a charge.

The production hoists its double standard in the very first scene: Mistress and maid conduct an expository conversation in a long corridor with a door at each end, to the accompaniment of much slamming and screaming. But while Trish Lindstrom as Silvia goes through these motions with a wit, an intelligence, and a command of shifting tones that gets even keener as the evening proceeds - this is her best performance to date - Gemma James-Smith's Lisette looks and sounds as if she were in a Carry On movie, all twitter and flutter and underlining of innuendo. This may be a blow for equality; usually in the classics, male comics have the monopoly on being lewd and crude.

When we get to see the full stage, it's a room full of mirrors: a thematically apposite design by Anick La Bissonniere. Linda Brunelle's costumes are modern, which doesn't really suit the social and sexual context, but they're stylish and unobtrusive enough for it not to matter. Nicolas Billon's translation is also modernish, as far as it's anything.

Harry Judge's Dorante oscillates between the production's two poles; mostly, sharing his scenes with Lindstrom, he's at the positive end, and he does hint at more complexity of feeling than anyone else. Arlequino is theoretically the star role; certainly Gil Garratt plays it that way: I suppose he deserves marks for intrepidity, but he's exhausting to watch and tormenting to hear.

As the lightly heavy father William Webster, with experience on his side, keeps his head while most around him are frenziedly clutching theirs; that especially goes for his son whom Zach Fraser, presumably obeying orders, plays as a smirking candymunching booby. He seems an unnecessary character, which may well be Marivaux's fault. Nothing else here is; this is a great rare play and a missed opportunity.

The Game of Love and Chance runs until May 12. For tickets, call 416-368-3110 or visit canadianstage.com.

Sometimes there can be truth in advertising. The Exquisite Hour does run for an hour, or something just over, and it is exquisite, or something just under. "Exquisite" is pitching it a bit high, but it's certainly charming. Its also cunning.

Its the work of Stewart Lemoine, a successful and prolific playwright from Edmonton whose work is hardly known here. The production is by an ad hoc collective of predominantly expat Edmontonians calling themselves the Theatre Department. The director is Ron Pederson, best known (to me, anyway) as one of the guiding lights of the group of improvizational parodists who call themselves the National Theatre of the World. The actors are the up-and-coming Daniela Vlaskalic and the very-much-arrived Ted Dysktra.

We begin with Dykstra in his backyard, getting busy with a watering can. He plays Zachary Teale, who is in his late thirties and has a managerial position in a department store. Into his flower-rimmed garden comes Vlaskalic in a flower-rimmed hat. Wearing it she looks middle-aged but she sheds about half her seeming years when she takes it off. She announces herself as a Mrs. Darimont; maybe I should have mentioned that the play is set in 1962, before the '60s became the Sixties.

Mrs. Darimont is here to change what Mr. Teale admits to be his fairly sheltered life. She wants to open him up to the world of knowledge; in other words, as Zachary shrewdly and rapidly realizes, she's in the encyclopedia business. She has, naturally, brought along a specimen volume, one simply - and, if my memory serves, atypically - labelled with a single letter, in this case H. Mrs. D suggests, more or less, that dropping salient facts on alphabetically allied subjects might improve Zacharys chances with women, which have hitherto been non-existent. All she asks is an hour of his time.

Zach tells, rather touchingly and very amusingly, of his married sisters repeated failed attempts to fix him up with eligible young women over dinner, primarily due to her own habit of hogging all the talk at the table. It may seem implausible that he should open up so quickly to a total stranger on so delicate a subject but the conversation is being lubricated with lemonade, which Zach likes to lace with bourbon. It's a Teale family tradition, apparently. There's free lemonade available in the Factory Studio lobby; Id say it was to get us into the spirit of the thing except that the spirits come extra.

Up to this point the piece is, at best, superior dinner theatre. Its also a role-reversed version of the Lanford Wilson two-hander Talley's Folly in which a man sets himself to win the affections of a woman in a bucolic setting and in a stated period of real time.

I don't think Im giving anything away in saying that its plain early on what Mrs. Darimont's game is and it isn't just selling encyclopedias; I found myself counting the minutes before Zach would nerve himself to enquire as to the whereabouts and precise earthly status of Mr. Darimont. What kicks the play into a higher gear is when the two of them start play-acting. They act out situations into which encyclopedic knowledge of the letter H could actually be introduced. This may not be terribly likely but, as written and acted here, its delightful. Its also, I suspect, catnip to Pedersen as director; he errs in underlining the fantasy with lighting changes and music cues but in all other respects his touch, and that of his actors, is featherlight.

Vlaskalic takes time to reach that state. She seems at first to be offering a caricature of a busybody, wellmeaning but overbearing. Once the games begin, though, she's transformed as well as transforming. A trial conversation about St. Hubert (dedicated hunter, converted to an ascetic life after encountering a miraculous stag with a blazing forehead) somehow becomes a re-enactment of the legendary meeting in which she is so enchantingly demure and flirtatious that one shares the disappointment of both parties when reminded that she's meant to be the antlered kind of venison rather than a deer, a female deer. She tops even this as a dental patient whose waiting-room agonies Zach attempts to soothe with fascinating facts about the Hohenstaufens (ruling family of medieval Swabia, distinguished by the frequency with which its members were named Frederick or Agnes).

Dykstra is superb from beginning to end, a lovely portrait of shy wonderment in which perfect comic timing is a vehicle for truth. Both he and the play rise to surprising heights when he contemplates the 60 minutes he has just enjoyed, so fleeting and so precious. It makes him want to return to the book to look up the word Hour. He might also, if he dared, look up Happiness.

The setting, spare but pretty, is by Marzena Cegys. Meghan Hubley is aid de camp, which I mention because its the only other credit in the program and its one I've never seen before. I'm sure shes very good at it.

Talking of things fleeting and precious but possibly renewable: The show is only here for a short time (till tomorrow, in fact) and it deserves to resurface. The word that rises to ones mind at the end of it is "sweet"; the sound that rises to the audience's lips - I actually heard it - is what a songwriter once called a soft satisfied sigh.

The Exquisite Hour closes April 29 at the Factory Studio. Call 416-504-9971 or visit factorytheatre.ca for ticket information.

Max B. Telzerow / Daniela Vlaskalic and Ted Dykstra leave audiences wistful.;; Caption:

THEATRE REVIEW

You Can't Take It with You Young Centre, Toronto

As dysfunctional families go, the one in You Can't Take It with You is remarkably functional. They may have their disagreements with the outside world, but among themselves the Vanderhof-Sycamore clan - Mr. Vanderhof 's daughter married a Mr. Sycamore, and the generations and their many associates all live together in a cozy New York house within whistling distance of Columbia University - never exchange a cross word. This probably makes them unique among theatrical families. It would certainly make them unusual among real ones.

That isn't a problem while you're actually watching the play, certainly not in as good a production as Soulpepper's, which finds the company at its warm-hearted, quickwitted best. In 1936, Moss Hart and George S. Kaufman, the joint gold standard-bearers of interwar Broadway, wrote what may be the prototypical screwball comedy, a handsomely structured celebration of principled fecklessness.

Grandpa Vanderhof retired from (unspecified) business years ago, having apparently made enough of a pile to subsist ever after in nonconforming comfort; he occupies himself in attending college commencement ceremonies and comparing their merits. His daughter Penny writes un-performable plays because a typewriter was once delivered to the house by mistake. (I've seen plays that could have been written for worse reasons.) Her husband Paul spends most of his time in the basement, making fireworks with the help of Mr. de Pinna, who once came to make a delivery and never left. Their elder daughter Essie makes candies, and takes ballet lessons from a wannabe Diaghilev who genially confides that, as a dancer, "she stinks." And so it goes.

The first external threat comes from the IRS, who have discovered that grandpa owes them big-time and are unimpressed by his objections to how they might spend his money. A second, more serious threat arises when younger granddaughter Alice falls for the son of her prosperously proper boss, and he for her. Not that anybody in either family objects to young love - the Sycamores, as you might expect, go positively gaga over it - but Alice fears that her prospective in-laws, Mr. and Mrs. Kirby, may object to her family's eccentricities; and her fears, when the two sides have an unscheduled collision, prove justified.

The play is directed by Joseph Ziegler, and it fits beautifully with his unrivalled instinct both as director (Harvey) and actor (The Time of Your Life, A Christmas Carol) for shrewd, joyous benevolence. For the presiding Vanderhof he has Eric Peterson, who commands the scene even before uttering a word, standing on a step, his eyes darting around like those of the pet snakes he keeps in an onstage tank. (Yes, it's that kind of play.) All the same, Ziegler's greatest triumph is to structure the story around Alice, the one character with an emotional stake both in the house and outside it. Krystin Pellerin, who seems more and more to have greatness in her, is instantly, unpretentiously radiant; we not only see but feel the play through her eyes. She's every youngster, both loving her family and embarrassed by them, only more so. The courtship scene she shares with Gregory Prest is a delight, gauche and detailed and surprisingly deep; you're happy for both of them.

Nancy Palk, capping a rather extraordinary run of performances, turns up again as a very good Penny from whom kindness and eccentricity flow unforced. Derek Boyes is admirably gentle as her husband, as is Mike Ross as Essie's husband, who likes to print things and who plays the xylophone, which is about the only thing I've never seen Ross play before.

Essie herself is Patricia Fagan, delightfully and continually en pointe; Diego Matamoros plays her self-appointed inspiration with a rich Russian voice and even richer Russian hair; and Maria Vacratsis is low-key but hilarious as his emigre compatriot, a blintz-dispensing former grand duchess whom the authors craftily introduce to pep up the play in its closing stages.

The play's politics, as far as they can be pinned down, are an odd mixture of liberal and libertarian; there's a depression on, and a war looming, but they're hardly mentioned, though at some level the play knows about them. It's a knowledge that was to be brought to the surface a few years later in the aforementioned The Time of Your Life, whose portrayal of the wealthy drop-out is more apparently fantastical but also more painful.

It's wryly appropriate, too, that for a few days You Can't Take It with You should have co-existed in Toronto with Clybourne Park, which effectively dynamites the whole American family-comedy genre, especially those descendants of Kaufman and Hart who have gone heavy on their progenitors' whimsy and much lighter on the wit. But the original stands up irresistibly. A final word of commendation for Christina Poddubiuk's set and especially for her costumes which, for the women in particular, are beautiful or funny or, quite frequently, both.

You Can't Take It with You runs in repertory until June 20. For tickets, call 416-866-8666 or visit soulpepper.ca.

2012-05-05-depth-of-a-salesman-michel-tr:
I like The Real World? better than any other Michel Tremblay play I have seen. (There are quite a few I haven't.) It dates back to 1988, and it concerns a playwright who has written a play about his own family. That is something Tremblay himself had already done and would do again, so we are in effect watching the autobiography of an autobiographer. It gets quite dizzying.

The Tremblay surrogate is a young Montrealer named Claude. His father Alexis suggests Willy Loman mixed with Homer Simpson, with the more lovable parts of both surgically removed; he's a philandering travelling salesman who prides himself on his philistinism, his conviviality and his talent for telling off-colour jokes. (Oddly, we never get to hear any of them.) Alexis' wife Madeleine might be described as long-suffering, and it's Claude's view that she's suffered altogether too long; one of his reasons for writing his play was to give her the voice, and maybe the actions, he thinks she should have found for herself. The family is completed by Claude's sister Mariette, who's a go-go dancer and who still lives at home.

Claude has moved out; disregarding paternal pressure to go selling and travelling himself, he works at a grunt job by day and writes by night. Having finished his play, he's given it to his mother to read, and is appalled to find that she's appalled. At first it seems to him - or maybe just to us - that it's just good old-fashioned fear of what the neighbours might think. She objects both to what Claude has reported and what he's invented; she's especially furious that he's credited her with a taste for Mendelssohn rather than the middle-of-the-road pop to which she actually listens. But it goes deeper. There's nothing Claude can tell her about her husband that she doesn't already know. And she has no intention of behaving the way Claude thinks she should.

While Madeleine tells her son just what she thinks of his play, we get to see the scene in question for ourselves: a device that Tremblay continues to use, with increasing audacity and success. Everything is in double focus; weighing one perspective against another proves a witty, stimulating and occasionally scarifying exercise. The fictional Madeleine delivers a tirade on why she is about to leave. The real Madeleine makes an even more effective speech, explaining just why she intends to stay where she is. It's an excoriating outburst - perhaps the only thing in the evening that is actually moving - and, in this Tarragon revival, it's excoriatingly well delivered by Jane Spidell.

Her rage is streaked with embarrassment, and also enriched by it; she keeps confessing that of course she's never read a play before. You can see why Tremblay, years later, felt he had to atone by according her a theatrical apotheosis in For the Pleasure of Seeing Her Again, one of whose premises is that his mother had never seen any of his shows.

As the current play progresses, the focus shifts from the mother and towards the father, to whom Claude remains resolutely unforgiving. We're told just why or partly why, in a late revelation about which reviewers have been asked to remain silent. It is, in fact, fairly predictable, but not too easy to credit, though Tremblay, by piling on the emotional pressure, does wear us down. This revival, directed by Richard Rose, is uneven; though not, as you might expect, because of the play's two levels. There's good or bad on both. Spidell's "real" Madeleine is complemented, but not equalled, by Meg Tilly, whose performance as her alter ego is that the kind that critics like to call brave, meaning that, physically and vocally, it's way over the top, full of strange cadences and odd angles. Meanwhile, Tony Nappo's real Alex is little more than a shouting shell, while Cliff Saunders as his opposite number at least suggests a man with his own case to make. It's a shame that he isn't actually given one; the fictitious devil is, in fact, given better tunes than the actual one but they aren't allowed to sway us. Claude thinks that his papa is a resentful oaf, weeping crocodile tears, and Tremblay does nothing to contradict him; we're primed to expect something more complex but it never arrives.

Sophie Goulet and Cara Gee are decorative as the two Mariettes, which is about all that's asked of them; fact or fiction (and in this case there's very little difference), she's more a device than a character. There's only one Claude; as his mother acidly remarks, he's kept himself out of his own play. His defence is he thought that would be fairer; he might have added that the author is traditionally his own least compelling character. Still, on the ground floor that he does get to inhabit, Matthew Edison - who, just to make things even more meta, is a playwright himself - avoids that fate. He has us wondering, as he should, just how any playwright or novelist expects to face his family after using them as identifiable material: No wonder that O'Neill forbade any performance of Long Day's Journey into Night until after all concerned were dead, including himself. He looks down his nose at those around him with a fascinating air of pain and disdain, whose vocal equivalent is his response to his father's taunting reference to beatniks: "They went out a lo-o-ng time ago." Rose's production rises to a character's thrilling display of angry violence; then spoils it by having the set join in the self-destructiveness; finally redeems itself by having Edison's Claude take a silent look at his real-time dad, as if he too were a character in a play: conceivably, the play we've just seen.

Talking of levels: Upstairs in the same theatre, The Innocents, by the promising Daniel Karasik, is probably not autobiographical, but it is an attempt to put representative figures of his own twenty-something generation on stage. The trouble is that they're more representative in a general sense, and less in a specific, than the play cracks them up to be; circumstances, like economics and access to drugs, may change but every age has had equivalent problems. Also, despite some sparky dialogue, the symmetry between two young men of similar Candian-Jewish upbringing - one a hot-shot lawyer with no personal life, the other a drop-out with nothing but - seems forced, as does their exchanging of girlfriends and, eventually, identities. Of the four young performers, Amelia Sargisson comes closest to finding a personality behind her lines, with the author himself the runner-up as the lawyer who ends up shedding, very literally, the trappings of worldly success.

The Real World? runs through June 3 at the Tarragon Theatre; The Innocents runs through May 13 at the Tarragon Near Studio. For more information, call 416-536-5018 or visit tarragontheatre.com.

THEATRE REVIEW

Bring It On: The Musical Ed Mirvish Theatre, Toronto

One thing I learned from Bring It On: The Musical is that in U.S. high schools, cheerleading has become an end in itself. Maybe I should have known that already; all the same, it was a shock to find that the batontwirling and formation-forming has no connection to the sport that it's meant to support. I suppose that sport is football, but for all anyone actually says it could be tiddlywinks. Whatever it is, it could hardly be more fiercely adversarial than the cheerleading itself, whose teams compete against one another at regional and national levels. Ask not for whom the leaders cheer, they cheer for themselves. And they want you to join in.

Competitive cheerleading is not the deepest of dramatic subjects, and Bring It On - based, loosely, on a series of movies - is not the deepest of shows. It is, to be frank, shallow, but it turns out to be an enjoyable kind of shallow. The writers have pedigree. The book is by Jeff Whitty (Avenue Q), the music is split between Tom Kitt (Next to Normal) and Lin-Manuel Miranda (In the Heights), while the lyrics are part Miranda and part Amanda: Amanda Green, that is, who has no famous shows in her resume but is the daughter of Adolph Green who, with his collaborator Betty Comden, personified all that is best in the more urbane traditions of Broadway and Hollywood.

The show concerns two schools in the same area. Truman High is suburban in feel and uniformly pale in complexion. Jackson High is innercity and predominantly black. Truman seems to be defined by its cheerleaders' squad. Jackson doesn't know from squads; it has a crew. Hence, conceivably, the divided score, with Miranda on previous evidence handling the hip hop and Green and Kitt the rest. However it worked out, the music is lively if not classic and the lyrics are smart. I especially liked the peace offering of Danielle (crew) to Campbell (squad), which goes something like: "At first I thought you were a white, stuck-up bitch; now I just think you're white."

Campbell, who has dreamed all her life of captaining a winning squad, has achieved that eminence at Truman: the captaining part anyway. Just as she's about to approach the winning stage she's transferred, courtesy of a sudden rezoning decision, to Jackson, along with a misfit contemporary named Bridget, who had never got closer to the squad than being team mascot in a fat suit.

Campbell, impressed by the crew's moves, urges them to apply their talents by forming a squad and, after some misadventures, succeeds, as do they. Campbell is partly influenced by the suspicion that her transfer from Truman had been engineered by Eva, who has become captain despite having been only third in line when Campbell herself departed.

We are left in doubt for some time as to whether Campbell's theories are justified or whether she's just a spoiled kid with paranoia. The second possibility would be more interesting and plausible but - well, I mustn't give it away. I will say that the device by which the truth about Eva is revealed is beyond incredible, but it does give rise to an entertainingly hysterical song in which she tells how she managed to lower one rival's grades while infecting the other with mono - oh dear, I think I have given it away.

The show communicates several messages. One is that it's all right to be manipulative, as long as you're the heroine. Another is that if you're entering a high-level cheerleading contest, it helps to have spectacular gymnastic and choreographic routines that look as if they've been staged by a first-rate Broadway professional, which both schools of course have.

Andy Blankenbuehler, the choreographer responsible, is also the director, and he has done a sharp job on a mobile set mostly composed of lighting gantries. There are lively and likeable performances from Taylor Louderman (Campbell), Adrienne Warren (Danielle), Elle McLemore (Eva) and Ryann Redmond (Bridget).

Campbell also gets a romantic subplot that may be the most perfunctory on record. Her gradual acceptance of, and by, her new surroundings is, however, very well handled, and are eventually quite stirring; I'm not a great one for inspirational musicals but in this show the racial and social tensions and harmonies feel organic rather than - as, in say, Hairspray - sanctimoniously imposed.

The show also has an attractive vein of self-mockery that stops way short of being selfdestructive. It's also the first show to open at what used to be the Canon since it was renamed the Ed Mirvish: an honour well deserved, though I wish they'd gone the whole route and called it Honest Ed's Theatre.

Bring It On runs until June 3. For tickets visit mirvish.com.

In High, Kathleen Turner commands the stage with square shoulders and a hoarse but powerful voice suggestive of a heavy cold. She also has canny, forthright comic timing, which though the play is far from being a comedy, comes in very handy, given that her role is that of a nun who swears a lot. Her prime antagonist, a 19-year-old gay drug addict who would seem to have seen and heard it all, doesn't like her doing this. He says it creeps him out. I agree, though probably for different reasons.

I thought the language an easy shock effect, though I admit that its laugh value declines steeply as it gets repeated, and that it does have traceable roots in the characters early life. Turner plays Sister Jamison Connelly, who works in a Catholic rehab institution where shes acknowledged to have an exceptional record of turning difficult patients around. She meets her greatest challenge yet in young Cody who has been on just about every known drug; who has been found with the dead body of his 14-year-old boyfriend; and whose dead mother was both a user and a prostitute. The sister is reluctant to take the case, but is pressured into it by her priestly superior, who has a special interest in the boy. And not the one you might pruriently have suspected.

The play's author, Matthew Lombardo, is Catholic and gay and a recovering addict, though judging from his autobiographical program note, he comes from a background more settled than Cody's and has had, fingers crossed, a more fortunate trajectory. In fact, he has probably put more of himself into the character of the nun, who is a former street person - hence the salty vocabulary - and, though she isnt very explicit about it, has had first-hand experience of dope, drinks and sex. She was saved by faith, but is all too aware of the possibility of relapse, spiritual and physical. She has a particularly hideous secret in her past, which she helpfully reveals to us in the second act, when the story needs some pepping up. She is the only one of the plays characters who's allowed to have monologues, which seems unfair, especially as they aren't as revealing as theyre obviously intended to be.

The play does hit nerves on the subject of addiction, but its less persuasive when offering religion as an antidote. I don't deny the possibility; I just don't think its been effectively dramatized. To his credit, the author avoids a facile redemptive ending, at least on the level of plot. He does, though, go for another kind of easy out: Like Doubt, that other pseudo-serious play about a nun, this ends with the central character repeating the title word - here signifying both a trip and the empyrean - as if, all by itself, it meant something.

Turner, who comes out swinging and goes right on that way, gives a compelling if unvaried performance, and she has two good supports. Evan Jonigkeits Cody goes through the required motions - bedraggled, defiant, despondent, despairing - without transcending a stereotype that goes back at least as far as Equus. Father Michael's personal conflicts are potentially the most interesting in the play, but during most of it he's just a plot device. Tim Altmeyers best moments come at the end, when he gets to appear with his cassock off; the character comes out from under wraps and so does the actor. Though he has a neat line at the start, when Sister Connelly asks why hes guilt-tripping her and he replies, "I'm a Catholic priest."

High is the kind of quasi controversial play that can make it to Broadway (at least if there's a star involved). Gruesome Playground Injuries belongs in the growing list of imaginative, sometimes remarkable, American pieces that, commercially at least, stay in the margins. Like High, its about addiction, though not of the chemical kind. Also like High, it has characters who are Catholic, though by upbringing rather than conviction and certainly not by vocation. And both plays involve an offstage funeral scene in which people keep telling someone who doesnt actually miss the departed that they're sorry for his or her loss. High holds the attention; Gruesome Playground Injuries rivets it.

What the two people in Rajiv Joseph's play are addicted to is pain: their own and one anothers. We first meet them in the nurses room at school when they're both aged eight. Doug, inspired by Evel Knievel, has ridden his bike off the roof and bloodied his head. Kayleen throws up; she often does. This sets a pattern for their subsequent behaviour. We last see them, 30 years later, at an ice rink: a perfect place for Doug to hurt himself again, though by now he isn't up to it. In between weve witnessed other stages of their relationship, though not in chronological order. Each time one of them is in some kind of hospital. Generally its Doug, who seems perversely to enjoy being accident-prone. But it can be Kayleen, whose psychological wounds go deeper. Doug at one point falls into a coma; Kayleen seems constantly to be on the verge of one. Doug comes from a loving family; Kayleen from very much the reverse. They stay away from one another for years on end, but each returns when the other is most in need. They have, it seems, the power to kiss one another better: sometimes literally. Indeed they share a first kiss; Doug, who wants it, suggests it's practice for their real first kiss, though Kayleen, who's resistant, is quick to point out the logical fallacy. Whether their physical relationship ever went any further is something the play leaves in doubt; over the years they both acquire and shed other partners, with jealousy resulting. Whats clear is that this, in its bizarre way, is the finest and most touching love story our theatre has told in years.

Peter Mooney and Janet Porter give performances that manage to seem both disciplined and spontaneous; Porter may have the edge, if only because Kayleen is the one who has edge. Doug, whatever his problems, remains the good-natured goof; Kayleen is allowed anger and introspection. Shes also the one whose ages and stages are more clearly differentiated; perhaps girls really do mature more than boys.

This play, too, comes with a program note: an impenetrable one by director Stefan Dzeparoski that seems to be about urban blight and the human body. Well, the second part is relevant. His actual production is admirably clear; the stage, a wide open space, is adorned with bubble-wrapped torsos, dummies of mummies, a couple of which fall to the ground with a thud at the start of things, to put us in the mood. The detritus of future scenes lies all around, ready for use; at the back there's a wheelchair, which, one accurately feels, does not bode well. Don't be discouraged; this, on occasion, a graphic play, is also a tender one. It's presented by BirdLand Theatre whose track record, though marred by a few grievously injurious missteps, continues outstanding.

High closes May 13 at the Royal Alexandra Theatre. Visit mirvish.com or call 416-872-1212 for details. Gruesome Playground Injuries closes May 13 at Theatre Centre. Visit theatrecentre.org or call 416-534-9261 for more information.

Well, we all make mistakes. A couple of months ago I was going into modified raptures over two then-new TV series, Smash and Luck, and anticipating increasingly good times for both. I was wrong in both cases, though for different reasons.

Luck ran out of it, and will not be back, though its first and only season just kept getting better. Its last episode drew all its threads together, while keeping some menacing options open for a sequel. It had more narrative clarity, and indeed more narrative, than all the previous instalments combined. I have to admit in previous weeks I was often content to let the dialogue and atmosphere wash over me. But the real emotional touchstones of this race-track story were the horses; and the second season has been cancelled on the humane grounds that too many of them were getting fatally injured. It may also be, of course, that the show was halted because not enough people liked it, while a sizable number actively hated it. The elusive (and allusive) storytelling apparently baffled them. Personally I cant see why anyone, or anyone interested in acting, would not want a weekly TV drama starring Dustin Hoffman.

Smash will be coming back, though apparently without its creator and showrunner Theresa Rebeck, which may be unfair. The show's first four episodes were its best, and Rebeck wrote the first three of them, though admittedly it was the fourth that was the best of all. It was in the wake of that opening quartet that I wrote my enthusiastic report. In those weeks Smash promised to be what it was advertised to be: a reasonably truthful and very entertaining story about the creation of a Broadway musical. It's been downhill since. The show is still watchable, but it doesnt seem to know whether its a show about a musical, or a musical in its own right.

It's a failure of style, or rather a failure to establish a style. Every episode will contain two or three numbers. There'll be something from the musical about Marilyn Monroe - at first simply called Marilyn, now rashly retitled Bombshell, which should really give the New York critics something to feast on - that the characters are supposedly putting together. Weve typically seen these songs staged in a bare rehearsal studio, which at some point magically transforms into a fully set and-costumed theatre. Fair enough; thats fantasy, but it's consistent fantasy. Do it often enough and you've got yourself a convention.

But there are also songs not from the show - pre-existent pop songs, mostly - that characters get up and sing because theyve been asked to perform at a party, or because theyre auditioning for something. And there are others that they sing to themselves, into a mirror usually, as an expression of their inner feelings but with full accompaniment, which is a different, non-naturalistic convention entirely.

There have been even less believable occasions on which whole ensembles have gone into impromptu song-and dance routines in a bowling alley, or the entire cast appeared in a grotesque Bollywood spectacle because in genue Karen (Katharine McPhee) was in an Indian restaurant and having hallucinations.

Two weeks ago Bombshell, as it now is, left New York for its Boston tryout. Composer Tom (Christian Borle) got into the spirit of the thing by sitting down at his piano and singing Cole Porter's apparently to impress his new boyfriend. Nice; but then suddenly the whole company were assembling on the Grand Central concourse (wrong station for the Boston train, but possibly chosen for the identification factor) cavorting around their suitcases like - well, like characters in a musical.

Now, it's true that in the golden age of Hollywood musicals, all these ways of doing a number could turn up in the same picture without anyone being bothered. But musicals in those days were an accepted genre whose practitioners had the time and the experience to play around a bit. Smash is trying to invent the TV musical, and to do it afresh every week with only 60 minutes minus commercials to do it in. Two songs in one hour do not make a musical, and in Smash they all seem to come out of nowhere. The guiding principle seems to be to try everything and hope something sticks.

That seems to be the narrative approach as well. Previously on Smash: I said that it wouldnt necessarily have been a better show if it had been done for cable. Wrong: done to cable standards, it might have been a musical Slings and Arrows, with the offstage narrative reflecting but subordinate to the business of putting on, not just a show, but one particular show. We still have no idea what these fictitious creators are trying to say about Monroe, and the occasional moments in which the aspirant actresses ask themselves, "What would Marilyn do?" are pathetic.

Apparently terrified of confusing their audience, the writers have settled for multipronged soap opera. One appreciates that the participants in a production will sometimes find themselves romantically entangled, but all of them, all the time? In fact, the parts of Smash that work are those most directly, even realistically, concerned with the theatre. I believe in Derek (Jack Davenport), the shoulder-chipped British director, when hes being a talented bastard at rehearsals; I couldn't care less about his relationship with Ivy (Megan Hilty), the bitchier and more insecure of the two standby Marilyns.

Tom and Julia (Debra Messing) are a thoroughly credible songwriting partnership, and I look fondly back on the episodes when they were actually shown writing songs; I also sympathize with Messing for having to act Julia's adulterous spree with a thoroughly boring actor, whose re-engagement in the role of Joe DiMaggio has demonstrated a remarkably cavalier attitude on the shows part to little things like authors rights and actors' contracts. The actual Bombshell songs have been well staged, and (by Marc Shaiman and Scott Wittman) cleverly written, though it's hard to see how theyd fit together. This score seems to consist of pastiche production numbers linked by no conceivable book. I used to think that Id like to see the finished product onstage. I now just think that the numbers placed end to end might make a terrific DVD.

Last week's episode was one of the better ones. It showed us Bombshell in previews, which meant it had largely to stick to business. I've grown to like Anjelica Huston as the producer, and it was touching to hear her talk-sing her way through September Song, which her grandfather Walter talkedsung definitively in 1938.

Rebecca (Uma Thurman), the star brought in to play Monroe and a well-observed character in her own right, prudently bowed out. We wait for tonights season finale to reveal whether Karen or Ivy will replace her; though Ive heard it suggested that Ivy's monster diva of a mother might be enlisted, which, since she's played by Bernadette Peters, sounds like a swell idea that would serve her daughter right. The crazy thing is, I don't really care, but I still want to know.

Smash's season finale airs May 14 at 10 p.m. on CTV and NBC.

Steven Sutcliffe, playing the central role of Garry Essendine in the Shaw Festival's production of Noel Coward's Present Laughter, makes a wonderful first impression. He emerges from his bedroom, in the middle hours of a weekday morning, to complain about the terrible racket that's deprived him of his beauty sleep. Since Garry is pretty much a surrogate for Coward himself, he's wearing a splendiferous dressing gown; the first, it turns out, of several. What issues from Sutcliffe's mouth, summing up his character perfectly, is a passionate whine, liberally laced with sheer cheek.

The cheek is especially apparent because the noise in his house is entirely his own fault. Garry, who when cornered admits to 39 (which was both Coward's own age, and that of the 20th century, when he wrote the play) is London's premier matinee idol; the previous night he brought home the latest in an obviously long line of adoring young females (on gender issues, the play does depart from strict autobiographical accuracy) who has woken up to find herself alone and abandoned in the spare room. Come the morning after, her host has pretty much forgotten who she is and why she was there. For him, she's just another of the people, both strangers and intimates, who want something from his infinitely forbearing self. He actually believes this.

And in some ways he's right. He has an inner circle of assistants and associates on whom he certainly depends but who also depend on him. Without his fame and talent where, as he constantly and rhetorically asks them, would they be? Garry, as everybody says including himself, is always on, always acting. His performance though, is totally sincere; and it's that mix, that contrast, that makes the play tick. Sutcliffe conveys it, for the most part, dazzlingly well; there's also (as there hasn't been in some actors of the role) a sunniness about him that makes his status as everybody's confidant thoroughly believable. He only falls off the tightrope at what seem to be Garry's (and Coward's) most heartfelt moments, most notably his crucial lecture on the hard graft it takes to become a professional playwright. Here earnestness takes over: We get the message but lose the messenger, who should still be playing a role, even though he's playing it sincerely. Sutcliffe, unwisely, lets the mask drop. Though so, come to think of it, did Coward himself. Because Garry here talks like a writer, though there's no indication elsewhere that he, unlike Coward, is anything but an actor.

Present Laughter is my own favourite of Coward's major comedies, partly because it's the loosest; the plot takes some time to get into gear, but while it does we're diverted by a relaxed genre painting of the comings and goings in Garry's luxurious studio, and in his even more luxurious ego. When the evening does shift into situation farce, with everyone and everything converging on Garry at once, it feels initially like a letdown, but the author's expertise in these matters gradually asserts itself. The play heads, easily and logically, for the quintessential Coward showdown; the finale tableau, common to all his best plays, in which one group of characters furtively departs the scene, leaving another group to its own raucous devices.

David Schurmann, a favourite Festival actor making his directorial debut, deals admirably with both the relaxed and frenzied moods on a peach of a set by William Schmuck that features startling murals, the obligatory staircase and, through a stage-sized back window, a stunning daylight vista of the Thames, with Big Ben prominently featured; at night, the sky is illumined by a half-moon that seems to have been flown in from one of Garry's musicals. There is, again, no mention of Garry actually doing musicals but, also again, one feels that he, like Coward, should have done them. The production does, in fact, feature between-scene selections of song, not by Coward, but by his American visa-vis Cole Porter, including one that's Porter's parody of a Coward song. Neat on several levels.

Among the supporting actors Mary Haney surpasses even Sutcliffe's presence and timing as his acerbically devoted secretary. You know the type, but she humanizes it; asked whether she finds Garry more charming onstage or off, she replies, "I can never quite make up my mind." You wouldn't think so simple a line could be so lethal. A raven-haired Moya O'Connell does an even more spectacular, though slightly less consistent, rehabilitation job on the vamp who threatens that old personal and professional gang of Garry's; she brings real personality - and real sexuality - to what could be a mechanical role. The men of the group are usually cardboard, but they're enlivened here by Gray Powell and especially by Patrick McManus, whose adoption of an American accent does wonders for the role of Garry's producer (and may well be a nod to Coward's real-life producer-lover Jack Wilson). As Garry's not-quite-ex-wife, Claire Jullien is off the sophisticated beam, while Julia Course as his latest conquest never gets anywhere near it. Jonathan Tan, however, as the angry young playwright (from Uckfield) who comes to lecture Garry and stays, immovably, to worship, gives a scenestealing and eventually show-stealing performance that involves an intimate relationship with furniture; when he isn't leaping over sofas, he's curling up on them, exuding excitement. In the smallest roles, we have, delightfully, Corinne Koslo as a psychic Scandinavian housekeeper, wreathed in shawls and cigarette smoke; James Pendarves as a Cockney valet whose untroubled self-assurance is everything that Garry thinks he envies; and Jennifer Phipps who, as a titled granny, moves mountains with a line about a mountain.

Present Laughter is in repertory through Oct. 28 at the Festival Theatre, Niagara-on-the-Lake. For show times and ticket information, call 1-800-511-7429 or visit shawfest.com.

THEATRE REVIEW

A Man and Some Women

Court House Theatre, Niagara-on-the-Lake

Misalliance

Royal George Theatre, Niagara-on-the-Lake

There are three women, no men, on stage at the start of A Man and Some Women. One of the ladies is sewing and talking, another is playing patience (or, as you might have it, solitaire) and replying, and the third is reading and keeping very quiet. The tableau is so reminiscent of the beginning of Chekhov's Three Sisters that I immediately assumed that Githa Sowerby's characters were three sisters, too. It took me ages to realize that only two of them are. The third, the quiet one, is a distant cousin who happens to be in love with the sisters' brother. This is awkward, because he's already married, not happily.

Sowerby, a pioneering English female playwright from the early years of the 20th century, never had the career she deserved. The Shaw Festival has already successfully revived two of her plays, Rutherford and Son and The Stepmother. A Man and Some Women opened in Manchester in 1914; the war scuppered its chances of production in London and it's barely been seen since; in fact this Niagara production is probably its most prominent airing to date. It's a less sturdy piece than the other two, but it's a fascinating and, once it gets going and we've sorted out who everybody is, an exciting one.

The Shaw's previous Sowerby plays registered as impressive studies of female anger, long contained but finally and explosively bursting forth. A Man and Some Women is an impressive - and impressively magnanimous - study of male anger, similarly repressed and released. For years Richard Shannon has supported his sisters, pharisaical Rose and timid Elizabeth, and his wife Hilda, in the process sacrificing both his dreams of a scientific vocation and his undeclared love for cousin Jessica. Richard's widowed mother has just died and the women await his return from the funeral and from the revelation of how much money they may all be inheriting.

Also in the house is a small illegitimate boy named Jack. Elizabeth is ineffectually nice to him, and Jessica actively kind, but Rose and Hilda treat him as some kind of pestilence, rather as if they were all living in a Victorian novel. Rose at least has religion on her side (the sins of the fathers - or mothers - and all that); Hilda gives the impression of having been born nasty. It's pretty clear where our sympathies are meant to lie, and when Richard arrives it's plain that he shares them. He bears news that puts the women in his power; and, when Rose pushes him by spying on him and Jessica, he uses it. Having told them all exactly what he thinks of them, he leaves the house, exulting that he will finally be free from being nagged. It's an exhilarating scene, at least from a certain point of view and certainly as played here by Graeme Somerville.

Alisa Palmer's production is an extraordinary mix of good and bad acting. Its beating heart is Somerville, hitting every note dead centre as a man who's spent his life being guiltily amiable and is determined that his new freedom will last; you can feel the audience cheering him on. It may be a comment on the play that the closer the others get to his orbit, the better they seem; that goes for Sharry Flett, whose Elizabeth starts in near-anonymity and gradually becomes a touching study in principle and independence painfully acquired, and for Marla McLean as Jessica, the new woman who seems, in this staging, to be asserting her independence by being a painter; I say "seems" because though in the last act we see her working at an easel, it's never actually mentioned in the dialogue; maybe it's just a hobby. But Kate Hennig (Rose) and Jenny L. Wright (Hilda) are, respectively, stilted and sullen; admittedly they've been handed the roles of monsters, but they do little to humanize them.

The play makes a conscientious attempt, if not to justify them, then to place them sociologically and economically; Rose has persuaded herself that denying love is a virtue, Hilda exemplifies marriage as legalized prostitution; it must have been thrilling to hear these things said on an English stage in 1914. But they are said rather than dramatized; by a similar token, I couldn't follow Jessica's reasoning in forcing Richard to choose between her and a career in tropical medicine; why can't he have both? The play is full of loose ends, and it hits its peak too early, but it's a discovery worth discovering.

Shaw's Misalliance is one of his most unabashedly - indeed exultantly - discursive plays. Its barrage of rhetoric and paradox can, if fired off with wit and rhythm and poise, be irresistible; without them, it's unbearable. The latter is the case in the new festival production, or at least in its first half. Only two of the actors can do it. One, mercifully since he has the leading role of John Tarleton, philosophical and philanthropical underwear magnate, is Thom Marriott who in a cheeky blond wig looks unsuitably younger than usual but whose gusto and humour - at once self-indulgent and self-deprecating - are irreproachable. The other is Jeff Meadows as his hearty, grinning, and defiantly non-intellectual son; he has energy plus focus.

The director, Eda Holmes, has moved the action, or at least the set and costumes, from 1910 to 1962: an idea she tries but fails to explain in her program note. A thorough updating to now might be stimulating; this halfway house is the worst of both worlds. Mostly you forget about it, but then you're jolted by references to Tarleton's Free Libraries (in a country which by the '60s had a national network of free libraries, all state-funded) or to sums of money that nobody has bothered to adjust for inflation.

Things do improve after the intermission, partly because Tara Rosling comes crashing through the roof in an airplane, an even blonder wig and a Polish accent through which she transmits her own sense of serious mischief: how nice to see this actress in a role in which she isn't required to suffer. The great difference, though, is that the plane crash, followed by another character's emergence from a Turkish bath with a revolver in his unsteady hand and revenge in his even less steady head, signals the play's transition into eccentric farce, a mode that sweeps the actors along with it. Even so, the production manages to muff the play's punch line.

A Man and Some Women is in repertory until Sept. 22; Misalliance until Oct. 27. For tickets, call 1-800-511-7429 or visit shawfest.com.

David Cooper / Jenny L. Wright as Hilda Shannon, Graeme Somerville as Richard Shannon and Kate Hennig as Rose Shannon in the Shaw Festival production of A Man and Some Women.; Caption:

THEATRE REVIEW

42nd Street

Festival Theatre, Stratford

When David Merrick, also known as Broadways Abominable Showman, purchased the stage rights to the 1933 Warner Bros. movie musical 42nd Street, he didnt stop there.

There are only four real songs in the movie so, to eke them out, Merrick also bought up the entire catalogue of numbers that Harry Warren, the composer, and Al Dubin, the lyricist, wrote for Warner Bros. in the '30s. One of the most famous of these was Lullaby of Broadway, which is from Gold Diggers of 1935. It became, in many ways, the defining number of the new stage show. (Well, new in 1980, when Merrick produced it.) It sums up the appeal of the show. It also indicates what's wrong with it.

The song happens when Peggy Sawyer, the eager and naive but super-talented young chorine from Allentown, has to be wooed back into the musical Pretty Lady to take over from the star Dorothy Brock, who has broken her leg. Peggys sensitive soul has already been badly bruised by the rehearsal process and shes about to catch the train home, so Julian Marsh, the tough and tyrannical but (we assume) also super-talented director, descends on the railroad station to persuade her to change her mind, closely followed by the entire company. They beg her to consider their jobs, their hard work and - most of all - the theatre itself. Lullaby of Broadway is the medium through which they deliver their message.

It is, as it has always been, an irresistible toe-tapper of a tune with a highly evocative lyric. Except that, if you actually listen to that lyric, what it evokes has nothing to do with what the performers are supposedly trying to say. The song is a down-to-earth celebration of New York's underside: subways, taxis, laterising good-time-girls and their sugar-daddies, "the daffodils who entertain at Angelo's and Maxies." In the Gold Diggers movie, it climaxes in a suicide. About the one feature of Broadway it doesnt mention is the theatre.

Well, I guess nobody does listen to lyrics. The calculation is that we will just hear the word Broadway and melt. The same goes for Julian's pre-song invocation of "musical comedy - the most marvellous words in the English language." Nobody really thinks that, and a musical that feels the need to proclaim it obviously doesn't. This one is saying, Look at all these outdated sentiments we dont believe any longer; arent they sweet and ridiculous? The word for that is camp.

I should add that in Gary Griffin's Stratford production of Lullaby of Broadway is very well staged: better, in fact, than I remember it being in Gower Champion's 1980 original. Griffins version, choreographed by Alex Sanchez, is less clangorous, more playful, more seductive, especially in the way Sean Arbuckle as Marsh moves around Peggy on her bench before the reinforcements arrive. The scene finds Arbuckle at his best; elsewhere hes damagingly miscast, ineradicably gentle, neither driven nor driving enough.

However many pills he pops, he can't convince us that Pretty Lady is his all-important last chance. This, admittedly, is something on which the show itself goes easy, and why it's a betrayal of the film on which its based. The book (by Michael Stewart and Mike Bramble) does throw in the odd reference to breadlines, and the interpolated numbers include the sardonic Were in the Money, but the Depression becomes a faraway fantasy. In the movie, within its backstage limits, it looks and feels real.

All that said, I had quite a good time. This very proscenium show takes surprisingly well to the open stage, letting the audience peer down into the centre of the production numbers; and Griffin, a master of musical storytelling, moves it smoothly along. There are some neat scenic jokes, plus a few involving Michael Barber's invigorating onstage band; indeed the production's own shafts of self-mockery are defter than those of the script, which often seems to be hedging its bets between hand-on-heart and tongue-in-cheek.

Cynthia Dale as Dorothy gets the stylistic balance, along with the modulation from spoiled diva to sympathetic professional, exactly right; as she sings it, About a Quarter to Nine is the best number in the show, and not just because its the simplest. Steve Ross and C. David Johnson do more for her rival suitors than the roles probably deserve. Jennifer Rider-Shaw has an appealing pudgy earnestness as Peggy and justifies the storys claims for her singing and, especially, her dancing, while Kyle Blair is relaxed dynamite as the juvenile lead who takes her under his wing and into his heart.

The chorus, not all of whom pass strict muster as "kids," come in an unusual variety of shapes and sizes, but not of colours; of course a musical company in 1933 wouldn't have been integrated, but this show doesn't seem to be going in much for historical realism. Anyway, as a tap extravaganza, it doesnt measure up to My One and Only a few seasons back. Geoffrey Tyler (oil) and Gabrielle Jones (vinegar) add flavour as Pretty Ladys writers, reminding us how much TV's Smash must owe to 42nd Street; Peggy is really a Karen without an Ivy. It's even harder here than in Smash to imagine what plot the show-within-a-show could possibly have, but its nice that the authors get to perform Shuffle Off to Buffalo, the number thats gets closest to the surreal suggestiveness of the Busby Berkeley original.

Berkeley's more elaborately kaleidoscopic routines of course could never be recreated in a theatre; which of course raises the question, why try? James Magruder's program note tells us that the 50-year delay in moving 42nd Street from screen to stage "isnt so mysterious." It isnt mysterious at all; in 1980 people weren't doing that kind of thing. It's only in later years that the theatre has become dependent on pointless imitations of things that were done perfectly the first time around and that still exist. Its a depressing and ultimately disastrous trend.

At least 42nd Street can claim to have been ahead of the curve; it wasnt quite the first, but it's still probably the best.

42nd Street is in repertory until Oct. 28. For tickets, call 1-800-567-1600 or visit stratfordfestival.ca.
