It may be hard to claim Ragtime as the great Canadian musical. It's an adaptation of an American novel, with an American composer, lyricist and librettist, and it was originally staged by an American production team with mostly American principal performers, and its very subject is America. Nevertheless, it was first produced by a Canadian company, Livent Inc., and its conceivable that its choice for revival at the Shaw Festival may have been influenced by those Canadian origins. Whether or not thats the case, it's regrettable, to put it politely, that the copious Shaw program makes only the barest small-print mention of Livent, and none at all of Garth Drabinsky, without whom the show would never have existed.

As it happens, Jackie Maxwell's Shaw production can stand comparison with the Livent original. It uses the Festival Theatre stage superbly; Sue LePages skeletal mobile sets and variously beautiful costumes and Alan Brodies superlative lighting make it both spare and spectacular. There's a surge of excitement right from the great opening title number that sets up the three groups of characters in pre-First World War America: the middle-class whites of New Rochelle, the emancipated but still submerged Negroes (the word at the time), and the European immigrants who escaped poverty and starvation to find, initially at least, more of the same. There are at least two occasions on which Valerie Moore's choreography betters my memories of the original; one is this opening, which she saves from looking like an imitation of the concentric Tradition number in Fiddler on the Roof, and the other is the vaudeville number in which glamour girl Evelyn Nesbit burlesques the trial of her husband for murdering her lover.

Evelyn is one of the historical figures in E.L. Doctorows novel and in the musical; others are Harry Houdini, Henry Ford, Booker T. Washington and Emma Goldman. Theyre the illustrative background figures in a tapestry whose principal characters are representative fictions from each of the social and racial groups. Terrence McNally's book still seems a miraculously clever reordering of the original, keeping faith with Doctorow's dry impersonal narrative tone while clearing space for Stephen Flahertys music and Lynn Ahrens lyrics to supply the emotional amplitude both inevitable and essential in a musical. Sometimes this spills over into sentimentality; it's notable, but not surprising, that the numbers that raised the loudest cheers on the Niagara first night were the most bombastic and simplistic: Wheels of a Dream, the hymn of ragtime pianist Coalhouse Walker to his new bride Sarah and his new Ford Model T; Back to Before, in which the unnamed Mother of the white family sings all too consciously about her intellectual liberation; Let Them Hear You, the last message of Coalhouse, turned avenger (some would say terrorist) after the vandalizing of his car and the killing of his wife. What does Coalhouse want us to hear exactly? Because he's just singing platitudes, that ride roughsod over the complexities of a situation in which hes a killer as well as a victim.

Far better are the sharp comedic songs, of which my favourite is Henry Fords brisk celebration of himself and his assembly line. Better still are Our Children, a duet for Mother and Tateh, the immigrant street vendor turned movie director, a love song that's all subtext; and He Wanted to Say, which is actually about subtext. Then there's The Night That Goldman Spoke in Union Square, simultaneously stirring and searching. Best of all is New Music, in which Coalhouses ragtime arouses deep feelings, rapturous and troubling or both, in all who hear it: Sarah, in a speechless heart-stopping moment, gives herself to him; Father, Mothers husband, just returned from Admiral Peary's expedition to the North Pole, understands enough to know he doesn't understand.

Benedict Campbells Father is the one performance that surpasses its Livent predecessor. He becomes the pivotal figure in the piece, despite being the least obviously sympathetic - or perhaps because of it. Father is hearty (at least as Campbell plays him) and hidebound; he senses the changes around him, goes grudgingly along with some, resists more, has a final cry of outraged humanity, that echoes Coalhouses from an act earlier. Campbell portrays him in broad strokes that still accommodate complexity.

The obvious star role, though, is Coalhouse. Thom Allison has been a star in my book for years, illuminating his roles with a Satanic gleam that he moderates in the first half of this show to a charismatic glow, augmented by his ringing singing. Vocally, he's just as powerful in the second half, but not dramatically; he doesn't make a convincing brooder or fanatic. In a show that covers a lot of narrative ground very fast, the surprise love interest of Mother (Patty Jamieson) and Tateh (Jay Turvey) fails to fulfill its proper weight; Turvey is delightful in his transported shtetl rags, but he cant reconcile his later dual role of romantic lead and foppish pioneer of spectacle. Kate Hennigs watchful Emma Goldman is very fine, as are her lightning-sketched historical peers: Julie Martell's delectable Evelyn, Peter Millard's Ford and Kelly Wongs Houdini. One bit of the show, though, that never works are the Little Boys repeated admonitions to the Great Escaper to "warn the Duke." He means the Archduke Ferdinand, whose murder at Sarajevo will end the era of ragtime for ever. Houdini doesn't get the message and neither, until far too late to be of theatrical use, do we. All one can say is, it worked in the book, by which I don't mean it stopped the war. The musical Ragtime does so much, it's unfair to expect it to handle its era's demise as well. Did Doctorow ever consider writing a sequel called Jazz?

Ragtime is in repertory through Oct. 14 at the Festival Theatre, Niagara-on-the-Lake. Visit shawfest. com or call 1-800-511-SHAW (7429) for show times and ticket information.

THEATRE REVIEW

Cymbeline

Tom Patterson Theatre, Stratford

The most wonderful thing about Antoni Cimolino's production of Cymbeline, encompassing all the others, is that it takes the play as it comes, which is no mean feat, as it comes in any number of guises.

Among Shakespeare's plays, it's the ultimate confounder of categories. In the First Folio, the first-ever collected works, it's placed among the tragedies, though hardly anybody in it dies. It has a happy ending, in which long-lost family members get united, as do the central pair of lovers. It can hardly be called a conventional courtship comedy, however, as the lovers in question are already married when the play starts, though people and events conspire to keep them apart for the duration.

It's something of a history play. There really was an ancient British king called Cymbeline, or someone like it, who reigned after the invasion of Julius Caesar; the play shows him refusing to pay tribute to Rome, and getting re-invaded for his pains. This issue, however, only surfaces halfway through the action, and it has to jostle for space with several other plot lines, all of which eventually intersect.

When the Roman army arrives it looks, in this production, exactly as you would expect it to look. It's largely staffed, however, by characters whom we have met earlier as cynical Italians from the Renaissance; and who have also dressed the part. One of them has tried to seduce Cymbeline's daughter Innogen, has been repulsed by her and has lied about it to her husband, who has responded with a murderous rage at least as ugly and graphic as Othello's.

Innogen, by the way, is by current scholarly consensus the name Shakespeare intended for his heroine; all the girls who in subsequent centuries have been christened Imogen apparently owe their names to a Jacobean printer's error. I guess we just have to suck it up. Innogen's reunion with the father who kicked the play off by banishing her husband links it with the other father-daughter plays commonly known as the late romances. The tale it tells is, even by late romantic standards, uncommonly tall, broad and coincidence-crammed. It looks you in the eye and dares you not to believe. This time we do, joyfully.

This is a superb ensemble account of a play with some dozen leading roles. Cymbeline himself seems to owe his title status to rank (again as in a history) rather than intrinsic interest. Geraint Wyn Davies, though, makes a more compelling case for him as the centre of the play than any actor I have seen. We see him at the start, tossing on a bed, appropriating the play's first line. ("You do not meet a man but frowns.") If this is meant to suggest that the whole play is his dream then it doesn't work, because there's no visible payoff, even though beds (not his) are to play a vital part in the subsequent action. But it does enable him to play a grieved and haggard parent, rather than a cardboard tyrant, and even when later scenes force him into more conventional regal mode, there is a conflicted man behind the lines. "Pardon's the word to all," he decrees at the end, and you feel that he includes himself.

Stylistically, the play is a mixture of knotted verse and pungent prose. The production's straightforwardness makes both modes intelligible; its intelligence makes them intense. Graham Abbey's jealous Posthumus is another major piece of reclamation: charming in his initial confidence, overwhelming in his rage and taking on a grave, self-immolating urgency in a repentance that he thinks has come too late; within this comedy there's a neartragic curve.

Cara Ricketts' Innogen starts with some overdone grievanceacting, but quickly becomes the most enchanting Shakespearean heroine seen at Stratford in years. She's a woman both capable and ingenuous. In her long scene with Tom McCamus' wily seducer Iachimo, she registers every change of mood; her fairy tale joy when on her way (she thinks) to meet her husband is both heartwarming and heartbreaking. She also, when in male disguise, is as convincing a boy-girl as you could hope to meet.

The Queen, Snow White's stepmother as Lady Macbeth, is a role that starts strongly but peters out; Yanna McIntosh makes the silky most of it while it lasts. Her son Cloten is a far meatier part, a lecherous brainless lout who's a snob and a bully but, disconcertingly, not a coward. Mike Shara makes him unceasingly funny and alarmingly real. The goodies include Brian Tree's bluntly faithful Pisanio, Nigel Bennett's Roman general and Peter Hutt's expositional physician, who takes his Hippocratic oath very seriously.

John Vickery's orotund delivery seems, not for the first time, to come from a different and older world, but that rather suits his role as a banished courtier hanging out in the Welsh wilds, attended by a couple of young noble savages, Ian Lake being the nobler and E. B. Smith the more savage. It's one good performance after another.

With the move to the mountains, the production begins to open up visually. This continues with our first sight of the Roman army: the sign of an eagle, aloft and advancing. It seems to be all we need but then, when it comes to the battle, we actually get one: handto-hand combats arranged by Todd Campbell, that are not only exciting in themselves but make clear what's supposed to be going on: In my experience of this play, that's a first.

The last scene is a test of a different kind: a non-stop series of revelations and recapitulations at which it's impossible not to laugh. ("O gods," says the doctor, "I left out one thing that the queen confessed.") What's extraordinary is that the laughter turns to tears, of joy: the incredible becomes its own magic. It only works, though, if we care for the people in the story. Here we do, richly. This is a production that trusts its audience, trusts its actors, trusts the play, and meets all its challenges.

Cymbeline runs in repertory until Sept. 30. For tickets, call 1-800-567-1600 or visit stratfordfestival.ca.

David Hou / While not quite a tragedy or comedy, Shakespeare's Cymbeline is a joy to watch.; Caption:

The church scene in Much Ado About Nothing is one of the most notorious booby traps in Shakespeare. It's the point at which the comedy's two major plot lines collide. Claudio, the callow young army officer, is scheduled to marry Hero, daughter of the city governor on whom he and his fellows have been billeted. Tricked into believing that his fiancee has been unfaithful, he abandons her at the altar and stalks out, followed by all his comrades save one. The exception is Benedick, the previously confirmed bachelor, who's influenced partly by a basic decency and partly by his dawning love for Hero's cousin Beatrice, a love that she, a previously confirmed spinster, reciprocates. They too have been tricked, in this case benevolently, by friends and relations who have sensed, rightly, that they were made for one another. Benedick asks what he can do to prove his love, and Beatrice takes him up on it. She says "kill Claudio."

The abruptness of this has traditionally raised a laugh, and productions have often been judged on their ability to avoid it. I don't know whether Christopher Newton, in his new Stratford production, wanted to avoid it, but if he did, he hasn't succeeded - at least not at the performance I saw. Sought for or not, the laugh on this occasion doesn't sink the scene; it may even enrich it. Actors Ben Carlson and Deborah Hay bounce right back, riding a wave of mingled passion and absurdity, rich in action and reaction. They are fairly funny, but very moving.

This is the unexpected direction in which they have been tending throughout an uneven but generally intelligent production. Carlson has been pointing his lines with his usual adroitness, but the "merry war" in which he and Beatrice have been engaged (as distinct from the un-merry one from which he has just returned) doesn't seem all that witty. Maybe it's Shakespeare's fault. Hay as Beatrice makes the stronger impression, maybe because her character is more vulnerable. It's plain that she and Benedick have been around the block before, and that she still carries the scars. When she speaks the famous bittersweet lines about the dancing star under which she was born while her mother cried, she's very affecting.

Surprisingly too, when it comes to the twin eavesdropping scenes in which each is apprised of the other's supposed love, it's Beatrice who makes the stronger impression. Generally, her turn is an anti-climax, because it comes second and is in verse in a play whose liveliest scenes are in prose. In this production, though, Carlson is kept unobtrusively in the background for his deception while the deceivers talk among themselves - very entertainingly, as they seem as intent on scoring points off one another as they do on tricking him. Hay, by contrast, is allowed some spectacular reactions involving a staircase; her subsequent soliloquy of surrender is magic, a bold spirit made shy. Carlson's defiance of his former friends is an equivalent turning point for him; and in the play's home stretches both actors, alternately needling and nuzzling one another, are superb. Their union seems, as it should, like the happiest match in Shakespeare.

There's a 19th-century Brazilian setting (designed, naturally, by Santo Loquasto) that doesn't detract much, but doesn't add much either. The early scenes look and feel cluttered.

Newton writes at length in the program about the appropriateness of the period's politics, but really the causes of this war could hardly matter less; it's over before the play starts, and the only character who alludes to it later is the malcontent Don John (Gareth Potter, nicely neurotic), who's motivated solely by personal spite. The other males are allowed more complexity than usual. Juan Chioran's Don Pedro is especially distinguished, a lonely prince nursing a secret longing for women in general and, it seems, Beatrice in particular. Tyrone Savage makes a passionate case for the usually irredeemable Claudio, whose selfrighteous cruelty at the nuptials is presented as the triumph of inexperience over hope. It isn't just Hero's betrothed who disowns her; her father Leonato joins in too, at least initially. James Blendick, affably witty in prose, makes a very heavy meal of his anger in verse, but this at least enables Bethany Jillard's Hero to convey how much his rejection adds to her humiliation. It also cues Timothy D. Stickney, as the good angel Friar Francis, to give his best Stratford performance to date. The constabulary scenes are performed with a confounding lack of inspiration; even the minor villains (Michael Blake and Victor Ertmannis), having started out as interesting sketches, remain merely sketchy. These scenes are introduced by what sounded to me like Jobim's The Waters of March, but Jonathan Monro's musical score otherwise stays attractively within the chosen period.

A much later comedy of manners (i.e. of male sexual confusion), Terence Rattigan's initial 1935 hit French Without Tears gets an entertaining outing at the Shaw Festival. It's slow to find its groove, a recurring problem at Niagara this season. The characters are mainly budding English diplomats doing French immersion on the French coast, and the first ones we meet are played either unbearably loud or insufferably wet. Once settled in, though, Kate Lynch's production is extremely well paced, with Martin Happer outstanding as the senior student, a naval chap who graduates from caricature to real man, largely through impeccable comic timing. A ruminative, alcoholic scene shared with his two most sensitive juniors (Ben Sanders and Wade Bogert-O'Brien) is the evening's highlight, played with the chaps stretched out horizontally, one face hovering mere inches above another; are they trying to tell us something? The females who disturb their dreams are Robin Evans Willis, who looks appropriately delectable as the resident flirt, and Julie Martell, balancing her glamour girl from Ragtime with a practical mademoiselle who's more attractive than she thinks she is. The play spins out too many variations on its theme, but they're amusing, sometimes charming, variations. There's a surprise ending which - another besetting seasonal sin - is thoroughly mishandled; to say how would, of course, merely add to the spoiling.

Much Ado About Nothing: through Oct. 27 at the Festival Theatre, Stratford. Call 1-800-567-1600 or visit stratfordfestival.ca for details. French Without Tears: through Sept. 15 at the Royal George Theatre, NiagaraontheLake. Call 1-800-511-7429 or visit shawfest.com for more information.

THEATRE REVIEW

The Matchmaker Festival Theatre, Stratford

Unless I'm forgetting something, Thornton Wilders The Matchmaker, at the Stratford Festival, is the richest and funniest production of a farce that Ive ever seen in a Canadian theatre.

It's other things as well, as befits a play with a tangled but illustrious history, one that goes back to 1835 when an English playwright, John Oxenford, came up with a one-act trifle called A Day Well Spent.

A Day Well Spent has proved to be a play well spent. Seven years later an Austrian dialect dramatist, Johannes Nestroy, adapted and elongated it under the title Einen Jux will er sich machen, which is roughly translatable as he's going to have a good time if it kills him.

A classic in his own country, Nestroy is virtually unknown outside it, but the omnivorous and multilingual Wilder knew about him, and in 1938 came up with his own North American adaptation, The Merchant of Yonkers. It was a flop, but Wilder persevered and in 1955 he turned it into The Matchmaker, which was, and has remained, a hit. It became an even bigger hit in 1964, when it was musicalized as Hello, Dolly!

Meanwhile, or rather some time later, in another part of the forest, Tom Stoppard, apparently unaware that hed had competition, wrote his own version of Einen Jux, On the Razzle, which took the setting back to Vienna and contains more good jokes than any play since The Importance of Being Earnest. In a preface, Stoppard summed up the storys age-old appeal: it's the tale of the country mouse - or mice - out on the town.

In The Matchmaker, though, that's only half the story. We have Cornelius Hackl, head clerk, 33, and Barnaby Tucker, assistant clerk, 17, who escape from dry-goods servitude in Yonkers, N.Y., for a day and night of adventure in the big gas-lit city. Their employer, the tight-fisted demi-millionaire Horace Vandergelder, is bound there himself, in search of a bride. To help in the search hes engaged Dolly Levi, a bustling widow who, in need of both security and companionship, is determined to have Horace for herself. She is Wilders own addition to the mix, one that gives the play its own peculiarly complex, satisfying rhythm.

It works at two speeds. We have the helter-skelter excursion of the clerks, and we have the slow burn of Dolly's entrapment of Vandergelder for, as he comes reluctantly to realize, his good as well as hers. Dolly may be the play's title figure but its only in the last of its four elaborate scenes that she takes full control.

That at least is the pattern is Chris Abrahams masterful production, in which each location - store, shop, restaurant - is solidly and delectably conjured by Santo Loquasto's settings. There are also, this being an open stage, some delightfully inventive transitions, one of them evoking a train.

In both scale and style this is a departure for Abraham, previously best known for staging intense new plays in small spaces.

Cornelius and Barnaby agree that, when they know they're having an adventure, theyll shout out "pudding"; this production comes over as Abrahams own adventure, his own pudding, and it's a wonderfully satisfying one.

Farcically, Mike Shara's Cornelius makes a lot of the running, especially when he finds himself in the millinery establishment whose proprietress, Irene Molloy, is his own bosss temporary intended. He spends half the scene diving into closets to escape detection, the other half falling irretrievably in love. Its a treat merely to watch Shara rock, perplexed, on his heels when crisis approaches, as it continually does; an even greater one to hear him step forward and tell us how he feels about Molloy.

Laura Condolln is a totally charming Molloy, and Andrea Runge an unexpected treat as her shy bespectacled beanpole assistant. As Barnaby, equally shy but volcanically so, Josh Epstein is a sweet riot.

Wilder was the most selfconscious of playwrights, and part of his program was to break down the fourth wall by periodically having his characters confide in us. These soliloquies are beautifully presented here; farce meets sentiment and, though the combination shouldn't work, it does: perhaps because each element has so much tradition and so much conviction behind it.

Tom McCamus, muttonchopped and lobster-voiced, makes a crackling Vandergelder, whose crackle gets more desperately effective the more hemmed-in he becomes.

Seana McKenna, an unusually svelte Dolly, moves as stealthily in on us as she does on him, until, suddenly, with her speech about spreading his money judiciously around like manure, it's her play.

Then theres Geraint Wyn Davies as Horaces hastily hired help, who stops the show when he explains to us his philosophical reasons for not stealing a purse. This comes at the height of the mayhem in the Harmonia Gardens Restaurant, which brings all the characters together, most of them unwillingly, with a comic climax involving screens and disguises that, in intensity and elaboration, is beyond any production of this play that I've encountered.

There's yet another couple involved, too: Vandergelders tearful niece (Cara Ricketts deals deliciously with the tears, but has problems with her Victorian demureness when dry-eyed) and the young artist (Skye Brandon), whom her uncle has, naturally, forbidden her to marry. Chick Reid inhabits two worlds of her own as a pair of selectively deaf domestics, one at each end of the play; and the restaurant, at which I want a reservation, is superbly staffed at every level.

A critic once wrote that Wilder "arranges flowers beautifully but he doesnt grow them." Right, but this is his most creative arrangement: a tribute to comedy, in its many forms, that's also the thing itself. As done here, The Matchmaker is a match - many matches - made in heaven. Or, to put it another way, Pudding.

The Matchmaker runs in repertory until Oct. 27. For more information, visit stratfordfestival.ca.
2012-06-13-where-the-art-is:
THEATRE REVIEW

Home

Young Centre for the Performing Arts, Toronto

David Storey's play Home begins with two men conversing in polite but somewhat stilted tones: Two middle-aged English gents, names of Jack and Harry, who seem to know one another, but not very well. The play was first produced in London in 1970, and Storey has claimed that when he started to write it he had no idea who or where the men were; they and their words just came into his head.

I used to distrust, or flatly disbelieve, this idiot-savant approach to playwriting, but seeing the play again, in a fine production by Soulpepper, I have to confess theres something in it. It obviously worked for Storey, who does indeed seem to be discovering his characters and their background as he goes along. It also works, mostly, for me.

Jack and Harry, natty representatives of the southern English professional class, are shortly joined by two ladies, Kathleen and Marjorie, of roughly the same age but from a lower social stratum. Later we meet Alfred, a muscle-bound young man who enjoys lifting tables and chairs in the air and then walking off with them. This annoys the four older people, because there never seem to be enough chairs for them all to sit down on in the first place, and hes making it worse. All five characters, it seems, call this place home.

As far as I remember, no great mystery was made at the time of the original production as to what kind of home it might be; it might have taken Storey himself time to find out, but critics who gave his conclusions away were not accused of ruining anybody's fun. This was before the word "spoiler" came into common use. Now it's considered bad form to reveal anything.

What does rapidly become clear, though, is that the quintet, who have no previous association, have been thrown together in some kind of institutional setting, with regular communal meal times and with therapeutic activities laid on. In theory, it could be anything from a holiday camp to a mental hospital. I dont think myself that theres much doubt on which end of the scale it belongs, but then I've seen the play before. I don't think that my prior knowledge lessened my enjoyment: quite the opposite in fact.

Some years ago Albert Schultz directed a memorable Soulpepper revival of Harold Pinters No Mans Land, and it's conceivable that his attention was drawn to Home by the fact that the leading roles in both plays were created by the same two great English actors, John Gielgud and Ralph Richardson. (Home came first.) Whether that's the case or not, Home ranks with No Mans Land (and the more rambunctious A Chorus of Disapproval and The Time of Your Life) among Schultzs best productions. In fact, despite having no theatrical knights on tap, his production of Home improves on the original, which came all too self-importantly from what was then the Royal Court Theatre tradition of Plays That Are Good for You.

All I really remember from it is the sight and muffled sound of Gielgud crying: something that he could always do more affectingly than anyone else. I presume that Richardson cried, too, since both of Soulpepper's actors do, but Sir Ralph was always a more discreet and enigmatic sufferer than Sir John. Anyway, it was hard back then to think of the play as anything more than a wispy vehicle for its stars, and I doubted if it could be of any interest without them. Michael Hanrahan (Harry) and Oliver Dennis (Jack) prove that it can.

They play seemingly affable, cultivated men, whose gentle banter proves to cover great depths, certainly of sorrow and probably of shame. Both are dapper, but Dennis is the more dapper of the two, with a neatness and precision that have to be covering something up. Hanrahan is outwardly the more open and relaxed, the ruddy squire to Dennis's pale citizen, but he seems to have done something to his face; it isnt quite all there.

They exchange bluff anecdotes about their military or commercial experiences, in an amiably competitive manner that thrives on free association. Harry floats the theory that the Garden of Eden was actually located in Englands Vale of Evesham, though he stops short of claiming that Eve was named after it (or even vice versa). This, apparently, is Dennis's 50th production for Soulpepper, and his versatility is something we've long taken for granted; Hanrahans seems to be growing by leaps and bounds - compare this outwardly bland performance to his crazy gangbanger in Half Life - and on this occasion he is ultimately the more moving and disturbing of the two.

What pricks the two mens precarious bubble is the advent of the two women, who greet their stiff attempts at courtliness with the deepest suspicion. Where the gentlemen are elaborately reserved, the women are aggressively outspoken. Maria Vacratsis (Marjorie) is ceaselessly censorious, not least with her companion whom she is continually adjuring to "pull your skirt down, girl." Brenda Robins (Kathleen) complies, with a suggestive giggle: Her response to anything suggestive of a double entendre, which of course means just about anything. Individually and as a duo, these are far sharper performances than I recall from London. Andre Sills' eruptions and interruptions as Alfred are massive; he's abrupt in what he does, deliberate in how he does it.

Ken MacKenzies set consists of a brick wall, in front of which is lowered a screen with a slowly shifting cloudscape, It suggests an endless English summer afternoon. The hints that the play might be an allegory for the homeland itself strike me as facile, though 40 years on, when these social types have mostly disappeared, they can seem pleasantly nostalgic; Denniss performance, in particular, carries a whiff of Ealing comedy.

What keeps the play alive, and is captured in this production with musical exactness, is its feeling for the rhythms of the lost, the socially and psychologically unmoored. If everyone in it is yearning for a home it seems, sadly, that they have found it.

Home runs until June 20. For tickets, call 416-866-8666 or visit soulpepper.ca.

The National Theatre of Great Britain is going through what's generally agreed to be a golden age. It's lasted for "nine, nearly 10 years now," which is how long, by his own count, artistic director Nicholas Hytner has been in office.

His success has been twofold; he has directed a long line of outstanding productions himself, while presiding as an impresario over a comparable number of successes staged by others. Some shows in both categories have gone international. His production of Alan Bennett's The History Boys, which I caught on Broadway just before it swept the 2006 Tonys, was the most enjoyable evening - actually it was an afternoon - I have spent in a theatre in years.

More recently, his production of One Man, Two Guvnors, an update of the Italian comedy The Servant of Two Masters, has also conquered New York; its star, Jamie Corden, just won the Tony for best actor. Also from the National Theatre stable is War Horse, which at the moment seems to be everywhere, including Toronto; it was directed by Marianne Elliott, a comparative newcomer whose track record at the National is second only to that of Hytner himself.

I recently spent a week in London, during which I saw three of Hytner's own National Theatre productions and wrangled an interview with the man. Rumours have been circulating of his impending resignation; he would only say, smiling, that they were "exaggerated." He did allow, though, that he would be staying long enough "to see the renovations out."

The priority here, he says, is making the National Theatre "building closer to the river, rather than just a concrete fortress, facing Waterloo Bridge." The opening up of the South Bank of the Thames, from the National and the Royal Festival concert hall eastwards to the Globe Theatre, is the best thing to have happened to the city in years. It's a cultural wonderland that, Hytner says, "happened organically."

Making the National seem more fully part of it involves the closing for one year of the Cottesloe, the smallest of the building's three stages. When it reopens, Hytner wants it to be "more flexible - somewhere where you can put things on for just a couple of weeks." His own past policy for the Cottesloe has been "to put a moratorium on the great classic plays - before that, they'd been doing a lot of Shakespeare and Chekhov there. Actors were being seduced by doing great plays in small spaces."

This is hardly surprising, but Hytner thinks the place for the major plays is on the National's major stages - the platform Olivier and the proscenium Lyttelton. I remarked that in Stratford, Ont., the riskier Shakespeare works have been confined to the Tom Patterson theatre, our equivalent of the Cottesloe, eliciting from Hytner the transatlantic injunction, "Don't! The more fearful you are, the more conservative your audiences become."

The miracle of NT Live, beamed into your local multiplex, has demonstrated Hytner's own prowess at mounting big plays in big spaces; these have included Racine's Phedre, with Helen Mirren in the lead, and Hamlet, with the young Rory Kinnear, one of the few Hamlets who have actually moved me.

NT Live also brought us One Man, Two Guvnors with its original cast, the one that's appearing now in New York. In London, where the show's transferred to the West End, I saw the take-over cast. They aren't as unforced as their predecessors, but the show is still uproariously funny. Richard Bean, one of Britain's leading comedy writers, has transferred Carlo Goldoni's original to the seaside town of Brighton on the cusp of the 1950s, a time and place apparently rife with small-time gangsters and boasting - a dazzling new idea for the time - a pub serving food. This is the scene of the legendary set piece in which the hungry two-timing servant serves dinner simultaneously to both his employers, here a dangerous love-struck crook and an upper-class wonder.

In both story and spirit, the show is remarkably faithful to Goldoni; it's heartwarming that, nearly 400 years later, he should be a commercial success on two continents and on his own terms.

The idea was Hytner's: "I wanted to program something purely entertaining. I also wanted to bring back Jamie Corden." Corden had been one of the original History Boys, but one of the less-noticed. Corden had come back to Britain and written his own TV series, which Hytner describes as "very warm and human, not contemptuous." Those qualities infuse his performance in this show, and they're shared by his London successor, Owain Arthur.

Back at the South Bank base, I saw two more Hytner productions, both new plays with Russian settings.

The less substantial of the two was Travelling Light, by Nicholas Wright. The work is concerned with the birth of film, hence the too-clever title, and is mostly set in a shtetl; it's a surprise to enter a theatre expecting to encounter old Hollywood and to find yourself looking at what might be the set for Fiddler on the Roof.

The main action is framed by Hollywood scenes; an expatriate director is shooting a movie about how he got his start back in the old country, and there's magic in the way in which one period and location melt into another. I found it beguiling, if hardly major.

Collaborators, in the Olivier, also has movie connections; its author, John Hughes, is a screenwriter who's never written for the stage before. The collaborators of the title are Stalin and the playwright Mikhail Bulgakov, whom Stalin commissioned to write a celebratory play about him. This did in fact happen, though the play was never produced.

I wasn't crazy about some of the supporting acting, but the production is beautifully fluid and the central relationship is wittily written, and gorgeously played by two recurring ornaments of the Hytner regime, and of the British theatre in general.
2012-06-20-thank-you-for-the-music-disse:
Ihad the same knee-jerk reaction as everyone else to the announcement that the Stratford Festival would be producing Youre a Good Man, Charlie Brown: Why was Stratford, in a season already heavily freighted with musicals, scheduling a trifling piece thats basically a children's show? That wasn't fair of me: As originally written, Charlie Brown is, at the very least, a better musical than some Stratford has selected. (Its better, for example, than 42nd Street.) And, like the Peanuts strip on which its based, it wasn't principally intended for children, though it obviously, like other superior entertainment, from Alice in Wonderland to The Simpsons, has crossover appeal.

The trouble is--one of the troubles is -- the show Stratford is presenting isn't the original, which was a small, charming piece with a small, charming score by Clark Gesner; that was adulterated (not perhaps the mot juste) some years ago with, presumably, the consent of Gesner himself who was alive then but isnt now. Andrew Lippa wrote some new songs, which arent up to the standard of the old ones and, worse yet, caused some of the old ones to be eliminated. I especially miss the breezily cynical Little Known Facts ( "I know now that you can't trust a daisy / They tell, every chance they get.") The book, also by Gesner, has been interfered with as well. I may be imagining that it used to include a sketch--a better term than scene since the show is more a revue than a narrative--about Lucy kicking Charlie Brown's football away; but Im positive that there used to be one about Linus and the Great Pumpkin. Why lose them?

Gesners original score gets slurpy on its closing number Happiness, but that's forgivable given such a delight as the ensemble Book Report, with its five viewpoints on Peter Rabbit, culminating in Charlie Brown's own shout out to procrastinators everywhere: I work best under pressure / And therell be lots of pressure / If I wait till tomorrow. That, of course, is a prime example of the shows fidelity to the spirit of Charles M. Schulz; it presents varieties of adult angst and projects them on to a group of six-year-olds (and a dog).

It's a dark show masquerading as bland. It's also undeniably cute, but that element needs to be kept in check. Stratford, though, at both the programming and production levels, has bought into the idea that its all for the kids, and it goes to exhausting lengths to ingratiate itself with them, or maybe just to make itself feel youthful. Donna Feore, directing and choreographing, injects a lot of hip hop. Michael Gianfrancescos set design mainly consists of garish screen images, incorporating speech bubbles, just to remind us of the show's cartoon origins. Snoopy is also heavily into video--he's a gaming addict. This may make 21st century youngsters feel at home; it may also make them feel condescended to.

The cast is mostly very good, especially Ken James Stewart, whos Charlie Brown to the hopeful heartbreaking life; his monologue both hoping and fearing to be noticed by the little red-haired girl is the best thing in the show (and, not coincidentally, the quietest). Kevin Yees Linus is charming, likewise Andrew Broderick's Schroeder, and Erica Peck is a powerhouse Lucy. Amy Wallis works unbecomingly hard to provide an equally powerhouse Sally, which the show doesn't need; blame the new authorized version that put her in and put Peppermint Patty out. As Snoopy, Stephen Patterson has razzmatazz to spare, and keeps sharing it with the humans, though hes meant to be laid-back and aloof, except when hungry. His big number Suppertime is supposed to be a surprise, and being so can work very simply; this production, and this performance, have already upped the ante so far that they have no option but to overkill us some more. Left to his own devices, which might not include descending an illuminated staircase and having the other actors butt in as chorus, this Snoopy would probably be very effective.

Musical massacre on a larger scale comes in The Pirates of Penzance, Stratfords return to Gilbert and Sullivan. Ethan MacSweeney's production isn't without its pleasures; in a staging that takes us into the sea as well as beside it, I greatly enjoyed the surprise appearance of one character in a frogmans suit. Im also a sucker for elaborate scenes that take us backstage at a Victorian theatre before reversing perspective for the show proper, though in this case I couldn't see the ultimate point. What sinks this particular pirate ship--most surprisingly from a director who has professed his delight at finding how funny the piece is--is how hard it is to make out most of the words. C. David Johnson's difficulties with rhythm and enunciation may have been peculiar to the first night; all the same, if you splutter your way through Major General Stanleys major general patter song, you arent meeting the job description. Insult gets added to injury in an interpolated reprise commemorating Stratford's 60th year; this kind of self-celebration is faintly embarrassing anyway, and the notion that "gang of four" rhymes with Bangalore amounts, in a show with W.S. Gilbert's name on its cover, to a diabolical liberty.

Elsewhere, over-production runs riot, especially in an overextended fight scene that effectively kills the scripted ending. On the way, even such a traditionally infallible number as the police sergeants lament about his lot not being a happy one gets ruined, so tricked out with Scottish-accented-coppers in kilts that lift to reveal Union Jack underpants, that even the great Steve Ross cant save it. Sean Arbuckle plays the Pirate King on the same lines of accident-prone flamboyance that made Kevin Kline a Broadway star some years back; by now, this role could use less Errol Flynn and Johnny Depp and more Robert Newton.

There are some compensations: Gabrielle Jones makes a good, clean, efficient job of Ruth, the requisite G&S heavy lady. Above all, and blessedly, there is Kyle Blair who sings like an angel, moves like a demon, and makes of Frederic, the pirate apprentice and subtitular "slave of duty," a delightfully dedicated and demented idealist. Full-bloodedly tongue in cheek, this is likely a definitive performance. Amy Wallis, more happily cast here than in Charlie Brown, meets him on his vocal heights as a self-parodying kind of coloratura. Not that I'm convinced there's any other kind. Sullivan's taste for operatic parody is well-known. In Pirates, it seems to account for about 80% of the score.

robert.cushman@hotmail.caYou're a Good Man, Charlie Brown runs through Oct. 28, The Pirates of Penzance through Oct. 27, both at the Avon Theatre, Stratford. For ticket

2012-06-23-award-analysis-comparing-cont:
Its prize-giving time in Toronto theatre again, and even if it's not twice as exciting as it used to be, at least it's twice as populous. On Monday, the long-established Dora awards will be announced and presented. But this is also the second successive season for which the citys theatre critics have organized their own awards, whose recipients were released to a breathlessly expectant world at the end of last month. Our choices - five of us hacks argued it out, three from the dailies, two from weeklies - overlapped somewhat with those of the Dora nominators, but not as much as you might expect. Some of their choices make me roll my eyes, but I daresay some of ours make them - whoever they are - do the same. Anyway, some thoughts and forecasts on the Dora hopefuls in what, by general consent, has been an unusually strong Toronto season.

It hasnt been a crowded time for great new plays, but then no time is. The Doras hem themselves in by confining their outstanding new play category to plays that have received their world premieres in Toronto. The equivalent critical prize is for best Canadian play, which at least meant we could give serious consideration to Carole Frechette's The Small Room at the Top of the Stairs (an import from Quebec) even though we eventually lighted on Ins Choi's very Torontonian Kims Convenience. This is also on the Dora list, and the smart money must be on it to win, as its local without being parochial; it puts the everyday city recognizably onstage while being funny and touching in its own right. Among its competitors, Pamela Mala Sinha's Crash, while distinguished, is limited by being a monologue (maybe that should be a separate category - there are certainly enough of them every year); Ajax and Little Iliad was an oddball double bill, only half of which worked; and, going to the opposite extreme of scale, the choice of Luminato's One Thousand and One Nights is baffling. An international rather than a homegrown show, and more notable as a staging than as a script, it might have been expected to turn up, if anywhere, among the best touring productions. That it doesnt, while the very Canadian Ride the Cyclone does, suggests the rules are getting tangled. One notable feature of this years Dora picks for new play: not one of them is by an established playwright. Cyclone is the work of comparative newcomers as well, which is encouraging.

The Cyclone's regional origins also exclude it from the Dora lists for outstanding new musical for which, if admitted, it would surely have been a shoo-in; although lumping musicals and operas together, as the Doras do in all their musical categories, does muddy the waters somewhat. I wasn't even one of Cyclones greatest fans, but I cant see that it had any serious competition, given the inadmissability of the American Caroline or Change. The latter, though, is up for outstanding musical production (concentrate hard; there is a difference) and I can't see any defensible way it could lose. It won the equivalent critics' award; we also handed out prizes to two of its cast, Arlene Duncan (best actress in a musical) and Deborah Hay (best supporting actress in same.) Our enthusiasm, though, is nothing to that of the Doras jurors, who have handed four out of five nominations for outstanding female performance in a musical to ladies from that cast and two out of five for outstanding male performance to its gentlemen. One of the latter, Michael Levinson, is a very young gentleman indeed, and if he wins, he should be cheered for more than sentimental reasons; his was simply, singing included, one of the best child performances Ive ever seen.

Paul Sun-Hyung Lee, playing Kim of convenience fame, will likely take the principal male in a play award for the same good reasons that the play itself will win. His main competitors, I'd guess, are Nigel Shawn Williams and Kevin Hanchard, both for performances in Topdog Underdog that were fine when they gave them at the Shaw Festival and, by all accounts, even finer when they gave them again in Toronto. Also nominated are another Shavian, Jim Mezon, a wonderful actor who in Red gave, to my mind, one of his less wonderful performances; and Michael Healey, who in Clybourne Park, gave possibly his most wonderful performance - it certainly extended him. Anyway, it's good to see that show recognized for something; its the best American play to reach us in years, but the Doras have no mechanism for acknowledging plays from away. The critics introduced one this year; it went to The Golden Dragon by everyones favourite German, Roland Schimmelpfennig.

As for outstanding principal female: The critics' choice was Nicole Underhay (in The Small Room), and I'd also root for her among the Dora gals, despite competition from Pamela Sinha (but see my earlier caveat regarding monologues) and Maev Beaty. The other nominations I dont understand; one of them is for a performance that came close to being downright bad. The most shameful omission from the list is Megan Follows, who was amazing in The Penelopiad. Now, you might claim that she, along with all the other ladies in that cast, has been recognized, because theres a category labelled outstanding performance in a supporting role/ensemble, and the ensembles for both The Penelopiad and The Golden Dragon have been listed there. It's a cop-out. Since ensemble" means the entire cast, just whom are they meant to be supporting? A separate "ensemble" category might make sense; the current arrangement just puts an additional squeeze on a box that already has to accommodate performances straight and musical, male and female. The three individuals who made it this year are Fiona Reid (White Biting Dog), Jeff Lillico (The Glass Menagerie), and Ryan Kelly (The Normal Heart): all deserving cases, but there are so many others.

Finally, there's outstanding production of a play or musical (one award) and theres outstanding direction (two awards, one for each genre). As you might expect, theres a lot of overlap. In fact, the only production not nominated for direction is War Horse. The original director, Marianne Elliott, didn't travel with it, but it was obviously still her staging. And some staging it is, getting additional nods in the sound, costume and choreography departments. It may very well gallop home with all of them. It depends on how tender towards the commercial theatre (it's a Mirvish show here) the judges feel this year. Theyve been known to swing both ways. There are also lighting and sound nominations for The Small Room at the Top of the Stairs, as well there should be. It should also be up for best production and best direction, but it isnt. The director was Weyni Mengesha, also responsible for Kim's Convenience. You'd think the Doras, which love a multiple nominee, would have noticed.

2012-06-25-biggest-play-on-the-blocks-wh:
The musical hit in London at the moment, in fact the biggest in years, is Matilda, based on the classic children's novel by Roald Dahl.

It started as a holiday show presented by the Royal Shakespeare Company at their home base in Stratford-upon-Avon. Now installed in the West End, its attracted unanimous critical raves, sell-out audiences and a record number of awards. In other words, its overrated.

The best thing about it, though, is the staging. The show is directed by Matthew Warchus and, as designed by Rob Howell, it's a fluid, colourful and inventive production that unfolds on a set whose main building blocks are building blocks: outsized versions of the alphabetical aids by which schoolchildren have been taught to read. This suits a story that's set in a school, even though the heroine is already preternaturally literate, a devourer of Dickens and Dostoevsky and a formidable storyteller in her own right.

These accomplishments earn her the hatred of her parents, the Wormwoods; Mr. W, a crooked used-car salesman, wanted a boy anyway (and insists on referring to Matilda as such) while his wife regards motherhood as a tiresome interruption of her commitment to ballroom dancing.

As punishment for her incorrigible intelligence, five-year-old Matilda is sent to a school whose motto is children are maggots and whose principal, a Miss Trunchbull, acts vigorously and sadistically on that principle. Shes a teacher for whom phys ed is the only ed that counts. She confines recalcitrant pupils to a closet lined with nails, and is a world champion at throwing the hammer, though if no hammers are available, children will do.

If Miss Trunchbull can move humans with her muscles, then Matilda, at least in this version of the story, can move less animate objects with her mind. These extraordinary powers, acquired disconcertingly late in the action and just as suddenly dispensed with, allow her to do battle with her oppressor-in-chief and to champion the meek but kindly teacher who seems to comprise the whole school staff.

In fact this teacher, Miss Honey, gradually emerges as the shows real heroine, which leads to a damaging split in focus. This can't be blamed on the performers. There are five rotating Matildas, and the one I saw was excellent; so were all the children in the cast, and so were Haley Flaherty as Miss Honey and Melanie La Barrie as a friendly librarian.

In fact, and unexpectedly, the sympathetic characters come off better than the villains. The senior Wormwoods do their blowsy best, but have been handed ham-fisted material, the wrong kind of caricature. Mr. Wormwood's lecture to the audience on the virtues of TV is an especially low point.

At least, though, these two are cartoons of actual parental abuse. Miss Trunchbull is another matter. Yes, this is a fantasy and yes, there have always been sadistic teachers in English schools, but any remotely like this one would have been closed down; it isnt the 19th century any more.

Matilda herself, as a reader of Dickens, would be able to point out the difference between Mr. Squeers, a monster drawn from life, and Miss Trunchbull, a monster for the sake of having a monster, and therefore no real threat. The show itself unwittingly illustrates this by bringing in, just before the end, some representatives of the Russian Mafia who are funny but just about believable; or rather, funny because theyre just about believable.

Miss Trunchbull, by contrast, is an excuse for a thin-lipped drag act; the actor who plays the role, Bertie Carvel, has been rewarded with praise, but I couldn't love hating him. Ross Petty could do better and, come the Canadian production (the show's slated for Broadway next year, but will get here eventually) he probably will.

As for the score, music and lyrics are by Tim Minchin: It starts well, with an ensemble song about how wonderful parents think their children are, or how wonderful children think their parents think they are; given how the story develops, this is touchingly ironic. Thereafter, the simpler numbers are the best; the ones that try for wit or wordplay arent as clever as they think they are. Still, as with Billy Elliot, those anxious to proclaim the next "great British musical" arent bothered.

The RSC were also represented in London by Written on the Heart, a contrastingly sober piece about the birth of the English Bible, which is a more combustible subject than you might expect: literally so, given the fiery fates of some of the pioneer translators of the 16th century.

David Edgar has written an honest, sober if sometimes bafflingly detailed piece, served up with equally honest, sober acting in the principal roles and some either stiff or colourless among the supports.

This places it ahead of The Duchess of Malfi at the Old Vic, in which most of the performers seemed to be imitating, at a distance, some imagined style thought appropriate to Jacobean tragedy and basically consisting of not seeming to believe what you say. That doesn't apply to Eve Best, one of the most highly regarded of younger English actresses, though probably best known here as Edie Falco's tall doctor sidekick in Nurse Jackie; her choices were consistently fresh and thoughtful, though she overdid the haughtiness and was unexpectedly hard to hear.

For the rest, and especially remembering the last Stratford production of the play, it was hard not to feel that we generally act the classics better, the difference probably being not one of talent but of tradition. Or, to put it more prosaically, practice.
2012-06-29-high-standards-nellie-mckay-b:
Its worth checking out Nellie McKay on YouTube, although she might not want you to. She describes the Internet as a bag full of poison and refuses to be on Facebook or Twitter. She says these things, as she seems to say most things, with an enchanting whispery earnestness, which is a tone that's prevalent in her music as well.

McKay is a New York-based singer-songwriter whose birthdate is a secret to Wikipedia but whom I would peg at about 30. She's about to visit Canada to play at the Ottawa, Toronto and Montreal Jazz Festivals. This, like much else about her, is intriguing, because she isnt commonly thought of as a jazz performer, though jazz certainly figures among the many styles and influences that permeate her work.

On one of those YouTube clips youll find her singing, to her own piano accompaniment, the track Sari, which seems to be a pun on the song's key word "sorry"; it's a pounding mock-apologia for just about everything, from the way she dresses to losing a Monty Python CD, whose conclusion - most of all, Im sorry for you, suggests she isnt really sorry at all.

Better still is a clip that starts with her getting up from the piano (whatever she's been doing there remains a secret), picking up a small guitar and going into a song called Mother of Pearl, which begins with what is probably her most famous line, "feminists don't have a sense of humour," on which she elaborates with the more inventive theyve got a tumour on their funny bone.

The point of the song is, of course, that feminists do have a sense of humour - certainly this one does - but it sounds slyer here than it does in its official recorded version. On the CD, a male chorus chimes in with the sexist, derisive comments the song is lampooning; live, she delivers them herself, between barely audible quotation marks, which is funnier and more devastating. She then goes into a song she didnt write, one that in fact dates back to 1928: the sweet, yearning If I Had You, whose avowal "I could cross the burning desert" she makes more touching and fervent than any other singer I have heard.

Between 2004 and 2010, McKay recorded five CDs, four of her own material and one tribute to Doris Day that finds her, apart from her singing, taking turns on seven different instruments. That's more than she actually admits to playing.

I fool around on about four, she tells me in the first of three phone conversations this week and last. (She has a hectic schedule, even without preparing for Canada, and sounded gentle but frazzled.) "The number goes up when we run out of money." At the jazz festivals, it'll be just her, the piano and whatever else she cares to play, which I suspect is preferable. She writes some headlong, wordy, free-associating lyrics; and on record, with a band, they can get lost in the mix.

I hope, she says, "therell be a few less words as I go on."

Of course, live (or on YouTube) you get the bonus of seeing as well as hearing McKay: blond and blue-ribboned, simultaneously demure and outspoken, fragile and steely, with a wide-eyed look that matches her wide-eyed voice (if there is such a thing).

Shes nervous about meeting jazz festival expectations, but at least it seems her repertoire will match up. This festival season, she'll be concentrating on the standards. If it was up to me, I'd sing them all the time. Theyre fresh, theyre exquisite; there's a reason people can't stop singing them, she says. "It makes you a little embarrassed to record your own songs after all those beautiful melodies."

McKay is also quite the musical scholar. On Normal as Blueberry Pie, the Doris Day album, she sometimes sounds more authentic than her model. Day, in her movies, sang 1920s songs in 40s and 50s arrangements; McKay has gone back to the originals. On Crazy Rhythm, her inspiration was Whispering Jack Smith, a pioneering crooner of whom few artists of her generation can even have heard.

Those '20s arrangements, they change, they do repeats, she says, before asking earnestly, "have you ever seen Second Chorus? I love it." It's a 1940 Fred Astaire movie from which comes a Johnny Mercer song with the deathless title (I Aint Hep to That Step But Ill) Dig It. Day sang it in her band-singer days, because it was current; McKay excavates the Astaire original, complete with an intro on which she trades jivey rhythmic spoken phrases with the boys in the band. It's my favourite thing on the CD.

McKay says she doesn't know where her own songs originate. It could be a melody, it could be the lyric, which neatly pre-empts the old question about which comes first. "I always say, I only wrote them. I dont know why Mother of Pearl is called that," she adds. Maybe it has something to do with Janis Joplin. Or maybe its a drug reference.

McKay also says that most of her songs aren't autobiographical. Asked to name one that could be, she chooses The Dog Song, a ragtime romper in honour of a pet that had been put down: "I don't care bout your hatin and your doubt/ And I don't care what the politicians spout/If you want a companion/Well, just go right to the pound/And find yourself a hound."

It figures, since McKay is a fervent spokesperson for People for the Ethical Treatment of Animals and, naturally, a vegetarian: another of the accusations misogynistically hurled by the redneck chorus of Mother of Pearl. This may explain why, of all the great pop vocalists, she chose to honour Day, whose principal postretirement profile has been as an animal rights activist. (McKay also has a biting - in every sense - song about eating burgers.) But in other respects, she's hard to pin down.

Like Randy Newman and Dave Frishberg, two writers McKay admires, shes oblique, a musical actor. Shes appeared on Broadway in The Threepenny Opera, and both her (divorced) parents are actors; her mother, Robin Pappas, some of whose work I saw and admired in Britain in the early '80s, is now her sometime producer and fulltime manager.

She has extraordinary taste, McKay says. "She adds the good stuff; I supply the drive." And, more prosaically, It's good to have someone you can trust; who can take care of all the stuff that has to be planned: visas, flights. In this business, nobody wants to be the facilitator. I was very naive when I started. Maybe I should have some media training. I can't seem to stop getting into trouble.

She says things like that in a whimsically self-deprecating tone few others could get away with, as when she talks of her own work. "I take credit for the bad songs. The good ones come from someplace else."

Nellie McKay plays the Ottawa Jazz Festival on June 29, the Toronto Jazz Festival on June 30 and the Montreal Jazz Festival on July 2.

2012-06-30-politics-of-theatre-on-ken-ga:
Just over a week ago, the board of Toronto's Factory Theatre caused a sensation by announcing that they had fired their long-serving artistic director, Ken Gass. Gass's service has been exceptionally long, since he's had the job twice. He actually started the Factory way back in 1970 and, 15 years ago, returned to run it again, sinking some of his own money into it to save it from a threatened closure. This record obviously places him in a strong moral and artistic position. It's strengthened by the fact that the issues between him and the board are cloudy. Gass hasn't said much, and what the board has said sounds petty.

About all that seems agreed is that Gass wanted major structural renovations to the place that would, among other things, make it more wheel chair accessible. The board, while agreeing in principle, decided that Gass's proposals were too expensive. On Wednesday, they issued a statement citing unspecified "irreconcilable differences" and saying that "this wonderful institution - is in great shape, and we are moving ahead with our new season and plans to renovate our building." This, of course, is the kind of thing that always gets said in such circumstances, and it hardly addresses the difficulty of finding a new artistic director at short notice or of how that director will organize the next season, at even shorter notice and in a climate of inevitable suspicion. George F. Walker, Factory's senior playwright, has already, as a gesture of solidarity with Gass, announced the withdrawal of a scheduled new play of his own

The Factory building could certainly use a facelift. Still, it seems to me that, given the way theatres and other organizations are governed and financed, the board was within its rights - was, in fact, doing its job - in deciding what it could or could not afford. It also seems that the right thing in these circumstances would have been to state this position to Gass and to give him the option of accepting it or not. If he couldn't accept it, he would have had to resign. This would still have caused bad blood, but nothing like the amount that's been caused by simply ousting him. It might also have made for a relatively peaceable transition period. The present furore is reminiscent, if on a smaller scale, of the scandal that rocked the Stratford Festival in 1980 (and that's being rather clumsily memorialized in the current Festival production of The Pirates of Penzance), when the incoming artistic directors unofficially dubbed the Gang of Four were summarily dismissed because the board thought - wrongly as it turned out - that they could secure somebody more famous. The Factory board, though, don't even appear to have a glamorous replacement up their sleeve.

Gass was offered a severance package and the title of artistic director emeritus. It's hard not to agree with his description of the latter proposal as "a ludicrous token position." It's the kind of gesture that committees make when they're feeling embarrassed. If there are artistic, as opposed to architectural, disagreements between Gass and the board, then neither side is coming clean about them. The Factory's track record under Gass has been up and down, but I wouldn't expect that to be different under any conceivable successor. The theatre has built its identity on doing Canadian, and only Canadian, plays - mainly new ones. There are not, and are unlikely ever to be, enough of those to make up seasons composed entirely of winners.

Of course, you never know. The late John Hirsch, in 1981, did manage to save Stratford's bacon when all had thought it irretrievably lost. And who, a year or two ago, would have guessed that the Toronto house to emerge most triumphant at this season's Doras would be Theatre Passe Muraille? TPM housed and coproduced Ride the Cyclone, which took the award for best touring production (and would undoubtedly have taken more if the Doras' rules weren't so arcane), and Crash, which won in four categories, including two of the sexiest: best play and best female performance. Both of those statuettes went to the same lady, actress and playwright Pamela Mala Sinha. Since she was also in the cast of The Penelopiad, which won best ensemble, she this year received two-and-one thirteenth Doras. This probably isn't a record, but it's certainly noteworthy.

And there was I, absolutely confident that Kim's Convenience, a triumph of feelgood theatre, would win for best play and best male performance. It lost out in the latter to Nigel Shawn Williams in Topdog/Underdog; I suspect that I discounted Williams and his equally meritorious co-star Kevin Hanchard because I'd never registered that show, an import from the Shaw Festival, as a Toronto production. It was indeed co-produced by the city's own Obsidian Theatre, which also had a year, as it was responsible along with the musical specialists Acting Up Theatre, for Caroline or Change, which cleaned up on a scale that even I hadn't anticipated.

The Dora show itself was one of the better ones with Eric Peterson, in the home stretch, qualifying for an award himself as best scene-stealing presenter. Maybe next year they should make him the host. After all, he can even sing; though perhaps not as well as Thom Allison, who presided this year in glittering style, though his presumably satirical opening number might have been even more devastating if the sound system had let us hear any of the words.

While I'm on a mea culpa kick: I've been justifiably assailed on the National Post website for misattributing songs and sketches that I said were missing from Stratford's You're a Good Man, Charlie Brown. Actually they're from another show entirely, or almost entirely: a show called Snoopy!!! that was a follow-up to the original Clark Gesner show, but in the way of sequels, never caught on the same extent. It is, though, at least as good, and has an excellent score by the underrated Larry Grossman: not that I want to give anybody any ideas. Anyway, my bad: I'm currently in sackcloth, and have sent out for some ashes.

Peter Redman, National Post / Earlier this week, Ken Gass was fired as artistic director of Factory Theatre.; Caption:

'What kind of war is this?" asks someone, to which someone else replies, "It's like all wars, ugly and stupid." I think the someone is Laura Secord, but there's so much doubling going on that I could well have got it wrong. The someone else is a grievously wounded soldier; his response sums up VideoCabaret's view of wars, and indeed of history in general, and it can be pretty hard to argue with. The conflict dramatized here is The War of 1812, which is also the title of the relevant instalment of VideoCab's ongoing cartoon epic, The History of the Village of the Small Huts. Usually this unfolds in the backroom of the Cameron House in Toronto (where it's now on its second go-round) but this show, for obvious celebratory reasons, is being presented at Stratford in a space - the Studio Annex - new to public performance, that's been set up to replicate the troupe's customary black box as closely as possible.

The surroundings may be different but the quality is the same. That is to say the writing (by Michael Hollingsworth) is pungent, the staging (also by Hollingsworth) is brilliant, the set and lighting (Andy Moro) are superbly precise and economic, the costumes (Astrid Janson) are even more superbly garish, the actors are without exception quick-change virtuosi as they appear and reappear in a dizzying succession of frocks, wigs, accents and personalities. For those who have never seen a VideoCabaret show: The video part derives from the action taking place on a tiny oblong stage suggestive of a TV screen. Each brief scene is succeeded by a blackout (this isn't quite as efficient a process in Stratford as it usually is at the home base) during which the next group of actors takes position, faster and more accurately than you would think humanly possible. The dimensions of the stage mean that none of the performers is ever visible below the knee, thus lending a whole new meaning to the phrase "footloose and fancy free."

The brevity of the scenes also accounts for the cabaret part. It's cabaret as the Berlin of the 1930s conceived it: nasty, brutish and short. That's not an aspersion on the creators (Hollingsworth and his associate director Deanne Taylor are lovely people) but it is the view of life that they present. Everybody who figures in their dramatic universe is a buffoon, a poltroon or a dupe; some manage to score in more than one of those categories. As I've noted before, keeping the scenes so short is a vital part of the world view; no character sticks around long enough to exhibit any redeeming features, or indeed any complexity of any kind. This is certainly bracing, and it can also, though less frequently than you might expect, be extremely funny. It does, though, end up feeling monotonous.

There are eight actors in The War of 1812 and between them they play, if the program and I have counted correctly, 55 characters. The first one we meet is U.S. President James Madison who, with Britain busy fighting Napoleon on the other side of the world, decides to invade its northern dominion because - well, just because. His wife is concerned about the effect on her social calendar, and their murderous frivolity sets the tone for the evening. The powerful people are despicable and the powerless, with one important exception, deserve them.

My favourite of all the plays in the cycle has been The Great War, which, without ever sentimentalizing, did discover a vein of compassion for the soldiers caught in the never-ending crossfire. The one character in the current episode to be treated with comparable sympathy and respect is Tecumseh, the First Nations chief lured into allying himself with the Canadians. Anand Rajaram gives him wit, dignity and an ironic awareness of everybody else's incompetence. Dying early, Tecumseh was spared the final humiliation of seeing his treaties dishonoured and his lands lost, and one can't help wishing that the script had cheated history and left him alive to bear poignant witness to his own and his people's disillusion. That task falls instead to his brother the Prophet, who does it nobly, though as played by Michaela Washburn it's hard not to think of him as Tecumseh's sister. Before joining VideoCabaret, Rajaram was one of the jewels of Second City, specializing in Asian roles; in this show he is, to put it doubly incorrectly, one kind of Indian playing another kind of Indian, but he also appears as a halfdozen other characters and makes an economically devastating impression in each of them. Mac Fyfe, who may be the signature VideoCabbie, is especially effective here as blood-andguts Captain Fitzgibbon, who gains a kind of respect by at least being efficiently ruthless and doing it in a crisp Celtic accent. Richard Clarkin is contrastingly, and entertainingly, foppish as General Brock, and everyone else is absolutely fine.

Nobody could accuse VideoCabaret of making cheap patriotic fodder out of a bicentennial. Both the play and the program note end with the pointed reminder that, after all the bloodshed, the war ended with the borders exactly as they were when it began. Though, given that the intention of at least one side was forcibly to redraw or remove them, that may not be quite such an insignificant achievement. Anyway, anyone (and I include myself) who's avidly following the Canadian story as told by this company will find this chapter of it well up to snuff. Anyone encountering it for the first time will be knocked out.

The War of 1812 runs through Aug. 12 at the Studio Annex, Stratford. Visit stratfordfestival.ca or call 18005671600 for more information.
