THEATRE REVIEW

A Midsummer Night's Dream

High Park Amphitheatre, Toronto

The critic's prayer, offered up regularly every January, is, "Please let me get through the year without having to see A Midsummer Night's Dream again. And if I do have to see it, please let it be indoors."

There may, though, be a lesson here, on the lines of being careful what you wish not to happen. Good, fresh stagings of the Dream do come along every so often. In all my years on this job, I count three of them, of which two, I confess, were in the open air. Now along comes Richard Rose's production, also alfresco, to make it four. It's by far the best thing I've seen at what used to be known as the Dream in High Park but has now renamed itself Shakespeare in the Park, possibly to fend off any advances from rival playwrights.

One thing that distinguishes Rose's production from previous High Park offerings is that it seems to enjoy the park itself, and wants us to enjoy it, too. There's no built-up setting getting in the way of the natural one. Indeed, about the only scenic feature is an onstage painting depicting yet more parkland, or a small section of same. The proceedings are fresh, funny and fast, the last quality owing something to the fact that the text has been quite extensively trimmed: something of which I disapprove in theory but which I appreciated in practice. The cuts are playful and intelligent, as is most of the show.

Theseus's court on this occasion looks and sounds traditionally - indeed stereotypically - Canadian, with pipers piping and Mounties mounting guard. The duke himself arrives by golf cart, his bride in the passenger seat, and delivers his opening speech through a microphone, giving the populace official notice of the approaching festivities. As is now customary to the point of cliche, his Hippolyta strongly resents the arrangement, but the obvious objection to this interpretation (i.e. that not a single line in the text supports it) is more cleverly overcome than usual. The lady delivers her own, equally celebratory, speech over the same PA system, through gritted teeth and obviously under duress. Later in the scene, she responds to her lover's attempt to bring her back into the conversation by getting into the golf cart and driving off in it. That'll teach him to patronize an Amazon. So there is at least the skeleton of a relationship here, one that feeds logically into the couple's transformation (now equally traditional, though equally tendentious) into Oberon and Titania.

As far as I've ever been able to follow it, the argument behind the doubling is that the eventual reconciliation of their fairy surrogates allows the royal mortals to work out their own differences. But as Oberon brings Titania to heel by playing a cruel erotic trick on her and blackmailing her into handing over her adopted child, it seems about as much of a feminist victory as The Taming of the Shrew, if not less so.

Still, the immortal couple's initial confrontation gains enormously here by being staged as a one-on-one verbal duel, unhampered by giggly attendants; and also by having Titania carrying the disputed changeling around with her, obviously intent on doing an ill-met-by-moonlit flit. Tamara Podemski's Hippolyta and Titania make an excellent double, respectively sulky and sultry. Dmitry Chepovetsky is a jovial enough Theseus, but is hampered as Oberon by his inability to sustain a legato line. His chief vocal resource is a threatening snort, mainly employed to keep Gil Garratt's laboriously recalcitrant Puck in line; his more benevolent impulses are hardly credible.

Titaniaapart, it's the humans who come off best here, right down to John Dolan's heavy father Egeus, that grumpy advocate of honour killing; his entry down the middle of the auditorium disrupts the scene as passionately as it should. In his wake come the rival young men, who are contrasted studies in entitlement; Eric Morin's Lysander is a narcissistic macho man, much given to tearing of his own and other people's clothes, while Ali Momen's Demetrius, a more subtle portrait, is a bespectacled nerd driven to competing extremes of petulant frustration by the girl he loves and the one who loves him.

The latter is Sarah Sherman's Helena, the self-styled spaniel, revelling in her role as everyone's complaining victim; the former is Sophia Kolinas' pert Hermia, whose awakening in the forest is the most revelatory moment of the evening; she takes her solitude as a playful joke on her lover's part before realizing, terrified, that it's the real thing. Both these actresses are to be watched.

What about the workers? The script names six of them; here there are only four, and three of them have their names and ethnicities, and all of them their occupations, altered. Peter Quince is now Pierre Le Coing, a temperamental auteur whom Pierre Simpson makes uncannily convincing. Flute the bellows-mender (this must have been a specialized trade even in Elizabethan England) is now Francis Filchenkov, gaunt and Slavic and, in Mark Crawford's performance, amusingly enthusiastic in his drag role as Thisbe.

Tom Snout the tinker is now, courtesy of Richard Lee, Tom Chow the gofer and the only man among them to speak in the stage rustic generally known as Mummerset. Nick Bottom is still Nick Bottom but he's moved up from weaver to silk-scarved realtor, with airs to match; in John Cleland's enchanting performance he's unshakably sure of himself, and is the only aspiring Pyramus I remember to audition for the role of tyrant by underplaying rather than the reverse; it's very effective.

The fairies - Pease blossom, Cobweb & Co. - who attend on him after his transformation to an ass are played by his fellows, similarly transmogrified in skirts. This is funny, but it's also daft: Why should they worry what's happened to him when they've seen it for themselves? Or is this just random doubling, for the sake of economy? Those who know the play may be kept in pleasing suspense over just how, in these reduced circumstances, the mechanicals will mount their play-within-the-play.

Actually, it works out beautifully. Moonshine's part is taken by Monsieur Le Coing himself, and it's one of the best things he does. As for he - or she - who plays the Lion's part: A volunteer is enlisted from the audience, and you wouldn't believe how well that goes. Well, maybe you would.

And there's another extra character; in celebration of her 60th anniversary, Queen Elizabeth II makes a personal appearance - in a different person every night, apparently - in the onstage audience. Which, since the Dream may have originally been written as a court entertainment, is appropriate as well as amusing. The current monarch gets a show well worth her time and travel. OK, I have seen funnier performances of Pyramus and Thisbe. Not many, though.

A Midsummer Night's Dream runs until Sept. 2. For tickets and more information, visit canadianstage.com.

Chris Gallow / Tamara Podemski, John Cleland, Richard Lee, Mark Crawford and Pierre Simpson serve up a fine Midsummer Night's Dream.; Caption:

THEATRE REVIEW

THE MILLIONAIRESS

Court House Theatre, Niagara-on-the-Lake

Nicole Underhay, playing the title role in George Bernard Shaws The Millionairess, is miscast. To be fair, it's hard to think of an actress who wouldn't be. In this 1934 comedy, Shaw tried to create a heroine who was both monster and charmer, and he made the first ingredient far more convincing than the second.

Epifania Fitzfassenden - her married name, of which shes trying to rid herself when we first meet her - was born with money and with the talent for making more of it. She believes these attainments make her superior to everybody else, and gets furious when this opinion is challenged. She might say, like Popeyes Olive Oyl, that strong men are her weakness, though she can sometimes be mistaken about which they are. Unlike Olive, she's as selfish in love as in everything else.

All in all, she suggests Ayn Rand with a sense of humour; or rather - since she repeatedly insists that she doesn't have one - Rand envisioned by an author who did.

Epifanias maiden name is Epifania Ognisanti di Parerga, and its a pleasure to hear Underhay roll all those syllables around on her tongue. It's also possible to enjoy her whiplash timing, always useful in a comedy even when your character is not supposed to get any of the jokes, and to admire her looks and her clothes sense. Cameron Porteous, this production's designer, has endowed her with a preternatural capacity for dressing perfectly for every room she enters.

The plays first scene is done up in red, its second in blue, its third in green, its fourth and last in gold; and Epifania has an outfit for all of them. The colour coding, plus some ingeniously versatile furniture and a strong supporting cast, contribute to an overall stylishness in Blair Williams production. But the fact remains that the leading actress is temperamentally (and maybe physically) too small for her role, and is overcompensating.

Required to play a force of nature, she forces. That means a vocal delivery that substitutes volume for tone, and a physical demeanour that involves much twirling of her fur stole, and much hurling of herself around the stage. She hurls other people as well, and that's far more satisfying. Indeed, Underhay comes through when she's given something specific to do, whether its falling in love or taking care of someone elses business. Or rather taking it over, which is what Epifania really is good at, and where the play becomes interesting.

It takes a goodly time to do so. Shaw's powers were far from exhausted when he wrote it, but they were flagging, and the first scene and a half go round in circles. We start in the office of Epifania's solicitor, which as aforesaid is all red, right down to the incumbents desk and - I kid you not - his ukulele; talking or strumming, Kevin Bundy plays him with suavity and charm.

Epi wants to make her will before committing suicide, for motives that seem totally arbitrary and are soon abandoned for reasons equally unclear. They are joined by her estranged husband, a boxer huffed and puffed by Martin Happer, and his new squeeze who, as played by Robin Evans Willis, makes ordinariness seem very appealing.

In the next scene Epifanias current swain, a fashionable loafer rejoicing in the name of Adrian Blenderbland, says something tactless about her late dad, for which she breaks his bones. Later on, he will claim damages for his damages, and gets hysterical when informed that she will beat him in the courts because she's both rich and a woman. Steven Sutcliffe doesn't exactly underplay Adrians agonies, but he does them very well.

Meanwhile, Epi has met an Egyptian doctor who sees right through her but is enchanted by her pulse rate. Kevin Hanchard plays him with appropriately smooth serenity. It turns out that her father and his mother laid down similar conditions for their offsprings marriages: that the partner of each should demonstrate an ability to take a small amount of money and make it multiply. He fails, through being too charitable; she of course succeeds.

She goes to a sweat shop, and blackmails the owners into employing her. Here it's worth remembering that the play was written in the '30s, and this scene was set in Londons East End. Williams production tries to expunge period references, and he has the actors, in a possible Shaw Festival first, speaking in their own Canadian accents, but the specific traces of time and place are ineradicable.

The underlying issues, of course, are still painfully pertinent, and Michael Ball and Wendy Thatcher give searingly real performances as the exploited exploiters. Epifania does them good and she does them harm: a point elaborated in a later speech by Mark Uhre as a hotel manager whose rundown family business she has also appropriated.

He details the vast improvements she has made, and the human wreckage she has left in their wake. He's elegantly non-committal about it. But the matters are not pursued because Epifania makes another speech, about marriage. It's a fine one, but it has almost nothing to do with the rest of the play.

If its suggesting that Epifanias cruelty can somehow be redeemed by her having found the right man, then it's delusional. Shaw was far more plain-spoken in his preface than he is in his play: A society which depends on the incentive of private profit is doomed."

The Millionairess runs until Oct. 6. For tickets, call 18005117429 or visit shawfest.com.

THEATRE REVIEW

Come Back, Little Sheba Royal George Theatre, Niagara-on-the-Lake

The two best Canadian performances I have seen this year are being given by Corrine Koslo and Ric Reid, in the Shaw Festival's production of William Inges Come Back, Little Sheba. They have a fullness and an immediacy so true it hurts.

Koslo plays Lola Delaney, an early 1950s Midwestern housewife suffering from a severe case of emotional, and occasionally physical, voyeurism. To put it more kindly, she lives through other people because she has so little to live for herself. Reid is her husband, a reformed alcoholic whom she addresses alternately as Daddy and "Doc," though they have no children, and he dropped out of medical school and settled for being a chiropractor.

If it comes to that, we only hear Lolas name quite late in the action when at a time of crisis she puts in a longdistance call to her mother, who isn't much help. To the neighbours she's Mrs. Delaney, a messy woman with a messy house. Shes also Mrs. Delaney to her lodger, an art student named Marie who uses a campus stud known as Turk for a combination model and fill-in boyfriend, until such time as her legitimate fiance Bruce shall swoop in from their hometown of Cincinnati and claim her.

This two-timing is deeply upsetting for Doc, who - nursing a crush that he cant acknowledge to himself or anyone else - idealizes the girl and thinks Turk unworthy of her. His frustrations boil up inside him with predictable results. He keeps a quart of whisky in the kitchen, just to prove he can resist it, and it functions of course like Chekhov's revolver: you got it, you use it.

Lola, meanwhile, gets a vicarious thrill out of both of Marie's entanglements: She spies on her and Turk, and prepares a bang-up dinner for her and Bruce, apparently seeing no contradiction. She also invites the postman and the milkman into her house, not to seduce them a la Blanche DuBois but to absorb their lives and spin half-truths about her own. She also misses her dog, who wandered off years ago and never returned.

Hence, of course, the plays title, the most notorious and, as it turns out, least necessary thing about it. Once a day Lola steps outside her door and calls unavailingly for lost Little Sheba to trot back. I once heard of a competition for Lines That Would Stop a Play Dead in its Tracks. The winner, hands down, was "Good evening, my name is Godot." I now think that a runner-up might be, Hey, lady, is this your dog?

Little Sheba is clearly a stand-in for everything thats missing in Lola's life and marriage, but since the rest of the play spells out much of what that is, and strongly hints at the rest, it's superfluous, not to say pretentious: A prime example of the fake poeticizing that infested American drama in the 50s and is still there today. At least this play doesnt end by reprising the title line. Sorry if that's a spoiler.

I'm not sure, though, that the dog is any more meretricious a device than, say, the imaginary childin Whos Afraid of Virginia Woolf? And though Inge hardly has Edward Albees wit, his may be the more painful and penetrating dissection of a marriage, a ride on a bitter merry-go-round that, however good the riders' intentions, is fated to go on forever.

A big hit in its day, it preceded his more familiar Picnic and Bus Stop and may well be better than either of them. Certainly Jackie Maxwell, who's directed both those plays at the Shaw, does her best work with this one. It may seem an odd compliment to call Koslos performance "shapeless," but the great thing about her is that she doesnt fit Lola into any kind of mould.

Distress, anxiety, bewildered good-heartedness, forced cheer and efficiency flow out of her, all swirling around an aching void, an unappeasable sense of loss and, crowning everything, love. Reid, whose first action in the play is to get breakfast, starts out kindly, competent, friendly. Then a peremptory edge appears, as he alternately confronts and avoids things he would rather not think about. Finally, and violently, he explodes, pouring out grievances we've known about and others we'd hardly have guessed. Things are said that, if not technically unforgivable, will surely prove unforgettable.

Reid cant prevent his big drunk scene from appearing something of a set piece, but thats inherent in the play. Its sequel, as he pleads not to be taken to a hospital of which he's already told us horrible things, is terrifying, moving, disturbing, everything.

Christina Poddubiuk has designed a ramblingly evocative set, and there's a jazz score that sounds a bit hip for the house, but is very atmospheric. Music counts a lot in this play. Lolas and Docs happiest memories, recreated, are of dancing the Charleston. One of Doc's, and the play's, finest moments finds him transfixed by a stray classical piece on the radio. Lola, unthinkingly and quite unmaliciously, changes the station.

Come Back, Little Sheeba uns until Oct. 19. For tickets, call 1-800-511-7429 or visit shawfest.com

David Cooper / Corrine Koslo and Ric Reid have a fullness and an immediacy so true it hurts in Come Back, Little Sheba.; Caption:

Meet Robert Service, bankster and rhymester. In Wanderlust, Morris Panych's admittedly fanciful account of his life and work - and Stratford's fourth, smallest and best musical this year - Service is putting in time among the urban money changers while dreaming of life in the gold fields and mining camps of the Yukon and writing poems about them. The opening moments of the show find Service, in the person of Tom Rooney, boldly singing one of his verses and then getting stuck for a rhyme. While he stumbles and fumbles, the music, composed for the occasion by Marek Norman, goes implacably on, and so does he, and somehow, triumphantly, they manage to finish together. It's hard to resist the show after that.

Robert, a dreamer with an impulsive streak but only a streak, is surrounded by people who either don't understand him or who understand him all too well, and he makes all of them nervous. The bank manager, one Sam McGee, is a disconcertingly benevolent tyrant who continually seems on the verge of dispensing with Service's services but always ends up giving him sympathetic advice instead. Randy Hughson, finally getting his due at Stratford, endows Sam with his own unsurpassed capacity for saying things very fast and without apparent inflection, while still making them devastatingly funny. I also caught him at one point, standing in a far corner of the stage playing the mouth organ, adding atmosphere to a scene in which he does not otherwise belong. The assistant manager, well sneered by Dan Chameroy, is an unpleasant fellow called Dan McGrew, with whose fiancee Robert is in possibly requited love. She's a lady known as Louisa or, as it might be, Lou. I think you can see where all this is heading, but I'll spell it out. The show presents Service's best known poems, and some of his lesser known ones, as fantasies spun out of his bank-bound existence.

The show has resemblances to such other musicals as She Loves Me (whose source play, Parfumerie, Panych has memorably directed) and The Producers, or the bit of it before Leo Bloom breaks his chains. Wanderlust's hero is afforded no such apotheosis; Panych points out in a program note that Service never set foot in the Klondike until after he had written most of the verses in which he mythologized it, mainly for the benefit of readers even further removed from the scene than he was. It's a fair criticism of the show that, like its hero, it never goes anywhere. It spins out variations on a single situation. (Service's jingliness must be catching, though I admit that he would have come up with a perfect rhyme.) But it's so well done in every department that I can't say I mind.

Panych has written one of his wittiest scripts, especially on the subject of finance ("a sensible man earns his money or, preferably, borrows it" says the bank manager), and given it one of his most humane and inventive productions. He also takes credit for "additional lyrics." I don't know if he intends to make a career, or yet another career, as an additional lyricist; I would guess that on this occasion he's written the romantic stuff, which is well enough turned but cloudier than the versified narratives of Service himself that furnish the bulk of the score. Norman's settings for these are always spirited, sometimes beautiful; though even verse this undemanding can be quite hard to follow when sung. The most effective number is The Cremation of Sam McGee, which is spoken, by Rooney, to music with Hughson managing to transmit human warmth even as frozen corpse. The Shooting of Dan McGrew becomes a more elaborate set piece; it has firecracker saloon choreography by Diana Coatsworth, who in the office scenes works more decorous but equally bewitching wonders with desks and chairs.

And there is Rooney, a star at last, or, more exactly, given a star role at last. He combines the patient physical grace of a Buster Keaton with the relaxed vocal attack, in both speech and song, of - well, of a Tom Rooney. He presents shyness advancing, via sulkiness, into defiance, and then sidling or shuffling back again. Never sentimental, he's sharp and shining and moving. I suppose there are things he can't do, but I've yet to see them turn up. Robin Hutton makes an affecting, ambiguous Lou; theirs is a relationship that at first seems pure romance fiction, but later reveals honest and discomfiting depths. Lucy Peacock gives a Hogarthian account of Robert's amorous landlady, while back at base we get Ken James Stewart as the office sneak, Xuan Fraser as the office perennial, Troy Adams as a bank clerk turned balladeer, and a similarly admirable ensemble. Ken MacDonald's sets are economical enough to please Mr. McGee himself, and imaginative enough to delight everyone else.

The Shaw Festival's small-scale musical is also a beaut. It's Leonard Bernstein's one-act opera Trouble in Tahiti, a yearningly sardonic portrait of a post-war pre-Mad Men suburban marriage. Bernstein wrote the lyrics, more notable for point than polish, as well as the music, notable for both. The show is not, of course, set in the South Seas; the title refers to a song and-sarong movie that the heroine, a more desperate wanderluster, wishes her life were more like, while still dismissing it as romantic rubbish. The hero, meanwhile, commutes and also, on occasion, yearns.

Elodie Gillett and Mark Uhre are very fine as the couple; an eight strong chorus swirls around them, wittily and menacingly directed by Jay Turvey and choreographed by Linda Garneau. Turvey also puts in a very effective silent appearance as the lady's shrink. Not since Floyd Collins has the Court House space been so inventively used. There's the usual impeccable musical direction from Paul Sportelli. One thing: Husband and wife upbraid one another for missing Junior's high school play, but the show ends with them trying to save their marriage by spontaneously going off to see a movie: in fact, that movie. I hope they have a short-notice babysitter, or there'll be trouble a lot closer than Tahiti.

THEATRE REVIEW

Henry V

Festival Theatre, Stratford

The best parts of Des McAnuff 's production of Henry V, his last Shakespeare as Stratfords artistic director, are the beginning and the end.

The plays customary one person chorus has been eliminated and the lines distributed among the entire cast. This turns out to have its disadvantages, but it's undeniably stirring to see the company distributing themselves around the stage in their civvies and to hear them, to mounting drumroll accompaniment, sharing out the prologue, with its exhortations to the audience to use our imaginations and think about horses.

The one actor who doesn't get to partake in all this group storytelling, now or later, is he who plays the king. Not, that is, until the finale when hes left alone onstage to deliver the epilogue, telling how the French conquests weve just seen achieved were squandered under his successor. There's a satisfying sense here of a circle being completed: the hero joining in the telling of his own story while stepping outside his role to do so.

It's spoiled, though, by the fact that hes never seemed much inside it in the first place. Henry is played by Aaron Krohn, the young American actor who was so chillingly funny last year as Lenny in The Homecoming. Hes equally chilling as Henry, though not at all funny, and it's hard to tell how much of this is intentional. He speaks his lines intelligently and intelligibly, but that's about all that happens. Theres little personality there, no warmth, no discernible reason for his soldiers to follow him. Theres no sense of self-doubt, so the big speech about ceremony goes for nothing. So, in another key, does his broken-French wooing of the enemy princess; we don't care enough to laugh either with or at him.

Henry V is a very slippery play. On one side of it, we have the chorus exalting "the mirror of all Christian kings" and the choice cavaliers who follow him to France. On the other, we have a ruler waging aggressive war for questionable purposes, with an army some of whom are dogged but skeptical while others are skulking profiteers. It's possible that Shakespeare used a chorus in this play because he was nervous that, if he left the action to speak for itself, it would get away from him. Making the chorus a collective rather than an individual voice, though, has the unexpected result of weakening its role.

Meanwhile, this kings most notable characteristic becomes a kind of calculating callowness. Henrys is, after Hamlet and Richard III, the longest role in Shakespeare, and that's a lot of time to spend learning that the production doesn't like him very much. Theres plenty of anti-war material in the play as written; it doesnt need to be forced down our throats.

As it is, this may be the only production of Henry V in which the king is the villain, and the hero is, of all people, Pistol. Tom Rooney, whom I wrote just a couple of days ago could play anything, is here mired in contradictions. He does in fact rise above them, but he can't obscure them, and they mostly stop him from being funny or even, in the way of a confessed rogue, endearing. This Pistol is a champion of the underclass and of the underdog; he knuckles under to Fluellen (Ben Carlson, magnetic as ever, though with a strange beard) not because he's a coward but because the Welsh captain is a bully. The giveaway is the amount of textual fiddling that has to be done to get these and allied points across.

On the other hand - though Im afraid it makes for confusion rather than complexity - McAnuff has kept, in their entirety, the speeches in which the Boy (well played by Sophia Walker, though a real boy would be preferable) tells us, very persuasively, just what a craven loudmouth Pistol is. Theres also some unusually graphic corpse-robbing. What might be called the post-Falstaff scenes are generally well done, with Lucy Peacock making the Hostess's tragic-comic eulogy expectedly effective, and the mourners amusingly sagging under the weight of the fat knight's coffin.

Randy Hughson is an excellent Bardolph, though his hanging and Henrys reaction to it are even more sentimentalized than in the Kenneth Branagh film; the more they try to move us with it, the less they succeed. The kings disguised encounter with his troops pre-Agincourt, usually the play's great scene, is here remarkably ineffective; while having the principal soldier later defy the king to his face is psychologically implausible, historically impossible and - again - textually unsound.

The show looks good; the battles are exciting and the costumes medievally gorgeous, especially those for the French. There are some nice symmetries; the English bishops, those crafty war lobbyists, appear on symbolic horses, and the archbishop is also a silent, oily presence at the final peace conference. The French, too, get to appear on horses, even while talking about them; they're well played too, with Richard Binsley a gentle king, Michael Blake a dry sardonic Constable, and Gareth Potter a preening Dauphin properly presented as the bizarro Henry.

The final, unexpected image is of the Canadian flag: maybe a homage to Michael Langhams legendary bicultural production of 1956 (whose star, Christopher Plummer, was in the opening night audience), maybe a pious hope that French and English could finally get along. After a production apparently dedicated to showing that they couldnt, it did not seem earned.

Henry V runs until Sept. 29. For tickets and more information, visit stratfordfestival.ca.

THEATRE REVIEW

His Girl Friday

Festival Theatre,

Niagara-on-the-Lake

The Shaw Festival has mounted a very good production of what may be the most unnecessary play ever written.

His Girl Friday is the play of the movie of the play. In the beginning, which was 1928, there was The Front Page, written by Ben Hecht and Charles MacArthur: not only the best of newspaper comedies but one of the great American plays of any kind. (For sheer, jazzy energy and wit it ranks with Once in a Lifetime and Guys and Dolls.) Its been filmed three times: twice under its original title, once under the one that's now on the marquee in Niagara.

The name change is the result of a gender change, one that according to legend came about when a Hollywood producer discovered the lines for the play's male star reporter sounded even better when spoken by a woman, and then presumably hollered for someone to get him a rewrite. Because the character was already called Hildy Johnson (the name of an actual, though male, U.S. journalist of Swedish descent), the rewrite was off to a propitious start. The picture was made in 1940, with Rosalind Russell as Hildy, looking superb in stripes, and Cary Grant as her former editor, and now also former husband, Walter Burns. What emerged was a classic screwball comedy with social-conscience underpinnings and maybe the fastest dialogue ever filmed. Its as great a movie as The Front Page is a play.

In 2003 the British National Theatre had the bright idea of combining the two by, in effect, putting His Girl Friday onstage. They got John Guare, the noted U.S. playwright, to adapt the adaptation, but he and they were on a hiding to nothing. The movie hasnt disintegrated, so why compete with the incomparable? The Front Page still exists, so why not just revive it? As well as being unfair to its predecessors, the new hybrid is unfair to Guare, whose House of Blue Leaves and Six Degrees of Separation rank among the best modern American plays and whose Atlantic City is my favourite screenplay ever.

Jim Mezon's production at the Shaw Festival is a huge improvement on the one at the National; it's better cast, zippier and it got rid of the extra layer of superfluity that weighed down the British version and that involved the pretense that the onstage proceedings were themselves being filmed. Making it the movie of the play of the movie, Mezon maintains most of the spirit of The Front Page, even without being allowed to deliver the letter. (As far as I could tell only one too-good-to-lose line of Hecht and MacArthur has been retained by Guare; its tell him his poetry stinks and kick him downstairs. He has had, alas, to jettison Grants immortal and presumably ad-libbed line from the movie: "The last man who spoke to me like that was Archie Leach, the day before he cut his throat.") He can't conceal, though, that the original play has suffered more than a sex change. It's been updated, which may not matter, and sentimentalized, which does.

The Front Page is set in the press room of a Chicago courthouse on the eve of a hanging. (Oh yes, its also the best play ever written about Chicago.) The condemned man, a clueless self-styled anarchist, has unintentionally shot a black cop, and the mayor and sheriff, who are up for re-election and are courting what they call the coloured vote, are determined to see him swing. They even go to the lengths of concealing his governmental pardon.

The killer escapes, and stumbles into the arms of Burns and Johnson, the citys star muckrakers. For the sake of a scoop, and because they hate the mayor, they conceal him - in a rolltop desk. Guare's version, like the movie, brings the action forward to the eve of the Second World War, but makes far more a point of it. The accused is now a German-Jewish refugee, his police victim an American Nazi. Walter Burns, the stopat-nothing newshound, is now, at least in his nobler moments, a crusader for justice and the little man, and even makes speeches about it, while Hildy is a positive paragon. Their originals had no such scruples; their mission of afflicting the comfortable - they weren't so hot on comforting the afflicted - had desirable political side effects, but they were basically in it for fun and profit. For which we loved them.

Guares version makes us love them less by trying to make us love them more, partly by making them love one another. Their romantic involvement worked fine in the film, but it weighs, and slows, the play down. Hildy wants to quit, Walter wants to keep her; and that dynamic would work just as well, probably be more interesting, if they were just colleagues and comrades-in-arms.

Thats not to knock the performances here; Benedict Campbell is prowling, Nicole Underhay is crackling and their collisions and collusions are smashing. Kevin Bundy is delicious as Hildy's new fiance, an all-around wimp who seems to have lapped up fascist sympathies along with his mother's milk. Hes one of Guares more felicitous inventions; mama herself is one of his least, a battle axe who made me feel embarrassed for Wendy Thatcher, who plays her, especially during a speech denouncing women writers that must rank as one of the unfunniest set pieces ever written.

As in any version of this material, much of the running - and very speedy running it is - is made by the supporting corps of reporters; Kevin Hanchard and Neil Barclay are stand-outs among an excellent team, with Ric Reid in a class of his own as the hypochondriacal poetaster Bensinger. Thom Marriott's bullying mayor and Andrew Bunker's desk-bound fugitive are great cameos, and Lorne Kennedy has a show-stopping, if somewhat indulgent, turn as the inebriated Bearer of the Pardon. Peter Hartwell's set is a fine sparse machine for rushing around in.

The show offers a roaring good time. Only it might have been a roaring even better one.

His Girl Friday runs until Oct. 6. For tickets and more information, visit shawfest.com.

Emily Cooper, Shaw Festival / "So let me get this straight, we're in a play of a movie of a play? What a scoop!"; Caption:

David Mamet's Speed-the-Plow is Mamet lite. Its also Mamet funny, and Soulpepper, under David Storchs direction, has given it a tight and entertaining production: the best, I think, of the three or four I've seen. That I can't remember the exact number may well say something about me, but I think it also says something about the play.

Speed-the-Plow arrived in the world in 1998, five years after Mamets masterpiece Glengarry Glen Ross. Its a further exploration of the masculine jungle he'd charted in that play and American Buffalo, with the action transferred to happier hunting grounds, or at least to more luxurious ones. We've travelled from the worlds of Chicago junk dealers and desperate real-estate pitchers to that of Hollywood movers and shakers - or at least to that of those who would dearly love to move and shake. One of them may even, at long last, be in a position to do so. Bobby Gould has crawled his way up the studio ladder to the office of Head of Production, meaning he can say "no" to nearly everybody and yes to a favoured few whose ideas may end up doing him some favours. To him comes Charlie Fox, a long-time hanger-on (by his fingernails, chiefly) who has acquired a) the rights to a prison melodrama whose main attraction is that its like all other prison melodramas, and more importantly, b) the interest of an A-list star who, Charlie says breathlessly, has come to his house. The catch is, the star has only given him a 24-hour window to clinch the deal. Bobby promises to take this sweetheart proposition to the studio head the very next morning and get him to rubber-stamp it.

In the outer office sits Karen, Bobbys shy and self-effacing temp. Charlie, euphoric over his imminent riches, bets Bobby that he can't seduce her. On Bobby's desk sits a long novel, about radiation and the end of the world, to which he has promised to give a "courtesy read" as a necessary preliminary to declaring it unfilmable. Bobby asks Karen to read it, and to come to his house that evening with a report, which she does. She loves the book and - still shy but no longer so self-effacing, and terribly earnest - tells Bobby that its his duty to film it, as his contribution to saving humanity. (Its not quite clear how this would work out as, from what we hear, the author regards Armageddon as a benign necessity, and radiation as God's chosen instrument. I guess you have to take your divine radiance where you find it.) She convinces Bobby. She also falls into his bed. Charlie, arriving next day for his meeting, is furious to discover he's lost his bet, and a lot more furious to realize that, since Bobby is only allowed to green-light one project of his own, hes lost his one chance of a big score. Violence ensues, not all of it verbal.

Its a watertight parable whose moral is, once again, that everyone's a whore. It's satisfactorily worked out, but not quite satisfyingly. The stakes arent as high as in Mamets previous plays. Yes, there's more money at risk - millions, in fact - but nobody's going to go to jail, or even be thrown on the street, if the deal doesnt go through. Compare that to Shelley "the Machine" Levene ineluctably digging his own grave in Glengarry. Or, in a later Mamet, the professor in Oleanna doing much the same thing. Mamets ear for the poetry of profanity is as acute as ever, but the medium here outpaces the message; it's hardly news that Hollywood is corrupt and that pictures get made for all the wrong reasons, which may be why, for all the snappiness of the dialogue, this quite short play feels quite long. At least, it does if you've seen it before. Youre not so deep, play, and your case is rigged. Get on with it, already.

The unfair though certainly amusing wrinkle is that whatever choice Bobby made would probably be the wrong one. Each character gets a shot at reading extracts from the disputed novel and, though they all read it in different tones and for different reasons, none of them leaves us in any doubt that its a terrible, pretentious book that would make a terrible pretentious picture. Bobby is an insecure slob who likes to play genial and to disparage any suggestion that he might be in the art-making business but in fact, even on artistic grounds, Charlie's jailbreak story would be a better bet - at least somebody might enjoy it. It's hard to believe Bobby wouldnt realize this, even without Charlies prompting, maybe not while sleeping with Karen but certainly after waking up.

Ari Cohen plays Bobby brilliantly, all blubber and bluster, but it's still hard to believe in him: not in his character but in his choices. Except his last one, which does have the old Mamet inevitability. Jordan Pettle has an easier job as Charlie; he's a highenergy snake, jubilant at getting a break, terrified at the prospect of it slipping away, doing everything possible to hang on to it. He has, after years of humiliation, a love-hate relationship with his boss; Pettle, who has never been better, is unflaggingly on target. That includes his beating up on Bobby, of which the production, to its credit, makes less of a meal than others have done. Theres no suggestion that Charlie is out of control; on the contrary he knows exactly what hes doing.

So does Karen; but it's one of the play's and the productions best points that we can never be sure just what that is. She may be a genuine idealist; she may be a predatory cat posing as a mouse; she may well be all those things. Sarah Wilson makes her a sphinx with three faces; shes a different person, in a smarter outfit, the morning after than she was the morning before, never mind the night during. In the central scene, when she and Bobby are sounding one another out on his sofa, it's impossible to determine which of them is the seducer. Which is exactly as it should be.

Speed-the-Plow is in repertory at the Young Centre for the Performing Arts. Visit soulpepper.ca or call 416.866.8666 for more information.

Cylla Von Tiedemann / Ari Cohen and Jordan Pettle go head to head in Speed-the-Plow.; Caption:

Alon Nashman, an actor I greatly admire, is appearing at Stratford in a one-man play about John Hirsch, a director whose memory I revere. I wish I liked the results more than I do.

There can be no quarrel with Nashman's actual performance of Hirsch, which is nicely poised between creation and impersonation. He has some moments of being moving, and more of being very funny. The undoubted highlight of Hirsch comes when the director, rehearsing The Tempest during his tumultuous reign as head of the festival, puts the actor playing Caliban through his paces, and also through hell, when trying to get his first entrance right. He isn't showing enough anger at Prospero. He isn't showing enough lust towards Miranda. He isn't showing that, perversely, he really loves both of them. And as if all that weren't enough, the director can hardly hear him. (Do you realize, Hirsch asks parenthetically, just how much it costs to rehearse you? Do you know what we're paying Len Cariou?) One feels for the unfortunate actor, and there's an added piquancy if you happen to know that he was Miles Potter, himself to become a prominent Stratford director in later years. The point is made that Hirsch was a tyrant, could be a bully, but was a tyrant and a bully with insights and an inspirational fervour; by the end of the scene he has got some results, and expresses himself moderately pleased with them. You get the feeling that his rehearsals must have been great fun if you weren't the one being shot at, and maybe even if you were. In retrospect, anyway.

Hirsch, as is well known, was a Hungarian orphan of the Holocaust who emigrated to Canada when still a boy, and was both haunted and driven ever after by the sense of what, both personally and culturally, he had lost and yearned in some way to restore. In another of this show's best scenes, we find the stateless hero, standing at one consulate after another, answering the same questions, taking the same blood tests. It's pure chance that he was standing in line for Canada, which wasn't high on his list, when there happened to be a vacancy. Given a choice of destinations, he opted for Winnipeg because it seemed to be in the centre geographically and therefore safe. Growing up there, he was able to put it in the cultural centre as well. The Manitoba Theatre Centre, which he founded, became the benchmark for regional theatres all over Canada.

You can glean that from this show. But the piece itself - devised by Nashman and Paul Thompson, and directed by Thompson - is both scattershot and cumbersome. It leaves a lot out, maybe because it is trying to get too much in. There's a whole outer layer in which Nashman appears as himself, wondering how to set about doing justice to his subject. Halfway through he decides he hasn't managed it, and tries a new tack. This involves him half-reciting, half-chanting, a verse narrative, full of amusingly forced rhymes. (Hirsch, we are told, went wandering the earsch.) In terms of what we actually learn, though, there's very little difference. If anything, the narrative gets scrappier. Earlier on, Nashman has interrupted the story to broach the question of how, and when, a Jew can tell his children about the Holocaust. It's a good question, but it has little to do with Hirsch, who didn't have any children. This entire superstructure (or second-guessing second level, call it what you like) is either too much or not enough.

The staging further slows things down. In an effort to link Hirsch's life with his work, the production brings on Mother Courage's cart, referencing both a play he directed and the memories he was fated to drag behind him. Nashman is attended by a couple of stage-hands who bring him props and changes of costume; they loom so large that they seem on the verge of taking out Equity membership.

There's proper tribute to Hirsch's production of the Yiddish classic The Dybbuk, which inspired the youthful Nashman and so may be have said to have lit the long fuse that led to this performance. Dybbuk certainly ranks among the finest things I've ever seen in the Canadian theatre; so do Hirsch's later Stratford productions of Tartuffe and As You Like It, which go unmentioned here. You can't have everything, but Hirsch's own love-hate relation with the festival is under-explored. We do get snapshots of his time at the CBC, and a very entertaining scene in a New York diner, drawn from Hirsch's time working at Lincoln Center and enabling Nashman to create three characters while actually playing only one of them.

Towards the end we find Hirsch in Israel writing to someone, previously unmentioned, called "Brian." We have to wait for a still later scene to discover that Brian was actually Hirsch's lover, and we don't get much insight into the relationship even then. It's even more surprising that we are told literally nothing about the family with whom he was billeted in Winnipeg in a trial arrangement that, emotionally, turned out to last a lifetime; his surrogate mother was arguably the most important person in his life.

There are glimpses of his biological family in Europe that are first charming and then, for obvious reasons, wrenching. It's a miracle that he himself escaped; and, for Canada and its theatre, a blessing. To date, only Robert Lepage has challenged him as the greatest director ever to hold a Canadian passport. He's in danger of being undervalued, perhaps even forgotten, and it's good that he is receiving this tribute. It's heartfelt, and thoughtful, and not at all sentimental. But, not having a shape or a structure, it remains anecdotal.

Hirsch is in repertory through Sept. 14 at the Studio Theatre, Stratford. Call 1-800-567-1600 or visit stratfordfestival.ca for ticket information.

THEATRE REVIEW

The Best Brothers

Studio Theatre, Stratford

Daniel MacIvor's The Best Brothers may be the playwright's best play.

It's almost certainly his most conventional; in this case, and contrary to received wisdom, that's a good thing. It's far more believable and funny and engaging and purposeful than much of his earlier work involving more than one performer. (I confess: I've never seen Never Swim Alone). It doesn't have the mesmerizing power with which he as an actor invested his solo works, but after seeing several of those in fairly quick succession, I found the law of diminishing returns taking a rapid toll. They were scary, but even terror can get monotonous.

They could be charming, too, and MacIvor's charm, as a performer and especially as a writer, is in the ascendant here.

That doesn't make the play soggy or soppy. He's one of a cast of two, who do indeed play brothers. MacIvor is Hamilton Best, an architect. John Beale plays Kyle Best, a real-estate agent. You might say they're in the same business. Indeed, Kyle does say it, to Hamilton's chagrin. The opening scene finds them in separate professional locations, receiving the news of the sudden death of their mother, whose name is/was Bunny. Hamilton's response is to rush to the scene. Kyle is more about taking his time. This could mean that he's unfeeling. It could equally mean that he's practical. After all, whenever he gets there, it isn't going to make her any less dead.

The cause of death was a collision with a drag queen named Pina Colada, who fell from a float at a Gay Pride parade. Not, in Hamilton's uncontroversial opinion, a dignified way to go. He blames Kyle for Bunny's having been in the crowd in the first place. Kyle is gay, with a partner who's a sex worker, ("He isn't my sex worker," Kyle explains, "it's just what he does for a living.") Hamilton is straight and married, and proud of it, though there are cracks apparent in his life from the outset.

Underlying all the tension between them is, of course, an unspoken rivalry over which of them their mother loved the best (or the Best); add some songs and a Gold Rush setting, and they might be the squabbling siblings of the last Sondheim musical Road Show - except there it was the straight brother who was the feckless one. Tensions come hilariously to the fore in a funeral reception scene, in which the two boys jockey for position in the matter of eulogy delivery, and in which it finally becomes clear that there was and still is a third boy on the team, one who may have been the best brother, or perhaps the best son, of all. His name is Enzo.

Enzo is a dog. Bunny, an aggressively free spirit, found in Enzo, after a lifetime of experiences with less satisfactory two-legged males, the most reliable relationship of her life. At regular intervals in the play, Kyle and Hamilton take turns to don a pair of green gloves and become Bunny, who tells us how she felt about Enzo and, in amused tones, about them.

Meanwhile and - to my taste, more interestingly - the two men try to come to terms with their responsibilities towards the dog and to cope with the havoc, both mental and material, that he can and does wreak with their lives. Sorting that out helps clarify their feelings about their mother and each other.

It isn't the biggest subject in the world, and MacIvor certainly hasn't written the biggest play. But, under Dean Gabourie's adroit direction, it fills its space, physically and spiritually. Beale makes Kyle almost cartoonishly camp to begin with, but this might be a long-range strategy of deception; he gets, as the play progresses, stronger and more human by the moment.

MacIvor's Hamilton reveals, or at least emphasizes more than ever before, his strange duality as an actor: He can communicate any amount of emotion while appearing to repress it, but when called upon - by his own script, after all - to open out, he clams up, as he does here in a big speech about Lego. It seems, by the way, that the Best parents - one assumes that Dad had a voice back then, even if he doesn't get one in the play - displayed remarkable foresight in bestowing upon their sons names that would so perfectly suit their personalities in later life.

Also, by the way, the curtain call in this production comes with its own pay-off.

The Best Brothers runs until Sept. 16. For tickets and more information, visit stratfordfestival.ca.

Cylla Von Tiedmann / Daniel MacIvor and John Beale play the Best brothers in, um, The Best Brothers.; Caption:

THEATRE REVIEW

The Sunshine Boys Young Centre for the Performing Arts, Toronto

Soulpepper is bringing us American playwrights in matching pairs. They followed their production of David Mamet's Glengarry Glen Ross with his Speed-the-Plow, an attenuated variation on the same theme. They've now given us Neil Simon's The Sunshine Boys, which stands in rather the same relation to his The Odd Couple. Both the minor Mamet and the simpler Simon differ from their predecessors in introducing an explicit showbiz setting dear to the author's own heart and experience. Well, dear to his heart anyway.

His title characters are an oldtime vaudeville comedy duo called Lewis and Clark, names almost too perfect to have been made up. We meet them in the early 1970s, long after the act has broken up. Al Lewis went into stockbroking, and thence into comfortable retirement with his daughter and her family. Willie Clark lives, mostly in his pajamas, in a seedy New York hotel room where he's visited every Wednesday by his nephew, who's also his agent - and who brings him soup, the latest issue of Variety and no offers of work. Even Alka-Seltzer, a word that Willie declares inherently funny because it has a "k" in it, won't use him in a commercial because the word is out that he can no longer remember his lines.

On this particular Wednesday, however, there is some good news. CBS is presenting a nostalgic tribute to vaudeville, and they want Lewis and Clark to reunite and perform their famous doctor sketch. The only problem is that the two men, who were together professionally for 43 years, can't stand one another. At least, Clark can't stand Lewis.

The first scene gives us Willie, on the subject of the absent Al and practically every other subject, kvetching; and I use the term advisedly. This is one of Simon's more explicitly Jewish plays; its characters, and their whole world, are steeped in borscht and bagels and there's a problem if the actors aren't.

Eric Peterson has Willie's tetchiness and crankiness and transparent insecurities down perfectly; he gets the evening off to a fine start, nodding off in front of a recalcitrant TV set, awakened by the whistling of a kettle, and feverishly answering a phone that hasn't actually rung. Vocally he's fine on the rhythms but he doesn't get the tonality, with the result that the audience sits in glacial silence. The wisecracks as written aren't exactly vintage Simon but they should still make us laugh, even if we hate ourselves for doing so.

At that, Peterson is better than was Walter Matthau in the mechanically disagreeable film version. All the movie had going for it was the presence of George Burns, who had reached a state of comic grace in which every word he uttered sounded funny and who justified Willie's grudging admission that no one could time a line like Al could time a line. However, Kenneth Welsh, who plays Al here, is equally wonderful in a completely different way, one that has more to do with how he looks than how he sounds. He's patient and reserved behind thick glasses; an actor I've previously thought of as wiry has become preternaturally solid in bulk though intriguingly gelatinous in texture. His Al is, as indeed George Burns was in his own career, the ultimate straight man, guaranteed, in a reversal of traditional comic logic, to get all the laughs and his partner's goat.

Ted Dykstra's production takes off when the two men come together for a reluctant rehearsal, and it has a fair stab at the doctor sketch itself, although this is a style of comedy gone almost beyond recapture, even by the most conscientious actors. Or perhaps especially by the most conscientious actors. It's burlesque rather than vaudeville, the American stage equivalent of a British seaside postcard; its walking, or wiggling, emblem is a blonde and all-around pneumatic nurse, here deliciously, indeed toweringly, embodied by Sarah Wilson; funnier than either of the two men who spend the routine leering at her, she beats sexism by joining it.

She's one of two characters billed simply as Nurse; the other, a juxtaposition that probably makes a point in its own right, belongs to the real world, and is called in to minister to Willie in the second act. She will take none of his nonsense, and is rousingly played by Quancetia Hamilton. The play needs her even more than Willie does.

Like The Odd Couple, The Sunshine Boys keeps restating the same central dynamic. The earlier play, however, buttressed its two leads with solid supporting characters; the guys' poker buddies, and even the two English roses upstairs, were roles worth playing. Most of the support work here has to be done, with less grateful material, by Jordan Pettle, who does it nicely enough; he makes a more convincing nephew than he does an agent, but that's pretty much his uncle's complaint about him anyway.

Unlike The Odd Couple, though, the play does get better as it goes on. As often with Simon, it hints at depths that it can't bring itself to explore. In this case, the intimations are of a Sartrean hell composed of other people, or at least of one other person. Those depths can be pretty murky or pretty funny. It depends on how you look at it. Or on which Sunshine Boy you are.

The Sunshine Boys runs until Sept. 22. For tickets and more information, visit soulpepper.ca.

2012-08-04-beatlemania-beyond-backbeat-t:
There's a very good scene in the second act of Backbeat in which John Lennon and Paul McCartney write a song together. Paul is singing and strumming something closely resembling the ditty later known as Love Me Do, and John happens by with some ideas on how to sex it up, both musically and lyrically. It's not unlike those scenes in old Hollywood composer biopics, where we watch a future hit being born, though the script here has rather more bite and the process does seem a bit more like hard work. Anyway, were in at the birth, not just of a hit song, but of an epochal songwriting partnership. Or are we?

Backbeat is the Beatles backstory. Most of it is set in Hamburg, where the Liverpool lads learned their trades playing punishing six-hour gigs, seven nights a week, in clubs with - we gather here - dodgy owners and dodgier clientele. The group's name and most of its personnel were already in place, but their ultimate identity, the hairstyles and clothes and the playing of their own material, had yet to emerge; they were still an R&B grunt band, grinding out sweaty, energetic covers of Chuck Berry songs. Up until the Love Me Do scene, there's been no indication - other than a few bars of I Saw Her Standing There that have shown up unexpected and unexplained - that Lennon and McCartney have had any interest in writing songs at all, though Paul now refers back wistfully to when they used to play around with the idea back in school. And after the scene, the subject of songwriting is never mentioned again. Maybe it would be dishonest to present us with an epiphanic moment at which the boys realized this was their destiny - after all, things rarely happen that neatly in real life - but in passing it up, the show may be the victim of its own integrity. That, indeed, is its overall problem.

To backtrack on Backbeat: It starts with an excessively smarmy Brian Epstein c. 1962, telling us - in a show that uses direct address intermittently and inconsistently - of this local group hes heard about and whom he has tracked down to their Cavern. He tells the foursome he wants to manage them; they can take care of their sound, hell look after their look. Oh, they say, you mean like Stu used to do? We go into flashback mode, and stay there for most of the evening.

The show isn't about John and Paul, or even about John and the other Beatles. Most of the time it's about Stuart Sutcliffe, the aspiring painter with the James Dean looks and the minimal musical talent whom Lennon persuaded to join the band as bass guitarist, apparently because he was personally obsessed with the guy and conceivably because, as a former art student himself, he both envied and resented his talent. Once theyre in Germany, Stuart does yeoman service as a chick magnet and he particularly magnetizes Astrid Kirchner, an ice-cool blond and talented photographer, taking her away from her boyfriend Klaus, self-styled original Beatles fan. Klaus takes it like a man, prophesying with as much dignity as is possible while exiting climbing a staircase that, though the first victim of Beatlemania, he will not be the last. The new relationship survives the groups temporary deportation, when the authorities discover that George Harrison is underage. Astrid, both before and after the hiatus, sets about recalling Stuart to his proper calling, and much of the show becomes an emotional tug-of-war between her and John, with Stu stewing, or smouldering, in the middle.

Sutcliffe is a moderately interesting figure. But he isn't that interesting and he wouldn't exert any fascination at all if he hadnt been a Beatle. The writing here (by Iain Softley and Stephen Jeffreys) is too generic to fill the gap; the Stuart-Astrid scenes seem to go on forever repeating the same themes, with performers (Nick Blood and Isabella Calthorpe) who are competent but hardly compelling. A long tall Lennon (Andrew Knott) makes more of an impression, though his doubtless devastating one-liners are largely drowned by his thick Scouse accent and a muddy sound system.

The show suffers from an identity crisis. Its subtitled The Birth of the Beatles, rather than The Death of Stuart Sutcliffe, and it devotes enough time to the band in performance to qualify as a musical, of the jukebox variety. However, David Leveaux' production seems unhappy about this, cutting numbers short and doing its best to deny audiences the chance to applaud. They do anyway, because they feel it's expected of them, but the upshot is frustration. Meanwhile, hanging over the entire evening is everyones foreknowledge that Stuart will die of a brain hemorrhage and that Pete Best, the bands drummer in their Hamburg days, is fated to be Ringoed. That's a double downer.

It isn't even given its full dramatic due. "Petes the drummer," says John to Astrid, "thats all you need to know about him," and the show apparently agrees. Pete as a character hardly exists until the second act when, to set him up as the sacrificial lamb, he's allowed a monologue. Back in Liverpool, and back in the show's present tense, hes fired by Epstein, his former pals too cowardly to turn up. This shabby behaviour is, I believe, historically accurate, but there must have been some discussion back at base; it could be dramatically interesting to be told why Epstein wanted him gone and shown how the others took it. Like Klaus before him, Pete (Oliver Bennett) takes his dismissal, as he says, with dignity. Of the others, George (Daniel Westwick) seems as anonymous as George in such circumstances always does; Ringo (Adam Sopp) appears, of necessity, only at the last moment but looks and sounds exactly right; and Paul (Daniel Healy) is the most interesting person onstage, partly because hes playing, not just the most talented character, but the most dedicated, the one who pushes forward the part of the story that we actually care about. He's the one who gets them their first recording gig by impressing Bert Kaempfert, who here seems as unpleasant as his middle-of-the-autobahn music always made him sound.

Staging mainly consists of characters prowling along a catwalk or climbing up and down those stairs. Within the alcove thus created, the boys play, the young Hamburgers disporting themselves in the foreground like refugees from the Berlin nightlife of 30 years earlier as depicted in revivals of Cabaret. It seems that everyone's nostalgic for Weimar Germany, even the Germans. After the curtaincall, the show jettisons its sterner principles, and gives us a mini-rock concert, with Stuart and Pete back on the bandstand. Whether this qualifies as a happy ending is anyone's guess.

Until Sept. 2 at the Royal Alexandra Theatre, 260 King St. W. Visit mirvish.com or call 416-872-1212 for ticket information.

Cylla Von Tiedeman / Backbeat's Daniel Healy, Dan Westwick, Nick Blood and Andrew Knott.; Caption:
2012-08-08-books-for-beginners:
THEATRE REVIEW

A Word or Two

Avon Theatre, Stratford

Christopher Plummer has the devil's own charm. He has plenty of other accomplishments as well, of course, but even if he didnt it would be hard to resist the overwhelming casualness with which he takes his place onstage at the beginning of his new one-man show at Stratford.

He walks unassumingly on, then sits down on a pile of books. More precisely, he sits on one of the lower promontories of the leaning tower of tomes, arching upwards and backwards toward the stage ceiling that is the main feature of Robert Brills elegant - and in its way eloquent - set. There's an unspoken humorous conspiracy between the actor and the audience. He's both heightening and defusing expectation, inviting us to make ourselves at home while leaving us in no doubt that hes the host. He exudes self-deprecation and selfassurance simultaneously, making each a vital component of the other. Essentially, hes saying, "Here I am," and smiling while doing it.

A Word or Two is, or purports to be, an autobiographical anthology. Plummer performs some prized passages of verse and prose (the verse predominates) and tells us why they are important to him. These, to quote a text with which he remains rather closely associated, are a few of his favourite things.

At 82, Plummer remains - is indeed more than ever - Canada's premier actor: a position, it's sobering to recall, that he has held for more than half a century, or ever since 1956, when he made his Stratford debut as Henry V in a festival theatre that was still a tent. Greatness is a matter of timing as well as talent, and Plummers career has been rich in both, and continues to be, given his late-life Oscar-winning status.

Hes an old-school bravura romantic actor, with an ironic touch that has kept him permanently modern. He emerged as Canada's young Shakespearean star, just when the country needed one, and he has managed to preserve both his Canadian and theatrical identities even while working largely in other countries and other media. It's only in recent years that hes come back to the Stratford stage with any regularity, but theres always been the feeling that he'd be there when it needed him and vice versa.

Plummer says surprisingly little in this show about his acting career and accomplishments: Maybe he feels it isn't his place. The autobiographical part of the evening is heavily weighted toward his childhood in Montreal; as we get past that, we increasingly lose touch with personal details. He talks about his mother and other relatives, and about the jazz, cabaret and striptease performers he saw in his youth. But he doesnt make much personal or philosophical connection between his various enthusiasms and the extracts he chooses.

He does make something of a statement about his love of language (two languages, in fact) and how he fears this may be becoming obsolete. (I think its form, rather than language itself, that we're losing touch with, but that's a topic for another day.) It seems that he, like many fortunate others, was first turned on to words by reading Lewis Carroll. He says, for him, the touchstone was the White Knights poem in Through the Looking-Glass about the aged, aged man, asitting on a gate. He quotes it at the start of the show and recurs to it frequently thereafter, sometimes pronouncing "aged" with one syllable, which doesnt fit the metre, and sometimes with two, which does.

The title derives from Othello: "Soft you, a word or two before you go." Plummer doesn't actually speak the line here, but he does deliver, thrillingly, the speech that it heralds, the Moor's last oration, about loving not wisely but too well; its a part he should have played. More seriously valedictory, perhaps, is his bilingual rendition of the death of Cyrano de Bergerac: a part he has played. Two treatments of martial defiance in extremis, attended by a brief word on how he himself feels about death (hes afraid of it, but makes a joke of saying so) that, again, go by too fast to really tell us anything. Besides, he's an actor, not an actuary, and still demonstrably at the top of his game.

That being so, it's best to enjoy each of his samples as it comes: his portrayal of an epicene Herod, as imagined by W.H. Auden, explaining the absolute necessity of massacring all those innocents; his countrymans sympathy with Robert Frost on the subject of fences; his joyous rendition, which I wish had gone on longer, of Stephen Leacock in what now sounds like a pre-emptive parody of Downton Abbey; his accounting of Drunken Poets I Have Known, with Dylan Thomas at their head.

The diabolic charm takes definitive form when he becomes the Devil himself, declaiming his denunciation of human destructiveness in Shaws Don Juan in Hell. He plays Juan, too, but this is one occasion on which the devil definitely has the best tunes.

These are all jewels, but there isn't much of a string. Des McAnuff directs the show with taste and discretion, apart from having music playing under some of the purpler passages. It's a crutch that Plummer doesnt need; he can make his own moods. We do, though, lose sight of the man behind the masks; which wouldnt matter if the show didn't make such an implicit claim to the contrary.

It's strange, too, because in his published autobiography In Spite of Myself, Plummer creates a very convincing picture of swagger tempered by shyness. Theres only a faint echo of that here; maybe he can reveal himself - or an image of himself - more completely on the page than the stage, precisely because the latter is his natural metier. Or maybe there just isnt the time.

The shyness, for all his surface joviality, has a touch of embarrassment about it, as if Plummer knows that the actor's task is to reveal himself not directly but through other people, and can't wait to get to the next character. Which he does; he doesnt just recite the pieces hes chosen, he acts them; more tactfully, but also more full-bloodedly, than actors in such circumstances usually do. What's his next full-length role going to be?

A Word or Two runs until Aug. 26. For more information, visit stratfordfestival.ca.

David Hou, Stratford Festival / Christopher Plummer's solo show at Stratford is part autobiographical anthology, part charm offensive.; Caption:
2012-08-11-rapier-meets-wit-mixed-though:
In the first scene of Soulpepper's The Royal Comedians we meet Moliere, played by Diego Matamoros, giving a virtuoso display of crosstalk and pratfalls to acknowledge the presence of the most powerful and distinguished of patrons. The setting is Moliere's own Palais Royal theatre in 17th-century Paris; the patron is King Louis XIV, direct from his own royal palace. As he seems to like the show, this could be the great actordramatist's proudest hour. The last scene will find him in disgrace and despair, literally dying on stage while playing his own Malade Imaginaire, an ending too appropriate to be true, except that it apparently was. How did he get from there to here?

Mikhail Bulgakov's play, written in Moscow in 1936 but censored out of performance for decades afterwards, offers a variety of possible explanations, none of them conclusive. Moliere has offended the clergy by writing and performing Tartuffe, the great satire of religious hypocrites, and they are out to get him. A fire-breathing captain of the musketeers is also out to get him, preferably on the point of his rapier, having been duped by those same priests into believing that he is the original of Moliere's licentious and blasphemous character Don Juan. Moliere may have contracted an incestuous marriage, since his young wife Armande, whom he took to be the sister of a former flame, is actually her daughter. He suspects Armande of being unfaithful to him, principally with a young actor whom he first found hiding in a harpsichord and whom he brought into the company and called his son. These threads do, theoretically, tie together; the Archbishop of Paris who's also the arch-enemy of Moliere uses all of them to discredit him with the fickle-favoured king who, beginning as the playwright's apparent protector, ends by abandoning him. But in practice there's no propulsion; the domestic components in particular have disappeared long before the end. We grasp that Moliere feels angry and deserted, but there is no logical line leading to his death, which plays as a picturesque but autonomous event.

I have seen two productions of this play (the first in England, where it was titled Moliere), and in neither has it registered as more than a succession of scenes, some vivid, some vague. There's something intractably woolly about it. The most fascinating thing about the play is its background. It was Bulgakov's own remarkably daring commentary on the Stalinist regime under which he lived; and which he only survived because the dictator had, as Paula Wing's program note says, a soft spot for him. Stalin played the same kind of cat-and-mouse game with Bulgakov as the play's Louis does with Moliere. Their relationship has in turn been dramatized this year at the National Theatre in London in Collaborators, a new play that may be less distinguished and is certainly less risky than Bulgakov's, but is more rewarding to watch. It also makes use of scenes from The Royal Comedians just as that play makes use of scenes from the collected works of Moliere.

Those scenes are the highpoints of Laszlo Marton's Toronto production. He may have made more of them than Bulgakov envisaged, but he's done his author a favour. Moliere's uxurious vulnerability is illuminated by a passage from The School for Wives in which he's the farcically anguished cuckold, while his wife and her lover play, more or less, themselves. Then we get what is almost (not quite) the best performance of the Tartuffe seduction scene that I have ever seen, with Matamoros offering a superbly sanctimonious expose of the horny hypocrite, and Raquel Duffy a delightful mix of the practical and the provocative. The Imaginary Invalid finale is given the full comedieballet treatment, all slapstick and grotesquerie and music, that its text demands and, at least in English language productions, hardly ever gets.

The rest of Marton's staging veers from exciting to exasperating. Lorenzo Savoini has designed a whispering gallery of a set that serves for both varieties of palace and whose multiplicity of doors are put to use alternately farcical and sinister, the latter aspect much reinforced by Richard Feren's scary sound-score. Its other acoustic properties are questionable. A remarkable proportion of the play is hard to hear. Even the Soulpepper stalwarts in the cast sound muffled, while among those less experienced, inaudibility runs riot (if you can have a quiet riot). They do especial damage to the scenes in which Moliere gets busted by the church's secret police, for which the production goes into full 1930s NKVD mode, replete with black uniforms and threatening searchlights. Meant to reinforce the play's implicit metaphor, this merely succeeds in shortcircuiting it. Rule of thumb: When a period play has modern dialogue, it doesn't need modern dress as well.

I've now seen two virtuoso actors fail to bring this play's protagonist to life. Antony Sher in the British version was so hyper-kinetic that I wanted to yell at him to keep still and let me see the character; Matamoros, equally adept with limbs and lungs and more controlled, left me feeling that there was no character to see. Certainly there are no relationships, other than the self-abasing one with Gregory Prest's Louis, who almost justifies his more vocally indolent moments with some electrifying transitions into absolutist authority. Otherwise, even as a lover, this Moliere is a loner, whether intentionally or by default. He does have friends, or at least loyal employees, both of them actors with other responsibilities on the side, and both well played here: William Webster gives the most humanly detailed performance of the evening as a nervous and censorious candle snuffer; Michael Simpson as the 17-thcentury equivalent of a company manager also has to function, to no helpful end, as a narrator. On the other side of the social and psychological tracks, there are stage-seizing performances by Stuart Hughes and Michael Hanrahan as the lords temporal and (theoretically) spiritual. They express their contempt for one another with a spitting contest that captures the grotesque satirical spirit for which the whole play may conceivably be striving. The idea is that all the characters are royal comedians, professional or otherwise. The younger performances, mainly by members of the current Soulpepper academy are, with an exception and a half, lamentable, the exception being Daniel Williston as the king's tame shoemaker who's also his jester, and the half Paolo Santalucia, who has his moments, though not enough of them, as the boy from the harpsichord. That whole business is obscurely and confusingly presented. Marton's finest productions have been notable for their physicality and their clarity. The first is more in evidence here than the second.

In repertory at the Young Centre for the Performing Arts. Visit soulpepper.ca or call 416-866-8666 for ticket information.

Cylla Von Tiedemann / William Webster and Diego Matamoros in The Royal Comedians.; Caption:
