THEATRE REVIEW

Hedda Gabler Court House Theatre, Niagara-on-the-Lake

Even people who have never seen Hedda Gabler generally enter the theatre with a fair idea of how it ends. Ibsens play has one of the famous final curtains, not to mention one of the famous curtain lines. This alone lends almost any production a quality that we call inevitability if the show goes right and predictability if it doesnt. The Shaw Festival's revival is very inevitable.

There's a driving logic to it - to Martha Henrys direction, to Richard Eyres adaptation and to the performances of the entire cast - that makes the play come up fresh and exciting. If the protagonist's journey shows anything, it's that the road to hell is paved with bad intentions. In this production, the path is charted with mesmerizing exactness.

Mesmerizing rather than moving, though. But then Im not at all sure this play, and especially its heroine, can ever be moving; and Im especially bemused by attempts to turn Hedda herself into some kind of feminist icon. Hedda is the adoring daughter of a deceased general who bequeathed her his pistols and an overwhelming sense of frustrated entitlement. Having been the belle of, probably, several seasons of Norwegian balls, she has come to the end of the last one with her dance card unmarked and her future uncertain. So she has settled for marriage to a fusty and, it seems, mostly sexless academic (special subject: the arts and crafts of medieval Brabant) whose research grant has bought them both a long honeymoon and a big house.

She hated the honeymoon, hates the house and is devoting herself to making the lives of her husband, his aunts and the help moderately miserable. She also has past male admirers to toy with or to fend off, both of which she is good at.

Still, claims the Shaw's program note, compared to the other characters, Hedda is luminous - she shines with rage and despair - her refusal to accept a monotonous, meaningless life at the mercy of self-centred mediocrities gives her unforgettable dramatic power."

Well, the power is certainly there, and Hedda is unquestionably trapped by a society that considers her proper destiny to be marriage and motherhood, the latter a prospect whose looming imminence she loathes. But I can't see that shes any less self-centred (or, truthfully, any less "mediocre, whatever that means) than the other characters. And in fact the play explicitly - in this production, very explicitly - contrasts her with another woman, an old schoolmate who has made the hard choices that Hedda has avoided; this Mrs. Elvsted has had to work as a governess, and has left her husband for the man she admires and adores: a dissolute genius who, under her guidance, has dried out and written a fine book, and who happens to be both one of Heddas enforcedly platonic exes and, in his reformed state, a threat to her husband's professional future.

Hedda is furious that this mousy girl, whom she used to bully at school and whose name she can't remember properly, has done what she herself has always dreamed of doing: inspire a man - especially this man - and shape his destiny. So she sets out to destroy what they have: to kill their child," or more prosaically, burn their yetunpublished second book. Hedda Gabler is a play about jealousy, which is what Henrys production brilliantly brings out.

Moya OConnell is a Hedda of vampiric beauty, and also of vampiric power, spiced with a vicious wit. She lacks the vulnerability that should ideally complete the picture, but she does rise, finely and ineluctably, to the two extreme actions: the literary infanticide (in a stove that, as the lights go down, glows like a Halloween mask) and the final gunshots that, despite foreknowledge, truly make the audience jump. Claire Jullien as the despised and envied Thea is a splendid match for her; the character may not know her own strength, but the actress does.

As Lovborg, the man over whom they fight their undeclared war, Gray Powell is remarkable. A rakish lock of hair over his forehead matches a rakish mode of speech; Eyre's text has him saying that he wrote his first, popular book to have "an ingratiating smile on its face." His proud determination to stay on the wagon, and his equally proud fall off of it, make up a scene of extraordinary tension, as does the barely veiled eroticism of his first conversation with Hedda as they sit on a sofa, ostensibly inspecting her holiday snaps. Their whole prior relationship flashes before their eyes and ours.

Patrick McManus gives Hedda's hubby a pedants petulance but also a pedants nobility; his heartfelt admiration for his rival's achievement rings absolutely true. Indeed, the whole production, as distinct from the program, seems intent on giving the opposition its due. Mary Haney's Aunt Juliana, after being snubbed by Hedda, sees right through her and hardly misses an opportunity to twist a benevolent knife. Jennifer Phipps practically makes a subplot out of the maid Berthes relationship to her new mistress, sometimes delighting in being in the way, at others cowering and scampering to get out of it.

The nearest thing to a weak link is the one I had expected to be the strongest: Jim Mezon is so ideally equipped to play the fleshy, menacing Judge Brack that he could afford to let up on the oily, lecherous menace from time to time. He contributes vitally, though, to the orchestration of the climax, and to the final modulation, when he unknowingly echoes one of Heddas own favourite dismissive phrases.

Ibsen once said that Hedda was a self-portrait; like her, he had spent his life preaching a doctrine of dissent that he was too timid to practise. The ending can be taken as an ironic kind of wish fulfillment. Hedda finds that her husband and her old friend can do without her, and that the judge can very much do with her; the alternative may be public disgrace. So you could say she's a frustrated playwright who, having failed to arrange her characters' destinies, didnt want to stick around for the reviews. She takes, if not quite the noble, then the only way out. It doesnt always convince. This time it does.

Hedda Gabler runs until Sept. 29. For tickets and more information, call 1-800-511-7429 or visit shawfest.com.

Emily Cooper, Shaw Festival / Moya O'Connell is a Hedda of vampiric beauty, and also of vampiric power, spiced with a vicious wit.; Caption:
2012-08-16-an-elektrafying-take-on-a-gre:
THEATRE REVIEW

Elektra Tom Patterson Theatre, Stratford

No more need to beware of Greeks bearing gifts, not when they are as gifted as director Thomas Moschopoulos and his cohorts in the staging of Sophokles's Elektra at Stratford.

Those harsh unfamiliar spellings are laid down by Anne Carson, the Canadianborn and U.S.-based poet and scholar whose superb, jagged translation is used here. It encompasses the exultant and the despondent, insults and laments, tirades and one liners. Its also on occasion funny in a way that Greek tragedy rarely is, at least not on purpose. This Elektra, its tone and impact defined by Yanna McIntoshs stark and thrilling performance of the title role is, well, elektrafying.

Moschopoulos has an impressive resume in Athens and elsewhere, but there is no sign here of a production having been simply brought in; it feels as if it as has been created with its actors, from the ground up. It might be described as a conventional staging, in that it makes crucial use of at least one of the bedrock conventions of the ancient Greek theatre. I refer not to masks or built-up buskins, but to music; vital portions of the text get sung.

The chorus do most of the vocalizing, but the principals, too, are liable to break into song. Some of them do it better than others, but the bridge holds: The bridge between Greek tragedy's stylized external forms and the intensely real emotions beneath, which are played with unflinching, and unflagging, naturalism. The result is not so much to make the old seem new as to make the insistently modern feel eternal.

The audience arrives to find the stage roped off. Behind the barrier is a long, illuminated table, covered in sheets. When the play starts, the sheets are pulled off, and the table splits into three, as does the giant figure that lays upon it. We are at the tomb of the late king Agamemnon, his body split in death, as it was in life by the hand of the usurper Aigisthos, egged on by his lover and his victim's wife, Clytemestra. (Yes, those are the names spellings here.)

To this memorial comes Orestes, Agamemnons longabsent son, whose return is dreaded by his mother, longed for by his sister Elektra, whose grief and vindictiveness surpass even her brother's. But then of course she, unlike him, has had to go on living with their mother.

As Elektra herself, McIntosh looks like the eternal student, or perhaps the eternal student drop-out. She wears the blacksweater uniform, complete with threatening dark-rimmed glasses that have signified the brainy malcontent since at least the Paris of the 1950s. An orphan in her own family's house, she brandishes her solitude like a weapon. She also brandishes an actual weapon, but she still has to wait for her brother to do the real slaughtering.

As his game plan includes spreading the false report of his own death, she has to move from faint hope to fullblown despair to incredulous recognition, the last being the nearest thing to happiness shes ever likely to experience. Its also the one moment that finds McIntosh fractionally behind the curve; otherwise she plays with a force and spontaneity unequalled in her work since Skylight, 12 years ago. Her Elektra is a killer of a performance: a symphony of rage and hurt.

She has one sparring partner and one outright antagonist. The first is her temporizing sister Chrysothemis, played with sympathy and subtlety by Laura Condlln. The antagonist of course is Clytemestra, whom Seana McKenna makes a glittering self-elected trophy wife. She does have a reasonable defence for having killed her husband; he sacrificed their other daughter, Iphigenia, so the Greek ships could sail for Troy.

That's the beautiful thing about Greek mythology; there's so much of it that any character can cite some of it to justify anything. Sophokles is generally accounted the sanest of the three great Greek tragedians, but he tells this story more mercilessly than either Aeschylus or Euripides did.

Ian Lakes Orestes is another arresting study in arrested development. He made me wish that Euripides extraordinary tragic farce Orestes, which Carson has also translated, could be done as a sequel.

As his silent partner Pylades, E.B. Smith is a grim, hulking presence, always available to block anyone's path to remorse or escape. Peter Hutt escorts the two of them as the tutor, at once peremptory and protective, who's deputed to tell the tale of Orestes death in a chariot race, a sports commentary so gripping that we forget hes made it all up; he raps out the words while rapping his staff.

The beat goes on in the choruses, which are for once exciting rather than embarrassing. Whether talking, singing or something in between, the seven women emerge as individuals, while also functioning as a collective sounding board. They don't so much comment on the action as take its pulse, whether they're sympathizing with Elektra, chiding her intransigence, or beating on the palace doors, caught up in the thrill of the chase. The final prey is Graham Abbey's Aigisthos, a smug thug who first struts, then totters the way to his doom.

It used to be academically fashionable to hold that character was a modern concept, unknown to the Greeks. This is belied by the story of the Athenian actor Polus, who is said to have played Elektra while cradling an urn containing the ashes of his own dead son, thus qualifying as the first recorded Method actor. It used, similarly, to be theatrically fashionable to prate about "ritual" which was taken to be the opposite of realism and far superior to it.

Urns, filled with ashes real or fake, play a recurring role in Elektra, and the breaking and scattering of one of them is one of major visual and psychological climaxes of this production. It has its share of ritual but it has a greater share of humanity, which includes inhumanity.

It's the best production of a Greek tragedy I have ever seen.

Elektra runs until Sept. 29. For tickets and more information,

visit stratfordfestival.ca.

The 2b Theatre Company from Halifax has an excellent track record that's further enhanced by When It Rains, the show they've brought to this year's SummerWorks (at the Factory Mainspace). It begins as a slightly whimsical cartoon, and never really abandons that mode. But as it goes on, it cuts surprisingly deep.

Anthony Black, who's both author and director, gives us a brother and sister, and their respective spouses. We first glimpse the quartet as disembodied heads, poking through the holes of a stage-size black-and-white drawing. A voice-over tells us that the sibling's father -- who is never mentioned again--was a murderer, but that since they never knew him this is unlikely to have affected them much. Of course, we don't have to believe that. Both couples originally met through coincidence, but then who didn't? A recurrent theme is the statistical improbability of absolutely everything.

This sense of randomness both raises, and discounts, the old conundrum about bad things happening to good, or at least moderately well-intentioned people. Of the two partnerships presented, one is visibly falling apart while the other is doing the same thing in slower motion. A financial high-flyer makes a little mistake that costs millions; a woman who's longed to get pregnant has her hopes and her health dashed; a betrayed wife seeks a dubious salvation in mysticism; the faithless francophone she's cast out takes to sleeping on park benches and to singing Ne Me Quitte Pas, all four and a half minutes of it, beneath the window of his unresponsive ex; he also, as per the title, gets wet. The narrative voice of the opening is replaced by captions, at least one of them quite cruelly misleading. Projections, designed by Nick Bottomley, do service for sets, and they intersect brilliantly with the live bodies of the actors. One especially striking sequence shows a couple vertically in bed; the initial image is witty enough, but the ensuing scene doubles down on it. Visually one of the funniest scenes in the show, it's also emotionally one of the most painful. Never losing its lightness of touch, the play becomes a haunting depiction of the physical and psychological spaces between, theoretically, the closest of people.

Form and content feed off, and illuminate, one another in a way that hardly anything else I've seen at this year's festival manages to achieve. Terre Haute (Lower Ossington Theatre) comes closest. It's based on the correspondence between Gore Vidal and the Oklahoma City bomber Timothy McVeigh. Vidal wrote some sympathetic articles about McVeigh, which didn't win him many friends; Edmund White's play imagines them actually meeting, for a series of death row interviews. The names have been changed, presumably to protect the fiction -- Gore is now called James, and McVeigh Harrison -- but the play still depends on our fascination with the real people. Its problem is that not even his recent death can make Vidal seem, in this situation, like the more interesting of the two. Much of the play hinges on James's growing sexual fascination with Harrison; but it's the latter's mind that we want to get into, even as we know that it's probably impossible. The play does at least let us know his unknowableness. Both characters speak with improbably elaborate fluency. Terrence Bryant's James copes the better with the words -- playing a writer, he can perhaps afford to sound literary--while Todd Michael Sandomirsky's Harrison compensates with a remarkable physical presence, mostly calm and obviously dangerous.

Anton Piatigorsky's Breath in Between (Passe Muraille) concerns another killer, an invented one this time, though he might be considered the offspring of two real-life phenomena: assisted suicide and Internet dating. Roger, our hero, places an online ad offering his services to people who want to die. He has two takers, one of each gender, and duly shoots them. All this has happened before the play starts, but Roger is still naturally haunted by the memory of his clients/victims. So is Amy, the young woman whom he manages to attract, bed and impregnate before going to jail. (The play's timeline is by no means clear.) Brendan Healy ( Blasted, The Maids) is a director who seems to thrive on extreme scenarios, and can get his actors to thrive there as well. Amy Rutherford, playing her namesake, sometimes has to try too hard, though her monologue about unwilling motherhood is very powerful. Paul Fauteux as Roger is extraordinary throughout, quiet and centred whether playing himself or, from behind masks, each of the deceased. Design, credited to audio wizard Richard Feren, is otherwise, as you'd expect, exclusively sonic, and scary. Scary, too, is much of the writing. But I felt, not for the first time with this dramatist, that a literary conceit was being stretched beyond its useful limits.

Much the same goes, if less portentously, for Pieta (Passe Muraille Backspace), by Danish playwright Astrid Saalbach. A middle-aged woman wakes up in a hotel room, next to a strange man who -- I'm trying not to give too much away -- is in no position to tell her how either of them got there. So she talks, largely to him but really to us, about herself. Since her first action on waking with a hangover at 5:30 a.m. is to pour herself a drink, we can guess straight off that she's an alcoholic, and her life turns out to have fallen apart in other ways as well. It all adds up, sort of, but the problem, endemic to monologues, of justifying the character's volubility is never solved, and Tamsin Kelsey's performance, though praise-worthily sustained, never breaks free of the banal near-naturalism with which she is surrounded.

THEATRE REVIEW

THE CRUCIBLE

Young Centre for the Performing Arts, Toronto

Soulpepper now has two plays running in which a 20th-century dramatist digs back to the 17th to furnish a parable for his own time and for a regime under which he himself suffered.

After The Royal Comedians, Mikhail Bulgakov's searchlight on Stalinism transposed to the age of Moliere and Louis XIV, we have The Crucible, in which Arthur Miller holds up the Salem witchcraft trials as a mirror to the House Committee on Un-American Activities of the 1950s. Bulgakov's satiric farce is, I guess, a more daring piece than Miller's melodrama, stylistically and indeed physically given that even Joe McCarthy wasn't quite Joe Stalin. But there can be no doubt which play packs the more powerful punch, both as a piece of writing and in its current production. The Crucible has its audience on the ropes.

I doubt if any modern play offers more visceral excitement than this one, especially in the third of its four scenes. This provides the thrills of a trial scene, and of a scene of demonic possession, at the same time, topping them up with all the satisfactions of moral outrage. We watch John Proctor, the Salem farmer determined to expose the fraud by which a clutch of vindictive and/or hysterical girls hold a community to ransom, and in doing so to save his own wife from the gallows. We see her seal his fate by telling the only lie of her life: denying that he has committed adultery with the girl who now accuses her of witchcraft, and thereby providing us with the additional theatrical satisfaction of whiplash irony. It all adds up to magnificent melodrama.

That is not a putdown. Melodrama is a legitimate, indeed a hallowed, theatrical form that can be put to serious use. Miller was masterful in fashioning the historical record into a coherent story, illuminating both the period he wrote about and his own. Others, too: When Deputy-Governor Danforth, the top Salem judge, proclaims that "a person is either with this court or he must be counted against it," he wakes any number of contemporary echoes, and not just from south of the border. And though the United States has never again been quite the theocratic society it was in 17th-century Massachusetts, where ploughing on Sunday could be cited in court as proof of bad character, we're still waiting for a time when a candidate can dare run for election without claiming God as his sponsor.

Albert Schultz's Soulpepper production has tremendous grip, much of it exerted by Stuart Hughes, who as Proctor communicates a throaty, sweaty honesty, enflamed with anger and drenched with shame. All these qualities explode together in his final courtroom outburst of mingled despair and defiance ("I hear the boot of Lucifer, I see his filthy face" - he seems momentarily to have broken into verse). He also manages to keep the embers glowing through the play's protracted final scene, which requires him to be more conscience-wracked than seems strictly justified: We appreciate that he feels sexual guilt, but why does he accuse himself of failing to confront evil? We've seen him do nothing but. His quibble over his "name" (he'll make a false confession, but he won't sign it) also sounds like Miller working through his issues with Elia Kazan. Through all of this Hughes charts a coherent and ultimately moving course

He's matched in impact by Joseph Ziegler's Danforth - something of an actor's dream role, I imagine, since he has the first half of the evening off and then swoops in and takes over. Miller later believed that he had gone too easy on Danforth; but in fact there is dramatic value, including suspense value, in making him, as Ziegler plays him, an apparently suave and reasonable man, morally undone by superstition and by a tender regard for his own authority. The less tenable his position becomes, the more fanatically he upholds it.

Poised between these two poles, indeed in some ways the fulcrum of the play, is John Hale, the minister who comes into Salem as a witchcraft expert and gradually sees through the fraud. (He wrote a book about it afterwards, a remarkably perceptive one.) Oliver Dennis is excellent in his initial pastoral visit, brimming with good intentions while modestly flourishing his credentials; when the scales fall, though, he lacks the sheer decibel power to compete with Hughes and Ziegler, and the action falls short of its full crescendo.

Patricia Fagan's Elizabeth Proctor is also a little muted, but she does convey both the love and the distance of the woman whose kindness, in her husband's memorable phrase, "would freeze beer." An especial virtue of the production, especially in its first scene, is the way in which, on Lorenzo Savoini's spare but summoning set, it navigates the cross-currents of a village population where rancor thrives on closeness.

Once the witch hunt has started, there are many reasons for keeping it going, all vividly depicted. For Reverend Parris (Derek Boyes), a paranoid with enemies, it's an insecurity so deep he almost becomes sympathetic. For the rich Thomas Putnam (Michael Hanrahan), it's coveting his neighbours' land, now suddenly available; for his wife (Raquel Duffy) it's the need to blame someone for the loss of her children in infancy. On the other side, Nancy Palk, superb in serenity, makes you believe all the good things her neighbours say about the aged and saintly Rebecca Nurse.

As the even more aged but less saintly Giles Corey, William Webster strikes a fine line between the intransigently sublime and the obstinately ridiculous; "it were a fearsome man, Giles Corey," Elizabeth says after his death, though the way in which she says it here, amused rather than awed, has the unfortunate effect of casting him retrospectively as comic relief.

There are a couple of odd casting choices among the other elders, but the production only really falters with the girls. Abigail, their ringleader, is a role more showy than substantial, and her abrupt disappearance weakens the play's last scene. That's history's fault, not the actress's, but while she is around Hannah, Miller never makes manifest either her fascination with Proctor or her power over his friends. She does, though, lead them compellingly in their massed transports at the trial, which are superbly staged and performed.

For Abigail, it's coldly contrived; for the others, who knows? We do see Mary Warren, the one among them who was about to tell the truth, being partly terrified, partly hypnotized into compliance; Courtney Ch'ng Lancaster, a standout among the younger generation, here makes our hearts break, both for Mary and for those who will now be her victims.

I don't know what Schultz is up to in his final tableau (I prefer Miller's) but otherwise this is a truly stirring show.

The Crucible runs until Sept. 22. For tickets and more information, call 416-866-8666 or visit soulpepper.ca.

What used to be Shakespeare in the Rough is now Shakespeare in the Ruff. What used to be The Two Gentlemen of Verona is now just Two Gents. The company that, after a lapse of a few years, has restored open-air Shakespeare to Withrow Park commences operations with a show that signifies, by its change of title, that it has radical designs on its author's possibly first, and probably worst, comedy. Actually they turn out not to be as radical as all that. Which doesn't stop the show from being enthusiastic and enjoyable.

A refresher course: The two gents are Valentine and Proteus, and they both leave their Verona home for the bright lights of Milan. Valentine, carefree and heartfree, goes first; Proteus is paternally pressured into following him, though he'd rather stay home and court his beloved Julia, who fancies him right back. In this production, set fairly unobtrusively in the late 19th century, Verona is located in Ontario and Milan in Manitoba. No harm done, but who would have thought that in them there days Milan, Man., was ruled over by a Duke - or, in this dispensation, a Duchess - with absolute powers? Anyway, it's unsurprisingly ironic that Valentine, the scoffer at love, should immediately fall for the Duchess' daughter Silvia. Proteus, on arrival, falls for her too, and forgets Julia, which is tough, seeing as she's just decided to follow him to Milan. (In male disguise, natch.) Proteus, setting some kind of record for betraying best friend and best girl at the same time, informs the Duchess of Valentine's and Silvia's plans to elope. The Duchess, who has earmarked her daughter for someone wealthier and stupider, tells Valentine to get out of town. And he doesn't even have frequent train-travel points; he seems to be making his way home on foot when he's captured by outlaws who make him an offer he can't refuse - be our captain or we'll kill you. (They're impressed by his book learnin'. No kidding. It's in Shakespeare.)

Proteus, who doesn't seem to understand the precise ways in which absence makes the heart grow fonder, is miffed that his double-double-crossing does not endear him to Silvia. She runs away, and is captured by the very brigands who have adopted Valentine. She's rescued by Proteus who, when she still rebuffs him, threatens to rape her. At which point Valentine steps out from behind a tree and disarms Proteus - both literally and figuratively. So impressive is Proteus's repentance that Valentine makes him a present of Silvia. "All that was mine in Silvia I give thee," is the line; and though there have been attempts to prove that it doesn't mean what it appears to mean, or that it's a satire on exaggerated Renaissance ideals of friendship, it's very hard to make them stick. It certainly appalls Julia, who is still in disguise and, fearing that she may be about to lose her man again, faints dead away. This is the most notorious crux in the play and I wondered, given all the publicity, how Shakespeare in the Ruff were going to confront it.

They don't. They simply cut the line; and the play goes merrily on without it. Having skirted the big problem, the Shakespeare-in-the-Ruffians (their coinage, and I like it) set about solving a less obvious one. Julia, they reason, can't possibly take Proteus back without a murmur, not after all he's put her through. Throughout the evening, they've been buffing up an admittedly slender script by throwing in lines from elsewhere in the complete works; passages have been lifted from As You Like It, Measure for Measure and even Othello. Now, at the close, they borrow the bittersweet finale of another early but far wiser comedy, Love's Labour's Lost. As it's not every week that I get to withhold the ending of a Shakespeare play, I won't say precisely how this works. But work it does. And since the show is frankly advertised as an adaptation, with an abbreviated title, there's no call to get purist about it.

In fact, I could wish they'd gone further. In their version Valentine still pairs off with Silvia, with the production's full approval. But they might have made something of the fact that, in the last two pages of the text as written, neither lady gets to say a word. This isn't unusual in a Shakespeare comedy; even the most spirited and loquacious heroines tend to go very quiet at the end, probably because that's when the plot lines have to be tied up and it falls to someone in authority, in those days invariably a man, to sort them out. (The only exception is Portia, who's still in charge at the end of The Merchant of Venice by virtue of being the richest and therefore most powerful person on the scene, which happens to be her own house.) Still, it would be perfectly possible to suggest that Julia and Silvia are silently protesting the ways in which their destinies are being decided. I doubt if that crossed Shakespeare's mind, but he isn't around to tell us.

Brendan McMurtry-Howlett's production, though, has merrier and mellower ends in view. Among a hardworking and multi-tasking cast, there are especially alert performances from Lesley Robertson as Julia, and from Adrian Morningstar as a fresh-faced Proteus in whose mouth butter would not stand the slightest chance of melting and who really does seem capable of persuading himself that every lie he tells is justified. For his most villainous soliloquy the director has him cunningly flanked by the two people he's about to ruin. Trudy Weiss, who though Canadian was last seen by me at the National Theatre in London, shows what an advantage experience and authority can be when you have a Duchy to run. The clown scenes, often this play's salvation, are here subdued; even the dog, for whom the company may partly have been named, fails to take full advantage of what has been called the best canine role ever written. David Patrick Flemming, playing three parts, is best as the rejected suitor Thurio, a rich rube from Tennessee, or somewhere deeply Southern, whose departure with a line that couldn't be found in any Shakespeare play was, I confess, my favourite moment. I feel less tolerant about the substitution of a country ballad for the justifiably famous Who Is Silvia? Update the tune, by all means, but the words, the reiteration of her rival's name, have to be kept intact if they are to have their proper painful effect on the eavesdropping Julia.

A last look back at Summer Works and to a play of which we will surely hear more, called Iceland but set here: Nicolas Billon's best yet, a gripping story that makes a strong, witty statement about the ways we live now, in relation to how much or little money we have. It's constructed of three intertwined monologues, given performances - by Kawa Auda, Claire Calnan and Christine Horne - that ranged from the superb to the superlative.

Two Gents runs through Sept. 2 in Withrow Park. Admission is free. Visit shakespeareintheruff.com for more information.

THEATRE REVIEW

STUDIO THEATRE, NIAGARA-ON-THE-LAKE

Iloved Carole Frechettes The Small Room at the Top of the Stairs when it was at the Tarragon last season. I therefore approached the Shaw Festivals revival of an earlier Frechette play, Helen's Necklace, hoping I would like it more than when it, too, was produced at Tarragon a few years ago. It wasn't to be; if theres any light, I still havent seen it. The Niagara production is in fact inferior to the Toronto one, but the main problem is still the play. The Small Room has a story. Helen's Necklace has only an idea.

Helen has lost her necklace. It has no great monetary but much sentimental value. She wanders all over town in a taxi looking for it -- town" being in a far-off, war-battered country whose inhabitants have suffered losses far more serious than her own. This is something she comes to learn over the course of the play, though it's surprising she should need the lesson. Her most wrenching encounter is with a woman looking for a lost child whom she insists is a neighbours. In the course of the conversation the woman is brought to acknowledge that the child is her own, and dead.

The play belongs to what seems to be a subgenre of French-Canadian playwriting: one in which Westerners have their consciousness raised and their consciences stirred by visiting unspecified places in the Middle East and being lectured about them. Wajdi Mouawads Scorched is a more elaborate essay on the same theme. There are obvious differences -- Mouawad has the greater territorial ambition, Frechette the finer fingertips -- but they both present their characters as symbols before, or rather without, establishing them as people.

Frechette's characters here seem unnervingly aware of their place in their playwright's pattern. Helens second most crucial encounter is with a man on a building site who tells her exactly what he thinks she and her necklace stand for. Of his own and his peoples situation he cries out, "We cannot go on living like this." Helen adopts this mantra as her own, repeating it during the rest of the play.

The trouble with this is that we have almost no idea of how she's been living previously. (A brief flashback to a broken relationship is no help, apart from the fact that it violates the conventions of the rest of the play.) Reencountering the play again reminded me of how much The Small Room gained from having the Bluebeard story as a point of departure. It seems to have freed Frechette's imagination, and spurred her inventiveness, in a way unmatched by her own predetermined fable. Shes in good company; Shakespeare worked best with borrowed plot lines. So did the Greeks.

MichelineChevriersproduction departs from the Tarragon staging, and also from all previous plays in the Shaw studio, by opting for a conventional one-end-of-the-room staging. This means that a play constructed entirely of duologues (all the people Helen meets are played by the same actor, regardless of gender) gets lost in a lot of unused space, on a set (by Judith Bowden) that tries vainly to be evocative.

Tara Rosling is appealing as Helen, but I preferred Susan Coyne's more businesslike approach at the Tarragon; she suggested the possibility of an offstage professional life, whereas Rosling seems more like sensitivity waiting to happen. Sanjay Talwar repeats his multiple performance from before, and is lost, angry and perplexed as required. The perplexity comes in his recurring role as the taxi driver, continually setting the heroine down and picking her up again, and generally earning what one hopes was a handsome tip.

At its Toronto premiere, the play's counterpointing of a minor private grief with huge public ones felt meretricious. Nine years later, measured against events in Syria and elsewhere, it seems closer to offensive.

robert.cushman@hotmail.com Helen's Necklace runs until Aug. 31. For tickets and more information, call 1-800-511-7429 or shawfest.com.

You win some, you lose some. Second City won handsomely with their last show, which was the best in recent memory. They lose heavily with its successor, We've Totally (probably) Got This!, which may be the worst. Fair's fair. This is the rare Second City revue whose title has something to do with the goods on offer. In fact, it even turns up in the dialogue. The words are uttered by a mall security team dealing with a break-in at Reitmans. (Let no one say the show doesn't confront real-life events.) Two of the guards are young and male and reasonably spry, but they are obliged to defer to their supervisor, who is older and female and has to be helped up and down the ladders that she insists on scaling. This is fairly funny when it starts but it then does nothing but repeat itself. That's the problem with most of the evening. It oscillates between taking passable ideas and beating them into the ground, and taking hopeless ones and doing the same.

There is a theme, or a tone, going through the show. At its beginning, at its end, and at several points in between, we get to watch the cast of six rocking in their seats in what might be a bus, a plane or even a rather large car, while lights flash on and off like crazy and the sound levels do their best to terrify us. The message might be politely paraphrased as "something terrible is going to happen," and now, as at most times, that is hard to argue with. However, if this show is trying to get down to political cases, it's doing a very woolly job of it. A one-liner about Rob Ford's motoring mishaps isn't enough to save a painfully repetitive sketch about legal sharks capitalizing on driving disasters. (Repetition, in this context, means a running gag that won't run.) Nor does mentioning Stephen Harper automatically qualify as political satire, even in a sketch where one of the characters claims to be the PM's daughter, and sings a song about it.

The number in question is set in a Curves exercise salon, and it does have its moments: moments when the dictated moves become excessively, well, dictatorial, culminating in one called the Sieg Heil manoeuvre, which drives one of the shyer company members out of the room in silent and understatedly funny protest. There's a promising sketch at the beginning of the first half in which a married couple agree to sign any mortgage arrangement rather than go back and face the bank again (we've all been there) and then get down to telling their son to "check your attitude" every time his school assignments prove he's smarter than they are. But it, too, doesn't so much build as repeat. Ditto for an even more promising sketch at the start of the second half, in which two desperately cheerful Haitian entertainers called Marco and Paolo (or just Marco Polo) offer some mordant insights into the state of their country's health care, or just of their country. They also quiz the audience, one of whom on my night admitted to be studying for a degree in education. "Aah," said Marco, unless it was Paolo, "you're studying studying." Nice. And if insouciantly dark is what you're looking for, I recommend a sketch in which two soldiers cope with the request of their mortally wounded buddy not to die a virgin. It develops in a manner oddly reminiscent of Kiss of the Spider Woman.

That, though, is about all I can recommend. Well, that and a musical number in which the three ladies in the cast sing about how about how Canadian women envy Brazilian women their sexiness, and then switch accents to state the reverse. It's rather convincing. Far more typical, though, is a sketch - again, praiseworthily drawn from the recent news - about schoolkids bullying their bus driver. The cast get somebody up from the audience and egg him on (it was a "him" on the night I went) to do the tormenting for them. This means that the sketch ceases to be about the humiliation of the driver and instead becomes about the humiliation of a member of the public. All right, the victim in question didn't seem all that humiliated - in fact, his enforced adlibs compared favourably with those of the professionals - but it still left the number feeling pointless and bloated. Onstage audience participation - as opposed to just taking suggestions from the house and improvising, as in the Haiti sketch - has become far too common a crutch at Second City. It leaves the material looking pointless and bloated, which is what happens here. It doesn't help that they seem especially proud of this sketch and refer back to it later. This kind of subliminal reprise can be delightful when it works, but not when it reminds you of something that you didn't much enjoy in the first place.

Camellia Koo has designed a set suggestive of a large, bare room, incorporating an upper level that, other than in the mall number, hardly gets used. Its false proscenium is surmounted by two long rows of books, or at least by drawings thereof, which could be a comment on something, though I'm not sure what.

Seven talented performers are involved, though one of them, Melody A. Johnson, functions only as director, in which capacity she does not seem to be doing her funniest work. There's a lot of shouting and screaming, and a distinct - or rather indistinct - lack of clarity and point. Carly Heffernan does most of the heavy lifting among the women, with Ashley Comeau and Stacey McGunnigle as backup. Among the men, Alastair Forbes is an invaluable lanky raconteur and de facto master of ceremonies. Jason DeRosse, alternately bumptious and victimized, is appealing in both guises, though starved of good material. Similarly underserved is Nigel Downer, who gets his biggest moment as a rap poet, offering new twists on nursery rhymes suggested from the house. He looks great doing them, even though hardly any of his new spoken words are intelligible. In fact, he's best when flatly refusing a source and passing instantly on to the next. One that nobody came up with at my visit was the saga of the little girl with the curl, whose particular qualities would seem to be especially apposite to Second City: when they're good they can be very, very good. When they're not - well, you know how it goes.

Indefinite run. 51 Mercer St. Call 416-343-0011 or visit secondcity. com for ticket information.

Toronto has a new cabaret venue, the Flying Beaver Pubaret, which as its name might suggest, is in the back room - a long and surprisingly elegant one - of a pub (488 Parliament St., at Carlton). This past Wednesday night, singer John Alcorn took command of its stage for an evening of Cole Porter songs. It's the first in a weekly series of Songbook programs (next week, Jerome Kern; after that, Berlin and Gershwin) that Alcorn has planned for as long as the traffic will allow. Judging by the packed house he attracted this week, that could be quite some time.

I labelled Alcorn as a singer, but in fact he does, and is known for, other musical things as well. "I think of myself," he said when I spoke to him the evening before the Porter gig, "as a singer/composer." He does a lot of theatre work, and is especially known for providing the scores for the virtuoso puppet shows of his partner, Ronnie Burkett: "When I'm working on one of Ronnie's shows, I submerge myself in it for a few months." But when he re-emerges he gets back to singing.

Given these dual talents it's logical that he should have started as a singersongwriter, on the approved model from the 1970s. The emphasis changed when a journalist friend gave him a copy of Alec Wilder's book American Popular Song: The Great Innovators 1900-1950. Wilder, a composer and lyricist himself, codified and analyzed the work of his peers and predecessors in a way that had never been attempted before. First published in 1972, it was a triumphant bucking of the tide. It may have been the single greatest factor in the rediscovery and reassessment of what's become known as the Great American Songbook. Tony Bennett refers to it, every chance he gets, as "the Bible," and it has by now inspired two further generations listeners and performers. For Alcorn, it was an education but also, in a way, a re-education. "It goes back to when I was a kid. My mother's father was in a dance band; my dad was a big Sinatra fan. And there were also a lot of original Broadway cast albums in the house."

Alcorn was born in Toronto, but his family subsequently moved to New Brunswick and then Nova Scotia. But in the middle of this Canadian childhood, "when I was 12 or 13, we moved to New Hampshire for a couple of years." And there, in a flea market, he came across an old Victrola, going cheap. He bought it, and found that it came with "a stack of old 78s," including Ella Fitzgerald's original hit recording of A-Tisket, A-Tasket. In terms of musical and verbal sophistication that's a fairly far cry from Cole Porter, but it unquestionably swung.

Jump a few decades and find that, in Alcorn's words, "as the Baby Boom generation grows older, our tastes tend to grow more sophisticated. There's a different level of creativity going on in the music of Porter, Harold Arlen and the others, both in lyrics and music. It's not a question of what's better or what's worse, it's more in qualities of emphasis. For Bob Dylan and Leonard Cohen, they were more focused on words. But they didn't have great compositional chops. And," he added hurriedly, "they didn't need them."

When he started out, Alcorn accompanied himself on piano but he gave that up some years ago. At the Flying Beaver, he doesn't have keyboard accompaniment at all. The main reason for this is that the stage is only big enough for a small electric piano, which he understandably dislikes. He has two sidemen: Steve Wallace, bass, and Reg Schwager, guitar. Wallace persuaded him that Schwager could play as richly and supportively as any pianist. He's turned out to be right.

This was amply demonstrated at Wednesday's show, which began with three familiar songs - You're the Top, I Get a Kick Out of You, Anything Goes - all done uptempo. After the show was over, I asked Alcorn if he thought of himself as a jazz singer. He answered that he'd started to, once he'd begun winning jazz polls, and that he was certainly happiest when singing with jazz musicians. I remarked that he did daring things with rhythm (that's especially true when he comes in after one of Schwager's solos), and he said that those choices were dictated by how he wanted to phrase the lyric: "I learned a long time ago that I can't sell just anything; I need to have a personal commitment to what I'm singing about." Frankly, I didn't get that from those first three songs - the sense was there, but not the peculiar semi-jaded, semi-ardent Porter style - but I rapidly changed my mind.

The next song up was the obscurest selection of the night, the lovely rueful ballad After You, Who, and it was done delicately, with an affecting deep note on the crucial vulnerable word "care." Even better was What Is This Thing Called Love?, done much slower than usual. This song has a seldom-sung introductory verse, that's almost a song in itself. In fact, it has two, and Alcorn is the only singer I've ever known do both of them. The second, in particular, takes the song into far more despairing territory than we might have suspected, and Alcorn struck just the right balance of quizzical cut-glass introspection and baffled desolation. The inevitable Night and Day was rejuvenated by a surging vocal, and even more by some fine melodic re-invention from Schwager. I've Got You Under My Skin (which is really Night and Day's twin) was given a treatment that avoided all foredoomed comparisons with Sinatra's Swingin' Lovers version by opting for a slow, incantatory, almost unearthly treatment that brought out the song's driven hopelessness. That's a constant note with Porter; I Concentrate on You, which was Alcorn's closer, may be the only serene unshadowed love song he ever wrote, and even that has an obsessive note about it, if only in the title.

There were lighter treats as well: Too Darn Hot, in which Wallace's bass made a thoroughly persuasive substitute for the "full drum kit" that Alcorn said he originally envisaged; Let's Do It, all verse-and-five-choruses of it, with Alcorn providing especially amusing visual illustration of the old sloths who hang down from twigs while doing it; and, as an encore, Miss Otis Regrets, which managed to be both funny and mordant. "It all felt," Alcorn said to me afterwards, "very much like an opening night." I think it was a good one.

Max Telzerow / Alcorn will program Songbook nights as long as the venue will have him.; Caption:

THEATRE REVIEW

Cirque du Soleil's Amaluna Grand Chapiteau, Toronto Portlands

Theres a scene in The Tempest in which the magician Prospero, as an engagement present for his daughter Miranda and her princely intended Ferdinand, produces an entertainment to all of whose characters are goddesses. Its generally referred to as the Masque Scene. Attending Amaluna, the latest extravaganza from Cirque du Soleil, is like seeing that masque stretched out over an entire evening.

There's good reason for this. The Cirque show is confessedly based on the Shakespeare play. It also professes to be a celebration of women; it has a high proportion of female performers - which, this being Cirque, means contortionists, gymnasts and such - plus what was known in less enlightened times as an all-girl band.

The trend starts at the top. Prospero is now Prospera; she's still the ruler of an island - though this one is populated, mostly by unicyclists - and she still conjures up a storm, literally. For her prototype, this and the resultant shipwreck were part of a revenge plot; for Prospera, a devoted mother, its just an elaborate way of finding the right young man for her daughter.

Up until now, this Miranda seems to have been leading a happy enough existence, frolicking with an upstanding man-sized lizard who swishes an impressive and, it subsequently transpires, detachable tail. He suggests, at least initially, a cuddlier Caliban, and he is indeed called Cali. Im not sure which of Prospera's many attendant sprites corresponds to Ariel, but I figured it to be the one who hangs down from an air-borne hoop, which I thought of as Ariel's aerial.

Ferdinand, when the sea washes him up, turns out to have been renamed Romeo, presumably to reassure both Miranda and the audience that he is indeed lover-boy material. He even, alone in the cast, gets name-checked in the course of the action; Cirque shows being understandably short on dialogue, we can only work out who the other people are by checking with the program, but Romeo has apparently been hanging out with the clowns, and they do get to talk, at length.

Theres a male clown, who might be Shakespeares Trinculo or Stephano or both, and a female clown, who's in residence from the start, if not before; she does the welcoming-the-audience and turn-offyour-cellphones bit. When he and she collide, we temporarily leave the world of The Tempest and enter that of The Magic Flute. They shack up, and before you know it have produced a dozen babies, pretty much before our eyes. All this while Romeo and Miranda are still at the hand-holding stage; some relationships just move faster than others.

In themselves the clown scenes are every bit as tedious as these Cirque interludes usually are, and even more protracted. But at least they're used to provide a conscious counterpart to the central romance, thereby bringing the show to a level of dramaturgical sophistication hitherto unknown in these parts.

Of course, dramaturgical sophistication is not necessarily what you go to Cirque du Soleil for. A problem with Amaluna, though, is that its short on the things - the breathbating, credulity-defying things - that you do go there for. Its a case of swings and roundabouts, except that the swings aren't swinging very wildly and the roundabouts are turning slow.

The director, Diane Paulus, arrives with a solid record in non-circus entertainment (she's responsible for Broadways current Porgy and Bess and its recent Hair) and shes at her best here when she's telling the story. Most Cirque productions claim to have a story, and it usually boils down to someone going on a nebulous quest and arriving at a mysterious castle where people do tricks as if they were in, well, a circus. Amaluna, with its classical underpinnings, has far more of a spine.

Sometimes it relaxes too much for comfort; I had a hard time sorting out the various lady deities who are apparently meant to be assisting at, or presiding over, Miranda's transition into womanhood. Prospera herself (Julie Andrea McInnes) seems to be controlling everybodys destinies with the help of a magic cello, but she doesnt really do much except to extend a hand over whatever is going on as if to say, "Hey, I did this."

However, Miranda (Iuliia Mikhaylova) is a delight, whether as a bewitched spectator of the magic, or a bewitching participant in it; the fact that she's both is the show's greatest claim to unity. Shes an aquatic acrobat (an aquackrobat?) who performs her choicest feats inside a tank shaped like a giant goldfish bowl. Romeo (Edouard Doye) crosses a tightrope to win her, just as we were expecting him to do, but his most spectacular talent is for climbing; put him in Verona and hed be up that balcony in no time.

Cali (Viktor Kee) reverts unexpectedly to jealous type, pushing young Romeo into the fishbowl, shutting the lid on it, and then doing a gleeful juggling act on top; it isn't an especially impressive juggling act (not by Cirque standards, that is; just you try it) but we get the point.

There's some group-juggling much earlier on, some of it done by performers who are niftily balancing on the soles of other performers feet. Some local Amazons do some tumbling on uneven bars that involves them playfully kicking some minor male castaways in the face. The guys get their revenge, however, at the start of act two with a tumbling routine on a seesaw, the one act to induce the sheer physical exhilaration that has traditionally been this troupes trademark.

A less boisterous kind of magic is administered by Lara Jacobs who, using her feet, raises and meticulously reassembles a set of bamboo shoots. It's the most hypnotic display of picking up sticks you are ever likely to see.

Amaluna runs in Toronto until Nov. 4 and runs in Vancouver starting Nov. 23. For tickets and more information, visit cirquedusoleil.com.

2012-09-20-banking-on-grand-illusions-a-:
A man who, after working all his life for the same company, is no longer useful to them, is summarily dismissed, with the implication that really it's all for his own good. His new boss, son of his old boss, is embarrassed, but more interested in his new wire recorder, the latest technological toy. His own sons, brought up to believe they are the inheritors of a society in which anything is possible, are crushingly disillusioned by the discovery that it isn't. Home owners, car owners and just plain appliance owners find themselves "in a race with the junk-yard," yearning to possess just one item that is still functional by the time they've finished paying for it. Neighbourhoods that used to feel like open spaces are increasingly boxed in by high buildings. There's probably never been a time since its premiere in 1949 that Arthur Miller's Death of a Salesman hasn't seemed topical, but its pertinence at the moment is beyond painful.

Indeed, Soulpepper's revival, directed by Albert Schultz, is even more powerful now than when it was first presented two years ago. (Its remount, with just one major cast change, must count as a revival of a revival.) Some of this obviously has to do with the production playing itself in. Salesman is, above all else, a play about a family; actors and audiences respond to it fully and easily because we've all been there, caught in those same crosscurrents of love and resentment. On one level, it's the kind of identification that works for soap operas, but soaps don't give you the same sense of context, the same rich correlation between the characters' social and economic circumstances and their emotional conflicts. Willy Loman's role as a salesman doesn't determine his fate -- he'd find some way of screwing up his life, whatever his job was -- but it highlights and focuses it.

There's a scene at the end of the play's first act that takes off like a rocket, a scene in which we see the Loman family simultaneously pulling together and falling apart. Elder son Biff is back home in Brooklyn after years bumming around the countryside. In school, he'd been a football hero, with not just the ball but the whole world at his feet, or so everybody believed. (Only in America? I'm not sure.) But he dropped out, never tried for the college place that seemed guaranteed, and has become a bitter disappointment to everyone, including himself. He's briefly roused by the prospect of a new career selling sporting goods, egged on by younger brother Happy, who has a marketing scheme that seems to consist of re-enacting their boyhood. Willy, who a few moments earlier was all resentful accusation, is now all enthusiasm, his faith in the dream rekindled. Linda, his wife, is enthusiastic too, though she should probably know better -- but she's one person for whom love, family love, really does conquer all. But whenever she chimes in, Willy, who seems to think this is man talk, impatiently shushes her. He does it once too often, and Biff ( "Stop yelling at her!") explodes. Willy, punctured and momentarily ashamed, shuffles off. Linda tries to mend fences; Biff subsides. A whole domestic drama has unfolded before us in less than 10 minutes.

The key to it all is Willy's desperate volatility, his bounding from one feeling to another -- and from one opinion to its opposite -- in a second. He simply can't afford to look clearly at himself, or at anybody else. One way in which he differs from the traditional tragic hero is that it isn't the realization of truth that does him in, but the persistence of illusion. That may well be closer to the facts of life. And his is, in its way, quite a grand illusion. There is now a grandeur about Joseph Ziegler's performance that in no way obscures Willy's weakness or his occasional brutality; he always had Willy's chameleon quality down perfectly, but he now makes both the man's pride and his humiliation agonizingly real.

Nancy Palk, who has spent the last couple of years inhabiting several of the modern stage's major mothers, gets completely inside this one, a woman who can see through her husband and her sons while still protecting them; some of her finest moments are her angriest. The bond between her and Ari Cohen's Biff is very strongly portrayed; and he, in a play full of flashbacks, is equally convincing as golden boy and tarnished man. The moment at which he passes from one to the other, the moment when he loses all faith in his father and his world falls apart, is magnificently done. An abiding puzzle in the play is how much of this Willy has managed to blot out; much of the time he seems genuinely mystified about why Biff should have, as he says, given up on his life. A lesser mystery is why Happy, the less favoured son, should feel so un-resentful about it; his own life isn't going so well, and he lies about it in the family tradition, but it's for other reasons. Mike Ross, the production's newcomer, gets both Happy's brashness in company and his dependence at home. Michael Hanrahan and Gregory Prest are beautifully, quietly authoritative as the father and son next door who can help and support but, as the play's most moving scenes make clear, not save. William Webster, bathed in what seems to be his own private lighting design, is a haunting, taunting apparition as the rich Uncle Ben whom we only meet in Willy's tormented dreams. Lorenzo Savoini's set still seems cramped; it suggests that the Lomans live in a bungalow. Everything else is as good as before or better.

robert.cushman@hotmail.com Continues at the Young Centre for the Performing Arts until Oct. 6. For ticket information, visit soulpepper.caor call 416-866-8666.

THEATRE REVIEW

Julie Sits Waiting

Theatre Passe Muraille Backspace, Toronto

Julie is the middle-aged wife of a cop named Rick. She is having an affair with an Anglican priest named Mick. We don't meet Rick; we do very much meet Mick. The rhyming names are presumably meant to tell us something, this being a new avant-garde opera rather than one of those vulgar musical comedies with their snappy lyrics and rhymes used for comic effect. Being funny is about the last thing on this show's mind.

Tom Walmsley wrote the libretto, and Louis Dufort the music. One of the traditional differences between operas and musicals has been that in musicals the tunes are usually written first and the lyrics fitted to them, while the opera composer generally fashions his notes to what the librettist has given him. Nevertheless, and paradoxically, it's taken for granted that in opera the music is the most important element, to the extent that operas are often performed in languages their audiences don't understand and at pitches that make most of the words incomprehensible anyway.

Surtitles, employed these days even when the text is in the audience's native language, may ease this problem, but they don't eliminate it. They may even aggravate it, since they entail a double focus, detaching us from the total musical dramatic experience opera is advertised as providing.

In recent decades the two genres have been drawing closer together. Many musicals have been through-sung; Julie Sits Waiting, officially an opera, contains spoken passages, which certainly aren't intended to relax the tension. Dufort's score is officially described as electro-acoustic, with the electric part coming from the instrumentation and the acoustic, sometimes "enhanced," from the singers. Both are, in the main, nervejanglingly effective, which is what Walmsley's text demands of them. Whether it deserves all the effort is another matter.

Like the relationship it depicts, it starts out all right. Julie and Mick come together (I'm afraid, yes, I do mean that) in a vacant house that Julie's husband is renovating. They have never clapped eyes on one another before, having arranged their assignation electronically (the libretto's best line may be, "Thank God for the Internet"), but are enchanted and excited when they do meet.

After a decent amount of vocal foreplay, they retire offstage and get on with it. While they are gone, the space is filled with fizzy light-show projections, designed (by Jeremy Mimnagh) to suggest what a good time the couple are having, and succeeding better at it than so cliched a device probably has any right to. We gather, when the characters return, that the sex has been wild and violent and that they've both enjoyed it. The sensible thing would seem to be to let them get on with it.

Which, it appears, they do for a while, but their author throws rocks in their way. Both develop qualms of conscience. Julie's, involving her loyalties less to her husband than to their teenaged daughter, seem the more prosaic and believable though not, given what we were initially shown, insurmountable. Mick's are higher-strung and farther fetched. He turns out to be one in that long line of theatrical clergy who have lost their faith but kept their guilt. This leads him certainly to self-hatred, probably to hatred of others and eventually to acts of unmotivated mayhem.

It might all seem less contrived if Mick had been given words that sing, musically or dramatically, but his remain ploddingly explanatory: prosaic without sounding natural. They revived my unworthy suspicions about whether audiences would be able to take opera quite as seriously if they could hear the words. Which in this case you can: all of them. To be fair, the words in most pop operas, sometimes known as rock musicals, are worse. Although of course those shows are less pretentious. (Scratch that; they aren't.)

The piece is presented by a company who combine the irresistible name of Good Hair Day Productions with a praiseworthy commitment to championing new forms of music theatre. It's directed, by Heidi Strauss and Alex Fallis, on a sustained note of visual and aural intensity; and it gets, from Fides Krucker and Richard Armstrong, the virtuoso performances it demands, rigorously unglamorous but searingly passionate. Armstrong is, if anything, too sweatily believable; Krucker is white-hot (as opposed to her partner's red), making her closing moments crazily credible, however dubious the steps it's taken to get her there.

I'm unsure why she gets the title billing, when the two characters are equally important. Nor am I clear as to what she's waiting for, unless it's to be punished for experiencing pleasure. For all its assaults on the senses, this is a very puritanical show.

Julie Sits Waiting runs until Sept. 23. For more information, visit passemuraille.on.ca.
2012-09-22-brothers-in-arms-no-great-mis:
The best scene in No Great Mischief - really, the only good one - occurs in the second act and takes place in the 1960s, in a mine on Cape Breton. Most of the miners are members of the family, or clan, MacDonald, and a good proportion of those are named Alexander. One of them has just graduated from college, as a dentist, but hes helping out down the mine following the death there of another Alexander MacDonald, a cousin who used to bully him when they were at school. There now appears a third Alexander, a draft-dodging, guitarstrumming relative from the U.S., referred to as the California Cousin. They all get to talking about family history and traditions, and someone references the MacDonalds valiant service on the Plains of Abraham, where General Wolfe apparently remarked of them that, brave though they undoubtedly were, it was "no great mischief if they fall."

This is the only time that David S. Young's play makes direct reference to its title, which is also that of the Alistair MacLeod novel on which it's based. Coming where it does, its a rueful illumination, all the more powerful for its casualness, of both the anger and the stoicism of a family accustomed to being treated as cannon fodder, which translates fairly easily into coal fodder. The tradition goes back to the Scottish Highlands, where the MacDonalds had a long history of being used and butchered, a history that the program, though not the play, helpfully explains. The scene gives way to a longer and showier, but less satisfying, sequence in which the mines Scots contingent face off against their francophone counterparts in a contest of musical cultures. Everyone onstage, it seems, can play something, and the encounter develops from aggressive confrontation to uneasy, mutually, or musically, respectful truce. It's like a less amiable version of the tavern scene in Fiddler on the Roof; or, given the Cape propensity for dancing while playing, Fiddler on the Hoof. The peace, such as it is, doesn't last; there will, shortly, be blood, whose ultimate cause may be California Cousins dirty tactics when playing poker. He might be said to start the whole scene off with a rousing, and I guess relevant, rendition of The Times They Are a-Changin. But the music and the mayhem aren't well tied together, and the former seems to be prolonged mainly for its own roof-raising sake. (It does get the applause it begs for.)

The problem, as when the show was first done at the Tarragon in 2004, is that the play remains an undigested first-person novel. Dental Alexander, as we may call him, tells the story and hence does most of the talking, but he isn't the protagonist; hes somebody who sees things, and to whom things sometimes happen, and who tells us about them, but he hardly ever initiates them. The one, fatal, action he does take is done almost by accident, and even this he has to describe to us, while its being elaborately illustrated. (I think I could happily live without seeing another scene of slow-motion violence.) Otherwise, he's the bright boy whose family wants him to get on and get out, which he does: a perfectly believable situation but one that needs exploration and individualization if it's to avoid seeming stock, and that doesnt get it.

The more dynamic character is his elder brother Calum. The boys were orphaned when Alexander was a child; loss of parents, usually at sea, is another family tradition. Calum had to look after Alex; in later years, the roles were reversed. The plays framework is that Alex visits Calum who's now holed up in Toronto, practically dying of drink. This sets off the flood of reminiscences, personal and historical, that make up most of the evening. Eventually, we find out how Calum got to be the way he is, but it's the answer to a question that hasnt been asked. The action has been too diffuse for there to be any suspense. Richard Roses production includes some flashy lighting and sound effects, and amiable "character" cameos from various grandparents, but no unifying interest, other than a generalized sense of dynastic doom.

The two principal performers are, to an extent, the victims of their own virtues. R.H. Thomson is one of nature's interlocutors, but his corkscrewing carefulness adds to the evening's frustrations; he worries exquisitely rather than getting a move on. David Fox is, as always, powerful, but he drowns his words deeper than usual even before seriously hitting the bottle. Both actors, it must be said, have extraordinary visual moments, lit solely from within, of reverting to their characters far younger selves.

Ben Irvine lightens things up in a different way as California Cousin. He leaves far too early considering what an enlivening presence he is and how strong an influence he has on the action - another example of the gulf between what is effective in a novel and what in a play. Actors in the eight-strong cast not involved in a particular scene are lined up facing the back wall of Charlotte Deans set, looking for all the world as if they're standing at a row of invisible urinals. The play's last section devolves into a hymn to Cape Breton, as if this were a play about a place rather than, as its been insisting, a family. As a play about Canadian history, it left me nostalgic for the trenchant cartooning of VideoCabarets saga of the Village of the Small Huts.

No Great Mischief runs through Oct. 21 at the Tarragon Theatre. For more information, call 416-531-1827 or visit tarragontheatre.com.
