2012-09-27-graves-anatomy-el-velador-tak:
One of the last things we hear on the soundtrack of PBSs new production of El Velador is a television announcement. It's saying, "unstable conditions will affect the region for at least 24 hours." It's a weather report, but it could equally well apply to living conditions in a part of Mexico effectively ruled by organized crime. Except that with the weather, theres a chance of things getting better once the 24 hours are up.

El Velador means The Night Watchman and Natalia Almadas calm, haunting documentary film revolves around Martin, who has that job in the northern Mexican town of Culiacan, identified in the film's publicity as "capital of Sinaloa and [of] Mexico's drug heartland." The particular site that Martin guards is the city cemetery; if Culiacan is the epicentre of the drug trade, then the graveyard is the epicentre of Culiacan.

In itself its a splendid structure, or rather series of structures; the graves and memorials run an architectural gamut from peasant simplicity to Byzantine grandeur. Theyre beautifully photographed: Almada, who comes from the territory she depicts, has shot a visual tone poem, a requiem about requiems.

There's little dialogue. Martin, middle-aged and grizzled, says a few sentences to the camera. He tells us that at night you can't walk around the cemetery; its where the gangs have their parties, and also their shoot-outs. Every dawn finds a fresh crop of bodies, frequently hacked and tortured. We owe this information to news bulletins coming off the radio belonging to the mausoleums coconut seller; he does a brisk trade what with the number of mourners around, and the fact that most of them have young children.

We get glimpses of gravestones, and do the math on the ages of the victims; one I noted was 22. Fatalities in the past six years - the term of office of President Felipe Calderon, who promised a war on the drug lords - have been estimated in the high 50,000s.

Most of the film's words issue from the TV or the radio. We hear an interview with a U.S. government drug czar, regretting the carnage and self-flagellating over how little attention his country pays to Mexico (described as its most important neighbour - "along with Canada") as compared to all the millions it's poured into Afghanistan. He does not, strangely enough, suggest neutralizing the illegal drug trade by legalizing the drugs. His interview is immediately followed by a commercial for mattresses, maybe an easy ironic point but more likely an acknowledgment that life goes on.

Toward the end of the film, the newscasts announce that one of the leading gangsters - the capo of capos - has been run to ground and killed, "along with seven gunmen." Martins buddies, discussing the event in the films longest sequence of overheard conversation, aren't impressed. The dude wasn't any good anymore. They got rid of him. Therell be someone else.

Its a climate of lament and acceptance. Just once, and in the distance, we hear a cry of agony: a woman wailing, "My son, my son." This in not, in short, the contemporary Hispanic version of Boardwalk Empire. (I have to confess there were times when I wished it were.) It couldn't be said that we get to know Martin himself, but the film takes its tone from his stoical pertinacity; he seems watchful by nature as well as by trade.

At least he's in a growth industry: he and the florists. We see new tombs being constructed, gorgeous new wreaths being hung. For at least one young woman, widowhood seems to have become a vocation.

Meanwhile, the children eagerly buy coconut water from the vendor, or have it bought for them, and play hopscotch on the gravestones. Life, as I said before, as the film keeps saying, goes on. And so does death.

El Velador (The Night Watchman) airs Sept. 27 at 10 p.m. on PBS.
2012-10-02-a-pygmalion-for-the-political:
Michael Healey's Proud is notorious as the play the Tarragon Theatre wouldnt do, despite it being the last part of a trilogy with whose first two instalments the theatre had had considerable success. It was widely speculated that the Tarragon got cold feet on account of Proud being a play whose central character is the current Prime Minister. Although, as no official statement was ever made, we dont know if the cancellation was for that reason or if the Tarragon simply didn't think the play was good enough. If the latter's the case, I can only say that the Tarragon must have unrealistically high standards. Or, considering some of the plays that it has produced, that its fooling itself.

Proud, which has now reached the Toronto stage in a production essentially promoted by its author with himself in the leading role, is in fact a smaller, less formally adventurous play than its well-named predecessors Generous and Courageous, though on a minute-by-minute basis, its also a funnier one. (This last quality also has something to do with Healey's own presence on stage.) It's a counter-factual piece, in which Stephen Harper still has a majority, but a larger and more volatile one. In this alternate universe, hes won as large in Quebec as the NDP did in the real one and, like the NDP, he has a caucusful of rookie MPs as a result. Much of the play turns on the relationship between the PM and one of the most volatile of these recruits, a woman with the not-quite-persuasive name of Jisbella Lyth. (Ive never met a Jisbella. Have you? Has Healey?)

We start, in superior revue-sketch style, with the premier addressing his newly elected troops, promising huge but unspecified changes, warning of opposition from the opposition, and insisting on their unqualified loyalty. He finishes by directing them toward an open bar, which he promised will remain open for a full three quarters of an hour.

We then shift to his office, where he is directing Cary, his chief of staff, on house seating arrangements, stipulating that he does want to have to meet the gaze of any party member who has ever disagreed with him on any matter whatsoever. Cary says this will be difficult, and has a chart to prove it, but promises to do his best. And then Lyth bursts in, asking if either of them has a condom. It seems that Evan Solomon is interviewing her in her office, and she wants to have sex with him on her desk.

This development is fairly unlikely on several counts. (Spoiler: Solomon does not appear in the play.) It moves the tone into farce: not necessarily a bad move, but one it takes time to adjust to. Identifying Jisbella as a loose woman, which they don't much care about, and a loose cannon, which they do, her leaders set about firing her. When this doesn't work, she being smarter than they think, they decide to use her instead. She will sponsor an anti-abortion bill that has no chance of passing; shes an unlikely fit for this, being a single mother who has had a couple of terminations herself, but shell do as a piece of red meat thrown to the base while proving that her leader, who will not of course support her, isn't the fundamentalist fanatic of popular belief.

A double distraction in fact; and even more topical now than Healey must have thought when he wrote it. The scheme doesn't quite work out; the bill brings Jisbella attention, and even a certain amount of power, and she revels in it. It seems shes a Marxist,

of the Groucho persuasion: She has her principles, and if you dont like them, she has others. She also begins to fancy the Prime Minister something rotten, perhaps because she finds that seeming rigidity a challenge and a turn-on.

Healey has said that Shaw was a great influence on the writing of this play. People have pointed out the resemblances to Pygmalion (though to me the transformation of Jisbella rather suggests Frankenstein) while just last year at the Shaw Festival Healey adapted On the Rocks, another talkfest about a prime minister with transformational ambitions. Healey though adds an element that Shaw, at least at the explicit level, left out: sex. The mix isn't too comfortable. The plot requires us to accept the PM as a sex symbol, and I don't buy it. Still, Philip Larkin thought Mrs. Thatcher was sexy; it takes all sorts. But the play works best as crackling debate.

The stand-out scene has the PM passionately listing all the things that he doesnt feel passionate about, but that everybody thinks he does. ( "I dont care about Quebec. At all. I don't care about hospital wait times. I don't care about where the salmon went or why they came back." Im being very selective.) All he cares about is "an appropriately

sized government" and he wont even say what size that is. He makes all this sound, if not reasonable, then very appealing. After all, most of us don't care about the things we're supposed to care about.

Personally, I find it hard to believe that the real Prime Minister Harper doesnt believe in at least some of the things on his anti-hit-list. I also doubt, in my naive way, that the real Harper would swear as freely and engagingly as this one does, or that he could or would give his protegees young son such friendly and practical telephonic advice on how to turn potato latkes into hash browns. Healey's Harper is in fact a lot more likeable than his namesake, This is partly because of the way Healey writes him, and even more because of the way Healey plays him. It is, of course, impossible to write a decent play without falling in love with your central character, which is not the same as approving of him. Even reading the script, it's plain that Healey has given his protagonist his own sense of comic timing, which in performance is overwhelming. Healeys acting persona has generally been that of a bumbler with, increasingly, a backbone of steel. This is its definitive incarnation.

As Jis, a name the PM flatly refuses to use, Maev Beaty is sensationally good: switching from ditziness to determination and back again, with a quick flash timing to match Healeys slow burn. She's always had presence; she now has control. Tom Barnett plays fine third fiddle as Cary, and Miles Potter's direction doesnt let a moment slip.

There is a fourth character, a younger one, who moves the play into yet another dimension, and about whom I cant give anything away except to say that he also has an Evan Solomon connection and that he's played by Jeff Lillico, who's always welcome. The play needs him in order to transmit its darker implications, but its an awkward fit. Proud is not a conventionally well-made play, but it also isnt as radically and constructively ill-made as was Generous. But it's always sharp and sometimes hilarious, and though you may hope for more than that, you don't often get it. You don't usually get as much.

robert.cushman@hotmail.comProud runs through Oct. 6 at the Berkeley Street Theatre in Toronto, 416-368-3110.

THEATRE REVIEW

Between the Sheets

Tarragon Extra Space, Toronto

Nightwood Theatre's Between the Sheets is a gripping new play, terrifically performed. The rest of this review may constitute a spoiler, but I can't see any way of discussing it without.

Jordi Mand's play, her first, is set in a Grade 3 private-school classroom. It's the end of a parent-teacher evening. Teresa (Christine Horne), the young teacher, is just about to pack up and go home when Marion (Susan Coyne), a mother, appears to claim her interview slot to discuss her son Alex. This comes as a surprise to Teresa, since Marion hasn't made a booking, and anyway all Teresa's previous discussions about Alex have been with his father, Marion's husband, Curtis.

Marion is well aware of this, and is resentful about it. Well, more than resentful. Alex is a special-needs child, with what sounds like a serious case of ADD, and Marion doesn't like being left out of his loop. She certainly doesn't like Teresa's declaration that as Alex's teacher she spends more time with him than his career-woman mother does, and therefore understands him better. But what she likes least of all is her recent discovery, revealed after some initial thrust and parry, that her husband and Teresa are lovers.

That, plus Teresa's occupational paperwork, accounts for the failed pun of the title: the only clumsy thing about the play. The running time is a bare packed hour; we're a good 10 minutes into it before Marion drops her bombshell, and it's a measure of the author's skill that though we're not really surprised by it we're still shocked.

The same holds true for the other disclosures that come, thick and fairly fast, from one woman or the other for the rest of the play. About the unseen Curtis's incurably restless nature. About the plans he and Teresa seem to be making. About the economic pressures that keep Marion from her son while providing the money that sends him to school. About Teresa's own professional dedication, about her childlessness, and about her health.

Mand, her director Kelly Thornton, and their two actresses take the familiar technique of retrospective exposition, and imbue it with remorseless emotional logic. Each revelation is a revenge. Think Ibsen for long-range technique; Strindberg for short-haul intensity; and, for kinship of setting and subject, that other seat-clutching classroom duet, David Mamet's Oleanna. Like Oleanna, this play shows two people locked in mortal combat on the edge of a cliff. Also like Oleanna, it ends with one of them falling off, courtesy of an act that cannot be undone.

Mand, though, may be subtler than Mamet; she keeps the balance of power and of sympathy constantly shifting. Also unlike Mamet, she's charitable. Her two characters do have their moments, presented with tact and without sentimentality, of rapprochement. But then, as two women fighting over the same man, they would be likely to discover things in common. One telling detail is their varying use of one another's first names; it can signify patronage, guilt, sympathy or - the last time it happens - a horrific combination of all three.

The play might, as one psychological scar after another is laid bare, be accused of piling things on. But every person comes with issues, and every relationship automatically doubles them. Or, if you throw in this play's two offstage male characters, quadruples them. They interlock, and Mand makes each of them fresh and individual, with the possible exception of Marion's conflicted feelings over her enforced superwoman status; the situation is believable but the actual writing feels like an undigested magazine article.

The production can be wrenching without ever playing for pathos. There's a kind of hush all over the house while it's playing: the sound of an audience caught, held, rapt. It isn't something that you hear too often.

Between the Sheets runs until Oct. 7. For tickets and more information, visit nightwoodtheatre.net.

John Lauener / Between the Sheets is like David Mamet's Oleanna with notes of Ibsen and Strindberg mixed in.; Caption:

THEATRE REVIEW

Queen for a Day

Richmond Hill Centre for the Performing Arts

Soap opera, despite its name, does not need songs. Or maybe because of its name. A form whose whole reason for being is to push easy emotional buttons doesnt need to be made any more blatant than it already is. Queen for a Day is a soap musical, and the tautology sinks it.

It takes its name and its story from a 1950s radio (and later TV) show in which four women each day told the American public about their dreams and their problems, and in which the audience voted on which would have her problem alleviated and her dream made true. The musical's heroine, Claribel Anderson (based apparently on an actual contestant), gets on the show almost by accident and is pronounced the winner. She seems to have won the voters' hearts partly by the artless impetuosity with which she answers the hosts questions before he asks them, but mostly by her generosity when it comes to making her pitch; she asks that the wish of another contestant, in greater need, be granted in preference to her own. Whose heart wouldnt melt?

The radio program comes over as a slick mix of exploitation and compassion: a perennially popular combination that might more recently have been dubbed soap Oprah. The 20 minutes or so during which it's recreated onstage are by far the liveliest part of the evening. The program credits a bewildering number of people with book, "additional dialogue" and creative concept, but Chris Earle and Shari Hollett seem to be the primary writers, and their revue talents are probably responsible for the pace and sharpness with which the sequence unfolds.

The shamelessly recurring commercial jingles also seem to bring out the best in Linda Barnett, the musical's composer, lyricist and originator. Actor Alan Thicke, of whom my previous awareness was even vaguer, is perfect as our host Jack Bailey, gliding through the proceedings like a human oil slick. He keeps the persona going through a second-act appearance as a deus ex machina, as of a man programmed to do good deeds in his sleep. He should not, however, be called upon to sing.

Nor should anybody else in this show, including those who technically do it very well. That includes Blythe Wilson, who plays Claribel and is required to spoil the fun of the game show scene with a strenuously dramatic number called A Woman Has a Right to Change Her Mind. As weve already seen her change it, this doesnt add very much. That's the trouble throughout; the score takes obvious situations and makes them more obvious. The songs have the kind of generic titles (A Few Years from Now, One Wonderful Day, Maybe It's Time) that practically invite you to write your own synopsis, and though the tunes are reasonable facsimiles of the period, theyre never any more than that.

Claribel is a waitress in a Los Angeles diner. We learn that shes an independent spirit when she steps offstage to pump gas on the forecourt, and is roundly rebuked by her boss, who says that's man's work. He then goes into a number called Men Who Run the Show, in which he celebrates a surprisingly wide spectrum of red-blooded role models, from Hugh Hefner, who is a liberal, to Senator Joseph McCarthy, who on the whole wasnt. Soon after this Claribels husband, who keeps losing jobs and resents her having one, has a song called My Own Man, which says the same things all over again.

Having got us on its side on the subject of sexism, the show proceeds to tackle race; the fellow contestant whose cause Claribel champions is black. That Hollywood liberalism we keep hearing about seems to have made early inroads, since the game show staff, heartwarmingly if not quite believably, all back Claribel up. The studio audience are less enlightened, as the black contestant acknowledges when, thanking Claribel, she says that "those people wouldn't have voted for me for all the tea in China." It may not be the most original image, but it's a resonant and economical one, the best line in the show. But it, too, is vitiated when the actress (Angela Teek) has to go through the obligatory faux-gospel number. The show keeps fighting battles that have already been won, making brave statements that nobody in the audience is going to disagree with. The combination of cliche and uplift has admittedly carried many recent musicals to success. But they have generally applied the formula with a bit more know-how.

They have not, for example, weighed themselves down, as this one does, with a framework set 60 years after the main events. The elderly Claribel is a pack-rat whose apartment is being forcibly cleaned up by a juvenile offender doing community service. Of course the two apparent opposites bond while sorting through Claribels memorabilia, and the younger one learns some invaluable life lessons. What these might be, however, is unclear, since we are told absolutely nothing of what Claribels life has been like from that day to this. All we can take away is the knowledge that the veteran Denise Fergusson can hold a spirited end up in both speech and song; when her teenage help lays an angry rap number on her, she raps right back.

Meanwhile, back in the 1950s, the plot runs out and padding runs in. As queen for the day (and night), Claribel is taken to a nightclub, where a painfullyirrelevantCaribbean-crossed-with-Latin number happens. A mild romantic fling (Cory O'Brien, likeable) transpires out of nowhere and as speedily returns there. A squawky, screen-struck young friend (Marisa McIntyre) gets bewilderingly blackmailed. A more dubious acquaintance (Lisa Horner) is forced into a would-be show-stopper of vengeful hysteria that bears no relation to what has previously passed for her character. Even caricatures need consistency.

Tim French's production has one fine pictorial moment, posing the four aspirant queens against a bare studio backcloth. The musical staging operates on the assumption that anybody, regardless of narrative or persona, can be pressed into singing or dancing service at any time. They cant, not in an old-fashioned, quasi-realistic, dialogue-heavy show like this one. It puts serious, or at least solemn, sentiments into the mouths of dummies, and asks for brownie points.

The Queen for a Day phenomenon itself can be viewed as either liberating or degrading. To its credit, the musical sees both possibilities, but it never contrasts or reconciles them; it just grabs at whichever will make the easiest effect at any given moment. At the end, its implied that Claribel's day as queen was, pun made explicit, the crowning one of her life. That seems sort of sad. The show tries to present it as inspirational.

Queen for a Day runs until Oct. 7. For tickets and more information, visit queenforadaythemusical.com.

There are three theatres in Toronto that are pleasant to visit, irrespective of what happens to be playing in them. All of them are recent buildings. One is the Four Seasons Centre, more generally thought of as the Toronto opera house. Another is the Young Centre, home of Soulpepper. And the third, though apparently not for much longer, is the Princess of Wales.

This week David Mirvish, who owns the Princess of Wales and most of the adjoining territory, announced that the theatre is to be demolished as part of a new King Street development incorporating an art gallery that will make Mirvish's own legendary but largely unseen collection available to the public, a new campus for OCAD University, and three condominium towers, each a different shape. According to a letter sent to the media by Mir-vish, the Princess of Wales is "a beautiful facility of which I am proud, but it happens to be situated in the middle of the new project's path."

Well, it's Mirvish's property, he has a right to do what he likes with it, and he and his late father Ed have made huge contributions to the theatrical life of the city, indeed to its life in general. I share the widespread reaction that the last thing downtown Toronto needs is more condos, but quite possibly the new development will be the transformative addition to our cityscape that we are being promised. It's hard to tell from the preliminary sketches we've been shown; and as Frank Gehry, the architect, has said, they are only sketches. Much may change in what is apparently a multi-year project; one only hopes that there won't be too many second thoughts after the theatre has been levelled.

But if a theatre has to be sacrificed, why does it have to be this one? The Royal Alexandra is also a Mirvish property, and it's just down the street. Actually, I'm less shocked by the plan than by the cavalier reaction of some of my fellow theatre writers who claim that to shed tears over the loss of the Princess of Wales would be sentimental.

My objections aren't sentimental; they're practical. The late 1980s were Toronto's golden age of theatrical renovation. The Pantages - later the Canon, now the Ed Mirvish - was restored and reopened in 1989, as was the theatrical duplex of the Elgin and the Winter Garden. But the Princess of Wales was the first theatre, not just in Toronto but in Canada, to be built as a private enterprise since the Royal Alex back in 1907. (The Toronto Centre for the Arts, previously the North York Centre for the Performing Arts, was opened in 1993 as a combined private/ civic initiative. It's a great space in the wrong place. It's far easier to persuade North Yorkers to go downtown than the reverse.)

The Princess of Wales was opened, we're now told, merely as a "temporary facility" to house the Toronto production of Miss Saigon. Well, some temporary facility. It's lasted for 20 years, during which it's established itself as the most beautiful, audience-friendly big house in Toronto. The famous Frank Stella murals are the least of it, though we're promised that they'll mostly be retained in the new developments. The really rare achievement is the intimate contact between audience and performers, extraordinary considering the vastness of the stage and the spaciousness of the auditorium and equalled among big theatres only by the Festival Theatre at Stratford, which has a totally different configuration.

It's comfortable in less rarefied ways as well. Its lobbies are spacious. Despite its several levels, it's fully, and almost uniquely wheelchair accessible, which counts morally and, increasingly, legally. It has abundant legroom and excellent sight lines. Compare the cramped and cramping seats at the Royal Alex and the impassable crush in the foyer of the Ed Mirvish, Or, going outside the Mirvish empire, think of the Sony Centre, which for all its facelifts and name-changes, is an irreducible barn. Or the St. Lawrence Centre, which hardly ever feels right. The restored Elgin/Winter Garden has never established an identity. Even the Young Centre, which has the friendliest lobby in town, still has visibility problems in the actual theatres. Theatre architecture is a hard thing to get right. To take a successful example that's only two decades old and reduce it to landfill seems sort of wasteful.

Now it's true (though it hasn't been mentioned in the official announcements) that Toronto has more outsized theatres than it can use. They were built, or rebuilt, by competing impresarios at a time when it was thought that huge musicals, and the huge audiences for them, were forever. It turns out they weren't; the megamusical is becoming extinct (and just as well, if only for the extreme ugliness of the word itself). But big shows in themselves are unlikely to disappear, and the Princess of Wales is the best place in which to house them. The Royal Alex has history on its side, and as for the Ed Mirvish, one can hardly expect the organization to sacrifice a theatre named in honour of its founder. But if something has to go, I would rather it were one of them. If a beautiful new theatre is dispensable, while old ones aren't, then maybe our ideas of heritage need some re-examination.

It's true, too, that Toronto really needs purpose-built medium-sized theatres, able to originate work or - something the Mirvishes are already starting to do - house transfers from our small independent houses, whose best productions too frequently die on the vine. (Those small theatres are almost uniformly, if understandably, ramshackle. It's notable that the dispute at the Factory, Toronto's preceding theatrical furore, was sparked by opposing schemes for renovation.) No plans have been announced for incorporating a new theatre in the King Street development, but David Mirvish has said that he's always willing to build a theatre if it's needed, and I imagine that a smaller one would fit that bill. But I spend a lot of my time in theatres, and I'm going to miss the comforts, creature and otherwise, of the Princess of Wales. Even critics have the right to agitate for an agreeable workplace.

Mike Cassese, Reuters / The Princess of Wales is one of Toronto's few great theatre spaces.; Caption:

THEATRE REVIEW

Sister Act

Ed Mirvish Theatre, Toronto

So where do you hide if youve just witnessed a gangland killing, and the shooter wants to rub you out as well, to prevent you from squealing? Well, if you're a male musician (or two) in Prohibition-era Chicago, you dress up in drag and join an all-girls' band. Take it from Some Like It Hot. If youre an aspiring female soul singer in 1970s Philadelphia, as in Sister Act, which takes a lot from Some Like It Hot, you get into a nuns habit and join a convent.

The lady's name is Deloris, and though she doesn't much enjoy her new environment (its no vacation and she has no vocation) she makes the best of things by giving the nuns choir, previously tuneless and moribund, a hip new makeover. Under Deloris's guidance, they so rock the joint that both the pews and the collection box are soon full to overflowing. This is a godsend (so to speak) for the convent and the church to which it's attached, since theyve been under threat of closure unless they can bring in more business, just like the Save-a-Soul mission in Guys and Dolls.

As a narrative, Sister Act, based on the 1992 movie of the same name, is so eclectically derivative that it seems a triumph of restraint for the cop who arranges Deloriss refuge not to send her on her way with a song called Get Thee to a Nunnery.

If the religious house in Guys and Dolls suffered from a shortage of sinners, this one eventually finds itself with a glut of them. (So does the one in Guys and Dolls, but they're nicer.) Deloris's nemesis, who has the near-iconic name of Curtis Jackson and who also happens to be her married boyfriend, but isnt one to let sentiment stand in his way, tracks her down, to find her encircled and protected by all her new friends, from abbess to novice. They seem to have learned their pro-activity from the Nazi-defying sisters of The Sound of Music, and the show does have the decency to acknowledge this with an explicit shout-out.

Curtis pulls a gun on Deloris, thereby suggesting that either he or his authors have taken leave of their senses or, to put it another way, that theyve vacated their premises. Get this: The villain's whole motivation is to prevent the heroine from bearing witness to a murder, and to achieve this he proposes to commit another murder in front of a whole convent-ful of witnesses. He also, more understandably, fails to appreciate a rather delicious irony. He's been moving heaven and earth (fairly literally) to stop his ex-lover from testifying, meanwhile shes been testifyin in a whole different way. And doing it very well.

Just to point this up, the show starts with Deloris and a couple of wannabe supporting Supremes auditioning a song called Take Me to Heaven, which later, with a gospel swing and a more overwhelming vocal arrangement, becomes the singing sisters' first big hit. It sounds very good in both its fleshly and its spiritual guises; in fact, and for once, the best thing about this new(ish) musical is the music.

Alan Menken (Little Shop of Horrors, Beauty and the Beast) has supplied a pulsating set of tunes that make pop theatrical in a way unmatched by any composer since Cy Coleman; there are also a couple of unlaboured ballads with some rich turns of musical phrase. There are neat turns, too, in Glenn Slater's lyrics, and sometimes some whole neat ideas, such as Curtiss vengeful When I Find My Baby, which turns a familiar song-type inside out.

As often happens, the songs with the least wit are the ones that try hardest to be funny, like Its Good to Be a Nun, based on the notion that the mildest off-colour remark will sound hilariously naughty if it's done by a nun. The book (by Cheri and Bill Steinkellner) holds tightly and shamelessly to this idea, which might be called the Nunsense formula. There was once a revue of that name whose one joke was that all the performers wore wimples. Sister Act varies the recipe by adding uplift. Deloris doesn't get religion, but she does get friends; faced with a three-way choice between career, love (theres a vestigial romantic plot) and her sisters, she indulges in some soulful soul-searching, though there seems no good reason why she shouldnt have all three.

"Additional book material" is credited to Douglas Carter Beane; I can't prove that he's responsible for the great one-liners that occasionally turn up, but Im going to believe it anyway.

Jerry Zaks directs a slick production, incorporating one of those silent-movie chases in which people keep smiling while going in and out of doors and bumping into the other people they most wish to avoid. TaRea Campbell does everything possible with the role of Deloris except put an individual stamp on it. Hollis Resnik, though, does have a distinctive take on the Mother Superior, especially in her handling of the wryest lyric lines, throwaways that land. Much of the action pivots on her distrust and dislike of her new resident, though it's never clear whether this is down to piety or just jealousy; as in Billy Elliot, the conflict is painted in because otherwise there wouldn't be a show and painted out because otherwise there couldnt be a happy ending.

The other nuns are all called Sister Mary Something-or-Other; it might be funnier if just one of them wasnt. They're all the kind of crabby that's supposed to be endearing, except for a shy young postulant (Lael Van Keuren) who continually suggests conflicts that never get explored. (A loud song called The Life I Never Led doesnt count.) Among the men, Kingsley Legges Curtis is suitably menacing in his suit; Charles Barksdale droller than such a character has any right to be as his dim nephew; and E. Clayton Cornelious endearing as Sweaty Eddie, police officer and torch-carrier.

There's some blatant heartstring-tugging towards the end, and any suggestions of spiritual depth are best ignored, but the music and some genuine good-heartedness carry it.

Sister Act runs at the Ed Mirvish Theatre in Toronto until Nov. 4. For more information, visit mirvish.com.

Joan Marcus / Hmm, which one is the hip nun who wants to inject some soul in the church choir and which one is more in favour of the conventional ways? Hollis Resnik as Mother Superior and Ta'Rea Campbell as Deloris in Sister Act.; Caption:

Mixed media, multimedia, whatever, usually comes off as pointless and self-indulgent, an excuse for theatre directors to play at being movie directors without giving up the day job. Tear the Curtain!, which has come from the west coast to open the new season at Canadian Stage, is a different world. Its a seamless blending of stage and film, in the ironic but somehow fitting service of a story in which the two media are literally at war. The script isn't as good as the presentation but it's good enough, and the total effect, under Kim Colliers direction, is stunning.

Its a co-production of two Vancouver troupes - the Electric Company and the Arts Club Theatre - and it was first staged at the Stanley Theatre, a live house that was once a cinema. (This may sound like a reversal of the natural order, but it happens.) The Stanley opened in 1930 with a screening of Lillian Gish's first talkie The Swan. This factors into Tear the Curtain! itself, which is set in that same year and whose protagonist, name of Alex Braithwaite, is shown in the first scene arriving at another theatre for a performance of the play (by Ferenc Molnar) on which the movie is based, and being dangerously smitten by its leading actress. Our hero, in what may be a dramaturgical first, is a theatre critic, whom Jonathon Young (actor, co-author and co-director) endows with the intellect, charm, devotion to duty and suave good looks generally known to be characteristic of the trade. He has, naturally, a devoted and adoring secretary, Mavis, whom we see driving him to the theatre, dropping him off alone, and then going her winsome uncomplaining way. I should add that this whole episode is shown on film: film projected on to a theatre-sized screen, none of your video monitor nonsense. Not till Alex enters the imaginary theatre do we switch to live action in the real one, and the switch is so smooth that we hardly feel the join. We shuttle between the two modes for the rest of the evening, in a dazzling but strangely easeful display not just of synchronicity but of style. Collier's direction is visually flawless in both formats. Her design team comprises David Roberts (a versatile and hauntingly hued split-level set), Nancy Bryant (costumes), Alan Brodie (lighting), and Brian Johnson (cinematography), plus Peter Allen (music), Miguel Nunes (sound) and Alex Craig (editing). Their work is uniformly brilliant. The Bluma Appel, for which the show wasnt even conceived, has never looked better.

Theres also a story, quite a complicated one. In this 1930 Vancouver, which bears a strong resemblance to 1920s Chicago as depicted in things such as The Front Page, both the old theatrical empire and the budding cinematic one are controlled by gangsters, who are waging a turf war over a promising piece of real estate. Changes in culture are affecting the newspaper business too; Alex is appalled to learn that his free-standing theatre coverage is to be absorbed into an all-encompassing entertainment section. (Well, those sure were the days.) He's also absorbed in a different way by the history of the Stanley Theatre itself. In this telling there really was a Stanley, a visionary theatre director now dead. Except that someone claiming to be him, a derelict who lives in a tent in (naturally) Stanley Park, waylays Alex at his apartment, paints a portrait of him that might have been done by a drunken Modigliani, and charges him to spread the Stanley gospel. This, like most theatrical gospels, involves shedding all pretense and presenting Truth. Stanley's own group was called the Empty Space, a premature homage, perhaps, to Peter Brook (though I dont think Brook, a showman at heart, was ever that naive). Anyway Alex follows through, with a big think-piece called Tear the Curtain, which takes him weeks plus a lot of morale-building from Mavis, and which sets the town alight. All the factions want a piece of him, alive or dead, including a cadre of neo-or post-Stanleyites, who call themselves Liberty. They have seen the future and it works. They even show it to us, in a hilariously downbeat coup-de-theatre. Though that might not be the right term as what they present is, in the long run, anti-theatre.

It has to be confessed that if the medium here is the message, the former is far more crystalline than the latter. Theres a famous story about Raymond Chandler being quizzed about one of the plot twists in The Big Sleep (which he wrote) and confessing that he couldn't explain it either. Tear the Curtain! is comparably confounding as a narrative, even without the metaphors and metaphysics piled on top. Not to mention anachronisms; the film-noir style that Collier and her authors, Kevin Kerr and Mr. Versatility Young, have principally chosen to lampoon, is about a decade younger than the period they are ostensibly depicting. But they do it very well, and they have one continuing thread of suspense that sees us and themselves through. As Mavis keeps leaning physically and emotionally closer to Alex we ask ourselves, is the lucky idiot finally going to kiss her? I'm not kidding; it works, with great emotional effect. This is largely due to Dawn Pettens enchanting Girl Friday performance, tender-hearted and steel-willed, beautifully consistent (and consistently beautiful) from stage to screen and back again.

Laura Mennell also does well as the all-purpose siren, blond-tressed onstage, brunette-bobbed off it, who seems to be in with every faction in town. The rival moguls are Gerard Plunkett, promoting theatre but more convincing on screen than in the flesh, and Tom McBeath, the reverse. With the repurposing of theatres so much in the news, this play, which premiered in 2010, seems not so much timely as prophetic. As for its final import, I would say that it ends up championing not just illusion but escape, and blowing us away with it. As the man (not Stanley) incontrovertibly said, thats show business. And inescapable

Tear the Curtain! runs through Oct. 20 at the Bluma Appel Theatre. Call 416-368-3110 or visit canadianstage. com for ticket information.

Bruce Zinger / Our critic says Canadian Stage's Tear the Curtain! is a stunner.; Caption:

THEATRE

Bloodless: The Trial of Burke and Hare Panasonic Theatre, Toronto

Theatre 20 is a new company whose name derives from the number of accomplished performers who are its founding artists and whose mission is to revive interesting old musicals and to develop new ones. They've commenced operations with an example of the latter, which - good new musicals being even harder to come by than good new plays) - is a brave choice. It proves, on this occasion, a foolhardy one.

The foolhardiness stretches back to the actual conception of the piece. Bloodless, which began life a few years ago at the Winnipeg Fringe, concerns William Burke and William Hare, probably the most famous of all body-snatchers, and certainly the most innovative. The orthodox practice in their day was to dig up the recently deceased, present them to physicians in need of subjects for dissection, and pocket the reward.

Burke and Hare, Irish immigrants who flourished (if that's the word) in the Edinburgh of 1824, didn't sit around waiting for nature to take its course. They preferred to help it on its way. Hare and his wife kept a rock-bottom lodging house; Burke and his mistress, neighbours, persuaded them that they were sitting, in relative economic terms, on a gold-mine. First they dispatched a boarder who was in dire health anyway; then they moved on to prostitutes whom nobody would miss. Their preferred method was strangulation: hence the show's title.

Joseph Aragon, who wrote both book and score, is an avowed admirer of Stephen Sondheim, and it shows in his words and especially in his music. That being so, a set of gruesome murders among the underclass of 19th-century Britain was probably the last subject he should have chosen.

Comparisons to Sweeney Todd are inevitable, and he seems at times to have gone out of his way to invite them. His show starts, like Sweeney, with a jovially threatening chorus telling us about the horror of it all, and filling us in on the story. In this case the choristers are the lawyers and spectators at the killers' trial: hence the show's subtitle. But the framework disappears for long periods, and is never very effective when it's around.

Aragon's music has something of Sondheim's sinister, yearning plangency, and might be easier to appreciate in a less reminiscent context. But it's hard not to goggle at underscoring that sounds like a ghostly reprise from the murkiest depths of Sweeney's London.

Unfortunately, Bloodless fails to equal Sweeney's two main attractions: its exciting story (derived from Christopher Bond's extensive reworking of the original Victorian melodrama) and its characters. The real greatness in that show is the relationship between Sweeney, the possessed avenger, and Mrs. Lovett, the amoral opportunist: the symbiosis that makes atrocity possible. There are some faint echoes here, in a cheerful temptation song called The Bugger Is Better Off Dead, and in the attempted portrayal of Burke as a narcissistic tearaway and Hare as the disillusioned voice of caution, but the contrast is only fitfully pursued and the late addition of a sexual jealousy plot doesn't help much.

The Scots dramatist James Bridie wrote a play called The Anatomist whose main character was Dr. Knox, the surgeon and lecturer who bought the bodies, and who embodies medical-ethical problems more complex and absorbing than those of his suppliers. Bridie confined Burke and Hare themselves to supporting roles, and he was probably wise. At any rate, they never come to life here, and so neither does the show.

Knox and his students do figure, at one point singing a Gilbert and Sullivan parody based, like most Gilbert and Sullivan parodies, on the Major General's patter song from The Pirates of Penzance.

G&S's heyday was half a century later than that of B&H. The point, I suppose, is to paint the medics as opera-loving toffs, indifferent to the sufferings of those below. The show's main departure from the historical record is to make the villains' nemesis a crusading prostitute whose best friend was one of the victims. But the implicit arraignment of respectable society is nullified by the fact that once the murderers' guilt is known, nobody on stage cites the victims' status as a mitigating factor.

The populace ends up screaming for Burke's blood and ready to string up Hare by the hair, though their reasons may admittedly have little to do with social justice.

One positive thing the production reinforces is the extraordinary abundance (a fairly recent phenomenon, both here and abroad) of really good actors who can really sing. Evan Buliung makes a magnetic impression as Burke, a braggadocio in his own mind, and Trish Lindstrom, looking taller than ever before, an iron one as Mrs. Hare, the readiest to voice scruples and the most efficient at overcoming them.

Eddie Glen and Jan Alexandra Smith are their partners; theirs are more subdued roles, and in fact splitting the interest four ways may be one of the show's downfalls. With David Keeley as Knox, Jeff Irving as his most troubled assistant, and Carly Street as the avenging angel of the pavements, Theatre 20's company oozes talent.

Especially notable is Kaylee Harwood who plays two roles and gets sacrificed in both of them; in her first incarnation she shares a duet with Street so touching that we feel her loss as much on theatrical grounds as on moral ones. So the talent does extend to the writing; it's good to encounter a lyricist with some conception of what a rhyme is, though he does overdo them and some are dubious anyway. The tone wavers and so, fatally, does the story.

Bloodless runs until Oct. 28. For tickets, call 416-872-1212 or visit mirvish.com.

Time has been kind to La Cage aux Folles. When the musical premiered in 1983, it was an old-fashioned show with a newfangled premise. Its principal characters, Georges and Albin, are a middle-aged gay couple, married in all but name, running a transvestite cabaret club in St. Tropez; Georges is the manager and compere, Albin the drag queen and star. Putting them at the centre of a traditional show was a kind of coming out for the Broadway musical. It was also an artistic coming out for the composer-lyricist, Jerry Herman, whose previous big hits had been Hello Dolly and Mame. The heroines of those shows had always seemed, especially when doing their iconic numbers, like drag queens in disguise. When Albin, in La Cage's key number, sings about the release he feels in putting a little more mascara on, he's eliminating the middlewoman.

He's also going out on a limb, as is the musical itself. The thing that's always bothered me about Dolly and Mame, the latter especially, is that they're thoroughly conventional shows preaching about being unconventional. Mame even tells us, in roughly so many words, that the fellow we ought to be is unconventional. She's the ultimate safe rebel. But Albin, and Georges, too, do have something to fight against. And they don't, by and large, preach.

Georges has a son, Jean-Marie, the result of a one-night heterosexual fling. Georges and Albin have brought the boy up, and he now wants to get married -- to a girl. Unfortunately, Anne, his beloved, is the daughter of the most aggressively homophobic politician on the Riviera. Jean-Marie is bringing his future in-laws home to meet the folks, and he wants the swishy Albin to make himself scarce: something that embarrasses Georges and hurts Albin deeply. Harvey Fierstein's book, based on a French play, sets this situation up very well in its first act. The second, in which the visitors arrive, takes a nose-dive into uninspired farce, but redeems itself when Albin makes a surprise appearance that's a veritable coup and that I, not having seen the show since its first production, had forgotten.

That's another example of time's kindness. But the highly enjoyable revival that's touched down at the Royal Alex is its beneficiary in less trivial ways. In the 1983 production, the crusading politico and his wife were crude caricatures; they still are, but they carry more weight. It's a paradox: Gay marriage was barely an issue when the show was new; 30 years later, it's empowered a new generation of reactionary polemicists.

The current production is directed by Terry Johnson, a leading British playwright who has moved from staging his own work to staging other people's. Johnson started at a small theatre in London and eventually progressed to Broadway. That's the same trail that was blazed by the famous Sam Mendes production of Cabaret, and this La Cage takes a similar conceptual approach, emphasizing the tawdriness of the clubland setting and presenting the whole show as an extended club routine. There's some playful, but painless, interaction with the audience. The blurring of fantasy and reality makes for some very rich effects. When Albin, in everyday female garb, dances socially with Georges, they look like an old married couple. And then you realize that that is indeed what they are, but that Albin isn't really a woman, although that is how he feels most at home. The ambiguities are positively Shakespearean.

The glory of the show is Christopher Sieber's wonderful Albin, who can slide instantly from petulant complaint to deep pain, and also into hilarious anger, transmitted by steep vocal descents into gravelly basso profundo. He's also impeccably skilled in pure musical-comedy terms. He transforms The Best of Times, a Herman cheer-up song with a French accent, into genuine joy, for instance.

Albin has always been the star role of this show. Georges is just, pardon the expression, the straight man, though it must be possible to do more with him than is accomplished here by George Hamilton who, cast for road-company celebrity value, acquiesces by obeying the Woody Allen dictum that success is mainly a matter of just showing up. He deals with song and dance mainly by avoiding them; his acting is confined to some amusing raised-eyebrow moments when his plans fall apart and then come together again. If he does too little, Jeigh Madjus as butler-maid of the menage does much too much. Katie Donohue, though, makes all that can be made of the underwritten Anne, and the six Cagelles, given appropriately seedy choreography by Lynne Page, are a riot.

2012-10-26-a-try-in-the-sky:
THEATRE REVIEW

This Must Be the Place: The CN Tower Show Theatre Passe Muraille, Toronto

The problem with This Must Be the Place is that this doesn't have to be the place. Let me explain.

A few years ago a group called the Architect Theatre Collective came to Toronto with a play entitled Highway 63: The Fort Mac Show. It was set, as you might guess, in Fort McMurray, Alta., and though much of what it showed us, in terms of characters and relationships, didn't seem to be peculiar to that locale, it didn't matter too much: They were characters and they were relationships and it was a play, well-written and well-acted.

The same group now offers Toronto a show about Toronto, or professing to be; its contents turn out to be no more peculiar to Toronto than those of The Fort Mac Show were to Fort Mac. And it matters more because the new offering doesn't have its predecessor's traditional virtues. It isn't a play and doesn't pretend to be. It's more of a revue; or, to be franker, a grab-bag.

It does make regular references to Toronto areas and landmarks, including the one that provides if not a focus, then at least a subtitle. Indeed, it starts there, with a reasonable evocation of what it's like to have an evening out in an establishment more notable for the view than the cuisine. A much later scene suggests what a blessing it is that the CN Tower didn't become the focus for redevelopment that was initially intended. That's probably the most interesting point of the evening. We also hear testimony from people who have worked there, and who don't appear very enthusiastic about the experience.

Much of the show seems to have been assembled from interviews. This kind of theatre verite can produce exciting results when there's a story to be told or a thesis to be advanced. Here it just feels tepid and aimless. The overall impression is that Toronto is a big city that can be scary when you first arrive but can later turn out to be reasonably friendly. That's true enough. It would also be true of almost any big city you care to name.

The show's refusal to make big statements, about the CN Tower or anything else, does have an upside. It suggests honesty. Certainly the four performers - Georgina Beaty, Greg Gale, Ingrid Hansen, Thomas Olajide - are pleasant enough, though both Beaty and Gale showed in Highway 63 that they were capable of more. Gale and Olajide are the most aggressively ingratiating here, sometimes to the point of overplaying their hands.

Near the end they all inveigle members of the audience to come onstage and dance with them, which takes you back a bit, though not necessarily in a Torontonian direction. Ditto for some earlier audience-involvement games: There's nothing threatening about them, but there's nothing very relevant either. In fact they feel like padding, as if the company had taken on an assignment that it couldn't quite fulfill but couldn't very well walk away from.

I called the show a revue, but it doesn't seem to fulfill a revue's usual obligation to at least try to make every number funny. The only item that could be described as a sketch is a recreation of a City Hall debate about the plastic-bag levy. Real names are used and real people impersonated, with councillors Adam Vaughan and Giorgio Mammoliti especially prominent. It's quite lively, but gets nowhere; which may of course be the point.

The show's named creators, other than the actors, are JonathanSeinen(director)and Charlotte Corbeil-Coleman (fairly experienced playwright) "with Layne Coleman" (very experienced actor, author and director). The senior Coleman is a former artistic director of Theatre Passe Muraille and must know the city very well. Beaty, the first performer to identify herself, confesses to not being a resident, or at least not on any consistent basis. But it's never very clear whether we're getting an outsider's view, an insider's view or something in between.

The show is part of TPM's ongoing celebration/examination of Toronto: a town that Andy McKim, current artistic director, describes in his welcoming program note as "a vibrant, intercultural, progressive and worldly city that is home to the most extraordinary people possible." He's right. Making that description theatrically real is another thing. Soulpepper's Window on Toronto managed it, partly by concentrating on a single specific image that was also, literally, a viewpoint.

The present show is well-intentioned but scattershot. This, you feel, can't be the place.

This Must Be the Place: The CN Tower Show runs until Oct. 27 at Theatre Passe Muraille in Toronto. For tickets, call 416-504-7429 or visit passemuraille.on.ca.
2012-10-27-miss-caledonia-puts-on-the-ch:
Its worth going to Miss Caledonia just to experience Melody A. Johnson singing I've Been Everywhere while twirling a baton, and doing both at ever-increasing speeds. As she performs it, it's the climax of the beauty competition that gives her play its title. Its also the theatrical climax of the show, though it isnt quite the dramatic climax of the story.

Therein lies a flaw, though certainly not a disabling one. I referred to Miss Caledonia as her play" with reason; Johnson wrote it, she performs it all on her own, and at a certain level it seems to be about her. At a more literal level, it's about her mother, born Peggy Douglas, whom Johnson presents as a 1950s teenager, growing up in Ontario farm country, at driveable distance from the bright lights of Hamilton. Peggy is a movie fan who likes Roy Rogers, fantasizes about getting advice from Bing Crosby, and is especially stuck on Debbie Reynolds and on how she was "discovered." She sees her own path to similar fortune as leading through the plentiful array of local beauty pageants. She fails miserably in her first attempt, coming in 11th in a field of 12. However, Peggy perseveres, enrols in a local charm school and proceeds to the biggest contest in the region. Her ambitions meet firm opposition from her farmer-father, but are supported - morally, financially, logistically and semi-secretly - by her mother.

Miss Caledonia was first seen at Summerworks two years ago. It returns to Toronto, expanded and strengthened. The additions and improvements, if memory can be trusted, largely concern the character of Peggy's mother who reacts to the constricting circumstances of her life and home by plastering the walls of the living room with newspaper clippings, carefully selected to happy events. She especially dreams of having an indoor toilet and, when she and her daughter visit a prosperous neighbour, spends an inordinate amount of time wallowing in the well-appointed bathroom. Theres a lovely payoff to this in the plays final section.

As a performer, Johnson has brought self-deprecation to the sharpest comic level. She's a counter-charmer, inspecting the world with a deadpan scowl that insulates her against any suspicions of sentimentality. It's especially effective here where shes playing a character young in years but a veteran in disappointment. Peggy has her dreams, and pursues them, and we root for the pursuit. Determinedly downbeat, shes the last person you'd expect to play a cheerleader; which is why, when she gets to the routine, it's such a joy.

Along the way, she plays other people as well. Its impossible, seeing a self-authored one-woman play in the Tarragons Extra Space, not to make comparisons with Kristen Thomson's I Claudia. Miss Caledonia isn't in that league; it doesnt probe as deeply, or at such length, into as many characters. The farmland setting also prompts associations with the Beattie brothers Wingfield cycle, but Johnson isn't the wizard of vocal versatility that Rod Beattie is. She's a versatile actress, as witness her array of brilliant performances in Trout Stanley, 7 Stories and I Think I Can, but none of those were quick-change operations.

Minor individuals may be faintly presented, but the overall atmosphere comes over very strong. It all comes together at the crucial contest when Peggy is asked to recall a memorable incident from her life and comes up with one that effectively binds self, family and community together. It even suggests, without overstressing, a rapprochement with her father.

What, we wonder but are not told, happened to Peggy once the pageant was done? Well, we know one thing that happened. The play, in effect, spans three generations; Johnson plays her mother telling us about her mother. And yet it feels directly autobiographical. You have to keep reminding yourself that the girl it depicts didnt grow up to be Melody Johnson; she grew up to be Melody Johnsons mother, which on this and other showings, must be a proud accomplishment. The play was directed by Rick Roberts and Aaron Willis, with a choreographic assist from Jane Johan-son; one wonders if Johnson, even wearing two hats, didn't sometimes feel outnumbered at rehearsals. After the Toronto run, she's taking the show to British Columbia, Alberta, and three more locations in Ontario. She's going everywhere, man.

Miss Caledonia runs through Nov. 22 at the Tarragon Extra Space. Call 416-531-1827 or visit tarragontheatre.com for details.

2012-11-02-the-war-rugs-on-political-mot:
THEATRE REVIEW

Political Mother Bluma Appel Theatre, Toronto

For the second time straight, Canadian-Stage has housed the most spectacular show in Toronto. Well, maybe not counting War Horse. Right after Tear the Curtain, play and movie in one, came Political Mother, a dance-rock-theatre piece that's visually and aurally blistering but with beatific interludes. Its too-short run at the St. Lawrence Centre is already over, but it was only the first leg of a Canadian tour.

Its the creation of Hofesh Shechter, a composer and choreographer (a portmanteau of talents that may be unprecedented but is certainly useful and even logical), born and trained in Israel but now based in London. It starts, on a smoky stage, with a lone figure in medieval armour. I thought for a moment that it might be Joan of Arc; maybe I was misled by the gender implications of a show title that otherwise remains inexplicable. Although, if you take the Mother part to be an abbreviation, it does make a certain sense.

Anyway, the figure, which on later consideration is probably male, draws its sword and commits hara-kiri. And, with that image of martial self-destruction, the show is on.

Its about war: how people are incited to it, how enthusiastically they sign up for it, how quickly and bitterly they come to regret it and how they keep coming back for more. These are hardly new themes, but Shechter has found powerful ways of illustrating them. On the top level of a double-tiered set, a dictator-demagogue rants incomprehensibly. He fades in and out, vocally and also visually - Lee Curran's marvellous lighting is an integral part of the experience - to be replaced by a line of pounding guitarists. They alternate in turn with a line of equally pounding drummers, placed at ground level. And in front of them, there are Shechter's magnificent dancers, a dozen of them, responding enthusiastically to the beat. (There are times when the choreography suggests West Side Story gone nuts.) The intoxication is part-way understandable; the show, in addition to its other virtues, is a foot-tapper.

Sometimes the music changes. Bach is piped in, and the dancers enjoy lyrical passages of peace, the Four Minute Hate giving way to the Ten Minute Love. (My timings are approximate.) Other scenes depict the underside of war; the intoxicated warriors of earlier episodes become the haggard, stumbling inhabitants of death camps. Then theyre back in the ranks, the latest turn in an endless cycle. Its the message of Buffy Sainte-Marie's Universal Soldier but without the words, which is probably an improvement.

Regarding the lack of words, in a piece that's billed as theatre as well as "dance": it confirms that rock works best in the theatre when its nonverbal. Rock musicals are an oxymoron, since you cant tell stories or develop characters through monotonous music wedded to inaudible (or, where audible, woolly and pretentious) lyrics.

Political Mother, whose story is an endlessly recurring loop and whose characters are robots or archetypes, doesn't have that problem. It uses its music for visceral effect, which is tremendous. It may even constitute an unwitting indictment of rock. Its dictator figure, ranting gibberish, is a rock star twice-removed, and the drums and guitars are his method of inciting his subjects to frenzy. When the show wants to evoke tenderness it goes, as previously noted, for baroque.

The proceedings aren't entirely non-verbal. There are two outbreaks of distinguishable words, one written, one sung. Near the end, an electrical sign is displayed, reading "where there is pressure there is ..." Were kept waiting for the punch word for the longest time; when it arrives it turns out to be "folkdance." The anti-climax gets a laugh, but the purpose is unclear. It seems to be mocking the gentler steps that have punctuated the evening, or at best to be treating them as a naive delusion.

Even more perplexing is the recorded singing, at the last moment, of Both Sides Now: a vocal folk dance perhaps (though the selected performance is grittier than that). Well, Joni Mitchell did claim to have looked at love and life from both sides, and the show may possibly be claiming to have done the same, though more at life than at love, despite some nice pas de deux. (It doesnt much look at clouds, except perhaps mushroom ones.)

The use of the song has an ironic air about it, without much clue as to what it's being ironic about. I'm not convinced that Shechter knew how to finish his creation, but that could be the penalty of telling a never-ending story.

Meanwhile, both the way he tells it, and the way his dancers and musicians execute his telling, are conceptually and technically superb.

Political Mother plays in Montreal until Nov. 3, Quebec City (Nov. 5) and Ottawa (Nov. 9-10) For more information, visit canadianstage.com.
