2012-11-03-the-means-to-an-end:
The fabled swish of the curtain is a sound seldom heard in the theatre these days. It's especially not heard in Soulpepper's revival of Endgame despite the fact that this is the rare modern production that actually has a curtain. The noise it makes as it rises to kick off the evening is a combination of creak, whirr and rattle. It's both scary and funny, the perfect overture to a play and production that are both those things in spades.

Daniel Brooks directed Samuel Beckett's doomsday phantasmagoria in Soulpepper's second season back in 1999; and though I can't claim to remember that production in much detail, I do remember being very impressed by it. He's now revisited the play with the same design team (Julie Fox, set; Victoria Wallace, costumes; Kevin Lamotte, lighting; Richard Feren, sound) and together they have created a bleakly witty environment for the blind and chair-bound Hamm to await the end of the world. The end of his world, anyway; he doesn't much care what goes on outside, though he would prefer that nothing did. We may well be in a post-apocalyptic situation; when Clov, Hamm's shuffling manservant who can no more sit than his master can stand, laboriously climbs his set of steps to peer through one of the two impossibly high chamber windows and inspect the world outside he does just once see a sign of life, but it's soon snuffed out.

"Not an underplot!" prays Hamm, who tends to think in literary-dramatic terms ("haven't you ever heard an aside before? ... I'm gearing up for my soliloquy") when not picturing himself as a chess master, about to execute a grand checkmate. Somehow, though, his endgame never ends. He hopes for stasis but gets, at best, infinitely suspended motion. That at least is what I take from the final tableau which, even though Beckett and spoilers would seem to be notions from separate universes, I shall not describe. I will reveal though that the curtain comes down as bone-creakingly and as definitively as it went up.

What's extraordinary is that a play that seems to crave death should be so full of life, that dialogue so apparently barren should be so fertile. A script crammed with bookish references somehow flourishes as a sustained crosstalk act, with subsidiary turns for Hamm's parents whom, in the play's most celebrated image, he keeps at the side of the stage. Under Brooks' direction the tension, in a play that on the face of it has little to get tense about, never snaps.

It's a fine production but not a wholly satisfying one. The discontent stems, most unexpectedly, from the joint presence of two of Canada's finest. At text level, Joseph Ziegler's Hamm and Diego Matamoros' Clov are exemplary; not a nuance gets past them. But in the end neither seems ideally cast. Ziegler is an actor who exudes empathy, even when (as in The Crucible, A Whistle in the Dark and the pre-conversion parts of A Christmas Carol) it's negative empathy. Hamm is a monster of uncaringness, of not needing; and though Ziegler faithfully explores all his self-pitying grandiloquence, he never really embodies it.

Matamoros played Clov in the 1999 version and knocked me out, but then I spent that whole season being knocked out by the varied brilliance of an actor I had barely registered before. He's great at the physical comedy, the constant painful toiling over objects that he has always left in the wrong place, but something snapped for me when Clov, pulling himself together after a lapse, says "Now I'm intelligent again." That should seem like self-deception, but Matamoros is always intelligent; he can't avoid it. My disappointment may have something to do with my anticipation of seeing these two working as a team. Beckett doesn't really allow for teamwork; he writes competing solitudes.

On the other, stage-right, hand, Eric Peterson and Maria Vacratsis do wonders as the bin-bound parents, even importing some reciprocal tenderness or the memory of it. Beckett slams the trash-can lids down on the idea, but it's too late. We'll remember it well.

Endgame runs through Nov. 17 at the Young Centre (416-866-8666)
2012-11-07-coincident-report:
THEATRE REVIEW

Speaking in Tongues Berkeley Street Theatre, Toronto

Two men and two women are in a hotel room, with adulterous intent. For a moment we may think they're there for a foursome, but it soon becomes clear we are watching two distinct encounters played simultaneously. The fun is in hearing how exactly the words and reactions of the two couples duplicate one another. It is, if we are to believe them, the first infidelity for everyone concerned. At the end of the scene, though, the ways part. One pair decides to go through with it, the other walks away.

That's the beginning of Speaking in Tongues, by the Australian dramatist Andrew Bovell, whose When the Rain Stops Falling (at the Shaw Festival) was the most haunting and exciting new work seen in these parts last year. Speaking in Tongues, produced by Company Theatre under the auspices of Canadian Stage, may well carry off the same palm for the current season though; written some 10 years earlier, it's more abrupt and less polished in its use of fragmented structure and multiple points of view. It's interesting that those same techniques also figure, though in a more conventional format, in the only other Australian play to reach us recently, The Blonde, the Brunette and the Vengeful Redhead. Maybe that's a coincidence, but it's a fitting one, since coincidence is what drives all of these plays.

It especially drives Speaking in Tongues, so nakedly and eventually so powerfully that it ceases to be a mere device and becomes a metaphor for what the Greeks would have called fate and we might prefer to think of as the baleful interconnectedness of people and things. It reinforces the old truth that tragedy is the dark reflection of farce. It turns out that the two couples of the first scene were unknowingly engaged in husband-and-wife-swapping, the man in each duo married to the woman in the other. So we get another contrapuntal scene, with the partners who have only committed adultery in their hearts casting out those who have gone the whole hog.

Symmetry proliferates as the two husbands accidentally cross paths in a way that's more funny than painful, the two women in a way that's more painful than funny. Eventually, both errant spouses return to ask pardon of their mates, each with a story to tell concerning someone they've met or heard about, a story that throws their own problems into sharp relief. One involves a man who has spent years pining for a woman who left him and who has now reappeared without acknowledging him; the other is of a man who is suspected of murder, on strong circumstantial evidence, but whose wife unquestioningly believes in him. It's the strongest expression of trust that we're to hear, or hear about, all evening.

It's no surprise that in Act 2 we meet some of these people and others connected with them, nor that they're played by the same four actors we've already seen. The pattern is creatively varied by having one, though only one, of the first-act characters reappear in the second, though in a professional rather than a personal capacity. Once again we crosscut between different viewpoints, this time relayed through letters, phone calls, police statements, therapy sessions as well as plain old conversation. We learn more about the reported death, and how it might have been averted if somebody had picked up a phone.

This may sound like the cruellest, and dramatically crudest, of accidents, but it turns out to be the most crushing, and also the most inevitable, of all the coincidences. Although there's another one still to come. Everything connects in a play that is, ironically, about missed connections. Nearly everybody in it wants to connect; nearly everybody, to some degree, fails.

The play lost me just once: in a second-act sequence where all present recount their unpersuasively identical dreams. Philip Riccio's production is wittily precise and fleet-voiced in the early scenes and gets steadily deeper and darker as it goes on. The actors cohere as a team and shine as individuals.

Yanna McIntosh's double performance exemplifies the evening's progression; elegant and controlled before the intermission, even when in pain, she's frighteningly frightened after it, spending most of her time, and all of her change, calling for help from a deserted pay phone. This must be the most vulnerable performance she's ever given.

Jonathan Goad, initially your bluff average guy, transforms into a puzzled man, not so much protesting his innocence as explaining it. (Conceivably he's lying, but the play is undercutting itself if it wants us to think so. And come to think of it, though we're constantly shown people deceiving themselves or one another, there are very few outright lies.)

Helene Joy passes from puzzled near-innocence, disappointed in itself, to a glittering, rather scary account of the one character who survives by disdaining any kind of emotional commitment.

Finest of all may be Richard Clarkin, who alone in the cast gets to play three roles; in the last he seems to gain age and weight simply by turning toward us and revealing that he wears glasses. He's the most pitiable character and also, if guilt has to be apportioned, the guiltiest. It's largely through him that the play ends up cutting harrowingly deep. And Company Theatre's virtually unblemished record remains so.

Speaking in Tongues runs until Nov. 24. For tickets, call 416-368-3110 or visit canadianstage.com.

Shaun Benson / The cast of Speaking in Tongues cohere as a team and shine as individuals.; Caption:
2012-11-10-having-their-pie-eating-it-to:
Soulpepper has a new sub-group, known as the Creation Ensemble, that consists at present of Mike Ross (actor-musician), Ken MacKenzie (actor-designer), Ins Choi (actor-playwright), Raquel Duffy (actor-actor) and Gregory Prest (ditto). Their initial presentation is Alligator Pie, a freewheeling musical entertainment based on the Canadian children's verse of Dennis Lee.

It's an invigorating, sometimes enchanting show whose weakest element is its source material. The poems left me feeling dissatisfied, or maybe just disenfranchised. Having been written in the 1970s, they could hardly have been part of my own childhood (which wasn't Canadian anyway), but they weren't part of my children's childhoods, either. Encountered now, by someone who grew up on Lewis Carroll and tried to pass it on, they feel sub-Seuss: longer on whimsy than on wit, without the Seussian rhythmic insistence and, most of the time, without the narrative strength. That they mention Toronto landmarks in unexpected contexts doesn't quite compensate. Besides, setting existing verse to music is a dodgy enterprise at most times; the texts here are easier to follow than the e.e. cummings poems that were the basis of an earlier Soulpepper show, but even these comparatively simple words tend to be swamped rather than enhanced by the accompaniment.

No director or choreographer is listed; the show was staged, very inventively, by its performers. It's done in the round, with the space envisioned as an adventure playground for grown-ups; or for the child in every grown-up. The famous five begin proceedings by clambering up through a trap door, initially one at a time, though the pattern gets varied and syncopated. Their wear looks of mischief and wonder, and they keep wearing them throughout. They also wear elaborately strange coiffures (Ross and Duffy especially) and these do change in the course of the proceedings.

The staging makes much use of found objects, or of objects left purposefully lying about, never more effectively or infectiously than in a concluding dance on bubble-wrap, proving that squeaks can be as joyful as taps. (Further expanses of the same material are placed at the exits so that the departing audience can feel the joy.)

Homemade and original, too, are many of the musical instruments, many of them played by Ross, who presumably wrote most of the music. There's more orthodox instrumentation, too, some of it played by unlikely people in unlikely circumstances and prompting unlikely thoughts. For some reason I found myself convinced, while watching the lanky Prest blowing trombone, that here was a future Hamlet. And not so far in the future, either. This is momentous. One of Soulpepper's problems over the years has been finding - and holding on to - young male actors likely to inherit from their formidable list of founding members. Prest, who has succeeded in one demanding role after another in the last two years, demonstrating equal intensity as tragedian and clown, seems to be the man.

Ross is wickedly delightful as a superannuated wizard in the evening's most sustained sequence of storytelling. Duffy does some impressive instant re-stylings of hair and personality, and Choi looks wonderfully self-satisfied as a phenomenal infant. Music sounds predominantly country, theoretically incongruous for an urban poet, but in fact working nicely and varied in itself, taking in everything from ballad to square dance. But there are also excursions into Latin and rap, as well as an extended interlude of boyd percussion in which four-fifths of the cast turn themselves into so many Bobby McFerrins. The mention of "Mulligan stew" prompts a tone of sweet solemnity that is pretty much the show's signature. The title poem bookends the proceedings. It's hard to resist the quintet's rhythmic choral declaration that if they don't get their pie they're surely gonna die, and pleasant to welcome it back at the end. I wish the filling of the pie were more nourishing. But the flavour's appealing.

Alligator Pie runs through Nov. 25 at the Young Centre for the Performing Arts. Call 416866-8666 or visit soulpepper.ca for ticket information.

Jason Hudson / Ins Choi, left, and Mike Ross in Soulpepper's Alligator Pie.; Caption:
2012-11-17-it-s-just-a-matter-of-time-th:
Kate was a schoolgirl in the 1950s with a consuming interest in physics and mathematics.

She was especially obsessed with the nature of time. However her teachers thought that, as a woman, she did not have the right kind of brain to pursue a scientific career in what even they recognized to be a changing world. They persuaded her somewhat reluctant mother to enrol her in a vocational school: something secretarial perhaps. She dropped out, and spent the rest of her life, up until something resembling the present day, moving unhappily from one unfulfilling job to another. Always shy and abrasive, she became clinically depressed. After being institutionalized and theoretically cured, she settled for merely being bitter and withdrawn.

That is the narrative spine of John Mighton's The Little Years, a play more entertaining and even uplifting than I have probably made it sound. It was first produced by Theatre Passe Muraille in 1995; a revised version was staged at Stratford last year, and that production, with a few cast changes, has now been brought to the Tarragon. I liked it a lot at Stratford. I still like it; its sharp and economical and compassionate without being sentimental. But I now have more doubts about the relation of the story to its ideas, and I also feel that some of the life has gone out of Chris Abrahams production.

Mighton, himself a scientist as well as a playwright, writes in a program note that new and almost paradoxical ways of thinking about time and space" mean that "we may be forced to re-examine our unconscious beliefs about art. If time isn't linear, then art isn't eternal, because - Im struggling here - if time doesnt exist, then eternity has nothing to defy. I'm not sure that's such a revolutionary idea; George Orwell wrote long ago that like all writers, Shakespeare will be forgotten some day," and I doubt if Orwell was up on Einsteinian physics. Anyway Kate, who isnt by conventional terms an artist, has a brother, William, who is; hes a poet, acclaimed as a genius since childood. Kate probably adores him, as everybody else seems to, but growing up in his shadow hasn't helped. William dies in the course of the action, and we never meet him even when he's alive, though we do, in one of the plays wittiest touches, behold his funeral urn - by which time the value of his work is already being called into question. (But doesnt this often happen when a writer dies?) I can see the theoretical point of William's absence from the stage, but I found it more frustrating the second time around. We do meet his wife Grace, a social and environmental activist whose passion also wanes with the years; and through her we meet Roger, "the Barry Manilow of painting," a compliment when it was first bestowed but not so much later. He and Grace have an affair, which also proves fleeting though doubtless very nice at the time.

Mighton has honed his dialogue so that every mention of time, however casual, rings an ironic bell. It's here that the production has congealed; too many lines are delivered with a heavy weight of Significance. This affects Irene Pooles performance of Kate, but she can afford it; for one thing, her character specialises in saying things that make people uncomfortable, and for another her assumption of the role - vocal, physical, and psychological - is absolute. She ages with grave and impeccable conviction, and with no obvious external aids. Hunched in an anorak, she retreats ever further inside herself; she even looks monosyllabic. It takes the plays length for her to shed a tear; when she does it's infectious, or so I found it. She cannot, however, make the link between her preoccupations and the play's seem more than a convenient coincidence. She has to do double duty, proclaiming a theme and exemplifying it.

As Grace, Pamela Sinha also ages well; in her younger scenes she seems not so much naive as silly. Shes one of the two principal newcomers; the other is Ari Cohen whose Roger is magnificent, and far removed from anything else Ive seen him do; after his string of American tough guys he offers us a long-haired ponytailed artist, nervously craving validation, professional or sexual, but philosophical when it's withheld. His and Grace's scene of halting mutual seduction remains a highlight: ground-zero endorsement perhaps of the message that, if nothing lasts, we may as well grab the moment. Most revealingly, it has no noticeable consequences. Chick Reid reprises her role as Kates mother, at her best when gnarled and obstinate in a retirement home. Bethany Jillard doubles, beautifully, as the 14-year-old Kate and as her niece who, born into a less restrictive age, is Kate without the baggage. Her aunt, it turns out, was her inspiration. This is the plays epiphany, though to my mind an ambiguous one. It could be a defiance of time, as popularly conceived. It could also be a vindication of it.

The Little Years runs through Dec. 16 at the Tarragon Theatre.

Cylla Von Tiedemann / The Little Years's Giacomo Gianniotti, Hannah Anderson and Bethany Jillard.; Caption:
2012-11-24-the-wheel-deal-fare-game-look:
Judged as a play, Fare Game is feeble to the point of non-existence. To be fair (ouch) it isn't trying to be a play. Its an assemblage of documentary film clips, for which the links happen to be provided by live performers in front of a live audience. Even on that basis, it leaves a lot to be desired.

The shows subtitle is Life in Toronto's Taxis and its subject is the working conditions of Toronto taxi drivers. Three people with collective credentials as actors, writers, directors and video artists - Marjorie Chan, Ruth Madoc-Jones, Alex Williams - put it together as part of Theatre Passe Muraille's current Theatre Beyond Walls project, which is aimed at making a connection between the playhouse itself and the area around and outside it. Sometimes they take shows into the surrounding streets; other times, they bring the streets into the show. Fare Game does both. Its creators went out with cameras and recorders to interview drivers both in and out of their cabs, and they now run the footage for us.

One of the shows stated aims is to make us give more thought to the man or woman at the wheel (all but one of their interview subjects are male) the next time we get into a cab. In that, they probably succeed. They also leave us in no doubt that taxi-driving is a tough life: very long hours for, once all overheads have been deducted, very little money. Its also, we're told on two separate occasions, the most dangerous job in North America. The most effective of the video segments is the first-hand story of a driver who was knifed by a passenger at Yonge and Sheppard, which he might reasonably have believed to be a safe area; he could see the knife coming but still couldn't manage to escape.

We are told, which most of us probably already know, that cab driving has traditionally been an immigrant occupation with its constituency changing with each successive wave of newcomers; also that this results (and is probably more the case now than ever before) in a large number of cabbies working far below their educational qualifications. We learn - something we probably should have known already, but I have to confess I didnt - that the big taxi companies arent employers at all, but middlemen connecting drivers with passengers; which makes you wonder about the drivers, who are also the car owners, having to sport the company logo.

There's a lot about licensing: about the difference between "standard plates" and "ambassador plates" and how this can lead to cab drivers being exploited. Unfortunately, most of this information is anecdotally supplied to us by the drivers themselves, which doesn't make it too easy to follow. Maybe the show should have expanded its video resources to include some charts, or at least some captions. Some of the film sequences show drivers and their representatives, in search of a better deal, demonstrating outside City Hall and attending a hearing inside of it. They all come off as good-humoured and articulate. As for their civic and industrial opponents (who must exist, otherwise what are they protesting about?) they are neither seen nor heard from. This is a pity. The case for including them is not so much that it would be fairer (pun, this time, not intended) but that it would be more interesting. Or, that it would be more dramatic, which a documentary - on stage, film, TV or any combination thereof - needs to be, every bit as much as a scripted play.

Some of Fare Game actually is a scripted play, or a scripted something. As well as introducing the video segments (and, as interviewers, appearing in some of them) the three originators deliver statements from subjects who didnt want to appear on camera. This unavoidably entails the actors functioning as actors. They also do a few unexplained physical exercises, presumably to establish their theatrical cred, and each of them gets to jump on and off his or her own personal set of steps and rostra: again to no discernible artistic or informational end. They vary in their efficiency at fulfilling their dual functions. Chan, both as actor and narrator, goes through the whole evening sporting the same broad and uncommunicative grin. Madoc-Jones is engagingly informal as link-person but freezes when speaking other peoples lines. Williams, the least experienced performer of the three, makes a wooden, apologetic master of ceremonies, but comes to surprising life when playing characters. On opening night, though, the biggest hand went to the taxi drivers themselves, present in the audience, and that was certainly fair. (Ouch again, but a good ouch.)

Fare Game: Life in Toronto's Taxis plays through Dec. 8 at Theatre Passe Muraille. For tickets, call 416-504-7529.

Aviva Armour Ostroff / Fare Game: Alex Williams and Marjorie Chan; Caption:
2012-11-26-school-of-the-absurd:
THEATRE REVIEW

The Lesson

Lower Ossington Theatre, Toronto

Two celebrated European plays from the mid-20th century opened in Toronto last week. In fact, they had their official premieres on the same night: Thursday if anyone's counting. Max Frischs The Arsonists and Eugene Ionescos The Lesson have something else in common: They have both been tagged as belonging to the Theatre of the Absurd, a catch-all category whose boundaries are so porous as to be meaningless. Or, in another word, absurd.

It certainly has nothing to do with Frisch, the action of whose plays is thoroughly realistic, despite being carried out in the main by characters generic or representative. But if there ever was an absurdist playwright, it might well be Ionesco, whose plays, of which The Lesson is one of the first and best, depict people saying and doing things unlikely to be said and done in everyday life. Which doesn't mean of course that they don't reflect and illuminate things that are said and done. They could even, though Ionesco himself might have had mixed feelings about this, be called political. And that does point us to some common ground between The Lesson and The Arsonists. The Arsonists is a transparent allegory on the rise of Nazism. In The Lesson a Professor, who has done something awful, is admonished by his housekeeper to don an armband as self-protection: a red armband whose business side is turned away from the audience but that might well feature a swastika. It figures, as he has momentarily transformed into a gibbering, goose-stepping parody of Hitler.

Or at least he does in this production. The armband is in the text; the Great Dictator routine isnt. Its an invention of Soheil Parsa, the Iranian refugee director whose Modern Times Stage Company is presenting the play. Ionesco's Professor flatters, intimidates and finally terrorizes his young female Pupil (Ionesco does generic names, too) by showering her with pseudo-academic gobbledygook. The use of language as a weapon has obvious political implications. Parsa brings these to the forefront with a battery of design, sound, lighting and casting effects that range from the impressive to the ridiculous. Broadly speaking, they work best at the start when they're establishing an atmosphere, worst at the end when theyre underlining points that the script and the actors are making powerfully well on their own.

The set is a bare chamber, furnished only with two high-backed office chairs on castors, uncomfortable enough to frighten any student (or prisoner), mobile enough to empower any teacher (or interrogator). The air is full of noises, strident, screeching and threatening. The opening bars of Beethovens Fifth are briefly transmitted to signal the Professor's approach; it sounds as if he's descending from an upper level with Beethoven as his elevator music.

The Pupil, mindful of how much she has to learn, awaits his approach with trepidation. However, when he appears, clad in this version in gown and mortar board like everyones favourite caricature of a schoolmaster, he is initially all kindness. He takes her through her mathematics, delighted by her skill at addition (she has no problem with one plus one), but disappointed by her inability to master subtraction (one minus one consistently defeats her). He moves on to philology, despite the warnings of his Maid, whos been here before, that "philology leads to calamity." It certainly leads, in the Professor's case, to prolixity and paranoia. On and on he rants, in a cascading spiral of meaninglessness, about Spanish and Neo-Spanish and some kind of Romanian, and the less the Pupil understands him - in effect, the less she submits to him - the more enraged he becomes. It's a truism that language is a weapon; its being brandished here without regard to any Geneva Convention.

David Ferry plays the Professor and Michelle Monteith the Pupil, and theyre as superb together here as they were two years ago in Blasted. Ferry's performance traces a seamless arc (barring a few understandable verbal stumbles) from pedagogue to demagogue, getting increasingly enflamed on the way, before subsiding into a grotesque crumple.

It's a brilliant display; but though I think I can see how he does it (if not how he learned it), I havent a clue how Monteith arrived at her sublime incarnation of the Pupil. At first shes the picture of demure, Alice bemused at her entry into Wonderland, where she does indeed meet the maddest of Hatters. Under his onslaught, she cries out that she has a toothache; she repeats this countless times, and the gradations of fright and helplessness that she's able, without any obvious changes in intonation, to infuse into that one line are extraordinary.

The tension generated by these two actors makes the fancier touches of Parsa's direction seem increasingly superfluous. They include having the Maid played by a man (Costa Tovarnisky) in drag, with a bald head and a thick Eastern European accent, and having him come on as a sinister, controlling apparatchik instead of a faithfully clucking domestic, cleaning up her masters messes.

Not that the performance isnt compelling in its own right, especially in its brief appearances in the apertures of an otherwise featureless set. Parsa has narrowed the play in presenting it as a primarily political parable, but he hasn't distorted it. If there is such a thing as the Theatre of the Absurd, then one of its achievements is to present us with power-plays in their purest form. Ionesco, one considered a back number, has had a resurgence in recent years and that's a reason why. He leads us, by fantastic paths, back to theatrical basics.

The Lesson runs until Dec. 1. For tickets and information, visit moderntimesstage.com.

John Lauener / David Ferry, left, and Michelle Monteith's performances as The Professor and The Pupil suggest they've done their homework for The Lesson.; Caption:
2012-12-01-up-the-detroit-river-boblo-s-:
Toronto's Theatre Centre, about to move from its long-established address at Queen and Dover-court, takes leave of its old premises with a show that is itself a requiem for a shuttered place of entertainment. Boblo takes its name and its subject matter from an amusement park that flourished for nearly a century on an island in the river between Windsor and Detroit. Its name was a corruption of Bois Blanc. It finally shuttered in 1993. Among those who cherish its memory are Erin Brandenburg, writer, and Andrew Penner, musician and composer. They crafted this memorial tribute together, and their company Kitchen-band is presenting it.

It's an impressionistic piece, not a history. In fact, as somebody who had never heard of Boblo, let alone visited it, I left with a very hazy idea of what the place was like, or how it may have differed from any other carnival park.

Penner's music is the best part of the show, and as front-man and vocalist, he himself is the dominating presence in it. He provides, among other things, a great vocal that leads into a Charleston routine that itself leads into a challenge dance. I'm not sure why the 1920s should be privileged here above all other periods; maybe it's just because Charlestons generally look and sound like fun. Certainly this sequence is the liveliest part of the evening. Other times the music is mainly moody and folky, most effectively so in a number called Pelee String Club that comes right at the end: after the curtain call, in fact.

Boblo - the fairground, the island and the encircling Detroit River - are presented as sources of pain as much as of pleasure. Almost the first thing we hear is the lament of a parent, mourning the loss of a young son, desperately hoping that he will somehow resurface alive and unharmed. It's wrenching, and so is the near-concluding moment when the show circles back on itself to tell us what actually happened.

Similarly haunting is the testimony from beyond the grave of a drowned woman, buttressed by accounts of the man who tried to save her. The victim is played by Amy Rutherford, who's the only actor to make much of an impression. (That's as opposed to the musicians, who all have personalities and revel in them.) Rutherford also appears, posed in a picture frame, as one of a quartet of piquantly mismatched summer lovers; and she also spends a lot of time behind a scrim, meditating on radio waves and on the fact - possibly frightening, but more likely consoling - that they never disappear.

The show in fact is less concerned with specific memories than with the persistence of memory itself. This provides a few haunting moments, but as a theme it could apply to any place, any time. What we're told about Boblo itself seems vague and arbitrary. It's as if the authors expected their own nostalgia to be automatically self-validating. It's more like self-defeating.

Boblo runs until Dec. 2 at The Theatre Centre in Toronto. For tickets and information, visit theatrecentre.org.

Handout / As the frontman and vocalist, Andrew Penner is the dominating presence in Boblo.; Caption:
2012-12-05-a-sleepy-hit:
THEATRE REVIEW

Snow White

Elgin Theatre, Toronto

Ross Pettys Snow White is his best panto in years. When it comes to theatrical self-awareness, or admitting that a show is just a show, Bertolt Brecht and his alienation effect have nothing on the family musicals that Petty has been peddling for more Toronto holiday seasons than most of us can count, as a Canadian spin on the traditional English pantomime. Actually, in this context, "admitting" is a weasel word; Pettys productions revel in creating a context and then blithely stepping outside it.

It's got so that this year's panto comments not just on itself but on its predecessors. The perennial Eddie Glen, chirpy music-hall comic reincarnate, bounds on at the beginning to inform us that this years Snow White is the third show in the series with that name in its title, but also that its the first in which it's the entire title. Usually we get Snow White and Something with Seven in it. The traditional septet are apparently too politically incorrect to present though not, it seems, to mention; when the heroine in this version reaches the famous cottage she observes that it used to be owned by seven dwarves and wonders why they've vacated the premises. (Answer: Its the wicked queens fault. Like everything.)

I'm getting ahead of myself. This time Snow White (Snowie to friends) is partnered by just one seven with two zeroes in front. In other words, meet Bond, James Bond; played by Abbey, Graham Abbey. It's an old Petty custom to insert a classical actor into one of his extravaganzas and have him let his hair down, but never before has it been taken so far or done so well. Abbey has in fact been here before, as Prince Charming, going with the flow; now hes Prince Charmings dad, more or less, and he pretty much directs the flow.

On one level, he's giving a first-rate impersonation of Sean Connery: cinematically the first Bond, probably the best, and undoubtedly the most imitable. Listen to him roll the Connery burr on his tongue. On another, he offers a commentary on the whole double-0 ethos, making most of his points with a modest somersault or a lithe forward roll. (Bond, in this incarnation, isn't as young as he was.) On a third, hes contemplating - with a kind of incredulous satisfaction - the idea of him with his Stratford resume being there in the first place.

This leads to some particularly barbed banter with Petty, his co-star and employer, and with the small children brought up from the audience to render assistance at a crucial plot point. (My agent, he told one aghast infant on the first night, "is wearing the same expression as you right now.") I dont know how many of Abbey's ad libs were truly spontaneous but they all sounded as if they were. On all levels he's having and giving a very good time. Hes a trouper.

Of course, he isnt the whole story. The whole story is well underway before he even appears, holed up in the dwarves' former dwelling, managing his spy ops while surrounded by a bevy of beauties. Snowie turns up there because she's banished or is on the run from (its rather confusing) the Queen, who is of course her stepmother and is also of course Petty. She, too, is surrounded by a bevy of beauties, though in her case theyre male. They give her the admiration she craves, as she parades in a succession of gaudy outsize dresses, which is just as well as she doesn't get it from her jester (Glen, given and taking more opportunities than usual) or from her mirror (Dan Cham-eroy via hologram) despite the fact that that's what she pays it for. It insists, as it immemorially has, on telling the unpalatable truth about the Competition. It gets smashed.

Snow White (Melissa ONeil) is really more of a Cinderella; shes the usual sweet thing, though with a belting voice and a commitment to veganism. She wants to be a vet, and in the meantime has made friends with some of the lowlier beasts of the field, including a skunk and a couple of raccoons. When she hits the road, they go with her, and soon they're joined by an assortment of characters from other stories: a device owing equal debts to Into the Woods, other pantomimes and Shrek.

The extremely fine bunch includes Red Riding Hood, whom Bryn McAuley hilariously renders as a bossy but supportive valley girl, Snow White's BFF action with a GPS, and One Little Pig, brilliantly incarnated by Reid Janisse as a porcine Don Cherry who keeps score of the story as if it were a hockey game, and goes into impromptu Coachs Corner huddles with Pinocchio (Billy Lake) who has fewer opportunities but does have an understandable thing about wood. The group is completed by Jack the Giant Killer who has become a pacifist, thus qualifying as Snow Whites love interest. (He may of course simply have run out of giants.)

That's quite enough plot, except perhaps to note that the computer age gives a whole new meaning to the wicked queen's poisoned apple. The way-above-average script is by Rick Miller (the Rick Miller), Carolyn Bennett (not the Carolyn Bennett) and Malcolm Clarke. The program lists them in that non-alphabetical order, suggesting that Miller either did most of the work or has the toughest agent. Theres a smattering of Rob Ford jokes, the last of which is very funny.

The smart direction is by Tracey Flye. The songs seem irrelevant, even by pantomime standards, but they justify their existence at the end, when heroine and villainess square off in a moral and physical beauty contest: a play-off thats also a sing-off. This has become a convention of Elgin pantos, along with the tense finding-a-hidden-object-in-a-bedchamber scene. They are the parts of the show that give equal pleasure to children and adults. Otherwise the show, especially in its jokes, caters to the grown-ups. The kids - with a couple of tearful exceptions - didn't seem to mind.

Snow White runs until Jan. 5. For tickets and more information, visit rosspetty.com.

Racheal Mccaig / Ross Petty's Snow White: It's not quite Disney or Stratford, but it's a lot of fun.; Caption:
2012-12-13-as-the-dickens-women-miriam-m:
Many people, by Miriam Margolyes own account, know her best for her role as Professor Sprout in the Harry Potter films. Others, though probably not quite as many, think of her for her TV performances in Blackadder. And there are some fans who warmly congratulate her on her appearance in a recent London stage production of Samuel Beckett's Endgame.

Everybody seems to know her for something. And during the past year, audiences all over the world have come to know her as an acting ambassador for Dickens' Women -- the title and subject of a one-woman show that shes been taking on a global tour that winds up this week at the Young Centre in Toronto, part of the theatre houses Word Festival, which celebrates the bicentenary of Charles Dickens.

Margolyes isn't exactly a star, but she has a star personality, on and off the stage. Say the name Miriam to anyone in the British acting world and they will know exactly who you mean. This has been going on for a long time, something for which I can personally vouch.

We attended the same English university; I arrived the year after she left, and she was still a potent first-name legend. "She calls everybody darling," said a student newspaper, but, being Miriam, she means it.

For years she insisted that we had been contemporaries, and that I used to give her bad reviews. I've finally persuaded her, during the course of a phone call this past week, that she was wrong about this, but it wasnt easy. Miriam -- I cant call her by her surname at this late date -- is one of those people who seem shy after you get to know them --shy but determined.

The Dickens show has been part of her life for some 20 years, though her enthusiasm for the novels goes back to her childhood. She and another actress, Sonia Fraser, came up with the idea for a two-person show about Dickens.

"We wanted to make a parallel between his life and his work," Miriam tells me. We commissioned a script from a playwright, but it wasn't good. So I wrote it myself: the first and last time I've ever written anything.

They took the idea to the then-director of the Edinburgh Festival, who gave them a booking. It was a two-person show then, with an actor named David Timson playing Dickens himself, and several of his male creations. But "after Edinburgh, Timson got married and decided he didnt want to tour."

So it became a solo show, which she performed with great success, both in England and abroad. Norman Lear, the TV producer, had booked me for a show for a year, she says. "He thought Dickens would be interesting--and new to a Los Angeles audience."

He was right. She plays 23 characters in the show, 20 of them women, including herself. Id have thought this might come naturally to someone who's always been a great character actress and a great character, but she describes it as the bravest thing I do. I talk directly to the audience. I slightly startle them; I come in and out of character without warning.

This week in Toronto marks the end of the Dickens show, though she qualifies that by saying that at least she won't tour it again.

"Ill be a complete wreck when I get back on the plane. But Ill be a very satisfied one."

robert.cushman@hotmail.com Dickens' Women runs Dec. 12-15 at the Young Centre for the Performing Arts in Toronto. For tickets, visit youngcentre.ca.
2012-12-13-string-theory-prehistoric-pup:
The title of the latest show to reach Toronto from the Old Trout Puppet Workshop of Calgary is Ignorance. Its announced subject, though, is happiness. The message seems to be that the two are the same thing. Ignorance, after all, is proverbially associated with bliss. It makes sense; the moment you start asking whether you're having fun yet, it's plain that you aren't. I asked it a lot during the course of this show.

It presents us with three visible puppeteers -- Nicolas Di Gaetano, Trevor Leigh, Viktor Lukawski -- wearing moustaches, grey overalls, and single-horned Viking helmets. The set they inhabit suggests a cave, with the makings of a fire centre stage. The dolls they wield come in two flavours: prehistoric and contemporary. This is to contrast primitives who, it appears, were sometimes able to achieve happiness because they didn't worry about what it was, and moderns who worry all the time and thus can't have it at all.

A program note informs us that in 1934, an Andorran adventurer named Boris Skosyreff, hiding in a cave in the Pyrenees, discovered "the first palaeolithic puppet." I took this to be a joke, but if it is, then Wikipedia, which supplies a biography of Boris, is at least partially in on it. (It vouches for his existence, but doesn't mention puppets, palaeolithic or otherwise.) The note is credited to Sir Reginald Chute, GRMPH, who certainly is a joke, and one that pervades the show itself. His cod-scholarly style is reflected in the recorded narration, voiced by Judd Palmer in unctuous tones that might well be Sir Reginald's own, that is the dominating feature of the evening itself. Its pomposity is obviously intentional, and probably intended to be funny, but that doesn't make it any more pleasant to listen to.

Not that voice-over Sir Reginald doesn't make some good points. He tells us that the average person experiences only 14 minutes of pure happiness in a lifetime. That strikes me as an over-pessimistic estimate, but maybe not by much. He adds the even more telling statistic that most of these moments will have been experienced by the age of 12. Yes indeed: Childhood is the best shot we have at feeling unadulterated (there's a funny word), un-self-conscious pleasure. Of course by the same token, it's the best, or likeliest, time for feeling pure defenceless misery. There are no mental defences against either sensation. It's why cruelty to children is so horrible.

Anyway, the Old Trouts take us back to the childhood of the race. Here is prehistoric man discovering the delights of, among other things, prehistoric woman. He finds love; and isn't he lucky not to know the word, and hence not to have to wonder what it means. He also, though, discovers jealousy and loss. His cave is invaded by another, Alpha Male, who knocks him out and makes off with his mate. This presumably makes Alpha Male happy. Or, as the narrator tells us, "happiness is Mother Nature's reward for being a winner." That seems an unduly cynical definition. Happiness may well be when you stop worrying about winning or losing. Ask a child on a swing. Or rather don't ask; you'll spoil it.

The Stone Age, in this show's mythology, co-exists with the Garden of Eden. Eve gives Adam the apple, and with it the gift, or curse, of imagination: conceiving of something better and hence wanting it. So the human desire for happiness becomes a search for ever shinier toys, and the show plunges into the present to illustrate this. The puppets playing our predecessors are pudgy assemblages of sticks and stones, appropriately eager to break one another's bones.

Present-day humanity is represented by more compact creations who seem to have waddled out of old advertisements for lemon squash i.e. they look like squashed lemons. They try to manufacture happiness on mass-production lines, or to discover it in driving kiddie-cars. Filmed projections illustrate how deluded they are, showing us what might be outtakes from Modern Times or footage of cars proceeding in disconsolate lines along the highway, aimless and probably joyless. A similar lack of progression affects the show itself. It keeps cutting back from present to primeval, without telling us anything new. The satiric effect of the modern scenes quickly palls. The Stone Age at least offers the prospect that a woolly mammoth might drop by, or the near certainty that the males of our species will continue bashing one another up.

This they do with some ingenuity. The puppetry is very skillful. But it never makes you hold your breath or lifts your heart. There is some ingenuity but no joy. Ignorance, as they say in the courts, is no excuse.

robert.cushman@hotmail.comIgnorance runs through Dec. 15 at the Berkeley Street Theatre.

2012-12-14-the-drogheda-monologues:
THEATRE REVIEW

This Lime Tree Bower Berkeley Street Theatre, Toronto

The Irish are great soliloquisers. Or is it soliloquists? It must be, as spellcheck hasn't given me a hard time for using it.

Anyway, they give great monologue. Currently in Toronto there are two plays in which a trio of Dubliners line up to give us their separate, alternating portions of what turns out to be a single tale: Terminus by Mark O'Rowe and now This Lime Tree Bower by the foremost exponent of the genre, Conor McPherson.

McPherson wrote The Weir, which initially seems to be no more than an assortment of anecdotes, but which turns out to be both unified and moving; it's a long, shaggy-dog story composed of shorter shaggy-pup stories.

This Lime Tree Bower doesn't bother with that kind of naturalistic cover. It gives us the convention at its purest: three men, seated side by side, talking always to us, never to one another. The title derives, rather obscurely, from a poem by Coleridge: This Lime Tree Bower My Prison. The poet, temporarily incapacitated, sits in a tree and imagines all the fun his friends are having without him. Each of McPherson's three characters is, like everybody, confined in the cell of his own consciousness. Each of them tries, or is obliged, to reach outside it and achieve some degree of empathy with other people.

The theatre itself may be a lime tree bower in its own right. We sit there, watching and especially listening, and the longer we do so - in this case, anyway - the more amused, shocked and involved we become. It does take time.

In Sarah Dodd's plain but powerful production, the most accomplished performance is given, unsurprisingly, by the most experienced actor: Gray Powell's Ray is the consummate faculty-bar Lothario, volubly despising everyone else while silently loathing himself.

The newest player, Anthony MacMahon as Joe, starts tentatively, apparently uncertain of both the accent and the acoustics, but settles down into a funny, vulnerable performance, showing himself a young master of agonized suspense.

In between, Matthew Gorman as Frank blurs the edges of both character and text. He is, though, as artistic director of Cart/Horse Theatre, responsible for bringing us the play in the first place, and all credit to him for that.

This Lime Tree Bower runs until Dec. 22.
2012-12-15-victorian-ideals-dickens-wome:
My favourite line in the whole of Dickens concerns a very minor character in his very first novel, The Pickwick Papers. A junior barrister is momentarily singled out for notice during the breach of promise trial of Bardell v. Pickwick, and tried to look as if he didnt know that everybody was looking at him: an endeavour in which no man ever succeeded or in all probability ever will. Beat that for an insight into the human condition. It seems to me that if you cant enjoy Dickens as a gag writer, you're unlikely to enjoy him at all.

It's significant, too, that it happens in a law court: From first almost to last in Dickens a symbol of societys organized - or sometimes casually disorganized - injustice. I often wondered, in the days when Margaret Thatcher and her adherents were preaching about "Victorian values," just which values they had in mind. I especially wondered if theyd ever read any Victorian novels. The novelists of Victorian England produced the greatest, most enduring works of their time; and none of them could be said to be in tune with the governing ethos of their age. Implicitly or explicitly they denounced it for its cruelty, its complacency, its greed and its vindictiveness. None of them, of course, did this more persistently, more penetratingly or more hilariously than the one whose 200th birthday has been celebrated this year.

This week, the Young Centre is the site of a last-minute bicentennial celebration. Among other events, it plays host to Miriam Margolyes and her one-person show, now on the last leg of a world tour, Dickens' Women. That, she disarmingly announces after completing her opening item, "was Mrs. Gamp from Martin Chuzzlewit, and I'm Miriam Margolyes from Clapham." The workhouses and the Poor Laws are only an implicit presence in this recital, except in one scene. Departing slightly from the premise of her title, Margolyes gives us, from Oliver Twist, the courtship of Mrs. Corney, the workhouse matron, by Mr. Bumble the beadle, whose philosophy is that you should give the paupers what they dont want so that they wont keep coming back ungratefully for more. The exigencies of the scene confine Margolyes to rendering Corney in her coy rather than her later ruthless aspect, but she gives us, physically and vocally, the full Bumble, greasy, self-important, respectably avaricious and cautiously lecherous. She doesn't, I suspect, care much for Corney, but she loves Bumble, even while loathing and despising everything he represents. In all these respects she would, I am sure, have had her author with her.

That doesn't in itself make Dickens a misogynist. Plainly he adored Mrs. Gamp, the combination midwife and deathbed attendant (very similar functions, as she herself says) who so loved the human race that she would have laid all of them out for free if she could. He loved her, with her gin-tippling and her fantasy monologues, even while hating the economic conditions on which she battened. Margolyes revels in her, but in a very disciplined way. Mrs. Gamp doesnt only begin the show; she apparently began the idea of the show. Mrs. Gamp had very little neck and, in a book accompanying the show (and sold at performances) Margolyes reveals that "having very little neck ... I could ... use some of my unfortunate physical qualities to bring her into the theatre." I wouldnt have put it quite like that myself; still, Margolyes is a small but ample lady. She's also, though, a very dainty one, very precise and selective in her movements. As Mrs. Gamp she waddles. As Flora Finching, the decayed and ridiculous former beauty of Little Dorrit, she resembles a bloated Dresden doll.

Flora was Dickens' rather cruel revenge on Maria Beadnell, the pretty and shallow girl who broke his heart when he was young. In her linking narration (which is admirably informal and informative) Margolyes traces the relationships of the women in Dickens books to those in his life: the genteel, poverty-stricken mother who sent him to work in a blacking factory when he was a child; the sister-in-law he idealized and who died young in his perfectly platonic arms; the actress he fell for in his later years and who probably tortured him as much as Maria had. She also details his appalling treatment of his wife, whom he banished from their home while managing to regard himself as the victim, If he hadnt made us laugh so much, she says, speaking for herself and her director-collaborator Sonia Fraser, "he'd have made us very angry."

But then Dickens probably made himself angry. Though Margolyes claims that Miss Havisham, the avenging, forsaken woman of Great Expectations, was a Dickensian self-portrait, I think it's likelier to be true of Miss Wade, the confessed self-tormentor of Little Dorrit, the lesbian in thrall to a merciless younger woman. Margolyes, her face in profile on an otherwise blacked-out stage, brings her harrowingly to life: a brilliant contrast to the gossips and harridans who occupy most of her attention.

These she portrays with a wonderful appreciation of her authors genius for the evocative, crazy, inevitable word. Occasionally I felt that an irony might bite harder if it were faster or drier, but her taste, her relish and her rhythms are infallible. There are of course sins of omission. She reveals in her book that a gentleman in India once rose from his seat to demand of her, "Where, oh where is Betsey Trotwood?" I was glad to read that because Id been silently asking the same question myself: Betsey (from David Copperfield) is one Dickensian lady who is both richly eccentric and a force for good. She is, admittedly, almost the only one. Dickens' view of women was, to put it gently, selective, and this show makes no secret of the fact. It won't make you angry. But it will make you laugh, and wonder, and love.

Young Centre For The Performing Arts / Miriam Margolyes's taste, relish and rhythms are infallible in this wide-ranging look at the women in Charles Dickens' work and life.; Caption:
2012-12-20-the-years-best-bess-musical-o:
There are frightfully few days before the holiday season takes full effect, but still just enough shopping hours to get the Broadway lover in your circle a few of 2012's best offerings.

For starters, this year saw a Broadway production billed as The Gershwins' Porgy and Bess - a curious title since it omitted the name of DuBose Heyward, on whose novel Porgy the opera was based and who also wrote most of the libretto, with Ira Gershwin contributing only a few of the lyrics. Perhaps, more importantly, the title misrepresented the nature of the show itself.

The Gershwins' (and Heyward's) Porgy and Bess was an opera - an opera built of show music. This production, with new dialogue supplied in place of the original recitative and new orchestrations to replace the ones George Gershwin wrote himself, turned it into a musical.

I can't judge the success of the staging, since I didn't see it. I expected that on the cast album (from the in-valuable U.S. label PS Classics) the alterations would be unnoticeable, and I'd just hear a rendition of the score with Audra McDonald being wonderful as Bess. She does indeed sound superb, but the changes around her are impossible to ignore or to approve, literally from the start.

Gershwin wrote an instrumental prelude; here we get an overture compiled from the score's greatest hits, followed by a Summertime that's been changed from a solo lullaby to a duet with chorus, thereby losing most of its poignancy. The new script by the dramatist Suzan-Lori Parks seems, as far as I could tell from the copious extracts supplied, to have devoted itself to solving problems that don't exist: giving the drug peddler Sportin' Life a backstory, for example.

Out of context, the Porgy songs can sound great when given a jazz or pop treatment; those, after all, are the traditions Gershwin came from. But when sung as part of the score, the choppy staccato treatment that Norm Lewis affords to I Got Plenty o' Nuttin' actually sounds less hip than the buoyant, flowing original. He doesn't have the vocal heft for Porgy, and the adaptation makes it worse by trying to dignify him. The opera's Porgy was a cripple in a goat cart; this one merely walks with a cane. The women mostly come off better than the men, and the ensemble work is excellent.

Porgy and Bess was Gershwin's last work for the theatre. One of his first - indeed his first book musical on Broadway - was Sweet Little Devil (1924), written with his principal pre-Ira lyricist, the preternaturally hard-boiled B.G. (Buddy) DeSylva. A success in its time, it's never been revived. PS Classics has, like Porgy and Bess, now given it its premiere recording, the latest in this label's string of rescues of lost, loopy musicals (Gershwin and other) for which they have perfected the right high style: insouciance with a sting.

This one begins with a threatened strike by Ziegfeld chorus girls, without whose gorgeous pins, as they accurately sing, "The Follies won't have a leg to stand on." From here it abruptly switches to a typical '20s tale of ingenues and hucksters, except that the ingenues aren't that ingenuous and the handsome hero is as much mocked as celebrated.

The most arresting number, Matrimonial Handicap, has a couple of couples placing odds on their chances of a happy married future, expressing something of the mood of Company in the imagery of Guys and Dolls. None of the songs is a neglected classic, but together they add up to something very engaging. It's performed by a cast of musical revival reliables including Rebecca Luker, Philip Chaffin and Danny Burstein, who was a terrific Buddy in last season's Follies and here plays a dodgy operator with amorous delusions.

Songs from the Jazz Age - which doesn't necessarily mean jazz songs - are the meat of Diana Krall's latest CD, Glad Rag Doll, whose selections from the 1920s and early '30s include one treat I was delighted to discover You Know - I Know, Ev'rything's Made for Love. Krall can be breathily sad, as on the title track, or twangily cheery, as on the opener We Just Couldn't Say Goodbye, in which her tongue seems only just contained within her cheek. The guitar-heavy production (by T-Bone Burnett) lends the album a bluegrass feel, and also a certain sameness; it's probably best listened to a few tracks at a time.

The supporting musicians include one Howard Coward, a.k.a. Mr. Elvis Costello Krall, who is featured on mandola (there's versatility for you) and voice, supplying a fairground showman's intro to his wife's enjoyably doomy closing vocal, When the Curtain Comes Down. Composers' names, important to some of us especially on this kind of collection, are given in inexcusably small print.

Brian Stokes Mitchell, the original Coalhouse Walker of Ragtime and now one of Broadway's leading men, pays tribute to some of his predecessors and their medium on Simply Broadway. And it is simple, just him and a pianist, the terrific Todd Firth. It can be disconcerting when Mitchell tries to sound English (How to Handle a Woman) or Jewish (If I Were a Rich Man), at least in the spoken bits; when he sings he gets right inside the characters, accents and all.

Indeed he acts all the songs, but without overacting them; except for atrocities such as Stars (from Les Miserables) or The Impossible Dream, where it's probably unavoidable. He finds a snarky Manhattan tone for Sorry-Grateful, while his It Ain't Necessarily So is hugely better than the one on the Porgy album, both as characterization and as sheer vocal. He ends proceedings with Leonard Bernstein's Some Other Time, the best possible way to end anything.
2012-12-24-forget-about-me-anthony-rapps:
Ihated Without You. This was not because of its standard of performance, which is high. Some 15 years ago, Anthony Rapp created the role of Mark, the videographer-narrator of Rent, and his performance was the best thing in the show. His talents are still on display in the current offering, which is in part a memento of what apparently remains his finest hour. All alone, if you don't count his five back-up musicians, he looks back on his experiences auditioning for Rent, appearing in the workshop, rehearsing for off-Broadway. And then of course the catastrophe that has helped make the musical a legend: the death from an aortic aneurysm and just before the first preview, of Jonathan Larson, the show's author and composer.

Without You is partly Rapp's memorial to Larson. It's also, and more regrettably, a memorial to Rapp's mother, who died of cancer shortly after Rent's opening. (She had been ill before, but had had a lengthy period of remission.) Basing a public performance on private grief is a dodgy proposition, worsened in this case by the fact that Rapp has nothing to say about either person that can make them matter to anyone but him.

Larson makes the better subject of the two, partly because the audience is likely to have some knowledge of and interest in him before entering the theatre, and partly because Rapp can pay tribute to him -- and to his own past -- by singing his songs. Rapp still has an urgent, wiry voice, and it's stirring as well as nostalgic to hear him giving out with Rent's opening number, the one about being "in America, at the end of the millennium." His intensity and the surge of the music carry the lyric, which seemed vaguely pretentious (or pretentiously vague) even at the time. He recounts his initial, and understandable, dismay at the idea of a "rock opera" and how surprised and impressed he was to find that its subject matter included gayness and AIDS. "This" he asked himself, "is a musical?": a strange question, surely, in a New York that had already seen Falsettoland. But all we learn about Larson himself is that he was sort of a cool guy; well, that and the fact that his being cut off in, or quite possibly before, his creative prime was a cruel deprivation, but we already knew that. There's nothing about Larson's personal life, not even a mention of his other musical Tick Tick Boom: a better score than Rent and a show that, being itself self-referential, might have helped.

That Larson's death occurs quite early in Without You is chronology's fault. Still, it leaves Rapp's feeling about his mother to occupy the bulk of the evening. Of course he loved her; of course he was devastated by her illness and her death. We take that for granted. We're also quite willing to believe that she was a very admirable woman. She was, after an initial period of denial, accepting of his sexuality, which is a credit to her but, dramatically speaking, deprives the story of a possible conflict: so much so that we wonder why he bothers to mention it.

The only link between the show's two subjects -- other than that they're things that happened to him, or at least how they're presented -- is that appearing in Rent, with its themes of loss, helped Rapp to deal with his own. The connection involves him in honouring his mother by singing Seasons of Love, but since that's another song with stirring music but portentously sentimental words (never trust a song in which the word "love" has three syllables) the effect is mush. So are the various nostrums proffered by the grief counsellor first brought in to help the Rent company deal with the death of Larson and then consulted by Rapp to deal with his own loss. And it does come across as just his. We're told that he has a brother and sister; presumably they had feelings too, but we're never told what they were -- not even when his brother, also living in New York, travels back with him to the family home in the midwest.

It all seems to be another chapter in the history of the sanctimonious narcissism that's been with us since the 1960s: the belief that the intensity of someone's feelings automatically entitles them to be expressed in public without the mediation of focus and structure: In a word, of art. Rapp achieves this just once, though to be fair it is at his show's climax. He has the late Larson's help, but that's no crime; in fact it's the point. He sings the song from Rent that's his own show's title song, and it does become a moving statement about loss and survival: A summary of his own condition that we can also relate to ours. Not all the songs he sings are from his greatest hit; some are his own compositions, including one called Wild Bill about his mother's tumour that would probably be a low point if the words were audible. Towards the end he tells us about his mother's memorial service, and the show is probably meant to be an extended variation on that event. At a memorial, though, the audience doesn't pay to get in and nobody expects applause.

robert.cushman@hotmail.comWithout You runs through Jan. 6 at the Panasonic Theatre.

2012-12-29-reviews-in-review-a-fairly-fo:
Jessica Moss made a terrific debut as writer-performer of the hilarious Modern Love and somewhat cemented it in Was Spring, Tarragons puzzlingly titled minor MacIvor.

Megan Follows and Kelli Fox in The Penelopiad - the standouts and figureheads in an extraordinary female ensemble, with specially honourable mention for Pat Hamilton and for Pamela Sinha, who after her delectably self-obsessed Helen went on to do wrenching work as author-actress of Crash. Nightwood Theatre was the company of the year, following The Penelopiad with The Happy Woman and the hypnotically tense Between the Sheets. All three were directed by Kelly Thornton.

Everyone in The Golden Dragon, but especially David Fox, who as a flight attendant called Barbie was a scream, even in a play (German) and production (Ross Manson) built on age and gender reversal. The opening shot in a (mostly) exceptional year for Tarragon.

Paul Sun-Hyung Lee in Kim's Convenience - star representative of another stellar ensemble. Ins Choi's play, a candidate for best of the year, was certainly the warmest. A departure for Soulpepper, which generally does revivals; though since it had previously been done on the fringe, it maybe qualifies. And it was freshly directed by Weyni Mengesha.

Ronnie Burkett, actor-writer-puppeteer, in Penny Plain - this all-purpose Armageddon wasnt one of his major works, but hes still a multiple threat in everything he does. It was also the most notable thing to happen this year at Factory, unless you count the theatre board's extraordinarily clumsy dismissal of founder-director Ken Gass.

Arlene Duncan in Caroline or Change, which joined the forces and specialties of Obsidian (race) and Acting UpStage (genre). It was, hands down, the year's best musical - writing, staging (Robert McQueen), performance - additional special mention for young Michael Levinson and for the self-transforming Deborah Hay, later to score a minor Stratford triumph in Henry V and a major one in Much Ado About Nothing.

Theodore Bikel - not just for Visiting Mr. Green (actually he was Mr. Green), but for showing us how at 87.

Adam Paolozza in TheDouble, his own Dostoyesky adaptation. Pure theatre, including the musical contribution of Arif Miroldolbaghi, who, also for the first time, acted. From TheatreRUN, one of the small companies that made so much of this years running.

Nancy Palk in Long Days Journey into Night, heartrendingly completing a remarkable run of drama's legendary mothers. She was later delightful in You Can't Take It with You (another mother)andwonderfulinTheCrucible (a grandmother). Fine work too from Joseph Ziegler, Evan Buliung (as later in Bloodless) and Gregory Prest (as in, it seemed, just about everything - one of Soulpeppers finest finds).

Amy Nostbakken, Canadian-born and British-based, in The Big Smoke, a breakdown in a capella, and a revelation.

Eric Peterson - ideally scrappy and cranky in Seeds, impressive docudrama, ideally meek, cranky and garbage-canned in Endgame.

Oliver Dennis (eternally reliable) and Michael Hanrahan (who just gets better and better) in High Life and then again in Home, where they played a lovely duet.

Natasha Greenblatt - playing a boy in David Craigs The Neverending Story (YPT).

Nicole Underhay in The Small Room at the Top of the Stairs - superb play, production (Mengesha again) and performances - everyone, with Sarah Dodd (also in The Penelopiad) being outstandingly witty. Later at the Shaw, Underhay was defeated by the unplayable protagonist of The Millionairess, but victorious in His Girl Friday.

Maev Beaty Quality meets quantity: The Penelopiad (in a beard), The Happy Woman (knockout), Proud (even more so), Terminus (which I couldn't review, for family reasons, but in which she was spectacular).

Kawa Ada, a bright spot in My Granny the Goldfish; Clare Coulter, whose opening monologue in Was Spring held out unfulfilled promise.

Michael Healey in Clybourne Park - this, and his later performance in his own Proud, may be the most impressive acting he's ever done. Clybourne Park was an all-round fine production of a crackling, mercifully unsentimental, American play.

Petrina Bromley - fine in the soggy Newfoundland import Oil and Water.

Trish Lindstrom - redeeming feature of CanStages The Game of Love and Chance, and good later in Bloodless, in which I confused her with Jan Alexandra Smith: Sorry, they were both good. Peter Mooney and Janet Porter in Gruesome Playground Injuries - another fine, off-the-wall American play, another invaluable independent company (BirdLand),

Jane Spidell in The Real World? - uneven production of Michel Tremblays best play?

Brenda Robins and Maria Vacratsis - the other duet in Home. Albert Schultz, who didn't act this year, directed Soulpepper's best new productions, this and The Crucible, and also brought back Death of a Salesman. But is Soulpepper ever again going to give us a play written before 1900?

Ben Carlson in Much Ado - he and Hay (see above) dug deep into Bene-dick and Beatrice. Stratfords best all-round productions though were, by remarkably unanimous consent, Cymbeline, The Matchmaker and Elektra. Id add Wanderlust, though many wouldn't.

Kyle Blair in Stratford musicals; Martin Happer, jolly good chap at the Shaw.

Corinne Koslo and Ric Reid, heartbreaking couple in Come Back Little Sheba, the Shaw's best show, closely followed by Hedda Gabler. Honourable mention for Present Laughter, especially Steven Sutcliffe. For consistent distinction in the ranks: Gray Powell, Graeme Somerville, Patrick McMaus, Mary Haney, Kevin Bundy.

Stuart Hughes, magnificent in The Crucible. Ari Cohen in Speed-the-Plow, the revived Salesman and, at Tarragon, The Little Years.

Between the Sheets, Jordi Mands playwriting debut, apart from being maybe the years best new script, was also a riveting acting duet for Susan Coyne and the now consistently magnetic Christine Horne. And here's another duo: David Ferry and Michele Monteith in The Lesson.

Tear the Curtain, Kim Collier's production from Vancouver, gave mixed media a good name, and had acting, too (especially from Dawn Petten.) Seems like all the good stuff at Canadian Stage was a partnership with someone. Witness Company Theatres Speaking in Tongues, from the fascinating Australian dramatist Andrew Bovell. Cast were a fine fivesome, with Richard Clarkin maybe best.

Kaylee Harwood, two roles in Bloodless, so maybe counting as a multiple. As does, in spades, Melody Johnson as her own Miss Caledonia (and friends).

Christopher Sieber in La Cage aux Folles, best male performance in a musical, no contest. The show stood up surprisingly well, best in Mirvishs succession of fluffy imports. Their prize production of course was War Horse, but you didn't go to that for the acting. But don't forget that at the beginning of the year they brought us The Blue Dragon, prime Robert Lepage. You didnt go to that for the acting either, but it was good.

Cylla Von Tiedemann / Jean Yoon and Paul Sun-Hyung Lee in Soulpeppers Kim's Convenience.; Caption:
2013-01-05-heart-to-take-with-love-and-a:
Julia Lederer, author of With Love and a Major Organ, has a neat way with a digital simile. So does the young woman she herself plays, in a production at the Next Stage Theatre Festival. Having fallen heavily for a man with whom she briefly interacts on her subway commute every morning, she tells him, "You back me up better than any hard drive." Well, she doesnt exactly tell him; she confides the thought, along with many others of the same kind, to a cassette recorder and, one day, during one of their brief strap-hanging or pole-clutching encounters, slips the tape into his pocket. His response is minimal at best, so she tries harder. The next time around, she gives him her heart as well. I mean that literally. She detaches the beating organ (how, we are aren't told) and makes him a present of it. Physically, she suffers surprisingly few ill effects. Psychologically, of course, she's a mess. But then she always was.

Obviously, its all meant to be a kind of metaphor. But in what we actually see and hear, it functions as a piece of plot that everyone takes as a matter of course. The plays third character opens the show by reciting a fable about a girl who was born with a paper heart, but that doesn't solve any problems. Nor does the storyteller, an older, now-single lady, retain her narrator role in the rest of the show. Instead, we see her acting out a series of vignettes illustrating the hazards and frustrations of speed-dating. She also complains about her 29-year-old son, who's disappeared. The initially separate storylines eventually converge, in a manner more predictable than believable. Then again, literal credibility doesnt seem to be the point. But it isnt clear what is. I guess the experiences of both generations are meant to illustrate the perils and opportunities of relationships in the computer age. The older woman subscribes to online counselling. The younger constructs her life by Facebook, blog and GPS. The man in the middle is cowed and fazed by it all, and who can blame him?

Unable to establish a workable convention for itself, the play becomes a protracted exercise in whimsy. It's salvaged from ultimate tiresomeness by a reasonable supply of funny lines and by the acting. The author and Martha Ross give decent performances, and Robin Archer gives rather more. He's a tall, shy-seeming man, most of whose professional experience, according to the program, has been as a stand-up comic. He stands up a lot here too, many of his appearances taking place at rush-hour, but he talks far less than I would imagine he does when flying solo. That in itself makes him endearing, at least in this context. He conveys that his character has issues as well. With one woman trying to idealize and the other to infantilize him, he still comes across as the most grown-up person onstage.

Memorial, another three-hander at Next Stage, is another play, one of whose characters goes in for making mix-tapes. Tapes? In 2012 - sorry, 2013? Lederers heroine, insistently up-to-date in all other matters, defends this one antiquarian pursuit as being sort of nostalgic and romantic. Steven Gallagher, author of Memorial, has constructed his play largely in flashbacks; so when Dylan, his protagonist, offers a tape to his new boyfriend, Trevor, its part of the past. In the present, Dylan is about to get married to Trevor. He's also about to die of brain cancer. He's opted to remain at home, tended by Trevor and, to a lesser extent, by his older sister Ruth, the first person to whom he came out and his fractious confidante ever since.

The play begins with Ruths tribute at Dylans funeral and/ or memorial. Then Dylan interrupts her. It turns out this isn't fantasy; it's a rehearsal. Dylan is planning his own obsequies; and - attempting a feat attained by few people in life and maybe only by Tom Sawyer in fiction - he wants them to happen while he can still be around to enjoy them. (This latter point is slow to be revealed, but its stressed in the plays publicity, so it seems fair to mention it.) Dylan, you will gather, is mischievous, self-centred and a control freak; charges he mainly wouldn't deny but that he objects to having Ruth bluntly describe in what will shortly be public.

The play is somewhat awkwardly split between being a clinical study of the experience of dying, both doing it and watching it, and being a character study of Dylan himself. It is, though, magnetically well written on both levels and, under D. Jeremy Smith's direction, very tightly and fluently performed. Mark Crawford makes, at our chronologically earliest sighting of Dylan, a very convincing 16-year-old. He goes on being a very convincing 16-year-old even when Dylan has theoretically grown up and become a casting director, throwing adolescent tantrums and exerting infuriating adolescent charm. (A lifelong Muppets devotee, he still wears a Grover T-shirt. Though according to Kate, his real favourite was Miss Piggy which, she says, should have given them an early clue.) Pierre Simpson is as caring and supportive a stage-partner as his character is said to be a life-partner. His bio states thats hes appeared in John Osborne's Look Back in Anger; I don't know which role he played, but Memorial, with its self-pitying but charismatic protagonist and its enforcedly constricted setting, reminded me of that play but with its social and sexual tensions compressed and reordered. As in Osborne, the woman gets dealt the weakest hand: Kate is something of a dramatic convenience, but Mary Francis Moore brings her to jagged if partial life.

The Next Stage Theatre Festival is at the Factory Theatre through January 13. (416-966-1062)
