THEATRE REVIEW

This Is War Tarragon Extra Space, Toronto

The central event of Hannah Moscovitchs This Is War is an atrocity committed in Afghanistan, one in which Canadian forces are indirectly involved. It happens offstage, and its details only gradually become apparent. They're revealed to us by four Canadian soldiers who are testifying before an invisible military tribunal. At least, that's what we initially think theyre doing. It turns out that theyre answering questions from a broadcasting organization back home. It still looks - and, to them, feels - like an interrogation.

This ambiguity is, I think, needlessly confusing. Butthat's my only reservation about a play that grips unceasingly as a story, is brilliantly constructed, morally complex and takes us inside a world. Moscovitch was one of the writers on CBC Radio's Afghanada, and her play obviously owes a debt to that show, though the tone is much starker. The four characters - consummately acted in Richard Roses production - are all members of the same platoon.

One of them is a woman, a master corporal, and two of the men are in lust with her. The younger, a teenage private, seems besotted with her; for the other, the platoon commander, older and married, shes a diversion on an especially drunk and desperate night, following a game of poker. Her own degree of desperation and tedium at a given moment are likely to govern how lucky either of them gets with her. Jealousy results.

In the context of the war itself, these personal emotions may seem transient and trivial. Moscovitch, with superb cunning, lays a trail that leads inexorably from these apparently petty conflicts to the final catastrophe. It determines who goes on a mission and who gets left behind; how they behave under fire and how much responsibility the Canadians hand over to their less disciplined Afghan allies.

The corporal, the captain, the private take turns at telling the story to their interviewers and hence to the audience, and their separate accounts are acted out before us. Some scenes get repeated. In terms of actual events, the different viewpoints hardly vary. What changes is our appreciation of the emotional effect on each of the participants; a scene may go on a little longer because of whom it hurt or whom it made angry.

Underlying everything is a sense of guilt: the knowledge of having made mistakes in a situation where anyone, especially a child, could be either friend or foe, and the determination not to have it happen again. Some of the worst events in the play are the fruits of the best intentions. The characters are conscientious professionals, cynical but vulnerable, in a hopeless situation. Moscovitch gives them tense, searing, sometimes witty dialogue that, at least to this civilian, rings absolutely true. This is a text without an ounce of fat on it.

Rose's direction is similarly lean, in a set by Camellia Koo that places us with the actors in their camouflaged tent, and with lighting by Rebecca Picherack that it wields like a weapon. (One of the most effective scenes takes place in total darkness.) Lisa Berry's corporal is wonderfully tough and troubled. Ari Cohens captain, world-weary and battle-weary, has tremendous force, the more unsettling because the actor has the ability to turn his rages on and off in an instant. Ian Lakes private covers the most emotional territory, aging as much psychologically as physically; gauche and open-faced in the main action, elaborately bitter when giving his testimony.

One of the play's subtleties is the way the characters effectively close ranks when bearing witness; whatever their individual fates or differences, they are all soldiers facing down an alien authority. They may not have been coerced into talking, but they all behave as if they were. Another is the way the play takes us beneath the uniforms by reminding us in which parts of Canada each of them grew up.

Our fourth neighbour, played subtly and sympathetically by Sergio Di Zio, is an army medic who seems for much of the time to be outside the main action; he's everybodys friend and confidant, always appearing when needed, which suggests that hes more than fulfilling his job description. Reticent about himself, he isn't in the opening line-up of interview subjects. Eventually, though, he does get to speak for himself. In fact he has the last word, and it's a stinging one. It performs, in fact, everything the play's title promises. It caps what is, on every level, a magnificent evening.

This Is War runs at the Tarragon Extra Space until Feb. 3 before heading to the Prairie Exchange in Winnipeg Feb. 20 to March 10.

The theatrical year in Toronto looks like being a real Wiener-schnitzler. Soulpepper will be reviving La Ronde, probably the best-known play by Arthur Schnitzler, Viennese playwright and novelist of the late 19th and early 20th centuries. Meanwhile, at the Tarragon, we have Morris Panych's adaptation and production of Schnitzler's Anatol, its title extended to The Amorous Adventures of Anatol, so as to leave no doubt about the subject matter.

That of course is something that it shares with La Ronde, along with its episodic structure. There are differences. La Ronde is a linked series of sexual encounters, a theatrical daisy chain in which the first partner eventually reappears as the last. Anatol focuses on just one young man about town, showing him with a succession of different women, one per scene. Something else: the popularity and/or notoriety of La Ronde partly derives from the fact that in the course of all but one of its 10 scenes, the couple concerned actually do it. By contrast, Anatol's conquests are much described, especially by him, but never explicitly shown. His alliteratively amorous adventures consist of him being rejected or, less often, doing the rejecting himself. Somehow the stars never seem to align so that both parties get disillusioned simultaneously. Which, I guess, is life.

The first scene sets the tone. Anatol, partly to show off to his friend Max, puts his latest prey under hypnosis to determine whether she loves and is faithful to him. (His own fidelity doesn't enter into it; he may not have invented the double standard, but he flourishes it like his own personal banner.) The answers he gets seem satisfactory, but he can't quite be sure. He's doomed to frustration. Schnitzler apparently wrote this scene as a self-contained sketch, and it still feels sketchy. But he persisted, and found a remarkable resilience in the idea.

In the following scene, Anatol's doing his Christmas shopping (the staging recalls Panych's production of that lighter continental treat, Parfumerie) and encounters an older flame, a married or conceivably divorced or widowed woman - anyway a Mrs. Something - who proves jealous of whomever he's buying presents for now. It ends in a stand-off. And so it goes up to a final scene which finds Anatol about to set off to get married, but delayed by the presence of a hot date from the night before: A development that shocks even the unshockable Max. ("Oh, no, not LIONA").

Watching the play is a curious experience. It begins by being lightly entertaining. It then threatens to become tiresome: How many times do we need to be shown that Anatol is a narcissist who thinks he idealizes women while worshipping only himself, and is terrified that they will tire of him before he tires of them? But the repetition starts to justify itself, even to take on not just satirical edge but moral weight. It ends - in this version anyway - with the promise that Anatol's marriage heralds the revenge of all the furious women he has ever scorned.

The super-prolific Panych, mounting his first production in at least two weeks, has come up with a fluent, sometimes witty text (the laughs are surprisingly few but reassuringly good) and given it a fleet, crisply timed staging in a set by Ken MacDonald, whose back wall resembles a giant, elegant filing-cabinet, with one drawer for each chapter of Anatol's past. It's actually used that way in one scene, though it's typical of our hero that he can't file them under names, probably because he's forgotten what they are.

Mike Shara, who can shift from one foot to another more meaningfully and more energetically than any other actor I know, captures both the exterior Anatol, confident roue, and the interior one, nervous boy eternal. It's never revealed exactly how he maintains his apparently luxurious lifestyle. His lady-friends, or some of them, do have jobs: Dancer, actress, circus-performer - it seems that in old Vienna there was no business like show business. We meet seven of his partners altogether, all of them played by Nicole Underhay and nearly all of them (with handsome help from Charlotte Dean's costumes) dazzlingly differentiated. The first quick-change, from bouncing ingenue to wounded woman of the world, is especially striking; two opposite characters, fully inhabited. She's delightfully self-absorbed in her circus-town, off-handedly informing Anatol that she's ditching him, while tucking in to a restaurant meal at his expense. (Every play of this kind has one. Central European drama is the only drama that knows how to eat.) Her resources aren't quite inexhaustible; her jealous transports in her last scene closely resemble her jealous transports from earlier on. But both are dead-on in their own right.

Robert Perscichini makes a suitably tactful Max, alternately congratulated and upbraided by Anatol for not understanding women, though it's clear in at least one scene that that is another instance of Anatol's self-delusion. (Max is a psychologist, by nature and vocation; Schnitzler, a doctor as well as a writer, seems to have split himself between the two men.) Adam Paolozza plays a whole flock of flunkeys, to telling if generally silent effect.

Schitzler was one of the most penetrating of playwrights, and it would be good to see a Toronto production of one of his more elaborately constructed plays: Undiscovered Country perhaps, which Tom Stoppard has translated and which Chris Abraham directed, very well, some years ago in Montreal.

The Amorous Adventures of Anatol runs through Feb. 10 at the Tarragon Theatre.

THEATRE REVIEW

The Wizard of Oz Ed Mirvish Theatre, Toronto

When I first heard that Andrew Lloyd Webber and Tim Rice were adding songs of their own for their stage adaptation of The Wizard of Oz, my initial reaction was, "Isn't that illegal?"

Probably it should be, but in fact, apart from a near-to-closing inspirational anthem that's more like the worst of Disney than the best of MGM, the new numbers they have tagged on to the movie originals aren't bad. Rice's lyrics, indeed, may be the best he's ever written, with an accuracy and ingenuity in wordplay that are astonishing from the man who once tried to get away with rhyming "biscuit" and "district." He even manages to write some additional lines for Over the Rainbow and If I Only Had a Brain without embarrassing himself. The spirit of Yip Harburg must have rubbed off on him.

E.Y. Harburg, to give him his official billing, wrote the 1939 movie lyrics to the music of the great Harold Arlen. He was also one of the platoon of writers who worked on the screenplay; and to hear him tell it (and he told it a lot) he was the one responsible for giving the picture its tone: a mixture of heartfelt whimsy and social consciousness. The latter may not be too obvious now, but The Wizard of Oz is a story that starts in the Kansas dustbowl, filmed in the wake of the Depression and on the brink of war. Harburg saw it as his tribute to the New Deal, with FDR as the man who had restored brains, heart and courage to a nation of scarecrows, tin men and cowardly lions: a country that no longer knew its own strength.

It's this conviction, plus Judy Garland at her nervously pluckiest, that gives the film its urgency. Without that, it's just a story, a spectacle. Which is what it becomes in the new stage version that originated in London and is now in Toronto, with a Canadian cast and its sights set on New York.

The movie Wizard, of course, was itself an adaptation; and the original L. Frank Baum book has been the subject of stage musicals, quite independent of the film, both long before it and long after (The Wiz was a pretty good show). But it's the movie that's stuck, and Jeremy Sams' production (he's also the co-adaptor, with Lloyd Webber) is, like all such enterprises, torn between reproducing it and re-imagining it.

It starts out rather well in Kansas, with Dorothy's Uncle Henry and Auntie Em given a more detailed relationship to their orphaned charge than we're used to. (They're well played by Charlotte Moore and Larry Mannell, the latter doubling as the gatekeeper of Emerald City, British-accented like in the film.) But then we get to the twister, the hurricane that blows Dorothy to Oz; apparently deciding it can't be staged, the production team try to evoke it with a projected montage of flying images. In other words, they film it, which of course has already been done. The only time here when the new technology justifies itself is at the end, when Dorothy seems to be finding her way back to Kansas with the help of Google Earth.

Meanwhile, we have had set and costume designs (by Robert Jones) more garish than stylish. The sharp-suited inhabitants of Emerald City suggest Guys and Dolls gone green, but the effect is done to death in Arlene Phillips' choreography, which is lumpen almost throughout. The low point is reached by the snarling slinking of the Wicked Witch's underlings, which might just about do for a musical of Star Wars, but here only spoil her song, a covetous confection about the ruby slippers that finds Rice matching "clueless" with "shoeless" and "footwear" with "put where." No, it isn't Harburg, but its feet are in the right place.

But there's another thing. In the movie, the witch doesn't sing. In fact, the last third of the movie practically stops being a musical; it has too much story. The stage show, obliged to keep shovellinginsongs,slowsevery-thing down. Hollywood was so self-denying in this regard that it cut out a first-rate Arlen-Harburg rhythm number, The Jitterbug. I was rather surprised that the show hasn't reinstated it; I'd gladly sacrifice the Lullaby League and the Lollipop Guild in exchange. (To be honest, I could do without the Munchkins altogether. They're full-grown in this production, either for PC reasons or so they can be doubled with everyone else.)

I'm philosophically opposed to the idea of casting shows by TV talent contests, but it works out as well here in practice as it did in Sams' (far superior) production of The Sound of Music. As Dorothy, Danielle Wade - plucked from the CBC's Over the Rainbow talent show - is a troubled teen rising above her troubles, and does much to keep the show on the Yellow Brick Road (one of the better design elements, incidentally). It isn't her fault the song Over the Rainbow is now so crusted in mythology that it's impossible to accept as part of a story (and the rainbow itself looks very cut-rate).

Jamie McKnight is a charming Scarecrow; his solo dance is the most delightful thing in the show. Mike Jackson's Tin Man is all right but no more, while Lee MacDougall's Lion is much less. Harburg's inspiration of fashioning the role for Bert Lahr has made the role unplayable by anyone else, but turning him into a pussycat who's seen too many musicals (and proudly pronounces himself "a friend of Dorothy") is a terrible solution. I did like the annoyed reaction of the other two when Dorothy announced she'd miss the Scarecrow most (I'd often wondered how they must feel) and I loved Lisa Horner's Wicked Witch greeting Robin Evan Willis' Good Witch with a "hello, Glinda," like Jerry Seinfeld acknowledging the existence of nemesis Newman. Horner seems to be having a good time, and shares it with the audience.

Willis, meanwhile, is a Good Witch who's post-Wicked, and far more entertaining in her fairy godmother complacency than the sugary trilling of her movie prototype.

Cedric Smith is a pleasing Professor Wonder and a boomingeye-flashingWizard, whose exposure is weakened by being confusingly staged. In the film it's brought about, with a wonderful mixture of the inadvertent and the inevitable, by Dorothy's dog Toto, but perhaps they didn't trust the stage Toto to do it right. On the first night he was being fed with treats, as if they were prompts. He, incidentally, is of the same cairn-terrier breed as his cinematic predecessor but is reddish-brown rather salt and pepper. This must be colour-blind canine casting.

The Wizard of Oz is playing at the Ed Mirvish Theatre in Toronto. For tickets and more information, visit mirvish.com.

THEATRE REVIEW

Berkeley Street Theatre, Toronto

The best parts of Kristen Thomson's Someone Else are very good indeed. Thomson herself appears in it, opposite Tom Rooney; they play a couple in their forties whose marriage is crumbling, and they give lacerating performances. The most painful thing is that they arent playing people who hate one another. Theyre playing people who love one another, even though each of them has turned, in the other's eyes, into someone else. At least, that's how I take the title. Other interpretations are possible.

She, named Cathy, is a stand-up comic, he, Peter, is a doctor: not perhaps the most obvious match, come to think of it, though Ive known doctors who thought themselves comedians. Within the structure of the play - and heres where it begins to run into trouble - their two jobs function in different ways. Cathy's is a dramaturgical device; Peter's is part of the plot.

The play begins with Cathy doing her act; or maybe just rehearsing her act. Chris Abrahams production features a bare white room of a set featuring a lot of doors and not much else. With the house lights still on, she picks up a microphone and starts prowling the stage, telling us how much her life sucks. She makes especially fierce fun of the state of her marriage and the size of her bum.

Cathy takes her self-deprecation further still, into self-therapy; theres no "between us girls" element in her routine, no presumption of sympathy. It's all her. It's a brilliant, bravura performance that she intensifies later on, pouring out anger and desperation in a second monologue for which she doesnt have the stage to herself; her husband is running around behind her, apparently in search of a ceaselessly ringing phone.

Effective though it is as commentary, Cathys profession doesn't have much bearing on the story. Peter's does, partly as a source of jealousy. Cathy suspects his interest in a self-destructive 19-year-old called April. Peter does indeed become obsessed with her, though not, as far as we can tell, sexually. Part of the problem between him and Cathy is that hes as reticent as she is needy and effusive. Aprils demands are easier for him to cope with because he can at least tell himself that they're professional, and he doesn't have to live with them. April has a history of cutting herself; Peter asks her to teach him how, as a means of awakening his own frozen feelings.

Maybe hes attracted to women who talk a lot. April makes long speeches about her abused childhood and her attempts to transcend it, but they arent as amusing or arresting as Cathy's confessions. In fact they stop the play in its tracks. This is partly because the young actress (Bahia Watson) hasn't the vocal chops to get them cleanly across in this exposing space, but more because the character seems like an intrusion: The play isnt about her, but she takes up a lot of its time.

The productions geometry is also odd. Or maybe its arithmetic, since in principle all its elements could add up, they don't come out as a satisfactory sum. The cause of Peter's withdrawal is revealed to us when, like a recovering alcoholic, he engineers a meeting with someone hes wronged in the past. This is David, a paraplegic who has sat mute and presumably accusing in his wheelchair for several scenes before his presence is officially recognized.

Damien Atkins gives a tremendous performance in this role, a man who disdains sympathy and works himself into a blazing outpouring of pride and scorn. And, yes, it makes theoretical sense that Peters encounter with him could have had the effect we're told it had. But, coming as and when it does, it seems too pat.

There are some wonderful scenes throughout, though. Thomson as writer, she and Rooney as actors and Abraham as director strike deep at the raw pain of opposites not just attracted but bound - two incorrigibly smart people wrong-footing one another with every step. Early on we see Peter and Cathy in a therapist's office, answering regulation questions that are spelled out for us on a screen: Shes flip but anguished, hes logical and impatient, a cross-talk routine that only one of them is equipped to play.

Much later we see them suddenly reunited by shared terror at the apparent disappearance of their daughter; Thomson's hysteria, Rooney's desperate mask of practicality, the galloping speed of the whole thing - all are agonizingly believable, even a little bit funny, though I couldnt quite believe that she wouldnt have snatched the phone out of his hand rather than relying on him to relay information. As everyone knows, and as Cathy would certainly agree, there are some situations in which men just can't be trusted.

Someone Else runs until Feb. 2 at the Berkeley Street Theatre in Toronto. For tickets and more information, call 416-368-3110 or visit canadianstage.com.

Two years ago, the award for best new play in the Toronto Fringe Festival was given to Kim's Convenience, which went on to glory. Last year, the prize was won by a play called Help Yourself, which is unlikely to achieve the same wide success, partly because it isn't as sunny and partly because it isn't as good. It is, though, worth checking out; as can now be done courtesy of a re-mount at the Red Sandcastle, an intimate makeover of a theatre on Queen West, which is easy to miss but very welcoming once found.

Help Yourself is indeed about self-help, or about somebody who sells it. He's Donny, a high-living (in a condo), fast-talking young man who charges a cool $5,000 an hour to clients who want to find the courage to do something forbidden. He's consulted by Ted, an older man, or at least a man with less hair and worse posture, who wants to work up the nerve to kill his wife, whom he's convinced is cheating on him. Ted has some moral qualms about this, as well as the apparently less troubling fear that he might be caught. Also he's never fired, or even held, a gun. Donny undertakes to free him from his misgivings, especially the ethical ones.

His technique is aggressive brainwashing, involving press-ups, forced marches around the room, and making Ted take copious draughts of hooch at an ungodly hour of the morning. "Ungodly" is indeed the word, since the more cerebral part of Donny's technique includes philosophical disquisitions on the irrelevance of conventional morality, as mainly derived from religion. He also confuses Ted with citations from Hume, Kant and Machiavelli. (Neither man completed college, but while Ted flunked it, Donny dropped out, believing - obviously rightly - that he could make more money following his own star. Ted, on the other hand, is a security-guard in a jewellery store. This turns out to be a plot point.) Donny's method is to be fast, loud and in-your-face, often literally. Ted frequently threatens to leave, sometimes even does so, but always comes back.

Interspersed with these moments from a consultation are scenes from Donny's private life: visits, presented mostly in reverse chronological order, from his girlfriend, a fairly recent acquisition who would like him to find a nicer line of work, though she does appreciate the perks of this one. The eventual convergence of the play's two narratives is predictable from a long way off: From so far in fact that, by the time it's actually fulfilled, we've forgotten about predicting it, so it still has an element of surprise, even of shock. It also grows in the mind; some behaviour (Ted's especially) that seems inexplicable when it happens proves in retrospect to have been both logical and clever. This is the second time in a couple of weeks that I've had occasion to recall The Public Eye, a 50year-old one-act play by Peter Shaffer. I doubt that the creators of Help Yourself, a group called Theatre Brouhaha, have seen or even heard of it but, take it from me, there's a structural resemblance, though the Shaffer play is much gentler.

The principal creator here, as writer and director, is Kat Sandler, who contributes a program note about ours being a society in which everything is permitted, and of which a personality and profession like Donny's are the natural products. This strikes me as specious generalization, but it does produce some effective drama, rather like Theatre Brouhaha's previous brouhaha LoveSex Money, though that one was more varied in its attack. The problem with this one is that Donny's abrasiveness takes over the play itself; his humiliation of Ted is all it has to offer, and though the process is never boring, it's grating to sit through. This is probably accentuated by the performance as Donny of Daniel Pagett (who was also involved in the writing); he seems to be enjoying himself more and holding himself back less than is strictly necessary. As, respectively, his punching-bag and sparring-partner, Tim Walker and Tosha Doiron are thoroughly credible

Nightwood Theatre's The Penelopiad, Margaret Atwood's re-imagining of the Odysseus story from the point of view of the wandering hero's famously patient wife, is back for a well deserved second season. It isn't quite a play, more a feat of theatrical storytelling and illustration: What is meant to be its binding element - Penelope's guilt over the fate of her faithful maids, brutally executed by her returning husband - never really registers as a dramatic fact, however much she talks about it, and however much they continue to haunt her in the afterlife from which she now addresses us.

Their concerns have to share our attention with Penelope's bruised and amused recollection of her entire life story from neglected royal childhood to semi-happy, semi-aggrieved and highly resourceful royal wifehood. (Her travails include what she might, if she didn't happen to be in Hades herself at the time, describe as the mother-in-law from Hell.) It's written with understated passion and superbly sustained wit, and these elements are preserved and amplified in Kelly Thornton's production, distinguished by Monica Dottor's choreography, Denyse Karn's spare, versatile set and tasteful, graceful costumes, delightful choral singing and dancing, and a wonderful corps of 13 actresses, several of them of actual or potential star quality, and all but one of them playing maids (and just about everybody else).

The exception of course is Megan Follows, who must have to deliver half the text and, without a hint of strain, conveys every jest, thought and cry of pain within it. I can hardly call Follows our most underrated actress - everybody knows how good she is - but she may be our most under-used. I've hardly ever, for example, seen her play Shakespeare (she was Juliet at Stratford, opposite the festival's current director, but that was before my Canadian time) though she'd seem to be made for it, with a command of text and mood, and a fastidious unforced charm, second to none. She heads a remarkable team (the few newcomers including a spirited Telemachus from Neema Bickersteth) but this is her show. We don't just see the story through her eyes; we feel it.

When people talk about the theatre district in Toronto, they usually mean King Street West, where the Royal Alexandra and the Princess of Wales live. Even if you take the majority view among ticket-buyers that theatre in Toronto really means commercial theatre, that picture is geographically limited. It leaves out the Yonge Street strip between Queen and Dundas, guarded at one end by the Elgin and Winter Garden and at the other by what is now the Ed Mirvish. If your taste runs rather to what are sometimes called the independent theatres - the established non-commercial ones that we might call "institutional" if they were a bit bigger and a lot more comfortable - then the theatre district is a bit further west. New York has off-Broadway, we have off-Bathurst; which is where the Factory, Theatre Passe Muraille and, a little to the north, the Tarragon are all situated. Commercial or non, big or small, Toronto theatre is a west end deal (though not in the bright-lights London sense). Theatres east of Yonge, certainly east of the Don River, are rare creatures.

That may be changing. Near the Beaches, there's already the Red Sandcastle Theatre, housing a constantly changing slate of visiting small-company productions. And a more grandiose project is now taking shape in Leslieville, at Dundas West and Carlaw: not too far away, as the crow flies. Or as Crows flies, because this new theatre, scheduled to open in two years time, is the brainchild and the future home of the previously peripatetic Crows Theatre company, whose artistic director for the last seven years has been Chris Abraham.

Abraham himself lives in the east end - as does his administrator Monica Esteves, a vital partner in the enterprise - so for years now he's been travelling to work, or to see other people's work. Hes universally acknowledged as one of our leading young (well, younger) directors; he also has a reputation for having built his career with exemplary canniness.

When I mentioned this to him during a phone conversation this week, he denied having had any great master plan; hes gone where the work was. It's a challenge having a directing career, especially if you want to stay in this country. I've not thought hugely about what Im doing or where Im going.

Still, he's had an impressively varied freelance career both before and during his time at Crow's; he became known for directing new plays, most notably Kristen Thomsons I, Claudia, but he also directed classics and rarities with the late Bill Glasscos short-lived but exciting Young Company in Montreal and later with Soulpepper; for the last few years he's been a rising star at Stratford, culminating last year in his hilarious, loving production of Thornton Wilder's The Matchmaker.

"I definitely enjoy directing - I seize as many opportunities as possible to be in a rehearsal hall," Abraham says. Hell still be getting them, as in their new premises, Crows, which has been averaging two productions a year (currently Thomson's Someone Else, a co-production with Canadian Stage), will probably be mounting three. Even that of course hardly makes a full season, but that isn't the aim. The architect is Joe Lobko, whose previous projects include Wychwood Barns and the Brickworks.

This isnt, says Lobko, himself an east end resident, "just about building a theatre; its about sharing it with an area that needs it. For one third of the year, that will be theatre; for the other two-thirds, it will be available for community activities" - among which he lists musical performances, art exhibits, conferences, cooking classes (the planned facilities include a kitchen) and weddings. (Weddings, Lobko says, "are cultural events in some societies.") This, obviously, is a business model as well as a cultural one; the diversification is aimed to keep actual theatre ticket prices down to $20. Which, by current standards, is a steal.

There will be 200 seats, designed to be flexibly arranged, plus a rehearsal space (roughly the size of the stage - a luxury), and what Lobko calls "a generous lobby space, that can itself be used for community events." And it's all to take up the ground floor of what will otherwise be a condo. This seems to be one of the things that especially interests Lobko: There's an exciting history of making theatrical spaces in the bottom of large buildings. (He instances the Auditorium Building in Chicago, designed by Louis Sullivan, mentor of Frank Lloyd Wright). "And the acoustical buffering problem, from both directions, is an interesting technical challenge."

Abraham describes his own challenge as wanting to develop a different relationship with the audience. I am interested in getting to know the audience that is coming to see my plays. Recently Ive started to make myself available to audience members after performances and spent time speaking with them about their experiences, why they come to the theatre. I never used to do this. I think the new relationship I am looking for has to do with wanting to redefine for myself my relationship to the people I am making theatre for. What are my obligations to them? What is important to them when they come to the theatre?

I think thats healthy. Practitioners often give too little consideration to audiences, unless as pressure groups or as the abstract recipients of good intentions. Abraham is also unfashionably sanguine about the future of the theatre in the city,

"I'm not worried about future leadership. I think there'll be a renewal. I grew up in an era where many of us learned to do a lot with very little. Maybe we've tended to think too much inside the sandbox."

2013-02-02-making-the-familiar-strange-j:
It is only in the last stages of RARE that there is any explicit mention of Down's syndrome. This is despite the fact that nine of the play's 10 performers have the condition, making it, inescapably, the subject. Judith Thompson, who assembled and directed the show from the actors' own testimonies, made a canny decision here. We think, for the greater proportion of the piece's one-hour length, that we are being let off the hook, and probably feel guiltily grateful for it. When, finally, we are impaled, the process turns out to be bracing and then healing.

Partly it's because by then we've got to know them as individuals, which also, in the way of theatre, makes them more powerful as a group. The actors begin by putting on masks, giving the impression that they are looking at us: also, perhaps, shielding both us and themselves. Then they take the masks off and introduce themselves by their real names: Sarah Carney, James Hazlett, Nicholas David Herd, Michael Liu, Dylan Harman Livaja, Suzanne Love, Nada Marie Christiane Mayla, Krystal Hope Nausbaum and Andreas Prinz. Those are the full versions, as listed in the program. In the performance itself, they only use their first names.

They also tell us their ambitions. The method recalls, of all not too unlikely things, A Chorus Line, and the show does indeed include some song and dance. At the end, after the mood has changed and the stakes have risen, they give their names again, and again tell us what they most want. The terms are different, and they themselves seem older. Instead of "I'm looking for a girlfriend" (James), we have "I hope one day to have sex" (Dylan).

The first part of the show works by making the familiar strange. At times this spills over, perhaps unavoidably, into cuteness; when Suzanne does a dance routine, enthusiastically and well, the audience response is vociferous almost beyond the call of duty. The vocal and instrumental contributions of Victoria Carr, a singer-songwriter who's the 10th performer, supply an air of muzzy uplift to proceedings that are otherwise very precise. A friendship-into-love scene, tentative but determined, between Sarah and Michael, is charmingly specific to the characters themselves; it also seems like everybody's fumbling, hopeful youth, caught forever.

The text includes some formal poetry. What may be the two most famous speeches in Shakespeare - Romeo's "but soft, what light through yonder window breaks" and Hamlet's "to be or not to be" - are spoken, to remarkably freshening effect. In the first, especially, the careful, emphatic delivery, and the bold but spare accompanying gestures, make you hang on every word; this may even be how Elizabethan actors spoke the lines, when they were new and when acting would have been natural by its own lights, probably stylized by ours.

The Hamlet speech comes in the production's last movement, and is shared among the performers as they grapple with their own lives. Up to now, they've seemed cheerful, resilient, even innocent. The resilience remains, but they now talk unsparingly about being bullied and insulted, about their love for lost siblings and grandparents (this is especially moving), about their fears of what may happen when their parents die, and about their determination to survive it. There's an impassioned plea to impending parents of Down's syndrome children not to have those children aborted: A plea, it seems to me, that only those children and their parents have the right to make. There's anger, too. Dylan swears about his condition barring him from acting school. If ability to transmit a powerful emotion is a criterion for admittance, he has a case.

The pleasures and the pains recounted and enacted here should relate to everyone's remembrances of childhood, with the confounding difference that we're experiencing here through people who, physically and intellectually, are not children. (They're mostly in their twenties.) It's possible - actually very likely - to approach this production feeling queasy; or, equally, with a determination to avoid that feeling. Both apprehensions feel groundless. I'm not sure if the title is meant to be a description of the show itself; but if it is, it's justified.

RARE runs until Feb. 7 at the Young Centre for the Performing Arts. For tickets, visit youngcentre.ca

Young Centre / RARE at first seems like it will let us off the hook. It doesn't.; Caption:
2013-02-09-selfcentred-a-pair-of-plays-t:
Everybody, or so one hopes, wishes the new regime at the Factory Theatre well. Nigel Shawn Williams and Nina Lee Aquino, the joint artistic directors, were parachuted into their positions after the board's dismissal of their predecessor Ken Gass; but holding the way he was treated against the new duo would probably be unfair and would certainly be unproductive. It could result in there being no Factory at all. All that said, Every Letter Counts, the partnership's first offering, a play written by Aquino and directed by Williams, puts goodwill to a severe test.

Of the two partners, Williams comes off the better. His production sounds good, at least at the sound-effects level, and looks good, Anna Treusch having designed a handsome room of a set, on which Cameron Davis projects some striking images, of which the most important are a series of Scrabble tiles. These reinforce the play's main metaphor, driven home in its title. It's an autobiographical piece in which Aquino recounts how, when she was six, a kindly uncle helped her overcome her dyslexia by teaching her this most educational of board games. This may be a theatrical first; there are many plays that employ chess as a metaphor, but I don't know of any others that use Scrabble.

When not thus benevolently engaged, uncle Ninoy was a freedom-fighter in the Philippines, the most outspoken opponent of General Fernando Marcos, who imprisoned him, then released and let him leave the country, and finally - when he dared to return - had him shot as he got off the plane. Posthumously, he's a hero, with a museum in his honour in Manila. The museum is the play's ground zero. The grown-up Bunny (the author's surrogate name) visits it and gets to thinking about the four days she spent in her uncle's company in Texas, during his exile. She seems to feel guilty about letting him return, though what she could have done about it in such a short time and at her tender years is obscure.

Really it isn't, or wasn't, about her. But the play behaves as if it is, an effect compounded by having Aquino be not only the author and the heroine of the play but also its leading actor. Playing herself, she makes, for better or worse, no attempt to be a realistic six-year-old, except perhaps in the matter of sheer ill-tempered brattiness. This note, largely uninflected, infects her entire performance, and its monotony makes the chronology difficult to follow. There are flashbacks within the flashbacks: scenes of Ninoy's imprisonment, especially his meeting with a surprisingly suave and understanding General Marcos. Or perhaps not so surprising: Deceptively decent dictators are a theatrical staple. Earl Pastko seems to enjoy playing this one; you can understand why Ninoy might take the chance of returning, to reason with him. (Imelda and her shoes, alas, are referred to only in passing.)

Ninoy himself is played with dignity and charm by Jon de Leon. That he wasn't quite a saint is driven home to us by his brother and Bunny's father (Anthony Malarky), whose only apparent function is to balance the picture with some angry reminiscence. Not to devalue the heroine's dyslexia, or the efficacy of Scrabble in teaching her to arrange her thoughts as well as her words, but they don't seem very important compared to the fate of a country. Either this play is telling the wrong story or it's telling the right one in the wrong way.

An earlier theatrical essay in self-mythologizing has been revived by Heart in Hand Theatre. This one was a double. Seems that near the beginning of their respective careers Patti Smith, the singer, and Sam Shepard, the playwright, shacked up together. It was an ill-natured and short-lived alliance, but they reconciled enough to write a sort-of play, performed originally by themselves, in which they reconstructed their relationship as a series of quarrels and monologues. Slim (that's Sam) complains that Cavale (Patti) has stolen him away from his wife and children in a hopeless attempt to make him into a rock star. Cavale, who identifies with doomed poets, says that she's tired of telling stories about people killing themselves because they make her jealous: Roll that one around in your mind.

She also tells a poignant story about being cast as the Ugly Duckling in a school play, only to have another girl replace her for the transformation into a swan. This, the best speech in the play, is hauntingly delivered by Jessica Huras; the rest of her performance is loud but mopey. Slim, the amateur rocker, is played by a professional, Jason Collett (of Broken Social Scene), who brings to it the understated confidence often shown by musicians who turn actors; he's at home on the stage, if not quite in the play, and comes off better than she does because he doesn't seem to be trying so hard. The play has the kind of self-absorbed aimlessness, alleviated by flashes of lightning, that I associate with all but the best of Shepard's own plays; though in this case he seems to have written less well for his own role than Smith has for hers.

There is a third character, known as Lobster Man; he seems to be an unfortunate delivery boy whose employers make him dress up in a crustacean suit. Sam and Patti make fun of him, with explosive results that seem, in Esther Jun's production, both baffling and half-hearted. Once again, the best thing is the set: a cluttered, slummy mess of a room, designed by Akiva Romer-Segal.

Every Letter Counts runs through Feb. 24 at the Factory Theatre; Cowboy Mouth runs through Feb. 14 at Cameron House.

Factory Theatre / Writer-star Nina Lee Aquino's monotonous performance in Every Letter Counts makes the play difficult to follow.; Caption:
2013-02-14-the-perfect-villain-shakespea:
When Shakespeare wrote Richard III he accomplished something that was unprecedented, and something else that has remained unique. It was one of his earliest plays and, if not the first star vehicle in the English theatre, still the first to have attracted all the generations of subsequent actors. It is also the only viable play, ever, to have a recent historical monster at its centre. I don't know of any others that have done that, or even attempted it. If there are any successful plays with Hitler or Stalin as their protagonist, I haven't come across them.

Now of course there has long been debate as to whether the historical Richard was a monster, and it's been given new life by the discovery of his bones under the extremely unconsecrated ground of a Leicestershire parking lot. In at least one respect, the revisionists have now been vindicated. Richard, it appears, had a crooked spine, but was by no means the grotesque hunchback, born with a full set of teeth and a withered arm, so colourfully depicted by Shakespeare and the Tudor historians who were his sources. They wanted to make Richard look bad, and they took their assignment very literally.

Their motive, as has been often pointed out, was to make their own monarchs look good. Henry VII, first of the Tudors and grandfather of Shakespeare's own Queen Elizabeth, had come to the throne by defeating Richard in battle; his genealogical claim to the throne was tenuous, and he was no oil painting himself if actual paintings of him are to be trusted, but he could claim the moral high ground of having rescued England from the 30-year carnage of the Wars of the Roses, and that ground would be even higher if the king he had displaced were shown to be the devil's deputy on Earth. Henry's historians got right on it, the most eloquent of them being no less sanctified a figure than Sir Thomas More. One of the pleasures of Hilary Mantel's Wolf Hall novels has been seeing More taken down a few pegs from his position as the perfect Man for All Seasons. Mantel reminds us that this Catholic martyr had, in his day, been an enthusiastic prosecutor and persecutor of Protestant heretics. His book on Richard III shows him also to have been a disconcertingly brilliant purveyor of Tudor propaganda. Maybe it's to his credit that he never actually finished it.

The claims of Richard's detractors and of his defenders don't altogether cancel one another out; it's perfectly possible that Richard was a capable and even merciful governor of the north of England during the reign of his elder brother Edward IV and that, down south, he intrigued and murdered his way into being Edward's successor. It was a bloody period, where fighting at court could be as vicious if not as direct as on the battlefield. My own sympathies are with the pro-Richard party. I doubt, at the least, that he was much worse than his contemporaries, though I confess that, much as I would like to pin the murder of the Princes in the Tower on Henry VII, I fear the evidence points to Richard. I do believe that Shakespeare's immensely influential portrait of Richard traduces him. I still wouldn't wish it any different. (I admit to being tickled by the fact that the Canadian gentleman, "a 17th great-grand-nephew of Richard's older sister," whose DNA has been a crucial factor in identifying Richard's body, is a Mr. Ibsen. The namesake of a great dead playwright may have helped salvage a reputation that an even greater European playwright has lastingly savaged.)

It's a shame that Shakespeare can never have heard the word chutzpah, because his Richard embodies it. He does so, most famously, when the wins the love of his future wife, whose husband and father-in-law he had killed, right beside the coffin of the latter; this despite being, in his own words just one scene earlier, so ugly "that dogs bark at me as I halt by them." That's one of his rare moments of self-pity; more typical is his later description of himself, when off to seduce another princess: "To her go I, a jolly, thriving wooer." That, in its perfect mix of self-confidence and self-deprecation, is one of his very best lines.

Shakespeare wasn't short on chutzpah himself. He credits Richard with one murder - that of his other brother the Duke of Clarence - that even the historians hadn't thought of. (Clarence was popularly said to have been drowned in a butt of Malmsey wine. This seems merely to have been colourful slang for his having died drunk.) At the other extreme hedescribes the Princes in the Tower as the most beautiful babes that ever were born, here anticipating the style of modern tabloids (and not just of tabloids) who write as if the killing of children were not horrific enough in itself but must be bolstered with fulsome adjectives. The pouring-on of pathos when Richard is offstage, together with his gusto in villainy when he's on, have led Harold Bloom, writing recently in Newsweek, to suggest that Shakespeare was writing deliberate parody. Professor Bloom has an enviable confidence about what was going on in Shakespeare's mind, together with a less endearing habit of treating his own theories as if they were established facts, but I can only say that neither Richard nor the blood-soaked tragedy Titus Andronicus (another Bloom theory) feel like parody to me. I think Shakespeare meant them.

He might not have meant them at a later stage in his career, and even here he had to work his way up to it. Before Richard III come the three parts of Henry VI, which depict the Wars of the Roses in grisly detail. Richard appears about halfway through. At first he's just one bloodthirsty aristocrat among many, though wittier than most; gradually you feel him working his way, through that wit, to the forefront of Shakespeare's imagination. When all the plays are done in sequence he seems less a prodigy of evil, more the ultimate product of an age - which would also have made for good Tudor propaganda. In or out of order, Shakespeare never shortchanges Richard; he may end by offering his kingdom for a horse, but he doesn't do it so he can escape. He does it so he can continue to fight. And part of us - a large part - cheers him on. We know, morally, that he ought to lose. We just don't want him to.

It's the kind of ambivalence that drama thrives on, right down to The Wire. Or to The Sopranos, or Boardwalk Empire, or even Mad Men. Even more directly in the Richard line

is the British TV series of the 1990s, House of Cards, currently being aired in a new and inferior American adaptation. (I speak from prejudice. I haven't seen the U.S. version. But I bet I'm right.) Francis Urquhart, the English politician killing and blackmailing his way to the Premiership, is the Richard III of parliamentary politics, with his bland catchphrase - "you might very well think that; I couldn't possibly comment" - the latter-day equivalent of Richard's pious appeals to Holy Scripture. And both the British Urquhart, the late great Ian Richardson, and Kevin Spacey, his American successor, came to the role after playing Richard.

The significant difference is that Francis Urquhart (FU for short) is a fictional character. So are most of those other TV anti-heroes. Shakespeare himself never tried to do a Richard III again. True, there's Macbeth, who also murders his way to the throne; he was a historical figure. But he was a faraway and shadowy one, and though the play takes us, disturbingly, deep inside his head, it never asks us to enjoy, if only because he never gets to enjoy himself. And as I've said, modern monsters have gone undramatized.

Well, maybe that's not completely true: Bertolt Brecht wrote a Hitler play, The Resistible Rise of Arturo Ui, but it's a cartoon in which the Fuhrer is caricatured as a Chicago gangster who learns his oratorical skills from an old Shakespearean actor; he's Hitler and Al Capone and Richard III rolled into one. Last year in London there was Collaborators, which cut Stalin down to size by having him share the limelight with one of his victims, the writer Mikhail Bulgakov, and making him in effect a figure in Bulgakov's nightmares; that too was a cartoon. Portraying these men seriously on a stage may well be impossible; their crimes were too vast and too recent, their victims too numerous.

And Stalin died in his bed, which isn't satisfying, dramatically or otherwise. (There's no great play about Napoleon either.) Richard was a petty malefactor by comparison, his misdeeds affecting only his own country. With a world-class criminal, where do you start? Who, so to speak, owns the rights? The Elizabethans could both own and disown Richard. He was recent history, but a history they could tell themselves had been exorcised. We don't have that luxury. But, for as long as the play lasts, we're the beneficiaries of theirs.
2013-02-21-the-bard-reworked-soulpepper-:
'Who would have thought we were so important?" Rosencrantz asks Guildenstern towards the end of Tom Stoppard's theatrical memorial to the two of them. Or maybe Guildenstern asks Rosencrantz; one of Stoppard's running gags is that nobody, including themselves, is ever sure which of them is which. Whoever poses it, it's a pregnant question through which all the play's levels get levelled. It reflects on the two guys' literary status as minor characters in Hamlet; on their social status as functionaries or hangers-on at the Danish court; and on their status as human beings, condemned from birth to an end that, being universal, is statistically insignificant. "They really had it in for us, didn't they?" says one of them, and "they" could be Hamlet, Shakespeare or fate.

The title Rosencrantz and Guildenstern Are Dead is a direct quote from the last moments both of Shakespeare's tragedy and Stoppard's comedy, the words dispassionately delivered in both contexts by an English ambassador. Stoppard's signal achievement is that in the 45 years since his play appeared, it's become impossible for us to hear them dispassionately. We want to protest, say that they didn't deserve to die, that it isn't fair.

Stoppard shows us Hamlet's two university buddies on the road to Elsinore, ignorant of why they've been summoned, and wondering and worrying about it; then, at court, doing their ineffectual best to probe the cause of Hamlet's lunacy; and finally, escorting him to England for what is supposed to be his execution and turns out to be theirs. When they are, so to speak, off the Shakespearean stage, they talk in scintillating Stoppardian prose, mixing high philosophy and low verbal farce, a cross-talk of which they're both the executants and the victims; but every so often they fall subserviently into pre-determined blank verse as characters from the larger play sweep in on them and, even more disconcertingly, sweep out again.

In Shakespeare's play the duo really are indistinguishable; they are never on their own and, since they never get to say a word to one another, they have no relationship. Stoppard obviously had to change that; his characters share a predicament, and they both feel oppressed by it, but Rosencrantz is both the more innocent and the more transparently woebegone, while Guildenstern takes refuge in displays of intellectual superiority, like a Samuel Beckett tramp who may actually have seen Waiting for Godot. In Soulpepper's revival, Rosencrantz is wonderfully played by Ted Dysktra, a towheaded embodiment of existential dread, filled with boyish eagerness and boyish despair, and with almost unfaultable comic timing. Jordan Pettle, his opposite number, doesn't have the same verbal punch and precision, which means that some of the philosophic crosstalk threatens to outstay its welcome. But he comes into his own, as does Joseph Ziegler's whole production, in the last movement, where all the talk of death becomes more than talk; becomes indeed rather moving. It's the first time I've known this play ripen rather than fade as it progresses.

At every stage of their journey R&G, as they tell us in Hamlet, meet the Players, whose specialty is death and who are there to point out the difference between make-believe mortality and the real thing, each having its theoretical advantages; Kenneth Welsh, as First Player, brings a leathery down-at-heel authority to a role often played as farouche trickster. Visually the production is very impressive, from the pyrotechnic coin-tossing of the opening to the pirate attack of the last act.

This has been a week for Shakespearean knock-offs. It would have been even more of one if WorldStage's Othello, C'est Qui hadn't been cancelled, but we have more Moor at Stratford later in the year and, right now, in Joseph Jomo Pierre's Shakespeare's Nigga, a co-production of Obsdian and Theatre Passe Muraille. This gives us the poet himself looking back on his career, in high dissatisfaction. He dreams of having two black slaves, with the same names as the two leading black characters in his own plays, Othello and Aaron, the gleeful villain of Titus Andronicus. At least, a synopsis included in the press kit (maybe as last-minute insurance) says that he's dreaming; it's not at all clear in the production. Othello is, in the play's appropriation of Deep South parlance, the house nigga, entrusted with a whip; Aaron is the field one, on whom he uses it, and who spends most of the play chained-up and snarling. Othello nurses a love for Shakespeare's daughter Judith; Aaron actually has her. Both these passions, for different reasons and in different measures, displease Shakespeare, bringing in more potent echoes of the Prospero-Miranda-Caliban-Ferdinand dynamic in The Tempest than of anything in the other plays.

Obviously this isn't intended as a serious contribution to Shakespeare biography; he's there as a symbol of European culture and of what it's done to the disenfranchised. To that extent the play resembles Edward Bond's Bingo, but that has a real action, grounded in real documents. Pierre complains, in both play and publicity, that Shakespeare failed to give Aaron (whom he plays himself, beneath his previous good form as both actor and playwright) a voice: an odd accusation, given that he has the second longest role in Titus, and much the liveliest; if he isn't a fully fleshed character, then neither is anyone else in that play. And it's absurd to claim that Titus, a totally neglected piece until the last 60 or so years, has influenced how anybody sees anything. Othello probably has but, aside from a few moments that may reflect obliquely on the protagonist's relations with his wife and father-in-law, this play does nothing with them. Pierre's Othello and Aaron have nothing in common with Shakespeare's but their names and their colour. Anything goes, which means that nothing does.

2013-02-22-rising-to-the-occasion-with-d:
I'm very fond of a remark by the British playwright Howard Brenton, who said that there are only two kinds of play: plays set in rooms and plays not set in rooms. The implication was that there is domestic drama and there's epic drama and that, in the modern theatre, there's been more of the former than the latter.

The same holds true, with some variation, for movies, though of course a film, even on an intimate subject, is likelier than a play to go outdoors because it's easier to do. If it aspires to epic, then it's going to spend most of its time outside, with "outside" usually being a battlefield, or at least a riot-torn street.

That's one of the things that makes Steven Spielberg's Lincoln such a remarkable movie. It is an epic, but it's set in rooms.

Not entirely: It starts on the battlefield, with a brief, grim, muddy scene of hand-to-hand conflict, that gives a better idea of what fighting in the American Civil War (or any war of that period or earlier) must actually have been like than any other film I recall. The background is established; we don't get back there until the war has ended, and the film nearly has, when we're taken on a tour of artistically-posed corpses, that's one of the picture's falser notes. Between times, we've mainly been in the White House or in that grimier house known as Congress. We've been watching politics. Which means wheeling and dealing, depicted with notable relish and in notable detail. It's what gets left out of most ostensibly political films, whether historical or current.

Most of all, we're watching a head of state with a limited time-frame in which to achieve his aims. Like, say, a U.S. President at the start of his second term.

Lincoln may have temporised previously about emancipation, but the film doesn't mention it; we must assume either that he didn't mean it or that he changed his mind. The man we see is positive about his aims, convinced they're just, and unblushing about resorting to bribery, or equivocating about Confederate peace overtures, in order to achieve them. He seems, indeed, rather to enjoy it. But that's politics. And it's in an overwhelmingly good cause.

Of course, all political issues are ultimately moral ones, but some - environmental protection, gun control, abortion - are more obviously so than others. Slavery seems the most cut-and-dried of all, the least open to debate. The film reminds us, pointedly, that it wasn't always.

The characters talk; sometimes, especially when the house is in session, they shout, both excitedly and excitingly, but most of the time it's conversation, often conducted in poised, even witty sentences. This has obviously disappointed some people; the most common criticism of the film has been that it's "talky" (with the unspoken addition "don't they know there's a war on?"; they do, that's why they're talking).

As it happens, this Shavian kind of writing is a departure for its author, Tony Kushner, who is best-known for plays, chiefly Angels in America, that are certainly very verbal, but aren't naturalistically grounded in this way; I'd call them epic-fantastic.

It's audacious - anti-Hollywood really - for a film whose title suggests a full-dress biography to confine itself to just a few weeks of its protagonist's life. We see Lincoln, with the end of the war in plain sight, determined to push through the Thirteenth Amendment so that the outlawing of slavery will be a done deal before peace is declared. Basically, the picture is about him securing the required number of votes, and it's a nail-biting process, even though we already know the outcome. (It's like an action movie keeping us on the edge of our seats, despite our knowing from experience that the hero will triumph. Funny how often that happens.)

There are all sorts of amusing contemporary echoes; we see interested parties, keeping in touch by telegraph, tallying the score, doing everything but tweet their friends about it; just as earlier we've watched Lincoln himself hesitating over the wording of a wire like a man at a keyboard agonizing over whether to press send.

Lincoln, of course, was filmed during President Obama's first term - and conceived, we know, before then - but it's been prescient in its timing. It gives us the perpetual American drama of a bill, passed in one house, needing to be taken through another. It allows us to compare the partisan vituperation of their age with ours: probably about equal as far as media are concerned (their papers and pamphlets, our internet) though it seems that on the actual floor our representatives are a trifle more decorous than theirs were.

At least, it's hard to imagine one of our politicians publicly insulting an opponent in the terms that Tommy Lee Jones' foaming abolitionist Thaddeus Stevens applies to the aptly named congressman (Fernando) Wood: "Even a reptile like you, sir" he says, neatly turning the man's white supremacist arguments against him " deserves to be held equal before the law." Great satisfaction in the house: We'd been longing for him to make precisely that argument.

Stevens is actually reining himself in; he'd like to say more, but has been entreated not to alienate the undecided. Lincoln, like Obama, is under as much pressure from his left as from his right. (Watching this film, you have of course to keep performing mental and historical gymnastics, regarding Democrats and Republicans.) In fact, Stevens is the character in the movie undergoing the most moral conflict. Lincoln doesn't seem to have any.

One of the most revealing scenes shows Lincoln, after his victory, admitting to his black housekeeper that he doesn't know what comes next for her people: the film's tacit acknowledgment of how much further there was to go, and maybe another Obama connection: politicians who can do nuance. Not to mention those who, as Ulysses S. Grant says to Lincoln, graphically age on the job.

That housekeeper is otherwise an idealised figure, and the criticism that the film's black characters are tokens is probably justified. The movie might have been truer to itself, and made a subtler statement, if it had done without black characters altogether; but it probably couldn't have got away with it. Similarly, its creators would probably have preferred not to include Lincoln's assassination; but they must have felt they couldn't leave it out, and their supposedly clever way of showing it amounts to a cheap trick.

The soothsayers say that Lincoln probably won't win the Oscar for Best Picture: this despite having the traditionally victorious quality of making our pulses race in a righteous cause. Nobody doubts that Daniel Day-Lewis will win for Best Actor, and so he should; he presents a man who is believably great, and good, and human. Not to mention humorous, and shy, and tall.

I haven't always been a Day-Lewis fan, though we do have one thing in common: We both, on successive nights, walked out of his performance as Hamlet. He had a breakdown while playing it, in London in 1989, and left the stage half-way through, never to return. The previous evening, I'd left at intermission as his performance, for reasons I couldn't then know, was communicating nothing.

In his film career since, I've sometimes felt that I was watching his legendarily arduous preparation for a role, rather than the character. But his Lincoln goes beyond impersonation based on books; it's a full, autonomous creation. And so for the whole movie; like Schindler's List it shows Spielberg as the best kind of populist: someone who, even with lapses and compromises, can dramatise huge, hideous events without cheapening them. The film summons history; it also illuminates the way we live now.
