2013-04-20-about-the-law-race-is-mamet-i:
Nigel Shawn Williams, playing a lawyer in David Mamet's play Race, gives a tornado of a performance. The storm he raises reaches its highest level of force and velocity when, propelled by rage and frustration, he charges across his office, encountering a row of swivel chairs on his way, giving each of them a vicious shove as he passes, and setting them all spinning. It's a terrific image, electric in itself and a vital building-block in a relentlessly exciting evening.

Williams plays Henry, who is black; he shares the office and the firm with Jack, who's white, and with their junior, Susan, black. To them comes Charles, a rich young white man, accused of raping a young black woman in a hotel room. He claims innocence; says there was sex but it was consensual. The lawyers' initial response to that might be paraphrased as, "Sure. You would say that, wouldn't you?"

Henry has the first speech of the play: a summary of all the derogatory or patronizing things that white Americans might think about black Americans. Williams delivers it as a suave series of hammer-blows. "O.J. was guilty. Rodney King was in the wrong place, but the police have the right to use force ... Malcolm X was noble when he renounced violence. Prior to that he was misguided. Dr. King was of course a saint ... and you had a maid when you were young who was better to you than your mother." Charles protests that he would never say such things. Henry says of course he wouldn't; he wouldn't dare. He himself, being black, can, if only to make a rhetorical point. It's even possible that he believes them.

Charles says it isn't fair. Jack, speaking for the first time, says "It is neither fair nor unfair. None of us is immune. From a false accusation." He adds that if they take the case they will believe in his innocence, because it's their job. The play may have the wrong title. What it has to say about race is pungent and provocative, but it never really advances on that first speech. But if you go for portentous one-word titles then a better one here - Justice having been taken a century ago by John Galsworthy - might be Law. Jack and Henry delight in telling Charles how much his case, or any other, depends on performance, spectacle, manipulating the prejudices of the jury. "The law" says Jack "is an alley fight." He adds that "neither side wants the truth," or even knows what it is. "Each wants to prevail." None of this may be news either, but it's exhilarating to hear it expressed so nakedly and pursued so inventively. At the punchy, punch-line level - though not necessarily at all others - Mamet is writing as well as ever. And he follows it through, in words and action. Charles is cautioned against making any kind of confession to the press; they and the public would crucify him. There was a time when his class and colour might work in his favour; that time isn't now. Ken Burns' documentary on the Central Park Five, shown this week on PBS, reminded us just how recent that past time was. Both his film and Mamet's play perform a useful public service in reminding how far we've lost the meaning of the word "alleged".

Intertwined with race and law, especially race, there is of course a third issue, gender. Susan, though present, says nothing in the first scene, which is its own statement. The firm, for reasons you should discover for yourselves, takes the case; for a time, it even thinks it has one. Further developments are largely due to Susan, who is Jack's protegee, much resented by Henry who describes her as his white colleague's "science project." Henry volubly despises affirmative action, though it's perfectly possible that he's been the beneficiary of it: Susan sees him as an updated Uncle Tom. (Everybody, in or out of the courtroom, thinks they're innocent. We're all the heroes or heroines of our own melodrama.) There's a strong resemblance to Mamet's Speed-the-Plow in which the dreams of a couple of Hollywood shysters get derailed by a female with her own agenda. That was a slighter play, because it wasn't about much. Who doesn't know that Hollywood is a nest of bottom-feeders? And who in hell cares? (Mamet would put that more forcefully.) Race, by contrast, is about things that concern all of us. That, combined with its skill and drive, keep us on the edge of our seats. The only other current dramatist who can so consistently do that is Martin McDonagh. That he and Mamet may be our most misanthropic playwrights is probably no coincidence.

Mamet's two best plays, American Buffalo and Glengarry Glen Ross, have all-male casts, and he's often accused of not being able to write for women. Oleanna, whatever people say, proved the opposite; the trouble in Race is not that he hasn't written a good role for Susan - she has an interesting trajectory - but that he hasn't written her good lines. Cara Ricketts has to work hard to justify her character's actions, in both the verbal and the psychological sense. Matthew Edison, cast radically against previously unassuming type, shows as Charles that he can get powerfully angry. Jack is Jason Priestley, the production's presumed selling point, and also its weakest link; he hasn't been on stage in 13 years and it shows, in his limited range of both inflection and gesture. He doesn't actually distort the play but he lessens its moment-by-moment impact. Williams picks up most of the slack, though even he has his weak moments (about 5%, I'd say.) Mamet, we're told, sternly forbids any tampering with his stage-directions, but he doesn't seem to object to them being added to, and Williams' business with the chairs, which isn't in the script, is an inspired invention of the actor, or his director Daniel Brooks, whose production is a triumph of tautness, or both. It isn't a great play; you don't believe, as you did in Buffalo and Glengarry, that the characters have off-stage lives. But it's a searching and unsettling one, and its grip never slackens.

Race runs through May 5 at the Bluma Appel Theatre 416-368-3110

2013-04-27-water-logged-the-2004-boxing-:
David Yee's Carried Away on the Crest of a Wave is a talented piece of work - but it nonetheless comes close to drowning in its own ambition. Appropriately, it unfolds on a waterlogged stage.

The water is impressive and also vital since, though the title might suggest an ancient musical comedy, it actually refers to the Asian tsunami of Boxing Day, 2004. The play is a series of vignettes, designed to show the aftershocks of that catastrophe, across huge expanses of time and space. Some scenes take place as physically far from the epicentre as Toronto and Salt Lake City; some are as temporally far as, well, now. I think, though I'm not sure, that the events depicted are shown to us in chronological order. Each one presents us with an entirely different set of characters. The moral, emblazoned on the back page of the program and expanded in a long speech in the last scene, is that "we are all connected, and we are, none of us, alone."

It's no criticism to say that we've heard that before: from John Donne in one of the world's great one-liners; from Stephen Sondheim and James Lapine in a key song from Into the Woods and, more importantly, in that show's whole structure. It lived its meaning by taking four disparate stories and tying them inextricably together. Yee's episodic approach means he has to provide a separate coincidence - a shocking revelation, a long-delayed reunion - in each scene. The tsunami and its aftermath must of course have been full of such things; Yee's play isn't a documentary, but he's based it on interviews with survivors, whose stories he has freely - sometimes, by his own account, very freely - adapted. Some of them carry dramatic conviction; some don't, but there's no cumulative effect. It makes, inevitably, an uneven evening.

There are a few gestures towards continuity. Figures whom we think we may recognize from earlier scenes can sometimes be glimpsed gesticulating from behind a scrim. It may signify something that two separate characters are called Thomas; or that another makes a not-too-convincing reference to Samuel Beckett, while Beckett is the name of the character who delivers the play's opening monologue, a speech about imperceptible but devastating shifts in the Earth's balance that introduces us to the suggestive notion of "leap-seconds." The concluding scene introduces to another scientist, a meteorologist consumed with guilt at not having delivered an early warning. So that may close a circle. There are also two contrasting and consecutive scenes, one on either side of the intermission, featuring a prostitute and a client.

The set is a pool, with curtains behind it and a deck in front. Designed by Camellia Koo and lit by Michelle Ramsay, it's suggestive and efficient. Only one scene is actually set in a flood; physically, it's the highlight of Nina Lee Aquino's production. We see two brothers, designated the Swimmer and the Runner, perched on the roof of a doll's house, jettisoning their family possessions in an attempt to stay afloat; when this seems fruitless, Swimmer sets off to readjust the Earth's position to its proper place on the back of a turtle. We then switch to a different brand of religious belief. A Catholic priest is informed by an architect, who happens to be Muslim, that there's no scientific evidence that he and his flock were spared by having hung garlands on their statue of the Madonna; the Father is resistant, at least initially, to the suggestion that their survival is wonderful enough, and that he should thank Heaven for small miracles.

That's one of the play's best scenes. Another shows a Canadian DJ resolved to play his own song about the disaster, deemed by the higher-ups to be in bad taste, barricading his studio door, perhaps as if trying to hold back a tsunami. This segment is a bit over-stretched, but it's full of good lines. Indeed Yee writes many of them; perhaps the best is the suggestion in the second of the brothel scenes that a prostitute would regard the idea of love as unfair competition. That's another of the good scenes. Its predecessor, though not without tension, is one of the least believable, with a confusing shock-ending, feebly staged (though an apparent missed lighting-cue on the first night may have been partly to blame.)

An overall failing in Aquino's production is that it ain't got rhythm. The actors are too often left to flounder. Some can take care of themselves; Richard Zeppieri, who gives a trio of strong and very varied performances as intrusive North Americans, certainly can. So, most of the time, can Kawa Ada, especially as the imperturbably reasonable architect. Mayko Nguyen, the one woman in the cast, is fine when required to be cool and impassive, as when playing Second Sex Worker. But she flounders and gabbles as the Beckett-quoting Utah housewife, who gets an accusing visit from an FBI man (Richard Lee, unhelpfully stolid) with a literary background of his own. Whatever plane of reality this encounter is supposed to be occupying, the acting and direction fail to establish it; there's no pacing, no light, no shade. Unfortunate, because the basic situation, though strange, is not implausible. There's similarly no reason for Ash Knight to deliver the last big speech so over-emphatically that one loses the will to listen.

But there's delicacy on hand as well. Nguyen may be the only grown woman in the cast, but there is also a little girl, Eponine Lee, whose bio lists under upcoming engagements "being a first grader this coming September." She plays an orphan rescued by a gruff but compassionate man (John Ng, excellent) who knows from experience what it's like to be an orphan. There's a bond of sorts between them, however tenuous and temporary. And it's firmer on her part. Her every look and gesture, completely unstrained, communicate less fussily and more effectively than the verbalized efforts of some of her elders. At the end of the scene her uncle, as previously arranged, comes to collect her and doesn't even say thank you. This doesn't seem likely. It would also seem to undercut the theme of solidarity. But then that theme never establishes itself, and the play's own qualities undercut it. It's a special variety of curate's egg: good in unconnected parts.

Carried Away on the Crest of a Wave runs through May 26 at the Tarragon Theatre, 416-531-1827

THEATRE REVIEW

THE BOOK OF MORMON

Princess of Wales Theatre, Toronto

The best thing about The Book of Mormon is that it all comes right in the end. Or nearly. I'm not talking about plot; this is a hugely successful Broadway musical so obviously it has a happy ending. I'm talking about comic tone.

The Book of Mormon, as if you didn't know, was written by Trey Parker and Matt Stone (from South Park) and Robert Lopez (from Avenue Q, which I think of as a tidier section of the same neighbourhood), and concerns two eager young Salt Lake Citizens, just graduated from missionary college and sent out together on their qualifying two-year mission. ( "God loves Mormons And he wants some more.") There's elder Kevin Price, the star of his year and the straightest and most self-satisfied of arrows, and elder Arnold Cunningham, a plump well-meaning misfit with a weakness for, as he himself says, "making things up." elder Cunningham doesn't mind where they're sent; he's just tickled pink at the thought of going there with elder Price. elder Price was hoping -- as he tells us many, many times -- for a posting to Orlando, Fla., where he once spent a dream vacation. Instead, they find themselves in an especially squalid village in a remote part of uganda, plagued by AIDS and other diseases and threatened by a neighbouring warlord intent on performing mass clitorectomies.

Hard as it may be to believe, most of this played for laughs; even more incredibly, some of the laughs are forthcoming. The young elders win the villagers' confidence but are in danger of losing it; the tribal chieftain's brave and beautiful daughter, who had taken their teachings very literally, is especially disillusioned. Then one of her friends says something so sensible and so heartening and so hilariously surprising that the whole audience dissolves. We're about 20 minutes from the final curtain, and we ride there on a wave of goodwill, right up to the closing number, which is a reprise with variations of the opening number, which was the best number in the show anyway.

What goes between is mostly fun but underwhelming, never quite sure of its ground and trying desperately hard to pretend otherwise. This surprised me since I had detected no such insecurity in New york where I greatly enjoyed the show, far more in fact that I had expected to. (I'd entered determined to resist the hype: a kind of double bluff.) In this touring production it seems muffled: literally so, as whenever more than one person is singing, the sound system makes it impossible to understand the words. It isn't the fault of the performers, nearly all of whom are at least as good as their Broadway counterparts. Christopher John O'Neill's shambling Arnold is actually better since he seems from the start like a human being rather than a collection of nervous tics. Mark evans is equally good as his chin-jutting, strong-singing friend, the one who, in a reversal of expected convention gets humiliated (quite graphically, at one point). At least, it would be a reversal if the show were not so obviously a spoof in an age of spoofs. It's like a Hope and zzCrosby Road movie with Bob re-cast as the one who gets dorothy Lamour, who in this case is the delectable Samantha Marie Ware. They share a song that begins "I'm about to do it for the first time And I'm going to do it with a girl." It's about baptism.

The relationship of the two young Mormons, which includes some quite bitter soul-searching on the part of elder Price, is the strongest element in the show. They're backed by an entertainingly campy group of slightly older elders, who do a high-kicking routine about resisting temptation; like most of the songs it has only one idea, but it's one that Casey Nicholaw's choreography pursues with inventive vivacity. The show also pays tribute to, or borrows from, or just bears an uncanny resemblance to such earlier musicals as Guys and Dolls (the mission that will be closed down if it can't save a few souls) and The King and I (the natives who act out their own interpretation of a Western story and shock the authorities by doing so). There's also some broad parody of the Mormons' own founding fables. The show, though, isn't really a satire on Mormonism. It ends up an agnostics' celebration of faith: an assertion that there are things to be done in the world, and they can be done in the name of God, even if you're not sure that he exists. Its own great saving grace is that -- as opposed to such earnestly mushy entertainments as Wicked or Billy Elliot -- it's about something.

The trouble, at least on a second viewing, is that half the subject, the African half, has gone missing. The show has good fun with the patronizing white folks ( I Am Africa) and it gives the villagers their own cynical anthem (title untranslatable in a family newspaper). And there's that great debunking moment at the end. But it's still hard to see how, in converting them, these latter-day Latter day Saints have actually solved any of their problems. Things such as AIdS can't be laughed or sung out of existence; while, especially in the light of recent headlines, things like raping babies just can't be laughed at, though the show tries to pretend they can. But black humour (no racial reference intended) needs to have some depth; it can't just be a matter of blithely mentioning the unmentionable.

If the book is scattershot, the score is slapdash (the three authors take no separate credits for the various elements). The tunes are nothing much; the lyrics have their share of funny lines, but they rarely build and some of the rhymes are slipshod. On the occasions when even the basic joke doesn't work, no amount of production can flog it into life; a number set in Hell is truly infernal. Some local specifics: Kevin Mambo is excellent as the village headman; the sadistic warlord carries no threat whatever (he did in New york), which seriously impacts the overall impact. (It's not as if there's any shortage of real-life models.) There's a running gag about Arnold's mispronouncing his beloved's name, which I confess I fell for nearly every time. There's also a thread about Africa's being nothing like The Lion King, which pays off explosively well near the start but frays later. It does connect, though, with Arnold's creative substitution of themes from pop culture for the scriptures he's supposed to have studied. Who, he and the show implicitly inquire, needs Mormon when you have Mordor? I tend to agree. But then I'm the guy who liked the musical Lord of the Rings.

THEATRE REVIEW

Falsettos

Daniels Spectrum, Toronto

After Robert McQueen's superb productions of Light in the Piazza and Caroline, or Change we now have -for the same company, Acting up Stage - his equally fine version of a slightly older American musical, William Finn's Falsettos.

I call it a "version" because Falsettos has a complicated history. In 1981 there was March of the Falsettos, a musical comedy of manners concerning a Jewish New Yorker called Marvin, his wife, his son, his male lover, and a psychiatrist. In 1990 there was Falsettoland, a darker piece, in which the son prepares for his bar mitzvah and the lover dies of AIDS. In 1992 there was Falsettos, which consisted of revised versions of the two earlier musicals. The new Toronto Falsettos presents the same two shows, but goes back to their original texts. I did see the '92 production in New York but at this remove I can't identify specific differences, all I can say is that this staging seems a) a bit long and b) a lot better.

Patrick du Wors has designed a dual set for this dual show. Part One takes place on a bare, black-draped rectangle, Part Two on a white disc, clinically matched to the hospital setting in which the story reaches its climax. McQueen's other principal collaborators are carried over from his production of Caroline: Reza Jacobs provides impeccably sharp musical direction; Kimberly Purtell supplies beautifully concentrated lighting (how refreshing to see a show in which the actors aren't underlit); and Tim French contributes tight, witty and occasionally uproarious choreography. French's work is an especially vital component of the production's overwhelming virtue, its lucidity. Which in this piece, or these pieces, is a remarkable virtue to have.

Finn's ambition in the Falsetto shows - to musicalize complex relationships - is admirable. his realization of it is patchy. Officially Falsettos has a book (credited to Finn and his original director James Lapine); in reality, it's virtually through-composed. So all the work of story and characterization has to be done by the score, and especially by the lyrics. Finn's words, though, are often vague and fuzzy. Sometimes he uses rhyme as it should be used, to make or drive home a point; other times, he seems to be using it because it's expected of him; he rarely makes it sound effortless. "My father's a homo," sings Marvin's son Jason, "my mother's not thrilled." But then he's off, laboriously pairing "homo" with "chromo(somes)," while the music chugs off in pursuit, turning into formless recitative.

March of the Falsettos has two title songs. At one time the show was to be called Four Jews in a Room Bitching, and it starts with a song of that name, sung by the males in the cast; Trina, the wife, later joins in, upping it to Five Jews. (I should say at this point that Falsettos is presented "in association with" the Harold Green Jewish Theatre Company, and that it's their most distinguished association to date.) "Bitch, bitch, bitch" they sing "funny, funny, funny," which is a great abstract set-up, set to a pulsating tune, but one that the song never develops or particularizes. Nor does it herald the action that follows as accurately as it thinks it does. The official title tune March of the Falsettos, also by the four men is, especially as done here, a delight, very catchy and offbeat, but, again, what does it really mean?

It can't just be about being gay, because two of the characters are straight. It's set off, as is made unusually clear in this production, by Trina's complaint that there aren't any real men in her life. But the tone might be either abashed or triumphant with the words, apparently assembled on a free-association basis, giving no clue. The second half of the evening welcomes us to Falsettoland, which is even less defined. The cast is expanded to include "the lesbians next door," a doctor and a caterer. Both might be described as neurotic, but then who might not? On this showing, Falsettoland is a very inclusive locale - chances are, you don't even have to be Jewish - whose main function is to provide a bitter-sweet punchline.

A major reason that it's ill-defined as a collective is that its inhabitants are shadowy as individuals. There are actually three Marvin musicals (there was a prequel called In Trousers) so it's amazing how little we learn about him. We do gather that he has money, but there's no clue as to how he's earned it. We also find that he's a double-standard jerk who, after setting up house with another man, objects to his wife doing the same. he also strikes her, making him, at least for a moment, an ex-wife beater. Whizzer, his lover, is even more of a cipher; all we discover about their relationship is that Whizzer sucks at chess (Act One) and Marvin at squash (Act Two).

It's hard to get invested in them. But this matters less in the first piece, which is mainly comedic, and is buoyed up by McQueen's unyielding insistence on having each number flow logically out of what has preceded it and on having each character sing as if he or she were communicating something specific to someone specific.

It's also carried by two supercharged performances. Michael Levinson, the amazing young boy in Caroline, is equally phenomenal as Jason, puzzled and enquiring, taking refuge - at least until puberty strikes at the first act curtain - in his father's favourite board game. (Fair's fair: Falsettos is a much better musical about chess than Chess.) Darrin Baker is a tonic as Mendel the psychiatrist who, with a royal disregard for customary ethics, progresses from treating Marvin to treating and eventually marrying Trina to treating Jason; he even makes house calls. he's professionally and lasciviously anxious, shortish and balding, mole-like but expansive: imagine George Costanza as a shrink.

Stephen Patterson and Eric Morin do everything possible for Marvin and Whizzer, and Glynis Ranney, vocally more pungent than plangent, comes strongly through as Trina; her opening moment, exasperatedly pushing a vacuum-cleaner across the stage, gets the show off to the best possible start. Sara-Jeanne Hosie and Sarah Gibbons are fine as the second act cavalry, though McQueen's only misstep is not allowing Hosie, as the doctor, enough time and space for her ominous announcement that "something bad is happening," the first darkening mention of AIDS. It presages Whizzer's sickness and eventual death.

When the show was first done, he might have been moving just as a statistic; now, we need to know more about him and Marvin as people. Since we don't, the Falsettoland half of the proceedings seems drawn-out and sentimental. In the 10 years between the two original shows Finn's lyrics and music actually grew more skilful and sophisticated, but they don't have as much to be sophisticated about. The best numbers are, again, the comedy ones: the latest in the American musical's long line of baseball ensembles ("we're here to watch Jewish boys who can't play baseball/play baseball") and a bouncing, as in on the furniture, duet for Mendel and Jason entitled Everyone Hates His Parents. Jason, we notice throughout, finds it easier to confide in his parents' lovers than in his parents, which is a point worth pondering.

The staging of his bar mitzvah (what, no rabbi?) finally unites the two main strands of action in a manner that's become legendary but had better remain unspecified, just in case. Anyway, it's a great production, and most people don't seem to share my reservations about the piece itself, so you should go.

Falsettos runs through May 12. For tickets and information, call 1-800-838-3006 or visit actingupstage.com.

In 1998 in London, the royal Family in attendance, there was a gala tribute to Cameron Mackintosh, the most successful of musical theatre producers then, now, and conceivably ever. It was indeed called Hey, Mr. Producer! Perhaps its most memorable item was a pretaped duet between Stephen Sondheim and Andrew Lloyd Webber, two composers who, whatever their dissimilarities, share two things: a birthday and a track record of having their shows produced by Mackintosh. For this occasion, Sondheim wrote a parody lyric to music that alternated his own Send in the Clowns with Webber's Music of the Night. The moment that went viral, as people probably weren't saying in those days, was the one in which Sondheim sang "God, but he's rich!" to which Webber replied: "richer than me!"

Well, he ought to be. He's produced the longest-running of Webber's own musicals (Cats and The Phantom of the Opera)as well some comparably successful shows by other composers: most spectacularly, of course, Les Miserables. He also produced the movie version of that show, Blu-ray edition now available. Since this was his first film, ("apart", as he says, "from filming a few concerts") I was curious to know whether his had been a hands-on involvement. On the phone he replied, emphatically, that it was.

Not from the start, apparently. "I went into it" he said, "just as an executive producer. But Les Mis is my baby, as it were. I've been its catalyst since the beginning." He can even take some credit for being its inspiration. It turns out that Claude-Michel Schonberg and Alain Boublil, its French composer and lyricist, had been much influenced by seeing Mackintosh's revival of Oliver! in London. So the much-remarked similarity between their Parisian street-urchins and Lionel Bart's London ones was no fluke. Having seen their work as a song-cycle in Paris, Mackintosh took it to Trevor Nunn and the royal Shakespeare Company, and the rest is history, if not perhaps in a sense that would be recognized by scholars of 19th-century France.

When the movie came around, a quarter of a century after that London opening, Mackintosh found himself "in a very unusual position for a producer; I represent the authors. I didn't realize, originally, that I'd be there for 99% of the filming. But I was. I also worked a lot on the editing. It was incredibly complicated." Also, it seems, amazingly fast. "This time last year, we were just about to start filming."

As for how he feels about the result: "I'm thrilled and relieved. We achieved what we set out to do. We took the story apart - a theatrical, full-blown popular opera - and put it together as a movie. It was a challenge, but Claude-Michel was up for it."

Has it whetted Mackintosh's appetite to do more films? "Not hugely. If I was 40, I'd be jumping up and down." (He's 66, though he still looks comparatively boyish.) Besides, he has a theatrical empire to take care of.

"We're in an extraordinary situation. So many of our shows are in their third or fourth decades. And they're being done in new productions." This, at first blush, is unusual. Of course, plays and musicals get new productions all the time, but generally only a certain time after the original has closed. It's unconventional for a show to get a complete facelift during what is still its initial run. (Though come to think of it, Agatha Christie's The Mousetrap, which has been running in London since 1952, making the Mackintosh musicals seem like new kids on the West End block, has regularly brought in new directors with completely new casts.) In fact, Nunn's and John Caird's production of Les Mis, and Harold Prince's of The Phantom will continue in London. But everywhere else will see new stagings. That includes Toronto, where a re-vamped Les Mis is due at the Princess of Wales in October.

Meanwhile, "the new version of Les Mis is breaking box-office records on Broadway. The 25th anniversary production is in rehearsal in London ... thank God I can now do casting through video. Then I go to Japan at the end of April. I'll be in Australia for a new production in 2014. There's a new staging of Phantom in Birmingham."

Personally, I can't imagine Phantom without the Hal Prince staging, or maybe it's just that I don't want to, but Mackintosh says that "the new stagings work incredibly well. They're done by a different generation of people. They have a different energy. They're both darker and grittier than the originals."

The worldwide success of the Mackintosh generation of musicals is unprecedented. He advances two explanations. One is that, despite some demurs from critics and other skeptics, they have "universal subject matter. Miss Saigon is about the sacrifice of a mother for her child. Phantom is about a love that can't possibly be realized. you can't get a ticket for Les Mis now. Kids in schools see the truth in the characters." And kids, apparently, do their own productions. "We've released Les Mis for use in schools; Phantom, too, though it isn't done as much; the technical requirements are more daunting. I'm very attracted to shows where ordinary people triumph over their circumstances. My shows are nearly always powered by great stories; I don't come up with the ideas, but when somebody else presents one, I dive in. If I don't like the characters, then I don't want to work on it."

I suggested that Cats didn't quite fit this sociopolitical story-driven description; though, to be fair, its characters do represent the cat in the street (or the alley) rather than the cat on the lap in the drawing room. Mackintosh says "it wouldn't work - Andrew would agree with any lyricist other than Tom Eliot. There are wonderful allegories in their poem." They initially tried to impose a more complicated concept but eventually, "Trevor said we just need a simple story. We didn't impose a premise. The simple story of an outcast being redeemed is what made it work."

Mackintosh's second explanation for his shows' longevity is that "the musical started going global in the '80s, when cheap airfares started to happen. It put the shows in dozens of countries. Now it's cool to see musicals." I think that depends on your definition of cool, but there can be no arguing with Mackintosh's statement that "theatre was always a major business - now it's one of the biggest industries in the world."

And it's no longer a principally American business: not, at least, in terms of origin or subject-matter or - most importantly - sensibility. Mackintosh points out that the last comparably dominant musical-theatre brand - the Rodgers and Hammerstein shows - "were written for a 1950s American sensibility." And their success was parochial by comparison. "The musical of theirs to achieve the greatest worldwide success was The Sound of Music - their most European show."

It also, of course, owed much of that success to its film version, which in turn has sparked successful stage revivals that are essentially based on the movie. One myth that has been exploded - the one that kept the r and H shows off the screen for years - is the belief that making a musical available on film, let alone on video, would kill its chances with live audiences. The opposite has proved to be the case. "Films," Mackintosh says, "open up shows to a whole new audience." It's also, of course, led to attempts to short-circuit the process by turning successful films into stillborn shows: Mackintosh agrees that Shrek, for example, "doesn't have a reason to sing in its own right."

Mackintosh also owns seven London theatres ("I thoroughly enjoy being a landlord") only one of which currently houses one of his own shows. (Les Mis, at the Queen's.) But he has other people's musical hits (Mamma Mia, Jersey Boys) and, perhaps more remarkably, "four or five plays doing stonking business. The London theatre currently has a Pounds 10 to Pounds 15-million advance - the highest it's ever been in my lifetime." recession or no recession, "London hasn't been healthier for a long time."

Universal Pictures / Cameron Mackintosh produced last year's film version of Les Miserables, as well as the original stage version.; Caption:

A celebrated British actress once counselled a celebrated British actor against accepting the role of Figaro in a revival of the Beaumarchais play: "It never works, darling. That's why they had to turn it into a musical." The play in question was The Marriage of Figaro (1784), source of course of the Mozart opera (1786). The Marriage, though, was the second of Beaumarchais' Figaro comedies, the first being The Barber of Seville (1775), source of the equally famous, though paradoxically later, opera by Rossini (1810). It isn't true that the original plays never work; in France, they're staples of the classic repertoire. But their track record in English is certainly sparse, with productions of the Barber being even thinner on the ground than those of the Marriage. Soulpepper's Barber is an amalgam of play and opera, in which Beaumarchais' text is periodically interrupted by Rossini's music. The script, though not its setting, has been updated and otherwise mucked about with, and the tunes are served up with new words, in mostly altered contexts, and in much reduced orchestrations. In fact, they have turned it into a musical. And it still doesn't work. The first-night audience greeted it with hysterical enthusiasm, and it isn't devoid of good points, but overall it's a self-indulgent mess.

Michael O'Brien's adaptation (first done, if I may throw another date at you, by Theatre Columbus in 1996) isn't altogether at fault. Its dialogue is often racy, if equally often repetitive, and the lyrics, at least the ones that are audible, are neat. Its main impulse seems to be to democratize the play, both by adding in as many topical references and extended farcical gambits as possible, and by bringing to the fore political impulses that are at most latent in the original.

Actually what O'Brien has done is to read back the sequel into the prequel. Pierre-Augustin Caron de Beaumarchais was a Jacques-of-all-trades, whose non-literary activities included ship-owning, music-making, gun-running (to the rebellious American colonies), and some spells in jail. He was also a pungent polemicist, who prompted Louis XVI to exclaim of The Marriage of Figaro that it was seditious and could never be produced. (It was; to the applause of Louis' courtiers, who laughed all the way to the guillotine.) What aroused the king's shocked displeasure was a speech of Figaro the valet in which he questioned the aristocratic right of his master Count Almaviva to, for example, seduce Figaro's fiancee. That's in the future though. In The Barber of Seville Figaro's function, as endlessly resourceful servant, is to facilitate the union of his employer the Count with the beautiful Rosine who, in accordance with comedic custom immemorial, is being held virtually prisoner by her elderly guardian Don Bartolo who wants her for himself. O'Brien transforms the Count, a mere rake in the original Barber, into a cynical, not to say stupid, exploiter of women and servants, whose final relationship with Figaro would, as presented here, make the later play impossible. Meanwhile Don Bartolo gets gradually upgraded from possessive pantaloon to pathetic victim. The show ends with he and Figaro vowing revenge on their ill-users while bits of the set swing up in the shape of a barricade, as if we were about to embark on a production of Les Miserables. (Which isn't about the French Revolution, but try telling that to the fans.)

I'm not suggesting any of this should be illegal. O'Brien has aright to spin and re-order the material as he likes (it's billed as his play, not Beaumarchais') and the shout-outs to the gathering French storm are the most effective parts of the evening. That it's actually set in Spain was just the original author's safety-precaution. What does go horribly wrong is the general galumphing about that characterizes Leah Cherniak's production and that dilutes and obscures a fairly simple intrigue. The alternation of play and opera does justice to neither; it just prolongs the evening to intolerable lengths. People sing and dance on no provocation and with minimal relevance; the production number that closes the first half makes it impossible to discern what in the story is supposed to be going on. The idea seems to be that Soulpepper actors letting their hair down is a sufficient treat in itself. Which makes it ironic that the standout performance, the one that saves the show from being a complete shambles, is given by a company newcomer, Dan Chameroy. His Figaro is masterfully mercenary, tough and resilient and rather touching when wounded. He is also the only performer who can do justice to the music; his introductory number, the Largo al Factotum constructively rewritten, raises hopes for the evening that are never subsequently restored. The others seem undecided as to whether they're singing cod opera or the real thing. This is particularly the case with Courtney Ch'ng Lancaster's big aria as Rosina; her acting, though, of a heroine ruthlessly reconceived as an emerging New Woman, is splendid. She also plays a mean flute in the overture: another item that, under John Millard's musical direction, promises more than is subsequently delivered. Gregory Prest as her lover is less fortunate; having nicely established the Count as narcissist, he has to undertake a couple of overdone impersonations, mercilessly extended. Yes, they're in the original play, but not quite like that; in the second case, a bosomy drag act, not at all like that.

Oliver Dennis, an actor with modest musical pretensions (he didn't sing a note in The Fantasticks, but got a deserved award anyway), does charmingly with the two interpolated ditties Don Bartholo is given here, one of them borrowed from The Phantom of the Opera, perhaps as a comment on the domestic tyrant's taste. He's also beautifully at ease with this Don's alternating championship of reaction and revolution. His foil Don Basilio (William Webster) was written as a man who'll do anything for money. The production, never able to resist a gag, destroys that by making him a coward as well; there really are times when complexity isn't called for. Raquel Duffy provides some welcome moments of restraint as a loyal housekeeper.

One of the biggest successes in London and New York at the moment is One Man, Two Guv'nors, an adaptation of Goldoni's The Servant of Two Masters that takes great anachronistic liberties with its original while still remaining joyfully true to its spirit. This Barber of Seville has no spirit to be true to and, hard though it tries to seem otherwise, isn't joyful at all.

THEATRE REVIEW

Of a Monstrous Child: A Gaga Musical

Buddies in Bad Times Theatre

Staged and performed with immense style, Of a Monstrous Child is a musical-intellectual collage that centres on, or more accurately swirls around, the figure of Lady Gaga. Its title is a line from Michel de Montaigne on the subject of deformity, a line quoted by Stefani Germanotta in her pre-Gaga days as an art student in New york. It seems, from the sentences we hear quoted and see projected, to have been a very creditable student essay. And obviously it bore fruit. One thing the show firmly establishes is Lady Gagas intelligence.

She talks very sensibly about her audience being able to read into her anything they like. She also talks pretentiously about offering herself up to them as kind of saviour, living rather than dying for their sins. (The pretentious bits tend to come later in the show.) She's played here by a performer with the wonderfully appropriate name of Kimberly Persona, who functions beautifully as a walking Rorschach test. As a kind of epiphany, at the end of the show - and I mean really the end, after the curtain call - she gets to sit down at the piano and sing a whole song. This is a notable event, the kind of bonne bouche you might expect at the end of a jukebox musical.

Which up to then the show, as its author and director Alistair Newton has been insisting, very much isn't. (The production comes from Newtons group ecce Homo, and its their most ambitious and impressive to date.) What music we hear, and there isn't an enormous amount of it, isn't necessarily Gagas own. The most impressive number, the one that actually communicates something, is from way before her time; its the '50s show tune, turned jazz standard and gay anthem, The Ballad of the Sad Young Men. It's sung by three performers including Bruce dow, whose role is that of Leigh Bowery, a celebrated Anglo-Australian performance artist and sometime fashion designer (of whom I confess I had never heard) whom, far more than Gaga, the show is about. Though much of the script is made up of other peoples opinions of its heroine, Bowery doesnt have any, for the very good reason that he died, of AIDS, in 1994.

What the show seems to be telling us is that Bowery was a precursor of Gaga's, without her physical advantages and also without her reticence: an odd word here, perhaps, but where Gaga keeps everybody guessing, even when she's supposedly being frank, Bowery on this evidence was verbally unable to contain himself; he comes over as witty, blistering, a self-inventor like Gaga but also, completely unlike her, a self-destroyer.

According to Wikipedia (which the show invokes, so I dont see why I shouldnt), "As he got larger he used his costumes to exaggerate his size, and the effect was frequently overpowering and unforgettable for those who encountered him, the more so because of his confrontational style." dow certainly captures all of that; a performer whose previous stock-in-trade has been ingratiating ebullience, he is here ice-cold and diamond-hard - which, given his technical command as both actor and singer, actually makes him more likeable than ever before. For most of his appearances he's in drag; his last, though, is a long, spellbinding monologue delivered in the unforgiving, unapologetic nude. It caps a superb, noble performance.

One of Bowery's missions in life, he tells us earlier, is to redeem the concept of irony. To show how the word has been debased, the show gives us a very funny interpolated scene (written by Jacob Richmond, of Ride the Cyclone) in which a couple of hipsters compete in describing the awfulness of the music they prefer to listen to, rather like the flat-capped northerners of Monty Python, swapping memories of childhood deprivation; you might call this sport one-downmanship.

Gavin Crawford contributes a series of brilliant lightning impressions of figures who may have influenced Gaga, or have thoughts about her, including Bjork (putting the dead in deadpan), Cher (excessively gravelly, but never mind), Andy Warhol (very interesting), Marina Abramovic (a performance artist I have heard of, and indeed admire) and Camille Paglia, who declares the Lady to be a rip-off of Madonna, though I cant see theres much to choose, except that Madonna got there first.

Madonna herself is played by Chy Ryan Spain, as are Grace Jones (his best turn) and yoko Ono, while Kyle Travis young, one of the few guys in the cast who only plays guys, does especially well as a sniffy Boy George whose loftily approving comment on Gaga basically amounts to, Hey, I was her. Tyson James does extremely well as a Gaga-worshipper, the saddest of sad young men, who sees her as his salvation from suicide and speaks reverently of her music, without actually saying much about it.

And here lies a paradox that the showpokes at but doesn't illuminate. With Lady Gaga, as with Madonna, we've reached a time in which the success of pop singers has minimal connection with what theyre actually singing. Of course pop has always been about image as well as music, but the imbalance has never been as severe as now. It strikes me that Newton may have been canny as well as high-minded in declining to do a jukebox musical; he wouldnt have had a score.

I also think - though here I'm taking issue with his program note rather than his production - that Newton is off-beam in claiming that informer times "the star remained aloof, self-absorbed and unattainable, the fan vulnerable, devoted and available." Judy Garland? Billie Holiday? They were anything but aloof; they bled all over their audiences. Meanwhile, on Newton's own theatrical showing, Gagas fans are as vulnerable and available as fans have ever been.

How important this is, I dont know; I doubt that the world in general is as obsessed with Gaga as the show would have us believe. (A thought to live by: everything is a minority interest, except the weather). Anyway it's a beautifully wrapped package; and on the first night it broke - twice - the previously immutable theatrical rule that critics should be exempt from audience participation. Talk about transgressive.

Of a Monstrous Child runs until May 26. Tickets and info at buddiesinbadtimes.com.

There's a quaint belief, expounded in newspaper columns and letters to editors, that our own age is significantly less moral than previous ones. Almost any worthwhile piece of past literature, fact or fiction, will give the lie to that, even if morality is defined, as it generally and quaintly is, as sexual morality. Our Betters, a sardonically titled comedy by W. Somerset Maugham now on view in a good production at the Shaw Festival, is a case in point, suggesting that in this respect the only thing we've lost is hypocrisy.

Maugham's play (written in 1915, premiered in New York 1917, not allowed a British production until 1923) admittedly deals with a special subset of a specialized group. Set in or near London among the rich and/or fashionable, most of its characters are American, and most of them are millionaires' daughters who have married into the European aristocracy. (This, we're told, was a frequent occurrence before the First World War, though already on the wane when the play was written. It's easy, though, to find later equivalents.) We have a variant on the Henry James theme of the Yankee innocent abroad, though here the corruption is Yankish as well. In fact we have two (comparative) innocents: a young man, Fleming Harvey, who's vigorously shocked by everything he beholds, and Bessie Saunders, his former fiancee, who's inclined to be dazzled by it. Bessie is staying with her sister Pearl, wed to an English lord whom she rarely sees (and whom we never see). Meanwhile, she disports herself with other men of various ages. Her two closest compatriot chums are the Duchesse de Surennes, divorced, and the Princess Della Cercola, separated and devoting herself, at least partially and certainly atypically, to good works. Some people's ethics and others' sang-froid are tested during a country weekend at which the hostess is discovered in a thoroughly compromising situation in the summer house with somebody else's presumed erotic property.

Morris Panych's production captures the play's acrid attitudes, though it fluctuates in tone. There's a tendency for characters to hug the edges of Ken MacDonald's two economically dazzling sets (for Mayfair, and someplace called Abbots Kenton) and it's hard to tell whether this is conscious commentary, placing them outside the action, or just a consequence of the small Royal George stage. It's also quite hard, in a loquaciously expository first scene, to keep up with who is who, and whose boy-toy or sugar-daddy is whose. The acting varies, but Claire Jullien holds the play together as a shamelessly glittering Pearl, hard as her own manicured nails and magnificently unwilling to take the blame for anything whatever. Writhing most painfully beneath the tables she turns are Laurie Paton's Duchesse, torn between righteous indignation and terrified loneliness, and Lorne Kennedy's besotted tycoon, apparently modelled on the man who founded Selfridges; these are both expert performances, but they seem to exist in their own little worlds.

Maugham famously wrote that sincerity in society was like an iron girder in a house of cards. His play, and especially this production, show that girders can be not only effective but attractive. Wade Bogert-O'Brien rescues the noble Fleming from any suggestion of priggishness, and Julia Course makes Bessie's awakening fairly sympathetic and almost entirely believable. Panych may give them too strong a hint of a happy ending, but his filling out of the script's bald final sequences is generally both sensitive and inventive, though an 11th-hour ballroom-dancing sequence also escapes its frame, and seems besides to have hired the wrong kind of gigolo. I enjoyed Ben Sanders' unexpectedly decent English lord, Neil Barclay's asexual professional gossip (once I'd got used to the patches on his suit) and Anthony Bekenn's disapproving butler (is there any other kind?).

The Shaw's other two opening shows are a Salvation Army pairing; indeed Major Barbara and Guys and Dolls turn out to have an amazing amount in common, right down to the hero who bangs a big bass drum for love of the mission doll (a major in one show, a mere sergeant in the other). They are also both concerned with the extent to which sin, or the wages thereof, may be employed in the service of virtue, though the play, as you might expect, agonizes about it more than the musical; the theme of where charity begins also figures in a minor way in Our Betters. Jackie Maxwell's production of Major Barbara is - as one of its minor characters, a Mr. Charles Lomax, might put it - a corker, clad in a cunning set (by Judith Bowden) that, even when we're in a West End drawing-room, keeps us aware of East End poverty lurking behind. The play seems more and more to be Shaw's greatest, and certainly his most perennially topical. The arguments about arms and government, poverty and exploitation, religion and humanity, are wittily broached in the first act, superbly dramatized in the second, and explosively discussed in the third; though the principal speakers' eloquence can never quite overcome our rebellious inclination to say "Yes, but..." (occasionally a character does, but nobody listens).

Nicole Underhay's professional preachings in the title role can be, as the same Mr. Lomax would say, a bit much; but her moment of disillusion is electric, and she goes on radiating thereafter. Benedict Campbell plays her father, the munitions millionaire to whom, as devil's advocate, Shaw gave most of the best tunes; he too might vary his cunning charm at the beginning and his thunderous eloquence at the end, but he does both very well. Graeme Somerville is quite unfaultable as the drum-beating professor of Greek, shy and incisive and with a justified hint of an Australian accent.

Equally on the ball, and this time perfectly within the frame, is Laurie Paton as a most original Lady Britomart, dictatorial lomat rather than dragon and - a great help to the play - very much her daughter Barbara's mother, right down to their hair colouring. Also doing invaluable service on the high-society front are Ben Sanders' Stephen, a born leader-writer who looks like a shrunken John Cleese, and Wade Bogert-O'Brien as the quotable Mr. Lomax. The richly written scenes in the Army shelter are here comparatively colourless, the actors (except for Catherine McGregor's Rummy Mitchens) out of touch with their characters' vocal and psychological rhythms; it seems that younger Shaw actors these days can do posh but not poor. The smallest roles, though, are very well done: Thom Allison as a patient factory foreman and Anthony Bekenn as another disapproving butler; no, there isn't any other kind.

Tadeusz Bradecki's production of Guys and Dolls starts gloomy, both in its opening numbers and in Peter Hartwell's set; Times Square may be sleazy, but it shouldn't be monochrome. The designs, the performance and Parker Esse's choreography all brighten up considerably for the Havana sequence; while in the ensuing return to New York in the small hours, the chiaroscuro comes into its own for the love-duet of SkyMasterson and Sergeant Sarah and their subsequent (temporary, as if you didn't know) estrangement. Elodie Gillett's mission doll is very good throughout, whether determined or intoxicated or determinedly intoxicated. Kyle Blair's Sky is too soft-boiled and fresh-faced for the gambler of the world, but he sings beautifully, and acts through his singing and also, when tenderness is called for, through his acting.

The real treasure of the show is Shawn Wright's Nathan Detroit, rueful and rubber-faced; he might have stepped out of one of Nicolas Bentley's illustrations for Damon Runyon's stories, and looks especially good as the helpless centre of the song hymning his permanent floating crap-game, the best-staged number in the show. He's also the only actor who can effortlessly get his tongue around the script's appropriation (and approximation) of Runyon's unique, and uniquely funny, prose. Jenny L. Wright is all right as his Adelaide, but could be better if she honoured the innocence that makes this showgirl both touching and hilarious, not to mention the lyrical architecture that should make her Lament the best comedy song ever written. There's some of this innocence in Thom Allison's Nicely-Nicely, nervous instead of fat, which works surprisingly well, making Sit Down You're Rockin' the Boat a charmer if not quite a show-stopper. His fellow mugs seem to have been cast for their dancing rather than their acting, and their crap-game ballet is indeed a highlight - or, being set in a sewer, a lowlight. As in Major Barbara, though, the low-lifes are less convincing than the high-minded; Peter Millard's Uncle Arvide and Patty Jamieson's General Cartwright do their Mission proud. But then, in Frank Loesser's score, everybody has the best tunes. Bradecki's direction has an especially neat and novel touch at its conclusion. Finishing this show has always been a problem; mainly, I suspect, because nobody wants it to end.

Our Betters is in repertory at the Royal George Theatre, Niagara-on-the-Lake, through Oct. 27, Major Barbara at the Royal George through Oct. 19, Guys and Dolls at the Festival Theatre through Oct. 12. 1-800-511-7429

Part of the received wisdom on Romeo and Juliet is that it’s a tragedy that looks, for much of its length, as if it’s going to be a comedy. In this case, the received wisdom happens to be true. It certainly underpins the production at Stratford, an exhilarating start both to the new season and the new regime.

The comedy isn’t just a matter of individually humorous lines or even scenes, though Tim Carroll’s production is exceptionally adroit at discovering and delivering these. It’s a matter of how the play goes: that up until the deaths, half-way through the action, of Mercutio and Tybalt, maybe even beyond then, there seems no reason for there not to be a happy ending. The deaths of Romeo and Juliet themselves are caused less by their own personal qualities than by a series of external accidents.

This may well, as the purists are fond of saying, stop it from ranking with the greatest tragedies. It doesn’t prevent it from being a moving, suspenseful and, on this occasion, very involving play. For the first time in many years, I found myself desperately hoping that things would end differently, that Juliet would wake up before Romeo took the poison, that the Friar would get to the tomb on time.

The set (designed by Douglas Paraschuk) is Stratford’s original Tanya Moiseiwitsch arrangement of steps and balconies, with a few thatched additions on top that suggest both Shakespeare’s own Globe Theatre and the modern London reconstruction of it at which Carroll has been a frequent director. This production, like his work there, cleaves to what’s become known as Original Practices: an attempt, admittedly incomplete, to re-create some Elizabethan theatre conditions. It here involves putting the actors in 16th-century costume, keeping the house-lights on throughout, and dispensing with any furniture beyond the obligatory bed and tomb, both of which are solidly and beautifully realised. It also seems to involve having the actors not just address the audience directly but buttonhole them individually; I suppose Elizabethan actors may have done this, but it feels more like 21st-century wishful thinking.

The self-consciousness starts early with some minor Montagues and Capulets chatting us up in their own words. All the same, it’s a thrill when their language suddenly changes and we find ourselves, all at once, thrown into the midst of the play’s opening brawl. At the other end of the evening, with the play proper officially over, the company, deceased lovers included, break into a dance. This is presumably a nod to the Elizabethan custom of ending each play with what was called “a jig.” Its precise tone here is difficult to decipher, but it provides at the very least an ingenious way of getting the corpses off stage.

What goes between these extremities is freshly thought, freshly imagined, freshly told. The platform stage proves itself, yet again, an unrivalled base from which to launch a text and to explore the relationships of the people delivering it. It also encourages overlapping exits and entrances, which become increasingly frequent and increasingly exciting, and is especially helpful for the comings and goings all over the Capulet household on the eve of Juliet’s supposed wedding. The costumes also contribute to the domestic atmosphere; they evoke a society, a world. This isn’t the only way of doing Shakespeare, but it’s a valid and at this moment a revelatory one. It makes some of the overstuffed hi-tech productions of recent years look old-fashioned.



Photography by David Hou. Full Company.

It also makes great demands on the actors, which most of those here have the skill and experience to meet. Sara Topham’s Juliet may not exactly look like a fourteen-year old, but she conveys all the ardour and the joy and the suffering of one. A moment at which, desperate for reassurance, she collapses sobbing into the her nurse’s arms is heart-stopping. We’re assured that there are no lighting changes in this production so it must just have been in my mind’s eye that the stage darkened during Juliet’s nightmare potion speech (just as it seemed to lighten during the Prince’s ironic welcoming of daybreak at the play’s end.) Topham illuminates line after line of this familiar text that I could hardly remember hearing before. She also has a sense of fun: I loved her look of distaste when obliged to dance with Paris; while she and her Romeo, Daniel Briere, keep the balcony scene light until the last possible moment.

His performance is more problematic. In his opening scenes, mooning for the unseen Rosaline, he seems less in love with love that in love with words, which is fine; but he hardly seems to change even after he’s met Juliet. This may be intentional – you can make a case for him always being less mature than she is – but it isn’t very satisfying. He also has something of a moon face, not helped by the sombrero he’s required to wear in Mantua. Still, he isn’t the first Romeo to be more convincing when fighting than when loving.

The fights in this production (arranged by John Stead, like most fights) are terrific, and they give Jonathan Goad’s Mercutio, bitterly joking to the last, a great send-off; earlier he’s on the right vigorous lines but sometimes jumps the track. Kate Hennig’s Nurse is a wonderful combination of warmth and insensitivity; the breaking of her bond of trust with Juliet is superb, as is her discovery of the girl’s body.

Scott Wentworth enriches the play with a full-length portrait of Capulet, a henpecked tyrant who plainly has no time for his wife’s beloved Tybalt, and in fact is rather pleased to see the end of him. Tom McCamus’ Friar Laurence has a delightful line of holy patter that deepens sternly and impressively when trouble strikes.

Mike Nadajewski’s clown Peter is the best I’ve seen, his illiteracy becoming an excellently unforced running gag. And there could hardly be a better tragic-comic moment than that of Antoine Yared’s Paris, a well-meaning fop with a French accent conceivably inspired by his name, arriving at his fiancee’s deathbed, dancing what I take to be an ill-timed galliard. Talking of dances, the lovers’ first encounter at the ball is magically set up, she prancing merrily off stage and out of reach, then returning for their duet.

But the production is full of moments like that. Do you remember the audience in Shakespeare in Love, erupting in cheers at the end of this play’s first performance, as if they’d never seen anything like it before (as, historically, they hadn’t)? This production lets you know how they felt.

2013-06-01-the-duke-abides-stratford-cov:
Shakespeare set Measure for Measure in Vienna. (Well, he name checks the place twice.) Martha Henry's Stratford production places us in that ambiguously liberated city, just after the Second World War: Harry Lime time. It works, creating a climate of cankered bureaucracy and sexual unease, not to say disease, befitting a story in which a lax ruler takes leave of absence, bequeathing his powers to a notoriously puritanical deputy and then returning incognito to see how he gets on.

You couldnt hope to find better acting, direction or indeed writing than in the two scenes in which the newly empowered Angelo faces the novice nun Isabella whos come to plead for the life of her brother Claudio, condemned to death for impregnating his girlfriend, and finds himself, for the first time in his life, falling in lust. Tom Rooney gives a magnificent, searching performance of a man obsessed with law and morality, and convinced that they're the same thing. As his self-image crumbles he finds himself literally grasping at things: clutching at books, papers, finally and violently at Isabella herself, all of them slipping through his fingers. (This production is as full of props as Romeo and Juliet is empty of them, but both excel at seizing on the text's suggestions and making them real.) Rooneys isaquiet performance, very logical and measured, until it collapses, violently, into a new kind of fanaticism, desire and self-hatred mixed.

She speaks, and my sense breeds with it, is how he puts it; and it may be the way Isabella talks that first attracts him; theyre both great legalistic arguers, and the severe habit that envelops Carmen Grant's convent trainee (most Isabellas give themselves more leeway when they go a-calling) gives him little else to go on. She matches him as a logician, cool at first, then goaded into moral passion, feeling her own strength. Angelo's blackmailing bargain -her body for her brothers life - sends her into shock; left alone, she reaches for the phone on his desk (shes a prop person, too) before realizing she has no one to call. Her desperate summation - "more than our brother is our chastity" - sounds, for once, right: for her, anyway.

The tremendous force of these scenes, and of Isabella's subsequent one with Claudio (Christopher Prentice, passionate and perplexed), has its downside; it throws into even sharper relief than usual the drop in dramatic pressure when the disguised Duke emerges from the shadows to take over the action and steer it from disaster. He does it in rapid prose that suggests the playwright as well as the character is improvising his way out of an impossible situation. For one thing, he reveals discreditable things about Angelo that take the shine off what we had taken to be the corruption of a saint. The Duke himself seems in this production to have a past. He makes his first, pre-abdication entrance, through the door of a cage that's an impressive permanent feature of John Pennoyers set, in surprise disguise; either hes been getting some spying in early, or his taste for dress-up is already well developed, or the cynical Lucio was more right about the Duke's non-ducal habits than even he might have guessed. Talking (again) of habits: along with his friar's uniform, Geraint Wyn Davies Duke borrows a Welsh accent (which to this actor, of course, comes naturally) from one member of his host order and apair of spectacles from another. This gives him charm, along with his natural unforced authority, but its sometimes hard to tell whether it's the actor or the character who most enjoys exerting it. The Duke is a perennial puzzle - moral force or heartless manipulator? - and this production and performance, intentionally or not, leave him ambiguous.

A crowd of good performances cover all the play's bases. On the streets theres Stephen Ouimettes raddled Lucio, an irrepressible hard case, Randy Hughson's pockmarked pimp, and Brian Tree for whom the role of Elbow the indignant constable was probably written. On the bench there's Peter Hutts Escalus, finding a remarkable range of magisterial gradations. In prison, there are Stephen Russells properly gentle Provost, Robert Persichini huge and hairy as the unregenerate Barnadine, and Ruby Joy bringing unwonted pride to the pregnant Juliet. In the moated grange, here equipped with its own ferry, there's Sarah Afful's Mariana who sings her own song. Thelistgoes right down to the First and Second Gentlemen, the latter of whom (E. B. Smith) doubles as the executioner Abhorson, a true professional. Theres also a dog. The last scene, in which they all (except the dog) foregather, is very well-ordered, tense and exciting. The production is both riveting and perplexing: like the play.

Is there a better-constructed scene in any musical than the wedding in Fiddler on the Roof? Theres the joy of the ceremony itself, accompanied by the infallibly moving Sunrise, Sunset; then the celebration, including the immortal Bottle Dance; then the squabbling domestic comedy, centred around the unsuccessful suitor; then more dancing, with the joyous breaking down of barriers between men and women advancing the political plot; then its brutal interruption by the Czarist police; finally Tevye's brusque instructions to clear up, followed by the desperate shrug of his silent, questioning appeal to heaven. Donna Feore's Stratford production makes the pogrom scarier than the usual carefully choreographed furniture-smashing; this time, people get hurt. She also, as choreographer, blesses us with some spectacular Cossack leaps and splits in To Life, though the earlier parts of this number arent as incandescent as they were in the previous, unforgettable Stratford production.

Nor is the show as a whole, and not just because Scott Wentworths Tevye can hardly hope to be as supernaturally moving as was Brent Carver's. He's still good: fine in his singing and, in his acting, increasingly powerful the more rugged the character and the situation become. Its also a tickle to see him, the night after his Capulet in Romeo, playing another father with disobedient daughter troubles; maybe Juliets marital problems could have been solved if her dad had had the right dream. Keely Hutton is delightful as the girl who marries shockingly out, while Andre Morin and Mike Nadajewski, who just seems to get better and better, are suitably unsuitable suitors. The design incorporates a number of portable dollhouses, which don't do much to suggest Anatevka or anywhere else, and some motifs hanging from the ceiling too crude to be the Chagal-lian homage that must have been intended. The show itself is the hero here: Joseph Stein's superbly crafted book, Jerry Bocks lovely stirring music, and Sheldon Har-nicks lyrics, even if they tend to explain things too earnestly for the benefit of the Gentiles. It isn't quite indestructible (Harvey Fierstein proved that a few years ago) but it's the next best thing.

Measure for Measure is in repertory at the Tom Patterson Theatre, Stratford, through Sept. 21; Fiddler on the Roof at the Festival Theatre through Oct. 20.

2013-06-08-made-in-the-arcade-des-mcanuf:
Des McAnuff's Stratford production of Tommy is a superlative feat of visual storytelling. Returning to the piece 20 years after his original staging, McAnuff takes enthusiastic but perfectly disciplined advantage of his new technological opportunities. Sean Nieuwenhuis is credited as "projection designer" but that seems rather a niggling description of what amounts to a dazzling, constantly changing background, dovetailing perfectly with the bridges and catwalks of John Arnone's more formal set, and also with Howell Binkley's lighting and David C. Woolard's perfect period costumes.

The visuals, which here include the actors, are especially evocative in the early scenes. Pete Townshend was writing, again, about his generation, and the way in which the Second World War forever coloured the perceptions of those in Britain who were born into it without consciously remembering it. Also of their elders; the production leaves a lovely mostly unspoken impression of the meeting of the hero's future parents on an English airfield, and a later breathtaking one of the mission that led to dad's being missing, presumed dead. There is, too, the recurring presence, cunningly placed, of Steve Ross's Uncle Ernie, beginning his limping progress from black marketeer to celebrity mouthpiece via child molester. Wayne Cilento's jumping, jerking choreography -the best I've seen from him - comes into its own when we reach the 1950s and '60s, with the youth-clubbers and arcade dwellers, presided over by Paul Nolan's magnificently nasty Cousin Kevin who mock the afflicted Tommy before his emergence as pinball wizard and then slobber over him. The direction overall is precisely tuned to the pulse and excitement of Townshend's music. This is what McAnuff does best, and he's never done it better.

The word on the Stratford street is that the production is cold, but that can only be a disappointment if you think there's anything in the story itself to get hot about. The libretto remains what it has always been: a sickly piece of rock-hero mythology, pinball here being an admitted metaphor for music, in which the fans are shocked by the revelation that their idol is not the Messiah. I yearned for Tommy's long-suffering mother to tell them that he isn't a pinball wizard, he's just a very naughty boy. To be fair, Tommy himself comes to something like this conclusion when he finally opts for family over fame; it's what the fans can't forgive him for. So he does fulfill at least one traditional Messianic requirement: getting rejected. In the meantime, though, the show has played both sides by suggesting that his deaf-dumb-and-blindness really does make him mystically special. This is accentuated in the current version by having his older self (Robert Markus, who's good) periodically descend to offer ethereal counsel to the four-and-10 year olds (who were, on the first night, even better, hauntingly so; there are alternate child performers for both roles). Even the set-up is suspect; Tommy is traumatized when his father, thought dead, shoots his wife's new fiance. But dad was a POW; wouldn't he have been allowed to write home? You'd think, too, that Tommy's physical or psychosomatic disabilities, would be enough to gain our sympathy, without having him sexually assaulted and mercilessly bullied as well. Fine as Ross and Nolan are, these scenes come off as gratuitously nasty; like the interlude with Jewelle Blackman's full-throated Acid Queen, they're filler, incidents that don't lead anywhere. The failure to make them add up can largely be blamed on the words; in a stand-alone number like Pinball Wizard they're fine, but when it comes to developing narrative and character, the songs fall into vagueness, pretentiousness and banality: the unholy trinity of rock-lyric ineptitude. That's without even mentioning the deafness to rhyme and scansion, which at one point have the crucial word "mirror" pronounced with the emphasis on the second syllable. The most feeling, touching parts of the score are the simplest: the loving, guilt-ridden attempts of Tommy's parents (very well played by Kita Guiolen and Jeremy Kushnier) to reach their unreachable son. It's nice at least that Tommy reconciles with them. Meanwhile the production keeps us thrilled, if not moved, to the very end.

Miles Potter's production of The Three Musketeers, though low-tech by comparison, shows a similar mastery of stagecraft, and a similar disproportion between style and content. Peter Raby's adaptation, now getting its fourth Stratford airing, is something of a virtuoso job, in that it manages to get in nearly all the crowded plot of the Dumas novel. In saving the story, though, it has to sacrifice nearly everything else, notably the humour. The extended wit-combats of Dumas' musketeers are replaced by physical combats (fair enough, and up to fight-master John Stead's best swashbuckling standards) and by a lot of horseplay, none of it involving actual horses. Luke Humphrey's D'Artagnan keeps his end up well, and his three pals have been extravagantly strongly cast: Graham Abbey (D'Artagnan last time around) lending weight and a hint of real pain as Athos, Mike Shara delicately disdainful as Aramis the ladies' man with religious aspirations, and Jonathan Goad vigorous as Porthos, though the role might benefit from an actor who was, well, fatter: In the book he's afar more flavourful buffoon. Stratford is rightly proud of its company strength, but that can have its downside: We notice when actors like these three aren't given enough to chew on; when other major talents seem off-beam (Deborah Hay's Milady more kittenish than viperfish, Steven Sutcliffe's Cardinal a jellyfish); when still others turn up as glorified walk-ons or, at this production's tempo, run-ons, while some more important roles are plain inadequate. The pace and vigour of Potter's staging, plus the insouciant ability of Douglas Paraschuk's sets to throw us a rope-bridge out of nowhere, plus my unquenchable affection for the material, kept my attention; but, especially in the second half, it's hard to deny that though much is going on, nothing seems to be happening.

Blithe Spirit, perhaps because it manifests itself so often, has become my least favourite of the four of five major Noel Coward comedies. It ploughs a discordant domestic field that was more fruitfully explored in Private Lives, splitting the female interest in half, between dead wife Elvira and living wife Ruth, which means a lot of bickering. Madame Arcati, the happy medium, almost invariably runs, or more accurately cycles, off with the play; it's no detraction from Seana McKenna's conqueringly sporty and practical performance (which, coming on the regal heels of her Elizabeth in Mary Stuart, makes her the doubles champion of Stratford's opening week) that she benefits from being refreshingly free of past, or indeed any, romantic associations. The other major characters are throwing past entanglements - people of whom we've never heard and in whom we have no interest - at one another, right up to the final curtain. Ben Carlson, whether unruffled or ruffled, is pitch-perfect as the twice-haunted husband; Michelle Giroux has the traditional throaty charm of his revenant spouse; Sarah Topham as her replacement lets off some fiercely effective reproaches in her early scenes but then finds, please forgive me, that she can't top 'em, so that her exasperation becomes shrill and self-defeating. Brian Bedford's direction is suave and traditional. Coward revivals always seem to bring out the atavism in audiences: the urge to applaud pretty scenery (Simon Higlett's set here is a peach) and actresses' exits, especially when they deliver their parting shots while climbing stairs. One thing the production does bring out is how firmly rooted, though it never mentions it, the play is in wartime Britain: just like Tommy.

Tommy is in repertory through October 19 at the Avon Theatre, Stratford; The Three Musketeers through October 19 at the Festival Theatre; Blithe Spirit through October 20 at the Avon.
