THEATRE REVIEW

Mary Stuart

Tom Patterson Theatre, Stratford

Stratford's opening week reaches its peak with Mary Stuart, a play that, in the special dramatic world of counterfactuals, reigns supreme. Friedrich Schillers drama, first staged in 1800, has as its centre piece an encounter between Elizabeth I, Queen of England, and her cousin and captive commonly known as Mary Queen of Scots. This never happened. Mary, having fled her native Scotland, was indeed imprisoned for years under Elizabeths orders, and was eventually convicted of treason - at a trial she was not allowed to attend, on the extorted evidence of witnesses whom she wasn't permitted to confront.

She, a Catholic, was certainly the figurehead and inspiration for a succession of mostly young conspirators who dreamed of putting her on the throne (to which she had a certain dynastic claim) and restoring the old religion. Whether she connived at these plots is still a moot point; Schiller has her protest her innocence under seal of the confessional, so we're obviously meant to believe her. The play begins with her trial already over, but her sentence unpronounced. She dreams of meeting Elizabeth in person, knowing that the ties of blood and the spirit of queenly co-existence would have to result in her being pardoned. Elizabeths hard-headed counsellors know this too, and are determined to stop it happening. Others, with their own agendas, flatter her that it will be a golden opportunity of personally humiliating her rival. So, in the grounds of Fotheringay Castle, where Mary is imprisoned and near to where Elizabeth just happens to be hunting, the two come face to face.

Or, it sometimes seems, knee to knee. In Antoni Cimolinos hypnotically tense production, the scene is marked out by who gets closer to the ground. Lucy Peacock's Mary, painfully swallowing her immense pride, kneels and begs forgiveness. Seana McKenna's Elizabeth bends her own body downwards, but not in sympathy; rather in a spirit of mocking incredulity. She lays on the sarcasm until Mary can take it no longer, draws herself back up to her full height, and exultantly proclaims Elizabeth a usurping bastard (literally). Elizabeth is the one humiliated; Mary has metaphorically signed her own death warrant. Neither has got what she wanted. Its a superb scene.

Its a peculiar quality of the play that it makes something that didn't happen a stepping stone to something that famously did. Schiller, who was not innocent of sentimentalism, also wrote a Joan of Arc play in which the Maid dies on the battlefield rather than at the stake, but his Mary does indeed go to the block. Actually sending her there remains a political and psychological problem for Elizabeth, which she resolves by signing a non-metaphorical warrant and handing it to a hapless secretary with no specific instructions on what he's to do with it. The play is, among other things, an overlapping set of highly suspenseful cat-and-mouse games: a Schiller thriller.

Its also, of course, an unsurpassed vehicle for two star actresses. The governessy tones that sometimes afflict Peacock in her classical roles (though never in her modern ones) hinder her here in her opening scenes, but she blazes in the central duet, and is spare and moving in her concluding journey to the scaffold, where her self-abnegation becomes real. In its final sanctification of Mary, receiving the last rites from an old friend whos taken holy orders expressly for the purpose, the play cheats a bit; after triumphantly flouting historical facts, it starts relying on them; it dredges up Mary's past sins, involving people we haven't met, purely for the purpose of absolving her of them. But it does give the actress the opportunity to play hard-won serenity, an opportunity that Peacock beautifully takes. McKenna, from her first sweeping entrance (eo Sharps costumes are gorgeous and Elizabeth naturally has the best of them) is both superbly regal and rackingly insecure. Her wit coruscates; it is, on the surface, always at someone elses expense, but underneath it's at her own.

There is, or so it seems in this production, a third major character almost as important as the two queens; this is the earl of Leicester presented, not too historically, as Mary's admirer as well as Elizabeths and emerging, in Geraint Wyn Davies performance, as a master of real politik and of playing one side against another, almost - but not quite - as ruthlessly successful as the Tudor monarch herself; there's something shabby about his manoeuvres as there isn't about hers. (That, by the way, is a compliment to both performances.)

Schiller was a great political playwright, and his mastery of argument is electrically embodied in Ben Carlsons Burleigh, implacably hounding Mary to her death without, as far as we can tell, harbouring ashred of personal ill-feeling towards her. His counterpart is Brian Dennehys old earl of Shrewsbury, counselling compassion and exemplifying it, even towards his opponents; it's this actor's finest Stratford performance.

Then there are James Blendick as Marys immovably honourable jailer, and Ian Lake as his nephew Mortimer, a fictitious prototype of all the men who went to their deaths to save Mary, equally enflamed by religion and by her, and likely unable to distinguish between the two. When Soulpepper produced this play, I wrote that Mortimer might be a suicide bomber in the making. Six years on, the resemblance seems closer and scarier, especially given that the character initially seems to be, and seems to himself to be, the romantic lead.

Cimolinos production encloses its period sets and costumes within a modern fence of barbed wire; but even without this, and given Peter Oswald's equally barbed translation, the resonances are overpowering: what with Mary languishing unheard in her own private Guantanamo, and Elizabeth throwing her hapless bureaucrat under the Tudor equivalent of a bus. He's given a delightfully, even poignantly, bewildered performance by Dylan Trowbridge, whom I should have included on my roll of honour for Measure for Measure; Patricia Collins, too, comes up strongly in her quieter moments as Marys devoted nurse.

Like Measure, also at the Tom Patterson, this production offers the special luxurious thrill of a first-rate company operating at close quarters, with one another and with us. Its also the re-discovery of the world's great dramatists, one of whom we still know almost nothing. It's Stratford at the top of its bent.

Mary Stuart runs until Sept 21. For tickets and information, call 1-800567-1600 or visit stratfordfestival.ca.

Peter Hinton's Shaw Festival production of Lady Windermere's Fan is, both visually and tonally, a masterpiece. That's not a term that many people would have used for the play itself, one of the three "society comedies" with which Oscar Wilde limbered up for the full-blown farce of The Importance of Being Earnest, and which are generally regarded as maudlin melodramas periodically redeemed by quotable quips. Hinton's redemptive solution is to drill into the real and even complex feelings that underlie the histrionics; to make the jokes into commentary on the jokers themselves as much as on those they are joking about; and to place the whole within a shifting frame whose contents, as well as being beautiful in themselves, supply an ongoing assessment of the characters and the time and space they inhabit.

Lady Windermere is a high-minded young wife and mother whose happy sheltered life in equally high fin-desiecle London society is disrupted when she's informed that her husband has been paying calls on, and giving money to, a Mrs. Erlynne, widely regarded as a woman with a past. He has his reasons, but won't say what they are. He further humiliates his wife, atleast in her own eyes, by insisting that she receive Mrs. Erlynne at her upcoming ball; Lady W threatens that if Mrs. E is so brazen as to show up, she will strike her in the face with her fan. (does she? Find out.) A despairing Lady Windermere seems about to yield to the entreaties of the moderately dashing Lord Darlington to run away with him, and even arrives in his apartments. She's followed there by Mrs. Erlynne, who begs her not to throw her life away, and takes drastic measures to stop her doing it. By the end of the play, Lady Windermere has learned not to be judgmental, Lord Windermere has learned to be more trusting, and Mrs. Erlynne has learned, not too surprisingly, that she has a heart. The world in general, of course, has learned nothing at all.

That world is here revealed to us gradually, and in sections. Before the play properly starts, a line of fine ladies parades slowly across the stage, each carrying her own emblematic fan. The opening scenes are shown to us as through a camera lens, in expanding and retracting sections; in one interpolated vignette, we see the curdled cream of society in a theatre box, peering with delicious shock at the shamelessly fallen woman who's dared to attend. The previously compartmentalized stage opens to its full width for the ball itself, and remains so for all succeeding scenes, each of them gorgeously and precisely realized in Teresea Przybylski's set and William Schmuck's costumes. The various interiors are patterned after painters of the period, with glimpses of the indispensable drawings of Aubrey Beardsley. There are also fireworks, real ones.

For all this, it's the acting that drives the evening. Marla McLean's Lady Windermere may have a mysterious accent, and Martin Happer as her husband may rush some of his emotional fences, but they both trace detailed, and in her case moving, maps of the breaking down of prejudice; the image of the penitent McLean by her baby's cradle is unforced and unforgettable. Tara Rosling's Mrs. Erlynne looks too young to make the play's most startling revelation credible, and she's more convincing as passionate saviour than as femme fatale, but the former element may well be the more important. The supporting roles are superbly done. Gray Powell finds some moody variations in the seducer Darlington, Lady Windermere's greatest fan. The duchess of Berwick, a role traditionally played as a dragon, is magnificently re-imagined by Corinne Koslo, who presents her instead as a viper, a censorious gossip with the blandest but deadliest of bites. She regrettably fades out of the play after triumphantly marrying her daughter off to a lanky but wealthy Australian, but there's compensation in her replacement by a chorus of world-weary young men, headed by Kyle Blair and Patrick McManus, who foregather in the third and best act to make a sustained self-satirizing ensemble out of what might otherwise be an anthology of free-floating quotes. (The play contains an amazing number of Wilde's most famous lines.) Hovering amiably on the edge of this group is Jim Mezon as an older a risto who ends up a touchingly amusing amalgam of victor and victim.

Wilde reigns on the Shaw Festival's main stage, while GBS himself is confined to its smaller houses. At that, there are only one-and-a-half of his plays on view this year, the half being Peace in Our Time, John Murrell's adaptation of Geneva, which is somehow both one of Shaw's least-seen works and one of his most notorious. First staged in 1938, and constantly revised to keep up with events, Geneva is both a satire on, and a wistful celebration of, the League of Nations. Its finale is the appearance before the International Court at The Hague, and under only slightly disguised names, of Hitler, Mussolini and Franco. The play could hardly be accused of sympathizing with them, but it does go imaginatively easy on them. (It also fails to put Stalin up there with them, where he belonged.) Shaw was perennially incapable of recognizing, or at least of dramatizing, real monstrosity; nearly all his characters speak with the same suave eloquence, and these are no exception. Shaw's preface, written after the war and never explicitly mentioning the play, shows that he knew about the Nazi camps, but his shock seems to have been intellectual rather than visceral. In the play an anonymous Jew (nearly all the characters are anonymous) has Hitler brought up at The Hague on charges of persecution; the scenario now, a sit was then, blandly disproportionate to what was actually going on.

For all that, the play as written is witty and provocative. even in Murrell's version, all the play's best lines (apart from a very funny one about sheep) are Shaw's own. Murrell says that one of his aims was to "bring some of the offensively jingoistic language ... up to date"; though since Shaw's play is in large part a satire on jingoism, or on the murderous idea of any nation's exceptionalism, I'm not sure what that means. In a funny way, though, Shaw's play is patriotic; this displaced Irishman gave the most silkily persuasive speeches to an English diplomat. Murrell's adaptation does the same, with Patrick Galligan polishing off both authors' contributions very nicely.

Murrell's first act, and Blair Williams' direction of it, are rather a mess. Michael Ball puts in appearance as a Bishop, shocked into a fatal heart attack by meeting a Communist; I was sorry to see him go, as at this point he was almost the only person on stage who wasn't over-acting. Some other British characters have been turned into stereotypes of other nations; one of them is now Canadian, occasioning a fusillade of audience-baiting jokes that would be unforgivable if the actor in question, Andrew Bunker, weren't so good in the role. A South London typist, who's as near as anyone to being the major character, has become middle American; Diana Donnelly plays her with grating exaggeration though she improves later on when the character turns, more or less, into Sarah Palin. Claire Jullien (South American) and Moya O'Connell (Russian) contribute other national caricatures that are most charitably described as determined. O'Connell's commissar was male in the original, but another female role has been (unwisely) cut so the gender score remains as before.

The show's second half, though, meaning the court scene, is a rip-roaring success, largely owing to the arrival of the three anti-Marx brothers: Neil Barclay, a mountain of Aduce, Ric Reid, a furious Fuhrer, and Lorne Kennedy, a strutting bantam of a Generalissimo. All three exemplify the combined wisdom of Shaw and Laurence Olivier that actually there's no such thing as over-acting if you can go high enough to fill the space - though with Barclay it's more a case of going broad enough; he's spaghetti bolognaise made flesh, and topped off with a soothingly disdainful voice. All three, indeed, show a contempt for one another, only exceeded by their contempt for everybody else. Murrell has preserved their best Shavian material, and creatively supplemented it. The democratic opposition is strongly voiced by Jeff Meadows as the despairing League secretary, and by Sanjay Talwar as a more optimistic judge, though if he as he claims is a Dutchman, then I'm one. The ending Murrell has given him is, by today's lights, less facile than Shaw's; and here at least our blushes are spared.

Reverting to "mere" melodrama: it can, if honestly done, be both suspenseful and moving, as is proved by Benedict Campbell in A Wife for a Life, a very early Eugene O'Neill play let, in which he plays a prospector torn between revenge and forgiveness. Much of the writing is jaw-droppingly blatant, but that was to remain a problem with O'Neill, right the way through to Long Day's Journey into Night. ("you've told me your memories. Wanna hear mine?"). This revival is part of a lunchtime double-bill called Trifles, named after a roughly contemporary piece by Susan Glaspell: a play whose greater fame is probably justified but which is here the less powerful. One play takes place in "a lonely kitchen", the other in "a lonely cabin"; Meg roe's production, designed by Camellia Koo, emphasizes the similarities.

Lady Windermere's Fan is in repertory at the Festival Theatre, Niagara-on-the-Lake, through Oct. 19; Peace in Our Time and Trifles at the Court House Theatre through Oct. 12

For 15 years its been impossible to see or hear the word mafia without conjuring up a mental picture of james Gandolfini as tony soprano.

The word itself was rarely heard in The Sopranos, and when it did turn up it was uttered in tones of angry denial. most famously there was the early episode in which tonys daughter, meadow, asked him about his possible membership, and got the blustering reply that no such organization existed; it was just "an ugly stereotype."

There was a lot of Gandolfini's tony in that exchange: the forcefulness, the evasiveness, the desperate desire to be thought well of by his own family and, ultimately, by himself. also the perverse pride in his own heritage. (at the other end of the show's life, he denounced the movie made by his nephew, Christopher, as a very unflattering picture of italian americans, thereby both echoing and pre-empting critics of the story of which he himself was the protagonist.)

Tony, sensing Meadow was too smart to be altogether taken in, went on to admit that some of his income perhaps derived from businesses that werent strictly legal. Then, later in the hour, we saw him skilfully and enthusiastically garrotting an informer from his past. The brutality seemed to come as naturally to him as the earlier protectiveness.

It seems appropriate that the actor responsible for Tony Soprano should have died on a visit to Italy; mournfully fitting, too, that the apparent cause of death should have been a heart attack, a fate for which Tony himself, a conflicted man carrying a lot of physical and emotional weight, had often seemed a likely candidate. It was startling, as well as sad, to learn that Gandolfini was only 51 at his death; that means that in 1999, when he started playing Tony, he would have been in his late thirties. Thats not an implausible age for the character, but he always registered as older - though if you look again at the first season, he does seem more open and less creased than he subsequently became.

Because he aged with the character over several years, partly as well because he was little known before he took the role, James Gandolfini convinced us all that he was Tony Soprano. This, of course, had its unfortunate side-effects; it meant he could never shake the image of Tony in his subsequent movie roles (Zero dark Thirty, for example); we were always glad to see him, but we could never quite believe in him. (The magnificent edie Falco, who played opposite him as Carmela, has never had that problem; admittedly hers was a subordinate role, but I doubt that even Nurse Jackie, of which she's unquestionably the star, will haunt her career as Tony did Gandolfini's.)

A recurring and defining characteristic of Gandolfinis Tony was the way he would shake his head and smile whenever he held a secret advantage over his colleagues and/or rivals; when he knew what was going down, and they didnt know he knew. He was always a cut above them, more intelligent and in his way more sensitive; and it was Gandolfini's communication of this that, more than anything else, provided the tension that kept the show alive.

We always hoped and expected better of him, even while recognizing he was unlikely to provide it. We even dreamed (as he did) that he might some day get out of the Life altogether, while knowing (also as he did) that he never could. This conflict, explored at such length in such detail and reflected among the other characters, gave the show, as it

quickly became commonplace to point out, the density of a great novel.

We could never be sure of Tony: never know when he would scare us to death or when he would move us to tears. The latter was likeliest to occur in his fleeting, selfconscious relationship with his son, Anthony Jr.; sharing a furtive dish of ice cream with him early on, or showing him how to change a tire. ("We do it ourselves in this house.") In the final season, in one of his last consultations with dr. Melfi, he spoke of how, when your children are ill you long to change places with them and take their pain; Gandolfini made you aware both of the reality of the feelings and of the sinister limitations of the space in which they operated. It may, when it occurred, have been Tony's most moving scene, but it was topped by the wrenching, unforgettable episode in which AJ tried to commit suicide in his parents pool. Tony, seeing it just in time, threw down the sandwich he was eating, jumped in and rescued him. His first reaction after fishing the boy out was to shake him and say angrily, Whats wrong with you?

His next was to ask: "Are you all right?" And his third was to break down in tears, hold him and say, over and over, "Oh, my baby." In a way, it brought father as well as son back from the brink. Tony, who the previous week had murdered his surrogate son, Chris, now saved his real one, proving, I guess, that blood really is thicker even than the water of an attempted drowning. Keeping AJ happy and uninvolved would have been Tony's idea of salvation, but he seemed unlikely to get it; AJ too seemed by the end to be destined for life as a gangster, just not a very effective one.

We couldn't be sure, of course, any more than we could be sure of what would happen to Tony himself; the shows notorious non-ending, leaving us all hanging, was surely an acknowledgment that any conclusion to a story so layered, so complex, would have to seem glib, and that we were better off without one. (There have always been rumours of a sequel or a movie. Now, that can plainly never happen; and its hard to imagine that it could ever have been anything but a let-down.) It was appropriate, too, that the last scene should have been a family dinner; however wide it spread its net, The Sopranos was always a show about a family - and not, primarily, in the criminal sense. It's why, perhaps perversely, we think of it as a warm show, and of The Wire, its only rival for the title of best American drama series and one with its own supply of heart-breaking moments, as a cold one; its focus was professional rather than personal.

How much the superb acting and writing of The Sopranos owed to one another is impossible to know, though it's obvious that they grew symbiotically. At its centre was the greatest character television has ever created. A gangster walked into a psychiatrist's office, and walked out a legend: an outsider and an everyman.

Next Monday sees the annual presentation of Toronto theatre's dora Awards. As on all such occasions, the list of nominees provokes a mix of headnodding ("now, that's a good choice"), brow-smiting ("hey, I'd forgotten that one"), and eye-rolling ("what were they thinking?").

For the city's newspaper critics, these reactions can be especially acute, since for the last three years we've been giving our own prizes. The processes are rather different. The doras have a complicated nominating and voting process, involving multiple jurors from within the business, climaxing in a starstudded ceremony, for which you can buy tickets. The critics - three from the daily papers, two from the weeklies - foregather informally in some place of refreshment, and argue among ourselves until a consensus is reached. We announce the results, and a few weeks later re-assemble to hand out certificates to the chosen, all of whom know why they're there. There is absolutely no suspense. It's rather pleasant.

In each year so far, there's been very little overlap between critics' choices and dora nominations; which, awards being fallible by definition, is probably a good thing. This year, for example, the critics' awards in four categories went to a production called Terminus, a ticklish situation for me, since the play was directed and partproduced by a member of my own family. This meant I had to keep recusing myself. (I didn't have to have leave the room; I just sat in a corner, occasionally murmuring, "Oh well, if you insist.") In the doras, by contrast, Terminus appears in only one category.

The critics' choice for best new Canadian play was This Is War, Hannah Moscovitch's tight and powerful Afghanistan piece. It doesn't even figure in the dora nominations though another Moscovitch piece, Little One, does. Among the five plays on the dora list, Little One might well have my vote too, given that they've also left off Michael Healey's political satire Proud; I liked that one less than I liked Generous and Courageous, the two previous instalments of Healey's adjectival trilogy, but I still liked it.

The doras' other best play nominees range from bemusing to stupefying: Kristen Thomson's Something Else, which had stunning scenes of marital combat, but didn't hang together as a whole; Melody A. Johnson's Miss Caledonia, a lightweight acting vehicle for its author (also gaining her a deserved best actress nomination); and daniel MacIvor's Arigato, Tokyo which, despite a striking production such as we have come to expect from Brendan Healey at Buddies in Bad Times, was paralyzingly boring; though betting men might be well advised to consider it, given the huge number of categories (eight in all) for which it's been nominated. disgracefully absent from all dora categories was Jordi Mand's Between the Sheets, which was pin-drop tense, deserving nods (at the very least) for writing, acting, direction and design. It really wasn't such a bad season for new plays as the doras would have us believe.

Outsiders have long berated the doras for squeezing all acting nominees into two categories, male and female, without regard to whether they were leading, supporting, musical or framatic; they then further confounded the issue by including votes for ensemble, meaning they didn't like to choose between the actors in a show. This year they've gone some way to remedying this by giving the ensembles their own category, the nominees including such worthy candidates as Canadian Stage's THIS (though I would have singled out Alon Nashman, as the critics actually did) and Soulpepper's Rosencrantz and Guildenstern Are Dead (though I would have preferred a solo shoutout for Ted dykstra). There's also a citation for the Second City gang, though I can't see that their teamwork was any more admirable this year than it usually is. It all seems very arbitrary. I'm rooting for THIS, though, because I thought it was the season's best imported play, and the doras don't have a category for that.

As for the solo actors: Among the ladies, Maev Beaty is running against herself, as in truth she was in the critics' poll; we gave it to her for Proud, though she was equally deserving for Terminus. (I think I can allow myself to say that.) Actually she won our prize for supporting performance - we do allow ourselves those distinctions - while our best leading actress choice was Michelle Monteith in Little One, though it was frankly a toss-up between that and her equally uncanny performance in The Lesson - for which she has been doranominated in the independent (i.e. smaller theatre) division. yes, I know it's confusing. Anyway, Beaty and Monteith have been the two most exciting young actresses in Toronto for some years now, and it's good to see them being widely recognized, especially alongside Moscovitch, in whose plays they both first surfaced. Also in the dora actress stakes are Johnson, as mentioned, Clare Coulter for her remarkably moving King Lear, and Irene Poole in The Little Years: a strong team.

The doras don't agree with us so much about the men. Among those they've nominated, my faves would be Nigel Shawn Williams in Race and Tom rooney, taking time off from his apparently effortless brilliance at Stratford, to supply similar in Something Else. Stuart Hughes, critics' choice for The Crucible, isn't up there, though Albert Schultz's production is, deservedly, both for best direction and best production. (That means best all-around thing.) directing competition includes Chris Abraham, twice. richard rose should be there for This Is War, but isn't. unsurprisingly unnominated was Alan dilworth's La Ronde, the most underrated staging of the year, with a brilliant set by Lorenzo Savoini, who is also not nominated, though he is for The Crucible.

The doras may be stingier than the critics with acting prizes, but they're more generous regarding design; they have separate categories for sets, costumes, lighting and sound, while we lump them together in a single package. And maybe that's fairer. Actors get a lot of attention anyway,whilebackstagepeople don't. Maybe one day there'll be a dora for stage managers. As Adam Brazier has recently pointed out, they work harder than anyone. each of the dora design categories is dominated by a single person, Kimberly Purtell (lighting) getting three nominations out of five.

There's some confusion in the musical theatre and opera divisions: sometimes they overlap, sometimes they don't. Let me just note that best musical actor nominees include critical winners Bruce dow and darrin Baker (leading and supporting respectively, for us); that I wish some space could have been found for Christopher Siebert in La Cage Aux Folles, even if he was just passing through; and that I was glad to see Falsettos (musical) and Dialogue Aux Carmelites (opera) nominated for best production in their respective categories, though I was sad to see no mention of their respective directors, robert McQueen and robert Carsen. In the latter case, I'm more than sad; I'm incensed. Dialogue aux Carmelies was the COC's finest production of a fine season, maybe their finest production in years. It may also have been the best thing seen last season on any Toronto stage. robert.cushman@hotmail.com The Dora Awards are at the Bluma Appel Theatre on Monday June 24.

2013-06-29-speaking-shakespeare-whedon-s:
One of the great things - actually the greatest thing - about Joss Whedon's film of Much Ado About Nothing is how natural it sounds. All the reviews have enthused about the capacity of a group of youngish Hollywood actors, not best-known for their classical expertise, to get their tongues around Shakespeare's language with a minimum of apparent effort, and the maximum of point, wit and flavour. up here, we can get quite complacent about our overall competence in these matters. I've been saying for years that the relative permanence and stability of our companies at Stratford have long left standards in the u.K. in the dust. The theatrical ecology in Britain, not least at National Theatre and royal Shakespeare Company level, is hand-to-mouth. As for America: It is to laugh. Or so we patronizingly thought.

It turns out one very good way to practise is to do what Whedon did: Have regular Shakespeare-reading sessions with your chums and colleagues. Then, if you're happy with the results and want to share them, make a movie.

Something rather similar was done 20 years ago in New york with another classic playwright; the director Andre Gregory, and a group of high-powered buddies including Julianne Moore and Wallace Shawn, met periodically to rehearse Chekhov's Uncle Vanya; then Louis Malle came in and filmed them doing it. The result was Vanya on 42nd Street, a magical movie that started with the performers clutching their coffee cups while greeting one another and then, before we even had time to notice, moved into one of the most searching performances of Chekhov anyone could remember. The actors really inhabited the play.

Whedon's actors inhabit their play, too, in a rather literal way. More than any other Shakespeare comedy, even Twelfth Night, Much Ado is solidly set in and around a single house. Whedon's own California mansion does excellent duty for the governor's house in Messina, a hospitable place in a near-permanent state of party. That sense of location, deliciously explored in the movie, is one of two great gifts that Shakespeare's text hands to a modern-dress interpreter.

The other is that a huge proportion of the play, including all the best bits both comic and dramatic, is in prose. In fact, the only character handed testing chunks of verse is the governor himself, Leonato; and Clark Gregg, though looking young for the role, handles them and the whole role splendidly. But Benedick and Beatrice, the two people who make the play go, speak hardly a line of verse between them.

Part of the genius of Shakespeare's verse is the way its apparently artificial form captures actual speech rhythms. The prose, though, consists of actual speech rhythms: the rhythms of its own day, obviously, but also, by some magical coincidence, of ours. And, it seems, of every age in between. Whedon's leading players are hardly the first to prompt comparisons with Cary Grant and Katharine Hepburn. Alexis denisof's Benedick is, in truth, a little heavy-going, but his heart and mind are in the right place; Amy Acker's Beatrice, whether playing happiness or heartbreak or both together, is superb, finding the soul and the shape of every sentence, making them sound like classic screwball, classic sitcom, classic Shakespeare, all at once. down among the constabulary, I initially thought Nathan Fillion's security officer dogberry too low-key. But he grew on me, hilariously; if he played down the malapropisms, he precisely hit the innocent selfimportance. every generation has to find its own way into the great scripts. Shakespeare, especially in his prose ("the greatest prose writer of the age of Shakespeare" said T.S. eliot "was Shakespeare") can make the task both daunting and incredibly easy. There are stream-ofconsciousness passages in the two parts of Henry IV - slow with Justices Shallow and Silence; fast, obviously, with Mistress Quickly - that are like nothing else in english drama until you get to Pinter; Shakespeare seems to have been waiting for us. It's amazing too, how any actor of Shylock, Jewish or Gentile, finds the lines slipping naturally into modern Jewish cadences. It's as if our life is imitating his art.

As for what's going on in england: I used to think that the new cockney - estuary, east end, call it what you like, it's now a generalized British rather than London accent - was hopeless for Shakespeare, not because of its class associations (though the classlessness of North American and especially Canadian english is a blessing in these plays) but because it was ugly and sloppy and slid tunelessly and tonelessly over both the shape and the meaning of the words.

That can still happen, and too often does. But rory Kinnear's Hamlet at the National Theatre a couple of years ago proved that it can work magnificently in Shakespeare. Kinnear is the son of roy Kinnear, rotund comedian of a hundred Carry On movies; using his own undoctored voice he was magnificently supple, magnificently agile, witty, intelligent and vulnerable; he was indeed, I realized with something of a shock, the first Hamlet ever to move me emotionally as much as he did intellectually.

Currently (and coming in September to a movie theatre near you, courtesy of NT Live) he's playing Iago in Othello: a role more obviously amenable to tough-guy diction, and one in which he brilliantly explores the character's corrosive feelings of inferiority along with the impervious practicality that leads everyone to take him for "honest." His central duets with the Othello of Adrian Lester, improved beyond measure since his callow Henry V of 10 years go, achieve a rare level of contact, with the script and with one another.

Like Whedon's Much Ado, this is a detailed, modern-dress production, one in which the sights and sounds of a military occupation are meticulously captured. Both productions might count as site-specific Shakespeare, though in the case of Nicholas Hytner's Othello, the site has been constructed on a stage. The wide open space of the National's Olivier Theatre contracts for the final scene in desdemona's bedchamber, which for once actually feels like a bedroom: An intimate space into which the tragedy's victims, perpetrators and spectators are incongruously huddled. The tension is extraordinary. It isn't the only way to do Shakespeare. At the Stratford Festival, Tim Carroll's "original practices" (in quotes, because the term is inexact) production of Romeo and Juliet is aggressively unlocalized, but still creates a world onstage: even, in the helterskelter scenes in the Capulet household, a domestic one. It does so because the actors - not all of them, but most - are able to make the words live: the story looks elizabethan but sounds modern or, if you prefer, timeless. The average standard is actually higher than in the NT's Othello, in which most of the supporting performances are dull.

Or maybe I'm reacting against them because they aren't the english actors I grew up on. Michael Pennington would disagree with me. He's a unique combination of star actor, fine writer, and first-rate if uncredentialed Shakespeare scholar; in a recent and indispensable book called Sweet William, which has illuminating and sometimes revelatory things to say about all the plays, he writes: "Today's young actors who, whatever you may have been told, have an aspiration for classical work identical with ours, are an inspiring group - passionately engaged, resourceful, extremely talented and hard-working - in whose hands the future can confidently be left."

I've heard less exuberant assessments from British teachers and directors; it isn't the talent they doubt, it's the training or the lack of it. Successful practice really does come down to having the chance to practise. It can happen in the least expected places. Like at Joss Whedon's house.
2013-07-06-super-tramps-stratford-s-wait:
In Jennifer Tarver's beautifully proportioned Stratford production of Waiting for Godot, Tom rooneys Vladimir emerges, if not as the central character - impossible given the plays egalitarian structure - then as the defining one. Tarver's program note suggests Vladimir may even be a stand-in for Samuel Beckett himself: the stoic philosopher asking questions of the universe, and maybe foolhardy enough to expect an answer. He may even be that most doomed of Beckettian figures: an optimist.

For a tramp, he's remarkably dapper. But then the play never actually says Vladimir and his companion Estragon are tramps; its just a conclusion that a couple of generations of audiences, abetted by a tradition of bowler-hatted productions, have jumped to concerning the likely status of two men who sleep in ditches, subsist on rotting carrots and turnips, and spend their evenings in a barren stretch of country awaiting the arrival of a chronically non-appearing benefactor.

rooneys Vladimir seems to accept this situation but not altogether to belong to it. He can't help interrogating it, trying to put the best possible face on it. He appears educated; he might even be a lapsed academic. He certainly never tires of trying to make his pal see sense, or at least of making him admit some continuity in their existence, if only in the matters of recognizing his own pair of boots or recalling where he spent the previous night and how many people beat him up during it. There are vestiges of a humane tradition in Vladimir; faced with the plutocratic Pozzo and his slave Lucky, whose neck has been rubbed raw by the rope around it, he cries out - impulsively and even passionately in rooney's performance - its a scandal." Its only a passing moment of protest, quickly withdrawn under pressure, but it's something. Something more is his meditation as he watches his friend asleep (there are few things to be sure of in this play but friendship is one of them, even if it's defined as shared endurance) and reflects that someone, somewhere, is watching him; that he, too, is a character in a play, a tragicomedy both comic and cosmic. Theres no suggestion, by the way, that the person watching is a merciful God, let alone a merciful Godot. I confess there were times when I had difficulty accepting this Vladimir, because he departs so far from the norm: Even the late William Hutt wasnt this cultured. But that's my fault, not his.

If rooney's Vladimir is a fine performance, Stephen Ouimettes Estragon is a great one: as down at heart as at heels, and perversely glorying in his destitution. He understands very little of what Vladimir says, and what he does understand disgusts him. He certainly doesnt share his buddy's humane instincts: His reaction to Lucky's plight is to kick him when hes down, literally. Hes only afraid Lucky might kick back; and Ouimette keeps the balance between fear and vindictiveness beautifully tight. Morally considered, Estragon is a deplorable person, but we can't disown him, if only because Vladimir, and therefore Beckett, doesn't; hes us, give or take a vegetable or two. And hes the realist of the pair; when Vladimir boasts that at least they've kept their appointment and asks "how many can say as much?, Estragon replies millions." It's the cruel puncturing of a rhetorical question, and possibly my favourite moment in the play, both funny and final. Meanwhile, they suffer with their respective physical infirmities; Ouimettes Estragon continuously but resignedly with his feet, rooneys Vladimir spasmodically but agonizingly with his bladder.

However dark its ultimate meaning, Waiting for Godot is, line by line and moment by moment, an exceptionally lively play, kept brightly lucid by the cross crosstalk of its vagrant double-act. Tarver's production doesn't let a connection go by,

and makes most of them casually fresh. This goes for the physical content as well as the verbal; the juggling of three hats between two men rises to superb heights of puzzlement. The same goes for the rubbery facility with which they fall down and get up. The Tom Paterson stage, for the third time this season, comes up trumps; in Teresa Przybylskis set (at the furthest stylistic remove from her sumptuous Lady Windermeres Fan at the Shaw) it's sternly dominated by the essential unexpectedly flowering tree, mercilessly surveyed by a swivelling silvery moon, and bisected by a strip of road that, Tolkien fashion, appears to go ever onward. It is of course the highway for the two appearances of Pozzo and Lucky. Pozzo is Brian dennehy, who flashes a pearly-white grin worthy of Mack the Knife, and finds a perfectly matching vocal tone, as of one unbending to his inferiors from unimaginable heights, with which languidly to interrogate his new acquaintances about their ongoing appointment. Called upon, however, to articulate the encompassing despair of his second-act blindness, he merely shouts, without the genuine power to back it up. real despair is the province of randy Hughson's Lucky, taut and tortured at the end of his rope, and erupting on command into his one long speech. Most actors deliver this as a virtuoso display of sheer nonsense; here its something deeper and more painful: an anguished attempt to find hope and meaning through a mash-up of philosophical jargon, collapsing in the admission that despite such temporary distractions as "tennis of all kinds," there is none to be found. The speech has shape and meaning, even in denying it, like the play itself.

Though I have to question: If Pozzo and Lucky are returning in Act 2 from the fair to which they were en route in Act 1, why dont they re-enter from the direction in which they left? I've heard of the Absurd, but this is ridiculous.

Weekend Post robert.cushman@hotmail.com

2013-07-13-the-night-heir-macbeth-works-:
It begins on a blasted heath and ends on a field of battle; still, I doubt many people think of Macbeth as an outdoors play. Like most of the other tragedies, its a play that the dream in High Park, like most of the other pastoral Shakespeare operations, has avoided like - well, like Macbeth himself trying to keep out of the way of Macduff. My soul is too much charged with blood of thine already: High Park has the blood of any number of lighter Shakespeare plays on its lawns already: plays that were the victims of half-baked direction, haphazard casting, and a general confusion of the popular with the patronizing. Ker Wells' production of Macbeth is, in this context, a double revelation; not only does it show that you can do a tragedy alfresco but it really is a production, with a definite view of the play. It is, in some respects, a perverse view; but it's carried out with intelligence and imagination, and cast, for the most part, with actors who are equal to their roles.

The major exception in the latter category is, unfortunately, Macbeth himself: Hugh Thompson progresses conscientiously through the lines without putting an individual stamp on any of them and without making us feel the heat inside the murderers head. He is something of an automaton, which may even be the intention; hes the only Macbeth I've seen who, when he gets to "tomorrow and tomorrow and tomorrow" illustrates the words with some rather effective strutting and fretting of his own. The production's thrust, intentional or not, is to absolve him of much individual blame. Hes a soldier in a militaristic society; what else would you expect? That seems to be the reasoning.

So we start with an elaborately choreographed battle, the witches emerging from beneath the corpses to perform their opening ritual. They speak in sex-kittenish voices, rendered more mockingly sinister by the amplification; its unfortunate that the same sound system has a similarly inhuman, and less felicitous, effect on the other characters; about the only actor to escape the boom of doom is Kevin Macdonald, an understated and even humorous Banquo. duncan, whom the script keeps describing as some kind of saint, is played as a bloodthirsty martinet, who can't wait to hear that execution has been done on Cawdor; indeed he asks twice. His son Malcolm, in an arresting performance by Greg Gale, is a cool gum-chewing customer, whose proclamation as heir-apparent is one of the production's best moments; he takes it in his stride, while Macbeth goes to pieces. Most startling of all, the Thane of ross (Thomas Olajide), normally a mere well-intentioned bringer of bad news, here becomes Macbeths hit-man and an all-around time-server. Hes the Third Murderer at the killing of Banquo, subsequently and non-textually bumping off the First. (That's one theatrical cliche I would love to see the back of: the tyrant who lets none of his instruments escape alive.) He bears false tidings of comfort to Lady Macduff, preparatory to assisting at her murder too. He then switches to Malcolm's side, on hearing how big an army hes raised. In fact he displaces Macbeth as the true villain of the piece, which may be one reason why the supposed central performance fails to catch fire.

The productions other, and more legitimate, angle is its emphasis on the Macbeths' childlessness. This oddly makes no impact in the scenes between the couple themselves, but its implications are chillingly apparent elsewhere. Macbeth plays the jolly uncle with

Banquo's son Fleance, just a few scenes before arranging for the boy to be killed. The bloodstained child who figures among the witches apparitions is given haunting prominence. Macbeth himself turns up at the Macduff family massacre, and at its end makes off with one of the children; I doubt that he intends to adopt him. This makes a terrific buildup for the scene in which Macduff hears the news (from ross, of course) and ryan Hollyman plays it most powerfully. Excellent, too, is Philippa domvilles Lady Macbeth, switching in an uncanny instant from wifely exasperation at her husband's failure to pick up the daggers where she left them (if she's told him once, shes told him a thousand times) to the pang of conscience at duncans resemblance to her father; if I've seen the latter moment better done I don't recall it. In fact one of the great strengths of Wells production is its alertness to the echoes in the text. He sometimes juggles the order of things to bring this out, but its subtle and allowable. Thus, when the drunken Porter (Hume Baugh, not quite as drunk as all that, indeed promoted to something of a commentator) goes through his litany of the damned, Macbeth appears pat at the mention of the equivocator. The evening's final success is the setting itself. We're used to the fall of night bestowing magic on even the unworthiest of open-air comedy productions. It turns out to work for tragedy as well; certainly for this one which reaches its climax in a castle surrounded by a forest. Though I regret to say that there is no visible suggestion of Birnam Wood marching towards dunsinane; the High Park trees stand stubbornly still.

On the fringe: The Musical of Musicals: The Musical is an off-Broadway hit of a few seasons past in which the same basic situation - a lecherous landlord, a heroine who cant pay her rent - is presented as it might be treated by in order, rodgers and Hammerstein, Stephen Sondheim, Jerry Herman, Andrew Lloyd Webber, and Kander and Ebb. Non-payment of rent is, of course, a staple theme of melodrama, though I dont think it's been treated in any actual modern musical: except, of course, Rent. The minispoofs here are almost continuously hilarious, though they sometimes mistake mere quoting for satire, especially in the r&H section, whose heroine is called June, perhaps because she's bustin out all over. In Lloyd Webberland she becomes Juanita, an aspiring singer exploited by a cat. In the Sondheim segment, which is musically the acutest, shes the victim of a villain who wants first to paint her and then garrotte her, confirming my long-held belief that Sondheim's Sweeney Todd and his Georges Seurat have a lot in common. The Toronto production, directed by Vinetta Strombergs, is a delight with ace performances from a cast of four: Mark Cassius, Adrian Marchuk, dana Jean Phoneix and Paula Wolfson, who's wonderful as a succession of older-woman advicedispensers called Abbie (hear her nihilistic gloss on Climb Evry Mountain) who finally gets her own Jerry Herman vehicle called, naturally, dear Abbie. The audience applauds her says Michael Mulrooney, narrating from the piano, "even though she hasnt done anything yet". The show is at least as sharp on the staging of musicals as on the writing of them, with choreography, credited to Consensus & Theft, that does terrific hatchet-jobs on Agnes de Mille, Gower Champion and Bob Fosse, and throws in a curtain-call salute to Michael Bennett which I won't spoil for you except to say that it sure is a singular sensation.

Macbeth is in repertory through Sept.

1 at Shakespeare in High Park; The Musical of Musicals: The Musical runs through July 14 at the Factory Theatre.
