2013-07-19-being-frank-about-it:
Faith Healer Royal George Theatre, Niagara-on-the-Lake Enchanted April Festival Theatre, Niagara-on-the-Lake Brian Friel's Faith Healer consists of four lengthy monologues, only one of which contains any jokes. Its probably reprehensible of me to have taken against the play on such superficial grounds, but there it is. Still, of the three productions of it that Ive seen, the new one at the Shaw Festival is the best. It makes my vestigial respect for the piece somewhat less grudging.

The faith healer of the title is Francis Hardy, who tells us early on that his choice of profession may have been influenced by his sharing its initials. (This doesn't count as one of the jokes. Francis, a.k.a. Frank, doesn't go in much for humour. Mordant self-deprecation is as close as he gets, and he gets there often.) Irish by birth, hes mainly plied his trade in the village halls of Wales and Scotland but, with money and audiences drying up, he returns to the old country for what turns out to be a fateful gig in Ballybeg. His entourage consists of Teddy, his cockney manager, and Grace, his wife. At least she says shes his wife, and Teddy says so too. Frank himself prefers to call her his mistress.

This is the most glaring but probably the least consequential of the several discrepancies in the trio's recollection of events. Frank's on first, then Grace, then Teddy, then Frank again. It seems obvious that Teddy and Grace are telling the truth on the marriage question, while Franks version is a way of humiliating Grace while appearing to be quite the lad himself. Murkier are the precise circumstances in which Grace, unattended and in a remote Scottish village, gave birth to a stillborn child while Frank blithely absented himself. Most mysterious, a cliffhanger left hanging, is the course of events at the pub in Ballybeg, when Frank was asked to work his magic on a hopeless paraplegic, and to face some very threatening music from the mans friends if he failed to deliver.

The conflict of memories isn't nearly as compelling a theme as it's cracked up to be. The question that really fascinates is why Grace and Teddy stick with Frank over some 20 years; and the answer - that they love him - is no less powerful for being self-evident. Teddy, the ultimate small-time agent (God knows how hes survived on a percentage of Frank) ranks Frank with the great ones: from rob roy the Piping dog, most successful of his own former clients, to Sir Laurence Olivier. What they all had in common, says Teddy, was that none of them knew how they did what they did.

At Niagara this theory is tested by the presence as Frank of Jim Mezon, who really is a great actor. (I didnt realize this till about five years ago; others have known it longer.) At ground level, I'm sure that Mezon knows exactly what he's doing; but I can imagine that he, like all performers, might live in fear of the magic not working on a particular night, and equally of its working unaccountably and unrepeatably well on another. Even if he doesnt, he uses his physical bulk and vocal delicacy to tap unerringly into Franks twin veins of vanity and insecurity. He calls himself a mountebank; he also knows he has a gift, however unreliable, and he clings, eyes and voice glinting, to the memory of the one transcendent night when everything mysteriously clicked and he cured 10 out of 10.

In Craig Hall's production, this compulsive oscillation is illustrated by having Frank spend his first soliloquy setting out the chairs in Christina Poddubiuk's fine composite re-creation of all the draughty halls the act can ever have played. realistically, this makes no particular sense; Franks current address would seem to be limbo, and even when active he would never have condescended to be his own roadie; he would have left such drudgery to Grace and Teddy.

But it gives the actor something to do, and us something to look at; it also makes a fine contrast to the same rooms uncluttered aspect when Frank returns to complete his narrative. There's a wonderful image of Mezon standing upstage, his hat newly placed on his head and his back to us, before turning and advancing to confront and/or surrender to his demons. Frank tells us that he's in a state of unworldly suspension, and Mezon makes us believe it.

Grace, hugging the bottle while apparently re-enacting a therapy session, is another in Corinne Koslos fine line of wrenchingly devoted wives (or mistresses). As Teddy, Peter Krantz is handed two gifts: he has the only funny lines, and his gold smoking-jacket is the evenings one splash of colour; Bonnie Beecher's lighting, jabbingly stark elsewhere, brightens up to greet it. His performance, though, is so emotionally and rhythmically limited that his protestations, of caution or loyalty, amount to a series of exclamation marks. Teddy has been known to walk off with this play; this time it belongs, as it should, to Frank, an exemplar of star quality in a play that's about it.

If Faith Healer is excessively demanding but somewhat nourishing, its balanced by the Shaws other opening, Enchanted April, which is excessively undemanding and not nourishing at all. It's a Broadway-endorsed adaptation (by Matthew Barber) of the celebrated novel by Elizabeth von Arnim, which I haven't read.

Its first act is quite interesting; two young wives, frustrated by their lives in post First World War London and especially by their husbands, team up to rent a villa near Genoa, country of sunshine and wisteria for a month. (They dont tell their spouses about it until the day before their departure, which strikes me as behaviour more typically male than female.) They take two other ladies with them to share expenses: one a free-spirited young woman with a title and perhaps a past, or at least a present, the other an older, censorious widow. These scenes, especially the marital ones, set up some intriguing, even troubling, relationships. They are nt followed through. After intermission, we and the cast arrive in Italy to find the wisteria and sunshine present as advertised. Indeed, apart from minor problems with the plumbing and cooking, all is idyllic, which is nice for them but rather boring for us. A little matter of conjugal infidelity raises its head, but is swiftly swept under the rug, though the play doesn't seem to realize that there is a rug; it lurches in the direction of farce, and then lurches out again, a frustrating progress that Jackie Maxwell's production does nothing to iron out. Tara rosling provides some subtlety as the more reserved of the two central vactioners; Moya OConnell as proactive companion is certainly vivacious, but its hard not to sympathize with the character, who says that her high spirits "would make Pollyanna blush." Marla McLean smoulders in an underwritten role; donna Belleville, as the dragoness who predictably melts when someone offers her walnuts, gets the regulation laughs from the series of disparaging oneliners that seem to make up her role. Sharry Flett also gets laughs, though not from me, as a maid who demonstrates her ethnicity by periodically breaking into excerpts from Italian opera's greatest hits.

William Schmuck has designed a first-act set that reduces multiple London locations to a uniform drabness, and a contrastingly colourful second-act successor that provokes instant applause, even though, as they say in The Musical of Musicals, it hasn't done anything yet. What this second-rate confection is doing on the main stage of one of our two premier theatre festivals, I cannot say. It doesn't even have the excuse of being a musical.

National Post robert.cushman@hotmail.com Faith Healer is in repertory until Oct. 6; Enchanted April until Oct. 26. For tickets and information, call 1-800-511-7429 or visit shawfest.com.

David Cooper / Jim Mezon uses his physical bulk and vocal delicacy to tap unerringly into Frank's veins of vanity and insecurity in Faith Healer.; Caption:
2013-07-20-back-in-blackmail-entertainin:
Joe Orton's Entertaining Mr. Sloane was his first play and, when staged in London in the 1960s, made him an instant celebrity. Gay when it was a crime, and fresh from a six-month jail term for defacing library books, Orton conceived the piece as a comic revelation of the hypocrisies and sexual rapacities of lowermiddle-class British life. Its a theme he was to expand in his subsequent, more elaborately farcical plays Loot and What the Butler Saw, both of which are, in dialogue and action, bolder and funnier than their predecessor. It does, however, have one quality that they lack, and that is superbly brought out in Soulpeppers first-rate new production. Orton would probably have scoffed at the phrase, but Entertaining Mr. Sloane has human interest.

Not that that makes it sentimental. Mr. Sloane himself is a fair-haired hunk of 20 or so, taken as a lodger by Kath, a lady twice his age who says she picked him up at the library. (Joe's in-joke?) Kath has designs on Sloane's body. So does her brother Ed, but hes too repressed to act on them, which no one, except perhaps herself, could say about Kath. despite her protestations of virtue ("I had an upbringing a nun might envy") shes all over him from the first moment he sits on her settee. Before the play is done, she will find herself, for the second time in her life, pregnant. The first time was when she was young, by a man whom her family forbade her to marry; at least, that's her story. The child was given up for adoption; and one rather expects it to be revealed that Sloane is her long-lost son. In a later Orton play, it would have been after she'd bedded him. Even as it is, she keeps calling him her baby.

Ed, meanwhile, a selfproclaimed businessman who keeps boasting of his high-placed and high-living contacts without letting on who they are, engages Sloane as his chauffeur and does his best to pry him away from Kath. Theres another member of the household, the siblings elderly, ailing but peppery dada (that's what Kath calls him) who suspects, correctly, that Sloane may have murdered his, dada's, former employer. Sloane has to shut him up, thereby putting himself at the mercy of brother and sister, and each of them at one anothers. The game of three-sided blackmail that ensues is clever, icy, hilarious and disconcertingly believable, like the entire play. Its also, like the entire play, overextended. We know everything about these characters, long before they've finished telling us. The wit of the dialogue, self-satirizing epigrams couched in tones as prim as their Wildean predecessors were fruity, isn't quite enough to compensate.

Brendan Healeys production is staged in the round, the acting area surrounded by billowy red curtains that part to reveal a lounge (genteel speak for living room) thats

the pared-down essence of suburbia; yannik Larivee's set cunningly gives us the basics without smothering the play in chintz, as has been its fate in some earlier productions. A happy corollary of this is that none of the characters gets patronized. The performances capture every shift in tone, every laugh and every twinge of horror or - believe it or not - pity; and the accents, allimportant in this play, are spoton. As Kath, Fiona reid is, not too surprisingly, perfect. undulating in her undies, she's a model of sensual gentility, and also of domestic pride. (The landlady-lodger relationship owes something to Pinters The Birthday Party; the master returned the compliment, not altogether successfully, in the more ruthless moments of The Homecoming.) But shes also a touching figure of desperation, not least when her claws come out. A moment at which she replaces her false teeth, dislodged in a squabble, and favours the assembly with a radiant smile, sums up the play and the character for all time.

Stuart Hughes is less obvious casting for Ed, and sometimes the effort shows. But he still commands the stage, rocking back and forth on his heels in agonies of inadmissible lust; and his timing and pacing are sharp as a tack, or as the checked suit that proclaims him a man of the world, no matter if the world's a small one. What Sloane's own sexual preferences may be remains a mystery; I think we can safely assume that he doesnt have any emotional ones. In later Orton plays, his chilly amorality would infect the entire world; here its his own personal province. david Beazley, whiny when cornered, otherwise casually cruel, flawlessly embodies it. Michael Simpson brings a surprising dignity to dada, whose (comparative) honesty isn't as mercilessly mocked here as it would be in Loot; while in What the Butler Saw honesty hardly enters the equation. They, as already stated, are probably more considerable, certainly more deeply subversive plays. But, no doubt about it, as presented here Mr. Sloane is very entertaining.

Weekend Post robert.cushman@hotmail.com Entertaining Mr. Sloane is in repertory through August 17 at the Young Centre (416-866-8666)

Cylla Von Tiedemann / The back of David Beazely, the ever-perfect Fiona Reid and a commanding Stuart Hughes.; Caption:
2013-07-27-pip-pip-hooray-soulpepper-s-g:
With a running time of two and a half hours, Soulpepper's stage version of dickens' Great Expectations, adapted and directed by Michael Shamata, clocks in between the royal Shakespeare Company's two-part eight-hour Nicholas Nickleby, one of the great theatrical experiences of my lifetime, and the trim and perennial Soulpepper-Shamata Christmas Carol, based on a short story. Both those productions were matched in scale and feeling to their sources; they left you with the satisfying feeling that nothing had been left out. Great Expectations is, by dickensian standards, a medium-sized novel, and this dramatization doesn't have to skimp very much in terms of plot. The first half never feels rushed; it is in fact beautiful. The second lacks breathing space; the story is all there, but it becomes a concertina of coincidences.

Bless, however, the central performance. dickens' heroes often prove livelier onstage than on the page; and Pip, the narrator-protagonist of this one, starts with the advantage of having an inner life. He's the orphaned blacksmith's apprentice whose life is transformed when a mysterious benefactor gives him the money to move to London and become a gentleman. Snobbery overcomes him; he becomes ashamed of the people who have always loved him. If anything Pip, who's more corrupted in his manners than in his instincts, spends too much time beating up on himself for what seem like normal human failings, failings that are told rather than shown. Jeff Lillico, however, keeps us with him in an unshakably clear, lucid and responsive performance. He alternates at switchback speed between commentator and participant, rough and smooth, man and boy. As narrator, it's his prerogative to play himself at all ages, and he gives an especially vivid account of the frightened child in his parents' graveyard, surprised by the escaped convict Magwitch who will, in more ways than one, hold Pip's life in his hands.

Other characters are governed by different rules, so a child actress and an adult one divide between them the roles of Pip's two female contemporaries, the warm and sympathetic Biddy and the decidedly cold and unsympathetic Estella. young Naomi Agard, finds more to chew on in Estella, the ultimate spoiled little girl; with Leah doz, her grown-up successor, it's the reverse: She's better as Biddy. But then the grown Estella is a literary contrivance: a woman raised to be selfish, "to break men's hearts", who is yet unselfish enough to warn Pip about it.

There are some flavourful performances among the full-time adults. Kate Trotter forsakes the usual she-dragon accounts of Miss Havisham to give us a self-punishing faded beauty whose "sick fancies" are hauntingly believable; she does, though, run out of variations. Oliver dennis, who makes modesty magical, was obviously born to play Joe Gargery, ever the best of Pip's friends, embarrassed by his own embarrassment. He was equally born to play Mr. Wemmick, the lawyer's clerk who's all humanity at home and all business at business; sensibly, he plays both of them in the most notable of the evening's ongoing quickchange routines. C. david Johnson is punctiliously powerful as Wemmick's employer Jaggers, dickens' great embodiment of a decent instinct in an indecent system. Paolo Santalucia's Hebert Pocket has warmth and energy, if not quite enough of either, and Oliver Becker's Magwitch is suitably scary, though so vocally rough-hewn as to be often incomprehensible.

Shawn Kerwin's set, on a stage that bisects the auditorium, consists of some chairs and a mysteriously unnecessary pillar. Pip's arrival in London is bustlingly well staged but the fatal fire at Miss Havisham's is confusing. So, more damagingly, is the climactic steamboat tussle between Magwitch and his nemesis Compeyson, here transposed to dry land with Compeyson, a shadowy character to begin with, escaping alive, resulting in a lack of closure all around. Indeed the show gives short shrift to all the book's villains; old Orlick, who does for Pip's shrewish sister, is barely present and not at all accounted for, while Bentley drummle's, Pip's amorous rival and symbol of the society that engulfs him, is more talked about than seen. This is not an overpoweringly joyous event; but then Great Expectations isn't an overpoweringly joyous book. It's one of the late, great dark novels. dickens intended to give it an unhappy ending, but was talked out of it. It could, I think, be made ambiguous; and Shamata's staging of the last scene seems initially to be heading in that direction. Maybe next time.

In Anything Goes, by contrast, joy is pretty much unconfined. This 1934 Cole Porter musical takes us back to the days when all the best shows were set on Transatlantic luxury liners. Actually there was no such time, but there should have been. This show has established itself as the quintessence of all the song-and-joke-heavy products of its depressed decade, exuding what the great critic Eric Bentley once described as "a cockeyed devil-may-care philosophy that is certainly attractive and may even be rather useful." It's epitomized here by the moment at which rachel york as "nightclub evangelist" (get that) reno Sweeney gazes down on a scene in which a humble Wall Street runner has been mistakenly hailed - and celebrated - as a gangster, Public Enemy Number One. Cocking her own eye, she gives the only possible response: she goes into the title number which, as staged and choreographed with unstoppable verve by Kathleen Marshall, remains the definitive comment on celebrity culture.

Anything Goes was a work-inprogress even at its premiere, its book enforcedly rewritten at the last moment. The present script (by Timothy Crouse and John Weidman) has just the right amount of self-mockery and has been standard since Lincoln Center presented it in 1987. Marshall's direction now doesn't have the wit and style of Jerry Zaks' then, but it beats London's overstuffed National Theatre production. The book works in all but one of the songs (which include five standards) from the original score, plus five from other Porter sources, including one, the magnificent Easy to Love, which was meant for the show but replaced because the leading man thought it too difficult. (I think the song that replaced it is even harder, but maybe he didn't dare complain twice.) Its intended status may explain why it works so well now, dramatically as well as musically. It seals the love plot.

If anything there are too many songs, or at least too many extended treatments of them, but that seems a grudging complaint when they're all so good. More serious is the disconnect between york's singing and her acting, which sounds like an impersonation of Peggy Lee impersonating Mae West (Miss West in fact crops up here in two of Porter's list songs, suggesting even he could run out of ideas), and the further disconnect between her and the rest of the show. Both she and the audience seem to be under the impression that it's her star vehicle, a sort of Hello Reno, though it's an ensemble piece, and was so even when Ethel Merman played it in '34. If anything the central character is Billy, the playboy broker, who's both the romantic and comic lead; Josh Franklin is not quite to the debonair manner born, but you can't see him defeated by any song, any dance, any gag. Fred Applegate does wonders through understatement as his farcical foil, Public Enemy No. 13 (I wish they'd kept the original gag in which he was superstitious and wanted to bump somebody off to improve his rating), and dennis Kelly does similar as Billy's myopic employer. I initially doubted the wisdom of Edward Staudenmayer's playing the bemused Wodehousian Englishman with such devout seriousness, but he'd won me over by the end. The energy level is fabulous throughout; and who can resist the way the portholes change colour, several times in a number, in sympathy with the sky. Everyone go.

Great Expectations is in repertory through Aug. 17 at the Young Centre; Anyhing Goes runs through Aug. 25 at the Princess of Wales Theatre.

Joan Marcus / The Cole Porter musical Anything Goes, in contrast to the darkly themed Great Expecations, is pretty much unconfined joy.; Caption:
2013-08-03-pulling-out-stoppard-shaw-fes:
When the Shaw Festival announced, some years ago, that it was expanding its programming policy to include plays written later than gBS own lifetime, the first author who came to most peoples minds was Tom Stoppard who, in his wit and his fascination with ideas, is obviously the most Shavian of all contemporary playwrights. It was not to be, at least not for a long time. But now, at last, the Shawfest has brought us Arcadia, the play generally regarded as Stoppard's masterpiece, and has given it, by way of further amends, a sparkling production.

If you detect a guarded note in that phrase "generally regarded," you are right. I don't myself find Arcadia as intoxicating an experience as Stoppards earlier intellectual extravagances Jumpers and Travesties; while The Invention of Love, the play that followed Arcadia and that still awaits its Canadian premiere, contains what are for me his single funniest joke and his most wrenching emotional moment. It would also, being set very much in Shaws lifetime, have fit perfectly into the festival's revised mandate, while Arcadia only qualifies under its re-revised one. However, I've been going on about The Invention for a dozen years now, so I should probably shut up.

No doubts, anyway, that Arcadia is the most perfectly organized play of an author whos always been distinguished as much for his tidiness as for his audacity. Any number of conceptions, artistic or scientific but generally both, chase one another around in it, but the governing one is the Second Law of Thermodynamics: The universe will eventually run out of heat and die. This ultimately terrifying but comfortingly far-off eventuality is intuited in the play by Thomasina Coverly, a precocious mathematical genius who is 13 when we first meet her and 16 when we say goodbye. Thomasina is ahead of her time in more ways than one, as she comes up with her idea in 1812, a full 40 years before its official formulation. Shes the daughter of the aristocratic Croom family, in the schoolroom of whose English stately home, known as Sidley Park, both portions of the play are set.

About those portions: We alternate between the 19th century and the present day (1993, at the play's premiere) when the house, still in the same family, has been invaded by a couple of literary scholars, each with an axe to grind. Bernard Nightingale, a gaudy media don, is intent on proving that Lord Byron was once a guest in the house and that, when there, he duelled with and killed a very minor poet named Ezra Chater whose wife he had seduced. Hannah Jarvis, a far more reserved author, is interested in the Sidley Hermit who, around the same time, took up residence in the Park's capacious park, which had just been elaborately converted to what was taken to be a state of nature, i.e. a wilderness, naturally - or unnaturally - complete with hermitage. Hannah sees the hermits fate as emblematic of the decay of romanticism, she herself being a dedicated Classicist and (again in more ways this one, this being Stoppard) anti-romantic. Both Bernard and Hannah are wrong in their suppositions, but Bernard is the more recklessly and spectacularly wrong of the two.

Byron, as we know from the plays alternate sections, was a guest of the Crooms, and he did have sex with Mrs. Chater. (But then who, apparently didn't? As her husband, more than willing to trade her favours for a good review, puts it, there is nothing that woman would not do for me.) Other assumptions are due to the modern characters' misreading of the few surviving documents; we see for ourselves which evidence has been preserved and which destroyed; some things can disappear forever, even without the heat-death of the universe. It should be stressed that all characters in the play are fictitious, apart from Byron who doesnt appear. We do, though, meet his friend Septimus Hodge, Thomasinas tutor in mathematics and drawing and literature and everything else including, platonically and somewhat reluctantly, love. Septimus shares some of the Byronic temperament, and much of the cool Byronic wit. He is in fact the kind of character whom Stoppard most seems to enjoy writing, and to whom the audience certainly most enjoys listening; asked if sexual congress is the same as love, he replies: "Oh no, it is much nicer than that." In Eda Holmes' effervescently fast and intelligent production, gray Powell makes a capital Septimus, alert and amusing with an undertow of sorrow, while Kate Besworth is delightful as a Thomasina whose emotional development is catching up, rapidly and poignantly, with her intellectual.

This delectable couple has its latter-day counterpart in diana donnelly's prickly and practical Hannah, her best performance yet, and in Patrick McManus Bernard, whos wonderfully, self-satisfyingly pink, in costume and demeanour (I don't know about his politics); he's his own fireworks display. He in turn has his own fine foil in Martin Happer as Valentine, gauche present-tense scion of the Crooms and admirer of Hannahs, a quietly dedicated scientist who also finds his own findings anticipated by Thomasinas. Only she only had algebra and limited time; he has a computer and so, theoretically, infinity. Every idea in this play, indeed almost every line and especially the jokes, connects with another. It isn't true that Stoppard's plays are bafflingly intellectual; he explains the ideas as he goes along. But he does tend to wrap them in epigrams, and unwrapping them without spoiling them requires care. This production mostly supplies it, though Nicole underhay makes disappointingly heavy weather of Lady Croom (1800s edition) who stands sexually to the absent Mrs. Chater as Septimus does to the absent Byron and who also has most of the lines about landscape gardening, which are here so gabbled as to obscure one of the plays themes and one of its major plot developments.

Everything comes together in the plays famous last scene, a scenic and temporal overlap in which the classical and the romantic join hands, literally, while time is magically, heartbreakingly, suspended. At least, that's the idea. I get it, but I've never been as moved by it in practice as Im obviously supposed to be. I think the production might hint more powerfully than it does at Thomasinas eventual fate. However, the choice of Leonard Cohen's Dance Me to the End of Love as closing music is inspired (music is another of the play's crucial elements; sorry not to have mentioned it before) and the final use of Sue LePage's set is audience involvement at its very best.

Arcadia is in repertory through Sept. 7 at the Studio Theatre, Niagara-on-the-Lake (1-800-511-7429)

David Cooper / Kate Besworth as Thomasina Coverly and Gray Powell as the Byronically witty Septimus Hodge in Arcadia.; Caption:
2013-08-10-here-comes-the-bard-part-mart:
John Murrell's Taking Shakespeare is a modest but charming play with some stings and barbs to it. A young man named Murph, an undergraduate faced with flunking, is sent for special coaching in Shakespeare from an elderly female professor, known to us only as Prof. Murph is a mature student by undergrad standards, having dropped out for a few years. He never took to the Bard in high school, where they tried unsuccessfully to make him read Hamlet; now he is even more flummoxed by a volume of four comedies whose titles he thinks are too long. The anthology in question begins with The Comedy of Errors and ends with The Tempest: a selection that provokes shudders of disapproval from Prof herself. However, when she learns that the dean of Humanities, who also happens to be Murph's mother, has suggested he study Othello, she perks up.

Murph's own tastes run to video games and Game of Thrones. (Prof might have pointed out that the latter is just as long a title as The Tempest, but she doesn't.) Prof 's own feelings about Othello are deep and complex, though not very deeply explored. It seems she herself was turned on to Shakespeare by a professor who inspired her and who happened to be teaching that play. Maybe she saw herself as desdemona to his Moor, enthralled by his wonderful tale-telling, but we have to guess that for ourselves. Maybe it would have been all the same if he'd been teaching Macbeth.

Still, Othello it is, and after initial hesitation, Murph really takes to it. This is not exactly a surprise, and there's probably an element of wish fulfilment to it; it's what we'd all like to see happen. Still, as Murrell has written it, it's a delight to see Murph progress from the mechanics of the iambic pentameter (conscientiously counting feminine endings) to creative involvement. Prof takes him through the text at the rate of an act a week, giving Murrell's play its own miniature (and satisfying) five-act structure. Murph gets painstakingly but with inspired leaps into the character of Othello, comes up with a vision of Iago as nihilist that surprises even Prof and, under her goading guidance, arrives at an interpretation of Emilia that surprised even me. Meanwhile - also predictably but also touchingly - teacher and student develop a protective affection for one another.

Casting and acting are the main event here. The role of Prof was transparently written for Martha Henry who, as well as being the doyenne of Canadian Shakespeare or indeed of Canadian acting, is the head of Stratford's actors' conservatory; Luke Humphrey, who plays Murph, is a recent conservatory graduate and a rising festival star with a great oxymoronic talent for dogged impetuosity. (He's d'Artagnan in this season's Three Musketeers). In diana Leblanc's production, a mutual respect and admiration, not to mention a shared pride, ring round the theatre. A great actor is a kind of teacher anyway; Henry obviously relishes the chance to speak Shakespearean verse assigned to characters who would never have been on her resume; she also joyfully points up Prof 's asperities and eccentricities. Also her pain and an underlying golden-heartedness. Prof hasn't, we gather, had an easy life. She lives alone, and never seems quite certain which day it is; she has an uneasy relationship with the faculty that employs her (she speaks witheringly of the lack of humanity in the humanities), a conflict that comes to a head as the play progresses. Humphrey is matchingly perfect. It's a joy to hear the two of them speak the Othello extracts in different but complementary styles; they make a great trailer for Stratford's upcoming production of the tragedy itself. It's another joy, if a less refined one, to hear them trade nonsense syllables as characters from Murph's favourite game Bandwitch (which obviously should exist even if it doesn't). Michael gianfrancesco supplies a wonderfully cluttered set, all overflowing bookshelves and frowsty rugs, for the sitting-room where Prof reads and dozes and teaches and has her being.

The same designer's setting for the Shaw Festival's The Light in the Piazza is also cluttered, but less happily. Adam guettel's musical is set in Florence, where Margaret, a middle aged middle American woman, has come for a holiday with her daughter Clara, now in her mid-twenties and mentally disabled as a result of a childhood accident. In a city square they meet Fabrizio, a 20-year-old who speaks hardly any English. Clara and Fabrizio fall in love; Margaret, already guilty over Clara's condition, agonized over whether she has the right to stand in the way of her daughter's happiness and what, or whether, to tell Fabrizio and his family - who have their own concerns to agonize about.

In this production, Florence is represented by a set of arches that are not particularly evocative when they're standing still and are downright dangerous when the actors move them about, as happens far too often. Two contrasting numbers, one for the young people and one for the old, involve characters talking while walking; in Jay Turvey's production, they spend all their time negotiating the architecture, so we can hardly follow what they're thinking about. Nor is the actual light in this piazza anything to write postcards home about. under Paul Sportelli's direction, guettel's music, achingly romantic melodies over tricky rhythms and adventurous harmonies, sounds as beautiful as in Acting up Stage's production four years ago, but the emotional effect, of the songs and of Craig Lucas' book, gets shredded.

Jeff Irving is gloriously full-throated and full-hearted as Fabrizio. Jacqueline Thair's Clara matches him vocally but her psychological problems never seem to go deeper than shyness; she misses the sheer terror conjured by her predecessor when Clara gets lost in a strange city. Patty Jamieson repeats her Toronto performance of Margaret, who has the tricky role of observer as protagonist, returning to the town where she spent her own honeymoon and comparing Clara's dreams and hopes with her own faded ones. She's at her best when phoning home to her unresponsive businessman husband (Shawn Wright, always seen amusingly and impatiently tying his tie) but the tensions created here don't carry over into her bittersweet songs, which include Dividing Day (mostly bitter) and the closing number (mostly sweet). Juan Chioran, another repeat performer, is conqueringly impulsive and imposing as Farbrizio's papa, and he has terrific family support: Jualin Molnar as an understanding wife who keeps her own counsel while explosively confiding in us, Kelly Wong as philandering older son, and Kaylee Harwood, true trim dynamite as a jealous daughterin-law. The piece itself remains one of the finest American musicals of the new century. Listen to it.

V. Tony Hauser / Undergraduate Murph's preferences run to video games and Game of Thrones, but he expands his tastes under Martha Henry's Prof in the modest but charming Taking Shakespeare.; Caption:
2013-08-16-heaven-sent-theatre-review:
Angels in America

Performing Arts, Toronto

I first saw Angels in America, Tony Kushner's two-part sixhour gay fantasia on national themes at the National Theatre in London where it was staged, to rave reviews, ahead of its equally acclaimed New york debut in 1993. I had to write myself down a skeptic; I thought that a good little play about roy Cohn had been bloated to inordinate proportions by a lot of fancy stuff about angels. Too many angels, not enough America. I was wrong, as is proved by Soulpeppers new production, which lights up nearly every moment of the marathon while returning the company itself to the level of acting magnificence that distinguished its earliest days. Still Cohn, the one historical figure among the plays half-dozen principals, remains its most immediately compelling character, and he provides a good entry-point to the work as a whole.

Early in Part One Cohn, a hugely successful New york lawyer and former flunky and confidant of Joe McCarthy, is diagnosed with AIDS. He angrily denies that this means he's homosexual, his reason being that homosexuals are losers, while he himself is clout personified. No, he says, he isn't homosexual; he just likes to have sex with men. Nobody ever said that Kushner doesnt write great lines.

He also writes great scenes, and Cohns death and its aftermath are among them. Cohn enters hospital, under cover of having liver cancer, using his contacts, of whom he is inordinately proud, to procure a huge private stash of AZT. It doesn't save his life and when he dies - about halfway through Part Two - Belize, his gay male nurse, appropriates the drugs to distribute among his own stricken friends. Partly to cover this, and partly as a mark of grudging respect towards a man whose guts he reciprocally hated but with whom he had established a kind of rapport, Belize enlists Louis Ironson, the only other Jew he knows, to act as his drug-mule and to say kaddish over Cohn's body. Louis, definitely secular, is nervous about this, and initially gets the prayer confused with the blessing over wine, but he perseveres, prompted by the ghost of Ethel rosenberg, whom Cohn claims to have personally sent to the chair in the 50s and who has been balefully haunting his bedside, occasionally bemused by things like buttons on phones. The beneficiaries of Cohns unconscious bequest will include Prior Walter, Louis' partner whom he abandoned when Prior caught the plague. Prior's life will be not just saved, but transformed.

This scene buoyantly embodies the plays wild and apparently spontaneous blend of history and invention, realism and fantasy, laughter and pain. It also involves or invokes most of the main characters. Theres one notable absentee, Joe Pitt, legal clerk and protege of Cohn's, a self-denying gay man who eventually surrenders to a relationship with Louis, and who also happens to be a Mormon. All the main men in this play are gay; none of the women are. The most prominent females are Harper, Joe's unhappy wife, strung out on Valium and agoraphobia; and Hannah, Joes mother, who leaves Salt Lake City for New york after her son has come out to her over the phone.

Journeys, past or present, actual or imagined, are a key part of Kushners play; so is ancestry. The kickoff speech is delivered by a rabbi, at Louis' grandmother's funeral, recalling the trip from Lithuania to "the melting-pot where nothing melts." Prior, from an old WASP family, receives delirious sickbed visitations from two prior Priors. He lives further up to his name by wrapping himself, when he ventures back into the world, in what looks like a monastic cowl. Among the places he visits is a Mormon museum where both Pitt women have taken up residence and where the chief exhibit is a diorama of the Saints trek to utah, headed by a figure who looks very much like Joe and whom Harper addresses as if he were Joe. Whats more, he responds.

The staging of this tableau, poised between pathos and farce, is one of the triumphs of Albert Schultz's production. The method of the scene harks back to an earlier episode in which Prior, delirious with illness, finds his fantasy intersecting with that of Harper, whom he has never met and who imagines herself in Antarctica, saving the ozone layer. (It's 1985.) What, Prior asks Harper, "are you doing in my hallucination?" Thereby both getting a laugh and setting up a very handy method of making thematic connections while shortcutting exposition. And then there are those angels.

Or rather that angel. She drops down on wires through Priors ceiling, scattering plaster in her wake, to tell him that millennium approaches and that hes a prophet and has a mission. He demurs; but in Part Two, when he's feeling much better, he climbs the ladder she's brought with her and finds himself in what seems to be the American wing of heaven, a place apparently deserted by god in 1906 on what seems, by world cataclysmic standards, the rather flimsy pretext of the San Francisco earthquake. Prior declares that the celestial delegates should respond to the divine desertion by taking responsibility for their own affairs and returns to earth to put his principles into practice. Just how remains vague.

So I still have trouble with the plays mystical aspects; and indeed the heavenly conclave is one of the less satisfactory sequences of a generally swinging production. Schultzs direction thoroughly outclasses what I remember as the plodding British staging, not least in getting more exciting rather than more exhausting as it goes on. It unfolds fluently on a set (by Lorenzo Savoini) divided into three playing areas to accommodate the multifarious plotlines; occasionally an actor will invade somebody else's space without even a fantasy warrant, but they're mostly kept rigorously distinct.

Most impressive, though, is the productions undeviating sensitivity to the text, and the actors responsiveness to it and to one another. There's a great performance everywhere you look, each growing greater by feeding off its fellows, with Bonnie Beecher's refreshingly bright lighting throwing all of them into the sharpest relief. Hardly a laugh, a pang, an image or an argument goes missing.

Very Steven Spielberg says Prior when the angel first descends, striking, in damien Atkins superb performance, the note of the true movie maven, awestruck but detached. Even when Priors in extreme physical or emotional pain, Atkins never plays for self-pity. He focuses instead on Prior's bemused intellectual growth and above all on his reflexive wit; he sees and shares the quirky side of everything. Kushner's jokes are the highest proof of his talent, and Atkins as Prior has some of the best of them: in a secondary role - everyone here gets to play more than one - he has the very best.

Diego Matamoros Cohn begins as a virtuoso display of brute intelligence, deepens into a study of agonized, unforgiving (and mostly unforgiven) loneliness. Especially fabulous are his scenes with Troy Adams off-duty drag-queen Belize, a demon of deflation with people he likes, a conscientiously ministering devil with this man he loathes.

The consummate transformation artist is Nancy Palk, who starts out sublime and unrecognizable as the rabbi, and proceeds impeccably through four other roles, including a sedately implacable Mrs. rosenberg and, as her main assignment, Hannah the Mormon mama, who comes to town to save her son and finds less expected, more charitable, outlets for her innate practicality.

Which brings us to the ending. The russian word for restructuring is perestroika, which is the subtitle of Part Two. The last scene finds Louis and Belize in an obviously endless argument about the Middle East, Prior tolerantly shrugging, and Hannah playing den-mother; Joe is significantly absent. There's a shoutout to what was going on in russia under gorbachev, as a hopeful sign of the times in general. It might all seem rather facile; in fact it does. But time has been kind to the play by being cruel. Subsequent events, including those in russia and especially in the context of a "gay fantasia," have lent this epilogue an enriching layer of irony. Besides that, there's the impact of the event itself. Size and ambition have a habit of bringing out the best in actors. They certainly do here. They have a matching effect on audiences. They bond both sides of the house in a spirit of mutual generosity, of all-of-us-in-it-togetherness. At the last moment, Atkins steps modestly forward to, in effect, bless us.

On the first night - more exactly, the second first night - we responded in kind with a thunderous, heartfelt standing ovation. I cannot imagine subsequent audiences feeling any different.

robert.cushman@hotmail.com Angels in America runs until Sept. 14. For tickets and information, visit soulpepper.ca.

Cylla Von Tiedemann / Soulpepper's Angels in America bonds both sides of the house in a spirit of mutual generosity, of all-of-us-in-it-togetherness.; Caption:
2013-08-17-in-the-heat-of-the-night-othe:
The new Stratford Othello is red hot. That goes for the way it looks, sounds, feels and takes possession. Chris Abraham's electrifying production, superlatively designed by Julie Fox, unfolds

on a scarlet-drenched revolving rectangle, moved by humans rather than hydraulics, and itself backed by red panels. Billowing white curtains provide occasional contrast, functioning mostly to denote Desdemona's bedchamber, of which we're given a teasing glimpse a couple of scenes before the play and its hero move in for the sacrificial kill. This is presented right down on the lip of the stage and is as detailed and as shocking as I have ever known it.

The set is capable of thrilling instant transforma-tions; from the tumult of the Venetian streets to the full order of the senate, and from there to the storm that greets Othello's arrival at Cyprus. It goes up and down as well as round and round, and it tilts so as continually to bring the action and the characters closer to us, thus conquering the notoriously flat and distant Avon Theatre stage. In fact, the production complements Abraham's staging last year of The Matchmaker, an ostensibly proscenium-bound play that he made work joyously on the Festival Theatre platform.

Dion Johnstone, whom I'd feared might be too lightweight for the title role, in fact navigates his way through and around it very skilfully. Using an accent (West African?) that I've never heard from him before, he emphasizes the Moor's strangeness in the society that employs him, and the extent to which he not only accepts but enjoys it; making his case to the senate, he lingers on the word "anthropophagi" as if it summed up all the exotic experiences he has had and they never will: the ones for which Desdemona, living them vicariously, fell in love with him. That love, on both sides, is palpable to the end, however distorted; and Othello's final dying "upon a kiss" is logical. He holds on to his trust for her for the longest and firmest time the play

allows; in the temptation scene it's touch and go whether he'll succumb to Iago's poison or throttle the poisoner. Once it takes, he's a man possessed, and also a man made psychologically ugly, a transformation that Johnstone plays to the hilt. There are passages of verbal majesty and of volcanic passion that he can't encompass; but substantial proportions of the part and the play can come through without benefit of molten lava. His surrender to Iago is superbly acted and presented, again at the edge of the stage, the two kneeling men ("Now art thou my lieutenant," "I am your own for ever") effectively becoming one.

It's a truism that Iago is himself a victim of the jealousy with which he infects, and destroys, Othello. Graham Abbey's Iago doesn't merely suffer from jealousy; he's tormented by it. His "I am not what I am," delivered with the vocal tremor that in this actor denotes conviction rather than hesitation, is the utterance of a soul in hell, determined to drag everyone down there with him. He can act cheerful but he's fundamentally sombre. This is quite compatible with his opportunism and his relish for power - the click in his mind when Desdemona's father suggests that she will betray her husband as she did him is barely perceptible and yet unmistakable - but he doesn't notably enjoy his villainy; to adapt his own words, it is what he is. Among the myriad of motives he adduces for himself, one of the least remarked is a love for Desdemona; he then scornfully dismisses it, but in Abbey's performance it's plain that he does at least fancy her. Of all the masks he puts on, the most damnably convincing is that of her comforter, perhaps because at some level he wishes it were true. What this performance suggests - to me, anyway - is that Iago is consumed by the knowledge that he, alone in the play, is incapable of love. This includes his wife, Emilia, with whom he can put on an amorous act when necessary; she certainly loves him, obviously fears him, and is, in Deborah Hay's performance, visibly if quietly upset by his jokes about women. Their relationship is unusually believable, and her disillusion correspondingly intense. Iago always runs the first four-fifths of this play; Emilia, the one who undoes him, then takes over, and Hay's suspicion turned to anger is tremendous.

Bethany Jillard captures Desdemona's spirit, her innocence and, above all, her insistence; the quality that first enchants Othello and then, as she persists in pleading for Cassio, enrages him. She can't believe, until the very last moment, that he means to kill her; when she does realize it, she's terrifyingly terrified, while the murder itself - strangling followed by smothering - takes as long to accomplish as it realistically should. It drains Othello, even before he learns the truth.

Mike Shara is an exceptional Roderigo, passionate - even dangerously so - but infinitely suggestible, modelling his own moods on Iago's, taking every one of his suggestions and running with it. Brad Hodder brings unusual depth to Cassio's despair at the loss of his reputation; Peter Hutt overdoes Brabantio's anger in the opening scene (everybody's shouting here; it would be nice to have some variation) but is moving when he bitterly acknowledges his daughter to be lost.

The costumes are traditional Renaissance; Thomas Ryder Payne's brooding soundscore is contrastingly modern, and very effective. Also it never drowns out the actors. (Well, hardly ever.) This, as far as I know, is Abraham's first Shakespeare production - certainly his first major one, and of a play with an unlucky record at Stratford - and it's an extraordinary debut.

The Thrill

Studio Theatre, Stratford

Judith Thompsons The Thrill is a play that holds the attention while gradually forfeiting belief. It's stronger on speeches than on scenes, and has a large structural flaw. But it is extremely well acted.

Its protagonist is elora, selfdescribed "bedpan crip"; she's been in a wheelchair for the whole of what would otherwise have been her physically active life. In other ways, though, shes exceptionally active, indeed an activist. Shes a lawyer, and a crusader for the rights of the disabled. Top of her agenda are the right not to be sentimentalized or patronized, and the right not to be put out of what others might call her misery.

The first has led her to a years-long denunciation of Jerry Lewis and his telethons. The second leads her, in the play's present tense, to wheel herself onto the platform where a euthanasia advocate named Julian is making a book-plugging speech and to denounce him.

Elora is based on Harriet Johnson, a similarly handicapped lawyer and driving force of the Not dead yet movement, and the play is set in her hometown of Charleston, S.C.; though nothing specific, apart from the paying of respects and the occasional distant sound of the blues, is made of this. Julian is more loosely based on Peter Singer, an ethics philosopher who once shared a stage with Johnson at Princeton. They were, obviously, on opposite sides of the debate but they found themselves respecting and even liking one another. Thompson takes the relationship several degrees further. She has elora and Julian fall in love.

There are two other characters. One is Francis, elora's gay male nurse and devoted friend and confidant. The other is Hannah, Julians mother who is in failing physical and mental health and who, by convenient coincidence, is also living in Charleston, having arrived there by a circuitous route; she spent much of her married life in Ireland, where she bore three children including Julian, but she herself was born in england This distances Julian from the real Peter Singer, who is Australian; Julian also differs in not being a career academic but rather one who has chanced onto the college circuit by writing a single blockbuster book. The book was entitled Wheelbarrow, that being the vehicle in which his crippled younger sister was transported during her short, agonized life. He feels guilty for not having put an end to her suffering (and also probably guilty about feeling guilty). He has no desire, however, to abridge his mothers life; but why, even by his own professed standards, should he? She doesn't appear demented, merely crotchety and inclined to imaginary conversations. So Julian's double standards arent quite the irony the play seems to intend.

Elora and Julian find some common ground in their detestation of the institutions fate that she dreads for herself and her friends, and that Julian fears for his mother. That, though, wouldnt necessarily fuel a romantic relationship, and from the moment Julian, impressed by elora's intrepidity, shows up at her place and asks for a date, the play starts to feel forced and schematic. Both of them, of course, find their initial positions modified, though not by contact with one another, more by the ineluctable pressures of life. There's a suggestion, if only in the title, that what seems to be eloras sexual initiation hastens her decline. Appropriately enough in this Stratford season, she evinces a desire like Othello to "die upon a kiss"; theres a further connection with the other current studio play

Taking Shakespeare in that both present testy, indomitable, lonely women fighting impossible odds.

Except that elora isn't all that lonely. She has Francis; and each of them admits that the other is the most important person in their life, even though Francis has an offstage partner with whom he seems very happy. elora and Francis have a more credible and interesting relationship than elora and Julian; so, to a lesser extent, do Julian and his mother. The play is, on its own showing, skewed; livelier at its edges than at its supposed centre.

Lucy Peacock is terrific as elora, the hunched immobility of her limbs offset by the darting intensity and crackling wit of her voice, her mind and her eyes. Robert Persichini embodies unsentimental devotion as Francis who was once an actor and is now, professionally and otherwise, a moderately camp counsellor; acting and writing between them redeem what could easily be a stereotype. Patricia Collins' Hannah takes beautifully unforced of a last speech, chronicling the uneventfulness of her life, that shows Thompson at her best, pitiless and compassionate at once. everybody in this play gets to soliloquize; Julians monologue doesnt save him from being an authorial puppet, but Nigel Bennett animates him very well. dean gabourie's production welds the performances sensitively together, and also supplies some visual flash, which doesn't hurt.

When Scott Went worth's Shylock first comes up with his pound-of-flesh proposition, he's very cool and businesslike about it. Well, he is a businessman. Theres an undercurrent of humour there too; he does call it a "merry bond" and this Shyock seems truly tickled at the idea of making so outlandish a deal. Its a note he sounds again, more emphatically, when in his next speech the Jew throws up his hands in pious horror at the Christians' idea that he would ever collect so meaningless a forfeit. But there's a third layer as well. I hate him, Shylock has already said of Antonio; and the hatred, well earned by Antonios behaviour to him, burns beneath everything he subsequently says or does. The rare merit of Wentworths performance is that he can convey all these levels simultaneously.

His power and clarity are remarkable. This is an actor who can command the Stratford Festival stage with voice and stance, even when he has his back to us. He is not an especially sympathetic Shylock. Stern and narrow by temperament, he's a man rendered

bitter by persecution; Antoni Cimolino's production, set in 1930s Fascist Italy, presents a society in which traditional marginalization is inching its way toward outright statesanctioned brutality. But he does appreciate the irony by which the merchant who has delighted in insulting and humiliating him now needs his financial assistance, and it seems for a time that the dark humour of this situation, which he spells out with relish, will be enough in itself to sustain him; he has, after all, no good reason to expect that Antonio will default on his debt. He enjoys the idea that Bassanio may waste the "borrowed purse" for which his friend Antonio stands surety, but thats a side dish; it isnt going to stop Antonio's ships from coming in.

What tips him, of course, is the elopement of his daughter Jessica with a Christian and a casket of ducats. (Good to be reminded that there are four caskets in this play, not three.) He comes home, in this staging, to find the mezuzah torn from his gates by the revellers who have abducted her. Not that there's been much noticeable warmth in the father-daughter relationship; the fondest gesture is the guilt-laden hug that Jessica (Sara Farb) bestows on Shylock just prior to robbing and deserting him.

By the time he reaches the trial, Wentworths Shylock is twice obsessed: with revenge and with the law. The latter is as almost as important to him as the former; hes having his day in court (it may, in this production's context, be the last a Jew in Venice will ever

have, and he knows it) and he hugs the legal rightness of his cause. You get the feeling that if Portia could find a valid weakness in his case, he would give in, though probably not gracefully; he scans the bond very carefully to see if it requires a surgeon to be present.

And indeed, when Portia does defeat him, on hair-splitting grounds, his incredulous response is, "Is that the law?" Assured that it is, he tries, like the practical man he is, to make the best of it. Only when his opponents further turn the screws on him - again legally - does he momentarily, savagely, threaten to break out: a stunning moment, and one I don't remember seeing before.

Thanks largely, but by no means entirely, to its Shylock, this trial scene is immensely exciting. Well, all right, it usually is. Whats more surprising is that the big casket scene is almost equally suspenseful. This, too, has to do with context. The stage is thronged with Portias household and Bassanio's followers, all of them desperate to see him make the right choice, and their involvement communicates itself to us. Just as remarkable is the last scene: that awkward mixture of squabbling and celebration, in which everyone tries to behave as if Shylock had never existed. There's a palpable chill in the Belmont air; Lorenzos speech in praise of music is cued by his attempts to find a radio station that doesnt feature a frenzied oration by Hitler or Mussolini. The production does seem to suggest that there was no difference between the two, in terms of anti-Semitism; that wasn't the case, at least at that date, but it's a forgivable elision. No wonder Lorenzo, with a Jewish wife, is feeling uneasy; no wonder Michelle Girouxs highly intelligent Portia is perturbed and even somewhat guilty. Shes begun the play, like a regency or restoration heroine, making fun of her unwelcome pan-European suitors and mocking their accents; she gives herself most gracefully to Bassanio; and she discovers herself, both her talents and their consequences, in her male-lawyer disguise.

This is a fluent, thoughtful production, crammed with local colour, with douglas Paraschuk's gated set providing easy access from Venice to Belmont and back. (Full disclosure: my son is the assistant director.) There are some weak performances, but the key ones are strong, beginning with Tom McCamus' Antonio, flaunting a homoerotic melancholy, he never shakes off; he seems, at some level, to want to be sacrificed. Tyrell Crews thinks his way through a feckless Bassanio with unexpected philosophical depths; Tyrone Savage is a lyrical, trenchant Lorenzo; and Jonathan Goads Gratiano plays the fool with a selfconscious exaggeration that suggests, accurately, in terms of his later loutish behaviour, that he has something to hide; its a shame that the curtailing of his one melancholy speech denies him the chance to round the portrait off.

Some what similarly, Antoine Yared is a very funny Prince of Arragon, bearing himself like a cross between Salvador dali and a matador, but he flunks his final moment of self-realization. Sophia Walker's Nerissa is her best performance at Stratford but the production makes surprisingly little, in such a race-conscious play, of Portia's having a black maid.

I have a suspicion that the best play of both highlighting and reconciling this plays contradictions might be to give it an unromanticized 16thcentury setting. This production is thoroughly compelling on its own terms; coming one night after Othello, that other racial Venetian play, it constitutes a grand slam that might be a landmark for Stratford. Indeed thats not all; this season has given us four Shakespeare productions, all different, all good. I can't remember the last time that happened.

This is the summer of our discontent. At least, I seem to have spent much of it watching a prize assortment of Shakespearean grievance-huggers: Shylock and Iago at Stratford, Macbeth in High Park, and now Richard III, currently holding economical but extremely rewarding court in the more modest Toronto parkland known as Withrow.

The villainous company Ive been keeping has prompted me to make some distinctions. Shakespeares plotters and murderers divide into two categories: those with human ties and those without. Shylock, with his wounded love for his daughter and his more grudgingly expressed regard for the servant who also deserts him, clearly belongs in the first camp. So does Claudius in Hamlet, whose murder of his brother is partly caused by love for the brother's wife. So, really, does Macbeth, whose wife made him do it the first time, and whose descent into further crime coincides with her unravelling.

Then there are the loners, some of whom have a disconcerting habit of changing their spots at the last minute. Edmund in King Lear, who starts out cheerfully amoral, develops a conscience towards the play's close when it is, grimly, too late. His fellow bastard don John, in Much Ado About Nothing, gets closer to the model of unredeemed malevolence, but hes a shadowy figure in a predominantly cheerful play. Then theres Aaron the Moor in Titus Andronicus; he could be the villain's villain - he goes to his death regretting any day on which he may have passed up the chance of doing somebody harm, presumably by sleeping late - but even he spoils his record by displaying great tenderness for his newborn son. And so we reach Iago, the only one who admits no positive connection with anyone else at all and also, as graham Abbey is chillingly demonstrating at Stratford, the only one who, for that very reason, gets no fun out of life. Edmund and Aaron revel in their misdeeds; Iago achieves only a cold self-satisfaction. It's commonly and, I think, accurately believed that Shakespeare, when writing Shylock or indeed Falstaff, surprised himself with the depths of humanity he found in them. With Iago the reverse must have happened; he astonished himself by discovering previously uncharted levels of inhumanity. you keep waiting for Iago to crack. He never does.

Richard III does, though only near the last minute and only in a rather artificial speech prompted by artificial means. (He thinks hes had a bad dream. The play says that hes been visited by the ghosts of his victims.) He then pulls himself together and goes unrepentant to his death in battle. Alex McCooeye, the young actor who plays Richard in Withrow Park, deals splendidly with the last self-immolating defiance and better than most with the chop-logic nightmare. But his finest moments have already happened, the most surprising of all being his first appearance. Most richards hug the floor; the late Michael Redgrave once declared that he could never play the role because he was too tall. McCooeye, though, has him all beat in the height department; he looks to be about seven feet. This gives him a lot of limp to carry around, and to complain about.

The complaining, though, is less pervasive than we tend to remember. In diane D'Aquila's production, which is crammed with smart and helpful ideas, he makes his first entrance, shyly and slyly, from behind a tree. He then launches into the familiar lines about peacetime decadence, all that courting and dancing, delivered in high-pitched tones of delectable mockery. Then, suddenly, on the part about not being shaped for sportive tricks, a storm breaks, one of tormented and full throated bitterness; its electric. The cloud passes, and he gets cheerfully down to the business of outlining his homicidal, including fratricidal, path to the throne. And those are the parameters of the performance.

Richard, until the moment he achieves his ambition, belongs with the good-time villains. Once hes there, killing becomes a strategy of survival, still efficient, but increasingly frantic. The pace, of both performance and production, quickens; and it's been going at a good lick to start with. Shakespeare's second-longest play here comes in at less than two hours, and it isnt all down to cutting (though thats extensive and, for the most part, not to be regretted).

Richard doesn't dwell much on his deformity after that first speech. He mocks it, after his successful wooing of Lady Anne, a scene that in this production carries an exceptional erotic charge; he practically has her up against a tree (not the same one). He's mocked for it by his young nephew, the duke of york, one of the Princes not yet in the Tower, who more or less calls him a monkeys organ grinder; in this production the hurt is, for once, more physical than mental, and obviously very deeply felt. Here I must commend Charlie gould, the very promising young actress who plays both Anne and york; you feel that in the former role she might kill Richard as easily as submit to him; later she gets the further benefit of practically hearing her own death-sentence. Vocally, McCooeyes Richard doesn't have much middle ground between a high whistle and a low snarl, but he uses those extremes to capture Richard's menace, his charm, and the terrifying alternation of the two. Visually, hes such an extreme figure that you understand his contemporaries bewilderment; they never know whether to laugh or to tremble.

With a cast of 10 and no other scenery than nature's, D'Aquilas direction makes a superb virtue of economy. This is a modern-dress production, though you hardly notice except when Marc Bondys Buckingham, an operator's operative, is wielding his cellphone. There's no manpower for a funeral procession, so Anne carries her father-in-laws remains about in an urn (the text does helpfully mention his "ashes") that shes unwise enough to entrust to Richard's custody. We know that Richard, when about to secure the execution of Hastings, jocularly sends a bishop for some strawberries; this is the first time I've known him to be eating them when the severed head is delivered. Its about this time, too, that night helpfully descends, as if to signal the beginning of Richards reign of terror. I had thought that the ghosts might have to be cut, or reduced to offstage voices, but they're there, in gripping torchlight procession. Notable supporting in performances include Jesse Griffiths' Clarence and Jacklyn Francis Elizabeth, the second more ambiguous recipient of Richards treeside advances. The director herself adds authority as Richard's mother, the only person present who can cow him with a curse. Brandon McMurtry-Howlett is a richmond who actually gets to kill Richard in person, though you could hardly call it traditional single combat; his snipers already have his opponent in their red-dotted sights, He closes the play in the authentic accents of St. george, somewhat compromised by his brandishing a gun over his head while he does it. This actor is also the artistic director of Shakespeare in the ruff, not to be confused with its predecessor in the park, Shakespeare the rough. They made their debut last summer with a promising but uneven Two Gentlemen of Verona. This year, they really deliver.

Richard III runs through Sept. 1 in Withrow Park.

2013-09-07-physical-skitness-second-city:
The new Second City revue, We Can Be Heroes, contains the funniest beheading number I have ever seen. I'll admit that the competition in this category is limited but, still, this number is gloriously executed. I think thats the right word.

A medieval headsman, dour and as played by Connor Thompson increasingly aggravated, announces from his parapet the imminent death of a traitor. The malefactor, an entrancingly guileless Kevin Vidal confesses his guilt and proclaims his eagerness ("do with me what you will!) to take the consequences. His taking them, however, is only the beginning. youve heard the expression heads will roll"; this head rolls and rolls like Old man river, the result ofwhatmust be supernatural contortions by the parts of the victim's body that remain out of sight. meanwhile the onlookers, strategically positioned around the auditorium, provide mountingly hilarious commentary, whose best bits it costs me a supreme effort of will not to quote. If all this sounds very monty Python, it is, but homage worthy of its lineage. There's rarely been a Second City number that builds and builds and keeps topping itself as this one does.

But then there have been few Second City shows as consistently good as this one. Physically, under the direction of Kerry Griffin, it reaches new levels of agility and inventiveness, and it has a thoroughbred cast. Thompson, a newcomer with the square jaw and square voice of everybodys straight man, exploits and explodes that persona in a virtuoso solo spot as a vainglorious lifeguard who happens to be legally blind. (but he can hear you cry for help and, failing that, he can smell your fear.) After barking out answers to the audiences questions - I've seen the show twice, and he coped imperturbably with two different sets of them - he leaves us with the frightening twin thoughts that water is our enemy and that we're 80% composed of the stuff. The sketch is indeed a high-water mark, but its closely followed - actually its immediately followed - by another winner in which Vidal, another new Second Citizen, plays a black senior citizen, whose only friend and visitor is a plump and disconsolate schoolgirl, disappointed to discover that he can't solve all her problems for her like the nice old black men she sees on TV. (bullied by her peers, she says she would run away to Japan except that the people there are so small, the clothes wouldn't fit her.) Jan Caruana, also new, is the moppet who cant keep her knees or her frock still. both she and Vidal are, apart from anything else, excellent actors; Caruana indeed is unnervingly touching playing the same girl in one of Second Citys trademark sequel scenes, one whose tearful impact is only increased by the certain knowledge that its emotional balloon is going to be punctured by a punchline. I must admit though that the line itself turns out when uttered to be no great shakes. It seems that every time I review a Second City show, I complain that they rarely know how to end a routine. I hereby register that complaint again.

I must however suspend it for the item in which Stacey mcGunnigle, a comparative and consistently invaluable SC veteran, plays the curlywigged blunt-speaking voter of every progressive pollster's nightmares. (She doesn't know, and many of us will sympathize with her, what Nuit blanche is meant to be about. That isnt the punchline.) Craig brown is an unassuming but protean performer, whose turns range from a bumptious fellow shamed into undergoing a prostate exam to a tall small boy, persuaded that the bearded man beside him on the subway is Santa Claus en route to the North Pole via Finch. (Hes persuaded because he can't think of any other reason for anyone to be going to Finch.) Allison Price, a returning artist of delightful beanpole proportions, pairs off with biden in a dialogue for two figure-skaters wondering whether to boycott the russian Olympics, punctuating their discourse by describing light-fantastic patterns across invisible ice. This is the comic-choreographic highlight of a show in which everybody is a lovely mover, from Thompson as a provocatively terpsichorean bat first observed hanging coyly from the ceiling of an unwisely rented cottage to the volunteers, one per show, cajoled on to the stage to match limbs and poses with the professionals and, on each of my visits, more than holding their own. There's also a honey of a scene in which a husband feels his virility challenged by a pair of super-competent removal men who impress his wife, a delightful mcGunnigle, with words like "stud.

The weakest parts of the entertainment are, as usual, the musical ones. Nobody in the cast is a singer, though Price is nice in a song about the difficulty of distinguishing a hipster from a homeless person: a funny idea that isnt developed. Theres a title number that opens and closes the proceedings and, again as usual, has nothing to do with the rest of the show. In its first iteration it has one neat line, about the odds against being a Superman in a society that has abolished phone booths; the reprise endlessly and pointlessly repeats a joke from a preceding sketch, thereby exposing both of Second City's Achilles' heels - musicality and finality - at the same time. mostly though this is an uncommonly stylish and witty show, for which the invariable Camellia Koo has designed an unconventional, in this context, brick-walled set that comes in very handy for scenes that are set in houses and also for scenes that arent.

Stefan Dzeparsokis Birdland Theatre production of Fortune and Men's Eyes bears a family resemblance to his Gruesome Playground Injuries for the same company. Once again he has a wide open set, minimally furnished but hung and strewn with motifs. This time, though, neither the cast nor the text are strong enough to justify the treatment. John Herbert's 40-year-old Canadian classic" concerns four male prisoners, all homosexual by either nature or viciously enforced necessity, crammed into the same cell; the spaciousness could hardly be less appropriate or, once the first image has been absorbed, less helpful. Two of the actors, Cyrus Faird as the rooster rocky and Alex Fiddes as the queeny Queenie, give caricatured, vocally indistinct performances, rendered more obscure by having the theatres airconditioning running full blast almost throughout. Its turned off to allow us to listen to the big scene between david Coomber's mona and Julian deZotti's Smitty, both of whom are indeed worth listening to. deZotti is an intelligent and commanding actor, but he presses too hard to make some artificial dialogue sound natural; his journey from innocent to victim to new boss same as the old boss is a series of snapshots rather than a logical progression. Coomber plays a victim who has embraced victimhood as survival, almost as identity, and hes truthful and touching. The two jointly recite the Shakespeare sonnet that gives the play its title, and on which it relies to summon the emotion that it cant produce on its own. The situation is disturbing and persuasive; the writing is sentimental posing as tough. dzeparoski's last production was impressive; this one is just pretentious.

We Can Be Heroes runs indefinitely at the Second City Mainstage (416-343-0011); Fortune and Men's Eyes runs at the Dancemakers Studio, Distillery District, through Sept. 8.
