2013-09-10-frosty-the-showman-on-david-f:
London, Saturday, Nov.

24, 1962. (I've checked the date.) I was in my last year of grammar school - high school, to you over here - and came home late in the evening to find my family around the television. This was not unusual. The set was tuned to the bbC; that wasnt unusual either. What was unusual was the program they were watching. It was the premiere of what seemed to be some kind of variety show, but unlike most in that genre it was obviously going out live. even more surprisingly, it was making jokes about politics and politicians, quite rude and personal ones: the same kind of jokes that people in real life made all the time, but that you never, ever heard on TV. It was more than surprising; it was liberating.

The show was titled That Was The Week That Was, commonly known in very short order asTW3. And presiding over it was somebody who looked and sounded like an uppity undergraduate, and whose name was david Frost.

He was indeed a recent Cambridge graduate, and had made a name there as a performer with the universitys legendary and, over the years, extraordinarily influential intimate revue club, the Footlights. Since coming down he had made some cabaret and TV appearances, but essentially he was unknown. He had come up through the state-school system and spoke in a voice that seemed both fresh and familiar, individual and generic; it hinted at no particular region, no particular class, and managed to combine elements of both squeak and sneer while still being ingratiating. The voice remained pretty much unchanged for the rest of his career, though naturally the appearance didn't. In his later years he came to look quite elderstatesmanlike, his hair soberly sandy, but back when he started it was dark, with an accusatory widow's peak that one reviewer declared (approvingly) to be an affront in itself. The obituaries that followed his death last week on board the Queen elizabeth have mostly concentrated on his later activities as a multiple interviewerof presidents and prime ministers and as a TV mogul on his own account: Frosty the Showman. but that young persona and the use he made of it remain his most important achievement, and the most far-reaching.

What the look, the voice, and the persistent wagging finger conveyed was an indictment of the british ruling class (and it certainly was a class), not so much for being corrupt or inefficient as for being absurd. In 1962, with Harold macmillans Conservative government in apparently secure power, this wasnt just startling, it was practically revolutionary. Nor were the broken taboos exclusively political. One thing that struck me on that Saturday night was that, for the first time ever on british TV, people were being funny about sex. mentioning it at all, except perhaps on science programs, was practically unheard of. Later on, TW3 presented "a consumer's guide to religion", anticipating by some 40 years the much-missed God-slot that Stephen Colbert used to do on The Daily Show before he got his own Report. TW3's venture into sacrilege prompted at least one clergyman to write to the newspapers, demanding that this horrible programme be swept from the screens of a Christian country. Interestingly Frost, like the devoutly Catholic Colbert, was aChristian; he was the son of amethodist minister, and had considered entering the ministry himself.

TW3 did not of course come out of nowhere. The previous year had seen the London opening of the incomparably hilarious revue beyond the Fringe, in which four other recent graduates - Peter Cook and Jonathan miller from Cambridge, Alan bennett and dudley moore from Oxford - had expanded the targets and techniques of british stage comedy beyond what anybody had thought possible. It was inspired; I had never laughed as much in the theatre (still havent) and neither had anybody else, at least nobody else I knew. Cook capitalized on its success to open what was described as "a satirical nightclub" named, with an irony no less effective for being thumpingly obvious, The establishment.

Satirical. Satire. Those were the words. everybody wanted a piece of them. Theatres and clubs, though, were privileged zones. Putting this kind of thing on TV took real cheek. The man who possessed it, and who recruited Frost, was Ned Sherrin, a young bbC producer who had come up through a lively news program called Tonight but was more of a showbiz creature than a current affairs one. (He was a political animal only in the professional sense.) He caught a peculiar cultural moment in britain; it was the immediate pre-beatles era and the shows preferred music, what was cool at the time, was jazz. The improvisational spirit extended to the visuals; cameras, cables and microphone-booms were proudly visible. That's a cliche now, but it was immensely refreshing at the time. The casualness extended to the running-time; the show was the last thing on in the evening and could overrun or underrun according to what was in the week's news that could be made fun of.

And presiding over it all, giving it its tone, was Frost. He wasnt a great comedian (his solo bits usually fell flat) but he was the perfect front-man. He had a fine team of actors supporting him, and what seemed an inexhaustible stable of writers. One of them was Peter Cook, though it seems that he and Frost werent friends. Cook described Frost, with whom he had overlapped at the Footlights, as a bubonic plagiarist. Later on, when the non-swimming Frost was taking a dip in Cook's pool, Cook did save him from drowning; but according to Alan bennett, speaking at Cook's funeral, he always maintained that it was the one thing in his life he regretted doing. (A related legend holds that michael bentine, a gentler and zanier comic of the preceding generation, once sent Frost a telegram that read "dear mr. Frost, I think you are a cult" and signed it "michael beltine.") TW3 got lucky with history. The John Profumo-Christine Keeler scandal erupted in 1963, providing an endless source of material that it gleefully and relentlessly exploited. The commercial stations of the time would never have touched the show, and it had plenty of enemies within the bbC itself. Schedulers did their best to sabotage the second season, and were only foiled by the top-level intervention of Sir Hugh Carleton-Greene, brother of Graham Greene the novelist and the most enlightened director General that the corporation known, fondly and otherwise, as Auntie bbC ever had. There wasnt a third season; there was a general election coming up and it was decreed that satire, or whatever it was, would be tactless. The show could at least claim to have been the author of its own destruction; it had been widely credited with bringing down the macmillan government. This is unlikely, but it had certainly captured and fostered an increasingly skeptical national mood.

And, it turned out, an international mood. In 1964, with the british version off the air, the u.S. produced its own TW3 series, with Frost again involved, inaugurating a bicontinental career that at one point had him commuting by Concorde twice a week. (It seems fitting that he should have died while crossing the Atlantic.) Canada had This Hour Has Seven Days, similar to the british show in title and tone, and also in being cut off in its prime. Sherrin, without Frost, went on to produce two similar though less successful series, that incidentally were as hard on the new Labour prime minister, Harold Wilson, as their predecessors had been on Harold macmillan: harder, probably. Frost, without Sherrin, hosted and produced a show called The Frost Report that was less topically centred and lampooned social types rather than individuals. Always a good talent-spotter, he assembled a supporting team that included yet another Footlights graduate, John Cleese, who soon went on to be one-sixth of Monty Pythons Flying Circus. I was at Cambridge, and in the Footlights, in the years immediately after TW3, and the style was already more pre-Python than post-Frost. Frost might have been grooming the stable of comedy that was to replace his own.

Except it didn't. The Pythons were actually the anarchic heirs of TW3 (though they also owed a debt to Lewis Carroll). They didn't have to establish that english public life was ridiculous; that had already been done. They didnt have to attack individual targets; why ridicule a particular politician when you can invent the ministry of Silly Walks? Theyve been the dominant influence on british and North American comedy ever since.

Still, something had gone missing. Saturday Night Live has been inadvertently proving it for nearly 40 years now, imitating the TW3 formula, right down to the time slot, without approaching either its bite or its free-wheeling spirit. It wasn't until 1999 that there appeared on TV a direct descendant of TW3, a comedy show explicitly based on the news. It is of course The Daily Show with Jon Stewart, with- since 2005 - its spin-off The Colbert Report. People in britain used to say that they had to keep up with the news in order to appreciate the jokes of Frost and company; they now say exactly the same about Stewart and Colbert. (Well, there are worse reasons.)

There are obviously differences. America now is a more bitterly divided society than britain in the '60s ever was, and the shows reflect that. Then theres the matter of technology: the TW3 team did impersonations; the newguys can rely on video clips to have their targets convict themselves out of their own mouths. They are also more talented comedians than Frost; indeed Colbert,who combines traditional performance skills with a razor mind and whose blowhard persona is a great and brilliantly sustained creation in its own right, is a comedic genius, a consummate verbal tightrope artist. Stewart is playing a less complicated game, and hes prone to excessive mugging, but both he and Colbert have it all over Frost in the underlying seriousness department. They do irony where Frost did sarcasm. Frost's manner on TW3 never suggested that anything much was at stake; Stewart is at his best when the humour is coming out of barely-controlled anger. (This also distinguishes him from bill maher, whose nervous giggling at his own jokes makes him unwatchable.) Stewart is also the best interviewer on TV: the only one who asks a question as if he would actually like to know the answer and then follows it up as if he were conducting something resembling a conversation. I imagine that at some point he'll tire of having to cram these encounters into 10-minute segments, a portion of which have to be spent proving that he can still be funny; and that he will devote himself to full-length, if not full-time, interviewing. If he does, he will of course be following in Frost's later footsteps, as he already has in the earliest, most valuable ones. david Frost, at the dawn of his career, showed television, and the world, that it didn't have to respect respectability.

In the opening sequence of The Invisible Woman, the movie (screened at TIFF) about Charles Dickens late-life affair with a young actress, we meet the lady concerned, Ellen Ternan, in her own later life. Shes married and has given up the stage, though she's putting her early training to use by supervising juvenile amateur dramatics. Somebody asks her whether she was the inspiration for Lucie Manette, the heroine of A Tale of Two Cities. She doesn't deny it, but doesnt seem to want to dwell on the matter. Neither does the film, which is a pity.

A Tale of Two Cities is one of Dickens last three completed novels, the others being Great Expectations and Our Mutual Friend. It's generally believed that Dickens' relationship with Ternan influenced his portrayal of the young ladies in those books; theyre generally more temperamental, more teasing, than the monochromatic love-objects of the earlier stories. Lucie, admittedly, doesnt quite fit the new pattern; she's a pretty, virtuous nonentity, only interesting because she has a father, released from the Bastille, to mentally support. But two men love her: two men so identical in appearance that one of them, the dissolute Sydney Carton, can take the place of the other, the noble Charles Darnay, on the guillotine and thus do the far, far better thing that supplies the novel's celebrated climax.

Note that one of them has the same initials, indeed the same first name, as the author himself. And if ever an author was name-conscious, it was Dickens. So he gets to split himself between two look-alikes, and to enjoy both the satisfaction of getting the girl and the sweet noble agony of giving her up. Which, for a man experiencing both the guilt and the pleasure of an illicit affair, must have been quite a release. Though I have to say that The Invisible Woman goes easy on the guilt.

In fact The Invisible Woman makes dickens himself a none-too-visible man, or at least an opaque one. Its reasonably enjoyable, but ralph Fiennes, in his second outing as actor-director, brings to it neither the visual flair nor the performing authority that distinguished his brilliant modern-dress version of Coriolanus. Admittedly a writer writing is even harder to make dramatically interesting than a painter painting or a composer composing. but the film keeps hinting at connections that it doesnt pursue. Its main story is told to us in flashbacks, prompted by ellen's staging of a play written by dickens and his friend Wilkie Collins, and also by the friendly questioning of a quite unnecessary clergyman who fancies himself as an amateur psychiatrist. (everyone in her new life seems to know of ellen's association with dickens, but not how intimate it was.).One thing she tells him is that she was the model for estella, the heroine of Great Expectations whom Pip, the very autobiographical hero, loves but cannot have, up to and very much including their final meeting on the books last page. At least thats how dickens originally wrote it. he was persuaded by his close friend and future biographer John Forster that his public would never stand for so unromantic a conclusion. ellen, impressively anticipating generations of literary critics, says that the change was an artistic mistake.

What it's supposed to mean to her is uncertain. Is she bitter that dickens could never marry her, as Pip marries estella? Is she wishing that their affair had never happened at all? (There's some doubt as to whether the relationship was consummated, but the film, following Claire Tomalins book, takes the persuasive viewthat it was, and that ellen bore a child that died at birth.) And how does she feel about the novels whole depiction of estella who, raised by the crazedmisshavisham to break men's hearts, might be described as the tease of all time? dickens went on to create, in Our Mutual Friend, another, more everyday flirt in bella Wilfer who rejects the supposedly poor hero's addresses because she has her heart set on marrying money, and has to be educated into love. ellen, estella, bella: the names chime but, from what the film shows us, the fictional ladies are very unfair depictions of the real one, who doesnt lead dickens on, initially resists him as any well brought up young lady of the period might, gives in because shes come to love him, and is no kind of gold digger. (her mother apparently is; she urges ellen to become the great man's mistress, as she's never going to make it as an actress. Though it does seem for a moment as if Kristin Scott Thomas mrs Ternan, a fine figure of a woman, is about to offer herself to dickens in her daughters stead.) Fiennes' performance does capture the energy of the man who wrote like a demon and also edited, did public readings, socialized and even hiked like one; you can see why he would have needed a comparable sexual outlet, but there's no investigation of why, having found it, he would translate his lover into the tormenting figures of those last novels.

Maybe it was guilt. he certainly had plenty to feel guilty about, and not just by Victorian standards. The great glorifier of hearth and home treated his wife atrociously, sending her as a go-between to ellen and letting her learn of the marital separation from a selfrighteous letter published in the Times. This much the film does show us, very effectively; but mrs. dickens then disappears from the screen and, it seems, from her husbands mind. We arent shown his behaviour to his children, raised to emulate him and then frozen out when they failed to measure up to his own great expectations.

We are shown his social, as opposedto personal, conscience at work; and that's to the film's credit. he raises, with all the charmandpassion in the world, impressive sums for the rescue of fallen women. Sometimes the social and the personal coincide; hes embarrassed when a passing copper mistakes ellen for a prostitute, shocked when an actual prostitute accosts him and cant believe it when he offers her money not to have sex. These are the kind of scenes that lurk beneath the surface of dickens' novels and that the pieties of the time wouldn't allow him to depict Throughout dickens' work courts and prisons were to remain the symbols of organized injustice, and the happy endings were to get less definitively happy; the favoured enclaves into which the heroes and heroines and their friends and relations withdraw themselves in the last chapter seem more and more like fragile defences against an inhuman world. by the final books, the convention has been abandoned almost entirely; Our Mutual Friend, last and in some ways greatest of the novels, hardly has formal ending at all. Its image for society is a garbage dump, politely called a dust heap, and it offers its definitive comment on Victorian values in the character of mr. Podsnap, the businessman who combines pomposity, insularity and philistinism; who literally waves away all unpleasant subjects; and who judges life and art on whether they will bring a blush to the cheek of some mythical young Person.

None of this of course stopped dickens from doing very well-socially, financially, artistically - out of the world he criticized and, as far as we can tell, from enjoying his success. but he must have felt the contradictions; they may have fuelled the frenzied activity that shortened his life, and of which the ellen Ternan affair, which he must have seen as a refuge, was actually a symptom. his comparatively early death-he was 58-is something else that The Invisible Woman never gets around to mentioning. Consciously or not, the complexities of his life found issue in his books. Somebody should make a film about it.

Karl Marx famously said that history repeats itself, the first time as tragedy, the second time as farce. In fact he said it so famously that, if he were able to collect royalties for every time it was quoted, he would be a very rich anticapitalist indeed. As well, of course, as a very longlived one. Tom Stoppard's Arcadia,, which has just closed at the Shaw Festival but had better be revived, teaches a different lesson. Juxtaposing events in the same stately home 200 years apart, it says that history happens twice, the first time as farce, the second time as farce.

Or maybe Karl was right, because there is a tragic element hidden away in the older of the two storylines: Thomasina Coverly, the 16yearold mathematical prodigy whom the audience has come to cherish, is destined to die in a fire immediately after the play's last scene, her first love unconsummated, her genius unknown. The only reason we know about it is that it's one of the facts discovered by the presentday section of the cast, in the course of their (generally misguided) efforts to investigate the house's past. They only mention it in passing and it's quite easy to miss, as is their reference to the fate of Thomasina's beloved tutor Septimus who despaired and became a hermit. So, come to think of it, is the key to the play's title, taken from an iconic memento mori: "Et in Arcadia, ego," says Death; "Even in Arcadia, I am here."

Stoppard does like to make his emotional points in a sidelong, almost deflationary way; it's something that links him, surprisingly perhaps, to Chekhov. Think of A. E. Housman in The Invention of Love lamenting of a passion that dared not speak its name: "I would have died for you, but I never had the luck." Or of Rosencrantz exclaiming to Guildenstern after discovering that they're escorting Hamlet to his death: "But we're his friends" Or of Henry Carr in Travesties failing to stop the Russian Revolution in its tracks because he's too busy with an amateur production of The Importance of Being Earnest. Or of the fact that the most wrenching moment in any of the plays is a man stepping on a tortoise in Jumpers: tragedy and farce happening simultaneously.

The tragic undertones of Arcadia are especially hard to bring to the surface, there being so much else going on, and Eda Holmes' Shaw production didn't manage it; it was one of

the evening's few weaknesses. But perhaps, as Septimus tells Thomasina preconflagration, it doesn't matter: everything that's lost will be rediscovered. It would be nice to think that might be true of the production itself: that it should have a future. Even in Niagara, where it sold out before it opened, it was seen by very few people; given a short run in the Studio while Faith Healer, a play with far less obvious appeal (i.e. fewer jokes), was holding the larger stage of the Royal George. Though, to be fair, Holmes was able to use the Studio space in ways that wouldn't have been possible in more formal surroundings; the audience entered and exited through the playingspace, as if we too were part of the history of the house and of its allimportant garden.

Still, even if that effect had to be sacrificed, this production should be given a longer and wider life. There are precedents. Last year's Studio production of Topdog/Underdog was successfully transferred to Toronto (its being a coproduction with Obsidian may have made the process easier); the Tarragon has played host to the Stratford studio production of The Little Years and is about to do the same for The Best Brothers. The logistics of transferring a major mainstage production might well be insuperable, but it would be wonderful to have Arcadia and another recent Shaw studio triumph, When the Rain Stops Falling, playing in repertory at, perhaps, Berkeley Street or the Young Centre. And after they've played the centre of the universe, they could be shown off to the rest of Canada.

Let us now praise a famous actress; maybe I could be biased here the best one in the world. I'm always bemused when I hear TV comedians referring in mocksepulchral tones to "Dame Judi Dench" as if she were Dame Edith Evans intoning "A handbag." Actually, when Dench herself played Lady Bracknell, which she did with uncompromising rigour but also with a novel hint of flirtatiousness, she downplayed that line, as nearly all postEvans Bracknells must, in sheer selfdefence, have felt obliged to do. It didn't matter; she got every other possible laugh.

Anyway, she may be a Dame but it's hard to think of an actress, or a woman, less grande.

I'm lucky; I've been able to follow her career from its very beginning, which was in 1958 when, straight out of drama school, she played Ophelia at the Old Vic to John Neville's Hamlet. The critical consensus, which had my adolescent endorsement, was that she was ineffectual in the early scenes but very good, very real, when she went mad. And real, it turned out, was what she was about. She confirmed it later that season when she played a lively and funny Maria, the waitingwoman in Twelfth Night. This was an in genue with the soul of a character actress.

Ingenue was what she did for the next few seasons at the Vic, culminating in her Juliet for a generation, in a groundbreakingproduction by Franco Zeffirelli. (If you've only seen the Zeffirelli movie, without Judi, you haven't lived.) Jump forward 20 years to her playing the tough, loving Juno in Trevor Nunn's perfect production of Juno and the Paycock, brisk and warm and unsentimental, which is a good summation off her, onstage and off. Everyone's sweetheart had turned into everyone's mother. She was also the only Englishborn performer among a cast of Irish expatriates, and she fit right in. Now, after three further decades, she's again impeccably Irish in the movie Philomena (shown at TIFF), as a workingclass Catholic mother searching for the illegitimate son whom the nuns had torn from her and given up for adoption 50 years before. It's an overcute film with roadmovie ambitions, hobbled by the determination of writer and costar Steve Coogan to make it as much about him as about her. She has to play as much for mischief as pain, but you believe every moment of both. An added pleasure for me, and I imagine for her, is the casting, as the most monstrous of the sisters, of Barbara Jefford who, though only a few years older, was leading lady at the Old Vic when she was a beginner. Within a few years they were playing together, marvellously, as Gwendolen and Cecily in The Importance.

Philomena is one of two doubleacts I've seen her do this year. The other, live in London and opposite Ben Whishaw, was in Peter and Alice, about the embittered later lives of the children who were the models for Alice in Wonderland and Peter Pan; a pointless piece except for giving her the opportunity to play aged, hardbitten asperity while radiating undiminished, unforced star quality, onstage and off. An actor who worked with her at the English Stratford once said that even just sitting in the green room she knocked him out, and I know what he meant.

Repression exploded has always been one of the things she's done best. It can take many forms. In Harold Pinter's A Kind of Alaska, she played a woman awakened from years of sleeping sickness. Watching her take her first steps across the room, tentative but determined, as if her muscles were remembering what to do, was like watching human motion reduced to its essence. It was one of the purest pieces of acting I've ever seen.

And if you're wondering what any of this has to do with Arcadia: Well, if Tom Stoppard had got around to writing it earlier say in 1962 Judi would have been the perfect Thomasina. That was the year she played another young woman, from roughly the same period, also experiencing a doomed first love but surviving it better, in John Whiting's A Penny for a Song.

It was one of the plays in which the young Judi Dench showed how enchantingly good she was at falling in love, and what fun it could be to watch her and to share the feeling. It hasn't gone away.

Richard Sheridan Willis is a nicely grandiloquent name for an actor. Its owner-as he tells us in his autobiographical show Strolling Player - is not only an actor but the child of actors. He was born in Stratford upon-Avon, England, though not, as you might expect, because his parents were members of the company there. They had in fact made a special pilgrimage to Shakespeares birthplace so that it might be their son's as well. Biblical parallels come to mind.

The treatment took. Willis speaks Shakespeare very well, and his show is dotted with speeches from the plays, mostly the famous ones. His early theatrical experience, though, was far from Stratford, in terms of both geography and prestige. His father ran a company in Guernsey, one of the Channel Islands, in a period - the late 1960s - that must have been among the last days of weekly rep. Willis gives a vivid account of a childhood spent taking tickets, helping sets get built and dismantled and presumably playing the odd juvenile role. The repertoire was Agatha Christie, farce and the occasional Shakespeare or Ibsen to keep the actors from mutiny." The ambience, of both stage and auditorium, seems to have been an intriguing mixture of gentility and sweat.

From there, Willis progressed to drama school and then to a professional career that's been split, like that of most actors, between stage, film and TV; and also, unlike that of most actors, between three countries: the U.K., the U.S., and Canada where he now lives, having taken a Canadian wife. (Shes Heidi Reimer, an author, whos his co-writer here.) It's been, from what we gather, an up-and down life, symbolized perhaps in the outfit that he wears: a nice, cream-coloured suit in an extreme state of disrepair, one leg cut off at the knee. He has entertaining stories about fighting to retain his death scene in an episode of Dr. Who; understudying Antony Sher's marathon role in the West End production of Harvey Fiersteins Torch Song Trilogy (but never going on); marvelling at the ferocious power of an unknown young repertory actor called Daniel Day-Lewis; and falling incongruously off the stage while playing a suave man-about-town in an Oscar Wilde society drama. He also does a killer impersonation of Richard Burton, who figures in an anecdote with an especially good punchline.

Whats lacking is much sense of how these isolated incidents fit together. The show was apparently inspired by the exhaustive Canadian immigration form on which Willis was required to fill in his entire biography since turning 18: a daunting task for anyone, and especially for a self-described "strolling player. Having gone to all that trouble, he's turned the results into a performance.

A bureaucratic inventory can do without connective tissue; a play, though-or, if you prefer, a theatrical event - really can't. The Shakespeare extracts are plainly intended to serve this purpose, but they dont, good though they often are in themselves. Kicking off with all the worlds a stage" seems too flamingly obvious, but Willis won me over with the unusual sardonic emphasis he gave to the line about "the bubble reputation. It may even be meant to key into his own career, though we're never told what his own professional reputation has been: where, at any given moment, he has fit into the pecking order of British actors, or how often, on his own turf, he was able to put his love of Shakespeare into practice. I don't know what the inclusion of the kings repentance - or attempted repentance - speech from Hamlet is supposed to illustrate. This confession of a brothers murder here oddly prefaces an account of his father's funeral. The best integrated of these excerpts, and one of the best executed, is an anti-romantic speech of Benedick from Much Ado About Nothing: a role he happened to be playing while falling in love.

There's a lot about the actors love life, and its either too much or too little. Falling in and out of love and even of marriage is something that happens to most people, and if we're to be interested in one person's experience of it rather than anothers, then we need some specifics. Delicacy may well forbid him from naming names, but since he raises the subject one would like to know more about his first marriage and why it fell apart. Its aftershocks are felt in a longish section about his paparazzi-stalked relationship with a young actress (again unnamed but easy to detect) in Peter Halls production of The Master Builder, starring Alan Bates. This production, by the way, followed its London run with a season at the Royal Alex in Toronto, though it predated Willis' move here by several years. In the meantime, he seems to have spent much of his working life in America. Again one would like to know how this came about - green cards don't grown on trees - but theres a delightful account of giving a Shakespeare recital in the White House before President George W. Bush. (I liked him," says one of his fellow-performers afterwards; "its very confusing.) Indeed it seems to have been in the States, and especially in Chicago, that Willis' Shakespearean career has blossomed. Looking him up on the web, I found an interview that goes into far more detail on the theory and practice of playing Shakespeare than the show ever does, though I think the show would be better for the inclusion. It's a pleasant experience, though, one that left me wanting to see Willis in a play. Or in another play, since I did see that Master Builder when I myself was new in Canada, though I can't claim to remember much about it, except a feeling that Bates was too likeable for his role. At one point Willis describes himself as painfully shy and reticent." That's not uncommon among actors, even those doing first person, one-man shows. It would be another paradox worth exploring.

robert.cushman@hotmail.com Strolling Player runs through Sept. 27 at the Red Sandcastle Theatre

JohnCleese, currently embarked on what his title would suggest is a farewell tour of Canada, comes before us on an empty stage and a full video screen. When we enter the theatre, the screen is occupied by that title, Last Time to See Me Before I Die, spelled out in large letters. One of the letters is cheekily surmounted by the figure of the Grim Reaper, himself one of Cleese's own greatest roles. (See Monty Python and The Meaning of Life.) A few minutes before opening time, with the audience still fully lit and chattering, he wanders onstage, looks at his watch, gives an embarrassed grimace, and wanders off again. This means he has us laughing helplessly before his show even starts. I hope that isnt a spoiler.

When the lights do go down, the screen lights up to show us Cleese as Reaper moving menacingly through a montage of everybodys favourite clips from Monty Python and Fawlty Towers, all of them still jaw-breakingly hilarious. And then the man himself saunters back on, and furthers his disarmament program by copping to what he says we're all thinking, i.e. doesn't he look old? Actually, the shock isnt that he looks old onstage - in fact, hes 73 and well preserved, even if his socks are odd, his pants baggy and his waistline expanded-but that he looks so young onscreen. Admittedly, most of the scenes we're shown were shot in the 1960s and '70s, but even then Cleeses specialty was playing deranged authority figures. One remembers him as having always seemed middle-aged.

I cant recall him ever having done a solo turn on his TV shows. His scenes were always two-handers at the very least, and he isn't trying to reinvent himself as a standup comic now. What he's offering is an easygoing illustrated memoir, offhandedly and expertly delivered with the aid of a face-mic, a teleprompter, and a sense of timing thats fast, dry and unimpaired. Hes doing it, he tells us, to raise the money to pay an outstanding $2-million on a $22-million alimony settlement with his third wife, about whom his remarks are not charitable. He's also cutting, though rather more affectionately so, about his birthplace of Weston-super-Mare, described as a supernally dull English seaside town that got bombed during the war, despite the fact that there was nothing in it to destroy.Maybe, he muses, Goebbels had a relative there against whom he had a grudge. Or maybe the Germans were trying to prove that they did, so, have a sense of humour.

He tells us about his father, of whom he seems to have been fond, and about his mother, an undemanding person who wanted only one thing: "her way." She died at 101 having lived through all the upheavals of the 20th century without, he says, noticing any of them. (Well, he concedes, she did notice between 1939 and 1945 that there was a war on, started by somebody called Hilter.) She also suffered, it seems, from phobias both agora and claustro, making it very difficult for her to find a comfortable space. Thence to school, where he was bullied by boys smaller than himself. But then everybody in that school was shorter than the 12-year old Cleese, including the masters. His height, of course, was to prove a major factor in his comedy career - it fuelled his Silly Walk and Basil Fawlty's frenzies - though he does seem to have shrunk in more recent years. In time-honoured fashion he defended himself at school by making people laugh. He also made them laugh at university, becoming a member of the famous Cambridge Footlights, appearing in a show of theirs that, under the title of Cambridge Circus, transferred to London. (He downplays his contribution to this shows success; it was probably substantial.) After graduating, he was rescued from a career in law by a producer who sent Cambridge Circus to New Zealand (which, by his account, made Westonsuper-Mare seem up-to-date) and to New York. The show flopped on Broadway - thank you, New York Times - but Cleese was rescued by David Frost, a consistent benefactor, who engaged him as a writer/performer on his TV show The Frost Report on which he made a mark, and then gave him a TV showcase of his own, At Last the 1948 Show (also featuring the bugeyes Marty Feldman), which I could kick myself for having forgotten and of which I was very glad to be reminded. And from there to the shows and movies we all know about, the theatre audience torn between delight at the excerpts that are included and frustration over those that arent.

In the second half, Cleese talks about black humour, instancing the stage and TV shows that immediately preceded him: Beyond the Fringe, which he calls the best show he's ever seen (me, too) and That Was the Week That Was. I agree that their broaching of political and other subjects previously off limits were liberating, even intoxicating, but I don't know thatId call them black. He screens the limb-chopping scene from Monty Python and the Holy Grail which certainly is black, and hilarious, but also harmless and, in the Pythons own special sense, "silly": a sense that's its own kind of subversion. Maybe his own darkest joke is another, real-life, one about his mother: one that involves a murderous man from Fulham and that I'll leave you to discover.

There are illuminating memories of Peter Sellers, and sad and funny ones of Graham Chapman, who seems more and more the funniest of the Pythons, perhaps because he looked the most serious. He stresses that the Pythons were writers before they were performers and quarrelled over scripts, not over casting. He leaves out some things I wishhed included. Theres nothing from or about Life of Brian, which was the Pythons' furthest pushing of the envelope, and surely crucial to the points he's making.

Other omissions are the radio show Im Sorry Ill Read That Again, which was a bridge between Cambridge Circus and his TV career, and all of his post-comedy, though not post-humorous, activities. These range from making industrial training videos, and co-writing books with the psychiatrist Robin Skynner, books in which he's self cast as the curious everyman. There's a Cambridge tradition (exemplified by Jonathan Miller, Graeme Garden and Rob Buckman) of doctors turning into comedians; these books enabled Cleese to, in a sense, reverse that trajectory. They also underline the thoughtfulness that co-exists with the wildness and that has made his career, and this show about it, work.

THEATRE REVIEW

Buddies in Bad Times, Toronto

Bruce Dow, an actor whose spiritual stature grows by cubits, comes before the cur-tain - yes, there really is a curtain - and tells us that he believes in light. He goes on to name some other things he likes; cellphones are on the list, and DVDs very closely followed by porn and brutality. Finally, and lingeringly, he tells us that I believe in death.

Thus the opening of PIG, a British play by Tim Luscombe being given its world premiere at Buddies in Bad Times, apparently because it was deemed too hot to handle on its home turf. Dow appears as four separate but similar characters, as you may judge from their names which are Harry, Barry, Larry and Garry. I'm not sure which he is when hes speaking the prologue, but all four are various degrees of voyeur, with a particular taste for sado-masochism. There are two other actors, Paul Dunn and Blair Williams, each of

whom also plays a quartet of characters united by sexual role. We watch them, still be-fore the curtain, engaging in an online pick-up; Williams is the top and Dunn the bottom.

The curtains part and there are the same two actors, now apparently in a live-in relationship. We find out later that theyre married, though "later" in this play is a loaded word, as the writing juggles time frames, and also levels of reality. Stevie, the Williams half of the menage, is a writer struggling to repeat his initial success; Joe, his partner, has literary aspirations himself that are becoming, from Stevie's jealous point of view, embarrassingly close to being fulfilled. Stevie is writ-ing, or has written, a play mak-ing use of their relationship. It's unclear just how many layers of illusion are involved here, but Stevie has an alter ego called Knife, who takes his sadism seriously and professionally, and another whom the pro-gram lists as "Knife." Joe is similarly billed as Pig, both in and out of inverted commas, not to mention getting into the plays title in capital letters. I mean Luscombes play's title, but I could probably just as easily mean Stevie's.

The structural secret is re-vealed with exemplary deft-ness; the play turns out to have a false bottom. (Pun unintended but apposite.) Unfortunate-ly, it also turns out to have any number of false endings. The need to wind up the action in all its manifestations extends the second act unmercifully. This is a shame because what has gone before is often sharp, occasionally poignant and sometimes very funny, in a dark way.

Dark may be an understatement. Gay sex and S&M are presented as synonymous, which seems simplistic from either direction, and the cruelty here, though more discussed than demonstrated, is extreme. It takes in gang-rape and goes beyond to forcible - or, per-haps more disturbingly, willing - infection with AIDS. This is where the rhyming-with-Harry characters come in, or some of them; they want to see and inflict the worst, and are willing to pay good money for it. Dow plays them brilliantly and chillingly, though his best moments are as a comparatively benign figure: a jealous ex-lover of Joes who offers a hilariously barbed toast to the happy couple, and delivers an equally witty lament for the days when gay meant furtive. This is tradition-

al camp at a high level, from an author whose bio doesnt quite jibe with the bad-boy image of his play. (As a director he seems to have specialized in Coward, Rattigan and Ayckbourn, and as a playwright in adaptations of Jane Austen.) Dunn is equally fine as the variously Piggy permutations of Joe, which encompass shy, frightened and professionally aggrieved when requested to inflict pain rather than suffer it. He also at one point con-fesses to a coke addiction; it's rather charming to discover that he's referring to cola.

Williams, an actor whose natural mood is civilized, doesnt always convey the ex-tremes that lie beneath Stevie the Knifes veneer; when those extremes break through, how-ever, he's excellent.

All three actors help keep confusion somewhat at bay by switching flawlessly between accents and, this being Eng-land, classes. Brendan Healy's high-gloss direction is, again, superb; he injects style even into the cast's statutory re-arranging of the furniture.

PIG runs until Oct. 6 at Buddies in Bad Times Theatre. For tickets and information, visit buddiesinbadtimes.com.

2013-10-05-the-power-of-blood:
Kat Lanteigne's Tainted is an AIDS play that isn't about gays. It deals, as might be guessed from its title, with the events of the 1980s that resulted in a generation of Canadian hemophiliacs being infected with HIV and hepatitis C through contamination of the blood supplies on which they depended for survival. The 1997 Krever report brought in a finding of criminal neglect, public and private. Subsequent proceedings produced a verdict that it was all very sad but nobody, really, was to blame.

Tainted, perhaps surprisingly, isn't a documentary. It filters the facts through the story of one fictitious family, four of whose members, by lineage or marriage, become infected. There are obvious problems about superimposing fact on fiction in this way, and there are equally obvious flaws in the execution. The play though, in a terrifically acted production, rises above them. It's charming, frightening, and finally very moving.

We meet the Steeles, whose name, as they themselves are apt to insist, suggests a resilience that is to be severely tested. Greg and Molly Steele have three sons, Jeff, Scotty and young Leo.We also meet Jacklyn, Jeff 's wife, and Christine, Scotty's girlfriend. All three brothers suffer from hemophilia and are coping with it, cheerfully when we first see them. Then - well, it hardly needs to be spelled out. In addition to the physical problems, the family has to cope with the hostility of friends and neighbours to the carriers of a condition both feared as a plague and reviled as a stigma. (To that extent, this is a gaythemed play at one remove.) Their own reactions vary. Jeff, trained as a lawyer, becomes an activist, whose quest for revenge and redress grows in proportion to his body's decay. Scotty, who's in finance, seems for some time to be in denial; as he puts it "you can't have AIDS on Bay Street."

There's nobody in the cast from outside the family, so we have to rely on them for information about the outside world: a tactic that works surprisingly well. It's the stuff about the Steeles themselves that can feel forced.We're told that when Greg and Molly got married they were subjected to parental pressures because one of them was Catholic and the other wasn't; but the subject, once raised, is so completely dropped that I can't even

remember which was which. There's the same paint-by numbers approach to characterization in Molly's fear that her genes have caused her sons' condition; amoment's anguish, powerfully expressed, and then never mentioned again. Also, the author's ear seems fallible, and the characters sometimes talk more like mouthpieces than like people.

The actors though, under Vikki Anderson's direction, rescue them. Maria Vacratsis gives a seamless, titanic performance as Molly, a mother confronted by one disaster after another; Vacratsis finds a truthful response for every one of them, without a moment of either exaggeration or avoidance. She's a constant presence in the play as written; her husband tends to come and go, both physically and emotionally. It's he, though, who gives us the most concentrated account of the Steeles' encounters with other people; Richard Greenblatt brings this off splendidly, creating a whole man and a moral perspective, both at the same time. Owen Mason starts the play off as Leo - this is where the charm comes in - practising a speech about his puppy love for a lady lifeguard. This amazingly natural child actor has in the past been one of Soulpepper's long line of Tiny Tims: useful practice for a role in which, with help from some discreet writing, he gets to break our hearts without insulting our minds. Alex Furber (Albert in War Horse) also has charm, and more than that, as Scotty. Jeff, sarcastically angry at everyone, seems at first an impossible character-in both senses, incredible and unlikeable - but Gord Rand saves him, giving his bitterness passionate expression, and showing too how it fits into the total pattern; unlike the comparable hero of The Normal Heart, he isn't presented as the centre of everything, and the play's the better for it. Claire Calnan and P. J. Prudat do warm work as the brothers' partners. The ensemble work grows steadily in strength and responsiveness throughout the evening; by the end you really feel that you have met a family - even that you're part of it yourself.

The Flood Thereafter is as woolly a performance as Tainted is precise. Sarah Berthiaume's play (originating in Quebec and translated by Nadine Desrochers) is a mash-up of motifs from The Odyssey, though if it wasn't for the fact that one character is called Homere and another Penelope and that a program-note mentions the Sirens, I might not have noticed. It takes place in a village where the main entertainment is a perfunctory strip, performed nightly by a young lady named June whose effect on her audience - consisting, as far as can be seen, of the barman and one customer, but we're probably meant to imagine others - is to have them cover their heads and cry. This, it seems, is because any one of them might be her father; her mother, who owed her arrival years earlier to being caught in a fisherman's net, having proved irresistibly attractive to every man in town. (She now works in a diner and shows few signs of her earlier self.) Visitors are discouraged, though when a young trucker passes through town and is detained by a malfunctioning vehicle, June takes an interest in him and he in her, though he still professes devotion to the girlfriend back home, which makes June jealous. So he's Odysseus, and she's Circe as well as a Siren. As June, Courtney Ch'ng Lancaster, who was excellent in Soulpepper's The Crucible and even survived The Barber of Seville, is dogged but defeated - especially by a long speech that demands intensity without furnishing the tools to achieve it.Maggie Huculak is similarly undone by incessant speechifying, even though she proved in Divisadero that she can do narration better than anyone; she only comes to life here when as Penelope, who despite her name is not the trucker's girl, she's allowed to stop intoning and start acting, in a well-written scene of jealous resentment with her husband (W. Joseph Matheson) who of course isn't Odysseus but is Homere. The only character in whose fate I felt interested was the trucking intruder (Kevin Macdonald) though we aren't told what that fate is. Yannik Larivee's set is one of those that assembles elements of various scenes and piles them up in a big collage at the back of the stage. KerWells' production must be aiming at stylization but merely looks awkward. People have to edge around the stage just to get to where they're going.

Tainted runs through Oct. 12 at the Daniels Spectrum (1-800-204-0855); The Flood Thereafter is on through Oct. 6 at the Berkeley Street Theatre.

2013-10-11-we-have-lift-off-56-up-revisi:
Ive been catching up with Up. I'm referring to the British documentary series that started in 1964 when World in Action, a current-affairs program presented by the independent company Granada TV, interviewed 14 seven-year olds from a variety of social and geographical backgrounds. The resulting segment was called 7Up. Seven years after that, Michael Apted, a young director who had been a researcher on the show, had the idea of checking in on the young participants at age 14. Every seven years since then, he has repeated the process. The latest instalment is 56Up. It was aired in the U.K. last year, and is being screened on PBS on Monday. All eight shows are also available in a box set, which is how I've been watching them, over three days, after hearing about them all my adult life. Its an experience both inspiring and heartbreaking.

Its also been somewhat indigestible. The episodes get progressively richer but also longer as each new instalment includes, for purposes of both comparison and exposition, plentiful footage from the old ones. Again and again, we flash back to the seven-yearolds skipping down streets, riding bikes, acting up in class. It's hopeful and it's sad, as the sight of children playing always is - nobody ever gets to be that happy again - and the knowledge of their future lives makes both feelings the more intense. Here, a voiceover tells us as the kids enjoy a group outing to the London Zoo, is a glimpse of Britains future, the CEOs and shop stewards of tomorrow.

As it happens, none of them has grown up to be either of those things. Some of them have fulfilled their initial ambitions. The posh prep-school boys who intended to be a barrister or a solicitor have become those things, very successfully. At the opposite social extreme, or near it, is Tony, the East End boy who realized his childhood dream of being a jockey but lost every race and settled at 21 for his backup plan of being a London taxi driver- which he still is. Hes done well at it; he has a sideline as an actor (usually playing a cabbie) and he's become a celebrity, the public face of the Up series - something of which, he told me on the phone from London, he's very proud. "Im accessible, and Im enthusiastic about it- I know the importance of the films." Also the importance of his own honesty in them I've gotta make it truthful-there's no mendacity in there. As voluble and irrepressible now as he was at seven ("the mould was there") he may be the participant whos changed the least.

The one whos changed the most, the most troubling and the most troubled, must be Neil, the middle-class boy from Liverpool, the most open and enchanting of the sevenyear-olds, who dropped out of university, became a squatter and then homeless, admits to mental health issues (I'm not just afraid of going mad, he said at one point, "I know I am") but has somewhat reinvented himself as a, mostly unpaid, local councillor in a succession of localities. Alone among the 14, he has never married and has no children.

Neither Tony nor Neil expresses any doubts or regrets about being in the programs. Plenty of the others have, especially the three East End girls - Jackie, Lynn and Sue - who are in some ways the heart of the enterprise. All have had problems with relationships, health, work; all have had lives far beyond the limited horizons they first envisaged and that Apted may initially have prophesied for them. As the series proceeds they talk back to him, criticize the show itself for reducing their lives to a recurring set of soundbites, threaten not to come back. But they, and most of the others, always do; they seem committed to it. (Also perhaps, though the show doesn't make a great point of it, to one another. Tony told me that theres always a private screening for all the subjects and everyone always claps after each interviews finished. That's show business. But it's also humanity. And the sense of belonging to something big.) Suzy, the upper-class daughter of a broken marriage (that there are only four women in the lineup is something that Apted has publicly regretted, as well he might) has compared the show to a bad book she cant stop reading. Hers has been another transformation story: from a bitter, chain-smoking 21-year old to, at 28 and ever since, a happy, grounded (if admittedly privileged) wife and mother.

Theyre all articulate, all intelligent, all likable: even John, the barrister, who at first seems intolerably snobbish, and quits because he's been made to look that way, but returns to reveal that he's had his struggles too. He also at one point compares the program to a reality show "like Big Brother." Unfair, I think; the Up films arent competitions. (The only permanent dropout has been Charles, who became a TV producer himself. Conflict of interest?) The projects power is marvellously summed up by Nick, who grew up on a farm in the north of England, and moved to the U.S. to become a physics professor: The idea of looking at people over time is nifty ... it's a picture of everyman ... not an absolutely picture of me, but it's a picture of somebody. Tony, when I spoke to him, said much the same thing: "Were pioneers of what everybodys going to go through; good, bad or indifferent, it's going to happen to everyone." The Up series is television doing what no other medium could; a documentary comparable in sweep and emotional effect to what The Wire achieved in drama. And it's nice that it should have happened almost by accident.

robert.cushman@hotmail.com National Post 56 Up airs Oct. 14 at 10 p.m. on PBS.

2013-10-12-the-actor-s-revenge-venus-in-:
In the Canadian Stage production of The Flood Thereafter, which has just closed, there was a scene in which a woman who had her sights set on a man seized the man's cellphone to yell at his girlfriend and make her jealous. In the Canadian Stage production of Venus in Fur, which has just opened, there is a scene in which a woman who has her sights set on a man seizes the man's cellphone to yell at his girlfriend and make her jealous. Who says our theatres don't have consistent artistic policies?

David Ives' Venus in Fur arrives here as a big American success. It is, in both writing and staging, a much slicker piece than the homegrown Flood Thereafter, and it's far better acted, but its total effect is equally confused. It's a play about the mounting of a play based on a book. Thomas Novachek, a NewYork playwright with a European accent, is casting his own adaptation of Venus in Furs, the 19th-century novel by Leopold Sacher-Masoch about a dominating woman and a submissive man, whose subject and whose author's name inspired the psychiatrist Kraft-Ebbing to coin the word "masochism." (Poetic justice: Krafft-Ebbing's own name has given rise to its fair share of puns.) Curtain rise finds Thomas lamenting that he can't find an actress intelligent and attractive enough to play his female lead; it's been suggested that Ives is here presenting Thomas as criminally sexist, but actually his demands and his disappointment seem perfectly reasonable. There enters an actress with a ripe New York accent and an unquenchably enthusiastic manner who, despite auditions being officially over for the day, prevails on Thomas to let her read for the role. The character's name is Wanda and the actress' is Vanda, a coincidence that strikes Thomas deeply. He's also impressed by her having dressed, or more accurately undressed, for the part. And once she actually starts reading, he's knocked out; as are we. Her voice and manner change completely, and it's obvious that she knows the play - and, as it turns out, the novel - inside out. She also knows Thomas outside in.

"Who" he asks, "are you?" He seems to think she might be the novel's Wanda come to life, or maybe even the Venus whom the novelist invoked. Or the Aphrodite who was the Roman goddess' Greek equivalent. Thomas starts talking about The Bacchae, the Euripidean tragedy in which women tear a male voyeur to pieces, though he rather glosses over the fact that they were acting under the influence of a male god rather than a female one. (There's another link to The Flood Thereafter: Greek myth roots.) Anyway, what Ives' Venus infers is that Thomas is a masochist waiting to happen. She has him read his play's male role, and tells him that he's great in it and should play it himself. In fact, she starts directing him. She also, it seems, sets about seducing him: hence the call to the girlfriend. The play embarks on a series of role and even gender reversals, the latter linking up with The Bacchae, whose doomed hero was in drag when he was dismembered. But they seem mechanical and self-cancelling: titillating rather than interesting. They certainly don't go as deep or as disturbing as this season's other S&M play, Pig.

The play, and Jennifer Tarver's sharp direction, work best as black backstage comedy: the actor's revenge. Rick Miller, best known for switching between multiple lightning-quick sketches in his own one-man shows, here gets to play one character in depth, and he brings it off beautifully; first obstinate, then pliable. (I can do literary references, too.) As Vanda/Wanda/Venus/Aphrodite, Carly Street blazes. At first sight and sound, she seems almost too broad a broad, but that just throws her instant transformation into sharper relief. From then on, she alternates between voices and personae, and is in perfectly-timed command throughout. Street is probably best know for her appearances in musicals (Lord of the Rings, Bloodless) but she's also done superb work in little-seen productions of Shakespeare and Marivaux; she could, if anybody cares, be one of the best classical actresses we have. Meanwhile, in her flaming red hair and black undies, she comes closer to justifying this play's erotic pretensions than the text itself ever does.

From furs to hosiery: ...And Stockings for the Ladies is the arbitrary name - the line only crops up once and in passing - given to the new production by the Harold Green Jewish Theatre Company. The author, Attila Clemann, had drawn on the letters and reminiscences of two Second World War members of the Royal Canadian Air Force: a squadron-leader, Ted Aplin, and a sergeant whom he has renamed Daniel Friedman. Both were present at the liberation of Bergen-Belsen, and the play is mainly concerned with their efforts to provide succour to the inmates, beyond and in defiance of official guidelines. For no apparent reason except economy, both men, and everyone else involved, are played by the same actor, Brendan McMurtry-Howlett. He does pretty well, but as a ventriloquial actor he's hardly a Rod Beattie, or indeed a Rick Miller. His director, Zach Fraser, doesn't help by insisting that he perform everything; a scene in a taxi in which he has to keep shuffling between seats as passenger and driver is one of the clumsiest pieces of staging I've seen in ages. Concentration camp prisoners are represented by puppeteer's dolls; one can just about see the reason, but it doesn't justify the break in convention. Besides all this, and despite the horrors it relates, the script itself isn't very interesting. Of course, Squadron-Leader Aplin missed, and was missed by, his wife and children back home, but just reading out their letters isn't enough to make us care. There's one compelling passage: a quarrel between the two men while engaged on an apparently pointless rescue mission. McMurtry-Howlett (a singularly, or doubly, un-Jewish name) does get some tension into this. But he'd do far better if he had someone else to act with and either a real play or a thoroughgoing documentary to act in.

robert.cushman@hotmail.com Venus in Fur runs through October 27 at the Bluma Appel Theatre; ...And Stockings for the Ladies runs through October 24 at the Studio Theatre, Toronto Centre for the Arts

2013-10-15-you-say-you-want-a-revolution:
THEATRE REVIEW

Les Miserables Princess of Wales Theatre, Toronto

Jean Valjean, no evil-doer, Stole some bread though he was pu-er.

A detective chased him through a sewer.

The End

The above lyric is not from Les Miserables. It's from a 1940s revue number called Reader's Digest, written by Betty Comden and Adolph Green, and a refreshing example of wit and of the brevity that is its soul. It certainly refreshes me just to type it after spending an evening at Les Mis, a show to which both brevity and wit are strangers. The restaged version that has arrived in Toronto has some individual merits, but the musical itself is as miserable as ever.

Chief of the redeeming features is Ramin Karimloo's performance as the redeemed redeemer himself: Jean Valjean, saviour and faker and candlestick-taker.He has exquisite vocal control and an intensity that, in his vengeful pre-reformation state, suggests that he might turn into Sweeney Todd. Even when a compassionate bishop inspires him to choose the more tedious, and largely unexamined, path of sanctity, he pursues it with a passion whose climactic expression is his singing of the show's best song, Bring Him Home, where his fists clench as his voice rings. Even he, though, cannot do much for the finale, where the hero dies for no clear reason except that it's getting late and time to send everybody, onstage and in the auditorium, home feeling noble.

Apart from being the one moment in Claude-Michel Schonberg's score where simplicity doesn't tumble over into pounding banality, Bring Him Home works because it shows Valjean, praying for the survival of his adopted daughter's beloved, discovering the depth of his feelings. It explores a character and develops a situation; it does in fact what songs in musicals are supposed to do.

At the opposite extreme, and far more typical, is the appalling dirge I Dreamed a Dream, which, starting with its tautological title, repeats things we already know in the loudest and most shopworn of terms. Nothing in it is specific to the woman who sings it, Fantine, a prostitute who's had to abandon her child. It could be sung by any deserted heroine in any musical.

The same goes for the later On My Own. The titles here are real giveaways. Do you hear the people sing? It's hard not to at this volume, but harder still to discern what they're singing about. The number in question is a call to a French revolution, though not the French Revolution; that's already happened, 40 years earlier. What the singers are revolting about or against is never mentioned, even though the revolt itself takes up most of the second act. There is an irony here - the revolutionaries are mostly students whom "the people" fail to support-but it's barely stated, never explored.

To some extent, it's the form that's to blame. Les Miserables is a throughsung musical: a species that seems, mercifully, to be dying out but that survives in revivals and in endless original runs. It delegates the tiresome business of storytelling to intermediate musical passages that aren't dialogue, aren't recitative, are in fact miniature songs, subject to song rules. They place an enormous burden on the lyricist who, in this English version of the French stage version of the Victor Hugo novel, is Herbert Kretzmer. In a recent interview in The New Yorker, Kretzmer, a veteran pop song and theatre man, said that he avoided cliches "like the plague." I think, hope, that he was joking, but his work on Les Mis is one giant plague spot.

Hugo's novel is vast, partly owing to his compulsion to provide a back-story for everybody and everything, from the bishop to the sewers. The adaptation does cut a clear path through the jungle, though it leaves out such useful information as how the hero transformed himself from hunted convict to factory owner and mayor.

It also flattens his inner conflicts, and those of his hunter Inspector Javert,whose suicide, prefigured in the book, here seems arbitrary. The most powerful sustained passage is the prologue, Valjean's release from the galleys and subsequent turnaround. In this new staging (by Laurence Connor and James Powell) it might be called the pre-credits sequence as, once it's over, the show's title is flashed up and we're plunged into the murk which, in a design inspired by the thunderclap style of Hugo's own paintings, is often literal.

The previous production had a scale and spaciousness this one has lost; but it also had a ceaselessly turning stage that took revolution rather too literally. One definite improvement is the flight through the Parisian drains, which projections make far more exciting. A definite deterioration is in the quality of the sound; many of the words are muddied and, apart from Karimloo, only Earl Carpenter (Javert) and Melissa O'Neil (the on-her-own Eponine) pierce through, clear and unforced. Fantine (Genevieve Leclerc) is a real screecher.

Bizarrely unchanged, in a French story with a mostly Canadian cast, is the convention that the lower orders, especially the sex-workers, all have cockney accents. This doesn't quite apply to the dastardly Thenardiers (Cliff Saunders and Lisa Horner), the designated comic relief, who are in a bizarrely capering world of their own. They turn up at the end in presumably filched finery at the marriage of Marius, the revolutionary hero who seems to have joined the class he was rebelling against. Maybe there's an irony here, too; the choreography, half-heartedly grotesque, doesn't seem to have made up its mind.

And there you have it: a long-haul show dedicated to short-term effects.

2013-10-19-company-s-three-in-soulpepper:
Alan Ayckbourn writes plays about Scarborough. For many years he ran his own theatre in the spa town of that name in the North of England. He tried out and directed all his own plays there, and maintained extremely high standards of performance and production. It sometimes seemed to me that, in a country that kept preaching about "community theatre", his was the nearest thing to it that actually existed. He wrote and presented plays about the same middle-class people who, as residents or tourists, made up his audience. None of the plays was ostensibly set in Scarborough, but all of them might very well have been. Occasionally he would pursue characters and settings from one play to another. Over the years - and he's been extremely prolific - the plays, linked or not, built up into a British equivalent of Balzacs Human Comedy. Theyre addictive.

The Norman Conquests, now being given a smashing production by Soulpepper, is an early block in the Ayckbourn building, but in itself it typifies the whole enterprise, sharp in perception, modest in tone, crazily ingenious in scale. First produced in Scarborough in 1973, and done in London the following year, it is in fact a trilogy, and the funniest ever written. (The competition, from The Oresteia to O'Neill's Mourning Becomes Electra, isnt any competition.) Its constituent parts are Table Manners, Living Together, and Round and Round the Garden, and they take place in the dining room, the sitting room and, naturally, the garden of the same country house - this one definitely in the south of England, near the coast - over the same summer weekend. Only they dont happen sequentially. Their actions are roughly simultaneous, each showing us what was going on in one area while we and the cast were occupied in another. The author's always maintained that it doesn't matter which of the three plays you see first, but Id recommend seeing them in the advertised order; though admittedly Ive never seen them in any other order. They're a jigsaw puzzle, and part of the fun is fitting the pieces together. It's also, as it turns out, part of the sadness; and I mean that in a good way.

There are six characters in search of a solution. Three of them are siblings: Annie, who lives in the house and takes care of their bedridden mother; Reg, an estate agent, who arrives so that Annie can take the weekend off; and Ruth, a businesswoman, who arrives. The others are Tom, a vet, whos been hanging around for years in vague pursuit of Annie; Sarah, Regs bossy wife; and Norman. Norman is an assistant librarian, when he has the time, and Ruth's husband, perhaps when she has the time. His conquests are the three ladies in the cast: all of whom he virtually or actually overcomes between Saturday and Monday, even though at least two of them claim, with some reason, not to be able to stand him. Norman has appeared, less furtively than might seem advisable, to take Annie for a dirty weekend in East Grinstead (one of those English place-names whose intrinsic hilarity doesn't really travel). It doesnt happen, largely because Annie is dissuaded by Sarah, who claims that she isnt a prude but does have standards. So they're all stuck in the house together. Two unseen characters are the mother up the stairs and a cat up a tree, both apparently with very disagreeable dispositions.

Ayckbourn's specialty is that apparent contradiction in terms, delicate farce; the physical comedy, which can be a scream, always tells something about the people. He is also, and perhaps uniquely, a boulevard playwright who never tells lies. He exposes his characters without mercy, but also without contempt. Ive heard him described as speeded up Chekhov and there are passages, especially those involving Annie and the terminally ineffectual Tom, that are like crazy-house versions of the failed proposal scenes in Uncle Vanya and The Cherry Orchard. The garden play, drawing on our investment in its predecessors, goes especially deep; though it does also include a prolonged sequence of forced misunderstandings that seems to belong in some other play: perhaps Relatively Speaking, Ayckbourns first success and probably his funniest in terms of belly-laughs but something that for better or worse he went beyond. The final curtain of this one, an uneasy calm after a storm, ambushes you with its bleakness.

It's underplayed in Ted Dykstra's production, though theres little other cause for complaint; it gets both the mechanics and the psychology unforcedly right. Albert Schultzs Norman, an overgrown self-tickling puppy-dog, may be going too far in his skittishness but he's going in the right direction; Norman, who alternates between self-promotion and self-pity, describes himself as "a gigolo trapped in a haystack" and Schultz, with encroaching beard and encroaching waistline, brings out both the charm and the selfdeception; he's perceptive about other people, blinkered about himself, so he gets what he wants in the small things, while always feeling frustrated in the big ones. Fiona Reid, mistress of manic gentility, was obviously born to play Ayckbourn, though apparently she never has before; Sarahs obsessive orderliness, especially with somebody elses house and mother, gives her no trouble, but the real treat is to watch naughty thoughts cross her mind, reflected in her swivelling eye and quivering lip, as she realizes that Norman may be hitting on her too. She's wearing two expressions at once. She's also a treat to watch while eating toast.

The great performance, though, is Laura Condollns Annie, a wonderfully subtle and expressive portrait of a self-cast wallflower who has no need to be, and is continually on the verge of breaking out; when she actually does, in anger or in lust, we cheer her on. In jeans or, self-consciously, in skirt, she looks exactly right: she makes impatience attractive. She also communicates that, though Norman may be the most intelligent person on stage, shes the wisest. Derek Boyes gets the beamish enthusiasm of Reg, an amateur games inventor, whose finest moment comes when he satirizes the unnatural movements of a knight on a chess-board. Oliver Dennis is admirably obtuse as Tom, most extreme of the play's trio of oblivious males, though I confess to missing Michael Gambon, the role's London creator, whose was genial bulk made him deliriously funny when seated on a very low stool at the dinner-table with Norman patting him, literally and metaphorically, on the head. Sarah Mennell draws an accurate honey-coloured outline of efficient (and myopic) Ruth, but doesn't mine the material as deeply as she might. And Norman conquers, thrice.

The Norman Conquests run in repertory through Nov. 16 at the Young Centre robert.cushman@hotmail.com
