THEATRE REVIEW

Puppet Up! Uncensored Panasonic Theatre, Toronto

Puppetry is an enviable skill. So is improvisational comedy. The performers of Puppet Up! Uncensored are adept at both, which puts them in a special league of accomplishment. All the same, the mixture of talents can result in a kind of split focus. And that characterizes the whole show. Some of it is fun, but the total effect is aimless.

First, there's the question of where, and who, it's coming from. The show's originating company is called Henson Alternative, and BrianHenson himself is credited as co-creator and producer. Brian is of course the son of the late genius (and I mean that) Jim Henson, creator of the Muppets. Onstage at the Panasonic, there's a multi-tiered display case of puppets, all ready to be taken out and manipulated by the live ladies and gentlemen of the cast, and all carved and dressed in Muppet style. There are a few whom I thought I recognized from Sesame Street or The Muppet Show, but I can't be sure; it's been a long time. I did think I caught a glimpse of Kermit during the opening number, but he was in the back of the group and didn't reappear thereafter.

The "alternative" part is that we are seeing Muppet types in the kind of material they wouldn't be allowed to perform on family TV. Actually, as Brian Henson himself pointed out in an interview with this paper, the Muppets have always had an irreverent and even satirical edge, certainly on their own show and even on Sesame Street, so the only departure here is in having them being more explicit, sexually and anatomically and verbally, than we might expect them to be. But since they aren't individually recognizable Muppets, even the shock effect of that is blunted. (A member of the first-night house, in a show dependent on audience involvement, inquired as to the whereabouts of a favourite character, and was told that he's owned by a different company. That's telling.) And if you want to see the Muppets satirized, that's already been done by Avenue Q.

There are half a dozen puppeteerperformers, plus co-creator, director and host Patrick Bristow, whose manner is poised somewhere between cute and oily and who is there to tell the others what to do and when to stop doing it. In other words, he's the puppeteers' puppeteer. At the start of each number he commands them to Puppet Up, suggesting analogous concerns for their morale (as it might be "Man Up!"), their efficiency ("Hurry Up!") or even their physical safety ("Buckle Up!"). His more specific instructions are mostly dependent on suggestions from the audience, prompting among other things a sketch about Rob Ford ballet dancing in a Gay Pride parade. Our Host seemed hazy as to who Mayor Ford might be, but some of his team were able to put him right; they also seem to have been in town long enough to drop the name of the Brass Rail, the strip club up the street. Anyway, it's nice of these Americans to come up to Toronto and make our local jokes for us.

And they're good at what they do, both at making up stuff and blaming it on the dolls they're holding. To appreciate their prowess fully, however, you have to devote much of your attention to the onstage video monitors that allow you to watch the puppets in close-up: another, literal, example of split focus. There's always something dispiriting about attending a live event and having to spend your time looking at a screen; and it's worse when the screens aren't commenting on the stage action but just tacitly admitting that without them you wouldn't be able see anything properly anyway.

Most striking of the cast is a long red-haired drink of strong waters identified onstage as Colleen; I can't give you her full name or those of her colleagues since the program, presumably to allow the performing help to be economically rotated, doesn't supply them. Anyway, Colleen, apart from looking good, has a wry and ready wit, exemplified by her extemporization of a song for a James Bond sketch with the suggested title of The Spy Who Bought Me Groceries. The Bond idea was a given, as presumably was the music that came with it, but the groceries were ordered on the night, and she really ran with them. The second greatest personal impression was made by an engaged couple from the audience named Chris and Barbara. Chris turned out to be an employee of Mirvish Productions, the second time I've known this to happen in a Mirvish show; maybe the staff should be demanding danger money. They watched while puppets enacted their first date, and were asked to press buttons when anything struck them as true or false. Barbara, when her surrogate declared that she was an agnostic, hesitated forever over which button to push, which was outstandingly witty.

You will guess that the comedy finally counted for more than the puppetry. A reasonable number of hits were scored, but two hours is a long time to spend watching improv, a form in which every item is arbitrarily determined and can be arbitrarily ended. You end up with an evening devoid of forward drive. And there's another thing; I haven't seen the I Love Lucy show at the Royal Alex, but it's ominous to have two Toronto stages occupied by rip-offs, I mean spin-offs, of TV shows. Still, it could be worse. Many people, I think, approach puppet shows with a certain apprehension. The cast of Puppet Up address this in their closing number. They sing (I quote from memory, but I hope not too inaccurately), "We hope that you enjoyed yourselves and had a good time/If you didn't, just be thankful that we're not a bunch of mimes". My sentiments exactly.

robert.cushman@hotmail.com Puppet Up! Uncensored runs until Nov. 3. For tickets and information, visit mirvish.com.

Last year I raved about The Double, a crazily inventive Dostoevsky adaptation for two actors and a talking bassist, at the Factory Studio. It's now been re-mounted, apparently with some alterations, at the Tarragon Extra Space, and I hope to get back to it. In the meantime, highly recommended. While I'm in laudatory mood, Ben Heppner's mad scene in the wonderful Canadian Opera Company production of Peter Grimes is the greatest experience available on a Toronto stage: at least until tonight, when it closes. In its hushed intensity it's a joint triumph of composition, staging and performance. Earlier Heppner, even when he's not singing, even when he's just sitting brooding and mending his fishing nets, has extraordinary presence.

A happy memory from earlier this year is of a speech in John Murrell's Taking Shakespeare, at Stratford. A young man, newly turned on to Shakespeare in general and Othello in particular, pours out his enthusiasm for both. To create that play and its central character, he says, Shakespeare must have been to Venice. And Cyprus. And he must have been a soldier. And black. That reductio ad absurdum constitutes a brilliant demolition of the silly, recurring Shakespearean "authorship debate". It was good to hear it from a real playwright, as opposed to somebody with starry-eyed ideas about how playwrights actually work. Murrell, one of Canada's finest if less fashionable dramatists, has had a comeback year, what with a new play at Stratford, an adaptation at Shaw, and a revival by Soulpepper of one of his earlier successes, the 1982 Farther West.

This proves disappointing. It concerns May Buchanan, a real-life Ontario woman from the late-19th century who became a prostitute at 14 and a successful madam later on. We're told that her father, amused or appalled or both, told her to move "farther west" and that she took his words on both a literal level, moving and plying her trades in Calgary and Vancouver, and a symbolic one, refusing to stay still and let anybody, especially any man, tie her down. The play, though, never tells us anything about May other than that she existed, that she was attractive and efficient, and that men were obsessed with her. The locations may change, but the characters and situations stay the same.

It starts well, with Tara Nicodemo's May recounting her early life while disengaging herself from a somnolent customer and getting dressed. (This has been the year, with La Ronde and now this production, that nudity came to Soulpepper.) Nicodemo does well throughout, though not well enough to lift the character out of her repetitive rut. Of her two principal pursuers one, played with credible passion by Matthew MacFadzean, is an initially shy and respectable hanger-on who gets as far as marrying her but finds that doesn't count for much, with dire results. The other is a puritanical Bible-spouting policeman whose revulsion from May's profession masks a deep desire for her person; a pattern familiar in fiction from Somerset Maugham's besotted Reverend in Rain to the character Michael Shannon plays on Boardwalk Empire. (There's a minor case, come to think of it, in Peter Grimes.) As played by Dan Lett, this play's constable seems constantly on the verge of unintended comedy; though in Diana Leblanc's production life isn't made easy for him by a scene in which he's required to harangue May while apparently oblivious of the fact that one of his men and one of hers are locked in potentially mortal combat. It ends with them falling into a pool of water; leaving space for this is one of the problems that bedevils Astrid Janson's set, an all-purpose split-level construction on which nothing looks comfortable.

A strong-on-paper cast is largely wasted; an extreme example is Evan Buliung, held in reserve until the second act and then appearing to play, nicely, a gentle Englishman, yet another of May's admirers, whom the play hardly needs.Her female employees, of whom she's admirably protective, signal their appearances in the first act with much boisterous laughing and singing, always the same song. Sarah Berthiaume's Yukonstyle is a great improvement on her preceding play The Flood Thereafter, in which a supposed mythological overlay obscured a couple of good domestic scenes. Here, the personal relationships are all with any greater resonance being contemporary and emanating from the characters' TV screens. The overriding theme seems to be family responsibility, as exemplified in Japanese and native Canadian cultures but rejected by representatives of both who are taught, painfully, not to do it again. The Japanese, female, is Yuko, now a chef at a restaurant in Whitehorse where the temperature is "between cold and death." The native, male, is Garin, her dishwasher and uneasily platonic roommate. They take in Kate, a feckless, pregnant 17-year-old just off the bus, who says she wants an abortion but has come to the wrong place, and is unwilling to get back on the bus to Vancouver to obtain one; she shies off from more primitive means as well. The Robert Pickton trial is in progress and on the news, and Garin comes to believe that his mother, who vanished when he was two, may have been one of Pickton's victims. Under pressure, Garin's French-Canadian father, who has drunk himself into cirrhosis, tells the truth about their relationship. That they should never even have attempted to have this conversation before is one of the play's several implausibilities. But Berthiaume (translated by Nadine Desrochers) does demonstrate a knack for bringing her characters to the boil, even if she can't always deal with them once they've boiled over.

The same strengths and weaknesses are evident in her three younger actors (Grace Lynn Kung, Ryan Cunningham, Kate Corbett); papa (Louis Klanfer) is the only one who stays on a convincing keel throughout. He's also the only one not required to switch performance modes; the others all function periodically as narrators, either of their own stories or somebody else's. There are also awkward flashbacks and gratuitous symbolism, and the director, Ted Witzel, hasn't found a style to blend it all together. With his set and lighting designers (Gillian Gallow, Bonnie Beecher) he seems to be aiming at stark and arriving at dingy. But the scenes mostly hold, even if not all the speeches do. I don't know what the song at the beginning and end is meant to convey, but it gets things off to a jaunty start and finish.

robert.cushman@hotmail.com Farther West runs at the Young Centre through Nov. 9; Yukonstyle at the Berkeley Street Theatre through Oct. 27.

Bruce Zinger, Canadian Stage / Grace Lynn Kung as Yuko and Kate Corbett as Kate in Yukonstyle, a great improvement for the playwright.; Caption:

In seasonal flight from anything involving zombies or vampires, I arrived at the Downstage Theatre, underneath the Magic Oven restaurant on the Danforth. The play is Savage in Limbo, an early work by John Patrick Shanley, later celebrated as the screenwriter of Moonstruck, which deserved its success, and the playwright of Doubt, which didn't.

Like Doubt, whose characters were mainly priests and nuns, Savage in Limbo belongs to the new school of American Catholic drama, not so much lapsed as haunted, and most stimulatingly exemplified by Stephen Adly Guirgis (The Last Days of Judas Iscariot, Jesus Hopped the A Train). It also fits into the great American saloon tradition, in which the playwright corrals his characters in a symbolic watering-hole and watches them ferment. In Shanley's play, three of the bar-flies are 32-year-old Jersey girls who once went to convent school together. One of them is Denise Savage, who is a virgin and aggressively bitter about it, and about most everything else. Her opposite number is Linda Rotunda, who's far from virginal (three illegitimate births and counting) and is more of a single issue malcontent, the issue being that her boyfriend has recently ditched her, declaring that he wants to be with someone ugly, which Linda certainly isn't. These two seem to be regulars at the bar; the final member of the trio, April White, who once wanted to be a nun and whom the others initially fail to recognize, must practically live there, knocking back all the booze that a gruff but protective proprietor will allow her to pour into herself. She's unhappy, too, but in a more sodden and resigned way than the others.

Rounding out the personnel are the barman, name of Murk, and Tony Aronica, Linda's ex, who arrives to explain that his taste for ugly girls relates to a recent stimulating encounter with a woman whose pillow talk consisted of a two-hour lecture on Soviet Russia. (The play dates from 1984.) In other words he, like everyone else onstage, wants more out of life than he's been getting. That's relatable; and Shanley's dialogue zings, though it's unclear what his overall point is, beyond the reiterated one that we'd better do something with our lives - maybe love one another or die - while we have a chance. Denise, the titular savage, is especially insistent about this, but the least equipped to put it into practice. As starved for friendship as for sex, she suggests setting up house with the other two women, but their other options and her own abrasiveness inevitably get in the way. The limbo she inhabits, and that Murk's bar embodies, must be one of the antechambers of hell. Whether it's escapable depends on who you are and who's there to help you. Denise looks defeated on both counts.

Sarah Kitz's production, with the audience on three sides and at close quarters, is an entertaining, well-orchestrated workout. Diana Bentley as Denise is initially trapped on a sustained note of angry grievance; she improves considerably when the script allows her to modulate. The play may advertise her as its central figure, but it's really an equal opportunity piece, and all the parts here are well-taken. Melissa D'Agostino's Denise sizzles and sparkles in a leopard skin-printed top, and Nick Abraham is puzzled and pugnacious as Tony, the only member of the quintet with an imaginable offstage life. Caitlin Driscoll is both sad and funny as April whose thoughts walk but don't run towards suicide. Tim Walker as her drink dispensing guardian angel is given a really surprising surprise entrance to start things off, followed by a nifty passage of mime, which seems excessive at the time but feels justified in retrospect. He spends much of the rest of the play fixing the others (and us) with an uncanny gaze, compounded of control, compassion and a determination that everyone should pay for their drinks. He also, in the evening's stand-out sequence, gets to dress up as Santa Claus. The play still feels promising, even if the promise was made 30 years ago.

A mere two years ago I raved over The Double, the extraordinarily creative dramatization of a Dostoevsky novella created and performed (them's the credits) by Adam Paolozza, Arif Mirabdolbaghi and Viktor Lukawski. Paolozza directs and plays Golyadkin, the prickly and timorous government clerk (archetypal figure in Russian fiction) whose paranoia is both inflamed and embodied by the appearance of a lookalike namesake who possesses all the social graces he wishes he had himself. Paolozza is if anything too personable for the man whose heart, according to his author, had the habit of "beating on all other people's staircases" and who, on festive occasions, "almost always turned up inappropriately." Technically, though, he's a marvel, whether running on the spot in a desperate attempt to escape from himself or locked in ventriloquial combat with his other self. The same goes for his production, not least in the way it uses Andre du Toit's marvellous lighting to simulate a stage curtain. Lukawski plays the extensive role of Everybody Else, meaning all Golyadkin's persecutors, including most spectacularly a glutinous nightclub MC in a scene you won't find in Dostoevsky but that fits perfectly here.

Mirabdolbaghi plays double bass (and you can bet the pun is intentional) and narrates, doing both superlatively. He's also the figure in Golyadkin's mirror, reflecting our hero's chronic uncertainty over what to do next, and the possessor of the week's second uncanny stare, in this case incorporating a satanic grin. Smaller stringed instruments represent Golyadkin's shapely beloved: a mocking, vestigial romantic interest that is largely the play's own invention. The piece has changed since I first saw it, largely by getting too long; we're on the brink of a needless intermission when the main theme emerges. And though the casual updating works perfectly, the local references (Gordon Lightfoot?) are just too cute. The occasional up-chatting of the audience also worked better in the show's original cabaret setting. These, though, are tiny flaws in a haunting, hilarious whole.

Savage in Limbo runs through Nov. 7 at the Downstage Theatre, 798 Danforth Avenue; The Double runs through Nov. 24 at the Tarragon Extra Space

Courtesy Tarragon Theatre / Double or something: Viktor Lukawski and Adam Paolozza bring their inspired take on Dostoevsky back to the stage.; Caption:

A young man and woman, probably early twenties but maybe late teens, confront one an-other in front of what looks like a garbage dump, though it sports a sign saying that no garbage is allowed. Ain't that just like life. The pair are bobby and Tina, who got together, against the odds, in George F. Walker's play Tough! and whom we now meet again in a sequel, Moss Park, which reaches us two decades after its predecessor though the couple themselves have aged by only three years. but then the poverty trap, which grips them both, is ageless.

Bobby and Tina aren't married, or even living together. They do, however, have a toddler daughter; and, thanks to a one-night stand reunion, another child is on the way. bobby learns this from Tina in the course of the, mostly crackling, 60-minute conversation that makes up the play. bobby wants Tina to take him back - he's always wanted that - but she has serious doubts, as he's repeatedly proved himself incapable of holding down a job. Always, as he tells it, that's somebody else's fault, though it's doubtful that he's managed to convince even himself of that. He certainly hasn't convinced Tina, who seems both smart and practical. The ways of the heart, and of the body, are notoriously and perhaps mercifully strange, so it's easy to accept that she still loves him: less so, perhaps, that she might be prepared to build a life with him. bobby, it seems, has known success in only two areas of his life. Tina is one of them; the other is acting as lookout for a small-time break-and-enter gang, one of whom, a close friend, is now in jail.

One thing that together Tina and attention-deficient bobby have in common is they both come from, and are currently living with, colourfully dysfunctional families, whose antics sound quite funny when we hear them described, until we stop to think about what these situations actually entail. The strength of Walker's writ-ing here is his ability to depict

deep pain with a light touch; I actually prefer him in this mode to the more elaborate Gothic of his Suburban Motel plays. The comparative simplicity of Moss Park must owe a lot to its being designed for a young people's (not a children's) audience; it's staged here by the Green Thumb company of vancouver whose mandate that is. There's one plot-and-character twist that's hard to take - it's a relief, in more ways than one, when it turns out to be a false trail - but in general Walker spins his situation out resourcefully, making especially good use of crossed cellphone calls from Tina's dis-approving buddy and bobby's enabling one.

Despite its brevity, the play does run out of variations, as do the basically good perform-ances in Patrick Mcdonald's production. Graeme McComb's bobby is consistently the over-grown class clown. Haley McGee's Tina coruscates, not least when most desperate, but you do start wondering how somebody so smart and witty and strong got stuck in such a no-win situation. The play tells you why; the performance doesn't quite bear it out. Still, you root for the couple, hope the best for them, fear the worst; which I think is what the play wants of you. both actors, by the way, have great timing.

Timing is something nota-bly missing from Where's My Money?, with which Toronto's independent theatre scene continues its exploration of the plays of John Patrick Shanley. This one is billed as a Halloween play, and it does involve ghosts: deceased entanglements haunting, literally, the troubled marriages of a couple of couples. Staging these apparitions is a problem, not solved in this production which combines spooky lighting with awkwardly matter-of-fact appearances. Still, the ghosts are the play's trimmings rather than its heart. That resides with the spouses who converse in the brittle comic manner that, on broadway and off it, is the conventional mask for hatred and heartbreak. It isn't a style I especially like, but it can be effective if competently done. Here, whether through tone-deafness in the director (Jodi Sprung-boyd) or inexperience or simple incapacity in the ac-tors, nobody is suave, every-body shouts. In a play that introduces its characters one by one, the acting gets progressively more leaden; every time you think you've hit bot-tom, somebody worse comes on. The first to appear, Emily Coutts, is actually pretty good (and the most interesting character as written) but her role proves brief. After that, the only break in the depress-ing pattern is Michael Goldlist who's terrible in his first scene but improves thereafter. The play itself says some interest-ing things about dependence and co-dependence, but its people are puppets, and they need really skilled animation.

Moss Park runs through Nov. 16 at Theatre Passe Muraille (416-504-7529); Where's My Money? through Nov. 9 at the Sterling Studio Theatre, 163 Sterling, unit 5.

Courtesy Passe Muraille / Graeme McComb as Bobby and Haley McGee as an unusually witty Tina in Moss Park.; Caption:
2013-11-13-curtain-calling-soulpepper-20:
The standout productions at Toronto's Soulpepper theatre this year have been the marathons: the two-part Angels in America and the three-part The Norman Conquests. Both, its announced yesterday to nobodys surprise, are being revived in the company's 2014 season. Their success did leave some people wondering what Soulpepper intended to do for an encore. The Oresteia? Schiller's Wallenstein trilogy? Ibsens reputedly unstageable double-header Emperor and Galilean? Tom Stoppards The Coast of Utopia? That last triple-decker might actually make sense, since according to Soulpepper's artistic director Albert Schultz and to others as well, Stoppard is one of the surest box-office bets a prestige theatre can make.

As it turns out, all the other plays in next year's battalion are single spies. Arthur Millers The Crucible is being brought back from two years ago. Among the new entries are two other American plays: Reginald Roses familiar Twelve Angry Men and the decidedly unfamiliar Idiot's Delight by Robert E. Sherwood. Otherwise there'll be plays from Ireland (The Gigli Concert by Tom Murphy, whose A Whistle in the Dark rocked Toronto a few years back), South Africa (Athol Fugards The Road to Mecca) and of course Canada (David Youngs Glenn, which splits Glenn Gould four ways).

Canada may also claim at least a partial share in Of Human Bondage, which is an adaptation by Canadian playwright Vern Thiessen of the famous novel by Somerset Maugham: the first ever stage version apparently. What might be called canonical classics have one-and-a-half representatives. The half is A Tender Thing, described as a modern, moving reworking of Romeo and Juliet. The one is Moliere's Tartuffe, in the Richard Wilbur translation that's already a near-classic on its own account.

Two things to note about that list. First, in a departure from previous Soulpepper practice, it only takes us up to next September; the lineup for the remaining three months wont be revealed until next April. Schultz, when I spoke to him on the phone, said that "were too big an organization to do it all at once," and that he wants to leave the space to deal with unforeseen events from markets crashing to new plays arriving - or of course the desirability of extending the run of a successful show. That sounds sensible.

The second feature is that there have been no announcements of actors or directors. It seems that final phone calls have yet to be made and contracts signed. One directorial assignment can be revealed: Schultz told me that he'd "offered Albert Schultz the job of directing Idiot's Delight and that Schultz had accepted."

That play is the most intriguing choice on the list, for several reasons. One is that it will be the first play to open. Another is its rarity; some of us may have seen the MGM movie version but few will have seen it onstage; I certainly never have. A third is the nature of the play itself; first staged in 1936 its about dancing on a literal and metaphorical precipice; its setting, in Schultzs own description, is a resort hotel in the Italian Alps where English, German, Italian and American characters engage in a celebration of life - a recognition of it as an idiot's delight. And of course they're only three years away from apocalypse.

Schultz describes it, referring to two other American plays of the same era that have been successes for Soulpepper as "The Time of Your Life meets You Cant Take It with You," all, directly or indirectly about the imminence of war and the end of a society. This, apparently, will be a key theme of Soulpeppers programming in the next few years: a commemoration and examination - involving poetry, music and dance as well as plays - of two world wars and the space between and beyond them. There are hints that some of this will make itself felt in those blank three months of next year. It's reasonable to guess that at some point we'll see some kind of production of Journeys End, the classic First World War that was once given a notable production by the Stratford Festivals Young Company, some of whose members, including Schultz himself, went on to form the nucleus of Soulpepper.

About that word "classic"; in what might be called its vulgar sense - plays written before 1900 - it's an area that seemed a vital part of Soulpepper's identity when it started 15 years ago but has become steadily less important since. In that sense, Soulpepper has grown less adventurous. Schultz disagrees; he says that the 12 actors who started the company all had "a similar aesthetic", a similar classical background and training. They were people who wanted to do what we do in our own city, and for them nothing could have been less adventurous than doing Schiller and Moliere. Well, maybe, but theres a time when being reactionary is the most revolutionary thing you can do. Nobody else was doing those plays in Toronto at the time; more to the point, nobody is now either. Even toprank Shakespeare is hard to come by in Canadas largest city and supposed cultural capital.

Schultz's answer would be that, since moving into its own premises in the Distillery District, Soulpepper has been more adventurous, establishing what he calls "a creative village" and bringing on new generations of artists. Our core artists don't just do a play; they teach the next generation; they contribute curatorially. Were training actors, directors, designers; were even training producers - no one else is doing that. They're also doing it, as he continually points out, with very little subsidy: "We invest a million dollars every year. 92% of it we raise ourselves, from box office fundraising. We have a company of 150 artists, including poets and choreographers and composers. We employ more people than any four other theatres."

I wouldn't argue with any of that, though I can't claim to love all of the results. I'd still like them to do more old, preferably rare plays. It would be nice to have both. And there are hints that we yet might.
2013-11-16-how-she-forgets-the-gravitati:
Among other things The Gravitational Pull of Bernice Trimble is a tale of two kitchens. They occupy the same stage space, and our visual clue as to which we are in at a given moment is the presence or absence of salt and pepper shakers. Bernice herself is a great shaker-collector, and Camellia Koo's set, one of her best, gives us shelves and shelves of them, stretching in every direction as far as our eyes can see.

Bernice is also a lively, organized, recently widowed woman who, in her mid-50s, is diagnosed with earlyonset Alzheimers: the same disease that took her mother. She now has to communicate this news to her own three grown children. Theres Peter, a confessedly awkward" statistician, who takes conflict-avoidance to artistic levels; Sara who's just the opposite, constantly spoiling for a fight; and Iris, whom Sara fights with the most, and who falls temperamentally between the other two. Iris is also the inhabitant of the other, shakerless kitchen, and our narrator. We see and hear the action entirely through her eyes and ears. We find her at the beginning of the play preparing one of her mother's recipes, a sodiumheavy dish that Bernice jovially calls "the everything-that-is-bad-for-you casserole, and that consorts rather oddly with her extreme phobia about dirt. The casserole preparation also serves as a kind of countdown, something cunningly clarified in the plays last wracking moments.

One of the subtleties of Beth Grahams script is that while Sara is violently vociferous about the chances of Bernice's condition being passed on to her and eventually to her own baby daughter, Iris obviously feels equally threatened but keeps quiet about it. She is, she tells us, an expert at biting her own tongue; she's found that, in her family, its the best way to survive. She talks to herself, or to us (the play can get too cute about this) as compensation. The family tensions are as vivid and believable as in any play since Death of Salesman, and theyre faultlessly realized in Philip Akin's pitch-perfect production. Akin is the artistic director of Obsidian Theatre, who present the play and who are Toronto's leading black company. This isnt a black" play; the only ethnic touches in the dialogue seem to be Italian, and the author is white. What we have are four good actors, presenting a credible family in a situation that could affect anybody and tear them, individually and collectively, apart.

Making Iris rather than Bernice the centre of the play was a smart move. It means we get a drama rather than a clinical study. The play, as the title indicates, isnt so much about her as about her effect on those she loves and who loves her. Karen Robinson, indomitable even in disarray, shows us as much about Bernice as we need to know; she's almost cheerfully (and movingly) determined even when contemplating suicide, thus administering the ultimate family litmus test. Iris' narrator role is taken to another kind of extreme; she describes the others actions and even their tones of voice as theyre happening, as if she were doing closed-circuit captioning. The sheer length of the role places a heavy technical burden on the actress; Alexis Gordon, who's a year out of drama school and has spent most of that year doing musicals, shoulders it phenomenally well. There isn't a false or faltering moment in her performance.

Sara presents an opposite problem, which Lucinda Davis attacks, successfully, by aggressively going for it: by revelling in her compulsion to impart all the physical details about her little girl Heaven (great name for a future stripper, Iris muses sardonically), about her rage and denial and unforgivingness, all of it understandable if hardly endearing. As Peter, Peyson Rock is taciturnity eloquent, and occasionally hilarious. This is, for obvious reasons, an upsetting play; its also a riveting one.

Joan Macleods The Valley, another four-hander, ranges wider but not as deep. It's set in Vancouver. Each of the characters begins by telling us of his or her first encounter with the police, usually in childhood. One of them, Dan, grew up to be a cop. He married Janie, an ex-addict, and they have a baby son. One day Dan finds himself called to a troublescene; a young man, Connor, clearly disturbed, is alarming his fellow passengers on a train by brandishing what might be, but actually isn't a dangerous weapon. Connor is a possible prodigy, who wrote a whole fantasy novel as a youth, then dropped out of his first term at university, and is now living with his mother, a divorced bookstore employee named Sharon. Connors jaw gets broken in the confrontation, and Sharon accuses Dan of using excessive force. What the truth about this might be I cannot testify, as in Richard Roses production, with all locations simultaneously depicted and the audience on two sides, my view of the incident was completely blocked by a large sofa. That, I should add, is not typical of the staging, which is mostly clear and fluid and stunningly lit by Graeme S. Thomson.

The train scene comes towards the end of the first act. Before then, the two sets of characters have existed in separate alternating compartments, coming to life, like the play as a whole, only in fits and starts. The men get the best of it. Ian Lake's Dan, certainly not a brute, is an unshakably true-to-life conflicted cop (or maybe I should say he's true to the image of the cop in the best TV shows). Colin Mercer is equally unassailable as Connor, equal parts stubborn and volatile, railing at his mother for using adverbs, which she does, shamelessly and repeatedly. She also mysteriously tells him not to make fun of Thomas Hardy. Susan Coynes Sharon is fine when given specific strong emotions to convey, but has too often to fall back on generalized concern. As Janie, Michelle Monteith adds to her list of terrifying meltdowns, but earlier is something of a blur; her climactic scene is one that the play hasnt really earned. It gestures toward broad issues - strains on and by the police especially in Vancouver, lack of social services especially in Vancouver, the rift between those who live high up and those lower down, literally and figuratively, again in Vancouver - but the gestures aren't followed through. Where the play works, it works domestically.

The Gravitational Pull of Bernice Trimble runs through Dec. 1 at the Factory Theatre; The Valley runs through Dec. 15 at the Tarragon Theatre.

THEATRE REVIEW

Winners and Losers

Berkeley Street Theatre, Toronto

Marcus Youssef and James Long, fortyish independent theatre luminaries from Vancouver, sit at opposite ends of a table and play a game whose name is the same as the title of their show: Winners and Losers. The game goes like this: One player will say a word, drop a name, and the other will say whether the person or issue cited could best be described as a winner or as a loser. Then one of them rings a bell. (That is not a metaphor.) Some examples prove hard to categorize. Sylvia Plath, for example, is ranked as a winner for writing The Bell Jar and as a loser for killing herself. Then there's Stephen Hawking: Which, they ask, would he prefer to have, his legacy or his legs? That doesnt play as crass as it probably reads.

For all that, the idea of assigning everything and everyone to one team or the other gets to seem both arbitrary and superficial. Maybe thats the point, questioning a way of thinking and being that turns society into a contest. But it's hard to feel that they're criticizing a game that theyre so intent on playing. Also, when they do bring up an interesting topic - the suggestion that South African apartheid was modelled on Canadas treatment of its First Nations, or the likelihood that modern history would have been completely different if the Mensheviks had been the winners in the Russian Revolution instead of the Bolsheviks - the quickfire rules of their game prevent them for pursuing it. They're both very fast talkers, Youssef especially.

One of their glancing blows is really searching: The accusation that in our society the sick or just the old count as losers. This comes quite late in the show, and the proceedings do get more interesting around the halfway mark, starting when Long temporarily leaves the stage and Youssef slows down and gets confidential with us. The evening takes several of these sharp turns, marked off by charged pauses, reminding us that a director (Chris Abraham) has been at work and that the performers aren't making it up as they go along.

Indeed they confess that most of their exchanges are transcribed from months and months of conversation. Theyre performing a script with maybe a few topical adlibs thrown in. Impromptu or rehearsed, they do seem to enjoy wrong-footing one another. And it gets personal. When Long returns, he accuses Youssef, whose father is a high-up banker, of being a privileged dilettante, dabbling in left-wing theatre and left-wing politics while waiting to inherit a million. The actual word Long uses is "tourist," and he instances Youssefs long delay in visiting Egypt, where his family came from, and his spending his time there being photographed at the Pyramids.

Long's own upbringing was far from sheltered; Youssef expresses sympathy but remarks that Long, if not rich, is not currently doing too badly and spends more on a pair of jeans than he himself would ever dream of doing. Long cops to both charges. Everything they say about one another is, I'm sure, factual. Blood is drawn. (That is a metaphor.) A friendship shatters before our eyes. Except it doesnt really. Theatre is never as real as it might like to be and these actors, even using their own names and their own lives, are acting: acting well, too, with Long dominating the first half and Youssef the second. In that sense theyre both winners. Or both losers. Whichever: They take a curtain-call together, and you know they'll be colleagues, doing the show again, tomorrow night. We've been taken for a fairly enjoyable ride.

robert.cushman@hotmail.com Winners and Losers runs until Dec. 8. For tickets and more info, visit canadianstage.com.

I've lost count of the number of adaptations Ive seen in recent years of August Strindbergs Miss Julie, each of them transferring the 1906 Swedish original to some closer time and place. After Miss Julie, by the British playwright Patrick Marber, is the only one of them that works. If it weren't for the awkward fact that it couldn't exist without its predecessor, Id say that it was better than Strindberg.

In Strindbergs play, Miss Julie, a nobleman's daughter, loses her virginity to Jean, her father's valet, in the heat of a Midsummers Eve celebration. Daybreak finds her ashamed but inflamed, careering between excoriating her new lover and planning to run away with him, a project they both, for different reasons, realize is hopeless. Marber tells the same story, sometimes word for word, but sets it down in England, on VE Day, with a Labour government just voted in: so, a double celebration. The unseen father is now a Labour peer, though one whose politics are never going to get in the way of his privilege; as his chauffeur, John, the reincarnation of Jean, bitterly remarks. John, a demobbed soldier returned to the estate on which he grew up, is both a rebel against the class structure and a prisoner of it. So, in her way, is Julie, the English rose with thorns rampant. At every turn, and with nothing seeming forced, the new local and historical references make the play more immediate than Ive ever known it. Also more economical: always before, I've grown impatient with these class-crossed lovers' twists and turns. This time, I hung on every word and every silence.

In David Ferrys production (for the new-to-me Red One Theatre Collective) the intertwined tensions, social and sexual, could be cut with a knife. Ferry, who must be our most undervalued director (witness The Last Days of Judas Iscariot, and the similarly titled Life of Jude at this years Summerworks, and now this) knows when to linger things out and when to slam them violently shut. He also designed the set and lighting, which are moody and evocative. There's a radio onstage, playing 1940s dance music and rarely turned off; at first it threatens to be a distraction, but as the action progresses, its unheeding smoothness does more than provide an ironic counterpoint; it actually has the effect of turning up the heat, which in these performances is already extreme. They're

also dead accurate in time, place and status. Claire Armstrongs Julie is the image, visual and vocal, of ravaged English entitlement, temptress and tempted in one. Christopher Morriss John is a burning compound of resentment, calculation and desire. Amy Keating brings a biting northcountry practicality to Christine, the cook and John's fiancee, in whose kitchen the play takes place and who, alone of the three of them, knows her place and how to take advantage of it. Marber gives her one hilariously vindictive moment that Strindberg never thought of; though, to give the Swedish devil his due, his ending does possess a tragic inevitability that isn't quite encompassed here. In all other respects the emotional logic is impeccable; the first night audience, in a tiny makeshift space, was spellbound. This, with the possible exception of The Double, is the best show in Toronto.

Speaking of endings: The Sacrifice Zone, a words-and-action piece from a Canadian company working with an Australian playwright, has a denouement that rocks. It makes sudden sense of plot-points that until then have been kept mysterious. Its so effective that what has gone before seems for a moment more substantial than it did at the time. Then the spell lifts.

The play deals with an explosion at an industrial plant, fictitious but obviously meant to be emblematic, in which five people were killed. Most of the victims families accept a compensation package from The Company (thus referred to throughout, shades of Prison Break) that runs the town, but one bereaved husband and one bereaved wife hold out for a government inquiry. Meanwhile a Company geologist falls in love with another employee and marries him; but is dismayed by what she discovers about the firm's ecological practices. Her husband is less idealistic; so is nearly everybody else in town, faced with the possible shutdown or removal of the industry on which they all depend. The play weighs the human and moral costs of justice, and it recognizes ironies and complexities. But it doesn't flesh them out. Theatre Gargantua, a self-described multi-disciplinary theatre company, surrounds Suzie Millers skeletal script with electronic music, a set consisting of constantly reconfigured door-frames, and a great deal of mime. Well, all right, thats what they do; but it mostly seems fussy and repetitive, especially in the domestic scenes. Under Jacquie P.A. Thomas's direction, a cast of five, all grown-ups but playing characters of all ages, throws itself enthusiastically about; Michelle Polak and Sam Benson can be quite touching in scenes involving a mother and son, the latter with a superhero fixation that turns out to be trouble. But they all have trouble making the semaphore text sound natural.

Layne Coleman and Linda Griffiths face similar problems in Griffiths' play Heaven Above, Heaven Below, though for different reasons. Here the dialogue is too arch and brittle to be credible as conversation but not witty enough to be enjoyable for its own sake. Its a sequel to Griffiths 20-year-old play The Darling Family and maybe you need to have seen the earlier work (I haven't) to get invested in the newer one. Two people named only as He and She meet in a boutique hotel room to discuss the abortion She had as a consequence of their brief affair, also 20 years ago. So the play makes a pair with George F. Walker's Moss Park, the previous Passe Muraille twohander, also a sequel and also involving an abortion, though in that case contemplated rather than achieved, hence involving suspense and possibility rather than just recrimination. As He and She contemplate their comfortable surroundings, compare their comfortable careers, do pot and coke, and wonder whether theyll have drinks from the minibar or sex on the bed, I found myself in unexpected sympathy with Ford Nation. (Well, maybe that doesnt work for the drugs.) Coleman at least manages to give He an appealing shaggy slyness, though I found it hard to believe in him as the musician he claims to be. But maybe that too is all in the past.

robert.cushman@hotmail.com Weekend Post After Miss Julie runs until Nov. 30 at the Storefront Theatre, 955 Bloor West; The Sacrifice Zone until Nov. 30 at the Factory Studio; Heaven Above, Heaven Below until Dec. 7 at Theatre Passe Muraille Backspace.

THEAT REREVIEW

Ed Mirvish Theatre, Toronto

I doubt if anybody was expecting Aladdin, the Disney stage musical of the Disney film musical, to be more than just another knock-off. But just as we should be careful what we wish for, a principle that Aladdins Genie would certainly endorse, so we should be cautious as to what we despair of. This Aladdin turns out to be the best-ever stage version of a movie. Just confining comparisons to the Disney stable: It shows up the theatrical Beauty and the Beast for the drearily uninspired Xerox that it was; and though it may not be as outlandishly imaginative as The Lion King, it has its own kind of inventiveness and is frankly more fun.

And it has, obviously, a much better score. Alan Menken's music, and the lyrics of the late and much lamented Howard Ashman, have the kind of verve and wit that used to be taken for granted on Broadway and is now mostly a memory to be invoked for spoof purposes - meaning camp purposes - only. Aladdin redeems showbiz tradition by making fun with it, rather than of it: something that now may only be possible in a fantasy setting. Here the source material is doubly a fantasy: a cartoon derived from a fairy tale. The movie's songs - One Jump Ahead, Friend Like Me and, best of all, Diamond in the Rough - come up fresh and sparkling. So does the scene-andtone-setting Arabian Nights, to which Chad Beguelin, who wrote the shows adroit book, has added some new lyrics worthy of the Ashman tradition, so neatly rhymed as to be, on a couple of occasions, laugh-out-loud funny: a rare accomplishment.

The show also has the good fortune of being directed and choreographed by Casey Nicholaw, whose past credits (Book of Mormon, Spamalot and the Broadway version of The Drowsy Chaperone) have established him as the master of the comedy musical. I wouldnt claim that his choreography represents the second coming of Jerome Robbins but it keeps the stage humming, notably in the opening marketplace number. This, among other things, is a mobile showcase for Gregg Barnes' gorgeous costumes, which get only richer as the evening goes on; add these to Bob Crowley's sets (his Cave of Wonders, with its flashes of green lightning, is especially wonderful) and the production could probably franchise a couple of stagings of Kismet, which might not be such a terrible idea.

Staging, lighting and design come triumphantly together when the hero takes his princess for a breathtaking ride on a magic carpet with no visible means of support. I dont often find myself applauding a special effect but this one is really special. Beautifully, stunningly done, it has the benevolent side effect of taking our minds off the accompanying song A Whole New World, the scores one real dud with lyrics so dumb they can only have been supplied by Tim Rice after Ashman's death.

For a Toronto audience the show must seem at times like a Ross Petty panto with more money. Indeed Jonathan Freeman's villainous Jafar is, presumably by coincidence, a Petty sound-alike, especially in his fortissimo sneer; his sidekick Iago (Don Darryl Rivera) also strongly resembles the assistant villain usually played in Petty shows by Eddie Glen, except that he cringes rather than chortles.

Adam Jacobs is an engaging Aladdin somewhat altered from the movie; here hes a scamp trying to go straight even before he falls in love, owing to a promise he made his late mother (who in a British panto wouldnt be late at all; she'd be called Widow Twankey and would be running a Chinese laundry, in Baghdad). Aladdin's filial soul-searchings are explored in a song called Proud of the Boy, which is more touching and less sticky than you might expect. As for his beloved Princess Jasmine: the liberated heroine who was so refreshing in Beauty and the Beast had already become her own kind of stereotype by the time they filmed Aladdin: The presence of a charming flesh-andblood actress (Courtney Reed) makes her less of a cartoon in more than one sense.

When it comes to classical antecedents, you cant beat James Monroe Igleharts Genie, who is part Ariel from The Tempest (he wants the liberty his master promised) and, of course, part Robin Williams. He has to provide a stage equivalent of what the animators and Williams' voice created between them on film, and he does it superbly. Announcing himself in Friend Like Me, he has to cope with everything Nicholaw's staging throws at him, which is everything; the number is deliriously extended. But being a corporeal presence, and an imposing one, he's necessarily his own man, or whatever a genie is: a preeningly proud all-around entertainer, though slightly more impressive in singing than in dancing, extravagant in joy and, briefly and temporarily, in sorrow. This really is a legend, several legends actually, brought to life. And so is the whole show. What joy to encounter a big, splashy, funny musical that works.

robert.cushman@hotmail.com Aladdin runs until Jan. 5. For tickets and information, visit mirvish.com.

2013-11-30-kind-of-bleu-robert-lepage-s-:
One of Robert Lepages finest but least celebrated qualities is his humour. There are scenes in Needles and Opium that are the funniest in any Canadian play in ages. They owe their effectiveness, in roughly equal proportions, to Lepages writing, to his understated direction (the adjective isn't one he usually attracts, but it's appropriate) and to the performance of Marc Labreche, playing the role that the maestro himself created when the work first appeared, more than 20 years ago.

The role is that of a Quebecois actor, whose bilingualism has got him hired as narrator for a documentary film, shot in Paris, about the visit to that city in 1949 (just 40 years before his own trip) of Miles Davis and about the trumpeters affair there with the chanteuse Juliette Greco. We watch our hero, at the mike, expressing his frustration with both the script and the direction hes been given. We see him trying to place transatlantic calls from his hotel, and to get the lovemaking couple in the next room to keep the noise down, and being further frustrated by operators and receptionists on both continents. We see him visiting a hypnotherapist and being sidetracked into giving a hilarious summary of the history of his home province.

The reason for his seeking help, and for his being on edge generally, is that he's coping, or failing to, with a recent breakup; his lover has left him for someone and somewhere else, the somewhere being New York. This makes him feel a special and wrenching empathy with Davis who, we are told, broke up with Greco, and returned to the Big Apple, because he wanted to spare her the pains of an interracial romance. A second actor, Wellesley Robertson II, appears as Davis, and his story is acted out in counterpoint and in flashback. Those terms, though, hardly do justice to the physical and technological wonders that, more than the jokes, are the selling points of Lepage's work in general and of this piece in particular.

The narrator and his hotel rooms are encased, in Carl Fillions design, within a spinning cube that moves all over the stage, testing Labreches ability to keep his physical as well as his histrionic balance. Meanwhile Robertson's Davis prowls the streets of a Manhattan evoked by a stunning combination of documentary film footage, solid and perfectly dovetailed scenic elements, and his own recorded music is phenomenal. Labreche begins the play contemplating the merits of acupuncture; Davis, whose points of visual reference range from Grand Central to a pawnshop, seeks solace in the more lethal needles of heroin. Robertson also perfectly mimes his trumpetplaying; a coda finds him, cleaned-up and back in Paris, recording the improvised soundtrack for Louis Malle's Lift to the Scaffold.

So much for the needles. The opium is supplied by Jean Cocteau, on another feted postwar trip, this time from Paris to New York, and also played by Labreche. His scenes occasion their own share of visual marvels, re-creating some famous photographs in theatrical terms, but they arent as satisfying a fit, partly because Labreches French-Canadian imitation of a French-French accent lacks the casual grace, not to mention the comprehensibility, of the rest of his performance. The show's manner may in the end be more compelling than its matter, but we have a couple of superlative performances in a superlative production: one for which I return to that word understatement. One of the charms of Lepage's work is that it seems to take its own magic for granted. It has us gasping in amazement without gasping itself.

The Gay Heritage Project brings together three fine actors - Damien Atkins, Paul Dunn, Andrew Kushnir - who also have solid track-records as playwrights, to investigate the implications of their own title. They dont arrive at any final definitions of either "gay" or heritage (even "project" turns out to be problematic) but I doubt if they expected to. What, intriguingly, they present is an autobiographical show that (mostly) lifts the curse of self-indulgence. Each presents passages of his own life, including his own coming-out,

while also examining those of others. In one especially effective sequence, each in turn gets to depict one of his colleagues, while the one presented looks authoritatively on. (I think that this should come nearer to the end of the show than it does). The trio only perform together in song-and-dance interludes; otherwise the show is composed entirely of solo turns, though each actor may in that time play many parts. Kushnir, whose background is Ukrainians, conducts a dialogue with two gay men in the old country who can hardly understand the freedom he has attained in Canada. Dunn (Scottish-Irish) counterpoises his own experiences with the exponentially grimmer ones of homosexuals in Nazi Germany. But its Atkins (Australian, which I'd never suspected) who makes the most spectacular impression. In a spoof of The Wizard of Oz, he plays all the parts, Toto included, finally identifying the inscrutable Michel Foucault as the man behind the curtain; he details the frustrations of being typed as a gay actor, remarking that actors are never denied roles because they seem too straight (I'm not sure he's right about that); he finds himself, in what may be the most self-critical item of the evening, on board a metaphorical freedom bus, surrounded by members of minorities that overlap with his

own, thus raising the question of how anyone defines themselves. Atkins has become an actor of great versatility and extraordinary authority, most notably and recently as the hero of Angels in America, whose unsought quest might function as a supplement to the one he and his colleagues undertake here. Or maybe, since Angels is indisputably the larger work, the other way around.

Needles and Opium runs through Dec. 1 at the Bluma Appel Theatre, canadianstage.com; The Gay Heritage Project at Buddies in Bad Times through Dec. 8.

THEATRE REVIEW

Once

Royal Alexandra Theatre, Toronto

There's a party going on when you enter the theatre to see Once, and it's irresistible. The stage is crowded with people singing, playing, drinking, jigging about if not actually dancing. It all looks very Irish as, given the subject matter to come, it should. Some of the celebrants, it seems, are audience members who got there earlier than you did. They return to the auditorium but the party onstage continues, with cast members boisterously performing a couple of traditional, or at least unattributed, songs. Then one of them is cajoled into singing something that he himself has supposedly written. And this, as they used to say, is where the story really starts. We've been eased, delightfully, into the show proper. It isn't a wholly original idea, but it's brilliant.

From this point on, all the songs in Once, with a couple of broadly parodied exceptions, are the fictional creations of this same Dublin guy, whom the program identifies only as Guy and to whom the script gives no name at all. Guy meets Girl, who's a Czech immigrant with a talent for the piano, and who declares Guy's compositions to be masterpieces, just waiting to be snapped up by some fortunate record company; and indeed in real life they've made it as far as Broadway, where Once has been a great and deserved success. Even before that, they won an Oscar. As they come off the stage, though, the songs are pretty much indistinguishable, with keening and largely incomprehensible words, and tunes that typically start attractively and then wander off into inconsequence. The paradox of Once is that it's a very good musical with a poor score. A further paradox is that the songs, in their way, work. They're hopeless at advancing the story or, except at the most rudimentary level, depicting the characters, but they do create a mood. It's a mood that's superbly reinforced by the show's main attractions: its script and especially its staging.

Last week I described Aladdin as the best stage musical of a movie. I should have stressed that I meant the best stage musical of a movie that was already a musical. Once is adapted from a movie (hence the Oscar), one that I haven't seen; however, I trust the word of people who have, plus my own instincts, that it wasn't a musical but a film with songs. There is a difference: something in the way they move.

The stage show moves beautifully. There's nothing in John Tiffany's production that suggests another medium is being imitated or reproduced; it all feels warmly and indigenously theatrical.It follows in the path of John Doyle's Sondheim revivals by having its actors double as musicians (or vice versa). It departs from it by having them not just play their instruments but dance with them.

Steven Hoggett's choreography moves us rhythmically and enchantingly from scene to scene, with steps that have nothing to do with conventional Broadway stepping, everything with everyday body language.

In this way, it resembles the choreography of Spring Awakening, except that its prevailing mood is tender rather than tough. It's capable of sweeping, stagefilling collective gestures, and also of the most delicate detail. There's a small heartstopping moment in which an older woman sweeps a boy, who's just received crushingly bad news, up into her comforting arms.

It's emblematic of a show with its own flavour of bittersweet. Guy and Girl (whose characters apparently owe something to the show's actual composers, Glen Hansard and Marketa Irglova) look on track to be the predestined romantic couple: ill-sorted perhaps, but what would be the fun if they weren't? Girl has a child, whose absent father may or may not be wholly out of the picture. Guy is writing his songs in memory of a former girlfriend who left to go to New York, and with whom he may or may not wish to be reconciled. Guy comes on to Girl; Girl rebuffs him, but is obviously still interested.

Meanwhile she encourages him to follow his dreams, musical and romantic, all the way to America. That's all there is really; and it necessitates a fair amount of secondact padding. But the suspense of wondering which way they'll jump is enough to buoy the story up; and beyond that there's the city itself.

The show is in part a love letter to Dublin, and the musical's book (by the Irish playwright Enda Walsh) keeps it salty, funny and largely unsentimental. The songs are tied to the lamentable singer-songwriter principle that autobiography counts for more than craft or content, but they both suit and enhance the atmosphere, especially when Guy, Girl and a homemade band get to put them down at a 24-hour recording session.

Bob Crowley' designs are as magical as, though quite different from, his sets from Aladdin; they encase the whole roving action within an Irish snug with a long mirror on its back wall. Everything and everybody gets reflected, but there's nothing hectoring or pretentious about the device; it simply resonates.

Guy is played with casual charm by Stuart Ward and Girl with spiky, complex appeal by Dani de Waal. The supporting cast is splendid, not to mention multi-functional, with specially endearing work from Benjamin Magnuson as a bank manager rendered susceptible to the financial propositions of hero and heroine by the fact that he himself plays guitar (and, as it turns out, doubles on cello). The all-embracing musical metaphor does much to carry the evening. The show's good beginning is matched by its good ending: both logical and surprising - logical because surprising - as good endings should be.

robert.cushman@hotmail.com Once runs until Jan. 5. For tickets and information, visit mirvish.com.

There's never a boring moment in God of Carnage, but there are few really arresting ones, either. The characters are Alan and Annette and Michael and Veronica, two American married couples. In Yasmina Rezas original script they were French, like the play itself, and so they were in Christopher Hamptons English translation when it was first presented in London. They then underwent a transatlantic transplant for ease of North American consumption. This kind of parochial patronage isn't precisely what the play itself is satirizing but it is in the same, how you say, ballpark.

Alan and Annette, the more upscale of the pairs, have a son who got in a fight with the son of Michael and Veronica, and knocked out two of his teeth. (Both the unseen boys are 11.)

The victim's parents have invited the assailants parents over, so that a civilized apology may be drafted. At first all seems to be going politely, but then rifts appear, not just between the marriages but within them. What first tips things over are the calls Alan keeps getting on his cellphone, which he can never resist answering, in full hearing of the others. They and we learn that he is a lawyer counselling a pharmaceutical company on how not to accept liability for a potentially lethal drug. Veronica, who writes well-intentioned books about the worlds worst countries, is appalled by this. So is Annette, though not for moral reasons; she resents her husband's absorption in his work, of which his phone is an umbilical symbol. Michael, who runs an appliance business, is less affronted by Alan's ethics than by his superior airs. As the evening proceeds, the two men are revealed as, essentially, allies. In the plays title speech Alan proclaims his belief, exemplified by both his own and his sons generation, in a murderously aggressive spirit that, despite all the comforting lies we may tell ourselves, rules our thoughts and actions. Michael echoes him by copping to the inner Neanderthal he has been repressing in resentful deference to his wife's liberal values.

Linked to this is the assertion that good deeds - Veronica's for example - are motivated by the desire to think well of oneself. This is convincing if not especially disturbing; after all, its the results rather than the causes that count. It also has an ironic flip-side; even Alan is shamed at one point into doing a decent thing, and it hardly seems to matter whether hes impelled by conscience or by the knowledge that the others' eyes and ears are upon him. Anyway, that's about all the play has to say. It spins out variations, mostly verbal but sometimes ingeniously physical, on a single theme. Annette, after too much drink and dessert, throws graphically up over Veronicas cherished volume of Kokoschka illustrations, thereby putting her hostess into an un-pretty pickle of aggrieved indignation and hospitable compassion.

God of Carnage is an off-Mirvish production by Joel Greenbergs Studio 180 who recently brought us Clybourne Park, another conversation piece in which conciliation gave way to violence, but one in which both the issues and the construction were considerably more complex and far-reaching. That play was witty to the bone; this one is merely funny at the fingertips. The acting is good, though John Bourgeois' Alan gets too easily ruffled too often. Tony Nappo, with a strong physical and vocal resemblance to the late James Gandolfini who played the role on Broadway, slips easily into Michael's rages and resentments. The women, though, have the best of it, Sarah Orensteins damaged Annette falling elegantly apart and Linda Kashs Veronica trying and explosively failing to keep it together. Since it's her house that's the setting, John Thompson has honoured her taste with a striking design in red and black.

For social satire more biting and locally pertinent, travel a couple of blocks south on Yonge to The Little Mermaid. This, the latest and possibly the best of Ross Pettys holiday pantomimes, bears little resemblance to the Disney movie or the Hans Andersen story; as is gleefully acknowledged in an opening number hymning the freedoms and delights of The Public Domain. This mermaid is a social activist who resides on the bottom of Torontos harbour and uses her day at the surface to protest, and subvert, a scheme to turn her home into a site for "three casinos, a large airport, and 14 condos designed by David Mirvish." Given the way civic policy is going, I'd say she was swimming against the tide, but pantos are allowed, indeed required, to have happy endings. Besides, nobody could resist a heroine who looks and sounds like Chilina Kennedy, a super singer, actress, comedienne and dancer. She backs up every word and note she utters, and is even delightful when struck temporarily dumb. In Tracey Flye's production, choreographed by Marc Kimmelman, marine creatures travel on skates - quite a trick when you also have a tail - and Kennedys mermaid skates like an Angel, which happens to be her name.

Her chief antagonist is, of course, Petty himself as Ogopogo, a sea-vandal who also appears in an earthly entrepreneurial disguise so complete that I initially failed to penetrate it. The kids in the audience were far sharper; they booed him on sight. He is, as usual, excellent though he seems to be relinquishing star comic status to Dan Chameroy, in his accustomed drag as Angels Auntie Plumbum, who confuses gender still further by being less mermaid than Merman, of the Ethel variety; wherever she goes, themes from Gypsy go with her. He/she has mastered/mistressed being vulgar and delicate at the same time. There is equally reliable clown backup from Eddie Glen and Reid Janisse, the latter also billed, rather low down, as Writer; he's done a good job. Jordan Clark, a terrific dancer, plays Ogopogo's seductress-assistant. Angel has three flirtatious friends, one of whom is, like, a valley mermaid. She also has a love-interest (Marc Devigne) whom she meets rather late, but extremely cute; what first attracts him is the way she harmonizes, which shows him to be a young man of taste. Even the four hardworking male supers have personality while Lana Carillo, as a Shrimp whos the stern principal of her school of fish, gives possibly the most terrifying performance on any Toronto stage. Erika Connors costumes are a stylish delight, and Michael Gianfrancesco's sets, lavish within their means, are very attractive. The storyline forbids the inclusion of anything resembling a village square scene, which is a great relief. Petty's pantos have shaken free of most of the old conventions, even while establishing their own.

God of Carnage runs through Dec. 15 at the Panasonic Theatre; The Little Mermaid through Jan. 4 at the Elgin Theatre

Adevice that may work in a novel can seem like a thin literary conceit when transferred to the stage. That is the principal problem with the bold attempt by the independent company Unspun Theatre to adapt Gunter Grass's The Tin Drum. Oskar, the central character of both book and play, addresses us from the German mental hospital to which he's been voluntarily confined sometime in the 1950s. Oskar is 30, and he stopped growing - physically, not mentally - at the age of three. This was another conscious decision, taken to avoid the pangs and responsibilities of adulthood. These would have been especially onerous for Oskar since he grew up, or didn't grow up, in Danzig, the polyglot city whose disputed Polish or German identity was a flashpoint for the outbreak of the Second World War.

Oskar's own identity recapitulates that of his hometown in, so to speak, little. His father Alfred is German, and an early convert to Nazism; his mother's family is Polish, one of them being a cousin, Jan, who's also her lover and quite possibly Oskar's real father. This situation, which seems to be tacitly accepted on all sides, doesn't stop Alfred and Jan from being card-playing best buddies, but it finally brings death and destruction. There seems no particular reason for Oskar to blame himself for this, but the novel appears to think he should. Or at least the play does. Or at the very least the program-note does. It asks us to consider "what kind of burden do we bear when we watch history unfold but do not intervene?" By this reckoning, Oskar's indifference to the dramas in his own house (and a convenient hotel) are a dress rehearsal for his opting out of the greater cataclysm that engulfs his whole community. All he cares about - and here the story does begin to build a case - is his drum.

Or his drums. He goes through a lot of them, having been given his first, as a kind of pacifier, when he was three. Beating them, furiously, becomes his primary method of communication; his secondary method is a scream that really can shatter glass. Both these talents come in useful in his subsequent young-adult career as a professional entertainer. As a child, he's acquired his instruments from a friendly storekeeper, obviously Jewish, by whose eventual fate he is quite unconcerned. When the Danzig post office mounts a last desperate stand against the invading Germans, Oskar's greed for the city's last available drum causes the death of cousin Jan, who has been reluctantly conscripted into heroism.

The post-office siege is one of the most powerful sequences in an uneven production by Chris Hanratty, who's also one of the two adapters. An earlier pogrom is similarly effective, at least visually; in both scenes the noise, ingeniously created through the pounding of found objects, tends to drown out the dialogue and hence the narrative. Storytelling, though, is hazardous throughout, the difficulty being not so much making the events clear as making them count. As often happens with novels dramatized, we get one thing after another, rather than one thing leading to another. The adulterous triangle in Oskar's home takes up more time than it justifies. There is also the unstageableness of Oskar himself, played by a full-grown actor (Jesse Aaron Dwyre) who makes no pretence of being anything else, in a staging that isn't fanciful enough for us to make the necessary imaginative leap. We have to keep reminding ourselves that he's supposed to be a midget, a task made more complicated by scenes in which, temporarily deprived of his drum, he is said to have grown to full size. Played with some charm but little individuality, this Oskar is a more unreliable narrator than may have been intended. We're told that he's an omnivorous reader, much affected by early exposure to Goethe and Rasputin. But what they meant to him, and how they influenced him, is never explored. He remains opaque.

The general performance level is variable, very. Cyrus Lane, an actor of great sardonic power, plays Jan, indifferently at first but then quivering with terrified life in the face of death. He's even finer, later, as a liberated concentration-camp inmate saying a determined, demented Kaddish over the body of a man whom he doesn't know, but may possibly suspect, to have been an enthusiastic anti-Semite; it's the high point of the evening. (The word "Jew" is never uttered in the play, though the word "synagogue" is; decide for yourselves whether this represents subtlety or coyness.) There's much doubling by everyone but Oskar; Courtney Ch'ng Lancaster is good in all her guises, especially the shy ones, and Shira Leuchter (the other adapter) blossoms when she dons an Italian accent. She does this when playing a circus psychic, Oskar's lover (he's sexually active, in all his dimensions) and one of a troupe of selfstyled freaks who school him in the wisdom of remaining aloof: wisdom that comes back to bite them. Him too probably: but, despite a scene of choral guilt-tripping that attempts to tie everyone and everything together, you never really know.

Repetitive Strain Injury, from another indie group that calls itself Company Kid Logic, has already received some of the rudest reviews in memory, and Rob van Meenen's play does indeed live all too faithfully up to its title, especially the adjective part. But its second half does contain a couple of half-decent if essentially free-floating scenes. In one a married couple conduct a believable row, even though the issue that gives rise to it is well beyond belief. In the other a non-married couple seem to be approaching an interesting rapprochement: until, that is, it transpires that one of them is playing a trick not only on the other but on us. The two relationships do nothing to illuminate one another, and are tied together as narrative only by the thinnest pieces of string. These include a fifth character whose story and function I cannot bear to describe, except to say that she's a supposedly wise figure who exemplifies the play's wild erratic swings between failed comedy and attempted tragedy. It would take acting and direction of exceptional deftness to keep such a script afloat. It doesn't happen here.

The Tin Drum runs through Dec. 14 at the Daniels Spectrum; Repetitive Strain Injury runs through Dec. 15 at the Factory Studio.
