It is a truth universally acknowledged that Jane Austen's Pride and Prejudice has one of the most perfectly balanced opening sentences in English literature. Its words arent spoken in the adaptation of the novel at Campbell House, which doesnt have a narrator. It does nevertheless convey something of its author's amused but merciless voice.

The last time I visited Campbell House for theatrical or indeed any other purposes, it was to see a twoactor dramatization of The Turn of the Screw, which proved to be clever and ultimately scary. Pride and Prejudice, a novel that's theatrically harder to handle, or at least longer, has been staged, all over the stately house, by Burt & Werneburg, a company consisting of two actresses, Hallie Burt and Kate Werneburg, who take responsibility for the adaptation and for playing all the roles. They call their version Elizabeth - Darcy; and, as youd expect, even without that title, it focuses on the most popular courtship in English fiction, that between the proud Mr. Fitzwilliam Darcy and the prejudiced (against him, anyway) Miss Elizabeth Bennet. The results are, again as you might expect, uneven; but theyre ultimately enjoyable.

This is a site-specific production in a site that pretty much imposes its own rules. As with The Turn of the Screw we assemble in the hall, and are then led up and down the main staircase into a succession of dining rooms, sitting rooms and a subterranean kitchen. Unlike The Turn of the Screw, which is very much the story of one particular house, Pride and Prejudice moves between dwellings, so we have to imagine ourselves in some half-dozen establishments in four different English counties. The adaptation does a nifty job of letting us know where we're presumed to be and just who the actors, who don't have time for any but the most basic costume changes, are impersonating at any given moment. The direction, by Tom Arthur Davis, is especially neat in the manner of surprise entrances; you never know through which door somebody is going to enter or who theyre going to be when they get there. All the same, though I understand the desire to make use of every available space, I doubt that even so smug and insensitive a wooer as the Reverend Mr. Collins would have invaded Elizabeths bedroom in order to propose to her. Not in good British society in 1813.

Both performers appear as a multitude of characters, but they naturally take one title role apiece. Burt's Elizabeth is generally delightful, whether pert or hurt, as attractive and intelligent, and with as intuitive a sense of her own dignity, as Austen's readers have always taken her to be. Werneburgs Darcy doesnt initially get beyond a varnish of prim hauteur, inexpertly applied; she does though improve considerably when the character reveals his more vulnerable side.

As for their other assumptions: Burt's wit comes in handy for Lizzie's acerbic father, of whom one would like to see more than this version has time for. His most famous utterance, about Lizzies having to choose between being abandoned by her mother if she refuses Mr. Collins and by her father if she accepts him, is given its due, spoken through a door so as to spare the actress the necessity of talking to herself. Even better is the scene in which the reclusive Mr. Bennet accepts responsibility for neglecting his family, and asks to be allowed to indulge his guilt because - and here I paraphrase - it wont last long. Burt is, however, thoroughly off key as younger sister Lydia, the cause of the incipient family disgrace, whom she plays with a kittenish vulgarity that's out of style and out of period. Both Lydia and her seducer Wickham have been shortshifted by the adaptation, but that's probably unavoidable.

The same fault that hobbles Werneburgs Darcy - an insensitivity to phrasing, so that everything comes out squashed and hasty - also causes her to overplay both Mr. Collins and his rival in tactlessness Mrs. Bennet; the latter, the archetype of managing mothers, is great fun when you hear her cannonading from a distance but most uncomfortable to share a room with. Surprisingly, Werneburg plays the snobbish Lady Catherine de Bourgh, a role that might seem an invitation to Gorgonhood, with considerable and very effective restraint. She is similarly graceful with Elizabeths friend Charlotte, acceding with sad clear eyes to a future as Mrs. Collins, and Jane, eldest of the Bennet sisters; I never realized before how much Pride and Prejudice, with its harried and fractious parents and five marriageable daughters has in common with Fiddler on the Roof. Jane and her noble suitor Mr. Bingley are still not the liveliest company, but then neither are they in the book.

The show was first seen on the Toronto Fringe where, says the director in a program note, critics objected to his ending it with Mozart's Requiem. The irony, he says, is justified, because at least two of the story's marriages are obviously doomed. That's all very well, but the bride descending the staircase as the music plays is Elizabeth herself, with Darcy waiting for her; and the production doesn't seem to want to be ironic about them. Their union is a hard-won victory, in the play as in the book. The same program makes amends, though, by concluding the long customary list of acknowledgments with the name of Jane Austen, without whom.

robert.cushman@hotmail.com Elizabeth - Darcy runs through Dec. 29 at Campbell House Museum. 416-597-0227

It is, as Andy Williams really should have sung, the Most Repetitive Time of the Year: the time when the same, not necessarily good, old songs go into rapid rotation in every coffee-shop and supermarket. The time when an ersatz carol like The Little Drummer Boy goes around (and around, and around) long after outstaying any welcome it may once have had. The time when Bing Crosby singing White Christmas becomes inescapable. Except that it doesn't, not Bing's recording or anyone else's. Maybe the places I frequent have atypical tastes in muzak, but this year I can't recall hearing it anywhere. Maybe it doesn't like the company it would be keeping. Maybe the programmers feel that it would be just too familiar, though that doesn't seem to stop them when it comes to an ersatz carol like The Little Drummer Boy or even a real one like Silent Night, whose ubiquity has given it the status of an honorary pop song. Or maybe I'm just imagining things. Real or imagined, the absence of White Christmas has set me thinking about what a good, if taken for granted, song it actually is.

Irving Berlin of course wrote it, and Crosby introduced it in the 1942 movie Holiday Inn, a film built around the conceit of a hotel open only on public holidays and staging a separate floorshow for each one of them. This obliged, or enabled, Berlin to come up with themesongs for Lincoln's birthday (Abraham, an earnest anthem of emancipation with Bing in blackface, God forgive him) and for Washington's (Fred Astaire dancing around a cherrytree while cheerfully singing that he can't tell a lie - about being in love). There were also numbers about starting the New Year right and about having plenty to be thankful for (at Thanksgiving).

For Berlin, whose business instincts were as sharp as his verbal and musical ones, the assignment must have seemed heaven sent: an opportunity to write multiple songs with annually recurring hooks. As it turned out, only three of them caught on, One was Easter Parade, recycled from a Broadway revue of a decade before; another was Be Careful, It's My Heart, on which you have to concentrate hard to realize that it's about Valentine's Day; and the third was White Christmas, which also had originally been written for a revue, but an unproduced one, and is one of the soberest celebratory songs ever written. That's its genius and the source, however unexamined, of its lasting appeal. Well, that and Berlin's almost unfailing rightness in matching words to music, so that everything sings naturally, nothing sounds forced. There's an especial grace in the way this song ends, not repeating its title exactly but re-ordering it: "May all your Christmases be white." It's a hope, not a guarantee, sung by a character who at that point in the movie is having a down moment.

As it happens, Crosby's performance in the film, like his own and most other singers' subsequent recordings, is textually incomplete. The full version has an introductory verse:

The sun is shining, The grass is green, The orange and palm trees sway.

There's never been such a dayIn Beverly Hills, L.A. But it 's December the twenty-fourth, And I am longing to be up north.

That localizes and individualizes the song, which dramatically is the right thing to do. But it also diminishes it, makes it less everybody's story. And of course it was wartime, when loss and longing were everybody's story, even if they were spending Christmas at home, even if it were snowing. Even without a war, there's enough yearning in most people's lives for the song to touch a chord. We may think of it as aural greeting-card, but that isn't how we feel it. Cutting the verse was a canny decision, commercially and even artistically.

Curiously, the same thing had already happened in reverse with the other enduring anthem to come out of a Hollywood musical, an immediately pre-war one, The Wizard of Oz.

Over the Rainbow also had a verse, one that generalized the individual yearnings of the girl in the song into a philosophical statement about what happens "when all the world is a hopeless

jumble." In cutting it, the producers, or whoever was responsible, made the song all about Dorothy, eventually all about Judy Garland. Over the Rainbow achieved immortality by emphasizing the personal over the universal, White Christmas by emphasizing the universal over the personal. Each was right for its moment, onscreen and off, and, as it's turned out, for all subsequent moments.

The melancholy - or, heard another way, the dogged against-the-odds optimism - that distinguishes White Christmas also marks the other great seasonal song to come out of wartime Hollywood. I recently saw Have

Yourself a Merry Little Christmas described, disparagingly, as the most depressing of all Christmas songs. The complainant should have heard the lyric that Garland in Meet Me in St. Louis was originally required to sing to her kid sister as they faced being uprooted from their home city: "Have yourself a merry little Christmas, it may be your last ..." She protested that audiences would hate her if they heard her singing that to a child, so the song was rewritten. It still sounds bittersweet: "Some day soon we all may be together if the fates allow/Until then we' ll have to muddle through somehow ..." For commercial (i.e. non-cinematic) publication, that last line was changed to the anodyne "hang a shining star upon the highest bough" and "may" became "will," and that's how the song has mostly been sung since, transforming something touching and individual into just another Christmas number. Hugh Martin and Ralph Blane, who wrote it, were not, as far as I know, Jewish. This of course differentiates them from most classic American songwriters and especially, it seems, from those who wrote Christmas songs. If, as has been claimed, the 19th-century conception of Christmas was invented by Dickens, then the twentieth-century idea might be credited to Berlin.

It's a secular version, of course, though it couldn't exist without some taken-forgranted religious underpinnings. (And White Christmas itself is practically a hymn compared to Easter Parade, in which the holiday is a fashion show.) It's also, though very exportable, an American version. Berlin, the five-year-old Russian immigrant, came by his patriotism naturally; it always sounds honest, which is why it never sounds embarrassing. He wrote, sung, about America even when it wasn't his explicit subject. White Christmas does mention sleigh-bells and glistening treetops, but its central image is that of a man on his own writing Christmas cards and dreaming of family. It's about being lonely but linked; which is a very American thing. And a very wartime thing.

It's significant that none of the enduring American Christmas songs date from before World War Two. The post-war songs, exploiting the market that Berlin opened up, have been loaded with the seasonal cliches that he, and Blane and Martin, avoided. Mel Torme's Christmas Song ("Chestnuts roasting on an open fire") is a catalogue of them, though musically superior and with the grace to be mildly deprecatory about itself. Mitchell Parish's words to Sleigh Ride ("there's a birthday party at the home of Farmer Grey...") - a winter rather than a Christmas song but they're all grist to the seasonal mill - trades on the audience's nostalgia for an Arcadia that never existed. Rudolph the Red Nosed Reindeer (by Johnny Marks, if anyone cares) at least has an original story idea which may explain its survival in the face of words and music of surpassing banality. Though maybe they helped.

Did no writer in the great tradition ever protest? One did: Yip Harburg, the Wizard of Oz lyricist and a Hollywood blacklist victim, wrote a 1951 Broadway show entitled Flahooley, a fantastical satire on consumerism and ... well, just about everything, really. It included a choral number called Sing the Merry: a mock-carol in which the cash-registers musically jingled while the lyrics rhymed off the names of New York's biggest stores, culminating in the exhortation to "for Christ's sake, give Christmas back to Christ."

That final line, penned by a self-proclaimed Jewish atheist, was cut from the stage production. The entire number was cut from the cast album. It seems that all the best Christmas songs have been subject to some kind of censorship, some from their authors.

Of course there are other holidays to be sung about, once this one is over. Frank Loesser, another great wordsand-music man (he wrote Guys and Dolls), knew about that. Baby, it's cold outside. What are you doing New Year's Eve?

There are five musicals contained within The Musical of Musicals: The Musical!, and they all have the same plot. Heroine, whose name is June or Juny or Jeune or Junita or Junie Faye, cannot pay her rent. Sinister landlord, variously known as Jidder or Jitter or Mr. Jitter or Phantom Jitters or Jutter, tells her she can avoid eviction by succumbing to his whims, which are mostly marital. Hero, who might be called Bill or Billy or Villy or William or Big Willy depending on ethnicity or (he would have us believe) endowment, comes to heroines rescue, sometimes. Older woman, identified as Abby or Aunt Abby or Mother Abby or Fraulein Abby or Abigail Von Starr, dispenses advice, of a highly vocal nature, from the sidelines, secure in the knowledge that the outcome will not affect her in any way whatever.

Each of these musicals of musicals (the musicals!) is written in the style of a recognizable Broadway master or team of masters. Just to put the recognition beyond doubt, each portion of pastiche is preceded by a caption that tells us not just the title of the segment but just who it is "in the style of ": a concession to ignorance that strikes me as distinctly uncool and also as useless, since anybody who can't identify the models instantaneously will get nothing out of the show at all, and probably wouldn't be attending in the first place. The piece has music by Eric Rockwell, lyrics by Joanne Bogart, and book, what there is of it, by the two of them together. Their parodies are verbally clever and musically acute, sometimes even subtle. Theyve taken a long time to reach us; the show was done in New York in 2003, and had its Toronto premiere this year in a small production at SummerWorks. I thought it was great. Now that its been promoted to the glossier or at least more commercial precincts of the Panasonic, I have, in the curmudgeonly way so typical of critics, to revise that opinion. I now think it's good.

The one reservation that I expressed, back when the living was easy and the seats cheaper, now bulks larger than before. It is that the show too often confuses satire with mere quotation. This is especially the case in the first and longest segment, the one that lays down the ground rules for all the others. It's called Corn!, and its principal target is Rodgers and Hammersteins Oklahoma!, with side glances at the rest of their canon, starting with the characters names. Heroine June gets hers repeated in triplicate, like the month that was bustin' out all over in Carousel; villainous Jidder is but a double consonant away from the no-good Jigger in the same show; Mother Abby is the Mother Abbess of The Sound of Music, though her maternity seems purely secular. Big Willy doesn't have any R&H namesakes that I can call to mind, though he compensates by combining the avocations of cowboy and fairground barker. The state of Oklahoma itself has been relocated to Kansas where, you will recall, it is very corny, especially in August. The field, Big Willy sings on the beautiful mornin of his first appearance, is all ears, which is a line to die for. Rockwells pastiche of Rodgers' tunes is very sharp, as close to the originals as anyone could come without being sued, and he and Bogart do a delightful job in re-casting Carousel's Real Nice Clambake as a serenade to clam-dip, following the idea through in precise, affectionate detail. The problem, though, with this whole R&H section is that its too affectionate. It doesnt have an attitude.

The better parts of the evening have some poisoned darts to aim at their targets. Dear Abby! takes on the world, meaning the heroines, of Jerry Herman; the diva Dollys and managing Mames and their choruses of sycophants, on and off the stage. "The audience applauds her," says the production's pianist doubling as narrator even though she hasn't done anything yet, and the ensemble proclaim their own worthlessness and hopelessness when deprived of her presence, even though she still hasnt done anything. Even Mr. Jitters succumbs to her; sent away to put a little more mascara on, he returns sounding just like Carol Channing, thereby proving that Hermans earlier big ladies were really the drag-queens of La Cage Aux Folles waiting to happen. Aunt Abby's obligatory self-doubt number is splendidly titled Did I Put Out Enough? Aspects of Juanita, dedicated to aspects of Andrew Lloyd Webber, gets even more personal, giving us Sir Phantom Jitter, a masked operatic impresario who tells his protegee that she has the voice of a whiny self-absorbed angel but nevertheless wants her to sing for him. The authors fail, though, in the impossible task of satirizing Cats.

A Little Complex, located in the Sondheim part of town, presents Rockwell with his toughest compositional challenge, one to which he impressively rises. Bogart's lyrics, too, are aptly tongue-twisting. The setting is an alienated and alienating apartment building reminiscent of Company but called The Woods; indeed the writers reference most of the Sondheim oeuvre with the notable exception of Follies, perhaps because so much of that score is already pastiche. They are very perceptive about the resemblances between Sondheims two great obsessives: Sweeney Todd, artist in murder, and Georges Seurat, artist in art.

Sondheim of course uses pastiche, not just for its own entertaining sake, but to make dramatic points. This distinguishes him not just from Rockwell and Bogart but from John Kander and Fred Ebb, who are the objects of Speakeasy, the last and most narrowly focused of the evenings travesties. (I use the word in its original non-pejorative sense.) It summons the cynicism and the funny accents of Cabaret and Chicago, which it seems to regard, probably rightly, as the only two entries in Kander and Ebb's extensive catalogue that would be readily recognizable; though they do throw in a bit of Kiss of the Spider Woman as well. By this fifth go-round, the rent plot (which of course was also the Rent plot) has begun to seem tired, indeed perfunctory. But the real subject here is Bob Fosse, the directorchoreographer whose stage and screen visions of these dedicatedly decadent musicals have proved indelible.

The choreography in this Toronto production is, as it happens, excellent. It's the work of Vinetta Strombergs, whos also the director; her miniature takeoffs of Fosse, and of Gower Champion in his Hello Dolly mode, are very witty, but her tour-de-force, and that of her corps of four, is her take on the high-horse stepping of Agnes de Milles Oklahoma! dream ballet. The performers are unglamorous but expert; to judge from the New York cast album, they're better than their American predecessors, who included the composer and lyricist themselves. This production has a discrete (and discreet) narrator-pianist, Michael Mulrooney, who carries out both his duties with schoolmasterly aplomb Mark Cassius gets the Jitters and Adrian Marchuk the Willies, while Dana Jean Phoenix does the flaming Junes and Paula Wolfson takes us on a tour of the Abby's who consistently get the best material. In Corn!, her fortissimo admonition to Follow Your Dream is, like the Climb Evry Mountain that inspired it, magnificently irrelevant to the situation at hand; in Dear Abby she makes the conflicting exhortation to Take My Advice and Live sound divinely patronizing; and in Speakeasy, as old Berlins throatiest gift to Chicago nightlife, she's Lenya and Dietrich combined as she urges the permanently impoverished Juny to Sell Your Body ("Who are you? Joan of Arc? Find yourself an easy mark.")

The best is last. To a tune reminiscent of a familiar song from A Chorus Line and to the steps of the familiar hat-tipping dance that goes with it the entire cast, pianist this time enchantingly included, bow and twirl, and tell us that they are done ("So why are you still sitting there?") It is, in many ways, the wittiest and most refreshing thing in the evening. It sent me away happy before, and it sent me away happy again.

2014-01-04-12-plays-of-new-year-s-from-a:
Here, alphabetically, are some of the shows that stood out for me in the year just departed. I couldn't get it down to a Top 10 so here is my Divine Dozen (with others associated).

After Miss Julie Strindberg has rarely been so exciting or made so much political and emotional sense as in Patrick Marbers British update, masterfully directed by David Ferry with perfectly pitched performances by Claire Armstrong, Christopher Morris and Amy Keating. "Wow!" murmured one member of the spellbound first night audience and the feeling was unanimous. The tiny Storefront Theatre must take some credit for the intensity of the experience: one of a new wave of makeover sites for independent companies (the Red Sandcastle is another).

Angels in America Soulpepper had a peak-and-valley kind of year, but the peaks included a couple of mountain ranges: three evenings of The Norman Conquests, and two of Angels in America, Tony Kushners comic-cosmic-fantastic epic standing up superbly in Albert Schultz's production, with a breathtaking roster of major performances from the company's senior, junior and intermediate generations: Damien Atkins, Diego Matamoros, Nancy Palk, Gregory Prest, Mike Ross, Troy Adams. Other Soulpepper highlights: the aforementioned Conquests, with Fiona Reid relishing in her element and a lovely debut by Laura Condolln; Rosencrantz and Guildenstern Are Dead, with Ted Dysktra especially delightful; and the much underrated and very imaginative La Ronde.

Arcadia The Shaw Festivals revival of Tom Stoppards house-andgarden possible masterpiece might have filled one of their larger spaces, but Eda Holmes' production made clever use of the Studio space, while the demanding text was beautifully handled by Gray Powell, Diana Donnelly, Patrick McManus, Kate Besworth, others.

Lady Windermere's Fan At the opposite extreme of scale, Peter Hinton reclaimed Wildes society melodrama in a production that was a visual (designer, Teresa Przybylski), musical and emotional masterpiece. And funny too. Other Shaw highlights included Major Barbara, Jackie Maxwells intimate revival of what seems increasingly likely to be the house sage's best play.

The Little Mermaid Well, why not? Ross Petty's "family musicals" (or made-over English pantomimes) have become a tradition Toronto can call its own, and this may be the best of them. Also, you couldnt find a musical performance this year to top Chilina Kennedy on skates and tail.

Mary Stuart Antoni Cimolinos first production as Stratford's artistic director could not have been happier. A powerful and meticulous staging of the greatest female double-header ever written, with Lucy Peacock and Seana McKenna radiating in isolation and coruscating in conflict. And with a luxurious line-up of supporting males: Ben Carlson, Brian Dennehy (his best Stratford performance ever), Ian Lake, Geraint Wyn-Davies.

Needles and Opium Lepage, in glory. Ditto his two actors.

Once The year's best musical. Aladdin came in second; while among revivals there was Falsettos (Acting UpStage/Harold Green), a flawless presentation of a flawed work.

Othello With Romeo and Juliet, Measure for Measure and The Merchant of Venice, Stratford had its best all-round Shakespeare season in recent memory, but the crown was Chris Abrahams conquest of the usually unyielding Avon stage: red-hot designs by Julie Fox and performances by Dion Johnstone, Graham Abbey, Deborah Hay ... again, the list goes on. A great year altogether for what has recently seemed the most intransigent of the tragedies; in London, outgoing director Nicholas Hytner staged a marvellous production at the National Theatre; a scene from it can be glimpsed in the Nationals 50th birthday gala, well worth catching when it comes around again on NT Live. (Check your multiplex). Back at Stratford: special commendations for Sara Topham's Juliet, Scott Wentworth's Shylock and Tom Rooney and Stephen Ouimette in Measure; the last two were also terrific tramps in Godot, with Randy Hughson a revelatory Lucky.

Pig Not the greatest play, but a chance to pay tribute to Brendan Healys transformative directorate at Buddies in Bad Times. A mesmerizing production, fearlessly performed by Bruce Dow, Paul Dunn and Blair Williams. Fearless was also the word for Dow, earlier, in Of a Monstrous Child; while Dunn, later, teamed impressively up with Damien Atkins (possible actor of the year) and Andrew Kushnir in The Gay Heritage Project. Healy, meanwhile, also scored with Soulpeppers Entertaining Mr. Sloane.

This Best Play from Away, no contest. (The author's Canadian born, but this play and her career are essentially American). A bold staging by and at Canadian Stage, who later gave us Venus in Fur; again not the greatest play, but Carly Street was electric and Rick Miller a surprise.

This Is War By Hannah Moscovitch.

Best Play from Here. Again, no contest - including a couple of others from the same author. Finely observed, deceptively well constructed, and an especially gripping and wellacted production by Richard Rose.

Additional: family connections prevent me from including Passion Play on the list, still: It united the talents and resources of three of Toronto's independent companies (Convergence Theatre, Outside the March, Sheep No Wool) backed by a fourth (Crows Theatre), it was creatively site-specific in two separate sites, it brought us an impressively ambitious American play (by Sarah Ruhl) and it had eye-catching performances by Cyrus Lane, Mayko Nguyen and Andrew Kushnir, not to mention Maev Beaty as Elizabeth I, Hitler, and Ronald Reagan, the last of whom she devastatingly outacted. And, though its not strictly my turf, Canadian Opera Company's Dialogue des Carmelites and Peter Grimes were among the great theatrical events of the year. Dramatic companies should consider poaching.

2014-01-06-not-to-code-prior-to-hollywoo:
Though I would count myself a musicals buff, there is one group of classic movies in the genre that I had never got around to watching. I refer to the musicals made in Hollywood in the early years of the talkies by the expatriate German director Ernst Lubitsch. For years I had read that these films were the Champagne of musicals, frothy and sophisticated and explicitly but tastefully sexy in ways that would have been beyond the ken of any American-born director. So finally, for a holiday treat, I curled up with Lubitsch Musicals (Criterion Collection; Eclipse Series 8), a DVD box set of the four movie musicals Lubitsch made for Paramount between 1929 and 1932, and then topped up my frosted glass with The Merry Widow (WB Archive Collection), a one-off in the same tradition that he directed at MGM in 1934.

Well, most of it is true. Compared to the static movie musicals that preceded them, and that looked like literal reproductions of stage shows even when they weren't, the Paramount pictures are wonderfully fluid; Lubitsch seems not so much to be breaking the rules as never to have heard of them. That includes the perennial Hollywood convention by which singing could only be deemed acceptable in a performance situation; here the characters, none of them singers by trade, break into song simply because it's a natural way of expressing themselves.

It's probably wise to allow more time between viewings than I was able to do, as the characters, tones and settings are very similar. They all take place in Paris, or in some other European location equally imaginary. They all star Maurice Chevalier, Jeanette MacDonald, or both.

To be precise: Chevalier and MacDonald are teamed together in The Love Parade (1929), the first of the Paramounts, and in One Hour with You (1932), the last. In between, MacDonald is seen dallying with Jack Buchanan in Monte Carlo (1930), and Chevalier with both Claudette Colbert and Miriam Hopkins in The Smiling Lieutenant (also 1930).

MacDonald is a dream, and a revelation to all who have thought of her solely in her later guise as the virgin goddess of operetta movies opposite Nelson Eddy. Her typical role is that of a besieged beauty, living on her wits to keep the wolves - often amatory, sometimes economic - from her door. She's a sparkling comedienne, wonderful at putting men in their place, but with an underlying vulnerability, so that she melts enchantingly once she has decided which man it would be sensible to melt for.

All these pictures begin with some kind of parade; in Monte Carlo it's a throng of wedding guests, one of whom bears a sign reading "happy the bride the sun shines on." Then it rains. Meanwhile the bride, having discovered that her wedding dress doesn't fit and with no time to put on anything else, is off to the railroad station in search of freedom. She then sings Beyond the Blue Horizon, the one classic song to come out of any of these films, and an acknowledged landmark for the way it matches propulsive words, propulsive music, propulsive sound effects (the whizzing loco wheels), and propulsive visuals (peasants in the fields waving encouragement at Jeanette as she hurtles by them), all in the service of a propulsive character and situation.

Chevalier provokes more complicated feelings. For those who know him as the complacently aging boulevardier of Gigi, it's a shock to see him as a young man, already inordinately pleased with himself and with his effect on women. At least in Gigi, he's just remembering it. Here, he's a coy boy, constantly rolling his eyes and flashing his accent, and it isn't only in The Smiling Lieutenant that you wish someone would make him turn the smile off. That's the bad half of it. The good is that, as in any good sex farce or romantic comedy (these films are both), his ego, to his own great surprise, takes a pasting, and Chevalier plays both the incredulity and the hurt very well. His redeeming charm when successful is that he can't believe all the girls are happening to him; when rejected, he can't believe that they aren't happening to him What really deepens him is wedlock; he spends a surprising proportion of these films being married.

Part of the mystique of the Lubitsch films is that they pre-date the studios' self-imposed morality code; they show people, not always married, in bed together and conversing in entendres that hardly bother to be double.

The Love Parade starts by proclaiming La Vie Parisienne, illustrated by cancan girls, a short song about "a little bottle of Champagne," and the unexpected arrival in Chevalier's rooms of a man whom the young lady present shriekingly greets as "mon mari"; which Chevalier helpfully translates for us. He's playing a Count who gets recalled to his mythical homeland of Sylvania for having had such a scandalously good time. The queen who sent for him to punish him instead falls in love with him, after he woos her with the title song, which tells her that she's all his previous girls rolled into one; a queen has to take what a queen can get and she takes him. He settles into the life, and the ceremonial role, of a Prince Consort. He has opinions, but nobody wants to hear them. He asserts his independence, thereby bringing out the actor in Chevalier and a satisfying substance in the film.

He again gets royally wed in The Smiling Lieutenant, where a virginal princess (Hopkins) has her father buy Chevalier for her despite his being attached to the far worldlier leader of an all-girl band (Colbert). Both ladies are charmers, if not exactly great singers, but it's married love that wins out, perhaps surprisingly. (Or perhaps not; there were limits to how far you could flout the code, even before it was written down.)

Reunited for One Hour with You, Chevalier and MacDonald are married from the start, and so devoted a couple that the chorus of Parisian Keystone Kops who start the picture off cannot believe that they're legal. This is the best and wittiest of the Paramount cycle, though the one with the fewest ambitions as a musical; the only song to get any kind of extended treatment is the title number, its lyric shared between half a dozen characters to reflect their various states of mind.

For once Chevalier plays a man happily faithful, but thrown off course by the uninhibited attentions of his wife's best friend. In the meantime his wife becomes jealous, but of the wrong woman, and herself gives half-hearted encouragement to a devoted but ineffectual wooer. Cross purposes abound, most notably in a classic encounter between Chevalier and his seductress's spouse, who has seen all this before; he's understanding but unforgiving.

It was Lorenz Hart who wrote new words to the famous Franz Lehar melodies in The Merry Widow, including such poker-faced delights as "I think he said Maxim's/He's going there, it seems/I heard that's where a man can/See ladies dance the cancan." Dance it they do; Lubitsch fills the screen with whirling skirts, not to mention, in one dazzling image, a human staircase of waltzing couples extending as far as the eye can see.

The great operetta score is there, and so are the barest bones of the operetta situation: MacDonald plays the richest woman in the Ruritanian statelet of Marshovia, weary of widowhood and ready to be merry, and Chevalier is Captain Danilo, the practised Casanova sent to Paris to marry her and thus preserve the Marshovian economy. She's at her most gracious and glittering, he at his most endearingly resilient. In some ways this is their most old-fashioned pairing, the one in which their mating is postponed until the final scene. It actually spins out its situation too long, but that's true of all these pictures.

Obviously the most melodious of the Lubitsch musicals, The Merry Widow is also the funniest. The Hays code had come in by now, but nobody seems to have told the director; at any rate he worked around it, notably in the scenes between the fussy, harried King of Marshovia (George Barbier) and his perky, restless Queen (Una Merkel), who's able to give Danilo her own seal of approval. Discovering them virtually in flagrante the King asks only that they keep it secret; assuring him that they will Chevalier adds, with his patented air of rakish innocence, "We weren't even planning to tell your Majesty."

Paramount had style, MGM had gloss; and when the Marx Brothers, about the same time, moved from one to the other, they lost a lot of their edge. Lubitsch somehow managed to keep his, perhaps because it was more "civilized"; the urbane societies he conjured up were the kind the Marxes lived to destroy. He was more tolerant of pomposity than they were, but he too liked to make fun of it, especially when it involved politicians (he went on to direct Garbo's Ninotchka, which is a kind of spy drama, and the riotous Second World War comedy To Be or Not to Be) and The Merry Widow is his satiric as well as his romantic summit.

It's also his musical summit; the one in which, more than ever before, the camera dances even between the numbers. This film lives up to its legend, the first three Paramounts almost do, and One Hour with You is even better than I'd been told. Watching them was a great holiday treat. But you don't have to wait for a holiday.

2014-01-11-spoof-of-the-matter-killer-bu:
The Next Stage Theatre Festival, which began as a way of giving a longer life to shows that had been successful at the Fringe, has grown into a showcase of its own: one with a more rigorous selection process, or at least with fewer shows. I caught two of the more logistically ambitious productions at Fringe Mark Two on opening day this week.

Rifles is an adaptation by Nicolas Billon of Senora Carrars Rifles, a lesser-known play by Bertolt Brecht set in the Spanish Civil War. Its central figure is a widow in a fishing village whose sympathies are with the Republicans but who is determined, having lost her husband to the fighting, to keep her two sons out of it. Not having intimate knowledge of the original, I cannot say how much of the present script is Billon and how much is Brecht; it's a safe assumption, though, that in Brecht's text the soldier whose wounds Mrs. Carrar, as shes called here, solicitously dresses was not an English member of the International Brigade by the name of Eric Blair, later to be better known as George Orwell. He doesnt say much but he observes; and at one point, when we're told about a female teacher who fought against Franco for the freedom to continue saying that two and two make four, we see him noting it down for when 1984 rolls around. Other than that, it's hard to see what his presence adds to anything.

The plays political standpoint is unwavering: The Republicans are the good guys (and gals). Its moral compass is, at least until the end, harder to read and hence more interesting. The late Mr. Carrar left behind him a set of rifles; his firebrand brother Pedro has come to reclaim them for the cause, and also to recruit his two nephews: Juan, whos out in his boat, and Jose, who very much wants to join up. The senora is determined to stick to her guns, and to her sons. We sympathize with her, even while acknowledging the futility of her belief that war has nothing to do with the poor; as Pedro observes, the poor end up paying for it. Their opposing arguments are fairly but passionately thrashed out; the village priest is allowed to make a decent if doomed case for non-violence. This being Brecht, it's a foregone conclusion that Mrs. Carrar will donate her rifles in the end; as to how and why it will happen, we're kept guessing.

Michael Wheelers production (for Praxis Theatre) has the right hard practical aspect, perhaps best symbolized on Erin Gerofskys set by the peasant fireplace in which Senora Carrar bakes her bread. She herself is given a performance of matching granite, streaked with unshed tears, by a close-cropped Kate Hennig. Even finer perhaps is Barbara Gordon as one of this kind of play's indispensable neighbours, judicious but not judgmental, mourning but not regretting the death of her daughter the teacher. Not all the acting manages to keep the proper Brechtian cool (my vulgar translation of the alienation effect): as Pedro Cyrus Lane, though certainly strong, is inclined to have his foot on the gas when it should be on the brake, while some others are simply shrill. What should be the play's most shocking moment is shuffled through, in both staging and performance. Araya Mengesha is suitably fresh and eager as young Jose; Wade Bogert-O'Brien, recent ornament of the Shaw Festival, is his older brother, a role whose main requirement is stillness.

Killer Business (a possible alternate title for Rifles) comes with the all-too-familiar sub-head The Musical. Itsalso supposedly a thriller and it shows, like some glossier shows before it, that the two genres don't mix. It's hard to get caught up in the quest for the killer when the suspects keep holding up the investigation with song. Admittedly, the show doesnt seem to be asking us to be involved, but it isnt giving us much else to hold on to either. It's all-purpose, sprayedon spoof. It supposedly happens during the actual performance of a musical; suspicions are first alerted when a stage-weight falls from above, narrowly missing one of the cast. The identical plot device was used in Rodgers and Hammerstein's backstage musical Me and Juliet; whether its recurrence here counts as homage, plagiarism or accident I couldnt say.

Talking of musical echoes: The producer of the musical-within-the-musical is a short squat Italian-American named Tony, who addresses his late mama in song like his namesake in The Most Happy Fella. It turns out, though, that hes thinking more of Barbra Streisand in Yentl, because what he's always wanted to be, because you need it for success in showbiz, is Jewish. He sings the word with the accent on the second syllable, and compounds the offence by giving the same treatment at the very end of the song to the word Hebrew; though the line would make as much sense, and much better sound, if the punchwords were simply "a Jew." Even by current lyric-writing standards this is unforgivable. That's apart from the fact that the joke, such as it is, has already been made in Spamalot.

Tony is a poverty-row impresario who uses cardboard cut-out chorus girls because he cant afford real ones. The show hes presenting sounds like it was written in the 1920s, though there's no suggestion that it's either a parody or a revival and the outer setting seems to be contemporary. After that one number, Tonys would-be Jewishness is never mentioned again; which may be a blessing, considering the relentlessness of the shows other jests about being fat, being gay or being a dick. The last category is occupied by the evening's narrator-figure, a Marlovian private eye played by David Keeley, conspicuously the most experienced performer on stage, in an echo of his role in Urinetown.

For better or worse, most of the songs are drowned out by the piano accompaniment; one singer, Matthew G. Brown, does get to sing a few bars a cappella and he sounds good. He plays a lighting technician of a philosophical bent. There a few other nice ideas, including a couple of gabby, educated flesh-and-blood chorines, an overworked but everwilling allpurpose assistant (Julia Juhas) whose fate includes not getting a solo number, and a bit of funny choreography. Overall, though the show might best be described, in keeping with Tony's ethnic aspirations, as a fleet of ships that sailed already.

2014-01-18-love-and-or-death-in-flesh-an: There is a particular kind of acting that I constantly find myself railing against but for which I have yet to find a satisfactory name. Maybe I should call it explanatory acting. It consists of pumping more emotion into a line or a speech than either the words or the situation behind them can reasonably bear. It's intended to be passionate but instead sounds merely querulous. It cant be blamed on lack of talent, since it can crop up in otherwise good performances by good people, though it may well be a sign of lax direction. It can currently be found at the Tarragon in performances by Blair Williams, an actor of proven excellence who indeed has some fine moments here of both wit and pain, and Maria del Mar, who has many film and TV credits but is here making her professional stage debut, in a demanding role; I suspect that anxiety is causing her to overdo some things but when she relaxes she plays with spark and generosity.Theyre appearing in Flesh and Other Fragments of Love, a play by Evelyne de la Cheneliere (French-Canadian) derived from a novel by Marie Cardinal (French-French). They play Pierre and Simone, a married couple (from France) vacationing in Ireland in an attempt to repair a fractious and fractured marriage. Pierre goes for a walk on the beach and finds the body of a drowned young woman. He reports back to Simone, who's jealous of her husband's apparent fascination with the deceased; they have a theoretically open marriage, with plenty of separations, but it doesnt seem to work as its supposed to. Simone makes inquiries and finds that the corpse is that of Mary, a medical student who got pregnant, went to New York with her child, then came back home and killed herself. The tones in which Simone relays this information are an especially clear example of the kind of over-emphasis I'm complaining about. She seems, with her inflections rising even higher than her voice, to be blaming Pierre for what she's telling him. Now its true that the two of them go in for blame on a large scale, but this hardly seems to be the moment for it. Psychologically suspect, its also theatrically ineffective. There are times - many times - when a simple statement is the most powerful thing an actor can deliver. Enough with the colouring; we just want the facts.We especially want them here, so that there can be some solid ground to a play whose characters are naturalistic but whose action isn't; at least I find it hard to believe that, even in remote parts of Ireland, the authorities would let a corpse just lie there, festooned in seaweed, as a sort of bizarre tourist attraction. What happens is that Pierre and Simone each engage in a series of imaginary conversations with Mary, reconstructing her life in terms of what they would like to believe about their own; using her, in fact, as a supernatural marriage counsellor. Rich people's problems, you might think (and if an Anglo playwright were to pull this kind of stunt, youd probably think it a lot more dismissively). Marys situation obviously doesn't, or didn't, fall into this category; and she, ironically or not, is the most flesh-and blood person in the piece. Nicole Underhay, playing her, has the advantage of a lyrical Irish accent, to give her a local habitation as well as a name, and she sustains it beautifully; she too has been known, in other contexts, to overdrive her roles, but her appearances at the Tarragon always seem to find her at her best and here she is graceful but quite unsentimental; visually otherworldly - in our first glimpse of her prone in the water she looks, in Richard Roses production, like an Arthurian heroine as painted by Edward Burne-Jones - but in her feelings very much, and bitterly, of this world.Still, the play isnt really about her; and the central couple outstay the interest both of their situation and of the dramatist's device. It's not that their relationship isnt believable; it is, very, and there are some painfully accurate, even funny passages of mutual recrimination, along with the desperate attempts to cling on to something that may once have existed. Williams compromised attempts to assert his independence are especially engaging. He also does some memorable silent suffering at the end, his eyes suffused with terror and regret. By now though the play is making emotional demands that it hasn't justified and on which the actors, try as they might, cannot collect. That may partly account for why they overdo things earlier; they're trying to force into the light a drama that exists only in the playwrights (and maybe the novelists) head.An older Quebec play has been revived by Pleiades Theatre, at Buddies in Bad Times. This is Manon, Sandra and the Virgin Mary, in which Michel Tremblay reunites characters from two of his still earlier pieces. Well, he doesn't exactly reunite them; he has them sitting at opposite sides of the stage, engaging in parallel monologues, and converging, and then not physically, only at the end. Stage right in her rocking chair sits the puritanical Manon who, though not a nun, has given her life rigidly to God and has tormenting spasms of doubt as to what she's got in return; Irene Poole reaches into her mental and emotional centre, though on the way she sometimes ... well, go back to where I came in. Richard McMillan, on the other hand and on the other side, is in consummate control, technical and otherwise, of Manons spiritual (if thats the word) opposite: the selfcreated Sandra, ne Michel, the drag-queen of Hosanna grown even more scabrous and flamboyant with age, sitting enrobed at his dressingtable, and rhapsodizing about the male organ, his own and as many others as possible. He has fewer regrets than when we last met him, but those he has are choice. Like Manon, though less consistently, he's obsessed with the image of the play's third title character, which becomes gradually more visible as John van Burek's production proceeds. (Van Burek is directing his own excellent translation). Thoughts of the Madonna are what bring Manon and Sandra thematically together: that and some childhood reminiscences. A feeling of regret, of something missed, hangs in the air at the end, but it isn't as compelling as the monologues, respectively shaming and shameless. So, two plays with a Mary as their third figure and both concerned, at least in passing, with Catholic guilt.robert.cushman@hotmail.comFlesh and Other Fragments of Love runs through Feb. 16 at the Tarragon Theatre; Manon, Sandra and the Virgin Mary runs at Buddies in Bad Times through Feb. 2.Credit: Robert Cushman; Weekend PostIllustrationCylla Von Tiedemann / Maria del Mar in her professional stage debut, Nicole Underhay as a lyrical Irish body, with Blair Williams in the shadows.; Caption:Word count: 1158
2014-01-25-you-know-for-kids-wadji-mouaw:
Ken Gass' Canadian Rep Theatre - known in some quarters as the Factory-in-exile - begins operations with Pacamambo, a play by the Lebanese-Quebecois playwright Wajdi Mouawad that was originally designed for young audiences and should probably be approached with that in mind.

It begins with a contest in shouting: an infallible way of grabbing attention in the theatre (and outside it, for that matter) but one calculated to produce more heat than light. A psychiatrist is interrogating a young girl named Julie about some very peculiar behaviour; she had been found in a the basement of her grandmother's house, keeping watch over the grandmother's body, death having occurred 19 days previously. Julie initially refuses to offer any explanation, delivering her denials in Amy Keating's performance with a feral intensity that's very powerful in itself but doesn't have much to do with what she shows us later. The shrink, played by Karen Robinson, seems herself to have been driven round the bend, or at least to the end of her tether; she responds to Julie by yelling right back at her, an approach both ethically and dramatically dubious. You feel like sitting her down in front of Peter Shaffer's Equus, in which a psychiatrist dealt gently and patiently with an equally obstreperous child patient and got results.

Still, Julie does eventually open up, and flashes us back to the scene of the trauma. Her grandmother, called Marie Marie, had died when Julie was visiting, death being depicted here as a visit from The Moon, and causing grandma's bed to rise in the air, leaving her clinging to its now vertical frame: a strong image, though the sequence might benefit from some more balletically elaborate staging. Julie, whose only companion is now a talking dog named Growl, cannot accept the loss; she is torn between caring for the corpse and trying to resuscitate it, the latter process including emptying all the bottles of perfume that granny had stashed in her bottom drawer. Above all, she remembers what Marie Marie had told her about a land called Pacamambo, "the land of universal empathy" where people respond to one another as people, without regard to colour, which apparently is not the way they behave at Julie's school. These speeches seem preachy and simplistic, even for a young audience's play: perhaps especially for a young audience's play, though given the tensions in both halves of the author's own dual background, they have a certain theoretical sting.

It's unclear whether Julie wants to give her grandmother a nice sendoff to Pacamambo or actually to join her there; either way, she later disarmingly admits that she knows the place isn't real. It's one of the play's best moments, and keys also into the great strength of Keating's performance, which is to find the practicality in whimsy. Whimsy is here in plenty; you only have to look at the characters' names. Growl the dog admits, not quite so disarmingly, to her own inherent improbability, and is anyway delightfully played by Michelle Polak. Kyra Harper's Marie Marie is wise and endearing, even from beyond the grave. Robinson redeems her psychiatric excesses when she re-appears as Death herself, svelte and implacable though perplexed by the particular circumstances; she arrives to announce that though in the fullness of time she will indeed get Julie (and presumably her medium-sized dog too) that event is a long way off and right now she should get over herself. It works, which may be the point of the doubling. "I wish you" says Death in parting "a long life." It's the best moment in the best scene of the play. Whether it's the best way to acclimatize children to the idea that nobody goes on forever I'm not sure, but it resonates for grown-ups.

The whole play is an effective fable, far preferable to Mouawad's more grandiose attempts to forge his own mythology out of real-world ethic and political conflicts. For an adult evening out, though, and for all the virtues of the acting, it's thin.

robert.cushman@hotmail.com Pacamambo runs through Feb. 2 at The Citadel, 304 Parliament Street.

2014-02-01-songs-sung-true-this-verbatim:
Inherently and inescapably, theatre is artificial, and never more so than when it tries its hardest to be real. Such is the case with verbatim theatre, the form whose scripts are based on interviews whose subjects' words are taken down and then used in evidence. However scrupulous the transcription, there are always choices and selections to be made; however self-effacing the actors may try to be in reproducing the voices they've heard in the street or on tape, their own talents and personalities will keep breaking through. These paradoxes are exhibited, explored and exalted in London Road, a fascinating British piece given a momentous and fabulously cast production by Canadian Stage. It is, amazingly, a verbatim musical.

The road of the title isn't in London; it's a street in the medium-sized Suffolk town of Ipswich. Five women, all prostitutes, were serially murdered on this street in 2006, and the killer was subsequently discovered to have lived there. Alecky Blythe, a British playmaker, visited the place when the case was still under investigation and the neighbours in shock. She returned before, during and after the trial, discovering at the end of two years that the street's inhabitants had become a community. An impromptu organization that had started defensively as a Neighbourhood Watch had evolved into a beautifying project intent on reclaiming itself in the eyes of the world and in its own. Floral contests and displays were a major feature, though they'd been mentioned as a morale-building possibility from the very start. They are indeed the subject of the first and most beautiful of the show's musical numbers.

Ah, yes, the musical numbers. Blythe is known in Britain as a verbatim practitioner par excellence; she likes to reproduce not just her subjects' exact words but their every hesitation, repetition and nonverbal exclamation. The National Theatre brought her together with a composer, Adam Cork, to whom it said, more or less, "set that to music." And so he did, finding musical rhythms to match speechrhythms, not changing a word, counterpointing the characters when they're in disagreement, supplying choral settings for their moments of unanimity and doing especially exciting things when they're all saying the same thing but in different words. It's an extraordinary score. There are spoken passages too, but essentially this is opera, demanding from its performers (and here receiving) operatic precision and commitment, if not traditional operatic range.

That makes it of course very artificial; people in real life don't sing in impromptu chorus, any more than they talk in blank verse. But theatrical writing from Shakespeare to Sondheim has found a special thrill, and a special truth, in making artificial forms sound natural, in making the conversational sound inevitable (and vice, necessarily, versa). It draws out the heart of a situation, in concentrated form. That is what happens here when Deborah Hay and Glynis Ranney fearfully agree, each echoing and reinforcing the other's words, that with the killer at large, "you automatically think it could be him" of every man you encounter. A nervous keyboard accompaniment underlines their feelings and amplifies their fears; I don't know if Reza Jacobs, the show's MD, is conducting his own arrangements or as has inherited them from the National production, but he and his combo do superb work either way.

Hay is best known for her work in plays, Ranney for musicals. In fact, though, both can do both, and so it is throughout the cast. The director, Jackie Maxwell, has miraculously corralled eleven first-rate and first-ranking performers, allowing us the potent pleasure of seeing each emerge powerfully and pointedly from the ensemble and then merge seamlessly back into it. Each plays a named member of the Committee, and they also account between them for, by the program's count, 52 other roles. Nobody plays the murderer; he's revealed to be a truckdriver who resided on the street for eight months (there's no suggestion of any miscarriage of justice) but all we learn of the trial is the street's reaction to the news coverage. Nor do we hear any individual details about his victims; though Hay, Michelle Fisk and Fiona Reid share a memorable trio as three of their surviving colleagues, no longer able to work this particular street. The street's own reaction to this can be disconcerting, especially when voiced by Reid in her best house-and-garden mode as the horticultural lady-in-chief. Then we have George Masswhohl as an avuncular committee chair, caught making an illphrased promise about "tarting the street up"; Ben Carlson as a saloon-bar wiseacre insistently reiterating that his fund of knowledge about serial killers doesn't mean he is one; Damien Atkins hilarious as a TV reporter tripped up by the similar names of prosecutor and accused and also by scheduling-restrictions on the use of the word "semen" (this goes remarkably well into song); Sean Arbuckle, Julain Molnar, Steve Ross, Shawn Wright: they're a community in themselves. The evening is a carousel of knockout performances, beautifully contained in Maxwell's visually simple and logistically complex production; to which, considering the variety and accuracy of the accents on display, Jane Gooderham, the dialect coach, must have made a major contribution. As must whoever coordinates the myriad changes of Judith Bowden's costumes.

The show invents a format and makes a dazzling case for it. I am less sure what else it has to say. Maybe just that these things happened and that these people matter, but it cannot avoid at least the appearance of commentary. It ends with the street en fete, reprising its celebration of flowers. In the middle of this finale, there's a momentary freeze. We hear, briefly, the voices of the actual interviewed prostitutes (nobody here says "sex-worker" but, equally, nobody says "slut"): their real voices, not actors'. So here for a moment is reality, not artifice: in what is presented, though not of course in the choice of where. It's a shock effect that makes the merrymakers on stage, with their prizes and their lottery tickets, seem smug and insensitive. For most of the evening the show has been presenting a balanced view of its people, people who could easily be us: a view both critical and admiring. The end, though, feels less like complexity than like having it both ways. It's a significant blot but it hardly cancels out the glories of what has gone before.

A rather different kind of community musical is Once on This Island, the show that the Ragtime team wrote before they wrote Ragtime. The revival, by Acting Up Stage and Obsidian, hardly measures to their previous collaboration on Caroline or Change; Nigel Shawn Williams' production lacks the helpful bazazz of the Broadway original, and as simple storytelling - in a show that explicitly celebrates storytelling - it doesn't really get going until its final poignant and tender third. In this Caribbean companion to The Little Mermaid a peasant girl from the French Antilles falls in love with a scion of the Grand'hommes, the lighter-skinned and impenetrably snobbish people from the richer side of the tracks. She nurses him back to health after an accident and he, in his fashion, loves her: not enough, though, to throw over his arranged bride for her sake. She dies at his gate, but the gods take belated pity and work an arboreal transformation on her: girl gets boy, girl loses boy, girl turns into tree, becoming a posthumous emblem of reconciliation. Stephen Flaherty's music has grown on me over the years, and at least one of Lynn Ahrens' lyrics - the hero's blithe apologia for his own caddishness - is a treasure; it's called Some Girls, as in "some girls you marry, some you love." As she he loves Jewelle Blackman looks enchanting, acts with ardour, and hits some startling low notes in her singing; some of her high notes are startling as well, but in a less agreeable way.

robert.cushman@hotmail.com London Road runs to Feb. 9 at the Bluma Appel Theatre; Once on This Island runs through Feb. 9 at Daniels Spectrum.

2014-02-08-back-to-the-front-in-the-1936:
Albert Schultz, director of Idiot's Delight, has described this 1936 American play as The Time of Your Life meets You Can't Take It with You. To me it feels more like the meeting of The Time of Your Life and Casablanca. Like that famous film, it presents a cosmopolitan assortment of characters in an international watering-hole, though here the location is cold rather than hot: not a North African nightspot but an Italian hotel with ski-lodge ambitions, perched high in the Alps and commanding tantalizing views of Austria and Switzerland.

Also l ike Casablanca, Idiots Delight has a rootless American hero, surprised into a kind of commitment by the reappearance in his life of a woman he had loved and lost. Most crucially, both play and movie unfold against the background of the Second World War, though with a significant difference. Casablanca is set, historically if not geographically, in the thick of it; in Idiots Delight, we're on the brink, awaiting - nervously or fatalistically, according to temperament - a conflict that finally erupts. Robert E. Sherwood, one of the period's most successful if less remembered playwrights was writing, remember, three years before this actually happened. He got the mood prophetically right, even if he got the eventual historical details wrong. In his vision, the war starts when Italy bombs France and France retaliates. No suggestion of Germany invading Poland: indeed no mention of Poland at all, and not much of Germany: just one reference to Jews to hint at what National Socialism was actually like. Sherwood, whose extra-theatrical activities included speech writing for FDR, was a pacifist who turned when he found out about the Nazis; this play seems to have been written when that conversion was, at most, a work in progress. The Italian Fascists are here the heavies, and even they seem reluctant about it. Sherwood is mournfully arraigning self-destructive humanity in general and, if he exists, God: "Poor, dear God. Playing Idiots Delight. The game that never means anything, and never ends."

Im quoting Irene, the play's - for want of a better word -heroine: a self-described Russian adventuress whose story keeps changing and who may in fact be American; Harry, our hero, claims to have spent a night with her in Omaha when he was touring with a mindreading act, though right now he's touring Europe as frontman for a quintet of singing, dancing and (in this production) squealing blonds. Like most of their fellow guests, theyve arrived at the previously deserted hotel because their train was derailed, and want to get out before its too late. The play begins as a mobile genre-painting from those halcyon days when American plays could afford teeming casts, Depression or no Depression; their comings and goings and philosophical musings are where the Time of Your Life likeness makes itself felt, and Schultz orchestrates them here as masterfully as he did in his production of the Saroyan play. He has, again, a fine set by Lorenzo Savoini, high, wide, suggestively furnished, and mountain-viewed.

Gradually, through the bustle, the focus narrows down to Harry and Irene, roles in which Dan Chameroy and Raquel Duffy exceed themselves. He projects a kind of alert worldweariness, she a sophistication that's ambiguous, vulnerable and only slightly impaired by the tendency of her words to get lost in her accent. Their last scene reaches a high level of both mood and contact.

Harry's transformation is as decisive as that of Bogarts Rick in Casablanca, though it goes in the opposite emotional direction.

You must remember this: Ricks cafe derives much of its mystique from the playing of one song. Harry and his troupe provide the occasion for many more from American song's golden age, some of them specified by the author, some not, but all apposite. Especially haunting is Let's Face the Music and Dance, a number originally performed by Fred and Ginger on the edge of a precipice, and here employed to summon a whole world in the same situation. The production credits Sherwood with additional prophetic powers when Evan Buliung as a gentle Austrian waiter sings Ill Never Smile Again (which really does date from 1939) while clearing tables; its a charming moment in an altogether lovely performance by a man out of several of his elements.

Some of the play's actual writing is stuffy, but the actors humanize it, none more than Gregory Prest who, as an agonized French Communist, finds pain and passion in a role composed mainly of slogans. Gordon Hecht and Michaela Davies are delightful as a pair of young English honeymooners and William Webster powerfully impatient as a German doctor with an excruciating case of divided loyalties, plus a possible cure for cancer and a convoy of lab-rats. Diego Matamoros is all iron and irony as Irene's ambiguous protector, a munitions-king on whom, next to God, the play seems inclined to blame everything. Hes like Shaws Undershaft (from Major Barbara) without the intellectual muscle, and the play's ending, defying air-raids, definitely recalls that of Heartbreak House. Instead of Keep the Home Fires Burning, we have, authorially mandated, Onward Christian Soldiers: a mordant, bitter finale that Schultz's production, atoning for the sentimentality with which he spoiled Oh What a Lovely War, plays to the hilt. In all, a great rediscovery and a Soulpepper success.

Everybody knows the opening sentence of Franz Kafkas Metamorphosis, about Gregor Samsa waking up one morning to find himself changed into an insect. What follows is less known than Kafkas The Trial, but actually hits harder. Certainly it does in the stage version brought to Toronto by David Mirvish, adapted and directed by David Farr (of London) and Gisli Orn Gardarsson (of Reykjavik) and performed by a four-fifths Icelandic cast whose accents, not to mention their talents, give the text the right sense of jolting familiarity.

Josef K was betrayed by bureaucracy; Gregor is betrayed by his family. That hurts a lot more, especially when the prime rejector is his sister, the only one who initially showed sympathy. Even more poignant than his physical transformation is the fact that they can't understand a word he says, though he keeps trying. Gregor is the victim, among other things, of his inability to stop loving, and Bjorn Thors gives him a wonderfully sympathetic performance. Wonderfully acrobatic, too; he still looks like a man but he moves like an insect, hanging, gliding, clutching.

The upper half of the set, representing his bedroom, has been turned at an angle of 90 degrees, prompting physical feats and scenic images that recall Robert Lepage's Needles and Opium and, less expectedly, the opening number of Hairspray. Some of the family scenes go on too long, and analogies to Nazism are pushed too hard (Idiot's Delight in reverse), but this is a superb - well, a transformative - production. Weekend Post robert.cushman@hotmail.com

Idiot's Delight runs at the Young Centre in the Distillery District to March 14; Metamorphosis runs through March 9 at the Royal Alexandra Theatre.

Cylla Von Tiedemann / Raquel Duffy, Paolo Santalucia and Diego Matamoros, in a play that falls between Casablanca and The Time of Your Life.; Caption:
2014-02-15-listen-carefully-canadianstag:
In a dismal season for new plays, homegrown or imported, CanadianStage is doing something to pick up the slack, at least in the second category. On the heels of London Road it brings us Tribes, another British piece, and a magnetically interesting one.

The easiest way of describing Nina Raine's play is to say it's about deafness. Which it is, but it branches out from there to be a play about families and about communication, or the lack of it. With some acknowledgments to Twelfth Night: Some tribes you're born into; some you join; some absorb you. Billy, the central character here, experiences all three.

Billy, deaf since birth, is the twentyish son of an intellectual family in northwest London. (Their intellectual status is established by their above-average rate of swearing. The location is never precisely stated but trust me, I've lived there.) Billy's parents are Christopher, a former teacher who's now a full-time critic, by profession and by temperament; and Beth, who's started a new late-life career as a mystery novelist. So, they're both concerned with words; Christopher indeed is obsessive about them, and about their proper usage, and is merciless towards those who don't live up to them. Billy has two older siblings, Ruth and Daniel, who have moved back home in recoil from failed relationships and stalled careers. Ruth is an aspiring opera singer, currently doing cabaret gigs. Daniel is working on a thesis about, wouldn't you know, language. Billy has never learned sign language; his family thought it would make him feel self-conscious. Or maybe it's that they couldn't be bothered to learn it themselves. They are all, with the possible exception of Beth, very self-absorbed.

Then, Billy meets Sylvia, who is an expert signer; she comes from a deaf family, and is losing her hearing herself. Her signing and his lip-reading bring them together, in a scene that's witty, edgy, romantically charming and - like all first encounters - awkward, all at the same time; any failures of comprehension on the audience's own part are dealt with, as they are throughout the play, by projections of the words in question; the characters' problems become, by translation, ours. They become a couple and, through Sylvia, Billy becomes increasingly involved in the deaf community - to use a phrase that his father would, and does, volubly hate. Indeed, when Billy brings Sylvia home to meet the folks, Christopher in particular gives her a very hard time. This turns out, though, to be a standard rite of passage, one that she passes with (to use another expression Chris would probably hate) flying colours. They like her, though Daniel at least seems to have issues. Nor is Billy's and Sylvia's own relationship free of abrasion; she brought him both a new independence and a new sense of involvement, and both can work against her. Besides, her condition is in many respects harder than his; she knows what she's losing. When music plays, as it constantly does both between and during scenes, he may feel left out but he doesn't have to tune out; she, progressively and enforcedly, does.

Tribes is billed as a Theatrefront production in association with CanadianStage (who house it) and Theatre Aquarius. Daryl Cloran, artistic director of Theatrefront, directs the play; Lorenzo Savoini designed the barebones but sufficient set, whose major component is the all-important family dining table. There are especially fine performances, sympathetic but thoroughly unsentimental, by the central couple. Stephen Drabicki, a hardof-hearing actor himself, makes us feel Billy's hope, pain, his sharp humour and - perhaps most important - his stubbornness. The play's story takes Billy into a new world; Drabicki takes us into one as well. Holly Lewis shows Sylvia's attractive strength and also its frightened, and frightening, limits.

Billy's brother and sister are less well served by their author. Patricia Fagan vividly depicts Ruth's anger and frustration, but isn't given much chance to play anything else. If she has too few notes in her score, Dylan Trowbridge as Daniel has too many. He gives a high energy and highly watchable account of a young man who hasn't quite grown up. He tells us, though the play never really explores it, that he cares deeply for Billy and a) doesn't want him to be hurt and b) doesn't want to lose him. (There seem to be echoes here of the fraternal love-hate in Long Day's Journey into Night.) Maybe that's why he makes a pass at his brother's girlfriend: to defuse their relationship before it can cause any harm. It seems an awfully long-winded way of going about it; and anyway, from the moment Daniel first sets eyes on Sylvia, the production has suggested an attraction between them.

In its second half, the play loses its concentration, as if it were trying desperately to avoid becoming an "issues" piece, or had simply run out of ideas. In fact, the issues have been so strongly established and so artfully varied that they become themes. Every time somebody mentions writing, or texting, or talking or singing, it becomes another part of the pattern. When Joseph Ziegler's Christopher puts on a pair of headphones to shut out a conversation he wants no part of, it's the perfect image, multiply reverberant. Ziegler's performance is the upmarket counterpart of his great Irish dad in A Whistle in the Dark: an articulate man who, whatever his protestations of open-mindedness, will only converse on his own terms. His timing is a joy as, in a more sympathetic key, is that of Nancy Palk, whose role as Beth also recalls one of her own earlier appearances, as the wife in You Can't Take It with You, who took to playwriting because a typewriter had been accidentally delivered to her door. And was also, in her way, a caring mother. As for this playwright: Raine has had a meteoric career in London, and also in New York; it's good to have been introduced to her here, in a play and production that are alight and alive.

robert.cushman@hotmail.com Tribes runs at the Berkeley Street Theatre through March 2.
