2014-02-22-demographic-deja-vu-anita-maj:
Anita Majumdar's new piece Same Same But Different consists of two thematically linked one-act plays, which may be a sly reason for that perplexing title. It also makes for a long evening.

On a less fanciful level, the title refers to distinctions, especially racial and colour distinctions, in India and across the Indian diaspora. In the first piece, Majumdar, drawing on her own background and also on her own talents as a dancer, appears as Aisha, an Indian movie star who was born and grew up in Canada, and has now come back. Shes making a Bollywood musical, in Vancouver. Her director, who is unseen but very vocal, is overjoyed to have her in the picture, her being so famous, but he does keep interrupting her numbers and telling her to start again, which is entertaining for us, at least to begin with, but infuriating for her. And theres one other little thing: She's too dark. Too dark, that is, for the Indian audience whose compatriot he is. He keeps pressing skin-lightening creams on her - creams, it turns out, that she has plugged in commercials, but that she is indignantly opposed to using herself. She is up, in fact, against the kind of prejudice now officially known as shadeism. (It ought to be possible to combat injustice without crucifying the English language, but there you go.) Aisha's dance partner is Ben, who is Spanish-Filipino and to whom, perhaps because hes so pale, the director takes a fancy: so much so that he promotes him from chorusboy to leading man. This happens with improbable suddenness, but then the plays whole chronology is confusing. Its last section is an exact replay of its first, but it's unclear whether this is meant to denote a flashback or demonstrate that nothing ever changes - or just to be a cute way of rounding things off. One thing does progress; Ben, once over his excitement at his new status, encourages Aisha, of whom he is a long-time fan, to stand by her principles. This is good of him, because she's been exhibiting her own varieties of prejudice against him.

The most enjoyable sections here are the dance numbers, which involve the performers in imitating stereotypically ancient Egyptians, complete with jutting elbow movements, and which Majumdar herself has choreographed. She executes them with great skill, while radiating a delightful sense of disgust at what she has got herself into. Her expressiveness does not, on this occasion, extend into her spoken bits. She does communicate star quality, both on her own account and Aishas, but what you might call her conversational range is limited. Then again, she has written herself a role that confines her to distinguishing between sundry shades of pique. Her partner, Nicco Lorenzo Garcia, has a pleasing personality but even less variety. Brian Quirt, doing double duty as director and dramaturge, lets things sag alarmingly in both capacities.

The evenings second half both fulfills and betrays the title; it's somewhat different, but too much same same. It takes us back to Bombay, and back in time to when the city had that name. We're now in a recording studio, presided over by a sound engineer as dictatorial, as capricious and as invisible as the director from earlier (or later, depending on how youre counting). Garcia plays Felipe, a youthful but experienced session singer of the same ethnicity as his previous role, and Majumdar is Kabira, whos making both her professional debut and her professional farewell; she's about to depart for an arranged marriage in, yes, Canada. She is in fact, or will be, Aisha's mother; and some of the things we learn about her do connect with what weve heard of Aishas upbringing. But the links aren't very urgent; the proceedings are too nerveless for us to care. This second part is more interesting than the first but also, coming so late, more boring. The social and political pressures discussed here, both in India and the Philippines, are more acute and more compelling than any amount of agonizing about Bollywood. But discussion is all they get; this playlet, like its predecessor, is mainly composed of repetitive conversation, with a wisp of a love-plot thrown in. This time they're arent any dances, but there are songs: nicely disdainful covers of Michael Jackson numbers, which prompt a few more thoughts about skin tone. Theres also the sad, if hardly surprising, dashing of Kabira's dreams of vocal stardom: another future legacy for her daughter. Felipe, meanwhile, has a more pressing deadline; he wants, in spite of the dilatory sound guy, to get the session over with so he can make a midnight meeting that will help him leave the country. This does contribute some suspense; or maybe it's just that Felipes impatience is infectious. The best performance is given by Reza Jacobs, who plays both the director and the sound engineer, and who may not even be physically present; at least he didnt take a curtain-call. If his contribution was pre-recorded, then all concerned should be congratulated on a fine job of synchronization; though it may, on consideration, contribute to the overall deadness of the evening. Jacobs is one of Toronto's best and busiest musical directors, so he may well have other places to be; that he should be able to act as well seems unfair. I can't say he differentiates much between his two roles - both of them masters of sweet unreasonableness - but he takes full advantage of Majumdars best lines. On plagiarism: "It isnt stealing if you admit that you're doing it." And of an especially protracted Bollywood movie: "I walked in a boy, I walked out a man." I sympathize.

robert.cushman@hotmail.com Same Same But Different runs through March 8 at Theatre Passe Muraille

2014-03-01-the-real-fight-in-the-two-wor:
The grandiose title The Two Worlds of Charlie F. conceals a fairly simple production. It's a dramadocumentary about British service personnel invalided out of Afghanistan, and it grew from a rehab-come-therapy project in the U.K. Listening to the testimonies of these men and women injured, traumatized, permanently crippled or all of the above, it occurred to the organizers that their experiences might make a show. And so it has. A few private performances led to public ones, under professional direction, then to a U.K. tour, and now to a second longer one, with a Toronto detour as its opening date.

The performers are either actual vets or actual actors, plus one who qualifies in both categories. This is Cassidy Little, whose pre-military career included separate stints as a dancer and a standup comic, and who also happens, by blessed coincidence, to have been born and partly brought up in Canada, "and don't you forget it." (He says those last five words himself. I couldn't help wonder if they'd always been in the script, or if they were added for local consumption. Either way, they got first-night cheers.) Little was a medic in Afghanistan, where most of his right leg was blown off. He plays Corporal Charlie Fowler - the Charlie F of the title - who was similarly maimed. His two worlds are the beforeand-after of this event, and they are also inhabited, to one degree or another, by most of the other characters. A minor but abiding puzzle of the piece is how closely the fictional Fowler is meant to resemble the actual Little, a nagging uncertainty that extends itself to the rest of the cast; even with the actors brought in for the occasion, one wonders whether they're playing real individuals or composites. The show has a credited writer, Owen Sheers, but it's fairly clear that most of the script derives from interviews.

The show begins with Littleas-Charlie seen in silhouette on his hospital bed, in mental and physical agony and possibly hallucinating. He then comes forward in a wheelchair, stump plainly visible, and addresses us directly; this prologue done, he fades out for a time, but he comes back full force later on. It does seem that, by however unfortunate a road, he's found his vocation; he's an easy, magnetic performer with a fluency and authority beyond anyone else in the cast, amateur or professional. In fact, having noncombatants in the cast at all may be a mistake. Little apart, none of the performers makes any great individual impact. The show's power derives from its authority as firsthand collective testimony. The direction, by Stephen Rayne, is efficient but unimaginative. There are songs, specially composed and apparently included because having them is some kind of documentary theatre rule. They range from innocuous to terrible; definitely in the latter category is a rehab number consisting of the names of drugs. (Choreography is even worse. What's it doing there?) Charlie's opening line, therefore the show's, is "your hearing is the last thing to go and the first to come back"; it's arresting information, and in the second act he relays it to a therapist, but nothing is made of the idea in between. The best sustained sequence, by far, is a lecture on all the horrific things that can happen to a soldier who is shot or who steps on a mine. The chilling central message is that though armaments and areas of engagement change with the ages, the real battlefield is always the human body. The listening soldiers are not, at this point, being instructed in self-preservation. They`re being told how to tend to the fallen guy next to them. This is a constant theme: The soldier's primary loyalty is not to a cause or a country but to his mates.

Background to the conflict is confined to a whistle stop listing of previous attempts, British or Russian, to subdue Afghanistan; why the U.S. and its allies should have been there at this particular time, or how the British and commonwealth troops might have felt about it, is never explored, indeed hardly mentioned. Everything is kept local and personal. We are given the contrast between the blandishments of the recruiting office and the first experience on the parade ground. We watch the soldiers bonding over letters from home, and over estranged wives or girlfriends (never boyfriends, though some of the troops are female) in both the before and after worlds. Charlie's fiancee leaves him, rendering him uncertain of just how he feels. (Little conveys this very well. It seems that in real life, he's happily married.) Most of these things, though, we've encountered in other plays, films, books, about this or other wars, and they seldom rise here above the generic. Comparisons keep suggesting themselves. Oh What a Lovely War gave a far more pungent grunt's eye view, and its songs were authentic (and authentically double-edged.) London Road gave us professional actors delivering the actual utterances of actual named people, and music was its raison d'etre, not an add-on. Afghanada and This Is War have already given us a Canadian, if determinedly apolitical, view of the same campaign. One oddity here: Charlie, in his initial ramblings, claims to have been taken prisoner by the Taliban and tortured for weeks. How did he escape. Or is it meant to be a delusion? It probably is, but - in a show so dependent on the authenticity of experience, it would be good to have it cleared up. The production can only be moving - which it is - to the extent that we believe it's real.

robert.cushman@hotmail.com The Two Worlds of Charlie F. runs through March 9 at the Princess of Wales Theatre

2014-03-08-sorta-stephen-sondheim-a-mash:
It's all duologues at the Tarragon. In the extra Space, there's the all-talking Lungs; on the main stage the all-singing, and sometimesdancing, Marry Me a Little, which is a sort of Stephen Sondheim musical.

Sort of, because though Sondheim gave the show his blessing, he had nothing to do with its creation. It's a cross between a story-show and an anthology, assembled off-Broadway in 1981 by craig Lucas (later a successful dramatist in his own right) and Norman rene from songs written for Sondheim musicals that had never reached the stage or cut from shows that had. The conceit that bound the songs together involved a young man and a young woman both living in the same apartment building but each unaware of the other's existence. Alive and alone on a Saturday night (title number of Sondheim's first and, in 1981, still unproduced musical) each fantasizes about a relationship with an imaginary other ... and you can probably guess the rest. Their fantasies interlock, a development made scenically easier by the fact that their landlord has apparently supplied them with identical rooms; one set does duty for both, so that each character can invade the other's space without the audience worrying about where they're supposed to be.

Declaration of interest: I directed the British premiere of this show, a couple of years after the American one, so I find it hard to shake my own preconceptions of how it should go. As regards this production: I admire the inventiveness of Adam Brazier's staging, and envy him Ken Macdonald's set which, without raising the characters out of their struggling financial league, is far more detailed and welcoming than the one we came up with in London. I quarrel, though, with what I take to be his concept.

In this version the boy-girl fantasy is, as far as I can tell, all the boy's. There's a keyboard in his apartment, and he seems to be an aspiring composer-lyricist. Two songs in, there's a knock on his door; it's the girl (whom we've already seen and heard in her own environment, but won't again) come for an audition. She leaves, then comes back, and he sets about getting her into his pullout bed. Their romance shows promise, but falls victim to their conflicting fears and expectations. They end up bitter-sweetly accepting that, in the words of their closing number (one of many heartbreakingly deleted numbers from Follies) "it wasn't meant to happen."

Making this essentially the guy's story spoils the symmetry. Given that, there's a lot to enjoy. Brazier and his choreographer, Linda Garneau, have gone vigorously for narrative and conflict. even solo songs are confrontational rather than contemplative. This works spectacularly well with the title number, one of the discarded trial-runs for what eventually became Being Alive, in Company. elodie Gillett sings its passionate plea for a dispassionate relationship right in her partner's face and all over his bed, thereby heightening both its desperation and its unreality. Less happy is the decision to give the same treatment to Adrian Marchuk's performance of the succeeding song Happily Ever After, another lapsed candidate for the same spot in Company. Sung as a soliloquy, its rejection of any kind of commitment can seem painfully honest; flung directly at a possible lover, it just sounds cruel and insensitive, with its singer coming off as a jerk. (he's already spent a lot of stage time getting out of his pants as a hopeful prelude to getting into hers.)

Making every song a duet, virtual or actual, has other downsides. Some songs get sung in counterpoint before having a chance to establish themselves in their own right; Who Could Be Blue, another cut treasure from Follies and a melody whose simplicity and serenity are worthy of Jerome Kern, is especially shortchanged. But we get to hear a lot of lovely music; my favourite has always been, and remains, the exquisitely yearning All Things Bright and Beautiful, yet another cut-out from Follies (and still there, instrumentally, as part of its opening music.) The score of Marry Me has always been a mutable thing, with directors allowed to add to, or delete from, the original tune-stack.

This production lets us hear something new: Rainbows, a song written for the forthcoming movie of Into the Woods but apparently cut from it, thus validating its right to be here. A recurrent bleating tone mars the performances of both Marchuk and Gillet; other than that, they're both fine singers, and even better acting singers; Gillet, especially, is transformed when she gets dramatically invested in a song. Paul Sportelli's musical direction is, as usual, perfect.

Duets are the fashion of the day beyond the Tarragon. Indeed, Marry Me a Little sometimes seems like the recent Venus in Fur with music but without revenge. The volcano company has revived daniel MacIvor's A Beautiful View, the story of two women whose long fractious friendship is highlighted by a sexual encounter which each enters into in the belief that it's the other who's really the lesbian. This remains a teasing, elegant piece, in both style and structure. Ross Manson's production is excellently inhabited by Amy rutherford, cool and powerful as the waitress who claims to be a bartender and Becky Johnson, rash and shy and gangling as the ukulele-player who claims to have a band and who wears a nervous grin and long socks with stripes at the top. (She wears other things too, but those are what you notice). This isn't a musical, but Johnson does have a delightful sung interlude. The production's camping-ground conclusion, though, loses out to the author's original staging as regards being scare-ish and bearish.

Marry Me a Little runs through April 6 at the Tarragon Theatre; A Beautiful View runs through March 9 at the Factory Studio.

2014-03-10-baited-breath-a-couple-wonder:
THEATRE REVIEW

Tarragon Extra Space, Toronto

I'm not sure why Lungs is called Lungs. It could be because the plays two characters talk a lot about the state of the environment, and hence of course with the quality of the air they and everyone else breathe. Or it could just be because they talk a lot.

That is not meant to be disparaging. Lungs, a 2012 British play by Duncan Macmillan, is a terrific evening: a script crammed with wit and surprise, delivered here by performers whose own lungs, not to mention their hearts and brains, are up to the fearsome demands made upon them. They play a couple - ill-assorted like most but plainly devoted to a degree that would make separation dangerous - unmarried, in their thirties and consumed by the question of when or whether or to have children. We never learn their names, but the program labels them, for obvious gender-related reasons, as W and M.

It seems at first that the matter of whether or not to propagate is all the play is going to be about. In fact it goes much further, in more senses than it would be fair to reveal. It covers a lot of ground, speedily and without strain, its fluency enabled by the simple artfulness of its construction; its a continuous duologue made up of many smaller ones, their dates and subjects and locations changing, with no alteration in set or costume, as we watch.

When we first meet M and W, they're in the check-out line at IKEA (this is a play of international relevance), an awkward place, as they both agree, to raise the subject of impending parenthood, but then where wouldn't be? Well put it back in the box" they say, leaving me uncertain as to whether they were talking metaphorically about the lifechanging decision on their minds or literally about the purchase they were about to make. Before we know it theyre driving home, conversation apparently uninterrupted, and then they are home, still talking.

They're always a second ahead of us, but no more than that; the only time I felt thoroughly left behind was during what I had taken to be a later car scene but one in which neither character appeared to have a hand on the wheel. This seemed very irresponsible behaviour for people with such highly developed social consciences.

W, at the play's beginning, is a PhD student. M is a musician, though when W actually does get pregnant (I have to give something away), the responsibility goes to his previously irresponsible head and he becomes, in his own words, "a cog in the corporate machine; quite a dedicated one, too, which leads W to accuse him of neglecting her.

The two are never short of things to quarrel about, or of feelings and beliefs to agree about. They veer between blame and self-blame, doubt and self-doubt, notably on their pet preoccupation of whether its right to bring new life into an increasingly poisoned and fractious world. The question of who, if everybody refused to give birth for these reasons, we would be saving the planet for is left unexplored, but then it always is. Besides, the play makes clear that M and Ws ecological concerns, however genuine, are just another layer on the doubts and uncertainties that have beset impending parents of every generation. If it laughs at their desire to think of themselves as good" people, it does so by letting them intermittently laugh at themselves, or at least question themselves; after which they carry on exactly as before. We are watching a love story, a joyous one all told, but one in which the joy encompasses the dark or painful parts.

Weyni Mengesha directs, on a quadrilateral stage in one corner of the auditorium, neutrally set (designer, Ken Mackenzie). She gets immaculate, razor-sharp performances from her two actors. W is Lesley Faulkner, who knocked me out when she played the Marilyn Monroe equivalent (biographical, not physical) in an Equity Showcase production of Arthur Miller's After the Fall. That must have been a decade ago, and I haven't seen too much of her work since, but her intensity, her magnetism and above all her vocal control are undiminished (and she hardly looks a day older). Her role requires her to describe great parabolas of anger and guilt and blame and yearning, one thought or feeling free associating flowing into the next, seemingly without benefit of punctuation.

She is the one who sets the pace and the tone of nearly every scene; Brendan Gall's M, a self-confessed goofball who towers or at least sways over her, is content most of the time to act as her punching-bag, deferring to the unchallengeable fact that she will be the one carrying the baby. Aroused, though, he can give as good as he gets, with the same rhetorical force, though usually in shorter sentences.

The two of them are locked, like any couple, in recurring psychological patterns, and there are times when the repetitiveness of this jars on the patience, but the play always rescues itself. There are twists in the action, expected ones that make you nod your head in agreement, unexpected ones that make you gasp. The end is very moving; I was in tears. In part, though, they were tears of joy: delight in a play and production that got so much right, about both the big things that can weld people together and tear them apart, and the small ones - the shared jokes, the memories - that make both processes possible.

Lungs runs at the Tarragon Theature until March 30. For more information, visit tarragontheatre.com

2014-03-15-force-and-subtlety-sixteen-sc:
The new Second City revue, entitled Sixteen Scandals and one of the troupe's sharpest and funniest ever, begins by disposing, briskly and musically, of the weather. The customary half-dozen performers (three male, three female) line up to complain about how endlessly terrible it's been. We hear them. The run is scheduled to last until July, and by then of course this lament may have lost some of its bite. (Then again, perhaps not.) The show promptly moves on to Torontos second favourite object of complaint. A downtowner is visiting an old friend who has relocated to Etobicoke and who entreats him to do the same. Well, he doesnt so much entreat as threaten. Join us, he says direly, "or we'll elect him again." This is the evening's one Rob Ford joke, and it doesnt even mention Rob Ford, at least not by name.

The same force and subtlety are evident throughout the evening; the performers, as always, take joint credit for the script, but I suspect some writing as well as editorial input from the director, Chris Earle. Even the title turns out to be more than the usual random pun. It inspires a first-act closer in which five-sixths of the cast, in various and (for Second City) unaccustomed states of undress merrily carol, Mr. Rogers-style, about the scandals in your neighbourhood which turn out to be merely heightened gossip. The remaining performer, Connor Thompson, whose solid

presence conceals impressive reserves of angst, tries to remind them of the really scandalous things in the world. They pronounce him boring. Even when he takes off his own clothes, his nakedness camouflaged only by a placard arraigning child poverty, it stops them in their tracks for no more than a moment.

Kevin Vidal, who is black and who would be a good actor in any context, has a beautifully crafted monologue addressed to an unseen son who has come out - as black. The double entendre (reminiscent of Flanders and Swanns The Reluctant Cannibal if anyone does remember that one) progresses from denial through anger to the qualified acceptance of "maybe next year I'll march with you in Caribana." Denial is one Vidal's specialties; earlier hes given us an office worker near hysterical in his insistence that Toronto has to be the capital of Canada, just like New York is the capital of the U.S. (Well, he has a point. I mean, whoever heard of Canberra?) As a soloist, he yields only to Ashley Botting, in her motivational lecture on attaining happiness by becoming someone else. As she unanswerably asks, If you were happy being you, wouldnt you be happy by now?

Musically, this is the strongest Second City show I remember, running to a duet for a hit-man (the straight-arrow Thompson) and his neglected wife, sung through Andrew Lloyd Webber style, lugubrious underdone words set to lugubrious overcooked tunes. (Musical director, Matthew Reid). There are actually fewer marital or domestic skits than usual, and those there are tend to the refreshingly outlandish; a husband finds comfort in dropping through his very own Black Hole (it's in his very own closet) because, he says "I need my own space - and time." And then there are the cross-dressed sketches: a matched pair. The three ladies - Botting fitting in between Allison Price, who's tall, and Sarah Hillier, whos droll and compact enough to play a goblin, which she elsewhere does - appear as a trio of would-be jocks, united in their frustrated conviction that "bitches be crazy." Then - later enough in the proceedings for it to be a surprise as well as a treat - Thompson, Vidal and Craig Brown team up as a trio of mature, respectable lady shoplifters. The men-as-women have the wittier lines, but the womenas-men definitely win out on the moves, which in their case are balletically grotesque, or perhaps wincingly winsome. The show gets in to some refreshingly dark and astringent places. Camellia Koos set includes a large circular aperture that suggests a washing machine (and at one charming point, does more than suggest), and the customary Second City steep ladder, here confined to a corner of the set and used, as far as I could observe, only once.

There isn't always safety in numbers. If Sixteen Scandals is a triumph, Six Essential Questions is a disaster. It's a first play by Priscilla Uppal, based on a novel of hers that

Im told is autobiographical and, on the evidence here, would have to be. As staged, it presents Renata, a Canadian doctor, who comes to Brazil in search of the mother (billed as Mother) who abandoned her and her brother and their quadriplegic father years before. Renata has every reason to believe that Mother was a very bad mother, and the play takes a long and crushingly undramatic time to prove her absolutely right. There must have been more intended than this, but if Mother was supposed to have a case of her own it never emerges; shes a jolly sociopath, whose nonstop conversation mainly consists of a numbered list of the things she likes about herself. (It goes into the hundreds.) Her conviction that she's the life and soul of her own South American party is wearyingly reinforced by Elizabeth Saunders' performance and by Leah Cherniaks would-be carnival of a production. There is some respite in Maggie Huculaks graciously loopy account of Mother's own mother, and in Mina James' Renata, who has little chance to be anything but earnest. Veering between these poles of exhibitionism and restraint is Richard Zeppieri as Mothers brother, known as Doctor Garbage, and emerging from a symbolic pile of it: symbolic of what, I wouldnt know. The six essential questions are those that Renata asks, when she finally gets a word in, concerning her mother's selfishness; it's a relief to hear them, but a final letdown to realize that there is no answer to them. I have to ask a seventh, even more essential question why was this play that isn't a play put on?

robert.cushman@hotmail.com Sixteen Scandals runs through July at Second City; 6 Essential Questions runs through March 30 at the Factory Theatre

2014-03-22-bird-in-their-hands-the-chekh:
Chekhov's The Seagull famously flopped at its first production, and though there seem to have been purely local and technical reasons for this, the fundamental cause was that neither actors nor audience knew what to make of a play that could not be pigeonholed as comedy or tragedy, and that dispensed with an obvious plot line or protagonist. Instead it offered a shifting group of principal characters and shifting themes. It was ahead of its time in other ways, too. It is, as far as I can tell, the first play to focus on differing attitudes to the creation and appreciation of art. Put more prosaically, its the first play about fan-worship.

So here we have Irina Arkadina, famous Russian actress, spending a discontented summer at her brothers place in the country, accompanied by her lover Trigorin, famous novelist. We have her son Konstantin, aspiring author, who despises Trigorin and all his works, and is inclined to despise his mother and all hers, but is inhibited by the facts that she is his mother, and that he adores her. We have Nina, aspiring actress, for whom Konstantin has written an extremely abstract one-woman play and whom he adores; which is unfortunate for him, as she is entranced at the mere thought of meeting Trigorin and is swept off her feet, and eventually into his bed, when she does. Around this quartet, we have an array of friends and relations, most of them suffering from unrequited love or unfulfilled dreams, and nearly all of them with opinions to offer on the role of the artist (exalted) or the state of the theatre (in decline).

The new production at the Berkeley Street Upstairs is the work of the Chekhov Collective, who take their name and their principles not from the playwright but from his nephew Michael, a famous Russian actor and acting teacher. His techniques, according to the program, involved the actors meeting at intervals over a year "to build the ensemble and to explore the characters and the world of the play. I can't say that the results strike me as notably different from any other decent production of the play. But they are decent, and sometimes more than that.

Physically, and for reasons probably more economic than aesthetic, it's a modest staging, with a single set consisting of a slatted back wall with holes in it; some of these represent doors but not all, though it takes some time to work this out. In the meantime, you may find yourself wondering why the characters always seem to be taking the longest way round to reach the acting area. Peggy Coffeys production is at its most inventive in the first-act presentation of Konstantins play, beside a lake and before his mostly baffled acquaintances. He has Nina move among them, followed and covered by a large frame that sometimes threatens to engulf the onlookers as well; it makes him an early exponent of audience involvement, as well as of site-specific staging. (For which The Seagull itself might be an excellent candidate. We certainly have the lakes.) All this avant-garde stuff presumably adds to his mother's irritation and contributes to her appalling rudeness to her hyper-sensitive son.

Rena Polley, who plays her and who also wrote the adaptation, underplays this; indeed she hardly conveys Arkadina the famous actress at all. She's considerably better at playing the mother, trying to compensate for her neglect with a concern thats fulsome but genuine. Shes a bit of a Gertrude which Konstantin acknowledges by quoting Hamlet at her, thereby setting up Nina as Ophelia. The comparison holds since Nicole Wilson's Nina resembles most Ophelias by being a blur in her earlier scenes but maturing in madness, brought on by Trigorin's abandonment of her, the loss of their child and her frustrated acting career. All the same, the play seems to be saying, shell survive, personally and professionally. Konstantin doesnt; he may have the talent but he doesn't have the stuff, and Riley Gilchrist admirably charts his consequent descent into despair.

Patrick Garrow points up the contrast as Trigorin, careless about everything but his work, the dishevelled opposite of a matinee idol, but still a celebrity magnet for Nina; he's especially good too at showing the weakness that has him slithering between both women. Greg Ellwand, though almost too hale and tall for the role, is excellent as Irinas ailing brother, who laments a wasted life and physically declines before our eyes, but is close as anyone to being the plays moral centre; he's significantly absent from its final catastrophe, as is the hapless schoolmaster Medvedenko, who has at least commanded our attention with the play's famous opening line (Why do you always wear black?") and whom Andrei Preda plays with utter conviction. The world and the characters are there, all right; how completely depends on who at any given moment is embodying them.

The least satisfactory thing about The Seagull has always been the seagull: the bird that Konstantin shoots, that Trigorin forgets and that Nina identifies with? "Is this some kind of symbol? shes asked earlier, as if warding off the possibility that shell end up in an Ibsen play.

There's a flock of seagulls around right now; Peter Hinton has staged the play in Ottawa and next year, in a fine ornithological confusion, Crow's Theatre will be mounting it, also at Berkeley Street but downstairs. Currently, that space is occupied by Nightwood Theatres The Carousel. Denyse Karn designed the highly effective set for this, a hospital corridor stretching away from us in deep perspective and capable of becoming, at least in our imagination, a regional highway; shes also credited with projections, which are modest but help the imaginative process, and with costumes, though the plural is puzzling, since there's only one performer and she never changes her clothes. Allegra Fulton is the actress, and she's splendid. Megan Follows is the first-time director, and seems to have done a god job. The play, by Jennifer Tremblay, purports to present the same character as the authors earlier monologue The List, though its hard to see how they correspond. In this one the protagonist sits outside the room where her mother is dying, recalls her past travails and travels (mostly along that Route 138) and those of the mother and her mother, and about the men from whom they've had to take refuge. Despite Fulton's unfailing concentration and her prodigious technique, it's hard to know, or care, which generation she happens to be summoning. She also talks about her son, whom she takes for a ride on the titular merrygo-round in Paris, and whom she always addresses as my son". It's very lyrical, very sensitive and very dull.

robert.cushman@hotmail.com The Seagull runs at the Berkeley Street Upstairs through March 23; The Carousel runs at the Berkeley Street Downstairs through March 30.

Sean Sullivan and Greg Ellwand, members of The Chekhov Collective, in their sparse new production of The Seagull.; Caption:
2014-03-29-decadon-t-the-quebecois-group:
This af ternoon in Toronto Robert Lepage will be presenting the Glenn Gould Protege Prize to the Quebecois musical performance group known as Lorchestre dhommesorchestres: LODHO for short. The ceremony takes place at the Theatre Centre, which has just moved a few doors west from its previous home at Queen and Dovercourt, to gleaming new premises in what used to be the Carnegie Library; the lobby areas are still unfinished, but the main performance area looks and feels good and is also, I am told, thoroughly flexible. In its second week of existence the new Centre is already on to its second production: the prizewinning LODHO in a show called Cabaret brise-jour. On this evidence LODHO deserves its award. Its members are very good at what they do.

That doesn't mean I have to like what they do, and as a matter of fact I hated it. Cabaret brise-jour is an exercise in deconstruction - how intentional I'm not sure - conducted at the expense of the music of Kurt Weill. Weills German, French and American periods are all represented, and the program includes a laudatory biographical note about him. It isnt quite clear why, because while all the songs included are indeed Weill's, most of them might just as well be anybody's. Their musical lines are obscured, and most of their words are rendered incomprehensible. Weill seems to have been chosen because of the whiff of transgression that still attaches to his work; his Weimar or Brechtian period has - many times over - been identified with, and exploited for, a vaguely defined idea of "decadence.

LODHO begin by exploring this concept fairly conventionally; the eight performers are seen lounging about in various states of deshabille, swigging from bottles and swaying gently to accordion and guitar accompaniment. Later the images get bolder; one of the performers goes through much of the evening with a stocking over her face, and one song shares the stage with an elaborate demonstration of what seems to be a heroin injection. Theres also a great deal of dressing and undressing. In the most effective of all the numbers, the singer perseveres with her singing while doffing and donning an uncountable number of garments including a football jersey and boxing gloves, egged on by the rest of the cast who keep throwing clothes up in the air, eventually covering the stage with them. Its a fun piece of performance art, culminating in an arresting image; though what it's meant to be an image of is uncertain.

All the performers sing - with varying degrees of accomplishment, but that's hardly the point - and most of them play. Most of the instruments are conventional, with a bias toward those of the more piercing variety, but some are homemade, ranging from the humble musical saw to contraptions on a Heath Robinson level of ingenuity. The visuals are strong, but the effect most of the time is not so much to complement the songs as to cancel them out.

Occasionally a new treatment justifies itself; Mack the Knife (the only German song done in an English translation) works well as a slow, sour rap, with the protagonists name omitted, replaced by a sardonic our friend." Theres even a case of a lyric - Ogden Nash's for The Trouble with Women - getting laughs on its own merits, though it seems somehow typical that the actor (who recites rather than sings it) should screw up a crucial rhyme in the funniest stanza. The show seems to harbour a special contempt for the songs Weill wrote with the American verse playwright Maxwell Anderson; some perfectly viable satires of theirs on war and bureaucracy are screamed and snarled into oblivion, and I had to look at the program to discover that the cacophonous first-half closer had actually been a Weill-Anderson song called Big Mole. The final blow to their catalogue is saved for near the end: The torch song Will You Remember Me - hardly so familiar as to need refreshing - becomes an agonized and interminable punk rhapsody, yelled out by a guy in a smock; I could have sworn at one point that he was singing Will You Dismember Me, which could have been appropriate.

Acting Up Stage, devoted to offbeat musicals, celebrates its 10th anniversary by reviving one of its earliest successes, William Finn's Elegies: A Song Cycle: another composer showcase, but a more transparent one than

LODHOs Weill. Actually its a self-showcase, since Finn assembled it himself. He's an uneven songwriter, lyrically and melodically, though the words here are generally more lucid than those for his betterknown Falsettos. The songs, as the title indicates, are all memorials to actual dead friends of the author's, not all of them victims of AIDS. The best, now as it was a decade ago, is The Ballad of Jack Eric Williams and Other 3-Named Composers, the surviving triple threats being a generation of now middle-aged, mainly off-Broadway champs: Michael John LaChiusa, Jason Robert Brown and Ricky Ian Gordon, to whom the song is notionally addressed. Williams, unlike them, was never successful; indeed until I heard this song, I never realized he was a composer - I knew him only as the skilful and extremely bulky actor who created the Beadle in Sweeney Todd. Finn makes me wishId heard Williams songs; he died while still, as he complained and the song repeats, "out of fashion." Thom Allison performs the number with caressing compassion and dazzling wit; he is indeed superb throughout, in full command of nuance and attack, his held notes high and ringing, his vibrato immaculate. He's also relaxed about it all; his colleagues (Barbara Barsky, Steven Gallagher, Joel Gomez, Eliza-Jane Scott) are good but inclined to pile-drive. The evening suffers too from a built-in monotony of theme, accentuated by the facts that most of Finn's subjects mean less to us than they do to him, and that the great majority of the songs are solos. At its best, though, the show is fine.

Weekend Post robert.cushman@hotmail.com Cabaret Brise-Jour runs through March 29 at the Theatre Centre; Elegies: A Song Cycle runs through April 13 at Daniels Spectrum

Guillaume D.Cyr / A fun piece of performance art that culminates in an arresting image - but an image of what, exactly? And why?; Caption:
2014-04-05-when-irish-guys-are-singin-a-:
Irishmen are possessed by an overwhelming passion to sing like their idols. So, at least, Irish drama would have us believe. Recently Mark O'Rowe's Terminus introduced us to a fella who sold his soul to the devil in exchange for the ability to channel Bette Midler doing "Wind Beneath My Wings." Soulpepper now brings us Tom Murphy's 1983 play The Gigli Concert, one of whose characters takes less drastic measures in pursuit of a conceivably nobler ambition. He wants to sound like the classical Italian tenor who gives the play its name, and he seeks the assistance of a "dynamatologist," a species of self-help merchant invented by the playwright and one who demands only cash in advance. That at least is the only tangible payment he wants. It turns out that the physician is as much in need of healing as the patient - probably more.

The first thing to be said about the play, at least in Nancy Palk's production, is that it is magnificently acted. Diego Matamoros, who has set his bar impossibly high in a string of previous performances, may even clear it as JPW King, the English-born dynamatologist who lives in one-room bachelor squalor and who admits to having had only one previous client. Stuart Hughes is a figure of dark-suited bowler-hatted menace as the aspiring tenor, a self-made building magnate in private life, whose name we never learn and whom the cast-list identifies only as "Irish Man"; King calls him "Beniamillo," a presumably affectionate reduction of his hero's first name of Beniamino. Irene Poole completes the cast as Mona, a buxom married woman from whom we learn that the J in JPW stands for Jimmy, and who seeks solace in his pull-out bed, attentions for which he seems insufficiently grateful. All three actors make what would seem to be indelible physical impressions at their first impressions, and then do superb jobs of demolishing their own facades. Thomas Murphy is best known in these parts for his first play A Whistle in the Dark, whose belated Canadian premiere, at the hands of Company Theatre, was one of the great events of Toronto's last decade. That was a play with a clear and exciting storyline whose characters, in equal parts pitiless and pitiful, revealed themselves through their own violent actions. The Gigli Concert was written some 25 years later, and in the interim Murphy seems to have crossed over into his compatriot Brian Friel's territory: more inward, more indirect. I have to say I prefer him in his earlier mode; this play has some rich writing but it suffers, in direct contrast to its transfixing predecessor, from a woolliness of construction. The play be may taken as a sustained riff on the term "transference"; the two men, apparently like their author, disdain psychiatry, though Jimmy at least is not above resorting to both its practitioners and their practices. He takes on Irish Man's problems so that they blend into his own. The relationship between the two men, which is most of the play, takes place over the course of half-a-dozen sessions, but much of it seems to happen in the gaps between, assumed rather than demonstrated: They may be ships that pass in the night, but here they hardly even touch. This may conceivably be the fault of the production, which delights in giving the actors their individual heads, but I remember feeling much the same about the '83 original, which I happened to catch at that year's Dublin Festival (and which was, as far as I can trust my memory, less spectacularly performed).

Irish Man traces his love of singing, and some talent for it, to when he was Italian Boy, the youngest of a large family that emigrated early. So, at least, he says; none of the characters exactly qualifies as a reliable narrator. In the present tense, he is proud of his ability to stand on his own financial feet and seems to have a marriage that is troubled, but perhaps not irreparably.

We get a closer look at JPW's personal life, partly because the play happens at his place. It seems that "Steve," the founder of dynamatology, whose picture is the sole adornment of Jimmy's wall, split the scene long ago, leaving Jimmy his one remaining disciple. Jimmy claims, initially and unconvincingly, to be married; we see him making telephone contact with a lost idealized love; once, startlingly, he gets a call back.

Both men drink heavily (who, in an Irish play, doesn't?) but Jimmy is the further gone. Matamoros, red-cardiganed and white-undershirted, starts his day and the play in an alcoholic haze. His gait is a semicomatose trudge, a miraculous contrast to the spring that gets into his step when his spirits and his fortunes lift. He has a breakdown beyond anything I have seen him do before (he hasn't, in other roles, been much of a crier) and he has a near-to-closing sequence that is, to use his own word in an ironically different context, "transcendent." (The lighting helps). Its import, though, is ambiguous; I hope I'm not giving too much away in saying it depends on whether it's the actor or the character who's very good at miming to records. He has a smaller moment of triumph earlier when he puts on Hughes' hat, his opponent having been largely defined by his domineering dapperness; this Irish Man can threaten, alarmingly, and he can crack, movingly, but his physical guard hardly ever drops. Poole has far less to do than the two men, but her appearances are always welcome (actually they're a relief ); inclined to push too hard in other roles, she's beautifully contained in this one, with no loss of emotional impact - maybe the Irish accent is its own emollient. For two characters out of three, the play ends on a note of qualified hope, for the audience on one of enthusiasm tempered by frustration; one would like to have heard less, know more.

The Gigli Concert runs through May 16 at the Young Centre.

If you suspect the title Cock of having anatomical significance, your suspicions are justified. It also has metaphorical significance. Mike Bartlett, the British playwright who has won awards for this and other plays, conceives of it as a sequence of battles, fought one-to-one, no quarter given: cockfights, in fact. His concept pretty much dictates the play's staging; the actors stalk one another around the playing area, which in Studio 180's production is a bright green square in the middle of the auditorium. It's exciting.

Meet John, who within this structure ranks as a doubly privileged figure; he's the only one who fights in every round, and the only one afforded the dignity of an actual name. Not that he seems to feel privileged - or dignified, for that matter. He's inclined to feel sorry for himself, wanting only to be left alone. He also, though, wants to be loved, thereby ensuring that those closest to him are both infuriated by him and protective of him. We meet two of these people. One is M, the man who has had John as his live-in partner for an unspecified but clearly substantial period. The other is W, the woman of whom John regularly catches sight on his way to work and with whom he has his first heterosexual experience. He enjoys this so much that it becomes a serious threat to his relationship with M, already under stress through M's resentment of John's general helplessness and John's resentment of that resentment. Exhibit A (this alphabetical stuff is catching): M complains that John can't cook while he himself is a whiz in the kitchen; you can bet, though, that both of them prefer it that way.

Flailing around in an attempt to mollify M, John rashly (and inaccurately) describes W as "manly," thereby inspiring M, who has never met her, to embark on fantastical descriptions of her as some kind of outsized Amazon. He gets quite specific about it; he might conceivably be accused of vagina-envy, but it seems likelier that he's just protecting his own turf - to use an image that he doesn't but very well might. However, as bold as the play's language and situations get, its staging is very discreet. Clothing is presumed to be shed, and sexual congress to be occurring, but the actors remain fully clad and hardly even touch. In fact when, near the end of the evening, two people actually kiss, it's a real shock effect. In the meantime John's first nervous exploration of W's body, conveyed in words alone, has been made both touching and hilarious.

I don't think the title word ever crops up in the actual dialogue, metaphorically or otherwise, and even the sporting image doesn't seem too exact; the encounters we witness early on are more like boxing matches, each round concluding with the ringing of a bell and the participants sneaking the occasional glass of water. As a device, this outstays its welcome; it gets us interested in the characters but not truly involved with them. We hunger for some relief from the duologues, and eventually we get it; W is invited to M's place, so that John may choose between them (which of course is the last thing John wants to do). Sadistically, the author keeps us waiting for the longest time for W to cross the threshold. The wait is worth it; W may not be "manly" (she even wears a skirt) but she's a tough little bruiser whose confrontations with M up the play's stakes from mere squabbling to actual conflict. Then, having successfully broken his own mould, Bartlett proceeds with even greater effect to shatter it. We've noticed in the program that there's a fourth character, billed as F. This turns out to stand for father: M's dad, a widower, whom he's invited over for moral support. F confesses to having been taken aback when M first came out; now, however, he's firmly in his son's corner, and wants only his happiness, which he translates as getting rid of W. And it's between F and W that battle is finally and, in Joel Greenberg's production, most excitingly joined.

Challenged to decide who and what he is, John cries out that he doesn't want to be categorized: as straight or gay or, probably, as bisexual. It's a nice sentiment and a strong moment, but sexual identity, fixed or fluid, isn't really what's at issue. It's about what constitutes love, about whether domesticity can coexist with erotic excitement and in what proportions, and about how you choose. John of course wants everything, except responsibility; and he's charming enough almost to get away with it. As an acting role, he's something of a booby-trap: "I'm two different people" he says at one point but, as played by Andrew Kushnir, who excels at artless, tousle-haired likability, he's very much the same person whichever partner he's with: flustered, eager to please and apt to fall into a single apologetic rhythm. Kushnir is at his best when he too breaks his mould: when John is goaded into exploding. Much of the play's high tension depends on the audience's wanting John to decide (though I'd guess a poll would result in a sharp division on which way); much of its cleverness depends on its acknowledgment that any decision would seem, dramatically, like cheating. The uncertainty remains even after, in plot terms, John would seem to have made his choice; we leave him curled up on the floor, like a hedgehog in agony: the perfect position for him.

Jeff Miller, though somewhat self-conscious about his English accent, is fine and forceful as M, alternately upbraiding John and tempting him with cheesecake (his favourite). Jessica Greenberg is excellent as W, at first amused by John, then blisteringly aggressive; and she's matched by Ian D. Clark's F, solicitous turning to inquisitorial. John Thompson's set design is, obviously, neutral; it's the dialogue that sets the scenes, and it's notable that, while the early locations have been fairly vague, in the last section we're made very aware of the layout of the house. The play becomes a territorial struggle in the best Harold Pinter tradition, with a particular resemblance to The Collection, one of the best if least-known constituents of the Pinter canon. Cock has its limitations but it's tight within them. It's cocksure.

robert.cushman@hotmail.com Cock runs until April 27 at Studio 180 Theatre, studio180theatre.com
