Erin Shields' Soliciting Temptation is full of surprises. It unfolds in a series of narrative and character reversals. That makes it compelling. It doesn't make it believable.

It also makes it impossible to review without giving stuff away: stuff you would undoubtedly enjoy more if I hadn't told you about it. So you have been warned. For those still with us: Soliciting Temptation is a 90-minute two-hander whose characters are identified only as Man and Girl and whose setting is similarly unspecified. All we know is that it's a poor, hot country where prostitution is rife and where it's advisable not to drink the water; what with that, and the actress playing Girl being Hispanic, we might be as close to home as Mexico.

Man, whom we discover to be Canadian and even Torontonian (he has a 416 phone number), is a businessman whom we see, in rapid succession, crawling out of his mosquito-netted hotel bed, stubbing his toe, and phoning front desk to complain about the broken air conditioning. He asks to be moved to another room, but puts that request on hold when he hears a knock on the door. It's the Girl he ordered.

She looks young, younger it seems that he had expected. He's disconcerted, as he also is by the businesslike way in which she starts undressing and, most of all, by her failure to say a word. Maybe she doesn't speak his language. Then, suddenly, she does talk: in English. This is the play's first and most effective shock. It's also, when it happens, a relief. Derek Boyes has been playing the Man splendidly, and continues to do so; all the same, one didn't want the whole play to be his monologue.

One may have second thoughts about that. He certainly does. It seems that he's the victim of a sting operation, about to be locked up for procuring sex with a minor, or at

least with someone he believed to be a minor. In the meantime, she lectures him on the evils of the sex trade, and especially of sex tourism, and of his own complicity in same. He protests - convincingly at first, less so later on - that he doesn't make a habit of this kind of thing, and anyway that he's allowing sex workers (he's careful to use the term; she scoffs at it) a chance to improve their lot. She replies in terms that might - as he notes when he stops quivering - have come straight out of a pamphlet. The audience is put in the, I suppose, stimulating position of endorsing much of what she says and hating the way she says it.

Dramatically, it's hardly a fair fight. Boyes, in his many performances with Soulpepper, has specialized in playing goodnatured weak-willed men; that's also his starting-point here, but he advances from it to explore degrees of anger, authority, humiliation and fear to which he

has never had visible access before. His antagonist, Miriam Fernandes, doesn't have the same resources of technique or experience, and has to say things like "how very heteronormative of you." The fact that the play is inclined to laugh at her for saying them doesn't make the actress' task any easier. The author has to employ some fairly desperate plot devices (one in particular) to endow her with any complexity, and it still isn't enough to stop her from sounding shrill. The tension remains, and is stretched to the max in Andrea Donaldson's production. Ken Mackenzie's set offers a persuasive rundown hotel room, with an especially intriguing occasional glimpse of a green passage just beyond the door, a suitably mysterious zone from which the Girl emerges and into which she disappears; the costume plan had me wondering why, given the heat indoors and out, the Man was wearing an undershirt.

Shields' best-known play is If We Were Birds, a powerful reworking of the Greek myth of Philomela. Some of that power, and of Shields' literary skill, is evident here but maybe she's happier when working with somebody else's story. There is some kind of rapprochement between the characters here, but it isn't very persuasive. The play could be the kinder, gentler Canadian version of such American duels-to-the-sexual-death as Oleanna and Venus in Fur; it's less good than the former, better than the latter. It could even be the season's best new Canadian play. This season, though, that isn't much of an accolade.

Michael Hollingsworth's VideoCabaret, on its second comic-book trip through The History of the Village of the Small Huts (i.e. Canada), has reached Trudeau and the FLQ, one of the best of the cycle and, along with The Great War, the most emotionally affecting. The quick-change satirical cameos are as dazzling, and as dazzlingly lit, as ever. But the fact that the action zeros in on a couple of hostage-takings, one of them fatal, precludes sneering; and in Prime Minister Pierre himself, brilliantly portrayed by Mac Fyfe with all mannerisms fastidiously on display, the series may even have found itself a hero; at least it never shows him doing anything wrong and seems to applaud him doing everything ruthlessly right. (Mind you, there is a second Trudeau instalment in store, so the results aren't finally in. And that one will probably have more about Maggie, who is here only a teaser.) Fyfe is matched by Jacob James' Maurice Duplessis, earnestly studying revolutionary tactics through multiple viewings of The Battle of Algiers. The downside of VideoCab's innumerable short sharp scenes has always been a rhythmic monotony; to put it another way, the shows, however great, always feel long. This one, though, as cells divide and sub-divide, works up a real head of narrative steam. It's also, of course, in a retrospective way, very topical.

Soliciting Temptation runs through May 4 at the Tarragon Extraspace; Trudeau and the FLQ runs through May 8 at the Young Centre.

Michael Hollingsworth's latest VideoCabaret instalment, Trudeau and the FLQ, may have found the series' hero: a certain Prime Minister Pierre.; Caption:
2014-04-19-bloodletting-and-miraculous-r:
Two plays have now opened in Toronto in rapid succession in which a character's stubbing a toe turns out to be a defining moment. In Soliciting Temptation it's a middle-aged man's foot that gets bumped, and it's adduced, not least by himself, as proof of what an accident-prone doofus he is. In Belleville, the new production from Company Theatre, it does not so much indicate character as determine future action; it's a young woman who is hurt, hurt so bad that - in one of the most stomach-churning moments of a hypnotically gripping evening - she contemplates drastic action with a kitchen knife.

The woman's name is Abby, and in this play by the rising American writer Amy Herzog, she's living with her husband Zach in the Parisian district of the title (the one cinematically known for its triplets). They have expatriated themselves from the States because it's what Abby wanted. She went into severe depression after the death of her mother; Zach fortuitously landed a Parisian posting with Doctors Without Borders, so here they both are. At least that's Zach's story. At one point Abby claims that Zach had totally misunderstood her and that all she'd really wanted in Paris was a weekend. But the two of them are having a screaming row when she says it, so you really don't know who to believe. What you do realize over the course of the action is that faults and weaknesses are more equally balanced between this couple than is at first apparent. Zach and Abby are engaged in tearing one another apart, and then patching over the wounds, until they reach the point beyond healing.

The plight of two people unable to live with or without one another is a familiar dramatic staple. It can even be a tragic staple. Herzog can't, or at least doesn't, take it to that level, though she sometimes approaches it. She gives us unusually penetrating melodrama, one that escalates smoothly, if not quite inexorably, from a troubled but controllable situation to one beyond any mitigation. Abby and Zach may be special cases, necessarily unmoored from their own society (they call one another "homey," maybe in compensation), but their dance of avoidance and confrontation strikes some painfully believable chords.

It starts with Abby coming home early from the yoga class that she teaches part-time to find Zach, who should be at work, watching porn on his computer. She's recently come off her meds, and is extremely vulnerable. She can't help letting it all hang out; Zach, apparently the more balanced and affable, is the one with things to hide. Abby at least has a kind of support system; she's in constant, dependent cellphone communication with her father back home, largely about her sister's pregnancy and imminent delivery, about which she is extravagantly anxious; indeed, children seem to make her anxious, in any context. Zach's main solace is smoking dope with his landlord, a pleasure impaired by the fact that he's behind with the rent.

We haven't been short recently of intense plays about domestic situations. None of them, though, can match this one in the breath-holding, seat-clutching, eyeaverting stakes - largely, I think, because the suspense here dwells not in what the characters might do to one another but in what they might do to themselves.

It gets so you shudder every time one of them leaves the living-area that constitutes the set and goes into the kitchen or - especially, since they can lock it - the bathroom. It may also help that they have names, rather than, as so often recently, being identified as Man, Woman, He, She or by some letter of the alphabet.

Like much of Company Theatre's best work, including their unforgettable debut show A Whistle in the Dark, Belleville is directed by Jason Byrne, celebrated for his refusal to impose any set blocking on his actors - not just in rehearsal but in performance. This may or may not be a decisive factor (most plays after all, certainly realistic ones, come with a built-in supply of moves) but he does seem to get performances of exceptional force and, as far as I can tell, spontaneity. Christine Horne's Abby seems indeed less like acting than like living; she's an unstoppable electric current with a blond crop. I don't think I've ever seen a performer get closer to the nerve of mental and emotional imbalance, or convey such a sense of intelligence denied its proper emotional or professional outlet. I've also seldom seen so convincing or frightening a drunk scene. As Zach, Allan Hawco has initially the less spectacular role; he's the ordinary guy trying to survive and to help. As his mask slips, so both his aggressiveness and his defensiveness increase. Zach is out of his depth, frightened and frightening, and Hawco's performance combusts. The two remaining characters, the friendly landlord and his less friendly wife (Dalmar Abuzied and Marsha Regis) are decidedly subsidiary, but very valuable; and they share a highly effective, near silent scene at the end. At other times, the show can be quiet in less admirable ways; rather too many lines casually disappear up the actors' intensities. I'm still not sure if the word Belleville actually gets uttered. A good alternative title, if it hadn't already been taken, might be There Will Be Blood. Believe me.

Belleville runs through May 4 at the Berkeley Street Theatre.

Guntar Kravis / Christine Horne - an unstoppable electric current with a blond crop - and the combustible Allan Hawco shine in Company Theatre's Belleville.; Caption:
2014-04-26-animal-harm-beatrice-and-virg:
Yann Martel's Beatrice and Virgil is a novel with, effectively, two characters. They are engaged in the writing of a play, also effectively with two characters. So it makes apparent sense to turn the novel itself into a play for two actors, each of them playing one character from each of the two levels. That's the approach that Lindsay Cochrane, a first-time playwright, has taken in her adaptation. Technically, it works; but there isn't much juice in it.

The two people in Martel's book are both called Henry. I'll call them Henries I and II. Henry I is a writer with one highly successful novel behind him. He has ambitious plans for a followup, one that would combine novel and essay in alternating segments. His publishers reject it, and our hero, licking his wounds and living on his royalties, moves to another country and gives himself over to clarinet lessons and amateur dramatics. Here he's contacted by Henry II who requests his help with a play he's writing. He encloses a scene: two characters named Beatrice and Virgil sitting under a tree discussing, in luscious detail, the shape and flavour of a pear. (Beatrice has never seen or tasted one; Virgil is an expert.) Intrigued, Henry I tracks Henry II to his lair, which turns out to be a taxidermy store. There, among all the animals that have been lovingly and expertly stuffed, are the originals of Beatrice and Virgil; Beatrice is a donkey and Virgil a howler monkey. Henry II reads Henry I random scenes from his manuscript, though he'll never let him see the entire work. We learn that Beatrice and Virgil are friends making noble efforts to comfort one another, hunted creatures who have suffered grievously. They are victims of man's inhumanity to beast, a scarcely veiled metaphor for man's inhumanity to man.

Cochrane's script hews closely to Martel's original, though it moves a few things around and has, like all dramatizations of novels, to leave stuff out. Some of the omissions are forgivable; one at least isn't. The novel tells us, but the play doesn't, that Henry I's abandoned book was an attempt to deal with the Holocaust. That's also, it becomes clear, the subject of Henry II's play. His motives in writing it could not, it transpires, be called noble. It is, in fact, an exercise, in selfexculpation. Henry II cares a lot more for animals than he does for people. And, however much he may bemoan the disappearance of species, he may well, artist in taxidermy that he is, prefer dead animals to live ones.

Henry I has decided, the hard way, that to write narrative fiction about the Holocaust is selfdefeating. Better, he thinks, to leave it to the autobiographers: to Anne Frank and Primo Levi. He's probably right; one doesn't want to see such an event become the object of some outsider's beautiful prose. Martel himself may or may not agree with his fictional alter ego. He seems to want to have it both ways. He dreams up a Holocaust fable, milks it for its horrific value (which is considerable), and then disowns it.

Henry II's abortive play is mostly a duologue, but it does have three other characters, one of them referred to as A Boy. In this it resembles a more widely seen drama, Samuel Beckett's Waiting for Godot. Beckett's Boy was a bullied innocent; Henry II's is anything but. We can hardly help thinking of Beckett anyway, since Beatrice and Virgil, like Sam's tramps, spend their days at the side of the road, under a tree, always saying they'll leave but never making a move. (Mind you, their Godot does in a sort appear, prompting the thought that Vladimir and Estragon didn't know how lucky they were.) Martel may be suggesting that Beckett's play is itself a Second World War memento, reflecting its author's experience in the French Resistance and implicitly contrasting it with Henry II's more inglorious wartime record. The literary self-awareness is something else that's disappeared from the adaptation. So has much of the stylistic poise that is the book's main attraction. Martel's novel is told from Henry I's point of view, but not in his voice. Cochrane's play makes him the narrator, which is probably the simplest way of doing it, but it presents the narration as a talk at a lectern, to some unidentified assembly. It might have been bolder, and more in keeping with the spirit if not the letter of the book, to have the actor directly address us, the theatre audience.

What remains? The agonized reminiscences of Beatrice and Virgil, necessarily shortened, retain some power; they also, when coming off the stage rather than the page, usefully evoke some more recent genocides. But these are isolated passages. The fable in general seems more precious than illuminating.

In Sarah Garton Stanley's production, designed by Amy Keith, the taxidermist's emporium is represented by a set of receding acting areas, each giving way to the one behind as we

get deeper into the story: a neat image, though it does result in the most important scene being played in the remotest space. We don't, alas, get to see any of the preserved inhabitants except the two in the title. They are represented, not especially evocatively, by various means: as puppets, as silhouettes, and - in more extended passages - by the human actors, playing without masks, makeup or any other kind of disguise. Damien Atkins (Henry I) doubles as Beatrice, and Pierre Brault (Henry II) as Virgil, though there seems no particular reason why it shouldn't be the other way around.

Both performers, in both their roles, are accomplished but neutral. Brault is the more individual of the Henries, though he can't prevent an unbecoming geniality from creeping in. He extends his visitor a welcoming smile; in the book he never smiles, wouldn't know how to, is doggedly humourless; it's what's most unnerving about him, to the other Henry and, if that's communicated, to us. Atkins, who has had quite the season, here hardly has a character to play; his domestic life (in the book he's married, with a child on the way) has been excised: not a major loss to the narrative, but still one that knocks a colour out of what's already a limited spectrum. In another way, the actor colours too much. The most disturbing part of the play, as of the novel, is its epilogue: a series of unanswerable questions about reactions to atrocity. They should, for maximum shock, be posed deadpan; the actor doesn't need to show us, as Atkins does here, how shocked he is. Even as it stands, though, this is the one part of the play, as of the novel, that even begins to do justice to its subject.

robert.cushman@hotmail.com Beatrice and Virgil runs through May 11 at the Factory Studio.

Joanna Akyol / Pierre Brault plays an unexpectedly genial Henry II to Damien Atkins' colourless Henry I.; Caption:
2014-05-03-catholic-tastes-david-suchet-:
Plays about God move in mysterious, not to say frustrating, ways. Two of them are currently playing in Toronto.

The movement in The Last Confession is backwards and sideways. This play, a British success now commencing a world tour with an international Anglophone cast, concerns the brief papal reign of John Paul I (1978-1978), who suffered a fatal heart attack after only 33 days in office. By Vatican standards he was, or intended to be, a radical reformer, especially in the matters of birth control and financial corruption. This, together with the fact that no autopsy was permitted after his death, gave rise to the idea that he may have been murdered. These theories, neither proved nor disproved, are the underpinning of this first play by an American lawyer, Roger Crane.

John Paul, as Crane presents him, is an engaging and sympathetic figure, delightfully played by Richard O'Callaghan with a mixture of ingenuousness and determination that makes him seem at first an impossible Pope and then a formidable one. His is not, however, the star role.

That belongs to David Suchet as Cardinal Giovanni Benelli. (Both Suchet and O'Callaghan are reprising the roles they created in England,) Benelli is an accomplished ecclesiastical politician, with reforming and maybe papal ambitions of his own, who is largely responsible for securing John Pauls accession, but then leaves Rome in, apparently, a fit of pique at not being offered the key position of Secretary of State on sufficiently flattering terms. So he isnt around to support the new Pope during his battles with an implacably obstructionist Congress (sorry, Curia), something for which he never ceases to reproach himself. The last confession of the title is Benelli's own, a desperate one. He believes that in failing to help or save John Paul he effectively murdered him.

This is reminiscent of Salieri in Peter Shaffer's Amadeus, claiming responsibility for the death of Mozart in a testament that nobody believes (and that also has a spiritual dimension). The Last Confession also shares with Amadeus a cumbersome flashback structure and a clodhopping prose style. What it doesnt have is the fierce portrayal of

personal jealousy that makes Shaffers Salieri a compelling figure, and justifies his displacing his great contemporary as the focus of the drama. Benelli remains intractably on the sidelines. His only claim on our interest lies in his repeated protestations that he has lost his faith. But since we've never seen him in possession of it in the first place, that doesn't mean much.

You abandoned God? Benelli is asked, to which he replies "I think God abandoned me." Theres a lot of this automatic back-and-forth in the writing. It reaffirmed your belief in God?

"I began to believe in man." Or: Youre afraid you've lost God? "I'm afraid I might find him." It gets so you can predict the answer as soon as you hear the question. Cliched writing tends to breed cliched acting, and Jonathan Churchs production is full of it. Even Suchet, one of the best actors on the British stage (he was, among other things, my favourite Shylock) isnt immune; he has brought incisiveness, of both voice and gaze, to a fine art, and there's a commanding urgency about his performance, but he still succumbs to the play's own stock rhythms. He does, when heading a secondact murder investigation, share an invigorating shouting-match with Nigel Bennett, who plays an unrepentant but comparatively honourable reactionary. The various clerics can be hard to keep track of, and some of them are atrociously played, but Bernard Lloyd gives a fine, elegant performance as senior Cardinal. Donald Douglas is both touching and authoritative as the Pope-before-last, and David Ferry amusingly adapts his native Newfoundland accent in the service of an ambiguous Irish factotum. The identity of Benellis Last Confessor is revealed at the end of the play, and is one of those closing moments that makes you think the author should have gone back and started again. It raises central issues that the play has never begun to explore.

Something similar happens at the end of Sean Dixons A God in Need of Help, though somewhat more forgivably. In this concluding scene, and with some indebtedness to Euripides' The Bacchae (a play that has influenced nearly everything) the author, in a play set in 1606, raises the question of the persistence of paganism, into the era of the Reformation and Counter-Reformation. That must sound awfully remote, but the play makes its complicated historical background a lot more comprehensible than the far more recent one of The Last Confession. At least its people, though not devoid of stock characteristics, sound more or less like people. A giant painting of the Nativity is being bodily transported, by the four winners of a strong man contest, across the Alps from nominally Catholic but largely secular Venice to Prague, where its presence has been requested by the Holy Roman Emperor (who at this date was neither especially holy nor especially Roman). They're escorted, and bullied, by a mercenary military captain. In a German village theyre confronted by a group of the image-destroying extreme Protestants to whom we owe the term "iconoclast"; but both they and the painting are saved by an apparent miracle. The Virgin Mary walks bodily out of the picture, causing the villagers to fall to their knees and become Catholic. That, at least, is the story told by the picture-bearers when they return to Venice, where they are severally interrogated by a cynically nasty magistrate and a rather nice archbishop.

Their stories - told, yet again in flashback - vary, but not so much as to engender a Rashomon level of suspense. The last scene, featuring the youngest and unlikeliest of the four porters of the apocalypse, offers the most startling variation, but its so out of sync with the others as to make most of what has gone before seem irrelevant. Form and (eventual) subject seem at war with one another. Camellia Koo's set is dominated by a stunning reproduction of the painting itself (a Durer) with a detachable frame, which is brought forward in Richard Rose's production so that the various narratives can be enacted within it. The acting is unspectacularly decent, with Daniel Kash a standout as an ex-soldier who has seen it all.

The Last Confession runs through June 1 at the Royal Alexandra Theatre; A God in Need of Help through May 25 at the Tarragon.

Cylla Von Tiedemann / David Suchet brings both incisiveness and urgency to his performance, but he cannot escape the script.
2014-05-10-neatly-tied-up-in-a-woe-soulp:
Gregory Prest makes his first appearance in Of Human Bondage, in which he plays the hero, through a trap door in a blaze of red light. He looks as if hes just ascended from hell. As things turn out, it seems likelier hes just arrived there. In more prosaic terms, his character, Philip Carey, is attending a lecture at the London medical school where he is a student. A little later his professor will display a slide and announce it as "the crosssection of a diseased heart. He isn't actually referring to Philip's own mental and emotional condition, which is exacerbated by a club foot, but he very well might be Of Human Bondage is adapted by Vern Thiessen from the 1915 novel by Somerset Maugham, a book generally accepted as being partly autobiographical. Philip, like his author, is a young man of modest means who has turned to medicine despite deep longings to be an artist. Maugham, of course, was to become an immensely successful novelist and playwright; Philip, when we me meet him in this dramatized version (which starts later than the book) has behind him a failed fling as a painter in Paris. In Albert Schultzs Soulpepper production, visually his most striking and imaginative to date, both of Philips two worlds are continuously present. Lorenzo Savoini's set is dominated by a human skeleton, the emblem of Philip's medical career. His artistic aspirations are represented by a set of human-size picture frames, behind which members of the company function as live models. Or the frames can be empty, so that Philip may gaze into them as if into a mirror. Savoinis lighting does as much as his scenery to move time and place, and Mike Ross contributes an equally compelling music and sound score, the music mainly merry, the sound atmospherically grim. I did wonder why, when Philip takes his girl to The Belle of New York, an American musical, the number they actually see performed is the old British music-hall favourite Waiting at the Church. Philip chooses the show because its the kind of entertainment favoured by Mildred, the tea-shop waitress with whom he is unbreakably besotted. When he takes out a ladyfriend with more elevated tastes, they head for The Importance of Being Earnest in which, to judge from the offstage noises, Oliver Dennis is playing Lady Bracknell.

Philip and Mildred are what everyone remembers from the novel. She taunts and ignores him, says he physically repels her, takes his gifts and money while despising his dependence on her, leaves him for other men, even destroys his paintings. But she is no less dependent on him, and not just financially; the human bonds tie both ways. They may also stand for the murderous poverty that swallows Mildred, nearly engulfs Philip, and is shown to have most of the population in its grip. Prest makes Philip's emotional servitude, along with his other mental and physical struggles, hauntingly credible. Michelle Monteith does the same for Mildred, the shadow of her flirtatiousness persisting even in the direst circumstances; hers is a matter-of-fact attractiveness, one that she takes completely for granted, which is why Philip is so defenceless against it. Their relationship takes up much of the stagetime (and theirs are the only roles that aren't doubled) but it never quite becomes the centre of the action. Nothing does. Its decades since I read the book, but I wouldnt doubt that Thiessen's dramatization is the best and cleverest possible. It still isn't tightly wound enough to be a play. That isnt a condemnation (Of Human Bondage makes a better evening than many plays) but it does indicate a frustration. Philips story never comes to a point; he has experiences, he suffers, and he has a kind of redemption that's thought rather than felt, but there's no definite climax: something a novel can do without but a play cant. The various supporting characters, Philips fellow students and old bohemian associates, are presumably meant to echo and complement him, but they remain shadowy. They are also unevenly acted, both collectively and individually; the extreme case is Dan Chameroy whose alcoholic poet is overdrawn when we first meet him but whose eventual deathscene is the most moving thing in the production. Paolo Santalucia does well as an apprentice medic who's both aristocratic and disadvantaged, as do Sarah Wilson and Courtney Ch'ng Lancaster as the more suitable women who precede and follow Mildred in Philips affections. The adaptations refusal to go Hollywood, to be just a love story and neglect the broader social canvas, is obviously praiseworthy; but it does come at a price.

Soulpepper's other new production is a play, but one that takes a long time to offer any kind of satisfaction. Athol Fugard is so admirable a figure that one wishes he were a more effective dramatist. His The Road to Mecca (1987, set in South Africa in 1974) takes a long, discursive first act to set up its situation. Miss Helen, an Afrikaner widow living in a remote village in the Cape, faces being eased out of her house, apparently because her neighbours dislike the statues and other art-objects that she has devoted the last 15 years to creating, and that she collectively calls her Mecca" though from what we see their inspiration seems more pagan than Islamic. But they sure ain't Christian. A young friend, a schoolteacher from comparatively enlightened Cape Town, to offer her vociferous support; meantime they fill us, and one another, in on their recent life stories. At the very end of the first act there appears Pastor Marius, from all appearances the chief of Helens persecutors. Mercifully, he stays for most of the second, lifting the play and David Storchs production to a new and thrilling level. David Fox gives him a massive, and massively complicated, presence. He also brings out the best in Diana Leblanc, who has previously seemed like ideal birdlike casting for Helen and now proves to be so.

Fugard needs his third actor, though, to force a denouement, and force it he does; Shannon Taylor can hardly be blamed for shouting much of her role, but she doesn't have to be quite so ceaselessly exclamatory. The context, the sheer isolation of the community, might be richer, too, if Helen and the pastor actually sounded Afrikaans, though it's admittedly hard to wish Foxs personal speech rhythms, pausing in the middle of a sentence before hurtling with maximum force through the rest of it, any other than what they are. I wonder if Fugard is consciously echoing Ibsens Ghosts, another play in which a blinkered pastor tries to rein in a self-liberating lady, whose name is also Helen. His own play is a hard slog, but it's ultimately a rewarding one.

2014-05-15-the-ironic-woman-fiona-reid-d:
THEATRE REVIEW

The Charity That Began at Home

Court House Theatre, Niagara-on-the-Lake, Ont.

Arms and the Man

Royal George Theatre, Niagara-on-the-Lake, Ont.

Fiona Reid can divide a comic line into three parts, get a laugh on each without crowding the others, and still keep the sense and the rhythm unbroken. She can be equally hilarious, maybe more so, without saying a word. In The Charity That Began at Home she has a silent scene for the history books, a technical and imaginative triumph in itself and central to the play's meaning. She plays Lady Denison, an Edwardian chatelaine, who at this moment is having to deal with some serious misconduct among the help. She is later to admit that "I do so hate deciding things," and we watch as possible courses of action or inaction run through her mind and across her face, each of them leading her into an abyss of further doubt. I don't think I've ever seen such a superbly prolonged series of mental double-takes. You want it to go on forever; you also can't wait to find out how it will end. Don't worry: I'm not going to tell you.

St. John Hankin's play is sub-titled A Comedy for Philanthropists; it's also largely about them, Lady Denison's country house being the home in which the charity begins. Hankin, whose theatrical career lasted from 1903 to 1908 and whose ill-health drove him to suicide when he was still in his thirties, went in for mischievously sardonic titles. This play was published in a collection that he called Three Plays with Happy Endings; the Shaw Festival has already, and with great success, produced the other two. The Charity ... is the least known of them (not that the others are exactly standard items) but it may also be the best. It's irony made flesh.

Lady Denison and her daughter Margery are collectors of lame dogs. They open their house to decayed gentlefolk who are too dull or too impoverished or too disreputable to receive invitations anywhere else. (They do not, though, extend their hospitality to members of the lower orders. One must draw the line.) Their spiritual mentor is Basil Hylton, the youngish founder of what he calls "the Church of Humanity" which believes in forgiveness above all else. Lady Denison has occasional doubts about this ("if we don't punish the wicked people, it would be so discouraging to the good people") but then she could hardly be called the clearest thinker.

Hankin, a born playwright whose death was a major calamity for English drama, fills his stage with conflicting ideas and complementary actions. Christopher Newton, who has directed all the Shaw's Hankin revivals, orchestrates the sights, sounds, thoughts and feelings of this one magnificently. As costumed by Judith Bowden, some of the houseguests might have stepped out of the pages of Punch, the humorous magazine to which Hankin himself was a contributor: Sharry Flett, an etiolated witch of a German governess, or - a fine double cartoon - Neil Barclay, the last word in portliness, paired on first appearance with Jim Mezon as an unstoppable bore of an Indian Army general. The polite efforts of all concerned to find shelter from the General's name-dropping yarnspinning amount, as staged here, to a beautifully fluid social ballet. But his reminiscences are more than a joke; they serve a plot-function. This in turn leads to the General having, for the briefest moment, to face the truth about himself. As played by Mezon, it's almost moving.

That is the great thing about the play. It never lets you get comfortable about anyone. It is, to make proper use of an overused word, disturbing.

The play's final focus is on Margery and on the fiance whom she wants to reform and who, with the best will in the world, is uncertain whether he can measure up. Julia Course and Martin Happer give, barring the occasional casual slip out of period, fine performances, both probing and touching. The happiness of their ending is even more richly ambiguous than those of Hankin's other plays; there's more at stake, emotionally and intellectually. The servants, who have their own dramas going on, are excellently played by Edmund Stapleton, Andrew Bunker, and Darcy Gerhart who has a very expressive line in blubbing. This is the Shaw Festival at its very best.

Morris Panych's production of Shaw's own Arms and the Man isn't quite that, but it's excellent value. It starts with a chase through the auditorium; in the Balkan War of 1886 (eight years before the play's premiere) the victorious Bulgarians are pursuing the defeated Serbs, though the foe they have in their sights happens to be Swiss: the pragmatic mercenary Captain Bluntschli, the celebrated "chocolate cream soldier" who finds confectionary to be a more useful holster-filler than ammo. It makes an exciting prelude to the first scene proper, which finds Bluntschli taking refuge in the bedroom of Raina Petkoff, starry-eyed daughter of one of Bulgaria's first families. It also prompts Graeme Somerville to give a very convincing portrayal of the starved and exhausted fugitive, though at the expense of the crisp wit with which he punctures his protectress' illusions. By a similar token Kate Besworth's Raina glides over her last line, a surrender to romance, as if she hadn't noticed it were there. Vocally, this young actress has some way to go, but in mind and spirit she's already there; pert and dreamy, she excels at pointing up the false side of Raina's romanticism: the rapturous, hero-worshipping side.

As the hero in question, the peacocking Major Sergius Saranoff, Martin Happer is exactly right, vainglorious but vulnerable, stepping on and off his self-erected pedestal at a moment's notice. Louka, the maid who does the best job of tempting him off it, is voluptuously presented by Claire Jullien, though she seems less like Raina's rival and contemporary than, to put it as diplomatically as possible, her older sister. Norman Browning and Laurie Paton give conventional, meaning thoroughly appropriate, performances of the Petkoff parents. Ken MacDonald has set the play, or so says his director's program note, within a giant cuckoo clock, which seems fitting for a play with a Swiss protagonist; the cuckoo isn't too much in evidence but the machinery, certainly in the last scene, clicks, whirrs and rotates delightfully. So, more importantly, does the machinery of what, in traditional love-comedy terms, may be Shaw's most satisfying play. It's another play with a happy ending, but in this one there's no ambiguity about it. The good end happily, there are no bad to worry about, and we've been told some truths about war that we can live with. Talking of endings: the play's last line has been changed. Why, beats me.

The Charity That Began at Home is in repertory through Oct. 11; Arms and the Man through Oct. 18.

2014-05-17-visit-from-an-old-chum-shaw-f:
The Shaw Festival's Cabaret proves, again, that there will never be a production of this musical as good as the first one. History - including theatrical history - is against it.

That original 1966 staging, directed by Harold Prince, was a seduction. It lured you, titillated you, amused you with its evocation of the louche nightclubs of Weimar Republic Berlin. You knew, intellectually, that Nazism was on the horizon but for much of the evening it did no more than hover; it didnt frighten. Then two things happened. At the engagement party of Herr Schultz, the Jewish greengrocer, and Fraulein Schneider, his Christian landlady, a stone was thrown through the window: a minor act of violence but one that, coming apparently out of nowhere, sent shivers. Sometime later, we got to the gorilla number, the one in which the nightclubs master of ceremonies waltzes serenely with his simian lady-love and ends by sweetly crooning "if you could see her through my eyes - she wouldn't look Jewish at all.

The show wasn't actually accusing 1930 clubland Berlin of being anti-Semitic; it was depicting some apparently apolitical entertainers having a deliciously dangerous topical giggle. Reflecting the tenor of the times, they became complicit in it; and we, with the smiles wiped off our faces, realized what we had been getting into. That was shocking: one of the few really shocking theatrical moments Ive known. At the time, in fact, it was thought too shocking; early in the New York run, the songs last line was replaced with something meaninglessly anodyne; and the same thing happened in London (where I was lucky enough to see it on the second night, before the sting had been withdrawn). Nowadays, of course, we've got way beyond that; and besides, thanks largely to the film version, everyone knows the punchline anyway. So, given that the intention of the show is to shock, later productions have had to find ways of upping the ante.

The favoured method is to immerse us in the supposed decadence of the cabaret itself. This approach, with heavy emphasis on a leeringly androgynous MC and backup, has been institutionalized by the 1990s revival directed by Sam Mendes and Rob Marshall: a version so successful that it's just been revived itself in New York and, presumably for contractual reasons, is credited in the Shaw program as the original production. (The Prince production, a triumph of stagecraft, seems to have been written out of history.) The Mendes-Marshall treatment is so in its audiences faces from its opening number onward that it has nowhere to go. Peter Hintons Shaw production has loftier ambitions and some interesting ideas, but it's even more muddled and, despite some terrific performances, lacks even its predecessor's showbiz smarts.

It has a new beginning. Before we have heard so much as a wilkommen," we see our observer-hero Clifford Bradshaw sitting at his typewriter thinking up the title-speech of the John Van Druten play I Am a Camera, on which the musical is based, and which is itself based on the Berlin stories of Christopher Isherwood for whom Clifford is an Americanized substitute. Maybe, to adapt Fred Ebbs gorilla lyric, we are to see the show through his eyes. We would certainly like to, given the exceptional subtlety and authority of Gray Powells performance (his singing isn't great, but he doesn't have to do much of it); and indeed the notion is embedded in the sourcematerial and at least implicit in Joe Masteroff s Broadway script. But the production doesnt go through with this. Instead it complicates matters by having the MC mimic Clifford's writing position, and at the end having one of them ventriloquize the other. It's a notion that hovers on the verge of being intriguing without ever getting there. Are the two meant to be doubles? Isnt one narrator enough? To make it worse, Juan Chiorans costume as the MC makes him look both pointy-headed and pointy-bodied, and his performance, in a traditionally show-stealing role, never manages to break free of it.

It isn't the only visual constriction. The Prince production rigorously distinguished between the commentative cabaret numbers and the reallife story, only merging the two at the end when devil-maycare Sally Bowles returned to the Kit Kat Klub to, in effect, comment on herself. Later versions have made the club a framework for everything, unsubtly asserting that life is indeed a cabaret (old chum). Michael Gianfrancesco's set suggests that its more of a treadmill; the space is almost entirely taken up by an assemblage of huge revolving staircases. They can accommodate a lot of people, and occasionally they make a point; while the Money song is performed downstage, we see Clifford earning some deutschmarks of his own in his brief unwitting career as a Nazi courier; while Deborah Hay rapturously sings Sallys Maybe This Time we can also watch Herr Schultz and Fraulein Schneider enjoying their new brief happiness. The set, though, is hardly a choreographer's dream, and Denise Clarke (of the Calgary performance group One Yellow Rabbit) is hardly this show's dream choreographer. Mostly she confines herself to pointless echoing; when the Schultz-Schneider duo sing their Pineapple song, everyone on the stairs eats a pineapple; when the same couple sing about being Married, the corps divide up into their own nuptial pairings, all of them, it seems, same-sex.

Meanwhile, back in the 1930s, Benedict Campbell is a first-rate Herr Schultz, chipper and troubled. As his intended, Corinne Koslos acting is similarly rooted, though her singing (and she has the best songs, in pastiche Brecht-Weill style) may be too consciously ominous, summoning the period rather than the particular woman. Hays Sally is the best I have seen since Judi Dench, both in the tremulous sophistication of her book scenes, and her handling of the Kander and Ebb score. Her title number is a spine-tingling combination of false bravado (the character's) and true bravura (her own).

There's fine supporting work, too, from Jenny L. Wright as an incipient Nazi and Jay Turvey as a chillingly real one. Less happy is the productions attempt to bestow party membership on Max (Lorne Kennedy), the clubowner, and to outfit his entire staff with swastika armbands. In reality, the club would have been one of the first places the Nazis shut down. The stone through the window still chills as much as ever, but the proliferating sinister images of this productions final moments are self-defeating. We know already.

Correction: In Thursday's review of The Charity That Began at Home, I attributed the costumes to Judith Bowden. They were in fact designed by William Schmuck.

Cabaret is in repertory through Oct. 26 at the Festival Theatre, Niagara-on-the-Lake.

2014-05-24-art-imitating-death-judith-th:
The fancy name Watching Glory Die has been affixed to a decidedly plain play. The word Glory" in Judith Thompson's title may conceivably have some allegorical significance, but mostly its just a fictitious name bestowed on a real, now dead person. The play is a barely altered presentation of the case of Ashley Smith, the teenager who strangled herself to death in an Ontario correctional facility, under the eyes of guards forbidden to intervene until the very last moment.

The play consists of alternating monologues for three characters: Glory herself, her adoptive mother, and a correctional officer. The attentiongrabbing feature of Ken Gass production is that all three roles are played by Thompson herself, who trained as an actress but has not to my knowledge appeared on a stage in many years. She still has it; she's more than competent, and often compelling. She doesn't vary her characters very much; they all wear the same blue prison smock (she wouldnt have time to change anyway) and all speak in much the same tone and rhythm. But conceivably thats the point.

The most interesting of the three is Gail, the officer, because she's the only one who's conflicted. She has some sympathetic feelings for the women in her charge; but shes on guard against those same feelings. She doesnt want to be taken advantage of; she also has her orders, orders of which she doesn't always approve. In Glory's case, the conflicts come to a head. Glory has been in custody, at one facility or another and mostly in solitary, for six years; shes now within sight of release. During those last weeks Gail performs a rare act of kindness towards her; Glory takes advantage of it, which leads to her sentence being extended, which leads her to her suicide, strangling herself with a ligature. Gail knows and rails against the pointlessness of the new rules, born of exasperation, that prevent her and her colleagues from entering the cell until its too late for resuscitation attempts to be of any use. She also knows that she will take the blame. At our last sight of her, she's grimly contemplating a new career "as a crossings guard." It's a strangely haunting line.

Equally resonant is the announcement by Glorys mother thatshell never eat veal again: a decision prompted by her having seen the conditions in which the calves are kept, a sight that reminds her all too vividly of her daughter's plight. She also gives us useful information about the apparently harmless act that first caused Glory's incarceration, setting off a chain reaction: Glory in jail keeps acting up so Glory stays in jail. (Can you call her a recidivist if she never got out?) For the most part, though, Glorys mother can only tell us that she wants her daughter back, dreams of their reunion, and is angry at the system thats preventing it from happening. It's sympathetic but it's repetitive.

Glory herself brings out the expected intensity in Thompsons writing and the less expected intensity in her acting. But again we dont learn very much. Glory has fantasies about her mother (presumably her birth mother) as a crocodile; her resentment of what she's going through on a human level is easy to comprehend, self-defeating though it often seems. Dramatically, though, Glory remains as unreachable as her prototype was in real life. In the end the play's effectiveness depends on what it tell us about Ashley Smith, and it doesnt tell us much more than did the news reports at the time. There is an implicit claim, one with which I wouldnt quarrel, that watching Ashley die, at a decent artistic remove, is a worthwhile civic jolt in itself. Astrid Janson has designed a sternly effective set, lit with appropriate rigour by Andre du Toit. Glory inhabits the cell that's its centre. Her two fellow-victims - for that's what they are, but articulate ones, like her - address from outside it. Gass direction is mostly rigorous in keeping each one to her own corner of the stage, so thatwell know immediately who is who, though there's a confusing placement near the end. The show is produced by the Canadian Rep Theatre, founded by Gass after his ejection from the directorship of the Factory Theatre. Meanwhile, back at his former ranch, the new regime has mounted a new play by another Canadian playwriting icon, Daniel MacIvor. Bingo!, billed as a comedy, is an avowed attempt by its author to write something more popular, or maybe that should be populist, than the stark works for which he's best known. It concerns a Cape Breton high-school reunion, 30 years after its characters graduated (or, in one case, failed to) and its title is the victory shout in what seems, to an outsider, a spectacularly pointless drinking game. But then the whole play seems pointless, bearing as it does the startling news that people look back on their younger days with a mixture of fondness and regret, and that some move on, socially and/or geographically, while others dont. Also that they may resent the hell out of one another, and can be very aggressive about it. Nigel Shawn Williams production keeps the proceedings proceeding at a fair if relentless clip. There a couple of nice scenes, both involving John Beale and Sarah Dodd as the two most likable characters, or at least the two who don't shout. This is a low-key work from MacIvor, especially considering that he's given recent proof, in The Best Brothers and A Beautiful View, that he can be funny and compassionate without compromising any of his standards.

Watching Glory Die is at the Berkeley Street Theatre Upstairs; Bingo! at the Factory Theatre, both through June 1.

Wendy D Photography / Judith Thompson plays three roles in this one-woman show about a prison tragedy.
2014-05-26-the-year-of-lear-once-thought:
This is the year of the Lear. Tonight the Stratford Festival opens with Colm Feore playing King Lear in a production by Antoni Cimolino. There have been two productions in New York: one with Frank Langella, the other, less grand, at Brooklyn's Theatre for New Audiences with the British actor Michael Pennington heading an otherwise American cast. Meanwhile in London, Simon Russell Beale is playing Lear at the National Theatre, in a production directed by Sam Mendes. I missed the Langella version, but I saw Pennington on stage and Beale in a transmission from National Theatre Live. I admired both.

I heretically doubt if this abundance of 2014 productions signifies anything more timely than a confluence of actors' schedules. Lear has always been a popular play, at least since the middle of the 20th century (the new Stratford production is the fourth in 15 years); even in the 18th or 19th centuries, when it was thought "unactable" (or performed in heavily adapted versions) the neglect was a kind of tribute. The play was thought too painful, too titanic, simply too great, to be completely realized in performance. One thing we've learned is that it doesn't have to be. It is doubtful that there ever has been, or could be, a perfect production of Lear. It's equally unlikely that there have been many really bad ones. The size of the play calls out the best in the people who present it.

It can do the same for those who teach, study or write about it. There's a passage that has always moved me in Great Books, the film critic David Denby's account of a year spent as a mature student, re-taking the firstyear Literary and Humanities course at Columbia University. Lear is on the syllabus, and the man teaching it suddenly breaks off from textual analysis to say "Nobody can lay a glove on this play. This is the greatest thing written by anyone, anytime, anywhere, and I don't know what to do with it ... no one else knows what to do with it, either." This "hipster wit" is, Denby tells us, "on the verge of tears."

The play does that to you. It seems to have done it to Shakespeare. He took a source-play (King Leir, by Anonymous) with a happy ending, and made it merciless. (Not pitiless. There's a difference.) He doesn't just kill off the king, as tragedy might require. He has Cordelia, the good daughter of the king's three, her father's last refuge and only hope, hanged in prison, after Edmund, the man who ordered it, has had a deathbed change of heart and tried to stop it, but before Lear himself dies, so that he has to suffer this last agony too. "Is this the promised end?" asks one onlooker, invoking the end of the world. "Or image of that horror?" says another, agreeing. This is pretty nervy on Shakespeare's part. The deaths of Hamlet or Othello provoke a few awed words from the survivors, but nothing suggesting this unparalleled level of tragedy. And we accept it. The rhythm of the last scene sweeps us along, as it must have swept its author. It's a rhythm that shouldn't be tampered with. Mendes' production is one of many that have made heavy cuts in this scene, including (perhaps because it's thought sentimental) Edmund's fruitless repentance. This is so wrong. Lear's last despairing entrance, with the dead Cordelia cradled in his arms or (if the actor can't manage that) dragged at his feet, needs to surprise us if it's going to shock us. It did so superbly in the Brooklyn production where Pennington's "howl, howl, howl, howl" issued from a promontory at the edge of the stage that had hardly been used before. We had to swivel our heads to see where it was coming from. Then we were caught.

Lear fascinates as a ruler, as a father, and as an old man who misjudges his own strength and goes mad, discovering truths that he would never have faced when sane. Pennington, who in his early scenes made me think of a brisk English squire just back from hunting, brilliantly emphasized the man's mercurial nature. He told me in an email that he'd discovered in Lear that "nothing proceeds in a straight line ... he seems to shuttle between piercing good sense, riffs of madness, and a sort of overt mental torment." The Brooklyn production (directed by Arne Arbus) was a plain presentation, illumined by bolts of lightning: literally in the storm scene where a flash, and a pause in the thunder, set off Lear's crucial declaration that "my wits begin to turn".

This production was in nonspecifically modern dress. The National Theatre's is more elaborately (and expensively) modern and thus inescapably more political. Gloucester, excellently played by Stephen Boxer as a pinstriped bureaucrat, gets waterboarded before he gets blinded. Beale says, in an NT Live intermission interview, that Mendes' first instruction to him was to shave his head so that he would look "less like Santa Claus." Thus bulletheaded, not to mention short and solid, Lear somewhat resembles the Stalin whom Beale played last year in the play Collaborators. In that performance, the dictator's monstrosity was initially masked by modest self-deprecation; Lear, at least when we first meet him, wouldn't know what self-deprecation meant. Beale makes a bluff no-nonsense entrance to preside over his daughters' loyaltycontest, staged with the three of them lined up a table, a microphone before each of them. Goneril delivers her script with satisfactory unction; Regan, feeling the need to one-up her sister, is literally all over her dad, and he loves it. (Later, she's to take the same slinky tack - or tacky slink - with nearly every male in the cast. It's an arresting idea, and certainly fun to watch, but it does lack variety.) When Cordelia refuses to join in the game, Lear's fury is scarifying, as of an immense spoiled child. There was a famous moment in Peter Brook's legendary 1960s production when Lear's knights overturned a table, to show what rowdy houseguests they were. This Lear, at this moment, does his own table-turning. When the rebellious Kent confronts him, saying, "Be Kent unmannerly, when Lear is mad" he's stopped momentarily in his tracks, then turns his fury up yet further. Has the fear of madness already been haunting him? Is this the first time he's encountered it? Either way, it's a fascinating prelude to Beale's meticulous charting of how Lear comes to use, and even to embrace, the word. This fear rings through his scenes with his Fool, wonderfully played by Adrian Scarborough as a north-country comic in a Tyrolean hat: headgear that Lear himself appropriates for his most sustained mad scene, at Dover. Here we encounter both the power of modern dress and its limitations: I could take it when Lear's attendants stuck a straitjacket on him; jabbing him with a hypodermic seemed an anachronism too far.

If Lear is a political play, it is so in a different way from most Shakespeare's. It isn't about the jockeying for power of rival kings and queens; that's there but only for plot purposes. What resonates now - and probably always has, in different registers - is Lear's prayer for the "poor naked wretches" of his kingdom, forced to endure the storm; he even uses the word "homeless." Even more startling is his acknowledgment that when enthroned he had taken "too little care of this": not that he was responsible for it, but that he should have done more to alleviate it. He moves on to a stunning attack on all levels of authority: "a dog's obeyed in office." There's nothing else like it in Shakespeare. It's been suggested that he had to make his protagonist mad to get away with such sentiments, and that may well be true. Both the two recent Lears make these speeches burn and sizzle. But then so do most Lears.

In the post-madness reconciliation with Cordelia, Beale is very moving, partly because he plays it initially for anger and bewilderment rather than beatitude. Pennington had the edge, though, in their subsequent scene together - "let's away to prison ... we two will sing like birds in the cage." I agree with him that this is "the emotional heart ... the real beauty of the reunion ... and that's the last we see of them alive of course." Even if you've never seen the play before, it's heartbreaking because you sense it can't last. If you know what's coming, it's brutal. But, as with everything else in the play, you wouldn't want it any different.
