2014-06-21-best-in-shows-the-doras-have-:
The Dora Awards presentation gala, on Monday evening at Harbourfront, is being hosted by Naomi Snieckus and Matt Baram. The venue is a new one for the awards; the two funsters doing the hosting are holdovers from last years ceremony, at which they did a refreshingly entertaining job. Their return should at least guarantee that the Doras this year will be less tacky than their big American cousin, the Tonys whose host, Hugh Jackman, seemed under the embarrassing impression that the show was all about him.

The actual Dora nominations seem remarkably classy this year, which I suppose is a critics way of saying that nestled among the possible winners are most of those who were actual winners in this year's Toronto Theatre Critics' awards, plus many who were close contestants in our blood-spattered, furiously argued, marathon-length, closeddoor deliberations last month. (Actually our proceedings, as has consistently been the case in the four years weve been playing this game, were surprisingly short, refreshingly sweet, and conducted in a secluded corner of a public space.)

Its been a poor season for new Canadian plays. There hasn't been one that kept its eye on its object and that turned believable characters and speakable dialogue into action: nothing in fact to match Hannah Moscovitch's This Is War which lit up the previous season and has just been awarded the Trillium book prize. The critics choice this year was Robert Lepages Needles and Opium, a dazzler in writing, staging and performance; it had been seen before in Toronto but had been so extensively re-worked that we felt it qualified as new. The Doras have looked similarly outside the box in choosing as one

of their five Best Play nominees Tim Luscombe's PIG, which isn't Canadian. It was however a world premiere, since in its native Britain its presentation of gay sado-masochism had apparently been considered too hot to handle. The resurgent Buddies in Bad Times picked it up and gave it a superb production. The competition includes only one orthodox play, Sean Dixons A God in Need of Help; I was surprised that the lot didnt fall upon Joan Macleod's The Forest which everybody else seemed to like more than I did. The other contestants are The Gay Heritage Project (Buddies again), a collage of autobiographies; Winners and Losers, a semi-improvised cross-talk act, in which the talk got very cross; and Of Human Bondage, an adaptation of a novel. If I had a vote at this stage it would go to PIG, imperfect - indeed confusing - though it was, though if I were a betting man I'd put my money on Soulpeppers Of Human Bondage because of the number of other categories in which its been nominated. It's called momentum.

Those categories include both best production and best direction; in fact this year four out of five nominees in each of those categories figure in both: a comfort to those of us who have always wondered how you're supposed to tell the two apart. The other three doubles champions are the aforementioned PIG, directed by Brendan Healey; another British import Lungs which, if the Doras rules were different, would be an almost unbeatable contender for best play and was flawlessly directed at Tarragon by Weyni Mengesha; and - to my great satisfaction and delight - The Double, the impish Dostoevsky adaptation that was also a concerto for three performing virtuosi, one of them being the director Adam Paolozza; physical theatre has never been more delightful or more intelligent. All four double entries are shows of which Toronto can be proud. The ringer among the best production choices is Venus in Fur, which was (or is, since its coming back for a third run) a triumph of performance over material. It's certainly an event, which may be what best production is about. The remaining best direction nod has gone to Richard Rose for A God in Need of Help.

Albert Schultz has already won the critics' direction award for Of Human Bondage. Our production award was split; we divided it between Lungs and Soulpeppers other blockbuster Angels in America: a miniature and a mammoth, two shows that were, in the strict sense of the word, incomparable. Soulpeppers season has unquestionably been its best since the company took up residence in the Distillery; it included another, homelier epic The Norman Conquests and such a smaller-scale success as Entertaining Mr Sloane. Schultz's staging of Bondage has been justly celebrated, but Angels, which he also directed, is the more spectacularly acted; indeed it has the greatest concentration of superlative acting of any Soulpepper show since The Wild Duck. (Well, maybe The Time of Your Life.) It was also, most definitely, an Event.

A personal note: I left Angels in America, which came early in the season, convinced that Nancy Palk, who played three roles in it, already had a lock on best supporting actress; nothing that happened later shook that opinion, and she indeed received the critics' award in that category. There is no such slot, however, in the Doras which wastefully lump together performances principal and supporting. Anyway, Palk is in there but only for her performance in Angels Part II, which seems a pedantic distinction and anyway leaves out her amazing rabbi at the top of Part I. (For some inexplicable reason Angels seems to be counted as two plays but the three-part Conquests as one.) Its a daunting field altogether among the females: Carly Street (critics choice) in Venus, Lesley Faulkner (extraordinary) in Lungs, Fiona Reid (hilarious) in Sloane, and Holly Lewis (haunting) in Tribes. Major omission: Laura Condolln in Conquests. As for the males: I'll be very surprised if Damien Atkins, who has already won two awards for his performance in Angels, doesn't carry off a third. Its been his year; hes been in four shows (one of which he co-wrote) and was good to great in all of them. I'll admit that in contemporary plays any distinction between principal and supporting roles is increasingly hard to discover or justify. Hence, perhaps, the Doras' fallback category of best ensemble. This year that includes Bondage (but not, crazily, Angels), The Double, and - a really welcome surprise - Sixteen Scandals, the best Second City revue in, probably, decades.

There is a corresponding ensemble category in the musicals division, but here I cannot imagine the prize going to anything but Canadian Stages London Road; I will be equally horrified if the show itself doesnt get best production and if Jackie Maxwell doesn't win for her direction (and Reza Jacobs for his musical direction of an extraordinarily tricky score). Reid and Atkins are also nominated for their individual performances but, good as they were, I can't see that they were any better than their colleagues in what was, really, an incredible assemblage of Torontos finest. Besides, shouldnt we be spreading these things around a bit? As for your actual best new musical: the pickings are thin, as is demonstrated by the inclusion of The Barber of Seville (another Soulpepper show; nobody's perfect), though operas are included as well including the other Figaro story, Figaro's Wedding. Figaro here, Figaro there. For musicals per se,Id go with Ross Pettys The Little Mermaid if it were nominated, but it isn't. At least, there's a separate opera division in all other categories. For female performance theres a fair embarrassment of riches, but Sondra Radvanovskys Elizabeth I (Roberto Devereux) must surely be the richest of all.

I can't say much about the independent (i.e. small theatre) division, as I have family connections with two of the nominated shows. (I liked them both, by the way). But, among the nominees not involving relatives, I thought very highly of VideoCabaret's Trudeau and the FLQ and Mac Fyfes performance in it; of David Ferrys direction of After Miss Julie and Claire Armstrong's performance in that; and of Alex Mc-Cooeye's seven-foot alfresco Richard III: nice to see Shakespeare in the Ruff getting a nod. Reverting to the general division: the nominations for Of Human Bondage include scenic, costume, lighting and sound design: all thoroughly deserved. The critics simply gave the show an overall best design award. I do carry a subsidiary torch for Camellia Koo's set design for The Gravitational Pull of Bernice Trimble, a new Canadian play that was underrated in a season that could hardly afford to be sniffy. On which subject: the award for Show Most Consistently Shut Out of the Doras must go to Cock, a play not nominated in any category at all. It was another of the British plays without which this Canadian season would have been very sad indeed.

Jeremy Mimna GH / Tim Luscombe's PIG: Not technically Canadian, but since the British play did have its world premiere here, it picked up a Dora nomination.
2014-06-28-the-shirty-dozen-twelve-angry:
It's no great surprise that Soulpepper's production of Twelve Angry Men should turn out to be a spellbinder, not to say a humdinger. This TV play turned movie turned stage play pours all the traditional excitement of a courtroom drama into the jury-room adjacent, where it shows the tension to be even higher. A conventional trial drama offers us a series of one-on-one confrontations, with only the judge permitted to interrupt. Reginald Rose's play gives us a dozen characters in non-stop interaction over a matter of, literally, life-anddeath, enmities and alliances forming and re-forming, everyone's thoughts and feelings in continual flux. All that's needed to make it work is 12 good actors and it's true - the company in the Distillery has a plurality of these on tap and can order in the rest.

Actually, it has 12 plus one, since there's a 13th character, the guard who ushers the jurors in and out of their conferring chamber. He's very well played, too, by Andre Sills; I don't know if Alan Dilworth's production is intending to make a point by casting a black actor in this purely functional role; but one is made anyway. In Rose's play, which in its original TV form dates back to 1954, the case on trial is one of murder; a 16-year-old stands accused of knifing his father and will go to the chair if found guilty. Father and son belong, according to the more truculent jurors, to "these people"; their precise ethnicity is never specified (black? Puerto Rican?) but whatever it is, it has no representatives among the 12 males charged with reaching a verdict. As is well known, 11 of the deciders begin the deliberations convinced that that verdict should be guilty. The one holdout takes very seriously the judge's instruction about guilt needing to be established "beyond reasonable doubt"; the play tracks his efforts to persuade the others of just how reasonable his own doubts are and why they should share them.

Now, as in the 1950s, we accept his side as being that of the angels. It's a valid criticism of the play that it makes a safe case, one that few members of any likely theatre audience would dispute. The reasonable doubter, known to the program as Juror 8, is an architect by trade, though you may feel he missed a vocation or two; he should have been a private detective or a public defender. He ferrets out all kinds of possible holes in the prosecution's case, all of them mysteriously ignored by the prisoner's own court-appointed lawyer who had either decided the case was unwinnable or was just staggeringly incompetent. The play needs these assumptions in order to function, and it piles them on pretty thick. But we forgive them; the play's moral passion still glows while its mechanics are both physically and psychologically thrilling.

Dilworth's production renders the play's melodrama exciting by initially downplaying it. Yannik Larivee's set is a plain room on a strip of stage in the middle of the auditorium, with the audience on two sides. It's a hot day, waiting to rain; the storm will break, spectacularly, as we watch: the show's one technical indulgence, unless you count the pastiche TV theme music that Richard Feren has designed in cock-eared tribute to the play's origins. The actors troop on and take their places at a long table, reeking (the air-conditioning's on the blink) of the 1950s; with their shirt sleeves and their hair-partings, the performers are so completely absorbed into the period that even those we know by heart are hard to recognize, (Larivee's costumes are wonderful). The least colourful, at least initially, is the one who might be called the hero; as played by Stuart Hughes he's not the Henry Fonda type of the decent crusader (Fonda created the role) but a man whose conscience nags first at him and then at everybody else. It isn't that he believes the boy innocent, just that he isn't convinced he's guilty. He's fighting for the principle of reasonable doubt and also, as the debate goes on, for the souls of his opponents. This is a modest, tenacious performance that doesn't fully declare itself until the end - in one sharp mind-clinching line and then in compassionate silence - and that grows in the mind when the play is over.

Some of his conquests are fairly easy, men with sympathetic experience of being underdogs. Others are good-hearted or maybe just affable enough to be won over. The play is very hot on civic duty; the clearest exemplar of this is the jury-foreman who says little beyond calling his unruly, and often violent, flock to order but whose role, as played by Tony DeSantis, is shown to be pivotal; when his vote changes, so does the play.

This leaves three holdouts. One, played with brutal, loud-mouthed virulence by William Webster, is the room's one out-and-out racist, accurately pegged, in what may be the play's best line, as a man who always needs to have someone to hate; today, he'd be a compulsive contributor to online forums. At the opposite extreme of propriety is a businessman who prides himself on clear thinking, and is the only one who declines to take his jacket off; Tim Campbell's performance, implacably courteous behind his gleaming glasses and seemingly baked into his suit, would be the completest performance, if it were not for Joseph Ziegler as the angriest man of all, Hughes' ultimate opponent, the one whose weak spot he finds, probes, and may even attempt to heal. Ziegler's rage has a sociological veneer, but is deeply personal. Like another paterfamilias, the Irish patriarch whom Ziegler so devastatingly played in A Whistle in the Dark, this one self-destructs while ranting on top of a table. This being a more liberally hopeful play than Whistle, he's afforded a kind of redemption in surrender. It might all seem too neat, but the acting and the writing make it seem logical, raw power burning itself out before our eyes. This is a frightening, pitiful, self-transforming performance in a play of which the word "decent" can, for once, be honourably used.

Twelve Angry Men is at the Young Centre for the Performing Arts until July 19.

Cylla Von Tiedemann / This 1950s TV play, turned movie, turned stage play, pours all the traditional excitement of a courtroom drama into the jury-room adjacent, where it shows the tension to be even higher.
2014-07-05-bliss-this-miss-noel-coward-s:
Every production of Hay Fever has to have a staircase. Much of the action in Noel Coward's play about the worst weekend in the history of country house comedy consists of guests and residents going back and forth between the sleeping quarters upstairs and the eating and playing quarters at ground level. On the set that Douglas Paraschuk has designed for the new Stratford production, one of the stairs is missing. Or maybe it's just rotten; from a seat in the stalls, it's impossible to tell. We do, though, get a very good view of the characters negotiating this obstacle. The Bliss family, whose summer place it is, hop daintily or swing insouciantly over it. Their visitors are less knowledgeable, less adroit, and loaded down with suitcases. Naturally they keep tripping. And they never learn. Alisa Palmer's production has locked itself into a single running gag that isn't too hilarious to begin with and gets more relentlessly unfunny with each repetition. If it were cut, though, there might not be any production left.

Hay Fever is famously short on plot but what it has is strong, simple and symmetrical. Judith Bliss, star of the 1920s London stage, currently in rustic retirement, has invited an admirer down for the weekend. Similar invitations have been issued by her husband, David, who writes terrible romantic novels, and by their children Sorel and Simon. None of them has bothered to inform the others about this until immediately before their guests' arrival. When they do arrive, they are first ignored and then humiliated, forced to participate in charade-like games for which they possess neither aptitude nor interest. Games over, the players pair off for flirting purposes, the joke being that none of the hosts is partnered with his or her original intended - though how serious the intentions may ever have been is very much open to question.

Judith, who made her name in plays with titles like Love's Whirlwind, acts off-stage in

much the same way she used to act on, and the other Blisses can hardly help playing along. Come the end of the evening, their victims are flabbergasted to find that they have become engaged to a younger Bliss or have precipitated the divorce of an elder. By next morning, of course, the family have forgotten all about it - indeed seem unaware that they ever had any visitors at all. The civilians, cowed and sleepless (their rooms were uniformly horrible), make as speedy an exit as they can manage, thereby provoking the Blisses to deplore the extraordinary way in which some people behave.

Coward himself remarked on Hay Fever's popularity with amateur groups: "It has a small cast and only one set which must lead them, poor dears, to imagine that it is easy to act." He added that, since this "species of delusion" was universal among amateurs, he had no intention of disabusing them except to suggest, mildly, that "from the professional point of view, Hay Fever is one of the most difficult plays to perform that I have ever encountered." The Stratford program quotes that last sentence and proceeds, bizarrely, to theorize that the difficulty is a philosophical one, born of the play's "utter commitment to unconventionality." Actually half the characters are thoroughly conventional; that's where the fun is.

Coward's point, which he went on to make perfectly clear, was a purely technical one; the comedy, short on action, depends on behaviour: on the delivery, feather-light and rapier-sharp, of lines that look innocuous on the page but can be devastating in context, and on an overall rhythm that should bind the cast together, even while the people they're playing are locked in mutual incomprehension. It's a play for an ensemble, an ensemble of specialists.

There's another weird statement in the program, this one from the director herself, who says that the play is really about mothers and daughters. In her actual production, though, the relationship of Lucy Peacock (Judith) and Ruby Joy (Sorel) bulks no larger than any of the others in the criss-cross, and it's hard to see how it could.

What we actually get is a disconnected set of performances that never build into a show. Peacock, technically expert, covers all Judith's selfindulgent bases without quite taking possession of them - or, perhaps, letting them possess her; her natural quality is earthy rather than flighty. (It's hard to believe she would need to practise the names of the flowers in her garden.) Her husband, normally and I think correctly played as tweedily absent-minded, comes over in Kevin Bundy's performance as a fretful young man with a beard stuck on. Tyrone Savage's Simon starts off as a painfully exaggerated idea of a male Bright Young Thing, but relaxes and improves thereafter.

In general, the flies in the web come off better than the spiders. That, to be fair, is how they're written, though you wouldn't know it from Cynthia Dale's ineffectual stab at the vamp Myra Arundel, the only one who really fights back. The others are endearingly relatable, as they grapple with unthinkable things like the possibility of the Bliss family not serving tea.

Gareth Potter is splendid as the young boxer who finds himself going separate rounds with each of the ladies of the house; Sanjay Talwar is even better, pretty much perfect in fact, as the diplomatic diplomat who here seems to have taken the English garb of the English sahib, and internalized it. At least I think that's the idea; with non-traditional casting, you can never be sure whether or not you're supposed to notice. His initial scene with Ijeoma Emesowum's terrified flapper, the two of them making the smallest of talk while wondering whether they've come to the right place, is the best in the play, as Coward himself realized. Even here, though, the lines are drawn less tight than they should be. Sarah Orenstein's chain-smoking dresser turned maid is amusingly surly until the production either pushes her over the top or stops her from going there. The set is an applause-getter and the costumes are swank. But the overall laughter-level is painfully low. The comedy sinks like a fleet of lead balloons.

Cylla Von Tiedemann / There appears to be some kind of miscommunication in this early 20th century farce.
2014-07-09-relationship-material:
THEAT REREVIEW

Company

Berkeley Street Theatre Downstairs

In a way that's unique among musicals, the action of Company takes place in a split second. Robert, New York bachelor just turned 35, imagines a birthday party thrown for him by the five married couples who count themselves his best friends. Its a strange party, since the people giving it dont seem to know one another and the guest of honour never actually shows up.

At least he doesn't always. At different points of the show, he envisions the party three different ways. At the first he's a happy participant; at the second a disillusioned participant; and at the third a nonparticipant. In conjuring up these dubious celebrations Robert (also addressed as Bobby, Bob, Robbie even - God forgive them - Robbo), starts taking stock of his life, which seems mainly to consist of dropping in on his friends marriages and contemplating them with various degrees of incredulous amusement. We see him with them, and also with three representative girlfriends who lament his emotional, as opposed to physical, unavailability. Finally, something explodes in his head, and he decides to stop living vicariously and to embark on Being Alive: that being the title of the climactic song in Stephen Sondheims vertiginously brilliant score. Being alive doesn't necessarily mean being married, though the show up to this point has been so focused on marriage that it's hard to take it any other way. But it does seem to mean being involved with someone ("alone is alone, not alive") and taking responsibility.

In its day, 1970, Company was a controversial show, though the discomfort it aroused seems to have had more to do with its tone than with its structure. Sondheims lyrics, unerringly focused on social foibles and human weaknesses, had probably the greatest concentration of wit of any musical up to that time, and the music was thought to be disconcertingly harsh and angular when it wasnt being disconcertingly beautiful.

In Theatre 20's new production, The Company song is a traditional showstopper with a twist: Bobby's friends express their devotion; he, leading the dance, suddenly realizes he has no place in it. Marc Kimmelmans choreography, here and throughout, is both slick and characterful.

The Berkeley Street space has always been acoustically unfriendly but other musicals (Light in the Piazza, Caroline or Change) have overcome it. Ken MacDonalds Company set leaves the stage open to its brick walls, swallowing up too many of the sung words and even some of the spoken ones.

The solo numbers, though, come off intact, especially Dan Chameroy's in the lead, and this is where the production importantly delivers. George Furth's book derives from his own series of one-act plays, each involving a different couple and an observing friend. The musical rolls the onlookers into one, leaving the built-in problem of a displaced protagonist. Its been addressed over the years by some rewriting, notably by reinstating the cut song Marry Me a Little, which, in its new halfway position, shows us Bob fighting angrily against what he doesnt want to believe. Chameroy, whose emotional range these days just keeps expanding, keeps the baffled anger going into Being Alive, where it finally explodes and transforms.

Anger, too, informs Louise Pitre's magnificent delivery of the showpiece "The Ladies Who Lunch." It's harder than it used to be to equate a collection of well-heeled Manhattanites with the Human Condition, but we do get a wide and talented spread here; Brent Carver and Nora McLellan as the karate couple with their competing addictions (his alcoholism rather halfheartedly presented, compared to her gluttony), Steven Sutcliffe and Nia Vardalos excellent as the novice pot-smokers. Outside the marital circles, Marisa McIntyre is delightful as April, the flight-attendant whom Robbo takes to bed. Their morning-after duet is one of Company's paradoxes; in a non-narrative show, it tells a complete story of its own. It also has maybe the funniest, and most logical, opening line (Where you going? "Barcelona") of any song in any musical. And then, later on, one of the funniest lines of any kind Sondheim ever wrote. The line is "June". You have to be there.

Company runs through July 13 at the Berkeley Street Theatre Downstairs.
2014-07-12-leafy-highs-lows-shakespeare-:
Shakespeare in High Park, formerly The Dream in High Park, took a notable step forward last year with its production of Macbeth, which was less concerned than its predecessors with playing games and more with playing the play. The welcome trend is continued this summer with alternating performances of Shakespeare's most contemplative comedy and his goriest tragedy.

Nigel Shawn Williams' production of As You Like It is an especially pleasing case in point. Modern-dressed, but hardly so you'd notice, it possesses the cardinal virtues of any successful Shakespeare: Its actors speak the lines as if they mean something and as if they have an immediate connection to what the speaker before them has just said. You'd be surprised how many Shakespeare productions fail the test of basic conversational lucidity, and in doing so fail to tell the play's story. This one gets it right from the very beginning, with Alexander Plouffe's Orlando lamenting his plight as persecuted youngest son with exceptional point and gusto. It carries over into his confrontation with bad brother Oliver, played with silky venom by James Graham. Their physical confrontation, which Orlando naturally wins, is practically a dress rehearsal for the professional wrestling bout in the next scene (a good and detailed one, incidentally).

Both brothers fulfil their promise in the remainder of the play. Graham is as full-blooded in his repentance as in his villainy (it's probably a compliment to him that the two stages seem more than usually incompatible), while Plouffe finds the folly, the passion and the residual good sense in the lovesick Orlando, alternately comforted and tormented by having to make pretend-love to the supposed young man whom he has to call his Rosalind and who actually is. Amy Rutherford is a heroine of wit and charm, with a keen sense of her situation's ironies, ambiguities and heartaches, both suffered and inflicted. If she never takes full command of the play as great Rosalinds do, this may be partly due to the cuts inflicted on her role in the cause of getting the running-time down to the park's statutory 90 minutes. "Men have died from time to time, and worms have eaten them, but not for love"; a Rosalind who doesn't get to say that is operating under a heavy handicap. When Rutherford does get to take possession of an extended speech - the play's epilogue, in fact - she comes through very nicely.

The outstanding female performance, though, is given in a role written as male: the misanthropic Jaques, played by Jan Alexandra Smith as an acerbic bluestocking. Gender-changing can play havoc with a play's relationships, but in this case, Jaques having no relationships to speak of, it hardly matters. Smith is in fact the prime example of paying attention to what others are saying and taking off from it; her "all the world's a stage" is not a set-piece but an appreciative response to the Duke's preceding remark about a "universal theatre." Acting this intelligent is heartwarming in itself (though

the casting does make it seem odd that Jaques' "seven ages of man" are indeed all about Man, with Woman unrepresented). Smith could be one of our major Shakespearean actresses, a possible fine Rosalind herself, or better yet a Beatrice. Among what Jaques calls the country copulatives, Gwenlyn Cumyn makes an arrestingly caustic Phebe and Omar Alex Khan a Silvius whose lovesickness is both silly and touching; he doubles as usurping Duke Frederick and gets away with it.

Keira Loughran's Titus production has fewer acting treats and less sensitivity to text, but a more distinct visual identity, the play's ancient Rome being decked out as legendary Japan. This really neither helps nor hinders; stylizing the play's horrors, with red ribbons

denoting bloodshed, guards against unwelcome laughs; having the army of the Goths crawl on hands and knees toward Rome made me think of Napoleon's army marching on its stomach, though Nap only meant it as a metaphor. The action is distanced too much to be really affecting.

I can never think of the title character, the stoic Roman general whose family is decimated by war and intrigue, without remembering Ken Tynan channelling Lady Bracknell: "To lose one son may be accounted a misfortune; to lose twenty-four, as Titus does, looks like carelessness." Sean Dixon's finest moment in the role is the one where words almost fail him; "When will this fearful slumber have an end?" he asks in hushed tones, and in vain since his nightmare continues. He doesn't exactly plumb its

depths, but he does suggest the crazed logic of the man, if not his crazed humour. Comedy, to judge from his Touchstone in As You Like It, is not his strongest suit.

The laughs, and the human interest, go as usual to Aaron the happily psychopathic Moor, Beau Dixon's performance being both gleeful and, when he defends his black baby's life against the sons of his white mistress the Empress, rather moving, at least as moving goes in this play. His rhythmic delivery of his first speech had the first-night audience clapping along, past the point where he probably wished they would stop, and where I certainly did. (By the way, though the play is hardly toddler-appropriate, there were several present). It's a shame that Aaron's last defiance, repenting any good deed he might inadvertently have done, has been brought forward from its proper position at the end of the play, robbing both him and us of the limelight he deserves.

The brothers Plouffe and Graham play another fraternal pair, the former as one of the more agreeable characters (and hence one of the first to perish), the latter as a prototypical Roman emperor, writhingly degenerate. Of the two major survivors, Emilio Vieira has spark as the Andronicus son who gets to pick up the pieces; Jan Alexandra Smith again plays a male-written role, and again very well. This time it's Marcus, now Marcas, Titus's brother who comes upon his niece in the woods, after she's been raped and mutilated, and makes a long speech at her: one that at first seems impossibly artificial and then, by sticking to its own terms, becomes very affecting. It's the play's own way of keeping atrocity at a distance and thereby making it horribly real.

As You Like It and Titus Andronicus alternate through to Aug. 30 and 31 at the High Park Amphitheatre.

Da Vid Hou / Nigel Shawn Williams' As You Like It possesses the cardinal virtues of any successful Shakespeare: Its actors speak the lines as if they mean something and as if they have an immediate connection to what the speaker before them has just said.
2014-07-16-theatrebooks-last-bow-online-:
Friday July 18. A sad day for Toronto book lovers, and for theatre lovers both within and without the city. It's the day of the closure of TheatreBooks, after 39 years of much-loved existence. Its the place where both residents and visitors went to find scripts of plays, and books, both learned and popular, about drama, opera, dance and film. Leonard McHardy and John Harvey, the two men who founded it back in 1975, have run it for the whole of its lifespan.

TheatreBooks loss is, of course, part of a general winnowing of specialist and independent bookshops: victims not, as they might once have feared, of the big-box stores who have never attempted to duplicate their particular inventories, but of the online world, where you can get everything and get it cheap. Never mind that browsing on a screen can never compare, for pleasure or surprise, with browsing actual shelves: we're all complicit. When the news of Theatre-Books' closure broke, one of Torontos best young actresses tweeted that she felt both sorry and guilty; she regretted that she hadnt been in more, but she had been unable to resist the lure of the mouse. Possible customers would ask McHardy if he could pricematch Amazon; he had to confess, emphatically, "No, we can't."

Michael Healey, actor and playwright, told McHardy, You have every right to be bitter and angry. McHardy says, "I don't want to be bitter" and indeed he doesnt sound as if he is.

He does, obviously, feel sad. He had originally wanted to work in the theatre himself, as a director; he had spent a year in England on a British Council grant, working in a regional theatre. Returning home, I couldnt find a place in the Toronto theatre; Canadian theatrical nationalism was at its height and "everyone was doing plays by David French or David Freeman."

Around then he met Harvey (his partner in life as well as in business) and we said, 'We' ll open a bookstore.

John built the shelves himself. I helped him. They were in virtually unexplored territory, but one for which there proved to be a need. "Being a niche market", says McHardy, protected us for quite a time. People just couldnt find books on theatre elsewhere. They certainly couldnt, when TheatreBooks started, find books on Canadian theatre, because hardly any existed. It's a market that grew along with the store itself. "Now there must be 40 to 50 textbooks on Canadian theatre."

Their first location was at Yonge and Charles, where there were about seven other independent booksellers around us. About the time they opened, two British theatrical knights, John Gielgud and Ralph Richardson, were appearing at the Royal Alex in Harold Pinter's No Mans Land. "Gielgud," says Mc-Hardy, saw the store, came upstairs, carrying a Persian cigarette case. I think he rather fancied John, my partner.

Gielgud had written books, which they had in stock, and they asked him if hed sign them. "We asked him if he'd sign one of his own early books. He said, 'Id do anything for you. " (McHardy does a very good Gielgud impersonation.) And thus began a tradition, TheatreBooks became the preferred venue for book-signings and any other promotional events connected with the performing arts.

Yonge and Charles was the first of four locations in the store's lifetime. Its last resting place has been downtown, at Spadina and Adelaide, but the longest-serving address, 20 years, was on St. Thomas, just south of Bloor.

Wherever it's been, TheatreBooks has had the reputation of being the place where you could expect to run into friends and colleagues. One thinks of it as the preserve of professionals and fans, but its also performed an important educational role. Teachers have brought students there; aspiring actors have gone there to locate plays theyve heard about but never read or to find material for auditions. It's always been a very friendly place.

Harvey, a former teacher himself, says that that is what he will miss: Young people coming up to me and saying 'I nailed that audition with the monologue you suggested  - a monologue that staff may have devoted a couple of hours to helping them find. "Weve had wonderful young people working in the store. Neither Leonard nor I have drama degrees, and we've learned so much from them."

Harvey adds: "People looking elsewhere for books they couldn't find would say, Well, theres always TheatreBooks.' Well, guess what; there isn't TheatreBooks any more."
2014-07-19-oceans-of-emotion-a-masterful:
Edward Bond's The Sea is a great play up until its final scene. First staged in London in 1973, and more frequently revived than any of its author's other works, it's set in a British coastal village a few years before the First World War. It starts with a storm and a drowning; a young man, sailing home to get married, perishes, while his surviving friend and companion pleads in vain for help from the coast guard on duty, a man named Hatch who has his mind on other things.

More precisely, he has his own take on the situation. He's convinced that the world is being taken over by hostile forces from outer space (he seems, as fantasists go, to be ahead of his time) and that the drowned man is one of them in disguise. His paranoia, which reaches impressively hysterical heights, may partly be a reaction to the humiliations he suffers in his day job as a draper.

His principal oppressor is a Mrs. Rafi, the richest woman in town, a town she rules with an iron fist that she barely bothers to conceal in a velvet glove. Her habit of returning goods that fail to meet her standards has already driven Hatch to the twin verges of desperation and bankruptcy; she pushes him right over by refusing to accept an especially grand set of blue velvet curtains. His response is to pick up a pair of shears and start maniacally cutting them up into the ordered lengths. Even his own friends and employees - young men who have bought into his extraterrestrial theories - are appalled.

Mrs. Rafi represents privilege, and Hatch shows what privilege can do to those who don't have it. That's one way of looking at it, and one that Bond the ideologue would probably endorse. Bond the playwright might see it differently, or at least more sympathetically. For him they could be two dynamic people, trapped in a constricting society.

They are certainly both major creations, and in the Shaw Festival's production they get major performances. Patrick Galligan, having taken a huge leap forward in this season's When We Are Married, takes a further one as Hatch, eaten up with passion misdirected and misshapen, defiant even when cringing. Not being required to play the gentleman has released something in him; he's revealed as an active actor too often cast in passive roles.

For Fiona Reid, Mrs. Rafi is less of a stretch; she may actually overdo the imperiousness of this particular society dragon. But she's unbeatable when it comes to the high comedy of the role, especially when putting the more subservient ladies of her circle through a rehearsal of their annual dramatic pageant, in aid of (naturally) the lifeboat fund. Her particular butt is her paid companion (Patty Jamieson, timidly resentful and, in one extended sequence, hilariously musical) whom she deathlessly instructs to "stop trying to sound like a woman with an interesting past." Even better, one of the great speeches in modern drama flawlessly realized, her vision of her future self as an old woman in a wheelchair on whom her previous victims will be able to take what she admits to be a justified revenge.

The chatelaine, the draper and the play all reach their peaks in a brilliantly grotesque funeral scene (Neil Barclay a very funny vicar) in which the drowned man's ashes end up scattered in unexpected places. This is the play's climax, but not its finale. That is given over to a moralistic discussion between three characters of whom we know very little.

One of them, given a pleasingly positive performance by Wade Bogert-O'Brien, is an outsider, the dead man's friend and entitled to be mysterious. Another, the bereaved fiancee, is a shadowy figure whom Julia Course cannot bring to life. The third is a beachcombing recluse who speaks for the author in deploring the state of the world of which this community is a microcosm; Peter Millard gives him lucidity but not the prophetic fervour that he needs. He, like Mrs. Rafi earlier, advises the two high-born young people to go off together, which they do: a surprisingly traditional comedy ending, though perhaps appropriate in a play whose verdict on society's view of tragedy that "they'll make a law against it." Tragedy or comedy or something between, this is a play that operates, in scope and language, on a near-Shakespearean level. Eda Holmes' production, with its impressionistic evocations of sea and storm, certainly makes the case.

Tennessee Williams' late one-act A Lovely Sunday for Creve Coeur, is wonderful: the Shaw's best lunch time show since The President. It has the same director, Blair Williams, who again mines every moment for its full potential, while never slackening pace or losing balance.

In The President the mode was satirical farce; here it's tragi-farce. Dorothea, a fading southern belle, now a teacher, waits one Sunday morning for a phone call from the principal with whom she's had a fling and on whom she counts to take her away from all this. Meantime she does her exercises, and spars with her roommate Bodey, who wants Dorothea to marry her beer-swilling brother (Bodey`s family is of Germanic descent) and has planned a seaside outing to that end.

Dorothea is Blanche DuBois, transferred from New Orleans to the playwright's own St. Louis, with a mere third of Blanche's playing-time, which may well be preferable. Blanche too was a teacher, and this play has much talk of streetcars, which this time also fulfil a vital plot-function.

As Dorothea, Deborah Hay is miraculous, combining boldness of gesture (her ladylike keep-fit routine is a hoot) with delicacy of feeling; Kate Hennig brings the same qualities, in a gruffer key, to Bodey, both protective and scheming. Kaylee Harwood is effective, if too emphatically unpleasant, as a genteel visitor who arrives to burst everybod's bubble, to and of whom Bodey tartly remarks "you can't catch heartbreak if you don`t have a heart to break." Heartbreak is what Creve Coeur means; it's also the beach resort at which Bodey hopes questions will be popped. The play's living embodiment of heartbreak is the lady upstairs, a non-English speaker who has lost her mother, and over whom Julain Molnar makes us both laugh and cry ourselves. At the end Dorothea, acknowledging their kinship, tells her, "Tears are a release - but they enflame your eyes." You have to agree, though for the audience many of the tears are of delight.

The Sea is in repertory through October 12, A Lovely Sunday for Creve Coeur through October 11, both at the Court House Theatre, Niagara-on-the-Lake \

David Cooper / Shaw's production of Edward Bond's The Sea makes the case for the play as a major work.
2014-07-26-the-plotted-besotted-love-sav:
A lady and a gentleman are making love to one another in the drawing room." That is the opening stage direction of The Philanderer, Bernard Shaws second play, written in 1893. Given the date and the author, not to mention the location, its unlikely that "making love here means having sex"; but of course you never know. Lisa Peterson, an American director making her Canadian debut at the Shaw Festival, doesn't physically show us the lady and gentleman at it, but before the lights go up she lets us hear enough heavy breathing and rapturous moaning to make the libidinous point.

Even without this, we would probably not think that the emotional relationships in the play were platonic. Or maybe we would. The text contains no explicit sexual references, and though this may be partly due to the theatrical constraints of the time (Shaw's next play, Mrs. Warrens Profession, deals with prostitution without ever using the word) it probably points to something in the writer himself. His characters, certainly in this play, talk a lot about love, but give the impression that they would rather talk about it than do it. Still, they are supposed to be physical beings; and if Petersons mostly bold and imaginative production is untrue to the letter of the text, it's faithful to what one hopes is its underlying spirit. Or if not faithful, then certainly more interesting.

The play itself is much concerned with the virtues and limitations of fidelity. Its title character, the gent exerting himself in the drawing room, is Leonard Charteris, who is something of a Shavian self-portrait, though a satirical one: probably not the late sexual starter that Shaw himself was (though GBS does seem to have gone through an energetic phase of making up for lost time) but, like his author, a self-consciously liberated man who won't shut up about it. To the plays credit, it can endorse Charteris views, especially on marriage (constricting) and divorce (should be easier), while exposing his self-centredness; which is why Shaw was a dramatist, not a pamphleteer. His partner at curtain-rise is Grace Tranfield, a young widow, who shares her lover's views but not his egotism. Their idyll is interrupted by Julia Craven, an old flame of Charteris' who has no intention of being extinguished.

Julia wont let her ex-lover go, refuses indeed to believe that he really wants to be ex. Shes an emotional stalker and, as her first entrance demonstrates, a physical one as well. She throws fits, threatens suicide, drives people out of the room or into her arms; the latter tends to be Charteris' reaction, and whether it's primarily due to passion, compassion, or simple self-defence is unknowable, probably even to him. In the plays last festival outing, Julia was played as if she knew she was being outrageous and took a humorous delight in it. That was a mistake; Julia is the rare Shaw character who doesnt

have a sense of humour, even a sense of irony. Moya O'Connell, this time around, plays her with uncompromising masochistic passion, never once letting up. It's a dark, fearless performance, maybe her best. Gord Rand gives a louche compelling account of Charteris, only marred by the moments when the production, getting too high on its own concept, has him delivering key lines directly to the audience, as if to impress us with how relevant they are. (Honestly, wed notice anyway.) As the third and most level-headed member of the transient triangle, Marla McLean is charmingly cool.

Charteris, Grace and Julia are all members of something called the Ibsen Club, a haven for advanced thinkers or, as the clubs own promo material has it, for "unmanly men and unwomanly women." (Julia got in by having her nominators perjure themselves.) Shaw himself admitted, some 30 years later, that this aspect of the play was dated. What he didn't acknowledge was that it never had much point to begin with. The play's whole long middle section is set in the club, but it has hardly anything to say about the great Norwegian, except to treat him, lazily, as a standin for progressive thought in general. In fact, Ibsen was a congenital contrarian who, if I may plagiarize a line from my review of the Shaws 2007 production, would never have joined any club that would have him as a mentor. The characters here are swimming in some pretty shallow waters. Julias younger sister, a defiantly unwomanly woman sportingly and sportily played by Harveen Sandhu, is a member of the club; so, claiming that they're there to protect their daughters, are Julia's and Graces fathers, given enjoyably fruity performances by Michael Ball and Ric Reid. Both dads are proudly old-fashioned: Graces is a theatre critic (enough said); Julia's is a military man, resigning himself to an early death as a result of a liver complaint discovered by a young Dr. Paramore, who has named it after himself. Actually nearly everybody in the play might be said to suffer from some kind of paramour's disease, not least the doctor himself, whos besotted with Julia and is trying to nerve himself to propose to her, greatly encouraged by Charteris who sees this as his way out.

And this is where things, both in writing and production, get fascinating. In the plays official last act, Paramore does propose and is accepted, though Julia plainly doesn't love him. This act, though, was a replacement for the one Shaw originally wrote, and which no one at the time would accept. His original version took a time-jump, hurling us four bitterly disillusioned years into Paramore's and Julias marriage. This production restores that scene in place of the published one, and the change is electric. For one thing it enables Jeff Meadows Paramore to emerge as a feeling, rounded human being, rather than the amiable goof he has played in previous scenes. (His disease turned out to be a total bust, much to the disgust of Colonel Craven who had turned vegetarian when he thought he had it.) Indeed, everybody develops depths, most of them sombre, even the philandering Charteris himself, though he kicks against it. The entire scene feels more modern, not only than the play that's preceded it, but than practically anything else its author wrote. It certainly feels more sexual, even if the sex has gone sour. Here, too, Peterson's direction shows its hand. Sue LePage has designed two handsome, detailed interiors for the earlier scenes; this one she sets in what seem to be the ruins of a once-classical landscape. The characters, trying to escape an intolerable situation, are cast adrift from whatever certainties they may have had. Only the ending fails to convince. It seems intended to echo, or pre-echo, the union of Jack Tanner and Ann Whitefield at the end of Man and Superman. That ending, though is a believably happy one; Jack and Ann do seem made for one another, united in wit. You couldnt say the same about the corresponding couple in this play. The production, though, seems to be trying to.

The Philanderer is in repertory through October 12 at the Festival Theatre, Niagara-on-the-Lake
