Welcome to Gracepoint, Americas Last Hometown. That's how it announces itself to any visitors who care to read its billboards. Its main industry is whale-watching. Or rather, it's catering to the tourists who come to watch the whales. However, when we visit the place, its being roiled, and its reputation soiled, by what we are told is its first-ever murder case.

Gracepoint is the title, and the setting, of a new 10-part thriller serial on Fox. It has has a British twin. Or, to be less fancy about it, the show is an American re-make of the British series Broadchurch; Gracepoint has even imported Broadchurchs star, David Tennant, who repeats his role as a wild-eyed, control-freakish cop parachuted into the top detective job in this sheltered community after having mysteriously fouled up in a larger one. His English character name was Alec Hardy, which sounds almost too British detective-story to be true. His U.S. equivalent is called Emmett Carver; Emmett doesn't like his name, but then he doesn't like many things. Or many people, especially the ones hes thrown among in Gracepoint. Tennant, with his hair spilling defiantly over his eyes, plays him very well, and his accent is impeccable, at least as far as I could tell through the angry dismissive growl in which he delivers most of his lines.

Even better is Anna Gunn as Detective Annie Miller. Shes Emmett's professional partner, and neither of them enjoys the partnership. In fact, when the show starts, Anna has just come back from vacation to find that she's expected to work with the man who has taken job shed been promised. Professional resentment, however, has to go on the back-burner when, mere minutes after the opening credits, the body of a dead 12-year-old boy is discovered on the beach. The boy is the best friend of Ellies own son, and she herself is on close terms with his parents.

In fact, it seems that everybody in Gracepoint knows everybody else. And yet it's also big enough to support its own newspaper, the Gracepoint Journal, whose mission statement, dripping with retrospective irony, is "Celebrating the Everyday." It's like the Simpsons Springfield, which can transform from village to metropolis according to the needs of a particular episode.

Its also like Springfield in that everybody in it goes to church. The minister, though, is more like the priest in The Sopranos, being fairly young and twitchy, and with an obvious crush on a married parishioner, in this case the bereaved mother. He may have some more sinister secrets as well; the show certainly works overtime to make us think so. But then, of course, it has the whodunnit's vested interest in making everybody a suspect. The first episode begins with the still-unknowing father of the dead boy walking through town, greeting and being greeted by what turns out to be most of the cast.

At its primary level, the show works. I've viewed seven of the episodes and I really want to know what happens in the remaining three. (Never having seen Broadchurch, Im unspoiled.) But, given how susceptible we all are to suspense, that may not be setting the bar very high. Gracepoint hardly misses a manipulative trick. The background music is incessant, and there are more slow-motion sequences than I have seen in any other show. (Maybe the slow-mo is intended to drive home the point that Gracepoint is a sleepy town. No, probably not.).

Once again the gulf yawns wide between drama on cable and drama on the networks, even in police procedurals. Or especially in police procedurals. I wasnt a great fan of True Detective, which seemed far too enamoured of its own obscurity; still, one recognized, even while trying to make out what Matthew McConaughey was talking about, the presence of a certain depth and texture. Gracepoint seems to have ambitions in that direction - with the death of a child as its starting point, it can hardly afford not to have - and it has Tennant as the obligatory corroded cop. But the writing is very run-of-the-mill.

Maybe the British version was better; at eight episodes instead of 10 it was presumably tighter. Still, Chris Chibnall, who wrote Broadchurch, is also an executive producer on Gracepoint (and wrote the pilot), so it's presumably much the same animal. Nick Nolte turns impressively up as the town loner, the grizzled runner of an informal wildlife observation society for the town's youth; there should be sign over his shoreline shack reading Acting Done Here. He also has the shows best single line; interrogated by Tennant as to his whereabouts on the night of the crime (hes all too natural a suspect) he says that he was home reading: "Infinite Jest - you might not like it; hardly any pictures."

The acting in general is unspectacularly good, in the baseline way of most TV. Virginia Kull and Michael Pena build a believable agonized relationship as the bereaved parents, though pseudo-profound lines like "you learn to live with pain" don't do Kull any favours. I also lost count of the number of occasions on which people threatened to punish other people in unspecified ways that they would never forget. One who escapes unthreatened, though she certainly doesn't deserve to, is a lady journalist, who descends on Gracepoint from the big city, seduces (physically and otherwise) an impressive young local reporter and twists everything anybody tells her, with dire results; she also seems to have the goods on Tennant though, even seven hours in, I still dont know what they are. The smug unpleasantness of her character is obviously intended - theres an echo, given the show's origins, of the scandals over Britain's tabloids - but it's surprisingly dull to watch. Here, as in other ways, the show is in over its head.

Gracepoints airs Thursdays at 9 p.m. on Global.

David Tennant
2014-10-02-brothers-in-harms-tarragon-el:
Theat rereview

An Enemy of the People Tarragon Theatre, Toronto

I bsen scholars have generally ranked An Enemy of the People fairly low in their man's canon, maybe because of its spirited straightforwardness. That same quality, though, always makes it thrilling in the theatre: in the case of the new production at the Tarragon, immensely so.

Calling it new may be a stretch. It's a re-staging, by Tarragon's artistic director Richard Rose, of a production by the German director Thomas Ostermeier, one that he saw and admired at the Schaubuhne theatre in Berlin and that has since toured the world, though not as far as Canada. Rose's version reproduces the German design and staging, and he has had Maria Milisavljevic translate what was already Florian Borchmeyer's updated adaptation of the original. (Yes, we have an English translation of a German adaptation of a Norwegian play.) But of course Rose had to cast and direct the Canadian actors himself, and the results are superb.

It's surprising that Ibsen's play didn't get a rash of Canadian productions around the time of Walkerton. It could be even more topical now in a world where politicians at various levels discourage scientists and tells doctors to stick to their stethoscopes. The doctor here is Thomas Stockmann, consultant for the medicinal baths of a town that owes its new prosperity to the tourists who come to take its waters. He discovers that those waters are polluted by industrial waste, that they will cause disease rather than cure it, and that the whole system will have to be closed down and rebuilt, a process that will take a couple of years. He has the initial support of the local paper, which likes to think of itself as progressive, and of what the paper's proprietor calls, in the traditional translations, "the solid compact majority." He loses it when it's pointed out how much his proposals will cost. His principal opponent is his own brother Peter, identified in most versions as the Mayor, but in this one as just a member of the council. But he's also chairman of the baths; and when the doctor calls a public meeting to present his case, Peter stage-manages the proceedings so that they end with his brother being physically driven from the hall, denounced as "an enemy of the people."

All of that is still there in the new version. The scene, too, remains Norway; at least, no other place is mentioned and no characters' names have been changed. Some have been removed; sea-captain Horster, the only man in town to stand by Thomas and his family from first to last, has been eliminated. So has the doctor's similarly steadfast daughter, whose vestigial relationship with the newspaper's editor has now been transferred to her mother, by way of a few lines of dialogue that add nothing and go

nowhere. The Stockmanns' two school-age sons have also gone, replaced by a baby. The net result of all this is to make the doctor and what remains of his family more vulnerable. In the original, after briefly thinking of emigration, Thomas resolves to stay in town, home-school his boys, and preach his gospel of independence to however many of the uncorrupted will listen to him. This production ends with him and his wife, stripped of jobs and prospects and (a new touch) threatened with jail time, reeling against the wall.

That wall is none too solid. The set consists of chalkboards, decorated with drawings and slogans, telling us where we are, what time has elapsed, and what's on the characters' minds. When Thomas tells his brother just what bacterial demons are being unleashed, the words "e coli" take their place among the writings on the wall. The doctor's house is also the rehearsal space for an indie band consisting of him and his wife, Hovstad the editor, and a wannabe firebrand of a journalist named Billing who goes on singing and playing even when everybody else has had the decency to stop. ("Never have a couple in your band" says Billing, when the lady of the group goes off to attend to her infant: a line whose equivalent you would be hard-pressed to find in Ibsen.) Actors move the furniture around to transport the scene to the newspaper office.

In this production, the doctor holds his meeting in a theatre, represented of course by the theatre we're actually in. The houselights are turned on, and audience members are encouraged to participate. The night I went, most of us were too shy to contribute, and the vital questions were asked by people I took to be plants, who would be necessary anyway to keep the show on track and to give the actors their cues. Which is why I think this kind of theatre, though it can undoubtedly be exciting, is fundamentally dishonest; the performers have rehearsed, the spectators haven't, so it isn't an equal contest.

Forbidden, by bullying masquerading as democracy, to talk about the baths, Thomas instead takes aim at a bigger target: public ignorance, venality and stupidity. In this adaptation he does so by spouting an anarchist manifesto that on my visit escaped totally unheckled, possibly because its language is impenetrable. But he does in the end come back to Ibsen's original text, which is that the majority is always wrong. The majority then proves him right by physically and verbally assaulting him. Not that any of us actually in the Tarragon would have laid a finger on him, proving again the limits of audience participation.

Thomas, you may feel, has lost the plot; or at least enlarged it beyond recognition. But he was goaded into it. Ibsen, still smarting from the hostility directed at his previous play Ghosts, said that Thomas was like himself, only nicer; and he's usually played as an overgrown teddybear.

Joe Cobden, younger and slimmer than the norm, makes him more an overgrown student, still hanging with the other kids (hence the band); he's led a sheltered scientific life and, while his conclusions are unimpeachable, he's ill-equipped to confront or comprehend those who oppose them. Frustration leads him to hysteria, which seems to be a family trait. The revelation of this production has little to do with water-supplies or even cover-ups; it's that this is one of the great plays about siblingrivalry. Rick Roberts' Peter is a consummate portrayal of a politician, one with a skin as thin as his brother's but cunning enough not to expose it in public. (And he can think on his feet. At the performance I saw, he ad libbed a splendidly selfdeprecating response to an audience member's allegation that he was white and male.)

As the turncoats of the press Matthew Edison, Tom Barnett and Brandon McGibbon (painfully funny as the weathervane Billing) make a trenchant trio, while Richard McMillan oozes resentful malevolence as the doctor's factory-owning fatherin-law, the prime polluter on every level and the ultimate challenge to Thomas's integrity. All these performances are richly individualized while fitting perfectly into the frame. That it's a borrowed frame makes the achievement all the more remarkable. Anyone can have a concept; what counts is the execution, and this production executes in spades.

National Post robert.cushman@hotmail.com

An Enemy of the People plays until Oct. 26. For more information, tarragontheatre.com.

His primary opponent in making this happen is his brother, Peter, usually represented as a mayor, in this production a city councillor.

Clytemnestra is doing her ironing, patiently by the look of it. There's a knock at the door, and she admits an earnest young man who would like to interview her. He turns out to be a theatre director who wants to tell her story yet again, this time from her point of view. He thinks she's got a raw deal from previous playwrights. Surprisingly, she doesn't altogether agree.

So begins Bloody Family, a theatrical meditation on the roots of Western drama and indeed of Western civilization. Clytemnestra is the only character to appear in all three parts of Aeschylus' Oresteia, the one Greek tragic trilogy to have survived in complete form. In the first play she murders her husband Agamemnon; in the second she herself is killed by her avenging son Orestes; in the third she's a ghost, blaming the Furies for falling down on the job of tormenting her tormentor. The apparently endless chain of human and superhuman vengeance is only broken when the gods step in and establish the first ever courts of law. (Orestes gets off, with an Olympian caution.)

The story has been re-told and re-interpreted by countless other playwrights, beginning with Aeschylus' own near-contemporaries. In Bloody Family, we get to hear a scene from a play by Euripides, Iphigenia in Aulis (in, as it happens, a free translation by a couple of British guys who had their own agenda). It tells how, on the eve of the Trojan war, Agamemnon sacrificed his daughter Iphigenia to the gods, so that the winds might blow and allow his ships to sail to Troy. Clytemnestra never forgave him for allowing their daughter to be killed. According to Bloody Family, which simplifies the issues a bit, this was her main motive for killing her husband.

The show doesn't list a director, but it was "created" by Philip McKee and Tanja Jacobs. Jacobs plays Clytemnestra, and is wondrously enigmatic. Emotions pour out of her, and yet she maintains an outward serenity. (Ironing boards will do that to you; cf. Look Back in Anger). Answering her visitor's questions, or reading the Euripides scene with the actress slated to play her daughter, she gives full vent to the mother's terror and anger. And yet, when asked whether her husband's conduct was justified, she calmly replies that of course it was. There was a war on. And, by the way, she doesn't believe in art as an instrument of social change. And she doesn't like the theatre, because it isn't real.

McKee, a director by trade, here plays the director, and brings off a very entertaining piece of what I take to be selfsatire: an eager-beaver theorist, proudly brandishing his iPhone, and taken aback when his enterprising research project fails to yield the results he expected. We then shift into a different mode, one favoured by French dramatists of the last century; a situation from Greek myth is re-imagined in disarmingly domestic terms. Orestes, following a trail of bloodstains on the floor, comes home to kill his mother; she asks him to stay for a few days in hopes he'll change his mind. He can have his old room. The loving look she bestows on him while he's sleeping is a peak moment. She makes him sandwiches; he makes her a coffin. He doesn't like the theatre either, which surprises her given that he acts so dramatic. In the end, the story takes its predestined course.

We switch modes again. Director McKee calls his Orestes (Ishan Dave) in for a special rehearsal, despite the fact that said actor is feeling awful. We're at the last part of the Oresteia; Orestes has to be worked into an extreme state of mind and body befitting a victim of the furies whose fate can only be determined by the invention of democratic justice. The director subjects him to rigorous exercises ("do pushups during this speech ... I'll do them with you") and we laugh at the pretentiousness of it all; we also sympathize when the actress who read Iphigenia (Norah Sadava) arrives in a state of high indignation to rescue her colleague. And yet ... it does seem to work. When Orestes says "pain has taught me the wisdom of rituals," we believe him.

Bloody Family is partly the latest re-telling of an old story, and partly a commentary on current theatrical practice. Both aspects are fascinating, but they don't often mesh. When they do, though, the stage resonates; the justification for re-living the old saga of endless retribution is "these things don't stop happening." The project was partly prompted, in 2011, by a radio program about Afghanistan. It almost feels like a simpler time.

Life, Death and the Blues might well be an alternate title for Bloody Family (and for many other plays as well). In fact it belongs to an autobiographical show by Raoul Bhaneja, actor, writer and - we now learn - musician. It too is a piece with a double identity; the publicity calls it a "concert/theatre hybrid" and the concert part is much the better - great, in fact. The theatre, or drama, section begins enjoyably with Bhaneja in shades, as a composite of every gutturaltalking bluesman that was ever cartooned. He then tells us that that's quite enough of stereotypes and proceeds to tell us his own story: that of a part-Indian, part-Irish, North-of-England -born Canadian, who grew up with a passion for the blues but initially felt abashed about singing and playing them.

Quite why is never really clear, though he's given an on-stage antagonist in Divine Brown, a fine lady singer who tells him that he'll never sing the blues until he gets in touch with his "roots." This strikes me as malarkey, especially given how tangled his roots actually are. He does, with her prompting, sing a traditional tune from India, and he does it beautifully, but no more so than when he's singing black American music. He pays tribute to blues musicians who have helped or influenced him, though his historical memory seems to be short-term. (How do you chronicle blues singers without mentioning Bessie Smith? And was T-Bone Walker the first to blend blues and jazz? Would have been news to Louis Armstrong.)

Eda Holmes directs, and has staged the material better than she's shaped it. Projection design, by Cameron Davis, is excellent. But in the end, it's all about the music. The divine Divine enchants the joint, especially when singing gospel. Bhaneja is a commanding singer, and a demon of a harmonica-player. A terrific three-man band backs him up, and there's a guest musician winding up every show. On the first night, it was Chris Whiteley, whose guitarplaying could get you high.

Bloody Family runs through October 5 at the Theatre Centre; Life, Death and the Blues runs through October 19 at Theatre Passe Muraille
