Theatre Review

Julie Madly Deeply; The Boy with Tape on His Face

Panasonic Theatre, Toronto

Despite its awful title, Julie Madly Deeply is a delightful show. Part tribute, part biography, part impersonation, part affectionate satire, it's about Julie Andrews. But it's also about Sarah-Louise Young, who wrote and performed it, and it's that double focus that keeps it interesting and buoyant.

Young is a British cabaret performer who has mastered the art of being self-assured and selfdeprecating at the same time. She tells us frankly when she first comes on that she isn't Julie Andrews and never could be, thus striking the note that keeps her going throughout: She keeps a distance from her subject but not from us. Andrews is a singer with a - sometimes overlooked - flair for comedy. Young is a comedienne who can sing.

The distancing note has been struck before Young even comes on stage. Michael Roulston, her accompanist and an invaluable partner throughout, has played a brief overture consisting of songs that indeed come from Andrews' two biggest hits, My Fair Lady and The Sound of Music, but that were sung to or about her rather than by her.

When we get into the body of the show, too, Young contents herself with nibbling at the edges of the Andrews repertoire. When she gets to My Fair Lady she neglects the obvious "I Could Have Danced All Night" in favour of the less familiar "Show Me" ("say one more word and I'll scream") which she cleverly uses to illustrate her heroine's supposed impatience with voice teachers and directors. She gives us "Say a Prayer for Me Tonight" which was written for Andrews to sing as Eliza Doolittle off to the ball, but was cut (and later turned up in Gigi). Much later on she sings Stephen Sondheim's acidic "Could I Leave You," which Andrews performed in the anthology Putting It Together, and does it as well as anyone I have heard since Alexis Smith in the original Follies.

Pardon my show-buffery. One thing Young shares with her subject, or persuades us she does, is a very British no-nonsense briskness. She admits that her main strategy for getting inside the skin of her heroine is to wear a Sound of Music flaxen wig. She disparages her own vocal talents, though in fact she sings very well, even if she can't quite soar like Andrews in her prime. She does a very good Liza Minnelli impersonation (Minnelli subbed for Andrews in Victor/Victoria on Broadway), though perhaps not good enough to justify the number of times she repeats it; and the fact that she self-mockingly apologizes for the repetition doesn't make it better. She admits to having a limited repertoire of accents, though that couldn't reconcile me to the borscht-belt voice and delivery she imposes on the sophisticated Moss Hart (doesn't she know his plays?) or to the roughneck tones of her Richard Rodgers. (Oscar Hammerstein, in this rendition, is a silent partner.)

She's especially apologetic about the voice she uses for Julie's stepfather Ted Andrews, who was abusive, exploitative and Canadian. One thing that distinguishes Young from most visiting performers: When she pays compliments to Canada or makes jokes about Toronto, she actually sounds as if she means it. She may even have done some research.

Anyway, my own nostalgia kicks in here; growing up in Britain in the 1950s I used to hear the Andrews family on the BBC, billed as "Ted and Barbara Andrews and Julie." Then, suddenly, it was just "Julie Andrews," mother and stepdad having realized where the voice and the talent and the meal-ticket were.

There was Educating Archie, which had Julie playing straight-girl to a ventriloquist's dummy (on radio) and which I regret to say Young fails to treat with the respect it deserves. Still, her breakneck commentary on the teenage Andrews' rise to fame as if it were a horse-race (Petula Clark coming up on the inside) is irresistible. Then it's Broadway, with My Fair Lady celebrated and Camelot slighted, I think unfairly, even if Young does admit to a crush on Richard Burton; there should have been room for Alan Jay Lerner's tribute to Andrews' fortitude during the wreckage of that show's previews: "makes you wonder how the English ever lost India." Then the movies, of course, and Blake Edwards, and the decline from box-office sovereignty, and the tragic voice operation.

Young, both amused and amusing, keeps it all funny and honest and unsentimental and never gets cheap or manipulative. She doesn't manage to explain or explore - though she sometimes promises to - just why we all adore Julie Andrews, maybe because not all of us do. Some of us just like and admire her. (Others of course hate her, but that isn't reasonable, and isn't part of the present equation.)

At the end of the show Young gives us "Something Good," the song that Rodgers without Hammerstein wrote for the Sound of Music film and that is actually better than most that were carried over from the stage show. She sings it with the same restraint and simplicity as did Andrews himself, and it makes a lovely summation for both of them. They've both done something good.

Julie Madly Deeply, which isn't mad and isn't deep, comes to us direct - well, sort of - from the fringe of the Edinburgh Festival, as does The Boy with Tape on His Face; the two shows were shown to the critics on the same night but are now alternating.

Sam Wills, a New Zealander based in the U.K., is another writerperformer. He's also a mime, and he has masking tape over his mouth lest he should ever yield to the temptation to be anything else. He does some ingenious things with props, and gets props of his own, right off the bat, for consistently failing to perform a simple juggling trick. (Well, simple if you're a juggler. I assume. Actually it must take skill to get it wrong every time.)

But his main foils are his audience, whom he invites on stage in an unending succession and whom he directs by gesticulation. He gives them moves. When they get them wrong, he's scornful; when he gets them right, he's aghast. He communicates these feelings through what may be the most expressive eyeballs in show business. One spectator gets asked up repeatedly and is then summarily dismissed; until the end when he becomes the subject, or maybe that should be object, of an extended routine. The first-night victim exhibited a charming gift for resignation. Indeed, all the dragooned spectators turned out to have great stage personalities, thereby reinforcing my suspicion of performers who rely on the unpaid help to do most of the work. I also don't much like mimes. Nobody else seems to like them much either. And yet there's a public for them. So somebody must be lying.

Julie Madly Deeply and The Boy With Tape on His Face run until Oct. 19. Tickets and more info at mirvish.com.

Mirvish / Julie Andrews is a singer with a flair for comedy. Sarah-Louise Young is a comedienne who can sing.
2014-10-11-one-for-the-funny-second-city:
The new revue Rebel Without a Cosmos is good second-division Second City. That makes it a bit of a letdown after its predecessor Sixteen Scandals, which was very good first division. But let's concentrate on the happy things. These would definitely include Connor Thompson, a holdover from the previous show who, when not heavily disguised, could pass for a solid young leading man in a classical repertory company. A lot of the time, though, he is heavily disguised. The show's best single number finds him as a children's entertainer who, through a confusion of bookings, finds himself engaged at a Remembrance Day ceremony. Called upon to sing about the First World War he comes up with "The First World War was lots of fun /As World Wars go it was Number One," which I guess is incontrovertible, the second part anyway. He gets into deeper water when trying to make the number of casualties the subject of a counting game, while a similarly cheerful approach to the Second World War doesn't go down well at all. He also takes suggestions from the audience, demonstrating an impressive ability to improvise in rhyme. Later on in the show, we get a brief look at his opposite number, the war memorialist performing at a kids' party and scaring the daylights out of them.

Thompson also appears, beneath impenetrable hair, as Pete, who spends his days propping up the outside wall of a gas station in Owen Sound. (Owen Sound is a running gag in this show.) Pete is a kind of walking - well, sprawling - GPS, who can give you instant directions to any place at all, if you can decipher his high-speed mumblings, and can also hand out lifealtering advice, such as telling the young lady who's just hit town to leave it as soon as possible and to ditch the guy what brung her, an insufferable Film Studies major. Pete is a definite fount of wisdom.

Another for the books is Ashley Botting, accepting a Miss Average Canada award, while paying tribute to the 90% of other women in the room who must be equally deserving, as well as to Joe Fresh and Jackson Triggs who made her averageness possible. Botting also has a love song to and about Chris Hadfield, a number not only well-sung but well-written. Indeed musically this show is far above the Second City average.

Ethan Muskat and Kevin Whalen, both new Second Citizens, share a well-pointed sketch about Apple stores and their groundbreaking contributions to built-in obsolescence. (Old-fashioned customer: "I'll have you know I've been using the same razor for 20 years." New-fashioned clerk: "Gross.") The company is completed by Allison Price, tall and thin and generally helpful, though starved of good material. The director is Reid Janisse. The designer is Camellia Koo, whose set pays handsome tribute to the show's inter-galactic title, though not much else does. We're used to Second City naming its revues with inconsequential puns; usually they have some pretence to topicality but maybe this time, in taking a 60-year-old movie as their inspiration, they're going for timelessness.

Talking of titles: The Thing Between Us is the bond between Linda and Shannon who first meet as 10-year-olds, and whom we follow into womanhood. Shannon's father is dead, and her mother has gone away to a spa in Switzerland to recover. Linda's parents are Shannon's godparents, and they take the girl in, thereby providing their own daughter, an only child, with an instant sister. At first Shannon's behaviour suggests that she's been terribly spoiled; later it seems likelier that she was horribly neglected, emotionally at least. She lies, and manipulates, shearing Linda's long and beautiful hair and also taking her sex education in hand by leading her onto the roof to observe, through binoculars, her parents making love. (We never actually meet Linda's dad - he's usually on the road - but it seems that when he's home he makes up for lost time. At any rate Shannon is impressed. Linda, we later learn, is traumatized.)

Alison Lawrence's play sets the girls' relationship up economically and intriguingly but, as Shannon grows from problem child to full-blown sociopath, it can hardly help spinning its wheels. Shannon keeps getting into awful trouble and doing awful things, many of them to Linda; Linda keeps excusing and enabling her, and the main tension for the audience lies in waiting and hoping for the moment when she'll say "enough!" Rooting for her comes easy, as Emily Hurson, though tactfully restrained in Aaron Willis's production from any physical attempt at representing a 10-yearold, gets the young cast of mind and voice perfectly and then shows it growing. Mary Francis Moore, though, acts Shannon backwards; she sounds like an adult from the start, so there's no disturbing tension between how we'd expect a child to behave and how this one actually does. Randi Helmers does her best with Linda's mother whose continuing indulgence of Shannon may be even greater than Linda's own, and is certainly more inexplicable; well, an explanation is offered but it's late and unconvincing. She's also the occasion of Linda's final disillusion, in a scene that is certainly harrowing but is also crude and manipulative. At the end Linda learns that there was apparently more to Shannon than she had ever known. The news comes rather late for her to process, and altogether too late for us.

Rebel Without a Cosmos runs indefinitely at Second City; The Thing Between Us runs at Theatre Passe Muraille Backspace through Oct. 19.

Racheal McCaig / Connor Thompson (face covered, but a highlight of the production), Allison Price, Kevin Whalen, Ashley Botting, Etan Muskat in Second City's Rebel Without a Cosmos - a good second-division Second City.
2014-10-18-at-death-s-troubadour-what-ma:
It seems that hardly a show can open in Toronto that isn't a tribute to some troubadour or other. In the past few weeks weve had Sarah-Louise Young celebrating Julie Andrews and Raoul Bhaneja celebrating Raoul Bhaneja. Now comes What Makes a Man, in which two male and two female performers parcel out the words and music of Charles Aznavour.

Lets start at the end. The last thing we see and hear in this Necessary Angel production is the pivotal member of the foursome, Kenny Brawner, thoughtfully reciting the opening words of Tomorrow Is My Turn," an exceptionally buoyant and hopeful Aznavour tune that was memorably recorded by Nina Simone. We wait expectantly for him to get to the meat of the song; by this point of the evening we could use the lift. But no, the intro is all we're given; from there, we go straight to the curtain-call. It's typical of a show that seems fanatically dedicated to denying its audience a good time.

The idea seemed promising enough. If Jacques Brel can have a show, then Aznavour, a somewhat more inventive composer and a far less pretentious lyricist, certainly deserves one. The overture, too, is inviting; a six-piece jazzblues band, stationed by the

side of the acting area, makes an invigorating introductory noise that may not be quite what one expects in a chansonnier context but is probably none the worse for that.

Brawner then appears, announced by the MD as if we were in a nightclub (nobody else in the cast gets that kind of build-up), sits at an onstage piano, and goes into one of Aznavours best-known songs, "Yesterday When I Was Young. It seems a reasonable beginning, contemplative and retrospective; and if your mind runs that way (mine does) you may notice how Herbert Kretzmers portentously melodramatic English lyric anticipates his later work on Les Miserables. You may, though, have to struggle to make the connection, since this is the downstairs Berkeley Street Theatre, a venue whose acoustics have muffled many a play and are plain murder for a musical, however multifarious the mikes.

What Makes a Man is a cabaret. That's fine; so were Ain't Misbehavin and Side by Side by Sondheim, and they worked in the theatre. But I doubt if they would have worked in this theatre, certainly not on a set made up of blue-draped steps and backed by the spaces brick walls, the latter being a feature of which directors seem inexplicably fond and which help mightily to devour the sound. Jennifer Tarver, Necessary Angel's incoming artistic director and this production's originator, doesnt have to direct everything as if it were written by Samuel Beckett. Actually her Beckett productions are more fun.

Brawner, funky throughout and playful when permitted, is followed on stage by Andrew

Penner, whose initial impression is that of a Louisiana busker, a one-man band making simultaneous music with hand, foot and mouth. Later on, he reduces his self-accompaniment to just a guitar. This is altogether as musician-heavy a show as could be wished, with the two actor-guys doubling up on a band that already includes two guitars, and a piano and a keyboard, together with bass and drums. Penner has the most effective number of the evening, by far, and on this he just sings, with touching restraint. Its a song about a gay man who's a transvestite stripper. It's also the title number, though neither the song nor the show answers the title question. They dont even ask it.

First to appear of the two ladies is Saidah Baba Talibah, who sings well, in a jazz-rock fashion, but doesnt manage the essential theatrical trick of turning singing into storytelling. (I was intrigued and impressed, though, to learn from her bio that she's the daughter of Salome Bey, and the niece of Andy Bey, whom she describes as arguably the finest jazz vocalist on the planet." Arguably, she's right.)

Finally, theres Louise Pitre, the only member of the cast who suggests old rather than New Orleans, and whose forte here is barely controlled rage. This works best for her in A Young Girl, about a seduced 16-year old, abandoned and dying by a roadside. This has a fine English lyric, curt and sardonically compassionate, by the great and neglected Oscar Brown Jr. Hes especially neglected by this production's song list, which declines to credit any translators apart from the show's dramaturg Andrew Shaver. For that matter it doesnt let on that not all Aznavours music is by Aznavour. Some of his tunes, including this production's "I'm Gonna Sleep With One Eye Open, are by an American ex-pat named Jeff Davis.

Pitre spends a lot of time sitting at the top of the steps with her back turned to the audience and to the other performers. This isnt because shes rude, or is trying to dissociate herself from the proceedings. It's part of the concept, and it gradually spreads through the entire cast. The show becomes a study in sullen solitudes. Maybe the most dispiriting thing about it is that the four performers, all with excellent voices, are never allowed to sing together. The closest they get is to deliver successive lines of a single song, and even that only happens once.

Indeed, the nearest we get to group action is when Brawner sings Take the Chorus" (a good Shaver lyric) and exhorts the band to do just that; each member gets to play a solo. It makes a welcome change from the other solos, lugubrious vocal ones, that make up the overwhelming bulk of the show. It's just one doom-andgloom thing after another. I remember Aznavour from television appearances as an impish presence with a melancholy streak. The version of him we're offered here is all streak and no presence: not a fair exchange.

What Makes a Man runs through Nov. 2 at the Berkeley Street Theatre. For tickets, visit canadianstage.com

John Lauener / Kenny Brawner takes on some of Charles Aznavour's best-known songs in What Makes a Man.
2014-10-20-tough-nuck-as-boardwalk-empir:
They decapitated Deadwood and they've foreshortened Boardwalk Empire. HBO seems to have it in for ambitious drama series with recent historical settings.

The death of Deadwood was a cultural crime. That new look at the old West had a rhythm and flavour all its own; it belonged in the same bracket of achievement as The Sopranos and The Wire. Boardwalk Empire has never reached the level of those shows; indeed it has dwelt in their shadow, sharing a principal author (Terence Winter) and a principal subject (gangsters) with The Sopranos and inheriting actors from both. It hasn't had a protagonist as magnetic as Tony Soprano, and it hasnt made the steady progress through different levels of society that distinguished the five seasons of The Wire (as far as I know the only one of these "TV novels" to have covered all of its intended territory and then stopped). But it has been a consistently gripping and entertaining show and its fifth and last season, now winding down to its final episode this Sunday, has a sombre grandeur all its own.

Its had to do it quicker than was intended. Boardwalk Empire is a chronicle of Prohibition, meaning it had to cover the whole of the 1920s and the first few years of the 1930s. It proceeded through them in a fairly leisurely fashion. The fourth season let us off at 1924, after having ruthlessly disposed of the show's two most beloved characters: Eddie, Nucky Thompson's faithful German attendant, offed himself rather than betray his employer, while Richard Harrow, the hitherto invincible half-faced sharpshooter, took a bullet after having, for the first time in his life, hit the wrong target. That seasons last image was of Richard, collapsed on the Atlantic City boardwalk, hallucinating the happy domestic ending that we had all been wishing for him and that had seemed to be within his grasp. We may have seen him kill more people than any other character on the show, but we never held it against him.

At that rate, it would have taken another six seasons to reach the end of the decade. But, as in the ruthless world of the show itself, word came down ordering a hasty execution, and the fifth season has taken us straight to 1931. In the interim we lost another favourite character, his end decreed not by sadistic scriptwriters but by history; this was Arnold Rothstein, the New York gangster played with enchantingly chill soft-spokenness by Michael Stuhlbarg. We were sorry to see him go - he deserved a proper death scene.

Nucky and Margaret, meanwhile, are no longer estranged, their reconciliation occasioned by the necessity of making common cause against the vengeful Mrs. Rothstein. One of the pleasures of this season has been seeing Steve Buscemi and Kelly Macdonald return to striking wary sparks off one another, he obviously still wanting and respecting her, she reciprocating some of the want but holding off on the respect.

Its been a teasing, leisurely process. In fact it's remarkable that a season that one might expect to be hurtling to a finish - and in some respects is - should also be taking its time exploring byways. One obvious example of this is the flashbacks that have been filling us in on Nucky's childhood and early career, his gradual acceptance of venality, leading up to his real deal with the devil: his delivery of the 13-year-old Gillian to the all-powerful Commodore. These scenes arent telling us things we didnt know or couldn't guess, but they're bringing them home. Theyve also managed to find, for the emerging Nucky and his brother Eli, young actors who actually look and sound as if they could grow up to be Buscemi and Shea Whigham.

Slow build-ups to explosions of violence: that has been the pattern this season, and a very effective one. Weve lost two major characters. Chalky White (Michael Kenneth Williams) went down in dignity to a Harlem firing squad after a protracted game of catand-mouse with his long-time nemesis, Dr. Narcisse (a character whose carefully cultivated cadences have been far more tolerable this season than in the previous one when he unfolded them at much greater length). Chalky thrived in Atlantic City, but only under Nucky's patronage; Narcisse, who seemed all-powerful, is paying protection to Lucky Luciano; even in crime, it's a white mans world. Not that white men cant be humiliated, too.

We've been witness to the unlikely partnership of Eli, former sheriff now on the run, and Nelson Van Alden (the marvellously straight-backed and wild-eyed Michael Shannon), former Prohibition enforcer ditto, both of them in simultaneous bondage to Al Capone and to the feds who tracked them down. I'm not convinced that the writers had quite this character arc in mind for the fanatical Van Alden when they first conceived him, but theyve certainly capitalized on it. He and Eli have consistently had the best lines. (Van Alden, cuckolded: Ive been having problems at home. Eli, who did it to him: "I can attest to that.") Van Alden's death, struck down while hurling himself at Capone in a furious re-statement of his previous identity, was abrupt but strangely fitting.

I've left Buscemi till last, because his performance exemplifies both the achievement of Boardwalk Empire and its limitations. I love the way he plays Nucky, and relish his wit, his bite and the way he can switch from charming self-deprecation to chilling self-assertion. The problem is, the boardwalk may be his, but the empire isnt. When the show started we were led to believe that it would all be about Atlantic City, but soon it started taking in the organized crime scene in New York and Chicago as well. This was an irresistible choice, given the richness of the terrain; we must have met, or at least heard about, every famous gangster of the period. They have all had dealings with, or against, Nucky, but there has never been the sense, as there was with Tony Soprano, that all the threads somehow led to him and that he epitomized his era. (The Wire didnt have an overwhelming protagonist either, but then it never pretended to.)

You can't be half a gangster, Nucky was told, in what is probably the show's most famous line. It seems though that his historical prototype, Nucky Johnson, actually could be, and was. He was a corrupt all-powerful municipal pol, who waxed rich through bootlegging, and eventually went to jail for tax evasion (like Capone), but he never killed anybody. Nucky has taken that final step, several times over, but its made him less interesting, morally indistinguishable from the other hoods, and very much at the mercy of events. Ive lost count of the number of times he's risen and fallen and risen again.

So now we await his final fall. Or not. Nucky Thompson isn't Nucky Johnson, who lived to a ripe and even respected old age. Our Nucky could still go down; and we know from history that he cant dispose of his chief remaining enemy Luciano, who proved himself truly Lucky by also dying old.

I hope Nucky survives: not that I think he deserves to but that he doesnt deserve not to; unlike Chalky or Van Alden or even Eli, he's never reached tragic despair so shouldn't have a tragic end. Besides, I like him. Its hard to dislike a man who in his very first episode, and with all the scorn and disgust at Buscemis elegant disposal, could tell Mickey Doyle, that inexplicable survivor, to "read a f-king book," or who, more recently, could drunkenly recite the whole of Hiawatha to a couple of tarts, before being mugged by one of them.

That the focus has narrowed to Nucky vs. Lucky is evidence of how neatly the show has winnowed its field. It may have done so under duress, but now, in its final stages, it feels inexorable.

Boardwalk Empire's series finale airs Sunday at 9 p.m. on HBO Canada.
2014-10-22-yellow-perished-it-will-alway:
This past Sunday night, viewers sat down to once again take part in an annual tradition: The Simpsons Treehouse of Horror," the annual Halloween special of the longest-running TV cartoon series ever. This year's entry was divided, as is customary, into three parts. The first segment took the Simpson family to Hell: a city, it seems, very much like Springfield. It was amusing to begin with, but soon pointlessly repeated itself. The last segment had the family confronted by doubles of themselves: a comment, I think, on the endless proliferation of Simpson images and on the repetition compulsion referenced above. The middle segment - well, I can't tell you about the middle segment because Ive forgotten it already. Honestly.

Its true that the Halloween specials have always provided a concentrated dose of Simpsonian self-satire, and that the same element, in more discreet doses, used to crop up in regular episodes. In either format, it was funny because the show had a self to satirize. Now it's down to satirizing the idea of satirizing itself: to coasting on its own reputation. It's sad.

The Simpsons has now been bad for longer than it was good, but when it was good it was great. Television has never provided as many inspired jokes per minute, sometimes per second, as The Simpsons did; has never been as consistently, ruthlessly, creatively irreverent as The Simpsons was. It taught a generation to revere wit and to distrust authority, two hugely important achievements. Now the irreverence has shrunk to mere random rudeness, and the jokes are flabby and far between. Everythings gone slack.

Surprisingly, this seasons premiere was actually one of the better recent efforts. It showed Krusty the Klown's career crashing to earth, giving his father the rabbi a fatal heart attack en route. The rabbi is still being voiced by Jackie Mason, and it's encouraging to find that the thick kosher sauce of his delivery has not been diluted by issuing from beyond the grave. All the same, weve seen the Krusty-onthe-skids plot more than once before and this time it hardly sustained the running time. In the golden days it would have been supported by one or more parallel actions. Now, we just kept flashing back to aimless scenes of Lisa worrying over Homers weight. No story went with this; it was merely reiterations of a joke we've heard for years. The point of cartoon characters is that they never change - but they should find new ways of not changing.

Ironically, the Simpsons' finest recent moments have come on somebody elses show. Im referring to the season premiere of Family Guy in which the Griffin clan found themselves paying an unplanned visit to their Fox TV colleagues. There has long been an undeclared war between these two shows, or at least between their fans. People who love The Simpsons tend to loathe Family Guy; we (you may count me in) regard the later arrival as an ill-tempered scattershot rip-off. It may seem ridiculous to fault a cartoon series for being unrealistic, but a show about an American family whose members include a talking baby and a talking dog is not one I can take seriously enough to find funny. It's also monotonously obnoxious. Peter Griffin is a boor. So is Homer Simpson, but Homer, unlike Peter, believably loves his family. That may sound sentimental, but it's what gives the character, and the show, texture and tenure. Its not just a matter of Homer having a saving grace; its because of the constant conflict between that grace and everything else about him. And of course Marge is a genuinely, and credibly, good person.

The Griffin family's best line in their shared episode was actually a riff on the competition's mythology. Adrift, with their car stolen, they came upon a signpost pointing to Springfield. "What state is that in? they asked, the answer being Were not allowed to say." Its significant that the show had to depict the Griffins visiting the Simpsons; if it had been the other way around, there would have been no one there. The Simpsons live in a community, one that has been established over the years in extravagant detail. The Griffins also have an identifiable hometown (in an actual state) but there's nobody among its honchos with the personality, joyous even in monstrosity of a Mayor Quimby, a Police Chief Wiggum or a Mr. Burns. The famous cutaway gags are like Stewie's sarcasm: selfflattering hipness trying to pass itself off as humour. When the Simpsons nudge the fourth wall - and they do nudge rather than break it - they do it with style:

Lisa: "Dad, do you even know what rhetorical means?

Homer: Do I know what rhetorical means?" Or:

Marge: "Homer, you loved Rashomon.

Homer: Thats not how I remember it."

All right, those were a long time ago. But imagine Family Guy coming up with anything comparable, ever.

I dont know how the animation responsibilities were parcelled out for the confrontation, but both sides were visually very much themselves. The Simpsons, though, were the clear winners, playing on their own turf even if the other side owned the broadcasting rights. The visitors got to bathe in the reflected glory of a virtual parade of Springfield favourites; Apu was in especially good form in a Kwik-E-Mart scene almost of vintage quality. We even got a glimpse of Sideshow Bob.

The actual plot wasn't so much; it climaxed in an inordinately prolonged dust-up between the two dads, followed by their appearance in a court presided over by Fred Flintstone. That was a nice touch, since The Flintstones might claim to be the progenitor of both shows. A Simpsons episode once paid explicit homage, with Homer carolling his own version of the Flintstone theme song while driving his car into a tree. Family Guy, though, bears the stronger resemblance, The Flintstones being a supremely dumb show whose idea of being clever was to dress its characters in animal hides and have them talk about Brontosaurus burgers while adhering in every other respect to the corniest conventions of 1950s domestic comedy. (I tend to believe the rumour that it was based on unused scripts from The Honeymooners.)

There was a good Family Guy moment at the end, though, with Peter carelessly and callously tossing into the garbage the saxophone generously bequeathed by Lisa to Meg, the despised and downtrodden Griffin daughter, who had discovered a virtuoso talent for the instrument: the first time in her life she had ever been good at anything. It was reminiscent, too, of a particularly poignant and pitiless moment on The Simpsons itself: a flashback episode in which a kindergarten Bart displayed precocious abilities too original for his teachers to recognize, and so was condemned to a lifetime of underachievement. It happened in a flash, like all the best things on the show. But that too was long ago.

The Simpsons can teach Family Guy a thing or two when it invades their territory, but when left to its own devices it seems content to sink to Family Guy level. Do yourself a favour this season and watch reruns. Or download a vintage "Treehouse of Horror" episode, one in which those superbly superior extraterrestrials Kang and Kodos end up running the show. They weren't even in this one; thats the depressing news Ive kept till last. As Bart once said of a Where's Waldo in which the hero was hiding in the plainest of sight, they aren't even trying any more.
2014-11-01-god-save-the-queen-s-newspape:
'The historical novelist", or so I once read, "must necessarily turn history into romance, and romance will always lie with the deposed or threatened king."

Same goes for the historical dramatist, as Shakespeare will bear witness. It goes, too, for the counter-historical dramatist, as is currently being demonstrated by Mike Bartlett, whose King Charles III is the prestige hit of London.

Or maybe Bartlett should be called a future-historical dramatist. The situation with which he presents us is that the Queen of England has just died and her son has, after a lifetime in waiting, succeeded to the throne. Immediately the new King Charles finds himself faced with a major crisis, of conscience and of state. In the wake of the recent phonehacking scandals and of attacks on privacy generally, a bill has been passed that will effectively limit what has traditionally been regarded as the liberty of the press. All the bill needs to become law is the mere formality of the royal signature. At least, it's always been assumed to be a formality. Charles, though, refuses to play. He takes the idea of press freedom seriously, even while admitting that he and his family have suffered from its abuse. He is also a student of history and knows that a monarch has one weapon left when facing an intransigent parliament. He can dissolve it.

Bartlett, whose best-known play in Canada is Cock, has done some clever things. He has seized on two issues on which most will have mixed feelings. One is censorship; we abhor it, and don't want to see a government insulating itself against attacks from the media; we can still feel uneasy about some of the things those media can get away with.

The other is that strange institution known as a constitutional monarchy. Of course, we don't want to see a democratically elected government subordinated to the whims of somebody whose position derives from mere hereditary accident. On the other hand, when we look at the antics of the elected, it's hard not to yearn for somebody to at least knock their heads together. There's a whole line of plays pitting king against cabinet, the elect against the elected; the most famous is Shaw's The Apple Cart, whose King Magnus took the wind out of his opponents' sails by threatening to abdicate and run against them. In Bartlett's play, abdication is a threat to be used against the king. Shaw's play is a comedy. So is Bartlett's, and often a funny one, but it's a comedy with the lineaments of tragedy.

It brings off this neat trick by dressing itself up stylistically as a Shakespearean chronicle play. Bartlett isn't the most impeccable of pastiche artists, but he is sometimes eloquent and often trenchant. The style may be a stunt, but it sustains remarkably well.

It's a first-rate production by Rupert Goold. Tim Pigott-Smith, the official king, was sick when I attended but his understudy, Miles Richardson, was excellent. He's the son of the late Ian Richardson, one of Britain's best classical actors, and he seems to have inherited his father's aquiline voice and manner, an air of being both vulnerable and aloof.

If ever a play was destined to be overtaken by events, this one is; but that's all the more reason to enjoy it while it still seems plausibly prophetic. It should come to Canada, quick.

Like most interesting shows in the West End, it's a transfer from a non-commercial house, the small independent Almeida. From the National Theatre, at the top of the subsidized heap, comes another state-of-the-nation play, uncompromisingly titled Great Britain. That's about the only uncompromised thing about it. Where King Charles III alludes to the Rupert Murdoch empire hacking scandals that caused the closure of the News of the World, this play is wholly concerned with them, and tries in fact to dramatize them. The trouble is that the staged drama can hardly compete in farcical luridness with the real thing; the show strains mightily to pitifully small effect.

It certainly has pedigree; it was staged by Nicholas Hytner, about to step down from a mostly glorious reign as the National's artistic director, and its author is the insanely prolific Richard Bean, who wrote one of Hytner's and the National's most deserved successes, One Man Two Guvnors. His gagman's touch only asserts itself in scenes involving a hapless police commissioner with gay proclivities, an Indian or maybe Pakistani accent, and a talent for inserting foot in mouth at press briefings. Otherwise all is laborious.

Names in this play are changed, but where it counts identities are distinguishable. Murdoch is now an Irishman, Rebekah Brooks is a minor character, and the leading figure is a female journalist, given an unfortunate performance in which the actress seems as obnoxiously pleased with herself as the person she's playing. The character's name is Kate Brittain, which should give an idea of the degree of subtlety on view here. Still, to judge from the fullness of their respective houses, while King Charles III is doing well, Great Britain is doing better. It makes you see the kebab man's point.

Brinkhoff-Moegenburg / Lucy Punch plays a news editor in Great Britain; Johan Persson / Oliver Chris and Tim Pigott-Smith star in King Charles III.
2014-11-08-dead-and-loving-it-with-its-s:
Welcome to the graveyard.

You'll be amazed at how lively it is.

Spoon River is adapted, by Albert Schultz and Mike Ross, from Spoon River Anthology, a collection of mainly short poems by Edgar Lee Masters, first published in 1915. Schultz directed it; Ross composed, arranged and directed the music, which is omnipresent, and he is also in the cast. Its the fourth Soulpepper production for which Ross has set a body of verse to music, and by far the best. Masters poems, a pungent series of dispatches from the dead, are substantial enough to work dramatically, yet simple enough to be understood when sung or spoken rather than read. It's a further strength that many of them are spoken; Ross's musical settings are brilliant, and stylistically varied, but theyre all the more effective for not being continuous.

Spoon River is an imaginary small town in Masters own state of Illinois. Its deceased inhabitants regale us with what I can best describe as their own virtual epitaphs: What they would have liked to have had inscribed on their tombstones, if only tombstones told the truth. That truth, in the overwhelming majority of cases, is dark. The population of Spoon River seems to have divided between the exploiters and the exploited, social or sexual. Those last two categories, of course, frequently overlap.

The book gives us its characters and their utterances unadorned. The theatre version supplies a frame. We make our way to the auditorium through a long black passage, adorned with memorial portraits; blackclad attendants usher us along, and on our journey we pass a coffin. We are on our way to a funeral. The town cemetery is called The Hill and when we reach our destination, there it is, rendered on stage in all its unearthly moon-haunted glory. (All honour to Ken MacKenzie, who designed the set and the superb lighting.) The stage is filled with actors, all of them for the moment motionless. The one live presence is Diego Matamoros, who identifies himself, in the only prose speech we are to hear all evening and the only one not taken from the book, as the sole Spoon River citizen old enough to speak for the community but young enough to manage the climb. He's also a father recently bereaved of his son, though the corpse over whose burial he's presiding is that of a newly deceased young woman. He makes himself scarce, and the massed ghostly presences spring into ... well not into life, but into a rousing, swinging old-time country number, self-accompanied. There are 19 actors in the cast, ranging from company vets to academy recruits, and nearly all of them can play at least one instrument.

The set-up is reminiscent of an earlier benchmark Soulpepper production, Thornton Wilders Our Town, or at least of its graveyard-set last act. Its tempting to describe Masters' vision as a bracing antidote to Wilder's rosier view of small-town Americana, but Im not sure that would be true. The splashes of darkness on Wilders generally sunny canvas register all the more strongly through contrast, and his final message - that the dead forget - is bleaker than anything here, especially as we had got to know those dead people when they were alive. Masters' characters still have all their memories.

The poems sharply juxtapose those memories, especially where married couples are involved. Schultz's production finds a striking visual correlative; the successive husbands and wives appear on either side of a revolving upright tombstone. The first pair (Gregory Prest and Raquel Duffy) seem to have had a long and happy union, and they sing about it, beautifully. They turn out, though, to be thoroughly atypical. Far more representative are Mr. and Mrs. Benjamin Pantier (Prest and Nancy Palk), he an attorney who wound up living in his office with his dog, she lamenting that the only man you are legally permitted to have sex with is the very man that fills you with disgust.

The poems are, for their day, amazingly explicit: "The old, old problem: Should it be celibacy, matrimony or unchastity?" - so wonders a woman who could have been as great as George Eliot but instead married a druggist and had eight kids. Copulation thrives; some ruined girls leave for greener pastures; another is cast out by her husband when he discovers she was raped at age eight.

In the public world, Prohibition is the mark of virtue, drunkenness the norm. The effective ruler of the town seems to have been banker Thomas Rhodes, who also ran the church and the store; we meet an overworked, underpaid employee who might, since hes played by Oliver Dennis, be described as the anti-Cratchit; he dies of his own anger. In compensation, the same actor appears as Fiddler Jones, who died "without a single regret."

The most harrowing stories involve mothers. Duffy plays a seduced servant-girl whose child was raised by her employers as their own and who had to watch his subsequent rise to fame, wanting vainly to cry out, Thats my son. Even kindness can corrode; it's heart-rending. Even more so is Palk's quiet soliloquy as a woman whose son (Colin Palangio) went cheerfully to the Philippine war, and was first disillusioned, then killed. They buried him, too, in Spoon River with, he bitterly complains, a flag over his grave.

Stuart Hughes plays, among other memorable things, a Lothario invincible until he got too old or the women too young; Frank Cox OConnell is a looming deaths head presence; and there's the unexpected sight of Matamoros, in a funny hat, singing and playing bluegrass.

I should list everyone; this is one of those productions that comes over as a heartfelt gift from the actors to the audience, joyously offered, joyously received. Ross himself is an MD who leads from the front; he plays a thrusting guitar but denies himself a song until the end. Then he emerges as Matamoros's dead son, exhorting the just-buried girl, and everybody else, "Is your soul alive? Then let it feed." It builds to a showstopper. It might be accused of privileging one uncharacteristically cheerful thread from the original pattern, just as Masters own pessimism, taken in bulk, can sometimes seem facile. But thats show business.

And if one of the functions of an adaptation is to send you back to the original - well, this one did that for me, and what I found was richer than I'd remembered.

Spoon River runs through Nov. 15 at the Young Centre.

Cylla Von Tiedemann / Stuart Hughes, Frank Cox-O'Connell, Anthony MacMahon, Brendan Wall, Diego Matamoros and Gordon Hecht rest in peace in Spoon River's musical cemetery.
2014-11-15-heads-will-roll-two-new-ish-p:
Stephen Adly Guirgis is the New York playwright responsible for The Last Days of Judas Iscariot, whose Toronto production was one of the great theatrical events of the past 10 years. It established Guirgis, in my eyes anyway, as the most exciting dramatist now working in the U.S., though since then Bruce Norris (Clybourne Park) has provided some substantial competition. Guirgiss other plays that I've seen or read are on a smaller scale than Judas, physically and philosophically, but they have the same wit, the same unexpectedness, and the same concern with how we live, love and believe.

The Motherfker with the Hat, which may come to be known as the asterisk play, is Guirgis's latest, brought to us now by a new company called Bob Kills Theatre, operating out of The Coal Mine, whose fittingly subterranean location is beneath the Magic Oven restaurant at Pape and Danforth. The space is tiny but the performance and production team is top-flight.

The play takes us, giddily and profanely, into the working-class, and underclass, world of upper Manhattan. Our protagonist is Jackie, a recovering alcoholic with some good intentions, a short temper and an itchy trigger-finger. Recently out of prison, he comes home to his girlfriend Veronica, whom hes loved since high school, announcing that,

maybe for the first time in his life, he has a respectable job. How this works out for him we never have the chance to discover, since other concerns supervene. Jackie detects an unfamiliar male scent in Veronicas bed and an unfamiliar male hat on her table. Veronica, who has her own issues with vodka and cocaine, indignantly denies any wrongdoing. Thoughts of a cozy evening at their favourite pie-shop and/or in bed are banished. Jackie storms out.

He goes to see Ralph, his AA sponsor, who in his own recovery has become an avid consumer of, and evangelist for, health-food drinks. In addition to dietary advice and behavioural instruction, Ralph offers Jackie a couch on which to crash. This leads to complications with Ralph's wife Victoria: not, as you might expect, because she doesn't like Jackie but because she doesnt like Ralph. Meanwhile, there are other complications;

Jackie has shot up the apartment of the man in his building whom he believes to be the malefactor in the hat. He now needs to hide the weapon. So, with Ralph in tow, he turns to his Puerto Rican cousin Julio who agrees to take care of the gun, though not before reading Jackie a lecture on his selfishness and irresponsibility. It does indeed turn out that Jackie has been unfaithful to Veronica, with a previous, female, sponsor. Although it also turns out that Jackies behaviour may count as ethical, compared to the lines that Ralph has crossed. It all depends, as Jackie might say, on your code.

This is the only one of Guirgis's plays to have been produced on Broadway, which may account for the conventional feel-good vibe that surfaces in its last scene. The play begins with Jackie and Veronica, and it ends with them, but if their relationship is meant to be its heart, the emotional case isn't made. The womens roles arent as richly written as those of the men. Nor (by Melissa D'Agostino and Nicole Stamp) are they as distinctively played.

Sergio Di Zio's Jackie is a subtle performance that starts as a standard angry tough but goes on to find new levels of hurt, bewilderment and conscience. His final words to Ralph - that the fact he hasnt killed him doesnt mean that he might not do it in the future - are Guirgis at his best: a simple statement that radiates in all directions. Ted Dykstra's Ralph, with the strangest and greasiest ponytail ever sported, is drop-dead hilarious in the prose arias, both solicitous and self-serving, that his author has bestowed on him; he's also very persuasive in his discomfiting arguments that sex, with anybody at all, is no big deal, and that after the age of 25, there are no friends, only associates."

Speeches even more joyously spectacular go to Juan Chioran as Julio, the self-described "f-got cousin" (in boyhood anyway) with a threatening sideline in martial arts; he is blissfully absurd and, in one spellbinding speech of reminiscence, even more blissfully serious. Layne Coleman directs a very tight production, on a set by Steve Lucas that convinces as three separate locations. Simon Fon has arranged fights that look, at these close quarters, as dangerous as any Ive seen. The play is more successful at evoking a world than at making a point, but its still a dazzler.

It does, I guess, say one of the same things as Tom Stoppard's Arcadia, which is that theories, however cosmic, get messed up by people fancying people they shouldn't. Stoppards two-timing modern classic illustrates this more persuasively in its 19thcentury scenes than its 20th-century ones (the two periods alternate, and finally and famously co-exist) but the minor complaint is outweighed by the major compliment.

Eda Holmes studio production from last year's Shaw Festival has expanded into the Royal Alex with no loss of definition. In fact, it's gained; the actors now inhabit their roles and bandy their words with enchanting assurance. Gray Powell nails every line and thought as the tutor who might be called Lord Byron once removed; Kate Besworth is a poignant delight as his fated genius pupil; Diana Donnelly is splendidly dismissive in a cardigan as the modern lady academic; and Patrick McManus as her professional and psychological opposite is wonderfully uninhibited in a suit as her professional and psychological opponent, whose real name is Nightingale and whose assumed and far more suitable one, as he careers flamboyantly toward a fall, is Peacock. Like most Stoppard characters, indeed like most people, hes trying desperately to make himself feel important.

You get more out of this play every time you see it, not so much in wisdom as in the joy of picking up connections, some of them structural, some (like an allusion to the sub-title of The Importance of Being Earnest) thrown in for the fun of it. The production has gained, too, in gravitas, both at its end and in a passing image like that of Kyle Orzech, the one newcomer, as the mute boy Gus covering his ears against the intolerable noise (a keyword) of his squabbling elders. Festival casting means that we get major actors like Ric Reid, Sanjay Talwar and, as a butler, an immovable Michael Ball glorifying minor roles. There are Stoppard plays of which I am personally fonder but all right, I give in, this is his masterpiece.

The Motherf ker with the Hat runs through Nov. 30 at The Coal Mine; Arcadia runs through Dec. 14 at the Royal Alexandra Theatre.

David Cooper / Tom Stoppards Arcadia is enjoying a remount at the Royal Alex after a run at last year's Shaw Festival. The production shares some surprising similarities with the more profanely titled The Motherfker with the Hat.
2014-11-22-sextet-the-single-girl-two-ne:
The acronym NSFW stands for "not safe for work." The play of which the acronym is the title has a further subtitle: Money, Sex and Photoshop. It's the work of a notable young British playwright, Lucy Kirkwood, and it's being given its North American premiere by Studio 180. It's been widely described as a play about the objectification of women, but that is selling it short. It's about the objectification and humiliation of both sexes, by both sexes.

It's set in the London offices of two magazines, both of them, come to think of it, photo shops. First we're in the Doghouse, that being the name of a girlie mag trying to keep a foothold in an increasingly precarious print market.

The current issue features a picture of a big-breasted young woman who turns out to have been only 14; the photograph was submitted by her ex-boyfriend, and selected for prominent display from among hundreds of other offerings. The girl's father has come across the picture, and is naturally incensed. Aidan, the editor, has to set about damage control. Or, given the possible legal consequences, damages control.

He invites the father, a Mr. Bradshaw, down from his Manchester home, puts him up in a five-star hotel, offers him coffee and sympathy, and produces a cheque for a substantial amount, all signed and ready to go. Mr. Bradshaw declines both the coffee and the money; he wants blood. He remains immovable, even though Aidan, having taken expert and expensive advice, assures him that he doesn't have a legal leg to stand on.

Our sympathies, of course, are all with the aggrieved and disadvantaged dad up against the metropolitan smoothie, and they remain that way. But he, too, turns out to be compromised (how, among other things, did he come across his daughter's picture in the first place?); and though we hope that he will stand his ground, we realize increasingly that it's no sure thing.

This, in Joel Greenberg's production, is as tense and multi-faceted a scene as you could hope to encounter. Patrick Galligan slides effortlessly along Aidan's trail of slime, implicitly threatening even, or especially, at his most ingratiating; he exploits his opponent's weaknesses from behind the blandest of concerned smiles. Ian D. Clark is heartbreakingly flesh and blood as Bradshaw, voice, stance and raincoat all correct. There is a third player: Charlotte, Aidan's assistant who, the job situation being what it is, has compartmentalized her life. In the office, she's an efficient cog in her boss's machine, and possibly his girlfriend as well; outside it, she belongs to a women's group. Her function in this scene is to watch and wait, stiff-lipped; Jessica Greenberg makes that lip remarkably expressive, silently communicating disillusion with one party, disappointment in the other, and disgust at just about everything.

We've already met Charlotte, keeping her end up in off-colour banter with Aidan's two male subordinates. One, Rupert, is a trustfund kid, whose advantages enable him to tell Aidan to stuff it when asked to embarrass himself for the sake of a story. (Class resentments between the two men are alluded to, but I suspect it would take a British production to make them clear.) The other, Sam, just one step above an intern, declines a similar assignment out of loyalty to an adored fiancee. Both these men reappear in the play's second location, which moves us from David Mamet's territory into Caryl Churchill's. The Top Girl here is Miranda, editor of Electra, an upscale publication whose aim of empowering female readers amounts in practice to exposing their imperfections, in the hope they'll spend money to correct them.

Rupert now has a job at Electra and Sam is applying for one. Rupert's involves putting himself as a man through painful procedures routinely undergone by women: most ironic, considering his previous protests and also, in James Graham's enforcedly silent performance, most hilarious. Sam, endowed by Aaron Stern with a touching brand of eager shyness, is put to a test; Miranda asks him to identify flaws in the girlfriend to whom he remains passionately loyal.

Like Mr. Bradshaw before him, he squirms and protests and wriggles. Miranda is an even greater master of office doublespeak than Aidan; she's continually wrongfooting others, under the smiling guise of wrongfooting herself. Susan Coyne, in a splendidly considered and beautifully timed performance, makes clear that, underneath the assurance, there's a genuine layer of self-hatred. What unites all the play's characters is the desperate instinct for selfpreservation, whatever the cost. The final stage image, implicitly asking, "Is this what feminism has come to?" is sadly unsubtle. Up to that point, though, its wit is devastating. I didn't laugh all that often, but when I did I laughed loud.

The Sextet of Morris Panych's new play is a chamber group, marooned at a motel because of a blizzard. Harry is silently (except to us) and unrequitedly in love with Dirk, who fancies Sylvia, who is actually attracted to Harry; Otto, a test-tube baby, may have similarly impregnated Mavis, whose cross-dressing husband Gerard, despite certain physical difficulties, would like to believe that he himself is the father. It takes time to sort all this out, what with the dialogue moving very fast, and I'm still not sure I got it all right.

Panych, as usual, directs his own play and, also as usual, his staging is excellent, on a neatly terrifying set designed by Ken MacDonald, six unnervingly identical beds lined up in a row. But the play itself feels mechanical, with only two of the characters coming to life.

One is Damien Atkins' Harry, who has the advantage of functioning as a kind of a narrator with a direct line to the audience and who builds on it with a study of embarrassed frustration that may add up to 50 shades of green; the other is Laura Condolln's Sylvia, who is simply real. Matthew Edison (Dirk), Jordan Pettle (Otto) and Bruce Dow (Gerard) all contribute high expertise, though Rebecca Northan, a clown deprived of her red nose, is pallid as Mavis.

In addition to putting the sex into sextet (I'm not trying to deny paternity, but it's Panych's joke) these musicians, or most of them, care about their music, especially Gerard, who wants them to play Schoenberg, while the others would much prefer Schubert. Gerard gets his way, because he's the boss. And, judging from what we hear at the end of the play, his way, in this case at least, may be the right way. The show goes on; but I don't think it makes a metaphor.

NSFW runs through Nov. 30 at the Theatre Centre; Sextet runs through Dec. 14 at the Tarragon Theatre.

Cylla Von Tiedemann / Above: Jordan Pettle, Matthew Edison, Damien Atkins, Laura Condlln and Rebecca Northan in Sextet.; Karri North / Below: James Graham, Susan Coyle and Aaron Stern in NSFW.
2014-11-24-the-scottish-plays-the-royal-:
The last six kings of Scotland, before its union with England, were all called James. They didnt have an uninterrupted run; between the reigns of James the fifth and sixth came that of Mary Queen of Scots, a sovereign who has never lacked for theatrical attention. Her male predecessors, by contrast, have remained obscure, both on and off the stage. The James Plays are an ambitious attempt by a Scottish playwright and TV writer, Rona Munro, to even the odds.

She has written three linked plays, each devoted to one of the first three Jameses. They have been staged by the National Theatre of Scotland, a peripatetic company now eight years old, whose production of Black Watch was a sensation when it visited Toronto a few years ago. After opening at the Edinburgh Festival, the James trilogy has come to London as a co-production with the National Theatre of Great Britain (which presumably, and for the time being, includes Scotland, but let's not get into that), mounted in the South Bank complex's largest house the Olivier, a platform stage transformed for the nonce to a theatre-in-the-round. It deserves the honour.

The three kings it treats have more in common than a name. All were married off to foreign heiresses, and all met violent ends. Its the 15th century; the Jameses, from the Stewart family, are murderously opposed by greedy and obstreporous rival clans. James I passed his youth as a prisoner of Englands Henry V, victor of Agincourt, who helps us get our historical bearings by making a personal end-of-life appearance, foul-mouthed and foulblooded. He wants to teach James how to be a king; and he posthumously succeeds, better than he could have hoped. Returned to Scotland, James imposes something approximating a rule of law, and proves coolly efficient at disposing not just of enemies but of potentially embarrassing friends. His is the most straightforward tale of the three, and the most straightforwardly effective.

James II spent his early years as a frightened pawn of the feuding landowners who disposed of his father. His play starts with a long nightmare sequence showing him hiding in a series of boxes of increasing size. It's a brilliant image, superbly realized in Laurie Sansom's production; the boxes go whizzing about the stage, while their dreaming former occupant sees his younger boxed-inselves impersonated by puppets.

Unfortunately, the play never progresses once hes woken up. Like its hero, it pursues much the same political course as its predecessor; and the one new ingredient - James relationship with a feckless boyhood friend - never justifies the amount of space it occupies. James III, however, changes the pattern; instead of a king learning to impose his will on peers and parliament we have one who would rather just let them get on with it. His principal demand of them is that they fund a choir to follow him around and provide appropriate incidental music.

He is that familiar figure in historical drama: the aesthete king up against a philistine establishment. He's also, because of his wit and impudence, good dramatic value. The real power, however, both in the kingdom and the play, resides with his wife, a Danish princess played by a real Danish actress (Sofie Grabol, from TV's The Killing). She takes cool and constructive control of the familys, and the countrys, finances; she also imports, from Venice, a new brand of mirror, one that enables its users to see themselves as they actually are, to their almost universal embarrassment.

This is another fine stage image, from an author whose visual sense is matched by her verbal; Munro writes forceful, colloquial dialogue that bridges the centuries; it's modern without being embarrassing. She respects her characters, and the audience. I can't imagine any Canadian company would stage these plays, but World Stage or Luminato could and should import them.

From the Scots boys to The Scottsboro Boys: This is the John Kander-Fred Ebb musical that had a discouragingly short run on Broadway in 2010 but has triumphantly resurfaced in the West End. Its about the case of nine young black American men who were, literally, railroaded; travelling by train through Alabama in 1931, in search of work, they were accused of rape by two white women who were themselves trying to avoid arrest for prostitution. The nine were tried, convicted, and sentenced to death. Appeals and re-trials followed, but the verdicts stood, despite one of the accusers having recanted her testimony. One of the "boys" died in prison, 20 years after his arrest; the rest were freed or paroled, four of them briefly becoming a vaudeville act.

This last circumstance gives the musical its concept; its presented as an old-time minstrel show with the crucial difference that, instead of white performers in blackface, we have blacks playing whites and blacks, finally donning an extra layer of makeup to drive the point brutally home. A racist trope is turned against itself. This is the finest use of showbiz metaphor in any Kander and Ebb musical: better than Chicago, where the style is in paranoid excess of the subject; better than Cabaret, where the horrific subject cannot help dwarfing the style. Here, hand and glove are an exact fit.

Kander's music is dangerously, seductively tuneful; Ebb's lyrics are among his most polished and pointed. David Thompson's book places the story perfectly inside its theatrical frame. Susan Stroman has recreated her New York staging, bringing over four key members of the original cast; her direction and choreography are her best yet, stylish and inventive without a drop of superfluous splash. Her routines, terrifically executed really can make you, if not laugh and cry, then smile and wince at the same time.

The British recruits include, delightfully, a veteran classical actor, Julian Glover, in the one white role: a paternal Mr. Interlocutor who doesn't get it. It sometimes seems that every musical since the year 2000 has been trumpeted as the best of the new millennium. This one actually is.

James II: Manuel Harlan, Royal National Theatre /
2014-11-29-parish-the-thought-god-only-k:
Pierre Teilhard de Chardin was a French geologist and paleontologist whose crucial scientific work was done before the Second World War. He was also a Jesuit priest. De Chardin believed fervently in evolution, which the Catholic Church at this point officially didn't. So there was a conflict. The trouble with The De Chardin Project, Adam Seybolds biographical play, is that the conflict is all external.

The hero isnt defrocked or excommunicated, but he's posted to China; in effect he's banished. Exile turns out to be a kind of blessing, since on an archeological dig there, he discovers a previously missing link in the evolutionary chain, to be known thereafter as "Peking Man." When war comes, hes interrogated by the Japanese as to what hes done with the evidence. But fearsome as these pressures must have been, they don't mean much theatrically because the protagonist never seems in any danger of succumbing to them. He never seems to have doubts. The play maintains a high level of intellectual chat, but it's basically undramatic.

It also has a hackneyed framework. We enter the theatre to find our hero stretched out flat on the floor. It seems that he has had a heart attack, and is minutes away from death. A mysterious female figure makes a highly effective surprise entrance and proceeds, as his past life flashes before him, to impersonate the most unforgettable people the dying man ever met.

This turns out to be a good thing, as it enables Maev Beaty to play even more characters, faster, than she did last year in Passion Play. As de Chardins Jesuit superior relaying the bad news from Rome she strays into sentimentality, playing sympathy rather than rigour, but elsewhere she is irreproachable. She is steely and scary as the Japanese jailer, funny as a jovially skeptical colleague, and gets to inject some real tension into the proceedings as an American expat who does her best to get the priest into bed. Hes as committed to his spiritual vows as to his scientific quest (in fact he regards the two as one) so she has to settle for being his secretary, confidante and muse. But he does at least seem tempted, and we finally get to see him interacting with a character who's on stage long enough for there to be a relationship.

Alan Dilworth's production makes imaginative, haunting use of lighting and sound, on a set by Lorenzo Savoini that looks like a boxing ring riddled with trapdoors. Cyrus Lane plays de Chardin for the most part on one conscientiously worried note, but thats what hes been handed. He plays the arguments well, but they remain speeches. At the end he's vouchsafed a vision of discoveries that will vindicate him after his death. (He died in New York in 1955.)

We can work out for ourselves that his view of the Biblical creation story will become theologically mainstream: that it's metaphor rather than history or, as G.K. Chesterton wittily put it, that science proves not that God doesnt exist but that hes been much underrated. Maybe more heretical is his view of Original Sin: that it's a good thing that makes human striving possible. As a non-believer, I've always found it a persuasive doctrine; it accounts for the way things always go wrong. It accounts, in fact, for tragedy. Seybolds play makes a bold attempt to give these ideas theatrical shape but it doesnt show them working on or through its hero. It's a whistlestop bio.

Talking of tragedy: Ned Dickens wrote the monumental City of Wine cycle, a reimagining, and fleshing out, of the substantial portion of Greek drama that's set in Thebes. His new play Paulo and Daphne goes back to mythology, less successfully. It presents the story of Apollo and Daphne, as told in Ovids Metamorphoses, as the tale of a Canadian immigration lawyer and his assistant; he wants her, she obdurately resists. (Shes also smarter than he is, which isn't in the source.)

To them comes a refugee claimant, bearing a volume of Ovid, and calling herself Illyria, which Google tells them was another name for Thrace, which is now called Bosnia, and whose more ancient horrors included the Minotaur. This, Illyria tells them, is her story, though she keeps changing her own. Despite felicities in the writing, it all seems forced, out of scale; though it might be more persuasive in a more precisely weighted production than Adam Proszowski's (for Theatreworks Productions), in which two of the actors, Karen Glave and Daniella Forget, are overheated while the third, W. Joseph Matheson, is less consistently and slightly more effectively understated.

For an independent production that gets everything right, I have to cite Moment, an Irish play by Deirdre Kinahan, that ARC produced at The Grocery on Queen Street East. It has closed, but must be revived. It had the feel of a site-specific show without actually being one; the audience, limited to 30, sat around the walls of a kitchen re-created in mesmeric detail.

Within it unfolded a tale of family reunion; longed for by the unbalanced widowed mother of the house, dreaded by everyone else, notably by the artist-son returning years after being released from long imprisonment for a horrendous offence. Christopher Stanton, already known as an actor and sound designer, directed this one with, except at the very end, impeccable sensitivity. The exchanges around the dinner-table were superbly orchestrated; they felt like life. The actors were pretty much perfect but I have to single out Janet Porter as a resentful daughter, dragooned into attendance, sitting awaiting an inevitable explosion and, her face told us, both dreading and willing it to happen. That's two plays that invoke fate, one that made it real.

The De Chardin Project plays through Dec. 14 at Theatre Passe Muraille; Paulo and Daphne plays through Dec. 7 at the Pia Bauman Theatre.

2014-12-06-this-charming-man-petty-s-cin:
In Ross Pettys new Cinderella, the heroine is the proprietress of an organic vegetable store in St. Lawrence Market, whose evil stepmother keeps getting in her enlightened way. Her Prince Charming is a universally adored pop singer and environmental crusader whose fanatical female following keep getting in his enlightened way. This is not unlike - no more weasel words, its very like - the situation in last year's Petty extravaganza, The Little Mermaid, in which the romantic couple bonded over their shared dedication to keeping Toronto's lake free from pollution.

So this Cinderella is a re-tread: an entertaining re-tread certainly, with some great performers, but less fun than it was the first time. To be fair, pantomime itself - the traditional British panto on which Petty has been putting a Canadian spin for nearly 20 years now - is all about theme and variations. You take a traditional story, and mess with it. The more popular sources keep coming around at the Elgin like the more popular Shakespeares at Stratford. Topical jokes have always been part of the recipe, but in recent years theyve become more pointed. The shows are no longer set in some anonymous fairyland but in a fairyland called Toronto. Its quite a radical shift, and a welcome one. But this year's show, compared to last year's, suffers from there being too much theme and too little variation.

Cinderella, in accordance with the independent-heroine tradition that came in with Disneys Beauty and the Beast, is a lot less oppressed than she used to be. I mean, here she is, running her own business, quite successfully it seems, and with a whole singing and dancing chorus as her employees. Shes come a long way from the days when her only companions were mice. She does still have a wicked stepmother, one Revolta Bulldoza - played of course by Petty himself - who, to give the plot some traction, has the legal power to take over the market and remake it in her own evil image, so long as she can seal the deal before Cinderella turns 21. So, when none of the good characters are minding the store, she fills its shelves with an addictive product called Hypno Chips. The property they do have is that of rendering anyone who consumes them a zombie slave to Revolta's will. This is a fate that eventually, if temporarily, overtakes nearly every member of the cast. It obviously makes life easier for Revolta. It also becomes a narrative crutch, and a tiresomely repetitive one, for the show itself. The best part of the story turns out to be the most traditional: the transformation scene, which is suitably magic and involves a pair of real ponies to take Cinderella to the Eligi-Ball (nice one) at which Max Charming, on the advice of his manager, will choose himself a bride. (Or maybe not. The rules are a bit vague.) This sequence is a long time coming, but no more so than in more traditional versions. It makes it all the more effective when it happens.

Danielle Wade is a delightfully wholesome Cinderella and Jeff Lillico a charming Charming. The standout performance though comes from Dan Chameroy, playing his accustomed role of Dame Plumbum, but with a difference. Previous Plumbums have been minor villainesses, sharing the stage with Petty's major one. This Plumbum is a goodie, in fact the Fairy Godmother. This is good economy; no show needs two vain and malevolent drag queens. (Im not even sure it needs one. Pettys best performances have been as Captain Hook and the Sheriff of Nottingham. This time around he's reduced to coming on in a frock, leering and berating the audience for not booing loud enough.) Chameroy's Fairy Plumbum is a delectable creation, accident-prone and easily distracted, but coming triumphantly through in a crisis; the pantomime dame may be a coarse creation but here shes most delicately realized. Shes also a whiz at the ad libs, as is Eddie Glen, who was born to play Buttons and does. Unlike previous Buttonses he isn't lovelorn; another departure is that he gets to accompany Cinders to the ball as her footman, in which capacity he's renamed Zipper. His opposite number Dandini (aka Dan Dean), accurately described as Max Charmings clever little characteractor friend, is played by Reid Janisse, whos also the show's writer; and if you think I've slipped that information in too casually, you should see how modestly hes billed in the program.

A great season for independent theatre in unaccustomed venues continues with a new production of David Harrowers play Blackbird. David Ferry directs, and also plays Ray, a man approaching 60 who once had an affair with a 12-year-old girl and went to jail for it. Now, 16 years later, his victim Una tracks him down to his new workplace; he's apparently rebuilt his life, and has certainly changed his name. His new surname, Trevelyan, has aristocratic connotations of which Una is especially scornful; scorn and aggression are, initially, the dominant notes in her register; surveying the "pigsty" (his word) in which he works and which he seems intent on clearing up, she queries whether he is in fact the janitor. Apparently he isn't, but now that shes appeared, he dreads losing what position he has. Ferry plays him, brilliantly, as a compound of fear and shame, his face illuminated, in an especially striking moment, by the pale glow of a floor-lamp. Striking, too, is the desperate way he talks of "these people" in an attempt to distance himself from your run-of-the-mill pedophile. We blame him, but we find it increasingly hard to despise him. At the same time we watch Sarah Booths Una displaying new layers of vulnerability; at one point she's left alone in a darkened room, and her cries - adult cries as helpless a child's - are indelible; we lose any sense of an actor acting. From this point the play shifts into a different mode; the author says its a love story, and it seems he wasnt kidding. And then it shifts again. It's never obscure, but it's honestly ambiguous: not about facts but about feelings. The intensity of both performances sometimes slips into inaudibility (paradoxically a greater danger in a small space than in a big one) but this is a far better balanced production than the one a few years ago by Studio 180. Like its predecessor, it gives this British play a Canadian setting, or at least Canadian accents: no harm, though some of the video accessories are unnecessary. The setting is uncredited but then it's practically non-existent, which makes it bleakly perfect.

Cinderella runs through Jan. 4 at the Elgin Theatre; Blackbird runs through Dec. 11 at Artscape Studio 107, 180 Shaw St.
