2014-12-13-dahl-house-james-and-the-gian:
YPT's production of James and the Giant Peach, a musical based on the Roald Dahl book and directed by Sue Miner, has two great things going for it. One is the ensemble performance of the outsize insects who accompany the title character on his trip in the flying, floating title fruit. The other is the visual identity bestowed on the peach, and the creepycrawlies, and just about everything else in the show by its design team.

Yannik Larivee did the sets and Robin Fisher the costumes; Fisher also designed the puppets that represent the insects before a magic potion enlarges them to actor-size. They're a colourful bunch posttransformation, and they inhabit a colourful stage world in which the giant peach is first glimpsed as a silhouette on a screen before opening up and becoming the main acting area. Shadow play also serves to delineate the young hero's recurring nightmare about the death of his parents who, as you may or not remember, were eaten by a rhinoceros escaped from the London Zoo.

They must have been phenomenally unlucky. Rhinos in the real world have been known to gore or trample people to death, but never to eat them; they're vegetarians. Dahl is here indulging in the kind of brutal whimsy that makes his stories, as far as I'm concerned, so very resistible.

Take, for example, the two greedy and malicious aunts who have to adopt the orphaned James, and who mercilessly torment and exploit him. As with the sadistic school principal in the hugely successful stage version of Dahl's Matilda, we can't relate them to what we actually know about child abuse, because they are so camped-up and caricatured. These ugly sisters (one assumes they're sisters) make Cinderella's siblings look like thoroughly motivated case studies. They're spiritedly played here by Nicole Robert and Karen Wood, though their screechy pseudo-British accents hurt my ears. It's hardly their fault, though, that they aren't as darkly funny as the script clearly thinks they are. They're presented as petty cheats who think they've hit the big time when the giant peach in their garden. When it disappears they have to scarper, off to America on the Queen Mary, though since they apparently haven't yet collected on all the money they thought was coming their way, it's a mystery how they can afford it.

Meanwhile James himself, brightly and honestly played by Alessandro Costantini, is off on his own transatlantic trip, travelling by peach. His voyage is also one of self-discovery, shared with and prompted by his newly inflated friends. When marine disaster threatens, he proves a resourceful and inventive leader; they learn that not all humans want to tread on them; and they all become what they most want and have lacked, a family. In this new world of hug-a-bug, Lana Carillo's ladylike Ladybug naturally takes precedence, but both Saccha Dennis (Spider) and Stewart Adam McKensy (Grasshopper) are credits to entomology while Jacob MacInnis charms the house as a timorous Earthworm who, predictably but delightfully, proves a hero. Dale Miller is excellent as the incorrigibly suspicious Centipede; his conversion is the show's dramatic high point, and he can even do convincing Cockney. He's less happy as the Mysterious Man who gives James his magical recipe and then disappears without explaining himself, though not before delivering the most ill-fitting of the musical numbers. The score is by the off-Broadway team of Benj Pasek and Justin Paul, who wrote the pastiche songs for the TV show Smash and are still spoofing away here; you have your plaintive loneliness song, and your sneaky lowlife song, and your rhythmic rave-up (the highlight): nothing that's bad but nothing that feels inevitably right either. But if the material is sometimes lacking, the presentation is first-rate.

A much older story is the basis of The Brown Bull of Cuailnge, presented by the group known as The Room and written by their playwright-in-residence (though he actually resides in Buffalo) Neil Wechsler. In first-century Ireland, a queen sends an army to Ulster to capture a bull, the only one in the country bigger than the one owned by her husband. None of this exciting stuff actually happens on the stage, which is occupied by four soldiers in the queen's army wondering what they're doing in what seems to be the most frivolous war since The Iliad and trading doubts, fears, blows (eventually) and the occasional song. They also presume heavily on our knowing the legend, or at least the program's summary of it. The others accuse their leader, Fergus, of periodically deserting them, which indeed he does, though never for more than a minute at a time; they speak, though, in terms of thousands of years, so maybe they're meant to represent all soldiers in all wars. The conversation goes in frustrating, and eventually agonizing, circles; and Geoffrey Pounsett's production doesn't give it any contours. The youngest recruit is played, pointlessly, by a woman, Gabriella Colavecchio, who's monotonously plaintive; the angriest by Antonio Cayonne, who's monotonously loud. Dylan Roberts' Fergus is monotonously ferocious, but he is at least quite powerful at the start; Anand Rajaram, the musician in the case, keeps a quizzical distance which feels in context like a small blessing. However: Wechsler's bio tells us that he has adapted Ibsen's supposedly unstageable epic Emperor and Galilean, and that I would like to see.

James and the Giant Peach runs through Jan. 4 at Young People's Theatre; The Black Bull of Cuailnge runs through Dec. 14 at Sidemart Theatrical Grocery

2014-12-20-a-family-affair-in-the-best-w:
Red One Theatre Collective's production of Who's Afraid of Virginia Woolf ? is the first I have seen to make me believe in the imaginary son. Or rather, it's made me believe in why George and Martha believe it. For those who may not know: they, the couple at the black heart of Edward Albee's play, have no children but have indulged in the shared fantasy of having one. This is one of the ways in which they try to shore up their 20-year marriage, which needs all the shoring-up it can get. Their other principal resources are alcohol and savage jokes, mostly at one another's expense though other targets are welcome when available.

The time is the early 1960s: the Kennedy era. The place is a university town in New England. George is a history professor, though not - as Martha never ceases to remind him and everybody else - the head of it: this despite the fact that he should have had the inside track, what with Martha's father being the university president. When we meet them, the happy couple have just returned home from a faculty party. Martha, to George's initially mild displeasure, has invited two of the other attendees to drop in for a few extra drinks.

These guests are another. much younger married couple, also childless: Nick, a newly appointed biology prof, and his wife Honey. George and Martha, compulsive grudgeholders and character assassins, now have an audience to play to. Nick and Honey are both fascinated and horrified, though she leans more toward the fascination and he toward the horror. It becomes clear that their marriage has as shaky a foundation as that of their hosts, and fewer builtin defences.

Red One's production is a family affair. George is played by Booth Savage, Martha by his wife Janet-Laine Green, and the play has been directed, excellently, by their un-imaginary son Tyrone Savage. I don't know whether these intimate connections have contributed to the immediacy of the experience, but another kind of intimacy certainly does. Being an acknowledged modern classic, Who's Afraid usually gets produced in medium-to-large institutional spaces. Red One operates out of the tiny Storefront Theatre; the same venue in which the same company gave us last year's Strindberg adaptation After Miss Julie. That was another memorable Walpurgisnacht, Walpurgisnacht being the sub-title that Albee gave to one of the three acts of his marathon play. Being so close to the action certainly drives home the brutality of both pieces. But it also, perhaps less expectedly, emphasizes the compassion. Or to put it more prosaically, I felt sorrier for Albee's characters, as for Strindberg's, than I ever have before. Booth Savage's George is, in his scruffy cardigan and red shirt, the very image of a disappointed academic, taking it out on everybody else. He's wonderfully sly and waspish in his intellectual dismemberment of Nick, the scientist who Martha claims will deposit old humanists like him in the dustbin of history. Trouble is, George more than suspects she may be right; in the meantime he takes enormous pleasure in purposely misunderstanding everything Nick says about his work and pouncing on everything he inadvertently reveals about his life and wife. He's better at the one-liners than he is at George's longer prose arias, but he's splendidly sacerdotal when he comes to the Exorcism, Albee's sub-title for his last act. This is when George announces, in public, the death of their fictitious son. Martha is horrified; the boy, every detail of his life carefully fabricated, was meant to be their secret. George points out that she already had told Honey about it; she broke their agreement.

So his destroying the fantasy is partly judgment and partly revenge, for her breach of faith and for her at least attempting to cuckold him with Nick. (Nick had had too much to drink. That's the trouble with the younger generation. They can't hold their liquor.)

But it's also a kind of mercykilling. Martha really had come to believe in "the little bugger" and she'll be better off without it. The thing is this couple, unlike Nick and Honey, really do love one another. At the very least, they need one another, and this production makes that manifest. Green's Martha is commonplace in her earlier wisecracks and put-downs. But she flares into life in her seduction scene; hilariously self-aware in her slinkiness, she's putting Nick down as much as she's leading him on. Then, in the last act, hysterically fighting off disillusion before succumbing to it, she is piteous, beyond anything I have known in this play before. The play's title denotes fear of suicide. For once, it doesn't seem forced or sentimental.

Benjamin Blais perfectly captures the square-shouldered all-Americanism of Nick. while Claire Armstrong's Honey is extraordinary. Honey is the real hysteric here; it was a hysterical pregnancy that occasioned her marriage, and she spends a large part of the play, having drunk too much brandy and heard too many truths, offstage, face down on the bathroom tiles: a favourite position, according to her husband. When she's on, she's mostly on the sofa, registering barometrically every change in the dramatic weather. She's shocked, she's delighted, she's intrigued, she's appalled, over and over again. Armstrong communicates - in face, posture, voice giggle and continually rearranged costume - every transition, every facet. It's a totally truthful performance: always changing, always the same.

Some doubts about the play remain. George and Martha still seem too cut-and-dried: always announcing their own strategies, always knowing what they're doing. This time, though, there's a saving ambiguity. I had always thought the imaginary child to be a crutch for the playwright rather than for the characters. This production has changed my mind. Weekend Post

Who's Afraid of Virginia Woolf ? runs through Dec. 21 at the Storefront Theatre.
2014-12-27-top-11-theatre-productions-fr:
1. London Road That impossible beast, the verbatim musical, showing how the killing of five prostitutes affected the inhabitants of the British provincial town where it happened. Britain's own National Theatre production is unlikely to have been any finer than this one from Canadian-Stage. Jackie Maxwell directing 11 of our best actor-singers and musical director Reza Jacobs for steered them through an extraordinarily difficult score without a false note.

2. Metamorphosis Kafka's famous man-into-insect story theatricalized with unflinching imagination by an acrobatic and mainly Icelandic cast, in a script by David Farr (of London) directed by Gisli Orn Gardasson (of Reykjavik). Thanks to Mirvish Productions for importing it; the same team are about to offer us their take on Robin Hood. Quite some metamorphosis there.

3. Lungs A strikingly original British play, a continuous duologue that moves effortlessly through time and space, as the couple concerned wonder whether to bring a child into a polluted world. Mesmerizingly written, acted and directed, witty and moving. This was one of two outstanding shows at the Tarragon, the other being An Enemy of the People. 4. Of Human Bondage/Spoon River Anthology Two Soulpepper productions, both visually and aurally adventurous, that I'm going to pass off as one as they jointly represented an imaginative leap for their director Albert Schultz. Bondage, Vern Thiessen's adaptation of a Somerset Maugham novel, was also the year's nearest approach to a good new Canadian play. This was a hat-trick year for Schultz since he also directed the more conventional but comparably distinguished Idiot's Delight. This had a breakthrough lead performance by Dan Chameroy, who kept turning up this year in all kinds of contexts.

Soulpepper also did finely by another, more familiar American piece, Twelve Angry Men, directed by Alan Dilworth and a compendium of accurate acting with Joseph Ziegler in devastating form as the angriest and saddest man of all.

5. The Charity that Began At Home St. John Hankin, the acrid Edwardian, has been one of the Shaw Festival's major rediscoveries, and this take-noprisoners comedy of morals may be the best of the cycle.

6. King John Tim Carroll's Stratford staging moved with perfect control from formality to naturalism and back again. Tom McCamus and Graham Abbey gave the year's two best Shakespeare performances in the year's best Shakespeare production - unless you count the Canadian Opera Company's revelatory Falstaff: the only comic opera I have ever seen that was deeply and consistently funny. This multinational co-production was actually directed by a Canadian, Robert Carsen. Can't we keep him here and get him to do a play? A more modest adaptation: Cymbeline's Reign, from Shakespeare in the Ruff, which is now the premier Shakespeare company in Toronto.

7. A Lovely Sunday for Creve Coeur Lovely any day of the week. Another Shaw Festival discovery; a rare Tennessee Williams one-act, both laugh-making and heartbreaking. Blair Williams' lunchtime production was as perfect an hour as you could hope to find; Deborah Hay and Kate Hennig were sublime. Also at the Shaw and nearly as good: The Sea, Edward Bond's near-masterpiece, directed by Eda Holmes, whose last season's production

of Tom Stoppard's Arcadia came, joyously, to Toronto. 8. Tartuffe The first-best classical production and Soulpepper's peak, its finest in this area since the same director, Laszlo Marton, did The Wild Duck. Moliere's comedy was freshly thought through, stretched without distortion to its farcical and near-tragic limits. In the major roles, Diego Matamoros and Oliver Dennis were major. 9. The Beaux' Stratagem The last great Restoration comedy restored (not that we get to see the earlier ones much either). In Antoni Cimolino's crisp and beguiling Stratford production, the cherished memory is of Martha Henry's Lady Bountiful, brandishing

broadsword and cucumber with cheerfully hostile intent. 10. The Motherf-ker With the Hat/Moment/Blackbird/Who's Afraid of Virginia Woolf? The last part of the year brought a remarkable string of independent presentations: invigorating productions of exciting plays, staged in intimate spaces and attracting top-ofthe-line actors (though, as one of them said to me, "you have to go into debt to do them"). The Motherf-ker with the Hat reacquainted us with America's best current playwright Stephen Adly Guirgis; Moment was a recent Irish piece, pitchperfect in its family dynamics; Who's Afraid of Virginia Woolf ? was a revelation in close-up; and Blackbird, David Harrower's disturbing play about pedophilia was given its second Toronto production and the first to be truly harrowing. Like the vast majority of the best new(ish) plays seen in Toronto this year, starting with London Road, Blackbird was British. And another funny thing: most of them had one-word titles - Lungs, Cock, NSFW (if that's a word).

11. A Midsummer Night's Dream(s) The 11th entry in my Top 10. Neither of these two wildly different Stratford productions would have made the cut on its own, but taken together they offered interesting if tendentious views of the most familiar of plays. Chris Abraham's mainstage version, enchantingly set, celebrated gay marriage, and was particularly good with the fairies; Peter Sellers' studio abridgement seemed disinclined to celebrate anything, and was at its best with the quarrelling lovers. Neither made much of the rude mechanicals; Sellars, indeed, seemed hardly to know they were there. But if you were looking for funny: Sixteen Scandals was Second City's best revue in I don't know how long. Probably eons.

2015-01-03-out-with-the-old-in-with-the-:
Im looking forward to Infinity. Thats the title of a new play by Hannah Moscovitch, due at the Tarragon Theatre this March. Moscovitch is one of the two best playwrights now working in Canada. The other is Michael Healey, who doesn't have anything coming up, or at least nothing that I've been told about. Theyre opposites. Healeys plays are always identifiably Canadian; their themes and settings may be domestic or political, but they're always very much here. Moscovitch's interests, and her sensibility, are cosmopolitan. Her first success was The Russian Play; her greatest was East of Berlin, which despite its title was set largely in South America. Her most recent was This Is War, in which all the characters were Canadian, but which took place in Afghanistan.

I dont know where Infinity is set, but its press release, which is all I have to go on, suggests that its venturing into Tom Stoppard/John Mighton/Michael Frayn territory: physics and metaphysics. I quote: How does a new theory of time change everything we know about ourselves? A brilliant young woman and her parents smash together - like colliding particles in an accelerator." Well, that sounds like fun.

Preceding Moscovitch into the Tarragon are Waiting Room, a new play by Diane Flacks, and Abyss, the Englishlanguage premiere of a piece by German writer Maria Milisavljevic. Don't let anybody tell you that female playwrights are under-represented on Toronto's stages. That hasnt been the case for years. The Factory has two new plays coming up, one of them by Charlotte Corbeil-Coleman, the other by Yvette Nolan. The Factory-in-exile, also known as the Canadian Rep Theatre, has three plays lined up, two by women.

One is How Do I Love Thee, which, as might be guessed, is about the courtship of Robert and Elizabeth Browning, a fittingly poetic subject for Florence Gibson MacDonald; the other, by Colleen Murphy, is a two-hander on an African war theme, in fact entitled Armstrongs War. Theatre Passe Muraille, the remaining house devoted to new Canadian work, has R-E-B-E-C-C-A, the playwriting debut of Sara Farb.

Three years ago Passe Muraille gave us Crash, a prizewinning first play by another actress-playwright, Pamela Sinha. This year her second play Happy Place is being produced by Soulpepper. It isn't just the first new play by a woman the company has presented; it's the first new play. When Soulpepper started out, it was focused on the classics; it has drifted from that policy, re-defining it as "plays that have already been done somewhere else.

Even the successful Kims Convenience was the development of a piece that had premiered on the Fringe. Shows newly created - most recently Of Human Bondage and Spoon River Anthology - have still been adaptations of pre-existing texts. Meanwhile, theres been a heavy reliance on established plays from the American repertoire (Miller, Mamet and even Neil Simon) while - with its revivals of David French, John Murrell, Judith Thompson and David Young - the company has practically invented the category of Canadian classic." So Happy Place is a departure, though a logical one.

The Canadian male playwrights haven't disappeared. There's a new Daniel MacIvor at Tarragon, Cake and Dirt, whose publicity makes it sound as if its author is breaking fresh sociological ground while delving into familiar themes. The third production in Canadian Reps lineup is a revival of George F. Walkers Nothing Sacred, which is another adaptation of a literary classic, in this case the Turgenev novel Fathers and Sons. It also happens to be my favourite Walker, due to a production years ago at the Shaw Festival.

The Shaw's own bill this year includes tempting American morsels: Sweet Charity, maybe the last of the great unselfconscious showbiz musicals; Light Up the Sky, a rare piece by Moss Hart; and, trailing clouds of more recent New York glory, Peter and the Starcatcher and Tony Kushner's The Intelligent Homosexuals Guide to Capitalism and Socialism with a Key to the Scriptures.

It looks like a good year for catching up with recent American stuff. Soulpepper has Sarah Ruhls Eurydice. Acting UpStage are giving us one of the two American musicals of The Wild Party (and it's the more interesting of the two, with a score by Michael John LaChiusa). Company Theatre's residency at CanStage will yield Domesticated by Bruce Norris, whose Clybourne Park raised hopes that deep satire might not be dead on Broadway. Can-Stage have also programmed Harper Regan, which, alas, is not a lampoon of Canadian and American political leaders.

Stratfords season is built around the theme of discovery. This seems to mean plays about science, from the Jacobean charlatans of Ben Jonsons The Alchemist to the pretenders of Friedrich Durrenmatt's The Physicists, a play from the early 1960s that's been crying out for revival: the implications of its theme - was has been thought can never be unthought - grow more terrifying by the year. But it also takes in Sophocles Oedipus, whose hero certainly discovered stuff, and which marks an overdue Stratford debut for director Daniel Brooks.

The characters in the festivals four Shakespeares also make discoveries about themselves and each other; it's what drama's about. And, just to bring a few wheels full circle: the Tarragon season with which I began kicked off last year with An Enemy of the People, a free adaptation of a classic, and it ends with another, a "Bollywood version" of Much Ado About Nothing.

I dont know whether Im looking forward to that. But I can testify that the best Much Ado I've ever seen (by the Royal Shakespeare Company) was set in the British Raj, with Judi Dench and Donald Sinden as Beatrice and Benedick going around the block for the last time, and a Dogberry whose malapropisms were the result of his imperfect relationship with the English language. You couldn't get away with that now.
2015-01-10-provocative-work-from-a-to-b-:
The Next Stage Theatre Festival is an ambiguous animal. It began, or so I've always assumed, as a way of giving a second airing to shows that had proved successful at that older established festival, the Toronto Fringe. Now it seems more and more to consist of independent productions that have been in development, and are now ready to go to the Next Stage of confronting a live audience. The next Next Stage could be a run somewhere else: presumably not at the Fringe itself, though that would certainly be an interesting full circle.

Of the two plays I saw on the first day of this year's festival, one was surprisingly mainstream. For a Good Time, Call Kathy Blanchard could be the Canadian equivalent of an Alan Ayckbourn play, though the author, Michael Ross Albert, doesn't appear to have Ayckbourn's farcical inventiveness or his expertise in handling group dynamics; there are four characters in the play, but only rarely are they all on stage together. Also unlike Ayckbourn, the play is softcentred, or at least soft-ended. But like Ayckbourn it presents a comically bilious view of family life, with a tragedy going on in the background.

Well, perhaps not a tragedy but a drastic situation. Mother, we gather, is in hospital, suffering from dementia and from possibly fatal thirddegree burns. Lawrence, the eighth and youngest of her grown children, is chronically underemployed, and has fanciful ambitions of being a singersongwriter. The house is being run, dictatorially, by his sharptongued cousin Mary.

The two others who wander in are Sky, who is supposed to be renovating the place and has just been thrown out of his own house by Lawrence's sister to whom he is married, and Amanda, with whom Lawrence is in love and to whom he unexpectedly proposes.

All the characters have secrets to keep, all of them revealed to humorously discomforting effect. The biggest surprise, concerning his plans for the immediate future, is sprang by Lawrence himself, and it comes from so far out of left field as to blow a serious hole in the play's credibility. It's rivalled in this respect by the title, which turns out to refer to a sign that Lawrence once saw hung up somewhere. It has no other relevance, and it signals a dangerous taste for arbitrary whimsy.

There's some snappy writing, though, and a good instinct for extending comic tension to the limits of an audience's endurance. Jim Warren's production is well paced and well acted. Jennifer Dzialoszynski, who has done fine work at the Shaw Festival, makes Mary excessively high-speed and high-pitched, but one can see what she's getting at. As Lawrence, Daniel Pagett commands the stage by being ineffectual, which is quite a feat; Geoffrey Pounsett performs the same trick in reverse, finding the weakness in Sky who prides himself on practicality; and as Amanda, Caroline Toal is appealing which is all her role asks of her. There is an ongoing metaphor that involves all the quartet trying to watch the Stanley Cup final on a dysfunctional TV; the metaphor, like the TV, fails to work.

Mine, technically a more radical piece, presents two women, identified in the program as A and B, and in the dialogue as Abigail and Bea. The chronology is scrambled, but it seems they met when A was a TA, and B was a psychology major taking A's poetry course out of necessity rather than enthusiasm. A asks B out (something that would be frowned upon were teacher and student of different genders) and a relationship develops: one in which A seems to have the upper hand but in which B may call the important shots. A has the more assertive personality (Type A in fact) but B is the one with professional prospects.

One thing this play shares with For a Good Time... is a concern with young people's bleak employment situation; A may be teaching literature, but her real interest is astronomy. The best sustained scene has B signing the lease for a swish new apartment, something of which A is rapturously in favour of until she still considers what it signifies for their inter-personal dynamics. These, it's made clear, exist on the same shifting scale as those of any other menage; it's a constant battle of wills from which sex, graphically and gracefully presented, provides only a temporary diversion and of which it may well be an illustration.

Jenna Harris wrote the play, and she also plays B, very well, as 70% gaucherie and 30% assurance; a speech about how it feels to be a perambulating wallflower at a social gathering strikes especially home as both text and performance. As the more dominating A, Michelle Polak has paradoxically the less rewarding or certainly the less varied role, but she, too, does well. The physical production, by Clinton Walker, is very striking, on a set whose elements are symbolically constructed of books.

The play cuts back and forth between the couple's experiences at home, in school, at bars and clubs, and at a salsa class; the changes keep us on our toes but are not all that helpful.

To show what can be done with a relationship story, told chronologically but seamlessly, one scene melting into the next, last season's triumphant production of Lungs has returned. The acting (Lesley Faulkner, Brendan Gall), the spartan direction (Weyni Mengesha) and the writing (Duncan Macmillan) are as dazzling and ultimately as moving as before.

The Next Stage Theatre Festival runs at the Factory Theatre through Jan. 18; Lungs runs at the Tarragon Extra Space through Jan. 25.

Fraser Elsdon / Jenna Harris and Michelle Polak star in Mine.
2015-01-17-prince-of-thieves-and-men-in-:
So, there's this medieval thug called Robin Hood and he robs the rich. Period. He's obviously operating on the sensible maxim espoused by thieves of a later generation, that that's where the money is. He does not give any of the proceeds to the poor. That, according to the erudite program note to Mirvish Productions' The Heart of Robin Hood, a sentimental 16th-century addition to the original legend. In the show itself it's the brainwave of Marion, daughter of the Duke of York, who has heard of Robin's activities in the forest and has jumped to the conclusion that he must be acting benevolently. Where she can have got this idea is unclear; the romances couldn't have been written yet.

The Heart of Robin Hood is in fact a mess, with a few creative flashes. It was written by David Farr and directed by Gisli Orn Gar[eth]arsson: the same team that brought us last year's brilliant Metamorphosis. They aren't exactly repeating themselves; their new show is as relentlessly upbeat as its predecessor was devastatingly down.

There is the same emphasis on spectacular acrobatics, but here they aren't all executed by one transmogrified central character. This time everybody does it: goodies, baddies and in-betweens. The all-green set is dominated by a huge, practically vertical back wall. The preferred method of entrance is for the characters to appear from nowhere and slide down it. The first time this happens, it's astonishing. The subsequent hundred times it's still impressive, but decreasingly so. People also, with less intrepidity, climb up and down, which looks easier but may be harder. There are other visual trompes l'oeil scattered through the evening; I especially liked the duck that turns out to have unsuspected properties. As for plot: Marion ventures into the forest, and is duly disillusioned when Robin's robbers rob her. She returns, though, this time in male disguise, and sets up her own band public-spirited outlaws. She has a personal motive for going into the woods; she wants to avoid marriage to Prince John. He's taxing the peasantry so that he can raise an army to depose his brother King Richard the Lionheart, who is off on a crusade; or, as somebody puts it, fighting a meaningless war in the Middle East.

Marion, of course, falls for Robin at first sight, and he for her, though he's reluctant to admit it. He also finds her male alter ego easy to talk to, though as professional rivals they get off on several wrong feet. After they and others have outwitted John, the future king slinks off, threatening like Malvolio to be revenged on the whole pack of them. He doesn't put it in quite those words, but closely enough, as if to remind us that this show originated in Britain with the Royal Shakespeare Company, which I hope performed it with more finesse, though I wouldn't bet on it.

The script is full of Shakespeare allusions. Marion, like Kate in The Taming of the Shrew, has a petulant younger sister who can't be married until she herself is disposed of; like Viola in Twelfth Night she tells her lover, in male disguise, about her feelings as a woman; and like Rosalind in As You Like It, she flees to the forest accompanied by a jester and plays teasing verbal games with the object of her affections. Farr's script has a some nice moments in dealing with this last situation, but doesn't have the consistent wit to carry it off. The good jokes are few and very far-between.

Instead of jokes, there's jokiness. A country-rock band, Parsonsfield, provides songs whose relevance might be easier to judge if the words were distinguishable. As it is, the musicians seem to exist so that the real characters can draw attention to their non-dramatic presence. Haven't we had enough by now of shows that mock their own identity without creating one? The style is somewhere between Ross Petty and Monty Python, without the comic energy of either. Energy is not the same thing as mere physicality; the fights here are all done balletically, draining them of any sense of danger or excitement. Perhaps in compensation, there are scenes of nastiness. A lord has his tongue torn out. A tax-evader's hanged body is displayed, and John pursues a vendetta against the malefactor's two small children, one of whom is threatened with onstage decapitation. It seems the show wants to be taken seriously as well.

But it can't be, if only because, at the heart of The Heart of Robin Hood, there's a void, Gabriel Ebert's Robin having to oscillate between brute and patsy with nothing in between. It's Izzie Steele's Marion who makes all of the running, playing with guts and grace, and a self-deprecating humour in switching between genders; indeed this Maid outdoes even Rosalind, being not only smarter than her man but tougher. The production's final image is lovely. But it doesn't atone.

The Heart of Robin Hood runs through March 1 at the Royal Alexandra Theatre.
2015-01-22-for-the-birds-chekhov-s-the-s:
Theatre Review

The Seagull Berkley Street Theatre

It was once said - by Peter Ustinov, who was half-Russian himself - that teamwork and Chekhov are incompatible. It depends what you mean by teamwork. Its true that Chekhov, who learned his dramatic craft by writing farces, created self-absorbed characters who seldom understand or truly communicate with one another. They do, though, share a space. As a group, they find themselves in shared situations; as individuals, each reacts in his or her own way. Chris Abraham's production of The Seagull, for Crow's Theatre, honours both halves of the equation. It has a Grade A cast, each of them a distinct personality, with a particular rhythm. Those rhythms, however, are symphonically combined. In that sense, these actors are a team.

We see this in its purest form in the first act. All 10 of the plays characters are onstage. One of them has written a play of his own, another is performing it, and the other eight are their invited spectators, responding in eight identifiably different ways. When we, the real audience, file in we find Konstantin, the playwright within-the play, fussing nervously over last-minute preparations. His impromptu theatre is his mothers lakeside estate. She is Irina Arkadina, celebrated Russian actress, who greets her son's "experimental" play with barely concealed impatience, as if she were professionally threatened by it; we can sense her mentally fidgeting even while physically she's in gracious repose. Her lover Trigorin, successful novelist, says barely a word (hell make up for it later), and projects polite, slightly embarrassed boredom. Dorn, doctor and ladies man, seems genuinely fascinated.

So does Irina's brother Sorin, though he may mostly be motivated by avuncular affection. Masha, addicted to vodka and snuff, also loves Konstantin, unrequitedly, and is accordingly jealous of Nina who's performing his play, without much liking or understanding it, and whom he loves, also unrequitedly. Masha has her own hapless suitor, the schoolmaster Medvenko, constantly complaining in a self-deprecating way, about his impoverished lot; he seems uncertain how to respond, as if suspecting hes there on sufferance, which he probably is. Mashas unhappy mother Polina has eyes only for the doctor, who has been dallying with her. Her husband Shamrayev, the estate manager, is a very good audience; he stands up on his seat in his enthusiasm.

Tony Nappo's Shamrayev, the best I have ever seen, is an emblem of the production's success. There are two sides to this character, and he plays them both to the limit. One is the theatre fan, trying to ingratiate himself with his employers with his genial reminiscences of great performances past; nobodys interested, but he carries on anyway, because it makes him feel good. The obverse is his behaviour whenever hes asked a favour; no, he tells the dear lady whom he's just been buttering up, she can't have horses to drive into town; and he can switch in a calculated instant from sweet reasonableness to blackmailing rage. His attitude has apparently rubbed off on his daughter; Bahia Watson delivers Mashas famous opening line about being in mourning for her life on a note of sarcastic anger that turns out to be a self-fulfilling prophecy. It isnt the subtlest of performances, but it's hard to fault it at any given moment. Certainly it's consistent with how she treats poor Medvedenko after shes deigned to marry him; and Gregory Prest makes him consistent too, resigned to a perpetual fate of walking long miles in the rain.

Anger flourishes in this Russian landscape. Unusually and refreshingly, it fuels Philip Riccios electric Konstantin as he rails at the culture he despises and, Hamlet-like, at his mother's infatuation with a man who epitomizes it; rage, burning itself out, believably fuels his eventual suicide. Christine Horne's Nina turns out to be his opposite; oblique to begin with, an uncertainly aspiring actress, she matures when personal tragedy and professional failure hit her. She finds a lucidity in despair; she has a job to go to; she will survive. What fells Konstantin is the realization that she still loves Trigorin, of whom he is accordingly thrice-jealous. (He would die rather than admit it. And does.) Trigorin, ironically, can never acknowledge the havoc hes caused; his description to Nina of the novelists driven life is not the usual sedentary setpiece, but a roving monologue that physically mirrors the restlessness of which it speaks. Tom Rooney makes spinelessness magnetic; he surrenders into relationships. Irina, fearful of losing him, has to throw herself at her feet though Yanna McIntosh, thoroughly successful in her star-lady aspects, underplays the self-abasement: a loss, as it's one of the play's recurring themes. Its reflected, full-strength, in Polina begging Dorn to take her away with him, an entreaty with which he deals by ignoring it. In contrast to Trigorin, Tom McCamus urbane doctor is a self-aware philanderer, kind up to a point, with the courage of his lack of conviction. Tara Nicodemo's Polina shows us a subtle kind of revenge in her silence when he returns from his travels in the last act. It's hard, admittedly, to accept this Polina as old enough to be Mashas mother, just as Eric Petersons Sorin, a deliciously biting portrait of an old man feasting on his own futility, hardly seems to belong to the same age-group as his sister.

Those are minor cavils. These are 10 notable performances, enriching one another; make that 11, since Marcus Jamin does a remarkable amount with the nearsilent servant Yakov.

I do, though, have problems with the chosen script; George Calderon's century-old translation (the first English one, I believe) has been adapted by Chicago director Robert Falls; and pretty freely, to judge from the abundance of OKs and fourletter words. More importantly, Chekhov's soliloquies have gone, making Dorn sound less perceptive and Konstantin less articulately desperate. And the seagull itself has had its wings clipped. Admittedly the bird that Konstantin shoots and presents to Nina was never one of its authors best ideas, as he may have admitted by having her ask incredulously "is this a symbol?" Hornes success in her last scene may even owe something to her not having to keep talking about it. Still, it's the title, and we should be made more aware of it in the dialogue than we are. Its final personal appearance, though, is a great success. Nappo proudly presents Rooney with the stuffed bird he'd requested; Rooney, who once wrote a story about Nina and her seagull, professes not to remember it. And the sad and funny thing is that we believe him.

The Seagull runs until Feb. 8. For more information, visit canadianstage.com.

Handout / The Seagull has a Grade A cast, each of them a distinct personality, with a particular rhythm.
2015-01-24-think-big-whoa-maybe-not-that:
This week, Toronto welcomed tree plays on momentous topics, all presented with a high level of skill - and all suffering from a lack of focus.

Waiting Room, by Diane Flacks, begins silently and brilliantly. A married couple are in the hospital area of the title, nervous and impatient, doing everything but talk to one another. We wonder which of them is the patient and which the support. When they start talking, though, they refer to an unseen her, who turns out to be their baby daughter, who has brain cancer.

They will spend the play torn between hope and despair, getting mad at each other, and even madder at a pediatric surgeon with the worst bedside manner imaginable. This part of the play is movingly written, directed (by Richard Greenblatt), and acted; Jordan Pettle combines doggedness and impetuosity as the husband, while as the wife Michelle Monteith is devastating, naked in her pain, volcanic in her anger.

We've come to take Monteith's intensity almost for granted, but here she has the advantage of at least starting from normal, normal being something that she also does well when she gets the chance. Her character has forged a fortuitous bond with another mother whose son has been in and out of the same establishment and whom Jane Spidell plays acidulously well.

Meanwhile, on the other side of the stage, the doctor is having his own meltdown. Self-diagnosed with Alzheimers, he self-medicates, with an unlicensed experimental drug, enlisting a junior pediatrician to monitor his progress and also to keep it a secret; she has misgivings, but goes along because shes both a dedicated researcher and her boss's lover. (Ever wondered why doctors keep you waiting? It's because theyre having sex in the office.)

Trying to inject human emotion into an impossible situation, Ari Cohen and Jenny Young inevitably end up over-acting. Cohen does, though, become very moving later, even suggesting that his aloofness comes not from caring too little but from caring too much. Alone in the cast Cohen and Monteith are allowed monologues, suggesting that their roles are meant to illuminate one another, but it doesnt work out that way. The two stories overlap structurally but hardly ever emotionally. We seem to be watching two

different plays, one of them all too believable, the other anything but.

Boom, Rick Miller's new solo show, has come to the Panasonic Theatre, which I guess makes it a Panasonic Boom. The title actually refers to his parents' generation, and his show begins with brief filmed interviews with them and with a male contemporary of theirs whose relevance is kept a secret until the end. They all seem to be likable people; and, the clips over, Miller spends the rest of the show impersonating them, together with all the cultural figures who most influenced them during their Baby Boomers lifetime. Thats a lot of ground to cover, even given that, having started with VE-Day, he stops inexplicably short at the end of the 1960s.

The end result is scattershot and superficial; maybe if Miller had concentrated on his mother as a representative Canadian Boomer, his story might have had more coherence. As it is, the choice of events seems encyclopaedically arbitrary.

Technically, the show's a wonder. Miller, who directed it himself, spends most of inside a cylinder on a platform, fading in and out of view, constantly changing costume and position, seamlessly merging with David Leclerc's nonstop video footage. And of course he does all the voices. He isnt as accurate imitating real people as he once was when doing everybody from The Simpsons; his Winston Churchill and Harold Macmillan are approximate, while his Perry Como is a travesty. Hes more successful when spiritually closer to home; he does a succession of persuasive rockers, including an amazing Janis Joplin. He finishes with David Bowie, emerging to great effect from his cylindrical cocoon to do "Space Oddity." After which, and for no detectable reason, the show ends. It's true that it's touched on the space race, among many other things, but that hasnt exactly been a guiding theme.

Small Axe, from Project Humanity, is also an interview piece. Andrew Kushnir, writer, and Alan Dilworth, director, talked to gay Jamaican-Canadians; and five actors deliver, very well, verbatim excerpts from the conversations. Kushnir himself presides, talking through a microphone which he discards, as if sacrificing his own position of privilege. He, too, is gay, but white, and of Ukrainian heritage; and his efforts to establish common ground with his subjects results in his being told that it isnt about him. Fair enough; but the play continues as if it is.

Kushnir is a talented and sympathetic performer, and an autobiographical piece about his growing up and coming out in Canada might be very interesting; it's already happened, to an extent, in The Gay Heritage Project. Here, though, his self-punishment seems both excessive and distracting.

Waiting Room runs through Feb. 15 at the Tarragon; Boom through Feb. 1 at the Panasonic Theatre; Small Axe through Feb. 1 at The Theatre Centre.

David Leclerc / Boom goes the Boomers in Rick Miller's one-man show.
2015-01-31-sick-and-tired-but-not-tired-:
The problem with plays about illness is that there's no one to blame. They can hardly help being moving, but they are also frustrating. The suffering is unrelated to the sufferer, as far as any kind of cause and effect is concerned. To become dramatic, they have to shift focus away from the disease itself and on to the relationships of those affected by it.

Diane Flacks Waiting Room is a good current illustration. The patient is a cancer stricken baby, and offstage. The play succeeds to the extent that it makes us care about the childs parents, and on how much it persuades us that their current crisis exposes tensions that were latent in their marriage anyway. It fails when it goes looking for a scapegoat, providing a far-fetched parallel narrative about a pediatric surgeon battling his own self diagnosed dementia. In the new epidemic of medical drama, Sharr White's The Other Place, a recent off-Broadway success now mounted by Canadian Stage, succeeds better than most. Coincidentally, its protagonist may suffer from one or other of the two conditions presented in Waiting Room: brain cancer or early-onset Alzheimer's. Both are presented as possibilities, and it would probably count as a spoiler to reveal which one is correct. Two things keep the play afloat. One is the fact that its constructed as a psychological thriller, with liberal use of false trails and flashbacks. This turns out to have its disadvantages (you may end up feeling youve been had) but it mostly fits very nicely together and its unfolding is compelling to watch.

The other thing the play has going for it is that it too is a powerful portrait of a marriage, in this case undiluted by sub-plots. The heroine, Juliana, is a neurologist who has switched from clinical practice to shilling for pharmaceuticals. She's at a conference, promoting the benefits of (irony of ironies) a new anti-dementia drug when she feels something snap in her brain. This is a scary experience and not, we learn, an isolated one. Her husband, Ian, is an oncologist, both loving and concerned. His feelings, though, often translate into anger and frustration. For one thing, Juliana keeps insisting that they are going through a divorce, though Ian is pretty sure that they aren't.

The major skeleton in their closet is their daughter, Laurel, who left home propelled by her mothers intolerance.

For once in a disease play, character may be destiny. Julianas paranoid proclivities, it seems, go back a long way; we get to see Juliana and Laurel, in present time, talking on the phone, re-enacting a classic mother-daughter impasse. Juliana is also oppressed by the memory of another young person whom she drove away, her assistant Richard, who may or may not have been involved with Laurel. Sorry to be so vague about all this, but it's that kind of play.

I might have liked it less, had I encountered it in a production less exciting than the present one by Daniel Brooks. It features a rock-hard, attack mode performance by Tamsin Kelsey as Juliana; neither the character nor the actress ever solicit our sympathy and in consequence both, especially in the play's concluding scenes, receive it. As Ian, Jim Mezon is magnificent, radiating rage while still signalling supportiveness; Mezon, always a powerful actor but usually a quiet one, here operates at his highest decibel level ever, and its rather refreshing. There are two others in the cast. Haley McGee plays all the subsidiary females, including Laurel and a young shrink whom Julianna suspects of carrying on with her husband, and makes them all different. Joe Cobden performs the equivalent male function and makes as much of it as anyone could; his roles vary from tenuous to almost invisible, and its a surprise that an actor last seen as the lead in An Enemy of the People should have taken them on.

I'm not sure why the production begins with projections of Old Masters (we seem to have wandered into the Louvre or the Sistine Chapel) but they're certainly good to look at. Judith Bowden's settings, appropriately cool, later prove good at transforming themselves, with the cast helpfully pitching in. One of the locations gives the play its title. The Other Place is how Ian and Juliana refer to their country home - if they were Canadian it and the play would be called The Cottage - from which Laurel disappeared and which they could not bring themselves to keep.

Juliana nerves herself to re-visit it, and has an encounter with the remarkably understanding new occupant, a scene that is gripping in overall effect if suspect on details. The title can have other connotations, and the author is finally unable to restrain himself from playing games with them. He gets even cuter at the end, which has Juliana referring back to the vision of a nubile girl in a yellow bikini whom she jealously saw - or thought she saw - in the audience at the lecture that began it all. We wind up, in fact, where we came in.

This kind of facile rhyming is typical American drama, whether Broadway or off. So is the compulsion to leave us, if not with hope, then at least on a note of peace. This time, though, it almost feels earned. There isn't too much mush.

The Other Place runs through Feb. 8 at the Bluma Appel Theatre.

David Hou Haley McGee and Tamsin Kelsey star in The Other Place.
2015-02-07-a-ballet-legend-dances-in-the:
Prince Friedrich Arthur of Homburg commanded the cavalry of the German region of Brandenburg at the Battle of Fehrbellin in 1675, and defeated the invading army of Sweden by leading a charge without waiting for orders from above. That much is history; or at least historical legend. In The Prince of Homburg, an extraordinary play written in 1811, the German playwright Heinrich von Kleist took the legend and ran with it. The play is a classic in its own country, and over the past 40 years has begun to establish itself in England. It seems never to have been professionally performed here until last week, when Talk Is Free theatre in Barrie, Ont., gave it a courageous Canadian premiere. That production, the directorial debut of the renowned choreographer James Kudelka, has its final performance tonight. It's worth travelling to see.

Kleist changed the battle story by turning the Prince's victorious manoeuvre from an unauthorized act to one of actual insubordination. He'd been told at the pre-battle briefing not to make a move until instructed, but he wasn't paying attention. This is because, in the words of an old pop song, the kid's a dreamer.

We meet him at the beginning of the play, stretched out in the castle garden, in some kind of trance, plaiting himself a laurel wreath. Summoned to witness this strange sight the Elector, Brandenburg's ruler, he decides to have a little fun. He removes the wreath, entwines his own chain of office around it, and then returns it. Aroused from his halfslumber into half-waking, Friedrich catches sight of Princess Natalia, the Elector's niece, and cries out his love for her. He also finds himself in possession of Natalia's dropped glove. At which point, the Elector decides that the joke has gone quite far enough and departs, bidding the Prince to wake up and report for duty. "Victory," he says ominously, "cannot be won by dreams."

It turns out that it can, putting both ruler and ruled in uncomfortable positions. Prince Friedrich finds himself thanked and congratulated for his victory, and court-martialled for his disobedience. He is in fact condemned to death, but he takes the sentence with surprising lightheartedness. He's convinced that the judgment is for show, and that he'll be reprieved. He's only jolted out of this when he beholds his own prepared grave; the sight turns him to jelly, and he declares that in order to live, he will give up anything, including his requited love for Natalia. She, though, has her own plans.

Meanwhile, she makes a personal plea to the Elector, who was planning to marry her off as part of a treaty with the Swedes. Very well, he says in effect; if the prince wants life at the expense of honour, let him choose. We spend the last part of the play wondering which way the two men, ruler and ruled, will jump. The suspense is terrific.

Part of it is due to the fact that, once you accept the play's military ethos and its patriotic bias, there are no unsympathetic characters. We root for all of them, even when their aims seem incompatible.

Kudelka's production gets this hearteningly right, though, surprisingly given his background in ballet, it is sometimes physically awkward. Kleist was a writer with a luxuriant imagination but his plays seldom get the resources they deserve. Nick Blais' designs here are a serviceable cut above, though I wish the vital castle ramp could have been less cluttered.

Most of the men's scenes involve conference and camaraderie and these actors, largely from Stratford and Shaw, have the martial ensemble spirit down pat. These actors bring their own style. But the production can't find one for the women. Katherine Cullen as Natalia and Jean Yoon as the Elector's wife are reduced to playing line by line, with no connective tissue.

The play wakes any number of theatrical echoes, forwards and back. Its premature twin is Calderon's Life's a Dream, which I'd recommend as a future project for this theatre - or for any theatre. Natalia confronting the Elector cannot help reminding us of Isabella pleading for her brother's life in Measure for Measure. And the prince's conduct on the field is identical to that of the vainglorious Sergius, hero by accident in Shaw's Arms and the Man. Shaw, of course, treated it as comedy. So did Kleist, but he gave it the outward form of tragedy. The unsettling combination kept the play off even German stages for years. But its time has come.

Luca Ragogna / The Prince of Homburg looks like he's in a spot of trouble.
2015-02-11-making-a-farce-of-the-police:
The road may have started in 1970s Milan, but it led to 2015 Toronto. An Italian farce of relatively recent vintage has arrived on the city's stage, ruthlessly remodelled to tell a story of here and now.

Accidental Death of an Anarchist is the work of Dario Fo, veteran practitioner of a style that might be called commedia dellagitprop. (And I do mean veteran; if Soulpeppers program and my arithmetic are accurate, Fo is still writing and performing in the old country at the age of 89.) This play was inspired, or perhaps provoked, by the death in Milanese police custody of an admitted anarchist suspected of massacre by arson. During his interrogation he mysteriously fell out of a fourth-floor window. His death was declared to be suicide, and the policemen concerned walked away unindicted. Ring any bells?

In Soulpepper's production they ring loud if not always clear. Ravi Jain, directing, and Paula Wing, dramaturging, have recast Fo's carabinieri as Canadian cops, apparently graduated from a police academy with ancestral ties to Keystone; some are less corrupt or incompetent than others, but all are manic. The one male civilian present outdoes them all in that respect, but the difference is that he does it on purpose. Hes known as the Madman, and hes been brought in on a charge of Compulsive Imitation; he keeps pretending to be other people. Left alone, he chances on the files from a suspicious case of Anarchist Defenestration; posing as an investigating judge, he's able to get the station's senior brass to confess. Then, by offering to get them out of the pit hes dug for them, he has them digging it even deeper.

Some of the physical comedy in Jains production is inspired, especially an extended acrobatic sequence built on the possibility of the top cops hurling themselves out of the window. They're subsequently induced to sing a rousing chorus of a revolutionary anthem, and that's funny, too, though turning it into an audience singalong smacks of excess anxiety, and not just on the characters part.

Kawa Ada as the Madman gives something of a virtuoso performance, but only something. The role of this compulsive chameleon calls for the quick-change vocal gymnastics of a Robin Williams plus the wisecracking smarts of a Groucho Marx, which is a tall double order; Ada fills it with tremendous pace, but the speed of his transitions, especially in his early scenes, too often obscures what theyre transitioning to. That goes, too, for the production as a whole; it's so intent on tying the actors in knots, vocal and physical, that we lose sight of what the facts of the case might actually be.

That's part of a larger problem. Fo based his play closely on actual recent events; that gave it its kick. This adaptation tries for something similar, but though Canada, like

the U.S., has certainly had its recent share of suspect police activity, it hasn't had a specific incident quite like this one. So it all seems frivolous; and it isn't made any less so by a continuous stream of jokey local references.

To redress the balance Ada, near the end of the show, steps out of character and lectures us on how the media feed us minor scandals to keep our minds off major ones. The break of convention has a momentary shock impact but, apart from being factually dubious it devalues the rest of the play. Are the "accidental death" and its cover-up also of minor importance? If not, why not? If so, why have we been bothered?

Accidental Death of an Anarchist runs until Feb. 21 at the Young Centre in Toronto.
2015-02-19-into-the-abyss-but-first-some:
Well into the 20th century, the Victorians Robert Browning and Elizabeth Barrett Browning were cited in the textbooks as the only major English poets to have been married to one another. Their ownership of the marital Parnassus wasn't to be challenged until the union of Ted Hughes and Sylvia Plath.

But while the Hughes-Plath marriage was notoriously stormy, and eventually tragic, the Brownings relationship was popularly regarded as an idyllic meeting of minds and talents: celebrated in such things as the play and movie The Barretts of Wimpole Street and the musical Robert and Elizabeth. Now here, to shatter the idyll, comes Florence Gibson Mac-Donald with her play How Do I Love Thee? Her Robert and Elizabeth could give Ted and Sylvia a good, or bad, run for their money.

The title comes from Mrs. Brownings most famous poem; Elizabeth gets to count the ways quite late in the play, and the recitation, passionately done, is all the more moving for coming at a point where what might seem to be uppermost in both their minds is How Do I Hate Thee? Their early encounters have indeed been idyllic, conducted initially by letter. Robert's attention is drawn to something nice that Elizabeth has written about his work, and soon he's at her door and all over her sofa.

Although shes self-cast as a shut-in and invalid, her dashing young idol has her out and about in London, and even persuades her to elope with him to his beloved Italy. MacDonalds poets speak, for the most part, in her own rich prose, which is both worthy of them and gratifying for us.

Once they've set up house in Florence, it all falls apart: the relationship and, I'm afraid, the play. There are two subsidiary characters. One is John Kenyon, the couples mutual friend who brings them together; left behind in London, he necessarily fades out. Whereas he seems to love the pair mainly for their poems, Wilson, Elizabeths maid, loves the poems - Elizabeth's anyway - because it's her mistress, whom she calls "mum," whos written them.

The first, very telling, moments of the play find Elizabeth rhapsodizing on a swing; then Wilson creeps up behind her and administers what we subsequently discover to be a cocktail of laudanum, morphine and opium.

Wilson believes the drugs necessary to Elizabeths writing; so, even more damagingly, does Elizabeth herself; and, most distressingly, so apparently does the play. Its second act becomes the chronicle of Elizabeth's addiction, and Robert's increasingly angry and desperate attempts to wean of her off it (and to stop the apothecarys bills from bankrupting them). Cold turkey proves disastrous, and the lady wont keep to a regimen of gradual withdrawal. Two of the most monotonous things in the world are drug addiction and marital quarrels; both just keep repeating themselves, and so does the play.

One taunt that Elizabeth keeps throwing at Robert is that she's the one who's writing all the successful verse. This is outrageously onesided, but the play seems to agree with her; its notable that two of her major works, Sonnets from the Portuguese and Aurora Leigh, get mentioned by name, but none of his. The idea seems to be to make her a feminist heroine at his expense. (But dont trust me; I'd back Ted Hughes against Sylvia Plath.) Lurking somewhere in the background is Elizabeth's controlling monster of a father; and its frustrating that, though we often hear about him, we never meet him.

Ken Gasss production, for his Canadian Rep Theatre, is well manoeuvred and well acted. Irene Poole, whose intensity in other roles has sometimes seemed a bit much, gives a wonderfully uninhibited but still splendidly controlled performance as Elizabeth, as unbridled in joyous awakening as in rage and pain; her evocation of orgasm-through-verse is delicious.

Matthew Edison's Robert grows from fuzzy romantic symbol to passionate maturity. David Schurmann is an agreeable John, while Nora McLellan's Wilson gives a triumphant demonstration of the many possibilities of keeping mum.

Abyss is a translation by Maria Milisavljevic, of her own award-winning 2013 play. Its a three-hander, set in the authors native Germany, whose unnamed narrator has a former lover and current roommate called Vlado, a traumatized exile from the former Yugoslavia, and a sister called Sophia.

Vlado's present girlfriend disappears, and the play tells of the trio's increasingly desperate attempts to find her, despite getting minimal help from the police (Sophia) or disdaining it altogether (Vlado).

As an atmospheric thriller, it pretty much succeeds, despite getting murky towards the end. But it also seems meant as a metaphor for the traumatic aftermath of the Balkans war, and here it takes far too much for granted, not helped by verbal mannerism (Vlado keeps being referred to as "the one who finds") and gratuitous sub-plots (Vlado is jealous of the narrator's new boyfriend, played by the same actor).

It's given a very taut production by Richard Rose, the three actors whirling and writhing while holding and relinquishing hands. Cara Pifko is a most lucid and sympathetic storyteller; Gord Rand is magnetically hollow-eyed and hollow-souled; and Sarah Sherman copes in a businesslike fashion with a role that requires her to interrupt the action periodically with instructions on how to kill and skin a rabbit or, by sinister extension, a person.

How Do I Love Thee? runs through Feb. 22 at the Berkeley Street Theatre Upstairs in Toronto; Abyss runs through March 15 at the Tarragon Extraspace in Toronto.
2015-02-20-the-year-of-the-biopic:
Eight films are competing on Sunday for the Best Picture Academy Award. Four of them are biographical. That's a record.

Somewhere behind the movies', and the movie public's, fascination with true-life stories, is the belief that dramas are better for you if they are about people who actually existed. The reality factor makes a happy ending feel happier, a sad one sadder and both more ennobling. If the protagonist is heroic, and most are in some way, then we get to share vicariously in the heroism. Movies have always been about uplift.

We have The Imitation Game, with Benedict Cumberbatch as Alan Turing, famous for codecracking; and The Theory of Everything, with Eddie Redmayne as Stephen Hawking, famous for scientific genius combined with appalling physical disability; and Selma, with David Oyelowo as Martin Luther King, famous for freedom; and - though here the uplift is more controversial - American Sniper, with Bradley Cooper as Chris Kyle, famous for killing.

Even two of the other nominees might be described as biographically inflected; Birdman plays off the parallels between the fictitious career of its protagonist, formerly famous for acting superheroes, and the real career of Michael Keaton who plays him, while Boyhood is in part a meditation on the idea of biography, with its actors literally aging alongside the imaginary and not-at-all-famous people they portray.

Why the biopic should have crested this year is anybody's guess, but the genre itself is a venerable Hollywood tradition. The very first batch of Oscar nominees for Best Picture in 1929 included The Patriot, which, perhaps surprisingly, was not about George Washington or Abraham Lincoln, but about Paul I, the 18th-century Tsar of Russia who could hardly have been a household name, at least not in American households. Before long, however, both the studios and the academy were going more mainstream; nominated early talkies included Disraeli and The Private Life of Henry VIII, testifying to the industry's, and maybe the nation's, enduring belief that history is something that happens in England.

The success of the Turing and Hawking pictures certainly testifies to that; as also, in a bizarre way, does the fact that Selma, that most American of stories, has British actors playing both MLK and LBJ. Maybe it's some kind of nationalist backlash that has kept both Oyelowo and Tom Wilkinson from getting acting nominations, though both deserve them.

Both Cumberbatch and Redmayne are up for Best Actor, but of course they're Britons playing Britons. Cumberbatch is a biographical specialist. As well as playing Turing, he was Hawking (in a 2004 TV movie called Stephen Hawking) long before Redmayne was Hawking, and he was Julian Assange in the 2013 film The Fifth Estate. He's also played Vincent Van Gogh.

Two things can be guaranteed about any biographical or historical film: It will be attacked for getting facts wrong and defended on the grounds that drama necessitates the cutting of corners. The Imitation Game and The Theory of Everything have been especially vulnerable here, because they're both about scientists, and other scientists have been piling on, denouncing simplifications and falsifications. The simplifications are probably inevitable; science is a difficult movie subject because its practitioners must spend a lot of time talking about things the audience doesn't understand.

The experts have been especially scathing about The Imitation Game, even though - or perhaps because - on a lineby-line basis, it contains more technical dialogue than The Theory of Everything. It's also dialogue that should, on the face of it, be the more viscerally exciting. Hawking's discoveries about black holes weren't going to have any immediate effect on anybody's existence; Turing's breaking of the Nazis' war codes was literally a matter of life and death.

According to the film, he personally won the war. And yet it all rings false. It's written and shot like one of those stiff-upper British war movies that proliferated in the 1950s, only not as well. It grabs at cliches. It can't just present us with the moral dilemma of allowing Allied vessels to sink, so as not to tip off the enemy that they'd been deciphered; it has to give one of Turing's team a brother on one of the doomed ships and have him plead hysterically that it be spared. It has to drag in a historically unrelated spy plot and make a Blimpish caricature of Turing's unsympathetic superior.

It also, according to an article in The New York Review of Books, makes Turing himself far more of a socially clueless loner than he actually was, and more closeted a homosexual than he actually was. It's hard to believe that the latter subject could be considered taboo in a modern movie, so the alterations have to be put down to somebody's mistaken idea of what would seem dramatic. I don't think the filmmakers were trying to dumb anything down; I think they just couldn't help themselves. Even without the objections of the professionals, the science rings false because the character rings false.

The Theory of Everything starts with the advantage that the main character's life is as interesting as the science. That Hawking, who's now 71, has so triumphantly survived after being diagnosed with ALS and given two years to live, is phenomenal in itself.

Both Selma and The Imitation Game focus on specific crucial periods in their heroes' careers. That's the usual way of doing things, and a reasonable one. It goes back to The Story of Louis Pasteur and The Life of Emile Zola, formative back-to-back biopics (from 1936 and 1937 respectively), both starring Paul Muni, the Benedict Cumberbatch of his day, and both Oscar contenders. In '36, Muni won but the film didn't; in '37, it was the other way around. Between them, they set the image of the virtuous prestige picture. And both, despite their all-encompassing titles, concentrated on key moments: on Pasteur's triumph in persuading the world of the truth about microbes, on Zola's valiant advocacy in the Dreyfus case.

The Theory of Everything, though, gives us the whole life, because it's the endurance that's important; it belongs in the category of stuff that you couldn't make up, but that we know they didn't have to; therefore we accept it. Foreknowledge here is moving in itself; the film tears your heart out even in its lyrical earlier sequences when Hawking is courting his soon-to-be wife. It does follow the Muni movies in the sense of being a man-and-wife story, and in doing so, it skirts sentimentality. However, just when you think that Felicity Jones' radiantly sensible Jane Hawking is too self-sacrificing to be true, she develops wants and resentments. This is a love-and-marriage story that includes divorce.

The science is mostly pushed to one side (the movie's title is overreaching), but we believe what we're told about it because we believe the rest. There's a notorious tradition of actors getting prizes for playing characters with disabilities, the more severe the better, and by that yardstick, Redmayne should have it made, but he's remarkable anyway, communicating volumes through the smile around his eyes.

Were I an academy member, I might well vote for him. Though I might abstain altogether, to protest the fact that in this year of biopics, the best of them all has been shut out. Scientists may be hard subjects for the screen, but artists are impossible. Has there ever been a first-rate movie about a great author? (Shakespeare in Love doesn't count. It's a fantasy and it wears its artifice cheerfully on its sleeve.)

But there's one category of artist that's an exception: painters. And Mike Leigh's Mr. Turner was here to prove it. Watching a writer writing is about as exciting as - well, as watching paint dry. But you can watch a painter painting, especially if he applies the final strokes when the picture is actually being exhibited, as Turner does in the film and as, it's been attested, he did in life. You can show the finished works themselves, and reflect them in your own visual style, as Leigh does. You can recreate a society, and have it frame a central performance, like Timothy Spall's, that makes few concessions to loveability and none to victimhood. You can also sacrifice any chance of an Academy Award. I wouldn't say that Mr. Turner is too good for Hollywood, but I suspect that it's too honest.

National Post robert.cushman@hotmail.com

2015-02-21-who-ya-gonna-call-angela-lans:
Twice in Blithe Spirit, Angela Lansbury as Madame Arcati goes into a trance. The process involves traversing the stage while executing an Egyptian sand dance, minus the sand. As the madame herself says, its an exhausting process but a stimulating one, and besides, its her job. She's a medium, a happy one, and there are times when a trance may be the only way of raising a spirit or, as is later required, banishing one. Or two. She certainly raises our spirits. Lansbury, whose Mama Rose in Gypsy was the greatest performance I have ever seen in a musical and one of the greatest performances of any kind, doesn't have to explore as extensive a technical or emotional terrain in this role, but she brings to it the same commitment, the same acceptance of an extravagant character on the characters own terms. Not that Madame Arcati, as Lansbury plays her, would ever think of herself as extravagant; shes a disciplined professional who relishes her work, just as she relishes a long bike ride or a dry martini, but who approaches it with the utmost seriousness. Sadly accustomed to skeptics, she faces them down, politely but witheringly, with a sharp word or dismissive glance. She rules the room.

Lansbury is 89; it seems obligatory to mention it. This production of Noel Coward's spectral comedy is in fact a double triumph for octogenarians, since Michael Blakemore has staged it with the care and flair that have characterized his work since he began directing in the 1960s. A distinguishing feature of his productions is that they never confuse pace with rush; a former actor himself, he gives his performers room to breathe, to establish themselves and to build relationships. It's evident here from the opening moments, which find Susan Louise OConnor as Edith the maid stopped in her tracks through the living room by the sight of the billowing window curtains, disturbed by a breeze from who knows where: long-range preparation for her otherwise unaccountable metamorphosis into psychic sidekick. She also has, when her employer tips her at the end, a delightful moment of silent double entendre that Ive never encountered before.

Her boss is Charles Condomine, the researching novelist whose late first wife, Elvira, is summoned by seance, to the discomfiture of her successor, Ruth. Charles is the play's pacemaker, the one whose reactions steer the action. Charles Edwards finds an enormous amount of wit in a role that Coward himself thought too boring to play; he also finds a remarkable amount of feeling. Charlotte Parry is an unusually complex Ruth, and the two of them paint a persuasive picture of a cool, companionable marriage more troubled than either will admit. Conversely, there's a far greater sexual charge than usual to Charles scenes with the revenante Elvira, even though Jemima Rooper doesnt go much beyond the seductive throatiness that shows why the lady is a vamp. This is the first time I have ever believed in the existence of the past lovers whose names the characters keep hurling at one another.

The later parts of the play remain undisguisably drawn-out, and I doubt if Madame Arcati herself could explain the concluding comings and goings to my satisfaction, but all around this is the blithest Blithe Spirit I have seen.

In one of the numberless vignettes that make up The Dining Room, a young WASP student informs his old WASP aunt, whom he's been quizzing about tableware, that she is the object of his anthropological class project. She throws him out of the house, with a saltiness of language surprising in one of her breeding. A.R. Gurney's 1982 play is itself an anthropological study: an investigation of how the welloff lived in the northeastern United States; the earliest identifiable date is the 1920s, the latest is what would, when the play was new, have been now. Once families gathered around the dining table to eat and talk; now teenagers deface the old rituals or new owners devise ways of carving the room up.

The set is unchanging, but the room is generic; or at least, if its specific the house must have changed hands at a dizzying rate - which, to judge from some of the elders insistence on continuity, it can't have done.

The chronology leapfrogs; scenes occasionally overlap. The dining room outwears its usefulness as a symbol; some of the scenes, including an affecting one about a mother's dementia, could happen anywhere.

At times, with its abrupt series of crises, it seems like a succession of soap-opera clips without the vital ingredient of to be continued. Nor is it as critical its own world, either positively or negatively, as it purports to be. But its well-written, and Joseph Zieglers Soulpepper production is beautifully tuned.

Six actors play between them more than 50 roles; there's no gender-bending but there's plenty of age-swapping; I never thought to see Sarah Wilson playing Brenda Robins mother. Derek Boyes is appropriately boyish, even (or especially) when playing an adulterous husband; Jeff Lillico excellently plays a series of squirming adolescents, though hes less happy as a paterfamilias, in what is admittedly a cartooned scene out of step with everything else.

Courtney Ch'ng Lancaster drives deep as a divorced daughter, seeking succour in the family nest. Diego Matamoros has fun in his small-boy roles, and more than fun in his grown-up ones, including an affectionate family tyrant (well, one assumes he's affectionate) inveighing against the New Deal before it's happened. All the actors are company regulars, and knowing them so well adds to the attraction of the quick changes.

In a world where, in the words of the song, "Everybody Ought to Have a Maid," each of the actresses gets to play one; and their roles, like their sister's in Blithe Spirit, say a lot, even or especially when silent.

Blithe Spirit runs through March 15 at the Princess of Wales Theatre; The Dining Room runs through March 7 at the Young Centre.

2015-02-28-enjoy-the-party-excuse-the-gu:
There are two musicals and a poem called The Wild Party. The poem, rhyming coupleted, was published in 1926; it's the work of a New Yorker writer, Joseph Moncure March, and it's a Jazz Age wallow, a fascinated deadpan view of a louche backstage world where everything was publicly Prohibited and privately indulged.
