By some quirk of fate or rights availability, the two musicals based on the poem both debuted in New York in 2000, one off Broadway, the other on. By some other but probably similar quirk, it's taken another 15 years for either musical to be presented in Toronto. But now, finally, and courtesy of the Acting Up Stage and Obsidian companies, we have a production of the Broadway one, the more adventurous, musically and theatrically, of the two. It's an evening that starts out terrific but gradually runs out of steam, even while remaining steamy.

"Queenie was a blond, and her age stood still /And she danced twice a day in vaudeville." So begins March's poem, and so also begins Michael John LaChiusa's musical; he wrote the lyrics and music, which are practically continuous, and collaborated with George C. Wolfe on what there is of a book. The scene-setting opening number is performed by the full company, louche and loud and scornful and aggressive.

We meet Queenie and her boyfriend Burrs, who's also in the theatrical profession; he has a blackface act. Queenie asks Burrs to make some coffee; his reply is to threaten to beat her up. She says she'd like to throw a party, and that goes down much better. All their friends attend and a few of their enemies, most of them performers of one kind or another, and all of them sexually or professionally on the make. In its use of showbiz as metaphor, and its unwaveringly acrid tone, the show does for 1920s New York what Chicago does for Chicago. It also suffers from the same encroaching weakness; it tells us so unrelentingly how rotten everyone is, that it leaves itself no place to go.

The score, unlike Chicago's, doesn't go in much for straightforward pastiche. LaChiusa has his own style: his music, in its mocking mordancy, sounds like a George Grosz painting looks. There's a matching visual style to Robert McQueen's production, designed by Michael Gianfrancesco, costumed by Alex Amini, lit by Kimberly Purtell and choreographed by Stephanie Graham. Their apparently seamless collaboration is matched by that of the performers, so electrically confident as an ensemble, that we wait eagerly for them to declare themselves as individuals. Some of them do.

Queenie, who "was sexually ambitious," is played by Cara Ricketts, a usually fine actress in what appears to be her first musical. Her singing doesn't always get across; she also seems vulnerable from the outset, rather than becoming so, which hurts the show's most important narrative arc. Her best moment is a beautiful anomaly, for her and for LaChiusa's score; Queenie, to her own surprise, has fallen in love with an equally surprised gigolo, stylishly played by Dan Chameroy, and on the classic urban-pastoral setting of a fire escape, they share a guardedly rapturous duet. This sends her official lover, into a fury of jealousy; Burrs, as played by Daren A. Herbert, burns up the stage.

He has other reasons to feels incendiary; in this production, though not in the New York original, both Queenie and Burrs are black. So her blondness becomes more piquant, and his enforced blackface - as with many real black performers of the time, including the great Bert Williams - more grotesquely explosive.

"Uptown is looking more like downtown," sing a black voice-and-piano duo, who provide the party's official entertainment. "Black folks are sounding more like white folks /who are sounding more like black folks every day." The production reinforces their point, though in the reality of the time, they would probably have been the only blacks present, hired as cafe society's pet exotics. As brothers, they're biliously jealous of one another; by J. Cameron Barnett and David Lopez hit all the right buttons, musically and dramatically. Their counterparts, played with matching pungency by Josh Epstein and Larry Mannell, are a couple of Jews, would-be producers, both of them called Gold-something-or-other and set on changing that.

There are other arresting performances by Sterling Jarvis as a boxer, another kind of pet exotic, and Stephen Patterson as a playboy, sexually and socially voracious: intellectually to, if name-dropping counts.

The women blur, whether they're arrogant lesbians ("I made Alice B. Toklas cry"), exploited ingenues or jealous leading ladies; some are vague in outline, others short on detail. Susan Gilmour, as a desperate aging star, comes off best, Queenie's amorous rival is the weakest. Here, the cast's weaknesses conspire with those of the material. None of the characters are what you would call likable, but the men are at least interesting; still, when the show belatedly moves from genrepainting to narrative, it's hard to care, especially when the story turns to mayhem. (Chicago, never my favourite show, nevertheless knew better than to even try to move us.)

Involvement is further hampered by too many of the lyrics being indistinguishable, not because they're too soft but because they're too loud. Apart from this matter of balance, Bob Foster's musical direction is scintillating. There is a huge amount of talent at work here, but you have to sort through it.

The Wild Party runs through March 8 at the Berkeley Street Theatre.

Racheal McCaig Photography / Judging by this photo, The Wild Party lives up to its title.
2015-03-07-taking-it-from-the-top:
I have now seen Once twice. The Broadway-Irish musical was first in Toronto in its New York production, touring edition. It's now returned, but with a specially recruited all-Canadian cast. Honours between the two versions are more or less even. What was good about the show remains excellent. What was flawed stands out more sharply.

To begin at the beginning. Once may have the most charming opening of any musical since the beautiful mornin' of Oklahoma! We are in a Dublin pub, magically rendered in Bob Crowley's set-design, and full of music. Some lucky or intrepid audience members are invited on stage for a glass. After they have been returned to their seats, the cast members take over for more riotous renditions of songs from the catalogues of those great composers Trad, and Anon. Almost imperceptibly, we slide into the main action, when one of the characters is persuaded to give out with a song of his own. He's maybe shy, maybe just uncommunicative. But he does communicate to one chance hearer, a young woman with an accent that we discover to be Czech. She's more than impressed.

Guy tells Girl (those are the only names we ever have for them) that his day job is repairing vacuum cleaners. She says that's lucky as she has a vacuum cleaner that needs repairing. And so a relationship is born: undeclared love at first sight. Girl tells Guy that he should take his songwriting seriously, should move to New York, try to get a record deal. (She makes it all sound so easy.) She even offers to write lyrics for tunes of his that don't yet have them. Two things stand in the way of her becoming an active part of the dream. One is that she is married, with a sixyear-old daughter, and that her absent husband might reappear at any moment. The other is that he has an exgirlfriend whom he has yet to get over and who is in New York already.

Guy and Girl are inspired by, if not literally based on, the real-life songwriting partnership of Glen Hansard and Marketa Irglova; their songs are the score. Ian Lake, the new Guy, can't match his predecessor as a singer but surpasses him as an actor, conveying the raw pain of a recent breakup, and the bemused joy of finding someone to help heal it. Trish Lindstrom's Girl also comes with bitter baggage, and a practicality that enables her to rise above it. Her principal project is to secure the money, time and personnel that will enable Guy to make a demo. In plot terms, that's about all that happens, and the show has to be filled out with subplots involving others.

It turns out that just about everybody Guy and Girl knows can play an instrument of some kind: a state of affairs that may or may not be commonplace in Dublin, but that dovetails with the casting of the show; everybody involved is both actor and musician. When it comes to the climactic studio session, Girl plays piano herself, two of her expat relatives play drums and guitar, her volatile music-store employer also plays guitar and supplies the drum-kit (a source of manufactured tension in the second act), and the bank manager who's been cajoled into advancing the cash doubles on cello.

Laurie Murdoch gives an affectingly restrained performance as Guy's widowed Da; Brendan Wall has little to do as the studio manager, but he, too, is wonderful, rampaging through a ditty that once enjoyed pop-hit status in a version called The Thing.

I much preferred these old-time interpolations to the songs written by Hansard and Irglova, misty folk-pop creations that trade heavily on being autobiographical and thus, in some sense, "true" - a notion that's been responsible for a lot of bad songwriting. The only number here with stagefilling size is "When Your Mind's Made Up," the one we see and hear being done at the demo; Lake's does a passionate lead vocal, and the others support him with an intensity that belies the amateur status we are told they have; put it down to the transforming powers of music and theatre.

The direction (John Tiffany) and the choreography (Steven Hoggett) remain excellent; the script (Enda Walsh) is, as intended, a love letter to Ireland. The resolution of the love story, though, has become problematic. The first time around I thought it honestly ambiguous; this time, it feels merely inconclusive. We're left with a feeling of, "Is that all?" Having been eased beautifully into the show, we're ushered very abruptly out of it.

Once runs through May 31 at the Ed Mirvish Theatre.
2015-03-14-a-house-divided-molly-parker-:
I don't know what Harper Regan is about. That doesn't stop it from being both interesting and entertaining. But it does make it frustrating.

I know who it's about. It's about a young-middle-aged Englishwoman, the oddly named title figure, who takes unheralded leave of her home and immediate family to attend the deathbed of her father, in another town; and who during her absence discovers things about herself and others, some of which she would rather not have known.

The play's production by CanadianStage is also about introducing us to the work of Simon Stephens, the prolific young British dramatist who here demonstrates an impressive ability to construct tense encounters between characters who always seem to be at rightangles with one another; they oppose, sometimes violently, but they never quite confront. It's also about CanStage's repatriation, to Canada and to the stage, of Molly Parker, celebrated for her role in House of Cards, except in my house ,where she's celebrated for her role in Deadwood.

This, we are told, is only the second time in a 25-year career that Parker has appeared on a stage. I'm hidebound enough to find it shocking that a serious actor should become a star without a thorough theatrical grounding; but Parker takes to the boards as if she'd spent her whole career there. She does so, too, in a particularly demanding role. Most of the play's scenes are duologues, and Harper is in every one of them. But she seldom takes the initiative. She reacts, and Parker, apart from proving excellent at wry vocal colouring, imposes herself through stillness. At least she does after an opening scene in which she

doesn't seem to know what to do with her hands. But even this could be characterization; Harper is in an embarrassing situation, asking for compassionate leave from a boss who refuses to grant it. Hardee T. Lineham plays him with a manic stridency that seems excessive at the time but is justified in retrospect when someone describes him as "weird." His weirdness includes hardly listening to Harper, but instead rattling on about his own obsessions, which include young people who live their lives on the Internet or in their headphones. Or of course both. We seem to be set up for two well-worn British theatrical forms: the drama of noncommunication and the stateof-the-nation play. Matthew Jocelyn's production honours the first category; he gives us a stark and stylized staging in which actors sit in the halflight between their scenes, the scenes themselves being played on a newly constructed forestage - for which relief from the Bluma Appel's customary remoteness, much thanks. The nation, though, is nowhere to be seen, or rather nowhere to be heard; Canadian actors are generally wizards at English accents (see the Shaw Festival, any time) but they make no attempts at them here.

This is especially damaging, since the play switches between two distinct parts of the country. Harper lives, with her husband Seth and their daughter Sarah, in the extreme west end of London, at Uxbridge (one of those place-names guaranteed to get a laugh from an English audience for reasons incomprehensible to everyone else). They moved there after some scandalous allegations about Seth made their original home-life intolerable. They used to live up north, in Stockport near Manchester, and it's to there that Harper, risking unemployment, repairs to see her father (she's too late) and to confront her mother, who tells her things about both their partners that she would prefer not to believe but cannot dismiss.

The lack of local flavour has an unfortunate effect on the mother (Lynne Griffin) who comes off as a non-specific nag. It also turns Sarah (Vivien Endicott-Douglas) into a stereotypical bratty student, though the same actress does better as a tactlessly well-intentioned nurse. Philip Riccio is excellent as a slimy journalist who makes an ill-fated pass at Harper, and whose leather jacket she makes off with, feeling herself much empowered. Izaak Smith is a real find, bringing one major and one minor character to vibrant life; the major is a boy, another student, to whom Harper finds herself blamelessly attracted. Alex Poch-Goldin doubles as Seth and as a man with whom Harper hooks up, via the dreaded Internet, for a hotel tryst, and makes both of them ambiguously sympathetic. As Seth he has, rather surprisingly, the play's last speech, outlining an improbable retirement fantasy (he doesn't have a job); Harper, as usual, just listens, we imagine skeptically.

Jocelyn's program-note suggests a parallel between Harper's quest for the truth and that of a Greek tragic hero; this seems very far-fetched and besides, with the Greeks, we always find out what the truth was. Harper remains inscrutable, even to herself, and the play is similarly sphinx-like,

hinting at themes without developing them. The parts, or many of them, are good; the whole, not so much.

Daniel MacIvor's Cake and Dirt is a mere doodle. Its main point of interest is its construction: two cryptic scenes are followed by a flashback that explains some things. We then proceed to a final episode which makes everything that has gone before, and most of the characters, irrelevant.

The main point at issue is the destruction of a Toronto park; the blame goes to a man dubbed Councillor Flip-Flop, for his fickleness and his footwear. The other people are mostly spoiled and mostly drunk. In Amiel Gladstone's production, most of the actors start strong and then amp themselves wearyingly and repetitively up. The exceptions are Maria Vacratsis, who stays on an even keel throughout, and Patrick Kwok-Choon, who is unbelievable from first to last. In this play had any other author's mane on it, I doubt if it would have got on.

Harper Regan runs through March 22 at the Bluma Appel Theatre; Cake and Dirt runs through April 15 at the Tarragon.

David Hou / Vivien Endicott-Douglas and Molly Parker star in Harper Regan. Do not show up expecting to see Kevin Spacey.
2015-03-21-crying-uncle:
The Vanya of Christopher Durang's Vanya and Sonia and Masha and Spike is nobody's uncle. He is, though, a brother. Masha is his birth sister and Sonia was adopted. Masha is a famous actress with five marriages behind her - as well as, probably, as the best years of her career. Still, her success has enabled her to send money back to Pennsylvania where Vanya and Sonia have been tending to the house, and also to their now-deceased parents. These parents had been pillars of community theatre, and were devoted to the plays of Anton Chekhov. This accounts for them having given their children Chekhovian names. Christening, it seems, is destiny. Vanya and Sonia, marooned in the country, have grown into disconsolate middle age, mourning their lost potential, like their namesakes in Uncle Vanya. The parallels strengthen when Masha (who doesn't have much in common with the Mashas of Three Sisters and The Seagull) arrives, partly to attend a party but mainly to announce that she intends to sell the house out from under them.

This may be the place to mention that its grounds include 10 cherry trees; whether that's enough to constitute an orchard is a matter of fierce debate. With Masha on her trip to the country is Spike (his parents obviously weren't Chekhovians), a 25-year-old hulk attractive to both sexes until they get to know him.

That completes our roundup of characters who make it into the title. There are two others, who don't. One is Nina, the young lady next door, who like her counterpart in The Seagull wants to be an actress, and is overwhelmed at meeting a reallife movie star; she also seems to have designs on the star's boy-toy. The other is Cassandra, a cleaning-lady who, as her name suggests, has wandered in from another dramatic canon altogether. Like her ancient Trojan counterpart, she goes around uttering prophecies that everyone disregards, largely because they're incomprehensible. She also does things with voodoo dolls. She doesn't fit. But then, as we've been told, the local amateurs couldn't bring off Greek tragedy either. Maybe the curse persists.

Durang's play, a Tonywinner in 2010, arrives in Toronto in a first-rate production, directed by Dean Paul Gibson and presented by David Mirvish by way of the Royal Manitoba Theare Centre, and it contains some funny stuff, along with some that's irritating.

Some of the shadowboxing with Chekhov's originals is delightful. Vanya tells us that he could never decide whether Konstantin's play in The Seagull was meant to be ahead of its time or just a terrible play. (I hear you, brother). So he's written one of his own, expanding Konstantin's post-apocalyptic scenario into a scarifying fable on climate change; there's an impromptu reading of it with Nina, as in Chekhov, playing the leading role, in this case a Molecule. The performance sets off some unexpected, and

unconvincing, confrontations and role reversals.

Around here, Broadway wish-fulfilment sets in. It looks as if Durang's characters may actually change their lives. That's what Chekhov thought their prototypes ought to do, but he knew that they wouldn't and was honest enough not to pretend otherwise. Durang's play, like 90% of American drama, takes the easy way out.

Paying homage to Chekhov, Durang sentimentalizes him. He still provides treats for actors, two of them in particular. Steven Sutcliffe's Vanya, coming down to breakfast in a smock, actually looks Chekhovian; he proceeds to give a superb account of a man who has always gone along to get along, and knows it. In the second act something bursts; he's handed what I can only describe as a shy tirade celebrating the shared cultural experiences of his youth, as opposed to the atomized multi-tasking of Spike's generation. Some of his examples sound suspect, but he acknowledges this, tempering his defiance with apologetics but still plowing exhilaratingly ahead. It's a virtuoso display of changing tempi within an overall charging rhythm.

Having Fiona Reid in the role of Sonia is beyond a blessing, since her own comic style, and especially her timing, have always been of the Smith persuasion - though I think she may have bettered the instruction; she's easier to believe. Anyway, a scene in which she takes a phone call, alternating between Sonia's real voice and her assumed one, is a jewel. Nobody does hilarious indecision like Reid, and we're all pulling for her to make the right choice. (We're sentimentalists, too.)

The role of Masha is loaded with famous-actress cliches, but Jennifer Dale sails through them with a conquering mix of bravura and bravado. Ellen Denny's Nina is a delightful bluestocking ingenue, and Luke Humphrey brings a fitting shamelessness to Spike, who likes to parade in his underpants. Making Cassandra fit with the rest of the play may be an impossible task, but Audrey Dwyer might do better at it if she lowered the volume.

Blood Wedding (1933) by Federico Garcia Lorca is a play I've always half-wanted to see: only half because I feared that its Spanish poetry, verbal and visual, might wilt in an Englishlanguage production, or be swallowed in what directors like to call "ritual," and that its story might not hold tight. I was more than half wrong.

The wedding is that of a bashful but determined groom and a bride who has had amorous dealings with a family on the other side of a blood-feud. The ceremony goes ahead but the bride is then abducted on horseback by her former lover Leonardo, the only character allowed a name; the hoofs of Leonardo's horse are a recurring motif in the text (translated by Langston Hughes) and in Soheil Parsa's direction, which offers the diagram of a firstrate production: not quite the thing itself because some of the performances are lacking.

Derek Kwan's Groom and Carlos Gonzalez-Vio's Leonardo, however, are fine; and Beatriz Pizano as the groom's mother is a bodeful presence. The production is a joint venture by Parsa's Modern Times company and Pizano's Aluna Theatre. Trevor Schwellnus' design consists of windows, that darken or crack to thrilling effect; he also provides a lovely frame for the apparition of the Moon who appears, along with Death, to preside over the final pre-destined mayhem.

Vanya and Sonia and Masha and Spike runs until April 5 at the Panasonic Theatre; Blood Wedding runs until March 29 at Buddies in Bad Times Theatre.
2015-03-30-on-shanley-subways:
Beyond a doubt, John Patrick Shanley's most famous play is Doubt. But this American favourite has written many others, and in recent seasons Torontos independent theatre companies have fashioned a cottage industry of bringing us Shanley plays. That ante has now been upped. Three indie groups - Flip Jaw Productions, the Storefront Theatre and Side-Mart Theatrical Grocery - have joined forces to bring us, not just the Canadian but the world premieres, of no less than six Shanley plays. Or rather playlets, bundled together on a single evening, under the umbrella title A Woman Is a Secret.

Whether they are cumulatively worth doing is another matter. The first episode shows us a young man and his girlfriend at a restaurant, the two of them interacting with an aggressively French waitress who keeps bringing to the table things that havent been ordered. His date, meanwhile, is disturbed by his checking out the waitress's physical attributes, a charge he denies. It ends with the two women more or less ganging up on the man, and with the suggestion that the whole thing may be a dream, or perhaps a time warp. It's hard, despite some amusingly annoyed lines, to care.

As a trio, that first scene turns out to be, perhaps cleverly, misleading. Those that follow are all duets. Certain other features, though, stay constant. All the scenes feature a table, in one position or another. All are sexual, or pre-sexual, jousts. All involve the participants distrust or disbelief. Most hint at some degree of fantasy.

One is labelled Tennessee, which may indicate not just locale but a tongue-in-cheek homage to the playwright of that name. The two people here could certainly join the Williams line of acid-tongued no-hopers. The male is a perpetual adolescent who would rather be anywhere else; the female is a small-town psychic whose services he craves and who already knows more about him than is comfortable. The two of them are well drawled by Jade Hassoune and Katie Swift.

Tiny Tragedy is about a couple of insects, a spider and a moth. Or maybe thats just a metaphor, and what we have is an encounter between a sadistic time-biding man and a self-destructive woman: more shades of Tennessee. Trent Pardy and Holly Flood play them with appropriately languorous intensity.

In Poland (that's another title, though the scene isn't set there), an eastern European charmer attracts and teases an American multimillionaire who wants her to help him solve a jigsaw puzzle. She reads a lot into that: practically psychoanalyses him on the strength of it. The performances of Karen Knox and Jonathan Higgins are, again, flavourful.

All these mini-dramas involve the characters making pseudo-profound statements about life and love. Shanley, like many semi-serious American playwrights, can more or less get away with this, if his actors can; and these players - a mix of veterans, neophytes, and in-betweens - are nearly all up to the job.

Under Andrew Shavers direction, they find the right tone and rhythm for every scene. The only ones who dont are Anna Hardwick and Anand Rajaram, who play a newly and unhappily married woman and her reappearing old flame. Instead of gliding stylishly along the text, they plumb it for depths that aren't there; most of the scenes are a bit too long, this one is interminable. Redemption is at hand, though, from the two heaviest hitters in the lineup, cunningly kept in reserve until the end.

All the plays seem to say is that relationships are plagued by misunderstandings and that, contrary to the overall title, these are not the province of one gender. If a woman had written them and called them A Man Is a Secret, you wouldn't know the difference.

In Soulpeppers Subway Stations of the Cross, Ins Choi gives us a Toronto homeless person as intermittent preacher. He is hypnotic. His words arent always immediately clear; he seems, when he first shuffles into view, to be talking about eclairs. Actually he is, chocolate ones, but the word is there for rhyming rather culinary effect. Rhymes, rapid and clenched and inexhaustible, are his medium, and they are far more exact and exhilarating than those of most hiphoppers; Choi actually understand accents and syllables.

And they do sometimes connect, as advertised, with those of biblical prophets, Old Testament rather than New. He's very good when he's talking about Jerusalem. Periodically, theres a train rumble, and the lights go down, suggesting that our preacher has had to move on to another station. These various, and scattered, elements, though, hardly unify the piece or justify its title. Its impressive but fragmentary.

A Woman Is a Secret runs through April 5 at the Theatre Centre; Subway Stations of the Cross through April 4 at the Young Centre.

Nathan Kelly / Ins Choi's Subway Stations of the Cross gives us a Toronto homeless person as an intermittent preacher.
2015-04-07-where-the-tudors-fears-to-tre:
Some people dont know how to wait. Wolf Hall, Hilary Mantel's blockbusting, prize-wining historical novel, was published in 2009. It was the first part of a trilogy. Its successor, Bring Up the Bodies, appeared in 2012; the final instalment, The Mirror and the Light, has yet to appear but is scheduled for publication later this year.

From the start, the books have seemed irresistible subjects for dramatization. Set in the reign of Henry VIII, which seems to be stage and screen's favourite stretch of English history, they give their starring role to a man who has previously been a supporting character at best: Henrys minister Thomas Cromwell, traditionally a minor villain, here an ambiguous hero. So they combine familiarity and surprise. What could be better?

Cromwell rose to power by finessing the second and third of Henrys six marriages, and lost both his position and his life by mismanaging the fourth.

That last development is, of course, the province of Mantel's third book, yet unseen; and I had expected would-be adapters to hold their fire until the whole story was in.

In fact, though, there are two versions already out there, both based on the two existing books while using the title of the first one. The Royal Shakespeare Company has presented a stage Wolf Hall, now playing in New York, and now the BBC has brought out a six-part miniseries, about to be shown by PBS under its Masterpiece imprint, premiering April 6.

I can't speak for the stage version, but the TV production, directed by Peter Kosminsky, is excellent. And it comes of course with the built-in promise of a sequel. The last shot practically mandates it. Cromwell, having brought Anne Boleyn to the block so that Henry may marry Jane Seymour, receives a grateful embrace from his royal master, and squirms within it, simultaneously gratified and alarmed. Anne had once warned him that "those who are made can be unmade" and he had agreed. Fully made now, he can see his own unmaking as only too likely.

Mantels books are told entirely from Cromwells point of view, though not in the first person. We are told his thoughts and observations, but only at a distance; we don't have to agree with them. Peter Straughan's adaptation finds a dramatic equivalent for this. Mark Rylance as Cromwell is in practically every scene, and he spends a lot of time silently reacting; there are no voiceovers. His typical look is one of quizzical disbelief. He knows, always, that he is the smartest person in the room.

He also knows, at least at the beginning, that he is one of the least powerful, and that insecurity never quite leaves him. Its not just that we never know quite how he feels; he never does either. As for grudges, Cromwell is very good at holding those, and from our own plebeian point of view, they seem largely justified. Most of the time, were on his side.

Like the novels, like the history, the drama is thickly populated, but it's usually possible to tell who the important people are, even when scenes are lit, naturally, only by candles. (Although I did wonder whether, in Tudor England, people conducted all their conversations to lute accompaniment.)

We learn, again, that at this time all men were called either Harry or Tom. The principal Harry is of course the king himself, played with dangerous and mercurial friendliness by Damian Lewis; his minor namesakes are mostly improvident young bloods who find themselves accused of adultery with the queen.

As for the Thomases, apart from Cromwell himself, they include both his greatest friend and his greatest adversary. The ally is his protector Cardinal Wolsey who, perhaps because we see him only in decline, becomes in Jonathan Pryce's performance a surprisingly sympathetic figure, his wit flashing openly to the last. (Cromwell has to keep his own under wraps.)

The enemy is Sir Thomas More, the intransigent holdout against Henrys divorce and its necessary consequence, the Protestant Reformation. Well be the fools and oppressors says More, foreseeing their future reputations, "and he'll be the proud victim, with the better turn of phrase ... he wrote the play years ago." It was in fact written centuries later and called A Man for All Seasons, and Mantel's novel is in part a counterblast to Robert Bolts hagiographic play. It stresses the unamiable things Bolt left out, like Mores propensity for torturing and burning heretics.

These are stressed, graphically, in the TV version, too, but More gets a better deal on screen than in the novel because we actually see him, flesh-and-blood, in a fine performance by Anton Lesser, standing proud at his trial. Cromwell himself is averse to torture ("No, madam, we don't do that" he tells Anne when she urges him to put the screws to More) and we almost believe it. We'd certainly like to believe it. Rylances performance is, in its gentle inscrutability, one of the finest, and certainly one of the most restrained, things he has done.

Anne Boleyn herself (Claire Foy) is the least successful character; she looks good in the frocks but sounds merely shrill and spoiled in a repellently modern way. Admittedly, the script never lets her say a kind word to anybody; when it adds to Mantels dialogue, it doesn't tread the same fine line as its original between obscurity and anachronism. It also scrimps on Cromwell's domestic life, movingly depicted in the books. But it's a fine achievement, in what used to be the BBC's best style.

The difference between this and something like The Tudors is that Wolf Hall interprets history where The Tudors ignored it.

Wolf Hall airs Sundays on PBS.

BBC / Mark Rylance plays Thomas Cromwell, a minister to King Henry VIII, with a lot of looks of quizzical disbelief.
2015-04-11-the-string-theory-of-everythi:
Elliot is a theoretical physicist and Carmen a musician. So they are both deeply and professionally concerned with time. They are two of the three speaking characters in Hannah Moscovitch's new play, Infinity. The third is a young woman called Sarah Jean, whose role consists mostly of monologues, and who initially seems to exist in a different dramatic frame, and time-frame, from the others. It turns out that she's their daughter; that information is withheld for some time in the play, but it's freely available in the program notes, and the play wouldn't make much sense without it. This is a case where not giving something away would be a spoiler.

I tried not to keep repeating the word "time" in the above paragraph and failed miserably. This may prove Moscovitch's apparent point that time is both a slippery concept and an inescapable one. Elliot believes that it does not exist, at least as commonly conceived; and he devotes his life, starting with his PhD thesis, to proving it.

He and Carmen meet, in the play's first scene, at a postgraduate bash, a meeting that turns into a seduction in what must, even by academic standards, count as record time. (That word again.) Their relationship continues, and Sarah Jean is the result. They get married, and though they probably have a few happy moments, the play isn't concerned to show them. What we witness are quarrels and threats of separation. And those are the good times, at least compared with what is to come. It's no wonder, though no explicit connection is made, that Sarah Jean grows up with a jaundiced view of love and sex, one confirmed by her own later experiences, about which she tells us in graphic detail. When she goes into academe, her chosen field is mathematics, which could mean that she's splitting the difference between her parents' specialties or that she has rebelled against both of them by choosing the most intellectual and least emotional pursuit available.

The parents' rows are vividly written and powerfully performed, as are the daughter's reminiscences. Ross Manson directs, and the play is a co-production between his Volcano Theatre and the Tarragon. The other credits include Lee Smolin as "consulting physicist", and he's quoted in the program as follows: "What is time? ... Everything we think, feel, or do reminds us of its existence." True enough: but dramatically something that applies to everything might as well apply to nothing. We get a couple of fairly effective domestic stories tied together with a piece of string theory, and the string frays.

Paul Braunstein plays Elliot as a man whose lack of social graces is its own grace, and its own teddybear charm. The best scene is sparked not by his ideas but by his insistence on devoting himself to them even after he's won his doctorate. Carmen feels shut out and victimized by his single-mindedness, though it would seem likely that, as a composer, she would be as fanatically devoted to her own concerns as he is to his. Carmen is in fact severely underwritten; vocally, Amy Rutherford is compelled to strike a single recurrent note of angry grievance; physically, she's subtler. A significant part of her role has been contracted out. I said there were three speaking characters, but there is a fourth performer: a violinist, Andrea Tyniec, who wanders onstage to play what we must take to be Carmen's music, actually composed by Njo Kong Kie. The play's best single line is about music being "a sculpture in time" but the image is never pursued.

Haley McGee's Sarah Jean is a compelling study of young-adult anger, grown out of childhood belligerence. In her parents' story she figures as an eight-year-old, surprisingly ignorant of the facts of death. It's death that pokes a hole in Elliot's theories and converts him to what might be called the common-sense view of time, or at least the one that we rely on, if only by default, to get us through our days. After those days, there's only the infinity of the play's title, which might be either the negation of time or the ultimate confirmation of it. But these are themes that the play merely picks up and puts down again. It doesn't embody them.

Manson's production does its best to suggest higher things, with a set, designed by Teresa Przybylski, of black whorls on a white background, and choreography, by Kate Alton, that's an extended sequence of hand-jive, presumably meant to suggest the characters trapped in their own obsessive patterns. Like most of Moscovitch's plays, this one is gripping from moment to moment; unlike her best ones, it doesn't make those moments cohere.

Infinity runs through May 3 at the Tarragon Theatre.
2015-04-14-the-dame-game-at-82-years-old:
Theatre review

Dame Edna's Glorious Goodbye: The Farewell Tour

Princess of Wales Theatre, Toronto

On the first night of her valedictory sojourn in Toronto Dame Edna Everage, self-anointed gigastar, devoted a considerable portion of her precious time and inexhaustible energy to affectionately browbeating an audience member named Elaine. Well, she claimed she was doing it affectionately. Or at least for Elaine's own good. After lengthy interrogation, she elicited the information that Elaine lives in a detached house, meaning, the Dame helpfully translated, that you can walk all around it. She then raised her eyes to the patrons in the balcony and said "that's an impossible dream for you."

So she's at it again, playing off the folks in the expensive seats down front against those in the cheaper ones way up above, and hilariously insulting both groups. Dame Edna made her first public appearance back in 1955, when she was just an Australian suburban housewife; just how old that makes her I'm not sure, but Barry Humphries, the man behind her or perhaps inside her, admits to 82. But the razor-sharpness of both the character and her creator remains unblunted. Once again we marvel at, to use a phrase that might earn her censorious rebuke, the number of balls Edna that can keep in the air; having staked out, early in the proceedings, the five or six people on whom she is going to pick she keeps returning to them, making them the objects of both her criticisms and her confidences. I'm impressed that she can remember all their names, let alone their salient characteristics, and knocked out by the insouciant unexpectedness with which she brings each of them back into what, if it weren't so egomaniacal, you might call the conversation.

Her named victims from the orchestra seats are always women, helpfully lectured on their dress sense or lack of it ("saved up for that, did you?"); they don't have the Dame's advantages and wouldn't know what to do with them if they did. Those aloft she greets, as always, as "paupers," though this time she also, more compassionately, calls them "les miserables" (or "mizzies"). One of the great joys of the show is the recurrent upward tilt of the head that signifies that she is about to address these unfortunates, meaning that she has thought of a new way of insulting them. She also has a few kind words for those in the side-boxes ("the ashtrays") and an interestingly macabre explanation, that I would not dream of giving away, for the few empty seats. As always, Dame Edna gives new meaning to the phrase "target audience."

We don't have to feel sorry for the people she singles out. The routine is well-known by now, and I have it on good authority that ticket-buyers actually compete for the seats where they are likeliest to attract her attention. They're prepared, and they can give as good as they get. This is even, or especially, the case when they're brought physically onstage. It certainly was on the Toronto first night when a man and woman determined by the Dame to have matching DNA were ceremonially married by her, despite each having a spouse already, one being present in the house, the other reached by phone after the ceremony and apparently cool with it. Shy at first, the newly happy couple rapidly warmed up, and came close to stealing the star's thunder. Maybe what she says is really true; she isn't bullying them, she's empowering them. "I don't think of you as an audience" she says, "but as a focus group."

There's a sustaining tension in the Edna phenomenon between Humphries, the brilliantly intelligent standup comedian, and the impenetrably stupid woman who is his mouthpiece, He's endowed her with his own quickwittedness and her own closed-mindedness. There's more of course. With her purple hair, her amazing spectacles (in both senses), her glittering bangles and no less glittering frocks, and her complete confidence in her own superiority, she's the ultimate satire on celebrity culture. But she's also a great individual creation, the most sacred of monsters; and indeed part - slightly too long a part - of her second act concerns her spiritual awakening at an ashram, with the Dalai Lama himself, Dal for short. (She got pally with the Dali. You're welcome.) She also, game thing that she is, sings and dances with a supporting quartet, the tackiness of whose routines isn't quite excused by their being that way on purpose. More accomplished and enjoyable are a couple of video sequences. One is a ruthless expose of the sordid truth behind the Everage myth, including a very funny guest cameo by Hugh Jackman, who tells us about taking Edna's acting classes Down Under, with Mel and Cate and the rest of the gang. The other shows Edna's many apotheoses, encountering the rich and famous, even hobnobbing with Charles and Camilla in the Royal Box before excusing herself because she's got a better seat.

And there's a coda, that's a complete departure from all previous Edna shows. For one thing, it's moving. And it convinces you that this Farewell Tour really is Goodbye and that it really is Glorious.

National Post

Runs until April 19. For more information, visit mirvish.com.

Mirvish / "I don't think of you as an audience" Dame Edna addressed the crowd "but as a focus group."
2015-04-18-femmes-the-breaks-david-mamet:
David Mamet is famous, or notorious, for writing plays with either no roles for women or bad ones. The second part of the charge isn't altogether fair, but in 1999 he seems to have taken it seriously enough to have written a play with an all-female cast. The play, Boston Marriage, was a double departure for him, since it abandoned the edgy contemporary settings and dialogue of his other work, and settled instead in the genteel late 19thcentury world of Henry James and Edith Wharton.

Boston Marriage shows us two women trying desperately to keep their fragile footing in that world and a third without a hope of getting into it. Anna and Claire are somewhat estranged lesbian lovers. Anna has a rich male protector who has given her a diamond necklace and the means to maintain a fashionable house; against her own aesthetic judgment, she has re-decorated the place in chintz, thinking that Claire would like it. Claire has become attracted to a much younger woman and asks Anna's permission to use the house as a place of assignation. Anna is understandably not keen but, after a lot of fencing, agrees: on conditions. Meanwhile she takes her bad temper out on her maid, who is Scottish but whom Anna keeps insisting is Irish, with many a merry reference to the Great Potato Famine. Claire, when her own temper is frayed, which is often, is happy to join in the taunting.

In this respect the play is a female version of one of Mamet's best allmale pieces, American Buffalo: we have two comparatively advantaged, older characters and a third apparently helpless younger one whom they alternately patronize and victimize, though here the pattern's broken when, for plot reasons both complicated and implausible, they find they need her.

American Buffalo, of course, is written in Mamet's best manner: street speech as profane poetry. Boston Marriage uses ersatz Oscar Wilde spiked with intentionally jarring anachronisms. A line like "this fellow fancies you dead rotten" is followed a moment later by an entreaty to "only conceive, I pray you." He hasn't exactly lost his touch; lines that are intended to be funny quite frequently are, but the wit still feels strained. What he does demonstrate, devastatingly well, is a knack for running up great, non-chintzy curtain-lines. He remains committed to a two-act structure, and his Act One ends with a smashing instant reversal, a cliff from which the subsequent action can hang. Act Two doesn't fulfil that promise - in fact much of it feels like padding - but it too has a great ending, incorporating a splendidly suggestive pun and a slow-burn revelation that neatly and ironically ties up what has gone before.

Kelli Fox, for Headstrong Collective, directs a site-specific production, in a drawing-room at Campbell House. Scenically, it takes us right into the characters' world. Verbally, it halts on the threshold. The words drip, or should, with poise and poison; as an actress Fox, with her Shaw Festival background, could probably handle them perfectly. But there's little sense of phrasing or timing from Catherine McNally (Anna) or Deborah Drakeford (Claire); they mostly blunderbuss their way through their lines. They're better in their moments of vulnerability, especially Drakeford, who has more of them. As Catherine the maid Charlotte Dennis is delightful, dignified even when humiliated; she spends a lot of time standing patiently around, waiting to deliver messages that her betters, to their own detriment, refuse to hear. She may be the most positive character Mamet has ever created. Otherwise he depicts women here as manipulative or pitiable or both, which is just how he has generally depicted men.

Ubu and the Truth Commission, part of CanadianStage's Spotlight on South Africa festival, mixes together the puppeteering skills of the Handspring Company (who wrought the magic of War Horse), the historical subject of the post-apartheid judicial process, and the borrowed protagonist of Alfred Jarry's Ubu Roi, which was the original absurdist play and, like many of its successors, far more fun to read about than to watch. Jarry's Pere Ubu was the prototypical bourgeois, a greedy tyrant in his own home, a nonentity outside it. In this version he has a past as a secret policeman; Mere Ubu suspects of him sneaking out at nights to see other women, and is mightily relieved to find that he's only been killing and torturing people. Pa and Ma are given lifesize performances by David Minnaar, who's spectacular, and Busi Zokufa; other roles are played by three Handspring puppeteers, sometimes through their puppets, sometimes not.

The ingredients don't all add up. Mere's jealousy, in particular, seems like a gigantic red herring; and Pere's twists and turns, as his past threatens to catch up with him, are not always easy to follow. The actual trial testimonies, mainly from parents called to identify their butchered children, remain devastating, the more so for being understated and anonymous. Jane Taylor wrote the script; the director is William Kentridge, who's also credited with "animation"; this probably means the grim cartoon projections are a major part of the production, and in fact more visually striking than the puppetry which, however expert, is, by War Horse standards, merely serviceable. But then the show isn't trying to be War Horse. I think it may have bitten off more than it can reasonably chew. I have always thought South Africa's Truth and Reconciliation Commission to be one of civilization's more encouraging moments. This production, in which Ubu gets away with it, is a lot more skeptical.

Boston Marriage runs through April 26 at the Campbell House Museum; Ubu and the Truth Commission runs through April 19 at the Berkeley Street Theatre Downstairs.

Bonnie Anderson / Deborah Drakeford and Catherine McNally are best in their moments of vulnerability.
2015-04-25-home-sweet-home-tom-on-the-fa:
The least interesting character in Tom on the Farm is Tom himself. That is no reflection on Jeff Lillico's hyper-active and hyperintelligent performance. But he's playing someone who is both protagonist and reflective surface, and the two functions get in one another's way.

In Michel-Marc Bouchard's play, receiving a delayed English-language premiere in Linda Gabouriau's translation, Tom is a young advertising man whose male colleague and lover has died in an accident. The dead man grew up on a farm, miles from anywhere, and Tom makes the trek there for the funeral. Here he meets his partner's mother, Agathe, who didn't know her son was gay, and his brother Francis, who knew only too well. On Tom's first night at the farm, Francis pins him down on his bed (they share a room - like brothers) and threatens him with dire consequences should he even hint at the truth; he even insists that Tom invent a girlfriend for his boyfriend. Tom agrees, partly because he's terrified, but maybe also in part because, whatever the emotional cost to himself, he does want to spare Agathe's feelings.

The maybes pile up. Tom keeps up a continuous interior monologue, letting us know about the pain he's in and the lies he's forced to tell. At first, when it's in counterpoint to what the others are saying out loud, this is both touching and amusing. When it extends into long soliloquies, it defeats itself. However much Tom talks, he leaves questions unanswered, including the obvious one of why he sticks around, given that he has a job to go back to, and that Francis treats him appallingly; he ends up very bloodied.

One possible answer is that he finds life on the farm unexpectedly fulfilling, especially when it involves the delivery of a calf; he bonds with it, perhaps identifies with it, or finds the newborn to be a substitute for the life that was lost. Another is that he develops a sado-masochistic attraction to Francis, one that may very well be reciprocated. "Anything but normal round here is multiplied by twenty" says Francis, and he could be guiltily referring to himself as well as to his late brother. This could explain, on two levels, why he ratchets up the violence. This includes suspending Tom, upside down, over a giant cow-pat; Tom gamely continues to soliloquize.

The melodrama in the play involves several physical and psychological improbabilities, but it's brought to full atmospheric life in Eda Holmes' unimpeachable production. The slatted walls of Camellia Koo's set carry appropriate suggestions of prison bars; Rebecca Picherack's lighting is eerie and John Gzowski's sound design scary. There's humour too; about the least plausible thing Tom does is to summon a co-worker to impersonate the imaginary and supposedly francophone girlfriend, but it justifies itself in Christine Horne's bold comic turn, forced into speaking a language she barely knows.

The mother and brother, characters who, unlike Tom, develop before our eyes, are superbly played. Jeff Irving finds all the torment, of himself and others, in Francis, notably in his filial conflict between resentment and affection. As Agathe, Rosemary Dunsmore says the least (though she does have a funny aria about pasta salad) but conveys the most. She is religiously obsessed but also very practical. The play's most powerful irony is our gradual realization that she could have dealt with her son's sexuality had anyone told her.

The play rises to a violent climax that we wish for in advance but find hard to credit when it happens. But its brief aftermath, filled with a terrible tenderness, makes some sense of it. Two characters are left with what, it seems, they wanted.

Daniel Karasik's Little Death explicitly invokes the old meaning of its title phrase as a synonym for orgasm. (It casts a new and probably accurate light on a song in "A Little Night Music.") It also refers to an imminent bigger death; its hero Alex (the characters have names in the program, though they're never spoken in the play) having received the diagnosis, asks permission of the wife with whom he has been monogamous since they were both 16 to experiment while there's still time; she agrees but begins to wish she hadn't.

The play alternates his encounters with other women, or their beginnings in a hotel bar, with his returns to his increasingly angered and anguished spouse. This play, too, gets a beautifully tuned production, directed by Zachary Florence.

The text is in short-lined verse that plays as heightened prose, taut and full of echoes. Sometimes it's too brittle, as in the fencing of Alex (an ambiguously ingenuous Christopher Stanton) with a magazine writer (Shauna Black) and an actress (Elizabeth Tanner, a promising newcomer in an A-list cast). Sometimes it's conversationally perfect, as in a consultation with a doctor (Sarah Dodd, perfectly grounded in a brief role.) And sometimes it strikes ruthlessly and/or compassionately home, in the scenes of actual intimacy, physical or otherwise.

Kate Hennig is wonderfully warm and sensible as the maturest of Alex's pick-ups, though it seems she did the picking. Nicole Underhay is even better as the wife, nailing every loving or resentful word, thought or feeling with extraordinary quicksilver precision. The scenes seem to be chronologically ordered, though the last one cheats by diverting into fantasy; it's affecting, though, and the feelings behind it truthful.

Tom at the Farm runs through May 10 at Buddies in Bad Times Theatre; Little Death runs through May 3 at the Theatre Centre.

Jeremy Mimnagh / Rosemary Dunsmore co-stars in Tom at the Farm; Emily Lockhart / Christopher Stanton, Nicole Underhay in Little Death.
2015-04-29-mad-men-s-joke-is-on-us-after:
I like Mad Men. I would never miss an episode. I would rank it fourth among the great longform TV series of recent years, after The Wire, The Sopranos and Deadwood. But I'm not as invested in it as I was in the other three.

Maybe this is because it lacks their exoticism. The New York advertising world isnt mine but its closer to my experience than the streets of Baltimore, the New Jersey Mafia or the old Wild West. It's also blander. The stakes are lower. People in Mad Men can lose their jobs, their marriages can break up, and there have even been a couple of suicides. But they don't go around under the daily threat of violence. They dont have the dramatic advantage of being disadvantaged. And they dont constitute a society, even - as those in the other shows do - a society of outsiders.

This past Sunday's episode was a joke. That's a description, not a value judgment. It began, more or less, with the news that our friends at Sterling Cooper, the little agency that could, were about to be vanish into the maw of Mc-Cann Erickson, the big advertising devil with whom, last season, they had made a deal that seemed good at the time. Don Draper, resourceful as nearly always, came up with an identity-saving alternative plan; the old firm would preserve its independence by retreating to its office in Los Angeles, taking some choice clients with it. McCann then pulled the rug from under the partners feet by telling them not to worry, there were luscious accounts waiting for them in the big house. They - Don, Roger, Joan, Pete and Ted - seemed uncertain whether to laugh, cry or, the majority choice, get plastered.

If the joke was on them, it was also on us. We had spent an hour worrying about a threat that turned out to be no threat at all. It was well set up and well sustained, and there are no hard feelings. I was pleased things turned out as they did. I had no desire, with the show at the precise halfway point of its final season, to see it pick up sticks and live out its declining episodes in California. Its previous forays out west have been among its duller moments. It belongs in New York.

I know that Mad Men is generally regarded as reflecting a society, as mirroring the changes in mainstream American life from the 1950s to the 70s. It's certainly true that the show takes infinite pains in getting the clothes and furnishings right. But that's just decoration. You can get nostalgic if you were there at the time, or wish you had been, but that hardly constitutes dramatic interest. (I confess that Sundays instalment had me pining for the days of the personal answering service.)

The advertising business has traditionally been, in plays or movies, a subject for satire. Theres some of that in Mad Men, and it has the probably salutary effect of making the ads in the show's own commercial breaks look ridiculous. But there's something self-defeating about it; were being told that the characters are involved in a superficial business while also being asked to root for their success. One sales pitch comes to seem much like another, and the same goes for corporate guys in suits. The characters, outside the central group, are hard to keep track of; likewise the office politics. In memory even the mergers merge.

Mad Men is more than a soap opera, but it does face the dilemma common to workplace soaps; it has to keep switching between its characters business and personal lives. Unlike a routine soap, it has to establish some connection between the two. It doesn't always do this; there was an egregious lapse on Sunday when Pete Campbell got into fisticuffs with a descendant of his clan's historic foes, the MacDonalds. (See Glencoe, Massacre of; and talk about far-fetched.)

The character whose public and private lives have always most satisfyingly coalesced - for us if not for him - is Don Draper himself. Moralists like to cite him as a walking symbol of the emptiness of the world the show depicts. Why, his very existence is a fraud; he stole somebody elses name and identity. But the show hasnt made much of that recently; and besides, as the much-missed Bert Cooper said back in the first season, who cares?

In fact, Don's ability to create his own place in the world could be seen as admirable. It's also given him a capacity for empathy that in this show is practically unique; it takes extremes to bring it out, but when one of his colleagues is under the gun, Don is the only one with anything to say. All right, both his marriages fell apart, but they were impossible anyway. I like Don (and I especially like Jon Hamms performance now that Ive seen, from his performance in the BBC's Dark Mirror, that he can do other things, too).

He can't unify his show, the way Tony Soprano did his, but dramatically hes in reverse, the good points outweighing the bad. And, though it seems to be a minority view, I hope that the waitress whos his latest flame reappears. She won't be his salvation, and she knows it, but she's interesting. My favourite character, though, remains Dons perpetually solicitous secretary Meredith, whos finally been granted some depth. Don is an outsider, incurably, though posing as the opposite; unlike the patrician Roger whose wit, in John Slattery's performance, remains irresistible, or the incorrigibly decent Ted, both of them afflicted, in their current time frame, by fashionably outlandish facial hair. The other outsiders, their status unsparingly denoted in the show's very title, are of course Joan and Peggy, alternating being nice and mean to one another; one of the shows recurring strengths lies in showing how colleagues with little in common can nonetheless make common cause. Joan (Christina Hendricks is continually surprising) was last seen remarking bitterly that she, alone among the partners, had been promised no goodies at their new corporate HQ. In this very cool show, her advance - sometimes through her sexuality, sometimes in spite of it - has been the most moving ingredient; now she seems to have hit a glass ceiling without waiting for the phrase to be invented. What really awaits them all at McCann Erickson we have of course yet to learn, but the omens arent hopeful. (I'm always surprised, by the way, that Mad Men gets to use the names of real companies, especially when they're cast as the villains.)

We left with a sense of foreboding; Dons attempt to rally the troops with a motivational speech having sent the rank and file scurrying to their own corners, obviously skeptical, probably afraid. Perhaps its as well that there are only three weeks left for them, and us, to find out. It will he hard, after all the time we've spent with Sterling Cooper in its various formations, to see its constituents as cuckoos in somebody else's nest. For our favourite mad men, and women, disillusion surely beckons, maybe even despair. Don wouldn't even need to fall out of that window.

Elisabeth Moss, Jon Hamm and Rich Sommer star in Mad Men. The fictional Sterling Cooper advertising firm is about to vanish into the jaws of (the real) ad giant McCann Erickson.
2015-05-02-shakespeare-as-you-like-it-th:
Shakespeare's Much Ado About Nothing, the traditional version, begins with an army led by a Spanish prince but staffed largely by Italians billeting itself on another Italian, the governor of Messina, who is only too pleased to have them. In the self-styled "adaptation" at the Tarragon, the Mayor of Brampton, whose name is Ranjit, plays host to an even more diverse body of civilian guests, presided over by a certain Lord Tata, who seems to be his own corporation.

This Much Ado has been touted as "the Bollywood version," and it does include a lot of singing and dancing, Indian-style, though these are hardly the most distinguished parts of the evening. (They aren't a distortion, though; Much Ado, like many Shakespeare comedies, is practically a musical.) The main lines of the plot remain the same. Lord Tata's favourite assistant, an Iranian bearing the historic Persian name of Darius, falls for the Mayor's daughter Sita and she for him; villains persuade him that she's been pre-nuptially unfaithful and he brutally rejects her at the altar.

Meanwhile, Tata's chief financial officer Benedict, a confirmed bachelor and one of only two characters to retain, more or less, their Shakespearean names, and Thara, Mayor Ranjit's free-spirited niece, the lady formerly known as Beatrice, are more benignly tricked into believing that each is loved by the other which, underneath their habitual banter, happens to be the truth. Apart from changes in names and circumstances, some of them awkward, the actors speak the original lines, which are surtitled in Hindi. Except, that is, when the characters themselves are speaking Hindi, or in one case Italian, at which times the captioning is by Shakespeare.

Richard Rose directs, with Ravi Jain billed as "consultant director," and, as in his past productions at Stratford, he illuminates some unexpected corners of the play. The male characters lose a dimension from being de-militarized; CFO to CEO is a lesser bond than officer to general. Still, the visitors here are played with unusual strength and definition.

As Lord Tata, the former Don Pedro, Kawa Ada practically writes his own ticket to Stratford, assuming he wants to go there; he presents an urbane fixer, well-intentioned in his own head, but chillingly insulated from other people's feelings or even from his own. Paying temporary court to Thara, he almost sounds involved, then backs away. Ali Momen is less technically assured; angry verse turns him wooden. He does, though, make a strong case for Darius/Claudio's ardour and an uncompromising one for his meanness. It's best not to inquire how Tata acquired an illegitimate and thickly accented Italian brother, complete with accent, but Salvatore Antonio makes this Don Jovanni a splendidly malevolent presence. As the mayor whose hospitality they so thoroughly abuse, David Adams runs a satisfying gamut from genial to enraged.

These performances rather upstage the play's traditional star turns. Anusree Roy makes very little of Thara except, oddly enough, in her one speech in heartfelt verse. (Much Ado is predominantly, and gloriously, a prose play.) Her wit goes missing; Alon Nashman's as Benedict is fitful. The more serious he gets, the better - and sometimes the funnier - he is, whether rejecting his former friends or, at the end, embracing not just a new wife but a new culture - at which point the production concept justifies itself as more than fun. The broader fun of the constabulary scenes is, at best, intermittent.

Here there's been a lot of rewriting, as well as some ingenious cutting. John Cleland's Constable Verges is divine, but as Dogberry a.k.a.

Head Constable Dan Singh, Anand Rajaram has a mouth full of marbles - or maybe of doughnuts, since most of his malapropisms have been replaced by exaggerated flights into Tim Hortons Canadian. It seems effortful. Michelle Tracey's airy set is attractive, as are most of her costumes. (Sita's stripes are unfortunate; whether intentionally or not, I'm not sure.) The show is a mixed bag, but it has a nice spirit and some moments of real distinction.

George F. Walker's plays can be so bad they're good. He's embarked on a new cycle about schools, the first two of which have arrived in a double bill. Parents Night, as its title suggests, shows a teacher confronted by an angry father and an angry mother, of two different children. The situation of The Bigger Issue is similar, except that the teacher is reinforced by a principal, the parents are a couple, and their offstage kid is older. Low academic achievement is the flashpoint of play one; classroom violence is the bigger issue of play two.

The plays are presented by a company called Crazy Lady, which seems appropriate as between them the plays show us five crazy ladies plus a couple of crazy gentlemen. People in Walker's plays shout at one another, ceaselessly and with abandon. This is especially the case when he's his own director but the director here, Wes Berger, follows faithfully in the master's footsteps. It can be wearying, not to say monotonous, especially as the actors here are not the most technically accomplished.

The first play in particular repeats itself unmercifully, but it redeems itself with a table-turning, and wormturning, final scene. These characters' anger, and their author's on their behalf, is justified and eventually bracing, whether they're parents a desperate notch above homelessness or teachers doing their best in a society that despises them and a system that wears them out.

Sarah Murphy-Dyson is grimly exaggerated as the principal in Play 2 but engaging as the teacher of Play 1, especially when indignantly channelling her inner Julia Louis-Dreyfus; Dana Puddicombe plays essentially the same role in both plays, but seems well suited to it; Julia Heximer is a spirited and sympathetic rookie teacher in the second one, in which Matthew Olver reaps the benefit of being the one quiet person onstage; his earlier role is much louder and far less believable.

You won't get subtlety here. You will get some humour, more compassion, and uncomfortable truth. Both plays end with the characters continuing to talk while the lights fade. On stage, as opposed to film or TV, the fade-out finish is an ineffective device, but the point is clear. These things, like these people, go on forever.

Much Ado About Nothing runs through May 31 at the Tarragon Theatre; Parents Night and The Bigger Issue run through May 17 at Theatre Passe Muraille.

Cylla Von Tiedemann / Much Ado About Nothing, the Bollywood version
2015-05-09-organ-grinder-creditors-and-l:
Two independent theatre spaces with impressive track records - the Coal Mine on the Danforth and Storefront Theatre on Bloor West - are currently adding to them.

I do have a pedantic bone to pick with the Coal Mine's production of August Strindberg's Creditors, or at least with its publicity. It has been announced as "Strindberg's least produced play." You could have fooled me. It may not turn up on our stages as often as Miss Julie (thank God) and it may not have the textbook prestigeof The Father or The Dance of Death, though I've yet to see either of those in Toronto. But I have seen Creditors here before, and it's also had a strong presence in London and New York. Meanwhile, there are dozens of Strindberg plays that never get done anywhere, except presumably in Sweden.

Creditors is a short, intense and devilishly assembled piece that administers its author's obsessions in a concentrated dose. There are three characters: Tekla, a novelist; Adolph, who is her husband; and Gustav, who used to be. The play, set in a hotel, consists of three duologues. In the first, Gustav systematically poisons Adolph's mind against Tekla, who has been off on a junket somewhere, surrounded - as Gustav is at pains to point out - by adoring young men. Adolph does not know who Gustav is, and neither at this point do we, at least in theory. But it's easy for us to guess, and dramatically more effective as well. When Tekla returns, Gustav makes himself scarce, but he can hear from offstage the destruction he has wrought. Exhausted from quarrelling with his wife Adolph, who wasn't too well to begin with, leaves the room while Gustav re-enters it. Tekla, after the initial shock, is very pleased to see him; a rapprochement seems imminent. Adolph, too, has overheard; and for a brief, drastic moment all three are onstage together.

The adaptation, by the Scottish playwright David Greig, plays well, as does Rae Ellen Bodie's tense and intense production. It may, by its author's own feverish lights, go too easy on Tekla and too hard on Gustav. Gustav voices Strindbergian misogyny at full alarming strength. The possibility of infidelity is the least of the charges that he, in her absence, levels at Tekla. He persuades Adolph that she has emasculated him. He is an artist, and she's responsible for his doing sissy stuff like painting, instead of masculine forms like sculpture (though Gustav denounces that as old-fashioned as well); she has drained his talent to feed her own feeble efforts; she may even have brought him to epilepsy. Her pet name for him - "little brother" - says everything.

The scary and powerful and, yes, funny thing about all this is that Strindberg actually believed it, as a general truth about men and women; scarier and funnier still is that he wrote the role of Tekla for his own wife and that she played it. It wasn't all he believed; he did have the genius to recognize his own self-pity, but that never stopped him indulging it.

Gustav's assault on Adolph is comparable to Iago's on Othello, with Tekla cast as a combination of Desdemona and Emilia; jealous revenge is both the motive and the weapon. Like Iago, Gustav works by insinuation, but Hardee T. Lineham delivers his attack as a series of hammerblows; it certainly has impact but it dulls with repetition.

He is more effective with Tekla, with whom he has to be subtler and to whom, it seems, he nearly succumbs. She is, at least in part, the manipulator whom he accuses her of being, but Liisa Repo-Martell downplays that aspect of her. She has a hypnotic presence, though, and the moment at which she catches on to what Gustav is up to is a genuine game-changer.

Noah Reid has maybe the hardest task, Adolph being more acted-upon than active; but there can be passion in passivity and he thrillingly finds it.

Tekla and Gustav, though probably not Adolph, might agree with a proposition advanced in Kat Sandler's play Liver: that "hell is just your ex being immortal". (It beats Sartre.) Sandler's title, like much else in her play, is doubleedged; the liver in question has been surgically removed, with no replacement, from a man who nonetheless lives. So, has he come back from the dead and, perhaps more importantly, does he deserve to? He is, as those around him never tire of reminding him, an unlikely messiah: a drunken, philandering, sentimental slob, who never apologizes; he's also apparently rich, though this is only credible if the money were inherited rather than earned. As played by Shaun Benson, he's hard to stomach and impossible to forget.

The author directs her own play, with immaculate comic and dramatic timing. Sean Sullivan plays a surgeon with a devotion to research, and his own ego, far in excess of what would generally be regarded as ethics; this in a play that makes explicit reference to Josef Mengele and even lists some of his Auschwitz experiments. Then there's Katelyn McCulloch in the generic role of the surgeon's assistant's girlfriend (well, he thinks she's his girlfriend) who is curious to see a dead body and even more curious when she finds it isn't.

All these performances are fine but better still are the two who seem to speak for the author. Michael Musi is the surgical apprentice, an elongated Woody Allen figure in scrubs or a Hazmat suit, standing awkwardly up for what is good and right. Cautioning him from a slightly older perspective is the non-deceased's happily separated spouse, played by Claire Armstrong whom I have now seen give three first-rate performances at the Storefront, all different.

The play has no dull moments, and though it doesn't fully engage with all the issues it raises, it doesn't demean them either. It's also full of firecracker dialogue; I forget which character says "you don't get special treatment just because you're dead" but in context it's a great line.

Creditors runs through May 17 at the Coal Mine Theatre; Liver runs through May 16 at the Storefront Theatre.

Noah Reid and Liisa Repo-Martell star in Creditors, which is definitely not one of August Strindberg's least-produced plays, no sir.
2015-05-16-on-the-edge-of-their-sheets:
According to the Soulpepper program, Alan Ayckbourn has written, and on his home turf directed, 77 full-length plays. Few people can have seen all of them, so few are in a position to say which is the best. My own score comes in at under a third. But of the ones I know, the best is Bedroom Farce, the one that Soulpepper is currently presenting. It's a perfect play.

The title is a tease, but also the literal truth. The entire action takes place over one night in three bedrooms, which share the stage throughout. The sleeping-chamber at stage left belongs to Ernest and Delia, an elderly couple who are about to celebrate their wedding anniversary in a favourite restaurant.

("We're regulars. We go there every year.") Centre stage is occupied by Malcolm and Kate, newlyweds who are throwing a party. Over on the right we find Jan, who is attending the party, and her husband Nick, who isn't as he is confined to bed with an injured back about which he is vocally grumpy. There's a fourth couple, Trevor and Susannah, whom we never see at home as they are too busy invading the spaces of the other characters and laying them waste. Trevor is the son of Ernest and Delia and a former boyfriend of Jan. Trevor and Susannah are made for one another, only in the sense that they are both totally self-absorbed. The condition takes them differently. Trevor's default setting is a cheerful unconsciousness of anybody else's feelings. Susannah's is hysteria.

They too attend Malcolm and Kate's party, but separately, having quarrelled before leaving home. They keep it up after their arrival, thereby ruining everybody's evening. The proximate cause of their row is Trevor's having a nostalgic cuddle with Jan, in on which Susannah fatally walks. This leads to Susannah's running to her in-laws (who don't much like her) for comfort and counsel, and to Trevor's going round to Nick and Jan to Explain. Neither visit is much welcomed by its recipients, who by now are trying to get some rest.

This is something on which their erstwhile hosts have given up. Malcolm uses the unforeseen spare time to do some rather precarious DIY, ostensibly as a present for Kate who, delectable in her nightdress, looks neglected. This, then, is a bedroom farce in which nobody gets any sex and hardly anybody gets any sleep. The play's superbly constructed; without any apparent strain it tells its story within the scenic limits it's set itself; we hear just as much as we need of the world elsewhere, without ever needing to see it for ourselves. Voyages between the rooms are always strictly accounted for and superbly synchronized. Meanwhile the four marriages are, politely but remorselessly, stripped bare. The production in general is excellent, physically inventive and very funny. It's anchored by the performances of its senior couple. Derek Boyes' Ernest lacks something in asperity, but has an owlish geniality, as befits a man whose favourite bedside riding is that 19th-century Boys' Own classic Tom Brown's Schooldays. ("Always worth a re-read.") Delia is a blissfully brisk Corinne Koslo, contemplating her compliant husband, her unsatisfactory daughter-in-law, and her own curl-papered image in the mirror, with equally dispassionate efficiency. Malcolm and Kate are Gordon Hecht and Katherine Gauthier, who were the hilariously self-indulgent lovers in Soulpepper's Tartuffe and are even better here.

Nick and Jan are less convincing. Jan, as her husband complacently states, is a woman notable for her commonsense equability; it, too, can be strained on occasion but Caitlin Driscoll plays her as if anger were her natural state, and there's quite enough of that going around already. Nick is a self-styled high-flyer laid humiliatingly low; Alex McCooeye is immensely tall, and to see his length stretched out upon the bed is a comic treat in itself, even before misfortunes like a dropped book force him into elaborate contortions. He's less adept vocally, which is a particular shame as Nick has the most trenchant speeches in the play, most of them directed at Trevor, whose blithe insensitivity is precisely captured by Ron Pederson. He's partnered with equal conviction (which in her case means total lack of it) by Amy Matysio. These two, cuckoos in every nest, are the only characters who get to grab some sleep in one another's arms. Needless to say, it's on somebody else's bed.

robert.cushman@hotmail.com Bedroom Farce runs through June 20 at the Young Centre
2015-05-20-a-farce-to-be-reckoned-with-s:
Theatre review

You Never Can Tell Royal George Theatre, Niagara-on-the-Lake

The Shaw Festivals opening production of You Never Can Tell begins as a pain and ends as a delight. The pain doesnt have anything to do with the first scene being set in a dentist's office. Valentine, the philandering hero of this early and exceedingly popular Shaw comedy (it may hold the record for productions at the festival) does perform a couple of extractions there, but they're both under anaesthetic: with gas, five shillings extra, laughing gas being Shaws stock-in-trade as well as his autobiographical protagonists. Valentine plies his trade in an English seaside town, and we all like to be beside the seaside. But Jim Mezon's production lays on the atmosphere excessively thick and also with excessive coyness.
