We have to take on trust the idea of the workingguy playwright as a budding genius. As Charlie Gallant plays him, roughedged and impressionable but with an incipient chip on his shoulder, he's certainly the realest person around. He has a couple of well-played allies: Graeme Somerville is a worldly wise author offering counsel and comfort from experience; Fiona Byrne is a writer, ghosting the actress' memoirs, whom the play forgets about after she's served its expository purpose but whom the production cleverly places as a silent vessel of artistic conscience. But the most delightful performance is Shawn Wright's last-act cameo of a shy stage-struck Shriner, whose fellow conventioneers have been adding to the hotel hell. He's there to bring news of good reviews (though the team would surely have read them anyway) and to apologize for his colleagues' rowdy behaviour at the premiere, which we can presumably blame for the general perception of disaster. The Shriners are altogether good value in this production; we get a brief enchanting glimpse of them carrying drunkenly on before the curtain properly rises on the last act. Projections also give us a delightful look at the exterior of the Ritz-Carlton before we venture inside. And the play does give a fair if sketchy impression of the turn-on-adime Broadway mentality. Or theatrical mentality. Or human nature.

Weekend Post robert.cushman@hotmail.com

Light Up the Sky runs through Oct. 11 at the Festival Theatre, Niagara-on-the-Lake

David Cooper / Charlie Gallant as Peter Sloan, Claire Jullien as Irene Livingston and Thom Marriott as Sidney Black in Light Up the Sky, a play about a play that dramatizes that primal theatrical nightmare: trouble on the road.
2015-08-18-shakes-versus-shaw-festival-s:
Tim Carroll, the newly named artistic director of the Shaw Festival, has never directed a play by George Bernard Shaw. This may make him seem an unlikely choice for his new post, which he takes up in 2017. However, he does have what he himself calls a "shadow CV" - the mental list, common to all directors, of plays they would have done with huge success if only things had worked out as planned, and this includes a lot of Shaw. He has a longstanding enthusiasm for Shaw's plays, something he attributes in part to his mother - like GBS himself, "an Irish Protestant from Dublin."

He's British, but he has a Canadian profile, one connected not with the Niagara-on-the-Lake festival but with the other one: the Stratford one. He's staged two Shakespeares along with a production of Peter Pan. The last would probably be classified as "family entertainment" and he's returning to Stratford next year to direct another show in the same category: The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe. So he's going to have a bifurcated Canadian year in 2016: staging his own production at one festival while spending most of his time at the other, shadowing Jackie Maxwell, the outgoing director.

He's best known for his Shakespeare work, and especially for two productions, of Twelfth Night and Richard III, that went to Broadway with Mark Rylance as their star. These, like his Stratford Shakespeares, were productions that tried to re-create at least some elements of Elizabethan stagecraft. The "Original Practices" tag is one that has stuck to him, though when I talked to him on the phone last Thursday, just after his appointment was announced, he insisted that it only accounted for four of the 30 Shakespeares he has directed. "The notion has grown up," he said. "Actually, the majority of my Shakespeare productions have been in modern dress. But people love to put you in boxes."

What most attracts Carroll to Shaw's plays, and by extension plays in his tradition, is that they have "real intellectual meat. All Shaw's plays confront us with our prejudices - especially our comfortable, liberal ones." He takes that tradition to include musicals, which have become important to the festival, financially and otherwise. He himself directed Stephen Sondheim's A Little Night Music a few years ago; and Sondheim has "real literary juices."

He doesn't think intelligent theatre has to be dutiful or forbidding. "It shouldn't be like going to the dentist. It should be a great visceral experience." He's also open to extending the repertoire backwards: something that hasn't been done before. "If there

was an overwhelming reason to do an Aristophanes, we'd do it." That's interesting: Aristophanes, the great comic playwright of ancient Greece, was in some ways the GBS of his time, and some of Shaw's plays owe him an explicit debt - though, unlike Shaw, this most explicit of comedians never wrote Plays for Puritans.

Carroll inherits a performing ensemble that Jackie Maxwell herself inherited, in its spirit and largely in its personnel, from her predecessor Christopher Newton, who really created it. All three directors incidentally are British born, though both Newton and Maxwell were already established features of the Canadian theatre when they took over. Carroll admits, "I know there's a sense of nervousness when the new guy comes in. I don't want to lose the sense of ensemble. I want to make the ensemble the star."

Canada, where film and TV opportunities are limited, is an enviable place for actors, and for lovers of theatre acting. Carroll confirms that "in the U.S., where I've worked a lot, the reputation of Canadian actors is very high - especially for the classics, which in America of course means anything more than five years old."

Certainly classically inclined theatres from Chicago to San Francisco regularly borrow actors from Shaw and Stratford. As for the U.K., whose two major subsidized theatres created wonderful companies in the '60s and '70s: "The National Theatre doesn't have an ensemble, the Royal Shakespeare Company doesn't, though not necessarily because it doesn't want to - they just can't hold on to people."

Sounding rather like the late Robin Phillips, talking about "semaphore acting" when he moved here from the U.K. to take over Stratford, Carroll says, "A lot of theatre in Britain is living on past glories. There's a lot of demonstrative, shallow, fake acting there."

His substantial CV is remarkably varied, from formal - he's done a lot of opera - to decidedly informal. Building on his work at London's Elizabethan Globe theatre - "where every performance was different, because it was in the open air" - he started his own London company, the Factory, where he did a Hamlet "where we chose the cast by lottery before each show" and a dramatization of Homer's Odyssey where "each of the 24 books was performed in a different style chosen by the audience." How much of

this free-and-easiness can be applied at the Shaw I'm not certain, and neither I imagine is he, but it's intriguing.

The board that selected him started with a list of 30 candidates, whittled it down to twelve, then to six, then to four. Carroll was the unanimous choice, partly due to his philosophy about the business side. This, inevitably, includes reaching younger people; like most theatres, the festival is concerned about the age of its audience.

Shaw has begun to move into the family entertainment business, with The Wind in the Willows and Huckleberry Finn as future projects. Peter Jewett, the head of the Shaw's search committee describes his new employee as "very engaging, somewhat self-effacing." And one other thing: the actors to whom I've spoken have loved the experience of working with him.

Mike Dibattista, Niagara Falls Review / Tim Carroll is the new artistic director of the Shaw Festival, replacing Jackie Maxwell after the 2016 season.
2015-08-20-above-parr-marriage-as-a-fenc:
THEATRE REVIEW

The Last Wife Stratford Festival

'Six wives said Charles Laughton in the final frame of The Private Life of Henry VIII, and the last one is the worst of the lot." In that funny and fanciful movie, Katherine Parr, the queen in question, figures rather briefly as a combination of nursemaid and nag. Kate Hennigs play The Last Wife, which is also funny and fanciful as well as entertaining and absorbing, is devoted to proving that there was much more to her in addition to showing her perform those same two functions.

Katherine - known to her husband as Parr and to the program as Kate - wins some of the kings confidence by regularly dressing a suppurating legulcer that he is otherwise too proud, or too image-conscious, to acknowledge. As for the other thing: Hennig's script is not so much in modern English as in modern American; "nag is not a word that anyone in the play actually uses, but it's easy to tell that its what some of them, the male contingent, are thinking.

Kate is a woman who knows what she wants and sets about getting it, sometimes by direct confrontation, sometimes by clever strategy. When we first meet her, shes a young widow-to-be on whom the king has already made a move. She also has a lover-in-waiting, the courtier Thom Seymour, brother of the Jane Seymour who died in childbirth as opposed to being divorced or beheaded like Henry's other exes. Both suitors are waiting impatiently for Kate's husband to croak (they say hes 70; she counters that hes 49); when he does she makes the smart, indeed the inescapable, royal choice.

She offers to be the king's mistress, but he says that he can no longer perform out of wedlock. So she insists on a pre-nup: there shall be no sex unless she initiates it, something that later turns out to be a powerful political arrow in her quiver; and she shall supervise the education of the king's two daughters and one son, each the child of a different mother and each destined in turn to assume the throne.

The boy the play calls Eddie was always going to succeed his father as Edward VI, but it took an Act of Succession to extend the same dynastic privilege to his older half-sisters Mary and Bess, later to be famous as Bloody and Good Queen respectively. Its their stepmother Kate who pushes through this legislation, or persuades the king to. She also persuades him to appoint her regent of England while hes on his last campaign in France which, in the face of an allmale Privy Council, must have taken some doing.

What she cannot do is have him decree that this position shall endure after his death. The political reasons for this are left unclear; we have to put it down to Henry's mercurial feelings about this most capable of wives. He both respects and suspects her, both loves and resents.

And she, it seems, both fears and cares for him. There's a moment in their first interview when Maev Beatys Kate stands with her eyebrows raised, her chin drawn tight, wondering what she has got herself into and how she can survive it. We can see her mind work, and it works very fast. A second later, she is verbally fencing, volatile on the surface, steely underneath. The wittiest actress of her (under-forty) generation is playing a woman who has to live by her wits, and her humane good sense, and her sexuality. The results are superb, not a word or a move or a pause out of place. A star is born. Or, more accurately, confirmed.

Joseph Ziegler must be the only Henry VIII in theatrical history not to knock himself out trying to look like a bloated Holbein portrait, and not just because the production is in modern dress. Nor is he only a ruthless sexist pig. Hes other things as well: intelligent and artistic and with a special, dangerous kind of vulnerability, the kind that does monstrous things for fear of losing face or being taken advantage of. This king and queen make great fencing partners.

So, what's not to like? That's actually a line from the play, and it sort of answers its own question. Nobody wants a history play to sound archaic, but this script makes a point of being aggressively anachronistic. Hey, that was fun," says Kate, making a rapid post-coital exit from Thoms bed. Henry refers to the likelihood of the fat lady singing. The line that really crosses the line is "Im a conformist - that makes me a fascist, not a liberal." The audience apparently can't be trusted to make its own connections. The play comes to seem less like the author's idea of what really happened than her fantasy of what ought to have happened.

The writing is certainly racy, in the sense of both pungency and speed, and Alan Dilworths production puts it across with admirable clarity and economy. Yannik Larivees set sneaks in a couple of cheeky homages to the historical period: a miniature palace, probably Hampton Court, hangs upside down over the scene, and there's an actual throne, sparingly but powerfully used. Other furnishings are purposefully nondescript.

The scenes around the Tudor family dinner-table are a hoot. The princesses are arrestingly written and played. Sara Farb's Mary is all scarcely bottled resentment, Bahia Watsons Bess is a cheeky teen in the process of growing up. Eddie, the precocious boy-king who never got the chance to grow up, is played Jonas Q. Gribble, an exceptionally palatable and intelligent child actor. As his uncle Thom, Gareth Potter does well though he gets left behind by the plays secondact gallop to keep up with history.

Religious tensions are remarkably scanted, considering that this is a play about the Reformation and its aftermath. But Hennig, a fine actress as well as a promising playwright, is planning two further plays on the reigns of Mary and Elizabeth, so chances are she'll get to it.

In repertory as part of the Stratford Festival until Oct. 7.

David Hou / Joseph Ziegler as Henry and Maev Beaty as Kate in The Last Wife.
2015-08-22-for-the-ladies-shakespeare-s-:
The new Stratford production of Loves Labours Lost begins, brilliantly, with Mike Shara arriving late. Shara is playing Berowne, one of the three young lords who, in this great early Shakespeare comedy, sign up for the King of Navarre's program of turning his court into a model university, a "little academe." He is also the most skeptical about its chances of success, given that the proposed academy strongly resembles a monastery with strict prohibitions concerning eating, sleeping and - above all - contact with women. Berowne himself obviously likes to sleep in, which is why he's still plonking down his suitcase while his fellows, having made a ceremonial entrance, are already taking their vows. Berowne is both a realist and a compulsive joker. Its he who reminds the king that the no-woman rule will have to be broken, immediately, as the Princess of France is about to arrive on a diplomatic mission. She has three attendant ladies, and of course the four men fall in love with the four women. They send extravagant love letters, mostly in verse, which the ladies, though fundamentally favourably disposed, find ludicrous. To a large extent, this is a play about words, and like Berowne himself, it both mocks and revels in them. John Caird, a firstdivision British director making his Stratford debut, builds his production around them. The wit-combats, often involving multiple players, are elaborately orchestrated, and elaborately choreographed as well. Theres an action to suit every word.

Berowne has two great speeches, both about love. In the first he confesses that he, the cynic, has turned out the most hopeless of romantics, while remaining cynical even about that. Shara bounds about the stage, in an ecstasy of self-mocking selfflagellation. The second, undertaken to save the faces of himself and his forsworn friends, is a long lyrical aria in praise of love and of women; and this he delivers with a stillness, a concentration and a command, all the more compelling for their contrast with the hyper-activity that both follows and precedes them. It's a vindication of the Festival stage as an unrivalled launching-pad for language, and of the actor who, after innumerable and usually very funny successes in supporting roles, finally has a governing role and triumphs in it.

Of his fellow students, Sanjay Talwar is an engagingly indecisive king while Andrew Robinson, a supercilious Longaville, and Thomas Olajide, an acrobatic Dumaine, make individuals out of roles that are usually blanks. The women however, who are meant to be the repositories of sense and reason, largely fall down on the job; Ruby Joy is a graceful princess but she could use some lower notes in both her voice and her personality.

The young aristocrats are surrounded by humbler, and mostly older, folk, similarly word-drunk. Prince among them is Don Adriano de Armado, the fantastical (and deadbroke) Spaniard, whom Juan Chioran endows with moustachios spectacularly flared and with a bizarre dignity of soul. His diminutive page Moth is played by young Gabriel Long with remarkable fluency, verbal and on occasion musical, though the production's use of the latter element sometimes gets out of hand. Josue Labourcane is a find as the clown Costard and, as the country wench whose favours he shares with the Don, Jennifer Mogbock is a carnal delight. Then there are the pedants, the professional wordmerchants;

Tom Rooney is an unusual schoolmaster Holofernes, more robust and sensual than the average and also more humane, while Brian Tree, who must by now have played every rustic role in this play, flutters sententiously around him as the curate Sir Nathaniel. Hethen becomes touching in his role as Alexander the Great in the last act pageant of the Nine Worthies, trying uncomfortably to look martial on a hobby-horse. This whole interlude is spectacularly staged, with lots of props, though I wondered, not for the first time, how these well-meaning amateurs could have managed, at about a half-hours notice, to get it all together.

The play proper is prettily set and costumed, Cavalier-style, by Patrick Clark, and beautifully lit by Michael Walton. For all that, its less seductive, less funny, and less verbally adroit than Michael Langham's swan-song production of seven years ago. It's fussier, and its also less moving. What makes this play a masterpiece is its unique bittersweet conclusion. Some 10 minutes from the final curtain, all seems set for a happy ending; the ladies have forgiven the gentlemen their foolishness, the Jacks have won their Jills. Then, out of nowhere, a messenger appears. The princesss father is dead; games, romantic or verbal, must be set aside. Besides, the fact of death makes the women aware that the men still have some maturing to do. They're told to smarten up, sober up, devote themselves to good works for a year and a day, then report back. Here, the shock is muted. We can see the messenger coming (he enters down the auditorium steps) and there hasn't been enough rapport between the lovers for their separation to mean much. The final song of the Owl and the Cuckoo, all plain words and sweet music, helps out, as it always does, but the magic has gone. No other play ends like this, and the play knows it: Come, sir, it wants a 12-month and a day. And then twill end. "Thats too long for a play."

Weekend Post robert.cushman@hotmail.com

Love's Labour's Lost is in repertory through Oct. 9 at the Festival Theatre, Stratford

Da Vid Hou / The no-woman rule doesnt make it far in Loves Labour's Lost featuring Andrew Robinson as Longaville, Mike Shara as Berowne, Sanjay Talwar as King Ferdinand of Navarre and Thomas Olajide as Dumaine.
2015-08-27-a-brilliant-farce:
A very good Stratford season concludes with a grand production of one of the best plays from the Shakespearean period not to have been written by the house playwright. Ben Jonson's The Alchemist is, along with the same author's Volpone, among the classic English comedies of scam.

We're in a house in London in 1610, during one of the city's recurrent bouts of plague. The owner has fled to the country, leaving his butler in sole possession. He teams up with a con-man named Subtle and a prostitute with the enchanting name of Dol Common. Subtle's racket is to pose as a "cunning man", one whose supernatural knowledge can help his clients to financial or social success. The butler's function is to roam around town, reeling in likely dupes; he adopts the persona of a gamester and soldier, and calls himself Captain Face.

Most of the victims are small-timers, for whom Subtle functions as a glorified fortuneteller. But there is one outsized exception: Sir Epicure Mammon, a knight with fantastic dreams of monetary and sexual glory. For him Subtle assumes the role of alchemist, purveyor of the Philosopher's Stone, the magical substance whose touch can turn base metals into gold. Since Mammon has a lot of base metal already on hand, and is happy to turn it over, he and the gang seem made for one another.

The play begins with the thieves falling out, Subtle and Face both claiming to be the one who does all the work. Dol keeps telling them to calm down and stop yelling, so the volume-level in Antoni Cimolino's production is probably justifiable. Certainly, too, the quarrel is pungently staged and enthusiastically acted. Still, it's a relief when they quiet down and agree to compete over "who shall shark best" that day. The whole action is confined to that one day and that one house: a classical economy unique in Elizabethan/Jacobean drama. The concentration makes for brilliant farce. The play's unique in another way; of all the raucous comedies set in the London of the time, it's the only one to be written entirely in verse. The language is a heady mixture of lyricism and slang; Cimolino's production does an excellent job of keeping the words clear, the action furious, and the characters distinctive, compelling, and extremely funny.

It's hard to say which of the two male leads does in fact shark best. Stephen Ouimette's lank-haired Subtle is the purer charlatan of the two, so ascetically intent in his doubletalk that you almost suspect him of believing it himself. He can certainly be piously indignant when challenged: not that this prevents him from being the dirtiest of fighters with his own colleagues. Ouimette's timing, physical and verbal, is a thing of wonder. Jonathan Goad's Face paints with a broader and more cynical brush; he's a shape-shifter, a man of many Faces, switching between backslapping barfly and scuttling lab assistant at a moments' notice. His energy is unflagging; impressively, he never tries to ingratiate himself with the audience, not at least until the epilogue in which he, the tricksters' trickster, enlists us as his coconspirators. Brigit Wilson's Dol is the voice of exasperated common sense when mediating between the two men, and an enticing decoy when let loose on the more susceptible male customers.

It's when these customers start overlapping that the fun and the desperation move into the highest gear, as the trio wildly improvise to keep their stories straight. We've already had time to size up the visitors, as each in turn makes an introductory appearance. By their clothes we know them; Carolyn M. Smith's period costumes help individualize them, as well as giving us an agreeable window onto a past world. Antoine Yared's Dapper, a lawyer's clerk with gambling ambitions, is defined by his barrister's wig, presumably borrowed and slightly askew: a definition that the actor fills out with properly pedantic insistence. Steve Ross' delightful Abel Drugger, humble pharmacist, wears an apron and a shy smile, one that gets bolder the more thoroughly he is swindled. I felt, as never before in this play, just how these fellows are drawn in, how inevitably one step leads to the next; it's easy, without any modern-dress nudging, to recognize and even identify with them.

Scott Wentworth's Mammon is something else; in the most bloated bloomers ever fashioned, he rhapsodizes over the riches he'll disperse and the harems he'll furnish. There's a luxuriant grandeur to the visions of this Epicure, even a trace of public spirit. When his dreams go up in (literal) smoke and onlookers commiserate on the losses he's sustained he replies, sorrowfully, "not I: the commonwealth." As his skeptical friend Surly, who tries to cheat the cheaters and pays the penalty for his (comparative) honesty, Wayne Best displays an unwonted flair for sardonic humour, first as its mouthpiece, then as its victim. Jamie Mac, fresh-faced and pugnacious in the role of Kastril, the "angry boy" from the country, anxious to learn how to quarrel "by the book," a book, needless to say, in which Subtle is eager to instruct. Indeed, he probably wrote it.

Jonson's is a measured madness. The only characters with whom he reaches Shakespearean heights of spontaneous craziness are his favourite targets, the covetous puritans. Here, however, they fall short: Rylan Wilkie is far too reasonable for the perpetually angry deacon Ananias ("I hate traditions; I do not trust them"), leaving Randy Hughson in the awkward position of playing straight man to a straight man as his superior, Tribulation Wholesome.

The play itself isn't quite perfect; it blows its stack a little too early, condemning the alchemist himself to a rushed, inglorious exit. Or maybe it just seems that way because Ouimette, unlike some Subtles, has earned his titular status, the centrepiece of an explosive, hilarious show.

In repertory until October

Courtesy Of The Stratford Festival / From left: Jonathan Goad, Brigit Wilson and Stephen Ouimette in Ben Jonson's The Alchemist.
2015-08-29-internet-connection-second-ci:
The new Second City revue, most unusually for its species, has a title that bears some relation to the show itself. Click Bait Switch is a revue for the Internet age, with opening and closing routines that consist of the six-person cast delivering disconnected come-on lines designed to hook unwary or credulous surfers. Beyond that it has, intentionally or otherwise, a recurring theme. It depicts people behaving like automata.

Of course, a lot of comedy does that. Obsessiveness is what makes the wheels of comedy, and especially of farce, go round. But this show seems, well, obsessive about it. Its second half kicks off with Kyle Dooley, a notably tall performer with equally notable improv skills, as a muscleman ready to challenge all comers, real or fictitious, living or dead, and coming on like a cross between a cartoon figure and a wind-up doll. The same description might go, double, for the two senescent wheelchair-bound billionaires, married, whom we find wondering how to dispose of their wealth. This is an especially strong number whose major joke is all the more satisfying for being foreseeable a short way off. It also has that rarity in Second City or any other revues: a great punchline. And it has an Internet connection.

This is an unusually intelligent show: one that taps into today without going for easy topicality. (Such words as Harper and Duffy never cross a performer's lips.) The first extended sketch - to tell the truth, it's over-extended, but funny nonetheless - has the sextet at a barbecue, screeching "Don't Do That" - every time someone says something that might be considered shaming of someone else, which is all the time. A happy young couple, she an activist, he a CSIS agent, recall how they found compatibility,. ("Are you reading my mind?" "No, just your emails.") A darkskinned guy - Etan Muskat, versatile and ebullient - reveals to his two paleskinned buddies that his secret fantasy is to be white. ("I'd like to ask a waiter, how spicy is the pepper?") His friends aren't pleased. ("We're not racist, but without you - there's no proof.") This item also has a good payoff, physical rather than verbal. We visit a high-end restaurant that gives new meaning to the term "tasting menu", and where the dessert is rendered more delicious by having a hungry man (Dooley, on a leash and with his tongue hanging out) watch you eat it. There's a great ending to this too, all the better for connecting with an earlier scene.

There's also plenty of stuff that's just charmingly crazy. Becky Johnson, another tall performer, sabotages herself at a job interview, despite her potential employer's kindest intentions. (She refuses a relaxing drink on the grounds that alcohol makes her weird. She must have put away a few before she even got there.) Leigh Cameron sweetly delivers the evening's one and only song as a delectable pastry, cheerfully waiting to be devoured. ("It's OK, please don't cry /For I'm just a singing pie.") More manically musical - far more - is Kirsten Rasmussen as a demonically possessed clubber, whose moves drive the other guests to request music that she can't dance to. It turns out that no such music exists. Kevin Whalen, who has a knack for appearing simultaneously genial and worried, heads a trio of caterpillars all grossed out by the unexpected experience of turning into butterflies. Which probably they would be, not having had sexed. There's a sketch about that, too, and a good one, with very funny representatives of the puritanical, the permissive and the just-don't-know-yet There are creepy-crazy bits as well. Johnson and Whalen play a mother and son out for a drive, the former telling the latter things no boy should have to know. An ultrasound scene puts a new face, and body, on some familiar fears and feelings. (I know that sounds vague but I don't want to give everything away.) It has yet another effective ending; I don't know what I've been complaining about. Somewhere between the comforting and the forbidding is a twist on the old Lady and the Tiger theme: a traveller has to choose between two doors, one festive, one fatal, guided by two confusing oracles who are new on the job; this bit, like its protagonist, doesn't really know where it's going but has some fun on the way.

So it's a good show, mostly well written, always excellently performed, and with a tang that differentiates it from its predecessors. Paul Bates directed it.

Click Bait Switch runs indefinitely at Second City

2015-09-05-look-forward-to-looking-back-:
Summer bows out, the festivals wind down, and the Toronto theatres gear up for a new season. From what's been announced, it looks like being a nostalgic one. It's full of plays we've seen before, sometimes in productions we've seen before. That isn't necessarily a bad thing. enjoyable shows are there to be enjoyed, by as many people as want to see them.

Factory theatre The most throughgoing retrospective is at the Factory Theatre, which is offering a whole season of Canadian classics: a description, rather promiscuously employed, that seems to mean plays by Canadian writers that have already been done by someone else. The season's umbrella title is Naked, and it has a subtitle as well, of machine-gun briskness: "Text. Audience. Imaginations. The Possibilities Are endless." What this seems to mean is that these will be barebones productions, with no horrible decorations to get in the way. my own imagination runs to the possibility that this might be an economic necessity as much as an artistic choice, but that's probably unkind. "Naked" says Peter Hinton, who directs one of the plays, "is the invitation to engage the imagination fully."

Hinton is certainly a director who knows about engaging the imagination, as well as having plenty of his own, though lately he's been exercising it on a far larger scenic scale at Shaw Festival. The play he's staging at the Factory is bombay black, by Anosh Irani, previously seen at Theatre Centre in 2006. Set in an Indian dance hall, it concerns an exotic dancer, which doesn't mean there what it does here; her managing mother, who really is her manager; and a bookseller from their village who comes to see the dancer dance, despite being blind. I remember it as having first-rate dialogue but woolly construction. I look forward to seeing what Hinton, one of our very best, will make of it. (Factory mainspace: Nov. 17-dec. 6).

tarragon The Tarragon has an impressive lineup of new Canadian work, including plays by Gord rand (better known as an actor), Kit Sandler, and - someone we haven't heard from for a long time - Fabrizio Filippo. It starts however, with a couple of re-treads. One is a show previously seen at Harbourfront: blind date, in which clown-improviser rebecca Northan interacts each night with a different member of the audience, who presumably doesn't get paid even though he ends up doing a lot of the work.

The other is a re-tread of a re-tread. The Tarragon's most exciting production last season was An enemy of the People, a version of the Ibsen classic about a Norwegian doctor who alienates his community by pointing out that its water supply is contaminated. Since the town in question is a spa, this poses serious moral and economic questions. richard rose, Tarragon's artistic director, saw a modern-dress production that greatly impressed him at the berlin Schaubuhne theatre, and re-created it, in english, on his own stage. The play is now billed as "created by Henrik Ibsen," in tactful acknowledgement of the departures from the original. The crucial public meeting scene, for example, is revamped to include audience participation. The new staging will see a further departure: the protagonist, dr. Stockmann, is to be played as a woman, by the admirable Laura Condolln. For the trivia-minded: also new to the cast is the redoubtable david Fox who once played dr. Stockmann at Stratford (as a man). (Tarragon mainspace: Oct. 7-Nov. 1).

Soulpepper Soulpepper has a full slate of past hits, starting with The Play's the Thing, a stylish delight from their second season and one of their formative productions, and proliferating over the holiday season for a "family festival" so extensive that it will spill over from the company's own distillery stages onto that of the bluma Appel theatre in the St. Lawrence Centre. meanwhile, back at the ranch, a rarity: Peter Weiss's The Persecution and Assassination of Jean-Paul marat as Performed by the Inmates of the Asylum under the direction of the marquis de Sade, more conveniently known as the marat/Sade. This play, one of the most celebrated of the 1960s, has been little seen since then, at least in english, probably because Peter brook's London staging (subsequently seen in New york and then filmed) has been deemed an impossible act to follow. Albert Schultz, who follows it, has two Soulpepper regulars ideally cast in the title roles: Stuart Hughes as the carbuncled revolutionary marat, diego matamoros as the disillusioned philosopher Sade. And it has a new score - the play is virtually a musical - by the company's own mike ross. (young Centre, opening Sept. 14).

coal Mine Still, my choice for the season's most promising lineup is the one at the Coal mine, a basement space under a restaurant on the danforth, where some of our best actors have been doing some of their best work for what I take to be a pittance. They'll be doing four plays, and I feel compelled to list them all. First is The river, written by the british playwright Jez butterworth whose Jerusalem is one of the most justly acclaimed plays of recent years; it's directed by Ted dykstra, the Coal mine's "artistic curator." (Nov. 1-21). Then there's the promise of something Toronto rarely sees: high-level wintertime Shakespeare. Graham Abbey, Stratford luminary, makes his directorial debut with, fittingly, The Winter's Tale with a cast of other Stratford luminaries. (Jan. 28-Feb. 20). Then there's Killer Joe, by Tracy Letts, author of the American hit August: Osage County, which was one of the most unjustly acclaimed plays of recent years, but one shouldn't be prejudiced. (April 3-24). And finally - an actual new Canadian play: Instructions (To Any Future Socialist Government Proposing to Abolish Christmas) by michael mackenzie. I've no idea what it will be like but I love the title. (may 29-June 19).
