2015-09-08-the-historic-form-and-functio:
The historic role of the American musical has been to tell stories about America. They don't have to be true stories; they can be rooted in national legends or they can just reflect united states of mind. But, every so often, Broadway hosts a show that stages some crucial part of the nations own recorded past. Its doing so now, to huge acclaim, with Hamilton, a musical biography of one of the less-celebrated of America's founding fathers. Lin-Manuel Miranda's show, with a score built on hip-hop rhythms and hip-hop wordplay, may be turning - or returning - Hamilton into a household name.

Miranda wrote the shows book, music and lyrics; he also plays the title role. To find a similar quadruple threat, you have to go back to one of the musicals own founding fathers: George M. Cohan, who flourished at the beginning of the twentieth century. The two share more than versatility. Cohan's best-remembered songs include Give My Regards to Broadway, The Yankee Doodle Boy ("I'm a Yankee Doodle Dandy"), and Over There, the definitive First World War whoop. His stock-in-trade was a jaunty jingoism; he was famous for draping an American flag around himself while performing.

Cohan didnt write historical musicals and his patriotism was never what you would call subtle or ironic. Mirandas is both. But at the same time, his show is very much a celebration of America. Its national symbol is not a flag but a banknote. Alexander Hamilton, Washington's aide-de-camp in the War of Independence, later became America's first Secretary of the Treasury, the face on the 10-dollar bill. Or, as he himself raps it, hes a Ten-dollar Founding Father/Without a father. Hamilton was born out of wedlock, on a Caribbean island to a French mother and Scottish father. Or, as Aaron Burr, Americas third vicepresident and Hamilton's historical and theatrical nemesis, puts it, "the orphan, bastard son of a whore and a Scotsman." Burr was of old Puritan stock, and he wonders how Hamilton could have gotten so far, so fast. The musical's answer seems to be: by being blatant. And it exemplifies its own theme. Immigrants! exult Hamilton and his fellow revolutionary warrior the Marquis de Lafayette, "we get the job done." Its a line that rocks the Richard Rodgers Theatre.

The American musical itself is largely the creation of immigrants. One of the key American shows is Fiddler on the Roof; which of course is set far from America, but depicts people who, as the curtain falls, are making their way to a country in which they will fashion entertainments like the one weve been watching. Fiddler was the first major show in which Jewishness was a subject rather than a code. It gave us Jews played by Jews, or by actors who could pass. Hamilton gives ethnicity an extra, dizzying spin. Its characters, basically the men who made the American Revolution and the women who loved them, are white. Yet, only one of the performers is.

Miranda, a charming and funny performer in his own right, is Hispanic. Most of his colleagues are black. That includes the actor playing Burr. The show makes sparing mention of slavery, but the subject looms and the casting bites; Daveed Diggs, the rapper-turned actor who plays both Lafayette and Jefferson, is terrific. In the matter of racial casting as commentary, the show's most obvious antecedent is the 1976 Stephen Sondheim-John Weidman masterpiece Pacific Overtures, whose subject was the American opening up of Japan to Western culture in the nineteenth century, and whose style was a hybrid of Japanese and Broadway traditions. As the undeclared conquest continued, the staging and the music became more westernized. The cast was all Asian, and so were most of the characters. But the same actors played the American and European invaders as well, and they were presented in Kabuki fashion. The audience was jolted into a new look at its own history, just as in Hamilton.

A highlight of Pacific Overtures is the magnificent Someone in a Tree in which four outsiders offer contrasting accounts of what happened at a closed meeting. The most exciting number in Hamilton is The Room Where It Happens, in which Burr, like a frustrated Iago, rages about all the high-level wheeler-dealing from which he is shut out. Like its predecessor, this song grows in intensity, spurred on by its staging. The reviews of Hamilton hadn't prepared me for the brilliance of Andy Blankenbuehlers choreography, an almost ceaseless but never excessive swirl, precisely keyed to the beats.

The one character for whom this staging stands comparatively still, and the only one to be played by a white actor, is King George III, who periodically tells his ungrateful former subjects how much he loves them. He has a nice line in purring, playful threats: "When push comes to shove/I will send a fully armed battalion/To remind you of my love."

Compare Sondheims British envoy, buttering up the reluctant Japanese, Gilbert and Sullivan style: We don't foresee that you will be the least bit argumentative - So please ignore the man-of-war we brought as a preventative."

Miranda has his own shout-out to Gilbert and Sullivan: George Washington calls himself the very model of a modern major-general and rhymes it with "men are all which Miranda has claimed, accurately, to be a truer rhyme than Gilbert's mineral.".

As Sondheim himself has pointed out, Mirandas strength is his awareness of musical theatre tradition: the mutual reinforcement of words and music. The classic American musical grew up alongside the classic American popular song, flanked by jazz. Immigrants, or the children of immigrants, got the job done, revelling in the American language both verbal and musical, bending it to their will. For about 50 years, theatre music and popular music were practically synonymous. Rock changed that, downplaying lyrics or making them impenetrable, rendering them useless for telling stories. Rap can seem similarly self-enclosed, but its generally rooted in specific people in specific circumstances, and it can move from soliloquy to conflict.

Miranda's earlier show, In the Heights, pointed the way, and Hamilton follows it, finding in hip-hop's insistence a mirror for the assertive irreverence of the revolutionaries themselves. "Im not throwing away my shot," cries Hamilton at the shows start, and the image pursues him until it resolves itself in the duel that ends his life: shot by Burr. That's the overarching pun in a show that's full of them. The rhymes can seem relentless, but Miranda uses the form to restore the musical to its lost tradition of wit: the tradition that was almost destroyed by the humourless pop operas and hardly restored by the spoof shows whose only joke is themselves. Miranda applies the lightest of touches to the weightiest of subjects, without ever cheapening them.

Hamilton is a New York musical, as the smartest shows have traditionally been, ever since Cohan sent his regards to Broadway. New York is where Hamilton, before getting embroiled in war and politics, began his career as a lawyer, and its the place to which the show keeps returning. Its a town that shows like Guys and Dolls have turned into a mythical place, a city that has created its own legend: a core part of the larger national legend. Hamilton knows this, knows its place in the tradition, in all the traditions. It says so in its full title which, as displayed on posters and programs, is deliciously double-edged. The title is Hamilton: An American Musical.

News Service / Lin-Manuel Miranda wrote Hamilton's book, music, lyrics and also plays the title role. His awareness of musical theatre tradition shines through in a production that is as much about American musical theatre as it is about American history.
2015-09-12-send-in-the-clowns-half-heart:
Circuses are the original theatresin-the-round, meaning that half the audience gets a good view of the other half. The view on the first night of Empire, a sort of circus that's pitched its tent down by the Toronto lakeshore, revealed a lot of people taking pictures on their phones, whether of the show itself or of themselves taking pictures of the show. Most live entertainments begin with admonitions to the audience to refrain from the use of recording devices of any kind. Not this one: it exists to go viral. In that regard, it's a dispiriting look at the possible future, indeed of the probable present. It isn't the evening out that matters; it's the morning after.

This may also account for the curious half-heartedness of the show itself; it doesn't even officially start - with a clangorous call of "Welcome to Empire" - until we've already been watching it for half an hour. During this preliminary period, with the house lights on, performers have been milling around in fairly aimless fashion. One of them is a pirate sort of guy in a blue silk shirt; another is a lady who appears to be following the old theatrical maxim, "If you can't be funny, wear a big hat." There's some nondescript dancing, and a man who produces what I took to be an egg from inside his pants, then holds them open while other cast members, looking bored, pelt him what I took to be tennis balls. Somewhat more interestingly, a young woman in her underwear gyrates inside a revolving globe, receiving thunderous applause when she does the splits. As her act concludes, the air fills with soap bubbles, an effect that's pretty if hardly original.

Pre-show over, the lights go down and the performers get down: to, presumably, business. The title Empire seems to refer to the Empire State Building; from time to time people parade around the circus ring carrying little models of this and other New York landmarks. The show seems to have its roots in New York - at least it played there for a long time - and it makes occasional reverential mentions of Times Square; this must count as nostalgia since no one is likely to feel sentimental about that location, as currently constituted. Anyway, those moments don't seem to have any relevance to anything else that's going on. We merely get a succession of acts from anywhere. The publicity promises "somersaulting, slapsticking and stripteasing." The somersaulting parts are the best.

They amount to a semi-cirque: that is, they resemble Cirque du Soleil, but without the beauty or the danger. (To be fair, the show isn't pretentious, either, as Cirque productions sometimes can be.) A trio of intertwining female acrobats is accomplished and inventive, without being spectacular. A man spins hoops around himself. These Empire contortionists are doing things that you or I couldn't do, but we've all seen other performers doing things that these couldn't do. Or at least don't do. The slapsticking is best passed over. As for the stripteasing: the only nudity is male, and very brief. The nearest we get to tease is the caged lady early on.

No, I think I tell a lie. There's an extended scene in which a woman with Dietrich inflections pulls a male spectator onstage, dances with him until declaring that he has no sense of rhythm, then sits him down and vamps him, meanwhile asking personal questions about his sex life. (When she isn't talking she's singing, inexplicably, Brother Can You Spare a Dime?) She does take most of her clothes off in the process, and I wondered if she was going to turn out to be a man. She doesn't; but there's a coda that I wouldn't want to spoil, or indeed describe. I thought the whole routine repulsive and demeaning, though I'll admit the guy on the receiving

I long one day to see a victim of audience

participation refuse to participate end didn't seem to be objecting. All the same, I long one day to see a victim of audience participation refuse to participate, preferably throwing in a couple of obscenities to make the point. The performers always have the advantage in these scenarios, because they've rehearsed. It's actually bullying.

One routine stands apart from the rest. A male performer slowly and methodically assembles an elaborate contraption of long overlaying bamboo sticks, keeping them together, it seems, by sheer force of willpower. It's the most Cirque-like of all the acts; indeed I may have seen it before in a Cirque show. In a boring kind of way, it's hypnotic. It's probably the most distinguished item in the evening. It's also the last item, but as a climax it's an anti-climax, since it bears no relation to anything that has gone before, either in style or in what might charitably be described as substance. It certainly has nothing to do with New York. "Them's slim pickings under that little old big top."

Empire runs through Oct. 18 in the Spiegeltent, 318 Queens Quay West

Dani Elle Covin / Empire resembles Cirque du Soleil, but without the beauty or the danger.; Free Style Photography /
2015-09-15-canadian-voice-on-broadway-ch:
For some half-dozen years, a favourite question among Canadian theatre audiences was "how long can we hang on to Chilina Kennedy?" Or, more precisely," how long before Broadway snaps her up?" Kennedy, a small vocal dynamo and one of the prized products of Sheridan College's musical theatre program, spent three years at the Shaw Festival playing ingenue roles in musicals: most delectably Eileen in Wonderful Town. She then spent three more years at the Stratford Festival, playing leading roles in musicals; these included the best of all possible Marias in West Side Story and an Evita who actually played the character, rather than the idea of a generalized rock-opera.

And now, the Broadway snapping-up having happened, she's in New York, being real as another real person. She's playing Carole King in a show based on the lady's life and songs and entitled Beautiful. At the moment in the show when her character is urged to make the transition from pure composer to singer-songwriter, she asks dubiously "Who wants to hear a normal person sing?" That's the best line in a jukebox musical whose songs are great to hear but whose script makes Jersey Boys seem like a literary masterpiece. The second-best line is the response she gets from a musician-friend: "Uh ... other ordinary people?" Kennedy plays, charmingly and believably, an ordinary person with an extraordinary talent.

She also, both in and out of character, conveys a modest delight in her own success. Here she is: the centrepiece of a Broadway musical with her name firmly at the head of the cast. "There are" she says in a phone conversation "no words." Still, she finds some.

She didn't create the role. It was originated last season by the American actress Jessie Mueller, who won a Tony for it. Kennedy had auditioned for it the first time around. She was already somewhat known in New York having played Mary Magdalene in the Stratford Festival production of Jesus Christ Superstar that went to Broadway. At that point her career became bi-national. She appeared in Hartford, Conn., in the comedymusical A Gentleman's Guide to Love and Murder. But she also came back to Canada to appear in the new musical Evangeline, and - less expectedly - to play Cecily in a Halifax production of The Importance of Being Earnest, opposite another Sheridan grad, Michael Therriault. Both actors represent a healthy contingent of Canadian performers who can switch, apparently effortlessly, between plays and musicals. Both were also in the Birmingham Conservatory, Stratford's post-grad academy for classical acting; Kennedy had a non-musical Stratford success in John Steinbeck's The Grapes of Wrath.

When the chance came to reaudition for Beautiful, she was prepared. "Fortunately, I'd kept the music I'd been working on the first time; usually I throw it away." She was only just in time. "I was 33 weeks pregnant - they don't let you fly after 36. I did the audition; they put me on a tape for Carole. I flew back to Canada, and went into labour from the stress." Soon afterwards she got a phone-call from her agent saying "I'd like two tickets for your opening on Broadway." It took her a moment to realize what he meant.

The bulk of the show deals with King's early career, as a composer to the lyrics of her husband Gerry Goffin (played by Scott J. Campbell, yet another Sheridan graduate and another Canadian, though one whose career has been entirely American). Her solo flights are kept till the end, though these songs, from the legendary 1971 Tapestry album, are the ones that get the biggest response, from an audience that plainly grew up with them. It's also the part of the legend that weighs most heavily on Kennedy, even though she was born several years after the record came out. "So many people attach themselves to Tapestry - what it meant to them in their lives - so they have expectations of me and the character." King herself is "so private, she didn't want to come see the show in the beginning" though when she did, she approved. She's described in the show - by herself - as "always wanting to please", and the storyline is largely about her learning how to please herself as well to outgrow Goffin as both a professional and marital partner.

Beautiful is running at the Stephen Sondheim Theatre, New York.

Illustration
Joan Marcus, The O And M Co., The Associated Press / Canadian actress-singer Chilina Kennedy who is taking over for Jessie Mueller in Beautiful: The Carole King Musical.
2015-09-18-from-stage-to-screen-and-back:
The stage show London Road was one of a kind: a verbatim musical, the actual spoken words of actual people, taken down and sung. There'd been nothing like it before, and theres been nothing like it since - though admittedly theres hardly been time yet for it to have any followers. It opened at the National Theatre in London in 2011, and was a great success. It's had only one major production elsewhere: a very fine one by the Canadian-Stage company in Toronto.

The show depicts the aftershocks of the murders of five prostitutes in the English provincial town of Ipswich. London Road is the street on which it happened, the street on which the killer lived, and the core of the piece is his neighbours' reactions, both before and after the arrest.

Now its been filmed. Rufus Norris, who directed the National Theatre production has directed a movie, with an augmented version of the original cast. Its playing at this year's Toronto International Film Festival, and Norris came over for the occasion, along with the two authors of both play and film, Alecky Blythe (she did the interviews, transcribed and edited the words) and Adam Cork (he set them to music, a fearsome task, nearoperatic in sheer duration).

Norris, a trim and friendly 50-year-old whose rise to the summit position in British theatre has been a steady progression through acting and directing, readily admits that "adaptation from stage to screen is very dangerous - especially when you're doing it with the same people. The verbatim musical is theatrical enough, so everything else needs to be questioned. There can be no direct address in the film and there can be no doubling."

London Road on stage has a cast of 11, all playing multiple roles; part of the pleasure of the Toronto production was keeping track of the actors. Thats a strictly theatrical device that can only work on screen if the film is consciously winking at the audience. Otherwise, it would just be confusing. So, London Roads London cast are all in the movie, but as one character apiece. Other roles are played by other people, the best-known newcomers being Tom Hardy in a small part and Olivia Colman in a big one.

We were trying, Blythe told me, "to make the film as active as possible." She also said that the film feels darker than the show. It certainly begins differently. The stage version starts by plunging us into the middle of the story; the householders of London Road meet to form a residents' association, to counter the bad rep they're getting in the media. The instigator of the meeting welcomes the others in song, haltingly but warmly. It sets up the convention of the whole piece, and the community at its centre.

The show then flashes back to the murders, or rather to the streets reaction to the murders. Thats where the film starts, with dialogue sequences: interviews that could pass for documentary footage. The approach, chronological and gradual, may have seemed logical, given the almost inescapable realism of film, but it means that when the singing does start, it seems artificial: even more than the average musical, because it's trying so hard not to be. There are some beautiful moments; when, with the murderer still at large, the women sing "you automatically think it could be him" of every man who crosses their path. Cork's choral setting, catching speech rhythms in music, is a wonderfully effective method of conveying a group reaction in song. The effect is mordantly enhanced in the film when the sung suspicions extend to a dummy in a menswear store. Too often, though, the singing seems to be a long-winded way of conveying information that might just as well be spoken (and, in real life, was).

London Road has the same problem all film musicals face (and one that would also affect original film musicals, if anyone made them any more): people breaking into song seems odd. And the more seriously the story appears to be taking itself, the odder it seems. It wasnt always a problem. When musicals were common currency, nobody minded; habit is its own convention. It helped of course that there were stars who created their own vocabulary. Fred Astaire, Judy Garland, Gene Kelly made singing and dancing seem as natural as talking. Nobody today gets to have that kind of career in movie musicals. But then very few of the classic film musicals were based on shows, even when they claimed to be. When the studios bought Broadway musicals in the 30s and 40s, they usually kept only the titles and a couple of hit songs; everything else got censored out. Religiously faithful, though still somewhat expurgated, films of shows only arrived in the 50s, when everything from Oklahoma! to West Side Story got the treatment.

Some of them (Kiss Me Kate, The King and I, The Pajama Game) were pretty good, but none captured the excitement of their stage originals, or even of a good stage revival, and many floundered helplessly between stools. Like the movie versions of straight plays, they performed a public service; they brought the material to audiences who wouldnt otherwise get to see it, and provided starrier, though not necessarily stronger, casts than any theatre production would be likely to afford. Pauline Kael once decried the cinematic purists who condemned filmed plays as if they'd got on the screen illegally. They were, she sensibly argued, among the many possible kinds of film, and should be accepted as such. But she seldom claimed that they were great movies. She did make an exception for Sidney Lumet's film of Long Days Journey into Night, and it contains superb performances by Ralph Richardson and Katharine Hepburn. But there have been productions of Eugene ONeill's play at the National Theatre and the Stratford Festival that moved me more, and in which the drama's confinement to one room seemed liberating rather than oppressive.

Were all familiar with the groaning sensation of a play being "opened up" for the camera; it sacrifices concentration without gaining anything much in return. The extra locations almost invariably seem gratuitous. Filming a play is a very different exercise to filming a novel; a play is a dramatic machine to begin with. Though Ill confess that I came out of the movie of Driving Miss Daisy feeling that I had a very good time and that I had no desire to see the play. I didn't want to spend an evening watching two people being lovable in an on-stage automobile. This is one case where opening up was a blessing.

Of late, the traffic has started going the other way, with the odds of collision even higher. Famous movie musicals have been put on stage, 42nd Street being the most successful example. But even that show is a pale, if loud, shadow of its original, with all the grit taken out. And why would anyone want to see a stage version of Singin' in the Rain? Its perfect as it is, and its still there. The public service argument hardly applies here. Stage productions are ephemeral. Films are forever, setting impossible standards of comparison. Why not just rent the movie?

There are exceptions, or at least there are ironies within ironies. The movie of Cabaret was good, but the original stage production was better. All the same, recent stage revivals have essentially been adaptations of the film. One of the great American plays, The Front Page (1928), became one of the great American films, His Girl Friday (1940), a wholly different though still related animal. The trick was changing one of the male leads to a woman, decades before gender-neutral casting became a thing. Then, in 2003, the National Theatre (and later the Shaw Festival) put His Girl Friday on stage, hoping for the best of both worlds and, predictably, getting the worst. The wheel didn't come full circle; it stuck in the middle.

A staged film that actually worked - triumphantly in Toronto, and also apparently in London - was the dramatization of the Danish film Festen, which was a very special case; even as a film, it was practically a play. As Rufus Norris says "it gives you permission." He directed the London production, which subsequently went to New York, where it quickly closed. As he says, it didn't have name recognition. And thats the problem with plays into movies, and even more with movies into plays. People arent buying entertainment. They're buying a name.

National Post

London Road plays at The Bloor Hot Docs Cinema in Toronto at 6:00 PM on Sunday, Sept. 20.

Courtesy Of Tiff / London Road, a verbatim musical about the reactions of the murders of five prostitutes, is now a movie.
2015-09-19-meta-memory-lane-soulpepper-r:
Soulpepper first staged The Plays the Thing in 1999. It was the first production of the company's second season and it's the show that defined them. Their first two-play season had been a great success but it was still possible to attribute that to Robin Phillips who had directed both productions. There was then an interregnum production of Our Town: another success, and one that was to be often revived, but still a play that one would expect North American actors to know their way around. The Plays the Thing was something else: a Hungarian comedy from the 1920s, glorying in its own artifice. It gave Diego Matamoros his first Soulpepper leading role. And from the moment he stepped forward to deliver, with consummate cool, the plays opening speech, we knew we were home. Except that home had never been like this. There was a level of sophistication and assurance here unprecedented in Toronto. And so it went - in Beckett, Chekhov and Tennessee Williams - throughout the season.

The Play's the Thing was directed by an actual Hungarian, Laszlo Marton; his production was revived in 2003, and now it's back again. Matamoros still plays Sandor Turai, the boulevard dramatist who starts the play by remarking to his colleagues on how difficult it is to start a play. How much easier it would be if you could bypass all the customary contrived conversations and simply tell the audience who was who and what was what. He then proceeds to do just that, informing us that he, his longtime collaborator, and their new protege, a brilliant young composer, have just finished writing an operetta, and are currently holed up in a friends castle, awaiting the arrival of their leading lady who is also the composers fiancee. Exposition over, the action starts. The trio overhear their star in the next room, receiving the advances of an older married actor, and not resisting them as firmly as might be hoped. The composer is devastated; his friends fear for him, and fear even more for their own chances of having a hit. Sandor, forever unfazed, stays up all night and writes a play, incorporating all the shameless words that had emanated from next door. He then blackmails the guilty couple into performing it, so that his young musical genius will believe that he had unwittingly eavesdropped on a rehearsal. All ends happily, according to the ancient comic maxim that happiness consists of being well-deceived.

The production isn't quite the polished jewel it used to be; Matamoros, though stylish as ever, is almost too relaxed, and the first act moves slowly. The second, in which Sandor's overnight masterpiece gets rehearsed, is hilarious. There are two other survivors from the first staging: William Webster as second playwright, perpetually perplexed, and C. David Johnson in a gorgeous performance as the errant actor, sadistically saddled with an endless series of unpronounceable place-names. (The translation is by P. G. Wodehouse, the English master of pure comedy, and he really went to town here; or to a succession of towns.) Among the newcomers, Oliver Dennis is a perfect punctilious servant, Gordon Hecht a delightfully ingenuous young maestro, and Raquel Duffy the productions best prima donna to date. As a neurotically conscientious prompter Gregory Prest is funnily hysterical rather than hysterically funny; I preferred the quieter desperation of Jim Warren the first and second times around.

From old to new: Soulpeppers concurrent production of Happy Place is its first thoroughgoing world premiere, neither an adaptation (Of Human Bondage) nor a transfer from the fringe (Kim's Convenience). Pamela Mala Sinha's play does owe something to an earlier work; it takes off from her previous play Crash, a solo piece about a young woman surviving a rape. Happy Place gives us six women reeling from the same or similar traumas, all of them on suicide watch in a private care facility. But where Crash was a sustained creation, Happy Place has the feel of a diploma piece: a self-imposed assignment to write good roles for half-a-dozen actresses. In this it succeeds: a fine cast gets a succession of opportunities, some solo, some shared. But it doesnt add up to anything more organic.

It starts, like The Plays the Thing, magically, with the arrival on an empty stage of Samira, the patient whose experiences bear the strongest resemblance to the story of Crash; she proceeds to call the facility's communal area into being, one furnishing or appliance at a time. The elegance and simplicity of this prove typical of Alan Dilworth's production, but the device turns out to be structurally misleading. It suggests that Samira will be the focus of the play, but she turns out to be just one among equals; which is democratic but unsatisfying. Samira is played by Oyin Oladejo, who has tremendous presence but sometimes strays into orating rather than talking. The same pitfall periodically ensnares most of her colleagues, the shining exception being Diane DAquila who is scarifyingly good as an older woman with sulphurous reserves of anger. Liisa Repo-Martell is contrastingly, uncannily quiet as a patient nursing a possibly phantom pregnancy. Caroline Gillis is everybodys friend whom nobody likes; Irene Poole is a recently estranged lady apparently tormented by the fact that her adored son is only her stepson; and the author herself plays another woman with maternal issues. We learn more about some of them than about others, but not enough about any. Two of the inmates are discharged, or discharge themselves, but it's far from clear that they have become any less suicidal than those who remain. (And talking of loose ends, we're told that the facility charges $800 a day. Few of the characters look or talk as if they could afford it.)

There is a seventh character, the staff doctor; a role in which Deborah Drakeford looks right but sounds unconvinced. The ebbs and flows of institutional life are well captured, in writing and production, but there is little beyond that for the audience to hold on to. Sinha obviously didnt want to write a collective disease-of-the-week movie, and she probably wanted to avoid any kind of melodramatic climax, but if we are to be moved by the thought that life goes on, we need to be more fully involved in the lives in question. Soulpepper, true to eighteen years of form, offers another excellent ensemble but that, however much we enjoy watching actors interacting, cannot be an end in itself.

Weekend Post robert.cushman@hotmail.com

The Plays the Thing is in repertory through Oct. 14, and Happy Place through Oct. 12, at the Young Centre

Cylla Von Tiedemann / The Play's the Thing to see at Soulpepper.
2015-09-22-sightline-salutes-mirvish-pro:
On Monday, at the Royal Alexandra Theatre, Mirvish Productions announced their upcoming season. Or rather, they celebrated it. Most of the 2015-16 season has been public knowledge for some time. But this was an opportunity for those involved to sing a few songs (most Mirvish shows are musicals), screen a few video clips and tell a few jokes.

The principal joker, in his capacity as host, was Luke Kempner, a British actor about to open here in his one-man show Upside Downton, a spoof of Downton Abbey in which he plays thirty roles: that's more characters than most people could probably name from having watched the TV original. Once upon a time parodying a pop culture phenomenon would have been the job of a revue sketch, but the trend now is to make it last an evening. A few years ago Mirvish brought us a similar entertainment that derived from Harry Potter (and that played at the same theatre, the Panasonic).

"Without you, the audience, we on stage are nothing," said Kempner. "That's why this season is all about saluting you." That's true, of course, though I'm not sure why it should be truer of this season than of any other. Still, it's nice to hear some acknowledgment of the people it's all being done for, the people who laugh, cry, clap and buy subscriptions. Subscribers were actually represented at yesterday's event, via videotaped testimonials.

However, the bulk of the promotional activity concerned the bigger shows to which subscribers are being asked to subscribe. A quartet of performers from the Tonywinning musical A Gentleman's Guide to Love and Murder (touring version) breezed through a four-minute version of that show's extremely complicated plot. Bailey Ryon, currently playing the title role in the Broadway production of Matilda, flew up to sing one of the songs. This is the musical, based on a Road Dahl novel, that started in Stratford-on-Avon, then conquered London, and then New York. These two shows have something in common with one another, and indeed with Downton Abbey. They're all fantasies about England.

Matilda has oppressed schoolchildren with magical powers, rising up against a schoolmarm so monstrous that she has to be played by a man. Gentleman's Guide is about an oppressed young Edwardian gent with intellectual powers, who rises up against the relatives who have done the oppressing, murdering each of them until there's nobody left standing between him and the family title. This may remind you of Kind Hearts and Coronets, greatest of all English film comedies. Indeed, show and movie both acknowledge a common source, a long-forgotten novel. Gentleman's Guide, however, makes no explicit claim to being Kind Hearts: The Musical, and I'm sure the fact that, in both versions, all the victims are played by the same actor is merely a coincidence.

The designated holiday attraction is Cinderella, with music by Richard Rodgers and words by Oscar Hammerstein II. This, Kempner's narration assured us, "took Broadway

by storm." Well, no wonder: Broadway hasn't had a new RH score since The Sound of Music in 1959. This one, of course, isn't really new. It was a live TV special in 1957, starring Julie Andrews and attracting, we were told, 100 million viewers, more than have ever watched Downton Abbey, Kempner sportingly acknowledged. This isn't the first time somebody has attempted to put this Cinderella on stage: a cut-price version came through Toronto a few years ago. Maybe the new incarnation will preserve some of the original's wit along with its nice songs; Alexandra Zorn, who plays Cinders, sang one of them to whet our appetites.

Just about to open is Motown, a title that needs no explanation. A theoretically more adventurous musical than any of the above is If/Then, which has a score by Tom Kitt

and Brian Yorkey, who wrote Next to Normal, a musical about mental illness. This one is about life-choices; its opening song is called What If ?. The heroine gets to choose between two possible paths, and we get to watch her follow both of them. Idina Menzel won plaudits and prizes for playing this split personality on Broadway, but if she's playing it in Toronto the producers are keeping uncharacteristically quiet about it.

The most intriguing item, though, in the Mirvish Main Subscription package is a play, from the 1930s: Gaslight, a psychological thriller - actually, a psychological torturethriller - that became a famous film and is still a famous title, but has fallen off the theatrical radar. Patrick Hamilton, who wrote it, was a master of atmospherics, starting with his taste in titles. The noted British actor Owen Teale plays the charming villain. There's also The Judas Kiss, a play about Oscar Wilde by David Hare, starring Rupert Everett.

"For those looking for something a little more quirky, a little more challenging" there's the Off-Mirvish season, which has its own subscription system. It features two recent American plays, in new Canadian productions. One is Seminar, by Theresa Rebeck, whose central character is a cruelly demanding creative-writing teacher, to be played by the esteemed Tom McCamus. Disgraced, by Ayed Akhtar, is in the great American line of explosive dinner-party plays. Four diners: a Muslim lawyer, his WASP wife, a Jewish art-dealer, and his black wife. Raoul Bhaneja stars, in a role played off-Broadway by The Daily Show's Aasif Mandvi. (Later, on Broadway, Boardwalk Empire's Gretchen Mol joined the cast.) There's also Bigmouth in which a Belgian actor, Valentjin Dhaenens, delivers political speeches from Pericles of Athens to George W. Bush, each in the original language. It's described as "the ultimate press conference."

And - standing apart from the subscription seasons - there's the ultimate long-runner, The Phantom of the Opera. Again. However, this time it is being announced as "a spectacular new production by Cameron Mackintosh." The wording suggests that Mackintosh is directing it, which would be a departure for somebody previously content to be the most successful producer in the history of musical theatre. In fact, though, this is a new staging by Laurence Connor, who previously re-directed Les Miserables and improved it, if not to the extent of making it good. I must admit I find it hard to imagine that any production of Phantom could improve on Hal Prince's original. Mind you, I thought the same about Cabaret. Mind you, I was right.

Tyler Anderson , National Post /
2015-09-26-playing-with-power-the-20th-o:
A couple of weeks ago, reviewing the circus show Empire, I wrote that I longed to see somebody in a theatre audience refuse, as emphatically as possible, to become part of the show. Last week I almost got my wish. The show in question could not, on its face, have been less like a circus. It's a monologue, spoken by a would-be mass murderer, and entitled The 20th of November. On that date in 2006 a German man, aged 18, returned to his old school, intent on shooting as many of its staff and students as possible. He then committed suicide, leaving behind videos and blog entries justifying his actions. Lars Noren, described as Swedens leading playwright (Ill take that on trust), parsed the killer's words, which, shuffled and selected, make up the script of the play.

In one way it is like a circus, at least in Brendan Healy's production at Buddies in Bad Times. As at a circus, the audience sits in a ring around the auditorium. The actor, Sina Gilani, only enters it once when, hoarse from all his talking, he crosses it to get himself a drink of water, thus removing himself from most of our sights. This takes a long time, during which nothing happens. Though on the first night something did: two separate members of the audience, bored or exasperated or both, got up and left the building, the ultimate act of audience participation.

Both before and after this come more conventional attempts to involve the spectators. The actor sits among us, separated only by his intense look, his intense clothes, and the fact that he talks into a microphone while we dont talk at all. Not that he doesnt want us to; from time to time he looks at individual members of the audience and asks them to validate his thoughts or supply their own, getting only embarrassed silence in return. At the very end he seems ready to inaugurate a QA session: again, no takers. Which is hardly surprising; he's an actor, playing a rehearsed role, we're there as ourselves. There is no common ground.

Before I expand on the futility and dishonesty of this, I should acknowledge that the production, the performance, and even the text have considerable grip. This is Healys outgoing production as artistic director of Buddies. Like all his work there, its tense, thoughtful, and technically brilliant, even with the technology kept minimal. Gilani's vocal palette is kept minimal too, though he proves capable of modulating into a scary baby voice, making it eerily hard to tell whether he's laughing or crying. His phrasing is lucid even if the phrases themselves arent. He also has a scary way of fluttering his eyebrows.

His character, whose name is Sebastian, does have some good points to make, though as youd expect they tend to contradict one another. His speech is an oxymoron in itself: an aggressive apologia. He rails against the path that society wants him, and everybody else, to follow: what he calls STWRD (School, Training, Work, Retirement, Death). At the same time he seems to resent his own inability to follow it. He claims, accurately, to be one of a whole army of losers." "Hitler, he says, he was one of us." But he also says he hates Nazis. He also hates Tupperware, cats, and David Beckham: everything and everyone really. He seems to be making his best point when he says that he, like everyone, is going to die anyway, so why shouldn't he get it over with? It's hard to dispute that one, but it doesnt account for his desire to take as many other people as possible with him.

That all comes down to his having had a terrible time at school. The cool kids tormented him, girls wanted nothing to do with him, and everyone called him a geek. These are the grievances he keeps coming back to, obsessively. I can believe that in this respect the play faithfully mirrors its source material. I also believe that these could indeed be the makings of a psychopath. "Since I was six years old, he says, youve made fun of me, but now you will pay." But who is this "you? Are the audience meant to be stand-ins for his actual intended victims? Or are we just there to bear witness, as members of society? That Sebastian's repetitions become agonizingly boring is perhaps the point; the production's message, unstated but unmistakable, is that we arent there to be entertained.

Lars Noren," says the publicity "dares us to listen to the very things we try to ignore." But the apparent belief that were all just too smug and sheltered to have thought about the alienation of people like Sebastian, what causes it and what it may lead to, just isn't true.

At the risk of sounding callous: Sebastian might be a more interesting dramatic subject if he had been a more efficient murderer. In fact, though he managed to wound 30 people, the only person he succeeded in killing was himself. The 20th of November is a play that bullies its audience. The relationship between stage and auditorium is a power relationship. And though it may not always feel that way to actors sick with nerves, the power lies with the performers. So it shouldn't be abused. This play does abuse it: not outrageously but significantly. When people whove rehearsed and who have skills demand the participation of people who havent and don't, that's bullying. Thats the case even when, as here, the audience refuses to play. The implication is that its being done for our own good; that Lars Noren and his interpreters (including his translator, Gord Rand, who seems to have done a good job) have earned the right to lecture us, just by being artists. I don't think they have.

The 20th of November runs through Oct. 4 at Buddies in Bad Times Theatre.

Jeremy Mimnagh / Sina Gilani in The 20th of November, a monologue of a would be mass-murder.
2015-09-30-his-own-show-how-trevor-noah-:
Judging by his 10-minute spot as bizarro host on The Colbert Report, carried off with aplomb and excellent comic timing, Barack Obama would have made a strong replacement for Jon Stewart on The Daily Show. Though the show would have had to go on hiatus until he was through with his current gig. But it was Trevor Noah who got the job, making his debut Monday night.

Like Obama, Noah projects charm and intelligence. Also like Obama, Noah - the South African son of a black mother and a white father - is of mixed race. He had a very funny bit about this on a TV special, remarking that Obama's similarly complicated heritage was held against him during his candidacy, but that when he won the presidency people began falling over themselves to acclaim him as "our black." Though "black" wasn't actually the word Noah used.

His first night as host of The Daily Show had two themes: his blackness and his newness. The production had fun with our fears and preconceptions. Would it be the same? Would it be different? It turned out to be both. There was the same-old voice-over opening: the date, Comedy Central, The Daily Show ... only the name at the end had changed, for obvious reasons. The font for the titles had changed, too, and so had the desk, but there still was a desk.

Noah's style emerged as cheeky self-deprecation. He told us how thrilled he was to have realized two of his wildest childhood dreams; the host position on a late-night talk show, and an indoor toilet. He paid the obligatory tribute to his predecessor, but far less fulsomely than is usual on such occasions: "Jon might find he has a new stepson and he's black, which is not ideal."

He admitted that the producers had tried to find a woman or an American for the position, but they had been turned down, "so once again a job Americans rejected is being done by an immigrant." He then proceeded, in traditional Daily Show style, to address a couple of news stories: the Pope's arrival and John Boehner's departure. The clips of both elicited something strongly resembling Stewart's patented reaction of coy disbelief.

The Boehner resignation provided the stronger material, though Marco Rubio's announcement of it, to thunderous applause from Florida Republicans, really made any satiric comment superfluous. Correspondent Jordan Klepper rattled the host with the news that people were saying "John, please come back." This was funny, but better yet was an item about the discovery of water on Mars, bringing a face even newer, and considerably darker, than the host's: Roy Wood Jr., Senior Mars Correspondent. Will people like us, Noah asked him, soon be going to Mars? "Black people can't catch a cab" was the brusque reply, "how are they going to Mars?" Wood could be the black Lewis Black.

The show's last segment, an interview with "rock-star comedian" Kevin Hart, was the weakest. But showbiz promotional chats were always the worst parts of Stewart's shows too - they felt like filler - while his political or literary interviews were among the best. They were actual inquiries and they had meat. We don't know yet whether Noah has the authority to pull this off, or whether he will be able to move us as Stewart increasingly did when he got angry and voiced it to camera - something that depended on the trust he had built up over the years.

Last Saturday, Noah was able to quickly earn that level of trust from an audience in Toronto, headlining the Just for Laughs festival at the Sony Centre. Considering he was only two days away from his premiere, one could easily deduce he has nerves of steel. Or maybe it was good therapy. Anyway, he was brilliant.

Stand-up comedy too often signals a jerky succession of one-liners. Noah took a topic, explored it in loving detail, before moving seamlessly on to the next.

He offered a meditation on the probability of Idris Elba being the next James Bond, and on the unlikelihood of a black Bond being able to carry out a secret agent's duty of blending unobtrusively into the background, especially in Scotland, a country from which, Noah informed us, he had just returned and in which, according to him, blackness is unknown. That's unlikely to be true, but nobody could quarrel with his vocal transformation from light South African to heavy Scottish. It was hilariously perfect, as was each of the many accents that followed it. He has a flawless ear and a twisting tongue. He plainly loves language.

Race obviously figures heavily in Noah's act, but he isn't heavy about it: just disarmingly sharp. He told us that he had to move from South Africa to America to discover that he was black and that, having become a connoisseur of racism, he thinks he prefers the overt to the subtle kind. He illustrated his points with impeccable mimicry of incomprehensible brothers and of hearty or genteel Lexington, Kentuckians.

Noah's virtuosity with accents is obviously going to come in handy - it already has - and his traditional comedic skills are greater than Stewart's. I've never seen Stewart do stand-up but I can't imagine him holding the Sony Centre in the palm of his hand for an hour or more. Unlike the comparably gifted Stephen Colbert, currently hamstrung by weak scripts and an unyielding, antiquated format, Noah has landed in an environment that suits him and that he should be able to tweak.

It looks as though The Daily Show is in safe hands.

Brad Barket, Getty Images For Comedy Central / South African comedian Trevor Noah on his Daily Show premiere, two days after performing in Toronto.
2015-10-03-asylum-seekers-soulpepper-s-m: There can be few dramatic titles more generously informative than The Persecution and Assassination of Jean-Paul Marat as Performed by the Inmates of the Asylum of Charenton under the Direction of the Marquis de Sade. That, or its German equivalent, is the banner under which Peter Weisss play was first performed in Berlin in 1964. The same year it was done in London, by the Royal Shakespeare Company, who understandably wanted something snappier on the marquee. So, the play became Marat/Sade, and at least in the English-speaking theatre, it has remained.The RSC did more than change the title. They changed the nature of the play. Weiss wrote a dialectical drama: an imaginary conversation between Marat - one of the blooodthirstier idealists of the French Revolution, stabbed in his bath in 1793 - and the mordant hedonist de Sade - and added the frisson of setting it in a madhouse. The historical de Sade was indeed confined to the Charenton asylum during the Napoleonic era, and while there he organized theatrical performances as therapy for himself and his fellow inmates. His debate with Marat is presented as one of those psychodramas, the Marquis playing himself, the other patients playing everybody else. The British production, a virtuoso staging by Peter Brook, took the playwithin-a-play and spectacularly ran with it. The setting became the subject. The asylum took over the lunatics.Soulpepper's production, directed by Albert Schultz, follows in many of Brook's footsteps. It uses the same translation, credited to Geoffrey Skelton with verse adaptation by Adrian Mitchell. Mitchells contribution was crucial; he put much of the text into snappy, and often funny, rhyming couplets. (Of Marat and his partner Simonne Everard: "They shared one vision of the just and true /And furthermore, they shared her money too.") The shows entertainment value was further enhanced by its score; the play became virtually a musical. At Soulpepper, it's virtually an opera. What were once speeches have become songs, set by Mike Ross in a radiant panoply of styles, with only one misfire: a song purporting to bring us up to date, or to 1808, on French history has been set too choppily for the facts to be clear. It all provides another impressive demonstration of the Soulpepper company's musical talents, vocal and instrumental.Trouble is, the people theyre playing arent supposed to be skilled professionals; they aren't even supposed to be competent. The confusion's compounded by the addition of an extra frame to a play that already has more than enough. Were told that its being performed for us by contemporary Canadian mental patients who, in a device that might have alienated Bertolt Brecht himself, have to do all their acting behind bars; the stage is a cage. As in Soulpepper's Accidental Death of an Anarchist, new topical references have been written in, including a shout-out, or shout-in, to the company itself; it may mean to be provocative, but it comes over as cosy.We lose the sense of de Sade directing his play as we watch; in Diego Matamoros' performance hes just another character in a pre-written drama, and a distant one, kept remote and upstage. He only comes into his own in his culminating speech to Marat on the futility of revolution, here re-cast as a song in the manner of Brecht and Hanns Eisler. Theres a tortured power in Stuart Hughes' Marat and a perky wit in Oliver Dennis' herald-narrator; neither of them gives any indication of mental illness, but considering the amount of text they have to get through, thats probably a good thing. The mad ensemble are fine as a group, whether suffering or menacing, but they dont disturb with their individual obsessions as the Brook actors did. The sleeping sickness of the woman playing Charlotte Corday (Katherine Gauthier) is reduced to an inconsistent running gag; her lover Duperret goes very light on his supposed sex addiction,though Gregory Prest's performance is otherwise excellent. Unfortunately, their scenes together don't tell us much, either about their relationship or about Charlottes reasons for killing Marat.Thats the author's fault.Marat/Sade is a great idea for a play, but that's all. Its full of activity but has very little action. Marat and de Sade keep re-stating their positions, neither affecting the other. Charlottes three arrivals at Marat's door are pretentious padding. The chorus keep singing about how the poor stay poor and how they want a revolution now. Finally they attempt one, their real and theatrical identities merging, but are brought to heel by the asylum authorities. Schultz's updating suggests that the inmate-performers are political protesters, imprisoned by the Canadian government. That may be fine, but it doesnt justify a grossly sentimental new ending. The London version, as I remember, ended with the cast giving the audience the finger. Id probably hate that now, but it seemed like fun at the time.Motown The Musical, unlike most juke-box entertainments, spotlights not a performer or composer but a producer: Berry Gordy, founder of the eponymous label, the man who wrote the book. In fact, he wrote it twice; his own script is based on his own memoir. The dialogue is unbelievably wooden, but the show is rather well constructed, tracing the Detroit company's rise, triumph and commercial fall, all while doing a reasonable job of linking it to the politics of the '60s and 70s. Gordy must have discovered or promoted every important black act of the time, from Smokey Robinson (portrayed as his bosss glorified gofer) to the Jackson 5, and we get to hear most of the hits, snazzily framed and solidly sung with moves that likely surpass the originals. The songs in the first half sound better than those in the second, but that could just be my nostalgia kicking in.robert.cushman@hotmail.comMarat/Sade is in repertory through Oct. 17 at the Young Centre; Motown The Musical runs through Nov. 1 at the Princess of Wales TheatreCredit: Robert Cushman; Weekend PostIllustrationCylla Von Tiedemann / Soulpepper's company proves their musical talents even as inmates in Marat-Sade.Word count: 1007
2015-10-10-pardon-my-french-michel-tremb:
There's something in the program notes for the Soulpepper production of Michel Tremblay's Yours Forever, Marie-Lou that perplexes me. Actually there are two things. One is that the first two words of the title are given as Forever Yours, which was the order adopted in the plays first English translation but not in the one that the production is actually using.

Thats odd but probably not important. I doubt that either variant is more faithful than the other to Tremblay's original French. Or rather to Tremblay's original joual, since the play was written, in 1970, in that demotic Quebecois variant of French. Im ignorant of joual (even more than I am of French) but thats all right since, according to the same program note, "in their native French, Tremblay's plays can feel dated because the language remains fixed in the idioms of the 1960s." Now that's weird. Tremblays plays are generally touted as Canadian classics, and I have to feel skeptical of the classic status of plays whose original texts are dated and have to be "revitalized" by their translators, in this case the ubiquitous Linda Gaboriau. Of course, classics should survive in translation but its unusual to hear that they're improved by it.

Anyway in another program note, Diana Leblanc, who directs the Soulpepper revival, comes down firmly on the side of tradition. She writes of the original's spare elegance and describes it as "breathtaking." She agrees, though, in heaping praise on Gaboriaus translation. Just as well, as there seems these days to be a law against anyone else translating French-Canadian plays. The current text does include one superbly chilling line: An expectant mother declares that she will love her new child to death. The words come late in the play, by which time we have been told enough for them to carry a horrific charge.

Marie Lou is a split-level play, literally so in Leblancs production, which gives us two characters upstairs and two down. Up aloft we have Leopold, a garage mechanic, and his wife Marie Louise; the two despise one another. This will be their last day on Earth. We know this from the reminiscences, 10 years later but staged simultaneously, of their grown daughters, who occupy the space below: Manon, a religious devotee still living in her parents' house, and Carmen, a self-described free spirit who has left the family scene to become a country singer on the notorious Montreal strip known as the Main.

Glen Charles Landry's set is somewhat realistic, though dotted with symbols. Theres a crucifix, for the Catholicism that oversees both the believers and the skeptics in the cast, and the outline of a car, suggesting both the family vehicle (ill-omened in itself ) and the job that Leopold loathes. Marie Louise, sitting with her knitting, feels just as oppressed by her role as wife and mother. Theres a third child - a boy, whom we don't see - and she dreads the prospect of a fourth, though she does change her mind about this. Even that, though, seems to be a way of taunting her husband. They both feel, justly, that they're in a state of economic servitude. They start the proceedings by arguing over brands of peanut butter and go steadily downhill from there. The play, an hour and a quarter without an interval, is their short days journey into night.

It feels long, however; longer than Eugene ONeill's family marathon did in either Leblanc's great Stratford production or her good Soulpepper one. Tremblays play has traditionally been staged (or so I gather; Ive never seen it before) as a dramatic tone poem, with the four characters seated and stationary, in a Beckettian limbo. In Leblanc's quasi-naturalistic staging, the parents stay static but the daughters get to move around, just as their dialogue switches between verbal reminiscence and physical flashback. There's a gain in surface variety but probably a loss in intensity.

In fact, the elders, exchanging recriminations from opposite sides of the stage, have the best of it. Their grudges and grievances seem wearisomely familiar at first, but when they get around to discussing their sex life, or the lack of it, the play becomes powerful and shocking, not in the sense of breaching taboos but of telling dramatic truths. Theres poignance, too, in the one glimpse of former tenderness, as captured in the title, whichever way round you want to phrase it. The performances of Christian Laurin and Patricia Marceau are uneven, but at their best they do seem like stubborn, suffering people.

At other times, they seem like actors. This, though, puts them ahead of their younger colleagues, who never seem like anything else. Genevieve Dufours repressed Manon is a monotone wraith, Suzanne Roberts Smith's Carmen an automaton who never utters a believably conversational word. She is, to judge from her name and bio, the only Anglo in the cast, but she is less expressive with this English text than any of her francophone colleagues.

"You love to wallow in your misery" says Carmen to her sister, and it seems all too true of every character in the play, herself included, for all her boasts of independence. Is she the same character as the martyred country singer of Tremblay's later play, Saint Carmen of the Main? If so, she certainly changed. But maybe the author was just having a little joke. robert.cushman@hotmail.com

Yours Forever, Mary-Lou is in repertory through Oct. 17 at the Young Centre

Cylla Von Tiedemann / The performances of Genevieve Dufour and Suzanne Roberts Smith leave something to be desired.
2015-10-17-things-gone-wrong-native-eart:
There's a dull green chair, turned over on its side, and a low stool of the same colour, doing duty as a table, with a bottle on top of it. Theres also a dirty cloth on the floor. Thats what we see before the lights go down. When they do, we hear the voice of the one and only actor, sounding muffled. The reason for this becomes clear when we get a sight of him. He has a plastic bag over his head. He's playing a suicide game, how seriously we cannot decide. Neither, it turns out, can he.

The actor, who is also the playwright, is Cliff Cardinal, and the play is Huff, presented by Native Earth Performing Arts in its own fairly new black-box space, the Aki Studio at Daniels Spectrum. The play has been in various stages of development for several years, but this should probably be taken as its definitive version. It comes before us in two simultaneous guises: as a stark, sometimes darkly funny portrayal of neglect and abuse - substance and otherwise - among First Nations; and as a display piece for its authorperformer, one man playing several parts. Both aspects have their virtues but they get in one another's way.

The narrating protagonist, the suicide-tease at the plays start, is named Wind. Hes the middle one of three brothers, whose father left and whose mother subsequently committed a real suicide. Father then returned with a new woman in tow, and set about raising his sons with a mixture of violence and affection, the former predominating. Some protection was provided by the boys' stepmother, and rather more by their maternal grandmother, whose dislike of her son-in-law was heartily returned. Older brother was a sadistic bully. His two siblings, mutually protective, took refuge in a rich fantasy life that includes imagining that their dog can talk and that each of them is possessed of a sacred gift from the Creator." Wind's gift is shoplifting.

Experimenting with fluids, bodily and other, the boys accidentally start a forest fire. (Its complicated.) They subsequently hear that a local firefighter suffered a fatal heart attack while trying to put it out. This could have been coincidence but it supports Winds

belief that his and his brother's lives are at the mercy of a conscienceless practical joker, roughly equivalent to what the Greeks called Fate and Christians the Devil. Wind's name for it, or for him, is Trickster. Trickster is the spirit of things going wrong.

Tricksters tricks plague Wind and his family at home, at play and at school. Rather late on in the proceedings Wind says, with heavy but justified sarcasm, that we will have guessed by now that he and his younger brother have had all the benefits of a reservation education. We see them in class, making life hell for a teacher who more than returns the compliment. In fact, soon after making a sympathetically helpless first appearance, she transmutes into a clone of the monster schoolmistress in Roald Dahls Matilda, the hit musical coming soon to a theatre near us. (The fact that both ladies are played by a man may have something to do with this.) Some earlier parts of the play have whimsically dawdled but the schoolroom episode is the real deal, sad and savage. It is also, in Karin Randoja's production, inventively staged with the various students represented by a line of bottles, the one white pupil alone and aloof at the end of the row. This doesn't make him a victim, the reverse in fact.

School gives the play a booster shot, a momentum that it retains from there on in, as we move forwards to where we came in - to what, if I were more culturally sensitive, I might be able to resist describing as Winds game of Indian roulette. On the way we encounter some more-than-usually pointless gestures toward audience participation. These underline a pervasive cuteness in Cardinals performance, perhaps inseparable from the device of having a single actor play all the roles. This can work excellently when a play is constructed as a series of monologues (think I Claudia or The Blonde, the Brunette and the Vengeful Redhead). But when it goes in for quickfire dialogue, we get what I think of as ventriloquist's timing: the breathless rushing from one voice to the next with a consequent loss of flavour and conviction. Cardinal is a limber performer, but he isn't in Rick Millers virtuoso class as a vocal chameleon. On the other hand, he has more to say than Miller has usually had and when he allows his people room to breathe, he brings them to life. Wind himself, in the way of narrators, is a bit of a blur but his kid brother is a heartbreaker, his drunken dad and take-charge grandma are vivid lightning sketches, and his stepmom a more elaborate one, movingly out of her depth. Shes the most conflicted character in the piece, and therefore the most interesting.

Huff runs through Oct. 25 at the Daniels Spectrum
