2015-10-19-struggling-to-adapt:
Let us begin by admitting that Shakespeare's plays are not absolutely dependent on their original words for their effect. If they were, they wouldn't work in translation; and the histories of the French, German and Russian theatres offer plenty of evidence that they do.

Still, a play in translation is a different animal from a play in its original language. It doesn't have the original breathing down its neck. If you're re-writing Shakespeare in English, then you're going into competition with him. And you're going to lose. So the shivers that ran down James Shapiro's spine (The Dumbing Down of the Bard, Oct. 8) when he learned that the Oregon Shakespeare Festival was commissioning modernized versions of all 36 plays are fully justified.

The Oregon festival is a long-established event - older by 20 years than our own festival at Stratford -and to see a place turn its back on so much history is kind of depressing. It's also, as Prof. Shapiro describes it, funny. Apparently Oregon will continue to mount the plays in the authorized versions alongside the new revised texts. So, in a given season, one production or another will have the status of a freak-show, though I'm not sure which.

There are of course different kinds of adaptation. You can rewrite every single line of the original, in effect coming up with a new play on the same subject. Or you can just try to tidy up the hard parts. This seems, to judge from Shapiro's description of a specimen adaptation of Timon of Athens, to be what Oregon has in mind. The example he gives actually involves the addition of a single letter: the word "erection," which in context could be social or sexual or ambiguous, becomes "erections" which removes the ambiguity and leaves us with a dirty joke. In all fairness, that's probably how the line in question would strike a modern audience even if left unchanged. But we don't actually gain anything from the change, except a possible laugh in a context where it isn't needed.

Shapiro is right that, even if imperfectly understood, the original is more resonant, especially when that one example is multiplied over the course of an entire evening.

Still, there's a difference between ambiguity and obscurity. Words and phrases that simply get in the way of plain meaning can legitimately be altered. Stratford has been doing it for years. The late Michael Langham, as sensitive a Shakespeare director as you could hope to find, was ruthless about making small changes in the cause of clarity, and they were never objectionable. (Well, hardly ever.) It goes on in England too. I recently watched the video of what I still believe to be the best Shakespeare production I've ever seen: Macbeth, directed by Trevor Nunn in a small shed in Stratfordon-Avon in 1976, with Ian McKellen and Judi Dench in the leads. I remembered it as a model of making conversational sense of the language while still suggesting hidden depths beneath every line. I hadn't remembered that one or two of those lines had been changed. When Macbeth meets the witches on the blasted heath and they salute him with his present and future titles he says "by Sinel's death, I know I am Thane of Glamis." Who's Sinel? We never hear of him again. Presumably he was Macbeth's predecessor in the thanedom (if that's a word and even if it isn't). McKellen changed the line to "by my father's death" which makes sense. I doubt if anyone minded.

I have to admit, too, that another of my great memories - and of a production universally considered a landmark - involved adaptation on a large scale. This was an earlier Royal Shakespeare Company production, The Wars of the Roses: a tumultuous trilogy in which the three parts of Henry VI were reduced to two and then topped off with a full-length Richard III. It was a triumphant evocation of a medieval world in chaos, and the cuts to these very early plays could be justified on both artistic and financial grounds. They necessitated, though, the writing of new transition scenes, and John Barton, the scholar-director who prepared the text, duly supplied them. He was a master of pastiche, but he didn't just edit, he editorialized; his additions told us what to think; they had the feel of sore thumbs. A few years later Barton took this to extremes with a version of King John whose title might have referred to the director himself; power had gone to his head. Trying to make the Middle Ages seem contemporary, he added lines like "the price of goods soars, meteor-like, to heaven." He almost wrote a new play; but unfortunately not quite.

That's the problem with juxtaposing Shakespeare's words, even his second-best words, with your own; they make yours sound silly. Shapiro's article originally appeared in the New York Times, and it prompted a response in the New Yorker, pointing out that "authentic" Shakespeare is a comparatively new idea, and that from the 17th century to the 19th, the plays were heavily adapted and re-written, to fit "contemporary" tastes. That's true, but nobody now thinks those adaptations were a good idea, and even at the time some of the best minds rebelled against them. Charles Lamb lambasted Nahum Tate's happy-ending version of King Lear which effectively was a new play, though not a good one; staged today, it would seem like a parody.

Adaptations are sometimes justified on the grounds that Shakespeare himself was a shameless reworker of other men's works, but three things distinguish his rewrites from those who would rewrite him: a) he wrote better than his sources; b) with a couple of exceptions, those sources were not other plays but chronicles and prose fictions; c) his plays were offered on their own merits, rather than as parasites on the backs of famous originals. I don't see the Oregon trail-blazers beating those odds.

I quarrel with Shapiro's claim that "directors and actors ... too frequently offer up Shakespeare's plays without themselves having a firm enough grasp of what his words mean." At the literal level, whether in Britain, America or Canada, they usually do; and if they don't they're willing and able to look it up. Shapiro laments that programs list "a fight director, a dramaturge ... but rarely an expert steeped in Shakespeare's language and culture." I don't know if he's applying for the job, but I thought that's what a dramaturge on a Shakespeare production was supposed to be. He can hardly workshop the script with the author.

Shapiro may well be right about how the words sound; when it comes to counting the beats in a blank-verse line a generation, certainly of British actors, seems to have gone deaf. It is true that actors and audiences don't have the educational equipment they once had. I referred above to the "authorized version" and the scriptural echo was intentional. I'm all in favour of secular education but a generation raised on the King James Bible (my own was probably the last) was off to a flying start in understanding the Jacobean Shakespeare. In my school, we started reading the plays at 12 or 13. Not everybody enjoyed them; some were bored; but nobody was baffled.

Miramax Films / Colin Firth and Judi Dench in John Madden's Shakespeare in Love.
2015-10-24-godot-of-small-things-the-bec:
Samuel Beckett, I once wrote, is a gentleman and a showman. (He was alive at the time. Hence the tense.) It may seem odd to speak of Becketts showmanship. He was, after all, the low priest of theatrical minimalism. But the fewer effects you use, the more powerful they can be, if you know how to use them. Beckett always knew. And he made no secret of it. His stage directions are as detailed as, if less loquacious than, those of that other great Irish expatriate Bernard Shaw. And, unlike Shaw, he expected them to be carried out to the letter.

As they mostly are in The Beckett Trilogy, an hour's worth of his latest and shortest, performed by Lisa Dwan, Irish herself, who learned the trick of them from Billie Whitelaw, the English actress who first played them and who was Beckett's latelife theatrical muse. We start with Not I, the one in which a woman pours forth an unstoppable stream of high-velocity reminiscence. The text calls her the Mouth, and a pair of lips is all we see of her. Indeed, in this production, its all we see of anyone. But here the director, Walter Asmus, does depart from his authors stated intentions. Beckett's directions dictate the presence of a figure - shrouded, hooded and silent - referred to as the Auditor, the almost-impassive recipient of the Mouth's confessions. Paring down Beckett might seem impossible, but in eliminating the Auditor this production achieves it. The change, though, is for the worse. Every so often the Auditor is supposed to incline slightly, as if he or she might actually be listening. Without this both the Mouths speech and her plight become less tantalizing, less rich.

Her words suffer, too, from the record speed at which Dwan delivers them, too fast and too low for comprehension. When Whitelaw played the role, a little slower, you couldnt understand everything, but you could understand something. All that really registers in this performance of Not I are the reverse title-words: every so often the Mouth, who's been speaking entirely in the third person, pulls herself out and says -screams - what? ... who? ... no! ... she!, as if dissociating herself. (It's at these points that the Auditor is supposed to audit.) The cries, as Dwan emits them, are electrifying. Plainly she is denying something, probably the experience of pleasure. The script is full of clues, about her birth 70 years ago to unknown parents, about her growing up in a hellish and probably religious institution, about guilty moments of human contact in a pastoral setting. They would be worth hearing. But you cant.

Two things seem to have happened over the course of Becketts playwriting: he grew more interested in women and less interested in everything else, especially in what is commonly called action. The plays get progressively shorter. Waiting for Godot gives us four men and a boy, all capable of moving around. Endgame has four characters, three of them immobile, one of those three female and also the least voluble. Happy Days is a nearmonologue for a woman buried in sand, with a husband of whom we see little and hear less. The play called Play has three people - one male, two female - encased neck-down in funerary urns. Which brings us to Not I and its successors.

Footfalls, the first of these, is something of a reversal. Again a woman is on stage but this time she is glimpsed fulllength and - wonder of wonders - she moves. In fact, she paces, back and forth on an uncarpeted floor, patiently responding to the offstage questionings of her mother. (Dwan does both voices, brilliantly.) Mother, we learn, is 90. "So much?" she marvels. Daughter is in her forties. So little? she complains. Each is solicitous of the other, daughter offering to change her mother's sheets, mother entreating daughter to stop pacing and, above all, to stop remembering. The amount of naturalistic detail is, for Beckett, astonishing, not to say haunting. The play, short as it is, doesn't quite sustain; an uncertainty over whether the daughters name is May or Amy is cheap mystification, unworthy of its author.

And that, you can hear Beckett saying, is what movement gets you: dont ask me for it again. Which brings us to Rockaby, in which motion is reduced to a rocking chair going backwards and forwards, with a probably dying woman inside it, her recorded voice (Dwan haunting again) piped in as counterpoint. Hypnotic here, and what I mean by Beckett's showmanship, are the chair and its occupant rocking away from the light, what there is of it, and back in again. The stygian precision of James Farncombe's lighting here reaches its apogee. The message remains the same: life is something best ended but with occasional moments, or their echoes, that may make it worth living. Or at any rate enduring. The trilogy is a bracing experience, not fun exactly, but hard to shake off. Dwan, having taken us through it all, took her curtain calls with a radiant smile. She even blew us kisses. So shes a showperson too. She says in her bio that she "is also open to the possibility of comedy." I bet shed be great at it.

Matt Baram and Naomi Snieckus are more than open to such possibilities. It's what they do, usually very well. They are a married couple who are also alumni of Second City; and You and Me Both, their sketch comedy revue, is like an hour's worth of Second City marriage skits laid end to end. They're good skits, starting with a number in which, fully clothed, they play themselves in the shower, trying to be playfully nice with each other and not always succeeding. They also do nifty theatrical satire, as in a bit of updated Chekhov, in which they lament how hard it is to get to Moscow when you live in Liberty Village. "You should have given me a child," she upbraids him, "so we could use the HOV lane." They are appealingly retro, though I think their 1950s-style title song is something they could do without; likewise, their overly ingratiating chats to the audience. But they're a pleasure, and the more so the more you get to know them.

2015-10-26-the-bending-point-tarragons-g:
Theatre Review

Enemy of the People Revisited

A year ago Toronto's Tarragon Theatre presented an adaptation of Henrik Ibsen's 1882 play An Enemy of the People. Actually it was twice adapted: a Canadian version of a German production that had already taken considerable liberties with the Norwegian original. It was a deserved success, and is now back for a second run with an additional transformation. The principal role and its performer, both formerly male, are now female.

Ibsen's central character is, or was, Dr. Thomas Stockmann, medical consultant for a spa town that has staked its economic future on the tourists who will come to take its curative waters. He discovers that those waters are far from curative; that they are in fact fatally contaminated by industrial waste. He's naive enough to think that his fellow citizens will thank him for this information. Initially some of them do; the local paper sees it as great ammunition to use against its ideological foes. But when the councillor-in-chief, who happens to be the doctor's brother, points out to them how long it will take to fix the problem, and how much it will cost, and how taxes will have to go up to pay for it, tunes get changed. Stockmann, branded a public enemy, is hounded out of a public meeting and out of his livelihood.

All of this still happens in Richard Rose's Tarragon production, except that Thomas is now Thomasina, played - very well indeed - by Laura Condlln. Thomas' straight marriage is now Thomasina's gay one. There have been several other cast changes, but the role of the wife is played by the same actress as before, Tamara Podemski, whose performance I liked much better now than I did last year.

How much difference does the gender-switch make? Surprisingly little. The play isn't about the Stockmanns' marriage. Their domestic life was always the least interesting part of Ibsen's original (though a production some years ago at Britain's National Theatre did more with it than I would have thought possible) and the German-Canadian script reduces it still further. Ibsen gave the Stockmanns a grown daughter and two school-age sons; at the Tarragon this time around they have a single baby and - courtesy of Podemski's actual pregnancy - another on the way. But the family relationship that counts is the one outside the household. I wrote last year that the production showed the play to be the best ever written about sibling rivalry. It somehow seems even more acute when the siblings, the physician and the politician, are brother and sister. Condolln and Rick Roberts, repeating his performance as the dyspeptic Peter Stockmann, summon up a whole lifetime's fractious relationship, one of wary affection gone irredeemably, even hysterically, sour. Condlln's body language is remarkable, rangy and cheerful in her initial innocence, hunched and clenched and incredulous in her angry disillusion. There are, obviously, two kinds of cross-gender casting. One, as here, is to change the sex of the character or characters. The other is to leave them as written, but to cast across the line. Generally, not always, this involves having either an all-male or all-female cast. This of course is how Shakespeare's plays were first performed; actresses weren't allowed on the Elizabethan stage and the women's roles were played by boys.

This tradition has been revived from time to time at the reconstructed Globe Theatre in London, with the obvious difference that the female impersonators are now grown men. Mark Rylance played Cleopatra there, and he was the best I've ever seen. Freed from the female obligation to look like the most beautiful woman in the world he could concentrate on playing the character, to its uncompromising limits; he made Cleopatra's unpredictable rages more frightening, and more believable, than any actress has managed or perhaps would have dared. I was far less charmed by Rylance's Olivia in the Globe's all-male Twelfth Night when I caught it in New York; rapturously received and technically brilliant, this was an elaborate piece of female impersonation that unbalanced the play, a star turn in a less than star role.

Sometimes conventions can be mixed. Sarah Bernhardt used to play Hamlet, in productions otherwise conventionally cast. She was the most famous actress of her time, and it was accepted as her prerogative. (It may have helped that she did it in French.) Rather more recently Seana McKenna at the Stratford Festival played Richard III, in a production in which the other men were men, fastening on Richard's obsession with his own deformity to present him as asexual, a monstrous imp. It worked. So, some years ago in Toronto, did a much-underrated production of A Midsummer Night's Dream, directed by Kate Lynch with an all-female cast. It established the convention that the play was being performed by a troupe of victorious Amazons and followed it through, shining an ironic but not hostile light on the comedy's sexual politics. It stayed faithful to its own terms which, it turned out, were perfectly compatible with Shakespeare's.

Chris Abraham, directing the Dream at Stratford two years ago, offered three different varieties of what might be called intersexuality in one production. Maybe four, since he too had a frame; the play became the entertainment at a gay wedding. Male actors alternated as Oberon and Titania, but played them traditionally as male and female. This worked beautifully. The squabbling quartet of young lovers were re-imagined as a straight couple and a lesbian one; this sort of worked, but not without strain. Peter Quince, moving spirit of the Athenian workers' amateur dramatic society, was played by a woman, as a woman.

This didn't work at all. The dynamic of half-a-dozen men, buddies at that, is different from that of five men and one woman. The scenes went flat. The same is true of a string of well-intentioned open-air productions in Toronto, including a Merchant of Venice in which Shylock was transformed into a Jewish mother. Neither the family nor the commercial relationships made any sense.

A dead author's intentions may be unknowable but a play's logic isn't - or at least it makes audible creaking sounds when it's contradicted. But its identity can be surprisingly flexible. And it's not just a matter of gender. I read recently of a production of Othello in which Iago, as well as Othello, was black. It sounds crazy. But when you think about it: Iago says many vicious things about "the black Othello" but he never claims that he himself is white. You can play him as jealous of his compatriot's success in the white world without altering a line of the text or, more importantly, without in any way changing the relationship between them, which is what drives the play. It may even make more credible Othello's credulity. What this suggests is that the term "colour-blind casting" - as opposed to the idea behind it - is meaningless, and indeed seems to have fallen into disuse. An audience can no more fail to notice whether actors are black or white than whether they are tall, short, fat or thin. How much it matters, in a given play, is something infinitely variable. Often it doesn't matter at all. But if a production of Othello were to cast a black actress as Desdemona, it would be in trouble. The play would be pointless.

As, to take an example unrelated to race or gender, Sophocles' Oedipus Rex became in Daniel Brooks' Stratford production this year. The key scene in the tragedy is the one in which Oedipus extracts from an old shepherd the truth about his own origins. He's been warned that finding out will be fatal, but he has to know. The shepherd wants to spare him, but Oedipus' insistence, his sheer strength of will, is too much for him. In this production, Oedipus has a couple of goons beat it out of him. The play ceases to be about a man digging his own grave, from a mixture of pride and genuine nobility, and becomes about how big and tough the director is.

An Enemy of the People never makes this kind of mistake. It makes changes: "ch-ch-ch-changes" to quote the David Bowie song that the characters have an irritating habit of singing. It has a darker ending than the one Ibsen provided, and in this it follows its own logic. But that turns out to be a variation on Ibsen's, not a contradiction of it. The essential drama is there: the feuding of brothers, or in this case of brother and sister; the shifting tides of personal and political interest, coming to a thrilling head in the newspaper office. In fact the only time in which invention becomes distortion is in what the production plainly intends to be its innovative high point. This is the meeting scene, performed with the house lights up and the audience invited to join in. Trying to underline the play's perennial topicality, it actually dilutes it. On the first night Rick Roberts - who, as councillor Peter, was giving his best Stephen Harper - was peppered with questions that seemed to have less to do with the story than with the election, then five days away. He coped brilliantly, though I have to wonder if some of the fire may not have gone out of this scene since Monday.

Inhibited by being a critic, or maybe just inhibited, I failed to ask the question on my mind, which was just how the town expected to stave off financial ruin when people started dropping dead from the poisoned water. Roberts would probably have replied that it wouldn't happen and his sister's charges were unproven. But we knew that they were proven. We'd been watching the play. The pretence that we hadn't, or that we were characters in it, was even phonier than audience participation usually is. But the production picked up in the last scene, with Condolln and Roberts and Tom Barnett as the weasel publisher all desperately fine. Last year this was an excellent production. This year it's the most exciting show in town.

Cylla Von Tiedemann /
2015-10-31-move-over-jack-bauer-devilish:
There was an episode of 24 in which Jack Bauer extracted a suspects confession by threatening to do terrible things to his wife and family, driving the point home with a video link to the possible victims. It turned out that Jack was bluffing, though not before his flame of the season had told him that he had become as bad as the terrorists he was pursuing. There's a similar situation in Nicolas Billon's play Butcher, except that this time it isnt a bluff.

Or then again, maybe it is. Butcher is a devilishly clever piece of work, and one of the most diabolical things about it, for a reviewer, is that its almost impossible to describe without giving too much away. Butcher springs one surprise after another; and though a good play should of course be able to stand up to a second viewing, that hardly invalidates the first-time pleasures of suspense, which in this case are extreme. Billon keeps you on the edge of your seat throughout; his script would make a fabulous 24 episode. It digs deeper, though, than that show usually did; or at least it conscientiously tries to. There is, though, such a thing as being too clever for your own good, or at least for your own good intentions.

Anyway, here goes. We appear to be in a Toronto police station. It's Christmas Eve, and the inspector wants to get home to his children, the younger of whom needs reassurance about the existence of Santa. In the copshop itself, though, Santa has arrived; at least a man in a Santa hat has been dropped off, dazed and speaking no English, the only clue to his identity being a business card on which has been scrawled "please arrest me" and that bears the name of a local lawyer. The lawyer is summoned, but all he can contribute is that the man comes from a recently war-torn country called Lavinia, a theatrical stand-in for all the European hellholes of the post-Soviet era.

Around the stranger's neck is a butchers hook. Before the play is over, we will learn that just such a hook was a favourite implement of the commandant of a Lavinian concentration camp. He was in fact known as the Butcher, and is on Interpols wanted-list, as well as that of a group of victim-survivors who call themselves the Furies.

Atrocities beget atrocities, and the play is cunning about just how explicitly to present them: about when to let us off its own hook and when to impale us on it. Both its tact and its cruelty are precisely mirrored in Weyni Mengesha's excruciatingly excellent production. Tony Nappo makes a persuasive hardbitten copper; John Koensgen expresses fear and anger while speaking entirely in Lavinian

(a language invented for the occasion); and Michelle Monteith brings her uncanny practicality, plus a talent for lightning changes of front, to a nurse unexpectedly fluent in the same language. As the lawyer (specialty, copyright), raised in Britain and ostentatiously civilized, Andrew Musselman adjudicates, admirably and agonizingly, between the claims of the wild justice called revenge and the tamer and more dilatory justice called justice.

Which is the question the play finally poses.

It gets there ingeniously; initially incredible coincidences slide into place with perfect logic. A character whom we had taken, if not for a moral compass then at least for a reasonably decent Everyman, turns out to be no such thing. This, however demanded by the plot, is one twist too many. It makes you doubt - or made me doubt - the credibility, not just the narrative plausibility, of the play as a whole. The political thriller is a slippery theatrical genre; Friedrich Durrenmatt's The Physicists is one of the few to keep action and texture in balance to the end. The end of this one suggests that the authors head is in the right place. But it still feels like an exercise, though a riveting one.

Butcher is the first offering in a three-play season presented by Why Not Theatre (head honcho, Ravi Jain). Meanwhile the Factory has begun its own new Naked season, presenting remounts of local plays from the recent past - or, as theyre rather too promiscuously known, Canadian classics. The initial production, of Linda Griffiths' Age of Arousal, tends to confirm suspicions that the Naked imperative - no sets, off-the-peg costumes - might be economic rather than artistic. The Factory's normally dodgy acoustics are much worsened by the echoing void, particularly ruinous to this play, a whimsically panoramic study of late 19th-century English feminism, heavily dependent on its language.

The characters excursions into "thoughtspeak" - Griffiths term for the traditional "aside" - are here indistinguishable from their more conventional speakspeak, much of. which is indistinguishable on its own account. In Jennifer Brewin's production, it's every woman (theres only one man) for herself. They mostly muddle through; Juno Rinaldi is especially good at flicking off sarcastic commentary, while Julie Stewart excels at bestowing looks of worried concern. She plays the senior character, a former suffragette who teaches her juniors to type and thus acquire economic independence while leaving them to acquire the sexual and emotional variety on their own. The production has been twice trumped by the Shaw Festival: by a superior staging of the same play some seasons ago, and by this years lunchtime rediscovery of J. M. Barrie's The Twelve Pound Look, an earlier and far more trenchant and witty demonstration of the emancipating power of the Remington.

Weekend Post robert.cushman@hotmail.com

Butcher runs through Nov. 14 at the Theatre Centre; Age of Arousal runs through Nov. 8 at the Factory Theatre.

2015-11-07-on-the-hook-jez-butterworth-s:
'I waited, deepening, and the fish Listened for me." That's a line, or a line and a half, from a Ted Hughes poem, After Moonless Midnight. The central character of The River who is indeed a fisherman, amateur but passionate, has a copy of it lying around the cabin he calls home, and which is indeed by a river. At one point in Jez Butterworths play he beseeches a lady friend to read it aloud; an excerpt from it is also printed in the program. Heard or read, it mesmerizes. Or, to use the plays own metaphor, it hooks you, draws you in.

"They waited for me. The whole river Listened to me ... 'We've got him, it whispered." The Man (the play gives no names) is hooked himself, on his own devotion to fly-fishing and, by dangerous analogy, on the need to love and be loved. Over the years, it seems, he has brought a succession of women here on a succession of moonless midnights, taken them fishing, had sex with them, told them he loved them, but never obtained the same declaration in return. The sex, to judge from one of the best speeches in a play full of good speeches, was always fine but at the end of it the woman was turned off because the man turned away. Leaving everybody frustrated and the cycle primed to begin all over again. The play switches back and forth between two of these encounters, with partners identified as The Woman and The Other Woman. The Other Woman, at least in the Coal Mine Theatres Canadian premiere production, is younger. Butterworth is the British playwright who came to notice with the tough-guy play Mojo, and who achieved huge success with Jerusalem, a wild panoramic play that contains the best writing to grace an English-speaking stage in years. The River is a smaller play than Jerusalem, apparently written in conscious reaction to it, lyric rather than epic, melancholic rather than satiric. But there's continuity. Both plays have loner protagonists, though The River's is an introvert, where Jerusalems was decidedly the opposite. Both plays, as written, have English rural settings, richly evoked; though in The River the exact locale, like the characters, is anonymous. It goes quite beautifully into Canadian.

The play absolutely demands an intimate space, and the Coal Mine company, obliged to spend their new season shuttling up and down the Danforth, do it proud in their current lodging. Ted Dykstras direction is exquisitely tuned, and Steve Lucas' kitchen-table design perfect. David Ferry, who has given some extraordinary performances these last few years, excels himself here, with a study in watchful desolation that withstands the closest scrutiny. His smile is both childlike and Satanic. He also has impressive practical skills, gutting and cooking a fish under our very noses. He makes us share his terror when one of his ladies seems to have disappeared into the darkness, and both shocks and amuses us when he learns that she has merely gone fishing with another fisherman. The river proves a fertile spawning-ground for jealousy; baiting your hook the easy way counts as a particularly noxious form of cheating. The two Women are excellently contrasted: Jane Spidell amused and sensible, more inclined to read To the Lighthouse (another appropriate choice) than to witness a lunar eclipse, Dani Kind (the Other) flightier and more excitable; the two of them eventually alike in disillusion. The play's mechanics do become predictable, the characters and their situation intriguing rather than involving. But the writing holds, and a crafty piece of casting lends spice to an ending that might otherwise appear rather pat.

Gord Rands The Trouble with Mr. Adams is another play in which a man has a series of unsatisfying encounters with women, though in this case theyre presented sequentially rather than as a mosaic. Mr. Adams is a middle-aged gym teacher, and his trouble is that he may have made inappropriate advances to his star volleyball student when they were stranded in his car during a freak snowstorm and she was a day under 16. The first scene starts with a bang, Mr. Adams announcing to his wife that he's leaving her. He then has to backtrack when she tells him that she knows everything, and that the girl's parents are filing charges; shes had a terrible day in other ways too. Philippa Domvilles performance is emotionally and physically fearless. Scene two finds Mr. Adams consulting a lawyer (Allegra Fulton) who loathes him and shows it but, professional that she is, directs him toward a loophole through which he may crawl to an acquittal. After these two duets with aquiline actresses, the teacher finally gets a scene with his fresh-faced ex-pupil (Sydney Owchar). It's two years later and, having apparently been let off with a lot of cautions, he tracks her down in a motel room after her latest athletics meet. It's implausible that he would do this, and incredible that she would let him in; and their subsequent conversation does nothing to clear things up. He keeps protesting his essential innocence, she doesnt seem inclined to disagree, and her responses, then and now, remain cloudy. Shes always referred to by her full name of Mercedes McPfefferidge, suggesting a vein of dark or at least piquant comedy which surfaces in all the scenes but is never maintained. Mr. Adams' state at the end is pitiful but not pitiable; despite our having spent the whole play in his company, we simply don't know enough about him, and Chris Earles performance circles the character without getting inside it. Like The Man in The River he is, or believes himself to be, hopelessly in love but hes not so much mysterious as puzzling. robert.cushman@hotmail.com

The River runs through Nov. 22 at the Coal Mine Theatre, 982 Danforth Avenue; The Trouble with Mr. Adams runs through Nov. 29 at the Tarragon Extra Space

2015-11-14-fates-obscured-blood-soaked-h:
Challenging the play commonly known as Marat/Sade in the long-form title stakes is We Are Proud to Present a Presentation About the Herero of Namibia, Formerly Known as South-West Africa, From the German Sudwestafrika, Between the Years 1884-1915.

Also like Marat/Sade, We Are Proud... is a play about the production of a play, a play moreover about blood-soaked historical events. The Herero were an African tribe, wiped out by their German overlords during the period denoted by the title, after which the future Namibia was taken over by the British. The proud presenters assume, rightly, that this is a subject about which most of us know nothing, and they are here to educate us about it. The show they produce has the air of being something worked up in rehearsal by the actors themselves. In fact, it's a formal script by an American playwright, Jackie Sibblies Drury, brought to us now by a Canadian cast who - it's something of a shock to realize - are playing Americans. Or: they're playing Americans, playing at being Germans and Africans.

So they begin, if you're still with me, by providing us and themselves with a potted survey of the territory, historical and geographical, though it takes them time even to get started on this, as they keep interrupting and second-guessing themselves. For all I know, Drury's script intends these introductory skirmishes to be as hideously jokey and awkward as they appear in Ravi Jain's production. After a while, though, things begin to tighten up. By the end of the evening, they are very tense indeed.

A female director-figure is in nominal charge of the proceedings. She addresses her cast as White Man, Black Man, Another White Man, Another Black Man, and Sarah. The first major glitch comes when Black Man accuses the showin-progress of concentrating on white people's problems: more precisely, of basing its text on letters sent by German soldiers to their wives back home. (That, collectively, would be Sarah.) White Man counters that these letters, which skirt around the subject of slaughter, are the only documentation we have. This struck me as a straw-man conflict, the kind of scene that makes the audience want to bang the characters' heads together and tell them to stop shouting. There must be some record of the genocide, or nobody would have known it happened. Which everyone is agreed it did.

Anyway, the performers try other tactics. They work up a scene of a German soldier shooting a refugee African, even though he'd prefer not to. Black Man sees this too as, for want of a better word, whitewashing; and, to bring the real atrocity home, he plays an African brutally executed by the whites. Only the scene that transpires doesn't seem to be happening in South West Africa at all; it's the image of a lynching in the American South.

What seems to be in question here is cultural appropriation, the ultimate straw-issue. History and humanity are there, to be turned into art by whoever wants to try; the only criterion is how well and honestly it's done. The play, or the production, seem to acknowledge this when Another White Man (Brandon McMurtry-Howlett) gives the outstanding performance of the night as an African grandmother, a character different from himself in age, race and gender. The final lynching sequence, though, seems to be arguing otherwise. These American actors (let's not get into the fact that they're actually Canadian) are the prisoners of their own history. The scene is very well staged and it sends the actors into apparent shock: shared by the audience, the infallible proof being that we don't know whether or not to applaud. The play, again like Marat/Sade, plays games with us and with its own ideas. The final irony, I guess a conscious one, is that it obscures the actual fate of the Herero just as much as it accuses everybody else of doing.

The Immigrant, presented by the Harold Green Jewish Theatre, is a benevolent musical based by its librettist, Mark Gorelik, on the life of his grandfather, who came from Russia to the small town of Hamilton, Texas, and began his life there by selling bananas door to door. One of the doors belongs to a local banker and his Baptist wife; conquering their initial prejudices, they take him into their home and under their wing, and help him become a prosperous department-store proprietor. He brings his own wife over from the old country; she too has suspicions but she conquers them, mainly during the intermission. So we have four nice people getting on together, which is humanly warming but dramatically tame. When strife does break out, it's another of those manufactured conflicts that could be defused if everyone took a deep breath. It does, though, occasion the only number in which the show justifies itself as a musical; otherwise the score (Sarah Knapp, lyrics; Steven M. Alper, music) does nothing the script doesn't do better. The evening is salvaged by Robert Mc-Queen's firm unfussy direction and by a very high level of performance, musical and dramatic; the four actors (Sean Arbuckle, Tracy Michailidis, Kathryn Akin, Steven Gallagher) are strong, poignant and, on occasion, funny.

The most gorgeous theatrical experience around is Talking Heads, two alternating evenings of monologues written by Alan Bennett for BBC TV and transferring perfectly to the intimate setting of Campbell House, one small room per playlet. All are set in Bennett's native Yorkshire. I saw Program B, which begins with Deb Filler as an antiques dealer, superbly supercilious, who can't enter a sickroom without appraising the bedside table and is eventually hoist with the invalid's petard: irony shot through with unsentimental pathos. Then we have Richard Sheridan Willis, riveting as a youngish man, gay and repressed, living with his somewhat ailing mother and threatened by the arrival of an admirer from her distant past. Finally there's Fiona Reid, in the most detailed, most revealing, and most hilarious (or maybe it's just her) of the segments, as a vicar's alcoholic wife who finds brief erotic bliss with an Indian grocer, with whom she learns "what all the fuss was all about" and also about his god: "a god, not the God, not the definite article." After beginning as the picture of glum, she is transfigured - though this may owe something to the production's adroit use of the on-site lighting. John Shooter's direction is excellent throughout. Bennett's major plays (Kafka's Dick, The Madness of George III, The History Boys) have been neglected around here. These sketches are excellent appetisers and a meal in themselves.

We Are Proud to Present ... runs through Nov. 29 at Theatre Centre; The Immigrant runs through Nov. 22 at the Toronto Centre for the Arts; Talking Heads runs through Nov. 22 at the Campbell House Museum.
2015-11-25-first-act-questions-wormwood:
There is a wonderful image towards the end of Andrew Kushnirs new play Wormwood, beautifully realized in Richard Rose's production. A young man in a garden begs a young woman to come away with him while her father, previously opposed to their union, fervently advances a counter-proposition. Meanwhile, from a window above, the family next door - another father and daughter, plus a mother - look down in mingled fury and despair, beseeching the boy to take their girl instead. Out of the window they dangle two bedsheets tied together: an improvised ladder. This is how the young man, like the prince in a fairy tale, got into the garden in the first place. Now they want him to use it to get out again.

We are in Ukraine, in 2004: the time of the Orange Revolution. The young man is Ivan, a Canadian of Ukrainian heritage; he is one of two brothers who have come over to monitor what are supposed to be the country's first democratic elections. The other brother moves out (and fades out) while Ivan remains billeted with the trio in the window: a volubly irascible man known to us as the Professor, his housekeeper who may or may not be his wife and who doesnt talk much, and their daughter who talks a lot though not in English.

As for the neighbours, father and daughter: the Professor claims to hate them for being survivors of Chernobyl, and thus presumably vessels of contagion. But he has other reasons, though the play takes its time to reveal them.

The survivor-father is identified as "the Doctor", and indeed he is one. His daughter is called Artemisia, a name that linguists and herbalists (Im neither, but I can Google) may identify as the Latin term for the bitter herb of the play's title. There's yet a third significance to wormwood, one the play holds in reserve until near the end when its electric. Earlier, though, Artemisia the character has wafted around like somebody symbolic of something: maybe of the broken state, or broken heart, of Ukraine itself.

The entire first act, though it contains some lovely writing, leaves you wondering what the author (Canadian-Ukrainian himself ) has in mind. We get that Ivan is well-intentioned, probably out of his depth, enamoured of his ancestral country and of its attractive herbally equipped embodiment in the next house, but there is little sense of where either he or the play are going. Political details are scanted; we can just about tell that the contest is between reformers and oligarchs, but to fill that out you have to read the very helpful program. It names historical names, which the play never does. (Its not too generous with fictitious ones either, as you may have noted.)

The story has a storyteller: the Kobzar, a blind Cossack bard, modern in dress but with the glint of ages, who admits his own imperfections. "You can commit to memory", he tells us, but memory will not always return the compliment. Witty though this is, we still wonder why he's there. Again, we have to wait till after the intermission to find out.

It's worth the wait. The second half explodes, beginning with a dream sequence thats both nightmarish and hilarious, often at the same time. Ivans private dilemma becomes a convincing metaphor for a larger public one: whether to stay and help, or leave and help. Political specifics are still avoided, though it's a shock when the Doctor reveals which way he has voted; it seems that, against all expectation, he prefers the devil he knows.

Meanwhile he delivers a searing account of just how it felt to be caught up in the Chernobyl disaster, powerful on its own account and haunting as a token of a national tragedy, brutally exploited. The play, like most plays, reaches us after a development period of several years, and it takes no account of more recent developments in Ukraine. But we can still infer them. In that light, the characters and their situation seem even more desperate.

Rose's production has a spare, versatile set by Camellia Koo, and a top-notch cast giving top-notch performances. Luke Humphrey is a fine conflicted Ivan, both earnest and feckless. As Artemisia, Chala Hunter brings charm to a role thats overwritten in one sense, underwritten in another. Ben Campbell captures the Professors sound and fury and frustration, as he plays a long and cunning and finally desperate game. As his opposite number, the Doctor (a bee-keeper on the side), Scott Wentworth is superb, with a sober and commanding bedside manner, and a tragic trove of memories. Memory, it seems, has committed to him, with bitter results; so it makes sense - more than sense, eventually -that he also plays the Kobzar. As the Housekeeper, a scary female Cyclops, Nancy Palk holds most of her powers in reserve, until she unleashes them in a phantasmagoric speech about dentistry. As her daughter, Amy Keating communicates sad and funny volumes while speaking almost entirely in Russian; she also wields a hair-dryer like a benevolently intentioned weapon; later she lends a whole new meaning to the idea of buttering somebody up. Ken James Stewart has the disposable role of Ivan's brother, but his real value to the show is musical; he plays the blind Kobzar's Cossack guide (unlike the Kobzar, hes dressed for the part) and also supplies a vocal complement to Victor Mishalow, an Australian-Ukrainian-Canadian who provides invaluable atmospheric accompaniment on a zither-like instrument called the bandura.

This, after Nicolas Billons Butcher, is the second play to reach us recently on what Timothy Snyder's book calls the Bloodlands. Billon's play is the tighter and the more viscerally exciting, but Wormwood feels the more authentic, and not just because of the authors lineage. This is Kushnirs first major independent play, and it's a notable debut.

National Post

Wormwood runs through December 20 at the Tarragon Theatre, Toronto
2015-12-01-unsentimental-scandal-a-brill:
THEATRE REVIEW

Domesticated Berkley Street Theatre, Toronto

The great thing about Bruce Norris' plays is that they contain no sympathetic characters. Norris is the American playwright responsible for Clybourne Park, which we saw a few years ago, and Domesticated, which is running now. Most American drama is sentimental; Norris is a refreshingly astringent voice.

Like Clybourne Park, Domesticated has two contrasting halves. The earlier play spanned two periods in the life of a black family in a formerly all-white neighbourhood; among other things, it showed us two stages of competitive gentrification. Domesticated shows us two periods in the life, for want of a better word, of a marriage. Here, though, the division is a matter less of time than of dominant voice. Act One, at least in terms of number of words spoken, belongs to the wife, Act Two to the husband.

The husband is a man of Clintonian sexual appetite, and indeed his name is Bill. He isnt president, but he is a prominent political figure, one who has also achieved great professional success as a doctor: a gynaecologist in fact. Hes also a frequenter of prostitutes, including a young one who, when they were together, slipped and hit her head and went into a coma. Did she fall or was she pushed? Bill of course claims the former, but the optics are still terrible. We find him, at the start of the play, making the traditional public apology while his wife Judy, equally traditionally, stands tight-lipped by her man. Bill's aria of contrition is practically all he gets to say before the intermission, though we do see and hear him breaking into humiliated tears, probably genuine, at the family dinner table.

Bill and Judy have two daughters.

The younger, adopted and Cambodian, is silent, at least at home. The elder is volubly dismissive of both her parents, though mostly of course of her father, her contempt accentuated by the fact that there is now insufficient money to put her through the college of her choice. Judy has tried to exploit the situation by writing a book about it, but it hasn't sold as well as was hoped. Everybody in the play is in the exploitation business, financially or psychologically or both.

The comatose girls mother goes on an Oprah-like TV show, relishing her minutes of fame while her everso-empathetic host monopolizes most of the conversation. In Philip Riccios production (for Company Theatre and CanStage) these roles are not so much inhabited as impaled by Sarah Dodd and Akosua Am-Adem. Bill's lawyer (Torri Higginson in a jewel of a performance, i.e. hard and glittering) confesses to her old friend Judy, a little too artlessly, that she dallied with Bill in the front seat of his car. Bill's mother (Nicola Lipman, excellent too) tries to persuade her daughter-in-law that boys will be boys. Most devastating of all is Maria Vacratsis as the family maid, silently judgmental and shortly unaffordable.

Judy has a lot to put up with; she also has the moral high ground. Despite these circumstances, or maybe because of them, she isnt sympathetic, in either sense of the word; and Martha Burns admirably refrains from trying to make her so. She simply, and sharply, states her case. In Act Two, Bill, professionally down and domestically out, states his, at length; and its a fascinating mix of self-pity, self-loathing, and self-justification. Some of what he says is sensible, but none of it is likable; Paul Gross' performance, his best stage work that I've seen, is as unsparing as its eloquent. He has an especially bruising encounter with a transsexual (Salvatore Antonio, icily disdainful).

His most painful scene of all, though, is a date with his two daughters in a cafe, at which he says, and orders, all the wrong things. Kelly McNamee embodies pitiless teenage scorn; Abigail Pew says nothing, again. She does, however, speak between scenes, delivering a class assignment on mating habits in the animal kingdom, the male increasingly dispensable as the examples pile up. This, though, is one of those framing devices that outstay their welcome: a case of an author having an idea and being stuck with it.

The play, in general, is less tight than Clybourne Park, even while painting a smaller canvas; the traps it sets for its characters are less consummately sprung. Overall, though, its a brilliant piece of mercilessly serious comedy; and the production, on Nick Blais' elegant and economic set, gets it absolutely right. Near the end Bill and Judy, after exhaustively and explicitly rehashing their marital problems in and out of bed, show some small signs of getting back together again. The play's greatest distinction may be that, against all the accustomed rules of audience response, we fervently hope that they wont.

Bombay Black

Anosh Iranis Bombay Black is the second mainstage production in Factory's Naked" season of Canadian revivals, and a great improvement on its predecessor in at least one respect: you can hear it. Peter Hinton's production has enough drapery on stage to cushion the actors voices. Otherwise, everything visual is done with lighting and movement, this being a play about a dancer, a young woman who gives private performances, managed by her mother. All three characters are unconventionally cast: Kawa Ada (daughter) is male, Anusree Roy (mother) is young, Howard J. Davis (client) is, from where I sat, pale for the plays Indian setting. Ada is haunting, Roy is biting, Davis is initially pleasant but frustratingly weak at being anything else. The layers of artifice end up removing us from the story: a tale of blindness, revenge, rape and arranged marriage (not in that order) that is tenuous to begin with, being mainly told in retrospect. The play's original production had a tighter grip on its narrative and on its grace of language. The revival, for all its moodiness, feels interminable.

Domesticated runs through Dec. 13 at the Berkeley Street Theatre; Bombay Black runs through Dec. 6 at the Factory Theatre. robert.cushman@hotmail.com

Courtesy Of Canadian Stage / Domesticated, now at the Berkeley Street Theatre, is a play of two contrasting halves.
2015-12-05-look-who-s-40-40-middle-age-h:
Two anniversaries meet. Torontos Young People's Theatre is 50 years old this year, and Mordecai Richler's Jacob Two-Two Meets the Hooded Fang is 40, at least in book form. Three years after the storys publication, YPT put it on stage. It has been, in various incarnations, one of their most reliably popular offerings ever since.

On the strength of the latest version its hard to see why. Jacob is the sixyear old boy - or, as he would say, the two-plus-two-plus-two-year-old boy - who antagonizes his elders with his habit of saying everything twice. This, he says (twice), is the only way he can get anyone larger than himself, meaning everybody, to take notice of him. Entrusted with his very first errand, he incenses a greengrocer with his repeated request for tomatoes, and is arrested on the dread charge of annoying bigger people. He is found guilty by a kangaroo court (though not, alas, one presided over by an actual kangaroo) and sent to the children's prison on the fog-shrouded Slimer's Island, whose governor is the dreaded Hooded Fang, a personage who, the production suggests, has haunted his dreams even in his pre-convict days.

The Fang turns out, however, to be a softie, an ex-wrestler trying to be tough. Jacob sees right through him, and in doing so robs the story of any chance of excitement. However nasty and threatening the subordinate prison staff may be, however heroic Jacob may be in encouraging his fellow inmates to rise up and escape, there really is no contest. Drama is further defused by the musical component, of which there is far too much. The talented team of Britta and Anika Johnson have supplied a score that is plainly meant to carry the story but is likelier to obscure it. This is partly a matter of sound-balance; in a show thats close to being through-sung, the music too often drowns the text. There seems to be a message about Child Power but its bafflingly muffled. Damien Atkins, doubling as grocer and Fang, does manage to cut through. Darrin Baker, as Jacob's court-appointed lawyer Louie Loser, granted one of the rare sustained passages of dialogue, takes advantage.

Toronto has a too-brief opportunity to see Canada's greatest King Lear since William Hutt. David Fox is playing the king in somewhat reduced circumstances; of his supporting cast only Hume Baugh, a super-intelligent sweet-and-bitter Fool, approaches the lead actor in bite and presence. Rod Carley has set his production in what his program note calls "the colonial aping of the British court in preconfederation Upper Canada in 1837." Well, all right, but there was never a king of Upper Canada, and I doubt if there was a Dover cliff either. The setting does nothing to illuminate the play (or vice versa). But it doesnt obscure the play either, and some things are very clever. The storm scenes are especially well staged, with touches at once domestic and titanic, and the relationship of the multiply disguised Edgar and his blinded father Gloucester is beautifully developed, with an onstage epiphany that isnt quite in the text but in no way betrays it. Above all there is Fox, capable of roaring passion at one moment and unearthly quiet simplicity the next; the transitions are thrilling and unpredictable. I am firm he says, banishing Cordelia in the first scene; he says it quietly, with the ironclad whimsy of a tyrant-by-habit. Once unkinged, or self-deposed, he develops a wry troubled humour about his situation. Decidedly un-humorous is the curse of sterility he lays on Goneril; it too is quiet, clinically detached and reasonable, a revelation. The humour, turned up a few twisted notches, modulates naturally into sweetly reasonable madness; the mock-trial scene is a heartbreaker. So, of course, is the ending. "Why should a dog, a horse, a rat, have life?' he asks over Cordelia's body, and the question has never seemed more agonizingly appropriate: for any death, anywhere. As for the famous repetitions: "howl, howl, howl, howl, howled from offstage, is a lament worthy of the Greeks; the five nevers" occasion an extraordinary, inspired modulation, vocal and physical. To describe it would be to spoil it; discover it for yourselves. But hurry: There are only a few performances left. Otherwise, pray that he returns to the role - maybe in a setting that retains this productions best ideas while dropping the others. (The battle should be left offstage as in most other productions, as should the original stage directions.) Lear admits to "fourscore and upward." Fox is 74. He has time.

National Post

Jacob Two-Two Meets the Hooded Fang runs through Jan. 3 at the Young Peoples Theatre; King Lear runs through Dec. 6 at Theatre Passe Muraille

Cylla Von Tiedemann / Drew Davis and Damien Atkins in Jacob Two-Two, one of Young People's Theatre's most popular offerings.
2015-12-12-mashup-musical-when-peter-pan:
Ross Petty is finally slinging his Hook. After 20-years playing villains in his self-produced, self-described "family musicals" (read: traditional English pantomimes somewhat Canadianized) he's making his onstage farewell. The shows will go on, but from next year he'll be their impresario only, not their star. For his valedictory performance he takes up the role he was born to play, and in fact already has.

But that was in another script, one that was a closer spoof of J. M. Barrie's original Peter Pan. Peter Pan in Wonderland, as its title proclaims, is a mash-up of Peter Pan or some of its characters, with an even greater children's classic, Alice in Wonderland or some of its characters, the latter bunch being somewhat arbitrarily selected. The evening starts with Eddie Glen, a valued regular, and Jessica Holmes, a valuable newbie, temporarily tagged as Tweedle Dum and Tweedle Dumber, singing a song called Backstory, in which they skim through the details of their two revered sources, very few of which bear any relation to the entertainment that follows. Still, it's a fun number, spiritedly performed. "Lewis Carroll," they promise us, "will turn in his grave" and they predict a similar fate for Barrie. I don't know; it seems to me that their properties have taken so many beatings over the years that they must have grown very thick posthumous skins. At least this production doesn't pretend to be respectful. The world in recent years has been especially cold to Peter Pan knock-offs, most of them awful. There's even been a previous collision between Peter and Alice: a play of that name was seen in London a couple of seasons ago, presenting the mostly unhappy grown-up lives of the real-life children on whom the fictional hero and heroine were modelled. It wasn't good.

Peter Pan in Wonderland is not great but good. The prologue over, we move to the older-and-wiser Wendy's bedroom as she waits yet again for Peter to make one of his return flying visits, oft promised but never performed. This time he does turn up but too late; his impatient girlfriend has stepped inside what she takes to be a basket of goodies but which in fact precipitates her right down a rabbit-hole. So you know where she'll end up. Peter, informed of her flight by Nana, the unexpectedly talking dog, follows her down, followed in his turn by Tinker Bell's much bigger sister, Tinkerbum, who of course is closely related to the timorous and amorous Dame Plumbum whom Dan Chameroy has played in successive Petty Pantos, each time more delectably than the time before. My favourite moment in the present show is fairy Chameroy laboriously climbing through the Darling family window, which fortunately is a big one.

Anyway, they catch up with Wendy who meantime has made the acquaintance of Alice, the White Rabbit, the Mad Hatter and the Cheshire Cat, who exhibit few of their role-models' characteristics and even fewer of their own. It turns out that Captain Hook, having escaped the jaws of his nemesis the crocodile, has engineered the arrival in Wonderland of Peter and Co. so that, by nefarious and complicated ways, he may get his hands on the Tickle Trunk of Wonder, which resides at the centre of a maze somewhere and can be opened only with fairy dust that the unknowing Wendy has in her possession.

Chris Earle's script has the same basic script as all his previous pantos: there's something somewhere that will bestow giant destructive powers, and the Petty character must have it. (He Must! She Must! They Must!) The goodies, striving to prevent this, face many reversals, including imprisonment, but finally square off against the baddies in a TV-style contest, which here involves some fantastic rope-skipping by Anthony McPherson's altogether acrobatic Peter. There's a chase in which the coveted object passes from hand to hand to hand and back again. Earle's writing credit is again buried deep in the listings, somewhere between the stage manager and the music co-ordinator; I used to wonder at this but now suspect that it's because Messrs Petty, Chameroy and Glen (he plays Smee, Hook's conflicted, but loyal first mate) are so adept at making up their own lines when things go wrong and sometimes even when they don't.

The only character with a life of her own, and partly of Lewis Carroll's, is Holmes' lisping flirtatious Queen of Hearts, issuing sentences of execution that never get carried out. My second favourite is when she imperiously calls, "Five, Six, Seven, Eight," Chorus Line-style, and playing-card soldiers bearing those numbers troop on to do her bidding. The interpolated pop songs get in on very thin pretexts, but the dances that accompany them (choreographer, Marc Kimmelman) are impressively inventive. Indeed, everything in Tracey Flye's productions looks good; Michael Gianfrancesco's sets are a succession of truly wondrous vistas. And then there is the retiring actor-manager himself, about whom there is nothing Petty but the name. His Hook is a daintily stylish, world-weary villain, inviting our boos and hisses with the familiar contemptuous relish, now honed to perfection. He makes his final exit into his own infernal basket, singing that he did it His Way, which is no less than the truth, and with the insatiable crocodile in eager pursuit. It's quite a way to go.

Peter Pan in Wonderland runs through January 3 at the Elgin Theatre

2015-12-12-sinatra-good-and-bad-remember:
Elia Kazan, the great American film and stage director, hated Frank Sinatra, mainly because of what hed heard about the singer's arrogant and unruly behaviour on and off movie sets. But in 1968, with Sinatra at what might be called the last stage of his prime, Kazan was persuaded - by Raquel Welch, remember her? - to attend one of his shows. Halfway through the first song Kazan, who knew everything about acting, turned to his glamorous date and said My God! This (expletive-deleted) guy is the best actor I've ever seen in my life. Hes completely naked up there. Hes a genius.

I got that nugget from Sinatra: The Chairman by James Kaplan, the second half of a massive and probably definitive two-volume biography - a double-doorstopper from Doubleday - published to coincide with the centenary of its subject's birth, on Dec. 12, 1915. The first volume Frank: The Voice came out in 2010, and it contains an observation that should be considered in conjunction with Kazan's. Mitch Miller, of singalong fame, was the classical oboe virtuoso turned record producer, who masterminded whats generally considered to be the low-point of the Sinatra career: the early 1950s when, having fallen from his unprecedented teen-idol eminence of the previous decade, he was recording novelties and sub-standard ballads in a vain attempt to keep up with the musically depressing times. It was, however, the other Sinatra - the great interpreter of great songs - whom Miller seemed to have in mind when he decried the common notion that the singers best work was autobiographical. No, he said, he was singing his audience's emotions, not his own. This accords with the philosophy of one of Sinatra's primary influences, the godmother of New York cabaret, Mabel Mercer. A very modest and sensible lady, she always said that it was her job to make her hearers feel their own feelings, not hers.

The nakedness Kazan saw, the impersonality Miller described, are not incompatible.

Theyre what acting, which includes some kinds of singing, is about: the exploration of feelings that everybody has and can recognize, the revelation of a persona that relates to that of the performer but is not identical with it. In Sinatras case the situation is complicated by there being so much persona to relate to. There's the mother-dominated high school dropout from New Jersey who became a towering artistic, financial and even political success, an omnivorous reader and listener, but still felt like a social and intellectual outsider. There's the private and public philanthropist who spent and raised millions on a worldwide tour for childrens charities, declaring with undoubted sincerity that "an overprivileged adult ought to help underprivileged children," and theres the associate of gangsters who seems to have used their services, not to secure himself movie roles - Kaplan debunks that one pretty thoroughly - but to settle personal grudges. There's the friend who was passionately loyal until he discarded you. There's the doggedly passionate anti-racist, the man with the guts to be a liberal in a John Wayne Hollywood, the JFK booster who, apparently out of pique when he too was discarded, went over to Nixon and Agnew and Reagan. Theres the courteous, even chivalrous guy whose conquests Kaplan estimates to have been in the hundreds if not thousands. Theres the man who throughout his life stayed loyal if not faithful in his fashion to his first wife Nancy and the man whose second wife, Ava Gardner, apparently remained the great passion of his life and also the great friendship. A leitmotif of both Kaplan's books is Frank and Ava's perpetual pursuit and rejection of one another, before, during and after their marriage.

How to reconcile all this? Twenty years ago, on Sinatras 80th birthday, I wrote the tedious truth seems to be that he is capable, like most of us, of both good and bad behaviour, but that his position gives him more scope in both directions. I suppose I still believe that, but I have to admit that, reading Kaplans books, I find the bad behaviour more disturbing, the man himself harder to like, than before. The gang connections don't bother me so much - actually they become rather boring, not to mention confusing - but the verbal and even physical cruelty, often towards helpless subordinates, is really ugly. The cruelty, though, never gets into the singing which at the worst, which isn't very often, substitutes macho swagger. More often, theres vulnerability. I dont think this is dishonesty; more likely it's sublimation, the artist admitting to a weakness he could never admit in life, where instead he took it out on others. The Gardner marriage began when Sinatra's career was at its lowest ebb, and ended when it returned to high tide, with his Oscar-winning performance in From Here to Eternity and the beginning of his great string of recordings for Capitol. Popular wisdom holds (and Kaplan reiterates) that Gardner was on his mind when he recorded all those searching ballads, beginning with the great bittersweet LP, In the Wee Small Hours. Perhaps. But when I first heard his performance on that album of Richard Rodgers and Lorenz Harts Glad to Be Unhappy (talk about an emblematic title), I didnt even know about him and Ava. I just responded to the song. As he did.

That's the crux. Sinatra's career began (his first recording was in 1939) just as the greatest era of American songwriting was beginning to wind down; fine songs in the tradition variously known as standards or the Great American Songbook or (these days and tellingly) "Sinatra music," were still being written but there were fewer of them. Sinatra seized on them, in his band-singer and bobbysoxidol days, but he also collected the older ones, the Jerome Kerns and George Gershwins and Cole Porters and others less heralded but still inspired. He did so on a larger scale when the long-playing era came along, at Capitol and on his own label Reprise. He didnt work through the catalogue as systematically as Ella Fitzgerald in jazz or Bobby Short in cabaret, but he did so with an unerring sense of which songs would work for him. He explored them, and he inhabited them.

In fact he disappeared into them. Its depressing that so much Sinatra-worship should focus on the Rat Pack, a tawdry and short-lived phenomenon that's inspired some perverse nostalgia. If you look at the footage of Sinatra and company horsing around in Vegas, exchanging jokes and insults, it's pretty glum, not least because Frank himself (unlike his pals Dean and Sammy) was no comedian. But then the orchestra will strike up I Have Dreamed or My Heart Stood Still, and immediately you and he are in a different world. The audience at a Sinatra performance could hardly be unaware of the man himself, but speaking from within the song is a different voice; if its the man himself, then its the best in him, finding and sharing beauty.

Part of it of course is technique: the superfine breathcontrol, the inimitable voice that sculpts a song, the gravity with which he separates syllables, the phrasing that always knows which words to emphasize. His sensitivity in sad songs - what he termed saloon and others have called suicide songs - is legendary, but it extends to happy songs as well. Sinatra's recording of You Make Me Feel So Young lives in the memory as the quintessential uptempo celebration - what Cole Porter, who didn't write it, called "the quintessence of joy" - so its a surprise to listen to it again and realize that he actually delivers it at a jaunty medium pace, every word cherished and caressed but never oversold; his songs for swingin lovers are as ardent, as deep, as fastidious, as his songs for only the lonely. Even when he does ramp up the tempo, as on his brass-backed recording of Dancing in the Dark, the stoic desperation at the song's core comes clearly, crisply through.

When I said he was no comedian, I meant it only in the formal sense. He certainly relishes the wit in a song. Hand him Rodgers and Hart's I Wish I Were in Love Again, the definitive anti-love song, and he will give it his ironic best, italicizing nothing, communicating everything. Or in a broader swinging-brass context, he can give a wonderfully cheerful deadpan reading of Doncha Go Way Mad, a song about an acknowledged infidelity (Who would have dreamed your cousin/Would wander into that restaurant?) He freely admitted to loathing his two biggest late-career hits: Strangers in the Night too sappy, the anthemic My Way "too on the nose." No matter what the image may seem to be, I hate boastfulness, I hate immodesty, and that's how I feel every time I sing the song. You know what? I believe him, believe that in betraying himself as a singer, he was betraying himself as a man. But there are so many truths to outnumber the betrayals. There's his extraordinary quiet recording of the Antonio Carlos Jobim song Dindi, whose beauty and wonder he seems to be discovering, awestruck, as he sings. From She Shot Me Down, a very late album and one of his finest, theres I Loved Her which begins "she was Boston, I was Vegas" and goes on opposites attract, the wise men claim/still I wish that we had been a little more the same. The way he stretches out that word "little" - lit-tle - infusing it with anger, regret, bitterness, passion, pain and self-blame, all at once, is sung acting at its greatest, just as Kazan said. Its the accumulated power of the man, in the service of the song.

I've been writing about Sinatra in the present tense, which seems right because - a hundred years after his birth, 17 years after his death, he's still with us: as a legend, as a personality, and - most importantly - as a body of work unmatched in its field. When he left Capitol, the label hit back by releasing a triple LP package of some of his greatest tracks. The liner notes ended by asking "were better recordings by a singer ever made?" The question was rhetorical but I' ll answer it anyway: No, none ever were.

National Post robert.cushman@hotmail.com
