2015-12-29-2016-theatre-preview:
You've heard of feasts and famines: also of coincidences. One of the most compelling, and most surprising, Toronto theatre productions of 2015 was Blood Wedding, mounted at Buddies in Bad Times by the Modern Times company, an enterprising independent outfit who come among us at unpredictable intervals. Blood Wedding, by the poet-playwright Federico Garcia Lorca who was one of the casualties of the Spanish Civil War, is a lyrical tragedy much honoured in textbooks but seldom staged, at least in English, possibly because it's very hard. In decades of theatregoing I'd never seen it. Now I'm to get a second helping, with a different flavour and at a more settled address. The same play features in the 2016 lineup at Soulpepper, in a new version by the company's head of playwriting Guillermo Verdecchia, announced as "reset with the rhythms of rural Ontario," so presumably taking place there; though in what period has not been revealed.

Blood Wedding is one of two mainstream classics in Soulpepper's new season. The other is a far more familiar piece: the proto-feminist, and unshakably resonant A Doll's House, directed by Laszlo Marton, the recurring Hungarian maestro responsible for a healthy proportion of the company's best work, including one previous Ibsen, The Wild Duck, which was among the best of the best. A Doll's House is being presented in a translation by Frank McGuinness, noted playwright from Ireland, though presumably not set there.

Arthur Miller is a Soulpepper favourite (Death of a Salesman, The Crucible, The Price) who stubbornly refuses to go out of fashion; his 60-year old A View from the Bridge is currently the sensation of New York. His later Incident at Vichy has been neglected, though I remember being riveted by its London premiere with Alec Guinness as a European nobleman caught up in a roundup of Jews in Nazi-occupied France. Diego Matamoros has the princely role at Soulpepper in a production by Alan Dilworth, who gets to follows his thrilling Twelve Angry Men with a comparably tense play about eight terrified men.

A more recent American play - a 2015 prize-winner in fact - is the one billed as Father Comes Home from the Wars (Parts I, II, III). (There are other parts to come, though they haven't all been written yet.) Following in the footsteps of Eugene O'Neill, whose Mourning Becomes

Electra retold the story of the Oresteia by setting it in the American Civil War, Suzan-Lori Parks gives the same period treatment to the Odyssey, focusing on the country's racial divide as O'Neill didn't, at least not in that play. In Soulpepper terms the production would seem to continue the radical American-epic tradition of Angels in America.

Another company tradition, and a good one, is that of reviving - or keeping alive - successful productions. 2016 will offer three of these, all from the middlebrow or frankly populist, section of the repertoire: The Odd Couple (a re-revival), the backstage comedy Jitters, and, at the top end, those dozen angry guys. The current Family Festival, which continues to Jan. 3, is made up of such favourites; and it's fun to see old shows with some new faces. In A Christmas Carol, Oliver Dennis now alternates as Scrooge with the role's creator Joseph Ziegler (who has restaged Michael Shamata's original production, making no changes that I could detect, because none were necessary); Dennis's Scrooge is closer to the miserly profile of Dickens' illustrators than Ziegler, equally moving as he learns the truth about himself, less transportingly joyous in the conversion where Ziegler seemed to leap almost out of his skin. The show remains a delight, funny and honestly tearful, as does Parfumerie, another fruit of the Hungarian connection, with Gregory Prest and Michelle Monteith a new and beautifully detailed pair of mail-order lovers, Sarah Wilson a delectable acquisition as a Judy Holliday dumb blond, and the surrounding ensemble stronger than ever in an adaptation and production that seem wittier than ever.

Antoni Cimolino's personal production slate as artistic director at Stratford seems to have settled into a pattern: one Shakespeare tragedy, one non-Shakespeare comedy. Last season it was Hamlet and The Alchemist (the latter one of the festival's three best shows, along with The Taming of the Shrew and The Physicists); this time it will be Macbeth and The Hypochondriac, the latter being a Moliere adaptation by Richard Bean whose immortal One Man Two Guv'nors will presumably be seen in Canada sometime, somehow; Stephen Ouimette, farceur supreme, has the title role. This year's Macbeths are a youngish couple, Ian Lake and Kristin Pellerin: not an unprecedented choice but an unusual one. Stratford too has its Ibsen and its Miller; the latter All My Sons (Ziegler and Tim Campbell, father and son in Soulpepper's Salesman reprising the relationship in the play that preceded it); the former the great, late John Gabriel Borkman, one of the few plays to offer three walloping roles for mature actors, here Scott Wentworth and - in a re-match of their great Mary Stuart duet - Lucy Peacock and Seana Mc-Kenna. And talking of re-matches: I look forward to Stratford's studio premiere of a new Hannah Moscovitch play Bunny, fruit of one of her many commissions, starring Maev Beaty who first knocked me out a Moscovitch solo piece called USSR.

There's no Ibsen at the Shaw Festival, which spoils the classical symmetry, but there is Strindberg: The Dance of Death with the formidable couple of Jim Mezon and Fiona Reid in a marriage that makes Who's Afraid of Virginia Woolf look like a model of happy domesticity. And there's Chekhov: Uncle Vanya, in a production by outgoing director Jackie Maxwell, with Neil Barclay, an actor who seldom gets such breaks, in the title role. And there's Sondheim: Maxwell directs Sweeney Todd (Stratford has A Little Night Music. So that's symmetrical). There's Lewis Carroll: our theatres can't keep their hands off Alice, and - in what publicity is featuring as the festival's flagship production - Peter Hinton will give us his take on Wonderland, which will undoubtedly be imaginative, whatever else. There's Gilbert without Sullivan: a rare and thoroughly sardonic comedy called Engaged. Oh yes, and there's even some Shaw: a dramatization of the story The Adventures of the Black Girl in Her Search for God, and one actual play: Mrs Warren's Profession, last seen, or so it seems, only yesterday. When, he asked yet again, are they going to do Androcles and the Lion?

And ... and ... and: Crows Theatre, in cahoots with CanadianStage, are bringing Chimerica to Toronto. This is the 2013 play by the British playwright Lucy Kirkwood that shuttles between Tiananmen Square, 1989, and New York 2012. Large scale, large cast, and Chris Abraham directs. It's hard not to feel excited.

Don Dixon / Macbeth
2016-01-09-word-to-your-father-hamilton-:
The musical Hamilton is a phenomenon. That's evident at the Richard Rodgers Theatre in New York, and also on the cast album, a double CD on Atlantic. There are phenomena among American musicals, and there are hits, and there are classics. The categories can overlap. Phenomena are shows that create box-office frenzies and are also felt to have changed the form in some way. Examples are Oklahoma!, Hair, A Chorus Line, Rent, with honourable mentions to My Fair Lady, which was nobodys idea of a game-changer but which conquered the world by doing the expected things with extraordinary grace and assurance, and to West Side Story, which really did shift the ground under Broadways feet but was only a modest commercial success on its first run.

Phenomena don't necessarily endure. Hair has proved to be ephemeral and the same may well prove true for Rent. On the other hand, take Guys and Dolls and Gypsy, two shows that bookend a decade (Guys and Dolls was first staged in 1950 and Gypsy in 1959). When they first appeared they were greeted merely as good shows, at a time when good shows seemed plentiful; they have turned out to be the most revivable musicals of all. They're classics.

Commercially, Hamilton, the hip-hop show about a Founding Father, is clearly a phenomenon. To call it a hit is almost to insult it; tickets for its New York run are changing hands at thousands of dollars apiece. (The cheapest unscalped seats go for US$130.) Could it become a classic? I think it might. Like Hair and Rent, its rock predecessors, it uses a current pop style; unlike them, it doesnt give the impression that its creators decided on the style and then went looking for a story on which to hang it. (Hair never found one.) Hamilton feels as if the story came first. Lin-Manuel Miranda, who wrote the book, music and lyrics - and stars in it, says in interviews that he read Ron Chernows biography of Alexander Hamilton and knew immediately that he wanted to musicalize it. He also says that hip-hop ("my generation's music - it's only a little bit older than me") was the way to do it, because its an outpouring of words, and that Hamiltons life and career, his whole energy, were built on words. They made him and they destroyed him.

Here it seems obligatory to quote the first words of the score: How does a bastard, orphan, son of a whore and a/Scotsman, dropped in the middle of a forgotten/spot in the Caribbean by providence/impoverished, in squalor/grow up to be a hero and a scholar? The lines are sung, spoken, rapped by Aaron Burr, the man destined to kill Hamilton in a duel. They convey information, in packed but comprehensible form, about their subject and also about the man who says them. Burr was vice-president; Hamilton had been secretary of the treasury, founder of the American financial system, George Washington's righthand man in peace and war. Burr and Hamilton had been occasional allies and lifelong rivals. The biographical number is taken up by two more of Hamilton's enemies, Thomas Jefferson and James Madison, as well as by Hamiltons wife, Eliza, and by George Washington himself. Love him or hate him, they all speak his language. We dont hear from the man himself until Burr asks "What's your name, man?" and Miranda himself steps forward and says, with unassuming confidence, Alexander Hamilton. The night I saw the show, a week after the opening, we all broke into applause. Partly this was because the moment, built up so cunningly, was so quiet yet so devastating: an anticlimax that was also a climax. Partly it was because the buzz around the show had prompted us to cheer the man who created it. He deserved it.

The moment still comes through on the CD, which makes up in presence and clarity for what it loses in visual appeal. (Hamilton is an exceptionally well-staged show, economically spectacular.) It will probably still be a good show without Miranda, but it will not be quite the same show. His charm and his energy suffuse it. Still, the most important part of that energy is its passion for its own narrative, and that will survive. Every number forwards the story. In this very important way, Hamilton is not so much an innovation as a return to first principles; it's a rebuke to the pop-operas like Les Miserables, in which the songs solemnly tell us things we already know and the story has to be conveyed in the tuneless bits of quasirecitative that come between them. Another thing Hamilton has, that those shows lack, is humour.

This is most obviously present in the three solo appearances of King George III, singing in carefree early-Beatles style, at first about how much the rebellious colonials will miss him when hes gone, and later about his reaction to President Washingtons retirement: "I wasn't aware," sings the hereditary monarch that was something a person could do. And he concludes "They will tear each other into pieces. Jesus Christ, this will be fun!" (I suspect a hattip here to Sondheim's Company:

Its not so hard to be married/And, Jesus Christ, is it fun.). Georges numbers are set pieces, but other laughout-loud moments come, in the musical's best tradition, from apparently innocuous lines dropped into the right context: Hamilton's first flights of oratory elicit the deadpan response: "Lets get this guy in front of a crowd."

Theres great wit, too, in the casting; with the notable exceptions of the Hispanic Miranda, and of Jonathan Groff who plays the king, this show about the beginning of America has a black cast. Jefferson, the slave-owning founder recently returned from ambassadorial duties in France, has the most infectious RB number in the show, What'd I Miss (I've been in Paris meeting lots of different ladies/I guess I basiclly missed the late eighties).

The score, contrary to some of the composers assertions, is at most only 50 per cent hip hop; it can even change styles within a single song. Daveed Diggs, who plays Jefferson, doubles as Lafayette whose "immigrants: we get the job done" may be the show's most heartfelt line. Its greatest traditional theatre number, surging and torrential, is The Room Where It Happens, the outsider Burr's jealous diatribe against the political deals that get made behind closed doors. Its a perennially topical subject, and Leslie Odom Jr.s Burr actually comes over better on disc than on stage. So do the more romantic or contemplative songs involving the hero's wife, mistress and adored sister-in-law; or maybe it's just that theyve grown on me.

Other fine and adventurous composer-lyricists have appeared in the past couple of decades (Adam Guettel, Jason Robert Brown) but none has broken through in the way Miranda has. A Chicago production is currently in the works, but theres no word on when we might expect to see the show in Canada. The CD is great but it isn't the same. You wanna be in the room where it happens.

Joan Marcus, The Public Theater Via Associated Press /
2016-01-15-you-couldn-t-take-your-ears-o:
It was 1962. I was in my last term at Latymer Upper, a West London grammar school with a great tradition of drama. I was in a rehearsed reading of Serjeant Musgrave's Dance, a cult classic of the time. We complacent old-timers were jolted away from our scripts by the sight, and especially the sound, of an unfamiliar boy, three years

our junior, who - Latymer not having yet gone co-ed - was playing a barmaid. The boy's name, we discovered, was Alan Rickman. I can still recall the defiant heartbreak with which he imbued a line about being required to cradle a dead lover's skeleton and "make up songballads."

The same voice, preternaturally deep and hollowed out, was equally eloquent in expressing rage, sarcasm and humiliation. It was already the voice that was to make him a star.

When Alan left school he went to study graphic design. But he also joined an amateur drama group, one in which he met a sharp-witted young lady named Rima Horton, who was to become his companion for the rest of his life. It was obvious he would have to choose between vocations and he did.

He enrolled at the Royal Academy of Dramatic Art, Britain's premier drama school. After graduating, he was, as he once told me, never out of work.

His rise in the professional theatre was fast. We'd kept bumping into one another, usually on buses and subways, but he first crossed my professional radar in the early 1970s. I was theatre critic for The Observer and I saw him in regional productions and at the Edinburgh Festival. The voice, even deeper and craggier than before, and the saturnine demeanour, made him ideal for cynical roles in Jacobean drama, and allowed him to lend authority to others as well. He's probably the only actor to get rave reviews in the usually nondescript role of Friar Peter in Measure for Measure.

You couldn't take your ears off him. He played mediumsized roles with the Royal Shakespeare Company, left, and returned a few years later as a fully fledged lead, playing the melancholy Jaques in As You Like It and the musclebound Achilles of Troilus and Cressida. The RSC gave him his breakthrough role: the Vicomte de Valmont, career seducer, in Les Liaisons dangereuses, a performance in which he blended languid self-confidence with whiplash wit. The play went from Stratford to London to Broadway, and its success took him to Hollywood, where they seized on his talents as a villain.

I had just moved to Canada when Die Hard opened, and I remember looking at the posters outside a movie theatre. You never expect to see an old school friend emblazoned as a movie star. But there he was. Having grown up poor, it was a status he took to with an air of bemusement. He enjoyed the perks but never took it too seriously.

From a self-satirizing Sheriff of Nottingham in Robin Hood: Prince of Thieves to Severus Snape in the Harry Potter franchise, the villain roles continued. He could do wonders with a sneer and a drawl, and he made evil likable. One of my own favourites among his film roles, though, was his decidedly unvillainous Colonel Brandon in Sense and Sensibility. The portrayal had the same Rickman style, but this time it was deployed in the service of decency.

Offstage and off-screen, that was Alan. He was remarkably loyal, across decades and oceans. He was a generous host and a gracious guest. His relationship with Rima lasted 50 years. They had no children but they were extraordinarily kind to other people's. An actor friend described Alan as being "like a wonderful uncle." My own children certainly felt the benefit of that: he gave them career advice and encouragement, took them around the Harry Potter set, even got them work as extras on one of his movies.

He was also one of the most respected figures in the British theatre. Everybody sought his opinion, everybody wanted to act with him or, later, be directed by him. He was intelligent and outspoken and could be more critical than any critic, sometimes outrageously so. He once described a certain stage director as the worst he'd ever worked with. I protested that he always said that. "I know," he admitted, "but this time I mean it."

The last time I saw him in person was in Toronto in 2014 when the film A Little Chaos, which he directed, was shown at TIFF. He also appeared in it - reluctantly, he insisted - as Louis XIV. The studio wanted to add his star power to that of Kate Winslet. He couldn't stop talking about how wonderful she was in it, and he was right. He never seemed to belong to any group or clique. His career straddled media, attracting fans of all generations. He put a personal stamp on everything he did, everything he said. He was unique. And he will be missed.

Jaap Buitendijk / The late Alan Rickman as Professor Severus Snape with Maggie Smith in Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince.
2016-01-20-clinical-mistake-in-the-glass:
Through an incredible hospital foul-up, a woman becomes an unwilling surrogate mother. The embryo she is carrying is the biological property of Michael and Darah, a married couple in their forties who for the last six years have been trying, desperately and unsuccessfully, to have a child of their own by more orthodox methods. In other respects, they are extremely well off (Michael is a banker; Darah designs video games). The bearer of their test-tube offspring is named Linda; she and her husband Scott are in their thirties, have a daughter of their own and are scraping by (Scott is a poet; Linda is a musician).

Anna Chatterton's Within the Glass shows us the two couples meeting in person for the first time. Michael and Darah are hosting, and they're doing it in style (Julie Fox's living-and-dining-room set is luscious). This is partly because they can afford it, and partly because they're very nervous. They don't know which of the options open to Linda, now at the end of her first trimester, she will decide to take. Will she keep the child as her own? Will she have an abortion? Or will she carry the baby to term and then give it to Michael and Darah to adopt? The last choice of course is the one that Michael and Darah devoutly hope she will make. Linda herself seems disinclined to oblige.

The Tarragon has mounted a first-rate production of a problematic play, one that begins amusingly, and moves on to some powerful confrontations, but destroys itself halfway through. This is when one of the characters makes, offstage, a crucial decision whose reasons are never made clear. By way of cover-up we get an extended foray into the comedy of over-eager embarrassment. Even before this, the play has been split in its tone. Half of it is anguished personal drama, focusing on the agonies of sterility and with assumed socio-political overtones. The other is a comedy of manners, or perhaps a comedy of awkward hospitality. The richer couple don't want to appear patronizing, the poorer couple make it clear that they feel patronized.

This is all very amusing to begin with, and it offers some rich double meanings, especially when the subject is food. Michael, announcing dinner, says "we'll all feel a

little better with something in our bellies," not perhaps the most tactful thing to say to the pregnant Linda. She, a vegetarian, objects strongly to the offer of a chicken dish: "It's never just a chicken, it's a genocide for chickens." The chicken, in another biological double-entendre, is a castrated one: a capon.

When the foursome stop smiling and start shouting, the conflicts tend to be vivid but free-floating, unmoored from what surrounds them. They do, however, provoke some really exciting acting, beautifully orchestrated under Andrea Donaldson's direction. As Linda, the designated earthmother alternately resenting and glorying in her fecundity, Nicola Correia-Damude gives an appropriately overflowing performance, drawing on impressive reserves of anger and longing.

Where she's all curves, Philippa Domville's Darah is all angles, coyly flirtatious as she sets the table and welcomes the guests. Brittle and apparently hysterical as the evening proceeds, she too finally gets to release her rage, storming at the woman who has accused her of delaying child-bearing for the sake of her career.

Michael, it turns out, is even more frantic for parenthood than his wife. Rick Roberts, who starts out as the picture of a suave accommodating host, loses the suavity while ratcheting up the accommodation to self-immolating levels. Paul Braunstein's roughneck Scott could hardly be further from the conventional idea of a poet, but it takes all sorts, and his jovial cynicism, biting the hands that are feeding him while relishing the food, is an excellent contrast to the earnest concerns of everybody else. While the wives attack one another, the husbands grow closer together: self-defence perhaps, given that both couples will eventually get around to airing some longfestering grievances. There's a suggestion that Michael and Linda are attracted to one another, or at least that he is turned on by her fertility, but it seems to be there because that kind of thing is expected in a play. At a certain level the action is farcical. Once we had comedies about children swapped at birth, now we have them swapped in test-tubes. If one of the play's purposes is to discuss the ethics and consequences of in vitro ("within the glass") fertilization, then maybe the discussion shouldn't have been based on a clinical mistake.

Within the Glass runs through Feb. 14 at the Tarragon Theatre National Post robert.cushman@hotmail.com

Cylla Von Tiedemann / Philippa Domville and Rick Roberts star in the Tarragon's production of Within the Glass.
2016-01-26-he-made-me-believe-rememberin:
I never thought that Brian Bedford could move me to tears until I saw him play King Lear. But then I had never before seen him in a role in which he was required to.

Bedford, who died this month at the age of 80, played Lear at the Stratford Festival in 2007. It was the last great Shakespearean role he attempted, and he directed it himself: an impossible idea that didn't turn too badly. He wasnt known as a heavyweight tragedian, and his first few speeches as Lear were delivered at an alarmingly low sound level. In fact they were nearly inaudible. Then suddenly, when his authority was challenged, it reasserted itself. The voice, I wrote at the time "crackles, swells, and even roars, while the tottering old man turns into a tyrant fully capable of lifting a sword and, if not prevented, doing serious damage with it." His familiar ironic and comedic skills came into play in Lears madness, which he presented as a kind of baffled logic. He reached true greatness at the end when Lear thinks he sees the dead Cordelia's breath stirring; he was looking not at her but straight ahead, as if at some phantom in his own imagination. That's when we cried.

It might be said that, in his many seasons at the Canadian Stratford, Bedford reclaimed his British classical birthright. Bedford came from Bradford, in Yorkshire, and his childhood was exceptionally bleak. Acting seems to have saved him; he won admission to the Royal Academy of Dramatic Art, where his classmates included Albert Finney and Peter OToole, fellow-members of the new wave of working-class actors who emerged in Britain in the 1950s. Bedfords subsequent career as a master of drawing-room comedy may make that hard to credit, but he seems to have delighted in the occasional chance to return to his roots; at Stratford, his Bottom in A Midsummer Night's Dream was pure Bradford, and a delight because of it, especially when he confidentially corrected the Duke of Athens on the exact plot-line of Pyramus and Thisbe.

After RADA Bedford went into rep in Liverpool, where at the age of 21 he played Hamlet, prompting a local critic to salute him as one of the British theatre's rising stars. The prophecy proved true. Within a couple of months he was in London, making a reputation as an actor of sensitive young men. He also appeared at the English Stratford as Ariel in The Tempest, directed by Peter Brook; it was a controversial performance in a controversial production though I, a schoolboy at the time, remember liking both well enough. It was the only one of his English performances I saw; somehow I missed his breakthrough role in a breakthrough play, playing the tormented son in Peter Shaffers Five Finger Exercise. The play, and John Gielguds production, took him to New York, and there he stayed. He felt, he said, that he had found his home.

He was to find a second one in Canada. He had a decent American career, including some movies, some returns to London and - decisively - his emergence as a classical comedian, notably in Moliere. Then, in 1975, Robin Phillips, Stratford's newly installed artistic director, invited him to join the company there. He must have sensed in Bedford a wasted resource, waiting to be reawakened; Bedford may have felt the same. His first Stratford role was one of his neurotics, Angelo in Measure for Measure; it was, by common consent, magnificent, and I wish I'd seen it. I did catch his Richard III a couple of years later, and I still think it the best Ive seen: not especially funny, perhaps surprisingly, but electric with malice: one resentful, ambitious man against the world.

It was for being funny, though, that Bedford became most celebrated at Stratford: especially when Phillips persuaded Maggie Smith to come to Stratford; she and Bedford, high-wire artists in touch with the earth, performed a series of scintillating duets, most famously as the squabbling couple of Noel Cowards Private Lives. Bedford was a Coward specialist and a Coward friend.

To some people's surprise, Bedford's connection to Stratford outlasted both Smiths and Phillips; lasted in fact up till his death. He and the festival were good for one another. His technical command in comedy became so consummate that people were apt to take it for granted, but there was always more to it. As Sir Peter Teazle in The School for Scandal, he made me laugh every time he opened his mouth; he also made me believe. When he returned to Private Lives, this time opposite Seana McKenna, there was an unbroken current of thought connecting the epigrams.

He directed that Private Lives himself, and directing became an important part of his career. He started with tragedies (Richard Monette once told him that they were all he could direct): a Titus Andronicus that was a triumph and a Coriolanus that was pretty good. But he moved on to comedy, frequently directing himself in roles he'd previously played for other people. His masterpiece production was The Importance of Being Earnest, in which every line and every twist of plot made delirious sense, and in which every performance was impeccable, including his own Lady Bracknell: a dragon too sure of herself, or too afraid of being contradicted, ever to need to raise her voice. The production went to Broadway, though alas without most of its Canadian cast.

Bedford was a star, and he knew it. He was also, in my experience, charming and self-deprecating. I once asked him whether there'd been any difference between his two Stratford Malvolios; he smiled and said he shouldnt think so. (The one I remember had him roused from his bed, clutching a teddy-bear.) Hes the only actor I've interviewed to suggest, half way through, that we adjourn from the office to the nearest pub.

Last week also robbed of us another Stratford treasure. William Needles was a real veteran, part of the very first festival company in 1953. The following season gave him a star role: a paradoxically shy Petruchio in a Wild West Taming of the Shrew. He never again had a part that big, but he gave great authority to supporting roles, right up to the Henry VI history cycle of 2002. Jerry Franken, a third loss, was rarely thought of as a Stratford actor, though he was a good Polonius to Paul Gross' Hamlet, and once said, wisely, "The emotion is built into the text. You can't put anything on top of it .... Using tricks with Shakespeare is dangerous." But he will surely be best remembered for his wiry, vinegary performance as the farmer in Michael Healey's The Drawer Boy.

Peter Morgan, The Associated Press / British actor Brian Bedford had a long relationship with the Stratford Shakespeare Festival, and had a memorable cross-dressing turn as a dowager on Broadway. He died of cancer on Jan. 13 in Santa Barbara, Calif., at the age of 80.
2016-01-27-a-time-honoured-way-to-fight-:
On Jan. 13, 1898, the Paris paper L'Aurore published Emile Zola's open letter J'Accuse. The institution he was accusing was the French army, which had sentenced the Jewish officer Captain Alfred Dreyfus to penal servitude on Devil's Island for selling military secrets to the Germans and had suppressed the evidence of another officer's guilt. Zola was sued for libel and fled to England, but the effect of his letter was to blow the Dreyfus affair wide open and to expose the conspiracy behind it. Dreyfus was pardoned on the condition that he admit guilt which, as it was his only way of getting off the island, he did.

So the use of available media to protest a miscarriage of justice has ample, even noble, historical precedent. Zola used the press. The 10-part documentary Making a Murderer uses Netflix to tell the story (we're long past spoiler alerts here) of Steven Avery, scrap dealer, of Manitowoc, Wisc., who, beginning in 1985, served 18 years on a charge of rape before being exonerated. Two years after getting out he was accused and convicted of another crime, a murder, also possibly involving a rape; so now he's serving another term, this time with no prospect of release. He was clearly railroaded in the first case and many people, probably including the makers of the film, believe that he was framed again in the second.

There are obvious huge differences between the cases. Everyone knows that Dreyfus was innocent. With Avery, it's not impossible that he was both guilty and framed. Still, there are some odd parallels. After Dreyfus' conviction, a curious French officer found evidence pointing to the real traitor. The French court chose to disregard this and had the offending sleuth transferred overseas. In the Avery rape case, the Manitowoc police similarly chose to ignore suggestions from an adjoining jurisdiction pointing to the guilt of another man, a serial rapist who subsequently confessed and whose DNA testing led to Avery's exoneration. The crucial documents used to convict Dreyfus were forged by a Major Henry who, when his actions were discovered, committed suicide. Somewhat less dramatically, Ken Kratz, the district attorney who was the prosecutor in Avery's murder trial, had to resign his position five years later after complaints of online sexual harassment. His comeuppance was one of the few cheering moments in Making a Murderer, since Kratz as prosecutor had come over as both heartless and smug. His closing statement to the jury had included what may be the most extraordinary words ever uttered by a lawyer in a courtroom: "Reasonable doubts are for innocent people." It's hard to know where to start with that one.

You can't, as they say, make this stuff up; and Making a Murderer didn't have to. As well as its own interviews it had trial footage, recorded phone calls, and - most chillingly - video records of interrogations. It took the writer-producers, Laura Ricciardi and Moira Demos, 10 years to sort through and assemble the material, and no wonder. Tuning in for the first time, knowing little of the Avery story, I had assumed that episode one would deal with the rape case and episode two with the murder, and that would be that. I could hardly believe that I was in for 10 hours. John Moore in the National Post recently wrote that he thought it altogether too much, and I'll concede that they might have got through it in nine. Overall though, length was strength. This was especially true of the scenes in court, especially those of Avery's murder trial, which were hypnotic.

It's generally agreed that trials make for mesmerizing drama. Kenneth Tynan had a theory that their power derives from the witnesses on the stand having no choice

but to answer their inquisitors; they can't simply walk away from a painful or embarrassing question as one might in everyday life. "Nothing" Tynan said "is harder to write than a bad trial scene." Making a Murderer didn't even have to write a scene; it was already there, and, considered strictly as television, it was better than most madeup drama.

It worked, though, like drama. It even had the trappings. It presented itself as the most rigorous of documentaries - no narrative voice-over, the baldest of captions to keep us clear on chronology - but it indulged itself with mood music, bleak views of the rusting cars in the Avery junkyard, prolonged surveys of hopeless wintry landscapes, all very reminiscent of True Detective. Though this might have been called False Detective since much of the program's power lay in its indictment of the Manitowoc Sheriff 's Department who, with Avery suing them for millions of dollars over their mishandling

of the rape case, had every inducement to have him put away for the murder of Teresa Halbach. The evidence for the planting of evidence seemed overwhelming. Indeed one ended up rooting for Avery in part because the forces arrayed against him seemed so detestable, up to and including the judge, whose sentencing speech was as virulent towards the whitetrash Avery as the French judges were to Dreyfus the Jew. It was almost beyond belief that the same judge who had condemned Avery was allowed to preside over his appeal. As Steven himself sagely remarked, he didn't stand a chance.

Avery and his supporters got to speak directly to camera; their opponents didn't, though apparently not for want of being asked. (They then got to complain about the film-makers being biased against them.) They were still, thanks to the archive footage, vividly present: characters all. But then so was everybody who appeared. You couldn't make them up, either, though many writers and actors would surely love to. The defence lawyers, in particular, were a parade of casting director's dreams: the local lady, folksy but sharp, who was Steven's first resource on the rape charge and who declared that he wasn't smart enough to be guilty; the silky, avuncular public defender who succeeded her; the sophisticated dream team at the murder trial - clever, painstakingly decent men whose very names, Dean and Jerry, seemed to have predestined them to be a double act. (As did their statures: one short, one tall.)

Then there were Steven's parents: the defiant mother who could be a dead ringer for Ma Joad in The Grapes of Wrath, the father angry but resigned; unlike John Moore, I thought his final appearance tending his garden both moving and relevant.

There was Steven himself, perpetually baby-faced (they kept showing his baby pictures for comparison) even as the rest of him aged disturbingly; we were told he had an IQ of 70, though he always seemed remarkably logical and articulate; you may not have liked him but it was hard while watching not to believe him. (And, unlike Dreyfus, he never, on either charge, took the option of a guilty plea. Instead he immersed himself in law-books.) Even more disturbing was his nephew Brendan Dassey, a 16-year old boy, convicted as his uncle's accomplice; the two were tried separately, with the same DA presenting scenarios that cancelled one another out. We saw Brendan, educationally subnormal and with no parent or lawyer present, goaded and bewildered into making a confession - which he subsequently and repeatedly and unavailingly retracted. (When his mother, on the phone, asked him why he had told the investigators what he thought they wanted to hear, he said "that's how I do my homework." It's on tape. Like his request that, having confessed to murder, he be allowed to go home to complete a school project.) It's ironic: since interrogations have to be recorded, Brendan's questioners, coercing him into condemning himself out of his own mouth, condemned themselves out of theirs. Not that they've suffered for it.

Brendan's story must have left most viewers drained and angry; the only fictitious TV to have produced a similar effect, at least in my experience, is the abandonment of another lost boy, Randy, in the fourth season of The Wire. You can argue that it's unfair to use dramatic techniques to plead a real-life case, but I don't see it. Some of Zola's contemporaries doubtless thought he was one-sided as well; you use what resources you have and your opponents have the same option. It seems undeniable that Steven and Brendan deserve, at the least, a re-trial. Two sentences from Dean and Jerry linger most hauntingly in the mind. One, at the end of an episode, was "who better than a police officer would know how to frame someone?" The other, at the end of the series, was Dean's admission that a small part of him hoped Steven was guilty, because if he were innocent the thought of what has been visited upon him would be unbearable.

Morry Gash, The Associated Press Files / Steven Avery, the subject of the Netflix series Making a Murderer, listens to testimony in Chilton, Wis., in 2007.
2016-01-30-master-of-the-house-gaslight-:
Gaslight, by the English playwright and novelist Patrick Hamilton, is a 1939 thriller with a split personality: half fresh, half stale. Appropriately enough, it's been filmed twice; MGM, who made the second and more famous version, the one with Ingrid Bergman and Charles Boyer, apparently did their damnedest to have the earlier, British movie destroyed. They weren't successful, though their film was. It might be claimed that in their attempted ruthlessness, the Hollywood guys were merely mimicking the behaviour of their principal character.

This is a Mr. Manningham who lives with his wife in a big and luxurious house in late Victorian London; the play was a period piece, and a very effective one, even when it was new. Mr. Manningham, a smooth tyrant, is waging psychological war on Mrs. Manningham, who is timid and desperate to please. Mrs. M's mother died in an insane asylum, a fact of which Mr. M never tires of reminding her. He keeps accusing his wife of losing things, things of sentimental and practical value; in fact, he's removing them himself and hiding them. He varies the cruelty with tantalizing, not to say patronizing, shows of kindness; he promises to take her to the theatre, then withdraws the offer on the pretext that she has slipped back into her old careless ways. He further increases the pressure by varying the intensity of the gas-lamps that illuminate their home; the lady never knows when she will be plunged into semi-darkness. And, this being 19th-century London, it's foggy out.

It's perfectly possible, for most of the play's first act, to believe that the master of the house is motivated by an innate sadism, reinforced by traditional ideas of male superiority. Taken that way, the play works disturbingly well as a study of a respectable cruelty that its victim has been conditioned to accept. It turns out, however, that the gentleman has other motivations and that they are, by detective story standards, disappointingly commonplace. When he steps out, as it seems he does every evening, another man steps in. This is Inspector Rough, a retired policeman whose mind is still working on an unsolved case and who has found the clues to it in this very house. It involves that staple of stately home melodrama, missing jewellery of inestimable value. As a storyline it's perfunctory, though it takes the inspector a long time to expound it. He does succeed, though, in restoring the morale of Mrs. Manningham, who needs it.

The good in the play outweighs the bad, and the current Toronto production, which comes to us from England, is mostly excellent. Flora Montgomery gives an especially fine performance, quivering with life, as a woman delivered from an all-too-believable state of terror. We feel for her in her bewildered attempts to make sense of a senseless situation, and we root for her to escape. In a way she's a case of Stockholm Syndrome; she hasn't been kidnapped or abducted, exactly, but she has been separated from her family and she clings to her tormentor as if he were her protector. Mrs. Manningham may be trapped, but she has the theatrical advantage of being an original creation, struggling in her chains, unpredictable in her reactions. Mr. Manningham may be her jailer but he's the play's prisoner: the period's too. Owen Teale never actually twirls his moustache but he can't quite escape the stereotype of the gentleman-cad. He fills it out though with grim, sardonic presence, underplaying whenever possible; in his early sallies he might almost persuade you, as he does her, that he's acting from principle. He's snarlingly good at the end when the mask is torn off, when the gentleman vanishes and the cad remains, still trusting in his own charm. Ian McElhinney plays the oddly named Rough, who's actually rather gentle, as devoted to comforting the afflicted as to afflicting the comfortable, indeed in this performance rather more so; he lays on the whimsical charm excessively thick, playing a "character" rather than the character, and slowing the play down in the process. Both these actors are Game of Thrones regulars, and if the production is counting commercially on attracting that show's fans, then it made a good bet; on the third night, the house was packed.

The Manningham menage runs to a cook, unseen, and two maids, contrasted and highly visible, both admirably played. Victoria Lennox is the sympathetic older one, definitely in her mistress's corner; Emily Head is the flighty, flirty younger one, very much in her master's, or rather trying her best to lure him into hers. (He certainly has no objection; sexual humiliation, all but overt, is another of the crosses Mrs. Manningham has to bear.) David Woodhead has designed a handsomely menacing drawing-room set that manages to be spacious and claustrophobic at the same time. The production doesn't always sound as good as it looks; the actors are unreliably and unnecessarily miked, with distortion at the top end; when Teale, cornered, tried for a shout, all that came out the other end was a hollow boom. The director, David Gilmore, also reveals a taste for corny underscoring, as if he didn't trust the play and the actors to scare us on their own. Worst of all, he destroys the play's signature effect by accompanying the dimming of the gas with a chamber-of-horrors soundscore; the sound drowns out the sight. For compensation, though, there's Montgomery's handling of her last scene, in which the former worm turns. I have a hunch, completely unverifiable, that the author originally meant the play to end more drastically than it actually does, and that either he or his original producers got cold feet. As it is, the spectre of an alternative finale haunts the stage, the actress teasing both her stage partner and the audience, all of us squirming on tenterhooks.

Weekend Post

Gaslight runs through Feb. 28 at the Ed Mirvish Theatre.

Cylla Von Tiedemann / Owen Teale and Flora Montgomery in Gaslight. The good in the play outweighs the bad, and the current Toronto production, which comes to us from England, is mostly excellent.
2016-02-06-small-room-big-impact-groundl:
The new Groundling Theatre Company makes its bow with the best Shakespeare I've seen in Toronto. That isn't quite as bold a statement as it may seem. We mostly see the plays here in open air stagings, where interpretations tend to be half-baked and performances underpowered. Indoors theres Soulpepper, which has the acting strength but whose excursions into Shakespeare have been infrequent and uneven. The Groundlings production of The Winter's Tale has a cast of Stratford notables, with a sprinkling from the Shaw, all of them in the confined 100-seat space of the Coal Mine Theatre, acting at full exhilarating throttle, It's a pressure-cooker effect; the surroundings are spartan, but the experience is luxurious.

Graham Abbey, company founder and debutant director, though a (youngish) Stratford acting veteran on his own account, has mounted a production thats sensitive and intelligent with a few fascinating flourishes. It proves once again that good acting is contagious. Start, as the production unexpectedly does, with Tom McCamus Sicilian King Leontes caught, in an unassertively modern-dress staging, watching home movies of the happiest times of his life, the ones spent frolicking with his wife and young son before his jealousy destroyed everything. We then realize that we're seeing him after he's been deprived of both of them, enduring his 16-year penance in what would normally be the last part of the play. So in this production the bulk of the action becomes a flashback.

The new opening isnt especially deep but its arresting, and it pays emotional dividends. Seeing the young Prince Mamillius (Callum McAlister, a charming and accomplished 13-year-old) in cinematic close-up makes his eventual fate even more poignant than usual. It also gives McCamus the springboard for an unusually complex performance. When Paulina, his self-appointed guardian angel, reminds him yet again of his guilt, he permits himself a momentary snarl; he knows she's right, but enough already. It's a throwback to his insecurity at the beginning of the story; king he may be but he can never have the ease and grace of his queen Hermione (Michelle Giroux), or of their longtime guest and his fellow monarch Polixenes (Patrick Galligan), and the dormant knowledge eats him up. Watching the two of them bantering together, his resentment gives way to mad suspicion. We can follow all the twists of his mind, and of the dauntingly complicated verse that twists accordingly. In his domestic scenes, hes in shirt and suspenders; when he comes to accuse and arrest his wife, hes in a military jacket with medals, as if to give himself the assurance of rank. McCamus, a sometimes too easygoing actor, plays with bitter, warped lucidity and unfettered passion.

Giroux's Hermione matches him in power; her pride and hurt when brought to trial are superb. Lucy Peacock's Paulina is a thoroughly human, even humorous, avenging fury; confronting him with his newborn daughter she never gives an inch. When Leontes resistance finally breaks and he falls in agony to the floor, she joins him there, attacking his grief with her own. On a tiny stage, with the audience surrounding on four sides, these actors arent playing their emotions any smaller than they would at Stratford, but they never seem exaggerated either. For them and us, the encounter feels liberating.

The play's mood notoriously shifts halfway, when it moves from Sicilia to a pastoral Bohemia; where, however, Galligan's Polixenes proves as apt a tyrant as Leontes, if for a shorter time. The young lovers roles are tricky for moderns, bred on irony: Charlie Gallant brings unusual freshness and conviction to Florizel; Sarena Parmar is a too-pert Perdita, though shes very good earlier on as the waitingwoman Emilia. As Autolycus, the singing con-artist, Brent Carver, looking remarkably like Danny Kaye, gets on shockingly intimate terms with his audience (in this space, it works) but he's actually more interesting as Antigonus, the well-meaning courtier tricked into being Leontes' accomplice. This is the only production in which Ive actually believed in his marriage to Paulina, a relationship the play only gets around to mentioning after weve met them both individually. Antigonus' famous exit, pursued by a bear," has him, as far as I could tell, playing beast and prey simultaneously, one of those ideas that register as ingenious rather than convincing. Paulina's abrupt second marriage to Camillo (a jovial Roy Lewis) is managed with unusual tact. Back among the rustics, Robert Persichini gives a very complete account of the old shepherd, both earthy and poignant; as his son the clown, Mark Crawford is excessively boisterous but still amusing and mostly believable.

Nearly all the actors double in smaller roles. To accommodate this, the text has been cut, mostly sensibly. I was surprised that a song for Autolycus and two jealous shepherdesses was set up, but not sung. More seriously, Apollos oracle has disappeared; Im not sure whether this is for economic or rationalistic reasons, but it removes a final, crucial step in Leontes' downward trajectory. What's important, though, is that the lines that remain are spoken intelligently, intelligibly, and hence excitingly. Training, experience, talent and intimacy pay off, beautifully. The final scene of resurrection and reconciliation works its accustomed magic, but the whole performance had us primed for tears. It isnt all sweetness, even at the end. From where I sat, Hermiones forgiveness of her husband looked far from certain. I'm not sure I approve, but I was certainly intrigued.

The Winter's Tale runs through Feb. 20 at the Coal Mine Theatre.

Michael Cooper / Tom McCamus plays Sicilian king Leontes with bitter, warped lucidity and unfettered passion, while Lucy Peacock's Paulina is a thoroughly human, even humorous, avenging fury.
2016-02-17-the-importance-of-being-angry:
If you are a man named Ernest, you may be best advised not to marry a woman named Ernestine. And vice, of course, versa. It's probably advisable too to get to know your partner a bit before tying the knot and moving into a basement flat with no windows, a temperamental furnace, and only a drawbridge to connect you to the outside world. Oh, you may start out thinking you adore your home and your partner and calling the latter sweetie all the time, but your delight will dissipate, to be replaced by what was always there, bubbling beneath the surface: The Anger in Ernest and Ernestine.

Which is the title of the two-character play by Leah Cherniak, Robert Morgan and Martha Ross, first produced by Theatre Columbus in 1987 and since established, if not as a Canadian classic, then certainly as a Canadian standby. Its now been revived by Soulpepper as a studio (i.e. small-scale) production with Cherniak directing. It stands up well. Unfolding as much in action as in words, in accordance with the Columbus esthetic, it traces a funny and persuasively slippery slope. The downhill ride starts at breakfast, or over three successive breakfasts. Ernest, who at this stage doesnt have a job, lovingly counts out his cornflakes (in German, which is cute) while Ernestine, who has not merely a job but a career, ties herself into literal and increasingly frantic knots, trying to get ready, get dressed, get fed and get out. Raquel Duffy, struggling to fit into her heels while spraying cereal in all directions including her own, is a scream. Gregory Prest matches her in technical finesse, and is more intrinsically and endearingly comic: a matter partly of his own personality as a performer, and partly of the advantages the script hands him. He arrives catastrophically late for a marital date-night, due to the fascinating people and animals he encounters on the way home from work. (He has a job by this point, though hardly a good one.) Ernestine finds this behaviour unforgivable, and she's probably right, but the audience gets to hear Ernest's own description of the events and its charming. Anyhow, the way their argument develops, their common determination to make the worst of a bad situation is most acutely written and performed.

Theres one scene in which the two unite, to write an exaggeratedly angry letter in the wake of a traffic accident. One can see the point - that they're channelling their mutual resentment into an attack on a third party - but it's the wrong kind of grotesque and it feels like a roadblock. So, even more, does the presence of an intermission, stopping the flow and making the second half feel repetitious. Still, its an entertaining and uncomfortably believable tale, expertly told. Shannon Lea Doyles set is excellent, a room you can't wait to get out of.

Gregory Prest might someday make a good Cyrano de Bergerac: an idea prompted

by Soulpepper's other new studio show, Cowboy Versus Samurai. This is a 10-year-old play by an American writer, Michael Golamco, avowedly based on the classic tale of the long-nosed cavalier-poet, hopelessly in love with a beautiful woman and finding painful solace in furnishing a handsome rival with the words to win her heart. This new version takes us to the town of Breakneck, Wyoming: initial population 1,000, initial Asian population two. The two are Travis, an English teacher of Korean heritage, and Chester, whose adoptive parents never bothered to ask just where he was from and who therefore casts himself as an all-purpose Asian and very militant about it. A newcomer arrives in town and at school: Veronica, another teacher, also Korean but with a history of dating only white men. Travis, attracted but feeling racially as opposed to nasally disqualified, compensates by ghostwriting flowery letters for the man she really fancies, a parttime PE teacher named Del. This does not convince. In the original Cyrano, the lovemaking never got much beyond serenading under balconies, so the subterfuge was credible. But, this being the 21st century, Veronica and Del actually move in together, so its impossible she wouldnt notice. (And why would he be writing her all those letters anyway? They see each other every day.) Beyond this, the play is fatally split between being a study of a self-defeating love and a piece about race; sometimes the subjects seem to synchronize, but mostly they swim past one another. The race part yields the best or at least the funniest writing: Chester the firebrand is an all-purpose revolutionary, appropriating tropes equally from black power and the KKK (substitute yellow for white, he says of the latter, and it's the same speech). He has a very nice line in chastising Travis for his accommodating tendencies. ("You're like a Chinese waiter offering them a fork".) Miqelon Rodriguez makes the most of these opportunities, though he remains a cartoon figure in a play that aspires to be real.

Ins Chois production also boasts a first-rate performance from TJ Riley as Del, the sheepish tough guy, as far removed from a real cowboy as Travis from a real samurai. (The title is a real reach.) Jonathan Tan, charged as Travis with tying the threads together, makes a sympathetic job of it, best when watchfully reacting to everyone elses extravagances. The evening's most significant lack is that it can't make us care who Veronica (Rosie Simon) ends up with or why. That's a shame: the Cyrano story is the heartbreaker and/or tear-jerker of all time, and anyone who sees it must have yearned to see it furnished. somehow, with a happy ending. Here it's all attitudes struck, not feelings felt.

The Anger in Ernest and Ernestine and Cowboy Versus Samurai are in repertory at the Young Centre in Toronto through Feb. 20.

Cylla Von Tiedemann, Soulpepper / Raquel Duffy and Gregory Prest in The Anger in Ernest and Ernestine at Soulpepper in Toronto
2016-02-20-to-the-chef-condiments:
THEATRE REVIEW

Mustard Tarragon Theatre

At the Tarragon Theatre, a play called Mustard. My condiments to the chef.

The title denotes a character clad mostly and appropriately in yellow, with a jester's cap on top. He's the imaginary friend of a girl called Thai, and he's stuck around much longer than children's imaginary friends usually do, in plays or in life. Thai is 16, and still talks to him. So, as Kat Sandler's play progresses, does Thai's mother Sadie, whose husband walked out a year ago, leaving Sadie a pill-popping alcoholic. Thai and Sadie fight a lot, with words, and Thai is violent in other ways; she has a track-record of attacking her schoolmates and leaving them with, we are told, bloodied faces. Both ladies could use a friend, and for the time being Mustard is the one they could use.

He needs them too. Unlike any other imaginary friend in fiction, Mustard isn't all that imaginary. He isn't exactly human either. He belongs to a species called boons: as in, presumably "boon companion" or "a boon and a blessing." Boons are subject to rules, and Mustard has broken them by long outstaying what was meant to be his welcome. Two other boons are dispatched to drag him, kicking and literally screaming, from his refuge under Thai's bed to the place where all superannuated boons go, the Boon Hollows. (The author, who's pretty hot on wordplay, has heroically refrained from calling it the Boon Docks.)

The play, under Ashlie Corcoran's direction, unfolds on three unevenly distributed levels. The most successful is the most realistic, or shall we say the most domesticated: the feuding of the mother and daughter who would love to love one another but keep falling back on reciprocal resentment, pumped by the conflicted feelings they still have for their errant husband and father. Rebecca Liddiard burns through Thai's teenage rage while mostly maintaining our sympathy and, remarkably, never exhausting our patience; she's uncompromising and she's lost. Paolo Santalucia is charming and funny as the older man (by four years) who gets her pregnant and who's last seen with the bloodiest countenance she has yet inflicted; this doesn't necessarily mean their relationship is over. As Sadie, Sarah Dodd is glorious, her face a conduit of deep desolation that blossoms into nervy incredulity when she meets her Mr. Mustard (who isn't mean), and into wondrous joy as their relationship ripens and he invites her to go on a date: her first in years, his first ever. She never quite believes it's happening, but she goes for it anyway, happy to be bemused.

Mustard himself is caught, not just between two worlds but between two styles. He's meant to appeal to our feelings but he can't, because we don't believe in him. He's broken the rules of his fictional species, and the play, try though it might, can't invent a new system to supplant the old one, the one in which imaginary friends stay imaginary. What he does appeal to is our sense of humour; he's well-meaning and observant, and he has an inquiring wit. He's delightfully played by Anand Rajaram who, having charmingly shown us all these aspects, shows us some different ones in a brilliantly conceived near-final scene in which the author keeps us guessing while the actor keeps everybody hopping. Rajaram almost has us believing that the play has done what it needs and aspires to do: created its own mythology. When we get to the third level, though, it's clear that what we're getting is not new myth but old whimsy. Whenever the two boon-catchers appear, the heart sinks: partly in sympathy with Mustard, their destined prey, but mainly because as a duo, despite being perfectly decently acted, they feel so tired. One of them (Tony Nappo) is rough, the other (Julian Richings) smooth: like the pairs of cross-talking hitmen who recur in Harold Pinter's plays. They also have a strain of anxious pedantry, being much given to wondering whether certain words are actually one word or two. It seems to be a concern common to boons, as Mustard himself is ahead of them, pondering at his first appearance whether it's "for ever" or "forever." (No blame to him: it could be either.) The tic gets more creative when, told to "begone" he asks, very reasonably, "where should I bego?" The fizziest and deepest exchange, though, comes when he tells Sadie that "saying something makes it real" and she, with the bruised and tender wisdom of humanity, corrects him with "it's true - for the moment." That's Sandler's writing at its best, describing itself.

Mustard runs through March 13 at the Tarragon Extra Space

Cylla Von Tiedemann / Mustard, left, isn't all that imaginary. He isn't exactly human either. He belongs to a species called boons.
2016-02-27-a-tale-of-two-edies-this-retu:
So, there's Big Edie and theres Little Edie, mother and daughter. They live in Grey Gardens, a big house in the Hamptons. We first meet them in 1941 when Big Edie, full name Edith Bouvier Beale, is supposedly throwing a party to celebrate Little Edies engagement to Joe Kennedy Jr.: yes, one of those Kennedys. Also on hand are Major Bouvier, Big Edie's disapprovingly patrician father, and two little Bouviers, the future Lee Radziwill and Jackie Onassis. Jackie, of course, will pause on the way to marry her own Kennedy, which is more than Little Edie manages to do. A telegram arrives for her from her father Mr. Beale, announcing his imminent divorce from Big Edie. Little Edie commits the cardinal social error of reading it out loud to the assembled company, resulting in a scandalized Joe breaking off the engagement. Or rather, she sings it out loud, because this is Grey Gardens, the musical.

It was an esteemed show, if not quite a hit, on Broadway 10 years ago and has been brought to us now by Acting Up Stage, as the latest in its series of praiseworthy musical reclamations. It's an intelligent show, given an accomplished production, but it doesnt add up. Its avowed source is the celebrated documentary film by the Maysles brothers; there has also been an excellent made-for-TV movie with Jessica Lange and Drew Barrymore as the Edies. Their story has a built-in musical component: Big Edie was briefly a professional singer, and shes now a more than enthusiastic amateur, with a resident accompanist-cum-gigolo. For her daughter's engagement she has planned a program of nine songs though, when Little Edie complains of being upstaged, she graciously consents to reduce it to eight. She still contrives to sabotage the engagement, or so Little Edie believes. She has her own performing ambitions, and she storms off to New York to follow her dream. End of Act One.

Act Two takes place 32 years later. Big Edie, if not actually bedridden, never gets up. Little Edie, her career having failed to materialize, has returned to look after her though, by Big Edie's account, not nearly well enough. Grey Gardens is now a dump, overrun with garbage and cats; and the two Edies fight like felines themselves, each accusing the other of bad life-choices, especially regarding men and money. Doug Wright wrote the book, Scott Frankel the music, and Michael Korie the lyrics. The shows two halves are very different, obviously by design. Act One is full of bustle and upper-crust infighting; it plays like High Society with teeth. As in any conventional musical, everybody gets a number. In Act Two, as befits their shared solitude, only the Edies sing, except in one sequence thats Big Edie's fantasy. (It's a hallelujah thing, involving Norman Vincent Peale.) The problem with this is that Act Two makes Act One seem irrelevant; indeed even when its going on it feels curiously weightless. We dont care about these people. They're more intriguing in Act Two, but even this lacks forward motion. The mainspring of the action is the civic threat, spearheaded by an offstage Jackie O, to get Grey Gardens cleaned up, but there's never any dramatic urgency about it. (There was in the films, both of them.) Despite the title, and despite evocative sets (by Camellia Koo) and lighting (Bonnie Beecher), the house itself never seems much of a presence. At the end of the show Little Edie packs her bags again, but this time she cant leave. She and her mother are locked together. Its the Samuel Beckett musical.

The Big Edie of Act One and the Little Edie of Act Two are about the same 40-ish age, and they're both played by the same actress. This provides the opportunity for a star turn, but it makes it impossible to believe that the two Little Edies are the same person, which rather destroys the point of the story. Lisa Horner does the double here. She's efficiently brash in the first half and splendidly barbed and inward in the more interesting second. As a singer she deals beautifully with the two best songs in the score: the haunting Will You? (as Big) and the plaintive Another Winter in a Summer Town (as Little). Theres another intended show-stopper in The Revolutionary Costume for Today in which Little Edie, dressed as a sort of counter-culture nun, greets the 1970s; but she blares it, obscuring the words. Add Ann Hodges production to the list of shows, musicals especially, that have failed to conquer the Berkeley Street acoustics. Amplification means, perversely, that the orchestra drowns out the loud singers but not the quiet ones.

Nicola Lipman plays the older Big Edie with consummate crabbiness; Lisa Guloien does the younger little one with spirit. Jeff Lillico is a standout in two roles: the weak-willed Joe of the first act, victim of his family's expectations, and Jerry, a handy young fellow whom Big Edie virtually adopts because he really appreciates her sweetcorn. (As Little Edie tartly comments, he knows on which side it's buttered. Or, actually, margarined.) Of the rest, Matthew Brown makes a strong quiet impression as two generations of black retainer; he's especially good when registering pained disapproval of a Southern-fried rave-up called Hominy Grits. The song proves that the authors can do old-fashioned musical numbers; others show that they can write newfangled psychological ones too. What they haven't done is make one kind balance and illuminate the other.

Weekend Post robert.cushman@hotmail.com

Grey Gardens runs through March 6 at the Berkeley Street Theatre.

Racheal Mccaig Photography / Lisa Horner, middle, plays the Big Edie of Act One and the Little Edie of Act Two; / she is efficiently brash in the first half, and splendidly barbed and inward in the more interesting second.
2016-03-07-a-beguiling-salt-water-moon-p:
The Factory Theatre's Naked  season ("Canadian Classics Reimagined") has so far been a matter of passing off economic necessity as aesthetic choice. Ravi Jains production of Salt-Water Moon is a departure; its the first on the list to turn bare-bones staging, ingeniously and imaginatively, into a style.

David French's play - premiered in 1984, set in 1925 - has two characters. Jain's version gives it three. This may seem a paradoxical kind of economy but it works. We have Mayko Nguyen as Mary Snow, young small-town Newfoundland lady currently in domestic service, and Kawa Ada as Jacob Mercer, her former lover who returns from a stay in Toronto to woo her for keeps. But there is another person on stage with them: Ania Soul, billed in the program as "Musician." She sings and plays songs appropriate to the time and place. Now, these are all very nice atmospherically, but whats more important is that she reads or recites the plays original stage directions. These give meticulous descriptions of the play's picket-fenced waterside locale and of the clothes its people are wearing: descriptions that are in flagrant and sometimes amusing contradiction of what we see. The scenic details on which the author was so insistent are gone, replaced by an array of candles that Mary spreads around the floor as the action gets started. Her mandated yellow dress has given way to sweater and jeans; Jacob wears the same actor's uniform. Later on our narrator will describe actions that the performers never actually perform. In this context non-traditional casting is a non-issue. Both actors are ethnically unconventional choices for their roles but in this productions neutral convention, as if we had dropped in on a rehearsal, it doesnt matter either way.

Thanks to those candles the production, with no designer credited, is visually beguiling, as befits a play about a moonlit courtship: one in which the lunar references point the contrast between the practical woman and the fanciful man. In Jacob's absence Mary has got herself engaged to a suitor with more eligible prospects: one, moreover, against whom Jacob has a portfolio of grudges, some related to the still-recent war. Mary is an orphan who needs to look out for herself and still more for her younger sister, currently immured in a brutal-sounding institution. All Jacob has to offer are charm, a love that we presume to be both real and reciprocated, an ambiguous touch of urban glamour, and - most importantly for the play's purposes - the gift of the gab. Here, though, the production and the performances fall down. Both actors are proven talents, possessed of magnetism and range. Ada has a remarkable capacity for compelling attention by simply occupying space; his smile doesnt hurt either. But his actual lines, especially in the earlier parts of the play, come out here in a fast monotone. Responding to them, Nguyen protests rather too much. Neither actor is attempting a Newfoundland accent, and this could be damaging. The rhythms are not perhaps as important as the similar ones in an Irish play (try reading a line of Synge or OCasey without falling into the brogue) but they still add flavour. Its absence makes this revival less effective than the one at Soulpepper a few years ago. That had a more conventional setting but also, frankly, a more effective one. The play isn't a timeless masterpiece; it needs its scenic context. It also needs, or at least benefits from, its wider dramatic context. The Soulpepper production was part of a Mercer family cycle; we had already seen Leaving Home, a play written earlier but set much later, in which French introduced us to Jacob and Mary as a fractious older married couple, uprooted and living in Toronto. It made Salt-Water Moon, and especially its ending, more pungently bittersweet.

On its own terms, though, that ending in the Factory production is magically done. Jain's staging unmoors it from the rest of the play, brings it closer to us (literally). Thus exposed, Ada and Nguyen find their best form, he spinning rhapsodically between truth and fantasy, whichever he thinks will charm and impress her the most at any given moment, and perhaps unsure himself of which is which; she giving in with full consciousness of what shes doing, with no illusions about his illusions, and getting a firm and funny last word. They end happy, at least for the moment, and so do we.
