2016-03-16-culture-clash-a-personal-play:
'I still have an excellent memory," says Edouard Beauchemin, exquisitely played by R.H. Thomson, in a tone that's half-bluster, half-regret, and all pride. It's the opening line of You Will Remember Me, so the irony and pathos of Francois Archambault's play hits you from the start. Edouard, a retired history professor, is in the early stages of Alzheimer's and knows it. He does indeed have impeccable recall of his academic subject: mostly war, according to his wife Madeleine, who is standing supportively beside him with what we take at this point to be tart affection. What he can't remember, as she rather less supportively announces, is what he had for breakfast that morning.

The two off them are appearing on the only Quebec TV show of which Edouard still approves. Before his illness, he had been, we gather, quite the media personality. He despairs of present-day culture in general and of the internet and social media in particular, perhaps because they are so relentlessly present, so cut off from the past, so disdainful or oblivious of tradition. He could be right, he could be wrong. It's notable that by the end of the play Facebook will have helped destroy his marriage while YouTube will have allowed him to share his last message with the world - which, judging by the number of hits it gets, is more than willing to receive it. Not that Edouard will know, or remember.

You Will Remember Me was staged, in French, in 2014. It reaches Toronto, translated by Bobby Theodore and directed by Joel Greenberg, in a co-production by the Tarragon and Studio 180. It is, in varying degrees, a personal play, a family play and a political play. Madeleine, desperate for a break, deposits Edouard with their daughter Isabelle, a TV news reporter who declines the responsibility as she's off to cover a flood disaster whose victims, clinging to their own memories, she describes as crybabies off-camera. Patrick, Isabelle's live-in boyfriend, volunteers to pitch in, and the two men seem to get on well, even if Edouard can never remember Patrick's name or what it is he does for a living - though whatever it is or was, he isn't doing it now and is staying home pleading burnout. Nor is he above taking off for a night with his poker buddies, consigning Edouard to the care of his own daughter, Berenice. How many levels of separation is that?

Berenice, being teenaged and techno-addicted, is everything Edouard distrusts, while she regards him as a fossil. She's especially impatient of his nostalgia for the passions of 1980 and the referendum: living history for him, pre-history for her. Actually, it's hard not to sympathize with her. Even set in a province where memory is a fetish, the play doesn't work hard enough to establish its political dimension. Though it makes a better job of it than Michel Tremblay's Hosanna, whose two characters were said to stand for opposite sides of the Quebecois identity, on no dramatic evidence whatever. However, a bond develops between Edouard and Berenice: She reminds him of someone, and of a long-buried family secret.

The trouble with this, dramatically, is that it is buried and then abruptly disinterred. We are given few details about it, especially no clues as to how it affected Edouard's wife and daughter; and the actresses are given no chance to show us. The play is all Edouard, and the other characters only come to life in relation to him. Fortunately, he's a rich creation: selfish, obviously, and a habitual seducer of his students (or is that just what he'd like us to believe?), but witty and inquiring and with a darkly humorous awareness of his own decline. He is never, it seems, self-pitying. Thomson's performance has a craggy edge and a quicksilver centre; he gives you a perfect sense of the man's mind working, all the harder against odds. Even without an accent, there are fast French rhythms - French public-intellectual rhythms - in his speech. With the set of his hair and chin and glasses, he even looks Quebecois. His wife's decision to leave him, though it may work for her, is tough on the audience, depriving it of the pleasure of Nancy Palk's company, which is considerable. As daughter Isabelle, Kimwun Perehinec is stuck on a single aggrieved note, but Mark McGrinder is shiftily likeable as her partner, notably when spinning Edouard a yarn about being an astronaut. (Why not? He won't remember.) Michela Cannon's Berenice gets finer as Berenice herself gets gentler, or rather as her firmness takes the shape of empathizing with Edouard rather then dismissing him. This makes for the play's last and most beautiful movement: an unsentimental sense of youth inheriting from age, of raging against the dying of the light while doing something, however incomplete, to preserve its memory. It's the first new play in a long time to occasion honest tears.

You Will Remember Me runs at the Tarragon theatre in Toronto until April 10.
2016-03-31-brave-but-foolhardy-spanish-p:
The wedding in Blood Wedding is cursed before it happens, and the play makes no secret of it. The bride still has passionate feelings for an old flame, and he for her despite his having married somebody else. Even before all this, the families of the groom and his hovering rival were engaged in a bloodfeud, and the grooms mother cannot let go of the fact. Even as she strives to be an accepting mother-in-law, her thoughts and her words keep reverting to the knives that took the lives of most of her male relatives.

It all sounds very Latin, and Blood Wedding is indeed the work - maybe the best-known work though the all-female House of Bernarda Alba seems to get done more often - of the Spanish poet and playwright Federico Garcia Lorca, killed by Francos men in 1936, three years after this play was written.

Soulpepper's revival, though, re-locates it in Ontario farm-country. At least, I think it does; the publicity promised it, though the program-notes go on, rightly, about how Spanish the play is. There are no specific Canadian references in Guillermo Verdecchia's script, but the costumes have a local cut and so does the onstage band that comments on the action and sometimes seems to be substituting for it. At the wedding party itself the brides father (Oliver Dennis), hitherto a rather dour individual, surprises us all by getting up on the stand and exhorting everyone in song to Raise a Ruckus. You cant get more down-home than that.

There's something patronizing, to both parties, in the idea that audiences can only respond to a play if it's set in their own backyard. Still, the change of locale is a symptom, rather than the cause, of the failings in Erin Brandenburgs production. In fact, Verdecchias translation, stark in syntax but flowery in image, would probably work perfectly well if the play was still set in Spain. But there seems to be a conspiracy, probably unconscious, to lower the temperature. Diane D'Aquila's vengeful mother has the most commanding performance, the vengeance festering in her heart and on her lips in a society that gives her no scope for action; but she keeps having to switch tones, from Spanish fury to Canadian gossip.

Few of the others even try to reach her level. The prenuptial chat between the bride (Hailey Gillis) and her maid (Caroline Gillis) is just giggly. Theres no heat, indeed no connection, between the young lady and Leonardo (Colin Palangio), the lover who abducts her: they just stand around, speaking lines. Leonardo is the only character to whom Lorca gave a name, though here its been shortened to Leon, which doesn't have quite the same ring: indeed no ring at all. That's important, because the name is meant to reverberate, to send shivers through the community. Gordon Hecht starts off well as the groom, stolid and shy (his opening scene with DAquila is excellent, raising hopes for the production that are to remain unfulfilled) but when he has to turn avenger, he too seems merely to be going through the motions. When the text turns unavoidably formal, as when the wedding guests line up to offer lyrical salutations, the actors scamper dutifully through the lines, apparently hoping to be rid of them as quickly as possible.

To do Blood Wedding at all is brave; to do it in Toronto at this moment may be foolhardy. A production courts comparison with the admirable one mounted last year by the Modern Times and Aluna companies. That production, without going aggressively flamenco on us, had a style and a tone, the sense of a world different from ours but relatable. It had what this staging lacks: inevitability. The story had strength and purpose; here it seems thin and rather pointless. The fatal meeting of husband and lover is lost in the forest, literally; you cant see the actors for the trees.

In Soheil Parsa's production the hoofbeats of Leonardo's horse, a constant presence in the communitys consciousness, were a resonant recurring aural presence; in this one theyre just an isolated sound effect. The force and grace of Parsa's staging took us effortlessly through the play's trickiest transition: the appearance of two symbolic figures, the Moon and Death, to preside over the final mayhem.

In Soulpeppers production Andrew Penner, the lead musician, speaks the Moons lines; he does them decently but I doubt if anyone unfamiliar with the play would know who or what he was meant to be. Death becomes a cackling beggar-woman looking and sounding like one of those pantomime crones who, when someone is nice to them, turn out to be fairy godmothers, though this one definitely doesn't. D'Aquila plays this role too, before reverting in the last scene to bereaved mother, now more bereaved than ever. The production seems to intend her as the central figure, and there's a good case for that; the play begins and ends with her, and she embodies all the traditions of her world, good and bad. But here there's no world.

2016-04-06-the-illusion-of-foreign-intel:
You could hardly wish for a more exciting opening scene than the one that kicks off Chimerica, by the British playwright Lucy Kirkwood. It's 1989, and we are in a hotel room in Beijing, overlooking Tiananmen Square. It's the last gasp of the protests, crushed by the Chinese government troops. In the room is Joe Schofield, a rookie American photojournalist on his first major assignment. His editor is on the line from New York, beseeching him to get the hell out, and hes about to, but his attention is caught by a scene below: a man carrying shopping-bags standing in front of an oncoming tank, which doesnt mow him down. Joe takes the famous Tank Man photo. And then the police burst in.

Presumably, Joe (a fictional character) escapes unharmed and unbanned, since we now flash forward twenty-three years to find him flying back to Beijing on another story. The play will continue to alternate between past and present, and also between China and America: hence its portmanteau title, which also invokes the word "chimera," meaning illusion.

Chris Abraham's production - by Canadian Stage out of the Manitoba Theatre Centre - follows its thrilling prologue with equally resourceful handling of the constant, hectic transitions; Judith Bowden's rotating set, Deco Dawsons video design, Michael Waltons lighting and Thomas Ryder Payne's sound are all top-notch. They work seamlessly together, to create the impression that something really momentous is happening. In the broadest strokes, something is. The play contrasts a China, making huge economic strides while remaining repressive, with an America - well, I'm not sure what its saying about America, other that its in a state of uncertainty while being in economic thrall to a country it used to despise. The U.S. scenes all take place in the election year of 2012.

However, it's in human detail that the play falls apart. The story hinges on the friendship between Joe and his Chinese contact Zhang Lin, who as a student was one of the Tiananmen rebels and is now an English teacher, living alone and widowed; his wife was one of those massacred and her memory, physically evoked, still haunts him. Lin leads Joe to believe that the Tank Man, to whose image Joe owes his professional success, may be alive and possibly well and probably living in New York. This in turn leads to a succession of the kind of scenes in which a self-anointed sleuth goes from one seedy location to another, asking questions, proffering cash, and being sent somewhere else.

These scenes, and the ones in newspaper offices, are presented in the selfconscious tough-guy mode common to plays about journalists, especially when a British writer is trying to sound American. Joe himself is a puppet, there to push the story along; Evan Buliung does this with commendable urgency, adding a nervous sensitivity beyond what's furnished in the writing. Joe doesnt really have a character; he has issues, but these feel pasted on - hes egotistical, doesn't want children, but does want an English marketing consultant, who seems to be there because this is a play and there has to be a love-interest. Laura Condolln plays this functional character with skilled conscientiousness, and makes the most of the play's best American scene, in which she lets down her professional guard and warns her corporate clients against reducing the population of China to power-point stereotypes.

The scenes in China support her case; they can be repetitive, but theyre subtler and more affecting than the western ones. Zhang Lin has sunk into post-activist torpor, but he rouses himself to post a quickly-deleted email about Beijings levels of smog. It's enough; he's hauled in for correction and confession. Paul Sun-Hyung Lees performance is alight with mournful irony; his sad eyes, as he remembers and imagines his lost wife, are a spectacle to rival any of the productions technical wonders. All this performance has in common with the one he gave in Kim's Convenience is its sheer presence. He has a fine foil here in Richard Lee as Lin's practical businessman brother Zhang Wei, who has made philosophical peace with the regime and wonders why Lin cannot do the same.

Otherwise, the cliches in the writing infect the supporting performances, of which several are mediocre and a couple downright dreadful. The play does come together, somewhat, in its last scene. Joe, semipenitent after ruining several lives, is having an exhibition of his work. Among the visitors is Zhang Weis son Benny (Norman Yeung), a Harvard student with no desire to return home. He seems to be getting the best of both worlds, or maybe the worst. He brings a message from his uncle Lin, one bearing a revelation about the Tank Man, whose picture is, of course, the exhibitions centrepiece. It's the second revelation we've heard; the first was a legitimate shocker, genuinely thoughtprovoking. This new one is very neat, and momentarily effective. And then you start wondering why Zhang Lin kept it a secret all this time and realize its just because if he hadnt, there wouldn't be a play.

Chimerica runs until April 17 at the Bluma Appel Theatre in Toronto.

Dylan Hewlett / It's 1989, and we are in a hotel room in Beijing, overlooking Tiananmen Square. It's the last gasp of the protests, crushed by the Chinese government troops.; Dylan Hewlett / Evan Buliung and Laura Condolln co-star in "Chimerica", preformed at RMTC in Winnipeg.
2016-04-11-the-3-tv-program-that-bypasse:
Three dollars for the best writing and acting on television strikes me as a steal. Let me explain. Im hooked on Horace and Pete, a series that can be downloaded from American comedian Louis C.K.s website, and is not available legally in any other way. So far there have been 10 episodes, released at weekly intervals, offering great bingewatching for the foreseeable future. C.K. (I hate referring to him that way, but it's his choice of surname) writes and directs, and is also one of its stars. He charges a premium $5 for the first show, a loss-leading $2 for the second and $3 for all subsequent episodes. (Well, all right, they're U.S. dollars. But still.)

This method of bypassing the traditional distributors - network, cable, even Netflix - isnt completely unprecedented (this type of thing is becoming the norm in the music business), but I cant think of any drama or comedy - Horace and Pete is both - undertaken in this way and on this scale, which has been released exclusively on the web. And compared with the $50 The Screening Room proposes to charge for the privilege of watching movies at home on the day they come out, C.K.'s product is a bargain. It also, in contrast to schemes inveigling us into watching big films on small screens, has the esthetic advantage of being beamed to the medium for which it was intended.

C.K.'s high profile enabled his show to keep a low one. The first anyone knew that Horace and Pete existed was when the first episode, or the invitation to buy it, cropped up on the site. He had enough followers for word to spread, and it has.

Its cheering to see a new way of delivering content, without the middleman, taking off. C.K. financed the show himself. Im not sure if that makes him the Donald Trump of independent production, but it would be pleasingly ironic if it did, as C.K., on that same website, has posted one of the most passionately persuasive anti-Trump pieces I have ever read. (It takes a comedian to know a comedian?) The most heartening thing of all is that Horace and Pete justifies its independence. It's its own animal, unlike anything else on TV (I guess it counts as TV). Its tone is both too leisurely and too outrageous for the networks; its visual style is too basic for cable.

It's set in a Brooklyn bar called Horace and Petes, founded exactly 100 years ago by a couple of brothers called Horace and Pete. That Horace had a son called Horace, that Pete had a son called Pete, and so it has gone, through the generations, both the names and the ownership of the bar. Theres a tradition in American drama of presenting the barroom as a reflector of the national mood: hopeful or, as in this case, fractured.

C.K. himself plays the current Horace, Steve Buscemi is the current Pete and Alan Alda, in a show-stealing performance, is their uncle, wonderfully identified as "the previous Pete," a foul-mouthed and cantankerous old bigot who occasionally says something disconcertingly sensible. Edie Falco, America's greatest actress, plays Sylvia, the proprietors' sister, and Jessica Lange is Marsha, their late fathers final girlfriend, or, as Sylvia graphically puts it, his last pleasure-chest. That, anyway, is the family set-up at the start; some surprise skeletons have been rattled since, but I wouldnt want to spoil them for you.

C.K.'s control over both content and distribution is something that Orson Welles would have killed for and that even Woody Allen, as an actor-writerdirector still dependent on studios and outside finance, might envy. C.K. isn't bound by time slots or the conventional television structure. His first two episodes each run for over an hour; most subsequent ones are about half that. In some - but not all - theres a break in the action and a caption appears saying, "Intermission." Episode five concluded with the message: End of Act One. C.K., it seems, goes where he pleases.

What this suggests is that, where most TV aspires to the condition of film, Horace and Pete sees itself as a play. And this is how its written, staged and performed: in extended dialogue sequences that may be duets, trios or ensembles. In television terms, this is so oldfashioned as to be revolutionary - a throwback to how sitcoms used to be shot, minus the audience and the laugh-track. Often the camera will pull back and let us see the actors, as in a theatre, in equal opportunity long-shot; it sometimes looks clunky, but it gives a sense, unusual in TV, of the spatial relationships between characters, which is especially rewarding when they're as vividly portrayed as these are. And it lets us see the whole bar.

Mostly it's the bar in the afternoon. The customers are what C.K., when interviewed by Jimmy Kimmel (the networks do have their uses), has described as "day drinkers:" the hard core. Two other comedians play regulars. Steven Wright, taciturn and morose, brings his own coaster, which is a statement in itself. Kurt Metzger is a contrastingly voluble patron whose profane gloss on the biblical story of Sodom and Gomorrah is the shows most sustained comic cadenza. Hes also, in his own way, political. He has persuaded a conservative and a liberal that, if they actually listened to one another's principles, they would find very little to be hostile about. In a more mordant variation on the same theme, he has suggested that the ideal U.S. election outcome would be for Trump and Bernie Sanders to be co-presidents: Bernie will keep taking money from the rich people; Trump will give it back. This "will reveal the whole nature of the system." Eventually, nobody will be worth anything and they'll tear it all down.

Up-to-the minute references, invariably disenchanted, are a feature of the show, an entertaining byproduct of its fast turnover. They raise the question: does C.K. actually write a whole new show every week? If he does, its a phenomenal achievement, considering everything else hes doing. My guess, though, is that he stockpiled the bulk of the scripts, sprinkling in the topical bits at the last moment. They're nice, they're funny, but they feel like add-ons.

Most of the show isnt that funny (though when the laughs come theyre big, genuine ones). It is, however, comic.

It's comic like Chekhov is comic: the comedy of desperate people - sometimes wellmeaning, sometimes not - each trapped in an individual bubble of self-regard, itself part of a larger collective bubble. And, just as the family in Chekhov's most famous play were trying to hold on to their cherry orchard, so the family in Horace and Pete are trying to hold on to Horace and Petes. At least, some of them are.

Pete, heart-rendingly played by Buscemi, seems to be the nicest, and most of the time the gentlest, person around; he spent 10 years in a mental hospital, still has psychotic episodes when hes off his meds and has nowhere else to go. Sylvia, whose rage and pain in Falco's performance burn up the screen, wants to sell; she has cancer and desperately needs the money. Horace wavers, but he feels an overwhelming obligation to tradition - a tradition that includes selling no mixed drinks and a very limited range of beers. Pete calls him "passive aggressive" and C.K., who doesn't have his colleagues acting chops, stresses the passive (though his mode as a stand-up comic has been aggressive). His Horace goes along to get along, listening and responding, generally acting kind but sometimes cruel.

This country, says Sylvia, apparently out of nowhere but her own despair, "is going to s-t in a handcart" (her own less elegant variation of the proverbial phrase about hell and handbaskets). The grandest, darkest example of the barroom as American metaphor is Eugene ONeill's The Iceman Cometh, and Horace and Pete sometimes suggests the tight family drama of O'Neills other masterpiece, Long Days Journey into Night, superimposed on the sprawling canvas of his last-chance saloon. Except that O'Neill didn't do jokes.

Whats truly remarkable about Horace and Pete is its riveting succession of long confessional monologues, all of them delivered by the ladies of the cast - by Falco, Lange or by one of the guest females who appear on a weekly basis (Horaces exwife, for example, who turns up to tell him about her new liaison with a much older man, and to seek and disregard his advice). These speeches are so completely inhabited by the performers that one suspects them of being improvised, though it seems logistically unlikely. There are cat-and-mouse duologues, first dates or morning-after fencing matches that are almost as good. There's a cunning, and increasingly gripping, dramatic shape. Horace and Pete proves C.K. to be a great enabler of actors and a major American playwright. And he's done it in his own format and on his own dime. Not to mention his own mailing-list.

National Post robert.cushman@hotmail.com

2016-04-13-tensions-are-on-the-rise-disg:
A Manhattan couple has invited another Manhattan couple over for food and chat, and the hostess brightly announces that she has bought pork tenderloin for dinner. This might seem tactless, since her husband is a Muslim, at least by heritage, and her male guest is Jewish, but it turns out that neither of them has any objections. The Jewish guest indeed admits to a ravenous appetite for pig meat; he's making up for lost time.

Disgraced, a Pulitzer-winning first play by an American Muslim writer, Ayad Akhtar, is about a group of people trying to shake off traditions and stereotypes, and finding that it isnt that simple. At its centre is Amir Kapoor, a hard-driving corporate lawyer of Pakistani descent. Hes hoping for a partnership in the Jewishowned firm that employs him, and from the sound of things, fully deserves one.

His bosses apparently think he's Indian, hence Hindu, and one of them has made him a present of a statue of Shiva which now stands proudly in a corner of the desirable apartment where Amir lives with his WASP wife Emily. She's an artist who has found inspiration in ancient Islamic culture: ironic, since her husband is scathing about Islam and has done everything possible to distance himself from it. Emilys work has attracted the attention of an art-dealer named Isaac. Hes the Jewish man who's come to dinner, accompanied by his wife Jory, who is black and who also happens to be a colleague of Amir's.

Amir is tense when the guests arrive. At the urging of his nephew, who was born Hussein but goes by the name of Abe, he has reluctantly appeared as a character witness for an imam accused of advocating terrorism. The newspapers have exaggerated his support, and hes now in trouble at work. When conversation turns to 9/11 and then to the Middle East, Amir and Isaac, despite their avowed secularism, get nationalistically heated, Amir especially. Masks slip, the more painfully because neither man suspected he was wearing a mask.

The characters are, rather obviously, representative figures assembled as counters in an argument. An unavoidable recent comparison is Yasmina Rezas God of Carnage, another play about an exploding dinner-party. Akhtar's play is shorter on psychological detail, but has a greater impact because its issues are more substantial. In fact they're blazingly urgent.

If anything, time has made them crueller. The play, which premiered in 2013, references al-Qaida and the Taliban but not ISIL. It recalls Bruce Norris Clybourne Park in the way it booby-traps its characters and their beliefs, but without its wit and surprise, or its sophisticated structure. Though, to be fair, that plays racial tensions were strictly black and white, while Disgraced covers nearly as many ethnic waterfronts as it has characters. It also throws in an adultery angle which is completely gratuitous, except that it provides a short-cut to an outbreak of physical violence. This, if you can stand another comparison, resembles the climax of David Mamet's Oleanna, but it's less effective because it doesnt feel inevitable, and we arent as invested in the people.

For all that, Disgraced doesn't just hold attention, it grabs it. Amir may not be the most fully realized person you will ever see on a stage, but his predicament is real, and forcefully presented. How much of him is conviction and how much accommodation? How much principle and how much spite? Raoul Bhaneja plays him unsparingly well. Michael Rubenfeld's Isaac, situated somewhere between amiability and creepiness, is an admirable sparring partner. The womens roles are thinner, but Birgitte Solem and Karen Glave mine what there is. And then theres Abe, vividly played by Ali Momen, who reappears at the end, having reverted to Hussein. His path doesn't so much counter his uncle's as complement it: hes on the way to being radicalized by being marginalized. This is the most straightforward scene in the play, and the most powerful. Robert Ross Parker directs a taut production on a set, by Sue LePage, of streamlined plush.

From a newish American play to an oldish British one, revived as a vehicle for Rupert Everett, and passing through on its way to New York. The play is David Hares The Judas Kiss, which presents two moments in the life of Oscar Wilde.

In the first he's in his favourite London hotel in 1895, immediately following the first of his three trials. His friends, or some of them, urge him to escape to France before the police come for him. We know he won't, but there is a paradoxical kind of suspense in waiting for something not to happen. Wilde may be acting, or failing to act, from lassitude or self-destructiveness or loyalty to his lover Lord Alfred Douglas, aka Bosie, who wants him to stay and face his accusers down.

This first act had me wondering what all the extravagant fuss over Everetts Oscar was about. Hes much better in the second which shows us Wilde after his prison term, broken in health but not in spirit, living with Bosie in serious poverty in Naples. He spends most of this act sitting down in one place; when he gets up it's a legitimate major moment. Everett here projects a mournful perceptiveness that turns acid when, at very long last, he realizes that Lord Alfred, who had indeed kissed him in London immediately before deserting him, is his Judas.

The trouble with this is that Bosie is as unspeakable a person here as he apparently was in real life. He even claims that he, not Oscar, was the real victim: he may have been spared Reading Gaol but he suffered guilt by association, was disowned by his family, and was denied his comforts as an aristocrat and his due as a poet. History suggests that, on the last count at least, he was fooling himself.

He also, under his friend's eyes, cavorts with a beautiful fisherman, and goes out drinking and dancing with him till all hours. Love may be blind, but Wildes myopia here strains belief, or at least patience. If, as the title suggests, the play is about Oscar and Bosie, then what is the rest of it doing?

Scenes with Robbie Ross, Wildes first male lover and more-or-less faithful friend, may be intended as a counterweight, but they're either too much or not enough. If the play is intended as a portrait of Wilde, it leaves out too much, notably its subject's fabled wit. Hares dialogue is pleasingly true to period, but I only laughed once. I was touched, though, by Oscars interactions with the hotel staff: loyal and admiring, and intrigued by the hints of their off-stage lives. Supporting performances are competent; Neil Armfields's production handles timeshifts imaginatively. Both these plays have been brought to Toronto by David Mirvish, and it strikes me that Disgraced might serve equally well as a title for The Judas Kiss. Indeed, for its own play, it seems rather vague. But vaguely menacing titles, plus timeliness, may be the recipe for pulling in Pulitzers.

Disgraced runs through April 24; The Judas Kiss through May 1.

Cylla Von Tiedemann / From left, Karen Glave, Michael Rubenfeld, Raoul Bhaneja, Birgitte Solem and Ali Momen star in Disgraced, a Pulitzer-winning first play by Ayad Akhtar about a group of people trying to shake off traditions and stereotypes.
2016-04-20-the-american-family-reduced-w:
Tracy Letts became famous in 2007 as the author of August: Osage County, a long play about an American family behaving badly. It was not his first play. That had happened in 1990, when he wrote Killer Joe, a short play about an American family behaving even worse. He got it right the first time, and the Coal Mine Theatre's superb production is here to prove it. Its the best show in town.

August: Osage County was a rambling play in which the author dealt with any halt in the action by pulling yet another skeleton out of the extended family closet. Killer Joe, by contrast, is concentrated. It pursues a single story and squeezes every drop of juice out of it.

The characters in Killer Joe are mostly at the extremes of poverty, and its economic desperation as much as anything that drives them. We're in the Texas trailer home of Ansel Smith and Sharla, his second wife. Crashing back into their lives comes Chris, Ansel's son by his previous spouse. Chris owes a lot of money to drug dealers and has no hope of repaying it. But he has a scheme for raising the cash: have his mother killed and collect on the insurance. Everybody thinks this a good idea: Ansel, Sharla, and even Chriss sister Dottie who is mentally somewhat damaged, probably due to their mothers active neglect when she was a baby.

Everybody's blithe acceptance of the murder plan smacks of the kind of glib black comedy in which unspeakable things are discussed in the most casual of tones. But the play works its way past that, courtesy of its title character. Killer Joe Cooper, the man hired to do the deed, is a law-enforcement officer with a lucrative sideline as a hit-man. Asked if he ever finds himself investigating a death for which he is himself responsible, he replies that he does and that no, it isn't awkward, its convenient. Joe has a normally ironclad rule about requiring payment up front, which the Smiths of course cannot provide. But on this occasion he agrees to accept a retainer. The retainer is Dottie.

Letts is quoted in the program as having been inspired by Hollywood film noir, and the plot-line does suggest a down-market Double Indemnity. But the genre that comes most to mind is Southern Gothic: Cormac McCarthy and especially Tennessee Williams. When Joe comes to claim his collateral, he arrives for a dinner-date with Dottie, bearing flowers no less; its like a crazy-house version of the encounter between Laura and her Gentleman Caller in The Glass Menagerie. The upshot is predictably carnal; less predictable, though not altogether unexpected, is that Dottie and Joe become fond of one another. That's a complication.

So, even more, is the fact that Chris comes to regret the deal. He really loves his sister; the relationship may not be technically incestuous, since at curtain-rise Dottie is still a virgin, but it certainly has overtones. Chris wants Dottie to skip town with him. The play pivots on the contrast between Joe, immovable, and Chris, wavering. Both are terrifically embodied here. Matthew Gouveia is a brilliantly twitchy Chris, a character who starts out full-blown despicable and then gains our sympathy, maybe even our respect. Matthew Edison makes a stylish, lanky, drawling Joe, both menacing and charming, like the dark twin of the Gary Cooper whose surname he shares, surely not a coincidence.

The Smiths, by a similar token, could be an American Everyfamily reduced to its barest essentials. They are all vividly played: Vivien Endicott-Douglas' Dottie, a tough waif; Paul Fauteuxs Ansel, a vacillating husk; Madison Walshs Sharla, bold and with her own secrets that help precipitate the play's tumultuous conclusion. All the characters have to choose between love and business, and we're kept wondering which way each of them will jump.

Its funny as well as scary, and Peter Pasyks production is in total control of mood, timing and action. Steve Wilsher has arranged maybe the most ferocious stage fights I've ever seen, the scarier for happening in such confined quarters; Patrick Lavender's set makes constructive and imaginative use of every inch of space, down to the theatres own washroom. Christopher Stanton designed the sound, whose most memorable feature is the savage barking of the familys dog, kept chained, we presume, in the trailer-park outside.

If/Then is a musical, brought from Broadway, about the road you didn't take, contrasted with the one you did. In my innocence, I'd imagined that each act of the show would outline a different path, with perhaps some reconciliation at the end. In fact, though, the two strands alternate throughout the evening, which I suppose is more daring but is also confusing.

Our protagonist, Elizabeth, comes back to New York from a failed marriage in Arizona, hoping for some kind of career in urban planning. She goes to Madison Square, planning to meet up with an old, male friend and/or - the syntax is catching - a new, female one. One invites her to a protest, the other to hear some music. Which invitation she accepts will determine her future. One will lead her to a highpaying, high-flying city job, the other to teaching and a second marriage, ill-fated in a different way from her first, but with a couple of children. The same people figure in both trajectories, which makes them difficult to keep straight. We are offered a few signposts - Elizabeth is known either as Liz or Beth, she does or does not wear glasses. I was faced with my own existential problem: was my lack of interest due to my inability to follow both stories, or could I not follow them because I wasnt interested? Probably its both. The show never stays in one emotional place long enough for us to become invested in it.

The show is the work of the team who wrote Next to Normal, a show that had slightly more going for it. Tom Kitt's music is featureless contemporary wallpaper. Brian Yorkey's book has the odd sharp line, and its possible that his lyrics may as well; its hard to tell because the sound-level is pumped up into oblivion. This isn't just a mechanical thing; much of it is down to Jackie Burns who plays Liz/Beth. Whenever emotion seems indicated, which is often, she doesn't so much sing as bray. Like Idina Menzel, who created the role(s) on Broadway, she has done time in Wicked, a show that pioneered the idea that volume equals passion, especially for leading ladies. There are quieter, and thereby better, performances from Matthew Hydzik as an army medic who picks Elizabeth up, several times, and marries her; from Toronto favourite Darren A. Herbert as a boss with both professional and personal designs on her; and from Anthony Rapp as the old college chum who, given the shows structure, might be described as a bisected bisexual: hes gaily married in one plotline, the heroine's part-time lover in another.

One of the more effective numbers concerns her, and our, uncertainty as to which of these three men is in bed with her. The direction is by Michael Greif, who has been known to do better; choreography, consisting of aimless street-moves, is minimal and annoying.

Killer Joe runs through April 24 at the Coal Mine Theatre, Toronto; If/Then through May 8 at the Princess of Wales Theatre.

Photo: Coal Mine Theatre / From left, Madison Walsh, Vivian Endicott-Douglas, Matthew Gouveia and Paul Fauteux co-star in Killer Joe, a play about an American family behaving badly.

Theatre Smash, a company with a track-record of producing contemporary German plays, is billing their latest under its attractively euphonious original title of Das Ding. The actual performance, though, is in English, and the translated title of The Thing appears (in parentheses) as a helpful appendage.

So: what is the Thing of Das Ding? It's a bolt of cotton fibre, and the play belongs in that line of works - more often novels or stories than plays - that are united by an inanimate object passing from one character, or group of characters, to another.

Our first sighting of this object is as something big, flowing, bulbous, and stagefilling: solid and capacious enough for a man wearing a crown to be sitting on top of it. He turns out to be King Manoel I (died 1521) of Portugal, wearily granting an audience to Ferdinand Magellan (also died 1521), famous for discovering the Straits that bear his name, and at this moment in dire straits of his own.

He has been wounded in the royal service, and would like a new job, or a pension, or the king's support for a world-circling, tradeseeking voyage around the southernmost tip of the Americas. While he makes his case, his projected route is illustrated by clever little arrows projected onto the great big cotton ball: a delightful effect. Not that it does Magellan any good. All his requests are jovially rejected by a monarch who has had quite enough of explorers seeking handouts, even if they are subsequently vindicated by history. Nothing else in Philipp Lohle's play is as engaging as this prologue. We are thrust forward into the present, where circumnavigation has become commonplace and mainly electronic. It's a world in which those who plant cotton are still forgotten, and the fortunes of those who trade in it or make stuff from it can be equally precarious.

At first, we meet a pair of cotton-growing farmers, Siwa who is African, and Guy who's French-Canadian. Canada has replaced Germany in this production as the play's home-base, with Birgit Schreyer Duarte's translation snappy enough for the transference to be credible. Then, we're introduced to two Chinese men: Wang and Li, who manufacture and export cotton T-shirts. They also hire out janitors, though the cotton connection here is none too clear: if it's a sideline for them it's a sideshow for the play.

Back in Canada, there's Patrick, a young man - a boy, really - who has taken a photograph of his sister's bedroom that has gone viral, for reasons that are never very clear; maybe it's just meant to illustrate the randomness of social media. Patrick wears one of Wang and Li's T-shirts. He has another sister, Katherine, who's married to a man named Thomas and who, to his displeasure, has taken to exhibiting herself sexually on the Internet. One of her online admirers is Li, who crosses oceans in hopes of finding her and making her his own. Katherine and her husband wear Wang-Li Tshirts too.

All these roles are shared between five actors, who also serve as a chorus. The Thing cleverly splits apart to reveal them, reacting - always with interest, occasionally with alarm - to the various uses to which they are put. It's all very cute, or meant to be.

Drew Facey's set design, or rather Thing design, is as progressively ingenious as it's initially impressive, and the cast, under Ashlie Corcoran's direction, hurtle around the stage with great collective enthusiasm. As individuals, though, they're less effective. Naomi Wright comes off the best, as a series of international interviewers quizzing Patrick about his famous photo, hearing what they want to hear in his answers while hardly bothering to listen to them; a neat piece of cultural comment, both in writing and performance. She also gets the evening off to a good start as the suppliant Magellan, with Qasim Khan as a blithely uncaring king.

None of the other characters come to comparable life; the text gives the actors little beyond raw ideas and the actors return the compliment or lack of it. It's revue-sketch presentation but without revue-sketch wit. Commentary and captions help us keep track of where we are and whom we're dealing with; though in a play about competing cultures, ethnically-blind casting seems an idea more virtuous than helpful.

Das Ding runs through May 1 at the Berkeley Street Upstairs Theatre, Toronto.

James Heaslip / King Manoel I (died 1521) of Portugal atop Das Ding.

THEATRE REVIEW

Botticelli in the Fire /Sunday in Sodom

Up until last week I had never seen a play by Jordan Tannahill: this despite his being probably the hottest young playwright in Toronto. My fault, and also my misfortune: Tannahill, as Sandro Botticelli said of Leonardo da Vinci, is the real deal.

Well, all right, Botticelli probably didn't say that about Leonardo, at least not in those words. But he does say it in Botticelli in the Fire, the first in a double bill of plays by Tannahill, presented by Canadian Stage. Leonardo figures here as Botticellis apprentice, much admired by his master for his speed and dexterity in mixing paints, and also as his lover. Botticelli himself, riding high as Florences master painter of the late 15th century, is at work on his masterpiece The Birth of Venus.

In Tannahill's telling, the model for this painting was Clarice, wife of Lorenzo de Medici, Duke of Florence and source of all power and patronage. She's also Botticellis mistress, he being omnivorously omnisexual. This is a dangerous game for the painter to be playing, a point driven graphically home by a scene in which he and Lorenzo meet up for a round of squash; the ruler scores effortlessly while the artist gets winded.

This, you will have noticed, is a play that goes in wholeheartedly for anachronisms, verbal and physical. The whole-heartedness is the point, the style and the attraction. It isnt, as has been known to happen, just a matter of throwing in the odd self-conscious bit of modern slang. In one of the sharpest and most startling scenes, we find ourselves in a TV studio where Savonarola, the famous fanatical friar, is being interviewed, stating his case with all the apparent reasonableness of any contemporary puritan pundit offered a platform for his platform. Savonarola is out to purge Florence of its vices, which include painting and sex.

This of course makes Botticelli doubly if not triply vulnerable, and he agrees to throw his own works into the flames. Orthodox history holds that he had, at least temporarily, got religion. The play holds that he was acting out of a mixture of fear and cunning. He even comes up with the phrase Bonfire of the Vanities which Savonarola, after mulling it over, pronounces a good one. He does manage to salvage the Venus painting, by working it over in the manner of a Renaissance Jackson Pollock. How it got it back to its pristine state, for posterity's delectation, isn't explained, but doubtless Leonardo helped. Though on second thought, given the way the play develops, he probably didnt.

Botticelli acts, sparingly, as his own narrator, telling us his story in our terms, which means through a hand mike. He even gets to make the introductory cellphone announcement: an awkwardly ingratiating beginning that threatens the worst. But the play recovers, as does Salvatore Antonios performance, a masterful trip through bravado, panic and shame.

Christopher Morris gives a brilliant account of Lorenzo, switching in a second from boyishly bland to ducally dangerous, and keeping us in constant suspense as to which way he will jump. He's been cuckolded by the hired help, and their catand-mouse scenes together are the play's finest, for wit and suspense and general resonance. Theyre finer still for being shared with the Clarice of Nicola Correia-Damude, red-hot in passion and white-hot in contempt; these Medicis have an amusingly modern marriage. Stephen Jackman-Torkoff s Leonardo is also excellent, though his relationship with Botticelli, presented as crucial and consuming a lot of dialogue, is dramatically underdeveloped. It encompasses both betrayal and sacrifice, but they never seem more than words. Alon Nashman is unexpectedly mild as the firebrand Savanorola, though this could be another piece of mischievous revisionism.

Completing the cast, and doing it well, is Valerie Buhagiar as Botticell's mom, who recalls what he was like as a boy - i.e. very self-willed - and encourages him to keep on being it. Hers is the smallest role, but she's compensated in the evenings second and shorter play Sunday in Sodom, which she easily dominates despite being glued to one spot for the duration. This is because she has been turned into a pillar of salt; the Sodom Sunday thats being commemorated is the last and most famous day in that city's history, cheekily updated.

The play might easily have been called Lot's Wife or The Wifes Lot. Or, considering her fate and the plays use of it, The Saline Solution. She has to cope with everything, though at least she now has a name, Edith. She tells us that the day had been rough even before the apocalypse, what with Lot spending all his time watching the war news on TV and nephew Isaac phoning up, understandably traumatized by father Abraham's near-miss attempt to turn him into a ritual sacrifice.

When the angels arrive, they are American-sounding soldiers called Chris and Derek. While Edith stands and narrates, centre stage, the other characters, played by the same actors we met earlier, pop up around her and pop down again, as in a cartoon strip. Tannahill's writing remains lively but, shorn of its religious underpinnings and with nothing substantial replacing them, the story seems arbitrary, overloaded but unanchored. The Botticelli story has been creatively reimagined; this one, despite being set in a recognizably modern war zone with the Lot family as refugees, feels jokey rather than witty. One good joke, implicit in the juxtaposition of the two plays, is that there's no mention of sodomy in this Sodom. Savonarola might have given the place a pass.

Buhagiar's Edith starts her testimony, and wins our allegiance, by suggesting possible reasons, ignored by Scripture, for her fatal turnaround: Had she, for example, left the stove on? The real reason turns out to be equally human and considerably more poignant but, as with Sandro and Leonardo, stated rather than dramatized. Reservations aside, this is an impressive showcase of an evening, and not just for its author. Matjash Mrozweski directed the first play and Estelle Shook the second; both are graduates of the CanStage/York University training program and both have delivered fine productions, pictorially striking and emotionally acute.

Botticelli in the Fire/Sunday in Sodom runs through May 15 at the Berkeley Street Theatre in Toronto.

Cylla Von Tiedemann, Canadian Stage / Valerie Buhagiar easily dominates Sunday in Sodom, writes Robert Cushman, and does so despite being glued to one spot for the duration of the play - as a pillar of salt.

THEATRE REVIEW

The Summoned, Tarragon Theatre

Years and years ago I saw a play by a writer new to me, Fabrizio Filippo, entitled Waiting for Lewis. It was presented by Theatre Direct, a young people's company, but it struck me as being better worth taking seriously than many plays intended for adults. Filippo was an actor as well as a playwright, and he disappeared from Toronto to make his fortune in film and television. But hes now back as both author and lead performer of a new play The Summoned. This one is presented by the Tarragon, a theatre for grownups. But for much of its length, it seems a less-mature play than its predecessor. Or maybe it just needs an audience of especially tech-savvy kids.

Its premise is traditional enough. The characters who have been summoned in The Summoned are gathered for that age-old theatrical ceremony, the Reading of the Will. The deceased is an Internet-security mogul, fabulously rich of course, named Khan. Or maybe Kahn: since he does not, for obvious reasons, appear on stage and is therefore unlisted in the program, either spelling may be correct. But I ll go with Khan, for its megalomaniac associations.

The gathering takes place at an unglamorous Toronto airport hotel, owned and run by Annie, an old flame of Khan's who was also, we are told, Wozniak to his Steve Jobs; so he used and discarded her on two levels simultaneously, which may make him super-Jobs. The place has come in useful over the years as a rendezvous for Khan's more reclusive clients - think Edward Snowden or Salman Rushdie - but Annie has otherwise retired from the game, morally as well as emotionally disillusioned. Helping her run the place is a young man named Aldous; he is Annies son and, we assume, Khans as well. He may even have been named in ironic tribute to Khan's brave new world, the full extent of whose braveness and newness is to be posthumously revealed.

Aldous acts as our narrator, or our geek-lecturer. Filippo plays the role himself, and he comes over as precociously, inhumanly glib. There turn out to be good dramaturgical reasons for this but we have to wait a long time to discover them, and in the meantime we're stuck with him. It may be a tribute to Filippos performance that he comes off so insufferable, but his being the author makes the play seem insufferable, too.

The other characters are hardly better company. Annie is the only one granted anything approaching feelings, but Maggie Huculak has an uphill battle conveying them. Then theres Gary (John Bourgeois), a high-level ex-associate who can't decide whether he

loved or hated Khan but can't stop breaking into tears either way. Laura, a lawyer, has the reverse reflex; her shtick is non-stop hysterical laughter, always a difficult effect for an actor to bring off but one that Kelli Fox manages without embarrassing either us or herself. From another part of Khans life, and of Aldouss, there's Isla (Rachel Cairns) who comes on as ditzy and then back-pedals like crazy, or perhaps that should be like sane. Keeping them all more or less in line is Quentin, the security man's security man, barking messages on an apparently limitless succession of cellphones, each one of which he proceeds to break in two; Tony Nappo, alone in the cast, makes a personality out of a running gag.

Sets (Jason Hand), costumes (Charlotte Dean), and of course video (Kurt Firla) are all high-class, and for live action we get some instant replays of the groups previous relationships. The flash and the flashbacks are slickly, speedily and even on occasion wittily handled in Richard Roses production. But the characters remain cardboard, so the story stays uninvolving. Until, that is, we get to the unfolding of Khan's last will and testament, or rather to its theatrical codicil.

Aldous is detached from his companions, to play a scene with a disembodied robotic voice whose identity it would be unethical to disclose. Enough to say that it introduces Aldous to horizons previously undreamed of, while presenting him - and us - with some pretty, and genuinely perplexing, moral problems. The teasing pre-recorded voice, by the way, belongs to Alon Nashman, currently Toronto's most ubiquitous actor; you may hear him here and both see and hear him in the Jordan Tannahill double bill that opened almost simultaneously at CanStage. This scene galvanizes the play, and the energy sustains through our heros return to thrash things out with his companions. Were presented with a choice between the pain of mortality and the no-horizon promises of technology. The play turns out to be about something, and it proves in retrospect to have been cunningly constructed. For a moment, it almost feels worthwhile.

The Summoned runs through May 29 at the Tarragon Theatre.

Cylla Von Tiedemann / The Summoned's Fabrizio Filippo is detached from his companions to play a scene with a disembodied robotic voice.
2016-05-19-back-down-the-rabbit-hole-aga:
THEATRE REVIEW

Alice In Wonderland Uncle Vanya Mrs Warrens Profession Shaw Festival

Our first sight of the Shaw Festival's Alice in Wonderland raises expectations and raises them high.

A drop curtain depicts a Victorian proscenium theatre, enchantingly drawn in playingcard colours, with our heroine's face, as in an old photograph, surveying the scene through a peephole on top of the arch. When the curtain itself rises, we behold an equally magical riverside scene, complete with a rowboat on which Lewis Carroll will escort the three Liddell sisters - of which, Alice is the youngest - while he tells them the tale of Wonderland.

When that story begins to take shape, the pictures become more complex before our eyes: a mixture of live action and projection. Through the magic of video, Alice herself falls dizzyingly down the rabbit hole, though she does give the odd impression of falling upwards. Her constant changes of size are wittily depicted while, in more sombre vein, theres a beautiful seashore scene for Alices encounter with the Mock Turtle.

There are a few eyesores, mainly in the costumes, but the production, directed by Peter Hinton and designed by Eo Sharpe, is for the most part visually amazing.

In all other respects, it's a mess.

Hinton's adaptation takes the story to be a meditation on Victorian society and on growing up; which it may well be, but we dont have to be hit over the head with it. The satire here is very heavy-handed, especially when we get to the Queen of Hearts and her trial scene. Theres a lot of new dialogue, and not only is it less fun than the original, it's also less trenchant. Whatever happened to sentence first, verdict afterwards? The rewrites and additions extend to the songs; their words, to Allen Cole's music, are often difficult to make out but enough comes through to suggest that Hintons lyrics, sloppy in rhyme and meter, would have had Carroll, a master of light verse, reeling and writhing and fainting in coils.

The overall tone is literal rather than logical: precisely the reverse of the Alice books themselves. It is also unforgivably unfunny. Much of the original text remains, but few of the actors seem to know how to point it. Its a blessed relief when the Cheshire Cat appears, in full grin and in hologram form, with Jennifer Phipps' face clearly recognizable behind the whiskers, and with her voice speaking the words as if she knew what they meant and relished the knowledge. Graeme Somerville is also fine, as a gentle troubled Carroll whose commentary is acceptable because it's outside the story proper, and as a Mock Turtle whos similarly gentle and troubled and who even gets to sing his Beautiful Soup song with the proper mournfulness. His is the best sustained scene in the show containing, in the Lobster Quadrille, the best-looking and best-sounding musical number. He also makes the most of an apocryphal courtroom speech for the Mad Hatter, though the tea-party scene is soporific enough as to turn the audience into so many dormice. Finally Tara Rosling, flying on wires like Peter Pan, makes an intrepid forthright Alice: maybe too forthright, but the books Alice is never slow to lecture the creatures she meets and the play's is even less so.

There are modern classic plays in the Shaw's smaller theatres. Jackie Maxwell has directed a fine production of Chekhovs Uncle Vanya, in an adaptation by the rising American playwright Annie Baker. Its one that retains the original's time and place but whose dialogue is aggressively here and now. Waffles, the family hanger-on, now gets called a moocher, which is OK, though I found Dr Astrov's repeated description of himself, and practically everybody else, as a creep somewhat infelicitous; but then I dont know Russian.

Anyway, this is a close-quarters bare-knuckled production in which the actors respond beautifully to one another while making clear how the characters fail to. Everybody is suffering, and hardly cares who knows it; and the occasional well-intentioned effort to make things better only makes them worse.

Patrick McManus, radiating self-contempt through a droopy moustache, is the angriest Astrov I have ever seen, if not exactly the subtlest. His diatribes about deforestation can never have sounded more urgent.

Neil Barclay in the title role doesnt establish himself as the play's central figure, but titles aren't everything; understated at first, he works himself into the hysterics of his attempt to shoot the Professor, a scene that just about defines tragic-comedy, or rather tragic-farce. His subsequent agonized sullenness is touching and credible. Marla McLean is a Sonya less longsuffering than most; she can rage with the best of them, and its invigorating. She meshes beautifully with Moya OConnell's Yelena, a vibrant portrayal of a woman afraid of vibrancy, terrified by emotions (her own or others'), and desperately pleading to escape from them.

I believed why she, young and beautiful, had married her old professor, smug and irritable as David Schurmann properly plays him. Peter Millard strums along nicely as Waffles, and as everybodys nanny Sharry Flett is concern personified. About the only flaw is the servant who, while moving the sets around, sings what sounds like "ha, ha, ha," but maybe thats an ironic comment on Chekhov's insistence that his plays were comedies.

Eda Holmes has staged Mrs Warren's Profession - the seasons one actual Shaw play - as a rehearsed reading (though none of the actors carry books) in a present-day London club that has yet to admit women to membership.

The idea is to show that misogyny, theoretical and practical, is as alive now as when Shaw wrote his expose of prostitution and its economic causes back in 1899, when the play was banned and had to be presented by a different kind of private club.

I wouldnt have thought any audience could miss the contemporary point; it belongs to what Basil Fawlty called the special subject of the bleeding obvious, especially given a production as vividly acted as this one.

The concept, as sometimes happens, has had beneficent side effects: the constricted setting, with plush sofas doing furniture duty for scenes inside and out, focuses attention, ours and the performers'.

Nicole Underhay plays Mrs. Warren, the working-class girl who became a prostitute because it beat getting paralyzed in a factory and who now runs a string of brothels herself. She sometimes overdoes the coarseness and bravado but she's excellent when vulnerable, pleading for the understanding of her daughter Vivie, who has unknowingly gone through college on the proceeds of the trade.

Vivie, all pertness and practicality in Jennifer Dzialoszynskis performance, applauds her mothers initial decision when she finally learns of it, in a confrontation that seems more than ever one of the strongest scenes Shaw ever wrote. It's when she learns that the business is still going on - Mrs. Warren being too good a businesswoman ever to give it up - that Vivie revolts.

Sir George Crofts, business partner and gentlemanly blackguard, is toweringly played by Thom Marriott. He certainly towers physically over Vivie, to ironic effect since she bests him in every other way. Wade Bogert-O'Brien is ideally feckless as Frank, the younger suitor whom she rejects along with anything else that might reek of romance.

The plays four gentlemen - the others are Gray Powell as an ineffectual artist with an undefined place in the Warren orbit and Shawn Wright as Franks father, a caricature of a clergyman - act as the production's chorus, welcoming us to the club and reading some of the stage directions, including those at the end when Vivie settles down to her destiny in an actuary's chambers.

This is ambiguous. Are we meant to think that, even as she asserts her independence, the male sex is still pulling her strings? Or is the laugh on them? After all, the play was written by a man.

Alice in Wonderland is in repertory through October 16 at the Festival Theatre, Niagara-on-the-Lake; Uncle Vanya through September 11 at the Court House Theatre; Mrs Warren's Profession through October 16 at the Royal George Theatre.

Emily Cooper / From left, Jay Turvey, Kelly Wong, Marcus Nance, Andrew Broderick, Jahlen Barnes and Jonathan Tan as the Caterpillar and Tara Rosling as Alice.
2016-05-26-tackling-dark-tales-of-surviv:
THEATRE REVIEW

The Model Apartment (Harold Green) The Testament of Mary (Soulpepper)

So, how to dramatize the Holocaust? In The Model Apartment, the American playwright Donald Margulies does it by hereditary displacement. He gives us a now-elderly couple, Max and Lola, who met and married just after the war when both were survivors, she of a camp, he of the woods where he had been a partisan. They moved to America and had a daughter, Debby, who is more visibly traumatized by their experiences than they themselves appear to be. She has grown up mentally disturbed and physically obese.

Max and Lola have followed the post-retirement trail from Brooklyn to Florida. It seems their condo isn't ready, so they are offered a temporary apartment that looks good but in which nothing works: the TV is a hollow shell, theres nothing in the fridge and there isnt even a proper bed. They left New York without telling Debby where they were going, but she found out anyway and she follows them there. And she in turn is followed by her boyfriend Neil who seems only marginally more stable than she is, and whom she took in when he was homeless. The play happens during a long first night in the apartment. Max, whom we are told can sleep anywhere, gets some fitful rest on a pull-out couch, periodically rousing himself to join the others in their ongoing screamingmatch.

The "model apartment" to which Max and Lola are consigned may be intended to remind us of Theresienstadt, the model camp to which Jews and others were sent, before being transferred to hellholes less decorously disguised. The unseen "nice landlord" to whom they refer may even be an allusion to the soothing guides who escorted victims into the gas chambers. The play certainly isn't shy of waking more obvious echoes. Lola shares with Neil - and therefore with us - stories of her friendship in Belsen with Anne Frank: memories that are almost certainly fantasies, and that Debby has heard so often that she can recite them in unison.

Max says comparatively little about his own experiences, though he does occasionally let off complaints on the order of I came out of the woods for this? It turns out he named his daughter after a Deborah who was his own first (murdered) love.

Debby bears the scars of her parents' experiences. She screams incessantly, claims to see Nazis in every Howard Johnsons, and embarrasses her elders with her sexual explicitness. Its a possible situation. But having established it, the play can do little but repeat it. It's efficiently written, but it can't avoid the taint of exploitation, of tapping into available responses, even if at one remove.

The Harold Green theatre has given it a good production, directed by Tanja Jacobs. A tetchy Eric Peterson and a practically unrecognizable Clare Coulter provide a sold base-line for Lisa Nortons rather spectacular performance as Debby, fearlessly padded and even more courageously emoted. Tony Ofori completes the cast as Neil, and has the most effective moment of what I can only call camp about the camps, when he sees Lolas prisoner-number and cheerfully volunteers that he has tattoos too. It's the kind of jolting serio-comic shock for which the whole play may be aiming but which it cannot sustain.

Soulpepper also has a play about a Jewish family: The Testament of Mary, a monologue for the mother of Jesus. Nancy Palk doesn't play her as noticeably Jewish, though remembering her wonderful rabbi in Angels in America there were moments when I rather wished she would. Instead, she offers an accomplished and sensitive account of a highly intelligent woman forced to watch her son suffer unimaginable pain after reaching heights of, to her, unaccountable celebrity. Yes, she was at the marriage feast at Cana; yes, she heard about the walking on the water. And yes, she was there for the raising of Lazarus, but all she could think of, encountering him postresurrection, was that this was a man who was now condemned to die twice. Its the most haunting passage of Colm Toibins play, adapted from his own novella. We meet Mary in hiding, plagued, she tells us, by visits from a couple of visitors - presumably two of the evangelists - who want to hear her story as long as it's in accord with their own. They certainly don't want to hear that she fled in fear from the scene of the crucifixion, or to hear her skepticism about her sons resurrection. It seems she never cared much anyway for the men he hung out with.

Its hard not to be reminded of the skeptical mother of Monty Python's Brian ("he isn't the Messiah ...") but Toibins script, though not without a vein of sardonic humour, isnt written or played for laughs. It suffers from the curse that afflicts nearly all one-person plays: it has to tell rather than show. Though I felt, perversely, that there were things, especially the politics of the times, about which I would like to have been told more.

Aaron Willis's production injects some intelligent tension, with threatening sound effects (Richard Feren) and even more alarming light-changes (Lorenzo Savoini). Palk keeps her performance lucid and level, carefully husbanding her occasional outbreaks, one of which is actually about her husband. The most devastating is her cry that it - meaning, really, Christianity - "wasn't worth it": not worth the agony it caused a mother.

The Model Apartment runs through May 29 at the Toronto Centre for the Arts; The Testament of Mary is in repertory through June 18 at the Young Centre.

A Gentlemans Guide to Love and Murder is the musical adaptation of KindHearts and Coronets, greatest of all British film comedies. It only confesses, though - in very small print - to being "based on a novel by Roy Horniman," that being the 1909 book that inspired the 1949 movie. So, is it just a coincidence thatboth film and show are built upon the same conceit?

In each of them a single actor plays all of the eight aristocrats whom the hero, a poor relation, has to eliminate in order to succeed to the family earldom. And in the similarity lies the crucial difference between the movie and the musical.

Alec Guinness multiple performances in the film were a triumph of subtlety and tongue-incheek restraint with each role, including a couple of silent ones, filled so delicately to the brim the audience purred with delight the moment he appeared in a new disguise.

Delicacy is the last quality to be attributed to John Rapson, who in the show's Toronto production struts or minces or bellows through his various incarnations in what somebody apparently believes to be English high-comedy style. It isn't even high-farcical.

It also isnt altogether the actors fault. He's reproducing the Broadway performance of Jefferson Mays, who won a Tony for his pains and was equally obnoxious, though he did at least manage to make the songs comprehensible. The score - music by Steven Lutvak, lyrics by Lutvak and Robert L. Freedman - is not the greatest, but it does have its quaint and merry moments, and even a couple of good punch-lines.

In Rapson's performance, the words are just an amplified mumble.

Like his predecessor, hes most bearable as a couple of comparatively quiet (and non-singing) members of the ill-fated DYsquith clan. He's least bearable, again like his predecessor, in an agonizingly prolonged musical sequence in which he plays a philanthropic noblewoman who travels to a succession of tropical plague-spots and emerges infuriatingly unscathed from each of them. Compare, if you can bear it, Guinness' sublime silent cameo as a smiling suffragette whose balloon gets burst: Literally. Also as in NewYork, the real star turn is given in the role of Monty, the penniless son of a mother cast out by the insufferable DYsquiths, who on hearing of the connection devotes himself to getting rich by getting even. This performance also differs from its cinematic counterpart, but in this case the departure is creative.

In place of Dennis Prices suave heartlessness, Kevin Massey offers an initially bashful, increasingly confident young man who can hardly believe the depths to which he can sink or the heights that he can reach.

These heights are romantic as well as financial; once prosperous, he has to juggle the affections of a mercenary flirt (Kristen Beth Williams, campy but amusing) and a deadly serious female relative (Adrienne Eller, a self-satirizing coloratura).

A patter trio in which both dear charmers descend on Monty's chamber and have to be kept forcibly and athletically apart is the high point of Darko Tresnjak's production, which otherwise varies from the neat to the frantic, with the latter taking grisly precedence as the evening lengthens. An exchange of insults between the last of the DYsquiths and his lady is the crassest and least necessary scene Ive beheld in years.

But it gets worse. The film's last sublimely ironic moment has been replacedby a device whose feebleness beggars belief.

It's just as well that critics aren't allowed to give away endings.

A Gentleman's Guide to Love and Murder runs through June 18 at the Princess of Wales Theatre in Toronto.

THEATRE REVIEW

Incident at Vichy Soulpepper Theatre

All My Sons Stratford Festival

Its one year late for his centenary, but this is proving to be a golden time for Arthur Miller. New York has seen acclaimed revivals of The Crucible and A View from the Bridge. Now, up here, we have Miller productions from Soulpepper and Stratford, both of them outstanding.

Soulpeppers choice is a rare one: Incident at Vichy, a 1964 play that was gripping when new and mesmerizing now. Alan Dilworth's production starts with the sound of a train: a terrifying noise because it's 1942 and were in the supposedly free section of occupied France. Ten men sit in a line on a bench in a featureless room, all of them brought there by police working, it seems, in perfect concord. None of them knows why they have been caught in this dragnet; they try to tell themselves that its a random checkup but they can't help fearing that they have been picked up because of the way they look, the way they sound. Most of them are Jewish. A few have heard of what is going on in the rest of Europe. They know what the trains are carrying, and where they're going.

The play is unashamedly schematic. Its first part is a discussion between those who know or guess the worst and those who are in denial, trying to believe that they will be all right if their papers are in order. The audience of course knows the terrible truth, but this hardly lessens the suspense. In fact it increases it; we want to know which if any of the detainees will be allowed to leave. Greater even than that is the overarching tension that comes from waiting for an axe to fall.

Some of the characters believe that such atrocities could never happen in a civilized country on a civilized continent; others know only too well that they could. The positions are familiar and baldly stated, and some of the cast find it hard to put conversational flesh on the bones. They speechify rather than talk. But the texture deepens as the play proceeds.

As an army major with qualms, Oliver Dennis reclaims the stereotype of "the good German," resisting his Gestapo controllers, then surrendering to them, then trying to salvage a fragment of self-respect. Kawa Ada brings a nervous bravado to an actor trying to convince himself, against all experience, that his enemies respect for culture will save him. Its a recurring theme of the play: men can love literature, love music, and still be killers.

Finally, we reach the two men at the end of the line: Stuart Hughes as an ex-army doctor who came out of hiding to get medicine for his wife, and Diego Matamoros

as an Austrian prince apparently arrested because of his accent and the one prisoner who seems certain to be released. There is nothing as simple as a conflict between realism and idealism.

The doctor certainly has no illusions, and Hughes' bitter practicality drives the play. The prince, having lived through the annexation of his homeland, also knows about the Nazis; indeed he believes that the world may have entered a new age of barbarism, spurred by demagogues - on whom his thoughts seem, in 2016, chillingly apposite. But he has yet to take in the full scope and immediacy of the horror; he is still, with the best and most benevolent of intentions, above it all' "Are you all Jews?" he asks his fellows, in the nicest possible way. Matamoros, courtly and gentle throughout, lets us see, feel, the princes mind expanding, from awareness of pathos to awareness of tragedy. The interplay of these two actors is superb; they restore Soulpepper to a level of performance that, once upon a time, we took for granted.

Millers best plays are exciting stories plus. All My Sons, his first success, is a real breath-suspender. Inspired by actual events it tells of Joe Keller who, during the war, allowed faulty airplane parts to leave his Ohio factory, and let his partner take the rap when twenty-one American pilots met their deaths.

Joe's own son Larry, also a pilot, may not have been one of the 21, but he, too, died in action. Now, in 1946, the Keller family awaits the arrival of Ann Deever, the jailed partner's daughter; she was Larrys fiancee and is now being courted by his brother Chris, a beefy idealist. Joe is cautiously in favour of the match; his wife Kate is passionately against it. She cannot bring herself to believe that Larry is dead. Gradually it becomes clear that for her the possibility of his death is bound up with the probability of Joes guilt. She's trying, in her own way, to protect her husband. People think her disturbed, but she may be the clearest-sighted person around.

Martha Henry's Stratford production is dazzlingly acted. Its also dazzlingly designed by Douglas Paraschuk, in the round and on a greensward setting with an especially fetching gazebo for the use of Joes family and friends. Though the court exonerated Joe, a shadow hangs over him, and he's at great pains to dispel it, from the minds of others and his own: playing unofficial scoutmaster with the neighbouring kids, the concerned husband, the all-American dad. Joseph Ziegler gets all the swagger and the neediness, his hands rapping his knees as he makes his points or waits for others to make theirs. Cornered, his geniality fades and desperation descends as he makes his excuses: he wanted to make money for his family, everybody was doing it, it was too late to call a halt.

It's maybe the plays fault that Joes final despair, unlike Willy Loman's in Miller's next play Death of a Salesman, doesnt appear inevitable; you feel he would have weaseled out of it somehow. If theres a tragic figure here it's Chris, whose insistence that his father face the truth blows up in his face. Tim Campbell, reprising the father-son relationship he played with Ziegler in Soulpepper's Salesman, is visually

and emotionally perfect. So is Lucy Peacock as Kate, by turns the haunted mother and the desperately practical hostess and wife.

The Deever family in this production are black, as are the Kellers neighbours. This, given the plays immediate postwar setting, is implausible in some ways but suggestive in others. It casts new light on why Joe got off while his partner went to jail. It also provides for an excellent performance from E.B. Smith as the doctor next door and an electric one from Michael Blake as Ann's brother who returns from visiting his imprisoned father and jolts the whole play into higher gear. As Ann herself, Sarah Afful is less satisfying, her emotions float somewhere above the given situation. The group scenes in this production are a revelation: all manner of sparks flying on the surface and angry currents crossing thrillingly underneath.

Incident at Vichy is at the Young Centre, Toronto, through June 25; All My Sons is at Tom Patterson Theatre, Stratford, through September 25.

Cylla Von Tiedemann / In Incident at Vichy, 10 men sit in a line on a bench in a featureless room, all of them caught in a mysterious dragnet.
