Macbeth

As You Like It

Stratford Festival

Antoni Cimolino's Stratford production of Macbeth might be called traditional, though it's in a tradition that has recently fallen into disuse. The play is set firmly in its historical pre-medieval period. Julie Fox's set splits the difference between blasted mosscovered heath and craggy castle, complete with steps on which the embattled characters can rush vigorously up and down. The witches, and the apparitions they summon, are staged and acted with good old-fashioned shrieking abandon. It looks as if Scotland's destiny is to be ruled by a race of reindeer.

In all, the production provides a fitting barbaric background for a central performance both unkempt and verklempt. Ian Lake offers us Macbeth as neurotic thug, a blood-soaked soldier transformed into a bloodbolstered psychopath. He's good at registering Macbeth's disquiet when Malcolm is proclaimed as the kingdom's heir, and at his best in the total misanthropy that precedes his final battle: the lily-livered boy who brings him news of the advancing English can never have been more witheringly dismissed. But we never get inside Macbeth's head, which is where the play's real action resides.

We do, from her very first words, get inside Lady Macbeth's. To quote her own advice to her husband: Krystin Pellerin looks, and sounds like the innocent flower, there is a serpent underneath. Her apparent girlishness makes her selfpropelled journey to the dark side all the more chilling. Her impatience with Macbeth-asmurderer is very persuasive. Her sleepwalking scene is not only haunting but moving.

In her one scene as Lady Macduff, Sarah Afful is similarly able to make sense of the words and to make them her own: the most basic requirements of Shakespearean acting. She's impatient with her own husband's absence, but then she settles into nervous affectionate banter with her young son (Oliver Neudorf, aged nine and excellent). The ensuing massacre is brutal but brief, the stage blacking out on her cry of "Murder" which echoes in our minds through the next scene, affording an extra poignance and an extra force to the anguish and anger of Michael Blake's Macduff. "He has no children," he cries out when Antoine Yared's admirably cool Malcolm promises him revenge. There's nothing he could do to Macbeth that would equal what Macbeth has done to him.

Such reliable actors as Scott Wentworth (Banquo) and Joseph Ziegler (Duncan) are, well, reliable. They both make ghostly appearances at Macbeth's banquet which is usually Banquo's solo haunt: an interesting idea but one that weakens a well-staged scene. As the drunken Porter, Cyrus Lane stopped the show on the first night, which really shouldn't happen. John Kirkpatrick is unprecedentedly present as the Doctor: guessing only too well at what's wrong with his patient.

If Stratford's Macbeth is straightforward, its As You Like It is anything but. The director, Jillian Keiley, has honoured her heritage by setting the play in Newfoundland in the 1980s, home, according to her program note, to "a cultural revolution that changed our perception of time and place."

She also aims to re-create the atmosphere of the province's kitchen-parties, with loads of music and audience participation. Spectators are given goodie-bags containing, among other things, branches to wave about and boxes that produce sound effects. Presiding over all this is Hymen, god or in this case goddess of marriage who does in fact appear at the end of Shakespeare's play when everybody pairs off. Despite the buildup, that textual appearance goes for almost nothing here.

But then the whole play seems cut off from the production's chosen time and place. To bridge the gap, much of it is played for giggles. It's a bad sign in a highly verbal comedy when none of the laughs come from the lines. The shame of it is that when Keiley does get down to directing a scene, she can do it very well.

The opening quarrel between the brothers Orlando and Oliver is strong and clear and physical, and so too, with humour added, is the subsequent appearance of the wrestler Charles (Cory O'Brien). The big wooing scene between the crossdressed Rosalind and her Orlando (played by Cyrus Lane as not too bright but engagingly sincere) is mined for much of its wit, pain and paradox. Not enough, though, because the ground hasn't been sufficiently prepared.

Petrina Bromley has barely explored Rosalind's good sense or the depths of her love, and her male disguise. Seana McKenna gives a fine disdainful reading of Jaques' seven ages of man speech but making this character a woman means excising references to his libertine past, impoverishing the role and the play. The banished duke likewise becomes a banished duchess. Brigit Wilson is touching when reunited with her daughter, but we lose the rivalry of the ducal brothers, and - most damagingly - the moment when the usurping Duke Frederick turns on the similarly fratricidal Oliver with "more villain thou." It's a moment of either hypocrisy or guilty displacement which has been known to turn the whole play around.

Oliver himself is vigorously played by John Kirkpatrick who doubles as the play's other Oliver, the hedge-priest Martext, endowed with a Maritime accent so thick that the other actors have to translate his words. It's a funny idea that actually works. Sanjay Talwar's Touchstone isn't funny at all, but there's nice work from Jamie Mac as the lovestruck shepherd Silvius,.

The words As You Like It appear in the program with the "you" heavily emphasized. So, it's all our fault. Macbeth is in repertory until November 5, As You Like It until October 22, both at the Festival Theatre, Stratford.
2016-06-16-three-s-company-director-lesl:
A couple of years ago, I reported enthusiastically on The James Plays, as presented by the National Theatre of Scotland at the other National Theatre in London. They performed three plays (the Jameses in question are the first three Scottish kings of that name from the fifteenth century) in the platform-stage Olivier Theatre, which they transformed into a theatre-in-the-round.

Those who wished could take in all three plays in a single day, as I did. It was exciting, as theatrical marathons often are, but as I wrote at the time, I couldn't imagine any Canadian company putting on anything so ambitious, and so historically and geographically remote. I added, though, that World Stage or Luminato could and should import them."

Sometimes you get what you wish for.

The James Plays arrive at the Luminato Festival this week, somewhat revised and recast, but basically as their original productions. The director is Laurie Sansom, and I had coffee with him this week at his Toronto hotel.

Sansom is the outgoing artistic director of the National Theatre of Scotland. Hes 44, and hes been in the job for three years. The company itself is ten years old, and has no fixed abode; it tours the country, all of it. Sansom says that he was "intrigued by a national theatre that didn't have to be an iconic building and was in fact the first of its roving kind. The model has since been copied by the National Theatre of Wales.

According to Sansom, just last Saturday, we closed a show at a barn in Perthshire, about men, deserters, shot for treason in the First World War. We draw on pop art, performance art. In that sense, the James Plays are quite an anomaly for us."

They're the work of Rona Munro, a Scottish writer and historian. Sansom found the first draft of the plays on his desk when he took over from his predecessor, Vicki Featherstone.

"Vicki had asked Rona what her dream project was. Rona told her, and said, Youll never do that.' Vicki said, 'Do it. So she did. When I read them, I was struck by their use of contemporary language, by their storytelling, wit and invention. They were exploring how Scotland should be governed.

The three Jameses, though widely different personalities, had several things in common. They all married foreign princesses, they all faced virulent opposition from the local lords, and they all met violent ends. James I spent his early years as a prisoner: a hostage at the English court of Henry V, who appears in the first play in a less chivalrous light than that depicted in Shakespeare. When Henry died," says Sansom, "James returned to Scotland to take the crown, and to impose a tax-based regime on the English model. He wanted to bring an established government to a country that hadnt had one for 40 years.

James II spent the early years of his reign as a hunted, haunted child. His play starts with a nightmare sequence showing him hiding in a series of boxes of increasing size. It's a brilliant image which was superbly realized in Sansom's original production. The boxes were sent whizzing about the stage while their grown-up former occupant

watched his younger boxedup selves being impersonated by a succession of puppets. I was grieved to learn that the puppets, as part of a general clarifying operation, have now been eliminated. But I take Sansoms point that the great bonus is that the actor can now live through the traumatic events himself " rather than handing them over to a bunch of dolls.

When we get to James III, were introduced to an item that Sansom justly calls a "great dramatic device. His Danish wife imports a mirror from Venice which, unlike all previous looking-glasses, reveals people as they actually look. This queen Margaret is altogether a fascinating character. As Sansom says, She ruled Scotland for her last two years." She was certainly far more capable than her husband.

Where James I and II were forced by circumstances to become increasingly ruthless, James III was one of your artist-kings, asking only to be left alone with his own personal choristers. In Sansom's words, "Margaret takes over the play, as she took over the country.

Margaret has been neglected by historians. But so has the whole period. This, according to Sansom, is a period of Scottish history forgotten in Scotland. There have been only three books written about it: one for each king.

"The plays ask: How do you govern a country. Do you fight for it?" They were first staged at the time of the Scottish referendum, whose result seems to have been a bitter disappointment for most of the actors.

There's a large majority of Scottish artists who are in favour of independence. In The James Plays, there are twenty actors of whom all but two are Scottish. The exceptions are an English actress who plays James Is English wife (who would rather live in France where they have orchards and better weather) and a Swedish lady as Danish Margaret.

"At our best," says Sansom, "at the National Theatre of Scotland, weve taken a rough Scots tradition and brought a new aesthetic to it. We're both populist and rule-breaking; there's not much respect for rules in the Scottish theatre, generally."

High praise coming from Sansom, who himself is English.

Russell Millard / The James Plays are characterizations of the first three Scottish kings of that name from the 15th century. The Plays arrive at the Luminato Festival this week.
2016-06-22-dust-off-the-doth:
I grew up in Britain singing God Save the Queen. That isn't strictly true; in my day we hardly ever sang the national anthem, we were merely required to stand at attention every time it was played. Or at any rate to stand. Even when we did hear the words, we never paid them very close attention. They washed over us, as familiar words generally do. Still, decades later, my generation can at least claim that "Long to reign over us" is a prayer that's been answered, or a prophecy fulfilled.

That of course is in the first verse. There are others. The second one is a real eye-and-ear opener. Except that it's never sung. At least,

I didn't think it was. But maybe I was wrong. U.K. Labour Party leader Jeremy Corbyn seems to have heard it because he recently, and quite understandably, took serious exception to it. It goes like this: O Lord our God arise Scatter our enemies And make them fall. Confound their politics, Frustrate their knavish tricks; On thee our hopes we fix. God save us all.

Well, nobody could say that isn't vigorous. Especially the "knavish tricks" bit. It exposes, more nakedly than usual, the message of all national anthems: we're the good guys, and God is on our side. They all say that, which should logically mean that they cancel one another out. There's nothing ironic or metaphorical about them.

I bring up irony and metaphor because Andrew Coyne invokes them, along with "allegory," in his recent article on the changes to Canada's anthem. He says, quite rightly, that people can sometimes take words too literally, without reference to tone or context. I think he misses, though, the distinction between a conversation and a written text. Or, more to the point, between words used colloquially and words used officially.

So yes: when, to quote his own example, we "happen across a group of girls addressing

each other as 'you guys,' " we don't stop to wonder if there is some confusion going on. We probably don't give it a thought. If we do, we're unlikely to think that the word "guys" has become gender-neutral. We're likelier to relish the slight incongruity. We may even consider that, once upon a time when it first happened, there was some cheeky humour involved. Humour, though, is not something you go looking for in national anthems, though the world might be a more agreeable place if it were. Whatever the intentions of Robert Stanley Weir, who in 1914 revised the O Canada lyric that he had written in 1908, he wasn't trying to be funny.

He was trying to be timely, changing his original "thou dost in us command," which really is gender-neutral, to "all thy sons command," which really isn't. There was a war on, though it was only just getting started, so the words must have been meant less as a celebration of Canadian heroism (which has become the revisionist interpretation) than as an exhortation to it: a musical recruiting-poster, in fact. The soldiers doing the fighting, certainly in the front lines, would have been men. I doubt if anyone back then, hearing the word "sons," would have formed a mental picture that included daughters. And - despite Coyne's insistence that this literalmindedness would have meant that they were deaf to metaphor, irony and allegory - I think they would have been right.

Later generations have probably taken the words as much for granted as I did those of God Save the Queen. But if they do stop to think, they're as unlikely as their forebears to think that "all our sons" also accommodates "all our daughters." The word "sons" isn't in the same class as the word "mankind" which, rightly or wrongly, has been accepted as meaning "all humanity." "Sons" is a more specific term. It summons individuals. There's a good case, in this context, for replacing it, especially given that it's a replacement itself.

I don't think it's a big deal. I don't think anybody's life is going to be radically changed, for better or worse, either by amending the anthem or by keeping it as it was. And I have to admit that the women in my family are less bothered by the familiar version than the men seem to be. But there's another reason for amending it - it's clumsily written. "True patriot love/In all thy sons command." Is that "command" a noun or a verb? Weir's earlier version is much clearer: "True patriot love/In us thou dost command." It's a verb, with "Canada," three lines earlier, its subject. He got it right the first time.

All the same: what kind of love is it that has to be commanded? The proposed alteration to "in all of us command" gets rid of the gender issue, but it's watery, besides being as syntactically ambiguous as the line it replaces. I say, go back to 1908, thereby appeasing traditionalists, progressives and pedants alike. Of course the word "dost" may sound a bit dusty, but isn't that what one wants of an anthem? Weir in 1914 was trying to be up-todate and look where it got us.
2016-06-29-palpable-and-moving-a-1970s-c:
THEATRE REVIEW

A Chorus Line

Festival Theatre, Stratford

So how do you stage A Chorus Line - the very title of which would seem to demand a proscenium stage - on a three-sided platform like the one at the Stratford Festival? Simple. You build a proscenium on the platform. It's all done with mirrors. Or at least, some of it is.

The 1970s did not seem, to those who were there, like a great period in the history of the American musical. That was then. Seen from now, after decades of musical misery, it looks like a golden age. Consider the four shows that were up for the Best Musical Tony award in 1976. One was Bubbling Brown Sugar, an early jukebox musical, long and justifiably forgotten. But the others were Pacific Overtures, Chicago and, yes, A Chorus Line, all major works. A Chorus Line was the predestined winner: the awards show was built around it, rather like with Hamilton this year.

Its prestige has dimmed somewhat in the intervening years; Pacific Overtures now seems, as indeed it always did, a more intelligent and adventurous show, while Chicago, because of its phenomenally successful revival, has become far more visible. A Chorus Line is softer; it has a veneer of toughness, but its one of Broadways valentines to itself.

In particular, it's a tribute to the wonderful and seemingly inexhaustible breed of actor-singer-dancers. We're at an audition. Zach, a director-choreographer, needs eight people - four male, four female - to dance attendance on his leading lady. He has seventeen to choose from. On the thin pretext that they will also have lines to speak, he gets them to talk about themselves, about their growing up, about how they got into dancing and what they expect to get out of it. My favourite spoken line: "I dont want to hear that Broadway is dying, because I just got here."

The show has one of the most electric openings of any musical. It was great in Michael Bennetts legendary original production, and it's great again in Donna Feore's Stratford staging. Those auditioning are being put, rigorously, through their paces; and just the sight of them brings the house down. The number that follows has a documentary authenticity about it, an excitement thats maintained even when they burst, less realistically, into song with I Hope I Get It.

Nothing else in the show has quite that impact. Theres a gulf between this number, where they dance because they're dancers, and the subsequent autobiographical ones where they dance and sing because they're in a musical. The most extended of these is Hello Twelve, Hello Thirteen, Hello Love, in which they share with us their experiences of puberty. Though its supposed to give the show universal appeal, it actually distracts from the reason were interested in these characters in the first place: they are performers, on the line for a place in the line. And yet, it's a terrific number, masterfully conceived and thrillingly executed.

Feore's choreography, here and elsewhere, doesnt seem all that different from what I remember of Bennetts, but that's hardly a bad thing. Michael Walton's lighting is great - again like the original. Michael Gianfrancescos set gives us a false back wall, which periodically revolves to become the bank of rehearsal-room mirrors that have always been the shows signature. Laura Burton conducts a taut rendition of Marvin Hamlisch's music, a score that's serviceable in the best way; except, that is, for the atrociously non-specific What I Did for Love, a transparent attempt at a detachable hit song.

Among the cast I especially liked Ayrin Mackie, in the role of Sheila, oldest, tallest and sassiest of the chorines, and Matt Alfano, who has the evenings first solo and in many ways its best. Its called I Can Do That, and indeed, he can. Juan Chioran, acting mainly from the back of the auditorium, is a commanding martinet as Zach. Dayna Tietzen is Cassie, his ex-flame, who angers and embarrasses him by turning up for a place in the chorus when he thinks she should be a star. Their relationship has always been the least convincing thing in the show, and it still is. Cassie's cri de coeur solo, The Music and the Mirror, never seems to work. It's a dance of frustration that is itself frustrating, refusing to take off. A number that always works is the infernally catchy One. Its introduced, with sadistic cunning, in a rehearsal sequence in which we almost see, almost hear it, so that were left panting for the full experience. And then at the end of the show, after the lucky eight have been chosen and the others regretfully dismissed, we get it: a full-scale full-stage reprise, the entire company orbiting in gold suits around their invisible star. It's part epilogue, part curtain call. At least it was in 1976. This time it's just curtain call. The lights have gone firmly down on the preceding scene, and the audience dutifully applaud as if theyd been given a happy ending though it is, at the most, bittersweet.

We enjoy the closing number as a number, detached from everything else. Theres a strong vein of sentimentality in the show, and in this production it's stronger than ever. I still prefer it to the assembly-line cynicism of Chicago. And the performers' commitment is palpable and moving. After all, it's their story.

In repertory through Oct. 30. robert.cushman@hotmail.com

David Hou / Members of the company in A Chorus Line.

Theatre Review

Shakespeare In Love The Lion, The Witch and The Wardrobe

Avon Theatre, Stratford

Something has happened to Shakespeare in Love on its journey from London to Stratford: it's gotten good.

When I saw this stage version of the much-cherished movie in the West End a couple of years ago, I thought it a spectacularly pointless exercise. The film still exists, its script could hardly be improved upon, and neither could its actors. An ad hoc stage cast could hardly compete; the one assembled in London certainly couldnt.

The Stratford production has the same director, Declan Donnellan, working with his regular design partner Nick Ormerod. In Stratford, however, hes working with a company that makes all the difference, especially in a show that is, like the movie, a celebration of theatre.

I won't pretend that I didn't still miss the movie performers, and especially the casual yet precise way in which they flicked off Tom Stoppards jokes. Stoppard shared credit for the screenplay with Marc Norman, but it seems generally accepted that the original idea was Normans while the humour is Stoppard's: deliciously anachronistic in its appropriation of modern showbiz idioms (you're not going to do it that way, are you?), but somehow fitting right in with this piece about the birth of modern theatre.

Lee Halls stage adaptation keeps many of the great lines and moments, but it coarsens them. This affected the London actors and it infects the Stratford ones too: actors mostly playing actors, some of them carry individual rambunctiousness to generalized extremes. As a group, however, they make the story their own. Just the way they huddle when disaster threatens, or the way they cheer when its overcome, are enough to put us on their side.

Some of the individual performances are delightful: Tom McCamus as the stagestruck moneylender Fennyman, transformed from tyrant to acolyte at the offer of a walk-on role, and Stephen Ouimette as the manager Philip Henslowe, who historically was a loan-shark, but who figures here as an anxious and committed impresario, confident that the show not only must but will go on.

Above all, we have a central couple with real passion, real wit, and real chemistry. Luke Humphrey's is a dashing, spirited Shakespeare, released from a writer's block so severe that his friend and rival Christopher Marlowe, in a balcony scene apparently inspired by Cyrano de Bergerac, has to feed him the words to woo his lady. Shannon Taylor is truly inspiring as Viola, the lady in question, finding temporary release from court life by posing as a boy player.

Through one another, they discover love, changing the course of English drama; he gets to write Romeo and Juliet, she - for one night or afternoon only - gets to play its female lead. Then she sails for America and an arranged marriage as he writes Twelfth Night, naming its heroine after her: the great bittersweet comedy to commemorate a bittersweet affair.

Donnellans production is great fun and moves with speed and purpose. Ormerods set is cunning and versatile, a theatre within a theatre. One lament: I wish they had found some way of staging my favourite moment from the film. I love the scene in which a Puritan, who had been protesting outside the playhouse with the prophetic

slogan "their business is show," joins the crowd in throwing his hat in the air at the climax of the world's first great love tragedy.

Shakespeare in Love is history as fairy-tale. The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe, this year's childrens play at Stratford, is fairy-tale firmly rooted in history, and its a matching success.

Stratford this season is rich in good child actors and equally rich, it seems, in good grown-up actors playing children. Gareth Potter, Ruby Joy, Andre Morin and Sara Farb are not only believable as youngsters; they're dead-on convincing as English middle-class evacuees in the Second World War. Adrian Mitchell's stage version of the C.S. Lewis novel gives us an establishing scene in a railway station that sets up Narnia in both an ominous and reassuring fashion.

We reach it, as the four children do, through a world of books. The professors house in which they are billeted seems, in Douglas Paraschuks set designs abetted by Brad Peterson's projections, to be made of books: a tribute to a certain kind of imagination, the kind that's fed by literature. Narnia, on the other side of the wardrobe, is similarly book-bedecked.

Tim Carrolls production is ceaselessly inventive and imaginative. Its also excellently acted. Tom McCamus doubles as man and beast, professor and lion, and is actually fiercer as the first than as the second. That's clearly intentional; as Aslan he projects a regal gentleness from within a magnificent maned shell in the style of the War Horse; he's its voice and also its front legs. Yanna McIntosh makes a silkily, almost campily seductive White Witch, whose menace, when she unleashes it. is chilling. Mike Nadajewski is a charming Mr. Tumnus, and theres sterling work from good beavers, bad wolves and unclassifiable others.

The songs, which originated in this adaptations London production, might have been dispensed with. Or so I thought until we got to the musical assault of the witch's minions on Aslan's supposedly lifeless body. It was very effective, and needed the preceding jollier numbers to set it up. The Christian symbolism of Aslan's sacrifice and resurrection is played down: a relief in many ways.

This show and Shakespeare in Love inhabit the populist wing of the festival; their titles practically guarantee them an audience. This time they both deserve it.

National Post Shakespeare in Love is in repertory through Oct. 16; The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe through Nov. 5.

THEATRE REVIEW

Cam Baby Life After Toronto Fringe Festival

Two productions arrive on this year's Toronto Fringe Festival as winners of the festival's awards for Best Play and Best Musical. Giving prizes to shows before they have even opened is a new phenomenon. It turns out, though, that both pieces deserve their honours.

The play is Jessica Moss's Cam Baby, which begins as another comedy about the Internet. Clara and her boyfriend Tim, neither of them glamorous, are indulging in their favourite pastimes of texting, viewing and recording themselves. They don't know that Andrew, Clara's ineffectual landlord, and Matabang, his controlling self-described friend, have installed cameras in the house and are making videos of the couple, naturally including their most intimate moments.

They've made a small business out of it; they share their products with a select circle, and some of them go less selectively viral. Clara, who is overweight, is a great hit, or gets a lot of hits, on Ugly Porn. One of her admirers turns up in person, which leads to Clara finding out and being, naturally, very hurt and very angry.

Moss first burst on the scene as a writer-performer, doing hilarious monologues about, what else, relationships. It seems that she can write just as wittily and perceptively for other performers.

Her earlier scenes strike funny sparks off people's relationships to their toys; Matabang

in particular would likely die without his. But she goes on to cut deeper. For one thing she observes the Chekhovian rule that you should never bring a revolver on stage unless you intend to use it, though in her case the weapon is a hammer.

Most importantly, she lets nobody off the hook. Clara and Tim are sympathetic, especially Clara, but they're also complicit. They're victims of a culture in which they themselves partake. And it isn't something that just happened with the Internet. We're dealing with human qualities - cruelty, greed, loneliness, exhibitionism, indifference

- that may have found new technological outlets but are really eternal. Charlotte Gowdy directs an excellent cast. Clara is played by Ashley Botting, an ornament of Second City who is expectedly amusing here, but is also both touching and scathing. The others are Andrew Cameron and Brandon Coffey as two varieties of helpless; Christine Horne, the best known of the actors but playing the least rewarding role, one that's mainly plot-mechanical; Beau Dixon who doesn't so much forward the action as explode it; and Karl Ang, who conveys Matabang's self-admiring smoothness but delivers it too hard and fast for clarity. Actually too many words get lost throughout; casualties, yet again, of a hollow echoing stage.

The same problem bedevils the musical Life After, probably through no fault of Brandon Kleiman who designed both shows and is obviously a good-luck charm. The words here are especially precious, since Britta Johnson's lyrics are amazing; she knows what a rhyme is and how it can sharpen both feeling and meaning.

She also wrote the book, which is minimal, and the music. This doesn't quite make her Lin-Manuel Miranda, as she doesn't act in the show, but she does musically direct the music. And by playing piano, she's also half the orchestra; the other half is Kevin Wong on, of all things, viola. The only fault to be found there is that the accompaniment sometimes drowns the singers; voices without microphones are a blessing, but it must be confessed, a mixed one.

The life of the title is that of Alice Carter, beautifully played by Anika Johnson, the composer's sister, and what it comes after is the death of her father, killed in a car accident when he should have been attending Alice's sixteenth birthday. We watch

her coming to terms with the loss and with the suspicious circumstances surrounding it; though it's a mark of the show's honesty that what seems to be the big reveal turns out to be something that can be lived with.

Father himself is a ghostly or flashback presence, sung by Tim Funnell, appropriately haunting. He is, or was, a motivational speaker, though the show itself is refreshingly free of fake uplift. Alana Hibbert gorgeously sings Alice's mother, whose survival strategy is to re-decorate; Kate Blackburn is her tactlessly cheerful friend, and Janet Gigliotti plays her teacher whose friendship carries an unintended sting; and Kaylee Harwood is excellent as her older sister, wondering how much to tell her. A fine cast all around, under a director, Robert McQueen, who takes full advantage of the score's best feature: its capacity to make every song a piece of the action, physical or emotional or both.

That's a Sondheim quality, and we're in his territory in the musicalization of group scenes and in the probing of contradictory feelings. Musically we're more in the slightly later world, plangent and nervous, of Next to Normal or Fun Home, though I much preferred this show to either of those. It's more intelligent, less portentous. Its last scene had me tearing up.

These two shows must have a life beyond the fringe; ideally in more forgiving surroundings, though there really is very little to have to forgive.

The Toronto Fringe Festival runs until July 10. Cam Baby is at the Factory Theatre; Life After is at Theatre Passe Muraille. Check schedules for dates and times.

Toronto Fringe Festival / Nobody is let off the hook in Jessica Moss's Cam Baby, which deals with human qualities like greed and indifference.

THEATREREVIEW

Matilda The Musical Ed Mirvish Theatre

Dan Chameroy, playing Miss Agatha Trunchbull in Matilda The Musical, brings something to the role and to the show that I never thought to see. The something is subtlety.

Miss Trunchbull is the sadistic, sports-obsessed school principal to whose callous mercies the show's five-year old heroine is consigned by her hateful parents. The actor who played this harridan in London and New York gave a performance of lip-licking grossness that, depressingly if unsurprisingly, won him raves and awards.

Chameroy's triumph is to be chilling but delicate. He comes to the role with extensive cross-dressing experience: for years he's been the flirtatious Dame Plumbum in Ross Petty's Toronto pantomimes. Flirtatiousness would be out of place for Trunchbull, whose clothes are aggressively drab, and whose hair is a tight and savage bun. But a soft and silky vocal tone comes in handy, especially when it turns to ice, the character's preferred temperature for inspiring terror. Miss Trunchbull likes to invent misdeeds and then punish her pupils for committing them. Any child will do.

She was an Olympic champion at throwing the hammer, and she likes to pick up a little boy, spin him around her head, and then hurl him into the great beyond. Don't get too excited; the stage blacks out at the crucial moment. Underneath all this, and without strain, Chameroy shows us a terrible streak of insecurity. This is what drives her to inflict mental and physical tortures on the children she calls "maggots," with Matilda Wormwood the most maggoty of them all.

Matilda's greatest crime, in Miss Trunchbull's and her parents' eyes, is that she loves to read; she polished off Crime and Punishment, Nicholas Nickleby and halfa-dozen others in a week; like I said, the show doesn't go for subtlety. Her parents also resent that she was born a girl, or indeed that she was born at all. Her birth begins the story, with her mother registering annoyed amazement at the news that she's nine months pregnant and thus will not be able to participate in an upcoming ballroom dancing contest. Dennis Kelly's script is based on the book by Roald Dahl whose children's stories have always struck me as short on humour and long on gratuitous nastiness. Also, even within the limits of fantasy, short on believability. It's fair enough that Matilda's mum and dad, who loathe her, would send her to a hellhole of a school. But what about the other kids? There's no indication that their parents don't love them. Unlike the Dickensian Dotheboys Hall (the Nicholas Nickleby reference makes for a nice shout-out), Dahl's Crunchem Hall is a day-school, presumably with holidays, so the children could easily tell their folks what was going on. As a librarian friend of Matilda's (nicely played by Keisha T. Fraser) asks in a slightly different context, "Why doesn't somebody call the police?" And what are we to make of Miss Honey, the nice teacher - indeed, as far as we can see, the only teacher - in the school? She turns out to have a double relationship with Miss Trunchbull that only makes sense if she's a total idiot. But she's presented to us as intelligent if timid. In London, she was the best thing in the show. As played here by Paula Brancati, she's still good to have around; her song of self-doubt is the highlight of the score, neat and searching. Otherwise Tim Minchin's lyrics, at least the ones you can hear, are uneven while his music is undistinguished; the ballads are static, the attempted showstoppers have no bounce to them.

Matthew Warchus's direction is fast and slick, on a set by Rob Howell largely composed of alphabetical building-blocks. Perhaps I'm the oly person who preferred their collaboration on The Lord of the Rings. The biggest production number is one in which the children are terrorized into a display of advanced PhysEd, the terror somewhat undercut by the fact that they look to be having the time of their lives.

Three girls alternate as Matilda. Hannah Levinson, who played her on the first night, is a splendidly assured little know-it-all. It's odd that, despite the build-up it's given, her bookishness barely comes into play in defeating Miss Trunchbull. Instead, she has to develop occult powers that arrive late and depart early. The promised conflict hardly exists. But at least the headmistress is allowed a certain grandeur. Matilda's working-class parents, vain or crooked and obsessed with "the telly," are presented with odious condescension as screeching cockney caricatures. As Dad, a fruitlessly unscrupulous used-car merchant, Brandon McGibbon slips in a few moments of understated wit; Darcy Stewart as his lady has no truck with understatement, but she may well have felt it was pointless to try.

Best supporting grownup: Eric Craig in a stylish last-minute cameo as a Russian mafia boss. (Don't ask.) Best supporting tot: Isabella Stuebing, gleeful as Matilda's self-anointed best friend. Best musical for which this one made me feel nostalgic: Annie. I'd be perfectly happy to see Chameroy play Miss Hannigan.

THEATRE REVIEW

One of the rules at Shakespeare in High Park in Toronto is that no performance should run longer than an hour and a half. So its intriguing one of this summers two plays should be Hamlet, which usually clocks in at three hours and has been known to stretch to four.

Intriguing, and in many ways, rewarding. As you'd expect, Birgit Schreyer Duarte's production does a lot of cutting; it also does a lot of cross-cutting, juxtaposing bits of one scene with bits of another, with some illuminating results. The general speed and clarity make for excellent storytelling. They dont, though, allow much in the way of exploration. The play is Shakespeares longest for a reason. It twists and turns because its hero's mind won't stop working. Here, everything is over so quickly that nothing can take on weight. It seems particularly strange that Hamlet should keep beating up on himself for not getting around to killing his uncle. Hes hardly had time.

As it happens, Frank Cox-OConnell's Hamlet is especially good in his self-lacerating moods. Tall and thin and pale, a punk intellectual who seems to have majored in nihilism, he jabs at himself (cutting is catching) before considering whether to be or not to be. He then proceeds to bring that too famous speech to new and tingling life. But then he does that with every word he utters.

This actor has shone in independent productions, and he also staked a good claim as a director with Soulpepper's The Just. He now gives the best lead performance I have seen in the park, slicing as keenly as his knife through the muggy open-air acoustics. Hes a master of the unexpected, logical emphasis: "How ALL occasions do inform against me," he complains with exasperated weariness; at YOUR age, he lectures his mother with all the insufferability of the puritanical young. Pulling a cloth from the wedding-feast table, he wraps it around his head to embarrass his newlywed mother and uncle. Also, it seems, to protect himself: grief and anger have made him emotionally raw. He delights in playing the bitter fool even before the ghosts visitation gives him the excuse to play the madman.

His quicksilver moodiness ignites his scenes with Ophelia, hurtling between affection and disgust, each note sounding genuine. It's clearer than usual that his mother's marriage has unleashed the misogynist in him. Rose Tuongs Ophelia, here almost a joint protagonist, and a clearer-cut tragic figure, positively gains from the textual editing, which allows her to act out scenes that generally are only described. She goes on a fated journey from spirited lover to reluctantly obedient daughter to, if I can coin a word, sexhibitionist. It seems fitting her funeral, prefaced by a reggae-fan Gravedigger (Marvin L. Ishmael) should be one of the highlights. Nicky Guadagni plays a female Polonius (surely that should be Polonia): an idea that works well in her maternal scenes with Ophelia but collapses when Hamlet kills her thinking shes Claudius. Surely he would have noticed the difference.

It also seems strange that nobody should regard killing a woman as monstrous; chivalry must really be dead in Denmark. Other gender reversals give us a Rosencrantz without a Guildernstern, pressed into service as Hamlet's impromptu shrink ("glean what afflicts him" she's told, and she does her best), and a Princess Fortinbras who doesnt work at all. Alon Nashmans Claudius brings a booze bottle to his prayer scene, making it clear why he tries to repent, and why he fails. Elsewhere, he's less lucid: he rushes through the speech about his love for his queen, strange in a production that makes a big romantic deal of their relationship.

Hamlet seems quite a churl for resenting his elders' happiness. After all, whats a little incest so long as you keep it in the family? Or a little fratricide? The directors program note, which isn't nearly as good as her production, makes some startlingly unsupported claims about the play's action while deriding a sentimental interpretation that nobody has actually advanced in decades. In fact the sentimentality is all hers, as she ends the play with Horatios "good night, sweet prince" followed by a sequence of home movies. Fortunately, what has gone before is far more bracing. And theres that central performance.

All's Well That Ends Well, the companion play, offers almost nothing as good. It has the same cast and a comparably ingenious editing of text, but none of the actors is consistently on top of that text except perhaps Cox-O'Connell, whose First Lord has the same bite and authority as his Hamlet. These two roles are the same as were played by Ben Carlson in his first season at Stratford: a pleasing coincidence as we have here the best Shakespearean actor to appear among us since Carlson.

The driving role here, love her or hate her, should be that of Helen, the poor physicians daughter who cures the King of France of a fistula, wins the man of her dreams, and then has to win him all over again. Mina James has her moments, mainly the dejected ones, but her method with a long speech is to punch out every other word.

Ted Witzels production also has moments, especially in the last scene where he has the actors swinging about in military formation as if registering amazement at the ways of this play's peculiar world and the ambiguous happiness of its ending. His principal interpretive idea is to give the soldier Parolles a homosexual attachment to his young patron Bertram; it's an interesting notion but the acting isnt there.

Qasim Khan is excellent as a Horatio even more taciturn than usual by virtue of the lines hes lost, but his Parolles is colourless, his humiliation has nothing to fall from. But perhaps I was unfair in comparing this production to Hamlet. There is one commanding performance: Rachel Jones as the clown Lavatch, though the text she's on top of isn't all Shakespeare's; the director has written her some very long monologues saying how bittersweet everything is. It would be nice if the play could do that by itself. It has been known.

Hamlet and All's Well That Ends Well alternate through Sept. 4.
2016-07-27-there-is-still-no-exit:
THEATRE REVIEW

The Dance of Death Studio Theatre, Niagara-on-the-Lake Engaged Royal George Theatre, Niagara-on-the-Lake

Nobody ever accused August Strindberg, Sweden's premier playwright, of doing things by halves. In The Dance of Death, written in 1900, he gave us the most miserable married couple in the history of drama, and then drove the point home by having them live in a prison. Really it's a fortress but, certainly in Martha Henry's Shaw Festival production, it looks like a prison.

William Schmuck's set gives us bars on the windows, and a sentry marching on the platform outside, more visibly and more frequently than in any other production of the play I've seen. In fact there are two sentries, both played by the same actor: a young and vigorous patrolman in Act One and an older one with a conceivably symbolic limp in Act Two. The young one casts the occasional glance inside the living quarters, suggesting he's appalled by the suffering he sees and would like to help out, but wouldn't know where to start. He has our sympathy.

The couple in the castle are Edgar, a low-grade military captain who resents just about everybody, and Alice, a former actress who mostly resents Edgar. She blames him for ruining her career by marrying her, for alienating his colleagues and superiors whom he indiscriminately dismisses as "scum," for their consequent poverty and for the fact that they can never keep a servant. He blames her for there never being any food in the house. Almost their only link to the outside world is the telegraph; phones have been invented but Edgar is too paranoid to allow one on the premises. The play's first half-hour has them exchanging insults and grievances as in a game, one that's been going on for years. By way of illustration, they settle down to a game of cards, knowing it's going to provoke more argument. Still, the couple that plays together stays together, and these two, approaching their silver anniversary, are plainly in for life. The catalyst for action is the arrival of Kurt, Alice's cousin and one-time lover, newly appointed as this island outpost's quarantine officer. Husband and wife each try to enlist him against the other. He tries to be charitable to both. He enlists medical assistance for Edgar, who has a series of what appear to be strokes but keeps bouncing back, and he lets himself be re-seduced by Alice. But their combined malevolence defeats him, and he finally flees what he calls "this hell," leaving his hosts to wonder at the unaccountable way in which some people behave. The play unexpectedly anticipates Noel Coward's Hay Fever, though its more commonly cited successors are Jean Paul Sartre's No Exit, hell as an eternity of other people, and - for obvious marital reasons - Edward Albee's Who's Afraid of Virginia Woolf.

Albee's inferno is more fun, but Strindberg's feels more authentic. He really thought men and women were like this; he himself had been married twice before writing The Dance of Death and he went and did it a third time afterwards - his life plainly imitating his art. Line by tortured line, blow by psychological blow, much of the play is painfully believable. Strindberg took himself and his obsessions very seriously; any humour in his plays is unconscious.

Henry's production does have occasional comic touches, but what's best about it, in a streamlined adaptation by the Irish playwright Conor McPherson, is its lucidity. For the first time I could actually follow Alice's and Kurt's plot against Edgar. I could not, however, care.

Jim Mezon's Edgar, a selfintoxicated ramrod, grows in command as the captain grows in grotesquerie, notably when dancing to his wife's piano rendition of his favourite tune the Entry of the Boyars and - with his author's typical lightness of touch - collapsing at the end of it. The woman, for once in Strindberg, is a lesser monster than the man, but Fiona Reid unexpectedly falters in the mix of vulnerability and venom. She's best in her remorse and relief when her schemes go blessedly awry. Kurt could easily come over as a wimp, but Patrick Galligan gives him real passion, almost too much of it at points. An apt prelude to Strindberg's view of marriage is W. S. Gilbert's view of courtship, as presented in his 1877 comedy Engaged. Gilbert without Sullivan means we get the author's bracingly cynical view of human nature, unsweetened by pretty tunes. The hero, so to speak, is Cheviot Hill, a rich young man whose governing qualities are a fanatical stinginess and the compulsion to propose to every young woman he meets. He acquires three fiancees in the course of the play, every one of whom is after his money, as are their relatives and Cheviot's supposed friend Belvawney. The play's first act is set on the border between England and Scotland, whose differing marriage laws make it possible that Cheviot may have become unknowingly hitched. The second act, in London, makes hilarious hay of his predicament and its ramifications; the third flags a bit, as by now we've got the message that everyone is mercenary and have to wait around until they've all got paired off in a straight-faced parody of a happy ending.

By and large, though, the play is a delight, certainly as directed at the Shaw by Morris Panych on wittilyexaggerated sets, exteriorrural and interior-urban, by Ken MacDonald. Gray Powell gives a superb performance as Cheviot, distinguished by his capacity to change course multiple times in a single sentence without ever losing the thread. Diana Donnelly, trailing the longest of wedding trains (Charlotte Dean did the costumes) is comparably delicious as a self-proclaimed innocent who is also a self-confessed gold-digger; Nicole Underhay can be very funny as her rival, though she doesn't place her tragedyqueen outbursts in the right ironic perspective. Jeff Meadows is affable as Belvawney though without the hypnotic intensity the character is said to have when he takes his glasses off. Martin Happer is wonderfully lachrymose as a kilted peasant whose occupation is to block railway trains so that his neighbours may make money off the stranded passengers. Shawn Wright is admirable as a moderately heavy father, and out of this world when he sings an old music-hall song entitled My Mother Doesn't Know I'm on the Stage. Poor mother.

National Post

The Dance of Death is in repertory until Sept. 10, Engaged until Oct. 23.

The story so far: Naz Khan, a mild-mannered student of Pakistani parentage living in Queens, is invited to a party in Manhattan. His lift lets him down so he borrows, without asking, the taxi of which his father is one-third owner-operator.

He doesn't know how to turn off the on-duty sign so he gets repeatedly hailed. And one of his would-be passengers he actually picks up: an attractive young woman who invites him to her brownstone, plies him with drink and drugs, and takes him to bed. He wakes up next morning in the kitchen, looks into the bedroom, and finds his hostess dead, her body covered in knife-wounds. Terrified, he drives away but is caught making an illegal left turn. The cops who arrest him are called away to the real crime scene, taking Naz with them. And so, inexorably, he finds himself, on strong circumstantial evidence, up on a murder charge. Denied bail, he awaits trial on the notorious Rikers Island.

That's what's happened in the first three episodes of The Night Of, the eight-part miniseries that's the best thing to happen to TV drama in general, and HBO in particular, since The Wire. There's more, of course. Towards the end of Episode One we meet Jack Stone, a down-on-hisluck attorney (it seems like he's always been down on his luck) prowling the police station where Naz is first held, and pricking up his ears at the chance of snagging a high-profile case. When Naz protests his innocence and insists that he's telling the truth, Stone shuts him up: "I don't need to be stuck with the truth. Not till I have to be. I need to be flexible." But apparently he can't be flexible enough. He asks Naz's parents for a retainer of $55,000 - a low fee but astronomically more than they can afford. He's outmanoeuvred by a another lawyer, a far more elegant and successful brand of ambulance-chaser, who offers to take on the case pro bono. It hardly seems cynical to assume that the good in that Latin phrase will mostly accrue to her: win or lose, it will be great publicity.

The Night Of is based on a British series (which I haven't seen) called Criminal Justice: a title with more bite to it, and a better indication of the show's real concerns. We're used to American TV re-doing British shows and ruining them (that includes House of Cards; it very much includes House of Cards) but in this case, title apart, I find it hard to believe that the original could have been better than the imitation.

The New York setting counts for a lot. Richard Price, writer, and Steven Zaillian, director, play it - in an insistent, low-key way - for all it's worth. The police-station scenes, spread across two weeks, staffed by weary and hard-bitten, but by no means malevolent professionals, builds up an extraordinary head of tension just by going slow and realistic. We could be sitting in any waitingroom. There sat Naz, as yet accused of nothing worse than a traffic offence, and we wait for the net to close around him. I can't think of any show that has so powerfully communicated what it must be like to be caught up in the justice system, especially if you're innocent.

Of course we don't know that Naz is innocent. The show wants us to think so, at least for now, and we want to believe it because we like him, and because we've been seeing most of the story from his perspective. In Riz Ahmed's performance, sensitive and watchful, he's very sympathetic. It's possible that he committed a murder, before blacking out and forgetting, but it doesn't feel likely. We have glimpsed a couple of other conceivable suspects, but so far they've been peripheral. The show isn't behaving like a whodunit.

When we're not with Naz we are, mostly, with Stone, and we're similarly invested in him. However much he may profess indifference, we want to believe that he believes in Naz's innocence. The role was originally slated for James Gandolfini, and it's fascinating to imagine what he would have made of a character who is, on the face of it, so unlike Tony Soprano. Stone is a legal footsoldier, rather literally; he wears sandals all the time, as his feet are afflicted by terrible eczema. Robert de Niro was mentioned for the role after Gandolfini's death, but fortunately it went to John Turturro, who is wonderfully wry and tired and downbeathumorous. We certainly root for him against the lawyer who has supplanted him, and who commandeered an Indian junior from her office ("India? Pakistan? What's the difference?") to act as interpreter when she called on Naz's parents: this despite the fact that the Khan family all speak perfect English.

"It's a big club, the criminal justice system," says Detective Dennis Box, consummately played by Ian Camp, warning Naz against Stone because he scents competition. Stone might say the same about him, and with equal truth. Box is the quintessential good cop, both professionally and in the sense of the one who acts like he's on your side so that you'll confess. His demeanour isn't always that civilized, but he never loses his cool. "If I were to turn you upside down," he asks a black witness, "how much weed is going to fall out?" The same black man had previously greeted Naz on the street with, "Hey, Mustafa, you leave your bomb at home?" Another black guy, a client of Stone's, protests at being handed a longer sentence than the white-collar offender who preceded him, and is told by the judge, "You want Jew time, you do a Jew crime." This is the casual hierarchy of racism that the show suggests.

This show is real, freshly thought and written and performed, and truly disturbing. We not only want to know what happens next. We want to know how.

THEATRE REVIEW

Sweeney Todd

Festival Theatre, Niagara-on-the-Lake

Jackie Maxwell's outgoing production as artistic director of the Shaw Festival is a big musical. Thats fitting, as it was she who introduced musicals to the Shaws main stage with her 2005 staging of Gypsy. It's also gratifying: Sweeney Todd: The Demon Barber of Fleet Street is the best musical production ever to grace the Festival Theatre stage.

The satisfaction starts in the orchestra pit. From the first dark notes of the introductory Ballad of Sweeney Todd, this musical thriller musically thrills. I had forgotten the quivering excitement that Stephen Sondheim's score can generate when played by an orchestra of the right size. The Shaws production restores the Jonathan Tunick orchestrations from the shows 1980 premiere, and has the resources to do them justice. The string figure that underlies the opening number sounds, as it should, like something echoing from the murkiest depths of the River Thames. Paul Sportelli's musical direction is, as usual, immaculate.

Nearly as impressive as the orchestral work is the choral. The Ballad, with its racing rhythms and crashing chords, is introduced by a succession of isolated solo voices. In Maxwell's production, designed by Judith Bowden, theyre hanging menacingly out in a huge derelict building. Suddenly, as the song takes a hairpin bend into its middle section, we behold the rest of the ensemble - which here means everyone except the shows two leads - invoking the vengeance-mad protagonist: "Swing your razor wide, Sweeney, hold it to the skies." It's the evening's second electric shock, built into the writing but seldom realized as forcefully as here. And we havent even gotten to the main ingredient.

Thats Benedict Campbell, giving what must be the performance of his life in the title role. What's remarkable about it is how firmly grounded it is, and how terrifyingly it rises from that ground. The show's ultimate source is a Victorian melodrama in which the demon barber slits his customers throats while his accomplice Mrs. Lovett turns the corpses into meat pies, neither of them for any discernible reason beyond fun and presumably profit. It isnt clear how Sweeney built up his clientele. It can hardly have been through word of mouth, since all the mouths had been closed. In the 1970s, an English playwright, Christopher Bond, adapted the original, supplying Sweeney with a motive: a powerful judge had raped his wife, stolen their daughter, and had Sweeney himself transported to Australia on a trumped-up charge. He has escaped and has returned to London, bent on revenge. Bond's story is the one the musical tells, its reach extended and its impact intensified by Sondheim's music and lyrics, encased in a script by Hugh Wheeler thats short on dialogue, but strong on structure.

Of all the Sweeneys Ive seen, Campbell's is the most believable barber. He isn't a flashy demon at the start; hes an artisan, proud of his skills but consumed, naturally enough, with a terrible brooding bitterness. As he learns more of whats happened during his absence, the rage turns to obsession; reunited with the tools of his trade - my friends he calls them in one of the music's most dangerously lyrical passages - he's both professionally and murderously elated. When the judge escapes his clutches, obsession becomes possession, as he embarks on a career of mass murder; "they all deserve to die" he proclaims, not excluding himself. The meat-pie proposal tickles his new-found nihilism; for the first time, he laughs. But the practical craftsman never disappears; the immediacy of Campbells transitions, the intensity with which he lives each moment, had me constantly on the edge of my seat. In his handling of a demanding score, theres scarcely any detectable strain. I have never seen a better Todd.

In the damnable equation that makes atrocity possible, Mrs. Lovett is the indispensable other half: the amoral functionary to Sweeney's deranged visionary. Corinne Koslo starts out shrill; placed too far upstage, her celebration of The Worst Pies in London lacks both verbal and visual clarity. After that, though, she's wonderful: sentimental on the outside, ruthless underneath, not least in the precision of her comic timing. Her By the Sea is a joy, the best rendition ever. The productions storytelling is first-rate, sped along by Valerie Moores purposefully grotesque choreography, clarified and punctuated by Alan Brodie's lighting. The set turns into a cage for the madhouse to which Sweeney's daughter Joanna is confined, and from which she escapes with a homicidal readiness that shows her to be a chip off the old block. The inmates swarm onto the streets taking over the city, in a sequence whose staging matches the astonishing confidence of Sondheims non-stop score.

Notable supporting performances include Jeff Irvings fresh-voiced, lovestruck sailor, Patty Jamieson's tragically crazed beggarwoman, Jay Turvey's oily beadle, and Kyle Blairs vocally and physically acrobatic Signor Pirelli, rival barber and blackmailing mountebank. Tobias, his illused apprentice, is played by Andrew Broderick with exaggerated grotesquerie early on, but with real poignancy later. Its a pity, though, that the production, like others before it, underplays his final rebuke of the herovillain: "you shouldn't hurt people, Mr. Todd." It's the shows saving moral gesture, and the only one it needs.

There are a few other flaws. Marcus Nances judge is finely sung but weakly acted. Sweeney's trick-chair, dispatching his victims to Mrs Lovett's bakery basement, doesn't function with the proper cheerful efficiency. There are no oven doors for what should be the story's ghastly climax. Otherwise the production on the first night roared its way to a standing ovation, unanimous and deserved. The show has always been a tour-de-force. This time it feels like a masterpiece.

In repertory until October 19.

THEATRE REVIEW

Father Comes Home From the Wars (Parts I , II , III )

Young Centre , Toronto A black man, named Hero, is in the woods, somewhere in the South during the American Civil War. He wears a Confederate uniform, though he isn't altogether a soldier, more of a valet, attending on the colonel whose plantation slave he was before the war and whose military slave he is now. The colonel is there too, and so is a Union soldier, a captain apparently, whom they captured on the battlefield where he had been left with a wounded leg. The colonel, wanting to impress, puts a treasured white plume on his hat, says he used to wear it all the time: "Now I just mostly carry it around in a box." He adds, off-handedly, "Hero made the box."

This is called keeping your eye on the object: the writer's eye and the audience's too. Thought and feeling made flesh, words turned into action, action into words. A complex situation made achingly, wittily concrete. It's what drama is about. It happens time and time again in Father Comes Home From the Wars (Parts I, II and III) by the American playwright Suzan-Lori Parks, first seen in New York two years ago, and now given its Canadian premiere in Weyni Mengesha's soul-stirring Soulpepper production.

Six further parts, bringing the narrative up to the present, have yet to be seen, perhaps because they have yet to be written. It's best to regard what we have in the meantime as a single play in three acts. The act from which I've quoted is the middle one: the most naturalistic of the three, the most concentrated, the most gripping and suspenseful. The surrounding two are as powerful and as real, but more stylized, partly written in verse (though you hardly notice). It incorporates the equivalent of a Greek chorus.

It's all Greek, at least in outline. The template is Homer's Odyssey with Hero himself as Ulysses. He even adopts that name, having heard stories about northern general Ulysses S. Grant that lay especial emphasis on his craftiness. Hero would like to be crafty, but he comes off more as opportunist, and not always sure of which opportunity to grab.

Act One finds him on the Texas plantation, with his fellow-slaves making bets on whether or not he'll go to the war. The master has promised him his freedom if he goes, but he's made that promise before and broken it. Then there's the complication that if Hero does go and fight he'll be fighting against his freedom. His adoptive father and Penny, his almost-wife, give him conflicting advice; they even contradict themselves.

This is to be a recurring situation; in each part of the play, in varying circumstances, somebody will be faced with the agonizing choice of moving on or staying put: "Two sides of the same coin. And the coin ain't even in your pocket." Even before the play started, Hero, we learn, had made another kind of choice. Another slave had tried to escape, and Hero had betrayed him. He had then, on master's orders and tempted by master's promises, cut off the fugitive's foot. The victim is still very much around. His name is Homer.

So we have a Hero who isn't heroic and a Homer who is lame rather than blind. Parks is playful with her sources. Like his Odyssean prototype, Hero has a faithful dog, humorously named Odd-See; and when, in Act Three, he returns from the war, he too has to contend with his Penelope's rival suitors, or in this case with one. In other respects he appears in his homecoming less like the classical Ulysses than like Ulysses's supremely tactless comrade Agamemnon, as depicted in the Greek tragedy that bears his name. The play also references Shakespeare - especially Henry V - and, perhaps more surprisingly, Rodgers and Hammerstein.

Mengesha's direction is spare, clear and driving, on an impressively raw set by Lorenzo Savoini, lit with pitiless exactness by Kevin Lamotte. Dion Johnstone's Hero is remarkable in the sympathy he arouses for a character who hardly does an admirable thing. He's trapped, partly by his own choices, partly by history, and is aware enough to know it.

When Smith, the Yankee prisoner (a fine performance by Gregory Prest of an apparently open-hearted man with secrets to keep) tempts him with visions of freedom, he sees clear through to the present: "When a Patroller comes up to me, when I say, I'm my own and I own my ownself, you think they'll leave me be ?" The interplay between the three actors in this central section is beyond praiseworthy.

Oliver Dennis, who has never been better, is cunningly casting for the colonel; first seen singing and strumming a banjo, he seems a poorer, slighter man than the "Boss-Massa-Boss " whom we've imagined as the terror of the plantation. But that's the point. "I am grateful every day ," he says, "that God made me white;" it's all he has to cling to, that and owning other people. He asks the shocked Smith to guess Hero's monetary value. He enjoys baiting both of them. But his playing with Hero's freedom is only partly sadistic; it's a war between his own best and worst impulses. He is, unexpectedly, the most complex character in the play.

Runner-up would be Homer whom Daren A. Herbert, previously known for musicals, endows with an explosive mix of biting intelligence and frustrated devotion. All the actors meet the high emotional bars their author sets. Lisa Berry's Penny, a little stiff in the first act, rises in the third to thrilling levels of sustained angry passion. Walter Borden is a wily Oldest Old Man, Hero's fatherfigure. Peter Fernandes bounds and yelps delightfully as a messenger whose identity it would be unkind to reveal. Divine Brown supplies gorgeously sung commentary. The spoken chorus (Akosua Amo-Adem, Roy Lewis, Marcel Stewart) appear in the first act as Hero's fellow workers and in the last as fugitives from other plantations; they are individually compelling, though occasionally awkward in the semi-colloquial way that Greek choruses, real or imitation, tend to be.

The writing is hugely versatile, in tone, form, flavour and even period; "mark it " is a signature phrase at the beginning, "true dat " at the end. It's hardly a spoiler to say that the play concludes with Emancipation proclaimed, so it seems the runaways didn't have to run away. A greater irony, implicit but poised to erupt in future instalments, is that emancipation was only the first step on a still unfinished journey.

This is the most exhilaratingly ambitious American play to reach us since Stephen Adly Guirgis'The Last Days of Judas Iscariot. It has the feel of greatness.

robert. cushman @hotmail. com Father Comes Home From the Wars (Parts I , II and III ) runs until August 27 at the Young Centre in Toronto

With some plays, the more you update them, the more they date.

When Henrik Ibsens A Dolls House first hit the stage in 1879, it did so with the force of a thunderclap. Its presentation of a woman walking out of a stifling and infantilizing marriage was denounced as blasphemous by some, hailed as liberating by others. Productions since then, set in or near the original period, continued to seem topical, not so much in what they show as in what they foreshadow. Audiences have the double satisfaction of weighing how much has changed against how much has not. A modern-dress revival forecloses on that. Which is what happens in Daniel Brooks' Soulpepper production. It tries to force relevance down our throats instead of letting us discover it for ourselves.

Ibsen's Nora Helmer is the wife of a banker, Torvald Helmer, who calls her his squirrel" and his "little fritter bird." The latter is a reference to her spending and shopping habits which he finds somewhere between endearing and exasperating. Their lifestyle accurately reflects that of a middle-class family of the time: a fragment of humanity, but large enough for theatrical and political traction. Today, even within that fragment, they would be an anomaly. The Helmers have two children, a maid and a full-time nanny. Nora has never had a job. Talk about rich peoples problems.

And they do have problems.

Years before, when Torvald was ill, Nora secretly borrowed money for his recuperative holiday, forging a signature to get her hands on the necessary 48,000. (Dollars? Kroner? Frank McGuinness adaptation keeps the Norwegian names but everything else about it sounds North American.) Now a blackmailer appears, threatening to tell if she doesn't persuade her husband to give him a job at the bank.

Since the man has a criminal record, and Torvald prides himself on his respectability, this is a long shot. Eventually, all is revealed, and Torvald, as uptight as he's upright, proposes a cover-up while reading Nora a lecture on how criminally irresponsible she has been and how she can never be allowed to contaminate their children. Nora realizes she herself is being treated like a child, just as she always has been. Despite his entreaties, she leaves, slamming the door: a sound-effect that shattered the audiences of the time and still reverberates today.

Which doesnt mean that all the narrative details hold up in a contemporary setting. To make them fit, desperate measures seem called for, and the two leading performances certainly supply them. Katherine Gauthier is unafraid to go to extremes, as she proved to great comedic effect in Tartuffe a couple of years ago. Watching her Nora and, to a lesser extent, Christopher Morris Torvald, I was torn between admiring their audacity and doubting their veracity.

Gauthier plays the early Nora by sliding between different notes of giggly hysteria, without a hint of the steel that enabled her to carry through what was, after all, a fairly daring scheme. I doubted that she would be able to carry off the transition to self-awareness. She does manage it, but only by doubling down on the hysterics.

Morris matches her; having presented Torvald as a cartoon of boyish smugness, he now goes on a crying jag of his own. He also feels her up a lot and even strips, as if to remind us, contrary to what we may have heard, 19th century people had sex. When we get to their final confrontation, there seems to be nothing real at stake. There's no indication Nora has any qualms about giving up her children even though this production, unlike

some, has brought them on stage.

We merely feel they'll be better off without her, as they seem to have a very competent nanny; Michelle Fisk, who plays her, is very competent too.

Good productions of A Dolls House keep you on edge with the realization these are flawed but caring people with things to gain and to lose. They tell a good story, which Brooks production fails to do. It makes no narrative sense of Dr. Rank, the friend who's dying of an unspecified disease. Diego Matamoros at least makes him effective as the messenger of death; on that level it's a fine performance.

Theres a superlative performance, however, from Damien Atkins as the blackmailer Krogstad, a once-decent man desperate to regain that decency (and beyond caring what it takes); ruthlessness and shame come beautifully, scarily, even movingly, together.

The production, on an ice-cold set by Lorenzo Savoini, has a certain visual style, though with plenty of oddities: some but not all the characters make their entrances in zombie-ish slow motion. Perhaps theyre meant to be things in Nora's dream, one that she only escapes when she makes her final exit through the auditorium. If that's the idea, it hardly adds anything.

Soulpeppers production of The 39 Steps is also overwrought, though in a different way. It has a lengthy pre-history. John Buchans spy-novel appeared in 1915. Alfred Hitchcock famously filmed it in 1935. Fifty years after that, there was a British stage version of the movie, in which four actors played all the roles; that must have been fun, a straight dramatization with the constant quick-changes supplying a comic edge. But then, courtesy of another British writer, Patrick Barlow, came an adaptation of the adaptation in which the edge moved to the centre. This unrelentingly farcical parody, a huge hit in London and New York, is the version we have here.

I think it's dire: a 10-minute spoof stretched over more than two hours. Once again four actors play, by the program's count, more than 150 characters. Or rather, three actors play more than 149 characters while the fourth confines himself to merely one. This is Kawa Ada who, as the stiff-lipped hero Richard Hannay, reaps all the benefits of being the straight man when everyone else is playing the fool. He was the only performer who made me laugh, or at least elicited some appreciative chuckles. He also smokes a pipe very well.

His male cohorts, Andrew Shaver and Anand Rajaram, are billed as Clowns 1 and 2 and, under Ravi Jains undeniably energetic direction, they knock themselves out. Rajaram tends to be all over the place, especially vocally, but Shaver has some real distinction, especially as Mr. Memory, a music-hall artiste whos the unconscious repository of the secrets everybody seeks. Raquel Duffy is painful as a Germanic femme fatale, quickly and mercifully dispatched, but redeems herself as a neglected crofter's wife - I mean a crofter's neglected wife - even managing to smuggle in some human feeling. Ada does the same, when obliged to deliver a political stump-speech on the heels of an endless sequence involving two doddering Scotsmen.

Most of the action takes place in Scotland, where the accents seem based on the idea that incomprehensibility is automatically funny. I have a pet theory: an audience, given the hint of a plot, will do their damnedest to follow it and will resent anything that gets in the way. Judging by the hilarity that surrounded me, Im wrong.

All the same, the bits that work best here are the ones in which the narrative manages to assert itself. Most of the time, the show is making fun of a story that - again - it cant be bothered to tell.

A Doll's House runs until Aug. 27, The 39 Steps until Sept. 3.
