THEATRE REVIEW

Bunny Studio Theatre, Stratford

"Show, don't tell" is one of the cardinal rules of playwriting, and like most rules it can be broken.

Nobody has broken it more consistently and successfully than Hannah Moscovitch. She first came to wide notice with The Russian Play, which everybody remembers as a monologue but was actually a firstperson narrative with inset scenes involving two other actors. She retained and refined this format in several of her subsequent plays, and in her new one, Bunny, commissioned and premiered by Stratford, she returns to it, full-strength. The result is an often-scintillating piece that only slackens when, perversely, it doesn't tell us enough.

Bunny is the nickname that one of her friends gives to the play's protagonistnarrator

on account of the caught-in-the-headlights look that comes over her in social situations. Her actual name is Sorrel, bestowed on her by left-wing academic parents who "disapproved of beauty unless it was painted by Van Gogh." She inherits their politics and their scholarship but not their intellectual puritanism. (They approve of sex, at least in principle and when it isn't too loud.) Shy and gawky growing up, she has a passion for Victorian novels. At 17, she discovered boys and they discovered her. She found kissing very enjoyable, and did as much of it as possible, shortly making the logical progression to more intimate encounters. She became known as "a hot dork," the apparent contradiction making her all the more desirable; other girls came up with less affectionate descriptions.

We watch Sorrel as a highschooler, losing her virginity to a football hero; as an undergraduate, beginning a long-running affair with a married professor; as a career academic, marrying a politically ambitious businessman of whom her family would disapprove, whoever painted him. By the time we take our leave of her, she's a professor herself - of Victorian literature, unsurprisingly - responding, or not, to the advances of a young man in a canoe. This last scenario is forecast at the beginning of the play as part of a montage that's confusing at the time but falls into place later. All the while, Sorrel keeps up a retrospective commentary on herself and the men in her life, a running soliloquy whose tone varies between humorously self-deprecating and even more humorously self-deprecating. The sharper the humour, the deeper the sting.

This is a mode in which Moscovitch has always done well, and in which she does so again. It's also a formfitting style for Maev Beaty, who gave her first great performance in a lesser-known Moscovitch play USSR (which really was a monologue) and for whom this new one may well have been written. She uses impeccable technical poise to convey a character in constant apprehension of losing whatever poise she has. Every word, every wince, every nervous smile, is perfectly timed, perfectly true: wit in the service of feeling. Her male partners, all excellent, are Cyrus Lane as the adulterous lecturer; Tim Campbell the pink-shirted image of a robust politician in waiting; and Emilio Vieira and David Patrick Flemming as the younger guys at either end of the chronological spectrum.

The writing, the acting, and Sarah Garton Stanley's direction together offer something rare: good, frank theatre about sex, erotic without being exploitative.

We watch and listen to Sorrel trying to find her moral compass. She's vague about where it may be; the only trouble is, so is the play. The constant references to her Victorian literary heroines aren't much help. They might be more so if she was more specific about which ones they are; it's not as if all the female protagonists of Victorian novels were identical. My own guess is that Sorrel would like to be Dorothea Brooke (Middlemarch) while fearful of turning into an unexpurgated version of Becky Sharp (Vanity Fair), but, voluble though she is, she never lets on.

And then there's the one character in the play about whom Sorrel, in her storytelling capacity, says nothing: Maggie, her best, maybe her only, female friend, the one who names her Bunny, and who first appears riding a bicycle and offering cautionary advice. She offers more of it, though not from a bike, in later scenes, even as tragedy begins to envelop her own life. This, Sorrel eventually tells her, is the most important relationship she has (there's no suggestion that it's sexual), but we have to take that on trust, because their scenes together provide no proof beyond the bare statement. In fact, Sorrel as narrator seems to consider their friendship too strong or too sacred to require comment. It isn't, even though Krystin Pellerin as Maggie adds another to the production's roster of fine performances. (As does Jessica B. Hill in the late-arriving role of Maggie's daughter.)

Nonetheless, what seems meant to be the point is blunted, because the play won't show and Sorrel/Bunny won't tell. But what precedes and surrounds it should charm you.

National Post robert.cushman@hotmail.com

In repertory until September 24.

David Hou / Maev Beaty stars as Sorrel, left, and David Patrick Flemming as Angel in Bunny.

THEATREREVIEW

The Hypochondriac Festival Theatre, Stratford

Moliere's The Hypochondriac is famous as the comedy whose author-star, a far from imaginary invalid, collapsed on stage at the fourth performance, dying that same night because the doctors he had been mocking refused to come to his aid. That's a pretty hard act to follow, and I wouldn't want any production to try. Still, the legendary circumstances of that original run may have given the play a critical status in excess of its actual merits.

Or so I've often thought.

In what was - of necessity - his last play, Moliere was re-cycling a formula he had used many times before: middle-aged monomaniac wants to marry off his daughter, natural or adopted, though she's in love with somebody else. The obsessive protagonist may, in previous plays, have been a jealous guardian, a religious fanatic, or a miser. Argan, the central figure here, is miserly, but he's principally a man in rude health - the jokes about this are especially rude - who fancies himself at death's door, and wants to have a doctor in the family.

It had always seemed to me that a static satire on the medical profession and its victims was being padded out by a conventional and perfunctory love-plot. Antoni Cimolino's Stratford production comes closer than any before to changing my mind.

The success owes something to the choice of translation and more to the choice of leading man. Stephen Ouimette's Argan is a self-pitying tyrant who somehow remains likable. There's an innocence about his delusions, a toughness too. He's never hysterical; he simply cannot conceive that anyone could disagree with him, even though nearly everybody does. And in fact, on everyday subjects, he can be quite hard-headed; the most delightful parts of Ouimette's performance are his deviations, abrupt but seamless, into common sense; this includes his ability, almost unheard-of in classic comedy, to see through another character's disguise. He's also quite moving when some of the scales fall from his eyes. Everything about this performance is delicately done, but it still lands with maximum force. Or, given Ouimette's supremacy in the genre, maximum farce.

Delicacy is not perhaps the quality one most associates with this play. House-calls and pharmaceuticals don't seem to have come cheap in 17th-century France, and Argan's opening speech finds him resentfully counting the money he's spent on lotions, pills and enemas. Especially enemas. They seem to work: Argan's frantic excursions offstage to relieve himself become a running gag (if that's the expression I want) that Ouimette

manages to make palatable (again, if that's the word I want). It happens more frequently and more explicitly in Richard Bean's adaptation than in Moliere's original, but Bean, who made Goldoni live again in One Man Two Guv'nors, is only following where his master led him. He goes furthest perhaps in bringing on stage an outsized fully-operational anal pump.

He also supplies a steady stream of really funny lines, along with some that merely try to be, and makes the love-interest more interesting, and more entertaining, than I would have thought possible. Also more class-conscious: Moliere's Cleante, wooing Argan's daughter Angelique, is no gallant in particular. Bean makes him an apprentice in

a factory that has made Argan rich but that he never visits. In the evening's most dazzling scene, Cleante disguises himself as Angelique's music master, and the two of them improvise a comic opera, singing their love while deceiving their audience; the idea is Moliere's, the development Bean's, and the performances entrancing. Luke Humphrey and Shannon Taylor renew their chemistry from Shakespeare in Love, with Taylor adding a top-class soprano.

There's a fine quorum of quacks: Peter Hutt, David Collins, Rylan Wilkie and, as the prize idiot who's Argan's designated son-in-law, Ian Lake in a mountainous wig, declaiming his contempt for such newfangled notions as the circulation of the blood. As Toinette, the indispensable managing maid, Brigit Wilson is needlessly strident, and as Beline, Argan's scheming second wife, Trish Lindstrom leaves me wondering, for the second time this season, where her subtlety has gone.

She may well have felt though, that subtlety would be wasted on her role in this adaptation, which makes Beline not just rapaciously eager for her husband's demise but having it off on the side with the lawyer who's preparing his will.

This is one of Bean's less happy alterations; a better one comes when Argan is confronted and berated by his commonsensical brother Beralde, to whom Ben Carlson brings his customary vigour and lucidity. In the original Beralde is contemptuous of all doctors; here he has a certain respect for science, reserving his scorn for what we would now call alternative medicine. The play also gets a new frame. Moliere was persecuted by the clerical establishment of his day but protected, to some extent, by King Louis XIV, to whom he paid glowing, even cloying, tribute in Tartuffe. The production's conceit is to present the play as a command performance at court; we get a pre-show, the company going through their choreographic paces as they first await and then salute the royal arrival. It seems as if the play proper will never start, but the delay pays off with a surprise horizontal entrance by Ouimette.

From time to time thereafter, the players interrupt the action and go into full sycophantic mode, delivering interpolated panegyrics to the monarch, to whom they refer every time by his full name and number, as if he needed to be reminded. Moliere ended his play with a masquerade, a kind of dream, in which Argan, his faith in medicine undimmed, is inaugurated into the college of physicians, becoming doctor and patient in one. This is generally thought to be a brilliant satiric conclusion though in performance it always comes off as aimless and anticlimactic. So it does here, but this time it isn't the climax.

There's an ending after the ending. Now it's true that to appreciate it you have to know, from the program since the production doesn't make it clear, that the actor playing Argan is supposed to be Moliere and the actress playing his daughter is his young wife Armande. (Was Moliere the Woody Allen of his day?) If you do know this, the evening ends with a bang.

I won't give away the details, but if I say that at this point the play meets its legend you may well guess them. It's powerful and sobering anyway. The preceding production is uneven, but it has the pace and gusto of Cimolino's recent work in comedy. It isn't, Ouimette's title performance apart, in the same league as The Alchemist last year. But then neither is the play.

In repertory through October 14.

David Hou / From left, Stephen Ouimette as Argan-Moliere, Shannon Taylor as Angelique-Armand Bejart and Brigit Wilson as Toinette co-star in Moliere's The Hypochondriac.
2016-09-08-scandinavia-on-stage-in-canad:
A Little Night Music Avon Theatre, Stratford

Never marry a Scandinavian, advises the aged Madame Armfeldt in A Little Night Music. Canadian theatre this year has been doing its best to prove her right. We've had Ibsen at Soulpepper, Strindberg at Shaw, and at Stratford another Ibsen and Night Music itself, the musical of an Ingmar Bergman movie. Not a happy domestic arrangement in any of them, though the musical at least suggests that, after the final curtain, one might exist.

One hopes so, because Ben Carlson and Yanna McIntosh, the sadder-butwiser couple here, give performances that are terrific individually, and dynamite together. The show is based on Bergmans Smiles of a Summer Night and sticks remarkably close to it, in story if not in style.

The transforming factor is Stephen Sondheims score, a new kind of operetta, dry and sparkling. The Night Waltz that opens and underpins the action is as tantalizingly beautiful a tune as has ever been heard in a musical, a vocal overture that bewitches the ear even before we hear any lyrics. Stratford's production, like the Shaw's Sweeney Todd, has a large orchestra to do the score justice, and also some fine voices, especially those of the quintet who wander in and out of the action. The principal principals are Fredrik Egerman, Swedish lawyer, and Desiree Armfeldt, Swedish actress. They were lovers long ago; now hes on his second marriage, to a much younger and stillvirgin wife, shes involved with a vain and foolish and married dragoon. The musical's main project is to bring them together: two intelligent people, compromised by previous bad choices and almost trapped by them.

Carlson's Fredrik excels at snatching victory from the jaws of ridicule; hes the only actor ever to make me laugh out loud at the wit of his opening song, in which he fantasizes about seducing his untouched bride while undressing for bed, knowing all along that he will settle for falling asleep. McIntoshs Desiree is an unpretentious

diva who radiates humour and common sense. Their first scene together, when he visits her in her lodgings and ends up in her bed ("what are old friends for?"), is a delight. Their second, the one in which she, thinking she'll never reach him, sings Send In the Clowns, had me in tears: not just the song, though she sings it beautifully, but the feelings, subtly conveyed by both, that have brought them to this impasse.

At the end, when fate and other people have cleared the way for them and surging strings signal the song's reprise and they fall gratefully into one anothers arms because really theres nothing else they can do, we laugh and cry all over again.

Carlson shares another delightful duet with Juan Chioran's preening dragoon, the two of them warily sizing one another up while lamenting their enthrallments to the same woman. Elsewhere Chioran may be too visibly enjoying himself, but the enjoyment is infectious, and he rises with just the right mixture of nobility and absurdity to his one moment of dignity at the end. You can almost believe his wife would want him back, though Cynthia Dale endows her with so much wounded intelligence that you wonder why she'd bother.

Alexis Gordon plays Fredriks unawakened wife and Gabriel Antonacci, the gauche seminarian stepson who adores and eventually wins her, leaving his father ironically free.

They both sing gorgeously and act winningly, though Gordon overdoes the bubbling innocence; she doesnt let her character grow.

Somewhat similarly, Sara Farb as the Egermans' maid sings The Miller's Son, her hedonist anthem, excitingly, but it seems to come out of nowhere. Rosemarie Dunsmore gives an efficient account of Desirees mother, the rich retired courtesan as commentator, but she isnt one of nature's grandes dames, and she can't make her sub-Wildean epigrams sound funny; the only Madame As who have are Angela Lansbury, by being a great actress, and Hermione Gingold, by being Hermione Gingold.

Gary Griffins direction is strong on storytelling, both in and between the songs. Debra Hanson's sets are all right for the vernal second act, and very strange for the urban first one, which is dominated by a line of smokestacks. Mostly, though, this is a lovely production of a piece that seems to grow richer with the years.

A Little Night Music is in repertory through Oct. 23.
2016-09-14-first-rate-second-city:
THEATRE REVIEW

Come What Mayhem Second City, Toronto

Come What Mayhem!, Second City's 78th revue hits its peak, as a good revue should, at the end of its first half. The number in question is that hardy perennial, a game-show sketch. The game thats being played is called You Oughta Know. A hyper host puts questions to three contestants, two of them his fellow cast-members, the third a volunteer (well, she didnt actually say no) from the audience. Unusually for this kind of number, the questions are about what we may loosely call Current Affairs: fairly basic ones like "who is the president of Turkey?" or what do the initials of ISIS stand for. You can feel the theatre audience guiltily racking its own brains over that one.

The rehearsed performers, of course, come up with answers of inspired ineptitude, like identifying the capital of Syria as S. Their impromptu colleague naturally cannot be relied upon to get things so hilariously wrong but I have to say that the gallant lady on my night got thoroughly into the spirit. She did best of all, though, when on her last go-round she got an answer right. The question was "who is Kanye West married to?" At which point the host, who had reached increasing heights of righteous hysteria at each successive display of ignorance, finally exploded. Why he screamed, in the vocal equivalent of italics and capital letters combined "is that what you know?" He could have been indicting all of us.

Roger Bainbridge, a newcomer to Second City's mainstage, plays the demented quizmaster, and he's a find. He brings a comparable, though quieter, moral-satiric edge to the show's closing number which, again in the best revue tradition, represents a second peak. It has him speculating on what a terrorist attack might be like if it happened, say, close to where we were sitting. Or exactly where we were sitting. The show makes a good running gag out of ISIS. That is not a sentence I ever expected to write.

You may deduce that the title has more relevance than the pointless pun that generally adorns the Second City marquee. Not that every sketch is apocalyptic, at least not on the grand scale. The show can narrow its sights without blunting its aim.

One thing this revue does better than most is punchlines. Lindsay Mullan is a versatile performer who does a fine improv bit as a daydreaming checkout clerk, autobiographically riffing off minimal information proffered by yet another intrepid audience participant. This number is educational: it may make you better understand why you have to line up so long at Shoppers Drug Mart. Kyle Dooley and Brandon Hackett provide what is known in the trade as solid male support.

This isn't the most spectacularly performed Second City show ever, but it may be the best written, at least in recent years. Not all the material is great, but none of it is bad, which in a revue is remarkable. And since at this address the performers are the writers, they earn on the swings any bouquets that they may have lost on the roundabouts. Bouquets also go to Carly Heffernan who has directed with style and speed.
2016-09-19-tims-invades-britain:
Britain is about to be invaded by Tim Hortons. Or, to quote an article in the Financial Post, "Canada's biggest coffee chain is venturing into the land of tea and crumpets."

Somebody's obviously been watching too much Downton Abbey. I grew up in England, but most of the crumpets I've eaten have been bought in Canadian supermarkets. There's also no such thing in England as an English muffin.

Tea, of course, is another matter. They do indeed drink a lot of it in Britain. It's probably why it took them so long to get out of India. But here's a funny thing: the best tea I've had in Canada has been at Tim Hortons. It's the only chain where they boil the water hot enough. It's also the only place where the lady behind the counter (it's usually a lady serving at Tims) will ask you whether you want milk and sugar, and then put it in for you, rather than waving you over to an untidy assortment of cartons and containers at the far end of the room. It's the next best thing to being served tea by your mother. In fact, anybody pouring tea in England, regardless of gender, will ask, "Shall I be mother?" They don't say that at Timmys but the thought is there.

I should add that in mentioning sugar I was paying craven homage to convention. George Orwell, in his classic essay on How to Make a Cup of Tea, said that if you put sugar in tea, you weren't drinking tea, you were drinking sugar. He went on to advise sugar-drinkers to try drinking their tea without it for a few days, promising that, if they did, they would never go back. He was right. Orwell, of course, never crossed the Atlantic. If he had, he would have found people doing even more abominable things to tea than putting sugar in it. He would have found them topping it up with cream. Still, this practice seems to be dying out in Canada, if not in the United States. That's progress.

Yes, there is such a thing in Britain as cream tea, but the cream comes separately. You put it on scones, preferably with jam. It's delicious, though I wouldn't advise having it too often.

Now, I don't know how successful Tim Hortons will be in marketing its tea to British drinkers. (I wish I could avoid mentioning coals and Newcastle, but the best I can do is parentheses.) I realize that it probably isn't what the company has in mind, and it certainly isn't what it's best known for at home. Maybe it can bring something new to the coffee market. When I first came to Canada, I didn't know what a double-double was, and I was shocked when I found out. Actually, I still am.

Britons drink a lot of coffee as well, and they don't seem to mind if it's supplied by foreigners. Starbucks is big there. Still, in terms of the number of outlets, it comes in a distant second. First place belongs to a chain that's homegrown: Costa Coffee, named not, as you might expect, because its beans come from Costa Rica, but because it was founded by two immigrant brothers from Italy named Bruno and Sergio Costa. Sergio subsequently bought out Bruno - maybe there's a movie there - and the whole operation was later bought by Whitbread, the giant British-based conglomerate that started with beer. This year Costa made a deal with Shell Canada, so its coffee may be coming soon to a service-station near you.

Perhaps the traffic can also go the other way. Perhaps. But Tims isn't Starbucks. Starbucks has a North American glamour about it. Tims is more about homeliness than glamour - it has built its reputation on being quintessentially Canadian - and that may not be exportable. Still, it does have an extra weapon, what businesspeople call a "unique selling proposition:" it has food.

Nobody goes to any of those other chains to eat. They know about doughnuts in the U.K., of course. They may even know maple doughnuts. But there's no place where doughnuts have the same cachet as they do at Tims, and they could have exotic appeal over there.

The British have notoriously sweet teeth. Though I have to say that some of Tims' recently added flavours are altogether too exotic. They're so smothered in toppings, you can't even find the hole.

But it's not just the doughnuts. My wife and I had a gourmet Canadian friend, a businessman and world traveller, whose favourite dining place was London's justly celebrated Connaught Hotel. But he was equally passionate about the chili at Tim Hortons. So am I. During the few years when Tims was allied with Wendy's, I developed a gourmet combo of my own: I would buy a chili at Tims, then go to the adjoining Wendy's and buy one of their excellent baked potatoes with sour cream and chives (eat your heart out, McDonald's) and apply the cream to the chili. Now, with the link to Wendy's broken, maybe Tims could add potatoes and sour cream to their own menu. They could even forget about the potatoes. The British might lap it up.

They might even be able to persuade the great British public to roll up the rim. But I doubt that they'll ever be able to sell them on Timbits.

National Post robert.cushman@hotmail.com

2016-09-21-at-home-at-the-zoo-eloquence-:
Edward Albee, who died last week at the age of 88, arrived in the American theatre at just the right moment. When he came along, with The Zoo Story in 1960, Arthur Miller and Tennessee Williams - the great postwar duo - had their best work behind them, and there were no apparent contenders. There was certainly no-one of international stature. It had been a while since an American dramatist had produced a play of interest to any theatre outside America.

Albee changed that; he was international from the get-go. He was also seen, initially, as an American writer in a fashionable European mode. The Zoo Story was assigned to that catch-all category, the Theatre of the Absurd, and Albee was hailed as the American heir of Samuel Beckett and Eugene Ionesco. In fact the play, a conversation piece for two men on a park bench ending in a killing, presents a situation more naturalistically credible than anything from Ionesco and its characters come with more back-story than anyone from Beckett. Albee himself reinforced the point toward the end of his life by writing a new first act to his original one-act play, presenting the domestic life of one of the duo immediately prior to his showing up on that bench. He went so far as to insist that the original Zoo Story could no longer be produced without its prequel.

What really commanded attention about the play when it first appeared was the fizz and eloquence of its language. It restored the theatre to its place in the great crackling line of American wit, even of the American wisecrack: a humour employed not, as in the plays of Neil Simon, to reassure but to unsettle.

The same quality, writ large - very large - pervaded the play that in 1963 marked Albee's breakthrough and is still his best-known work: Who's Afraid of Virginia Woolf.

A wise British director once offered a persuasive diagnosis of the blight that afflicts most contemporary drama. There are no plays, he said, with characters one can imagine future actors passionately wanting to play. He was talking about British plays, but its true of American ones, too. Virginia Woolf is an exception; ever since Arthur Hill and Uta Hagen created the roles of George and Martha, the bogged-down history professor and his flamboyantly embittered wife, major actors have been lining up to play them.

Martha may be the more legendary role of the two. In the last decade or so I have seen three great Canadian actresses - Fiona Reid, Martha Henry, Nancy Palk - triumphantly take it on. But George, in his less demonstrative counterpunching way, carries an equal share of the plays weight, maybe more, which, as his wife belatedly acknowledges, is also true of their marriage. The play has been credited with all kinds of political and metaphysical overtones, but what carries it in the theatre is its linguistic virtuosity, embedded in two compelling characters who are a master and mistress of the rhythmic put-down, directed first against one another and then - because the couple who joke together stick together - against the outsiders who have strayed into their territory. It's a high-wire act, maintained over three long acts. The length was another quality that gained Albee instant respect; it placed him in the marathon tradition of Eugene O'Neill.

His subsequent plays have been more compact, though they havent always seemed so. Tiny Alice (1965) and All Over (1971) were soporific. They seemed weighed down with significance, while giving us no human reason to be interested. Its perfectly possible that future productions will reclaim them, but I don't see any theatres lining up to try. Still, such late Miller plays as The Price and Incident at Vichy have proved unexpectedly resilient, and so has Albee's A Delicate Balance (1966), a play that re-orchestrates the domestic dynamics of Virginia Woolf for a larger ensemble, overlaying them with a quasisymbolic menace that doesnt seem meretricious.

If Albee seemed to rule the American drama of the 1960s, in the following decades his fortunes, and indeed his plays, went into a prolonged slump. But in his last decades he rallied.

The Play About the Baby (1998) is a notably deft reworking of some of the themes of Virginia Woolf, light-handed though not lighthearted; at the end it reverts to its authors characteristic biliousness. Soulpepper once gave it an enjoyable workshop presentation, with a fine performance by Juan Chioran, but it still awaits a full Toronto production; come to that, it's never had a full Broadway production. The Goat or Who Is Sylvia? (2002) was outrageous - it is indeed about a man unabashedly in love with a goat - and exhilarating.

There cannot be many writers like Albee, who commenced operations halfway through the 20th century and were still going strong at the dawn of the 21st.

Jack Mitchell, Getty Images / Pulitzer Prize-winning playwright Edward Albee, pictured in 1965, died last week at 88.
2016-09-22-asking-the-difficult-question:
THEATREREVIEW

Aunt Dan and Lemon Theatre Passe Muraille Backspace

Lemon, short for Leonora, is a solitary insomniac woman of indeterminate age who subsists on fruit and vegetable juices. She doesn't watch TV or listen to the radio, and the play in which she appears predates the Internet, but she probably wouldn't have had much use for it even if it had existed. She likes to lie in bed and read about the Holocaust, though the word itself is unlikely to have passed her lips. The formative influence on her childhood was Dan, short for Daniella, a bisexual Oxford don with a passionate admiration for Henry Kissinger.

Aunt Dan and Lemon, first seen in 1985, is the work of Wallace Shawn, known apart from his plays for being a droll cameo performer in movies and for being the son of William Shawn, for many years the editor of The New Yorker.

Aunt Dan is Lemon's aunt only by courtesy; she's a close friend of Lemon's parents and a constant presence in their house. She's an American expat, as is Lemon's father who married an Englishwoman and stayed; he professes to love nearly everything about England, especially its crumpets. He's an executive in an auto-parts company; it's a job despised by his old friends from university but he likes to point out that it comes with a load of hiring-and-firing responsibility that they couldn't possibly handle. He also has regular rows with his wife over their daughter's eating disorders.

All this is recalled for us by Lemon as the play's narrator. But what she mainly remembers are her conversations with Aunt Dan, especially the ones that took place when she was 11. Dan's main topics are sex and Kissinger, with an occasional overlap between the two. She passionately defends Kissinger's aggressive foreign policies (in her admiring mind they always seem to be his, not any president's); she argues - or rather declares - that such actions are necessary to protect the lifestyles of people like themselves. She's also sure that Kissinger, like Lemon's dad, agonizes over every painful decision. She once caught a glimpse of Kissinger in a restaurant and could see how compassionate he was. Lemon's mother disagrees, but all she can really say is that it seems wrong. She's expressing the audience's instinctive feelings, and she isn't doing a very eloquent job of it.

At the beginning and end of this play, Lemon ruminates on the care the Nazis took to conceal from the Jews what was about to happen to them and on the brutality with which they drove them, women and children included, into the gas chambers when concealment was no longer possible. She then wonders whether we condemn the Nazis only because they were so unashamed about what they did, when in fact any society will kill when it thinks it has to. And any individual will do the same. And this "compassion" that people (like her mother?) go on about: she's felt it watching movies or reading novels, but never in real life.

This is purposely awkward stuff, the most unsettling piece of devil's advocacy since the heyday of George Bernard Shaw. If the play no longer feels as shocking as it reportedly did 30 years ago, that may be partly because the name Kissinger no longer presses as many buttons. It's still a thoroughly compelling piece of theatrical writing, despite being nearly all talk, no action. Indeed, when it does get physical is when the interest slackens. Lemon, as far as we can tell, is sexless; Aunt Dan certainly isn't, or wasn't. She loves telling Lemon about Mindy, a callgirl friend whom she fancied and who would do anything for money, including kill a client. Dan has no problem with this, but it's a problem for the play; it shifts her character from being a principled if misguided advocate of ruthless realpolitik to being turned on by violence for its own sake. The play proposes a continuum from Aunt Dan's apparent amorality to Lemon's theoretical rejection of any morality at all, and dares us to prove either of them wrong. Dragging in crime-fiction lets them, and us, off the hook.

The play gets an excellent revival from a new outfit, Shadowtime Productions, directed by Dan Spurgeon on a set, by Elizabeth Traicus, that elegantly combines elements from the drama's shifting times and locales. Joanne Latimer, a flamboyantly handsome Dan, makes every line count; Helen Juvonen does the same for Lemon, and has maybe the harder task since she has to be both nagging, at our consciences, and naive.

Both are idiomatically exact, as are the rest of the cast, including Breton Lalama as Mindy and Philip Cairns who plays a variety of roles and is a dead ringer for Seinfeld's Newman. In an essay quoted in the program, Shawn wrote "we might still be able to prevent the complete triumph of evil if we recognize that the complete triumph of evil really is a possibility and that the partial triumph of evil has already occurred." He wrote that in 1986.

Until September 25.

National Post robert.cushman@hotmail.com

Roger Humbert / A scene from Wallace Shawn's Obie-winning play Aunt Dan and Lemon.
2016-10-05-sounding-off-about-nothing-on:
THEATRE REVIEW

Noises Off Soulpepper

Michael Frayn's Noises Off is, famously, a farce about the rehearsal and performance of another farce, whose ingeniously matching title is Nothing On. Nothing On is an oldschool British caper revolving, at a furious rate, around doors and underwear and sardines. The sardines being a tasty new addition to the traditional recipe. We only get to see the first act of Nothing On, though we see or at least hear it three times. This is because Noises Off presents three episodes in the life of its inset show, each more desperate than the last.

Nothing On is, we gather, a touring production, underwritten by its leading lady, an ex-sitcom star called Dotty Otley, hoping to put something by for her retirement. She is also romantically involved with at least one of her fellow actors, with much jealousy resulting. The director has been busy as well, seducing both the ingenue and the assistant stage manager. Act One of Noises Off shows us the company at a combined technical and dress rehearsal, a doubly ghastly occurrence rendered even ghastlier by stretching into the early hours of the actual opening day. In Act Two the show is on the road and we are backstage, watching the company acting out their personal feuds with whatever props come to hand.

Theyre all professionals, though, so whenever their cues come they drop everything, literally, and rush on - or, from our perspective, off - to perform their roles. Part of the genius of this act is that we always know where theyve got to, even though we can't actually see it, so well has the ground been prepared. In Act Three, the tour is on its last leg - or, as the stage manager all too accurately puts it, its last legs - and chaos has come.

Frayn once told me that he had been besieged by offers from theatre managers, begging him to write the rest of Nothing On, since it was far better than the farces they were actually producing. The first act of Soulpepper's production bears them out; most of its laughs come from the play within the play. Nothing On seems funnier than Noises Off.

This is partly due to the physical adroitness of the company, under Ted Dykstras direction, a quality that sustains and multiplies through the rest of the evening. In Act Two, especially, the performers throw themselves into hilarious heaps, even to excess. Its sometimes hard to follow who is trying to do what to whom, and why.

They aren't as limber with the words. The British comic idiom defeats several of the players, surprisingly, considering Dykstra's mastery of it as both actor and director in Soulpeppers Alan Ayckbourn productions. Brenda Robins cant find the right tone for Dotty's chosen role of the housekeeper continually robbed of her sardines. Christopher Morris goes for low camp though he's supposed to be a heterosexual threat on both the plays levels. David Storch has the proper weariness for the director, a self-proclaimed intellectual selfhatingly slumming it, but not the proper sarcasm; without that, and the actors responses to it, much of the play's verbal wit goes missing.

Completely on top of the style is Oliver Dennis as the veteran actor whose drinking problem is everyone's problem. Matthew Edison is excellent as a lascivious leading

man, and spectacularly acrobatic when falling down a flight of stairs craftily shaped to inflict maximum damage. Raquel Duffy is bang-on as the relentlessly upbeat trouper who knows all the companys secrets except for those she doesnt, and Myrthin Stagg is endearingly accident-prone as the theatrical debutante who battles on regardless, except when her contact lenses fall out: a running gag of which the production might make more than it does. Anand Rajaram, in an intriguing world of his own, has some hysterical moments as the overworked stage manager. Oyin Oladejo some appealingly earnest moments as the equally exploited assistant stage manager, though the narrative bombshell she explodes at the end of Act Two is something else that's curiously muted.

Its lack of effect rebounds onto Act Three. The end of Noises Off has always been a problem. Every production seems to try something different and nothing works. The cause, I've come to realize, is that the play doesnt have a central character. Kenneth Tynan described tragedy as "the piling of agony on a human head until it splits" and the same is true of farce, except that the fatal split is always averted at the last moment.

In Noises Off, the agony is spread democratically around so the play, despite enormous hilarity on the way, finally lacks shape and even purpose. Theres no principal sufferer for us to fix on, no personto-whom-all-this-could-not-happened-at-a-worse-time. The director comes closest, but he's too often absent: admittedly a complaint that actors frequently make about directors. His final appearance is something that nobody has ever been able to explain. This production seems to be suggesting that the finale is fantasy but farce, of all genres, cannot afford a change in convention. It needs to be mercilessly consistent.

Noises Off runs until October 22 at the Young Theatre in Toronto.

Bronwen Sharp / Matthew Edison is a lascivious leading man; / Myrthin Stagg an accident-prone theatrical debutante.
2016-10-05-the-directors-dilemma-and-the:
You can be replaced."

Those words were spoken this year to George Bernard Shaw, on one of the stages at the Niagara theatre festival that bears his name. To be precise, and to be obvious, they were spoken to an actor impersonating him. GBS was drafted as a character in a play based on, or at any rate inspired by, his short prose parable The Adventures of the Black Girl in Her Search for God. And if Shaws shade was looking down from wherever it is freethinking playwrights spend eternity he may well have reflected, ruefully, that his dethronement seemed all too likely.

For at the only theatre in the world ostensibly dedicated to him, Shaw's plays have recently been conspicuous by - well, not their absence exactly but their modesty. Or the festival's modesty on their behalf. This season, only two plays have earned him any kind of authors credit. The Black Girl was a highly-praised lunchtime show at the small Court House theatre; Mrs. Warrens Profession, the year's one actual Shaw play, was presented at the slightly larger Royal George.

These last few seasons, Shaw has indeed looked like being replaced by his contemporary and fellow Irish expatriate Oscar Wilde. Wilde's Lady Windermeres Fan had a memorable production on the main Festival stage a couple of years ago, and this year the same big space has housed his A Woman of No Importance.

Wilde duly features on the bill for the 2017 season, the first under the festivals new artistic director Tim Carroll. But now it's his turn to be the subject of an adaptation and to occupy the lunchtime slot. Under the title Stories for Children, four of his tales have been dramatized by actress-playwright Kate Hennig, who achieves a rare double. She has a new play going on at the Stratford festival as well. Meanwhile, Shaw himself is making a comeback. Two of his plays are being presented, both directed by Carroll himself who has never directed a Shaw play before, and one of them in the big theatre.

This is Saint Joan, which Carroll, who made his reputation in Shakespeare, was drawn to by its "poetry and lyricism ... its shamelessly ecstatic language. The play presents an unconventional portrait of a saint, a Catholic martyred by other Catholics, and one who in Shaw's dispensation often sounds like an inspired Irish peasant. The play used to be thought of as Shaws masterpiece, perhaps because its subject made it a suitable choice for schools. More recently, it has slipped in esteem. In London, the National Theatre recently staged a production: rather grudgingly, it seemed, because the entire Shaw canon, once a prime source of both subsidized and commercial revivals, had fallen out of favour.

Saint Joan of course is a history play. So, in its own peculiar way, is Carrolls other choice, Androcles and the Lion, which takes the old legend of the man who won a lion's undying gratitude by removing a thorn from its paw and transports it to ancient Rome. The hero becomes an early Christian about to be thrown to the lions himself. There are no prizes for guessing how the story ends. But on the way the play has many scintillating things to say about religion: more, I think, than Saint Joan. It's always been one of my favourite Shaw plays (it was the first I ever read) and this will be only its second production at the festival. Carroll himself commends its open-endedness ... the questions it raises about faith and power ... it conducts a two-way conversation with the audience." Theres a lot in the 2017 lineup that should intrigue: some plays, like Androcles, that I have always thought the Shaw should do, others that I could kick myself for never having thought of. High among the latter is the seasons big musical Me and My Girl, a big London hit in 1937 and an even bigger one in 1984 when it was revived and extensively re-worked by Stephen Fry before he was famous. With its story of English toffs infiltrated and invigorated by lovable cockneys, it should play right to the festival company's accumulated strengths in both high and low comedy.

There's a prime piece of Canadian theatrical history about a prime piece of Canadian political history - 1837: The Farmers Revolt - its authorship jointly credited to Rick Salutin and Theatre Passe Muraille, dating from that theatres glory days. Salutin was known as a playwright before he was known as a journalist, and the play is generally cited as a key text in the flowering of theatrical nationalism. Carroll approached it warily, thinking it might reflect "the insecurity of Canadian theatre but found it to have none of that - it feels happy and ebullient. The audience is opened up by comedy and then punched in the gut. It's like Middletown."

Carroll is referencing another play on next season's bill: a response by the American playwright Will Eno to his own countrys classic Our Town, so a kind of sequel to this years Shaw production of the Thornton Wilder play. From closer to our own time and place, there's a new play about Joe Clark by Michael Healey, who's already done Stephen Harper.

Then theres Alan Bennetts The Madness of George III, about the English king who's currently enjoying great theatrical celebrity, courtesy of Hamilton in which he has the funniest numbers. Bennett got there first, however, with a play that was a success in London, New York and on film, but unstaged in Canada.

The Shaw's strength, like Stratfords, has always been its comparative permanence; and Shaw, which prints a complete list of its ensemble in every program, may even have the edge here. Certainly both as companies exceed anything to be found in the U.S. or even in the U.K., where the National hasnt had one since the end of Laurence Olivier's directorate 40 years ago.

You can definitely tell the difference. There's a twoweek training session at the beginning of each Shaw season, known as the Mandate Intensive, a chance for experienced actors to pass on their accumulated skills to new ones. Beyond that there are, says Carroll, "certain actors who are fitted by nature for this kind of work, able to pull off the level of wit in Shaw or Wilde or Stoppard."

Oh, yes, Stoppard. How about The Invention of Love, definitely set in Shaws lifetime; hes even referenced in it and Wilde actually appears. This is only the 17th time I've

mentioned it.

THEATRE REVIEW

Hosanna Soulpepper

Soulpepper's revival of Hosanna, Michel Tremblays famous study of a Montreal drag-queen, includes wonderful performances, but still comes across as dated.

The apartment Hosanna (a.k.a. Claude) shares with his biker-lover Cuirette (a.k.a. Raymond) is suddenly revealed, just before the intermission, to include a four-panelled floor-to-ceiling mirror. No matter how selfadmiring Hosanna may be, this can hardly be meant to be realistic. It paves the way, however, for the second halfs shift into formality: Hosanna tells the story of his humiliation at the party to which he had gone proudly dressed as Elizabeth Taylor dressed as Cleopatra while Cuirette, who was partly responsible, antiphonally apologizes.

Hosanna's long narration, shifting between shame and anger and self-recognition, is the spellbinding crown of Damien Atkins's superb performance: his third this year. From his and the plays first moments, hes been fully alive in every flounce, every sneer, every drag - if you'll pardon the expression - on his cigarette.

That's even before he starts talking. When he does, his vocal range and emotional control are extraordinary. Jason Cadieux Cuirette gives him sympathetic support, even when his character doesnt. Their duet, under Gregory Prest's direction, is beautifully orchestrated.

This is the best production of Hosanna I've seen.

It cant, however prevent the play, now 40 years old, from seeming technically old-fashioned. It withholds information so that it can have a second act while devoting most of its first to having the characters tell each other what they already know, with a shamelessness that would have raised Ibsens bushy eyebrows. Sentimentality is kept at bay, largely due to Atkins's performance, until the end when Hosanna proclaims/admits that he's a man. At which point the director has Cuirette pick him up and carry him to bed, like a groom carrying a bride across the threshold. Is this meant to be irony? Or just a nice stage-picture to finish with?

Hosanna runs until October 15 at the Young Theatre in Toronto.
2016-10-13-dramatic-poetry-of-teenage-ta:
THEATRE REVIEW

Concord Floral CanStage Bluma Appel Theatre

Jordan Tannahill's Concord Floral is a magnetic piece of theatre. It has two poles, ancient and modern. The old one is Giovanni Boccaccio's The Decameron, the Italian counterpart of The Canterbury Tales, in which ten young people, taking shelter while fleeing plague-stricken medieval Florence, beguile the time by telling stories.

The present-day inspiration, the one that gives the play its colourful title, is in Tannahill's own programnote description, "a million-square foot abandoned greenhouse in Vaughan."

He attended a party there five years ago, and what with "the piles of old cigarette butts, broken beer bottles, underwear, used condoms, and graffiti," it reminded him of the places where he and his friends used to hang out when they were teenagers.

Tannahill was reading The Decameron at the time of the party. He put the two pieces together, making his characters 10 Grade 12 students who are reading the book as a class project (they must have an enlightened teacher), and whose favourite gathering place, other than the school cafeteria, is their very own Concord Floral. And from that place they let loose their very own plague.

It's a deceptive piece in some ways, full of surprises. We assume, from the Italian connection, that the dozen teens are all going to tell their own tales, plain or fanciful. As it turns out, there's only one story and it involves the kids themselves. There are a few personal monologues operating at a tangent to that story but we are mostly caught up in a single, driving narrative.

Two girls, named Nearly Wild and Rosa Mundi, make a night-trip to Concord Floral; Rosa drops her cellphone through one of the many holes in the floor; Nearly descends to retrieve it, and finds a dead female body. They flee the scene, in horror and terror. That night Nearly gets a call, purporting to come from the dead girl using the missing phone.

Tannahill has written a bravura script that makes dramatic poetry of teenage talk. We respond to the writing, though, less for its own sake than as one element in a tightly-wound theatrical experience. The production, directed by Erin Brubacher and Cara Spooner, has been in development for three years and has been staged, with varying casts, in Toronto, Ottawa and Whitehorse. It has always been performed by real teenagers, some of them aspiring professional actors, some not. Its first full Toronto run puts the audience up with the actors. They perform on a platform at one end of the Bluma Appel stage; we sit on risers, facing them.

The Bluma audi torium yawns beside and beneath us. Concord Floral is thrillingly concentrated, a continuous symphony of speech, movement, lighting (Kimberley Purtell) and especially sound (Christopher Willes).

The actors are microphoned which, given the confined space, doesn' t bode too well for the future of Canadian acting. Still, their voices an immediacy that comes out well in the mix. Jovana Miladinovic is fresh and unsparing as Nearly who starts out sympathetic and then reveals unsettling complexities; there is ear-catching work too from Jessica Munk as her ghostly caller, and from Franco Pang and Theo Gallaro. Some of the young people get to double as wildlife; a fox and a bobolink help tell the story and have crucial roles in it. So do inanimate objects; a couch is given a voice and so is the greenhouse itself.

There's a built-in puzzle to the story, one that gets resolved in a way that's quite unexpected and perfectly satisfying. Emotionally it lets the audience off a hook, but it doesn't do the same for the characters.

The narrative involves shaming, ganging-up and teenage groupthink; the things that it's fashionable to blame on "youth today" and social media but that the play is honest enough to admit has always been around, even if technology has made it faster and easier.

The greenhouse, Concord Floral itself, has the last word, a quotation from Susan Sontag that's also printed in the program: "10 per cent of any population is cruel, no matter what, and 10 per cent is merciful, no matter what, and the remaining 80 per cent can be moved in either direction."

It then suggests that the 80 may be moving toward mercy. It's a nice thought, but on the play's own previous showing, a pious hope.

Canstage / Concord Floral has always been performed by real teens.
2016-10-19-controller-controller:
THEATRE REVIEW

All But Gone Berkeley Street Theatre Master Harold ... and The Boys Toronto Centre for the Arts

Jennifer Tarver directs Samuel Becketts plays with iron control. A prize example is All But Gone, a kind of Beckett anthology that's a joint production of Canadian Stage and Necessary Angel.

As a playwright, Beckett was quite the control freak: his stage directions practically dictate the staging for all of his plays. All that stands between the scripts and uniformity is the stubborn individuality of actors. The Beckett play that gives its actors most scope is of course the first and most famous, Waiting for Godot. Tarver directed a fine production of Godot at Stratford a few years ago, though to call it definitive, as the CanStage press release does, is ridiculous; the same is true for her Stratford production of the briefer Krapp's Last Tape. Tarver has continually returned to what are known as Beckett Shorts, which Ive always thought should be worn with Tom Stoppards Jumpers. The new program offers four of them, with musical interludes.

The music starts the evening, performed by two opera singers, Shannon Mercer and Kristina Szabo, who are costumed as Irish peasant women and whose singing also has a keening Hibernian quality, even though the lyrics (set by an actual Irish composer, Garrett Shouldice) are in Latin. It sets the proper note, haunting and foreboding, for Act Without Words I, a solo mime that's a gloss on the myth of Tantalus. A man (Paul Fauteux) down-at-heel and probably down-and-out, rushes back and forth at the command of offstage whistles, one coming from each side. A bottle of water is dangled before him, perpetually out of his reach. He does have access to a rope but when he tries to hang himself with it, it breaks. He faces similar humiliations in Act Without Words II, which finds him supine in a sack from which he emerges at the prodding of a long hooked pole, again issuing from the wings. He engages in a series of physical jerks, looking as dejected as ever. Beside him lies another sacked man (Jonathon Young) who's subjected to the same stimulus and performs the same exercises. He, though, is dapper and cheerful about it. Both men get to eat a carrot; Fauteux finds his carrot disgusting and spits it out, Young seems to relish his and, a neat and provident soul, tucks some of it away for later consumption. Optimist and pessimist, both are condemned to reenact the same routines at the whim of a merciless universe; theyre Godots tramps deprived of the words that gave them sustenance and an audience pleasure.

Fauteux's character gets revenge when he wields a spotlight to extract jerky confessions from the other three performers in the Beckett play called Play which seems to be the Play of the moment; it also currently features in The Unending, presented by the enterprising site-specific company Convergence Theatre. Its characters are a husband, wife and mistress recounting their relationship, possibly from purgatory, at warp speed and twice over.

"Repeat play exactly," says the stage direction and they do; Beckett is very much about obedience. The two singing ladies speak their lines resonantly but without much variation; Young, the actor between them, is good at ferreting out the humour in what is one of Beckett's wittiest inventions. The same cannot be said of Ohio Impromptu, the final selection, in which one man reads while the other hears the story of a lost love. Its like Krapps Last Tape rewound and has you wishing, for once, that its author had used fewer words. Tarver's perfect-on-its-terms production leaves you feeling that there must be more to life than this while fearing that there very likely isn't.

Philip Akins production of Athol Fugards Master Harold ... and the Boys, imported from the Shaw Festival and presented by Obsidian, is perfect on anybody's terms.

It's a play rooted in autobiography, set in 1950 South Africa. Like Fugard himself in that time and place, Master Harold is a white teenage schoolboy, whose mother keeps a tea shop while his alcoholic and disabled father languishes in hospital; both parents are unseen. The "boys" are of course men, black men, Sam and Willie, who work in the shop and have been Harolds companions all his life. Sam in particular has been a surrogate father, playing with him, helping him in his studies though Harold can hardly acknowledge it. Apartheid is beginning to bite, exacerbating prejudices that were always there. In the course of a late afternoon, the relationship crumbles.

James Daly gives a wonderfully unsparing performance of Harold: defensive, mean and torn. His accent alone deserves a citation. Allan Louis, last seen by me as Julius Caesar, is now Willie, whos anything but a leader. He spends much of the play silently reacting, generally in trepidation; the amount the actor conveys through facial and bodily movement is extraordinary. Andre Sills is passionate and eloquent as Sam, though there are moments when he is too obviously his author's mouthpiece, speaking for him now while Harold represents him then. The play has other flaws; Sam is coaching Willie for a ballroom dancing contest, and the dance as an embodiment of harmony between people is a metaphor of which the characters seem too volubly aware. But this hardly hampers the emotional effect of a show in which everything looks right (set design by Peter Hartwell), sounds right, feels overwhelmingly right.

For the first time in a theatre in a long time, I wept.

All That Gone runs through November 6, Master Harold ... and the Boys through October 23

Canadian Stage / Samuel Beckett

THEATRE REVIEW

Breathing Corpses Coal Mine Theatre, Toronto

The Coal Mine Theatre seems to specialize in contemporary plays that practically scream for performance but, as far as Toronto is concerned, have hitherto screamed in vain. They may be American (Killer Joe); they may even be Canadian (Instructions to Any Future Socialist Government Wishing to Abolish Christmas). Now comes a British entry: Breathing Corpses by Laura Wade, first seen at the Royal Court Theatre in London in 2005, and a genuine seat-clutcher.

It's also a puzzle. In its first scene a hotel maid discovers a dead male body in the bed of the room shes servicing. In the last scene the same maid finds another male body in the same bed. In between we meet two other sets of characters, five people in all, one of them the man who was a corpse in the first scene. So were flashing back. The play has drawn comparisons to La Ronde, probably because of the way it circles back on itself, with the maid appearing at both ends of the evening but nowhere in the middle. But the comparison doesn't really hold because the structure doesn't give us one character from each scene moving on to the next. It more closely resembles

Harold Pinters Betrayal, which moved steadily back in time to explain, or at least illuminate, its initial situation. But even this parallel isnt exact because the movement of Breathing Corpses isn't strictly reverse linear. It's more crabwise.

Oh, not, not again says Amy, the maid, when she pulls back the sheets in the plays opening moments. It seems that the downmarket inn where she works is a favourite spot for suicides, and this is the second one she has personally uncovered. Its got so that the other employees call her "the Angel of Death": a joke that becomes darker as the action proceeds. For the moment, though, as she reads the suicide note, she's all blithe sympathy and concern; Erin Humphry plays her Irish, with a winsome earnestness and a hint of steel beneath.

The dead man's name, we learn, is Jim; and he had a wife called Elaine. We meet them in the second scene. Jim runs a storage business, and theres a strange and nasty smell coming from one of the boxes. When Jim investigates, he too finds a dead body and the discovery sends him into a deep and, as we already know, fatal depression. Before this happens, he and Elaine seem to be muddling through. Theyre empty nesters; and Elaine, picking up on the image that obsesses both her husband and the play, describes their home as a box. She's cheerful enough, though, to come by with a treat of "bacon sarnies" for Jim and his young assistant Ray. All the performances in David Ferry's production are excellent, but Richard Sheridan Willis Jim and Severn Thompsons Elaine are top of the crop. He plays with a corrugated brow and voice that take him with total conviction from stoicism through anomie to despair. She has an aweinspiring command of London speech and, inseparable from it, London attitude. (The play was written Yorkshire but the production moves it south, to admirable effect.) Simon Bracken gives them fine support as Ray, who is brighter and certainly more practical than his employers give him credit for. We see this trio again in a later scene; and this time it's later in time as well. Jim has retreated to his house, and he's taken all the doors off. Hes trying to dismantle the box.

Wedged between these two episodes, in the dead centre of the play, we find another, younger couple. Kate, who runs a business from home, is angry at her malfunctioning computer, and at many other things. She, too, is haunted by having found a body, female this time, in some bushes, while out walking the dog. She hates that dog; Ben, her partner, loves it. The discovery that Kate has viciously kicked the dog rouses Ben to unaccustomed fury; generally hes the passive one in what seems to be a semi-consensual sado-masochistic relationship; he has, and shows, the scars to prove it. Kim Nelson isn't totally in control of Kate, but her rages are truly frightening. Benjamin Sutherland's as Ben may be even more so, since theyre plainly out of his usual character but logical in the context of the scene.

Kate and Ben provide some clues as to what may be in Jims box, but they aren't conclusive The actual concluding scene is still less so; we can't even be sure of its place in the time scheme. It introduces a final character: a travelling salesman, given an uneasy charm by Jonathan Sousa, whose stock includes an extremely sharp knife. Its presence produces extraordinary suspense; we dont know who may do what to whom, or when, or if.

Its this sense of tight, shifting dynamics, in speech and action and interaction, that gives the play its distinction. Overall it hardly says more than that death is a universal threat that some can disregard and that paralyses others. But though none of the relationships can be developed at length, all are uncommonly believable, first amusingly, then horrifyingly, and - finally - teasingly. But the tease isn't gratuitous. It stays in your mind and breeds there.

Breathing Corpses runs until November 13.

Coal Mine Theatre / Laura Wade's very British Breathing Corpses was first seen at the Royal Court Theatre in London in 2005.

THEATRE REVIEW

The (Post) Mistress Berkley Street Theatre

Tomson Highway has been absent from the Toronto theatre for a long time. It's been a quarter of a century since Dry Lips Oughta Move to Kapuskasing moved to the Royal Alex. Since then we've had only a revival of his other major play, The Rez Sisters. He returns with a more modest work, a show whose principal revelation is that Highway is a first-rate piano player.

The (Post) Mistress is a cabaret act dressed up as a play for which Highway wrote both words and music. It's been performed in various forms and various places since 2009, but its present production, a joint venture of Pleiades Theatre and Theatre Francais de Toronto, is its first one in Toronto. It's double or triple tongued, presented in French with a bit of Cree, and English surtitles; or in English with a bit of Cree, and French surtitles. The former version is the one I saw; the latter is the one that will be performed for the remainder of the Toronto run.

Marie-Louise Painchaud is the post-mistress of the title in the northern Ontario village of Lovely, near the mining town of Complexity. Marie-Louise is middle-aged and married, for the second time and not, she tells us, very satisfyingly. She appears to know the contents of all the letters that pass through her domain, the show being set in the 1980s when people still wrote letters. At first we suspect her of steaming them open, like the village postal lady in Dylan Thomas' Under Milk Wood, but her methods turn out to be far more rarefied. Most of them are love letters, telling of steamy encounters in exotic locales like New Orleans, Buenos Aires and Rio de Janeiro. These provide Marie-Louise, who has never even been on a plane, with a rich fantasy life. They also provide the show with its songs; Highway has written an effective series of musical pastiches.

The post-mistress' identification with the illicit affairs that she conjures up explains the punning parenthesis in the show's English title. One of the more passionate couplings that she describes is so craftily set up, and then so passionately bumped-andground, that we may come to believe, or at least hope, that it really happened to her, but we're soon disillusioned.

Patricia Cano is exhaustingly roguish when speaking but comes to vivacious life in her songs. The staging is generally smooth though it's a pity that madame's desk, on and around which much of the action happens, is placed far to one side, making much of the show feel, and especially sound, remote. Teresa Przybylski has designed an attractively cavernous set, dominated by seemingly endless shelves of sparsely-populated pigeonholes. These turn out to have an extra significance in the evening's last section whose revelations I must not reveal.

The show's worst faults are that it's dramatically and psychologically monotonous, and - with an intermission thrown in - too long. The (Post) Mistress runs through Nov. 6 at the Berkeley Street Theatre Upstairs in Toronto.

Bryan McNally / In The (Post) Mistress, Patricia Cano is exhaustingly roguish when speaking but comes to life in her songs.

THEATRE REVIEW

Ariodante

The Canadian Opera Company continues to provide some of the richest theatre in Toronto.

Its production of Bellini's Norma offers glorious singing; Handels Ariodante offers equally glorious singing plus inspired and meticulous staging by the British director

Richard Jones. Its full of Shakespearean echoes.

A villain seduces a waiting-woman into impersonating her mistress on the eve of that mistress' wedding, causing the bride's father and fiance to revile her as an premarital adulteress, just as in Much Ado About Nothing. A mysterious martial champion arrives at the last moment, just as in King Lear. The wronged heroine revolts against the happy ending and walks off in protest. just as in Measure for Measure; or rather as in modern productions of Measure for Measure. But here the departure, in both senses, is fully

thought out and stimulatingly presented.

The sung text, or the surtitles, give us the traditional story, the staging gives us the new one, in bracing counterpoint. The setting has been transposed from a Macbeth-like mythical royal Scotland to a tribal, more or less modern Hebridean island, where the local customs include much ceremonial shifting of furniture and a puppetry fetish; handmanoeuvred dolls enact tabletop routines of celebration or condemnation, the last one making a brilliant contribution to the ironic ending. Meanwhile the human action has been seamless, never a slack moment in performance or design.

The stage becomes one great hypnotic moving picture.

Ariodante is in repertory through November 4 at the Four Seasons Centre

Michael Cooper / The Canadian Opera Company's production of Ariodante is full of Shakespearean echoes.
2016-11-09-acrobat-eggs-you-can-have-you:
THE ATRE REVIEWS

Cuisine Confessions Princess of Wales Theatre Acquiesce Factory Theatre

The Seven Fingers company are a peripatetic, multi-ethnic, multi-disciplinary group based in Montreal. Their skills include acrobatics, music, storytelling and - for the purposes of their show Cuisine Confessions - cookery. They arrive in Toronto as a kind of culinary Cirque du soleil.

The acrobatics are the most important ingredient. They execute their manoeuvres with charmingly casual grace, and some of the feats are breathtaking. They put the audience in a pleasurable trance. We know in advance they can do these things, because otherwise they wouldn't be doing them.

Least important is the cooking; omelettes and pasta and banana bread are prepared on stage in real time and even served to the audience, but the food is really just there to provide a pretext and a framework. A juggling act acquires an extra piquancy when it's done with whisks.

The setting is an exceptionally spacious and wellappointed kitchen: the sum total, it seems, of the performers' own culinary memories and experiences. This is where the confessional part comes in. The cast-members tell us in turn what preparing food and eating it meant to them, especially when they were growing up.

There is some audience participation, too. On the first night, a young lady was enticed on stage to be wooed with an omelette and with the thought-provoking compliment, "the less I know you, the more I love you."

While little of the talking here communicates much (and neither does most of the singing), when Sidney Bateman and Melvin Diggs, both from the United States, take turns jumping through hoops at increasingly impossible angles, we're transported to a magical world. They're helping one another, they're competing, they're egging one another on (that seems the appropriate phrase) - they make it look both easy and impossible.

There is one sequence that overshadows all the others, one autobiographical monologue that is not so much a confession as a bearingwitness. Matias Plaul, from Argentina, tells of how, when he was a boy, his father was abducted, tortured, killed. To illustrate, Plaul climbs up what the program identifies as a Chinese pole, stretching from stage floor to somewhere out of sight. He then abruptly slides down, presenting an image of death as heart-stopping as I have seen in a theatre. As he goes on to tell how he and his family coped with the loss, he performs other feats on that pole, some of which cannot be believed even while they're happening; they defy gravity.

At the end of the show, pasta is served from the stage. I didn't brave the crowds to partake, but I did pick up some chocolate-chip banana bread on the way out and it was good.

David Yee, accomplished actor and playwright, combines the two roles in his new play, Acquiesce, the opening production in Factory Theatre's season of plays by authors of colour.

Yee plays Sin Hwang, an Asian-Canadian summoned to Hong Kong for the funeral of his father. Sin is a writer. We first meet him on the outward flight, trying to sleep while the man in the next seat badgers him with questions - first flattering, then insulting - about his one successful novel, also called Acquiesce. This is a funny scene, but our hopes for more are dashed when Sin arrives and is informed by his cousin Kai that jokes don't go down well in Hong Kong. A later scene involves a Buddhist monk who's a pretty fair joker himself and proud of it, but most of the play is heavy, or certainly feels so in Nina Lee Aquino's portentous production.

Sin, who is very Westernized, must come to terms with his Chinese heritage and also with the legacy of his father whom, as he keeps protesting, he hardly knew. Dad walked out when Sin was six, and was physically abusive while he was there.

Abusive to a six-year old: that's a thought to pull you up short, but the play doesn't dwell on it, or tell us anything at all about the rest of Sin's upbringing. His mother isn't even mentioned.

We gather the father's behaviour was learned from his own childhood, and that Sin fears he may have inherited it and therefore wants no children of his own, causing his girlfriend to leave him. But all that is just words. We're asked to respond to a father-son relationship that hasn't been dramatized. What we're finally told about it seems arbitrary and inconclusive.

Sin does learn his father suffered from hallucinations, and it seems this, too, may run in the family. Sin's flight companion asked him to explain a dream sequence in his novel, and the play goes on to give us dreams and flashbacks and even flashbacks of dreams. One of them involves a talking Paddington Bear, with a surprisingly rough London accent. Yee's presence as his own protagonist is a plus. He has strength and humour and an appealing wariness, a built-in psychological shrug: very useful when Sin is called upon to ritually wash his father's body or to deliver a eulogy in Cantonese, which he doesn't speak. But he acquiesces.

Richard Lee plays cousin Kai who is fastidious, or - in Sin's eyes - bossy, but who melts eventually. Yee and Lee build an initially amusing, finally touching relationship.

Two other actors play everybody else: John Ng provides a bright series of cameos, culminating in a surprise appearance as the deceased; Rosie Simon is defeated as the girlfriend, who exists only in unreliable memories, but is very entertaining as a funeral parlour attendant who walks and talks like a cartoon geisha.

Yee has written better plays: Paper Series and Carried Away on the Crest of a Wave. Or, since this one is apparently a revision of an early discarded work, you might say, more positively, that he has gone on to write better plays.

National Post

Cuisine Confessions runs until December 4, Acquiesce until November 27.

Alexandre Galliez / Montreal circus troupe The Seven Fingers.
2016-11-16-an-irresistible-temptation-tr:
THEATREREVIEW

Chasse-Galerie Soulpepper Young Centre, Toronto

In Chasse-Galerie the energy never lets up. It's a musical based an old Canadian legend that may itself have even deeper roots. The accepted Quebecois version tells of a group of loggers who make a deal with the devil to escape their frozen fastness for one night of tavern revelry. Of course, the bargain comes with escape clauses, and of course, Satan works hard to prevent his victims from exercising them. You might even say that he does his damnedest.

In this stage version the woodchoppers are four in number, and female; the lumberjacks are lumberjills.

So we have Alex, Michelle, Lea and Toba, all of them pining for hot lights and faroff loves (of both genders), when into their hut tumbles a smooth-talking tempter who gives his name as Damien. They know almost immediately who he really is, and what theyre getting into. If you want to take that phrase literally, it is the Chasse-Galerie itself: a flying canoe.

While they paddle vigorously onstage, their course is charmingly plotted by whimsical projections. When they arrive, everybody dances. But then everybodys been doing that since the show began.

Tyrone Savage wrote the adaptation and is also the director. James Smith wrote the music and lyrics, and is also the musical director; he plays piano and guitar, sometimes simultaneously. Ashleigh Powell is the choreographer, and her contribution is immense. The show begins before the story begins, giving us a preview of the bar, the club, the dive, that is to be the pleasureseekers' destination. The entire company are wildly stomping in what will turn out to be the production's signature style. Its exhilarating, but it courts monotony.

However, as the plot proceeds and conflicts get underway, the dancing takes on real dramatic power.

The steps and bends can be seductive, they can be threatening, they can even be witty.

What isnt danced is mostly sung. "You know how susceptible I am to the majesty of song," says one of the characters, and Smith's songs are indeed majestic: tuneful, rousing, clever and funny. He also acts; his depiction of a shy suitor is delightfully understated: a quality, to be honest, that isn't much evident in the other performances.

They still give a lot of pleasure. Tess Benger, Shaina Silver-Baird, Nicole Power and Kat Letwin are - in ascending order of rowdiness, though not necessarily effectiveness - the four Cinderellas who can beat the devil if they get home before dawn, provided that they also abstain from touching crosses on steeples and from swearing. The last prohibition is the hardest to observe, as it also entails their abstention from hard liquor, which is one of the things for which they hazarded their souls in the first place.

Damien/Satan (played, with rather too obvious enjoyment, by the author/director) thinks he has them there; he well knows how susceptible they are to the majesty of whiskey. But the ladies find an unexpected, and unacknowledged, protector in the heavily-disguised shape of the Archangel Uriel, Satans old foe from way back in Paradise Lost. This, for all its earthiness, is a very erudite show; it also invokes Dante and Shakespeare.

Uriel, who likes a challenge, agrees to conduct his campaign entirely in verse, which he has of course to make up as he goes along. This allows us to hear a lot of intentionally bad rhymes, in instructive contrast to the scrupulously good ones in

Smiths lyrics. Uriel's endgame, though, remains obscure even while he's playing it and irrelevant afterwards; we dont even see him in hell, which is where the show has its showdown. Its a protracted finale; there have apparently been additions to the production since its debut appearance last year at the Storefront

Theatre (which I didn't see) and it was probably better shorter. It shouldn't really have an intermission. There are also a couple of unready performances. None of that matters, though. The show is irresistible.

Chasse-Galerie runs until Nov. 26 at the Young Centre in Toronto.
