Peter Morgan has made a writing career out of the life and times of Queen Elizabeth II. He wrote the film The Queen, which focused on the royal reaction to a single moment of national trauma: the death of Princess Diana. He then wrote the stage play The Audience, a success in London and on Broadway. Like the film it starred Helen Mirren, but it took a more panoramic approach, showing us a series of meetings between Elizabeth and her successive prime ministers. A Canadian production is slated for next year, in Winnipeg and Toronto, with Fiona Reid in the lead. And now, to complete the trifecta, we have The Crown, a Netflix TV series that's an expansion of The Audience.

The first season of The Crown takes us from 1947, and the wedding of the then-Princess Elizabeth to Prince Philip, to the brink of the Suez crisis in 1956. That takes 10 episodes. A second season has already been commissioned.

In the meantime we have Claire Foy, doing a very credible job as the young Elizabeth. She has an air of brisk, polite common sense. One of her best moments comes when she's asked what name she will take as queen. Apparently surprised by the question she says that she, unlike her father and her uncle, will keep her own first name. So England gets its Elizabeth II. It's a pleasing coincidence that Foy has previously played Anne Boleyn, mother of Elizabeth I. The father and uncle - George VI and his elder brother, briefly Edward VIII - loom large. Alex Jennings, one of Britain's best, turns up in the third episode as Edward, returned from postabdication exile in Paris and New York, and pretty much steals the show: an intriguing mix of calculation, resentment, anger and resignation, all of them battling for supremacy when he drops in on his niece to offer her postaccession advice. A sense of duty seems ineradicable in this family, even in the one who got away. Not that this wins him any points with his mother Queen Mary (Eileen Atkins) who, in a flashback to 1936, berates him for deserting his post.

The charge sticks because Jared Lewis, who was the suicidal British partner in Mad Men, gives a comparably affecting performance as the king battling a disease whose fatal extent he is the last to know. When he dies, something goes out of the show's life as well as the lives and hearts of the people around him. A royal historian, writing in Britain's Mail, slammed the show for what he deems its apocryphal vulgarities, including this King George's fondness for obscene limericks. It seems to me one of the most believable things in the script.

The production reportedly cost 100 million British pounds (US$124 million) - a Netflix record. Visually, it's money well-spent: a parade of stately houses, populated by hundreds of meticulouslycostumed extras. As royal soap-opera - no, that's unfair, as royal domestic drama - it's persuasive.

Alex Bailey, Netflix Via The Associated Press / Claire Foy as Elizabeth and Jared Harris as George VI.

THEATRE REVIEW

The Realistic Joneses Tarragon Theatre

In Will Eno's The Realistic Joneses, American family drama meets, explosively, that other dear old thing, the Theatre of the Absurd. In Eugene Ionesco's The Bald Soprano, the primary absurdist play, we met two married couples who spoke exclusively in polite cliches to illustrate the futility of language and hence of what we used to call bourgeois existence. One of those couples was named Smith, as if to say "how average can you get?" Eno's play does Ionesco one better. It also gives us two couples, but both of them are named Jones. It may be worth noting that, once this point has been established in the play's first scene, it is never mentioned again.

Bob and Jennifer Jones are a 40-ish couple, living in a small town with a nice view of the mountains. John and Pony Jones are a very slightly younger couple who have just moved into a neighbouring house, and who kick the play off by paying a neighbourly visit. "We know that house," says Bob, adding as one conversationally might, "someone else used to live there." "Wow" says John, "who knew the place had such an interesting history." It does not seem at this point that he is being sarcastic, though he certainly will be later.

Language in this play is very slippery. What distinguishes Eno from Ionesco is that his characters are in on the joke, while dizzyingly aware that the joke is on them. John has found a website that offers transcripts of any audio-book, prompting Jennifer, the most grounded of the four, to ask "wouldn't that just be the book?" John also says "We communicate pretty well, even without words" to which skeptical Bob replies "Yeah?" Failure of communication is a staple of modern drama, but Eno takes it to a more immediately recognizable plane than Beckett or even Pinter. Compared to their characters, his Joneses are indeed realistic. They come with biographies. They also come with medical conditions, the men anyway. Bob and John both suffer from a (fictitious) neurological disease. It's why they're neighbours; they've moved to be near the doctor who specializes in their complaint and who gave his name to it. It apparently causes seizures, blackouts, temporary blindness and forgetting words. Bob mostly accepts his situation, even exploits it, while wanting to know as few of the details as possible; he suggests that Jennifer keep his doctor's appointment for him and bring him back a report. John is nobody's stoic; he rages and plays word-and-mind games. Jennifer seems to be a fine caregiver, though she chafes in the role; Pony, who shrieks at the sight of a dead squirrel, could hardly be less suited to it.

There is some flirtation across the marriage lines but it's inconclusive. This isn't one of those American plays in which family members yell at one another while pulling skeletons out of cupboards, the plays (The Humans is the current exhibit) that win awards and have profitable Broadway runs and that turn up in Canada some five years later, making us wonder what all the fuss was about. The Realistic Joneses did play on Broadway but its honesty about relationships, coupled with its paucity of plot, must have made audiences uncomfortable.

The night I saw it, there were walkouts. That production, with a starry cast, was good, but the Tarragon one, directed by Richard Rose, is better. It's certainly much funnier, the four actors feast on the wrong-footing and secondguessing with which these Joneses strive to keep up with one another. Susan Coyne as Jennifer begins with good humour and common sense; the latter remains a constant but, increasingly, she burns underneath. Tom Barnett as Bob shows, with alarming conviction, a man declining into a slug. Jenny Young is a fine neurotic Pony. Patrick McManus as John is the play's dynamo, insecurity fuelling aggression. All four discharge their parts with crack-shot timing but McManus has the hottest ammunition.

Charlotte Dean's set revolves elegantly between one couple's deck and the other's kitchen, with a side-trip to the local grocery store. Thomas Ryder Payne has created a soundscape that alternately lulls and frightens, while Graeme S. Thomson's lighting rises to virtuosity in a backyard encounter involving the two men and some unsettling blackouts. The best scenes, though, are the first and last, where all four Joneses get to interact. The first finds them uneasily sounding one another out; in the last they're replete and dangerously calm. "I don't think anything good is going to happen to us," says Bob. "But, you know, what are you going to do."

National Post

The Realistic Joneses runs until Dec. 18 at the Tarragon Theatre in Toronto.

Cylla Von Tiedemann / Patrick McManus and Susan Coyne star in The Realistic Joneses at the Tarragon Theatre in Toronto.
2016-11-30-the-show-must-go-on-how-new-y:
Two days after the U.S. election, I was in the lobby of the Public Theatre in New York. It was crowded with people, many of them milling around a buffet table at the side. Eventually, the milling stopped; the crowd formed itself into a circle, stretching right around the room. Then, one by one, the people in the circle identified themselves. They were all, it seemed, members of the Public Theatre's staff. I, standing on the periphery peering in, was the only civilian present. When it came to my turn to declare myself, I had to admit that I was only a member of the Publics public.

Into the middle of the ring stepped Oskar Eustis, the Publics artistic director, to rally his troops. Nothing", he said, "that happened Tuesday night changes what we do. It just makes it more important. It was a great morale-building moment.

One of the things the Public is currently doing is a play called Women of a Certain Age. The play, written by the long-serving American dramatist Richard Nelson, is the last part of a trilogy whose overall title is The Election Year in the Life of One Family. The family name is Gabriel, and its members live in upstate New York. The assembled women of a certain age are the wife, ex-wife, mother, sister, and sister-in-law of a recently deceased novelist and playwright. This final instalment takes place on Election Day itself, but since it obviously had to be written well before that date, the story tactfully stops at 7 p.m., before any results could be in. The exwife is an ex-actress, who is rehearsing a solo tribute to Hillary Clinton. All the Gabriels seem to be Hillary voters, though none of them appear terribly enthusiastic about it. One tells of her son emerging from the polling station, literally holding his nose.

Most Broadway theatres were closed on Election Day, not wanting to compete with the cliff-hanging action outside, but this play, off-Broadway, actually opened that night. The performance, with nobody knowing the real-world outcome, was apparently a cathartic experience. The Canadian Stratford veteran Roberta Maxwell is in the cast, and she gives a magnificent performance as the grandmother whose body is frail but whose words are acerbically strong. Maxwell told me that the actors had emerged euphorically for the first-night party, only to find joy draining out of them, as the news came in.

That must have been the whole city's story, and not just that of the arty crowd. When I first arrived in New York, a cab-driver informed me: The Trump party is over at the New York Hilton ... and our future president is holding hers at the Javits Centre." New York, of course, isn't America. That lesson has been driven home. But what was notable about Women of a Certain Age was its premonitory elegiac quality. When I saw it, two days after the premiere, the explicit references to Trump and Clinton had become the least persuasive things about it; they felt, in fact, like sore thumbs. But the play as a whole tapped into a national mood.

The Gabriels wouldnt qualify as working class, but theyre white middle class and they're struggling. They're dyed-in-the wool Democrats but they have the same economic concerns as the most rabid Republicans. The late Thomas Gabriel apparently made a success of his writing, but his first wife has had to give up acting for teaching, while her successor, a retired doctor, sees no way of returning to her former job and will also have to teach. Thomass brother is yet another teacher, of piano; hes also a cabinetmaker and greatly resents some of his richer clients.

His wife has been working in catering, part-time, but is about to commence work as a hotel maid; the grandmother informs her that is the same job, in the same place, at which her own mother had worked a century ago. Grandma is responsible for the family's overarching fear; she had been sweettalked into taking out a reverse mortgage as result of which the

Gabriels are about to lose their home.

Many of the fears and prepccupations it presents overlap symptomatically with those of another family drama The Humans, currently the most lauded play on Broadway. I saw the two shows on successive nights, and sometimes felt as if I were watching the same play twice. The one at the Public, though, is clearer, subtler and less pretentious.

I don't know what Donald Trump would make of it. Its common knowledge, though, that he has been much exercised, even though he hasnt seen it, by another show that started its life at the Public, before transferring to become a Broadway phenomenon. I refer of course to Hamilton: An American Musical. Mike Pence recently attended and was roundly booed by members of the audience.

Then, after the show proper had ended, Brandon Victor Dixon, who now plays Aaron Burr, stepped forward, on behalf of the musical's creators and his fellow performers, to express the hope that the vice president elect had taken its message of inclusiveness to heart. (Hey, an actor playing a past VP addressing a real-life future one. How's that for fourthwall-breaking.) Pence seems to have taken this in good part, even commending it as an example of free speech, but his boss was greatly offended by it, tweeting that it was "rude and insulting and that there should be an apology.

Im torn on this. The purist in me feels that the show should have been content to make its own statement, which is powerful and, I would have thought, unmissable. This is the musical in which a cast of black and Latino actors stake a claim to their countrys history by playing America's founding fathers. It's the show in which the line immigrants, we get the job done," uttered jointly by Hamilton himself and the Marquis de Lafayette, was already raising the roof when I saw it, a week into its Broadway run. On the night of the Pence visit, it stopped the show. Its been argued that the tradition of criticising living politicians from the stage stretches back to Aristophanes, who in one comedy had his chorus step out of the story to attack the demagogue Cleon and in another put him on stage as a character. But these were parts of the plays as written; they werent extra-dramatic add-ons.

On the other hand: Dixon's speech was very far from being insulting. He actually began by asking the audience to cease their booing, and his words were reasonable and respectful. A man about to ascend to the second-highest office in the land should be able to handle public disagreement, as indeed it seems Pence was.

Trump, undeterred by this, further tweeted that he had heard that Hamilton was "much overrated which, true or not, is startlingly irrelevant. It's also petulant, of a piece with his spoiled-child characterization of the protests that followed his electoral victory as unfair;" How dare they rain on his parade? Meanwhile, at a performance by Hamiltons Chicago company, the "immigrants line was greeted by a man in the audience getting up and shouting: We won! Get over it!" That really was rude, to put it mildly.

Unlike some, I cant pretend to know what goes on in the president-elect's head. My guess is that he believes every word he says - however selfcontradictory - at the moment he says it. Perhaps it's the secret of his success. I suspect that he will have to get used to being attacked from the stage; sooner rather than later, there will be off-Broadway plays in which he is a character.

Hes already inspired theatrical comparisons. In The New York Times, a few weeks before the election, a leading Shakespeare scholar was comparing him to Richard III. This, I think, was unfair to both parties. Theres more to Shakespeare's Richard than Trump with a hump. And, nobody has accused the Donald of murdering his relatives to get to the throne. There is also the fact that Richard has a great line of ironic self-deprecation, which includes casting doubt on his attractiveness to women. That does not sound very Trumpish.

The great Trump analogs come from a dramatic source less exalted and more recent. It's been pointed out that, 16 years ago, The Simpsons showed a future President Lisa inheriting the office from a disastrous President Trump. It seemed like an incredible flight of fancy at the time. But there was a more acute if unconscious prophecy in another Simpsons episode, the one in which Sideshow Bob runs for office against Mayor Quimby. His platform is that Quimby is soft on crime; his proof is that Quimby let Sideshow Bob out of jail.

This sounds uncannily like Trump claiming that he was the right man to fix tax loopholes because he himself had so thoroughly exploited them. That was also the episode in which Bart and Lisa, like reluctant Clintonians, campaigned with signs reading "Vote for Quimby. This time he really is the lesser of two evils." The more skeptical of Richard Nelson's characters might have empathised. Oskar Eustis would, I think, have recognised the spirit of wit as part of what he and his team intend to preserve at the Public, even if this example came from California.

I have been visiting New York for 50 years, and have never fallen out of love with it. Right now, I love it more than ever.

National Post robert.cushman@hotmail.com

Hamilton Llc, The Associated Press / Actor Brandon Victor Dixon, who plays Aaron Burr in Hamilton, speaks to vice president-elect Mike Pence from the stage after the curtain call in New York Nov. 18.

THEATRE REVIEW

Come From Away Royal Alexandra Theatre, Toronto

I confess that I approached Come from Away with some skepticism. A musical about how the people of Gander, Nfld., opened up their hearts and homes to the 38 planeloads of people stranded there as a result of 9/11 has an inspiring premise. But once the situation had been established, where could the show go from there? I anticipated a lot of sentimental filler, perhaps focusing on made-up romances between residents and visitors.

I could not have been more wrong. Come from Away is indeed a heartwarming show, but there's almost nothing sentimental about it. Both in its substance and in its treatment, it's outstandingly sensible. It drives but it doesn't rush. The cleverest but also the most honest thing about it may be the way it deploys its cast of 12. The opening number shows the people of Gander dealing with their own issues; there's a school bus driver strike, and the mayor is trying to get both sides to - in his own recurring phrase - come to the table. Then the news breaks.

We switch to the inside of one of the planes; the crew aren't clear about why they've been diverted and the passengers of course know even less. The scene change is effected, instantly, by a re-arrangement of chairs. The performers don't have to change; the same actors who were at the council meeting (held in Tim Hortons) are now in the air. And so it goes throughout the evening, sometimes back and forth in the course of a single song. It's ingenious, it's invigorating, and it's never confusing.

It was a rewarding decision to devote so much time to the fears and confusion of the new arrivals while they're still airborne and then for the long hours when they're waiting on the tarmac. It builds tension and lets us get to know them. Meanwhile, we also get better acquainted with the townspeople, as they realize the full scope of the situation, making multiple frenzied trips to scour the shelves of Shoppers Drug Mart in anticipation of each possible future demand. Irene Sankoff and David Hein, who wrote the book and score (there's more score than book) assembled their show from interviews they conducted with both locals and with those from away. They give us both groups in microcosm. The passengers and crew of one plane stand in for those of all 38. The Gander citizens we meet represent the town's population of 9,000. They have to play host to a sudden influx - from all over, but predominantly American - of 7.000. That the two parties are almost equal in number makes the interchangeable casting even more apt.

It's appropriate, then, that this is a joint Canadian-American production (and bound for Broadway), the authors from here, most of the production team from there. The director, Christopher Ashley, has staged the show superbly, much aided by Beowulf Boritt's simple set design and Howell Binkley's evocative lighting. I fancy that it would be poetically just if the casting were to be split equally between the two countries; in fact there are three times as many of them than there of us. But everyone on stage is so good that it's pointless to quibble, let alone to rank them in any order of merit.

It's best just to list them: of the three Canadians, Petrina Bromley (this year's Stratford Rosalind) plays an SPCA official, passionately concerned with the welfare of the animals on board, and especially with the incipient birth of Gander's first ever bonobo chimpanzee. Lee MacDougall is, impeccably, a British passenger who's one half of the love-plot that the show does in fact provide. Astrid Van Wieren gives an overflowing but disciplined performance as a teacher who takes instant charge of what amounts to an impromptu refugee centre.

Of the nine Americans, Geno Carr plays the top local cop. Jenn Colella is the airline captain who, as befits her rank, gets the one solo number in a score otherwise made up of ensembles; it's a good song about her pride in becoming American Airlines' first female pilot and her horror at how the planes she loves have been turned into vehicles of destruction.

She also talks of how planes suffer when they're grounded too long, not something that would have occurred to most of us. Joel Hatch, rubicund and conscientious, is the image of a small-town mayor, and indeed gets to play a whole quick-change succession of them as the influx spreads out to neighbouring townships.

Rodney Hicks is a black American who can hardly believe that none of these hospitable strangers wants to kill or even rob him. Kendra Kassebaum is a local TV reporter who comes to cover a strike and stays, wide-eyed, to bear witness to history.

Chad Kimball is a gay man named Kevin, travelling with his partner, also named Kevin; they say that once this seemed cute but is now tiresome, which is a pretty good description of how their whole relationship is presented. Caesar Samayoa is the other Kevin, and also plays a Muslim exposed to the new distrust of his fellow passengers; also, as the new security comes in, to a humiliating body-search witnessed with disquiet by the lady captain. Q.

Smith plays an elderly woman from New York who bonds with the teacher over each of them having a son who is a firefighter - and who lives in fear when the full implications of the day's inferno dawn on her. Sharon Wheatley is the other half of the love-interest, a Texan whose involvement with the Englishman has to be true because nobody would dare to make it up All these characters, plus the subsidiary ones that all the actors take on, add to a mosaic of people coming together and recoiling from differences.

A favourite moment: a bus comes to a dead halt when it encounters a moose in the road; happens all the time, the newcomers are informed. The atmosphere is warm, but never insultingly folksy. The score, mostly tight and rockish, goes traditional for one ebullient sequence celebrating the appointing of four of the visitors as honorary Newfoundlanders.

It's one of the few times when the show stops for applause. Otherwise it barrels seamlessly through, without an intermission. It's the only musical I've seen in which the band are granted their own curtain-call. They play on through it, 10 of them, each in turn taking a solo. There couldn't be a better ending.

National Post

THEATRE REVIEW

Who Killed Spalding Gray?

Berkeley Street Theatre, Toronto

I have to declare an interest.

About halfway through Who Killed Spalding Gray?, Daniel MacIvor's tribute to the late American monologist, the actor pauses to read extracts from a couple of reviews, naming the reviewers names.

One of them is the revered Pauline Kael, who was disgusted by Gray. His juxtaposition in the film version of his Swimming to Cambodia between his personal problems with the horrors inflicted by the Khmer Rouge was distasteful to her. I havent seen the movie or read the whole review, but on the evidence presented here it sounds to me like Kael was right.

The other review I have read, because I wrote it. It concerned an earlier oneman MacIvor play with the punning title Here Lies Henry. Henry was a man who might or might not have been lying in everything he told the audience, and my response to this was, Who cares? I also said that no actor in Canada was better than MacIvor at doing what he does and that his skill was spellbinding, but I can understand, and not just because I've been there myself, that it's the perceived slight that would have lingered. It causes MacIvor to say here that, though hes not comparing himself to Gray, he does know how it feels to be hurt.

I cant think of anything to say about his new show that is likely to hurt him, but of course you never know. My description of it as a tribute wasn't quite accurate, but I can't think of a term that would be. Its a piece that moves around and bounces off the man in its title; a man who in 2004 provided the most literal answer to the question in MacIvors title by jumping (or falling) off the side of the Staten Island Ferry after spending most of the day riding back and forth on it.

Three narrative streams flow through the play, feeding into one another. One is an account of Gray's last days, emphasizing the fact that the night before his fatal ferrytrip, Gray had been to see a Tim Burton movie, Big Fish, accompanied by his son. Sons figure prominently in much of what MacIvor tells us in this show. The last lines of Big Fish are: "A man tells a story over and over so many times he becomes the story. In that way, he becomes immortal." Maybe Gray, a professional storyteller, was putting his own immortality to the test.

Talking about Gray, MacIvor goes someway towards becoming Gray. At any rate he adopts the Gray pose, sitting behind a desk with a glass of water and a microphone. When he talks about himself, in the play's second stream, hes more himself as we know him from his other solo shows: roaming around the stage, amplification in hand. The personal story he tells is about being informed by an ex-lover that there is an entity attached to him, that this could be fatal, and that hed better take himself to a "psychic surgeon" to have it removed. So he did. MacIvor is very funny detailing the grim surroundings in which he found himself, as well as the offhand inquisitorial manner of his surgical practitioner. It seems that the entidectomy (I'm guessing that's the word) was successful. Unfortunately it exactly coincided with the death of Spalding Gray, leaving MacIvor feeling, as per his title, uneasily, if irrationally, guilty.

I dont know whether this story is true. Rationalist that I am, I rather hope it isnt, but rather suspect that it is. The point is that here, as not in Here Lies Henry, I cared to know, perhaps because MacIvor is an unquestionably real person while Henry was a fiction. An acknowledged fiction is the third element in Killing Spalding Gray. It's the story of a man named Howard who wanted to commit suicide and found the go-to guy to help him do it. But their plan misfired, for reasons too delicious to reveal, and Howard found himself sitting by the ocean, more disconsolate than ever. A mysterious woman greets him there (everyone in a MacIvor show is mysterious), speaking in the voice of Helena Bonham Carter. As well as enabling MacIvor to do a pleasing impersonation, this connects with the narrative of Spalding Gray's last days, since Carter starred in Big Fish and was Tim Burtons partner at the time. Its a theatrical practical joke that contributes to the play's total effect, which is to be agreeably unsettling, linking things without tying them up.

The agreeableness is a function of MacIvor's own performing personality which - here at least - is devastatingly unassuming. He gets applause at the top of the show, simply by walking on. He then proceeds to interrogate a member of the audience. I dont know what the point of this is but it does enable MacIvor to ingratiate himself still more by confessing that he doesnt feel very comfortable doing it.

In the main body of the show, MacIvor rises, seemingly effortlessly, to every one of the challenges he has set for himself in his script's three intersecting modes. His unobtrusive director is, as usual, Daniel Brooks who, years ago, was co-creator-and-performer of The Noam Chomsky Lectures - the only other production in which I have heard myself being namechecked from the stage.

That's probably a coincidence, but then Killing Spalding Gray seems to be suggesting that theres no such thing as coincidence.

Who Killed Spalding Gray Runs At The Berkeley Street Theatre In Toronto Until December 11.

Canadian Stage / Daniel MacIvor rises to the challenges in his scripts three modes, the Post's Robert Cushman writes.

THEATRE REVIEW

Sleeping Beauty Elgin Theatre, Toronto

This holiday season brings us the first Ross Petty pantomime, or "family musical," without Ross Petty. Well, not altogether without. He does pop up at one point via video, in full Captain Hook garb and with full Captain Hook leer, asking - no, demanding - "Do you miss me?" In truth, we do. But more of that later. This Sleeping Beauty, recognizably a Petty production even without Petty on stage, has many things going for it, not least the way it spins out some theatrically unpromising material. As legends go, the original Sleeping Beauty is short on plot. Princess gets cursed, princess gets pricked, princess goes to sleep, prince awakens princess with kiss. That's about all there is. Jeremy Diamond's script ingeniously expands this with some good jokes, not all of them selfreferential, and a second act set almost entirely in Dreamland, where things get positively metaphysical.

We're in Dreamland because that's where the show's Princess Rose goes during her prolonged enforced siesta. We first meet Rose at her christening where the wicked fairy Malignicent, furious at being denied an invite, puts a spell on her that obliges her royal family to keep her away from all sharp objects. We then flash forward 18 years, during which Rose has definitely grown, though no one else at the court has changed their looks or even their clothes, which by rights should be quite messy because cutlery has been banned throughout the realm.

Rose has been further protected by being enclosed in a rotating glass bubble. This is obviously frustrating for her but it gives her one heck of a first entrance. Anyway, the curse has nearly reached its expiry date so she leaves her bubble, rejoicing at being able to enjoy herself and do good in the world. Like all fairy-tale princesses these days, she's a social justice warrior. But she isn't quite safe yet and Malignicent, with devilish cunning, arranges for her nemesis to be the lad who loves her. He's an aspiring musician, of troll parentage but not bad-looking if you don't mind green hair, named Luke. Tricked into becoming a DJ, he turns up at the castle with his disc scratching equipment, and you can undoubtedly guess what happens.

James Daly plays Luke, and his singing, dancing and clowning are awesome; also, when called for, is his acting. Talk about versatile: This performance, coming right after his searing dramatic work in Master Harold and the Boys, proclaims him the theatrical find of the year. AJ Bridel, late of Kinky Boots, is a sweet and spunky princess, especially notable for making an individual impression in some lively but standardized dance-routines (choreography by Julie Tomaino). By some elaborate plot-twists possible only in Dreamland, the story is given a feminist twist (I think) by having the heroine be the one to wake the hero up. And they still live happily ever after, or at least through the curtain-call.

The interpolated songs are mainly generic pop, apart from the witty opening number, a new Petty tradition, in which the Brothers Grimm in lederhosen clap hands, bump rears and promise that the ensuing story will be truly Grim (as opposed to deviously Disney). The brothers are Eddie Glen - who goes on to do his regular welcome turn as a reluctant bad guy - and Laurie Murdoch - whose principal role is the King of Torontonia which, as I probably should have mentioned, is the place that Rose is princess of. The king is an endearing bumbler, but Lisa Horner's acerbic queen keeps him in line. Professionals, the two of them.

The royal Torontonians seem to reside in Casa Loma, as why shouldn't they. The place has been attractively made up by Michael Gianfrancesco, who has also done a sumptuous job on the costumes, especially those for the sheep who do the choral work in Dreamland. The one person who has problems with the look of the place is the malevolent Malignicent, who wants to redesign it, this being the motive for her malignity. Hilary Farr, who plays her, is the reason we miss Petty; she brings no comic flair to her villainy and is really hardly worth booing. Also standing in for an absent standby is Paul Constable, who plays Sparklebum, "a fairy in training" and sister of the flirtatious Dame Plumbum generally played by Dan Chameroy. He too has to compete with a patched-in appearance by his predecessor, and in his scripted moments he does little more than go through the motions. When he gets to ad-lib, with the trio of tots who troop on in time-honoured fashion from the audience, it's a different story, and a very funny one. It isn't quite true that in pantomime anything goes but here, under Tracey Flye's direction, most things do.

Sleeping Beauty runs at the Elgin Theatre in Toronto until Jan. 7.

BOOK REVIEW

Swing Time By Zadie Smith Hamish Hamilton 464 pp; $34

He isnt doing that right." Fred Astaire apparently used to say that when watching himself dancing on screen. Zadie Smith tells us so in her novel Swing Time - or rather her narrator, unnamed throughout a long book, tells us. The quotation reverberates through the story on several levels.

The narrator, whom we follow from her childhood right through her 20s, is obsessed with Astaire. In fact, she's obsessed with dance generally, especially with dance on film, readily available through the VCR when she's growing up, in Smiths own northwest London in the 1980s. The book takes its title from one of the Astaire-Ginger Rogers movies of the 1930s: the one with perhaps the greatest score and performance, though hardly the greatest script. But "Swing Time also reflects the way the novel itself moves, swinging back and forth between different decades, different continents.

Astaires comment about himself resonates with the narrator when she encounters it as a pre-teen. For Astaire the person in the film was not especially connected with him. And I took this to heart, or rather, it echoed a feeling I already had, mainly that it was important to treat oneself as a kind of stranger ... I thought you needed to think like that, to achieve anything in this world." On the face of it, she has taken the opposite tack.

This, Smith's fifth novel, is the first to be written in the first person. But that too can be a way of distancing, at least to the reader. Who, after all, can see themselves whole? It may be significant that we never learn the narrator's name. She has a wonderful voice - the book is infinitely quotable - but an amorphous personality, especially given the kaleidoscopic narrative shes called upon to unify. The effect is partly intriguing, partly frustrating.

The narrator loves dance, but has no talent for it. Her best childhood friend - who does have a name, Tracey - is brilliant at it, and makes it her career. The two complement one another in other ways. The narrator has a black mother and a white father; Traceys parentage is the reverse. Tracey's father is almost entirely absent, apparently often in jail; Tracey fantasizes that the reason for his absence is that he's a back-up dancer with Michael Jackson.

The narrators father is around, at least to begin with. Hes kind but ineffectual, intimidated by his wife, a dedicated and ambitious Open University student and a determined achiever, other than domestically. ("My mother, who aspired to healthy eating, could not spend fifteen minutes in a kitchen without being reduced to a sort of self-pitying mania ... We would end up eating Findus Crispy Pancakes again. Round Tracey's things were simpler: you began with the clear intention of making Findus Crispy Pancakes.) We're told that Long before it became her career my mother had a political mind: it was in her nature to think of people collectively." A memorable scene shows the grown-up narrator having lunch with her mother, now indeed a professional politician, attended by an acolyte, colleague and lover named Miriam. Miriams "favourite thing in life was to see a conflict resolved, any conflict, and so my mother was a great resource for her: everywhere she went she made conflict.

One source of conflict is her daughters own job, as personal assistant to a pop megastar named Aimee, who suggests Madonna with a dash of Angelina Jolie. Aimee has announced her commitment to global poverty reduction" and wants to build - in fact does build, or at least finance - a girls' school in a West African village. "'White woman saves Africa says mother, is that the idea? Very old idea."

Aimee was born in Australia, but she acknowledges no roots and "has no tragic side. She goes through life as her own creation, and through the book as an entertainingly observed one. But when the story itself moves to Africa - followed, at carefully chosen photo-op intervals, by Aimee herself - the life goes out of it. There are some thematically crucial moments: the narrators exposure to African dance, which thrills her, and her realization that the villagers think of her as white.

She makes a new friend, Hawa, that relative rarity in the village, a middle-class girl." Hawa is the substitute for the definitely (and defiantly) un-middle-class Tracey, from whom the narrator has grown apart. The rift gets increasingly bitter. That's believable, but it isn't fleshed out. And yet its clearly meant to be the fulcrum of the book.

Maybe I should confess an interest here. Im a West Londoner myself; and though I grew up a couple of decades earlier than both Smith's narrator and Smith herself - and a little more south and east - Smith's novels, starting with the amazing White Teeth, still make me feel London as no other current writer does. I also share the narrators obsession with classic musicals and especially with their songs: one aspect of the book that Smith has admitted to be autobiographical.

The narrator may not be able to dance, but she can sing; with limited range but an intuitive sense for phrasing a lyric (like Astaire, though she has to be taught to acknowledge it). I believe it. That sympathy established, I feel entitled to pick a few nits. The book gets a couple of song-titles wrong: They All Laughed becomes We All Laughed, and All of You is confused with All of Me, mistakes which if followed through would make nonsense of the lyrics, and hence of a vital part of the narrators sensibility. Tracey gets into the chorus of a West End production of Guys and Dolls, her and the narrator's favourite musical - that shows their impeccable taste - but the number that's described, a pussycat routine called Pet Me Poppa, was only in the movie, where it replaced the far superior A Bushel and a Peck (Ive never known it to be done on stage).

Later, Tracey lands another chorus gig in a revival of Show Boat; the narrator is moved to wonder why neither Tracey nor any performer of colour (she calls that phrase, in another context, "the new euphemism) ever gets the plum role of Julie. But as far back as 1971 I saw the part played in a highly successful London production by the mixed-race Cleo Laine, and I dont know of any subsequent staging that has or would cast a white performer. This is important because race, and the degree to which it can or cannot be fluid, is a central theme of the book. The author's general point may be valid, but she's chosen the wrong example.

Show Boat proves to be Traceys last theatrical engagement. When the narrator pays her a last call, Tracey is a multiple single mother who throws class, and implicitly race, in her visitors face as she never has before. (Final musical irony: her kids are glued to the TV, watching South Pacific.) The narrator herself is childless, parentless and partnerless - though her romantic life has always been, as far as we can tell, shadowy. She's also jobless. The details have been hinted at in a prologue - it was the first day of my humiliation" - from which the rest of the book is a flashback. When you first read it, this introduction is mysterious to the point of confusion, but if you go back to it at the end (as I suspect the author knows you will) things fall into place. It includes a reviewing of the Bojangles of Harlem number from Swing Time the movie, in which the narrator notices - apparently for the first time - that Astaire, paying tribute to the great Bill Robinson, is dancing in blackface. "I'd managed to block the childhood image from my memory," she says, and I imagine everything else follows from that. I don't think it does; the book sprawls too much. But it does swing.

Weekend Post

THEATRE REVIEW

It's a Wonderful Life, Bluma Appel Theatre, Toronto CIBC Radio I think I heard that right "presents the Cabbagetown Players in It's a Wonderful Life." Thus begins Soulpeppers stage version of the 1946 Frank Capra movie, the perennial hearttugger presented as if it was being done as a Christmas radio play, also in the postwar 1940s.

It isnt a homegrown Soulpepper version. It's an existing adaptation by an American writer, Philip Grecian, that has been seen before in Toronto. CanadianStage presented it in 2008 in the very same theatre. The two productions share a contributor: John Gzowski, billed as sound and foley designer.

The latter part of that job description is anachronistic for the '40s and indeed for radio. But it chimes with the determination of Albert Schultzs Soulpepper production to make a supersized meal out of the conventions of broadcasting. Everybody, not just the actors playing studio techies but the actors playing actors, participates enthusiastically in the simulation of sound effects. Lorenzo Savoinis set lovingly evokes the period and the season and the medium, though the snowflecked windows struck me as excessive. Every radio drama studio I've been in was subterranean.

Anyway, here they are to tell the story of George Bailey, the smalltown boy who gave up his dreams of college to take over his family's savingsandloan business, running it so generously and humanely as to earn the undying gratitude of his fellowcitizens and the enmity of Mr. Potter, the tycoon who owns most of the town and wants all of it. I described him last time around as "Montgomery Burns without the nuance."

Georges take is that Potter "hates everybody who has anything he cant have." A run of bad luck, plus Potter's knavery, brings George to the brink of ruin and suicide. An apprentice angel named Clarence has to be dispatched from heaven to rescue him, and to earn his wings in the process, having waited for them nearly 300 years. Clarence shows George what life would have been like had George never been born.

Schultz, in an interview in this paper, has pointed out the resemblances between this story and A Christmas Carol (whose deservedly immortal Soulpepper dramatization is back again at the Young Centre). The protagonist of each has his destiny altered by supernatural visitation, timed for Christmas Eve. But there are important differences, and the advantage is all Dickens'.

We learn about Scrooges past as he himself relives it, courtesy of the spirits. We learn about Georges through an extended flashback, as a superior angel brings Clarence up to speed on his case history. This takes up much of the play, and it's clumsy. Even more crucially, we watch Scrooge change. George doesn't change at all; he was always a nice guy and he remains one. A Christmas Carol is both moving and delightful. Its a Wonderful Life, certainly in this incarnation, is sentimental. It gets to you, especially in scenes involving George and his children, but you may hate yourself afterwards.

Sentimentality also infects the staging. Lights are dimmed, even blacked out, at what are deemed to be affecting moments. But were supposed to be in a radio studio where the actors have to see to read their scripts, and where the effects would anyway be wasted on the listeners.

The production betrays its own convention in other ways. In commercial radio tradition, the action periodically stops for some words from our sponsors who in this case include Telus and, as noted, CIBC. There are also plugs for Soulpepper's other current holiday shows. But we're supposed to be in the 1940s. This kind of thing can be great in a Ross Petty pantomime, where anachronism is part of the fun, but here it seems smug. Also, the spoken puffs arent as witty as Pettys video clips. In fact they aren't witty at all.

Still, in the concluding stages you forget the trappings and get caught up in the story, which I guess is the intention. The acting, mainly from Soulpepper trusties, is fine. Gregory Prest has all the shy urgency of George. He doesn't do a James Stewart impersonation, but theres something about the set of his mouth and his chin when he squares up to opposition that does recall the original. As his loving wife, Raquel Duffy brings 1940s womanhood to life.

Michelle Monteith gives the evenings most creative performance as the presumptive bad girl: first sly, then tremulous. Diego Matamoros captures the commanding boom of an oldtime radio announcer, more menacing if anything than his subsequent sneering Mr Potter. One of the script's weaknesses is that he and George don't have a final showdown. Up in the celestial realms, Oliver Dennis plays Clarence and William Webster is God; or, as the program would have it, The Boss.

Its A Wonderful Life runs until Dec. 31 at the Bluma Appel Theatre in Toronto.

Cylla Von Tiedemann / Right down to simulated sound effects, Soulpeppers stage version of Frank Capra's It's a Wonderful Life is a loving homage to the radio dramas of yesteryear.
2016-12-28-the-very-best-of-this-year-s-:
Will Eno, a true original among American playwrights, was in Toronto recently for the closing performance at the Tarragon of The Realistic Joneses, his most successful play to date. We had a phone conversation during which he said, I hope there's something in it that promotes the view that kindness is necessary, crucial, a great thing.

I can't say that those sentiments, true and humane though they are, were what has stayed with me from a witty and unsettling play about two couples suffering from the same illness and the same surname; a play whose last words are "I dont think anything good is going to happen with us, but what are you going to do?" But I am happy to report Enos enthusiasm for the acting, the design and the overall impact of Richard Rose's production (It was coherent in a deep way - made the funny stuff funny and the sad stuff sad.).

There will be more Eno on our stages next year when the Shaw Festival presents his Middletown, which he insists is not a response to Thornton Wilder's Our Town. It is set in a smallish town, not unlike Carlyle, Mass. ("a library, a fire station, one store - a lonely place in some ways") where Eno himself, now 51, grew up. "I was trying to create a little place that represented a larger place. We tend to look for meaning in our birth, which we cant remember, and our death, which we wont be able to respond to. Mathematically, we are usually in the middle of things."

Meanwhile, The Realistic Joneses certainly makes my list of the best theatrical things to happen here in 2016. And since it opened near the end of the year, I propose to list my other choices in - roughly - reverse chronological order.

COME FROM AWAY

A certifiable no-seats-available hit. A musical about the welcome extended by the citizens of Gander, N.L., to the airplane-loads of unwitting refugees from 9/11, it proved to be more suspenseful and less sentimental than anyone could have hoped. Simply, fluently and imaginatively staged, it was one of two outstanding new Canadian musicals, the other being James Smith's Chasse-Galerie, brought in from the fringe to the Distillery. Also note that another Canadian musical, Ride the Cyclone, has made it to New York's Public Theatre, though both the Public and The New York Times insist on describing it as coming from Chicago. (The NY production originated there but the show didnt.) And a friend remarks that, even in Come from Away which has Canadian writers and an American production team, though Newfoundland is frequently mentioned, Canada never is.

MASTER HAROLD ... AND THE BOYS

This came from the Shaw Festival, but I caught it at the Toronto Arts Centre. Athol Fugards reminiscence of early apartheid was brought to heartbreaking life by director Philip Akin and actors Allan Louis, Andre Sills, and James Daly whose subsequent singing-dancingclowning appearance in the Sleeping Beauty panto proclaims him this year's Mr Versatility.

THE UNENDING

Aaron Willis' and Julie Teppermans site-specific Convergence Theatre offered a terrific triple bill that included Becketts Play, in an inventive staging by Willis that beat out the concurrent one at CanadianStage, and a penetrating new play by Tepperman with a tremendous performance by Mayko Nguyen.

FATHER COMES HOME FROM THE WARS (PARTS I, II, III)

It was a great year for new and old American plays. Suzan-Lori Parks' sardonic epic about the Civil War from the slaves' perspective - or perspectives - was a breath-taker, as directed by Weyni Mengesha. It was a fine ensemble showing, with possible personal-best performances from Dion Johnstone and Oliver Dennis. We now await the next parts. Arthur Millers neglected Incident at Vichy proved both tense and intense, offering insights on demagogy that seemed pertinent at the beginning of the year, and downright frightening at the end. Alan Dilworths production was another ensemble achievement, culminating in a soul-shaking duet between Diego Matamoros and Stuart Hughes. These two shows were beacons in an otherwise middling Soulpepper season - along, that is, with Damien Atkins' emergence, through revelatory supporting performances in The Heidi Chronicles and A Doll's House and a star turn in Hosanna, as Actor of the Toronto Year.

ALL MY SONS, ANOTHER MILLER

Given a probing, pitch-perfect production by Martha Henry, Joseph Ziegler, Lucy Peacock and Tim Campbell were great as the central family; Michael Blake gave a breakthrough performance (reinforcing his admirable Macduff) as the outsider who shatters their illusions. This was Stratfords prize production this year, though The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe and Shakespeare in Love were populist choices that earned their artistic keep; Stephen Ouimette in The Hypochondriac confirmed his position as farceur supreme; and A Little Night Music triumphed over inexplicable set-designs by virtue of the piece itself and the performances of Ben Carlson, making you laugh, and Yanna McIntosh, making you cry.

ENGAGED

The highlight of the Shaw Festival was Morris Panychs production of this bracingly cynical comedy by W. S. Gilbert-without-Sullivan. Gray Powell's susceptible skinflint, turning on an endless succession of dimes, was a serious contender for performance of the year. Other Shaw goodies: outgoing director Jackie Maxwell's farewell duo of Uncle Vanya and Sweeney Todd (a good year for festival Sondheim) with Benedict Campbell a rivetingly realistic Sweeney, down to earth and high on hate.

BOTTICELLI IN THE FIRE/SUNDAY IN SODOM

Jordan Tannahills Botticelli was the best new Canadian play of the year; Sunday, its double-bill partner, wasnt but was still worthwhile. Tannahill offered himself serious competition, though, when Concord Floral finally reached Toronto, though the staging and the young performers were the real knockouts here.

KILLER JOE

American Tracy Letts' inexorably compelling first play (far better, and shorter, than his August: Osage County) was given a perfect production by Peter Pasyk, making inspired use of the Coal Mine Theatre space. Is this tiny house the most reliably exciting theatre in Toronto? That's a rhetorical question. Its other prize offerings included Instructions to Any Future Socialist Government Wishing to Abolish Christmas, which would have been the new Canadian play of the year, if it hadnt taken so many years to get here; Breathing Corpses, the only good new British play to arrive this twelvemonth; and the new Groundling Companys The Winter's Tale, top-flight Shakespeare in an intimate setting, such as Toronto hardly ever sees.

Cylla Von Tiedemann / Patrick McManus and Susan Coyne in The Realistic Joneses, one of critic Robert Cushman's top performances of the year in Toronto.
2017-01-04-canadians-russians-and-the-gr:
Musicals are in the air at the moment, even more than usual.

Hamilton's success and its prestige continue undiminished, despite the illadvised mixtape. (Ironic, considering that is what the stage show was originally intended to be.) Meanwhile, in the movies, everyone's raving about La La Land. I'm eager to see it, though I can't help noticing that no review I have read has had much to say about the actual songs. I had to go to IMDb to discover their titles and who had written them. But the fact that it's an original, rather than an adaptation of a stage show is encouraging, after the false musical dawns of Chicago and Mamma Mia. Well, I must confess: I haven't seen the movie of Mamma Mia. The stage version was more than enough. Much more.

And of course there are musicals lining up for the coming year in Toronto and environs. Here are some of the more intriguing: Passing Strange is a Tony-winner from 2008 (though set in the 1970s). It's described as "a coming-of-age story told through sex, drugs, and rock 'n' roll." I can see how it might be told through the last of those, but it's surely being told about the first two. Anyway, it has a score by Mark Stewart (a.k.a Stew) that got a lot of attention at the time. It reaches us this month in a co-production by Obsidian who have collaborated on a few musicals in their time, and Studio 180 who haven't - though their director, Joel Greenberg, staged a lot of them in a former life. The venue is an unaccustomed one: the Opera House at Queen and Broadview.

The Elgin Theatre is the more familiar setting for the muchawaited Sousatzka, marking the return to producing of Garth Drabinsky. Confession of interest: I worked for Drabinsky's Livent organization for 18 months, and had a great time. My biased opinion is that the best of Livent's work (Kiss of the Spider Woman, Show Boat, Ragtime, Parade) constitute a track record unmatched by any commercial theatre organization since, or indeed for some time before.

The new show's director is Adrian Noble, former head of the Royal Shakespeare Company and responsible here for a memorable Stratford Hamlet; the choreographer is Graciela Daniele of Ragtime; and the cast includes Victoria Clark, renowned on Broadway for her performances in The Light in the Piazza and other things, and Montego Glover, who did a great turn here a few years ago in an otherwise misbegotten musical that claimed to be about Alberta Hunter.

However, the names that interest me most are those of Richard Maltby Jr. and David Shire, lyricist and composer respectively. They have been writing together since they were students in the late 1950s, and were primed to be the great American team of the post-Sondheim generation. Shire's music being both melodic and adventurous and Maltby's words sharp and character-driven. They certainly haven't lacked for success: Shire as a composer of film scores and Maltby as director of Ain't Misbehavin' and English lyricist of Miss Saigon. Together they wrote Baby, one of the few good musicals of the 1980s, and two whole heaps of wonderful songs collected in the anthology shows Starting Here, Starting Now and Closer Than Ever. But they've never had a Broadway hit together.

Sousatzka is set mainly in London but with tentacles spreading outwards in both place and time. It's based on a novel by Ruth Prawer Jabvala that also gave birth to the Shirley MacLaine movie Madame Sousatzka. Both book and film portray a Russian piano teacher instructing a gifted student from India. The show makes one major alteration: the young prodigy is now African. This was a great relief to Maltby and Shire, who didn't relish the idea of writing an Indian-flavoured score; they had attended a sitar concert in preparation, and Maltby told me that as they emerged he said to his collaborator, "Let's go back to your place and modulate." Now they can have jazz.

I confess - this seems to be my confessional week - that I have doubts about the title. The source material doesn't have great name recognition and, to quote a lyric from the musical Fiorello!, "Nobody likes a candidate whose name they can't spell." Yes, I too wish there were more Canadians in the cast of this "Broadway tryout," especially given the number of first-rate actor-singers we have on tap.

Meanwhile, we can also look forward to a couple of classic British shows: the Shaw Festival's Me and My Girl, from the 1930s (but an even bigger success in the 1980s) and, from the 1870s, the Stratford Festival's H.M.S. Pinafore, which in its day was the grand-daddy of all hit transatlantic transplants. Also at Stratford is Guys and Dolls, for the third time (and it cropped up not too long ago at the Shaw). No question that it deserves the exposure - it's the greatest of all musicals. But it does point up how few titles count as guaranteed cash-cows.

One wishes they could take a chance on something less familiar. I mentioned Fiorello!. A Pulitzer winner in the 1950s, when that award was rare for a musical, it deals with New York's fabled crusading Mayor LaGuardia. The line I quoted comes in a song called "Politics and Poker," Other shows have taken us into those legendary smoke-filled rooms, but it was left to the team of Jerry Bock and Sheldon Harnick, later of She Loves Me and Fiddler on the Roof, to give us a song you can really choke on. It might be a good choice for the Shaw, probably in one of their smaller theatres. I yearn for a staging of an earlier political show, the Gershwin brothers' Strike Up the Band, a satire on warmongers much harder-hitting and perennially pertinent than their more famous election lampoon Of Thee I Sing. It exists in two versions, both given sumptuous studio recordings in recent years. It must be possible to combine the best of both.

And of course there are current Broadway shows we will be itching to see. Natasha and Pierre and the Great Comet of 1812 (Great Comet for the listings) is already the hottest Broadway thing since Hamilton. The irresistible long-form title clues us in that this is a musical of War and Peace. And to judge from the CD of the original off-Broadway production, it's a good one, combining irreverent comment ("It's a complicated Russian novel/Everyone's got nine different names") with truthful, touching adaptation. Less lauded but still running is Something Rotten, a romp about a couple of Elizabethan theatrical wannabes, trying haplessly to compete with an apparently unstoppable phenomenon. Judging again from the recording, some of it is crass but some of it, especially when the man himself appears rhyming off his best-selling quotations, is truly funny. Stratford might have a ball with it.

THEATRE REVIEW

Next Stage Theatre Festival, Factory Theatre

In the musical Blood Ties, at the Next Stage theatre festival, there's a song whose singer is exploring the clothes-closet of someone recently deceased and who is impressed by what he finds. It goes, in part, like this: His suits are tailored with skill and finesse. Each shoe is a small work of art. This was a man who knew how to dress; It's a shame that he had to depart.

You don't often hear lyrics as neat as that in a new musical - Canadian or otherwise. And it gets even better. We hear, concerning the sartorial choices of defunct celebrities "from JFK to Marvin Gaye" that "they wore the right costume so even posthumously they could impress." Imagine that: an internal rhyme.

Lyricists who can rhyme with point and accuracy at the end of a line are rare enough these days; those who can do it in the middle of one are phoenixes.

Need I add that the words sit perfectly on the music, and that the music is also fine, theatrical and contemporary at once? The words, sung and spoken, and the music are the joint work of Anika Johnson and Barbara Johnston; near-namesakes but not related.

Although some confusion may arise from the fact that Anika has also been known to collaborate with her equally talented sister Britta.

The Johnson and Johnston of Blood Ties are also performers. Johnson plays Sheila, who is about to get married; Johnston plays Franny, her friend.

Judged from moment to moment, Blood Ties is dark, funny and a joy. But I have to admit that its separate pieces don't hold together very well.

The clothes-conscious corpse at its centre is Sheila's uncle who appears, most inconsiderately, to have blown his brains out in the bathroom on the eve of his niece's nuptials. The bride's three best buds - Franny and two guys - come to the house, and find themselves commandeered into cleaning up the mess.

Sheila herself is very tightly wound, a condition that seems to derive from the death of her parents in a car accident, a disaster for which her three friends were partly responsible.

This event is set up, with great verbal and musical tension, in the show's opening number, and it must be meant to overhang all the subsequent action. But it doesn't.

For much of the time, we forget about it. The authors also say that the show explores what weddings mean in today's secular society. But, again, it doesn't.

It branches out into other stories, entertaining ones that are not so much sub-plots as parallel plots. For a 75-minute piece, it's pretty diffuse. The authors have no trouble with dialogue but they do have problems with structure.

The virtues far outshine the flaws. The performances, under Ann Merriam's direction, are spirited and precise. In addition to Johnson and Johnston, there's delightful work from Carter Hayden as an earnest medical intern, aching to make the girl next door see him as something more than the boy next door, and from Jeremy Lapalme as the friend with the wardrobe fixation. He's gay, and I may convey the show's exhilarating quality by quoting more of his big song: If I had a closet that held this much clout, I'll tell you one thing: I'd have never come out.

The Next Stage festival, also known as the son-and-daughter of the Toronto Fringe, is spread over three spaces at the Factory Theatre, which between them house 10 shows. I've seen three.

Kawa Ada, esteemed actor, turns playwright-director for The Death of Mrs. Gandhi and the Beginning of New Physics (a Political Fantasy). This is a past-and-future play. In 1984, four female leaders, actual and potential, are assembled for the funeral of Indira Gandhi.

The gathering comprises Margaret Thatcher (who convened it), Imelda Marcos, Benazir Bhutto and a young Kim Campbell. Suddenly there erupts among them, from the year 2030, Malala Yousafzai. She claims, plausibly, to have grown richer, and certainly seems harder.

We're in Caryl Churchill territory, with a whiff of Shaw and a hint of Stoppard. Malala has come, she says, to awaken them to their full personal and political potential.

As in Churchill's Top Girls, there's the danger that they'll merely replicate men's mistakes. It looks, indeed, as if this is what will happen though it seems to be Thatcher's fault, a point that Churchill also made but with more subtlety and more clarity. The play's argument is muddy, and the physics, relating to Malala's time-travel, merely get in the way of the politics.

The laughs are few and forced. Ada's staging is good but the acting, with the honourable exceptions of Trenna Keating's Campbell and Tennille Read's Bhutto, stridently reinforces the obscurity: Ellen-Ray Hennesy's Thatcher looks at first glance as if she's wearing a mask and sounds, for much of the play, as if she's speaking through one.

The play lasts 90 minutes. Date Me, an improv piece, clocks in at a pleasant 30.

Two performers, Ted Hallett and Lisa Merchant, play out a first date between people randomly selected from descriptions in Internet ads, in locations selected by the audience.

So, it's a different show every time. The one I saw was amusing enough, with Hallett, already the taller of the two, standing most of the time on a platform, to denote macho insecurity.

I can't help feeling that some of their material could be re-used for any dating scenario, shared awkwardness being a given in such circumstances, but I'm mean that way.

The Next Stage Festival runs through Jan. 15.

Photo By Tanja Tiziana / Anika Johnson, left, and Barbara Johnston star in their own musical Blood Ties at the Next Stage Theatre Festival, one of 10 shows being put on at the Factory Theatre in Toronto.
2017-01-18-a-stage-divided-sequence-crac:
THEATRE REVIEW

Sequence, Tarragon Theatre

On my left, the self-proclaimed luckiest man in the world, giving a motivational address on how he does it, meaning essentially that he doesnt know and you can too. On my right, a sternly rationalist stem-cell researcher, addressing her students on the classically vexed subject of chickens, eggs and their pecking order.

That, as viewed from out front, is the opening set-up of Sequence, a play that comes to Toronto after winning prizes in Calgary and Bloomington, Ind. Its author, also from Calgary, is Arun Lakra, who by day is an eye surgeon.

Sequence belongs to the growing genre of scientific-mathematical-philosophical plays that proceed through argument, usually spiced with melodrama. Its particular preoccupation is the intersecting claims of chance and design, and it tells two stories that also intersect, at least in their staging. Theo, the lucky guy, and Dr. Guzman, the scientist, deliver their introductory spiels from their opposite sides of the stage, Theo makes flamboyant use of a ladder and a mirror, Dr. Guzman more fastidiously relies on chalk and a whiteboard. Each of them then receives a visitor who turns out to be an opponent. As the two confrontations proceed, each spills over into the other's space, creating some moments of visual irony and none of confusion. That certainly scores one for design over chance.

Theo has made a fortune by betting on the Super Bowl according to the toss of a coin. Somehow his call has always turned out to be the right one. He is confronted by Cynthia, a young lady who wants to prove that Theo's choices have been governed, unknown to him, by a mathematical progression. She cant afford to believe in luck because hers, on the face of it, has always been bad. Her health, and maybe that of her unborn daughter, has been genetically compromised. She also accuses Theo of having a sexual interest in her, though this doesnt seem terribly relevant.

Over in the science lab, Dr. Guzman also faces a terrible misfortune. She is going blind, with a crucial piece of her research still incomplete. Through her door there rolls, in a wheelchair, a Mr. Adamson, one of her students, who recently pulled off the statistically astonishing feat of getting every question in a 150-question test wrong. He was born with cerebral palsy, and a traffic accident has made him a paraplegic. He could be the unluckiest man in the world, but he's also deeply religious, and thinks that his misfortunes, like everything else in the world, are part of God's plan. The doctor naturally finds his ideas appalling, and he of course thinks the same of hers.

The debates, especially on the academic side of the fence, crackle enough to hold attention. But the characters are counters at best, ciphers at worst, so interest flags and has to be artificially boosted. Parallels between the two scenarios have to be inserted. Sinister briefcases figure in both, quite effectively; so do firearms, quite desperately. Tricks are played, but not resolved, with coincidence and chronology; and these just seem cheap.

The director, Andrea Donaldson, goes for loud and fast: a plausible choice in a battle of words but one that proves hard on the actors. Ava Jane Markus winds up playing Cynthia on one aggressive note; so does Nancy Palk as Dr. Guzman, though her note at least encompasses some nicely tossed-off moments of bitter sarcasm. Kevin Bundys opening monologue is excessively kinetic, even by snake-oil standards, but when Theo starts to feel some pain, he is able to dig deep into it. The most flexible and therefore the best performance comes from Jesse LaVercombe, making a case for religious fundamentalism thats urgent and, in a Toronto theatre context, surprisingly persuasive. However, it's a sure sign that something has misfired when the audience applauds the start of the last scene, thinking it's the curtaincall.

THEATRE NOTES

Footnotes on a couple of memorable one-off events. One of them was actually a three-off: three concert performances of the Marsha Norman-Lucy Simon musical The Secret Garden by a bakers dozen of fine actor-singers, some familiar, some new and very young. They did especial justice to the English folksong aspects of Simons score and, as a real treat, were accompanied by a fine full orchestra under the baton of Mark Camilleri, a fearless accompanist (as I can testify) revealed as a sparkling conductor. He's also one of the guiding spirits of Podium Concert Productions.

Also last week, the Barbara Hamilton Memorial Award for excellence in the performing arts was presented to Christopher Newton, whose production of The Audience opens at the Royal Alex on Thursday. Newton is best known for his phenomenal 22-year artistic direction of the Shaw Festival, an institution to which he brought both continuity and surprise. Ben Carlson, in a witty and charming tribute to the man under whose auspices he blossomed into one of Canada's best actors, spoke of Newtons "overview" of the repertoire he presented. Newtons mandate, for most of his regime, was to stage plays written in Shaw's own lifetime: a century's worth of theatre of all kinds that he searchingly and eclectically illuminated. And his acceptance speech was charming too.

National Post Sequence runs through Feb. 12 at the Tarragon Theatre in Toronto

Cylla Von Tiedemann / Nancy Palk, Ava Jane Markus, Kevin Bundy and Jesse LaVercombe in Sequence.

THEATRE REVIEW

The Audience Royal Alexandra Theatre, Toronto

The Audience stands, in Peter Morgan's royalist oeuvre, between The Queen and The Crown, not perhaps the safest place to be. At any rate, this stage piece lacks both the concentration of the film, which focused on the death of Princess Diana, and the capaciousness of the TV show, the first season of which has only taken us as far as the eve of Suez. The Audience is a set of duologues: guesswork reconstructions of the weekly briefings of Elizabeth II by eight of her thirteen-to-date prime ministers, the most surprising of the absentees being Harold Macmillan and Edward Heath and the most understandable - because the play was written before her elevation - Theresa May.

They aren't presented chronologically; rather, the play jumps around in time. This deprives The Audience's audience, not to mention its leading actress, of any sense of dramatic development. The format also means that there's no room for the queen's inner or domestic life. In The Crown, these ingredients mix with the politics to provide compelling drama. The TV Elizabeth may or may not resemble the real woman (though she certainly sounds like her), but she's a real person on the screen. Lacking this scaffolding, the play becomes glorified gossip while Fiona Reid in the lead is reduced, initially at least, to just doing the voice. But she rallies. As always, she deals perfectly with the good lines that come her way (one being "that started out as a compliment but ended somewhere else"), while the performance gets deeper as her character ages.

Like the actors in Crow's Theatre's The Wedding Party, she has a lot of costume changes, but hers are covered by her chatting from just beyond our sight to her younger pre-monarchical self; exchanges that reek of contrivance. Even worse is having an offstage chorus moan "Suez! Suez!" when Anthony Eden mentions the fatal canal. If that's in the text, a director with Christopher Newton's taste and intelligence should have cut it. There's also a needless coronation sequence.

Still, the assorted PMs are a fine character-actorly bunch. Top of the crop is Kate Hennig, whose Margaret Thatcher scores high as both creation and impersonation. Her meeting with the queen, who plainly dislikes her, strikes more sparks than anything else on stage. The one she does like, or so we are literally told, is Harold Wilson, who in Nigel Bennett's salt-of-the-north performance, is certainly a more endearing figure than the one I remember. Then we have Benedict Campbell's downright Gordon Brown and Paul Essiembre's gaunt Eden, each battling their own physical demons; John B. Lowe, gamely contending with John Lithgow as a Churchill whose scene was partly recycled for The Crown; Kevin Klassen's Tony Blair, getting easy rueful laughs when he talks about democratizing Iraq; Evan Buliung almost unrecognizable as a John Major drawn in more delicate detail than most of his mates; and, bringing up the rear, Ben Carlson, a David Cameron whose crisp timing matches that of his sovereign.

Perhaps it's the fact that she's constitutionally powerless that makes most of the encounters seem pleasant rather than urgent. They are linked by an Equerry who fills us in on the decorative details that we aren't allowed to see for ourselves, which is most of them; Anthony Bekenn does these honours, and does them honourably.

The Audience runs until Feb. 26.
